## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries, and furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture and in which places of their works they did so.*

*The most accurate edition, and easily to be preferred to all others, if one considers the cleanliness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—one, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library gathers together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.*

### First Series

In this series appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

## [Complete Works of Jerome of Stridon]

[Column 0009]

# Preface

Although the prefaces placed before the individual books of this second volume relieve me for the most part of the burden of writing a general preface, I nevertheless see certain matters about which it will not be unwelcome to warn the reader at the very outset.

First, I must explain the reason for my undertaking. I have gathered into a single volume the minor works of Jerome that had been scattered here and there—whether occupying foreign places in the sequence of the Letters, or mixed into the writings of other authors, or not yet incorporated into the Jerome collection to which they belong—in such a way that this nearly new and properly substantial volume might arise.

I proposed this especially in order to give my edition value and dignity: that each work should be arranged in as correct an order as possible. I considered this the principal matter to which those who seek support for their studies in reading the holy Fathers ought to attend. Therefore, if I restored, as it were by right of return, to their native places those treatises whose composition is not long enough for separate publication, and whose character, nature, and manner of discussion do not permit them to be mixed with books of different subjects and different genius, I thought that the addition of new material and new order would provide them with the greatest praise and illumination.

The disorder of the editions prepared hitherto was scarcely tolerable, since they continually mix these little books with the Letters. Erasmus, followed by Victorius, whose concern was the arrangement of subjects, placed certain works in a second class or volume, taking occasion repeatedly from the Letters to place there works that contained *ἐλεγκτικὰ καὶ ἀπολογετικά*—that is, writings of refutation and defense—or matters relating to various heresies and the calumnies of detractors. He listed others at the end of the first volume, although the proposed purpose and the dissimilarity of the subject sometimes resisted him.

The recent Benedictine editor, who had undertaken a chronological order for the Letters, interrupted that order here and there with immense gaps in order to insert these writings. In arranging them, however, he paid no attention to the times to which they belonged, but perhaps only to their subjects. Thus, while trying to follow both paths at once, he often departed from both, and by disturbing both the order of subjects and that of time, carried the reader across the track.

Two books alone will serve as evidence—so that I need not remain longer in this criticism—of the places occupied by these works in that recension. One, the *Life of St. Paul the Hermit*, surpasses all the other works of the holy Doctor in age; the other, the *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, is later than nearly all the rest. Yet the former is placed after the Letters written to Marcella and Paula ten years later, although the whole sequence of subjects is extraordinarily different; the latter, which belongs to the year 415, is placed before Letters written from the year 386 onward.

Nature has arranged matters in such a way that unlike things have no natural association. If one compels them to be referred together to a single sequence, one cannot avoid this sort of confusion. If one follows the chronological order of the Letters and demands that the Treatises follow it as well, one must commit the error of an ugly transposition and scatter the monuments of a single subject here and there. If one prefers to follow the traces of the subjects, one must overturn the rules of chronology, which is almost the soul of the Letters.

I do not deny that there are three or four minor works to which individual Letters would lend additional illumination because of their proximity of subject. I say that it is better to warn the reader about them than to tear them forcibly from their proper places, transfer them to alien ground, and, under the pretext of borrowing illumination, become a delay and obstacle to readers.

In this respect, the more accurate editions of other ancient Fathers have also been prepared. In them, each kind of writing is assigned its proper place, so that plain epistolary speech is not mixed with dissertations and books, nor Commentaries, Homilies, and other works born under different auspices are mingled together.

Two further reasons moved me to do this with still greater justification in arranging Jerome. First, certain of his minor works were wandering in other volumes—for example, Didymus’s book *On the Holy Spirit*, translated from Greek into Latin—or had not yet been added to the Jerome collection, such as the Rule of St. Pachomius, likewise translated from Greek into Latin, to mention nothing else. It was worthwhile to add these here, and through this increase of writings the collection had grown to the size of a separate volume.

Second, with the single exception of the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, it was easy to arrange the abundant material of all the others not only according to subject but also according to time.

All these minor works naturally fall into two classes. They are either ascetic, dealing with the lives and rules of monks, or—forming the greater part—polemical, as they are now commonly called, written against the founders of various heresies. Once this division of subjects has been established, the individual works follow one another so suitably according to their several periods that they retain throughout the recension the place they received by virtue of their origin.

If the result has succeeded according to my intention, learned readers will spontaneously affirm that my labor has been well placed. I shall now briefly indicate how I accomplished it.

I gave the first place to the ascetic books, both because of the excellence and dignity of their subject and because they begin with the *Life of St. Paul the First Hermit*, which, as the Author himself testifies, precedes all Jerome’s other works by the testimony of time.

These are followed by the two lives of Malchus and Hilarion, respectively. Then come the Rule of St. Pachomius, his Letters, and his Mystical Sayings, which the holy Doctor rendered into Latin from a Greek translation. These now enter the collection of his works for the first time and complete this first part.

There is one matter about them of which I must still warn the reader: the enigmatic formulas of speech by which the classes of monks are designated through letters of the Greek alphabet, and which are entitled “mystical words,” are explained with particular care by Kircher in the supplement to his *Prodromus* and *Coptic Lexicon*. Anyone interested in his interpretation should consult it.

From this point the writings of another kind begin: those composed in a sharper style against heretics or patrons of heretics. They offer a brilliant example of how great the virtue of the holy Doctor was in his struggle against the enemies of the Faith, although he excelled merely by teaching within the walls of his cell.

The first is Didymus’s book *On the Holy Spirit*, explained by Jerome in Latin from Greek. It is presented as one continuous work, not, as it had hitherto been, divided into three by a kind of foolish *περιεργία*—curious meddling or over-subtle fussiness.

It is written against certain opinions concerning the Holy Spirit that were found neither in Scripture nor employed by any of the ancient ecclesiastical writers. Some learned men maintain that this was the reason why Jerome translated the work—not a reason belonging to Didymus as author, but to Jerome as translator.

Next comes the *Altercation of the Luciferian and the Orthodox*, which ought in strict chronological order to have preceded the preceding book, unless the arrangement based on the Author’s period had then seemed preferable to that based on the translator’s.

This is followed by the book against Helvidius on the perpetual virginity of Mary, and by the two books against Jovinian. Since I have said much about this man elsewhere, I shall add only one observation here. A law was issued against him under the consuls Honorius IX and Theodosius V, that is, in the year 412. It is found both at the end of the work in several Jerome manuscripts and in the Theodosian Code, title 5, *On Heretics*, law 53, where the distinguished Gothofredus records it.

I have suspected either that this law is spurious, or—and this seems still more probable—that the name of the heretic against whom it was issued has been corrupted, and that it falsely gives “Jovinianus.”

To the arguments drawn there from Jerome, add this further testimony from Gennadius, chapter 75, in his notice of Paul. There he mentions the heretic Jovinianus, a preacher of pleasures and lust, to whom the discipline of a continent and chaste life was so opposed that he “vomited out his soul” amid luxurious banquets.

From this it will also be clear that the heretic did not lead a miserable life, beaten with leaded scourges in exile on the island of Dalmatia, famous for such exiles, as the law commands; rather, amid the delights of a life crowded with every kind of pleasure, he expelled his soul together with his drunken excess.

Next comes the short work against Vigilantius in defense of the veneration of the saints and their relics, followed by another written with a fuller pen against John of Jerusalem, the standard-bearer of the Origenist faction.

The prerogative of age, as I myself assert it, may seem to require that this book also be placed before the preceding one. But since learned men offer different judgments on the matter, and since the book itself was neither brought to completion by its Author nor reached the hands of the public until much later—so that even Rufinus, looking for a knot in a rush, failed to notice it—I have left the matter intact in this order, allowing each reader to adopt whichever opinion he prefers.

I append three apologetic books against Rufinus, followed by the apology of Rufinus himself, the Aquileian priest, to Pope Anastasius, and by the latter’s letter to John of Jerusalem concerning Rufinus. These two most distinguished monuments, although previously not counted among the materials necessary for a proper understanding of the Jerome writings, are in fact indispensable.

Next come Rufinus’s books of invective against Jerome. The preconceived opinion—or, more truly, the hallucination—of learned men concerning their number must finally be removed here.

It is commonly accepted that he wrote three books, not merely the two that survive, and that the third was lost through the violence of time. Jerome responds in an equal number of books, and at the beginning of the second *Apology*, section 2, he himself clearly testifies that his adversary had composed “THREE books against him with Attic elegance.”

The printed copies indeed give this reading, and we have not departed from them by even a finger’s breadth without the support of manuscripts. Yet I think that either “two” must be restored there or the number entirely removed. Certainly I maintain that no more than two books were written by the Aquileian priest.

My chief argument is drawn from the Epilogue, in which the Author both concludes his own work and reviews, chapter by chapter, the matters to which he had responded piecemeal in his own defense. It is enough to examine it at the end of the second book, section 41 and following, to have no further doubt that it contains the whole substance of the work of invectives and that there could have been no additional book whose complete chapters he did not recall in this *ἀνακεφαλαίωσις*, or recapitulation.

The sequence of Jerome’s exchanges, especially the final one that he composed after receiving Rufinus’s books, refutes only those two. It knows nothing at all of the third book that they imagine.

Finally, Gennadius knows only two, in chapter 17. I consider his testimony of the highest authority in this matter, since no one was more concerned for Rufinus’s reputation or more familiar with his works.

“Rufinus,” he says, “responded to the detractor of his minor works”—namely Jerome—“in TWO volumes, arguing and proving that, with the Lord’s help, he had exercised his talent with regard to God and for the benefit of the Church, whereas the other, driven by the spur of rivalry, had turned his pen to slander.”

But let this have been said in passing and also in my own defense, since in the preface I seem, from a preconceived opinion, to have counted three.

After these come the three books, or, as some manuscripts call them, parts, of the *Dialogues against the Pelagians*. With them this series of polemical writings ends.

Finally I append the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. I delayed it until later chiefly because, by the nature of its subject, it could conveniently be assigned to neither class.

Since it was also necessary, following the example of earlier editions and manuscripts, to append Gennadius’s catalogue of illustrious men, whom he commemorates by following Blessed Jerome, it was highly convenient to defer it to the end of the volume, lest the sequence of Jerome’s works should be unattractively interrupted by another author’s writing. It is appended here in the manner of an appendix.

So that no one, because of the place it occupies, might think it more recent, I shall first give a warning about its date. I have devoted the same care to determining the proper period of each of the preceding books and to prefacing the other relevant matters.

Only one thing remains: to explain why I undertook this labor, so that you may turn over these offspring of Jerome’s mind with day-and-night devotion.

All the literary monuments left to posterity by that teacher of the Churches are certainly useful and distinguished, but I consider those contained in this second volume far more excellent and far richer. Every one of them either supplies strength and weapons for guarding the deposit of true Faith against the poisonous doctrines of heretics, or provides the greatest assistance for wisely establishing a proper way of life. Finally, they contribute greatly to the education and knowledge of noble and well-disposed minds.

# Minor Works of St. Eusebius Jerome of Stridon, or Books on Various Subjects

[Column 0013]

## Preface to the Following Three Lives of Paul, Hilarion, and Malchus

Jerome recounts the lives of three especially distinguished monks—Paul, Hilarion, and Malchus—in these three short works. In an equal number of Letters, which we present in their proper places in the first volume, he celebrated the virtues of three women eminent for the praise of holiness—Fabiola, Paula, and Marcella—in a manner almost equivalent to biographies.

There are no other lives of holy Fathers composed by the holy Doctor, although several ancient writers assign many more to him, especially those that Heribert Rosweyde listed in his second book. The testimony of these writers, however, has misled scholars of later ages.

“Gelasius,” or whoever the ancient author of the decree *On Authentic Books* may be, says in chapter 4: “We receive with every honor the Lives of the Fathers Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the Hermits, which the blessed Jerome nevertheless wrote.”

But it is established that the Life of Antony was written in Greek by Athanasius and rendered into Latin by Evagrius of Antioch.

Much later Gratian says in Part II of the *Decree*, cause 27:

“As Blessed Jerome relates, Macarius, pre-eminent among Christ’s hermits, after celebrating a wedding feast, when at evening he was about to enter the bridal chamber, departed from the city, set out for lands beyond the sea, and chose the solitude of the desert for himself.”

Yet this is not transmitted by Jerome at all, but by the genuine authors of Macarius’s Life, Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus.

I pass over testimonies of this kind drawn from spurious Jerome writings, as well as the overly subtle conclusions that some derive from Cassiodorus’s *Divine Readings*, chapter 32, and from Cassian’s preface to the books of the *Institutes*.

Certainly there are extremely ancient manuscript books that seem to guarantee these and many other lives. We once examined two such Vatican manuscripts, formerly belonging to the Queen of Sweden; the distinguished Montfaucon testifies that many are held among the Coislin manuscripts.

But one indication alone makes it clear that they are deceptive: these Lives differ in no respect from those circulated under the name of Palladius.

One Colbertine manuscript, according to Cangius, adds the following after the *Lausiac History*:

> “Another history concerning the lives of the holy Fathers of Egypt—[the word ‘Fathers’ is supplied]—written by Jerome, monk and priest from Dalmatia.”

But Fabricius notes, on Cangius’s own testimony, that Palladius is copied in it word for word. Nor does it seem doubtful that some Greek writer falsely attached Jerome’s name to it because that collection also contains these three genuine histories of the holy Father.

This must first have deceived Gelasius. Since the collection had long begun with the Life of Paul, the entire book was entitled under the name of the author displayed on its title page.

Furthermore, I do not doubt that, both to avoid the ill repute attached to the names of Rufinus and Palladius and to serve the convenience of scribes, this fraud was sometimes deliberately undertaken.

Thus these three alone proceeded from the pen of our holy Doctor. They are commended both by their outstanding elegance of language and by their exceptionally splendid examples of ascetic life.

Indeed, no work among Jerome’s writings has been reprinted more often, found more editors, or received more learned treatment.

The first two are also available in Greek. Indeed, one of them was translated into Greek by Sophronius scarcely after it had been published by the Author. Nevertheless, learned men prefer to attribute the Greek text that now survives, beginning:

> “In Palestine there is a city no less than forty-five stades distant from Gaza”

to Symeon Metaphrastes.

In Latin, besides the editors of Jerome’s works, Surius and Lipomanus include them. Rosweyde, Bollandus, and those who continue that great undertaking have again polished and illustrated them with very learned annotations.

It may seem that little remained for our diligence. Nevertheless, so that our labor should not be fruitless, we have exerted ourselves wherever the texts could be more fully corrected and improved.

Four ancient Vatican manuscripts, formerly belonging to the Queen of Sweden, were available: numbers 432, 500, 589, and 797. We also consulted one of our own manuscripts, kept privately in our home—not one of the most remote antiquity, certainly, but of good quality.

Above all, however, one manuscript of the most illustrious Veronese Chapter deserves praise. It easily surpasses all those known to this day.

It was written in the year 517 by a certain Ursicinus, reader of our church, whose name I do not know, and who himself records the fact in these words, somewhat corrupt according to the pronunciation of that period:

> “This codex was written on the Kalends of August, in the tenth indiction, under Agapitus, most distinguished man, by Ursicinus, reader of the Church of Verona.”

**Note:** This manuscript codex, the oldest and most excellent of all, was taken by a man who was not indeed uneducated—out of consideration for his name I refrain from identifying him—and compared only with the printed edition. He did not collate it carefully enough, nor, as had been intended, with the Benedictine edition, but with a certain Cologne edition that he had at hand. Hence it happened that he repeatedly transcribed false variant readings and made us excessively credulous toward him. In the present edition of this short work we have met and remedied this defect at each individual place.

The year in which the Life of Paul was written seems scarcely doubtful: it was 374 or the following year. Certainly at that time it was sent to Paul of Concordia, his namesake, together with Letter 10 in our recension.

**Note:** In the *Chronicle*, under the nineteenth year of Constantius, Jerome states that he had explained the death of Paul the Theban in a short work.

In the *Catalogue*, however, it occupies the first place among all Jerome’s writings.

We assign the other two to the year 390, guided by the same argument—namely, the order in which they are listed in the *Catalogue*, after the translation of Origen’s Homilies on Luke, which we assign to the preceding year, 389.

**Note:** Written about the year 374.

# Life of St. Paul the First Hermit (C)

[Column 0017]

Jerome recounts the life of Paul, from whom the desert first began to be inhabited, lowering his style somewhat for the sake of simpler readers. He shows that Paul, about sixteen years old, sought the desert under Decius and Valerian in order to escape the persecution raging against Christians, and that he lived there for ninety-eight years with extraordinary abstinence and holiness, until, visited by the great Antony after Antony had been divinely warned, he met his final day.

He dedicates the history to Paul of Concordia, his namesake.

## 1

**Note:** We have supplied this division of the Prologue, which is absent from the printed editions, from three Vatican manuscripts formerly belonging to the Queen of Sweden—422, 500, and 589—with which we also collated the whole history. Nevertheless, we do not deny that in our oldest Veronese manuscript, mentioned immediately above in the preceding Preface and written by the reader Ursicinus in 517, this is merely the title of the short work: “Here begins the Life of the blessed Paul, monk of the Thebaid,” without any mention of a prologue.

## Prologue

[Column 0017A]

### 1

People have often disputed who first caused the desert to be inhabited by monks. Some, tracing the matter farther back, took its beginning from blessed Elijah and John.

**Note:** Compare the testimonies concerning Elijah and John, the earliest inhabitants of the desert, collected by Rosweyde from the Fathers and historians. Soon afterward the same Rosweyde and a few other printed books seem to read “he was a prophet,” whereas most other books, and especially the manuscripts, are silent about the word “prophet.” In our preceding edition we thought that we had correctly supplied it on the authority of the highly praised Veronese codex. But, deceived by the negligence of the person who had undertaken to compare that codex with the printed editions, we have now become more certain of the codex’s true reading and have removed that gloss.

Of these two, Elijah seems to us to have been more than a monk; and John began to prophesy before he was born.

Others, in agreement with the opinion accepted by the whole common people, assert that Antony was the founder of this way of life. This is true in part: he was not so much the first of all as the one who stirred up the zeal of all the others.

**Note:** In the *Chronicle* he numbers three great disciples of Antony: Sarmata, Amathas, and Macarius. Likewise, in the Life of St. Pachomius, Macarius is said to have buried his teacher’s body, not Amathas, as Jerome here suggests.

Amathas and Macarius, disciples of Antony—the former of whom buried his teacher’s body—even now affirm that a certain Paul the Theban was the founder of this movement, not of the name.

**Note:** Our manuscripts, together with the older edition, support the printed reading. Other manuscripts in the possession of Rosweyde, Bollandus, and Martianay read either “was almost the founder of this matter only in name” or “but not in name,” followed by the opinion expressed here; or “was the founder of this name and order”; or “was the founder of the name and order of this matter.” Most printed editions read “was the founder of this matter,” followed by “which we approve not so much by opinion as by name.”

Jerome’s meaning is that Paul was indeed the founder of that institution, or of the eremitical life, but that the common name “hermits” did not originate from him.

If I may conjecture, I would prefer “was the founder not of this matter but of the name,” so that the meaning would be that there were indeed people living in solitude before Paul, but that the name “hermits” first took its beginning from him.

A learned Anonymous’s *Response to the Book on the Primacy of St. Paul the Theban* appeared long ago, in 1750, at Strasbourg. It discusses the matter at length and approves this, our more accurate interpretation of the passage.

The older and better manuscripts read: “was the founder of this matter, not ...” Other manuscripts preserve the following variant readings:

- The Avignon manuscript and another belonging to the Friars Preachers of Toulouse: “was the founder of this name and order.”
- Two Paris manuscripts: “the founder of this matter was the name and order.”
- Finally, the printed editions display the following reading, fabricated by Erasmus: “was the founder of this matter, which we also approve not so much by names as by opinion.”

**Martianay.**

Some people loudly proclaim these and other claims as their fancy dictates, saying that he was a long-haired man living in an underground cave, with hair reaching to his heels, and inventing many incredible tales that it would be tedious to pursue.

**Note:** The word “was” is absent from the Veronese manuscript, as it is also from several printed books.

Since their lie was shameless, the opinion itself does not even seem to require refutation.

Therefore, since the life of Antony has been carefully handed down to memory in both Greek and Latin, I have decided to write a little about Paul’s beginning and end—more because the subject had been neglected than because I trusted my own ability.

But how he lived during the middle period of his life, and what snares of Satan he endured, is known to no human being. ━
## 2. Decius and Valerian, Persecutors of the Christians

[Note: The title is absent from our Verona manuscript. Then, unquestionably corruptly, two manuscripts in Martianus read “under Diocletian and Valerian”; nor does it matter that the insufficiently careful author Nicephorus, in Book VII, relates the appended story of the young man tempted by a prostitute under Diocletian. Shortly afterward, the two words *felici cruore* (“with blessed blood”) are missing in two of our manuscripts. The Verona manuscript and some others have *felici cruore damnati sunt* (“were condemned with blessed blood”). Under Decius: the manuscripts of Avignon and Toulouse read “under Diocletian and Valerian.” We note this because Nicephorus, *History* VII.13, reports that the story of the young man related immediately afterward occurred under Diocletian. MARTIANUS.]

Under the persecutors Decius and Valerian, at the time when Cornelius suffered martyrdom at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage by a blessed shedding of blood, a savage storm devastated many churches in Egypt and the Thebaid. At that time Christians’ wish was to be struck down by the sword for the name of Christ [Verona: “to endure it”]. But the cunning enemy, devising slow punishments leading to death, desired to slaughter souls, not bodies. As Cyprian, who himself suffered at his hands, says:

[Note: Saint Cyprian, Letter 53: “especially since those wishing to die were not permitted to be killed” (read, with Jerome, in the singular: “he was not permitted to be killed”). Seneca, *Thebaid*: “To kill is to forbid one who wishes to die.”]

“Those who wished to die were not permitted to be killed.” To make his cruelty better known, we append two examples for the record [Note: Previously *subjecimus* (“we have appended”), contrary to the manuscripts. With their help we have also removed *igitur* (“therefore”) from the following verse, where the sense is disturbed: “Therefore persevering in the faith,” etc. These martyrs are mentioned in the Martyrology under 28 July.]

## 3. Two Distinguished Martyrs

He ordered a martyr persevering in the faith, victorious amid the torture-horse and the metal plates, to be smeared with honey and, with his hands tied behind his back [Note: We preferred, on the basis of the Verona manuscript and other manuscripts of the highest quality, to restore this passage to its more correct sense: “to be placed with his hands tied behind his back,” instead of “with his hands tied and his body laid backward,” as others have it.] placed beneath the fiercest sun, so that he might succumb to the stings of the flies, having previously overcome the heated frying pans.

He ordered another young man in the flower of his age to be led away [Others: “brought”] to delightful little gardens. There, amid gleaming lilies and red roses, while a stream crept along nearby with a gentle murmur and the wind brushed the leaves of the trees with a soft whisper [Others: “touched”], he ordered him to be laid on a bed piled with feathers and, so that he could not throw himself from it, to be left entangled in the gentle bonds of garlands.

[Note: Some later editions read “upon a bed spread with feathers,” and then the older editors Erasmus, Rosweyd, and Victorius altered *sertorum* (“of garlands”) conjecturally to *serico* (“silken”). They also altered *ac lectulum* and *supinari*.]

[Note: “With the gentle bonds of garlands.” The printed editions read “with gentle silken bonds”; but all the manuscripts read as we have printed it, “with the gentle bonds of garlands.” This reading ought not to have been altered merely on the basis of Erasmus’s conjecture. MARTIANUS.]

When everyone had withdrawn and a beautiful prostitute had come, she began to clasp his neck with delicate embraces and—and it is a crime even to say it—to touch his genitals with her hands, so that, when his body had been aroused to lust, the shameless victor might throw herself upon him.

[Note: Three manuscripts of the Queen’s Library read: “What was the soldier of Christ to do? Where was he to turn? Whom …” This is more correct. Immediately afterward one manuscript reads: “Abominable pleasure alone prevailed.” Others read: “Pleasure might prevail”; this too is more correct. But most correctly, two words—“inspired from heaven”—are found in the Verona manuscript and are omitted elsewhere.]

“What was the soldier of Christ to do, and where was he to turn? The man whom tortures had not conquered, pleasure overcame.”

At last, inspired from heaven, he bit off his tongue and spat it into the face of the woman kissing him; and so the magnitude of the pain that followed overcame [Others: “seized and snatched away”] the sensation of lust [Verona: “trampled it down”].

[Note: The printed editions have *morsu* or *morsibus* (“with a bite” or “with bites”). But the reading of the Verona manuscript and other manuscripts, which we have preferred, is supported by a similar passage of Jerome, Letter 88, or Theophilus’s Synodical Letter, §1: “One man bit off a part of his tongue.”]

## 4. Paul’s Qualities and Learning

At the same time, therefore, when such things were happening in Lower Thebaid, Paul, with his sister already married, was left, after the death of both parents, in possession of a wealthy inheritance, about sixteen years old [Note: So read all the manuscripts after Martianus; one of the older manuscripts in my possession is mutilated in its upper portion. Victorius, however, following Erasmus, counts only fifteen years. Bollandus nevertheless correctly observes that Jerome does not say that Paul fled immediately after being deprived of his parents, but afterward, when persecution broke out following the killing of the emperors Philip.] He was thoroughly educated in both Greek and Egyptian letters [Verona manuscript: “fully educated”], gentle in spirit, and a great lover of God.

When the storm of persecution thundered, he withdrew to a more remote and secluded estate.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “He lived more secretly in a more remote estate”; others: “He remained in greater seclusion”; still others: “He was more remote and secluded.” The printed reading gives the better sense: Paul withdrew and reserved himself for the Lord, to use Cyprian’s expression. See Tertullian’s book *On Flight in Persecution*. “To an estate.” In other manuscript books: “He lived more secretly in an estate,” or “He was more remote and secluded in an estate.” MARTIANUS.]

But what does the accursed hunger for gold not compel in human hearts? [Virgil, *Aeneid* II.] His sister’s husband began intending to betray the man whom he ought to have concealed. Neither his wife’s tears, as is customary, nor the bond of blood, nor God, who sees all things from on high, recalled him from his crime [Verona manuscript: “recalled them”].

[Note: Two words, as is usual, are absent from all our manuscripts and other books, and I would prefer to delete them. Immediately afterward some read: “To this he pressed on”; the older printed editions also adopt this reading and further alter it to “cruelty, which seemed to imitate piety.” The printed reading is preferable; Jerome borrowed it with great elegance from Florus, Book III, chapter 5, concerning Mithridates: “He was present, he pressed on; he used savagery as though it were virtue.”]

“He was present, he pressed on; he used cruelty as though it were piety.”

[Note: “He was present, he pressed on.” Several manuscripts read: “To this he pressed on; he used cruelty as though it were piety.” Jerome borrowed this from Florus, who has in Book III, chapter 5: “He was present, he pressed on; he used savagery as though it were virtue.” Erasmus and Marianus, unaware of this, fabricated another reading: “To this cruelty pressed on, seeming to imitate piety.” MARTIANUS.]

## 5. A Secret Mint

When the very prudent young man understood this, he fled to the deserted mountains and, while awaiting the end of the persecution [Others: “while awaiting”], turned necessity into free choice. Gradually proceeding and repeatedly stopping [Note: Three manuscripts of the Queen’s Library have, instead of *subsistens* (“stopping”), *tantumdem* (“the same distance”); our exemplar retains the word *subsistens*, which is not excluded by the preceding phrase, and again reads *subsistens tantumdem*, and so repeatedly. The Verona manuscript has: “proceeding, and again the same distance.”], and doing the same thing again and again, he finally discovered a rocky mountain [Note: Some manuscripts have *excisum* (“cut away”), others, as do some printed editions, *exesum* (“hollowed out”), and others *extensum* (“extended”). But Saint Jerome here uses *saxeus* (“rocky”) in the elegant manner of Sallust, *Jugurtha* 92: “Among the rest of the plain there was a rocky mountain, sufficiently spacious for a moderate fortress.” Similar passages occur in Florus III.1 and Frontinus III.9. In what follows we have preferred to follow the evidence and agreement of all the manuscripts we collated. The printed editions seem to err by inserting certain words that produce a different and awkward sense. They say: “At its foot, not far away, there was a large cave, which was closed by a stone.” Other manuscripts, preserved by Gravius, read: “He saw a cave whose mouth was closed by a stone not very large.” Immediately afterward most manuscripts also vary, though the sense remains intact in both forms, as human eagerness tends to recognize hidden things avidly: “he noticed inside,” etc. The Verona manuscript reads: “desiring more eagerly to recognize hidden things.”]

At the foot of it was a not very large cave, closed by a stone. When he had removed it—for human beings are eager to investigate hidden things—he explored more avidly and noticed inside a great vestibule, which, with the sky open above, an ancient palm tree covered with its spreading branches, displaying a very clear spring.

[Note: The phrase “displaying it” is set against the immediately preceding word *contexerat* (“had covered”). The palm tree, whose branches covered the vestibule above, displayed the spring plainly; that is, it not so much allowed it to be seen as indicated it by its position. This should have been noted for the benefit of the recent editor of Severus Sulpicius, who considers the passage entirely corrupt and, by attempting to understand it, understands nothing. The Verona manuscript is shortened in this brief section, with the words “whose living …,” then “bursting forth immediately through a small opening,” and finally “the waters”; I do not altogether reject this reading.]

The stream flowing out only a short distance was immediately swallowed by the earth through a small opening, by the same earth that had produced the waters.

Moreover, throughout the hollowed-out [Others: “rocky”] mountain were quite a few dwellings, in which rough anvils and hammers, with which money is struck, could be seen. Egyptian writings report that this place had been a secret mint at the time when Antony was joined to Cleopatra.

## 6.

Having therefore fallen in love with the dwelling—as though it had been offered to him by God [Verona manuscript: “as though the dwelling were offered by God”]—he spent his entire life there in prayer and solitude. The palm tree provided him with food and clothing.

Lest this seem impossible to anyone, I call Jesus and his holy angels to witness that, in that part of the desert adjoining Syria and the Saracens [Note: “In that part of the desert that borders Syria and the Saracens.” Thus we read in two ancient manuscript copies, from which it is clear to us that Jerome published the Life of Paul in the desert. MARTIANUS.], I have seen monks and also seen one who lived enclosed for thirty years on barley bread and muddy water, and another who was sustained in an old cistern—called by the Syrians in their native language *gubba* [Note: I believe that the Syrians do not call it *gubba* in their native language, but, as Victorius reads, *kubba*, a word meaning a cistern, pool, or similar place. When Jeremiah, chapter 6, also says that *gubba* means “cistern” in Syriac and Hebrew, he may have been referring to the pronunciation of the Syrians of his own time. The word may indeed be derived from the Chaldean term meaning “pit” or “pond,” but that word has no such meaning in Syriac. It may also be added that monks of this kind, who enclosed themselves in cisterns, are called in Greek ἐγκλείστοι (*enclausists*, “the enclosed”).]—on five dried figs each day.

These things, therefore, will seem incredible to those who do not believe that all things are possible for those who believe [Verona manuscript: “for one who believes”].

## 7. The Ages of Paul and Antony

But to return to the point from which I digressed: when the blessed Paul had already been living a heavenly life on earth for one hundred thirteen years, and Antony—so he himself used to assert—was living in another desert at the age of ninety, this thought entered his mind: no monk more perfect than himself had settled in the desert [Others: “no monk beyond himself”].

[Note: The word *perfectum* (“perfected”), which we find in no manuscript copy, could easily be deleted, unless the statement immediately following it—that another had been revealed to be much better than he—provided some support for it. Formerly we thought that *profectum* (“advanced”) ought to be read, so that the sense would be simply that he had advanced far beyond Paul into the more inward and remote parts of the desert; but we do not approve this very much. We prefer, with the Verona manuscript, to read: “that no monk in the desert was farther beyond him.” In the third line after this, the same manuscript has *properare deberet* (“he ought to hasten”) instead of *proficisci deberet* (“he ought to set out”).]

But while he was resting during the night, it was revealed to him that there was another, farther within, much better than he, whom he ought to set out to see [Others: “farther away and on earth”].

As soon as the light broke, the venerable old man, supporting his infirm limbs with a staff, began to go where he did not know. By midday the sun was already blazing overhead, yet he was not diverted from the journey he had begun [Verona manuscript: “was not led onward”], saying:

“I believe in my God, who will one day show me the fellow servant whom he promised me.”

Before he could say more, he saw a man half horse, to whom popular belief had given the name Hippocentaur.

[Note: One manuscript reads *onocentaur* (“ass-centaur”). Others discuss this kind of monster of two species and show, not implausibly, that it is attested by Pliny VII.3 and Alexander ab Alexandris III.8. See the note on the following page.]

When he saw it, he armed his forehead with the saving sign [of the cross] and said: “Hey, you! In what direction does this servant of God live?”

The creature, growling something barbarous and breaking off words rather than speaking them, sought a friendly address amid its bristling mouth [Note: Victorius reads “of the old man”; others “sufficiently.” But *setis* (“bristles”), which we have taken from two manuscripts, seemed more correct.]. Extending its right hand, it indicated the desired path, and then, flying across the open fields with winged speed, vanished from the eyes of the astonished old man.

But whether the devil had fashioned this apparition to terrify him, or whether—as is customary—that desert, fertile in monstrous animals, also produced this beast, we do not know.

## 8. Fauns and Satyrs: A Satyr Brought Alive to Alexandria

Amazed, therefore, and turning over in his mind what he had seen [Two Vatican manuscripts: “he proceeded more quickly”], Antony went farther [Verona manuscript: “turned back”]. Soon, in a rocky valley, he saw a little man, not very large, with hooked nostrils and a forehead roughened by horns; the lower part of his body ended in goats’ feet.

[Note: Up to this point the reading *Infractusque* (“and unshaken”) had wrongly prevailed, although no manuscript has it, despite the manuscripts varying greatly among themselves. Here we follow the second manuscript of the Queen’s Library, or 432. Others read *attonitus* (“astonished”) instead of *Antonius*, perhaps more correctly in this sequence: “His body ended in goats’ feet; astonished at this spectacle, the good soldier seized the shield of faith.” The words “and the breastplate of hope,” inserted between these clauses, are not recognized by the Verona manuscript, which reads: “astonished at the spectacle.”]

At this spectacle Antony seized the shield of faith and the breastplate of hope like a good soldier. Nevertheless, the aforementioned creature offered him palm fruits for his journey, as though they were pledges of peace [Others: “brought”].

When Antony recognized this, he pressed forward and, asking who the creature was, received this reply:

[Note: This little story about a Faun or Satyr, which may seem to require a charitable reader, is made more credible by many testimonies from other highly authoritative writers. Augustine, *City of God* XV.23: “There is a very famous report, and many affirm that they have experienced it themselves, or heard it from those who experienced it, whose reliability cannot be doubted: that the Silvani and Fauns, whom the common people call Incubi, have been wicked toward women.” Jerome again, on Isaiah 13: “The hairy ones, or Incubi, or Satyrs—certain wild men whom some call Goat-Fauns.” Eutropius XII and Isidore, *Etymologies* IX, contain similar accounts. They are generally believed, according to popular opinion, to have been demons. Heraclitus, *On Incredible Things*, chapter 25, says that there were mountain men who had “the hair and legs of goats” (Greek: τράγων δὲ τρίχας καὶ σκέλη ἔχειν). To the authors cited and praised in the preceding column on this subject add Plutarch, in his *Life of Sulla*. He says that, near Dyrrachium, a curious observer saw with his own eyes and examined a living Satyr of this kind and spoke with it, although the creature could not form words; its voice resembled the neighing of a horse or the cry of a goat. Tertullian, Justin, Cyprian, Athenagoras, Clement of Alexandria, and Lactantius—highly learned authors—are also said to have lent an ear to such a story and to have thought that these Satyrs were among the rebellious angels whom God, in punishment, ordered to dwell upon the earth, while others were compelled to remain in the air and others in Hell. The whole religion of the pagans, by common agreement, regarded them as gods or demigods. I pass over the foolish conjectures of the rabbis, especially Rabbi Abraham, who held that they were real creatures from the hand of the Almighty, but imperfect because, when God was creating them, night overtook him on the Sabbath and he refused to put the finishing touch to them.]

“I am mortal, and one of the inhabitants of the desert. Deceived by various errors, the Gentiles worship us, calling us Fauns, Satyrs, and Incubi [Note: Our manuscripts do not contain the word *illud vocans* (“calling it that”).]. I am carrying out the mission of my people. We ask you to pray on our behalf to the common Lord, whom we have learned to have come long ago for the salvation of the world, and whose sound has gone out into all the earth.”

As he spoke these words, the long-lived traveler drenched his face with abundant tears, which the greatness of his joy poured forth as signs of his heart. He rejoiced at the glory of Christ and the destruction of Satan, while at the same time marveling that he could understand the creature’s speech. Striking the ground with his staff, he said:

“Woe to you, Alexandria, which worship monsters in place of God. Woe to you, prostitute city, into which the demons of the whole world have gathered [Col. 0023C: “Woe to you, prostitute city, into which the demons of the whole world have gathered.”]. What will you say now?”

Beasts speak of Christ, while you worship monsters in place of God.

[Note: This repetition of the preceding sentence—“while you worship monsters in place of God”—is not found in our manuscripts.]

He had not yet finished speaking when the insolent creature fled away as though on wings.

Lest this disturb anyone’s credulity, the account is supported by the testimony of the whole world under the emperor Constantius.

[Note: Previously the text read “under Constantine,” as in most of the common editions. But all our manuscripts, especially the Verona manuscript itself, have “Constantius,” and we have restored that name in accordance with their testimony, supported by the chronology and history. As the recent editor of Severus Sulpicius also noted, it cannot be asserted that Constantine had his seat at Antioch, whereas there is no doubt that Constantius did, at least during the first twelve or thirteen years of his reign.]

For when such a man was brought alive to Alexandria, he provided a great spectacle for the people. Later, his lifeless corpse was carried to Antioch, after salt had been applied so that it would not be dispersed by the summer heat, to be viewed by the emperor.

## 9.

But to continue with my subject, Antony proceeded through the region he had begun to explore, looking only at the tracks of wild animals and the broad desolation of the desert. He did not know what to do or where to turn his steps. Another day had already passed. One thing remained: to trust that Christ could not abandon him.

He spent the second night awake in prayer. At the uncertain light of dawn, he saw not far away a she-wolf panting from the burning thirst [Note: The negative particle was absent: “he saw from a distance.”] and creeping into the foot of a mountain. He followed it with his eyes, and, when the beast had gone, approached the cave. He began to look inside [Verona manuscript: “began to look within”], but curiosity accomplished nothing, because the darkness kept his sight from penetrating.

But, as Scripture says, “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Carefully suspending his step and moderating his breathing, the resourceful explorer entered and proceeded little by little, repeatedly stopping and listening for a sound [Note: The two words “as a clever explorer” are omitted by the Verona manuscript; immediately afterward it reads *capiebat* (“was capturing”) instead of *captabat* (“was listening for”).].

At last, through the horror of the blind night, he caught sight of a distant light. As he hurried toward it more eagerly, he struck a stone with his foot and caused a noise [Note: Other manuscripts read: “Having struck a stone with his foot, he caused a noise”; our manuscript has “against the foot.” Immediately afterward they read “opening” instead of “closing.” The Verona manuscript has “by the striking of his foot.”].

After the sound, the blessed Paul closed the door, which had stood open, and fastened it with a bolt [Verona manuscript: “opened it”].

Then Antony fell before the door and, until the sixth hour and even longer, begged for admission, saying:

“You know who I am, where I come from, and why I have come. I know that I do not deserve to see you; nevertheless, unless I see you, I will not leave. You receive wild beasts—why do you reject a human being? I sought, and I found; I knock so that it may be opened. If I do not obtain this, I shall die here before your doors. At least you will bury my corpse [Note: Elsewhere Gravius found: “or my lifeless body.”].”

He persisted in saying such things and remained fixed there.

To him the hero replied briefly:

“No one asks in such a way as to threaten; no one makes an accusation with tears [Note: Victorius and Gravius annotate: “does an injury.”]. And do you marvel that I do not receive you, when you have come intending to die?”

And so, smiling, Paul opened the entrance.

When it was opened, they embraced one another, exchanged their names, and gave thanks together to the Lord.

## 10.

After the holy kiss, Paul sat down and began speaking to Antony:

“Here is the man whom you sought with such labor. His unkempt gray hair covers limbs rotten with old age. Here you see a man soon to become dust.

“But because charity bears all things [Verona manuscript: “endures all things”], tell me, I beg you, how the human race is doing. Are new buildings rising in the ancient cities? By what government is the world ruled? Are any people still being carried away by the error of demons [Others: “captured by the error of demons”]?”

During this conversation they saw a raven sitting on a branch of a tree. It flew gently down from there [Note: Some manuscripts read “flying lightly down”; Victorius preserves the fuller reading. The Verona manuscript reads: “flying gently down, carrying a whole loaf,” etc.] and placed a whole loaf before the eyes of the astonished men. After it departed, Paul said:

“See, the Lord has sent us breakfast, truly kind, truly merciful. For sixty years now I have continually received half a loaf [Others: “a fragment”]. But at your arrival Christ has doubled the ration for his soldiers.”

## 11.

After giving thanks to the Lord, they both sat down beside the edge of the glass-clear spring [Verona manuscript: “sat beneath it”]. A dispute then arose over which of them should break the bread, and it nearly lasted until evening. Paul, in accordance with the law of hospitality, insisted; Antony, by right of age, refused.

At last they decided that, each taking hold of the bread from opposite sides and pulling toward himself, his portion would remain in his hands [Note: The Verona manuscript adds “to pull”; the older editions then read “each one’s portion.”].

Afterward they drank a little water from the spring, bending their mouths to it [Others: “with their mouths bent toward the spring”]. Offering God a sacrifice of praise, they spent the night in vigils.

When daylight had been restored to the earth, the blessed Paul spoke to Antony:

“Long ago, brother, I knew that you lived in these regions. Long ago God promised me that you were my fellow servant. But now the time of my falling asleep has arrived, and, since I have always desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ, after completing my course there remains for me the crown of righteousness. You have been sent by the Lord to cover my little body with earth—indeed, to return earth to earth.”

## 12. Athanasius Gave Antony a Cloak; Antony’s Monastery Was Occupied by the Saracens

When Antony heard this, he wept and groaned, begging Paul not to abandon him and to accept him as a companion on such a journey.

But Paul said: “You ought not to seek what is yours, but what belongs to another. Once the burden of the flesh has been cast off, it is good for you to follow the Lamb. It is also good for the other brothers that they should still be instructed by your example. Therefore, I beg you, proceed if it is not burdensome, and bring the cloak that Bishop Athanasius gave you, to wrap my little body in.”

Paul asked this not because he greatly cared whether his decaying corpse was covered or naked—for during so long a period he had clothed himself in woven palm leaves—but so that, as Antony departed, the grief of Paul’s death might be eased [Note: In the Verona manuscript, with one or two errors: “so that, departing from him, the memory of his death might be relieved.”].

Antony was therefore astonished at what he had heard about Athanasius and his cloak. It was as though he saw Christ in Paul and revered God in his breast; he dared not answer further. Weeping silently, he kissed Paul’s eyes and hands and returned to the monastery, which was later occupied by the Saracens [Note: Bollandus notes that this occurred in the same year in which Saint Antony died. See the *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 356.].

His steps, however, did not keep pace with his spirit. Although his body was exhausted by fasting and even his old age had broken him, he conquered his age by the strength of his spirit [Note: The manuscripts read: “But although his body, emptied by fasting, and his years had broken him, in spirit he conquered.” The Verona manuscript agrees.].

## 13. Antony’s Humility

At last, tired and breathless [Verona manuscript: “exhausted”], he reached his dwelling after completing the journey. Two disciples who had begun to minister to him in his advanced old age [Note: The reading in all the common editions, “who had long been accustomed to minister to him,” is not sufficiently appropriate and certainly contradicts Jerome’s intention and the evidence of the manuscripts.] came to meet him, saying:

“Father, where have you been for so long?”

He replied:

“Woe to me, a sinner, who bear the false name of monk. I saw Elijah; I saw John in the desert; and truly I saw Paul in paradise.”

Then, with his lips compressed and striking his breast with his hand, he brought the cloak out of his cell.

When the disciples asked him to explain more fully what had happened, he said:

“There is a time for keeping silence, and a time for speaking” (Ecclesiastes 3:7).

## 14. Paul’s Soul among the Choirs of Angels

Then he went outside, taking not even a little food, and returned by the road along which he had come, thirsting for him, longing to see him, and embracing him with his eyes and with his whole mind.

For he feared—and what he feared happened—that, while he was absent, Paul would give back to Christ the spirit owed to him [Note: The word *debitum* (“owed”) is absent from two Vatican manuscripts. Immediately afterward, instead of “the journey might remain,” the reading we have taken from the consensus of the manuscripts is “three hours’ journey remained”; the former reading had prevailed up to this point in the opposite sense, even though the following context compels the latter.].

When another day had already dawned and three hours of the journey remained, he saw Paul, shining with snowy radiance, ascending on high among the hosts of angels and the choirs of prophets and apostles [Note: The Verona manuscript has “he sees,” in the present tense.].

Immediately falling on his face, he heaped sand upon his head and, weeping and wailing, said:

“Why are you leaving me, Paul? Why are you departing without greeting me? Why, known so late, are you departing so soon?”

## 15.

The blessed Antony afterward related that he ran the remaining distance with such speed that he flew like a bird—and not without reason. For when he entered the cave, he saw the lifeless body with its knees folded, its neck erect, and its hands extended upward [Verona manuscript: “he sees”].

At first he himself believed Paul to be alive and prayed beside him. But when he heard none of the sighs of a person praying that he was accustomed to hear, he rushed into a mournful embrace and understood that even the corpse of the saint was praying by the gestures of the body to the God to whom all things live [Note: So read the manuscripts and Victorius. Martianus, following Erasmus, is wrong to read: “that the holy corpse was also praying to God,” etc.].

## 16. Christian Tradition

After wrapping the body and carrying it outside, Antony sang hymns and psalms according to Christian tradition [Note: The Verona manuscript and other manuscripts read: “After carrying the body outside and singing psalms according to Christian tradition, Antony was distressed,” etc.]. He was saddened because he had no hoe with which to dig the earth.

[Note: The Verona manuscript has “he possessed.” “And wavering amid conflicting thoughts,” it says, “he reflected: If …,” without an intervening verb.]

Thus, wavering amid conflicting emotions and turning many thoughts over in his mind, he said:

“If I return to the monastery, it is a four-day journey [Others: “three-day journey”]. If I remain here, I will accomplish nothing further. I shall therefore die, as is fitting, beside your warrior, O Christ, and, falling down, pour out my final breath.”

While he was turning these things over in his mind, behold, two lions came running from the inner part of the desert, their manes flying around their necks. At the sight of them he was terrified at first. But turning his mind again to God, he remained fearless, as though he were seeing doves.

They ran directly to the body of the blessed old man and stopped there. Fawning with their tails, they lay down around his feet, roaring with an immense growl, so that you would understand that they were mourning as best they could [Others: “so that he would understand”].

Then, not far away, they began to scratch the earth with their feet [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “to scrape”; another “to hollow out” and “to dig out a space large enough”; immediately afterward, one has “moved by their ears” instead of “with movement of their ears.” The Verona manuscript reads “about to ask.”]. Ejecting the sand in rivalry, they dug a space large enough for one person [Verona manuscript: “dug out.”].

Immediately, as though asking for payment for their work, they approached Antony with a movement of their ears and their necks lowered, licking his hands and feet [Note: The manuscripts have in one sequence: “so that he might notice”; shortly afterward the two Vatican manuscripts read *sibi servirent* (“served themselves”) instead of *Deum esse sentirent* (“perceived that he was God”); the other reads: “so that he might perceive that even mute animals recognized him.” The Verona manuscript omits “that he was God.”].

He understood that they were asking him for a blessing. Without delay, pouring himself out in praise of Christ because even mute animals perceived that he was God, he said:

“Lord, without whose will neither a leaf falls from a tree nor one sparrow falls to the ground, give them what you know.”

He waved his hand at them [Others: “signaled to them”] and ordered them to depart.

When they had withdrawn, he bent his aged shoulders beneath the burden of the holy body. He laid it upon the excavated earth and, gathering earth over it [Note: “Into the grave” was incorrect. One manuscript of the Queen’s Library more correctly reads “in the grave.” But the reading of the other manuscripts seemed most accurate: “the earth that had been dug out,” that is, “the earth,” etc. The Verona manuscript then has “another day had dawned.”], raised a mound according to custom [Others: “constructed it”].

When the next day dawned, lest the pious heir possess anything from the intestate’s estate, he claimed Paul’s tunic for himself, the one Paul had woven for himself from palm leaves in the form of a basket.

Thus he returned to the monastery and related everything in order to the disciples. On the solemn days of Easter and Pentecost he always wore Paul’s tunic.

## 17. A Comparison of Paul and the Rich of This World

At the end of this little work, I wish to question those who do not know the limits of their patrimonies, who clothe their houses in marble, and who sew estates into a single thread of villas [Note: The reading was *lino* (“linen”), which Victorius noted as faulty; Martianus has *praedia pro pretia* (“estates instead of prices”), as is customary with him when copying Erasmus without consulting the other books. Jerome imitated this passage from Tertullian’s *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 9: “Ten thousand sesterces are inserted into a single thread.” It is a thread into which pearls and gems are inserted, forming necklaces. Nevertheless, the Verona manuscript has *lino* (“linen”) instead of *filo* (“thread”), and *pretia* (“prices”) instead of *praedia* (“estates”).]:

“What did this naked [Others: “nearly naked”] old man ever lack? You drink from gems; he satisfied himself with the hollowed hands of nature [Note: See below, Book II *Against Jovinianus*, and Diogenes Laertius on Diogenes. Immediately afterward two manuscripts read: “I care about woven tunics.”].

“You weave gold into your tunics; he did not even possess the clothing of the cheapest slave belonging to you.

“But, on the other hand, paradise stands open to that poor man, while Gehenna will receive you in your gold. Although naked, he preserved the garment of Christ; clothed in silk, you have lost Christ’s garment.

“Paul lies covered with the cheapest dust, destined to rise in glory; elaborate stone tombs [Others omit *saxi*, “of stone”] weigh you down, and you will burn with your possessions.

“Spare yourselves, I beg you—spare at least the riches you love. Why do you wrap even your dead in gilded garments? Why does ambition not cease amid mourning and tears? Do the corpses of the rich not know how to decay except in silk?”

## 18. I beseech you, whoever reads this, to remember Jerome the sinner: if the Lord were to give him a choice, he would much rather choose Paul’s tunic together with Paul’s merits than the purple robes of kings together with their punishments.

[Note: The Verona manuscript has “with his merits”; other copies have “with kingdoms” instead of “with punishments.” Martianus appended both readings. One Vatican manuscript adds the following at the end: “Here ends the life of the blessed Paul the Monk, written by Jerome the presbyter, who came before Saint Antony, whom he himself buried in the desert. He was never in the cities after he had dwelt in solitude.”]

[Col. 0029]

[Note: Written approximately in A.D. 390.]

# LIFE OF SAINT HILARION (C)

[Col. 0029]

The monk Hilarion, born at Thabatha, a village of Palestine, and a disciple of the great Antony, lived with such abstinence and holiness, and became renowned in the desert for such great miracles, that Jerome describes him at length and presents in him a model of the perfect monk.

13 [Note: In the *Lives of the Fathers*, the following appeal is prefixed to the Prologue: “In your holy prayers remember me, Nonna Asella, glory and dignity of virgins”; and likewise at the end of the Life: “I desire that you remain in Christ and remember me in your prayers, most sacred virgin.” Hence some have thought that Jerome dedicated this history to Asella; but since those words are found neither in other printed editions nor in any manuscripts, I see no basis for establishing the matter with certainty.]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0029A]

### 1.

As I am about to write the Life of blessed Hilarion, I invoke his indwelling Holy Spirit, so that he who bestowed virtues upon Hilarion may grant me the speech with which to recount them, and so that deeds may be made equal to words. For the virtue of those who have acted, as Crispus says, is esteemed as great as distinguished talents have been able to exalt it in words.

[Note: Victor has “virtues,” and, as Crispus says, “their merits are as great as …,” but this is incorrect. See Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 8.]

Alexander the Great of Macedon—whom Daniel calls either a ram, or a leopard, or a he-goat of the goats—

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have “beast” instead of “ram”; the latter word is more correctly omitted in another manuscript.]

when he had reached the tomb of Achilles, said:

[Note: “Fortunate are you.” The Avignon manuscript reads: “You are fortunate, young man, you say, who …” The same account is given by Arrian in Book I of *The Deeds of Alexander the Great* and by Plutarch in his *Alexander*. Alexander’s words are quoted by Vopiscus in *Probus*: “Fortunate are you,” he said, “young man, who have found such a herald of your virtues.” MARTIAN.]

“You are fortunate, young man, who enjoy such a great herald of your merits!”—plainly referring to Homer.

But I must describe the conduct and life of so great and distinguished a man that even Homer, if he were present, would either envy the subject matter or succumb to it. For although Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, who spent much time with Hilarion, wrote a short letter praising him, which is commonly read—

[Note: This letter of Epiphanius did not survive to his time.]

nevertheless, it is one thing to praise the dead by means of commonplaces, and another to recount the dead man’s particular virtues. Therefore, as we undertake the work begun by him—more out of respect for him than as an affront to him—we disregard the voices of detractors. Those who once disparaged my Paul will perhaps now disparage Hilarion also: they slandered Paul for his solitude, while they will reproach Hilarion for his crowds, so that the one who was always hidden may be considered not to have existed, and the one seen by many may be judged worthless. Their predecessors, the Pharisees, once did the same. They were pleased neither by John’s desert and fasting nor by the crowds, food, and drink of the Lord and Savior. But I shall lay my hand to the work I have undertaken and, with stopped ears, pass by the dogs of Scylla.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

### 2.

[Note: Compare Sozomen, Book III, chapter 14: “His homeland was Thabatha, a village situated south of Gaza”; and shortly afterward: “While attending a grammarian in Alexandria,” etc.]

Hilarion was born in the village of Tabatha, situated about five miles south of the Palestinian city of Gaza. Although his parents were devoted to idols, a rose, as the saying goes, blossomed from thorns. They sent him to Alexandria and entrusted him to a grammarian. There, as much as his age allowed, he gave great evidence of intelligence and character; in a short time he became dear to everyone and skilled in speaking. And, greater than all these things, having believed in the Lord Jesus, he took no pleasure in the frenzies of the circus, the blood of the arena, or the extravagance of the theater; his entire desire [Al. pleasure] was in the assembly of the Church.

### 3.

When he heard the famous name of Antony, which was being proclaimed throughout nearly all the peoples of Egypt, he was inflamed with a desire to see him and went out to the desert. As soon as he saw him, he changed his former clothing and remained near him for nearly two [Ms. three] months, observing the order of his life and the gravity of his conduct: how constant he was in prayer, how humble in receiving the brothers, severe in correcting them, and cheerful in encouraging them; and how no illness ever broke his continence or the austerity of his food.

But he could no longer endure the crowds of people who flocked to Antony on account of various illnesses [Note: The two Vatican manuscripts have “various illnesses and afflictions”; shortly afterward they read “saying” instead of “leading.”] or attacks of demons; nor did he think it fitting that the people of the cities should inhabit the desert. Thus, he judged that he ought to begin for himself as Antony had begun: Antony was receiving the rewards of victory as a strong man, whereas Hilarion had not yet begun to serve as a soldier. He therefore returned to his homeland with some monks.

When his parents had died, he distributed part of his property to his brothers and part to the poor, reserving absolutely nothing for himself and fearing the example—or punishment—of Ananias and Sapphira in the Acts of the Apostles. Above all, he remembered the Lord’s saying: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

He was then fifteen years old. Thus naked and armed in Christ, he entered the wilderness that, for travelers going along the coast toward Egypt, turns to the left at the seventh milestone from the emporium of Gaza, Majoma.

[Note: The manuscripts have “Majuma” and “Mauma.” See Sozomen, Book V, chapter 3.]

Although the region was bloody with brigandage, and his relatives and friends warned him of the impending danger, he despised death in order to escape death.

### 4. Hilarion’s fasting

Everyone marveled at his courage; everyone marveled at his age. Yet a certain flame of the breast [Col. 0031A]

[Note: The word “breast” is almost entirely absent from the manuscripts.]

and sparks of faith shone in his eyes.

[Note: “His cheeks were smooth.” In Erasmus’s edition we read “his cheeks were soft,” but incorrectly, since all the better manuscripts, both ancient and recent, retain the word *smooth*. Through the fraud or incompetence of earlier copyists, *soft* may have slipped in for *smooth*. Genesis 27:11: “But I am smooth.” MARTIAN.]

His cheeks were smooth [Al. soft], his body delicate and slender, unfit to endure any hardship, and liable to be afflicted by the slightest cold or heat. Accordingly, covering his limbs only with a sackcloth and wearing a leather cloak, an *ependytes* which blessed Antony had given him when he departed, together with a coarse rustic mantle, he enjoyed the vast and terrible solitude between the sea and the marsh, eating only fifteen figs after sunset.

Because the region was notorious for brigands, he never made a habit of living in the same place. What could the devil do? Where could he turn? He who had formerly boasted, saying, “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14), saw himself defeated by a boy and trampled underfoot by him before the boy was old enough to sin.

### 5.

[Note: “Thus his senses were tickled.” The Avignon and Toulouse manuscripts read: “Thus his senses were tickled by the natural heat of the flesh, and …” MARTIAN.]

Thus his senses were tickled, and he suggested to his adolescent body the customary fires of pleasure. The novice of Christ was forced to think about what he did not know and to turn over in his mind the spectacle of something whose experience he had never known.

Angry with himself and beating his breast with his fists—as though he could drive out thoughts by slaughtering them with his hands—he said:

[Note: Saint Paulinus expresses this very elegantly in Poem XXI:

“Let the soul be strong, mortifying its ass,” namely, the body inclined toward lust.]

“Little ass, I shall see to it that you do not kick. I shall not feed you with barley, but with chaff. I shall wear you out with hunger and thirst; I shall load you with a heavy burden; through heat and cold I shall track you down, so that you will think about food rather than wantonness.”

Accordingly, he sustained his failing spirit with the juice of herbs and a few figs every three or four days, praying and chanting psalms frequently and digging the soil with a hoe, so that the labor of work might double the labor of his fasts. At the same time, weaving small baskets from rushes, he imitated the discipline of the Egyptian monks and the Apostle’s saying: “If anyone will not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Thus he was emaciated, his body so thoroughly wasted that it scarcely clung to his bones.

### 6.

One night he began to hear the cries of infants, the bleating of sheep, the lowing of oxen, the lamentation of little women [Al. women], the roaring of lions, the rumbling of an army, and again monstrous sounds of various kinds, so that he was terrified and gave way more from the sound than from the sight. He understood that these were the mockeries of demons. Falling on his knees, he made the sign of Christ’s cross on his forehead. Armed in this way, he fought more resolutely as he lay there, desiring in some manner to see those whom he dreaded hearing, and looking anxiously around him in every direction.

Meanwhile, unexpectedly, with the moon shining, he saw a chariot with fiery horses rushing upon him. When he cried out to Jesus, the entire spectacle was suddenly swallowed up before his eyes by a cleft in the earth. Then he said: “He cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exodus 15:1). And: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we will glory in the name of our God” (Psalm 20:7).

### 7.

His temptations were many, and the snares of demons varied by day and night. If I wished to recount them all, I would exceed the limits of the book. How often, while he was lying down, naked women appeared to him; how often, while he was hungry, lavish banquets appeared! At times a howling wolf and yelping fox leapt over him while he prayed; and while he was chanting psalms, a gladiatorial combat was staged before him. One gladiator, as though wounded and collapsing at his feet, asked to be buried.

### 8.

Once he prayed with his head fixed to the ground, and, as human nature dictates, his mind was drawn away from prayer and was thinking about something else. A charioteer leapt upon his back—

[Note: Victor has “a swift charioteer,” instead of the former “gladiator.” Shortly afterward the two Vatican manuscripts read “you are sleeping?” instead of “why are you sleeping?”]

—and, kicking his sides and striking his neck with a whip, said: “Come now, why are you sleeping?” Laughing from above, he asked whether, if the man had failed, he wanted to receive barley.

### 9. Hilarion’s little hut

From the age of sixteen to twenty, he avoided heat and rain in a small hut that he had covered with reeds and rushes. Later he built a small cell, which remains to this day. It was five feet high—that is, lower than his own stature—and slightly longer than his little body required—

[Note: Two manuscripts have a word meaning “he walked about,” perhaps with another or more harmonious sense.]

—so that you would think it a tomb rather than a house.

### 10. Hilarion’s clothing and way of life

Once a year, on Easter Day, he cut his hair. He lay on the bare ground and on a mat of reeds until his death. He never washed the sackcloth with which he had once clothed himself, saying that it was SUPERFLUOUS to seek cleanliness in a hair shirt. He did not change to another tunic unless the first had been completely torn apart.

He also retained the sacred Scriptures by heart and recited them after prayers and psalms as though in the presence of God. Since it would be tedious to recount his progress in fragments over the various periods of his life, I shall briefly set it before the reader’s eyes, presenting his life as a whole; afterward I shall return to the order of the narrative.

### 11. Hilarion’s food

From his twenty-first year to his twenty-seventh, for three years he ate half a sextarius of lentils soaked in cold water, and for another three years dry bread with salt and water. From his twenty-seventh year to his thirtieth, he was sustained by wild herbs and the raw roots of certain shrubs. From his thirty-first year to his thirty-fifth, he had six ounces of barley bread and a small quantity of cooked vegetables, without oil, as food.

When he perceived that his eyes were becoming dim and that his whole body was contracting with a skin disease and a certain pumice-like roughness, he added oil to the diet described above. He continued this degree of abstinence until his sixty-third year, tasting nothing else—neither fruit, nor vegetables, nor any other food.

Then, when he saw that his body was exhausted and thought that death was near, from his sixty-fourth year to his eightieth he abstained from bread, with incredible fervor of mind, so that at that time he might approach the service of the Lord as though a new recruit, when others customarily live more indulgently. His food and drink consisted of a little gruel made from flour and chopped greens, weighing scarcely five ounces. Thus he completed the course of his life, never breaking his fast before sunset—not on feast days, nor even in the most serious illness [Al. sickness]. But now it is time to return to the order of the narrative.

### 12. Robbers come to Hilarion by night
