When he was still living in his little hut, at the age of eighteen, robbers came to him at night, either thinking that he had something they could steal or considering it an insult to themselves if a solitary boy did not fear their attack. Thus they ran about between the sea and the marsh from evening until sunrise, but were never able to find the place where he slept.

In broad daylight, when they had found the boy, they asked him almost jokingly: “What would you do if robbers came to you?” He replied: “A naked man does not fear robbers.” They said: “Certainly, you can be killed.” “I can,” he said, “I can; and for that reason I do not fear robbers, because I am ready to die.”

Then, astonished at his steadfastness and faith, they confessed their nighttime error and that their eyes had been blinded, promising that thereafter they would live a more upright life.

### 13. A barren woman is the first to dare to break in upon him

He had already spent twenty-two years in the desert, known to everyone only by reputation, and his fame had spread throughout all the cities of Palestine. Meanwhile, a certain woman from Eleutheropolis, seeing herself despised by her husband because of her barrenness—for she had borne no fruit of marriage for fifteen years—was the first to dare to break in upon blessed Hilarion.

He suspected nothing of the kind when suddenly she fell at his knees and said: “Forgive my boldness; forgive my necessity. Why do you turn your eyes away? Why do you flee from a woman who is asking you for help? Do not look at a woman, but at a wretched person. This sex gave birth to the Savior. Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke 5:31).

At last he stopped and, after seeing a woman for so long a time, asked the reason for her arrival and her tears. When he learned it, he raised his eyes to heaven and told her to trust. He accompanied her departure with tears and, after a year had passed, saw her with a son.

### 14. A noblewoman, wife of the prefect of the praetorium. There were no monks in Syria before Saint Hilarion

This beginning of his signs was enhanced by another, greater sign.

[Note: The manuscripts give the Greek form *Aristaenete* (Ἀρισταινέτη). Libanius praises her highly in Book IV, Letter 44, to Helpidius: “I have come to know the excellent Aristaenete.” Marcellinus, however, is somewhat unfair to Helpidius, evidently because of his hostility toward the Christian name. “Aristaenete of Helpidius.” For Helpidius, prefect of the praetorium, see Marcellinus, Book 21. MARTIAN.]

Aristaenete, the wife of Elpidius, who afterward became prefect of the praetorium, was highly distinguished among her own people and even more distinguished among Christians. Returning with her husband and three children from blessed Antony, she stayed at Gaza on account of their illness. There, either because of the corrupted air or—as later became clear—because of the glory of Hilarion, the servant of God, all were seized alike by the semitertian fever.

[Note: *Hemitritaeus* means a fever occurring every third day and a half, Greek ἡμιτριταῖος πυρετός, “semiter­tian fever.” Galen, *To Glaucon*: an imperfect tertian approaching a quotidian, because it recurs sooner than a true tertian. See Celsus, *On the Kinds of Fevers*. MARTIAN.]

All were given up by the physicians. The mother lay howling and, as though moving among the three corpses of her children, did not know which one she should mourn first.

When she learned that there was a monk in the neighboring desert, she forgot the pomp of a married woman—for she knew only that she was a mother—and went there accompanied by maidservants and eunuchs [Al. household servants]. Only with difficulty was she persuaded by the man to travel seated on a little donkey.

When she reached him, she said:

[Note: The two Vatican manuscripts read more elegantly: “I beseech you, by Jesus …”]

“I beseech you by Jesus, our most merciful God; I adjure you by his cross and blood: restore my three sons to me, so that the name of the Lord and Savior may be glorified in the city of the Gentiles, and that his servant may enter Gaza, and that the idol Marnas may fall.”

[Note: Our manuscripts do not recognize the word “idol.” Our author speaks again below of Marnas, as does his letter to Laeta; Arnobius and Marinus likewise mention him in the *Life of Proclus*. Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*, chapter 108: “Marnas, the slave of Asterius the Cretan, is worshiped by the Gazans.” Shortly afterward the manuscripts have “about to depart” instead of “having departed.”]

He refused, saying that he had never left his cell and was not accustomed to entering not only a city but even a village. She prostrated herself on the ground, repeatedly crying out: “Hilarion, servant of Christ, restore my children to me. Those whom Antony preserved in Egypt, let them be saved by you in Syria.”

Everyone present wept, but he himself wept as he refused. What more is there to say? The woman did not leave until he promised that he would enter Gaza after sunset.

When he arrived there, he marked each of their beds and their burning limbs with the sign of the cross and invoked Jesus.

[Note: Other copies have “dry,” but “burning” is more fitting for the semitertian fever, that is, the fever occurring every third day and a half. Earlier printed books made the shameful error of reading “they considered” instead of “he marked,” which means “he marked with the sign of the cross” or “blessed” in ecclesiastical writers and is found in all the manuscripts we consulted.]

And, marvelous to relate, as though from three springs, sweat burst forth from all three at once. At that very hour they received food; recognizing their grieving mother and blessing God, they kissed the holy man’s hands.

When this became known and spread far and wide, people flocked to him competitively from Syria and Egypt, so that many believed in Christ and professed themselves monks. For at that time there were not yet monasteries in Palestine, and no one in Syria had known a monk before Saint Hilarion. He was the founder and teacher of this way of life and discipline in that province. The Lord Jesus had the old man Antony in Egypt; in Palestine he had the younger Hilarion.

### 15. A blind woman for ten years

Facidia is a little village of the Egyptian city Rhinocorura.

[Note: It was absurdly printed as *vicula*—“little village”—instead of *viculus*—“village”; we have restored the correct form from all the manuscripts. In the old editions, the following was incorrectly printed as “it has now been ten years,” which Rosweyd corrected, and the manuscripts confirm.]

From this village, a woman who had been blind for ten years was brought to blessed Hilarion.

[Note: “For ten years already.” The older editions mislead the reader by printing “it has now been ten years,” as though the miracle of the blind woman’s healing were said to have occurred ten years earlier. MARTIAN.]

When she was presented to him by the brothers—for many monks were already with him—she said that she had spent all her property on physicians. He replied: “If you had given to the poor what you lost on physicians, the true physician, Jesus, would have healed you.”

When she cried out and begged for mercy, he spat into her eyes, and immediately the same power that had followed the Savior’s example followed here also.

### 16. The charioteer of Gaza

A charioteer from Gaza was also struck by a demon while in his chariot and became completely rigid, so that he could neither move his hand nor turn his neck [Al. could]. He was therefore carried on a bed. While he could move only his tongue to pray, he heard that he could not be healed until he believed in Jesus and promised that he would renounce his former profession.

He believed, he promised, and he was healed. He rejoiced more over the salvation of his soul than over that of his body.

### 17. Marsitas, a very strong young man

Moreover, a very strong young man named Marsitas—

[Note: Three of our manuscripts have *Messicas*, others *Mesitas*; shortly afterward they read “inspired” instead of “affected.” The older printed editions incorrectly have “afflicted.”]

—from the territory of Jerusalem took such pride in his strength that he could carry fifteen *modii* of grain for a long distance and a long time; and he considered it the crown of his strength if he could surpass donkeys.

He was afflicted by a most wicked demon and tolerated neither chains, fetters, nor intact door-bars. He had bitten off the noses and ears of many people; he had broken the feet of some and the legs of others.

[Note: Earlier editions had “he seized the throat” instead of “he broke the legs,” which seemed worth correcting from the two Vatican manuscripts. One of them, retaining both readings, has: “He had broken the throats of these and the feet—or legs—of those.”]

He had inspired everyone with such terror that, loaded with chains and ropes pulled in opposite directions by those straining against him, he was dragged to the monastery like a most savage bull. When the brothers saw him, they were terrified—for he was of enormous size—and they reported him to the father.

The father, just as he was sitting, ordered him to be dragged to him and released. When he had been unbound, he said: “Bow your head and come.”

The man trembled, bent his neck, and did not dare look him in the face. Having laid aside all his ferocity, he began to lick the feet of the seated man. The demon who had possessed the young man was adjured and tormented, and on the seventh day departed.

### 18. Orion, a man of distinction

Nor should it be left unmentioned that Orion, a man of distinction and the wealthiest citizen of the city of Aila, which overlooks the Red Sea, was brought to Hilarion possessed by a legion of demons.

His hands, neck, sides, and feet were weighed down with iron, and his fierce eyes threatened the violence of his madness. As the holy man was walking with the brothers and interpreting something from the Scriptures, Orion broke free from those holding him. He embraced Hilarion from behind and lifted him into the air.

Everyone cried out, for they feared that he would dash to pieces the saint’s limbs, wasted by fasting. The holy man smiled and said: “Be silent [Al. let me be], and release my wrestler to me.”

Then, bending his hand over his shoulders, he touched Orion’s head; seizing him by the hair, he brought him before his feet. He gripped both his hands directly in front of him and stamped on both his feet with his own feet, repeatedly saying: “Torture them, you crowd of demons, torture them.”

When Orion howled and, with his neck bent backward, touched the ground with the crown of his head, Hilarion said: “Lord Jesus, release the wretched man; release the captive. It is yours to conquer one, and likewise many.”

I relate something unheard-of: different voices issued from one human mouth, and the sound resembled the confused shouting of a crowd.

When Orion had been healed, he came to the monastery not long afterward with his wife and children, bringing many gifts as though to return thanks. The holy man said to him: “Have you not read what happened to Gehazi (2 Kings 5) and to Simon (Acts 8), one of whom accepted a price and the other offered one—so that the former might sell the grace of the Holy Spirit and the latter purchase it?”

When Orion, weeping, said, “Accept them and give them to the poor,” Hilarion replied: “You can distribute your own possessions better, since you travel through the cities and know the poor. I, who abandoned my own possessions, why should I desire another’s?”

Many people use the name of the poor as an occasion for greed; mercy, however, has no artifice. NO ONE distributes more effectively than one who reserves nothing for himself.

When Orion, sorrowful and lying on the ground—

[Note: All the manuscripts read “in the arenas” instead of “on the ground.”]

—the saint said to him: “Do not be distressed, my son. What I do for myself, I do also for you. For if I accept these things, I too shall offend God, and the legion will return to you.”

### 19. A paralytic is healed

Who could pass over in silence the fact that a Gazan from Majoma, not far from Hilarion’s monastery, was cutting stones from the seashore for building and became completely paralyzed? His fellow workers carried him to the holy man, and he immediately returned healthy to his work.

[Note: We have added “healthy” from the manuscripts.]

The shore that stretches [Possibly: extends] before Palestine and Egypt is naturally soft, but becomes rough as the sands harden into stone; and, gradually clinging together, the gravel loses its touch, though it does not lose its appearance.

### 20. A spell undone at the circus

An Italian, a Christian citizen of the same town, was also raising circus horses against the Gazan duumvir, who was devoted to the idol Marnas.

[Note: Earlier editions, contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts, read “is preserved at present.” Then, instead of “for Consus,” they formerly read “by Consus himself.” It was preferred to read more emphatically “for Consus himself.” Concerning this god of counsels, for whom quadrigas ran in a sevenfold circuit, monuments occur everywhere; among them is an ancient inscription once excavated in the Circus Maximus, cited by our Panvinius in *On Circus Games*. Most elegant is Propertius, II: “Or does she seek the prize before, by skill, / Her wheel has worn the seventh turning-post in its unfinished course?” For the matter at hand, Varro, Book V of *On the Latin Language*: “The Consualia are so called from Consus, because then public festivals are held for that god, and in the circus games are celebrated at his altar by the priests—the games at which the Sabine maidens were carried off.” And Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*: “Thereafter the games were called Consualia, which at first honored Neptune. For they call him also Consus.” And immediately: “Although they also defend the Consualia by reference to Romulus, because he dedicated them to Consus, the god, as they maintain, of Counsel—namely, of that counsel by which he then devised for his soldiers the abduction of the Sabine maidens for marriage.” Saint Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*: “Consus, whom Romulus wished to be worshiped as the god of deceit, or as it were the god of counsels, after his treachery had succeeded in the abduction of the Sabines.” See also, if desired, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book I; Valerius Maximus, Book II; and Plutarch, *Roman Questions*.]

[Note: “For Consus, as it were.” On Consus, the god of counsels, and the circus games, consult Book III of Festus Pompeius’ fragments and Book V of Varro’s *On the Latin Language*. MARTIAN.]

This custom had indeed been preserved in Roman cities from the time of Romulus, so that, in honor of the successful abduction of the Sabine women, quadrigas would run seven circuits for Consus, regarded as the god of counsels, and victory would consist in breaking the horses of the opposing side.

The Italian’s rival had a sorcerer who, by certain demonic incantations, hindered the Italian’s horses and urged the rival’s horses to run. The Italian therefore came to blessed Hilarion and begged not so much that his adversary be harmed as that he himself be protected.

It seemed foolish to the venerable old man to waste a prayer on such trifles. He smiled and said: “Why do you not instead give the price of the horses to the poor for the salvation of your soul?”

The Italian replied that this was a public duty, and that he wished it not so much as he was compelled to perform it. A Christian could not use magical arts; rather, he should seek help from a servant of Christ, especially against the Gazan adversaries of God, who were insulting not so much him as the Church of Christ.

The brothers who were present therefore urged Hilarion to help him. He ordered that the earthen cup from which he usually drank be filled with water and given to the Italian. When the Italian had received it, he sprinkled his stable, his horses, his charioteers,

[Note: The word “chariot” is absent from all the manuscripts we use. One older Vatican manuscript reads “the bars of the wagons” instead of “the barriers of the starting gates,” perhaps more correctly.]

his chariot, and the barriers of the starting gates with the water.

The crowd waited in wonder. The rival had mocked and publicized the incident, while the Italian’s supporters exulted, promising themselves a certain victory. At the signal, the one team rushed forward and the other was hindered. Beneath the former’s chariot the wheels burned, while the others could scarcely see the backs of the team flying past.

The crowd’s shouting grew enormous [The manuscripts read: “the enormous shouting of the crowd rose up”], so that even the Gentiles themselves shouted together: “Marnas has been defeated by Christ!”

The furious opponents then demanded that Hilarion, the Christian sorcerer, be punished.

[Note: The manuscripts read “the sorcerer of the Christians.” Ancient authors often note that the sorcerers who drove horses hindered the horses of opponents by demonic imprecations and urged their own toward faster running. Cassiodorus, Book III of the *Variae*, Letter 1, says of a certain noble charioteer: “The frequency of his victories caused him to be called a sorcerer.” For victory in horse racing cannot be attributed to merit unless it is referred to perverse magic. Arnobius, Book I *Against the Gentiles*, on the arts of magicians: “Who does not know this … in the racecourse to weaken, urge on, delay a horse,” etc. See also the Theodosian Code, on the law concerning magic, Book IX, and Ammianus Marcellinus in several passages.]

Thus the unquestionable victory became an occasion of faith both for them and for many others at numerous subsequent circus games.

### 21. He frees a virgin from a love-spell

In the same town of the emporium of Gaza, a neighboring young man was consumed with desire for a virgin of God.

[Note: In three or four manuscript copies: “A young man who lived near the virgin of God was wasting away from love.” MARTIAN.]

Since he had accomplished nothing by repeated touches, jokes, nods, whistles, and other such actions—which are commonly the beginnings of a dying virginity—he went to Memphis so that, having confessed his wound, he might return armed with magical arts against the virgin.

[Note: Isaiah 19 has a similar passage: “Memphis, devoted to magical arts, displays traces of its former error down to the present.” And in chapter 65, concerning the shrine of Aesculapius, in which the Gentiles used to lie upon the skins of sacrificial victims in order to learn future things in dreams.]

After a year, having been instructed by the prophets of Aesculapius, who did not heal souls but destroyed them—

[Note: Some copies read: “By the prophets of Aesculapius, who did not remedy but destroyed souls,” etc. MARTIAN.]

—he returned, carrying in his mind the intended violation. Beneath the threshold of the girl’s house he buried certain monstrous words and monstrous figures engraved on a sheet of Cyprian bronze.

Immediately the virgin went mad. Throwing off the covering of her head, she twisted her hair, gnashed her teeth, and called out the young man’s name. The greatness of her love had turned into madness.

Her parents therefore brought her to the monastery and entrusted her to the old man. At once the demon howled and confessed:

“I have suffered violence; I was dragged away against my will. How well I used to deceive people in Memphis through dreams! O crosses! O torments that I endure! You force me to leave, yet I am bound and held beneath the threshold. I will not leave unless the young man who holds me releases me.”

Then the old man said: “Great indeed is your strength, since you are held fast by a thread and a sheet of metal. Tell me: why did you dare to enter the virgin of God?”

“To preserve her virginity,” he replied.

“You would preserve her, traitor to chastity? Why did you not rather enter the man who sent you?”

“Why,” he answered, “should I enter the man who had my fellow demon of love as his companion?”

Before he had cleansed the virgin, however, the saint did not wish to order either the young man or the signs to be sought out,

[Note: Earlier editors, through the omission or insertion of this one small phrase, acted contrary to the truth of the story and Jerome’s intention, making it appear that Saint Hilarion also healed the young man. On the contrary, he did not even permit the young man to be sought, lest he seem to give credence to his incantations. We have supplied the wording from all our manuscripts, with the support of Gravius. We have also corrected another error of the earlier editors, who read “released”—that is, the demon departed—for “customary,” namely, incantations. We correct several lesser matters below.]

lest the demon appear to have departed after being released by incantations, or lest Hilarion himself appear to have placed faith in the demon’s speech. He asserted that demons are deceitful and skillful at pretending. After restoring the virgin to health, he rebuked her more severely for having done things through which the demon could have entered.

## 22. He frees Constantius’s Candidate from a demon. The local decurions.

Not only throughout Palestine and the neighboring cities of Egypt and Syria, but also in distant provinces, his fame had spread. For Candidatus [Note: All the manuscripts, including those consulted by Martianay, read *Constantini*. Concerning the *Candidati*, who constituted a military rank, see the ancient authors, especially Ammianus Marcellinus, passim.] of the emperor Constantius, red-haired and indicating his province by the whiteness of his body—for among the Saxons and Alemanni there is a people [Note: In place of *ejus*, which all the manuscripts, together with Victorius, have, Martianay reads *est*. Concerning the boundaries and name of ancient Francia, see Eumenius, in the *Panegyric to Constantine*, where not only that part but Germany as a whole is called by the name of Francia. Ammianus Marcellinus likewise, book XXVII, chapter 8, says that the Franks and Saxons, whose territories bordered them, were laying waste the districts of Gaul. Francia lay between the Saxons and the Alemanni, as is also clear from the Peutinger Table.] which historians call Germania, but which is now called Francia, and whose territory was not so extensive as it was powerful—had, from ancient times, that is, from infancy, been possessed by a demon. The demon compelled him by night to howl, groan, and gnash his teeth. He secretly asked the emperor for an *evection* [Note: An imperial diploma granting permission to use the public transport system. In Greek, *sýnthema* (σύνθημα). See what we noted in *Epistle* 118, no. 1. The word belongs to legal terminology and is used elsewhere by Saint Jerome and by Sulpicius Severus, book 2 of the *History*: “Through the Vicar and the Governor, permission for an inquiry having been granted, he is compelled to appear, although the Emperor had issued no specific order concerning him.” It also occurs in Symmachus, book VI, letter 6; book VII, letters 48 and 105; and book IX, letter 20.], simply stating the reason. After receiving letters also from the governor of Palestine, he was escorted to Gaza with great honor and a large retinue.

When he asked the decurions of that place where the monk Hilarion lived, the Gazans were greatly terrified [Note: Two Vatican codices read: “Thinking that he had been sent to him by the Emperor, they went to the monastery.”] and, supposing that he had been sent by the Emperor, brought him to the monastery, both to render honor to the man commended and to erase, by this new service, any resentment that might remain from former injuries done to Hilarion.

The old man was then walking on the soft sands and murmuring something from the psalms to himself. When he saw such a large crowd approaching, he stopped. After returning everyone’s greeting and blessing them with his hand, he ordered the others to depart after an hour, but commanded the man to remain with his servants and attendants; for from his eyes and face he had recognized why he had come.

At once, when the servant of God questioned him, the man became suspended, scarcely touching the ground with his feet. Roaring terribly, he answered in the Syrian language in which he had been questioned. You would have seen Syrian words sounding perfectly from the mouth of a barbarian who knew only the Frankish and Latin languages, so that no harshness, aspiration, or peculiarity of Palestinian speech was lacking.

He confessed in what manner the demon had entered him. Then, so that his interpreters—who knew only Greek and Latin—might understand, Hilarion questioned him also in Greek. When he likewise answered in the same words and pleaded many opportunities for enchantments and necessities of magical arts, Hilarion said: “I do not care how you entered; but I command you, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to depart.”

When he had been cured [Note: The manuscripts add *homo*, “the man.” We correct a few minor matters below.], he offered ten pounds of gold with rustic simplicity and received from Hilarion a barley loaf, having heard that those who were nourished by such food regarded gold as mud.

## 23. Dumb animals cured.

It is too little to speak of human beings: dumb animals, too, were daily brought to him in their madness. Among them was a camel from Bactria, of enormous size, which had already crushed many people. More than thirty men brought it with shouts, stretched out by the strongest ropes.

Its eyes were bloodshot, its mouth foamed, its writhing tongue swelled, and over all the terror there resounded an immense roar. The old man therefore ordered it to be released. Immediately all who had brought it, and all who were with the old man, fled in every direction, not one remaining [Col. 0040B].

But Hilarion alone went forward to meet it and said in the Syrian language: “Do not frighten me, devil, with such a mass of body. In a little fox and in a camel you are one and the same.” Meanwhile he stood with his hand extended.

When the raging beast had reached him, as though it were about to devour him, it immediately collapsed and lowered its head until it was level with the ground. Everyone present marveled that after such ferocity there had suddenly appeared such gentleness.

The old man taught that, for the sake of harming human beings, the devil also seizes animals, burning with such hatred of them that he desires not only the people themselves but also whatever belongs to them to perish. As an example of this he offered the fact that, before permission was granted to tempt blessed Job, the devil killed all his possessions.

Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that, at the Lord’s command, two thousand swine were killed by demons (Matthew 8 and Mark 5); for those who witnessed it could not otherwise have believed that such a multitude of demons had come out of the man unless a great number of swine, as though driven by many forces, had fallen all at once.

## 24. M. Antony honored Hilarion.

Time would fail me if I wished to recount all the miracles performed by him. For he had been raised by the Lord to such glory that blessed Antony himself, hearing of his way of life, wrote to him and gladly received his letters.

Whenever sick people came to him from the regions of Syria, Antony would say to them: “Why did you take the trouble to come so far, when you have my son Hilarion there?”

Through his example, innumerable monasteries therefore began to arise throughout Palestine, and all the monks eagerly ran to him [Col. 0041A]. When he saw this, he praised the grace of the Lord and exhorted each one to make progress in the soul, saying: “The outward form of this world is passing away; and the true life is that which is purchased at the cost of hardship in the present life.””

## 25. Hilarion visited the monasteries.

Desiring to give them an example both of humility and of duty, on fixed days before the grape harvest he visited the monks’ cells. When the brothers learned this, they all flocked to him; and, accompanied by such a leader, they went around the monasteries, carrying their provisions, since sometimes as many as two thousand people gathered.

As time went on, each village gladly offered food to the neighboring monks for the reception of the saints.

How great his diligence was in not passing by any brother, however humble or poor, is shown by the following incident. When he was going into the desert of Kadesh to visit one of his disciples, he reached Elusa [Note: The manuscripts of Avignon and Toulouse retain *Elusium*; others read *Eolesa*. Martianay.] [Alternative readings: *Elusium* and *Eolesa*], accompanied by an endless multitude of monks [Note: “He reached Elusa.”], on the very day when the annual festival had gathered the entire population of the town into the temple of Venus.

They worshipped her because of Lucifer; the nation of the Saracens is devoted to her cult [Note: The same Gordianus the Monk bears witness to this in the *Life of Saint Placidus the Martyr*, no. 61. He says that Abdala, emperor of the Saracens, in order to erase the practice of the Christian religion completely from the earth and increase the worship of the temples of Moloch and of Lucifer, assembled an expedition of one hundred ships. Our Jerome likewise says in his commentary on Amos 5: “To this day the Saracens worship Lucifer.”].

The town itself was also largely half-barbarous because of the character of its location. When they heard that Saint Hilarion was passing by—for he had frequently cured many Saracens possessed by demons—the people came out in crowds with their wives and children to meet him. They bowed their necks and shouted in the Syrian language, “Barech,” that is, “Bless!”

He received them kindly and humbly and begged them to worship God rather than stones. At the same time he wept profusely, looking toward heaven and promising that, if they believed in Christ, he would come to them frequently.

By the marvelous grace of the Lord, they would not let him depart until he had laid out the plan of a future church; and their priest, who was a *Coronatus* [Note: The order of pagan priests was that of the *Coronati*, who are mentioned in Innocent’s letter to the bishops assembled at the synod of Toledo [Col. 0042D]. There he denies that those who, after baptism, had either been crowned or held what is called the priesthood could enter the ecclesiastical order. Firmicus Maternus says more clearly: “They will be either crowned, or placed over the priests, or bearers of sacred images.”], was marked with the sign of Christ.

## 26. The miserly monk.

Another year, when he was about to set out to visit the monasteries and was arranging on a list where he should stay and whom he should visit in passing, the monks, knowing that one of the brothers was excessively frugal and wishing at the same time to cure him of his fault, asked Hilarion to stay with him.

He replied: “Why do you wish to wrong yourselves and trouble the brother?”

When that frugal brother heard this [Note: In certain printed editions: “And out of affection of mind each one,” etc.], he was ashamed. With everyone’s urging, he could scarcely prevail upon the unwilling man to put his own monastery also on the list of places where Hilarion would stay.

On the tenth day they came to him. The guards had already been arranged in the vineyard [Note: Two Vatican codices read: “In the vineyard, as though it were a village, he had stationed them”; another older manuscript: “Already in the vineyard, as though it were a village, he had stationed them,” etc. Gravius found in other manuscripts: “As though it were someone else’s vineyard and he were the guardian of a village.”], so that as the visitors approached they might frighten them with stones, clods, and the whirling of a sling. The visitors departed in the morning without eating a grape, while the old man laughed and pretended not to know what had happened.

## 27. Sabas, the generous monk.

They were then received by another monk named Sabas—for we ought to conceal the name of the frugal man, but name the generous one. Since it was the Lord’s Day, Sabas invited everyone into the vineyard so that, before the hour of the meal, they might relieve the labor of the journey by eating grapes.

But the saint said: “Cursed is the one who seeks refreshment for the body before refreshment for the soul. Let us pray, sing psalms, and render our service to the Lord; then we shall hasten to the vineyard” [Alternative reading: “Then you will hasten to the vineyard.”].

When the service had been completed, he stood on high, blessed the vineyard [Col. 0042B], and released his sheep to feed. Those who were eating numbered no fewer than three thousand.

When the entire vineyard had still been valued at one hundred jars, after twenty days it produced three hundred. The frugal brother, however, gathered far less than usual and later grieved that even what he had possessed had turned into vinegar.

The old man had foretold this to many brothers. Above all, he detested monks who, out of a kind of lack of faith, stored up their possessions for the future and took care over expenses, clothing, or any of those things that pass away with the world.

## 28. The excessively cautious brother.

Finally, he had driven away from his sight one of the brothers who lived about five miles from him, because he had discovered that the man was an excessively careful and fearful guardian of his little garden and possessed a small amount of money.

The brother, wishing to reconcile himself with the old man, often came to the brothers, especially to Hesychius, in whom Hilarion took the greatest delight [Note: The manuscripts consistently read *Isicium*; Sozomen calls him *Hesycha*, following the Syrian pronunciation, by which Syrian speakers distorted Greek names.].

One day he brought a bundle of fresh chickpeas, still on their plants. When Hesychius had placed it on the table toward evening, the old man cried out that he could not endure its stench and asked where it had come from.

When Hesychius replied that a certain brother had brought the first fruits of his little field to the brothers, Hilarion said: “Do you not perceive the most dreadful stench, and avarice rotting in the chickpeas? Send them to the oxen; send them to the dumb animals, and see whether they will eat.”

When Hesychius had placed them in the manger according to the command, the oxen, terrified and bellowing more than usual, broke their bonds and fled in different directions.

The old man had this gift: from the odor of people’s bodies and clothing, and of the things that someone had touched, he could know to which demon or vice the person was subject.

## 29. Hilarion was an enemy of crowds.

In the sixty-third year of his life, seeing that there was a large monastery and a multitude of brothers living with him, and that crowds of people afflicted by various illnesses and unclean spirits were being brought to him, so that the solitude was filled all around with every kind of person, he wept daily and remembered with incredible longing his former way of life.

When the brothers asked him what was wrong and why he was wasting away, he said: “I have returned to the world and received my reward in my lifetime. Look: the people of Palestine and the neighboring provinces think that I am someone of importance, while under the pretext of administering the monastery and the brothers I possess paltry [Possible reading: useful] household goods.””

The brothers watched over him, especially Hesychius, who was devoted to the old man’s honor with extraordinary love. After he had lived [Alternative reading: continued] in mourning for two years, Aristaenete, whose mention was made above, then the wife of the prefect but possessing none of the prefect’s pomp [Note: The printed editions read *Aristeneta*, as noted above. Shortly afterward two manuscripts read *habitu* (“habit”) instead of *ambitu* (“pomp”).], came to him, wishing also to go to Antony.

Weeping, Hilarion said to her: “I would gladly go myself, if I were not held shut in the prison of this monastery, and if there were any benefit in going. For today it is two days since the whole world was deprived of such a father.”

She believed him and stopped. A few days later, when a messenger arrived, she heard of Antony’s death [Note: Compare this vision concerning the death of Antony with what is explained at the end of the following section.]

## 30. A marvelous contempt for glory. Bishops Dracontius and Philo in exile.

Let others marvel at the miracles he performed [Note: All the manuscripts add “and wonders”; then one has *humanitatem* (“humanity”) instead of *humilitatem* (“humility”), and shortly afterward *celare* (“to conceal”) instead of *calcare* (“to trample”).]. Let them marvel at his incredible abstinence, knowledge, and humility. I am astonished by nothing so much as by his ability to trample glory and honor [Col. 0043C].

Bishops, priests, and throngs of clerics and monks flocked to him. Christian matrons also came—a great temptation [Note: Our codices, together with Victorius, read: “Christian matrons also,” etc. Some codices read: “Matrons also and Christians,” etc. Thus there is a great temptation in Christian matrons, whom monks and clerics ought therefore to avoid if they have any wisdom. Martianay.]—as well as, from here and there, the common people of cities and countryside.

Powerful men and judges also came, so that they might receive from him blessed bread or oil [Note: This was an ancient custom of piety in the Church: men distinguished for holiness were offered oil or bread to bless, which would later be useful to them in warding off evils. Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* III, chapter 3: “It should not be omitted that the wife of Count Avitianus sent Martin oil, which, as is customary, he was to bless as necessary for various causes of illness.” Shortly afterward: “A glass vessel with oil, which Martin had blessed.” See also Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* II.4, where he tells of a man whose limbs were paralyzed and who immediately recovered after being anointed with blessed oil by Antony’s disciples. Sozomen confirms this in book VI, chapter 20.].

But Hilarion thought of nothing except solitude, to such an extent that one day he decided to depart. He had a little donkey brought and attempted to set out—for he was so emaciated by fasts that he could scarcely walk.

When this became known [Note: “And as though devastation,” etc. Other manuscript books read: “And as though devastation and mourning were being proclaimed throughout the Palestinian *justitium*.” For the meaning of *justitium*, see the dictionaries. Martianay.], and as though devastation and a suspension of legal business (*justitium*) had been proclaimed throughout Palestine, more than ten thousand people of every age and sex gathered to hold him back.

Unmoved by their entreaties, and striking the sands with his staff, he said: “I will not make my Lord a liar; I cannot see churches overturned, Christ’s altars trampled, and the blood of my children.”

Everyone present understood that some secret had been revealed to him, which he did not wish to confess; nevertheless, they guarded him so that he could not depart.

Therefore he declared publicly, calling everyone to witness, that he would take neither food nor drink unless he were released. After seven days, at last released from his fast and bidding farewell to many, he came with an endless procession of those accompanying him to Betilium [Note: The printed editions retain *Betilium*; the manuscripts read *Betuliam*. Others read *Bethelium*, concerning which see Sozomen, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 15. Martianay. — *Betulium*: Before Martianay, the printed editions had *Betilium*; he himself read *Betuliam* from certain manuscripts, none of which we have found. Our manuscripts generally have *Vetilium*, but two Vatican codices prefer *Vetulium*. Some are also said to read *Bethelium*. Certainly Eusebius or Jerome nowhere mentions *Betuliam* in the *Book of Places*. Suidas, however, records only this: “Betulaia, the city belonging to the Jews” (βαϊτυλαῖα ἡ τῶν Ἰουδαίων πόλις). I therefore readily think that the village of the Gazans called *Bethelia* by Sozomen, book V, chapter 15, is meant. The conjecture gains very strong support from Sozomen himself, who says that the inhabitants of that place were converted to the Christian faith by Saint Hilarion and that his own grandfather received baptism there. He further says that Bethelian was so called from the Pantheon that stood there, “the name being translated from the language of the Syrians into that of the Greeks as ‘dwelling-place of the gods,’ because of the temple of the Pantheon” (ἐκ τῆς Σύρων φωνῆς, εἰς τὴν Ἑλλήνων ἐρμηνευόμενον θεῶν οἰκητήριον ὀνομάζεσθαι διὰ τὸν τοῦ Πανθέου ναὸν).].

There, after persuading the crowds to return, he chose forty monks who had provisions and could travel fasting—that is, after sunset. After visiting the brothers who were in the neighboring desert and at a place called Lychnos [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read *Lichonos*, a third *Lignos*, and others *Lichognos*. It seems that *Lycos* should be read, which is a town at the extreme end of the Thebaid. Pliny, book V: “Lycos, where the mountains end.” Shortly afterward, other codices have *Thonbaston* and *Thabaston*, while one has the closer *Thaubaston*. We easily think that *Thauba*, which Ptolemy places in the Arabian Desert in chapter 19, should be understood.], he went after three days to the fortress of Theubatus to see Bishop Dracontius and confessor, who was in exile there.

The presence of so great a man consoled Dracontius beyond measure. After another three days Hilarion reached Babylon with great labor, to visit Bishop Philo, who was also a confessor. For King Constantius, favoring the heresy of the Arians, had deported both men to those regions.

Leaving there, after three days he came to the town of Aphroditon. There he met the deacon Baisane [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read *post biduum* (“after two days”). In Martianay there was an error shortly afterward, where he had *equis locatis, dromadibus*, etc. Victorius was also not entirely satisfactory, reading *locatis camelis et dromedis*, as though these were two kinds of beasts, contrary to what Vopiscus teaches in his *Aurelian*: “When Zenobia fled with camels, which they call dromedaries,” etc. We have restored the passage in accordance with the agreement of the manuscripts.], who, having hired dromedary camels, was accustomed, because of the scarcity of water in the desert, to lead travelers going to Antony.

Hilarion confessed to the brothers that the day of blessed Antony’s death was approaching and that he owed it to Antony to keep vigil for him through the night at the very place where he had died.

After three days through a vast and dreadful desert, they finally reached a very high mountain. There they found two monks, Isaac and Pelusianus; Isaac had been Antony’s interpreter.

## 31. Saint Antony’s dwelling. Antony’s cell. The unknown tomb of blessed Antony.

Since the occasion presents itself, and we have come to the place, it seems fitting to describe in a brief account the dwelling of so great a man.

A rocky and lofty mountain, extending about one thousand paces, sends water forth at its foot. Some of the water is drunk up by the sands; other streams descend toward the lower ground and gradually form a brook. On both banks innumerable palms provide the place with great beauty and convenience.

You would have seen the old man running here and there with the disciples of blessed Antony. “Here,” they would say, “he used to sing psalms; here he prayed; here he worked; here, tired, he used to sit. He himself planted these vines and these little trees; he himself arranged that garden plot with his own hands. He built this pool [Manuscripts: “small pool”] for watering the garden with much sweat. He kept that hoe for digging the earth for many years.”

He lay on his bed and kissed the couch, as though it were still warm. His cell was no larger in area than a sleeping man could occupy when stretched out.

Moreover, at the summit of the mountain, as one ascended by a kind of spiral stairway and with very arduous effort, two cells of the same size could be seen. Fleeing the crowds of visitors and the company of his disciples, Antony had lived in them. They had been cut into the living rock, with only doors added.

When they had come to the garden, Isaac said: “Do you see this orchard [Alternative reading: enclosure], planted with small trees and green with vegetables? About three years ago, when a herd of wild asses was ravaging it, Antony ordered one of their leaders to stand still. Striking its sides with his staff, he said: ‘Why do you eat what you have not sown?’ From that time onward, except at the waters where they came to drink, they never touched either a tree or the vegetables.”

The old man also asked them to show him the place of his tomb. When they had led him aside, whether or not they showed it to him is unknown.

They said that the reason for concealing the place was Antony’s command [Note: See Saint Athanasius, *Life of Saint Antony*. We correct a few minor matters below.], lest Pergamius, who was the richest man in those regions, should take the saint’s body to his estate and build a *martyrium* [Note: A *martyrium* is a church dedicated in honor of martyrs or confessors. Martianay.].

## 32. Hilarion obtains rain.

Returning to Aphroditon, Hilarion retained only two brothers with him and remained in the neighboring desert. His abstinence and silence were so great that he said it was then, for the first time, that he had begun to serve Christ.

For three years the closed heavens had dried up those lands, so that people commonly said that even the elements were mourning Antony’s death.

Hilarion’s fame had not escaped the people living nearby. Men and women, pale of face and wasted by hunger, vied with one another in begging rain from the servant of Christ, that is, from the successor of blessed Antony.

When he saw them, he was deeply grieved. He raised his eyes to heaven and lifted both hands on high, and immediately obtained what they had asked.

But behold: after the thirsty, sandy region had been irrigated by the rains, it suddenly produced such a multitude of serpents and venomous animals that countless people, when bitten, would have died immediately unless they had run to Hilarion.

After the oil had been blessed, all the farmers and shepherds touched their wounds with it and recovered certain health.

## 33. He proceeds to other regions.

Seeing that he was also being honored there with remarkable honors, Hilarion went to Alexandria, intending from there to cross into the farther [Manuscripts: inner] Oasis desert.

Since he had never stayed in cities from the time he became a monk, he turned aside to some brothers known to him in Bruchion, not far from Alexandria [Note: The reading *Brutium*, here and below, prevailed improperly and contrary to the manuscripts. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXII, chapter 16, also advised reading *Bruchion*. Epiphanius likewise testifies that the region called Bruchion (Βρούχιον κλίμα), that is, the district of Bruchion, was deserted in his day. The author of the *Life of Apollonius Dyscolus* calls it Προύχιον: “in Prouchion, near the *dremon* [as printed]” (perhaps the text should read τὴν ἔρημον, “the desert”), “in a place called Hypo [as printed], near Alexandria.” This was a district of Alexandria, perhaps called πυρουχεῖον, from which the word *Bruchion* was altered; it should therefore be written with a diphthong, as Petavius argues in his notes on Epiphanius concerning weights and measures.].

They received the old man with extraordinary joy. Since night was already near, they suddenly heard his disciples saddle the donkey and prepare him to depart.

They therefore fell at his feet and begged him not to do this. Prostrate before the threshold, they declared that they would rather die than be deprived of so great a guest.

He replied: “For this reason I am hastening to leave, so that I may not cause you trouble. From what happens afterward you will learn that I did not depart suddenly without reason.”

The next day, the Gazans entered the monastery with the prefect’s lictors, for they had learned that Hilarion had arrived the day before. When they did not find him, they said to one another: “Are the things we heard not true? He is a magician and knows the future.”

For after Hilarion had departed from Palestine, Julian had succeeded to the imperial power. The monastery was destroyed, and, after petitions had been presented to the emperor, the Gazans obtained the death of Hilarion and Hesychius. A written order had been sent throughout the entire world that both were to be sought.

## 34. Concerning the disciple Hadrian.

Leaving Bruchion, Hilarion entered the trackless desert and reached the Oasis. After spending about a year there, he considered sailing to the remote islands, since his fame had reached that place as well and he seemed no longer able to remain hidden in the East, where many knew him both by reputation and by appearance.

He wished that the seas might at least conceal the man whom the land had made famous.

At about the same time his disciple Hadrian arrived from Palestine, saying that Julian had been killed and that a Christian emperor, Jovian, had begun to reign. Hilarion, he said, ought to return to the remnants of his monastery.

When Hilarion heard this, he rejected it with indignation. Hiring a camel, he crossed the vast desert and reached the Libyan coastal city of Paretonium.

There the wretched Hadrian, wishing to return to Palestine and seeking his former glory under the name of his master, inflicted many injuries upon him. Finally, having packed up what he had brought that had been sent to him by the brothers [Note: Two manuscripts read: “Having summoned all the things which,” etc.; another: “With the vessels which,” etc. Victorius observed that *convasatis* means the same as “collected into bundles,” so that the things might be carried away.], he departed without Hilarion’s knowledge.

Since there is no other place to mention this, I will say only this, as a warning to those who despise their teachers: after some time Hadrian rotted away from jaundice [Col. 0047B].

## 35. He had written out a copy of the Gospels in his own hand.

Taking the old man Gazanus with him [Note: The same manuscripts read *Senem Zazanum*.], Hilarion boarded a ship sailing to Sicily.

When he had sold a copy of the Gospels that he had written with his own hand as a young man, intending to pay the fare, about midway across the Adriatic the shipmaster’s son was seized by a demon. He began to shout and say:

“Hilarion, servant of God, why are we not allowed, through you, to be safe even on the sea? Give me time until I reach land, lest, being thrown out here, I fall into the abyss.”

Hilarion replied: “If my God grants you permission to remain, remain. But if he casts you out, why do you make me, a sinful and beggarly man, an object of envy?”

He said this so that the sailors and merchants on the ship would not betray him when they reached land.

Not long afterward the boy was cleansed. His father gave his word, as did the others who were present, that none of them would speak to anyone about Hilarion’s name.

## 36.

When he entered Pachynus, a promontory of Sicily, Hilarion offered the Gospel to the shipmaster as payment for the passage of himself and Gazanus. The shipmaster refused to accept it, especially when he saw that, apart from that book and the clothes they wore, they possessed nothing else. At last he swore that he would not take it.

The old man, fired with confidence in the consciousness of his poverty, rejoiced all the more that he possessed nothing of the world and was thought by the inhabitants of that place to be a beggar.

## 37. He flees to the inland regions. A man with dropsy is cured.

Reflecting that merchants coming from the East might make him known [Note: Compare Sozomen, book V, chapter 10. For the sake of brevity, we give only Valesius’s Latin translation:

“At about the same time”—namely, during the reign of the emperor Julian—“the monk Hilarion, sought by the Gazans, withdrew to Sicily. There he gathered wood from the deserted mountains, carried it into the city on his shoulders, and sold it; in this way he obtained the daily food sufficient for life. At last he was identified by a nobleman who was being tormented by a demon. After he had freed him from the unclean spirit, he crossed to Dalmatia,” etc.

Two points relevant to our matter should be noted. First, Sozomen is mistaken in saying that Hilarion crossed to Sicily in order to escape the Gazans’ ambushes, since Jerome’s preceding narrative shows that Hilarion remained hidden in the Oasis until Julian was killed and only then came to Sicily.

Second, Gravius is wrong to suspect that the man who revealed Hilarion’s holiness was not a *scutarius*, or that the word should be read *scrutarius*, meaning one who sold rags, as in Horace’s verse:

“Selling cheap rags to the tunic-wearing crowd.”

On the contrary, Sozomen calls him ἄνδρα τῶν ἐπιστήμων, “an eminent man,” whether by birth or dignity, and identifies the name *Scutarius*.], Hilarion fled to the inland regions, twenty miles from the sea. There, in a certain deserted little field, he daily tied up a bundle of wood and placed it on his disciple’s back.

They sold it in the nearest village and bought a little food both for themselves and for those who happened to come to them.

But, as it is written, “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14), a certain Scutarius, while being tormented in the basilica of blessed Peter at Rome, cried out through the unclean spirit:

“Hilarion, servant of Christ, entered Sicily a few days ago, and no one knows him; he thinks himself hidden. I will go and betray him.”

Immediately the man boarded a ship in the harbor with his servants, reached Pachynus, and, led there by the demon, prostrated himself before the old man’s hut [Note: One manuscript reads: “The demon leading him, he prostrated himself before the old man, and was immediately cured,” etc.], and was at once cured.

This was the beginning of Hilarion’s miracles in Sicily. Thereafter an innumerable multitude of the sick, and also of devout people, came to him. So great was the number that one of the leading men, swollen with dropsy [Note: We have supplied the word “water,” which was previously lacking, from the manuscripts.], was cured on the very day on which he came to Hilarion.

Afterward, when he offered him immeasurable gifts, he heard the Savior’s saying to the disciples: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10:8).

## 38. The disciple Hesychius seeks Hilarion.

While these things were taking place in Sicily, his disciple Hesychius searched throughout the whole world for the old man, visiting the shores and penetrating the deserts. He had only this confidence: wherever Hilarion might be, he could not remain hidden for long.

After three years had passed, Hesychius heard at Methone from a certain Jew who sold cheap rags to the people that a Christian prophet had appeared in Sicily, performing so many miracles and signs that he was thought to be one of the saints of old.

He questioned the Jew about the man’s clothing, gait, language, and especially his age, but learned nothing [Note: Until now the text incorrectly read *interrogatus* (“having been questioned”) instead of *interrogans* (“questioning”), and *nihil dicere* (“to say nothing”) instead of *nihil discere* (“to learn nothing”); we correct this from all the manuscripts.]. The man who reported the matter testified only that news of such a person had reached him.

Hesychius therefore entered the Adriatic Sea and came swiftly to Pachynus. In a little village on a curved shore, he asked about the old man’s reputation and learned from everyone, in a unanimous voice, where Hilarion was and what he was doing.

Everyone marveled at nothing so much as this: after so many signs and miracles, he had not received even a fragment of bread from anyone in those regions.

To avoid prolonging the account, the holy man Hesychius threw himself at his master’s knees, wetting his feet with tears. At last Hilarion raised him up. After speaking with him for two or three days, Hesychius heard from Gazanus that the old man could no longer remain in those regions but wished to go to certain barbarian nations where both his name and his fame would be unknown [Note: The manuscripts consistently read: “where both his name and his fame would be unknown,” etc.].

### 39. He burns the serpent called a boa

And so he led him to the Dalmatian town of Epidaurum, where, although he stayed for a few days in a nearby little field, he could not remain hidden. For a dragon of extraordinary size—which in the language of the pagans they call *boas*, because they are so large that they are accustomed to swallow oxen—was laying waste to the whole surrounding province. It devoured not only herds and flocks, but also farmers and shepherds, dragging them to itself by the force of its breath and swallowing them. When he had ordered a pyre to be prepared, and, after prayer had been offered to Christ, had summoned the creature and commanded it to climb the pile of wood, he set fire beneath it. Then, while the whole populace watched, he burned the monstrous beast.

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “by the violence of its savage breath”; another reads, “of its own breath.”]

[Note: “And after prayer had been offered to Christ …”: The printed books read incorrectly, “and after prayer had been offered to Christ and the people had been summoned, he commanded,” etc. For Hilarion summoned the serpent and ordered it to climb the pile of wood so that it might be burned. MARTIAN.]

[Note: The manuscripts read more elegantly and more briefly: “He set fire beneath it, and while the whole populace watched …”]

36. Therefore, burning with anxiety about what he should do and where he should turn, he was preparing another flight. As he surveyed deserted lands in his mind, he grieved [variant: wondered] that, while every tongue was silent about him, miracles were being spoken of.

### 40. The sea is restrained after leaving its boundaries

At that time, during the earthquake that occurred throughout the whole world after Julian’s death, the seas left their boundaries. It was as though God were once again threatening a flood, or as though everything were returning to the ancient chaos: ships, carried onto the precipitous slopes of the mountains, hung there.

[Note: “Carried onto the precipitous slopes of the mountains.” This is how it is written in all the manuscript codices I examined. Marianus reads: “They were carried to the precipitous slopes of the mountains and hung there.” MARTIAN. —Martianaeus restored the Erasmian reading on the authority of his manuscripts, taking *delatae* as a separate word rather than *delate*; we prefer this reading of Victorius, which is confirmed by all the manuscripts we consulted.]

[Note: “At that time, during an earthquake.” In the Eusebian Chronicles the same Jerome writes that, in the second year of Valentinian, when an earthquake had occurred throughout the whole world, the sea left its shore and overwhelmed the cities of Sicily and many islands, together with countless peoples. Concerning the same event he writes in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 15: “During a great earthquake, to my disgrace, when the seas crossed the shores of the whole world,” etc. See also Orosius, book VII, chapter 32, and Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 3. MARTIAN. —This is the same earthquake that Ammianus Marcellinus describes elegantly at the end of book XXVI, and he says that it occurred under Valentinian I, together with his brother Valens; this is assigned to the year 365 (see the *Chronicle* under the second year of Valentinian). In the Alexandrian Chronicle: “In this year the sea left its own boundaries, in the month of Panemus, before the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.” See Socrates, book IV, chapter 3.]

When the people of Epidaurum saw this—the roaring waves, the masses of water, and the mountains of the flood being driven against the shores—they feared what they already saw happening: that their town might be utterly destroyed. They entered to see the old man and, as though they were going out to battle, placed him on the shore.

[Note: “They entered.” Previously it read “they went in,” certainly against the testimony of the manuscripts. See Sozomen, book V, chapter 20.]

When he had drawn three signs of the cross in the sand and stretched out his hands toward the sea, it is incredible to say to what height the swelling sea rose and stood before him. Roaring for a long time, and seeming to resent the obstacle, it gradually fell back into itself.

Epidaurum and that whole region proclaim this event to the present day, and mothers teach it to their children so that the memory may be handed down to posterity. Truly, what was said to the Apostles—“If you believe, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move into the sea,’ and it will happen” (Matthew 17:19)—can also be fulfilled literally, provided that someone possesses the Apostles’ faith, and faith of the kind that the Lord commanded them to have. For what difference does it make whether a mountain descends into the sea, or whether immense mountains of waves suddenly grow rigid and stand before the old man’s feet like stone, while on the other side they flow gently away?

### 41. He flees to Cyprus

The whole city was amazed, and the greatness of the sign had become known even at Salona. When the old man realized this, he secretly fled by night in a small boat. After finding a merchant ship two days later, he proceeded to Cyprus.

When, between Malea and Cythera, pirates in two fairly large *myoparones* encountered them—their abandoned vessel on the shore being steered not by a mast but by a pole—and when waves again came rushing from both sides, all the rowers who were in the ship began to tremble, weep, run about, and prepare their poles. As though one messenger were not enough, they vied with one another in telling the old man that pirates were approaching.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “while the rower was sweeping the waves”; this may perhaps be the more correct reading.]

He looked at them from a distance and smiled. Turning to his disciples, he said: “O you of little faith, why are you afraid?” (Matthew 14:32). “Are these men more numerous than Pharaoh’s army? Yet, when God willed it, they were all drowned.”

He was speaking, yet the hostile ships, their prows foaming, threatened them from only a stone’s throw away.

He therefore stood at the prow [variant: edge] of the ship and, extending his hand toward those approaching, said: “Thus far is enough to have come.”

O marvelous truth of the event! Immediately the little boats sprang backward, and, although the oars drove against them, their momentum turned back toward the stern. The pirates were amazed that they were being carried backward despite their efforts. Straining with all their bodily strength to reach the ship, they were carried to the shore much more swiftly than they had come.

### 42. He cures many of unclean spirits

I pass over the rest, lest I seem to lengthen the volume of my narrative with accounts of miracles. I shall say only this: while sailing with a favorable wind among the Cyclades, he heard from the cities and villages on either side, and from people running to the shores, the voices of unclean spirits crying out.

[Note: The reading “were heard” was contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts.]

He entered Paphos, the famous city of Cyprus celebrated in the poets’ songs. Since it had frequently collapsed in earthquakes, it now showed what it had once been only by the traces of its ruins. He lived two miles from the city in an obscure place, rejoicing that he might live in peace for a few days.

But before twenty full days had passed, everyone on that island who was possessed by unclean spirits began to cry out that Hilarion, the servant of Christ, had come, and that they ought to hasten to him. Salamis proclaimed this, Curium proclaimed it, Lapetha proclaimed it, and so did the other cities. Many insisted that they knew Hilarion and that he truly was a servant of God, but that they did not know where he was.

Within thirty days, or little more, nearly two hundred people, men and women alike, gathered around him. When he saw them, he grieved that they would not allow him to rest and, in a manner, raged against them in revenge for himself. He scourged them with such persistence in prayer that some were cured immediately, others after two or three days, and all within a single week.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “not more than”; another incompletely reads, “twenty,” etc.]

### 43. He ascends to a more secluded place. The Bucolia of Egypt. A paralytic is cured

After remaining there for two years, and constantly thinking of flight, he sent Hesychius back in spring to Palestine to greet the brothers and visit the ashes of his monastery.

When Hesychius returned, Hilarion wished to sail back to Egypt, that is, to the region called Bucolia, because there were no Christians there, but only a barbarous and savage people. Hesychius persuaded him instead to climb to a more secluded place on the island itself.

[Note: Some manuscripts read *Batholia*. Heliodorus says: “The whole region is called Bucolia among the Egyptians,” etc. Hence the Bucolic soldiers mentioned throughout Egypt by Capitolinus and others, from the common name of this place, which they occupied.]

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “to withdraw.”]

After exploring the whole area for a long time, Hesychius found such a place and led him twelve miles inland from the sea, among secluded and rugged mountains, to a place that could scarcely be climbed except by crawling on hands and knees.

When Hilarion entered, he saw a very terrible and remote place, surrounded here and there by trees. It also had waters irrigating it from the brow of the hill, a very lovely garden, and many orchards, whose fruit he never took as food. Nearby stood the ruins of a very ancient temple, from which—as he himself reported, and as his disciples testify—the voices of so countless a number of demons resounded day and night that one would have thought an army was present.

[Note: The manuscripts read “testified”; and a little later, “because he had, as was evident, so many opponents,” etc.]

Hilarion was greatly pleased with the place, since he would have adversaries close at hand, and lived there for five years. Hesychius often visited him, and at this final period of his life Hilarion was refreshed by the fact that, because of the harshness and difficulty of the place and the multitude of apparitions—as people commonly reported—either no one or only a very few could or dared to climb up to him.

One day, when he had gone out of the garden, he saw a man lying before the doorway, paralyzed throughout his entire body. He asked Hesychius who he was and how he had been brought there.

Hesychius replied that he had been the steward of the little village, to whose jurisdiction the garden in which they were living also belonged.

[Note: Victorius reads, “to whose boundary the garden also belonged,” etc.]

Hilarion wept with him, stretched out his hand toward the man lying there, and said: “I say to you, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: rise and walk.”

The speed of the cure was marvelous. The words were still turning in the speaker’s mouth, and already the man’s limbs, strengthened for standing, were raising him to his feet.

When this became known, necessity overcame even the difficulty of the place and the trackless route. Nothing was observed so carefully throughout all the surrounding villages as that he should not somehow escape. For rumor had spread about him that he could not remain long in the same place. He did this not because he was overcome by fickleness or childishness, but because he fled honor and annoyance; for he always desired silence and an obscure life.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “to allow him to remain.”]

### 44. Hilarion’s testament

A daughter and son-in-law of Constantia cured by anointing with oil.

In the eightieth year of his life, while Hesychius was absent, Hilarion wrote with his own hand a brief letter, as though in place of a testament, leaving all his possessions to him—namely, the Gospel, a sackcloth tunic, a hood, and a little cloak—for his servant had died a few days earlier.

Many devout men came from Paphos to the sick man, especially because they had heard him say that he was soon to depart to the Lord and be freed from the bonds of the body. There was also a certain holy woman named Constantia, whose son-in-law and daughter he had rescued from death by anointing them with oil.

He adjured them all not to keep his body even for an hour after his death, but immediately to cover him with earth in that same garden, dressed as he was in a haircloth tunic, a hood, and a rustic cloak.

### 45. His death

A small amount of warmth still lingered in his chest, and nothing remained of a living man except consciousness. Yet, with his eyes open, he spoke:

“Go forth. What are you afraid of? Go forth, my soul. Why do you hesitate? You have served Christ for nearly seventy years, and are you afraid of death?”

With these words he breathed out his spirit. They immediately covered him with earth and buried him before the report of his death had reached the city.

### 46. Hesychius steals the body of Saint Hilarion. Hilarion’s body remains whole and his clothing undamaged

When the holy man Hesychius heard this, he went to Cyprus. Pretending that he wished to live in the same garden, so as to remove from the inhabitants any suspicion of his assiduous watch over it, he stole Hilarion’s body at the risk of his own life after approximately ten months.

He brought it to Maiuma and, accompanied by crowds of monks and townspeople, buried it in the ancient monastery. The tunic, hood, and little cloak were undamaged, and the whole body remained intact as though he were still alive. It gave off such abundant fragrance that one would have thought it had been drenched in perfumes.

### 47. Constantia dies of grief because Saint Hilarion’s body was stolen

I do not think that, at the end of this book, I should leave unmentioned the devotion of that most holy woman Constantia. When the news was brought to her that Hilarion’s body was in Palestine, she immediately died, proving even by her death the genuine love she bore for the servant of God.

She had been accustomed to spend wakeful nights at his tomb and, as though speaking with him while he was present, to converse with him in order to assist her prayers.

Even today you may see the remarkable contention between the Palestinians and the Cypriots: the former competing to possess Hilarion’s body, the latter claiming to possess his spirit. Yet great miracles occur every day in both places, though more in the little garden of Cyprus, perhaps because he loved that place more.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “because he loved the little place.”]

---

## The Life of Malchus, the Captive Monk (C)

[Note: Written in the year 390. In two Vatican manuscripts formerly belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden, numbers 432 and 500, it begins: “The Acts of the Captive Monk, dictated by Jerome the Presbyter.” In another, number 797, it is simply entitled “Concerning the Captive Monk”; likewise in another, number 589: “The History of Malchus, the Captive Monk, written by Blessed Jerome.” The entire text of the Life is established from these copies.]

[Note: The work presents to readers the life of Malchus, a monk from the Syrian village of Maronia—a life harassed by various dangers and misfortunes and crushed beneath captivity.]

### 1. Jerome intended to write an ecclesiastical history

Those who are going to fight a naval battle first, in harbor and on calm seas, turn the rudders, pull the oars, and prepare grappling irons and hooks. They accustom the soldiers arranged along the decks to stand firmly despite the hanging steps and slipping footing, so that what they have learned in a mock battle they will not fear in the real contest.

So I too, who have long been silent—for the man whose speech is his punishment forced me to keep silent—wish first to exercise myself in a small work and, as it were, scrape away a certain rust from my tongue, so that I may proceed to a more extensive history.

For I have decided to write—if only the Lord grants me life, and if my detractors will at least cease pursuing me while I flee and remain shut away—from the coming of the Savior down to our own age; that is, from the Apostles to the dregs of our own time: how and through whom Christ’s Church was born and grew to maturity, how it increased through persecutions and was crowned with martyrdoms, and how, after it came to Christian emperors, it became greater in power and wealth but lesser in virtues.

But that belongs elsewhere. Let us now explain what lies immediately before us.

### 2. As a young man Jerome lived in Syria

Maronia [manuscripts: *Maronias*] is a modest village situated nearly thirty miles east of Antioch, a city of Syria. After passing through many owners or patrons, it eventually came into the possession of Pope Evagrius, a relative of mine, while I was living as a young man in Syria. I have named him now so that I may show how I know what I am about to write.

There was there an old man named Malchus—whose name we can render in Latin as “king.” He was a tenant-farmer of a little estate near Nisibis.

[Note: Clearly from *melech*, which means “king” in Hebrew. Hesychius likewise writes, “Malchus, King” (*Μάλχος Βασιλεύς*). See Eunapius, *Life of Porphyry*.]

He was Syrian by nationality and language, and truly a native of that same place.

[Note: We restore this reading from five manuscripts, especially one from our monastery at Jumièges, which reads, “truly a native of that same place.” The other four—that is, one Parisian manuscript belonging to D. le Peletier, formerly to the jurist Pierre Pithou; another from the Dominican Friars at Avignon; a third also from the Dominican Friars at Toulouse; and a fourth from the monastery of Fontfroide at Narbonne—all read as follows: “He was Syrian by nationality and language, and lived as a native of that same place.” In the printed editions of Erasmus and Marianus nothing is genuine, but the entire phrase has been fabricated in Greek. MARTIAN.]

[Note: The older printed editions give, for the words “a native of that same place,” the Greek *αὐτόχθων*. Although I have found this word in no manuscript, I by no means believe that it was invented by Erasmus and approved by Victorius. In several codices Thebaston thought he had found *indigena* (“native”), but perhaps a copyist wished, in somewhat corrupted Latin letters, to render the Greek word *αὐτόχθων*, from which some less learned person wrote *Thebaston*. *Αὐτόχθων* means the same as “a native of that place.”]

An extremely aged old woman also lived with him, seemingly already close to death. Both were so devout and so constantly wore down the threshold of the church that one would have taken them for Zechariah and Elizabeth from the Gospel, except that John was not present among them.

When I carefully asked the inhabitants who they were to each other—married, related by blood, or joined in spirit—they all answered with one voice that the pair were holy, pleasing to God, and involved in some marvelous relationship that I could not understand.

Attracted by this curiosity, I approached the man and questioned him more closely about the truth of the matter. I received the following account from him.

### 3. The story of Malchus

“I,” he said, “my son, was a tenant-farmer of a little estate near Nisibis and the only child of my parents.” When they compelled me to marry, as though I were the offspring and heir of their family, I replied that I preferred to be a monk.

“How greatly my father persecuted me with threats, and my mother with entreaties, so that I might betray my chastity, is shown by this one fact: I fled both my home and my parents.

“Since I could not travel eastward because of nearby Persia and the guard of the Roman soldiers, I turned my feet toward the west, carrying a tiny amount of provisions—just enough to protect me from starvation.

“What more need I say? At last I reached the desert of Chalcis, which lies between Immas and Beroea, farther toward the south.

[Note: The manuscripts retain *Himminas*, *eminos*, or *immus*, but all consistently read *Beroea*, not the corrupt *Essa*. MARTIAN. —Martianaeus reads *Hymmas*; Ptolemy calls the city *Ἱμμάμ* in Seleucid territory. But in place of *Beroea*, the older printed editions read *Essa*; one Vatican manuscript has *Bessa*, incorrectly, since it has been established that Beroea, a city of Cyrrhestica—now called Aleppo—is meant. Compare Ptolemy, book V, chapter 15.]

“There I found monks and placed myself under their instruction, seeking my livelihood through manual labor and restraining the wantonness of the flesh by fasting.

“After many years, the desire came upon me to return to my homeland. My mother was still alive—for I had already heard that my father was dead—and I wished to comfort her widowhood. Then, after selling my little property, I would distribute one part to the poor, establish another part as a monastery, and—why should I be ashamed to confess my faithlessness?—reserve a part to meet my own expenses.

[Note: The manuscripts likewise read, “and establish part of it as a monastery.”]

“My abbot began to cry out that this was a temptation of the devil, and that, under the pretext of an honorable undertaking, the snares of the ancient enemy lay concealed. He said that this was the dog returning to its vomit; that many monks had been deceived in this way; that the devil never revealed himself openly.

“He set before me many examples from Scripture, including the fact that in the beginning he also overthrew Adam and Eve through the hope of divinity. When he could not persuade me, he fell at my knees and begged me not to abandon him, not to destroy myself, and not, while holding the plow, to look behind me.

“Woe to me! I defeated my adviser with a disastrous victory, thinking that he sought not my salvation [manuscripts: advantage] but his own consolation.

“Thus he accompanied me out of the monastery as though he were carrying out a corpse, and, bidding me farewell at the end, said: ‘I see that you are marked with the brand of the son of Satan. I seek no explanations and accept no excuses. A sheep that leaves the fold is immediately exposed to the wolf’s bites’ [variant: jaws].”

### 4. He is brought into captivity

For those traveling from Beroea to Edessa, there is a deserted region near the public road through which the Saracens continually wander here and there, without fixed settlements.
