The expectation of danger gathers travelers in those places, so that the impending peril may be avoided through mutual assistance.

There were about seventy people in my company: men, women, old people, young people, and children. Suddenly Ishmaelites mounted on horses and camels rushed upon us. Their heads were long-haired and bound with ribbons, and their bodies were almost naked; they dragged cloaks and broad trousers. Quivers hung from their shoulders; they brandished slack bows and carried long spears. They had not come to fight, but to plunder.

We were seized, scattered, and dragged in different directions. Meanwhile, I, a hereditary possessor returning after a long exile and repenting too late of my decision, was assigned with another little woman to serve the same master.

We were led—or rather carried aloft on camels. Through the vast desert, always fearing a fall, we hung more than we sat.

[Note: All the manuscripts read, “we cling rather than sit.”]

Half-cooked meat was our food, and camel’s milk our drink.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript adds, “the hands of the barbarians”; three French manuscripts later read *caligas*, and another *calliculas*. See below, the Rule of Saint Pachomius.]

### 5. He is ordered to tend sheep

At last, after crossing a great river, we reached the inner desert. There we were ordered, according to the custom of the people, to worship the mistress and her children, and we bent our necks.

Here, as though confined in a prison, I learned to walk after changing my clothing—that is, naked.

[Note: Three manuscripts read: “For the harshness of the climate of that place allowed nothing except the private parts to be covered”; one reads “the climate.”]

For the harshness of the climate allowed nothing else to be covered except the private parts.

I was assigned sheep to pasture. In comparison with other evils, I enjoyed this consolation: I saw my masters and fellow slaves less frequently. I seemed to possess something of the holy Jacob; I remembered Moses, who had himself once been a shepherd in the desert.

I lived on fresh cheese and milk. I prayed continually and sang the psalms I had learned in the monastery. My captivity pleased me, and I gave thanks to God’s judgment, because I had found in the desert the monk whom I would have lost in my homeland.

### 6. He is compelled to take his fellow captive as his wife. The captive woman’s courage

O nothing ever safe from the devil! O his manifold and ineffable snares! Even here envy found me lying concealed.

The Lord, seeing that his flock was increasing and finding no deceit in me—for I knew that the Apostle had commanded that masters should be served faithfully as though they were God (Ephesians 6, etc.)—and wishing to reward me and make me more faithful to him, handed over to me that fellow captive of mine as a wife.

When I refused and said that I was a Christian and that I could not take the wife of a living husband—for her husband, who had been captured with us, had been carried away by another master—that implacable master, driven into a rage, drew his sword and began to attack me.

[Note: We have corrected the text in accordance with the agreement and authority of the manuscripts. Up to this point the printed editions, with the adverb *rursus* prefixed, read “that savage and implacable man,” which is entirely irrelevant.]

If I had not immediately extended my arms and seized the woman first, he would at once have shed blood.

[Note: Four manuscripts read, “unless, swiftly extending my arms, I had seized the woman first”; another reads, “unless I had quickly held the woman and seized her with my arm,” etc.]

It had now grown darker than usual, and night had come too soon for me. I led my new wife into a half-ruined cave. With sorrow serving as our wedding attendant, each of us detested the other, though neither confessed it.

Then I truly felt my captivity. Prostrate on the ground, I began to mourn the monk I was losing, saying:

“Was I, wretched man, preserved for this? Have my sins brought me to the point that, with my head already turning gray, I should become a virgin husband? What good did it do to despise parents, homeland, and property for the Lord, if I do what I despised those things in order not to do? Unless perhaps I endure these things for this reason: because I desired my homeland.

“What shall we do, my soul? Are we perishing, or are we conquering? Shall we await the hand of the Lord, or shall we pierce ourselves with our own sword? Turn the sword against yourself. Your death is more to be feared than the death of the body. Chastity, when preserved, has its own martyrdom. Let the witness of Christ lie unburied in the desert. I myself shall be both persecutor and martyr.”

Having spoken thus, I drew the sword, which even in the darkness flashed, and turned its point toward myself.

“Farewell,” I said, “unhappy woman. Consider me a martyr rather than a husband.”

Then she fell at my feet and said:

“I beg you, by Jesus Christ, and I adjure you by the necessity of this hour, do not shed your blood so as to make me guilty.

“If you wish to die, turn the blade against me first. Thus we shall be joined to one another instead. Even if my husband returned to me, I would preserve the chastity that captivity has taught me; I would rather die than lose it.

“Why do you delay, so as not to be joined to me? I would die if you wished to be joined to me.”

“Take me, then, as a wife in chastity, and love the union of our souls more than that of our bodies. Let our masters hope for a husband; let Christ know a brother. We shall easily persuade them to the marriage when they see that we love one another in this way.”

I confess that I was stunned. I admired the woman’s courage and loved her more as a wife.

Yet I never looked upon her naked body; I never touched her flesh, fearing to lose in peace what I had preserved in battle.

Many days passed in such a marriage. The marriage had made us more pleasing to our masters. They had no suspicion of flight, and sometimes I was absent for an entire month, faithfully tending the flock through the desert.

### 7. He is stirred by the example of ants

After a long interval, while I was sitting alone in the desert and saw nothing except sky and earth, I began silently to turn many things over in my mind. Among them I remembered the fellowship of the monks, and especially the face of my father, who had instructed, kept, and lost me.

[Note: Martianaeus reads, “and nurtured, and destroyed me.” Thus, while I was thinking, I saw, etc. This is contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts, although the rest is sound.]

As I was thinking in this way, I saw a swarm of ants bustling along a narrow path. You could see them carrying burdens larger than their bodies. Some dragged seeds of grass with the pincers of their mouths; others removed earth from their holes and blocked the channels of water with embankments.

Some, mindful of the coming winter, cut up the seeds they had carried in, lest the damp earth turn their storehouses into grass. Others, with solemn mourning, carried away the bodies of the dead.

What is more remarkable, in so great a crowd one ant did not obstruct another that was entering. On the contrary, if they saw one that had fallen beneath a burden, they helped it by placing their shoulders underneath.

What more need I say? That day offered me a beautiful spectacle. Recalling Solomon, who sends us to the industry of ants (Proverbs 6 and 30) and rouses sluggish minds through such an example, I began to grow weary of captivity, seek the cells of the monastery, and long for the likeness of those ants, where labor is undertaken for the common good and, since nothing belongs privately to anyone, everything belongs to everyone.

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “to long for their diligence”; one of these adds, “where labor is held in common.”]

### 8. He flees

When I returned to our dwelling, the woman met me. I could not conceal the sadness of my spirit from my face. She asked why I seemed so lifeless.

[Note: Victorius reads, “She heard the reasons and urged flight.”]

She heard the reasons; I urged flight; she did not reject the proposal. I asked her to keep silent; she gave me her word. In constant whispering, we fluctuated between hope and fear.

There were two goats of extraordinary size in my flock. After killing them, I made wineskins from their hides and prepared their flesh as provisions.

At the first evening, while our masters thought that we were secretly sleeping in our quarters, we set out, carrying the wineskins and portions of meat.

When we reached a river—for it was ten miles away—we climbed onto the inflated skins and entrusted ourselves to the waters, gradually paddling with our feet. We hoped that, as the river carried us downstream and set us out on the opposite bank much farther from the point where we entered, our pursuers would lose our tracks.

But meanwhile the meat became wet and partly fell away, promising scarcely three days’ food. We drank until we were satisfied, preparing ourselves for future thirst.

We ran, constantly looking behind us. We advanced more at night than by day, either because of the ambushes of the Saracens wandering widely about, or because of the excessive heat of the sun.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “we advance.”]

In my misery I was afraid even as I reported the events; and although I was secure in my whole mind, I trembled throughout my whole body.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “Although miserable, I was still secure in fear”; three others read, “I am afraid, wretched man, even as I tell it, although I was secure.”]

### 9. The master catches the fugitive

On the third day, looking uncertainly ahead, we saw two men approaching rapidly from a distance, seated on camels.

Immediately my mind, presaging evil, began to imagine that my master was plotting my death; I saw the sun growing black.

While we were afraid and understood that our tracks in the sand had betrayed us, a cave appeared on our right, extending far beneath the ground.

Fearing poisonous animals—for vipers, king-snakes, scorpions, and creatures of that kind, avoiding the sun’s heat, usually seek shade—we did enter the cave, but immediately, at the very entrance, we entrusted ourselves to a hollow on the left and went no farther, lest, while fleeing death, we should run into death.

We reflected among ourselves: if the Lord takes pity on the wretched, we have salvation; if he despises sinners, we have a tomb.

What do you think our state of mind and terror were, when our master and fellow slave were standing before the cave, not far away, and had already reached the hiding place by following the tracks?

O death expected, far more dreadful than death actually inflicted!

Again, with difficulty and fear, my tongue stammered; and although my master was shouting, I did not dare even to murmur.

He sent the servant to drag us from the cave. He himself held the camels and, with his sword drawn, awaited our appearance.

Meanwhile, when the servant had entered approximately three or four cubits, and we saw his back from our hiding place—for eyes are so constituted that those entering shadows after sunlight are blind to everything—a voice rang through the cavern:

“Come out, you gallows-birds! Come out, you doomed men! Why are you standing there? Why are you delaying? Come out; your master is calling. He is waiting patiently.”

[Note: These words, “He is waiting patiently,” seem to have been inserted incorrectly; we have found them in no manuscript.]

He was still speaking when, through the darkness, we saw a lioness attack the man and, after choking him by the throat, drag him bleeding into the cave.

Good Jesus, what terror and what joy were ours then! We watched, without our master knowing, as our enemy perished.

When the master saw that the servant was delaying, he suspected that two men were resisting one. Unable to postpone his anger any longer, he came toward the cave with the sword he was holding. Rebuking the servant’s sluggishness with a furious shout, he was seized by the beast before he reached our hiding place.

[Note: The printed books read “his madness”; the manuscripts reject this. Victorius then reads, “Who would believe such a thing?”]

Who would ever have believed that, before our very faces, a beast would fight on our behalf?

When that fear had been removed, a similar death still hovered before our eyes, except that it was safer to endure the lion’s rage than a man’s anger.

We trembled inwardly, and did not even dare to move. Amid such dangers, protected as though by a wall, we awaited the outcome, armed only with the consciousness of our chastity.

The lioness, wary of a trap and aware that she had been seen, carried away the cub she had seized in her teeth at dawn and yielded the shelter to us.

[Note: Thus read all our manuscripts, and four others used by Martianaeus, who nevertheless reads *mature* rather than *matutina*. Victorius, and the older manuscripts, have neither reading. In four manuscript codices we read *matutina* instead of *mature*, that is, “she carried away the cub at dawn.” MARTIAN.]

Yet, still not sufficiently trusting, we did not immediately burst out. We waited for a long time, and, while considering whether to leave, imagined that the lioness might meet us.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “but we watched for a long time”; then all have *figuramus* instead of *figurabamus*.]

### 10. Freed from danger, he returns to the monks

[Note: [Col. 0059B] The Vatican manuscript likewise reads: “And so, under such guard, when that day had passed”; another has: “And so, under such terror,” etc.]

When the terror had subsided and that day had passed, we went out toward evening. We saw camels—called dromedaries because of their extraordinary speed—rolling in their mouths the food they had previously eaten and drawing back into their bellies what they had already swallowed. After mounting them and being refreshed with a new supply of provisions,

[Note: [Col. 0059B] More correctly, *isthaec*, that is, “provisions”; the other reading is the gloss of some over-clever person, and the better manuscripts omit it.]

that is, with provisions, at last on the tenth day we reached the Roman camp through the desert. Brought before the tribune,

[Note: [Col. 0059B] The manuscripts read: “We set out the sequence of events, and from there were sent on to Sabinianus.” Formerly the text had *Sabinum*, and in Martianaeus perhaps, through a printer’s error, *Sabianum*. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVIII: “Sabinianus, having suddenly obtained power, puffed up with pride,” whom a little later he calls “a man of narrow and mean spirit.”]

we laid out the course of events; from there, sent on to Sabianus, commander of Mesopotamia,

[Note: [Col. 0060B] “Sent on to Sabinianus,” etc. Ammianus Marcellinus wrote about Sabinianus, commander of Mesopotamia, in Book XVIII. MARTIAN.]

we received the price of the camels. And since that abbot of mine had already fallen asleep in the Lord, when I had been brought to these places I returned myself to the monks, while I handed this girl over to the virgins, loving her as a sister, yet not entrusting myself to her as to a sister.

[Note: [Col. 0060B] “The old man Malchus told me this,” etc. The manuscript copies preserve various readings here. The codex of Petrus Pithoeus reads as follows: “The old man Malchus told this to me as a young man. I, now an old man, tell this to you: to the chaste, a history of chastity. I set this forth to the virgins; I exhort them to virginity. Tell it to those who come after,” etc. The other Avignon and Toulouse codices read: “The old man Malchus told this to me, the young Jerome. I, now an old man, have told this story of chastity to the chaste; I have explained it. I have shown virgins how to preserve virginity. Finally, I exhort you to tell it to those who come after, so that,” etc. MARTIAN.]

The old man Malchus told this to me when I was a young man. I, now an old man, have therefore told this story to you; to the chaste I have explained a history of chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0060B] Two manuscripts read: “I explain a history of chastity to the chaste, and of virginity to virgins. Tell it,” etc. The words inserted here—“I exhort virgins to preserve chastity”—are found in only one manuscript.]

I exhort virgins to preserve chastity.

[Col. 0060B] Tell it to those who come after, so that they may know that, amid swords, deserts, and wild beasts, chastity is never taken captive; and that a person devoted to Christ can die, but cannot be defeated.

[Col. 0059]

## Latin Translation of the Rule of Saint Pachomius by Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon

[Col. 0061]

## Prefatory Notice on the Following Rule of Saint Pachomius, Rendered into Latin by Saint Jerome

To the collection of Jerome’s works which we are preparing, there is added first this Rule of Saint Pachomius, father of the Tabennesian monks. It was originally composed by the author himself in Syriac, then rendered into Greek, and enriched—as it is reasonable to believe—with the precepts and institutions of Theodore and Orsiesius. Jerome explained it in Latin letters at the request of the priests Leontius and Silvanus.

This work had not yet emerged from the recesses of the libraries into public view when Erasmus, and afterward Victorius as well, prepared their editions. Since it has subsequently been published so many times, however, it ought by no means to have been omitted from the edition of Martianaeus, in which Jerome’s own letter, serving as a preface, is reproduced in the eighth class, incomplete in its own section and disfigured by very many errors.

To offer a preliminary account of Pachomius’ original composition itself: among the ancients scarcely anything was more celebrated. Palladius relates in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 38, that a bronze tablet containing the rules of monastic discipline was delivered to Pachomius by an angel; he also explains its contents. Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 7, says:

“Pachomius, a monk, a man endowed with apostolic grace both in speech and in the working of signs, and founder of the Egyptian coenobia, wrote a rule suitable for both kinds of monks, which he had received at the dictation of an angel.”

Sozomen has the same account in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 3: according to widespread tradition, a holy angel appeared to Pachomius and gave him a tablet, which the monks still preserve. Written on it was the instruction that he should grant each person liberty to eat, drink, work, fast, or otherwise act only to the extent permitted by nature. Those who ate more generously were to be assigned more arduous tasks; easier tasks were to be given to those who disciplined their bodies with fasting and abstinence. He also prescribed that there should be many small dwellings, and so forth; these matters are related there in sufficient detail, but they can be repeated much more fully from the *Life* composed by an author whose identity is uncertain, although he professes to have lived in the same period as Pachomius.

To these witnesses may be added the *Roman Martyrology* on the day before the Ides of May; Cassian; Nicephorus; Callistus; Saint Benedict of Aniane; Smaragdus; and, not to pursue the testimony of each individually any further, Rupert, abbot of Deutz, at the beginning of Book IV of *On the Apostolic Life*. He says:

“Blessed Pachomius delivered the Rule of the monks, dictated to him by the angel from heaven, not, evidently, as a human work, but as a divine oracle.”

As for this Latin translation of the Rule by Jerome, there can be no doubt that a wholly genuine product proceeded from the pen of the holy Doctor. I therefore consider those to be quite foolish who, for this one reason, dare to deny its authenticity: namely, that Jerome does not list Pachomius among ecclesiastical writers, although he would certainly have mentioned one whose book he had in fact translated into Latin. Their argument is intrinsically extremely weak, and it also rests upon a false assumption. This translation did not precede the *Catalogue*; on the contrary, it followed it after an interval of nearly thirteen years, as I shall demonstrate more clearly below.

Among the surviving copies of this work by Jerome, our first debt is owed to Saint Benedict of Aniane, who flourished around the year of Christ 820. He appended it to his *Codex of Rules*, together with the letters mentioned by Gennadius in the chapter cited above and several others. Since the collection of the Abbot of Aniane had not yet emerged from the corners of the libraries, this Latin Rule was taken from other manuscript codices. Achilles Statius first published it at Rome in 1575; Ciacconius did so there in 1588; afterward others reprinted it with additional editorial work at the end of Cassian’s *Collations* and in libraries of the Fathers.

Those editions, however, contain neither the whole Rule as it is presented here, nor the sections entitled *Judgments*, *Laws*, and *Admonitions*, nor, finally, the *Letters*, *Mystical Sayings*, and other works of that kind, which the Preface itself makes clear were also translated into Latin by Jerome.

Full credit must therefore be given to the diligence of the distinguished Luca Holstenius. Having come upon a copy of Saint Benedict’s work transcribed from one said to be preserved at Saint Maximinus near Trier and to be extremely ancient, he compared it with other old codices that contained some of these rules and published it in print, first at Rome in 1661 and then at Paris two years later.

We use this copy, since it is the fullest and most accurate of all. Moreover, because the learned man was prevented by death from presenting the variant readings which he had extracted from other books, and the notes which he had prepared for inclusion at the end of the work, we carefully compared it, insofar as it was useful to us, with the first edition, that of Achilles Statius, and then with the second, enlarged edition of Petrus Ciacconius; and whatever was lacking from Holstenius’ work, insofar as possible or seemed relevant, we supplied.

The time when Jerome prepared this Latin translation can easily be inferred from the fact that, at the very beginning of the Preface, he professes that he had remained silent for a long time while mourning the death of the holy and venerable Paula, until, in embellishing this work, he broke his long silence under what is called a favorable omen.

This indicates the year 404. At its beginning, the holy and blessed Paula died on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, on the third day of the week after sunset, during the sixth consulship of Honorius Augustus and the consulship of Aristenetus; Jerome records this most clearly in her epitaph. This translation may therefore conveniently be assigned to the end of that same year, or, if one prefers, to the following year, 405, when he composed it after having swallowed his grief in prolonged silence.

## Preface

[Col. 0061A] 53

### 1

Although a sharp and polished sword, if it is kept hidden in its sheath for a long time, becomes soiled with rust and loses the brilliance of its former beauty, so I too, mourning the death of the holy and venerable Paula—not as though I were acting against the Apostle’s command, but because, wounded by her death, I sighed for the consolation of many—received books sent to me by the man of God, the presbyter Silvanus. He had received them after they had been sent from Alexandria, so that he might also assign them to me for translation.

For he said that in the coenobia of the Thebaid, and in the monastery of Metanoea, which was changed from Canopus into repentance by the happy transformation of its name,

[Note: [Col. 0063C] That is, *Metanoea* means “repentance” in Greek. Canopus, formerly an island notorious for luxury and extravagance, was called Metanoea after monks were transferred there by Theophilus or Cyril to lead a life of penitence. The presbyter Athanasius, in the little work which he presented to the Council of Chalcedon against Dioscorus, writes: “Μετάνοιαν προάστειον τῆς μεγίστης Ἀλεξανδρείας, ὁ πότε Κάνωπος καλούμενος,” that is, “Metanoea, a suburb of the greatest city Alexandria, formerly called Canopus,” etc. See also Eunapius, in the *Life of Aedesius*, where, after the shrines of Canopus had been destroyed, he says that monks were brought there.]

many Latins lived who did not know the Egyptian or Greek language in which the precepts of Pachomius, Theodore, and Orsiesius had been written. These men were the first to lay the foundations of coenobia throughout the Thebaid and Egypt, according to the command of God and of the angel who had been sent to them for this very institution.

[Note: [Col. 0063D] The first edition, and the more accurate Roman edition of 1580, read: “who was sent by God under this institution,” etc.]

### 2

And so, because I had remained silent for a long time and had swallowed my grief in silence, while the presbyter Leontius and the other brothers with him, who had been sent to me for this very purpose, pressed me—having summoned a secretary—to dictate in our language what had been translated from Egyptian into Greek, I obeyed such distinguished men in their command—or, rather, their request—and under what is called a favorable omen broke my long silence.

I returned to my former studies and brought consolation to the soul of the holy woman who had always burned with love for monasteries and had meditated here on earth what she was going to see in heaven. Her venerable virgin daughter Eustochium would also have something to give the sisters to do,

[Note: [Col. 0063D] I would prefer the reading which gives a more elegant sense.]

and our Egyptian brothers—that is, the monks of Tabennesis—would have examples to follow.

[Note: [Col. 0063D] Cassian, Book IV, chapter 1, calls them “Tabennesiots.” They take their name from Tabenna, an island in the Nile where Pachomius had founded a notable monastery, from which the other establishments of the same institution were, as it were, cut off from a mother-city. See Palladius and Sozomen.]

They have in each monastery fathers, stewards, weekly officers, servants, and superiors of the individual houses. Thus, in one house approximately forty brothers live, obeying its superior; and, according to the number of brothers, thirty or forty houses exist in one monastery. Three or four houses are joined into one tribe, so that they may either go together to their work or succeed one another in weekly service in an orderly fashion.

### 3

Whoever first enters the monastery is first to sit, first to walk, first to recite the psalm, first to extend his hand toward the table, and first to receive Communion in the church. Age is not asked about among them, but profession.

[Note: [Col. 0063D] In former times psalms were not customarily sung in their entirety antiphonally by monks or clerics, as they are today; rather, they were sung individually in turn, so that while one person sang the psalm, the rest listened in complete silence. See our notes on Epistle 125, to Rusticus, no. 15.]

### 4

They have nothing in their cells except a *psiathium*,

[Note: [Col. 0064D] The old printed editions do not recognize this or the words written below. Holstenius later notes in his *Index*, after Rosweidus and Menardus, that a *psiathium* was a mat made from rush or papyrus, which the monks used as a bed or covering. The glossaries interpret *lebitonarium* as *colobium* and *colobarium*. Cassian, Book I, chapter 5, describing the Egyptian monks, says: “They wear linen *colobia*, which scarcely reach to the lower arms, and otherwise go about with their hands bare.” See below, chapter 11. As for the *melotes*, the deacon Paul, writing in the name of Abbot Theodemar to Charlemagne, says: “That garment which the Gallic monks call a *cuculla*, and which we call a *capa*, which properly signifies the dress of monks, we ought to call a *melotes*, just as some people in this province have until now called it.”]

and what is written below: two *lebitonaria*—a kind of sleeveless garment among the Egyptian monks—and one already worn out, for sleeping or working; a linen cloak; two hoods; a goatskin, which they call a *melotes*; a linen belt; Gallic shoes,

[Al. *caligas*: boots or shoes.]

and a staff as a companion for travel.

### 5

The sick are supported with extraordinary attentiveness and with food prepared in full abundance; the healthy practice greater abstinence. Twice a week, on the fourth and sixth days of the week, everyone fasts, except during the periods of Easter and Pentecost. On the other days, those who wish eat after midday. A meal is likewise served at supper, for those who work, for the old, for children, and because of the very great heat.

Some eat a little for a second time; others are content with only one food at lunch or supper. Some, after tasting a little bread, go out. All eat together. Whoever does not wish to go to the table receives only bread, water, and salt in his cell, whether he wishes to do so for one day

[Note: [Col. 0064D] Holstenius reads: “or after two days.”]

or for two days.

### 6

Brothers of the same craft are gathered into one house under one superior. For example, those who weave linen are together; those who make mats are counted as one household; tailors, carpenters, fullers, and shoemakers are governed separately by their own superiors. Every week they report an account of their work to the father of the monastery.

### 7

One head is regarded as the chief of all the monasteries. He lives in the monastery during the days of Easter. Except for those who are needed in the monastery, everyone gathers with him, so that nearly fifty thousand people may celebrate together the feast of the Lord’s Passion.

### 8

In the month called Mesore, that is, August, days of remission are observed in the manner of a Jubilee, and sins are forgiven to everyone. Those who have had any quarrel are reconciled with one another. The heads of the monasteries, the stewards, the superiors, and the servants are appointed according to necessity.

### 9

The Thebans say that an angel gave Pachomius, Cornelius, and the Syrian—who is said still to be living beyond the age of one hundred and ten years—the knowledge of a mystical language, so that they might write to one another and speak by means of a special alphabet concealing hidden meanings in certain signs and symbols.

[Note: [Col. 0065A] Holstenius reads “not,” perhaps through a printer’s error.]

We have translated their letters into our language as they are read among the Egyptians and Greeks, retaining the same characters as we found them. Insofar as we have imitated the simplicity of the Egyptian language, this is the fidelity of the translation: so that rhetorical speech would not alter these apostolic men, wholly devoted to spiritual grace.

I have not wished to give a preliminary account of the other matters contained in their treatises, so that those who delight in the pursuit of holy conduct may learn them from their own authors and drink from the springs rather than from the streams.

# Rule of Our Father Pachomius, Man of God, Who Founded the Monastic Way of Life in Coenobia at the Beginning by the Command of God

[Col. 0065]

## Prologue to the Precepts

[Col. 0065B] 57

### I

Whoever, being untrained, enters the assembly of the saints, and whom the doorkeeper has led in order from the door of the monastery and seated among the gathering of the brothers, shall not be permitted to change his place or order of sitting until Totihioc—that is, the superior of his house—transfers him to the place properly assigned to him.

### II

He shall sit with complete dignity and gentleness. He shall wear a goatskin over his shoulder, tucking it beneath his buttocks on the side and lower portion; and he shall carefully fasten his garment—that is, the sleeveless linen tunic called a *lebitonarium*—so that it covers his knees.

### III

When he hears the sound of the trumpet calling the assembly, he shall immediately leave his cell, meditating on something from the Scriptures until he reaches the door of the meeting place.

[Col. 0065C]

### IV

And when he begins to walk in the place of assembly, so that he may reach the place where he is to sit or stand, he must take care that no harm comes to the monastery, even through another’s negligence.

### V

But if the signal sounds at night, he shall not stand by the fire which, according to custom, is kindled to warm the bodies and drive away the cold. Nor shall he sit idle in the assembly. Rather, he shall quickly prepare cords for the mat straw with his hands, except in the case of bodily illness, for which permission to rest is granted.

### VI

When the superior, or the prior standing in his rank, strikes his hand while reciting something from Scripture by heart, so that the prayer may end, no one shall rise more slowly than the others; all shall rise together.

[Note: [Col. 0065D] We have emended this chapter in accordance with the first edition. Holstenius presents it with an incomplete sense as follows: “When the prior standing in his rank strikes his hand and recites something from Scripture by heart, so that, when the prayer ends, no one,” etc.]

[Col. 0066B]

### VII

No one shall look at another who is twisting a cord or praying. With his eyes fixed on his own work, he shall remain intent upon it.

[Note: [Col. 0065D] Statius and Ciacconius add: “working or praying.” One of them completes this Prologue with this chapter and thereafter begins the Pachomian Rule as follows: “Here begins the Rule of Pachomius. These are the precepts handed down by the three elders,” etc.]

### VIII

These are the life-giving precepts handed down by our elders.

[Note: [Col. 0066D] Holstenius has *a nobis majoribus* incorrectly; we have restored *a nostris*. More elegantly, as indicated above, the old editions read: “handed down by the three elders,” namely Pachomius, Theodore, and Orsiesius.]

If it happens that, during the singing of psalms, prayer, or in the middle of a reading, someone speaks or laughs, he shall immediately undo his belt

[Note: [Col. 0066D] Holstenius’ *vinculum* is incorrect.]

and, with his head bowed and his hands lowered, stand before the altar and be rebuked by the head of the monastery. He shall do the same in the assembly of the brothers when they have gathered together to eat.

### IX

When the trumpet’s blast summons the assembly during the day, whoever comes late to one prayer shall be corrected according to the order of the preceding rebuke

[Al. “shall be rebuked”]

and shall stand in the place of the meal.

### X

At night, since somewhat more allowance is made for bodily weakness, whoever comes after three prayers shall be corrected in the same manner both in the assembly and at the meal.

### XI

When the brothers are praying in the assembly, no one shall leave without the permission of the superiors, unless he has asked and received permission to go out for a natural necessity.

### XII

No one shall divide the reeds for weaving cords except the person serving that week. If he is detained by proper work, he shall await the superior’s command.

### XIII

From among the weekly officers of one house, no one shall be chosen to stand in rank and repeat something from Scripture before the whole assembly. Rather, all shall repeat from memory, according to the order of sitting and standing, what has been commanded to them. If one of them forgets something and hesitates while speaking, he shall undergo correction for negligence and forgetfulness.

### XIV

On Sunday, or at the time of the offering, none of the weekly officers shall be absent. He shall sit in the place of Ebiyymius and respond to the one singing psalms, with only one house serving during the principal week. There is also a lesser week, performed by fewer men in each house.

### XV

But if a larger number is necessary, others from the same tribe shall be summoned by the superior of the house serving that week. Without his command, no one from another house of the same tribe shall come to sing psalms, and no one may come for another house’s weekly service or from another house unless he belongs to the same tribe.

[Col. 0067B]

### XVI

A single tribe consists of three or four houses, depending on the size and population of the monastery. We could call these “families,” or “peoples” of one nation.

### XVII

On Sunday and at the assembly in which the offering is to be made, no one shall have authority to sing psalms without the superior of the house and the recognized elders of the monastery.

### XVIII

Whenever one of the elders sings, that is, recites the response, if anyone is absent, he shall immediately undergo the prescribed order of penitence and rebuke before the altar.

### XIX

From the assembly in which the offering is to be made, whoever leaves without the command of a superior shall immediately be rebuked.

[Col. 0067C]

### XX

In the morning, when the prayers have ended in each house, they shall not immediately return to their cells. Rather, they shall discuss among themselves what they heard the superiors debating, and only then enter their sleeping quarters.

### XXI

The superiors of the houses shall hold such a discussion three times each week. During the discussion, whether sitting or standing, the brothers shall not change their order, according to the order of the houses and of the individual men.

### XXII

If anyone falls asleep while sitting as the superior of the house or the head of the monastery is speaking, he shall immediately be compelled to rise and shall stand until he is ordered to sit.

[Note: [Col. 0067D] The old editions read: “until it seems good to him.”]

### XXIII

When the signal sounds for them to assemble and hear the precepts of the elders, no one shall remain behind. The fire shall not be kindled until the discussion has been completed. Whoever omits one of these matters shall be subjected to the correction prescribed above.

[Note: [Col. 0067D] The same manuscripts read: “Whoever omits one commandment from these,” etc.]

### XXIV

The weekly officer shall not have authority, without the command of the head of the monastery, to give anyone cords or any other vessels. Unless he commands it, he shall not be able to give the signal for them to assemble for the midday assembly or for the evening assembly of six prayers.

[Col. 0068A]

### XXV

After the morning prayers, the weekly servant to whom this task has been assigned shall ask the head of the monastery about each matter he considers necessary, and how many workers should go out to work in the field.

[Al. “workers” rather than “to work.”]

According to his command, he shall go around the individual houses and learn what each person needs. If they ask for a book to read, they shall receive it; and when the week is over, they shall return it to its proper place for the sake of those who succeed them in the service.

### XXVI

If they are making mats, the servant shall ask the superiors of the individual houses in the evening which houses need reeds, and how many.

[Note: [Col. 0067D] I would rather read “from the superior,” followed immediately by “what, or how much, for whom.”]

He shall then soak the reeds and distribute them to each person in order in the morning. If in the morning he sees that others also need reeds, he shall soak them and carry them to the individual houses until the signal for eating sounds.

### XXVII

The superior of the house who is completing the week, the one who will take up the coming week, and the heads of the monastery shall take care to see what work has been omitted or neglected. They shall have mats made, of the sort customarily spread over the floor in the assembly. They shall count the cords twisted during each week, record their total on tablets,

[Col. 0068B]

and preserve them until the time of the annual assembly, when an account is to be rendered and sins are forgiven to everyone.

### XXVIII

When the assembly has been dismissed, each person, as he goes out toward his cell or toward the place of eating, shall meditate on something from Scripture. No one shall have his head covered during the time of meditation.

[Col. 0068C]

### XXIX

When they have come to eat, they shall sit in order in the designated places and cover their heads.

### XXX

As soon as a superior orders you to move from one table to another, you shall offer no resistance whatsoever. You shall not dare to extend your hand toward the table before the superior of your house, nor look around at those who are eating.

### XXXI

Each superior shall teach in his house how they are to eat with discipline and gentleness. If anyone speaks or laughs while eating, he shall do penance and be immediately rebuked in that same place. He shall stand until another of those eating rises.

[Note: [Col. 0068D] I think the old editions more correctly read: “until the others rise from eating,” that is, until the end of the meal.]

### XXXII

If anyone comes late to eat,

[Col. 0068D]

unless he has been commanded to do so by a superior, he shall likewise do penance or return fasting to his house.

### XXXIII

If anything necessary is wanted at the table, no one shall dare to speak. Instead, he shall give a signal by making a sound to the servants.

[Col. 0069A] 61

### XXXIV

If you have left the meal, do not speak on the way back until you have reached your place.

### XXXV

The servants shall eat nothing besides what has been prepared in common for the brothers, nor shall they dare to prepare different food for themselves.

[Col. 0069A]

### XXXVI

The person who strikes the signal for eating and gathers the brothers shall meditate on something while striking it.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] The old editions read: “while they are gathering.” The striking is the giving of a signal by striking something.]

### XXXVII

The person who distributes *tragemata*—sweets—to the brothers leaving through the doors of the dining area shall meditate on something from Scripture while distributing them.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] The same editions read *dulciamina*, “sweetmeats,” instead of *tragemata*.]

### XXXVIII

The person who receives what is distributed shall accept it not in his hood but in his goatskin; nor shall he taste any of what he has received before reaching the house.

### XXXIX

The person who distributes the portions to the others shall receive his own portion from the superior. The other servants shall do the same, receiving from someone else and claiming nothing for themselves on their own authority.

What they receive shall be enough for three days. If anything remains for anyone, he shall take it back to the superior of the house, who shall store it in the storeroom until it is mixed with the rest and distributed to all the brothers.

[Col. 0069B]

### XL

No one shall give one person more than another person has received. If illness is alleged, the superior of the house shall go to the servants of the sick and receive from them whatever is necessary.

### XLI

If one of the servants themselves falls ill, he shall not have permission to enter the kitchen or storeroom and take something for himself. Instead, the other servants shall give him whatever they see that he needs. Nor shall he be permitted to cook for himself whatever he desires. The superiors of the houses shall obtain from the other servants whatever they see to be necessary for him.

### XLII

No one who is not sick shall enter the place of the sick. Whoever falls ill shall be led by the superior of his house into the dining room of the sick. If he needs a small cloak, a tunic, or other things necessary for covering himself or eating, the superior himself shall receive them from the servants and give them to the sick.

A sick person shall not be able to enter the dining room of those who are eating and eat whatever he desires unless he is led to eat by the servant appointed for this purpose.

[Col. 0069C] 62

### XLIII

He shall not be permitted to carry anything that he has received in the place of the sick back to his cell—not even a piece of fruit.

### XLIV

Those who cook the stews shall in turn serve the servants and those who are eating.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] The first edition reads: “They themselves shall serve those who are eating,” with *edentes* perhaps in the margin. Ciacconius reads: “They shall serve those who are eating without tasting anything themselves.”]

### XLV

No one shall touch wine or fish sauce except in the place of the sick.

### XLVI

If one of those who have been sent abroad falls ill on the road or on a ship,

[Note: [Col. 0070D] The same editions read “on the road” instead of “on a ship,” and shortly afterward, with the negative particle, “which they are not accustomed to eat.”]

and has a need or desire to eat fish sauce or something else which they customarily eat in the monastery,

[Col. 0069D]

he shall not eat with the other brothers but separately. The servants shall give him an abundant supply, so that the sick brother may not be distressed in any way.

### XLVII

No one shall dare to visit a sick person without the permission of a superior. Not even a relative or brother shall have permission to enter without the command of the superior of the house.

[Col. 0070A]

### XLVIII

If anyone omits or neglects one of these provisions, he shall be corrected by the customary rebuke.

### XLIX

If someone comes to the door of the monastery wishing to renounce the world and be added to the number of the brothers, he shall not have freedom to enter. The matter shall first be reported to the father of the monastery. He shall remain outside before the door for several days and shall be taught the Lord’s Prayer and as many psalms as he can learn by heart.

He shall carefully be put to the test, lest he may have done something evil and, being troubled, depart in fear after only a short time, or lest he be under some authority. They shall also determine whether he can renounce his parents and despise his own possessions.

If they see that he is suited to prayer and to everything else, he shall then be taught the remaining disciplines of the monastery, which he must preserve and practice, and whom he must serve—whether in the assembly of all the brothers, in the house to which he is to be assigned, or in the order of eating—so that, instructed and perfected in every good work, he may be joined to the brothers.

Then they shall strip him of his secular clothing, dress him in the monastic habit, and hand him over to the doorkeeper, who shall bring him before all the brothers at the time of prayer. He shall sit in the place where he has been instructed to sit.

The clothing which he had brought with him shall be received by those appointed for this task and placed in the storeroom; it shall remain under the authority of the head of the monastery.

### L

No one living in the monastery shall have authority to receive anyone for a meal. Instead, he shall send him to the door of the guesthouse, so that he may be received by those appointed for this purpose.

### LI

When some people come to the door of the monastery, if they are clergy or monks, they shall be received with greater honor. Their feet shall be washed, according to the command of the Gospel,

[Al. “they shall observe”]

and they shall be led to the guesthouse, where they shall be provided with everything suitable for the use of monks.

If they wish to come to the assembly of the brothers at the time of prayer and assembly, and if they are of the same faith, the doorkeeper or the servant of the guesthouse shall report this to the father of the monastery, and they shall then be led to pray.

If secular persons, the weak, or more fragile vessels—that is, women—come to the door and wish to pray,

[Note: [Col. 0070D] The words “and to pray” are more correctly absent from the old printed editions.]

they shall receive each one in separate places, according to the order proper to their position and sex. They shall especially care for women with greater honor and diligence,

[Col. 0070D]

with complete fear of God, and assign them a place separate from all proximity to men, so that there may be no occasion for blasphemy.

If they come in the evening, it is wrong to drive them away. Instead, as we have said, they shall be given a separate and enclosed place with complete discipline and caution, so that the flock of brothers may freely perform its duty and no one be given an opportunity to find fault.

### LII

If someone stands before the door of the monastery saying that he wishes to see his brother or relative, the doorkeeper shall report it to the father of the monastery. The father shall summon the superior of the house and ask whether the person sought is staying with him.

With the superior’s permission, the brother or relative who is in the monastery shall take as a companion for his departure someone whose fidelity has been tested. He shall then be sent to see his brother or relative.

If the visitor has brought some food which is permitted to be eaten in the monastery, the monastery resident himself shall not be able to receive it. Rather, he shall call the doorkeeper, who shall accept what has been brought.

If the food is of the sort to be eaten with bread, the person to whom it was brought shall receive none of it; everything shall be taken to the quarters of the sick. If it consists of sweets or fruit, the doorkeeper shall give him as much as he may eat, and shall carry the rest to the cell of the sick.

The doorkeeper himself shall not be able to taste anything that has been brought, but shall return to the person who brought it *lapsania*, a kind of inferior herb, or bread, or uncooked vegetables.

As for the foods which, as we have said, are brought by parents or relatives and are of a kind that must be eaten with bread, the person to whom they were brought shall be led by the superior of the house to the cell of the sick, and there he shall eat from them only once. The rest shall remain in the hands of the servant of the sick. The servant himself shall not be permitted to eat from them.

[Col. 0071B] 64

### LIII

If it is reported that one of their relatives or kinsmen who lives in the monastery is ill, the doorkeeper shall first report it to the father of the monastery. He shall summon the superior of the house and question him.

They shall select a man whose fidelity and discipline have been tested and send the monk with him to visit the sick person. He shall receive only as much travel provision as the superior of the house determines.

[Col. 0071C]

### LIV

But if necessity compels him to remain outside and eat in the house of his parents or relatives, he must by no means do so; rather, he shall stay either at the Lord’s house or in a monastery of the same faith. And if his relatives or kinsmen prepare food and set it before him, he shall not accept it at all, nor shall he eat except what he is accustomed to eat in the monastery. He shall not taste a sauce, drink wine, or consume anything else whose eating is not his custom. If he receives anything from his parents, he shall eat only as much as will suffice for the journey; whatever remains he shall give to the superior of his house, and he shall carry it to the cell of the sick.

### LV

If someone’s relative or blood relation dies, he shall not have permission [Al.: authority] to accompany the funeral, unless the Father of the monastery has ordered it. [Col. 0071D]

### LVI

No one shall be sent outside alone on any business, unless another has been joined to him.

### LVII

When they have returned to the monastery, if they see someone waiting before the door for one of their relatives who live in the monastery, they shall not dare to go to him, report to him, or call him. And, in general, they shall not be able to recount in the monastery anything they did or heard outside.

[Col. 0072A] ### LVIII

If the signal has been given for them to go out to work, the superior shall go before them; and no one shall remain in the monastery except the one whom the Father has ordered to remain. And those who are going shall not ask where they are going. [65]

### LIX

When all the houses have been gathered together in one place, the superior of the first house shall lead them all, and they shall proceed according to the order of the houses and of the individual men. They shall not speak with one another, but each shall meditate on something from the Scriptures. If someone happens to meet them and wishes to speak with one of them, the monastery porter assigned to this duty shall meet him and answer him, and they shall use him as their messenger. If the porter is not present, the superior of the house, or another to whom this has been entrusted, shall answer those who meet them.

[Col. 0072B] ### LX

While working, they shall say nothing secular; rather, they shall either meditate on what has been written [Note: [Col. 0071D] The older printed editions read *quae sancta sunt*, “the things that are holy.”] or simply remain silent.

### LXI

No one shall take a linen mantle with him when going to work, unless perhaps by permission of a superior; and while walking in the monastery after the assembly, no one shall use that mantle.

### LXII

A worker shall not sit down without the superior’s order.

### LXIII

The leaders of the brothers on a journey, if they have need to send someone, shall not be able to do so without the superior’s command. But if the one who is leader is compelled [Al.: is compelled] by necessity to go somewhere, he shall entrust his office to the one who is next after him in rank.

### LXIV

Brothers who have been sent out, or who are stationed outside, if they eat away from the monastery, shall receive food from the weekly server who accompanies them, without cooked stew; and he shall carry water around, with a glass [Note: [Col. 0071D] I would prefer to delete the conjunction *et* and read *juxta virum*, “according to the man”; [Col. 0072D] that is, according to the order of each individual, not “a glass.”]. No one shall have permission to rise, draw water, or drink.

### LXV

When they return to the monastery, no one from the group shall remain behind.

### LXVI

When they have reached their houses, they shall hand over the tools with which they worked and the *gallicae* to the one who is second after the superior of the house; he shall bring them in the evening to a separate cell and lock them there. When the week is complete, all the tools shall be brought back to one house; and those who succeed to the weekly duty shall know again what they are to distribute to each house.

### LXVII

No one shall wash the *levitonarium* or anything else belonging to the monks’ clothing on Sunday, except sailors and bakers.

### LXVIII

Nor shall they go to wash until the one signal has sounded for everyone; they shall follow their superior and wash silently and with discipline.

### LXIX

No one shall wash with his garments drawn up higher than has been prescribed; and when they have washed, they shall all return together. If anyone remains behind at the time when they are going to wash, or is not present at that moment, he shall inform his superior, and the superior shall send another with him; after washing the garment, they shall return home.

[Col. 0073A] ### LXX

In the evening they shall take up the dry *levitonaria* and give them to the second—that is, to the one who is after the superior—and he shall put them away in the cell.

### LXXI

But if they are not dry, they shall be spread out in the sun the next day until they dry; nor shall they be left in the heat of the sun beyond the third hour. When they have been collected, they shall be softened slightly.

### LXXII

Nor shall individuals keep them with themselves; rather, they shall hand them over to be stored in the cell until Saturday.

### LXXIII

No one shall take vegetables from the garden unless he has received them from the gardener.

### LXXIV

No one shall take palm leaves, from which baskets are woven, on his own authority, without the one to whom the palms have been entrusted.

[Col. 0073B] ### LXXV

No one shall dare to eat grapes or ears of grain while they are still unripe, contrary to the order of discipline; and, in general, no one shall eat separately of anything in the fields or orchards before everything has been presented equally to all the brothers. [Note: [Col. 0073D] Statius reads, “until he has presented an equal portion”; others more correctly read, “until the father has presented it.”]

### LXXVI

The one who cooks shall not taste anything before the brothers eat. [Al.: They shall not dare to eat.]

### LXXVII

The one who is over the palms shall not eat of their fruits unless the brothers have eaten first.

### LXXVIII

If they are ordered to gather the fruits of the palms, the superior of those gathering shall give each of them a small amount to eat in that same place; and when they come to the monastery, they shall receive their portions among the other brothers. But if they find apples fallen beneath the trees, they shall not dare to eat them; instead, they shall place what they find along the path beside the roots of the trees. The one who distributes the fruit to the other gatherers shall likewise not be able to taste it; rather, he shall carry it to the steward, who shall distribute it with the rest to the brothers and shall give him his portion as well.

### LXXIX

No one shall store anything for eating in his cell except what he has received from the steward.

### LXXX

As for the small loaves given to the superiors of the houses for distribution to those who do not wish to eat in common with the others, but devote themselves, as it were, to greater abstinence: they shall observe the following rule. They shall give them to no one according to personal favor, not even to someone setting out on a journey abroad. Nor shall they be placed in the common supply; rather, whenever the recipients wish to eat, the loaves shall be given to them with discipline in their cells, and they shall eat nothing with them except salt. [Col. 0073D] No one shall have authority to cook food anywhere except in the monastery kitchen. And whenever they go outside, that is, to work in the fields, they shall receive vegetables seasoned with salt and vinegar and prepared for extended use during the summer.

### LXXXI

No one shall have in his house or cell, apart from the things prescribed by the common law of the monastery, a woolen tunic, a cloak, a skin softer than the unshorn wool of rams, a few coins, [Note: [Col. 0073D] The older printed editions have instead: “nor anything of his own apart from his clothing.”] not even a little cushion for his head, or any other varied household furnishing, except those things distributed by the Father of the monastery through the superiors of the houses: namely, his armor, two *levitonaria*, one of them worn and damaged from use, a *sabanum*—that is, a longer linen cloth wrapped around the neck and shoulders—a little skin hanging at the side, *gallicae*, two hoods, a belt, and a staff. Whatever else you find besides these things, you shall take away without objection.

### LXXXII

No one shall separately possess a small sharp implement [Read: *pavula*] for pulling out thorns if he should step on one, without the superior of the house and the second-ranking brother; and it shall hang in the window where the books are placed.

[Col. 0074B] ### LXXXIII

If anyone is transferred from one house to another, he shall not be able to take anything with him except the things mentioned above. [Note: [Col. 0073D] The same books explain that these are the things necessary for daily use and clothing.]

### LXXXIV

No one shall have permission either to go out into the fields, walk about in the monastery, or go outside the monastery wall unless he has asked the superior and the superior has granted permission.

### LXXXV

Care must be taken that no one carries words from one house to another, or from one monastery to another, or from the monastery to the fields, or from the fields to the monastery.

### LXXXVI

If anyone has walked on the road, sailed, or worked outside, he shall not speak in the monastery about what he saw being done there.

[Col. 0074C] [68] ### LXXXVII

No one, when sleeping, shall lay himself down unless he reclines in his assigned cell [Note: [Col. 0073D] Statius, who read in a manuscript, “Let him not sleep except on a reclining seat,” had ingeniously conjectured the emendation “a reclining little chair.” But I retain the rest as it stands, since the passage could not be restored. Now that this conjecture has shed light on the matter, I would reconstruct the whole passage as follows: “No one, while sleeping, shall place anything beneath himself except a reclining little chair. Neither in his assigned cell, nor in the buildings in which they rest at night to avoid the heat, nor in the fields, when he has lain down to sleep, shall he speak to another after he has fallen asleep.” Palladius, praised by Statius, has: *καθευδέτωσαν δὲ μὴ ἀνακλινόμενοι, ἀλλὰ θρόνους οἰκοδομητοὺς ὑπτιωτέρους πεποιηκότες*, “Let them sleep, not reclining, but having constructed seats that are somewhat tilted backward,” etc. “Let them take sleep not lying down, but on constructed chairs that recline slightly,” etc.]. Neither in his cell, nor in the buildings where they rest at night to avoid the heat, nor in the fields, when he has settled down to sleep, shall he speak to another after he has fallen asleep. If he wakes during the night after sleeping, he shall pray; if he begins to thirst, but it is a day of fasting, he shall not dare to drink.

### LXXXVIII

Apart from a *psiathium*, that is, a mat, he shall place absolutely nothing else beneath himself in his cell for sleeping.

### LXXXIX

It is forbidden to enter another’s cell unless one has first knocked at the door.

### XC

They shall not go to food unless they have been summoned by the general sound; nor shall they walk about in the monastery before the common signal has sounded.

### XCI

No one shall walk in the monastery without a hood and a little skin garment, nor shall he go to the assembly or to eat without them.

### XCII

In the evening, to anoint and soften their hands, worn by work, with oil, they shall not go without another. No one shall anoint his entire body except on account of illness; nor shall he wash with water while naked unless his illness is evident.

[Col. 0075A] ### XCIII

No one shall wash or anoint another unless he has been ordered to do so.

### XCIV

No one shall speak to another in the dark. No one shall sleep with another on a *psiathium*. No one shall hold another’s hand; rather, whether standing, walking, or sitting, each shall remain one cubit from the other.

### XCV

No one shall dare to pull a thorn from another’s foot except the superior of the house, the second-ranking brother, or another to whom this has been ordered.

### CXVI

No one shall cut his hair without the judgment of a superior.

### XCVII

No one shall dare to exchange with another what he has received from the superior; nor shall he take the better and give the worse, or conversely give the better and receive the worse. In his clothing and dress he shall introduce nothing new, for the sake of elegance, beyond the others.

### XCVIII

All the skins shall be fastened and hang from the shoulders.

### XCIX

The hoods of each individual shall bear both the sign of the monastery and that of the house.

[69] ### C

No one going to the assembly or to eat shall leave behind an unbound book. The books that are placed in the window—that is, inside the wall—at evening shall be under the care of the second-ranking brother, who shall count them and lock them up according to custom.

### CI

No one shall go to the assembly or to eat wearing *galliculae* on his feet or wrapped in a linen mantle, whether in the monastery or in the fields.

[Col. 0075C] ### CII

Anyone who allows his garment to remain in the sun beyond midday, when the brothers are summoned to food, shall be rebuked for negligence.

### CIII

And if anyone passes over, in contempt, even one of the things mentioned above, he shall be corrected with a similar rebuke.

### CIV

No one shall make *galliculae*, or repair or assemble anything else that requires joining, except the one to whom the superior of the house has assigned this service.

### CV

If one of the brothers has been injured or struck, but does not remain lying on a bed and instead walks about weak, and needs something—a garment, a small cloak, or other utensils—the superior of his house shall go to those to whom the brothers’ clothing has been entrusted, and shall receive and give it to him. [Note: [Col. 0075D] We have supplied the words “and shall give” from the first edition.] When he has recovered, he shall return it without any delay.

### CVI

No one shall receive anything from another unless the superior has ordered it.

### CVII

No one shall sleep with his cell closed, nor shall anyone have a room that can be locked, unless perhaps the Father of the monastery has granted this because of someone’s age or illness.

### CVIII

No one shall go to the village unless sent, except herdsmen, ox-drivers, and farmers.

[Col. 0076A] ### CIX

Two men shall not sit together on the bare back of a donkey, nor on [Note: [Col. 0075D] Again the same reading as in the older editions, and apparently the more correct one: “on the pole of a wagon.”] the covering of a wagon.

### CX

If someone arrives seated on a donkey, except in the case of illness, he shall dismount before the monastery gate; then, walking ahead of the donkey, he shall lead it by a rope in his hand.

### CXI

Only the superiors shall go to the workshops of the various trades, in order to obtain what is necessary.

### CXII

They themselves [Al.: he himself] shall not be able to go before midday, when the brothers are summoned to eat, unless some necessity happens to arise; and, with the counsel of the Father of the monastery, the weekly server shall send someone to carry what is necessary. And, in general, no one shall dare to enter another’s cell without the command of a superior.

[70] ### CXIII

No one shall accept anything entrusted to him by a fellow brother.

### CXIV

No one shall store anything in his cell without the superior’s command—not even the most worthless apples [Note: [Col. 0075D] The older editions do not have “these” and similar words.].

### CXV

If the superior of another house has gone somewhere, another superior shall be leader of that group, shall take charge of the one who has departed, and shall exercise his powers, carefully arranging everything. He shall divide the instruction concerning the two fasts in such a way that he conducts one in his own house and the other in the house of the one who has departed. [Note: [Col. 0075D] The same books add: “or the one who is second”; then they read, “Let him exercise care for the one who has departed,” or “the one whom the superior himself has chosen from among the brothers and to whom he has entrusted his care.”]

### CXVI

When they sprinkle flour with water and knead the dough, no one shall speak to another. In the morning also, when they carry the loaves on boards to the oven or baking ovens, they shall observe the same silence, and shall sing [Al.: meditate on] something from the Psalms and the Scriptures until the work is completed. If they need anything, they shall not speak, but shall give a sign to those who can bring what they need.

[Col. 0076C] ### CXVII

When they have been summoned to mix the flour, no one shall sit in the place where the bread is baked; except for those needed for the baking and those who have been ordered to do so, no one shall sit.

### CXVIII

There is a similar discipline on ships as well. No one shall cast off the ship’s rope without the Father’s command—not even the small boat. [Note: [Col. 0076D] Statius reads *navigium*, “ship,” and *funiculum*, “rope”; other printed editions have “the ship’s rope.” But even *lembum*, “small boat,” and the words “in the place of the bilge” are lacking.]

### CXIX

In the place of the bilge and in the inner part of the ship, while the other brothers rest on the crossbeams and planking, no one shall sleep; and no one shall allow secular persons to sleep with them in the ship. The weaker vessels shall not sail with the others unless perhaps the Father of the monastery has ordered it. [Al.: has ordered it.]

### CXX

No one shall dare to make a fire in his own house unless one is lit in common for everyone.

### CXXI

Anyone who comes late to one of the six evening prayers, or who mutters, speaks to another, or smiles during the remaining prayers, shall perform penance according to the established order.

### CXXII

When they sit at home, they shall not be permitted to speak about anything secular; but if the superior teaches anything from the Scriptures, they shall discuss it among themselves in turn, and report what each has heard or retains by memory.

[71] ### CXXIII

No one shall do any work, carry around cups filled with water, or even twist a rope unless the superior has ordered it.

### CXXIV

No one shall take soaked reeds for himself to work with unless the weekly master has given them to him.

### CXXV

Anyone who breaks an earthen vessel [Note: [Col. 0077C] The first edition adds, “or any useful object,” meaning “or any useful thing for the monastery’s use.”] or soaks the reeds a third time shall perform penance in the evening during the six prayers.

### CXXVI

After the six prayers, when everyone has separated for sleep, no one shall be permitted to leave his room except for a matter of necessity.

[Col. 0077B] ### CXXVII

If a brother sleeps, the entire brotherhood shall accompany him. [Note: [Col. 0077C] The older printed editions read: “No one shall go outside, no one shall speak, no one shall remain behind,” and so forth.] No one shall remain behind without the superior’s command, nor shall anyone sing psalms unless ordered to do so; nor shall anyone join one psalm to another without the superior’s permission.

### CXXVIII

Two men shall not sing psalms simultaneously during a time of mourning, nor shall they be wrapped in a linen cloak [Perhaps: *lineo*, “linen”]. No one shall fail to answer the one who sings the psalm; rather, he shall join him in step and with a matching voice.

### CXXIX

The sick man shall have a servant at the funeral to support him; and, in general, wherever the brothers are sent, they shall have among the weekly servers those who serve the sick, in case illness should come upon someone during the journey or in the fields.

### CXXX

No one shall walk before his superior and leader; no one shall remain behind his assigned order.

### CXXXI

If anyone has lost something, he shall be rebuked publicly before the altar. But if what was lost belonged to his personal clothing, he shall not receive anything for three weeks; in the fourth week, after performing penance, he shall be given what he lost.

### CXXXII

Anyone who finds something shall hang it up for three days before the brothers’ assembly, [Perhaps: “so that the one who recognizes it may take it.”]

### CXXXIII

For all rebukes and instructions that have been written down and established, the superior’s correction shall suffice; but whatever is new in the offense he shall report to the head of the monastery.

[Col. 0078A] [72] ### CXXXIV

No one shall carry out any washing in the house without him; and every new matter shall be arranged according to his judgment.

### CXXXV

Every correction shall be carried out in such a way that those being corrected are separated from the others; they shall stand at the principal assembly and at the place of eating. [Note: [Col. 0077D] The same editions read *disjuncti*, “separated,” in the margin as *distincti*, “set apart.” Other editors followed Statius’s conjecture and likewise read the rest of this chapter as: “those who are being corrected, with their hands lowered and their heads bowed, shall ask forgiveness, promising that they will amend the faults of which they are accused.”]

### CXXXVI

Anyone who has left without the brothers’ admonition, and later returns after doing penance, shall not be in his own rank without the command of a superior.

### CXXXVII

If the superior of a house and the steward have slept for one night without the brothers, and afterward come to the brothers’ assembly after doing penance, he shall not be permitted to enter the house or stand in his rank without the command of a superior.

### CXXXVIII

Everything they have heard debated in the brothers’ assembly they shall be compelled to repeat among themselves, especially during the fasts, when they are taught by their superiors.

### CXXXIX

Anyone who enters the monastery uneducated shall first be taught what he ought to observe; and when, having been instructed, he has agreed to everything, they shall give him twenty Psalms and two Apostolic Letters, or a portion of another Scripture. If he does not know letters, at the first, third, and sixth hours he shall go to the one who can teach him and who has been assigned to him; he shall stand before him and learn with the greatest diligence and with all thanksgiving.

### CXL

Afterward the letters, syllables, words, and names shall be written for him; and even if unwilling, he shall be compelled to read. In the monastery there shall be no one who does not learn letters and retain something from the Scriptures—at the very least, as far as the New Testament and the Psalter.

### CXLI

For the assembly, psalm-singing, and prayer, no one shall invent occupations for himself by which he claims to be occupied, as though he could not go. [Note: [Col. 0078D] The same editions read: “Let no one invent excuses for himself.”]

### CXLII

Whether he is on a ship, in the monastery, in the fields, on a journey, or engaged in any service, he shall not omit the times for prayer and psalm-singing.

## Rules and Institutions of Our Holy Father Pachomius

[Col. 0077]

How the assembly ought to be held and how the brothers are to be gathered to hear the word of God, according to the precepts of the elders and the teaching of the holy Scriptures, so that they may be freed from the error of the soul [Note: [Col. 0077D] The edition of Statius reads “the soul of the converts,” and so forth], and glorify God in the light of the living, and [Al.: so that they may] know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God without ruin or scandal; so that they may not become intoxicated by any passion, but stand within the measure of truth and in the traditions of the apostles and prophets; and so that they may observe the order of the solemnities, imitating their conduct [Al.: their congregation] in the house of God, and completing fasts and prayers according to custom. For those who serve well follow the rule of the Scriptures.

[Col. 0077D] [73] ### CXLIII

This, then, is the service that the ministers of the Church ought to perform [Al.: complete]. [Col. 0078D] Let them gather the brothers at the time of prayer and do everything that ought properly to be completed, giving no opportunity for refusal [Al.: so that they give no opportunity for refusal], nor allowing anyone opposed to discipline to walk about.

### CXLIV

If they ask for a book, let them bring it to them.

### CXLV

If someone comes from outside in the evening and has not arrived in time to receive the work he is to do the next day, let it be assigned to him in the morning.

### CXLVI

If the work he had in hand comes to an end, let him refer the matter to the superior’s knowledge [Al.: judgment], and let him do what the superior orders.

### CXLVII

The one who is in charge shall take care that no work is lost in the monastery in any craft whatsoever practiced by the brothers. But if anything is lost and has been wasted through negligence, the Father shall rebuke the minister of each individual work, and he in turn shall rebuke the one who lost the work—always according to the will and judgment of the head, without whom no one shall have authority to rebuke a brother.

[Col. 0079B] ### CXLVIII

If someone finds a garment spread out in the sun on the third day [Note: [Col. 0079D] We have supplied the word “day,” which, as elsewhere above and below, is of lesser importance, from the first edition], its owner shall be rebuked and shall perform public penance in the assembly. [Note: [Col. 0079D] The same edition adds: “and shall stand at the place of eating.”] If a little skin garment, *galliculae*, a belt, or anything else has been lost, the one who lost it shall be rebuked.

### CXLIX

If anyone has taken something that is not his, he shall carry it on his shoulders and perform public penance in the assembly, and shall stand at the place of eating. [Note: [Col. 0079D] The same edition again adds: “But if he is caught in theft, they shall beat him thirty-six times [Al.: thirty-nine], and outside they shall give him only bread and water to eat; clothed in sackcloth and ashes, they shall compel him to perform penance at each time of prayer. The same law shall be observed for fugitives.”]

### CL

If one of the brothers is found stubbornly doing something or contradicting a superior’s command, he shall be rebuked according to the measure of his offense.

[74] ### CLI

The Father of the monastery shall hear of anyone who lies, or is found to hate someone, or is disobedient, or is excessively devoted to joking, or is idle, or answers harshly, or has the habit of slandering the brothers or those outside; and, in general, of anything contrary to the rule of the Scriptures and the discipline of the monastery. He shall punish each according to the measure and nature of the offense.

### CLII

The superior of a house shall be subject to blame and rebuke if he has not reported to the Father within three days anything lost on the road, in the fields, or in the monastery; and he shall perform public penance according to the established order. If someone flees and he has not reported it to the Father within three hours, he shall be guilty of the fugitive’s loss—unless he later finds him again.

### CLIII

This is the punishment for one who has lost a brother from the house: he shall perform public penance for three days. But if he reports it to the Father in the same hour in which the brother fled, he shall not be held guilty.

### CLIV

If the superior sees an offense in his house and does not immediately rebuke the offender or report it to the Father of the monastery, he himself shall be subjected to the order of correction.

### CLV

In each house they shall complete six prayers and psalms in the evening, according to the order of the principal assembly, which is celebrated by all the brothers together.

### CLVI

Each week the superior shall complete two discussions, that is, catechetical instructions.

### CLVII

No one shall do anything in the house except what the superior has ordered.

[75] ### CLVIII

If all the brothers who are in one house see that the superior is excessively negligent, or rebukes the brothers harshly and exceeds the measure of the monastery, they shall report it to the Father, and he shall be rebuked by him.
