The superior himself shall do nothing except what the Father orders, especially in a new matter. For what descends from custom, he shall observe the rules of the monastery.

### CLIX

The superior shall not become drunk. He shall not sit in the lower places beside the monastery’s vessels, lest he break the bonds that God established in heaven to be observed on earth. He shall not mourn on the feast day of the Lord the Savior. He shall rule his flesh according to the measure of the saints. He shall not be found in high beds, imitating [Al.: having imitated] the custom of the Gentiles. He shall not be double-minded. He shall not follow the thoughts of his heart, but the law of God. He shall not resist higher authorities with a swollen spirit. He shall not rage or [Note: [Col. 0080D] The older printed editions read *inruat*, “rush upon.” But *hirrire*, properly the growling of dogs when they are angered, is used by Sidonius in his letters.] growl at those beneath him. He shall not move boundaries. He shall not be deceitful, nor entertain tricks in his thoughts. He shall not neglect the sin of his soul. [Note: [Col. 0080D] Older printed editions add “to root it out.”] He shall not be overcome by the lust of the flesh. He shall not walk carelessly. He shall not quickly utter an idle word. He shall not place a stumbling block before the feet of the blind. He shall not teach his soul pleasure. He shall not be dissolved [Al.: released] by the laughter and jokes of fools. His heart shall not be carried away by those who speak foolish and flattering words. He shall not be overcome by gifts. He shall not engage in the talk of children. [Note: [Col. 0080D] The same editions more correctly read, “Let him not be led by speech.”] He shall not be distressed in tribulation. He shall not fear death, but God. He shall not become a transgressor because of impending [Al.: eminent] fear. He shall not abandon the true light for the sake of small portions of food. He shall not waver or fluctuate in his works. He shall not change his judgment, but shall be firm and steadfast in his decision, considering and judging everything justly and in truth, without desire for glory, manifest before God and men, and far from fraud [Al.: distancing himself from fraud]. He shall not be ignorant of the conduct of the saints, nor blind to their knowledge. He shall harm no one through pride, nor follow the desires of his eyes. The incitements of vices shall not overcome him. He shall never pass over the truth. He shall hate injustice. He shall never judge according to persons in return for gifts, nor condemn an innocent soul through pride. He shall not laugh among children. He shall not abandon the truth when overcome by fear. He shall not eat bread gained by fraud. He shall not desire another’s land. He shall not oppress a soul for the sake of another’s spoils. He shall not despise those who need mercy. He shall not give false testimony, seduced by profit. He shall not lie through pride. He shall not contend against the truth because of arrogance. He shall not abandon justice because of weariness. He shall not destroy his soul because of shame. He shall not look toward the dishes of a more luxurious table. He shall not desire beautiful clothing. He shall not neglect himself, so that he may always scrutinize his thoughts. [Note: [Col. 0081A] In another sense, and one again more smoothly expressed, the earlier version was: “Let him not neglect the old; let him always discern his thoughts.” Soon afterward, with different punctuation: “Let him possess humility joined to truth when he judges.” What follows is: “Let him follow,” etc.] He shall not become drunk with wine; rather, he shall join humility to truth. When he judges, he shall follow the precepts of the elders and the law of God, which has been proclaimed throughout the whole world.

If he has passed over any of these things, a measure shall be rendered to him according to the measure with which he measured, and he shall receive according to his works, because he has committed adultery [Note: [Col. 0081B] Formerly: “in wood and stone,” and shortly afterward “of the wicked” instead of “of the pagans.”] in his wood and stones; and because of the brightness of gold and the splendor of silver he abandoned judgment, and through desire for temporal profit clothed himself in the snares of the pagans (Jeremiah III). And there shall come upon him the ruin of Eli and his sons (1 Samuel IV); the curse of David which he invoked against Doeg (Psalm LI); the sign with which Cain was marked (Genesis IV); the burial of a donkey, of which Jeremiah speaks (Jeremiah XXII); the destruction by which the chasm of the earth swallowed sinners (Numbers XVI); the annihilation of the Canaanites; the breaking of the water jar at the fountain; and the crumbling of sand [Note: [Col. 0082B] Older editions read “on shores battered by salty waves.”] on shores and rocks battered by waves (Ecclesiastes XII); and the breaking of the glorious staff from Isaiah, so that he is like a blind man groping with his hand along a wall (Isaiah V and LIX). All these things shall befall the one who did not preserve truth in judgment and acted unjustly [Al.: unjustly] in all the things entrusted to him.

## Rules and Judgments of Our Holy Father Pachomius

[Col. 0081] [77] ### CLX

The fullness of the law is love, for those who know the time, because the hour is already near for us to rise from sleep, and salvation is nearer than at the time when we believed. The night has passed, the day has drawn near: let us put away the works of darkness (Romans XIII), which are quarrels, slanders, hatreds, and the pride of a swollen spirit.

Anyone who is quick to slander and says what is not true, if he is found in this sin, shall be admonished twice; and if he scorns hearing the admonition, he shall be separated from the assembly of the brothers for seven days and shall receive only bread and water, until he promises and confirms that he will abandon this vice; then he shall be released.

### CLXI

If an angry and furious man becomes angry frequently without cause and over something empty and worthless, he shall be admonished six times. On the seventh occasion they shall make him rise from his place in the order of seating and place him among the last; they shall teach him to cleanse himself of this disturbance of mind. When he has brought three trustworthy witnesses who will make a promise on his behalf that he will never do anything similar, he shall receive his seat again. Otherwise, if he persists in the vice, he shall remain among the last, having lost his former place.

[Col. 0081D] ### CLXII

Anyone who wishes to prove a false charge against another in order to oppress the innocent shall be admonished three times; afterward he shall be held guilty of injustice, whether he is one of the senior or one of the junior brothers.

### CLXIII

Anyone who has the very bad habit of troubling his brothers with speech and corrupting the souls of the simple shall be admonished three times. If he scorns the admonition and persists stubbornly in hardness, they shall separate him from the monastery, and he shall be beaten before the gates. [Note: [Col. 0081D] The first edition adds “thirty-nine times,” that is, “he shall be beaten.” See above, chapter 149, and the note corresponding to this passage.] They shall give him bread and water to eat outside until he is cleansed of his filth.

### CLXIV

Anyone who has the habit of murmuring and complains that he is oppressed as though by heavy labor shall be taught five times that he murmurs without cause, and they shall show him the evident truth. If after this he is disobedient, and is of mature age, they shall treat him as one of the sick and place him among the infirm; [Col. 0082C] there he shall be fed in idleness until he returns to the truth. But if his complaint is just and he is being unjustly oppressed by a superior, the one who has caused his scandal shall be subject to the same sentence.

### CLXV

If anyone is disobedient, quarrelsome, argumentative, or a liar, and is [Note: [Col. 0082D] The same editions add: “and is of mature age,” as in the preceding chapter.] shameless, he shall be admonished ten times to desist from his vices. If he refuses to listen, he shall be rebuked according to the laws of the monastery. But if he has fallen into these vices through another’s fault, and this has been proved, the one who was the cause shall be held liable for the punishment.

### CLXVI

If one of the brothers is found willingly laughing and playing with children and maintaining friendships with immature persons, he shall be admonished three times to withdraw from their company and remember propriety and the fear of God. If he does not stop, he shall be corrected as he deserves, with the severest correction.

### CLXVII

Those who despise the precepts of the elders and the rules of the monastery, which have been established by God’s command, and make light of the counsels of the seniors, shall be corrected according to the established order until they are amended.

### CLXVIII

If anyone who is judge of all offenses abandons the truth through perversity of mind or negligence, twenty holy men who fear God—or ten, [Col. 0083A] or as few as five—of whom all shall give testimony, shall sit and judge him, and they shall demote him to the lowest rank until he is corrected.

### CLXIX

Anyone who disturbs the minds of the brothers and is quick [Note: [Col. 0083B] Again the same reading: “quick to slander.”] to speak, sowing quarrels and disputes, shall be admonished ten times. If he is not corrected, he shall be rebuked according to the order of the monastery until he is amended.

### CLXX

If anyone among the superiors and provosts sees his brother in distress and is unwilling to inquire into the cause of his distress, and despises him, the cause shall be investigated by the judges mentioned above, between the brother and the Provost. If the Provost’s negligence is discovered, or if he has oppressed the brother through pride and judged him [79] not according to the truth but according to his personal standing, he shall be reduced from his seat until he is corrected and cleansed from the filth of injustice—because he did not consider the truth but persons, and served the perversity of his own mind rather than God’s judgment.

[Note: In another version: “the distress of his brothers,” etc.]

### CLXXI

If anyone promises that he will observe the regulations of the monastery and begins to do so, but then abandons them, and afterward returns and does penance, alleging weakness of body by which he cannot fulfill what he had said, let him remain among the sick and be fed among the idle until, having performed penance, he fulfills what he promised.

[Variant: “what you promised.”]

### CLXXII

If boys in the house devote themselves to games and idleness, and cannot be corrected even after admonition, the Provost himself must admonish and correct them for up to thirty days. If he sees that they persist in their perversity, does not report them to the Father, and some sin is discovered in them, he himself shall be subject to the guilt, according to the sin that is found in them.

[Note: Earlier printed editions add “of the monastery.”]

### CLXXIII

All boys who are not afraid to be put to shame because of sin, who through thoughtlessness do not consider God’s judgment, and who do not mend their ways when corrected by word, shall be beaten for as long as is necessary for them to receive discipline and fear.

[Note: Holstenius reads *saltem*—“at least”—instead of *autem*.]

### CLXXIV

Whoever judges unjustly shall rightly be condemned by others.

### CLXXV

If one, two, or three of the brothers, having been scandalized by someone, withdraw from the house and later return, the matter shall be examined between them and the one who caused the scandal before the judgment. If he is found guilty, he shall be corrected according to the regulations of the monastery.

### CLXXVI

Whoever consents to sinners and defends another who has committed an offense shall be accursed before God and human beings, and shall be corrected with the most severe rebuke.

[Variant: “the worst rebuke.”]

But if he was deceived through ignorance and did not think the matter was as it really was, he shall be forgiven. Everyone who sins through ignorance will readily receive pardon; but whoever sins knowingly shall endure correction according to the measure of his deed.

[Note: Formerly: “according to the measure and character of his sin.”]

# Precepts and Laws of Our Holy Father Pachomius

[Col. 0083]

## Concerning the six evening prayers and the assembly held in each house for the six prayers

### CLXXVII

The Provost of the house and his second-in-command shall weave twenty-five *orgyai* [fathoms] from palm leaves, so that the others may work according to their example. If they are not present, whoever is in charge in their place shall devote himself to this work and its prescribed measure.

### CLXXVIII

After they have been summoned, they shall come to the assembly; before they are summoned, no one shall leave his cell. If anyone despises these precepts, he shall be subject to the customary rebuke.

### CLXXIX

The brothers shall not be compelled to do excessive work; rather, moderate labor shall summon everyone to work. Let there be peace and concord among them, and let them willingly submit to their superiors, whether sitting, walking, or standing in their proper order, striving with one another in humility.

[Variant: “caring for one another in humility.”]

### CLXXX

If any offense has been committed, the Fathers of the monasteries may correct it and establish what ought to be followed.

### CLXXXI

The Provost of the house and his second-in-command shall have only this authority: to compel the brothers, in the assembly of the house or in the greater assembly—that is, the assembly of all the brothers—to submit to penance.

[Note: Earlier authorities read: “to compel the brothers, in each individual offense, to submit to penance in the assembly,” etc.]

### CLXXXII

If the Provost is away on a journey, the second-in-command shall take his place, both in receiving a brother’s penance and in any other matter that is necessary in the house.

[Variant: “necessary for the master.”]

### CLXXXIII

If anyone goes to another house without the knowledge of two persons, or asks a brother of another house to lend him a book for reading, or requests anything else, and is caught doing this, he shall be rebuked according to the order of the monastery.

### CLXXXIV

Whoever wishes to remain—or, according to another reading, “to live”—without stain and without contempt in the house to which he has been assigned must observe before God everything that has been prescribed.

### CLXXXV

Whatever is necessary in the monastery or on the farm, if the Provost of the house is occupied, the second-in-command shall carry out.

[Note: Formerly the text read otherwise: “The Provost also shall carry out what has not been requested.” Statius read *implicatus*—“entangled”—instead of *non postulatus*—“not requested.”]

### CLXXXVI

To perform the six evening prayers according to the example of the greater assembly, in which all the brothers gather together, is a matter of the greatest delight. They are performed so easily that they carry no burden—and perhaps, “so that weariness may arise from the burden.”

### CLXXXVII

If someone comes from outside and is suffering from the heat while the other brothers are celebrating the prayer, he shall not be compelled to go if he cannot.

[Variant: “while the other brothers have celebrated the prayer.”]

### CLXXXVIII

When the Provosts of the houses teach the brothers about the conduct of a holy life, no one shall be absent without the gravest necessity.

[Note: The earlier text also had “and the gravest illness”; and immediately afterward: “and whoever of the brothers is sent,” etc.]

### CLXXXIX

The superiors who are sent outside with the brothers shall have the authority of Provosts for as long as they are there. Everything shall be governed—or, according to another reading, “carried out”—according to their judgment, and they shall teach the brothers for the appointed days. If some dispute should perhaps arise among them, the superiors themselves shall hear and decide the matter, and shall rebuke the one deserving blame, so that at their command they may immediately restore peace among themselves with a full heart.

### CXC

If one of the brothers is troubled against the Provost of his house, or if the Provost himself has some complaint against a brother, brothers of proven conduct and faith must hear them and judge between them. If the Father of the monastery is absent or has gone somewhere, they shall first await him. But if they see that he is remaining away for a longer time, they shall then hear the case between the Provost and the brother, lest greater sorrow arise from a judgment long suspended. The Provost, the one subject to him, and those who hear the case shall do everything according to the fear of God and shall give no occasion for discord in anything.

### CXCI

Therefore, those who desire to be of one mind and have resolved to live with a common spirit should serve the counsels of their superiors. Whatever proceeds from the counsels of the Fathers, let them do.

### CXCII — Concerning small garments

If anyone possesses more of the things that have been prescribed, without the permission of his superior, he shall hand them over to the keeper of the cell and shall have no authority to enter or request them; instead, they shall be subject to the discretion of the Provost and his second-in-command.

[Variant: Earlier editions more correctly read “without the permission of the superior.”]

### CXCIII — Concerning the discipline of girls

No one shall go to visit them, etc.

[Note: Holstenius placed the remainder of this chapter elsewhere, among the Rules for Virgins, on the authority of a manuscript which does not recognize it as belonging among the precepts of Saint Pachomius.]

### CXCIV

Whoever neglects any of these commands, without any doubt through negligence and contempt, shall perform penance, so that we may be able to possess the kingdoms of heaven.

# Admonitions of Saint Pachomius

[Col. 0085]

Honor God, and you will prosper. Remember the groans that the saints endured. Let us become of one mind, remaining in the calling to which we have been called; caring for everyone, so that we may be able to complete the life we have undertaken and may earn the completion of our course of formation in a manner pleasing to God. Let us not be found like those who rejoice in vain and fleeting things; lest our mind, abandoning the straight line of the right path, fall into sin and be deprived of eternal hope.

For in understanding it is supremely good to know the will of God. The person who obeys the truth is made superior to all. For it is worse than all evils to resist God’s law and yield to one’s own will. Whoever fulfills his own will shall be deprived of divine knowledge; nor, by fulfilling his own will, will he be able to walk in the way of the saints. At the end he will find destruction and lamentation.

Now, therefore, is the time to please the Lord, because salvation is acquired in a time of tribulation. Let us not retain the confidence of faith only in a time of joy and then withdraw from it in a time of tribulation. For it is written: “If you make a vow to the Lord, do not delay in fulfilling it” (Eccles. V), and in tribulation do not fail; rather, be patient and beseech the Lord.

The fullness of steadfast faith will be bestowed by God—the faith that the prophets acquired through the Holy Spirit and in which the apostles were also strengthened. For faith they endured various tribulations of persecution and reached the promised rewards. Knowing this, let us not be carried away, deceived by the seduction of errors; rather, let us remain firm and immovable, restraining by constant remembrance of the divine law the wanderings of our thoughts, which boil up like waters. Through that law, destroying the law of carnal desire, may we be able to seek everything that is pleasing to God.

May we be guarded unharmed from worldly cares and from every kind of exaltation, which is the worst madness, worse than all evils. Always keeping the Lord before our eyes, let us remember the passion and death of his cross, through whom we were redeemed and brought to life. Let us therefore hate the world and everything that is in it; let us also hate every bodily rest. Let us renounce this life, so that we may be able to live for God.

[Col. 0086D]

Therefore, dearest ones, let us remember our profession and how we promised to serve God; for this very thing will be required of us on the day of judgment. Let us hunger, thirst, endure nakedness, keep watch, and, occupied with psalms and prayers, pour out tears while groaning from the depths of our hearts. Let us test ourselves by careful examination, to see whether in any respect we may deserve to be found worthy of God because of his immense mercy. Let us not flee the anguish of tribulation, so that we may attain the rest of the Lord’s consolation and may deserve to receive the rest of immortal and eternal life.

# Letters and Mystical Sayings of the Holy Fathers Pachomius and Theodore

[Note: Concerning these letters, Gennadius says in chapter 7: “Pachomius wrote letters to the fellow Provosts of his office, in which he enclosed an Alphabet covered with mystical mysteries, exceeding the understanding of ordinary human usage; I believe it was revealed only to those endowed with grace or merit. One letter was to Abbot Syrus, and one to Abbot Cornelius. He wrote one letter to the Provosts of all the monasteries, so that, gathered into one ancient monastery called *Baum* in the Egyptian language, they might celebrate the day of Easter as though by an eternal law. Similarly, he wrote one letter concerning the day of remission, which is observed in August, so that the Provosts might gather together; and one letter to the brothers who had been sent outside the monastery to work.”]

## Letter of Our Father Pachomius to the holy man Cornelius, Father of the monastery of Mochanseos

In this letter he speaks according to the language that had been delivered to both of them by the Angel, whose sound we heard but whose powers and meaning we cannot understand.

### I

The wise God, the good God without any pretext, the God without any complaint, has given rest to your spirit; and you, give rest to your soul, so that Zion may rejoice in the days of her birth. Perform the work of Iota, which in ancient days was called Y; and place Delta before your eyes, so that it may be well with your soul.

Ro stretched out his hand to reach you; that is Iota: this is the tomb of your chamber. Sing Ω yourself, lest the most shameless age sing Ω to you. Let it rejoice with you, lest you rejoice with the most brazen age.

Remember Heta; do not forget the Kalends, which are the days of your poverty and your bed. Take for yourself Iota, which is the chief among them; for there was no Lambda in Heta, and therefore you were nourished without garments.

Return to the Kalends, which are Xi. From Y the princes of the tribes prepared wagons for the tabernacle and offered them joyfully, with every gift and complete gladness. And you, as a wise person, recognize the hair of your head on the way, so that grace may come upon those things that belong to the days of your innocence.

Are not the Kalends Tau? Heta is Passover. In all these things do not forget Simma, which is indeed called Simma but has communion with Ro: he gave him his portion so that he might become rich in Ω.

The letters of this Letter are written as Delta and Iota. Greet the head, the feet, the hands, the eyes, and the remaining parts of your spirit, which are Alpha.

## Letter of Our Father Pachomius to Father Syrus of the monastery

He too had received, together with Pachomius and Cornelius, the grace of the angelic language.

### II

Remember what I wrote to you: Y, in the Letter written because of Tau; and remember, and write Ni, because of what is written as Simma. Is Xi not Y, which is changed into Kappa? In all these things remember, and write Ni and Iota, so that Alpha may be beautifully written for the grace of those on high.

Is Moe not Y and Kappa? Is Kappa not Tau? Open your mouth and lift your face, so that your eyes may see and you may be able to read what has been written. Pay close attention, and beware lest you write Delta over Phi, your days grow old, and your waters diminish. Remember and write Theta and Ro, so that Ro may be written well.

## Letter of Our Father Pachomius to Father Cornelius of the monastery called Mochanseos

### III

Honor the Lord, and you will be strengthened. Remember the groans of the saints. Let Simma and Phi be made: let your house be ordered according to your years, according to the examples of the saints—not in temporal foods, nor in any likeness of the things that are seen in heaven or on earth.

Have Ω, so that you may be able to meet God on the day of visitation, freed from Martha’s rebuke. Prepare your house according to its boundaries. Observe Theta, lest you be liable to the rebuke of the one to whom it was said: “Give an account of your stewardship” (Luke XVI); or of the one who ate and drank with drunkards when he refused to dig and would not give food to his fellow servants at the proper time (Matt. XXIV).

For this reason they repaid him, because he had forgotten God’s law and had despised visiting the sick. And therefore he began to drift and to lack bread, imitating the most self-confident and arrogant people, who did not wish to make the house Hi.

Man, understand what is being said, because the Lord’s battle is in their hands, and it was entrusted to them to rule their flesh and make it stand—if perhaps they might escape Daniel’s rebuke, Esau’s ruin, Moab’s hardness, Ishmael’s apostasy, and the allurements of satiety and the belly, because they savored the things that are upon the earth.

A person’s abundance is his wisdom. O man, submit your heart to discipline, lest through your contempt and negligence you multiply the dead because of the error of your heart. O man, do not despise visible things. A hired man is not a shepherd; in darkness foxes eat.

Hold the sword of your glory; recognize the breastplate of righteousness; and do not despise the dwelling-place of wisdom. Make for yourself little bags that will not grow old, so that you may be able to put your hand into the hole of an asp.

Do not become drunk with wine, from which innumerable destructions arise and people walk naked upon the earth. Consider that the law was given concerning a menstruating woman, so that she should be cast outside the camp; for her paths are paved with thorns. Poverty humbles a man, and the house drips where hands are idle.

Do not grow weak from the blows of the woods—Tau and Ro. The madness of the belly is worse than all evils. The error of the eyes diminishes the prudence of the wise. The wise man fails because of the desire of the flesh in the flesh, so that blood is mingled with blood.

All you who are fellow workers with God, do not lose your glory. Know above all that if you are in Alpha, God will agree with you. But when you have agreed with God, in whom your course lies, you will not be able to rejoice in every vain thing; if you care for it, your prudence will be turned into folly.

A drunk person cannot help another drunk person. How will one who is astray show the way to another who is astray? Woe to the one who wishes to use him as a guide. For the blind will lead the blind into a pit.

Wisdom is among the saints, and in them the will of God is found—not in those who oppose God. Those who say, “God is in us,” will have their joy turned into mourning. For they did not know the mystery of God, nor did they find the way of the servants in which they should work. They were scourged and did not grieve; they were deceived and did not understand.

In all these things, O man of God, return to what is on high; that is, to the knowledge of wisdom. It is written, “You shall not covet” (Exod. XX), and again, “You shall not become drunk.” Desire does not concern only one thing.

The sinner is praised in the works of his hands. It was said also to others: “What kind of house will you build for me?” (Isa. LXVI)—those who for forty years heard the word of God but did not offer him sacrifices, nor fast for him for seventy years. Their heart was after idols, and they did not wish to be free for God, who said: “Be still and know that I am God” (Ps. XLV); and to this day they are not free for God!

It is said to you, man: “Why do you love vanity?” (Ps. IV). Or is your heart weighed down? Cain worked the ground in order to offer sacrifices to God and built a city, but he did all these things not according to the knowledge that pleases God.

Noah and his entire household were saved in the ark from the shipwreck of the world. Abraham was rich. Isaac left the blessing to Jacob. Jacob himself understood whom he ought to love, and they held his blessing as though it were a law.

Joseph was a helper to his people because he fled sin and detested pleasure. He showed his descendants that God would visit them, revealed the mysteries of future things, and left behind a memorial of his wisdom.

Afterward Moses arose. He conquered the allurements of the world, regarded riches as nothing, and showed that the wisdom of the Egyptians was foolish. Therefore Jesus ministered to him, having understood their teaching, and he had Caleb as his companion.

Foolish people did not understand these things, and therefore they called light darkness. God gave his ordinances so that the people might walk in them; but in all these things they did not find their heart, nor did they conduct themselves according to God’s commandments. Rather, they were free for their own desires and not for the works of God.

O man, how long will you not hear the one saying to you: “Be still and know that I am God” (Ps. XLV), while each person follows the thoughts of his own soul? Have you not visited the sick? Why will you die? Why do you run toward the snare?

These are the life-giving precepts that the saints received, so that they might conduct themselves in them, think of nothing else, and perform works worthy of immortality. The birds of the sky neither sow nor reap, and God has given them the power to seize from every kind of fruit and to live without payment.

The unjust and most wicked person who desires the property of others is an imitator of the worst birds: he seizes and eats what is not his. We must avoid such people, understand the parables, and not be robbers and unjust; rather, we must imitate our superiors, who pleased the Lord and rebuked Adam because he ate at Eve’s persuasion.

Before he ate, he had given names to all things, and even now they are called by their own names. But after he ate, he was expelled from paradise, worked the ground, and fathered Cain and Abel, who grew up and worked according to their own will.

Abel’s work pleased God more than Cain’s because he offered God what was chosen and foremost. Cain, on the contrary, offered God whatever was inferior. They went before as examples of the human race.

All who offer what is chosen to God are like Abel; those who offer what is inferior are compared with Cain’s works, with the one who mocked his father and reported his nakedness to his brothers, and with the one who built a tower in the plain of Shinar, forgetting the mercy of God, by whom he had been saved in the ark and delivered from the flood, and by whom his fathers had been blessed.

In a kind of fury they urged their companions, saying: “Come, let us quarry stones and cut down sycamores and cedars, and let us make a tower for ourselves,” without considering the punishment of the tower of Chalanne.

[Note: The author understands Chalanne—thought to be the same city as Ctesiphon on the Tigris—as the place where the Babylonian tower was built. After Eusebius, Jerome and many Greek writers generally support this view, on the basis of the passage in Isaiah X according to the Septuagint: “The region above Babylon and Chalanne, where the tower was built.” These words, however, are absent from the Latin manuscripts.]

Consider how God divided the languages of those who wished to build a tower of pride reaching to heaven and who were leaving the eastern region, because they had forgotten the law of God, which they had received in their hearts.

Now, therefore, take heed and understand the punishment of the tower. Though it was high, it could not reach heaven; and “not one stone will be left upon another” in the temple where the impiety of the Pharisees was assembled against Christ. It is written: “This generation will not pass away until all these things take place” (Luke XXI).

[Note: The Vulgate, and likewise the Greek text, has *αὐτή*—“it.”]

Now is the time for us to work for the Lord, because our salvation is found in the time of distress, if we are able to tread in his footsteps and always say: “May the Lord be magnified by those who love his salvation” (Ps. XXXIX). And again: “But I will hope in you always” (Ps. LXX).

For it is not faith if it exists only in a time of joy and fails in a time of tribulation. It is written: “Whatever proceeds from your mouth, take care to do” (Deut. XXIII). And again: “If you make a vow to the Lord, do not delay in fulfilling it, lest the Lord require it of you and it become sin for you.”

Therefore, if you have said, “But I will hope in you always,” and have made this promise, fulfill it in deed, so that in tribulation also you may merit salvation from the Lord.

Remember what is written: “Do not fail, and guard my counsel and knowledge, so that your soul may live” (Prov. III). Whoever guards the commandment of the law preserves his soul.

It is written: “The shadow of death covered us, and we did not forget the name of our God. If we spread out our hands to a foreign god” (Ps. XLIII). And again: “The snares of death surrounded me; the dangers of hell found me. I found tribulation and sorrow. In all these things our heart did not turn back, but I called upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. XVII).

Another believer speaks with the firmest heart: “I will not fear the thousands of people surrounding me” (Ps. III). He says this because he has confidence in God.

Son, do not fail; raise up your friend, for whom you gave your pledge, knowing that all nations are like shoots from a fire, like light stubble carried here and there by a swift breeze, and like dust swept up by a whirlwind.

Know what has been written for you: when you see horse and rider and an uncountable multitude, do not fear in your heart; rather, remember the Lord your God, who gave you strength to conquer in battle, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. II).

If you have heard the voice of God saying, “I fill heaven and earth,” you will not fear, but will say: “Our Lord is in heaven above and upon the earth below.” Do not hear the words: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” Instead, you will answer again: “If the Lord had not been with us when people rose against us, they might have swallowed us alive.”

Often they fought against you from your youth, and you bore the yoke of faith from your childhood. Your back was not struck by Egyptian burdens, nor did your hands serve at the basket, because you loved spiritual circumcision, which gave occasion for the salvation of your soul.

In brief, you have heard: there is great danger for a person while the new wine is fermenting, lest it boil over.

## Letter of Our Father Pachomius to Father Syrus of the monastery of Chnum and to John, Provost of the same house

### IV

We passed by you and, because of excessive haste, could not discuss the divine word with you; therefore we speak now through a letter.

Strive with all your strength to fulfill the custom of the monastery and to do what has been prescribed, lest you prepare yourself for the correction of the future and be condemned to the bonds of sins, and be offered to God because of negligence—not only your own, but also that of the brothers who are with you and work alongside you, knowing that what he gave us we have faithfully handed on to them.

Remember also the ministry and labor of the saints, and your friend, who came to know the will of God, so that they too may become co-heirs of the same promise and may have from God the immortal faith created through the spirit of the prophets and strengthened by the apostles. They endured every distress and persecution for it. For they believed in his promise and therefore prepared for themselves the fragrance of a good odor.

Let us therefore consider those to whom God has granted authority, to see whether we may perhaps deserve to serve them and adhere to their teaching, having abandoned all pride and sin, resisting with the greatest strength Alpha, which works without fear in bodies.

For death has been swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. XV). How, then, are we again weak in the present time, knowing that the Church has been established and must be directed toward the good, just as he foretold to you?

You know that the axe must not boast without the one who cuts with it, and that the Scriptures teach us to have a response concerning death (2 Cor. II), which, if we consume it, saves our soul.

Destruction is not to be feared in the place of our pilgrimage; rather, we must fight so that we may be able to have peace with those who keep God’s ordinances.

Heta, if you gain the whole world and have hostility against God, what benefit is there? Therefore it is fitting that we should at last understand what is being said to us, knowing that the world and its desires are passing away.

Watch and see how you walk. We know that death comes upon the uneducated. And do not understand the times in which there is error and seduction.

Consider the hours and moments, and the spans of the months by whose course human life rolls onward. By their number it is known how long each person has lived, so that they may gather their strength, fill their storehouses from it, prepare seed for future harvests, and so that at the time of harvest they may find the labors of cultivation, and possess what is necessary before God and all people, having overcome the fear of death.

When the world has passed away, let them not celebrate feast days in old garments.

Cities have been destroyed and filled with foreigners who, being impious, do not enter wisely into counsel. Water flowed in the desert, and beasts and birds rejoiced. The wise and temperate person will not anoint himself with perfume that has been ruined by dying flies and that has been compounded for the sons of the field.

Therefore we must keep watch and provide with every care for future stones, so that we are not put to shame when the times of refreshment come, and so that we are not found subject to slavery, but may be a new lump of dough, knowing that beauty is with us.

The divine word also says elsewhere: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. XLIX). Therefore let us not be carried about by every wind of doctrine, because the time has come for the saints to receive the kingdom.

Zion stretched out her hands, and there is no one to comfort her. Young men have grown weak beneath blows of wood, scattering the waters of their journey.

The myrmecoleon perished because it had no food (Job IV). Whoever shares with a thief hates his own soul. Avoid profane and novel doctrines. Let the stranger be among you as one born among you.

He killed their vines with hail and their sycamores with frost (Ps. LXXVII). An intelligent servant is acceptable to the king. You have found honey; eat what is sufficient, lest you become filled and vomit it up.

Remember judgment, mercy, and faith: judgment, by which inhabited regions are made secure; mercy, through which God is glorified; and faith, which is the foundation of the dead and the living, so that through this we may be able to possess hope.

Fight and strive, and so must the brothers who are with you, because I have written to you in figures and parables, so that you may seek them wisely, following the footsteps of the saints and not falling under God’s judgment, instructed by his words.

Let the winter of the present age not prevent us from walking; rather, let us always and without ceasing perform God’s righteousness, remembering that testimony: “Until the winter passes and the rain departs and withdraws” (Song II).

May God be our helper in peace, whose generosity has no measure, and may that peace be in our houses until the evening time passes.

I have written all these things to you so that, though laboring now, you may be able to have rest in the future.

## Letter of Our Father Pachomius to All the Monasteries

That all the brothers may gather in the greater monastery called Baum during the days of Easter, and that there may be one solemn celebration for all.

V. You ought to undertake the care of gathering your prudence, so that your door may be open before you depart from this world. When a poor man eats, he eats according to the measure of his poverty. I told you this so that you might know the hours and seasons of your youth, and not be anxious about the house, which is your prepared hunting-ground. And when you come to us, take care to provide a bed for the sick, so that you may spread it for him and not lack bread. If you can find a mattress or a pillow for the head, so that the weak may rest, then the memorial written for us may be fulfilled: “But if anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. V). “Gith is beaten out with a rod, and cumin is eaten with bread” (Isa. XXVII). If you have touched the hair of your head and found the ointment of your beard, which descends even to the fringe of your garments, you will be able to fulfill everything that has been written for you. We read elsewhere: “Let not your eyes fail; for your reward is more vigorous for your works.” Therefore let your eyes flow with water, and let your tears stream day and night, without failing.

I want you to be like those who did not know their right hand from their left. Keep watch, and bend your bows. “For the adversaries have bent their bow: a bitter thing” (Ps. LXIII). Remember that the saints open their door to everyone who passes by. We are commanded to enter our room and shut the door, and not be carried about by every wind. Therefore we must pay closer attention, lest we be swallowed up in seasons of goodness, but imitate those times which existed before the Flood, when each of the righteous pleased God with all his household and children, and no sin was found in them.

But afterward, when iniquity increased and the whole earth clung to the vices of the flesh, they offended God. In their condemnation, Noah alone, with his household and children, was saved when the Flood inundated the earth; and while the world was perishing, he held the rudder of righteousness and was overcome by no storm of sinners. The man who had mocked him and reported his nakedness to his brothers was cursed together with his offspring, and at that time what is written was fulfilled: “He who dishonors the righteous sins” (Prov. XVII).

And again: “Cursed is he who curses his father and mother” (Exod. XXI), as Esau despised his parents. Therefore it is written of him: “Let there be no fornicator or profane person, such as Esau” (Heb. XIII). Through Rebecca’s diligence it came about that he did not obtain the blessing or receive the garment of the firstborn, since he had offended his parents. They, returning his treatment and provoking his pride to emulate a good work, clothed Jacob in his garments. He did not deserve to use the garments of those whom, proud and harsh, he neglected. For that reason they did not divide their possessions among his sons, but gave everything to Jacob, who dwelt innocently in the house and obeyed their commands.

Solomon also speaks of Esau: “An undisciplined son is headed for destruction.” And Moses, with the same meaning, says: “Cursed is the man who curses his father or mother” (Exod. XXI). Again Solomon says: “Nothing good will come to a deceitful son” (Prov. XIV). Thus he lost the blessing and was deprived of his paternal inheritance.

What shall I say of Adam, who from the beginning of the human race went before us as an example of disobedience and contempt? Dominion over all the beasts of the earth had been given to him, just as the firstborn are commanded to receive a double portion of everything. But after he despised God’s command, he not only lost his dominion; he was also expelled from the place he had received as a dwelling, like a fornicator expelled from the Church and deprived of his glory. All that he suffered will be endured by those who despise God’s commands, and those who walk in pride will experience what is written: “He spoke, and the earth devoured them” (Num. XVI).

We, however, should imitate the example of the righteous man who wisely preserved his household and, when the pride of the giants was struck down, was preserved through humility. It is no wonder that he, his children, and their wives were preserved from the whole human race, since even the beasts and birds escaped death and were freed through obedience. Noah sent a dove from the ark. Obeying the will of the one who sent it, it went out and returned, and by its obedience condemned contemptuous human beings, because a bird obeyed the righteous man while human beings did not obey God. All the beasts and every living creature were likewise delivered through obedience. And because they were such, he offered sacrifices from them to God.

This history teaches us what things are offered in sacrifice to God [variant: “sacrifices”]; and if they are obedient to his command, they are rescued from the snares of the devil and enjoy his blessings—not according to their own works of righteousness, but according to his mercy, through which we have all drawn near to him. Knowing what is to come, let us join ourselves to one another in love, so that we may escape the sentence of God that hangs over us.

Do not be provoked to anger by anyone, lest he perhaps die and you be left bound, and all his sorrow be transferred to your soul, and God pour out his anger upon you because you have poured out your fury upon your brother. Do not forget God’s commandments, lest it be said of you: “They turned their backs to me and not their faces, and in the time of their affliction they will say, ‘Rise and save us’” (Jer. II). And he himself will answer: “I will rebuke their delights, and I will not make them reach the Pasch to which they are summoned.”

Let us labor, bearing one another’s burdens, just as Christ bore our infirmities in his body and did not fail. If Christ is our teacher, let us be his imitators and bear his reproaches, lest in the time to come we be separated from our brothers who have suffered tribulations. Others have also suffered—those who were unwilling to devote themselves to virtues but to vices. Our judge and witness is God, who sees everything from heaven and on the day of visitation will repay each according to his works. Let all follow the footsteps of his saints, whose commands we too ought to hear. I have spoken to you through my weakness.

**95–96. LETTER OF OUR FATHER PACHOMIUS to Syrus, father of the monastery called Chnum, and to John, superior in that same monastery of one house.**

VI. I want you to understand the letters that you wrote to me and which I wrote back to you, and how it is necessary to know all the elements of the spiritual Alphabet. Write Moe above Heta and Theta, and write Zeta above Xi; and Moe, Lambda, and Iota. When you have completed these letters in reading, write them down for yourselves, so that you may understand the mysteries of the letters. Do not write Moe above Xi, Eta, and Hi; rather, write Zeta above Xi, and Moe above Heta and Theta.

As soon as I received your letters, I wrote back, and I too answered the sacred mysteries. For I noticed that Heta and Theta were the limits of your letter; therefore I also agreed with the same meaning and words, lest I should appear unequal to your negligence and you should suffer some loss through us. I therefore wrote to you Simma Phi; write back Chi. Thus, in these days, we do not write Theta Moe.

And do not say: “We can write N, Heta, Phi, Labda, OYYOYY, Labda, Iota, Labda.” Behold, I have written to you Xi, whole and complete in circles. You too write Xi and Phi, so that you may be able to write Simma Moe. Behold, Theta was written earlier. Let it suffice for you to take care of Kappa and Tau.

But if you are going to depart, we have written Hi to you, because of your labor, so that you may exercise every care before you set out. For we have the same concern as you, and we have not written Kappa and Tau. I wrote to you by name; therefore, when you see Kappa and Tau written, write back Zeta. When you see Simma and Phi, write back Moe. When you see Labda, Iota, Labda, write back Xi. When you see YOYY Kappa, Ro—for we found it written—while we wrote Simma Phi, take care.

For in these days this is written: Ro, “be concerned.” These letters are called in Egyptian Orez and Thei. For we found written the letters which are called in Egyptian Bei and Thei. Therefore take care of Hi, and write Alpha, because I gave you that in place of Hi. Write also Simma, because Tau and Delta are written, so that you may be able to reach us.

Take care not to forget to write Psi above Kappa, because it was written earlier, and Ro was written before it; and do not perhaps say that Theta and part of Xi have been written. Therefore we write the whole as Beta, lest you say that Gamma has been written.

In every letter that I have written to you there is mention of your sitting and of your resurrection, and of the shadow of the outer wall, which is outside the wall. The fragrance of your wisdom has reached us and compelled us to write these things to you. And you, as wise men, understand what I have written to you, and show yourselves to be as my speech has chosen to describe you.

**LETTER OF OUR FATHER PACHOMIUS to all the monasteries, so that all the heads of the monasteries and the superiors of the houses may assemble in the monastery called Baum on the twentieth day of the month which the Egyptians call Mesore [Latin: August], so that the remission of all sins and works may properly be completed.**

VII. The time is near for you to come together, according to the former custom and the ancient observance, so that the remission of all things may be duly celebrated and you may come to know one another; so that each may, according to the Gospel command, forgive his brothers their debts, as well as their sorrows and quarrels; and if there is any dispute, let it be driven away from the choir of the saints.

Let them free their hearts through the fear of God; and when falsehood has been driven away, let truth rule. When wars have ceased, let the tranquillity of peace return, and may you be able to walk in it before God and human beings. May you all love one another equally; may you serve God and concord, and not varied lusts, the error of your eyes, the deceits of swelling knowledge, and the vices of the flesh.

From these arise schisms, contempt for God’s law, contention, evil thoughts which, boiling with the fire of anger, eventually burst forth and foam over into bodily pleasures. For this reason the law of God was written, so that the laws and rights of the bodies may be dissolved, and those who walk in their lusts may be ashamed; and so that at last they may return to God and, spurning temporal things, seek eternal ones.

Let them be prepared for the inheritance of the saints, who despised the present life for the life of the age to come; for wickedness, hoping for kindness; for tumult and discord, peace and concord; for adoption by the flesh, service to God. Let them seek those things which please his will, overcoming the impulses of the flesh.

For it is written: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses” (Matt. VI). And again: “Let each forgive his brothers from his heart.” And again: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Matt. XVIII). And further: “Do good to those who hate you” (Luke VI). And elsewhere: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Matt. V). And this: “Do not say, ‘Avenge me against my enemy’” (Luke XVIII). And elsewhere: “Not returning evil for evil” (1 Pet. III). And again: “Providing good things before all human beings” (Rom. XII). And this: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “Be kind to one another, doing good to all” (Eph. IV). And again: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; pray for those who persecute you” (Luke VI).

Let us therefore consider, dearly beloved brothers, by how many testimonies the faithful person is bound by God so that he may not sin—if only he is willing to hear his law, incline his ear to his commands, open his eyes, and direct his heart, so that he may fulfill what is said.

For there are many who indeed desire good things, seek God with tears, and groan day and night; but, deceived by the desires of their eyes and overcome by the ticklings of the flesh, they have slept amid groaning and anguish of heart because they could not rule their flesh or restrain the incitements of their seething thoughts, pursuing fleeting and empty things instead of what is firm and everlasting.

They desire the law, but by their deeds they destroy God’s will. They judge things true, yet they are overcome by lies. Therefore, according to the sayings of the prophets, they groan and continually waver in terror until they fail; they waste away in their ways and sleep in their sorrows. But those who are truly righteous and possess peace within themselves enjoy everlasting joy.

**LETTER OF OUR FATHER PACHOMIUS to the brothers who sheared goats in the desert, from whose hair cilicia are woven.**

VIII. God seeks those who love him. Just as he found Israel like a grape in the desert and like an early fig, so Jacob too was found in Mesopotamia when he wandered like a grape in solitude, and Joseph in Egypt like an early fig. God recognized him among all his brothers and gave him authority after many hardships.

We ought to imitate him, because he conquered his flesh, overthrew sin, and trampled underfoot the snares of his eyes. He did not pursue the fullness of his belly, so that he might preserve his holy soul for God, become a temple of the Holy Spirit, and exchange captivity for freedom. God will not forget those who fear him and do his righteousness.

Thus also that young man, placed at the slippery age of life, whom the blandishments of the flesh did not conquer, overcame bonds and prisons and pleased God in a place of confinement. Let us therefore trust that God is with us in the desert, and let his remembrance always be in our heart. Let us preserve our holy flesh and soul in the desert, just as Joseph preserved himself in captivity, so that God may remember us and be with us to the end.

**WORDS BY LETTERS OF OUR FATHER PACHOMIUS, in a hidden language, concerning things that are to come.**

IX. **ΑΩ.** The ages have boiled over in evil, which is Delta. **ΒΥ.** The completed fruit is on the lips, which is Tau. **ΙΧ.** God has made me forget my poverty in my house, from the head of the mountains to their summit, which is **ΡΟ**. **ΛΦ.** Because of the widow’s drowsiness and the glory of the poor, which is **ΟΥ**. **ΕΥ.** The mountains heard the joy of the earth, which is **ΞΞΙ**. The hidden earth was without price, which is **Ν**. **ΝϹ.** They will be level before the eyes until evening, **Ι**. **ΕΡ.** Do you suppose they will look toward the well, which is **Π**. **ΙΥ.** They drank what was hidden in joy, which is Iota. **ΡΟ.** The spoils of the earth were made without blood. **ΝΑΞ.** The depths of the abyss were made in the grief of the heart, which is **ΞΕ**. **ΗΝ.** The hidden ones fled without fear, which is **ΟΑΩ**.

Who knows whether he will return and repent—God? **ΤΒΨ.** Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult. **ΘΙΧ.** Dan awaits the salvation of God. **ΟΑΦ.** “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” **ΒΙ ΕΥ.** Blessed is God; he has given food to those who fear him. **ΩΚΖΤ.** The fruit of my mouth has become sweet upon my lips. **ΙΝϹ.** The Lord gives me a disciplined tongue. **ΛΘΡ.** “I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the Lord.” **ΙΩ.** “He who enters through me will be saved.” **ΤΚΟ.** The judgment of the Lord is sought for his people—Damascus. **ΟΛΖ.** Because God has had mercy on Israel and consoled the humble of his people. **ΜΝ.** As cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a distant land. **ΘΡΝΙΝΖΟΡΙΠ.**

**WORDS SPOKEN BY OUR FATHER PACHOMIUS, in a vision instructing the brothers in the monastery of Mochansi concerning what would befall them; and as he spoke and discoursed in the spirit, the brothers recorded what the heads of the monasteries would either do or suffer.**

**ΑΝΝΑΜΜΜΑΑΒΝΙΡΙΖΖΟΙΓΙΘ ΡΗϹΩΨΥΤΥΧ ΨΑΟΜΝΠΦΧΓΘΙΛΨΒΙΜΞΤΑΖΑΡΕΤ.**

X. The heads of the monasteries have practiced iniquity in their baskets; the sword of their destruction is beneath their armpit, which has arisen. They lie in wait at the gates of hell.

The abundance of the earth and the good things that God had bestowed upon the children of human beings said: “Come, let us scrutinize our ways and see whether we can find leaven, and put it into the mass of flour, so that it cannot rise or swell upward, but may fail through hunger.”

They prepared snares for their feet, a bow in their hands, and carried an axe upon their shoulder. They came to a man who had a saw, and he said to them: “Go and cut wood.” But they said to him: “By no means; rather, we are scrutinizing our ways and have found leaven, so that we may put it into the mass, which does not rise and cannot swell upward, but has failed through hunger.”

The man therefore called his friends, and they flayed their feet and the tips of their hands—that is, their fingers—and these flowed down upon the earth. Then the young ravens came and carried them away, made a nest there, and the ravens bred in their places; and through them the earth was inhabited.

**WORDS BY LETTERS OF OUR FATHER PACHOMIUS, in a hidden language, concerning things that are to come.**

XI. God is truthful in all things, who says **ΡΝ**: “All the streams flow into the sea,” **Κ**. The Lord looked down from heaven. **Α.** There is no longer wisdom in you. **ΜΑΝΥΤ.** The Lord is pleased with those who fear the Lord. **ϹΘΟΜ.** “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord?” **Θ.** The eyes of the wise are in their head. Patience is the pledge of the poor. **ΗΘΑΜ.** It is the joy of the righteous to execute judgment. **Ν.** A wise son is judgment. **ΦΥ.** The pain of the fool is to abandon discipline. **Τ.** Take away his garment, for the injurious man will pass away, **ΥΦ**, and he will insult others. **ϹΝ.** A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise. **ΚΜ.** How long will you look upon those who despise you and remain silent? **ΤΜΑ.** My eyes have failed while waiting for your salvation. **ϹΘ.** A wise heart understands a parable. **Τ.** We saw that Zion had stripped herself of the glory she possessed from the beginning; therefore **Ϲ** did not burn with anger.

Between the letters **ΝΥ** do not write **Ζ**, but rather write **ΑΟΑ** from what is superfluous. **ΑΙΑ.** I know that you write from yourself. In all these things remember **Α**; hasten to write **Ι**, and say that it belongs to him. Thus far **Ε** has been written. **ΙΝΩΧ.** He himself wrote **Ξ**. And if **Κ** too has been written in the same way, keep **Ο** expanded again. It is necessary for you to count, and so I write again **Α** and **ϹΗΙ**.

Place **Ω** before your eyes, so that it may be well with your soul. Remember **Ϲ**, which has returned to the Kalends, namely **ΖΘΟ ΟΥ**. Remember also and write **Ζ**, because of **Κ**, which is written—not according to what I now tell you, but because I trust that you have heard this day.

**Ρ** again stretches out its hand toward us in these days. Before your eyes our heart grieves over **Ϲ**, because it truly is **Ϲ**, and they have forgotten the Kalends.

As for what you wrote, **Α ϹΗΙ**, another before us did this same thing and said: “Behold, I send you like sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matt. X). Again we heard from **ΕΙΝΩ** that “two are grinding together; one will be taken, and the other will be left.”

[Note: Gennadius mentions several letters of this kind written by Theodore and composed in the language of the Holy Scriptures, chapter 8.]

**LETTER OF OUR FATHER THEODORE to all the monasteries, concerning Easter.**

XII. The solemnity of Unleavened Bread has drawn near, during which Easter is to be celebrated. Concerning it Moses also commanded the people departing from the land of Egypt, saying: “Eat it with all haste” (Exod. XII). The righteous king Josiah likewise celebrated Easter most diligently in his days, and his zeal is still recounted (4 Kings II). Concerning this the Apostle also speaks: “Our Passover has been sacrificed, Christ” (1 Cor. V).

Therefore let us celebrate the feast in him, as has been commanded to us. Gird your loins and put on your feet the Gospel sandals, holding staffs in your hands and burning lamps, so that we may eat the Passover with haste and ascend to Jerusalem six days before Easter, sanctifying ourselves so that we may celebrate the holy day in holiness, without malice and wickedness, in sanctity and truth, as the Apostle and our Father also commanded us—the Father from whom the life of the coenobia was founded.

Let us assemble together in peace, according to the boundaries which it is unlawful to pass, so that none of us may desire to remain in the monasteries without the arrangement of our superiors, and so that, when we have assembled, no one may come without the command of the superiors [text uncertain: *veninat*]. We too, who appear to be superiors of the brothers and to show them the rules of their way of life, must not, without grave necessity, allow them to remain at home. The Paschal gathering must not be abandoned on our account, lest we be found to empty our Father’s commands; rather, let us regard what he wrote, in our contrition, as the standard of truth. And let God be glorified, who has appointed families like sheep. Let the upright see and rejoice, and let every iniquity close its heart.

Let all of us, the council of the children of Israel, and with them those who come second, come to Easter, and let none of us be found left behind who does not fulfill the bounds of our Father. Let the stewards of the monasteries, the superiors of the houses, the whole order of the brothers, and all the members come together into one body, so that they may raise up the temple of God.

Let us assemble in peace and concord, so that we may fulfill the bounds of the saints and the rules of our Father. And let the catechumens who are in the monasteries and await the fearful remission of sins and the grace of the spiritual mystery hear from you that they ought to weep and mourn their former sins and prepare themselves for the sanctification of souls and bodies, so that they may be able to endure the Blood and Body of the Lord and Savior; even to think upon this is terrifying.

As for the other things that you ought to do, you know them very well, and there is no need to admonish you by letter: prepare yourselves at the appointed time which our Father ordained. We and all the brothers who are with us send you our most earnest greetings, and likewise the whole brotherhood that is in your monasteries.

**THE INTERPRETATION OF THE BOOK OF DIDYMUS ON THE HOLY SPIRIT BY SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON**

**NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING BOOK OF DIDYMUS ON THE HOLY SPIRIT**

Didymus of Alexandria, who displayed a remarkable achievement in that, although deprived of sight from early childhood and ignorant of the very elements of reading, he was nevertheless thoroughly trained in every branch of learning, even in those disciplines that depend most heavily upon sight, was compelled by the frequent urging of the brothers to write this book on the Holy Spirit, among the other monuments he left of his intellect, in order to refute certain opinions about the Holy Spirit which had neither been read in Scripture nor used by any of the ancient churchmen.

Jerome, who especially admired Didymus’s learning and had used him as a teacher at Alexandria, first, while living at Rome at the urging of Damasus, Roman pontiff, began to explain him in Latin words. Then, after returning to Jerusalem, he translated and published the work afresh at the urging of his brother Paulinianus.

The book is a single work, as Jerome himself indicates whenever he praises it—for example, in chapter 109 of the *Catalogue* and in Book II against Rufinus—and as all the manuscripts we have examined testify. Augustine too, in Book II of the *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 25; Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 17; and Ratramnus, who read this very version of Jerome, in *Against the Greeks*, Book II, chapter 5, call it a single book. Only through an inconvenient *periergia* (περιεργία, meddlesomeness) has it happened that, contrary to the intention of both author and translator, editors and critics down to the present day have commonly divided it into three books.

The division of the books itself is accidental and useless. For example, the third book is ordered to begin in the middle of the exposition of a prophetic passage, a fault utterly foreign to the mind of a learned writer. It can, however, conveniently be distributed into three parts or sections. First, he establishes by many arguments and testimonies that the Holy Spirit is of a nature different from that of the angels. Next, he proves that invocation of his name in baptism is also necessary, so that the person who omits it baptizes imperfectly and does not fully free the baptized person from sin. Third, he teaches that the Spirit is indivisible and impassible, *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος, consubstantial) with the Father and the Son, and endowed with the other attributes of the divine substance.

The Greek text of Didymus has perished, and Jerome’s interpretation itself perhaps removed it from the hands of learned men. Nevertheless, some appear to disparage the fidelity of the translation without sufficient caution, alleging that much was sewn on which did not proceed from the Alexandrian author, and that many other things—especially errors of the Origenist doctrine to which Didymus was attached—were purged by the translator.

I would consider very slight the force of the argument, although it is the chief one, drawn from the terms *homoousios* and *anomoousios* (ἀνομοούσιος, dissimilar in substance), from which the followers of Adamantius [Origen] strongly maintain that they recoiled. Didymus was not so bound to every individual article of Origenist teaching that he thought himself permitted nothing of his own; nor, when his Greek exemplar is missing, can it in any way be proved that he ventured nothing further. The remaining arguments brought forward on this matter are much weaker.

The period to which this translation of Jerome is to be assigned cannot be confined precisely to a single year, as is generally the case with his other treatises. It was begun at Rome in the year 384, as is perfectly clear from his preface, while Damasus was still alive; he died toward the end of that same year. Certainly Saint Doctor Jerome seems to indicate no other work of Didymus than this little treatise, which he had proposed to translate, when he says that he wished to babble a little about the Holy Spirit and dedicate the work he had begun to the pontiff of that same city.

But it does not appear to have been completed before the year 389, when, avoiding the envy of his rivals, he had withdrawn to Jerusalem and was likewise at Bethlehem with his brother Paulinianus, Paula, and Eustochium. Approximately the same year is indicated in the *Catalogue*, where he mentions this labor between the book on Hebrew Names and the homilies on Luke from Origen.

For the rest, we have corrected this edition of ours against the testimony of three manuscripts: first, one in the Vatican, no. 4945; then another exceedingly elegant manuscript which we found in the library of the Roman College of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus; and finally the Toulouse manuscript, from which Martianaeus had relegated the excerpted variant readings to the end of the book.

Among the editions published before the Erasmian collection, we frequently consulted the earlier one of 1496, without place of publication, and also the Venetian edition praised by Barthius in his *Adversaria*. We have likewise considered several of Barthius’s conjectures on this book wherever it seemed worthwhile. There are other editions of this work, which there is no time to list individually and which may readily be found in bibliographical works.

[Note: It is said that Cardinal Passionei found most of Didymus’s works in a Greek manuscript in his library, and that the distinguished Mingarelli, a canon regular at Bologna, was laboring to publish them, etc.]

**JEROME’S PREFACE TO PAULINIANUS**

[Note: Namely, to his brother; for some older books incorrectly address it to Paulinus of Nola, and add that Jerome translated the work into Latin because of the ignorance of someone who had written about the Holy Spirit.]

When I was living in Babylon [that is, Rome], and was a tenant of the purple-clad prostitute, and lived according to the rights of Roman citizens, I wished to babble a little about the Holy Spirit and dedicate the little work I had begun to the pontiff of that same city.

And behold, that pot which in Jeremiah is seen behind the staff, burning from the face of the north, began to blaze; and the Senate of the Pharisees cried out [variant: “began to cry out”]. No scribe [Note: There is considerable suspicion that the reading of this passage is corrupt. Vatican manuscript 4945 has *nullum scriba vel fictum*; the old edition of 1496 has *nullus scriba in eis fictus*. Barthius thinks it should be restored as *ut nullus scribae in eis sit ictus*, so that the meaning would be that no one attacked Jerome individually for wishing to babble something about the Holy Spirit, but that all, as soon as battle was declared, agreed to condemn his ignorance. This interpretation, however, scarcely—or rather not at all—pleases us as an emendation. Some would prefer *nullus scriba relictus*, which is equally unattractive. Therefore consider whether, instead of the two words *vel fictus*, it might be better to read the single word *velificatus*, meaning “favoring” or “eagerly complying”; for then the one clause would be elegantly opposed to the other, and the meaning would be that no one showed himself more favorable to him, but that all conspired against him. Cicero writes in a letter, “lest you be said to have spread sail for anyone,” etc. See letter 127, no. 9, concerning the disturbed school of the Pharisees.]

or pretender [reading uncertain], but the entire faction conspired against me, as though a battle of doctrines had been declared, because of my ignorance [Note: One Toulouse manuscript, in the possession of Martianus, who relegated the variant readings from it to the end of the book, has here *impetus*. The old edition reads *imperitiae convincendum factio*, etc.].

Immediately I, as though by right of return, [to] Jerusalem [Note: This is discussed more fully in the *Life*. Concerning Romulus’s hut, consult Ovid, *Fasti* III, verse 183. Prudentius, Book XI:

“May the Romulan people themselves cover the huts with fragile straw.”]

Thus they relate that Remus lived, etc.] I have returned: and after Romulus’ hut and the games of the Lupercalia, I saw Mary’s lodging and the cave of the Savior. Therefore, my brother Paulinianus [Al. Pauline], since the aforementioned Bishop Damasus, who had first urged me to undertake this work, now sleeps [Al. has fallen asleep in the Lord] in Christ, aided now by your prayers as well as those of the venerable handmaids of Christ, Paula and Eustochium [Al. exhortation], I murmur here among you in Judaea the song that I could not sing in a foreign land, considering that place far more august which gave birth to the Savior of the world than that which gave birth to a brother’s murderer. And, to acknowledge my source by its title: I preferred to become the translator of another’s work rather than, like certain people, adorn myself as a misshapen jackdaw with another’s colors.

[Col. 0104A] Some time ago I read a little book by a certain author on the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0104B] Rufinus contends in Book II of his *Apology* that St. Ambrose is attacked by insinuation, with his name suppressed, and accused of plagiarism; for this reason he launches a very serious accusation against Jerome. But it can be demonstrated by arguments that are by no means weak that this was not the holy Doctor’s intention. See the Benedictine Fathers’ Preface to Ambrose’s books *On the Holy Spirit*, p. 598.]. And, in accordance with the Comic poet’s [that is, Terence’s] judgment, from Greek goods I saw Latin things that were not good. There was nothing dialectical there, nothing manly or forceful, that might draw the reader, even unwillingly, to assent; rather, everything was flaccid, soft, polished, and beautiful, and everywhere scented with carefully selected perfumes [Note: [Col. 0104B] Perhaps *coloribus* should be restored. Certainly Rufinus read it that way long ago in Book XI.].

But my Didymus, having the eye of the bride from the *Song of Songs*, and those eyes which Jesus commanded to be raised on high so as to behold the shining harvest-fields, looks far more deeply into the distance (Matthew XIII and John IV) [Note: [Col. 0104B] Barthius understood *candelabra* quite incongruously as lampstands capable of holding candles inserted in many places. Jerome is in fact alluding to John IV, 9; explaining that passage in the cited chapter of his *Commentary on Matthew*, he says: “Blessed are the eyes which Jesus commanded to be raised aloft, so that they might see the white harvest-fields.” See Epistle 76, to Abigaus, no. 2, at the end.]. And he has restored to us the ancient custom, so that the Prophet may be called “the Seer.” Certainly, whoever reads him will recognize the thefts of the Latins and will despise the streams once he has begun to draw from the springs. He is unskilled in language [Al. but not in knowledge], expressing an apostolic man through his very speech [Al. style], in the light of his meaning as much as in the simplicity of his words [Note: [Col. 0104C] We read this thus from the Vatican manuscript and the old Venetian edition; previously it was *nomine*, as we do not deny that it is also found in Epistle 65, no. 19, where he says that beauty lies more in the force of meaning than in the flower of words. In reality, however, neither reading is entirely satisfactory. The manuscript of the Roman College of the Society of Jesus has *tam suo nomine*.].

[Col. 0103D] THE BOOK OF DIDYMUS OF ALEXANDRIA ON THE HOLY SPIRIT, TRANSLATED BY ST. JEROME [Note: [Col. 0103D] In some books it is entitled: “Of Saint Didymus, Greek monk of Alexandria.” See Epistle 71 to Lucinius, no. 5, note b.]

[Col. 0103]

[Col. 0103D] 107

### 1

We ought to attend to everything divine with reverence and intense care, but especially to what is said concerning the divinity of the [Al. Holy] Spirit—particularly since blasphemy against him is without forgiveness [Note: [Col. 0103D] Consult St. Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book [Col. 0104D] and page 611, where the meaning of unforgivable blasphemy is discussed.]—so that the punishment of the blasphemer extends not only throughout the present age but also into the future. For the Savior says that there is no forgiveness for one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, neither in this age nor in the age to come (Mark III).

Therefore, we must attend all the more carefully to what the Scriptures report concerning him, lest the error of blasphemy creep upon anyone, at least through ignorance [Note: [Col. 0104D] The Vatican manuscript, together with the older printed editions, reads: “lest someone at least,” etc.]. It would indeed have been expedient for a faithful and fearful person, one who moderated his own strength, to pass over in silence the magnitude of the present question and not draw a matter fraught with danger into his own peril. But since certain people are lifted up toward heavenly things with rashness rather than by the right path, and proclaim concerning the Holy Spirit things that are neither read in Scripture nor employed by any of the ancient ecclesiastical writers, we have been compelled to yield to the brothers’ very frequent exhortation and to confirm by Scriptural testimonies what our opinion of him is, lest ignorance of so great a doctrine deceive those who advance contrary arguments and immediately drag into the adversaries’ view those who, without careful examination, are at once drawn over to it.

### 2

The designation “Holy Spirit,” and the substance indicated by that designation itself, are wholly unknown to those who philosophize outside sacred Scripture. For both its concept and its name are found only in our writings, in the New as well as in the Old Testament. David, a man of the Old Testament who had become a participant in it, prayed that it might remain in him, saying: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm L). And God is said to have stirred up the Holy Spirit in Daniel while he was still a boy, as though it were already dwelling in him.

Moreover, in the New Testament those men who are reported to have pleased God are full of the Holy Spirit. John, sanctified while still in his mother’s womb, leaps for joy; and Jesus, rising from the dead, breathed upon the faces of the disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (Luke I). The volumes of the divine Scriptures are full of such statements, the accumulation of which I have refrained from arranging in the present work [Note: [Col. 0105D] The Tholosan manuscript reads: “It is superfluous, if it is easy to find from these,” etc.], because it is not difficult for each reader to find similar passages for himself from those we have selected.

### 3

No one should suppose that there was one Holy Spirit in the holy men before the Lord’s coming and another in the apostles and the other disciples, as though the same name applied to different substances [Note: [Col. 0105D] From the Vatican and Roman College manuscripts we have adopted *homonymum*, since previously the faulty reading was *nomina*.]. We can produce testimonies from the divine Scriptures showing that the same Spirit was in the apostles and in the prophets.
