In the Epistle that Paul writes to the Hebrews, bringing testimony from the book of the Psalms, he states that it was spoken by the Holy Spirit: “As the Holy Spirit says here: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts,’” and so forth (Hebrews III, 7, from Psalm XCIV, 8) [Note: [Col. 0105D] This article was previously absent and is also lacking in the Latin copies; Didymus, however, presses it very strongly.].

Likewise, at the end of the Acts of the Apostles, while arguing with the Jews, he says: “As the Holy Spirit spoke through the prophet Isaiah to our fathers, saying: ‘You shall indeed hear, and you shall not understand’” (Acts III). Paul did not possess one Holy Spirit and therefore write these things concerning a Spirit who had been different in the Prophets before the Lord’s coming; rather, he wrote of the Spirit of which he himself was also a participant, as were all who were carried forward in the faith of perfected virtue.

Thus, when he mentions it with the article, he testifies that it is solitary and one. He does not say simply *Πνεῦμα ἅγιον*—that is, “Holy Spirit”—but, with the addition of the article, *τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον* [Note: [Col. 0106D] We have added the second *τὸ* from the Greek exemplar; it is especially necessary both to the context and to the author’s intention.]—that is, “this Holy Spirit.”

He also recalls that Isaiah prophesied with the articulated expression *διὰ τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον*, that is, “through this Holy Spirit,” and not simply *Πνεῦμα ἅγιον* [Note: [Col. 0106D] The same manuscripts have, in the genitive case, *διὰ τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος* and shortly afterward *διὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος*. More correctly.]. Peter too, in the speech by which he persuaded those present, says: “The Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit spoke” (that is, *τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον*) “through the mouth of David concerning Judas” (Acts I, 16), showing that the same Spirit worked both in the prophets and in the apostles.

### 4

We shall treat this more fully in what follows, when we begin to say that not only was the Lord, the Word, made known to the prophets, but also the Holy Spirit, since he is possessed inseparably together with the only-begotten Son of God.

The very expression “Holy Spirit” is not an empty designation but a demonstrator of the underlying essence: associated with the Father and the Son [Al. joined to them], and wholly alien to creatures. Since creatures are divided into visible and invisible—that is, bodily and incorporeal—the Holy Spirit is not among bodily substances, being the inhabitant of souls and of perception, and the producer of speech, wisdom, and knowledge; nor is he among invisible creatures. For all these things are capable of wisdom and of the other virtues and of sanctification. But the substance of which we are now speaking produces wisdom, knowledge, and sanctification.

For no power or operation of sanctification and virtue can be found in the Holy Spirit that he receives from something external [Note: [Col. 0106D] The Tholosan manuscript, together with our manuscripts, reads, perhaps more correctly: “a power which he receives from some external operation of sanctification and virtue.”], since such a nature is mutable. The Holy Spirit, however, by the confession of all, is immutable: the sanctifier of divine knowledge, the giver of all good things, and, to put it more briefly, himself subsisting in those goods that are bestowed by the Lord.

For when Matthew and Luke describe the same passage of the Gospel, one of them says: “How much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” (Matthew V, 11), while the other says: “How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke XI, 13). From these passages it is evident that the Holy Spirit is the fullness of God’s gifts [Al. good things], and that the things administered by God do not subsist apart from him, because all the benefits received from the grace of God’s gifts flow from this source.

What is substantially good cannot be receptive of goodness from something external, since it itself bestows goodness on others [Col. 0106D] 110. Therefore, it is clear that the Holy Spirit is alien not only to bodily creatures but also to incorporeal creatures, because the other substances receive this substance of sanctification, whereas he is not merely incapable of receiving alien sanctification but is himself its giver and creator.

Finally, those who enjoy communion with him are called participants in the Holy Spirit, being sanctified by him. For it is plainly written: “And he who does insult to the Spirit of grace” (Hebrews X, 29)—without doubt referring to one who has sinned after receiving him [Note: [Col. 0107D] The text previously read incongruously and incorrectly: “it is written that he who insults the spirit of grace, in which he has been sanctified, will be punished by a grave sin.” We have corrected it on the basis of the cited manuscripts. The Tholosan manuscript agrees with our reading, although it abounds in errors in the preceding and following context.].

If, then, a person has been sanctified through communion with the Holy Spirit, it is shown that he has been a participant in him, and that the Holy Spirit is the giver of his sanctification. The Apostle also, writing to the Corinthians and listing those who will obtain the kingdom of heaven, adds: “And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified, in the name of Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians VI, 11), asserting that the Spirit of God is none other than the Holy Spirit.

Indeed, in what follows he confirms the same point, saying: “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus’; and no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians XII, 3), affirming that the Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit.

### 5

If, then, he is the sanctifier [Al. sanctification], he is shown to be a substance not mutable but immutable. The divine utterances plainly teach that only God and his only-begotten Son possess an immutable substance, while proclaiming that every created substance is changeable and mutable.

Therefore, since the substance of the Holy Spirit has been shown to be not convertible but inconvertible, he will not be consubstantial (*ὁμοούσιος*) with creation. For creation too would be immutable if it were placed with the Father and the Son, possessing the same inconvertibility.

Everything that is receptive of goodness belonging to another is separated from this substance. All creatures are of this kind. God, however, since he is good, is the source and beginning of good things; therefore he makes those to whom he imparts himself good, while he himself is not made good by another but subsists in goodness. For this reason he is capable of containing [*capabilis*], but not receptive [*capax*] [Note: [Col. 0107D] From this you can understand well in what sense Didymus says that the Holy Spirit is *capabilis* and not *capax*. If he had called God receptive of some good or virtue—say, wisdom or truth—he could have seemed to have received these from elsewhere, not to possess them from himself, and thus to be able at some point to lose what he had once acquired. He should be believed to be *capabilis* for this reason: Scripture testifies in many places that he fills the hearts and souls of the faithful. Other Fathers agree. The author of the *Altercation with Pascentius the Arian*, formerly counted among Augustine’s letters as Epistle 177, says: “Is the Father incapable of being contained, whom the Son wholly contains?” … Then, after certain intervening remarks: “He who contains all things, whom no one contains—but men, for he is wholly contained by the Son.” In the *Conflict of Arnobius and Serapion*, p. 543: “God is capable, not containable.”].

Likewise, the only-begotten Son, who is the wisdom and sanctification of the Father, is not made wise but makes others wise; he is not sanctified but sanctifies [Col. 0108A] 111. Therefore he too is *capabilis*, not *capax*.

Since an invisible creature—which it is customary to call a rational and incorporeal substance—is not *capabilis* but *capax*, for if it were *capabilis* it would not be receptive of any good, being simple and subsisting through itself, while receiving another good; it has goodness by participation, and it is to be understood not as possessing things that are possessed by others but as being possessed by those who possess other things—the Father and Son being possessed more than possessing, whereas creation possesses and is not possessed [Note: [Col. 0108D] Formerly: “Let us treat of the Holy Spirit.”].

Let us reconsider the Holy Spirit also. If he too is holy through participation in another holiness, let him be numbered among the other creatures. But if he makes holy persons capable of himself, let him be placed with the Father and the Son.

That the Holy Spirit is received by others, and does not receive others, we have expressed both here and in the book *On Sects* [Note: [Col. 0108D] He mentions that book again shortly below, where he says: “of which we have already argued abundantly in the book *On Sects*.” Heraclides also mentions it in *Paradise*, chapter 1; Jerome mentions it especially in his *Catalogue*, chapter 109, where the book is called *On Doctrines*. It was easily entitled *Περὶ Δογμάτων* (“On Doctrines”), as can be gathered from Didymus himself somewhat farther below, where he says that he has already briefly shown in the book *On Doctrines* that the Holy Spirit is Creator. Certainly it was not entitled *Περὶ Αἱρέσεως* (“On Heresy”), as some have thought. See Theodoret, *History*, Book IV, chapter 29.], insofar as we have been able; and it is very easy to support our argument from the whole of Scripture.

The blessed Apostle, writing to the Ephesians, also says: “In whom, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (Ephesians I, 13). If some are sealed with the Holy Spirit, assuming his form and appearance, the Holy Spirit is among those things that are possessed and do not possess, since those who possess him are impressed with his seal.

Writing similarly to the Corinthians, he says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed” (Ephesians IV, 30), testifying that those who had received communion with the Holy Spirit were sealed. For just as the one who takes on discipline and virtue receives its seal and figure, so to speak, into his own understanding, in accordance with the knowledge he has acquired, so the one who becomes a participant in the Holy Spirit becomes spiritual and holy through communion with him [Note: [Col. 0108D] The Tholosan manuscript reads: “becomes a spiritual participant and holy.”].

### 6

But if the Holy Spirit were one of the creatures, he would at least have a circumscribed substance, as all created things do. For although invisible creatures are not circumscribed by place and boundaries, they are nevertheless limited by the particularity of their substance.

The Holy Spirit, however, since he is in many, does not possess a circumscribed substance. When Jesus sent out the preachers of his teaching, he filled them with the Spirit; and, breathing upon their faces, he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit, and go, teach all nations” (John XX, 22), as though he were sending all of them to all nations.

For the apostles did not all travel together to all nations; rather, some went to Asia, some to Scythia, and others were dispersed among other peoples, according to the dispensation of the one whom they had with them, the Holy Spirit. So too the Lord says: “I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII, 20).

The following also agrees with this: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts I, 8). If, then, these men, stationed at the furthest boundaries of the earth for [Al. according to] the testimony of the Lord, were separated from one another by the greatest distances, while the Holy Spirit, their indwelling inhabitant, was present with them, he is shown to possess an uncircumscribed substance [Note: [Col. 0109D] The Tholosan manuscript incorrectly reads, as it does in many other places: “the substance of an uncircumscribed inhabitant.”].

The angelic power is wholly different from this. An angel who was present, for example, with an Apostle praying in Asia, could not at that same time be present with others situated in the other regions of the world. But the Holy Spirit is present not only to human beings separated from one another; he also dwells with each individual angel, principality, throne, and dominion.

And just as, by sanctifying human beings, he belongs to a nature other than theirs, so by sanctifying the other creatures he is other than their substance, since every creature is made holy not from its own substance but through communion with another holiness.

### 7

The angels are indeed called holy in the Gospel, when the Savior says that the Son of Man will come in the majesty of himself and of the Father and of the holy angels (Luke IX, 29). And in the Acts of the Apostles, Cornelius is said to have received a response from a holy angel [Al. is reported to have been addressed by a holy angel] (Acts X, 22), so that he might summon Peter, Christ’s disciple, to himself.

But the angels are holy through participation in the Holy Spirit and through the indwelling of the only-begotten Son of God, who is holiness [Note: [Col. 0109D] The old edition reads: “and through the communication of the Father.”], and the communion of the Father. Concerning him the Savior says: “Holy Father” (John XVII, 11).

If, then, the angels are not holy from their own substance but from participation in the Holy Trinity, it is shown that the angels’ substance is other than the Trinity. For just as the sanctifying Father is other than those who are sanctified, and the Son is other than those whom he makes holy, so the Holy Spirit is of another substance than those whom he sanctifies through his gift.

But if heretics propose that angels are holy by the nature of their creation, they are consequently forced to say that they are *ὁμοούσιοι*—of the same substance—with the Trinity, and that according to their substance they are holy immutably. If, to avoid this, they say that angels are of one nature with the other creatures but do not possess the same holiness as human beings, they will necessarily be driven to say that human beings are of a much better substance: for human beings possess holiness through communion with the Trinity, while angels, holy by their own nature, are alien to it [Note: [Col. 0109D] Barthius says: “They will necessarily be driven to this conclusion,” etc.].

But it is the desire of perfected human beings, those advancing toward the consummation of holiness, to become equal to the angels [Note: [Col. 0109D] Origen attributes one and the same nature to angels and human beings, at least to those who have attained the summit of holiness. Consider how far Didymus, who is often said to have adopted Origenist doctrines, departs from that teaching. Compare also what we have noted in Volume I, in the letter to Theophilus accompanying the Synodical Letter, and in the letter to Avitus.]. For angels grant assistance to human beings, not human beings to angels: they minister salvation to them and announce to them the more abundant benefits of God [Note: [Col. 0110D] The Vatican manuscript, together with the ancient edition, reads: “announcing to them its giver.” From this…].

From this it is clearly shown that angels are more honorable and much better than human beings, through what one might call a more genuine and fuller reception of the Trinity.

### 8

Therefore, since the Holy Spirit is other than those whom he sanctifies, he is not of one nature with the other creatures that receive him. But if he is of another nature than creatures and subsists in his own essence, he is shown to be uncreated and not made.

There are many passages of Scripture that prove without ambiguity that he is of a nature different from all created things. Certain people are also said to be full of the Holy Spirit; but no one is said, either in Scripture or in ordinary speech, to be full of a creature [Col. 0110A] 114. Scripture does not claim this for itself, nor does common speech permit one to say that someone is full of an angel, throne, or dominion. This language belongs only to the divine nature.

We do, however, say that certain people are full of virtue and discipline, as in the statement: “He was filled with the Spirit” (Exodus XXXI, 3), meaning nothing other than that they were full of perfected and complete virtue.

It is written of John: “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (Luke I, 15). Again: “Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 41). And later: “His father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 67). There is no doubt that John also prophesied.

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, concerning many believers who had gathered together, it is reported: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts II, 4). Since the Holy Spirit is capable of being shared, like wisdom and discipline, he does not possess the substance of knowledge merely in empty names; rather, through a nature that sanctifies and fills all things with good, he himself subsists as good. According to this, certain people are said to be filled with the Holy Spirit.

Thus it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with confidence” (ibid.). For just as one who is full of a discipline, possessing it perfectly, can speak about it learnedly and subtly, so those who have received the Holy Spirit completely, so as to be filled with him, speak the word of God with confidence, because the present Holy Spirit supplies a voice worthy of God.

Hence someone says with haughtiness: “Thus says the Holy Spirit.” And the Apostle says: “But be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Ephesians V, 18). In many places in the Acts of the Apostles, the Lord’s disciples are also recorded as having been full of the Holy Spirit.

“Therefore, brothers, select from among yourselves seven men who have a good testimony, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom” (Acts VI, 3). And concerning Stephen: “But being full of the Holy Spirit, he looked up into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (ibid., 5). And concerning the chosen vessel it is said: “Saul, who is also Paul, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said…” (Acts XIII, 9). And generally concerning all the believers it is recorded: “The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 52).

The presence of angels, or of any other excellent created nature, does not fill the mind and understanding, because that nature itself is filled from elsewhere. For just as one receives from the Savior’s fullness and becomes full of wisdom, virtue, righteousness, and the word of God [Note: [Col. 0111D] Two manuscripts, together with the old edition, read: “and truth.”], so the one who is full of the Holy Spirit is immediately filled with all God’s gifts: wisdom, knowledge, faith, and the other virtues.

Therefore, the one who fills all creatures that are nevertheless capable of receiving virtue and wisdom is not himself one of those whom he fills. From this it follows that he is of another substance than all creatures.

We have also said elsewhere that, in the substance of the Holy Spirit, the fullness of divine gifts is to be understood [Col. 0111B] as well.

### 9

Finally, it is impossible for anyone to obtain the grace of God unless he possesses the Holy Spirit, in whom we affirm that all God’s gifts subsist [Note: [Col. 0111D] The alternative reading is *approbantur*; shortly afterward the Tholosan manuscript has *consurgere* instead of *consistere*.].

That the one who possesses him has also perfectly obtained the word of wisdom and the other good things is demonstrated clearly by the present discussion, and we said this shortly before when we established that the Holy Spirit is the substance of God’s good things, citing the example: “The Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke XI, 13), and: “The Father will give good things to those who ask him” (Matthew V, 11).

We must not think that the Holy Spirit is divided according to substances [Al. according to substance] because he is called by a multitude of names for good things. For he is impassible, indivisible, and immutable; but according to his different operations and meanings he is called by many names of good things, because he grants his participants communion with himself not according to one and the same power, since he is suited to the benefit of each individual and fills with good things those whom he judges ought to have his presence.

Finally, Stephen—that first witness to the truth, and one worthy of his name, since *Stephanos*, Στέφανος, means “crown” in Greek and “crown” in Latin [Note: [Col. 0111D] It is well known that Stephen, Greek *Στέφανος*, is interpreted in Latin as *corona*, “crown.”]—is said to have been full of wisdom and the Holy Spirit, wisdom being understood as present in him while the Holy Spirit dwelt in him, as Scripture says: “And the apostles chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit” (Acts VI, 5).

And again: “Stephen, full of grace and power, performed wonders [Note: [Col. 0112D] The manuscripts consistently have *portenta*, “wonders.”] and great signs among the people” (ibid., 8). And concerning the same man: “They were unable to resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke” (ibid., 10).

For the blessed man, full of the Holy Spirit, also became a participant in faith, which comes from the Holy Spirit, according to the statement: “To another, faith, in the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians XII, 9). Possessing grace and power according to that same Spirit, he performed great signs and wonders among the people. He also abounded in those gifts according to the same Spirit that are called gifts and powers of healings. These too are placed among God’s gifts, which are given by the Spirit and according to the Spirit, in the First Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Corinthians.

Stephen was so full of divine grace that none of those who contradicted him or argued against him could resist the wisdom and the Spirit who spoke in him [Note: [Col. 0112D] The Vatican and Tholosan manuscripts and the old edition read: “for he was wise according to God and the Holy Spirit,” etc.]. For he was wise through the Holy Spirit.

Therefore Jesus plainly declares to his disciples: “When you are brought before rulers, authorities, councils, and synagogues, do not be anxious about what you ought to say or what you should speak at that time. For words of wisdom will be given you by the Holy Spirit, against which not even those who are highly skilled in debate will be able to argue.”

### 10

But let us set down the testimony itself, which runs as follows: “When they bring you into the synagogues before rulers and authorities, do not be anxious about how or what you should answer; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that hour what you ought to say” (Matthew XII, 12).

And in another Gospel: “Therefore settle it in your hearts not to rehearse beforehand how you will answer. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or answer” (Luke XIV, 14).

Since the Holy Spirit grants the apostles words against those who opposed the Gospel, it is clearly shown that in his substance the word of wisdom and knowledge is to be understood. How the Savior, in that hour, bestows a mouth and wisdom upon the disciples—wisdom against which not even those considered most eloquent among human beings can prevail—is not for us to discuss at this time, because our present purpose has been to show that the gifts of the virtues are always understood to be present in the Holy Spirit, so that the one who possesses him is regarded as full of God’s gifts.

Thus in Isaiah God himself says to someone: “I will put my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessings upon your children” (Isaiah XLIV, 3). For no one ever receives the spiritual blessings of God unless the Holy Spirit has preceded. Whoever receives the Holy Spirit will consequently possess blessings—that is, wisdom, understanding, and the other things of which the Apostle writes:

“For this reason we also, from the day on which we heard, have not ceased praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, walking worthily of God” (Colossians I, 9).

He says that those who walk worthily before him through their works, words, and prudence are filled with the will of God, who places the Holy Spirit upon them, so that they may be filled with wisdom, understanding, and the other spiritual goods [Note: [Col. 0112D] The Tholosan manuscript reads: “so that they may be filled with the wisdom and understanding that are given by God in the Holy Spirit.”].

Wisdom and understanding, however, which are in the Holy Spirit, are given by God. “The Lord,” it says, “will give wisdom; and from his presence proceed wisdom and understanding” (Ecclesiasticus I). The wisdom that comes from human beings is not spiritual but fleshly [Col. 0113A] and human.

Of this wisdom the Apostle writes: “We conducted ourselves in the world not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God” (1 Corinthians I and II) [Al. “in this world”], calling fleshly the wisdom that subsists in bodily matters from human reasoning [Note: [Col. 0113D] The same manuscript reads: “which subsists in the bodies of these things and in human thought,” etc.].

Spiritual and intellectual wisdom, on the other hand, remaining concerned with invisible and intelligible things, grants its presence through the operation of the Holy Spirit to those who receive it.

In many other places also the Apostle recalls that God’s gifts dwell [Al. are mentioned] in the substance of the Holy Spirit, as in the passage: “But may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope through the power of the Holy Spirit” (Romans XV, 13).

### 11.

But God, the giver of good things, will restore the hope that he promised, through the power of the Holy Spirit, to those who possess him, filling them with joy and peace—those who, possessing an undisturbed and tranquil mind, have cheerful thoughts and are calm, free from every storm of agitation.

Those who have obtained the aforementioned goods through the power of the Holy Spirit will also attain right faith in the mystery of the Trinity. Elsewhere in the same epistle he says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XIV, 17). By affirming that righteousness—that is, complete virtue—and the peace mentioned above are joined with the joy of God in the Holy Spirit, he very clearly proves to those who were able to hear him that these goods are nothing other than the substance of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, since these goods come to human beings from the generosity of the Holy Spirit, the calling of the nations, which he introduced through the teaching of the Gospel, is made acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit. For in this work also the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies and makes acceptable, is the substance of God’s blessings. And whoever is full of him does everything rationally: teaching rightly, living irreproachably, and truly and perfectly displaying signs and wonders. For he possesses the power of the Holy Spirit as an outstanding treasure and the source of the fullness of every good.

[Note: The Tholosanus manuscript lacks “strength” (*fortitudinem*).]

Peter, the disciple of the Lord Jesus, knows that the bestowal of the Holy Spirit is the nature of God’s gifts. For he says to those who reproached him for entering the house of Cornelius:

“If, then, God gave them an equal gift, granting the Holy Spirit to them as also to us at the beginning, who was I that I could prevent the Lord?” And again to his own people: “God, the knower of hearts, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV, 8 ff.).

The same meaning is also appropriate to what is said in many passages, that the Holy Spirit is given by the Lord:

“Jacob is my servant; I will receive him. Israel is my chosen one; my soul will receive him. I have given my spirit in him” (Isa. XLII, 1).

And again:

“He who gives breath to the people established upon it”—without doubt, the earth—“and spirit to those who tread upon it” (ibid., 5).

But above we demonstrated that the Spirit of God and the Holy Spirit are not different.

Paul likewise says: “The love of God has been poured out in your [or: our] hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to you” (Rom. V, 5).

And also: “How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke XI, 13).

This Spirit is also said to have been poured out by God upon all flesh, so that those who receive him may prophesy and see visions, according to Joel, who speaks in the person of God:

“I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel II, 28).

[Note: Vaticanus and the old edition add: “They shall see visions.”]

For the outpouring of the spirit is the cause of prophesying and of seeing the meaning and beauty of the truth. The very term “outpouring” proves that the substance of the Holy Spirit is uncreated. For when God sends an angel or another creature, he does not say, “I will pour out from my angel,” or from a principality, throne, or dominion.

[Note: The Tholosanus reads, “I will pour out an angel,” or “from my angel”; he and Vaticanus append this gloss at the end of the sentence. This is an incredible—indeed, deceptive—statement of that kind.]

For this expression applies only to those things that are shared by others, just as we have now and shortly before spoken of the love of God, which has been poured out in the hearts of those who have received the Holy Spirit:

“The love of God has been poured out in your hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to you” (Rom. V, 5).

The Savior also, because he too is capable of being received, is said to have been poured out in the likeness of ointment:

“Your name is ointment poured out” (Song I, 2).

For just as ointment contained in a vessel possesses the substance of fragrance but is prevented from spreading farther because it is enclosed within the vessel, whereas, when it is poured out from the vessel, it releases its pleasant scent at a distance, so the fragrant name of Christ, before his coming, was present only among the Israelite people, as though enclosed in the vessel of Judea:

“God is known in Judea; his great name is in Israel” (Ps. LXXV, 2).

But when the Savior, shining forth in his flesh, extended his name throughout the whole earth—indeed, throughout every creature—fulfilling what is written, “How wonderful is your name in all the earth” (Ps. VIII, 2, 10), then the Apostle’s words were fulfilled:

“There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts IV, 12).

And the Psalmist says to the Lord:

“You have magnified your holy name above all things” (Ps. CXXXVII, 2).

Then was fulfilled: “Your name is ointment poured out.” The word “outpouring” signifies the broad and abundant richness of a gift.

### 12.

Therefore, when one person somewhere, or two, receive the Holy Spirit, it is not said, “I will pour out from the spirit”; rather, this is said when the gift of the Holy Spirit has overflowed upon all the nations.

The Apostle also recalls to Titus that salvation was granted to the nations:

“Not from works of righteousness that we ourselves have done, but through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly” (Tit. III, 5).

[Note: Vaticanus reads *omnes* (“all”) for *nos* (“we”), contrary to the Greek text itself.]

Here also the word “outpouring” indicates the generous bestowal of the Spirit.

From all these passages we learn that the substance of the Holy Spirit is capable of being received, and therefore uncreated. A “receivable” substance is one that is received by many and grants them participation in itself; a “receptive” substance, however, is one that is filled through communication with another substance, and, while receiving something else, is not itself received by another.

To what is receivable, immutability immediately belongs, and to what is immutable, eternity; conversely, what receives is changeable, and what is changeable is created. Nothing among created things is immutable, and therefore nothing is everlasting.

Thus not only what is rational in human beings is changeable and created; this same change is also found in all creatures. For the divine words demonstrate the changes and falls of angels. Although the multitude of angels and of the other exalted powers persevere in blessedness and holiness, nevertheless, since they have been changed into something possessing a similar nature, it is clearly shown that they remain in their original state not through the immutability of their substance, but through more diligent service to the Lord. For the nature of equals cannot be different.

Since the entire human race is mortal, and individual human beings are mortal, so likewise, if some of the higher beings are immortal, undoubtedly all those constituted within the same genus and species are immortal.

### 13.

Since these things are so, even if one angel should appear changeable, all will be changeable, although those who have not changed may persevere in blessedness—just as all human bodies are divisible, although not all are divided. For some bodies, having undergone division, reveal the nature of the others like themselves.

With these matters explained, the Holy Spirit is shown to belong to a substance other than that of the visible and invisible creatures. If this is true, then certain people impiously count the Holy Spirit among all things, saying that, in the statement that all things were made by God through the Word, the creation of the Holy Spirit is also signified.

For the Holy Spirit is not one among all things, but is shown by substance to be something else outside all things, distinct from both kinds. For if, as we demonstrated above, creation is divided into corporeal and incorporeal things, then the Holy Spirit, if he was created, must be either a visible or an invisible creature, that is, corporeal or incorporeal.

But he will in no way be a body, as we said earlier, since he teaches, grants knowledge, and is received by the mind and soul. Nor will he be an invisible creature, as we argued shortly before.

Therefore the Apostle, in the Epistle he wrote to the Hebrews, demonstrates that he is other than all the angels, saying:

“To which of the angels did he ever say, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’? Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are about to inherit salvation?” (Heb. I, 13).

And afterward:

“How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? It received its beginning in being proclaimed through the Lord, and was confirmed to us by those who heard, while God bore witness with signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will” (Heb. II, 4).

The words “to which of the angels” are equivalent to saying “to none,” the angelic name signifying the substance of all invisible creatures. For God did not say to any angel, or to any other rational creature, “Sit at my right hand.”

The statement therefore declares generally that God did not say to any creature, “Sit at my right hand.” This is stated generally concerning creation. And, speaking generally of all invisible creatures, he says that they are ministering spirits. Therefore he adds:

“Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service?”

Although not all invisible creatures individually have been sent, nevertheless, because some of the same genus and rank have been sent, they too are in a certain way sent by possibility: participants in the sending and of equal substance.

Therefore, just as the Lord, through whom that great salvation received its beginning in proclamation, is other than all creatures—the salvation whose neglect the Apostle does not want us to commit when he says, “How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation, which received its beginning in being proclaimed through the Lord and was confirmed to us by those who heard”; and just as God, who bears witness to this salvation through signs and wonders, is other than all ministering spirits, so also the Holy Spirit—through whose distributions God bears witness according to his will, distributing him not in divided portions but through communion to those to whom he has decided to grant him—is himself of another substance than those into whom he is poured and among whom he is distributed.

### 14.

Therefore, since we have established according to the sense of the Scriptures that the Holy Spirit is other than every creature, certain people who vainly, indeed impiously, wish to show that he is created make use of the testimony by which all things are said to have been made through the Word, so that, as they claim, his eternal substance may also be included among all things.

And because, to prove his created condition, they also appropriate a prophetic statement in which God says, “I create spirit,” we must show that in this too they are completely alien to an understanding of the truth.

For the Prophet’s statement was not about the Holy Spirit, as is understood from the very sequence and context of the speech. For the prophet Amos, speaking in the person of God, says:

“Prepare to call upon your God, O Israel, for I am he who establishes the thunder, who creates spirit, and who announces his Christ to human beings; who makes dawn and mist, and ascends upon the heights of the earth: the Lord God Almighty is his name” (Amos IV, 13).

[Note: Incorrectly, and contrary to the writer’s meaning, the text formerly read *concedere* (“to concede”); we emend it from the Vatican manuscript, which also has, more neatly, *pariter effatus*, etc. (“having likewise declared,” etc.) in place of the words *et facere* (“and to make”). Shortly afterward Tholosanus reads *formare* (“to form”) for *firmare* (“to establish”), a reading which other manuscripts also interchangeably prefer below.]

For the God who had declared beforehand that he creates spirit and makes things, also said that he establishes thunder and makes dawn and mist. If, therefore, we maintain the order of the preceding account—that is, of the thunder, dawn, and clouds—we must preserve the same order of the account also with regard to spirit, so that what is said by God may have this meaning:

“Prepare to call upon me, who am God, who provide for all things, who am also the creator of everything, who establish thunder and create wind, who make dawn and mist for certain human uses. Prepare, O Israel, so that you may call upon me. When you have prepared yourself to call upon me and have prayed to me, who establish the things mentioned above, you will enjoy favorable seasons and the abundance of other blessings, while I supply you each year with all things according to the order of nature: so that the year may flow fruitfully, so that the moments of the hours may pass in their appointed intervals, so that thunder may roar at its proper time, and so that a health-giving breeze may blow with timely gusts.”

But if thunder, dawn, mist, and the creation of spirit are understood allegorically, they will signify not the substance of the thing but a figurative interpretation.

### 15.

But if, conversely, someone should clearly object that these words are spoken about the Holy Spirit, because the statement “and announcing his Christ to human beings” is added to the creation of the Spirit, the following must be answered.

[Note: Neither our manuscripts nor the text of Amos has the word “all”; I would certainly prefer that it be deleted. I am persuaded that the annotation was derived from Hebrew through Jerome, not from Didymus’s own ingenuity, since he was entirely ignorant of Hebrew letters. For Saint Ambrose, who also answers this objection from Amos in Book II *On the Holy Spirit*, indicates that he did not find this solution from Hebrew in Didymus; he passes over it entirely. The heretics argued from this passage that the Holy Spirit was created in order to announce Christ to human beings. In reply, Jerome asserts that the Hebrew source does not read as it does in the Septuagint, but has “announcing his utterance to a human being.” He interpreted and explained it in this way in his commentaries, where he notes that the Septuagint translators were deceived by the similarity and ambiguity of the word. For, he says, if we read “his Christ,” which in Hebrew is *Messio*, it is written with the letters mem, sin, yod, heth, and vau, as the Septuagint translators supposed. But if, as it appears in Hebrew and among the other interpreters, it is written with mem and beth, it is *ma*, that is, “what” or “which.” Then sin, yod, heth gives what we read as *sia*, that is, “utterance.” The final element, written with the single letter vau, *αὐτοῦ* (*autou*), that is, “his,” has the same meaning, and, joined together, is read as *masio*. Hence he concludes that through the prophets God indicates his will, and that those who introduced another being outside the Creator, the Father of Christ, were shamefully mistaken, since Amos speaks not of the Spirit but of wind, and not of Christ but of God’s utterance.]

“If the words that follow are brought forward as referring to the creation of the Spirit—‘and announcing to all human beings his Christ’” (ibid.)—in Hebrew it says, “announcing his utterance to a human being.” The meaning is that he who is the creator of all things also inspires the prophets and makes his will known to human beings through them.

The answer must also take account of the fact that certain heretics invent another Lord outside the Creator, the Father of the Savior, and proclaim this impiously. Their wicked suspicion is refuted by God, who says:

“I am he who forms [Vaticanus: establishes] thunder, who creates spirit, who makes and governs the other parts of the world, and who announces my Christ to human beings. For this too is the work of my providence above all my works: that I should be the source not only of external things, but also of those things that pertain to the soul’s benefit and the mind’s advantage [variant: humility].”

I think that the statement “I create spirit” is equivalent to “creating wind.” For by his arrangement God directs those breaths that are produced by the movement of the air, according to what we read elsewhere:

“He brings forth winds from his treasuries” (Ps. CXXXIV, 7).

It is rightly said that he does not say, “I created,” but “I create spirit.” If the statement concerned the substance of the Holy Spirit, he would certainly have said, “I created.” For he does not continually create the same Spirit. But now the statement appropriately concerns breath: “I create,” because winds were not made only once, but, in the fact that they subsist, are made daily.

Nor is it without reason that spirit is here said to be created without the article, which in Greek indicates singularity. It is not the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit is almost always named with the article, as in the phrase:

“αὐτὸ τὸ Πνεῦμα”—that is, “the Spirit himself”—“bears witness to our spirit” (Rom. VIII, 16).

And elsewhere:

“αὐτός ἐστιν τὸ ζωοποιοῦν”—that is, “he is the one who gives life” (John VI, 64).

[Note: The printed editions and manuscripts have this form, but incorrectly. It should be corrected from John’s own text to *τὸ Πνεῦμα ἐστὶ τὸ ζωοποιοῦν*, “the Spirit is the one who gives life.”]

And again:

“Thus no one has known the things of God except τὸ Πνεῦμα, that is, the Spirit of God; τὸ γὰρ πνεῦμα, that is, ‘for the Spirit, searches all things, even the depths of God’” (I Cor. II, 10).

Many other examples can also be extracted from the sacred Scriptures.

Wherever the Holy Spirit is rarely named without the article, it should be understood that he is named with an addition signifying his majesty. Sometimes he is named without the article when it is not the Spirit himself in his own person that is indicated, but participation in him—for example, “the Spirit of Elijah,” and “walk by the Spirit” (IV Kings II, 15; Gal. V, 16), and whatever resembles these expressions.

### 16.

Since it has been demonstrated from the passages I have mentioned and from many others that the Holy Spirit is not a creature, he is nowhere counted among created things, but is always placed with the Father and the Son. Let us now see what equality [variant: difference] he has with both.

At the end of the second Epistle that Paul writes to the Corinthians, he says:

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, be always with you all” (II Cor. XIII, 13).

The present statement shows one participation in the Trinity, since the person who has received the grace of Christ possesses it both through the administration of the Father and through the generosity of the Holy Spirit.

For grace is given by God the Father and by Jesus Christ, according to the words:

“Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. I, 7; I Cor. I, 3; Colossians I, and elsewhere).

The Father does not give one grace and the Savior another. For Scripture describes grace as given both by the Father and by the Lord Jesus Christ, and as completed through the communion of the Holy Spirit.

The Spirit himself is also called grace, according to the statement:

“And insulting the Spirit of grace, by whom he was sanctified” (Heb. X, 29).

In Zechariah God also promises that he will pour out upon Jerusalem—that is, grant in greatest abundance—the spirit of grace and mercy (Zech. XII, 10).

When someone has received the grace of the Holy Spirit, therefore, he has received it from God the Father and from Jesus Christ our Lord. Thus one grace, completed through the operation of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, demonstrates that the Trinity is of one substance.

Elsewhere he says:

“The love of God” (II Cor. XIII, 13), which is both granted and confirmed by the Trinity, “be with you all.”

For the Savior says:

“Whoever hears my words and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him” (John XIV, 21).

[Note: Tholosanus manuscript: “He who has my commandments and keeps them,” etc.]

The Savior’s love for those who are loved is not different from the Father’s love. For God loves for salvation:

“God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him [variant: in the Son] should not perish but have eternal life” (John III, 16).

Likewise, the Son, who is life and gives life and salvation, loves those whom he wishes to become better. Therefore he says that he loves the one who is loved by the Father. And of him it is written in the Prophet:

“He himself will save them, because he loved them” (Isa. XXXIII, 21; XXXV, 4).

### 17.

The Apostle testifies that this love is the fruit of the Holy Spirit, as are joy and peace, which are supplied by the Father and the Son, saying:

“But the fruit of the Spirit is joy, peace, love” (Gal. V, 22).

This love has been poured out in the hearts of believers through the Holy Spirit. For he says:

“The love of God has been poured out in your hearts [Tholosanus: our hearts] through the Holy Spirit” (Rom. V, 5).

Everyone who shares in the Holy Spirit shares through participation in him, according to the words:

“And the communion of the Holy Spirit be always with you all” (II Cor. XIII, 13).

And elsewhere:

“If there is any communion of the Spirit.”

When someone possesses the wisdom and word of God, and truth in all things, he will also possess a share in holiness with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“God is faithful, by whom you were called into the communion of his Son” (I Cor. I, 9).

[Note: Vaticanus here and below consistently reads *communionem* (“communion”) for *communicationem* (“participation”); shortly afterward it reads, “Therefore whoever,” etc.]

John also writes concerning the Father:

“If we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have communion with him” (I John I, 7).

And again:

“Our communion is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.”

Therefore whoever shares in the Holy Spirit immediately shares in the Father and the Son. And whoever has the love of the Father has it from the Son, communicated through the Holy Spirit. Likewise, whoever is a participant in the grace of Jesus Christ possesses that same grace, given by the Father through the Holy Spirit.

For it is established in every case that the operation of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is the same. And of those whose operation is one, the substance is also one. For things that are *homoousia* (ὁμοούσια), “of the same substance,” have the same operations; whereas things that belong to another substance and are *anomoousia* (ἀνομοούσια), “of unlike substance,” are discordant and different.

[Note: The text formerly read *ejusdem* (“of the same”), contrary to Vaticanus, which nevertheless incorrectly has *ἀνούσια* instead of *ἀνομοούσια* shortly afterward.]

### 18.

The unity of the Trinity is not taught only by the passages we have already cited, but also by innumerable others, of which we shall again set down a few in their proper order.

Peter, reproving Ananias because he had committed fraud in the sale of the field whose entire price he claimed to have offered, established the unity of the Holy Spirit with God—not according to number but according to substance—saying:

“Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back part of the price of the field? While it remained, did it not remain yours? And after it was sold, was it not in your power? Why have you put this matter in your heart? You have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts V, 3 ff.).

[Note: The old edition reads *ex dimidio* (“part of it”), more smoothly.]

For if one who lies to the Lord lies to the Holy Spirit, and one who lies to the Holy Spirit lies to God, no one can doubt that the Holy Spirit shares in communion with God. And just as holiness subsists in God, so divinity is understood to subsist in the Holy Spirit.

This Holy Spirit, whom we have said to be of the same nature as the Father, also does not differ from the divinity of the Son. The Savior says to his disciples:

“When they bring you into synagogues and before rulers and authorities, do not be anxious about how or what you should answer. For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that hour what you ought to say. Place it in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how to answer. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom which they will not be able to resist or contradict” (Luke XII, 11 ff.).

[Note: Vaticanus, together with the old edition, adds “that is, speech.”]

Here also, after saying that they should not be anxious about what they should answer those who contradict them, because in that same hour they would be taught by the Holy Spirit what they ought to say, he immediately added the reason for their confidence:

“Place it in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how to answer; for I will give you a mouth and wisdom which they will not be able to resist or contradict” (Luke XXI, 14).

After saying that, at the time of answering, they would be taught by the Holy Spirit what they ought to say, he says in what follows:

“For I will give you a mouth and wisdom,” and so forth.

### 19.

From these statements it is shown that the wisdom given to the disciples by the Son is the wisdom of the Holy Spirit, and that the teaching of the Holy Spirit is the teaching of the Lord. The Holy Spirit therefore shares one nature and one will with the Son.

Since it was demonstrated above that the Spirit is by nature the companion of God’s Only-Begotten Son and of God the Father, and since the Son and the Father are one, according to the statement:

“I and the Father are one” (John X, 30),

the Trinity has been shown to be not divided [variant: undivided] and inseparable according to nature.

In another Gospel it is said:

“For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 20).

If, therefore, the Spirit of the Father speaks in the apostles, teaching them what they ought to answer; and if what is taught by the Spirit is wisdom, which we cannot understand as anything other than the Son, it plainly appears that the Spirit is of the same nature as the Son and as the Father, whose Spirit he is.

The Father and the Son are one. Therefore the Trinity is joined by unity of substance.

### 20.

Through another example from the Scriptures, the unity, nature, and power of the Trinity are also demonstrated.

The Son is called the hand, right hand, and arm of the Father. As we have frequently taught, these names demonstrate the indistinguishability of one nature [variant: that the indistinguishability of one nature is demonstrated].

The Holy Spirit is likewise called the finger of God, in accordance with the union of nature between the Father and the Son.

In one of the Gospels, when those who disparaged the Lord’s signs said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the ruler of demons” (Matt. IX, 34), the Savior asked:

“If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke XI, 19).

Another Evangelist, describing this same passage, introduced the Son as saying:

“But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God.”

From these statements it is shown that the finger of God is the Holy Spirit.

If, therefore, the finger is joined to the hand, and the hand to the one whose hand it is, then without doubt the finger refers to the substance of the one whose finger it is.

### 21.

But take care lest, having been brought down to lowly matters and having forgotten the subject now under discussion, you picture in your mind the differences among bodily limbs and begin to fabricate for yourself magnitudes, inequalities, and other larger or smaller bodily members, saying that the finger differs from the hand, and the hand from the one whose hand it is, by many inequalities.

For Scripture is now speaking of incorporeal things, intending to demonstrate unity alone, not a measure of substance. Just as the hand is not divided from the body, through which it accomplishes and performs all things, and is in the one whose hand it is, so the finger is not separated from the hand whose finger it is.

Therefore, when you think of God, reject inequalities and measurements, and understand the unity of the finger, the hand, and the whole substance—by that finger with which the law was written on tablets of stone.

[Note: Vaticanus likewise reads: “the unity of the whole body, with which finger the law,” etc.]

It is also very easy to establish the proof of our faith through another Scripture.

God alone is called wise. He does not receive wisdom from another, nor is he called wise through participation in someone else’s wisdom. Many are called wise, not from their own nature, but through participation in wisdom.

God, however, is called the only wise one, not through participation in another wisdom, nor because he became wise from elsewhere, but because he generates wisdom and makes others wise.

This Wisdom is our Lord Jesus Christ, who is called the power of God and the wisdom of God. The Holy Spirit is also called Wisdom.

[Note: The Tholosanus manuscript reads, “The Spirit is called Wisdom.”]

For the ancient books also report that Joshua son of Nun was filled by the Lord with the spirit of wisdom.

Therefore, just as God alone is wise, receiving wisdom from nowhere else but making others wise and generating wisdom, so he alone is wise, beyond all who are called wise by the naming of him:

“For the multitude of the wise is the salvation of the world” (Wis. VI, 26).

And again:

“Those who know themselves are wise.”

And again:

“When you are with the wise, you will be wise” (Prov. XIII, 20).

So also the Holy Spirit, not receiving wisdom from elsewhere, is called the spirit of wisdom. For his very subsistence is the spirit of wisdom, and his nature is nothing other than the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of God. We have already discussed these matters at length in the volume *Against the Sects*.

[Note: See above, p. 111, note b.]

Therefore, lest we repeat the same things unnecessarily, let us be content with the previous discussion.

### 22.

[Note: From this point the published editions begin the second book, contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts and to the intention of the Author and Translator themselves. See the Admonition prefixed to this work.]

Since, therefore, the Spirit of wisdom and truth is inseparably with the Son, he himself also subsists as Wisdom and Truth.

For if he were capable of wisdom and truth, he would at some point come to the point of ceasing to possess what he had received from elsewhere—that is, wisdom and truth.

And since the Son himself subsists as Wisdom and Truth, he is not separated in substance from the Father, who is proclaimed by the words of Scripture to be the only wise one and the Truth.

We see that the Holy Spirit, insofar as he is the spirit of wisdom and truth, shares with the Son this same circle of unity and substance [reading: “We see the Holy Spirit to share…”]. And again, the Son does not differ in substance from the Father.

[Note: The earlier text read, “we see him possessing,” but Barthius, deleting the first occurrence of “Spirit,” argues that it should be corrected to: “we have hitherto seen him possess with the Son.”]

Since the Son is the image of the invisible God and the form of his substance, all who are shaped and formed according to this image or form are brought into the likeness of God, though they attain such form and image only according to the capacities of human progress.

Likewise, since the Holy Spirit is the seal of God, those who receive the form and image of God, marked by him, are led through him to the seal of Christ’s wisdom and knowledge, and are also filled with faith.

“For there are distributions of operations, but it is the same Spirit who works all things in all” (I Cor. XII, 4).

Therefore, while the Father operates the manifold fullness of spiritual gifts, the Son multiplies that fullness, making it subsist through the Holy Spirit.

“For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit,” and the other gifts enumerated by the Apostle.

To these he adds:

“But all these things the one and same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid., 8 ff.).

[Note: Vaticanus and the old edition give the fuller text: “For there are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and divisions of operations, but the same Lord who works all things in all.”]

### 23

Hence, when we call the Holy Spirit an operative and, so to speak, distributive nature—[Note: The word has been supplied as we have it from the Vatican manuscript.]—let us not be led away from those who say that the Spirit is God’s operation and not his substance. The subsistent nature of the Holy Spirit is also demonstrated in very many other passages, as in what the apostles write: “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28). For the expression “it seemed good” signifies not an operation but a nature, especially since a similar expression is found concerning the Lord: “As it seemed good to the Lord, so it came to pass” [Col. 0123B] (Job 1).

Finally, his words are also very frequently read, as in the passage: “While they were fasting and ministering”—that is, the 130 disciples of Christ—“the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2). This voice, an indication of divinity and authority, shows a substance that is not created but uncreated. For the Holy Spirit did not call Barnabas and Paul to some work other than that which belongs to the Father and the Son, since the ministry that the Spirit entrusted and assigned to them is the ministry of the Father and the Son.

Paul says to the Galatians: “For he who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked also through me for the Gentiles and through Barnabas” (Gal. 2:8). [Note: The Toulouse manuscript has: “worked also through me and Barnabas among the Gentiles”; and immediately afterward: “they were sent by Christ; the Spirit cooperating in the Apostles, the ministry was completed.”] They were likewise sent to the nations by the authority of the Holy Spirit. While Christ also worked in the apostles, the Spirit’s ministry was completed [Col. 0123C], as the apostles themselves confess: that they speak in Christ, and that they saw with their own eyes and became ministers of the word—namely, of Christ—and stewards of the mysteries of God. [Note: A manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, marked no. 497, whose variant readings, recorded on loose sheets, now first come to my attention and which I shall cite here and there below, has here “of Christ’s discourse,” without the words “that is”; and a little later, “Go and teach,” without “Go.”]

Finally, as though possessing primacy in the priesthood and having been shown by Christ to be initiators of the faith, they are told: “Go, go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). And, as the Apostle writes with complete correctness: “There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism.” Who would not be compelled by the truth itself to accept the undivided unity of the Holy Trinity, since there is one faith in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and baptism is given and confirmed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit?

### 24

I do not think that anyone will be so foolish and insane as to regard as perfect the baptism that is given in the name of the Father and the Son, without the addition of the Holy Spirit; or again, baptism in the name of the Father and the Holy Spirit, with the name of the Son omitted; or certainly baptism in the name of the Son and the Holy Spirit, without the name of the Father being placed first.

For although someone might be so stony-hearted, so to speak, and completely out of his mind as to attempt to baptize while omitting one of the prescribed names—clearly acting as Christ’s contrary legislator—[Note: The Toulouse manuscript wrongly has “only, without perfection.”] nevertheless he will baptize without perfection; indeed, he will not be able to free from sins those whom he supposes to have been baptized by him.

From this it is gathered how undivided the substance of the Trinity is; that the Father is truly the Father of the Son, and the Son truly the Son of the Father; that the Holy Spirit is truly the Spirit of the Father [Note: The just-mentioned Queen’s manuscript has: “truly the Spirit of the Father and the Son.”] and of God; and, moreover, that he is the Spirit of wisdom and truth, that is, of the Son of God.

This, then, is the salvation of believers, and the administration of ecclesiastical discipline is perfected in this Trinity. For when the Savior sent his disciples to preach the Gospel and to teach the doctrines of truth, the Father is said to have established in the Church—[Note: The Queen’s manuscript deletes the word “Father.”]—first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, in agreement also with the Apostle’s statement concerning this matter: “Just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the Gospel, so we speak, not as pleasing human beings, but God, who has tested our hearts” (1 Thess. 2:4).

These same men whom Christ commanded to be teachers, and whom the Father approved, are reported to have been established by the Holy Spirit as stewards and overseers in the Church [another reading: “are truly forbidden”]. For when the Apostle Paul had gathered at Miletus presbyters from different places and many churches, he said: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, over which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to govern the Church of the Lord, which he acquired through his own blood” (Acts 20:28).

If, then, the Holy Spirit placed over the Church those whom Christ sent to evangelize and baptize the nations, appointed by the Father’s decision, no one can doubt that the operation and approval of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, and consequently that the substance of the Trinity is the same. [Note: The Toulouse manuscript has: “thus that the operation and approval are one,” and so forth.]

We must also consider that a creature cannot dwell in the heart and mind unless God and his Word dwell there in the Holy Spirit, just as the Father says to certain people: “I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them” (2 Cor. 6:16). And someone addresses him himself: “But you dwell in the sanctuary, O praise of Israel” (Ps. 21:4). For the Creator of the whole creation dwells on high, in the highest places.

The Only-Begotten Son also dwells in a pure mind and in the hearts of believers. [Note: The words “and the Only-Begotten Son” are deleted in the Queen’s manuscript.] “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, in the inner person, in the Spirit,” the Apostle writes: “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith in the inner person” (Eph. 3:17). He himself also says of himself: “Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). And again: “Christ speaks in me” (2 Cor. 13:3).

The Savior likewise says: “We will come, I and the Father” (John 14:23)—clearly referring to the one who has kept his commandments, and saying that “we will make our dwelling with him.” For the passage is joined together as follows: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word. And my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (ibid.). Elsewhere too, the whole nature of rational creatures is called the Savior’s house.

### 25

[Note: In the Queen’s manuscript: “the Savior’s house; but Christ over his own house, whose house we are,” and so forth.]

Just as the Lord Jesus is over his own house, whose house we are, so the house of Christ is the temple of God, in which his Spirit, the Spirit of God, dwells. Writing to the Corinthians, Paul says: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16).

If, then, in the house and temple in which the Father and the Savior dwell, the Holy Spirit is immediately found as well, the undivided substance of the Trinity is thereby demonstrated. A little later in the same epistle [Col. 0125B] he says: “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God?” (ibid.).

Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit is taught to dwell in the mind and inner person in the same way as the Father and the Son, it is not merely foolish but impious to call him a creature. Disciplines—by which I mean virtues and arts—and the disturbances, ignorance, and passions opposed to them can dwell in souls; yet they do so not as substances but as accidental qualities. It is impossible, however, for a created nature to dwell in the mind.

If this is true, and the Holy Spirit is without any ambiguity a subsistent inhabitant of the soul and heart, no one can doubt that he must be believed uncreated together with the Father and the Son. From all, therefore, that the preceding discourse has discussed, the Holy Spirit has been shown to be by nature incorruptible and eternal, like the Father and the Son; he has removed every ambiguity and suspicion concerning himself, so that he might not be thought one of the created substances.

[Note: We have supplied from the Queen’s manuscript the words “Nor can it be doubted that,” since they are necessary to complete the sense, although they are absent from the other manuscripts and printed books known to us so far.]

Nor can it be doubted that he is the Spirit of God whom the Savior’s words in the Gospel declare to proceed from the Father. “When the Consoler has come,” he says, “whom I will send to you—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26).

He calls the Spirit the Holy Consoler, giving him this name from his operation, because he not only consoles those whom he finds worthy of himself and makes them free from every sadness and disturbance, but also grants them an extraordinary joy and gladness, so that someone, giving thanks to God for being considered worthy of such a guest, may say: “You have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4:7). Eternal joy indeed dwells in the heart of those whose inhabitant is the Holy Spirit.

This Holy Spirit, the Consoler, is sent by the Son—not according to the ministry of angels, prophets, or apostles, but in the manner in which it is fitting for the Spirit of God to be sent by wisdom and truth, possessing an undivided nature with that same wisdom and truth. For the Son, sent by the Father, is not separated or divided from him, remaining in him and possessing him within himself.

Likewise, the Spirit of truth, sent in the manner mentioned above by the Son, proceeds from the Father; he does not migrate from one place to another. For this is equally impossible and blasphemous. [Note: We judged this to be the more correct and coherent reading of the sentence, and have taken it from the old edition so often cited and from the Vatican manuscript. Martianay and other editors had: “For if this Spirit of truth is confined, according to the nature of bodies, within a definite spatial extent, he has left one place and migrated to another.” The Toulouse manuscript is no better: “For if he is found from place to place, and the Spirit of truth, according to bodily nature, is confined within a definite spatial extent,” and so forth. In the earlier, erased reading of the Queen’s manuscript, the following is written in the margin: “For if the Spirit of truth comes from place to place, bodily according to the law of nature and confined within a definite spatial extent,” and so forth. The reading we have restored is supported by the disagreements among the manuscripts themselves.]

For if the Spirit proceeds from one place to another, then the Father himself will also be found in a place, and the Spirit of truth, confined according to the nature of bodies within a definite spatial extent, will leave one place and migrate to another. But just as the Father, not existing in a place, is beyond the whole nature of bodies, so the Spirit of truth is in no way enclosed by the limits of places, since he is incorporeal; or, to speak more accurately, he surpasses the whole rational creation. [Note: The Vatican and Toulouse manuscripts have: “surpassing the essence of all rational creatures.”]

### 26

Since, then, it is impossible and impious to believe these things concerning incorporeal beings, the statement that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father must be understood in the same way in which the Savior testifies that he himself proceeded from God, saying: “I came forth from God and came” (John 8:42).

Just as we separate places and changes of place from incorporeal beings, so also we distinguish expressions of coming forth—whether inward or outward, as I may put it—from the nature of intellectual beings, because such expressions belong to bodies that can receive touch and possess extension.

Therefore, by an ineffable expression known through faith alone, we must believe that the Savior is said to have come forth from God, and that the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father, with the Spirit saying: “the Spirit who proceeds from me.” [Note: The Queen’s manuscript reads “of faith alone”; and then, “to proceed from the Father,” as in the statement, “with the Spirit speaking, who proceeds from the Father.”] For although he could have said “from God,” or “from the Lord,” or “from the Almighty,” he touched none of these expressions but said “from the Father.” This does not mean that the Father is something other than the almighty God—for it is a crime even to think this—but the Spirit of truth is said to proceed from him according to the particular relation and conception of a parent. [Note: The same reading as the old edition: “according to the property of a father and the understanding of a parent,” and so forth.]

Although the Savior frequently says that he came forth from God, he nevertheless claims for himself the particular relation and, so to speak, intimacy of which we have often spoken from the designation “Father,” saying: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10). And elsewhere: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), along with many other similar statements that the attentive reader will find in the Gospel.

This Holy Spirit, then, who proceeds from the Father, will bear witness, the Lord says, concerning me, bearing testimony similar to the Father’s testimony, of which he says: “The Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John 12:49). When the Son sends the Spirit of truth, whom he called the Consoler, the Father also sends him at the same time. For the Father does not fail to send him when the Son sends him, since the Spirit comes by the same will of the Father and the Son.

The Savior also speaks through the Prophet: [Note: As will be clear to anyone who reads the entire passage, these words are absent from the Queen’s manuscript. I restore from the Vatican manuscript and the old edition “his Spirit,” in place of which the text had in the nominative, contrary to the author’s meaning, “his Spirit.”] “And the Lord sent me, and his Spirit.” For God sends not only the Son but also the Spirit.

The Apostle likewise says: “These things have now been announced to you through those who preached the Gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven” (1 Pet. 1:12). And in the book entitled Wisdom, a voice of thanksgiving to God is attributed to those who have received divine gifts: “Who has searched out the things that are in heaven? And who has known your will, unless you gave wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from on high? And thus the paths of those who were upon the earth were made straight, and human beings were taught the things pleasing to you” (Wis. 9:17).

In the present passage also, it is not only the wisdom of God—that is, his Only-Begotten Son—that is given by the Father, but the Holy Spirit too is sent.

### 27

In the Gospel itself also, the Holy Spirit is proclaimed to be given by the Father and sent, when the Savior says: “And I will ask my Father, and he will give you another paraclete, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16). And again: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything” (ibid., 26).

In these words also, the Father is said to give another Paraclete—not another than [MSS: “without”] the one who is sent by the Son, according to the statement: “When that Paraclete has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth” (John 15:26). He called him “another Paraclete” not because of a difference of nature but because of a diversity of operation.

Since the Savior assumes the role of mediator and ambassador, and, as high priest, pleads for our sins, saving forever those who draw near to God through him, because he always lives to intercede for them before the Father [the manuscript reads “for us”], the Holy Spirit, according to another significance of the word, was named Paraclete because he consoles those placed in sadness. [Note: Previously it read “from which,” as in the Queen’s manuscript, and “as if.” The Toulouse manuscript has “in which.” See Letter 64 to Fabiola, no. 19. I likewise correct the punctuation, the faulty form of which made the sentence meaningless.]

But do not infer different natures from the different operations of the Son and the Holy Spirit. For elsewhere the Spirit is found acting as Paraclete in the role of an ambassador to the Father, as in the passage: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings. But he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, how he pleads for the saints according to God” (Rom. 8:26). [Another reading: “when he pleads.”]

### 28

The Savior likewise performs in the hearts of those who need it the consolation from which the Holy Spirit is called Paraclete. For it is written: “And he consoled the humble of the people” (Ps. 17 and 32). Hence he who had received this benefit, proclaiming him, said: “Lord, according to the multitude of the sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my heart” (Ps. 93:19); or, “have loved my soul,” for both forms are found in different copies. [Another reading: The words “in my heart, your encouragements will delight my soul” are found in the Toulouse manuscript. Another version has “your consolations,” and so forth. This is a gloss produced by the audacity of critics. The difference in the reading urged by Didymus lies in the words “they gladdened” and “they loved.” In fact, some Greek books have ἠγάπησαν, “they loved,” while others have εὔφραναν, “they gladdened,” as in the Latin copies.]

The Father too is called the God of all consolation, consoling those who are in tribulation, so that from those very afflictions they may first attain salvation through patience and afterward the crown of glory.

Therefore the consoling and holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth, is given by the Father so that he may always dwell with Christ’s disciples, with whom the Savior himself also is, saying: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Since the Holy Spirit and the Son are always present with the apostles [another reading: “assist them”], it follows that the Father too is with them, because whoever receives the Son receives the Father also; and the Son makes his dwelling with the Father among those who have proved worthy of his coming.

Moreover, wherever the Holy Spirit is, the Son is immediately found as well. For when the Holy Spirit is in the prophets, causing them to foretell future things and perform the other works proper to prophecy, the Word of God is said to have come to them, so that, in addition to the prophetic formula “Thus says the Lord,” [Note: The text previously read, incorrectly, “it was prophesied.”] the expression “The word that came to Isaiah,” or to the other prophets, is added.

### 29
