That the prophets had the Holy Spirit we learn clearly from God’s own speech. He says: “Whatever I commanded by my Spirit to my servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7).

The Savior also indicates in the Gospel that righteous men, and those who before his coming had sung beforehand [Vatican: “had foretold”] to the people of things that were to come, were filled by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. For when he asked the Pharisees what they thought about Christ, and heard that he was the son of David, he said: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand’? If David therefore calls him Lord in the Holy Spirit, how is he his son?” (Matt. 22:43). [Note: The old edition more correctly reads: “that he was the son of David, said, ‘David, speaking in the Holy Spirit, said, The Lord said to my Lord,’” and so forth. The Toulouse manuscript differs: “that he was the son of David, he said, for David speaks concerning God, ‘The Lord said to my Lord,’” and so forth.]

Peter also says to his fellow believers: “The Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas,” and so forth (Acts 1:16). Again, in the same book: “You spoke through the Holy Spirit, by the mouth of your servant David: ‘Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise futile things?’” (Acts 4:25).

Isaiah too, when he had been moved by the word of God to prophesy, is said to have prophesied by the command of the Holy Spirit, as is written at the end of the Acts of the Apostles: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying: Go to this people and say: You will hear with your ears,” and the rest (Acts 28:25). [Note: The text previously read “the Holy Spirit by command,” an ungrammatical expression. Everyone would regard this as a printer’s error and restore “of the Holy Spirit,” as in the very ancient edition that I follow. I would nevertheless prefer to retain “holy” in the nominative and read “through him,” that is, through Isaiah, in place of “by command.” This is plainly the author’s meaning, and the entire following context confirms the conjecture.]

This prophecy, then, which the Apostle Paul affirms was spoken by the Holy Spirit, the prophet’s own book records as having been spoken by the Lord. “And I heard,” Isaiah says, “the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And I said: Here am I; send me. And he said: Go and say to this people: You will hear with your ears” (Isa. 6:9).

After other words, the Lord himself says: “And they will turn, and I will heal them.” Immediately the prophet asks: “How long, Lord?” For when the Lord had told the prophet to speak the things that are written, and the prophet had answered the commanding Lord, “How long, Lord?”, Paul affirms that the things spoken by the Lord in the prophet were recalled as having been spoken by the Holy Spirit.

From this it is plainly shown, as we have often said, that the Lord and the Holy Spirit have one will and one nature, and that in the designation “Spirit” the name “Lord” is also understood. For just as, in the passage to the Corinthians, the designation “God” applied to the Father and “Lord” applied to the Son neither takes lordship away from the Father nor divinity away from the Son—since, in the same way that the Father is Lord and the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is also called Lord—so, if he is Lord, consequently he is also God, as we said shortly before when we cited the Apostle Peter’s words to Ananias, who had held back the money, because divinity is understood in the Holy Spirit as well. [Note: The text incorrectly had “in these two words, thus indeed.”]

### 30

But since the order of the question arose from the passage: “When the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, has come, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything” (Luke 12:12), let us now inquire from the very wording whether we can find anything in it that agrees with what has been said.

The Savior affirms that the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father in his own name, since the Son is properly the Savior’s name. For this expression signifies a sharing of nature and, so to speak, the particular relation of the persons. In this designation of the Son, the Holy Spirit sent by the Father must not be understood [another reading: “is understood”] as a servant, another being, or someone separated from the Son.

Just as the Son comes in the Father’s designation, saying: “I have come in my Father’s name” (John 5:43)—for it belongs only to the Son to come in the Father’s name, while the particular relation of the Son to the Father and of the Father to the Son remains intact—so, conversely, no one else comes in the Father’s name, but, for example, in the name of the Lord, God, or the Almighty.

You can recognize this clearly if you read the prophets attentively. Moses, the great minister and servant of God, came in the name of him who is; and Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob came in the name of God, when God spoke to Moses: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:15). And again: “You shall say to them: ‘The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob has sent me to you.’”

The mission of righteous servants—such as those of whom he said, “I will command my Spirit to my servant prophets” (Zech. 1:6)—was carried out in the name of God. And because [perhaps: “who”] they showed themselves worthy of God, they are said to have come in the name of God. Again, advancing to something greater and remaining under the command of the one God, they came under the designation of almighty God.

But because the children of Israel, while dwelling in Egypt, had learned to worship those who are not gods as though they were gods, and to venerate the world’s fathers with divine honor [Note: The text previously had “the parts of the world,” in place of “the fathers.” The Queen’s manuscript, in a second hand, reads “the rulers of the world.”], it followed that Moses should be sent to them under the designation of him who is, freeing them from false gods and leading them to the true divinity and to the Lord of the fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

### 31

Just as servants who come in the name of the Lord, by the very fact that they are subject and serve, indicate the Lord and bear his particular designation—for they are the Lord’s servants—so the Son who comes in the Father’s name bears the Father’s particular relation and name, and by these he is shown [another reading: “called”] to be the Only-Begotten Son of God.

Therefore, because the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father in the Son’s name, possessing the Son’s particular relation according to the fact that he is God, but not possessing sonship so as to be his Son, he shows that he is joined to the Son in unity. Hence he is also called the Spirit of the Son, making those who wished to receive him into sons by adoption. “Because you are sons,” he says, “the Father sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15). [Note: All the manuscripts have “in unity”; the printed editions have “uniquely.” The Vatican manuscript, together with the Toulouse manuscript, then reads “making sons through his adoption,” and so forth.]

This Holy Spirit, who comes in the Son’s name and is sent by the Father, will teach everything to those who are perfect in the faith of Christ. By “everything” he means all spiritual and intellectual things; and, to summarize everything briefly, all the mysteries of truth and wisdom.

He will teach not as a teacher and instructor of a discipline that he acquired elsewhere—for that belongs to those who have learned wisdom and certain arts through study and industry—but as art itself [another reading: “the art itself”], teaching, and the Spirit of wisdom and truth, he invisibly insinuates into the mind the knowledge of divine things. [Another reading: “invisibly.”]

The Father also teaches his disciples in this way, as the one who had been taught by him says: “God, you taught me wisdom.” And another cries out boldly: “You taught me, O God, from my youth” (Ps. 70:17); and thus all become taught.

The Son of God, too, who is the wisdom and truth of God, teaches his participants in such a way that he does not teach the discipline as an art but by nature. Hence the disciples are taught to call him their only teacher.

These same disciplines, given by the Father and the Son into the hearts of believers, the Holy Spirit administers to those who have ceased to be merely natural persons [another reading: “who cease”]. For the natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit, considering what is said to be foolishness (1 Cor. 2:14). But whoever has purified his mind from disturbances will be filled with the disciplines of the Holy Spirit—that is, with words of wisdom and knowledge—so fully that he who has received them says: “But God has revealed them to us through the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 10).

To those who have prepared themselves in this way, God grants the Spirit of wisdom and revelation so that they may know him. Those who receive the Spirit of wisdom become wise not from another source but through the Spirit himself; through him they understand the Lord and whatever is God’s will, and through his revelation they come to know the Spirit himself, so that they may understand that these things have been given to them by the Lord.

Thus, whoever has received the spirit of revelation and wisdom is sufficient to proclaim the doctrines of truth, supported not by human skill but by God’s art, as we can hear one of the apostles saying: “My preaching and my message were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in a demonstration of the Spirit” [Note: The Vatican manuscript likewise has “and of God’s truth,” which is contradicted by the Greek text.] “and of the power of God” (ibid., 4).

We cannot interpret the power equal to the Spirit as anyone other than Christ our Lord. For he himself says to his disciples: “You will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you” [the Vatican manuscript: “of the Holy Spirit who is coming”] (Acts 1:8). And the angel [another reading: “archangel”] says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

Therefore the creative power of the Most High, when the Holy Spirit came upon the virgin Mary, fashioned Christ’s body; using it as a temple, he was born without the seed of a man.

### 32

From these things it is shown that the Holy Spirit is Creator, as we briefly demonstrated in the volume *On Doctrines*. [Note: Recall what we said about this work, *On Doctrines* (*περὶ Δογμάτων*), above, p. 111, note b.]

And in the Psalm it is said to the Lord: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their earth. Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:30).

It is no wonder that the Holy Spirit is the creator of the Lord’s body alone, since, joined to the Father and the Son, he created by the same power everything that the Father and the Son created. For he says: “Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created.”

We have already frequently shown that the Holy Spirit belongs to the same operation as the Father and the Son, and that in the same operation there is one substance; and, conversely, that the operation of those who are ὁμοούσια—“of the same substance”—is not different.

To offer another testimony that may assist us in our faith concerning the Holy Spirit, the discourse in the Gospel is joined together as follows: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth has come, he will guide you into all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me [another reading: “will honor me”], because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine. Therefore I said to you that he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16:13–15).

### 33

From these sacramental words we learn that, after Jesus had taught his disciples many things, he said: “I still have many things to say to you.” For the statement “I still have many things to say to you” is addressed not to any newcomers, [Note: There is very great disagreement among the copies here. The old edition has: “and directs those completely ignorant of God’s wisdom”; the Vatican manuscript: “is directed to those ignorant of God’s wisdom”; the Queen’s manuscript: “to those unacquainted with God’s wisdom”; the Toulouse manuscript: “and directs those filled with God’s wisdom, as were the righteous and the prophets,” but continues: “not to those who had not yet become hearers of his words,” and so forth. The Vatican manuscript then again has: “who had not yet acquired everything that they would afterward be able to endure for his name, but, handing on to them in part the things that were greater, postponing the rest for later, commending also those things which he deferred to a future time, so that the remaining discipline of his Holy Spirit—which they could not bear if at the outset the instruction and form of the cross did not precede in our Head—could be supplied. For whatever they were able to endure,” and so forth. The Toulouse manuscript places nearly the same material first, but more correctly reads “unless the instruction and form of the cross first went before,” since this was before the coming of the Lord’s passion, and so forth. From these variants the reader may extract whatever is useful.] and completely empty of God’s grace, but to those who had heard his words yet had not acquired everything.

Having handed on to them whatever they were able to bear, he postponed the remaining things to a future time, since they could not know them without the discipline of the Holy Spirit. For before the coming of the Lord’s passion the Holy Spirit had not yet been given to human beings, as the Evangelist says: “For the Spirit had not yet been given to anyone, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39). By saying that Jesus was glorified, he means that he tasted death for all. [Note: The Toulouse manuscript has: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. What does it mean to say that Jesus had not yet been honored? By ‘glorified’ he means,” and so forth.]

Therefore, after the resurrection, appearing to his disciples and breathing upon their faces, he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). And again: “You will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you” (Acts 1:8).

When he comes into the hearts of believers, they are filled with words of wisdom and knowledge; thus, having become spiritual, they receive the discipline of the Holy Spirit, which can lead them into all truth.

For the hour had not yet arrived [perhaps: “was not yet impending”] in which it was necessary for them to be filled with the Holy Spirit, when he said to them, “I still have many things to say to you”; consequently he added: “But you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12).

Still serving the type of the Law, its shadow, and its images, they could not behold the truth, of which the Law bore the shadow, [Note: The text previously had “spiritual things.” The old edition has “nor finally”; the Vatican manuscript has “and not.”] and therefore could not endure spiritual things.

“But when he has come,” he says—that is, the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth—“he will guide you into all truth,” transferring you through his teaching and instruction from the death of the letter to the life-giving Spirit, in which alone the truth of all Scripture is contained.

The Spirit of truth himself, entering a pure and simple mind, will impress the knowledge of truth upon you, and, continually adding new things to the old, will guide you into all truth.

### 34

Someone, addressing prayers also to God the Father, says: “Direct me in your truth” (Ps. 24:5)—that is, in your Only-Begotten, who testifies in his own voice: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). God grants this perfection by sending the Spirit of truth, who directs believers into the whole truth. Then, in what follows, concerning the Spirit of truth who is sent by the Father and is the Paraclete, the Savior—who is also the truth—says: “For he will not speak from himself” (John 16:13)—that is, not without me and without my and the Father’s will, because he is inseparable from my will and the Father’s. Since he is not from himself but from the Father and from me, this very fact—that he exists and speaks—comes to him from the Father and from me. I speak the truth: that is, I inspire what he speaks. For he is the Spirit of truth.

To say and speak in the Trinity must not be understood according to our custom, by which we converse and speak with one another, but according to the nature of incorporeal beings, and especially according to that of the Trinity, which implants its will in the heart of believers and in those who are worthy to hear it: that is, to “say” and “speak.”

[Note: [Col. 0133D] Gratianus formerly read: “inserts it into the hearts of believers and implants it in their hearts, who …” Soon afterward the Toulouse manuscript has: “to say, to know, to understand, and to speak.”]

### 35

We human beings, when we speak to another about something, first conceive in our mind what we wish [to say]. Then, wishing to transfer it into the understanding of another, we move the organ of the tongue and, striking it against the strings of the teeth like a kind of plectrum, emit vocal sound.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] The older edition has: “we conceive it in the mind; and because we cannot transfer it into another’s understanding without speech, we move the organ of the tongue. Thereupon the tongue and teeth, colliding like a kind of plectrum of the heart …”]

Just as we strike the tongue against the palate and teeth and modulate the struck air into different utterances, so that we may communicate to others what is known to us, so also the hearer must necessarily offer open ears, constricted by no impediment, and direct them toward what is said,

[Note: [Col. 0133D] I agree with Barthius, who wrote *arrigere* (“direct toward”) instead of *erigere* (“raise up”), the reading formerly accepted.]

so that he may know what is uttered in the same way as the speaker who utters it knows it.

But God, being simple, immaterial, and spiritual in nature, has neither ears nor organs by which a voice is emitted; rather, as a solitary and incomprehensible substance, he is composed of no limbs or parts. The same things are to be understood similarly of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

### 36

Whenever, therefore, we read in the Scriptures, “The Lord said to my Lord” (Ps. 109:2), and elsewhere, “God said, ‘Let there be light’” (Gen. 1:3), and anything similar to these passages, we must receive it in a manner worthy of God [alternative reading: *digna*].

For the Father does not announce his will while the Son—who is wisdom and truth—is ignorant of it, since everything he speaks, being wise and truly subsisting, possesses wisdom [and substance].

[Note: [Col. 0134D] Formerly: “and in truth, substance.”]

When, therefore, the Father speaks and the Son hears, or conversely, when the Son speaks and the Father hears, this signifies the agreement of the same nature and the same will in the Father and the Son. The Holy Spirit also, who is the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom, cannot, when the Son speaks, hear what he does not know, since he himself is what proceeds from the Son—that is, proceeding from the truth, the Consoler flowing from the Consoler, God from God, the Spirit of truth proceeding.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] Gratianus has: “God proceeding from God, the Spirit of truth proceeding from the truth, the Consoler flowing from the Consoler,” and so forth; this is more correct.]

Finally, lest anyone separate him from the will and fellowship of the Father and the Son, it is written: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak” (John 16:13). The Savior likewise says of himself: “As I hear, I judge” (John 5:30). And elsewhere: “The Son cannot do anything from himself except what he sees the Father doing” (ibid., 19).

[Note: [Col. 0134D] We have supplied the words “from himself” from the Vatican manuscript, with the Greek text also agreeing: ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ (*aph’ heautou*, “from himself”). The older edition then reads: “For if the Father and the Son are one, not according to Sabellius’ statement …” The Vatican and Regina manuscripts have “Sabellius’ error.”]

For if the Son is one with the Father—not according to Sabellius’ statement, which confuses the Father and the Son, but according to the indivisibility of essence or substance—he cannot do anything apart from the Father, because the works of those who are separated are different. Rather, seeing the Father at work, he himself also works, not as working in a second rank and after him. The works of the Father and the Son would begin to be different if they were not performed equally. It is written, however: “Whatever he does”—there is no doubt that “he” means the Father—“these things the Son also does in the same way.”

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The Regina manuscript has, more correctly, “when the Father works”; shortly afterward the Vatican manuscript also agrees: “the same and similar things subsist.”]

If, then, when the Father and the Son work, all things that are made subsist not according to an order of first and second but according to the same time of working, as identical and undivided; and if the Son cannot do anything from himself because he cannot be separated from the Father, so also the Holy Spirit, in no way separated from the Son because of their fellowship of will and nature, is believed not to speak from himself, but to speak everything that he speaks according to the word and truth of God.

The Lord’s following words confirm this opinion: “He will glorify me” [Al. *glorificabit*]—that is, the Paraclete—“because he will take from what is mine.” Here again, “to take” [or “he will take”] must be understood in a manner appropriate to the divine nature.

### 37

Just as, therefore [Al. *enim*, “indeed”], the Son, when giving, is not deprived of what he bestows, nor does he impart it to others at his own loss, so the Spirit does not receive something he previously lacked. For if he received what he had not previously possessed, then, once the gift had been transferred to another, the giver would become empty, ceasing to possess what he gives.

As, therefore, we understood the matter above when discussing incorporeal natures, so now also we must understand [Al. *intelligendum*, “comprehend”] that the Holy Spirit receives from the Son what belongs to his own nature. This does not signify one who gives and another who receives, but one substance. For the Son is also said to receive from the Father the very things by which he subsists. The Son is not something other than those things given to him by the Father, nor is the substance of the Holy Spirit other than what is given to him by the Son.

These things are said so that we may believe that the Holy Spirit has in the Trinity the same nature as the Father and the Son.

### 38

Since every human voice can judge nothing except bodies, while the Trinity, which is now the subject of our discussion, surpasses all material substances, no word can properly be fitted to it or signify its substance. Everything we say, therefore, is *καταχρηστικῶς* (*katakrēstikōs*), that is, abusively or figuratively, both concerning incorporeal beings generally and especially when we speak of the Trinity.

Thus the Holy Spirit glorifies the Son, displaying him and bringing him into the open before those who are worthy to understand and see him with a pure heart, and to know the splendor of his substance and the image of the invisible God. Again, the image itself, displaying itself to pure minds, glorifies the Father by making him known to those who did not know him. For he himself says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

The Father also, revealing the Son to those who have deserved to reach the summit of knowledge, glorifies his Only-Begotten, displaying his majesty and power. The Son himself, too, by granting the Holy Spirit to those who have prepared themselves as worthy of his gift, and by disclosing the sublimity [or “distinctive character”] of his glorification and the power of his greatness, glorifies him.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] The same manuscripts, together with the older edition, have: “and revealing his [or ‘to them his’] sublimity of glorification and greatness, glorifies him.”]

Then, having introduced the interpretation, after saying a little earlier, “He will take from what is mine,” he immediately added: “All things that the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16:14).

[Note: [Col. 0135D] I emend this according to Barthius’ conjecture, since the text had incorrectly been printed as a single word, *quomodo*.]

He is speaking, in a sense, as follows: “Although the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father, and God gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him, nevertheless, since all things that the Father has are mine, and the Spirit of the Father is also mine, he will take from what is mine.”

But when these things are said, beware lest you fall into a serious error of understanding and suppose that there is some thing or possession held by the Father and the Son. Rather, whatever the Father has according to substance—that is, eternity, immutability, incorruption, and immutable goodness subsisting from and in himself—the Son also has these same things.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] The word “immutable” is superfluous here and is not found in the Regina manuscript. Immediately afterward, I restore, on the agreement and authority of all the manuscripts: “And, to say more, whatever the Son himself subsists as, and whatever belongs to the Son …”]

And, to say more, whatever the Son himself subsists as, and whatever belongs to the Son, the Father also has. Far from this let the snares and sophisms of dialecticians be driven away from the truth—those who, taking an occasion for impiety from a pious proclamation, say: “Then the Father is also the Son, and the Son the Father.”

For if he had said, “Everything that God has is mine,” impiety would have had an opportunity to fabricate this conclusion, and the falsehood would have seemed plausible. But since he said, “All things that the Father has are mine,” by the name “Father” he declared himself to be the Son; he did not usurp the Fatherhood, since he was the Son. Nevertheless, through the grace of adoption, he too is the Father of many saints, according to what is read in the Psalms: “If your sons keep [your covenant]” (Ps. 131:12). And again: “If his sons forsake my law” (Ps. 88:31).

In the present statement and its intended meaning, therefore, the Son also has the things we said above belong to the Father, and the Holy Spirit has the things that belong to the Son. For he says: “He will take from what is mine”; therefore, “he will also announce the things that are to come.”

Through the Spirit of truth, certain knowledge of future things is granted to holy men. Hence the prophets, filled with this same Spirit, foretold them with understanding and, as though viewing them in the present, perceived what was afterward to occur.

Let what we have said about the present Gospel passage, according to the poverty of our ability, suffice—indeed, suffice abundantly. But if the Lord reveals better things to some, and they have been brought near to the truth and can see it more clearly, let us yield to their discussion the better insights, with the support of him who is the Spirit of truth. And we ask those who will read this to pardon our ignorance and grant indulgence to our zeal, which desires to offer to God everything it has been able to produce, although it has not been able to fulfill its own desire.

### 39

Let us set forth also the testimony of the Apostle’s Epistle to the Romans and examine whatever in it appears relevant to the present subject.

“[So that] the justification of the law might be fulfilled in you, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who are according to the Spirit perceive the things of the Spirit. For the wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the Spirit is life and peace, because the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God. Indeed, it cannot be. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

“But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the spirit lives because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you.

“Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. For you did not receive again the spirit of slavery in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God. But if sons, then heirs also—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him” (Rom. 8:4 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0136D] “Brothers” was absent; we have supplied it from the manuscripts.]

In the present passage of the Apostle, many things are demonstrated concerning the fellowship that the Spirit has with the Father and the Son. The Apostle says that divine justification and the spiritual law are fulfilled in those who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

The person who walks according to the flesh—one who, through pleasures, joins the vices of the flesh to the body and does everything that belongs to the flesh and body—is described by the apostolic statement.

[Note: [Col. 0137A] Alternatively: “everything that is of the flesh”; alternatively, “is described” may read “describes.”]

On the other hand, the person who walks according to the Spirit is one who advances according to the commandments of the spiritual order, in the precepts of God’s law and the Gospel. For just as it is the vice of the carnal to set one’s mind on the things of the flesh and to think about bodily things, so conversely it is the virtue of the spiritual always to think about heavenly and eternal things and to deal with the things of the Spirit.

But the wisdom of the flesh, immediately joined to death, kills those who walk and think according to the flesh; whereas the wisdom of the Spirit grants eternal life to those who possess it, together with tranquility of mind and peace. Once they possess it, they will have all disturbances, every kind of vice, and even the demons themselves—who strive to suggest such things—under their feet.

Since the wisdom of the flesh is joined to death, it is hostile to God. It makes enemies of those who live according to its laws, always contrary and opposed to the will and law of God. For it cannot happen that one who possesses the wisdom of the flesh should keep God’s commands and submit to his will.

As long as we serve pleasures, we cannot serve God. But when we have brought wantonness, which tickles us, beneath our feet and, transferring ourselves wholly to the Spirit, are no longer in the flesh—that is, in the passions of the flesh—then we shall be subject to God.

The Apostle’s statement does not concern this flesh in which we live and in whose vessel our soul is contained, for all the saints, surrounded by body and flesh, pleased God. Rather, it concerns what is perpetrated against God’s commandment through human society, as in: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:5), and: “What you do not wish to be done to you …” (Tob. 4:16).

“But you,” he says—clearly meaning the disciples of Christ, who have received the wisdom of the Spirit and life and peace—“are not in the flesh,” that is, in the works of the flesh, nor do you perform its works, since you have the Spirit of God within you.

The same Spirit of God is also the Spirit of Christ, leading and joining to the Lord Jesus Christ the person who has him within. Hence it is written in what follows: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.”

### 40

Again, in the present passage we learn the fellowship that the Holy Spirit has with God and with Christ.

In Peter’s Epistle also, the Holy Spirit is shown to be the Spirit of Christ: “Searching and investigating,” he says—that is, the prophets, of whom he had spoken earlier—“into what time and what circumstances the Spirit of Christ who was in them was indicating, testifying beforehand to the sufferings destined for Christ and the decrees that were to follow. To them it was revealed that they were serving not themselves but us, announcing the things that have now been proclaimed to you through the Holy Spirit” (1 Pet. 1:10 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0137D] The text was previously corrupt and meaningless: “in which he says, what time …” Nor was the scriptural passage written correctly; we pass over the other errors of punctuation and the like with which this entire book abounded.]

This Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of God not only in the present passage but also in many other places, as in: “No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (Rom. 8:9). Then, after the statement, “If anyone does not have the Spirit of God, he does not belong to him,” there follows: “But if Christ is in you,” and it is most clearly demonstrated that the Holy Spirit is inseparable from Christ.

For wherever the Holy Spirit is, there also is Christ; and wherever the Spirit of Christ departs, Christ likewise departs. For if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ.

If someone takes the converse of this statement, he can say: “If anyone belongs to Christ, so that Christ is in him, in that person the Spirit of God is.” The same may likewise be asserted concerning God the Father: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of God, he does not belong to him.” Conversely, someone may say: “If anyone belongs to God, in that person is the Spirit of God.”

Hence it is written: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). And in John’s Epistle: “By this God dwelling in certain people is recognized, when the Spirit whom he gave remains in them” (1 John 4:2).

From all these passages the indivisible and undivided substance of the Trinity is demonstrated.

### 41

When, therefore, he says, “If Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin” (Rom. 8:10), this does not mean that the body, serving vices and wantonness, is stirred toward vices; rather, being put to death because of sin, it is no longer alive to sin.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] The Vatican manuscript has “if” instead of “but.” For the sense to agree at all events with the Apostle’s preceding statement, some word must be supplied, perhaps: “he means that it in no way …,” or something similar.]

After the body has been put to death because of sin, Christ, present in those who have put their bodies to death, displays the Spirit of life through righteousness, or through the correction of the works of immortal virtues, or through faith in Jesus Christ, in those who conduct themselves according to his faith.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] Consider whether the Regina manuscript’s reading should be preferred: “Christ shows life through the present Spirit to those who have mortified their bodies, through the righteousness of works, or through the correction of mortal vices, or through faith in Jesus Christ,” and so forth.]

Then the Apostle uses another connected syllogism, which dialecticians more significantly call an *ἀξίωμα* (*axiōma*, “axiom”), and says:

[Col. 0138D] “But if the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:9).

Does he not seem to say this to you? If the Spirit of him who raised Christ Jesus—that is, the Spirit who belongs to that same Jesus Christ—dwells in you, then consequently your mortal bodies also will be given life, together with immortal souls, by him who raised Christ Jesus from the dead, the leader and firstborn of the resurrection?

[Note: [Col. 0139D] This is how the older edition and the Regina manuscript read. Previously it had: “together with the souls of the immortals.” Immediately afterward the same older edition has: “displaying him as the firstborn of the resurrection.” Hence, “And to those to whom such and so great a gift …”]

To those who have been granted by God through the Spirit such a great gift, we are debtors to the Spirit, not to the flesh, so that we may live according to it [i.e. the flesh].

For whoever has lived according to the flesh will die by that death which follows sin. For sin, when it has been completed, gives birth to death (James 1:15), according to James. Ezekiel too writes that the sinful soul dies (Ezek. 18). It is separated from the life that is placed in the wisdom of the Spirit.

### 42

But if anyone has transcended the life of the flesh and by the Spirit has put to death the works of the flesh, he will live a blessed and eternal life, counted among the sons of God and directed onto the right path because of the Holy Spirit, who is also called the Spirit of God.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] The Regina manuscript has the fuller and more coherent reading: “If anyone has transcended the life of the flesh and by the Spirit has put to death the works of the flesh.” Previously it had only: “If anyone has transcended the life of the flesh …”]

“For if you live according to the flesh, you will die. But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Rom. 8:13). And in what follows: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God.”

Again refreshing, consoling, and urging those to whom he spoke to hope for better things, he says: “For you did not receive again the spirit of slavery in fear”—that is, you do not abstain from vices in the manner of slaves, through fear and dread of punishments—

[Note: [Col. 0139D] The Vatican manuscript has: “abstain from vices, having with you the gift …,” and afterward: “who is himself the Spirit of the Son, and of Christ, and of truth …”]

because you have received from the Father the Spirit of adoption, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is himself called the Spirit of God, of Christ, of truth, and of wisdom.

If this Spirit adopts as sons of God those in whom, through his favor, he becomes an indwelling presence, I leave to you the understanding of what power over those who follow can consequently be attributed to him.

[Col. 0139C] 42. Moreover, in this Spirit of adoption those who possess him cry out to God as Father, as the statement shows: “In whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (ibid., 15). The Spirit himself, who adopts us as sons, bears witness through his participation in us to what is possessed by our spirit: that we are sons of God.

It follows that God, as our Father, has conferred on us hereditary riches, spiritual gifts; and that we are fellow heirs with Christ, because through his grace and kindness we are called his brothers. We shall be heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ if we suffer with him, so that through fellowship in his sufferings we may deserve also to be glorified with him.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] The Regina manuscript has: “which is possessed by our spirit,” and shortly afterward, together with the older edition: “as a father, to be inherited by us”; “fellow heirs with Christ,” without the words “having bestowed spiritual gifts.”]

### 43

But since this too has been expounded according to our ability, let us set forth a passage from the Prophet containing certain things concerning the Holy Spirit, so that we may be taught not only from the New Testament but also from the Old concerning faith in him and understanding of him.

For we said above that the grace of the Holy Spirit has been active in all the saints, both those who lived after the coming of our Lord and those of earlier times—namely, the Patriarchs and Prophets—and that he filled them with various gifts and virtues.

For just as those who possessed the grace of the one God and of his Only-Begotten—both those who lived before his coming and those who lived afterward—raised the banner of righteousness and attained knowledge of the truth, so they also possessed the grace of the Holy Spirit, since we have shown in many passages above that the Holy Spirit is inseparable from the Father and the Son.

It is therefore written in the Prophet:

“I remembered the mercies of the Lord and his power in all the things that he bestowed on us. The Lord is a good judge to the house of Israel, bringing upon us according to his mercy and according to the multitude of his righteousness. And he said:

‘Surely my people are sons, and they will not transgress.’

“And he became salvation for them from all their tribulation. Not an ambassador, nor an angel, but he himself saved them, because he loved them and spared them. He himself redeemed them, received them, and exalted them throughout all the days of the age. But they did not believe and provoked his Holy Spirit, and he turned against them in hostility. He himself fought against them and remembered the ancient days—he who brought up from the land the shepherd of sheep, who placed his Holy Spirit within them, gathering Moses with his right hand” (Isa. 63:7 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0140D] It will be worthwhile to reconsider this notable passage from Isaiah against the Greek exemplar, on whose authority we have corrected several points. Instead of “Were not my people sons?” the text formerly had, in a negative sense, “My people were not sons,” contrary to the testimony of the Regina and Vatican manuscripts. The Greek likewise has Οὐχ ὁ λαός μου … (“Was not my people …”).]

### 44

Those who have frequently received God’s benefits, knowing that they obtained them more through his grace and mercy than through works originating from themselves, speak as though united in one agreement and one mind: “I remembered the mercies of the Lord.”

Reflecting on the gifts they had frequently received from him through Moses, they give thanks and, together with his mercy, remember the Lord’s powers—whether the miracles he repeatedly performed for them among the nations, or the advances of the soul by which they were instructed through the Law, the Prophets, and his salutary commandments.

For in the Scriptures the word “power” has both meanings.

They say that they remember his mercy and his powers in all that he has bestowed upon them—not according to their own righteousness, but according to the mercy and goodness of him who is the good judge of the house that sees,

[Note: [Col. 0140D] The older edition has: “and of the pure understanding that sees God.”]

and of the understanding that sees the Lord with a pure heart.

For this is what “Israel” is interpreted to mean in our language from the Hebrew expression: “a mind seeing God.”

[Note: [Col. 0140D] Previously, contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts, the text had “the Lord.” This etymology of the name Israel—*νοῦς ὁρῶν Θεόν* (“a mind seeing God”)—was especially welcomed by Greek writers, including Olympiodorus on Ecclesiastes 1, Leontius *On the Sects*, Theophanes Cerameus, and others. Among Latin writers, it may be found in Optatus of Milevis, book II at the end, and also in Jerome, though according to the opinion of others. Elsewhere we have discussed what can be extracted from that word.]

Although the judge sometimes inflicts punishments and torments upon those who deserve judgment, nevertheless the person who looks more deeply into the causes of things, seeing the purpose of his goodness—for he desires to correct the sinner—confesses that he is good, saying: “Bring upon us according to his mercy.”

For if the Lord were to consider the iniquities of those whom he judges, who could endure? But because there is forgiveness with the Lord, the Lord—our Lord and Savior—brings upon us according to his mercy everything that advances us toward salvation.

[Col. 0141D] He also brings it according to his mercy, doing this in judgment, when in righteousness he bestows on us what he has granted with mercy and goodness mingled together.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] The words “and doing this” are deleted in the Regina manuscript; shortly afterward the Vatican manuscript has: “he bestows on us, because he granted these things according to the goodness of his mercy.”]

### 45

[Note: [Col. 0141D] Other editors begin the third book here, a matter discussed above in the prefixed Admonition. It is especially incongruous that they should have begun it in the middle of the exposition of the passage from Isaiah.]

The present passage refutes the error of heretics who, separating goodness from justice, invented one good God and another just God.

For here the same God is both good and judge, restoring according to his mercy and justice, and subsisting equally as good and just.

It is therefore futile, by fabricating an unjust doctrine, to maintain that the God of the Gospel is good while the God of the Old Testament is just, since in many other passages as well, and now in the Prophet’s statement, God is written to be a good judge. Conversely, contrary to what they wish, in the Epistle of the Apostle Paul—who is certainly a preacher of the New Testament—God is reported as a just judge: “There is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:8).

The God of the New and Old Testaments is therefore the same, whether they wish it or not—the creator of visible and invisible things. The Savior also clearly bears witness in the Gospel that the Father is just and good: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John 17:11). And in another place: “No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10:18).

In the Old Law too, God is called just in one place and good in another. In the Psalms: “The Lord is just, and he has loved righteousness” (Ps. 10:8). Conversely, in Jeremiah: “The Lord is good to those who wait for him.” Again, in the Psalms: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. 72:1).

These things have been said briefly, as it were incidentally, against the heretics. It is now time to continue the Prophet’s intended sequence, which proceeds as follows:

“And he said”—there is no doubt that the Lord said it—“Surely my people are sons, and they will not transgress” (Isa. 1:5).

[Note: [Col. 0141D] The Regina manuscript reads: “They defend the one as good from the Gospel and the other as just from the Old Testament.”]

“They were not,” he says, “like those who were begotten and exalted and despised him who begot them.” And he became salvation for them—that is, for those concerning whom the Lord says, “Surely my people are sons, and they will not transgress.”

The very fact that they did not transgress or despise the Father became salvation for them; or, alternatively, the fact that they were called sons became the cause of salvation for them.

This salvation, bestowed by Christ the Lord, is also confirmed by the voice of the angel to the shepherds, who says: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:10).

[Note: [Col. 0142D] The Vatican manuscript has: “a great Gospel,” and “there has been born for you,” differing from the Greek text itself.]

He became for all who believe in him an occasion of eternal salvation; and he is the Savior of the world, who came to seek what had perished. He is also the one of whom the choir of saints sings: “Our God, the God of salvation” (Ps. 67).

[Note: [Col. 0142D] The Toulouse manuscript has: “God, God, God of salvation.”]

### 46

Since it was God who provided eternal salvation, it was said: “Not an ambassador, nor an angel”—that is, not a prophet, not a patriarch, not Moses the lawgiver—“saved them.”

All those whom I have named could act as ambassadors before the Lord on behalf of the people. Thus Moses, interceding with him for the sinful populace, says: “If you forgive them their sin, forgive it” (Exod. 32:31). But he begged for pardon, fasting for forty days and urging God’s mercy through the affliction of his soul.

Yet no one from among these ambassadors can be the savior, since he himself requires the one who is truly the giver of salvation.

The angels too, although they are spirits and are sent for various ministries on behalf of those who are to receive salvation, are not the authors of salvation. Rather, they interpret and announce the one who is the fountain of salvation.

Hence it was said: “Not an ambassador, nor an angel, but the Lord himself saved them.” He did so for no other reason than that he loved them and spared them.

To spare is said of them as of his creatures, according to what is written elsewhere: “But you spare all things, Lord, lover of souls, because they are yours; for you do not hate anything that you have made” (Wis. 11:29).

Therefore, for their salvation, the Father did not spare his own Son but handed him over to death, so that through the death of his Son, after the one who held the power of death—that is, the devil—had been destroyed, he might redeem all who were held by him in the bond of captivity.

Hence it follows: “He himself redeemed them, received them, and exalted them.” He receives those who have been saved and exalts them; he lifts the redeemed on high on the wings of virtues and by instruction and knowledge of the truth—not for one day or another only, but throughout all the days of eternity—dwelling in them and with them, granting them life until the consummation of the age and remaining the author of their salvation.

Illuminating their hearts throughout all the days of the age, he does not allow them to remain in the darkness of ignorance and error. I think this is what is meant by the statement that they were exalted throughout all the days.

### 47

[Col. 0142D] Because they were changeable and willingly prone to vices, after such great benefits they proved unbelieving toward God, abandoned his commandments, and provoked the Holy Spirit of God, who had bestowed many good things upon them. They fell into a sin like that of those who, after being begotten and exalted, despised their father.

Or perhaps the same people are being described here who were described earlier, since there too, after their sin, it is said to them: “You have abandoned the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger”; and here: “They did not believe and provoked his Holy Spirit.”

From the present passage, therefore, the Spirit’s fellowship with the Lord is demonstrated. The person who abandons the Lord, is unbelieving, and provokes the Holy One of Israel to anger also provokes his Holy Spirit. The same indignation against sinners is referred both to the Holy Spirit and to the Holy One of Israel.

Hence, in what follows, a similar conjunction of the Trinity is shown when Scripture says that the Lord turned to hostility against those who provoked his Holy Spirit and handed them over to everlasting torment, after they had blasphemed against his Holy Spirit not merely in speech but in their actions.

He, therefore, who turned against them in hostility fought against them and subjected them to manifold and prolonged torments, so that they might obtain forgiveness for their sins neither in the present age nor in the future. For they provoked his Holy Spirit and blasphemed against him.

### 48

But if you wish to understand this of the Jews, who crucified the Lord the Savior and therefore provoked the Holy Spirit, the statement “He himself defeated them” must be referred to the interpretation that they were handed over to the Romans, when the wrath of God came upon them to the end. For throughout the whole world and in every region they alone, exiled from their homeland, wander in a foreign land, possessing neither their ancient city nor their own dwellings; and they have received in return what they did to the Prophets and to their Savior. Because they were bloodthirsty and always seized by mad fury [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Regius manuscript, together with the old edition, read “seized by fury.”], they not only killed the 155 Prophets and stoned those who had been sent to them, but, advancing to the height of impiety, betrayed and crucified the Lord the Savior, who had deigned to descend to earth for the salvation of all. Therefore they were expelled from the city which they had stained with the blood of the Prophets and of Christ.

According to this meaning, then, we must understand that they were defeated by the Lord, not for a short time, but for the entire age to come, until the consummation of the world [Note: A full stop had been placed here. “Until the consummation of the world,” as we have said, etc.; the manuscripts correct the passage.]. For, as we have said, fugitives and captives, they wander among all nations, possessing neither a city nor a territory of their own.

Nevertheless, because the one who defeated them is by nature kind and merciful, he granted them a place for repentance, if they should wish to turn to better things. Hence it is also said, “He remembered the days of the age.” For, remembering future times, he opened the closed door to them to some extent [Note: The printed editions had the words in part in a faulty transposition; some of the manuscripts correct them.], so that, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel—whoever shall be worthy of this name—will be saved.

Although they burst forth into such recklessness that they killed the one who had been sent for their sake, saying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25), nevertheless God raised him from the earth, in whose heart he had dwelt for three days and three nights, as the shepherd of his sheep. For the passage continues: “He who brought up from the earth the shepherd of his sheep” (Isaiah 63:12).

### 49

That the God who is the shepherd of the sheep, who is now described in the prophetic utterance, is the Lord, we learn more clearly in the Gospel, with the Savior himself bearing witness: “I am the good shepherd, and I lay down my life for my sheep” (John 10:11). And again: “My sheep hear my voice.”

After all these things the Prophet says: “Where is he who placed his Holy Spirit upon them?” (Isaiah 63:11) [Note: In the manuscripts, *Prophetes* is frequently written in the nominative, following Greek usage; hence the printed editions, quite improperly, read *Prophetis*. It is Isaiah, however, whose exposition is continuing here.]. For he marvels at the great happiness from which they have fallen into such great misery [Note: The printed editions, and even some manuscripts, wrongly read “and how does he speak?” The old edition has: “who redeemed them, who exalted them, who placed [his Spirit among] them,” etc.]. In a manner he says:

“He who redeemed them, who placed his Holy Spirit among them, dwelling with them—where is he now? Where has he gone?” He abandoned them because they had first abandoned him and provoked the Holy One of Israel.

God had placed his Holy Spirit in them long ago, when they were still good and were striving to obey his commandments. For the Holy Spirit is inserted only into those who, having abandoned vices, pursue the company of virtues and live in faith in Christ according to those virtues and through them.

But if, as negligence gradually creeps in, they begin to drift toward worse things, they stir up against themselves the Holy Spirit who dwells in them, and they turn the one who gave him toward hostility [Note: The printed editions, through the prompting of negligence, read less correctly: “if they should begin to drift toward worse things.”].

Something similar to this the Apostle also says in writing to the Thessalonians: “For God did not call us to impurity, but to sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:7).

### 50

Therefore whoever despises—or, as is better found in the Greek, whoever transgresses [Note: Another reading has *praevaricantur*, “they transgress”; the Greek is ἀθετήσωσι, “they reject” or “set aside.”]—does not transgress against a human being, but against God, who gave his Holy Spirit in you.

For in these words God, calling through faith to sanctification—that is, so that believers might become holy through the Holy Spirit—gave them the Holy Spirit. And as long as they kept God’s commandments, the Holy Spirit whom they had received remained in them. But when they fell through slippery love [Note: The Vatican manuscript has a corrupt reading; the old edition has “through love of vices,” etc.] and sank into impurity, they despised—or transgressed against—the Lord who had given them the Holy Spirit, so that they might not serve impurity but might be sanctified.

Therefore those who committed these things will suffer punishment, despising not a human being but God. And so that we may know that the Holy Spirit who is given to believers is the Lord, let us learn it from the words of Isaiah himself, who introduces someone saying to the Lord: “My Spirit is in you, and I have placed my words in your mouth” (Isaiah 59:21).

The present passage shows that whoever has received the Spirit of God possesses with him also the words of God, namely, words of knowledge and wisdom. Again, in another place the same Prophet has God say: “I have placed my Spirit upon him” (Isaiah 42:1).

He who placed the Holy Spirit among them recalls that Moses was sanctified by his right hand—whether this means that illustrious man and initiate into the mysteries of God, concerning whom the Lord says to Joshua son of Nun, “Moses my servant,” or whether it means his Law, which was written in the Old Instrument. For I remember frequently reading that Moses is used as a name for the Law, as in the Apostle: “Until this very day, whenever Moses is read” (2 Corinthians 3:14). And Abraham says to the rich man who was suffering torment: “They have Moses and the Prophets” (Luke 16:29). It is clearly established there that Moses does not signify the man mentioned above, but the Law.

### 51

Furthermore, what is the right hand of God that brought forth Moses, unless it is our Lord and Savior? For he is the right hand of the Father, through whom he saves, exalts, and accomplishes mighty works, as it is said elsewhere of God: “His right hand and his holy arm saved him” (Psalm 97:1) [Note: The same books read “his right hand saved him.” The Greek is ἔσωσεν αὐτῷ, “saved for him.”].

And again: “The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me. I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the Lord” (Psalm 117:16).

This voice is certainly spoken in the person of the Lordly Man [Note: Some of the Fathers formerly objected to calling the Savior “the Lordly Man,” suspecting that this expression separated man from the Lord and divided Christ by some novel subtlety. In fact, this formula of speech belonged particularly to the Apollinarians; Gregory of Nazianzus criticizes it in Letter 1 to Cledonius. Hence Rufinus also invented against Jerome the story which he himself relates in *Apology*, book II: that when the Apollinarians received Athanasius’ book, in which *Lordly Man* was written, for reading, they altered it so that they rewrote in the erasure what they had scraped away, in order that it might seem not to have been falsified by them but added by Jerome. Finally, when Augustine had used this expression in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 36, he later wished it corrected in *Retractions*, book I, chapter 19, because, since Christ is Lord, it was improper to call him “Lordly,” as though it meant that he was not God and Lord but merely “lordly”—that is, a human subsistent united to the Lord, or to the Lord’s subsistent being. In this way two subsistent beings would be posited in Christ, as Nestorius blasphemed.

Nevertheless, other writers, especially Greeks, use the expression without hesitation. Saint Gregory of Nyssa, *Second Oration on Saint Stephen*: ὁ μὲν κυριακὸς ἄνθρωπος τοῦ σωτῆρος, “the Lordly Man of the Savior.” Saint Epiphanius likewise, in *Ancoratus*, no. 95, and others. Among the Latins, Cassian, *Conferences*, II.13: “That Lordly Man,” he says, “who redeemed the human race.” For this expression, as also in the present passage of Didymus, which is the reason for writing this note, the explanation of Saint Thomas should be applied, *Summa Theologiae*, III, question 16, article 3: “The Lordly Man can be defended in a certain respect, namely, because one may say that ‘Lordly Man’ is said with reference to the human nature, which the word ‘man’ signifies, and not with reference to the subsistent being.”].

The passage itself clearly proves that this is spoken of the Lordly Man whom the only-begotten Son of God deigned to assume from the Virgin, because he is the right hand of God. Thus it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, born of a virgin, when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her.

Concerning him David prophesied in the Spirit that, rising from the dead, he was taken up into the heavens and raised by the right hand of God [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “raised to the right hand of God”; this is not correct.]. It is written there as follows:

“David, foreseeing this, spoke concerning the resurrection of Christ, that he was not abandoned in Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. God raised this Jesus, and of this we are all witnesses. Therefore, having been exalted by the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit, he poured out this gift upon us, which you see and hear; for David did not ascend into the heavens” (Acts 2:31–34) [Note: The old edition reads, “his soul was not abandoned in Hades.” A little farther below, the words “the gift among us” are missing.].

There can be no doubt that the Lord Jesus, exalted by the right hand of God and risen from the dead, is the one of whom Scripture itself bears witness. Therefore this one who rose from the dead says: “I slept and took my sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord raised me” (Psalm 3:6).

### 52

Therefore he who, taken up into heaven by the word of God, is proclaimed to have been raised by that right hand of God of which we spoke above, both received from the Father the promises of the Holy Spirit and poured him out upon believers, so that they spoke in every tongue of the mighty works of God [Note: Another reading is: “Therefore this one who, rising from the dead by the word of God,” etc.].

The Lordly Man also received a communication of the Holy Spirit, as it is written in the Gospels: “Jesus, filled with the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1; the supplied citation reads Luke 1:67). And in another place: “Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee” (Luke 4:14; the supplied citation reads Luke 8:55).

These statements about the Lordly Man, who is the whole Christ, the one Jesus Son of God, must be received without any slanderous implication, in a pious sense—not as though he were one person and another, but because the discussion concerns one and the same being, considered according to the nature of God and according to the nature of man. For God the Word, the only-begotten Son of God, receives neither change nor increase. Indeed, he himself is the fullness of every good thing [Note: These words are absent from the old edition: “who is the whole Christ, the one Jesus Son of God.” Certainly, to prevent “Lordly Man” from being understood in the Apollinarian sense, they were added either by Didymus or by Jerome, or by others—I cannot determine. Recall the preceding note.].

### 53

Enough, and more than enough, has been said concerning the Prophet’s testimony. Let us not proceed to the remaining matters, so that we may know that just as the Father and the Son perfect the holy and good through their participation in them, so also the Holy Spirit makes believers good and holy through participation in himself, and that from this he is also shown to be of one substance with the Father and the Son [Note: The words “we know that” are absent from the Vatican manuscript and the old edition. A little farther on, the Regius manuscript reads “makes his believers good.”].

It is said to the Lord in the Psalms: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a level land.” We know that in some copies it is written, “Your Holy Spirit” (Nehemiah 9). In Ezra, however, he is unambiguously called the Good Spirit: “You gave your good Spirit to make them understand” (Ephesians 3:4).

That the Father sanctifies, the Apostle writes, saying: “But may the God of peace sanctify you completely” [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “sanctify you in all things,” in agreement with the Vulgate. The Greek is ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς, “you wholly” or “completely.”]. And the Savior says: “Holy Father, sanctify them in the truth, because your word is truth” (John 17:11).

He says plainly: “In me”—who am your word and your truth—“sanctify them through faith in me and participation in me.”

God is also called good elsewhere: “No one is good except one, God” (Luke 18:19). Above we also showed that the Son sanctifies, with Paul agreeing in the same words: “For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.” He indicates that Christ is the one who sanctifies, and that those are sanctified who can say: “Christ Jesus became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

He is also called the Spirit of sanctification. Hence it is said to him: “All the sanctified are under your hands and are under you.”

Our Lord Jesus Christ is good, and he was begotten from the good Father. Of him we read: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Psalm 117:1). Let those give thanks to him who either beseech him for forgiveness of sins or return thanks for the benefits granted by his clemency.

The Holy Spirit also sanctifies those whom he deigns to fill, as has already been demonstrated above, when we showed that he can be participated in and received by many at once. And now, in Paul’s present testimony, he is shown to be the giver of sanctification, where Paul says: “But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose us as firstfruits for salvation, in sanctification of the Holy Spirit and belief in the truth” (1 Thessalonians 2:13) [Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “in the sanctification of the Spirit the Father and the truth are possessed.”].

For in this passage also the gifts of God are implicitly understood to be in the Spirit, since in the sanctification of the Spirit faith and truth are possessed together.

### 54

Since, therefore, we have spoken correctly, piously, and in accordance with the truth, the designation “sanctification,” as well as “goodness,” is equally referred to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, just as the designation “Spirit” itself is.

For the Father is also called Spirit, as in the statement: “God is Spirit” (John 4:24). The Son too is called Spirit: “The Lord,” he says, “is Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:17) [Note: I restore and punctuate these two Scriptural texts, which had been very badly received. In one copy the reading was “the Lord” or “of the Lord, his Spirit,” instead of “is.”].

The Holy Spirit, however, is always designated by the title “Holy Spirit,” not because he is named with the Father and the Son merely through sharing the word “Spirit,” but because he possesses one nature and one name with them.

Since the word “spirit” signifies many things, we must briefly enumerate the things to which this name is applied.

“Spirit” is used for wind, as in Ezekiel: “You shall scatter a third part into the spirit”—that is, into the wind (Ezekiel 5:2). If you wish to understand historically the statement, “With a violent spirit you will break the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm 47:8), there too “spirit” means nothing other than wind.

Solomon also received among many gifts from God the ability to know the violence of spirits; by this he shows that he received nothing other than knowledge of the swift blasts of winds and of the causes by which their nature is sustained.

“Spirit” is also used for the soul, as in the Epistle of James: “Just as your body without spirit is dead,” and what follows (James 2:26) [Note: The Regius manuscript substitutes another passage from the Epistle of James, namely 4:5: “The Spirit that dwells in you desires to envy”; it then adds, “For the spirit means nothing other than,” etc. In the passage presented here, the Vatican manuscript does not have the word “your,” nor does the text of James itself.].

For it is perfectly clear that here “spirit” is nothing other than the soul. In accordance with this understanding, Stephen also calls his soul his spirit, saying: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:58).

We must also consider the statement in Ecclesiastes: “Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward and the spirit of the beast goes downward to the earth?” (Ecclesiastes 3:2). Are the souls of animals also called spirits?

Apart from the soul, and in addition to our spirit, another spirit is said to exist in a human being, concerning which Paul writes: “For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him?” (1 Corinthians 2:11) [Note: The printed editions, and generally the manuscripts as well, had hitherto read: “and except the Holy Spirit, another spirit,” etc. I have substituted “our spirit,” following the Regius manuscript, and especially on the basis of sound reasoning and the meaning of Paul’s testimony.].

If someone should insist that “soul” is signified here by “spirit,” what human being is there whose thoughts, hidden matters, and secret things of the heart another human being does not know, except his own spirit? For it would be utterly foolish to try to understand this of an isolated body.

### 55

But if someone attempts to creep in through clever deceit, asserting that these words are written about the Holy Spirit, he will cease to maintain this falsehood if he carefully considers the words themselves.

For it is written: “Who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also the things of God no one knows except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

Just as a human being is one thing and God another, so also the spirit of the human being that is in him is distinct from the Spirit of God who is in him—the Holy Spirit, as we have often shown.

In another passage too the same Apostle distinguishes the Spirit of God from our spirit, saying: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit” (Romans 8:16). By this he signifies that the Spirit of God, that is, the Holy Spirit, bears witness to our spirit—the spirit which we have just said is the spirit of the human being.

He also says to the Thessalonians: “May your spirit and soul and body be kept whole” (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

For just as the soul is one thing and the body another, so the spirit is one thing and the soul another, which is specifically named in its own place. Concerning this spirit he prayed [Alternative: “he prays”] that it might be preserved whole together with the soul and body, because it is incredible and blasphemous to suppose that the Apostle prayed for the Holy Spirit to be preserved whole, since the Holy Spirit can receive neither diminution [Note: I read this from the old edition; in the others the reading was “change”] nor increase.

Thus, as we have said, the Apostle’s statement here bears witness to the human spirit.

### 56

The heavenly and rational powers, which Scripture usually calls Angels and Powers, are also called “spirits,” as in the statement: “You make your angels spirits” (Psalm 103:4) [Alternative: “he makes.”]. And elsewhere: “Are they not all ministering spirits?” (Hebrews 1:14).

I think that the statement in the Acts of the Apostles should also be referred to this meaning: “The Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more” (Acts 8:39); that is, the Angel of the Lord, lifting Philip up on high, carried him to another place.

Other rational creatures also, voluntarily falling away from good into evil, are called evil spirits and unclean spirits, as in the statement: “But when the unclean spirit has gone out of a person.” And shortly afterward: “He takes seven other spirits more evil than himself” (Matthew 12:43).

Demons are also called spirits in the Gospels. But this must also be noted: the contrary spirit is never designated simply as “spirit,” but with some qualification, such as “unclean spirit” or “spirit of a demon.” Those who are holy, however, are called “spirits” simply, without any qualification.

### 57

We must also know that the word “spirit” expresses both the human will and the mind’s judgment.

For the Apostle, wishing a virgin to be holy not only in deed but also in mind—that is, not only in body but also in the inward movement of the heart—says: “So that she may be holy both in body and in spirit” (1 Corinthians 7:34). By “spirit” he signifies the will, and by “body” the works.

Consider whether this same meaning is expressed in Isaiah, where it is written: “And those who err in spirit shall know understanding” (Isaiah 29:24). Those who, through error of judgment, regard one thing instead of another as good will receive understanding, so that their error may be corrected and they may choose what is right instead of what is perverse [Alternative: “instead of what is chosen with good intention.”].

Consider also whether the statement, “The one strength of your spirit” [Alternative: “our spirit”], expresses the same thing.

Above all, however, the word “spirit” signifies a higher and mystical understanding in the Holy Scriptures, as in the statement: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). By “letter” he means the simple and manifest narrative according to history; by “spirit,” the holy and spiritual understanding of what is read [Note: Again I follow the same edition and the Vatican manuscript; previously the reading was “to know” instead of “to understand.”].

This meaning is also in agreement with the statement: “We are the circumcision, who serve the Lord in spirit and do not trust in the flesh” (Philippians 3:3).

Those who do not cut the flesh according to the letter, but circumcise the heart in spirit, removing all its excess—that which is close and friendly to generation—are truly circumcised in spirit, Jews inwardly and true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit [Note: The text was corrupt and disjointed: it had “and these” instead of “truly,” followed by the new error “true Israelites” instead of “truly” or “true.”].

Transcending the shadows and images of the Old Testament, true worshipers worship the Father in spirit and truth: in spirit, because they have transcended bodily and lowly things; in truth, because, abandoning types, shadows, and copies, they have come to the substance of truth itself. And, as we have already said, rejecting the lowly and bodily simplicity of the words, they have reached a spiritual knowledge of the Law.

### 58

For the present, according to the ability of our understanding, we have touched upon the number of things signified by “spirit.” At the proper time, if Christ grants it, we shall explain what each signifies.

Sometimes the Spirit is also called our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, the Son of God. For the Spirit is kind and is the Spirit of wisdom.

And elsewhere: “The Lord is Spirit,” as we said earlier, adding there also the statement, “God is Spirit” (John 4:24)—not merely according to a sharing of the name, but according to participation in nature and substance.

For just as it sometimes happens that things whose substance is different are called by a common name, and these are called *homonyms* (ὁμώνυμα), so, when things have the same nature and substance, equality of nature is joined to their sharing of a name; the discipline of dialecticians calls these *synonyms* (συνώνυμα).

Therefore the word “Spirit,” and whatever other terms are customarily used of the Trinity, is a *synonym*: for example, “holy” and “good,” and other expressions of this kind, which we touched upon shortly above [Note: I correct the text from the old edition: “Holy, good,” since “good spirit” was contrary to the author’s meaning.].

### 59

We have necessarily been led to these matters because, since the designation “Spirit” is frequently scattered throughout the divine Scriptures, we must not slip through misunderstanding of the name, but must take each occurrence according to the variety of its contexts and meanings.

Therefore, contemplating with every effort and care where and how the word “Spirit” is used, let us crush the sophistries and fraudulent snares of those who assert that the Holy Spirit is a creature.

For when they read in the Prophet, “I am the one who establishes the thunder and creates the spirit” (Amos 4:12) [Note: Instead of “I am the one who establishes,” the Greek has στερεῶν, “establishing”; the reading was “I confirmed.” Some manuscripts have “I am the one who forms.”], they ignorantly supposed from this expression that the Holy Spirit was being indicated, although in this passage the name “spirit” means wind.

Likewise, when they hear in Zechariah that the Lord said he is the one who creates the spirit of a human being within him, they thought that the Holy Spirit was signified even in that chapter, failing to notice that the designation “spirit” means either the human soul or the spirit—which, as we have already said, is a third element in the human being.

Therefore, as we stated at the outset, let us consider how each expression is used, lest through ignorance we fall into the abyss of error.

For when error arises from a sharing of names in other matters, it brings confusion and shame upon the one who has erred. But a fall from heavenly and divine matters into wickedness leads to eternal punishment and Tartarus [Alternative: “the abyss”], especially when someone, once deceived, refuses to recover but shamelessly defends his error.

It was also fitting, and the magnitude of the book required it, that the discourse should now come to an end.

### 60
