But because a question arises against what we discussed above—which we then set aside so that it would not break into the texture of the discourse and place an impious controversy amid a pious exposition—I think it necessary to respond to it according to the subject and leave the judgment concerning these matters to the reader.

When we argued above that no creature can fill the soul or mind of a human being according to its substance, but that the mind is filled by created things only according to their operation and according to the error or virtue of the will, our question arose as though it dissolved this position: the created substance called Satan in the Scriptures is said to enter certain people and to fill the heart of some.

For to the man who had kept back part of the price of the field he had sold, claiming otherwise, the Apostle Peter said: “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart?” (Acts 5:3). And the Savior himself says concerning Judas that Satan entered into him.

This must be answered later. For the moment, let us argue against the statement that is written: “Why has Satan filled your heart?” How can Satan fill someone’s mind and the ruling faculty of the heart [Note: In Greek, ἡγεμονικόν, “the ruling faculty”; see the *Commentaries on Matthew*], without entering into him and into his understanding and, so to speak, entering through the doorway of his heart? Such power belongs to the Trinity alone.

Rather, Satan fills it as a certain crafty, wicked, deceitful, and fraudulent deceiver who draws the human soul toward an inclination to evil through thoughts and incitements to vices, with which he himself is full.

Thus Elymas the magician, himself a son of the devil, existing in accordance with wickedness and depravity, is written to have been full of every deceit and wickedness. His father Satan had implanted this will in him, as though by custom [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “as though by custom, almost introducing a second nature.”].

The Apostle Paul therefore reproves and rebukes him, saying: “O man full of all deceit and all wickedness, son of the devil, enemy of the righteousness of God!” (Acts 13:10).

Because he had received into himself every deceitful fraud, being crooked and crafty, he is called a son of the devil, because he filled that one's entire ruling faculty with fraud, iniquity, and every wickedness, enticing and deceiving him so greatly that Satan himself was thought to have filled his soul and to dwell in that same man whom he had prepared as a minister and servant for all the deceptions of his perversity [Note: The same manuscript reads, “whom he had prepared for himself as a minister and son.”].

### 61

As for the second example we had proposed [Vatican manuscript: “had proposed” instead of “had placed”], namely, that Satan had entered Judas, this must be said.

The devil observed through certain movements and signs of action toward which vices Judas’s heart was especially inclined. He discovered that Judas was open to the snares of avarice. Having found an entrance through greed, he put into his mind how he might obtain the money he desired and, through the opportunity for profit, become a betrayer of his teacher and Savior, exchanging piety for silver and accepting the price of his crime from the Pharisees and Jews.

This opportunity for thought therefore gave Satan a place, so that, entering his heart, he might fill him with the worst intention.

He entered, then, not according to substance but according to operation, because to enter into someone according to substance belongs to the uncreated nature which can be participated in by many. The devil, therefore, is not a being who can be participated in, but exists as a creature, not as the Creator.

Consequently he is changeable and mutable; he fell from holiness and virtue. Above we said that what is *participable* (μετοχικόν; the manuscript has μετοχικῶς), that is, what is received through participation, is incorruptible and immutable and, consequently, eternal. But what can change has been made and has a beginning. What is incorruptible, on the other hand, exists eternally both backward and forward.

Therefore the devil does not fill anyone, as some think, through participation in nature or substance, nor does he become the inhabitant of anyone in that manner. Rather, through fraud, deception, and wickedness, he is believed to dwell in the one whom he has filled.

Through this deception he also entered the elders who had turned their love toward Susanna into cruelty [Note: The old edition reads, “who had turned their love toward Susanna into cruelty.” The Vatican manuscript reads, “who were raging against Susanna; he turned them toward cruelty and filled their souls,” etc.], filling their souls with the fire of lust and the belated pleasure of old age.

For it is written: “Then two elders came, full of an evil thought” (Daniel 13:28).

Through these snares he also filled the entire Jewish people, as the Prophet says concerning them: “Woe, sinful nation, a people full of sins, an evil seed, unrighteous children” (Isaiah 1:4).

The devil is an evil seed, and his children, because of their iniquity and fullness of sin, are called sinners [Note: The Regius manuscript reads “children of the Devil.” A little farther on, the Vatican manuscript has “were called children of sinners”; both senses are acceptable unless the latter is preferable.].

If, then, the devil is not received by those who are called his children in Scripture according to participation in substance [Alternative: “are not named in that way”]—since it has frequently been shown to be impossible for this to occur among creatures—no one else can receive him by participation in substance, but only by assuming a most fraudulent will.

We have said that operations and pursuits—not only of good works but also of evil—can be participated in among creatures; but nature and substance can enter into others only in the case of the Trinity [Note: The Regius manuscript expresses this more fully: “but also of evil things can be participated in among creatures, whereas we said that the nature and substance of the Trinity alone can enter into others.”].

### 62

The proposed question has, I think, been sufficiently answered.

But since it seems inept and foolish to respond to foolish statements, and to wish to refute whatever may fall from the mouths of the impious [Alternative: “whatever may rush forth”], for it is not so great an impiety to propose wicked things as to wish to debate wicked things in opposition to them [Note: The text had an awkward reading: “at least wishing to resist.” In the next passage, with a certain error, it read “what they usually handle” instead of “what they usually boast or proclaim,” which is found in the better manuscripts.], I therefore pass over what they habitually boast, proclaiming against us with sacrilegious audacity:

“If the Holy Spirit was not created, then he is either the brother of God the Father, or the uncle of the only-begotten Jesus Christ, or the son of Christ, or the grandson of God the Father, or he himself is the Son of God. And then the Lord Jesus will no longer be the only-begotten, since he has another brother.”

Wretched and pitiable people! They do not understand that one may not reason about incorporeal and invisible beings according to the nature of corporeal and visible things.

“Brother,” “uncle,” “grandson,” and “son” are names for bodies and terms belonging to human weakness. The Trinity transcends all these designations. Whenever any of these terms is applied to it, it does not speak of its own nature through our names and inappropriate vocabulary [Note: The text improperly had “not according to its own nature”; the Vatican manuscript and the old edition correct it.].

Since, therefore, Holy Scripture says no more about the Trinity than that God is the Father of the Savior and that the Son was begotten by the Father, we ought to hold only what has been written. And once it has been shown that the Holy Spirit is uncreated, we should consequently understand that, since his substance is not created, he is rightly joined in fellowship with the Father and the Son.

63. Let these statements suffice for the present, in view of the poverty of our eloquence, indicating my fear at having dared to speak about the Holy Spirit. [Note: The Regina manuscript and the Vatican edition read: “I have indicated only my fear in this, that I have dared to speak about the Holy Spirit.”] For whoever blasphemes against him shall not be forgiven—not only in this age but also in the age to come. Nor is any mercy or pardon reserved for one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God and insulted [another reading: “subjected to contumely”] the Spirit of his grace, in whom he was sanctified. The same must also be understood of God the Father. For whoever blasphemes against him and acts impiously will be tormented without pardon, [Note: The same Regina manuscript reads: “with no one in any way interceding with the Lord for him.”] with no one interceding with the Lord for him, as it is written: “But whoever sins against the Lord God, who will pray for him?” Nor will the one who denies the Son before human beings be acknowledged by him before the Father and his angels.

Therefore, since no pardon is granted to those who blaspheme against the Trinity, we must take every care and precaution lest, even in a brief and very short discussion of it, we slip. Rather, if anyone wishes to read this volume, we ask that he cleanse himself from every evil deed and from the worst thoughts, so that, with an enlightened heart, he may understand what is said; and, filled with holiness and wisdom, forgive us wherever the outcome has not fulfilled our intention. Let him consider only with what mind something has been said, not in what words it has been expressed. For just as we boldly claim for ourselves, in accordance with our conscience, the sense of piety, so, as far as concerns speaking about it, we frankly confess that rhetorical elegance and eloquence, in keeping with the sequence and texture of the discourse, are far from us. [Note: The word “us” was improperly inserted here, and the sense was defective. I have deleted it with the help of the Regina manuscript, which likewise omits the word and reads somewhat more smoothly: “eloquence in accordance with the sequence.”] Our aim, when discussing the Holy Scriptures, was piously to understand what has been written and not to be unaware of the limits and inadequacy of our own speech.

[Col. 0153]

# DIALOGUE AGAINST THE LUCIFERIANS

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Book

It is well known that this was the position of Lucifer, bishop of Calaris: those who had subscribed to the perfidy of Arius at the Council of Ariminum could no longer enter into communion with the Church, even if they repented. He therefore completely withdrew even from communion with those who, after satisfaction or penance, had received the lapsed. For, says Sulpicius, *History*, book II, chapter 45, “he condemned those who had been at Ariminum to such an extent that he even separated himself from communion with those who would receive them after satisfaction or penance.”

From this arose the heresy of the Luciferians, who rashly asserted that the Holy Spirit was not conferred by Arians and by bishops who had once agreed with them; that such men had fallen from the episcopate and the priestly office in such a way that every power of administering the sacraments had been taken away from them; and that they themselves were unwilling to receive even those baptized by them except through the laying on of hands and the invocation of the Holy Spirit.

On this matter a Luciferian and an Orthodox Christian once disputed. As commonly happens, however, each wrangled more through insults than arguments, and each had broken his opponent rather than defeated him. It was therefore agreed that they should meet on the following day; and, as they argued, what each said in support of his own position was taken down by notaries. In this book Jerome presents the matter as a dialogue, as though the words proceeded from the mouths of the disputants. Yet there is no doubt that the holy Doctor carefully composed and polished the work in order to defend the faith of Catholic truth.

For he introduces a large part of the proceedings of the Council of Ariminum and speaks of its history and of the Arians’ devices and deceptions—especially of the fact that the heretics prevailed upon the Orthodox to reject the term *ousia* in order to restore peace, while pretending to agree with them in all other respects; but, once they had bound the bishops by that wicked subscription, they revealed their fraud and proclaimed victory on their own behalf.

He also discusses the baptism of heretics at length and with such correctness of meaning that the opinion of those who say that certain statements about heretical baptism slipped from the Doctor in this book, but were later recalled by him when his judgment had become more mature with age, is hardly credible. Such, too, is the passage refuted by Victorius: namely, that Saint Jerome thought a morally upright life necessary in priests in order for them either to absolve or to celebrate the Eucharist. On the contrary, especially in section 5, he clearly establishes that, if elsewhere he seems to assert the contrary, he does so lest priests, while boasting of their priestly power alone, abandon the norm of right living and destroy by their example what they build by their authority.

Scholars do not agree sufficiently about the year in which this work was composed. Some are influenced by the fact that Jerome mentions Lucifer with great praise in the *Chronicle*, and it seems unlikely that he would celebrate the constancy and faith of someone whose position—or rather whose error—he attacks in a published book, unless this book, in which Lucifer is disparaged, was later than the one in which he is praised. Since it is certain that the *Chronicle* was written in the year 380, they consequently wish to place this dialogue after that date.

But you will see that this argument has no force if you weigh those testimonies carefully and understand that Jerome regarded many things in Lucifer with suspicion. He attacks not the bishop himself in the strict sense, but his followers, who abused his name in defense of their error. Indeed, in this very book Lucifer is spoken of favorably, as in the words: “I am compelled to think something different about blessed Lucifer from what both his merit and my humanity require.”

From the sequence and position in which Jerome lists this book in the *Catalogue*, and from the fact that it immediately precedes the *Chronicle*, it is clear that it either predates the year 380 and surpasses the period of his departure from the desert, or belongs to the year 379, as is noted in the chronological headings of the letters. It is therefore easy to assign the book to the year 379 itself, when Jerome, fleeing from the desert of Chalcis, stopped at Antioch. A Luciferian and an Orthodox Christian had disputed at Antioch, and Jerome declares that he wrote immediately after that dispute.

# DIALOGUE AGAINST THE LUCIFERIANS OF SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON

[Note: The editions of Martianay and Vallarsi have: “Here begins the Dispute between the Luciferian and the Orthodox, written by Saint Jerome.” An old manuscript of the Sorbonne preserves the following heading: “Here begins the Letter of Jerome the presbyter against the Luciferians.” It then continues: “Recently a follower of the Luciferian heresy approached, contending with hateful loquacity against a certain member of the Church,” and so forth. —Martianay.]

## 1

[Note: A manuscript of Cluny reads: “Recently it happened that a certain follower of Lucifer,” and so forth.]

Recently it happened that a certain follower of Lucifer, contending with another member of the Church in hateful loquacity, exercised a dog’s eloquence. [Manuscripts: “exercised.”] He maintained that the whole world belonged to the devil and—as it is now familiar for them to say—that the Church had been made into a brothel.

The other, by contrast, defended—reasonably indeed, but at an inappropriate place and time—the position that Christ had not died without cause, nor had the Son of God descended merely on account of Sardinian [Note: A term noted by lexicographers. The *mastruca* was a Sardinian garment. Another reading is *mastruga*. Prudentius writes:

> “To strip the nobles of their *mastrucae*, and clothe the wearers of the toga.”

Quintilian is especially apposite, *Institutio Oratoria* II.10: “Cicero deliberately mocked the *mastruca*, since it is Sardinian.” Paulinus likewise writes to Macarius of poor clothing, “the Sardinian *mastruca*.” Manuscript codices read *mastrugam*. The *mastruca* was a garment made from skins, or an ill-smelling animal-hide garment worn by the Sardinians. —Martianay.]

*mastruca*.

What more need be said? While the lights already kindled in the streets were dispersing the audience and gathering, and night interrupted their disorderly debate, they withdrew with their faces almost spat upon by one another. Yet those who had been present decided that they should meet early the next morning in a secluded colonnade. When they had all assembled there as agreed, it seemed best that the speech of each should be taken down by notaries.

## 2. A Heretic Must Be Discussed as a Pagan

When everyone had taken his seat, Helladius the Luciferian said:

**HELLADIUS.** I want this first question answered: Are Arians Christians or not?

[Note: An old edition has Jerome himself speaking in the role of the Orthodox: “I, Orthodoxus,” and so forth.]

**ORTHODOXUS.** I ask a more comprehensive question: Are all heretics Christians?

**L.** By calling someone a heretic, you have denied that he is a Christian.

**O.** Then all heretics are not Christians?

**L.** You heard the answer already.

**O.** If they do not belong to Christ, they belong to the devil.

**L.** No one doubts that.

**O.** But if they belong to the devil, it makes no difference whether they are heretics or pagans.

**L.** I do not dispute that.

**O.** Therefore we have settled between us that a heretic must be spoken of as a pagan.

**L.** Completely settled.

**O.** Now ask whatever you wish, since we agree that heretics are pagans.

**L.** What my question was forcing you to admit has been made explicit: heretics are not Christians. What remains is the conclusion. If Arians are heretics, and all heretics are pagans, then Arians are pagans. But if Arians are pagans, and it is established that the Church has no fellowship with Arians—that is, with pagans—it is clear that your Church, which receives bishops from the Arians, that is, from pagans, receives not so much bishops as priests from the Capitol. Consequently, it ought to be called more a synagogue of Antichrist than the Church of Christ.

## 3. The Eucharist

**O.** “He has dug a pit for me, and he himself has fallen into it.” The prophecy has been fulfilled.

**L.** How so?

**O.** If Arians, as you say, are pagans, and the gatherings of the Arians are the camps of the devil, how do you receive someone baptized in the devil’s camps?

**L.** I receive him—but as one who repents.

**O.** You plainly do not understand what you are saying. Does anyone receive a pagan who repents?

**L.** At the beginning of our discussion I simply answered that all heretics are pagans. But since your question was deceptive, I concede you the palm in the first question and proceed to the second, in which I assert that a layman coming from the Arians ought to be received as a penitent, but a cleric ought not.

**O.** Yet in the first question, which you say I won, I also won the second.

**L.** Explain how you won it.

**O.** Do you not know that laymen and clerics have one Christ, and that God is not one for the newly baptized and another for bishops? Why, then, should he not receive clerics who receives laymen as penitents?

**L.** It is not the same thing to shed tears for sins and to touch the Lord’s body. It is not the same thing to fall at the knees of the brethren and to distribute the Eucharist from the elevated place. It is one thing to grieve over what you have been; another, while neglecting sin, to live gloriously in the Church.

You who yesterday were proclaiming sacrilegiously that the Son of God was a creature; you who every day, worse than the Jews, were hurling stones of blasphemy against Christ; whose hands are full of blood, whose stylus was the soldier’s lance—will you, an adulterer, enter the virgin Church after an hour’s conversion? If you regret that you sinned, lay down the priestly office. If you are confident that you sinned, remain what you were.

## 4

**O.** You are practicing rhetoric and rushing from the thorny paths of debate into the open fields of free declamation. But please stop with generalities and return again to the steps and lines of the argument. Later, if you wish, we shall discuss the matter more broadly.

**L.** There is no declamation here. Pain overwhelms patience. State your case as you wish, argue as you wish: you will never persuade me that the bishop who confesses his error is in the same position as a penitent layman.

[Note: Gravius directs that this be read: “that the bishop who confesses is the same as the penitent layman”; this appears more correct.]

**O.** Since you obstinately maintain that the position of a bishop is different from that of a layman, for the sake of bringing our dispute to a conclusion I grant what you demand. Since you have provided the setting, I shall not hesitate to join battle with you. Explain to me why you receive a layman coming from the Arians but do not receive a bishop.

**L.** I receive a layman who confesses that he has erred; and the Lord prefers the sinner’s repentance to his death.

**O.** Then receive the bishop too, since he both confesses that he has erred and the Lord prefers the sinner’s repentance to his death.

[Note: An old edition reads: “I too receive the bishop.”]

**L.** If he confesses that he has erred, why does he remain a bishop? Let him lay down the priesthood; I grant pardon to the penitent.

**O.** I shall answer you in your own terms. If a layman confesses that he has erred, how does he remain a layman? Let him lay down the priesthood of the layman—that is, baptism—and I too grant pardon to the penitent. For it is written: “He made us a kingdom and priests for his God and Father” (Revelation 1:6).

[Note: The name “priesthood” was also formerly shared by the people in a certain sense, especially in the earliest times of Christianity, as has been learnedly noted from 1 Peter 2:9: βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα, “a royal priesthood,” which is cited immediately afterward; Martianay omitted this passage because he had not found it in his manuscripts.]

[Note: The old edition expresses the negative particle.]

[Note: Published books add: “And again, a holy nation, a royal priesthood, a people for his possession.” Our manuscripts do not read this. —Martianay.]

And again: “A holy nation, a royal priesthood, a people for his possession” (1 Peter 2:9). Whatever is not permitted to a Christian is equally forbidden to a bishop and to a layman. The person who does penance condemns [another reading: “despises”] his former conduct. If a penitent bishop may not continue as he was, neither may a penitent layman remain in that condition for which he confesses penance.

[Note: In the Sorbonne manuscripts: “Neither may a penitent layman remain in what he was, because of which he confesses penance.” The Cluny manuscript likewise reads, except that it has *licet* (“it is permitted”) where the others have *liceat* (“may it be permitted”). —Martianay.]

[Note: Martianay notes that the words “in that” are absent from two manuscripts. Gravius reconstructed the passage as: “Neither may a penitent layman remain what he was, for which he confesses penance.”]

**L.** We receive laymen because no one will be converted if he knows that he must be rebaptized. Thus, if they are rejected, we shall become the cause of their destruction.

**O.** By receiving the layman, you save one soul; by receiving the bishop, I associate with the Church not merely the people of one city but the whole province over which he presides. If I reject him, he will drag many down with him into ruin. Therefore I ask you to extend to the salvation of the whole world the principle you believe you observe when receiving a few.

But if this displeases you, and you are so harsh—or rather so irrationally unmerciful—as to regard the one who gave baptism as an enemy of Christ but the one who received it as a son, we do not contradict ourselves. Either we receive the bishop together with the people whom he makes Christian, or, if we do not receive the bishop, we know that we must reject the people as well.

## 5. The Bishop as the Seasoning of His Church. The Church’s Weeping for Penitents. The Book of the Twelve Prophets. The Bishop as the Church’s Eye

**L.** I ask you: have you not read what is said of bishops? “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt becomes tasteless, with what shall it be salted? It is useful for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled underfoot by people” (Matthew 5:13).

And also that the priest should entreat God for the sinful people, while no one else should intercede for the priest (1 Samuel 3). These two passages of Scripture converge upon one meaning. Just as salt seasons every food, and nothing by itself is so pleasant that it delights the taste without it, so the bishop is the seasoning of the whole world and of his own Church. If he becomes tasteless—whether through denial, heresy, lust, or, to put it in a word, through every kind of sin—from whom can he receive seasoning, since he himself is the seasoning of all?

The priest offers his oblation for the layman, lays his hand upon the subject, invokes the return of the Holy Spirit, and thus reconciles to the altar the one who had been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved, after prayer has been made for the people. Nor does he restore one member to health before all the members have been healed together.

[Note: In another sense, and one not wholly useless, the old edition reads *conflaverit* (“has fused together”), and shortly afterward *consequitur veniam* (“obtains pardon”).]

For a father readily forgives his son when the mother pleads from the depths of her heart. If, therefore, the penitent layman is restored to the Church by the rank we have described, and pardon follows where mourning has preceded, it is clear that a priest removed from his rank cannot be restored to that same place. [Note: Gravius notes that *absque* (“without”) is read in the old codices.] Either, as a penitent, he will lack the priesthood, or, if he remains in office, he cannot be brought back into the Church according to the order of penitence.

You, with your now tasteless salt, contaminate the flavor of the Church. You place upon the altar the one who, having been thrown outside, ought to lie in dung and be trampled underfoot by everyone. And where is the Apostle’s command: “A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (Titus 1:7)? And again: “Let each person examine himself, and then let him approach” (1 Corinthians 11:28)? Where is the Lord’s warning: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7:6)?

[Alternative reading: “Let us not cast our pearls before swine.”]

If you understand this as having been said generally of everyone, how much more must caution be exercised concerning priests, when even in the case of laymen such care is required [another reading: “such is held to be the case”]. The Lord says through Moses: “Separate yourselves from the tents of these most wicked men, and do not touch anything that belongs to them, lest you perish together in their sin” (Numbers 16:26). [Note: Gravius prefers the active form “touch” (*tangere*), with both the Hebrew text and the Latin translator in agreement.]

And again in the Twelve Prophets: “Their sacrifices are like bread of mourning; all who eat them will be defiled” (Hosea 9:4). And in the Gospel the Lord says: “The lamp of the body is the eye”—that is, the bishop is the light of the Church. “If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light” (Matthew 6:22). When the priest proclaims the true faith, darkness is driven from the hearts of all.

And he gives the reason: “No one lights a lamp and places it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for everyone in the house” (Matthew 5:15).

[Note: The old edition reads: “for everyone who is in the house. For this lamp is God’s spark of knowledge,” and so forth.]

That is, God kindles in the bishop the spark of his knowledge so that it may shine not for him alone but benefit everyone. And immediately afterward: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark. If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?” (Matthew 6:23).

And rightly so. For since the bishop is appointed in the Church to restrain the people from error, how great will the error among the people be when the one who teaches is himself in error? How can one who is himself a sinner forgive sins? How can a sacrilegious man make something holy? From where will light enter me when my eye is blind? Alas! A disciple of Antichrist governs the Church of Christ.

And where is the saying: “You cannot serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24)? And also: “What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial?” (2 Corinthians 6:14–15).

We read in the Old Testament: “A man in whom there is a blemish or defect shall not approach to offer gifts to the Lord” (Leviticus 21:17). And again: “The priests who approach the Lord God to sacrifice must be clean, lest the Lord perhaps abandon them.” And in the same place: “When they approach to minister in the holy things, they shall not bring guilt upon themselves, lest they die.”

There are many other passages that it would be endless to pursue, and I omit them for the sake of brevity [another reading: “but I omit them for the sake of brevity”]. For it is not the number of testimonies but their authority that matters. From these passages it is shown that you have corrupted the whole mass of the Church with a little leaven, and that today you receive the Eucharist from the hand of one whom yesterday you were spitting upon as though he were an idol.

[Note: Victorius preferred, following the Brixian manuscripts, “as though he were an idolater.”]

## 6. Sacrifice in the Church. Christ Cleansed the Waters by His Washing

**O.** You have quoted many passages from the sacred Books, abundantly and from memory. But after circling the entire forest, you are caught in my nets.

[Manuscripts: “you will be caught” or “you are caught.”]

Let the bishop of the Arians be, as you wish, an enemy of Christ; let him be tasteless salt, a lamp without a spark, an eye without a pupil. You will nevertheless reach the point where salt cannot season if it itself has no salt; where the blind cannot illuminate, nor the extinguished kindle anything.

But when you eat the food seasoned by him, why do you accuse the one who seasoned it of being tasteless? Your Church shines by his spark, and you denounce his lamp as extinguished? He supplies you with eyes, and yet he is blind?

Therefore I ask you either to grant him permission to sacrifice, whose baptism you approve, or to reject the baptism of one whom you do not regard as a priest. For it cannot be that one who is holy in baptism is a sinner at the altar.

[Note: Another reading was: “in the baptistery,” which forms a more elegant contrast with “altar.”]

**L.** But I receive a penitent layman through the laying on of hands and the invocation of the Holy Spirit, knowing that the Holy Spirit cannot be conferred by heretics.

**O.** All the paths of your propositions converge upon one crossroads, and, like frightened deer, while you avoid the empty flights of feathers, you become entangled in the strongest nets.

[Note: They were suspended by cords beyond the area occupied by the nets, so that the animal, attempting to avoid their flight as a danger, would throw itself into the nets. Virgil, *Georgics* 3:

> “They are driven neither by unleashed dogs, nor by any nets, nor by fear of the crimson feathers.”

]

For when a person baptized in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit becomes the temple of the Lord, when, after the old dwelling has been destroyed, a new sanctuary of the Trinity is built, how can you say that sins can be forgiven among the Arians without the coming of the Holy Spirit? How is a soul cleansed of its ancient filth if it does not possess the Holy Spirit?

Water does not wash the soul; rather, the water itself is first washed by the Spirit, so that it may be able spiritually to wash others. Moses says: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Genesis 1:2). From this it is clear that baptism does not exist without the Holy Spirit.

The pool of Bethesda in Judea, unless the Angel came to it, could not heal bodily weakened limbs. [Note: This is the Pool of Bethesda mentioned in John 5:2, λεγομένη Ἑβραϊστὶ Βηθεσδὰ, “called in Hebrew Bethesda.” The reading *Bethsaida* now prevails even in Jerome manuscripts.] And you produce a soul washed by ordinary water, as though from a bath?

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who was not so much cleansed by washing as who cleansed all waters through his own washing, received the Holy Spirit as soon as he raised his head from the stream. This was not because he had ever been without the Holy Spirit—for he was born in the flesh from the Holy Spirit—but so that it might be shown to us that baptism is genuine when the Holy Spirit comes upon it.

[Note: This clearly refers to the question over which the ancients disputed on various occasions: whether certain sacraments administered by heretics, or by those bound by an anathema, were valid. We therefore point out that Jerome does not absolutely deny that Arians can baptize, but defends the practice of the Church, which received bishops coming from the Arians. In this sense Saint Augustine also freely admits in Letter 185.47 that the Holy Spirit cannot be possessed outside the unity of the Body of Christ.]

Therefore, if an Arian cannot give the Holy Spirit, he cannot even baptize, because baptism in the Church is nothing without the Holy Spirit. But when you receive someone baptized by him and afterward invoke the Holy Spirit, you must either baptize him, because he could not have been baptized without the Holy Spirit, or, if he was baptized in the Spirit, cease invoking upon him the Spirit whom he received at the time of his baptism.

## 7. What Is Necessary for True Baptism? What of John’s Baptism? No Baptism Exists without the Holy Spirit. The True and Legitimate Baptism of the Church

**L.** I ask you: have you not read in the Acts of the Apostles that those who had already been baptized by John, when the Apostle questioned them, replied that they had not even heard whether there was a Holy Spirit, and afterward received the Holy Spirit? From this it is clear that someone can be baptized and nevertheless not have the Holy Spirit.

**O.** I do not think those who hear us are so ignorant of the divine Books that a lengthy speech is needed to resolve this little question. But before I say anything on the subject, listen to how great a confusion of the Scriptures arises according to your own view.

What does this mean: that John could not give the Holy Spirit to others in his baptism, though he gave it to Christ? And who is this John? He is “the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isaiah 40:3; Matthew 3:3). He is the one who said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). To say less, he is the one who cried from his mother’s womb: “And how has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43).

He did not give the Holy Spirit, whom the deacon Philip gave to the eunuch (Acts 8), and whom Ananias gave to Paul (Acts 9)? Perhaps I may seem bold in placing John above everyone. Hear the Lord speaking: “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11). For no prophet was granted both to announce Christ and to point him out with his finger.

And why do I need to linger over the praises of such a man, when he is even called an Angel by God the Father? “Behold,” he says, “I send my Angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” (Matthew 11:10).

Indeed, an Angel who, after dwelling in his mother’s womb, pursued the deserts of the wilderness, played as a child among serpents;

[Note: Victorius notes an allusion to Isaiah 11:8: “The infant shall play over the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand into the serpent’s den.” The passage describes a person whom no crime harmed, even from infancy.]

who, with Christ before his eyes, deigned to look upon nothing else; who trained his voice to be worthy of God in proclaiming the words of the Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. And, not to delay the question, it was fitting that such a Forerunner of the Lord should increase.

This John, then, so great and such a man, did not give the Holy Spirit, whom the centurion Cornelius received before he was baptized? Answer me, please: why did he not give him? Do you not know? Hear what the Scriptures teach: John’s baptism did not so much forgive sins as constitute a baptism of repentance unto the remission of sins—that is, unto a future remission, which was subsequently to follow through the sanctification of Christ.

For it is written: “John was in the wilderness, baptizing and preaching the gospel of repentance for the remission of sins.” And shortly afterward: “They were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.” Just as John himself was the Forerunner of the Lord, so his baptism was preliminary to the Lord’s baptism.

“The one who is from the earth,” he said, “speaks of earthly things; the one who comes from above is above all” (John 3:31). And again: “I baptize you in water; he will baptize you in the Spirit” (Matthew 3:11).

But if John, as he himself confessed, did not baptize in the Spirit, consequently he did not forgive sins either, because sins are forgiven to no human being without the Holy Spirit.

Or if you argue contentiously that John’s baptism forgave sins because it came from heaven, explain what greater thing we obtain in Christ’s baptism. That which forgives sins frees from Gehenna. That which frees from Gehenna is perfect. But no baptism can be called perfect except that which is found in the cross and resurrection of Christ.

Thus, while perversely religious, when John himself says, “He must increase, but I must decrease,” you assign more to the baptism of the servant than it possessed and destroy the Lord’s baptism, leaving it nothing greater.

[Note: Erasmus, together with the older edition, reads: “you are led into irreligion.” Victorius reads: “perversely religious.” Jerome, Letter 44: “Although perversely, your gifts agree.”]

What is the purpose of this assertion? Clearly, that you may not find it surprising that those baptized by John later received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the Apostles’ hands, since it is established that they had not even received remission of sins without the faith that was to follow.

But you receive one baptized by the Arians and attribute to him the baptism that is perfect. How, then, do you summon the Holy Spirit as though something minor were lacking in him, when the baptism of Christ is nothing without the Holy Spirit?

But I have gone on too long; though I could have repelled the attack of my opponent face-to-face, I have cast lighter weapons from a distance.

[Note: Manuscripts read *minus* (“lesser”) instead of *leviora* (“lighter”).]

For John’s baptism was so imperfect that those who had been baptized by him were afterward baptized with Christ’s baptism. The account tells us:

“It happened that, while Apollos was at Corinth, and Paul was passing through the upper regions of Asia, he came to Ephesus. When he found certain disciples, he said to them: ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they answered: ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ He said: ‘Into what, then, were you baptized?’ They answered: ‘Into John’s baptism.’ Paul said: ‘John baptized the people with a baptism of repentance, telling them to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus, for the remission of sins.’ When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them immediately” (Acts 19:1 and following).

Therefore, if they were baptized with the true and legitimate baptism of the Church and afterward received the Holy Spirit, follow the authority of the Apostles, baptize those who do not possess the baptism of Christ, and you will be able to invoke the Holy Spirit.

## 8. The Practice of the Churches in the Laying on of Hands. The Authority of Tradition

**L.** Those who thirst in their sleep greedily fill their throats with rivers. The more they drink, the more they thirst. You seem to me likewise: in response to the little question I proposed, you have sought arguments here and there and nevertheless remain thirsty in the same dispute.

Do you not know that this is also the custom of the Churches: that hands are afterward laid upon those who have been baptized and that the Holy Spirit is then invoked? Do you demand where this is written? In the Acts of the Apostles.

Even if the authority of Scripture did not support it, the agreement of the whole world on this matter would have the force of a command. For many other practices observed in the Churches through tradition have claimed for themselves the authority of written law—for example, dipping the head three times in the font; afterward, on emerging, tasting the harmony of milk and honey as a sign of infancy; and, on the Lord’s Day and throughout Pentecost, not worshipping on one’s knees and breaking the fast; as well as many other practices that are not written down but which reasonable observance has claimed for itself.

[Note: Martianay read: “returning to signify infancy,” but this made no sense. We have restored the reading found elsewhere: “on the day,” instead of “returning.”]

From this you see that we follow the custom of the Church, even though it is established that someone was baptized before the invocation of the Spirit.

[Col. 0164B] **9. The bishop hastens to the laying on of hands. The blasphemies of the Arians. Why is the laying on of hands reserved to the bishop? The bishop’s right to baptize.**—O. I do not indeed deny that this is the custom of the Churches: that the bishop should hasten to those who have been baptized by presbyters and deacons far from the major cities, in order to lay his hand upon them for the invocation of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] “To those who are far away.” The Sorbonicus manuscript reads: “who are far from the major cities,” etc. MARTIANAEUS.—With Gravius and the older printed editions I read *who are far away*. Previously it read: “who are far away in smaller cities,” although the very structure of the sentence rejects this. Moreover, I think that cities, even smaller ones, had not lacked a bishop before and after the Sardican canon; rather, villages, fortresses, and more remote places from the cities are meant, as is indicated below.]

But what sort of thing is it for you to transfer the laws of the Church to heresy, and to endure your virgin’s integrity amid the brothels of prostitutes?

[Note: [Col. 0163D] “To allow it to be polluted in brothels.” The printed editions add the verb *to be polluted*, which the manuscript copies do not retain. MARTIANAEUS.—Formerly the reading was “to allow it to be polluted,” but Martianaeus testifies that the preceding verb is not found in the manuscripts. I do not like the isolated *to allow*, and would rather read *to divide*, so that, just as he disapproves of transferring the laws of the Church to heresy, he would likewise disapprove of dividing virgin integrity among brothels.]

If a bishop lays on his hand, he lays it upon those who have been baptized in the right faith, who have believed in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three persons, one substance. But since an Arian believes nothing else—close your ears, I beg you, those who are about to hear, lest you be polluted by the voices of such great impiety—than that the Father alone is the true God, that Jesus Christ the Savior is a creature, and that the Holy Spirit is the servant of both, how will he receive the Holy Spirit from the Church, when he has not yet obtained remission of sins?

For the Holy Spirit does not dwell in a dwelling that is not clean; nor does he make the temple his habitation when it does not have true faith as its bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0164D] I restore *dwelling* from an old edition instead of *faith*. That edition likewise has *which has him as bishop* instead of *which does not have a bishop*, and then *you object* instead of the reading at this point, *you ask*.]

But if at this point you ask why one baptized in the Church does not receive the Holy Spirit except through the hand of the bishop, although we maintain that he is bestowed in true baptism, learn that this practice derives its authority from the fact that, after the Lord’s ascension, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles. We find the same thing being done in many places,

[Note: [Col. 0164D] He clearly asserts the right of presbyters to confer the seal, and in his letter to Evangelus he indicated that this practice was sometimes permitted: “For what does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do?” Likewise, in the commentaries published under Ambrose’s name on Ephesians 4: “In Egypt, presbyters confer the seal if the bishop is not present.” The ancient Author of the *Questions from Both Testaments*, mixed among Augustine’s works, says the same; and this practice is still said to prevail among the Greeks. [Col. 0165D] Innocent, however, in that famous letter to Decentius, says: “With regard to sealing infants, it is clear that it may be done by no one other than a bishop. For although presbyters are second in rank, like priests, they do not possess the fullness of the episcopate. That this episcopal office belongs to bishops alone, so that they may either seal or impart the Spirit, the Paraclete, is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by that passage in the Acts of the Apostles,” etc. Compare Gregory the Great, Book IV, letter to Januarius; the First Council of Toledo, canon 20; likewise the First Council of Orange, canon 11, etc.]

more for the honor of the priesthood than as a matter of necessity.

Otherwise, if the Holy Spirit flows down only at the bishop’s invocation, those who were baptized by presbyters and deacons in villages, fortresses, or more remote places, and died before they were visited by bishops, must be mourned.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] Martianaeus is wrong to read *in little beds* instead of *in villages or hamlets*.]

**182** The salvation of the Church depends upon the dignity of the supreme Priest;

[Note: [Col. 0166D] Several printed editions have: “consists in dignity and veneration.”]

and unless a certain authority, exceptional and preeminent above all, is granted to him, as many schisms will arise in the Churches as there are priests.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] “To whom, unless an exceptional authority is granted.” The manuscript copies read as follows: “To whom, unless this certain lot and a power elevated above men is granted,” etc. But it seems that *this lot* has been put for *exceptional*, which they did not sufficiently understand. MARTIANAEUS.]

Hence it follows that, without chrism and the bishop’s authorization, neither presbyter nor deacon has the right to baptize. Nevertheless, when necessity compels, we know that this is also frequently permitted to laypeople. For as someone receives, so he can give—unless, perhaps, the eunuch baptized by Philip the deacon must be believed to have been without the Holy Spirit. Scripture speaks of him in this way: “And they both went down into the water; and Philip baptized him” (Acts 8:38). “And when they came up from the water, the Holy Spirit came upon the eunuch.”

But if you think this should be brought against us, that “when the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them; and when they had come, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, for he had not yet fallen upon any of them” (ibid.), learn in what follows why this happened. For he himself says: “They had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit.”

If at this point you also claim that you act in the same way, because the heretics did not baptize in the Holy Spirit, know that Philip had not been separated from the apostles, that he belonged to the same Church, and that he preached the same Lord Jesus Christ; indeed, he was a deacon of those who later laid on hands. But since you say that among the Arians there is not a Church but a synagogue, and not clergy of God but worshipers of creatures and idols, how can you claim that you follow the same rule in a different case?

**10.** L. You indeed drive me back forcefully, standing firm and fighting me face-to-face; but you are struck from behind and leave your unarmed back unprotected. Let it be granted that among the Arians there is not even baptism, and that therefore they cannot give the Holy Spirit, because they have not yet received remission of sins. All this advances my victory, and the arena of your arguments sweats the palm of victory for me. An Arian has no baptism—and how can he have the priesthood? Among them he is not a layman—and how can he be a bishop? I am not permitted to receive a beggar, while you receive a king? You hand over the camp to the enemy, while a deserter from our side must be rejected?

**11.** O. If you remembered what came before, you would already know that you had been answered; but while you pursue the love of contradiction, you have fallen away from the lines of the argument—in the manner of certain talkative rather than eloquent men, who, although they do not know how to debate, nevertheless do not cease quarreling.

For I am not so much now condemning or defending the Arians as circling the goal of my argument: that we receive a bishop from them by the same reasoning by which you receive a layman from them. If you grant pardon to one who has gone astray, I also forgive one who repents. If the person baptizing one baptized in his own faith could not harm him, then the person appointing as priest one established in his own faith did not defile him.

Heresy is subtle, and therefore simple souls are easily deceived. The deception of both layman and bishop is common. But the bishop could not have erred. Indeed, men are chosen for the episcopate from the bosom of Plato and Aristophanes.

[Note: [Col. 0166B] Another reading has *are elected*.]

For how many are there who are not thoroughly educated in these authors? Finally, of all the learned men ordained today, their concern is not how to drink in the marrow of the Scriptures, but how to charm the ears of the people with the rhetorical blossoms of declaimers.

Furthermore, the Arian heresy agrees more closely with worldly wisdom and borrows its streams of argument from the fountains of Aristotle. Therefore, like little children quarreling with one another, whatever you say, I will say: you affirm, I will affirm; you deny, I will deny. An Arian baptizes, therefore he is a bishop; he does not baptize, then reject the layman, and I will not receive the priest. I will follow you wherever you go; either we shall both remain stuck in the mud, or we shall both get free.

**12. The solemn interrogation at baptism.**—L. But the layman must be forgiven for this reason, **184** because, thinking it was the Church of God, he approached in simplicity and was baptized according to his faith.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] In the contrary sense, the old edition has “An Arian coming,” that is, one coming from the Arians to the Orthodox.]

O. You assert something new: that someone became a Christian through one who was not a Christian. When he approached the Arians, in what faith was he baptized? Clearly, in the faith that the Arians possessed. Or if he himself already believed correctly, and knowingly was baptized by heretics, he does not deserve pardon for his error.

But it is utterly absurd that a disciple, going to a teacher, should be an artisan before he has been taught; that someone newly converted from the worship of idols should know Christ better than the one who teaches him.

But you say: “He believed simply in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and therefore obtained baptism.” What, I ask, is this simplicity—to be ignorant of what one believes? He believed simply. What did he believe? Certainly, either, hearing three names, he believed in three gods and became an idolater; or, believing God to be three-named in three words, he fell into the heresy of Sabellius.

Or, taught by the Arians that the Father is the one true God, he believed the Son and the Holy Spirit to be creatures. What else he could have believed beyond these alternatives, I do not know—unless perhaps, already instructed in the Capitol, he had learned the Trinity as *homoousion* (“of the same substance”).

He knew that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are divided not in nature but in persons. He knew also the name of the Son in the Father and the name of the Father in the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The point is that the Father cannot be conceived without the thought of the Son occurring. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book VII: “For the name of the Father also contains within itself the name of the Son.”]

It is utterly ridiculous to have someone discuss faith before believing; to know the mystery before being initiated; for the baptizer to think one way about God and the baptized person another.

Moreover, since it is customary in the font to ask, after the confession of the Trinity: “Do you believe in the holy Church? Do you believe in the remission of sins?”

[Note: [Col. 0167D] “Do you believe in the holy, etc.” The preposition *in* was unnecessarily added in the Cluniacensis manuscript; the Sorbonicus does not read it in the subsequent phrase, “after ‘Do you believe in the holy Church.’” Whether it is read or not, the sense is the same. MARTIANAEUS.—Victorius notes that he removed the little word, repeated several times here, because the more accurate copies did not contain it; and more correctly, as in the Creed, it is attached to only one God, to express the greater faith.]

Which Church do you say that he believed in? The Church of the Arians? But they do not have one. Ours? But, being baptized outside it, he could not have believed in the Church that he did not know.

**13.** L. Since you quibble over everything and evade the darts hurled by us with the shield of your speech, I shall cast one spear that will pierce, by its force, the boss of your covering and your clattering words; nor will I allow strength to be defeated by artifice.

**185** A layman baptized outside the Church in the faith is received when he repents; but a bishop either does not do penance and remains a priest, or, if he does penance, ceases to be a bishop. Therefore we rightly receive the layman when he repents, but reject the bishop if he wishes to remain in the priesthood.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] An old edition reads: “baptized outside the faith of the Church.” The printed reading may be understood faithfully, whether the formula is complete or not; for below, in the person of the Orthodox, it is stated that heretics do not possess baptism—namely, those among the Arians who denied the divinity of the Son in the words of the sacrament.]

O. An arrow directed from a drawn bowstring is difficult to evade. It reaches the one at whom it is shot before it can be thwarted by the shield’s barrier. By contrast, your propositions, because they are launched without an iron point, cannot pierce the enemy.

This spear, then, which you have hurled with all your strength, and with which you threaten us, I shall repel, as they say, with one little finger. For the question is not whether a penitent bishop may be one and a layman may be another; it is whether a heretic possesses baptism. If, as is established, he does not possess baptism, how can he be penitent before he is a Christian?

Prove to me that a layman coming from the Arians possesses baptism, and then I will not deny him penance. But if he is not a Christian—if he has not had a priest who could make him a Christian—how can a man who does not yet believe do penance?

**14.** L. I beg you, setting aside the arguments of philosophers, to speak with me in Christian simplicity—if indeed you follow not the dialecticians but the fishermen. Does it seem right to you that an Arian should be a bishop?

O. You approve him as a bishop because you receive from him one who has been baptized; and for this you are to be reproached: why do you separate yourself from us by walls when in faith and in receiving Arians you agree with us?

L. I already asked above that you speak with me not philosophically but as a Christian.

O. Do you wish to learn, or are you arguing?

L. Certainly I am arguing, because I demand from you the reason for what you do.

O. If you are arguing, you have already been answered. For I receive a bishop from the Arians by the same reasoning by which you receive one who has been baptized. If you desire to learn, cross over into my battle line. An adversary is defeated; a disciple is taught.

**186** L. I cannot become a disciple before I hear the teacher preaching.

O. Since you are evading the issue and wish to be taught by me while retaining me as your complete adversary,

[Note: [Col. 0168D] “while I have the adversary entirely behind me,” etc.]

I shall teach you according to your own mind. We agree in faith; we agree in receiving heretics; let us agree also in assembling.

L. This is not teaching but arguing.

O. Because you seek peace with a shield, while we insert an olive branch into a sword.

L. Look, I raise my hands; I yield; you have won. But when I lay down my weapons, I ask for the reason for the sacrament into which you compel me to swear.

O. Meanwhile I congratulate you, and I give thanks to my God Christ, because with a good disposition you have transferred yourself from the falsehood of the Sardinians to the taste of the whole world, and you do not say, as some do: “Save me, O Lord, for the holy man has failed” (Psalm 11:1).

[Note: [Col. 0168D] “From the falsehood of the Sardinians.” This passage is very corrupt in the earlier printed books, which read “from the heat of falsehood” or “from the odor of falsehood,” etc. The Cluniacensis manuscript preserves the correct reading, “from the falsehood of the Sardinians,” by which the Luciferian was held. —Formerly the reading was “from the heat or odor of falsehood.” But even *from the falsehood of the Sardinians*, which Martianaeus restored from the Cluniacensis manuscript, does not seem sufficiently emended to me. For although the name *Sardinians* is most elegantly set against the whole world, it responds awkwardly to *falsehood*. Perhaps Jerome wrote *insipidity* instead of *falsehood*, or, if expressed in Latin, *saltiness*. Everyone says that the island of Sardinia suffers from pestilential air; it is also well known that the Sardinians are reputed liars. MARTIANAEUS.]

Their impious voice empties Christ’s cross of its power, subjects the Son of God to the devil, and understands that lamentation which was uttered by the Lord concerning sinners as now spoken concerning all human beings: “What profit is there in my blood, while I go down into corruption?” (Psalm 29:10).

But far be it from us that God should have died in vain. “The strong man has been bound, and his vessels have been plundered” (Mark 3:27). The Father’s address has been fulfilled: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8). “The fountains of waters appeared, and the foundations of the inhabited world were revealed” (Psalm 17:16). “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun, and there is no one who can hide himself from its heat” (Psalm 18:6).

The Psalmist, filled with God, sings: “The swords of the enemies have failed utterly, and you have destroyed their cities” (Psalm 9:7).

**15.** And where, I ask, are those excessively religious—or rather, excessively profane—men who assert that there are more synagogues than Churches? How have the cities of the devil been destroyed, and how, at the end—that is, at the consummation of the ages—have the idols fallen?

If Christ does not possess the Church, or possesses it only in Sardinia, he has become exceedingly poor. And if Satan possesses Britain, Gaul, the East, the peoples of India, barbarian nations, and the whole world at once, how have the trophies of the Cross been erected at a corner of the earth?

[Note: [Col. 0168D] Victorius had added from the manuscripts *spread throughout the whole world*; the old edition had only *throughout the whole world*. Martianaeus, following Erasmus, deleted it.]

Surely the powerful adversary granted Christ the Iberian monster, pale men, and a poor province, disdaining to possess them.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] “The Iberian monster.” At this point the Sorbonicus manuscript is superior to the Cluniacensis and presents the true and genuine reading: “the Iberian monster, pale men, and a poor province,” etc. Jerome also speaks of the Iberian, or Iberian monster, in his letter to the deacon Julian. MARTIANAEUS.—He calls it the Iberian monster as an insult, namely, the most dreadful of all monsters, whether the word is used of a man, as in Letter 6 to Julian, or of a region, as here, or of some other subject. Perhaps he means Sardinia, a hydra of evils that daily grows larger. Formerly the reading was: “Iberia and the Celtiberians, pale men, and the province of the Ethiopians,” etc.]

But if they take comfort in that saying written in the Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8), let them know that the faith spoken of there is the faith of which the Lord himself said: “Your faith has saved you” (Matthew 9:22).

[Note: [Col. 0169D] Victorius observes that *faith* here is to be understood as confidence, or more ardent belief, which contains hope and love within itself; it is clear that by this a person is justified.]

And elsewhere concerning the centurion: “I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matthew 8:10).

[Note: [Col. 0170D] “Such faith in Israel.” The same Sorbonicus manuscript adds *nor*, that is, “nor in Israel.” MARTIANAEUS.]

And again to the apostles: “Why are you fearful, O men of little faith?” (Luke 7:9). And also in another place: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move” (Matthew 14:31).

For neither the centurion nor that little woman who had been wasting away for twelve years from an issue of blood had believed in the mysteries of the Trinity, which were revealed to the apostles after Christ’s resurrection, so that their faith in this mystery might rightly be praised. Rather, the simplicity of their mind and the soul devoted to its God were approved. For she said in her heart: “If I only touch his garment, I shall be saved” (Matthew 9:21).

This is the faith that God declared to be rarely found. This is the faith that even among those who believe correctly is rarely found in perfection. “Let it be done for you,” God says, “according to your faith.”

I do not wish this saying to be applied to me. For if it were done to me according to my faith, I should perish. And certainly I believe in God the Father; I believe in God the Son; and I believe in God the Holy Spirit. I believe in one God, and yet I do not want it to be done to me according to my faith.

For the enemy often comes and sows weeds among the Lord’s harvest. Nor do I say that anything is greater than faith in the sacrament or purity of soul; but unwavering faith in God is difficult to find.

Let the following example be offered so that what we mean may become clear: I attend prayer. I would not pray if I did not believe. But if I truly believed, I would cleanse the heart through which God is seen; I would strike my breast with my hands; I would water my cheeks with tears; my body would shudder; my face would grow pale; I would lie at the feet of my Lord; I would drench them with weeping and wipe them with my hair; certainly I would cling to the wood of the Cross and would not let go until I had obtained mercy.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The same edition adds: “I would become tender-hearted.”]

But now, very often during my prayer, I either walk about beneath the porticoes, or calculate interest, or, carried away by a shameful thought, do even things that I am ashamed to mention. Where is faith? Do we suppose that Jonah prayed in this way? Or the three youths? Or Daniel among the lions? Or surely the thief upon the cross?

I have offered these examples to make the point intelligible. For the rest, let each person examine his own heart, and throughout his life he will find how rare it is for a faithful soul to be found—one that does nothing for the sake of desire for glory or the gossip of men.

For one who fasts does not immediately fast for God, nor does one who stretches out a hand to the poor lend at interest to God. Vices lie close beside virtues. It is difficult to be content with God alone as judge.

**16.** L. You anticipated my question. I had reserved this Scripture for the end, for all our people—or rather, now no longer my people—use it as a battering ram in their debates. I rejoice greatly that it has been broken and crushed. But I beg you to explain the whole reason why the Church receives those coming from the Arians, not as to an adversary but as to a disciple. For although I cannot answer you with words, I still do not agree inwardly.

**17.** O.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] “Under King Constantius, Eusebius and Hypatius being consuls.” Eusebius and Hypatius were brothers of Faustina, the wife of Julian. See Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXI. They were consuls in the year of Christ 357, that is, the twelfth year of Constantius. MARTIANAEUS.]

Under King Constantius, when Eusebius and Hypatius were consuls, unbelief was written under the name of unity and faith, as is now recognized.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The passage that follows concerning the Council of Ariminum was compared with an old manuscript of Saint-Germain in Paris and other copies by the distinguished Baluzius and inserted into his edition of the Councils. There, instead of *unbelief*, one finds *lack of faith*; and this is what is now understood by *unbelief*.]

For at that time nothing seemed so pious, nothing so fitting for a servant of God, as to follow unity and not be cut off from the communion of the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] In the manuscript in Baluzius’s possession: “for the servants of God, and also for the communion of the whole world,” without the preposition *from*.]

Especially since the surface meaning of the statement no longer presented anything sacrilegious: “We believe,” they said, “in one true God, the almighty Father.” We too confess this. “We believe in the only-begotten Son of God, who was begotten from God before all ages and before every beginning.”

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The same manuscript has: “in the one and only true God,” etc.; and shortly below, “the Son like his begetter, the Father.”]

“The only-begotten was begotten from the Father alone: God from God, like his begetter, the Father, according to the Scriptures. No one knows his birth except the Father, who alone begot him.”

Was it inserted here: “There was a time when he was not”? Or: “The Son of God is a creature from things that did not exist”?

[Note: [Col. 0170D] Again the same manuscript reads: “except the one who alone begot him,” and shortly afterward, more correctly: “the Son of God is from God, not from created things that did not exist.”]

It is a perfect faith to believe God from God. And they said that the only-begotten was born from the Father alone. What does “born” mean? Certainly not “made.” Birth removed the suspicion of creaturehood.

They added: “He who descended from heaven was conceived from the Holy Spirit, born from the Virgin Mary, crucified by Pontius Pilate, rose from the dead on the third day,”

[Note: [Col. 0171C] We have supplied “from the dead” and “ascended into heaven” from Victorius’s manuscripts and Baluzius’s copy. From the same source and the old edition we read “such honey of praise” instead of “so much praise,” as was previously printed.]

“ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will come to judge the living and the dead.”

The words sounded pious, and amid such honeyed praise no one suspected that poison had been inserted.

**18. Why the term *ousia* was removed. Valens, Bishop of Mursa. The public archives of the Churches. The acts of the Council of Ariminum.**—As for removing the term *ousia*, a plausible reason was offered.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] Sulpicius narrates the matter in Book II, chapter 43: “The Arians abolished the word *ousia* as ambiguous, rashly used by the Fathers, and not derived from the authority of Scripture, under the pretext of a false argument, lest the Son be believed to be of one substance with the Father. The same confession of faith declared the Son to be like the Father. But inwardly there was a fraud: he was to be like, but not equal.”]

“For,” they said, “it is not found in the Scriptures, and by its novelty scandalizes many of the simpler-minded; it has therefore pleased us to remove it.” The bishops were not concerned about the word, since the meaning was secure.

Finally, at that very time, when popular rumor was spreading that there had been fraud in the statement of faith, Valens, Bishop of Mursa, who had written it, in the presence of Taurus, the prefect of the praetorium, who had attended the synod by order of the emperor, declared that he was not an Arian and that he utterly abhorred their blasphemies.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] An old manuscript reads: “and that he had withdrawn from their error.” But this did not extinguish popular opinion; shortly afterward, a crowd of laypeople also gathered.]

The matter, having been conducted privately, had not extinguished popular suspicion. Therefore, on another day, in the Church at Ariminum, when crowds of both bishops and laypeople had gathered, Muzonius, bishop of the province of Byzacena, to whom, because of his age, precedence was accorded by all, spoke as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0171D] Through a shameful error, *Byzantine* has until now been read instead of *Byzacene*. Baluzius also wishes to restore from an ancient manuscript “precedence was accorded by all” instead of “the first place was accorded and they were given.” Finally, the old edition failed to recognize certain words because of their antiquity.]

“We order that someone among us read to your holiness the things that have been made public and brought even to us, so that whatever is evil and ought to be abhorrent to both our ears and our heart may be condemned with one voice by all.”

[Note: [Col. 0172C] Previously: “the things made public.” Then the old manuscript in Baluzius’s possession has “someone among you” instead of “someone among us,” and “from the ears of our hearts” instead of “from our heart,” etc.]

All the bishops answered: “It pleases us.”

Accordingly, when Claudius, bishop of the province of Picenum, had begun, at the command of all, to read the blasphemies attributed to Valens, Valens, denying that they were his, cried out and said:

[Note: [Col. 0172D] So Baluzius’s manuscript. Other editions read: “Christ God.” Shortly afterward, the same manuscript supplies *and*; the missing words are restored.]

“If anyone denies Christ the Lord, the Son of God, begotten from the Father before the ages, let him be anathema.” All responded with one voice: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone denies that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures, let him be anathema.” Everyone answered: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone does not say that the Son of God is eternal with the Father, let him be anathema.” All shouted: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone says that the Son is a creature, as the other creatures are, let him be anathema.” The same response was given: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone says that the Son is from things that did not exist, and not from God the Father, let him be anathema.” All shouted: “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone says, ‘There was a time when the Son was not,’ let him be anathema.”

[Note: [Col. 0172D] The same old copy supplies: “All responded: Let him be anathema.”]

At this, all the bishops and the whole Church together received Valens’s words with applause and rejoicing. If anyone thinks that we have invented this, let him search the public archives. They are certainly full of the records of the Churches,

[Note: [Col. 0172D] It was incorrectly printed *certain*. Baluzius’s manuscript has: “The chests of the ecclesiastical Scriptures.” Below, the old edition reads: “and those who confirm the truth, who,” etc.]

and the memory of the event is still fresh. There remain men who were present at that synod; and, what confirms the truth, the Arians themselves do not deny that these things happened as we have said.

When, therefore, everyone was praising Valens to the skies and condemning their suspicion of him with repentance, the same Claudius, who had begun the reading above, said:

“There are still certain matters that escaped my lord and brother Valens. If it seems good to you, let us condemn them together, so that no scruple may remain.”

[Note: [Col. 0172D] One manuscript reads: “All said, and Valens himself; and all answered: Let him be anathema.” Shortly afterward, instead of *condemned*, it reads: “condemned in a clear voice.”]

“If anyone says that the Son of God existed before all ages, but not before absolutely all time, so that anything could precede him, let him be anathema.”

They all said: “Let him be anathema.” And Valens condemned many other things that seemed suspect, at Claudius’s pronouncement.

Whoever wishes to learn these matters more fully will find them in the acts of the Council of Ariminum, from which we too have taken this brief account.

**19. Valens and Ursacius. The Body of the Lord in the Church. Why the Council of Nicaea was convened.**—After these things had happened,

[Note: [Col. 0172D] Martianaeus, following Erasmus, adds: “After these things had therefore happened.”]

the council was dissolved. Everyone returned joyfully to his provinces. For the emperor and all good men had been concerned that East and West should be bound together by the bond of communion.

**BUT CRIMES DO NOT REMAIN HIDDEN FOR LONG**, and a badly closed scar bursts open when the unboiled pus beneath it breaks through.

Afterward Valens and Ursacius, and the other associates of their wickedness—those distinguished priests of Christ, of course—began to boast of their palms, saying that they had not denied the Son to be a creature, but had denied him to be like the other creatures. Then the name *of the same substance* was abolished; then the condemnation of the Nicene faith was proclaimed. The whole world groaned, and was astonished to hear itself called Arian.

[Note: [Col. 0172D] For he was not Arian in his intention; indeed, he held the correct view, but was astonished that he was being publicly declared and heard to be Arian in a sense he did not wish.]

Accordingly, some began to remain within their communion, while others began to send letters to those confessors who were exiled under the name of Athanasius. Some lamented in despair the alliance they had entered, wishing that it had been better.

A few, however—as is the nature of human beings—defended error as though it were deliberation.

The apostles’ little boat was in danger; the winds pressed upon it, and the waves battered its sides. Nothing now remained but hope. The Lord awakens and commands the storm; the beast [namely, Constantius] dies, and tranquility returns.

I shall speak more plainly. All the bishops who had been driven from their own sees returned to their Churches through the clemency of the new ruler [namely, Julian]. Then Egypt received its victor Athanasius; then the Church of Gaul embraced Hilary returning from battle; then Italy changed its mourning garments for the return of Eusebius [namely, of Vercelli].

Bishops came together who, ensnared by the deceits of Ariminum, were regarded, without awareness, as heretics. They protested that, in the Body of the Lord and in everything holy in the Church, they had suspected no evil in their faith. “We thought,” they said, “that the meaning agreed with the words; and in the Church of God, where there is simplicity and a pure confession, we feared that one thing might be concealed in the heart while another was spoken on the lips.”

A good opinion of evil things deceived us. We did not suppose that the priests of Christ were fighting against Christ.

They asserted many other things, which I omit for the sake of brevity, weeping as they spoke, and prepared to condemn both their former signature and all the blasphemies of the Arians.

At this point I ask those excessively religious men what they thought should be done with the confessors.

“They should have deposed the old bishops,” they will say, “and ordained new ones.” It was attempted. But how many people of sound conscience allow themselves to be deposed? Especially when all the people, loving their priests, rushed almost to the point of stoning and killing those who deposed them?

“They should have remained within their own communion,” they say.

That is to say, they should have surrendered the whole world to the devil through irrational cruelty.

Why would they have condemned those who were not Arians? Why would they have split the Church while it remained united in faith? Why, finally, would they have made those who believed correctly into Arians through their obstinacy?

For since we know that at the Council of Nicaea, which was convened because of the Arian perfidy, eight Arian bishops were received, and since there is now no bishop in the world except those whom that synod ordained, how could they have acted against the very council for whose sake they endured exile?

[Note: [Col. 0173C] Some think that Jerome slips here through a failure of memory when he says that Arius himself was received at the Council of Nicaea. For the Synodical Letter of Nicaea, after imposing an anathema upon those who shared the Arian position, deliberately says nothing about what end Arius met, lest it seem to insult the man’s misfortune; these words clearly indicate that the emperor imposed the punishment of exile upon him.
