Yet we learn from Sozomen, Book II, chapter 16, that Arius, being led into exile—or, rather, at the very time when he was being deported into exile—was recalled. Socrates likewise records that he was recalled immediately from exile, before Eusebius and Theognius sent their petition of repentance. You now see, therefore, in what way Jerome’s statement can be understood and reconciled.]

## 20. The Authors of the Arian Heresy. The Men Who Had Attended the Council of Nicaea Still Survived. What Was Determined at the Council of Alexandria. What Lucifer Did.

**L.** Or were the Arians received even then? Who, I ask?

**O.** Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia; Theognis [Al. Theogonius], bishop of Nicaea; Saras, then a presbyter of Libya; Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine; and the others, whom it would take too long to enumerate. Arius himself also—the head and source of these men and of their evils—and the deacon Euzoius, who was bishop of Antioch after Eudoxius; and Achillas the lector. These three, after all, were clerics of the Church of Alexandria and became the authors of this heresy.

[Note: I restore the reading of Victorius, in whose place Martianus, together with Erasmus, has “who afterward, under Theodosius, was bishop of Antioch,” and—what is least tolerable—entirely conceals Victorius’s diligent work. It is certain, however, that Erasmus is mistaken, and that this was not Jerome’s intention in mentioning Theodosius, nor did Jerome write it in that way. On this subject Socrates, book II, chapter 44, says: “When the Antiochenes learned that Eudoxius, having despised their Church, had leaped over to the wealth of the see of Constantinople, they summoned Meletius from Beroea and placed him in the see of Antioch. He . . . began to assert the doctrine of consubstantiality. When the Emperor learned this, he ordered him to be exiled; but he promoted Euzoius, who had formerly been deposed together with Arius, as bishop of the Church of Antioch.” It was for this reason, evidently, that Jerome said “after Eudoxius.” But I prefer to reproduce Victorius’s wording. That Euzoius succeeded Eudoxius in the episcopate of Antioch is established by the Tripartite History—namely, by Socrates, book II, chapters 43 and 44, and by Sozomen, book IV, chapter 12. Nicephorus Callistus explains all this more fully, book IX, chapter 48. Jerome, who here lists the Arian heretics, omits Meletius, who held that see between the two others: for he was a Catholic and, having been expelled by the Emperor Valens, was driven into exile. Both the others were Arians, although Eudoxius was also of the Aetian faction. This passage had previously been corrupted by Erasmus. He read: “and Euzoius the deacon, who afterward under Theodosius was bishop of Antioch,” as though Theodosius the Emperor had lived in the time of Arius, whose associate Euzoius was. Another Euzoius of that period deceived him—the one mentioned in the Catalogue, who was a Catholic and to whom Gregory of Nazianzus wrote. With the support both of the histories and of the manuscripts, we have corrected the passage in this way. We are always glad, when possible, to confirm the authority of ancient books by the testimony of historical works.]

**L.** If someone denies that they were received, how can he be refuted?

**O.** Men who attended that council still survive. And if this is insufficient, since because of the antiquity of the period they are now exceedingly rare and witnesses cannot be present everywhere, let us read the acts and names of the bishops of the Council of Nicaea. There we shall find, among the others, that those whom we mentioned above were received and signed the *homoousion*—the confession of consubstantiality.

**L.** If you can, show that after the Council of Nicaea they declined into perfidy.

**O.** You have put the question properly. Those who do not believe are accustomed, with their eyes closed, to deny that something happened which they do not wish to have happened. But how did they not afterward decline, on whose account the council had been convened, and whose letters and books of impiety, published before the council, still exist to this day? Therefore, since at that time three hundred and more bishops received a few men whom they could cast out without injury to the Church, I am astonished that certain people—and certainly followers of the Nicene faith—should be so hard-hearted as not to think that three confessors returning from exile—Athanasius, Hilary, and Eusebius of Vercellae—

[Note: The holy Athanasius, Hilary, and Eusebius of Vercellae.]

ought to have done, for the salvation of the whole world, what so many and such men did voluntarily.

But, as we had begun to say, after the confessors’ return, it was later determined in the Council of Alexandria that, with the exception of the authors of the heresy, whom error could not excuse, penitents should be restored to communion with the Church—not because those who had been heretics could be bishops, but because it was evident that those who were received had not been heretics. The West assented to this judgment; and through so necessary a council [Perhaps: *plan*], the world was snatched from the jaws of Satan.

We have come to a most difficult passage, in which, against my will and intention, I am compelled to judge concerning the blessed Lucifer somewhat differently from what both his merit and my humaneness require.

[Note: An old edition adds: “with what good will I feel toward Lucifer.”]

But what shall I do? Truth opens its mouth and compels my unwilling tongue to express what my conscience bears within. At such a crisis for the Church, amid such madness of wolves, after separating a few sheep, he abandoned the rest of the flock.

He was indeed a good shepherd, but he left much prey to the beasts.

I pass over those arguments which certain slanderers defend as though they were sufficiently well established:

[Note: The same edition reads: “that he did this not from love of the Church, but from glory,” etc. Martianus reads: “that he did this not from love of glory,” but later removed the negative particle in the list of errata.]

that he did this out of love of glory and in order to transmit his name to posterity; and also because of the hostility he had taken up against Eusebius [that is, Eusebius of Vercellae] on account of the dispute at Antioch.

[Note: The well-known disagreement arose from the election of Paulinus, which Lucifer conducted contrary to the agreement, although with good intentions, and which Eusebius disapproved.]

I believe none of these things concerning such a man.

[Note: The old edition reads: “There is one point which I shall state, since it is even now established.”]

There is one point which even now I shall state plainly: he differs from us in words, not in substance, since he receives those who obtained baptism from the Arians.

## 21. Hilary, Deacon of the Roman Church. There Is No Church That Does Not Have a Priest.

**L.** How different were the things formerly brought to me—and, as I now understand, things more conducive to error than to hope! But thanks be to Christ God, who infused the light of truth into my heart, so that I would no longer, with sacrilegious speech, call his virgin the harlot of the devil. One thing remains, which I ask you to explain: what can be said against Hilary, who does not even receive those baptized by the Arians?

**O.** Once Hilary, a deacon, has departed from the Church and, as he thinks, the world has become a mere crowd, he cannot celebrate the Eucharist, since he has neither bishops nor presbyters; nor can he confer baptism without the Eucharist. And since the man himself is now dead, his sect also died with him, because a deacon could ordain no cleric after himself.

There is no Church, moreover, that does not have priests. But, setting aside a few insignificant men who are themselves both laymen and bishops, listen to what should be thought concerning the whole Church.

**L.** You have dissolved so great a question in three words, as they say; and while you speak, I seem to agree with you. But if you become silent, I do not know what new scruple arises again: why are those baptized by heretics received?

**O.** This is precisely what I also said: listen to what should be thought concerning the whole Church. For this scruple, as you say, troubles many. I shall perhaps be lengthy in explaining it; but the gain of truth is worth the effort.

[Note: The same edition adds: “so that I may not remain silent.”]

## 22. Noah’s Ark as a Type of the Church. The Number Eight in the Psalms and the Gospel. The Degrees of the Church. No One Can Judge Human Beings before the Day of Judgment.

Noah’s ark was a type of the Church, as the Apostle Peter says: “In Noah’s ark a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water; and now baptism of a similar form saves us also” (1 Peter 3:20).

As in that ark there were kinds of every animal, so in this Church there are people of every nation and every character. As there were there the leopard and the kid, the wolf and the lamb, so here the righteous and sinners—that is, golden and silver vessels dwell together with wooden and earthen ones.

The ark had its nests; the Church has many dwelling places.

Eight human souls were saved in Noah’s ark. And Ecclesiastes (chapter 11) commands us to give a portion to seven and also to give a portion to eight—that is, to believe in both Testaments. For this reason certain psalms are entitled “For the Eighth,” and in Psalm 118 the righteous person is instructed through groups of eight verses, each assigned to one letter.

The beatitudes also, which the Lord pronounced to his disciples on the mountain, thereby outlining the Church, are eight. Ezekiel likewise employs the number eight in the building of the Temple. You will find many other things signified in this manner throughout the Scriptures.

A raven is therefore sent out from the ark,

[Note: According to the sense of the Septuagint translators: “it did not return” (*ouk anestrepsen*).]

and does not return; afterward a dove announces peace to the earth. So also in the baptism of the Church, after that most foul bird—the devil—has been expelled, the dove of the Holy Spirit announces peace to our earth.

Beginning at thirty cubits and gradually decreasing down to one cubit, the ark is constructed. Similarly, the Church, established through many degrees, ends at last with deacons, presbyters, and bishops.

The ark was endangered in the flood; the Church is endangered in the world.

Noah went out and planted a vineyard, and, drinking from it, became drunk. Christ, born in the flesh, planted the Church and suffered.

The elder son mocked his father when he was uncovered, while the younger covered him; so the Jews mocked God crucified, while the Gentiles honored him.

The day would fail me if I explained all the mysteries of the ark by comparing them with the Church.

Who among us are the eagles, who the doves, who the lions, who the deer, who the little worms, who the serpents? I shall briefly settle what concerns the present matter.

[Note: “Servants” was perhaps a typographical error.]

Not only do sheep dwell in the Church, nor do only clean birds fly about; but grain is sown in the field, and among shining cultivated ground, burdocks and thistles, barren oats also hold sway.

(From Virgil, *Georgics* I.151.)

What is the farmer to do? Should he pull up the weeds? But the whole harvest would be overturned at the same time. Every day rustic diligence drives away the birds with noise and frightens them with scarecrows; here the whip cracks, there scarecrows are stretched out. Nevertheless, either swift does or a wanton wild ass rushes in; here mice carry grain into barns dug beneath the ground, there ants in a seething column ravage the crop.

[Note: The old edition reads: “in a frequent column.”]

Such is the situation. No one possesses a field in safety. While the master of the house slept, the enemy sowed weeds over the wheat. When the servants proposed going to uproot them, the Lord forbade them, reserving for himself the separation of the straw and the grain (Matthew 13).

These are the vessels of wrath and of mercy that the Apostle proclaims to be in the house of God (Romans 9 and 2 Timothy 2).

The day will therefore come when, after the Church’s treasury has been opened, the Lord will bring forth the vessels of his wrath. As they go out, the saints will say: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

No one can claim Christ’s palm for himself; no one can judge human beings before the day of judgment. “There is a way that seems right to human beings, but its end leads down into the depths of hell” (Proverbs 14:12).

In this error of judgment, what certain verdict can there be?

## 23. Ecclesiastical Tradition. Heretics of the Primitive Church. Heretics among the Jews. Heretics against the Gospels.

The blessed Cyprian attempted to flee from broken cisterns and not drink from another’s water. For this reason, rejecting the baptism of heretics, he sent an African council concerning the matter to Stephen, then bishop of the city of Rome, who was the twenty-second after blessed Peter.

[Note: “The twenty-second.” In the later book of the *Chronicle* we read: “Lucius holds the episcopate of the Roman Church as the twenty-first, for eight months; after him Stephen, the twenty-second, for eleven years.” Letters of Cyprian to both men survive. Others make him the twenty-third. —Martianus.

It is altogether established, after reckoning the succession, that Stephen held the twenty-second place after Peter. Therefore we did not hesitate to correct the error by which he had hitherto been called the twenty-sixth. Perhaps the Roman numeral was once written XXII, which a copyist, through haste in writing or reading, took for XXVI. Shortly afterward, in place of *sent* or *directed*, the edition perhaps more correctly reads *announced*.]

But his attempt was in vain. Finally, those very bishops who had decided with him that heretics should be rebaptized returned to the ancient custom and issued a new decree.

[Note: We learn this only from Jerome; elsewhere you will find no mention of this new decree. Indeed, the very dispute between the Donatists and Saint Augustine knows nothing at all of it. Pamelius cites Saint Dionysius of Alexandria as a witness to this matter, but, along with Baronius, he is mistaken.]

What are we to do? Our predecessors handed this down to us, and theirs handed it down to them.

But why should I speak of later times? While the Apostles were still in Judaea, with the blood of Christ still fresh, the Lord’s body was asserted to be a phantom. The Apostle again gives birth to the Galatians, who had been led back to observance of the Law. He attempts, with many arguments, to draw the Corinthians, who did not believe in the resurrection of the flesh, back to the true path.

At that time Simon Magus and his disciple Menander asserted that they possessed the powers of God. At that time Basilides devised Abraxas as the supreme God, together with 365 [powers, rulers, or angels].

[Note: The editions read “powers, rulers, and angels,” whom Basilides distributed into 365 classes according to the number of the heavens—for he imagined that there were 365 heavens—and thus he preferred to call the spheres through which the sun travels in its daily motion. Abraxas was the supreme God and ruler of these, since that name, in its letters, yields the same number. But some read “aeons” instead of “editions” or “classes.” Many defend Nicolas from heresy, although they do not deny that he gave the Nicolaitans an occasion for devising it.]

Then Nicolas, who was one of the seven deacons, imagined obscene and even shameful sexual unions by practicing marriages day and night.

I say nothing of the heretics among the Jews, who, before Christ’s coming, dispersed the Law that had been handed down: how Dositheus, leader of the Samaritans, rejected the Prophets; how the Sadducees, springing from his root, also denied the resurrection of the flesh; how the Pharisees, separated from the Jews because of certain superfluous observances, derived their name from this separation.

[Note: Origen, in his commentary on Matthew, after saying that the Sadducees denied the resurrection and rejected the immortality of the soul, adds: “The Samaritans to this day hold the same doctrine as the Sadducees concerning the soul of human beings” (*to de auto tois Saddoukaiois dogma peri tes ton anthropon psyches, phronousi mechri tou deuro Samareis*, etc.). As for the Pharisees, whom he says soon afterward received their name from the division, it is known from the Hebrew term, meaning “division,” that they were so called.]

The Herodians accepted Herod the king in place of Christ.

I come now to the heretics who tore apart the Gospels: a certain Saturninus, the Ophites, the Cainites, the Sethians, Carpocrates, Cerinthus, and his successor Ebion, together with the other plagues, most of whom erupted while the Apostle John was still alive. Yet we do not read that any of them was rebaptized.

[Note: “The Ophites and Cainites.” In manuscript codices, “Chaldaeans” occurs in place of “Cainites.” See this material in Epiphanius and others. —Martianus.

Victorius reads “Gnostics” and “Carpocrates”; and in other books “Chaldaeans” is often found instead of “Cainites.”]

[Note: Some learned men assert that there was never an Ebion, preferring to think that those heretics received the name “Ebionites” from their impoverished view of Christ. But none of the ancients denies that he existed; many affirm it. Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 33; Pacianus, letter 1; Philaster, heresy 37; Hilary, *On the Trinity*; Theodoret; Rufinus; and Epiphanius, who additionally reports that he lived in the village of Cochabe in the region of Bashan, heresy 32. He does not conceal the allusion to the poverty expressed by his Hebrew name.]

## 24. Heretics Should Be Granted Penance without Baptism.

Since we have mentioned such a man, let us also establish from his Apocalypse that heretics ought to be granted penance without baptism.

The angel of Ephesus is charged with having abandoned charity. In the angel of the Church of Pergamum, the eating of food sacrificed to idols and the doctrine of the Nicolaitans are condemned. Likewise, in the angel of the Thyatiran Church, the prophetess Jezebel, food offered to idols, and fornications are rebuked.

Yet the Lord exhorts all these to penance, also threatening future punishment unless they convert. He would not command them to repent if he were not going to grant forgiveness to those who repent.

Did he say, “Let those who were baptized in the faith of the Nicolaitans be rebaptized”? Or, “Let hands be laid upon those who believed among the Pergamenes while they held the teaching of Balaam”? Rather, he says: “Repent; but if not, I will come to you quickly and fight against you with the sword of my mouth” (Revelation 2:2).

## 25. Saint Cyprian’s Letter to Stephen. The Same Man’s Letter to Jubaianus.

But if those who were instructed by Hilary, and who have begun to be sheep without a shepherd, wish to produce from the Scriptures what the blessed Cyprian left in his letters concerning the rebaptizing of heretics, let them know that he did not publish these things with a curse against those who were unwilling to follow him.

[Note: Compare Eusebius, book VII, chapter 3, and Augustine, book V against the Donatists, chapter 23. They say that Stephen ordered that nothing be innovated and threatened an anathema, but that he did not actually break communion with Cyprian and the Africans. On the contrary, Firmilian’s letter says: “What Stephen has now dared to do, breaking the peace against us which his predecessors always maintained with you in mutual love and honor.” Some therefore accuse Jerome of error.

I would more gladly accuse Firmilian himself of falsehood. Certainly Augustine, book V of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 25, said of Stephen: “Although they were more deeply stirred, they nevertheless expressed their indignation as brothers; yet the peace of Christ prevailed in their hearts, so that no evil of schism arose between them.”

Moreover, these documents show how much confidence should be placed in such records, in Augustine’s testimony in Letter 92: “There are some who contend that Cyprian did not at all hold this view, but that it was fabricated under his name by presumptuous and deceitful men.”

The old edition reads: “Let them know that he did not hate the opinion of those who were unwilling to follow him.”]

For he remained in communion with those who opposed his judgment. Rather, because of Novatian and the many other heresies then arising, he urged that no one should be received without condemnation of his error.

He concluded the discourse which he delivered on this matter to Stephen, the Roman pontiff, as follows:

> “We have brought these matters to your conscience, dearest brother, both for the sake of our common honor and out of simple affection, believing that, because of the truth of your religion and faith, you too will approve what is both religious and true. For the rest, we know that some people are unwilling to lay aside what they have once absorbed and do not easily change their purpose. Yet, while preserving the bond of peace and harmony among colleagues, they retain certain practices of their own which they once adopted among themselves. In this matter we use force against no one, nor do we impose a law, so as to prevent each person from having free discretion in the administration of the Church according to his own will. Let each preside over his own affairs, destined to render an account of his actions to the Lord.”

Writing also to Jubaianus concerning the rebaptizing of heretics, he spoke at the end of his short treatise in this way:

> “We have written these matters to you briefly, dearest brother, according to our modest ability, prescribing or prejudging nothing, so as to prevent any bishop from doing what he thinks right, since each has free power of judgment. As far as lies in us, we do not quarrel with our colleagues and fellow bishops concerning heretics, with whom we maintain divine harmony and the Lord’s peace, especially since the Apostle says: ‘If anyone thinks that he is contentious, we have no such custom, nor has the Church of God.’ We patiently and gently preserve the charity of the spirit, the honor of the college, the bond of faith, and the harmony of the priesthood.”

## 26. Against Hilary, the Deacon of the Roman Church.

There is another argument which we shall bring forward, against which Hilary, the Deucalion of the world, will not even dare to mutter.

For if heretics do not possess baptism, and therefore must be rebaptized by the Church because they were not in the Church, then Hilary also is not a Christian. He was baptized in that Church which has always received baptism from heretics.

Before the Council of Ariminum was held, before Lucifer went into exile, Hilary, a deacon of the Roman Church, received those coming from heretics with the baptism they had previously received.

Unless perhaps only the Arians are heretics, and it is forbidden to receive those baptized by them but permitted to receive those baptized by others.

You were a deacon, Hilary, and you received those baptized by the Manichaeans.

[Note: The old edition reads: “and you received the Manichaeans.” What is called below the “new bath” is explained by Victorius as “a new baptism.”]

You were a deacon, and you approved the baptism of Ebion.

Suddenly, after Arius arose, you began to find the whole world displeasing. You separate yourself with your little servants and open a new bath.

If some angel or apostle rebaptized you, I do not challenge what you follow. But if you were born in my bosom and nourished by my breasts, and now raise the sword against me, return what I gave you and, if you can, become a Christian in another way.

I am a harlot, but I am still your mother. I do not preserve the chastity of one marriage bed; such was I when you were conceived. When I committed adultery with Arius, I had done so previously with Praxeas, Ebion, Cerinthus, and Novatian. You embrace these men; you now receive these adulterers into your mother’s house.

I do not know why one adulterer offends you.

## 27. Heretics Have Always Been Received.

If anyone should think that it must be denied that heretics were always received by our predecessors, let him read the letters of the blessed Cyprian, in which he tears apart the error of the long-established custom before Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome.

[Note: More correctly, the same edition reads: “in which, before Stephen, bishop of the city of Rome, he attacks the error of the long-established custom.” Jerome is referring to Cyprian’s Letter 72, addressed to Pope Stephen concerning the council, and at the same time to another letter mentioned by Crescens, bishop of Cirta, in the Council of Carthage, though that letter has not come down to us. In it, evidently, many scriptural testimonies were brought forward against Stephen’s judgment concerning the baptism of heretics.]

Let him also read the treatises which Hilary himself published against us concerning the rebaptizing of heretics. There he will find Hilary himself confessing that, by Julius, Mark, Sylvester, and the other ancient bishops, all heretics were likewise received into penance.

Yet custom ought not to prejudice the truth for him.

The Council of Nicaea also, which we mentioned shortly before, received all heretics except the disciples of Paul of Samosata. And, greater still, if a Novatian bishop should be converted, it preserves for him the rank of presbyter.

This judgment attacks both Lucifer and Hilary, since the same man is both a cleric and baptized.

## 28. In Which Church One Must Remain. Conclusion and Fruit of the Discussion.

I could occupy the day with a discourse of this kind and dry up all the streams of argument with the one sun of the Church. But since we have already talked at length and the length of the debate has wearied the attention of the listeners, I shall offer you a brief and clear statement of my mind: one must remain in that Church which was founded by the Apostles and endures to this day.

If anywhere you hear those who are called Christians named not after the Lord Jesus Christ but after someone else—for example, Marcionites, Valentinians, Montenses, or Campites—know that they are not the Church of Christ but the synagogue of Antichrist.

[Note: Montenses, or Campites. From Jerome’s *Chronicle* we learn that Donatus’s followers were called Montenses because they had their church on a mountain at Rome. Concerning the Campites and Tharsensian heretics, see above, the first letter to Pope Damasus.

—Martianus.

I think that the Donatists were called Campites as an insult because they lived in fields or mountains, as the word itself indicates. In the records of the purification of Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, published by Baluzius, the deacon Nundinarius said: “The Campites and the arena-men made him bishop.” The first edition and Erasmus read “Campates.” Both they and Victorius, however, ridiculously interpret Montenses from the heresy of Montanus.]

By the very fact that they were established later, they show that they are those whom the Apostle foretold would come.

Nor should they flatter themselves if they seem to confirm what they say from passages of Scripture, since the devil too has spoken certain things from Scripture, and “the Scriptures do not consist in reading but in understanding.”

[Note: This sentence is taken in the same words from Saint Hilary, *To Constantius*, book II, section 9: “For the Scriptures are not in reading but in understanding; nor are they in transgression but in charity.” See Saint Augustine, Letter 120 to Consent; and Athanasius, *Oration 2 against the Arians*.]

Otherwise, if we follow the letter, we too can construct a new doctrine for ourselves, asserting that those who wear shoes and possess two tunics must not be received into the Church.

**L.** Do not imagine that you alone have won. We have both won; each of us carries away the palm: you carry away the palm over me, and I over error. Would that I might always have the opportunity to debate in such a way that, advancing toward better things, I abandon what I was wrongly holding. Yet I confess one thing to you: because I know the character of my people extremely well, they can more easily be defeated than persuaded.

[Col. 0181]

# ON THE VIRGINITY OF THE BLESSED MARY (C)

## Notice Concerning the Following Book

Helvidius, relying on several improperly understood testimonies of Sacred Scripture and insufficiently considering the authority of two ancient Fathers—namely Tertullian and Victorinus of Pettau—had composed a book in which he attempted to prove that Mary the Virgin, after giving birth to Jesus the Son of God without any human agency but through the Holy Spirit, afterward bore several children by Joseph her husband, according to the common practice of other human beings. These children, he claimed, are called the Lord’s brothers in the Gospel.

To cover this madness with some coating of argument, he compounded it with a new error. He loudly declared that virginity was in no way superior to marriage, and attempted to prove this with arguments—or rather falsehoods.

He was apparently an ordinary man from the common people, rustic, and scarcely instructed even in the rudiments of letters. His name was so obscure that, although he lived at Rome at the same time as Jerome, Jerome had never recognized him by sight and did not know whether he was white or black, as the saying goes.

Gennadius adds that he was a disciple of Auxentius, the most impious of the Arians who had seized the see of Milan, and an imitator of Symmachus, that pagan senator who had defended idolatry in writing. But Gennadius’s testimony troubles me for more than one reason, and I think it suffers from a serious transposition.

For why would Jerome, in replying, have passed over Auxentius as Helvidius’s teacher? And how could Helvidius have imitated Symmachus except in the intention to do harm and in impiety—he who had published a book polished neither in language nor in reasoning, and indeed full of solecisms? Again, if he imitated Symmachus’s impiety, how can Gennadius say that he wrote from devotion to religion? These things plainly do not agree with sound reasoning and cannot equally be referred to Helvidius.

At the request of the brethren, Jerome eventually replied to Helvidius’s little book, although he had long delayed doing so, lest by answering he should make Helvidius worthy to be defeated.

Accordingly, preparing to enter the contest, he attacks each proposition of the heretic in order, expounding the passages of Scripture—and especially Matthew 1:18, which his opponent chiefly abused—in such a way as most clearly to establish that Mary the Mother of God remained perpetually a virgin and never knew a man even after giving birth to the Savior. This is the faith of the Catholic Church.

For this reason he gave the book the title *On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary*. Gennadius, in a manuscript at Corbie, again calls it an excellent and welcome little book, in which it is shown that the most blessed Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, remained a virgin after giving birth just as she was a virgin before giving birth.

As for the authority of the ancients, Jerome is content to say that Tertullian was not a man of the Church; but he emphatically denies that Victorinus of Pettau held the same opinion as his opponent. He then says that he could summon and set against Helvidius an endless succession of writers.

Finally, he explains at length the praise of virginity, whose excellence he extols, after presenting Paul’s splendid testimony to the Corinthians, also by describing the disadvantages of marriage that he places before the eyes.

When he wrote about this matter to Pammachius ten years later, in Letter 48, section 17, he said:

> “While Damasus of holy memory was still alive, we wrote a book against Helvidius on the perpetual virginity of blessed Mary. In it, in order to proclaim the blessedness of virginity, it was necessary for us to say many things about the burdens of marriage. Did that distinguished and learned man, an expert in the Scriptures and a virgin, the teacher of the virgin Church, find anything to criticize in that discourse?”

From this testimony it can also readily be determined when the book was written. According to the testimony of the ancient martyrologies, Damasus died toward the end of the year 384. Jerome did not reside at Rome with Damasus before the end of the year 382, as has been established by the chronological arguments of Letters 19 and 20. The intervening period of two years proves that the earlier year, namely 383, must be assigned to the book. This is confirmed by another testimony from Letter 22:

> “How many burdens marriage has and by how many anxieties it is beset, I think has been briefly expressed in the book which we published against Helvidius on the perpetual virginity of blessed Mary.”

That letter belongs, as we have shown in its proper place, to the first part of the year 384. Therefore the book against Helvidius which it praises, and which it indicates was already in the hands of the public, must be assigned to the preceding year, 383.

# Saint Eusebius Jerome, Presbyter of Stridon,  
## One Book on the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary, against Helvidius

[Note: The editions of Martianus and Vallarsi have the title: “Here begins the book of Saint Jerome against Helvidius on the Virginity of Blessed Mary.”

—Editor.

“Here begins the book,” and so forth. In four or five manuscript copies this book is entitled “The Letter of Saint Jerome.” This is because the work was always written among the letters, or in manuscripts of the letters. Jerome mentions this book several times in his commentaries and in his letter to Eustochium, among other places.

—Martianus.]

[Col. 0183]

# Book One
[Col. 0183A] 205

### 1.

Recently, when I was asked by the brethren to reply to the little book of a certain Helvidius, I postponed doing so—not because it would have been difficult to refute, concerning the assertion of truth, a rustic man scarcely even instructed in the first elements of literature, but lest, by replying, I should make him worthy to be defeated.

[Note: To this was added the fact that the man, etc. The printed editions read this passage thus: “To this was added that I feared lest a turbulent man, and the only person in the whole world at once layman and priest—who (as he himself says) considers loquacity, etc.” We have followed the manuscript codices, which do not read the word “I feared,” added in the printed editions, and which retain *sibi* (“for himself”) in place of *simul* (“at once”), with an appropriate sense: for Helvidius was layman and priest for himself, not for the Church of Christ, in which he was regarded as a monster, not as a priest. —Martianus. The older printed editions have “because I feared lest the man.” A little later Victorius reads *simul* instead of *sibi*, which he nevertheless does not disapprove, and notes is found in manuscripts. We follow chiefly the authority of the Veronensis, which easily surpasses all known to this day in antiquity and excellence.]

To this was added the fact that the man was turbulent and, alone in the whole world, both layman and priest for himself (who, as he himself says, considers loquacity eloquence [Alternative reading: “should consider loquacity eloquence”] and regards reviling everyone as a sign of a good conscience).

[Note: He indicates Tertullian without naming him, from chapter 1 of the book *Against Hermogenes*: “A man,” he says, “in the world, and by nature also a heretic, even turbulent, who considers loquacity eloquence, counts impudence as steadfastness, and judges that reviling individuals is the duty of a good conscience.”]

Having received material for disputation, he would begin to blaspheme still more and, as though from an elevated place, pronounce judgment upon the whole world; and because he could not attack me with truth, he would tear me apart with insults [Alternative reading: “tear me apart”]. But since all these very just reasons for my silence, on account of the scandal of the brethren who were agitated by his madness, have now come to an end for a still more just reason, the axe must now be laid to the roots of the fruitless tree of the Gospel (Matt. 3:10),

[Note: “And with the barrenness…” Marianus argues here against Erasmus; but both are mistaken. Jerome does not refer either to the unfruitful Gospel fig tree or to the righteous man of the First Psalm, but to the leaves of words in speech, whose barrenness was found in the rustic and none too eloquent Helvidius. —Martianus.

He plainly alludes to Matthew 3:10: “Already the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” He calls the leaves barren because their very abundance and excess turns all the moisture into leaves without fruit. Such was the fig tree upon which the Lord pronounced a curse. I therefore more readily agree with Erasmus’s interpretation, although the question is almost about nothing.]

and, together with the barrenness of its leaves, it must be handed over to the flames, so that the one who never learned to speak may at last learn to keep silent.

### 2.

Therefore the Holy Spirit must be invoked by me, so that he may defend the virginity of blessed Mary with his meaning through my mouth. The Lord Jesus must be invoked, so that he may protect from every suspicion of intercourse the lodging of the sacred womb, whose inhabitant he was for ten months.

[Note: See Aulus Gellius and the notes on Epistle 127 and elsewhere.]

God the Father himself must also be entreated, so that he may show the mother of his Son to have remained a virgin after childbirth, she who was a mother before she was married.

[Note: Namely, because she had conceived from the Holy Spirit before she became Joseph’s wife from being his betrothed. There are, however, some who understand *to marry* and *married* as referring to bodily intercourse with a man. Thus, in the scholia of Saint Cyril on the Incarnation of the Lord, chapter 25: “For he was born from a Virgin, and alone has an unmarried mother,” that is, one who had never had intercourse with her husband. Tertullian likewise understands the matter in this sense in the *Apologeticus*, when he asserts that the Son of God had a mother untouched by unchastity: “Even she whom he seemed to have, had not married.”]

We do not seek a field for rhetorical eloquence, nor the snares of dialecticians, nor do we search out the thorny thickets of Aristotle. The very words of Scripture must be set forth. Let him be refuted by the very testimonies that he has used against us, so that he may understand that he was able to read what was written but was unable to recognize what had been confirmed by piety.

[Note: The Veronensis manuscript has: “and was unable to understand what was written.” “His first,” etc.]

[Col. 0185B] ### 3. Helvidius.

His first proposition was this:

“Matthew says: ‘Now the generation of Christ was as follows. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to have conceived in the womb from the Holy Spirit. But Joseph her husband, being righteous and unwilling to expose her, wished to dismiss her secretly.’

[Note: The Veronensis does not have the words “her” and “but.”]

“While he was considering this, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: ‘Joseph, son of David, do not fear to receive Mary your wife. For what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 1:18 ff.).

“Behold,” he says, “you have a betrothed woman, not merely one entrusted to you, as you say—and certainly she was betrothed for no other reason than that she would eventually marry. For the Evangelist would not have said of people who would not come together, ‘before they came together,’ since no one says of a person who will not dine, ‘before he dined.’ Then she is called both wife and united to him by the angel. Let us now hear what Scripture declares: ‘Joseph, rising from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and took his wife, and did not know her until she had given birth to her son’ (Matt. 1:24–25).”

### 4. Jerome.—What the preposition “before” indicates. Why Mary conceived as a virgin betrothed.

Let us run through each point, pursuing his impiety along the same tracks by which it entered, and show that he has said things contradictory to one another. He admits that she was betrothed, and immediately wants her to be a wife whom he has confessed to be a betrothed woman. Again, of the woman whom he calls a wife, he says that she was betrothed for no other reason than that she would eventually marry. And lest we think this insufficient:

“‘You have,’ he says, ‘a betrothed woman, and not one merely entrusted to you—that is, not yet a wife, not yet joined by the marital bond.’”

But when he says, “For the Evangelist would not have said of people who would not come together, ‘before they came together,’ since no one says of a person who will not dine, ‘before he dined’”—whether I should grieve or laugh, I do not know. Should I accuse him of ignorance or charge him with rashness?

Suppose someone said: “Before I dined in the harbor, I sailed to Africa.”

[Note: The earlier text had “he sailed”; and instead of “unless he must dine in that harbor,” I accept from the Veronensis “unless he had to dine in the harbor.”]

The statement could surely stand without implying that he would at some later time have to dine in that harbor. Or suppose we wished to say: “Before the Apostle Paul went to Spain, he was thrown into chains at Rome.” Or certainly: “Before Helvidius did penance, he was overtaken by death.” Would it follow immediately that Paul had to go to Spain after his imprisonment, or that Helvidius had to do penance after death, when Scripture says: “But in hell, who will confess to you?” (Ps. 6:6).

Would it not rather be understood that although the preposition *before* often indicates a sequence, nevertheless it sometimes points only to things that were previously contemplated? Hence it is not necessary that what was contemplated should occur, since something else may intervene precisely so that what was contemplated does not occur.

Therefore, when the Evangelist says, “before they came together,” he indicates that the time of the wedding was near and that the matter had already reached the point at which she who had previously been betrothed was about to begin to be a wife. It is as though he had said: “Before they mingled kisses and embraces; before they carried out the act of marriage, she was found to have conceived.”

She was found, moreover, by no one other than Joseph, who detected the swelling womb of his betrothed with almost marital permission and inquisitive eyes.

[Note: In his commentary on the first chapter of Matthew, he says that Joseph knew nearly everything about his future wife by marital permission.]

Yet it does not follow, as we have shown by the preceding examples, that he came together with Mary after the birth—he whose desire to come together had been removed by the conception in her womb.

As for what is said to Joseph in a dream, “Do not fear to take Mary your wife,” and again, “Joseph, rising from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and took his wife,” no one should be disturbed as though, because she was called a wife, she had ceased to be betrothed. For we know this to be the custom of divine Scripture: to call betrothed women wives.

This is demonstrated by the following testimonies from Deuteronomy. “If,” it says, “a man finds a virgin betrothed to a man in the field and, using force, sleeps with her, he shall surely die, because he has humbled his neighbor’s wife” (Deut. 22:25).

And elsewhere: “But if a young woman has been betrothed to a man, and a man finds her in the city and sleeps with her, you shall bring both of them out to the gates of that city, and they shall be stoned with stones and shall die: the young woman because she did not cry out, although she was in the city; the man because he humbled his neighbor’s wife. And you shall remove the evil from your midst” [Alternative reading: “the wicked one”] (Deut. 22:23–24).

Again, elsewhere: “Who is the man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man take her” [Alternative reading: “will take her”] (Deut. 20:7).

If anyone is troubled by the question of why a betrothed virgin, rather than a virgin without a bridegroom—or, as Scripture calls him, a husband—conceived, let him know that there were three reasons.

[Col. 0187B] First, so that through Joseph’s genealogy, since Mary was his kinswoman, Mary’s ancestry also might be shown.

[Note: Victorius notes that this was done for the purpose of showing Mary to have belonged to the same tribe, so that she would not appear to have been taken as a wife from another tribe, which was prohibited by the Law (Num. 36).]

Second, so that, according to the law of Moses, she would not be stoned by the people as an adulteress.

Third, so that, when fleeing to Egypt, she would have the protection of a guardian rather than of a husband.

For who would have believed a virgin at that time if she said that she had conceived from the Holy Spirit? Who would have believed that the angel Gabriel had come and delivered God’s command? Would they not rather have condemned her as an adulteress, following the example of Susanna, by the judgment of everyone, when even today, although the whole world now believes, the Jews argue that Isaiah, when he says, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son” (Isa. 7:14), wrote in Hebrew “young woman,” not “virgin”—*AALMA*, not *BETHULA*?

[Note: “As Isaiah says.” Many additions and alterations are found in the ancient editions of this little work, including here: “Isaiah teaching about Mary and her virginity.” These words are found in no manuscript exemplar and will seem superfluous to an educated reader if he pays careful attention for a moment to Jerome’s context. —Martianus.

Before Martianus’s edition, the printed editions add, incorrectly, “teaching about Mary and her virginity.” Immediately afterward, the Veronensis gives the form *HAALMA*, which Jerome elsewhere explains very fully in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* and in his commentaries on Isaiah.]

We shall discuss this matter more suitably in another place.

Finally, with the exception of Joseph, Elizabeth, and Mary herself, together with a very few others whom we may suppose to have heard from them, everyone thought Jesus was Joseph’s son. So much so that even the Evangelists, expressing the common opinion—which is the true law of history—call Joseph the Savior’s father.

[Note: These words, which are the true law of history, are absent from the Veronensis manuscript; hence I doubt whether they proceeded from a pen other than Jerome’s.]

As in the passage:

“He came in the Spirit into the Temple”—there can be no doubt that this refers to Simeon—“and when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law” (Luke 2:27).

And elsewhere: “His father and mother were marveling at the things that were said about him” (ibid. 2:33).

And again: “His parents went every year to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover” (ibid. 2:41).

Then: “When the days were completed and they were returning, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it” (ibid. 2:43).

Mary herself, who had answered Gabriel, saying, “How will this be, since I do not know a man,” listen to what she says about Joseph:

“Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I, grieving, have been searching for you” (ibid. 2:48).

[Note: The preferred reading, found in all the manuscript codices, is “This is not the voice of the Jews.” Erasmus and Marianus retain it. —Martianus. The Veronensis likewise does not have the name Joseph here, which is somewhat more elegant.]

This is not, as many argue, the voice of Jews or of mockers. The Evangelist calls Joseph the father; Mary acknowledges him as father—not because Joseph was truly the Savior’s father, as I indicated above, but because, for the sake of preserving Mary’s reputation, he was considered father by everyone. Before he was warned by the angel:

“Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife, for what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20),

he was considering secretly dismissing her.

[Note: The Veronensis has “by people” instead of “by everyone”; “Mary as his wife” instead of “as his spouse”; and below “he confessed” instead of “he thought.”]

He was so convinced that the one who had been conceived was not his own. But enough has now been said in the interest of teaching rather than replying: why Joseph was called the Lord’s father, why Mary was called his wife; and in this is also briefly contained the reason why some are said to be his brothers.

### 5. Helvidius.

But since we reserve this little question for its proper place, and our discourse is hurrying on to the remaining matters, we must now discuss how Scripture says:

“Joseph, rising from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and took his wife, and did not know her until she had given birth to her son, and he called his name Jesus” (Matt. 1:24–25).

Here the opponent first wastes his labor uselessly by insisting that the word “know” refers more to intercourse than to knowledge, as though anyone had denied this, or as though some sensible person could ever have suspected the absurdities that he refutes.

Next he wants to demonstrate that *until*, or *up to*, an adverb indicates a definite time, at the completion of which what had not been happening until the prescribed time begins to happen, as in the present case:

“And he did not know her until she had given birth to a son.”

“It is clear,” he says, “that he knew her after the birth, since he had merely postponed knowing her until the birth of the child.”

To prove this he piles together very many examples from Scripture,

[Note: Like an Andabates brandishing a sword in the darkness. It was the custom of the Andabatae, or gladiators, to fight with their eyes closed. Hence Jerome himself says below, in Book I *Against Jovinianus*: “It is better to fight with closed eyes, as an Andabates does.” See Erasmus’s *Adagia*, “Chiliades.” —Martianus.]

swinging his sword in the darkness like an Andabates and shaking the sound of his tongue only to stab the limbs of his own body.

[Col. 0189A] ### 6. Jerome.

To this we reply briefly that, in the Holy Scriptures, both “knew” and “until” are understood in two ways.

He himself has argued that the word “knew” in the passage must refer to intercourse, since no one doubts that it often refers to knowledge, as in the passage:

“The child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.”

Now it must be shown that, just as he followed the custom of Scripture in that matter, so also he may be refuted concerning *until* by the authority of the same Scripture. For *until* often indicates a definite time, as he himself argued when it is used in that sense, but often an indefinite time, as when God speaks through the Prophet to certain people:

“I am he, I am he, and until you grow old, I am” (Isa. 43; Jer. 7).

Will God cease to be after they have grown old?

And in the Gospel the Savior says to the Apostles:

“Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Will the Lord therefore depart from his disciples after the consummation of the age? And at that time, when they will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19:38), will they be deprived of the Lord’s companionship?

The Apostle Paul also writes to the Corinthians:

“Christ the firstfruits; afterward those who are Christ’s, who believed at his coming; afterward the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he destroys every principality and every authority and power. For he must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet” [Note: The Veronensis does not have “for he has subjected all things under his feet.”] (1 Cor. 15:23, 26).

Let us suppose that this was said of a man—not denying that it refers to the one who suffered the cross and was afterward commanded to sit at the right hand. What does this mean:

“For he must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet”?

Will the Lord reign only until his enemies begin to be under his feet, and after they have been placed under his feet will he cease to reign, when surely he will begin to reign all the more once his enemies have begun to be under his feet?

David also says in the fourth Psalm of Degrees:

“As the eyes of a maidservant are toward the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Ps. 122:3).

Will the Prophet therefore keep his eyes directed toward the Lord only until he obtains mercy, and after mercy has been obtained will he turn his eyes toward the earth?

In another place he says:

“My eyes have failed in longing for your salvation and for the word of your righteousness” (Ps. 118:123).

[Note: The Veronensis has a very different reading: “Before I pile up countless examples on this subject and conceal all the insolence of the challenger beneath a cloud of testimonies, I will still add a few.”]

I could gather countless examples on this subject and conceal all the insolence of the challenger beneath a cloud of testimonies; but for now I shall add only a few, so that the reader himself may find similar examples.

### 7.

The divine word speaks in Genesis:

“They gave Jacob the foreign gods that were in their hands, and the earrings that were in their ears. And Jacob hid them beneath the terebinth that is at Shechem, and they remained lost to this day” (Gen. 35:4 ff.).

[Note: The Veronensis likewise has “he hid them,” whereas Erasmus read “them” in the masculine and Victorius “them” in the neuter in both places. The Greek likewise has αὐτά, “them.”]

Likewise, at the end of Deuteronomy:

“Moses, the servant of the Lord, died in the land of Moab by the word of the Lord, and they buried him in Geth, near the house of Phogor; and no one knows his tomb to this day” (Deut. 34:6, according to the Septuagint).

Certainly “this day” must be understood as the day of the time in which the history itself was composed—whether you wish to say that Moses was the author of the Pentateuch or that Ezra restored the work. I do not object.

[Note: Tertullian says in *On the Cult of Women*, chapter 3: “The whole instrument of Jewish literature is acknowledged to have been restored through Ezra.” Many Greek and Latin Fathers adopted this view.]

The question now is whether what is said, “to this day,” refers to the period in which the books were published or written. Let him then prove that, after that day, so many years having passed through the volumes down to our own time, either the idols that had been buried beneath the terebinth were found or Moses’ tomb was investigated—because he emphatically asserts that after *until* and *up to* there begins to exist what did not exist for as long as the *until* and *up to* remained incomplete.

Rather, let him observe the idiom of Holy Scripture and understand with us that matters about which doubt might arise are marked when they are written, while other matters are left to our understanding.

[Note: The older edition reads: “Let him understand the things about which he hesitated.”]

For if Moses’ tomb could still have been unknown in recent times, while those who had seen Moses were alive, how much more could it remain unknown after so many centuries had passed.

Accordingly, the passage concerning Joseph is also understood in this way: the Evangelist indicated that he had not known her until childbirth, because this was the point concerning which scandal might arise, so that we might understand all the more clearly that he did not know her after childbirth—the one from whom he abstained at a time when he could still have been uncertain because of the vision.

### 8.

In sum, I ask why Joseph abstained from her until the day of childbirth.

He will surely answer: because he heard the angel say:

“For what has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20).

To this we reply: Certainly Joseph had also heard:

“Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife” (ibid. 1:20).

He had been forbidden to abandon her, lest he regard her as an adulteress. Was he also separated from intercourse with his wife, when he had actually been admonished above all not to separate from her?

“And did the righteous man,” he says, “dare to think of intercourse with his wife when he heard that God’s Son was in her womb?”

Excellent.

The man who believed a mere dream so completely that he did not dare touch his wife—after he had learned through the voice of shepherds that the angel of the Lord had come from heaven and said to them:

“Do not fear. Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:10 ff.),

and when the heavenly host sang praises with him:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will”;

who had seen the righteous Simeon, while embracing the child, proclaiming:

“Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; because my eyes have seen your salvation” (ibid. 2:27);

who had seen Anna the prophetess, the Magi, the star, Herod, and the angels—this man, I say, who had learned of so many miracles, dared to touch the temple of God, the dwelling of the Holy Spirit, the mother of his Lord?

And certainly Mary “kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (ibid. 2:51).

And lest you impudently [Alternative reading: “imprudently”] deny that Joseph knew these things, Luke says:

“His father and mother were marveling at the things that were said about him.”

Although you may contend, with astonishing impudence, that these words have been corrupted in the Greek manuscripts,

[Note: At least the words “his father” are absent from the Greek manuscripts, except for the Cambridge manuscript and one of the Stephanic manuscripts; they are found, however, in the Vulgate and the Coptic version.]

they were not only preserved by nearly all the Greek commentators in their volumes, but some Latins have also adopted them, just as they stand in the Greek manuscripts.

[Note: The plural was printed incorrectly. The Veronensis reads “to argue from the variety of copies,” instead of “to discuss.”]

Nor is it necessary now to argue from the variety of copies, since the whole body of both Old and New Scripture has been translated thence into Latin speech, and the water of the fountain should be believed to flow much purer than that of the streams.

### 7. Helvidius.

“You say that these things are trifles to me, and that your arguments are superfluous and your discussion more curious than true. Could Scripture not have said: ‘He took his wife, and afterward he did not dare to touch her’ (Gen. 38:26), just as it said this concerning Tamar and Judah? Or did Matthew lack words by which he could express what he wished to be understood? ‘He did not know her,’ he says, ‘until she had given birth to a son’ (Matt. 1:25). Therefore he knew her after the birth, since he had postponed knowing her until the birth.”

### 8. Jerome.

If you are so contentious, you will now be overcome by your own argument. I do not want you to insert any interval between childbirth and intercourse. I do not want you to say:

“Any woman who has conceived and given birth to a male child shall be unclean for seven days; according to the days of the separation of her impurity, she shall be unclean; and on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised. Then she shall sit for thirty-three days in the blood of her purification; she shall touch nothing holy,” and so forth (Lev. 12:2–3).

Let Joseph rush upon her immediately. Let him immediately hear Jeremiah say:

“They became frenzied horses toward women; each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. 5:8).

Otherwise, how can the statement stand:

“He did not know her until she had given birth to a son,”

if he waits until the period of purification; if desire is again postponed for forty days and delayed for so long a time?

Let the woman who has given birth be defiled with blood; let the midwives receive the crying infant; let the husband hold his exhausted wife. Thus let the marriage begin, lest the Evangelist have lied.

But far be it from us to think this of the Savior’s mother and the righteous man. There was no midwife there; no attentiveness of little women intervened. She herself wrapped the infant in swaddling clothes; she herself was both mother and midwife.

“And she placed him,” it says, “in a manger, because there was no room for him in the lodging” (Luke 2:7).

This statement also refutes the ravings of the apocryphal books, since Mary herself wrapped the infant in swaddling clothes; and it prevents Helvidius’s desire from being fulfilled, since there was no room for marriage in the lodging.

[Note: In truth, the singular book concerning Saint Mary and the midwife is rejected among the apocrypha in the decree of Gelasius; it is also mentioned in the *Protoevangelium of James*, chapter 19. The Veronensis and Erasmus read “desire” instead of “pleasure,” while the other printed books have “pleasure.”]

### 9. Helvidius.

But since we have now answered sufficiently and abundantly the points he had proposed—“before they came together” and “he did not know her until she had given birth to a son”—we must come to the third question, so that, following the order of his discussion, the order of our reply may also proceed.

For he wants Mary to have borne other sons as well, and he attempts to prove this from what is written:

“Joseph also went up to the city of David, to register with Mary his pregnant wife. And it happened that, while they were there, the days were completed for her to give birth, and she gave birth to her firstborn son” (Luke 2:4 ff.).

He endeavors to establish that no one can be called firstborn unless he has brothers, just as an only-begotten son is called one whose parents have no other child.

### 10. Jerome.

We, however, define the matter as follows: Every only-begotten son is firstborn, but not every firstborn is only-begotten. A firstborn is not merely one after whom others are born, but one before whom no one was born.

The Lord says to Aaron:

“Everything that opens the womb, from all flesh that is offered to the Lord, from human beings to cattle, shall be yours. Only the firstborn of human beings they shall redeem for a price, and the firstborn of unclean animals” [Note: The Veronensis has “and the firstborn of unclean animals,” without “of cattle.”] (Exod. 34:19–20; Num. 18:15).

The word of God has defined what a firstborn is:

“Everything,” it says, “that opens the womb.”

Otherwise, if only the one followed by brothers is firstborn, firstborn children would not be owed to the priests until other children had also been born, lest the child should later prove to be only-begotten and not firstborn because no later birth followed.

“Its redemption,” it says, “shall be from one month, according to the valuation of five” [Note: Likewise, “five shekels, according to the sacred shekel.” A little later: “so that every male that opens the womb…”] “shekels. The shekel, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, is twenty obols. But you shall not redeem the firstborn of calves, the firstborn of sheep, or the firstborn of goats, because they are holy” (Num. 18:16–17).

The word of God compels me to vow to God everything that opens the womb, if it is from clean animals; but if it is from unclean animals, to redeem it, paying the price to the priest.

I can reply and say: Why do you confine me to the interval of one month? Why do you call him firstborn when I do not know whether brothers will follow? Wait until a second is born. I owe nothing to the priest unless another child is born, through whom the one previously born begins to be firstborn.

Will not the very letters speak to me and rebuke me for my stupidity, showing that he was called firstborn who opens the womb, not one who has brothers?

Finally, I ask about John, whom it is certain was only-begotten: was he also firstborn? Was he likewise subject to the whole law according to the Law?

There can be no doubt. Certainly Scripture speaks of the Savior as follows:

“When the days of their purification were completed according to the Law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the Law of the Lord: ‘Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord’; and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, ‘a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons’” (Luke 2:22 ff.).

If this law applies only to firstborn children, and if later children are what make a child firstborn, then the one who did not know whether brothers would follow him ought not to have been bound by the law of the firstborn.

But because he is bound by the law of the firstborn even though no other brothers follow him, it is concluded that he is called firstborn who opens the womb and before whom no one exists, not one whom a brother born later follows.

Moses writes in Exodus:

“It happened at midnight that the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat upon his throne to the firstborn of the captive woman who was by the pool, and every firstborn of cattle” (Exod. 12:29).

Answer me: Those who were then killed by the destroyer—were they firstborn or also only-begotten?

If only those who have brothers are called firstborn, then the only-begotten were spared from destruction.

But if they were killed although only-begotten, this contradicts your position: only-begotten sons would have died among the firstborn.

Either you will free the only-begotten from punishment and be ridiculous, or, if you confess that they were killed, we shall prevail against you despite your unwillingness, and the only-begotten will be shown to be called firstborn.

## 11. The final proposition of Helvidius

His final proposition was this (although he wanted to establish the same point from the word “firstborn”): that the Lord’s brothers are named in the Gospels, as in the passage: “Behold, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him” (Luke 8:20). And elsewhere: “After this he went down to Capernaum, he himself and his mother and his brothers” (John 2:12). And again: “Therefore his brothers said to him, ‘Depart from here and go into Judea, so that your disciples also may see the works that you do. For no one who acts in secret seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, manifest yourself to the world’” (John 7:3–4). John adds immediately afterward: “For even his brothers did not believe in him at that time” (ibid. 5).

Likewise Mark and Matthew say: “And he was teaching them in their synagogue, in his own country, so that they were astonished and said: ‘Where did this man get all this wisdom and miraculous power? Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas, and are not all his sisters here with us?’” (Mark 13:5; 5:24 [the references are as printed]).

Luke also reports in the Acts of the Apostles: “All these were persevering with one accord in prayer with the women and Mary, the mother of Jesus, and his brothers” (Acts 1:14) [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads: “with one accord in prayer with the women, and she who was the Mother of Jesus,” and so forth.].

The Apostle Paul likewise agrees, in the same historical truth, saying: “Then I went up according to revelation, and I saw no one except Peter and James, the brother of the Lord” (Galatians 2:2). And again elsewhere: “Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to lead about [Note: Victorius reads *mulieres* (“women”) instead of *uxores* (“wives”), and strongly accuses the printed reading of being false, chiefly because, although in Jerome’s own understanding the Greek word γυνή is common to the meanings “wife” and “woman,” it is nevertheless certain that the Apostle here means the women who ministered to the Apostles. As evidence he cites the holy Doctor’s exposition from the first book *Against Jovinianus*: “But if he should oppose to us that all the Apostles had wives, to prove it, ‘Do we not have the right to lead about women, or wives, since γυνή among the Greeks signifies both, as do the other Apostles, Cephas, and the brothers of the Lord?’ Let him add what is also found in the Greek manuscripts: ‘Do we not have the right to lead about sisters, women, or wives?’ From this it is apparent that he spoke of other holy women who, according to Jewish custom, ministered to their teachers from their own possessions, just as we read that this was also done for the Lord himself, and so forth.” Yet from these passages it is by no means proved that he read *mulieres* instead of *uxores*; rather, they show what is to be understood by that word. The question is therefore not simply whether *wives* or *women* should be read, but whether the phrase is joined as “a woman who is a sister,” as in the Latin interpreter, or “a sister who is a woman,” as in the Greek text, ἀδελφὴν γυναῖκα. Several ancient writers, however, read *mulieres* in the plural: Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, chapter 8, and *On Modesty*, chapter 14; Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew 27 and in his Letter 22 to Eustochium; Ambrosiaster, Sedulius, and others. We have so far found no one who simply read *uxores*.]

“wives,” as do the other Apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas?” (1 Corinthians 9:4–5).

And lest some Jew refuse the testimony of those who also gave the names of his brothers, claiming [variant: *asseris*, “you assert,” for *asserens*, “asserting”] that they too had been deceived by the same error concerning the brothers by which “they had stumbled in determining the father,” he prudently anticipated the objection and said that the Evangelists name these same persons elsewhere, and that they are the same people whom they call the Lord’s brothers, the sons of Mary.

Matthew says: “There were also many women there [Note: Through a faulty transposition, the earlier editions had *erat ibi et mulieres* (“there was there also a woman”), undoubtedly referring to the women before the Lord’s cross. The Veronese manuscript corrected the reading.] watching from a distance—those who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him. Among them were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee” (Matthew 27:55–56).

Likewise Mark: “There were also women watching from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and Joseph, and Salome” (Mark 15:40); and shortly afterward: “And many other women who had come up with him to Jerusalem.”

Luke likewise says: “There were Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James, and the others with them” (Luke 24:10).

## 12. Jerome

We have repeated these things so that he may not slander us and loudly protest that the points favoring his position have been suppressed by us, and that his opinion has been overturned not by the testimonies of Scripture but by slippery argument.

“Behold,” he says, “James and Joseph, the sons of Mary—the very [Note: We supply the word *iidem* (“the same”) from the Veronese manuscript, which consistently reads *Josephtis* for *Josetis*.] men whom the Jews called brothers. Behold Mary, the mother of James the younger and of Joses. He is called ‘the younger’ in distinction from James the elder, who was the son of Zebedee, just as Mark states elsewhere: ‘Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James and Joses saw where he was laid; and when the Sabbath was past, they bought spices and came to the tomb.’ And surely,” he says, “it would be pitiful and impious to think this about Mary: that while other women took care of Jesus’ burial, we should say that his mother was absent; or that we should invent some other Mary whom we do not know—especially since the Gospel of John testifies that she was present there, when the Lord entrusted her, now a widow, to John as a mother [Note: From this, Victorius says, it is clear that Joseph, Mary’s husband, had already died by the time Christ suffered on the cross.]. Or are the Evangelists both mistaken and deceitful, so that they called those men Mary’s sons whom the Jews said were Jesus’ brothers?”

## 13.

O blind madness, and mind rushing headlong toward its own destruction! You say that his mother was present at the Lord’s cross; you say that, because of her widowhood and loneliness, she was entrusted to the disciple John—as though, according to your position, she had not [Note: Helvidius evidently maintained that Joseph had four sons and innumerable daughters. Cotelerius thinks that “innumerable” is used because the daughters are not numbered in the New Testament, neither in Matthew 13:56 nor in Mark 6:3. In reality, however, the ancients vary both in the number and in the names of Joseph’s daughters. In the *Chronicle of Hippolytus of Thebes*, published by Canisius, we read: “For Joseph had four sons and two daughters, Esther and Martha, by his wife Salome, who was the daughter of Haggai, the brother of Zechariah,” and so forth. Epiphanius likewise lists two, but under other names, Mary and Salome. Saint Hilary, however, in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 1, says: “The most wicked men presume upon the authority of their opinion, claiming that our Lord is reported to have had several brothers. If they had been Mary’s sons, and not rather sons whom Joseph had from a former marriage, she would never, at the time of the Passion, have been transferred as a mother to the Apostle John,” and so forth.] four sons and countless daughters, whose companionship she might enjoy?

You also call her a widow, although Scripture does not say so. And while you set forth all the examples from the Evangelists, the words of John alone displease you. You mention in passing that she was present at the Lord’s cross, so that you may not seem deliberately to have omitted her; yet you are silent about which women were with her. I would forgive ignorance if I did not see that you are deliberately withholding the truth.

Listen, then, to what John says: “There stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene” (John 19:25).

No one doubts that two Apostles were called by the name James: James the son of Zebedee and James the son of Alphaeus. This James the younger, whoever he may be—the one whom you want to be the son of Mary, although Scripture does not identify that Mary as the mother of the Lord [Note: See Jerome himself in his Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 17. The old and stale question concerning the three James has been debated in many discussions by both ancient and modern writers.]—do you want him to be an Apostle or not?

If he is an Apostle, he will be the son of Alphaeus; he will believe in Jesus; and he will not belong to those brothers of whom it is written: “For even his brothers did not believe in him at that time.”

If he is not an Apostle but some third James whom we do not know, how is he to be considered the Lord’s brother? And how will he be called “the younger” in distinction from “the elder,” since “elder” and “younger” ordinarily establish a distinction not between three but between two? And the Lord’s brother is an Apostle, for Paul says: “Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and I stayed with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other Apostles except James, the Lord’s brother” (Galatians 1:18–19). And in the same Epistle: “When they recognized the grace that had been given to me, Peter and James and John, who were reputed to be pillars” (Galatians 2:9).

And lest you think that this was James the son of Zebedee, read the Acts of the Apostles. He had already been killed by Herod.

The conclusion remains that this Mary who is recorded as the mother of James the younger was the wife of Alphaeus and the sister of Mary, the mother of the Lord—this Mary whom the Evangelist John calls Mary of Clopas, whether he gave her this name from her father, from the gentile designation of her family, or for some other reason.

If this seems to you otherwise [variant: *Sin* for *Si*], because elsewhere she is called “Mary the mother of James the younger,” while here she is called “Mary of Clopas” [variant: *Cleophe* for *Cleophae*], learn the customary usage of Scripture: the same person is called by different names.

Raguel, Moses’ father-in-law, is also called Jethro. Gideon, with no reason for the change of name having been stated beforehand, is suddenly read as Jerubbaal [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads: “with no reasons for changing the name having first been stated,” and so forth.]. Uzziah, king of Judah, is alternately called Azariah. Mount Tabor is called Itabyrium. Again, the Phoenicians call Hermon Sanir, and the Amorites call it Senir. The same region of the sky is called by three names—Negeb, Teman, and Darom, as you may read in Ezekiel. Peter is also called Simon and Cephas. Judas the Zealot is called Thaddeus in another Gospel. The reader himself can collect many other examples throughout Scripture corresponding to these.

## 14.

Now we are attempting to show how those who are called the Lord’s brothers may be the sons of his maternal aunt, Mary—those who formerly did not believe but afterward believed.

It could have happened that, when one believed immediately, the others remained unbelieving for a long time; and that this Mary was the mother of James and Joses—that is, Mary of Clopas, the wife of Alphaeus—and that this is the Mary called the mother of James the younger.

If she had been the mother of the Lord, the Evangelist would have called her his mother, as he does everywhere else, rather than, by calling her the mother of other men, intending another Mary to be understood.

But on this point I do not engage in contentious dispute. Let Mary of Clopas be one person and Mary the mother of James and Joses another, provided it is established that the Mary who was the mother of James and Joses was not the mother of the Lord.

“And from what source,” you ask, “were those called the Lord’s brothers who were not his brothers?”

You will now be taught that in the divine Scriptures people are called “brothers” in four ways: by nature, by nation, by kinship, and by affection.
