By nature: Esau and Jacob, the twelve patriarchs, Andrew and Peter, James and John [Note: Isidore, quoting this passage from Jerome in *The Etymologies*, book 9, chapter 6, omits the words “the twelve patriarchs.” The Veronese manuscript reads: “By nature, as Esau and Jacob and the twelve,” and so forth.].

By nation: all Jews are called brothers among themselves, as in Deuteronomy: “If you buy your brother, who is a Hebrew, or a Hebrew woman, he shall serve you six years; and in the seventh year you shall release him from your service” (Deuteronomy 15:12). And in the same book: “You shall indeed appoint over yourself as prince the one whom the Lord your God chooses, one who is from among your brothers. For you cannot appoint over yourself a foreign man, because [perhaps: who] he is not your brother” (Deuteronomy 22:1–2).

And again: “When you see your brother’s calf or his sheep straying on the road, do not neglect them; you shall lead them back to your brother. But if your brother is not near you and you do not know him, you shall gather them inside your house; they shall remain with you until your brother seeks them, and you shall return them to him” (Deuteronomy 22:1–2) [the reference is printed as Deuteronomy 17:11]. [Note: The Veronese manuscript adds: “and you shall return them to your brother.”]

The Apostle Paul says: “I could wish that I myself were accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Romans 9:3–4).

By kinship, brothers are called those who belong to one family, that is, to one *patria* [Note: “That is, fatherland.” This is the genuine reading of the manuscript copies, and it is easy for the reader to understand if he supplies *patriae*, that is, those whom the Latins interpret as “fatherlands” or “families,” namely, paternal relations. See above, the commentary on Ephesians, chapter 3. Martianus says: “I would prefer to read the Greek πατριᾷ, as Victorius does, since previously *patriae* had been written incorrectly; although the Latin manuscripts and Isidore give *patria*. This word *patria* was also preserved by Tertullian in *Against Marcion*, poem 4, where he writes of Christ:

‘To whom every knee, plainly, confesses that it must bow,

from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.’

This is taken from Ephesians 3:15: ‘from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.’ In this passage our Jerome says: ‘The fatherhood which in Greek is πατριὰ and in Hebrew *Mesphath*, that is, kinship or family,’ and so forth. Martianus, who here requires the reader to supply *patriae*, that is, “those whom the Latins interpret as fatherhoods, namely families,” does not seem to have understood our Author’s meaning.].

When a multitude of one lineage spreads from a single root, as in Genesis: Abraham said to Lot, “Let there be no quarrel between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds, because we are brothers” [Note: Previously *omnes* (“all”) was found here incorrectly, whereas the Greek also has ἄνθρωποι ἀδελφοὶ, “men who are brothers.”]. And there: “Lot chose for himself the region around the Jordan, and Lot departed from the east, and each withdrew from his brother” (Genesis 13:8) [Note: Earlier editions wrongly had *omnes* (“all”), although the Greek too reads ἄνθρωποι ἀδελφοί, “men [are] brothers.”].

Certainly Lot was not Abraham’s brother, but the son of his brother Aram. Terah fathered Abraham, Nahor, and Aram; and Aram fathered Lot.

And again: “Abraham was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. And Abraham took Sarai his wife and Lot, his brother’s son” (Genesis 12:4).

If you still doubt that a brother’s son may be called a brother, receive another example. “When Abraham heard that Lot his brother had been taken captive, he counted his household servants, three hundred and eighteen” (Genesis 14:14). And after describing the slaughter carried out by a nighttime attack, he added: “And he brought back all the cavalry of the Sodomites, and recovered Lot his brother” (ibid. 16).

These examples would be sufficient to prove what we have said. But lest you wriggle away like a slippery serpent and quibble over some point, you must be bound by the chains of these testimonies, so that you may not hiss complaint and say that you have been defeated more by twisted arguments than by the truth of Scripture.

Jacob, the son of Isaac and Rebekah, fearing his brother’s plots, went to Mesopotamia. He approached and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well and watered the sheep of Laban, his mother’s brother (Genesis 28 and 29). “Jacob kissed Rachel, and cried aloud, and wept. And he told Rachel that he was her father’s brother and that he was Rebekah’s son” (Genesis 29:11).

Here again, by the same rule as above, a sister’s son is called a brother.

And again: “Laban said to Jacob, ‘Because you are my brother, shall you serve me for nothing?’” (Genesis 29:19). “Tell me what your wages shall be.”

After twenty years had been completed, Jacob returned to his homeland with his wives and sons, without his father-in-law’s knowledge. Laban overtook him on Mount Gilead. He searched for the idols that Rachel had concealed but did not find them among the baggage. Jacob answered and said to Laban: “What is my fault, and what is my sin, that you pursued me? And why did you search through all my possessions? What have you found among all my belongings [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads: “among all your belongings”]? Set it here before my brothers and your brothers, and let them judge between us two” (Genesis 31:36–37).

Answer me: who were these brothers of Jacob and Laban who were present there at that time? Esau, Jacob’s brother, was certainly absent; and Laban, the son of Bethuel, had no brothers except Rebecca, his sister.

## 15.

There are countless examples of this kind inserted throughout the divine books. But, so that I do not become tedious, I shall return to the final division: that people are also called brothers by affection. This is divided into the spiritual and the common.

Spiritually, all Christians are called brothers, as in the Psalm: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together” (Psalm 133:1). And in another Psalm the Savior says: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Psalm 22:22 [printed as Psalm 11:23]). And elsewhere: “Go, tell my brothers” (John 20:17).

In the common sense, because all are born from one father, we are joined to one another by equal kinship. “Say to those who hate you, ‘You are our brothers’” (Isaiah, final chapter, according to the Septuagint).

And the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator [Note: The Vulgate interpreter reads: “if anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or greedy,” and so forth. The difference in Jerome’s reading derives from the Greek particle ἤ. If ἤ is read, it means “or”; but ᾖ means “is.” The Greek is: Ἔαν τις ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος ἤ (or ᾖ) πόρνος. Nicephorus of Constantinople explains the reading appropriately in chapter 37 of Cotelerius’s third volume of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*: “If anyone who is called a brother—or is known as such—is a fornicator: he does not seem to speak of one whom some person has seen fornicating, but of one who is so called, that is, known by everyone.”], or greedy,” and so forth. The difference in Jerome’s reading derives from the Greek particle ἤ. If ἤ is read, it means “or”; but ᾖ means “is.” The Greek is: Ἔαν τις ἀδελφός ὀνομαζόμενος ἤ (or ᾖ) πόρνος. Nicephorus of Constantinople explains the reading appropriately in chapter 37 of Cotelerius’s third volume of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*: “If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator—or is known as such—it does not seem to say that someone saw him committing fornication, but that he is called such, that is, known by everyone.”], or greedy, or an idolater, or reviler, or drunkard, or extortioner, with such a person not even to eat” (1 Corinthians 5:11), and other things of the same kind.

I now ask you: according to which of these meanings do you understand the Lord’s brothers to be called brothers in the Gospel?

According to nature? But Scripture does not say so, calling them neither sons of Mary nor sons of Joseph.

According to nation? But it is absurd that only a few Jews should be called brothers, since all the Jews who were there could have been called brothers by this rule.

According to human and spiritual affection? But if so, who were more truly brothers than the Apostles, whom he taught inwardly and whom he called mothers and brothers?

Or if all human beings are brothers because they are human [Note: These words—“or if all human beings are brothers”—are absent from the Veronese manuscript.], it was foolish for the message to be announced as though it concerned something particular: “Behold, your brothers are seeking you” [another reading: “are seeking”], when by this right all human beings are generally brothers.

It therefore remains that, according to the exposition given above, you should understand them to have been called brothers by kinship, not by affection [Note: In the same manuscript *non istud* is deleted, perhaps more correctly.]; not by the privilege of nation, and not by nature.

In the same way Lot is called Abraham’s brother; Jacob is called Laban’s brother; the daughters of Zelophehad receive a portion among their brothers; and Abraham himself took Sarah his sister as his wife. For he says: “Indeed, she is my sister by my father, but not by my mother” (Genesis 20:11)—that is, she was the daughter of his brother, not of his sister [Note: He means that, in Abraham’s time, it was unlawful to marry sisters who had one parent in common; this is also the opinion of other Fathers, especially Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 22, chapter 35. Many others disagree, however, and do not doubt that Sarah was Abraham’s sister, since Abraham himself expressly declares it at Genesis 11:9. Some also hold that this was permitted in David’s time; otherwise Tamar would not have told her brother Amnon to ask their father for her in marriage (2 Kingdoms 13), although we know that each interprets these matters differently according to his own view.].

Otherwise, what sense would it make for Abraham, a righteous man, to take his father’s daughter as his wife, when Scripture, out of reverence for the first human beings, does not even name this practice, preferring that it be understood rather than stated openly, and when God later establishes a law and threatens: “Whoever takes his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness and she sees his nakedness, it is a disgrace; and they shall be exterminated before the sons of their people. He has uncovered the nakedness of his sister; he shall bear his sin” (Leviticus 18:9).

## 16.

Most ignorant of men, you had not read these things; and, abandoning the entire sea of Scripture, you directed your madness against the Virgin, after the example of the man whom the fables say was unknown to the common people and could devise no good deed by which he might become famous, and who is said to have set fire to the temple of Diana. When no one exposed the sacrilege, he is said to have stepped forward publicly, shouting that he himself had committed the arson. When the leading men of Ephesus asked him why he had wished to do this, he replied: “So that, since I could not become famous through good deeds, I might become known to everyone through an evil one.”

This is what Greek history relates [Note: See Strabo, book 14; Solinus, book 43; Valerius Maximus, book 8, chapter 15; and others.].

But you have set fire to the temple of the Lord’s body [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads: “you have polluted the sanctuary from which,” and so forth.]; you have contaminated the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, from which you want a whole crowd of brothers and sisters to have proceeded.

Finally, joining your voice with that of the Jews, you say: “Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joses and Simon and Judas, and are not all his sisters with us?” (Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3).

The word “all” is not said unless the sisters are from the crowd. Who, I ask you, knew them before this blasphemy? Who had reckoned them in dupondii [two-asses coins]?  You have achieved what you wanted: you have become famous through crime.

I myself, who am writing against you, although I live in the same city as you, do not know whether you are, as they say, white or black [Note: This expression is found in Cicero, *Philippics* 2; Quintilian, book 11, chapter 2; and Horace, book 2 of the *Epistles*, to Julius Florus. The note then discusses a variant involving *alvus* (“belly”) and compares it with *uter* (“wineskin” or “womb”), as well as an old gloss: “Why do you stammer and blush?” The proverb is known from Cicero, Quintilian, Horace, and others, as noted by Gravius. Shortly afterward, instead of *ridiculum exordium* (“a ridiculous beginning”), the annotator prefers *ridiculum exodium* (“a ridiculous ending”), noting theatrical beginnings and comic endings. Catullus, poem 91, writes:

“Nothing do I strive too much, Caesar, to please you,

nor to know whether you are a white or black man.”].

I pass over the faults of expression with which your entire book teems. I am silent about its ridiculous beginning. “O the times! O the morals!” I do not seek eloquence, which you yourself do not possess, although you demanded it from your brother Craterius [Note: Other books have *Carterius*. The Veronese manuscript, with aspiration, has *Cartherius*. Does this refer to that Canterius whom Jerome mentions in his letters to Marcella and Saint Augustine and in his commentary on Jonah?].

I am not, I say, demanding polish of language; I seek purity of soul [Note: Martianus, following Erasmus, reads *pietatem* (“piety”) instead of *puritatem* (“purity”). Victorius, however, restored *puritatem* from more accurate manuscripts and noted that it agrees better with the word *nitor* (“polish”)].

Among Christians it is a great solecism and a disgraceful vice to say or do something shameful [Note: Cicero writes to Atticus, book 2, letter 11: “I do not enjoy watching the games at Antium, for it is ὑποσόλοικον, since I wish to avoid every suspicion of luxury.” Sidonius writes in his letter to Faustus: “There is a barbarism of morals, pleasant speech, and a troubled mind”; and Lucian, in *Hercules on the Stage*, says that to perform a monody, μονωδεῖν, seems to be a σολοικία, and so forth.].

I come to the end, and I shall conclude you with a horned question, dealing with you as though I had accomplished nothing earlier:

The Lord’s brothers were called brothers in the same way that Joseph was called father. “I and your father,” she says, “have been seeking you in sorrow” (Luke 1:48). It is the mother who speaks these words, not the Jews. And the Evangelist himself, reporting the event, says: “His father and mother were astonished at what was said about him” (ibid. 33), together with the similar passages that we have already enumerated, in which they are called his parents.

And lest you make an excuse from the variation among copies, because you have foolishly persuaded yourself that the Greek manuscripts have been corrupted, I turn to the Gospel of John, in which it is written most plainly: “Philip found Nathanael and said to him: ‘We have found the one of whom Moses in the Law and the Prophets wrote, Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth’” (John 1:45).

Certainly this is contained in your own manuscript. Answer me: how is Jesus the son of Joseph, when it is certain that he was begotten from the Holy Spirit? Was Joseph truly his father? Though you are dull-witted, you will not dare say so, will you? Or was he thought to be so? In the same way, let the brothers be considered brothers in the manner in which the father was considered father.

## 17.

But since the discourse has now sailed away from the rocks and rugged places, the sails must be spread, and we must attack the epilogue of his work. In it, thinking himself learned, he calls Tertullian as a witness [Note: I think the citation comes from *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 6, section 48, or from *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 23, section 164. Helvidius produced Tertullian’s authority.], and sets forth the words of Victorinus, bishop of Petabion [Note: Of Victorinus, bishop of Petabion. The error of the older editions returns here: as above, in the book *On Illustrious Men*, they read “bishop of Poitiers” instead of “bishop of Petabion.” See our notes above on Victorinus in the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Martianus.].

As for Tertullian, I say nothing more than that he was not a man of the Church.

But concerning Victorinus, I assert what I have also asserted concerning the Evangelists: that he called them the Lord’s brothers, not the sons of Mary. He called them brothers in the sense explained above—by relationship, not by nature [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads: “by relationship, not by the mother,” and more correctly below: “to disturb the succession of the ancient Greek writers.”].

But we are wasting time on trifles, leaving aside the fountain of truth and pursuing the streams of opinions. Can I not bring against you the entire succession of ancient writers—Ignatius, Polycarp, Irenaeus, Justin Martyr, and many other apostolic and eloquent men—who wrote volumes full of wisdom against Ebion, Theodotus, Byzantium, and Valentinus, sharing this same opinion [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads *Byzantinum* and does not recognize Valentinus. Victorius also testifies that Valentinus is absent from many manuscripts. Cotelerius, however, found *Byzantinum* in a certain royal manuscript and in others, but says that Valentinus is marked in the royal manuscript in the margin as a variant reading alongside *Byzantinum*.]?

If you had ever read these authors, you would be wiser. But I think it better to answer each point briefly than to prolong the discussion and expand the volume.

## 18.

I now attack the point in which, by comparing virginity and marriage, you wanted to display your eloquence. We laughed at the proverb as applied to you: “We saw a camel dancing” [Note: The proverb concerns those who do something ineptly or disgracefully. See our Jerome, commentary on Isaiah, chapter 68.].

You say:

“Are the virgins better than Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who had wives? Are not little children fashioned every day by the hands of God in the wombs, so that we ought rightly to blush that Mary married after childbirth? And if this seems shameful to them, it remains that they should not believe that God was born through the genitals of a virgin. For in their view it is more shameful that God was born through a virgin’s private parts than that a virgin married her husband after childbirth” [Note: Taken from Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 39, where he argues against Marcion: “Come now, proclaim the uncleanness of the generative organs, the elements in the womb, the fluid and blood, the foul coagulations of flesh to be nourished from the same mire for nine months; describe the womb growing larger day by day, heavy, anxious, entirely bound, inserted into lusts of nausea and appetite. Attack even the shame of the laboring woman . . . You shudder at the infant, as it emerges with its bodily impediments, certainly smeared and befouled,” and so forth.].

If you wish, add the other insults against nature: the womb swelling for nine months, nausea, childbirth, blood, and swaddling clothes. Let the infant himself be described to you, wrapped in the customary covering of membranes. Let hard feeding-troughs, the child’s crying, circumcision on the eighth day, and the time of purification be brought forward, so that he may be proved unclean.

We do not blush; we do not remain silent [Note: Saint Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, who flourished around the middle of the seventh century after Christ, explains this passage of Jerome in his sermon *On the Birthgiving and Purification of Saint Mary*. Although his words may exceed what the brevity of the notes permits, it is nevertheless worthwhile to reproduce them:

“Christ is therefore rightly called the firstborn from the Virgin—not because he violated the Virgin’s womb and opened the chamber of her modesty, but because he who was from the beginning the firstborn of all creation was himself born from her, both only-begotten and firstborn, in the manner he willed, without the groaning or pain of the woman giving birth.

“By these rules of Catholic truth, the meaning is clear on every side: for no one but a heretic says that Christ was born according to the common law of nature, or otherwise than other infants are born. Although Doctor Jerome, in the work he composed against Helvidius, may seem to have yielded to him—especially where he speaks of the lodging of the nine-month womb and of the reality of birth, which that heretic had proposed mockingly as unworthy of divine majesty, as though it were beneath him to humble himself so far as to move among the Virgin’s uterine organs or to be born between female thighs amid such filth—in fact he opposes everything in the manner of a heretic in order to destroy the truth of Catholic faith.

“To the contrary, that distinguished defender of truth, not yielding as these men suppose, but commending all the more the dignity of God’s most glorious humility, says: ‘The more lowly and dishonorable those things were which the divine majesty endured or accepted for us, the more dearly he redeemed us, and the more earnestly he is to be honored.’

“In this sense, although not, as I recall, in the same words, he appears to answer that heretic without inflicting upon the blessed Virgin the disgrace of any defilement or the punishment of sin, but rather reverently commending the divine condescension and immeasurable self-emptying in the form of a servant. He did not show the Virgin as assaulted and dishonored by the Lord, but demonstrated even to such heretics the clemency of the compassionate Creator.

“For this reason he did not yield to those who, with Helvidius, were in error, but rebuked them, so that they might learn not to defame the Virgin or diminish the Lord’s humility in the form of a servant. He does not teach that her chastity was harmed in any way, since he triumphs so greatly in her praise; nor did he yield even for an hour to his adversaries, since he fought for her so long and so earnestly with the sword of the word. God granted him such grace to resist her enemies and such power to defeat them that no one dares rise up against him.”].

The more humiliating were the things he suffered for me, the more I owe him. And when you have repeated everything, you will bring forward nothing more shameful than the cross—which we confess, believe in, and by which we triumph over our enemies.

## 19.

But just as we do not deny what has been written, so we reject what has not been written.

We believe that God was born from a Virgin because we read it. We do not believe that Mary married after childbirth because we do not read it.

We do not say this in order to condemn marriage—for virginity itself is the fruit of marriage—but because we are not permitted to form rash opinions about holy men.

By this reasoning concerning what is possible, we could also contend that Joseph had several wives, because Abraham had several wives and Jacob had several wives; and that the Lord’s brothers came from those wives—an idea that many invent with a boldness that is not so much pious as reckless.

You say that Mary did not remain a virgin. I claim even more for myself: that Joseph himself remained a virgin through Mary, so that from a virginal marriage a virgin son might be born.

For if fornication cannot be attributed to a holy man, and Scripture does not say that he had another wife, while he was rather the guardian than the husband of Mary, whom he was thought to have had, it follows that he remained a virgin with Mary—the man who deserved to be called the father of the Lord.

## 20

And because I am about to say something concerning the comparison between virginity and marriage, I beg those who will read this not to think that I have disparaged marriage in praising virgins, or that I have made some distinction between the saints of the Old Testament and those of the New—that is, between those who entered into marriage and those who withdrew entirely from the embraces of women—but rather that, according to the conditions of the times, the former were then subject to one decree, and we to another, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

As long as that law remained in force—“Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28)—and “Cursed is the barren woman who does not bear seed in Israel” (Isaiah, final chapter, according to the Septuagint). [Note: [Col. 0203D] Alternatively, “she who does not produce seed,” etc. This sentence is not found in the Vulgate Latin edition; we have discussed the matter elsewhere.] Everyone married and was given in marriage; and, leaving their parents, they became one flesh.

But when that voice thundered, “The time is shortened: it remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; cleaving to the Lord, we become one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 7:29), why is that? Because “the unmarried man thinks about the things of God, how he may please God. But he who is married is anxious about the things of this world, how he may please his wife. And the woman and the virgin are divided [Note: [Col. 0203D] Recall what we said concerning the reading of this passage in Epistle 22, to Eustochium, p. 104, note c.]: she who is unmarried thinks about the things of God, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But she who is married thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (ibid., 32–33 and following verses).

Why do you protest? Why do you resist? The chosen instrument speaks these things. He says, “The woman and the virgin are divided.” See how great is the happiness of the woman who has even lost the name of her sex: a virgin is no longer called a woman.

“She who is unmarried thinks about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit.” The definition of a virgin is that she is holy in body and spirit, because it is of no benefit to have virgin flesh if one has married in mind.

“But she who is married thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.” Do you think it is the same thing to devote oneself day and night to prayer and fasting, and, at the arrival of one’s husband, to adorn one’s face, alter one’s gait, and feign endearments? The virgin does this in order to appear more unattractive and to obscure nature’s gift by the injury she inflicts upon it. The married woman paints herself before a mirror and, in contempt of the Maker, attempts to be more beautiful than she was born.

Then infants babble, the household resounds with noise, the children hang upon kisses and lips, expenses are reckoned, and outlays are prepared. [Note: [Col. 0203D] The Veronese manuscript: “the children hang upon kisses and lips; expenditure is reckoned,” etc.] Here the cooks, with hands girded for work, pound the meats; there the crowd of weavers murmurs. Meanwhile, word is brought that the husband has arrived with his companions.

Like a swallow, she inspects every inner room: whether the bed is firm, whether the floors have been swept, whether the cups have been arranged, whether the meal has been prepared. [Note: [Col. 0203D] Likewise: “whether the floors have been swept, whether the cups have been set in order”; and shortly afterward, “and this is the happy household.”]

Tell me, I beg you: amid all this, where is the thought of God? And these are happy households?

Moreover, when drums sound, the flute shrieks, the lyre chatters, and the cymbal clangs, what fear of God is there? The parasite boasts in insults. Victims displayed for lust enter, and, naked because of the scantiness of their clothing, are thrust before shameless eyes.

The unhappy wife either rejoices at these things and perishes, or is offended, and the husband is provoked to quarrels. [Note: [Col. 0204D] The old edition: “or she is distressed; the husband is offended, and thus quarrels are stirred up.”]

Hence discord—the seedbed of divorce.

Or, if some household is found in which these things do not occur—a rare bird indeed—still, do not the very management of the household, the upbringing of children, the husband’s needs, and the correction of servants distract her from thinking about God?

Scripture says, “Sarah’s womanly functions had ceased” (Gen. 18:11). After this it is said to Abraham: “Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice” (Gen. 21:12).

She who is not involved in the anxieties and pain of childbirth, and who, when the functions of menstrual blood have ceased, has ceased to be a woman, is freed from God’s curse. Her turning is no longer toward her husband; rather, the husband is subjected to her, and the Lord’s voice commands him: “Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice” (Gen. 3).

And so they begin to devote themselves to prayer. For as long as the marital debt is being paid, the urgency of prayer is neglected.

## 21

We do not deny that widows or married women [alternative reading: “wives”] may be found who are holy; but they are women who have ceased to be wives, who, even amid the necessity of marriage, imitate the chastity of virgins.

This is what the Apostle briefly testified, with Christ speaking through him: [Note: [Col. 0204D] “The unmarried woman thinks about the things of God, how she may please God”; but the following adverb is absent in the Veronese manuscript.]

“The unmarried woman thinks about the things of God, how she may please God; but the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (1 Cor. 7:34).

He leaves us room here for interpretation. Yet he imposes no necessity or snare upon anyone; he recommends what is honorable. [Note: [Col. 0204D] The correct reading seems to be: “but what is honorable.”] He wishes all to be as he himself is.

And although he does not have a command of the Lord concerning virginity—for it is beyond human beings, and in a certain sense it would have been shameless to compel nature by saying, “I want you to be what the angels are”—therefore the virgin is of greater reward, since she refrains from what, if she were to do it, would not be a sin. [Note: [Col. 0205B] Older printed editions read “is of greater merit.” The Veronese manuscript reads “is of greater reward”; Martianaeus has “of greater recompense,” and says that he found “of greater price” in some manuscripts. But he and others made the mistake of reading *dereliquit* shortly afterward instead of *delinquit*, as we correct from the Veronese manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0206B] “Is of greater recompense.” Printed editions have “is of greater merit,” but manuscript codices have “is of greater recompense” or “is of greater price”; none has “is of greater merit.” — Martian.]

Nevertheless, in what follows he says: “But I give advice, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord so as to be faithful. I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity, because it is good for a person to be so.”

What is this necessity? “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in that day” (Matt. 24:19; Mark 13:17).

For this reason the forest grows up, so that it may later be cut down. For this reason the field is sown, so that it may be harvested. The world is already full; the earth cannot contain us. Every day wars cut us down, diseases carry us off, shipwrecks swallow us, and yet we quarrel over boundaries.

Among this number are those who follow the Lamb, who have not defiled their garments—for they remained virgins (Rev. 2).

Observe what “defiled” signifies. [Note: [Col. 0206B] The negative particle originally stood before the verb; we have removed it on the authority of the Veronese manuscript.]

I do not dare to explain it, lest Helvidius bring an accusation against me.

But when you say that there are some virgins who keep taverns, I tell you more: among them there are also adulteresses; and, what may astonish you even more, there are clerics who keep inns and monks who are immodest.

But who would not immediately understand that a tavern-keeping virgin cannot be a virgin, that an adulterous monk cannot be a monk, and that a cleric cannot be an innkeeper?

Is it virginity’s fault if someone who pretends to virginity is guilty? [Alternative reading: “Is virginity itself at fault?”]

For my part, leaving other persons aside and coming to the Virgin: she who practices the trades of a shopkeeper—I do not know whether she remains a virgin in body, but what I do know is that she does not remain a virgin in spirit.

## 22

We have been rhetorical and, in the manner of declaimers, have played for a little while.

You, Helvidius, compelled us to this, since now, while the Gospel is shining forth, you wish virgins and married women to possess the same glory.

And because I think that, overcome by the truth, you have turned to disparaging my life and to insults—for petty women also commonly do this, wishing evil upon victorious masters in corners—I say this in anticipation: your abuse will be a glory to me, when you wound me with the same mouth with which you disparaged Mary, and when the servant of the Lord and his mother alike experience your canine eloquence.

[Col. 0205]

# The Two Books of Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, Against Jovinianus (C, S)

## Editorial Notice on the Following Books Against Jovinianus

Jovinianus was, by profession, a monk; but if one examines his manner of life, he was a man devoted to luxury and dissipation, abusing ill-gotten riches, and one who, because of the infamy of his name, deserved to be called the Epicurus of the Christians. If one seeks refinement of mind and learning, he was plainly ordinary, neither eloquent nor learned; but, as is characteristic of such worthless minds, in insolence and arrogance he was second to none.

From what city he came—or rather from what monastery he emerged—is uncertain. Since then, following Baronius, many have maintained that he was Milanese; others, with Purricello, make him Roman. I would rather adopt the latter view, for Saint Augustine records in his book *On Heresies* that the seeds of his wicked doctrine were first sown at Rome, and that there some consecrated virgins, already advanced in age, were deceived by him into marrying men.

It is also established from Siricius’s letter that his followers, condemned in the Roman synod, afterward hastened to Milan to win the emperor’s favor. That they arrived there as strangers and newcomers is declared by Ambrose’s synodical letter to the same Siricius toward its end:

“When,” he says, “they had already received from their master and teacher—that is, at Rome and before the Pontiff—the fitting reward for their treachery, these Jovinianists came all the way here, so that no place might remain in which they had not been condemned.”

And shortly afterward:

“All who saw them fled from them as from some contagion.”

### 2

When he wished to burst forth into open heresy, so that he might corrupt people’s minds more freely, he is said to have abandoned the profession of monastic life. Some think so, and Jerome seems to indicate as much when, in Book I, section 40, he reproaches him for having turned, after a filthy tunic, bare feet, food-bread, and water to white garments, polished skin, mulsum, elaborately prepared meats, the sauces of Apicius and Paxamus, baths, fried delicacies, and taverns.

Then, in Book II, around the middle, he says:

“Formerly you were barefoot; now you are not merely shod but adorned. Then you were clothed in a rough tunic and a black undergarment; now you walk adorned in linen and silken garments, in fabrics from Atrebatum and Laodicea.”

Saint Ambrose likewise says in his *Rescript to Siricius*:

“These men,” he says—meaning the followers of Jovinianus—“lament that they were for a time subjected to hardship, and they avenge their own injury by wishing to drive away the labor of abstinence through daily banquets and a life of luxury.”

I say that these statements can be understood and discussed in both ways. If someone corrupts monastic life by his conduct, he must be thought to have bid farewell to it; Jovinianus ceased to be a monk. Conversely, if vices do not destroy the profession, he continued to be a monk. He himself certainly boasted impudently of being a monk, a point which Jerome attacks in the earlier passage, as though he had falsely assumed the name in deeds.

Some understand the change of clothing to mean that, before his perverse preaching, his affected filthiness is reproached even more sharply in contrast with the softness he later assumed. Perhaps, however, anyone could profess himself a monk in whatever clothing he wished.

### 3

The chief points of his heresy were these. First, that virgins, widows, and married women who have once been washed in Christ are of the same merit if they do not differ in the remaining works of life. Second, that those who have truly been baptized cannot be overthrown by the devil. Third, that there is no difference between one who eats food and one who fasts, provided that he eats with thanksgiving. Finally, that in the kingdom of heaven the reward of all who have preserved their baptism will be equal.

Saint Augustine attributes to him two further blasphemies, both nearly more destructive than the others. One is that all sins are equal; the other, that the Virgin Mary, Mother of Jesus, was violated not in conceiving but in giving birth.

Jerome for the most part passes over these two points, or at least does not oppose them in a specific response in these books. This has led Erasmus and others after him to conclude that Augustine unjustly attributed certain doctrines to Jovinianus, having rashly learned from popular rumor that they were being spread about him.

For my part, although the bishop of Hippo declares that he received what he wrote about this heresy from others, I do not think that he allowed anything false to be imposed upon him, or that he piled up Jovinianus’s errors beyond what was true.

Indeed, the absurd doctrine of the equality of sins flows from the same Stoic sources from which the heretic had drunk, and follows almost necessarily from the equality of merits which he asserted so shamelessly. Jerome refutes this throughout his books.

The other blasphemy, concerning the corruption of Blessed Mary’s virginity in childbirth, is shown by Saint Ambrose’s own *Rescript to Siricius* to have been impiously propagated by him and his followers:

“But,” he says, “they are exposed as uttering the wandering assertions of perversity: ‘A virgin conceived, but a virgin did not give birth.’”

Ambrose proceeds to refute this throughout that chapter and the following one.

Jerome himself also repeatedly presses and reiterates against the heretic that the integrity of the Mother of God remained inviolate both in conception and in childbirth, and that Christ’s body came forth through the closed barriers of the sacred womb just as he entered to the disciples through closed doors.

Likewise, against Helvidius, and against Tertullian’s very slight testimony in Book 32 of *On the Flesh of Christ*, he writes:

“When the Apostle declared that the Son of God was born not from a virgin but from a woman, he acknowledged the nuptial opening of the womb and had confirmed it by many prophetic utterances of Scripture.”

This may perhaps be why he was content to refer the reader to that work, so that he would not weave the same fabric again here.

### 4

This new teacher of the churches was therefore dispensing his poisons to Roman ears. So that they might spread more widely, he even dared to commend them to posterity in published little commentaries.

From those very brief fragments which Jerome preserves at the beginning of the first book, it is easy to gather how abnormal that work was: uncultivated and tasteless, in which the opinions of a madman were wrapped in the darkest language, while its most disgraceful barbarity of style itself turned the stomach.

Nevertheless, as happens when the reins are loosened on vices—to use Augustine’s words—he had such influence in the city of Rome that he was said to have cast even some religious women, whose chastity had previously been above suspicion, into marriage. He also weakened the holy celibacy of holy men by invoking the Fathers and by comparison with them.

But one must marvel at the man’s wickedness. He himself, who by equating the merit of virgins with conjugal chastity had urged everyone to take a wife, could not be persuaded to bring a wife home and join her to himself. He offered the highly unjust excuse that he did not want to be hindered by the troubles of marriage—not at all that he might gain any merit from it; that is, not to be better, but to be freer.

He had several Roman followers, as is written in Siricius’s letter: Auxentius, Genialis, Germinator, Felix, Plotinus, Martianus, Januarius, and Ingeniosus. In his letter to the Vercellenses, Saint Ambrose adds a certain Barbatio and Sarmatio, evidently among those whom Jovinianus had joined to his retinue when he came to Milan.

Jerome, however, judged that many more had adhered to him, when toward the end of Book II he says:

“Do not boast that you have many disciples. The Son of God taught in Judaea, and only twelve Apostles followed him.”

Augustine testifies that the number was indeed large by saying that Jovinianus was unable to draw any priests or clergy of reputation into his error.

### 5

Pammachius, that famous friend of Jerome, the most distinguished of Christians and the most Christian of the nobility, immediately rose up against the insane heresy. Together with other “most faithful Christian men, noble by birth and distinguished in religion,” as Siricius puts it, he diligently petitioned the Pontiff that the dreadful writing—Jovinianus’s *Commentaries*—once exposed by priestly judgment as contrary to divine law, should be erased by a spiritual sentence.

Understand this to have occurred from the sequence of events in the year of Christ 390, to which year Siricius’s celebrated letter is usually assigned, when the evil, which had been spreading secretly for scarcely two full years, had occupied people’s minds.

After the heretics were struck with anathema and expelled from Rome, they immediately hastened to Milan, as noted above, to the emperor Theodosius. Historical records of those times testify that the emperor had returned there on the Kalends of September of the preceding year, after having long before celebrated a triumph at Rome over Maximus.

Immediately afterward, presbyters sent from Rome with Siricius’s letter to Ambrose arrived: Crescens, Leopardus, and Alexander, burning with holy zeal. Through their efforts the assembled synod subscribed to the condemnation of the heretics and, having condemned them to universal execration, drove them from Milan as fugitives.

Some argue from Jerome himself, at the beginning of Book III against the Pelagians, that they afterward wandered through other lands outside Italy, since he says that Jovinianus’s doctrine had once been condemned at Rome and long afterward in Africa. It is much more credible, however, that he alluded to the doctrine of Caelestius concerning impeccability, which Jovinianus had also defended, rather than to Jovinianus himself by name, whom, according to Augustine, Africa entirely ignored.

Finally, it is commonly believed that the emperor’s rescript was directed against the heretic. Appended to it is Law 53 in the *Theodosian Code*, title 5, *On Heretics*, which the distinguished Gothofredus edited and which Martianaeus found at the end of Jerome’s work in the Carnotensis manuscript.

## Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Felix, Praetorian Prefect

The bishops’ complaint deplores that Jovinianus [alternative reading: Jovianus] is conducting sacrilegious assemblies outside the walls of the most sacred City. Therefore we order that the aforesaid man be arrested and, together with all his accomplices and ministers, crushed with lead and restrained in exile. The instigator himself is to be conveyed with all speed to the island of Boa; the others, wherever it may please, provided that their superstitious conspiracy is dissolved by the separation of their exile, are to be deported forever to solitary islands situated at a great distance from one another.

If anyone, with stubborn wickedness, repeats what has been forbidden and condemned, let him know that he will undergo a more severe sentence.

Given on the day before the Nones of March at Milan, in the consulship of Honorius for the ninth time and Theodosius for the fifth time, Augusti.

### 6

But, to say freely what I think, either this law is not genuine at all, or its subject’s name has been corrupted, and it does not concern Jovinianus.

No one should persuade himself that Jerome could have been mistaken in the history of this event. Writing against Vigilantius in the year 406—the year entered in the consular lists under the sixth consulship of Arcadius Augustus and the first of Anicius Probus—he gives the most certain testimony that Jovinianus had long since departed this life.

At the beginning of that book he says:

“Just as Euphorbus is said to have been reborn in Pythagoras, so in this man—Vigilantius—the perverse mind of Jovinianus arose again. He, condemned by the authority of the Roman Church, did not so much give up his spirit among Phasian birds and pork as belch it forth.”

The law therefore contains an anachronism of at least seven years, if it was issued in the consulship of Honorius IX and Theodosius V, that is, in the year 412; for it would have punished by exile a man who had already died long before.

If one supposes that the error lies in the date, or in the consular inscription, which may have resulted from a copyist’s negligence, and assigns it to any earlier year, one still cannot make the sentence agree with Jerome’s testimony.

Suppose—as Gothofredus also approves—that the heretic, already condemned in 390 and then a fugitive from both Rome and Milan, withdrew to the Roman diocese and habitually conducted assemblies outside the walls. Could the man who was arrested for this reason, crushed with lead, and deported to an island of Dalmatia famous for exile, have been said to have vomited out his spirit among Phasian birds and pork because of excessive gluttony?

The more credible account, based on the testimony of the holy Doctor, is that the infamous monk, devoted to luxury and condemned once and again, had nothing he preferred to indulging his appetite, and that, stuffed with food and wine, he died prematurely.

### 7

Having thus given a preliminary account of this wicked heresy—matters either little known or everywhere obscured by error—you may now approach with profit the reading of Jerome’s refutation, which commends the memory of Catholic doctrine.

In the year 393, or toward the end of the preceding year, the holy Doctor opposed these two books to Jovinianus’s little commentaries, at the urging of Pammachius, who had previously accused the heretic.

The strongest evidence for this date is that Jerome does not list these works in his catalogue of writings, which he extended down to the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius, 392; yet he mentions them in other books which he composed shortly afterward.

In the preface to his commentaries on Jonah he says:

“About three years have passed since I interpreted five prophets—Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Haggai—and, being occupied with another work, I could not complete what I had begun. For I wrote a book *On Illustrious Men*, and two volumes against Jovinianus. I also wrote the *Apology* and *On the Best Kind of Interpreting* to Pammachius, and so forth.”

Baronius and other learned men who adopt another chronology and assign the year 390 to these books were misled by a patch which some diligent student sewed onto this very preface at the final place in the catalogue. It is certain from Book I against Jovinianus, section 26, that the work on *Illustrious Men* which he mentions preceded it in time.

It would be tedious now to anticipate the whole argument. In the first book he attacks Jovinianus’s first proposition; in the second, three others. He explains innumerable passages of divine Scripture, historical testimonies, and philosophical doctrines with remarkable diligence.

For the slippery heretic had so bewitched the minds of many with seductive allurements that it was commonly said Jerome could not answer him with praise of virginity without censuring marriage.

The Manichaeans were also still present, condemning marriage. Jerome therefore had to proceed cautiously, lest, while wholly devoted to commending virginity, he should appear to incline toward the opposite side against a man who equated virginity with marriage.

Yet this care did not spare him the slanders of his opponents. He seemed to some rumor-bearing monks, and to several devout defenders of the Catholic faith, to have despised marriage.

Pammachius himself tried to recall the published books. When his diligence achieved nothing, he advised Jerome to meet the offense caused to many by a new writing.

Jerome replied with the *Apologetic Letter*—number 48 in our recension—to Pammachius, which it is worthwhile to recall after reading these books.

Meanwhile, for our part, we collated these works with the greatest care against manuscript codices, especially one Veronese manuscript written in majuscule letters, extraordinarily ancient and more accurately corrected than can be said; next, another Cistercian manuscript, or that of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Rome, which most closely approaches its antiquity; and finally the Casanatense manuscript, of a later age but of reliable character.

# Book One

[Col. 0211]

## 1. The Epicurus of the Christians. The defects of Jovinianus’s speech

Only a few days ago, some holy brothers from the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0211C] The name “Rome” is not found in either the excellent Veronese manuscript or the rather elegant manuscript of the Casanatense Library.] sent me certain little commentaries by a Jovinianus, asking me to answer their absurdities and to crush the Epicurus of the Christians with Evangelical and Apostolic vigor.

When I had read them and understood absolutely nothing, I began to reread them more frequently, examining not only the words and sentences but nearly every syllable, wishing first to discover what he was saying and thus either approve or refute what he had said.

But such barbarity is found in the writing, and so filthy a discourse is confused by such enormous defects, that I could understand neither what he was saying nor by what arguments he wished to prove what he said. [Note: [Col. 0211C] Siricius likewise seems to mark the same barbarity of style in Jovinianus’s writing in his *Letter to Various Bishops*, where he calls the writing dreadful, not only because of its blasphemies but also because of its defects of language.]

For the whole thing swells, and the whole thing collapses. It raises itself in each phrase and, like a weakened serpent, breaks in the very effort. It is not content to speak in our manner—that is, in human fashion—but attempts something higher.

## 238

“The mountains are in labor; a ridiculous mouse will be born.” (*Horace, On the Art of Poetry*)

As the poet himself says:

“Let mad Orestes swear that the man is not sane.” (*Persius, Satire 4*)

Moreover, he so wraps everything up and confuses the whole work in certain inextricable knots that this verse from Plautus may be applied to him:

“No one will read these lines except the Sibyl.” (*Pseudolus*)

For one must divine what he means. We read of Apollo’s frenzied prophetesses; and there is Virgil’s line:

“He gives sound without understanding.” (*Aeneid* 10)

Even the philosophers scarcely understand Heraclitus, who is surnamed *σκοτεινός* (*skoteinos*, “the obscure”). [Note: [Col. 0211C] The Ephesian Heraclitus is meant, whom everyone accuses of obscurity. Theodorus says that his books are βιβλία σκοτεινά (*biblia skoteina*, “dark books”) in the *Progymnasmata*, as do Demetrius in *On Style* and others; from them Jerome borrows *skoteinos* as a surname. See below, *Apology Against Rufinus*, Book I.]

But what is he compared with our *αἰνιγματισταί* (*ainigmatistai*, “riddle-makers”), whose books are much more difficult to know than to conquer? Although even victory over them is not easy. For who can overcome a man whose assertion he does not understand at all?

And, not to delay the reader longer, the beginning of his second book will show what sort of eloquence he possesses and with what verbal flowers he proceeds adorned. It belches forth the remains of yesterday’s drunkenness in this fashion:

## 239

### 2

[Note: [Col. 0212C] “I offer satisfaction to those who have invited me.” Earlier printed books read *Satisfacto invitatis*; but eight manuscript codices—the Corbeiensis 1, Sangermanensis 1, Regius 1, Colbertinus 1, three Carnotenses, and Sancti Ebrulphi Uticensis 1—retain the reading we have printed. Likewise below, *novella*, not *novellas*, and *eludere*, not *illudere*. — Martian.]

“I offer satisfaction to those who have invited me, not so that I may run with a famous name, but so that, cleansed of empty rumor, I may live.

I beg the field, the young planting, the tender saplings, torn from the whirlpools of vices, an audience fortified by ranks. We know the Church to be inaccessible and unconquerable through hope, faith, and charity.

[Col. 0212B] There is no immature person in it; everyone is teachable. No one can burst into it by force or elude it by cunning.” [Note: [Col. 0212C] In the Casanatense manuscript, after “he belches forth” appears: “Here begins Jovinianus’s disputation,” followed by “I offer satisfaction to those invited,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0212C] The Casanatense manuscript adds: “Jovinianus’s disputation ends.”]

## 3. Tatian, the founder of the Encratites; virginity, the fruit of marriage; what the numbers 30, 60, and 100 signify in the Gospel; Jovinianus’s heresies

I ask: what are these monstrosities of words? What disgrace of composition? Would you not think that he was dreaming in a fever, or seized by a phrenetic illness and requiring restraint in Hippocrates’ bonds?

Whenever I read him, wherever my breath fails, there is the punctuation. Everything begins, everything hangs upon something else. You do not know what is connected to what; and, except for the testimonies of Scripture, which he did not dare to alter with that most charming flower of his eloquence, the rest of his discourse suits every subject because it suits none.

This circumstance gave me some suspicion that he wished to praise marriage in such a way as to disparage virginity. For whenever lesser things are equated with greater, comparison with the inferior is an injury to the superior.

Nor do we disparage marriage by following the doctrines of Marcion and Manichaeus; nor, deceived by the error of Tatian, the founder of the Encratites, do we consider every sexual union impure. Tatian condemns not only marriage but also the foods which God created for use, and rejects them.

We know that in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay. And upon the foundation of Christ, which Paul the architect laid, some build gold, silver, and precious stones; others, on the contrary, hay, wood, and straw.

We are not ignorant of the words, “Honorable marriage, and the undefiled bed” (Heb. 13:4). [Note: [Col. 0213C] The manuscripts of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Rome and the Veronese manuscript read “the undefiled bed.”]

We read the first judgment of God: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). But we receive marriage in such a way that we prefer virginity, which is born from marriage.

Is silver not silver if gold is more precious than silver? Or is a tree and a field insulted if apples and fruits are preferred to the root and leaves, the stalk and ears? As apples come from the tree and grain from the stalk, so virginity comes from marriage.

Although the hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit arise from one earth and one seed, there is nevertheless a great difference in number.

Thirty refers to marriage. For the very joining of the fingers, as though embracing one another with a gentle kiss and forming a covenant, depicts husband and wife.

Sixty refers to widows, because they are placed in hardship and tribulation. Hence they are represented by the upper finger being pressed downward; and the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the allurements of pleasures once experienced, the greater the reward.

The number one hundred—pay close attention, I beg you—is transferred from the left hand to the right, and, although the same fingers are used, it is not represented by the same hand with which married women and widows are signified on the left. By forming a circle, it expresses the crown of virginity.

[Note: [Col. 0213C–0214C] This explains the ancient practice of counting by the fingers, concerning which several testimonies can be found among the ancients. The entire method is stated more explicitly by the Venerable Bede and most exactly by the Greek writer Nicholas of Smyrna, whose nearly unknown little work was published by Posinus. Bede says: “When you wish to indicate thirty, join the nails of the index finger and thumb in a gentle embrace. When you say sixty, bend the thumb and carefully encircle it with the curved index finger.” See also Apuleius, *Apology*, Oration 2.

Jerome’s statement that the number one hundred is transferred from the left hand to the right is known from Cassian, *Conferences* 24.26: “The number one hundred is transferred from the left hand to the right; and although it may appear to retain the same figure in the reckoning of the fingers, it nevertheless grows greatly beyond it in magnitude.”

Juvenal also writes in Satire 19, line 246, of the king of Pylos:

“…Happy indeed is he who through so many ages

Postponed death and now counts his years on his right hand.”

See also the epigram of Nicarchus, the ancient poet, in the *Anthology*, Book II, chapter 9.

Our own Jerome also says in Letter 123, to Ageruchia, that the thirtyfold number testifies to the marriage covenant by the joining of the fingers.

Incidentally, Victorinus should be noted, since he thinks that the gesture used for thirty differs from that described by Apuleius: he says that the index finger and thumb are to be opened, that is, their tips are to touch gently.]

I have said these things more from impatience than in accordance with the order of the argument. For while I am scarcely yet leaving the harbor and raising the sails by the ropes, a sudden rush of speech carried me into the midst of the sea of questions.

Therefore I shall check my course and draw in my sails for a little while; nor shall I indulge the blade that even now longs to strike on behalf of virginity. A ballista launches its missile more forcefully the farther it is drawn back.

Delay is not a loss when delay makes victory more certain. I shall briefly set forth my opponent’s opinions, and from his dark books, as from caves, I shall drag out the serpents. I shall not allow the poisonous head to remain hidden among the coils of its spotted body.

[Note: [Col. 0214D] As is customary, the Casanatense manuscript places “Jovinianus’s disputation” first, then distinguishes the propositions themselves with Roman numerals, and finally adds, after “reward,” “Jovinianus’s disputation ends.”

The synodical letter of Saint Ambrose to Pope Siricius attacks two propositions of Jovinianus, specifically the first and the last: that no grace of virginity and no order of chastity should be preserved; that he wished to confuse everything indiscriminately; that he abolished the degrees of different merits; and that he introduced a certain poverty of heavenly rewards.

It also reproaches him, in section 4, with another error concerning Mary’s integrity in childbirth: namely, that he said Christ could not have been born from a virgin. Although Jerome suppresses this blasphemy in silence, it is explicitly attributed to that heretic by Augustine as well, in *On Heresies*, chapter 82, and frequently in *Against Julian*, as elsewhere.]

Let what is harmful be exposed, so that it may be crushed once it has been exposed.

[Col. 0214B]

“He says that virgins, widows, and married women who have once been washed in Christ, if they do not differ in their other works, are of the same merit.

He endeavors to prove that those who have been reborn in baptism with complete faith cannot be overthrown by the devil.

Third, he proposes that there is no difference between abstaining from food and receiving it with thanksgiving.”

[The supplied source ends here, incomplete.]

“Fourth, and the last, [he proposes] that all who have preserved their baptism receive one and the same reward in the kingdom of heaven.”

### 4. The Devil’s Arts. Among the Pagans, Virtue Is Preferred to Pleasure

These are the hisses of the ancient serpent; by these counsels the dragon expelled man from paradise. For by preferring satiety to fasting, he promised that they would become immortal, as though they could never fall; and while promising them a divinity equal to God, he expelled them from paradise, so that those who, naked and unencumbered, virgins without any stain, had enjoyed the fellowship of the Lord, once cast down into the valley of tears, would be clothed in stitched tunics and skins.

But lest I delay the reader longer, [Note: The Casanatensis manuscript reads: “the steps of the proposition having been set forth.”]

I shall follow the sequence of the exposition already set out, and against each of his propositions I shall rely especially upon testimonies from Scripture, so that he may not complain that he has been defeated more by eloquence than by truth.

[Col. 0214D] If I complete this task and overwhelm him with the cloud of both Testaments, I shall also take up examples from secular literature, to which he himself appeals. I shall show that even among philosophers and distinguished men in public life, virtues are ordinarily preferred by everyone to pleasures: Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristides to Aristippus, Epicurus, and Alcibiades.

I ask you, virgins and continent persons of both sexes, as well as husbands and men married twice, to assist my efforts with your prayers. Jovinianus is the enemy of all alike. For by asserting that everyone has equal merits, he wrongs virginity when he compares it with marriage, [Col. 0215B] and he wrongs marriage as well, by asserting that marriages are lawful in such a way as to include second and third marriages. He is also an adversary of men married twice and three times, placing former fornicators and most lustful men, after repentance, in the same position as those who have married twice and three times—except that men married twice or three times ought not to grieve on this account, since the same adulterer and penitent is made equal in the kingdom of heaven even to virgins.

I shall therefore present his arguments and examples concerning marriage in clearer language and with some coherence, arranging everything in the same order in which he stated it. Let it not trouble the reader if he is compelled to read his nausea and vomiting. He will more willingly drink Christ’s antidote once the devil’s poisons have gone before it.

Listen patiently, virgins; listen, I ask you, to the most pleasure-loving preacher—or rather, pass by with closed ears, like the songs and tales of the Sirens. Bear your wrongs for a little while; think of yourselves as crucified with Christ, listening to the blasphemies of the Pharisees.

[Note: Again, the Casanatensis manuscript places the heading first: “The Disputation of Jovinianus.”]

### 5. Jovinianus. The Book of Deuteronomy Discovered in the Temple under Josiah

“God’s first judgment,” he says, “is this: ‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’” (Gen. 2:24; Matt. 19:5).

And lest we perhaps say that this passage is found in the Old Testament, he asserts that the same thing is also confirmed by the Lord in the Gospel: “What God has joined, let no human being separate.” Immediately he adds: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). Then, in order, he repeats that Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, [Note: Gravius would prefer “Methuselah.”] Methuselah, Lamech, [Col. 0215D] and Noah all had wives and begot children according to God’s judgment—as though the order of generation and the history of the creation of humanity could have been narrated without wives and children:

“Here,” he says, “is Enoch, who walked with God and was taken up into heaven. Here is Noah, who, although there were certainly many virgins because of their age, was alone preserved with his sons and wives when the world was shipwrecked. Again, after the flood, as though at a second beginning of the human race, pairs of men and women are joined, and the blessing of generation is restored anew: ‘Increase and multiply and fill the earth’” (Gen. 8:17; 9:1).

Moreover, permission to eat meat is also granted:

“Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you; just as I gave you all green plants, so now I give you everything” (ibid., 9).

He hastens to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: the first married three times, the second once, and the third had four wives—Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah. He asserts that Abraham received the blessing in the generation of a son because of the merit of his faith. He says that Sarah, as a type of the Church, whose womanly functions had failed, exchanged the curse of barrenness for the blessing of childbirth.

He says that Rebecca went, as a prophetess, to inquire of the Lord and heard from him: “Two nations and two peoples are in your womb” (Gen. 25:23). He says that Jacob served for a wife; and when Rachel thought that it belonged to her husband to give children, and said, “Give me children, or else I shall die” (Gen. 30:1), he replied: “Am I in the place of God, who has prevented you from having children?” (ibid., 2). “To such an extent,” he says, “he knew that the fruits of marriage belonged to the Lord, not to the husband.”

He says that Joseph, a holy and most chaste man, and all the patriarchs had wives, whom God equally blessed through Moses. He also brings forward Judah and Tamar, and touches briefly on the death of Onan, who was struck down by the Lord because, envying his brother, he deliberately wasted the work of marriage.

[Note: Another reading has “and not properly, he deliberately wasted the seed of marriage.” Ancient books more often give “Aunan” rather than “Onan.” The Veronese manuscript correctly has “Aunan,” from the Greek Αὐνάν, and below “Chaber” for “Haber.” Regarding “because, envying his brother’s seed”: in the Sangermanensis manuscript we read, “because, envying his brother, he wasted the work of holy marriage.” In one manuscript of the Colbert Library: “he poured the seed of marriage upon the ground.” Other manuscripts read as we have printed it; that this is the genuine reading can be proved from the context of the Septuagint interpreters, Genesis 38: “And Aunan, knowing that the seed would not be his … poured it upon the ground, so that he would not give seed to his brother.” He therefore envied the seed to his brother, and for that reason wasted the work of marriage. MARTIAN.]

He brings forward Moses and Miriam’s leprosy, because, speaking against her brother on account of his wife, she was immediately struck by God’s vengeance.

[Note: Vallarsius corrects the text in this way; Martianus V, 10 has “because.”]

He praises Samson and extols the married Nazarite with remarkable encomiums. He also repeats the story of Deborah and Barak: without the advantages of virginity, they defeated Sisera, Jabin, and the iron chariots. He introduces Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, and praises her hand armed with a tent peg.

Between Jephthah the father and his virgin daughter, who was sacrificed to the Lord, he says there was no difference; indeed, he prefers the father’s faith to that of the girl who was killed in mourning.

He comes to Samuel, another Nazarite of the Lord, who was raised from infancy in the tabernacle and clothed in the *ephod bad*, which is interpreted as linen garments. He says that Samuel fathered children and that priestly chastity was not diminished by the embrace of a wife.

[Note: In other books, “with the servant-girl Ruth.”]

He places Boaz with his Ruth on the threshing floor, and from them produces Jesse and David.

He says that David himself, by means of two hundred foreskins, and even at the risk of his life, sought intercourse with the king’s daughter.

[Note: “With two hundred foreskins.” In the editions of Erasmus and Marianus we falsely read “one hundred foreskins,” although the foreskins of two hundred men were counted. MARTIAN.]

[Note: In three of our manuscripts the reading is “even at the risk of his life,” without “of life.”]

What shall I say about Solomon, whom, placing him in the catalogue of husbands, he asserts to be an image of the Savior? He wants this passage to refer to him: “Give the king your judgment, O God, and your justice to the king’s son. And he shall be given the gold of Arabia, and they shall pray for him continually.”

Then suddenly he passes on to Elijah and Elisha and recounts, as though it were a great mystery, that the spirit of Elijah rested upon Elisha; but he says nothing about why he mentioned this—unless perhaps he thinks that Elijah and Elisha also had wives.

He passes to Hezekiah. While lingering over his praises, I wonder why he forgot to say: “From now on I shall beget children” (Isa. 38, according to the Septuagint).

He reports that Josiah, a most righteous man, under whom the book of Deuteronomy was discovered in the Temple, was instructed by Huldah, the wife of Shallum.

He also places Daniel and the three youths among married men.

[Note: The Cistercian, or Holy Cross, manuscript reads: “adopt one defense.”]

[Col. 0217B] Then suddenly passing to the Gospel, he places Zechariah and Elizabeth, Peter and his mother-in-law, and the other Apostles among married people. And he continues as follows:

“But if they wish to adopt a vain defense and allege that the world, being still new, needed increase, let them hear Paul speaking: ‘I want younger widows to marry and bear children’” (1 Tim. 5:14).

[Note: None of our manuscripts contains the words “to bear children,” just as none contains the two other words “her husband.”]

“And: ‘Marriage is honorable, and the marriage bed undefiled’” (Heb. 13:4).

“And: ‘A woman is bound to her husband as long as her husband lives. But if her husband has died, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord’” (1 Cor. 7:39).

“And: ‘Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor. Yet she will be saved through the bearing of children, if she continues in faith and love and holiness with sobriety’” (1 Tim. 2:14).

Certainly here that Apostolic saying ceases: “Those who have wives should live as though they had none”—unless perhaps you will say that he wants them to marry because some have already turned back after Satan, as though no virgin falls and their ruin were not greater.

From this it is evident that you follow the doctrine of the Manichaeans, who forbid marriage and the eating of foods that God created to be used, possessing a conscience branded as with a hot iron.”

[Note: That is, a lost and depraved conscience. The sentence is taken from the First Epistle to Timothy 4:1, where it alludes to slaves branded with a glowing iron after being convicted of a crime. Hence κεκαυτηριασμένον is transferred to signify some utterly depraved person. Saint Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 9, says of women deceived by the Marcosians: “who,” he says, “have a conscience branded as with a hot iron” (αἵτινες … κεκαυτηριασμέναι τὴν συνείδησιν). Shortly afterward, for *otiosum*, some manuscripts have *odiosum*.]

And after many other matters which it would now be tedious to rehearse, he shakes himself free, as though entering upon a rhetorical topic, and makes an apostrophe to a virgin, saying:

“I do not wrong you, virgin: you chose chastity because of present necessity; it pleased you to be holy in body and spirit; do not be proud. You are a member of the same Church as married women.”

[Note: The Casanatensis adds, as usual: “The Disputation of Jovinianus ends.”]

### 6. Jerome

Perhaps I have been excessive in explaining his propositions and have caused weariness to the reader. But I thought it useful to set all his efforts against me like a drawn-up battle line, and to gather the entire hostile army with its companies and commanders, lest, after the first victory, other battles should subsequently arise for me.

Therefore I shall not fight against individuals, [Note: Gravius would prefer “a passive engagement” for “a scattered engagement,” and so forth.]

nor be content with a scattered engagement against a few; the whole army must be confronted, and the disordered wedges of the enemy, fighting in the manner of brigands, must be driven back by a prepared and ordered battle line.

I shall place the Apostle Paul on the first front and, as the strongest commander, arm him with his own weapons—that is, with his own pronouncements. For when the Corinthians asked about this question, the teacher of the nations and master of the Church replied most fully. Whatever he establishes, let us regard as the law of Christ speaking through him.

And lest the reader’s silent thought, when we begin to dissolve the individual propositions that have been put forward, should always reserve itself for the Apostle and, neglecting the earlier and most powerful arguments, hasten toward the end—

[Note: The Casanatensis, omitting *priora*, reads: “hastening to the end,” and so forth.]

### 7. Nothing Is Contrary to Good Except Evil. The Outward Human Being Is Corrupted

Among other matters, the Corinthians had written to ask whether, after believing in Christ, they ought to remain celibate and dismiss the wives they had for the sake of continence, or whether, if virgins had come to faith, they should enter into marriage.

They also asked whether, when one of two pagans had believed in Christ, the believer should leave the unbeliever; and, if wives were to be taken, whether he should be ordered to marry Christians only or also pagan women.

Let us therefore see what Paul wrote in answer:

“Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman.

[Note: The manuscripts have the plural, “because of fornications,” corresponding to the Greek τὰς πορνείας. Likewise below. Soon afterward they have “the husband of her body,” without the word “own”; moreover, they do not recognize the verb “return” here or below. Finally, they read “But I say,” rather than “But this,” and so forth.]

But because of fornications, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the marital due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer. And return again to the same relationship, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

But I say this by way of concession, not by way of command. I wish all people to be as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that.

But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:1ff.).

Let us return to the head of the testimony: “It is good,” he says, “for a man not to touch a woman.” If it is good not to touch a woman, then touching is evil; for nothing is contrary to good except evil.

But if it is evil and is forgiven, it is therefore permitted lest something worse than evil should result. What kind of good is that which is permitted on the condition of something worse? For he would never have said, “Let each man have his own wife,” unless he had first stated, “But because of fornications.”

Take away fornication, and he will not say, “Let each man have his own wife.” It is as if someone should define matters thus: “It is good to eat wheat bread and to consume the purest fine flour; nevertheless, lest someone compelled by hunger should eat cow dung, I permit him also to eat barley.” Does wheat therefore lose its purity if barley is preferred to dung?

That is naturally good which has no comparison with evil and is not overshadowed by the preference for something else. At the same time, one must observe the Apostle’s prudence. He did not say, “It is good not to have a wife,” but, “It is good for a man not to touch a woman,” as though there were danger even in touching; as though the man who touched her would not escape the woman who snatches away men’s precious souls and makes the hearts of young men fly away:

[Note: All our manuscripts, and the old edition as well, have “captures” (*capit*), in accordance with the Greek ἀγρεύει.]

“Can a man carry fire in his bosom and his clothes not be burned? Or can he walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched?” (Prov. 6:27–28).

Therefore, just as the person who touches fire is immediately burned, so a man’s touch of a woman feels its own nature and recognizes the difference of sex.

The tales of the pagans also recount that Mithras and Erichthonius were generated either from stone or from the earth, from the mere heat of lust.

[Note: The fables of Mithras and Erichthonius. If Eubulus still existed—the author who explained the history of Mithras in many volumes—we would easily understand how Mithras was generated from the mere heat of lust. But this pagan tale is still insufficiently known both to us and to learned men. There is no difficulty concerning Erichthonius, or Erichthaeus: we know that he was believed to be the son of Vulcan, who, when he wrestled with Minerva, is said to have spilled his seed upon the earth; from this, they say, a boy was born with serpents’ feet, and so forth. He was the first inventor of silver and of the chariot. See Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book II; Lactantius, Book II, chapter 17; and Servius on Book III of Virgil’s *Georgics*. MARTIAN.]

[Note: Ancient writers commonly teach that Mithras was generated from a stone; and this was the traditional saying in the Mithraic mysteries: “God from the rock” (Θεὸς ἐκ πέτρας). Justin, in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, says: “For those who transmit the initiations of Mithras relate that he was born from a rock.” Commodianus, *Instructions*, Book I:

“Unconquered, born from the rock, if he is regarded as a god,
