Now turn back from these things and give priority to the former;

The rock conquered the god; the creator of the rock must be sought.”

The story of Erichthonius is better known.]

Thus our Joseph, because the Egyptian woman wanted to touch him, fled from her hands and, as though from the bite of a rabid dog, cast away the cloak which she had touched, lest the poison gradually spread.

“But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.” He did not say, “Because of fornication, let each man take a wife”; otherwise, by this excuse he would have loosened the reins of lust, so that whenever a wife died, another should be taken lest we commit fornication. Instead he says: “Let each man have his own wife.”

“His own,” he says: let him have his own and use his own—the woman whom he had before he believed, whom it was good not to touch, and whom, after faith in Christ, he should know only as a sister and not as a wife, unless fornication made touching her excusable.

[Note: We have removed the word “wife” from this passage; it was falsely inserted and occurs in none of our manuscripts or in the old edition.]

“The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”

The whole question concerns those who have been found in marriage: whether they may dismiss their wives—which the Lord also prohibited in the Gospel.

[Note: The Casanatensis reads: “those who have been found in marriage, whether …”]

Hence the Apostle says, “It is good for a man not to touch a wife.”

[Note: The same reading as in the old edition, and more correctly, “a woman,” not “a wife.”]

But because a man who has once taken a wife cannot abstain without mutual consent, nor dismiss a wife who is not sinning, he should render the marital due to his spouse; for he bound himself voluntarily so that he would be compelled to render it.

“Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.”

I ask you: what kind of good is that which prevents prayer? Which does not permit one to receive the body of Christ?

[Note: The reading was *accipi*, “to receive”; the manuscripts reject it.]

As long as I fulfill the duty of a husband, I do not fulfill the duty of a continent person.

[Note: “I do not fulfill the duty of one who practices continence.” Several manuscripts retain *continentis* in place of the word *Christiani*, which Erasmus and a few manuscript copies read. MARTIAN.]

The same Apostle commands elsewhere: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5). If one must always pray, then one must never serve marriage, since whenever I render the marital due to my wife, I cannot pray.

The Apostle Peter, who had experience of the bonds of marriage, see how he instructs the Church and what he teaches Christians:

“Likewise, husbands, live with your wives according to knowledge, granting honor to the female vessel as to a weaker one, and as co-heirs of the manifold grace, so that your prayers may not be hindered” (1 Pet. 3:7).

Behold, in the same sense—and therefore also by the same Spirit—he says that prayers are hindered by the duty of marriage.

But when he says “likewise,” he urges husbands to imitate the example of what he had already commanded wives, saying:

“So that husbands may see your chaste conduct in fear, whose adornment should not be external—the arrangement of hair, the wearing of gold, or the ornament of clothing—but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a gentle and quiet spirit. This is pleasing before God” (ibid., 2–3).

Do you see what kind of marriage he prescribes between husbands and wives? “Living together according to knowledge,” so that they may know what God wills and desires, and may grant honor to the female vessel.

If we abstain from intercourse, we grant honor to our wives; if we do not abstain, it is clear that insult is contrary to honor.

To wives also he says:

“So that husbands may see your chaste conduct in fear, and the adornment of the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a gentle and quiet spirit.”

[Note: The Casanatensis again reads: “so that husbands may see, he says, your chaste conduct in fear,” and so forth. Then, in “the hidden person of the heart,” I think *homine* should be read instead of *hominem*, and that the word *ornatum* should be understood substantivally. The Greek is κόσμον. The most carefully corrected Veronese manuscript supports this, as does Jerome’s own text.]

O truly worthy word of an Apostle and of Peter, the rock of Christ! He gives a law to husbands and wives; condemning the adornment of the flesh, he proclaims chastity and the adornment of the inward person, in the incorruptibility of a gentle and quiet spirit, saying in a certain sense:

“Since your outward person has been corrupted, and you have ceased to possess the blessedness of incorruptibility, which properly belongs to virgins, imitate at least the incorruptibility of the spirit through a delayed abstinence; and what you cannot provide in the body, provide in the mind.”

For these are the riches Christ seeks, and this is the adornment he seeks from your union.

### 8.

But lest anyone think that, from what follows—“so that you may devote yourselves to prayer, and return again to the same relationship”—the Apostle intends this, rather than granting it because of a greater downfall, he immediately adds:

“Lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”

A beautiful concession, indeed—and “return again to the same relationship.” What he is ashamed to call by its own name, what he sets before Satan’s temptation, what has lack of self-control as its cause, we labor to explain as though it were obscure, although he himself has explained what he wrote:

[Note: Our manuscripts read more elegantly: “although the very man who wrote it has explained himself.”]

“But this,” he says, “I speak by way of concession, not by way of command.”

And still we mutter that he does not call marriage a concession but a command—as though second and third marriages were not granted in the same way, or as though the doors of the Church were not opened through repentance even to fornicators, and, what is greater than this, to incestuous persons.

For the man who violated his stepmother, whom he had handed over to Satan in his First Epistle to the Corinthians “for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved” (1 Cor. 5), he recalls in the Second Epistle (2 Cor. 2), and labors lest the brother be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

To want something is one thing; to forgive is another.

[Col. 0221C] In the will we earn merit; in forgiveness we abuse mercy.

Do you wish to know what the Apostle wills? Join to this what follows:

“But I want all people to be as I myself am” (1 Cor. 7:7).

Blessed is the person who will be like Paul. Happy is the person who hears the Apostle commanding, not forgiving.

“This,” he says, “I want; this I desire: that you be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

He was a virgin from the Virgin, incorrupt from the incorrupt. Since we are human beings and cannot imitate the Savior’s birth, let us at least imitate his conduct. The former belongs to divinity and blessedness; the latter belongs to the human condition and labor.

“I want all people to be like me,” so that, while they are like me, they may also become like Christ, whose likeness I bear. For the person who believes in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked (1 John 1:6).

“But each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Cor. 7:7).

[Note: In the Veronese and Holy Cross manuscripts, both of the most ancient kind, the following is inserted: “In a command there is glory; in a concession scarcely any remission. What he commands, he crowns; what he relaxes, he marks for repentance. There the highest goal of action is to escape punishment; here, to have attained a crown is a matter of due. Concession and grace run by different roads. What, he says …”]

What he wants is obvious. But since there are different gifts in the Church, I also grant marriage, lest I seem to condemn nature.

At the same time, consider that the gift of virginity is one thing and the gift of marriage another. For if the reward of married women and virgins were the same, he would never have said, after commanding continence:

[Note: The text formerly read “of married women,” less well.] “But each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that.”

Where there is an individual distinction, there is mutual difference. I grant that marriage is also a gift of God, but there is a great difference between gift and gift.

Finally, the Apostle says concerning the same man who repented after incest: “On the contrary, you should forgive and comfort him; and if you have forgiven anyone anything, I have also forgiven him” (2 Cor. 2:7, 10).

And lest we think that a human gift should be despised, he added: “For whatever I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I did so for your sake in the presence of Christ” (ibid., 10).

Christ’s gifts are different. Hence Joseph, as a type of Christ, had a garment of many colors. And in the forty-fourth Psalm we read:

“The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded by variety” (Ps. 44:10).

And the Apostle Peter says: “As co-heirs of the manifold grace of God” (1 Pet. 3:7).

[Note: Current Greek manuscripts generally prefer χάριτος ζωῆς, “the grace of life,” and only rarely χάριτος ποικίλης, “manifold grace.” The Vulgate likewise has *gratia vitae*, “the grace of life,” which misled Victorius, who thought that he should praise the reading in 1 Peter 4:10, where the Greek and Latin have “manifold grace.” For this reason he judged that the preceding word *co-heirs* should necessarily be changed to *stewards*, on the basis of both texts; and in his *Apology to Pammachius*, or Epistle 48, he altered it in accordance with this preconceived opinion.]

In Greek this is expressed more significantly as ποικίλης, that is, “varied.”

### 9.

It follows:

“But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:8–9).

After granting married people the use of intercourse and showing what he himself wished and what he conceded, he passes to the unmarried and widows, proposes his own example, and calls them blessed if they remain as he does.

“But if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry”—the same point as above: “because of fornications,” and “lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”

He gives the reason why he said, “If they do not exercise self-control, let them marry”: “For it is better to marry than to burn.”

Marriage is therefore better because burning is worse. Take away the heat of lust, and he will not say, “It is better to marry.” For “better” always looks toward a comparison with what is worse, not toward the simple goodness of something good in itself and incomparable.

It is as if he said: “It is better to have one eye than none; it is better to lean on one foot and support the other side of the body with a staff than to crawl with broken legs.”

[Note: Martianus reads: “For it is better to have one …,” and then: “What are you saying, Apostle?” and so forth.]

What are you saying, Apostle? I do not believe you when you say: “Although unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge.” How does that arise from humility—“because I am not worthy to be called an Apostle,” and “the least of all the Apostles”? And, “As to one born prematurely”—I think this too was said in humility.

[Note: Previously the text had *puto*, “I think”; the manuscripts reject it.]

You know the peculiarities of expressions, which is why you take certain testimonies from Epimenides, Menander, and Aratus.

When you speak of continence and virginity, you say: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” And: “It is good for them if they remain as I am.” And: “I think that this is good for them because of the present necessity.” And: “It is good for a man to be so.”

But when you come to marriage, you do not say, “It is good to marry,” because you cannot join the words “than to burn”; rather, you say, “It is better to marry than to burn.”

If marriage is good in itself, do not compare it with fire; simply say, “It is good to marry.”

I distrust the goodness of that which the magnitude of another evil compels to be regarded as the lesser evil. I want not a lesser evil, but a simple good in itself.

### 10. Faithful Women Joined to Unbelievers. Matrons Preparing to Rage against Jerome. Abraham Binds His Servant by an Oath in Christ

Thus far the first chapter has been fully explained. Let us proceed to what follows.

“To those who are joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband. But if she does depart, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let the husband not dismiss his wife.”

[Note: We have removed the word “his” from this passage; it appears neither in our manuscripts nor in the current Vulgate.]

“But to the others I say—not the Lord: If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her,” and so forth, up to the place where he says:

“Let each one walk as God has called him, and as I teach in all the churches” (1 Cor. 7:10ff.).

This passage does not pertain to the present controversy. For, in accordance with the Lord’s judgment, it teaches that a wife is not to be repudiated except for the cause of fornication, and that a wife who has been repudiated, while her husband is alive, should not marry another, or at least should be reconciled to her husband.

But to those whom faith found in marriage—that is, if one of two people believed—he commands that the believer should not repudiate the unbeliever.

After setting out the circumstances, namely, that the unbeliever is a candidate for faith if he does not wish to depart from the believer, he commands conversely that if the unbeliever repudiates the believer because of faith in Christ, the believer ought to depart, lest he prefer a spouse to Christ, to whom even the soul must be subordinated.

But now very many women, despising the Apostle’s command, join themselves to pagans and prostitute Christ’s temples to idols. They do not understand that they are members of his body, whose ribs they also are.

The Apostle forgives the union with unbelievers of those who, while already having husbands, afterward believed in Christ; but he does not forgive those who, while they were Christians, married pagans. Elsewhere he addresses such women:

“Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership is there between righteousness and lawlessness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever? What agreement does the temple of God have with idols? For you are the temple of the living God” (2 Cor. 6:14ff.).

[Note: Our manuscripts consistently have “Christ and Belial,” corresponding to the Greek Χριστῷ πρὸς βελιάρ. We also find *Beliae* for *Belial*.]

Although I know that very many matrons will rage against me; although, with the same shamelessness with which they have despised the Lord, they will savagely attack me, a flea and the least of Christians, nevertheless I shall say what I think and speak what the Apostle has taught me: that they belong not to righteousness but to lawlessness; not to light but to darkness; not to Christ but to Belial; not to temples of the living God but to the shrines and idols of the dead.

Do you wish to learn more openly that it is altogether impermissible for a Christian woman to marry a pagan? Hear the same Apostle:

“A woman,” he says, “is bound for as long as her husband lives; but if her husband has fallen asleep, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:39)—that is, a Christian.

[Note: Victorius adds *legi*, “according to the law,” so that the text agrees with the Vulgate. In the Greek manuscripts, however, τῷ νόμῳ is often absent, and the Hieronymian manuscripts do not have it here. The Casanatensis shortly afterward reads: “that is, to a Christian, not to a pagan, who grants second marriages,” and so forth.]

He who permits second and third marriages in the Lord forbids first marriages with a pagan.

Hence Abraham binds his servant by an oath at his thigh—that is, in Christ, who was to be born from his seed—that he should not bring a foreign woman as a wife for his son Isaac.

And Ezra restrains God’s offense by the repudiation of such wives (2 Esdr. 10).

The prophet Malachi also says:

“Judah has acted treacherously, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem. For he has profaned the sanctuary of the Lord, and he has loved and taken as his wife the daughter of a foreign god. May the Lord destroy the man who does this, teacher and disciple, from the tents of Jacob, and the one who offers gifts to the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:11–12).

[Note: The Casanatensis incorrectly reads: “and not offering.”]

I have said these things so that those who compare marriage with virginity may at least know that such marriages are to be placed beneath second and third marriages.

### 11. He considers his interpretation open to criticism. Faith properly belongs to Christians.

In continuation of the preceding discussion, in which he had taught that a believer ought not to separate from an unbeliever, but should remain in the marriage as faith had found them, and that each person, whether celibate or married, should continue as baptism in Christ had found him, he suddenly introduces analogies concerning the circumcised and the Gentile, the slave and the free person; and under their metaphor he discusses the married and the unmarried.

“Was someone called while circumcised? Let him not bring on the foreskin. Was someone called in the foreskin? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and the foreskin is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God. Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called as a slave? Let it not concern you. But even if you are able to become free, make better use of it. For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman. Likewise, the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave. You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Let each person, therefore, remain before God in the calling in which he was called” (I Corinthians 7:18ff.).

First, since I think that some will criticize this interpretation, I should like to ask what the connection is by which, while discussing husbands and wives, he suddenly passes to a comparison of Jew and Gentile, slave and free person, and, when this discussion has ended, returns again to virgins, saying, “Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord” (I Corinthians 7:25).

[Note: The word “therefore” is found neither in the Greek nor in Jerome’s manuscripts. Here and below, they have *brothers* in the plural, not *brother*, likewise corresponding to the Greek ἀδελφοί (*adelphoi*). Finally, instead of “what the connection is,” they read “what the consequent meaning is.”]

What has the comparison of Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free persons, to do with marriage and virginity?

Second, how can the statement “Was someone called while circumcised? Let him not bring on the foreskin” be understood (ibid., 18)? Can someone who has once had his foreskin cut off, if he wishes, bring it on again?

[Note: He understands “bringing on the foreskin” to be impossible, contrary to what we have perhaps said elsewhere at greater length than necessary. See the interpreters of that passage.]

Next, in what sense should the words “For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise, the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave” be explained (ibid., 22)?

Fourth, how can the man who commanded slaves to obey their fleshly masters now say, “Do not become slaves of human beings” (ibid., 23)?

Finally, what does the statement “Let each person remain before God in the calling in which he was called” have to do with slavery or circumcision? For it is also contrary to the preceding statement. If we heard, “Do not become slaves of human beings,” how can we remain in the calling in which we were called, when many have believed while having fleshly masters whom they are now forbidden to serve? Moreover, what does remaining in the calling in which we were called have to do with circumcision, when in another passage the same Apostle cries out, “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians 5:2)?

It remains, therefore, that circumcision and the foreskin, slave and free person, must be fitted to the preceding meaning and depend upon what comes before.

[Note: In the very ancient manuscripts of Verona and Cîteaux the following is added: “By the designation of circumcision, he teaches abstinence from lust, because that part of the body is to be cut off from which danger is expected in shameful matters.” Below Jerome himself says, “Let them first learn marital abstinence.”]

“Was someone called while circumcised? Let him not bring on the foreskin.” At the time, he says, when you were called and believed in Christ, if you were called while circumcised by your wife and were celibate, do not take a wife—that is, do not bring on the foreskin—lest you burden the freedom of circumcision and chastity with the load of marriage.

Again, if someone was called in the foreskin, let him not be circumcised. You had a wife, he says, when you believed; do not suppose that the faith of Christ is a cause of separation, because God called us in peace.

“Circumcision is nothing, and the foreskin is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God” (ibid., 19). For celibacy and marriage are of no benefit without works, since even faith, which properly belongs to Christians, is said to be dead if it has no works. By this rule, the virgins of Vesta and the one-husband women of Juno could also be counted among the saints.

“Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called” (ibid., 24). When he believed, whether he had a wife or did not have one, let him remain in the condition in which he was called. Thus he does not so much compel virgins to marry as forbid repudiation. Just as he removes from those who have wives the permission to dismiss them, so he takes away from virgins the opportunity to marry.

“Were you called as a slave? Let it not concern you; but even if you are able to become free, make better use of it.” Even if you have a wife, he says, and are bound to her, and pay the debt, and have no power over your own body—and, to speak more plainly, are your wife’s slave—do not on that account be sad or sigh over your lost virginity. But even if you can find some grounds for separation, so that you may enjoy the freedom of chastity, do not seek your salvation through another’s destruction. Keep your wife for a while; do not outrun one who is delayed. Wait until she follows. If you act patiently, your wife will be changed into a sister.

“For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise, the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave.”

He gives the reasons why he does not want wives to be abandoned. Therefore he says: I command that those who believe in Christ from paganism should not abandon the marriages they entered before faith, because the believer who has a wife is not so much occupied with the service of God as virgins and unmarried women are; he is, in a certain sense, freer, and the reins of his servitude are loosened. While he is, so to speak, his wife’s slave, he is the Lord’s freedman.

But the man who, without a wife, believed and was called by the Lord free from the servitude of marriage—he is truly Christ’s slave. What great happiness it is not to be a wife’s slave but Christ’s; not to serve the flesh but the spirit! “For the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (I Corinthians 6:17).

And lest it should seem that, in the words he had said above—“Were you called as a slave? Let it not concern you; but even if you are able to become free, make better use of it”—he had mocked continence and handed us over to the service of spouses, he adds a statement that cuts off every quibble: “You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings.”

We were redeemed by the most precious blood of Christ. The Lamb was sacrificed for us, and, sprinkled with the warmest dew of hyssop, we have burned away every secretion of harmful pleasure. In baptism Pharaoh died for them,

[Note: There is no doubt that “Pharaoh” signifies sin or the Devil, of whom Pharaoh is a type. This is a familiar allegory among the ancients.]

and his entire army was drowned. Why do we seek Egypt again, and, after manna, the food of angels, desire garlic, onions, melons, and “meats of Pharan”?

[Note: Up to this point the reading *various meats* (*carnes varias*) had prevailed, although Martianus himself admits that *Pharian meats* (*carnes Farias*) is found in most manuscripts. Thus indeed do our two outstanding manuscripts read, and their authority must not be abandoned. I preferred to aspirate the word and read *Pharian*, explaining it as named from the place where the Hebrew people craved meat—that is, in the wilderness of Paran, where, scorning heavenly bread and desiring Egyptian meats, they received quails and devoured them to nausea and vomiting, as Jerome himself explained in the *Letter on Places*, section XIII. See Numbers 16:13ff.

I also know that *Pharian* is commonly understood as “Pharaonic,” in accordance with Prudentius:

> “This dissolves the savage kingdom of the Pharian king.”

And we sigh for various meats. Thus reads the manuscript of Saint-Germain and another of Chartres. The first hand of the Corbie manuscript reads *Pharian meats*, but a later hand changed *Pharian* to *various*, adding in the margin, “that is, Pharaonic.” One Royal manuscript and another Colbertine manuscript both read *Pharaonitic meats*. One manuscript of our monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres reads *wild meats*. Finally, the manuscript of Saint-Evroul reads *various meats*, that is, “Pharaonic meats.”

We have wished here to show the curious reader this disagreement among the manuscripts, so that from such great variety he may infer how large a forest of various readings there is in other, less important statements, though we have not recorded them all. —Martianus]

### 12. Why God did not command virginity. What are the festivals of marriage? Why Christ loves virgins more. The significance of the words must be considered.

After the preceding discussion of married people and the continent, he finally comes to virgins and says:

“Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord; but I give advice, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord, that I may be faithful. I think, therefore, that this is good because of the present necessity, since it is good for a person to be thus” (I Corinthians 7:25–26).

[Note: This clause—“since it is good for a person to be thus”—is not found in our manuscripts.]

Here the opponent rages with every expression of triumph, shaking the wall of virginity with this supposedly mighty battering ram:

“Behold,” he says, “the Apostle professes that concerning virgins he has no command of the Lord; and although he had issued authoritative orders concerning husbands and wives, he does not dare to command what the Lord did not command. Rightly so. For what is commanded is imposed; what is imposed must be done; and what must be done, if it is not done, incurs punishment. For a command is given in vain if it is left to the discretion of the person to whom it is given.”

If the Lord had commanded virginity, he would have seemed to condemn marriage and to remove the human stock from which virginity itself is born. If he had cut away the root, how would he seek fruit? If he had not first laid the foundations, how could he raise the building and place a roof above it to cover everything?

With great labor mountains are overturned by excavators; the depths almost beneath the earth are penetrated so that gold may be found. When, first by the smelting of the furnace and then by the skillful hand of the craftsman, a necklace has been fashioned from tiny grains, the person who grew gold out of clay is not called blessed, but the one who uses the beauty of gold.

[Note: On the agreement of the manuscripts and the old edition, we have supplied the word *terrarum* (“of the earth”).]

Do not therefore be surprised that, amid the ticklings of the flesh and the kindling of vices, we are not compelled to live the life of angels but are taught to do so. Where advice is given, the choice belongs to the one offering it; where there is a command, there is necessity for the one who serves.

“I have no command of the Lord,” he says, “but I give advice, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord” (I Corinthians 7:25).

If you do not have a command of the Lord, why do you dare to give advice about something for which you have no order?

The Apostle will answer me: Do you want me to command what the Lord offered rather than commanded? The Creator and Potter, knowing the fragility of the vessel he had made, left virginity in the power of the hearer. Should I, the Teacher of the Gentiles, who became all things to all people “that I might win all” (I Corinthians 9:22), immediately place the burden of perpetual chastity upon the necks of the weak who believe?

Let them first learn marital abstinence; let them devote themselves for a time to prayer, so that, having tasted chastity, they may desire always to possess what they enjoyed for a little while.

The Lord, when tempted by the Pharisees as to whether it was lawful according to the law of Moses to dismiss wives, entirely prohibited it. His disciples, considering this, said to him: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” He answered them: “Not everyone receives this word, but those to whom it has been given. For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb; there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by human beings; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matthew 19:10ff.).

It is clear why the Apostle said, “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord”: evidently because the Lord had first said, “Not everyone receives this word, but those to whom it has been given,” and, “Let the one who can receive it receive it.”

He sets before them the prize as a presiding judge of the games (*agonothetes*), invites them to the race, and holds in his hand the reward of virginity. He shows a perfectly pure fountain and cries out: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink.” “Let the one who can receive it receive it” (John 7:37).

He does not say, “Whether you wish it or not, you must drink and run,” but the one who wishes and is able to run and drink will win; he will be satisfied.

Therefore Christ loves virgins more, because they freely offer what was not commanded them. It is a greater grace to offer what one does not owe than to return what is demanded.

The Apostles, observing the burdens of a wife, said: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” Their Lord, approving their judgment, said: “You rightly understand that it is not expedient for a man who is making his way toward the kingdom of heaven to take a wife; but it is a difficult matter, and not everyone receives this word, but those to whom it has been given. Some are made eunuchs by nature, others by human force. I am pleased by those eunuchs whom not necessity but will has castrated. I gladly receive into my embrace those who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven and, for my worship, did not wish to remain what they were born to be.”

At the same time, the statement itself must be examined: “They made themselves eunuchs,” he says, “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.” If the castrated receive the reward of the kingdom of heaven, then those who have not castrated themselves cannot receive the place of the castrated. “Let the one who can receive it receive it.”

It is a great faith and a great virtue to be God’s perfectly pure temple, to offer oneself wholly as a burnt offering to the Lord, and, in accordance with the same Apostle, to be holy both in body and in spirit.

These are the eunuchs who, thinking themselves a dry tree because of their barrenness, hear through Isaiah (chapter 56) that a place in heaven has been prepared for them in place of sons and daughters.

Their type is Ebed-melech,

[Note: The manuscripts have *Abdamelech*.]

the eunuch in Jeremiah (chapter 28), and that eunuch of Queen Candace in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 8), who, because of the strength of his faith, obtained the name of a man.

Clement also, the successor of the Apostle Peter, of whom the Apostle Paul makes mention, wrote letters to them and composed almost his entire discourse on the purity of virginity.

[Note: Saint Epiphanius also testifies that Clement spoke of virginity in his letters, *Against Heresies* 30, chapter 15; and a passage of this kind does occur in his earlier letter to the Corinthians.]

After him came many apostolic men, martyrs, and distinguished figures, notable both for holiness and eloquence, whom it is very easy to know from their own writings.

“For I think,” he says, “that this is good because of the present necessity” (I Corinthians 7:26).

[Note: The printed editions have “this good work,” but both our manuscripts and the Greek and Latin texts showed that *work* is redundant. Elsewhere above and below we correct certain matters of lesser importance.]

What is that necessity which, spurning the bond of marriage, seeks the freedom of virginity?

“Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in that day” (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14; Luke 21:23).

Here it is not prostitutes or brothels that are condemned—there is no doubt about their condemnation—but swollen wombs, the cries of infants, and the fruits and works of marriage.

“Since it is good for a person to be thus” (I Corinthians 7:26). If it is good for a person to be thus, then it is bad for a person not to be thus.

“Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife” (ibid., 27).

Each of us has his own boundaries: give me what is mine, and keep what is yours. If you are bound to a wife, do not divorce her. If I am released from a wife, I will not seek a wife. Just as I do not dissolve marriages once they have been joined, so you must not bind what has been released.

The significance of the words must also be considered. The man who has a wife is called a debtor; he is in the foreskin, a wife’s slave, and—what is characteristic of bad slaves—bound. But the man without a wife is first of all no one’s debtor, then circumcised, thirdly free, and finally released.

### 13. Virgins who marry after consecration commit incest. The whole span of life is short. Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome’s teacher. What virginity is as Christ’s sacrifice. The difference between marriage and virginity.

Let us run through what remains, for the size of the volume does not allow us to linger longer over each point.

“If you take a wife, you have not sinned.” It is one thing not to sin and another to do good. “And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned” [another reading: “will not sin”].

That is not the virgin who has once dedicated herself to the worship of God. If any of these should marry, she will incur condemnation, because she has made her first faith void. If someone should object that this was said about widows, how much more will it prevail concerning virgins, since even those for whom it was once permitted are not allowed to do so now!

Virgins who marry after consecration are not so much adulteresses as incestuous women. And lest he should seem, by saying “If a virgin marries, she has not sinned,” to invite celibates once more to marriage, he immediately restrains himself and, adding something else, weakens what he had conceded, saying: “Yet such people will have tribulation in the flesh.”

Who are these who will have tribulation in the flesh? Those to whom he had just shown indulgence: “If you take a wife, you have not sinned,” and “If a virgin marries, she has not sinned” [another reading: “will not sin”]. “Yet such people will have tribulation in the flesh.”

We, ignorant of these matters, had supposed that marriage at least possessed joy in the flesh. But if those who marry have tribulation even in the flesh, in which alone they seemed to have pleasures, what remains for them to marry for, when there is tribulation in spirit, soul, and the flesh itself?

“But I spare you.” Thus, he says, I mention tribulation in the flesh as though there were not greater reasons why you ought not to marry.

“Therefore I say this, brothers: the time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none.”

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads, “so that those who have wives may also be as though they had none.” The Greek has ἵνα καὶ οἱ, “so that those also who …”]

I am no longer discussing virgins, whose happiness is beyond all doubt. I come to married men.

The time is short; the Lord is near. Even if we lived nine hundred years, like the men of ancient times, the time would still have to be considered short, because it would eventually have an end and cease to exist. But now, when it is not so much the joy as the tribulation of marriage that is brief, why do we take wives whom we will soon be forced to lose?

“And those who weep,” he says, “and those who rejoice, and those who buy, and those who use this world should be as though they did not weep, rejoice, buy, or use this world. For the form of this world is passing away” (I Corinthians 7:30).

If the world passes away—the world within which everything is enclosed—indeed, if the form and way of life of this world pass away like a cloud, then, among the other works of the world, marriage too will pass away. For there will be no marriages after the resurrection.

But if death is the end of marriage, why do we not turn necessity into willingness? What must be wrung from unwilling people, why do we not offer to God in hope of rewards?

“The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided.”

Let us observe the difference between the concerns of the virgin and those of the married man. The virgin desires to please the Lord; the married man desires to please his wife, and, in order to please his wife, he is anxious about the things of the world, which will surely pass away with the world. He is divided—that is, distracted among many anxieties and miseries.

It is not the place here to describe the narrow confines of marriage and to exult rhetorically, as though in a commonplace exercise. I think I have dealt with the matter more fully in my work against Helvidius and in the book I wrote to Eustochium.

Certainly Tertullian too, while still a young man,

[Note: He may perhaps be indicating a poem on virginity written by Tertullian in his youth. For it cannot be said that he “played” in the work entitled *Exhortation to Chastity*, which was composed near the end of his life and dealt deliberately with the troubles of marriage, as Jerome himself testifies. We find “Nazianzenus” added immediately afterward in none of the manuscripts.]

played with this subject. And my teacher Gregory of Nazianzus, discussing virginity and marriage, explained the matter in Greek verses.

I now briefly point out that in the Latin manuscripts this passage is read as follows: “The virgin and the married woman are divided.”

[Note: The manuscripts read, as in the text, “the woman and the virgin.” He explained this meaning in the book against Helvidius and in Letter 22 to Eustochium; see note c, section 21.]

Although this has its own meaning, and I too have explained it in this way in accordance with the character of the passage, nevertheless it is not the Apostle’s meaning. For the Apostle wrote as we translated above: “The married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided.” Having established this point, he passes over to virgins and continent women and says:

“The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit.”

Not every unmarried woman is a virgin. But every virgin is certainly unmarried. Yet, for elegance of expression, he may have repeated the same thing in another word—“the unmarried woman and the virgin”—or he may have wished to define what an unmarried woman is, namely, a virgin, lest we consider prostitutes unmarried merely because they are joined to no fixed marriage.

What, then, does the unmarried woman and virgin think about? The things of the Lord, so that she may be holy both in body and spirit.

Even if no other reward followed the virgin, this one distinction would be enough for her: that she thinks about the things of the Lord. He immediately teaches what this very thought is: that she may be holy in body and spirit.

For some are virgins in the flesh but not in the spirit: their body is intact, but their soul is corrupted. But that virginity is Christ’s sacrifice

[Note: Again the manuscripts of Verona and Cîteaux add: “a difficult command transcending human nature; for when a command is given, it lays bare the innermost parts, since they command what is beyond one’s strength and release the subject from the necessity of what has been begun.” They also sin through a faulty transposition and suggest an alien undertaking.]

whose mind no thought and whose flesh no desire has stained.

Conversely, the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband. Just as the man who has a wife is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife, so the married woman thinks about worldly matters, how she may please her husband.

But we are not of this world, which lies in wickedness, whose form is passing away. Of this world it is said to the Apostles: “If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own” (John 15:19).

And lest he should seem to be imposing the very heavy burden of chastity upon unwilling people, he immediately adds the reasons for his exhortation and says:

“But I say this for your benefit, not to throw a snare over you,

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads *sed ad id*, “but toward this,” without *ut*, “so that,” which is also absent from the Greek text. Formerly *vos adhorter*, “that I may exhort you,” was added in the line.]

but for what is honorable and fitting, and for serving the Lord attentively, without distraction.”

The Greek expression cannot be fully represented in Latin. What words could convey the phrase:

Πρὸς τὸ εὔσχημον καὶ εὐπρόσεδρον τῷ Κυρίῳ ἀπερισπάστως?

“Toward what is honorable and fitting for the Lord, without distraction”?

[Note: Πρὸς τὸ εὔσχημον. Erasmus and Marianus, in their customary corrupt manner, printed this passage most incorrectly. First, they supplied in the Latin “that I may exhort you,” which is not found in the manuscript codices; then they recited the entire Greek verse, although Jerome retains only its final part, which is not expressed because of the difficulty of translation, in accordance with the testimony of all the manuscripts. Worse still, they do not inform the reader what they themselves have added and thrust into Jerome’s text, without any legitimate necessity. It is also noteworthy that in the manuscript of Saint-Germain, after the word *edicere* (“to express”), the scribe placed “GRE.” Hence—and so forth—as if to indicate that he neither read nor supplied the Greek. All the other manuscripts retain all the Greek words that we have printed.

The manuscripts of Verona and Cîteaux clearly read ΕΥΠΑΡΕΔΡΟΝ rather than εὐπρόσεδρον. The meaning is not different, but the reading is by no means negligible.]

For this reason the Latin manuscripts, because of the difficulty of translation, do not contain this expression at all. Let us therefore use what we have translated.

The Apostle does not throw a snare over us or compel us to be what we do not wish to be. He advises what is honorable and fitting, and what enables us to serve the Lord attentively, always to remain watchful and to await the Lord’s will, ready to fulfill immediately whatever he has commanded, like a vigorous and armed soldier, and to do so without any distraction

[another reading: “distension”].

This distraction, according to Ecclesiastes (chapter 3), has been granted to the people of this world, so that they may be stretched and pulled apart by it.

[Note: The two manuscripts of Verona and Cîteaux again add, with equal agreement: “The virgin is said to boil over”—perhaps *N. R. E.*, that is, *natura*, “by nature”—“that is, concerning modesty: when the heat of carnal desire boils up in the limbs, the vigor of the soul is extinguished.”]

But if someone considers his virgin—that is,

[Note: The Casanatensis manuscript reads: “the flesh that is wanton boils over,” and so forth.]

if he sees the flesh become wanton and boil over with lust, and he cannot restrain himself, and a double necessity rests upon him, either to take a wife

[Note: Previously the text had, in an unsuitable sense, “or to fall,” instead of “or to reject,” which we have restored on the authority of all our manuscripts. Moreover, instead of “if she marries,” they read “if he takes a wife.” Properly speaking, *nubere* is used of a woman, not of a man.]

or to fall—let him do what he wishes; he does not sin if he marries. Let him do, he says, what he wishes, not what he ought.

He does not sin if he takes a wife; nevertheless, he does not do well if he takes one. For the man who stands firm in his heart, having no necessity,

[Note: These same manuscripts read “but having power, and having judged this in his heart,” corresponding to the Greek ἔχει, “has,” and κέκρικεν, “has judged.”]

but having power over his own will, and has judged in his heart to preserve his virgin, does well.

Therefore both the man who joins his virgin to marriage does well, and the man who does not join her does better (I Corinthians 7:37–38).

He had said deliberately and precisely above, “The man who takes a wife does not sin”; here he says, “The man who preserves his virgin does well.” But it is one thing not to sin and another to do good.

“Turn away from evil,” he says, “and do good” (Psalm 36:27). The former we turn away from; the latter we pursue. In the one there is a beginning; in the other, perfection.

But lest anyone should think that, in saying “the man who joins his virgin to marriage does well,” he has undermined our observance, he immediately diminishes and overshadows this good by comparison with the better and says, “And the man who does not join her does better.”

Unless he had been going to say “does better,” he would never have first said “does well.” Where there is good and better, the reward of the good and the better is not one and the same; and where the reward is not one and the same, the gifts are certainly different.

Thus the difference between marriage and virginity is as great as that between not sinning and doing good—or, to put it more mildly, as great as that between good and better.

### 14. Widows supported by the alms of the Church.

When the discussion of marriage and virginity had ended, he had proceeded between the two with the cautious moderation of his commands, turning neither to the left nor to the right but walking along the royal road and fulfilling the saying, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Ecclesiastes 7:17).

Now once again he compares monogamy with digamy. Just as he had subordinated marriage to virginity, so he subjects digamy to first marriage, and says:

“A woman is bound for as long as her husband lives; but if her husband should fall asleep, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my advice. I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (I Corinthians 7:39–40).

He grants second marriages, but to those who wish them and to those who cannot remain continent, lest, having grown wanton in Christ, they wish to marry and incur condemnation because they have made their first faith void. He grants this because many have turned back after Satan (I Timothy 5:15).

But they will be happier, he says, if they remain as they are. Immediately he adds apostolic authority: “according to my advice.” And lest the Apostle’s authority should seem weaker as belonging merely to a human being, he adds: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

Where he calls them to continence, it is the counsel not of a human being but of the Spirit of God. Where, however, he grants permission to marry, he does not mention the Spirit of God, but weighs the advice according to prudence, allowing each person as much as he is able to bear.

In accordance with this meaning, all those passages must be understood:

“The woman who is under a husband, while her husband lives, is bound by the law. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man. But if her husband dies, she is released from the law, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man” (Romans 7:2–3).

And the passage to Timothy:

“I therefore want younger widows to marry, bear children, manage households, and give the adversary no opportunity for reviling. For some have already turned back after Satan” (I Timothy 5:14–15), together with the other similar passages.

For just as he grants marriage to virgins because of the danger of fornication and makes excusable what is not desired for its own sake, so, in order to avoid that same fornication, he grants widows second marriages.

For it is better—though it may be a second or third marriage—to know one man than many; that is, it is more tolerable to be prostituted to one man than to many.

For that woman in the Gospel, the Samaritan,

[Note: The name “John” is absent from both our manuscripts and the old edition.]

who said that she had had a sixth husband, is reproved by the Lord because he was not her husband (John 4:17). For where there is a number of husbands, the husband, who properly is one, has ceased to exist.

At the beginning, one rib was turned into one wife. “And they will be two in one flesh,” he says (Genesis 2:24)—not three or four; otherwise they are no longer two,

[Note: We read *if there are several* rather than *but several* from the most carefully corrected Verona manuscript. The following passage is taken from Tertullian’s *On Monogamy*, where he says: “The first crime, murder, was consecrated in fratricide; a crime worthy of the second place was not that of two marriages. Once, then, the institution of God suffered violence through Lamech; afterward it remained until the end of that race. The flood of Asia was provoked by iniquities; once defended, such things were not defended seventy-seven times, as two marriages deserved.”]

if there are several.

The first Lamech, bloodstained and murderous, divided one flesh between two wives. Fratricide and digamy were destroyed by the same punishment of the Flood. The one was avenged sevenfold, the other seventy-sevenfold. As they differ in number, so also do they differ in crime.

How sacred digamy is

[Note: I would prefer to read *monogamy*, following the old edition, instead of *digamy*, but the manuscripts do not support it.]

is shown by the fact that a digamist cannot be chosen for the clergy. Therefore the Apostle says to Timothy: “Let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old and has been the wife of one man” (I Timothy 5:9).

Here the entire command concerns widows who are supported by the alms of the Church. For this reason an age is prescribed, so that only those who can no longer work may receive the food of the poor.

At the same time, consider that a woman who has had two husbands, even if she is old, decrepit, and needy, does not deserve to receive the Church’s charity. If the bread of almsgiving is taken away from her, how much more is that bread which descended from heaven! Whoever eats it unworthily will be guilty of violating the body and blood of Christ.

## 15. Paul Was Compelled to Will Many Things

Although some interpret the testimonies I cited above, in which widows are permitted, if they wish, to marry again, as referring to widows whom the faith of Christ finds in that condition after they have lost their husbands, [Note: [Col. 0234D] Our copies: “nor would it follow that,” etc.] it would not follow that the Apostle, after a husband’s death following baptism, commands a woman to marry another, since he also commanded those who have wives to live as though they did not have them; nor did he define the number of wives for this reason: because after the baptism of Christ, even if a woman has been a third or fourth wife, she is to be reckoned as though she were a first wife. Otherwise, if after baptism, when the first husband has died, a second is taken, why should a sixth and the others not be taken when the second, third, fourth, and fifth husbands have died? [Note: Manuscripts read “when they have died”; shortly afterward, by common agreement, “let her cast off several husbands” instead of “let her take”; and a little later, “the second Adam, a virgin” instead of “let us act as a second Adam.”]

It can happen that, through some misfortune or by God’s judgment cutting short repeated marriages, a young woman takes several husbands and becomes widowed from her first husband in old age. The first Adam was monogamous; the second was unmarried. Let those who approve digamy produce a third Adam, a digamist, for others to follow.

But suppose that Paul granted second marriages: by the same law he also grants a third, a fourth, and as many as there are deaths of husbands. The Apostle is compelled to will many things that he does not will. He circumcised Timothy, shaved his own head, practiced going barefoot, grew his hair, and cut it at Cenchreae. Yet he had rebuked the Galatians and reproached Peter because he separated himself from the Gentiles on account of Jewish observances.

How, then, in the other disciplines of the Church, he became a Jew to the Jews, a Gentile to the Gentiles, and all things to all people in order to win them all, so also he granted digamy to the incontinent and did not define the number of marriages, so that, when women saw that a second husband was granted after the death of the first in the same way that a third and fourth were granted, they would be ashamed to take another, lest they be compared with trigamists and quadrigamists. For when one has been exceeded, it makes no difference whether the next is a second or a third, since the person ceases to be monogamous.

“All things are permitted, but not all things are beneficial” (I Cor. VI, 12; X, 23). I do not condemn digamists, nor even trigamists, and, if it may be said, not even octogamists. I will go further: I receive even a fornicator who repents. Whatever is permitted equally must be weighed on an equal scale.

## 16. Chastity Has Always Been Preferred to Marriage. The Number Two Is Not Good

But since he draws us back to the Old Testament and, beginning with Adam, reaches Zachariah and Elizabeth, and then brings forward Peter and the other apostles, [Note: [Col. 0235C] Casanatensis: “and the other apostles had wives, but we,” etc.] we too must proceed through the same sequence of questions and show that chastity has always been preferred to the work of marriage.

Concerning Adam and Eve, this must be said: before the offense, they were virgins in paradise; after the sin, and immediately outside paradise, there was marriage. Moreover, the Apostle interprets this very matter: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother [Note: [Col. 0235D] Neither our copies nor the Greek epistle to the Ephesians contain the word “his.”] and shall cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Eph. V, 31; Gen. II, 24). And immediately he adds: “This is a great mystery. But I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (ibid., 32).

Christ is a virgin in the flesh and monogamous in the spirit. For he has one Church, concerning which the same Apostle says: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Eph. V, 25; Col. III, 19). If Christ loves the Church in holiness, chastity, and without any stain, husbands too should love their wives in chastity, and let each person know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God. “For God did not call us to impurity, but to sanctification” (I Thess. IV, 7).

Let us put off the old man with his works and put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of his Creator: “where there is not [Note: [Col. 0235D] We have not deleted the words “male and female,” which are inserted here in the printed editions against the testimony of all the manuscripts we consulted, and indeed against the text of Paul in Colossians III, 10, which is the source of this passage. For below Jerome explains something concerning the distinction of the sexes, which in some measure supports those words. We read, with the same manuscripts and the Greek text, “but Christ is all and in all.”] male and female, Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free, but Christ is all and in all” (Col. III, 10–11).

The image of the Creator has no marital union. Where the distinction of sex is removed, where we put off the old man and put on the new, there we are reborn into Christ the virgin—who was both born from a virgin and reborn through a virgin.

But when he says, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I, 28), it was necessary first to plant the forest and allow it to grow, so that there would later be something to cut down. At the same time, we must consider the force of the words “fill the earth.” Marriage fills the earth; virginity fills paradise.

This too must be observed, at least according to the Hebrew truth: when Scripture says on the first, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days, after the completion of each day’s works, “And God saw that it was good,” on the second day it completely omits this statement, leaving us to understand that the number two is not good, because it divides what was united and prefigures the bonds of marriage. [Note: [Col. 0235D] That is, it divides from unity. See the letter to Eustochium, Letter 22, p. 101, note b (in our edition, col. 406, note d).]

Hence, in Noah’s ark, all animals that enter two by two are unclean (Gen. VII–VIII). An odd number is clean. Yet the number two also displays another mystery: not even among beasts and unclean birds was digamy approved. For the unclean enter two by two, while the clean enter by sevens, so that after the Flood Noah might immediately offer to God what he could take from the odd number.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] Manuscripts read “for they enter two and two”; shortly afterward, in the Casanatensis, the name Noah is absent. Those who understand that seven pairs, rather than seven individual clean animals, entered the ark interpret the passage in this way: Augustine, *The City of God* XV, 27; Ambrose, *On Noah’s Ark*, chapter 12; Theodoret, *Questions on Genesis*, question 50; and others. It is nevertheless known that other ancient writers likewise understand seven pairs.]

## 17. But If Enoch Was Translated

[Note: [Col. 0236D] The first person to call upon God, or upon the name of the Lord, was not Enoch but Enos, son of Seth (Gen. IV); the one whom Scripture says was translated (Gen. V) was not Enos but Enoch, son of Jared, of whom the Apostle speaks in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Perhaps Jerome, writing hastily, was misled by the similarity of the names.]

But if Enoch was translated and Noah was preserved through the Flood, I do not think Enoch was translated because he had a wife, but because he was the first to call upon God and believe in the Creator [Note: [Col. 0236D] “In the Creator.” The printed editions falsely read “in the Savior,” whereas all the manuscript codices retain “in the Creator,” without a single exception. Moreover, Enoch was not the first to call upon God, but Enos, son of Seth—unless Jerome perhaps means Enoch’s special practice of faith, of which the Apostle speaks in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter XI, where nothing is said of Enos, son of Seth. MARTIAN.] [Alternative: “the Savior”], concerning whom the Apostle Paul teaches fully in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Heb. X, 5).

Noah, who was preserved as a second root for the human race, certainly had to be preserved with his wife and sons. Yet there is a mystery in this passage of Scripture. That ark, according to the Apostle Peter (I Pet. III), was a type of the Church, in which eight souls were saved. When Noah enters it, both he himself and his sons are separated from their wives; but when he goes out onto the earth, the pairs are joined. What had been separated in the ark—that is, in the Church—is united in the conduct of the world.

At the same time, if the ark had many chambers and nests, and was divided into two and three levels, and contained various animals, and if its dwellings were larger or smaller according to the kinds of animals, I think that this variety of dwellings prefigured the diversity of the Church.

## 18. Permission to Eat Meat

As for his objection that permission to eat meat was given in God’s second blessing, though it had not been granted in the first, he should know how divorce, according to the Savior’s teaching, was not given from the beginning but was granted to the human race through Moses because of the hardness of our hearts. In the same way, the eating of meat was unknown until the Flood.

After the Flood, however, just as quails were given to a murmuring people in the wilderness, so sinews and [Note: [Col. 0236D] He prefers “meat full of broth”; Casanatensis has “poisonous meat,” while Veronensis has, somewhat more elegantly, “brothy meats.” Tertullian, *On Fasting* IV, Origen, *Commentary on Genesis*, book XXIX, Basil, Chrysostom, Theodoret, and others likewise teach that before the Flood permission to eat meat had not been given.] poisonous meats were thrust upon our teeth.

The Apostle teaches, writing to the Ephesians (chapter I), that God had purposed, in the fullness of times, to recapitulate all things and [Note: [Col. 0237D] Our manuscripts read “to draw back to the beginning in Christ Jesus.” See Tertullian, book V *Against Marcion*.] bring back to the beginning in Christ Jesus the things that are in the heavens and on earth. Hence the Savior himself says in the Apocalypse of John: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end” (Apoc. I, 18; XXII, 13).

From the beginning of the human creation, we neither ate meat, nor granted divorce, nor removed the foreskin from ourselves as a sign. In this course we came down to the Flood. After the Flood, however, together with the giving of the Law—which no one could fulfill—meat was introduced for eating, divorce was granted because of hardness, and the knife of circumcision was applied, as though the hand of God had created more in us than was necessary.

[Note: [Col. 0237D] Elsewhere and in the Veronensis: “the hardness or hard-heartedness that permitted divorce.” Others shortly afterward read *creaverint*, plural.]

[Note: [Col. 0237D] This passage is taken from Tertullian, *On Monogamy*: “The Apostle also says, writing to the Ephesians, that God purposed in himself, for the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things to their source—that is, to their beginning—in Christ, the things in heaven and the things on earth in him. Thus the Lord also took upon himself the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, the figures of beginning and end converging in him, so that, just as Alpha and Omega are brought together, he might show that in himself there is both the course of the beginning toward the end and the return of the end to the beginning.”]

But after Christ came at the end of the times, and the Omega revolved back to the Alpha and drew the extremity back to the beginning, we are no longer permitted to divorce, nor are we circumcised, nor do we eat meat, since the Apostle says: “It is good neither to drink wine nor to eat meat” (Rom. XIV, 21). Wine, too, was consecrated for use with meat after the Flood.

## 19. Isaac as a Figure of Christ

What shall I say about Abraham, whom he himself calls a trigamist and who received the sign of faith in circumcision? If we imitate the number of his wives, let us imitate his circumcision as well. He is not to be imitated in one respect and rejected in another.

Isaac, the husband of one Rebecca, prefigures Christ and the Church, [Note: [Col. 0238D] These words, which ridicule the wantonness of digamy and smell of a foreign hand, are found in none of the manuscripts we use.] and censures the wantonness of digamy.

But if Jacob had two teams of wives and concubines, and the opponent refuses to admit that bleary-eyed, deformed, and fertile Leah prefigured the synagogue, while beautiful and long-barren Rachel signified the mystery of the Church, let him know that Jacob did this when he was among the Assyrians and was serving Laban, the harshest of masters, in Mesopotamia.

But when he wished to enter the Holy Land, and built a heap of witness on Mount Gilead, among whose baggage the possessor of Mesopotamia had found nothing, swearing that he would never return to the place where he had served; and when he wrestled with the Angel at the torrent Jabbok and began to limp, and his πλατὺ νεῦρον [that is, the thigh muscle] withered, he immediately received the name Israel.

Then that once-beloved wife for whom he had served, near Bethlehem, where the Lord—the herald of virginity—was to be born, was killed by the son [namely, Benoni] of her sorrow (Gen. XXXV, 18); and the Mesopotamian associations die in the Gospel city.

## 20. The Clean Must Receive the Body of Christ

I wonder why he has proposed Judah and Tamar to us as an example, unless perhaps he also delights in prostitutes; or why he mentions Onan, who was killed because he begrudged his brother his seed [the manuscripts read “Aunam”], as though we approved any emission of semen apart from the work of producing children.

It is clear concerning Moses that he would have perished at the lodging place unless Zipporah, whose name means “bird,” had circumcised her son and cut away the foreskin of marriage with the Evangelical knife. This indeed is the Moses who, when he saw the great vision and the Angel—or the Lord speaking [Note: [Col. 0238D] Veronensis: “or the Lord or God speaking.”]—in the bush, could not approach him unless he had loosened the strap of his sandal and cast off the bonds of marriage.

Nor is this surprising in the case of God’s friend, prophet, and lawgiver, since the entire people, when they were about to approach Mount Sinai and hear God’s word, were commanded to sanctify themselves for three days and abstain from their wives.

We know that this was also said—although I am improperly confusing the order of the history—to David when he was fleeing, by the priest Ahimelech: “Are the young men clean from women?” And he answered: “They have been, from yesterday and the day before” (I Sam. XXI, 4). For they could not eat the bread of the Presence, which was like the body of Christ, after rising from the beds of their wives.

We must also consider in passing what he said: “Are the young men clean from women?”—namely, that with regard to the purity of the body of Christ, every sexual act is unclean.

The Law also commands that the high priest take no one but a virgin as his wife (Lev. XXI), and that he not take a widow. If the condition of a virgin and a widow is the same, why is one accepted and the other rejected? A priest’s widowed daughter is commanded to remain in her father’s house and not to know a second marriage.

If a priest’s virgin sister dies, he is commanded to approach her funeral just as he is commanded to approach the funerals of his father and mother. [Note: [Col. 0238D] The printed editions had previously read falsely: “how he himself is to approach his father’s funeral, so the father is to approach hers.” I restored the genuine reading from the Veronensis and the manuscripts of Santa Croce, with the Casanatensis offering partial support. See Lev. XXI, 1 ff. A more decisive argument also supports it, since the difference lies only in the word “approach,” *accedere*, instead of *incedere*.]

But if she is married, she is disregarded as belonging to another. Whoever has taken a wife, and whoever has planted a vineyard as though they were propagating children, is forbidden to go forth to war (Deut. XX). A servant of a wife cannot serve in the army of the Lord.

From the mirrors of the fasting women, as though from the purest bodies of virgins, the basin is cast in the tabernacle. Inside the sanctuary, the cherubim, the mercy seat, the ark of the covenant, the table of the Presence, the lampstand, and the censer are all made of the purest gold. For silver could not be brought into the Holy of Holies.

## 21. The Names of Joshua. The Second Circumcision with a Stone Knife. The Kingdom of the Five Senses

Why do I linger over Moses, when my purpose is to touch briefly and rapidly upon each point as I dictate, and to draw certain outlines for understanding? I shall pass to Jesus son of Nun, who was earlier called Ause [Note: [Col. 0239C] The manuscripts read “Auses,” which is the same name. Jerome also censures this slight difference in the name at the beginning of his *Commentary on Hosea*, and Pseudo-Jerome in the final verse of Psalm LXXVI. The same kind of variation is the one noted above from the same manuscripts, “Anna” instead of “Onam.” Shortly afterward, in the Casanatensis, the word “marriage” is absent.] or, as it is more correctly found in Hebrew, Osee, that is, “savior.”

According to the Epistle of Jude, he saved and led the people of Israel out of Egypt and brought them into the Promised Land. As soon as this Jesus came to the Jordan, the waters of marriage, which had always flowed in the Law, dried up and stood still. The entire people crossed with dry and bare feet and came to Gilgal, where they were circumcised a second time.

If we take this literally, [Note: [Col. 0239D] He consistently presses the interpretation concerning the foreskin suggested above in section 11. In Isaiah LII he says: “For it is not within our power to bring back the foreskin after circumcision,” referring to those in the Book of Maccabees who are said to have made foreskins for themselves. He drew this from Origen, book IV of *On First Principles*, chapter 2, although in chapter 1 of the *Philocalia* he does not deny that many existed who, to conceal the deformity of circumcision, restored the skin by medical procedures. Certainly the method of restoring the foreskin was not unknown to the ancients; the rabbis themselves report that Esau first adopted it in order to depart completely from the religion of Abraham and Jacob, and that the Israelites mentioned here did so in the wilderness under Joshua, so that they had to be circumcised again. The Scriptures and their testimonies also provide the clearest examples. Epiphanius likewise says in *On Measures and Weights*: “By a certain medical art, having the subcutaneous skin of the limbs dissected beneath by means of what is called a scalpel . . . they again make it into a foreskin.” Cornelius Celsus himself teaches the procedure, as do other physicians; the most learned interpreters certainly do not doubt the matter.] it cannot stand at all. For if we had a double foreskin, or if the skin that had been cut away were born again, a second circumcision would rightly have a place.

But now this is signified: Jesus circumcised with the knife of the Gospel the people who had come through the wilderness, and he circumcised them with a stone knife, so that what had previously been prefigured in a few persons through the son of Moses might be fulfilled in all under Jesus.

The foreskins themselves, gathered into one heap [manuscripts: “tumulus,” a mound], buried, and covered with earth, together with the removal of the reproach of Egypt and the name of the place Gilgal, which is interpreted as “revelation,” show that, while the people walked through the wilderness in their foreskin, their eyes had been blinded.

Let us look also at what follows. After the circumcision of the Gospel and the consecration of the twelve stones at the place of revelation, Passover is immediately celebrated: a lamb is sacrificed for them, and they eat the produce of the Holy Land.

Jesus goes out, and the Commander of the army meets him holding a sword, either showing that he was prepared to fight on behalf of the circumcised people or cutting apart the glue of marriage. Likewise, just as Moses had been commanded, this man too is commanded: “Loosen your sandal.” [Note: [Col. 0240D] The old edition and all our manuscripts read: “Loosen the strap of your sandal,” etc.] “For the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III, 5).

Since the army of the Lord was armed in this way with priestly trumpets, as though for the preaching of the Gospel, the world is overthrown under the figure of Jericho.

And, to pass over innumerable matters—for it is not my purpose at present to unfold all the mysteries of the Old Testament—the five kings who previously ruled in the Promised Land and resisted the army of the Gospel are defeated while Jesus fights (Josh. X).

I think the meaning is clear: before the Lord led his people out of Egypt and circumcised them, sight, smell, taste, hearing, and touch reigned, and everything was subject to them as to rulers. Jesus entered the body, where these senses had fled for refuge into a cave and a dark place, and killed them, so that they might be slain by the very means through which they had previously ruled. [Note: [Col. 0240D] We emended the passage on the authority of three manuscripts. It previously read: “a dark place, that is, entering the body itself with either no sense or a thoroughly corrupted sense.” As you see, he now alludes to this and compares the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, and its victory over the senses, with Joshua as conqueror of the five kings. See Joshua X, 20.]

## 22. Moses Signifies the Law. The Number Twenty Is Unlucky. Belphegor among the Hebrews Is Priapus. Jesus Is Not Mourned When He Dies

But now it is time to raise the standard of Jesus’ chastity.

Moses is said to have had a wife. Moses, however, is interpreted as the Law both by our Lord and by the Apostle: “They have Moses and the Prophets” (Luke XVI, 29); and, “From Adam until Moses sin reigned, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. V, 14). No one doubts that in both testimonies Moses signifies the Law.

[Note: [Col. 0240D] Jerome seems to have taken this from Tertullian, who says in *On Monogamy*, chapter 6: “The second Moses”—namely, Jesus son of Nun—“of the second people, who brought our image into the promise of God, in whom the name of the Lord”—namely, Jesus—“was first consecrated, was not a digamist.” Our Jerome goes further, however, making him unmarried and a virgin. This opinion is supported by the interpolated letter of Saint Ignatius to the Philadelphians.]

Therefore, just as we read that Moses—that is, the Law—had a wife, show me that Jesus son of Nun either had a wife or had children, and, if you can show it, I will admit that I am defeated.

He certainly received a very beautiful portion of the land of Judea in its division, and he dies not in the twenty-number, which is always unlucky in Scripture—the number in which Jacob served, Joseph was sold, and Esau, whom he loved, received certain gifts—but in the ten-number, whose praise we have often discussed. He is buried at Thamnath-sare, that is, in the most perfect rule, or in the number of the new covering, so that he might signify the flocks of virgins covered by the Savior’s help on Mount Ephraim—that is, the fruitful mountain—north of Mount Gaash [manuscripts: Gaes], which is interpreted as “commotion.”

“For Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king” (Ps. XLVII, 3), is always set against envy and, through each temptation, says: “But my feet almost slipped” (Ps. LXXII, 2).

When the book that bears Jesus’ name has been completed with his burial, he is again described in the Book of Judges as though alive and rising again; and under ἀνακεφαλαίωσις [recapitulation], his works are proclaimed. We read:

“Jesus sent away the people, and the children of Israel went, each to his inheritance, to possess the land.” And: “The people served the Lord throughout all the days of Jesus,” and so forth.

Immediately afterward it is added: “And Jesus son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died at the age of one hundred and ten years.”

Moses, however, saw only the Promised Land, could not enter it, and died in the land of Moab. “And the Lord buried him in the valley in the land of Moab, opposite the house of Phogor, and no man has known his grave to this day” (Deut. XXXIV, 5–6). [Note: [Col. 0241D] Veronensis and the Septuagint read: “And they buried him in the valley in the land of Moab,” in accordance with the Greek text, καὶ ἔθαψαν αὐτὸν. Yet Jerome seems to cite this passage from the Hebrew, although he heightens its ambiguous meaning—“and he buried him in the valley,” adding the word “Lord,” which neither the Vulgate nor Jerome’s own translation has. See Letters 39, section 3, and 60, section 6.]

Let us compare the burials of the two. Moses dies in the land of Moab; Jesus in the land of Judea. The former is buried in a valley opposite the house of Phogor, which means “shame” (for in the Hebrew language Phogor properly means Priapus); the latter on Mount Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.

There is always a more exalted meaning in the simple words of divine Scripture. Since among the Jews glory lay in pregnancies and childbirth, and the barren woman who had no seed in Israel was accursed, and blessed was the one whose seed was in Zion and whose household was in Jerusalem, and since the greatest blessing was expressed in the words, “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children like olive shoots around your table” (Ps. CXXVII, 3), for this reason his tomb is described as being in a valley opposite the house of the idol that is devoted specifically to lust.

But we who serve under the leadership of Jesus do not know to this day where Moses was buried. We despise Phogor [alternative: Phegor] and all his shame, knowing that those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
