The Lord also said before the Flood: “My spirit shall not remain in these people, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI, 3).

Therefore, when Moses died, the people of Israel mourned him; but Jesus, as one who would live again, was not mourned. Marriage ends in death; virginity begins to be crowned after death.

## 23. Jephthah Is Accused of a Rash Vow. Many Priests Were Married. The Dress of the Levites. The Error of the Encratites

Samson too is brought forward, but the writer does not consider that the Lord’s Nazirite, once shorn by a woman, although he bears the type of the Savior in that he loved the Church from the Gentiles as a prostitute, and although he killed many more of the enemy in his death than during his life, nevertheless provides no example of marital chastity.

And certainly he is the one who, according to Jacob’s prophecy (Gen. XLIX), when carried along with the speed of a swift horse, was struck by a serpent and fell backward.

Why he has included Deborah and Barak, and the wife of Heber [manuscripts: Chaber] the Kenite, I entirely fail to understand. It is one thing to list the leaders of wars and weave together the sequence of history; it is another to signify certain figures of marriage, which are entirely absent from these people.

Moreover, the fact that he prefers Jephthah’s fidelity to the tears of his virgin daughter works in our favor. For we too praise not so much the virgins of the world as those who are virgins for Christ’s sake.

And by many of the Hebrews the father of the rash vow is censured, the man who said: “If you truly deliver the children of Ammon into my hands, then whoever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon shall belong to the Lord, and I will offer him as a burnt offering” (Judg. XI, 30–31). [Note: [Col. 0241D] Casanatensis, together with Veronensis, reads “because he said”; shortly afterward: “but whoever comes out,” etc.]

“If a dog,” they say, “or a donkey had come out to meet him, what would he have done?” From this they wish it to have happened by God’s providence that the man who had vowed thoughtlessly should learn the error of his vows through the death of his daughter.

But if Samuel, brought up in the tabernacle, took a wife, what bearing does this have on the prejudice against virginity? As though even today very many priests did not have marriages, and the Apostle did not describe a bishop as the husband of one wife, having children with complete chastity (I Tim. III).

At the same time, it must be understood that Samuel was a Levite, [Note: [Col. 0241D] Those ancient writers who oppose Jerome’s assertion that Samuel was excluded from the priesthood seem to be understood in this sense: they take “Levite” to refer to the priestly order or class, so to speak. Thus our Zeno says in treatise 16, section 14: “Samuel, that distinguished priest,” etc. But Josephus, an ancient Christian author, in *Hypomnesticon*, chapter 7, asks: “Who were Samuel’s ancestors from the priestly line?” and gives the following judgment: the first was Korah, who led a rebellion in Moses’ time; the second, his son Elkanah; the third, Exaud; the fourth, Eliud; the fifth, Tevaam; the sixth, Elkanah; the seventh, Samuel, from whom were born two sons who were judged unworthy of their ancestral succession. We have copied out the passage so that you may safely compare it with the genealogy proposed by Jerome.] not a priest, not a high priest.

Hence his mother made him an ephod of linen, that is, a linen shoulder garment, which is properly the dress of Levites and of the lower order (I Sam. II). Hence in the Psalms he is not named among the priests but among those who call upon the name of the Lord: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Ps. XCVIII, 6). [Note: [Col. 0242D] I have removed the word “says,” which is absent from the manuscripts. Shortly before, Casanatensis reads “is not counted” instead of “is not named.”]

Levi fathered Kohath; Kohath fathered Amminadab; Amminadab fathered Korah; Korah fathered Assir; Assir fathered Elkanah; Elkanah fathered Sub; Sub fathered Tohu; Tohu fathered Elihu; Elihu fathered Jeroham; Jeroham fathered Elkanah; Elkanah fathered Samuel.

There is no doubt that priests were descended from the line of Aaron, Eleazar, and Phinehas. Since they too had wives, they would rightly be brought forward against us if, led astray by the error of the Encratites, we argued that marriages must be rejected.

But our High Priest, according to the order of Melchizedek, was “without father, without mother, ἀγενεαλόγητος [without genealogy],” that is, without marriage.

And indeed Samuel reaps great fruits from his children: because he himself pleased God, he begot children who would displease the Lord.

But if he brings forward Boaz and Ruth to prove digamy, let him know that, because of her typological representation of the Church, even Rahab the prostitute is listed in the genealogy of the Lord in the Gospel.

## 24. Why David Was a Man of Blood. When Solomon Built the Temple

As for his boast that David bought a wife with two hundred foreskins, he should know that David had many others as well; that he later took back Michal, the daughter of Saul, whom her father had given to another; and that, already an old man, he was warmed by the embraces of the young Shunammite woman.

I do not say this because I dare to detract anything from holy men, but because it is one thing to live under the Law and another to live under the Gospel.

David killed Uriah the Hittite [“Gittite,” according to the Septuagint] and became an adulterer with Bathsheba. And because he was a man of blood, he was forbidden to build the Temple of the Lord—not, as most think, on account of his wars, but on account of his homicide. [Note: [Col. 0243D] This is more or less the opinion of the Hebrews: the blood that made David unfit to build the Temple of the Lord was the blood of the innocent Uriah, an opinion Jerome also follows. Ancient and modern writers, however, recognize the very reason he rejects, namely, David’s wars. See Josephus, *Antiquities* VII, 11; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* IX, 30; and indeed Scripture itself, I Chronicles XVII, 4; XXVIII, 3; and explicitly XXII, 8: “You have shed much blood and waged many wars,” spoken to David. The chronology also supports this, since David had conceived the plan of building the Temple before Uriah’s murder.]

But if we cause one of the least to stumble, if we say to a brother, “Raca,” and fail to see correctly, it is better that a millstone be fastened around our neck and that we be liable to gehenna; and adultery will be counted against us for a mere look.

He proceeds to Solomon, through whom Wisdom herself sang, and although he calls him a man devoted to wives and lingers over his praises, I wonder why he does not add the words from the Song of Songs: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and young women without number” (Song VI, 7). Nor does he add the passage from the Third Book of Kings, that he had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, as well as innumerable others (III Kings XI, 3).

These were the women who turned his heart away from the Lord. Yet before he had many wives and stumbled through the vices of the flesh, at the beginning of his reign and in his youth he built the Temple for the Lord. For each person is judged not by future things but by present ones.

But if Solomon’s examples please him, he will no longer be merely a digamist or trigamist. Unless he has seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, he will not be able to fulfill Solomon’s type and merit.

I beg you, reader—and I remind you of this very often—to understand that I say these things out of necessity, not to detract from those who came before us under the Law, but because they served their own times and conditions and fulfilled that saying of the Lord: “Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. I, 23), and, what is greater, provided types of things to come.

But for us, to whom it is said, “The time has been shortened,” it remains that those who have wives should live as though they had none, and that virginity should be consecrated by the virgin Savior.

### 25. The Rule of the Scriptures. He proves the history of Susanna.

As I have shown, it is clear how foolishly he has placed Elijah and Elisha in his catalogue of married men. For if John the Baptist came in the spirit and power of Elijah, and John was a virgin, then surely he came not only in Elijah’s spirit but also in the chastity of his body.

As for what may be recalled concerning Hezekiah—although in his customary stupidity he did not see this—namely, that after recovering his life and having his years prolonged by fifteen years he said, “From now on I shall beget children,” let him know that this is not found in the Hebrew volumes. Instead of this, they read: “A father shall make your truth known to his children.” [Note: The Casanatensis reads, “He would make your will known.”]

Nor is it surprising that Huldah, the wife of Shallum, a prophetess, was consulted [another reading: “comforted”] by Josiah, king of Judah, when the captivity was already near and the Lord’s anger was dripping upon Jerusalem. For this is the rule of the Scriptures: when holy men fail, women are praised in the reproaches directed against men.

It is superfluous to speak of Daniel, since the Hebrews still maintain that both he and the three youths were eunuchs, on the basis of that sentence of God which Isaiah speaks to Hezekiah: “And of the sons who shall be born from you, they will take them and make them eunuchs in the house of the king” (4 Kings 20:18).

Again, in Daniel we read: “And the king said to Ashpenaz, chief of the eunuchs, that he should bring in from the sons of the captivity of Israel, and from the royal offspring, and from the *phorthommim* [another reading: *phortemmim*] youths, in whom there was no blemish, handsome in appearance, and understanding wisdom” (Dan. 1:2–3). [Note: The same reading as the old edition: “and from the sons of tyrants”; another reading: “to the boys.” Two manuscripts have *Asphanezech* instead of *Asphanez* above.]

They argue that, if Daniel and the three youths were chosen from the royal offspring, and Scripture had foretold that eunuchs would come from the royal offspring, these must be the ones who were made eunuchs. [Note: Mark this passage.]

But if he should also object that Ezekiel says (chapter 14) that Noah, Daniel, and Job, in a sinful land, would not be able to rescue sons and daughters, the answer must be that this was said according to a hypothesis. For at that time Noah and Job were not living, as we know that they had lived many centuries earlier. The meaning is: “If such and such men were in a sinful land, they would not be able to rescue their sons and daughters,” because a father’s righteousness will not rescue his son, nor will another person’s sin be charged to someone else. “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:4).

This too must be said: according to the history of his book, Daniel was captured together with King Jehoiakim at the time when Ezekiel also was led into captivity. How, then, could he have had sons, when he was still a boy? After completing three years, he was brought into the king’s service.

And lest anyone suppose that Ezekiel was already speaking of Daniel as a grown man rather than as a boy, he says: “And it came to pass in the sixth year”—that is, of King Jehoiakim—“in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month” (Ezek. 8:1); and, “I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were sitting before me” (Ezek. 14:14). On that same day it was said to him: “If Noah, Daniel, and Job were present …”

Daniel, therefore, was still a boy, yet known to the people either because of his interpretation of the king’s dreams or because of the deliverance of Susanna and the execution of the elders. [Note: The Casanatensis, together with the Veronensis, reads: “because of the history and occasion of Susanna,” etc.] It is clearly established that, at the time when these things were said concerning Noah, Daniel, and Job, Daniel was still a boy and could not have had sons and daughters whom his righteousness might rescue.

Thus far concerning the Law.

### 26. The Gospel did not exist before Christ’s cross. Jewish women ministered to the teachers’ needs. John the Evangelist was a virgin; his age is commended; the time of his death; his privileges.

Let us come to the Gospel. He sets before us Zechariah and Elizabeth, Peter and his mother-in-law, and in his customary senselessness does not understand that these too ought to have been counted among those who served the Law. For the Gospel did not exist before Christ’s cross; it was consecrated by his passion and blood.

According to this principle, Peter and the other Apostles—although for the moment I grant him the point—did have wives, but they had taken them at the time when they did not know the Gospel. Later, when they were called to the apostolate, they abandoned the marital office. For when Peter, speaking on behalf of the Apostles, says to the Lord, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you,” the Lord answered him: “Amen, I say to you, there is no one who has left house, or parents, or brothers, or wife, or children for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this age, and in the age to come eternal life” (Matt. 19:27). [Note: Three manuscripts read: “Behold, we have left all our possessions and followed you”; they likewise do not recognize the word “Apostle” a little below.]

But if he should raise this objection to prove that all the Apostles had wives—“Do we not have the authority to lead about women or wives, as do the other Apostles, and Cephas, and the brothers of the Lord?”—since among the Greeks *γυνή* (*gynē*) signifies both “woman” and “wife,” let him join to it what is found in the Greek manuscripts: “Do we not have the authority to lead about sister-women, or wives?” [Note: Tertullian, *On Monogamy*: among the Greeks, “women” and “wives” are designated by a common word.]

From this it is evident that he was speaking of other holy women who, according to Jewish custom, ministered to the teachers from their own resources, just as we read that this was also done for the Lord himself. For the order of the words indicates this: “Do we not have the authority to eat and drink, or to lead about believing sisters, women?” (1 Cor. 9:4–5). Since eating and drinking, and the provision of expenses, are mentioned first, and sister-women are introduced afterward, it is clear that wives are not meant, but those women who, as we have said, ministered from their own resources. The same is written in the Old Law concerning the Shunammite woman, who was accustomed to receive Elisha and set before him a table, bread, a lampstand, and the rest. [Note: The same manuscripts introduce the sentence in this form.]

Or, certainly, if we take *γυναῖκας* (*gynaikas*) to mean “wives,” rather than “women,” the addition “believing sisters” excludes wives and shows that they were sisters in spirit, not spouses. [Note: The Casanatensis reads, “that they were spouses in the Spirit.”]

Nevertheless, apart from the Apostle Peter, it is not explicitly related of the other Apostles that they had wives. When something is written of one and nothing is said of the others, we should understand that those of whom Scripture indicates nothing of the kind were without wives.

Yet let the man who objected to us with Zechariah and Elizabeth, Peter and his mother-in-law, know that John was born from Zechariah and Elizabeth: that is, from marriage came a virgin; from the Law came the Gospel; from marriage came chastity, so that the virgin Lord might be both announced and baptized by a virgin prophet.

We may say of Peter that he had a mother-in-law at the time when he believed, but no longer had a wife, although in the *Periods* it is read that both his wife and his daughter were mentioned. [Note: It is read in the *Periods*. Clement is credited with the *Periods* above, in chapter 1 of the *Epistle to the Galatians*, where he says of Peter: “Or, as Clement relates in his *Periods*, he was bald on his head.” Martianaeus: Peter’s wife is indeed mentioned in books 7 and 9 of the *Recognitions*, but his daughter is not mentioned at all. We therefore suspect that the holy Doctor had before him a copy differing from the edition. In this passage, it seems that he implies that Peter dismissed his wife after he believed. He certainly states the same in Epistle 118, no. 4, to Julian, where he says that Peter left her behind together with the boat and the nets.]

But our entire dispute now concerns the canon. Since he appealed to the Apostles on the ground that the leaders of our discipline and guides of Christian doctrine were not virgins, let us for the moment grant that they were not virgins—for this cannot be proved concerning anyone except Peter. Let him know that these are the Apostles of whom Isaiah prophesies: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we would have been as Sodom, and we would have become like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:9).

Since they were Jews, they could not possess in the Gospel the virginity which they had lost in Judaism. Yet John, one of the disciples, who is reported to have been the youngest among the Apostles and whom faith in Christ had found a virgin, remained a virgin. For this reason he is loved more by the Lord and reclines upon Jesus’ breast.

Peter, who had had a wife, does not dare to ask a question; he asks John to ask it. After the resurrection, when Mary Magdalene announced that the Lord had risen, both ran to the tomb, but John arrived first. When they were in the boat fishing on the lake of Gennesaret, Jesus stood on the shore, and the Apostles did not know whom they were seeing. The virgin alone recognizes the Virgin and says to Peter, “It is the Lord.”

Again, after hearing the statement that Peter would be girded by another and led where he did not wish to go, and after the passion of the cross had been prophesied for him, Peter said, “Lord, what about this man?” Unwilling to leave John, with whom he had always been closely united, the Lord said to him: “What is it to you if I want him to remain so?” (John 21:22). [Note: Instead of *if I want him to remain so*, the old edition reads *if I want him to be so*, and below, with the best manuscripts, *he recognizes a virgin* rather than *he acknowledges a virgin*. The words “What is it to you, if …” represent a similar error of ancient copyists, which entered the Gospel text as “I want him to remain so.” In three manuscripts it is read in this form: “What is it to you? I want him to be so,” instead of the genuine reading, “If I want him to be so.” Martianaeus: All our manuscripts prefer this reading, and the old edition also agrees: “If I want him to be, what is it to you?” Nevertheless, we do not deny that long ago, through the error of copyists, “I want him to remain so” came to stand in John’s Gospel; Martianaeus also found this in several Hieronymian manuscripts. See our notes on that Gospel passage.]

Hence the saying went out among the brothers that this disciple would not die. From this it is shown that virginity does not die, nor does it wash away the stains of marriage with the blood of martyrdom; rather, it remains with Christ, and his falling asleep is a passing-over, not death.

But if he should insist that John was not a virgin, although we have said that virginity was the cause of the special love shown him, let him explain why, if John was not a virgin, he was loved more than the other Apostles.

“But,” you say, “the Church is founded upon Peter.” Although the same thing is stated elsewhere concerning all the Apostles, and although all receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the strength of the Church is established equally upon them all, nevertheless one among the twelve is chosen for this reason: that, once a head has been appointed, the occasion for schism might be removed. [Note: See Jerome, who prefers the merit of the Apostle John because he remained a virgin, although he does not deny that Peter, not John, was constituted head of the Church by the Lord. Indeed, in these words he expressly declares that the other Apostles were equal to Peter in both honor and power, because all alike received from Christ the authority to preach, bind, and loose; nevertheless, one head, Peter, stood above them all. Saint Leo the Great calls this distinction of power in Epistle 12, no. 14: “Among the most blessed Apostles, although there was a certain distinction of power amid the likeness of honor, and although their election was equal, nevertheless one was given precedence over the others.” This is mentioned in passing for the benefit of those who quibble over this passage of Jerome. See also Pope Gelasius, *Treatise* 4, no. 5, and Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, book 21, no. 26, concerning John’s perpetual virginity.]

But why was John, the virgin, not chosen? Consideration was given to age, because Peter was older, lest a youth, almost still a boy, should be preferred to men of advanced age. The good teacher, who ought to have removed every occasion for quarrelling among the disciples and who had said to them, “My peace I give you, my peace I leave you” (John 14:27), and, “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be the least of all” (Matt. 20:26), might otherwise have seemed to provide a cause for envy by preferring to them the young man whom he loved.

That John was then a boy is shown most clearly by the histories of the Church: he lived until the reign of Trajan, that is, he fell asleep sixty-eight years after the Lord’s passion. We also briefly touched upon this in our book *On Illustrious Men*. [Note: In the book *On Illustrious Men*. From this passage we establish most clearly that the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* was written and published before Jerome wrote against Jovinian. Martianaeus.]

Peter is an Apostle; John is an Apostle, a married man, and a virgin; but Peter is an Apostle only. John is both Apostle and Evangelist and Prophet.

He is an Apostle because he wrote to the Churches as a teacher; an Evangelist because he composed the book of the Gospel, something which, apart from Matthew, the other Apostles of the Twelve did not do. He is a Prophet because, on the island of Patmos, to which he had been banished by the ruler Domitian on account of the Lord’s martyrdom, he saw the Apocalypse containing innumerable mysteries of future events.

Tertullian relates that, when John was sent at Rome into a vessel of boiling oil, he came out purer and more vigorous than he had entered. [Note: Instead of “at Rome,” several manuscripts read “sent by Nero.” Martianaeus: All the manuscripts and the old edition read, “when he was sent by Nero,” etc. Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 36: “The Apostle John, after being plunged into boiling oil and suffering no harm, is banished to an island.”]

His Gospel itself also differs greatly from the others. Matthew begins to write as about a man: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.” Luke begins with the priesthood of Zechariah. Mark begins with the prophecy of the prophet Malachi and Isaiah. [Note: We have removed here the word “prophet,” which the manuscripts do not recognize.]

The first has the face of a man because of the genealogy; the second, the face of a calf because of the priesthood; the third, the face of a lion because of the voice of one crying in the wilderness: “Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight” (Isa. 40:3; Luke 3:4).

But our John, like an eagle, flies toward the heights and reaches the Father himself, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God,” and so forth.

Virginity explained what marriage could not know. To sum up much in a brief statement and to show the privilege belonging to John—or rather, to virginity in John—the virgin mother is commended by the virgin Lord to the virgin disciple.

### 27. The loss of the mother’s virginity compensated by the virginity of her children.

Yet we labor in vain. Our adversary brings against us the Apostolic statement and says: “Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was made a transgressor. Yet she will be saved through the bearing of children, if they remain in faith, love, and sanctification with sobriety” (1 Tim. 2:13–15).

Let us consider why and from where the Apostle arrived at this statement: “I therefore wish men to pray in every place, lifting up holy hands without anger and disputation” (ibid. 8). Consequently, he gives women rules for their way of life and says: “Likewise, women in becoming apparel, with modesty and chastity, adorning themselves not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but, as is fitting for women who profess piety through good works. Let a woman learn in silence with complete submission. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but to be silent” (ibid. 9 ff.).

And lest the woman’s condition should seem harsh, reducing her to servitude under her husband, he recalls the ancient Law and returns to the original example: Adam was made first, then the woman from his rib; Adam could not be deceived by the devil, but Eve could; and after the offense against God she was immediately subjected to the man, with her turning toward her husband.

He also recalls that the ancient error of the woman who had once been joined in marriage and reduced to Eve’s condition would be wiped away by the begetting of children—but only if she educated those children in faith and love of Christ, and in sanctification and chastity. For it is not “sobriety,” as it is wrongly found in the Latin books, that should be read, but “chastity,” that is, *σωφροσύνη* (*sōphrosynē*). [Note: Our manuscripts have neither the word “according to” nor does the Vulgate translator himself have it.]

See, then, how by this testimony itself you are defeated, and how you are compelled to understand as concerning virginity what you thought concerned marriage. For if a woman is saved through the bearing of children, and the number of children is the salvation of mothers, why did he add, “if they remain in love and sanctification with chastity”? [Note: Three manuscripts read, “if the children remain in faith and love,” etc. The Greek has *ἐν πίστει* (“in faith”), a reading also found in some other editions of the text.]

The woman, then, will be saved if she has borne children who will remain virgins; if she acquires in her children what she herself lost, and compensates for the injury to the root and its decay with blossom and fruit.

### 28. The vices of women. The devil and his insatiable daughters. What does love of a woman bring with it?

Earlier, in passing, when our adversary had set before us Solomon, who had many wives and had built the Temple of God, I answered briefly, intending to hasten through the remaining questions. Now, lest he shout that we have rashly attacked this and other patriarchs, prophets, and holy men in the Law, let us set forth the view on marriage held by this very man who had many wives and concubines. For no one can know better what a wife or a woman is than one who suffered it.

He therefore speaks in Proverbs: “A foolish and bold woman is destitute of bread” (Prov. 9:13). Whose bread? Surely, the bread that came down from heaven. Immediately he adds: “The earth-born perish with her and fall into the depth of hell.”

Who are the earth-born who perish with her? Surely those who follow the first Adam, who is from the earth, and not the second, who is from heaven.

Again, in another place: “As a worm in wood, so a wicked wife destroys her husband” (Prov. 25:20). But if you insist that this was said about bad wives, I shall answer you briefly: What necessity compels me to run the risk of not knowing whether the woman I take will be good or bad? “It is better,” he says, “to dwell in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and angry wife” (Prov. 21:9). He who has taken a wife knows how rare it is to find one without these vices.

Hence Varius Geminus, a lofty orator, aptly said: “He who does not quarrel is unmarried.” [Note: Varius Geminus. There is profound silence about this eminent orator Varius Geminus among historical authors. Therefore I cannot know who Varius Geminus was, nor do I wish, with rash speech, to invent some unknown orator who might perhaps one day become famous among grammarians and diviners. There was, moreover, another Varius, a tragic poet and associate of Virgil and Horace, as well as another poet of this name mentioned by Virgil. See Horace, *Satires* 1.5 and elsewhere. Martianaeus. Martianaeus: Seneca mentions Varius Geminus, the eminent orator, so often in the *Suasoriae* and *Controversiae* that I am astonished that Martianaeus asserts that there is profound silence about him among authors and historians. Gravius, moreover, cites a witty epigram to the same effect: “Ho, traveler, a marvel here: husband and wife do not quarrel.”]

“It is better to dwell in a corner of the roof than with a contentious wife in a common house” (Prov. 25:24). If the common house of husband and wife raises the wife to arrogance and causes her to insult her husband, how much more so if the wife is richer and the husband remains in her house! She begins not to be a wife but a mistress; and if she has offended her husband, he must leave.

“Drippings drive a man from his house on a winter day; likewise a contentious woman drives him from his own house” (Prov. 27:15). By continual quarrels and daily chatter she makes his house drip through, and drives him from his dwelling—that is, from the Church. Hence the same Solomon also commands above: “My son, do not overflow.” And the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “Therefore we ought to pay greater attention to the things that are spoken, lest perhaps we overflow” (Heb. 2:1). [Note: The manuscripts seem to read more correctly *and to drip through*, and shortly afterward *you may drip through*, and *let us drip through*, instead of *overflow*, etc.]

Who could be silent about what is written under an enigma? “The leech had three daughters, dearly beloved, but these were not satisfied; and the fourth cannot say, ‘It is enough’: hell, and the love of a woman, and earth that is not satisfied with water, and fire do not say, ‘It is enough’” (Prov. 30:16). [Note: The same manuscripts read, “They will not say, ‘It is enough,’” in accordance with the Greek *οὐ μὴ εἴπωσιν*; then, with the old edition, they place the particle *si* (“if”) before *sanguisuga* (“leech”).]

The leech is the devil. The devil’s daughters are the dearly beloved ones who cannot be satisfied with the blood of the slain: hell, the love of a woman, dry earth, and blazing fire (Prov. 30:16).

This is not said about a prostitute or an adulteress; rather, the love of a woman in general is accused. It is always insatiable: when extinguished, it is rekindled; after abundance, it is again needy; it makes a manly mind effeminate; and, apart from the passion it endures, it allows nothing else to be considered.

We read something similar in the following parable: “By three things the earth is moved, and the fourth it cannot bear” [the manuscripts read “cannot be borne]: “if a servant reigns; if a fool is filled with bread; if a hateful wife has a good husband; and if a slave-girl drives out her mistress” (Prov. 30:21 ff.). Here too a wife is placed among things of great evil.

If you answer, “But it is a hateful wife,” I shall say to you what I said above. “Yet this risk falling upon me is grievous.” [Note: Instead of “yet this risk falling upon me,” our manuscripts, perhaps having been corrected by a later hand, read “but this risk threatens to occur.” Terence, *Andria*: “But that danger befalling a daughter is grievous.”]

For he who takes a wife is uncertain whether he is taking a hateful or a lovable one. If he takes a hateful one, she cannot be endured. If a lovable one, her love is compared with hell, with dry earth, and with fire.

### 29. The wisdom of the flesh and of the spirit. We were created good by God but fell through our own fault.

Let us come to Ecclesiastes, setting forth a few testimonies from it as well:

“For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven: a time to give birth and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to uproot what has been planted” (Eccles. 3:1 ff.).

We gave birth in the Law with Moses; let us die in the Gospel with Christ. We planted in marriage; let us uproot through chastity what was planted. “A time to embrace and a time to be far from embracing; a time to love and a time to hate; a time for war and a time for peace.”

At the same time he warns us not to prefer the Law to the Gospel, nor to think the purity of virginity equal to marriage. “The end of a speech is better,” he says, “than its beginning” (Eccles. 7:9). Immediately he adds: “Do not say, ‘Why were the former days better than these?’ For you have not asked this wisely” (ibid. 11). He then gives the reason why the later days are better than the former: “Wisdom,” he says, “is good together with an inheritance.”

In the Law, wisdom of the flesh was followed by death, which slew; in the Gospel, wisdom of the spirit is awaited by an eternal inheritance.

“Behold, this I have found,” says Ecclesiastes: “I found one man among a thousand, but I did not find a woman among all these. Yet I found this: that God made man upright, but they themselves sought out wicked thoughts” (Eccles. 7:29). He says that he found an upright man. Consider the force of the word. “Man” includes both male and female; yet he says, “I did not find a woman among all these.”

Let us read the beginning of Genesis, and we shall find that Adam—that is, “man”—is the name given both to male and female. Since, therefore, we were created good and upright by God, we ourselves, through our own fault, fell into worse things. What had been upright in us in paradise was corrupted when we went out from paradise.

But if you object that, before they sinned, the sexes of male and female had already been divided, and that they could have been joined without sin, the answer is: What would have happened is uncertain. We cannot know God’s judgments or prejudge his decision according to our own choice.

What has happened is clear: those who remained virgins in paradise were joined after they had been expelled from paradise. Or what harm would there have been if paradise had received marriage, and if there had been no distinction between a married woman and a virgin, for them to have been joined even in paradise? They are expelled from paradise; and what they did not do there, they do on earth, so that from the beginning of the human condition paradise consecrated virginity, and earth consecrated marriage.

“At all times let your garments be white” (Eccles. 9:8). The perpetual whiteness of garments is the purity of virginity. “In the morning we sowed our seed; let us not cease toward evening.” We who served marriage in the Law, let us serve virginity in the Gospel.

### 30. The Song of Songs does not signify carnal love

I proceed to the Song of Songs, and I shall show that what our opponent thinks is entirely in favor of marriage contains the mysteries of virginity. Let us hear what the bride says before her bridegroom comes to earth, suffers, penetrates the underworld, and rises again:

> We shall make likenesses of gold for you, with ornaments of silver, until the king is on his couch (Song 1:10–11).

Before the Lord rose and the Gospel shone forth, the bride did not possess gold, but only likenesses of gold. The silver, however, which she promises to have at the wedding, she possessed in varied and distinguished forms among widows, continent women, and married women.

Then the bridegroom replies to the bride and teaches her that the shadow of the old Law has passed away and that the truth of the Gospel has come:

> Rise, come, my nearest one, [Col. 0252A] my bride, for behold, winter has passed; the rain has gone away (Song 2:10).

**[Note: Again the same manuscripts read, “my beautiful one, my dove,” etc., and do so consistently below as well; this accords with the Greek *καλή μου*, from which they likewise repeat twice the word “has gone away,” *ἀπῆλθεν, ἐπορεύθη*.]**

This concerns the Old Testament. Again, concerning the Gospel and virginity:

> Flowers have appeared on the earth; the time of pruning has come (ibid., 12).

Does this not seem to say the same thing as the Apostle:

> It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none (1 Cor. 7:29)?

And more clearly concerning the proclamation of chastity:

> The voice of the turtledove, he says, has been heard in our land (Song 2:12).

The turtledove, a most chaste bird, always dwelling in high places, is a type of the Savior. Let us read the natural historians [see Pliny, Book X, chapter 34], and we shall find that this is the nature of the turtledove: if it loses its mate, it does not join itself to another. Thus we shall understand that remarriage is rejected even by mute birds.

**[Note: The editions up to this point incorrectly read *multis* (“many”) instead of *mutis* (“mute”), a correction I had previously made conjecturally and now confirm by the authority of the Veronese manuscript; I also see that Gravius approves it.]**

Immediately the turtledove says to the turtledove:

> The fig tree has put forth its green figs (Song 2:13),

that is, the precepts of the old Law have fallen away, and the flourishing vines of the Gospel have given forth their fragrance. Hence the Apostle also says:

> We are the good fragrance of Christ (2 Cor. 2:15).

[Col. 0252C]

> Rise, come, my nearest one, my bride, and come. You are my dove in the cleft of the rock, beside the outer wall; show me your face and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful (Song 2:13–14).

When you covered your face with Moses, and the veil belonged to the Law, I neither saw your face nor deigned to hear your voice, when it said:

> Even if you multiply your prayers [perhaps: “your prayer”], I shall not hear you even then (Jer. 11:11).

But now, with unveiled face, contemplate my glory, and hide yourself beside the outer wall of the firmest rock.

Hearing this, the bride reveals the mysteries of chastity:

> My kinsman is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies (Song 2:16),

that is, among the most radiant choirs of virgins.

Do you wish to know what kind of throne our true Solomon, the peacemaker, has, and what kind of guards he possesses? Behold, he says:

> The bed of Solomon: sixty mighty men surround it, from the mighty men of Israel, all holding swords and trained for war; each man’s sword is at his thigh (Song 3:7–8).

**[Note: The manuscripts read: “all holding swords, and men trained for war; a sword at each man’s thigh,” in accordance with the Septuagint. Gravius insists that *vir* (“man”) should be read throughout and argues that this is a Hebraism.]**

Those who surround Solomon have a sword at their thigh, like that judge Ehud, **ἀμφοτεροδέξιος**—that is, ambidextrous—who killed the exceedingly fat and wholly flesh-devoted enemy, cutting off every pleasure (Judg. 3).

**[Note: The same manuscripts read: “I shall go, he says, for myself to the mountain,” and so again in accordance with the Greek *πορεύσομαι ἐμαυτῷ*; shortly afterward they likewise read “my nearest one” instead of “my beloved,” corresponding to *πλησίον μου*.]**

> I shall go, he says, to the mountain of myrrh (Song 4:6),

namely, to those who have put their bodies to death; and to the hill of Lebanon, that is, to the most pure flocks of virgins. And I shall speak to my bride:

> You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you (ibid., 7).

Hence the Apostle also says:

> That he might present the holy Church to himself, not having spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27).

> Come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon. You shall come and pass through: from the beginning of faith, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards (Song 4:8).

Lebanon, **λευκασμός**, is interpreted as “whiteness.” Come, therefore, most radiant bride, [Col. 0253B] of whom it is elsewhere said:

> Who is this who comes up whitened?

And pass through the way of this world: from the beginning of faith, and from Sanir, which is interpreted as “the tooth of a lamp,” in accordance with what we read in the Psalm:

> Your word, Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths (Ps. 118:105).

And from Hermon, that is, “consecration.” Flee the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards, which cannot change their markings. Flee, he says, the dens of lions; flee the pride of demons, so that, after you have been consecrated to me, I may say to you:

> You have wounded my heart, my sister-bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes, with one ornament of your neck (Song 4:9).

**[Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “our heart” instead of “my heart,” adhering consistently to the Greek version, *ἐκαρδίωσας ἡμᾶς*.]**

What he says means this: I do not reject marriage; you have a left eye, which I gave you because of those who cannot see what is straight. But the right eye of virginity pleases me more; if it is blinded, the whole body is in darkness.

And lest we think that he signifies carnal love and bodily marriage, he immediately excludes this meaning and says:

> You have wounded my heart, my sister-bride.

Where the name “sister” occurs, every suspicion of shameful love is excluded.

> How beautiful are your breasts, beyond wine (Song 4:10),

of which he had also said above:

> My kinsman is mine, and I am his; he shall dwell among my breasts (Song 1:16),

in the ruling faculty of the heart, **ἡγεμονικόν**, where the word of God has its dwelling.

> How beautiful are your breasts, beyond wine.

What is this wine that makes the bride’s most beautiful breasts beautiful and makes them fruitful with the milk of chastity? Surely it is the wine of which the bridegroom speaks afterward:

> I drank my wine with my milk. Eat, my nearest ones, and drink; drink deeply, brothers (Song 5:1).

Hence the Apostles were said to be full of new wine:

> They are full of new wine, he says (Acts 2),

not old wine, because new wine is put into new wineskins (Matt. 9); and they did not walk in the oldness of the letter, but in the newness of the Spirit (Rom. 7).

This is the wine which, when it has intoxicated young men and girls, immediately makes them thirst for virginity; they belch forth in the excess of chastity. Thus that prophecy of Zechariah is fulfilled—at least according to the Hebrew Truth, where he prophesies concerning the virgins of the Church:

> Its streets shall be filled with boys and girls playing. For what is its good, and what is its beautiful thing, except the grain of the chosen and the wine that makes virgins sprout? (Zech. 8:5)

These are the virgins of whom it is written in the forty-fourth Psalm:

> Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you in joy and exultation. They shall be brought into the temple of the king.

### 31. “A garden enclosed”

It follows:

> A garden enclosed is my sister-bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain (Song 4:12).

What is closed and sealed resembles the Mother of the Lord, both mother and virgin. Hence, in the new tomb of the Savior, which had been hewn from the hardest [or: purest] rock, no one was placed either before or afterward. Yet this perpetual virgin is the mother of many virgins.

For it follows:

> Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruit of orchard trees (Song 4:13).

In the pomegranates and fruits, the harmony of all virtues in virginity is signified.

**[Note: The Casanatensis manuscript, together with the old edition, reads “conception.”]**

> My kinsman is white and red: white in virginity, red in martyrdom.

And because he is red and white, it is immediately added:

> His throat is sweetness [another reading: “his taste”], and he is altogether desirable (Song 5:10).

The virgin bridegroom, praised by the virgin bride, in turn praises the virgin bride and says to her:

> How beautiful your steps are in sandals, daughter of Aminadab,

which is interpreted as “of the people who offer themselves willingly” (Song 7:1).

[Col. 0254C]

For virginity is voluntary; therefore the Church’s steps are praised together in the beauty of chastity.

It is not appropriate at this time, in the manner of a commentary, to unfold all the mysteries of virginity in the Song of Songs, since I do not doubt that even these remarks will make a fastidious reader wrinkle his nose.

### 32. Isaiah’s prophecy of the Virgin

Let Isaiah speak the mystery of our hope and faith:

> Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel (Isa. 7:14).

I know that the Jews are accustomed to object that in Hebrew the word **ALMA []** does not mean “virgin,” but “young woman.” And indeed, a virgin is properly called **BETHULA []**, whereas a young woman or girl is not called **ALMA**, but **NAARA []**.

What, then, does **ALMA** signify? A hidden virgin—that is, not merely a virgin, but a virgin with emphasis; for not every virgin is hidden or removed from the accidental sight of human beings.

Finally, Rebecca too, in Genesis, because of her extraordinary chastity and because of the type of the Church that she signified in her virginity, is written **ALMA**, not **BETHULA**, as can be made clear from the words of Abraham’s servant, which he speaks in Mesopotamia:

**[Note: The printed editions incorrectly read “and he says” instead of “and I said,” which begins the scriptural passage.]**

> And I said, Lord, God of my lord Abraham, if you direct my way by which I am traveling, behold, while I stand beside the spring of water, the virgin who comes out to draw water; and I say to her, “Give me a little water to drink from your jar”; and she answers, “You drink, and I shall draw water for your camels”—she shall be the wife whom the Lord has prepared for my master’s son (Gen. 24:42ff.).

In that place where it says, “the virgin who comes out to draw water,” the Hebrew has **ALMA**, that is, “a hidden virgin,” carefully guarded by the extraordinary diligence of her parents.

Or let them show me where married women are called by this word, and I shall confess my ignorance.

> Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son.

If virginity is not preferred to marriage, why did the Holy Spirit choose neither a married woman nor a widow? For at that time there was Anna, daughter of Phanuel, from the tribe of Asher, [Col. 0255B] distinguished for chastity and always devoted to prayers and fasts in the temple of God. If a way of life, good works, and fasts without virginity merit the Holy Spirit’s coming to oneself, she too could have been the mother of the Lord.

Let us hasten to what follows:

> He has despised you and rejected you, virgin daughter of Zion (Isa. 27:22).

The one whom he had called “daughter,” he also called “virgin,” lest, if he had named her only “daughter,” you should think her married as well.

This is the virgin daughter to whom it is elsewhere said:

> Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry out, you who do not travail, for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband (Isa. 54:1).

This is she of whom God speaks through Jeremiah:

> Will a bride forget her ornament, or a virgin her breast-band? (Jer. 2:32)

In the same prophecy there is a great miracle: a woman shall enclose a man, and the virgin’s womb shall contain the Father of the universe.

### 33. Jeremiah the virgin and his privileges. What is the true temple of God?

“But,” he says, “suppose the condition of marriage and virginity is different; what can you say about this? If a virgin and a widow are baptized and remain as they are, what difference will there be between them?”

What we said earlier about Peter and John, and about Anna and Mary, may serve us here. For if there is no difference between a baptized virgin and a baptized widow, because baptism makes a new person, then prostitutes and harlots, if they have been baptized, will be made equal to virgins. If previous marriage does no harm to a baptized widow, then previous pleasures among prostitutes, and bodies exposed to public lust, will receive the rewards of virginity after the washing.

It is one thing to join to God a most pure mind, polluted by no recollection; it is another to remember the embraces of a husband under the compulsion of shameful necessity, and to imitate in memory what one does not perform bodily.

Jeremiah, who was sanctified in the womb and known in his mother’s womb, enjoys this privilege because he had been destined for the blessedness of virginity. When all others were captured, and even the vessels of the Temple were seized while the Babylonian king laid waste to everything, he alone was free from the enemies and knew nothing of captivity’s injuries. He received wages from the conquerors, and Nabuzardan, whom Nebuchadnezzar had not instructed concerning the Holy of Holies, was instructed concerning Jeremiah.

For this is the true temple of God, and these are the Holy of Holies: those consecrated to the Lord by the purity of virginity.

By contrast, Ezekiel, who was held captive in Babylon, who had seen the storm coming from the north and the whirlwind sweeping everything away, says:

> My wife died in the evening, and I did in the morning as I had been commanded (Ezek. 24).

For the Lord had foretold to him that on that day his mouth would be opened and that he would speak and no longer be silent. Pay close attention: as long as his wife lived, he did not have the freedom to admonish the people. His wife dies, the marital bond is dissolved, and without any fear he is always engaged in the prophetic office.

For the one who has been called free is truly Christ’s servant.

I do not deny that widows are blessed if they have remained so after baptism; nor do I detract from the merit of those who persevere in chastity with their husbands. But just as these have a greater reward before God than married women serving the marital duty, so let them also endure with equanimity that virginity is preferred to them.

For if late chastity raises widows up against married women, after the pleasures of the body have been exhausted, why should they not recognize that they stand below perpetual chastity?

### 34. Lighter precepts were given to the still-infant Church. Various reasons for elections. The offense is that of the wicked, not of the good. An ancient fault in the Church. Names of offices, not of merits

“You speak these things in vain,” he says, “because bishops, presbyters, and deacons are appointed by the Apostle as husbands of one wife and as men having children.”

Just as the Apostle says concerning virgins that he has no commandment, yet gives advice—as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord—and throughout that discussion seeks to place virginity above marriage, urging what he does not dare command lest he seem to cast a snare and impose a burden heavier than human nature can bear, so also, when ecclesiastical order was being established, because a Church was being formed from the Gentiles while still inexperienced, he gave recent believers lighter precepts, lest, frightened, they should be unable to bear them.

Thus the Apostles and elders from Jerusalem send a letter instructing that no greater burden be imposed upon those who had believed from the Gentiles than that they abstain from idolatry, fornication, blood, and things strangled. And, as though giving milk to little children and infants, they give them milk to drink, not solid food. They neither command continence nor mention virginity nor summon them to fasts; nor do they say what is addressed to the Apostles in the Gospel:

> Let them not have two tunics, a bag, bronze in their belts, a staff in their hand, or sandals on their feet;

or, at any rate:

> If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you possess and give to the poor; and come, follow me (Matt. 19:21).

For if that young man who had boasted that he had fulfilled everything prescribed by the Law, on hearing this went away sorrowful because he had many possessions, and the Pharisees mocked such a saying of the Lord, how much more did such a vast multitude of Gentiles—whose highest virtue was not stealing what belonged to others—have no need of a commandment concerning chastity and perpetual continence, when they were being instructed to abstain from idols and fornication, and when fornication, indeed such fornication as does not even occur among the Gentiles, was being heard of among them?

The very election of bishops also supports my position. It does not say: “Let a bishop be chosen who takes one wife and fathers children,” but: “one who has had one wife, and whose children are obedient in every discipline” (1 Tim. 3; Titus 1).

Certainly you admit that one who fathers children while a bishop cannot be a bishop. Otherwise, if he is discovered doing so, he will not be treated merely as a husband but will be condemned as an adulterer.

Either allow priests to perform the works of marriage, so that virgins and married men are the same; or, if priests may not touch their wives, they are holy in this respect because they imitate virginal chastity.

This too must be added: if a layman or any believer cannot pray unless he abstains from marital duty, then a priest, who must always offer sacrifices for the people, must always pray. If he must always pray, therefore he must always abstain from marriage.

Under the old Law also, those who offered sacrifices for the people were not only absent from their homes but were purified for a time by separating from their wives; they did not drink wine or strong drink, which tend to provoke lust.

Married men are chosen for the priesthood—I do not deny it—because there are not as many virgins as priests are needed. Does the fact that the strongest men must be chosen for the army mean that weaker men will not also be enlisted, since all cannot be strong? If an army consisted only in strength and not also in the number of soldiers, the weaker would be rejected. But now men of the second and third degrees of strength are also enlisted, so that the army may be filled in both crowd and number.

“And how,” you ask, “does it frequently happen in the ordination of priests that a virgin is neglected and a married man is chosen?”

Perhaps because he has none of the other qualities suitable to virginity; or he is thought to be a virgin but is not; **or his virginity is disgraced**.

**[Note: “Or his virginity is disgraced.” He appears to call that virginity disgraced which is produced by human injury and violent action in those who have been made eunuchs by human beings, or who were born that way from their mother’s womb. This virginity is disgraced and prevents eligibility for ecclesiastical rank and election to the clergy. MARTIAN.]**

Or perhaps virginity itself produces arrogance in him, and while he congratulates himself on bodily chastity alone, he neglects the other virtues. He does not support the poor; he is more eager for money. Sometimes a gloomy face, a raised eyebrow, and a gait resembling the bearers of ceremonial displays offend the people, and because they find nothing in his life to criticize, they hate only his appearance and his walk.

**[Note: “A gait resembling the bearers of ceremonial displays.” Above, in the letter to Rufinus, column 4: “Let anyone shine with gold and glitter with ceremonial displays, and let metals gleam from his burdens.” There you have ceremonial bearers. MARTIAN.—Cicero, *De Officiis* 1.36: “One must beware of using excessively slow steps in walking, lest we seem like the bearers of ceremonial displays.” These were certain litters on which images of the gods were carried in processions. See Letter 3 to Rufinus at the end, and the letter to Rusticus, and elsewhere.]**

Many are chosen not from love for themselves but from hatred of another. In many cases simple-mindedness alone wins support, and is opposed to another’s prudence and cleverness as though these were wickedness.

Sometimes the judgment of the people and the crowd is mistaken, and when priests are being approved, each person favors his own character, seeking not so much a good superior as one like himself.

It sometimes happens that married men, who form the larger part of the people, applaud married men as though applauding themselves, and think that they are not inferior to virgins if they prefer a married man to a virgin.

I shall say something that perhaps I shall say to the offense of many; but good people will not be angry with me, because their conscience of sin will not trouble them.

Sometimes this also happens through the fault of bishops, who bring into the clergy not the better but the cleverer men, and consider the more simple and innocent unfit; or, as though distributing offices of earthly service, they give them to relatives and kinsmen; or they obey the commands of the rich.

What is worse, they grant clerical rank to those whose services have captivated them.

Otherwise, if, according to the Apostle’s statement, only married men are to be bishops, the Apostle himself ought not to have been a bishop, since he said:

> I wish that all were as I myself am (1 Cor. 7:7).

John too would be judged unworthy of this rank, as would all virgins and continent persons, with whom the Church’s necklace is adorned as with the most beautiful gems.

Bishop, presbyter, and deacon are names of offices, not of merits. It does not say, “If someone desires the episcopate, he desires a good rank,” but, “he desires a good work”—so that, established in the higher order, he may, if he wishes, have the opportunity to practice the virtues.

### 35. The rule of sobriety. Virtue makes the ecclesiastical ranks blessed

Therefore a bishop must be irreproachable (1 Tim. 3), so that he is enslaved to no vice: a husband of one wife, one who has had one wife, not one who currently has one; sober—or, as it is better expressed in Greek, watchful—**νηφάλεον** [another reading: **νηφάλιον**]; chaste, for this is what **σώφρον** [another reading: **σώφρονα**] signifies; adorned both in chastity and in conduct; hospitable, so that he may imitate Abraham and receive Christ with strangers, indeed in strangers.

He must be a teacher, for it is of no benefit to enjoy the consciousness of virtues unless he can also instruct the people entrusted to him, so that he may be able to exhort through teaching and refute those who contradict.

He must not be a drunkard, because one who is always in the Holy of Holies and offers sacrifices must not drink wine or strong drink, since there is wantonness in wine.

Thus let a bishop drink that it may be unknown whether he has drunk.

He must not be a striker—that is, one who strikes the consciences of individuals. For the apostolic passage does not describe a boxer; it instructs a bishop regarding what he must not do.

It now teaches, conversely, what he should do:

> But modest, not quarrelsome, not greedy; ruling his own household well, having children obedient with all chastity.

See how much chastity is required of a bishop: if his children are unchaste, he himself cannot be a bishop, and he offends God by the same fault by which the priest Eli offended him. Eli had indeed rebuked his sons, but because he had not expelled the offenders, he fell backward and died before the lamp of God was extinguished (1 Sam. 2, 4).

> Women likewise must be chaste,

and so forth.

In every rank and sex, chastity holds the chief place.

You see, therefore, that a bishop, presbyter, and deacon are not blessed merely because they are bishops, presbyters, or deacons, but if they possess the virtues corresponding to their names and offices.

**[Note: We supplied the word “if” from four of our manuscripts and the old edition. Shortly afterward, the same manuscripts have “whether because he is inferior,” in the form of a question.]**

Otherwise, if a deacon is holier than his bishop, will he be worse before Christ merely because he is lower in rank? Or will Stephen the deacon, who was first crowned with martyrdom, be lesser in the kingdom of heaven than many bishops—and than Timothy and Titus, whom I do not dare place beneath him, but neither do I dare place before him? (Acts 6, 7)

Just as in legions and armies there are commanders, tribunes, centurions, light infantry, lightly armed troops, common soldiers, and companies, and when battle has been joined the names of rank fall silent and only courage is sought, so in this field and battle in which we fight against demons, names are not sought but deeds; and under Christ, the true commander, the more glorious person is not the nobler but the stronger.

### 36. We suffer one another’s ardor. In the resurrection there will be the same substance

“But,” you say, “if all were virgins, how would the human race continue?”

I shall answer like with like. If all were widows, or continent within marriage, how would the race of mortals be propagated? By this reasoning nothing at all would exist, lest one thing cease to be something else.

For example, if everyone were a philosopher, there would be no farmers. What shall I say of farmers? There would be no orators, no lawyers, no teachers of the remaining arts. If everyone were a commander, who would be a soldier? If everyone were the head, whose head would they be called when the other members were absent?

Do you fear that if many desired virginity, prostitutes and adulteresses would cease to exist, and that children would no longer cry in cities and villages?

Every day the blood of adulterers is poured out, adulteries are condemned, and amid the very laws, executions, and tribunals, burning lust holds sway.

Do not fear that everyone will become a virgin. Virginity is difficult, and therefore rare because it is difficult:

> Many are called, few are chosen (Matt. 20:16; 22:14).

To begin belongs to many; to persevere, to few. Hence the great reward of those who persevere.

If all could be virgins, the Lord would never have said:

> Let the one who can receive it receive it (Matt. 19:12),

nor would the Apostle have hesitated in urging it:

> Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord (1 Cor. 7:25).

**[Note: The Veronese and Casanatensis manuscripts generally read more elegantly without the negative particle: “the Apostle would not hesitate in urging it.”]**

“And why,” you ask, “were the genitals created, and why were we fashioned by the most wise Creator in such a way that we suffer one another’s ardor and burn with desire for natural intercourse?”

We risk the embarrassment of answering, and, as though between two crags—certain **συμπληγάδες** of necessity and chastity—we suffer shipwreck on either side, whether of modesty or of the argument.

If we answer what has been proposed, we are suffused with shame. If shame obtains silence, we shall seem to yield the ground and give our adversary an opportunity to strike.

Nevertheless, it is better to fight, as the saying goes, with closed eyes, like the **Andabatae**, than not to repel with the shield the arrows aimed directly at the truth.

I could say: just as the posterior part of the body and the passage through which the excrement of the bowels is expelled have been removed from the eyes and placed, as it were, behind the body, so this organ, situated beneath the belly, was created by God to digest the fluids and drinks by which the body’s veins are irrigated.

**[Note: The earlier edition had “for directing”; all our manuscripts correct this to “for digesting.”]**

But since the organs themselves, the structure of the genitals, the distinction between men and women, and the receptacles of the womb, created to receive and unite offspring, proclaim the difference of sex, I shall answer briefly:

Then let us never cease from lust, lest we carry such members in vain. Why should a husband abstain from his wife? Why should a chaste widow persevere if we were born only to live like animals?

Or what harm will come to me if another man has intercourse with my wife?

For just as it is the function of the teeth to chew and send what has been chewed into the stomach, and the person who has given bread to my wife is not guilty, so, if it is the function of the genitals always to enjoy their natural use, let another’s strength overcome my weariness,

**[Note: The Veronese manuscript reads *supparent* (“should be equal/sufficient”).]**

and let accidental lust quench my wife’s, so to speak, most burning appetite.

But what does the Apostle mean by exhorting us to continence if it is contrary to nature? What does the Lord himself mean by teaching about the varieties of eunuchs?

Certainly the Apostle, who calls us to imitate his chastity, ought consistently to hear the question: Why do you carry a male organ, O Paul? Why are you distinguished from the female sex by your beard, hair, and other bodily characteristics? Why do your nipples not swell, your loins not widen, and your chest not become narrow?

The voice is old-fashioned, the speech more ferocious, and the brow more shaggy. You possess all these things of men in vain if you do not make use of the embraces of women.

I am compelled to say something and become foolish; but you forced me to dare to speak.

Our Lord and Savior, who, though he was in the form of God, deigned to assume the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross—why was it necessary for him to be born with those members which he would not use?

Certainly, to show his sex, he was also circumcised.

Why did he castrate the Apostle and Baptist John through his love for them, when he had caused them to be born men?

Therefore, we who believe in Christ should follow Christ’s examples.

And even if we have known him according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him according to the flesh.

**[Note: The manuscripts read: “but now we no longer know him according to the flesh.”]**

Certainly, in the resurrection the substance of the bodies will be the same as that which we now use, although with greater glory.

For the Savior also possessed the very same body after the underworld—[the old edition reads “after the resurrection”]—in which he had been crucified, so that he showed the hands pierced by nails and the wound in his side.

Moreover, if he entered through closed doors, something that the nature of human bodies does not permit, then we must also deny that Peter and the Lord had true bodies, because they walked upon the waters, which is contrary to nature.

> In the resurrection of the dead they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but they shall be like angels (Matt. 22:30).

What others will later be in heaven, virgins have begun to be on earth.

If we are promised likeness to angels—and among angels there is no distinction of sex—then either we shall be without sex, as the angels are; or, as is clearly proved, rising again in our own sex, we shall not perform the function of sex.

### 37. But what are we doing with arguments, and why do we eagerly wish to overcome our opponent’s propositions by a clever reply?

“The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5:17). I shall run through the sayings of the apostles; and just as, in discussing Solomon’s examples, I added brief explanations for ease of understanding, so now I shall repeat examples of Christian chastity and continence. From many testimonies I shall fashion, as it were, a single body, both omitting nothing relevant to purity and avoiding the weariness of excessive length.

Among other things, the Apostle Paul writes to the Romans:

> “What fruit, then, did you have at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death. But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and your end is eternal life” (Rom. 6:21–22).

[Note: Manuscripts do not recognize the words “in those things.”]

I think that the end of marriage, too, is death. But the fruit of sanctification, which belongs either to virginity or to continence, is requited with life.

And afterward:

> “Therefore, my brothers, you also have been put to death through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, who was raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit” [another reading: “in order that you may bear fruit”] “for God. For when we were in the flesh, the passions which worked through the Law were active in our members, so that they might bear fruit for death. But now we have been released from the law of death by which we were held captive, so that we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter” (Rom. 7:4–6).

[Note: Our manuscripts read: “the passions of sins, which worked through the Law in our members,” together with the old edition and, in accordance with the Greek text, τὰ παθήματα τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν (“the passions of sins”); indeed, also with the Vulgate translator.]

He says: “When we were in the flesh, and not in the newness of the spirit but in the oldness of the letter, we did the things that belonged to the flesh and bore fruit for death. But now, because we have died to the Law through the body of Christ, let us bear fruit for God, so that we may belong to him who rose from the dead.”

Likewise, in another place, after saying, “I know that the Law is spiritual” (Rom. 7:14), and after discussing at greater length the violence of the flesh, which repeatedly drives us to do what we do not wish, he concludes:

> “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24).

And again:

> “I myself, therefore, with my mind serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25).

And:

> “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh. For the law of the Spirit in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 8:1–2).

Then, more explicitly, he teaches in what follows that Christians do not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit:

> “For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those who are according to the spirit perceive the things of the spirit. For the wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace, because the wisdom of the flesh is hostility toward God. For it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. 8:5ff.).

And so on, up to the place where he says:

> “Therefore, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, so that we should live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.”

If the wisdom of the flesh is hostility toward God, and those who are in the flesh cannot please God, I think that those who serve the marital obligation, because they love the wisdom of the flesh, are in the flesh.

Drawing us away from this and joining us to the spirit, the Apostle continues:

> “I beseech you, brothers, through the mercies of God” [the Veronese manuscript has “through the mercies of God” in the plural, in agreement with the Greek διὰ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν τοῦ θεοῦ], “to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service. And do not conform yourselves to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God. For I say, through the grace given to me, to everyone among you: do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think toward purity” [not “toward sobriety,” as it is wrongly read in Latin manuscripts], “but,” he says, “think toward purity” (Rom. 12:1ff.; Phil. 4:18).

For in Greek it is written εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν (“toward self-control/purity”).

Let us consider the Apostle’s meaning. He says: “Be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.” What he says is of this kind: God does indeed permit marriage; he permits a second marriage; and, if necessity should arise, he even prefers a third marriage to fornication and adultery. But we who ought to present our bodies as a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice to God, our reasonable service, should consider not what God permits but what he wills, so that we may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.

Therefore, what he permits is neither good, nor pleasing, nor perfect.

He gives the reasons why he offers this advice:

> “Knowing the time, that it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep. For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed. The night has passed, and the day has drawn near.”

And at the end:

> “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires.”

The will of God is one thing; indulgence is another.

Therefore, writing also to the Corinthians, he says:

> “I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able to receive it, and even now you are not able. For you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

One who is merely natural and does not receive [another reading: “perceive”] the things of the Spirit of God—for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them because they are spiritually discerned—is nourished not by the food of perfect chastity but by the immature milk of marriage.

> “As through a man came death, so through a man also came the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. We served the old Adam in the Law; let us serve the new Adam in the Gospel. For the first man, Adam, was made a living soul, and the last Adam a life-giving spirit. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly. Now I say this, brothers, because flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor can corruption possess incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:21ff.).

[Note: Manuscripts read “corruption will not inherit incorruption,” in accordance with the Greek κληρονομεῖ (“will inherit”).]

This is so clear that it cannot be made more explicit by any interpretation: “Flesh and blood,” he says, “cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor can corruption possess incorruption.” If corruption refers to every sexual union, while incorruption belongs properly to chastity, marriage cannot possess the rewards of purity.

For we know that:

> “If the earthly house of this dwelling is destroyed, we have an edifice from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. In this we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling which is from heaven” [the same manuscripts read “desiring to put it on over us”]. “For we wish to depart from the body and dwell with Christ; and for this reason we strive most earnestly, whether in the body or outside the body, to please God” (2 Cor. 5:1ff.).

And, to explain more fully what sort of people he did not wish them to be, he teaches elsewhere, saying:

> “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

If you wish to refer this to the whole Church of believers, and to include in this betrothal to Christ married women, those married twice, widows, and virgins, this too works in our favor. For, while he invites everyone to purity and to the reward of virginity, he shows that virginity is superior in every rank.

Again, to the Galatians:

> “By works of the Law no flesh will be justified” (Gal. 2:16).

The works of the Law include marriage; hence those who do not have children are cursed in it [another reading: “those things which do not have children”]. If these things are permitted even in the Gospel, it is one thing to grant indulgence to weakness and another to promise rewards to virtues.

### 38. I shall say this also to my married men, who, after chastity and prolonged continence, rush back to sexual intercourse and behave wantonly like beasts:

> “Are you so foolish that, having begun with the spirit, you are now being completed in the flesh?” (Gal. 3:3).

“Did you suffer so many things in vain?”

When the Apostle loosens certain bonds of continence and lets the reins fall for those who are running, he does so because of the weakness of the flesh. Writing against this, he says again:

> “Walk by the spirit, and you will not fulfill the desire of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:16–17).

It is not necessary now to speak about the works of the flesh, since that would be lengthy, and anyone who wishes can easily take them from the Apostle’s Epistle [another reading: “because anyone who wishes can…”].

I shall speak only about the spirit, whose fruit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, [the Casanatensis manuscript adds “modesty,”] gentleness, and continence.

Continence sustains and protects all the virtues of the spirit, as though it were their most solid foundation and lofty summit. Against such things there is no law.

> “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. If we live by the spirit, let us also walk by the spirit” (Gal. 5:24–25).

Since we have crucified our flesh, its passions, and its desires with Christ, why do we again wish to do the things of the flesh?

> “Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. The one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but the one who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit” (Gal. 6:8).

I think that one who has a wife, as long as he returns to sexual relations so that Satan may not tempt him, sows in the flesh and not in the spirit. But one who sows in the flesh—and it is not I but the Apostle who speaks—reaps corruption.

God the Father chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless before him. We walked in the desires of the flesh, doing its will and that of our thoughts, and we were children of wrath, like the rest.

But now he has raised us together with Christ and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, so that we may put off, according to our former way of life, the old man who is corrupted according to the desires of error, and so that the blessing may be applied to us which the mystical Epistle to the Ephesians concludes in this way:

> “Grace be with all who love our Lord in incorruption” (Eph. 6:24).
