[Note: “Missa” (“sent”) had falsely prevailed up to this point instead of “mystical,” despite the manuscripts’ rejection of it. Jerome calls the Epistle to the Ephesians “mystical” because the Apostle gathered in it, or especially in it, obscure meanings and unknown mysteries of the age, as Jerome himself says in the preface to his Commentary on that same Epistle. Shortly afterward, manuscripts read “Grace with all,” without “with you,” since the Greek text likewise does not recognize that word.]

> “Our citizenship is in heaven. From there also we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20; 4:8).

Therefore, whatever things are true, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are just, whatever things pertain to purity: let us join ourselves to these and follow them.

Christ reconciled us to God the Father in his body through death, and presented us holy, blameless, and without reproach before him. In him we were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping away of the body of the flesh, but with the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which we also rose with him.

Therefore, if we have risen with Christ, let us seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; let us set our minds on the things above, not on those upon the earth. For we have died, and our life is hidden with Christ in God.

> “When Christ, our life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 2:12; 3:1ff.).

[Note: Manuscripts read: “No one serving as a soldier is entangled in worldly business,” in accordance with the Greek text οὐδεὶς στρατευόμενος ἐμπλέκεται (“no one serving as a soldier becomes entangled”), etc. Estius believes that “in order to please God” was added by the Vulgate translator himself, although it seemed to him to be required for completeness of meaning.]

> “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one who chose him” (2 Tim. 2:4).

For:

> “The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all human beings, training us to deny impiety and worldly desires, and to live chastely, justly, and devoutly in the present age” (Tit. 2:11–12).

### 39. The virgin daughters of Philip in Caesarea. James, the brother of the Lord. The shadow and image of truth in the Old Law.

My time would fail me if I wished to recall all the Apostle’s commands concerning chastity. These are the things about which the Lord was speaking to the Apostles:

> “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:12–13).

Immediately after Christ’s cross, the Acts of the Apostles presents the household of Philip the Evangelist as producing a team of four virgin daughters, so that Caesarea—where the Church from the Gentiles had been established through the centurion Cornelius—might also offer examples of young virgins.

Although the Lord said in the Gospel, “The Law and the Prophets were until John,” these women, because they were virgins, are reported to have prophesied even after John. For they could not be held [another reading: “detained”] by the law of the Old Testament, since they had shone with the splendor of virginity.

Let us pass to James, who was called the brother of the Lord. He possessed such holiness, such justice, and perpetual virginity that Josephus, the historian of the Jews, reports that Jerusalem was destroyed because of his death.

[Note: I do not find this testimony of Josephus concerning James in his present books. But Origen had also once read it, in Books I and II Against Celsus and in his Commentary on Matthew 13. Eusebius quotes the very Greek words in Ecclesiastical History 2.23; our Jerome also quotes them in the Catalogue, chapters 2 and 13. See what we note there.]

James was the first bishop from the Jews of the believing Church at Jerusalem. Paul went to him with Titus and Barnabas. In his Epistle he says:

> “Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect donation is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning” [we have preferred, in agreement with our manuscripts and the old edition, “shadow of turning away” instead of “shadow of variation”; the Greek is τροπῆς]. “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures” (James 1:16–17).

The virgin teaches virginity mystically. Every perfect gift descends from above, where there are no marriages; and it descends not from just anyone but from the Father of lights, who says to the Apostles:

> “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14).

With him there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile; nor does that shadow which existed in the Law oppress those who have believed from the nations. Rather, he brought us forth by the word, and by the word of truth, because a shadow, image, and certain representation of the truth preceded in the Law, so that we might be the firstfruits of his creatures.

And just as he himself, the firstborn from the dead, raised all the dead in himself, so he himself, being a virgin, consecrated in himself the firstfruits of his virgins.

Let us also consider what Peter thinks about the calling of the Gentiles:

> “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, according to his great mercy, regenerated us into a hope of life through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, kept in heaven for you, who are guarded by the power of God through faith for salvation, prepared to be revealed in the last time” (1 Pet. 1:3ff.).

Where an inheritance is proclaimed incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, prepared in heaven and reserved for the last time, and where the hope of eternal life is found—when “they neither marry nor are given in marriage”—there, in other words, the privileges of virginity are described.

For in what follows he teaches this very thing:

> “Therefore, girding the loins of your mind and keeping perfectly watchful, hope in the grace that is to be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. As obedient children, do not conform yourselves to your former desires in your ignorance” [our manuscripts, adhering more closely to the Greek, read “in your ignorance,” ἐν τῇ ἀγνοίᾳ ὑμῶν; afterward, “with silver or gold,” ἀργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσίῳ, and several other details of lesser importance], “but, according to the one who called you, the Holy One, be holy yourselves in all your conduct. For it is written: ‘Be holy, because I am holy.’ For you were redeemed not with corruptible silver and gold but with the precious blood of Jesus Christ, an immaculate lamb, so that we might purify our souls in obedience to the truth, having been born again not from corruptible intercourse but from incorruption, through the living and abiding word of God; and, like living stones, may we be built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices through Christ our Lord” (1 Pet. 1:13ff.).

We are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition. Christ died in the flesh for us. Let us arm ourselves with the same way of life as Christ, because the one who suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so that for the remaining time in the flesh we may live not according to human desires but according to the will of God.

For the time that has passed is sufficient, when we walked in wantonness, desires, and other vices.

He has given us great and precious promises of virginity, so that through it we may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through desire (1 Pet. 2:9ff.).

The Lord knows how to rescue the devout from temptation and to reserve the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment, especially those who walk after the flesh in desires of pollution and despise dominions, bold and presumptuous.

These people, like irrational beasts, are inclined toward the belly and lust, blaspheming; and in their corruption they will themselves be corrupted. They will receive the reward of unrighteousness: indulgence in luxury—those who consider injustice a pleasure, stains and blemishes, thinking of nothing except pleasures.

They have eyes full of adultery and insatiable lust, and they deceive souls not yet strengthened by the love of Christ. For they speak swelling words and easily entangle the unlearned in the snares of the flesh, promising them freedom while they themselves are slaves [our manuscripts read “while they themselves are slaves of corruption,” without the inserted words “of vices and luxury,” entirely in accordance with the Greek αὐτοὶ δοῦλοι ὑπάρχοντες τῆς φθορᾶς, to which the Vulgate translator also agrees. Shortly afterward, the same Greek text has “of the Savior Jesus,” without “our,” and a little later “after having come to know him, to turn back and abandon,” etc.] of vices, luxury, and corruption.

For each person is subject to the passion by which he is overcome. If, having escaped the pollutions of the world through knowledge of our Savior Jesus Christ, they are again overcome by the same things which they had previously overcome, their final condition has become worse than their former one.

It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after coming to know it, to turn back and abandon the holy commandment delivered to them.

And the truest proverb has been fulfilled in them:

> “The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (2 Pet. 2:9–22).

[Note: I did not wish to set out the entire passage of the Second Epistle of Peter, lest I become lengthy; I merely showed that by the prophecy of the Holy Spirit the teachers [another reading: “teacher”] and heresy of this age had been foretold. Jerome says above that the canon is beyond all dispute; consequently, both he and Jovinianus admitted Peter’s Second Epistle as belonging to the canon of the sacred books. MARTIAN.]

Finally, he identifies them more plainly, saying:

> “For in the last days mockers will come, walking according to their own desires,”

and so forth.

### 40. The monk Jovinianus, a dog returning to his vomit. The tribe of Levi substituted for the tribe of Dan. All works are imperfect without purity. Heretics condemn marriage. The Church approves and regulates it.

The Apostolic discourse has depicted Jovinianus speaking with swollen cheeks and weighing inflated words, promising freedom in heaven while he himself is a slave of vices [another reading: “of corruption”] and luxury—a dog returning to its vomit.

For although he boasts that he is a monk, after his filthy tunic, bare feet, coarse bread, and water to drink, he turns to white clothing [another reading: “a white garment”], shining skin, mulled wine, elaborate meats, the sauces of Apicius and Paxamus [another reading: “Paxamis”], baths, fried delicacies [another reading: “fritillas”], and taverns.

[Note: In Ambrose’s reply to Siricius concerning Jovinianus and his followers, these men lament that they were for some time subjected to hardship and are taking revenge for their own injury; through daily banquets and the practice of luxury they wish to drive away the labor of abstinence. The name Apicius is well known. Columella, in Book 12 of On Agriculture, and Suidas mention Paxamus; he wrote ὀψαρτυτικά (“culinary recipes”). Some manuscripts read “Paxamii.” For fricticulas, Gravius prefers fitillas. Certainly Arnobius, Book 7: “What are fitillae, what is frumen, which are names for fleas?” On the change in Jovinianus’ clothing, see what we note below in Book 2.]

[Note: As for “baths and fried delicacies,” no manuscript reads, with the printed editions, fritillas, but rather ficticulas or fricticulas. Jerome calls fricticulae culinary dishes of fried foods; therefore he aptly joins fricticulas with taverns. MARTIAN.]

It is evident that he prefers earth to heaven, vices to virtues, the belly to Christ, and supposes that the purple color of Christ is the kingdoms of heaven.

[Note: For the word “belly,” our manuscripts read “they will receive air” or “airs.” Although I do not understand their meaning, I am nevertheless warned that this passage of Jerome has been corrupted. For what else do they intend after these words than that he prefers something to Christ for himself and supposes the kingdoms of heaven to be the purple of Christ’s color? I am surprised that none of the editors has noticed this.]

And yet this handsome monk—fat, shining, whitened, and always walking about like a bridegroom—should either take a wife, so that he may demonstrate by marriage that virginity is equal to it, or, if he does not take one, he argues against us in vain by his words, since in practice he is with us.

John also agrees in the same words:

> “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of this life, which is not from the Father but from the world” (1 John 2:15ff.).

And:

> “The world is passing away” [another reading: “will pass away”], “and its desire. But whoever does the will of God remains forever. I have written to you a new commandment, which is true both in Christ and in us: because the darkness has passed away and the true light is already shining” (1 John 2:8).

And again:

> “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure. In this our love is perfected, if we have confidence on the day of judgment, so that as he is, so also are we in this world” (1 John 3:2–3; 4:17).

The Epistle of Jude also signifies something of this sort:

> “Hating even the garment polluted by the flesh” (Jude 23).

Let us read the Apocalypse of John, and there we shall find the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with him 144,000 sealed ones, having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads. They sing a new song, and no one can sing that song except those who have been purchased from the earth.

> “These are the ones who have not defiled themselves with women, for they remained virgins. These follow the Lamb wherever he goes. They were purchased from among human beings as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb, and no lie was found in their mouth; they are without blemish” (Rev. 14:1ff.).

[Note: It seems, Gravius says, that the tribe of Manasseh, the son of Joseph, was substituted for the tribe of Dan, since Levi is the third of the twelve patriarchs, the sons of Jacob.]

From each tribe, except Dan, in whose place the tribe of Levi is substituted, twelve thousand sealed virgins are said to be destined to believe; they were not defiled with women.

And lest we suppose that this refers to those who have never known prostitutes, he immediately adds:

> “For they remained virgins.”

From this he shows that all who did not remain virgins are polluted in comparison with the purest and angelic chastity, and with our Lord Jesus Christ himself.

These are the ones who sing the new song, which no one can sing except one who is a virgin. These are the firstfruits of God and of the Lamb, and they are without blemish.

If virgins are the firstfruits of God, then widows and those who are continent within marriage will be after the firstfruits—that is, in the second and third rank. Nor will the lost people be able to be saved beforehand unless they offer such sacrifices of chastity to God and reconcile the immaculate Lamb with the purest victims.

It would be endless to expound from the Gospel the mystery of the ten virgins, five foolish and five wise. For now I say only this: just as virginity alone does not save without the other works, so all works without virginity, purity, continence, and chastity are imperfect.

Therefore, what our opponent objects—that the Lord was at Cana of Galilee and celebrated a wedding feast when he changed water into wine—cannot hinder us.

I shall answer this very briefly: the one who was circumcised on the eighth day, and for whom a pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons were offered on the day of purification, approved the Jewish custom, together with the other customs, before he suffered, so that he would not appear to give them a just occasion for killing him, as though he were destroying the Law and condemning nature.

And yet this too works in our favor. For the one who came to a wedding once taught that one should marry once.

It could then have harmed virginity if we did not place marriage after virginity and the chastity of widowhood in the third rank.

[Note: From these remarks infer the falsity of the rumor circulated by heretics, as Augustine reports in Book 2, chapter 12, of his Retractions: that Jerome had been unable to answer Jovinianus with praise but only with condemnation of marriage.]

But since it belongs to heretics to condemn marriage and despise God’s creation, whatever he has said in praise of marriage we gladly hear.

For the Church does not condemn marriages but subjects them to regulation; she does not reject them but administers them, knowing—as we said above—that in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay; that some are for honor and others for dishonor; and that whoever cleanses himself will become a vessel for honor, useful and prepared for every good work.

## 41. Examples from the histories of the ancient world. Virginity among the pagans. Virgins always held in honor among the Romans. Spartan virgins. Other examples of virgins.

We have supplied sufficient, indeed abundant, examples of Christian modesty and angelic virginity from the divine books. But since I have understood from the commentaries of my opponent that we are also challenged to appeal to the wisdom of the world—on the grounds that this way of life was never approved in the world and that our religion has introduced a new doctrine contrary to nature—I shall briefly run through Greek, Latin, and barbarian histories, and shall show that virginity has always held the first place among forms of modesty.

The fables relate that Atalanta of Calydon, a perpetual virgin, always hunting and always in the woods, loved not the swelling wombs of women and the inconveniences of conception, but an active and chaste virtue. The distinguished poet also describes Harpalyce, a Thracian virgin (Virgil, *Aeneid* I), as well as Camilla, queen of the Volscians. When Turnus wished to praise her, since she had come to his aid, he had nothing more to say than to call her a virgin: “O glory of Italy, virgin!” (the same author, book XI).

> **Note [Col. 0269D].** Chalcioecus also, etc. So far as I know, this story is not found in the authors of mythology. For other virgins and the Sibyls, see Naso, books VIII and X of the *Metamorphoses*; Lactantius, book I of *The False Religion*; Augustine, *City of God* XXIII, chapter 23; Livy, First Decade, book VIII; Valerius Maximus, book VIII, chapter 1, and elsewhere. —MARTIAN.
>
> Our two copies read *Chalcooecos*. The Casanatensis has *Calcooequos*, another *Calcodecus*; we do not know which reading is preferable. *Chalcioecus* was the name of Minerva’s temple in Lacedaemonia, and for this reason Minerva herself is also called *Chalcioecus* by many Greek writers. Victorius thinks that one of these women is meant—the women whom Suidas records under other names, namely Theopes, Eubules, and Pasitheas. One of them, he says, appeased a plague and the anger of the gods by a voluntary death, and was perhaps given the surname *Chalcioecus* after Pallas. Meursius, in the *Ceromica*, cites a history from many authors [Col. 0270D] reporting that three women were all sacrificed for the safety of the city of Athens; hence the Leocorion was solemnly dedicated in their memory. Accordingly, the aforementioned Meursius wishes *Chalchioecus* to be corrected into the two words *Haud secus*, which I cannot approve in any way. Perhaps, however, we may preserve the Hieronymian reading if we recognize that *Chalcioecus* is an appellative, not a proper name, and understand that one of the four priestesses of Minerva who carried the *Arrephoria* for the goddess was called by this name at the famous Athenian festival, which was likewise called τὰ χαλκεῖα (*ta chalkeia*, “the bronze festival”). If desired, consult Suidas under this word and Meursius, *Attic Lessons* IV, chapter 19.

Chalcioecus too, the daughter of Leo, is said to have been a perpetual virgin who freed her country from pestilence by a voluntary death; and the blood of the virgin Iphigenia appeased the hostile winds. Why should I mention the Erythraean and Cumaean Sibyls, and the other eight? For Varro maintains that there were ten. Their distinguishing mark was virginity, and the reward of virginity was divination. If, in the Aeolic form of speech, the Sibyl is called Θεοβούλη (*Theoboulē*, “God’s counsel”), virginity is rightly said alone to know the counsel of God.

We also read that Cassandra and Chryseis were prophetesses of Apollo and virgins of Juno.

> **Note [Col. 0270D].** Elsewhere we read that the prophetesses of Apollo Actius were virgins only. For the others, see Lactantius, book I, chapter 6, *The False Religion*, and chapter 22, *The Anger of God*; Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 23; Livy, book VIII, First Decade; likewise Valerius Maximus, book VIII, chapter 1; and finally Ovid, in the *Fasti*, where such histories are recounted more fully.

There were also countless priestesses of Tauric Diana and of Vesta. One of them, Minutia, was buried alive because she was suspected of fornication—a punishment unjust, in my opinion, unless the violation of virginity was thought a grave crime.

Certainly, it is clear from the following how greatly the Roman people always honored virgins: consuls and emperors, men celebrating triumphs in chariots and bringing back trophies from conquered nations, and persons of every rank and dignity, were accustomed to give way to them in the street.

When the Vestal virgin Claudia came under suspicion of fornication, and the statue of the Idaean Mother had become stuck in the shallows of the Tiber, she is said, to prove her chastity, to have drawn the ship by her girdle—a ship which many thousands of men had been unable to move.

“Yet,” says the uncle of the poet Lucan [that is, Seneca, Nero’s tutor], “it would have been better if this had happened to her as an adornment of tested chastity rather than as a defense of doubtful chastity.”

Nor is this surprising among human beings, since the error of the pagans also fashioned Minerva and Diana as virgin goddesses, and placed a Virgin among the twelve signs of heaven by which they believe the universe to revolve. What a great insult to marriage, that they did not even force a wife and husband together among scorpions, centaurs, crabs, fishes, and goat-horned creatures [that is, Capricorn].

When the Thirty Tyrants of Athens had killed Phidon at a banquet, they ordered his virgin daughters to come before them, strip in the manner of prostitutes, and dance indecently upon floors stained with their father’s blood. Concealing their grief for a little while, when they saw that the drunken banqueters were going out as though to answer nature’s call, they embraced one another and threw themselves into a well, preserving their virginity by death.

> **Note [Col. 0271D].** On the deposition of the Areopagites. It was never my intention to write commentaries on the works of Saint Jerome, except perhaps on the book of Hebrew Names, which I knew was held in contempt by many. Therefore the diligent reader should seek here a pure and genuine edition of Jerome, not the diligence of schoolmasters displaying in their own books their learning in Greek and Roman mythology. Whoever wishes to know where the holy man Jerome gathered so many monuments of antiquity should consult Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, Strabo, Justin, Polybius, L. Florus, Xenophon, Herodotus, Plutarch, Theophrastus, and the others whom he himself so frequently cites. —MARTIAN.

The virgin daughter of Demotion, chief of the Areopagites, hearing of the death of her betrothed Leosthenes, who had provoked the Lamian War, killed herself, asserting that although her body was untouched, if she were compelled to accept another husband, it would be as though she were accepting a second, since she had already married the first in her mind.

> **Note [Col. 0271D].** Something seems to be missing here to complete the elegance of the sense.

The Spartans and Messenians had long maintained friendship with one another, to such an extent that they even sent virgins to one another for certain religious rites. At one time, then, when the Messenians attempted to violate fifty Lacedaemonian virgins, not one of so many consented to the outrage; rather, all gladly died for their chastity. Consequently a severe and very long war was provoked, and after a considerable time Mamertia was destroyed.

> **Note [Col. 0271D].** Consult Orosius, book II, chapter 21; also Strabo, book VI; Justin, book III; and Eustathius on Dionysius. Soon afterward the Casanatensis reads: “The virgins of Lacedaemon had gone, and the Messenians …” In place of *Mamertia*, which appears below, our manuscripts have *Mamertina*, as in the *Chronicle* under the year of the world 1430: “Messana, also called Mamertina,” etc. Pliny, book III, chapter 8: “The town of Messana, whose Roman citizens are called Mamertines.” Recall Eusebius again under the year 3670. Below, in place of *Arcadia*, the Casanatensis has *Achaia*.

Aristoclides, tyrant of Orchomenus, fell in love with the virgin Stymphalis. After her father had been killed, she fled to the temple of Diana, grasped the statue of the goddess, and could not be torn away from it by force. She was stabbed to death in that same place. Because of her death, all Arcadia was so deeply stirred by grief that it took up war publicly and avenged the death of the virgin.

Aristomenes of Messenia, a most righteous man, after defeating the Lacedaemonians while they were celebrating certain nocturnal rites called the Hyacinthia, seized fifteen virgins from the dancing choruses and, fleeing swiftly throughout the night, passed beyond the borders of Sparta. When his companions wished to violate them, he warned them as forcefully as he could not to do so; finally, he killed some who would not obey, while restraining the others by fear.

> **Note [Col. 0272D].** It falsely read *Hyacinthina*. These were nocturnal rites celebrated for Apollo or Liber. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 18: “Among the Lacedaemonians, even in the rites which they celebrate for Apollo, called the Hyacinthia, they are crowned with ivy according to the Bacchic custom.” Shortly afterward, in place of *fifteen*, the old edition has *twelve*. Then the Casanatensis reads *quamdiu potuit* (“as long as he could”) instead of *quantum* (“as much as he could”).

Later, when the girls had been ransomed by their relatives and saw Aristomenes being accused of the slaughter, they did not return to their homeland until they had seen their defender acquitted, clinging to the knees of the judges.

How should one fail to praise the daughters of Scedasus at Leuctra in Boeotia? They are said, while their father was absent, to have received two young men passing by under the law of hospitality. The young men, indulging excessively in wine, violated the virgins during the night. Unwilling to survive the loss of their chastity, the girls struck one another with mutual wounds.

It is also right not to pass over the Locrian virgins [or Lucrian], who, when they were sent to Ilium according to custom for approximately a thousand years, never gave rise to any story of obscene rumor or violated virginity.

Who could pass over in silence the seven Milesian virgins who, when the Galatians’ attack was devastating everything, fled shame by death so that they would not suffer anything dishonorable at the hands of the enemy, leaving an example to all virgins that honorable minds should care more for chastity than for life?

> **Note [Col. 0272D].** See on Jonah, chapter I: hence, during persecutions, one may not perish by one’s own hand, except where chastity is in danger.

After Thebes had been defeated and destroyed, Nicanor was overcome by love for a captured virgin. Seeking marriage with her and voluntary embraces—what a captive ought, of course, to have desired—he learned that to chaste minds virginity is worth more than a kingdom. He killed her with his own hand and, as her lover, held her while weeping and mourning.

Greek writers report another Theban virgin whom a Macedonian enemy had violated. She concealed her grief for a little while and later cut the violator’s throat while he was sleeping. Then she killed herself with a sword, unwilling either to live after losing her chastity or to die before becoming the avenger of her own wrong.

> **Note [Col. 0272D].** An old manuscript in Gravius reads *et aliam* (“and another”) instead of *Aethaliam*.

## 42. Fables about those born from virgins.

Among the Gymnosophists of India, the authority of this belief is handed down, as it were, from hand to hand: that a virgin bore Buddam [or Buldam], the founder of their doctrine, from her own side.

> **Note [Col. 0273D].** Some wish this person mentioned by the holy Father, Buddam or Buttam, to be the same as the most ancient figure mentioned by Clement of Alexandria, the leader of the Samanaeans and Gymnosophists. But Clement did not say that he was born of a virgin; certainly he would not have remained silent about this if such a story had been told about him. We believe that this tale was introduced by the Manichaean Budda after the time of Christ.

Nor is this astonishing among barbarians, since learned Greece likewise invented the stories that Minerva was born from Jupiter’s head and Liber Pater from his thigh.

> **Note [Col. 0273D].** The first hand of the Veronensis reads *de femina* (“from a woman”), which another altered to *de semine* (“from seed”); the codex of Santa Croce likewise has *de femina*. Another manuscript apud Gravium reads *de femina*.

Speusippus, the son of Plato’s sister, Clearchus in his praise of Plato, and Anaxilides in the second book of his *Philosophy* report that Perictione, Plato’s mother, was overcome by an apparition of Apollo, and they believe that the prince of wisdom was brought forth only by a virgin birth.

> **Note [Col. 0273D].** The Veronensis has *Amaxilidis*, the Casanatensis *Masciliadis*, and shortly afterward *fasmate* instead of *phantasmate*. Diogenes Laërtius, book III: “And Anaxilides, in the second book concerning philosophers …” This work was *On Philosophers*, and perhaps Jerome himself wrote a *Philosophical History* rather than a *Philosophy*.

Timaeus also writes that Pythagoras’s virgin daughter presided over a chorus of virgins and instructed them in the teachings of chastity.

Diodorus the Socratic is said to have had five daughters, all skilled in dialectic and renowned for their extraordinary modesty; Philo, the teacher of Carneades, also writes a very full account of them.

> **Note [Col. 0274D].** Receive this passage from Clement, *Stromata* IV: “For the daughters of Diodorus, surnamed Cronus, all became dialecticians, as Philo the Dialectician says in the *Menexenus*. He gives their names as follows: Menexene, Argia, Theognis, Artemisia, Pantaclea, and so on.” The daughters of Diodorus, whose surname was Saturn, were all dialecticians, as Philo the Dialectician says in the *Menexenus*. These are the names he gives: Menexene, Argia, Theognis, Artemisia, Pantaclea, and so forth.

And lest Roman power reproach us for believing that our Lord and Savior was born of a virgin, the founders of its city and nation believe that they were born from the virgin Ilia and Mars.

## 43. Pagan widows.

Thus, in passing rapidly through many histories, my hurried discourse has touched upon the virgins of the ancient world. I shall proceed to married women who did not wish to survive their husbands when they had died or been killed, lest they be forced to experience a second union, and who loved their only husbands with remarkable devotion, so that we may know that remarriage was also disapproved among the pagans.

Dido, the sister of Pygmalion, gathered a great quantity of gold and silver, sailed to Africa, and there founded the city of Carthage. When King Iarbas of Libya sought her in marriage, she postponed the wedding for a while until she had founded the city. Not long afterward, she built a funeral pyre in memory of her former husband, Sychaeus, and chose to burn rather than marry.

A chaste woman founded Carthage, and again that same city ended in praise of chastity. For when the city had been captured and burned, the wife of Hasdrubal, seeing that she was about to be captured by the Romans, seized her little sons with both hands and leapt into the fire burning beneath her house.

## 44. What shall I say of the wife of Niceratus?

Unable to endure the outrage inflicted upon her husband, she killed herself so that she would not suffer the lust of the Thirty Tyrants whom Lysander had imposed upon Athens after defeating it.

Artemisia, the wife of Mausolus, is also reported to have been a woman of remarkable chastity. She was queen of Caria and is celebrated in the praises of distinguished poets and historians, but she is especially extolled for this: she always loved her dead husband as though he were alive, and built him a tomb of extraordinary size.

> **Note [Col. 0274D].** The Casanatensis inserts, with letters only lightly erased, *de more*, “as usual.”

It was so magnificent that even to this day all costly tombs are called *mausoleums* after her name.

> **Note [Col. 0274D].** All manuscripts, as well as the old edition, add *et pulchritudinis*, “and beauty.” For the histories that follow, consult Polybius, book I; Florus in the *Epitome*; Cicero below, *Tusculan Disputations* V; Propertius, book V; and others. All manuscripts and the old edition read *Tanta Illyricorum Regina* (“Such was the queen of the Illyrians”) instead of *Teuta Illyricorum*; Florus calls her Teuta.

Teuta, queen of the Illyrians, surely owed it to the miracle of chastity that she ruled for a long time over the bravest men and often defeated the Romans.

The Indians, like nearly all barbarians, have many wives. Among them there is a law that the dearest wife is to be burned with her dead husband. These wives therefore compete with one another for the husband’s love; and the greatest ambition of the contestants, and the proof of their chastity, is to be judged worthy of death.

Thus the victor lies beside the corpse in her former clothing and adornment, embracing and kissing it, and, despising the flames laid beneath her, wins the praise of chastity. I think that a woman who dies in this way does not seek a second marriage.

That Socratic Alcibiades, after the Athenians had been defeated, fled to Pharnabazus. Pharnabazus, having received a payment from Lysander, commander of the Lacedaemonians, ordered Alcibiades to be killed. After he had been strangled and his head cut off and sent to Lysander as evidence that the killing had been completed, the rest of his body lay unburied.

His concubine alone, in the midst of strangers, in defiance of the command of his most savage enemy and with danger threatening, performed the funeral rites. She was prepared to die for the dead man whom she had loved while he was alive.

Let married women imitate this fidelity of a concubine—at least let Christian married women imitate it—and let free women provide what a captive woman preserved.

## 45. Strato, petty king of Sinope, wishing to stab himself with his own hand so that he would not become a laughingstock to the Persians, whose alliance he had rejected in association with the king of Egypt, was held back by fear. He kept looking at the sword he had seized and awaited the enemy’s arrival in terror.

When his wife understood that he was about to be captured at any moment, she wrenched the dagger from his hand and pierced his side. Then, according to custom, she threw herself dying upon his prepared corpse, so that after the marriage of her virginity she would not endure intercourse with another.

Xenophon writes in his account of the early life of Cyrus the Great that, after Abradates had been killed—a man whom his wife Panthea had loved with extraordinary affection—she placed herself beside his mutilated body, pierced her breast, and poured her blood into her husband’s wounds.

> **Note [Col. 0275D].** The Veronensis has *Abradate*, the Cisterciensis *Abrate*, and the Casanatensis *Abradite*. See Xenophon, book VII. Shortly afterward our manuscript also has *Phantia* instead of *Panthea*.

A wife thought it a just reason for killing the king that her husband had shown her naked and unaware to his friend.

> **Note [Col. 0275D].** Martianaeus incorrectly reads *quam amicus nudam*, “whom the friend [saw] naked,” instead of *maritus*, “whom the husband had shown naked,” as all the manuscripts and earlier printed editions have. Herodotus tells this story of Candaules, or Myrsilus.

For she judged that she was not loved if she could be shown to another.

Rhodogune, daughter of Darius, after her husband’s death, killed the nurse who was persuading her to enter a second marriage.

> **Note [Col. 0275D].** The Casanatensis has *Rhodone*. See Philostratus, *Imagines*. For Alcestis, consult Euripides. The remaining histories and myths are more familiar.

The fables relate that Alcestis willingly died in place of Admetus; and Penelope’s chastity is celebrated in Homer’s poem. Laodamia too is sung by the poets: after Protesilaus was killed at Troy, she refused to survive him.

## 46. Distinguished Roman women.

I shall now turn to Roman women and shall place first Lucretia, who, unwilling to survive the violation of her chastity, wiped away the stain upon her body with her blood.

Duillius [or Duellius], the first man at Rome to celebrate a naval triumph, married Bilia, a virgin of such chastity that she was an example even in that age when immodesty was considered a monstrosity rather than a fault.

When he was already old and his body trembled, he heard, during a quarrel, that his breath had been reproached as foul, and he returned home sadly. When he complained to his wife that she had never warned him so that he might remedy the defect, she replied: “I would have done so, if I had not thought that all men’s breath smelled in the same way.”

This woman, chaste and noble, deserves praise in both respects: whether she did not know her husband’s defect, or whether she endured it patiently; and also because her husband learned of his bodily misfortune not through his wife’s disgust but through the insult of an enemy.

Certainly a woman who takes a second husband cannot say this.

Marcia, the younger daughter of Cato, was asked why she did not marry again after losing her husband. She replied that she could not find a man who wanted her more than he wanted her possessions.

> **Note [Col. 0275D].** The manuscripts read: “By this remark she elegantly showed …” Victorius thought *Porcia* should be read instead of *Marcia*, since Marcia, as is stated immediately below, was not Cato’s daughter but his wife.

By this remark she showed that wealth is more often chosen in wives than chastity, and that many men marry wives not with their eyes but with their fingers. Excellent indeed is the union that greed brings about.

While she was mourning her husband, married women asked her what day would be the last of her mourning. She replied: “The day that is also the last of my life.”

> **Note [Col. 0275D].** The words *quo dicto eleganter ostendit* (“by which remark she elegantly showed”) are found in the manuscripts.

I believe that a woman who sought her absent husband in this way was not thinking about a second marriage.

Brutus married Porcia as a virgin; Cato married Marcia, who was not a virgin. But Marcia passed between Hortensius and Cato, and Marcia was able to live without Cato; Porcia could not live without Brutus.

> **Note [Col. 0276D].** Marcia passed between Hortensius and Cato, since she was the wife of both and, after bearing children, returned to her former husband. —MARTIAN.
>
> Hortensius obtained Marcia from Cato, her husband, for the purpose of having children; after she had borne them to him, she returned to Cato. On Porcia, see Plutarch, *Life of Brutus*.

Women attach themselves more strongly to one husband, and knowing nothing else is a great bond of closer affection.

When a relative urged Annia to marry another husband—for she still had a sound age and a beautiful appearance—she replied: “I shall certainly not do this. If I find a good husband, I do not want to fear losing him; if he is bad, why should I, after a good one, endure the worst?”

> **Note [Col. 0276D].** The words *ut ante habui* (“as I previously had them”) are supplied here by the more accurate manuscripts and the old edition.

When a certain woman of good character who had a second husband was praised in her presence, Porcia the younger replied: “Happy and chaste is the married woman who never marries except once.”

When Marcella the elder was asked by her mother whether she was glad to have married, she replied: “So very glad that I do not want to do so again.”

Valeria, the sister of the Messalae, did not wish to marry anyone after losing her husband Servius. When asked why she did this, she replied that Servius, her husband, was always alive to her.

## 47. Theophrastus’ book on marriage. The disadvantages of taking a wife. Why wives are said to be taken. The uncommonness of human folly.

I realize that in my catalogue of women I have said far more than the usual number of examples allows, and that an educated reader may justly criticize me for it. But what am I to do, when the women of our time thrust the authority of the Apostle upon me, and, before the funeral of their first husband has even been carried out, recite from memory the rules of remarriage?

Let those who despise the faith of Christian chastity at least learn chastity from the pagans.

A golden book by Theophrastus, *On Marriage*, is said to exist, in which he asks whether a wise man should take a wife. After defining the conditions under which a wise man might sometimes marry—if she were beautiful, well behaved, born to respectable parents, and if he himself were healthy and wealthy—he immediately adds:

> **“Yet these conditions rarely all coincide in marriage. Therefore a wise man should not take a wife. First, his philosophical studies will be obstructed; no one can devote himself equally to books and to a wife. There are many things necessary for a married woman’s needs: expensive clothing, gold, jewels, expenditures, maidservants, varied furniture, litters, and gilded carriages.
>
> “Then there are whole nights of her talkative complaints: ‘That woman goes out in public more elegantly dressed; everyone honors her, while I am despised in the assembly of women. Why were you looking at your neighbor? What were you saying to the little maidservant? What have you brought home from the forum?’ We cannot have a friend or companion. She suspects that another woman is loved and that she herself is hated.
>
> “If a very learned teacher is staying in any city, we cannot either leave our wife behind or travel with our burden. It is difficult to support a poor wife; it is torture to endure a rich one.
>
> **Note [Col. 0277D].** The manuscripts add *Adde quoniam*, “Add also that …”
>
> “Add also that there is no choice in selecting a wife: whatever woman happens to come one must have. If she is angry, foolish, ugly, proud, foul-smelling—whatever defect she may have—we learn it only after the marriage. A horse, donkey, ox, dog, and the most worthless slaves, as well as clothing, cauldrons, a wooden seat, a cup, and a clay jug, are inspected beforehand and then purchased. Only the wife is not displayed, lest she displease us before she is taken.
>
> “Her face must always be attended to, and her beauty praised, lest, if you look at another woman, she think that she displeases you. Her mother must be called ‘mistress’; her birthday must be celebrated; one must swear by her welfare and wish that she may outlive one; her nurse and wet nurse must be honored, as must her father’s servant, her fosterling, her handsome attendant, her curled-hair steward, and the eunuch castrated for long and secure sexual service. Under these names adulterers conceal themselves.
>
> “Everyone whom she loves must be loved against one’s will. If you entrust the management of the entire household to her, you become her servant. If you reserve anything for your own judgment, she will think that she is not trusted; this will turn into hatred and quarrels, and unless you intervene quickly, she will prepare poison.
>
> “If you admit old women, diviners, fortune-tellers, and merchants of jewels and silk clothing, your chastity is endangered; if you exclude them, you suffer the injustice of suspicion.
>
> “But what does even vigilant guarding accomplish, since an unchaste wife cannot be guarded, while a chaste wife ought not to be guarded? Necessity is an unreliable guardian of chastity; for that woman should truly be called chaste who was permitted to sin if she wished.
>
> “A beautiful woman is quickly loved; an ugly woman readily feels desire.
>
> **Note [Col. 0277D].** Publilius the Mime: ‘What many desire is difficult to guard.’
>
> “What many people love is difficult to guard. It is troublesome to possess what no one considers worth having. Yet it is a lesser misery to have an ugly woman than to guard a beautiful one. Nothing is safe when the desires of the entire people sigh after it. One man courts her with beauty, another with intelligence, another with wit, another with generosity. In one way or another, what is attacked from every side is eventually conquered.
>
> **Note [Col. 0277D].** The word *aliquando* (“at some time”) is absent from two manuscripts, and Gravius rejects it.
>
> “If wives are taken for the sake of managing the household, for comfort during illness, and to avoid solitude, a faithful servant manages the household much better, obeying his master’s authority and submitting to his arrangements, than a wife who thinks herself mistress when she acts against her husband’s will—that is, doing what pleases her rather than what she is commanded.
>
> “Friends and household servants bound by kindness can sit beside a sick man more effectively than a wife who charges us for her tears, sells her filthiness in expectation of an inheritance, and, by displaying her anxiety, disturbs the mind of the sick man with despair.
>
> “If she herself falls ill, one must fall ill with her and never leave her bedside. Or if she is a good and agreeable wife—for such a creature is rare—then we groan with her in childbirth and are tormented when she is in danger.
>
> **Note [Col. 0278D].** Abaelard, who cites this passage, has *quae rara*, “which is rare,” or *vix est*, “which scarcely exists.”
>
> “A wise man, however, can never be alone. He has with him all good men who now exist and who have ever existed, and he transfers his free mind wherever he wishes. What he cannot encompass bodily, he embraces in thought. And if there is a lack of human company, he speaks with God. He will never be less alone than when he is alone.
>
> **Note [Col. 0278D].** Cato writes that Publius Scipio used to say that he was never less at leisure than when he was at leisure, and never less alone than when he was alone. Cicero, *On Duties* III, at the beginning. See also Plutarch, *Apophthegmata*.
>
> “Moreover, to take a wife for the sake of children, either so that our name may not perish, or so that we may have support in old age and make use of reliable heirs, is the height of stupidity.
>
> “For what does it matter to us, as we depart from the world, if someone else is called by our name? A son does not immediately bear the father’s name, and countless people may be called by the same name.
>
> “Or what support for old age is there in raising at home someone who may perhaps die before you or have the most perverse character? Or, when he has reached mature age, in appearing to him to die too slowly?
>
> “Friends and relatives whom you choose by judgment are better and more reliable heirs than those whom, whether you wish it or not, you are compelled to have. Even if inheritance is more certain, while you are alive it is better to make good use of your property than to leave what you acquired through your labor for uncertain uses.””

> **Note [Col. 0276D].** The book of Theophrastus, *On Marriage*, in which he discusses the marriage appropriate to a wise man, has been lost, and the whole value of this fragment is owed to Jerome.

> **Note [Col. 0277D].** All manuscripts, including the old edition, read *servus paternus, alumnus* (“the father’s servant, the fosterling”), and so forth. Shortly afterward, in place of *exsectus*, the reading was *exectus*.

> **Note [Col. 0277D].** In place of *aruspices*, the manuscripts unanimously, along with the old edition, have *aurifices* (“goldsmiths”).

> **Note [Col. 0277D].** The reading *dispensationi* is less good; all manuscripts have *dispositioni* (“arrangement”).

> **Note [Col. 0278D].** The manuscripts have *alius non vocatur* (“another is not called [by our name]”), since a son also does not immediately bear the father’s name, and so forth. A little farther below, the Casanatensis reads: “When you have reached mature age, you will seem to him to die too slowly.”

### 48. All evils arise from women. Epicurus, advocate of pleasure. Jupiter Gamelius and Genethlius

When Theophrastus discusses these and similar matters, what Christian—whose manner of life is in heaven and who daily says, “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23)—would not blush? Will a man who is heir, indeed a co-heir of Christ, desire a human heir? Will he wish for children and take delight in a succession of grandchildren, whom perhaps the Antichrist will overtake, when we read that Moses and Samuel preferred others to their own sons and did not regard as children those whom they saw displeasing to the Lord?

Cicero, when Hirtius asked him to marry Terentia’s sister after divorcing Terentia, entirely refrained from doing so, saying that he could not devote himself equally to a wife and to philosophy. Meanwhile that excellent wife, who had drawn wisdom from Tullian fountains, married Sallust, his enemy, and then Messala Corvinus, and, as though descending by certain steps, came down from eloquence.

Socrates had two wives, Xanthippe and Myron, the granddaughter of Aristides. Since they frequently quarrelled with each other, and he was accustomed to mock them for disputing on his account—an exceedingly ugly man, with a snub nose, a receding [manuscripts: crooked] forehead, hairy shoulders, and bowed legs—they finally turned their attack upon him and, after beating him badly, pursued him as he fled for a long time. On one occasion, when Xanthippe was pouring endless abuse upon him from an upper story and he had stood his ground, she drenched him with filthy water. He replied nothing more than this, wiping his head: “I knew,” he said, “that after such thunder there would be a shower.”

Metella, the wife of Lucius Sulla Felix (see Plutarch, *Life of Sulla*), was openly immoral—if only he had not had a wife. And since we learn our own misfortunes last, this was being sung about at Athens while Sulla knew nothing of it; he first learned the secrets of his household from the insults of his enemies.

Mutia, the wife of Gnaeus Pompey (see the same author, *Life of Pompey*), was immoral; the eunuchs of Pontus and the hordes of Mithridates courted her. While the others thought that Pompey knew and tolerated the matter, a fellow soldier revealed it to him during the campaign and, to the victor of the whole world, delivered the crushing news.

Marcus Cato the Censor had a wife, Actoria Paula, born in a low station, fond of wine, unrestrained, and—what no one could believe—arrogant toward Cato.

**Note:** The Casanatensis does not have *vinolentam* (“fond of wine”); two other manuscripts read *violentam* (“violent”), and the old edition has *mentis impotem* (“lacking self-control of mind”) instead of *impotentem*.

I say this so that no one may think that, if he marries a poor woman, he has made sufficient provision for harmony.

When Philip, king of the Macedonians, against whom Demosthenes’ *Philippics* thunder, entered the bedchamber as usual, his angry wife shut him out. Excluded, he remained silent and consoled himself for the injury by quoting a tragic verse.

**Note:** The name “Georgias” was printed erroneously.

The rhetorician Gorgias recited at Olympia a splendid book on harmony, at a time when the Greeks were divided among themselves. His enemy Melanthius said to him: “Here is a man prescribing harmony to us who could not make the three—himself, his wife, and his maidservant—live harmoniously together in one house.” His wife, in fact, was jealous of the maidservant’s beauty and harassed her most chaste husband with daily quarrels.

All of Euripides’ tragedies are denunciations of women. Hence Hermione says: “The counsels of wicked women have deceived me.”

**Note:** This saying is identified in Euripides’ *Andromache*: *κακῶν γυναικῶν εἴσοδοι μ᾽ ἀπώλεσαν*, “the assaults of wicked women have ruined me.”

In the half-barbarous city of Leptis, situated in a deserted region, it is customary for a daughter-in-law, on the day after her wedding, to ask her mother-in-law for a cooking pot on loan. The latter immediately refuses her, so that Terence’s saying may be recognized as true—the saying he deliberately expressed ambiguously: “What is this? All mothers-in-law hate their daughters-in-law.”

**Note:** Stobaeus, *Sermon* 72, reports the following from Plutarch’s *Advice on Marriage*:

> “A Roman, when his friends reproached him for sending away a prudent, wealthy, and beautiful wife, held out his shoe to them and said: ‘This shoe, too, which you see, appears beautiful and new to you; but no one knows where it pinches me except me.’”

We read that a certain noble Roman, when his friends reproached him for divorcing a beautiful, chaste, and wealthy wife, extended his foot and said to them: “This shoe, too, which you see, appears to you new and elegant; but no one knows, except me, where it presses.”

**Note:** Herodotus writes—not in the seventh book, as has been noted elsewhere, but in the first book, chapter 8—that Gyges says to Candaules:

> Ἅμα δὲ χιθῶνι ἐκδυομένῳ συνεκδύεται καὶ τὴν αἰδῶ γυνή  
> “When a woman removes her tunic, she removes her modesty as well.”

Saint Cyprian likewise says in *On the Discipline of Virgins*: “There all modesty is stripped away; together with the garment, the honour of the body and its shame are laid aside.”

The plural forms Pasiphaes, Clytemnestras, Eriphylas, and so forth are found shortly afterward in the Casanatensis manuscript.

Our own comic poet considers fortunate the man who has never married. What need is there to mention Pasiphae, Clytemnestra, and Eriphyle? The first, overflowing with luxury—for she was the wife of a king—is said to have desired intercourse with a bull; the second killed her husband for love of an adulterer; the third betrayed Amphiaraus and preferred a golden necklace to her husband’s safety.

Whatever swells in tragedy and overturns households, cities, and kingdoms is the quarrel of wives and mistresses. The hands of parents are armed against their children; unspeakable banquets are served; and because one little woman was carried off, Europe and Asia clash in a ten-year war.

**Note:** The manuscripts and the old edition read: “Europe and Asia wage ten-year wars.”

We read that some women, after being divorced, married again immediately on the following day. Both husbands deserve blame: the one to whom his wife became displeasing so quickly, and the one to whom she became pleasing so quickly.

Epicurus, the advocate of pleasure—although his disciple Metrodorus had Leontion [or: Leontium] as his wife—says that the wise man should rarely enter into marriage, because many disadvantages are mixed with weddings.

Just as wealth, honours, bodily health, and the other things that we call indifferent are neither good nor evil, but, being placed as if in the middle, become good or evil through use and circumstance, so wives also lie on the boundary between good and evil. For a wise man, however, it is a serious matter to fall into uncertainty as to whether the woman he is going to marry will be good or bad.

Chrysippus absurdly instructs the wise man to marry, lest he violate Jupiter Gamelius and Genethlius. In that case, however, among the Latins there would be no need to marry, since they do not have a Nuptial Jupiter. But if, as he thinks [or: they think], the names of the gods prejudice human life, then he would offend Jupiter Stator if he sat down willingly.

### 49. The sources from which he drew what he said about marriage. Chastity, chief among women’s virtues

Aristotle, Plutarch, and our Seneca wrote books on marriage. Some of the preceding statements come from them, as do the following:

“Love of beauty is forgetfulness of reason and close to madness: a shameful vice, wholly unfitting for a sound mind. It disturbs counsels, breaks lofty and noble spirits, drags them down from great thoughts to the lowest concerns; it makes them querulous, angry, reckless, harshly tyrannical, servilely flattering, useless to everyone, and finally useless even to love itself. For when it burns with an insatiable desire for enjoyment, it wastes many periods in suspicions, tears, and lamentations; it makes a person hate himself, and finally love itself becomes hateful to him.”

**Note:** The Veronensis and Cisterciensis manuscripts read *novissime odium est*, “finally it is hatred”; the Casanatensis reads *novissimum odium est*, “it is the final hatred.”

The whole attack on love is set forth by Plato in the *Phaedrus*, and Lysias explains all its disadvantages: it is governed not by judgment but by frenzy, and, above all, a most burdensome guardian keeps watch over the beauty of wives.

Seneca further reports that he knew an elegantly dressed man who, when he was about to go out in public, fastened his wife’s breasts with a band, and could not endure to be without her presence even for an hour’s instant. Husband and wife drank no liquid unless their lips had touched the same vessel in turn. They did other things no less foolish, into which the thoughtless force of a burning passion burst forth.

The origin of the love was honourable, but its excess was deformed. It makes no difference from what honourable cause a person goes mad.

Hence Xystus says in his *Sayings*: “An overly ardent lover is an adulterer toward his own wife. In another man’s wife every love is shameful; toward one’s own wife it is excessive.”

**Note:** Nearly all the manuscripts read *Sextus*. See the notes on Epistle 133, p. 124. The following saying about Otho agrees with this view:

> “He had begun to be the adulterer of his own wife.”

Gravius prefers to read: “For all love toward another man’s wife is shameful; toward one’s own it is excessive, most shameful.”

A wise man ought to love his wife by judgment, not by passion. Let the impulse of pleasure be governed, and let him not rush headlong into intercourse. Nothing is uglier than loving one’s wife as though she were another man’s adulterous partner.

Certainly, those who say that they join themselves to wives and raise children for the sake of the commonwealth and the human race should at least imitate animals: after their wives’ wombs have swollen, they should not lose interest in their children. They should not present themselves as lovers to their wives, but as husbands.

Some men’s marriages have been bound together by adulteries; and, disgraceful as it is, the very men who had taken away chastity imposed it upon others. Thus such marriages were soon dissolved by satiety. As soon as the pandering of lust had disappeared, what had been pleasurable became worthless.

For what, says Seneca, shall I say about poor men, many of whom are hired under the name of “husband” to evade the laws enacted against celibates? How can a man govern morals, prescribe chastity, and maintain the authority of a husband when he himself has married?

It is the voice of a most learned man that chastity must be preserved above all things; once it is lost, every virtue collapses. In it lies the pre-eminence of women’s virtues. It commends a poor woman, raises up a wealthy one, redeems an unattractive one, and adorns a beautiful one. It serves the interests of her ancestors, whose blood she does not corrupt with secret offspring; it serves the interests of her children, who need neither be ashamed of their mother nor uncertain of their father; and, above all, it serves her own interests, since it protects her from the insult of an outsider’s body.

No captivity is more disastrous than being dragged into another person’s lust.

The consulship gives distinction to men; eloquence raises them to eternal renown; military glory and triumph consecrate them as founders of a new lineage. There are many things that ennoble outstanding talents. A woman’s particular virtue, however, is chastity.

It made Lucretia equal to Brutus—perhaps even superior to him, since Brutus learned from a woman that it was impossible to remain in slavery. It made Cornelia equal to Gracchus, and Porcia equal to the other Brutus.

Tanaquil is more famous than her husband. Antiquity has now concealed him among the many names of kings. Her rare virtue among women, however, has fixed her more deeply in the memory of all ages than to be capable of falling from it.

Therefore let married women imitate Theano, Cleobulina, Gorguntes, Timocleia, the Claudias, and the Cornelias. And when they see that the Apostle forgave women for a second marriage, let them read that, before our religion shone upon the world, having only one husband was always regarded as an honour among matrons. Through such women the rites of the Female Fortune were customarily performed; there was no priest who had married twice and no Flamen who had married twice.

**Note:** The manuscripts read *Theanum*, but the Greek form θεάνω is indeclinable. Concerning the exceedingly wise wife of Pythagoras herself and other distinguished women, see Plutarch near the end of *Advice on Marriage*. In Polyenus, *Stratagems* II, “Cleobulina” is printed erroneously as “Deubulina” in the *Chronicle*.

**Note:** The Casanatensis reads “no twice-married priestess.” On the Hierophants and the drinking—or, more correctly, the application to the male organs—of hemlock, see Origen, *Against Celsus* VII. Jerome has also reproduced this passage from Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, final chapter: “They do not place a crown upon Female Fortune except upon a woman of one husband . . . . The High Priest and the Flaminica marry once,” etc. By *Flamen*, Jerome means the *Flamen Dialis*, as is clear from Aulus Gellius, X.15, which records several laws concerning the *Flaminica Dialis*.

The Hierophants of the Athenians, moreover, are even today castrated by drinking hemlock; and after they have been chosen for the priesthood, they cease to be men.

## BOOK TWO

### 1. Jovinian’s second proposition

The second proposition is that those who have been baptized cannot be tempted by the devil. And lest this appear to have been foolishly asserted, he added:

> “But whoever has been tempted, I shall show to have been baptized only with water and not with the Spirit; this is what we read concerning Simon Magus. Hence John also says: ‘Everyone who has been born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God. By this the children of God and the children of the devil are revealed’ (1 John 3:9). And at the end of the Epistle: ‘Everyone who has been born of God does not sin, but the generation of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him’ (1 John 5:18).”

### 2. Jerome: Sin drives Christ away and brings in the devil

The objection is indeed strong, and would remain insoluble unless it were answered by John’s own testimony. For he immediately adds: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21). If everyone who has been born of God does not sin and cannot be tempted by the devil, how does he command them to beware lest they be tempted?

Again, in the same Epistle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us” (1 John 1:8 and following).

I think that John, himself baptized, wrote to baptized people, and that every sin comes from the devil. John confesses himself a sinner and hopes for the forgiveness of sins after baptism; but my Jovinian says: “Do not touch me, for I am clean” (Isa. 65, according to the Septuagint).

What, then? Does the Apostle contradict himself? Certainly not. In the same passage he immediately explains why he said this: “My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone has sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the expiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world. And by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments. Whoever says that he knows him and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But whoever keeps his word, truly in him the love of God is perfected. By this we know that we are in him. Whoever says that he remains in him ought to walk just as he walked” (1 John 2:1 and following).

“Therefore,” he says, “I write to you, my little children: ‘Everyone who has been born of God does not sin,’ so that you may not sin, and may know that you remain in the generation of the Lord as long as you have not sinned. Indeed, those who persevere in the generation of the Lord cannot sin. For what fellowship is there between light and darkness, between Christ and Belial?” (2 Cor. 6:14).

Just as day and night cannot be mixed, so neither can righteousness and iniquity, sin and good works, Christ and Antichrist. If we receive Christ as a guest within our breast [or: body], we immediately drive out the devil. If we sin and the devil enters through the door of sin, Christ immediately departs.

Hence David, after his sin, says: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Ps. 50:14)—the joy, clearly, that he had lost by sinning.

“Whoever says that he knows him and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him” (John 2:4). Christ is called Truth: “I am,” he says, “the way and the life and the truth” (John 14:6).

**Note:** The old edition adds *immo est* (“indeed, he is”). In the following Johannine verse, the words “and life” have been supplied from all the manuscripts and from Victorius. We boast in vain of belonging to him if we do not do his commandments.

For one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin. Just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead. Let us not think it a great thing merely to know one God, since even the demons believe and tremble.

“Whoever says that he remains in him ought to walk just as he walked” (1 John 1:6).

Let the opponent choose whichever of the two he wishes; we grant him the choice. Does he remain in Christ, or does he not remain? If he remains, then let him walk as Christ walked. But if it is rash to promise a likeness to the Lord’s virtues, then he does not remain in Christ, because he does not walk as Christ walked.

He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Pet. 2:22), and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:9). The prince of this world came to him and found nothing in him. Though he had committed no sin, God made him sin for us (1 John 3:5).

But we all sin much, according to the Epistle of James, and no one is free from sins, even if his life were only one day long (Jas. 3:2). “For who can say, ‘I have made my heart clean’? Or who can say, ‘I am pure from my sins’?” (Prov. 20:9). We are held guilty in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.

Hence David says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50:7).

And blessed Job says: “If I am righteous, my mouth will speak impiously; and if I am without guilt, I shall be found perverse. Even if I were purified in snow and washed with clean hands, you would stain me sufficiently with filth, and my garment would be abhorrent” (Job 14, according to the Septuagint, and 9).

**Note:** Two manuscripts read “she gave birth to me,” but the Greek has ἐκίσσησέ με, “she conceived me.” Shortly afterward, the Casanatensis reads “and my garment was accursed,” omitting *me*.

But lest we despair completely, thinking that after the sins committed following baptism we cannot be saved, he immediately qualifies this very point: “If anyone has sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the expiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world” (1 John 2:1).

He is speaking here to believers after baptism and promising the Lord as advocate for their offences. He does not say, “If you have committed any sin, you have an advocate with the Father, Christ, and he is the expiation for your sins,” lest you should say that they had not received baptism with complete faith. Rather, he says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, and he is the expiation for our sins,” not merely for the sins of John and of those to whom he writes, but also for those of the whole world.

**Note:** Martianus had omitted the words “with the Father.” The Casanatensis reads: “for the sins of John and of those to whom he writes; but also . . .”; Victorius preferred “and of others only.”

In the whole world are included all the Apostles and all believers. From this it is clearly proved that sin can be committed after baptism. For we have Jesus Christ as advocate in vain if sin cannot be committed.

### 3. The error of Montanus and Novatian condemned. We were created with free will. A new faction of ignorance

The Apostle Peter, to whom it had been said, “He who has been washed has no need to wash again” (John 13:10), and, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18), denies Christ when frightened by a serving girl.

And the Lord himself says: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has asked for you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Matt. 16:26).

In the same passage he says: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

If you reply that this was said before the cross, then certainly after the cross we say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:12).

If we do not sin after baptism, why do we ask that sins be forgiven us—sins that have already been forgiven in baptism? Why do we pray not to enter into temptation and to be delivered from evil, if the devil cannot tempt those who have already been baptized?

It would be another matter if this prayer belonged to catechumens and did not apply to the faithful and to Christians.

Paul, the chosen vessel, disciplines his body and brings it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should be found rejected (1 Cor. 9). “And there was given to me,” he says, “a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Cor. 12:7).

**Note:** Two older manuscripts do not have the words “a thorn in the flesh,” which are nevertheless present in the Greek text, σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί. That they were once absent from certain copies is indicated by the old Ethiopic version, which does not contain them. In the following verse all the manuscripts read “lest, as the serpent …”; the Greek likewise lacks μή πως. Finally, farther below the words “if I forgave anything” are absent from the manuscripts, with the Ethiopic version supporting this absence.

And to the Corinthians: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:3).

And elsewhere: “To whom you have forgiven anything, I also forgive. For whatever I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I have forgiven for your sake in the person of Christ, lest we be outwitted by Satan. For we are not ignorant of his devices” (2 Cor. 2:10–11).

And again: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human. But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; rather, with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure” (1 Cor. 10:13).

**Note:** The Veronensis manuscript reads “and the outcome” (*eventum*; Greek *ἔκβασιν*). Shortly afterward, *revertimini* (“return”) is absent, as below are *concupiscit* (“desires”) and the following *enim* (“for”), in all the Hieronymian manuscripts.

And: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.”

And to the Galatians: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Gal. 5:7).

And elsewhere: “We wanted to come to you—I, Paul, once and again—but Satan hindered us” (1 Thess. 2:18).

And to husbands: “Return again to the same union, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (1 Cor. 7:5).

And again: “I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfil the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these oppose each other, so that you do not do whatever you wish” (Gal. 5:16–17).

Since we are composed of both, it is necessary that we suffer the battles of the two substances against each other.

And to the Ephesians: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

**Note:** Earlier editions read “princes,” against the manuscripts. The Casanatensis reads, “and that after baptism we are asleep.”

Does anyone suppose that after baptism we ought to be secure and asleep?

And again, to the Hebrews: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and who have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and exposing him to public disgrace” (Heb. 6:4 and following).

We cannot deny that those who have been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, and who have tasted the good word were baptized.

**Note:** The name “God” has been removed here on the authority of the Veronensis codex and Victorius. But if the baptized cannot sin, how does the Apostle now say, “And they have fallen away”?

Yet lest Montanus and Novatian rejoice here—men who contend that those who crucified the Son of God for themselves and exposed him to public disgrace cannot be renewed through repentance—he consequently resolves this error and says:

“But we are confident concerning you, beloved, of better things and things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way. For God is not unjust, that he should forget your work and the love which you showed in his name, when you ministered to the saints and continue to minister” (Heb. 9:10).

**Note:** After Erasmus, Martianus adds here *boni*, “of the good,” contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts and to Victorius’ correction.

Indeed, it would be a great injustice on God’s part if he punished sins alone and did not accept good works. “I have spoken,” the Apostle says, “in order to draw you back from sins and make you more cautious through fear of despair. But I am confident concerning you, beloved, of better things and things nearer to salvation. For it is not consistent with God’s justice that he should forget good works and the ministry which you have shown and continue to show toward the saints for his name’s sake, and remember sins alone.”

The Apostle James also, knowing that the baptized can be tempted and can fall by their own will, says: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love him” (Jas. 1:12).

And lest we suppose, on the basis of the passage in Genesis where Abraham is said to have been tempted by God, that we too are tempted by God, he says: “Let no one, when he is tempted, say, ‘I am tempted by God.’ For God is not a tempter of evils; he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, produces death” (Jas. 1:13 and following).

God created us with free will; we are driven by no necessity either toward virtues or toward vices. Otherwise, where there is necessity, there is no crown.

**Note:** “Where there is necessity, where is the crown?” Earlier books falsely added: “nor condemnation.” The manuscript of Saint-Germain reads the sentence interrogatively: “Otherwise, where there is necessity, where is the crown?” Older printed editions may more correctly add “nor condemnation.”

Just as God is the one who perfects good works—for it is “not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy and assists us, so that we may be able to reach the finish”—

**Note:** “Of God who assists us, so that we may reach the goal.” We read the same thought at the beginning of our holy father Benedict’s Prologue to his Rule: “Whenever you begin any good work, beg of him with most earnest prayer that he bring it to completion.” Here God is the one who perfects good works. Let our theologians now take care not to twist the words of the saints to their own meanings, but interpret them with pure and simple faith, turning neither to the right nor to the left.

—so, in evils and sins, our seeds are the incitements, and the devil brings them to completion. When he sees us building hay, wood, and straw upon the foundation of Christ, he sets the fire beneath it.

Let us therefore build gold, silver, and precious stones, and he will not dare to tempt us—although even in this there is no certain or secure possession. For the lion sits in ambush and in secret places in order to kill the innocent.
