**Note:** The Veronensis manuscript and the old edition read, “that he may kill in secret places.” Shortly afterward, other manuscripts read “temptation and tribulations.”

The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, but temptation and tribulation test righteous men.

And elsewhere it is written: “My son, when you approach the service of God, prepare yourself for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1; 2:6).

James says again: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks at the face of his birth in a mirror. He looked at himself and immediately went away and forgot what he was like” (Jas. 1:22 and following).

**Note:** Martianus, after Erasmus, omits the word *verbi*, “of the word,” here.

He would have warned them in vain to join works to faith if they could not sin after baptism. “Whoever keeps the whole law,” he says, “but sins in one point, has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2:10).

Who among us is without sin? God enclosed all things under sin so that he might have mercy upon all (Rom. 11:32).

Peter also knows how to rescue the devout from temptation. “The Lord,” he says, “knows how to rescue the devout from temptation” (2 Pet. 2:9).

And concerning false teachers: “These are springs without water and mists driven by storms, for whom the gloom of darkness has been reserved. For speaking proudly and vainly, they entice in the desires of the flesh and in debauchery those who had barely escaped and have returned to error” (ibid. 2:17–18).

Does not the Apostolic discourse seem to you to have painted a new faction of ignorance? They open, as it were, springs of knowledge, because they promise a rain of teachings which they do not possess, like prophetic clouds through which the truth of God might reach us; yet they are driven about by the storms of demons and vices.

**Note:** Victorius reads, “who do not have the water of teachings.”

They speak grandly, and all their speech is pride. “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God” (Prov. 16, according to the Septuagint).

Thus those who had barely fled from sins return to their own error, and they persuade them toward luxury and the pleasures of food and the flesh.

**Note:** All the manuscripts read “the delicacies of food and the flesh.” Shortly afterward, where the text has *pravos*, “wicked,” the earlier form was *parvos*, “small.” Gravius suspects that *patruos* should be read; previously the phrase was “wisely prudent.”

For who would not gladly hear: “Let us eat and drink, and we shall reign forever”?

They call the wise and prudent wicked, while they listen more eagerly to those who are sweet in speech.

The Apostle John—or rather the Saviour writing through John—to the angel of the Church at Ephesus says: “I know your works, your labour, and your endurance, and that you have endured for my name and have not grown weary. But I have this against you: that you have abandoned your first love. Remember from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works. Otherwise I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you repent” (Rev. 2:2 and following).

Similarly, he calls the other churches—Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea—to repentance, and threatens them unless they return to their former works.

And in Sardis he says that he has a few who have not defiled their garments; they will walk with him in white, because they are worthy.

To whom else does he say, “Remember from where you have fallen”? And: “Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, so that you may be tested.” And: “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is.” And: “Keep in mind how you received and heard; preserve it and repent.”

All these and similar things he says to one who believed and was baptized, and who, although once standing, fell through sin.

### 4. All the saints of former times possessed the same merit as Christians now. Solomon departed from God through his love of women. Jesus son of Jehozadak as a type of the Savior. Angels can receive sin.

I had for a little while postponed examples from the Old Testament, because whenever they argue against them they are accustomed to say, “The Law and the Prophets lasted until John” (Matt. 11). But who is unaware that, under another dispensation of God, all the saints of former times possessed the same merit as Christians now do? As marriage was pleasing before Abraham, so virgins now please God through perpetual chastity. He served the law and his own time; [Note: The Casanatensis together with the Veronensis reads, “let us also serve the law and our own time.”] let us also serve the Gospel and our own time, toward which the ends of the ages have run their course (1 Cor. 10).

David, chosen according to the heart of the Lord (1 Sam. 13), who had done all His will and who had said in one of the Psalms, “Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence, and, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened. Test me, O Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. 25:1–2), is afterward tempted by the devil, and, repenting after his sin, says: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 51:1). He wishes a great sin to be erased by great mercy.

Solomon, beloved of the Lord, to whom God had twice revealed Himself, because he was a lover of women departed from the love of God. Manasseh, the most impious king, is reported by the Book of Chronicles to have been restored after the Babylonian captivity to his former dignity. Josiah, a holy man, was struck down in the plain of Megiddo by the Egyptian king.

Jesus, son of Jehozadak, the high priest, although he had preceded the Savior as a type—who bore our sins and joined to Himself a Church from among the Gentiles—is nevertheless presented according to the literal sense as defiled after his priesthood, and the devil stands at his right hand; afterward white garments are restored to him.

It is superfluous to write about Moses and Aaron, that they offended God at the water of contradiction and did not enter the promised land, since blessed Job declares that even angels and every creature can sin, saying: “For is a man clean before God? Or is a man without blemish in his works? If he does not believe in his servants, and finds something perverse against his angels, how much more in those who dwell in houses of clay” (Job 4:17ff.), since we too are made from the same clay! [Note: The Veronensis reads, “Is a man clean before the Lord, or [clean] in his works,” etc.] “The life of man upon earth is a temptation” (Job 7:1).

And Lucifer fell, he who was sending himself against all the nations. And he who was nourished in paradise of delights among twelve stones, wounded by the mountain of the Lord, descended to the underworld. Hence the Savior also says in the Gospel: “I was watching Satan fall from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10:18). If that highest sublimity fell, who cannot fall? If there are ruins in heaven, how much more on earth?

And yet, when Lucifer fell—or rather, after his fall, the ancient serpent—“his strength is in his loins, and his power is over the navel of his belly. [Note: The manuscript reads “his strength is in his loins” in place of “his strength.”] The great trees are shaded by him, and he sleeps beside the rush and the reed and the sedge. He is king over all that are in the waters” (Job 40ff.): that is, where there are pleasure and luxury, procreation, and the irrigation of marriage. “For who will strip the face of his garment? And who will open the doors of his face? Nations are fattened upon him, and the Phoenician peoples divide him among themselves” (Job 41). [Note: I delete here the word “Ethiopians,” which editions hitherto add; it occurs in no manuscript or old edition, and neither the Hebrew text nor any translation admits it—not even the ancient translation which Jerome published with obeli and asterisks, and which it will be worthwhile to compare with these Greek citations. Shortly afterward, in place of “has been given,” read “is to be given.”]

And lest the reader’s silent thought perhaps suppose that only those Phoenician nations and the Ethiopian people are meant, to whom the dragon was given as food, immediately, concerning those who cross the sea of this age and hasten to reach the harbor of salvation, it is said:

> “And in the ships of fishermen his head stands like an indefatigable anvil [or: like an anvil]. He regards iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood. And all the gold of the sea beneath him is like clay. He makes the abyss boil like a bronze vessel; he considers the sea as a wiped-out thing, and the abyss of Tartarus as a captive. He sees every lofty thing” (Job 40, at the end, and 41:5).

[Note: “And in the ships of fishermen.” From this passage, which Jerome subsequently repeats, we can learn how much was omitted from the Book of Job according to the Septuagint, if we consult the first volume of our edition—that is, the Divine Library of St. Jerome—where the Book of Job is printed in its proper place with asterisks and obeli. —Martian.]

The Greek has *ἐξάλειπτρον*, which is a vessel for ointment, according to Pollux and Suidas; other interpreters likewise understand it so, and Jerome himself suggests this in his version from the Hebrew. But the old Latin translator, through an easy slip of the eyes, read *ἐξάλειπτον*, from *ἐξαλείφω*, “erased.”

And my Jovinianus supposes that he can easily make him yield. What shall I say about holy men and angels, who, since they are creatures of God, can certainly receive sin? He dared to tempt the Son of God, and, rebuffed by His first and second sentence, nevertheless raises his head; wounded a third time, he withdraws for a while, postponing rather than removing the temptation. And we flatter ourselves because of baptism, which, just as it forgives former sins, cannot preserve us from future ones unless the baptized guard their hearts with all vigilance.

### 5. The third question.

At last we have reached the subject of foods, and the difficulty of the third question is brought against us:

> “Everything was created for this purpose: that it might serve the use of mortals. And just as man, a rational animal, as a kind of inhabitant and possessor of the world, is subject to God and venerates his Creator, so all living creatures were created either for human food, clothing, cutting the earth, transporting crops, [Note: The Casanatensis adds, “and of man himself.” Jerome later recalls this passage in Isaiah 1; Lactantius, Book 2, chapter 11: “They are called beasts of burden because they were made to help in cultivating the earth.” See Columella at the beginning of Book 6.] or for man himself; hence they are called *jumenta*, beasts of burden, from the fact that they help.

> “What is man,” David says, “that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and moreover the cattle of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea” (Ps. 8:5ff.).

> “Granted,” he says: let the ox have been created for plowing, the horse for riding, the dog for guarding, goats for milk, sheep for wool. What use are pigs apart from eating their flesh? What of roe deer, fawns [or: stags], fallow deer, boars, hares, and hunting of this kind? What of wild and domestic geese? What of ducks, fig-peckers, partridges, coots, thrushes? Why does a hen run about in houses? If these things are not eaten, they were all created by God in vain.

> “But what need is there of arguments, when Scripture most clearly teaches that everything that moves, like the vegetables of the herbs, was given to us for food (Gen. 9), and the Apostle cries out: ‘All things are clean to the clean, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving’ (Rom. 14:20); and that in the last days there will be people who forbid marriage and the eating of foods that God created for use (1 Tim. 4)?

> “The Lord Himself is called by the Pharisees a wine-drinker and a glutton, a companion of tax collectors and sinners; He did not refuse the meal of Zacchaeus, and went to the wedding feast. It is another matter if, out of foolish contentiousness, you say that He went to the meal in order to fast [Note: We have substituted *prandium*, “meal,” for the former reading *nuptias*, “wedding,” as all the manuscripts require.] and, like an impostor, said: ‘I eat this, I do not eat that; I do not wish to drink the wine which I created from water.’ As a type of His blood, He offered not water but wine.

> “After His resurrection He ate fish and a honeycomb, not [Note: ‘Not sesame, nuts, etc.’ The manuscript codices read *sisima* or *sisama*. *Sesama*, feminine, is taken as the name of a kind of Indian grain by Pliny, Book 18, chapter 10: ‘We have mentioned summer grains: sesame, millet, panic grass.’ *Sesamum*, neuter, and *sesama* in the plural are more often listed among legumes by Columella, for example in Book 2, chapters 7 and 10. In fact, in our Basque country *sesama* are the very legumes which elsewhere are called peas, but in my homeland are called *seses*, as though one said *sesames*. For our Basque language favors monosyllables and contracted Latin words: thus we call bread *pan*, and say *un can* for one dog. Likewise the elder tree, *sambucus*, we contract to *sauc*. As for the following word, *sorbitiunculas*, I would not venture to determine whether they were the *lagana* or cakes of 2 Kings 13, or small service berries, of which Martial says in Book 13:

> ‘We are service berries, too hard and softening bellies.’

> —Martian. The old edition has *caricas*; the manuscripts variously have *sisama* and *sesama*. At the end the Casanatensis adds *exspectat*, as appears below.]

> “sesame, nuts, and little morsels of fruit.” The Apostle Peter did not wait for the star according to Jewish custom, but at the sixth hour went up to the housetop to eat his meal. Paul breaks bread in the ship, not figs. To Timothy, whose stomach was suffering, he recommends drinking wine, not pear juice.

> “As for their abstinence from foods, is not the *Castum* of the Mother of the Gods and of Isis also a Gentile superstition?”

[Note: It is falsely and contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts that *Cossum* has until now appeared here instead of *Castum*. When Martianus tried to explain this reading, he compounded the error with a new one. He says that *cossi* refers to worms growing in oaks, which Jerome himself describes below and calls *ξυλοφάγοι*, “wood-eaters,” and says that to eat them in Pontus and Phrygia was an extravagance; Pliny likewise says in Book 17, chapter 24: “Luxury makes use of the more delicate *cossi* of oaks as food.” But these matters are entirely irrelevant here, and the worms called *cossi* have nothing to do with the mysteries of Cybele and Isis; in that sense, to take notice of *Cossum* is pointless.

On the contrary, some ancient authors mention the *Castum* of Isis and Cybele. Tertullian, *On Fasting against the Psychics*, chapter 16: “By introducing blasphemies into our xerophagies, you make them equal to the chastity of Isis and Cybele.” Arnobius, Book 5: “Why do you abstain from food made of bread, to which you have given the name *Castus*?” A similar account is found in an uncertain author quoted by Suidas under *Μητρῳακαί*, who calls them *καστεῖαι*:

> “The Motherly observances among the Romans, or even earlier among the Phrygians, were solemnly practiced as *kasteiai*, and he kept them holy each month.”

Some interpret this as a chaste observance, others as an expiation; I would rather understand it as a rite of abstinence in food. This is certainly suggested by the cited testimonies of Tertullian and Arnobius, which I believe agree with Jerome’s own letter 107 to Laeta, section 10: “The worshipers of Isis and Cybele, through gluttonous abstinence, devour Phasian birds and smoking turtle-doves, lest, forsooth, they contaminate the gifts of Ceres.” Clearly, they abstained from bread.

Still more clearly, below in this very book, he says: “Just as the imitation of the Devil’s virgins does not prejudice true virginity, so neither does the *Castum* of Isis and Cybele, nor perpetual abstinence from certain foods, prejudice true fasts, especially since among them fasting from bread is compensated by fattening on meat.” See what we have additionally noted there.

—Martian.

[Note: *Castum* of the Mother. The *cossi* are said to be worms that grow in oak trees. Pliny testifies that they were once considered a delicacy. To eat them in Pontus and Phrygia was an extravagance, as Jerome observes below. The priests of the mother Cybele abstained from these worms through ridiculous superstition, as though they were sacred. —Martian.]

### 6. Jerome. Physicists who wrote in prose and verse. Our religion educates the pursuit of wisdom. The opinion of Epicurus condemned.

I shall therefore follow the steps of the proposition set forth, and before I come to the Scriptures, and show from them the fasts pleasing to God and acceptable continence, I shall set the arguments of the philosophers alongside the arguments of our own case. I shall prove that we do not follow the doctrine of Empedocles and Pythagoras, who, on account of *μετεμψύχωσις*, transmigration of souls, think that nothing which moves and lives should be eaten, and judge guilty of the same crime anyone who cuts down a fir or an oak, since such people are murderers and poisoners. Rather, we venerate our Creator, who created everything for human use [or: produced everything].

And just as oxen were created for plowing, horses for riding, dogs for guarding, goats for milk, and sheep for wool, so pigs, deer, goats, hares, [Note: The Cistercian manuscript together with the Casanatensis reads: “and other creatures of this kind were not created immediately for eating,” etc.] and the rest were created not immediately for eating, but for other human uses.

For if everything that moves and lives was made for consumption and prepared for the appetite, let them answer me: why were elephants, lions, bears, leopards, and wolves created? Why vipers, scorpions, bugs, mosquitoes, and fleas? Why the vulture, eagle, raven, and hawk? Why whales, dolphins, seals, and tiny shellfish? Which of us has ever eaten a lion, a viper, a vulture, a stork, a kite, or the little worms that creep along the shores [or: will ever eat them]? Just as these have their particular uses, so we can say that the remaining beasts, fish, [Note: We have supplied the word “birds” from all the manuscripts and the old edition.] and birds were created not for eating but for medicine.

In the end, physicians know for how many purposes the flesh of vipers, from which theriac is prepared, is useful. Pieces of ivory are employed in various remedies. [Note: Formerly the reading was “of ears” in place of “various”; shortly afterward, “eagle’s” stood in place of “hyena’s,” a reading approved by Gravius. See Pliny, Book 29, chapter 6; Dioscorides; and Galen’s *On Simple Remedies*, from which nearly all these details are drawn.] The gall of a hyena restores clarity to the eyes, and its dung and rotten dog matter heal wounds.

And—and this may perhaps seem surprising to the reader—Galen teaches in *On Simple Remedies* (*ἐν ἁπλοῖς*) how many cures human excrement benefits. Physicists say that the skin shed by a snake, boiled in oil, wonderfully relieves earache. What seems so useless to those who do not know as bedbugs? If a leech has stuck in the throat, when its smoke is inhaled it is immediately vomited up; and difficulty in urination is relieved by its application.

As for the usefulness of the fats of pigs, geese, hens, and pheasants, all the books of physicians make it clear. If you read them, you will see as many remedies in a vulture as there are limbs. Peacock dung reduces the heat of gout. I would describe the diseases for which cranes, storks, eagle’s gall, hawk’s blood, the ostrich, frogs, chameleons, and the dung and flesh of swallows are suitable, if it were my purpose to discuss the healing of bodies.

Let whoever wishes read Aristotle and Theophrastus in prose, Marcellus of Side in verse, [Note: “And our Flavius.” Of this same Flavius, the book *On Illustrious Men* says in the notice of Firmianus: “Firmianus, who is also Lactantius … having been summoned under the emperor Diocletian together with Flavius the Grammarian, whose books composed in verse on medical subjects are extant,” etc. —Martian.

Understand him as the grammarian whose books on medical subjects composed in verse he himself says are extant in the *Catalogue*, chapter 80. Some think that he is the same person as Flavius Capro; others, wrongly, read *Fannius* instead of *Flavius*; the Casanatensis has *Flavus*. —Martian.] and our Flavius discussing these matters in hexameter verse; and likewise Pliny Secundus, Dioscorides, and all the other physicists and physicians, who refer every herb, every stone, and every animal—whether creeping, flying, or swimming—to the usefulness of their art.

Therefore, when you ask me why the pig was created, I shall immediately answer you, like boys arguing with one another: Why the viper? Why the scorpion? Nor will you judge God to be the creator of useless things merely because there are many beasts and birds which your jaws reject.

But lest this appear more contentious and combative than true, hear why pigs, boars, deer, and the other animals were created: so that soldiers, athletes, [Note: “Sailors, rhetors.” Marianus considers it a foul error to read *nautae, rhetores*, assigning *sectores* to the rhetors. Gravius, in his notes on this passage, wished to argue as follows: “Sailors, rhetors, etc. A great error has crept into the copies; correct it by reading *vectores*, carriers.” Read likewise in Book 2 *Against the Pelagians*: “Sailors and carriers speak”; and he joins the same two in Ezekiel 17 and Matthew 14, etc.

But, with the permission of Marianus and Gravius, let us adhere to the authority of the manuscript codices and defend the reading of Erasmus, since the context itself of Jerome teaches that it should be retained. The holy Doctor says that pigs, boars, deer, and so forth were created so that soldiers, athletes, sailors, rhetors, and miners might have food. He later adds what applies to each group: those who carry weapons are soldiers; those who weaken their bodies with punches and kicks are athletes; those who pull oars are sailors; those whose sides are strong for shouting and speaking are rhetors; those who overturn mountains are miners.

Jerome then adds: “Our religion does not educate a boxer, athlete, sailor, soldier, or miner, but a pursuer of wisdom,” etc. Certainly, if he had earlier read *sectores* or *vectores*, he would say here: “Our religion does not educate carriers or cutters.” But because Christianity educates rhetors and orators, he omitted that word while rejecting the other names. The word *rhetors* must therefore be retained. Apart from what has already been said, this is supported by Cicero, *On Old Age*: “I would have argued the Voconian Law in a loud voice and with strong lungs.” In the same work he says explicitly: “For the office requires not only intellect, but also lungs and strength.” Strong sides, therefore, for shouting and speaking must be attributed not to cutters or carriers but to rhetors and orators. —Martian.]

sailors, rhetors, miners, and all others enslaved to hard labor might have foods, for whom bodily strength is necessary: those who carry weapons and provisions; those who weaken one another’s limbs with punches and kicks; those who pull oars, whose sides are strong for shouting and speaking; those who overturn mountains and sleep under the open sky and in rain. [Note: The Casanatensis and the old edition have *sub divo*; read *sub dio*, “under the open sky.”]

But our religion does not educate a *πύκτης*, a boxer; nor an athlete; nor sailors; nor soldiers; nor miners; but a pursuer of wisdom, who has dedicated himself to the worship of God and knows why he was created, why he lives in the world, and toward what destination he hastens.

Hence the Apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12:10). And: “Although our outward man is corrupted, the inward man is renewed from day to day” (2 Cor. 4:16; and Col. 3). And: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). And: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14).

Was everyone commanded not to have two tunics, not to carry food in a bag, bronze in a belt, a staff in the hand, [Note: The manuscripts have *calceamenta*, “sandals,” in the plural. Below, “and give to the poor” is absent from the Casanatensis.] or footwear on the feet; to sell everything they possess, give it to the poor, and follow Jesus (Matt. 10; Mark 6)? No, but these instructions were for those who wish to be perfect.

Otherwise John the Baptist gives one command to soldiers and another to tax collectors. The Lord, moreover, says in the Gospel to the man who had boasted that he had fulfilled all the commandments of the law: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). Lest He seem to impose a burdensome load upon one unwilling, He left the matter to the listener’s own will, saying: “If you wish to be perfect.”

Therefore I too shall say to you: If you wish to be perfect, it is good not to drink wine and not to eat meat. If you wish to be perfect, it is better to fatten the soul than the body. But if you are a child [or: immature], and the rules of cooks delight you, no one snatches savory dishes from your jaws.

Eat and drink, and, if it pleases you, rise up and play with Israel, singing: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Cor. 15:32). Let him eat and drink who expects destruction after his meals, who says with Epicurus: “After death there is nothing, and death itself is nothing.”

We believe Paul when he thunders: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6:13).

### 7. The food of various nations. John the Baptist’s locusts. Valens’ law against eating calves. Customs of various peoples. Each Egyptian city worshiped a particular animal.

We have set down these few passages from Scripture in order to show that our teaching agrees with the philosophers. [Note: The manuscripts read, “These few passages from Scripture, in order that we might show [our teaching] to agree,” etc.] But who is unaware that each nation is accustomed to eat not according to the common law of nature, but according to what is plentiful among them?

For example, the Arabs and Saracens, and all the barbarian peoples of the desert, live on the milk and flesh of camels, because an animal of this kind is easily bred and nourished among them in accordance with the climate and barrenness of their regions. [Note: The same manuscripts read *pro tempore*, “according to the season,” rather than *pro temperie*, “according to the climate.”] They regard it as impious to eat pork. Pigs, which are accustomed to be fed on acorns, chestnuts, fern roots, and barley, are either rare among them or not found at all; and if they are found, they lack the foods mentioned above.

By contrast, if you compel northern peoples to eat the flesh of asses and camels, they will consider it as though they were forced to eat a wolf or a raven. [Note: Martianus mistakenly had *simulque* in place of *simile*, “as though”; the manuscripts and Victorius correct it.] In Pontus and Phrygia, householders demand as a great source of income the fat white worms with black heads that are born in decaying wood. And just as among us the partridge, fig-pecker, mullet, and scarus are counted delicacies, so among them it is an extravagance to eat the *ξυλοφάγον* [or: *ξυλοφάγιον*], the “wood-eater.”

Again, among the peoples of the East and Libya, because clouds of locusts are found throughout the desert and the hot wilderness, it is customary to eat locusts. John the Baptist also proves this to be true. Compel a Phrygian or a Pontic to eat a locust, and he will regard it as impious. Force a Syrian, African, or Arab to swallow Pontic worms, and he will despise them as much as flies, millipedes, and lizards. [Note: Another reading is *millepedias*. A *millepeda* is a kind of worm supported by many feet. Shortly afterward some have *raritatem*, “rarity,” instead of *charitatem*, “charity.”] Yet Syrians are accustomed to eat land crocodiles, and Africans green lizards as well.

In Egypt and Palestine, because oxen are scarce, no one eats a cow; instead they use the flesh of bulls, oxen, and calves as food. But in our province people consider it a crime to devour calves. Hence the emperor Valens recently issued a law throughout the East forbidding anyone to eat the flesh of calves, both providing for the needs of agriculture and correcting the wicked custom of the Judaizing populace, which consumed calves instead of fattened animals and sucklings. [Note: This is what they call tender piglets, which the Greeks also call *γαλαθηνοί*. See Diogenes Laertius in his account of Pythagoras.]

Nomads, Troglodytes, Scythians, and the new savagery of the Huns eat half-raw meat. The Ichthyophagi, a wandering people on the shore of the Red Sea, roast fish on rocks burning with the sun’s heat, and live on this food alone.

Sarmatians, Quadi, Vandals, and countless other peoples take pleasure in the flesh of horses and foxes.

Why should I speak of other nations, when, as a young man in Gaul, I myself saw the Atticoti [or: Scots], a British people, eating human flesh? Although they find herds of pigs and cattle and flocks of sheep throughout the forests, they are accustomed to cut off the buttocks of shepherds, as well as the breasts of women, and to regard these alone as delicacies of food? [Note: “I saw the Atticoti.” Erasmus and Marianus read *Scotos* here, a British people; but all the manuscript codices retain *Atticotos* or *Aticottos*. As for who the Acticottae or Atticotti were, see Buchanan, Book 2 of *Scottish History*, page 17, and the book *On the Military Offices of the Romans throughout the Provinces*. Ammianus Marcellinus says of them in Book 27: “The Actacoti, a warlike nation of men, and the Scots wandering in various places.” Here the Atticoti are distinguished from the Scots, as they are in Jerome’s context. —Martian.

Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 26, chapter 4, reads *Atacottos*: “The Picts, Saxons, Scots, and Atacotti harassed the Britons with continual hardships.” See Jerome, Letter 69, section 3.]

The nation of the Scots does not have individual wives; and, as though it had read Plato’s constitution and followed Cato’s example, no man among them has a wife of his own, but they indulge promiscuously like animals. [Note: Plato wished wives to be held in common in his *Republic*. Cato lent his own wife to Hortensius, as noted near the end of the preceding book.]

The Persians, Medes, Indians, and Ethiopians, kingdoms of no small size and equal to the Roman Empire, join themselves to their mothers and grandmothers, their daughters and granddaughters. [Note: A learned man contends that the word *regno*, “kingdom,” should be deleted. The manuscripts, however, have *imperio*, “empire,” in place of *regno*, and this is preferable. What Jerome reports of the Persians, Medes, and the rest is also related by other authors.]

[Note: Jerome borrowed the following accounts of various peoples, like many other passages, from Porphyry’s book *On Abstinence from Animal Life* (*περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων*); indeed, he translated it almost word for word. I add here some material from which St. Doctor’s text may to some extent be polished and restored:

> “It is reported that the Massagetae and Derbices consider those who die naturally to be the most wretched of their people. Therefore, before that happens, they sacrifice and eat their dearest ones when they have grown old. The Tibarenians throw their nearest elders alive from a precipice. The Hyrcanians and Caspians expose the living to birds and dogs, and the dead likewise. The Scythians bury the living together with the dead and slaughter them upon the funeral pyres, those whom the dead had loved most. The Bactrians throw their aged alive to dogs; and when Stasanor, Alexander’s governor, attempted to abolish this custom, he nearly lost his authority.”]

The Massagetae and Derbices consider those who die from illness the most miserable, and when their parents, relatives, and close kin have reached old age, they slaughter and devour them, believing it better that they be eaten by them than by worms. [Note: The Casanatensis reads “believing it better,” followed by all the other manuscripts; *consummantur*, “are consumed,” appears instead of *comedantur*, “are eaten.” Concerning the Massagetae, who are a Scythian people, Sextus Empiricus tells much the same story in *Pyrrhonian Outlines*. Concerning the Derbices, see Aelian, Book 4, chapter 1, *Various History*. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 9: “They say that among certain Gentiles each dead Scythian is eaten by his own people.” More accurately, *Against Marcion*, Book 1: “They eat the corpses of their parents, slaughtered with the animals, at a feast; those who do not die in such a way as to be fit for food have suffered an accursed death.”]

The Tibarenians hang the old people they loved on gallows. [Note: Porphyry says *κατακρημνίζουσιν*, which properly means “they cast down from a precipice,” as is also clear from Theodoret’s discourse on laws.] The Hyrcanians cast the half-living to birds and dogs; the Caspians cast the dead to the same beasts. The Scythians bury alive those who were loved by the dead, together with the bones of the dead. The Bactrians throw old men to dogs trained for this very purpose. When Stasanor, Alexander’s prefect, wished to correct this practice, he nearly lost his province. [Note: All printed books had until now falsely read *Nicanor* instead of *Stasanor*, a name preserved by two manuscripts, the Veronensis and Cisterciensis. The Greek text of Porphyry likewise has *Στασάνωρ*, and the historical evidence supports it.]

Compel an Egyptian to eat sheep’s milk; if you can, force a man of Pelusium to eat an onion. Almost every city in Egypt venerates a particular animal and a particular monster; whatever they worship, they consider inviolable and sacred. Hence their cities too are named from the names of animals: Leonto, Cyno, Lyco, Busiris, Thmuis, which means “goat.”

And to show what sort of gods Egypt had always received, recently one of their cities was called Antinous after Hadrian’s favorite. [Note: “Their city, Antinous.” Concerning Antinous, see our annotations in volume 3 of our edition, on Isaiah 2. —Martian.

Previously the form was *Antinois*. But *Antinous*, as found in the manuscripts, frequently occurs among ancient authors for *Antinoupolis*, and the city is almost never called otherwise. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 22: “Antinoon, which Hadrian founded in honor of the youth Antinous.” The Greeks say *Ἀντινώ*; hence *Antino* for *Antinopolis*, as *Pano* for *Panopolis*, and as Jerome himself has *Cyno* for *Cynopolis*.]

You see, therefore, that not only in eating, but also in burials, marriages, and every form of social life, each nation lives according to its own rite and characteristics, and considers to be the law of nature whatever it has learned.

But suppose that the eating of meat is common to all nations, and that whatever grows everywhere is everywhere permitted. What has this to do with us, whose citizenship is in heaven? Above Pythagoras and Empedocles and all the followers of wisdom, we do not belong to the one from whom we are born, but to the one from whom we are reborn. We subdue the resisting flesh, which drags us toward the incitements of lust, by fasting.

The eating of meat, the drinking of wine, and the satiety of the belly are the seedbed of lust. Hence the Comic Poet says:

> “Without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold.”

### 8. The five senses, entrances of the vices. Love of women is close to madness.

Through the five senses, as through certain windows, the vices gain entrance to the soul. The metropolis and citadel of the mind cannot be captured unless the hostile army has rushed in through its gates. The soul is weighed down by disturbances of these senses and is captured by sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.

If someone delights in the Circus games, in the contests of athletes, in the movement of actors, in the forms of women, in the brilliance of gems, clothing, and metals, and in other things of this kind, the soul’s freedom has been captured through the windows of the eyes, and the prophetic saying is fulfilled: “Death entered through your windows” (Jer. 21). [Note: Victorius preferred “our windows,” against the Greek *ὑμῶν*, “your.” Shortly afterward the Veronensis has “modulations” in place of “inflections”; finally, the old edition with Victorius has “comedian performances” in place of “comedies.”] Again, hearing is soothed by the varied music of instruments and the inflections of voices; by the songs of poets, the comedies, and the wit and tricks of mimes—whatever, entering through the ears, makes the manliness of the mind effeminate.

But the sweetness of odors, various incense, amomum, cyphi, oenanthe, [Note: Consult Dioscorides concerning these perfumes. Examples of eagerness for food may be found in Petronius’ *Satyricon*. The *mulsum* he mentions, in the poet Macer, whom Sigebertus records, is wine or even water diluted with honey.] musk, and the foreign skin of the mouse—things suitable, as people say, to the dissolute and the lovers—no one who is not dissolute denies.

Moreover, who is unaware that greed for food is the mother of avarice, and that it holds the mind, as though weighed down by fetters, fixed upon the earth? For the brief pleasure of the throat, lands and seas are searched; and so that honeyed wine and costly food may pass through our throats, we labor through the work of our entire life.

But the touching of other bodies and the more ardent desire for women are close to madness. Because of this sense we desire, become angry, rejoice, envy, emulate, and remain anxious; and once pleasure has been completed, we are inflamed again through a kind of regret. [Note: The Casanatensis does not contain “these things: we envy, emulate, remain anxious.” The old edition has “fullness” in place of “regret”; all the manuscripts have “we are inflamed” in place of “we inflame,” which has been restored.] We seek to do what, once we have done it, we shall again regret.

Therefore, when through these gates, as though wedges of disturbance, they have entered the citadel of our mind, where will its freedom be? Where its strength? Where its thought of God? Especially when touch also paints for itself past pleasures, and by recalling vices forces the soul to suffer with them and, in a certain way, to practice what it is not doing?

## 9. Crates of Thebes [Cols. 0298B–0299D]

Moved, then, by these considerations, many philosophers abandoned the crowds of the cities and the suburban gardens, where there were irrigated fields, leafy trees, the whispering of birds, the mirror-like surface of a spring, a murmuring stream, and many enticements for the eyes and ears—lest, through luxury and an abundance of resources, the strength of the soul should grow soft and its chastity be violated. For it is useless—indeed dangerous and harmful—to look frequently upon the things by which one has at some time been captivated, and to expose oneself to the experience of things from which one can scarcely abstain. Thus the Pythagoreans too, avoiding such company, customarily lived in solitude and deserted places.

[Note: The manuscripts read “were accustomed.” A little later we emend *locis* to *lucis*—“in the shrines of temples”—because the former gives an unsuitable and pointless sense and conflicts with the evidence of the more carefully corrected codices. Gravius too preferred *lucis*, though long ago Abelard, when quoting this passage in Book II of *Christian Theology*, had already read it in that form.]

The Platonists and Stoics likewise spent their time in the sacred groves and porticoes of temples, so that, reminded by the sanctity of a more confined dwelling [variant: “more august”], they might think of nothing except the virtues. Plato himself, although wealthy and although Diogenes trampled his couches with muddy feet, chose, so that he might devote himself to philosophy, a villa called the Academy, far from the city—not merely deserted but also pestilential—so that the force of lust might be broken by the care and continual presence of illnesses, and his disciples might experience no pleasure except in the things they were learning.

We read that some men put out their own eyes, lest through their sight they be drawn away from contemplation of philosophy. Hence that Crates of Thebes, having thrown a considerable weight of gold into the sea, said:

> Begone, you evil desires; I shall drown you, lest you yourselves drown me.

[Note: Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in his *Oration in Praise of Saint Basil*, attributes this other saying to Crates: “Crates gives the Theban Crater freedom.” See also Letter 118 to Julian, §5.]

If anyone supposes [variant: “judges”] that he can both indulge in an abundance of food and drink and devote himself to wisdom—that is, both live amid delicacies and not be held captive by the vices of delicacies—he deceives himself.

[Note: The old edition reads “always indulge”; the Veronese manuscript, “amid delicacies.”] For if, while far removed from these things, we are often captured by the enticements of nature and compelled to desire things of which we have no supply, how much more so when surrounded by the nets of pleasures we imagine ourselves free! Our sense perceives what it sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches, and it is drawn toward desire for the thing by whose pleasure it is captured.

It is also an ancient saying that the mind sees what the mind hears; and that we could neither hear nor see anything [variant: “could”] unless the sense were directed toward the things we perceive and hear. It is difficult—indeed impossible—for those who overflow with delicacies [variant: the Casanatense manuscript reads “riches”] and pleasures not to think about what they are doing. Certain people pretend in vain that, while preserving faith, chastity, and integrity of mind, they make use of pleasures, when in fact it is contrary to nature to enjoy an abundance of pleasures without pleasure. The Apostle, guarding against this very thing, said:

> But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives. (1 Timothy 5:6)

[Note: I have removed the word “widow,” which neither the Hieronymian manuscripts nor the text of Scripture itself recognizes, whether Latin or Greek.]

## 10. The body as a child, the soul as its tutor. Simpler food that sustains the body [Cols. 0299C–0300D]

The senses of the body are like horses, running without reason, while the soul, like a charioteer, holds back the reins of those who run. And just as horses without a guide rush headlong [variant: “are headlong”] to destruction, so the body, without the reason and command of the soul, is carried toward its own ruin.

Philosophers offer another comparison of soul and body, saying that the body is a child and the soul its tutor.

[Note: Recall Cicero’s words, cited by Augustine from Book III of *On the Republic* in *Against Julian* IV.12 and *The City of God* XIX.11: “God rules man, the mind the body, reason lust,” and so forth.]

[Note: Hence also “the Historian.” Jerome frequently calls Sallustius Crispus by this title, as though he were the most distinguished among historical writers. In the beginning of his history of the Catilinarian conspiracy Sallustius wrote as follows: “But all our strength resides in mind and body. We employ the authority of the mind and the service of the body: the one we share with the gods, the other with the beasts.”]

Hence also the Historian says:

> We make greater use of the authority of the soul and the service of the body. The one we share with the gods, the other with the beasts.

[Note: Sallustius, *Catiline* 1, where *animi* occurs instead of *animae*. Chrysippus, in Claudianus Mamertus, *On the Status of the Soul* 11, says: “He assigns to the soul the right of command and imposes upon the body the law of servitude.”]

Therefore, unless the prudence of the tutor governs the vices of the adolescent [variant: *adolentis*] and the child, all his efforts and impulses hurry toward wantonness. We can live without four senses—that is, without sight, hearing, smell, and touch. But without taste and food it is impossible for the human body to subsist.

Reason, therefore, must be present, so that we take foods of such kinds and in such quantities as will not burden the body or weigh down the freedom of the soul; for one must eat, walk, sleep, digest, and afterward endure the incentives of lust when the veins have been swollen.

> Wine is a wanton thing, and insolent drunkenness. (Proverbs 20:1)  
> Everyone who associates with these will not be wise.

[Note: This is the text of Scripture according to the Septuagint, Proverbs 20:1, a fact previously overlooked. Accordingly, together with the Veronese and Cistercian manuscripts, we read “and insolent drunkenness,” where the text formerly had “and tumultuous.” The Greek itself also differs, reading καὶ ὑβριστικόν—“and insolent.” Gravius approves the emendation. We correct several other minor matters below.]

Nor should we take foods that are difficult to digest, or that cause us, after eating them, to regret the great labor by which they were obtained and prepared. Vegetables, fruits, and legumes are easier to prepare; they require neither skill nor the expense of cooks. They sustain the human body without anxiety, and, since they are consumed moderately—for what does not stimulate the appetite is not devoured greedily—they are digested more easily.

No one is burdened with one or two foods, and those inexpensive, to the point of abdominal swelling; that swelling is produced by the variety of meats and the pleasure of flavor.

[Note: From the same manuscripts, we read “is produced,” namely, the swelling; formerly the reading was “is perceived.”]

When dishes smoke with various aromas, they drag us as captives toward eating them. Hence diseases too are stirred up by excessive satiety; and many cure their inability to restrain their appetite by vomiting, expelling more shamefully what they had shamefully taken in.

## 11. Final chapter of the exhortatory discourse on the arts. The source of the soul’s great exultation. A lighter diet. Examples of frugality [Cols. 0300B–0301D]

Hippocrates teaches in the *Aphorisms* that thick and obese bodies, which have reached the measure of their growth, unless they are quickly reduced by the removal of blood, break out into paralysis and the worst kinds of disease. For this reason reduction is necessary, so that they may again have room in which they can grow. Nature does not allow bodies to remain in one condition; they must either continue growing or diminish, and an animal cannot live unless it is capable of growth.

Hence Galen, a most learned man and interpreter of Hippocrates, says in his *Exhortation to Medicine* that athletes, whose life and profession consist in stuffing themselves, can neither live long nor remain healthy. Their souls, he says, are so wrapped in an excess of blood and fat, as though in mud, that they think of nothing refined or heavenly, but always of flesh, belching, and the gluttony of the belly.

[Note: The work is properly entitled *Προτρεπτικὸς λόγος πρὸς τὰς τέχνας*—“An exhortation addressed to the arts.” The following is the substance of the passage, which Jerome explains in Latin: “For by continually gathering together a mass of flesh and blood, they keep their soul extinguished, as it were, in much mud, unable to understand anything precisely, but mindless like irrational animals.”]

Diogenes asserts that tyrants [variant: “destroyers”] of cities, and wars, whether foreign or civil, are stirred up not for the sake of a simple diet of vegetables and fruits, but for meat and the delicacies of banquets.

And, remarkable as it may seem, Epicurus, the advocate of pleasure, filled all his books with vegetables and fruits and says that one ought to live on inexpensive foods, because meats and elaborate banquets are prepared with immense care and misery, and their penalty in seeking them [variant: “searching for them”] is greater than their pleasure in consuming them. (See Lactantius, Book III, chapter 17.)

Our bodies, however, need only food and drink. Where there is water and bread, and other things like them, nature’s needs have been satisfied. (See Diogenes Laertius, Book X, and Seneca, Book III of the *Letters*, Letters 2 and 25.) Whatever is beyond this does not concern the necessity of life, but the vice of pleasure.

We should drink and eat not for the ardor of delicacies but to extinguish thirst and hunger. [Variant: *crassiore*, “coarser,” is read as *grossiori*, “grosser.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “for the ardor”; formerly the text had “ardor is.” Victorius preferred “for the ardor of delicacies.”]

Those who eat meat also need things that are not meat. But those who make use of a simple diet do not require meat. Nor can we devote ourselves to wisdom if we think about an abundant table, which requires great labor and care.

Nature’s need is quickly satisfied. Cold and hunger can be driven away by simple clothing and food. Hence the Apostle says:

> Having food and clothing [variant: “garment”], let us be content with these. (1 Timothy 6:8)

Delicacies and varieties of banquets are fuel for greed. The soul experiences great exultation when, content with little, you have the world beneath your feet and exchange all its power and banquets and lusts—for the sake of which riches are acquired—for cheap foods and compensate for them with a coarser tunic.

Take away the luxury of banquets and lust, and no one will seek riches, whose use is either in the belly or beneath the belly.

One who is ill does not recover health except through light food and a disciplined diet, which is called λεπτὴ δίαιτα—“a light diet.” Therefore, by the foods through which health is restored, health can also be preserved, lest anyone think that diseases are provoked by vegetables.

But if vegetables do not supply the strength of that Milo of Croton—vegetables that grow and are nourished from meat—what need has a wise man and philosopher of Christ for such great strength, which is necessary to athletes and soldiers, and which, once acquired, provokes him to vices?

[Note: The word *ex* (“from”) was formerly missing. A little above, Tertullian calls a diet disciplined by God *castigatum victum*, and Cassian calls a meal so disciplined *castigatam refectionem*. Macrobius too, *Saturnalia* II.1, says: “Heroes sit down to disciplined meals.” For Milo, see Galen at the place cited above and Pliny VII.20.]

[Note: The reference is to the strength of Milo of Croton. Milo is said to have possessed such great strength that, in the Olympic contest, he carried an ox through the stadium; afterward he killed it with a blow of his fist and devoured the whole animal in a single day. See Galen at the place cited above and Pliny, Book VII, chapter 20.]

Let those think [variant: “they think”] meat conducive to health who wish to abuse lust and, submerged in the mire of pleasures, are always inflamed toward intercourse. A Christian needs health without excessive strength.

Nor should it trouble us if followers of this way are rare, since good and faithful friends, chaste and continent people, are also rare, and virtue is always rare. Read about the continence of Fabricius and the poverty of Curius, and in so great a city you will scarcely find a few whom you might imitate.

Do not fear that, if you do not eat meat, fowlers and hunters will have learned their crafts in vain.

## 12. The treatment of gout. All satiety must be avoided [Cols. 0302A–0302D]

We read that certain people suffering from joint disease and the humors of gout recovered after their property had been confiscated and they had been reduced to a simple table and poor foods. They had been relieved of the anxiety of managing a household and of the abundance of banquets, both of which weaken the body and the soul.

Horace mocks the appetite for foods that, once consumed, leave regret:

> Reject pleasures; pleasure purchased with pain is harmful.

And when, in a most delightful field, he portrayed himself as fat and sleek, a morsel for pleasure-loving people, he played with these verses:

> You will see me fat and shining, with well-tended skin,  
> When you wish to laugh, a pig from Epicurus’ herd.

But even with the cheapest foods satiety must be avoided. Nothing so overwhelms the mind as a full and overheated stomach, twisting this way and that and breathing out through belches or the expulsion of intestinal winds.

What kind of fast is that, or what kind of meal after a fast, when we are stretched out by the previous day’s banquets and our throat becomes the preparatory chamber of latrines?

[Note: “Our preparatory chamber.” Read this way with Erasmus and all our manuscript codices. The same word occurs in the letter to Fabiola on the forty-two encampments of the Israelites in the desert, Volume II of our edition, column 604, at the end. A *meditatorium* is a place of exercises or practices. Jerome therefore aptly called our throat a *meditatorium*, because what is later received and devoured by the latrine begins and is prepared there. See Tertullian, *On Fasting*.]

[Note: Elsewhere the reading is *mediatorium*, which is less satisfactory. This passage and the word are taken from Tertullian’s *On Fasting against the Psychics*, chapter 6: “When that whole dwelling of the inner man, stuffed with foods and flooded with wines, already boiling with the digestion of excrement, becomes a preparatory chamber for latrines.” See also the letter to Fabiola on the Encampments, Encampment 42.]

While we wish to acquire a reputation for a prolonged fast [variant: “to lack repute”], we devour so much that scarcely the night of a second day can digest it. Thus it should not so much be called a fast as gluttony—a stinking and troublesome digestion.

## 13. Dicaearchus, Xenophon, and Chaeremon [Cols. 0302C–0303D]

[Note: From the same passage of Porphyry: “Dicaearchus the Peripatetic, who, in recounting the ancient life of Greece …” and so forth, if the reader wishes to consult it. See also Suidas and Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book II, chapter 1, where he repeats the same matter from Dicaearchus. A little farther below, compare Cicero, *Letters to Quintus*, Book I: “And if not …”]

Dicaearchus, in his books on antiquities and his description of Greece, reports that under Saturn—that is, in the golden age—when the earth produced everything, no one ate meat, but everyone lived on grains and fruits, which the earth brought forth spontaneously.

Xenophon explains the life of Cyrus, king of the Persians, in eight volumes, asserting that they lived on porridge, cress (*cardamum*), salt, and coarse bread.

Xenophon, Theophrastus, and nearly all the writers of Greece bear witness to the frugality of the Lacedaemonians’ tables and way of life.

Chaeremon the Stoic, a most eloquent man, relates, in his account of the life of the ancient Egyptian priests, that, setting aside all the affairs and concerns of the world, they were always in the temple and contemplated the natures of things, their causes, and the principles of the stars. They never had intercourse with women; after they had begun to serve the divine worship, they never saw their relatives or kinsmen, not even their children. They always abstained from meat and wine because of the weakness of their senses and the dizziness of the head that they suffered from scanty food, and especially because of the impulses of lust that arise from these foods and this drink.

[Note: Up to Josephus’ testimony, this entire chapter is translated from Porphyry; I mention this only for the sake of brevity. The name formerly printed was “Cheramon.”]

They ate bread rarely, lest they burden the stomach. And whenever they did eat, they took crushed hyssop [variant: *consum et tusum*, uncertain] with their food, so that by its heat they might digest the heavier food. They knew oil only in vegetables, and even then only a little, to relieve nausea and the harshness of the taste.

“What need I say,” he asks, “about birds, when they avoided even eggs as though they were meat, and milk? They said that one of these was liquid flesh and the other blood, with the color changed.”

[Note: Porphyry had written: “Their bed was woven from the shoots of the palm, which they call *baias*.” Jerome translates: “Their bed was made from palm leaves,” and so forth. But in Porphyry *σπαδίκων*—“palm shoots”—should easily be read instead of *ὀπεδίκων*, and the phrase should be translated “from palm shoots.”]

Their bed was woven from palm leaves, which they call *baias*. They placed beneath their heads, on the ground in place of a pillow, an inclined footstool, sloping obliquely on one side, and they endured a fast of two or three days. They dried up the bodily humors [variant: “And the bodily humors”] produced by idleness and remaining in one place through an excessively austere diet.

[Note: The former reading was “inclined.” In the Rule of Saint Pachomius, according to our emendation: “Let no one who is sleeping place anything beneath himself except a reclining little seat.” See above, page 68, first note.]

## 14. The sects of the Jews. Three classes of Magi among the Persians. The Gymnosophists of India. Three precepts in the temple of Eleusis. Who was Antisthenes? [Cols. 0303C–0306D]

Josephus, in the second history of the Jewish captivity, in Book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, and in two volumes *Against Apion*, describes three doctrines of the Jews: the Pharisees, the Sadducees, and the Essenes. He extols the last of these with extraordinary praise because they had always abstained from wives, wine, and meat [variant: “were always abstaining”] and had turned daily fasting into a way of life.

[Note: Nowhere does Josephus—even in the book *Against Apion*—say that the Essenes abstained from wine and meat or fasted daily. Indeed, he teaches the opposite in Book II of *The Jewish War*. It was Philo who commended the Essenes in writing as perpetually fasting and never using meat or wine. Jerome is not to be blamed, however, since he does not report this from Josephus but from Porphyry, who quotes much from Josephus’ Book II *Against Apion* that is not found today. See *On Abstinence* IV.11–13.]

Philo too, a most learned man, published a separate volume on their life.

Neanthes of Cyzicus and Asclepiades of Cyprus write that, at the time when Pygmalion was reigning in the East, the eating of meat did not exist.

[Note: The printed editions, and even the manuscripts, had incorrectly read *Eantes*, while Erasmus read, even worse, *Evantes*. Diogenes Laertius, Book VIII, in his account of Empedocles, indicated that the correction should be *Neanthes*, calling him by that name and reporting that he had written about the Pythagoreans. Above all, Porphyry’s testimony establishes the reading, which Jerome consistently translates: “As time advanced, as Neanthes of Cyzicus says, and Asclepiades of Cyprus, under Pygmalion, who was a Phoenician by race but ruled the Cypriots, the eating of flesh was accepted, from such lawlessness …” See also Justin, Book XVIII.]

Eubulus too, who explained the history of Mithras in many volumes, relates that among the Persians there were three classes of Magi. The first, who were the most learned and eloquent, took no food beyond flour and vegetables.

[Note: Eubulus’ books do not survive today. Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 8, writes *Mitres* instead of *Mithras*, saying that he ruled in the city of the Sun.]

[Note: It is worth comparing Porphyry’s text again: “They were divided into three classes, as Symbulus says”—read *Eubulus*, “who recorded the history of Mithras in many books. The first and most learned neither eat living things nor kill them. They remain faithful to the ancient abstinence from animals.” Compare also Diogenes Laertius in the Prologue, where he repeats from the same Porphyry the examples of Bardesanes, Euripides, and Xenocrates.]

At Eleusis too it is customary to abstain from birds, fish, and certain fruits.

Bardesanes, a Babylonian man, divides the Gymnosophists of India into two doctrines. He calls one the Brahmans and the other the Samanaeans. They are so continent that they live either on fruits from trees beside the river Ganges or on publicly supplied rice or meal. When the king comes to them, he customarily worships them and considers the peace of his province to rest upon their prayers.

Euripides reports in *Cretans* that the prophets of Jupiter abstained not only from meat but also from cooked foods.

The philosopher Xenocrates writes that, according to the laws of Triptolemus among the Athenians, only three precepts remained in the temple of Eleusis: honor parents, revere the gods, and do not eat meat.

Orpheus thoroughly detests the eating of meat in his poem.

[Note: I have supplied the adverb “thoroughly” in accordance with the manuscripts. A little later the old edition reads “would require the service of his own work.”]

I would recount the frugality of Pythagoras, Socrates, Antisthenes, and the others for our own shame, were it not both lengthy and in need of a work of its own.

This, certainly, is Antisthenes, who, after teaching rhetoric with distinction and hearing Socrates, is said to have told his disciples:

> Go away and seek a teacher; for I have already found one.

He immediately sold what he possessed and distributed it publicly, reserving for himself nothing more than a little cloak.

Xenophon, in the *Symposium*, and his innumerable books bear witness to his poverty, labor, and exertion; some of these he composed [variant: “wrote”] in a philosophical style, others in a rhetorical one.

That famous Diogenes was his follower—more powerful than King Alexander and victorious over human nature. Since Antisthenes accepted no one as a disciple, and could not drive away Diogenes, who persisted, at last he threatened [variant: *minitatus*] him with a club unless he departed.

[Note: Victorius adds from ancient copies “arguing about poverty.” See Cicero’s discussion of Antisthenes in *On the Orator*, Book III, and Diogenes Laertius, who reports that Theopompus praised one Antisthenes among the disciples of Socrates.]

Diogenes is said to have presented his head to him and replied:

> No stick will be so hard that it can separate me from your service.

Satyrus, who writes the histories of illustrious men, relates that Diogenes used a double cloak because of the cold; that he used a wallet as a storeroom; and that he carried a club because of the frailty of his little body, with which, already an old man, he used to support his limbs. He was commonly called *hemerobios*—“living for the day”—because he asked each person for food for the present hour and accepted whatever he received.

[Note: Jerome again praises this learned Satyrus in the Prologue to his book *On Illustrious Men*. See Volfius, Book III, *On Greek Historians*.]

Diogenes lived [variant: “used to live”] in the vestibules of gates and in the porticoes of cities. When he curled himself up in a barrel, he joked that he possessed a house that could roll and that changed with the seasons. In winter he turned the mouth of the barrel toward the south; in summer toward the north; and however the sun inclined, Diogenes’ palace turned with it.

[Note: The reference is to an elegant and magnificently constructed house. *Praetoria* were understood as urban villas and places of luxury. Examples may be found in Suetonius.]

On one occasion, while he had a wooden cup for drinking, he saw a boy drinking from his cupped hand. He is said to have dashed the cup to the ground, saying:

> I did not know that nature too had a cup.

[Note: I have restored *caucum* in place of *caveum*, the reading of Martianus, or *cavum*, found in other editions. A *caucum* is a kind of drinking vessel, mentioned by Spartianus, who relates that Pescennius forbade soldiers, during an expedition, to drink from a silver cup. I do not deny that *caveum* may also have been a type of drinking vessel, as can be inferred from Trebellius Pollio’s account of Claudius—“eleven pounds in cups and goblets, likewise eleven pounds in cups and *zuma*”—unless that passage too is corrupt. But the reading we prefer is confirmed by two of the better manuscripts and also by Gravius. Diogenes Laertius has *κοτύλην*, “a cup.”]

His virtue and self-control are also shown by his death. For when, already an old man, he was traveling to the Olympic contest, which was attended by a great gathering from Greece, he is said to have been seized by a fever on the way and to have lain down [variant: “to have lain upon it”] on the roadside. When his friends wished to lift him onto a beast of burden or into a vehicle, he refused. But, moving into the shade of a tree, he said:

> Go away, I beg you, and continue on to the spectacle. This night will prove me either victor or vanquished. If I conquer the fever, I shall come to the contest; if it conquers me, I shall descend to the underworld.

There, during the night, after crushing his throat, he said that he was not so much dying as excluding the fever through death.

I have offered the example of only one philosopher, so that our pretty boys and—

[Note: The manuscripts read *trosuli*. See what we have said more than once in the letters about this word: *trossuli*, as though derived from *torosuli*, meaning “well-built” and strong in the muscles of manhood. Nonius notes: “And Persius: ‘The *trossulus* exults for you among the smooth benches.”]

—our well-built young men, who scarcely sketch footprints with the tips of their toes, whose words are in their fists and whose syllogisms are in their heels, may at least imitate the frugality of the Gentiles. They either do not know or despise the poverty of the Apostles and the hardship of the cross.

## 15. Examples from Scripture. The Second Inscription of the Tablets. [Col. 0305C] The Praise of Fasting. The Beginnings of Monasticism

[Note: [Col. 0306D] The printed editions read, “These things concerning the arguments,” etc., though the manuscripts reject this. Almost everything that follows here concerning the praise of fasting has been taken from Tertullian’s *On Fasting*, chapters 3 and 4, which the diligent reader may compare at leisure. We shall occasionally add some notes.]

I have discussed these matters concerning the arguments and examples of the philosophers. Now, turning to the beginning of the human race—that is, to our own history—I shall show that Adam first received the command in paradise to eat the other fruits but to fast from one tree. The blessedness of paradise could not be established without abstinence from food. As long as he fasted, he remained in paradise; he ate, and he was expelled; once expelled, he immediately took a wife. The man who, fasting, had been a virgin in paradise, once filled with food was joined in marriage on earth. Yet, after his expulsion, he was not immediately granted permission to eat meat; only the fruits of trees, the produce of crops, and the vegetables of herbs were given to him as food, so that, even as an exile from paradise, he might feed not on meat—which had not existed in paradise—but on the likeness of the fruits of paradise.

Afterward, when God saw that the heart of man had been carefully inclined toward wickedness from his youth, and that his spirit could not remain in such things because they were flesh, he condemned the works of the flesh by the Flood. Then, testing the exceedingly greedy appetite of mankind, he gave them permission to eat meat, so that, while they understood that everything was permitted to them, they would not greatly desire what was forbidden, lest they turn the commandment into an occasion of transgression.

[Note: [Col. 0306D] Formerly it read, “they greatly desire what was not permitted.” The old edition immediately adds: “that a fast concerning unclean animals had been commanded.”]

Nevertheless, even then a partial fast was imposed. For since some animals are called clean and others unclean, and since two of the unclean animals but unequal numbers of the clean were brought into Noah’s Ark—and certainly the eating of the unclean animals had been taken away, lest they be called unclean without reason—fasting was established in part, teaching abstinence from all things through the cutting off of certain ones.

Why did Esau lose his birthright? Was it not on account of food? He could not remedy his gluttonous impatience even with tears. The people of Israel, expelled from Egypt and destined to be brought into the land of promise flowing with milk and honey, desire the meats of Egypt, its melons, [Note: [Col. 0306D] More fully: “melons, leeks, and garlic,” etc. Immediately afterward, *Domino erat Deo* (“it was the Lord God”) occurs in place of *Deo* (“God”), contrary to Jerome’s manuscripts and the text of Scripture itself.] and other foods:

> Would that we had died, struck down by the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat beside pots of meat (Exodus 16:3).

And again:

> Who will feed us meat? We remember the fish that we ate freely in Egypt, and the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. But now our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing but manna (Numbers 31:4–5).  
> [Note: [Col. 0306D] Victorius substituted *pasceret* (“would feed”), because he did not find *vescet* (“will feed”) in Latin. The Vulgate reads, “Who will give us food?” At the end of the testimony, the Veronese manuscript does not have the word *conspiciunt* (“they see”), but has only “the eyes of our.”]

Despising the food of angels, they sighed for the meats of Egypt. Moses fasted for forty days and nights on Mount Sinai, at that time also proving, while speaking with the Lord, that man lives not by bread alone but by every word of God. The people, however, once filled with food, fashion idols. He, with an empty stomach, receives the law written by the finger of God. They, eating and drinking, then rising to play, melt gold into a calf and prefer the Egyptian bull to the majesty of the Lord. The labor of so many days is destroyed by the satiety of a single hour.

Moses boldly breaks the tablets, for he knew that drunken men could not hear the word of God:

> The beloved grew fat, became thick and broad, and kicked; he abandoned the God [Al. Lord] who had made him and departed from God [Al. the Lord], his Savior (Deuteronomy 32:15).

Hence also in the same Deuteronomy it is commanded:

> When you have eaten and drunk, and built fine houses, and your sheep and cattle have multiplied, and silver and gold have increased, let your heart not be lifted up, and do not forget the Lord your God (Deuteronomy 8:12–14).

Finally, the people ate, and their heart became fat, so that they could not see with their eyes, hear with their ears, or understand with their heart [Al. contain it]. They could not endure Moses, who was fasting and, according to the Hebrew Truth, made horned by his conversation with God, nourished and grown fatter.

[Note: [Col. 0307D] From Tertullian’s book cited above: “Since the fatter people could not steadfastly contemplate Moses himself fed by God, nor his abstinence nourished in God’s name.” And shortly afterward: “Therefore the Lord also rightly appeared to him in the flesh, as a companion no less of his fasts and of Elijah’s.”]

For this reason our Lord and Savior, not because of any indifference between virginity and marriage, as some think, but because of their fellowship in fasting, displayed Moses and Elijah with himself in glory when he was transfigured on the mountain. Although Moses and Elijah specifically prefigured the Law and the Prophets, as the Gospel Scripture plainly bears witness:

> They spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31).

For it is the Law and the Prophets, not virginity and marriage, that announce the Lord’s Passion. But if they contentiously claim that marriage is represented in Moses and virginity in Elijah, let them hear briefly that Moses died and was buried, while Elijah, carried away in a fiery chariot, began to be immortal before he died.

Nor could the second writing of the tablets be obtained without fasting. What drunkenness had lost, hunger recovered. From this it is shown that through fasting we can return to paradise, from which we had been expelled through satiety.

In Exodus, against Amalek, the battle was waged by the prayer of Moses and the fasting of the whole people until evening (Exodus 17). Jesus son of Nun commanded the sun and moon to stand still, and prolonged the victorious army’s fast beyond a single day (Joshua 10). [Note: [Col. 0307D] Understand fasting in the usual ecclesiastical sense, or at least an allusion to the double meaning of the word. Tertullian: “He commanded a station even upon the elements themselves.” See the note appended below.]

Saul, as it is written in the First Book of Kings, said:

> Cursed is the man who eats bread before evening, until I have taken vengeance on my enemies [Al. my enemy].

And none of his people tasted food, and the whole land [Note: [Col. 0307D] Some insist that, with the negative particle, it should also be read here, “and the whole land did not eat,” as Jerome has it, just as Pamelius reads it in Tertullian’s *Against the Psychics*, chapter 10. The Vulgate translator, however, with a very different meaning, has, “and the whole land came into the forest.” But, to say nothing of the reading of the Hebrew text, which it would be worthwhile to compare with the Septuagint, I maintain that the Greek *καὶ πᾶσα ἡ γῆ ἠρίστα* (“and the whole land ate breakfast”) became, in the old Latin version, *et tota terra prandebat* (“and the whole land ate breakfast”), without the negative particle, which Pamelius and others had no right to insert into the writings of the ancients.] ate breakfast (1 Kings 14:24).

So great was the authority of a fast once dedicated to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0308D] Martianaeus, following Erasmus and contrary to the evidence of the more accurate manuscripts, and less appropriately, reads “so that the lot might discover Jonathan …” Tertullian again has: “God gave such authority to that appointed fast—that is, to the fast—that Jonathan,” etc.] that Jonathan, who had been the cause of victory, was discovered by lot and could not avoid the charge of ignorance; he even provoked his father’s hand against himself and was scarcely saved by the people’s prayers.

Elijah, prepared by a forty-day fast, saw God on Mount Horeb [Al. Choreb] and heard him say:

> What are you doing here, Elijah?

[Note: [Col. 0308D] Again from Tertullian: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” This voice is much more friendly than “Adam, where are you?” For the former threatened a man who had eaten, while the latter spoke gently to one who was fasting.]

That voice was far more intimate than the one in Genesis, “Adam, where are you?” The first terrified a man who had eaten and was lost; this one gently addressed a fasting servant.

Samuel strengthened the people gathered at Mizpah by proclaiming a fast and made them stronger against their enemies. The tears, sackcloth, and humbled condition of Hezekiah the king broke, overthrew, and conquered the assault and power of Sennacherib.

Conversely, the city of Nineveh turned aside the Lord’s impending anger through the mercy obtained by fasting. Sodom and Gomorrah too would have appeased him if they had been willing to repent and reconcile him through tears of repentance supported by fasting.

[Note: [Col. 0308D] The same author says, “Sodom and Gomorrah too would have escaped if they had fasted.” Shortly afterward: “Anna also, the wife of Elkanah, barren and seeking a child, easily obtained from God that her empty belly should be filled with a son.”]

Ahab, the most wicked king, obtained through fasting and sackcloth that he might escape God’s sentence and that the destruction of his house might be postponed for his descendants. Anna, the wife of Elkanah, deserved to have her belly, empty of food, filled with a son.

The magicians are endangered in Babylon; every diviner, soothsayer, and augur is killed (Daniel 1 and 2). Daniel and the three boys obtain revelation through fasting; nourished on legumes, they are more handsome and wiser than those who ate meat from the king’s table.

Then it is written that Daniel fasted for three weeks; he did not eat pleasant bread, meat and wine did not enter his mouth, and he was not anointed with oil. [Note: [Col. 0308D] Here too Tertullian should be compared: “Come, I shall show you how pitiable you are—that is, by fasting,” etc.] And an angel came to him, saying:

> Daniel, you are a pitiable man (Daniel 9:23).

He who had appeared pitiable to God was, after his fast, terrifying to the lions in the pit. What a beautiful thing fasting is, which appeases God, tames lions, and terrifies demons (Daniel 14)!

Habakkuk is sent to him—although we have not found this in the Hebrew books—carrying the meal of the reapers. By a week’s fasting he had deserved such a bearer of a dish.

David, when his son was in danger, after his adultery, made an ἐξομολόγησις (*exomologesis*, confession) in ashes and fasting, saying:

> For I ate ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with weeping (Psalm 101:10).

And:

> My knees are weakened by fasting (Psalm 108:24).

And certainly he had already heard from Nathan:

> The Lord has taken away your sin (2 Samuel 12:13).

Samson and Samuel do not drink wine or strong drink. For they were sons of promise, conceived through abstinence and fasting.

Aaron and the other priests, when they are about to enter the Temple, do not drink anything that can intoxicate, lest they die (Exodus 10). [Note: [Col. 0309D] Tertullian has nearly the same words: “Indeed, those who minister in the Church without sobriety will die.”]

From this we understand that those who minister in the Church without sobriety die. Therefore Israel is reproached:

> You gave wine to my Nazirites to drink (Amos 2:12).

Jonadab, son of Rechab, commanded his sons not to drink wine forever. [Note: [Col. 0309D] The Veronese and Cistercian manuscripts read, “when Jeremiah offered them to drink,” without *wine*.] When Jeremiah offered them wine to drink and they refused to drink, the Lord spoke through the prophet:

> Because you obeyed the command of Jonadab your father, no man from the line of Jonadab son of Rechab shall fail to stand in my presence all his days (Jeremiah 35:8).
