[Note: [Col. 0309D] Also from Tertullian: “At the threshold of the Gospel, Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, who both recognized the infant Lord and proclaimed many things about him to those awaiting Israel’s redemption, is further honored, after the distinguished title of widowhood following a marriage to one husband, by the testimony of fasts, showing in what duties the churches ought to be served and that Christ is understood by none more than by those married once and fasting often.” Immediately afterward: “The Lord himself also consecrated his baptism, and that of all, through fasts,” etc. And shortly afterward: “Even against fiercer demons we must fight by fasts.”]

At the threshold of the Gospel, Anna, daughter of Phanuel, is introduced as a one-man woman, always fasting; and the Lord was received by long chastity and long fasts.

His forerunner and herald, John [Note: [Col. 0310D] The more authoritative manuscripts do not recognize the name “John” here.] is nourished on locusts and wild honey, not on meat; and the dwelling in the desert, the cradle of monks, begins with such foods.

The Lord himself also consecrated his baptism through a forty-day fast and taught that fiercer demons can be overcome only by prayer and fasting.

Cornelius the centurion, in order to receive the Holy Spirit before baptism, earned it through almsgiving and frequent fasts. The Apostle Paul, after hunger and thirst and his other labors, dangers from robbers, shipwrecks, and solitudes [Al. shipwreck and solitude], enumerates frequent fasts.

To his disciple Timothy, who suffered from an aching stomach and endured many illnesses, he recommends a moderate drink of wine:

> No longer drink water (1 Timothy 5:23).

To one to whom he says, “No longer drink water,” he shows that Timothy had previously drunk water. He would not have granted this permission unless frequent illnesses and stomach pain had demanded it.

## 16. Heretics Rejecting Foods

The Apostle does indeed condemn those who prohibit marriage and command abstinence from foods that God created to be used with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4), but he also indicates Marcion, Tatian, and the other heretics who impose perpetual abstinence in order to destroy, despise, and abominate the works of the Creator.

We, however, praise every creature of God; and we prefer leanness to fattening, abstinence to luxury, and fasting to satiety. For:

> A man who labors labors for himself and does violence to his own destruction (Proverbs 16:26, according to the Septuagint).

And:

> From the days of John the Baptist—the faster and virgin—the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it (Matthew 11:12).

For we fear that, at the coming of the eternal Judge, we may be found, as in the days of the Flood and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage. For both the Flood and the fire from heaven found satiety and marriages alike—things that they would destroy.

Nor is it surprising [Note: [Col. 0310D] Tertullian: “If he handed you the keys of the marketplace, permitting everything to be eaten in order to establish the exception concerning sacrificial food, he did not, however, enclose the kingdom of God in the marketplace.”] that the Apostle commands everything sold in the meat market to be bought and eaten (1 Corinthians 10), since for idolaters, and for those still eating sacrificial food in the temples of idols, the highest form of abstinence was merely to abstain from the foods of the Gentiles (1 Corinthians 10).

But when he says to the Romans:

> Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats (Romans 14:3),

he is not distributing equal merits between fasting and satiety. Rather, he speaks against those who, believing in Christ, were still Judaizing, and he warns those who had believed from the Gentiles not to scandalize by their food those who were still weaker in faith.

Finally, the following passage has the same meaning:

> I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, except to the one who considers something unclean; to that person it is unclean. For if your brother is grieved because of food, you are no longer walking according to love. Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died. Therefore let not our good be blasphemed. For the kingdom of God is not food [Al. food’s] and drink (Romans 14:14ff.).

And lest anyone think that this concerns fasts rather than Jewish superstition, he immediately explains:

> One person believes that he may eat everything; but the one who is weak eats vegetables (Romans 14:2).

And again:

> One person judges one day to be above another; another judges every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord. And the one who eats eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God. And the one who does not eat does not eat for the Lord, and gives thanks to God (Romans 14:5ff.).

Those who were still weak in faith considered some meats clean and others unclean, and thought that one day differed from another—for example, that the Sabbath, the new moons, and the Feast of Booths were holier than the remaining days. They are commanded to eat vegetables, which everyone eats indiscriminately. Those who were stronger in faith, however, believed that all meats and all days were equal.

## 17. The Fast of Christians. The Graves of Desire Persist. The Sanctification of Fasting [Col. 0311A]

[Note: [Col. 0311D] Earlier, “he dared.” Tertullian says: “How unworthily you interpret the Lord according to your lust, as one eating and drinking everywhere! But I think that he also fasted, who pronounced blessed not those who were full, but those who were hungry and thirsty; who declared that he had food—not what the disciples supposed, but the completion of the Father’s work,” etc.]

But concerning the claim he dared to make [Al. “he dared”]—that the Lord was called by the Pharisees a glutton and a drinker of wine, and that he went to a wedding feast and did not despise the banquets of sinners—I think the matter stands with us as follows.

This is the Lord whom you suppose to be a glutton: the one who sanctified the Christian fast through forty days [Al. “sanctifies”]; who calls the hungry and thirsty blessed; who says that he has food, not the food the disciples suspected, but food that would not perish forever; who forbids concern for the following day; who, although he is said to have been hungry and thirsty and to have frequently gone to meals, apart from the mystery which he expressed as a type of his Passion and the proof of the reality of his body, is recorded as having served neither his appetite nor his belly.

He is the one who tells of the rich man dressed in purple in Tartarus because of his banquets, and of poor Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom because of his hunger. When we fast, he commands us to anoint our head and wash our face [Note: [Col. 0311D] Some manuscripts read: “He commanded us to anoint our head and wash our face”], so that we may fast not for the glory of men but for the Lord.

After the resurrection he did eat a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb, not because of hunger or the sweetness of the throat, but to prove the reality of his body. For whenever he raised someone from the dead, he commanded that food be given to him, lest the resurrection be thought a phantom. For this reason Lazarus too is said, after his resurrection, to have entered into a banquet with the Lord.

We do not say this because we deny that fish and other foods, if there is a desire for them, may be eaten. But just as we prefer virginity to marriage, so we prefer fasting and the spirit to satiety and meats.

If Peter went up to the upper room at the sixth hour intending to eat, accidental hunger does not prejudice the practice of fasting. In this way the same necessity would fall upon everyone, whether they wished it or not, to drink at that hour, because the Lord, tired, sat beside the Samaritan woman’s well at the sixth hour and wanted to drink.

It may have been the Sabbath or the Lord’s Day; and after a fast of two or three days he may have become hungry at the sixth hour. I could never believe that an apostle who had dined the day before and had been stuffed with feasting was hungry at midday on the following day. But if he had dined the day before and became hungry before the meal on the following day, I do not think that he had eaten to satiety, since he was able to become hungry so quickly.

Moreover, if God speaks through Isaiah that he did not choose such a fast, saying:

> During your fasts your desires are found, and you strike those subject to you; you fast for judgments and quarrels, and you strike with your fists. I have not chosen such a fast, says the Lord (Isaiah 58:3ff.).

He teaches what kind of fast he did choose:

> Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor without shelter into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him; and do not despise those of your own flesh (Isaiah 58:7).

He did not, therefore, reject fasting, but showed what kind he desired. For the hunger of the belly is not acceptable to God when quarrels, robbery, and lusts destroy it.

If God [Al. the Lord] does not want fasting, how does he command in Leviticus that, in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, the whole people should fast until evening, and that whoever does not afflict his soul should die and be exterminated from his people?

Why do the graves of desire, where the people devoted to meat fell, remain in the wilderness to this day? And why is it written that the fattened people belched up *ortygometra*—quail—until they were sick? [Note: [Col. 0311D] Tertullian: “The monuments of desire still remain, where the people most avid for flesh were buried, gorging themselves on quail until bile arose,” etc., etc.]

Why was the man of God (1 Kings 13), at whose prophecy the hand of King Jeroboam had withered, immediately struck down because he ate against God’s command? And why did the lion that guarded the ass untouched spare no mercy for the Prophet when he rose from his meal? He who had performed miracles while fasting, once he had eaten, immediately paid the penalty of satiety.

Joel too cries out:

> Sanctify a fast; proclaim healing [Al. an assembly] (Joel 1:14; 2:15),

so that it might be shown that fasting is sanctified by other works, and that sanctified fasting contributes to the healing of sins.

Just as the imitation of the devil’s virgins does not prejudice true virginity, so neither does the “chaste one” [*castus*] of Isis and Cybele, nor the perpetual abstinence from certain foods, prejudice true fasts, especially since among them a fast of bread is compensated by a stuffing of meat.

[Note: [Col. 0311D] All the manuscripts read this way, and it must certainly be read so, as we explained above; see what *castus* means, page 330 and following, note (column 291, note b). Martianaeus, from a preconceived opinion, also reads *cossus* here and thinks it an error of the ancient scribes that they wrote *castus*, being unaware that *cossus* is a little worm. He himself completely failed to understand the matter. — *Cossus* of Isis and Cybele. The manuscript codices read, “the *castus* of Isis and Cybele”; but this is an error, unless I am mistaken, of the ancient scribes, who did not know that *cossus* was the worm from which the priests of Isis and Cybele abstained, as we observed earlier. MARTIAN.]

And just as the signs Moses performed were imitated by the signs of the Egyptians but were not true—for Moses’ staff devoured the staffs of the magicians—so, in everything the devil does by imitation of God, not the superstition of our religion but our negligence is condemned: our refusal to do what even the men of this world recognize as good.

## 18. Jovinian’s Fourth Proposition

“His fourth proposition, which is also the last, is that there are two orders: of sheep and of goats—the one of the righteous, the other of sinners; that some stand on the right and others on the left; and that the righteous hear:

> Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matthew 25:34).

But to sinners it is said:

> Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared [Al. ‘is prepared’] for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41).

A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit. Hence the Savior also says to the Jews:

> You are of your father the devil, and you desire to do your father’s wishes (John 8:43).

He presents the ten virgins, foolish and wise: five who had no oil remained outside, while the other five, who had prepared for themselves the light of good works, entered the bridal chamber with the bridegroom.

He turns to the Flood and says: Those who were with Noah, the righteous, were saved; but those who were sinners all perished together. At Sodom and Gomorrah, apart from the two categories of good and evil, no distinction is found. The righteous person is rescued; the sinner is consumed by an equal fire. There is one salvation for those who are delivered and one destruction for those who remain. That one must not deviate even slightly from righteousness is shown by Lot’s wife.

“But if,” he says, “you object to me: Why should a righteous person labor in peace or under persecutions, if there is no progress and no greater rewards? Know that he does this not to earn more, but so as not to lose what he has received.

In Egypt too all sinners experience the ten plagues equally: the same darkness threatens master and slave, noble and ignoble, king and common people. But the saints of God and the people of Israel had one light.

In the Red Sea likewise the righteous cross together, while sinners are drowned together. Six hundred thousand men, apart from the weak in age and sex, fall equally in the wilderness, and the two who were equal in righteousness are equally delivered. For forty years all Israel labors and dies in the same way.

For every age there is one measure of an omer of manna as food; garments are not worn out, hair does not grow, beards do not grow in common, and shoes last equally for all. Feet do not become calloused; food tastes the same in everyone’s mouth. They traveled to one dwelling with equal labor and reward.

Every Hebrew has an equal Passover, equal festivals of Booths, an equal Sabbath, and equal new moons. In the seventh year of rest, release is granted without distinction of persons; and in the jubilee all debts are cancelled for everyone, and the seller returns to his ancestral possession.”

## 19.

He divides into two orders the parable in the Gospel (Matthew 13 and Luke 8) of the sower, in which the good soil produces a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit, while, conversely, in the bad soil a threefold variety of barrenness is indicated: the orders of good soil and bad.

“And just as, in one Gospel, the Lord promises the Apostles a hundredfold, and in another sevenfold, for abandoned sons and wives, and in the future eternal life (Matthew 19; Mark 10; Luke 18)—and there is no difference between one hundred and seven—so too in this Gospel [Note: [Col. 0313D] That is, in this Gospel or Gospel example. Earlier, *in hoc numero* (“in this number”) had been wrongly read instead of *in hoc* (“in this”). Shortly afterward the manuscripts have: “without any difference or degrees, Christ,” etc.] the number does not create a distinction, where the fertility of this soil is praised, especially since the Evangelist Mark counts backward, thirty, sixty, and one hundred.

The Lord says:

> Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him (John 6:55).

Therefore, just as Christ is in us without any distinction of degrees, so we too are in Christ without degrees.

> Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him (John 14:23).

The righteous person loves; and when he loves, the Father and Son come to him and dwell in his lodging. Wherever such a resident is found, I think that nothing can be lacking to the guest.

But when he says:

> There are many dwellings in my Father’s house (John 14:2),

he does not signify different dwellings in the kingdom of heaven, but the number of the churches throughout the world, which are established as one through seven. “I go,” he says, “and I shall prepare a place for you” (John 14:2), not places.

If this promise belongs specifically to the twelve Apostles, then Paul has been excluded from this place, and the chosen vessel will be considered superfluous and unworthy. Did John and James, because they asked for more than the other Apostles, fail to obtain it? Yet their dignity was not diminished, because they were equal to the remaining Apostles.

> Do you not know that your bodies are the temple [Note: [Col. 0313D] Two manuscripts have *estis* (“you are”); shortly afterward the Cistercian manuscript has “those who will believe in me,” and, with the Veronese, “so that, as I, Father, am in you, and you in me, we are one,” etc. This reading seems much older, or belongs to the old Latin translation that Jovinian had before his eyes, although it does not correspond to the Greek original. The same reading occurs again below. See page 370, first note. Finally, the manuscripts have *dilexisti eos* (“you loved them”) instead of *dilexi* (“I loved them”).] of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19)?

He says “temple,” not “temples,” so that he might similarly show that God dwells in all.

> I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, they too may be one in us. The glory that you gave me, I have given them; I loved them as you loved me (John 17:20).

And just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, so there may also be one people in them—that is, as beloved sons, sharers in the divine nature.

Bride, sister, mother, and whatever other names you may think of: they are the assembly of the one Church, which is never without a bridegroom, brother, or son [Al. bride]. It has one faith; it is not defiled by a variety of doctrines or divided by heresies. It remains a virgin. Wherever the Lamb goes [Al. “will go”], it follows him; it alone knows the Song of Christ.

## 20.

“But if,” he says, “you object to me, ‘Star differs from star in glory,’ you will hear that one star differs from another—that is, spiritual people from carnal people.

We love all the members equally; we do not place the eye before the finger, nor the finger before the ear. But when any individual member is lost, the common body suffers.

We enter this world equally, and we leave it equally. There is one earthly Adam and another heavenly one. Whoever belongs to the earthly is on the left and will perish; whoever belongs to the heavenly is on the right and will be saved.

Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ and ‘Raca,’ will be guilty of Gehenna. And whoever is a murderer or adulterer will likewise be sent into Gehenna.

In persecution, whether someone is burned, suffocated, beheaded, flees, or dies shut up in prison, the kinds of struggle are different, but the victorious receive one crown.

Between the brother who had always been with his father and the one who was later received after repentance, there is no difference. To the laborers of the first, third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, one denarius is returned equally; and, to make the matter still more astonishing, the reward begins with those who labored less in the vineyard [Al. “labor less in it”].”

## 21. Jerome. The true preaching of Antichrist

By testimonies such as these, and others of the same kind from the divine Scriptures, which the crafty disputant bends toward the perversity of his doctrine, who would not be tempted, even among God’s elect? And since the Apostle John says that many Antichrists have come (1 John II), this is the true preaching of Antichrist: that it makes no difference between John himself and the final penitent.

At the same time, I marvel how our slippery serpent and Proteus changes himself into monsters of various forms. For although he is an Epicurean in sexual intercourse and satiety, suddenly, in the matter of the recompense of merits, he becomes a Stoic. He changes Jerusalem into Citium, Judea into Cyprus, and Christ into Zeno.

> [Note: Zenon, the founder of the Stoics, was from the city of Citium on the island of Cyprus. Hence he is called in Greek Κιτιεὺς or Κιττιεὺς, and in Latin Cittieus. See *Questions on Genesis*, chapter X, and *On Jeremiah*, chapter II.]

If it is not permissible to deviate even slightly from virtues, and all sins are equal, and he is guilty of the same crime who steals bread while hungry and he who kills a man:

> [Note: He compares the lightest fault with the gravest offense. Against this, the reading that has hitherto prevailed in printed books and in most manuscripts was: “he would compare a very grave offense with another equally grave one.” The point was that stealing bread from a hungry person was supposedly the same as killing a man; for even one who does not give food to the hungry kills him. The well-known saying from Ambrose is: “If you have not fed him, you have killed him.” On the other hand, if the hungry man himself steals, he sins more lightly than anyone; and this is what Jerome intends to compare, and what he in fact compares in the Veronese manuscript, from which we have corrected the passage.]

then you too are held guilty [Al. “will be held”] of the greatest crimes. But it is one thing if you say that you have not even the smallest sins, and, while all the Apostles, Prophets, and Saints lament themselves as sinners—according to what I discussed in the second proposition—you alone glory in your righteousness.

Before, you went barefoot; now you are not merely shod but adorned. Then you wore a fine-combed (*pexa*) tunic and a black undergarment, dirty and pale, carrying a hand hardened by work; now you walk about adorned in linen and silk clothing, and in garments from Atrebatum [Al. “of the Atrebates”] and Laodicea.

> [Note: He borrowed this from Horace: “If by chance beneath the smooth tunic there lies a worn undergarment.” The sense, however, is probably quite different, unless *impexa* should be read here in Jerome instead of *pexa*. For Latin writers, especially Horace, *pexa tunica* means a new, elegant, and costly tunic. Perhaps Jerome understood it as “shaggy,” or as something that ought to be combed because of its hairs. The Greeks call such a garment μαλλώτιον (*mallōtion*). Prudentius writes in the hymn: “The virgin shaggy with bestial hairs.” And our author, in the preceding book, number 40, called it a “dirty tunic.”]

Your cheeks are red, your skin shines, and your hair is trimmed toward the back of your head and your forehead:

> [Note: Gravius preferred *propensus*, from Persius: “The fat paunch stands out, protruding a foot and a half.”]

your belly projects, your shoulders rise, your throat swells, and words scarcely forced through your fattened throat are uttered. Certainly, amid so great a difference in food and clothing, sin must exist either here or there. Not that I assert that there is sin in food or clothing, but that variation and deterioration are close to deserving reproach. What is reproved is far from virtue; what is far from virtue is enslaved to vice; what is condemned as vicious is joined to sin. According to your view, sin belongs on the left side and is assigned to the herd of goats.

> [Al. “ascribed.”]

Therefore either return to your former purpose, so that you may be a sheep on the right; or, if by a perverse repentance you change your earlier opinion, whether you wish it or not—although you have shaved your beard—you will be numbered among the goats.

## 22. The sequence of Jovinian’s propositions. What the boys used to recite in school

But what benefit is there in calling a squinter a squinter and exposing the inconsistency of the accuser, when the sequence of the propositions must be dissolved?

> [Note: Again from Persius, *Satire* I: “And one who could call a squinter a squinter.”]

We do not deny that the sheep and goats on the right and left are two orders, respectively of the righteous and the sinners. No one doubts that a good tree does not produce bad fruits, nor a bad tree good ones. We also divide the ten virgins into the wise and the foolish, the good and the bad. We know [Al. “we do not deny”] that in the Flood the righteous were delivered and the sinners overwhelmed by the waters. In Sodom and Gomorrah, it is plain to all that the righteous man was rescued and the impious consumed by fire. We know also that Egypt was struck by ten plagues, while Israel remained unharmed. That the righteous crossed the Red Sea, while Pharaoh and his army were drowned, even little boys sing in school.

Six hundred thousand fell in the wilderness because they were unbelieving, and only two entered the promised land: the Scriptures teach this, along with the rest of what you have described up to the laborers in the vineyard, arranging them into two orders of good and evil. But what sort of argument is it that, because there is a division between the good and the evil, you assert that among the good themselves—or conversely among the evil—there is no distinction, and that it makes no difference whether someone among the flock is a ram or a little ewe; whether they have first-quality wool or second-quality wool; whether the sheep is scabby and diseased or vigorous and leaping?

Especially since Ezekiel, by the authority of his prophecy, demonstrates that there are rational sheep and a distinction between one flock and another, saying:

> [Note: The same manuscripts read *ecce ego judicabo*, in accordance with the Greek διακρινῶ, “I will distinguish/judge.”]

> “Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, and between rams and goats, and between fat sheep and lean sheep. Because you pushed with your sides and shoulders and butted with your horns all the weak sheep, until they were scattered” (Ezek. XXXIV, 17, 20).

And so that we might know what these sheep are [Al. “are”], he immediately added:

> [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads: “My flocks, the flocks of my pasture”; and shortly afterward, “because he is once on the right.”]

> “But you are my flocks, the sheep of my pasture; you are men.”

Will Paul, then, be the same as that penitent who had slept with his father’s wife, because he was received into the Church after repentance? And because he is likewise on the right, will he shine in the same glory as the Apostle?

And how, in one field, do weeds and wheat grow together until the harvest [Al. “and”], at the consummation of the world? By what logic are good and bad fish contained in Christ’s seine [Al. “sagina,” ‘net’] and the Gospel net? Why, in the type of the Church, the ark of Noah, are different animals present, and, according to the quality of their merits, different dwellings? Why did the queen stand at the Lord’s right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded by variety?

> [Al. “at your right hand.”]

Why did Joseph, in the likeness of Christ, have a variegated tunic? Why does the Apostle say to the Romans:

> “According as God has divided to each the measure of faith”?

> [Note: Two manuscripts read: “according to what God has apportioned.”]

> “For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another. Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: whether prophecy, according to the measure of faith; or ministry, in ministering; or the one who teaches, in teaching; the one who exhorts, in exhortation; the one who gives, in simplicity; the one who presides, with diligence; and so forth” (Rom. XII, 3 ff.).

And elsewhere:

> “One person judges one day to be above another; another judges every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own understanding” (Rom. XIV, 5).

And to the Corinthians:

> “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters are one. But each will receive his own reward according to his own labor. For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s agriculture, God’s building” (1 Cor. III, 6 ff.).

> [Note: The same manuscripts read: “You are God’s agriculture, God’s building”; and shortly afterward: “as a wise architect.”]

And again elsewhere:

> “According to the grace of God given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will become manifest.”

> [Note: “Faith”; “the day will disclose it,” without “of the Lord,” since that word is not found in the Greek either. Then: “and the work of each,” and finally: “but whose work has been burned.”]

> “For the day of the Lord will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work which he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss. But he himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (ibid., 10 ff.).

If the one whose work burned and perished, and who suffered the loss of his labor, will indeed lose the reward of his labor,

> [Al. “of his work.”]

but he himself will be saved—not, however, without the testing of fire, then if the work of the one who built remains, he will be saved without the testing of fire. Therefore there will certainly be some difference between one salvation and another.

And elsewhere:

> “Let a person regard [Al. “esteem”] us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God [Al. “his mysteries”]. Here, moreover, what is sought among stewards is that one be found faithful” (1 Cor. IV, 1–2).

Do you wish to know that there is a great difference between steward and steward—not, I say, between the bad and the good, but among the good themselves who stand on the right? Hear what follows:

> “Do you not know that those who perform the sacrifices eat from the sacrifices, and those who serve at the altar share in the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. But I have used none of these rights. I have not written these things so that they might be done in my case. For it is better for me to die than that anyone should deprive me of my glory. For if I preach the Gospel, it is no glory to me; necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not [Al. “unless I”] preach the Gospel. For if I do this willingly [Al. “do it”], I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship. What, then, is my reward? That, when preaching the Gospel, I may present the Gospel of Christ without expense, so as not to make use of the authority given to me in the Gospel. For although I was free from all [Al. “from everyone”], I made myself the servant of all, that I might win the more” (1 Cor. IX, 13 ff.).

Can you say that those who live from the Gospel and share in the sacrifices are sinning? Certainly not. For the Lord ordained that those who preach the Gospel should live from the Gospel. But the Apostle, who does not abuse this permission, works with his hands so as not to burden anyone, and labors day and night, and ministers to those who are with him. He does this precisely so that, laboring more, he may receive something more in reward.

## 23. Let us proceed to the rest

There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of workings [Al. “of working”], but the same God, who works all things in all. But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit according to what is useful (1 Cor. XII, 4 ff.).

> [Note: Earlier the reading was *operatio*, “operation.” Against all the manuscripts, we have restored *adapertio*, “manifestation/opening,” also supported by the Greek text, φανέρωσις. Shortly afterward: “For just as the body is one and has many members.”]

And again:

> “Just as the body is one and has many members, but all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (ibid., 12).

But lest you say that the different members in one body have one and the same merit, he immediately describes the ranks of the Church and says:

> “God has appointed some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, gifts of healings, helps, administrations, kinds of tongues.”

> [Note: Previously there was incorrectly *denique*, “finally,” instead of *deinde*, “then.”]

> “Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all powers? Do all possess gifts of healings? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? But desire the greater gifts, and I show you an even more excellent way” (ibid., 28 ff.).

And after he had discussed the virtues of charity at greater length, he added:

> “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when perfection comes, what is partial will be abolished” (1 Cor. IX, 10).

And in what follows:

> [Note: Previously it read *et in continentibus*; then the manuscripts: “but charity is greater than these.”]

> “But now faith, hope, and charity remain—these three. But the greatest of these is charity” (ibid., 13).

> “Pursue charity, desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy” (1 Cor. XIV, 1).

And again:

> “I wish that you all spoke in tongues, but especially that you prophesied. For the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues” (ibid., 5).

And again:

> “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you” (ibid., 18).

> [Note: We supply the word *magis*, “more,” from the manuscripts, with which the Greek text also agrees: μᾶλλον, “more.”]

Where gifts differ, and one person is greater while another is lesser, and all are called spiritual, they are certainly sheep and stand on the right; and there is some difference between sheep and sheep.

The Apostle Paul indeed speaks of humility:

> “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored more abundantly than all of them. Yet not I…”

> [Note: “But the grace of God which is in me.” In our Sangerman manuscript and in another from the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres we read: “but the grace of God with me.” The other older manuscripts retain: “but the grace of God which is in me.” *Martianus.* In a certain Corbie manuscript, as also in two others held by Martianus: “but the grace of God with me.”]

> “…but the grace of God which is in me” (1 Cor. XV, 9–10).

Nevertheless, in humbling himself he shows that some apostles can be lesser and others greater. And since he is called the vessel of election and labored more than all, God is not unjust so as to forget his work and compensate unequal merit with an equal reward.

Then we read:

> “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive, but each in his own order” (1 Cor. XV, 22).

When each will rise in his own order, the merits of those rising are certainly different.

> [Note: The word “of those rising” is absent from the Veronese and Cistercian manuscripts.]

> “Not all flesh is the same flesh, but there is one flesh of human beings, another of animals, another of birds, and another of fish. There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but one is the glory of the heavenly, another of the earthly. One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars. For star differs from star in brightness. So also is the resurrection of the dead” (ibid., 39 ff.).

You, of course, learned interpreter, have explained this in such a way as to say that the spiritual differ from the carnal. Therefore the spiritual and the carnal will both be in the heavens, and now not only your sheep but also your goats will ascend into the kingdoms of heaven.

“Star differs from star in brightness”—not sheep from goats, but sheep from sheep, that is, star from star. Finally, he says:

> “One is the brightness of the sun, and another the brightness of the moon.”

Lest you assert that “star and star” signifies the entire human race, he set down the sun and the moon, which you certainly cannot number among the goats.

Thus, he says, will be the resurrection of the dead: the righteous will shine with the brightness of the sun,

> [Al. “will gleam.”]

and those who are in the next rank will glow with the splendor of the moon, so that one will be Lucifer, another Arcturus, another Orion, another Mazuroth, and so forth—the names of the stars contained in the sacred book of Job.

> [Note: These are the names of the stars in Job, which he explains in Letter 64 to Fabiola, number 19. See there the note on page 367, for us column 618.]

For he says:

> “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. V, 10).

And lest you perhaps say that we appear before the tribunal of Christ so that the good may receive good things and the evil evil things, he teaches in the same Epistle:

> “The one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows in blessings will also reap from blessings” (2 Cor. IX, 6).

Certainly both the one who sows more and the one who sows less belong to the right side. And although there is one kind of seed, they differ in measure and number.

The same Paul writes to the Ephesians:

> “So that now through the Church the manifold and varied wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavens” (Eph. III, 10).

Do you see that in the various ranks of the Church the varied and manifold wisdom of God is proclaimed?

And in the same Epistle:

> “To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s grace.”

This does not mean that Christ’s measure is different, but that as much of his grace is poured into each as we are able to receive.

> [Note: Other manuscripts have less appropriately: “as much as we are able to hear.”]

## 24. Therefore it is useless to repeat the examples of sheep and goats, the five and five virgins, the Egyptians and the Israelites, and other things of this kind

For the recompense is not in the present but in the future. Hence the day of judgment is promised at the consummation, because there is no judgment now. The final day would be called the day of judgment without reason if God is judging now.

At present we sail, struggle, and fight, so that at the end we may reach the harbor, be crowned, and triumph. But you perversely and slipperily propose the conduct of the present age as an example of future things, although here there is injustice and there justice:

> “Until we enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny.”

Does the holy man die in one way and the sinner in another? Is tranquility and storm different for those sailing on the same sea? Is the thief killed in one way and the martyr in another? Are children born in one manner from adultery and brothels, and in another from chaste marriages?

Certainly the Lord and the thieves were crucified under an equal judgment. If the judgment of this age and of the future is the same, then those who were crucified alike here will likewise be treated alike in the future.

Paul and those who had bound him sail together, endure the storm together, and, when the ship is shattered by the waves, escape together to the shore. You cannot deny that there are different merits between the one who was bound and those who bound him. And how can there be one shipwreck of an Apostle and soldiers?

> [Note: The manuscripts read: “the shipwreck is,” and then more correctly do not recognize the word “Apostle.”]

The Apostle Paul later reports a revelation and says that those who were in the ship were granted to him by the Lord. Surely the one to whom they are granted and those who are granted are not of equal merit.

Ten righteous people can rescue a sinful city. Lot was rescued from the conflagration with his daughters; his sons-in-law too would have been saved if they had been willing to leave. And certainly there is a great difference between Lot and his sons-in-law.

One city, Zoar, is delivered from the Pentapolis, and although it had the same merit and was subject to the same sentence as Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, it is preserved through the prayers of the holy man. Behold the different merit of Lot and Zoar, and yet they escape the conflagration together.

The bandits who, while David was absent, had devastated Ziklag and carried off their wives and children as booty are slain in the field on the third day, while four hundred men mount camels and flee. Tell me that there is a difference between those who were slain and those who were able to flee.

We read in the Gospel that the tower of Siloam fell upon eighteen men and killed them by crushing them. Certainly, according to the Savior’s judgment, they alone had not been sinners; rather, they were punished as a warning to the rest, so that when a pestilent person is scourged, the fool might become wiser.

If there is one punishment for all sinners, then one person is unjustly killed and another is warned by the death of someone else.

## 25. We receive the body of Christ equally. What do the ten virgins signify? Pilate unwillingly pronounced the sentence. The six days of this age

You oppose me with the gomor of manna, one measure, and with the clothing, hair, beard, and shoes of the Israelites, as though we too did not receive Christ’s body equally.

There is one sanctification in the mysteries—for Lord and servant, noble and base, king and soldier—although, according to the merits of those who receive it, what is one becomes diverse.

> “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily will be guilty of profaning the body and blood of Christ” (1 Cor. X, 27).

Since Judas also drank from the same cup from which the other Apostles drank,

> [Note: Two manuscripts read: “from which Christ and the other Apostles drank”; shortly afterward: “we eat the same foods.”]

will he therefore have the same merit as the others? And if you do not wish to accept the Sacrament, certainly we all live equally: we draw the same air, are watered by the same moisture, and are nourished by the same foods.

But if foods are transformed for the better by the skill of cooks, and something is made more pleasant by seasoning, such foods satisfy not nature but pleasure. We hunger equally and suffer cold equally; together we contract from cold, and we are dissolved by heat and warmth.

The sun itself, the moon, the entire host of stars, the rains, and the world move equally for us all; and according to the Gospel, we are all watered by the same rains—good and evil, righteous and unrighteous.

If present things are examples of future things, then the sun of righteousness will also rise equally upon the righteous and sinners, upon the impious and the holy, upon Christians, Jews, and Gentiles, since Scripture says:

> “But for those who fear the Lord the sun of righteousness will rise” (Mal. I).

If it rises for those who fear him, then it will set for the contemptuous and the false prophets.

> [Note: Victorius: “The sheep who stand on the right go into the kingdoms of heaven,” with nearly all the manuscripts agreeing.]

The sheep who stand on the right are brought into the kingdoms of heaven; the goats are thrust down into Tartarus. This parable does not describe the merits of sheep among themselves, nor, conversely, those of goats; it establishes a distinction only between sheep and goats.

For not everything is taught in every passage; each likeness is referred to that of which it is a likeness. Thus the ten virgins are examples not of the whole human race, but of the diligent and the sluggish: the former always await the Lord’s coming, while the latter, giving themselves over to sleep and idleness, do not believe in the coming judgment.

Hence at the end of the parable it is said:

> “Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matt. XXV, 13).

> [Note: Formerly: “But in the Flood,” incorrectly. Shortly afterward, Victorius supplies the verb “to be.”]

If Noah was delivered in the Flood and the whole world perished, all were flesh, and therefore they perished. Either you will say that the sons of Noah and Noah, on whose account the sons were delivered, were not of equal merit; or you will place the curse of Ham in the same category as the father, because he too was delivered from the Flood.

In Christ’s Passion all turned aside and together became worthless; there was no one who did good, not even one. Will you therefore dare to say that Peter and the other Apostles who fled denied him in the same way as Caiaphas, the Pharisees, and the shouting crowd:

> “Crucify, crucify such a man”?

And, to say nothing of the Apostles, will Annas, Caiaphas, and Judas the traitor seem to you guilty of the same crime as Pilate, who, unwillingly and under compulsion, pronounced sentence against the Lord?

> [Note: See Lactantius, Book IV, chapter 18. Then the manuscripts: “so much greater is the crime.”]

The greater Judas’s merit had been, the greater was his crime; and the greater his crime, the greater also his punishment.

> “For the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI, 7).

A bad tree does not produce good fruits, nor a good tree bad fruits. If this is so, answer me: how did Paul, when he was a bad tree persecuting Christ’s Church, afterward produce good fruits?

And how did Judas, when he was a good tree performing signs with the Apostles, afterward, having turned into a traitor, produce bad fruits?

Therefore neither does a good tree produce bad fruits nor a bad tree good ones for as long as each persists either in its goodness or in its wickedness.

Moreover, the fact that every Hebrew celebrates Passover equally, is set free in the seventh year, and in the Jubilee—that is, the fiftieth year—every possession returns to its owners: this is not spoken of the present but of the future. For having served during the six days of this age, on the seventh day, the true and eternal Sabbath, we shall be free,

> [Al. “we shall be set free.”]

if indeed we wish to be free while we are still serving in the world. But if we do not wish to be free, our ear will be pierced as a testimony to disobedience, and with our wife and children, whom we preferred to freedom—that is, with the flesh and its works—we shall serve perpetually.

## 26. What is the parable of the seed? The false Jovinian. The custom of Scripture

The parable of the seed, which produces threefold fruit on both sides, and, according to the Apostle, in which one builds upon Christ’s foundation with gold, silver, and precious stones, while another builds with wood, hay, and straw—since in a great house also there are different vessels—makes the matter perfectly clear [Al. “because”]. To wish to contradict this is the height of impudence.

> [Note: Thus the more accurate manuscripts and Victorius; previously it read “of the sower.”]

Nevertheless, lest he exult in his falsehood and bring forward the example of the Apostles as a prejudice against the numbers one hundred, sixty, and thirty, let him know that in Matthew and Mark a hundredfold was promised to the Apostles who had abandoned everything of their own.

But in Luke’s Gospel there is much more—that is, πολὺ πλείονα (*polu pleiona*, “many more”)—and nowhere in the Gospel is “seven” written in place of “a hundred.” He must therefore be held either a falsifier or guilty of ignorance.

> [Note: Victorius has πολλὰ πλασίονα, as it is found in Luke 18. Elsewhere the reading is πολυπλασίονα.]

Nor does it harm us that in one Gospel the enumeration begins with a hundred and in another with thirty, since all Scripture, especially the Old Testament, places the smaller number first and gradually ascends to the greater.

For example, it may say that someone was seventy-five and one hundred years old; yet seventy-five cannot be more than one hundred, though it was named first.

If you do not take the difference between the numbers one hundred, sixty, and thirty in a good sense, neither will you take it in a bad sense; and the same fault will belong to the seed that fell beside the road, on the rocks, and among thorns.

But if those three kinds and these three kinds are each understood either in a good or in a bad sense, it was foolish to count six categories for two things—especially since the Savior, in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, always added when recounting the parable:

> “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI, 15; XIII, 9; Mark IV, 9; Luke VIII, 18; XIV, 35).

Where nothing lies hidden inwardly, we are summoned in vain to mystical interpretation.

## 27. Christ’s manifold dwelling in believers

If the Father and the Son make their dwelling among believers, and you think that wherever Christ is a guest nothing is lacking, I suppose that Christ dwelled in one way among the Corinthians and in another among the Ephesians—that is, in one way among those in whom the Apostle Paul discovered many sins, and in another among those to whom he expounded mysteries unknown for ages.

In one way in Titus and Timothy, and in another in Paul.

Certainly:

> “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist.”

But when one is called greater, it is necessary that he have others who are lesser. And:

> “The one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

> [Note: Al. “and the one who is lesser.” The Cistercian book reads: “The one who is least in the kingdom, he says,” and so forth.]

You see, therefore, that in heaven there is a greatest and a least; and among the angels also, and among invisible creatures, there is a manifold and infinite diversity.

Why do the Apostles say:

> “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XVII, 5),

if there is one measure for all? And why does the Lord say to the disciple:

> “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. XIV, 31).

In Jeremiah also we read about the future kingdom:

> “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Jacob, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers” (Jer. XXXI, 31–32).

And shortly afterward:

> “I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they will be my people. And a man will no longer teach his neighbor, nor a man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord.’ For all will know me, from the least to the greatest” (ibid., 33–34).

> [Note: Most manuscripts read *cognoscite*, “know”; shortly afterward, “But the one who teaches and does not do some things,” and so forth.]

The context of that passage plainly shows that the Prophet is describing Christ’s future kingdom. And how, on that account, will there be a least and a greatest if all are to be equal? Certainly in the same way as it is said in the Gospel:

> “The one who teaches and does this will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. But the one who teaches and does not do it will be called least” (Matt. V, 19).

At a banquet the Savior commands us to take the lower place, lest, when someone greater arrives, we be disgracefully thrust down from the higher place (Luke XIV).

If we cannot fall but are only raised up through repentance, what does that ladder at Bethel signify, by which angels descend and ascend, coming from heaven to earth?

Certainly they were standing among the sheep and on the right while they were there. Angels descend from heaven, while Jovinian is secure in possession of their realm.

## 28. Many dwelling places in heaven. The orders of the Church. The orders of the heavenly powers.

Who, indeed, could restrain his laughter at someone who thinks that the “many dwelling places” with the Father are churches spread throughout the whole world, when Scripture most clearly teaches—according to the Gospel of John—that the Lord was speaking not of the number of churches but of heavenly dwelling places and eternal tabernacles, which the prophet longs for? “In my Father’s house,” he says, “are many dwelling places. Otherwise I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you; and if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be” (John XIV, 2–3).

The place and the dwelling places which Christ says he is preparing for the apostles are, of course, in the house of the Father—that is, in the kingdom of heaven—not on earth, where for the present he was leaving the apostles. At the same time, the sense of Scripture must be considered: “I would have told you,” he says, “that I am going and will prepare a place for you, if there were not many dwelling places with the Father”—that is, if each person did not prepare a dwelling place for himself by his own works, rather than by God’s generosity. Therefore it is not my task to prepare it, but yours, since the place prepared for Judas was of no benefit to him: through his own fault he lost it.

In accordance with this sense, we must also understand what is said to the sons of Zebedee, one of whom wanted to sit on the left and the other on the right: “You will indeed drink my cup; but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you, but it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Matthew XX, 23). It is not the Son’s to give—and how, then, is it the Father’s to prepare? “Prepared,” he says, “are in heaven diverse and very numerous dwelling places, for the many and diverse virtues; and it is not persons but works that receive them. Therefore you ask me in vain for what depends upon you, what my Father has prepared for those who, possessing virtues worthy of it, will ascend to such great dignity.”

Moreover, when he says, “I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be” (John XIV, 3), he is speaking specifically to the apostles, concerning whom it is also written elsewhere: “That just as I and you, Father, are one, so they also may be one in us” (John XVII, 21)—those who have believed, who have been perfected, who can say, “The Lord is my portion” (Psalm XXVII, 26).

But if there are not many dwelling places, how is it that both in the Old Testament and in the New the high priest has one order, the priests another, the Levites another, the gatekeepers another, and the temple-servants another? In the book of Ezekiel, too, where the order of the future Church and heavenly Jerusalem is described, the priests who had sinned are degraded to temple-servants and doorkeepers; and although they are in God’s temple—that is, on the right—they are not among the rams but among the smallest sheep.

**Note:** [Col. 0325D] Alternatively, “on the threshold.” The passage is Ezekiel XLIV, 10: “But the Levites who went far away from me through the error of the children of Israel, and strayed from me after their idols, and bore their iniquity, shall be attendants in my sanctuary and gatekeepers of the gates of the house, and ministers of the house; they themselves shall slaughter,” etc.

In that river also which flows out from the temple, waters the salt sea, and gives life to everything, many kinds of fish are described. Why, then, are there in the kingdom of heaven Archangels, Angels, Thrones, Dominions, Powers, Cherubim, and Seraphim, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come? The diversity of names is meaningless if there is no diversity of merits. An Archangel is certainly greater than the other, lesser Angels. Archangels, Powers, and Dominions possess other beings over whom they exercise authority and whom they rule as subjects. This exists in heaven; this exists in the service of God—lest you mock and jeer at us in your customary fashion if we place there emperors, prefects and counts, tribunes and centurions, companies, and the rest of the military order.

**Note:** Two manuscripts read: “things over which they may exercise authority, then: ‘This exists in the ages; this exists in the service of God.’” Perhaps both readings are more correct.

## 29. The practice of Sacred Scripture. Elisha’s double spirit.

But what he says—“Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Corinthians VI, 19)—is a trivial objection, since divine Scripture commonly calls one thing plurally and many things singularly. Yet even in the temple itself he should know that there are many chambers: an outer court, an inner court, vestibules, the holy place, and the Holy of Holies. There are also kitchens in the temple, small storerooms, winepresses, and repositories for vessels.

So too, in the temple of our body there are different merits. God does not dwell equally in everyone, nor is he poured into all according to the same measure. The spirit of Moses is taken and given to the seventy elders. I think the abundance of a river is one thing, and that of streams another. A double spirit is given to Elisha from Elijah; hence, possessing a double grace, he performed greater signs. Elijah raised a dead man while alive; Elisha raised a dead man after his own death. Elijah called down famine upon the people; Elisha, when a city was besieged, supplied hostile forces in a single day.

Although what he says—“Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit?”—may refer to the whole Church of believers, who, gathered together, form one body of Christ, the question now concerns the body: who is worthy to be Christ’s feet, who his head, who his eye, and who his hand. The two women in the Gospel—the penitent and the holy woman—signify this: one holds his feet, the other his head. Yet some think that there was only one woman, who began at the feet and gradually reached the head.

And when he objects: “I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word: that just as I and you, Father, are one, so all may be one in us”; 

**Note:** We have explained above (no. 19, note b) that the manuscripts give this wording of the passage, and it is natural to believe that the old Latin edition had it as well.

and when he objects: and that the entire Christian people are one in God, like beloved children, sharers in the divine nature—above we have already said, and now it must be impressed more fully, that we are one in the Father and the Son not according to nature but according to grace.

For the human soul and God are not of the same substance, as the Manichaeans customarily claim. But he says, “You loved them as you loved me.” You see, then, that we are taken into fellowship with his substance, not by nature but by grace. And therefore he loves us because the Father loved the Son; and the members are loved, namely, in the body.

“For all who received Christ, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name: who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John I, 12). The Word became flesh so that we might pass from flesh into the Word. The Word did not cease to be what it had been, nor did the human being cease to be what he was born. Glory was increased, not nature changed.

Do you wish to know how we become one body with Christ? Let him who created us teach you: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 55ff.).

The Evangelist John, too, who had drawn wisdom from Christ’s breast, agrees in the same words, saying: “By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God—God remains in him, and he in God” (1 John IV, 13, 15).

If you believe in Christ as the apostles believed, you will become one body with them in Christ. But if it is presumptuous for you to claim their faith and works when you do not possess the same faith and works, you cannot occupy the same place.

**Notes:** The same manuscripts read: “It is very frivolous,” etc., together with the old edition. Other manuscripts read: “He dwells in all.”

The Cistercian manuscript reads: “but according to grace to be in the Father and the Son, without ‘one.’” Another manuscript reads: “and therefore he loves us”; other books add “namely, from the body.”

## 30. The order of the Church. Grave and light sins.

Moreover, your claim that “bride,” “sister,” “mother,” and all these names refer to one Church, and that all believers are signified by these names, works against you. For if there is one order of the Church, and it does not have many members in one body, why must she be called bride, sister, and mother—unless she is the bride of some, the sister of others, and the mother of still others?

All indeed stand on the right; but one stands as bridegroom, another as brother, another as son. “My little children,” he says, “for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians IV, 19). Do you suppose that those who are being born in labor and the one who gives birth possess the same merit?

Thus you foolishly wished to assert that all the members love us equally, that the eye is not preferred to the finger, nor the hand to the ear; and that when individual members are lost, the pain is common to all. Yet the Apostle teaches the Corinthians that “some members are more honorable, while others are more shameful,” and that those which are more shameful are surrounded with greater honor, whereas those which are honorable in themselves do not need our care (1 Corinthians XII, 22–23).

**Note:** The Veronese manuscript, with the Cistercian, reads: “to surround [them] with greater honor.”

Do you consider mouth and belly, eyes and the passages through which feces and urine are discharged, to be of the same order and merit? “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is blind, your whole body is in darkness” (Luke XI, 34). If you amputate a finger or the tip of an ear, there is pain, but not as much loss, nor disfigurement accompanied by as much pain, as when you tear out the eyes, cut off the nose, or dissect the mouth. We can live without some members; without others we cannot live at all.

There are light sins and grave sins. It is one thing to owe ten thousand talents and another to owe a farthing. We shall indeed be held accountable for an idle word and for adultery; but it is not the same thing to blush and to be tortured, to feel shame and to suffer torment for a long time.

Do you think that what we say is our own? Hear the Apostle John: “Whoever knows his brother to be committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and he will give life to him who sins not unto death. But whoever sins unto death, who will pray for him?” (1 John V, 16).

You see that if we pray for lesser sins, we obtain forgiveness; but if we pray for greater ones, obtaining it is difficult. There is therefore a great difference between sins and sins. Hence, because the people of Israel had committed a sin unto death, it is said to Jeremiah: “Do not pray for this people, nor take up supplication for them, and do not oppose me, because I will not hear you” (Jeremiah VII, 16).

But if all alike enter the world and leave the world, and if this is a determining principle for future things, then the righteous and sinners alike will be regarded equally by God, because they are now born and die in the same way.

If you insist that there are two Adams, one earthly and the other heavenly, and that those who are in the earthly Adam are on the left while those who are in the heavenly Adam are on the right, answer me for the moment while I ask you about two brothers: Was Esau in the earthly Adam or in the heavenly? There is no doubt that you will answer that he was in the earthly. In which was Jacob? You will immediately say, in the heavenly. And how was he in the heavenly Adam when Christ had not yet come in the flesh, who is called the second and heavenly Adam?

Either, then, you will count all those who lived before Christ’s incarnation as belonging to the old Adam, so that even the righteous will be in the earthly human being and on the left among your goats; or, if it is impious to place Isaac where Ishmael is, Jacob where Esau is, and the saints where sinners are, the last Adam will be counted from the time when Christ was born of the Virgin. The argument about the two Adams will therefore not benefit your sheep and goats, because we have proved that both sheep and goats were in the first Adam, and that in one and the same human being some stood at God’s right and others at his left.

“For from Adam to Moses death reigned over all, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Romans V, 14).

**Note:** Formerly, “to be on the left”; the Cistercian manuscript reads “on the left,” as below.

## 31. In the martyr, the will is crowned.

As for what you strive to prove—that insult and homicide, “raca” and adultery, idle speech and impiety are repaid with one punishment—I have already answered you above, and I shall answer briefly now.

Either you will deny that you are a sinner, so that you will not be liable to Gehenna; or, if you are a sinner, you will be led to Tartarus even for a light offense. “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom I, 11). I suspect that at some time, as a human being, you have lied—for “every human being is a liar” (Psalm CXI)—so that God alone may be true and may be justified in his words and prevail when he is judged (Psalm L).

Either, then, you will not be human, so as not to be a liar; or, if, because you are human, you have been a liar, you will be punished with parricides and adulterers. For there is no difference among sins. Nor will those whom you raise from the lowly to the sublime thank you as much as those will be angry whom, because of a light and daily sin, you have thrust into the outer darkness.

But if, in persecution, the one who is suffocated, the one who is beheaded, the one who flees, and the one who dies shut up in prison receive one crown of victory amid various kinds of struggle, this too works in our favor. In the martyr, the will—from which death itself arises—is crowned.

It is my task to oppose the fury of the Gentiles and not deny the Lord. It is in their power either to behead me, burn me, imprison me, or inflict various kinds of punishment. If I flee and die in the wilderness, the dying person will not receive the same crown, because Christ is not the same cause of death.

**Note:** Two manuscripts and the old edition have, with the opposite meaning—but, in my view, more correctly—“and if I die in the wilderness, the crown of the one who dies will be the same, because Christ is the same cause of death.” The context above also supports this: the punishments that must be endured in the wilderness in order to evade persecution for Christ.

As for what you say, that there is absolutely no difference between the brother who was always with his father and the one who was later received back after repenting, I add, if you wish, that the one drachma which had been lost and found was joined to the others, and that the one sheep which the good shepherd sought and brought back after leaving the ninety-nine sheep completed the number one hundred.

But it is one thing to repent and ask forgiveness with tears, and another always to be with the father. Hence, through Ezekiel, the shepherd and father speaks concerning the sheep that has been brought back and the son who was once lost: “I will raise up my covenant with you, and you shall know that I am the Lord; and you shall remember and be confounded, so that you will no longer dare to open your mouth because of your shame, when I have been reconciled to you in all that you have done” (Ezekiel XVI, 62–63).

For penitents to have nothing less than what is just, their shame alone is sufficient for every punishment. Hence elsewhere it is said to them: “You shall remember your most evil ways and all your crimes by which you were polluted, and you shall be displeased with yourselves in your own sight, because of all your wicked deeds that you committed; and you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have done good to you for my name’s sake, and not according to your evil ways or your most wicked crimes” (ibid.).

The son is also rebuked by the father because he begrudges his brother’s salvation, and while the angels rejoice in heaven, he is tortured by envy.

Although the likeness of the two brothers—the frugal and the luxurious—does not refer to the merits of the whole human race, it may refer either to the persons of the Jew and the Christian, or to the saints and penitents. On this parable I dedicated a little book to Bishop Damasus while he was still alive.

## 32. The time of the various callings. It is our task to prepare our reward.

Moreover, if the workers of the first, third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours are paid one denarius, and the reward begins with those who worked last in the vineyard, these do not describe people of one time and one age. Rather, from the beginning of the world to its end, they are the mysteries of various callings.

At the first hour Abel and Seth were called; at the third, Enoch and Noah; at the sixth, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; at the ninth, Moses and the Prophets; at the eleventh, the people of the Gentiles. They receive their payment first because, believing in the crucified Lord, they earned a great reward through the difficulty of their faith. Many kings and prophets desired to see what we see, and did not see it.

The one denarius is not one reward but one life and one deliverance from Gehenna. Otherwise, just as at the principal pardon the guilty of different crimes are released from prison, and each person, according to his labor or works, is in this or that condition of life, so the denarius, as the pardon of the true Prince, releases everyone from prison through baptism. It is now our task, according to the diversity of our virtues, to prepare diverse rewards for ourselves.

**Note:** Saint Augustine also says this in *On Holy Virginity*, chapter XXVI, replying to this objection of Jovinianus: “What else,” he says, “does that denarius signify except what all will possess in common, such as eternal life itself, the kingdom of heaven itself? Since eternal life itself will be equally shared by all the elect, one denarius was assigned to all; but since within that eternal life they will shine distinctly with the light of their merits, there are many dwelling places with the Father. Thus, in the equal denarius, one will not live longer than another, but in the many dwelling places one is honored more brightly than another.” See the book in which much is assembled against Jovinianus.

## 33. Jonathan between David and Saul.

Thus far we have answered the proposed points individually. The following discourse will answer all of them together.

The Lord says to his disciples: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be the least of all” (Matthew XX, 26). If we are all to be equal in heaven, we humble ourselves here in vain so that there we may be greater.

Of the two debtors, one owing five hundred denarii and the other fifty, the one to whom more is forgiven loves more. Hence the Savior also says: “I tell you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much. But the one to whom little is forgiven loves little” (Luke VII, 47).

**Note:** Two manuscripts read: “I tell you, her sins are forgiven,” etc. Whoever loves less, and to whom less is forgiven, will certainly be in a lower rank.

When the master of a household was leaving, he entrusted his possessions to his servants: to one five talents, to another two, to another one (Luke XIX), to each according to his own abilities.

A similar account is written in another Gospel: a nobleman, going away to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and return, summoned ten servants and gave them ten minas, one each. One of them made ten minas, another five; and each, according to his ability and profit, received either ten or five cities.

Another, who had received one talent or one mina, buried what he had received, or wrapped it in a cloth, and kept it for his master’s arrival.

First, we must consider that if the righteous do not labor in hope of advancement, as our Zeno maintains, but merely so that they do not lose what they have received,

**Note:** The manuscripts read: “lest they lose what they have.”

then the one who buried the mina and talent so as not to lose what he had received did not sin. Indeed, the caution of the one who preserved it should be praised more than the fruitless labor of those who toiled without a reward for their labor.

Next, the very talent that is taken away from the timid or negligent servant is not given to the one who had made the smaller profit, but to the one who had made the greater profit—that is, to the one who had been placed over ten cities.

If number does not establish order, why did he say, “He gave to each according to his own abilities”?

**Note:** Some copies, as Victorius reports, read *virtues* instead of *abilities*; Matthew, however, has δύναμιν [“capacity”], and above too he says, “to each according to his own abilities.”

If the profits from five talents and ten are the same, why are ten cities not given to the one who had made the smaller profit, and five to the one who had made the greater profit?

That the Lord is not satisfied with what we possess, but always desires greater things, he himself shows when he says: “Why did you not give my money to the bankers, so that when I came I might have collected it with interest?” (Philippians III).

The Apostle Paul, knowing this, forgets what lies behind and reaches forward to what lies ahead; that is, he advances daily, and does not preserve delicately in a cloth the grace he has received. Rather, as a greedy merchant, he is renewed from day to day, and considers himself to be diminishing unless he has continually increased (Numbers XXXV).

Six cities of refuge are described in the Law for those who unintentionally killed human beings; and these cities themselves are priestly cities.

I ask: will you place these fugitives among your goats or among our sheep? If they were goats, they would be killed like the other murderers, nor would they enter the cities of God’s ministers. If you say they are sheep, they will certainly not be such sheep as graze in complete freedom without fear of wolves.

And it will be proved to you that they are indeed sheep, but wandering ones: they are on the right, but do not stand; they flee until the great Priest dies and, descending to the underworld, frees the souls of the fugitives.

The Gibeonites approach the children of Israel and, while the other nations are slaughtered, are preserved as woodcutters and water-carriers (Joshua IX). They possess such great merit before God that Saul’s line was destroyed because of the injury done to them (2 Samuel XXI).

Among whom will you place them? Among the goats? But they were not killed, and the Lord’s sentence vindicates them. Among the sheep? But divine Scripture says that they do not possess the same merit as the Israelites. You see, therefore, that they stand on the right, but at a much lower rank.

Between David, the holy man, and Saul, the most wicked king, stood Jonathan. We cannot place him among the kids, since he was worthy of the prophet’s love; nor among the rams, lest we make him David’s equal, especially since he too was killed. He will therefore be among the sheep, but in a lower order.

And just as there is a distinction between David and Jonathan, so you are compelled to acknowledge distinctions between sheep and sheep.

“The servant who knew his master’s will and did not prepare, nor act according to his will, will be beaten with many blows. But the one who did not know and did what deserved blows will be beaten with few. From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from the one to whom much has been entrusted, more will be demanded” (Luke XII, 47–48).

Behold: more or less is entrusted to one servant and another, and according to the quality of what was entrusted and of the sin, a corresponding number of blows is imposed.

**Notes:** Some copies, according to Victorius, read “who killed a human being,” as it is in the Septuagint. Formerly they read “to kill” instead of “killed.” Victorius also notes that “to ask” occurs here.

## 34. The type of the future Church on earth, and so forth.

The whole description of the land of Judea and of the tribes is a type of the future Church in heaven. Let us read Joshua son of Nun; let us read the final portions of Ezekiel; and we shall see that whatever is distributed in the one on earth as history is promised spiritually in the other in heaven (Joshua XIII; Ezekiel XLVIII).

What do the seven and eight steps in the description of the Temple mean? And again, why, in the Psalter, after the elements of Psalm 118, by which we are instructed in the mystical alphabet, do we ascend through fifteen steps until we can sing: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Joshua XIII)?

Why do two and a half tribes live beyond the Jordan, where there are very many animals, while the remaining nine and a half either drive out the former inhabitants from their dwelling places or live together with them?

Why does the tribe of Levi receive no portion in the land (Numbers XVIII), but the Lord is its portion? And among the Levites and priests, why does only the high priest enter the Holy of Holies, where the Cherubim and the mercy seat are?

Why do the remaining priests use only linen garments and not wear clothing woven with gold, hyacinth-blue, scarlet, purple, and fine linen?

The Levites and priests of lower rank receive wagons and oxen; those of higher rank carry the ark of the Lord on their shoulders.

**Note:** “If you remove the order.” We read neither more nor less in the manuscript codices, and I cannot sufficiently marvel at Erasmus and Marianus, who retain a fabricated text and wholly false and futile annotations. They read it in this way:

“If all who are on the right are one body—and, as the saying goes, ἕν κόνιον [one dust-particle]—bishops are useless, presbyters are in vain, and deacons are without purpose.”

After printing this form of the text, Marianus admits in his notes that it is corrupt and thinks it should be restored as follows:

“If all who are on the right are, as the saying goes, ἕν χῶμα [one mound], bishops are useless,” and so forth.

Gravius conjectures that σύνθημα [the military term “signal” or “watchword”] should be put in place of ἕν χῶμα. But none of these learned men has followed the evidence of the manuscript copies or Jerome’s meaning.
