Jovinianus was mocking Catholics because they wished to establish different ranks and offices in the Christian army; he himself wanted all the good to be one ἕνσωμα—that is, an undifferentiated body, as though many should grow together into one body. Hence Jerome adds above, after describing the angelic orders:

“This exists in heaven; this exists in the service of God, lest you mock and jeer at us in your customary fashion if we place there an emperor, prefects, counts, tribunes, centurions, companies, and the rest of the military order.”

Thus Saint Jerome says here: If all the righteous placed on the right are one ἕνσωμα, and it makes no difference whether one is a ram or a little sheep, and if in the army it makes no difference whether someone is an emperor or an ordinary soldier, then there are certainly no bishops in the Church, presbyters are useless, and deacons are without purpose.

Since this was most absurd to assert, Jovinianus, refuted by such a chain of consequences, paid the penalty for his audacity and impiety. Those who know Greek should take care not to divide the word ἕνσωμα into two words by reading ἕν σῶμα [one body], for the Latin word *unum* placed above by Jerome compels us to read ἕνσωμα—namely, “one embodied thing,” or “one body compacted from many.”

**MARTIAN.**

If you remove the order of the Tabernacle, the Temple, and the Church; if all who are on the right are one, as the common expression has it, *encoma*, the measure by which one is approved for military service, then bishops are useless, presbyters are in vain, and deacons are without purpose. Why do virgins persevere? Why do widows labor? Why do married women practice continence? Let us all sin, and after repentance we shall be the same as the apostles.

**Note:** The interpreters have been extraordinarily perplexed by this passage, and continue to be so today. Erasmus reads: “one, as the saying goes, ἕν κόνιον [one dust-particle], bishops are useless,” and so forth, omitting the words concerning military service and taking ἕν κόνιον as a Greek proverb equivalent to μία κόνις, “one little particle of dust.”

Victorius copied the passage in Erasmus’s corrupt form, adding only in his notes, after the printing, how the Greek word might be restored. “It should be read,” he says:

“If all who are on the right are, as the saying goes, ἕν χῶμα [one mound], bishops are useless,” and so forth—that is, “if all the blessed will be one heap, and there will be no difference among the blessed, then the distinction of sacred orders is given in vain.”

Later, Gravius, rightly dissatisfied with Victorius’s emendation, wished to substitute: “one, as they say, σύνθημα [a military watchword], approved for military service,” and so forth. Although the Greek word is supported by no manuscripts, he extracted from it a meaning more or less consistent with Victorius’s explanation.

But Martianaeus criticizes these attempts of the interpreters rather severely. Assuming that Christian warfare is indicated, he rewrites the passage: “one, as the saying goes, ἕνσωμα [one body], approved for military service; bishops are useless,” and so forth. He wishes the statement to be understood according to Jovinianus’s meaning: that all in the Christian army are one ἕνσωμα, that is, a body without distinctions of parts, and therefore there should be no different ranks and offices.

I would not readily say how many faults this reading contains, or how much more false it is than the others. If it means anything, ἕνσωμα, with the word repeated, means “one one body”; nor can it be written ἕνσωμα or understood as “embodied,” but rather ἓν σῶμα, “one body.” How Martianaeus finally explains this, there is nothing in it that is relevant.

Nor is Clericus much more successful, since he thinks that εὔσωμον should be read, meaning “one good body.” Although his Greek is somewhat inelegant, he is guilty of errors no fewer than Martianaeus, and perhaps more serious ones.

The restoration of this passage is nevertheless not especially difficult if one adheres faithfully to the manuscript copies. In them appears **E N C O M A**. If the word is taken as Greek, it should be written ἔγκομμα; if Latin, as it stands, *encoma* or *incoma*.

What this name means is explained by Isidore’s *Glossary*: “*Incoma*, a measure of soldiers.” Vegetius likewise says in Book I, chapter 5: “I know that the height of recruits has always been tested against the *incoma*.” It was a staff or stake against which the stature of soldiers was tested, to determine whether they possessed the required height. Hence *encoma* or *encuma* became ordinary military terms, and the verb *incumare* and the adjective *incumatus* occur in the *Acts of Saint Maximilian* with this meaning of measuring: “Since he is of suitable stature, I order that he be measured.”

The meaning of Jerome, therefore, is this: just as soldiers are tested for military service according to one bodily measure, so the measure of the glory of those who are in heaven on the right is not equal. And just as bishops, presbyters, and deacons are useless if the order of the Church—the hierarchical order—is removed, so it is pointless for virgins to persevere, widows to labor, and married women to practice continence if the merit of all in heaven will be equal and there will be one rank.

Jerome himself explains the passage in this sense in Book II *Against Rufinus*, where he attacks Origen, who asserted that at the restoration of all things, when the principal pardon comes, the Cherubim, Seraphim, Thrones, Principalities, Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Archangels, Angels, the Devil, demons, and the souls of all human beings—Christians, Jews, and Gentiles alike—will be of one condition and one measure.

## 35. Epilogue of the discussion. Every creature except God is subject to fault.

But now we have begun to sight land from the sea, and after the mountains of the deep, the foaming waves, and the ship—whether raised aloft or plunged into the depths—a harbor gradually opens to those who are weary and exhausted.

We have spoken of married women, widows, and virgins. We have preferred virginity to widowhood, and widowhood to marriage. The Apostle’s *pericope* concerning these questions has been set forth, and each objection has received an answer.

Secular literature also entered the discussion: which women were virgins, which were *univirae*—women married only once—and, conversely, what troubles the marriage bond sometimes entails.

We passed to the second division, in which he denies that those who have received baptism with complete faith can afterward sin. We showed that, except for God, every creature is subject to fault—not because all have sinned, but because they can sin, and the fall of others should make those who stand fearful.

Third, we came to fasting. Since the adversary’s proposition had two parts—either appealing to philosophers or appealing to examples from divine Scripture—we answered both.

**Note:** The Cistercian manuscript, with the Veronese, reads: “either to the philosophers,” etc.

The fourth and final division had distributed sheep and goats, the right and the left, the righteous and sinners, into two orders, wishing to show that there is no difference between one righteous person and another, or between one sinner and another. To prove this, he had amassed countless examples from Scripture, as though they agreed with his own interpretation. We answered this question with arguments and examples from Scripture, and we crushed the ancient opinion of Zeno both by common sense and by divine reading.

### 36. Jovinianus Had Many Disciples. What Does a Doctrine of Pleasure Accomplish?

Now it remains for us to address our Epicurus, rutting [Al.: sweating] in his little gardens among young men and little women. The fat, sleek, and whitened favor you. Add, if you wish, in the manner of Socratic mockery, all the swine and dogs; and since you love flesh, vultures as well, [Al.: eagles] eagles, hawks, and owls.

The multitude of Aristippus will never frighten us (see the Commentary on Ecclesiastes, chapter IX). Whoever is handsome, whoever is curled, whoever I see with carefully arranged hair and reddening cheeks, belongs to your herd—indeed, they grunt among your swine.

Those of our flock are gloomy, pale, filthy, and, as though strangers in this world, speak by their clothing and bearing, even if they are silent in speech:

“Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Ps. 119:5).

[Note: Victorius reads “with the inhabitants,” together with the Vulgate, against the manuscripts.]

that is, in the darkness of this world, because “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”

Do not boast that you have many disciples. The Son of God taught in Judaea, and only twelve apostles followed him. “I have trodden the winepress alone,” he says, “and of the peoples there was no man with me” (Isa. 63:3). He remained alone in his Passion, and even Peter’s steadfastness toward him faltered. But the whole people applauded the teaching of the Pharisees, saying:

“Crucify him, crucify him!”  
“We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:6, 15),

that is, we follow vices, not virtues; Epicurus, not Christ; Jovinianus, not the Apostle Paul.

The fact that many assent to your opinion is an indication of pleasure: they do not approve you so much when you speak as they favor their own vices. In the circles of the streets, a counterfeit soothsayer daily beats his buttocks, and with a twisted club strikes the teeth of those who bite him; yet there is never a lack of someone who can always be duped.

[Note: Victorius reads “nostrils” (*nares*), a reading for which he invents many arguments. See our notes on Letter 127, to Principia, no. 9, and the passage from Lucian’s *On the Death of Peregrinus*. The same occurs below in Book I *Against Rufinus*.] And you consider it a sign of great wisdom if more swine run after you—swine whom you nourish for the slaughter of Gehenna?

After your proclamation and [note: Most of the Fathers utterly execrate the indecency of the public baths approved by Jovinianus: Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus* III.5; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* XXX.7; Chrysostom, *On the Education of Children*; and others. The canons also—Laodicean 3 and Trullan 77—as well as imperial decrees and laws condemned it.] the baths in which men and women wash together, all the shamelessness that previously protected its burning lust, as though beneath the garments of modesty [Al.: concealed], has been stripped bare and exposed. What was formerly hidden is now out in the open.

You have displayed such disciples; you have not made them. Your teaching accomplished this: that sins should not even have repentance. Your virgins, whom you taught from the Apostle by the wisest counsel—counsel no one had ever read or heard—“It is better to marry than to burn,” have changed secret adulterers into open husbands.

The Apostle did not advise this; nor did the chosen vessel. It is Virgil’s counsel:

> “He calls it marriage, and under that name conceals the fault.”  
> (*Aeneid* IV)

[Note: The old edition reads: “so that not even sin has repentance.”]

### 37. Basilides, the Teacher of Luxury. False Prophets Always Promise Pleasant Things. Jovinianus’s Words

It is nearly four hundred years since the preaching of Christ has shone in the world. Since innumerable heresies tore apart his tunic, nearly every error proceeded from the Chaldaean, Syrian, and Greek languages. Basilides, the teacher of luxury and of the most shameful embraces, after so many years was transformed into Jovinianus as though Euphorbus were transformed into Pythagoras, so that the Latin language too might have its own heresy.

[Note: He thinks that Jovinianus was the first heretic among the Latins—a point Victor also records, though I do not know how true it is if one takes Montanus, Novatian, and others into account, certainly Latins.]

[Note: In the following book, *Against Vigilantius* 1: “Just as Euphorbus is said to have been reborn in Pythagoras, so in this man—Vigilantius—the wicked mind of Jovinianus arose.” Pythagoras dreamed that the soul of Euphorbus, slain at Troy, had migrated into him. He claimed that he had first been Aethalides, then Euphorbus, afterward Hermotimus and Pyrrhus, then Delian the fisherman, and finally, from Pyrrhus, had become Pythagoras.]

Was there no other province in the whole world that would receive the proclamation of pleasure, into which the crooked serpent might creep, except the one in which Christ had founded Peter’s teaching upon the rock?

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “upon the rock of Christ.” The old edition reads: “except in the one in which Christ had founded Peter’s teaching upon himself, the rock.” Shortly afterward: “the authority of preaching.” Jerome plainly indicates the Roman Church, in which Jovinianus first raged as a heretic. See the Admonition prefixed to these books.]

The standard of the cross and the austerity of preaching had destroyed the temples of idols; now, in opposition, luxury—of the penis, belly, and throat—tries to overthrow the strength of the cross. Therefore God speaks through Isaiah:

“My people, those who call you blessed, lead you astray, and confuse the paths of your feet” (Isa. 3:14).

And through Jeremiah:

“Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his own soul; and do not believe the false prophets who say, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace—who continually repeat, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord’” (Jer. 51:6).

“Your prophets saw false and foolish things for you; they did not expose your iniquity in order to summon you to repentance. They devour the people of God [Al.: God] like food; they did not call upon God.”

Jeremiah, announcing captivity, was stoned by the people. Hananiah son of Azur was breaking wooden yokes for the present and preparing iron ones for the future.

[Note: From Jeremiah 28: “You have broken wooden yokes; you shall make iron yokes in their place.” Victor notes that this was spoken against those who flatter people and promise prosperity. Two manuscripts read “wooden collars” and “iron ones.”]

False prophets always promise pleasant things and please for a short time. Truth is bitter, and those who preach it are filled with bitterness. For in the unleavened bread of truth and sincerity the Lord’s Passover is celebrated, and it is eaten with bitter herbs (Exod. 12).

This is certainly an excellent utterance, and one that the bride of Christ should hear, among virgins, widows, and celibates—whence the name itself was given, because those who abstain from intercourse are worthy of heaven.

[Note: “Virgins, widows, and celibates.” Quintilian I.10: “Gaius seemed ingeniously to have called celibates *caelibes*, as though *coelites*, because they are free from a very heavy burden.” Martial. Two manuscripts omit *et*, reading “widows, celibates.” Gravius explains the appended etymology from Quintilian II.10: “Gaius seemed ingeniously to have called celibates *caelites*, as though blessed by heaven,” and so does Isidore, *Etymologies* X, letter C: “A celibate is so called as though blessed by heaven.”]

“Fast rarely; marry more frequently. You cannot perform the works of marriage unless you have taken honeyed wine, meat, and nuts. Lust requires strength. Flesh quickly consumed withers. Do not fear fornication. Whoever has once been baptized in Christ cannot fall, for he has the consolation of marriage with which to work off his lusts. And even if you fall, repentance will restore you; and you who were hypocrites in baptism will be of solid faith in repentance. Do not be disturbed, thinking that there is any difference between the righteous person and the penitent, or that repentance grants forgiveness to a lower rank but removes the crown. There is one recompense. Whoever has stood at the right hand will enter the kingdoms of heaven.”

By these counsels your swineherds are richer than our shepherds, and your goats drag many she-goats along with them. They have become horses raging toward women:

“As soon as they see women, they neigh” (Jer. 5:8),

and, shamefully, they console their lack of self-control with examples from Scripture.

Those wretched little women too, and not deserving of pity, chanting the words of their teacher—“For what else does God require but seed?”—have lost not only chastity but also modesty; and they defend the lust they practice with greater shamelessness.

[Note: From Ovid’s verse in the *Ibis*: “May you always be wretched, and may no one pity you.”]

Moreover, in your army you have many reserves; you have buffoons and light infantry in the outposts—fat, [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads “fat, carefully groomed, sleek.”] groomed, sleek, and shouting—who defend you with fists and kicks. Noblemen yield to you in the road; the wealthy kiss your head. If you had not come, drunkards and belchers could not enter paradise.

Bravo for your courage—or rather, for your vices! In your camp you also have Amazons, bare-breasted, with naked arms and knees, coming against men and provoking them to the battle of lust (see the Commentary on Jeremiah, chapter XVI). And because you are a wealthy householder, your aviaries nourish not turtle-doves but hoopoes (see also the Commentary on Zechariah, chapter V), which fly all around the haunts of foul pleasure.

Attack me, cast me aside, bring whatever charges you wish, accuse me of luxury and indulgence. You will love me all the more if I am such a person, for then I shall belong to your herd.

### 38. He Addresses Rome

But I shall speak to you, who erased the blasphemy written upon your forehead by confessing Christ. Powerful city, mistress of the world, city praised by the Apostle’s voice (Rom. 1), interpret your own name.

[Note: The text was corrupt, partly Greek and partly Latin: ΡΩΜΗ. In Greek, Ῥώμη (*Rhōmē*) means “strength”; in Hebrew, [the supplied text is incomplete] means “height” or “sublimity.”]

Rome is either a name of strength among the Greeks or of sublimity according to the Hebrews. Preserve what you are called: let virtue make you lofty, not pleasure make you low.

The curse that the Savior threatened you with in the Apocalypse (chapters XVII and XVIII) you can escape through repentance, taking the example of the Ninevites.

Beware the name Jovinianus, which is derived from the idol Jupiter. The Capitol lies neglected; the temples and rites of Jupiter have fallen. Why should his name and his vices flourish among you?

Even under the kings and under Numa Pompilius, your ancestors more readily embraced the continence of Pythagoras than, under the consuls, the luxury of Epicurus.

[Note: Victor maintains that this does not refer to the famous Pythagoras, founder of the Italian school, but to another Spartan Pythagoras; Martianaeus agrees. The commonly accepted view, based on the testimony of Dio Chrysostom XLIX and Nicephorus Gregoras XXXIII, makes Numa later than the Samian Pythagoras, although other ancient writers wished the two to have been contemporaries because of the agreement between their doctrines. I do not think, however, that Jerome is indicating Pythagoras’ person here, so that it is necessary to debate his age or invent another man of the same name, but rather the teaching that survived in writings and was especially pleasing to Numa. Livy XL.29, Pliny XIII.13, Lactantius XXII, Augustine, *City of God* VIII.5, Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Men* 3, and others actually speak of Pythagorean books found in Numa’s tomb.]

[Note: “They embraced luxury.” In the manuscript of Saint Peter of Chartres, a sentence of condemnation against Jovinianus follows:

“Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Felix, Prefect of the Praetorium.

‘Jovinianus …’”

This is Law 53 in the Theodosian Code, title 5, *Concerning Heretics*. —Martianaeus.]

---

## [Against Vigilantius]

### Admonition Concerning the Following Book, *Against Vigilantius*

We printed Jerome’s letter against Vigilantius, addressed to the presbyter Riparius two years before this little work, in the second part of the first volume, under number CIX. Since Jerome had not yet received the comments of that heretical man, he anticipated the battle in a certain way, revealing his own faith rather than attacking the other man’s unbelief.

Now that we have come to the book itself, in which he contends against the man’s madness with the utmost ardor, it is necessary to state beforehand who Vigilantius was and what he rashly believed against the true faith, so that you may have the circumstances of the case clearly before you.

Gennadius says that he was a Gaul by nation; Jerome says that he was from the Calagurritans, or from a little village near the city of Convenae called Calagurris. From this you may understand that he came from lower Aquitaine, at the foot of the Pyrenees.

According to Gennadius, he was a man seduced by human praise and presuming beyond his powers, polished in speech but not trained in the meaning of Scripture. If you listen to Jerome, however, he was unskilled both in words and in knowledge, and uncultivated in speech.

By the practice of his former life he had kept an inn—or was still keeping one when he wished to be heard as a new teacher of the Churches and was ordered to become a presbyter. He attained this rank and held a church in the Spanish diocese of Barcelona, to use Gennadius’ words. Since it bordered on the parishes of the holy presbyters Riparius and Desiderius, they continually grieved that the proximity of a diseased shepherd endangered their own sheep’s salvation.

The bishop under whose authority he lived also seemed to protect him and indulge his madness, since, although warned, he delayed correcting the madman or entirely neglected to do so.

### 2. The New Doctrines Invented by His Deranged Mind

The new doctrines that he devised in his insane mind can be reduced approximately to the following points.

1. He denied that there were martyrs, or that their relics should be venerated, or that vigils should be kept at their tombs in the churches, or that any of the other honors customarily offered to them in Christian assemblies should be paid.

2. With even worse madness he said that we are in no way helped by the prayers of the saints, nor are the heavenly beings moved by earthly necessities; hence the signs sometimes performed through them benefit only unbelievers.

3. He called certain ceremonies of the Church, especially the lighting of candles during the day at Mass or during the reading of the Gospel, a rite of pagan superstition; and he did not want the Alleluia sung except at Easter.

4. He held that each person could retain his wealth and that renunciation of worldly possessions was not so good after all; indeed, he called the poverty and solitude of monks idleness and shameful flight. For this reason he disapproved of the alms customarily sent to Jerusalem, and perhaps at times even prohibited them. He maintained that if wealth was to be distributed for the use of the poor, it should not be poured out all at once but given gradually.

5. Finally, he blurted out that clerics above all should not be celibate. He hated continence so much that he called it heresy, and chastity so much that he called it a seedbed of lust, that he even persuaded bishops that chastity should be trusted to no one and that no celibates could be ordained. Unless they saw women’s bellies swollen, they were to consider their husbands unworthy of Christ’s ministry.

### 3. Jerome’s Response to These Heresies

Jerome responds to these monstrous heresies point by point in this little book. You will admire it all the more because he dictated it in the labor of a single night.

He himself testifies that it was written nearly two years after he sent the previously mentioned letter to Riparius concerning vigils and overnight watches in the basilicas of the martyrs. We have shown that this letter belongs to the year 404, and therefore that this book must be assigned to 406.

This is also established by the sudden journey to Egypt of Sisinnius, the brother whom Jerome mentions at the end. This is the same Sisinnius who at one time received from the holy Doctor both this book, to be delivered to Riparius and Desiderius, and the commentaries on Zechariah, to be returned to Exuperius of Toulouse. Jerome testifies in the Preface that he composed those commentaries in the year 406, the year identified in the consular records by the sixth consulship of the Emperor Arcadius Augustus and the name of Anicius Probus.

It will also be clear that the work must be dated toward the end of that year from another letter, number 129 in our recension, addressed to Minervius and Alexander. In it Sisinnius, who had arrived at Bethlehem toward the end of autumn and was said to be staying there until Epiphany, is described as having shortly afterward suddenly arrived, declaring that he would depart immediately.

## One Book of the Holy Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, Against Vigilantius

[Note: The editions of Martianaeus and Vallarsius give the title as follows: “Here begins the book of the presbyter Saint Jerome against Vigilantius.” —Edition.]

[Here begins the Book.]

[Note: Jerome’s works are corrupted in certain manuscript books to such an extent that one can learn the fact from a single Cluniac manuscript. In it the present treatise against Vigilantius begins as follows:

“Here begins [the book] against Vigilantius, who agrees with Jovinianus. Many monsters have indeed been generated in the world: sirens, sea-monsters; the onocrotalus, a bird whose name means ‘long beak’; the crotalon, that is, a cymbal; owls, that is, birds named from their hooting; Leviathan, that is, a great whale, whose name means ‘their addition’; Behemoth, which means ‘animal’; the Stymphalian birds, that is, harpies from the river Stymphalus. We read of centaurs, sirens, owls, and onocrotali in Isaiah,” and so forth.

Who would not shudder at such extensive corruption and deformation of a sound text in the Cluniac manuscript, otherwise an excellent codex and more carefully written in many other places? These defects can easily be removed from other copies, of which this edition always has an abundance. —Martianaeus.]

### 1. Jovinianus’s Condemnation and Death. Vigilantius’s Errors and Blasphemies

Many monsters have been generated in the world. We read of centaurs, sirens, owls, and onocrotali in Isaiah (Isa. 13 and 35).

[Note: The earlier reading was “onocratuli.” Martial: “The foul throat of the Ravenna onocrotalus.” The Bologna codex of the monastery of Saint Saviour does not have “we read in Isaiah.”] Job describes Leviathan and Behemoth in mystical language (Job 3 and 40). The poets’ fables tell of Cerberus, the Stymphalian birds, the Erymanthian boar, the Nemean lion, the Chimera, and the many-headed Hydra. Virgil describes Cacus (*Aeneid* VIII). Spain has handed down the story of the three-formed Geryon.

Gaul alone had no monsters, but was always rich in brave and eloquent men. Suddenly Vigilantius arose—or, more truly, Dormitantius—fighting with an unclean spirit against the Spirit of Christ. He denies that the tombs of the martyrs should be venerated; he says that vigils should be condemned; he insists that the Alleluia should never be sung except at Easter; he calls continence heresy and chastity a seedbed of lust.

[Note: See the notes above, near the end of the second book against Jovinianus. The manuscripts of Bologna read “Euphorbius.”]

And just as Euphorbus is said to have been reborn in Pythagoras, so in this man the wicked mind of Jovinianus arose, so that against both men we must respond to the ambushes of the devil. To him it is rightly said:

“Wicked seed, prepare your children for slaughter because of the sins of their father” (Isa. 14:21, according to the Septuagint).

Jovinianus, condemned by the authority of the Roman Church, gave up his spirit among pheasants and pork—or rather, he belched it out.

This Calagurritan innkeeper, a mute Quintilian perversely named after his village—

[Note: This does not mean, as Victor thinks, that Vigilantius was Quintilian’s fellow countryman, but that both men had the same native city, Calagurris. Quintilian’s city was the Spanish Calagurris; Vigilantius’ was the village near the city of Convenae. Hence Jerome calls him “the mute Quintilian,” perversely named.]

—mixes water with wine. From his former trade he tries to mingle the poisons of his unbelief with the Catholic faith: to attack virginity, hate chastity, and proclaim himself against the fasts of the saints at secular banquets; while philosophizing among goblets, and while greedily eating pastries, he is soothed by the melody of the Psalms, so that he deigns to hear David, Jeduthun, Asaph, and the songs of the sons of Korah only amid his feasts.

[Note: The allusion appears to be to Isaiah 1: “Your wine is mixed with water,” which various Fathers, and especially Jerome, commonly interpret as referring to heretics. Tertullian, *On the Soul* 3, calls heretics innkeepers who mix water with wine. Jerome elegantly reproaches Vigilantius with both heresy and the innkeeper’s trade in a single expression.]

I poured out these words more from a grieving heart than a laughing one, because I cannot restrain myself and cannot pass by with deaf ears the insult done to the apostles and martyrs.

### 2. The Celibacy of Clerics

Shame upon the crime! He is said to have bishops as accomplices in his wickedness—if they are to be called bishops, since they do not ordain deacons unless they have first taken wives. They trust chastity to no celibate; indeed, by suspecting everyone, they show how saintly they themselves live. Unless they see the wives of clerics pregnant and infants crying in their mothers’ arms, they do not confer the sacraments of Christ.

What will the Churches of the East do? What will Egypt and the Apostolic See do, which accept either virgins as clerics [Note: All the manuscripts read “accept,” suggesting that the reference is to the Roman custom alone. Recall the statement in Book I against Jovinianus: “A man who fathers children while a bishop cannot be a bishop; otherwise, if he is discovered, he will not be treated as a man but condemned as an adulterer.” Siricius, Letter 1 to Himerius; Innocent, Letter 1 to Victricius; Ambrose, *On the Duties* I.50 and Letter 61 to Vercellae; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 59; and, to omit others, Augustine at the end of Book II *On Adulterous Marriages* support this.] or continent men? Or, if they have wives, cease to be husbands?

This is what Dormitantius taught, giving free rein to lust and doubling by his exhortations—or rather extinguishing through intercourse with women—the natural heat of the flesh, which usually grows hot in youth. Thus there would be nothing by which we differed from swine, nothing by which we differed from brute animals, nothing by which we differed from horses, of whom it is written:

“Raging horses toward women, each one neighed for his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. 5:8).

This is what the Holy Spirit speaks through David:

“Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 32:9).

And again concerning Dormitantius and his associates:

“Bind their jaws with bit and bridle, who do not draw near to you.”

### 3. Riparius, Desiderius, and Sisinnius. Vigilantius’s Ignorance

But now it is time for us to set down his own words and try to answer each one. It may happen that a malicious interpreter will again say that I fabricated the material to which I respond with rhetorical declamation, just as he did with the letter I wrote to Gaul concerning a mother and daughter who were quarreling with each other.

The holy presbyters Riparius and Desiderius are the authors of this little composition of mine. They write that their parishes have been stained by the proximity of this man, and they sent his books through their brother Sisinnius—books that he vomited up while snoring amid drunkenness. They assert that some people have been found who, favoring their own vices, assent to his blasphemies.

He is indeed ignorant both in words and in knowledge, and uncultivated in speech; he cannot defend even the truth. But because of worldly people and little women burdened with sins, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth, I shall answer his nonsense in a single night’s labor, lest I seem to have rejected the letters of the holy men who begged me to do this.

### 4. The City and Homeland of Vigilantius. It Was Called Pompeiopolis. Vigilantius’s Words

Naturally, he answers to his ancestry: born from the seed of robbers and the Convenae—whom Gnaeus Pompey, after subduing Spain and hastening to return for his triumph, brought down from the heights of the Pyrenees and gathered into a single town, from which the city received the name Convenae—he continues to rob against the Church of God.

[Note: The distinguished de Marca, in a special dissertation on Vigilantius’ homeland, argues that the passage should be restored by reading *nec* rather than the conjunction *et*. He wants the meaning to be this: if Vigilantius can draw authority from Origen for practicing robbery, that license must be restrained outside his own city, which was once formed from the peoples of the Vectones, Arevaci, and Celtiberians, peoples who practiced brigandage in war rather than military service; he must not be permitted to raid the other churches of Gaul any farther, since he does not carry the standard of the Cross, but is himself marked by the insignia of the devil. No manuscript, however, supports this conjecture. It is better, with Pagius, to correct the faulty punctuation with which the period was formerly burdened, as we have done, retaining the conjunction *et*. In that sense Vigilantius is said naturally to answer to his ancestry: being born from the seed of robbers—namely, the Vectones and Arevaci—he robs more and more, raids the churches of Gaul, and carries not the standard of the Cross but the insignia of the devil. In the Bologna manuscript *Arvaci* appears for *Arevaci*; in others these names are strangely corrupted.]

Descending from the Vectones, Arevaci, and Celtiberians, he raids the churches of Gaul and carries not the standard [Al.: of Christ] of the Cross, but the insignia of the devil.

Pompey did the same thing in the regions of the East: after conquering the Cilician and [Note: The Bologna manuscript reads: “after overcoming the Isaurian robbers.” Pomponius Mela I.13 says: “It is a city once possessed by the Rhodians and Argives after piracy, assigned to Pompey; now Pompeiopolis, formerly Soli.”] Isaurian pirates and robbers, he founded a city bearing his name between Cilicia and Isauria.

But this city still preserves the customs of its ancestors, and no Dormitantius has arisen there. Gaul endures a native enemy and sees a man of deranged mind, one who ought to be bound in Hippocratic restraints, sitting in the Church. Among his other blasphemous words, he also says:

“Why is it necessary for you not only to honor with such great honor, but also to adore that something-or-other which you worship while it is carried in a small vessel?”

And again in the same book:

“Why do you kiss and adore dust wrapped in linen?”

And in what follows:

“We see a practice almost pagan introduced into the churches under the pretext of religion: while the sun is still shining, masses of candles are lit, and everywhere people kiss and adore some little bit of dust, wrapped in a precious linen cloth in a small vessel.”

[Note: Two manuscripts read specifically “the rite.” This was indeed a pagan institution: lighting candles before idols. Jerome himself says in Book XVI, chapter 57, on Isaiah: “Honoring the protection of idols with candles and lamps.” Lactantius likewise writes in Book VI of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 2: “A person who offers candles and the light of wax candles as a gift to the author and giver of light should not be considered to possess a sound mind.” He was criticizing the pagans. In Christian worship, however, as I may say here once for all, the ancient Fathers approve the mystical use of lights during the day: Saint Epiphanius, *Letter to John of Jerusalem*, now numbered among Jerome’s letters as 51, section 9; and the celebrated verses of Paulinus, *Natale* 3 of Saint Felix:

> “The altars are crowned with dense lamps,  
> The lights burn fragrant in waxen reeds;  
> Night and day they shine, so that night with the splendor of day  
> Gleams, and day itself, bright with heavenly honor,  
> Shines more brightly, its light doubled by countless lamps.”

Our Jerome explains perfectly below that the candles are lit not to dispel darkness but to create a sign of joy. Isidore agrees in Book VII, chapter 12, of the *Etymologies*, as do others who thereafter expounded the many sacraments symbolized by these lights.]

“They offer great honor in this way to the most blessed martyrs, whom they think must be illuminated by the most worthless little candles, although the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne illuminates them with all the splendor of his majesty.”

### 5. The Relics of the Apostles and of Samuel

Who, you madman, has ever adored martyrs? Who has considered a human being to be God? Did not Paul and Barnabas, when the Lycaonians considered them Jupiter and Mercury and wanted to sacrifice victims to them, tear their garments and declare that they were human beings? (Acts 14.)

This was not because they were not better than Jupiter and Mercury, human beings long dead, but because, under the error of paganism, an honor due to God was being offered to them.

We read the same about Peter: when Cornelius wished to adore him, Peter raised him up with his hand and said:

“Rise, for I too am a human being” (Acts 10:26).

And you dare to say: “That something-or-other which you worship while it is carried in a small vessel”? I want to know what that “something-or-other” is.

“Explain yourself more clearly, so that you may blaspheme with complete freedom: some little bit of dust, wrapped in precious linen in a small vessel.”

You are pained that the relics of the martyrs are covered with precious cloth, rather than being bound in rags or sackcloth or thrown onto a dung heap, so that Vigilantius alone, drunk and asleep, may be adored.

Are we therefore sacrilegious when we enter the basilicas of the Apostles? Was the Emperor Constantius sacrilegious when he transferred the holy relics of Andrew, Luke, and Timothy to Constantinople?

[Note: See Philostorgius III.2 and Idatius in the *Fasti*; indeed, Jerome himself in the *Chronicle* under the years 19 and 20 of Constantius, not 21 as Scaliger reports; and in the *Catalogue* chapter 7, at the end.]

At Constantinople demons roar beside those relics, and the inhabitants confess that they sense their presence.

Must the Emperor Augustus Arcadius also be called sacrilegious, because long afterward he transferred the bones of blessed Samuel from Judaea to Thrace?

Must all bishops be judged not only sacrilegious but foolish, because they carried a worthless object and disintegrated ashes in silk and a golden vessel?

Must the peoples of all the churches be called fools because they went out to meet the holy relics and received them with such joy, as though they saw and welcomed the prophet present and alive?

[Note: The old edition adds “and rejoiced,” and shortly afterward “they might see” and “they might receive.” The Bologna manuscript reads “and might see him alive,” omitting “the prophet.”]

From Palestine as far as Chalcedon, crowds of peoples came together, and with one voice resounded in praise of Christ. Clearly they adored Samuel, and not Christ, whose Levite and prophet Samuel was.

You suppose that he is dead, and therefore blaspheme. Read the Gospel:

“The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. He is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matt. 12).

If they are therefore alive, then, according to your view, they are not confined in an honorable prison.

## 6. The Opinion of the Heretics of This Age. Apocryphal Books Are Not to Be Read. Basilides’ Monstrous Fictions of Words.

“For you say that the souls of the apostles and martyrs are seated either in Abraham’s bosom, or in a place of refreshment, or beneath God’s altar, and cannot leave their tombs or be present wherever they wish.”

[Note: This was the rule of the old judicial practice concerning persons conspicuous for their rank among the accused: before conviction they were not to be confined in prison. See law 1, *On the Custody of the Accused*, and Venuleius in the same Code, book 5. Soon afterward the old edition reads *recludantur* (“let them be confined”); then the Bologna manuscript has *leges ponis* (“you impose laws”).]

They are, forsooth, of senatorial rank; they are shut up not among murderers in the most dreadful prison, but in honorable and unrestricted custody, on the Fortunate Isles and in the Elysian Fields. Do you impose laws upon God? Do you put chains upon the apostles, so that they may be kept under guard until the day of judgment and not be with their Lord, of whom it is written: “They follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4)?

[Col. 0344B] If the Lamb is everywhere, then those who are with the Lamb must also be believed to be everywhere. Yet while the devil and demons wander throughout the whole world and are present everywhere with immense speed, are the martyrs, after the shedding of their blood, to be shut up beneath an ark and confined so that they cannot leave it?

[Manuscripts: *ara* (“altar”), not *arca* (“ark”). Thus shortly above, *subter aram Dei* (“beneath God’s altar”).]

You say in your little book that while we are alive we can pray for one another, but after we have died no one’s prayer can be heard on behalf of another—especially since the martyrs, when they pleaded for vengeance for their blood, were unable to obtain it (Rev. 6:9).

[Note: The Bologna manuscript reads: “can pray for all, when they still have to be concerned about themselves,” and continues, “But I wonder and grieve that heretics still quibble over this legitimate argument of Jerome’s—or rather, that they utterly fail to understand it. If the saints could pray for others while they lived amid the cares of this age, much more, once they have been received by God, secure in their own safety, will they be concerned for our salvation.”]

If the apostles and martyrs, while still in the body, can pray for others when they must yet be concerned for themselves, how much more after their crowns, victories, and triumphs? One man, Moses, obtains pardon from God for six hundred thousand armed men (Exod. 32; Acts 7). Stephen, the imitator of his Lord and the first martyr in Christ, pleads for pardon for his persecutors. After they have begun to be with Christ, will they have less power? The apostle Paul says that two hundred and seventy-six souls were granted to him on the ship; once he has begun to be released and to be with Christ, will he then close his mouth in prayer and be unable to utter even a word for those who throughout the whole world have believed in his Gospel? Will “a living dog” be better than “a dead lion” (Eccl. 9:4)?

I would rightly apply this to Ecclesiastes if I confessed that Paul was dead in spirit. Finally, the saints are not called dead but sleeping. Thus Lazarus, who was going to be raised, is said to have slept (John 11). And the Apostle forbids the Thessalonians to grieve concerning those who sleep (1 Thess. 4).

You are awake, yet you sleep; and while sleeping, you write. You present me with an apocryphal book, one that is read by you and your kind under the name of Ezra:

[Note: The book under the name of Ezra is apparently the Fourth Book of Ezra, for Vigilantius’ false opinion seems to have been taken from chapter 7, verses 36–44. MARTIAN.]

[Col. 0345A] where it is written that after death no one should dare to intercede for others—a book that I have never read. Why is it necessary to take into one’s hands something that the Church does not accept? Unless perhaps you should bring forward for me Balsamus, Barbelus, the Treasure of Manichaeus, and the ridiculous name Leusibora:

[Note: “The Treasure of Manichaeus.” Manichaeus taught that there were two natures, one good and the other evil, and asserted that they had been drawn out, as it were, from some eternal treasure. See these ridiculous monstrosities of Manichaeus and Basilides in Irenaeus, Epiphanius, and Augustine. MARTIAN.

Martianaeus thinks that the two natures, one good and the other evil, are indicated as having been drawn from some eternal treasure according to Manichaeus; Victorius does not differ from him, judging that *treasure* is meant in its ordinary sense. But, on the contrary, Jerome frequently indicates that “Treasure” was one of the monstrous names devised by Basilides and Manichaeus: “the monstrosities of Basilides, Balsamus, and Treasure, and also of Barbelus and Leusibora, and of the remaining names,” in his commentary on Isaiah 64. He says the same in the letter to Theodora and in the letter to Pammachius *On the Best Method of Translation*: “Among the Phoenician gods, Melkatharos and Thesauron” (*Μελκάθαρον*, “Melkatharos,” and *Θησαυρόν*, “Treasure”). Codinus likewise lists Thesauron in his *Origins of Constantinople*, number 66, although others substitute *Θύσῳρον* for *Θησαυρόν* and accuse Codinus of a false reading. Certainly, as the recently published author of the *History of the Manichaean Heresy* reports, the name “Treasure” was the title of the fourth book that Scythianus, the founder of this heresy, composed against the orthodox faith. See Eusebius, *Oration on the Praises of Constantine*, and what we noted in note b on Letter 25 to Theodora, no. 3. The word *proferas* (“you should bring forward”) is absent from the Bologna manuscript.]

and because you live at the foot of the Pyrenees and are a neighbor of Iberia, you pursue and put forward the unbelievable monstrosities of Basilides, that most ancient heretic and man of ignorant learning, proposing what the authority of the whole world condemns.

For in your little commentary, as though it supported your case, you take a testimony from Solomon that Solomon never wrote at all. Thus, since you have another Ezra, you may also have another Solomon. And if it pleases you, read the fabricated revelations of all the patriarchs and prophets:

[Note: Perhaps the book indicated is the one entitled *Patriarchs* (*πατριάρχαι*) in the synopsis of Athanasius and in the canon of Nicephorus of Constantinople.]

and once you have learned them, sing them among women’s weaving-rooms—or rather, display them for reading in your taverns, so that through these nursery tales you may more easily entice the uneducated crowd to drink.

## 7. Why Are Candles Lit in Churches? Christians Are Born Again. Why Are Lights Lit at the Gospel?

We do not light candles in broad daylight, as you foolishly slander us, but so that by this consolation we may temper the darkness of night and keep watch by the light, lest, blind, we sleep with you in the darkness.

[Note: The Bologna manuscript reads, “lest we sleep with you,” omitting “blind.”]

But if some, through ignorance and the simplicity of secular people—or certainly of devout women, of whom we can truly say, “I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2)—do this in honor of the martyrs, what do you lose by it? The apostles once complained that the ointment was being wasted, but they were corrected by the Lord’s words (Matt. 26; Mark 14). Christ did not need ointment, nor did the martyrs need the light of candles; nevertheless, that woman did this in Christ’s honor, and her devotion of mind is accepted.

And all who light candles receive their reward according to their faith, as the Apostle says: “Let each be fully convinced in his own mind” (Rom. 14:5). Do you call such people idolaters? I do not deny that all of us who believe in Christ came from the error of idolatry. For we are not born Christians; we are born again as Christians. And because once we worshiped idols, must we now not worship God, lest we seem to honor him in the same way as the idols?

That was done for idols, and therefore it is detestable; this is done for martyrs, and therefore it is to be accepted. Indeed, throughout all the Churches of the East, even without the relics of martyrs, when the Gospel is to be read, lights are lit while the sun is already shining—not to dispel darkness, but to signify joy. Hence those evangelical virgins always have their lamps lit (Matt. 25). And to the apostles it is said: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). And of John the Baptist: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35), so that under the figure of bodily light that light might be revealed of which we read in the Psalter: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:105).

## 8. The Roman Bishop Offers Sacrifices over the Bodies of the Apostles. Vigilantius’ Foolish Opinion or Objection. Eunomius, the Originator of the Heresy against Relics. Montanus. Tertullian’s Book *Scorpiace*. The Cainite Heresy Revived.

Does the Roman bishop therefore act wrongly when, over the remains of the dead Peter and Paul—bones that we regard as worthy of veneration, but which you call worthless dust—he offers sacrifices to the Lord and regards their tombs as Christ’s altars?

[Note: The proper term for the reverence owed to the relics of the saints is *veneration*. St. Hilary, in book 1 *Against Constantius*, no. 8, calls them “the venerable bones of the blessed martyrs.” Eusebius of Gaul, or, as it seems, Eucherius, in his homily *On Saint Blaudina*, laments that “the venerable bones” were reduced to ashes by the impious. Then he says: “Where are those who say that veneration should not be offered to the sacred bodies of the martyrs?” For *vilem* (“worthless”), some books and the Bologna manuscript have *vile* (“worthless”).]

And do not the bishops of the whole world, not merely of one city, err when, scorning the tavern-keeper Vigilantius, they enter the basilicas of the dead, in which some utterly worthless dust and ash lies wrapped in a linen cloth:

[Note: The old edition, together with the Bologna manuscript, reads “wrapped in a linen cloth.”]

so that it pollutes everything that has been polluted, and as though the Pharisaic tombs were whitewashed on the outside,

[Note: The Bologna manuscript again reads: “and inside they are filthy with unclean ash; according to you, everything unclean smells foul,” omitting the words inserted here. Victorius also observed that these words are absent from the ancient copies and thought it might have been better to delete them.

“While inside they are filthy with unclean ash”: several manuscripts omit some words here and read, “while they are filthy inside with unclean ash.” The Cluniac manuscript preserves this variant reading: “and inside the unclean ashes pollute and defile everything unclean according to you.” MARTIAN.]

while inside they are filthy with unclean ash, so that, according to you, everything unclean smells foul and is defiled?

And after this, vomiting from the sewer of his heart a muddy filth, he says: “So the souls of the martyrs love their own ashes and fly around them, always present, lest perhaps, if some petitioner should come, they might be unable to hear him while absent?”

[Note: Elsewhere and in the manuscripts: “if some sinner should come.”]

O monstrosity fit to be carried off to the ends of the earth! You laugh at the relics of the martyrs and, together with Eunomius, the originator of this heresy, heap abuse upon the Churches of Christ. Does it not alarm you to join such company, so that you say against us the same things that he says against the Church?

For none of his followers enters the basilicas of the apostles and martyrs, so that they may worship the dead Eunomius, whose books they consider more authoritative than the Gospels and believe that the light of truth is in him:

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “that the summit of truth is in him.” Shortly afterward the Bologna manuscript has “calling it, in a notable volume, the *Scorpiace*,” which is not correct.]

just as other heresies assert that the Paraclete came into Montanus, and even say that Manichaeus himself is the Paraclete.

Against your heresy—which long ago broke out against the Church, lest you boast in this also as the discoverer of a new crime—Tertullian, a most learned man, wrote a notable volume, which he calls *Scorpiace*, a name entirely appropriate, because it pours venom into the body of the Church through a wound shaped like a bow. It was formerly called the Cainite heresy; after lying dormant or buried for a long time, it has now been raised up by Dormitantius.

I am surprised that you do not say that martyrdoms should by no means be endured: for if God does not seek the blood of goats and bulls, much less does he seek that of human beings. Once you have said this—or even if you have not said it—you are regarded as though you had said it. For when you assert that the relics of the martyrs are to be trampled underfoot, you forbid the shedding of blood that deserves no honor.

## 9. Vigils and All-Night Watches in the Basilicas. The Fault of a Few Does Not Prejudice Religion. What Is Good When Done Once Cannot Be Evil When Done Frequently.

Concerning the frequent celebration of vigils and all-night watches in the basilicas of the martyrs, I answered briefly in another letter, which I wrote nearly two years ago to the holy presbyter Riparius.

But if you think that they should be rejected because otherwise we may seem to celebrate Easter repeatedly and not hold solemn vigils only once a year, then sacrifices must not be offered to Christ on Sunday either, lest we celebrate the Lord’s resurrection as Easter again and again, and begin to have not one Easter but many.

The error and fault of young men and of very lowly women, often discovered during the night, must not be imputed to religious people. For something of this kind is also often found to occur at the Easter vigils, yet the fault of a few does not prejudice religion:

[Note: The same Bologna book reads, “They can go astray either in their own houses or in others’.” A little below it has, “but if there is some fault,” and then, “lest a wife find an occasion for sinning.”]

and people can go astray even without vigils, whether in their own homes or in those of others. Judas’s betrayal did not destroy the faith of the apostles. Therefore the evil vigils of others will not destroy ours. Rather, those who sleep for lust will be compelled to keep watch for chastity.

For what is good to do once cannot be evil if it is done more frequently. Or, if some fault must be avoided, it is not culpable because it is done often, but because it is done at all. Let us therefore not keep watch during the days of Easter, lest the long-awaited desires of adulterers be fulfilled, lest a wife find an opportunity for sin, lest the marital door be unable to be locked. Whatever is rarer is desired more ardently.

## 10. Vigilantius’ Arguments against Miracles

I cannot go through everything contained in the writings of the holy presbyters; from his little books I shall bring forward a few examples.

He argues against the signs and miracles performed in the basilicas of the martyrs and says that they benefit unbelievers, not believers—as though the question now were for whom they are performed, rather than by what power they are performed.

[Note: The same manuscript, together with the old edition, again reads: “Therefore let them be signs,” and so forth.]

Let it be granted that they are signs for unbelievers, who, because they refused to believe the word and teaching, are brought to faith by signs. The Lord also performed signs for unbelievers. Yet the Lord’s signs are not therefore to be disparaged because those people were unbelievers; rather, they were more worthy of admiration because they possessed such power that they could tame even the hardest minds and compel them to faith.

Therefore do not say to me, “They are signs for unbelievers”; instead, answer how such an abundance of signs and miracles can be present in the most worthless dust and some ash of which I know not what kind.

I understand—I understand, most miserable of mortals—what grieves you and what you fear. That unclean spirit which compels you to write these things has often been tormented by this most worthless dust; indeed, it is tormented by it even today. Though it conceals its wounds in you, it confesses them in others.

Unless perhaps, in the manner of the pagan and impious Porphyry and Eunomius, you invent the claim that these are demonic illusions,

[Note: The Bologna manuscript reads: “inventing against you that they are demonic illusions,” and so forth.]

and that the demons do not truly cry out but merely imitate their torments.

I give you this advice: enter the basilicas of the martyrs, and at some point you will be cleansed. There you will find many companions of yours. You will not be burned by the martyrs’ candles, which displease you, but by invisible flames. Then you will confess what you now deny, and you will freely proclaim your name—you who speak in Vigilantius—as either Mercury, because of your greed for money, or Nocturnus,

[Note: More precisely, ancient mythographers generally enumerate three nights. Eusebius likewise says in *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 2, that they relate that Jupiter doubled the nights; hence Hercules was called *Τριέσπερος* (“Three-Nights”) and *Τρισέληνος* (“Three-Moons”). Ovid, however, like Jerome, notes two nights in book 1 of the *Amores*, elegy 13:

“He joined two nights together for his desires.”

Plautus, whom our author cites, writes:

“I believe Nocturnus slept through this night.”]

or Nocturninus, according to Plautus’ *Amphitryon*, when Jupiter joined two nights together while Nocturnus slept, so that Hercules might be born of his adultery with Alcmena; or certainly Liber Pater, because of your drunkenness, the cup hanging from your shoulders, your ever-flushed face, foaming lips, and unrestrained abuse.

## 11. The History of Vigilantius

Hence, in this province also,

[Note: “When a sudden earthquake occurred.” Prosper, in his *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Arcadius IV and Honorius III, reports that there was an earthquake for many days and that the sky seemed to burn. MARTIAN.

The *Chronicles* of St. Prosper and Marcellinus report this under the year 396: “In the consulship of Arcadius V and Honorius III there was an earthquake for many days,” and so forth. Shortly below, the old edition has “thus they prayed after being expelled from Paradise.”]

when a sudden earthquake in the middle of the night had awakened everyone from sleep, you, the wisest and most learned of mortals, prayed naked and recited to us Adam and Eve in Paradise. They, indeed, opened their eyes and were ashamed when they saw that they were naked, and covered their private parts with the leaves of trees. But you, naked both of your tunic and of faith, terrified by sudden fear and still bearing something of the night’s drunkenness, thrust the obscene part of your body before the eyes of the saints, so as to display your wisdom.

Such are the Church’s adversaries. These are the commanders who wage war against the blood of the martyrs. Such speakers thunder against the apostles—or rather, such rabid dogs bark against Christ’s disciples.

## 12. Jerome Sometimes Feared Entering the Basilicas of the Martyrs

I confess my fear, lest it perhaps arise from superstition. When I have become angry and conceived some evil thought in my mind, and a nocturnal apparition has deceived me, I do not dare to enter the basilicas of the martyrs; I tremble so completely, in body and in mind.

Perhaps you will laugh and mock the ravings of little women. I am not ashamed of the faith of those women who were the first to see the risen Lord, who were sent to the apostles, and who, as the mother of the Lord and Savior, were commended to the holy apostles.

You may belch along with worldly men; I will fast with women—or rather, with devout men who display chastity in their faces and, carrying pale countenances marked by continual self-restraint, show forth the modesty of Christ.

## 13. What Did Vigilantius Prohibit? Collections on Sunday. The Custom of Almsgiving among Hebrews and Christians

You seem to me to grieve over something else as well: namely, that if continence, sobriety, and fasting become established among the Gauls, your taverns will no longer make profits, and you will be unable to conduct the devil’s vigils and drunken banquets throughout the night.

Furthermore, I have been informed by letters sent to me that, contrary to the authority of the apostle Paul—and indeed of Peter, John, and James, who gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship and commanded them to remember the poor—you forbid any financial assistance to be sent to Jerusalem for the needs of the saints.

Clearly, if I answer this, you will immediately bark that I am pleading my own cause, since you bestowed such great gifts upon everyone that, unless you had come to Jerusalem and poured out your own money or that of your patrons, we would all have been threatened with starvation.

I am saying what the blessed apostle Paul says in nearly all his letters. He commands the Churches of the Gentiles, on the first day of the week—that is, on Sunday—to make a collection of everything that is to be sent to Jerusalem for the relief of the saints, either through his disciples or through those whom they themselves approve. And, if it is suitable, he himself is to send or carry what has been collected.

[Note: The Bologna manuscript reads, “or bring forward,” and shortly afterward, “I came to offer offerings and vows,” omitting “to Jerusalem.”]

In the Acts of the Apostles also, speaking to the governor Felix, he says: “After many years I came to bring alms to my nation, and offerings and vows, in which they found me purified in the temple” (Acts 24:17).

Could he not have distributed in some other part of the world, and among the Churches that he was instructing as they came to birth in the faith, what he had received from others?

[Note: The same reading is found approximately in the old edition, but with “to give to the poor saints.”]

But he wished to give to the poor of the holy places, who, leaving behind their small possessions for Christ, had turned with their whole mind to the service of the Lord.

It would take too long now to review all the testimonies from his letters in which he labors and hastens with his whole mind to have money sent to Jerusalem and to the holy places for believers—not for greed, but for refreshment; not to accumulate wealth, but to sustain the weakness of the little body and to escape cold and hunger.

This custom continues in Judaea to the present day, not only among us but also among the Hebrews: those who meditate day and night on the law of the Lord and have no father on earth except God alone are supported by the resources of the synagogues and of the whole world (Ps. 1; Deut. 18).

[Note: The learned Father Bacchinius explains the order of this matter and collects many examples in his book *On Metropolises*. The Bologna manuscript adds: “then, according to equality,” and so forth.]

Only according to equality—not so that some may have relief and others affliction, but so that the abundance of some may support the poverty of others (2 Cor. 8).

## 14. To Which Poor Should Alms Especially Be Given? Wicked Poor People

You will answer that each person can do this in his own homeland and that there will be no shortage of poor people who ought to be supported by the resources of the Church.

We do not deny that alms should be extended to all poor people, including Jews and Samaritans, if generosity is great enough. But the Apostle teaches that almsgiving is to be practiced toward everyone, especially toward those who belong to the household of faith (Gal. 6).

The Savior likewise said in the Gospel: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness”—or “unrighteous mammon”—“so that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

Can those poor people among whose rags and bodily filth burning lust rules possess eternal dwellings, when they possess neither what is present nor what is to come? For it is not poor people in general who are called blessed, but “the poor in spirit.” Of them it is written: “Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. 40:1).

In supporting the poor of the common crowd, no understanding is required, but almsgiving. Among the holy poor there is the blessedness of understanding, so that one may give to the person who is ashamed to receive and who, after receiving, grieves—reaping material things and sowing spiritual ones.

But when he asserts that those do better who use their possessions and gradually distribute the fruits of their estates to the poor than those who sell their possessions and give everything away at once, the answer will come not from me but from the Lord:

“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me.”

He is speaking to the one who wishes to be perfect, who rightly leaves behind father, boat, and everything else together with the apostles. The person whom you praise stands on the second or third step,

[Note: Some manuscripts read *et* (“and”) instead of *aut* (“or”).]

a step that we too accept, provided that we know the first is to be preferred to the second and third.

## 15. The Life and Condition of a True Monk. A Monk Must Avoid the Sight of Women

You must not deter monks from their vocation with your viperous tongue and most savage bite. You argue and say: “If they all shut themselves away and live in solitude, who will celebrate the Churches? Who will win secular people? Who will be able to exhort sinners to virtue?”

[Note: I think the manuscripts’ reading is more correct: “if they all shut themselves away,” as Martianaeus himself testifies—that is, if by shutting themselves in they separate themselves from others. An example is found more than once in Justin.]

By this reasoning, if everyone were foolish like you, who could be wise? Nor would virginity be approved. If everyone were virgins, there would be no marriages; the human race would perish; infants would not cry in their cradles; midwives would beg without payment; and in bitter cold Dormitantius alone, loose—or “solitary”—and hunched up would keep watch in his little bed.

Virtue is rare and not sought by many. Would that all were what the few are, of whom it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16; 22:14); then the prisons would be empty.

A monk does not have the office of a teacher but of one who mourns: one who grieves either for himself or for the world and awaits the Lord’s coming in fear; one who knows his weakness and fears to offend, knowing the fragile vessel that he carries, lest he stumble, fall, and be broken.

Therefore he avoids the sight of women, especially young women, and is so strict with himself that he fears even what is safe.

## 16. Vices and the Occasions of Vices Must Be Avoided. Certain Things Must Not Be Abandoned and Uncertain Things Pursued

“You are going to the desert,” you will say. “Obviously, so that I may neither hear nor see you; so that I may not be stirred by your fury; so that I may not suffer your wars; lest the eye of a prostitute seize me; lest a very beautiful form lead me into illicit embraces.”

You will answer: “This is not fighting but fleeing.”

Stand in the battle line and resist your adversaries while armed, so that after you have conquered you may be crowned.

I confess my weakness. I do not wish to fight in the hope of victory, lest at some point I lose the victory. If I flee, I have avoided the sword; if I stand, I must either conquer or fall.

But why is it necessary to abandon what is certain and pursue what is uncertain? Death must be avoided either with a shield or with one’s feet. You who fight can both be overcome and conquer. When I flee, I do not conquer the thing from which I flee; I flee so that I may not be conquered.

[Note: Martianaeus reads, “I will not be conquered.” Victorius disapproves this. We read with two manuscripts, “I am not conquered,” or “I have not been conquered.”]

There is no safety in sleeping near a serpent. It may happen that it will not bite me; yet it may also happen that at some point it will bite me.

We call sisters and daughters “mothers,” and we are not ashamed to cloak our vices in names of affection.

[Note: Recall Letter 147, no. 5, to the fallen Sabinianus, where women superiors of monasteries are called “Mothers.” St. Optatus also writes in book 2 *On the Donatist Schism*: “They found Mothers, whom they had made from consecrated women.”]

What is a monk doing in women’s cells? What is the purpose of private conversations held in isolation and eyes that avoid witnesses?

[Note: At the beginning of Letter 46 to Paula and Eustochium: “Love has no measure, and impatience knows no limit,” and so forth. Here, however, *impatientia* is used in the sense of lack of restraint, as indicated above.]

Holy love does not lack restraint. What we have said of lust may be applied to greed and to all the vices avoided through solitude. For this reason we avoid the crowds of cities, lest we be compelled to do what nature does not so much force us to do as our will.

## 17. Open Blasphemy Demands Indignation

These words, as I said, I dictated at the request of holy presbyters in the labor of a single night, while my brother Sisinnius was hastening very much

[Note: “Brother Sisinnius.” Concerning this same Sisinnius, the following is read in the preface to book 2 of the commentary on Zechariah: “While brother Sisinnius is hastening to Egypt, so that he may carry there also the fragrance of the good odor that you have sent to the brothers,” and so forth. He therefore wrote this little work against Vigilantius in the year of Christ 406, that is, in the sixth consulship of Arcadius Augustus, as he himself testifies in the preface to the third commentary on the prophet Amos. We have spoken about this brother Sisinnius in the prefatory *Admonition* to this work. MARTIAN.]

and was preparing to go to Egypt for the refreshment of the saints. Otherwise, the subject itself called not so much for a multitude of testimonies as for the writer’s indignation, since it contained open blasphemy.

If Dormitantius wakes up again in response to my invectives and thinks to disparage me too with the same blasphemous mouth with which he tears apart the apostles and martyrs, I will keep watch not merely through a short night’s labor but throughout the entire night against him and his companions—or rather, his disciples and teachers—who think husbands unworthy of Christ’s ministry unless they see their wives’ swollen bellies.

[Col. 0351]

# Against John of Jerusalem (C)

## Admonition to the Following Book Against John of Jerusalem

[Col. 0351] 1. John of Jerusalem, who before attaining the episcopate had been a monk and had adhered to the Arians and Macedonians, after being elevated to the episcopal dignity lent an ear to the Origenists, who were numerous in that province. All the good men, and especially St. Epiphanius, bore this with the greatest displeasure. Epiphanius met him at Jerusalem and personally exhorted him in person to withdraw from his error; John, on the contrary, became so enraged that he did not hesitate publicly to accuse Epiphanius himself of the heresy of the Anthropomorphites.

Moreover, being a man eager for quarrels and seeking grounds for revenge, he complained that Epiphanius had injured him because he had ordained as presbyter Paulinian, St. Jerome’s brother, who was living in a monastery in Palestine—namely, without the authorization of the bishop of Salamis. Although Epiphanius gave a sufficient defense, maintaining that he had done this not in a parish subject to John, and protesting that there was only one cause of the dispute, namely the violation of the right faith by Origenist doctrines, John made this ordination alone the pretext for his anger. For this reason he also hated Jerome, the brother of that same Paulinian, but much more because of Origenism. For since the holy Doctor took Epiphanius’ side, knew well that his brother’s ordination had been carried out without injury to anyone and according to the established custom among the bishops of Cyprus, and fiercely attacked Origen’s errors both in speech and writing, he so provoked John’s anger that John expelled him from communion with the Church, although Jerome remained continuously in communion with the whole Church of Jerusalem.

## 2. Archelaus the comes immediately tried to calm such great agitation of minds, and, having agreed upon a place where peace should be undertaken, proposed that, since suspicion of violated faith had produced the disagreements, they should reach agreement through each man’s profession of faith. John, however, though Archelaus invited him again and again to make peace, offered now one, now another very flimsy excuse and did not comply.

But John wrote to Theophilus of Alexandria—as one may reasonably believe—informed him of the growing discord, and perhaps also begged him to rebuke his adversaries. Theophilus wrote gently to Jerome, as he ought to have done on John’s behalf, informed him of what he had learned from John, and invited him to peace. To him our author replies in Letter 132 of our recension. In it he declares that he is seeking peace of his own accord, disposes of the charges one by one, and traces the causes of the disputes and of the violated faith to John.

Then, wishing to come to the aid of the Church, which was suffering more and more, Theophilus sent to Jerusalem as his legate the presbyter Isidore, a man renowned for his reputation for piety and other virtues, but one who had been seized by the Origenist stain, with a letter in which he sought to reconcile the minds of the dissidents. But when this evil intermediary of peace arrived at Jerusalem, he announced his embassy; nevertheless, he refused to deliver the letter entrusted to him to Jerome. When Jerome asked him, “If you are an ambassador, hand over the letters of your embassy; if you do not have the letters, how will you prove that you are an ambassador?”, he replied that he did indeed have the letters, but that John had asked him not to deliver them. He therefore preferred to depart with his mission unfinished rather than remove the suspicion that he favored the Origenist party.

Nevertheless, he advised John to write an Apology to Theophilus on behalf of his cause, and lent his assistance in composing it, so that, as Jerome says, he might be both its “dictator” and its letter-carrier. Thus John, disdaining to reply to Epiphanius’s letter, sent that Apology everywhere, but especially to the West, so that he might preoccupy the ears of the Roman priests as far as possible in his own favor.

Pammachius in fact writes to Jerome that the minds of many had been drawn into opposing positions, with some defending the cause of the bishop of Salamis and others that of the bishop of Jerusalem. Stirred by this, he asks the holy Doctor to explain what the matter was. Jerome now complies with him in this book, and shows that the cause of the dispute was so far from being the ordination of Paulinianus, Jerome’s brother, that—apart from the fact that Paulinianus was ordained in the territory of Eleutheropolis, not in that of Aelia—the quarrel between John and Epiphanius had already taken place on account of Origen before Paulinianus’s consecration.

He reduces Origenism to eight propositions, of which John’s Apology cleared him only of three:

1. That the Son cannot see the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the Son.
2. That souls, having fallen from heaven because of their sins, have been cast into the body as into a prison.
3. That the devil will one day repent and be converted, and will reign with the saints.
4. That Adam and Eve lacked bodies before they sinned, and that the bodies indicated by the “garments of skin” were given to them after the sin.
5. That the flesh will in no way be raised, and that we shall be without sex in the resurrection.
6. That the earthly paradise is to be understood allegorically.
7. That the waters said in Scripture to be above the heavens are angels, while those beneath the heavens are demons.
8. That human beings lost the image of God through sin.

He therefore again charges John with these errors and attacks the evasions of his Apology, addressing the bishop of Jerusalem directly throughout.

## 3.

There are, moreover, those who think that this book was not completed by its author. They suppose that this happened because, at the very time when it was being written, peace was finally established through the efforts of Theophilus. Yet it is no less plausible to suppose that, through the ravages of time, its final and very brief portion was lost.

Whatever the truth may be, Rufinus was certainly unaware of this composition; otherwise he would not have failed to attack it vigorously in his books of Invectives. Learned men differ astonishingly in assigning its date: some place it as early as the year 393, others as late as 406, while others assign it to one of the intervening years according to their preference.

We are persuaded to assign it to the year 399 or 400 by the following two arguments, which we have already set forth in the chronological notes on the Letters.

First, Jerome says that he composed the Commentaries on Ecclesiastes and the exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians nearly ten years earlier. Speaking only of the Commentaries, he himself testifies elsewhere, and especially in their Preface to Paula and Eustochium, that he undertook this work about the year 390, when nearly five years had passed since he had escaped from Rome. If nearly ten years are added to this, the year 399 or 400 results.

We derive the second argument for the same date from the fact that, near the end of the little work, he says that thirteen years earlier he had abandoned Antioch, that most celebrated city, in order to turn aside to the countryside and solitude and, mourning the sins of his youth, to draw Christ’s mercy upon himself.

These thirteen years cannot in any way be reckoned except from the completion of the year 386, since it is established that he remained at Rome until August of the preceding year, 385. At that time, after sailing to the East and traveling through various regions in succession, he finally settled at Antioch. He says that he left that city because, although he could have honorably exercised the priestly office in its Church, to which he seemed to belong by virtue of his ordination, he preferred to seek the countryside and solitude, so that he might erase the sins of his youth through repentance.

Thus, when thirteen years are added to 386, the year 399, or the beginning of 400, emerges—the date to which one may more readily assign this book, before Isidore, the Alexandrian presbyter, was condemned by the synod of that year and place through Theophilus.
