[Note: See our Annotation on the Preface to the Chronicle, where we discuss Vincent, the companion of our holy Father.]

# ONE BOOK OF SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, AGAINST JOHN OF JERUSALEM, TO PAMMACHIUS

[Note: Vallarsius’s edition gives the title as follows: “Here begins the book of Saint Jerome the presbyter to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem”; Martianay’s has “against the heresies of John,” and so forth.

Editor’s note.—“Against the heresies of John of Jerusalem.” In a more recent manuscript of the Sorbonne it is entitled: “Here begins the book of Saint Jerome to Pammachius against John, bishop of Jerusalem, and Rufinus, defender of Origen.” In the Cluniac manuscript: “Here begins the book of Saint Jerome the presbyter on the creation of the soul, or on the resurrection of the flesh, against the letter of Rufinus, who writes in this way: ‘Our subject is all visible things,’” as these words are read in the middle of this Epistle. At the end, too, much is missing in that manuscript, for before the words “in an inverted order,” it has *EXPLICIT*. The San-Cygiranus manuscript begins and ends in the same way, but retains this heading: “Here begins the book of Saint Jerome on the resurrection of the flesh.” Martianay.]

[Col. 0355]

## 1. It is dangerous to judge another person’s mind

If, according to the Apostle Paul, we cannot pray for what we feel [Romans 8:26], and speech does not express the thought of our own mind, how much more dangerous is it to judge another person’s mind and to investigate and declare the meaning of each individual statement and word?

Human nature is inclined toward leniency, and each person pities himself in another’s sin. If, therefore, you rebuke someone as guilty in his speech, he will call it simplicity; if you accuse him of craftiness, he will confess ignorance, in order to avoid the suspicion of malice. Thus it will happen that you, who bring the accusation, will be judged a slanderer, while the one who is reproved will be judged not a heretic but a rustic.

You know, Pammachius—you know that I have undertaken this work neither out of hostility nor from a desire for glory, but because your letters provoked me through the ardor of faith; and, if it could be done, because I would wish everyone to hold the same judgment. Nor can I be reproached for impatience or rashness if I speak after three years.

Finally, unless you had said that many people’s minds had been disturbed and were wavering between the two sides because of the Apology about which I have now begun to write, I had resolved to remain in the silence I had undertaken.

[Note: John wrote this Apology to Theophilus in defense of his own cause with the assistance of Isidore, and Jerome attacks it in this book.]

## 2. Novatian and Montanus. Whoever believes purely ought to speak purely. No one should be patient when heresy is suspected

Let Novatian, then, depart, extending no hand to those who err; let Montanus be overthrown along with his frenzied women—he who hurls the fallen headlong into the abyss lest they be raised. We all sin daily and stumble in some respect. Therefore, although we are lenient toward ourselves, we do not maintain strictness toward others. Rather, we pray, ask, and implore that he either plainly confess our faith or openly defend what belongs to another.

I do not want ambiguities of words; I do not want to be told something that can also be understood in another way. Let us contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face [2 Corinthians 3:18].

Formerly the Israelite people limped on both feet. But Elijah—whose name means “the strong one of the Lord”—

[Note: The name is derived from *El*, “strong,” and either *Elohim*, “God,” or *Adonai*, “Lord.” See 1 Kings 17–18. In the Book of Names it is interpreted as “God the Lord.”]

—said: “How long will you limp on both legs? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal is God, follow him” [1 Kings 18:21]. The Lord himself says of the Jews: “Foreign sons have lied to me; foreign sons have grown old and have limped from their paths” [Psalm 17:46].

Certainly, if there is no suspicion of heresy—as I desire and believe—why does he not express my meaning in my own words? What he calls simplicity, I interpret as malice. He wants to persuade me that he believes purely; then let him speak purely as well.

If a single word or a single meaning were ambiguous—if there were two or three—I would grant indulgence to ignorance. Nor would I judge what was obscure or doubtful by what was certain and clear. But now, what sort of simplicity is this: to walk as though suspended over eggs and ears of grain, with hesitant steps amid theatrical tricks? Everywhere doubt, everywhere suspicion! One would think that he was writing not an exposition of faith but a figurative controversy.

We learned long ago in the schools what this man now seeks. Our own armor fights against us. Even if he believes correctly, his speaking cautiously and timidly arouses suspicion in me through its excessive care. “He who walks simply walks confidently” [Proverbs 10:9].

It is foolish to endure infamy without cause. A crime is charged against him of which he has no consciousness. Therefore, since the entire charge depends upon a word, let him deny it confidently and freely bring discredit upon his adversary, Saint Epiphanius. With the same boldness with which the other accuses, let this man defend himself.

When he has said everything he wishes and everything he has proposed—once he has removed all grounds for suspicion—if the slander persists, let him bring the matter into court and confront his accuser openly. I do not want anyone to be passive when heresy is suspected, lest, among those who do not know his innocence, his silence be judged an admission of guilt—even though it is superfluous to seek out and extort silence from someone whose letters you possess.

## 3. He addresses John himself

We all know what he wrote to you, what he accused you of, and in what respect—as you claim—he slandered you. Respond to each point; proceed through the steps of this letter, passing over not even a dot or a stroke of the slander.

For if you act carelessly and, as I believe when you swear to it, happen to pass over something, he will immediately shout and say: “Here, here I hold you defeated [perhaps: bound]; here lies the hinge of the whole affair.”

Enemies and friends do not listen in the same way. An enemy looks for a knot even in a reed; a friend judges even what is crooked to be straight. The writings of the world say that the judgments of lovers are blind—words that, being occupied with the sacred Books, you may perhaps have entirely neglected.

Never boast of the judgment of friends. The true testimony is that which comes from an enemy’s voice.

[Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, where he renders Plato’s saying in Latin. The old edition reads: “which is uttered by an unwilling voice.”]

Otherwise, if a friend speaks on your behalf, he will be thought not a witness or judge but a partisan. Such things, and things like them, your enemies will say—people who perhaps do not believe you and wish to provoke resentment.

For my part, although you have never knowingly injured me, and although you are always compelled to toss my name about in your letters, I advise you either openly to proclaim the faith of the Church or to speak as you believe. For this careful management and balancing of words can deceive the unlearned. A cautious hearer and reader will quickly detect the ambushes and will plainly expose in the light the tunnels by which the truth is being undermined.

The Arians too, whom you know very well, pretended for a long time, because of the scandal attached to the name *homoousios* (“consubstantial”), to condemn themselves, and coated the poisons of their error with the honey of words.

[Note: The old edition reads: “the crooked serpent appeared, and the harmful head, which the spiritual [sword] had pierced, while the coils covered the whole body.” It soon adds: “and when the sins had been overcome through forgiveness,” and so forth.]

But at last the coiled serpent disclosed itself, and its harmful head, which had been covered by the coils of its entire body, was pierced by the spiritual sword. As you know, the Church receives penitents; and, while it is overcome by the number of sinners and cares for deceived flocks, it forgives the wounds inflicted by shepherds.

The same practice is now maintained in both the old and the new heresy: the people hear one thing, while the priests preach another.

## 4. Many in Palestine did not communicate with John, the bishop. Saint Epiphanius called John a heretic. Athanasius and Paulinus were the only Catholics in the East

Before I insert into this volume your letter, which you wrote to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, after translating it, and show you that I understand your excessive caution, I wish to remonstrate with you.

What is this great arrogance: not to answer those who question you about the faith? Do you regard the great multitude of brothers and the choirs of monks who do not communicate with you in Palestine as public enemies?

For the sake of one diseased sheep, leaving the ninety-nine in the mountains, the Son of God endured blows, the cross, and scourges; he bore that delicate sinner patiently on his shoulders up to heaven.

Do you, most blessed pope and disdainful bishop,

[Note: The same old edition reads: “and haughty prelate.”]

—you alone rich, you alone wise, you alone noble and eloquent—look down upon your fellow servants and those redeemed by the blood of your Lord with wrinkled brow and sidelong eyes?

Is this what you learned at the Apostle’s command: “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you” [1 Peter 3:15]?

Suppose that we are seeking an opportunity and, under the pretext of faith, sowing disputes, creating schism, and stirring up quarrels. Remove the opportunity from those who seek an opportunity,

[Note: The old edition reads: “Take away the opportunity from those who desire an opportunity, and then let it clearly be evident to all that the dispute is not about doctrine,” and so forth.]

so that, after you have given satisfaction concerning the faith and untied all the knots woven against you, you may then clearly prove to everyone that the contest concerns not doctrines but ordination.

Unless, perhaps, by a prudent plan you remain silent when questioned about the faith so that, once you have given satisfaction, you may not appear to have been a heretic. People ought not, therefore, to refute all the charges of which they are accused, lest, after denying them, they become guilty.

But you despise laymen, deacons, and presbyters. For, as you boast and proclaim, you can make a thousand clerics in a single hour. You have Pope Epiphanius, who in letters sent to you openly calls you a heretic.

Certainly, you are not greater than he in age, learning, merit of life, or the testimony of the whole world. If you appeal to age, a young man is writing to an old man. If to learning, an unlearned man is writing to a learned one—even though your supporters may claim that you are more eloquent than Demosthenes, more acute than Chrysippus, and wiser than Plato, and may perhaps have persuaded you of this yourself.

As for life and faith, I shall say nothing more, lest I seem to injure you.

At the time when the heresy of the Arians and Eunomians possessed the whole East, except for Pope Athanasius and Paulinus, and when you did not communicate with the confessors among the Westerners and those in the midst of exile, he was either heard as a presbyter of the monastery by Eutychius,

[Note: This Eutychius was the bishop of Eleutheropolis. Because of his hatred for Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, he supported the Arian party of Acacius of Caesarea, although, as Epiphanius reports, he was himself inwardly and in his heart a Catholic. A little earlier, the old edition reads “in the exile of Judaea” instead of “in the midst of exile.”]

or later, as bishop of Cyprus, was left untouched by Valens. For he was always held in such great veneration that heretical rulers considered it a disgrace to themselves if they persecuted such a man.

Write, then, to this man. Answer his letter. Let the others perceive your conclusion, eloquence, and prudence, lest you seem eloquent only to yourself. Why, when challenged by one person, do you turn your weapons against another? You are questioned by the Palestinians, and you answer Egypt. When others have sore eyes, you apply ointment to eyes that do not hurt. If you speak to someone else in order to please us, that is sufficiently arrogant; if you say something other than what we ask, it is sufficiently superfluous.

## 5. What Theophilus approved

But you say that the Alexandrian bishop approved my letter. What did he approve? That you spoke well against Arius, against Photinus, and against Manichaeus. For who is accusing you at this time of being an Arian? Who now charges you with the crime of Photinus or Manichaeus?

Those matters were corrected and refuted long ago. You were not so foolish as openly to defend a heresy that you knew displeased the Church. You knew that, if you did so, you would immediately have to be removed from office, and you sighed for the delights of your throne.

Thus you tempered your position so that you would displease neither the simple nor your own supporters. You wrote well, but nothing relevant to the case. How did the pontiff of the Alexandrian Church know what charges were being brought against you, or what confession was being demanded from you? You ought to have stated the charges brought against you and then answered each one.

An old story tells of someone who spoke eloquently, was carried along by the force and fluency of his words, and did not touch the matter at all. A prudent hearer and judge said: “Well, well—but what has this to do with the matter?”

Inexperienced physicians use a single eye-wash for every pain of the eyes. A person who is accused on several counts and omits something in his dismissal of the charges confesses whatever he has left unmentioned.

Did you not answer Epiphanius’s letter and yourself set forth the points that you intended to resolve? Surely you answered with this confidence: “No one is struck forcefully by himself. Choose whichever of the two you wish.”

You will be given a choice: either you answered Epiphanius’s letter or you did not. If you answered, why did you leave aside the greatest and most numerous of the matters charged against you? If you did not answer, where is that Apology of yours in which you boast before the simple-minded and, as though they were ignorant of the case,

[Alternative: “as though those ignorant of the case”]

scatter it here and there?

## 6. John answered three of the eight questions

Eight propositions concerning the hope of the Christian faith were brought against you, as I shall immediately prove. You touch upon only three and pass over the rest. In the others there is a profound silence.

Even if you had answered seven of them with complete clarity, I would nevertheless have remained fixed upon the one charge, and I would have held fast to what you had left unsaid. But now, as though you had seized a wolf by the ears, you can neither hold it nor dare to release it.

[Note: From the Greek proverb, *tōn ōtōn echō ton lykon, out’ echein out’ aphienai dynamai*, “I hold the wolf by the ears; I can neither hold it nor release it.” Terence renders it approximately in Latin in *Phormio* 3.2.21: “I hold the wolf by the ears.”]

Even those three matters you treat as though careless and unconcerned, as though occupied with something else. You fly over and brush past points where there is either no question or only a minor one.

Thus you proceed covered and concealed, so that by your silence you confess more than you reject in argument. Who could not immediately say to you: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?” [Matthew 6:23]

If the three little questions on which you seemed to say something are not free from suspicion and guilt, and if they are shown to have been written fraudulently and evasively, what shall we do with the remaining five? Since in them there was no opportunity for ambiguous speech, and you could not mock your hearers, you preferred to remain entirely silent rather than openly confess what was right.

## 7. The eight propositions of Origen’s errors brought against John by Epiphanius

The first concerns the book *On First Principles* (*Peri Archōn*), in which he says: “For just as it is incongruous to say that the Son could see the Father, so it is inappropriate to suppose that the Holy Spirit could see the Son.”

The second is that souls are bound in this body as in a prison, and that before the human being came into existence they dwelt among rational creatures in the heavenly places. Hence, for its consolation, the soul says in the Psalms: “Before I was humbled, I sinned” [Psalm 118:67]; and, “Return, my soul, to your rest” [Psalm 114:7]; and, “Bring my soul out of prison” [Psalm 141:8], and other things of this sort.

The third is that he says both the devil and the demons will at some time repent, and that at the end of time they will reign with the saints.

The fourth is that he interprets the “garments of skin” as human bodies, with which Adam and Eve were clothed after the offense and expulsion from paradise. There is no doubt, he says, that previously they had been in paradise without flesh, sinews, or bones.

The fifth is that he most openly denies the resurrection of the flesh and the structure of the limbs, as well as the sex by which men are distinguished from women—both in his exposition of the first Psalm and in many other treatises.

The sixth is that he allegorizes paradise in such a way as to remove the truth of the historical account: understanding angels in place of trees and heavenly powers in place of rivers, and overturning the whole content of the paradise narrative through a tropological interpretation.

[Note: Understand this as referring to what is contained and narrated in the account of paradise.]

The seventh is that he considers the waters said in Scripture to be above the heavens to be holy heavenly powers, while those above the earth and beneath the earth are opposed to them and demonic.

The eighth and final charge is that he says the image and likeness of God, in which the human being had been created, was lost by humanity and was not present in the human being after paradise.

## 8. Epiphanius’s humility and charity. The consul designate Praetextatus and what he used to say. Pure faith does not brook delay. What zeal for the faith ought to be

These are the arrows by which you have been pierced; these are the weapons with which you are wounded throughout the entire letter—apart from the fact that Epiphanius, falling upon his knees before you and, setting aside for a little while the honor of the priesthood, humbling his holy gray head,

[Alternative: “supporting rather than humbling”]

begs for your salvation and speaks these words:

“Grant both to me and to yourself that you may be saved, as it is written: ‘From a crooked generation’; and withdraw from the heresy of Origen and from all heresies, most beloved.”

And below:

“Because you arouse hatred against me in defense of heresy, you break the charity which I have shown toward you, to such an extent that you have even made us regret that we communicated with you, since you defend the errors and doctrines of Origen.”

Tell me, excellent disputant, about the eight propositions to which you have replied. For a little while I shall say nothing about the others.

With what weapons did you pierce that first blasphemy—that neither the Son can see the Father nor the Holy Spirit the Son?

He says:

“We believe in the holy and venerable Trinity, of one substance and coeternal, of one glory and divinity; and we anathematize those who say anything in the divinity of the Trinity is great or small, unequal, or visible. But just as we call the Father incorporeal, invisible, and eternal, so we call the Son and the Holy Spirit incorporeal, invisible, and eternal.”

Unless you said this, you would not hold the Church. Yet I am not asking whether you said it before. Nor shall I parade before the public whether you favored those who preached such things, or whether you were with them when they endured exile for saying them.

Who was the man who, while the presbyter Theon was preaching in the Church that the Holy Spirit is God,

[Alternative: “the Spirit of the Lord”]

closed his ears and hastily fled outside with his followers so as not to hear such an impious teaching?

“I want you to become faithful at once,” he says, “though your conversion comes late.”

Miserable Praetextatus, who died consul designate! This sacrilegious man and worshiper of idols used to say jokingly to blessed Pope Damasus: “Make me bishop of the city of Rome, and I shall immediately become a Christian.”

[Note: See Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 27, chapter 3, where he speaks of the magnificence of the Roman pontiff.]

Why do you demonstrate to me in a long speech and elaborate periods that you are not an Arian? Either deny that the man accused said this,

[Note: The old edition reads: “or, if he said such things, condemn the one who said them.”]

or, if he said such things, condemn him because he said them.

Do you wish to know how great is the ardor of those who believe rightly? Hear the Apostle: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be anathema” [Galatians 1:8].

To lessen the charge against you, you conceal the name of the guilty man, as though everything were safe and no one could be accused of blasphemies; and you weave an “idle faith” in elaborate speech.

[Note: We have restored *otiosam* (“idle,” “useless”) from the manuscripts and older editions, since the context itself demands it. It may mean an empty, useless, or superfluous faith. Quintilian uses *otiosus sermo* in this sense, to omit other examples. Erasmus preferred *enodam* or *enodem*, “a clear, uncomplicated faith.” Victorius and Martianay read *erosam*, “corroded faith.” The manuscript copies read *otiosam fidem*, not *aerosam*. Erasmus conjectures *enodam* or *enodem fidem*, that is, a simple faith containing nothing distorted. Martianay attacks this in his notes and argues that *erosam fidem* should be read, meaning a faith that is not whole or sound. Martianay.]

Say at once—and let your letter begin with this—that the one who dared to write such things is anathema. Pure faith does not brook delay. As soon as the scorpion appears, it must immediately be crushed.

David, who was found to be according to the Lord’s heart, says: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred” [Psalm 138:21].

If I had heard my father, mother, or brother saying such things against my Christ, I would have torn their blaspheming mouths like a mad dog, and my hand would have been first against them. Those who said to father and mother, “We do not know you,” fulfilled the will of the Lord. “Whoever loves father or mother more than Christ is not worthy of him” [Matthew 10:37].

## 9. Angels are invisible. Jerome’s pure faith and sincerity

You are accused of having said that your teacher, whom you call Catholic and whom you vigorously defend, said:

“The Son does not see the Father, and the Holy Spirit does not see the Son. And you say to me: ‘The Father is invisible, the Son is invisible, the Holy Spirit is invisible,’”

as though angels, Cherubim, and Seraphim were not also, according to their nature, invisible to our eyes.

Certainly David, even while doubting whether the heavens could be seen, says: “I shall see the heavens, the work of your fingers” [Psalm 8:4]. “I shall see,” not “I see.” I shall see when, with unveiled face, I have contemplated the glory of the Lord; but now “we see in part and we know in part” [1 Corinthians 13:9].

The question is whether the Son sees the Father, and you say, “The Father is invisible.” The question is whether the Holy Spirit sees the Son, and you answer, “The Son is invisible.” The question is whether the Trinity sees one another; human ears cannot endure such great blasphemy, and you say, “The Trinity is invisible.”

You wander into other praises and deliver speeches on matters that no one is asking about. You draw the hearer elsewhere so that you will not say what we are asking.

But let these words have been spoken as an excess. We grant you that you are not an Arian—indeed, we grant you more: that you never were one. We concede that, in your exposition of the first proposition, there is no suspicion against you, and that you spoke wholly purely and wholly simply. With the same simplicity, we speak with you.

Did Pope Epiphanius accuse you of being an Arian?

[Note: “Or of Eunomius.” The Sorbonne manuscript reads: “Or did he charge you with the heresy of Eunomius, that is, of the godless one, or of Aerius?” The printed editions omit the name Aerius, who was himself a famous Arian and heretic. See Epiphanius, Book III *On Heresies*, and Augustine, *Book to Quodvultdeus*. Martianay.]

Did he charge you with the heresy of the godless Eunomius, or of Aerius?

[Note: Martianay incorrectly has *Aerii* instead of *Aeri*, which is the name of the well-known heretic.]

This is what is being asked throughout the whole letter: whether you follow the errors of Origen’s doctrines and have certain associates in this heresy.

Why, when questioned about one matter, do you answer another? Why, as though you were speaking with fools, do you conceal the charges contained in the letters and repeat what you said in the Church in the presence of Epiphanius?

You are asked for a confession of faith, and you thrust your most eloquent treatises upon those who do not want them.

I ask you, reader, to remember the tribunal of the Lord and to understand that you will be judged by your own judgment. Favor neither me nor my adversary; consider not the persons speaking but the case itself. Let us therefore say what we began to say.

## 10. Isaiah, the herald of the Virgin

You write in your letter that before Paulinianus became a presbyter, Pope Epiphanius never confronted you concerning Origen’s error.

The first matter is doubtful, and I am arguing about the persons. He says that he brought the charge; you deny it. He produces witnesses; you refuse to hear those produced. He also recalls that there was another meeting, while you conceal both matters. Through his cleric he sends you a letter and demands a response. You are silent and dare not utter a sound; challenged by Palestine, you speak about Alexandria.

It is not mine to say to whom, between him and you, faith ought to be given. I think that you yourself would not dare to assign truth to yourself and falsehood to such a great man as he. But it may be that each man speaks for himself.

I shall summon you yourself as a witness against yourself. For if there was no question concerning doctrines, if you had not stirred the old man’s anger, if he had said nothing in reply to you, what need was there for you, in a single discourse of the Church, to debate every doctrine—about the Trinity, the assumption of the Lord’s body, the cross, the underworld, the nature of angels, the state of souls, the resurrection of the Savior and our own—and about the earth, which perhaps you forgot to mention—to say all this fearlessly before the assembled people and such a great man, continuing everything in one uninterrupted stream?

Where are the ancient interpreters of the Church, who could scarcely explain individual questions in many volumes? Where is the chosen vessel, the trumpet of the Gospel, our lion’s roar, the thunder of the nations, the river of Christian eloquence, who marvels at the mystery hidden from past generations and at the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge more than he speaks of it [Romans 11:33; Colossians 1:26]?

Where is Isaiah, the herald of the Virgin, who, overcome by a single question, says: “Who shall declare his generation?” [Isaiah 53:8]

A little man of no great stature has been found in our own age who, in a single turn of the tongue, flashed more brightly than the sun concerning every question of the Church.

If no one was asking this of you and everything was peaceful, you were foolish to undertake such great dangers of disputation. But if you were already speaking in defense of the faith, then the presbyter’s ordination is not the cause of the discord, since it is clear that he was appointed much later. You deceived those who were absent, and your letters flatter foreign ears.

### 11. The Anthropomorphites

We were present here and know everything, when Pope Epiphanius was speaking against Origen in your church, [Col. 0364A] when, under his name, darts were hurled against you [Al. us]. You and your chorus, with doglike grimaces and contracted nostrils, scratching your heads, spoke about the delirious old man by gestures [Note: [Col. 0363D] The word *nutibus* is absent in the old edition. From the passage that follows, observe the very ancient office of the archdeacon.] Was it not before the Lord’s tomb that you sent the archdeacon and ordered him to be silent while discussing such matters? Who among bishops ever commanded—or [Al. secured] this from—his own presbyter before the people? Was it not when you were going with Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0363D] Victor reads *ἀναστάσει*, “from the place of the Resurrection to the place or station of the cross.” The old edition, incorrectly, reads: “when you were going together with God’s servant Anastasius,” etc.] to the cross, and a crowd of every age and sex flocked to him, offering their children, kissing his feet, and tugging at his fringes? Since he could not advance, but could scarcely withstand the waves of the inundating crowd in one place, you, twisted with envy against the glorious old man, shouted; nor were you ashamed to say to his face that he was deliberately and intentionally delaying.

Recall, I beg you, that day when the people, invited for the seventh hour, were being kept there in hope alone, as though they were afterward going to hear Epiphanius. What did you preach then? Clearly, raging and indignant against the Anthropomorphites, who in rustic simplicity suppose that God has the bodily members described in the divine books, you directed your eyes, hands, and whole bodily frame against the old man, wishing to make him suspect of the most foolish heresy.

After you had fallen silent, exhausted, with dry mouth, head thrown back, and trembling lips, and at last the wish of the entire people had been fulfilled, what did the delirious and foolish old man do to you? He rose to show that he intended to say only a few words, and, greeting the Church with voice [Note: [Col. 0364D] Namely, by bringing his hand to his mouth and then extending it; this was an ancient custom of greeting, also in the Church. The Greeks say *τιμᾷν τοῖς διὰ χειρῶν φιλήμασι*, “to honor with kisses made by the hands.”] and hand, said:

“Everything that the brother who spoke to the assembly—my son in age—has said against the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, he has said well and faithfully, and it is also condemned by my voice. But it is right that, just as we condemn this heresy, we should also condemn Origen’s perverse doctrines.” [Note: [Col. 0364D] The old edition reads: “It is right that we clearly explain how we condemn this heresy.”]

I suppose you remember what laughter and acclamation followed from everyone. This is what you say in your letter: that he spoke to the people whatever he wished, and in whatever manner he wished. Clearly, he was delirious, speaking against your opinion in your kingdom. “Whatever he wished,” you say, “and in whatever manner he wished.” Either praise him or reject him. Why do you proceed uncertainly here as well? If what he said was good, why do you not openly proclaim it? If it was bad, why do you not consistently censure it?

But let us consider how the pillar of truth and faith, who dares to say of so great a man that “he spoke to the people whatever he wished,” reports about himself—how prudently and modestly, how humbly:

“When,” he says, “one day we too had spoken before him, and the reading that was being delivered had prompted us, while he and the entire Church were listening, we spoke on the faith and on all ecclesiastical doctrines—those which, by God’s grace, we always teach unceasingly in the Church and in the catecheses.”

### 12. Epiphanius, Father of Bishops

I ask: what sort of confidence is this, what such swelling of spirit? All philosophers and orators condemn Gorgias of Leontini because he dared, with a public chair set out, to promise that he would answer whatever anyone wished to ask him. Unless the honor of the priesthood and reverence for your name restrained me, and unless I knew the Apostle’s saying, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people’” (Acts 23:5; Exod. 22), with what shouting and indignation of words would I complain about your narrative!

You yourself diminish the dignity of your name when, in deed and speech, you despise the father of almost all bishops, the surviving remnant of ancient holiness. You say that one day, when the reading being delivered had prompted you, while he and the entire Church were listening, you discussed the faith and all ecclesiastical doctrines. [Note: [Col. 0365D] Thus the manuscripts read; the editors substitute *non*—“not”—on the basis, as they claim, of the ensuing sequence of the argument. But suppose Jerome is speaking ironically.]

Now we should marvel at Demosthenes, who is said to have spent a long time composing his splendid speech against Aeschines. In vain we admire [Al. receive] Tully [Cicero]. Cornelius Nepos reports that, in his presence, the defense for Cornelius, the seditious tribune, was delivered in almost the same words in which it was published. [Note: [Col. 0365D] Our Nepos may have written this in his lost books On the Life of Cicero. Yet it conflicts with Pliny’s testimony, who in Book 1, Letter 20, says that Cicero pleaded for Cornelius for four days, “so that we cannot doubt,” he says, “that what he said more extensively over several days, as necessity required, he afterward cut down and polished into one large book—large indeed, but still only one.” In the old edition the words appear absolutely in the same form; and the words “for a long time,” found shortly before, are absent.]

Here is our Lysias; here is Gracchus; and, to introduce someone more recent, Quintus Haterius, who possessed his eloquence ready at hand, so that he could not keep silent without a prompter. Caesar Augustus spoke of him splendidly:

“Our Quintus,” he said, “must be held back.” [Note: [Col. 0365D] Our man must be restrained. Erasmus incorrectly reads *sufflammandus*; the old codex has *inflammandus*. Concerning this word I have read the following among learned writers: *sufflamino* means “to restrain and hold back with a brake.” Seneca, in the Fourth Declamation, says: “His speed of speech was so great that it became a fault. Therefore the divine Augustus said most aptly: ‘Our Haterius must be held back.’” Elsewhere it is read *sufflammandus*, and elsewhere *suffibulandus*. A *sufflamen* was a restraint on a descending wheel, preventing it from running too fast. In French, *sufflamine* means *enrayer les roues d’un carrosse*, “to brake the wheels of a carriage,” etc. The ignorant cleric John misused this word in his Questions on Jerome, as though he feared that the studies of sacred literature might now be carried headlong into ruin by some kind of rotation. MARTIAN. — Seneca, in the Fourth Book of the Declamations: “His speed of speech, Haterius’s, was so great that it became a fault. Therefore the divine Augustus said most aptly: ‘Our Haterius must be held back.’” See also On the Death of Claudius.]

### 13. The Church’s Custom Concerning Those to Be Baptized

Would any prudent and sane person claim that, in a single discourse in the Church, he had discussed the end and all ecclesiastical doctrines? I ask you to show me what that reading was, steeped in the entire flavor of the Scriptures, that prompted you suddenly to descend into the danger of displaying your eloquence. And unless the river of your eloquence had overflowed you, you could have been accused of being unable, offhand, to speak about all doctrines.

But what is this? You promise one thing and produce another. Our custom is of this sort: for those who are to be baptized, we publicly hand down the holy and worshipful Trinity [the creed of faith] for forty days. If the reading being delivered prompted you to speak about all doctrines in a single hour, why was it necessary to repeat the instruction of forty days? But if you were recounting what you had said throughout the entire forty-day period, how could a single reading on one day have prompted you to speak about all doctrines?

Here too he speaks ambiguously. For it may be that what he usually delivered in the Church to those being baptized over forty days, he touched upon on this occasion under the stimulus of a single reading. For it belongs to the same eloquence to say little in many words and much in few words.

This too may be understood: after one reading had prompted him, he was inflamed by the ardor of speaking and never fell silent for forty days. Meanwhile, the idle old man, hanging upon his words while desiring to learn unheard-of things, nearly fell asleep. In any event, these matters must be endured; perhaps he spoke even these things simply, according to his custom.

### 14. John Ordered Epiphanius to Be Silent. Epiphanius’s Letter to Siricius

Let us set out the remainder, in which, after the labyrinths of his tattered disputation, he states not a doubtful but an open opinion, and concludes his remarkable treatments with this ending:

“When we had spoken these things while he himself was present, and afterward, out of regard for the honor that we had shown him beyond all measure, he had been prompted to speak, he praised and admired our preaching and declared to everyone that it was the Catholic faith.”

How much honor you showed him beyond all measure is demonstrated by the insults you inflicted beyond all measure: when you ordered him to be silent through the archdeacon, and when, because he was delaying among the crowds, eager for praise, you struck him with your shouts.

The present teaches us about the past. For three full years afterward he swallowed his injuries, disregarded private hostility, and asked only for the correction of the faith. You, who abound in resources [Al. “are wealthy,”] and for whom the religion of the whole world is a source of profit [Note: [Col. 0366D] “The religion of the whole world.” You see how, in Jerome’s time, priests were enriched by the offerings of Christians who traveled to Jerusalem for the sake of religion. MARTIAN.], send your most imposing legates here and there and rouse the sleeping old man to give an answer.

And indeed, since you had conferred so much honor upon him, it was just that he should praise especially your extemporaneous speeches. But since people sometimes praise what they do not approve, and nourish another’s foolishness with empty praise, he not only praised your words, but praised and admired them; and, lest the marvel itself be too small, he declared before the whole people that they were of the Catholic faith.

How truthfully he said these things, we too are witnesses, who heard him—he came to us shaken and lifeless by your words, saying that he had rashly entered into communion. The prayers of the entire monastery had asked him to return to you from Bethlehem, and, unable to withstand the entreaties of so many, he returned in the evening, only to flee in the middle of the night. His letter to Pope Siricius also proves this. If you read it, you will see clearly how he admired your words and declared them Catholic.

But we are wasting time on trifles and, by a long speech, refuting old women’s tales and superfluous songs.

### 15.

Let us pass to the second question, in which, as though nothing had been proposed to him, he pretends to sleep, secure and belching, so as to make readers drowsy. [Note: [Col. 0367C] From this point begins the oldest manuscript of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, written almost in papyrus-like letters, or, as they appear on Egyptian papyrus, under this heading: “Here begins Eusebius Jerome’s On the Resurrection of the Flesh.” Some diligent person had copied such a fragment for himself from the complete work.]

“But our discussion concerned the remaining matters pertaining to the faith: namely, that one and the same creator made all visible and invisible things, the heavenly powers and earthly creatures.” [Note: [Col. 0367C] The word *Deum*, “God,” is absent in the aforementioned manuscript; shortly afterward it likewise has *quod simpliciter*, “which simply.”]

“That is, the holy Trinity, in accordance with blessed David’s saying: ‘By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host’ (Ps. 32:6). The creation of man also demonstrates this plainly. For he is the one who, taking dust from the earth, formed man and, through the grace of his own inbreathing, gave him a rational [Al. reasoning] soul, and one possessing free will—not some part of his nature (as certain people impiously proclaim), but a creature proper to itself. [Note: [Col. 0367C] This refers, presumably, to the Manichaeans. Shortly afterward the Holy Cross codex reads “likewise believing”; the old edition has “likewise beginning.”]

And concerning the holy angels they likewise believe, according to the divine Scripture that speaks of God: ‘He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire’ (Ps. 104:4). Scripture does not permit us to believe that these are of an immutable nature, for it says: ‘The angels who did not keep their own rank but abandoned their proper dwelling he has kept in eternal bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day’ (Jude 6). [Note: [Col. 0367D] Up to this point the editions had incorrectly read *Dei*, “of God,” instead of *diei*, “of the day”; we correct it from the Holy Cross codex, with the Greek text, *ἡμέρας*, agreeing, as does the Vulgate translator. The same codex then reads more smoothly, though not with a different meaning, *quia mutati sint*, “because they have been changed.” The old edition then reads: “from their own dignity and glory, rather than God’s, they went into the order of demons,” etc.] We know [Al. “recognize”] that they were changed and, from their own dignity and glory, went over into the order of demons.

But we have never believed, nor taught—far be it from us—that human souls are produced from the fall of angels or from their conversion; and we confess that this is alien to ecclesiastical preaching.”

### 16. Origen’s Errors

We ask whether souls, before man was made in paradise and Adam was formed from the earth, existed among rational creatures; whether they possessed their own state, lived, remained, and subsisted; and whether Origen’s teaching is true when he said that all rational creatures, incorporeal and invisible, if they became more negligent, gradually slipped toward lower things and, according to the qualities of the places to which they descended, assumed bodies for themselves—for example, first ethereal, then aerial bodies.

When they reached the vicinity of earth, they were surrounded by denser bodies [Note: [Col. 0367D] The Holy Cross codex reads: “surrounded by bodies, and finally even bound to human flesh, and the demons themselves,” etc.; shortly afterward, “when they had subsequently received repentance.”] and were finally bound to human flesh. Even the demons who by their own will withdrew from God’s service with their prince, the devil, if they began to recover somewhat, were clothed in human flesh, so that, after subsequently doing penance, they might return after the resurrection by the same circle through which they had come into flesh [Note: [Col. 0367D] Martianaeus says: “At this point the old editions of Erasmus and Marianus Victorius—and he could have added other still older editions—introduce a theological error, where they read ‘they may return to the vision of God,’ as though demons could ever have enjoyed the blessed vision of God.” But the sense explained here is not Catholic but Origenist. Is it, moreover, a lesser error for demons, after doing penance, to return to the vicinity of God rather than to the vision of God? Origen in fact held this view in Volume III of his Commentary on Matthew, p. 332: It is possible that, just as a human being is converted from unbelief to faith, from lack of self-control to chastity, and generally from wickedness to virtue, so an angel entrusted with the care of a soul immediately from its birth may at first be evil, but afterward, in the same proportion as the one entrusted to him believes, may himself believe as well and make such progress “as to become one of the angels who continually behold the face of the Father who is in heaven.” I therefore do not know whether the old editions read more correctly *visionem*, “vision,” although our manuscript too prefers *viciniam*, “vicinity,” without a different meaning.]

—freed even from aerial and ethereal bodies—and then all knees, heavenly, earthly, and infernal, would bow before God, and God would be all in all.

Since these are the questions at issue, why, leaving aside the matters over which the dispute turns, do you depart from the arena [Note: [Col. 0368D] “From the arena.” Marianus rightly cautions and corrects Erasmus, who reads *de stammate*, etc., whereas all the manuscripts read *de scammate*. MARTIAN. — The ancients called the ditch enclosing the stadium the *scamma*; competitors were not permitted to go beyond it. The old edition reads “from the order of your number”; Erasmus, “from the *stamma*.”] and the place of contest and linger over foreign and wholly unrelated discussions?

### 17. What Origen Said in the Books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*). When Jerome Published His Commentaries on Ecclesiastes

You believe that one God made all visible and invisible creatures. Arius too would confess this, since he says that all things were created through the Son. If you were being accused of Marcion’s heresy, which posits one good God and another just God [Note: [Col. 0368D] “Positing God.” I found *inferens*, “introducing” or “positing,” written in the old codices, not *serens* or *ferens*. MARTIAN.] and asserts that the former is creator of invisible things and the latter of visible things, you would rightly have satisfied me on such a question.

You believe that the Trinity of the universe is creator. The Arians and Semi-Arians deny this [Note: [Col. 0368D] “The Arians and Semi-Arians.” Thus the Sorbonne manuscript reads; in the Cluniacensis, not in the same words but with the same sense, “the Arians and Eunomians deny” it. MARTIAN.], blaspheming that the Holy Spirit is not creator but created.

But who is accusing you of being an Arian at this time? You say that human souls are not part of God’s nature—as though you were now being called a Manichaean by Epiphanius. You reject those who assert that souls are produced from angels and say that our substance is their fall.

Do not conceal what you know, nor pretend to possess a simplicity you do not have. [Note: [Col. 0369C] The Holy Cross manuscript reads: “nor the simplicity which you do not have,” etc.] Origen never said that souls are produced from angels, since he teaches that the angels themselves are a name for an office, not for a nature.

For in the books *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* he says that angels, thrones, dominions, powers, rulers of the world and of darkness, and every name that is named (Eph. 1:21), not only in the present age but also in the future, are the souls of the bodies that they have taken upon themselves either from desire or from service. He says that the sun itself and the moon and the entire choir of stars are likewise souls of rational [Note: [Col. 0369C] The same manuscript reads “of certain” [*quarundam*]. See what we have noted in the Letter to Avitus and elsewhere; see also Saint Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] and once-incorporeal creatures. These creatures, now subjected to vanity—that is, to bodies of fire, which we ignorant and uneducated people call the lights of the world—will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. Hence all creation groans and labors in childbirth.

And the Apostle laments, saying: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24). It is not appropriate at this time to write against a doctrine that is pagan and partly Platonic. Nearly ten years ago, in my Commentaries on Ecclesiastes and in my exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians, I think I explained the view of my mind to prudent readers.

### 18.

Now I ask you, who say so much and expound the truth concerning all subjects in a single treatment, to give a brief and complete answer to those who ask:

When God formed man from clay and, through the grace of his own inbreathing, granted him a soul, did that soul exist beforehand and subsist, and where had it been, the soul that was afterward granted by God’s inbreathing? Or did it, on the sixth day, when the body had been formed from clay, receive existence and life by God’s power? [Note: [Col. 0369C] In the same manuscript: “or on the sixth day, when the body …”; shortly afterward it reads *videre*, “to see,” instead of *vivere*, “to live.”]

You are silent about this. You conceal what is being asked and occupy yourself with superfluous questions. You leave Origen untouched and rage against the follies of Marcion, Apollinaris, Eunomius, Manichaeus, Arius [Note: [Col. 0369D] The name Arius is supplied from the Holy Cross codex; according to it, shortly afterward we likewise read *retices*, “you are silent,” where previously there was *retines*, “you retain.”] and the remaining heretics.

You are asked for a hand and extend a foot; yet you secretly insinuate the doctrine that you retain. You appease us country folk in such a way that you do not thoroughly displease your own people.

### 19.

You say that demons, rather than souls, are produced from angels, as though, according to Origen, the demons themselves were not souls of an aerial body [Note: [Col. 0369D] In the old editions, a glossator’s hand reads: “This is pious: they are souls of an aerial body; and this is impious: from demons,” etc. The following words, “You write that angels are mutable,” are absent from the Holy Cross codex.], and as though, after they repent, they will not become human souls. [Note: [Col. 0369D] “They are souls,” etc. The same Cluniac manuscript omits the words “this is pious,” which are needlessly found in other books. MARTIAN.]

You write that angels are mutable, and under what is pious you introduce what is impious, so that, through many stages, souls come to be not from angels but from those names into which the angels were previously changed.

I want what I am saying to become clearer. Imagine someone who, because of his own fault, has been demoted from tribunician authority and, through the successive offices of the equestrian service [Note: [Col. 0369D] He calls it the palatine service, as I think, that is, the service or corps of soldiers who kept watch for the palace.], has fallen down to the status of a recruit. Does he immediately become a recruit from a tribune? No; first he becomes a *primicerius*, then a senator, a *ducenarius*, a *centenarius*, a *biarchus*, a *circitor*, a cavalryman, and finally a recruit. [Note: [Col. 0369D] A learned man, arguing that *senator* denotes a civic rather than a military dignity, thought the word had been wrongly inserted here or was corruptly read. But there was no reason for suspicion: although rarely, *senator* does occur among the military ranks in the Acts of the Martyrs of Agaunum, written by Saint Eucherius. At that time Saint Maurice was the great source of encouragement to faith; he was then, as is reported, *primicerius* of the legion and, together with Exsuperius, whom the army calls the *campiductor*—read *campidoctor*, for the Greek is *ὁπλοδιδάκτης* and *ὁπλοδιδάσκαλος*—and Candidus, a military senator, kindled each man by exhortation, etc. The same appears in Theodosius’s Novel 29, “Concerning the Scholars,” where the authority to beat and demote senators and *ducenarii* is denied to the counts of the scholars; shortly afterward senators, *ducenarii*, and *centenarii* are again mentioned. Constantine the Great, in Book 1 of the Justinian Code, *On the Office of the Master of Offices, on the Agents in Affairs*, responds as follows: “With the privileges formerly granted to your Schola preserved and kept intact, no one shall reach the *ducenaria*, *centenaria*, or *biarchia* by influence, but each by labor,” etc. Thus in the School of the Agents in Affairs, in the equestrian or palatine service—or in other cohorts that handled the emperor’s public or private affairs—there were definite grades through which one had to advance gradually: first cavalrymen, then *circitores*, then *biarchi*, and so forth. The name *centenarius* was missing here in Jerome and is supplied from the Holy Cross manuscript. For *circitor*, other learned men read *cirmicitor*, but, so far as I know, no mention of that name or dignity occurs among authors. A *circitor*, Greek *περιοδευτής* and *κελευτής*, was one who made the rounds of the watches and reported whether any offense had been committed. Vegetius, Book 3, chapter 8: “Now,” he says, “a rank has been established in military service, and they are called *circitores*.” Others read *circatores*.]

Although a tribune was once an ordinary soldier, nevertheless he became from a tribune not a recruit but a *primicerius*. Origen teaches, through Jacob’s ladder, that rational creatures descend gradually to the lowest degree, namely flesh and blood. It cannot happen that someone plunges suddenly from the number one hundred to the number one, unless he reaches the final point through each number, as though through the rungs of a ladder; and that they change as many bodies as the abodes they have changed in descending from heaven to earth.

These are your tricks and deceptions, by which you call us Pelusians, beasts of burden, and merely animal men because we do not accept the things that are spiritual (see the Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus [at the end]). You Jerusalemites even ridicule the angels. Your mysteries are dragged into the open, and a doctrine woven from pagan fables is published to Christian ears.

What you admire [Al. “imitate”] we long ago despised in Plato. We despised it because we accepted the foolishness of Christ [Al. “accept it”]. We accepted the foolishness of Christ because “the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1:25).

Are you not ashamed that Christians and priests of God, as though they were dealing with matters of amusement, cling to doubtful words and weigh ambiguous opinions, by which the speaker is deceived more than the listener? [Note: [Col. 0371D] The Holy Cross codex has the doubtful word *quaerere*, “to seek”; the lesser readings are noted in the margin.]

### 20. These Words Concern a Certain Origenist

When one of your chorus was being held by me and asked to say what he thought about the soul—whether it had existed before the flesh or had not existed—he replied that both body and soul had existed together. I knew that the heretic was seeking traps in his speech.

At last I discovered that he meant the soul to be called a soul from the moment it animated a body; before that it had been called either a demon, or an angel of Satan, or a spirit of fornication [Note: [Col. 0371D] The manuscripts, including those examined by Father Martianaeus, read *fortitudinis*, “of strength,” instead of *fornicationis*, “of fornication.”], or, on the opposing side, a dominion, power, ministering spirit, or messenger.

If the soul existed before Adam was formed in paradise, and lived and did something in whatever state and order it occupied—for we cannot imagine an incorporeal and eternal thing lying motionless and torpid like a dormouse—then some cause must have preceded, on account of which what had previously existed without a body was afterward surrounded by a body.

And if it is natural for the soul to exist without a body, then it is contrary to nature for it to exist in a body. If it is contrary to nature to exist in a body, then the resurrection of the body will be contrary to nature. But the resurrection will not be contrary to nature; therefore, according to your opinion, the body that rises, although contrary to nature [Note: [Col. 0371D] The word *resurgens*, “rising,” is absent in the Holy Cross manuscript.], will not possess a soul.

### 21. To Name Manichaeus Is Pollution

You say that the soul is not of God’s substance. Good. For you condemn the most impious Manichaeus, whom merely to name is pollution.

You say that souls are not produced from angels. For the moment I agree, although I know in what sense you have said it. Since, therefore, we have learned what you deny, we want to know what you believe.

“Taking clay from the earth,” you say, “God formed man and, through the grace of his own inbreathing, gave him a rational soul and one possessing free will, not some part of his nature—as certain people impiously proclaim—but a creature proper to itself.”

See how, with what a circuitous route, he expresses what we are not asking. We know that God formed man from the earth; we know that he breathed into his face and that he became a living soul. [Note: [Col. 0371D] The same manuscript reads: “and that man became a soul,” etc. Then: “We know that God created it and that it is his creature.”] We do not fail to know that the soul is rational, possesses its own will, and is God’s creature. No one doubts that Manichaeus is in error when he says that it is God’s substance.

What I now ask is this: When was this soul—a creature of God, possessing free will and reason, and not of the Creator’s substance—made? Was it at the time when man was made from clay and the breath of life was breathed into his face? Or had it previously existed [Al. “had previously been made”] and lived among rational, incorporeal, and invisible creatures, and was afterward given through God’s inbreathing?

Here you are silent; here you pretend to be simple and rustic. Under the words of Scripture you conceal what Scripture does not mean. In the place where you say what no one is asking—namely, that it is not some part of his [Al. “the divine”] nature, as certain people impiously proclaim—you should rather have said what we are all asking: that it was not something that had previously existed; not something he had created earlier; not something that had already been dwelling for a long time among rational, incorporeal, and invisible creatures.

You say none of these things. You bring forward Manichaeus and conceal Origen. Just as attendants offer amusing objects to little children asking for food, to distract their minds, so you distract us country folk with other matters, so that, while we are held by the novelty of another person [Note: [Col. 0371D] The Holy Cross manuscript reads: “while we are frightened.”], we do not ask what we want to ask.

### 22. Eve as a Type of the Church. God Daily Forms Rational Souls. A Free Confession of Faith

Suppose you do not say this, and suppose your simplicity contains nothing that you cunningly conceal. Since, then, you had begun to speak about the soul and, concerning so great a matter, to return to the beginning of the creation of humanity, why, while the argument remained unfinished, do you suddenly leap to angels and to the dispensation of the Lord’s body? Why, leaving such a great obstacle in the middle, do you allow us to remain uncertain and stuck in the mud?

If God’s inbreathing—which you do not wish to affirm and which you now leave ambiguous—is the creation of the human soul, where did Eve, into whose face God did not breathe, obtain her soul? I say nothing of Eve, who, as a type of the Church, was built from the man’s rib and should not, after so many centuries, have to endure the calumnies of her descendants.

From where did Cain and Abel, the first sons of the first human beings, obtain their souls? From what beginnings of souls is the whole human race thereafter reckoned? [Note: [Col. 0372D] See, if you wish, Letter 81 in our recension, concerning the origin of souls. Shortly afterward the Holy Cross codex reads: “gradually descended to earthly things,” etc.]

Are souls produced by transmission, like brute animals—so that, just as body comes from body, soul is generated from soul? Or are rational creatures, through desire for bodies, gradually fallen to earth and finally bound even to human bodies? Or, certainly—as is ecclesiastical teaching according to the sayings of the Savior—“My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). [Note: [Col. 0372D] *Meus*, “my,” was missing; it is supplied by the manuscript and confirmed by the Greek text. For “Isaiah,” Victorius reads “Zechariah,” and Martianaeus likewise advises that it should be restored, since these are the words of that prophet in chapter 12:1; but the manuscripts do not support this.]

And also that saying of Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0372D] “And that saying of Isaiah.” For “Isaiah,” read “Zechariah”: these words are found in Zechariah, chapter 12:1, although Isaiah says many things in chapters 42 and 57 about the creation of the soul and the breathing of the spirit. MARTIAN.]: “He forms the spirit of man within him.” And in the Psalms: “He who fashions their hearts one by one” (Ps. 33:15). God daily forms souls, for with him to will is to have made; nor does he cease to be Creator.

I know what you usually say against this, and how you bring before us adulteries and incestuous unions. That is a longer dispute and cannot be confined within the limits of this occasion. The same controversy can also be turned back against you; and whatever appears unworthy of the Creator of the present age is not unworthy of him when he grants it as well. [Note: [Col. 0373D] We read this from the Holy Cross manuscript. Previously it had the opposite sense: “what appears unworthy of the Creator of the present age, this too, with him granting it, is not unworthy.”]

To be born from adultery is not the fault of the one who is born, but of the one who begets. Just as, in the case of seeds, the earth that nourishes them does not sin, nor the seed cast into the furrows, nor the moisture and heat by which the tempered grains sprout into growth—but, for example, the thief and robber who by deceit and force steals the seeds—so, in the generation of human beings [Al. “of the human race”], the earth, that is, the womb, receives what belongs to it; and what it receives it nourishes, what it nourishes it gives bodily form to, and what it gives bodily form to it divides into members.

And amid those hidden confines of the womb, God’s hand is always at work; he is the creator of body and soul alike. Do not despise the goodness of your potter, who formed you and made you as he wished. He is the power of God and the wisdom of God who built himself a dwelling in the Virgin’s womb (Heb. 11). Jephthah, numbered among holy men by the Apostle’s testimony, was the son of a prostitute.

But listen: Esau was born from Rebecca and Isaac—hairy and rough both in mind and body—as good wheat degenerates into darnel and oats. For the cause of vices and virtues lies not in the seeds but in the will of the one who is born. [Note: [Col. 0373D] The words “But listen” are absent in the Holy Cross manuscript. Some lesser readings below are corrected from the same manuscript.]

If birth through human bodies is an offense, how were Isaac (Gen. 18), Samson (Judg. 13), and John the Baptist (Luke 1) born from a promise?

Do you understand what it means to profess one’s faith boldly and freely? Suppose I am mistaken: I openly say what I think. Therefore, either freely profess our position, or consistently state your own.

Do not place yourself in my battle line so that, under a feigned rusticity, you may keep yourself safe and, whenever you wish, stab the fighter in the back. It is not appropriate at this time to write against Origen’s doctrines. If Christ grants life, we shall devote another work to that subject.

The question now is whether the person being accused has answered what was asked, and whether his answer is simple and clear.

### 23. He speaks with fear of God and wishes to be heard. John’s confession

Let us pass from here to the very famous question concerning the resurrection of the flesh and the body, in which, reader, I wish to warn you again that you should know that I speak with fear and judgment of God, and that you ought to listen to me. For I am not so foolish that, if his exposition contains genuine faith and no suspicion of disloyalty, I should seek an opportunity to accuse him; and, while wishing to mark another with guilt, should myself be marked with slander. Read, therefore, what follows concerning the resurrection of the flesh; and when you have read it, and it has pleased you—for I know that it will please the ignorant—suspend your judgment, wait a little, and restrain your verdict until the end of our reply; and if afterward it pleases you, then you may mark us with slander.

> “We also confess his passion on the cross, his death and burial, all of which he truly underwent, and his resurrection in reality, not merely in appearance: he who is the firstborn from the dead (Colossians XVIII), the firstfruits of the mass of our bodies, which he raised after they had been placed in the tomb and carried up to heaven, giving us the hope of resurrection in the resurrection of his own body. Hence we all hope to rise from the dead in the same way as he rose. Not in certain other foreign bodies and bodies belonging to others, which are assumed in a phantasm; but just as he rose in that body which, having been laid in the holy tomb among us, rose again, so we too hope to rise in these very bodies with which we are now surrounded and in which we are now buried, in the same manner and vision.

[Note: The manuscript of Santa Croce reads, “we hope to rise in the same manner and by the same command,” etc.]

For what is sown, according to the Apostle, in corruption will rise in incorruption; what is sown in dishonor will rise in glory. ‘The natural body is sown; the spiritual body will rise’ (1 Corinthians XV, 42). Concerning these things the Savior also spoke when teaching:

> “‘Those who are deemed worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage; nor can they die any longer, but they are like the angels of God, being children of the resurrection’ (Luke XX, 35–36).”

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “like the angels in heaven, since they are,” etc. The Vulgate translator renders the Greek more fully: “they are equal to the angels and are children of God, since they are,” etc.]

[Note: The published editions after Erasmus read this sentence with a threefold negation up to this point—“and if they have not pleased you, I know that they will not please you”—and then, shortly afterward, “if afterward they have not pleased you.” But from the entire context, the sequence of the speech, and the author’s intention, it is clear that the sense must be read in the opposite way and that the threefold negative particle must be removed. For it is not, as Martianay wrote rather carelessly, the faith of the Church that is appended and displayed, but John’s faith—that of a deceitful heretic—which is so artfully woven that at first sight it pleases, especially those who are ignorant and suspect no deception; but after Jerome’s response, if he wishes, he himself is to be marked with slander. The eminent manuscript of Santa Croce reads it in the same way as I have corrected it, as do two old editions, one printed at Venice in 1496 and the other in the following year by Nicolaus Kesler, a citizen of Basel; the latter also has in the preceding line, “concerning the resurrection of the Lord’s flesh.”]

### 24. Again in another part of the Epistle

Again, in another part of the Epistle—that is, at the end of his treatises—in order to deceive the ears of the uninformed, he balanced the sound and pomp of the resurrection by this ambiguity of words:

> “Nor have we omitted the second glorious coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will come in his glory to judge the living and the dead. For he himself will raise all the dead and make them stand before his tribunal, and will repay each according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil: that is, either to be crowned in the body in which he acted chastely and justly, or to be condemned in the body that served pleasures and iniquities alike.”

We find operative in this chapter what we read in the Gospel: “At the consummation of the world, if possible, even the elect will be led astray” (Matthew XXIV).

[Note: The old edition reads, “works in this chapter, when the unlearned crowd, or populace,” etc.; and later, “confess not merely in appearance, and the firstfruits of the mass of our bodies, and God in a body,” etc.]

The uneducated crowd hears of the dead and buried; it hears of the resurrection of the dead in reality and not merely in appearance; it hears that the firstfruits of the mass of our bodies have reached the heavenly places in the Lord’s body; it hears that we shall rise—not in foreign bodies belonging to others, which are assumed in a phantasm, but just as the Lord rose in the body that lay buried among us in the holy tomb—so we too shall rise on the day of judgment in those very bodies with which we are now surrounded and in which we are buried.

And lest anyone should regard this as insufficient, he adds at the end of the chapter:

> “And he will repay each according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil: that is, either to be crowned in the body in which he acted chastely and justly, or to be condemned because it served pleasures and iniquities.”

[Note: Earlier the reading was “in the body.”]

When the uneducated crowd hears this, amid such a din of the dead, the buried body, and the resurrection, it suspects no trickery and no ambush. It believes that what is said is what is meant. For the ears of the people are more holy than the mind of the priest.

### 25. Again and again

Again and again, reader, I warn you to have patience and to learn what I too learned through patience;

[Note: The manuscript of Santa Croce reads, “through much patience.” A little later it read, “briefly concerning the resurrection,” etc.]

yet before I reveal the dragon’s face and briefly explain Origen’s doctrine concerning the resurrection—for you cannot know the power of the antidote unless you have first seen the poisons—observe this carefully and, rereading it cautiously, count it: although he names the resurrection of the body nine times, he does not insert the word “flesh” even once. Let it therefore be suspect to you that he omitted it deliberately.

Origen says in many places, and especially in the fourth book *On the Resurrection*, in his *Exposition of the First Psalm*, and in the *Stromata*, that a double error is current in the Church: that of our people and that of the heretics:

> “We simple people and *philosarcs*—that is, lovers of flesh, from φίλος (*philos*, ‘lover’) and σάρξ (*sarx*, ‘flesh’)—say that the same bones, blood, and flesh, that is, the face and limbs and the whole structure of the body, will rise on the last day: so that we shall walk with our feet, work with our hands, see with our eyes, hear with our ears, and carry about an insatiable belly and a stomach digesting food. It follows that those who believe these things must also say that we shall eat and drink, digest excrement, discharge bodily fluid, marry wives, and beget children. For what purpose would the genital limbs exist if there were no marriages? What purpose would teeth serve if food were not to be ground? What purpose would belly and food serve if, according to the Apostle, both this and that are to be destroyed? For he cries out again: ‘Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, nor does corruption possess incorruption’ (1 Corinthians I, 15).”

He asserts that we innocent and uncultivated people say these things.

> “But the heretics—among whom are Marcion, Apelles, Valentinus, and Manes—

[Note: *Manes* is a Persian name meaning “a slave”; Jerome, however, connects it with Greek Μανία, “madness” or “insanity,” or with μανός, “mad.”]

—completely deny the resurrection both of flesh and of body, and attribute salvation only to the soul. They say that we speak foolishly when we claim that we shall rise according to the Lord’s example, since the Lord himself also rose in a phantasm; and not only his resurrection but his very birth also was τῷ δοκεῖν—that is, merely apparent, more a thing seen in appearance than a reality. He himself rejects both opinions: he avoids both the flesh of our people and the phantasms of the heretics, because each side goes to excess in the opposite direction—some wishing us to be what we were, others wholly denying the resurrection of bodies.

> “There are four elements, known also to philosophers and physicians, from which all things and human bodies are composed: earth, water, air, and fire. Earth is understood in the flesh, air in the breath, water in the bodily fluid, and fire in the heat. When, therefore, the soul has abandoned this frail and cold little body at God’s command, everything gradually returns to its original substances: flesh falls back into earth, breath mingles with air, fluid returns to the abysses, and heat flies upward to the ether. And just as, if you pour a sextarius of milk and wine into the sea and wish afterward to separate what has been mixed, the wine and milk that you poured in have not perished, but what has been poured out cannot nevertheless be separated, so the substance of flesh and blood does not perish in its original materials, yet it does not return to its former structure, nor can it remain wholly the same as it was.”

When these things are said, the solidity of the flesh, the fluidity of blood, the thickness of the sinews, the interweaving of the veins, and the hardness of the bones are denied.

[Note: “*Philosarcs*,” that is, lovers of flesh, from φίλος and σάρξ.]

### 26. Origen’s opinion

> “In another way we confess the resurrection of bodies: of those bodies that have been placed in tombs and dispersed into ashes—the body of Paul as Paul’s, Peter’s as Peter’s, and each person’s as his own. For it is not right that souls should have sinned in one set of bodies and be tormented in another, nor is it fitting for the just Judge that one set of bodies should shed blood for Christ and another be crowned.”

Who, hearing this, would think that he denies the resurrection of the flesh?

> “And,” he says, “a certain principle has been implanted by God the Creator in each individual seed, which preserves the future materials in the beginnings of the marrow. Just as the great size of a tree—its trunk, branches, fruit, and leaves—is not seen in the seed, yet exists in the principle of the seed, which the Greeks call the *spermatikón lógon* (σπερματικὸν λόγον), so in a grain of wheat there is internally either marrow or a vein which, when it has dissolved in the earth, draws neighboring materials to itself and rises into a stalk, leaves, and ears. One thing dies, and another rises.

> “For in a grain of wheat the roots, stalk, leaves, ear, and chaff are not separately dissolved. So also in the principle of human bodies certain ancient beginnings of rising remain, and something like an ἐντεριώνη—alternatively ἀννερία—that is, a seedbed of the dead, is cherished in the bosom of the earth.

[Note: As though ἐντεριώνη. Erasmus was unfortunate in restoring this word too; Marianus still more so, changing it as though it were ἀντέριαν in order to substitute ἀνθέριον. Neither is Jerome’s true reading, as he himself teaches below. Speaking of this same seedbed of the dead and of the resurrection according to the heretics, he says later in this Epistle: “Do you slander the power of God …? He can from that marrow and your seedbed … ἐντεριώνη, not flesh only,” etc. Ἐντεριώνη means marrow, heart, and matrix, or the inner part of anything. Thus marrow and matrix were warmed in the bosom of the earth, like a seedbed for the resurrection of the dead, if Origen were to be believed. MARTIANAY.]

> “When the day of judgment arrives, and the earth trembles at the voice of the archangel and the final trumpet, the seeds will immediately be stirred, and in an instant of time they will make the dead germinate; yet they will not restore the same flesh, nor restore them in the forms that they formerly possessed. Do you wish to know that what we say is true? Hear the Apostle: ‘But someone will say, How are the dead raised? With what body will they come? Fool, what you sow is not the body that will be, but a bare grain—for example, of wheat, or of the vine, or of a tree’ (1 Corinthians XV, 36–37).”

[Note: The Greek word is σπερματικόν. The Greek term is extremely corrupt in the manuscript codices. After much labor Erasmus attempted to restore it as σπινθηρισμόν, which Erasmus proposed as the Greek term. Marianus, following Erasmus, testifies that it was written thus in the Greek manuscripts. Therefore the manuscripts used by Marianus Victorius have perished, since today there is no one who can recover the word σπινθηρισμόν. To avoid deceiving learned readers, the Greek word must first be represented from the old exemplars, where it is written in these Greek letters: ϹΠΕΡΤΙΠΟΠΑΡΟΠ, which the Greeks call *ceratiromason* or *snectiromason* when written in Latin characters in other, more recent copies. These expressions, plainly corrupt, seem nevertheless somehow to point toward σπερματικόν, σπερματίζων, or even σπερματισμόν. We retain the last word in the text, since among the Greeks σπερματισμός, “the emission of seed,” appears to be equivalent to “the principle of the seed.” I do not wish to contend over doubtful matters.

MARTIANAY: In the manuscript of Santa Croce, σπερατικὸν λόγον is read, from which I understood that σπερματικὸν λόγον should be restored by a slight change, as I shall immediately show. Martianay printed σπερματισμόν from his manuscripts, and although the reading is plainly fabricated, he labors at length to defend it, severely criticizing Victorius, who after Erasmus had read σπινθηρισμόν. Yet the Latin words “the principle of the seed” would themselves have been sufficient to restore the expression, since the Greeks would render or could have rendered them σπερματικὸν λόγον. Origen, whose meaning is under examination here, very often mentions *spermatikoi logoi* and discusses them.
