Take, for example, the beginning of the twentieth tome on John, where he also holds that “seminal principles” (σπερματικοὺς λόγους συγκαταβαλλομένους τισὶν ψυχαῖς) are implanted in certain souls; on this matter consult the learned Huet in his notes. See also Diogenes Laertius, Book VII, §136. Sextus Empiricus also mentions, *Against the Physicists* I, σπέρμα λογικοῦ, “the seed of the rational principle,” which among all kinds of seeds—or the *seminal principles* with which the world is filled—includes those by which human beings are generated, called λόγοι σπερματικοὶ λογικοῦ.]

And because we have already spoken partly about the grain of wheat and the seed of trees, let us now discuss the grape seed. The grain is so small that it can scarcely be held between two fingers. Where are its roots? Where is the twisting complexity of its roots, trunk, and branches? Where are the shade-giving leaves and the beauty of the grapes that will produce future wine? What is held is dry and scarcely visible; yet in that dry grain, through God’s power and the hidden principle of the seed, foaming musts will pour forth.

You will grant this to a tree but not to a human being? What is destined to perish is so adorned; what is to remain will not recover its former lowliness.

[Note: I transcribe this whole period from the manuscript of Santa Croce, with which the old edition also agrees somewhat. The sense seemed fuller with the supplied words, “Will you grant this to wood, but not grant it to a human being?”, which could easily have escaped a copyist’s eye because of the preceding *tribues* (“you will grant”); the comparison between the renewal of wood and of human beings is also more apt and truer. Until now all other books had the contrary sense: “You grant this to wood, which is destined to perish: thus what will not remain is adorned and will not recover its former lowliness; and do you again wish bones, blood,” etc.]

And do you want flesh, bones, blood, and limbs again, so that, as your hair grows, you will need a barber; your nose will digest mucus; your nails will have to be cut; and through the lower parts either excrement or lusts will flow?

[Note: The manuscript has “without the word *and*,” then *seminantis* instead of *sementis*; an old edition reads *sinuantur* instead of *fundentur*.]

If you bring forward these foolish notions of uncultivated people and of flesh—as though you forget that in the flesh, which is hostile, we cannot please God—and forget the resurrection of the dead, then hear: “It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown a natural body; it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians XV, 42–44).

Now we see with our eyes, hear with our ears, act with our hands, and walk with our feet. But in that spiritual body we shall see wholly, hear wholly, act wholly, and walk wholly; and the Lord will transform the body of our lowliness, making it conform to the glory of his body. When he says “he will transform”—that is, μετασχηματίσει—the diversity of the limbs that we now use is denied.

[Note: The same manuscript reads *transfiguravit*, “he transformed,” that is, μετεσχημάτισε.]

Another spiritual and ethereal body is promised to us: one that is not subject to touch, cannot be seen by the eyes, and is not weighed down by bodily weight; and it will be changed according to the variety of the places in which it will exist.

Otherwise, if the same flesh and the same bodies will exist again, then there will again be males and females, again marriages; men will again have hairy eyebrows and long beards; women will have smooth cheeks and narrow breasts, and their bellies and thighs will have to be enlarged for conceiving and bearing children.

[Note: Earlier editions read “smooth”; a little later the manuscript of Santa Croce reads, “the former will need to be nourished, the latter supported by staffs. Nor, O simple souls, should the resurrection,” etc.] Infants will rise again, and old men will rise again: the former will need to be nourished, the latter supported by staffs.

Nor should the Lord’s resurrection deceive you, simple people, because he showed his side and hands, stood on the shore, walked on the road with Cleopas, and said that he had flesh and bones. That body possesses privileges of another kind, since it was not born from a man’s seed and the pleasure of flesh. After his resurrection he ate and drank, appeared clothed, and offered himself to be touched, in order to establish the faith of the Apostles who doubted. Yet he does not conceal the nature of an ethereal and spiritual body. For he enters through closed doors, and at the breaking of bread he vanishes from their eyes.

Therefore, will we too after the resurrection have to drink and eat, and after eating discharge excrement? And where will that promise be: “This mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians XV, 53)?

[Note: In the same manuscript: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal,” and so forth.]

### 27. Flesh and body are different. The cleverness of the heretics

This is the whole reason why, in your exposition of the faith, in order to deceive the ears of the ignorant, you name the body nine times and do not name the flesh even once, while people think that you confess flesh in bodies and that flesh is the same as body. If it is the same, then it signifies nothing different.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “and you do not signify something different.”]

I know that you will say: “I thought that body was the same as flesh; I spoke simply.” Why do you not rather name flesh in order to signify body, and use now “flesh,” now “body,” indifferently, so that body may be shown in flesh and flesh in body?

But believe me, your silence is not simple. The definition of flesh differs from that of body: every flesh is body, but not every body is flesh. Flesh properly means that which is bound together by blood, veins, bones, and sinews. Although body is also called flesh, it is sometimes called ethereal or aerial, because it is not subject to touch or sight, and yet is often visible and tangible. A wall is a body but not flesh; a stone is a body but is not called flesh.

[Note: These words were missing: “A stone is a body but is not called flesh.” They have been supplied from the exemplar of Santa Croce.]

Hence the Apostle calls certain things heavenly bodies and others earthly bodies: the heavenly body of the sun, moon, and stars; the earthly body of fire, air, water, earth, and the other things reckoned among these elements without a soul.

Do you see that we understand your subtleties and the secrets that you discuss in private rooms and among the perfect—things that the people standing outside are not worthy to hear—and that we bring them into the open? This is what you say, laughing, with your hand held to your ear and your fingers snapping: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm XLIV, 14); and, “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs I, 3).

It is clear why you said “the resurrection of the body” and not “of the flesh”: namely, so that we uneducated people would think that you were saying “flesh” within “body,” while those who are perfect would understand that flesh is denied within the body.

Finally, the Apostle, wishing to demonstrate that Christ’s body was fleshly and not spiritual, aerial, or subtle, spoke significantly when he said:

> “And although you were once alienated from Christ and enemies in your understanding through evil works, he reconciled you in the body of his flesh through death” (Colossians I, 21–22).

And again in the same Epistle:

> “In whom you were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping off of the body of the flesh” (Colossians II, 11).

If “body” signifies only flesh and is not an ambiguous term capable of being drawn toward different meanings, then he says “bodily” and “fleshly” quite unnecessarily, as though flesh were not understood in body.

[Note: In the manuscript, “and flesh” is attached to “body” quite unnecessarily, as though flesh were not understood in body.]

### 28. The creed handed down by the Apostles

In the creed of our faith and hope, which was handed down by the Apostles and is not written on paper and with ink but on the fleshy tablets of the heart, after the confession of the Trinity and the unity of the Church, the whole mystery of Christian doctrine is concluded with the resurrection of the flesh.

[Note: The article concerning eternal life was thought to be contained in the article concerning the resurrection of the flesh. See Rufinus’s exposition.]

And you dwell on “body,” then again “body,” and a third time “body,” indeed “body” up to nine times, whether in word or in number, and you do not name flesh even once, whereas they always name flesh and remain silent about body.

But also understand that we perceive what you craftily append and cautiously conceal. For with these testimonies you prove the truth of the resurrection by which Origen denies it; and, confirming uncertainties with doubtful matters, you suddenly overturn the secure house of faith.

“It is sown,” he says, “a natural body; it will rise a spiritual body. For they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels in heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:44; Matthew XXII, 30; Luke XX, 35).

What other examples would you adopt if you wished to deny the resurrection? You claim, as you put it, to confess the resurrection of the flesh in reality and not merely in appearance. After those words with which you have flattered the ears of the ignorant—that we shall rise in the very bodies in which we died and were buried—add this instead, and say:

> “Just as the Lord after his resurrection showed the marks of the nails in his hands, displayed the wound of the spear in his side, and replied to the Apostles who doubted and thought they were seeing a phantasm, ‘Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have’ (Luke XXIV, 39); and specifically to Thomas, ‘Put your finger here in my hands, and put your hand into my side; and do not be unbelieving but believing’ (John XX, 27), so we too after the resurrection shall possess the same limbs that we now use, the same flesh, blood, and bones. In Scripture their works, not their substance, are condemned.

> “For it is written in Genesis: ‘My Spirit will not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh’ (Genesis VI, 3). And the Apostle Paul, speaking of the wicked teaching and works of the Jews, says: ‘I did not yield to flesh and blood’ (Galatians I, 16). And to the saints, who were certainly in the flesh, he says: ‘But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you’ (Romans VIII, 9).”

By denying that they were “in the flesh,” although it was evident that they were in the flesh, he condemned not the substance of the flesh but its sins.

[Note: A lacuna of six lines has been supplied here from the manuscript of Santa Croce, since all the earlier editions had a defective sense: “add and say, Since a spirit does not have flesh,” omitting the words now supplied concerning the Lord’s comparison, which the context of the speech below and the very adverb of comparison require. Without them the sense was not only incomplete but contrary to the author’s intention.]

### 29. The true confession of the resurrection. Elijah and Enoch

This is the true confession of the resurrection, which grants glory to the flesh without removing its reality. When the Apostle says, “This corruptible and mortal” (1 Corinthians XV), he points to this very body—that is, the flesh that was then visible.

When he joins the words “to put on incorruption and immortality,” he does not say that this clothing, this garment, abolishes the body that it adorns in glory. Rather, what was previously inglorious is made glorious, so that after laying aside the meaner garment of mortality and weakness, we may be clothed with the gold of immortality and, so to speak, with the blessedness of firmness and strength. We wish not to be stripped of the flesh but to be clothed over with glory, desiring to put on over it our dwelling that is from heaven, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Certainly no one is clothed over unless he was clothed beforehand.

Thus our Lord too was transfigured in glory on the mountain (Matthew XVII; Mark IX), not so that he lost his hands, feet, and other limbs and suddenly rolled around in the roundness of the sun or a sphere, but so that the same limbs, shining with the brilliance of the sun, dazzled the eyes of the Apostles. Hence his garments too were changed into whiteness, not into air—lest you should perhaps assert that his garments were spiritual. “And his face,” he says, “shone like the sun” (Matthew IX, 2). When his face is mentioned, I judge that his other limbs too were seen.

Enoch was transferred in the flesh. Elijah, in the flesh, was snatched up into heaven (Genesis V, 4; 2 Kings II). Though they have not yet died and are already inhabitants of paradise, they possess the limbs with which they were snatched up and transferred. What we imitate through fasting, they possess through communion with God. They feed on heavenly bread and are filled with every word of God, having the same Lord as both Lord and food.

Hear the Savior saying: “And my flesh shall rest in hope” (Psalm XV, 9). And in another place: “His flesh did not see corruption” (Acts II, 31). And again: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah XL, 5).

And you continually repeat “body”? Bring forward Ezekiel instead, who joins bone to bone, brings them out of their graves, makes them stand upon their feet, binds them together with flesh and sinews, and covers them above with skin (Ezekiel XXXVII).

[Note: “And he covers it above with skin.” In the printed editions we read without sense, “and he covers it above,” until the sentence continues, “Job, victor over torments.” Then, in Job’s text, learned and unlearned alike think that *certe* should be read, or at least “let them be carved in flint.” But they do not notice that Jerome expressed the Hebrew word *jebhats[.....]hun*, “they are sharply carved,” in order to indicate the instrument of carving. MARTIANAY.]

### 30. Job, the athlete of the Church before Christ. Job seems to write against the future Origen

Let Job thunder, victor over torments; let him scrape the pus of his rotting flesh with a potsherd, and console his miseries with the hope and reality of the resurrection:

> “Who will grant me that my words may be written? Who will grant me that they may be inscribed in a book with an iron stylus and a sheet of lead, or carved with a chisel in flint? For I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God. I shall see him myself, and my eyes shall behold him, and not another. This hope has been laid up in my bosom” (Job XIX, 23 and following).

[Note: There are critics of considerable reputation who insist that *certe* must be read instead of *celte*. Indeed, many manuscripts of the Book of Job prefer *certe*. More will be said about this in volume IX, at this passage from Jerome’s version.]

What prophecy could be clearer? No one after Christ speaks so openly about the resurrection as this man before Christ. He wants his words to endure forever, and, so that they may not be erased by age, he wants them inscribed on a sheet of lead and carved in flint. He hopes for the resurrection; indeed, he knows and sees that Christ his Redeemer lives and that he will rise from the earth on the last day.

[Note: In the manuscript of Santa Croce: “he knows and is faithful”; and later, “your Redeemer.”]

The Lord had not yet died, and the athlete of the Church saw his Redeemer rising from the underworld.

But when he adds, “Again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God,” I think he is not speaking as a lover of flesh, flesh that he saw putrid and stinking, but out of confidence in the resurrection he despises present things for the consolation of future ones.

Again he says: “I shall be clothed with my skin.” Where is the ethereal body here? Where is the aerial body, like spirit and breath? Surely where there is skin and flesh, where there are bones, sinews, blood, and veins, there is the structure of flesh; there is the distinctive character of sex.

[Note: In the same manuscript: “where there are bones and sinews”; then, “where there is the structure of flesh.” A little later: “he will see the salvation of God,” that is, Jesus the Lord.]

“And in my flesh,” he says, “I shall see God.” When all flesh shall see the salvation of God and Jesus God, then I too shall see my Redeemer, Savior, and God. I shall see him in this flesh that now torments me, which now drips because of pain. For this reason I shall behold God in the flesh: because by his resurrection he has healed all my weaknesses.

Does it not seem to you that even then Job was writing against Origen and undertaking another contest against the heretics on behalf of the reality of the flesh in which he endured torments? He grieves if he suffered so much in vain and if, while another rises spiritually, this flesh was tormented carnally.

Therefore he repeats and emphasizes the point, and concludes all the secrets of his slippery confession in a clear voice, saying:

> “Whom I shall see myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another.”

[Note: The manuscript reads, “if he is not to rise in his own sex.”]

If he is not to rise in his own sex, if he does not rise with the same limbs that lay in the dung, if he does not open the same eyes to see God with which he then saw the worms—

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “with which he then saw the worms and scraped them away.”]

—where, then, will Job be? You take away the things in which Job existed and give me the empty name of one who rises. It would be as though you wished to restore a ship after shipwreck while denying the individual parts from which the ship is constructed.

### 31. Where the truth of the resurrection lies. Where the likeness of angels promised to us lies

I shall speak freely, and although you twist your mouths, pull your hair, stamp your feet—

[Note: Elsewhere Jerome often says *applodere pedem*; here I would more readily read *applodatis* for *applaudatis*.]

—and seek the stones of the Jews, I shall confess the faith of the Church with the utmost clarity.

The truth of the resurrection cannot be understood without flesh and bones, without blood and limbs. Where flesh, bones, blood, and limbs are, there must necessarily be a difference of sex. Where there is a difference of sex, there are John and John, Mary and Mary.

Do not fear the marriages of those who, even before death, lived in their own sex without the activity of sex. When it is said, “On that day they will neither marry nor be given in marriage” (Matthew XXII, 30), it is said of those who are able to marry but will not marry. No one says of angels, “They will not marry, nor be given in marriage.” I have never heard of marriages of spiritual Powers being celebrated in heaven. But where there is sex, there is male and female.

Therefore, although unwillingly and compelled by the truth, you too have confessed this when you said:

> “Either to be crowned in the body in which he acted chastely and justly, or to be condemned in the body that served pleasures and iniquity.”

Remove body and put flesh in its place, and you have not denied male and female.

For who lives with the glory of chastity if he has no sex through which unchastity could be committed? Who has ever crowned a stone because it remained a virgin?

[Note: The manuscript reads, “For what benefit did the glory of chastity bring him who did not possess…”]

The likeness of angels is promised to us: that is, the blessedness in which angels exist without flesh and sex will be granted to us while we remain in our flesh and sex. My uncultivated understanding believes and understands that sex will remain without the works of sex: that human beings will rise and thus be made equal to the angels.

Nor will the resurrection of limbs immediately seem superfluous because they will no longer perform their proper functions, since even while we remain in this life we strive not to carry out the works of our limbs. The likeness to the angels is not a transformation of human beings into angels, but an advance in immortality and glory.

### 32. Enoch and Elijah again

*[Col. 0383C]*

The arguments, however, concerning boys and infants, old men, food and excrement, which you use against the Churches, are not yours: they have flowed from the fountain of the Gentiles. For the pagans make the same objections against us. You who claim to be a Christian, lay down the weapons of the Gentiles. Let them rather learn from you to confess the resurrection of the flesh than for you to learn denial from them. Or, if you too belong to the number of the enemies, openly show yourself an adversary, so that you may receive the wounds of the pagans.

I grant you your nurses, lest infants cry; I grant you decrepit old men, lest they shrink from the winter cold. The barbers have also learned their craft to no purpose, knowing that for forty years the Israelite people experienced neither the growth of their nails nor of their hair.[^c0039-1] And, what is greater than these things, their garments were not worn out, nor did their sandals grow old.

*[Col. 0383D]*

Enoch and Elijah, of whom we spoke earlier, remain for so long in the same age in which they were taken up. They have teeth, a belly, and genitals, and yet they need neither food nor wives.[^c0039-2] Why do you malign the power of God? He can draw not merely flesh from flesh, but a body from that marrow and “seed-store” of yours, ἐντεριών,[^c0039-3] and make one thing from another;[^c0039-4] and from water—that is, from the lowliness of flesh—change precious wines of an airy body.[^c0039-5] Surely the same power by which he fashioned all things from nothing can restore what once existed, since it is much less to restore what has been than to make what had not been.

*[Col. 0384A]*

Do you wonder if, from infants and old people, the resurrection produces the age of a mature man, when from the clay of the earth, without any stages of growth, a fully formed human being was made? A rib is changed into a woman; and, in a third mode of human formation, the lowly and shameful elements of our birth are changed into flesh: they are bound together in the limbs, run through the veins, and are hardened into bones.[^c0039-6]

Do you wish to hear a fourth kind of human generation? “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Adam was one way, Eve another, Abel another, and the man Jesus Christ another. Yet, in all these different beginnings, the one nature of humanity does not differ.

### 33. Testimonies that prove the true resurrection. What the word “resurrection” signifies

*[Col. 0384B]*

If I wished to prove the resurrection of the flesh and of all the members, and to add explanations to each individual testimony, many books would be required; but the present case does not demand this. For I proposed not to answer Origen in every respect, but to expose the secrets of his fraudulent defense. Nevertheless, since I have been lengthy in asserting the contrary position, and fear that, while striving to uncover his frauds, I may have left the reader offended, I shall set down the testimonies in a heap and touch upon them briefly, so that we may fight against the poisonous argument with the whole weight of the Scriptures.

The person who does not possess a wedding garment, and has not kept the command, “Let your garments always be white” (Matt. 12:13), is bound hand and foot, lest he recline at the banquet, sit upon the throne, or stand at the right hand of God; he is sent into Gehenna, where there is the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of teeth (Matt. 22). “The hairs of your head are numbered” (Luke 12:7). If the hairs are numbered, I suppose the teeth are more easily numbered. Yet they were numbered in vain if they are eventually destined to perish.

*[Col. 0384C]*

“The hour will come when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth” (John 5:25). They will hear with their ears and come forth with their feet. Lazarus had already done this.

*[Col. 0384D]*

They will come forth from the tombs—that is, those who had been brought into the tombs will come forth dead, and rise from their graves.[^c0039-7]

*[Col. 0385A]*

For the dew that comes from God is medicine for their bones. Then what the Lord speaks through the Prophet will be fulfilled: “My people, enter into your storerooms for a little while, until my anger passes” (Isa. 26:20, according to the Septuagint). The storerooms signify the graves, from which what had been laid up there will surely come forth. “And they will come out from their graves,” like young deer released from their bonds. “Their heart will rejoice, and their bones will rise like the sun.” “All flesh will come into the presence of the Lord, and he will command the fish of the sea, and they will disgorge the bones which they had eaten; and he will join structure to structure, and bone to bone.” “Those who slept in the dust of the earth will rise: some to everlasting life, others to everlasting reproach and confusion” (Dan. 12:2).

*[Col. 0385B]*

Then the righteous will see the punishments and torments of the wicked, “for their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched, and they will be before all flesh” (Isa. 66:24). Therefore, since we possess this hope, just as we presented our members as servants to impurity and iniquity leading to iniquity, so let us present them as servants to righteousness leading to sanctification, so that, rising from the dead, we may walk in newness of life (Rom. 6:19).

*[Col. 0385C]*

Likewise, “the life of the Lord Jesus is manifested in our mortal body”; and “he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will give life also to our mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in us” (2 Cor. 4:14). For it is just that those who have always carried the death of Christ in our body should also have the life of Jesus manifested in our mortal body—that is, in mortal flesh according to nature, but eternal according to grace.

Stephen also saw Jesus standing at the right hand of the Father (Acts 7), and Moses’ hand was changed to the whiteness of snow and then restored to its former color (Exod. 4). In both states the hand remained the same.

That potter of Jeremiah, whose vessel was broken because of the hardness of the stones, remade from the same mass and the same clay what had fallen apart (Jer. 18). The very word “resurrection” also signifies not that one thing falls and another is raised, while the addition “of the dead” demonstrates the proper flesh: for what dies in a human being is also what is given life.

The man wounded on the road to Jericho is brought whole to the inn, and the wounds of his sins are healed by immortality (Luke 10).

### 34. The truth of the resurrection proved by forty days. Why Christ ate after the resurrection. The error and blasphemy of Marcion. Apollonius of Tyana before Domitian

*[Col. 0385D]*

The tombs were also opened during the Lord’s Passion, when the sun fled, the earth trembled, and many bodies of the saints rose and appeared in the holy city (Matt. 27).

“Who is this,” Isaiah says, “who comes up from Edom, his garments shining from Bosor, so beautiful in his white robe?” (Isa. 63:1, according to the Septuagint). Edom is interpreted either as “earthly” or as “bloody.” Bosor means either “flesh” or “in tribulation.” In a few words he displays the whole mystery of the resurrection: both the reality of the flesh and the increase of glory.

*[Col. 0386A]*

The sense is this: Who is he who has ascended from the earth, who has ascended from blood? (Gen. 49; Isa. 63). His garments, according to the prophecy of Jacob, who tied his colt to the vine and trod the winepress alone, are red with new wine from Bosor—that is, from flesh or from the tribulation of the world (John 16), for he himself conquered the world.

Therefore his garments are red and shining, because he is “more beautiful in form than the sons of men” (Ps. 44); and, because of the glory of the triumphant one, they have been changed into a white robe. Then, truly, the following was fulfilled in Christ’s flesh: “Who is this who ascends, made white, leaning upon her kinsman?” And in the same book: “My kinsman is ruddy and white” (Song 8:5; 5:10).

*[Col. 0386B]*

Those who have not defiled their garments with women imitate him (Rev. 3); for those who castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven remained virgins. Therefore they will be in white garments.

At that time the Lord’s sentence will be shown to have been accomplished in deed: “Everything that the Father has given me I will not lose anything from it, but I will raise it up on the last day” (John 6:39)—namely, the whole human being, whom he had wholly assumed in being born.

Then the sheep that had been lost and was wandering in the lower regions will be carried whole upon the Savior’s shoulders; and she who had been weakened by sins will be supported by the judge’s mercy (Luke 15). Then they will see him whom they pierced, they who cried out, “Crucify, crucify such a man!” (John 19:6). Tribe after tribe will beat their breasts, they and their women—the women to whom the Lord spoke while carrying the cross: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children” (Luke 23:28).

*[Col. 0386C]*

Then the prophecy of the angels will be fulfilled. They spoke to the astonished Apostles: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand gazing into heaven? This Jesus who has been taken up from you into heaven will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).[^c0039-8]

*[Col. 0386D]*

What sense does it make to say that the Lord ate with the Apostles for forty days after the resurrection so that he would not be thought a phantom, and that by this very act of eating—appearing in flesh and limbs—he confirmed that he was a phantom? Either what was seen was true or it was false. If it was true, then he truly ate and truly possessed limbs. But if it was false, how did he wish to display false things in order to prove the truth of the resurrection? No one proves the truth by something false.[^c0039-9]

“Then,” you will say, “will we too eat after the resurrection?” I do not know. For it is not written. Yet, if the question is asked, I do not think we will eat. For I have read that the kingdom of God is not food and drink, while promising us things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart” (Rom. 1). Moses and Elijah fasted for forty days and nights (Isa. 65:4; Deut. 9).

*[Col. 0387A]*

Human nature cannot endure this; but what is impossible for human beings is not impossible for God (1 Kings 19). Just as, when someone foretells the future, it makes no difference whether he declares something destined to happen after ten years or after a hundred, because the knowledge of future things is one and the same, so whoever can fast and live for forty days—or rather, cannot fast but lives by the power of God—will be able to live without food and drink for all eternity.

Why did the Lord eat honeycomb? To prove the resurrection, not to allow honey to your throats. He asked for a fish roasted on the coals in order to strengthen the doubting Apostles, who did not dare approach him because they thought they were seeing a spirit and not a body (John 12).

*[Col. 0387B]*

The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is raised and receives food; Lazarus, dead for four days, rises and is brought in to dine (Mark 5; John 11)—not because he was hungry in the underworld, but because the difficulty of the deed required the scrupulousness of faith.

Just as he displayed true hands and a true side, so he truly ate with the disciples; truly walked with Cleopas; truly spoke with human beings by means of a tongue; truly reclined at the meal; truly took bread with true hands, blessed it, broke it, and handed it to them.

But the fact that he suddenly vanished from their eyes was the power of God, not the work of a shadow or phantom. Otherwise, even before the resurrection, when they had led him out of Nazareth to throw him from the brow of the mountain, he passed through their midst—that is, he escaped from their hands. Can we, in accordance with Marcion, say that his birth was therefore a phantom because, contrary to nature, he who was being held escaped? What is permitted to magicians is not permitted to the Lord?

*[Col. 0387C]*

Apollonius of Tyana is said, while standing before Domitian in the council chamber, suddenly to have disappeared. Do not compare the Lord’s power with the tricks of magicians, so that he may seem to have been what he was not, and be thought to have eaten without teeth, walked without feet, broken bread without hands, spoken without a tongue,[^c0039-10] and displayed his side without ribs.

### 35. And how, you ask, did they not recognize him on the road?

*[Col. 0387D]*

“And how,” you ask, “did they not recognize him on the road, if he possessed the same body that he had possessed before?” Hear the Scripture saying: “Their eyes were held, so that they would not recognize him” (Luke 24:16). And again: “Their eyes were opened, and they recognized him” (ibid. 31). Was he one person when he was not recognized and another when he was recognized? Certainly he was one and the same.

Therefore, recognizing and not recognizing belonged to the eyes, not to the one who was seen, although they also belonged to him insofar as he held their eyes so that they would not recognize him. Finally, so that you may know that the error present among them belonged not to the Lord’s body but to their closed eyes, Scripture says: “Their eyes were opened, and they recognized him” (John 20).

Thus Mary Magdalene, as long as she did not recognize Jesus and was seeking the living among the dead, thought he was the gardener. She recognizes him and calls him Lord.

*[Col. 0388A]*

After the resurrection Jesus stood on the shore, while the disciples were in the boat. When the others did not recognize him, the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord” (John 21:12). The former virginity recognizes the virginal body.[^c0039-11]

He was the same, yet he did not appear the same to everyone. Immediately it is added: “No one dared ask him, ‘Who are you?’ knowing that it was the Lord.” No one dared, because they knew that he was God. They ate with him as he dined because they saw a human being and flesh—not that one was God and another human being, but that one and the same Son of God was recognized as human and worshiped as God.

Clearly I must now philosophize that our senses are uncertain, especially sight, and summon some Carneades from the underworld to bring forward the truth:[^c0039-12] an oar appears broken in water; porticoes narrower at a distance; the angles of towers round from afar; and doves’ necks changing color at every turn.

When Rhoda announced Peter and told the Apostles that he had escaped because of the danger, they did not believe her and suspected a phantom (Acts 12).

*[Col. 0388B]*

But the fact that he entered through closed doors was an exercise of the same power by which he vanished from their eyes. Lynceus, as the stories tell, could see through a wall. Will the Lord, with doors closed, be unable to enter unless he was a phantom? Eagles and vultures sense carcasses across the sea. Will the Savior be unable to see his Apostles unless he opens a door?

Tell me, sharpest of disputants, what is greater: to hang the vast magnitude of the earth upon nothing and balance it upon the uncertainty of the waters,[^c0039-13] or for God to pass through a closed door, and for creation to yield to the Creator? You grant him the greater thing and malign the lesser.

*[Col. 0388C]*

Peter walks upon the waters with a heavy and solid body (John 20). The yielding wave does not give way; his faith hesitates for a moment, and immediately the body recognizes its nature, so that we may know that it was not the body but faith that walked upon the waters.

### 36. The Marcionite argument

*[Col. 0388D]*

I ask you, who use such extensive arguments against the resurrection, to speak with me plainly. Do you believe that the Lord truly rose, in the same body in which he died and in which he was buried, or do you not believe? If you believe, why do you advance arguments by which the resurrection is denied? If you do not believe, why do you thus flatter the souls of the ignorant and parade the resurrection under an empty name?[^c0039-14]

Listen. Recently someone from Marcion’s school said: “Woe to him who rises in this flesh and in these bones.” A joyful spirit immediately replied: “For we have been buried and have risen together with Christ through baptism” (Rom. 6:4). Are you speaking of the resurrection of the soul or of the flesh? I replied: Not of the soul alone, but of the flesh, which is reborn together with the soul in the washing.

*[Col. 0389A]*

And how will that perish which has been reborn in Christ? “Because,” he says, “it is written: Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (2 Cor. 15). Attend, I beg you, to what is said: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.” Does this mean that they will not rise? Far from it; it means that they will not possess it.

Why will they not possess it? Because what follows says: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” Therefore they will not possess the kingdom of God as long as they remain merely flesh and blood. But when the corruptible has put on incorruption, and the mortal has put on immortality (1 Cor. 15:53), and the clay of the flesh has been baked into pottery, that which had previously been pressed down to the earth by its heavy weight will, having received the wings of the spirit and of transformation rather than abolition,[^c0039-15] fly to heaven in a new glory.

*[Col. 0389B]*

Then what is written will be fulfilled: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting?” (Hos. 13:14; 1 Cor. 15:55).

### 37. John’s letter to Theophilus. Caesarea, metropolitan city of Palestine; Antioch, of the entire East. The presbyter Isidore

*[Col. 0389C]*

We have answered in reverse order concerning the state of souls and the resurrection of the flesh; and, omitting the beginning of the letter, our entire discussion has been directed against his distinguished treatises. For we preferred to speak about God’s affairs rather than about our own injuries.

“If a man sins against a man, they will pray for him to the Lord. But if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. 2:25). Yet now, in the opposite direction, we pursue our adversaries with hatred above all things: toward those who blaspheme God, we extend a merciful hand.

He writes an apology to Bishop Theophilus, whose beginning is as follows:

> “You, as a man of God and adorned with apostolic grace, take care of all the Churches, especially the one that is in Jerusalem, although you yourself are occupied with very many concerns for the Church of God that is under you.”

*[Col. 0389D]*

He flatters him to his face and invokes the standing of rulers.

You who seek ecclesiastical rules, who make use of the canons of the Council of Nicaea, and who strive to claim for yourself foreign clerics living with their own bishops, answer me: what does Palestine have to do with the bishop of Alexandria? If I am not mistaken, it is decreed there that Caesarea is the metropolitan city of Palestine and Antioch of the entire East.[^c0039-16]

Therefore, either you ought to have referred the matter to the bishop of Caesarea, whose communion you had rejected, though you knew that we were in communion with him; or, if judgment had to be sought from a distance, the letters ought rather to have been sent to Antioch. But I know why you did not wish to send them to Caesarea, and why not to Antioch. You knew what you were fleeing and avoiding. You preferred to trouble occupied ears rather than render the honor due to your metropolitan.

I do not say this because, apart from the friendships that generate suspicion, I find anything else to criticize in your embassy; rather, I say it because you ought to have defended yourself before those who were questioning you and in their presence.

*[Col. 0390A]*

> “You sent the most religious man of God, the presbyter Isidore, a man powerful both in the dignity of his very bearing and appearance and in divine understanding, capable even of caring for those who are seriously ill in soul—if only they recognize the nature of their illness. A man of God sends a man of God.”

There is no distinction between presbyter and bishop: the dignity of the sender and the one sent is the same. This is sufficiently inept: shipwreck, as they say, in harbor.

This Isidore, who is raised to heaven by your praises, is accused in Alexandria of the very thing of which you accuse him in Jerusalem; thus he appears to have arrived not as an envoy but as a companion.[^c0039-17]

*[Col. 0390B]*

Moreover, letters written in his own hand, bearing error, had been sent to us three months before the embassy and were delivered to the presbyter Vincent,[^c0039-18] and he still retains them to this day. In them he encourages the commander of his army to stand with a firm foot upon the rock of faith and not to be frightened by our nonsense.[^c0039-19]

He promises that, before there was any suspicion of an embassy, he would come to Jerusalem and that, upon his arrival, the entire host of his adversaries would immediately be trampled underfoot. Among other things, he uses these words:

*[Col. 0390C]*

> “As smoke is dissolved in the air and wax melts near the fire, so those who have always resisted the ecclesiastical faith, and who now attempt through simple people to disturb that same faith, will be scattered.”

### 38.

I ask you, reader: when the man who writes this is still to come, what does he seem to you to be—an adversary or an envoy?

This is the man whom we may call most pious or most religious, and, to render the word literally, θεοσεβέστατον, “most God-fearing” or “most devoted to God.” This is the man of divine understanding, so powerful and possessing such dignity of bearing and appearance that, like a spiritual Hippocrates, he might have been able to soothe the illness of our souls by his very presence, if only we had wished to submit to his medicine.

Let him heal himself with such a remedy, since he has been accustomed to heal others. To us, that divine understanding is folly for Christ’s sake. We willingly languish in our rusticity, lest we learn through your eye-salve to see impiously.

*[Col. 0390D]*

> “We beseech the Lord day and night in the holy places that your holiness, having been brought as though to its final perfection by your excellent intention, may receive from him a complete reward and be granted the crown of life.”

You give thanks appropriately—unless Isidore had come, you would not have found so faithful a companion in all Palestine. Unless he had brought you the assistance he promised, you would have remained among the crowd of rustics, who could not understand your wisdom.

*[Col. 0391A]*

This very apology of which we are now speaking was dictated in Isidore’s presence and with his extensive assistance, so that he was both their dictator and the bearer of the letters.

### 39. Count Archelaus. The prudence of Saint Epiphanius

*[Col. 0391B]*

> “When he had therefore come here, and had approached us three times, and had brought words containing the medicine both of your divine wisdom and of his own understanding, he benefited no one, and no one benefited him.”[^c0039-27]

This man, who is said to have approached us three times so that he might preserve a mystical number in his coming, and who was conveying to us the command of Bishop Theophilus, refused to deliver the letters sent to us by him.

When we said, “If you are an envoy, deliver the letters of your embassy; if you have no letters, how will you prove that you are an envoy?” he replied that he did indeed have letters for us, but that he had been adjured by the bishop of Jerusalem not to deliver them.

Behold the constancy of an envoy! In order to make peace and to exclude suspicion of partiality toward either side, he showed himself equally fair to both. And because he had come without a plaster and possessed none of the physicians’ equipment, his medicine therefore accomplished nothing.

*[Col. 0391C]*

“Jerome and those who are with him, both privately and before everyone, very frequently and with the testimony of an oath, assured him sufficiently that they had never entertained any uncertainty concerning us [variant: you] in respect to faith, saying: ‘Just as at the time when we were in communion with him, so now we have the same attitude concerning the matter of faith.’”[^c0039-20]

See what agreement in doctrines accomplishes. Isidore was his companion in communicating these things, a man of God and a most religious presbyter, θεοσεβέστατος, a powerful man, with sacred and venerable bearing and divine understanding; he is called the Hippocrates of Christians.

I, poor wretch, while hiding in the wilderness, suddenly cut off by so great a bishop, have lost the name of presbyter. And yet what did this Jerome, with his ragged crowd and filthy flocks, dare to answer that thunderbolt-like man, Isidore?[^c0039-21]

*[Col. 0391D]*

But lest he perhaps refuse to yield and crush them by his presence and the mass of his body, they swore—not once, not three times, but very frequently—that they knew the man in question to be orthodox and had never suspected him of heresy.[^c0039-22]

O manifest and shameless lie! O testimony offered on one’s own behalf, not even worthy of Cato’s belief! For “every word stands by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 27:6; Matt. 18:16; 2 Cor. 16:1).

Was it ever said to you or entrusted to you anywhere that we would enter into your communion without a satisfaction concerning the faith? When, through the most eloquent and most Christian man, Count Archelaus, who was the mediator of peace, an agreed place for the covenant had been appointed, was it not first demanded that the faith of the future agreement should lay its foundations?

*[Col. 0392A]*

He promised that he would come. The day of Easter was approaching; a large crowd of monks had gathered; you were being awaited at the appointed place; you did not know what to do. Suddenly you sent word that some woman or other was ill and that you could not come that day.

Is it a jester or a bishop who speaks this way? Grant that what you say is true: for the sake of one little woman’s indulgence, lest, in your absence, she suffer a headache, experience nausea, or become chilled in the stomach, do you neglect the cause of the Church? Do you disregard the presence of so many men—Christians and monks?[^c0039-23]

We did not wish to provide an occasion for this, for we saw through the trick of your delay; we overcame the injury by patience.

*[Col. 0392B]*

Archelaus wrote back, urging you to remain for a second and third day if you wished to come. But he was occupied: the little woman did not cease vomiting; once she had escaped her nausea, she completely forgot us.

After two months, therefore, Isidore finally came, not—as you pretend—to give testimony on your behalf, but to hear the case for which satisfaction had been demanded. When he asked us why we had been in communion with you if you were a heretic, he heard from everyone: “We were in communion with him, suspecting nothing of heresy.”

But after you were summoned by the blessed Pope Epiphanius, both by speech and by letters, and contemptuously refused to answer, Epiphanius sent letters to all the monks instructing them not to enter rashly into communion with you without satisfaction concerning the faith.

The letters are at hand, and there can be no doubt about this matter. This is what the crowd of brothers replied—not, as you argue, that you are not a heretic because you were not called one at some earlier time. By this reasoning, a person who was healthy before his illness ought not to become ill.

### 41. Paulinian’s ordination

*[Col. 0392C]*

> “When discussion began concerning the ordination of Paulinian and of the others who are with him, and, seeing themselves censured, they were being granted everything on account of charity and concord, while this one thing alone was required of them—that, although they had been ordained by others contrary to the rules, they should nevertheless be subjected to the Church of God, so that they would not divide it and make a principality of their own—when they would not consent to this, they began to raise the issue of faith and to make known to all that, if those who were with the presbyter Jerome were not accused, they found nothing to criticize in us. But if they were accused of error and fault, then, since they were entirely unable to argue about such questions and could find no satisfaction for their own error, they would resort to these matters—not because they hoped that we could be convicted, but because they were attempting to injure our reputation.”

### 41*. Paulinian was living in Cyprus. Jerome ordained by Paulinus

*[Col. 0392D]*

Let no one think that this is a fault of interpretation merely because the speech is perplexed. The Greek text is of the same character. For the moment I rejoice that, although I thought I had been beheaded, I suddenly see the head of my presbyterate restored to me.

He says that we cannot possibly be convicted, and he shudders at coming to battle. If the cause of the disagreement does not arise from a difference of faith but proceeds, as you say, from Paulinian’s ordination, what madness is it, when people wish to provide you with an opportunity, to refuse to answer?

Confess the faith; but nevertheless answer what you are asked, so that it may be clear to everyone that the dispute concerns not the faith but the ordination. For as long as you remain silent when questioned about the faith, your adversary can say to you: “The cause is not ordination, but faith.” If the cause is ordination, you act foolishly by remaining silent when questioned about the faith. If it is faith, you foolishly put forward ordination.

*[Col. 0393A]*

Furthermore, when you say that you requested that they be subjected to the Church of God and not divide it or establish a principality of their own, I do not sufficiently understand of whom you are speaking.

If you mean me and the presbyter Vincent,[^c0039-24] you have slept for a very long time, since, awakened after thirteen years, you are now saying these things. For this reason I left Antioch and he Constantinople, cities of the greatest renown—not to praise you while you were preaching among the peoples, but to weep over the sins of our youth in the fields and in solitude, and to turn Christ’s mercy toward us.

*[Col. 0393B]*

But if you are speaking of Paulinian, you see that he is subject to his own bishop, lives in Cyprus, and sometimes comes to visit us—not as your man, but as another’s, namely, the man by whom he was ordained.

And if he too wishes to remain here and live quietly in solitude in our exile, what does he owe you except the honor that we owe to all bishops? Suppose that you ordained him: you will hear from him the same thing that Bishop Paulinus of blessed memory heard from me, a wretched man:

*[Col. 0393C]*

> “Did I ask you to ordain me? If you grant the presbyterate in such a way that you do not take away from us our monastic life, you must answer for your own judgment. But if, under the name of presbyter, you take away from me that for which I abandoned the world, I still possess what I have always possessed: I have suffered no loss through the ordination.”

[^c0039-1]: He may have said this on the basis of Hebrew opinion, since the Hebrews are accustomed to exaggerate marvels. They commonly proclaim that their nails and hair did not grow during the forty years.

[^c0039-2]: The Codex of Santa Croce has “nor wives.” Immediately afterward, the old edition has *interiori* for the Greek word ἐντεριών, while our manuscript, as above, reads *enterian*, almost in agreement with Erasmus and Victorius. See Martianay’s annotation at the end.

[^c0039-3]: In your manuscript, ἐντεριών. Manuscripts read here *enterian*, *enteriore*, or *entria*. The Cluniac manuscript has: “from your seed-store and interior.” Ancient scribes changed the Greek word, which they did not understand, into a Latin form. See above what was said about Origen’s same “seed-store.” —Martian.

[^c0039-4]: The Cluniac manuscript preserves a variant reading of this kind: “And from water—that is, from the lowliness of flesh—to change precious, ethereal wines; surely the same wisdom by which he made everything from nothing…” —Martian.

[^c0039-5]: The manuscript of Santa Croce has: “precious wines of the ethereal [realm]”; *of the ether* would not be objectionable.

[^c0039-6]: The same manuscript has: “they are bound together in the limbs, run through the veins”; and immediately afterward: “and then the kind of human formation.” A little farther below, the manuscript has “and nevertheless from different beginnings,” and so forth.

[^c0039-7]: The same manuscript reads: “those who had been carried into the tombs will live, dead,” and so forth. Shortly afterward, the manuscript and several other editions read *medulla* (“marrow”) instead of *medicina* (“medicine”), but the Greek has ἴαμα (“healing” or “remedy”).

[^c0039-8]: Here and consistently below, the manuscript of Santa Croce reads *fulvida* (“shining”). In the following phrase, the manuscript lacks the word “ate”; it then reads: “either what is said is true or false,” without separately recording every scribal error.

[^c0039-9]: The manuscript lacks the word *comedisse* (“to have eaten”). It then reads: “either what is said is true or false”; the note records the omission without listing every scribal error.

[^c0039-10]: The manuscript adds: “without tongue or head, and [displayed] his side,” and so forth.

[^c0039-11]: The manuscript of Santa Croce reads: “the virginal body recognizes its fellow-virginal body,” and so forth.

[^c0039-12]: The corrected and supplemented reading from the manuscript of Santa Croce is *ut proferat verum* (“that he may bring forward the truth”). Earlier editions falsely read: “that he may bring forward an oar appearing broken in water, porticoes …” —Martian. The older editions do not contain the word *verum* (“truth”).

[^c0039-13]: The word *appendere* (“to hang”) is absent from the manuscript.

[^c0039-14]: “I beg you,” and so forth. Here too the reading was formerly corrupt: “I beg you, who, merely thinking against the resurrection, argue whether you speak with me plainly.” —Martian.

[^c0039-15]: The same manuscript reads: “with the wings of the spirit changed, not abolished.”

[^c0039-16]: This refers to Canons 6 and 7 of Nicaea, by which Caesarea is not so much established as recognized as the metropolitan city of Palestine, and this prerogative is confirmed to it.

[^c0039-17]: The old edition reads: “Moreover, let the letters also be produced.”

[^c0039-18]: It may be necessary to correct the text to *portantis errorem* (“bearing error”), but perhaps *portantes terrorem* (“bringing terror”) is more accurate, as Wastelius thinks in the *Vindiciae*.

[^c0039-19]: The same manuscript reads: “and not be frightened by our threats.”

[^c0039-20]: Wastelius reports that an older edition reads: “At that time we likewise had the same attitude.” He unsuccessfully attempts to defend this reading, since the sense is either nonexistent or plainly incongruous and contrary to Jerome’s meaning.

[^c0039-21]: The reading *fulmine* (“thunderbolt”) is found in some editions; the manuscript has *fulmineo* (“thunderbolt-like”).

[^c0039-22]: Isidore belonged to the group whose members, because of their great height, were called the “Long Brothers”: Dioscorus, Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, whose memory is well known in ecclesiastical history.

[^c0039-23]: The old edition adds: “and test the patience of the monks.”

[^c0039-24]: Presbyter Vincent, not Innocent. This is clear from what was said above and from the third book against Rufinus, where it is said that Vincent boarded a ship safely in the Roman harbor with Jerome when Jerome was returning to Jerusalem. Elsewhere, in the chronological notes, we shall explain from what time the thirteen years mentioned here are to be counted. —Martian.

[^c0039-27]: P. Wastelius maintains that *ad eos* (“to them”) should be read, although the manuscripts offer no support for it.

42. Those seeking baptism in the Church. Jerome prohibited from the Lord’s grotto.—“So that they would not divide it,” he says, “or make the principate their own.” Who divides the Church? We, whose entire household at Bethlehem shares communion in the Church? Or you, who either believe rightly but keep silent about your faith in pride, or believe wrongly and truly divide the Church?

Are we dividing the Church, who a few months ago, around the days of Pentecost, when the sun was darkened and the whole world feared that the Judge was already almost upon us, brought forty people of different ages and sexes to your priests to be baptized? Certainly there were five priests in the monastery who could, by their own right, have baptized them; but they did not wish to do anything contrary to your displeasure, lest this too give you an occasion to remain silent about the faith.

Or do you not rather divide the Church, you who instructed your priests at Bethlehem not to administer baptism at Easter to our candidates, whom we sent to Diospolis (Lydda), to Dionysius the confessor and bishop, to be baptized?

> **Note:** This is that Dionysius of Lydda, or Diospolis, whose previously unpublished Letter concerning the condemnation of the Origenists we published earlier, in volume one, under number 94.

Are we said to divide the Church, when outside our cells we have no place in the Church? Or do you not divide the Church, you who order your clergy that, if anyone calls Paulinianus—a presbyter consecrated by Bishop Epiphanius—a presbyter, he is to be prohibited from entering the Church? From that time to the present day we see only the Lord’s grotto, and, standing at a distance, we sigh while heretics enter it.

43. Are we the ones who divide the Church, or the one who denies the living a dwelling-place and the dead a tomb, who demands the exile of the brothers? Who specially stirred up that most powerful beast, threatening the necks of the whole world, against our necks?

> **Note:** I read *specialiter* with the manuscripts; this is what ought to be read instead of *spiritualiter*. Gravius likewise taught that this was required, and the sense demands it. As for that beast whom John had roused against Jerome, some wish to understand Rufinus, the guardian of Arcadius—the traitor who summoned the Gothic leader Alaric against Arcadius so that he himself might seize Arcadius’ empire; but when Alaric was repulsed, Rufinus himself was killed, in the declining year 395. Jerome himself speaks more clearly of this in his Letter 82 to Theophilus, against John: “Recently,” he says, “he demanded and obtained our exile; and would that he had been able to carry it out,” etc.—perhaps because, once Rufinus had immediately been killed, that rescript had no authority.

Who allows the bones of the saints and their innocent ashes to continue to be beaten by the rains? With such blandishments the good Shepherd invites us to peace, and accuses us of making the principate our own—although we share communion and charity with all bishops who hold the right faith. Are you alone the Church, so that whoever has offended you is excluded from Christ? If we defend our own principate, show that we have a bishop in your parish. The fact that we have not shared communion with you concerns the faith; answer us, and it will concern ordination.

44. “They also invent an occasion from other letters, which they say Epiphanius wrote to them. Although he will give an account before Christ’s tribunal for everything that was done, where the greater and the lesser will be judged without any respect for persons, nevertheless how can they rely upon that letter which he wrote after we had reproved him concerning the unlawful ordination of Paulinianus and of those who are with him, as the letter itself indicates at its beginning?”

I ask: what blindness is so great—wrapped, as they say, in Cimmerian darkness? He says that we are inventing an occasion and do not possess Epiphanius’ letters against him, and immediately adds: “How can they rely upon that letter which he wrote after we had reproved him concerning the unlawful ordination of Paulinianus and of those who are with him, as the letter itself indicates at its beginning?”

We do not possess the letter. And what is that letter which, at its beginning, speaks about Paulinianus? There is something after the beginning whose mention you are afraid to make. You were reproved by him concerning the age at which Paulinianus was. You ordain a presbyter and send him as an envoy and associate; and you have such confidence that, where you falsely claimed that Paulinianus was a boy, you send a boy there as a presbyter.

Likewise, you make Theosebas [or: Theosobius], a deacon of the Church of Tyre, a presbyter, and arm him against us, using his eloquence against us. You alone are permitted to trample upon the rights of the Church: whatever you do is the standard of doctrine. And you are not ashamed to summon Epiphanius with you to judgment before Christ’s tribunal.

What follows after this chapter is as follows: He charges Epiphanius with sharing his table and household, and writes that Epiphanius never spoke with him about the doctrines of Origen. He confirms this under oath, saying: “He did not even show himself to have, as God is my witness, any suspicion of faith hostile to us.”

I do not wish to answer and argue sharply, lest I seem to convict a bishop of perjury. Several letters of Epiphanius are available: one to the man himself, others to the Palestinian bishops, and recently one to the pontiff of the city of Rome. In them he says that he did not receive a reply from him when he accused him before many people concerning the doctrines; and the entire monastery of our littleness bears witness to this.

> **Notes:** From this conclusion of the work learned men argue that the book was not completed by Jerome.  
> See the Admonition prefixed to this book on this matter.

[Col. 0395]

## The Apology of the Holy Eusebius Hieronymus, presbyter of Stridon, against the books of Rufinus, sent to Pammachius and Marcella. (C)

> **Note:** “To Pammachius, etc.” In the manuscripts of Saint Audoenus of Rouen this defense is entitled as follows: “Here begins the Defense of Jerome, the distinguished Doctor, against the three little books of Rufinus, the slanderous and envious accuser, sent to Pammachius and Marcella.” In the previously printed books the same Apology was falsely entitled *to Marcellinus* instead of *to Marcella*. —Martianay.

## Admonition concerning the books against Rufinus

The history of the disagreement between Jerome and Rufinus is far too well known to require our explanation. The cause of so great an evil was the Latin translation of Origen’s books *On First Principles* (*Peri Archon*, περὶ Ἀρχῶν), which the presbyter of Aquileia had prepared at Rome around the year 398, with faithfulness that was certainly suspect.

For, so that he might serve the poisons of Origen’s doctrine more safely to Latin ears, covered with the disguise of deceptive interpretation, he prefixed to the work a preface in which he extolled Jerome with figurative praises, as though he were a supporter of the opinions of Adamantius [Origen] and a partner in his own judgment. He boasted that by his own labor he had purged the book itself of the errors attributed to it.

But since much still remained that disturbed Christian ears and was judged insufficiently Catholic, Pammachius and Oceanus urged Jerome himself to publish an exact interpretation of that book, without concealing its errors, so that they might openly reveal themselves; and thus to clear away the suspicion of favor toward Origen which his rival had cast upon him, lest, if he delayed to refute the accuser, he might seem to agree with him.

The holy Doctor first wrote to Rufinus, complaining as a friend. Then, in the year 400, he translated Origen’s book itself, in such a way that the heresies immediately became apparent. At the same time he sent Letter 84 in our recension to Pammachius and Oceanus, in which he completely removes the charge from himself and explains in what spirit he had once read or praised Origen without danger to piety.

From this there arose a vast conflagration in the Church. For Rufinus, compelled to write an Apology for his faith to Pope Anastasius, did not so much strive to satisfy him on his own behalf as to construct new slanders against Jerome in his own defense. Then, as the wound of hostility grew increasingly inflamed, he forged three books of invective against the holy Doctor in the following year, that is, in 401.

Jerome, who had not yet read them but had heard portions of them only from the mouths of friends, answered with these three Apologetic books. I assign them to the year 402 on the basis of two statements by Jerome himself.

The first occurs near the end of the first book, where he declares that he is writing after two years have passed since he answered Rufinus’ praises in a short book. That short book is the aforementioned Letter 84 to Pammachius, which belongs to the year 400.

The second occurs after the middle of Book II, where he says that he wrote *On Illustrious Men* nearly ten years earlier. It is established that that book appeared in 392; therefore, by this calculation, these books must be assigned to 402.

Their general content is as follows: In the first, he excuses his own translation by many arguments and refutes the charges brought against him. In the second, he attacks Rufinus’ Apology sent to Pope Anastasius. In the third, finally, he answers the letters Rufinus had sent him together with the volume of invectives.

### 2.

Now let us explain what we have done in reprinting them.

First, we have moved Rufinus’ invectives, which P. Martianay had placed continuously in the opposite column alongside Jerome’s Apology, and have attached them after Jerome’s own books. For the sentences do not answer one another in order, nor, when the rival makes an accusation in one column, is there a refutation of the charge in the other. On the contrary, one follows the impulses of his anger and engages in combat as he pleases; the other, without having read the books directed against him but having learned the accusations from common report, responds to them.

Therefore no one has failed to disapprove of Martianay’s misguided arrangement, which was devised to create labor for the reader and to interrupt the text of the holy Doctor on every page.

Second, since it is useful and convenient for students to append to an author’s writings the authentic documents that occasioned those writings or that are attacked by the author himself, we have included here, first, Rufinus’ little book—that is, his Apology or confession of faith—which he sent to Pope Anastasius and which Jerome refutes throughout Book II. Then we have also included Anastasius’ own letter concerning Rufinus’ name, which the holy Doctor repeatedly introduces, both elsewhere and especially in these books.

Previously these documents had been rejected into the volume containing foreign and spurious material. But in the ancient manuscripts, as P. Coustantius reports concerning the old Corbie manuscript, they are appended quite sensibly to Jerome’s books; and Jerome himself seemed to the learned man to have been the author of this arrangement.

Finally, we have collated almost all the treatises with the ancient editions, and one or another with the most ancient Palatine-Vatican manuscript 234; we have also frequently corrected them.

# Book One

[Col. 0397]

### 1.

[Col. 0397A] From your letters and those of many others I have learned that I am accused of having been “in the school of Tyrannus,” and that, “with the tongue of my dogs among the enemies” (Psalm 67:24), I translated Origen’s books *On First Principles* into Latin.

> **Note:** “In the school of Tyrannus.” Read this with nearly all the manuscript copies, in conformity with Acts 19:9: “disputing in the school of a certain Tyrannus.” —Martianay.  
>   
> Martianay thinks that this alludes to Acts 19:9: “disputing in the school of a certain Tyrannus.” But Jerome is properly identifying Rufinus’ homeland; among the ancients Rufinus is called Tyrannius, Toranius, or Turanius. His exposition of the Creed is entitled “To Rufinus Toranus, presbyter of the Church of Aquileia.” The place may have been called Tora or Tyra. Below, in Book III, Jerome says that it was a small town. Rufinus’ cognomen was therefore Tyrannius, as we show in the appropriate places.

What singular impudence! They accuse a physician because he has exposed poisons, so that they may defend their own “seller of drugs” (*pharmacopola*, φαρμακοπώλην), not on the ground of innocence but by sharing the crime—as though the number of sinners diminished guilt and the accusation concerned persons rather than facts.

Books are written against me and thrust upon everyone to hear; yet they are not published, so that they may strike the hearts of the simple while depriving me of the opportunity to answer on my own behalf. A new kind of malice: to accuse what you fear will be exposed; to write what you conceal. If what he writes is true, why did he fear to make it public? If false, why did he write it?

Long ago, as boys, we read: “I think it characteristic of an intemperate man to write anything he wishes to keep concealed” (Cicero, *Academic Questions*, Book I).

I ask: what is this anguish? What are they agitated about? What drives them mad? That I rejected a disguised herald? That I did not wish to be praised with a deceitful mouth? That under the name of a friend I detected the ambush of an enemy?

I am called “brother and colleague” in the little preface, and my crimes are explained plainly enough: what I wrote, and with what praises I lifted Origen to heaven. He says he acted with good intentions. How, then, does an enemy now bring against me the very things he had praised as a friend?

He had wished to follow me as a guide in his translation and to borrow authority for his work from my little writings. It would have been enough to say once what I had written. Why was it necessary to repeat the same things again and bring them forward so often—as though no one would believe a man praising himself unless he repeated his own statements?

A simple and sincere commendation is not so anxious about the faith of its hearers. What does he fear? That without testimony from my own words no one will believe him when he praises me?

Do you see that we understand his prudence, and that we have often played in the schools with the tricks of his mocking praise?

> **Note:** This is not “a commendation derived from tearing apart,” as Erasmus has it, nor “from disparagement,” as Victorius has it. Here *diasyrtic* praise is so called from its raising up of matters that are difficult to answer.

He cannot claim simplicity when he is caught practicing malice. To have erred once, or at most twice, might be accidental. But why does he err prudently and repeatedly, and cover his error throughout in such a way that I cannot deny what he praises?

It would have been the conduct of a prudent friend, after the reconciliation of a quarrel, to avoid even slight suspicions, lest what he had done accidentally should be thought deliberate. Hence Tullius, in his *Commentaries on the Cases*, in defense of Gabinius, says:

> “Although I have always thought that all friendships must be preserved with the greatest reverence and fidelity, I have thought this especially of friendships restored from enmity to harmony. For when friendships are intact, an omission of duty can be defended by the excuse of imprudence—or, if we interpret it more severely, negligence. But after reconciliation, if anything is committed, it is thought not to have been neglected but violated; nor is it usually assigned to imprudence but to treachery.”

Flaccus Horace likewise says in the *Epistle* he writes to Florus: “Badly mended, Grace joins together in vain, and is torn apart.”

### 2. Hilary, interpreter of Origen, and Ambrose and Victorinus. Rufinus’ three books.

What benefit is it to me now that he swears he simply made a mistake? Here his praises are brought against me, and the simplest of friends is charged with a commendation that was neither simple nor pure.

If he was furnishing his work with authority and wished to show whom he followed, he had Hilary the Confessor readily available, who translated nearly forty thousand lines of Origen on Job and the Psalms. He had Ambrose, whose books are almost all filled with this man’s language. He had the martyr Victorinus, who proves his own simplicity by plotting no ambush against anyone.

Of all these he says nothing. Passing over the pillars of the Church, he pursues me alone through the corners as though I were a flea and a man of no account. Unless perhaps, with the same simplicity with which he unknowingly accused his friend, he swears that he did not know those men either.

And who will believe him, a most learned man possessing such knowledge of ancient writers, especially Greek ones, that while pursuing foreign matters he has nearly lost his own—that he does not know men of recent memory and Latin writers? From this it is apparent that he praised not so much me as refrained from accusing them. Whether that praise is praise, as he tries to persuade fools, or accusation, as I feel from the pain of my wound, I would have neither the glory of my peers in the praise nor consolation in the blame.

### 3.

I have your letters, in which you write that I have been accused, and you urge me to answer my accuser, lest, if I remain silent, I seem to acknowledge the charge.

I did answer them, I admit. Although wounded, I preserved the rights of friendship in such a way that I defended myself without repeating the accuser’s accusation. What one friend had charged at Rome, I said had been spread by many enemies throughout the world, so that I might appear to answer not a man but his accusations.

It is another matter if, by the right of friendship, I ought to have remained silent when accused, and, while I have a muddy face and—as I may put it—am covered with heretical stench, ought not even to wash it away with plain water, lest he be thought to have inflicted this injury upon me.

> **Note:** Victorius reads “and his face, namely Rufinus’, made muddy” instead of *habeo*. Jerome seems to have taken the phrase from Tatian, who wrote of the philosopher Crescens that he had “a muddy face,” which was therefore unbecoming to a wise man.

This is neither the language of a man nor language addressed to a man: openly to attack a friend and expose his crimes under the guise of praise, while not even leaving him the freedom to prove himself Catholic and to answer that the praise of a heretic attributed to him arose not from agreement with heresy but from admiration for talent.

He had been pleased—or, as he wishes to appear, had been compelled—to translate into Latin what he did not want to translate. Why was it necessary to insert me, who was concealed and separated by such great expanses of sea and land, into the controversy? Why expose me to the envy of so many, so that by praising me he might harm me more than he benefited himself by his example?

Now also, because I refused to be his praiser and, with my pen turned in another direction, showed that I was not what my close associate had proclaimed me to be, he is said to have raged and to have composed three books against me with Attic elegance—accusing me of the very things he had previously praised and charging me, in my translation of Origen, with impious doctrines, although in the little preface to his praise he had said:

> “I will follow the rule of my predecessors, and especially of the man whom we mentioned above. Although he translated into Latin more than seventy of Origen’s little books, which he called homilies, and also several books from the volumes written on the Apostle, in which the Greek contains some stumbling-blocks, he so polished and cleansed everything by his interpretation that the Latin reader finds nothing in them contrary to our faith. We too, therefore, although not in eloquence, shall follow him as far as we can in the rules of method.”

### 4. The faith of the Roman Catholics.

Certainly these are his words; he cannot deny it. The elegance of the style itself, the composed speech, and—more important than these—the Christian simplicity prove the character of their author.

It is another matter if Eusebius corrupted these things, and the accuser of Origen and devoted admirer of me testified in one and the same work that both he and I had either erred or thought rightly.

An enemy cannot now call me a heretic when he previously declared that I did not depart from his faith. At the same time I ask him what he means by this restrained and ambiguous statement: “The Latin reader will find nothing in them that differs from our faith.”

What faith does he call his? Is it the faith in which the Roman Church is strong? Or is it the faith contained in Origen’s volumes? If he answers, “the Roman faith,” then we are Catholics, since we translated nothing of Origen’s error. But if Origen’s blasphemy is his faith, then, while he charges me with inconsistency, he proves himself a heretic.

If my praiser believes rightly, by his confession he takes me as his associate. If wrongly, he shows that I was previously praised because he thought me a participant in his error.

But against those books that chatter in corners and bite me through secret accusation, when they have been published and have come forth from darkness into the light, and have reached us either through the diligence of friends or the recklessness of rivals, I will try to respond.

For there is no great reason to fear books whose author is afraid to publish them and has decided that they should be read only by his confederates.

> **Note:** In the old edition: “to disclose them to his own people.”

Then I will either acknowledge the charges, dissolve them, or turn back upon the accuser the accusations brought against me. I will show that my silence until now arose from modesty, not from a bad conscience.

### 5. The author excuses himself.
