Meanwhile I wished to be cleared in the silent judgment of the reader and to refute the gravest charge among friends, lest the one who was first to inflict the wound appear to be the injured party, although I have directed no weapons against my persecutor in return; I have merely laid my hand upon my own wound.

I ask him to assign the blame, without prejudice arising from the persons involved, to the one who provoked the attack. Not content with injuring me, as though he were dealing with someone without a tongue and always destined to remain silent, he has worked out three books, and has fashioned Marcion’s *Antitheses* from my little writings.

> **Note:** “And *antitheses*.” Gravius calls the reading in this passage a prodigious error—and truly it is prodigious, because Erasmus’ fantasies, not Jerome’s text, are represented. Moreover, all the manuscript copies retain not Erasmus’ *artiōseis* but Marcion’s *antitheses*. Tertullian speaks of these in Book I *Against Marcion*: “For these are Marcion’s *antitheses*, which attempt to establish discord between the Gospel and the Law.” Then in Book IV: “The work was given the name *Antitheses* from its oppositions of contrary statements and was composed for the separation of the Law and the Gospel.” Rufinus constructed similar contrary oppositions from Jerome’s little work, so as to make the author appear inconsistent and opposed to him in the matter of Origen’s praise. —Martianay.  
>   
> *Antitheses of the Old and New Testament* is the title of Marcion’s book, which he composed by setting statements of Moses and Christ against one another. Tertullian was among the first to attack it. The reading formerly was *artiōseis*; this is erroneous.

My spirit eagerly desires to learn both his sudden doctrine and my unexpected madness. Perhaps in a short time he has learned something that he ought to teach us, and the sudden stream of his eloquence will display what no one thought he knew.

“Thus may that father make God his father; thus may great Jesus” (from Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book X). Let him begin to join battle.

Although he has poised the spears of his accusation and hurled them against us with all his strength, we believe in the Lord our Savior that his truth will surround us with a shield, and that we shall be able to sing with the Psalmist:

> “The arrows of the little ones have become their wounds” (Psalm 63:8).

And:

> “Though an army encamp against me, my heart will not fear. Though battle rise against me, in this I will hope” (Psalm 26:3–4).

But that belongs elsewhere. Now let us return to what we began.

### 6. Why did he translate Origen’s *Peri Archon* into Latin? Didymus, defender of Origen.

His followers bring charges against me and, weary from affairs, “prepare their grain-bearing weapons” (*Aeneid*, Book I): why did I translate Origen’s books *On First Principles*—harmful books opposed to the faith of the Church—into Latin?

The answer to them is brief and concise: the letters of you, brother Pammachius, and of your companions compelled me, saying that they had been fraudulently translated by another, with certain passages interpolated, added, or altered.

And lest I place little trust in your letters, you sent copies of that same translation, together with my flattering preface. When I had read them and compared them with the Greek, I immediately noticed that what Origen had impiously said about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit had been changed by the translator into a better sense—things that Roman ears could not endure.

But his other doctrines—concerning the fall of the angels, the fall of souls, the illusions of the resurrection, the world or Epicurus’ worlds between worlds, the restoration of all things to an equal condition, and much worse than these, which it would take too long to enumerate—he either translated as he had found them in the Greek, or expanded and strengthened them from the little commentaries of Didymus, who is Origen’s most open defender.

Thus one who had read a Catholic doctrine concerning the Trinity would not guard against heresy in the other matters.

### 7.

Another person, perhaps, who was not his friend, would say: either change everything that is bad, or expose everything that you consider excellent. If, for the sake of the simple, you cut away everything harmful and pretend that those things added by heretics are not to be transferred into a foreign language, then I yield: remove everything harmful.

But if you preserve the truth of the text in your translation, why do you alter some things and leave others untouched? Yet the open confession in the same Prologue is that you corrected what was wrong and left what was excellent. Consequently, you will be held responsible not with the freedom of a translator but with the authority of a writer, if anything heretical is proved in what you translated.

You will be accused of an evident crime because you wished to smear the cup of poison with honey, so that the feigned sweetness might conceal the worst venom.

An enemy would say these things, and much harsher ones, and would drag you before the judgment of the Church not as the translator of an evil work but as its supporter.

For my part, content merely to defend myself, I expressed in the books *On First Principles* exactly what was contained in the Greek—not so that the reader would believe what I was translating, but so that he would not believe what you had translated earlier.

My work had a double usefulness: it exposed the heretical author and accused the false translator. And lest anyone think that I agreed with what I translated, I fortified the necessity of translation with a preface and taught what the reader ought not to believe.

The first translation contains praise of the author; the second contains blame. The former invites the reader to believe; the latter moves him not to believe. In the former I am unwillingly taken up as a praiser; in the latter I praise the person I translate so little that I am compelled to accuse his praiser.

The same matter was not accomplished with the same intention; rather, one path had different outcomes. He removed things that were there, saying that heretics had corrupted them; and he added things that were not there, asserting that the same author had discussed them elsewhere. Unless he shows those very passages from which he claims to have translated them, he will not be able to prove this.

My concern was to alter nothing of the truth. For this reason I translated it: to convict the false translation.

> **Note:** Elsewhere: “so that what was badly translated might be convicted.”

Do you think me a translator? I was an exposer. I exposed the heretic in order to vindicate the Church from heresy.

Why I had previously praised Origen in certain matters is shown by the book that preceded this work. Now only the reason for my translation is at issue. Since that reason has the intention of piety, I ought not to be accused of impiety for exposing an impious man who was being handed over to the churches as though he were pious.

### 8. Eusebius, standard-bearer of the Arian faction.

I had translated his seventy books, as my close associate charges, into Latin, and many passages from his volumes. There had never been any controversy about my work; Rome had never been disturbed.

Why was it necessary to deliver to Latin ears what Greece detests and the world accuses? For so many years I translated so much and was never a scandal. You, previously unknown, have made yourself famous through recklessness in your first and only work.

The preface itself shows that you translated the book of the martyr Pamphilus in defense of Origen. And you do this with all your strength so that the Church will not reject one whose faith a martyr approves.

Eusebius of Caesarea, formerly the standard-bearer of the Arian faction, wrote six books in support of Origen—a very extensive and elaborate work—and proved by many testimonies that Origen was Catholic according to himself, that is, Arian according to us.

You translate the first of these books under the name of the martyr.

> **Note:** Here and below Jerome rejects Saint Pamphilus’ *Apology for Origen* as apocryphal and spurious. Yet Eusebius, in Book VI, chapter 33 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, states at the end that what it is necessary to know concerning Origen’s case may be learned “from the Apology composed by us and by Pamphilus, the holy martyr of our time, for his defense” (*ἐκ τῆς ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ πεπονημένης ἡμῖν τε καὶ τῷ καθ’ ἡμᾶς ἱερῷ μάρτυρι Παμφίλῳ ἀπολογίας*). It therefore seems false that Rufinus alone published this Apology under the martyr’s name, as the holy Doctor maintains, since the Greek manuscripts too, according to Photius, codex 118, and elsewhere, attributed it to Pamphilus. Nor is the argument valid that Eusebius wrote that Pamphilus published no work of his own. For Eusebius himself expressly testifies that Pamphilus devoted his efforts to this defense, although he did not compose the whole work alone but was assisted by another—namely Eusebius himself, who at that time was imprisoned in the same place. See Photius again, chapter 120.

And we wonder that you want me, a little man of small worth, to be a praiser of Origen, when you have slandered a martyr. Changing only a few testimonies concerning the Son of God and the Holy Spirit—things you knew would displease the Romans—you left everything else intact to the end. You did the same in the Apology attributed to Pamphilus as you did in your translation of Origen’s *On First Principles*.

If this is Pamphilus’ book, which of the six books will be the first book of Eusebius? In the volume that you pretend belongs to Pamphilus, mention is made of the following books. In the second book and in the remaining books as well, Eusebius says what he had already said in the first book and says that he ought not to repeat the same things.

If the whole work belongs to Pamphilus, why do you not translate the remaining books? If it belongs to someone else, why do you change the name? You are silent; the facts themselves speak—clearly, so that those who would have detested the leader of the Arians might believe the martyr.

### 9. The martyr Pamphilus wrote absolutely nothing.

What shall I say was your state of mind, most simple-minded friend? You were able to place the name of a martyr upon the book of a heretical man and make the uninformed defenders of Origen under the authority of Christ’s witness?

Because of the learning in which you excel, and because you are praised in the West as an illustrious *syngrapheus* (συγγραφεύς, “author” or “writer”), so that all your party call you a *coryphaeus* (κορυφαῖος, “leader”), I do not think that you were unaware of Eusebius’ *syntagma* (σύνταγμα, “compilation”) or that the martyr Pamphilus had produced no work whatsoever.

> **Note:** “And the illustrious *syngrapheus*.” Erasmus also changed the Greek word here—not because *syngrapheus* was absent from the manuscript copies, but because *syntactes* (“compiler” or “composer”) pleased him better. Reader, marvel at the editor’s fidelity: although he found the word *syngrapheus* in all the older books of Jerome, he rejected it into the scholia in order to force his own *syntactes* into the text, because it pleased him more. In what follows, for *coryphaeus*, the Cluniac manuscript reads *Coryphaeum*; other manuscripts change the Greek word into the Latin *incorruptum*, and the ancient copyists or correctors evidently did not sufficiently understand what *coryphaeus* meant. —Martianay.  
>   
> Erasmus did not read *syntactes* badly; he did not invent the word from his own imagination, since the older printed books also prefer it, although somewhat corruptly. I too prefer it. For *syntactes*, “syntactes” or “worker,” is the cognomen given to Origen, as is clear from Epiphanius at the beginning of Heresy 63: “of Origen Adamantius, who was called *Syntactes* by cognomen” (*Ὠριγένης τοῦ Ἀδαμαντίου καλουμένου τοῦ Συντάκτου*). I consider it highly probable that Jerome intended to mock his opponent with this same name.

Eusebius himself, the lover, herald, and companion of Pamphilus, wrote three very elegant books containing Pamphilus’ life. In them, while praising everything else with remarkable commendation and exalting his humility to heaven, he added this in the third book:

> “Who among those devoted to learning was not a friend of Pamphilus? If he saw anyone lacking the necessities of life, he generously supplied what he could. He also distributed the holy Scriptures readily, not merely for reading but for possession. He did this not only for men but also for women whom he saw devoted to reading. For this reason he prepared many copies, so that when necessity required, he could give them freely to those who wished them.  
>   
> “He himself wrote absolutely no work of his own, except for letters that he happened to send to friends; so far had he humbled himself. But he read the treatises of the ancient writers with the greatest devotion and was constantly engaged in meditating upon them.”

### 10. Theophilus and Anastasius called Origen a heretic

The defender of Origen and praiser of Pamphilus says that Pamphilus wrote absolutely nothing and composed no work in his own words. He says this now that Pamphilus has been crowned with martyrdom, so that, after Eusebius’s books have been published, you may have no escape by claiming that Pamphilus wrote this. What will you do? In the book that you published under the martyr’s name, the consciences of very many people have been wounded. [Col. 0404C] Among them the authority of the bishops concerning Origen’s condemnation has no force, because they believe that Origen was praised by the Martyr. What will they make of the letters of Bishop Theophilus? What of those of Pope Anastasius, who persecute the heretic throughout the world, when your book, published under Pamphilus’s name, fights against their letters and the testimony of the Martyr is set against the episcopal name? What you did in the books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*), do the same in this falsely titled volume. Listen to the advice of a friend; do not regret your own craft: either say that it is not yours, or that it was corrupted by the presbyter Eusebius. From what source could it be proved to you [Col. 0405A] that what has been translated was translated by you? Your handwriting is not in evidence; nor are you so eloquent that no one could imitate you. Or certainly, if the matter should come to proof and the testimony of many should overwhelm the shamelessness of your brow, sing a recantation in the manner of Stesichorus. It is better for you to repent of your deed than for both the martyr to persist under calumny and those who have been deceived to persist in error. Do not blush at changing your judgment: you are not of such authority or reputation that you should be ashamed to have been wrong. Imitate me, whom you love exceedingly, without whom you can neither live nor die; and cry out with me what I, praised by you, said in my own defense.

### 11. What Eusebius objected to the martyr Methodius. The minor works of Eusebius translated by Jerome

Eusebius of Caesarea, the bishop whom I mentioned above, in the sixth book of his *Apology for Origen*, makes this same objection against Bishop and Martyr Methodius that you make against me while praising me, and says: “How has Methodius dared now to write against Origen, when he said this and that concerning Origen’s doctrines?” It is not the place here to speak on behalf of the martyr; for not everything must be discussed in every place. For now, it is enough to have touched upon the fact that this was objected by an Arian to a most distinguished and eloquent martyr—the very thing that you, as a friend, praise in me and, when offended, accuse.

You have an opportunity, if you wish, to construct a calumny against me from the present passage also: why do I now disparage Eusebius, whom I praised previously in another place? The name, of course, is a different one—Eusebius [Note: For Jerome himself also had Eusebius as his first name.]; but the calumny is the same as that concerning Origen’s name.

I praised Eusebius in the *Ecclesiastical History*, in the *Chronological Summary*, and in the description of the Holy Land; and, translating these very works [Note: In translating them into Latin. Beware lest you understand Jerome here to mean that he translated Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* into Latin. For he translated only the *Chronological Canon* and the book *On Hebrew Places*, which he lists here together with the *Ecclesiastical History*. — MARTIAN. — That is, understand the *Chronological Canon* and the book *On Places*; he says merely that he praised the *Ecclesiastical History*, not that he rendered it into Latin.], I gave them to speakers of my language. Am I an Arian on that account, because Eusebius, who composed these books, was an Arian?

If you dare to call me a heretic, remember the preface to *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, in which you testify that I am faithful to your faith; and at the same time I beg you patiently to listen to a former friend who is making a complaint. You fight with others, either making a calumny or enduring one. Those whom you accuse and by whom you are accused belong to your own rank: whether rightly or wrongly, you yourselves must see to it. I dislike even a true accusation against a brother; I do not rebuke others, but say what I myself would not do.

Separated from you by such great distances of land, what have I done against you? What have I deserved? Is it because I answered that I am not an Origenist? Is my defense an accusation of you? And if you are not an Origenist, or were not one, I believe you when you swear it; if you were, I welcome you as one who repents. Why are you distressed if I am what you say that you are? Is it because I dared to translate Origen’s books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* after you, and my translation is thought to be a disparagement of your work? What could I do? Your praise of me was sent to me—that is, my accusation. You had praised me so boldly and at such length that, if I had acquiesced in your praise, everyone would have thought me a heretic.

See what the conclusion of the Roman letter addressed to me contains: “Clear away people’s suspicions and refute the accuser, lest, if you remain silent, you appear to consent” (*Letter of Pammachius and Oceanus*). Bound by such a necessity, when I was about to translate the same books, listen to what I wrote:

“My friends have imposed this upon me—I did not say ‘my friend,’ lest I seem to accuse you—so that, if I remain silent, I am judged guilty; but if I answer, an enemy. Both conditions are harsh, but of the two I shall choose the lighter. Hostility can be restored to friendship; blasphemy deserves no pardon” (*Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus*).

You see that this burden was imposed upon me against my will and resistance, and that the hostility arising from such a work was dealt with by an appeal to necessity. If you had translated the books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* without my name, you would rightly complain that I had later translated them in order to criticize you. But now you grieve unjustly that I answered you in a work in which I was accused by your praise. For what you call praise, everyone understands as accusation. Let it be clear to you that you accused me; and do not be indignant that I answered.

Suppose that you wrote with a good intention, as an innocent man and a most faithful friend, from whose mouth no lie ever proceeded, and that, without knowing it, you wounded me: what does that matter to me, who have been struck? Must I therefore not be healed because you wounded me with a good intention? I lie pierced through; the wound hisses in my breast; my limbs, previously white, are disfigured by blood; and you say to me, “Do not apply your hand to the wound, lest I seem to have wounded you.”

Moreover, the translation itself accuses Origen more than it accuses you. You corrected what you thought had been added by heretics. I exposed what all Greece proclaims to have been written by him. Which of us has judged more correctly is not for my judgment or yours to decide. Let the writings of both of us undergo the reader’s censorial stroke.

That entire letter in which I defend myself is directed against heretics and my accusers. What is it to you, who say that you are both orthodox and my praiser, if I am harsher toward heretics and bring their public tricks to light? Rejoice in my attack; otherwise, if you grieve, you may appear to be a heretic. When one writes against vices without naming anyone, the person who becomes angry is his own accuser. It would have been the part of a prudent man, even if he was distressed, to conceal his conscience and dispel the cloudiness of his heart by serenity of face.

### 12. The letters of Theophilus and Epiphanius, and the writings of the emperors against Origen

Otherwise, if you think that whatever is said against Origen and his followers is said against you, then the letters of Pope Theophilus [Note: See these letters, first published by us, in the preceding volume, no. 92 and following.] and Epiphanius, and of the other bishops, which I recently translated at their own command, attack you and tear you apart. The writings of the emperors ordering that the Origenists be driven from Alexandria and Egypt were also dictated at my suggestion. That the pontiff of the Roman city should detest them with such extraordinary hatred was my counsel. That the whole world should blaze with hatred of Origen after your translation, although previously it read him innocently, was accomplished by my pen.

If I have such power, I wonder why you do not fear me. I was that moderate man in the public letter (*Letter 81 to Rufinus*) who carefully took precautions lest you think that anything was said against you. I immediately wrote you a brief letter, complaining about your praises. Since you were not in Rome, my friends refused to send it to you, saying that you were boasting among your companions about my way of life in a manner unworthy of the Christian name [Note: The old edition reads: “because they were distressed that you, together with your companions, …”]. I have appended a copy of it to this volume, so that you may know how great a grief I restrained with such moderation of affection.

### 13. Jerome’s Jewish teacher. Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome’s teacher. The Jew Huillus. The untitled Psalms

I also hear that you criticize certain things in my letter in a philosophical fashion, and that you, a man of wrinkled brow and drawn-down eyebrow, play upon me with Plautine wit because I said that the Jew Bar-Anina was my teacher. It is no wonder that, where there is some similarity of words, you wrote “Barrabas” for “Bar-Anina,” since you have such license in changing names that you have made Pamphilus from Eusebius and a martyr from a heretic.

A dangerous man—and one whom I especially must avoid—lest, while I am unaware, you suddenly call me, instead of Jerome, Sardanapalus. Listen, then, summit of wisdom and standard of Cato-like severity. I did not call that man my teacher; I wished to demonstrate my zeal for the Holy Scriptures, so that I might show that I had read Origen in the same way in which I had heard him. [Col. 0407C] For I was not obliged to learn Hebrew letters from you. [Note: “The same thing—or an insult to you,” and so forth. A little later, where he speaks of Nazianzenus, the reading was formerly: “who among Latins is his equal,” as though someone had thought that he knew Latin to some degree, although Nazianzenus himself denies that he knows that language in Letter 71 to Posthumianus.]

Was it an insult to you that, in preference to you, I followed Apollinarius and Didymus? Could I not in that letter have named Gregory, a man of the greatest eloquence? [Note: “Who among Latins is his equal?” This passage, badly printed in Erasmus and Marianus, has exercised the ingenuity of scholars. They, together with some manuscript copies, read: “Could I not in that letter have named Gregory, a man of the greatest eloquence, who has no equal among Latins, in whose instruction I glory and rejoice?” From this corruptly printed passage many thought that Gregory knew Latin, but not as well as Greek; hence he was considered “unequal to himself among Latins.” We have restored Jerome’s genuine reading on the authority of the very ancient Corbie manuscript and another manuscript of no inferior quality from the Sorbonne. The Corbie manuscript is marked 147 in our Library of Saint-Germain; the Sorbonne manuscript has number 642 on its title page. — MARTIAN.]

Who among Latins is his equal? In him as my teacher I glory and rejoice. But I mentioned only those who were being criticized, so that I might testify that I had read Origen not because of the truth of his faith but because of his learning.

Origen himself, Clement, Eusebius, and many others, whenever they discuss something from the Scriptures and wish to establish what they say, commonly write: “A Hebrew told me”; “I heard from a Hebrew”; “This is the opinion of the Hebrews.” Certainly Origen also names the patriarch Huillus [Note: Some think that “Hillel” should be read instead of “Huillus.” Origen certainly calls this Jewish patriarch Ἰοῦλλος, “Jullus,” and says that he learned from another learned Jew who lived at the same time as Huillus, or Hiullus. Jerome may have attributed to Huillus what the other Jew had taught in Huillus’s presence and with his approval. As for his being called a patriarch, although no such person is mentioned among the patriarchs of Tiberias, he may perhaps have been patriarch of some lesser Sanhedrin, for example, of Diocaesarea. Concerning his name, whose Hebrew spelling is omitted or uncertain in the source, see the Jerusalem Gemara, tractate *Megillah*, chapter 1, and tractate *Horayot*, chapter 3. See also Origen’s first previously unpublished work in Montfaucon, volume I of the *Hexapla*.], who lived in his time. At the end of his thirtieth book on Isaiah, in which he explains “Woe to you, city Ariel, which David captured,” he concludes with Huillus’s interpretation; and although he says that he had previously thought otherwise, he admits that, having been taught by him, he now holds what is more truthful.

He also thinks that the eighty-ninth Psalm, which is written, “A prayer of Moses, the man of God,” and the other eleven Psalms that have no titles, belong to the same Moses according to Huillus’s interpretation; nor does he disdain, as he interprets the Hebrew Scripture passage by passage, to insert what seems correct to the Hebrews.

### 14. Origen condemned

After recently reading the letters of Pope Theophilus, in which he sets out Origen’s errors, he is said to have stopped his ears, condemned the author of such great evil in a loud voice before everyone [Col. 0408B: *coram* in some copies], and said that until that time he had not known that Origen had written anything so impious.

I do not refuse this, nor do I say what someone else might perhaps say: that he could not have been ignorant of what he translated, since he published an *Apology* for Origen, written by a heretic under the name of a martyr, and even professed his defense in a work of his own. Against this, if I have room to dictate, I shall argue in what follows. I say this about something which he cannot contradict.

If he was permitted not to have understood what he translated, why am I not permitted to have been ignorant of the books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, which I had not previously read, and to have read only those Homilies that I translated, in which his own testimony says that there was nothing evil? But if he now accuses me in these matters contrary to his own former judgment, he will be trapped on every side. Either he praised me as a heretical man because he shared the same doctrine with me, or he now falsely accuses as an enemy the man whom he previously proclaimed orthodox. But perhaps at that time, as a friend, he concealed my errors, and now, being angry, brings forward what he had previously hidden.

### 15. He defends his Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians

Although inconsistency deserves no credence and avowed hostility gives grounds for suspicion of falsehood, I shall nevertheless advance boldly, wishing to know what I have written that is heretical, so that either I may repent with him and swear that I was ignorant of Origen’s errors, having learned his impieties for the first time now from Pope Theophilus [Note: This is how it appears in the synodical letter, number 2: “We stopped our ears and condemned both Origen and his disciples with one accord,” and so forth], or else I may show that I indeed thought correctly, but that he, following his usual practice, does not understand.

For it cannot happen that in the same books on the Epistle to the Ephesians, which, as I hear, he condemns, I spoke both rightly and wrongly, and that from the same source there proceeded both sweetness and bitterness. I could not have condemned throughout the work those who believe that souls were created from angels, and then, suddenly forgetting myself, defend what I had previously condemned.

He cannot charge me with stupidity, since he proclaimed me to be most articulate and eloquent in his own works. Otherwise, such foolish verbosity must be considered the mark of a litigious declaimer and chatterer rather than of an eloquent man.

I do not know what, specifically, he accuses in the books. For reports of his accusations, not his writings, have reached me; and, according to the Apostle, it is foolish to beat the air with one’s fists. Nevertheless, I shall answer on uncertain ground [Col. 0409B] until I reach what is certain:

“I shall teach my *ἀντίζηλος* when I am old what I learned as a boy: that there are many kinds of expression; and that, according to the character of the subject, not only the meanings but also the words of the Scriptures vary.” [Note: “I shall teach my *antizelos*.” From this passage, which is not very difficult, I wish the diligent reader to understand how much confidence and learning belong to the ancient editors of Jerome: they were unable even by conjecture to recover *ἀντίζηλον*, which we have restored with the agreement of all the manuscripts. Thus Marianus Victorius restored the present passage and illustrated it in his notes: “I shall teach my *antipalon* as an old man what I learned as a boy.” This word signifies an adversary, that is, *ἐναντίον καὶ ἐχθρόν* (“an opponent and enemy”); and the sense is exactly the same if *ἀντίμαχον* is read. But the proposal that either *ὁμογέροντα* or *ἀθηνογέροντα* could be read is an Erasmian dream. Apart from the fact that this reading makes no sense, in all the printed and manuscript copies that we have seen we find either *ἀντίπαλον* or *ἀντίμαχον*. Thus far Marianus. To him I reply that no manuscript copy now survives among us which retains either *antipalon* or *antimachon*, but that all our manuscript books preserve the pure word *antizelon*, or unmistakably report it in the traces of the Greek letters. Jerome’s *antizelos*, meaning “rival” or “jealous competitor,” was Rufinus, as his invective and calumnies can prove even to fools. Compare Leviticus 18:18: “You shall not take a wife in addition to her sister, as a rival (*ἀντίζηλον*).” See the Septuagint. — MARTIAN. — Victorius says that he found *ἀντίπαλον* in his copies, or *ἀντίμαχον*, both of which mean “adversary”; at the same time he censures Erasmus, who thought that *ὁμογέροντα* or *ἀθηνογέροντα* could be read. Martianaeus restored *ἀντίζηλον* from his manuscripts.]

[Note: “But also the words of the Scriptures.” In several manuscripts we read, “but also the words of constructions are corrupted.” — MARTIAN. — Martianaeus testifies that several manuscripts read, “but also the words of constructions.” I would prefer, “but also the words vary in meaning,” and so forth.]

### 16. What sort of work Commentaries contain. Donatus, Jerome’s teacher

Chrysippus and Antipater move among thorns. Demosthenes and Aeschines hurl thunderbolts against one another. Lysias and Isocrates flow sweetly. There is wonderful diversity in each, but all are perfect in their own kind.

Read Cicero’s books *To Herennius*; read his *Rhetorical Works*. Or, since he says that those earlier efforts slipped from his hands unfinished and crude, turn over the three volumes *On the Orator*, in which he introduces the most eloquent orators of that period, Crassus and Antonius, disputing; and the fourth, *The Orator*, which he wrote to Brutus when already an old man. Then you will understand that History is composed in one way, Speeches in another, Dialogues in another, Letters in another, and Commentaries in another.

In my Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians I followed Origen, Didymus, and Apollinarius in such a way—although they certainly hold doctrines contrary to one another—that I did not surrender the truth of my faith.

What kind of work do Commentaries contain? They explain the statements of another person and make obscure things clear in plain language. They repeat the opinions of many and say: “Some explain this passage in this way; others interpret it in that way. Those people try to establish their meaning and understanding by these testimonies and by this reasoning.” Thus the prudent reader, after reading various explanations and learning what in the opinions of many should be approved or rejected, may judge what is more truthful, and, like a good money-changer, reject counterfeit currency. [Note: The old edition reads “of a different interpretation.”]

Is someone who has set down in a single work the explanations of many to be held guilty because of different interpretations and mutually contrary meanings? I suppose that, as a boy, you read Asper’s Commentaries on Virgil and Sallust, Vulcatius’s on Cicero’s speeches, Victorinus’s on his Dialogues and on Terence’s Comedies, and equally those of my teacher Donatus on Virgil [Col. 0410B], as well as those of others on other authors: Plautus, Lucretius, Flaccus, Persius, and Lucan. Accuse their interpreters: why did they not follow one explanation alone? Why did they enumerate what seemed correct either to themselves or to others concerning the same matter?

### 17. The faults of Rufinus’s language

I pass over the Greeks, whose knowledge you boast of, and in pursuing foreign things have almost forgotten your own language, lest I seem, according to the old proverb, to have a pig teach Minerva, or to carry wood into a forest. I am surprised that you, the Aristarchus of our time, did not know these childish matters. [Note: “Gamium,” that is, a grammarian and critic of great reputation; yet these roles certainly fit Rufinus less well than Jerome himself.]

Although, absorbed in meanings [Note: “And for constructing.” One old manuscript, together with the printed editions, reads *ad struendam mihi calumniam cernuus*. *Cernuus*, or *cernulus*, means a slanderer, one bent down and turned toward constructing a calumny. — MARTIAN.], and bent down to construct a calumny against me [Note: So Martianaeus. Other printed editions, supported by some manuscripts, have *cernuus*. See whether *cervulus* can be read, referring to an animal (*ὀξυδερκές*) of sharp or exceptionally keen sight, and comparing Rufinus to it because he sees sharply in order to construct a calumny. Pacianus of Barcelona is said to have titled one of his books *Cerus*, or *Cerulus*, a name which seemed to mean the same as “calumniator”; hence *cerulum facere*, “to slander.” See our notes on the relevant passage in the catalogues.], you have despised the precepts of grammarians and orators, you care little about restoring *ὑπέρβατα* after winding constructions, avoiding harsh combinations of consonants, and fleeing gaping diction.

It is ridiculous, when the whole body is weak and broken, to point out only a few wounds. I do not choose what I should criticize; let him choose something that is free from fault.

He ought not even to have known that Socratic maxim, “I know what I do not know”:

> The man ignorant of steering a ship is afraid to command it;  
> no one but one who has learned dares give wormwood to the sick. What belongs to physicians,  
> physicians promise and undertake; smiths handle smiths’ work.  
> Learned and unlearned alike compose poems everywhere.  
> *(Horace, Epistle I to Augustus)*

Unless perhaps he will swear that he has not learned letters; and we readily believe this of him even without an oath. Or he will flee to the Apostle, who confesses: “Even if I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not in knowledge” (1 Corinthians 11:6).

That man, learned in Hebrew letters and educated at the feet of Gamaliel, whom he does not blush to call his teacher even after attaining apostolic dignity, either despised Greek eloquence or, in humility, concealed his command of it, so that his preaching might rest not on persuasive words but on the power of signs. He rejected another’s wealth, being rich in his own. Yet even to an unskilled man who collapsed with every sentence, Festus would never have said before the tribunal: “You are mad, Paul; you are mad. Your many letters are driving you to madness” (Acts 26:24).

You, who mumble in Latin and move with a tortoise’s gait rather than walk, ought either to write in Greek, so that among people ignorant of the Greek language you may appear to know a foreign language, or, if you attempt Latin, first listen to a grammarian, withdraw your hand from the schoolmaster’s rod, and, as an *ἀθηνογέρων* among little boys, learn the art of speaking. [Note: “Little *athenogerontes*. *Ἀθηνογέρων* means an old schoolboy who begins to devote himself to literature in old age. The compound is formed from *Ἀθήνη*, Minerva, who was thought to preside over studies, and *γέρων*, old man. — MARTIAN. — At the beginning of the third book he says: “Nor do I attempt to teach my *athenogeron* letters with the schoolmaster’s strap and blows.” The Greek name denotes an elderly pupil.]

Though one may breathe Croesuses and Dariuses, letters do not follow the purse. They are companions of sweat and toil; partners of fasts, not of satiety; of self-restraint, not of luxury. Demosthenes is said to have spent more oil than wine and to have outstripped all craftsmen by his continual nightly vigils.

What he did in expressing a single letter, so that he might learn the letter rho from a dog, you criticize in me: why, as one human being from another, I learned Hebrew letters. That is why certain people remain uneducated wise men, because they refuse to learn what they do not know. Nor do they heed Horace’s warning:

> Why, when I cannot and do not know, am I called a poet?  
> Why should I be perversely ashamed not to know,  
> when I prefer to learn?

[Note: “Why should I be prudently ashamed not to know?” Marianus, with the manuscript copies, reads: “Why should I prudently be ashamed not to know, when I prefer to learn?” Erasmus reads: “Why should I prudently be ashamed not to know?” In Horace, *The Art of Poetry*, addressed to the Pisones:

> “Why, if I cannot and do not know, am I called a poet?  
> Why should I be perversely ashamed not to know, when I prefer to learn?”

— MARTIAN.]

Wisdom also speaks, as we read under Solomon’s name: “Wisdom will never enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sins. For the holy spirit of instruction will flee deceit and withdraw from foolish thoughts” (Wisdom 1:4–5).

It is another matter if, content with the reading of the common people, they despise the ears of the learned and scorn that saying by which insolent ignorance is marked:

> … Did you not, ignorant man,  
> once in the crossroads destroy  
> your wretched song with a shrill reed?

As though the crowd of curled-haired boys should not chant the Milesian fictions in the schools, and shake their limbs with the *Testament of the Sow* to the laughter of the Bessi, and such trifles be common amid the banquets of buffoons. [Note: “As though the crowd of curly-haired boys …” We have spoken above, in the Letters, about curly-haired boys. Persius refers to the same people in Satire 1:

> “Nor the curly-haired troop of the morning teacher.”

— MARTIAN. — He means boys with elaborate hair, in keeping with the very common saying:

> “Do you count for nothing the dictated lessons of a hundred curly-haired boys?”

Up to this point, *Milesiorum* had wrongly prevailed instead of *Milesiarum*. The ancients used *Milesiae* as a feminine noun, not a neuter one; they called poems and stories of a lascivious, or even old-womanish, fanciful, and amorous kind by this name. See Plutarch, *Crassus*, on Surena; Lucian, *Dialogues*, “Loves”; and others. See also the *Testament of the Sow* in Brissonius, *On Legal Formulas*, book VII.]

Every day a counterfeit soothsayer in the streets beats the buttocks of fools [Note: Martianaeus reads “noses.” See what we said above, book II of *Against Jovinianus*, no. 36.], and with a twisted scorpion shakes the teeth of those who bite; and we wonder if the books of ignorant people find readers?

### 18. They are indignant that I wrote that the Origenists are bound together in orgies of lies

I named the book in which I read this written—that is, the sixth *Stromateis* of Origen. In it, while adapting Plato’s opinion to our doctrine, he speaks as follows:

Plato, in the third book of *The Republic*: “Truth must also be pursued with the greatest zeal. For if, as we rightly said a little earlier, a lie is dishonorable and useless to God but sometimes useful to human beings, so that they may use it as a condiment and medicine, no one can doubt that such permission ought to be granted to physicians and removed from the imprudent. You speak truly, he says. Therefore the rulers of cities, if this is permitted to others as well, ought sometimes to lie, either against enemies or for the sake of their country and fellow citizens. But from others, who do not know how to use falsehood, every lie must be removed.”

Origenes: “Therefore, remembering that command, ‘Speak truth, each one with his neighbor’ (Ephesians 4:25), we must not ask, ‘Who is my neighbor?’ but consider how cautiously the philosopher spoke: that a lie is dishonorable and useless to God, but sometimes useful to human beings; and that God must not be thought to lie even for the sake of a dispensation.

“But if the advantage of the hearer demands it, he speaks in ambiguous words and presents what he wishes through riddles, so that the dignity of truth may be preserved with him, and what could have been harmful if presented nakedly to the common people may be brought forth covered with a kind of veil. [Note: Compare what he says in book I, chapter 2, of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*: “Useful dissimulation,” and so forth. Also compare Clement of Alexandria, book VII, p. 730. Cassian, chapter 17: “That the saints used lies pardonably, as though they were hellebore.”]

“But a person upon whom the necessity of lying falls must carefully attend to using a lie occasionally as a condiment and medicine, preserving its measure and not exceeding the limits used by Judith against Holofernes, whom she overcame by the prudent dissimulation of her words. Let him imitate Esther, who, after remaining silent for a long time, corrected the sentence of Artaxerxes by revealing the truth about her people. And above all, let him imitate the patriarch Jacob, whom we read to have obtained his father’s blessings by a cunning lie. From this it is clear that unless we lie in such a way that some great good is thereby sought for us, we must be judged enemies of him who said, ‘I am the truth’ (John 14:6).”

We cannot deny that Origen wrote this. He wrote it in books in which he addressed the perfect and his disciples. He teaches that teachers should lie, but that disciples ought not to lie. Therefore, the person who lies well and without any shame invents whatever comes into his mouth against his brothers, and proves himself an excellent teacher.

### 19. He defends his interpretation of Psalm 2. Kissing as an expression of veneration among the Hebrews

He is also said to criticize the fact that, when interpreting the second Psalm, I wrote in my little Commentaries, instead of what we read in Latin—“Take hold of discipline”—and what is written in the Hebrew book, *NESCU BAR*, “Worship the son.” [Note: See volume I, in the general Preface, what we said about these little Commentaries.]

Again, when translating the entire Psalter into the Roman form of expression, I supposedly placed “Worship purely,” as though I had forgotten my earlier explanation, although it is obvious to everyone that this contradicts the former wording.

And truly, one must pardon him if he is ignorant of the truth of the Hebrew language, since he sometimes stumbles even in Latin. *NESCU* [Note: Martianaeus reads the passage awkwardly in this way: “he stumbles, so that I interpret *Nescu* word for word,” and so forth. A little below, the words “and idols” are absent from some copies; we have placed the passage in parentheses and corrected the defect caused by punctuation. For notable examples of this manner of worship, see 1 Kings 19 and Ecclesiasticus 29. What Jerome adds about those who worship submitting their heads is explained by a passage in Lampridius concerning Alexander. He was greeted with the name “Hail, Alexander.” If anyone bowed his head or said anything too flattering, he was rejected, since Alexander had forbidden people to worship him. Pliny, book 28, chapter 2: “In worshipping, we bring the right hand to the mouth and turn the whole body around,” and so forth.]

To interpret the word literally, *καταφιλήσατε*, that is, “kiss,” is what it says. But because I did not wish to translate this literally in an inelegant fashion, I followed the meaning more closely and said “worship.” For those who worship commonly kiss the hand and bow the head—something that blessed Job denies having done with the elements and idols, saying:

> “If I saw the sun when it shone,  
> and the moon moving brightly,  
> and my heart rejoiced in secret,  
> and I kissed my hand with my mouth—  
> this would be the greatest iniquity  
> and a denial against the Most High God”  
> (Job 31:26–27).

And since the Hebrews, according to the character of their language, use “kissing” for veneration, I translated what they themselves understand, since the word belongs to them.

But *BAR* has various meanings among them. It means “son,” as in *Barjona*, “son of a dove”; *Bartholomew*, “son of Tholomaeus”; *Bartimaeus”; *Barhiesu”; and *Barrabas*. It also means “wheat,” “a bundle of ears,” “chosen,” and “pure.” What, then, have I done wrong if I translated an ambiguous word in different ways? And when, in the little Commentaries, where there is freedom to discuss, I had said “worship the son,” why, in the body of the work, so as not to seem a violent translator and to give occasion for Jewish calumny, did I say “worship purely,” or “worship in a choice manner,” as Aquila and Symmachus also translated it?

What harm, then, does it do to the faith of the Church if the reader is taught in how many ways a single verse is explained among the Hebrews?

### 20. Origen’s errors

Your Origen is permitted to discuss *μετεμψύχωσις*—the transmigration of souls—to introduce innumerable worlds, to clothe rational creatures in one body after another, and to say that Christ suffered often and will suffer still more often, so that what, once assumed, benefited may always benefit. You also assume such great authority for yourself that you make a martyr out of a heretic and falsely claim that Origen’s books are adulterations by heretics. But am I not permitted to discuss words and, in a Commentary, teach Latins what I learned from the Hebrews?

If it were not lengthy and redolent of self-glory, I would now show you the usefulness of wearing out the thresholds of teachers and learning an art from its practitioners; and you would see what a great forest of ambiguous names and words exists among the Hebrews. This produced the material for differing interpretations: while each person, amid uncertainties, translates what seems to him more consistent [Col. 0414B: *more suitable*].

Why should I send you to foreign examples? Turn over Aristotle, and Alexander’s volumes explaining Aristotle; from reading them you will learn how abundant ambiguities are, so that at last you may stop criticizing your friend for something that you have never learned, not even in a dream.

## 21. Commentary on Ephesians

Since my brother Paulinianus reported that certain things in the Commentary on Ephesians had been criticized by him, handed down a few of them from memory, and showed me the passages themselves, I ought not evade the matter. I ask the reader to pardon me if, in presenting and refuting the accusations, I become somewhat lengthy, as necessity requires. **477** For I am not accusing another; I am striving to defend myself and refute the charge of heresy brought against me. [Col. 0414C]

Origen wrote three volumes on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians. Didymus and Apollinarius likewise composed works of their own. What I wrote in the Prologue to that same work, whether translating or imitating them, I shall set out here:

> “I also give this warning in the Preface, so that you may know that Origen composed three volumes on this Epistle, and that we too have followed him in part; Apollinarius also and Didymus published certain brief Commentaries. From these we have selected a few passages, and have added or removed some things that seemed appropriate to us, so that the diligent reader may recognize immediately at the beginning whether this work is another’s or our own” (Prologue to the Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians).

Whatever fault, therefore, may be demonstrated in the explanation of this Epistle, if I cannot show it in the Greek volumes from which I said I translated it into Latin, I shall acknowledge the charge, and whatever was not another’s will be mine. Yet, lest I again seem to quibble and, by this device of excuse, shrink from engaging the issue, I shall set out the very testimonies that are being brought as accusations. [Col. 0414D]

## 22. The commentator’s duty. The date of composition of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians [Col. 0415A]

In the very first volume, we interpreted Paul’s statement, “Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him” (Ephesians 1:4), in such a way that we did not, following Origen, say that the chosen were those who had previously existed; rather, we referred the matter to God’s foreknowledge. Accordingly, we said:

> “The fact that he testified that he chose us to be holy and blameless before him—that is, before God—before the creation of the world pertains to the foreknowledge of God, for whom all future things are already accomplished and all things are known before they come to be. Thus Paul himself is predestined in his mother’s womb; and Jeremiah is sanctified, chosen, and strengthened in the womb, and is sent to the Gentiles as a Prophet in the type of Christ.” [Col. 0415B]

Certainly there is no accusation in this exposition; although Origen says the contrary, we followed the ecclesiastical understanding. And because it is the commentator’s duty to set forth the opinions of many—and I had promised in the Preface that I would do so—I also included Origen’s explanation, without prejudice arising from his name, saying:

> “Another, however, who strives to demonstrate that God is just, in that he chooses each person not through a prejudgment arising from his knowledge but on the basis of the merits of the elect, says that before the visible creatures—heaven, earth, the seas, and all that is in them—there were other invisible creatures, among them souls which, for reasons known to God alone, had been cast down into this valley of tears, into the place of our affliction and exile, in which the saint, established there, prayed that he might return to his former station, saying: ‘Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar [one Cistercian manuscript: “with the dwellings”], my soul has long been an exile’ (Psalm 119:5). [Col. 0415C] And the Apostle says: ‘Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?’ (Romans 7:24); and, ‘It is better to depart and be with Christ’ (Philippians 1:23); and elsewhere, ‘Before I was humbled, I sinned’ (Psalm 118:67),”

and other similar passages, which it would take too long to write out.

Observe what I said: “Another, however, who strives to demonstrate that God is just”—I say, strives to demonstrate; I did not say that he demonstrates it. If you are scandalized because I compressed Origen’s very extensive discussion into a brief statement and disclosed his meaning to the reader, and if you therefore seem to yourself to have found in me a hidden follower of his because I omitted nothing that he said, consider whether I did this to avoid your calumny: lest you say that I had concealed what he had argued with force, and that he had argued more powerfully in Greek. [Col. 0415D]

I therefore included everything that I found in the Greek, though more briefly, so that his disciples would have nothing new to thrust upon Latin ears. We more easily despise what is familiar than what is sudden. After setting out his interpretation, listen to what we said at the end of the chapter:

> “For the Apostle does not say, ‘He chose us before the foundation of the world, when we were holy and blameless,’ but, ‘He chose us so that we might be holy and blameless’—that is, we who previously were not holy and blameless, so that afterward we might become so. The same may be said of sinners who are converted to better things; and the statement will stand: ‘No living person will be justified in your sight’ (Psalm 142:2)—that is, throughout his life, during all the time he has lived in this world [in the Commentary: “spent”]. This, properly understood, also stands against him who says that souls were chosen before the world was made because of their holiness, and that they had no defect of sin.” [Col. 0416A]

For, as we have already said, Paul and those like him are not chosen because they were holy and blameless; they are chosen and predestined so that in the life that follows they may become holy and blameless through works and virtues. And after such a statement, does anyone dare accuse us of Origen’s heresy?

Eighteen years, more or less, have passed since I dictated these books [editorial note: we have shown in the Life of the holy Father, at the appropriate place, that this number cannot possibly stand], at the time when Origen’s name was flourishing throughout the world, while his work *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) was still unknown to Latin ears. Yet I openly declared my faith and showed what displeased me. Even if an enemy could have pointed out something heretical in the other matters, I would have been held guilty not so much of the perverse doctrines that I have often condemned here and in other books as of an incautious error. [Col. 0416B]

## 23. The faith of the Church

The second passage that my brother showed me had been criticized by him is so frivolous and so plainly displays its own calumny that I shall set it out briefly. In the passage where Paul says, “Having seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come” (Ephesians 1:20–21), after a many-sided exposition, when I had reached the duties of God’s ministers and was speaking of principalities, authorities, powers, and dominions, I added this: [Col. 0416C]

> “They must necessarily have subjects who fear them, serve them, and are strengthened by their power. These distributions of duties will exist not only in the present age but also in the future age, so that through their several advances and honors, ascents and descents, someone may either increase or diminish, and may come to be under one or another authority, power, principality, and dominion.” [Col. 0416D; see our notes from the Commentary on this passage.]

And after giving the example of an earthly king, and describing the whole palace through which I was illustrating the various offices of God’s ministers, I added:

> “Do we suppose that God, Lord of lords and King of kings, is content with only a single ministry?”

Just as one is not called an archangel unless he is the chief of the angels, so principalities, authorities, and dominions are not so called unless they have subjects of some kind and ranks beneath them. **480** But if he thinks that I follow Origen for this reason—that I included advances and honors, ascents and descents, increases and diminutions in my exposition—he should understand that there is a great difference between saying that angels, seraphim, and cherubim become demons and human beings, as Origen asserts, and saying that the angels themselves have been assigned different kinds of ministerial duties, which is not contrary to the Church. [Col. 0417A]

Just as among human beings the order of ranks differs according to the diversity of labor—since a bishop, a presbyter, and every ecclesiastical rank have their own order, while all remain human beings—so among angels there may be different merits while all nevertheless continue in angelic dignity. Human beings do not become angels, nor are human beings again transformed into angels.

## 24. He discreetly omitted the names of the commentators

The third passage criticized is the one in which, when the Apostle says, “That he might show in the ages to come the abundant riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus,” we set out a threefold exposition. In the first, we stated what seemed to us; in the second, what Origen proposed in opposition; in the third, what Apollinarius explained straightforwardly. [Col. 0417B]

If I did not give their names, pardon my discretion. I ought not to attack those whom I partly imitated and whose opinions I was transferring into the Latin language.

“But,” I said, “the diligent reader will immediately inquire and say so.” And again, at the end: “Another, however, transfers what he says—‘that he might show in the ages to come the abundant riches of his grace’—to that understanding.” [Col. 0417D; elsewhere and in the Commentary: “will transfer.”]

“There,” you will say, “under the guise of the diligent reader, you explained Origen’s opinions.” I confess my error: I ought not to have said “diligent,” but “blasphemous.” Had I done so, and had I known by some prophecy that you would pursue such nonsense, I would even have avoided the language of calumny. [Col. 0417C]

What a great crime it is that I called Origen a diligent reader, when I translated seventy of his books, praised him to the skies, and two years ago was compelled to respond in a short book to your praises of him (the Letter to Pammachius, written two years earlier). [Col. 0417D]

**Editorial note:** Rufinus does not, in fact, accuse Jerome of calling Origen a diligent reader, but of holding, on this passage of Paul, that demons would return to heaven after the final judgment and would share the same will as Jesus Christ. You object in your praises that I called Origen a teacher of the churches, and you think I ought to fear being accused by an enemy because I called him a diligent reader. We customarily call extremely frugal merchants, thrifty slaves, troublesome tutors, and very clever thieves “diligent.”

**481** In the Gospel, too, the dishonest steward is said to have acted prudently in certain matters (Luke 16), and it is said: “The children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16:8). Also: “The serpent was wiser than all the beasts which the Lord God had made upon the earth” (Genesis 3:1).

## 25. What is the body of death?

The fourth passage criticized occupies the beginning of the second book. There we explained Paul’s statement: “For this reason I, Paul, am a prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles” (Ephesians 3:1). Since the passage itself is clear, I shall set out only that part of the explanation which is exposed to calumny:

> “That Paul was a prisoner of Christ Jesus for the Gentiles may also be understood of martyrdom: having been thrown into chains at Rome, he sent this Epistle at the time when we have shown that the letters to Philemon, the Colossians, and the Philippians were written elsewhere. Or certainly, since it is read in many places that the body is called the soul’s bond, by which it is held as though enclosed in a prison, we say that Paul was therefore restrained by the bonds of the body and did not return to be with Christ, so that the preaching entrusted to him for the Gentiles might be completed—although some introduce another meaning in this passage, namely, that Paul, predestined and sanctified from his mother’s womb for the preaching of the Gentiles, received the bonds of the flesh after his birth” [in the Commentary: “let them introduce in this passage, that …].” [Col. 0418A]

Here too I set out a threefold exposition, as above: first, what seemed to me; second, what Origen maintained; third, what Apollinarius, proceeding against Origen’s doctrines, thought. Read the Greek Commentaries; unless you find it so there, I shall acknowledge the charge. [Col. 0418B]

What is my sin in this passage? Clearly the same for which I answered above: why did I not name those from whom the statements came? It was superfluous to give, at each of the Apostle’s testimonies, the names of those whose brief works I had announced in the Preface that I would translate.

Yet it is not an absurd interpretation to say that the soul is bound by the body until it returns to Christ and, in the glory of the resurrection, changes the corruptible and mortal body into one incorruptible and immortal. Hence the Apostle also says: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” He calls it the body of death because it is subject to vices, diseases, disturbances, and death, until it rises with Christ in glory, and the fragile clay that was formerly ours is fired by the heat of the Holy Spirit into the most solid pottery, changing its glory but not its nature. [Col. 0418C]

## 26. The fifth passage

The fifth passage is the strongest. In explaining the Apostle’s statement, “From whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, makes the body grow for its own edification in love” (Book II, chapter 4), we compressed into a brief statement Origen’s very extensive exposition, which repeated the same ideas in different words, taking away none of his examples or assertions. **482**

When we reached the end, we added the following:

> “Therefore, also, at the restoration of all things, when Christ Jesus, the true physician, comes to heal the body of the whole Church, now dispersed and torn apart, each person will receive his own place according to the measure of faith and knowledge of the Son of God—he is said to recognize him for this reason, because he previously knew him and afterward ceased to know him—and will begin to be what he had been. Yet this will not be according to the other heresy, that all should be placed at one age, that is, that all should be transformed into angels; rather, each member will be perfect according to its own measure and office [editorial note: we have supplied *placed* (*positi*), a word found in the Commentary and confirmed by the following reconsideration of the passage]. For example, the fallen angel will begin to be what he was created to be, and the human being who had been expelled from paradise will be restored again to the cultivation of paradise,” [Col. 0418D]

and so forth.

## 27. Two heresies

I am astonished that you, so prudent a man, did not understand the method of my exposition.

> “For when I say, ‘Yet this will not be according to another heresy, that all should be placed at one age, that is, that all should be transformed into angels,’ I show both that the matters under discussion are heretical and that they differ from another heresy.”

What, then, are the two heresies? One says that all rational creatures will be transformed into angels. The other asserts that, at the restoration of the world, each thing will become what it was created to be. For example, since demons come from angels, demons will again become angels; and the souls of human beings, as they were created, will be restored not into angels but into that for which they were created by God, so that the just and sinners alike may become equal. [Col. 0419A]

Finally, so that you may know that I was not explaining my own opinion but comparing heresies with one another—both of which I had read in Greek—I concluded my discussion with these words:

> “Therefore, as we said above, these matters are more obscure to us because they are expressed metaphorically (*μεταφορικῶς*) in Greek; and every metaphor, when it is transferred literally from one language into another, chokes the meaning and growth of the discourse with certain thorns, as it were.”

Unless you find these same things in the Greek, consider whatever has been said to be mine. **483**

## 28. The sixth and final passage

The sixth passage, which is said to be the last that he brings against me—if, indeed, my brother has forgotten nothing in between—concerns my interpretation of the Apostle’s statement, “He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church” (Ephesians 5:28–29). [Col. 0419C]

After a simple exposition, I set out Origen’s question, speaking in his person without naming him:

> “It may be objected to us that the statement of the Apostle is not true: ‘No one has ever hated his own flesh,’ since those suffering from jaundice, consumption, cancer, and catarrh prefer death to life and hate their own bodies.”

Immediately I added what I myself thought:

> “The statement should therefore be referred more properly to a figurative understanding.”

When I say “figurative,” I show that what is said is not literally true but is veiled in an allegorical obscurity.

Let us nevertheless set out the very words contained in the third book of Origen:

> “Let us say that the soul loves and nourishes and cherishes that flesh which is destined to see the salvation of God, instructing it through disciplines, fattening it with heavenly bread, and watering it with the blood of Christ, so that, restored and cleansed, it may be able to follow its husband on a free course and not be weighed down by any burden of weakness [in the Commentary: “and by no weakness or weight be burdened”]. It is also beautifully in keeping with the likeness of Christ, who nourishes and cherishes the Church and says to Jerusalem, ‘How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling’ (Matthew 23:37), that souls also cherish their bodies, so that this corruptible body may put on incorruption and, suspended by the lightness of wings, may be more easily lifted into the air (1 Corinthians 15). Let us therefore, as husbands, cherish our wives, and let our souls cherish our bodies [the Commentary supplies: ‘let them cherish’], so that wives may be changed into husbands and bodies into souls, and there may be no distinction of the sexes whatever. But just as among the angels there is neither male nor female, so let us also, who are to be like the angels, begin already to be what has been promised to us in heaven.” [Col. 0419D–0420A]

## 29. The simple exposition

Above, we expressed what seemed to us to be contained in this testimony, saying:

> “So far as the simple sense is concerned, we are now commanded, by the precept of holy love between husband and wife, to nourish and cherish our spouses—that is, to provide them with food, clothing, and whatever is necessary.” [Col. 0420B]

This is our opinion. Therefore, everything that follows, and that may be brought against us, we showed must be understood as coming not from our own person but from the person of those who offer the objection.

Although this is a brief and complete answer, and although, in accordance with what we said above, their argument has been distorted by allegorical shadows from what exists toward what did not exist, I shall nevertheless approach more closely and ask what displeases you in this discussion.

It is presumably because I said that souls, as husbands, should cherish their bodies as their wives, so that this corruptible body may put on incorruption and, suspended by the lightness of wings, may be more easily lifted into the air. When I say, “Let this corruptible body put on incorruption,” I do not change the nature of bodies but increase their glory. Likewise, when what follows says that, suspended by the lightness of wings, it may be more easily lifted into the air, the one who assumes wings—that is, immortality—so that he may fly more lightly toward heaven does not cease to be what he had been. [Col. 0420C]

“But,” you will say, “what follows troubles me:

> ‘Let us therefore, as husbands, cherish our wives, and our souls cherish our bodies, so that wives may be changed into husbands and bodies into souls, and there may be no distinction of the sexes whatever; but just as among the angels there is neither male nor female, so let us also, who are to be like the angels, begin already on earth to be what has been promised to us in heaven.’” [Col. 0420D]

They would rightly trouble me if I had not said earlier, “Let us already begin to be what has been promised to us in heaven.” When I say that we should begin here on earth, I do not abolish the nature of the sexes; I abolish lust and sexual intercourse between husband and wife, as the Apostle says: “The time is short; henceforth let those who have wives live as though they had none” (1 Corinthians 7:29).

And when the Lord was asked in the Gospel which of seven brothers would have the woman as his wife in the resurrection, he said: “You are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 22:29–30).

Indeed, where chastity exists between man and woman, neither the male begins to be male nor the female female; but while they still dwell in the body, they are changed into angels, among whom there is neither male nor female. **485** The same Apostle says elsewhere:

> “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:27–28). [Col. 0421A]

## 30. Rufinus’s false accusations. Rufinus had learned Greek without a teacher. He had translated Gregory of Nazianzus

Since the discussion has now sailed away from the rough and difficult passages, and we have rejected the charge of heresy with complete frankness [manuscripts: “repelled”], let us pass to the other parts of his accusation, by which he strives to attack us. [Col. 0421B]

The first of these is that I am a slanderous man, a detractor of everyone, and that I have always sunk my teeth into my predecessors. Let him name a single person whose work I have attacked in my writings, or whom I have struck with figurative praise according to his own method.

But if I speak against the envious, and if the point of my style pierces Luscius Lavinius, or Asinius Pollio of the family of the Cornelii, and if I remove from my company a man of a theatrical and envious disposition and direct all my missiles against a single trunk, why does he distribute his wounds among many? Why does he reveal, through his impatience to answer, that he is the one being attacked? [Col. 0421C]

**Editorial note:** Victorius prefers *infringere*, both because of the nature of genuine teeth, which break food, and because of the verse of Persius, to which Jerome seems to allude:

> “Lucilius cut up the City:
>
> ‘You, Lupus; you, Mutius; and he broke his tooth on them.’”

**Editorial note:** “And Luscius,” etc. Seneca, in the *Declamations*, teaches that Luscius Lavinius was a rival of Terence, and Asinius Pollio a rival of Cicero; Rufinus and another monk, who boasted of descent from the Cornelii, imitated those rivals. Compare this with the Commentary on Jonah, where the gourd is discussed. —Martianus.

**Editorial note:** Lanuvinus is also frequently used by Jerome, although in Donatus it is Lavinius; the two are the same. In Letter 112 to Augustine, written many years earlier, the gourd came into discussion, when the Cornelius and Asinius Pollio of that period asserted that I had translated *hedera* as “gourd.” See, if there is room, Jonah, chapter 4. Seneca mentions Lucius Lavinius, Terence’s rival, in the *Declamations*, as well as Asinius Pollio, Cicero’s rival. Is our Rufinus, then, or Rufinus’s associates—and especially the monk who boasted that he was of the family of the Cornelii—being attacked by these names? [Col. 0421D]

He accuses me of perjury mixed with sacrilege because, in the book in which I speak for the instruction of Christ’s virgin (Letter 22, to Eustochium), I promised, while sleeping before the tribunal of the Judge, that I would never again devote myself to secular literature, and nevertheless sometimes recalled the learning I had condemned.

[Editorial note: All manuscripts consistently preserve *histriculae*. Marianus, following Erasmus, altered this reading; Rufinus’s mind was theatrical and envious, and Jerome removed him from his friendship. The printed editions read *histricosae*, a sense that fits poorly. —Martianus: Victorius preferred the reading *histricosae*.]

Clearly this is that Sallustian Calpurnius who, through the great orator Magnus, had raised a not very great question for us, to which we gave a brief answer. [Col. 0422A]

**Editorial note:** “This is the Sallustian.” Below, in the Letter to Magnus: “But through you a question is put to me by another, who perhaps, because of his love of Sallust’s histories, is Calpurnius by name, Lanaerius.” See Cicero, *On Duties* III, and *Against Piso*. —Martianus.

**Editorial note:** See what we noted at the end of the Letter to Magnus concerning this Sallustian Calpurnius.

Now I must answer the charge of sacrilege and perjury concerning the dream. I said that henceforth I would not read secular literature; the promise concerns the future, not the obliteration of memories of the past.

**Editorial note:** The old edition reads: “A pledge concerning the future was made,” not concerning the past.

“And how,” you ask, “can you keep your promise if you reread nothing for so long?” If I answer anything about the ancient books, and say, “It is of great importance to become accustomed to something in one’s tender years” (Virgil, *Georgics* 2), then, while I deny the charge, I incur it, and by producing testimony in my defense I am accused by the very means by which I defend myself. **486**

Surely I must now weave a long discourse about what each person’s conscience confirms. Who among us does not remember his infancy? I certainly do, so as to make you, so severe a man, laugh and perhaps imitate Crassus, of whom Lucilius says that he laughed only once in his life. [See Letter 7, note 4.]

I remember running about the little cells of the household slaves as a boy, spending a holiday in games, and being dragged captive from my grandmother’s lap to the fierce Orbilius. [Col. 0422B]

**Editorial note:** “And to Orbilius.” Suetonius discusses Orbilius the grammarian in *On Illustrious Grammarians*; Horace, *Epistle* 1 to Augustus; and Martial, Book II of the *Epigrams*, 12. Jerome figuratively means his teacher by the celebrated name of the pedagogue. See Horace, Suetonius, and others concerning Orbilius. —Martianus.

And, to make you wonder still more, now that I am gray-haired and bald, I often seem in dreams to be a boy with flowing hair, putting on my toga and declaiming a little controversy before a rhetorician. When I awaken, I congratulate myself on having escaped the danger of public speaking.

**Editorial note:** “And against Piso.” See Cicero, Book III of *On Duties*, and *Against Piso*.

Believe me, much of infancy is remembered in its purity. If you had learned literature, the vessel of your little mind would still smell of whatever had once saturated it. No waters wash the purple dye from wool. Even asses and dumb animals, though traveling a long road, recognize the familiar turning points.

Do you wonder that I have not forgotten Latin literature, when you learned Greek without a teacher? Dialectic taught me the elementary forms of the seven modes of conclusion; what *axioma* (*ἀξίωμα*) means—a statement, as we may call it; how no proposition can be formed without a verb and a noun; the stages of the sorites; the subtleties of the *pseudomenon*; and the tricks of sophisms. [Col. 0422C]

**Editorial note:** “The subtleties of the *pseudomenon*.” See Cicero, *Academic Questions*, Book IV, and Book II of *On Divination*, where Cicero calls the *pseudomenon* by the Latin term *acervalis*.

**Editorial note:** Martianus is mistaken in stating that Cicero calls *pseudomenon* *acervalis* in Latin. In Book II of *On Divination*, §4, Cicero calls *pseudomenon* “the liar”; he calls the sorites *acervalis*, correctly, as is clear.

I can swear that after I left school I never read any of these things at all. I would therefore have to drink from the waters of Lethe, according to the poets’ fables, lest I be accused of knowing what I had learned. [Col. 0422D]

Now you, who accuse me of having little learning and consider yourself a minor literary man and a rabbi, answer this: why did you dare to write anything, and to translate a most eloquent man, Gregory, with equal splendor of expression? Whence came to you such abundance of words, such brilliance of thought, such variety in translation, when in adolescence you scarcely tasted rhetoric with your first lips? **487**

Either I am mistaken, or you secretly read Cicero. That is why you are so eloquent, and why you bring against me the charge of reading him: so that you alone among ecclesiastical writers may glory in the flood of eloquence.

You may appear rather to follow the philosophers—the thorns of Cleanthes and the twisted arguments of Chrysippus—not through an art you do not know but through the greatness of your intellect. And since the Stoics claim logic for themselves while you despise the ravings of that discipline, in this respect you are an Epicurean: you do not ask how you should speak, but what you should say.

What does it matter to you if someone else does not understand what you mean, since you speak not to everyone but to your own people? Finally, when I reread your writings, although at times I do not understand what you are saying and think that I am reading Heraclitus, I do not grieve or regret my slowness.
