**Editorial note:** The ancients describe Heraclitus as the most obscure of all philosophers. Lucretius calls him famous because of his obscure language. Hence he was also surnamed *σκοτεινός* (“the obscure”). See what we noted in *Against Jovinian*, Book I.

In reading, I experience precisely what you experience in writing.

## 31. He defends the dream. The renown of the holy places and the gathering there from the whole world. Why Rufinus attacked Jerome

I would say this if I had promised something while awake. But now, in a new form of shamelessness, he brings my dream as an accusation.

Would that the renown of this place and the gatherings here of holy people from the whole world allowed me to read the divine Scriptures! I have no time to meditate on foreign matters. Yet let the man who accuses a dream hear the voices of the Prophets: dreams are not to be trusted, because neither does a dream of adultery lead me to Tartarus, nor does a martyr’s crown lift me to heaven. [Col. 0423C]

How often have I seen myself dead and placed in a tomb! How often have I flown over the earth and crossed mountains and seas by swimming through the air? Let him therefore compel me either not to be alive or to have wings along my sides, since my mind has often been deceived by wandering images.

How many people are rich in dreams and suddenly become beggars with their eyes open? The thirsty drink rivers, and when they awaken their dry throats burn.

You demand from me an oath concerning a dream; I shall bring a truer and stricter charge against you. Have you fulfilled everything you promised at baptism? Have both of us fulfilled whatever the name “monk” demands? Take care, I beg you, lest through your own beam you see my splinter.

I speak unwillingly, and pain compels my reluctant tongue to utter words. The things you invent against me while I am awake are not enough for you unless you also accuse my dreams. You have such curiosity about my actions that you investigate what I did or said while asleep.

I pass over the fact that, by speaking against me, you have disfigured your own purpose—what you have done in word and deed to the disgrace of all Christians. **488**

This one thing I declare and, repeating it again and again, warn you: you are attacking a horned beast. If I were not restrained by the Apostle’s words, “The slanderous shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10), and, “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15), you would already feel that, from a small and deceptive harmony, a great discord had arisen in the world. [Col. 0424A]

What benefit is it to you to heap curses against us before people both known and unknown? Is it because we are not Origenists and do not know that we sinned in heaven, that we are accused as sinners on earth? And did we therefore return to harmony so that I would not be permitted to speak against heretics, lest, if I described them, you think yourself the target?

As long as I did not reject your praise, you followed me as a teacher, called me brother and colleague, and acknowledged me as Catholic in all things. After I did not accept your praises and judged myself unworthy of the commendation of so great a man, you immediately turned your style against me and began to condemn everything you had previously praised, uttering both sweetness and bitterness from the same mouth.

Do you sense what I am keeping silent about, because I will not lend words to an agitated heart? With the Psalmist I shall say:

> “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and keep watch over the door of my lips. Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness” (Psalm 140:3).

And elsewhere:

> “When the sinner stood against me, I was silent and humbled myself, and kept silent even from good things” (Psalm 38:1–2).

And again:

> “I became like a man who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth” (Psalm 37:12).

But the Lord, my avenger, will answer you for me. Through the Prophet he says:

> “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19).

And elsewhere:

> “You sat and spoke against your brother, and you placed a stumbling block against the son of your mother. You did these things, and I was silent. You thought, wicked man, that I would be like you; I shall rebuke you and set you before your own face” (Psalm 50:20 and following), [Col. 0424C]

so that you may see in yourself the things condemned which you falsely accuse in others.

## 32. Chrysogonus, a follower of Rufinus

Moreover, I hear that Chrysogonus, a follower of Rufinus, objects to me: why did I say that in baptism all sins are forgiven, and that, when a man married twice has died, a new man rises in Christ; and that there are some such priests in the Churches? I shall answer him briefly: they have the booklet [the *Letter to Oceanus*] which they bring forward as a charge. Let him answer it, overturn it by his own discussion, and refute writings with writings. Why does he weigh hollow words with a stern expression, contracted and wrinkled nostrils, and counterfeit holiness before the ignoble crowd by a pretended severity?

Let him hear us again proclaiming that the old Adam dies wholly in the laver, and that the new Adam is raised with Christ in baptism; that the earthly being perishes and the heavenly being is born. We say this, not because we ourselves, by Christ’s favor, are bound by this question, but because our brothers asked what we thought, and we replied, prejudging no one, so that each might follow what he wished, nor overturning by our opinion another’s decree.  
[Note: Perhaps this was the decree of Pope Siricius, as we note in the aforementioned letter to Oceanus. Or rather, that of Innocent.]

For we do not seek the priesthood, since we lie hidden in our cells; nor, with humility condemned, do we hasten to purchase the episcopate with gold; nor do we desire, with a rebellious mind, to stab the pontiff chosen by God; nor, by favoring heretics, do we teach that we are heretics. We neither have money nor wish to have it: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content” (1 Tim. 6:3). We continually chant that saying about the one who ascends the Lord’s mountain: “He has not lent his money at interest, nor accepted gifts against the innocent. Whoever does these things shall not be moved forever” (Ps. 14:5–6).  
[Note: This refers to the beginning of the Psalm, “Who shall ascend the Lord’s mountain?”]

Therefore, whoever does not do these things has already fallen forever.

# BOOK TWO

## 1. He wishes to defend himself, not accuse others

Thus far I have answered, with restrained grief [variant: effort], not as I ought but as I could, concerning—indeed, on behalf of—my own alleged crimes, which my former deceitful praiser thrust upon me and which his disciples accuse more insistently. My purpose is not so much to accuse others as to defend myself.

I shall come to his *Apology*, by which he attempts to satisfy the holy Anastasius, bishop of the city of Rome, and again constructs a slander against me in his own defense.

[Note: We append this below, after the third book.] He loves me so greatly that, carried away by the whirlwind and plunged into the depths, he seizes my particular foot—  
[Note: That is, as Victorius observes, he grasps the foot of a swimmer at the same time, so that he may not be submerged.]  
—so that either he may be saved with me or perish with me.

## 2. Rufinus’ *Apology*. In ordinary speech, “parents” meant relatives and relations by marriage

He says that he is first answering the rumors by which the reputation of that most excellent man is being attacked at Rome, a man most approved both in faith and in the love of God. And, unless after thirty years he had been restored to his parents, he would not have wished to abandon those whom he had seen only after so long a time, lest he be thought inhuman or harsh, or, weakened by the hardship of so long a journey, be too feeble to undertake repeated exertions. Since he did not do this, he says that he sent against his barking detractors a staff of letters, which he would hold in his right hand and use to drive away the dogs raging against him.

If he has been approved by everyone, and especially by the very bishop to whom he writes, in faith and the love of God—  
[Note: An old edition has “most approved.”]  
—how is he being bitten and attacked at Rome, and how is the reputation of his sought-after standing growing?

Next, what humility is it to call himself approved in faith and the love of God, when the Apostles ask, “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke 17:5), and hear, “If you have faith like a mustard seed” (ibid., 6)? And to Peter himself it is said, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31).

What shall I say about love, which is greater than both faith and hope, and which Paul desires rather than presumes upon; without which even blood poured out in martyrdom and a body handed over to the flames receive no crown of rewards? He claims both of these for himself in such a way that he nevertheless has detractors against him—who, unless they are driven back by the staff of the renowned pontiff, do not cease barking.  
[Note: The same old edition reads, “unless they are struck down by the pontiff”; Victorius has “unconquered.”]

But it is ridiculous that he boasts of having returned to his parents after thirty years—a man who has neither father nor mother—and that, having abandoned them alive as a young man, he desires them dead in old age. Unless perhaps by “parents” he means relatives and relations by marriage, according to military and ordinary speech:  
[Note: Elsewhere Rufinus, in *Ecclesiastical History* 5.24, translating a fragment from Polycrates’ letter into Latin, renders the Greek word συγγενεῖς (*syngeneis*) by “parents,” meaning relatives or kinsmen. Eutropius likewise, in book 1, chapter 7, calls Brutus “the parent” of Tarquinius; and Jordanes, chapter 17, calls the Goths and Gepids “parents.”]  
those whom, because he does not wish to abandon them lest he be thought inhuman or harsh, he therefore does not abandon his homeland but lives at Aquileia.

That most highly approved faith of his is in danger at Rome, while this lethargic and weary man cannot come by carriage, after thirty years, along the very gentle road of the Flaminian Way. Thus he pleads the weariness of a long journey, as though he had been running for thirty years without interruption, or as though, sitting at Aquileia for two years, he had been exhausted by the exertion of the journey already completed.

## 3. Rufinus’ words

“Let us take up the remainder and set down the very words of his letter:

‘Although, therefore, our faith was proved, during the time of the persecution of the heretics, when we were living in the holy Alexandrian Church, in prisons and exiles, by the sufferings inflicted on behalf of the faith—’”

[Note: In the Corbie manuscript, preserved by P. Constantius, the reading is “which were inflicted in the faith.”]

I am amazed that he did not add: “A prisoner of Jesus Christ, and delivered from the mouth of the lion; I fought with beasts at Alexandria; I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; henceforth the crown of righteousness awaits me.”

What exiles and what prisons does he name? I am ashamed of such blatant lying, as though prisons and exiles were imposed without judicial sentences.

[Note: I can scarcely believe—or perhaps not at all—that Rufinus lied so shamelessly on his own behalf. From Socrates, book 4, chapter 22, however, it can clearly be inferred that he suffered grievous things during the persecution of the Arians. Yet he himself could not, I think, have produced the records and judicial sentences by which punishments were imposed upon him, since during that persecution everything was done without legal procedure, at the arbitrary will of factious men. Others free Rufinus from the charge of lying by understanding him to mean not his own person, but the faith itself that he describes as having been proved by the prisons and exiles of so many martyrs who died for that same orthodox faith.]

Nevertheless, I want him to identify the very prisons and the provinces whose exiles he claims to have endured. Surely, from the many prisons and countless exiles available to him, he can name at least one. Let him produce the records of his confession, which until now we have not known, so that we may recount his deeds among the other martyrs of Alexandria, and so that he may say against his barking detractors: “From now on let no one trouble me, for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:17).

## 4. The question concerning Christ’s soul

[Note: Elsewhere: “Yet even now, if anyone exists…”]

“Yet even now, if there is anyone who wishes either to test our faith, or to hear it, or to learn it, let him know that concerning the Trinity we believe thus,” and so forth.

Above, you offer the bishop a staff against your dogs, with which he may proceed armed on your behalf. Now, as though uncertain, you say, “If there is anyone who wishes to test our faith.” Once again you hesitate, although the barking of many has reached your ears.

I shall not for the moment examine your expressions, which you yourself despise and disregard; I shall answer only the substance. You are asked about one matter and give an answer about another. You had already fought against the doctrines of Arius at Alexandria, in prisons and exiles—not with your voice but with your blood. Now you are accused concerning Origen’s heresy.

Do not concern yourself with healing wounds that are healthy. You say that the Trinity is of one Godhead. Since the whole world now believes this, I suppose that even the demons confess that the Son of God was born of the Virgin Mary and assumed human flesh and a human soul.

If I ask something more precise, you will call me contentious. If you say that the Son of God assumed flesh and soul belonging to human nature, I beg you to answer without irritation: did this soul which Jesus assumed exist before he was born of Mary? Or was it created together with the body in the virginal conception that was born of the Holy Spirit? Or, once the body had been formed in the womb, was it immediately made and sent down from heaven? Of these three possibilities, I wish to know what you think.

If it existed before he was born of Mary, then the soul of Jesus did not yet exist, and it was doing something; afterward, because of the merit of its virtues, it became his soul. If it began from transmission, then the condition of human souls—which we acknowledge to be eternal—and that of irrational animals, which dissolve together with the body, is one and the same. But if it is created and sent immediately when the body is formed, admit this plainly and free us from our scruple.

## 5.

You say none of these things. Occupied with other matters, you take advantage of our simplicity and, by tricks and a display of words, do not allow us to remain with the question.

“What?” you will say. “Was the question not about the resurrection of the flesh and the punishments of the devil?”

I admit it [variant: Admit it]. Therefore answer briefly and clearly. I am not asking about what you write—that the same flesh in which we live will rise, with no limb amputated and no part of the body cut away; for these are your words. Rather, I ask what Origen denies: whether bodies will be raised in the same sex in which they died—Mary as Mary, John as John—or whether, with the sexes mixed and confused, there will be neither male nor female, but both or neither.

And will those bodies themselves remain incorruptible and immortal, and—as you cleverly announce in advance—spiritual forever, according to the Apostle? And not merely bodies, but flesh and blood, poured through the veins and irrigating the bones, which Thomas touched? Or will they gradually be dissolved into nothingness and be drawn back to the four elements from which they were composed?

You ought either to have stated or denied these things, rather than saying what Origen slyly professes, as though mocking fools and children: “with no limb amputated and no part of the body cut away.” Indeed, this was what we feared: that we might rise without noses and ears, and that, with our genitals amputated and cut away, a city of eunuchs might be established in the heavenly Jerusalem.

## 6.

Moreover, concerning the devil he moderates his position as follows:

“We also say that there will be a judgment, in which each person will receive his own bodily condition, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. But if human beings are to receive what corresponds to their works, how much more the devil, who exists as the cause of sin for all? Concerning him we hold what is written in the Gospel (Matt. 25): that the devil himself, and all his angels, together with those who do his works—that is, those who accuse their brothers—will likewise obtain the inheritance of eternal fire.

[Note: A certain Coislin manuscript reads “fathers” for “brothers”; the latter reading is clearly required by Jerome’s criticism.] Therefore, if anyone denies that the devil is to be consigned to eternal fires, let him receive a portion of eternal fire with him, so that he may experience what he denied.”

[Note: Elsewhere the reading is “to be handed over.”]

Let us repeat each point. “‘We say,’ he says, ‘that there will be a judgment; in which judgment,’” and so forth.

I had resolved to remain silent about defects of wording; but since his disciples marvel at the eloquence of their teacher, I shall touch briefly upon a few matters. He had said that there would be a future judgment; but this cautious man feared simply saying “in which,” and inserted “in which judgment,” lest, if he did not repeat the word “judgment” a second time, we, having forgotten what came before, should take “ass” for “judgment.”

The statement he adds afterward—“those who accuse their brothers will likewise obtain the inheritance of eternal fire”—has the same elegance. For who has ever heard of possessing fires or enjoying punishments? But this Greek seems to me to have wished to interpret himself and, instead of the expression used among them, κληρονομήσουσιν (*klēronomēsousin*), which can be rendered in our language by the single word “they will inherit,” to have said, in a more elaborate and ornate fashion, “they will obtain the inheritance.”

His entire discourse bristles with such trifles and improprieties of expression. But let us return to the meaning.

## 7. Rufinus’ words ridiculed. Eternal fire according to Origen

The devil is struck by a mighty spear: he who exists as the cause of sin for all, if he is to render an account for his works like a human being and is to obtain the inheritance of eternal fire with his angels. This was the only thing lacking: that, while human beings were subjected to torment, he should possess the eternal fires which he had desired for so long.

[Note: An old edition, with a negative particle, reads: “that he should not possess.”]

[Note: There are learned men who defend Rufinus from this unfavorable interpretation. In truth, we do not free from guilt even the one who became the cause of another’s sin by suggestion, since we do not deprive the person who obeyed him of freedom of choice.]

And you seem to me to slander the devil in this passage and to accuse the accuser of all by false accusations. For you say, “who exists as the cause of sin for all.” By referring crimes to him, you free human beings from guilt and remove freedom of choice, although the Savior says that from our heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, and blasphemies (Matt. 15:19).

Again, concerning Judas we read in the Gospel: “After the morsel, Satan entered into him” (John 13:27). Before the morsel he had sinned of his own will and had not been bent toward repentance either by the Savior’s humility or by his mercy.

Hence the Apostle says: “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20). And elsewhere: “I have handed such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (1 Cor. 5:5). He handed them over to Satan as to an executioner for punishment; before they were handed over, they had blasphemed by their own will.

And David says: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18:13), briefly indicating both the error of his own will and the incitements of vices.

We read also in Ecclesiastes: “If the spirit of one who has power rises over your heart, do not leave your place” (Eccles. 10:4). From this it clearly appears that, if we give a place to the spirit that rises, we have sinned by giving it that place and by failing to hurl down headlong the enemy who climbs our walls.

But when you call down upon your brothers—that is, upon your accusers—eternal fires with the devil, you seem to me not so much to oppress your brothers as to raise up the devil, since he is to be punished in the same fires as Christian human beings.

[Note: They are looking for a knot in a reed who understand these words as Jerome understood them: namely, that Christian people who have violated God’s commandments will not suffer eternal punishments, unlike unbelievers and the Devil; and therefore, in that sense, Rufinus raises up the Devil and oppresses Christians when he invokes the same punishment upon both. For Jerome says nothing here about the eternity of punishments; he does not deny that the punishments imposed upon all the condemned are eternal, but he considers them more severe for the Devil, and thinks that the Devil is raised up if he is assigned the same punishment as wicked Christian people.]

I think it cannot escape you what Origen customarily understands by eternal fires: namely, the conscience of sinners and the inward repentance that burns the heart. Isaiah also speaks of this: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24).

And it is written concerning Babylon:

[Note: The Vulgate translator has it differently: “There are no coals with which they may be warmed, nor a hearth beside which they may sit.”]

“You have coals of fire; you shall sit upon them; they shall be your help” (Ps. 27:14).

[Note: “Thus have these things become for you, in whatever matters you labored.”]

And in the Psalm the penitent hears: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with desolating coals” (Ps. 119:4). Thus the arrows of God’s commandments—which the Prophet says elsewhere, “I was miserable while the thorn was being fastened into me” (Ps. 31:4)—may wound and pierce the deceitful tongue and make it desolate through its sins.

There is also that testimony in which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already kindled” (Luke 12:49).

[Note: An old edition reads, “and which I always wish to burn,” and so forth. Consult the Greek text.]

He interprets it thus:

“I desire all people to repent and to boil away their vices and sins in the Holy Spirit. For I am the one of whom it is written, ‘Our God is a consuming fire’ (Deut. 4:24). Therefore it is not a great thing to say this about the devil, since it has also been prepared for human beings.”

You ought rather, to avoid any suspicion that the devil may be saved, to have said: “You have become destruction, and you shall not exist forever” (Ezek. 28, according to the Septuagint); and, in the person of the Lord speaking to Job about the devil:

“Behold, his hope shall deceive him, and he shall be cast down while all look on” (Job 40:28). “I shall not stir him up as though I were cruel. For who can resist my face? Who has given to me beforehand, that I should repay him? All things under heaven are mine. I shall not spare him, either for powerful words or for words composed to plead” (Job 41:1ff.).

Yet these statements can perhaps be excused as the words of a simple man; and, even though they do not escape the learned, he can display before the uneducated the appearance of innocence.

## 8.

What follows concerning the condition of souls cannot be excused at all. He says:

“I hear that questions have also arisen concerning the soul. As to whether a complaint about this matter should be accepted or rejected, you must decide.

“But if it is also asked what I think, I admit that I have read differing opinions on this question among very many writers. I have read some who say that souls are diffused together with the body through the transmission of human seed, and they supported this with whatever arguments they could. I think that among the Latins Tertullian held this view, or Lactantius, and perhaps some others as well.

“Others assert that, once bodies have been formed in the womb, God creates and infuses souls each day. Others say that souls, having been made long ago—that is, when God created all things from nothing—are now, by his judgment, appointed to be born in the body.

“Origen and some other Greeks hold this view. But I, after reading each of these positions—this I say with God as my witness—because up to the present I hold nothing certain or definite concerning this question, leave it to God to know what is true, and whether he may deem it worthy to reveal it to anyone.

“Nevertheless, I neither deny that I have read each of these positions nor fail to confess that I still do not know them, except for what the Church clearly teaches: that God is the creator of souls and bodies.”

[Note: The earlier text incorrectly had “of the body” instead of “of seed”; the repetition by the holy Doctor makes the latter reading clear. Some manuscripts read “that the soul may be infused.”]

[Note: The wording elsewhere is “creator” rather than “maker.”]

## 9.

Before I discuss the substance, I shall marvel at Theophrastus’ words:

“I hear,” he says, “that questions have arisen concerning the soul. As to whether a complaint about this matter should be accepted or rejected, you must decide.”

If questions about the condition of souls have arisen in the city, what kind of complaint or accusation is this, whose acceptance or rejection is left to the judgment of bishops? Unless perhaps he thinks that “question” and “complaint” mean the same thing because he found such a figure of speech in Caprus’ *Commentaries*.

Next he writes:

“I have read some who say that souls are diffused together with the body through the transmission of human seed, and they supported this with whatever arguments they could.”

I ask: what license of figures of speech is this? What disturbance of moods and tenses? “I have read those who said—they supported it with whatever arguments they could.”

And in what follows:

“Others assert that, once bodies have been formed in the womb, God creates new souls each day and infuses them. Others say that souls, having been made long ago—that is, when God created all things from nothing—are now, by his judgment, appointed to be born in the body.”

Here too, what a beautiful order! “Others,” he says, “assert this or that; others, having been made long ago—that is, when God created all things from nothing—are now, by his judgment, appointed to be born in the body.”

He speaks so disgustingly and confusedly that I labor more in criticizing him than he did in writing. Finally he added:

“But I, after reading each of these positions”—and while the sentence was still hanging unfinished, as though he had brought forward something new, he added—“Nevertheless, I neither deny that I have read each of these positions nor fail to confess that I still do not know them.”

## 10. The mystery of the Trinity unknown to the ancients

O unhappy souls, wounded by so many spears of vices! I do not think that, according to Origen’s error, they suffered so much when they fell from heaven to earth and were clothed in heavy bodies, as they now suffer, battered here and there by words and sentences. I shall pass over the *cacēmphaton* [obscene or incongruous expression] by which souls are said to be diffused through the transmission of human seed.

[Note: An obscene or inappropriate reading.]

I know that defects of wording are not ordinarily criticized among Christians; but I wanted to show from a few examples what sort of recklessness it is to teach what one does not know and write what one does not understand, so that we may expect similar prudence in matters of substance.

He sends a letter—that is, a very strong staff with which the bishop of the city of Rome may be armed—and in the very question over which the dogs are barking he says that he does not know what is being asked. If he does not know the matter over which he is being accused, why is it necessary to send an *Apology* that contains not a defense of himself but a confession of ignorance? This is not to silence people’s suspicions but to sow them.

He sets out three opinions concerning the condition of souls and concludes at the end:

“I do not deny that I have read each of them, and I confess that I still do not know.”

You might think him Arcesilaus or Carneades, who pronounce everything uncertain, although he surpasses even them in caution. They, unable to endure the envy of all the philosophers because they removed truth from life, discovered probabilities in order to temper their ignorance of things with a plausible assertion.

[Note: “That they removed truth.” Apart from the old manuscript of our monastery at Floriacum, all the others we have seen, following Erasmus, read “that they removed life from life.” But the history of Arcesilaus and Carneades compels us to retain “truth,” since these philosophers removed truth from life by declaring everything uncertain and moderated their ignorance of things by a probable assertion or judgment. Arcesilaus was called a sophist because, while saying that he knew nothing and allowing no one else to claim knowledge, he confused everyone with sophisms. See Cicero, *On Ends*, book 2. M. Cato said that Carneades should be guarded against in the Senate because, through his eloquence and ability to argue, he could easily obtain whatever he wished. See Gellius, book 16, and Quintilian. —Martianus.]

[Note: Victorius restored this reading with the help of manuscript copies; previously the text had “life from life.” The reading is further supported by the character of Arcesilaus and Carneades, one the founder of the Middle Academy and the other the leader of the Third.]

This man says that he is uncertain and entirely does not know which of the three is true. If this was what he intended to answer, what reason compelled him to make so great a Pontiff a witness to his ignorance? Surely this is that weariness of which he speaks: exhausted by a journey of thirty years, he could not come to Rome.

How many other things we do not know, and yet we do not seek witnesses to our incompetence! Concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; concerning the birth of the Lord and Savior, about which Isaiah cries, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8)—on these matters he speaks boldly and claims for himself knowledge of a mystery unknown throughout all past ages. Yet the only thing he does not know is the very thing whose ignorance causes scandal to everyone.

He knows how the Virgin gave birth to God, and he does not know how he himself was born.

He confesses the Lord as creator of souls and bodies, whether souls existed before bodies, or were born with the beginnings of bodies, or were inserted once bodies had already been formed and shaped in the womb. In all these matters we acknowledge the Lord as author.

But the present question is not whether God or someone else made them. Of the three positions he set forth, he says that he does not know which is true. Take care lest someone immediately object to you that you confess ignorance of all three precisely so that you will not be forced to condemn one; and that you spare Tertullian and Lactantius so that you will not slay Origen along with them.

As far as memory suggests—unless I am mistaken—I do not recall having read that Lactantius said that the soul was *syspeirōmenē* (συσπειρομένη), that is, sown together or transmitted through descent.

[Note: In the third book he openly denies that Lactantius wrote of the soul as *syspeirōmenē*, that is, sown together or transmitted. You write that there are three opinions about souls: one followed by Origen, another by Tertullian and Lactantius, although you lie most clearly about Lactantius. In fact, in book 7, section 12, Lactantius assumes that he must prove that the soul derives its origin from heaven. I am therefore even more astonished that some learned men count the transmission of the soul among his errors. It is not our purpose to excuse Rufinus; according to Jerome himself, in Letter 126, the presbyter of Aquileia could have cited most Westerners in support of him, apart from Tertullian and Apollinaris.]

Since you say that you have read it, tell us in which book you read it, lest you appear to have slandered him, dead though he is, just as you would have slandered me while I slept.

But even here you proceed hesitantly and cautiously. For you say:

“I think that among the Latins Tertullian held this view, or Lactantius, and perhaps some others as well.”

You are uncertain not only about the condition of souls but also about the opinions of the authors, and yet there is some difference. Concerning souls, you plainly do not know and confess your ignorance; concerning the authors, you say that you know in such a way that you merely think rather than assert. Only about Origen are you not uncertain. For you say, “Origen holds this view.”

I shall ask you: does he hold it rightly or wrongly?

“I do not know,” you say.

Why, then, do you attempt, by sending messengers and frequent dispatches, to teach me so that I may know what you do not know?

And lest I perhaps not believe your ignorance, and think that you are cleverly concealing what you know, you swear, with God as your witness, that up to the present you hold nothing certain or definite concerning this question, and that you leave it to God to know what is true and whether he may deem it worthy to reveal it to anyone.

For so many ages, did no one seem worthy to you to whom the Lord might reveal the truth about this question? No patriarch, no prophet, no apostle, no martyr? Did such mysteries not become clear even to you when you were staying in prisons and exiles?

The Lord says in the Gospel, “Father, I have revealed your name to human beings” (John 17:6). He who revealed the Father remained silent about the condition of souls. And you wonder if the scandals of your brothers are stirred up against you, when you swear that you do not know what the Church of Christ confesses that it knows?

## 11.

Having set out his faith—or rather, his confession of ignorance—he passes to another matter and attempts to excuse himself for translating the books *On First Principles* into Latin. He writes the following word for word:

“Certainly, because I hear that discussion has also arisen on that account, since, at the request of the brothers, I translated certain works of Origen from Greek into Latin, I think that everyone understands that these things are being condemned out of sheer envy. For if there is something displeasing in the author, why is it diverted onto the translator? As they exist in Greek, I was asked to show them to Latin readers. I gave Latin words only to Greek meanings. Therefore, if there is any praise in those meanings, it is not mine; if there is blame, it is likewise not mine.”

“I hear,” he says, “that discussion has also arisen on that account.”

How prudently he calls his accusation a “discussion”!

“Certain works of Origen which, at the request of the brothers, I translated from Greek into Latin.”

What are those “certain works”? Do they have no name? You are silent? The booklets of the accusers speak.

“I think,” he says, “that everyone understands that these things are being condemned out of sheer envy.”

Envy of what? Are they jealous of your eloquence? Or have you done what no human being has ever been able to do? I too have translated many works of Origen, and apart from you no one envies or slanders me.

“For if,” he says, “there is something displeasing in the Author, why is it diverted onto the translator? As they exist in Greek, I was asked to show them to Latin readers. I gave Latin words only to Greek meanings. Therefore, if there is any praise in those meanings, it is not mine; if there is blame, it is likewise not mine.”

And you wonder if people think badly of you, when, concerning manifest blasphemies, you say, “If there is something displeasing in the author.”

Everything said in those books is displeasing; and you alone hesitate and complain that what you praised in the preface to your translation is being diverted onto the translator.

You were asked to translate into Latin what existed in Greek. Would that you had done what you pretend you were asked to do! No one would now be subject to envy on your account. If you had preserved the fidelity of the translation, I would not have been forced to overthrow a false interpretation with a true one.

Your conscience knows what you added, what you removed, and what you altered in either direction, according to your own judgment. After all this, you dare to say that both the good and the bad should be attributed not to you but to the author.

And, oppressed by envy, you still moderate your words, proceeding as though walking on the tips of your toes over ears of grain:

“Whether there is praise in those meanings or blame.”

You do not dare to defend it, yet you do not wish to condemn it. Choose whichever of the two you want; the choice is yours. If your translation is good, praise it; if it is bad, condemn it.

But he excuses himself and adds another rhetorical flourish. For he says:

“Indeed, I also added something else, as I indicated in my brief preface, so that, insofar as I could, I might omit a few things; those, however, which seemed suspicious to me because they appeared not to have been said in that way by Origen himself, but to have been inserted by others, for the reason that I had read orthodox statements about the same matters elsewhere in works by the same author.”

[Note: Other printed editions read “into suspicion,” against the manuscripts and Jerome, who mocks this phrasing.]

What extraordinary eloquence, varied with Attic brilliance: “Indeed, also”; and “those which seemed suspicious to me.” I marvel that he dared to send such monsters of language to Rome.

You might think that his tongue was fettered and bound with inextricable knots, scarcely able to break forth into human speech. But let me return to the case.

## 11. Origen’s blasphemy

Who gave you this license to omit so much from the translation? You were asked to translate Greek into Latin, not to correct it; to present another person’s words, not to compose your own. You confess that you did not do what you were asked, since you cut out so much.

Would that you had cut out the bad things and not inserted so much of your own in support of them! I shall produce one example, so that the rest may be recognized from it.

In the first book of *On First Principles*, where Origen blasphemed with sacrilegious speech by saying that the Son does not see the Father, you also supply reasons, as though speaking in the person of the writer; and you interpret a *scholion* (σχόλιον) of Didymus, in which he tries, with wasted effort, to defend another person’s error. You say that Origen indeed spoke correctly, but that we simple people—and Ennius’s tame creatures—  
[Note: In the brief commentaries that he entitled *Scholia* on this book of *On First Principles*, Didymus defended Origen as holding an orthodox position, distinct from that of the Arians. See below, p. 508.]  
[Note: “And the tame creatures of Ennius.” Ennius, the celebrated poet, undoubtedly meant animals and domesticated beasts, since he lived on the Aventine, content with very modest expense and the service of a little maidservant. Or perhaps he himself knew how to tame wild animals; hence the “tame creatures of Ennius” mentioned here. In a manuscript of the College of Navarre in Paris we read, “and the girdle of Sennianus.” —Martianus. Some learned man thinks it should be read “the girdled creatures of Ennius,” referring to barbarian peoples, such as the earliest inhabitants of Italy, whom Horace calls *cinctutos* in *Ars Poetica*, verse 50.]

To invent unheard-of things for the girded Cethegi. I do not wish anything to be altered; although, since this very passage does not survive among Ennius’s historical fragments, I would hardly wish to conjecture. Yet Tertullian too, toward the end of *Against the Valentinians*, or in chapter 37, spoke of “the Ennian tame creatures” of a more distinguished master. Or perhaps he indicated “wild natures, or barbarians, taught gentleness under ill omens and with futile effort.” But we cannot understand either the Ennian tame creatures, or his wisdom, or yours, who interpreted him.

Your preface, which you mention, and in which you adorn me with astonishing praises, makes you guilty of the worst translation. For you say that you omitted much from the Greek, although you are silent about what you added. What you omitted—was it bad or good? Bad, of course. What you kept [Col. 0434D]—good or bad? Good, of course. For you could not have translated what was bad. Therefore you cut away what was bad and left what was good? No one doubts it. Yet almost everything that has been translated is shown to be bad [Col. 0435A]. Whatever, therefore, I demonstrate to be bad in the translation will be charged to you, since you translated it as good.

It is another matter if, as an unjust censor guilty of the same crime [Note: It seems to me that *reos* should be read in the accusative, referring to those whom he would condemn in some cases and acquit in others.], you expel some from the senate while retaining others in the curia. But you say: “I could not change everything; I thought that I ought to cut away only those things which I judged had been added by heretics.” Fine. If you cut away what you thought had been added by heretics, then what you left belongs to the author whom you interpreted [Variant: *whom you were interpreting*]. Answer: is it good or bad? You could not translate what was bad. For you cut away, once and for all, what had been added by heretics. Unless, perhaps, you ought to cut away the heretics’ bad material while translating Origen’s errors intact into Latin.

Tell me, then, why you translated Origen’s bad material into Latin: to expose the author of the evil, or to praise him? If you expose him, why do you praise him in your preface? If you praise him, you are shown to approve a heretic. It remains, then, that you presented these things as though they were good. If all these things are proved bad, both the author and the translator will consequently be guilty of one and the same crime, and that saying will be fulfilled: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him; and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Ps. 49:18).

There is no need to make a clear matter uncertain by argument. Let what follows answer where the suspicion arose that these things had been added by heretics. “Because,” he says, “I had read the same author speaking catholically about the same matters in other places.”

### 12. Origen’s Heresies

Let us examine what comes first, so that we may proceed in order to what follows. Among Origen’s many errors, I prove these especially heretical [Note: See what we have said about each of these errors of Origen in the Synodical Letter of Theophilus, in the Letter to Avitus, and elsewhere.]: that the Son of God is a creature; that the Holy Spirit is a minister; that there are innumerable worlds succeeding one another through everlasting ages; that angels have been changed into human souls; that the soul of the Savior existed before he was born from Mary; and that this is the soul which, “being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped” (Phil. 2), but emptied itself, taking the form of a servant.

He teaches that the resurrection of our bodies will occur in such a way that they will not possess the same members, because, when the functions of the members cease, the superfluous members will be discarded; and that the bodies themselves, being subtle and spiritual, will gradually disappear and be dispersed into a thin vapor and into nothingness.

He teaches that, at the restoration of all things, when the original indulgence arrives, the Cherubim and Seraphim, Thrones, Principalities, Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Archangels [Col. 0435D], Angels, the Devil, demons, and the souls of all human beings—Christians, Jews, and Gentiles alike—will be of one condition and measure. And when they have reached the form and balance of equality, and the rational creatures, having cast off all the dross of their bodies, have displayed a new army of a people returning from the exile of the world, then another world will again be made from another beginning, together with other bodies in which the souls slipping from heaven will be clothed. Thus we must fear that those of us who are now men may later be born as women, and that she who is a virgin today may then [Variant: later] perhaps be a prostitute.

These are the heretical doctrines I show to be found in Origen’s books. You show where, in one of his works, you have read contrary statements.

### 13. Origen’s Six Thousand Books

Do not say, “I had read him speaking catholically about the same matters in other places,” lest you send me to the six thousand books of his which you accuse blessed Pope Epiphanius of having read. Name the actual passages; nor will this suffice for me unless you produce the same statements word for word.

Origen is not a fool, and I know that; he cannot speak contradictions. Therefore from this reckoning the following conclusion arises: what you cut away did not belong to the heretics, but to Origen. You interpreted his bad material for the very reason that you thought it good. And both his good and his bad must be charged to you, since in your Prologue you approved his writings.

[Note: Rufinus was perhaps misled by a faulty understanding of this passage in Epiphanius, *Against the Heresies* 64, concerning the Origenists, no. 63. There, addressing Origen himself, Epiphanius says: *εἰ γάρ ἐστιν ἀληθές ὃ περὶ σοῦ ᾄδεται, ὅτι ἐξακισχιλίους βίβλους συνεγράψω, ὦ ματαιοπόνε*—“For if it is true what has become widely reported about you, that you have written six thousand books, O laborer in vain.” But Epiphanius nowhere affirmed the number of the books, nor said that he himself had read that many. Jerome again below, and elsewhere, warns against the same hallucination on Epiphanius’s part and reproaches Rufinus for it.]

### 14. Hilary and Ambrose as Translators of Origen. Anastasius’s Letter to John of Jerusalem

The following occurs in the same *Apology*:

> “I am neither Origen’s defender, nor his advocate, nor his first translator. Others undertook this same work before me [Variant: had undertaken it]; I did it last, at the request of the brothers. If it is ordered that the work not be done, the order is usually observed thereafter. If those who acted before the order are blamed, let the blame begin with the first.”

At last he vomited out what he wanted, and all the swelling of his spirit burst forth in the malicious accusation of me. When he interprets the books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (“On First Principles”), he says that he follows me; when he is accused of why he did this, he offers my example. Secure or endangered, he cannot live without me.

Let him therefore hear what he pretends not to know. No one reproaches you for interpreting Origen—for otherwise Hilary and Ambrose would also be held guilty of this charge—but because, by interpreting heretical material, you confirmed it with the praise of your Preface.

I myself, whom you summon into the case, translated seventy of his Homilies and some passages from his *Tomoi* in such a way that I both removed the bad material in my interpretation of the good and plainly showed, in the books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, what a reader should avoid in order to expose the defects of your translation.

Do you wish to translate Origen into Latin? You have many of his homilies and *tomoi* in which moral instruction is treated and the obscure passages of Scripture are disclosed. Translate these; give these to those who request them. Why does your first labor begin with infamy? When you are going to translate heretical material, why do you preface its defense with a book presented as though it were a martyr’s work, and thrust upon Roman ears what, once translated, the whole world shuddered at?

Or, if you translate him in order to prove him a heretic, change nothing from the Greek, and testify in your preface to this very intention. The most prudent Pope Anastasius did exactly this in the letter he wrote against you to Bishop John: he acquitted me, who did this, and accused you, who refused to do it.

And lest you perhaps deny this as well, I have appended his example [Note: We attach this letter below in its proper place, in keeping with Jerome’s intention, since he thrusts the letter he had copied upon Rufinus.], so that if you do not wish to hear a brother giving warning, you may hear a bishop condemning [Variant: slandering] you.

### 15. Rufinus Shown to Be Origen’s Defender. Eusebius, Leader of the Arians. Rufinus’s Preface to Pamphilus’s *Apology for Origen*

You say that you are not Origen’s defender or advocate. I will now produce your own book, about which you speak in these words in that famous little preface to your excellent work:

> “I have set forth more fully the reason for this difference in the *Apologeticus* which Pamphilus wrote in his books, publishing it in a very brief additional volume. In it, with proofs that are evident, as I believe, we have shown that his books have been corrupted in very many places by heretics and malicious persons, especially those which you now demand that I translate, namely, *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*.”

Eusebius’s—or, as you prefer, Pamphilus’s—defense of Origen was not enough for you unless you added, as though you were wiser and more learned, what you thought they had said too little.

It would be a lengthy task if I wished to insert your entire book into this work and answer each chapter individually, showing what defects its language contains, what assertions are lies, and what incoherence appears in the very sequence of its words. Therefore, avoiding the weariness of its sprawling argument and compressing my words, I will answer only its meaning.

Immediately upon leaving harbor, he struck the ship. For, while reporting on the *Apology of the martyr Pamphilus*—which we have proved to be Eusebius’s, the leader of the Arians—and after saying, “We arranged it in the Latin language as best we could, or as the matter required,” he added:

> “This is what I want you, Macarius, as a man of desire, to understand: that this rule of faith which we set forth above from his books is such that it must both be embraced and held. For it is plainly proved that a Catholic understanding is present throughout all these matters.”

Although he removed much from Eusebius’s book and tried to alter what it said about the Son and the Holy Spirit in a favorable direction, it nevertheless contains many scandals and the most open blasphemies [Col. 0437D], which he cannot deny to be Catholic after declaring them so.

Eusebius—or rather, as you would have it, Pamphilus—says in this volume [Note: “The Son a minister of the Father.” All our manuscripts support this reading; nor do the printed books preserve Jerome’s true wording. Jerome did not say, “the Spirit the minister of the Son and the Father,” but that Eusebius said the Son was the Father’s minister, while the Holy Spirit was not of the substance of the Father and the Son. MARTIAN.—Older printed editions read, “the Holy Spirit the minister of the Son and the Father.” Perhaps the original wording was: “the Son the minister of the Father, the Spirit of the Son, not of the same substance,” etc. Jerome shortly above: “Origen’s most especially heretical teachings: the Son of God a creature, the Holy Spirit a minister,” etc.], that the Son is the Father’s minister; that the Holy Spirit is not of the same substance as the Father and the Son; that human souls have fallen from heaven; and that, since we have been changed from angels into what we are, at the restoration of all things we shall be equal to angels, demons, and human beings alike; together with many other things so impious and unspeakable that even to repeat them is criminal.

What will the defender of Origen and translator of Pamphilus do? If such blasphemy is found in the passages he corrected, how many sacrileges must be contained in those which he pretends were falsified by heretics? He suspects that the reason for this is that a man who was neither foolish nor insane could not have spoken contradictions.

And lest we perhaps think that he wrote different things at different times and published contradictions according to his age, he added:

> “What are we to do when, sometimes in the same passages, and, so to speak, in almost the immediately following chapter, a statement of contrary meaning is found inserted? Could he have forgotten himself in the same work, in the same book, and sometimes, as we have said, in the immediately following chapter? For example, could one who had said above that nowhere in all Scripture is the Holy Spirit said to have been made or created immediately add that the Holy Spirit had been made among the other creatures? Or again, could one who had designated the Father and the Son as being of one substance, which in Greek is called ὁμοούσιον, immediately in the following chapters say that he was of another substance and created—the one whom shortly before he had declared to have been born from the very nature of God the Father?”

### 16. Eusebius and Didymus Concede Origen’s Opinions

These are his own words; he cannot deny them. I do not want you to say, “For example, one who had said above”; name the book itself, where he first spoke correctly and afterward incorrectly; where, while writing that the Holy Spirit and the Son are of the substance of God the Father, he immediately afterward asserted that they were creatures. Do you not know that I possess all of Origen? That I have read very much of him?

> “To the people, trappings; I know you within and under your skin.”  
> (Persius, *Satire* 3.)

The highly learned Eusebius—I said “highly learned,” not “Catholic,” lest, as usual, you construct a calumny against me on this point as well—does nothing throughout six volumes except show Origen to share his faith, that is, Arian perfidy. He presents many examples and proves this consistently.

In what dream, then, revealed to you in the prison of Alexandria, did you learn to call false what he professes as true? But perhaps, as an Arian, he attributed to heretics what had been added, in order to turn it into an occasion for his own error, so that he would not seem to have been the only one to think wrongly against the Church.

What will you answer on behalf of Didymus, who is certainly Catholic concerning the Trinity? We too translated his book on the Holy Spirit into Latin [see above]. Certainly he could not agree that those passages had been added by heretics to Origen’s works. Yet in the very books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* which you translated, he composed brief commentaries, in which he did not deny that what had been written was written by Origen, but tried to persuade us, simple people, that we could not understand what was being said and in what sense it ought to be taken favorably. This he did only concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit.

In the other doctrines, however, both Eusebius and Didymus most openly concede Origen’s opinions and defend as Catholic and pious what all the churches reject.

### 17. Rufinus on the Adulteration of Origen’s Books

Let us nevertheless examine the arguments by which he tries to prove that Origen’s writings were corrupted by heretics.

> “Clement,” he says, “a disciple of the Apostles, who was bishop and martyr of the Roman Church after the Apostles, published books called *ἀναγνωρισμὸς*, that is, *Recognition* [Note: These are called *ἀναγνωρισμὸς*. There is no manuscript in our possession that does not correctly read *ΑΝΑΓΝΩΡΙΣΜΟΣ*, although inexperienced readers and scribes wrote *anatheorismos* in the margins of some copies; the printed books before ours retain this error. MARTIAN.]. In them, although doctrine is expounded in very many places in the person of the Apostle Peter, as though it were truly apostolic, the doctrine of Eunomius is inserted in certain passages so that one would think Eunomius himself was speaking, asserting that the Son of God was created from things that did not exist.”

And after other things which it would be lengthy to write, he says:

> “What, I ask, are we to think about this—that an apostolic man wrote heretical doctrines [Note: Rufinus’s editions add: “indeed, almost an apostle”]? Or should we rather believe that wicked men, in support of their doctrines, inserted under the names of holy men, as things more easily believed, what one must believe they neither thought nor wrote?”

He also writes that Clement, the presbyter of the Alexandrian Church, a Catholic man, sometimes says in his books that the Son of God was created; and that Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, a most learned man who argued against Sabellius in four volumes, slipped into Arian doctrine.

By these examples he endeavors to establish that ecclesiastical and Catholic men did not think wrongly, but that their writings were corrupted by heretics. Finally, he concludes by saying:

> “Concerning Origen also, in whom a similar diversity is found, as in those whom we mentioned above, let it not suffice to hold or understand what is already held or understood concerning men judged Catholic, lest an excuse for a similar case prove sufficient for a similar cause.”

If it is granted that whatever harmful material is found in books has been corrupted by others [Variant: “if this is so, then nothing,” etc.], nothing will belong to those whose names it bears; rather, it will be assigned to those by whom it is said to have been corrupted. Indeed, it will not belong even to those whose names are uncertain. Thus it will come about that, while everything belongs to everyone, nothing belongs to anyone.

By this confused defense neither Marcion, nor Manichaeus, nor Arius, nor Eunomius can be accused, because whatever we bring forward as impiously said by them, their disciples will answer that it was not published [Variant: said] by their teachers in that form, but violated by their enemies.

By this method even this book of yours will not be yours, but perhaps mine. And my book, in which I answer your accusation, if you find anything to criticize in it, will not be mine but yours, since you are the one criticizing it. And while you refer everything to the heretics, what will you assign to ecclesiastical writers, for whom you leave nothing of their own?

“And how,” you ask, “are there some defective things in their books?” If I answer that I do not know the causes of the defects, I will not immediately judge them heretics. It may be that they simply erred, or wrote with another meaning, or that their writings were gradually corrupted by inexperienced copyists. Or certainly, before Arius arose in Alexandria like a noonday demon, they may have spoken certain things innocently and less cautiously—things unable to escape the calumny of perverse men.

Crimes are brought against Origen, and you do not defend him but accuse others; you do not deny the crime but seek a crowd of criminals. If you were asked whom Origen has as associates in heresy, you would rightly bring these examples forward. But now you are asked whether what is found written in Origen’s books is good or bad. You are silent and speak of other matters in their place.

“Clement says this.” “Dionysius is caught in this error.” [Note: Bishop Athanasius. Several manuscripts retain the name Anastasius instead of Athanasius, through the error of earlier scribes. MARTIAN.] “Bishop Athanasius [Variant: Anastasius] defends Dionysius’s error in this way: the writings of the Apostles have likewise been corrupted.”

Just as others now bring against you the charge of heresy, and you remain silent on your own behalf while confessing on mine, so too I say: I am not what you accuse me of being. If you are what you are accused of being, you must see to that yourself. Neither my acquittal will prove you innocent, nor your guilt prove me liable to the charge.

### 18. Origen’s Letter to His Friends in Alexandria. The First Part of the Origenian Letter

After prefacing the matter with the claim that the writings of the Apostles, of both Clements, and of Dionysius had been falsified by heretics, he comes to Origen and speaks as follows:

> “We have proved this from the writings and words of Origen himself, who complained and lamented. For what he himself suffered, while still living in the flesh [Note: Rufinus’s editions read, “while he was living in the flesh.” In the manuscript of the Roman College, the following word, *sentiens* (“perceiving”), is absent.], perceiving and seeing, from the corruption of his books or speeches and from adulterated editions, is clearly demonstrated by a letter which he wrote to certain dear friends in Alexandria.”

He immediately adds an example from the letter. And he who charges heretics with falsifying Origen’s writings begins himself with a falsification: he does not interpret the passage as it appears in Greek, nor convey to Latin readers what Origen himself professes in his letter.

Although the entire letter attacks Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, and inveighs against the bishops and clergy of the whole world, and although Origen says that he has been excommunicated by the churches unjustly and does not wish to repay curses with curses, lest he appear to be a cursing man—so cautious in cursing that he does not dare curse even the devil—and although he thereby gave Candidus, a follower of Valentinian doctrine, an opportunity to slander him by saying that he had declared the devil’s nature to be capable of salvation, Rufinus, suppressing the letter’s argument, invents on Origen’s behalf what Origen does not say.

Accordingly, I translated a short portion of the letter from the preceding context and joined it to what Rufinus himself translated, deceitfully and clause by clause, so that the reader may recognize for himself why he suppressed what came before.

Arguing generally against the priests of the Church, by whom he had been judged unworthy of communion with them, Origen added:

> “Why is it necessary to speak of the words of the prophets, by which they very often threaten and rebuke shepherds, elders, priests, and rulers of the people? You can draw these things for yourselves from the holy Scriptures and clearly see that perhaps this is the time of which it is said: ‘Do not believe your friends, and do not put your hope in rulers’ (Mic. 7:5). And now the prophecy is fulfilled: ‘The leaders of my people did not know me; they are foolish children and are not wise. They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good’ (Jer. 4:21–22). We ought to pity them rather than hate them and pray for them rather than curse them. For we were created to bless, not to curse.

> “Thus, when Michael was disputing against the devil concerning the body of Moses, he did not dare, even against so great an evil, to pronounce a judgment of blasphemy, but said: ‘May the Lord rebuke you’ (Jude 9). We read something similar in Zechariah: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, O devil; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you’ (Zech. 3:2). Therefore we desire that the Lord rebuke those who do not wish to be rebuked humbly by their neighbors.

> “When Michael says, ‘May the Lord rebuke you, O devil,’ and Zechariah likewise, whether God rebukes the devil or does not rebuke him, let God himself see to it. And if he rebukes him, let him himself know how he rebukes him.”

And after much else which it would be lengthy to record, he adds:

> “We hold that not only those who have committed great sins will be cast out of the kingdom of heaven—for example, fornicators, adulterers, and those who lie with males, and thieves—but also those who have committed lesser offenses, according to what is written: ‘Neither drunkards nor revilers shall possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Cor. 6:16); and that there is a measure both in the goodness and in the severity of God.

> “Therefore we strive to do everything with deliberation, including the drinking of wine and the moderation of speech, so that we dare not curse anyone. Thus, while out of fear of God we refrain from directing curses against anyone, remembering the statement, ‘He did not dare to pronounce a judgment of blasphemy,’ which is said of Michael in relation to the devil, and in another passage, ‘The dominions indeed they reject, but they blaspheme the glorious ones,’ certain people who gladly seek quarrels attribute blasphemy to us and to our teaching. Let them see for themselves how they hear the statement: ‘Neither drunkards nor revilers shall possess the kingdom of God,’ although they say that the father of the evil and destruction of those who will be cast out of God’s kingdom—that is, the devil—can be saved, something that not even a mentally deranged person could say.”

From the same letter Rufinus translated other material in place of the words of Origen which we interpreted at the end:

> “Thus, because out of fear of God we refrain from directing curses against anyone,”

and what follows. Having deceitfully cut away the preceding material, on which the later material depends, he began translating the letter as though the earlier passage had had this meaning [Note: Victorius preferred: “as though this were the beginning of the meaning,” that is, as though the sense began there, although it had begun earlier.], and said:

> “Some of those who gladly accuse their neighbors attribute to us and to our teaching the charge of blasphemy, which they have never heard from us. Let them see to this, since they do not wish to observe the commandment which says, ‘Revilers shall not possess the kingdom of God.’ They say that I assert that the father of the evil and destruction of those who are cast out of the kingdom of God—that is, the devil—is to be saved; something that not even a person mentally deranged and manifestly insane could say.”

### 19. Candidus’s Dialogue with Origen. Novatian’s Book on the Trinity

Compare Origen’s words, which I translated above word for word, with those which Rufinus did not translate but overturned, and you will see how great their discord is—not only in words but also in meaning. I ask you not to find the longer translation burdensome. We translated everything for this very reason: to prove why he suppressed the preceding material.

Among the Greeks there is a dialogue between Origen and Candidus, a defender of the Valentinian heresy, in which I confess that I seemed to be watching two *Audabatae* fighting one another. Candidus says that the Son is of the Father’s substance, erring in asserting that this is a *προβολή*, that is, a “prolation” or production [Note: The words “that is, a prolation” are not found in Victorius, who is certainly mistaken in supposing that *προβολή* signifies excellence, or *ἐξοχή*, and consequently that Candidus errs because he says that the Father is more excellent than the Son. Rather, *προβολή* means production, in which sense it frequently occurs among ancient ecclesiastical writers, especially Irenaeus. Candidus blasphemed in this respect: together with Valentinus, he asserted such a *προβολή*, or production, by which Jesus had been generated from the Aeons. In this understanding he imagined the Son as a prolation and proclaimed a “prolative Word,” so that the Word who is the Son would not be such a Word of God the Father as every word, through the implanted nature of speech within us, is produced into a voice, as Saint Hilary also testifies in book 46 of *On the Synods*. On this matter see also Saint Epiphanius, *Heresy* 31. This interpretation is condemned by canon 8 of the Council of Sirmium and by the Roman synod under Damasus in the year 378; indeed, the Arians themselves rightly rejected the term, although they did so deceitfully. But Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 8, while condemning Valentinus’s interpretation, defends the use of the word:

> “I acknowledge God the Son. Then, if anyone thinks that by this I introduce some *προβολή*, that is, a prolation of one thing from another, as Valentinus did when he produced an Aeon from an Aeon, I will first say: Is truth therefore not to use both the term and the reality and meaning of it merely because heresy uses it? On the contrary, heresy received from the truth what it constructed for its lie.”

Certainly there is nothing to prevent one from calling the production of the Word a *προβολή*, and the Father is called the *προβολεύς* (“producer”) of the Word by Saint Gregory of Nazianzus and other Fathers.]

On the other side, Origen, in agreement with Arius and Eunomius, rejects the idea that the Son was either produced or born, lest God the Father be divided into parts. Instead, he says that the Son came into existence by the Father’s will as a sublime and most excellent creature, just like the other creatures.

They return again to the second question. Candidus asserts that the devil is of the worst nature and can never be saved. Origen rightly answers against this that the devil is not of a substance destined to perish, but fell by his own will and can be saved. Candidus turns this into a calumny, as though Origen had said that the devil’s nature was to be saved. Candidus had falsely alleged this; Origen refutes it.

We understand that in this dialogue alone Origen’s heretical falsehood is attacked, and not in the other books about which there was never any question. Otherwise, if everything that is heretical does not belong to Origen but to the heretics, and almost all of his *tomoi* are filled with these errors, nothing will belong to Origen but to those whose names we do not know.

It is not enough for Rufinus to slander Greeks and ancient writers, concerning whom, because of the distance of time and remoteness of place, he has the freedom to lie about anything he wishes. He comes to the Latins and first introduces Hilary the confessor, claiming that after the Council of Ariminum his book had been falsified by heretics [Note: Recall the entire story concerning Hilary and his falsified book in Rufinus’s *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*, where he recounts the matter at greater length. Jerome here protests that Rufinus invented the story; but if we consider for a moment where the story arose, the presbyter of Aquileia should be charged with error rather than bad faith. Suppose that the book mentioned by Rufinus was the one in which Hilary had narrated the history of the Councils of Seleucia and Ariminum, and that it had already been falsified and corrupted by the Arians. It is well known, moreover, that when Hilary had met Auxentius at Milan, and Auxentius had craftily pretended to be Catholic while about ten bishops, the quaestor, and the master were present, Valentinian ordered Hilary to leave Milan and himself joined Auxentius’s communion. When Rufinus heard this, he may honestly have thought that it was not Hilary’s book that had been mutilated, but that it had been disfigured by heretical errors, and that Hilary, the author of the book, had been punished with exile because of those errors.].

And for this reason, when the matter was raised against him in a council of bishops, he ordered the book to be brought from his house. It was being kept among his chests as a heretical book, without his knowledge. When it had been brought out and judged heretical by everyone, the author of the book, having been excommunicated, departed from the council’s assembly.

Rufinus thinks himself so authoritative that, when he tells this dream to his friends, no one dares contradict him as he pretends these things against the confessor.

Answer me, please: in what city was the synod by which he was excommunicated held? Name the bishops. Produce the decisions with their signatures, or show their differences or agreement. Tell us who the consuls were in that year, which emperor ordered this synod to be convened, whether only the bishops of Gaul were present or also those of Italy and Spain, and, certainly, for what reason the synod was convened.

You mention none of these things. Instead, you accuse a most eloquent man, the trumpet of Latin speech against the Arians, of having been excommunicated by a synod, in order to defend Origen.

The calumny against a confessor might somehow be tolerated. He moves on to the renowned martyr Cyprian and says that Tertullian’s book entitled *On the Trinity* is read at Constantinople under Cyprian’s name by heretics of the Macedonian party. In this accusation he lies in two ways. For the book is neither Tertullian’s [Note: There is no surviving book of Novatian, although Jerome himself, in *Catalogue* chapter 70, calls the work *On the Trinity* an *ἐπιτομή* (“epitome”) of Tertullian’s work, and many, not knowing this, think it Cyprian’s. Compare what we note on that passage.], nor is it attributed to Cyprian; rather, it is Novatian’s, whose name also appears in its title. The author’s eloquence and the distinctiveness of his style demonstrate this.

### 20. The Little Story about Jerome

I think it superfluous to refute obvious absurdities when my own little story is thrust upon me [Note: “From the synod, evidently.” In very many manuscripts we read “with a lyre for an ass” (*asino videlicet lyra*), but this is due to the ignorance of scribes who did not know about the synod convened by Damasus against the Apollinarians, at which Jerome was entrusted with dictating ecclesiastical letters. See this sort of story in Rufinus. MARTIAN.—This appears to have been the ecumenical synod held at Rome under Damasus in the year 382. Jerome does not accuse the corrupted Athanasian book of being false, but merely places the story among those things unsuitable to serious argument. Concerning the expression “the Lord’s man,” used to signify Christ—a phrase which some ancient writers rejected and others defended—we have collected much material in the notes to book 2 of Didymus’s *On the Holy Spirit*, no. 51; consult them if you wish.], from the synod, that is, and I am attacked under the name of a certain friend of Damasus, bishop of Rome, to whom he entrusted ecclesiastical letters to dictate. The story says that the cunning of the Apollinarians was exposed because, after receiving Athanasius’s book for reading, where “the Lord’s man” was written, they corrupted it in such a way that they rewrote on the erased place what they had scraped away, so that it would appear not to have been falsified by them but added by me.

I ask you, dearest friend, that in ecclesiastical treatises, where the truth of doctrines and the salvation of our souls are at issue and the authority of our predecessors is demanded, you abandon such ravings and do not treat stories of lunches and dinners as arguments for the truth.

For it may happen that, even if you have heard the truth from me, someone else who is ignorant of the matter will say that you composed it yourself, like a theatrical trick of Philistion [Note: Saint Epiphanius mentions Philistion in *Heresy* 36, concerning the Gnostics, no. 1; Tertullian mentions Lentulus in *On the Pallium*, chapter 4. That saying of Marullus is indeed a delightful one, addressed to a gluttonous parasite: “You imitate Hector; you never leave Ilium.” Marius Mercator mentions all three together in his *Commonitorium*: one Philistion, one Lentulus among the Latins, and one Marullus whom you should be compared with.], Lentulus, or Marullus, fabricated in elegant language.

## 21. Complaint concerning Saint Epiphanius

To what lengths will unbridled recklessness, once unleashed, not go? After Hilary’s excommunication, after Cyprian’s spurious book of heresy, and after the erasure—and at the same time the inscription—of Athanasius, while I was asleep, it eventually burst forth against Pope Epiphanius. He arranges the pain of his heart—that Epiphanius had accused him of heresy in a letter which he had written to Bishop John—in his *Apology for Origen*, and consoles himself with these words:

> “Rather, the truth hidden here must be brought to light. For it is not possible that anyone should employ so unjust a judgment as to form an unequal opinion about an equal case. But the authors of his detractors are those who either customarily dispute at length in the Church or even write books which speak or write entirely about Origen. Therefore, lest more people come to know their thefts—which certainly would not appear criminal if they were not ungrateful toward their teacher—they deter the more simple-minded from reading him. Finally, one of them, who thinks that he possesses the necessity of evangelizing among all nations and in every language, confessed, while a very large crowd of the brethren was listening, that he had read six thousand of Origen’s books, in order to speak ill of him. If, as he himself is accustomed to say, he was reading them in order to learn about Origen’s evils, ten books would have sufficed to discover them, or certainly twenty, or at most thirty. **[515]**

> **[Note: [Col. 0445D] See above, no. 13, note e.]**

> “But to read six thousand books is no longer to wish to learn his errors and evils; it is to devote almost one’s entire life to his teachings and studies. How, then, should this man rightly be heard when he condemns those who, for the sake of their instruction, have read a very few of Origen’s works—while preserving the rule of faith and undiminished piety?”

## 22. Epiphanius knew five languages

Who are these people who customarily dispute at length in the Church? Who write books? Who speak and write entirely about Origen? Who, because they do not want their own thefts to be known and are ungrateful toward their teacher, therefore deter the simple-minded from reading him? You ought to name them and identify the men themselves.

Therefore, should blessed bishops Anastasius, Theophilus, Venerius of Milan, and Chromatius of Aquileia, together with the entire synod of Catholics of both East and West, be judged thieves of his books because, with one and the same judgment—and therefore with one and the same spirit—they denounce him as a heretic to the peoples? And when they preach in the churches, do they recall not the mysteries of Scripture but the thefts of Origen?

> **[Note: [Col. 0445D] Blessed bishops Anastasius, etc. Anastasius was bishop of Rome, Theophilus of Alexandria, Venerius of Milan, and Chromatius of Aquileia. MARTIAN.]**

Is it not enough for you to disparage everyone indiscriminately, unless you specifically direct the spear of your pen against a blessed and distinguished priest of the Church?
