Who is this man who thinks that he possesses the necessity of evangelizing among all nations and in every language, in order to speak ill of Origen, and who confessed, while a very large crowd of the brethren was listening, that he had read six thousand of his books?

You too were in the midst of that crowd and assembly of the brethren when he complained in his letter that, on account of Origen’s abominable heresy, you had put forward doctrines [Col. 0446A] of your own.

> **[Note: [Col. 0445D] Labbe reports, *Conciliorum* vol. V, p. 658, the entire Western synod, which accepted and approved the judgment pronounced against the impious Origen by the Church of Alexandria, as Theophilus says in the sermon praised by the emperor Justinian. See Theophilus’s synodical letter and the three other letters which follow it, edited by us in vol. I, nos. 92 and following. [Col. 0446D]]**

Is it to be held against him that he knew Greek, Syriac, Hebrew, and Egyptian, and to some extent Latin? Then the Apostles and apostolic men who spoke in languages are also guilty; and will you yourself laugh at me, a man of three languages, as “double-tongued”?

> **[Note: [Col. 0446D] Jerome appears to be playing on the term “double-tongued” (*bilinguis*), so as to mark his detractor rather than someone knowledgeable in two languages. Jerome below, book III: “You are double-tongued, possessing such knowledge of Greek and Latin speech that Greeks think you Latin and Latins think you Greek.”]**

As for the six thousand books which you falsely claim that he had read [variant: “was learned”], who will believe either that you are telling the truth or that he could have lied? If Origen had written six thousand books, it could have happened that a most learned man, trained in the sacred Scriptures from childhood, had read the works of another out of curiosity and for the sake of knowledge. But what he did not write, how could this man have read?

Count the lists of his books contained in the third volume of Eusebius, in which he wrote the life of Pamphilus; you will find not six thousand, but not even a third of that number. [Col. 0446B] We possess a letter of the aforementioned Pontiff in which, while you were still in the East, he answered this calumny of yours and refuted your most blatant lie with the open face of truth.

## 23. He intended to write against Pamphilus’s *Apology*. The *Book of Illustrious Men* addressed to Dexter. He translated Origen’s homilies in his youth

After all this, and daring so much in your *Apology*, you say that you are not Origen’s defender or his advocate, although Pamphilus and Eusebius seemed to you to have said too little in his defense. Against those volumes—if the Lord grants me time in this life—I shall attempt to respond elsewhere.

For now, it is enough to have confronted your assertions and, briefly, to have instructed the prudent reader that I first saw the book circulated under Pamphilus’s name written in your own manuscript. Since I had no concern for what was said on behalf of a heretic, I always regarded it as though it were a different work by Pamphilus and Eusebius. Later, when the question was raised, I wished to answer their writings; for this reason I read what each of them thought on behalf of Origen. I clearly discovered that the first book of Eusebius’s six-volume work was itself the book which you published under Pamphilus’s name, both in Greek and in Latin, with only the passages concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit altered—passages which presented open blasphemy.

Accordingly, nearly ten years ago, when my friend Dexter, who had administered the prefecture of the praetorium, asked me to compile for him a catalogue of the authors of our religion, I included this book among the other writers, thinking it had been published by Pamphilus, as it had been disseminated by you and your disciples.

But since Eusebius himself says that Pamphilus wrote nothing except brief letters to friends, and since the first book of his six-volume work contains the same material, in the same words, as that which you fabricated under Pamphilus’s name, it is clear that you wished to disseminate this book for the purpose of introducing heresy under the person of a martyr.

And since you have distorted much in this very book which you pretend is Pamphilus’s, and since it differs in Greek and Latin, you ought not to attribute your fraud to my error. I believed the book to be his because its title declared it to be so, just as with *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) and many other works of Origen and of numerous Greek writers, which either I had not previously read or which, now that the question of heresy has been raised, I am compelled to read, so that I may know what I ought to avoid and what I ought to approve.

For this reason, in my youth I translated only those homilies of his which he delivered to the people—homilies in which there were not such great scandals—simply, at the request of those who asked me, without thereby prejudging that, from what is approved, one should accept what is manifestly heretical.

Certainly, to make a long speech brief: just as I show that I received the book from those who copied it from your manuscript, so you should show from whom you received your exemplar, so that the person who cannot name another author of the book may himself be held guilty of falsification.

“A good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (Matthew 12:35); and from the sweetness of fruits a tree of noble seed is recognized.

## 24. A letter falsely attributed to Jerome

Brother Eusebius writes that he found among African bishops who had come to the imperial court on ecclesiastical business a letter allegedly written in my name. In it, I was said to be doing penance and to confess that, in my youth, I had been led astray by the Hebrews into translating Hebrew books into Latin, books in which there was no truth.

When I heard this, I was astonished. And because “every word shall be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 17:6; Matthew 18:16; 2 Corinthians 13:1), and not even Cato is believed on the testimony of a single witness, letters from many brothers in the City informed me of the same matter. They tearfully inquired whether it was true and indicated by whom the letter itself had been spread among the people.

Whoever dared to do this, what else would he not dare? It is fortunate that malice does not possess as much strength as it possesses ambition. Innocence would have perished if wickedness had always been joined to power, and if slander had prevailed in everything it desired.

A most eloquent man could not reproduce my style, whatever its quality, or the form of my speech. But amid the very tricks and the assumed identity with which he had deceitfully disguised himself, he revealed who he was.

Thus the man who had fabricated, under my name, a penitential letter alleging that I had badly translated the Hebrew books is said to have charged me with interpreting the sacred Scriptures in condemnation of the Septuagint, so that, whether what I translated is false or true, I remain guilty: either I confess in the new work that I was mistaken, or the recent edition is [variant: “becomes”] a condemnation of the old one.

I wonder why, in that same letter, he did not say that I was a murderer, adulterer, sacrilegious person, and parricide, or attribute to me whatever disgrace silent thought can turn over within itself. I ought to thank him that, although there is such a forest of crimes, he has charged me with only one crime of error or falsity.

Have I said anything against the Septuagint translators, whom many years ago I carefully emended and gave to those devoted to my language, whom I expound daily in the gathering of the brethren, whose Psalms I sing in continual meditation? Was I so foolish that, having learned something in childhood, I wanted to forget it in old age?

All my treatises are woven from their testimonies. My commentaries on the Twelve Prophets expound both my own edition and that of the Septuagint.

O the labors of men, always uncertain! O the pursuits of mortals, sometimes having contrary ends! Where I thought I was doing a service to my fellow Latins and stirring up the minds of our people to study—since even Greeks do not disdain to translate from the Latin after so many translators—there I am summoned to account and force food into a nauseated stomach.

And what is safe in a human being if innocence is criminal? While the master of the house was sleeping, an enemy sowed weeds over the seed (Matthew 13:25). The boar from the forest destroyed the vineyard, and a solitary wild beast devoured it (Psalm 79:14).

I keep silent, and writings that are not mine speak against me. I am ignorant of the crime, and I confess the crime throughout the world. Alas for me, my mother, why did you give birth to me, a man who is judged and discerned by the whole earth (Jeremiah 15:10, according to the Septuagint)?

> **[Note: [Col. 0447D] Martianaeus has “who judges and discerns”; elsewhere, “who would judge.” In Greek, however, the reading is δικαζόμενον καὶ διακρινόμενον πάσῃ τῇ γῇ, “who is judged and discerned by the whole earth.”]**

## 25. From the Prologue to Genesis

All the brief prefaces to the Old Testament, examples of which I have partly supplied, bear witness to this matter. It is superfluous to write what is said in them differently from the way it is said there.

I shall therefore begin with Genesis, whose prologue is as follows:

> “I have received the desired letters of my Desiderius, who, by a certain foreknowledge of the future, was allotted Daniel’s name, and who entreats me to deliver to the ears of our people the Pentateuch translated into Latin from the Hebrew language.

> “Certainly, it is a dangerous undertaking and exposed to the barking of detractors, who assert that, in disparagement of the Septuagint translators, I am forging new things in place of old ones. Thus they test my talent as though they were testing wine, although I have very often testified that I offer in God’s tabernacle whatever I can according to my ability, and that the wealth of one person is not defiled by another’s poverty.

> **[Note: [Col. 0447D] The preface itself adds “of my detractors.” In this and the passages that follow, we do not dwell on such points in the present edition, since we supplied them in their proper place before the books of Scripture themselves. [Col. 0448D]]**

> **[Note: [Col. 0448D] Two manuscripts, one belonging to the Roman College and the other Palatine, read *pro vili*, “for what is common” or “for what is of little worth.”]**

> “Origen’s scholarly work urged me to undertake this task. He combined Theodotion’s translation with the ancient edition, marking the whole work with an asterisk (+) and an obelus (÷)—that is, with a star and a spit—either bringing to light what had previously been lacking or striking through and piercing whatever was superfluous, especially material which the authority of the Evangelists and Apostles had proclaimed.

> **[Note: [Col. 0448D] Elsewhere, *obelos*. Shortly afterward, instead of *illucere* (“to make shine”), Erasmus and Victorius read *illustria* (“illustrious things”), presumably because they thought it more harmonious, not because it was more accurate. It seems preferable to me to supply the word *illustria* after *fuerant*, without altering the text. Thus in the preface to Chronicles he says, “marking with asterisks what had previously been lacking.”]**

> “Among these we read many things from the Old Testament which are not found in our copies, such as: ‘Out of Egypt I called my son’ (Hosea 11:1); and, ‘He shall be called a Nazorean’ (Matthew 2:23); and, ‘They shall look on him whom they pierced’ (Zechariah 12:10); and, ‘From his belly shall flow rivers of living water’ (John 7:38); and, ‘Things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him’ (1 Corinthians 2:9); and many other passages which require their own compilation (*σύνταγμα*).

> “Let us therefore ask them where these things are written. When they cannot say, let us produce them from the Hebrew books. The first testimony is in Hosea; the second in Isaiah; the third in Zechariah; the fourth in Proverbs; the fifth likewise in Isaiah.

> **[Note: [Col. 0449D] I take this to refer to the *Ascension of Isaiah* and the *Apocalypse of Elijah*, books from which the Gnostics were thought to have drawn Paul’s passage to the Corinthians. Through this occasion, women in Spain and Lusitania were deceived by heretics, as Jerome himself says in his commentary on Isaiah 64. For the same reason he calls them “Iberian drivel” here.]**

> “Many, ignorant of this, pursue the ravings of apocryphal books and prefer Iberian drivel to authentic books. It is not my task to explain the causes of their error. **[520]**

> “The Jews say that this was done by deliberate policy, lest Ptolemy, a worshiper of the one God, should also discover among the Hebrews a double divinity. They did this especially because the matter seemed liable to fall under Plato’s doctrine. Finally, wherever Scripture gives sacred testimony concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they either interpreted it differently or kept entirely silent, so that they might both satisfy the king and not divulge the secret of the faith.

> “And I do not know which first author fabricated, by his lie, the story of the seventy cells of Alexandria, in which the translators, separated from one another, wrote the same things independently. Aristeas, Ptolemy’s defender (*ὑπερασπιστής*), and, much later, Josephus reported nothing of the sort; rather, they say that the translators gathered in one basilica and compared their work, not that they prophesied.

> **[Note: [Col. 0450D] The reading of the older edition is not to be despised; and Josephus himself, not long afterward, reported nothing of this sort, but wrote that they compared their work in one basilica, etc. The word “one” was lacking here in Martianaeus.]**

> “For it is one thing to be a prophet and another to be a translator. In the former case, the spirit foretells future things; in the latter, learning and abundance of words transfer what the translator understands.

> “Unless, perhaps, we should suppose that Cicero translated Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus*, Plato’s *Protagoras*, and Demosthenes’ speech *For Ctesiphon* under the inspiration of a rhetorical spirit, so that the Holy Spirit wove testimonies concerning the same books differently through the Septuagint translators and differently through the Apostles, and so that the Apostles falsely claimed that what the Septuagint had omitted had been written.

> “What then? Do we condemn the ancients? Certainly not. After the labors of our predecessors, we labor in the Lord’s house with whatever ability we possess. They translated before Christ’s coming, and they expressed in uncertain formulations what they did not know. We, after his passion and resurrection, write not so much prophecy as history. Things heard are reported one way, things seen another. What we understand better, we also express better.

> “Listen, then, rival and detractor; listen: I do not condemn or criticize the Septuagint, but I confidently prefer the Apostles to all of them. Through the mouth of the Apostles Christ speaks to me; I read that they were placed before the Prophets among the spiritual gifts, while the translators occupy almost the lowest rank.

> “Why are you tortured by envy? Why do you stir up the minds of the ignorant against me? If I seem to you to have erred somewhere in translation, ask the Hebrews and consult the teachers of different cities. What they possess concerning Christ, your copies do not possess.

> “It would be another matter if they had subsequently approved testimonies employed by the Apostles against themselves, and if the Latin copies were more accurate than the Greek, and the Greek more accurate than the Hebrew.”

## 26. From the Prologue to the Books of Kings

In the books of Samuel and Malachim—which we call the four Books of Kings—after the catalogue of divine Scripture, I also wrote the following:

> “Since these things are so, I ask you, reader, not to regard my labor as a criticism of the ancients. In God’s tabernacle each person offers what he can. Some offer gold, silver, and precious stones; others offer fine linen, purple, scarlet, and violet. We shall have done well if we offer skins and goats’ hair.

> “Yet the Apostle considers our more contemptible things more necessary (1 Corinthians 12:21). Thus the whole beauty of the tabernacle, and the distinction signified by each of its parts as referring to the present and future Church, is covered with skins and sackcloth; and the things that are of lower worth keep off the heat of the sun and the violence of the rains.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0450D] In the preface itself: “we shall have done.”]**

> See how arrogantly I swell against the Septuagint translators, claiming that they offered gold, precious stones, and purple in God’s tabernacle, while I offered skins and goats’ hair.

## 27. From the Prologue to Chronicles. The translation of the Septuagint translators corrupted

I shall add another testimony, lest you say that necessity has now compelled me to change my position. In the Book of Times—that is, Chronicles, called in Hebrew *DABRE JAMIM*—I used the following brief preface addressed to the holy Pope Chromatius:

> “If the pure edition of the Septuagint translators, as it was translated by them into Greek, had remained intact, you would be urging me needlessly, my most holy and learned bishop Chromatius, to transfer the Hebrew books into Latin speech. For what had once occupied the ears of human beings and strengthened the faith of the nascent Church ought rightly to have been confirmed even by our silence.

> “But now, since different copies are circulated according to the variety of regions, and since that genuine and ancient translation has been corrupted and violated, you consider it within our discretion either to judge from several copies what is true or to forge a new work within the old work, and, as the saying goes, to put out the eyes of crows—that is, to deceive those who claim that others are accustomed to deceive them.

> **[Note: [Col. 0450D] That is, to deceive those who profess that they themselves are accustomed to deceive others. See Cicero, *Pro Murena*, chapter 11, and *Pro Flacco*, chapter 20; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VII.5.]**

> “Alexandria and Egypt praise Hesychius as the author of their Septuagint copies. Constantinople as far as Antioch approves the copies of the martyr Lucian. The provinces between these regions read Palestinian copies, which Eusebius and Pamphilus published after Origen had prepared them. The whole world contends among itself through this threefold variety.

> “And certainly Origen not only composed copies of four editions, writing the individual words in parallel columns so that the one differing reading might immediately be convicted when the others agreed with one another;

> **[Note: [Col. 0451D] Martianaeus has *exapla* here, although long before, when printing the Preface itself in the first volume of his edition, he had rejected this reading. As Victorius also notes in correcting Erasmus, the *Hexapla* could not have consisted of four editions; rather, they would have been the *Tetrapla*. The reading restored by us is supported by the manuscripts.]**

> “but, what is more daring, in the Septuagint edition he mixed in Theodotion’s edition, marking with asterisks what had been lacking and with strokes what seemed to have been added unnecessarily.

> “If, then, others were permitted not to retain what they had once undertaken, and, after the seventy cells which are commonly proclaimed without an author, to open individual cells; and if what the Septuagint did not know is read in the churches, why should my Latins not accept me, since, without violating the old edition, I have fashioned a new one in such a way that I prove my labor by the authority both of the Hebrews and—what is more important—of the Apostles?

> “I recently wrote a book *On the Best Kind of Translation*, showing that the following Gospel passages—‘Out of Egypt I called my son’ (Hosea 11:1); ‘He shall be called a Nazorean’ (Matthew 2:15, 23); ‘They shall look on him whom they pierced’ (Zechariah 12:10); and the Apostle’s words, ‘Things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the heart of man, which the Lord has prepared for those who love him’ (1 Corinthians 2:9)—and other passages like them are found in the books of the Hebrews.

> “Certainly the Apostle and the Evangelists knew the Septuagint translators. How, then, could they say that these things are contained in the Septuagint when they are not?

> “And Christ our Lord, the author of both Testaments, says in the Gospel according to John: ‘Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly’ (John 7:38). What the Savior testifies to have been written must certainly be written. Where is it written? The Septuagint does not have it; the Church knows no apocryphal source. We must therefore return to the Hebrew books, whence the Lord speaks and the disciples take their testimonies.

> “I say these things with due respect for the ancients, and I answer only my detractors, who gnaw at me with a dog’s tooth: they slander me publicly while reading in corners, being at once accusers and defenders, approving in others what they disapprove in me, as though virtue and vice lay not in the things themselves but changed with their author.

> “For the rest, I remember that long ago I gave my people an edition of the Septuagint translators corrected from the Greek, and no one ought to think me an enemy of those whom I continually expound in the gathering of the brethren.

> “As for what I have now translated—*DABRE JAMIM*, that is, ‘Words of Days’—I did so in order to arrange more clearly the inextricable delays and the forest of names confused through the fault of scribes, as well as the barbarism of the meanings [variant: ‘labyrinths’], dividing them by the cola of the verses, and, like Antigenides, singing for myself and my own people, if the ears of others are deaf.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0451D] Antigenides’ pupil was a singer whom the public did not approve because he sang poorly. Antigenides said to him: “Sing to me and to the Muses.” [Col. 0452D]]**

## 28. From the Prologue to Ezra

In the volume of Ezra, too, I said similar things in the preface, and after much else I added the following:

> “What I am about to introduce is entirely just. I have published something which is not found in Greek, or which is found differently from the way I translated it. Why do they tear the translator apart? Let them question the Hebrews, and, with the Hebrews themselves as authorities, let them either grant or deny credibility to my translation.

> “But it is another matter if, with what is called closed eyes, they wish to curse me and do not imitate the zeal and goodwill of the Greeks, who, after the Septuagint translators, when the Gospel of Christ was already shining, carefully read the Jewish and Ebionite interpreters of the ancient Law—namely Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion—and through Origen’s labor dedicated them to the churches in the *Hexapla* (*ἐν ἑξαπλοῖς*).

> **[Note: [Col. 0452D] Martianaeus omitted the words *ἐν ἑξαπλοῖς* here, although earlier, in his edition of the Preface itself, he had approved them, and Victorius himself showed that they ought to be restored.]**

> “How much more grateful my Latins ought to be that they see rejoicing Greece borrow something from them! For, first of all, it requires great expense and infinite difficulty to possess all the copies. Moreover, those who possess them but are ignorant of the Hebrew language will err more, since they will not know which of the many translators has spoken more truly.

> “This happened recently even to a certain very wise man among the Greeks, so that at times, abandoning the meaning of Scripture, he followed the error of one interpreter [variant: “of each individual interpreter”].

> **[Note: [Col. 0452D] Here Apollinaris of Laodicea is intended, whom he explicitly identifies near the end of this book.]**

> “But we who possess at least a small knowledge of the Hebrew language, who are not entirely lacking in Latin speech, and who are therefore better able to judge among the others and express in our own language what we ourselves understand…”

## 29. From the Prologue to Job

I shall pass to the Book of Job. After the edition of the Septuagint translators, which Origen marked with obeli and asterisks and which had long ago been given over into Latin speech, when I was translating it anew according to the Hebrew itself, I spoke as follows:

> “I am compelled, in each individual book of divine Scripture, to answer the curses of my opponents, who accuse my translation of being a criticism of the Septuagint translators—as though among the Greeks also Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion had not expressed either a word-for-word translation, or a sense-for-sense translation, or a mixed and moderately balanced kind formed from both;

> **[Note: [Col. 0452D] In the most ancient Vatican-Palatine manuscript, no. 24: “whether by word, sense, or both,” etc.]**

> “and as though Origen had not marked all the volumes of the Old Testament with obeli and asterisks, inserting into the ancient translation what had been added or taken from Theodotion, thereby proving that what was added had been lacking.

> “Let my detractors therefore learn to accept in full what they have accepted in part, or else let them erase my translation together with its asterisks. For it cannot be that, once they have seen that the translators omitted much, they will not also admit that they erred in certain matters—especially in Job, which would be mutilated in its greater part if you removed what has been added under the asterisks.

> **[Note: [Col. 0453D] The same manuscript, as also Martianaeus in the Preface itself, reads “have accepted more omissions,” etc.]**

> “And this is so only among the Greeks. Among the Latins, before the translation which we recently published with asterisks and obeli, nearly seven hundred or eight hundred verses were missing, so that the shortened, lacerated, and gnawed book displayed its ugliness publicly to its readers.”

After much else which I omit for the sake of brevity, I added the following at the end:

> “Let my dogs therefore hear that I labored over this volume not to criticize the ancient translation, but so that what in it is obscure, omitted, or certainly corrupted through the fault of scribes might be made clearer through our translation. We have learned the Hebrew language in part, and in Latin we have been worn down almost from its beginnings among grammarians, rhetoricians, and philosophers.

> “If, among the Greeks, after the Septuagint edition, when the Gospel of Christ was already shining, the Judaizing heretics Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion were received—although they concealed many mysteries of the Savior through deceitful translation—and if they are nevertheless contained in the *Hexapla* among the churches and explained by ecclesiastical men, how much less should I, a Christian born of Christian parents and bearing the standard of the cross on my forehead, be rejected by fastidious or malicious readers?

> “My purpose was to restore what had been omitted, correct what had been corrupted, and open the mysteries of the Church in pure and faithful speech.”

## 30. From the Prologue to the Psalter

The Psalter, too, which Rome had previously received through our labor as a very carefully emended work according to the Septuagint translators, I translated anew according to the Hebrew and fortified with a preface. In part of the prologue I spoke as follows:

> “Since recently, while disputing with a Hebrew, you brought forward from the Psalms certain testimonies concerning the Lord our Savior, and since he, wishing to mock you, maintained in almost every sentence that the Hebrew text did not contain them as you alleged from the Septuagint translators, you earnestly requested me to produce a new edition in Latin speech after Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion.

> “For you said that you were more troubled by the variety among translators and that, because of the love by which you are carried away, you would be content either with my translation or with my judgment.

> **[Note: [Col. 0453D] Codex Regio-Vaticanus, no. 11, reads: “he, wishing to mock you.”]**

> “Moved by you, to whom I cannot and ought not to deny what I can and ought to grant, I once again delivered myself to the barking of detractors. In our friendship, I preferred that you seek my strength rather than my willingness.

> **[Note: [Col. 0453D] In his edition of the Prologue, Martianaeus reads: “to whom I cannot deny what I can, and ought not to deny what I cannot,” followed by “again,” etc. The old edition, with which another Regina manuscript, no. 1286, agrees, reads: “to whom I owe what I can, and what I cannot,” etc.]**

> “Certainly I shall speak confidently and call many witnesses to this work: I changed nothing knowingly from the Hebrew truth.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0454D] The old edition reads, “knowingly in the matter of meaning.”]**

> “If my edition therefore differs anywhere from the ancient ones, question any Hebrew you please, and you will clearly see that I am being needlessly torn apart by rivals who prefer to seem to despise excellent things rather than to learn them.

> “Most perverse men! Since they are always seeking new pleasures and the seas near their gullets are not enough for them, why are they content with the old taste only in the study of Scripture?

> “I do not say this because I am attacking my predecessors or think that anything should be taken away from them. I formerly gave their most carefully emended translation to those who use my language. I say it because reading the Psalms of believers in the churches of Christ is one thing, and answering Jews who slander every individual word is another.”

## 31. From the Prologue to the Books of Solomon

When I was translating the books of Solomon, which I had formerly rendered into Latin according to the Septuagint with obeli and asterisks, from the Hebrew, and dedicating them to the holy bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus, I added the following at the end of my brief preface:

> “If anyone prefers the edition of the Septuagint translators, he has it from us, formerly emended. For we do not forge new things in such a way as to destroy the old.”

## 32. From the Prologue to Isaiah

I shall come also to Isaiah and append part of his prologue concerning the Septuagint translation. Since I called Isaiah more an evangelist than a prophet, because he pursued all the mysteries of Christ’s Church so fully that he seemed not to prophesy about the future but to weave a history of past events, I added this as well:

> “Hence I infer that at that time the Septuagint translators did not wish to reveal openly to the Gentiles the mysteries of their faith, lest they give what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine.

> **[Note: [Col. 0454D] Martianaeus reads “who,” although the holy women Paula and Eustochium are being addressed, and although he himself has in the preface, “when you [feminine plural] have read.”]**

> “When you read this edition, you will observe what they concealed. I am not unaware how much labor it requires to understand the Prophets, nor that no one can easily judge a translation unless he has first understood what he has read.

> “We too are exposed to the bites of many who, provoked by envy, despise what they cannot attain. Knowing this, and knowingly so, I put my hand into the flame.

> “Nevertheless, I ask this of fastidious readers: just as the Greeks, after the Septuagint translators, read Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion either for the sake of their own learning or so that they may understand the Septuagint more fully by comparison with them, so these readers should at least deign to have one translator after the earlier ones.

> “Let them read first and despise afterward, lest they appear to condemn what they do not know, not from judgment but from the presumption of hatred.”

### 33. On Daniel

As for Daniel, I shall answer briefly that I did not deny that he was a prophet—a prophet whom I immediately acknowledged to be such at the beginning of the Prologue—but wished to show what the Hebrews said and by what arguments they sought to prove their position. I also taught the reader that the churches of Christ read this prophet according to Theodotion, and not according to the translators of the Septuagint. If, in this book, I said that their edition differed greatly from the truth and had rightly been rejected by the judgment of the churches of Christ, the fault is not mine, who said it, but theirs who read it.

Four editions are readily available: those of Aquila, Symmachus, the Septuagint, and Theodotion. The churches read Daniel according to Theodotion. What fault have I committed if I followed the judgment of the churches? But when I report what the Hebrews customarily say against the story of Susanna, the hymn of the three boys, and the tales of Bel and the Dragon—which are not found in the Hebrew volume—the man who accuses me proves himself a foolish slanderer.

[Note: From this passage one can understand the disposition with which the holy Doctor, both in the Preface to Daniel and in the introduction to his explanation of the same prophet, collected the arguments and quibbles of the Jews and Porphyry against the story of Susanna, Bel, and the Dragon, as well as against the hymn of the three boys. For he was not, as some have thought, finally forced by Rufinus’s arguments—found below in Book II of the Invectives—to sing a recantation here; nor was he ever of the opinion that, against the judgment of the Church, he himself should argue that these tales (for even very genuine histories are sometimes called by that name) were spurious. See Africanus’s letter to Origen on this subject, and Origen’s reply to Africanus, from which Jerome had previously drawn no small amount.]

For I explained not what I myself thought, but what they are accustomed to say against us. If I did not answer their opinion in the Prologue, I was pursuing brevity, lest I should seem to be writing not a preface but a book; and I think I immediately added the reason, for I said: “It is not appropriate to discuss this at the present time.”

Otherwise, from the fact that I asserted that Porphyry had said many things against this prophet, and called as witnesses to the matter Methodius, Eusebius, and Apollinarius, who answered that madness in many thousands of lines, he could accuse me of failing to write in the brief preface against Porphyry’s books. Let the man who pursues such foolish chatter, and does not wish to accept the truth of the Hebrew Scripture, hear me proclaim freely: “No one is compelled to read what he does not wish to read.” I wrote for those who asked, not for the fastidious; freely, not for the envious; for the studious, not for the drowsy. And yet I wonder how he reads Theodotion, a heretic and a Judaizer, while disdaining the translation of whatever Christian sinner I may be.

### 34.

I ask you, dearest friend, who are so inquisitive that you know even my dreams and summon to accusation everything I have written over so many years without fear of future slander: how can you answer for your ignorance of the prefaces to the books you accuse? Those prefaces, by a kind of prophecy, answered the slander that was to come, fulfilling the proverb: “The antidote before the poison.”

What harm does our translation do to the churches? You bought, at great expense, as I know, the Jewish translators Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, as well as the fifth and sixth editions. Your Origen—and, lest you complain that I have struck you with figurative praise, our Origen (I call him ours because of his intellectual learning, not because of the truth of his doctrines)—in all his books, after the Septuagint translators, explains and expounds the translations of the Jews. Eusebius and Didymus do the same.

I pass over Apollinarius, who, with good zeal indeed but not according to knowledge, attempted to sew together the translations of all into a single garment, and to weave the sequence of Scripture not according to the rule of truth but according to his own judgment. The apostolic men use the Hebrew Scriptures; it is clear that the apostles and evangelists themselves did so.

Whenever the Lord and Savior recalls the ancient Scripture, he cites examples from the Hebrew volumes, as in the passage: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says: Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). And on the cross itself: “Eli, Eli, lema azabathani,” which is interpreted: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”—not as it is given by the Septuagint: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21:1)—and many similar examples.

Nor do we say this in order to disparage the translators of the Septuagint, but because the authority of the apostles and of Christ is greater; and wherever the Septuagint does not differ from the Hebrew, there the apostles took examples from their translation, while wherever they differ, they placed in Greek what they had learned from the Hebrews.

Therefore, just as I show that many things placed in the New Testament are taken from the ancient books but are not found in the Septuagint, and demonstrate that these things are written in Hebrew, so let my accuser show that something is written in the New Testament from the Septuagint translators that is not found in Hebrew—and the dispute is over.

### 35. Conclusion of the Work

From all this it is proved that the edition of the Septuagint translators, strengthened by the antiquity of its readers, is useful to the churches, since they hear that Christ is to come before he comes; and that the other interpreters are not to be rejected, because they translated not their own but divine books. It is also proved that my friend ought to receive from a Christian and a friend what he hastened to have copied for himself from the Jews at great expense.

I have exceeded the limits of a letter; and although I had already fixed my pen against a wicked heresy [Note: That is, the Origenist heresy; against it he had at that time written quite a few letters or treatises and was planning to produce more daily.], I was compelled to answer on my own behalf, awaiting the three volumes of my friend and held in total suspense by the heap of his accusations—with this exception: it is less difficult to guard against an acknowledged enemy than to endure a hidden enemy under the name of a friend.

[Note: The editions of Martianaeus and Vallarsius here have the title: “Here begins the final reply of Jerome the presbyter against the writings of Rufinus the presbyter.” EDITOR.—In the manuscript copies of Saint Ouen of Rouen: “Here begins the final reply against those books after their reading.” In the Corbie codex: “Here begins Jerome the presbyter’s invective against the writings of Rufinus the presbyter.” The Cluniacensis and Navarricus treat this as a letter, or an extended book separate from what precedes, and retain this title: “The Letter of Jerome against Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia”; or: “Jerome writes to Aletius against Rufinus.” From all these witnesses we have separated the true title of the work, removing the false references to Aletius. We thought it appropriate, however, to leave Erasmus’s argument intact, since it explains the matter sufficiently. MARTIAN.]

## BOOK THREE, OR THE FINAL REPLY OF SAINT JEROME AGAINST THE WRITINGS OF RUFINUS

[Col. 0457]

### 1. Having received Rufinus’s books of invective, he replies

Having read the letter of your prudence, in which you attack me and now challenge to a reply the man whom you once praised—whom you called your true colleague and brother—and terrify me with accusations, I understood that Solomon’s saying has been fulfilled in you: “In the mouth of the fool is the rod of insult” (Prov. 14:3). And: “A fool does not receive the words of wisdom unless you say what is in his heart” (Prov. 18:2). And Isaiah says: “The fool will speak foolishly, and his heart will understand vanity, so that he may complete iniquities and speak falsehood against God” (Isa. 32:6).

For what need was there to send volumes of accusation and bring curses into the open, if, in the final part of your letter, [Note: Apparently after bringing an accusation before a magistrate; hence below: “You terrify me with your swords and threaten an accusation not now ecclesiastical but judicial.”] after threatening me with death, you frighten me from daring to answer your accusations—or rather, your praises? You both praise and accuse the same person, and from one spring proceed both sweet and bitter waters.

Therefore I beg you to display first the modesty and shame that you demand from me; and you who accuse another of lying, stop lying yourself. I cause no one scandal, nor am I presently your accuser. For I do not consider what you deserve, but what is fitting for me; and I fear the Savior’s saying: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Mark 9:41). And: “Woe to the world because of scandals. For scandals must come; but woe to the person through whom the scandal comes” (Matt. 18:7).

I too could heap falsehoods upon you and say that I had either heard or seen things that no one else had noticed, so that among the ignorant shamelessness might be considered truth and frenzy steadfastness. But far be it from me to imitate you and do in myself what I censure in you. Let the man who can commit filthy acts speak filth: “The evil man brings forth evil things from the evil treasury of his heart. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12:35; Luke 6:45).

For the present, count it as gain that your former friend, now accused by you, does not wish to cast shameful things in your face. And I say this not because I fear the swords of your accusation, but because I would rather be accused than accuse, and suffer injury than inflict it, knowing the Apostle’s command: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath; for it is written” (Deut. 32:35): “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord. But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Rom. 12:19–21). For the person who avenges himself does not deserve the Lord’s vengeance.

### 2. The apostles disagreed while preserving their friendship

Yet before I answer your letter, I wish to remonstrate with you, most ancient of monks [Note: “Most ancient of monks.” I read not *venustissime* (“most handsome”), but *vetustissime* (“most ancient”) in all the manuscripts; Rufinus was not a handsome monk, but an old one—that is, one from his earliest years. MARTIAN.—Victorius reads, “Yet before I answer,” and then *venastissime monachorum* for *vetustissime*, a reading which he nevertheless approves.], good presbyter, imitator of Christ: can you kill your brother, whom, if you hate him so much, you are a murderer? Did you learn this from the Savior, that when struck on one cheek you should offer the other? He himself answered his assailant: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23).

You threaten me with death, which even serpents can inflict. Death belongs to everyone; murder belongs to the worst. What then? Unless you kill me, will I be immortal? Rather, I am grateful that you make virtue out of necessity.

Did not the apostles also disagree while preserving their friendship, when Paul and Barnabas became angry over John, who was called Mark, and the journey separated those whom the Gospel of Christ joined? Did not the same Paul withstand Cephas to his face because he was not walking rightly in the Gospel? And yet he calls him his predecessor and a pillar of the Church, and explains the preaching with him, lest he should be running or have run in vain. [Note: Here Victorius restored the words “with him,” from Paul’s testimony: “I laid before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles,” etc.]

Do not even free persons in religion disagree with their parents, and wives with their husbands, while preserving reverence? If you hold what we hold, why do you hate us? If you believe otherwise, why do you wish to kill us? Is anyone who disagrees with you to be killed?

I call Jesus, the witness of my conscience, to testify that I wished, at the request of the holy pope Chromatius, to keep silent about these matters, to put an end to our quarrels, and to overcome evil with good. But because you threaten me with destruction unless I remain silent, I am compelled to answer, lest by my silence I seem to acknowledge the crime and you interpret my gentleness as a sign of a bad conscience.

### 3. The words of Rufinus’s letter

This is your true dilemma—not produced by the dialectical art that you do not know, but by the workshop and deliberation of executioners. If I remain silent, I shall be a criminal; if I answer, I shall be a slanderer. Thus you both forbid me and compel me to answer. In this I shall exercise restraint, so that I may both refute the charges and avoid insult.

For who would not fear a man who is prepared to kill? I shall follow the course of your proposition, leaving the rest to those highly learned books which I refuted before I had read them.

You say that “you sent your accusation only to those who had been injured by my words, and not to more people, because one ought to speak to Christians for edification, not for ostentation.” And from where, I ask, did the report of your books reach me? Who spread them through Rome? Who through Italy? Who through the islands of Dalmatia? If they were hidden in your chests and those of your friends, how did your crimes come to me?

And you dare to say that you speak as a Christian, not for ostentation but for edification, although, an old man yourself, you invent about an old man things that a murderous robber would not say about another robber, a prostitute about a harlot, or a jester about a mime. You bring forth mountains of accusations against me and sharpen, long beforehand, the swords with which you intend to strike my throat.

Did your Cerealian and anabasian messengers therefore run through the various provinces so that they could read my praises? So that they could recite your panegyric in corners and streets and in the weaving shops of little women? This is your holy modesty, this is Christian edification. You are so restrained and so chaste that crowds arriving from the West have reported your curses to me—so accurately and consistently that I was compelled to answer not your writings, which I had not yet read, but the opinions about those writings, and to catch the darts of falsehood flying throughout the world upon the shield of truth.

[Note: Victorius derives the name from the story of Ceres, who is said to have pursued her daughter Proserpina, after her abduction, everywhere, even among the dead. He explains *anabasii* from the Greek verb ἀνάβασις, meaning “ascent,” because they were swift after mounting chariots or horses.]

### 4. The monk Rufinus’s agent stole Epiphanius’s letter

Your letter continues: “Do not buy my secretary for a large amount of gold, as your friends did with my rough drafts concerning *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*—not yet corrected, not yet brought into a polished form—so that they could falsify them more easily, since no one or very few possessed them. Freely accept from me the codex that you would have desired to purchase at great cost.”

Are you not ashamed of such an introduction? [Note: Erasmus substituted *paroenii*, meaning drunken debauchery, from the Greek *παροινία*; quite ingeniously.] Would I buy your secretary with gold? And who is such a great person that he would dare to contend in wealth with Croesus and Darius, and not fear Demaratus suddenly appearing or Crassus? Have you become so hardened in the face that you place your hope in a lie, think that you can be protected by a lie, and suppose that whatever you invent must be believed about you?

Who stole from the bedroom of your brother Eusebius at Bethlehem the laudatory letter addressed to you? By whose contrivance, and through whose agents, was the codex found at the lodging of the holy Fabiola and of the Christian and prudent man Oceanus—a codex that they had never seen? Or do you think yourself innocent for that reason, if you transfer whatever belongs to you onto others? Whoever has offended you, however simple or innocent he may be, will immediately become a criminal? For you have the means by which Danaë’s chastity was overcome, by which Gehazi preferred his master’s sanctity, and because of which Judas betrayed his Lord.

### 5. He does not approve a Christian’s accusation against a Christian. He defends Eusebius of Cremona. The errors of the book *Periarchon*

“Let us nevertheless see what my friend has falsified from your rough drafts, not yet corrected and not yet brought into a polished form; and for that reason they were more easily falsified, since no one or very few possessed them.”

I have written this before, and now, with God as my witness, I protest the same thing: I did not approve his accusation, nor that of any Christian against a Christian. For what need is there to bring into the scandal and ruin of many what you could correct or amend privately?

But since each person lives according to his own temper, and a friend is not immediately master of another’s will, just as I censure even a true accusation, so I do not accept the falsification of the rough drafts by a holy man. For what could a Latin have altered in a Greek translation? Or what could he have removed or added in the books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, where everything is so interwoven and one part depends upon another that whatever you wish to remove or add immediately appears like a patch on a garment?

Therefore do yourself what you advise me to do: assume at least a little human, if not Christian, shame, lest, with your conscience despised and trampled underfoot, you think yourself cleansed by words when circumstances press you.

If Eusebius bought the uncorrected rough drafts in order to falsify them, produce your own copies, which have not been falsified; and if you prove that there is nothing heretical in them, then he will be held guilty of falsification. However much you alter or correct them, you will not prove them Catholic. [Note: That is, the rough drafts. Martianaeus, however, following Erasmus, reads “Catholic.”] For if the error were in the wording or in a few meanings, the bad material could be cut away and good material substituted. But when the entire argument is uniform—that all rational creatures, which had fallen by their own will, are afterward to return to a single state, so that again from the same beginning there may be other falls—what can you correct unless you change everything? If you wish to do that, you will no longer be interpreting another person’s books but composing your own.

I do not understand what sort of argument this is: “The rough drafts,” he says, “were uncorrected and not yet brought into a polished form; therefore they were more easily falsified by Eusebius.” Either I am duller than I should be, or this seems to me quite foolish and obtuse.

If the rough drafts were not yet corrected or brought into a polished form, their error will not be attributed to Eusebius but to your delay and slowness, since you postponed correcting them. He will be guilty only of this: that he quickly disseminated your writings among the public, although you had decided to correct them gradually.

But if, as you claim, Eusebius falsified them, why do you complain and allege that uncorrected and not-yet-polished writings burst into public view? Corrected and uncorrected writings alike are susceptible to the same falsification.

“No one possessed the books,” you say, “or very few did.” What great contradiction in a single statement! If no one possessed them, how were they in the possession of a few? If a few possessed them, why do you falsely say that no one possessed them? When you say that they were in the possession of a few, and by your own admission it is disproved that no one possessed them, where is your complaint that your secretary was bought with gold?

Name the secretary; state how much gold was given, where, through whom, and to whom. Surely you have cast away your betrayer from you and separated the guilty party in so great a crime from your company.

Take care lest the truth be rather that copies were given by those few friends of yours, Eusebius and the others, and that they agree and correspond with one another so closely that not even a point differs between one and another.

Further, what prudence is it to give others a copy that you had not yet corrected? The rough drafts had not been polished, and others already possessed the errors that you intended to correct. Do you not perceive that the lie does not hold together?

And what did it profit you at the critical moment to evade the judgments of the bishops, when you are shown to have been exposed and refuted by your own words? From this it is clear, in accordance with the saying of the celebrated orator Cicero, that you have the will to lie but not the art of fabrication.

### 6. What is the difference between “to compare” and “to buy”?

I shall follow the order of the letter and append the very words in which you spoke:

“Your eloquence, as you say, I admit that I praised in my Preface; and even now I would praise it, unless you made it hateful by your many boasts, contrary to the judgment of your Tullius.”

Where did I boast of my eloquence, when I did not gladly accept even the praise given by you? Or do you say this because you do not wish to be flattered by subtle praise? You will be openly accused, so that, having rejected the man who praises you, you may feel the man who accuses you.

As for your ignorance, I was not so foolish as to criticize it, since no one can accuse you more powerfully than you yourself do when you write. But I wished to show your fellow students, who did not learn letters with you, what you have achieved during thirty years in the East: you, an *ἀγράμματος συγγραφεύς*—an illiterate writer—who regard shamelessness, loquacity, and cursing everyone as signs of a good conscience.

[Note: Taken from Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 1: “A man,” he says, “of the world, and by nature also a heretic, turbulent besides, who thinks loquacity eloquence, counts shamelessness steadfastness, and judges that cursing individuals is the duty of a good conscience.” See also the beginning of the book *Against Helvidius*.]

Nor, as you say, do I apply rods to you, nor do I seek to teach my “old pupil” (*athenogeronta*, “an old disciple”) letters with whip and blows. But because none of us can endure the thunderbolt [variant: “flood”] of your eloquence and learning, and because you pierce our eyes with the sharpness of your intellect to such an extent that you think everyone envious of you, we all strive eagerly to suppress you, lest, if you once gain first place in writing and stand upon the citadel of eloquence, none of us who wish to know something may be allowed even to mutter.

I am a philosopher, rhetorician, grammarian, dialectician, Hebrew, Greek, Latin—a man of three languages.

[Note: An uncertain author, in a poem praising Jerome:

“First Latin in tongue; but, wondrous to say,

You gave Greek and Hebrew Chaldean words,

Now wise, and desiring Jesus . . . . .”]

In this way you too will be bilingual, since you possess such knowledge of Greek and Latin speech that Greeks think you Latin and Latins think you Greek; and Pope Epiphanius is *πεντάγλωττος* [manuscripts: *πεντάγλωσσος*], “five-tongued,” because he speaks against you and your Amasius—Origen—in five languages.

At the same time I marvel with what audacity you dare say this against a man of so many arts: “You who keep watch with the eyes of so many disciplines—how can you be granted pardon if you make a mistake, and not be covered by perpetual silence of shame?”

When I read this, and thought that I had slipped somewhere in speech—for “whoever does not sin in word is perfect” (James 3:2)—and suspected that he was about to expose some of my faults, he suddenly added: “Two days before the bearer of this letter departed, the things that you declaimed against me came into my hands.”

Where, then, is your threat when you say, “How can you be granted pardon if you make a mistake, and not be covered by perpetual silence of shame?” Unless perhaps, because of the shortness of time, you were able to arrange them in order; or perhaps you intended to hire someone from the learned to search through my little works for the jewels of your eloquence.

Earlier you wrote: “Freely accept from me the codex that you would have greatly desired to purchase, and now you speak through the artifices of humility. I wished to imitate you; but because the man returning to you was hurrying, I preferred to write a few words to you rather than write more broadly to others concerning your curses.”

Meanwhile, you boldly enjoy your ignorance. For you once admitted this, saying: “Your criticism of a few things was superfluous, since what we have professed is understood to apply to everything.”

Nor will I criticize you for using “compared” for “bought,” since comparison belongs to equals, while purchase is the counting out of a price; nor will I criticize the *περισσολογία*—excessive verbosity—of the most wretched expression, “while the man returning to you was hurrying.”

I shall answer only your meanings, and I shall prove you not at all a solecist or barbarian, but a liar, deceitful, and shameless.

[Note: Victorius, following the manuscripts, reads *fruitor*, a word expressing mockery and irritation.]

[Note: The same Victor. reads: “And I shall prove you in every respect by no means a solecist,” and so forth.]

### 7. In the Preface to the book *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*

If you write a letter to me only to admonish me and wish me corrected, so that I may not cause scandal to others and others may not be slaughtered by other madmen, why do you write books against me to others and scatter them throughout the world to be read through your agents?

Where is your syllogism by which you attempt to ensnare me [Note: Earlier the text was corruptly printed: “if to those to whom …”], when you say: “Whom were you seeking to correct in this, excellent teacher? Those to whom you write, if they had committed no offense; or me, whom you accuse, if you had not written to me?”

I shall answer you in your own words: Whom were you seeking to correct, ignorant teacher? Those who had not sinned, or me, to whom you had not written?

You think your readers are stupid and that no one understands your prudence—or rather, your malice, by which the serpent was wiser than all the beasts in paradise—so that you demand a private admonition from me while pursuing me with a public accusation. And you are not ashamed to call your accusation an Apology?

You complain that I oppose a shield to your dagger, and, like a very religious and saintly man, you put on the role of humility and say: “If I had erred, why do you write to others and not rebuke me personally?”

I shall turn this very question back upon you: Whatever you accuse me of not having done, why did you not do it yourself? It would be as if someone were striking another with fists and kicks, and, when the other wished to resist, said to him: “Have you not been commanded: ‘Whoever strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also’?” (Matt. 5:39).

What command, good man, have you received to beat me, gouge out my eye, and, if I move even slightly, sing the commandments of the Gospel to me?

Would you like to know all the twisted turns of your sophistries and the tricks of your little foxes that dwell in the walls, of which Ezekiel speaks: “Like foxes in the desert are your prophets, Israel” (Ezek. 13:4)? Listen to what you have done.

You praised me in your Preface in such a way that your praises were brought against me, and unless I had declared myself unworthy of so great a praiser, I would have been judged a heretic. After I rejected the accusations—that is, your praises—and answered, without envy toward your name, the accusations rather than the accuser; and in order to prove myself Catholic, though defamed by you, attacked the heretics—you became angry and raged, and forged brilliant books against me.

After you had handed them over to everyone to read and recite, writings came to me one after another from Italy, from the city of Rome, and from Dalmatia, in which you, my former praiser, had adorned me with eulogies.

### 8. He cleared himself of the suspicion of heresy

I confess that I immediately answered the charges and tried with all my strength to prove that I was not a heretic. I sent these very books of my Apology to those whom you had wounded, so that your poisons might be followed by our antidote.

For this offense you send me both your earlier books and your recent letter, full of insults and accusations. What do you want me to do, good friend? Should I remain silent? I shall seem to acknowledge the crime. Should I speak? You terrify me with your swords and threaten an accusation not now ecclesiastical but judicial.

What have I done? What have I deserved? In what have I injured you? Because I denied that I was a heretic? Because I considered myself unworthy of your praises? Because I openly described the frauds and perjuries of heretics?

What is that to you, who boast that you are both Catholic and truthful, yet more willingly accuse me than defend yourself? Is my defense your accusation? Or will you be unable to be orthodox unless you prove me a heretic?

What benefit do you gain from my association? Or what kind of prudence is this? Accused by others, you accuse another. You are attacked by one person; turning your back on him, you provoke against yourself someone who is at rest.

### 9. The old men Rufinus and Jerome. In his youth he praised Origen’s learning

I call Jesus the Mediator to witness that I have descended unwillingly and reluctantly to these words [variant: “to answer”], and that, unless you had provoked me, I would always have remained silent. In short, do not accuse, and I shall cease defending myself.

For what edification is there for those listening when two old men fight with one another over heretics, especially when both wish to appear Catholic? Let us set aside the patronage of heretics, and there will be no dispute between us.

With the same fervor with which we once praised Origen, let us now condemn him, condemned as he is throughout the world. Let us join right hands and unite our minds; let us follow with eager step the two *τροπαιοφόροι*, “triumph-bearers,” of East and West—Theophilus and Anastasius.

We erred when young; let us correct ourselves in old age. If you are my brother, rejoice that I have been corrected. If I am your friend, I ought to congratulate you on your conversion. As long as there is quarrel between us, we will seem to be embracing the true faith from necessity rather than from free will. Our enmity deprives us of one another’s testimony to genuine repentance.

If we believe one thing, if we both will and reject the same things—for even Catiline bears witness that firm friendships arise from this—if we hate heretics equally and condemn the former error alike, why do we turn our weapons against one another when we attack and defend the same things?

Forgive me for praising Origen’s learning and devotion to Scripture in my youth, before I had fully understood his heresy; and I shall forgive you for having written an Apology for his books in your gray-haired old age.

### 10.

You testify that my little books came into your hands two days before you wrote your letter to us, and that for this reason you had no leisure to answer; otherwise, if you had spoken against us after deliberation and preparation, you would have seemed to hurl thunderbolts rather than accusations.

And who will believe you, most truthful man, like a merchant of Eastern goods who had to sell the merchandise carried from here and buy there what he would bring back here, that you were in Aquileia for only two days, so that you were compelled to dictate a letter against us hurriedly and extemporaneously?

For are your books, which you polished for three years, more eloquent? Unless perhaps there was no one at hand to correct your foolish chatter; and therefore the whole course of your speech, without the art of Pallas, is cut up by ridges and chasms of faults.

The lie about the time is so obvious that I will not say you could have answered my writings, but that you could not even have read them in two days. From this it is clear either that you wrote that letter over several days, as the elegance of its style demonstrates, or, if it was hurried dictation [variant: “composition”], that you are negligent—since, if you are such a poor extemporaneous writer, you must be still worse when you have time to prepare.

[Note: It may perhaps be written without the question mark, as in Victorius; but, in addition, with the negative particle, as I think, the words are no more lucid, as the following context indicates. Otherwise, Father Martianaeus rather unhappily understood Jerome here to be calling Rufinus himself a merchant and mocking his business dealings and greed.]

### 11. The custom and rule of commentaries

I do not sufficiently understand what you mean when you evade the issue and say that you translated from the Greek what I had first translated into Latin—unless perhaps you are still accusing me concerning the Commentaries on Ephesians, and, as though nothing had yet been answered to you about this, you harden the shamelessness of your face and, with your ears stopped, refuse to receive the words of the enchanter.

In the Commentaries—both those and the others—we explained both our own opinion and that of others, openly acknowledging which things were heretical and which Catholic. This is the custom of commentaries and the rule of interpreters: to pursue various opinions in the exposition and explain what seems right either to themselves or to others.

This is done not only by interpreters of the sacred Scriptures but also by expositors of secular literature, in both the Latin and Greek languages.

You cannot make the same claim concerning the books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*. Your own Preface will convict you, for in it you promise that, once the bad material has been cut away and what had been added by heretics removed, the best material will remain. Thus whatever good or evil you say there will no longer be attributed to the person whose work you are translating, but to you, who translated it—unless perhaps you ought to have corrected the errors of the heretics and brought Origen’s evils into the open.

But on this matter, since you send us back to the codex, we answered you before we had read your writings.

### 12. An Absurd Matter and a Laughable One. The Roman Faith Does Not Admit Such Deceptions

Regarding Pamphilus’s book, I experienced—perhaps—a matter not ridiculous, as you write, but ridiculous: after asserting that it belonged to Eusebius, not Pamphilus, I finally said that I too had believed for many years that it was Pamphilus’s, and that I had borrowed a copy of this volume from you. See how much I fear your laughter, since even now I repeat the same thing.

We received from your manuscript what we took to be a copy of Pamphilus’s work. I believed a Christian, and I believed a monk; I did not think that you could fabricate so great a crime. Afterwards, however, because of your translation—which stirred up throughout the whole world the controversy against Origen—I became more diligent in seeking copies, and in the Caesarean Library I found six volumes of the *Apology on behalf of Origen* (Ἀπολογίαι ὑπὲρ Ὠριγένους).

[Note: Ἀπολογίας ὑπέρ. Erasmus read this Greek without the preposition; Marianus, however, read περί instead of ὑπέρ, although the former is not found in the manuscript copies. MARTIAN.]

When I had read these, I first discovered that book which you alone published under the name of the martyr: on the Son and the Holy Spirit, with most of the blasphemies altered into an acceptable sense.

[Note: The old edition perhaps more correctly reads: “which you alone,” that is, merely the first book.]

I do not know whether Didymus, or you, or someone else did this. Yet you are most clearly convicted of having done the same thing in the books *On First Principles* (περὶ Ἀρχῶν), especially since that same Eusebius—as I have already shown in the two preceding books—writes that Pamphilus published no work of his own.

Tell us, then, from whom you received the copy. Do not name some dead person merely to evade the charge, so that, when you cannot produce the author, you may bring forward someone unable to answer. But if that little stream has its source in your own chests, you do not doubt what follows, even if I remain silent.

Still, let us suppose that the title of this book and the author’s name were altered by some other admirer of Origen. Why did you translate it into Latin? Obviously so that, on the testimony of the martyr, everyone would believe Origen’s writings, after first being fortified by the authority and testimony of so great an author. Nor was the most learned man’s *Apology* sufficient for you, unless you also wrote a separate volume in his defense. Having disseminated these works widely, you now safely translate the books *On First Principles* from Greek, and recommend those very books in your Preface, saying that some passages in them were corrupted by heretics, which you corrected by reading Origen’s other books.

You praise me as well, so that none of my friends might contradict you. You proclaim me Origen’s herald (κήρυξ, “proclaimer”); you raise my eloquence to the heavens in order to cast my faith into the mud. You call me brother and colleague, and confess yourself an imitator of my work. Yet although you boast of the seventy homilies of Origen translated by me, and of several volumes on the Apostle, in which I so carefully polished everything “that the Latin reader would find nothing in them contrary to the Catholic faith,” you now denounce those same books as heretical. With your style reversed, you accuse the man whom you had praised because you considered him your associate, since you see him to be an enemy of your perfidy.

Who among the two of us is slandering the martyr? I, who say that he was not a heretic and did not write the book criticized by everyone; or you, who published the volume of an Arian under the martyr’s name after altering its title? Is the scandal you have caused in Greece not enough, unless you also thrust it into Latin ears and, insofar as you can, deform the illustrious martyr by your translation?

You acted with another intention—not to accuse me, but to defend through us Origen’s writings. Nevertheless, know that the Roman faith, praised by the apostolic voice, does not accept such tricks; and that, fortified by Paul’s authority, it cannot be changed even if an angel should announce something different from what was preached once for all.

Therefore, brother, whether the book was falsified by you, as many think; or by someone else, as you may perhaps try to persuade us, and you rashly believed it to be the martyr’s work, change its title and free Roman simplicity from so great a danger.

[Note: Victorius: “as perhaps you will try to persuade,” etc.]

It is not to your advantage that so distinguished a martyr should be judged a heretic, or that one who shed his blood for Christ should be proved opposed to Christ’s faith. Say rather: “I found the book and thought it belonged to the martyr.” Do not fear repentance. I shall no longer press you, nor ask from whom you received it. Name some dead person, or say that you bought it in the street from an unknown man. We are not seeking your condemnation, but your conversion.

It is better that you should have erred than that the martyr should have been a heretic. For the present, extricate your foot somehow from this fetter. At the future judgment, you will see what answer you can give to the martyr’s complaints against you.

### 13. A Slander Concerning the Commentaries. Apollinarius and Didymus Are Different

You also raise an objection which no one makes and refute an accusation which no one brings. For you say that you read in my writings: “Tell me, who permitted you, when translating, to remove some things, alter some things, and add some things?” Immediately you answer yourself and speak against me:

“Here is my answer to you: I ask, who permitted you, in your Commentaries, to write some things from Origen, some from Apollinarius, and some from yourself, rather than writing everything from Origen—or from yourself, or from someone else?”

Meanwhile, while doing something else, you have revealed against yourself a most serious charge and forgotten the old proverb: “Liars ought to have good memories.” For you say that in my Commentaries I inserted some things from Origen, some from Apollinarius, and some from myself.

If, then, the passages I attributed under other names belong to Apollinarius and Origen, how can you charge me in your books when I write, “Another says this; someone suspects this,” on the ground that that “other” and that “someone” are myself?

There is a great difference between Apollinarius and Didymus in explanation, style, and doctrine. When I set out different opinions in one chapter, am I to be thought to follow contradictory views? But more on this elsewhere.

### 14. What He Condemns in the Translation of the Book *On First Principles*. Translators of Origen

Now I ask you: who accused you of either removing, adding, or altering something from Origen, and questioned you as though you were hanging on the torture-horse, asking whether the things you translated were good or bad?

You pretend innocence in vain, attempting by a foolish question to weaken the real inquiry. I did not accuse you of translating Origen according to your own will. I did the same myself, and before me Victorinus, Hilary, and Ambrose did so as well. Rather, I accused you of strengthening a heretical translation by the testimony of your Preface.

You force me to repeat the same things and retrace my own lines. For in that same Prologue you say that you cut out what had been added by heretics and replaced it with good material. If you removed the heretics’ bad material, then what you left or added must belong either to Origen or to you, since you plainly inserted it as good.

Yet you will not be able to deny that much in these books is bad. “What does that have to do with me?” you will say. “Charge it to Origen; I changed only what had been added by heretics.”

Explain, then, why you removed the heretics’ bad material but left Origen’s intact. Is it not obvious that you condemned some of Origen’s errors under the name of the heretics, while accepting others because you judged them not bad but good and consistent with your own faith?

These are the matters about which I asked whether they were good or bad: the things you praised in your Preface and confessed remained as excellent after the worst had been cut away. I placed you on the torture-horse of genuine argument, so that if you call them good, you will be proved a heretic; but if bad, you will immediately hear: “Why, then, did you praise what is bad in your Preface?”

Nor did I add the point which you slyly pretend was my accusation: “Why did you translate what was bad for the knowledge of Latin readers?” For sometimes it is the duty not of a teacher but of one who warns against something to display evils: so that the reader may beware of errors, not follow them; so that he may recognize and reject what, because it is unfamiliar, may occasionally seem marvelous.

And after all this you dare to say that I am the author of such writings, while you, as translator, did more than a translator wherever you could correct something, and were merely a translator wherever you could not. You would be right to say this if your books *On First Principles* did not contain the Preface.

Hilary did the same when translating Origen’s Homilies, so that both the good and the bad might be attributed not to the translator but to their author. If you had not said that you cut out the worst and left the best, you might somehow have escaped from the mud.

This is what demolishes the tricks of your small talent and prevents you from escaping, bound on both sides. Do not abuse the reader’s simplicity so greatly, and do not think all who will read your writing so dull that they will not laugh when, having allowed wounds to fester, you apply plasters to a healthy body.

### 15. On the Resurrection

We have already learned from your *Apology* what you think concerning the resurrection of the flesh: “With no member amputated and no part of the body cut away.” This is your pure and open confession, which you assert was accepted by all the bishops of Italy.

I would believe you if this book—not Pamphilus’s—did not make me doubt you. Yet I wonder how Italy approved what Rome rejected: that bishops accepted what the Apostolic See condemned.

### 16. Two Letters of Theophilus Rendered into Latin by Jerome

You also write that I indicated in a letter that Pope Theophilus had recently issued an exposition of the faith which had not yet reached you, and you promise that whatever he wrote, you would follow.

I do not know that I wrote this, nor that I ever sent such a letter. But you agree to uncertainties for this reason: to avoid certainties, and not to be bound to assent to things whose future character you do not know.

I translated two of his letters against Origen and his disciples—the synodical and the paschal letters—and others against Apollinarius and that same Origen, over approximately these two years, and I gave them to be read by people of our language for the edification of the Church. I do not know that I translated any other of his works.

[Note: We first brought this letter out of the darkness in the preceding volume, where it bears the number 92.]

Yet you, who say that you follow Pope Theophilus’s judgment in everything, must be careful that your teachers and fellow disciples do not hear this, and that you do not offend very many people who call me a robber and you a martyr—lest he become angry with you who, when sending letters to you against Pope Epiphanius, urged you to remain in the truth of the faith and not change your judgment out of fear.

[Note: Isidorus the presbyter had written similar things to John of Jerusalem and his followers against Saint Epiphanius before he came as Theophilus’s envoy, as noted above in the book against John.]

That letter is held by those to whom it was delivered in autograph form.
