[Note: Not complete, as Victorius explains; understand “the original,” or “written in the author’s own hand.” Sidonius, *Letters* IX.11, used *holographa membranae* in this sense, and *holographum testamentum* for a will written entirely by the testator himself, to omit many other examples.]

After this, in your customary manner, you say: “As to what you had said above, I shall satisfy you even in your frenzy. Now you say, ‘What do you think? Do you have anything further with which to stretch the sinews of your loquacity?’”

And you are indignant if I accuse you of speaking offensively, although, as an ecclesiastical writer, you adopt the obscenities of comedies and the jests of prostitutes and their lovers.

### 17. On the Bishop Paul

Moreover, when you ask when I began to follow Pope Theophilus’s judgment and entered into communion of faith with him, you answer yourself:

“I believe it was then, when you defended Paul, whom he had condemned, with the greatest effort and every available means; when you urged him, through an imperial rescript, to recover the priesthood which he had lost by episcopal judgment.”

I shall not answer on my own behalf before speaking about the injuries done to others. What humanity or mercy is it to insult other people’s misfortunes and expose everyone else’s wounds? Did that Samaritan teach you to carry the half-dead man to the inn, pour oil into his wounds, and promise payment to the innkeeper? Did he teach you that the recovered sheep, the found drachma, and the prodigal son were received?

Suppose I had injured you and, as you say, provoked you by certain goads to the madness of insults. What had the man who was lying hidden deserved, that you should uncover his scar and tear open healed skin with unexpected pain? Even if he deserved insults, ought you to have inflicted them?

Either I am mistaken, or this is true, as many loudly proclaim: you are pursuing the enemies of the Origenists in him and, under cover of attacking one person, are raging against both.

If you delight in Pope Theophilus’s judgments and think it sacrilegious to overturn the decrees of bishops, what do you say about the others whom he himself condemned? What do you say about Pope Anastasius, whom—as you claim—no one can regard as having been capable of injuring either an innocent man or one who was absent, since he was the priest of so great a city?

I do not say this because I judge the bishops’ decisions or wish their decrees to be rescinded, but because each person should do at his own peril what seems right to him, and should know for himself how his own judgment ought to be judged.

In our monastery hospitality is dear to us, and we receive all who come to us with a cheerful expression of kindness. For we fear that Mary and Joseph may find no place in the inn, and that Jesus may say to us, when excluded: “I was a guest, and you did not receive me” (Matthew 25:43).

We receive no heretics—the only people you receive. Our purpose is to wash the feet of those who come, not to investigate their merits.

Remember his confession, brother, and the breast cut by scourges. Remember the prison, darkness, exile, and the mines, and you will not be indignant that a passing traveler was received as a guest. Do we seem rebellious to you because, in Christ’s name, we offer a cup of cold water to those who thirst?

### 18. The Heretics’ Faction Driven Out. Theophilus Praised

Do you wish to know why we ought to love him more, and you ought to hate him more? The faction of the heretics, recently driven out of Egypt and Alexandria, went to Jerusalem and wished to join itself to him, so that those whose suffering was one might also have one common accusation.

He rejected, despised, and cast them away, saying that he was not an enemy of the faith and was not taking up wars against the Church; that what he had attempted earlier had proceeded from grief, not perfidy; that he had not sought another person’s innocence but wished to prove his own.

Do you think it impious that an imperial rescript should follow the judgments of bishops? Let the one who deserved it know what that rescript was like. What do you think of those who, after being condemned, besiege palaces and, forming a wedge, persecute Christ’s faith in one man?

As witnesses to my communion and to that of Pope Theophilus, I shall call no one else except the very man whom you pretend was injured by me. You know that his letters were always sent to me, even at the time when you were forbidding them to be returned to me; and that, by sending messengers every day, you repeatedly claimed that his enemy was our friend and most intimate associate. You lied about the things you now write so shamelessly, in order to stir up his hatred against us, so that the pain of an injury might become an oppression of the faith.

But that prudent man, possessed of apostolic wisdom, proved by time and circumstances both our attitude toward him and your plots against us. If, as you write, my disciples stirred up plots against you at Rome and, while you slept, stole your uncorrected sheets, who stirred up Pope Theophilus against the rebels in Egypt? Who stirred up the imperial decrees? Who obtained the agreement of the world on this matter?

You boast that you have been Theophilus’s hearer and disciple from youth, although, before he became bishop, his innate humility never allowed him to teach, and after he became bishop here, you were not in Alexandria.

And you dare say, in reproach of me: “I neither accuse nor change my teachers.” If this is true, you make your conversion suspect to me.

[Note: Other manuscripts read *conversione*, “conversion,” which is not itself an unsuitable reading, since Rufinus had among his teachers at least one heretic—Didymus, for example, whom he heard at Alexandria. Therefore, unless he accused them or withdrew from their heresies, he would make his conversion to Christ and the faith he received at his conversion suspect. Nevertheless, *conversationis*, “way of life,” is more appealing both in wording and in sense.]

For I do not condemn my teachers, as you accuse me of doing; rather, I fear Isaiah’s warning: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isaiah 5:20).

But while you drink both the honeyed words and the poisons of your teachers, you have departed from the apostolic Teacher, who teaches that neither an angel nor himself is to be followed if they should err in the faith.

### 19. A Slander Concerning Vigilantius

I do not know what you dream up in connection with the name of Vigilantius. Where did I write that he was stained by heretical communion at Alexandria? Produce the book—you will find it nowhere at all.

Yet with the same license, or rather shamelessness, in lying, by which you think everyone will believe your words, you add: “When you applied a testimony from Scripture to him so insultingly that I do not dare repeat it in my own mouth.”

You do not dare repeat it, yet by remaining silent you accuse him more strongly. Since you have nothing to bring against me, you pretend modesty, so that the reader may think you are sparing me, although by lying you spared not even your own soul.

What is that testimony from Scripture which cannot come out of your exceedingly modest mouth? Or what can be mentioned in the sacred books that is disgraceful? If you are ashamed to say it, at least write it down, so that your own words may convict us of insolence.

To say nothing of the rest, I shall prove from this one chapter that you possess an iron forehead for deceit. See how much I fear your accusation. If you produce what you threaten, everything that belongs to you will become mine.

I answered you concerning Vigilantius. For he accused the same things which you afterward praise as a friend and accuse as an enemy. I know by whom his rage against me was stirred up; I know your underground passages. I am not unaware of the simplicity that everyone praises.

Through his stupidity your malice raged against me. If I drove it back in my letter, so that you would not seem to be the only one possessing the staff of literary argument, you ought not to pretend shame concerning words which you never found there at all. You ought instead to understand and confess that, through his madness, a response was made to your slanders.

### 20. Pope Anastasius’s Letter to John of Jerusalem Concerning Rufinus

In the letter of the holy Pope Anastasius you have proved slippery; confused, you cannot find where to plant your foot. For now you say that it was composed by me, and now that it ought to have been sent to you by the person to whom it was sent.

Again you accuse the writer of injustice. Even if it was written by him—or was not written by him—you declare that it has nothing to do with you, since you possess the testimony of his predecessor and, although he invited you to Rome so that you might honor him by your presence, you rejected him out of love for your little town.

If you suspect that I fabricated the letter, why not have it sought in the archive of the Roman Church? Then, when you discover that it was not given by the bishop, you may hold me manifestly guilty of the crime, and you will no longer set spider-web snares against me, but bind me with the strongest and most solid net.

But if it belongs to the Roman bishop, you act foolishly by asking for a copy of the letter from the person to whom it was not sent, rather than from the one who sent it, and by expecting testimony from the East when you have its author and witness nearby.

[Note: I would prefer to omit the negative particle: “to whom it was sent.” Rufinus maintained that the letter ought to have been transmitted by the person to whom it was sent—that is, by John—to himself. Jerome, on the contrary, calls it foolish for him to seek a copy of the letter from the one to whom it was sent rather than from the one who sent it, namely Anastasius. Nevertheless, I alter nothing without manuscript support.]

Go instead to Rome and, in his presence, demand to know why he insulted you, both when you were absent and though you were innocent.

First, why he refused to receive your exposition of the faith, which, as you write, all Italy approved, and refused to use your letters as a staff against your dogs. Then, why he sent letters against you to the East and, while you were unaware, burned into you the cautery of heresy, saying that the books of Origen *On First Principles*, translated by you and handed over in good faith to the simple Roman Church, would cause them to lose through you the truth of the faith they had learned from the Apostle.

[Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, adds *quod tibi*; less correctly.]

And, to bring greater odium upon you, he dared to accuse these very books, strengthened by the testimony of your Preface.

It is no small matter that the pontiff of so great a city has charged you with this—or has rashly accepted the charge from someone else. Shout and cry out through the crossroads and streets: “The book is not mine! And if it is mine, Eusebius stole my uncorrected sheets. I published it differently—or rather, I did not publish it at all. I gave them to no one, or certainly to very few; and so wicked was the enemy, so careless were the friends, that all their copies were falsified by him alike.”

[Note: The old edition and several manuscripts in Victorius read: “It is not mine; it is not a book,” etc. This repetition, for emphasis, is strongly approved.]

This is what you ought to have done, dearest brother, rather than turning your back on him and directing the arrows of your overseas insults against me. For what good does it do your wounds if I have been wounded? Is it consolation for the stricken man to see his friend dying alongside him?

### 21. You Produce a Letter of Siricius, Now Sleeping in the Lord, and Despise the Words of the Living Anastasius

What harm, as you say, can it do you that he either wrote or perhaps did not write it without your knowledge? And if he did write it, the testimony of the whole world is enough for you—that no one can regard it as true that the priest of so great a city could have injured either an innocent man or one who was absent.

You call yourself innocent, although Rome trembled at your translation. You call yourself absent, although, when accused, you do not dare to answer. And you flee the judgment of the city of Rome so completely that you would rather endure a barbarian invasion than the sentence of a peaceful city.

[Note: The incursion of Alaric with the Goths into Italy, from Aquileia, around the year 401.]

Suppose that I fabricated last year’s letter. Who sent the recent writings to the East? In them Pope Anastasius adorns you with such a profusion of flowers that, when you read them, you will begin to wish more to defend yourself than to accuse us.

At the same time, consider your incomparable prudence, your Attic wit, and the charm of your holy eloquence. You are sought by some, pierced by the accusations of others, and, raging against me, you boast and say:

“Can I not also recount how you departed from the City? What was judged concerning you at the time? What was written afterward? What oath you swore? Where you boarded the ship? How religiously you avoided perjury? I could disclose these things, but I have decided to keep more than I report.”

These are the ornaments of your words. And after this, if I say anything harsh about you, you immediately threaten me with proscription and swords.

Meanwhile, the most eloquent of men, by rhetorical skill, plays with words and pretends to pass over what he says, so that, since he could not prove the things alleged, he may make them appear criminal under the guise of having omitted them.

This is your entire simplicity: this is how you spare a friend and reserve yourself for the courts of judges, so that, while sparing me, you heap up a mass of accusations against me.

[Note: The whole sentence is supplied from the old edition and from Victorius.]

### 22. The Order of Jerome’s Departure from the City

Do you wish to know the order of my departure from the City? I shall tell it briefly.

In the month of August, with the Etesian winds blowing, I safely boarded a ship in the Roman port with the holy presbyter Vincentius, my young brother, and other monks who now live in Jerusalem, while a great multitude of holy people accompanied me.

I came to Rhegium and stayed for a short time on the coast of Scylla, where I learned the ancient stories: the precipitous course of deceitful Ulysses, the songs of the Sirens, and the insatiable whirlpool of Charybdis.

When the inhabitants of that place told me many things and advised me to sail not toward the Pillars of Proteus but toward the harbor of Jonah—for the former was the course of fugitives and troublemakers, while the latter belonged to a man at peace—I preferred to proceed through Malea and the Cyclades to Cyprus.

[Note: Martianus, with Erasmus, perversely reads: “the course of this man of fugitives and the troubled, while that is the course of a man at peace.” We correct this with the old edition. Victorius likewise restored the passage, as the sense itself plainly shows. The Pillars of Proteus are near Egypt, while the harbor of Jonah is Joppa. Jerome speaks of this elsewhere and in Letter 108 to Eustochium, II.8: “Joppa also, the harbor of the fleeing Jonah,” etc.]

There I was received by the venerable bishop Epiphanius, whose testimony you boast of. I came to Antioch, where I enjoyed communion with the bishop and confessor Paulinus. Escorted by him in midwinter and in the most severe cold, I entered Jerusalem.

I saw many miracles and confirmed by the judgment of my eyes what rumor had previously conveyed to me. From there I went to Egypt, visited the monasteries of Nitria, and saw asps lurking among the choirs of the holy.

Immediately I returned at a hurried pace to my Bethlehem, where I breathed in the manger and the cradle of the Savior. I also saw the famous lake, and did not surrender myself to idle leisure; rather, I learned many things I had not known before.

As for what was judged concerning me at Rome and what was written afterward, do not keep silent—especially since you possess the testimony of the Scriptures, and I should be convicted not by your words, which you can fabricate and boast of with impunity in a lie, but by ecclesiastical writings.

See how much I fear you: if you produce even a small document against me from the Roman bishop or from another Church, I shall confess that everything written about you is my own crime.

Could I not also examine your journey? How old you were; from where and at what time you sailed; where you lived; and in what events you took part? But far be it from me to do to you what I criticize in you, or to join the ravings of old-women’s quarrels to an ecclesiastical dispute.

Let this alone suffice for your prudence: beware of saying against another anything that can immediately be turned back against you.

### 23. Rufinus’s Insults Against Epiphanius. Epiphanius’s Letter to John

In the matter of the holy Epiphanius, your evasiveness is extraordinary. After a kiss and after prayer, you deny that he could have written against you—just as if you were arguing that one who had been alive shortly before could not have died, or that your rebuke were more certain than excommunication after peace.

“They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us” (1 John 2:19). The Apostle commands that a heretic be avoided after one or two admonitions; yet before he is avoided and condemned, he was certainly part of the ecclesiastical flock (Titus 3:10).

At the same time, I cannot restrain my laughter that, when warned by a certain prudent man, you declaim in praise of Epiphanius:

“This is that delirious old man; this is the anthropomorphite; this is the man who, with you present, recited six thousand books of Origen; who thinks that he has been charged to preach against Origen in the languages of all nations; who therefore forbids him to be read, lest others discover his thefts.”

[Note: Victorius preferred *pertonas*, “you thunder forth.”]

Read your own writings and his letter—or rather, his letters—from which I shall produce one as testimony to your faith, so that he may rightly appear to have been praised by you now:

“But may God deliver you, brother, and the holy people of Christ entrusted to you, and all the brothers who are with you, and especially the presbyter Rufinus, from the heresy of Origen, from other heresies, and from their destruction. For if, because of one or two words contrary to the faith, many heresies have been charged by the Church, how much more will this man be held among the heretics, who devised so many perversions and such evil doctrines against the faith and became an enemy of the Church of God!”

This is the holy man’s testimony concerning you; thus adorned and thus praised, you walk about.

This is the letter which you produced from the chamber of your brother Eusebius with gold coins, in order to slander the translator and make me plainly guilty of the crime of having translated *honorable* as *dearest*.

[Note: Epiphanius’s letter to John is number 51 in our recension. Recall also Jerome’s letter to Pammachius, *On the Best Kind of Translation*, which is number 57.]

But what does this concern you, who regulate everything by prudent counsel and walk in such a middle course that, if you find people willing to believe you, you may claim that neither Anastasius nor Epiphanius wrote against you—unless the letters themselves cry out against you and shatter the audacity of your forehead? Then you immediately disregard the judgment of both and declare that it does not concern you whether they wrote or did not write, since they could not have written against an innocent and absent man.

Nor should these evils be attributed to the holy man, “so that it may be shown that he gave peace with his mouth and kiss, but kept evil and deceit in his heart.” Thus you argue, and these are the words of your defense.

Both the world acknowledges that the letter is his, and we prove that the authentic letter came into your hands. I am amazed at the shamelessness—or rather, at what modesty you possess—that you deny what you do not doubt is true.

Will Epiphanius, then, be polluted because he gave you peace while keeping deceit in his heart? Would it not be truer that he first admonished you and wished to correct you and lead you back to the right path; that he did not reject Judas’s kiss, but by patience broke the betrayer; and that, after realizing that he was laboring in vain, that a leopard cannot change its spots or an Ethiopian his skin, he indicated in writing what he had conceived in his mind?

[Col. 0475B] **24. The calumny concerning a fabricated peace. The friends of Jerome sent to the West.**—You argue something of this sort even against Pope Anastasius: because you possess a letter of Bishop Siricius, he could not have written against you. I fear you may suspect that an injury has been done to you. I do not know how you, so sharp and prudent, have descended to such absurdities, so that, while you suppose your readers foolish, you prove yourself foolish. After your splendid argument, you place at the conclusion:

> “Far be this from holy men. Such things ordinarily proceed from your school. You gave us peace as we were departing, and from behind you hurled darts armed with poisons.”

And in this same prudence—or rather, in this declamation—you wished to appear eloquent. We gave peace; we did not accept heresy. We clasped right hands; we escorted you on your departure, so that you might be Catholics, not so that we might be heretics.

Nevertheless, I want to know what these poisoned darts are that you complain we hurled behind your back. Vincentius, Paulinianus, Eusebius, and Rufinus, presbyters—Vincentius came to Rome long before you; Paulinianus and Eusebius departed after your voyage had been completed for a year; Rufinus was sent in Claudius’s case after two years—all of them either on account of their family affairs or for the sake of another’s danger.

Could we possibly have known that, as you were entering Rome, [Note: [Col. 0475D] Macarius, to whom Rufinus dedicated Pamphilus’s *Apology* and explained the difficulties concerning Fate; not, as Martianaeus falsely and quite incongruously notes, Pammachius.] a nobleman would dream that a ship full of merchandise was entering with swollen sails?

[Note: [Col. 0475D] Erasmus reads, “that he might resolve all the questions of the opponents,” whereas Marianus reads, “that he might resolve all the questions against Fate”; so too the Cluniac manuscript. But all the others have, “the questions against Fate,” etc. Jerome therefore says that a nobleman dreamed that a ship full of merchandise had entered Rome when Rufinus entered that city with his companions; a dream which a foolish interpretation would not resolve, nor all the questions against Fate—because, plainly, that ship was full of blasphemies, as he teaches elsewhere and as we shall read shortly: “Therefore, unless you had come from the East, that most learned man would still be lingering among the astrologers, and Christian men would not know what to argue against Fate.” MARTIAN.—Victorius wrongly reads “against the fool.” Rufinus himself boasts that he had disentangled for Macarius the difficulties concerning Fate, or the *Mathesis*. See below.]

Could not a foolish interpretation resolve all the questions against Fate? That you might translate Eusebius’s work under the name of Pamphilus? That you might place your own covering, as it were, upon a poisoned dish? That you might transfer the most notorious work *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*) through the majesty of your eloquence?

This is a new kind of calumny: we sent accusers before you committed what was to be accused. It was not, it was not, I say, our plan, but God’s providence, that those sent for another purpose should fight against the heresy as it was arising, and, like Joseph, should relieve the coming famine through the ardor of faith.

[Col. 0476A] **25. Concerning the false letter to the Africans. Rufinus had corrected Latin texts from the Greek.**—Where does reckless audacity, once unbridled, not break forth? He attributed another’s crime to himself, so that we might seem to have invented it. Whatever was said without a name, he takes as having been said against him; and, while clearing himself of external offenses, he is concerned only with his own innocence.

For he swears that he did not write, under my name, a letter to the Africans in which I confess that I had been led astray by the Jews and had translated falsehoods; and yet he sends books containing precisely all the same things that he swears he did not know. I marvel how his prudence could agree with another’s wickedness, so that what someone else had lied about in Africa he here consistently declared to be true, and so that, I do not know which unskilled person could imitate the elegance of his style.

You alone are permitted to transfer the poisons of heretics and to pour out the cup of Babylon for all nations. You will correct the Latin Scriptures from the Greek and give the churches something different to read from what they once received from the Apostles. But I am not permitted, after the Septuagint edition which I gave to speakers of my language many years ago, having corrected it with the greatest care, to translate even those exemplars which the Jews themselves acknowledge to be the most accurate, in order that, whenever Christians debate with them, they may have no evasive byways for escape but may be struck especially by their own sword?

I remember having written more fully on this matter, and on many others, in many places, and at the end of the second book, where I answered your accusation. I restrained your popularity-seeking, by which you strive to stir up envy against me among the simple and uneducated, with a clear argument; and I think the reader should be referred there.

[Col. 0476C] **26. Rufinus called martyr and Apostle by his own people.**—I will not allow this to pass untouched, lest you grieve that the falsifier of your papers possesses, in my judgment, the glory of a confessor, while you, guilty of the same crime, after Alexandrian exile and dark prisons, are called martyr and apostle by all the followers of Origen.

I have already answered you concerning your excuse for ignorance. But since you repeat the same things, and, as though you had forgotten your earlier defense, again admonish us that, after devouring Greek volumes for thirty years, you do not know Latin, attend for a little while. I am not reproving a few words in you—otherwise your entire Scripture must be erased—but I wished to show your disciples, whom with great effort you have taught to know nothing, how shameful it is to teach what one does not know and write what one does not understand, so that in your very ideas they might recognize the same wisdom of the teacher.

And when you add, “Sins stink, not words: falsehood, calumny, detraction, false testimony, and every insult; and the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11), and warn me “not to let that stench penetrate my nostrils,” I would believe you if I did not detect deeds to the contrary—as though a fuller and a leatherworker were warning a perfumer to pass by their shops with his nostrils stopped.

I shall therefore do what you command: I shall close my nostrils, lest they be tormented by the sweetest fragrance of truth and [Note: [Col. 0477D] Does he allude to the *Benedictions of the Patriarchs*, on whom Rufinus wrote commentaries?] your blessings.

[Col. 0477B] **27. In one person we praise and accuse different things.**—Since you proved inconsistent in praising and disparaging me, you argued with remarkable acumen that you are as entitled to speak both well and ill of me as I am to criticize Origen and Didymus, whom I had previously praised.

Listen, therefore, most wise man and head of Roman dialectic: it is not a fault to praise one person in some respects and accuse him in others; rather, the fault is to approve and disapprove of the same thing. I shall give an example, so that the prudent reader may understand with me what you do not understand.

In Tertullian we praise his talent but condemn his heresy. In Origen we admire his knowledge of the Scriptures, yet we do not accept the falsity of his doctrines. In Didymus, moreover, we praise his memory and the purity of his faith concerning the Trinity; but in the other matters in which he wrongly believed Origen, we withdraw from him. For it is not the vices of teachers that ought to be imitated, but their virtues.

A certain African had in Rome a most learned grammarian, and he thought himself an imitator of his teacher if he reproduced only the hiss of his tongue and the faults of his speech.

In the preface to *On First Principles* you call me your brother and say that I am your most eloquent colleague; you praise the truth of my faith. You will not be able to detract from these three points; attack the rest as you please, lest you appear to contradict your own testimony about me.

When you call me your brother and colleague, you confess that I am worthy of your friendship. When you praise me as eloquent, you no longer accuse me of ignorance. When you profess me to be Catholic in every respect, you will not be able to lay the charge of heresy against me. If you find anything to criticize in me apart from these three points, you will not appear to contradict yourself.

From this reckoning arises the conclusion: you are wrong to criticize in me what you had previously praised, while I am not at fault if, in the same persons, I proclaim what deserves praise and criticize what deserves blame.

[Col. 0477D] **28. Concerning the question of souls. Didymus’s book to Rufinus, and the Explanation of Hosea to Jerome.**—You move on to the condition of souls and more fully reproach my “fumes”; and, so that you may be permitted to be ignorant of what you deliberately pretend not to know, you first ask me about heavenly matters: what are angels and archangels like? What sort of dwelling, or what dwelling, do they have? What difference is there among them—or is there none at all? What is the nature of the sun? Whence come the moon’s increase and waning? What is the course, or what sort of course, do the stars follow?

I marvel that you have forgotten to include those verses:

> Whence comes the trembling of the earth, by what force the deep seas swell,  
> Then, their barriers broken, settle back into themselves;  
> The various eclipses of the sun, and the labors of the moon;  
> Whence comes the race of men and cattle; whence rain and fires,  
> Arcturus, the rainy Hyades, and the twin Bears.  
> Why do the winter suns hasten so eagerly to bathe themselves in Ocean,  
> Or what delay obstructs the slow nights?

(Virgil, *Georgics* II.473; *Aeneid* I.746.)

Then, abandoning heavenly things and descending to earthly matters, you philosophize about lesser subjects. For you ask me: “Tell us what is the nature of springs? What of winds? What is hail? What is rain? What is the salt sea? What are fresh rivers? What are clouds, showers, lightning, thunder, or thunderbolts?”

Thus, after I have answered that I do not know these things, you may safely be permitted not to know about souls, and may compensate for ignorance of one matter with ignorance of so many others.

You, who fan my fumes through every page, do not understand that we see your darkness and storms. For, so that you might appear to be a little scholar and retain the glory of learning among your [Note: [Col. 0477D] “Among the Calpurnians.” Rufinus is repeatedly called “Calpurnius” by Jerome; hence his disciples are called “Calpurnians”—namely Macarius, Apronianus, and the rest of his group. MARTIAN.—One interpretation holds that Rufinus’s disciples are called Calpurnians because Rufinus himself was called Calpurnius by Jerome as an insult. But see what we observed below, section 32, note f.] Calpurnian disciples, you set the whole of natural philosophy before me—so that Socrates, when turning to ethics, said in vain, “What is above us is no concern of ours.”

Therefore, unless I give you an account of why an ant, a small animal and, so to speak, a mere point of a body, has six feet, while an elephant’s enormous bulk walks on four; why snakes and serpents glide upon their bellies and breasts; why the little creature commonly called the millipede swarms with such a multitude of feet—shall I be unable to know about the condition of souls?

You ask me what I myself think about souls, so that, as soon as I have made my declaration, you may immediately attack it. And if I say that text from Ecclesiasticus, “God creates souls every day and sends them into the bodies of those being born,” you will at once produce your teacher’s snares: Where is God’s justice, if he gives souls to those born of adultery and incest? Is he therefore a co-worker in the crimes of wicked people, and, while adulterers sow bodies, does he himself fashion souls?

As though the fault lay in the wheat-seed because it is said to have been stolen, and not in the one who stole the grain; and as though the earth ought not to cherish seeds in her womb because the sower cast them down with an unclean hand.

Hence comes that secret question of yours: why do infants die, if they received bodies on account of sins?

There exists a book by Didymus addressed to you, in which he answered your inquiry that they had not committed many sins, and that therefore it was enough for them merely to have touched the prisons of bodies.

My teacher and yours, at the time when you were asking him these things, dictated to me, at my request, three books of explanations on the prophet Hosea. From this it is clear what he taught me and what he taught you.

[Col. 0479A] **29. Natural questions.**—You press me to answer concerning the nature of things. If there were room, I could expound to you either the opinions of Lucretius according to Epicurus, or of Aristotle according to the Peripatetics, or of Plato and Zeno according to the Academics and Stoics.

And, to pass over to the Church, where the standard of truth is found, the books of Genesis and the Prophets, as well as Ecclesiastes, offer us much concerning questions of this kind.

Or, if we are ignorant of these matters, you ought, in your *Apology*, to have confessed ignorance of all things and asked your calumniators why they shamelessly demanded one thing from you when they themselves did not know so many things.

O richest three-decked ship, which had come to enrich the poverty of the city of Rome with Eastern and Egyptian merchandise!

[lacuna]

You [Note: [Col. 0479C] You are that Maximus. This line is from Ennius concerning Fabius Maximus: “The one man who, by delaying, restored the state to us.” MARTIAN.—From Ennius’s line concerning Quintus Fabius Maximus:

> One man restored the state to us by delaying,

which Virgil almost copied in Book VI.]

You are that Maximus,

> The one who restores the state to us by writing.

Therefore, unless you had come from the East, that most learned man would still be lingering among the astrologers, and all Christian men would be ignorant of what to say against Fate.

It is with good reason that you ask me about astrology and the course of heaven and the stars, since you have brought a ship full of such merchandise. I confess my poverty: I am not enriched in the East as you are. For a long time Pharos taught you what Rome did not know; Egypt equipped you with what Italy has until now lacked.

[Col. 0479C] **30. Various opinions concerning the soul.**—You write that among Ecclesiastical writers there are three opinions concerning souls. One is followed by Origen. Another by Tertullian and Lactantius—although you lie most openly about Lactantius. The third is held by us simple and foolish men, who do not understand that, if this is so, God would be accused by us of injustice.

And after this you swear that you do not know what is true. Tell me, I beg you: do you think there is something outside these three in which truth lies, while falsehood lies in the three? Or is one of the three true?

If there is something else, why do you confine the freedom of disputants within such narrow limits, and, although you have produced falsehoods, remain silent about the truth? But if one of the three is true and the other two false, why, with a similar ignorance, are you ignorant of the false opinions together with the true? Or do you conceal the truth for this reason, so that it may be safe for you to defend falsehood whenever you wish?

These are the fumes, these the darknesses by which you attempt to remove the light from human eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] **Aristippus of our time.** Aristippus, a Cyrenian, was a pupil of Socrates and the first to philosophize for pay. He possessed a disposition extremely ready to imitate anything according to time, place, and person. See Diogenes and Horace. Hermagoras and Gorgias were distinguished rhetoricians. It is said that Gorgias was the first to dare to ask in an assembly what anyone wished to hear, and to declare that he could speak at length on every subject, whatever matter might be brought forward for discussion and debate. MARTIAN.—Understand Aristippus of Cyrene, Socrates’ associate, a philosopher of courtly disposition, concerning whom Horace says:

> Every circumstance, condition, and situation taught Aristippus.

For, according to Suidas, he was the first to demand payment from his students. Hermagoras, who follows, was a Carian; Suidas reports that he established a particular method of speaking, which many followed. See Quintilian. As for Gorgias of Leontini, he is said to have been the first to dare to say in the theater at Athens to his audience, “Put forward”—that is, “Propose what each of you wishes to hear.” Jerome compares Rufinus with all these men.]

You are the Aristippus of our time, bringing a ship laden with every kind of merchandise into the Roman harbor, and, with a public platform set up, presenting us with Hermagoras and Gorgias of Leontini; yet, while hastening to sail, you forgot in the East the merchandise of a single little question.

And again you shout and boast that at Aquileia and Alexandria you learned what God is, the creator of souls and bodies.

[Col. 0480B] The question being debated here is, plainly, whether God or the devil made souls—not whether souls existed before bodies, as Origen wishes, and did something on account of which they were bound to thick bodies; or whether, in the manner of dormice, they lay sluggish, asleep, and buried in slumber.

These are the matters everyone demands, and you are silent about them; you answer those about which no one asks.

[Col. 0480C] **31. You also frequently mock my “fumes,” because I pretend to know what I do not know, and by listing learned men deceive [Al. lead astray] the untutored crowd.**—You, naturally, are fiery—or rather thunderous—thundering as you speak and unable to contain in your mouth the flames you have conceived; and, like that [Note: [Col. 0480D] **That Bar-Chochabas.** Bar-Chochabas is found in Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 6, and Salmoneus in Virgil. MARTIAN.—Eusebius, who relates this history in Book IV, chapter 6, calls him Barchochebas, Βαρχωχεβᾶς. Salmoneus’s well-known story is found in Virgil, Book VI.] Bar-Chochabas, the author of the Jewish revolt, who fanned a burning straw in his mouth with his breath so that he seemed to vomit flames, so you, another Salmoneus, illuminate everything upon which you tread, and accuse us of being smoky—of us it might perhaps be said, “You touch the mountains, and they smoke.”

You do not understand what the smoke of the locusts signifies in the Prophet [Note: [Col. 0480D] John in the Apocalypse, whose words are these: “Out of the smoke of the pit came locusts upon the earth, and power was given to them,” etc.], nor that the beauty of your eyes cannot endure the bitterness of our smoke.

[Col. 0481A] **32. Concerning the oath in the dream.**—As for the charge of perjury, since you refer me to your book, and since I answered you and Calpurnius for the most part in other books, [Note: [Col. 0480D] From this one may understand that Jerome is referring to a man other than Rufinus named Calpurnius, contrary to the common opinion of scholars. Here Victorius understands either Apronianus or Macarius, Rufinus’s friends, or finally Palladius, as P. Martianaeus also suspects. He is certainly the same person whom Jerome mocks by that name in his letter to Magnus. See what we noted concerning that passage of the letter.] it is enough to say briefly now that you demand from a sleeping man what you never supplied while awake.

I am guilty of a serious offense if I said to the girls and virgins of Christ that secular books should not be read, and if I promised, after being warned in a dream, that I would not read them.

Your ship, promised to the city of Rome by a revelation [Note: [Col. 0481D] Namely, the dream of Macarius, which he mocks above.], promises one thing and accomplishes another. It had come to resolve the questions of the astrologers, and it resolved the faith of Christians. It had sailed with full canvas through the Ionian and Aegean seas, the Adriatic and Tyrrhenian [Al. “sea”], and was shipwrecked in the Roman harbor.

Are you not ashamed to collect such ravings and to impose upon me the necessity of making similar charges against you? Suppose that someone else had seen a glorious dream concerning you. It would have been consistent with your modesty and prudence to conceal what you had heard, rather than to boast, as though it were a great testimony, about another person’s dream.

See what difference there is between your dream and mine. I report that I was humbly reproved; you repeatedly boast that you were extravagantly praised. Nor can you say, “It makes no difference to me what another person saw,” since in your most splendid books you say that you were moved by this very consideration in interpreting the dream, so that the distinguished man would not lose his dream about you.

This is your entire effort: if you prove me perjured, you will not be a heretic.

[Col. 0481C] **33. A calumny concerning disloyalty.**—I come to the gravest charge, in which, after our friendship had been restored, you accuse me of disloyalty. I confess that, among all the insults you either bring or threaten, nothing must be rejected by me so thoroughly as fraud, deceit, and disloyalty. To sin is human; to lay snares is diabolical.

Therefore, did we clasp right hands after sacrificing a lamb at the Anastasis [Note: [Col. 0481D] Martianaeus is quite wrong to read “at Anastasius,” when Victorius had noted the error and restored the Greek ἀναστάσει. What the Anastasis was—that is, the temple or site of the Lord’s Resurrection—we explained above in Book I *Against John of Jerusalem*, section 11.] so that we might steal your papers in Rome? So that dogs sent in might gnaw your uncorrected sheets while you slept? And is it credible that we prepared accusers before you committed the crime? Surely we knew what you were turning over in your mind? What another person would dream about you [Note: [Col. 0482D] The old edition reads, “what he was going to dream.”]?

Thus the Greek proverb would be fulfilled in you, and [Al. “so that”] the sow would teach Minerva.

If I had sent Eusebius to bark, who incited Aterbius [Mss. Atarbius and Atarbius] against you and against the madness of the others? Was he not the man who also judged me a heretic because of my friendship with you? When I had satisfied him by condemning Origen’s doctrines, you, shut up at home, never dared to see him, lest you either condemn what you did not wish to condemn or, by openly resisting, incur the odium of heresy.

Or will he be unable to testify against you because he is your accuser?

Before Saint Epiphanius came to Jerusalem and gave you peace with mouth and kiss, while keeping evil and deceit in his heart; before we dictated to him letters attacking you, so that he might write that a man was a heretic whom he had proved orthodox by his kisses, Aterbius [Al. Atervius] was barking against you at Jerusalem; and, unless he had departed quickly, he would have felt the staff not of [Note: [Col. 0482D] Martianaeus less aptly reads “of letters.”] letters, but of your right hand, with which you are accustomed to drive away dogs.

[Col. 0482A] **34. Concerning the uncorrected papers.**—“Why,” he says, “did you accept my falsified papers? Why, after my translation, did you dare to set your pen to the books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*? If I had erred as a human being, ought you not to have approached me by private letters and flattered me in the way I now flatter you in my letters?”

This is entirely my fault: accused by deceptive praises, I wished to clear myself, and to do so without bringing envy upon your name, so that what you alone had accused me of I might refer to many—not charging you with heresy, but defending myself against the charge.

Did I know that you would become angry if I wrote against heretics? You had said that you had removed heretical material from Origen’s books. I believed that you were no longer a supporter of heretics, and therefore I attacked not you but the heretics. If I was too vehement in this, forgive me. I thought that I would also please you.

You say that, by the theft and plotting of my attendants, your papers were brought into public view, papers that lay hidden in your bedroom or were held only by the man whom you had entrusted with the matter.

[Col. 0482B] And how do you confess above that either no one possessed them or very few did? If they lay hidden in your bedroom, how were they with the man whom you had entrusted with the matter? But if the one to whom they had been written had taken them for concealment, then they were not hidden only in your bedroom, nor were they possessed by the few whom you testified had possessed them.

You accuse us of having stolen them, and again you accuse us of having bought them for a great sum of money and countless commodities. In one matter, and in a short letter, what variety and contradiction in your lying!

You may accuse, but I may not defend myself? When you make accusations, you do not think of friendship. When I answer, then the rights of friendship come to your mind.

Tell me, I beg you: did you write the papers to be concealed or to be published? If they were to be concealed, why did you write them? If they were to be published, why did you conceal them?

[Col. 0482C] **35. He guarded against the suspicion of hypocrisy.**—But I am to be criticized for this: why I did not restrain your accusers, who were my friends. Do you wish me to produce their letters, in which they accuse me of hypocrisy because, knowing you to be a heretic, I kept silent; because, while heedlessly offering peace, I had undertaken civil wars within the Church?

You call those men disciples who suspect that I am your fellow disciple. And because I was too sparing in refuting your praises, they think that I am your fellow initiate. Your preface brought this upon me: you injured me more as a friend than an enemy could have done.

They had once persuaded themselves—whether rightly or wrongly, let them see to it—that you were a heretic. If I wish to defend you, I shall achieve only this: that they will accuse me equally with you.

Finally, they bring your praise against me, and they do not think that you wrote deceitfully but truthfully; and they vehemently charge me with what you had always previously praised in me.

What do you want me to do? Regard the disciples as accusers on your behalf? Receive in my own breast the darts twisted against a friend?

[Col. 0483A] **36. Concerning the books *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, you ought also to thank me.** [Note: [Col. 0483D] Victorius preferred: “You ought also to thank me.”]

For, as you say, you cut away whatever was harmful and inserted better material. I reproduced them as they were found in the Greek. From this your good faith is also revealed, as well as the heresy of the man whom you translated.

Men of the highest standing in Christ at Rome—Pammachius and Oceanus—were writing to me: “Answer the accuser, lest, if you remain silent, you appear to have consented.” With one voice they all demanded that I expose Origen’s subtle devices and show Roman ears that the poisons of heretics must be avoided.

What does this have to do with injuring you? Did you alone translate these books, and do you have no other associates in this work? Are you one of the seventy translators, so that after your edition no one else may translate?

Behold, I too translated many little books, as you say, from Greek into Latin. You also have the power to translate them again as you wish; for good and evil alike are attributed to their author.

The same would have happened to you, unless you had said that you had cut out the heretical material and translated what was excellent. This is your knot, which cannot be untied. But [Al. “Or”] if you erred as a human being, condemn your earlier judgment.

[Col. 0483B] **37. Rufinus was translating Latin books into Greek.**—But what will you do about your *Apology*, which you wrote on behalf of Origen’s works? What about Eusebius’s volume? In it, although you altered many things and, under the name of a martyr, translated the writings of a heretical man, you nevertheless inserted many passages that do not accord with the faith of the Church.

You also translate Latin books into Greek; will you forbid us to give foreign works to our own people?

If I had answered in another work, in which you had not injured me, I might have seemed to transfer what you had translated in order to injure you, so as to show you either ignorant or deceitful. But now there is a new kind of complaint: you grieve that I answered you in the very work in which I was accused by you.

Rome was being thrown into confusion by your translation, and everyone demanded from me a remedy for this matter. Not because I myself was of any importance, but because those who asked thought that I was.

You were my friend, and you had translated those works. What do you want me to do? Is it more necessary to obey God or men (Acts 5:29)? To guard the Lord’s property, or to conceal the theft of a fellow servant? Will you not be appeased unless I too commit the very offenses for which you must be accused?

If you had made no mention of my name; if you had not adorned me with splendid praises, I might have had some refuge and could have alleged various excuses so as not to transfer what had again been translated.

But you, [Note: [Col. 0483D] Victorius adds from Brixian manuscripts a second “you” for emphasis: “You, my friend, you compelled me,” etc.] my friend, compelled me to spend several days on this work, to bring into the open what Charybdis ought to have swallowed. And yet, although injured, I preserved the rights of friendship toward you and, insofar as I could, defended myself without accusing you.

[Col. 0484A] You are excessively suspicious and quarrelsome, referring to yourself words directed against heretics. But if I cannot be your friend unless I am also the friend of heretics, I shall endure your enmity more lightly than their friendship.

[Col. 0484A] **38. Concerning the letter to Rufinus.**—You also suppose that I invented a new falsehood, composing in my own name a letter to you as though it had been written long ago, so that I might appear good and modest—a letter which you had never received at all.

This matter can easily be proved. Many people in Rome possess copies of it [Note: [Col. 0484D] The letter to Rufinus is number 8 in our recension, to which we assigned the year 399.], written approximately three years ago, but they refused to send it to you, knowing what claims you would make concerning my name and what things unworthy of a Christian profession and impious things you would fabricate.

I wrote it without knowing what would happen, as though to a friend. They did not return it to one whom they knew to be an enemy, sparing both my error and your conscience.

At the same time you argue that, if I had written such a letter to you, I ought not to have written many harsh things against you in another little book. This is your entire error and the substance of your justified complaint: that you pretend that what we say against heretics is said against you; and unless we spare them [Note: [Col. 0484D] Martianus reads, “unless we spared them.”], you think yourself violated.

Do we therefore refuse to give you bread because we strike a stone against the brains of heretics?

And, so that you may not approve our letter, you say that Pope Anastasius’s letter too is supported by a similar fraud—an objection to which I answered you earlier. If you suspect that it is not his, you have an opportunity to accuse us of falsehood before him. But if it is his, as the letter of this very year against you also proves, you strive vainly and falsely to accuse a true letter of being false, since from his genuine letter we demonstrate that ours too is genuine.

### 39. The Disciples of Pythagoras. Pythagorean Precepts and Symbols. What Pythagoras First Discovered among the Greeks

How elegant you wished to be in excusing your lie—or, alternatively, your falsehood! And lest you produce the six thousand books of Origen, you demand from me the records of Pythagoras. Where is that confidence with which, puffing out your cheeks, you so frequently proclaimed that you had corrected what you had read in Origen’s other books in his books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*), and had restored to his own works what was not alien but his own? From so vast a forest of books you cannot produce one little bush or shoot. These are the true smoke-clouds, these the mists which, while you accuse me of them, you recognize as extinguished and dispersed in yourself through me. Yet you do not lower your broken neck, but with greater shamelessness than ignorance you say that I deny what is readily available—so that, although you promised golden mountains, you cannot produce even a leather coin from your treasures.

I acknowledge the just hatred directed against me, and the genuine frenzy with which you rage against us. For unless I boldly demanded what does not exist, you appeared to possess what you do not possess. You demand from me the books of Pythagoras. Who told you that any volumes of his survive? Are these not the words in my letter, which you accuse?

> “But suppose that in my youth I erred, and, educated in the studies of philosophers—that is, of the Gentiles—at the beginning of my faith was ignorant of Christian doctrines, and supposed that the Apostles taught what I had read in Pythagoras, Plato, and Empedocles.”

I spoke of their doctrines, not of their books—doctrines which I could have learned from Cicero, Brutus, and Seneca. Read the little speech *For Vatinius*, and the other places where associations are mentioned.

**Editorial note:** Justin, book XX: “Thirty young men, bound by an association under a certain oath, lived a life separate from the other citizens,” etc. See also Aulus Gellius, book I, chapter 9. Cicero had said much of the same Pythagorean associations in his speech *For Vatinius*, since Vatinius himself boasted of being a Pythagorean, as Cicero likewise testifies in his speech against Vatinius. Valerius Maximus, book IV, chapter 2, mentions Cicero’s speech *For Vatinius*. Turn over Cicero’s dialogues. Look throughout the coast of Italy, once called Magna Graecia, and you will recognize the Pythagorean doctrines engraved on public bronze tablets. Whose, indeed, are those “golden precepts” (*χρυσᾶ παραγγέλματα*)? Are they not Pythagoras’s?

**Editorial note:** In Martianus they are called *χρυσᾶ ἔπη*, “golden verses,” if indeed these are the works Jerome indicates here. He seems rather to speak of Pythagorean sayings and symbols than of those *Golden Verses* which are commonly, though falsely, ascribed to Pythagoras. In them all his doctrines are briefly contained, and Iamblichus has discussed them in a very extensive work, partly following Moderatus, a most eloquent man, and Archippus and Lysis, hearers of Pythagoras. Archippus and Lysis had schools in Greece—that is, at Thebes. Memorizing their teacher’s precepts, they used their own ingenuity in place of books. From them comes the following:

> “Flee by every means, and cut away with fire, iron, and every kind of device—from the body, sickness; from the soul, ignorance; from the belly, luxury; from the city, faction; from the household, discord; and, in common, intemperance in all things.”

**Editorial note:** The Greek words beginning *Φυγαδευτέον πάσῃ* were wholly unknown to Erasmus and Marianus, because they left them for us to recover from manuscript copies only through considerable labor and mental anguish. They preferred to invent foreign material and force many false readings into Jerome’s text rather than restore the genuine wording through careful investigation. Accordingly, they published Jerome in the following corrupted form:

> “It must be avoided altogether, and weakness of body, lack of education of the soul, indulgence of the belly, faction in the city, discord in the household, and intemperance in all things must be cut away.”

These are the fabulous Greek words of Erasmus, with which he has long deceived everyone who thought that he had published Jerome’s works according to the authority of the most ancient manuscripts, rather than from his own empty and futile conjectures. The manuscript copies, moreover, omit the material enclosed within angular brackets; they taught us that the Latin of Jerome supplied what was needed.

**Martianus.**

The Greek passage may be rendered:

> “Everything must be driven away by every means, and cut off with fire, iron, and every sort of device: disease from the body, ignorance from the soul, luxury from the belly, faction from the city, division of mind from the household, and, altogether, immoderation in all things.”

**Editorial note:** Martianaeus supplied from Jerome’s Latin version, which follows below, certain Greek words missing from the manuscripts. We have restored one or two places from the very life of Pythagoras by Iamblichus—or by Porphyry, whom Iamblichus frequently copies. Martianaeus had read *ἀκολασίαν* (“licentiousness”) where the life has *πολυτέλειαν*, that is, luxury or extravagance; *οἰκίας* instead of *οἴκου*; and *παναμετρίαν* instead of the two words *πάντων ἀμετρίαν*, which Jerome interprets as “intemperance in all things.” For the rest, see Diogenes Laertius, book VIII.

These, too, are Pythagorean precepts:

- Everything belongs in common to friends.
- A friend is one’s other self.

**Editorial note:** Malchus has the same saying in his *Life of Pythagoras*: “A friend is another self” (*τὸν δὲ φίλον ἄλλον ἑαυτὸν*). I wished to record this because Diogenes states it differently in his account of Pythagoras: “Everything belongs in common to friends,” and “friendship is equality” (*καὶ φιλίαν ἰσότητα*). The subsequent precepts and symbols may be found in the same Diogenes Laertius, *Lives of the Philosophers*, book VIII.

One should take particular care of two times: morning and evening—that is, of what we are about to do and of what we have done. After God, one must cultivate truth, which alone makes human beings close to God.

There are also those riddles which Aristotle discusses at length in his books:

- Do not step over the balance—that is, do not transgress justice.
- Do not stir the fire with a sword—that is, do not provoke an angry and swollen spirit with abusive words.
- Do not pluck the crown—that is, preserve the laws of cities.
- Do not eat the heart—that is, cast grief out of the mind.
- “When you have departed,” he says, “do not turn back”—that is, after death do not desire this life.
- Do not walk along the public road—that is, do not follow the errors of the multitude.
- Do not receive a swallow into the house—that is, do not keep garrulous and talkative people under the same roof.
- Place a burden upon those already burdened; do not associate with those who lay burdens down—that is, increase the precepts for those advancing toward virtue; abandon those who give themselves over to idleness.

And since I had said that I had read Pythagorean doctrines, hear what Pythagoras first discovered among the Greeks: that souls are immortal and pass from one body into another. Virgil, too, following this doctrine, speaks in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*:

> When these, after a thousand years have turned the wheel,  
> The god summons in a great company to the river Lethe,  
> So that, forgetful, they may behold the vault above,  
> And begin again to desire to return into bodies.

### 40. Other Doctrines of Pythagoras. Origen Transferred Plato into His Own Books

He was first Euphorbus, second Callis, third Hermotimus, fourth Pyrrhus, and finally Pythagoras; and after fixed cycles of time, what had existed would come into being again, so that nothing in the world could be seen as new.

Philosophy is a meditation on death: every day it strives to lead the soul out of the prison of the body.

> “Learning is recollection” (*μαθήσεις ἀναμνήσεις*),

that is, “things learned are recollections.”

**Editorial note:** The printed Latin editions omit here the Latin explanation of the Greek words, although all manuscript copies retain it: “learning consists in recollection.” Victorius adds *εἶναι* (“to be”), though I do not know whether more correctly, and does not have the interpretation “things learned are recollections”; Martianaeus added that from certain manuscripts.

And many other doctrines, which Plato develops in his books, especially in the *Phaedo* and the *Timaeus*. For after founding the Academy and acquiring countless disciples, recognizing that much was lacking from his teaching, he came to Magna Graecia. There he was instructed in Pythagorean doctrine by Archytas of Tarentum and Timaeus of Locri, and combined Socrates’ elegance and charm with their teachings. All of this, with the names changed, Origen is clearly shown to have transferred into his books *On First Principles*.

In what, then, did I err if, as a young man, I said that I had supposed the Apostles taught what I had read in Pythagoras, Plato, and Empedocles? Not, as you slanderously claim and invent, what I had read in the books of Pythagoras, Plato, and Empedocles, but what I had read as having been in them, and what the writings of others taught me that they had possessed.

This manner of expression is extremely common. For example, if I say, “I read doctrines in Socrates and thought them true,” I do not mean that Socrates wrote any books:

**Editorial note:** Some writers, including Leo Allatius, attribute writings of various kinds to Socrates; but nearly all the ancient authors emphatically deny that he committed anything to writing.

Rather, I mean that I read in Plato and in other Socratics what they said Socrates had held. Again, I might say, “I wished to imitate the deeds I had read in Alexander and Scipio.” This does not mean that they themselves had recorded their own deeds, but that I had read in other authors what they had done and what I admired in them.

Therefore, even if I could not prove that records of Pythagoras himself exist, nor establish that they had been approved by his son, his daughter, and his other disciples, you could not convict me of lying, because I said that I had read doctrines, not books. You are therefore foolishly mistaken in wishing to protect your own lie, so that unless I produce a single book of Pythagoras, you may claim that the six thousand books of Origen have been lost.

### 41. Rufinus Threatened Jerome with Death

I shall come to your conclusions—that is, your curses—in which you exhort me to repentance; and unless I am converted, that is, unless I fall silent under your accusation, you threaten me with destruction. You declare that this scandal will rebound upon my own head, because I, by my reply to your insane writing, have provoked you, the gentlest of men and one of Mosaic meekness.

You boast that you know crimes which I confessed only to you, as my closest friend, and that you will bring them into the open. You say that I must be painted in my own colors, and that I ought to remember how I lay at your feet, lest you cut off my head with the sword of your mouth.

After much more in which you exult furiously, you draw back and say that you desire peace—with the one proviso that I remain silent thereafter: that is, that I do not write against heretics and do not dare to answer your accusations. If I do this, I shall be your brother and colleague, a most eloquent man, a friend and companion; and, greater than all these titles, you will judge everything I have translated from Origen to be Catholic.

But if I change my mind and stir myself, immediately I shall be impure and a heretic, unworthy of your friendship. These are my praises; in this way you exhort me to peace, and do not even permit me to release a groan or a tear for my grief.

### 42. He Rebukes the License of Slander. Fulvia and Herodias

I, too, could paint you in your own colors, rage against one who rages, and say whatever I know or do not know. With the same license—or rather, frenzy and madness—I could heap together falsehoods and truths, so that you would be ashamed both to hear me speak and of what I said. I could bring against you charges that would condemn either the accuser or the accused, and by the hardness of my face make the reader believe me, so that what I wrote shamelessly would be judged to have been written truthfully.

But it is far from Christian conduct that, while seeking the blood of others, people should offer their own and become murderers in intention without a sword.

**Editorial note:** The old edition reads: “while others seek their blood, they offer their own,” and so forth.

This is suited to your goodness, your gentleness, and your simplicity—you who draw from one dungheap of a breast both the fragrance of roses and the stench of corpses, and, contrary to the Prophet’s sentence (Isaiah 5), call bitter what you had praised as though it were sweet.

There is no need for us to discuss matters belonging to the courts in ecclesiastical treatises. You will hear nothing further from me on this subject except the saying from the street:

> “When you have said what you wish, you will hear what you do not wish.”

Or, if a common proverb seems beneath you, and as a very wise man you prefer the sayings of philosophers and poets, read the Homeric line:

> “Whatever word you speak, such a word you will also hear.”

**Editorial note:** This is Homeric. Homer, *Iliad* Υ. The manuscripts add something after *ἔπος*, namely: *ἔπος τοῖον καὶ ἐπακούσαις*—“such a word as you speak, such you will also hear.” The reference is *Iliad* Υ, verse 250: “As the word you speak, so also shall you hear.”

This alone I ask of your exceptional holiness and judgment—whose purity is so great that demons snarl at your towels and girdles: whose example in writing are you following? Which Catholic has ever, in a debate with members of opposing sects, cast personal shame at the one against whom he was arguing? Is this what your teachers taught you? Were you trained in such disciplines that, when you cannot answer someone, you cut off his head and sever the tongue that cannot remain silent?

Do not boast greatly if you do what scorpions and dung-beetles can do. Fulvia did the same to Cicero, and Herodias to John: because they could not bear to hear the truth, they pierced the truth-speaking tongue with a executioner’s needle.

Dogs bark on behalf of their masters, and you do not want me to bark on behalf of Christ? Many have written against Marcion, Valentinus, Arius, and Eunomius. Who cast personal shame at them? Did they not devote themselves entirely to refuting heresy? These are the devices of heretics—that is, of your teachers: when convicted of treachery, they turn to curses.

Thus Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, found sons without knowing them.

**Editorial note:** Theodoret relates that Eusebius of Nicomedia, together with other supporters of Arian impiety, came to Antioch and there hired a woman who claimed that she had had intercourse with Eustathius, the bishop, and had borne a child by him, whom she was nursing. They caused him to be deposed. Although Socrates says that Eustathius was deposed on account of Sabellianism, he clearly hints at the slander involving adultery.

Thus Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, cut off the third hand of Arsenius. The man who had first been falsely represented as dead was later shown to be alive and to possess two hands.

Your fellow disciples and teachers are now fabricating such stories about a priest of that same Church, and with gold—that is, with the resources of you and your associates—they attack the truth of the faith.

What shall I say about heretics who, although outside, nevertheless call themselves Christians? Against the utterly impious Celsus and Porphyry, how many of our people wrote? Who, abandoning the case itself, occupied himself with superfluous accusations of crimes? Such matters belong not in ecclesiastical writings but in judicial pamphlets.

What does it matter if you lose the case but prevail through accusation? There is no need to accuse someone at the risk of your own head. Hire a single executioner, and you can satisfy your desire.

You pretend to fear scandal, although you are ready to kill one who was once your brother, now your accused opponent, and has always been your enemy.

Yet I wonder how a prudent man, overcome by fury, wishes to grant me the favor of bringing my soul out of prison and refuses to allow it to remain with you in the darkness of this age.

### 43. He Could Not Spare the Heretics

Do you want me, then, to be silent? Do not accuse me. Lay down your sword, and I will throw away my shield.

There is one matter on which I cannot agree with you: I cannot spare heretics if I am to prove myself Catholic. If this is the cause of our disagreement, I can die, but I cannot remain silent.

I ought indeed to have answered all your madness from all of Scripture and, like David playing the harp, to have soothed the fury of your heart with divine words. But I shall be content with a few testimonies from a single book, and I shall set wisdom against folly, so that if you despise human authority, you may at least not disregard divine authority.

Hear, then, what wise Solomon says about you and about all the envious, slanderous, and abusive:

> “When fools are eager for insults, they become impious and hate understanding. Do not devise evil against your friend. Do not become an enemy to a man without cause. The impious exalt insult. Cut away from yourself a crooked mouth, and drive wicked lips far from you: the eyes of the abusive, the tongue of the wicked, the hands that shed the blood of the righteous, the heart that devises evil thoughts, and the feet that hasten to do harm.
>
> “He who relies on a lie feeds the winds and pursues flying birds. For he has abandoned the paths of his vineyard and caused the rows of his cultivation to go astray. He walks through a dry and deserted place and gathers barrenness with his hands.
>
> “The mouth of the insolent draws near to destruction, and he who utters curses is the greatest fool. Every simple man is a blessed soul; a high-spirited man is dishonorable.

**Editorial note:** Perhaps, with altered punctuation, it should be read: “Every simple man is a blessed soul; a high-spirited man,” etc. The passage is Proverbs 11:25: *Ψυχὴ εὐλογουμένη πᾶσα ἁπλῆ*. It should also be noted that here Jerome, like St. Chrysostom in Homily 16 on John and Ambrose in book *On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 2, takes *εὐλογοῦμαι* in a passive sense, less suitably if not according to the meaning of the Septuagint, at least according to the truth of the Hebrew. In Hebrew idiom, “to bless” means “to do good.”

You will seek wisdom among the wicked and will not find it. The reckless will be filled by his own ways. The wise man, fearing, turns away from evil; the fool, confident, mixes himself with it.
>
> “A patient man is rich in prudence; the fainthearted is exceedingly foolish. He who slanders the poor insults his Maker. The tongue of the wise knows what is good, but the mouth of fools speaks evil. An angry man prepares quarrels, and everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God.
>
> “Hand laid against hand unjustly will not go unpunished. He who loves life spares his mouth. Before destruction comes insult, and before ruin comes an evil thought. He who hardens his eyes devises perverse things and provokes every evil with his lips. The lips of a fool lead him into evil, and the bold mouth calls for death.
>
> “A malicious man will suffer many losses. A righteous poor man is better than a lying rich man. It is glory for a man to turn away from curses; but the fool binds himself to such things. Do not love slander, lest you be uprooted. The bread of deceit is sweet to a man; afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel.
>
> “He who gathers treasures with a lying tongue—or, according to another reading, ‘of a liar’—pursues vanity and will fall into the snares of death. Do not say anything in the ear of a fool, lest he mock your wise words.
>
> “A club, a sword, and a deadly arrow are like the man who bears false witness against his friend. As birds fly away, and sparrows, so a groundless curse will not come upon him. Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him; but answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself.
>
> “He who plots against his friends, when he is seen, says, ‘I was joking.’ As a grate is to coals, and wood to fire, so is a malicious man to the kindling of strife. If your enemy entreats you, restrain your loud voice and do not consent to him, for there are seven evils in his soul.
>
> “A stone is heavy and sand scarcely bearable; but the anger of a fool is heavier than either. His indignation is cruel, his anger sharp, and his jealousy intolerable.
>
> “The impious slanders the poor, and he who trusts in the boldness of his heart—or, according to another reading, ‘in his greed’—is the greatest fool. The fool pours out all his anger; the wise man distributes it in portions.
>
> “An evil son has teeth like swords and molars like knives, to consume the weak from the earth and the poor from among human beings.”

(Proverbs 10, 18, and elsewhere, according to the Septuagint.)

Taught, then, by these examples, I did not wish to bite the one who bites me or repay injury in kind. I preferred to exorcise the madness of a madman and pour the antidote of a single book into your poisoned breast—or, according to another reading, insert it into your breast.

But I fear that, accomplishing nothing, I may be compelled to sing David’s words and console myself with this speech:

> “Sinners are estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly. They have spoken falsehoods; their fury is according to the likeness of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears and does not hear the voice of those who charm, or of the enchanter who charms wisely.
>
> “God will crush their teeth in their mouth; the Lord will break the molars of lions—or, according to another reading, ‘God will break them.’ They will come to nothing, like water running away. He bends his bow until they are weakened. Like wax that melts, they will be taken away; fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun.”

(Psalm 57:4 and following.)

And again:

> “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees the vengeance upon the impious; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner. And the man will say: ‘Surely there is fruit for the righteous; surely there is a God judging them on the earth.’”

(Psalm 57:11.)

### 44. At the End of the Letter You Write in Your Own Hand: “I Wish You to Love Peace”

To this I shall reply briefly: If you desire peace, lay down your weapons. I can yield to one who speaks soothingly; I do not fear one who threatens. Let there be one faith between us, and peace will immediately follow.

**Editorial note:** Vallarsius appends to Jerome’s work against Rufinus Rufinus’s *Apology against Jerome* in an appendix. Since we reprinted a very complete edition of Rufinus’s works in the preceding volume, it will be enough for us to refer the reader there; the reader will no longer wonder about the lacuna visible here between the numbers printed in heavier type.

# Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Priest of Stridon  
## Dialogue Against the Pelagians, under the Persons of Atticus the Catholic and Critobulus the Heretic

### Notice Concerning the Following Dialogues Against the Pelagians

1. Hardly had the Christian world, wherever it extended, condemned Origenist impiety and submitted its neck to Jerome when suddenly the Pelagian war broke out, spread widely through the Churches, and roused the great teacher—already worn down by old age, yet born, as it were, for the destruction of such monsters—to descend into the battle line. Thus, I think, no praise could ever belong to the slaughter of this heresy unless he alone, or at least the first, received the credit.

Pelagius, who had learned the execrable doctrine at Rome from a certain Syrian named Rufinus, imported it into Palestine around the year of Christ 412 and taught it at Jerusalem. With the bishop John of that city consenting, he advanced so far that there were people who came to be called by his name.

At that time the essence of the heresy was this: human beings can be without sin if they wish; the necessity of divine grace obstructs freedom of choice; and—apparently proclaimed then with less emphasis—that sin is not transmitted by descent.

In the books which he composed from that time onward, especially in his commentaries on Jeremiah, Jerome did not cease to rebuke this detestable arrogance whenever the opportunity arose. Yet he continually spared the names of the men involved, preferring that they be corrected rather than disgraced.

After nearly two years, however, and when he had scarcely completed the first book on the prophet in question, he sharpened his pen against the heretic and sent to Ctesiphon the letter which we printed in the preceding volume under number 133. In it he destroys the *apatheia* (*ἀπάθεια*) that had arisen from the sources of the ancient Stoics, while nevertheless threatening that, unless the heretics should come to their senses through that skirmish, he would compose books in which he would overturn all the tunnels and hiding places of the impious faction.

In fact, shortly afterward, at the request of the brethren, he published these three books. In them, following the Socratic manner, he set out what could be said for and against the heresy and introduced the persons of Atticus and Critobulus debating with each other, so that he might both explain orthodox doctrine more clearly and attack the heretic more forcefully.

Saint Prosper praises this in his most elegant verses, *Carmen de Ingratis*:

> Then also the guest of illustrious Bethlehem,  
> Jerome, graceful in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin speech,  
> An example in conduct and a teacher of the world,
