> Cut up the enemy in books of great excellence,  
> And made known by what whirlwind the darknesses that had arisen  
> Wished to obscure the true light.

2. The year in which these books were written may be learned from the *Apology* of Orosius, the Spanish presbyter who at that time sat at Jerome’s feet. I shall briefly explain its occasion as well, so that you may understand at the same time what the orthodox position was at that period, what the state and sequence of events were, and how much strength and confidence the heresy had acquired.

Since the question of the origin of the soul, debated intensely in both directions, was troubling Churchmen, Saint Augustine, to prevent minds from continuing to waver, judged that the greatest teacher of the Churches, Jerome, should be consulted. Orosius, who was then staying with him, was therefore encouraged by Augustine to go to Jerusalem, and Augustine gave him letters to deliver to Jerome on this subject. We present those letters in the first volume under numbers 131 and 132, together with Augustine’s books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* and his letter to Hilary, writings in which he refuted the evil doctrines that the Pelagian disciples—and especially Coelestius—had secretly uttered.

Equipped with these documents, Orosius approached Jerome. He also explained orally what had been done against Coelestius at Carthage. The matter immediately reached the ears of the common people, and disagreement arose, with many supporting Jerome and some even supporting Pelagius. John of Jerusalem, who was favoring the heretic, wished to suppress the dispute and summoned Orosius to Jerusalem. There, after a synod of the entire clergy had been convened, with Pelagius himself absent, the parties were ordered to explain what had been brought from Africa against his teaching and by what arguments he defended himself.

To settle the matter as briefly as possible: Pelagius, using as judge a man devoted to his party and employing interpreters of his faction who rendered Orosius’s Latin words into Greek with deceptive fidelity, escaped the synod’s judgment in such a way that he turned dangerous hostility against his accuser. Orosius, after publishing his *Apology*, was forced to remove every suspicion of heresy from himself.

In this *Apology* the Spanish presbyter recounts what happened in each of its stages and, above all, specifies the time at which the Jerusalem assembly was held: namely, forty-seven days before the first day of the Encaenia of that temple. According to Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, that festival fell on September 14. Calculation therefore establishes that the synod was held at the end of July.

There can be no doubt about the year: it must be understood as 415. For Orosius, who had arrived at Bethlehem that year, sailed back to Africa again around the following spring.

Now, speaking in that year, in that month, and about that synod, against Pelagius’s error—that a human being can easily keep God’s commandments without grace, if he wishes—Orosius says:

> “The blessed Jerome, whose eloquence the whole West awaits like dew upon a fleece—for many heretics have already been crushed, together with their doctrines, by his opposition—condemned this in a letter which he recently published to Ctesiphon; likewise, in the book which he is NOW writing, he refutes it through a debate conducted in the manner of a dialogue.”

Nor is it reasonable to suppose that the work was postponed until the following year, since, when Orosius was departing in the spring, Jerome gave him the letter which in our recension is number 134, to carry to Augustine. Addressing the bishop of Hippo in that letter, number 1, Jerome says:

> “Certainly, in the Dialogue which I recently published, I remembered your blessedness as was fitting.”

He wrote this near the end of the third book, and therefore when the work was already complete. No one, then, can doubt that it belongs to the end of the year 415.

3. It is reported that Anianus of Celeda, commonly called a deacon, first sharpened his pen against the books published by the holy Doctor; then, not long afterward, Pelagius himself, after deceiving the wretched synod at Diospolis; and finally Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia.

Yet the evidence of the ancient authors who mention the matter seems to indicate that the writings of Anianus and Pelagius were not two works, as is commonly believed, but one and the same work, which they composed through collaboration.

Orosius calls Anianus Pelagius’s armor-bearer:

> “There stands the most monstrous Goliath of pride, Pelagius, with his armor-bearer behind him. Although the latter does not himself fight, he supplies every support of bronze and iron.”

Jerome, in letter 143 to Augustine, says that Anianus was “fed most abundantly so that he might supply frivolous words for another’s blasphemy.” Gennadius does not even name him, although he does not conceal Pelagius’s writings in support of his heresy. Sigebert, however, who lists other books of Anianus—books which he says Anianus wrote against Jerome—does not acknowledge these.

But however the matter may stand, the later age badly destroyed writings born under evil auspices. The holy Father himself, while postponing their refutation for too long, eventually despised them, as though it were beneath his dignity to answer the most foolish drivel. He merely hinted to Augustine that it would be better if Augustine undertook the task:

> “Lest we be compelled to praise ourselves against the heretic.”

As for Theodore of Mopsuestia, my fellow countryman, Cardinal Henry Noris, the historian of Pelagianism, reports the following from Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 117:

> “A work of Theodore of Antioch was read—he is that bishop of Mopsuestia, as we gather from certain of his letters—with the title *Against Those Who Assert That Human Beings Sin by Nature, Not by Will*. The discussion is completed in five books, which he wrote against Westerners infected with this error. He says that the originator of this heresy was then living in some regions of the East and had composed books on the heresy recently devised by him, sending them to his countrymen at home. By this method he had already drawn many to his opinion and infected entire Churches with those absurd doctrines. He calls the author of the books Aram, uncertain whether this was his name or surname.
>
> “He also says that this man fabricated a fifth Gospel and that he found it in the libraries of Eusebius of Palestine. In addition, having rejected the divine and ancient version of the Old Testament which the Seventy translators produced jointly, as well as the interpretations of Symmachus, Aquila, and others, he dared to prepare some new version of his own, although he had not, like them, been accustomed to the Hebrew language from childhood, nor had he learned the meaning of Holy Scripture. He had merely entrusted himself for instruction to certain low-born Hebrews, and from that point had begun to write his own edition.”

The heretical slanderer could scarcely have described Jerome more clearly without naming him. The reason he calls him Aram seems to be nothing other than that this Pannonian lived in the East.

But the holy Doctor did not answer these books either; indeed, he does not even seem to have seen them or to have known that they had been written against him. Again, only certain excerpts survive from them, which Marius Mercator thought had been written against Augustine and inserted, translated into Latin by himself, in his *Commonitorium*.

4. Among the other services which we have performed, as far as possible, to increase the dignity of this work of Jerome, we have transferred here, after the Dialogue, those very fragments (*ἀποσπασμάτια*) from the edition of Marius Mercator by Baluzius, so that you may see what a man who seemed to himself to be the only one who knew anything clamored against the conqueror of the Pelagian sect—for why should I hesitate to honor Jerome with this title?

We have edited the entire work according to the authority of the ancient books, especially the manuscripts Vaticanus 4985 and the very old Regina Suecorum 286. With their help, readings that were previously corrupt have been corrected throughout.

**Editorial note:** In the Vatican manuscript formerly known as Regina 286, the work is entitled:

> “Prologue of the Dialogue of Saint Jerome, presbyter of orthodox faith, with Pelagius, discoverer of heretical doctrine, whom he wished to designate under the names of Atticus and Critobulus.”

## Prologue
[Col. 0495A] 693

### 1. He writes in response to the persistent appeals of the brethren

After the letter already sent to Ctesiphon (Epistle 233), in which I replied to his questions, there was frequent insistence from the brethren as to why I was postponing the work I had promised. In it I had pledged that I would answer all the little questions of those who preach ἀπάθεια (*apatheia*, freedom from passions). For no one doubts that this is the controversy of the Stoics and Peripatetics—that is, of the Old Academy: some of them maintain that the πάθη (*pathē*), which we may call disturbances—distress, joy, hope, and fear—can be uprooted and eradicated from human minds; others that they can be broken, governed, and restrained, as though they were unbridled horses curbed by bit and bridle. Cicero explains their opinions in the *Tusculan Disputations*, and Origen attempts to mingle them with ecclesiastical truth in his *Stromata*—to say nothing of Mani, Priscillian, Evagrius the Iberian [or Hiborian and Hyperborean], Jovinian, and nearly all the heretics of Syria, whom they call, in the local language, perversely (διεστραμμένως) Massalians, and in Greek εὐχίτας (*Euchites*, “those who pray”).

[Note: [Col. 0495B] “In the local language”—the Messalians. The old editions of John Andrea, Erasmus, and Marianus thrust many words into Jerome’s text; all of them wished to read: “whom in the local language they call Abin and Paanin, that is, ‘perverse,’ and in Greek they call Massalians.” Certainly the name of nearly all the heretics in Syria was “Messalians”; or, “in the local language of Syria,” they called the heretics Messalians, while in Greek they called them εὐχίτας. Apart from these facts, all the other words are superfluous and lack genuine meaning. The Corbie manuscript no. 146 contains nothing except the text printed by us, consistently with Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, book III, heresy 80, who says: “They are called Messalians, that is, εὐχόμενοι, ‘those who pray.’” Theodoret likewise has this in book IV, chapter 11, of his *Ecclesiastical History*: “At that time the heresy of the Messalians arose. Those who translated their name into Greek call them Εὐχίτας.” He also adds: “They have another designation, ἐνθουσιασταί; for they are called ‘enthusiasts.’” The old editors were led into error by the reading found in many manuscripts of Jerome, where the following appears: “whom in the local language they call ΔΕΙΗϹΤΡΑΜΗΝΙ, that is, ‘perverse Massalians,’ in Greek ΕΥΧΙΤΑϹ.” But this text is clearly fabricated from what I have just said about Epiphanius and Theodoret. Augustine incorrectly read “Psallians” in his *Book on Heresies*; although they could have been called that on the basis of their practice, since they often recited psalms and always prayed. MARTIAN.]

The Greek word that we received from the Regina manuscripts and have partly emended was not understood by the old editors; they distorted it into Latin letters as “Abin and Paanin, that is, perverse,” and so forth. Martianaeus, believing that these words had been falsely inserted and fabricated, ordered them to be removed entirely from the text, contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts that he himself used. In most of them, as also in the Regius manuscript, the word appears as ΔΕΙΗϹΤΡΑΜΗΝΙ, that is, “perverse”; and the explanation of this word immediately suggests to those who know Greek how it can be restored to its correct form. For if, with the slightest alteration—or rather merely by correcting the letters—you write ΔΙΕϹΤΡΑΜΜΕΝΩϹ, you will have struck the mark, since διεστραμμένως in Greek means the same as *perverse* in Latin, from the verb διαστρέφω, meaning “to pervert” or “to corrupt.” Hence things done contrary to what is proper are called διεστραμμένα, “crooked” and “perverse.” In this sense, then, Jerome writes that the heretics of Syria are called, in the local language, διεστραμμένως—that is, “perverse”—Massalians, or “those who pray,” in Greek εὐχίτας. Since the name “Massalians” is derived from a root meaning “he prayed,” and since the heretics themselves prayed continually, the holy Doctor says that they were called “perverse pray-ers.”

Appropriately, after Epiphanius, Augustine notes in his *Book on Heresies* that although the Lord said, “One ought always to pray and not grow weary,” and the Apostle, “Pray without ceasing,” this is most soundly understood to mean that set times for prayer should be omitted on no day; these men—the Massalians—carried it to such excess, understanding the Lord’s and the Apostle’s statements perversely, that on this account they were judged worthy to be numbered among the heretics.]

Their common opinion is that human virtue and knowledge can attain perfection—and I will not say merely likeness to God, but equality with God—so that they assert that once they have reached the summit of perfection, they cannot sin even in thought or through ignorance. Although in my preceding letter to Ctesiphon, written against their errors, I briefly touched on the matter because of the pressure of time, this book, which we are now attempting to compose, will follow the Socratic practice: it will explain what can be said on both sides, so that the truth may become clearer when each person has set forth his own opinion.

This, however, is proper to Origen: that it is impossible for human nature, from its beginning to its death, not to sin; and again, that it is possible, when someone has turned toward better things, to attain such strength that he no longer sins.

[Note: [Col. 0497C] Martianaeus and other printed editions read, “so that he can no longer sin,” contrary to the authority of the manuscripts, namely Vaticanus 4945 and Regius 286. Pelagians at times fell into this doctrine, which Jerome says was proper to Origen, when they were hard pressed by the arguments of Catholics. Thus Pelagius at the Council of Diospolis, Jansenius, and even Huetius wrongly criticize Jerome here.]

### 2. He was not moved by envy

To those who say that I am writing this work inflamed by the torches of envy, I shall give a brief reply: I have never spared heretics, and I have acted with every effort so that the enemies of the Church might also become my enemies. Helvidius wrote against the perpetual virginity of holy Mary. Did I answer him because I was moved by envy, although I had never seen him in the flesh? Jovinian,

[Note: [Col. 0497C] The old editions of Erasmus and Marianus falsely and ignorantly thrust the name “Pelagius” upon us, since no manuscript retains that name; Jerome here used assumed names so as not to injure anyone by naming him. MARTIAN.—The Regina manuscript reads: “whose heresy is stirred up by you.” The old editions falsely insert “O Pelagius,” although it is certain that Jerome never called him by name in these books.]

whose heresy is now being revived, disturbed the Roman faith in my absence; he was so devoid of eloquence and so foul in speech that he deserved pity more than envy. I answered him as best I could.

Rufinus brought the blasphemies of Origen and the books *On First Principles* (*περὶ Ἀρχῶν*) not merely to one city but to the whole world, insofar as he was able. He even published Eusebius’s first book of the *Defense of Origen* under the name of the martyr Pamphilus, and, as though that were not enough, spewed out a new volume in its place. Do we envy him because we answered him, and because such streams of eloquence flowed from him that they might have deterred me from the practice of writing and dictating?

[Note: [Col. 0498C] So the manuscripts and the old edition read; elsewhere the reading is *fulmina*, “thunderbolts.”]

Palladius, a man of servile wickedness,

[Note: [Col. 0498C] That is, he openly professes ἀπάθεια (*apatheia*); and in the life of Ammon and his wife in the *Lausiac History* he says that both attained impassibility, while he also babbles lies concerning others.]

attempted to restore the same heresy and to fabricate a new accusation against my translation of the Hebrew. Do we envy his talent and distinction?

[Alternative reading: *invidimus*, “did we envy.”]

Even now he is carrying on the mystery of iniquity, and each person chatters whatever he thinks: I alone am attacked by the glory of them all, and am so wretched that I envy even those who do not deserve envy. Therefore, to prove to everyone that I do not hate people but errors, that I seek the disgrace of no one, and that I am rather grieved for those who are deceived by knowledge falsely so called, I used the names Atticus and Critobulus, through whom I might express what both our side and that of our opponents thought.

Indeed, all who follow the Catholic faith hope and desire that the heresy be condemned and that the people be corrected. Or, if they wish to remain in error, then the fault is not ours, who have written, but theirs, who preferred falsehood to truth.

We reply briefly to the slanderers who heap their own reproaches upon them: it is the doctrine of the Manichaeans to condemn human nature, take away free will, and remove God’s help.

[Note: [Col. 0498C] We have supplied the sentence, which was previously lacking, from the manuscripts and the old edition. Shortly afterward, one Vatican manuscript reads: “this man says that he is what God is,” and so forth.]

Again, it is the height of madness for a human being to say that he is what God is. We must proceed along the royal road, turning neither to the left nor to the right, and we must always believe that the impulse of our own will is guided by God’s help.

If anyone falsely complains that he has been defamed, and boasts that he shares our views, he will prove his agreement with the true faith when he openly and without deceit condemns the opposing errors, lest he hear the prophetic saying: “And in all these things her treacherous sister Judah has not returned to me with all her heart, but falsely” (Jer. 3:10).

It is a lesser sin to follow what one has thought good than not to dare to defend what one knows with certainty to be good. If we cannot endure threats, insult, and poverty, how shall we overcome the flames of Babylon?

[Alternative reading: “Babylonian.”]

Let not a feigned peace take away the warfare that has been preserved. I do not wish to learn treachery through fear, since Christ has entrusted the true faith to my will.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0497]

[Col. 0497C] 697

### 1. Whether a person can be without sin if he wishes

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Atticus is introduced first; Martianaeus omitted the name.]

**ATTICUS.** Tell me, Critobulus, is it true what I hear you have written: that a person can be without sin if he wishes, and that God’s commandments are easy?

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Compare Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 6, section 16.]

**CRITOBULUS.** It is true, Atticus, but my rivals do not understand it in the same sense in which I stated it.

**A.** What ambiguity is there in the statement that gives occasion for different interpretations? I am not asking you to answer about both matters at once. You have proposed two claims: first, that a person can be without sin if he wishes; second, that God’s commandments are easy. Although they have been stated together, let them nevertheless be discussed separately, so that, even though they seem to constitute one proposition, there may be no disagreement in the diversity of the statements.

**C.** I said, Atticus, that a person can be without sin if he wishes—not, as certain slanderers falsely allege, without God’s grace (which it is sacrilegious even to think), but simply that he can, if he wishes, with the implication that this occurs with God’s grace.

**A.** Then God is also the author of the evil works within you?

**C.** Not at all, as you suppose. But if I have anything good in me, it is completed through his prompting and assistance.

**A.** I am not asking about nature, but about action. Who doubts that God is the Creator of all things? Answer me this, please: the good that you do—is it yours or God’s?

**C.** It is mine and God’s: I act, and he assists.

**A.** And how is it that everyone thinks you remove God’s grace and assert that whatever we human beings do is solely the product of our own will?

**C.** I am amazed, Atticus, that you demand from me the cause and explanation of another person’s error, and ask for something that has not been written, when what I have written is plain. I said that a person can be without sin if he wishes. Did I add, “without God’s grace”?

**A.** But because you did not add it, you appear to deny it.

**C.** On the contrary, because I did not deny it, I should be considered to have stated it. For we must not suppose that everything we do not say, we deny.

[Col. 0499A] 698

**A.** Then you confess that a person can be without sin if he wishes—with God’s grace?

**C.** I not only confess it; I proclaim it freely.

**A.** Then the one who removes God’s grace is in error?

**C.** He is in error. Indeed, he must be considered impious, since all things are governed by God’s will, and the fact that we exist and possess the inclination of our own will is a benefaction of God the Creator. To possess free will, and by our own will to incline either toward good or toward evil—whose grace is it that made us such, in his image and likeness?

### 2. Whether it must be attributed to God’s grace

**A.** No one, Critobulus, doubts that everything depends upon the judgment of the one who is Creator of all, and that whatever we possess must be attributed to his beneficence. But I ask whether this very thing that you attribute to God’s grace you refer to the benefaction of creation, or whether you think that his assistance is present in the individual actions we perform, so that we use his help in everything; or whether, having once been created by him with free will, we act by our own will or strength as we choose.

For I know that many of you refer everything to God’s grace in such a way that they understand the power to lie not in particular matters but in general—in other words, not in each individual action but in the creation of free will.

**C.** It is not as you suppose. I affirm both: that it is due to God’s grace that we were created as we are, and that in each individual work we are supported by his assistance.

**A.** Then we agree that in good works, after our own will, we rely on God’s help, and in evil works on the devil.

**C.** We agree, and there is no dispute about this.

**A.** Then those are wrong who remove God’s help from each individual thing we do, and attempt, by perverse—or rather laughable—interpretations, to twist to other meanings what the Psalmist sings: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Ps. 126:1–2), and other passages of this kind.

### 3. That God’s assistance is necessary in every action

**C.** Why do I need to speak against others, when you have my answer?

**A.** What sort of answer is yours? That they think rightly or wrongly?

**C.** What necessity compels me to state my opinion against others?

**A.** The order of the discussion and the reasoning of truth. Do you not know that everything said either exists or does not exist, and must be classified either among good things or among evil things? Therefore, this matter about which I am asking you must, whether you like it or not, be acknowledged as rightly or wrongly stated.

**C.** If God’s assistance must be used in every action we perform, then without God’s help we shall be unable even to sharpen a pen for writing, rub the sharpened pen with pumice, fit the hand to the letters, be silent, speak, sit, stand, walk, run, eat, fast, weep, laugh, and do other things of this sort?

**A.** According to my understanding, it is clear that we cannot.

**C.** In what, then, do we possess free will, and how is God’s grace preserved toward us, if we cannot even do this without God?

### 4. How free will was given; God’s grace does not hinder freedom

**A.** The grace of free will was not given in such a way that God’s assistance is removed from each individual action.

**C.** God’s assistance is not removed, when created beings are preserved through the grace of the free will once given to them.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Alternative reading: “when the grace of free will once given to the creature is preserved.”]

For if, without God, and unless he helps me in each individual action, I can do nothing, then he will neither justly crown me for good works nor punish me for evil ones; in both cases he will either receive or condemn his own assistance.

**A.** Then say plainly: why do you remove God’s grace? For whatever you take away in particular matters, you necessarily deny in general.

[Note: [Col. 0500D] Victorius argues that the text should be emended on the basis of ancient copies to read “why you remove God’s grace” rather than “for why,” and so forth.]

**C.** I do not deny grace, since I maintain that God created me in such a way that, through God’s grace, it was given to my will either to do something or not to do it.

**A.** Then God sleeps during our actions, once the power of free will has been given; and he need not be asked to help us in each individual work, since it belongs to our will and our own free choice either to act if we wish or not to act if we do not wish.

[Col. 0500D] 700

### 5. As the order of creation is maintained in the other creatures, so everything has been left to our will once the power of free will has been granted

**C.** As the order of creation is preserved in the other creatures, so, once the power of free will has been granted, everything has been left to our will.

**A.** Then, as I said, I ought not to ask God for help in each individual matter, since it has once been given over to my own judgment?

**C.** If he cooperates in everything, the action is not mine but his who assists—indeed, his who cooperates in me—especially since I can do nothing without him.

**A.** I ask you, have you not read: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16)?

[Note: [Col. 0500D] Vaticanus: “Have you not read?” At this point, an evidently very old marginal note has been added: “Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*: Behold, God acts so that we may will and believe; but to consent or dissent from the call belongs to one’s own will.”]

[Col. 0501A] From this we understand that willing and running are indeed ours; but that our will and our running are brought to completion belongs to God’s mercy. Thus free will is preserved both in our willing and in our running, while the completion of our will and running is left entirely to God’s power.

Of course, I must now repeat the testimonies of Scripture showing how the saints continually seek God’s help and desire to use him as their helper and protector in each of their works. Read the entire Psalter: all the voices of the saints are nothing but petitions to God in all their actions. From this it is clearly demonstrated that you either deny God’s grace, which you remove from particular matters; or, if you grant it in particular matters—which it is evident you do not wish to do—you must cross over to our position, in which we preserve free will for human beings while not denying God’s assistance in every individual action.

### 6. The Pelagian doctrine is strangled

**C.** This is a sophistical conclusion, descended from the art of dialectic. No one will take away from me the power of free will, lest, if God has been my helper in my actions, the reward be owed not to me but to him who has worked in me.

**A.** Enjoy the power of free will, then, so that you may arm your tongue against God, and prove yourself free if you are permitted to blaspheme. But no one doubts what you think about this, and the tricks of your confession have become evident in the clearest light.

Now let us return to the subject with which we began our discussion. Tell me, if you please: what you said earlier with God’s assistance—that a person can refrain from sin if he wishes—are you saying this can be true forever, or only for a temporary and brief period?

[Col. 0501C] 701

**C.** The question is superfluous. For if I say “for a temporary and brief period,” it will nevertheless be referred to eternity. Whatever you grant for a brief period, you grant also for eternity.

**A.** I do not understand what you are saying sufficiently.

**C.** Are you so dull that you do not perceive what is obvious?

### 7. Whether a person can abstain from sin temporarily or forever

**A.** I am not ashamed to admit that I do not know what I do not know. And before the discussion proceeds, it must be agreed between us what the statement means.

**C.** I assert that one who can abstain from sin for one day can do so on the next; one who can do so for two days can do so for three; one who can do so for three can do so for thirty; and in this way he can do so for three hundred days, for three thousand, and for as long as he wishes to abstain.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Other books read: “as long as he wishes to persist in abstaining.”]

**A.** Then say plainly that a person can be without sin forever if he wishes. Can we do everything we wish?

**C.** Certainly not. I cannot do whatever I wish; I say only that a person can be without sin if he wishes.

**A.** Please answer me this. Do you think I am a human being or a beast?

**C.** If I doubt whether you are a human being or a beast, I shall confess that I myself am a beast.

**A.** If, then, as you say, I am a human being, how is it that, when I wish and greatly desire not to sin, I nevertheless sin?

**C.** Because your will is imperfect. For if you truly wished it, you certainly would not sin.

**A.** Then you, who accuse me of not truly desiring it, are without sin because you truly desire it?

**C.** As though I were speaking about myself, whom I confess to be a sinner, and not about the few, if there are any, who may wish not to sin.

### 8. No example of this exists

**A.** For the moment, by both your judgment and mine, both I who ask and you who answer are sinners.

**C.** But we can be without sin if we wish.

**A.** I have said that I wish not to sin, and there is no doubt that you hold the same view. How, then, can neither of us do what both of us wish?

**C.** Because we do not wish it fully.

**A.** Then produce those among our ancestors who fully wished it and were able to do it.

**C.** That is not easy to demonstrate. For when I say that a person can be without sin if he wishes, I am not asserting that there have been any such people; I am simply saying that he can be without sin if he wishes. For it is one thing to be able to be something—what is called in Greek τῇ δυνάμει (*tē dynamei*, “in potentiality” or “by possibility”)—and another thing actually to be something, which they call τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ (*tē energeia*, “in actuality,” or “in actual operation”). I can be a physician, but for the moment I am not. I can be a craftsman, but I have not yet learned the trade. Whatever, therefore, I can be—even though I am not yet so—I shall be if I wish.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] The Greek is τῇ δυνάμει. Erasmus and Marianus consistently print the Greek words corruptly: here they read δύναμις instead of τῇ δυνάμει, and ἐνέργεια instead of τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ; below, in the opposite sense, they read περὶ ἀδυνάτου instead of περὶ δυνάτου. MARTIAN.]

### 9. Whether what never occurs in the future can be possible

**A.** Skills are one thing; what is accomplished through skills is another.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] Victorius, together with the old edition, reads: “what is beyond skills.”]

Medicine, craftsmanship, and the other arts are found in many people; but to be perpetually without sin belongs solely to divine power. Therefore, either produce an example of someone who has been without sin forever, or, if you cannot, acknowledge your weakness and do not set your mouth against heaven, mocking the ears of fools with the distinction between “to be” and “to be able to be.” Who will grant you that a person can do what no human being has ever been able to do?

[Note: [Col. 0502D] Compare Augustine, book III of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*. Shortly afterward Victorius reads: “Are you not even trained in dialectic?”]

Are you not even trained in dialectic? If a person can do it, then “cannot” is removed. But if he cannot, “can” is overturned. Either grant me that someone has been able to do what you maintain can be done; or, if no one has been able to do it, you will unwillingly be compelled to acknowledge that what you loudly declare possible is impossible.

Between Diodorus and Chrysippus, the most powerful dialecticians, there is this dispute περὶ δυνάτου (*peri dynatou*, “concerning the possible”). Diodorus says that only that can happen which either is true or will be true; and whatever will be true must necessarily happen. Whatever will not be true cannot happen. Chrysippus, however, says that even things that will not happen can happen—for example, that this pearl may be broken, even if it will never in fact be broken.

Therefore, those who say that a person can be without sin if he wishes will not be able to prove this true unless they show that it will happen. But since all future things are uncertain, especially those that have never happened, it is clear that they are calling future something that will not be future. The *Ecclesiastes* confirms this opinion: “Whatever is to be, has already been in former ages.”

### 10. God’s commandments are possible

**C.** I ask you to answer me this: did God give possible commandments or impossible ones?

**A.** I see where your argument is heading. But this must be discussed later, so that, by mixing question with question, we do not leave the listeners with an obscure understanding. Let us therefore reserve the point—which we acknowledge, namely, that God gave possible commandments, lest he himself be the author of injustice if he demands that what cannot be done should be done—and for now complete what you proposed: that a person can be without sin if he wishes.

Either you will produce those who were able to do so; or, if no one was able, you will plainly confess that a person cannot avoid sins forever.

**C.** Since you press me to give what I ought not to give, consider, I ask you, that the Lord said it is easier for a camel to pass through a needle’s eye than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19; Mark 10). Yet he said that something could happen which has never happened. For no camel has ever entered through a needle’s eye.

[Col. 0503A] 703

**A.** I am amazed that a prudent man should have proposed testimony that works against him. For it does not say here that the matter is possible; rather, an impossibility is compared with an impossibility. Just as a camel cannot enter through a needle’s eye, so a rich person will not enter the kingdoms of heaven. Or, if you can show that a rich person enters the kingdoms of heaven, it follows that a camel too can enter through a needle’s eye.

Do not propose Abraham and the others whom we read of as rich in the Old Testament as examples to me. They entered the kingdoms of heaven as rich men only because they used their riches for good works and ceased to be rich for themselves; rather, they were rich not for themselves but for others, and ought to be called stewards of God more than rich men.

But we must seek the perfection of the Gospel, in which it is commanded: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

### 11. He answers the objection from the Lord’s saying and dissolves the examples of Job, Zechariah, and Elizabeth

**C.** Without realizing it, you have been caught in your own trap.

**A.** How so?

**C.** You assert, on the basis of the Lord’s saying, that a person can be perfect. For when he says, “If you wish to be perfect, sell everything you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me,” he shows that a person can be perfect if he wishes and does what has been commanded.

**A.** You struck me with a very powerful blow, so that darkness has begun to pass before my eyes. Nevertheless, the very words, “If you wish to be perfect,” are addressed to one who was unable—or rather unwilling—and therefore was unable. But you must show me someone who both wished and was able, as you promised just now.

**C.** What necessity compels me to show who has been perfect, when it is clear that people can be perfect from the fact that the Savior said to one person—and through one person to everyone—“If you wish to be perfect”?

**A.** You are evading the issue; you remain stuck in the same mud. Either what can happen has happened at some point, or, if it has never happened, admit that it cannot happen.

### 12.

**C.** Why should I delay any longer? You must be overcome by the authority of Scripture. To pass over everything else, will you not be silenced by these two testimonies, in which Job, and Zechariah and Elizabeth, are praised?

Unless I am mistaken, it is written of Job: “There was a man in the land of Ausitis, whose name was Job, and that man was true and without fault, a true worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil thing” (Job 1:1, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: [Col. 0503D] “In the land of Ausitis.” All the manuscripts read this, in accordance with the Septuagint. The printed books falsely read “Hus” instead of “Ausitis.” MARTIAN.]

And again: “Who is he that accuses the just man without sin, and speaks through ignorance in his words?”

In the Gospel according to Luke, likewise: “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame” (Luke 1:5ff.).

If he is a true worshiper of God, without blemish and without fault, and if those who walked in all the Lord’s ordinances are righteous in his sight, I think they are free from sin and lack nothing pertaining to righteousness.

**A.** You have proposed testimonies that are not taken from some other passage of Scripture but from the very books in question. Job, after he was struck by many afflictions and, contrary to God’s decree, summoned him to judgment, is shown to have said: “Would that a man might be judged with God, as the son of man is judged with his companion” (Job 16:21)!

And again: “Who will grant me a hearer, so that the Almighty may hear my desire, and that he himself who judges may write a book” (Job 31:35)?

And again: “For if I am righteous, my mouth will speak impious things; and if I am without fault, I shall be found perverse. Even if I were cleansed with snow and washed my hands, you have plunged me deeply in filth. My garment has abhorred me” (Job 9:20–21).

[Note: [Col. 0504D] The old edition and Erasmus, whom Victorius corrects, read “my garment has been abhorred in me.”]

And it is written of Zechariah that, when the angel promised the birth of a son, he said: “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in age.” For this he was immediately condemned to silence: “You will be silent and unable to speak until the day when these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time” (Luke 1:18, 20).

From this it is clear that people are indeed called righteous and blameless, but that, if negligence creeps in, they can fall. A human being is always placed midway, so that he may descend from the summit of virtues into vices and rise from vices to higher things. He is never secure, but must always fear shipwreck in calm weather. Accordingly, a person cannot be without sin, as Solomon says: “There is no righteous person upon the earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. 7:20).

And in the same book of Kings: “For there is no one who does not sin” (1 Kings 8:46).

And blessed David says: “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18:13).

[Note: [Col. 0505D] In most books “Lord” is added, although the Hebrew and Greek texts reject it.]

And again: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2).

And there are many other passages with which the holy Scriptures are filled.

### 13. He refutes the argument from the Gospel of John

**C.** What, then, will you answer to the example given by the Evangelist John: “We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin; but the generation of God preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him. We know that we are of God, and the whole world lies in the evil one” (1 John 3:9)?

**A.** I shall answer like with like, and show that the Evangelist’s short Epistle, according to your interpretation, contradicts itself. For if everyone who is born of God does not commit sin—because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin because he has been born of God—how does the same writer say in the same place: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)?

You do not understand the matter; you hesitate and are confused. Hear the same Evangelist: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (ibid., 9).

We are righteous, then, when we confess ourselves to be sinners; and our righteousness consists not in our own merit but in God’s mercy, as the holy Scripture says: “The righteous person is the first to accuse himself” (Prov. 18:17).

And elsewhere: “Declare your sins, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26, according to the Septuagint).

For God has shut up all things under sin, so that he may have mercy on all (Gal. 3:22). And this is the highest righteousness of a human being: whatever virtue he may possess, not to regard it as his own, but as belonging to the Lord who bestowed it.

Therefore, the one who is born of God does not sin so long as God’s seed remains in him, and he cannot sin because he has been born of God. But because, in the Lord’s field (Matt. 13), while the master of the household sleeps, the enemy sows weeds over the grain, and, while we are unaware, the nocturnal sower inserts darnel and sterile wild oats among the good wheat, this parable of the master of the household in the Gospel is to be feared: he cleanses the threshing floor and, after storing the grain in the barns, leaves the chaff to be scattered by the winds and consumed by fire.

Hence we also read in Jeremiah: “What has straw in common with grain? says the Lord” (Jer. 23:28).

The chaff, however, is separated from the grain at the consummation of the age. From this it is proved that, while we are in this mortal body, we are mixed with the wheat.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] Victorius wished to read “mixed,” namely, “the chaff.”]

But if you object, asking why he said, “And he cannot sin because he has been born of God,” you will hear in reply: Where, then, will the reward of the will be? For if he does not sin because he cannot sin, free will will be taken away, and the good will no longer be ours but will belong to nature, which is incapable of sin.

## 14. Two Other Examples from the Old and New Testaments

**C.** A little while ago I proposed easier questions, in order to train you for more difficult ones. What can you say to this, which, clever though you are, you will be unable to overturn by any skill? I shall first take an example from the Old Testament, then one from the New. Moses is the chief figure of the Old Testament; of the New, the Lord and Savior. Moses says to the people: “You shall be perfect before the Lord your God” (Deut. 18:13). And the Savior says to the Apostles: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48). Either those who hear these commands can do what Moses and the Lord commanded, or, if it is impossible, the fault lies not with those who cannot obey but with the one who commanded the impossible.

**A.** To the uneducated, and to those without practice in, or knowledge of, meditating upon the Holy Scriptures, this passage at first sight seems to flatter your opinion. But when examined, it is easily resolved. When you compare scriptural testimonies with other testimonies, so that the Holy Spirit may not seem, according to the differences of places and times, to contradict himself—according to what is written, “Deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts” (Ps. 41:8)—then the truth will appear: namely, that Christ commanded what is possible when he said, “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect,” and yet that the Apostles were not perfect.

**C.** I am not saying what the Apostles did, but what Christ commanded. For the fault lies not with the one who commands, but with those who hear the command; and that it could indeed be done is acknowledged from the justice of the one who commanded.

**A.** Well said. I do not want you, then, to tell me that a human being can be without sin if he wishes, but that a human being can be what the Apostles were not.

**C.** Do you think me so foolish that I would dare say this?

**A.** Even if you do not say it, nevertheless, from your proposition, by the consequence itself and the order of the argument, you say it unwillingly. For if a human being can be without sin—and it is clear that the Apostles were not without sin—a human being could exist above the Apostles. I say nothing of the Patriarchs and Prophets, whose justice under the Law was not perfect, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by the grace of God, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation” (Rom. 3:23–24).

[Col. 0506D. Note: The same manuscript reads, “being justified freely through his grace”; the Greek agrees: δικαιούμενοι δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι, “being justified freely by his grace.” Alternative reading: adds “his.”]

## 14. He Opposes a Testimony of Paul to the Philippians

**C.** This argument is tortuous, enclosing ecclesiastical simplicity amid the thorns of philosophers. What has Aristotle to do with Paul? What has Plato to do with Peter? For just as Aristotle was chief among philosophers, so Peter was chief among the Apostles, upon whom the Lord’s Church was founded with solid mass, and is shaken neither by the force of a river nor by any storm.

**A.** You are indulging in rhetoric; while reproaching me with philosophy, you cross over to the camp of the orators. But hear what that same orator of yours says: “Cease from commonplaces: these matters arise at home for us” (Cicero, *Academica*, book 4).

**C.** There is no eloquence here, no rhetorical grandiloquence—for the definition of orators is to speak suitably for persuasion. We seek truth in pure language: either that the Lord did not command the impossible, so that those who failed to do what was possible are at fault; or, if these things cannot be done, that not those who do not do the impossible, but the one who commanded the impossible—which it would be impious to say—should be convicted of injustice.

**A.** I see that you have been violently aroused against your usual character, and therefore I shall stop arguing. But I shall ask you briefly what you think of that passage of the Apostle which he writes to the Philippians: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect. But I pursue, if I may apprehend that for which I was apprehended by Christ Jesus. Brothers, I do not consider myself yet to have apprehended. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to my purpose I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus. Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think this way; and if you think otherwise in anything, God will reveal this to you also” (Phil. 3:12 ff.), and the rest, which I do not doubt you know and which, for the sake of brevity, we pass over.

[Col. 0507D. Note: Victor again reads, “in which I was also apprehended,” in agreement with the Greek ἐφ’ ᾧ καὶ κατελήφθην.]

He says that he has not yet apprehended, and is by no means perfect, but, like an archer, directs his arrows toward his purpose and toward the mark—which the Greeks more significantly call σκοπός (*skopos*)—so that, if the arrow deviates to one side, it may not reveal an unskilled archer.

[Alternative reading: “what,” rather than “which.”]

He asserts that he is always forgetting the past and always stretching toward what lies ahead. Through this he teaches that past things must be neglected and future things desired, so that what he considered perfect today, while he stretches toward better and more advanced things, may be proved imperfect tomorrow. Thus, through successive stages, since he is never stationary but always in motion, he teaches that what we had thought perfect is imperfect, and that perfection alone and true justice are to be fitted solely to the virtues of God.

“I pursue,” he says, “according to my purpose, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus.”

O Apostle Paul, forgive me, a mere little man confessing my faults, if I ask you boldly. You say that you have not yet received, not yet apprehended, and are not yet perfect; that you always forget the past and stretch toward what lies ahead, in order somehow to attain the resurrection of the dead and obtain the prize of the heavenly calling. How, then, do you immediately add: “Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think this way,” or “let us have this understanding”? The manuscripts differ; an alternative reading adds “we are.” And what are we to understand—are we perfect? Have we apprehended what we have not apprehended, received what we have not received, and are we perfect when we are not yet perfect?

What, then, are we to understand—or rather, what ought we to understand—since we are not perfect? We ought to confess that we are imperfect, that we have not yet apprehended and have not yet received. This is the true wisdom of a human being: to know that one is imperfect. Indeed, to speak in this way, the imperfect perfection of all the righteous in the flesh is precisely this.

Hence we also read in Proverbs: “For understanding true justice” (Prov. 1:3, according to the Septuagint). For unless there were also a false justice, the justice of God would never be called true. And in the same passage of the Apostle it follows: “And if you think otherwise in anything, God will reveal this to you also” (Phil. 3:13).

[Col. 0507D. Note: In the Regina manuscript, by a second hand, here and below, together with the old edition, the reading is “has revealed.”]

I hear something new. A little earlier he had said, “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect”; and the chosen vessel, who, because of his confidence in Christ dwelling within him, dared to say, “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3)—and yet he plainly confessed that he was not perfect. Now he casts into the crowd what he had specifically denied of himself, joins himself with the others, and says: “Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think this way.”

But why he said this he explains in what follows. Let us have this understanding, he says, if we wish, according to the measure of human weakness, to be perfect: that we have not yet received, not yet apprehended, and are not yet perfect. And since we are not yet perfect, and perhaps think otherwise than true and complete perfection requires—if we think and understand otherwise than God’s knowledge possesses—God will reveal this to us also, so that we may pray with David and say: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your Law” (Ps. 118:18).

## 15. Two Kinds of Perfection and of Justice

From this it is clear that in the Holy Scriptures there are two kinds of perfection, two kinds of justice, and two kinds of fear. The first perfection, and the comparable truth and perfect justice, and the fear that is the beginning of wisdom, are to be fitted to the virtues of God; the second, which applies not only to human beings but also to every creature, corresponds to our weakness, according to what is said in the Psalms: “No living being shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2). This is the justice that is said to be perfect not by comparison, but according to God’s knowledge.

[Col. 0507D. Note: In the Regina manuscript, the words “and the fear that is the beginning of wisdom,” and what follows, are marked with dots as though they were to be deleted and rejected. In Victor’s edition, as also in the old edition before Erasmus, which we often use, they are entirely absent. Martianay restored them, but in addition read incorrectly “the beginning of the wisdom of God,” whereas it is clear that “of God” belongs with “virtues,” not with “wisdom.” A little earlier, too, the text says “perfection alone and true justice, to be fitted solely to the virtues of God,” not “the justice of God alone to the virtues,” and so forth. Moreover, he added “holy” to “human beings,” although we find this in no manuscript. We have made these small corrections from the Vatican manuscript, retaining in the text only what its authority warrants. It is obvious to everyone that the remaining discourse is fragmentary and confused in meaning, especially from what follows. Several words have easily dropped out, as the manuscripts indicate.]

[Col. 0508D. Note: The Regina manuscript likewise reads “according to that justice,” as Victor also reads. It would, however, seem necessary to read in the contrary sense: “that justice which is said to be perfect by comparison, but not according to God’s knowledge.”]

[Col. 0508D. Note: “That justice,” etc. The passage is greatly corrupted because it is very obscure and varies widely in the manuscripts. Two manuscripts read after the verse of Scripture: “according to that justice which can at some time be changed into injustice,” etc., and omit: “which is said to be perfect not by comparison but according to God’s knowledge. Job too, and Zechariah and Elizabeth are called just according to it.” A clear sense may be obtained from what follows, where a certain justice is called perfect by comparison among human beings, though no such justice can exist in relation to God’s majesty and knowledge. Thus the first justice of which Jerome speaks here is that fitted to the Virtues and blessed Angels, or incomparable perfection and the justice of God; the second, which belongs to our weakness, is that which can be changed into injustice. —Martianay.]

Job, too, and Zechariah and Elizabeth are called just, according to the justice that can at some time be changed into injustice, and not according to that justice which can never be changed, concerning which it is said: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6).

[Col. 0508D. Note: The Regina manuscript again reads “and by which it is said.”]

This is also what the Apostle writes elsewhere: “For even that which was glorified was not glorified, because of the surpassing glory” (2 Cor. 3:10)—that is, the justice of the Law, in comparison with the grace of the Gospel, does not seem to be justice. For, he says, “if what is being destroyed was glorious, much more will what remains be in glory” (ibid., 11).

And again: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when the perfect comes, what is in part will be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13:9). And: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (ibid., 11). And in the Psalms: “Wonderful is your knowledge beyond me; it is strengthened, and I cannot attain it” (Ps. 138:6). And again: “I thought I could understand this; it is a labor in my sight, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny” (Ps. 72:16–17). And in the same place: “I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you” (ibid., 25). And Jeremiah: “Every human being has become foolish through knowledge” (Jer. 10:14). And the same Apostle Paul says: “The foolishness of God is wiser than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:25). There are many other passages, which I omit for the sake of brevity.

## 16. A Person Is Called Just in Comparison with Other People, Not with God

**C.** You have argued cleverly, Atticus, and have recited your testimonies from memory. But your labor and your repeated multiplication of testimonies benefit my side. For I do not compare a human being with God, but with other human beings; and by comparison with them, one who applies himself can be perfect. Accordingly, when it is said that a human being can be without sin if he wishes, this is said according to the measure of a human being, not according to the majesty of God, in comparison with whom no creature can be perfect.

**A.** O Critobulus, in recalling these things you are agreeing with me. I too hold that no creature can be perfect according to true and complete justice. But that one person differs from another, and that human beings possess different kinds of justice, no one doubts. One person may be greater and another lesser, and yet, according to his own condition and measure, one may be called just who, in comparison with another, is not just.

[Col. 0510D. Note: Perhaps one should read: “may be called just in comparison with others who are not just.”]

For example, the Apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, who labored more than all the Apostles, was certainly just when he wrote to Timothy: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of justice is laid up for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to all who love his coming” (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

His disciple and imitator Timothy was also just. Paul teaches him what he ought to do and what path of virtue to follow. Do we think that the same justice existed in both, and not that the one who labored more than all possessed greater merits? “There are many dwellings with the Father” (John 14:2), because merits also differ.

“Star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41), and in the one body of the Church the members are different. The sun has its radiance, and the moon also moderates the darkness of night. There are five other stars called planets, which traverse the heavens with different courses and lights. There are innumerable other stars which we see shining in the firmament. Their lights differ individually, and yet each is perfect in its own order—only so, however, that in comparison with a greater one it lacks perfection.

In the body too, whose members are different, the eye performs one function, the hand another, and the foot another. Hence the Apostle also says: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I do not need you’; or again the head to the feet, ‘I do not need your service.’ Are all Apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all possess all the virtues? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? Strive for the greater gifts. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:21 ff.).

[Col. 0510D. Note: The Regina manuscript reads, “distributing what is proper to each one as he wills”; the Vatican manuscript, “distributing to each one as he wills.”]

In this passage observe carefully that he did not say, “according to what each member desires,” but “according to what the Spirit himself wills.” For a vessel cannot say to its potter, “Why have you made me this way or that?” Does the potter not have authority over the same lump of clay to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor? (Rom. 9:21).

Accordingly he added: “Strive for the greater gifts,” so that in faith and diligence we may deserve to have more than the other charisms and may be better than those who, in comparison with us, have been placed in a second or third rank.

In a great house there are different vessels: some gold, some silver, bronze, iron, and wood. Yet, according to its own measure, while a bronze vessel is perfect, it is called imperfect in comparison with a silver vessel; and again, silver is inferior in comparison with gold. In this way, while they are compared with one another, everything is both imperfect and perfect.

In good soil, from one seed there arises a thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold crop. The numbers themselves show that what is produced is unequal, and yet each thing is perfect in its own kind.

Elizabeth and Zechariah—whom you use as an apparently impenetrable shield—can teach us how much they are inferior in holiness to blessed Mary, the mother of the Lord. She freely proclaims, with the consciousness of God dwelling within her: “Behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed. For he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. And his mercy is from generation to generation upon those who fear him. He has shown strength with his arm” (Luke 1:41 ff.).

In this observe that she calls herself blessed not because of her own merit and virtue, but because of the mercy of God dwelling within her.

John himself, than whom no one was greater among those born of women, was better than his parents. For by the testimony of the Lord he is compared not only with human beings but also with angels. And yet he who was greater than all human beings on earth is said to have been lesser than the least in the kingdom of heaven.

## 17. The Same Point Is Also to Be Understood in a Comparison of Sinners

What is surprising about some saints being better and others inferior in comparison with one another, when, conversely, the same thing can be understood in a comparison of sinners?

To Jerusalem, which had been pierced through with many wounds of sin, it is said: “Sodom was justified in comparison with you” (Lam. 4).

This does not mean that Sodom was righteous in itself—for it fell into eternal ashes (Gen. 19) and hears through Ezekiel: “Sodom shall be restored to its former state” (Ezek. 16:52)—but that, in comparison with a more wicked Jerusalem, it appears just.

For Jerusalem slaughtered the Son of God; Sodom, because of an abundance of bread and the excess of luxury, went beyond the limit of lust.

[Col. 0511D. Note: The Vatican manuscript appears to fill the lacuna with these words: “whose impiety is greater than anything”; then it continues, “but this one became proud because of abundance,” and so forth.]

The publican in the Gospel (Luke 18), who struck his breast as though it were a treasury of evil thoughts and the consciousness of his sins, and who did not dare to raise his eyes, becomes more just by comparison with the proud Pharisee.

Tamar also deceives Judah under the appearance of a prostitute, and by the judgment of the man who was deceived deserves to hear: “Tamar is more just than I” (Gen. 38:36).

From all this it is proved not only that human beings are by no means perfect in comparison with the divine majesty, but not even in comparison with angels or with other human beings who have climbed the heights of virtue. For even you, who are better by comparison with another whom you have shown to be imperfect, are in turn surpassed by another who goes before you. Accordingly, you do not possess true perfection, which, if it were perfect, would need nothing.

## 18. How We Are Commanded to Be Perfect

**C.** How, then, Atticus, does the divine word urge us toward perfection?

**A.** In the manner I have explained: each person should stretch himself according to his strength, as far as he has been able, and try somehow to reach and apprehend the prize of the heavenly calling.

[Col. 0511D. Note: We restored the word “us” from the Vatican manuscript. In the editions published hitherto the text read, “each one of ours, as far as,” etc. “Our” or “of the righteous” would not have been objectionable; but since that word occurs neither in the Vatican nor in the Regina manuscript, we judged it better to delete it.]

Finally, almighty God—to whom, as the Apostle teaches, the Son must be subjected according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh, so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15)—clearly demonstrates that not everything is subject to him.

[Col. 0511D. Note: We supplied the negative particle “by no means” from the manuscripts, since it is necessary to the sense. Victor also inserted it; Martianay should at some point have consulted him and corrected Erasmus’s shameful error.]

Hence the Prophet also anticipates his own subjection at the end, saying: “Is not my soul subject to God alone? For from him comes my salvation” (Ps. 61:1).

[Col. 0512D. Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “Is not my soul subject to God,” and so forth, without “alone”; as far as I know, no text or version accepts this word.]

And because Christ is the head in the body of the Church, while certain members still resist, the body also appears not to be subject to the head. For if one member suffers, all suffer with it, and the whole body is tormented by the pain of one member.

What I am saying will become clearer in this way. As long as we have this treasure in earthen vessels, and are surrounded by fragile flesh—indeed, mortal and corruptible flesh—we consider ourselves blessed if in each individual virtue and in the several parts of virtue we are subject to God [alternative reading: “are subject”].

But when this mortal has put on immortality, and this corruptible has been clothed with incorruption, and death has been swallowed up in the victory of Christ, then God will be all in all. Wisdom will not be found only in Solomon, gentleness of spirit only in David, zeal only in Elijah and Phinehas, faith only in Abraham, perfect love only in Peter, to whom it was said, “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:15), and zeal for preaching only in the chosen vessel, with twofold or threefold gifts in the others. Rather, he will be wholly in all, and the whole number of the saints will glory in the entire choir of virtues, and God will be all in all.

## 19. As Long as We Live, We Cannot Possess All the Virtues

**C.** Then no saint, as long as he is in this little body, can possess all the virtues?

[Col. 0512D. Note: See the book *On the Deeds of Pelagius*, chapter 14, no. 32.]

**A.** No one can, because now we prophesy in part and know in part. For everything cannot exist in all human beings, since the son of a human being is not immortal.

**C.** How, then, do we read: “Whoever possesses one virtue appears to possess them all”?

[Col. 0512D. Note: The word appears to be missing in the Regina manuscript. Compare also Augustine’s letter to Jerome, numbered among the Hieronymian letters in our recension as 132, concerning the passage in James: “Whoever stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.”]

**A.** By participation, not by possession. Each person must excel in certain things; yet I do not know where what you say you have read is written.

**C.** Do you not know that this is a philosophical maxim?

**A.** But not an apostolic one. I am not concerned with what Aristotle teaches, but with what Paul teaches.

**C.** I beg you: does not the Apostle James write (James 2:10) that whoever offends in one point is guilty of all?

**A.** The passage interprets itself. He did not mean the subject from which the discussion began—that one who gives preference to a rich man over a poor man is guilty of adultery or murder. This is where the Stoics rave, maintaining that sins are equal. Rather, he says: “The one who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill.’ Even if you do not kill but commit adultery, you have become a transgressor of the law” (ibid.).

Light things are compared with light things, and serious things with serious things. A fault worthy of a rod is not to be punished with a sword; nor is a crime worthy of a sword to be corrected with a rod.

**C.** Granted that no saint possesses all the virtues; surely you will grant this: in the matter that he can do, if he does it, he is perfect.

**A.** Do you not retain what I said above?

**C.** What was that?

**A.** To be perfect in what one has done, and imperfect in what one could not do.

**C.** But just as he is perfect in what he has done, because he wished to do it, so also, in that by which he is imperfect because he did not do it, he could have been perfect if he had wished to do it.

**A.** Who does not wish to do what is perfect? Or who does not desire to flourish in all the virtues? If you demand the whole from everyone, you abolish the diversity of things, the distinction of gifts, and the variety of the Creator and craftsman, whose sacred Prophet sings: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24).

Let Lucifer be indignant that he does not possess the moon’s radiance. Let the moon complain about its phases and labor, asking why it does not complete the sun’s yearly circle in each month. Let the sun ask what offense it committed that it should be slower than the moon’s course. Let us too, little human beings, cry out about what cause brought it about that we were made human beings and not angels.

Although your teacher—the ancient one—from whose fountain these things proceed, asserts that all rational creatures were created with equal rights, so that, like chariots and wagons leaving their starting-gates, they may either fall in the middle of the course or rush past and reach their desired destination.

[Col. 0513D. Note: “That is, the ancient one.” By this name Erasmus intended Plato. Victor and Martianay understand Origen. See Garnerius, *Dissertatio in Marium Mercatorem*. It is also quite plausible that Origen was called ὁ ἀρχαῖος, “the ancient one,” as a kind of insult because he was the author of the work *On First Principles*, and that he is mocked with a certain playfulness of expression.]

Let elephants, with their enormous bulk, and griffins, with their own heaviness, complain about why they walk on four feet, when flies, gnats, and other such creatures have six feet beneath their little wings, and when there are some worms so teeming with feet that no sight can grasp their countless simultaneous movements.

[Col. 0513D. Note: This was evidently a famous question, which philosophers had also proposed to Saint Barnabas in the *Recognitions* attributed to Pseudo-Clement, in order to mock him. Earlier, in book 3 against Rufinus, Jerome himself had raised this question and dismissed it as a useless difficulty.]

Let Marcion and all the heretics who mock the works of the Creator say these things. Your doctrine will proceed this far: while they slander individual things, they lay hands upon God and ask why God alone exists, why he has begrudged creatures the possession of the same majesty by all.

Although you do not say this—for you are not so insane as openly to resist God—nevertheless you speak in other words, attributing to a human being what belongs to God, so that a person may be without sin, as God is.

[Col. 0513D. Note: The printed editions read “you resist,” contrary to the manuscripts.]

Hence the Apostle, proclaiming over the diversity of graces, says: “There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but it is the same God who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:4–5).

## 20. How Greatly a Human Being Differs from God

**C.** You are excessive on one and the same question, trying to persuade us that a human being cannot possess everything at once—as though God either begrudged his image and likeness or were unable to grant it that it should correspond to its Creator in all things.

**A.** Am I excessive, or are you? You put forward confused propositions and do not understand that likeness is one thing and equality another: the former is a picture, the latter reality.

[Col. 0513D. Note: The manuscripts read, “the reality of the body.”]

A real horse flies across the fields; a painted horse clings to the wall in a chariot.

The Arians do not grant the Son of God what you grant to every human being. Others do not dare to confess Christ as perfect human being, lest they be compelled to acknowledge that he assumed human sins—as though creation were more powerful than the Creator, and the son of a human being were the same as the Son of God.

Either propose other matters to which I can respond, or cease to be proud and give glory to God.

**C.** You are forgetful of your own reply. While you link argument to argument and rage through the broad fields of Scripture with the freedom of an unbridled horse, you have entirely kept silent about the very difficult question to which you promised to respond later, pretending to have forgotten it in order to evade the necessity of answering.

But I was foolish enough, for the moment, to grant what you asked, thinking that you would voluntarily offer what you had received, and not that you would have to be reminded to return what you owed.

[Col. 0513D. Note: Victor restores “of your promise” from the manuscripts and from what Jerome adds below: “concerning the very difficult question to which you promised to respond.”]

**A.** Unless I am mistaken, the reply concerning the possible commandments was postponed. So formulate it as you wish.

## 21. How God’s Commandments Are Possible

**C.** Either God gave possible commandments or impossible ones. If possible, it lies within our power to do them, if we wish. If impossible, we are not guilty even if we do not do what we cannot fulfill. Accordingly, whether God gave possible commandments or impossible ones, a human being can be without sin if he wishes.

**A.** I ask you to listen patiently. We are seeking not victory over an opponent, but truth against falsehood.

God made all the arts possible for the human race, since very many people have learned them (Plato, *Symposium*). I say nothing of those which the Greeks call βάναυσοι (*banausoi*), which we may describe as belonging to manual labor—for example grammar, rhetoric, the three branches of philosophy, physics, ethics, and logic, geometry as well, astronomy, astrology, arithmetic, music,

[Col. 0514D. Note: Before us, Victor supplied the word “music” from other manuscripts. For the Greek words that follow, the old edition, adapting them to the understanding of modern physicians, read, from the hand of a glossator, Διαιτητικόν, “the regulation of diet”; φαρμακευτικόν, “the preparation of medicines”; χειρουργικόν, “manual work”; and also jurisprudence. The Greek word βάναυσος properly refers to arts practiced in a forge or around a furnace; from there the term was extended to signify mechanical arts generally, since they were considered illiberal and their practitioners were excluded from public honors. Saint Clement, in his First Letter to the Corinthians, calls those who have served liberally ἀβαναύσως μεμαρτυρημένους, “those whose service has been attested as liberal.”]

which are themselves branches of philosophy—medicine as well, which is divided into three parts, δόγμα, μέθοδον, ἐμπειρίαν, “doctrine, method, and experience,” and also the knowledge of law and statutes.

Who among us, however ingenious he may be, could comprehend everything, when the most eloquent orator, Cicero, discussing rhetoric and the knowledge of law, said: “Few can do one; no one can do both”?

You see, therefore, that God commanded something possible, and yet that, by nature, no one can fulfill what is possible [alternative reading: “could fulfill”]. He therefore gave diverse precepts and various virtues, all of which we cannot possess at once. Thus it happens that what in one person is primary or complete exists in another only in part. Yet the person who does not possess everything is not guilty, nor is he condemned because of what he lacks; rather, he is justified by what he possesses.

The Apostle defines what sort of person a bishop ought to be when he writes to Timothy: “The bishop must be irreproachable, the husband of one wife, sober, chaste, orderly, hospitable, teachable, not a drunkard, not a striker, but gentle, not quarrelsome, without avarice, managing his own household well, having children subject to him with all modesty” (1 Tim. 3:2 ff.). And again: “Not a recent convert, lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil. Moreover, he must have a good testimony from outsiders, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil” (ibid., 6–7).

[Col. 0515D. Note: Our manuscripts here and below prefer “teachable.” A little later they do not contain the word “good,” which belongs to “testimony.”]

Writing also to Titus his disciple about what sort of bishops he ought to appoint, he demonstrates it in a brief statement: “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might set right what remains and appoint presbyters in each city, as I instructed you. If anyone is without crime, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or disobedience. For the bishop must be without crime, or without accusation—for this is what ἀνέγκλητος more precisely signifies—as God’s steward, not arrogant, not irascible, not a drunkard, not a striker, not desirous of shameful gain, but hospitable, kind, chaste, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast to the faithful word according to the teaching, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it” (Titus 1:5 ff.).

To pass over for now the various commands concerning different persons, I shall confine myself to the commandments concerning a bishop.

## 22. From the example of the virtues which bishops are commanded to possess

Certainly God wishes bishops—or presbyters—to be such as the chosen vessel teaches. First, the quality he mentioned, “blameless,” is either possessed by no one or by very few. For who is there who does not have, as it were on a beautiful body, either a mole or a wart? If the Apostle himself says of Peter that he did not walk with a straight foot in the truth of the Gospel, and was so blameworthy that even Barnabas was led into the same hypocrisy (Gal. II), who will be indignant that this should be denied to him which the chief of the Apostles did not possess?

Next, to find a man who is the husband of one wife, sober, chaste, well ordered, hospitable—and then, as follows, “apt to teach” (διδακτικός), able to teach—is difficult. This does not mean, as the simple Latin interpretation renders it, “teachable,” for you will scarcely find these virtues together. The Apostle also rejects the drunken, the striker, and the lover of sordid gain; instead, he desires a gentle man, free from quarrels, without avarice, one who rules his household very well—and what is most difficult of all, one who has children subject to him with complete chastity, whether children of the flesh or children of faith.
