“With complete chastity,” he says.

**Editorial note:** The Vatican manuscript, together with Victorius and the Brixian codices, reads: “For it is not enough for a bishop to possess his own [chastity], etc.”

It is not enough for him to possess chastity himself unless his children, companions, and ministers are also adorned by the modesty of that chastity, as David says: “He who walks in the blameless way, he shall minister to me” (Ps. C, 6).

**Editorial note:** Victorius, from the Brixian codices, reads “ministered.” The Septuagint likewise has ἐλειτούργει, “he ministered”; the Hebrew, however, is in the future tense. A little later, where the text reads *indecencies* (*impudicitiis*), our manuscripts have *unchaste persons* (*impudicis*).

Let us also consider the intensification (ἐπίτασιν; alternatively, σύντασιν) of chastity: “having children subject in all chastity”—so that they abstain from indecencies not only in deed but also in speech and gesture. Otherwise what happened to Eli might occur. He certainly rebuked his sons, saying: “No, my sons, no: I hear no good report about you” (I Sam. II, 24). He rebuked them and was punished, because he ought not merely to have rebuked them but to have cast them out. What will the man do who rejoices in vices and does not dare to correct them—who fears his own conscience and pretends not to know what the whole people cries aloud?

**Editorial note:** “Who fears his own conscience.” Marianus here adds the negative particle, reading “who does not fear his own conscience,” and calls it a foul error on Erasmus’ part that he read without the negation, “who fears his own conscience.” But Marianus himself is mistaken, not understanding Jerome’s meaning: Jerome says that a criminal bishop does not dare to rebuke the vices of others because he fears his own conscience, and therefore pretends not to know what the whole people proclaims. Moreover, all our manuscript codices read without the negative particle. *Martianus.*—The Vatican manuscript reads, “fears the conscience of his own person.” Victorius, failing to grasp the author’s meaning, added the negative particle on his own: “does not fear,” and so forth.

**Editorial note:** What follows is ἀνέγκλητον. In the Apostle, at I Tim. III, what follows is μὴ νεόφυτον, “not a novice”; but in place of this I read ἀνέγκλητον, “without crime,” in all the manuscript copies—or, as Jerome said above, “without accusation”—which suits this passage, so that he may be accused by no one. This compelled me to alter the old reading of the printed books. *Martianus.*—Formerly the reading was μὴ νεόφυτον, which is discussed a little below.

And then comes “blameless” (ἀνέγκλητον), so that he may not be accused by anyone; so that he may have a good reputation among outsiders; so that he may also be free from the curses of his opponents; and so that, although his teaching displeases them, his conduct may please them. I think it is not easy to find such a man—especially one who is able to resist opponents and crush and overcome perverse doctrines.

**Editorial note:** Our manuscripts do not recognize the word *wishes* (*vult*).

He wishes a bishop not to be ordained while still a novice, which in our own times we see being chosen as the highest standard of justice. If baptism immediately made a person just and filled him with every virtue, the Apostle would certainly never reject a novice. But baptism cuts away former sins; it does not bestow new virtues. It releases a person from prison and, once released, promises rewards if he labors.

Either no one, I say, or very few possess everything which a bishop ought to possess. Nevertheless, if one or two items from the catalogue of virtues are lacking in some bishop, he will not on that account—or, alternatively, immediately—be deprived of the name “just”; nor will he be condemned for what he does not have, but crowned for what he possesses.

**Editorial note:** The Vatican manuscript reads: “To possess everything and to lack no virtue belongs to him who…” The copy from the Regina manuscript agrees in part.

To possess everything and to need no virtue belongs to the one who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found; who, when he was cursed, did not answer with a curse (I Pet. II, 22);

**Editorial note:** Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “did not curse.” A little below Victorius reads “but emptied himself,” from the Greek ἑαυτόν.

who spoke confidently from the consciousness of his virtues: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30). Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as a prize to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Therefore God bestowed on him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. II, 6 ff.).

If, therefore, in the single person of a bishop you will find only a few of these commandments—or scarcely find them at all—what will you do with the whole human race, which ought to fulfill every commandment?

## 23. Even in bodily matters, not everyone possesses everything

From bodily matters let us consider spiritual matters. One man is swift on his feet but not strong in his hand. Another is slow in walking but steadfast in battle. One has a beautiful face but a hoarse voice. Another has an ugly face but sings with sweet modulation. We see one as gifted but forgetful, another as retentive but slow in intellect.

Even in those controversies in which we once played as boys, not everyone conducts himself in the same way—in introductions, narratives, digressions, arguments, abundance of examples, or the sweetness of conclusions. Rather, they differ from one another in different parts of their eloquence.

I shall speak of men who are more particularly ecclesiastical. Many discourse well on the Gospels but are unequal to themselves in explaining the Apostle. Others, although they have understood the New Testament very well, are mute in the Psalms and the Old Testament. I say all this because “we cannot all do everything” (Virgil, *Eclogue* VII); and there is scarcely any rich man—or perhaps none—who possesses equal abundance in every part of his wealth.

God has commanded what is possible, and I admit this. But none of us can possess all these possibilities individually—not because of the weakness of nature, lest you bring an accusation against God, but because of the weariness of the soul, which cannot possess all virtues simultaneously and always.

And if you accuse the Creator because he made you such that you grow weak and weary, I shall say again that your accusation will be greater if you wish to charge him with not having made you God. But you will say: “If I cannot do it, then I have no sin.” You have sinned in failing to do what another was able to do.

Again, the person who is worse than you in comparison with you, or worse than another in some other virtue, will himself be a sinner by comparison; and so it happens that whoever you think is first is inferior to the person who is greater than he in another respect.

## 24. God can preserve a person without sin

**C.** If a human being cannot be without sin, how does the Apostle Jude write: “To him who is able to preserve you without sin and to set you immaculate before the presence of his glory” (Jude I, 24)? By this testimony it is proved that a human being can be without sin and without stain.

**A.** You do not understand what you have proposed. The human being cannot be without sin, as your position has it; but God, if he wills, can preserve a human being without sin and guard him immaculate by his mercy. This too is what I say: all things are possible for God. But not everything a human being wishes is possible for him—especially something which you read no creature has possessed.

**C.** I am not saying that a human being is without sin, which perhaps seems possible to you; I am saying that he can be so if he wishes. For it is one thing to be, and another to be able to be. “To be” seeks an example; “to be able” demonstrates the truth of power.

**A.** You are talking nonsense, and you do not remember the proverb: “Do not do what has already been done; you are rolling about in the same mud—or rather, washing a brick.” You will hear nothing else from me except what is obvious to everyone: you wish to establish a thing which neither is, nor has been, and perhaps never will be.

And, to use your own expression and expose the folly of an incoherent (ἀσύστατος; in the manuscripts, *asystatae*, “inconsistent”) argument, I say that you are claiming that something can be which cannot be. For this proposition of yours—that a human being can be without sin if he wishes—is either true or false. If it is true, show us who has been such. If it is false, whatever is false can never come to pass.

But let these matters, as though rejected with contempt, be silenced, and let them merely mutter in your little chests, afraid of the public eye.

## 25. He refutes the book of Pelagius

Let us pass to other matters, in which we must use continuous discourse, though in such a way that you retain the power to refute and question anything you wish.

**C.** I shall listen patiently—though I shall not say willingly—and I shall marvel even more at your talent, whose falsity leaves me astonished.

**Editorial note:** Two of our manuscripts read: “and I shall marvel at the talent whose falsity I am even more astonished by.”

**A.** Whether what I am about to say is false or true, you will determine that only after you have heard it.

**C.** Speak as you wish. I have resolved that, if I cannot answer, I would rather remain silent than assent to a lie.

**A.** What difference does it make whether I overcome you while you are silent or while you are speaking, and, according to the story of Proteus, seize you while you are awake—or while you are asleep?

**Editorial note:** Martianus mistakenly printed *non* rather than *an*, which all the manuscripts prefer. Victorius likewise restored *num* with the same meaning. It is well known that Proteus was captured while asleep by the shepherd Aristaeus, who was fleeing through the Vale of Tempe in Thessaly, as Virgil sings in *Georgics* IV.

**C.** When you have said what you wish, you will hear what you do not wish at all. Truth may suffer hardship, but it cannot be defeated.

**A.** I would like to examine your propositions briefly, so that your followers may understand how divine a talent they admire in you.

You say that no one can be without sin unless he possesses knowledge of the Law. By this you exclude a large part of Christians from righteousness; and although you proclaim the possibility of sinlessness, you declare almost all Christians to be sinners. For how many Christians possess knowledge of the Law—a knowledge which you will find only rarely, or with difficulty, even among many teachers of the Church?

Yet you are so generous that you win favor among your Amazons, since elsewhere you have written that women too ought to possess knowledge of the Law, even though the Apostle teaches that women should keep silent in the church and, if they wish to learn anything, should ask their husbands at home (I Cor. XIV).

Nor is it enough for you to have given your troop knowledge of the Scriptures unless you also delight in their voices and songs. For you add and place in a heading: “That women too ought to sing psalms to God.”

Who does not know that women ought to sing psalms in their bedrooms, away from the presence of men and from the gathering of crowds? But you grant what is not permitted, so that what they ought to do modestly and without any witness they may proclaim publicly under a teacher’s authority.

## 26. He again refutes the book of Pelagius

**Editorial note:** The oldest Regina manuscript adds the number of each title, as do the printed editions before Erasmus. It would indeed be worthwhile to reproduce in the text the individual chapters of the Pelagian book from which these propositions are taken, as Jerome himself did something similar. But since some other very ancient copies have no numerical notation, while those that do have it sometimes differ in their numbers, and since the book of the heresiarch himself has long since perished, so that it is not readily possible to establish the reading from it, we have thought it better to place those notes in the margin from the royal manuscript, indicating only the variants.

Moreover, you add (Title XIII, alternatively XIV) that a servant of God ought to utter nothing bitter from his mouth but should always say what is sweet and pleasant. Then, as though a servant of God were one person and a teacher and priest of the Church another, forgetting your earlier statement, you write in another title (Title XXVII, alternatively XXII) that a priest or teacher ought to watch over everyone’s actions and rebuke sinners boldly, lest he have to render an account for them and their blood be required from his hands [alternatively: “lest you have to render an account for them”].

Nor are you content to have said this once: you repeat and insist on the same point (Title XXXI), that a priest or teacher ought to flatter no one but should rebuke everyone boldly, lest he destroy both himself and those who listen to him.

Is there such inconsistency in a single work that you do not know what you said first? For if a servant of God ought to utter nothing bitter from his mouth but only what is sweet and pleasant, then either a priest and teacher is not a servant of God—although he ought boldly to rebuke sinners and flatter no one, but courageously reproach everyone—or, if a priest and teacher is not merely a servant of God but holds the foremost place among his servants, you have reserved flatteries and sweetness uselessly for the servants of God. That is properly the practice of heretics and of those who wish to deceive their hearers, as the Apostle says: “For such persons do not serve Christ our Lord, but their own belly; and by sweet words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. XVI, 18).

Flattery is always treacherous, crafty, and smooth. Among philosophers, the flatterer is beautifully defined as “a pleasant enemy.” Truth is bitter, has a wrinkled and sorrowful brow, and offends those who are rebuked.

**Editorial note:** The Vatican manuscript reads: “a wrinkled and sorrowful brow indeed offends those who are rebuked, etc.” Hence the Apostle also says: “Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?” (Gal. IV, 16).

And the Comic poet says:

> Compliance wins friends; truth produces hatred.

Therefore we eat the Passover with bitter herbs, and the chosen vessel teaches that the Passover is to be celebrated in truth and sincerity (I Cor. V): let truth be sincerity in us, and bitterness will immediately follow.

## 27. All things are governed by God’s will

But what you place elsewhere (Title XXXI)—“All people are governed by their own will”—which Christian can bear to hear? If not one, nor a few, nor many, but all are governed by their own will, where will God’s help be? And how do you explain the following passages?

“The steps of a man are directed by the Lord” (Ps. XXXVI, 23); and, “A man’s way is not his own” (Jer. X, 22); and, “No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from above.” Elsewhere: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

The Lord and Savior says: “I have not come down from heaven to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John V, 30). And elsewhere: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Luke XXII, 42). “Nevertheless, not what I will, but as you will.”

**Editorial note:** Some manuscripts read, “if it is possible.” Immediately afterward the Vatican manuscript, together with the royal manuscript, reads: “not what I will, but yours.” Finally, “as in heaven, so also on earth.”

And in the Lord’s Prayer: “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth” (Matt. VI, 10).

With what rashness of opinion do you remove all God’s protection? And what you try in vain to add elsewhere—“not without the grace of God”—and how you wish this to be understood is clear from the present passage: you do not refer his grace to individual works, but to the power of nature, Law, and free choice.

**Editorial note:** See *The Proceedings against Pelagius*, chapter 3, no. 5 and following. In place of *sentiri*, which the manuscripts prefer, *sentire* had been printed. It is especially clear from what follows that the Pelagians wished by this proposition to remove the necessity of grace.

## 28. The distinction between the ungodly and the unrighteous

But what you place in the following chapter (Title LXII, alternatively LXXII)—“On the day of judgment the unrighteous and sinners are not to be spared, but are to be burned in eternal fires”—who can endure it?

**Editorial note:** The manuscripts more correctly omit the word “and.” This proposition of Pelagius was false because it was too general and absolute, and did not distinguish those guilty of graver crimes from those guilty of lighter ones. Moreover, as will be shown below from the letter of Hilary of Syracuse to Augustine, the Pelagians called “unrighteous” and “sinners” those who remained in wealth, even if they gave alms from that wealth and performed other good works; thus they urged people toward greater and more perfect things in such a way as to deter them from lesser ones. See below, Book II, near the end; also *The Proceedings against Pelagius*, chapter 3, no. 9.

You would forbid God’s mercy and judge before the day of judgment the sentence of the Judge, so that, if he wishes to spare the unrighteous and sinners, he may not be able to do so because you have prescribed otherwise.

For you say:

> “It is written in Psalm 103: ‘Let sinners perish from the earth and the unrighteous, so that they are no more.’ And in Isaiah: ‘The unrighteous and sinners shall be burned together, and those who abandon God shall be consumed.’”

Do you not understand that God’s threat sometimes sounds like clemency? For he does not say that they are to be burned in eternal fires, but that they are to perish from the earth and cease to be unrighteous. It is one thing for them to cease from sin and unrighteousness, and another for them to perish forever and be burned in eternal fires.

Finally, Isaiah, from whom you take your testimony, says: “Sinners and the unrighteous shall be burned together”; he does not add “for eternity.” “And those who abandon God shall be consumed.” He is speaking particularly of heretics, who, abandoning the straight path of the faith, will be consumed if they do not wish to return to the Lord whom they abandoned. The same sentence awaits you if you neglect to turn to better things.

Moreover, what presumption it is to join the unrighteous and sinners with the ungodly! We define them in this way: Every ungodly person is unrighteous and a sinner, but the terms are not interchangeable, so that we could say that every sinner and unrighteous person is also ungodly. Ungodliness properly belongs to those who do not possess knowledge of God, or who, after knowing him, have exchanged that knowledge for transgression.

Sin and unrighteousness, however, according to the character of their vices, receive healing after the wounds of sin and unrighteousness. Hence it is written: “Many are the scourges of the sinner” (Ps. XXXI, 10), not “everlasting destruction.” Israel is corrected through every scourge and torment. “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6).

It is one thing to strike with the affection of a teacher and parent; it is another to rage against enemies with a cruel spirit. For what reason, then, does the first Psalm also sing: “For the ungodly do not rise in judgment”? They have already been sentenced beforehand to destruction.

**Editorial note:** Martianus warns that this passage should be read cautiously. Servatus Lupus cites it in his *Collection on Three Questions* to support his doctrine of predestination; he also quotes other testimonies from Jerome, from the third book of this work at the end, and from the *Commentaries on Isaiah*. From this passage the Pseudo-Jerome evidently drew the statement in his *Brief Commentary on the Psalter*: “It does not say that they do not rise again, but that they do not rise in judgment; for they have already been judged in advance.”

“Nor sinners in the counsel of the just” (Ps. I, 5). It is one thing to lose the glory of rising again; it is another to perish forever.

“For the hour is coming,” he says, “when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 5).

In the same sense, and therefore by the same Spirit, the Apostle says to the Romans: “For whoever sinned without the Law will also perish without the Law; and whoever sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law” (Rom. II, 12). The ungodly person is without the Law and will perish eternally. The sinner under the Law is one who believes in God and will be judged by the Law, but will not perish.

If sinners and the unrighteous are burned in eternal fires, do you not fear your own sentence, since you say that you are unrighteous and a sinner? And you argue that a human being is not without sin but can be without sin. Then let only the person be saved who never was and is not, but will be—or perhaps will not even be—and let all those whom we read existed in the past perish.

You yourself, who puff yourself up with Cato’s pride—alternatively, Catoniaca—and swell with Milo’s shoulders, with what presumption do you, a sinner, assume the name of teacher?

**Editorial note:** He implies that Pelagius was a man of tall stature. In the preface to Book III on Jeremiah, Jerome calls him an “Alpine” dog—properly, an “Albinian” dog—large and corpulent, and one who could rage more with his heels than with his teeth.

Or if you are just and, out of humility, pretend to be a sinner, we shall marvel and rejoice that you alone possess, together with your associates, what none of the patriarchs, prophets, or apostles possessed.

But if Origen says that all rational creatures are not to be destroyed and grants repentance to the devil, what has that to do with us? We say that both the devil and all his satellites, together with all the ungodly and transgressors, perish forever; but that Christians, if they have been overtaken by sin, are to be saved after punishment.

**Editorial note:** Almost everyone attacks and slanders this passage. Not only heterodox writers, such as Stanislaus Pannonius the Anabaptist, who uses it in his book *On Divine Philanthropy* to construct an impious heresy, but also learned and highly Catholic men, such as Daniel Huetius, bishop of Avranches, in his *Origeniana*, pronounce it foreign to the true faith. There is no doubt that, if Jerome is interpreted as they interpret him, he assigned everlasting punishments only to the devil and to ungodly human beings who lack knowledge of God, while assigning merely temporal punishments to unrighteous Christians, even when guilty of grave crimes.

But I maintain that this was not his meaning, if the passage can suitably be understood in a Catholic sense, so that the teaching of the holy Father is not exposed to the most malicious slander. If only the suspicion arising from this passage had to be cleared away, I could readily do so by explaining it according to the natural meaning of the discourse: Christians who are not, however, transgressors—those whom he has just counted among the ungodly—if they have been overtaken by sin, certainly a lighter sin, since what is not against the Law is not transgression, are to be saved after punishments, namely purgatorial punishments by which sin can be removed.

But we know that the opponents wish the meaning of this passage to be judged by comparison with two other passages.

The first they bring forward from the final chapter of the *Commentaries on Isaiah*: “Just as we believe that the devil and all deniers and ungodly people who said in their hearts, ‘There is no God,’ are destined for eternal torments, so we judge the sentence of the Judge concerning sinners who are nevertheless Christians, whose works must be tested and purified by fire, to be measured and mixed with mercy.”

The second they take from what the holy Doctor likewise scattered through his *Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians*. Avoiding Rufinus’ criticisms, Jerome wrote in Book II of the *Apology*, no. 7: “When you call down eternal fires with the devil upon the brothers—that is, upon those whom you accuse—you seem not so much to oppress the brothers as to raise up the devil, since you assign him to be punished in the same fires in which Christians are punished.”

If we set against these six hundred testimonies of Jerome in which he explicitly teaches that everlasting punishments await wicked Christians who have died without repentance, the opponents wish to prove nothing more than that he changed his opinion at some point and did not always adhere to a single view. As though, in the passages they so vehemently slander, his teaching contained some abnormal error!

He said that he considered the sentence concerning “sinners, but nevertheless Christians, whose works must be tested and purified by fire” to be “measured and mixed with the Judge’s mercy.” The testimony of Paul in I Cor. III, 13–15 concerns precisely this: the works of Christians are to be tested and purified by fire so that they may receive their reward—that is, so that lighter offenses, and even graver ones already forgiven through repentance, may be cleansed by purgatorial fire.

Our author did not say this indiscriminately of all Christians, but of those “whose works must be tested and purified by fire.” By these words he signifies nothing other than punishments which, in ecclesiastical language and according to ecclesiastical understanding, last for a time and are inflicted upon the faithful who are guilty of light faults, or even of grave faults after repentance.

As for the other testimony drawn from the *Apology*, I shall not linger over it. Above, in the note on that passage, page 495, note c, I have shown, as I believe, clearly enough that the holy Doctor is not speaking of the eternity of fire, but only that it seemed to him that Rufinus was raising up the devil by assigning him to the same torments as Christians—since Rufinus thought that more severe punishments were owed to demons, according to the gravity of their crimes, than to condemned believers.

Therefore, whether we examine the difficulty proposed here on its own or compare it with other passages scattered elsewhere, Jerome does not appear to have spoken rashly or imprudently.

But, to leave no room for slander, we must recall that the holy Doctor was writing against the Pelagians, and that his purpose was to dispute against their madness concerning the merits and remission of sins, just as Saint Augustine did. For this was the hypocrisy of the Pelagians, born from the polluted springs of the Stoics: they called what were light sins extremely grave, or—as was noted a little above—they did not distinguish between those guilty of lighter and those guilty of graver crimes, so that they themselves might appear to be devotees of a stricter justice.

Let us give an example from the letter of Hilary of Syracuse to Augustine, which is said to have been publicized by the Pelagians:

> “A rich man who remains in his riches cannot enter the kingdom of God unless he has sold all that he possesses; nor can it benefit him if, from those same riches, he happens to fulfill the commandments.”

According to their view, such people had to be counted among the unrighteous and sinners and burned in eternal fires, even if they gave alms from their riches and faithfully kept all the commandments.

Jerome attacks this sort of nonsense throughout the whole chapter, and shows that their position entails that no one ever obtained eternal salvation before, or could obtain it in the future. It is therefore entirely clear that he is speaking of lighter faults, in which the heretics babbled that Christians who had been overtaken by sin were to be condemned forever, whereas he, in Catholic fashion, judged that they were to be saved after the punishment of purification.

In conclusion, I do not conceal that Saint Augustine, in his book *On Faith and Works* and in the *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity*, deliberately attacks the position which the opponents attribute to Jerome. But since the bishop of Hippo does not name the author against whom he is arguing, I think this charge cannot justly be turned against our holy Doctor, whom we have shown to have held an orthodox view.

## 29. Two chapters of Pelagius contradicting one another

Moreover, you join together two mutually contradictory chapters, and, if they are genuine, you will be unable to open your mouth:

“Wisdom and understanding of the Scriptures cannot be known unless one has learned them.”

And again:

“An unlearned person ought not to claim knowledge of the Law” (Title XX).

Either you will be forced to produce the teacher from whom you learned, so that you may be permitted to claim knowledge of the Law; or, if such a teacher did not learn from another and taught you what he himself did not know, it follows that you are acting wrongly when, being unlearned, you claim knowledge of the Scriptures, and that you began to be a teacher before you became a disciple.

Unless, perhaps, with your customary humility, you boast that your teacher is the Lord, who teaches all knowledge; and that, with Moses (Exod. XXXIV), you hear the words of God face to face in cloud and darkness, and then come forth among us with a horned forehead.

Nor is this enough. Suddenly you become a Stoic, and from Zeno’s brow thunder at us that a Christian ought to possess such patience that, if someone wishes to take away his property, he should gladly surrender it (Title LXXIII, alternatively LXIV).

Is it not enough for us patiently to lose what we possess, unless we also thank the violent man and the robber and follow him with every blessing? The Gospel teaches (Matt. V) that to one who wishes to contend with us in court and, through lawsuits and quarrels, take away our tunic, we should grant the cloak as well.

**Editorial note:** Two Vatican manuscripts mark this with an emphatic interrogative: “Does he command us…?”

It does not command us to give thanks and joyfully lose what is ours. I say this not because there is anything criminal in the proposition itself, but because everywhere you pass over moderate things hyperbolically (ὑπερβολικῶς) and pursue what is extreme.

Hence you add: “The glory of clothing and ornaments is contrary to God.”

What hostility to God is there, I ask, if I have a cleaner tunic, if a bishop, presbyter, deacon, and the rest of the ecclesiastical order appear in the administration of the sacrifices in a white garment?

**Editorial note:** From this passage learned men infer that in the earliest centuries of the Church clerics used no other garments than secular clothing, except that these were cleaner and finer in the administration of the sacrifices; thus they interpret the white garment. Compare what Jerome says in his *Commentaries on Ezekiel* XLIV, 17, and the notes there. This appears to have led to the result that, while those finer and better garments were used more rarely and guarded more carefully, they gradually became distinctive, as the ordinary form of clothing subsequently changed; and so those garments were assigned to the administration of the sacrifices. Otherwise, the opinion of Pope Celestine is well known: “We are to be distinguished from the people and others by teaching, not by clothing; by conduct, not by dress; by purity of mind, not by adornment.” *Letter to the Bishop of Vienne.*

Take care, clerics; take care, monks; widows and virgins, you are in danger unless the crowd sees you filthy and dressed in rags. I say nothing of secular people, against whom open war is declared, and enmity against God, if they use costly and shining garments.

## 30. Contradictory chapters of Pelagius

Let us hear the rest:

“Enemies are to be loved as neighbors” (Title CLXIV, alternatively CXLIV).

Immediately afterward, overcome by the deepest lethargy, you write and say:

“An enemy is never to be trusted” (Title CLXI, alternatively CXLVI).

That these statements contradict one another is clear even without my saying so.

But you will say—or rather, you say—that both expressions are contained in the words of Scripture, without noticing in what sense they were spoken in their respective contexts.

I am commanded to love my enemies and pray for my persecutors. Was I therefore commanded to love them as neighbors, relatives, and friends, so that there should be no difference between a rival and an intimate companion? If I love my enemies as neighbors, what more shall I show to my friends?

**Editorial note:** Earlier the reading was *dixeris* (“you will have said”), and shortly afterward *videaris* (“you may seem”) for *videreris* (“you might seem”), against the manuscripts.

Or if you had said this, you ought to have kept silent about the other, lest you appear to utter contradictory statements in the same place: “An enemy is never to be trusted” (Exod. XXIII).

But the Law itself also teaches how an enemy is to be loved (Deut. XXII, 4): “If the beast of your adversary has fallen, it must be lifted up.” And the Apostle says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head” (Rom. XII, 20)—not as a curse and condemnation, as many suppose, but for correction and repentance, so that, overcome by benefits and refined by the fervor of charity, he may cease to be an enemy.

**Editorial note:** One Vatican manuscript reads: “Once the coldness of hatred has been burned away, he may cease to be an enemy of charity.” Another, less satisfactorily, reads: “Once the fire of hatred has been burned away, through the coldness of charity, the enemy…” For Pelagius’ subsequent proposition, recall Saint Augustine, *The Proceedings against Pelagius*, chapter 5.

## 31. Whether the Kingdom of Heaven Was Promised in the Old Testament

Moreover, you add that the Kingdom of Heaven is also promised in the Old Testament (Title 123), and you set forth testimonies from apocryphal writings, although it is perfectly clear that the Kingdom of Heaven was first preached in the Gospel by John the Baptist, by the Lord and Savior, and by the Apostles. Read the Gospels. John the Baptist cries out in the desert: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:1). And concerning the Savior it is written: “From that time Jesus began to preach and to say: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4:17). And again: “Jesus went about the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues [variant: synagogue] and preaching the kingdom of God” (Matt. 9:35). And he commands the Apostles: “Go and preach, saying: For the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

Yet you call them Manichaeans because we prefer the Gospel to the Law, saying that in the Law there is shadow, but in the Gospel truth; and you do not understand that your stupidity is joined to your shamelessness. It is one thing to condemn the Law, as the Manichaean does; it is another to prefer the Gospel to the Law, which is apostolic doctrine. In the Law servants speak; in the Gospel the Lord who is present speaks. There the promise is made; here it is fulfilled. There are the beginnings; here is perfection. There the foundations of works are laid; here the summit of faith and grace is placed.

We have set this forth so that the teaching of the excellent instructor might be exposed.

*Note:* Martianay and others have corruptly read *cur legi*, “why I read,” whereas the intended reading is *quia Legi*, “because we prefer the Law,” etc.

## 32. He Attacks the Principal Opinion of the Pelagians

The hundredth title is: “That man can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes,” a matter about which enough has already been said. Although he professes himself an imitator—indeed, a fulfiller—of the work of the blessed martyr Cyprian, who wrote to Quirinus [manuscripts: Cirinus], he does not understand that in the same work he has stated contradictory things.

In the fifty-fourth title of the third book, Cyprian declares that no one is “without stain and without sin” [note: The text had hitherto been corruptly given as “can be without sin,” contrary both to Cyprian’s writing and Jerome’s argument; the manuscripts used here and a Corbie manuscript used by the Benedictine editors of Augustine all lack *can be*], and immediately joins testimonies in which it is written in Job: “For who is clean from uncleanness? Not even if his life upon the earth is only one day” (Job 14:4). And in the fiftieth Psalm, verse 6: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” [two Vatican manuscripts: “in sins she gave birth,” etc.]. And in the Epistle of John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

You, on the other hand, assert: “Man can be without sin”; and, to make it appear that you have spoken truly, you immediately add: “and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes”—commandments which either very few or no one has fulfilled. For if they are easy, they ought to be kept by many. But if, as we grant you, scarcely anyone can fulfill them, it is evident that what is rare is difficult.

And to heighten this claim and display the greatness of your virtue—so that you may appear to be pouring forth something from the good treasure of your conscience [the old edition and the Regina manuscript read: “so that you attempt to pour forth”]—you place in the title: “Not even lightly is one to sin” (Title 123). And, lest anyone should suppose that you said “lightly” in the body of the work, you append what “lightly” means: “Evil is not even to be thought” (Title 136, or 131) [the manuscripts and editions generally read this way. The Benedictine editors of Augustine read “evil is not even to be thought,” which would be acceptable if they had added “ought to be.” See Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 4, no. 12].

Nor do you remember that saying: “Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18:13). Yet the Church acknowledges that even those things in which we offend through ignorance, and in which we sin by thought alone, are offenses; so much so that it commands sacrifices to be offered for error (Heb. 2), and the High Priest who intercedes for the whole people first offers victims for himself. Certainly, he would never be commanded to offer for others unless he himself were righteous; nor would he again offer for himself if he were free from the sin of ignorance.

Apparently, I must now travel through the vast expanses of Scripture [Martianay incorrectly emends this to “to be traversed,” against the manuscripts and the more accurate editions] in order to show that error and ignorance are sin.

## 33. That Sins of Ignorance Exist

**C.** I beg you, have you not read: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28)? Therefore it is not merely the sight and the incitements of vices that are reckoned as sin, but also those things to which we give our assent. Either we can avoid an evil thought, and consequently can be free from sin; or, if we cannot avoid it, it is not reckoned as sin [strictly speaking, formal sin, to introduce a term from the schools, not material sin; the Pelagians were fond of confusing these two. Similar is that well-known saying of Augustine: “Who sins in what cannot be avoided?” He defended it against the Pelagian calumnies in such a way that he did not thereby deny either original sin—which certainly cannot be avoided—or the necessity of material sin. See both works against Julian], since what cannot be avoided is not culpable.

**A.** You argue cleverly, but you do not understand that your argument is directed against the sacred Scriptures. For the utterances of Scripture teach that ignorance itself is also sin. Thus Job offers sacrifices for his sons, lest perhaps they sinned in thought through ignorance (Job 1). And when a man cuts wood, if someone is killed when the axe slips from the wood because of the iron, he is commanded to flee to a city of refuge and remain there until the high priest dies (Deut. 19)—that is, until he is redeemed by the blood of the Savior, either in the house of baptism or in repentance, which imitates the grace of baptism through the Savior’s ineffable clemency [one Vatican manuscript reads: “who does not wish anyone to perish,” etc.]. For he does not wish anyone to perish, nor does he delight in the deaths of sinners, but rather that they should turn and live (Ezek. 18).

**C.** I ask: what sort of justice is this, that I should be held in the sin of error, when my conscience bears no guilt for it? I do not know that I have sinned, and I pay the penalty for a thing I do not know. And what more would I do if I sinned deliberately?

**A.** Do you demand from me the reasons for God’s judgment and arrangement? The Book of Wisdom responds to your foolish question: “Do not seek what is higher than you, and do not investigate what is stronger than you” (Ecclus. 3:22). And elsewhere: “Do not be excessively wise, and do not argue beyond what is fitting” (Eccles. 7:17). And in the same place: “Seek God in wisdom and simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1:1) [Victorius restores “and in another place,” since the first testimony is from Ecclesiasticus and the second from Wisdom; Jerome here calls Ecclesiasticus the Book of Wisdom].

And lest you contradict this book, hear the Apostle, sounding forth the evangelical trumpet: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11:33–34) [elsewhere, where this verse occurs, we note that it is scarcely credible that Jerome read *investigabiles*, “searchable,” instead of *ininvestigabiles*, “unsearchable”].

These are the questions about which he also writes elsewhere: “Avoid foolish and ignorant controversies, knowing that they produce quarrels” (2 Tim. 2:23) [the reference in the supplied text reads “2, 3”]. And Ecclesiastes—in whose book there is certainly no ambiguity—says: “I said, ‘I will become wise’; but it was far from me. Deep is the depth: who will find it?” (Eccles. 7:24–25).

You ask me why the potter made one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, and you refuse to listen to Paul answering on behalf of his Lord: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:20).

## 34. He Sets Forth Testimonies from Scripture

Hear, then, briefly, the testimonies of Scripture, so that your foolish—or rather impious—questioning may fall silent forever.

God speaks in Genesis: “I will not again curse the earth because of the works of human beings, since the mind of man is diligently inclined to evil from his youth” (Gen. 8:21).

Abraham and Sarah, after hearing the promise of the son Isaac, laugh in their hearts, and their silent thought is not hidden from the knowledge of God. They are reproved for their laughter, and the thought itself, as a part of unbelief, is censured. Yet they are not condemned for having laughed, but because afterward they believed, they received the palm of righteousness.

Lot does not know what he has done in intercourse with his daughters, and, having been made drunk by them, he bears no guilt in his conscience; yet the error is still a fault.

Reproach the holy man Jacob: why did he love beautiful Rachel, for whom he also served for a long time, and why was he saddened at his first intercourse with Leah? Then yield at last to human frailty, which loves beautiful bodies and detests misshapen ones.

Jacob mourns the death of his son Joseph and for a long time refuses to accept consolation from his sons. He says: “Mourning and lamenting, I shall go down to the underworld” (Gen. 37:35). He proves himself human, while the righteous man does not know what has happened to his righteous son Joseph.

In Exodus it is written: “If someone strikes another person and he dies, let him be put to death. But if he did not do it intentionally, and God delivered him into his hands, I will appoint for you a place to which the one who killed him may flee” (Exod. 21:12–13). Here it must be observed that God delivered the man into his hands, and yet the one who killed through ignorance is condemned to exile.

In Leviticus the Law is set forth [the old edition explains the law]: “If a soul sins unintentionally before the Lord, and does one of the things which the Lord’s commandments forbid, whether he is the high priest, or the whole assembly, or the rest of the people, and afterward learns of his sin, which he committed through ignorance, he shall offer a gift: an unblemished male goat. He shall lay his hands upon its head and kill it in the place where the burnt offerings are slaughtered before the Lord, because it is for sin” (Lev. 4:2, 13 ff.).

And immediately afterward: “If he touches anything unclean which he is not permitted to touch, and does so through ignorance, and afterward learns of it; or if he makes a promise and forgets it, he shall declare the sin in which he recognizes that he has sinned, and shall offer to the Lord for what he has sinned a female lamb or a female goat for his sin. The priest shall pray for him over his sin, and his sin shall be forgiven. But if his hand cannot afford a sheep for his sins which he has committed, he shall offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the Lord, one for sin and the other as a burnt offering. He shall bring them to the priest, and the priest shall offer first what is for sin; and through it he shall be reconciled for the sin he committed, and it shall be forgiven him” (Lev. 5:3 ff.) [the manuscripts read: “for his sin which he committed,” agreeing with the Greek text, *περὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας αὐτοῦ, ἧς ἥμαρτε*, “for his sin which he committed”].

There are many other similar passages, which I omit for the sake of brevity, lest I cause your stomach to recoil.

In what follows Moses also recounts (ibid., 8) that, at the consecration of Aaron and his sons, he offered a calf for sin; Aaron and his sons laid their hands upon it, namely upon the head of the calf that was for sin; he slaughtered it, took some of its blood, and with his finger placed it around the horns of the altar, and cleansed the altar. He did the same with a ram, and with its blood touched his right ear, his right hand, and the tip of his right foot.

After many other matters, which would take too long to recount, when the seven days had been completed, we read:

“On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and all the elders of Israel, and said to Aaron: ‘Take a calf from the herd for sins [variant: for sin], and an unblemished ram for a burnt offering, and offer them before the Lord. And speak to the elders of Israel, saying: Take one male goat from the goats for sin, and an unblemished year-old calf for a burnt offering.’ And Moses said to Aaron: ‘Approach the altar and make offering for your sin,’ and the rest. Again Aaron lifted his hands over the people and blessed them. And when he had made offering for sin and for the burnt offering and the sacrifice of well-being, he descended” (Lev. 9:1 ff.).

A woman gives birth to children by the law of nature, and she is unclean for forty days if she has borne a male child, and for eighty days if a female. Accuse the Creator: why does he call unclean something that he himself created? And not only is she herself unclean, but everything she touches is unclean.

“When the days of her purification for a son or daughter have been completed, she shall offer a year-old unblemished lamb, and a young pigeon and a turtledove for sin, at the door of the tent of testimony to the priest. He shall offer them before the Lord, and the priest shall make atonement for her” (Lev. 12:6 ff.) [a Vatican manuscript reads “tent of the covenant,” contrary to the Greek, *τοῦ μαρτυρίου*, “of the testimony”].

Of the leper also it is said that on the day of his purification a victim is offered for him as a sin offering, together with two turtledoves and two young pigeons: one for sin and the other as a burnt offering (ibid., 13). And the one who suffers a discharge of semen is freed by the same order of sacrifice, for sin and as a burnt offering.

Finally it is added: “Warn the children of Israel concerning their uncleannesses, and they shall not die for their sin if they defile my tent of testimony” (Lev. 15:31).

Aaron himself is also commanded not to enter the Holy of Holies at all times, lest he die. “When he wishes to enter,” it says, “let him offer a calf for sin and a ram as a burnt offering, and let him take two goats from the whole people. Let him offer one of them for his own sin, and the other for the sin of the people, and a ram as a burnt offering” (Lev. 16:3).

The other of the goats takes upon itself all the sin of the people as a type of the Lord and Savior and carries it into the wilderness; thus God is appeased for the whole multitude.

Finally it is said: “If anyone eats of the holy things through ignorance, it is reckoned to him as iniquity and offense, and he shall be liable for his vow.” Hence the Apostle warns that the Lord’s Eucharist must be received with caution, lest we take it to our condemnation and judgment (1 Cor. 11).

If ignorance is condemned under the Law, how much more conscience under the Gospel!

## 35. From the Book of Numbers

Let us pass to Numbers, and, in order to refute the shamelessness of contentious people, let us gather only the principal points.

The Nazirite, venerable for his sacred hair, is stained by the sudden death of another person, and all the days of his consecration that had elapsed are annulled. Afterward two turtledoves and two young pigeons are offered for him, one for sin and the other as a burnt offering. On the day of his completion, a lamb is also offered as a burnt offering and a ewe lamb for sin.

After many other passages, it is written: “And now let the strength of the Lord be magnified, as you have spoken, saying: ‘The Lord is patient and of great mercy, taking away iniquity and transgressions, and cleansing; he will not make innocent’” (Num. 14:18) [previously, even in the manuscripts, the text incorrectly read *locutus est*, “has spoken”; the text has *es*, “you are,” in all languages. For the following sentence, “and cleansing, he will not make innocent,” compare the rendering of the Septuagint with the version from the Hebrew, in which, as also in the Vulgate, it reads “and leaving no innocent person.” In the Hebrew text itself the phrase can be rendered “and making innocent, he will not make innocent.” In Greek it is *καὶ καθαρισμῷ οὐ καθαριεῖ τὸν ἔνοχον*, “and by cleansing he will not cleanse the guilty.” I have compared all these passages so that you may judge which version Jerome praises here and which he understands to have been expressed from the Septuagint].

For this the Septuagint translated: “and cleansing, he will not cleanse the guilty”—namely, that even after forgiveness a person remains guilty in his own conscience.

“And when the people have sinned unknowingly and have done one of those things which they ought not to do,” after a long order of ceremonies it is added and said: “Offer one male goat for sin, and the priest shall make atonement for the whole assembly of the children of Israel, and it shall be forgiven them, because it was ignorance. And they shall offer their offering as a sacrifice to the Lord for their sin before him, because they did not know” (Num. 7:28–29).

There too it is added: “If one soul sins through ignorance, he shall offer a year-old female goat for the sin of ignorance before the Lord. The priest shall pray for him because he was ignorant, for the sin of ignorance before the Lord, and he shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him” (Lev. 4:27 ff.).

At the new moon of each month, a male goat is offered to the Lord for sin. At Passover also, for eight days—from the fourteenth day of the first month to the twenty-first day—there is a sacrifice for sin. At Pentecost a male goat is offered for sin; and at the new moon of the seventh month, when the trumpet blast resounds, the same observance of the goat for sin is maintained.

On the tenth day of that same seventh month, when there is fasting until evening, a male goat is offered for sin, in addition to the goat which, before the burnt offering, is slaughtered for sin according to the Law.

During the days of the Feast of Booths, when the tabernacles were erected, from the fifteenth day of that same seventh month to the twenty-second day, among the other victims a goat was always offered for sin, so that the saying of blessed David might be fulfilled: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50:5).

Six cities are chosen as places of exile for those who sinned not intentionally but through ignorance—whether by throwing a stone, pushing with the hand, in jest, or in wantonness, without enmity, sinning more through misfortune than through will. Yet they are not without guilt, since they are banished forever, and before the appointed day their return and release cannot be obtained or purchased either by entreaty or by money.

## 36. From Deuteronomy

In Deuteronomy, which is a recounting of past events, it is clearly demonstrated that we are preserved not by our works and righteousness but by God’s mercy. The Lord says through Moses:

“Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God has overthrown them from before you: ‘The Lord brought me in to possess this land because of my righteousness,’ since the Lord will destroy these nations from before you because of their impiety. You will not enter to possess their land because of your righteousness and the uprightness [variant: love] of your heart; rather, the Lord your God will destroy them from before you because of their impiety, in order to establish the word that he spoke to your fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And you shall know that the Lord your God does not give you this excellent land to possess because of your righteousness, for you are a stiff-necked people.”

The sense in which he said, “You shall be perfect with the Lord your God” [one Vatican manuscript reads: “before the Lord your God,” etc.], is confirmed by what follows.

“When you have entered the land which the Lord your God will give you, do not learn to do the abominations of those nations. Let there not be found among you anyone who passes his son or daughter through fire. You shall not serve divinations, omens, auguries, magical arts, or incantations, nor consult magicians, diviners, or the dead. For everyone who does these things is an abomination to the Lord. And because of these abominations the Lord your God will destroy them from before you. You shall be perfect with the Lord your God” (Deut. 18:9–13) [one Vatican manuscript adds: “divinations and omens and auguries,” etc.].

Finally he adds: “For these nations which you will possess listen to diviners and soothsayers. But the Lord your God has not given you such a practice.” Immediately he continues: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among you, from your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him.”

From this it is shown that the perfect person here means not one who possesses every virtue, but one who follows the one perfect God.

He likewise recounts the condition of those exiles who sinned through ignorance, where and for how long they should flee, and then adds:

“When you build a new house, you shall make a parapet around your roof, lest you become guilty of blood when someone falls from it.”

And again: “If there is among you a man who is not clean because of a nocturnal discharge, he shall go outside the camp and shall not enter the middle of the camp. When evening comes, he shall wash himself with water, and after sunset he shall enter the midst of them” (Lev. 15:16).

## 37. From the Book of Joshua

From Jesus the son of Nave I shall set forth only two testimonies.

Achan sinned, and the whole people offended. The Lord said to Joshua: “The children of Israel will not be able to stand before their enemies; they will turn their backs before their adversaries, because the accursed thing has come among them. I will not continue to be with you unless the accursed thing is destroyed from your midst” (Josh. 7:12).

When the sacrilege was investigated and the lot had discovered the hidden culprit, Achan’s sons and daughters, oxen, donkeys, sheep, tent, and everything he possessed were killed with him and destroyed by fire.

Granted that he himself sinned: what did his sons commit? What did the oxen? What did the donkeys? What did the sheep? Bring an accusation against God: why, when one person sinned, was part of the people slaughtered? Why was he himself stoned, and why was he himself stoned [variant: “let him be stoned”], and why did avenging fire consume everything he possessed?

Let us give another example. “There was no city,” it says, “which the Lord did not deliver to the children of Israel, except the Hivite who dwelt in Gibeon. They captured them all in battle, because it was done by the Lord that he might harden their hearts and that they might fight against Israel, so that they would be destroyed, and that no mercy might be shown them, but that they might perish, just as the Lord commanded Moses” (Josh. 11:11–12).

If it was done by the Lord’s will that they should not accept peace or receive Israel, let us say with the Apostle: “Why then does he still find fault?” [previously the editions read *quid ergo quaeritur*, “what then is sought?”; the manuscripts and the Greek text, *τί ἔτι μέμφεται*, support the corrected reading]. “For who can resist his will?” (Rom. 9:19).

## 38. From the Books of Kings

Concerning Samuel and the Books of Kings:

Jonathan tasted a honeycomb on the tip of his staff, and, when his eyes were enlightened, he was placed in danger because he had done it unknowingly. Scripture testifies that he did not know that his father had commanded that no one should taste anything until the Lord’s victory had been completed.

The Lord was so angry that the lot discovered the hidden offender, and Jonathan himself confessed, saying: “I tasted a little honey on the tip of the staff that is in my hand; and behold, I am to die.” Later he was delivered through the intercession and prayers of the people, who said to Saul: “Shall Jonathan die, who has accomplished this great salvation in Israel? Far be it! As the Lord lives, not a hair of his head shall fall to the ground, because he acted with God on this day.” And the people delivered Jonathan, and he did not die (1 Sam. 14:45 ff.) [the published texts previously and falsely read “the Lord delivered Jonathan” instead of “the people,” which all the manuscripts prefer and which the scriptural text itself supports].

Samuel becomes angry with Saul and refuses to go with the king (1 Sam. 16:6–7). Later he is overcome by entreaties, to show the change of the human mind in opposite directions.

He goes to Bethlehem and thinks that each of Jesse’s sons is the one whom the Lord seeks. When he sees Eliab, he says: “Behold, before the Lord stands his anointed.” And the Lord says to him: “Do not look upon his face or the height of his stature, for I have rejected him. For man sees one way, but God another. Man sees what is before his eyes, but God sees the heart.” In this way he errs concerning them all and is corrected concerning them all, so that the weakness of the human mind may be evident.

Ishbosheth [the manuscripts here and below consistently read *Miphiboseth*, a form Erasmus also evidently intended when he wrote *Mephinoseth*; Jonathan’s son was killed by Baanah, as related in the book of 1 Samuel], the son of Saul, is killed by the treachery of Rechab and Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite. When they announced it to David and showed him the head of his adversary, they were killed by David, who said: “Wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house and upon his bed.”

Certainly Ishbosheth was not righteous; nevertheless, he is called righteous in this respect: that he was killed without guilt.

Uzzah the Levite, when the Ark of the Lord was being transferred to Jerusalem and the unruly oxen had made the cart turn to one side, put out his hand to support the tilting Ark. Immediately it follows: “The anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him there because of ignorance, and he died beside the Ark of God.”

David was grieved because the Lord had struck Uzzah, feared the Lord on that day, and said: “How shall the Ark of the Lord come to me?” (2 Sam. 6:7–8).

David, righteous, a prophet, and anointed as king (Ps. 77), whom the Lord chose according to his heart so that he might do all his will, when he sees ignorance punished by the Lord’s anger is terrified and saddened. He does not ask the Lord why he struck one who was ignorant, but trembles before a similar judgment.

David commanded Joab, commander of the army, to count the people. Immediately Scripture records: “David’s heart struck him, and he said to the Lord: ‘I have sinned greatly, because I have done this’” (2 Sam. 24:10).

When he commanded that it be done, he evidently did not know what he was saying; yet he himself reproved himself, and for this fault seventy thousand men were slaughtered by the angel’s sword.

When Solomon had completed the rites of the Temple, he stretched out both palms toward the Lord and said: “When your people sin against you—for there is no human being who does not sin” (1 Kings 8:46).

Ahijah the prophet, the Shilonite, did not know that Jeroboam’s wife was coming to him. The Lord said to him: “Behold, Jeroboam’s wife is entering to ask you for a word concerning her son, who is ill; thus and thus you shall speak to her” (1 Kings 14:5) [variant: “say to her”].

Elisha was sitting on the mountain. A woman whose son had died came to him and, embracing his feet, cried out. When Gehazi tried to drive her away, the man of God said to him: “Leave her, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden it from me and has not announced it to me” (2 Kings 4:27).

## 39. From the Book of Chronicles and from the Prophets

In the Book of Chronicles we read: “These were the sons of Shobal, the father of Kiriath-jearim, who prophesied in part” [two manuscripts here and shortly afterward read *qui prophetabat*, “who prophesied,” in the singular].

And again: “The sons of Salma, father of Bethlehem and the Netophathites, the crown of the house of Joab, and those who prophesied in part of Zareah, and the rest” (1 Chron. 2, according to the Septuagint).

Those who prophesied were certainly holy, and yet they did not deserve to receive perfect prophecy—not prophecy concerning the future in an allegorical sense, but prophecy concerning present matters according to the historical sense.

The prophet Habakkuk gives his song this title: “The prayer of Habakkuk the prophet for ignorances” [variant: “for the ignorant”]. For he had spoken boldly to the Lord and had said:

“How long, Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear? I shall cry to you, suffering violence, and you will not save me? Why have you shown me iniquity and labor, so that I see plunder and injustice? Judgment and contradiction have risen against me. Because of these things the law is torn apart, and judgment does not reach its end; for the impious prevails against the righteous. Therefore perverse judgment goes forth” (Hab. 2:2 ff.).

Then, reproving himself because he had spoken through ignorance, he writes a song of repentance. If ignorance were not sin, he would have written the book of repentance in vain and would foolishly have wished to mourn what was not sin.

At the end of Ezekiel, where, through the building of the Temple situated on the mountain, the mysteries of the Church that would exist many centuries later are narrated, on the first and seventh days of the first month victims are offered for the sin of all who have sinned through error or ignorance. For seven days of Passover a goat is always slaughtered for sin. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month the same order of sacrifices for sins is celebrated.

After many other matters, which it is not appropriate to repeat here, it is written: “There was a place to the west, and he said to me: ‘This is the place where the priests are to boil the sacrifice for sin and for ignorance’” (Ezek. 46:1).

Jeremiah speaks to God: “I know, Lord, that a person’s way does not belong to him, nor does it belong to a man to walk and direct his steps. Therefore the heart of man is perverse and inscrutable, and who will know it?” (Jer. 10:23).

In Proverbs we read: “There is a way which seems right to human beings, but its end comes down into the depths of hell” (Prov. 14:12).

Here too ignorance is plainly condemned, since a person thinks one thing, yet under the appearance of truth descends to the underworld.

“There are many thoughts in the heart of a person” (Prov. 19); yet it is not his will—which is uncertain, wavering, and changeable—that prevails, but God’s counsel.

“Who can boast that he has a pure heart? And who can trust that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. 20:9).

“For a person’s bread is sweet deceit, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel. Human steps are directed by the Lord; but how can a mortal understand his ways? Every person seems righteous to himself, but God corrects the hearts of all.”

The wicked son makes himself righteous and does not cleanse his outcome. The wicked son has lofty eyes and lifts himself up with his eyelids. There is a righteous person who perishes in his righteousness (Prov. 20:16 ff.) [this entire passage is drawn here and there from the Septuagint version, not as present-day copies give it. Moreover, the verse “The wicked son makes himself righteous,” etc., is read differently by Augustine in Epistle 93: “The wicked son himself calls himself righteous, but does not cleanse his way out.” This verse is absent from the Vulgate, but in Greek it is inserted in chapter 24 and under another chapter, 30:12; compare it in the Greek. In the old edition, the words “but God corrects the hearts of all” are placed after “he does not wash his way out.”]

Therefore it is said to him: “Do not be excessively righteous, and do not seek beyond what is fitting, as though through wisdom, lest you become bewildered. For whatever a person labors to seek, he will not find. If a wise person says that he understands, he will not be able to discover it. For the heart of the children of men is filled with evil” (Eccles. 7:17 ff.).

[Note: The Vallarsian edition adds: “Here ends the first book.” It appends the following note: “Two Vatican manuscripts read: ‘The first part of the preceding book ends here. The second part of the same book begins.’”]

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0533]

[Col. 0533D] 741 **1. Sacrifice for ignorance, error, etc.**—CRITOBULUS. You have indeed cited many passages from the Holy Scriptures, abundantly and from memory, and, as though through certain clouds, you have endeavored to cover the clear light of truth; but what has this to do with the matter?

[Note: “As though through certain clouds.” The sense retained by the manuscripts is entirely clear; Marianus and others, failing to attain it, wished to read: “And, as though after certain clouds had been dispersed, you seemed to open the clear light of truth.” Erasmus has *visus* (“you seemed”) for *nisus* (“you endeavored”).—MARTIANUS.] For by all these testimonies you seem to accuse human nature and thereby to direct resentment against God, if he created such human beings that they cannot be free from the sin of forgetfulness and ignorance. From this it is evident that a human being can, if he wishes, refrain from sinning. He did what he could not avoid. But when possibility is removed, fault is removed as well; for no one is condemned for what he could not do.

ATTICUS. I have often said that you do not understand my arguments or consider what I am arguing, but only what God commanded. God ordered sacrifices to be offered for forgetfulness, error, and ignorance, as though for sin—whether, in your view, wrongly, or, in mine, rightly. My duty is to observe what he commanded; yours is to criticize God’s commands.

C. Since you do violence to evident truth and drag me toward blasphemy, I will grant that this was commanded in the Old Law, concerning which it is written: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (II Cor. V, 17). But can you also establish this from the Gospel, so that someone may be punished for what he does not know and suffer punishment before he is guilty in conscience [another reading: of ignorance]?

A. While we are disputing this, Manichaeus suddenly rises against us, declaring that the Law has been abolished and that only the books of the New Testament should be read.

C. What have you heard from me that makes you suppose this?

A. The Law, too, which was given to the fathers, was just and holy for its time; and when the perfection of the Gospel arrived, the lesser things ceased.

A. Then must what is prescribed by the Law in no way be observed?

[Col. 0535C] C. Some things must be observed, others omitted.

A. Since I see that you are exceedingly learned, tell me which things from the Old Testament I ought to observe and which to leave aside.

C. We ought to observe the commandments that concern life and the correction of conduct, about which it is said: “The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII, 9). But the things that concern the ceremonies of the Law and the rites of sacrifices must be left aside.

A. Forgive me: while you boast of your knowledge of the Law and of all the Scriptures, you do not notice what I mean to say.

C. I understand what you say, not what you keep silent about.

A. Do I seem to you to be keeping silent, when by so many examples I have wished to teach you that a human being sins through ignorance, and that, just as victims are offered for sin in the Law, so repentance is to be offered in the Gospel?

[Col. 0535D] **2. An example from the New Testament in the person of the Apostle.**—C. Give me testimony from the New Testament showing that error, ignorance, and the impossibility of fulfilling a command are held as guilt.

A. It is not necessary to produce many passages. I shall produce one against which you certainly cannot object. The chosen vessel speaks plainly: “I consent to the law of God according to the inner man. But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 22 ff.).

C. You have produced testimony that supports my position. Therefore, once freed from this body of death through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, we ought no longer to sin.

A. We have indeed been freed by the Savior’s baptism. But explain to me why he said: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members.” What is this law reigning in a human being’s members and resisting the law of his mind? Answer plainly. Are you silent? Hear the same Apostle proclaiming most openly: “For I do not understand what I do. For I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate. But if I do what I do not want, I consent to the law, that it is good. Now, however, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me. For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For willing is present with me, but I do not find the ability to do good. For I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want. But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (ibid., 15 ff.).

C. I am astonished that you, a prudent man, understand the Apostle in such a way that you think he is speaking these words in his own person and not in that of others. For how could the one who freely proclaims from the consciousness of Christ speaking within him, “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (I Cor. XIII, 3), and elsewhere, “I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (II Tim. IV, 7, 8), say of himself, “I do not find the ability to do good,” and, “I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want”? What was the good he wanted to do but could not? And what was the evil he did not want, yet could not avoid? Therefore he is not speaking in his own person, but in the person of the human race, which is subject to vices because of the weakness of the flesh.

[Note: See Saint Augustine, *Retractations* and *Against Julian*, book I, where he attacks at length this interpretation, which the Pelagians assigned to Paul’s passage and which he himself had embraced in his earlier works.]

**3. In whose person Paul spoke, and another testimony of his.**—A. You take little away from me in order to attribute everything to yourself. I understand one human being, even though an Apostle, to be subject to sin; you assert that the whole human race is. If this is true of the genus, then it is also true of the species. For the Apostle is a human being; and if he is a human being, he speaks either about others or about himself as a human being: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” And: “Because good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. VII, 24). “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind occupied with many concerns” (Rom. IX, 15).

[Note: Victorius reads *multa cogitantem* (“occupied with many concerns”) from the Brixian manuscripts and the Greek νοῦν πολυφρόντιδα (“a mind full of cares”), as he explains.]

C. You speak as though I accept this in the person of the human race and not in the person of the sinner [another reading: sinners].

A. And who will grant you that the Apostle speaks this in the person of the sinner? If you understand it as spoken in the sinner’s person, he ought to have said, “Wretched sinner that I am,” and not, “Wretched man that I am.” “Human being” belongs to nature; “sinner,” to the will. Unless perhaps you also refer what is written—“Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. I, 2)—to sinners and not to all human beings. And again: “Nevertheless, a human being walked about in an image” (Ps. XXXVIII, 7); and afterward: “A human being has been made like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow” (Ps. CXLIII, 4).

[Note: The Vatican manuscript and Victorius read *pertransit* (“passes through”), with the Vulgate edition and the Greek διαπορεύεται. Martianus follows Erasmus.]

If you are not moved by this testimony of Paul, hear another of his that you cannot contradict: “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” and so forth.

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript and the old edition add, “he rehearses the testimonies.” In another Vatican manuscript the passage is joined thus: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, nor do I judge myself,” etc., omitting what is inserted.] “Marvelously,” he says, “neither do I judge myself: I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified.” The one who said this was certainly conscious of no sin in himself. But because he had read, “Who understands his offenses?” (Ps. XVIII, 13), and, “There are ways that seem right to a man, but their ends look toward the depth of hell” (Prov. XIV, 12), and again, “Every man seems righteous to himself, but God directs human hearts” (Prov. XXI, 4), he moderated his judgment, lest perhaps he had sinned through ignorance, especially since Scripture testifies: “There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness” (Eccles. VII, 16). And elsewhere: “You shall pursue what is just, what is just” (Deut. XVI, 20), lest by an appearance of truth [another reading: purity] we depart from righteousness, remembering Saul and Agag.

[Note: In the Vatican manuscript, *puritatis* (“of purity”) is perhaps more correct than *veritatis* (“of truth”). Shortly afterward, instead of the name Agag, which we have restored from the manuscripts, *Achan* had previously been printed. The history of Achan is entirely irrelevant here; the story of Saul and Agag, recalled from I Samuel chapter XV, fits the argument quite well.]

**4. That there are many righteous persons, but no one without sin.**—C. So that I may not seem to quarrel and pull the rope endlessly in the opposite direction, at least grant me this: that many are called righteous in the Scriptures.

[Note: Vatican: “you grant,” and shortly afterward, “what evil have I said,” etc.]

A. Not merely many, but innumerable.

C. If there are innumerable righteous people, and this cannot be denied, what wrong have I said in asserting that a human being can be without sin if he wishes? In other words, I have said that a righteous person can be without sin insofar as he is righteous.

A. I grant that there are righteous people, but I absolutely do not agree that anyone is entirely without sin.

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript, together with the old edition and another Corbie manuscript held by the Benedictines, reads: “For to be without fault, which in Greek is called ἀναμάρτητον [‘without sin’], belongs to God alone, and every creature …”; omitting the intervening words *κακία*, “I assert that a human being can be,” and “I deny that he can be without sin.” Recall the familiar statement: ὁ μόνος ἀναμάρτητος Θεός, “God alone is without sin.”]

For I assert that a human being can be without fault, which in Greek is called κακία [*kakia*, “evil”]; but I deny that he can be ἀναμάρτητος [*anamárτηtos*, “without sin”], for that belongs to God alone. Every creature is subject to sin and needs the mercy of God, as Scripture says: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. XXXII, 5; CXVIII, 64).

And lest I seem to be scrutinizing certain blemishes in holy men, in which they have fallen through error, I shall offer a few passages that do not concern individuals separately but everyone in common. In Psalm XXXI, verse 5, it is written: “I said, I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart.” Immediately it follows: “For this”—that is, for this wickedness or iniquity, for either meaning is possible—“every holy person shall pray to you at an opportune time.” If he is holy, how does he pray for iniquity?
