If he has iniquity, how is he called holy? Clearly according to the sense expressed elsewhere: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. XXIV, 16). And: “The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. XVIII, 13).

And elsewhere: “Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehoods” (Ps. LVII, 4). Either, as soon as they were born, they were subject to sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is the pattern of the one to come; or certainly, as soon as Christ was born from the virginal womb—of whom it is written, “Everyone who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exod. XIII, 2; XXXIV, 19)—all the heretics went astray because they did not understand the mystery of his birth. Indeed, what is said, “He who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Ezek. XI, 43, 44), can be referred more appropriately to the Savior’s particular birth than to the birth of all human beings.

[Note: It is the teaching of the best part of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, and also the decree of the Council of Ephesus, confirmed by the perpetual consensus of the Catholic Church and strengthened by the oracle of Ezekiel XLIV, 2, that Christ’s body came forth through the closed barriers of the holy Virgin’s womb in the same way that he entered to the disciples through shut doors. For this reason some people slander this passage of Jerome, among them Genebrardus, *Collections*, chapter 6, as though it supported Origen’s opinion concerning the opening of the virginal enclosure during childbirth. But, as the learned Huetius points out, the words should be understood with the qualification that Saint Thomas used to explain a similar passage of Ambrose, *Part III*, question 28, article 2. The Fathers spoke thus when they explained the Evangelist’s words, “Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”: this expression is used according to ordinary biblical usage, not to signify the opening of the virginal enclosure, but only the exit of offspring from the womb. Jerome therefore immediately adds that the doors nevertheless remained perpetually closed. See also his discussion of the matter *Against Jovinian* and in book *Against Helvidius*, no. 18.]

For Christ alone opened the gates of the virginal womb, though they nevertheless remained perpetually closed. This is the eastern gate that is closed, through which the Pontiff alone enters and departs, and yet it is always closed.

There is also what is written in the book of Job: “Will a human being be clean before God, or will a man be blameless in his works? If he does not trust his servants and finds perversity in his angels, how much more in those who dwell in houses of clay” (Job IV, 17, 18)—and we too are made from the same clay.

If you assert that this is spoken in the person of Eliphaz the Temanite, understand that it is not spoken by him, but by the one who, under the persona of an angel, speaks to him in vision and revelation the judgments of God. But let us grant that Eliphaz speaks it: what the angel plainly says—does Job himself not say this in his own person? “Human life is a trial upon the earth” (Job VII, 1). And: “If I have sinned, what can I do?” (ibid., 20). And: “Why have you forgotten me and not removed the iniquity from me, nor cleansed me from my sin? For how can a human being be righteous before God on earth?” (ibid., 21). And again: “If I am righteous, he will not hear me; I shall need his judgment” (Job IX, 15, 29).

[Col. 0539D] And again: “Since I am impious, why do I labor in vain? If I wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands, you have stained me sufficiently with filth. If I sin, you will watch me; but you will not make me innocent of iniquity” (ibid., 30).

[Note: Erasmus, following the old edition, wrongly reads “with natron”; then the Vatican manuscript reads, “and clean in hands.” The Queen’s manuscript, with the same edition, reads, “and clean with clean hands.”] And: “If I act impiously, woe to me” (Job X, 15). And: “If I am righteous, I cannot breathe; for I am full of disgrace” (ibid.). And again: “For who will be clean from filth? No one—not even if his life upon the earth were but a single day and his months were innumerable” (Job XV, 14).

If you say that the pronoun “who” is understood not as impossible but sometimes as difficult, I shall answer you: What becomes of the assertion you rashly made, that God’s commandments are easy and can easily be fulfilled? Scripture says: “A man labors for himself in hardship and does violence to his own destruction” (Prov. XVI, 26, according to the Septuagint), so that, when the flesh is weighed down, subdued, and dying, the spirit may live in him.

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “A man labors in labors,” and so forth. The Greek likewise has ἀνὴρ ἐν πόνοις πονεῖ, “a man labors in toils.”]

I pass over your ridiculous interpretation of Demosthenes, in which you endeavor to prove that Job did not say, “Who will be clean from sin,” but “Who will be clean from filth,” and that the filth of clothing is meant, signifying infancy rather than the vices of sin. Or, if he does not understand it in this way, tell us what he does mean. His statement is so confused and covered with such a filthy mass of words that it offers the reader suspicion rather than understanding.

[Note: Victorius reads *Dictator*, judging *dictor* to be due to printers’ carelessness.]

[Note: I understand Pelagius to be mocked under the name Demosthenes, and what follows confirms this. Nevertheless, Origen, whose words the Pelagians often used, was the earlier author of this interpretation. Here are his words, rendered into Latin from *Homily 12 on Leviticus*: “Everyone who enters this world is said to be made in some contamination. Therefore Scripture also says, ‘No one is clean from filth, not even if his life were but a single day.’ By the very fact that he is placed in his mother’s womb and receives the material of his body from his father’s seed, he can be said to be contaminated in father and mother. Or do you not know that, when a male child has been formed for forty days, he is offered at the altar so that he may be purified there, as one who has been polluted in the conception itself, whether by the father’s seed or by the mother’s womb?”]

Finally he adds: “But what shall I answer to these things? I shall put my hand over my mouth. Once I have spoken, I shall not add a second time” (Job XXXIX, 34). Behold our Job, a man immaculate, righteous, and blameless, abstaining from every evil:

[Note: In one Vatican manuscript *vere* (“truly”) stands in place of *vir* (“man”); the other has neither reading.] by what conclusion of righteousness is he crowned, so that he needs the mercy of God? This is what we read in Proverbs: “Who can boast that he has a pure heart? Or who can trust that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. XX, 9).

[Note: The word “who” is absent from the manuscripts.]

Suppose that here too “who” is understood not of impossibility but of difficulty. Remove, then, and erase from your book the claim that God’s commandments are easy.

[Col. 0540A] **5. He meets an objection from the Gospel of John.**—If you oppose to this the words of the Apostle John, “His commandments are not burdensome” (I John V, 3), and from the Gospel, “My yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 30), you are very easily refuted. It is certain that he called the commandments of the Gospel light in comparison with Jewish superstition, in which various kinds of ceremonies were required—ceremonies that, according to the letter of the Law and the judgment of the Apostle Peter, no one could fulfill.

Accordingly, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Now therefore, why do you tempt God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are” (Acts XV, 10).

[Note: The manuscripts add “God” or “Lord.” One of these names is found both in the Greek and in the Vulgate translator.]

The Apostle James writes: “If you judge the Law, you are not a doer of the Law but a judge” (James IV, 11). He judges the Law who says that something was not rightly commanded, that ignorance does not involve sin, and that victims are offered in vain for error, since error carries no consciousness of sin. For in the Law the question is not reason but authority.

The same Apostle says in the same Epistle: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James I, 20). And who among us can be free from anger, about which it is written: “Anger destroys even the wise” (Prov. XV)?

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “even the prudent.”]

Significantly, he says not “the anger of God,” but “the anger of man.” The anger of God is just; human anger proceeds from a disturbed mind. Hence it is also said in the Psalm: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 26). What this verse means the Apostle explains: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV, 5), so that it is altogether sinful even to become slightly angry, while righteousness consists in quickly calming anger through repentance.

Accordingly, we shall have to give an account on the day of judgment even for an idle word. And in the same Gospel we read: “He who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment” (Matt. V, 22).

Although in many ancient manuscripts “without cause” is not added, so that we should understand that we must not become angry even with cause.

[Note: In his *Commentaries on Matthew* and book III of his *Epistle to the Ephesians*, he argues that the phrase “without cause” should be removed from the Latin manuscripts. See meanwhile what we noted on this matter in Epistle 13, to Castorina.]

Who among human beings can say that anger, which is without righteousness, is perpetually free from fault?

[Note: I would prefer *irae*, “of anger,” that is, of the vice by which someone might say he could remain free forever. Or, according to another Vatican manuscript, I would exclude the word *vitio*, “from the fault.”]

And again: “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the approaching day will bring forth” (Prov. XXVII, 1). Hence it is written: “Do not call anyone blessed before death.” As long as we live, we are in combat; and as long as we are in combat, there is no certain victory—a victory that is reserved for the future age even for the Apostle, though he fought with the greatest courage.

The Lord and Savior speaks under the persona of the assumed human being: “For I am the most foolish of all human beings, and the prudence of a human being is not in me” (Eccli. XI). And in Psalm LXVIII: “God, you know my foolishness”; but “the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (I Cor. I, 23).

In Ecclesiastes too it is written: “In the abundance of wisdom there is an abundance of knowledge; and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccles. I, 18): understanding that he lacks perfection and, from what he knows, how much he does not know.

“And I hated life,” he says, “because the work done under the sun is evil.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “because the work that I do over myself is evil.” The Greek is τὸ ποίημα τὸ πεποιημένον ὑπὸ τὸν ἥλιον, “the work that is done under the sun.”] For all is vanity and striving of spirit. No one knows what will happen; for, as it is, who will announce it to him? There are righteous people to whom what is like the work of the wicked comes; and there are wicked people to whom what is like the work of the righteous comes (Eccles. VIII, 14).

This is said because certain judgment belongs to God alone. Those whom we think righteous are often found to be sinners, while those whom we consider sinners are righteous in God’s knowledge. However much a human being may labor to investigate, he will not discover it. And if a wise man says that he knows, he will not be able to find it.

“For all have one fate,” and the hearts of the children of men are full of wickedness and instability (Eccles. X, 1), which in Greek is called περιφέρεια [*periphéreia*, “instability” or “being carried about”]. Flies that are dying, or, as the Hebrew has it, dead flies, destroy and corrupt the sweetness of oil.

Who among mortals is not seized by some error? Whom do the poisons of heretical and false doctrines not stain?

“It is time,” he says, “for judgment to begin from the house of God. And if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel? And if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear?” (I Peter IV, 17, 18).

Certainly the righteous person is one who is scarcely saved on the day of judgment. He would be saved easily if he had no stain in himself. Therefore he is righteous in that he flourishes with many virtues, and he is scarcely saved in that, in certain respects, he needs the mercy of God.

[Col. 0541D] **6. The disturbances of the human race.**—There are four disturbances by which the human race is afflicted: two belonging to the present and two to the future; two concerning good things and two concerning evil things. There is grief, which in Greek is called λύπη [*lýpē*], and joy, which they call χαρά [*chará*] or ἡδονή [*hēdonḗ]; although most people call ἡδονή “pleasure.” One belongs to evil, the other to good.

We exceed the proper measure if we rejoice over things in which we ought not to rejoice—wealth, power, honors, or the misfortune and deaths of enemies—or, conversely, if we are tormented by grief over present evils: adversity, exile, poverty, sickness, and the deaths of relatives. The Apostle forbids this. Likewise, we exceed the measure if we desire what we consider good: inheritances, honors, prosperity in all things, bodily health, and the other matters whose presence gives us joy; or if we fear what we consider adverse.

According to the Stoics—Zeno and Chrysippus, that is—it is possible to be entirely free from these disturbances; according to the Peripatetics, it is both difficult and impossible. The authority of all Holy Scripture agrees with the latter view.

Thus Josephus, the historian who wrote the account of the Maccabees, said that disturbances of the mind can be broken and controlled, but not eradicated; and Cicero’s five books of the *Tusculan Disputations* are filled with arguments of this kind.

[Note: I think he had in mind the following passage from Josephus’s book *On the Maccabees*, chapter III: Οὐ γὰρ ἐκριζωτὴς τῶν παθῶν ὁ λογισμὸς ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ ἀνταγωνιστής—“For reason does not eradicate the passions, but opposes them by contending against them.” Indeed, the entire preface to that excellent book, up through section four, could serve as a commentary on Jerome’s purpose here.]

For, according to the Apostle, the weakness of the body and “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” fight against us (Eph. VI, 12). The works of the flesh and the works of the spirit are manifest, and these oppose one another (Gal. V, 19), so that we do not do what we want.

If we do not do what we want, but do what we do not want, how can you say that a human being can be without sin if he wishes? Behold, the Apostle and all believers are unable to accomplish what they want.

“Love covers a multitude of sins” (I Peter IV, 8)—not so much past sins as present ones, so that we may not sin further while God’s love remains in us. Hence it is said of the sinful woman: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII, 47).

From this we understand that it is not solely within our power to do what we wish; it also depends upon God’s mercy, if he assists our will (I John I).

[Note: From this passage it may be understood that the Pelagian *anamartēsia*—ἀναμαρτησία—was intended to mean that a human being would be free from every sin, including even materially unavoidable ignorance, forgetfulness, and similar things. Otherwise whatever a human being cannot avoid would in no sense be called sin.]

[Col. 0542C] **7. God alone immortal, wise, and perfect by nature.**—God is called light, and there are no darknesses in him. When he says that no darkness is found in God’s light, he shows that all other lights are stained by some impurity.

Finally, the Apostles too are called the light of the world. But it is not written that there are no darknesses in the Apostles’ light. And concerning John it is written: “He came for testimony, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light. He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I, 7, 8).

Hence it is also written concerning God: “He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (I Tim. VI, 16). Certainly we read of immortal angels, immortal Thrones and Dominations, and the other Powers. But God alone is immortal, because he is so not by grace, as the others are, but by nature.

For this reason the same Apostle writes that God alone is wise (Rom. XVI), although Solomon and many other saints are called wise, and it is said, according to the Hebrew, to the prince of Tyre: “You are wiser than Daniel” (Ezek. XXVIII, 3).

How, then, is he called alone the light, alone immortal, and alone wise, when many are immortal, lights, and wise? It is because human perfection does not come from nature but from grace; and this demonstrates that those who seem to be perfect are imperfect.

[Note: The punctuation obscured the meaning. The text had been printed: “lights and wise are?” as a question, followed by a new sentence beginning, “Thus the perfection of man …” The punctuation has been corrected.]

As for what is written, “The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from every sin” (I John I, 7), this must be understood both in the confession of baptism and in the mercy of repentance.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts add, “He does indeed cleanse us from every sin both …”; and shortly afterward they do not contain the words “it must be understood.”] But being cleansed by God is one thing; being without fault in oneself is another.

For if, according to Job, “the moon does not shine and the stars are not clean in his sight,” how much more is a human being “rottenness, and the son of man a worm” (Job XXV, 5, 6)!

“For every mouth is stopped, and the whole world is liable before God, because no flesh will be justified before him by works of the Law” (Rom. III, 19, 20). There is no distinction of persons. “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (ibid., 23, 24).

But when he writes, “We reckon that a human being is justified by faith without works of the Law, since God is one, who justifies circumcision by the Law and uncircumcision through faith” (ibid., 28, 30), he plainly shows that righteousness lies not in human merit but in God’s grace, who accepts the faith of believers without the works of the Law.

Hence it follows: “Sin will not rule over you.” Why? “Because you are not under the Law but under grace” (Rom. VI, 14). “It is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16).

Hence the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness—righteousness, that is, from faith. But Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness, because it was not from faith but from works. “For they stumbled over the stone of stumbling” (ibid., 30 ff.).

“For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4).

[Col. 0543C] **8. From the Apostle’s Epistles.**—Almost all the Apostle’s Epistles begin with these words: “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord” (I Cor. I, 3), and they are closed with a similar ending.

To the Corinthians too it is written: “So that you lack no gift, awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will also confirm you to the end, without accusation, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., 7, 8).

Although, therefore, we lack no gift, we nevertheless await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will then confirm us in all things and show us to be without accusation, when the day of our Lord Jesus Christ and the end of the world arrive, so that no flesh may glory in his presence.

“Paul planted, Apollos watered” (I Cor. II, 6), but the Lord gave the increase. Therefore neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but he who gives the increase, God. We are his field, his building.

“According to the grace of God,” he says, “as a wise architect, I have laid the foundation.” “Do not deceive yourselves. If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God” (I Cor. III, 19). “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile” (Ps. XCIII, 11).

And again: “For I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified, because the one who judges me is the Lord” (I Cor. IV, 4).

The same is said to you who claim to be without sin: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? You are already filled; you have already become rich” (ibid., 8).

And so that we may know that everything depends not upon ourselves but upon God’s judgment, he says: “I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills” (ibid., 19). For the one who says, “I will come to you,” shows that he wills it, reveals that he desires it, and promises his coming. But so that he may speak more cautiously, he adds, “if the Lord wills.”

For if anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.

**9. Again from the Apostle.**—The chosen vessel, cast down in humility—or rather, speaking from consciousness of his weakness—says: “I am the least of the Apostles, who am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty; rather, I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God that is with me” (I Cor. I, 9, 10).

He says that he labored more than all the Apostles, and immediately refers his labor to God’s assistance: “Not I,” he says, “but the grace of God that is with me” (II Cor. III, 4).

[Note: Thus according to the Greek. See the note above on the reading of this passage and Saint Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*.]

As he also says elsewhere: “We have such confidence through Jesus Christ toward God, not because we are sufficient of ourselves to consider anything as coming from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us competent ministers of the New Testament” (II Cor. III, 4–6).

For a human being is not justified by works of the Law except through faith in Jesus Christ. Hence he adds: “We have believed in Jesus Christ, so that we might be justified by the faith of Christ and not by works of the Law, because no flesh will be justified by works of the Law” (Gal. II, 16). “For if righteousness is from the Law, then Christ died for no reason” (ibid., 21).

There is a curse in the Law; for it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them.” “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us” (Gal. III, 10, 13).

For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly be from the Law. But Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ.

Therefore the Law was our pedagogue in Christ, so that we might be justified by faith (ibid., 21–24). Hence he adds, comprehending everything in a single verse: “You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the Law; you have fallen away from grace” (Gal. V, 4).

## 10. That no one has fulfilled the Law

I review all these points [Col. 0545A] to show that no one has fulfilled the Law, meaning by “the Law” all the commandments contained in it. For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish. The Apostle labors (Philippians II), and although he conducted himself without complaint according to the righteousness that is in the Law, he counts everything as refuse for Christ, in order to be found in Christ, possessing not his own righteousness, which comes from the Law, but that which comes from the faith of Christ and is from God.

Thus he writes to the Thessalonians: “But the Lord is faithful, who will strengthen you and guard you from evil” (II Thessalonians III, 3). Therefore we are preserved not by the power of free choice but by God’s mercy.

And lest you think that the truth of the faith can be overthrown by empty arguments that raise questions for those who hear them, the same Apostle writes to Timothy: “O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you, avoiding profane novelties of words and the contradictions of falsely named knowledge, which some professing have gone astray from the faith” (II Timothy I, 13–14).

“For the goodness and mercy of our Savior,” not from the works of righteousness that we have done, “but according to his mercy, he saved us, so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus III, 5–6).

We have plucked these points briefly, as it were from the broadest and most beautiful meadow of apostolic teaching, so that the shamelessness of an unyielding brow may be crushed.

## 11. From the precepts of the Gospel

Let us pass to the Gospels and complete the apostolic sparks with Christ’s most brilliant lamp. “Everyone,” he says, “who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment. But whoever says, ‘Raca’”—which is interpreted as “empty” and “without a brain”—“will be liable to the council,” undoubtedly the council of the saints and the angelic senate. “But whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew V, 22).

**[Note: The word is commonly derived from [Greek term], meaning “empty.”]**

Who among us can fail to be subject to this vice, when we shall even have to give an account for an idle word on the day of judgment? If anger, verbal abuse, and sometimes even a joke are consigned to judgment, to the council, and to the fires of Gehenna, what will the desire for shameful things deserve, and avarice, which is the root of all evils?

“If,” he says, “you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew V, 23–24).

It is within my power not to have anything against my brother. But whether he has something against me or not depends on his will. What, then, shall I do if he does not wish to be reconciled? Shall I beg him? Shall I bend my knees? He will disdain to listen. Or shall I drag him against his will into the jurisdiction of friendship by force? [Col. 0546A] And what greater enmity is there than to unite friendships by compulsion?

For he did not say, “Ask him to be reconciled to you,” but, “Be reconciled first to your brother, and then offer your gift at the altar.” Not that God commanded impossibilities, but he ascended to such a summit of patience that, because of its extreme difficulty, he seems almost to have commanded the impossible (Matthew XVIII and Mark IX), thereby overturning your statement that God’s commandments are easy.

**[Note: Perhaps *in recto patientia* should be restored, so that the sense is: the virtue of patience is commanded us as so perfect that attaining it appears almost impossible.]**

We are commanded to cut off the hand, eye, and foot that causes scandal. Granted that this is said figuratively of our dearest friends, blood relations, and those joined to us by brotherly and marital love: can we really think it easy, because of certain offenses, suddenly to cut off so great an affection?

And as for the statement, “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; anything beyond this is from evil” (Matthew V, 37), perhaps someone from your school may be found who has never lied and has never heard that prophetic and apostolic saying, “I said in my alarm, ‘Every human being is a liar’” (Psalm CXV, 2), and who does not know what is written elsewhere: “The lying mouth kills the soul” (Wisdom I, 11).

When someone strikes our cheek, we are commanded to offer the other. To the one who takes our tunic, we must also grant our cloak. To the one who compels us to go one mile, we must offer ourselves for two miles. “Give to everyone who asks you, and do not refuse the one who wishes to borrow from you” (Luke VI, 30).

**[Note: Two manuscripts, with the old edition, read: “and do not turn away from one wishing to borrow from you,” etc.]**

If I have two small coins and another asks for them, either I shall give them to him and must myself become a beggar, or, if I do not give them, I shall be found a transgressor of the Law.

As for the saying, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Luke VI, 27–28), perhaps such a person is found in your assembly; among us he is a rare bird.

Those who confess their sins simply deserve, through their humility, the Savior’s mercy. But as for what follows—“Take care not to perform your righteousness, that is, your almsgiving, before people in order to be seen by them” (Matthew VI, 1)—I do not know who could fulfill it.

A herald is hired to give away a piece of bread and two small coins, and when we extend our hand, we look around in every direction; if no one sees us, the hand becomes more tightly closed. Granted that one out of a thousand may be found who does not do this.

## 12. He presses the point from the same precepts

Answer me, I ask: where are the commandments that are easy? “Do not be anxious about tomorrow,” he says. “For tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matthew VI, 34).

Do you not think about tomorrow and, like birds, remain content with what is present?

**[Note: “Whose letters are bibline.” He said this wittily to indicate the avarice and pleasure-seeking of Pelagius and Julian, who sent papyrus letters to distant places so that gifts might return from there; he also alludes to the foreign gifts sent to Solomon in admiration of his wisdom. — Martianaeus.]**

Martianaeus thinks that these words indicate the avarice and pleasure-seeking of Pelagius and—what is truly remarkable—also of Julian, who had not yet joined Pelagius, as is clear from Marius Mercator, *Commentary* III, and Gennadius. They are said to have sent papyrus letters to distant places so that gifts might return from there.

Still more absurdly, John Clericus says that books are meant here—those of Origen translated into Latin by Rufinus—and that they are called “bibline letters” because Origen, an Alexandrian by birth, wrote on Egyptian papyrus.

It is clear, however, that an allusion is made to the passage of Isaiah XVIII, 2, according to the Septuagint: “Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, the one who sends hostages upon the sea, and letters of papyrus” (*epistolai biblinai*). Eusebius interprets these words in his *Commentaries* as referring to slanderous letters. He explains them as concerning the envoys of the Jews, who were then called apostles and who devised slanders against Jesus Christ the Savior:

“Their apostles, carrying papyrus letters, sailing above the waters and voyaging across the sea, traversed the whole earth, slandering the report concerning our Savior.”

This seems also to have been the sense in which Saint Epiphanius understood it, *Epistle* among the Hieronymian letters 51, no. 1.

Nor is it inappropriate to understand this passage as referring to followers of the Pelagians sent into distant provinces with letters full of deceit and slanders, by which they might strengthen their faction in remote regions and detract from the Catholic understanding.

Yet although Jerome by no means excludes this interpretation, he suggests something further concerning the avarice of the Pelagians, which is likewise extracted from another reading of the Isaian passage. In the preface to the third book on Jeremiah, speaking of Pelagius himself, he says: “He sends letters throughout the whole world, formerly golden, now accursed”—plainly indicating that the “golden” letters are those he attacks here.

The text of Isaiah, however, has the words which, with the common translator, you render “in vessels of papyrus.” I believe that the Prophet meant very swift little boats woven from papyrus. But the Septuagint, through its customary slight alteration of the letter, reading [a different form] instead of [the Hebrew term], translated it as *biblinas*, as though it were a proper name, *Biblos*; and they called what was made from papyrus—namely, paper—*letters*.

Finally, it is closer to the truth to understand “papyrus letters,” by allusion to that passage in Isaiah, as private letters of a single society, letters privy to a crime, which, by agreement, were understood only by those to whom they were sent.

Procopius of Gaza indicates something similar in his commentary on that passage. After recounting the story of Adonis, loved by Venus even in the underworld, and of the festivals instituted so that his absence might be mourned in alternate months and his return celebrated, he says that the Jews too, forgetful of true piety, adopted such a ritual of orgies. He refers to what Ezekiel records in chapter VIII: women sitting and mourning Tammuz, that is, Adonis.

“Something similar,” he says, “was done by the inhabitants of that city”—that is, Alexandria. They wrote letters on a potsherd to the women who were in Byblos, as though Adonis had been found; they cast the sealed potsherd into the sea after first performing certain sacred rites over it. According to those who sent it, it traveled of its own accord to Byblos, and by its arrival announced to the women of that city that the time of mourning had ended.

He then interprets the words “Woe to them”:

“Woe to them”—that is, to those who have exchanged among themselves pledges of crime and fellowship, suffering from the same impiety; they do not send ships, but release the potsherd upon the back of the sea.”

“Whose papyrus letters fly across the rivers of Ethiopia,” [Col. 0547A] so that among monkeys and peacocks new gifts from Ophir may be sent to Solomon.

Do you wish to hear how easy God’s commandments are? Listen to what is said: “How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matthew VII, 14)! He did not say, “those who walk along it.” That is the more difficult thing, but “those who find it.” For few find it, and far fewer enter upon it.

“The Son of Man,” he says, “has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke IX, 58)—he who says in Isaiah, “Receive the weary, and this is my rest” (Isaiah XXVIII, 12). If he has nowhere to lay his head or to rest, and says elsewhere, “Upon whom shall I rest except upon the humble, the peaceful, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah LXVI, 2), where is the ease of the commandments?

**[Note: Victorinus has “the ease of God’s commandments.”]**

Many take simply the statement that is written, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew IX, 19), according to the sense of that other saying: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Mark II, 16).

Others interpret it more forcibly: “I have not come to call the righteous” (Mark II, 17; Luke V, 31), since no one is righteous to perfection, but everyone is a sinner in some respect; “but sinners,” with whom the world is filled, as David says: “Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed,” and, “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their devices. They have all turned aside; together they have become useless; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm XIII, 2–3).

“Do not possess,” he says, “gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts; no bag for the journey, no bread, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff” (Matthew X, 9).

“You will say that these are apostolic commandments.” Certainly the Apostle Peter is reported to have had boots, when the Angel said to him: “Fasten your belt and put on your boots” [another reading: “Put on your boots”] (Acts XII, 8).

As for two tunics, to say nothing of the rest, I think that both you and I possess them, provided that we do not have more than that.

I say these things—and will repeat them again and again, pressing them upon you point by point—so that you may blush at your statement that God’s commandments are easy.

## 13. Again from the Gospel

“Brother,” he says, “will hand over brother to death, and father his son; children will rise against their parents and put them to death. And you will be hated by all people because of my name” (Matthew X, 22).

And because he had commanded easy things and knew that they could easily be fulfilled, he joined the following words to demonstrate the ease of the matter: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew X, 22).

“I have not come,” he says, “to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword. I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Matthew X, 34).

And lest he lengthen his statement by going through everything, he summed it all up in one sentence: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matthew X, 36).

And after saying, “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew X, 37), in consideration of the ease of the commandments he added: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matthew X, 38; Luke XIV, 27).

The cross of Christ is easy; to go naked after Christ is a game, a joke. And where are the rewards that are sought after overcoming difficulty?

The weeds are not gathered in the present age, lest the wheat also be uprooted at the same time.

**[Note: Up to this point the reading “the Lord’s chaff” was incorrectly printed, as though it meant chaff belonging to the Lord and allegorically interpreted in a negative sense. A *pala* is instead a rustic instrument with which grain is winnowed on the threshing floor. Matthew and Luke call it a winnowing fan. Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 3: “He carries the fan in his hand to cleanse his threshing floor. Let the chaff of a shallow faith fly away as much as it will; the purer mass of grain will be stored in the Lord’s barns.” We have corrected the text with the aid of the Vatican manuscripts.]**

The Lord’s winnowing shovel is reserved for the future judgment, when the righteous will shine like the sun, and the Angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous.

Peter sinks and deserves to hear: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matthew XIV, 31). If there is little faith in him, I do not know in whom there is great faith.

“From the heart,” he says, “come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are the things that defile people” (Matthew XV, 19). Let anyone come forward who can testify that these things are not in his heart, and I shall acknowledge full righteousness in this mortal body.

“Whoever wishes,” he says, “to save his soul will lose it; and whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it” (Matthew XII, 25).

**[Note: In the old edition these words are placed afterward: “These are the easy commandments. Again I say, woe to the world,” and so forth.]**

Again I ask: Are these the easy commandments? “Woe to the world because of scandals! For it is necessary that scandals come” (Matthew XVIII, 7).

Therefore it is written elsewhere: “In many things we offend, or err—all of us” (James III, 2). He did not say “a few sins,” but “many”; nor “some people,” but “all”: “For all seek what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s” (Philippians II, 21).

God alone is called good, and the goodness of the teacher, as a human being, is rejected. In the Law a man highly learned in it says that he has done everything, and therefore is loved by the Lord; yet he does not possess complete righteousness, because he was unwilling to distribute his possessions to the poor.

Thus difficulty is compared with difficulty—or rather, impossibility with impossibility—for neither can a camel pass through the eye of a needle, nor can the rich enter the kingdom of heaven.

Who among us does not wash the outside of the cup and dish while leaving the inside not at all cleansed of filth? Who can avoid resembling whitewashed tombs, lest Jesus say to us also: “Outwardly you appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matthew XXIII, 1)?

Even if we can be free of other vices, to lack the stain of hypocrisy is the achievement of few, or of none.

**[Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, has “cannot have,” although Victorinus had previously deleted *can*, with the aid of the Brixian manuscripts, which our manuscripts likewise unanimously support.]**

## 14. From the example of Christ the Lord and the Apostles

“Father,” he says, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew XXVI, 39).

The Son of God, who spoke and they came to be, who commanded and all things were created (Psalm CXLVIII, 5), moderates his judgment insofar as he is called the Son of Man: “Father, if it is possible; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew XXVI, 40). Yet my Critobulus, with raised eyebrows, says: “A human being can be without sin if he wishes.”

The Apostles hear: “So you could not keep watch with me for one hour?” (Mark XIV, 37). He did not say, “You would not,” but “You could not.” The Apostles cannot keep watch for one hour, overcome by sleep, sorrow, and the weakness of the flesh; and you can overcome all sins simultaneously for a long period?

The Evangelist Mark writes concerning the Lord: “And he could not perform a single miracle there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them,” and “he marveled because of their unbelief” (Mark VI, 5).

**[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read: “because of their unbelief.”]**

The Lord is said not to have been able to perform even one miracle in Nazareth, and is held back by amazement at another’s unbelief; yet you are able to do everything you wish.

Finally, what follows is written: “He went into the regions of Tyre and Sidon, and entering a house he wanted no one to know; yet he could not remain hidden” (Mark VII, 24). He certainly wished to remain hidden. Why, then, could he not do what he wished, so as to avoid everyone’s awareness of his arrival?

Do you ask why he could not remain hidden?

**[Note: You may learn how vehemently the Pelagians attacked this passage from Augustine’s *Unfinished Work*, and below, section 17.]**

Consider the reality of the human being he assumed, and you will be free of all scandal. If the Son of God is said to have been unable to do something in the flesh and on account of the flesh, shall we, who are wholly flesh and daily struggle against the works of the spirit, do everything we wish, contrary to the Apostle’s statement?

The Apostle Peter wants to make three tabernacles on the mountain—one for the Lord, another for Moses, and a third for Elijah—without knowing what he is saying, terrified by fear. And are we to belch forth the arrogance of Pythagorean philosophy?

**[Note: He calls the pride of Pythagorean philosophy *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια, “freedom from passion”) and *anamartēsia* (ἀναμαρτησία, “freedom from sin”), that is, the doctrine of perfect righteousness, which Jerome is accustomed to attribute especially to Pythagoras.]**

He answered that neither the Angels of heaven nor the Son knew the day and hour of the final consummation, while we profess complete knowledge?

**[Note: More probably, with the Regina manuscript and the old edition, the text reads: “and you profess complete knowledge.” The Vatican manuscripts soon add the interpretation of the Greek word, namely, “figuratively” (*putative*).]**

The weakness of the flesh rejoiced in having God as its inhabitant; nevertheless, it could not exceed the measure of its own frailty, so that, not according to mere appearance (*to dokein*, τῷ δοκεῖν), as the ancient heretics held, but truly, he might be believed to be both the Son of God and the Son of Man.

Leaving the Apostles for a little while, he fell prostrate upon the ground and prayed, saying: “Father, if it is possible” (Matthew XXVI, 39).

Why, I ask, did he express an uncertain judgment, when elsewhere he had said, “What is impossible with human beings is possible with God” (Matthew XIX, 26; Mark X, 27; Luke XVIII, 27)?

**[Note: The same two Vatican manuscripts express the thought of one in doubt.]**

But as a human being about to suffer, he speaks in the words of a human being. He says, “If it is possible, let this hour pass.” You say, “It is possible to avoid sins at all times.”

## 15. From other Gospel narratives

In certain copies, especially in the Greek manuscripts, the following is written at the end of Mark’s Gospel: “Afterward, when the eleven had reclined at table, Jesus appeared to them and reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had risen” (Mark XVI, 14).

And they, making their defense, said: “This age of iniquity and unbelief is a substance [or condition] that does not allow the true power of God to be apprehended through unclean spirits; therefore reveal your righteousness even now” (I John V, 19).

**[Note: Most manuscripts read, “their unbelief and hardness of heart,” and so forth. Moreover, the verses that follow, beginning with the words “And they made their defense” and continuing to the end, are not regarded by the Church as genuine. They are found neither in any Greek manuscripts that have reached us nor in the authoritative versions. The earlier verses, however, are genuine by the agreement of all the books.]**

**[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “under Satan,” a reading I would certainly prefer if it then had “which” in place of the following word. The preceding word, “they made their defense,” has been observed by learned men to mean the same as “they confessed their guilt.”]**

If you contradict this, at least you will not dare to deny the following: “The world is placed in the evil one” (I John V, 19), and that Satan dared to tempt his Lord, and, having been defeated and confounded, withdrew “until a time,” namely, the time of the Passion.

He is tempted, while the successor of Jovinian dares to say that “those who have received baptism with complete faith cannot be tempted”; or, in other words, that “a baptized person, if he does not wish to, can by no means sin thereafter.”

**[Note: See *Against Jovinian*, book II, sections 2 and following. The Pelagian doctrine of *anamartēsia* (ἀναμαρτησία, freedom from sin) was of this kind as well.]**

The righteous Zachariah hears from the Angel: “Because you did not believe my words, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day of his birth” (Luke I, 20).

The father of the lunatic says concerning the Apostles: “I asked your disciples to cast him out”—that is, the demon—“and they could not” (Matthew XVII, 15).

And the disciples themselves ask the Savior: “Why could we not cast him out?” They hear: “Because of your unbelief.” Why, I ask? Because the power to do everything was reserved for the Lord.

A thought entered the Apostles: which of them was the greater? They are corrected by the Savior’s teaching, when the lesser is recognized as greater and humility is exchanged for exaltation.

He is not received by the Samaritan town because his face was set toward Jerusalem. James and John, truly sons of thunder and burning with the ardor of zeal, wish to bring down fire from heaven like Phinehas and Elijah, and they are rebuked by the Lord. They would certainly not have been rebuked if they had wished such things without error.

Crowds were traveling with him—that is, with the Lord—and he turned and said: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 26). And: “Whoever does not carry his cross and follow me cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 27).

And here I shall rashly proclaim: “A human being can, if he wishes, avoid every sin, for his commandments are easy.”

They deserve to hear from the Lord and Savior: “You are those who declare yourselves righteous before people, but God knows your hearts, because what is exalted among people is an abomination before God” (Luke XVI, 15).

“It is impossible,” he says, “for scandals not to come” (Luke XVII, 1). I think that the sin which comes through scandal is itself a scandal. For, unless I am mistaken, *skōlon* (σκῶλον) and *skandalon* (σκάνδαλον) among the Greeks received their names from stumbling and falling.

Therefore, “In many things we all offend” (James III, 2). Suppose that I have not fallen; certainly I have stumbled, and not in one thing but in many. I think that to have offended in some respect is sin.

The Apostles said to the Lord: “Increase our faith.” He answered them: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed” (Matthew XVII, 19), which is certainly the smallest of all seeds. Yet my Critobulus swells with mountains of faith.

## 16. That freedom from sin can be granted by God

“He was also telling them a parable,” it says, “that they ought always to pray and never lose heart” (Luke XVIII, 1). We pray always in vain if it lies within our free choice to do whatever we wish.

The Apostles said: “And who can be saved?” They hear from the Lord: “What is impossible with human beings is possible with God” (Mark X, 26–27).

Therefore some things that are impossible with human beings are certainly shown to be possible by the fact that they are possible with God. Let it therefore also be possible for God, if he wishes, to grant a human being freedom from sin—not by that person’s merit, but by his mercy—while among human beings it is by no means possible through the power of free choice; rather, it is received through the will of the giver.

It had not been enough for the Apostles earlier to inquire about precedence—who among them was the greater—but at the very moment of necessity and the Passion it is written of them: “A dispute arose among them as to which of them was the greater” (Luke XXII, 24). Truly, an excellent time to dispute about rank, with the cross imminent.

“Simon, Simon,” he says, “behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII, 31).

**[Note: Gravius had read “requested” instead of “demanded.” Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*; Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*; Saint Augustine, on Psalm C; and others read it in the former manner.]**

And certainly, according to you, it lay within the Apostle’s power, if he wished, for his faith not to fail; for when it fails, sin necessarily enters.

In certain Greek as well as Latin copies one finds Luke writing: “An Angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke XXII, 43), unquestionably referring to the Lord and Savior. “And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling down upon the ground” (Luke XXII, 44).

**[Note: Saint Hilary also says this, *On the Trinity*, book X, section 41: “Nor should we be unaware that in very many Greek and Latin manuscripts nothing is written either about the Angel who came or about the sweat of blood,” and so forth. Today copies lacking these verses are much rarer, and Mill produces only three.]**

The Savior is strengthened by an Angel in his Passion, while my Critobulus has no need of God’s help, possessing the power of free choice. He prayed so intensely that drops of blood burst forth—a portion of the blood which he was soon to pour out entirely in his Passion.

“What are you sleeping?” he says. “Rise and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew XVI, 21).

According to you, he ought to have said: “Why are you sleeping? Rise and resist, for you possess free choice, and, once the power granted you by the Lord has been bestowed, you need the help of no one else. For if you do this, you will not enter into temptation.”

## 17. Again from the Gospel narrative

“I can do nothing from myself,” he says, “but as I hear, I judge” (John V, 30).

The Arians bring forward a slander, but the Church responds that these words are spoken from the person of the human being who was assumed.

You, by contrast, say: “I can be without sin if I wish.”

He can do nothing from himself, so that he may indicate the reality of his humanity. You can avoid every sin, although you still remain in the body—

**[Note: “Being established” (*constitutus*) is *antitheon* (ἀντίθεον). Beware the false interpretation of Marianus Victorius, who thought that here *antitheon* meant “contrary and opposed to God.” It is certain that Jerome understood it to mean “demigod,” “extraordinary,” “equal to God,” or “divine”—that is, *isotheon* (ἰσόθεον), “equal to God according to virtue” (*kat’ aretēn*, κατ’ ἀρετήν). — Martianaeus.]**

That is, “to be compared with God,” in which sense Homer frequently uses the word, as in *Iliad* Ψ, verse 360:

“Godlike Phoenix, companion of his own father.”] You show yourself to be ἀντίθεος (*antitheos*), that is, opposed to God. He denies to his brothers and relatives that he will go up to the Feast of Tabernacles; and afterward it is written: “But when his brothers had gone up, then he also went up to the feast, not openly, but as if in secret” (John 7:10). He denied that he would go, and did what he had previously denied.

Porphyry barks, accusing him of inconsistency and change, not knowing that all stumbling-blocks must be referred to the flesh.

[Note: Julian the Pelagian maliciously attacks this passage in Augustine, *Against Julian: An Unfinished Work*, book 4, ch. 88, in order to impute to Jerome the blasphemy of having said that Christ possessed not only natural but also voluntary sin. Having objected another passage from Dialogue 3, which we shall cite later, he adds: “By another testimony too, from John the Evangelist, he fastens upon him [Christ] the disgrace of falsehood. Of this work you [Augustine], in the letter which you sent to Alexandria, boast that Pelagius, crushed by its masses of Scripture, cannot vindicate free choice. But that work was answered by a Catholic man who had been attacked,” etc. Jerome, however, simply expounds the Gospel history in order to answer Porphyry, who interpreted it maliciously. See Augustine, book 3 *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, ch. 6, and Pelagius’s confession of faith to Innocent, which among the spurious works of Jerome is entitled *Explanation of the Creed to Damasus*, near the end: “We also anathematize those who say that the Son of God lied by the necessity of the flesh, and that, because of the assumed man, he was unable to do everything that he willed.”]

“Moses,” he says, “gave you the law, and none of you keeps the law”—that is, the law that was possible to keep—and yet no one had fulfilled what was possible; for the fault lies not with the one who commands, but with the weakness of the one who hears, so that the whole world may become subject to God.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript: “For neither was the frailty of the hearer to be blamed, so that the whole world,” etc.]

In the Gospel according to John, the account of the adulterous woman who was accused before the Lord is found in many Greek and Latin manuscripts.

[Note: Learned men who have inspected libraries attest that this history of the adulteress is commonly absent, or is not reported in the same words, in the surviving Greek manuscripts, whereas it occurs in Latin manuscripts, indeed in all Latin manuscripts. Some Greek Fathers also cite it, among them Chrysostom, Homily 60, and the much earlier Ammonius and Tatian; the Latin witnesses are too numerous to enumerate. St Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book 2, ch. 7, explains why it was removed from some books and ancient versions: “Certain persons of little faith, or rather enemies of the true faith, I suppose, fearing that their wives might be granted impunity for sinning, removed from their manuscripts what the Lord did in forgiving the adulteress, as though he who said, ‘Sin no more,’ had granted permission to sin.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 3, says that the history added to John came from the Gospel entitled *According to the Hebrews*. See Jansen’s Harmony.]

The scribes and Pharisees were accusing her and pressing their demand vehemently, wishing to stone her according to the law. But Jesus, bending down, wrote with his finger on the ground (John 8:6)—namely, the sins of those who were accusing her, and of all mortals, according to what is written in the Prophet: “But those who forsake you shall be written on the earth” (Jer. 17:13).

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the old edition read: “shall be written upon the earth.”]

[Note: In the Greek manuscript of the Gospels used by Wagenseil in his *Commentary on Sotah* occurs: “with his finger he wrote the sins of each one of them” (τῷ δακτύλῳ ἔγραφεν ἑκάστου αὐτῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας). Here Jerome preserves a trace of this gloss; some wrongly charge him with having invented it, and maintain that the Greeks took it from him. But the simpler form of the gloss in the manuscript shows itself to be older. Ambrose, Epistle 58 to Studium, is not dissimilar: “Foreseeing this, the Lord Jesus, with head bent down, wrote on the ground. What did he write, unless that prophetic saying [Jer. 22:9]: ‘Earth, earth, write these men as disowned’?” Victorius, following the Vulgate, added “bending down with his finger,” etc.]

Finally, raising his head, he said to them: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:10).

What is said here, “without sin,” is written in Greek as ἀναμάρτητος (*anamartētos*). Therefore, whoever says that “without sin” means one thing and ἀναμάρτητος another must either express the Greek word by a new Latin term, or, if it has been rendered into Latin—as the truth of the translation requires—it is clear that ἀναμάρτητος means nothing other than “without sin.”

And because all the accusers fled [another reading: “flee”]—for the most compassionate Judge had granted their shame time to withdraw—and because he again wrote on the ground, looking down at the earth, they gradually began to depart and avert their eyes from him. He alone remained with the woman, to whom Jesus said: “Where are those who accused you? Has no one condemned you?” She replied: “No one, Lord.” Jesus answered her: “Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on sin no more” (John 8:10–11).

The Lord commanded her not to sin any longer, just as he similarly commanded other things in the Law. But whether she did so or not, Scripture does not say.

“All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John 10:8). If “all,” no one is excepted. He says “who came,” not “who were sent”; concerning these the Prophet says: “They came of themselves, and I did not send them” (Jer. 17:12). By this statement the power of Christ alone is reserved: he came to his own, and his own did not receive him.

“While I was with them in the world, I kept those whom you gave me in your name, and none of them perished except the son of perdition” (John 17:12).

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript and another Vatican manuscript read: “I kept in your name those whom you gave me,” etc. This is a reading much to be adopted, although, so far as I know, neither the Greek text nor the testimony of ancient authors supports it.]

He did not say, “I gave them the power of free choice, so that they might save themselves by their own labor,” but, “I kept them; I saved them.” Finally he adds: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil.”

In the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 15), we read that a disagreement arose between Paul and Barnabas because of John, who was called Mark, so that they separated: Barnabas took Mark, and Paul took Silas into the ministry of the Gospel. Paul was stricter, the other more lenient; each is fully persuaded in his own judgment. Yet the disagreement contains something of human weakness. [Another reading: “was fully persuaded.”]

In the same volume we read: “They passed through Phrygia and the Galatian region [another reading: ‘Galatia’], having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia” (Acts 16:6). By this curse, I think, even today many heretics who act against the Holy Spirit are found in that province.

“And when they had come to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16:7).

Notice that the Spirit of Jesus is the Holy Spirit, who elsewhere, because of the unity of substance, is called the Spirit of the Father. They wished [another reading: “wished” in the preterite] to speak in Asia, and were forbidden by the Holy Spirit. They attempted to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them. It would be quite unreasonable if he had once given them the power of free choice to do or not to do something.

### 18. It follows

“Overlooking the times of ignorance, God now commands people everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30).

[Note: Vatican manuscript: “all everywhere,” etc., which agrees with the Greek exemplar, πᾶσι πανταχοῦ μετανοεῖν, “that all should repent everywhere.”]

Significantly, he indicated that the past times under the Law were times of ignorance.

Again he says: “I will come to you, if God wills.” Why did he insert the will of God, if he possessed the power of his own free choice?

The Apostle James says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James 2:10). Who among us has never sinned in anything? But if he has sinned—which cannot be denied—and through one sin is guilty of all sins, he is saved not by his own strength but by God’s mercy.

“If anyone does not sin in speech, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2). If you have at some time sinned in speech, where is your claimed perfection, especially since what follows says: “The tongue no one can tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison” (ibid., 8)? I ask you to answer me: if the tongue is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison, and no one can tame the tongue of mortals, and you are guilty of so great a crime, where is the perpetual avoidance of sins?

### 19. He pursues the same argument

“From where do wars and quarrels arise among you? Is it not from the pleasures that wage war in your members?” Either you do not have human members, or, if a human being cannot exist without members, confess that pleasure and wantonness wage war in your limbs.

David had confidently said: “Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart, for your mercy is before my eyes, and I have pleased in your truth” (Ps. 25:2–3). And again: “But I walked in my innocence, and my foot stood on level ground” (ibid., 11).

Although God’s mercy softened the truth of the judgment, nevertheless, because he dared to say this, he is left for a while to his weakness and, as you say, to free choice; and having fallen through adultery into murder, he later says: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy. And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity” (Ps. 51:1–2).

Nor do I say this to accuse the holy man, of whom it is written that he did all the will of God, but because he made up for these faults with many other good deeds and was saved by the mercy of God, whose judgment is exercised with proper measure. To him Asaph says: “You will feed us with bread of tears, and give us drink in tears by measure” (Ps. 80:6). For the Lord is not unjust, condemning sins alone and not remembering good works.

Thus, in another place, the same David sings: “I said in my abundance, ‘I shall never be moved.’ Lord, by your favor you had given strength to my beauty [a Vatican manuscript adds “good things”]. You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled” (Ps. 30:7–8).

For I said: “I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Ps. 32:5).

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript and old edition read “iniquity” for “injustice”; finally, all the books we use read “of my heart” for “of my sin.”]

And the righteous man is commanded: “Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act. He will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like midday” (Ps. 37:5–6). “For the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord” (ibid., 39), because there is no healing in their flesh before his wrath.

And daily, in accordance with the Apostle who said, “For no good dwells in my flesh” (Rom. 7:18), they groan, saying: “My kidneys are filled with mockeries, and there is no health in my flesh” (Ps. 38:8). He made our days brief, and our substance is as nothing before him. “Every living human being is utter vanity” (Ps. 39:6)—whether living in the body or living in virtues—and yet everything is vanity.

For he fluctuates in an uncertain condition, and while he feels no fear, he suffers a storm in calm weather. “When he was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.” “For nothing,” he says, “he will save them” (Ps. 56:8)—clearly the righteous, who are saved not by their own merit but by God’s clemency.

“And my sins are not hidden from you” (Ps. 69:6). This is said in the person of Christ. If he who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found, grieved for us and bore our sins, how much more ought we to confess our own faults?

“My soul refused consolation” (Ps. 77:3), considering the offenses I had committed. “I remembered God and rejoiced” (ibid., 4), thinking that I would be preserved by his clemency. “At night I meditated in my heart and swept my spirit. And I said: Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (ibid., 7).

This is the voice of the righteous man who, after the meditation of sleep and the crosses of conscience, finally says: “Now I have begun”—either to practice repentance or to enter the threshold of knowledge.

[Note: Martianay, following Erasmus, rather incongruously prints “to enter the light of knowledge,” whereas all our manuscripts read *limen* (“threshold”), and Victorius had earlier restored that reading from the Brixian manuscripts.]

This very change from good things to better things is not the work of my strength, but of the right hand and power of God.

### 20. He is endowed with God’s power

“Mercy shall be built up forever” (Ps. 89:3). There is no time when mercy is not being built up in each of the saints and in those who pass from sins to virtues.

Who among us can be delivered from “the arrow that flies by day, from the business that travels in darkness” (Ps. 91:6)? For behold, “sinners have bent the bow, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. 10:3). They do not wish to wound the crooked, but the upright in heart.

The arrow flies by day through heretics, through their interpretation of the sacred Scriptures. The business travels in darkness and night through philosophers, who desire to wrap the truth in the obscurity of their arguments.

“Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of our God” (Ps. 92:14). Those planted in the house of the Lord are the righteous, established in the Church. But they will flourish not in the present, but in the future, in the courts of the Lord, where possession is sure and secure.

“The Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and rich in mercy” (Ps. 103:8). “The Lord is good to all, and his mercy is over all his works” (Ps. 145:9).

[Note: One Vatican manuscript: “The Lord is good to all,” etc.]

You hear of such great mercies, and yet you dare to trust in your own virtue?

“Let all your works confess to you, Lord” (ibid., 10). If human beings are among all the works of God, then let all human beings confess their sins.

In Samuel we read that it was said concerning Solomon: “He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son” (2 Sam. 7:14).

[Note: The same Vatican manuscript, with the Royal manuscript, reads: “I will establish the throne of his kingdom.” In Greek: τὸν θρόνον αὐτοῦ, “his throne.”]

And again: “If he acts wickedly, I will chastise him with the rod of men, but I will not remove my mercy from him” (ibid., 19).

When David had given thanks to God, he concluded: “And this is the law of man: Lord God, always look to your clemency, and sustain the weakness of the flesh by divine help.”

[Note: The editor does not know whether these two verses are cited from some passage of Scripture; Victorius doubts whether Jerome is speaking in his own sense, as interpreter of the words “This is the law of man.” Certainly we find them neither in the Hebrew text nor in any version.]

“What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let Shimei curse, for the Lord commanded him to curse David. And who shall say to him, ‘Why have you done this?’” (2 Sam. 16:10). For God’s will is not to be scrutinized, but endured with thanksgiving.

And elsewhere: “The Lord commanded that he should thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that he might bring evil upon Absalom” (3 Kings 17:14), although his counsel was certainly like the counsel of God. By what reasoning, then, was the power of free choice overthrown by a greater power?

Jeroboam, who caused Israel to sin [the manuscripts read: “who caused the people Israel to sin”; others: “my people,” etc.], is reproved for having abandoned the Lord’s command, and it is said to him: “I gave you the kingdom of the house of David, and you were not like my servant David, who kept my commandments, followed me with all his heart, and did what was pleasing in my sight” (1 Kings 14:8).

Therefore God’s commandments are possible to fulfill, as we know David fulfilled them, and yet the saints grow weary in maintaining righteousness perpetually.

### 21. Many of the fathers were preserved through merit

In the case of many kings descended from David, we read that they were preserved not through their own merit but through the virtues of David their father, who had done what was pleasing in the sight of God.

Then we come to Asa, king of Judah, concerning whom it is written: “Asa did what was right in the sight of the Lord, like David his father” (1 Kings 15:11). And although the narrative had dwelt on many of his praises, it concluded: “Nevertheless he did not remove the high places. Yet his heart was perfect with the Lord all his days” (ibid., 14).

Behold, he is called righteous, since his heart was perfect with God; yet he erred in this, that he did not remove the high places, which we read that Hezekiah and Josiah removed.

Elijah, in whose spirit and power John the Baptist came, at whose prayer fire descended from heaven and the waters of the Jordan were divided, feared Jezebel and fled. Exhausted, he sat beneath a tree and, overcome by anguish, asked for death, saying: “It is enough for me, Lord; take my life, for I am not better than my fathers” (1 Kings 19:4).

Who can deny that this man was righteous? Yet to fear not merely a woman but a human being arose from disturbance of spirit, which cannot be free from fault, as David says: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. 56:11; 118:6).

Concerning Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, it is written: “The Lord was with Jehoshaphat, who walked in the former ways of David his father” (2 Chron. 17:3). From this it is understood that he possessed David’s earlier righteousnesses, but not his later sins.

“He did not hope in the Baals, but in the God of his father, and walked in his commandments, and not according to the sins of Israel.” The Lord strengthened his kingdom in his hand, and all Judah gave gifts to Jehoshaphat; he acquired immeasurable wealth and riches, and much glory (ibid., 3ff.). And when his heart had acquired courage because of the ways of the Lord, he also removed the high places and sacred groves from Judah.

He was related by marriage to Ahab, the most wicked king. When he returned from battle, Jehu son of Hanani the seer met him and said: “You give assistance to the wicked and join yourself in friendship to those who hate the Lord. Therefore you deserved the Lord’s wrath, but good works were found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah and prepared your heart to seek the Lord” (2 Chron. 19:2–3).

And lest we think that his former righteousnesses were erased by this sin and prophetic rebuke, afterward it is written concerning Ahaziah, of his line [another reading: “stock”], that Jehu found him hiding in Samaria, brought him out, and killed him: “And they buried him,” it says, “because he was the son of Jehoshaphat, who had sought the Lord with all his heart” (2 Kings 9:28).

Concerning Hezekiah it is written: “He did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, according to all that David his father had done. He removed the high places, shattered the images, burned the sacred grove, and broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made” (2 Kings 18:3–4).

And again: “He trusted in the Lord, the God of Israel, and after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah who were before him. He clung to the Lord and did not depart from him; he kept his commandments, which the Lord commanded Moses. And the Lord was with him, and in everything he undertook he acted wisely” (ibid., 5–6).

When Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, had captured all the cities of Judah, Hezekiah sent to him at Lachish, saying: “I have sinned; withdraw from me. Whatever you impose upon me, I will pay.” The king of Assyria imposed on Hezekiah three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. Hezekiah gave him all the money found in the house of the Lord and in the treasuries of the royal palace. At that time he cut down the doors of the temple of the Lord and the shields that he had overlaid with gold, and gave everything to the king of Assyria (ibid., 14).

Although so much is said about him, when necessity compelled him he was not afraid to offer to the king of Assyria what he had consecrated to the Lord. And it is said to him: “I will protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant” (2 Kings 20:6)—not for your sake, because of what you did previously, when the angel struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army.

### 22. The examples of the kings Hezekiah and Josiah

It must also be considered more carefully that Scripture records: “Hezekiah became sick unto death, and Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said: ‘Give orders to your household, for you shall die.’” He turned [two Vatican manuscripts: “who turned”] his face to the wall and prayed to the Lord, saying: “I beg you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes.” And Hezekiah wept with great weeping (2 Kings 20:1ff.).

Certainly Hezekiah was righteous and had a perfect heart. He was about to go to the Lord; he ought not to have wept. Do you seek the reason for his tears? If you consider that he was human, you will not wonder at the causes of his grief. For no one possessing a consciousness of sins goes without fear to the judgment of the Lord.

When he had wept, the word of the Lord came to Isaiah the prophet, saying: “Return and say to Hezekiah, my leader” (ibid., 5). He is called God’s leader, although his death had been announced, because he had been prostrated in humility: “Thus says the Lord God of David your father: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears.” His life was prolonged, and he was delivered from the hands of the Assyrians. Yet he asked for a sign so that he might believe that what God had promised was true; this was at least an indication of imperfect faith.

The king of Babylon also sent messengers and ambassadors to congratulate him on the restoration of his bodily health. He showed them all the treasures of spices, as well as the gold and silver, and the furnishings of his vessels. “There was no object,” it says, “that Hezekiah did not show them in the house of the Lord and in all his dominion” (Isa. 39:2).

[Note: Victorius, from the Brixian codices and the Greek text of Isaiah, reads “in his own house” (ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτοῦ; likewise in Hebrew), whereas the Hieronymian manuscripts consulted, with nearly all printed editions, read “of the Lord.”]

From this we understand that he showed the ambassadors even the vessels of the temple.

Therefore the Lord’s anger was aroused, and afterward, through Isaiah’s prophecy, he learned: “Your sons shall be eunuchs, and all the vessels of the temple shall be carried away to Babylon.” For this fault [manuscripts with the old edition: “because of which fault”] it is also written in the Book of Chronicles: “Hezekiah was lifted up in the pride of his heart” (2 Chron. 32:25).

Certainly no one but an impious person will deny that Hezekiah was righteous. You may say: “He sinned in certain matters, and for that reason ceased to be righteous.” But Scripture does not say this. He did not lose the name of righteousness because he committed minor sins; rather, because he did many good things, he possesses the title of righteous.

I say all this to establish by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures that people are not righteous because they have at some time sinned, but remain righteous because they flourish in many virtues.

Concerning Josiah it is written: “He did what was right in the sight of the Lord and walked in the way of David his father. He did not turn aside to the right or to the left” (2 Chron. 34:2). Yet although he was righteous, in a time of necessity and distress he sent to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Sellum, son of Tecua, son of Aaras, keeper of the garments. “She,” it says, “lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter”—clearly indicating a part of the city enclosed by an inner wall.

And she answered: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Go and say to the man who sent you to me.” Here there is a hidden rebuke of the king, the priests, and all the men: no holy man could be found among them who was able to foretell the future.

Finally Josiah was killed by Pharaoh, king of Egypt, because he did not wish to heed the words of the Lord spoken through the prophet Jeremiah; or, as it is written in Chronicles: “Josiah would not turn back, but prepared for battle against him and did not heed the words of Neco, which came from the mouth of God” (2 Chron. 35:22).

And it follows: “He died and was buried in the tomb of his fathers, and all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him, especially Jeremiah. All his male and female singers repeat laments over Josiah to the present day, and it became like a law in Israel. Behold, it is recorded in the Laments” (ibid., 24–25).
