[Note: Earlier printed books wrongly insert the name “Israel” here, reading “all Israel, Judah, and Jerusalem.” Our manuscripts and the Scriptural text recognize no such reading. The same manuscripts read “male singers” for “female singers.”]

### 23. Other examples of the saints in Scripture

I think that not to obey the words of God, whoever may speak them, is a sin.

Jeremiah himself speaks of this, although many understand it allegorically of the Lord and Savior: “The breath of our face, Christ the Lord, was captured for our sins. To him we said: Under your shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lam. 4:20).

Moses, to whom the Lord spoke face to face (Exod. 33), and whose soul was saved, offended at the waters of contradiction and did not deserve to enter the Promised Land with his brother Aaron.

Concerning them the Psalmist also sings: “Their judges were swallowed up beside the rock; they will hear my words, for they were pleasing” (Ps. 140:6).

[Note: Martianay says that all the manuscripts he used read “were able”; ours all read “were pleasing,” as Victorius also found in his manuscripts. The Greek, ἡδύνθησαν (“were made sweet”), and the Doctor’s ensuing exposition—“which are intrinsically most sweet”—support “were pleasing.” Martianay: “For they were able: thus all our manuscript codices read. Marianus reads from the Septuagint, ‘for they were pleasing.’”]

The meaning is this: the judges of the Jewish people, Moses and Aaron, were swallowed up by the sin of the people beside the rock from which streams of water flowed. Certainly they themselves were righteous and obeyed the words of God, which are intrinsically most sweet.

Finally, concerning the corpses of those who died in the wilderness, it follows: “As the fatness of the earth, they were shattered upon the earth. Our bones were scattered beside the grave” (Ps. 140:7–8).

In Hosea God says: “I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and judgment” (Hos. 2:19). He immediately adds: “And in mercy and compassions, and in faith,”

[Note: Vatican manuscript: “and in mercy and in compassions,” etc.]

so that by the reward bestowed by the giver she may recognize that he himself is the Lord.

In the same book it is written: “I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not enter the city” (Hos. 11:9)—that is, the gathering-place of vices. He alone does not enter this city, which Cain built in the name of his son Enoch. All this the mouths of the priests of the Most High celebrate daily, saying: ὁ μόνος ἀναμάρτητος (*ho monos anamartētos*), “he alone is without sin” in our language.

[Note: Observe that daily the mouths of priests celebrate in the churches the perfection attributed to the supreme God, saying *ho monos anamartētos*, that is, “who alone is without sin.” Vatican manuscript: “which all,” etc. I think the hymn intended is that now called *Glory to God in the highest*, and that the Latin doxology’s “for you alone are holy” corresponds to the words ὁ μόνος ἀναμάρτητος. Hence our manuscripts too read: “you alone are without sin.”]

This praise is reckoned to God in vain according to your view, if it is shared with others. For, in accordance with Amos, we turn justice into wormwood and the fruit of judgment into bitterness (Amos 6).

The sailors and passengers say in the Book of Jonah: “We beg you, Lord, do not destroy us because of this man [the printed editions until now wrongly read ‘because of the righteous man’; our manuscripts and the Scriptural text in every language read ‘this man’], and do not bring innocent blood upon us. For as it has pleased you, so it has happened, Lord” (Jon. 1:14).

They do not know the reasons for what the Prophet, a runaway servant [the word “servant” is more correctly absent from our manuscripts], deserves, yet they justify God and acknowledge innocent blood, whose works they do not understand. Finally they say: “As it has pleased you, Lord, so it has happened.” They do not question the justice of God’s sentence, but confess the truth of the just Judge.

Micah bears witness in a voice full of tears: “The holy one [another reading: ‘seed’] has perished from the earth, and there is no upright person among human beings. All lie in wait for blood; each hunts his brother to death. They call the evil of their hands good” (Mic. 7:2–3). And again: “The best among them is like a thornbush, and the upright like a thorn from a hedge” (ibid., 4).

This is human righteousness: according to the words of the same prophet, one must trust neither friend, nor spouse, nor children, because “a man’s enemies are his household” (Mic. 7:6). The Lord’s saying also confirms this judgment (Matt. 10).

Therefore, through the same prophet, counsel is given: “I will show you, O man, what is good and what the Lord seeks from you: certainly, to do judgment, to love mercy, and to walk carefully with your God” (Mic. 6:8). Did he say, “Possess equality with God”? No; what is greatest is to walk carefully with your God.

Never be secure in yourself. Guard your heart with every care. Consider that you are walking amid snares and entering beneath the battlements of walls, so that you may meditate daily on this saying: “They placed a stumbling-block beside the path for me” (Ps. 140:6). For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

### 24. The Timid Person Can Avoid Sins for a Time

The cautious and timid person can avoid sins for a time; but the person who is confident in his own righteousness resists God and, deprived of his help, lies exposed to the ambushes of enemies. “Let my bones,” says Habakkuk, “rot, and let worms swarm beneath me, provided only that I may rest in the day of distress, that I may ascend to my strong people” (Hab. 3:16). Here he implores tribulations, distress, and anguish of spirit so that in the future he may be joined to the company of men already reigning with Christ. From this it is clear that for these people there is battle and struggle, and victory in the future.

Jesus son of Josedec, whose name is interpreted as “righteous of the Lord” [Note: In the Book of Names, from Haggai, “righteous of the Lord,” or “justified.”], is described as the high priest clothed in filthy garments (Zech. 3). He had committed no sin, and yet bore our sins; Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him. After the struggle and victory it is said to him: “Take away the filthy garment from him”; and, “Behold, I have taken away your iniquity from you.” And Jovinian’s heir speaks:

“I am wholly without any sin whatsoever; I have no filthy garments; I am ruled by my own judgment; I am greater than the Apostle. He does what he does not wish, and does not do what he wishes; I do what I wish and do not do what I do not wish. The kingdoms of heaven have been prepared for me—or rather, I myself have prepared them for myself by my virtues.”

In this way Adam is held guilty, as are the others who consider themselves guilty in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, while I alone, with my band, am not held guilty. Others, shut up in cells and not seeing women because they are wretched, are tormented by desires because they do not hear my words; but even if I am surrounded by troops of women, I have no lust whatsoever. For it was said of me: “The holy stones roll upon the earth” (Zech. 9:16, according to the Septuagint); and therefore I feel nothing, because by the power of free choice I carry about Christ’s trophy.

Let us hear God crying out through Isaiah: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and overthrow the path of your feet” (Isa. 3:5). Who overthrows God’s people more: the person supported by the power of free choice who despises the Creator’s help and is confident in his own will, or the person who fears judgment at each of the Lord’s commands?

To people of this kind God speaks: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and intelligent according to your own judgment” (Isa. 5:21). Isaiah, according to the Hebrew text, mourns and says: “Woe is me, because I was silent, because I have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips; yet I saw the Lord of hosts with my own eyes” (Isa. 6:5). He enjoyed the sight of God by the merit of his virtues, yet, conscious of his sins, he confessed that his lips were unclean. This was not because he had said anything contrary to the Lord’s will, but because he had been silent, overcome either by fear or by shame, and had not rebuked the sinful people with prophetic freedom.

When do we sinners rebuke others, we who flatter the rich and show partiality to sinners for shameful gain? [Note: The manuscripts read, “When we sometimes rebuke sinners,” which is equally good. But a little further below, from the same manuscripts, we have preferred “that we may not do such things,” where previously it read “that we may not do other things,” etc.] Unless perhaps we speak [or: “may speak”] with complete confidence to those on whose resources we depend? That we may not do such things and abstain from every kind of sin, certainly to have kept silent about the truth is a sin. Although the Septuagint does not read, “Because I was silent,” but “Because I was pierced,” that is, by the consciousness of sins, so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled: “I was afflicted in misery, while a thorn was fixed in me” (Ps. 31:4).

He is pierced by the thorn of sin; you blossom in the flowers of virtues. “The moon,” he says, “shall be ashamed, and the sun shall be confounded, when the Lord of hosts visits on high” (Isa. 24:23)—that is what is written elsewhere: “The stars also are not clean in his sight”; and, “Against his angels he found something crooked” (Job 25:5; 4:18).

The moon is ashamed, the sun is confounded, and heaven is covered with sackcloth; yet we, fearless and rejoicing as though we were entirely free from fault, shall confront the majesty of the Judge, when the mountains—namely, those raised up in pride—and all the host of heaven, whether stars or angelic dignities, shall waste away; they shall be folded up like the books of heaven, and all their army shall fall away like leaves.

### 25. The Righteousness of God

“For my sword has been made drunk in heaven, and now it shall descend upon Idumea” (Isa. 34:5). God’s sword is made drunk in heaven, and shall your throne be secure in holiness? [Note: Our manuscripts have, in very different words and with a more harmonious sense: “And shall it be sober only in your holiness? In Idumea …”] It shall descend upon Idumea, whose name is interpreted either as “bloody” or “earthly,” so that by prophetic authority we may learn that the whole earth needs judgment.

Hence what follows: “The sacrifice of the Lord is in Bosra”—which is interpreted as “flesh”—“and great slaughter in the land of Edom,” that is, “in blood” (Isa. 34:6), in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50).

Woe to the one who contradicts his maker; woe to the one who says to his father, “Why did you beget me?” and to his mother, “Why did you give me birth?” (Isa. 45:9–10). This applies to those who say, “Why was I created such a person, unable to be without sin forever?” Why was such a vessel fashioned, so that I should not remain adamantine, but should be earthen and fragile at every touch? [Note: Some manuscripts read, “useless and breakable at every touch”; others, including one Vatican manuscript, read, “worthless and breakable.”]

“We all have gone astray like sheep, and the Lord has laid upon us all our sins” (Isa. 53:6). For he looked and examined carefully, and found no one who judged justly, no one who did his will in everything. Therefore his arm brought salvation, and his righteousness saved all things, so that the whole world might be subjected to God and preserved by his mercy.

For we were unclean—not a few of us, but all. “All our works in the Law have been reckoned like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. 64:6). In Ezekiel God speaks to Jerusalem: “You were perfect in my beauty” (Ezek. 16:14). The meaning is: not in your works, not in your conscience, not in the boasting of your heart, but in my beauty, with which my mercy had freely endowed you. [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “with the freedom of my mercy”; another, “with the generosity of my mercy.”]

Finally, in what follows, he speaks to her when she is saved not by her own merit but by his mercy: “I shall remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I shall raise up for you an everlasting covenant; and you shall remember your ways and be ashamed” (ibid. 16:60–61). And again: “I shall raise up my covenant with you, and you shall know that I am the Lord, so that you may remember and be ashamed and no longer dare to open your mouth because of your shame, when I have been reconciled to you for all that you have done, says the Lord God” (ibid. 16:62–63).

Behold, divine speech plainly shows what he said elsewhere: “And when cleansing you, he shall not make you innocent”—for even the righteous, after sin and restoration to their former state, do not dare to open their mouths, but say with the Apostle: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

Finally, elsewhere through the same prophet he speaks to those who have obtained his mercy. [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “who have been preserved by his mercy.” Shortly afterward, from all the manuscripts and in accordance with the Greek μνησθήσεσθε, we have printed “you shall remember” with Victorinus, instead of “remember,” found in the manuscript of Martianay. It should be noted here that Jerome refutes the Pelagians, who said that at the day of judgment the wicked and sinners should not be spared, because they did not distinguish between those guilty of graver and those guilty of lesser faults. See what we have observed above.] God says: “You shall remember your ways and all your crimes by which you were polluted, and you shall be displeasing to yourselves in your own sight, for all the evils that you have done; and you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have done good to you for my name’s sake, not according to your evil ways nor according to your worst crimes” (Ezek. 20:43–44).

Let us be ashamed and say what those who have already received their rewards say. Let us, sinners upon the earth and established in a frail and mortal body, speak what we see the saints in heaven say, although they have also been endowed with incorruption and immortality.

“And you say,” he says, “‘The way of the Lord is not right,’ whereas your ways are crooked” (Ezek. 18:25). [Note: The author of the Apostolic Constitutions, book 6, chapter 6, says that the Pharisees attributed the works of sinners to Fortune and Fate. Josephus, however, *Antiquities* 13.9 and 14.2, acknowledges that the Pharisees attributed some human things, or even all things, to Fate, but nevertheless did not wish free choice to be removed. Yet their opinion was so entangled that Jerome rightly asserts that they attributed the sins of their own will to the injury of the Creator.]

This is the arrogance of the Pharisees: to refer the sins of their own will to the injury of the Creator and to malign his righteousness. The priests of the mystical temple—which is interpreted as “the Church”—the sons of Zadok, do not go out to the people in their ministerial garments, lest, sanctified by human intercourse, they should be defiled (Ezek. 44). And you, in the midst of the common crowd, one of the people, believe yourself to be pure?

### 26. From Jeremiah

Let us run briefly through the prophet Jeremiah, examining him more by meaning than by wording. “Go around,” he says, “through the exits of Jerusalem, and seek in its streets whether you can find a man who lives according to justice and faith, and I shall be merciful because of him” (Jer. 5:1). Although they say, “The Lord lives,” they swear deceitfully, and this very oath is a lie (Jer. 7:8–9).

He rejects the sacrifices of sinners. He takes away food from those offering victims [Note: Perhaps more correctly, two Vatican manuscripts, with the old edition, read: “he gives food to those offering sacrifices.”], saying that he did not command such sacrifices to their fathers when he led them out of the land of Egypt. He did not command them by his will, but in comparison with idols, preferring that victims be offered to him rather than to demons.

“All have turned away from him; there is no one who speaks good and repents of his sins.” They follow their own wills, like a horse ready for battle. They stretch out their tongue like a bow; everything they say is false, and there is no truth in them. He also commands that the ambushes of friends be avoided and that no one trust his neighbors. Each one lies in wait for his friends, brother is deceived by brother; and this is done not through an evil of nature but through one’s own will, because “they have taught their tongue to speak lies” and rush headlong toward injustice.

“If the Ethiopian changes his skin and the leopard his spots, you too will be able to do good when you have learned evil” (Jer. 13:23). Therefore the Ethiopian skin and the leopard’s spots concern discipline, not nature: they are taught and learned. Nevertheless, the defect of ingrained evil cannot be removed except by him for whom all things are possible.

### 27. Hence He Speaks to the One Who Alone Is the True Physician

“Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, Lord, and I shall be saved; you are my glory [or: my boast] and my hope” (Jer. 17:14).

For if I look upon my condition and misery, I can say nothing other than this: “Cursed is the man who announced to my father, saying, ‘Behold, a male child has been born to you.’ May that man become like the cities that the Lord overthrew. Why did I not perish at once in the womb? Why was my mother’s womb not my tomb, and her womb not an everlasting underworld? Why did I come out of the womb, to see labors and miseries, and for my days to be consumed in anguish?” (Jer. 20:15–18). [Note: One Vatican manuscript places before this verse the following: “Cursed be the day on which I was born, and may that day on which my mother bore me not be blessed.” It then continues, “Cursed is the man,” etc. It is easy to suppose that this verse dropped out of other books because of the occurrence of a similar word, with which the following verse begins.]

He is so certain of his condition and trusts so completely in his strength that he prefers death to life. For he knew his wound and the power of him from whom nothing can be hidden, who says through the Prophet: “Am I a God who draws near, and not a God who is far off?” (Jer. 23:23). [Note: Victorinus reads “through the same prophet,” namely Jeremiah, lest a prophet other than the one praised hitherto seem to be indicated.] Since he fills heaven and earth, no one can escape his knowledge or conceal the secrets of the heart.

“He who searches the kidneys looks within.” [Note: A Vatican manuscript reads, “who looks into the inner parts of the kidneys,” etc.] And so that we may know that every good thing we do belongs to God: “I shall plant them,” he says, “so that they will never be uprooted, and I shall give them thought and understanding, so that they may know me” (Jer. 24:6–7). If thought and understanding are given by God, and knowledge of the Lord springs from the root of him who must be known, where is the proud boasting of free choice alone?

If we wish to know our condition, let us hear history. King Jehoiakim of Judah, and all his companions and princes, after hearing the words of Uriah, wanted to kill him (Jer. 26). When he learned of this, he fled to Egypt, terrified by fear. Why did he fear death, when he had explained the Lord’s sentence and knew that he had been sent to announce the Lord’s will?

We disdain God’s help in every circumstance and neglect to conduct everything at his command, although we read that holy men themselves needed the protection of human beings. Jeremiah is in danger, and it is explicitly said that the hand of Ahikam son of Shaphan helped him, so that he would not be handed over to the power of the crowd and overwhelmed with stones.

### 28. The Grace of the Gospel

When the ceremonies of the Law and the harsh burden of the ancient commandments have been abolished, the grace of the Gospel is promised, and the Lord promises a law by which all will know him, from the least to the greatest, saying: “I shall forgive their sins, and I shall remember their iniquities no more.”

But what kind of righteousness the holy men possessed under the old Law, he demonstrates in what follows: “The children of Israel and the children of Judah continued to commit iniquity in my sight, from their youth to the present day; and the city of Jerusalem, from the beginning of its foundation until the day of its overthrow, provoked me to anger.”

Pay attention to what he says: join the end to the beginning; the entire intervening time is in sin.

Jeremiah, sanctified in the womb before he was born (Jer. 1:5) [Note: In another Vatican manuscript and the old edition, the words “in the womb” are absent.], a virgin and a prophet of the Old Testament, trembles before Zedekiah and tearfully pleads, saying: “Now therefore, my lord the king, hear my petition, and let my supplication prevail with you: do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the scribe, lest I die there” (Jer. 37:19).

O Prophet, why do you fear an impious king? Why are you afraid of one whom you know is about to perish? Why do you dread the prison for which paradise is being prepared? [Note: Victorinus thought that *respondebis* (“you will answer”) should be read, as he restored it from Florentine and Brixian manuscripts, although it seems to us that Jerome continues to address Jeremiah, not Pelagius, as Victorinus believed. Our manuscripts are silent.]

He will answer me: “I am a human being established in mortal and corruptible flesh. I feel pain; I shudder at tortures, which my Lord himself will also feel for my salvation.”

God has mercy on the human race and does not wish what he made to perish. “Do not fear, Jacob,” says the Lord, “for I am with you, and I shall destroy all the nations among whom I scattered you. But I shall not destroy you; I shall chastise you in justice, and I shall have mercy on you in such a way that I shall not leave you innocent” (Jer. 30:10–11).

### 29. Let Us Be Saved by God’s Mercy

Therefore we also say that holy men are righteous [Note: Victorinus contends that the word “and” should be added for a more harmonious sense.] and, after sins, pleasing to God—not solely by their own merit, but by the mercy of him to whom every creature is subject and whose mercy every creature needs.

Let the heretics hear this, those who are lifted up by pride and say, “We have made horns for ourselves.” Let them hear what Moab heard: “We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is exceedingly proud” (Amos 6:14). “I know,” says the Lord, “his height, his arrogance, his boasting, and the swelling of his heart, because his strength is not according to his swelling” (Isa. 16:6).

And it is said to people of this kind: “Their enemies”—there is no doubt that he means the Lord’s flock—“strengthen them, saying: ‘We have not sinned,’ although they have sinned against the beauty of righteousness and the hope of their fathers.”

Do you wish to know when all sins will end? Hear the same prophet: “At that time, says the Lord, iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and it shall not exist, and sin in Judah, and it shall not be found” (Jer. 50:20). Why? It follows: “Because I shall be merciful to them.” But wherever there is mercy, sin has preceded it.

Remove, then, “ability” [Note: namely, the ability to act by one’s own powers and without God’s help], and I shall grant that everything subsists by God’s gift.

“It is good to wait in silence for the salvation of the Lord” (Lam. 3:26); it is good to place one’s mouth in the dust, to offer one’s cheek to the one who strikes, to be filled with reproaches, and to hope in the Lord (ibid. 3:27–30). “For if he has cast off, he will have mercy according to the multitude of his mercies; for he has not humbled and cast off the children of men from his heart.”

Man complains in vain about his sins. “Let us examine our ways, seek, and return to the Lord” (ibid. 3:40–41). Let us lift our hearts and hands to the Lord in heaven, and say to him: “We have acted wickedly and provoked you to anger; therefore you are inexorable” (ibid. 3:42).

### 30. We Know the Reasons for the Divine Will

The prophet Daniel says to Nebuchadnezzar that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men, gives it to whomever he wishes, and sets over it the most abject and rejected person. Ask him why he sets the lowest and most despised person as king and does whatever he wishes; and examine whether his will is just—he of whom it is written: “He raises the humble from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to place him with princes, with the princes of his people” (Ps. 112:7–8).

Or perhaps, in your view, does he seek glory and popular applause without judgment or justice, so that he may raise the humble to kingship and change the powerful into the lowly?

Hear the Prophet saying: “All the inhabitants of the earth are regarded as nothing before him” (Isa. 40:17). For he has done whatever he wished in heaven and on earth, and no one can resist his will [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “resist his strength,” etc.] or say, “Why have you done this?” All his works are in truth, his ways are justice, and he can humble those who are proud.

Antiochus Epiphanes, a most cruel king, overthrew the altar and caused righteousness itself to be trampled underfoot because this had been permitted by the Lord; and Scripture gives the reason: “Because of the many sins” (2 Macc. 5). Therefore he did not do only what he himself wished, but what the Lord permitted because of the people’s sins. Finally, it follows that he did not act by his own strength, but by the command of him who ordered it to be done.

But what he says in his prayer—“We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have done wrong, and we have departed from your commandments and ordinances” (Dan. 3:29)—and other statements of this kind, you are accustomed to say were spoken by David, Daniel, and all the prophets not on their own behalf, since they were holy, but in the person of the people. [Note: The name David is absent from all our manuscripts; perhaps this is more correct.]

Against this opinion he himself will answer and say: “While I was still praying and confessing my sins and the sins of the people of Israel” (Dan. 9:20). You see, therefore, that he entreated the Lord and poured out his prayers before the Lord his God both for his own sins and for the sins of the people.

Do you wish to know again when sin and iniquity will end? Although interpreters differ, hear the same Prophet: “Seventy weeks have been completed for your people and your holy city, so that iniquities may be completed, sin may receive its end, iniquity may perish, and everlasting righteousness may be revealed” (Dan. 9:24). [Note: He discusses their various interpretations in his *Commentary*, chapter 9.] Therefore, until that end arrives and this corruptible and mortal nature is changed into incorruption and immortality, we must remain subject to sin—not through the defect of nature and creation, as you slanderously claim, but through frailty and the changing of the human will, which varies from moment to moment, because God alone is unchangeable.

You ask where Abel, where Enoch, where Jesus son of Nun, where Elisha, and the other saints sinned. There is no need to look for a knot in a reed. Would that I could also keep silent about manifest sins. If you wish to hear the truth from me, I do not know.

“I am conscious of nothing against myself,” he says, “yet I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4:4). “Man looks upon the face, but God upon the heart” (cf. 2 Sam. 16:7). No one is justified before his conscience and his sight. Hence Paul also speaks confidently: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23); and: “God has shut up all things under sin, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:32), together with the other passages that we have often repeated. [Note: After this, Vallarsius’s edition has: “The second book ends.” To these words he appends the following note: “In the manuscripts: ‘The second part of the book ends. The third part begins.’”]

## BOOK THREE

### 1. Baptism Forgives Only Past Sins

**CRITOBULUS:** I have been delighted by the abundance of your speeches, concerning which it is written: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. 10:19). But what has this to do with the matter? Surely you will admit that those who have received Christ’s baptism do not have sin. And if they are without sin, they are righteous. Once they have become righteous, if they act carefully, they can preserve righteousness forever and thus avoid every sin.

**ATTICUS:** Are you not ashamed to follow the opinion of Jovinianus, which has been rejected and condemned? He too relies upon these testimonies and your arguments—or rather, you follow his inventions, wishing to teach in the East what was long ago condemned at Rome and, until recently, in Africa. [Note: It is not that Jovinianus’s explicitly named opinion had also been condemned in Africa, as Martianay notes; it had scarcely spread beyond Italy, as appears from Augustine’s *Book on Heresies*. Rather, Jerome said this because the impeccability defended by Jovinianus “long ago”—that is, recently—had been condemned in Africa, since at the African council of 412 or 413 the error of Coelestius concerning impeccability had been condemned, which Jerome regards as the same as Jovinianus’s error. Augustine appears to have held the same view in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, numbers 15 and 18. “Boast in order to fulfill Jovinianus’s measure more perfectly.”]

Read, then, what answer was given to him, and regard it as an answer to yourself. For in discussing doctrines and questions, one must seek not the person but the issue.

Know this nevertheless: baptism grants forgiveness for past sins; it does not preserve future righteousness, which is guarded by labor, effort, diligence, and always, above all, by God’s mercy. Thus it is ours to ask, and his to grant what is asked; ours to begin, his to complete; ours to offer what we can, his to fulfill what we cannot. [Note: “Ours to begin.” From this passage Saint Benedict may have taken the words in the Prologue to his Rule: “First of all, whenever you begin any good work, ask him with most earnest prayer to bring it to completion,” and the rest. Martianay adds: “To prevent a wrong interpretation, add the conclusion which Jerome himself, explaining himself in an entirely orthodox manner in Letter 130 to Demetrias, attached to a similar statement: ‘Even that which is ours is not ours without God’s mercy.’”]

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. 127:1–2). Hence the Apostle also commands: “Run in such a way that you may obtain the prize.” All run, but one receives the crown (1 Cor. 9:24). And in the psalm it is written: “Lord, with the shield of your good will you have crowned us” (Ps. 5:13).

Our victory, and the crown of victory, are prepared by his protection and shield; we run here so that we may obtain the prize in the future. There the one who has been victorious in this world will receive the crown. And after baptism it is said to us: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). And: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:16–17). And elsewhere: “The Lord is with you as long as you are with him; if you abandon him, he will abandon you” (2 Chron. 15:2).

In whose sanctuary and holy place, do you suppose, does Christ’s purity remain, and the serenity of the temple is saddened by no cloud? We cannot always have the same face—what philosophers falsely boast about Socrates [or: the philosopher]; how much less can we always have the same mind. Human faces are many, and so also are hearts diverse.

If it were possible to keep us always immersed in baptismal water, sins fluttering down upon us from above would not touch us; the Holy Spirit would protect us [or: protects us]. But the enemy attacks, and once defeated he does not withdraw; rather, he is always lying in wait to shoot those who are upright in heart.

### 2. From the Gospel According to the Hebrews

In the Gospel according to the Hebrews—which is written in the Chaldaic or Syriac language but in Hebrew letters, and which the Nazarenes use to this day—the history is narrated, whether according to the Apostles or, as most people maintain, according to Matthew; the book is also held in the library at Caesarea. [Note: Here Jerome explicitly teaches that the Gospel according to the Twelve Apostles, the Gospel according to the Hebrews, and the Gospel of the Nazarenes are the same. Bede therefore wrongly distinguishes the first two at the beginning of his Commentary on Luke, classifying the Gospel of the Twelve Apostles among apocryphal writings produced by heretics, but the Gospel according to the Hebrews among ecclesiastical writings. “Among these,” he says, “it should be noted that what is called the Gospel according to the Hebrews is to be numbered not among the apocrypha but among ecclesiastical histories. For it appears that Jerome himself, the interpreter of Sacred Scripture, drew many testimonies from it and translated it into Latin and Greek.”]

“Behold, the mother of the Lord and his brothers were saying to him: ‘John the Baptist baptizes for the forgiveness of sins. Let us go and be baptized by him.’ But he said to them: ‘What sin have I committed, that I should go and be baptized by him?’” [Note: Julian the Pelagian seized upon this as an occasion for slander. Augustine quotes these words in book 4, chapter 88, of his *Unfinished Work*: “But when these matters have been fulfilled as the situation requires, it is useful for you [Augustine] to agree with Jerome, at least to some extent. With what confidence can you praise Jerome’s writings and say that there was no sin in Christ, when he, in that dialogue which he composed under the name of Atticus and Critobulus with remarkable elegance, as befits such a faith, relies even upon the testimony of a fifth Gospel—which he says he translated—to show that Christ possessed not only natural but also voluntary sin, because he recognized that he needed to be cleansed by John’s baptism,” and so forth. Augustine answered this manifest slander: “If you had set out Jerome’s words, perhaps I could show how they should be understood without the blasphemy you seek to import into them. Even if they could not be so understood, I would not therefore think that the faith which he held with the other outstanding doctors of the Catholic Church should be rejected merely because something might be found that he said without agreeing with them. Against you, however, it is enough for me, speaking of this man, that although he holds the view concerning original sin which you so detest that you call me a Manichaean because of it, you nevertheless do not dare to call him one.” Jerome’s words plainly show that he neither grants authority to this Gospel nor regards its meaning as being that Christ was stained by any kind of sin which needed to be washed away by John’s baptism. Julian, who maliciously interpreted these words with the intention of slander, is also mistaken in saying that Jerome here refers to a version of the Nazarenes’ Gospel; Jerome records that Gospel in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the section on James, the brother of the Lord.]

“Unless perhaps this very thing I have said is ignorance.”

And in the same volume:

“If your brother sins in a word,” he says, “and makes satisfaction to you, receive him seven times a day.” His disciple Simon said to him: “Seven times a day?” The Lord answered and said to him: “Yes, I say to you, up to seventy times seven” (Matt. 18:22; Luke 17:4).

For among the Prophets also, after they had been anointed with the Holy Spirit, words concerning sin were found. Ignatius, an apostolic man and martyr, writes boldly: “The Lord chose Apostles who were more sinful than all other human beings.” [Note: The name Ignatius is absent from a Vatican manuscript, which leaves a blank space. In fact, Saint Ignatius did not write this about the Apostles; it occurs in the Epistle of Barnabas, page 16: ὅτι δὲ τοὺς ἰδίους, τοὺς μέλλοντας κηρύσσειν τὸ εὐαγγέλιον αὐτοῦ ἐξελέξατο ὄντας ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν ἁμαρτίαν ἀνομωτέρους—“because he chose his own Apostles, who were more lawless than all sin,” that is, “who were worse than all sinners.” Origen does not deny the same thing in *Against Celsus*, book 1, number 63: “It is true that in the Epistle of Barnabas, from which perhaps Celsus drew his material, where it says that the Apostles were infamous and exceedingly wicked, it is written that Jesus chose Apostles who were immoral, so that none were worse.” Saint Gregory of Nazianzus again presents this in the *Philocalia*, from Origen’s *Sentences*, chapter 18. We should therefore attribute this to a lapse of memory on Jerome’s part: he ascribes to Ignatius something found nowhere in his letters. It is not an implausible conjecture that the book itself, a collection of apostolic writings in which the Ignatian works came first and those of Barnabas and Clement followed, was responsible for the error. The whole collection may have been entitled with Ignatius’s name, or the Epistle of Barnabas, inserted among it, may not have had its own title in the book Jerome used. See Maenardus’s notes on that Epistle.]

The Psalmist sings of their swift conversion: “Their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they hastened” (Ps. 16:4).

If you do not use these testimonies as authority, use them at least as evidence of antiquity—of what all ecclesiastical men believed.

Suppose that someone baptized is immediately, or within those very days, taken away by death, and I will grant you what I ought not to grant: that he neither thought nor said anything in which he might fall through error and ignorance. Will he therefore be without sin, because he seems not to have overcome sin but to have fled from it? Or will it not rather be because, by God’s mercy, he was released from the prison of sins and departed to the Lord?

This too is what we say: God can do whatever he wishes; but a human being, by himself and by his own will—as you assert—cannot be without sin. If he can, then you needlessly join grace to the claim, since one who is powerful does not need it. But if he cannot without God’s grace, then you foolishly said that he can do what he cannot. Whatever depends upon another’s will does not belong to the one whom you claim to be able; it belongs to the one without whom it is evident that he cannot.

### 3. How far being differs from being able

**C.** I ask you: what is this perversity—or rather, this irrational contention? Will you not even grant me this, that a person emerging from the waters of baptism is without sin? [784] [Col. 0572A]

**A.** Either I am unable to explain my meaning in words, or, when I explain it, you are slow to understand.

**C.** How so?

**A.** Recall both what you said and what I am saying. You asserted that a person can be without sin if he wishes.

> **[Note: Victor: “You asserted that a person can be without sin,” etc. He says that from Critobulus’s own proposition it is clear that the word *can* was added by him; and below: “For you say that a person is not without sin, but can be so.” A little farther on: “This which you assert—that a person can be without sin if he wishes,” etc. Our manuscripts, however, are silent on this point.]**

I reply that this is impossible for a human being—not because a person immediately after baptism is not free from sin, but because the time during which he is without sin is attributed not at all to human ability, but to the grace of God. Remove the word “can,” therefore, and I will grant the word “is.” For how can someone do what he cannot do by himself? Or what sort of sinlessness is that which ends immediately with the death of this body?

> **[Note: That is, in one who dies immediately after baptism.]**

Or certainly, if his life is prolonged, he remains exposed to the danger of sin and ignorance. [Col. 0572B]

**C.** You ensnare me with dialectical skill and do not speak with Christian simplicity, contriving for me certain knots between “being” and “being able to be.”

**A.** Am I playing with verbal tricks, when this has proceeded from your own workshop? For you say that a person is not without sin, but can be so,

> **[Note: The manuscripts, together with the old edition, read: “whereas, on the contrary, I ascribe to you,” etc. Victor agrees; shortly afterward he also wrote *per se esse non posse*—“cannot exist by himself”—and restored *esse* on the basis of the manuscripts.]**

whereas, on the contrary, I attribute to you what you denied: that a person is without sin through the grace of God, and yet cannot be so by himself.

**C.** Then commandments are given in vain, if we cannot fulfill them.

**A.** God commanded what is possible; no one doubts this. But because human beings do not do what is possible, the whole world is therefore subject to God and needs his mercy. Or certainly, if you can point out someone who has fulfilled everything, then you will be able to demonstrate that there is a person who does not need God’s mercy. For everything that can be done is situated in three times: either the past, the present, [785] or the future. This which you assert—that a person can be without sin if he wishes—show that it has happened in the past, or at least that it is now happening; as for the future, we shall see later.

If you cannot point out anyone who either is or has been entirely without every sin, it remains that the dispute concerns only the future. For the present, you are defeated and held fast in two times, the past and the present. If later there should be someone greater than the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles who is free from sin, then, if you can, persuade us concerning the future. [Col. 0572C]

### 4. That a person can refrain from sin for a time

**C.** Speak as you wish and argue as you please: you will never wrest from me the free will that God once granted, nor will you be able to take away what God bestowed on me—that I can do so if I wish.

> **[Note: Victor removed the word “God” here as superfluous.]**

**A.** Let us use one testimony merely by way of example: “I have found David, the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my desires” (Acts 13:22; Psalm 88:21). That David was holy is beyond doubt; and yet the one who was chosen to do all God’s desires is criticized for having done certain things. Certainly it was possible for him to do this, since he was chosen for the purpose of doing all God’s desires. Nor is God at fault, who foretold that he would do all the desires of his commandments; rather, the fault is his who did not do what had been foretold.

For he did not say that he had found a man who would do all the desires of his commandment forever,

> **[Note: The words “but one who would do all the desires” were necessary to complete the sense and were missing from the printed editions. We supplied them from the Vatican manuscript.]**

but only one who would do all his desires. This is what we too say: a person can refrain from sin if he wishes—for a time, in a particular place, and in accordance with bodily weakness—as long as the mind remains attentive, as long as the string on the lyre is not loosened by any defect. [Col. 0573A]

But if he relaxes even slightly,

> **[Note: The manuscripts read: “But if he relaxes even slightly, without himself knowing it.”]**

just as someone drawing a small boat against the current, if he lets go with his hands, is immediately carried backward and borne by the flowing waters where he does not wish to go, so human nature, if it relaxes even slightly, learns its own frailty and recognizes that it cannot do many things.

Do you suppose that the Apostle Paul, when he wrote, “When you come, bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, and the books, especially the parchments” (2 Timothy 4:13), was thinking at that moment about heavenly mysteries and not about the things necessary for ordinary life and the body?

[786] Give me a person who is never hungry, never thirsty, never cold, never in pain, never feverish, never tormented by colic or difficulty in urinating, and I will grant you that a person can think of nothing except virtues.

The Apostle is struck by an attendant (Acts 23:3), and he directs a sentence against the high priest who ordered him to be struck: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall” (Isaiah 53).

Where is that patience of the Savior, who, “like a lamb led to the slaughter, did not open his mouth,” but speaks gently to the one striking him: “If I have spoken wrongly, testify about the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 18:29)? [Col. 0573B–C]

We do not disparage the Apostle; rather, we proclaim the glory of the Lord, who, having suffered in the flesh, surpasses the injury and frailty of the flesh. I say nothing of the passage in which he records: “Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; the Lord, the righteous judge, will repay him on that day” (2 Timothy 4:14).

### 5. Nor is the Creator’s constitution to be blamed

**C.** You compel me to say what I have long been eager to say, and yet I do not bring forth the words that are bursting out. [Col. 0574A]

**A.** Who, then, prevents you from saying what you think? Either what you are about to say is good, and you ought not to deprive us of something good; or it is bad, and for that reason you have kept silent—not out of consideration for us, but out of shame.

**C.** I will say it—at some point I will say what I think.

Your entire argument slips toward this: that you accuse nature and refer the blame to God, who created a human being such as this.

**A.** So this was what you wanted, and did not want to say? Say it, I beg you, so that everyone may enjoy your wisdom. You criticize God for having made a human being human? Let the angels also criticize him for being angels. Let every creature complain about why it is what it was created to be, rather than what it could have been created to be.

Clearly I must now amuse myself with childish declamations and proceed from the gnat and the ant all the way to the Cherubim and Seraphim, asking why each was not created in a better condition. And when I come to the exalted Powers, I shall complain and say why God alone is so completely God, and why he did not make everything gods.

Either, according to you, he is guilty of inability, or of envy. Criticize him also for allowing the devil to exist in this world, and take away the crown once you have removed the contest. [787]

> **[Note: Martianay, following Erasmus, had omitted the words after “inability”; we supplied them from the manuscripts and the old edition. Victor had already restored them from the Medicean, Fesulan, and other manuscripts. The following context confirms them, where Critobulus’s dilemma is rejected. Shortly afterward, the Vatican manuscript reads “to be able only in this world” instead of “to exist in this world.” The Regina manuscript, together with the old edition, reads equally well “only to exist.”]**

**C.** I am not so foolish as to complain that the devil exists, through whose envy death entered the world; but I grieve that ecclesiastical men, and those who usurp for themselves the title of teachers, take away free will. Once it is removed, the sect of the Manichaeans is constructed. [Col. 0574B]

**A.** Do I take away free will, when throughout my entire argument I have done nothing except preserve God’s omnipotence together with free will?

**C.** How do you preserve free will, when you say that a person can do nothing unless God is always helping?

**A.** If the one who joins God’s assistance to free will is at fault, then let the one who removes God’s assistance be praised.

**C.** I do not remove God’s assistance; indeed, through his grace we can do everything that we can do. But we assign each to its proper limits: what God’s grace gives is the power of free will, while it belongs to our will to do or not to do something; and a reward is reserved for those who do, and punishment for those who do not.

### 6. What God crowns in us

**A.** You seem forgetful to me, and, as though nothing had been said above, you return along the same lines of argument. For this was established by a lengthy discussion: that the Lord, by his grace through which he granted us free will, helps and sustains us in each individual work. [Col. 0574C–D]

**C.** What, then, does he crown and praise in us, if he himself has brought it about?

> **[Note: The printed editions read up to this point, “What, then, does he help and crown?” The words “helps and,” wrongly inserted and contrary to the author’s meaning—as the entire context makes clear—have been removed on the authority of the manuscripts, in none of which do we find them.]**

**A.** He crowns our will, which offered everything it was able to offer; our labor, which strove to accomplish it; and our humility, which always looked toward God’s assistance.

**C.** Then, if we did not do what he commanded, either God wanted to help us or he did not. If he wanted to help us and did help us, yet we did not do what we wished, then it was not we but he who was defeated.

But if he did not wish to help, the one who wanted to act is not at fault; rather, the fault is his who could have helped but did not wish to do so.

> **[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, with the opposite meaning, “and yet we did what we wished.” See Augustine, *On Perfect Righteousness*.]**

**A.** You do not understand that your *dilemmaton*—διλήμματον—has fallen into a great abyss of blasphemies: so that from either side God is either powerless or envious, and he receives not as much praise for being the author and helper of good as he receives blame for not restraining evil.

> **[Note: Not *dilemma*—δίλημμα—as the printed books have it, but *dilemmaton*—διλήμματον—all the manuscript copies read; and Hermogenes, *On Invention*, book 4, teaches that this is the correct reading. Suidas distinguishes them thus: *dilemma*, “a proposition understood in two ways,” and *dilemmaton*, “understood doubly,” that is, understood in two alternatives. MARTIAN.]**

Let him therefore be blamed for allowing the devil to exist, for having permitted this, and for still allowing some evil to occur daily in the world even to this day. Marcion asks this question, as do all the dogs of the heretics [788] who tear apart the Old Testament and are accustomed to construct syllogisms of this kind.

Either God knew that the human being placed in paradise would transgress his commandment, or he did not know. If he knew, then the one who could not avoid God’s foreknowledge is not at fault; rather, the fault lies with the one who created him so that he could not avoid God’s knowledge. If he did not know, then when you remove foreknowledge from him, you also remove divinity.

By this reasoning, the one who chose Saul as the future impious king will be at fault. And the Savior will be held guilty either of ignorance or of injustice for having said in the Gospel: “Did I not choose you twelve Apostles, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71). Ask him why he chose Judas as a traitor. Why did he entrust the money-box to one whom he knew to be a thief?

Do you wish to hear the explanation? God judges the present, not the future. He does not condemn in advance one whom he knows will later become such that he will displease him. Rather, he is of such great goodness and ineffable mercy that he chooses one whom he presently sees to be good, while knowing that he will become evil, granting him the opportunity for conversion and repentance, in accordance with the Apostle’s words:

“Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each according to his works” (Romans 2:4–5).

Adam did not sin because God knew that this would happen; rather, God, as God, foresaw what Adam was going to do by his own will.

Accuse God, then, of lying, because he said through Jonah: “Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3:4). But he will answer you through Jeremiah:

“At one moment I shall speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot it, to destroy it, and to overthrow it. If that nation turns from its evil against which I have spoken, then I too shall repent of the evil that I had thought to do to it. And at another moment I shall speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build it and to plant it. If it does evil in my sight, so that it does not hear my voice, I shall repent of the good that I had spoken of doing to it” (Jeremiah 18:7–10). [Col. 0575A–D]

Once, Jonah was indignant that he had seemed to lie at God’s command; but he is convicted of unjust grief, preferring to speak the truth to the destruction of [789] an innumerable people rather than to lie for the salvation of so many.

An example is given to him:

“You pity the ivy—or the gourd—for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow; it came into being in one night and perished in one night. And should I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which there are more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know the difference between their right hand and their left?” (Jonah 4:10–11).

If there was such a multitude of people at the age of infants and of the simple—people whom you certainly cannot prove to have been sinners—what shall we say about the various ages of both sexes, which, according to Philo,

> **[Note: The old edition reads “Philo the most prudent,” without the conjunction “and”; the Vatican manuscript reads “the most prudent of philosophers,” namely Plato in the *Timaeus*.]**

and the most prudent of philosophers, proceed from infancy to decrepit old age in a sequence of seven-year periods, with the stages of life succeeding one another so imperceptibly that, when we pass from one to another, we are scarcely able to perceive it? [Col. 0576A–B]

### 7. God is in no way the author of sin

**C.** Your entire argument tends toward this: that you ascribe what the Greeks call *autexousion*—αὐτεξούσιον—and what we call free will in name, but take it away in reality.

> **[Note: What the Greeks call *autexousion*. Here likewise all the manuscript codices read αὐτεξούσιον, not αὐτεξουσίαν, as Erasmus incorrectly printed it. *To autexousion* means free will, or free choice; hence Gregory of Nazianzus says, “honored with the faculty of free will” (*τῷ αὐτεξουσίῳ τιμηθείς*). MARTIAN.]**

For you make God the author of sins, when you assert that a person can do nothing by himself, but only with God’s assistance, to whom everything we do must be attributed. We, however, say that the power of free will is attributed, whether a person has done good or evil, to the one who did what he wished, and not to the one who once granted free will. [Col. 0576C]

**A.** Although you evade the issue, you are caught in the snares of truth. For in this way, even if God himself does not help, he will nevertheless, according to you, be the author of evil, because he could have prevented it and did not. There is an old saying that the person who, when able to save someone from death, does not save him, is a murderer.

**C.** Now, now—I lower my hand and yield; you have won, if winning means trying to overturn the truth by words rather than by realities, that is, not by truth but by falsehood.

For I can answer you with the Apostle’s words: “Even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge” (2 Corinthians 11:6). When you speak under compulsion through the twists of argument, you seem to me to agree with me; but when you fall silent, you again slip away inwardly, so that it becomes clear that your argument proceeds not from the fountains of truth [Col. 0576D] and Christian simplicity, but from the subtleties and artifice of philosophers. [790]

**A.** Do you wish me, then, to use the testimonies of Scripture again? And how do your disciples boast that no one can answer your arguments and problems?

**C.** I not only wish it, but desire it. Teach me from the holy Scriptures where, once the power of free will has been removed, a person does what he either did not wish, or could not do by himself.

> **[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “or wishes not to do.” The punctuation, whose fault had obscured the sense, has been corrected below.]** [Col. 0577A–D]

### 8. Testimonies from Scripture

**A.** Scripture must be employed not as you propose, but as truth and reason demand. Jacob speaks in his prayer:

“If the Lord God is with me, and guards me on the way by which I go, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear, and brings me back safely to my father’s house, then the Lord shall be my God; and this stone which I have set up as a pillar shall be the house of God; and of everything that you give me I shall offer you tithes” (Genesis 28:20 and following).

Did he say, “If you preserve my free will, and I obtain food and clothing by my own labor, and return to my father’s house”? He assigns everything to the will of the Lord, so that he may deserve to receive what he requests.

When Jacob was returning from Mesopotamia, an army of angels met him, and they were called “the camp of God” (Genesis 32). Afterward he wrestles with an angel in human form and is strengthened by the Lord; from *Jacob*, “the supplanter,” he receives the name *Israel*, “God’s most upright one” (*rectissimus Dei*).

> **[Note: “Jacob, most upright before God.” Marianus is foolish in his notes, as though in six hundred passages of Jerome the name Israel were not interpreted as “upright before God.” MARTIAN. —That is, Israel. For in his commentary on Isaiah 44 he says: “Properly, according to the Hebrews and the evidence of the letters, Israel is called *euthutatos theou*—εὐθύτατος θεοῦ, ‘upright before God.’” See the *Book of Names*. Victor preferred “most upright.”]**

For he would not have dared to return to his most cruel brother unless strengthened by the Lord’s protection.

It is written in what follows: “The sun rose upon him after he passed through Phanuel” (Genesis 32:31), which is interpreted as “the face of God.” Hence Moses also says:

> **[Note: “Hence Moses also speaks.” The words are Jacob’s, but they were written down by Moses; therefore Jerome attributes the same words to Moses. MARTIAN. —Although they were spoken by Jacob, he attributes the words to Moses as historian. So Christ, in Matthew 19:4, reports as spoken by God what Adam said, since Adam spoke it at God’s command.]**

“I have seen the Lord face to face, and my life has been preserved”—not by the property of nature, but by the condescension of the merciful one.

Therefore the sun of righteousness rises for us when we are strengthened by the face of God.

Joseph is confined in prison in Egypt, and it is related there that the keeper of the prison entrusted everything to his power and fidelity. The reason is given: “Because the Lord was with him, and whatever he did, the Lord prospered in his hands” (Genesis 39:23). [Col. 0577B–C]

Hence dreams are also suggested to the eunuchs (Genesis 40), and Pharaoh sees an inexplicable dream (Genesis 41), so that through this opportunity Joseph might be liberated (Genesis 42 and following), [791] his father and brothers fed, and Egypt saved during the famine.

It follows:

“God said to Israel in a vision by night: ‘I am the God of your fathers. Do not be afraid to go down into Egypt, for I will make you there into a great nation. I shall go down with you into Egypt, and I shall bring you back from there; and Joseph shall place his hands upon your eyes’” (Genesis 46:3–4).

Where here is the power of free will? Is not everything involved in his daring to go to his son and entrust himself to a nation that did not know the Lord the assistance of the God of his fathers?

The people are delivered from Egypt by a strong hand and an exalted arm—not by Moses and Aaron, but by the one who delivered the people through miracles of signs and finally struck down the firstborn of Egypt, so that those who had previously held them back stubbornly were compelled to send them out eagerly (Exodus 11 and 12). [Col. 0578A]

Solomon says:

“Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not exalt yourself in your own wisdom. Acknowledge him in all your ways, so that he may make your paths straight” (Proverbs 3:5–6).

Understand what he says: We must trust neither in our wisdom nor in any virtues, but in the Lord alone, by whom human steps are directed.

Finally, we are commanded to show him our ways and to make known to him those ways that become straight not through our own labor, but through his assistance and mercy.

Hence it is written: “Make your way straight before me,” or, as other copies have it, “Make my way straight before you” (Psalm 5:9): so that what is straight for you may also appear straight to me.

The same Solomon says: “Roll your works upon the Lord, and your thoughts will be established” (Proverbs 16:3). Our thought is established when we roll everything we do upon the Lord’s assistance, as upon a stable and exceedingly solid rock, and attribute everything to him. [Col. 0578B]

### 9. From the New Testament

When the Apostle Paul had recounted God’s benefits in rapid speech, he finally added: “And who is sufficient for these things?” (1 Corinthians 2:16).

Hence in another place he says:

“Such confidence we have through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us sufficient ministers of the new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but [792] the Spirit gives life” (1 Corinthians 3:4–5).

Do we still dare to be proud through free will and abuse God’s benefits as an insult to the giver, when the same chosen vessel writes most openly:

“We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the abundance of our power may be from God and not from us” (1 Corinthians 4:7)?

> **[Note: The word “our” is absent from the Regina manuscript and from the old edition; it is found neither in the Greek nor in the Vulgate translator. Some Greek copies, however, are thought to read *καὶ ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ*—“and from God.”]**

Hence, in another place, rebuking the shamelessness of the heretics, he says:

“Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord. For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends” (2 Corinthians 10:17–18).

And again: “For I was lacking in nothing among those who are exceedingly Apostles, although I am nothing” (2 Corinthians 12:11).

Peter says to the Lord, troubled by the greatness of his signs: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8).

And the Lord says to his disciples:

“I am the vine and you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing” (John 1:55).

> **[Note: Servatus Lupus, who quotes this passage from Jerome in his *Collection on Three Questions*, reads *afferet*—“will bear”—in the future tense; then he reads *folia vitium*—“leaves of vines”—incorrectly instead of *flagella*, “branches”; finally, he omits *nisi*—“unless”—before the name “Father.”]**

Just as the branches and shoots of vines immediately wither when they have been cut off from the trunk, so all human strength withers and perishes if it is abandoned by God’s assistance.

“No one,” he says, “can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). When he says, “No one can come to me,” he breaks the pride of free will:

> **[Note: The manuscripts read, “Even if someone wishes to go to Christ,” etc.]**

even if someone wishes to go to Christ, unless what follows takes place—“unless my heavenly Father draws him”—he desires in vain and struggles fruitlessly. At the same time, we must observe that the one who is drawn does not run voluntarily, but is brought either resisting and slowly or unwillingly. [Col. 0579A]

### 10. He argues from the passages cited

One who cannot come to Jesus by his own strength and labor—how can he avoid all sins at once? How can he avoid them forever and assume for himself the name of God’s power?

For if he is *anamartētos*—ἀναμάρτητος, “without sin”—and I too am *anamartētos*, what difference will there be between me and God?

I shall add one more testimony, so as not to weary you and your audience. Ahasuerus, whom the translators of the Septuagint call *Artaxerxes*—Ἀρταξέρξης—

> **[Note: Or “Artaxersen.”]**

is deprived of sleep, so that, while reviewing the records of faithful servants concerning himself, he may discover Mordecai, through whose information he had been rescued from plots; so that Esther might also become more highly esteemed (Esther 6), and the entire Jewish people might escape [793] the death threatening them.

Certainly that most powerful king, who possessed the entire East from India to the North and Ethiopia, after the most lavish banquets and foods gathered from throughout the world, wished to sleep and rest in sleep, and to exercise the free will of sleeping—unless the Lord, the provider of all good things, had interrupted the order of nature, so that the cruelty of the tyrant might be overcome contrary to nature. [Col. 0579B–C]

It would be too long if I wished to produce all the examples from the holy Scriptures. The entire speech of the saints is prayer to God; every prayer and supplication wrests the Creator’s mercy, so that we who cannot be saved by our own strength and effort may be preserved by his mercy.

Where there is mercy and grace, free will ceases in part—namely, insofar as it consists in our willing and desiring, and giving assent to what is pleasing.

> **[Note: Jerome seems here and above, in section 1, note b, to teach that the beginning of good will and faith comes from us. There is no need to mention that the second Council of Orange, especially canons 3 and 25, opposed this view. He is nevertheless excused by the example of certain other Fathers who wrote before the Pelagian heresy: since all the deceptions and sophistries of the Pelagians had not yet been exposed, they appear verbally to attribute somewhat more than was proper to human will, in order to preserve the integrity of free will. At that time there was, as it were, a proverbial saying: “Willing is ours.” Hence in a certain unpublished sermon on the Creed, in the Veronese parchment manuscripts: “Even if willing is ours, nevertheless we do not find that we can complete it without him”—that is, God. Hilary, on Psalm 118: “Our will must have from itself the power to wish; God will give increase to the one who begins,” etc. Optatus, book 2: “Willing is ours, running is ours, completing is God’s,” etc. Finally, Augustine himself, in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 32, explains this view admirably: “Everything must be attributed to God, who both prepares the human will to be helped and helps it once prepared. For a good human will precedes many gifts of God, but not all; and in those which it does not precede, it itself is also present.”]**

It is now in the Lord’s power to enable us, by his aid and assistance, to accomplish what we desire, labor for, and strive toward.

### 11. Bodily health is compared with the soul’s health

**C.** I had simply said that God’s assistance is perceived not in each of our individual works, but in the grace of our constitution and of the law, so that free will might not be broken. Otherwise, there are many among our people who say that everything we do is accomplished through God’s protection. [Col. 0579D–0580A]

**A.** Whoever says this will cease to be one of yours.

> **[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “He has ceased.” Martianay had this corruptly, with an interrogative mark.]**

Therefore either you too must say these things and begin to be one of ours, or, if you do not say them, you will be an outsider together with those who do not speak as we do.

**C.** I shall be yours if you say what I say—or rather, you will be mine if you do not say the opposite. You acknowledge healthy bodies, yet deny health to the soul, which is stronger. Just as disease and a wound are found in the body, so sin is found in the soul. Therefore, if you acknowledge that a person is sometimes healthy in the part that is flesh, why do you not also call him healthy in the part that is spirit?

**A.** I shall follow your proposition. You will not escape today; I shall come wherever you are summoned.

**C.** I am ready to listen.

**A.** And I am ready to speak to deaf ears.

[794] I shall therefore answer the question before us. Composed of soul and body, we derive the nature of both substances. Just as the body is called healthy when it is troubled by no illness, so the soul is healthy when it is shaken by no fault. [Col. 0580B]

And yet, although the body is healthy, whole, vigorous, and strengthened by the integrity of all its senses, it suffers from frequent or occasional illnesses; even when it is at its strongest, it sometimes experiences the discomfort of phlegm. In the same way, the soul, enduring the assaults of thoughts and disturbances, sails through shipwrecks but not without danger; and, considering its frailty, it is always anxious about death, in accordance with what is written:

“What is the person who shall live and not see death?” (Psalm 87:12).

This is the death that threatens all mortals—not the dissolution of nature, but the death of sin, in accordance with the prophetic saying:

“The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4).

Otherwise, we know that Enoch and Elijah have not yet experienced that common death by which even brute animals are dissolved.

Give me a body that has never been ill, or one that, after illness, is secure in perpetual health, and I will give you a soul that has never sinned and that, after acquiring virtues, will never again sin—especially since vices lie close beside virtues. If you turn aside even slightly, you must either go astray or fall headlong.

For how far apart are obstinacy and perseverance, parsimony and thrift, generosity and extravagance, prudence and cunning, courage and rashness, caution and cowardice? Some of these are reckoned among good things, others among evil.

The same is found in bodies. If you take care to regulate the gall, phlegm increases. If you hasten to dry up the bodily fluids, the blood grows inflamed, the bile is corrupted, and a yellow color spreads over the face.

Certainly, even if we employ all the diligence of physicians, live on carefully regulated foods, and avoid the sources of illness and indigestion, nevertheless, through certain hidden causes [795] known to God alone, we sometimes shiver from cold, sometimes burn with fever, sometimes cry out in colic, and implore the help of the true physician, the Savior. We say with the Apostles: “Master, save us; we are perishing!” (Matthew 8:25). [Col. 0580C–D; 0581A]

## 12. He Answers Several Objections from Scripture

**C.** Granted that no one could have avoided every sin in childhood, adolescence, and youth: can you deny that very many just and holy men, after their vices, devoted themselves wholeheartedly to the virtues and through them remained free from sin?

[Note: That very many just and holy men, after vices, devoted themselves to virtues and were through them free from sin was a doctrine proper to Origen, into which Pelagius too fell at the Synod of Diospolis. See Saint Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*. The Vatican reading is: “Can it be denied that very many just persons, etc.?”]

**A.** This is what I told you at the beginning: that it lies within our power either to sin or not to sin, and to extend our hand either toward good or toward evil, so that free choice may be preserved—but this according to the measure, time, and condition of human frailty. Perpetual sinlessness, however, is reserved for God alone, and for him who, having become the Word made flesh, did not suffer the weaknesses or sins of the flesh. Nor, because I can do something for a short time, will you compel me to be able to do it continually. I can fast, keep vigil, walk, read, sing psalms, sit, and sleep—but can I do so forever?

**C.** And why are we summoned in the holy Scriptures to perfect righteousness, as in the saying, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8); and, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118:1); and in God’s words to Abraham: “I am your God; be pleasing in my sight, and be without blemish or reproach, and I will establish my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly” (Gen. 17:1)? For if what Scripture affirms cannot be done, it commanded it to be done in vain.

**A.** By means of various Scriptural testimonies you wear away the same question in theatrical tricks, which bring forward one and the same man, changing him into different characters, as Mars and Venus, so that the man who previously walked rigid and savage is afterward dissolved into feminine softness. This thing that you now put forward as though it were new—“Blessed are the pure in heart,” “Blessed are the undefiled in the way,” “Be without blemish,” and other sayings of this kind—has been refuted by the Apostle’s reply: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part”; and, “Now we see through a glass in an enigma; but when that which is perfect has come, that which was in part will be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13:9–10). Thus the pure heart, which will afterward see God, and the blessedness of an undefiled life, and living undefiled with Abraham, we possess in shadow and in image.

Although someone may be a patriarch, a prophet, or an apostle, these words are spoken to them in the Lord our Savior: “If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (Matt. 7:11).

Finally, Abraham himself, to whom it had been said, “Be without reproach and without blemish,” fell face down upon the ground, conscious of his frailty. And when God had said to him, “Your wife Sarai shall no longer be called Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name; and I will bless her, and I will give you a son by her, and I will bless him; she shall become nations, and kings of nations shall come from her” (Gen. 17:15 ff.), it immediately follows: “Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed, and said in his heart: Shall a son be born to a hundred-year-old man, and shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?” And Abraham said to God: “May Ishmael live in your sight.” God replied to him: “Yes. Behold, Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac,” and the rest.

[Note: Victorius supplied “and I will bless her,” restoring the first three words from manuscripts at Brescia; and that the blessings are repeated in the Hebrew manuscripts as well is clear, the first being promised to Sarah herself and the second to her son.]

Certainly he had heard God say, “I am your God; be pleasing in my sight, and be without blemish” (ibid., 1). Why, then, did he not believe what God had promised, but laughed inwardly, thinking that he could conceal it from God and not daring to laugh openly? Finally, when he explains the reasons for his unbelief, he says in his heart: “How can it happen that a hundred-year-old man should father a son by a ninety-year-old wife?”

[Note: In all editions published up to the present, “shall bear a son” occurs here, though most manuscripts reject it. Immediately afterward the Vatican manuscript reads, “I do not seek difficult and great things.”]

“Let Ishmael live,” he says, “in your sight, whom you once gave me. I do not seek difficult things; I am content with the benefit I have received.” Rebuking him by an implicit reply, God says, “Yes.” The meaning is: “What you think will not happen shall happen. Your wife Sarah shall bear you a son, and before she conceives him, before he is born, I shall give the child a name.” For because of your error, in which you laughed silently, your son Isaac shall receive the name “Laughter.”

[Note: The manuscripts add the little word “and”; one of them, the Regina manuscript, does not recognize the name Isaac.]

But if you think that God is seen in this world by those who are pure in heart, why did Moses, who had previously said, “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Gen. 32:30), later ask that he might see him knowingly? Since he had said that he had seen him, he hears from the Lord: “You cannot see my face. For no human being shall see my face and live” (Exod. 33:20). Hence the Apostle also calls God invisible, dwelling in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see (1 Tim. 1). And the evangelist John bears witness in sacred words, saying: “No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him” (1 John 4:12). He who sees and declares does not disclose how great the one who was seen is, nor how much the one who declares knows, but only as much as mortal understanding can receive.

## 13. True Perfection Is Reserved for Heaven

As for your belief that the person who is undefiled in the way and walks in the Lord’s law is blessed, understand the earlier statement from what follows. You have learned above from many testimonies that no one has been able to fulfill the law. But if [alternative reading: “therefore”] the Apostle, in comparison with the grace of Christ, regarded as loss the things that he had previously counted as gains in the law, and considered them as dung in order to gain Christ, how much more ought we to understand that the grace of Christ and the Gospel succeeded the law precisely because no one could be justified in the law?

But if no one is justified in the law, how is the person who is still walking and hastening to reach the end “undefiled in the way unto perfection” [alternative reading: “perfection”]? Certainly the person who is running and walking on the road is inferior to one who has reached the destination. If, therefore, the person who is still walking on the road and progressing in the law is undefiled and perfect, what more will the person have who has reached the end of the road and of the law?

Hence the Apostle speaks of the Lord (Eph. 5), saying that at the end of the world, and at the completion of the virtues, he will present to himself a holy Church, without stain or wrinkle.

[Note: Saint Augustine refutes the Pelagians’ slander in almost the same words.]

You suppose that it is already perfect in this mortal and corruptible flesh, and you deserve to hear with the Corinthians: “You are already perfect; you have already become rich; you reign without us”—or, according to another reading, “you reigned”—“and would that you did reign, so that we also might reign with you” (1 Cor. 4:8).
