True perfection, however, without any defilement, is reserved for heaven, when the bridegroom will say to the bride: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4:7).

In accordance with this, the saying is also understood: “That you may be blameless and simple, like undefiled children of God” (Phil. 2:15). He did not [alternative reading: “did”] say “you are,” but “you may be”: he postpones it to the future, rather than affirming that it exists in the present, so that here there may be labor and struggle, and there the rewards of labor and virtue.

Finally, John writes: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Although, therefore, we are children of God, likeness to God and true contemplation are promised to us then, when he appears in his glory.

## 14. Pelagius’ Pride in His Letter to Juliana

From this swelling of pride comes the audacity with which, writing to a widow, you proclaim how the saints ought to pray:

[Note: This widow is Juliana, the mother of Demetrias, concerning whom more will be said below. Meanwhile, the words cited by Jerome appear to be Pelagius’ own; for Augustine reports in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* that the bishops at Diospolis charged him with teaching how the saints ought to pray and saying: “That person raises his hands worthily to God and pours forth his prayer with a good conscience who can say: ‘You know, Lord, how holy, innocent, and clean from every wickedness, iniquity, and robbery are the hands that I extend to you; and how righteous and pure, and free from every lie, are the lips with which I offer you my supplication, that you may have mercy on me.’” These words seem to have been translated into Latin from the Greek acts of the Council of Diospolis.]

“For he,” you say, “raises his hands to God with good reason; he pours forth prayers with a good conscience who can say: ‘For you know, Lord, how holy, how innocent, how pure from every fraud, injury, and robbery are the hands that I stretch out to you; how righteous, how undefiled, and free from every lie are the lips with which I pour out prayers to you, that you may have mercy on me.’”

Is this the prayer of a Christian, or of a proud Pharisee? The Pharisee also spoke in the Gospel: “God, I thank you that I am not like other men—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this publican. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke 18:11). He gives thanks to God because by God’s mercy he is not like other men, detesting sins rather than claiming righteousness. You say: “Lord, you know how holy, how innocent, how pure from every fraud, injury, and robbery are the hands that I stretch out to you.” He says that he fasts twice a week, afflicting the flesh that revels in vices, and gives tithes of all his substance. “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own wealth” (Prov. 13:8).

You glory with the devil, who says: “I will ascend above the stars; I will set my throne in heaven, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14). David says: “My loins are filled with mockery” (Ps. 37:8); and, “My wounds have become foul and festering because of my foolishness” (ibid., 6); and, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant”; and, “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2).

You boast that you are holy, innocent, and pure, and that you stretch clean hands toward God. Nor is it enough for you to glory in all your works unless you also declare yourself clean from every sin of speech and mouth, asserting that your lips are righteous, undefiled, and free from every lie.

The Psalmist sings: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:2), and apostolic authority confirms this: “Let God be true, and every human being a liar” (Rom. 3). Yet you possess lips undefiled, righteous, and free from every lie.

Isaiah laments: “Woe is me, for I am pierced through; because I am a man and have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips” (Isa. 6:5). Afterward a seraph carries a burning coal, grasped with tongs, to cleanse the prophet’s lips—not so that he might speak arrogantly, but so that he might confess his own faults.

[Note: Victorius wishes *Seraphim* to be read in the singular, indicating one seraph rather than several.]

In accordance with the Psalm’s saying: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals of desolation” (Ps. 119:4).

After such swelling, and such boasting and confidence in holiness, you attempt, like a fool persuading fools, to conclude by saying: “With these lips I pour out prayers to you, that you may have mercy on me.”

If you are holy, innocent, cleansed from every stain, and have sinned neither in word nor in deed—for James says, “The person who does not sin in speech is a perfect [alternative reading: “righteous”] man”—and, “No one can [alternative reading: “is able to”] restrain his tongue” (James 3:2, 8), how do you ask for mercy, apparently lamenting and pouring out prayers because you are holy, pure, innocent, with undefiled lips, and free from every lie, like God in power?

Thus Christ prayed on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words of my offenses” (Ps. 21:1); and again, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. 30:6); and, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). On our behalf he had given thanks, saying: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth” (Mark 11:25).

## 15. From the Lord’s Prayer

Thus he taught his Apostles, so that each day, believing in the sacrifice of his body, they would dare to say: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matt. 6:9).

[Note: The manuscripts read “in the sacrament.” Saint Gregory also praises the apostolic custom of reciting the Lord’s Prayer at Mass, *Letters* 7.64: “We say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the prayer because it was the custom of the Apostles to consecrate the sacrificial offering with that very prayer.” The older Optatus of Milevis likewise says in Book 2: “You cannot, after turning toward the altar, fail to recite the Lord’s Prayer first,” and other Fathers agree. Here Jerome indicates the preface of that prayer itself, in which, in nearly all liturgies, the priest confesses that he is unworthy to dare address God as Father. See Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, Book 2, chapter 15. It is customary among the Fathers, especially Augustine in opposition to the Pelagians, to argue from the Lord’s Prayer.]

They desire that God’s name, holy in itself, should be sanctified in them; you say: “You know, Lord, how holy, innocent, and pure my hands are.”

They add: “Your kingdom come,” awaiting the hope of the kingdom in the future, so that, when Christ reigns, sin may in no way reign in their mortal body. And they join to this: “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth,” so that human frailty may imitate the angels and the Lord’s will be fulfilled on earth.

You say: “A person can, if he wishes, be entirely without sin.”

The Apostles ask for their daily bread—or, “bread above all substances,” or “bread to come”—so that they may be worthy to receive the body of Christ. But you, through your excessive holiness and secure righteousness, boldly claim heavenly gifts for yourselves.

It follows: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Rising from the baptismal font, and regenerated in the Lord our Savior, they fulfill what is written concerning themselves: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1). Yet immediately, in their first communion of Christ’s body, they say: “Forgive us our debts”—debts that had been forgiven them in their confession of Christ. You, arrogant and proud of the purity of your holy hands and the cleanliness of your speech, boast instead.

Even if a person’s conversion is perfect, and after vices and sins he possesses virtues in abundance, can he be as free from fault as those who immediately emerge from Christ’s font? And yet they are commanded to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:13)—not through the lie of humility, as you interpret it, but through fear of human frailty, which makes them apprehensive about their conscience.

They say: “Do not lead us into temptation.” You, with Jovinian, say that those who have received baptism in full faith can no longer be tempted or sin.

Finally they add: “But deliver us from evil.” What do they ask from the Lord that they possess within the power of free choice?

O man, now you have been made clean in the washing, and this is said of you: “Who is this who ascends, whitened, leaning upon her kinsman?”—so that although she has been washed, she is unable to preserve her purity unless she is supported by the Lord God. How do you desire to be freed by God’s mercy when you have just been freed from sins? Only in the manner we have stated: that when we have done everything, we confess that we are unprofitable servants.

## 16. Pelagian Pride

Your prayer therefore surpasses the pride of the Pharisee and is condemned by comparison with the publican. The publican stood far off and did not dare raise his eyes toward heaven, but struck his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Hence the Lord’s judgment is proclaimed: “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted.”

The Apostles humble themselves in order to be exalted. Your disciples lift themselves up in order to fall.

[Note: This is Juliana, as noted above, the mother of Demetrias, to whom Pelagius had written. Marius Mercator teaches, in the *Commonitorium under the name of Caelestius*: “Finally, the booklet of his [Pelagius] which we have in our hands is addressed to a certain Livania.” He used Livania for Juliana, either to conceal his purpose or because, just as the ancients generally used Julia and Livia interchangeably, Livania was customarily used for Juliana. Augustine further reports in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* that at the Synod of Diospolis this was objected to him: writing flatteringly to the widow, he said, “May piety find in you a place which it finds nowhere; may righteousness find a seat everywhere in its exile; may truth, which no one now recognizes, become domestic and friendly to you; and may the law of God, which is despised by almost all people, be honored by you alone.”]

Flattering the same widow, you are not ashamed to tell her that piety—which is found nowhere on earth—and truth—which is everywhere an exile—dwell especially in her. You do not remember the saying: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and subvert the paths of your feet.”

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “You praise her with words from God, and you say…”]

You praise her in these words and say: “O how exceedingly happy and blessed are you, if that righteousness which is now believed to exist only in heaven is found in you alone on earth!”

Is this teaching, or killing? Is it lifting her from the earth, or casting her down from heaven—to attribute to a little woman what the angels do not dare claim?

But if piety, truth, and righteousness are found on earth nowhere except in one woman, where will your just people be, whom you claimed to exist on earth without sin? These two passages of prayer and praise you customarily swear to your disciples are not yours, although the brilliance of your style clearly shines through them, and such is the elegance of Ciceronian speech that, moving with a tortoise’s pace, you dare not publicly profess—or publish—what you teach secretly and send out for sale.

O happy you, whose disciples alone write books, so that whatever seems displeasing to you may be declared not yours but another’s. And who could possess such great talent as to imitate the charm of your speech?

## 17. How Infants Can Be Without Sin

**C.** I can no longer delay: everyone’s patience is overcome by the iniquity of your words. Tell me, please, what have little infants done wrong? Their guilt cannot be charged to their conscience, nor to ignorance, since, according to the prophet Jonah, they do not know their right hand from their left (Jonah 4:11). They cannot sin, yet they can perish. Their knees give way; their cries do not form words; their babbling tongue is mocked, and the torments of eternal misery are prepared for the wretched.

[Note: The old edition reads “laughs”; the Vatican manuscript then reads, “and the torments of eternal punishment are prepared for the wretched,” etc.]

**A.** Ah! You have begun to be excessively eloquent, so that you are [reading uncertain: perhaps “not merely eloquent”], after your disciples have been turned into teachers. The distinguished orator Antonius, whom Cicero extols in his praises, said that he had seen many eloquent men but not yet a single truly articulate speaker.

Do not therefore play with the flowers of orators rather than your own—flowers by which the ears of the ignorant and of children are usually deceived—but tell me plainly what you think.

**C.** This is what I say: grant me at least that those who cannot sin are without sin.

**A.** I will grant it if they have been baptized in Christ, but you will not immediately, on the basis of faith, compel me to agree with the proposition you stated, that a person can be without sin if he wishes.

[Note: The manuscripts supply “immediately, on the basis of faith.”] These children neither can nor wish to sin; but by God’s grace, which they received in baptism, they are without any sin.

**C.** You compel me to come to that unpopular point and say to you: “What have they sinned?”—so that you may immediately cast the stones of the crowds at me and kill by your will the person whom you cannot kill by force.

**A.** The person who allows a heretic to remain a heretic kills him. Otherwise, our correction is life-giving: by dying to heresy, you may live to the Catholic faith.

**C.** If you know us to be heretics, why do you not accuse us?

**A.** Because the Apostle teaches me to avoid a heretic after the first and second correction, not to accuse him, knowing that he is perverse and condemned by his own judgment (Tit. 3:10–11). Otherwise it is most foolish for my faith to depend upon another’s judgment.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript and the old edition read: “It is foolish for my faith to depend upon another’s judgment.”]

What if someone else calls you a Catholic? Shall I immediately assent? Whoever defends you and says that you think rightly while believing perversely is not freeing you from disgrace, but bringing disgrace upon himself for his treachery. A multitude of associates will by no means prove that you are Catholic; it will prove that you are a heretic.

But let these matters be trodden underfoot with an ecclesiastical step, lest some rather gloomy image be displayed, as though to little children who are crying. May the fear of God grant us this: that we despise every other fear. Therefore either defend what you believe, or abandon what you cannot defend. Anyone whom you bring forward in your defense you will name not your patron but your associate.

## 18. Why Infants Are Baptized, and the Testimony of Cyprian

**C.** Tell me, please, and free me from every question: why are little infants baptized?

**A.** So that their sins may be forgiven in baptism.

**C.** What sin have they committed? Is anyone released who has not been bound?

**A.** Are you asking me? The evangelical trumpet will answer you—the Teacher of the Gentiles, the golden vessel shining throughout the world: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is the form of the one to come” (Rom. 5:14).

If you object that some are said not to have sinned, understand that they did not commit the sin that Adam committed by transgressing God’s command in paradise.

[Note: The same Vatican manuscript reads, “that there are some here”; the old edition, with the Regina manuscript, reads, “that this is said here,” etc.] Nevertheless, all human beings are held liable either in the name of their ancient ancestor Adam or in their own name.

The child is released in baptism from the bond of his parent.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript does not recognize the word “parent,” and reads shortly afterward: “He is freed from another’s and his own sin by the blood of Christ.” The Regina manuscript reads: “He is held liable for another’s or his own sin, and by the blood of Christ…”]

The person who has reached an age at which he can understand is freed from both another’s sin and his own by the blood of Christ.

And lest you suppose that I understand this in a heretical sense, the blessed martyr Cyprian—whose skill in arranging Scriptural testimonies you boast of emulating—records the following in his letter to the bishop Fidus concerning the baptism of infants:

[Note: In Cyprian himself, the wording is *multum*, “much,” and *remissa*, “forgiven,” both in the Vatican and old editions; likewise *atque* occurs below, and later *de ope nostra* and *de divina misericordia*. The text seems to require correction here, as also in Jerome. Martianaeus did not understand that the latter part of this passage belonged to Cyprian.]

“Moreover, if remission of sins is granted even to those who have committed very serious offenses and have sinned greatly against God, when afterward they believe, and if no one is prevented from baptism and grace, how much more ought an infant not to be prevented—an infant who, being newly born, has committed no sin except that, having been born carnally according to Adam, he has contracted the contagion of ancient death through his first birth?

He approaches to receive the forgiveness of sins all the more easily because the sins forgiven him are not his own but another’s. And therefore, dearest brother, this was our position in the council: that no one should be prevented by us from baptism and the grace of God, who is merciful, kind, and gracious toward all.

Since this is to be observed and maintained concerning everyone, consider that it must be observed all the more concerning infants and those newly born, who by this very fact deserve more from our assistance and from divine mercy: at the very beginning of their birth, crying and weeping, they do nothing except make supplication.”

## 19. He Praises Saint Augustine

The holy and eloquent bishop Augustine wrote some time ago to Marcellinus, who afterward was killed, though innocent, under the charge of Heraclian’s rebellion by the heretics, two books on the baptism of infants against your heresy, by which you wish to assert that infants are baptized not for the remission of sins but for the kingdom of heaven, in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.”

[Note: Saint Augustine refers to this passage in Letter 134 to Augustine, section 1: “Certainly, in the Dialogue that I recently published, I remembered Your Blessedness as was fitting,” and so forth.]

[Note: Martianaeus incorrectly printed *Heraclini*. The Vatican manuscript has *Heracleani*; the old edition has the reasonably correct *Heraclianae*. Other books read *Heradiani*, *Heradii*, or *Eradii* for *Heraclianus* or *Heraclius*. To avoid entirely passing over the historical event: this Heraclianus, governor of Africa, defected from Honorius and advanced toward Italy and Rome with a huge fleet. He was defeated at Utriculum by the forces of the governor Marinus and fled back to Carthage, where he was eventually captured and beheaded. Marcellinus, whom Honorius had sent to Africa as tribune and notary to act as intermediary in the conference between Catholics and Donatists, was falsely accused by the heretics—or, more precisely, by the Donatists, whose hatred he had incurred by acting with great determination on behalf of the Catholics—as an accomplice in Heraclian’s rebellion. By order of the same Marinus, he was executed with his brother Apringius in September 413. See, if desired, Augustine, Letter 151, and our Norisius, *History of Pelagianism*, Book 1, chapter 5. Orosius, Book 7, chapter 42, says: “Marinus, governor, killed Saint Marcellinus at Carthage—whether driven by zeal or corrupted by gold is uncertain.”]

He also wrote a third book to the same Marcellinus against those who say, as you do, that a person can be without sin if he wishes, without God’s grace.

[Note: Servatus Lupus, in his *Collection on Three Questions*, quotes this passage from Jerome at length and reads it as in the printed editions. But two manuscripts, one of them the Regina manuscript and the other the Corbie manuscript, preserved by the Benedictine editors of Saint Augustine, read “that is, you,” followed by “can.” One Vatican manuscript likewise has “you.” Pelagius did not say this without the grace of God.]

And recently a fourth book to Hilary, against your doctrine, since he invents many perverse claims.

[Note: This Hilary was the bishop of Syracuse, whose Letter 156 is preserved among Augustine’s letters and whom we have often mentioned. Augustine’s reply to him is Letter 157, which Jerome indicates here.]

Other works are also said to be forged expressly under your name, but they have not yet come into our hands. Therefore I think this labor should be set aside, lest Horace’s words be applied to me: “Carrying wood into the forest” (*Satires* 1.10).

Either we would repeat the same things unnecessarily, or, if we wished to say something new, the better material has already been occupied by a most distinguished intellect.

I will say only this, to bring the speech at last to an end: either you ought to introduce a new creed, so that after the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit you may baptize infants into the kingdom of heaven, or, if you have one baptism both for little ones and for adults, infants too must be baptized for the remission of sins, in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.

But if the remission of other people’s sins seems unjust to you—a remission not needed by someone who could not sin—go over to your beloved Origen, who says that past and ancient sins committed in heaven are released in baptism, so that, in following his authority in other matters, you may also follow his error in this one.

[Note: Here, adding “The Dialogue of the presbyter Jerome is concluded,” Vallarsius adds the following note: “In many manuscripts, Jerome’s Dialogue is followed by the *Apologetic Book* of the presbyter Orosius, concerning which we spoke in the prefatory Notice.”]

---

[Col. 0589]

# Fragments of Theodore, Bishop of Mopsuestia

## I.

[Note: Excerpts from the fourth book of Theodore of Mopsuestia against Hieronymus, or Jerome, have been inserted here from Marius Mercator, who translated them into Latin and incorporated them into his work in the Baluze edition, p. 339. They were first published by our eminent fellow citizen Henry Noris in *Pelagian History*, Book 1, chapter 9. Garnerius also published them twice, because they pertain partly to the affair of Pelagius and partly to the case of Nestorius.]

From the second codex of the fourth book, the tenth folio: against the blessed Augustine, who defends original sin and argues in Catholic fashion that Adam was made mortal through transgression.

[Note: Read “Jerome.” Recall what we said in the prefatory Notice to Jerome’s *Dialogue*, section 3. The annotations that follow are transcribed from Baluze.]

807. “With so many facts demonstrating that Adam was formed from the earth in such a way that he was altogether mortal, he nevertheless wished to occupy the discussion with the question of the proper food and, unable thereafter to discern the truth, attached, in place of true doctrine, a defence arising from deceitful falsehood. [Note: Henricus de Noris published *volens*, as it stands in the Vatican manuscript, which he used.] He did not say (Genesis II), ‘You will be mortal,’ but ‘You will surely die,’ threatening to inflict the experience of death upon those who were already mortal by nature—an experience which, in accordance with the custom of his own benevolence, he nevertheless deferred from bringing to effect. [Note: The same edition has *adminationem*; I suppose this is because of what follows, namely, ‘threatening to inflict the experience of death.’] For just as, when he says, ‘Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed in return’ (Genesis IX, 6), he does not say this because the person who kills another will become mortal, but because he is worthy to be condemned to such a death, so also here he said, ‘You will surely die’: not that they would then become mortal, but that they would be worthy to receive the sentence of death [Note: Noris: ‘through transgression,’ as in the Vatican manuscript.] for their transgression.

“But observe also the divine sentence which God appears to impose upon Adam after the sin. For he says: ‘Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I had commanded you, saying, “From this alone you shall not eat,” you have eaten from it; cursed is the earth in your labors. In sorrow you shall eat it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field; and in the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth’ (Genesis III, 14 ff.). [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: ‘But through all these things he was born for this, that he would have a sorrowful life.’ From this the same learned man derived the following sense: ‘But through all these things man was born for this, that he would soon have a true course (*verum mox ambitum*).’ We have restored the true reading from the Beauvais manuscript, which the following passage also supports.]

“But through all these things he threatened that Adam would have a life of toil: thereafter he would obtain from the earth, with labor, the fruits by which he would be nourished and sustained, having nothing like the former abundance that had been set before him, such as he had enjoyed from the richness of paradise. For God did not assign the working of the earth as a punishment, as though transferring human beings from an immortal nature into mortality, since he had also commanded him to work and guard paradise. Rather, in return for the former abundance and pleasure of paradise, he threatened that Adam’s sustenance would be laborious, drawn from the fruits of the earth.

“For, having become mortal, he needed the fruits of paradise then, just as he now seeks the fruits of the earth; and, deprived as a punishment of his former delights, he is chastised by this most sorrowful and laborious mode of life. Hence, finally and consistently, he added: ‘Because you are earth, and you shall return to earth’ (Genesis III), [Note: Noris reads *Haec etiam*, and shortly afterward *significant* instead of *significans*. But he took this latter reading from the Vatican manuscript.] thereby also signifying the mortality of his nature. For Scripture did not apply this designation to one who was immortal and only then beginning to receive the sentence of death, as those very wise defenders—rather, astonishing fathers—of original sin assert; [Note: Noris: *imposuit*.] rather, because it judged this designation appropriate to one naturally made mortal from the beginning, divine Scripture repeatedly adopts this name for human beings as an indication of their corruptible [Note: The words *et resolubilis* were omitted from the edition of the same distinguished man.] and dissoluble nature.

“For it says: ‘He remembered that we are dust; man, his days are like grass, and like the flower of the field, so he shall blossom, because the spirit has passed through him, and his place shall be no more’ (Psalm CII, 14). [Note: The same edition has *vitam ducimus* in place of this reading, as we have already said.] He means that we are all corruptible and dissoluble, like grass that blossoms for a short time and soon afterward perishes. For we lead our lives only briefly; thereafter we altogether come to nonexistence.

“So also Abraham says, ‘I am earth and ashes,’ as though he were saying: ‘I am not worthy to converse with so great a God, a man made from earth and destined to become this in every respect.’ He ought therefore rather to have said: ‘Because you will be earth, and you will return to earth,’ since nature would only then be becoming mortal.”

## II. From the second codex, book three, four folios before the end of the book

809. “But none of this could the remarkable defender of original sin foresee, since he had never been at all trained in the divine Scriptures and, from infancy, had not learned the sacred writings, in accordance with the words of blessed Paul (II Timothy III). Yet whether declaiming about the meanings of Scripture or about doctrine, he frequently put forward many absurdities, both specifically and generally, concerning the Scriptures themselves and numerous doctrines. [Note: Noris reads *proposuit*, namely, that he shamelessly put forward things contrary to the very doctrines of Scripture.] For fear of powerful persons prevented anyone from speaking against him; only those who possessed knowledge of the divine Scriptures secretly disparaged him.

“Finally, he fell into this novel doctrine: that God, in anger and fury, had decreed Adam to be mortal and, because of his single offense, had condemned all human beings, even those not yet born, to death. Yet when arguing in this way he feels neither fear nor shame at attributing to God things that no one has ever attempted to attribute even to sane human beings who possess some concern for justice. Nor did he remember that divine utterance: ‘It shall no longer be said in Israel: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge, for thus says Adonai the Lord: The teeth of those who ate the sour grape shall be set on edge’ (Ezekiel XVIII, 1 ff.). [Note: The Beauvais manuscript reads this way. The Vatican manuscript has *obstipuerunt*. Noris reads *obstupescunt*.] [Note: The Vatican manuscript has *obstipescent*.] By this he shows that God does not punish one person in place of another, as some mistakenly believe, but that each person will render an account for his own offenses.

“Blessed Paul likewise adds statements consonant with this: ‘God,’ he says, ‘who will repay each person according to his works’ (Romans II, 6); and, ‘Each of us will bear his own burden’ (Galatians VI, 5); and, ‘Why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ’ (Romans XIV, 10).

“But this remarkable man judged that God had been so greatly angered by one offense [Note: The old books have the reading that we have printed. Henricus de Noris restored: ‘He judged that God had been so greatly angered by Adam’s sin that he wished to subject him to the most atrocious punishment.’ Garnerius, however, reads: ‘He judged that God had been so greatly angered by the sin, and him to the most atrocious punishment,’ and so forth.] that he subjected Adam to the most atrocious punishment, proclaimed an equal sentence against all his descendants, and among them there were innumerable righteous people.

“From this he ought especially to have considered how extremely incongruous it would be for Noah, Abraham, David, Moses, 810 and the innumerable other righteous persons to have been made liable to punishment [Note: That is, to Adam’s punishment, to the punishment of the man whom God had formed. All the books have this reading; Garnerius and Noris restored *ob unius*, ‘because of one.’] on account of that one offense of his, approved by the tasting of the tree, and for God to have extended his anger beyond all measure, so that he rejected all the virtues of so many righteous people [Note: This is the reading of the Beauvais exemplar. The Vatican manuscript has *totius quorum*. From this Noris produced *posterorum*, ‘of the descendants.’] and subjected them to such punishment because of Adam’s one sin.

“For even if he considered nothing else, he ought at least to have reflected upon Abel’s case and formed a fitting judgment. Abel, the first righteous man, was the first to die. If God had appointed death as a punishment for human beings, how could it not have been the height of impiety for the one who was the cause of sin to live—indeed, for him and Eve, the inventor of wickedness, to continue living (I pass over the devil, who has continued in immortality until now)—while the first righteous man, the first discoverer of virtue, and the first to undertake the care of divine worship was struck down before almost all sinners? [Note: The old exemplars have this reading. The same distinguished men substituted *poena*, ‘punishment,’ an emendation that may perhaps be sound.]

“But the wisest man ought also carefully to have considered Enoch, who did not die. For he was not endowed with such virtue or piety that he was better than all others—than Moses, I mean, and the Prophets and Apostles, or all the others of whom blessed Paul says that the world was not worthy (Hebrews XI, 38)—so that, after their deaths, he alone should continue without experiencing death. Rather, from the beginning God had determined this within himself: that human beings should first be mortal, but afterward enjoy immortality, arranging this himself for our benefit.”

And shortly afterward:

“God,” he says, “made these same things more clearly evident when he transferred Enoch and made him immortal. For if God had introduced death as the cause of punishment through sin, and had not long ago determined this within himself while dispensing all things ineffably for our sake according to his own wisdom, then Enoch would certainly not have remained immortal, while the Lord Christ would have come to experience death.”

And shortly afterward:

“For this reason,” he says, “the Lord became the author of all good things for human beings, so that, just as Adam was the initiator of the first and mortal condition, so he himself, existing as the initiator of the second and immortal condition, might first preserve the natural features of the former Adam: being born of a woman, being wrapped in swaddling clothes, and gradually attaining the growth of age [Note: The Italian edition incorrectly has *Lucas enim*: ‘For Luke.’] (for he says, ‘Jesus advanced in age and wisdom 811 and grace before God and human beings’ [Luke II, 52] [Note: These words were omitted from the same edition]), receiving circumcision, standing before God in the temple according to the legal custom, being subject to his parents, and being devoted to the lawful manner of life.

“Thus also, to complete the remainder, he finally accepted death, as something assigned to nature, so that, dying according to the law of human nature and rising from the dead by divine power, he might become the beginning for all human beings who receive death according to their own nature, so that they may rise from the dead and be changed into an immortal substance. For just as we have all been made conformed to Adam according to our present condition, so in the future we shall be made conformed to the Lord Christ according to the flesh.

“He ‘transfigured the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the glory of his body’ (Philippians V), and, ‘as is the earthly, such are the earthly, and as is the heavenly, such are the heavenly; and just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly’ (I Corinthians XV). He shows that, having become participants in the first condition of Adam, we necessarily also attain participation in the future condition of the second Adam, the Lord Christ, according to the flesh, since he arose from this same nature, assumed everything that belonged to nature, and therefore endured death, so that, by assuming the death of nature and rising from the dead, he might perfect nature as free from death.

“He assumed death for this reason, but by no means sin; rather, he remained entirely free from it. What belonged to nature—that is, death—he unquestionably assumed; but sin, which did not belong to nature but to the will, he did not assume in any way. And if sin had been in nature, then, according to the statement of this wisest man, he would necessarily have assumed sin, since sin would have existed entirely in nature.”

## III. From the second codex, book three, folio eighteen

“If,” he says, “God did not know that Adam would sin, let this be the wisdom of the wisest men, and let this be their answer: that it is utterly insane even to entertain such a thought. It is clear that he knew Adam would sin and, for this reason, undoubtedly that he would die.

“How, then, is it not the height of madness to believe that at the beginning [Note: I do not doubt that the emendation of the very learned men who edited this passage—*eum immortalem*, ‘that he made him immortal’—is sound. Nevertheless, all the books oppose it.] he made him mortal within six hours? (For that much time elapsed from his creation until the transgression, since he was made from the earth on the sixth day and, eating against the divine command, was expelled from paradise.) How, then, could he have shown him to be mortal after the sin? It is certain that, if he had wished him to be immortal, even the intervening sin would not have altered God’s sentence, since he did not make the devil mortal from being immortal, although the devil is the source of all evils.” [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads *commissionem*. The Beauvais manuscript has *commixtionem*. Henricus de Noris, thinking something missing here, added *peccati*, ‘of sin.’ I would readily believe that *comestionem*, ‘eating,’ should be read.]

## IV. From the second codex, book three, folio twenty-five

[Note: The following does not appear in the Italian edition. This title was added from the Vatican manuscript, since it is absent from the Beauvais manuscript. Garnerius nevertheless placed the title as though it existed in ancient exemplars: ‘Of the same Theodore, from another book, against the Lord Jesus Christ and his incarnation.’ He immediately adds that Theodore entitled these final books *περὶ ἐνανθρωπήσεως τοῦ μονογενοῦς* (“On the incarnation of the Only-Begotten”), but because they do not explain the reality of the incarnation but overthrow it, Mercator preferred to write “against the Lord and his incarnation.” The true title of the following fragment, recovered from the Vatican manuscript, proves this to be incorrect.]

“Those who lived from Adam until the coming of the Lord Christ in such impieties and injustices as blessed Paul expressed in his own words, as was made clear above by his statements, will not receive a great reward of resurrection if he delivers them to certain punishments without end and without correction. For where will resurrection be counted as a gift if punishment without correction is inflicted upon those who rise?”

And shortly afterward:

“Who,” he says, “is so mad as to believe that so great a good becomes the source of infinite punishment for those who rise, for whom it would have been more beneficial never to rise at all than, after the resurrection, to endure the experience of so many and such great evils under infinite punishments?”

## V. From the eighth sermon of the catechism, folio seven

[Note: Or “of the catechism,” as is clear from Facundus, who in book IX, chapter 3, cites the opening lines of this fragment from another version and says that they were taken from the book *To the Baptized*. Yet in the fourth collation of the Fifth Council it is consistently written *ad baptizandos* (“to those being baptized”), not only in the editions but also in ancient manuscripts written by hand; this seems preferable.]

“And if we say that there are two natures in Christ [Note: In Facundus: ‘Nor does the fact that we say two natures compel us by any necessity either to say two sons, or two men, or two Christs, since to think so is the height of madness.’ Here everyone can see that the word *men* should be deleted and *lords* substituted. Facundus indeed has this reading in the very ancient Verona manuscript.],” he says, “it does not necessarily follow that we must assert two sons or two lords, since to think this is evidently the height of madness. For everything that is two in one respect is one in another; the unity of both does not destroy their division. ‘I and the Father are one’ (John XX, 30). Yet because they are one, the distinct property of each is not to be denied.

“And elsewhere, speaking of husband and wife, he says: ‘They are no longer two, but one flesh’ (Matthew XIX, 6). But because husband and wife are one flesh, it does not follow that they are no longer two and only one flesh; they remain two in respect of being two, and one in respect of being one.

“In this manner, here too there are two by nature, but one by conjunction: two by nature, because there is much diversity of natures; but one by conjunction, because what has been assumed receives indivisible veneration together with the one who assumed it, remaining his indivisible temple.

“For everything that is called two includes the usage of two when one is believed to be indifferent from the other, in accordance with which it receives the designation and enumeration of two. For example, divine Scripture mentions four beasts (Daniel VII, 3): a bear, a leopard, a lion, and another that surpasses these in ferocity. They are four because each beast is shown to be no less, in substance, than the remaining beasts.

“‘The testimony of two men is true’ (John VIII, 17), because each is by nature what the other is. Likewise, ‘No one can serve two masters’ (Matthew VI, 24), because, for the one who offers service as to a master, neither is less than a master.

“Thus also here, if each were by substance a son and a lord, they could in some way be called two sons and two lords according to the number of persons. But since the one is by substance a son and lord, while the other according to essence is acknowledged to be neither son nor lord, yet through the conjunction made between him and the other is known to have shared in these designations, we therefore say that there is one son and one lord.

“We understand primarily that person to be the son and lord who is believed and called truly to be both according to substance; but in our thought we also embrace the one who is inseparably joined to him and is considered to share in sonship and lordship through an ineffable union with him.

“Therefore, whenever divine Scripture mentions this son who was assumed, we say, by reference to the one who assumes him and according to the unity, that he is called son. For when it says, ‘concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh’ (Romans I, 3), [Note: It is clear from the same decree of Pope Vigilius and from the Fifth Council that *non Deum*, ‘not God,’ must be read.] it does not yet speak of the Word [Note: The fragment is cited from another translation in the First Constitution of Pope Vigilius and in the same collation of the Fifth Council, and there it is more complete.] but of the assumed form of a servant. For he is not God according to the flesh, nor was God made from the seed of David—the one whom blessed Paul clearly calls son.

“We understand him to be called son not because he is said to be son in himself, but because through the conjunction he has with the one who truly is son, he is designated in this way. [Note: Garnerius rightly conjectured that this fragment also belongs to the book entitled *To Those Being Baptized*, and he thinks that after the final words of this fragment there should follow the words found in the council cited above: ‘that he might indeed make much his concern, but make everything his own,’ and so forth. They are also found in the decree of Vigilius.]

“The creator took pity on the ruined creature and, without mixture, formed the infant; he brought him to mature age, indicating through the gradual progress of growth, in accordance with the measure of belief, the likeness of nature, while secretly existing joined to the same person. He was not absent when he was formed; he was not divided when he was born. He was joined and present with him as he spoke, continuing in his actions and preserving his own connection with him there without sin.”

## VI. From the fifth book of the *Commentary on the Creature*

[Note: We have added the following from the Fourth Collation of the Fifth Council because Noris thought that they were excerpts from the same work of Theodore against Hieronymus. But since this is not so thoroughly established that another opinion is impermissible, we have introduced them only as a specimen, so that anyone who wishes to consult the remainder of his book may repeat it from the same collation of the council, numbers 57 through 71.]

“Therefore he did not impose death upon human beings unwillingly and contrary to his own judgment, nor did he give sin an opening that served no purpose; for, had he not wished it to happen, he could have prevented it. Rather, because he knew that it was useful to us, and especially to all rational beings, first for evils and inferior things to gain entry, and afterward for these to be destroyed and better things to be introduced, God therefore divided the present creation and the future into two conditions.

“In the future condition he will lead everything to immortality and immutability; in the present, meanwhile, he permits creation to remain subject to death and mutability. For if he had made us immortal and immutable immediately from the beginning, we would have no distinction from irrational beings, since we would not know our own good.

“Not knowing mutability, we would not know the good of immutability; not knowing death, we would not know the gain of immortality; not knowing corruption, we would not praise incorruption; not knowing the burden of sufferings, we would not marvel at freedom from suffering.

“To say it briefly, so that I do not make the discussion lengthy: without experiencing evils, we could not attain knowledge of those good things.”

## SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON

[Note: Hieronymus discussed this *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* frequently. First, concerning its title, in the letter written to Augustine, whose beginning is: “Three letters together,” and so forth. Hieronymus says: “You say that you received my book from a certain brother, who found that it had no title, in which I enumerated ecclesiastical writers, both Greek and Latin. And when you asked him—to use your own words—why the opening page had not been inscribed, or by what name it was to be called, he replied that it was called *Epitaphium*, and you argue,” and so forth. Therefore this book should be called either *On Illustrious Men* or, properly, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, although most ignorant correctors have given it the title *On Authors*.

“Second, concerning Dexter, to whom the book is dedicated, the same Hieronymus says in book II of his *Apology against Rufinus*: ‘About ten years ago, when my friend Dexter, who had administered the prefecture of the praetorium, asked me to compose for him a list of the authors of our religion,’ and so forth.

“Finally, in the letter to Desiderius, which begins ‘Having read the discourse,’ he writes as follows: ‘I wrote a book on Illustrious Men, from the Apostles to our own age, imitating Tranquillus and the Greek Apollonius. After cataloguing many people, I also placed myself at the end of the volume, as an abortive and the least of all Christians. There I had to record briefly what I had written up to the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius.’ In the preface to his commentaries on Jonah he similarly says that he wrote a book on Illustrious Men. Thus we can add nothing to a complete and distinct knowledge of this work, whether concerning its title and inscription or the time and circumstances of its composition. MARTIAN.”]

# BOOK ON ILLUSTRIOUS MEN, TO DEXTER, PREFECT OF THE PRAETORIUM

With an ancient Greek translation appended, which Erasmus published under the name of Sophronius. (C)

## ADMONITION CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK, *ON ILLUSTRIOUS MEN*

In this book on Illustrious Men, whether among Hieronymus himself or among other ancient writers, there is scarcely anything more distinguished or celebrated. The holy Author seems to have been pleased with the usefulness of the work, since in the books that he subsequently prepared he repeatedly seized every opportunity to mention it to his readers.

Immediately afterward he wrote *Against Jovinianus*. When the discussion turned to John and the statement was made that he had lived until the reign of Trajan—that is, that he had fallen asleep sixty-eight years after the Lord’s Passion—he said: “We also touched upon this briefly in the book *On Illustrious Men.”

Shortly afterward, in Letter 47 to Desiderius, he wrote: “I wrote a book on Illustrious Men, from the Apostles to our own age, imitating Tranquillus and the Greek Apollonius. After cataloguing many people, I also placed myself at the end of the volume, as an abortive and the least of all Christians. There I had to record briefly what I had written up to the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius.”

He says the same in the preface to his commentaries on Jonah; but in book II against Rufinus he expresses it especially clearly:

“About ten years ago, when my friend Dexter, who had administered the prefecture of the praetorium, asked me to compose for him a list of the authors of our religion, among other treatises I included this book, published by Pamphilus,” and so forth.

### 2

In a letter replying diligently to Augustine, Letter 112, he explains the inscription that he had given the book and, in a certain sense, its character:

“You say that you received my book from a certain brother, who found that it had no title, in which I enumerated ecclesiastical writers, both Greek and Latin. And when you asked him—to use your own words—why the opening page had not been inscribed, or by what name it was to be called, he replied that it was called *Epitaphium*. You argue that it would rightly be called this if you had read there only the lives or writings of those who had already died; but since the little works of many people who were living both when it was written and still now are mentioned, you wonder why I gave it this title.

“I think I understand your prudence: you were able to understand the title from the work itself. For you have read both Greeks and Latins who described the lives of illustrious men, and none of them ever entitled such a work *Epitaphium*, but rather *On Illustrious Men*—for example, on commanders, philosophers, orators, historians, epic poets, tragedians, and comic poets. An epitaph, properly speaking, is written for the dead; I know that I once composed one upon the falling asleep of Nepotianus, a presbyter of holy memory.

“Therefore this book should be called either *On Illustrious Men* or, properly, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, although most ignorant correctors have given it the title *On Authors*.

“Now hear what else Augustine wished him to undertake,” in Letter 67 among the Hieronymian letters:

“In the book,” he says, “in which you commemorated all the ecclesiastical writers whom you were able to recall, together with their writings, I think it would have been more useful if, after naming those whom you know to be heretics—for you did not wish to omit even them—you had added also the points concerning which they should be avoided. Although you have also passed over some, I would like to know the reason for this.

“Or, if you did not wish to burden that volume, so that, after mentioning the heretics, you would not add the matters in which Catholic authority condemned them, I ask that it not be burdensome to your literary labor—by which, through the grace of the Lord our God, you have greatly kindled and assisted the studies of the saints in the Latin language—to publish, if your occupations permit, a brief account in a single book of the perverse doctrines of all the heretics who, up to the present time, have attempted to corrupt the integrity of the Christian faith, whether through impudence, ignorance, or obstinacy. Let this be made known to those who either have no leisure to read and learn so many things because of other business, or are unable to do so because of an unfamiliar language.”

### 3

If I wished to review the testimonies of others, I should become too lengthy. Gennadius continued the same labor down to his own times in a book with the same title. In chapter 1, while discussing Jacob of Nisibis, he says:

“Blessed Hieronymus names this man in the *Book of Chronicles* as a man of great virtues. He can easily be excused for not placing him in the *Catalogue of Scribes,” and so forth; these matters we shall examine below in their proper place.

Facundus of Hermiana, book VI of the *Defense of the Three Chapters*, chapter 2, writes:

“Our Hieronymus, a very learned man, who had such extensive reading that he read all, or almost all, the interpreters of the divine Scriptures, whether in Greek or Latin eloquence, wrote a book entitled *On Illustrious Men*. In it he mentioned not only Catholics but also heretics who had written something concerning the holy Scriptures in either language. He did not conceal who had founded heresies, who had defended them, or who had been accused of heresy by some while others defended them.”

Finally Cassiodorus, *Divine Institutes*, chapter 17:

“Read the book of Saint Hieronymus, *On Illustrious Men*, where he briefly both honors and touches upon their various labors and little works.”

To these may be added Saint Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 6; Marcellinus Comes in his *Chronicle*; John of Salisbury, Letter 172; and almost innumerable others in later times.

4. The prominence of this work itself brought it about that it enjoyed better fortune than all the other books of Jerome: at various times it found several learned men whose efforts caused it to be increasingly revised and enriched, and it was published now separately, now together with other works. The more distinguished among them are Erasmus, Victorius, Gravius, Suffridus Petri, Johannes a Fuchte, Aubertus Miraeus, Ernestus Tentzelius, Salomon Cyprianus, Martianaeus, and, most recently of all, Albert Fabricius, who appended to his sufficiently careful recension the scholia and annotations of other editors as well.

Yet no undertaking was more remarkable than that of a certain Sophronius, who recast this entire book in Greek. Since learned men have argued much both for and against this man and this version, something must be said about them. Erasmus—who, as he himself says, was the first to obtain an ancient and corrected copy of Sophronius’s version—and most of the editors who followed him are convinced that this Sophronius was the same man whom our Jerome praises in chapter 134 of this Catalogue as an elegant translator of some of his shorter works from Latin into Greek. Their opinion rests first upon the title of the book itself, and then is strengthened by the preconceived judgment of learned men, based upon Jerome’s testimony.

Others, by contrast, regard him as a recent writer who falsely assumes the identity of that Sophronius, Jerome’s friend. Nor was there lacking a man otherwise learned and well educated—I mean Vossius—who suspected that Erasmus himself had fabricated the work, or at least maintained that it came from some Greek impostor of Erasmus’s age. They argue from the fact that in many places the version is neither Greek in character nor expressive of Jerome’s meaning, but seems to have been made from a corrupt Latin copy. They further argue that it has never been found in any ancient manuscript in the libraries examined hitherto by students of this kind of literature.

Between such widely separated opinions, the middle position approved by the more prudent men—Bosius, Huetius, and others—is also much the more probable. I mean that the Sophronius who was Jerome’s friend and to whom the work is commonly attributed was certainly not its author, but that it cannot at all be believed to have been fabricated by Erasmus or by some impostor of his age. The style itself first supports this conclusion, since it reasonably appears to bear the stamp of later Greek. The errors and false readings too, although not as numerous as Vossius exaggerates, are nevertheless of such a kind as to suggest a translation prepared from a more recent Latin copy, at a time when barbarism had gradually entered the language and negligence among scribes or rashness among critics had infected good books.

Most especially, however, the interpolations concerning Apostles or other ancient Fathers who wrote nothing at all and had not been listed by Jerome among ecclesiastical writers unmistakably bear the character of a mind utterly alien to Sophronius’s reliability and nobility.

The other point is easily established by the testimony of writers who flourished not merely one or two but many centuries before Erasmus. Suidas praises this version in many places and reproduces it in almost the same words in his notices of Basil, Caesarius, Gregory, Damasus, Epiphanius, Eusebius Pamphilus, Justin, Justus of Tiberias, Josephus, Methodius, Origen, Polycarp, Philo, and others.

“But,” you will say, “Suidas himself is of uncertain date, and seems to have lived in the twelfth century, since passages from Michael Psellos, who flourished under Alexius Comnenus, are quoted by him.” That is true; but no one will deny that his date cannot be determined from a few words added by a later hand. Although it is difficult to say in what year the author actually lived, learned men have established that he is nevertheless more ancient than is commonly believed.

Nor do I insist upon this one testimony alone. There is another, most clear and decisive. Photius, who certainly published his *Bibliotheca* before the year 850, read this very Greek translation and derived from it a considerable fragment of several lines. To establish the truth of the matter, compare Sophronius’s Greek translation of Jerome’s chapter 61, on Hippolytus, with the following passage from Photius, codex 121:

> It is also said that he—Hippolytus—addressed the people in imitation of Origen, whose companion and devoted admirer of his teachings he was. He even persuaded him to comment upon the divine Scripture, providing him with seven shorthand writers and as many others who copied their work neatly; he himself supplied the expense. While assisting him in this way, he demanded that he complete the work without fail, and for this reason Origen called him a “taskmaster” in one of his letters.

Since it is plainly evident that these words were copied from that version, and consequently that the version preceded Photius, it is no recent work but must be assigned, at the latest, to the beginning of the eighth century.

Whether the author himself was called Sophronius, or whether someone lies concealed beneath the name of an ancient translator of Jerome, I do not think it worth investigating with excessive curiosity. Nevertheless, one or two Sophronii lived at that time who could conveniently be thought capable of undertaking such a task.

5. We must now say at what time the holy Doctor published this book. In the final chapter, speaking of himself, he writes: “Up to the present year, that is, the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius, I have written these things.” No one doubts that this corresponds to the year 392 from Christ’s birth; I would rather understand it as the later part of that year, so that the other evidence may fit more exactly.

This may be gathered from the testimony of the book *Against Jovinianus*, mentioned above. Jerome himself did not mention that work in the Catalogue, since he had not yet prepared it; rather, the reference was added by some diligent reader who also recalls several later commentaries, contrary to the author’s intention and to the evidence of the ancient copies.

Again, this may be inferred from the Preface to the Commentaries on Jonah, where the holy Doctor lists the sequence of his labors over a period of three years, beginning with his exposition of five Prophets; and, to add this as well, from the second book *Against Rufinus*, where he testifies that he composed this Catalogue approximately ten years earlier.

6. Finally, you should learn briefly what we have contributed to a new edition of this book after the diligence of so many men. First, we have placed beside the text the Greek version, which the Benedictine editor omitted—certainly on poor advice—and which undoubtedly repeatedly assists in establishing Jerome’s reading. We have excluded only ten names, which derive from the hand of paraphrasts, or rather of a glossator, and do not belong to the archetype of the holy Father; these we have relegated to the end as illegitimate offspring.

Next, following the sufficiently commendable diligence recently displayed before us by the Hamburg editor, we have printed Jerome’s text in such a way that whenever he translated Eusebius’s Greek words into Latin in preparing this work, or at least departed only slightly from his traces, we have placed the Greek beside the text itself.

After the Catalogue we append two appendices. One is the work *On the Lives of the Apostles*, which Erasmus found under the name of Sophronius in his manuscript copy of the Greek version and translated into Latin. The other bears the titles *Jerome’s Work on the Twelve Doctors, to Desiderius*, and *Bede’s Work on the Luminaries of the Church*. This latter little work is indeed sufficiently foolish, as we shall point out in the prefatory judgment; but it could not be omitted under any circumstances, lest anything be lacking to the reader, whether learned or unlearned.

We give Gennadius fourth, since he continues the Catalogue of the holy Father and supplements it in several places. Thus, by a certain right of his own, he demands to be counted with Jerome’s work, or rather he does not permit himself to be removed from the position he has held in manuscripts and in most editions. For his sake we have postponed the Jerome Catalogue itself until the end of the volume, lest, if Gennadius were placed immediately after it, the sequence of Jerome’s writings would necessarily be interrupted.

Finally, a point to be mentioned fifth, we have checked all these materials against the most excellent manuscript copies, especially one from Verona, for which it would be difficult to find many equals in antiquity and correctness; and then another from Cîteaux, or from the monastery of Santa Croce in Jerusalem at Rome, of greatly valued antiquity and quality. I shall also add the Lucca manuscript, which is said to precede the ninth century, and from which I obtained a list of Gennadius’s chapters very different from that found in other manuscripts and printed books; and the Corbie manuscript praised by Mabillon, whose variant readings Martianaeus places at the end of Gennadius’s book. Finally, we have examined what earlier editors have noted from other manuscripts, and we openly and candidly acknowledge that we have sometimes benefited from their work.

## PROLOGUE

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### 821

You urge me, Dexter, to follow Tranquillus and arrange the ecclesiastical writers in order, and I shall do among our own writers [Alternative: “I shall do this”] what he did in enumerating the illustrious men of pagan literature—that is, briefly to set forth for you all who, from the Passion of Christ up to the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius, have committed anything concerning the holy Scriptures to memory or to writing.

[Note: Thus the Verona manuscript, the oldest of all; elsewhere *me* is lacking. Jerome himself praises this Dexter, to whom this book is dedicated, as prefect of the praetorium above, in Book II *Against Rufinus*; Gothofredus discusses him at length in the *Prosopography* of the Theodosian Code.]

[Note: Learned men have observed that the Greek phrase *τοὺς τὰ ἐθνικὰ συντάξαντας* properly denotes those who wrote about the vocabulary of some particular nation; it does not correspond well to the Latin phrase “illustrious men of pagan literature,” namely grammarians, rhetoricians, and poets, whom Suetonius catalogued.]

The Greeks indeed did the same: Hermippus the Peripatetic, Antigonus of Carystus, the learned Satyrus, and the musician Aristoxenus, by far the most learned of them all.

[Note: Smyrnaeus is meant, whom Josephus in Book I *Against Apion* calls a man most diligent and careful in investigating all history, and whom many of the ancients praise. Athenaeus and Laertius testify that Antigonus wrote *Lives of Philosophers*. Jerome himself mentions Satyrus elsewhere, in Book II *Against Jovinianus*: “Satyrus, who wrote a history of illustrious men.” Finally, Plutarch and Gellius celebrate the *Lives of Men* of Aristoxenus.]

Among the Latins there were Varro, Santra, Nepos, Hyginus, and Tranquillus, whose example you call upon us to follow.

[Note: Varro’s first six books of *Antiquities of Human Affairs* are apparently indicated. Donatus mentions Santra in his *Life of Terence*, as do others. Everyone knows our Nepos, a writer of great elegance. Finally, do not think of the Hyginus whose book of ancient mythology is in circulation, but of another and older Hyginus, a freedman of Augustus, whom Gellius praises in Book II, chapter 21. Shortly afterward Martianaeus appeals to him, against the manuscripts.]

But my situation is not like theirs. They, by unrolling ancient histories and annals, could weave, as it were from a vast meadow, a not inconsiderable garland for their little work. What can I do, following no predecessor, but having myself as the worst teacher, as the saying goes?

Although Eusebius Pamphilus, in the ten books of his *Ecclesiastical History*, has been of the greatest assistance to us, and the books of each of those about whom we are going to write will often provide testimony concerning the periods of their authors.

Therefore I beseech the Lord Jesus Christ that, through your encouragement, I may worthily accomplish among the writers of his Church what your Cicero—who stood at the summit of Roman eloquence—did not disdain to do in his *Brutus*, composing a catalogue of the orators of the Latin language.

[Note: “Among the writers of that Church.” The manuscript of the most eminent Cardinal Ottoboni reads here, “among ecclesiastical writers”; but the sense is the same in either reading. Martianaeus. In several manuscripts, according to the testimony of Martianaeus and Gravius, the better reading is “among ecclesiastical writers.”]

If any of those who have continued writing [Alternative: “have written”] down to the present day have been omitted by me in this volume, they will have themselves, rather than me, to blame [Alternative: “they have to blame”].

For since they concealed their writings, I could not know what I had not encountered; and what may perhaps be known to others was unknown to me in this corner of the world, Bethlehem.

[Note: The manuscripts rightly prefer this reading; all printed books and the Greek version agree with it. One manuscript in Fabricius’s possession reads *Moseensis*, “which are far away.”]

Certainly, once they have become famous through their writings, they will not sigh greatly over the losses [Alternative: “loss”] caused by our silence.

Let Celsus, Porphyry, and Julian, those rabid dogs against Christ, learn this; let their followers learn it as well—those who think that the Church has had no philosophers or men of eloquence, no teachers. Let them learn how many and what sort of men founded, built [Alternative: “constructed”], and adorned her, and let them cease accusing our faith of possessing only rustic simplicity; rather, let them acknowledge their own ignorance.

[Note: “Let Celsus, etc., learn.” These three philosophers and sages of the age were the most pernicious enemies of the Christian Church. Origen overthrew Celsus in his writings, Methodius overthrew Porphyry, and Cyril of Alexandria overthrew Julian. Martianaeus.]

Farewell in the Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: The Verona manuscript has “Farewell in the Lord Jesus Christ.” This greeting is omitted in other manuscripts and is also absent from the Greek.]

### 822

You urge me, Dexter, to follow Tranquillus and arrange the ecclesiastical writers in order, and to do among our own writers what he did when enumerating the illustrious men who wrote on pagan subjects. That is, from the Passion of the Savior up to the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius, I shall briefly make known all who wrote about the divine Scriptures and handed anything down to memory.

The Greeks did the same: Hermippus the Peripatetic, Antigonus of Carystus, Satyrus, a man learned in many things, and Aristoxenus the musician, who was far more learned in many matters.

Among the Romans there were Varro, Santra, Nepos, Hyginus, and Tranquillus, whose example you wish to set before us.

But my undertaking is not like theirs. They, rolling out ancient histories and the records of each year, were able, as though from a great meadow, to weave at least a small wreath for their own work. What shall I accomplish, following no guide, but having myself as the worst teacher, as the saying goes?

Even so, Eusebius Pamphilus, in the ten books of his *Ecclesiastical History*, has provided us with the greatest assistance, and the writings of each person about whom we are preparing to write will offer testimony concerning their own times.

Therefore I beseech our Lord Jesus Christ that, through your encouragement, I may accomplish, in enumerating the writers of his Church, what your Cicero—standing at the very summit of Roman eloquence—did not disdain to do in his *Brutus*, when he composed a catalogue of the orators of the Roman language.

If any of those who have written down to the present day have been omitted by me in this volume, let them charge themselves rather than me.

For since they concealed their own writings, I could not know what I had not come across; and what is sometimes known to others was unknown to me in this corner of the world.

Nevertheless, once they become manifest through their own writings, they will not complain of our silence as though they had suffered the greatest injury.

Let Celsus, Porphyry, and Julian, those mad dogs against Christ, learn this; let their followers learn it too, those who think that the Church has had neither philosophers and eloquent men nor any teachers. Let them learn how many and how great were the men who founded her, built her up, and adorned her; and let them cease censuring our faith as merely rustic simplicity, acknowledging instead their own ignorance.

[Note: The following chapters begin. I transcribed this Catalogue from the very ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and another from the abbey of Cluny. They sometimes have variant readings, but these are of little importance. For example, at no. 58 the Saint-Germain manuscript reads only “Adamantius the presbyter.” At no. 109 it does not contain the Greek words in Didymus, “ὁ βλέπων,” that is, “he who sees.” Finally, at no. 129 it reads “John the bishop.” Again, the Cluny manuscript at no. 132 retains nothing except the word “Dexter.” At no. 82 likewise, in the entry on Reticius, it omits the word *Eduorum*. But these variants are either of no importance or of little importance; I would not have mentioned them had it not been courteous to inform curious readers even of the smallest details. Martianaeus.]

## THE BOOK BEGINS

### CHAPTER ONE

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### 827

Simon Peter, son of John,

[Note: Many manuscripts, including those inspected by Victorius, read “son of Jonah.” This reading, besides the Greek version of Sophronius, is supported by the traditional ancient interpretation of this name, namely, “son of the dove.” But see John 1:42 and 21:15ff.]

of the province of Galilee, from the village of Bethsaida, brother of the apostle Andrew (Matthew 4:18), and chief of the Apostles, after serving as bishop of the Church of Antioch and preaching to those of the circumcision who had been dispersed and believed in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia (1 Peter 1:1), went to Rome in the second year of the emperor Claudius to defeat Simon Magus.

[Note: Eusebius, *History*, Book II, chapter 14: “In that same reign of the emperor Claudius.”]

[Note: He says the same in the *Chronicle*: “The apostle Peter, after first founding the Church of Antioch, was sent to Rome, where, preaching the Gospel, he remained bishop of that city for twenty-five years.” Since there are many questions and opinions concerning these twenty-five years, it is preferable to consult Pagius under the year 43 after Christ, Baluzius on Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 2, and others. Among earlier writers, Rufinus, Book II of the *Invectives*, counts twenty-four years—namely, the year 68 after Christ.]

There he held the priestly chair for twenty-five years, until the final year of Nero, that is, his fourteenth. By that emperor he was fastened to a cross and crowned with martyrdom,

[Note: In precisely the same words—something remarkable—Saint Gaudentius of Brescia speaks of Saints Peter and Paul, formerly included among the twenty *Zenonian Sermons*: “Peter is crucified with his head turned toward the earth and his feet raised aloft, declaring himself unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord.” Perhaps, therefore, both writers drew these words from some more ancient source. It is by no means likely that Jerome copied Gaudentius, even if the chronology permitted it; nor is the opinion of those convincing who derive the passage from the apocryphal Acts circulated under the name of Linus.]

with his head turned toward the earth and his feet raised aloft, declaring himself unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord.

[Note: Eusebius, *History*, Book III, chapter 1, quoting Origen: “He was crucified head downward.”]

He wrote two Epistles called Catholic,

[Note: Some manuscripts and printed editions less correctly read “canonical.”]

of which the second is denied by most to be his, because its style differs from that of the first.

[Note: See the discussion below in chapter 8 and Eusebius, *History*, Book III, final chapter.]

The Gospel according to Mark is also said to be his, since Mark was his hearer and interpreter.

The books of which one is entitled *His Acts*, another *The Gospel*, a third *The Preaching*, a fourth *The Apocalypse*, and a fifth *The Judgment* are rejected among the apocryphal writings.

[Note: In Eusebius, *History*, Book III, chapter 3, from whom Jerome seems to have taken this material, there is no mention of a book called *The Judgment*. Rufinus mentions it in his *Explanation of the Creed*: “The book called *The Shepherd*, or *Hermas*, which is entitled *The Two Ways*, or *The Judgment of Peter*.” It may have been called *The Judgment of Peter* because of 2 Peter 1:11ff. It is called “Judgment” in the same way that Prodicus once described the “Choice of Hercules” between two ways, one of virtue and the other of pleasure.]

He was buried at Rome in the Vatican, beside the road called the Triumphal Way, and is honored with the veneration of the whole world.

[Note: Martianaeus takes this reading from three manuscripts of the highest quality. Other manuscripts and printed editions read “the veneration of the whole city,” a reading also supported by the Greek version. “Of the whole world” is found in the Saint-Germain manuscript and is likewise retained by the manuscripts of Saint-Martin of Sées and Saint-Cyran; the rest, together with the printed editions, read “he is honored with the veneration of the whole city.” Martianaeus.]

### 828

Simon Peter, apostle, son of Jonah, of the province of Galilee, from the village of Bethsaida, brother of the apostle Andrew and chief of the Apostles, after the episcopate of the Church of Antioch and the preaching to those who had been dispersed and had believed from the circumcision in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, in the second year of Claudius came to Rome to wage war against Simon Magus. There he held the throne of the priesthood for twenty-five years, until the final year of Nero, that is, the fourteenth. Under him also he was crucified and bore witness, with his head toward the ground and his feet raised aloft, declaring himself unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as the Lord of all.

He wrote two Epistles called Catholic, of which most do not accept the second as his, because of its style and its disagreement with the first Epistle.

The Gospel according to Mark is also said to be his, since Mark became his disciple and interpreter.

His writings—that is, first, the one entitled *His Acts*; second, *The Gospel*; third, *The Preaching*; fourth, *The Apocalypse*; fifth, *The Judgment*—are rejected as apocryphal.

After being buried at Rome in the Vatican, near the road called the Triumphal Way, he is venerated by the Romans with every mark of reverence.

## CHAPTER II

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0609A] 829 James, who is called the brother of the Lord (Gal. I, 19), surnamed Justus—as some think [Note: [Col. 0609D] Namely, Eusebius, book II, and Ambrose on chapter I of Galatians. See Jerome, Against Helvidius, no. 13, and our notes there. His view, according to which James is called the brother of the Lord because he was his cousin, is more pleasing than the alternatives.]—was Joseph’s son by another wife, or, as seems to me, the son of Mary, the sister of the Lord’s mother (John XIX, 25), whom John mentions in his book [Note: [Col. 0609D] The Greek version does not recognize these words in its text.] He was immediately appointed bishop of Jerusalem by the Apostles after the Lord’s Passion [Note: [Col. 0609D] Eusebius gives the same account in book II, chapter 1, although he contradicts both Jerome and himself in book VII, chapter 19, where he writes that James was made bishop of the Jerusalem Church by the Lord himself and by his Apostles. Some among the ancients also support that view.]. He wrote only one Epistle, which is one of the seven Catholic Epistles; and this too is alleged to have been published by someone else under his name [Note: [Col. 0609D] The Sangerman manuscript, in Martianay’s edition, reads “by some,” referring this to “is alleged,” not to the printed reading.] although, as time gradually passed, it gained authority.
