[Note: [Col. 0610C] Eusebius, book II, chapter 23: “Hegesippus, who lived during the first succession after the Apostles, records the following account of him in the fifth book of his Memoirs: ‘James, the brother of the Lord, surnamed Just by all, succeeds the Church together with the Apostles, from the time of the Lord until our own day, since there were many named James. He was holy from his mother’s womb. He drank neither wine nor strong drink, ate no living creature, no razor came upon his head, he did not anoint himself with oil, and he did not use the bath. To him alone it was permitted to enter the holy places; for he wore no wool, but linen garments. He alone entered the temple, and he was found lying on his knees and asking forgiveness for the people, so that his knees were believed to have become hard like those of a camel.’”] Hegesippus, a contemporary of the Apostolic age, narrating the story of James in the fifth book of his Memoirs, says:

“He took over the Church of Jerusalem after the Apostles, James the brother of the Lord, surnamed Just.” [Note: [Col. 0610C] Eusebius has μετὰ τῶν Ἀποστόλων, that is, “with the Apostles.” [Col. 0610D] We noted above the tradition of several ancient Fathers, according to which James was appointed bishop of Jerusalem by Christ himself: Chrysostom, Homily 38 on First Corinthians: “For he is said to have ordained him himself and made him first bishop in Jerusalem.”]

“For many were called James. This man was holy from his mother’s womb. He drank neither wine nor strong drink, ate no flesh, was never shorn, was never anointed with ointment, and never used the bath.” [Note: [Col. 0610D] “To him alone it was permitted.” In several manuscript copies we read, “This man alone was accustomed,” or “To this man alone it was customary,” and so forth. MARTIANAY.—Several manuscripts cited by Martianay read “This man alone was accustomed,” or “To this man it was customary.” The Gembloux manuscript, examined by Sufridus Petrus, and Miraeus read, “He was accustomed to enter,” as does the Greek version, ἔθος δὲ ἦν αὐτῷ εἰσελθεῖν. Eusebius, however, has τούτῳ μόνῳ ἐξῆν εἰς τὰ ἅγια εἰσιέναι, “To this man alone it was permitted to enter the holy places.” Jerome correctly translates εἰς τὰ ἅγια as “into the Holy of Holies”; that is what Hegesippus intended, not merely “the holy places,” which any priest of Aaron’s order was permitted to frequent. Rufinus likewise translates it. I do not conceal that Hegesippus’s statement seems exceedingly difficult to believe, since it is unlikely that the Jews would have allowed James, a Christian, access to the Holy of Holies, where no one but the high priest was permitted to enter. As for the statement that he did not use wool but linen garments, that indeed accords with the custom of the high priest, Leviticus XVI, 4.]

“To this man alone it was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies, for he did not wear woolen garments but linen ones. He alone entered the temple, and, kneeling, prayed for the people, to such an extent that his knees were believed to have acquired the hardness of camels’ knees.” [Col. 0611A] 831

He says many other things as well, which it would take too long to enumerate. [Note: [Col. 0611C] The Greek version has ὑπερβαίνειν, “to surpass,” as though it had read “to have surpassed.” See these matters in Eusebius, book II, chapter 23.] But Josephus too [Note: [Col. 0611C] See Josephus, book XX, chapter 9, at the beginning. Some manuscripts in Martianay read “Ananias and the son of Ananias.”] in the twentieth book of his *Antiquities*, and Clement in the seventh book of the *Outlines*, report that, after the death of Festus, who governed Judea, Nero sent his successor Albinus; but before he had reached the province, [Note: [Col. 0611C] “Ananus,” he says, “the high priest.” The Sangerman, or Corbie, manuscript preserves another reading: “Annianus, the high priest, a young son of Ananias.” MARTIANAY.] Ananus, the high priest, a young man, the son of Ananus, of priestly descent, taking advantage of the opportunity created by the absence of a governor, convened a council and publicly compelled James to deny that Christ was the Son of God. When James contradicted him, Ananus ordered him to be stoned. [Note: [Col. 0611C] Josephus relates this much; what follows is taken from Clement through Eusebius.]

When he had been thrown down from the pinnacle of the temple, with his legs broken, and, while still half alive, was stretching his hands toward heaven and saying, “Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34), he was struck on the head with a fuller’s club, the kind used for wringing out wet garments [Note: [Col. 0611C] This word is absent from some manuscripts, and the Greek translator does not recognize it either. Other editions read *rudia*, “a rough club.”], and died.

Josephus likewise reports that he possessed such holiness and such renown among the people that, because of his death, it was believed that Jerusalem had been overthrown. [Note: [Col. 0611D] Origen cites this in book I *Against Celsus* and in his Commentary on Matthew as something reported by Josephus: “These things happened to the Jews as punishment for James the Just, who was the brother of Jesus called Christ, because the Jews killed him, although he was exceedingly just.” Eusebius derives the account from Origen, whom Jerome follows here. But Origen may have suffered a lapse of memory, applying to James what he had read about the death of John the Baptist at the hands of Herod. Certainly these words are found neither in Josephus’s works today nor, apparently, ever had a place in them.]

This is the man about whom the Apostle Paul writes to the Galatians: “I saw none of the other Apostles except James, the brother of the Lord” (Gal. I, 19). The Acts of the Apostles also repeatedly bear witness to this (Acts I, 13; XXII, 17; XV, 13).

The Gospel also called *According to the Hebrews* [Note: [Col. 0611D] Jerome discusses this Gospel according to the Hebrews at length elsewhere, in ways that seem at first sight to conflict with one another. Here he says that he himself translated it into Greek and Latin, yet he does not list that labor in his catalogue of works. In the following chapter, 3, he praises as authentic Matthew’s Gospel whose Hebrew autograph he had copied from the Caesarean library. Above, in book III *Against the Pelagians*, no. 2, he says: “In the Gospel according to the Hebrews, which is written in the Chaldaic or Syriac language but in Hebrew letters, and which the Nazarenes use to this day according to the Apostles—or, as most suppose, according to Matthew—which is also kept in the Caesarean library, etc.” And in his Commentary on Matthew XII, 13: “In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes and Ebionites, which we recently translated into Greek from the Hebrew language, and which is called by most people Matthew’s authentic Gospel.” These statements can be reconciled if one understands this to have been a particular copy of the same Gospel, written in the Chaldaic or Syriac language but in Hebrew letters—not by Matthew himself, but by the Nazarenes, who had long before prepared this translation into the Syriac-Chaldaic language and had appended many things that seemed to them to have been omitted by Matthew, such as those which Jerome occasionally notes. The Ebionites, by contrast, had removed the genealogy. Both groups declared their own copy authentic, and Saint Jerome copied the Nazarene version preserved in the Caesarean library, translating it from there into Greek and Latin. Yet I do not understand why he would recast the book in Greek if it already existed in Greek, since Origen had read it. Elsewhere, and in the admonition prefixed to the books *Against the Pelagians*, it has been noted that for this reason Theodore of Mopsuestia, in Photius, codex 177, called its author the fabricator of a fifth Gospel.]—which I recently translated into Greek and Latin, and which Origen frequently uses, reports the following after the Savior’s resurrection:

“But the Lord, having given the linen cloth to the servant of the priest, went to James and appeared to him.” [Note: [Col. 0612D] The Sangerman manuscript does not read “having given the linen cloth to the servant of the priest.” MARTIANAY.]

For James had sworn that he would not eat bread from that hour when he had drunk the Lord’s cup until he saw him [Col. 0613A] rising from among the dead. [Note: [Col. 0613C] Some copies read “from the dead.” Gregory of Tours, book I of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 22; Sedulius Scotus on First Corinthians XV, 7; and others report the same from Jerome. It should also be noted that the words “having given the linen cloth to the servant of the priest,” mentioned above, are absent from the Sangerman manuscript examined by Martianay. Moreover, the Greek text had incorrectly read “opened” for “appeared,” just as shortly afterward it incorrectly has “the Lord,” ὁ Κύριος, instead of “of the Lord.”]

And again, shortly afterward: “The Lord says, ‘Bring a table and bread.’” Immediately it is added: “He took bread and blessed it, broke it, and gave it to James the Just, and said to him: ‘My brother, eat your bread, for the Son of Man has risen from among the dead.’”

Thus he governed the Church of Jerusalem for thirty years—that is, until [Note: [Col. 0613D] The sixty-second year of Christ. The rest is taken from Hegesippus through Eusebius, book II, chapter 23: “And they buried him in the place, and his monument still remains beside the temple.” See, concerning the inscription, the Greek scholion which Valesius found in the margin of the Mazarin manuscript of Eusebius’s history: “It should be known that this monument was nothing other than an unshaped stone bearing the name of the buried James as an inscription. Hence Christians even now set up stones in their tombs, either writing letters upon them or engraving the sign of the cross.” “It should be understood that this monument was nothing other than an unshaped stone into which the name of James buried there had been cut. Hence Christians still set up stones in their tombs, on which they customarily inscribe letters or carve the figure of the cross.”]

the seventh year of Nero—and was buried near the temple, where he had also been thrown down. His memorial inscription was very well known until the siege of Titus and Hadrian’s final siege. Some of our people thought that he had been buried on the Mount of Olives, [Note: [Col. 0613D] Quaresmius and other learned men nevertheless prefer this opinion to the other, both because the Jews buried corpses outside the city and because it is not plausible that they would have allowed a man condemned to death by stoning—and, in their opinion, a seducer—to be buried near the temple and honored with a monument. Since the Mount of Olives lies opposite the temple, Quaresmius maintains that Hegesippus does not contradict this view.] but their opinion is false.

[Col. 0610A] 830 James, the brother of the Lord, an Apostle and surnamed Just—whom some suppose to have been Joseph’s son by another woman, but who, as it seems to me, was the son of Mary, the sister of the Lord’s mother—was immediately appointed bishop of Jerusalem by the Apostles. He wrote only one Epistle, which is one of the seven Catholic Epistles; and some say that this Epistle was published by someone else under his name, although, as time gradually advanced, it acquired a certain authority.

Hegesippus, a contemporary of the Apostolic age, narrating the story of James in the fifth book of his *Memoirs*, said:

“James, the brother of the Lord, surnamed Just because many were called James, took over the Church of Jerusalem after the Apostles. This man was holy from birth. He drank neither wine nor strong drink, never ate meat or any other sacrificial food, never cut his hair, and had no dealings with ointments or baths. It was his custom to enter the Holy of Holies wearing no woolen garment but a linen one. He alone was permitted to enter the temple; and, bending his knees, he prayed for the people so persistently that his knees were thought to have surpassed the hardness of camels’ knees. He says other things as well, which it would take too long to list. Josephus too, in the twentieth book of the *Antiquities*, and Clement, in the seventh book of the *Outlines*, have stated that after the death of Festus, who governed Judea, Nero sent his successor Albinus; and before Albinus reached the province, Ananus, he says, a young priest, the son of Ananus, of priestly descent, taking advantage of the absence of a governor, convened a council and compelled James publicly to deny Christ, the Son of God. When James contradicted him, he ordered him to be stoned. After James had been thrown from the pinnacle of the temple, with his legs broken, while still half alive he raised his hands toward heaven and said: ‘Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.’ Then, struck on the head with a fuller’s club, with which they customarily press out garments, he died.”

Josephus adds that James possessed such holiness and such religious renown among the people that everyone was persuaded that Jerusalem had been destroyed because of his death.

The Apostle Paul also says of him to the Galatians: “I saw none of the other Apostles except James, the brother of the Lord.” The Acts of the Apostles bear witness to this as well.

The Gospel entitled [perhaps, “entitled,” ἐπιγραφόμενον] *According to the Hebrews*, which I have now translated into Greek and Latin and which Origen also frequently uses, says after the Savior’s resurrection:

“But the Lord, having given the linen cloth to the servant of the priest, went to James and appeared to him.”

For James had sworn not to taste bread from that hour when the Lord had drunk the cup until he saw him risen from the dead.

And again, a little later: “The Lord says, ‘Bring a table and bread.’” Immediately it adds: “Having taken bread, given thanks, he broke it and, giving it to James the Just, said to him: ‘My brother, eat your bread, for the Son of Man has risen from the dead.’”

Thus, after governing the Church of Jerusalem for thirty years—that is, until the seventh year of Nero—he was buried near the temple, where he had been thrown down. He had a famous monument until the siege of Titus and the final revolt of Hadrian. Some among us think that he was placed on the Mount of Olives, but their supposition is false.

## CHAPTER III

[Note: [Col. 0613] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0613A] 833 Matthew, also called Levi, an Apostle from the tax office (Matt. IX, 9; Mark II, 14; Luke V, 27), first in Judea, for the sake of those who had believed from the circumcision, composed the Gospel of Christ in Hebrew letters and words. It is not sufficiently certain who later translated it into Greek. The Hebrew text itself is still preserved today in the Caesarean library, which the martyr Pamphilus assembled with the greatest diligence. I too was granted by the Nazarenes, who use this volume in the Syrian city of Beroea, the opportunity to copy it. In it one must observe that whenever the Evangelist, whether speaking in his own person or in the person of the Lord and Savior, uses testimonies from the ancient Scriptures, he does not follow the authority of the translators of the Septuagint but the Hebrew text. Two examples are these: “Out of Egypt I called my son,” and “For he shall be called a Nazarene.” [Note: [Col. 0614C] Papias, in Eusebius, *History* III, 39, reports the same, as do Eusebius himself in the same book, chapter 24, and book V, chapter 10. It is much more credible that Matthew himself wrote in Greek; and since the tradition concerning his translator is highly uncertain—some claiming James, others Paul, others Luke, and still others John—it seems that Papias and other ancient writers took the Nazarenes’ Gospel, mentioned above in chapter 2, for Matthew’s authentic Gospel, as Jerome himself notes in his Commentary on Matthew. Yet the Fathers cite this Gospel only in Greek and reject the Hebrew text, and I know of no one who suggests that the Greek was translated from Hebrew. See the preceding chapter and our notes there on this matter.]  

[Col. 0614A] 834 Matthew, also called Levi, an Apostle from the tax office, composed in Judea, first for those who had believed from the circumcision, the Gospel of Christ in Hebrew letters and words; the person who later translated it into Greek is unknown. The Hebrew text is still preserved today in the library of Caesarea, painstakingly established by the martyr Pamphilus. I was granted permission by the Nazarenes in Beroea of Syria, who use this book, to make a copy of it. From this copy one can establish with certainty that whenever the Evangelist, whether speaking in his own person or in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ and Savior, uses testimonies from the ancient Scriptures, he does not follow the authority of the seventy interpreters but the Hebrew text. Two examples are these: “Out of Egypt I called my son,” and “For he shall be called a Nazarene.”

## CHAPTER IV

[Note: [Col. 0613] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0613C] Judas, the brother of James [Note: [Col. 0614D] Victor and others observed “the brother of the Lord” in ancient manuscripts, and approve that reading, since Hegesippus also calls him this in Eusebius, book III, chapter 20. But most manuscripts more correctly read “of James,” as does Freculphus from Jerome, and the Greek translator from Luke VI, 16 and from Judas himself. The James understood as his brother is James the younger, discussed above in chapter 2. Hence Epiphanius correctly joins the two: “Judas, called the brother of James and of the Lord.” See also Clement of Alexandria on the Catholic Epistles.] left a short Epistle, which is one of the seven Catholic Epistles. And because it cites testimony from the book of Enoch, which is apocryphal [Col. 0615A] [Note: [Col. 0615C] Chapter V, verse 14. When Jerome, in his usual manner, says “by most,” understand “by some,” not οἱ πλείους, “the majority.” Thus Eusebius says that it was regarded as genuine “by many,” τοῖς πολλοῖς. It is not the place here to report the other ancient testimonies. See Huet, *Demonstratio Evangelica*, proposition I, and so forth.] it is rejected by many; [Col. 0615A] 835 yet it has already earned authority through antiquity and use and is counted among the sacred Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0615C] “Yet authority.” The very ancient Sangerman manuscript reads: “Yet it has now merited authority through antiquity, age, and use,” and so forth. MARTIANAY.—The Sangerman manuscript in Martianay reads: “Yet it has now merited authority through antiquity and use,” as does the Greek version.]

[Col. 0614C] Judas, the brother of James, left a very short Epistle, one of the seven Catholic Epistles. And since it draws testimony in it from the book of Enoch, which is apocryphal, it is rejected by many; nevertheless, by reason of its antiquity and the authority of its use, it has been judged worthy to be counted among the divine Scriptures. 836

## CHAPTER V

[Note: [Col. 0615] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0615A] The Apostle Paul, formerly Saul (Acts VII, 58), outside the number of the twelve Apostles [Note: [Col. 0615D] As he distinguishes himself in First Corinthians XV, 5, 8.], was of the tribe of Benjamin and came from the Judean town of Giscala [Note: [Col. 0615D] He says the same in the Epistle to Philemon: “They say that the parents of the Apostle Paul came from the region of Giscala in Judea; and when the whole province was devastated by Roman force and the Jews were scattered throughout the world, they were transferred to Tarsus in Cilicia, and the young Paul followed the condition of his parents.” Paul says of himself in Acts XXII, 3: “I am a Jewish man, born in Tarsus of Cilicia.” Josephus calls Giscala a πολίχνη, that is, a small town of Galilee, in book IV of *The Jewish War*, chapter 2.] When it was captured by the Romans, he migrated with his parents to Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts XIII, 12). Sent by them to Jerusalem for the study of the Law, he was instructed by Gamaliel, a most learned man whom Luke mentions. When he had taken part in the death of the martyr Stephen and, having received letters from the high priest, was traveling to Damascus to persecute those who had believed in Christ, he was compelled by a revelation to embrace the faith described in the Acts of the Apostles and was changed from a persecutor into a chosen vessel.

When Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus, first believed through his preaching, Paul took the name Paulus because he had brought Sergius under the faith of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0615D] “He took the name Paulus.” More fully in the Commentary on the Epistle to Philemon: “Just as Scipio, having subdued Africa, took the name Africanus for himself, so Saul, sent to preach to the Gentiles, carried back the trophies of his victory from the first spoil of the Church, the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and raised the standard so that he might be called Paulus.”] Taking Barnabas as his companion, traveling through many cities, and returning to Jerusalem, he was appointed by Peter, James, and John as the Apostle to the Gentiles.

Since the Acts of the Apostles gives a very full account of his career [Note: [Col. 0616C] Miraeus and others incorrectly read “conversion.” The same sense appears below, in chapter 8: “Philo wrote a book about their conduct”; and the Greek has διαγωγῆς, “conduct.”], I shall say only this: twenty-five years after the Lord’s Passion—that is, in the second year of Nero, when Festus succeeded Felix as governor of Judea [Note: [Col. 0616C] Eusebius, book II: “Festus was sent by Nero as Felix’s successor; before him Paul made his defense and was taken in chains to Rome.” Luke ends his history at this point, noting that Paul spent two full years at Rome without restraint and preached the word of God without hindrance. By equating Nero’s second year with the twenty-fifth after the Lord’s Passion, Jerome agrees with Eusebius, whose Chronicle, translated by Jerome into Latin, places Christ’s Passion in the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar’s reign after Augustus’s death, under the consulship of Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Marcus Fulvius Camillus Scribonianus. From the Pascha of that year to Nero’s second year there are in fact twenty-five years, which coincide with Nero’s second year at least once it had advanced somewhat.]—he was sent to Rome in chains. Remaining there for two years in open custody, he argued daily against the Jews concerning the coming of Christ. [Col. 0615C] 837

It must be understood [Note: [Col. 0616D] The Greek has ἀπολογίᾳ, “defense,” from II Timothy IV, 16, quite correctly; in this sense the best writers use *satisfactio* for a defense by which either an accusation is removed or an excuse offered.] that, at his first defense, while Nero’s rule had not yet been firmly established and he had not yet burst into the enormities that histories relate about him, Paul was released by Nero so that the Gospel of Christ might also be preached in the western regions, as he himself writes in the Second Epistle to Timothy, composed while he was in chains at the time when he also suffered:

“At my first defense no one stood by me, [Col. 0617A] but everyone deserted me; may it not be counted against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the Gentiles might hear, and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion” (II Tim. IV, 16). [Note: [Col. 0617C] The Greek version lacks the words “but everyone deserted me” through “may it not be counted against them.”]

He most clearly means Nero by the lion, on account of his cruelty. [Note: [Col. 0617C] The Greek translator has no corresponding text for the Latin words “And afterward, I was delivered … and will save me for his heavenly kingdom.” Conversely, Eusebius’s Greek text contains additional material from οὐκοῦν ἑξῆς onward, which explains more clearly that in his second imprisonment Paul did not write that he would again be delivered from the lion’s mouth, as he had on the former occasion, but that through martyrdom the Lord would wholly deliver him and transfer him to the heavenly kingdom. We had suspected that a copyist, in copying Jerome, had been misled by the words “from the lion’s mouth,” which ended the omitted second period; but our manuscripts do not enable us to emend the text.] [Note: [Col. 0617C] Eusebius, in the cited passage: “He clearly shows through these words that he had previously been delivered from the mouth of the lion, apparently calling Nero this because of his savagery. Accordingly he immediately adds something similar: ‘The Lord will deliver me from the mouth of the lion.’ For in his spirit he saw the death that was soon to come. Therefore, after ‘I was delivered from the mouth of the lion,’ he adds: ‘The Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will save me for his heavenly kingdom,’ signifying the martyrdom that was immediately impending. He predicts it more clearly in the same writing when he says: ‘For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure has arrived.’”]

And shortly afterward: “I was delivered from the mouth of the lion.” Immediately he adds: “The Lord will deliver me from every evil work and [Note: [Col. 0617D] Thus the reading *will save*, from our manuscript, although earlier it has *delivered*, not *will deliver*. All other printed and manuscript copies incorrectly read *delivered* and then *will save*. See II Timothy IV, 18.] will save me for his heavenly kingdom”—for he evidently understood that martyrdom was then impending. For in the same Epistle he had already said: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand” (II Tim. IV, 6). [Note: [Col. 0617D] Two very ancient manuscripts, one from Verona and the other from Santa Croce in the city, read “thirty-sixth.” Recall what we noted concerning the second year of Nero, which he connects with the twenty-fifth year after the Lord’s Passion. It may now seem to me that the beginning of Nero’s fourteenth year coincided with the thirty-sixth year after Christ’s Passion.]

Thus, in Nero’s fourteenth year, on the same day on which Peter was beheaded at Rome for Christ, Paul too was beheaded and buried on the Ostian Way, in the thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s Passion.

He wrote nine Epistles to seven Churches: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, and two to the Thessalonians. In addition, to his disciples he wrote [Note: [Col. 0618C] Miraeus adds: “four.”] two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon. The Epistle said to be addressed to the Hebrews is not believed to be his, because of the difference of its style and language [Note: [Col. 0618C] The ancient editions read “difference.” See Origen in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 25.], but is attributed either to Barnabas, according to Tertullian [Note: [Col. 0618C] Tertullian, *On Modesty*, chapter 20.], or to the Evangelist Luke, according to some [Note: [Col. 0618C] Eusebius, book III, chapter 38; Theophylact and Gobarus in Photius, codex 222, mention this opinion. I would prefer to remove the words “joined to him” as a mere gloss, since neither any of our manuscripts nor the Greek translator recognizes them.], or to Clement, later bishop of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0618C] Clement of Alexandria in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 14. See also Philaster, *Heresies*, 88.], who, they say, arranged and adorned Paul’s sayings in his own language. Or perhaps, since Paul was writing to the Hebrews and, because of their hostility toward his name, he omitted the title at the beginning of the greeting [Note: [Col. 0618C] Thus Clement of Alexandria in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI, 14: “That ‘Paul, Apostle’ was not prefixed is reasonably explained,” and so forth. See Chrysostom, Homily 64 on passages of the New Testament.].

For he had written as a Hebrew in Hebrew—that is, most eloquently in his own mode of expression—so that what had been eloquently written in Hebrew might be translated more eloquently into Greek [Ms. “to have translated”]. [Note: [Col. 0618C] We entirely reject the cacophonous common reading “a Hebrew wrote to Hebrews in Hebrew.” One of our manuscripts omits “to Hebrews,” another “a Hebrew”; the Greek likewise has only ἑβραῖος ἑβραϊστί, “a Hebrew, in Hebrew.” Our manuscript should be read: “For he had written as a Hebrew in Hebrew,” or “but” in place of “for.” Learned scholars convincingly maintain, however, that the Apostle wrote the Epistle not in Hebrew but in Greek. Jerome was led to the contrary view chiefly by Clement of Alexandria’s *Outlines*, cited by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI, 14, and especially by Eusebius III, 38; Theodoret, Preface to Hebrews, the anonymous writer cited by Oecumenius in a similar preface, and many moderns followed them. Yet their authorities are outweighed by reason: the text itself shows that it was first written in Greek through Greek allusions that would mean nothing in Hebrew, its continuous phrasing and style, its citations of Scripture from Greek, and interpretations for Hebrew readers, all of which would be pointless if it had first been composed in Hebrew. Moreover, Clement can scarcely be called its Greek translator, since, whether Greek or Roman, he could readily have been ignorant of Hebrew.] This is the reason why it seems to differ from Paul’s other Epistles. Some also read an Epistle to the Laodiceans, but it is rejected by everyone.

[Col. 0616A] Paul the Apostle, who was outside the number of the twelve Apostles, came from the tribe of Benjamin and from the town of Giscala in Judea. When that town was captured by the Romans, he settled with his parents in Tarsus of Cilicia. Sent by them to Jerusalem for the practice of the Law, he studied under Gamaliel, a most learned man whom Luke also mentions. But when he was present at the killing of Stephen the martyr, and, having received letters from the high priest for the persecution of those who had believed in Jesus Christ, arrived at Damascus, he was changed by revelation into the faith recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, from a persecutor into a chosen vessel.

When Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus, first believed in his preaching, Paul was allotted the name Paulus from him, because he had subjected Sergius to the faith of Christ. Taking Barnabas with him, visiting many cities, and then departing again for Jerusalem, he was appointed by Peter and James as the Apostle to the Gentiles.

Since much has been said in the Acts of the Apostles about his conduct, I shall say only this: twenty-five years after the Lord’s Passion—that is, in the second year of Nero, when Festus, governor of Judea, succeeded Felix—he was sent in chains to Rome. Remaining there for two years in open custody, he continually explained to the Jews the coming of Jesus.

It must be understood that, at his first defense, while Nero’s reign had not yet become firmly established and he had not yet committed the many crimes reported by historians, Paul was released by Nero in order to preach the Gospel of Jesus Christ in the western regions, as he writes in the Second Epistle to Timothy, at the time when he suffered and, while in chains, wrote:

“At my first defense no one stood with me, and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion”—clearly referring to Nero because of his cruelty. For, evidently aware that martyrdom was impending, he had said in the same Epistle: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure has arrived.”

Likewise, in the fourteenth year of Nero, on the same day on which Peter was beheaded at Rome for Jesus Christ, Paul was buried on the road called Ostian, in the thirty-seventh year after the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ.

He wrote nine Epistles to seven Churches: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, and two to the Thessalonians; and to his own disciples, two to Timothy, one to Titus, and one to Philemon. Some think that the Epistle to the Hebrews is not his, because of its style and the difference of its language, but that it belongs to Barnabas, according to Tertullian; or to Luke the Evangelist, as some think; or to Clement, later bishop of the Roman Church, who, they say, arranged and adorned Paul’s sayings in his own language; or, more probably, that Paul, writing to the Hebrews, omitted the designation “Apostle” at the beginning of the greeting because of the envy directed against him.

For he had written as a Hebrew in Hebrew—that is, eloquently in his own style—and what had been composed eloquently in the Hebrew language was translated even more eloquently into Greek. This is the reason why it is thought to differ from Paul’s other Epistles. [Col. 0620A] Some also read an Epistle to the Laodiceans, but it is rejected by everyone.

## CHAPTER VI

[Note: [Col. 0619] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0619A] 839 Barnabas of Cyprus (Acts IV, 36), also called Joseph the Levite, who was appointed with Paul as the Apostle to the Gentiles (Acts XIII, 2; Gal. II, 9), composed one Epistle pertaining to the edification of the Church [Note: [Col. 0619C] This is based on the title by which the Epistle was commonly known at that time; for immediately afterward Jerome calls it apocryphal, as he says in the Epistle to Leta: “Let her know that apocryphal books do not belong to those whose titles they bear.” Yet he cites it in chapter 43 of his Commentary on Ezekiel.] It is read among the apocryphal writings. Later, because of John the disciple, who was also called Mark (Acts XV, 37), he separated from Paul; nevertheless, he carried out the work of evangelical preaching entrusted to him.

[Col. 0620A] 840 Barnabas of Cyprus, also called Joseph the Levite, appointed with Paul as the Apostle to the Gentiles, composed one Epistle for the edification of the Church; it is counted among the apocryphal writings. Later, having separated from Paul because of John the disciple, who was also called Mark, he nevertheless fulfilled the work of the evangelical proclamation entrusted to him.

## CHAPTER VII

[Note: [Col. 0619] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0619B] Luke the physician, an Antiochene—as his writings show—was not ignorant of the Greek language. A follower of the Apostle Paul and his companion throughout his journeys, he wrote a Gospel, concerning which Paul himself says: “We sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the Churches” (II Cor. VIII, 18). And to the Colossians: “Luke, the beloved physician, greets you” (Col. IV, 14). And to Timothy: “Luke alone is with me” (II Tim. IV, 11).

He also published another distinguished volume, entitled *Acts of the Apostles* [Note: [Col. 0619D] The very ancient and better manuscripts read “under the title *Apostolic*.” The Vatican manuscripts preserve the following readings: “the practices of the Apostles,” 348; “under the title *Apostolic Practices*,” 349; “the practice of Apostolic actions,” 344. The Latin copyists’ errors were followed by Erasmus and Martianay, who read Πράξας Ἀποστόλων. The manuscript exemplar of Saint-Cyran is headed by the title *Apostolic Actions*, Πραξέων. MARTIANAY.—The Verona manuscript correctly reads “Acts of the Apostles,” πράξεις Ἀποστόλων, as does Vatican manuscript 384. The other variant readings reported here by Martianay are merely copyists’ errors. The older editions preferred to read πράξεις Ἀποστόλων.] The history of this book extends through the two years Paul spent at Rome, that is, until the fourth year of Nero (Acts II, 8, 30). From this we understand that the book was composed in that same city. [Note: [Col. 0620C] The Syriac tradition says that Luke wrote the Acts in Alexandria, not Rome, and also counts Theophilus, to whom the book is addressed, among the first and most distinguished believers of Alexandria. Bar-Bahlul, a Syriac author cited by Castellus, reports this. Euthalius, however, in Zacagni’s edition, p. 351, agrees with Jerome and says that Luke wrote the Acts while he was in Rome as Paul’s companion in captivity.]

We therefore count the *Journeys of Paul and Thecla* [Ms. *episodes*] and the entire story of the baptized lion among the apocryphal writings. [Note: [Col. 0620C] Manuscripts examined by Erasmus and Gravius read “vision” instead of περιόδους. In the present printed editions, this tale of the baptized lion is not found in the *Acts of Paul and Thecla*; only the lioness rushing upon Thecla and the baptism of Thecla are mentioned.] For how could it be that Paul’s inseparable companion, among all his other deeds, knew nothing of this one?

Tertullian too, a contemporary of that period [Note: [Col. 0620D] The manuscript of Santa Croce belongs to the same period. Tertullian’s passage is now in *On Baptism*, chapter 17: “If anyone reads the writings falsely attributed to Paul and uses the example of Thecla to defend the permission of women to teach and baptize, let him know that, in Asia, the presbyter who constructed that writing, as though adding it to Paul’s name from his own resources, was convicted and confessed that he had done it out of love for Paul, and withdrew from office. Jerome seems, however, to have used not the Latin text of Tertullian that we now possess, but a Greek manuscript, which he says he had commented upon in Greek before producing the Latin version, chapter 15. This may be inferred from the Greek title of the apocryphal book, περιόδους, and from the fact that the words found here do not occur in Tertullian’s Latin text, especially from the Greek term σπουδαστήν, “devotee” or “follower.”], reports that a certain presbyter in Asia, a devotee of the Apostle Paul, was convicted before John [Col. 0621A] [Note: [Col. 0621C] “Convicted before John.” This is the reading of the Sangerman and Cluniac manuscripts and of one manuscript in the Ambrosian Library, no. 281. Other copies likewise read this, despite the contrary preference of Marianus Victorius, who reads “convicted by John,” not “before John.” MARTIANAY.—All the manuscripts examined by us and by Martianay read this way; hence Victorius incorrectly read “by John.” The other printed copies add “and therefore from office,” but the manuscripts do not recognize these words, nor does Tertullian.] as the author of the book. He confessed that he had done this out of love for Paul and was removed from office.

Some suppose that whenever Paul says in his Epistles, “according to my Gospel,” he refers to Luke’s volume [Note: [Col. 0621C] See Eusebius, book III, chapter 4. Among those who supposed this—or rather, held it to be so—seems to have been Marcellus of Ancyra, in his Epistle to Julius, cited by Epiphanius, *Heresy* 72, no. 2. There he cites Luke I, 33, “of whose kingdom there shall be no end,” according to the Apostle’s testimony, “as the Apostle testifies.” Yet below he cites it under Luke’s own name. Most interpreters more correctly understand “my Gospel” as the Gospel that Paul himself preached. Compare Romans XVI, 11, 16, 25; Galatians I, 2.] and that Luke learned the Gospel not only from the Apostle Paul, who had not been with the Lord in the flesh, but also from the other Apostles. Luke himself makes this clear at the beginning of his work, saying: “Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered it to us.”

Therefore he wrote the Gospel as he had heard it, but composed the Acts of the Apostles as he himself had seen them. [Note: [Col. 0621D] Most editions lack the word “himself,” which we have restored from our manuscript. They also add the words “He lived eighty-four years without a wife,” of which there is not even a trace in the ancient manuscript copies consulted by Erasmus, Victorius, Martianay, ourselves, and others.]

He was buried at Constantinople, to which city, in the twentieth year of Constantius, his bones were transferred together with the relics of the Apostle Andrew. [Note: [Col. 0621D] “He was buried at Constantinople.” The words falsely added here are: “He lived eighty-four years without a wife,” followed by “and in Achaia.” No trace of these words exists in the manuscript copies, nor do I know from where these absurd additions arose. MARTIANAY.] [Note: [Col. 0622C] One manuscript I have seen, from Santa Croce, adds “from Achaia.” Victorius preferred to replace Constantius with Constantine; the Greek version also read Constantine. See Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, at the beginning, and Philostorgius, book III, chapter 2.]

[Col. 0620B] Luke, a physician of Antioch—as his writings show—not unfamiliar with Greek, a devoted follower of the Apostle Paul and his companion throughout all his foreign journeys, composed a Gospel, concerning which Paul himself says: “We sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the Churches.” And to the Colossians: “Luke the beloved physician greets you.” And to Timothy: “Luke alone is with me.”

He also published another excellent work, entitled *Acts of the Apostles*. Its history extends through the two years Paul spent at Rome, that is, until the fourth year of Nero. From this we are persuaded that the book was composed in that same city.

For the *Journey of Paul and Thecla* and the whole tale of the lion—as though a lion had been baptized—are to be reckoned among the apocryphal writings. For it was not possible that Paul’s inseparable companion should have been unaware of this among his other deeds.

Tertullian too, a man of that period, reports that a certain presbyter in Asia, a devotee of the Apostle Paul, was convicted before John because he had composed a book as though it had been written by Paul. He confessed that he had done this under the influence of his love for Paul, and for that reason, some suppose, he was expelled.

Whenever Paul says in his own Epistles, “according to my Gospel,” it is clear that he refers to the volume according to Luke; and Luke learned the Gospel not only from the Apostle Paul, who at that time had not been present bodily with the Lord, but also from the other Apostles. He himself plainly says this at the beginning of his own work: “Just as the eyewitnesses from the beginning delivered it to us.”

Therefore he wrote the Gospel as he had heard it, but composed and arranged the Acts of the Apostles as he himself had witnessed them.

His remains were brought and placed at Constantinople; in the twentieth year of Constantius, his body was transferred to that city together with the relics of Andrew the Apostle.

# CHAPTER VIII

[Note: [Col. 0621] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0621]

[Col. 0621B] **Mark**, Peter’s disciple and interpreter, wrote a brief Gospel at Rome when the brethren requested it, in accordance with what he had heard Peter relating. When Peter heard it, he approved it and published it with his authority for reading in the churches, as Clement writes in the sixth book of the *Hypotyposeis* and Papias, bishop of Hierapolis.

[Note: [Col. 0622C] From Irenaeus, cited by Eusebius, Book V, chapter 8: “Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, also wrote down what he heard from Peter …” What follows is taken almost entirely from Eusebius; compare Book II, chapter 15.]

[Note: [Col. 0622C] “And for reading in the churches.” The manuscript copies differ in this sentence; we have followed the older ones. In others we read: “And he gave the Church authority to read it.” MARTIAN.]

[Note: [Col. 0622C] The Veronese Codex has this reading. Some other manuscripts and printed editions have: “He gave the Church authority to read it.” Then our same codex reads: “As Clement writes in the sixth book of the *Hypotyposeis*, and Papias.” From this one may also conclude that Martianaeus’s punctuation should be corrected, since he places a period before “and Papias.”]

Peter also mentions this Mark in his First Epistle, figuratively indicating Rome by the name Babylon:

[Note: [Col. 0622D] “She who is in Babylon greets you,” and so forth. Here too I find three divergent manuscript readings. Besides the reading we printed from the older copies, three or four manuscripts preserve another: “She who is in Babylon, together with the elect woman, greets you, and Mark …” The remaining manuscripts read: “She who has been gathered in Babylon.” MARTIAN. Sophronius incorrectly has σὺν τῇ ἐκλεκτῇ (“together with the elect woman”) instead of συνεκλεκτῇ (“the co-elect woman”); likewise certain Hieronymian manuscripts, and two of ours, read “with the elect” or “with the gathered” instead of “the co-elect woman.” One reads: “The Church that is in Babylon, the elect one, greets you.”]

“She who is co-elect in Babylon greets you, and so does Mark, my son” (1 Peter 5:13).

Having therefore taken up the Gospel that he himself had composed, Mark went to Egypt and, being the first to proclaim Jesus Christ in Alexandria, established a church. He excelled in such learning and austerity of life that he compelled all Christ’s followers to imitate his example.

[Col. 0621C] Finally, Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, seeing that the first church in Alexandria was still observing Jewish practices, wrote a book about their way of life, as though in praise of his own people.

[Note: [Col. 0622D] Our codex does not contain the word “book,” but it is clear that he means Philo’s work *On the Contemplative Life*, or *On the Supplicants*. Eusebius, and Jerome after him, as well as other ancient and modern writers, thought that this book concerned the conduct and holy institutions of Christians, whereas in reality Philo describes the Alexandrian Therapeutae, “acquaintances of Moses,” as Philo himself states.]

(Acts 2:44). And just as Luke relates that the believers in Jerusalem held everything in common, so Philo recorded what he saw taking place in Alexandria under Mark as teacher.

But Mark died in the eighth year of Nero and was buried in Alexandria, with Annianus succeeding him.

[Note: [Col. 0623C] Eusebius does not affirm this; Jerome otherwise follows him, but Eusebius merely writes in Book II, chapter 24, that in Nero’s eighth year Annianus assumed the administration of the Alexandrian Church, first after Mark. Many writers, especially Eastern ones, say that this occurred while Mark was still alive, although they differ concerning the year of his death.]

[Note: [Col. 0623D] The Veronese Codex has “Annianus.” The Greek has Ἀνανίου, whom the Arabs call Ananias.]

[Col. 0622B] **Mark**, Peter’s disciple and interpreter, having heard Peter explaining the matter, composed a short Gospel when the brethren in Rome requested it. Peter read it, approved it, and published it with his authority for reading in the Church, as Clement writes in the sixth book of the *Hypotyposeis*, and Papias, bishop of Hierapolis. Peter also remembers this Mark in his First Epistle, figuratively signifying Rome by the name Babylon: “She who is in Babylon, together with the elect woman, greets you, and Mark, my son.”

Having therefore received the Gospel that he himself had composed, Mark reached Egypt and, being the first to proclaim Jesus Christ in Alexandria, established a church. He distinguished himself by such instruction and steadfastness of life that he caused all who followed Christ to imitate his way of life.

For this reason Philo, the most distinguished of the Jews, seeing in Alexandria the first church still practicing Judaism, composed a book about their way of life, as though in praise of his own nation. And just as Luke relates that those who believed in Jerusalem had everything in common, so Philo committed to memory what he saw being done there in Alexandria under Mark the teacher.

Mark died in Nero’s eighth year and was buried in Alexandria, with Annianus succeeding him.

# CHAPTER IX

[Note: [Col. 0623] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0623]

[Note: [Col. 0623D] Clement, cited by Eusebius (VI.14), says that John was requested by his acquaintances (ὑπὸ τῶν γνωρίμων); Eusebius himself (III.24) merely says that he was requested (παρακληθέντα).]

[Col. 0623A] The apostle **John**, whom Jesus loved greatly (John 13:23; 19:26; 20:2; 21:7), son of Zebedee and brother of the apostle James (Matthew 4:21; 10:2; Mark 10:35; Luke 5:10), whom Herod beheaded after the Lord’s Passion (Acts 12:2ff.), wrote the Gospel last of all. He was requested to do so by the bishops of Asia, against Cerinthus and the other heretics, and especially against the doctrine of the Ebionites, which was then emerging. They assert that Christ did not exist before Mary. Hence John was compelled to proclaim his divine birth.

[Note: [Col. 0623D] The Veronese Codex reads: “But there were also other reasons.” Our author derived this and what follows from Eusebius, Book III, chapter 24.]

They also report another reason for this writing. When John had read the books of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, he approved the substance of their history and affirmed that they had spoken truthfully, but said that they had composed the history of only one year—the year in which Christ suffered—after John’s imprisonment.

[Note: [Col. 0623D] The manuscript omits “of John.”]

Accordingly, passing over the year whose events had been set forth by the three, he narrated what had occurred in the earlier period, before John was imprisoned. This will be evident to those who read the four Gospels carefully. This circumstance also removes the apparent **disagreement** (*διαφωνία*) between John and the others.

He also wrote one Epistle, whose beginning is: “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked upon, and what our hands have touched, concerning the word of life.” It is approved by all ecclesiastical and learned men.

The other two Epistles, whose beginnings are, respectively, “The elder to the elect lady and her children,” and “The elder to Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth,” are attributed to John the presbyter.

[Note: [Col. 0624C] Irenaeus likewise attributes one of the two to another disciple of Christ named John, when he cites testimony from it in Book I, chapter 13. We record this to answer those who accuse Jerome of error, as though no one before him had expressed this view.]

[Note: [Col. 0624C–D] Papias distinguished two Johns and two tombs; Eusebius (III.39), citing him, reports that there were two tombs at Ephesus and that each was still called John’s: “There came to be two monuments at Ephesus, and each is still called John’s.” Jerome therefore did not interpret correctly a statement made generically about the name John by applying it to John the apostle and evangelist, as though it signified two memorials of one and the same person. This should be understood if, as seems likely, he translated the passage from Eusebius; if he learned this view of some persons from another source, I have no reply to make to one reporting an opinion of his own time.]

His other tomb is still shown at Ephesus, although some think that the two memorials belong to the same John the Evangelist.

[Note: [Col. 0625B] This is how we read it from the manuscript of Sainte-Croix and Fabricius’s edition, in place of “and some people.” The Greek likewise has καί τινες, “and some people.”]

[Note: [Col. 0625C] “Two memorials.” I read this in all the manuscript copies, and the preceding phrase “his other tomb” shows that it must be read so. Thus the Ephesian church had two memorials, or two tombs, of the same John, apostle and evangelist; just as our own church today has two memorials of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris and our patron: one in the chapel of Saint Symphorian, where the place of burial is; the other at the high altar of the church, where, besides the tombstone set beneath the altar, the sacred bodily relics are kept in a most precious gold casket adorned with gems, now supported in the hands of images of two angels of metal, amid six columns of the finest marble and beneath a gilded cornice of most elegant workmanship. The zeal and industry of the Reverend Father Arnulf de Loo, prior of our monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, procured for us the construction of this new altar. I have gladly noted this for perpetual remembrance, taking the occasion from the double memorial of Saint John the Evangelist. MARTIAN.]

When we come in due order to Papias, his hearer, we shall discuss this matter.

In the fourteenth year—when Domitian, in the second persecution after Nero, was stirring up persecution—John was confined to the island of Patmos and wrote the Apocalypse, which Justin Martyr and Irenaeus interpret.

[Note: [Col. 0625D] Christ’s year 95.]

After Domitian was killed, and his acts were annulled by the senate on account of his excessive cruelty, John returned to Ephesus under the emperor Nerva. Remaining there until the emperor Trajan, he founded and governed all the churches of Asia. Worn out by old age, he died in the sixty-eighth year after the Lord’s Passion and was buried near that same city.

[Note: [Col. 0626C] Christ’s year 100.]

[Note: [Col. 0625D] In the *Chronicle*, under Domitian: “The apostle John, confined to the island of Patmos, saw the Apocalypse, which Irenaeus interprets.” The Greek of Eusebius has ὡς δηλοῖ Εἰρηναῖος, “as Irenaeus explains,” or “as Irenaeus interprets.” I take this to refer to the title *Apocalypse*: Justin and Irenaeus called John’s vision by that name, but these Fathers certainly did not publish commentaries on the Apocalypse. Jerome himself does not mention such commentaries when listing their writings, nor does any ancient author. This is noted because the name *Apocalypse* is found nowhere among the ancient Greek writers and may have received its title from Justin and Irenaeus. It is astonishing how much this passage has perplexed learned men, who search everywhere for a few verses of the Apocalypse cited by Irenaeus and Justin.]

[Note: [Col. 0625D] “Under the emperor Nerva.” Many manuscripts, especially those of the Ambrosian Library, read “under Nerva Pertinax”; others, even very ancient ones, falsely retain “under Pertinax.” MARTIAN.]

[Note: [Col. 0626B] All the manuscripts we have examined incorrectly read “under Pertinax he returned to Ephesus.” Several others, including very ancient ones, retain this reading, as does the copy used by the Greek translator, which formerly read ἐπὶ Περτίνακος, “under Pertinax.” According to Martianaeus, some manuscripts, especially those of the Ambrosian Library, read “under Nerva Pertinax” instead of “under the emperor.” This gave rise to another error, whereby copyists entirely omitted Nerva.]

[Col. 0624A] **John**, whom Jesus loved greatly, son of Zebedee and brother of James, who was beheaded by Herod after the Lord’s Passion, wrote the Gospel last of all. He was requested to do so by the bishops of Asia, against Cerinthus and the other heretics, and especially against the Ebionite doctrine then emerging, whose adherents claimed that Christ had not been born before Mary. Hence John was compelled to proclaim his divine birth.

They give another reason for this composition. After reading the books of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, John approved the style of their histories and confirmed that they had spoken the truth, but held that they had composed the history of only one year, the year in which Christ suffered, after John’s imprisonment.

Leaving aside the year whose events had been set forth by the three, John narrated the events of the earlier period, before John was thrown into prison. This can be made clear to those who carefully read the four Gospels. This also removes the apparent disagreement between John and the others.

He wrote one Epistle, whose beginning is: “What was from the beginning,” and which is approved by all ecclesiastical and learned men.

[Note: [Col. 0624D] The Greek translator attributes only the opening words, Ὃ ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, “What was from the beginning,” to the Epistle, and perhaps Jerome had quoted no more. The Veronese Codex reads: “What we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes,” and so forth.]

The other two, whose beginnings are, first, “The elder to the elect lady,” and, second, “The elder to the beloved Gaius,” are said to be by John the presbyter. His other tomb is still located at Ephesus. Some think that the two memorials are those of John the Evangelist; when we reach Papias, his hearer, in due order, we shall explain the matter.

In the fourteenth year, when Domitian was stirring up the second persecution after Nero, John was confined to the island of Patmos and composed the Apocalypse, which Justin Martyr and Irenaeus translated.

After Domitian was killed and his acts were annulled by the senate because of his great cruelty, John returned to Ephesus under Nerva. He remained there until the reign of Trajan, founding and building up all the churches of Asia. Having grown very old, he died in the sixty-eighth year after the Lord’s Passion and was granted burial near the city mentioned above.

# CHAPTER X

[Note: [Col. 0625] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0625]

[Col. 0625B] **Hermas**, whom the apostle Paul mentions when writing to the Romans—“Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brothers who are with them” (Romans 16:14)—is said to have been the author of the book entitled *The Shepherd*. It is already read publicly in certain churches of Greece.

[Note: [Col. 0626C] Some incorrectly call him “Hermes.”]

[Note: [Col. 0626C] One of our manuscripts omits Asyncritus; another omits Hermas and Hermes; a third reads “Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas,” together with the Greek translator.]

It is truly a useful book, and many ancient writers have employed testimonies from it.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] We now read “already” from our manuscript, in place of the reading that had hitherto prevailed. Eusebius likewise has ἤδη καὶ ἐν τίσιν ἐκκλησίαις, “already also in certain churches”; see Rufinus, *On the Creed*. The same manuscript lacks the words “It is truly a useful book,” though the Greek translator reads them, as does Origen in the passage cited above: “This writing,” he says, “seems very useful to me.”]

[Note: [Col. 0626C] He did not understand the force of the verb, and the Greek translator rendered it as ὑπέκλεψαν, “they secretly took.”]

But among the Latins it is almost unknown.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] Tertullian, the author of the homily *On Dice-Players* among Cyprian’s works, Philaster, Cassian, Prosper, and several others do cite it. Indeed, only the very ancient Latin translation of this book has survived.]

[Col. 0626B] **Hermas**, whom the apostle mentions in writing to the Romans—“Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, and Hermes”—is said to have been the author of a book entitled *The Shepherd*, which is publicly read in certain Eastern churches. The work is truly useful, and many ancient writers secretly appropriated testimonies from it, but it seems to be unknown among the Romans.

# CHAPTER XI

[Note: [Col. 0625] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0625]

[Col. 0625B] **Philo the Jew**, an Alexandrian by birth and of priestly descent, is placed by us among ecclesiastical writers because, when writing about the first church of the evangelist Mark at Alexandria, he praised our people. He says that they existed not only there but also in many provinces, and calls their dwellings monasteries.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] The Greek translator has “born in Alexandria,” as Suidas also relates.]

[Note: [Col. 0626D] It was already noted above, in the discussion of Mark, that Jerome derived this opinion concerning Philo’s book *On the Contemplative Life*, or *On the Supplicants*, from Eusebius, Book II, chapter 17, and translated it. Learned men commonly reject the opinion because Philo is speaking of Jews, “acquaintances of Moses,” not Christians; but it is not the place here to present their arguments.]

He says that their dwellings were monasteries.

[Note: [Col. 0627C] Certainly in that book. In praising his Therapeutae, Philo says: “For each one there is a sacred dwelling called a sanctuary and monastery,” and so forth.]

From this it is clear that the first church of those who believed in Christ was such as monks today strive and desire to be: no one possessed anything as private property, and among them there was neither rich nor poor. Their estates were distributed to the needy; they devoted themselves to prayer, the Psalms, instruction, and self-restraint, as Luke reports the first believers to have done in Jerusalem (Acts 2:44; 4:32).

They say that under Gaius Caligula Philo faced danger at Rome, where he had been sent as an envoy of his people. When he came a second time to Claudius, they say that he conversed in the same city with the apostle Peter, became his friend, and for that reason adorned with his praise the followers of Mark, Peter’s disciple, in Alexandria.

[Note: [Col. 0627C] Eusebius indeed relates this in Book II, chapter 17; but in Philo there is not the slightest trace of this conversation with Peter.]

[Note: [Col. 0627C] The Veronese manuscript supplies “also,” where Victorius had read “the Church” in his copies. He preferred to delete the word, which had evidently been corrupted by the copyists.]

Philo’s distinguished and innumerable works survive, including works on the five books of Moses; one book *On the Confusion of Languages*; one *On Nature and Invention*; one *On What We Pray for and Renounce in Our Minds*; one *On Education*; one *On the Heir of Divine Things*; one *On the Division of Equal and Opposite Things*; one *On the Three Powers*; one *On Why Certain Names in Scripture Have Been Changed*; two books *On Covenants*; one *On the Life of the Wise Person*; one *On Giants*; five books *That Dreams Are Sent by God*; five books of *Questions and Solutions in Exodus*; four books *On the Tabernacle and the Decalogue*; and works *On Victims and Promises, or Curses*; *On Providence*; *On the Jews*; *On the Conduct of Life*; *On Alexander*; *That Brute Animals Possess Their Own Reason*; *That Every Fool Is a Slave*; and one book *On the Life of Our People*, about which we spoke above—that is, concerning the apostolic men—which he entitled *On the Contemplative Life of the Supplicants*, because they contemplate heavenly things and continually pray to God.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] This book, *On the Division of Equal and Opposite Things*, is not listed in the Codex Reginae Suecorum 342. It is certainly one and the same with the preceding work, indeed the second part of its title, as Eusebius reports. I therefore do not think that Jerome was entirely wrong to divide it into two, as some confidently assert; rather, I think that the word “or,” or something similar, dropped out of Jerome’s text through an easy scribal error. It should read: “or, *On the Division* …” For Eusebius likewise joins the titles with ἢ περὶ τῆς εἰς τὰ ἴσα, “or, *On the Division into Equal Things*.” This is also evident from Jerome’s context, since he does not add “one book” or “two,” as he does with the other works, but simply says “book,” although the Greek translation is wholly incorrect in having λόγος εἷς, “one treatise.”]

[Note: [Col. 0628C] In editions of Philo this work is incorrectly divided into two.]

[Note: [Col. 0628C] The Veronese manuscript does not recognize this work; Eusebius and the Greek translator nevertheless mention it, and Suidas follows them. Philo did not write *On Nature and Invention*, but *On Flight and Finding*, entitled *On Fugitives*. Jerome therefore seems to have used a corrupt copy of Eusebius, reading περὶ φύσεως, “on nature,” instead of περὶ φυγάδων, “on fugitives,” just as Rufinus also translated it.]

[Note: [Col. 0628D] “On the Tabernacle and the Decalogue” is a single title for four books. The first book, together with part of the second, has perished; the third remains, together with part of the fourth, under the title περὶ ψευδομαρτυριῶν, “On False Testimony.” Some manuscripts have only “four books On the Tabernacle.”]

[Note: [Col. 0628D] The Veronese Codex reads “remissions”; but the Greek translator has ὑποσχέσεων, “promises,” and Philo has περὶ τῶν προκειμένων.]

[Note: [Col. 0628D] Some fragments of *On Providence* survive in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* VII.21 and VIII.14; the following *Apology for the Jews* is wholly lost.]

[Note: [Col. 0628D] Some printed editions and manuscripts read, “On Alexander, saying that …”; Philo’s book itself is now lost. The work following it appears to be the same as that entitled in Philo, περὶ τοῦ πάντα σπουδαῖον εἶναι ἐλεύθερον, “That everyone devoted to virtue is free.”]

[Note: [Col. 0629C] The Veronese Codex reads “On the Life of Our People, concerning which we spoke above,” without “one book.” This more strongly refutes the mistaken opinion of those who invent that Jerome here alludes to another lost work of Philo, *On the Conduct of Christians*.]

Under other headings there are two books *On Agriculture* and two *On Drunkenness*.

[Note: [Col. 0629C] Our manuscript does not list the two works *On Drunkenness*; in printed editions of Philo they are joined into one.]

There are also other monuments of his intellect that have not reached our hands.

[Note: [Col. 0629C] These can be seen in editions of Philo’s works. As for his omission here of the book *On the Interpretation of Hebrew Names*, which he had already translated from Greek, I think this happened because it was better known under Origen’s name.]

A Greek proverb is commonly said about him: ἢ Πλάτων φιλωνίζει, ἢ Φίλων πλατωνίζει—“Either Plato follows Philo, or Philo follows Plato.” Such is the similarity of their thought and expression.

[Col. 0626B] **Philo the Jew**, born in Alexandria and of priestly descent, is placed among ecclesiastical writers by us because, when writing about the first church of Mark the Evangelist in Alexandria, he turned to praise our people. He says that they existed not only there but also in many provinces, and calls their dwellings monasteries.

From this it is clear that the first church of those who believed in Christ was like the monks of today, whom they strive and desire to imitate: no one possessed anything privately, and among them there was neither rich nor poor. They distributed their possessions to the nations [as printed] and devoted themselves to prayers, psalms, instruction, and self-restraint, like those whom Luke reports to have first been believers in Jerusalem.

They say that under Gaius Caligula Philo faced danger at Rome, where he had been sent as envoy of his own people. When he came a second time to Claudius, they say that he conversed in that same city with the apostle Peter and became his friend; for this reason he adorned with praise the followers in Alexandria of Mark, Peter’s disciple.

His distinguished and innumerable works include the following: works on the five books of Moses; one treatise *On the Confusion of Languages*; *On Nature and Invention*; one treatise *On What We Pray for and Renounce in Our Minds*; one *On Education*; one *On the Heir of Divine Things*; one *On the Division of Equal and Opposite Things*; one *On the Three Powers*; one *On the Changes Made in the Scriptures*; two treatises *On Covenants*; one *On the Philosophical Life*; one *On Giants*; five treatises *That Dreams Are Sent by God*; five treatises of *Questions and Interpretations of Exodus*; four treatises *On the Tabernacle and the Decalogue*; works *On Sacrifices*; *On Promises or Curses*; *On Providence*; *On the Jews*; *On the Conduct of Life*; *On Alexander*; *That Brute Animals Possess Their Own Reason*; *That Every Fool Is a Slave*; and *On the Conduct of Our People*, concerning which we spoke above—that is, concerning the apostles—which he entitled *On the Contemplative Life of the Supplicants*, meaning that they gaze upon heavenly things and always pray to God. There are also two treatises *On Agriculture* and two *On Drunkenness*.

There are other works of his that have not yet come into our hands. Concerning him there is the Greek proverb: “Either Plato follows Philo, or Philo follows Plato.” Such is the similarity of their thought and expression.

# CHAPTER XII

[Note: [Col. 0629] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0629]

[Col. 0629A] **Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Corduba**, a pupil of the Stoic Sotion and the paternal uncle of the poet Lucan, led a highly austere life. I would not have placed him in the catalogue of saints if those letters had not prompted me—letters widely read as being from Paul to Seneca and from Seneca to Paul.

[Note: [Col. 0629D] Two of our manuscripts, and those used by Honorius, incorrectly read “Photinus”; the Greek translator also formerly read σώζοντα. Seneca himself calls him Sotion in Letter 49—that is, the Alexandrian Stoic whom Jerome mentions in his *Chronicle* under the fifty-fifth year of Augustus—and many others do likewise.]

[Note: [Col. 0629D] The finest Vatican Codex 342, formerly belonging to the queen, reads not “in the catalogue of saints” but “in the catalogue of treatise-writers.” I greatly prefer this reading and regard it as Jerome’s, although Pseudosophronius, who encountered a corrupt copy of Jerome, translates τῶν ἁγίων, “of the saints.” Perhaps Jerome wrote “in the catalogue of sacred writers,” a category that could include not only Seneca and Philo but also the heresiarchs whom he lists, and anyone who had spoken about sacred matters. But after the second word was lost, the scribes corrupted the whole passage.]

[Col. 0629B] While he was Nero’s teacher and the most powerful man of that time, Seneca said that he wished to hold among his own people the position Paul held among Christians.

[Note: [Col. 0630C] The Veronese manuscript reads “or Seneca.” These letters still exist: five under Paul’s name and eight under Seneca’s. Everyone admits that they are spurious. Jerome does not assert that they are genuine, but only that they were commonly attributed to and read under those names. Saint Augustine also mentions them in his letter to Macedonius.]

[Note: [Col. 0630C] Seneca’s sixth letter to Paul: “What position I hold with you, may you hold with me; what position you hold, I wish were mine.”]

Two years before Peter and Paul received the crown of martyrdom, Seneca was killed by Nero.

[Note: [Col. 0630C] That is, in Christ’s year 66, according to Jerome’s reckoning.]

[Col. 0630A] **Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Corduba**, a pupil of the Stoic Sotion and the paternal uncle of the poet Lucan, was extremely self-controlled. I would not have counted him in the catalogue of the saints if his letters had not encouraged me—letters read by many as letters from Paul to Seneca and from Seneca to Paul.

As Nero’s teacher and a powerful man at that time, he wished to have among his own people the position Paul held among Christians. Two years before the apostles Peter and Paul suffered, Seneca was killed by Nero.

# CHAPTER XIII

[Note: [Col. 0629] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0629]

[Col. 0629B] **Josephus**, son of Matthias, a priest from Jerusalem, was captured by Vespasian and retained with his son Titus. Coming to Rome, he presented to the two emperors, father and son, seven books on the Jewish captivity. These were also delivered to the public library, and, because of the glory of his talent, he deserved a statue at Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0630C] The printed editions and manuscripts followed by Martianaeus have “Mattathias,” but “Matthias” should be read with the other copies; Valesius established this in his notes on Eusebius, Book III, chapter 9.]

[Note: [Col. 0630D] Josephus, in his *Life*, says δημοσιεῦσαι προσέταξεν, “he ordered that they be made public,” which Jerome has not rendered very precisely as “they were delivered to the public library.” Titus ordered that they be published; indeed, he wrote several words with his own hand in Josephus’s books to attest that what had been written there about the war was true.]

He also wrote twenty books of *Antiquities*, from the beginning of the world to the fourteenth year of Caesar Domitian, and two books of *Antiquity* against the Alexandrian grammarian Apion, who, having been sent as an envoy from the Gentile side under Caligula, had also written a book against Philo containing an attack on the Jewish people.

[Note: [Col. 0630D] The excellent manuscript used by us does not contain “and others,” nor does the Greek translator recognize it.]

Another of his books, entitled *On the Sovereignty of Reason* (περὶ Αὐτοκράτορος λογισμοῦ), is considered highly elegant; in it he also arranged an account of the martyrdoms of the Maccabees.

In the eighteenth book of the *Antiquities* he most explicitly confesses that, because of the magnitude of his miracles, Christ was killed by the Pharisees, that John the Baptist was truly a prophet, and that Jerusalem was destroyed because of the killing of the apostle James.

[Note: [Col. 0631C] The subject is discussed above, in chapter 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0631C] He also wrote about the Lord. Here is the famous testimony of Josephus concerning the Lord Christ, translated into Latin by Jerome with such prudence and learning that he anticipated all the learned men who admit that Josephus’s Greek words, ὁ Χριστὸς οὗτος ἦν, “he was the Christ,” cannot be understood as they stand but according to the author’s meaning. Jerome expressed this excellently by saying, “and he was believed to be the Christ.” See the *Evangelical Demonstration* of the learned P. Daniel Huet, Proposition III, pp. 27ff. MARTIAN.]

He wrote about the Lord as follows:

“At that time there was Jesus, a wise man—if indeed one ought to call him a man. For he was a performer of marvelous works and a teacher of those who gladly receive the truth. He attracted many followers, both Jews and Gentiles, and he was believed to be the Christ. When Pilate, at the instigation of our leading men, condemned him to the cross, those who had first loved him nevertheless did not cease to do so.

[Note: [Col. 0631D] Freculphus, who often cites this passage, does not have the word “to be”; the Nuremberg Codex instead reads “also.” Josephus’s words, ὁ Χριστὸς οὗτος ἦν, cannot possibly be understood as having been written by Josephus in the sense conveyed by Jerome, if they are genuinely his. The question of the testimony’s authenticity is not to be discussed here. Rather, observe that Sophronius cites it as it stands in Josephus’s Book XVIII, chapter 4, not, as he often does elsewhere, expressing it through a new translation by Jerome.]

“For he appeared to them alive again on the third day. The divine prophets had foretold these and countless other things about him. And to this day the tribe of Christians, named after him, has not disappeared.”

[Note: [Col. 0631D] The same Freculphus and the Veronese Codex omit the first occurrence of “who”; several manuscripts add “in faith” after “persevered”; Freculphus has “in him.” The same source below does not recognize the name “Christians.”]

[Col. 0630B] **Josephus**, son of Matthias, a priest of Jerusalem, was captured by Vespasian and kept with his son Titus. When he came to Rome, he presented seven treatises on the Jewish captivity to the two emperors, father and son; these were deposited in the public library. Because of the reputation of his talent, he was honored with a statue.

He also wrote twenty books of the *Antiquities*, from the beginning of the world to the fourteenth year of Caesar Domitian, and two books of *Antiquities* against the Alexandrian grammarian Apion, who, having been sent as an envoy from the Gentile side under Caligula, wrote a book against Philo containing an accusation of the Jews.

He also wrote another treatise, *On the Sovereignty of Reason*, very distinguished indeed, in which he mentioned the suffering of the Maccabees.

In the eighteenth book of the *Antiquities* he openly acknowledges that Christ was killed by the Pharisees because of the magnitude of his signs, that John the Baptist truly became a prophet, and that Jerusalem was devastated because of the killing of James the apostle.

He also wrote about the Lord as follows:

“At that time there arose Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it is proper to call him a man. For he was a worker of extraordinary deeds and a teacher of people who gladly receive the truth. He won over many Jews and also many from the Greek world; this man was the Christ.

“And when Pilate, at the accusation of our leading men, had condemned him to the cross, those who had first loved him did not cease. For he appeared to them alive again on the third day, while the divine prophets had spoken of these and countless other things about him. And to this day the tribe of Christians, named after him, has not ceased.”

# CHAPTER XIV

[Note: [Col. 0631] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0631]

[Col. 0631B] **Justus of Tiberias**, from the province of Galilee, also attempted to compose a history of Jewish affairs and to compile certain brief commentaries on the Scriptures. But Josephus accuses him of lying (*Life of Justus*). It is certain that he wrote at the same time as Josephus.

[Note: [Col. 0631D] The Codex of the Holy Cross and others, as well as Honorius, incorrectly read “Justin.” See Eusebius III, 10.]

[Note: [Col. 0631D] In some editions the words “on the Scriptures” are omitted; Suffridus Petri himself thought that they were superfluous. The Greek formerly had περιγράφειν, “to outline” or “describe.”]

[Note: [Col. 0632C] Our manuscripts do not add the verb “to compose,” nor does the Greek translator. The writings of this author have perished.]

[Col. 0632B] **Justus of Tiberias**, of the province of Galilee, also attempted to compose a Jewish history and certain notes on the Scriptures. But Josephus exposes him as a liar. He wrote at the same time as Josephus.

# CHAPTER XV

[Note: [Col. 0631] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0631]

[Col. 0631C] **Clement**, whom the apostle Paul mentions in his letter to the Philippians when he says, “with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are written in the book of life” (Philippians 4:3), was the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter. Linus was second, Anacletus third, although most Latins think that Clement was second after the apostle Peter.

[Note: [Col. 0632C] Origen, in his work on John; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 15; Epiphanius, *Against the Heresies* 27; Rufinus, *On the Adulteration of Origen’s Books*; Primasius, in his commentary on this passage of the Epistle to the Philippians; and many other more recent writers agree with Jerome. Nevertheless, others argue, on substantial grounds, that the Clement whom Paul names was a different person and was a presbyter of the Philippian Church.]
