[Note: [Col. 0632D] “Anacletus was third.” All the manuscripts agree in this reading. Let Marianus therefore explain where he introduced “Cletus” into Jerome’s text in place of Anacletus. MARTIAN. Martianaeus and all the manuscripts we examined read “Anacletus”; only the Veronese has “Anencletus,” and Irenaeus has Ἀνέγκλητος. Freculphus, Ado, Honorius, and others also read this way. Victorius preferred “Cletus,” as it appeared in the Greek translator. However one writes it, learned men do not regard Cletus as a person different from Anacletus.]

[Note: [Col. 0632D] The name “Peter” is absent from our manuscript and from the Greek translator. What follows is taken from Eusebius, Book III.]

He wrote, on behalf of the Church of Rome, a very useful Epistle to the Church of the Corinthians. It is publicly read in some places, and it seems to me to correspond in style to the Epistle circulated under Paul’s name to the Hebrews. It also makes extensive use of that Epistle, not only in its ideas but even in the order of its words. The resemblance between the two is altogether great.

A second Epistle is also attributed to him, but it is rejected by the ancients. There is also a lengthy *Disputation of Peter and Apion*, which Eusebius refutes in the third book of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

[Note: [Col. 0633C] This *Disputation of Peter and Apion*, mentioned by Photius in Codex 125, has perished. The first Epistle survives, but is defective in one place; the second survives for the greater part.]

Clement died in Trajan’s third year.

[Note: [Col. 0633C] That is, in Christ’s year 100. The Codex of the Holy Cross has “and his name,” which is preferable.]

A church built at Rome preserves his memory to this day.

[Col. 0632C] **Clement**, whom the apostle Paul mentions in writing to the Philippians—“with Clement”—was the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter. Linus was second and Anacletus third, although many Romans suppose that Clement was second after the apostle.

He wrote, on behalf of the Church of Rome, a very remarkable Epistle to the Church at Corinth. It is publicly read in public places and agrees in character with Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, not only in meaning but also in wording. In short, the resemblance between the two is very great.

Another Epistle is circulated under his name, but it is rejected by everyone. There is also a *Dialogue of Peter and Apion*, composed as a lengthy work, which Eusebius censures in the third book of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

Clement died in Trajan’s third year, and a church built at Rome preserves his memory to this day.

# CHAPTER XVI

[Note: [Col. 0633] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0633]

[The supplied source ends here.]

[Col. 0633B] 855 Ignatius, third bishop of the Church of Antioch after the Apostle Peter, was condemned to the beasts when Trajan stirred up persecution and was sent to Rome in chains. While sailing, he came to Smyrna, where Polycarp, a hearer of John, was bishop. He wrote one Letter to the Ephesians, another to the Magnesians, a third to the Trallians, a fourth to the Romans; and, departing from there, he wrote to the Philadelphians and to the Smyrnaeans, and separately to Polycarp, commending to him the Church of Antioch. In that letter he also cites, concerning the person of Christ, a testimony from the Gospel that was recently translated by me, saying:

[Col. 0633C] Eusebius, Book III, chapter 36, confesses that he does not know this; Jerome testifies that the passage was taken from the Gospel of the Nazarenes. See also Book XVIII on Isaiah. It is also found in another apocryphal book, namely the *Teaching of Peter*. Ignatius, however, does not quote it in the Letter to Polycarp, as the holy Doctor suggests, but in the Letter to the Smyrnaeans. Learned men have therefore thought that this passage could be corrected if enclosed in parentheses.

[Col. 0633D] It should be noted that the Greek lacks the words ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ, “by me,” although Jerome says “translated by me.” See chapters 2 and 3.

[Col. 0633D] Ignatius, *Letter to the Smyrnaeans*, chapter 3: “But I know that he was in the flesh even after the resurrection, and I believe that he exists. And when he came to those around Peter, he said to them: ‘Take hold of me, touch me, and see that I am not a bodiless demon.’ And immediately they touched him and believed.”

> But I also saw him in the flesh after the resurrection, and I believe that he exists. And when he came to Peter and to those who were with Peter, he said to them: “Behold, touch me [Col. 0633C] and see, for I am not a bodiless demon.”

[Col. 0633D] The Greek text has οἶδα, whence Rufinus’s *novi*: that is, “I know that he truly rose again.” For, I think, Ignatius did not see our Savior in the flesh, nor does he argue from autopsy (αὐτοψία, personal observation).

[Col. 0633D] “A bodiless demon.” Erasmus incorrectly read “bodily” on the basis of several manuscript copies. But “bodiless,” not “bodily,” is what Jerome himself teaches us to read in the Preface to his eighteenth book of *Commentaries on Isaiah*. Consult the passage, where “spirit” and “bodiless demon” are treated as equivalent. Moreover, our oldest of all manuscripts, the Sangermanensis, reads “bodiless”; so too the highly distinguished codex of Cardinal Ottoboni, formerly of the Altemps library, already mentioned. MARTIAN. — The Greek translator incorrectly has σωματικόν, “bodily,” as do certain Latin manuscripts. All ours, and those consulted by Martianay, have “bodiless,” as Jerome himself has elsewhere in the Preface to Book XVIII on Isaiah: “For when the Apostles thought that he was a Spirit, or, according to the Gospel read by the Nazarenes, a bodiless demon.”

And immediately they touched him and believed. Since it seems appropriate, now that we have mentioned so great a man, to set down a few passages from his Letter to the Romans [another reading: “which he wrote”].

[Col. 0634D] Ignatius, *Letter to the Romans*, chapter 5: “From Syria to Rome I fight with beasts, by land and sea, night and day, bound to ten leopards—that is, a military detachment—which, even when treated well, become worse. By their wrongs I am instructed more fully; yet for this I have not been justified. May I enjoy the beasts prepared for me, which I pray may be found swift for me, and which I shall entice to devour me quickly—not like some who, frightened, did not touch me. And even if they do not wish it, I shall force them. Bear with me: I know what is advantageous for me. Now I am beginning to be a disciple; may nothing visible or invisible arouse my jealousy, so that I may attain Jesus Christ. Let fire and cross, companies of beasts, scattering of bones, cutting apart of limbs, grinding of the whole body, and punishments of the Devil come upon me, provided only that I attain Jesus Christ.”

> From Syria to Rome I fight with beasts, on sea and land, night and day, [Col. 0635A] bound to ten leopards—[Col. 0635C] that is, soldiers who guard me [Note: Saint Paul likewise called Nero a lion.]—who, even when treated well, become worse. Their wickedness, however, is my instruction, but for that reason I have not been justified. May I enjoy the beasts prepared for me, which I pray may be found swift for my destruction, [Col. 0635C] All our manuscripts and certain editions likewise read “for my destruction” and “I shall entice them to eat me,” and quite rightly; not, as Martianay and others add, “and for punishments,” which is contradicted by the Greek text and its translator. From the word *alliciam*, imperfectly understood by copyists, arose the two corrupt readings “for punishments” and “to entice them,” wrongly intruded into the text. and I shall entice them to eat me, lest, as with certain other martyrs, they dare not touch my body. But if they are unwilling to come, I shall use force; I shall thrust myself upon them, so that I may be devoured. Forgive me, little children: I know what is beneficial for me. Now I am beginning [Col. 0635D] to be a disciple of Christ [Note: The name “Christ” is absent from the excellent Verona manuscript and others, as well as from the Greek text and translator.] desiring nothing of the things that are seen [Note: Ignatius and Eusebius add τῶν ὁρατῶν καὶ ἀοράτων, “the things that are seen and the things that are not seen”; the former phrase easily dropped out of Jerome’s text.], so that I may find Jesus Christ. May fire, cross, beasts, breaking of bones, division of limbs, crushing of the whole body, and [Col. 0635D] all the torments of the Devil come upon me, provided only that I may enjoy Christ.

[Col. 0635D] The word “whole” is found neither in the Greek text nor in our manuscripts. They correctly have “punishments,” followed by “roaring,” without the additional “him,” which is redundant. The Gembloux manuscript has “with impatient heat,” less correctly.

When he had already been condemned to the beasts, and, consumed by his eagerness to suffer, heard the lions roaring, he said: “I am Christ’s grain; I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, so that I may be found pure bread.” He suffered in the eleventh year of Trajan.

[Col. 0635D] The Vatican manuscript and certain others incorrectly read “the eleventh.” Trajan’s tenth year corresponds to A.D. 107, although John of Antioch and others assign it to 115.

His bodily remains lie at Antioch, outside the Daphne Gate, in the cemetery.

[Col. 0636C] The gate was so called from Daphne, a suburb of Antioch to the east. See Evagrius, Book I, chapter 16.

[Col. 0634B] 856 Ignatius, third bishop of the Church at Antioch after Peter the Apostle, was sent to Rome in chains when Trajan had stirred up persecution and ordered him to fight with beasts. While sailing and arriving at Smyrna, where Polycarp, a hearer of John, was bishop, he wrote one Letter to the Ephesians, another to the Magnesians, a third to the Trallians, and a fourth to the Romans. Departing from there, he wrote to the Philadelphians, to the Smyrnaeans, and separately to Polycarp, entrusting to him the Church at Antioch. In it he also makes mention, speaking in the person of Jesus Christ, of the Gospel previously translated, saying:

> “But I also saw him in the body after the resurrection, and I believe that he exists. And when he came to Peter and those who were with him, he said to them: ‘Touch me, for I am not a bodily demon.’” And immediately [Col. 0634C] they touched him and believed.

[Col. 0634D] It should be read as we have printed it, ἅψαντες, “having touched”; I do not know why a recent editor changed it to ὄψαντες, “having seen,” without informing the reader.

Since it seems fitting, now that we have commemorated such a man, to present a few passages from his Letter to the Romans:

> “From Syria to Rome I fight with beasts on sea and land, night and day, bound to ten leopards—that is, soldiers who guard me, [Col. 0636A] who become worse even after receiving benefits. For their lawlessness is my instruction, but I was not justified because of this. May I enjoy the beasts prepared for me—which I pray may be found exceedingly swift for my destruction—and may they persist in devouring me, lest, as happened with the other martyrs, they dare to touch my body. For if they are unwilling to come, I shall force them, longing to be devoured. Forgive me, children; I know what is beneficial for me. Now I am beginning to be a disciple; I desire none of these visible things, so that I may find Jesus Christ. Let fire, cross, beasts, breaking of bones, tearing apart of limbs, crushing of the whole body, and torments of the Devil come upon me, so that I may enjoy Jesus Christ.”

Having therefore been condemned to fight with beasts, and, from his desire to suffer, having heard the roar [Col. 0636B] of the lions, he said:

> “I am the grain of Jesus Christ, and I pray to be ground by the teeth of the beasts, so that I may be found pure bread.”

He suffered in the tenth year of Trajan. His remains lie outside the Daphne Gate of Antioch, in the cemetery.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Note: [Col. 0635] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0635]

[Col. 0635B] Polycarp, a disciple of the Apostle John, who was appointed bishop of Smyrna by him, was the leading man of all Asia. For he had as teachers, and had seen, some of the Apostles and of those who had seen the Lord. Because of certain questions concerning the day of Easter, under the emperor Antoninus Pius, while Anicetus governed the Church in Rome, he came to Rome, where he brought back to the faith many believers who had been deceived by the persuasion of Marcion and Valentinus. When Marcion happened to meet him and said:

[Col. 0636C] Thus all our manuscripts and many others read; others likewise have “do you know us?” Similarly, some read “of Satan,” others “of the Devil.”

> “Recognize us,”

he replied:

> “I recognize the firstborn of the Devil.”

Afterward, during the reign of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, in the fourth persecution after Nero, at Smyrna, while the Proconsul was seated and the whole people were shouting against him in the amphitheater, he was handed over to the fire.

[Col. 0636D] This was Lucius Aurelius Verus, who was also called Commodus. Accordingly, some learned men, following Jerome, date Polycarp’s martyrdom to A.D. 166; others maintain that he suffered under Antoninus Pius in A.D. 147. The letter of the Church of Smyrna also relates his manner of death differently: when the fire did the holy martyr no harm, a κομφέκτορας—that is, an executioner—was summoned and killed him with a dagger.

[Col. 0636D] This was Statius Quadratus, Proconsul of Asia.

He wrote a very useful Letter to the Philippians, which is still read today in the assembly of Asia.

[Col. 0636D] This passage does not seem to refer to the daily gatherings of Christians, but to some other assembly that used to take place annually in Asia, at which Christians, consulting about religion, would read this Letter.

[Col. 0636B] Polycarp, a disciple of the Apostle John, appointed by him bishop of the Smyrnaeans, became the leader of all Asia, because he had met many of the Apostles and of those who had seen Christ, and had had them as teachers. For certain reasons concerning Easter, while Antoninus Pius was reigning and Anicetus was bishop of the Church of Rome, he came to Rome, where he recalled to the faith many who had believed the teaching of Marcion and Valentinus. When Marcion happened to meet him and said to him, “Recognize us,” he replied, “I recognize the firstborn of the Devil.”

After this, while Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus were reigning, when the fourth persecution after Nero had arisen, and the Proconsul was presiding at Smyrna while the whole populace in the amphitheater shouted against him, he was delivered to the fire. He wrote a very remarkable Letter to the Philippians, which is read to the present day in the Asian assembly.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Note: [Col. 0637] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0637]

[Col. 0637A] 859 Papias, a hearer of John and bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, wrote only five books, which he entitled *Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord*.

[Col. 0637C] Eusebius, Book III, chapter 39, understands John here to be the other John, the presbyter, not the Apostle and Evangelist; Baronius follows him in the *Martyrology*. Jerome himself, however, in Letter 75 to Theodora, as do the other authors of martyrologies and a host of other writers, takes him to be the Apostle.

In them, asserting in his preface that he did not follow various opinions but had the Apostles as his authorities, he says:

[Col. 0637C] Only certain fragments of this work, *Exposition of the Lord’s Sayings*, survive.

[Col. 0637C] Papias in Eusebius, Book III, chapter 39: “I considered what Andrew or Peter had said, or Philip, or Thomas, or James, or John, or Matthew, or any other of the Lord’s disciples; and what Aristion and the elder John, disciples of the Lord, were saying. For I did not suppose that things from books benefited me so much as what came from a living and abiding voice.”

> I considered what Andrew had said, what Peter had said, what Philip had said, what Thomas had said, what James had said, what John had said, what Matthew had said, or any other of the Lord’s disciples; and also what Aristion and the elder John, disciples of the Lord, were saying. For books do not benefit me so much for reading as does a living voice, still resounding in its authors to the present day.

[Col. 0637D] The manuscript of the Holy Cross has “Ariston” here and below, as does another manuscript at Gembloux, according to Suffridus Petri. The Verona manuscript shortly afterward reads “they speak” instead of “they were speaking,” more accurately corresponding to Papias’s text, λέγουσιν.

From this very list of names it is clear that there was one John who is counted among the Apostles and another elder John, whom he lists after Aristion. We have said this because of the opinion mentioned above, which we reported as handed down by many: that the last two Letters of John belong not to the Apostle but to the Presbyter.

[Col. 0637D] Above, chapter 9. The Verona manuscript reads: “which we reported as handed down by many.”

This man is said to have published a Jewish *δευτέρωσις*—a “secondary exposition”—of a thousand years, which was followed by Irenaeus, Apollinarius, and the others who say that after the resurrection the Lord will reign bodily with the saints. Tertullian also, in his book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, as well as Victorinus of Petabium and Lactantius, were led by this opinion.

[Col. 0637D] It is well known that Jewish traditions are called by this name. See Irenaeus, Books IV and V. The writings of Apollinarius have perished, as has the book of Tertullian that he cites, *On the Hope of the Faithful*. Jerome, in his commentary on Ezekiel 36, says: “The Jewish doctrine, which many of our own people also promise—especially Tertullian’s book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, the seventh volume of Lactantius’s *Institutions*, and the frequent expositions of Victorinus, bishop of Petovium, as well as our recent Severus in the Dialogue to which he gave the name *Gallus*—and, to name Greeks and join the first with the last, Irenaeus and Apollinarius.”

[Col. 0638A] 860 Papias, a hearer of John and bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, composed only five books, which he entitled *Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord*. In them, saying in his preface that he did not follow diverse reports but regarded the Apostles as his authorities, he said:

> “I considered what Andrew had said, what Peter had said, what Philip had said, what Thomas had said, what James had said, what John had said, what Matthew had said, and what the other disciples of the Lord had spoken; and also what Aristion and the elder John, disciples of the Lord, had said. For books do not benefit me so much for reading as does a living voice, which to the present day flourishes in those who composed them.”

It is shown by this list of names that one John was the Apostle, while another was the elder John, whom he numbers afterward, after Aristion. We have said this because of what was mentioned earlier, where we said that the last two Letters were not those of John the Apostle but of the Presbyter. This man is said to have published a Jewish *δευτέρωσις* of a thousand years, which was followed by Irenaeus, Apollinarius, and the rest, who maintain that after the resurrection the Lord will reign bodily with the saints. Tertullian also, in his book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, together with Victorinus of Petabium and Lactantius, was drawn toward this opinion.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Note: [Col. 0637] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0637]

[Col. 0637B] Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles, was appointed in his place as bishop of Athens after Publius, who was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, and he gathered together by his faith and diligence the Church, which had been scattered in great terror.

[Col. 0638C] The Verona manuscript reads “crowned by martyrdom for Christ,” supported by the Greek translator, ὑπὲρ τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Jerome consistently identifies here, and in Letter 78 to Magnus, the Quadratus who was bishop of Athens with the man who presented an Apology for the Christian religion to Hadrian. Nevertheless, learned men—Valesius, Tillemont, and others—imagine two different Quadratuses.

When Hadrian had spent the winter at Athens, visiting Eleusis and having been initiated into nearly all the sacred rites of Greece, he gave those who hated Christians an opportunity to harass believers without an imperial order. Quadratus presented him with a book composed in defense of our religion, very useful and full of reason and faith, worthy of apostolic teaching. In it, demonstrating also the antiquity of his own age, he says that he had seen many persons who, under the Lord, had been healed of various afflictions in Judaea, and some who had risen from the dead.

[Col. 0638D] We have preferred the reading of our manuscript, “visiting Eleusis,” which is also retained by the Gembloux manuscript examined by Suffridus. All the others, including the printed editions, incorrectly read “Eleusinian.” Jerome explains what it means to visit Eleusis—or, as he says in the Letter to Magnus, “to visit the rites of Eleusis”—in his *Chronicle* under Hadrian’s seventh year: “to be initiated into the rites of Eleusis,” in Greek τὰ Ἐλευσίνια ἐποπτεύειν. Facundus of Hermiane quotes this entire chapter of Jerome.

[Col. 0638D] Our manuscript shortly afterward reads “very necessary”; the Gembloux manuscript has “for his action.” Both are incorrect. This *Apology*, by which the most serious persecution was calmed, as Jerome testifies in the Letter to Magnus mentioned above, no longer exists. It is preferable to suppose that it was presented to Hadrian when he came to Athens a second time, not the first, as is commonly believed—namely, in A.D. 126, not three years earlier.

[Col. 0638B] Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles, succeeded to the same position after Publius, bishop of Athens, had suffered for Christ, and he gathered together the Church, which had been scattered in great confusion. When Hadrian spent the winter at Athens, having come to Eleusis and been initiated into nearly all the mysteries of Greece, he gave an opportunity to those who hated Christians to punish them even without an imperial command. Quadratus presented a book composed in defense of our religion, very useful and full of reason and faith, worthy of apostolic instruction. In it, showing the antiquity of his own age, he said that he had seen many people who, while suffering various illnesses in Judaea under the Lord, had been healed, and that some had risen from the dead.

## CHAPTER XX

[Note: [Col. 0639] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0639]

[Col. 0639A] Aristides, an Athenian philosopher of the greatest eloquence, and, while still wearing his former [Col. 0639C] attire—that is, the philosophical dress or cloak—[Note: The Holy Cross manuscript below incorrectly has “under the emperor Hadrian.” Jerome’s Letter to Magnus reads: “Aristides the philosopher, a man of great eloquence, presented to that same prince [Hadrian] an Apology for the Christians, composed from the opinions of philosophers.” One writer has claimed that this distinguished Apology lies hidden among the monks at the monastery of Midilli.] a disciple of Christ, presented to the emperor Hadrian, at the same time as Quadratus, a volume containing an account of our doctrine—that is, an *Apology for the Christians*. It survives to the present day and is, among scholars of literature, evidence of his talent.

[Col. 0640A] Aristides, an eloquent Athenian philosopher, and, according to his former way of life, a disciple of Jesus Christ, presented to the emperor Hadrian, at the time when Quadratus also did so, a work filled with reasoning concerning our doctrine—that is, an Apology on behalf of the Christians—which remains preserved to the present day among men of letters.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 0639] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0639]

[Col. 0639B] Agrippa, surnamed Castor [Note: Martianay has “Castor,” as does Eusebius, Ἀγρίππα Κάστορος. The Gembloux manuscript and the *Index of Heresies* attributed to Jerome have “Pastor,” entirely incorrectly.], a very learned man, argued most vigorously against the twenty-four books of the heretic Basilides, which he had composed as an exposition of the Gospel [Note: Agrippa’s work has perished, as have the books of Basilides, which may perhaps have been entitled *Gospel*. Jerome and others seem to mention them elsewhere by this name.]. He exposed all his mysteries and enumerated his prophets, Barcaban and Barcob [Note: The manuscripts read “Barcaban and Barcob.” Some have “Berthaham and Barcobeth.” For these monstrous names and the name Abraxas, see our indexes above in Volume IV and in the preceding Volume III of our edition. See also the discussion of Antinous below in Hegesippus. For Cocheba, see the commentary on Daniel 9, column 1117, and the Letter *Lectis litteris*. For Abraxas and the other names, consult Irenaeus, Book IV, chapter 23. MARTIAN. — It is remarkable how variously these two barbarous names appear in printed books and manuscripts, and how corruptly. Ours first read “Barchabbam,” with double b, as do Eusebius and other Greek witnesses, Βαρκαββᾶν. The second is “Barcob” or “Barcho.” I would prefer restoring “Barcop,” which better corresponds to Eusebius’s Βαρκώφ. In Theodoret, *Haereticarum Fabularum Compendium* I.4, and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* X.5, and in Jerome’s Letter to Paula on the alphabet, it sounds like “son of calling,” just as Βαρκαββᾶν in Epiphanius XXVI.2 means “son of fornication” or “parricide.” Hence those who read “Barchobeth,” “Berthabam,” “Marcob,” “Barchon,” “Barcobbam,” or “Barcobbet” are certainly corrupt.], and, to terrify his hearers, certain other barbarous names. He also discussed his greatest god, Abraxas, whose name, when calculated according to the Greek numerical system, contains the number of a year [Note: I would prefer “contains” or “is reckoned as,” with the particle “if” deleted, since it was imported here from the *Index of Heresies*. The letters composing the name Ἀβράξας, when reckoned according to the Greek numerals, yield 365, the number of days in the year. See our notes in the Letter to Theodora.].

Basilides, from whom the Gnostics arose, lived in Alexandria during the reign of Hadrian, at the same time when Cochebas, leader of the Jewish faction, put Christians to death by various tortures.

[Col. 0640D] “He lived,” not “he died”: the Sangermanensis manuscript and many others read “he lived.” MARTIAN. — All our manuscripts, the Sangermanensis cited by Martianay, and other royal manuscripts read this way. Jerome himself, in the *Chronicle* under A.D. 133, says: “Basilides, founder of the heresy, resides in Alexandria; from him come the Gnostics.” See the *Chronicle*, page 709. As for the reading preferred by some, namely “he died,” because we supposedly read *moratus* for *mortuus*, just as in the *Chronicle* *commoratur* is read for *moritur*, we pray that our wretched detractor may acquire better judgment.

[Col. 0640D] In certain Jerome manuscripts the name is “Chozebas.” Thus that impostor, “son of falsehood,” was sometimes called, although his proper name was Cochebas, “son of the star.”

[Col. 0640B] Agrippa, surnamed Castor, a very learned man, argued vigorously against the twenty-four books of the heretic Basilides that he had composed as an exposition of the Gospel. He exposed all his mysteries and enumerated the prophets, Barcaban and Marcob, together with certain other barbarous names intended to frighten the hearers, and his greatest god, Abraxas, who, as though containing a year, is calculated according to the Greek numerical system. When Basilides was nearing death, the Gnostics were called so in Alexandria during the reign of Hadrian; at that time Cochebos, the leader of the Jews, also destroyed many Christians by various tortures.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Note: [Col. 0639] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0639]

[Col. 0639C] Hegesippus, who lived near the times of the Apostles, weaving together histories of ecclesiastical events from the Passion of the Lord down to his own age, and gathering from various sources many things useful to readers, composed five books in a simple style, so that he might reproduce even in his manner of speaking the character of those whose life he followed.

[Col. 0640D] Only certain fragments of this distinguished work remain, which Halloix and Grabe collected. See Eusebius.

He says that he came to Rome under Anicetus, who was the tenth bishop after Peter, and remained there until Eleutherus, bishop of the same city, who had formerly been Anicetus’s deacon.

[Col. 0641C] These are the words of Hegesippus in Eusebius IV.22: “When I was in Rome, I composed the succession down to Anicetus, whose deacon was Eleutherus. And after Anicetus, Soter succeeded; after him, Eleutherus.” This may be rendered in Latin: “When I was in Rome, I arranged the succession down to Anicetus, whose deacon was Eleutherus; and Soter succeeded Anicetus, and after him Eleutherus.” Jerome, as learned men have already noted, does not interpret διαδοχὴν ἐποιησάμην correctly when he renders it “I remained in Rome,” or, as Rufinus himself does, “I stayed there,” instead of “I composed or arranged a succession.”

Moreover, while arguing against idols and explaining from what original error they first grew, he inserted a history showing in what period he flourished. For he says:

[Col. 0641D] In Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* II.8: “They made tombs for the dead and temples, as we still see to the present day. Among these is Antinous, the slave of Hadrian Caesar, for whom a gymnastic contest is held at [Note: It was not at the city of Antinous that a gymnastic contest was customarily held for Antinous, but at Mantinea, as Pausanias writes in the *Arcadica*: ‘The king established honors and a festival for him at Mantinea … and a contest is held for him every fifth year.’ I would therefore prefer to correct the text on the authority of our excellent manuscript: ‘a contest in honor of Antinous is held, and a city was founded in his name,’ especially since the same Hegesippus says οὗ καὶ ἀγὼν ἄγεται Ἀντινόειος, and so forth.] the city of Antinous, which he founded in his name, [Note: These final words, κατέστησεν ἐν τῷ ναῷ, “he established in the temple,” have dropped out of Hegesippus’s text; Jerome translated them “and established prophets in the temple.” For just as one can say ἔκτισεν πόλιν, “he founded a city,” one cannot say ἔκτισεν προφήτας, “he founded prophets.” On the prophets of Antinous, see the excellent passage in Origen, *Against Celsus* III.36. See also Spartianus, *Hadrian*. The following sentence, “Hadrian is also said to have kept Antinous among his favorites,” is wholly absent from the Holy Cross manuscript.] and established prophets in the temple. Caesar Hadrian is said to have kept Antinous among his favorites.

[Col. 0640C] Hegesippus, who lived in the times of the Apostles, weaving histories of all ecclesiastical events from the Passion of the Lord to his own times, and gathering from every side many things contributing to the benefit of readers, composed five books in a very simple style, so as to express the character of those whose way of life he followed. He says that he came to Rome under Anicetus, the tenth bishop after Peter, and remained until Eleutherus, bishop of the aforementioned Rome, who had been Anicetus’s deacon. In his exposition against idols, explaining from what error they first grew, he composed a history showing in what times he flourished. For he says:

> “They made tombs for the dead and temples, as we see to the present day. Among them is Antinous, the slave of Hadrian Caesar, for whom a gymnastic contest is held at Antinous, and the city received its name from him, and he established prophets in the temple.”

[Col. 0642D] I do not understand what the Greek means here. It seems that he took the words “among the favorites” as referring to “aedilician,” a title of rank. The interpretation is rather careless.

Some writers say that Hadrian kept Antinous among his *aedilician* honors.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Note: [Col. 0641] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0641]

[Col. 0641B] Justin the philosopher, who also wore the dress of philosophers, from the Palestinian city of Neapolis [Col. 0642C]—more accurately, it should be called a city of Samaria, known to its inhabitants as Mabortha and formerly called Shechem—son of Priscus Bacchius [Note: Jerome treats Bacchius as a surname of Priscus, although it is the name of Priscus’s father, as Suidas states according to Lipomanus, Part II. Valesius proves this from the fact that Justin adds in the plural, τῶν ἀπὸ Φλαυΐας, evidently referring to both father and grandfather.], labored greatly for the Christian religion. To such an extent that he presented to Antoninus Pius, to his sons, and to the Senate a book written against the Gentiles—his longer *Apology*—and was not ashamed of the reproach of the Cross; and another book—his shorter *Apology*—to the successors of that same Antoninus, Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

There also exists another work of his against the Gentiles, the *Address to the Greeks*, in which he discusses the nature of demons; and a fourth work against the Gentiles, which he entitled *Refutation* [Note: It is now entitled λόγος παραινετικός, “hortatory discourse,” by which name Damascenus also calls it in the *Parallels*.]. There is also another book on the monarchy of God, and another which he entitled *Psalmist* [Note: The Verona manuscript has Ψάλτης in Greek letters. This book has perished, as has the following work, *Scholastic Treatise on the Soul*, and the works against Marcion mentioned below.], and another on the soul.

There is the *Dialogue against the Jews*, which he directed against Trypho, a leader of the Jews; and also distinguished works against Marcion, which Irenaeus mentions in Book IV of *Against Heresies* [Note: The printed editions, together with the Greek translator, have “in Book V,” but our very ancient manuscript corrects this. Irenaeus actually cites Justin’s work in Book IV, chapter 14: “Justin rightly says in his composition against Marcion …”]. There is also a book against all heresies, which he mentions in the *Apology* that he gave to Antoninus Pius [Note: The Holy Cross manuscript does not list this book against all heresies. It certainly does not exist today, although perhaps it never came into the hands of men. Justin himself said in his longer *Apology* that he kept it within his own household and would publish it if necessary.].

While he had a school in Rome, he rebuked Crescentus the Cynic, who blasphemed many things against the Christians, exposing him as a glutton, fearful of death, and a follower of luxury and lust. At last, accused through Crescentus’s zeal and plots because he was a Christian, he shed his blood for Christ.

[Col. 0643C] What Tatian said in Eusebius IV, τῇ μεγάλῃ πόλει, Jerome understands as referring to Rome; others prefer to understand it as Megalopolis, a city of Arcadia, about which Tatian speaks elsewhere.

[Col. 0642B] Justin the philosopher, who also wore the dress of philosophers, from the region of Neapolis in Palestine, son of Priscus Bacchius, labored greatly for the Christian religion. Thus he presented to Antoninus, surnamed Pius, to his sons, and to the Senate a book composed against the Gentiles, not being ashamed of the reproach of the Cross, and another book to the successors of that same Antoninus, namely Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

He also has another book against the Gentiles, in which he discusses the nature of demons, and a fourth discourse likewise against the Gentiles, which he entitled *Refutation*, and another on the monarchy of God, and another called *Psalmist*, and another on the soul; a *Dialogue against the Jews*, directed against Trypho, leader of the Jews; and distinguished works against Marcion, which Irenaeus mentions in the fifth book against heretics. There is also another book against all heresies, which he mentions in the *Apology* given to Antoninus Pius.

While he had his school in Rome, he corrected Crescentus the Cynic, who blasphemed against the Christians, calling him a glutton, fearful of death, a profligate, and an impure man. Finally, through his activity and plotting, Justin suffered as a Christian for Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Note: [Col. 0643] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0643]

Melito of Asia, bishop of Sardis, who was a disciple of the orator Fronto [Col. 0643C]—I think he wrote in order to refute Fronto’s own slanders, for Fronto had heaped reproaches upon the Christians in a notorious declamation; Gellius, Julius Capitolinus, Ausonius, and others mention him—presented to the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus a book on behalf of Christian doctrine.

He also wrote other works, of which the following are those we have listed: two books *On Easter*; one book *On the Life of the Prophets*; one book *On the Church*; one book *On the Lord’s Day*; one book *On the Senses*; one book *On Faith*; one book *On Creation*; one book *On Soul and Body*; one book *On Baptism*; one book *On Truth*; one book *On the Generation of Christ*; one book *On His Prophecy*; one book *On Hospitality*; another book entitled *The Key*; one book *On the Devil*; one book *On the Apocalypse of John*; one book *On the Incarnate God*; and six books of *Selections*.

[Col. 0643C] The Verona manuscript does not list *On the Lord’s Day*, although Eusebius knew it and calls it περὶ κυριακῆς in Book IV, chapter 26.

[Col. 0643C] The Vatican manuscript does not recognize this book *On Creation*; our Verona manuscript reads *On Plasi*, which I judge to be the more accurate reading. Eusebius calls it περὶ πλάσεως. The Gembloux manuscript intended the same title by reading *On Phase*, where *On Plasi* should be read.

[Col. 0643C] Eusebius does not seem to be understood in this way. He does not say περὶ προφητείας αὐτοῦ, “on his prophecy,” but αὐτοῦ περὶ προφητείας, “his work on prophecy,” although Rufinus also translates it as Jerome does.

[Col. 0643D] At this point two manuscripts, the Vatican and Holy Cross, differ. One has ΚΑΙΤΟΙΤΕΡΙΕΝΣΩΜΑΤΟΥ, where καὶ τὸν περὶ, “and the book on,” should be read; the other immediately adds, after the words ἐνσωμάτου θεοῦ, “incarnate God,” “one book *On the Eternity of God* and one book of *Selections*.” Apparently this was a marginal interpretation of the Greek words: “On the Incarnation of God.” The copyist, not fully understanding it, inserted it into the text and read “On the Eternity,” although there is no evidence anywhere that Melito wrote such a book. This supplies a new argument against the distinguished scholars Cotelerius, Valesius, and others, who interpret the title as “On the Bodily God” and attribute to Melito the error of the Anthropomorphites. If Melito had wished to establish that God was bodily, he would never have used the word ἐνσώματος, which properly means “clothed in flesh,” as Rufinus translates it, or “incarnate.” Nor would Jerome himself have merely listed the title of the book if it contained the doctrines of so wicked a heresy. Yet a testimony of Origen cited by Theodoret, *Questions on Genesis*, question 20, causes difficulty: “Melito, who left writings on the proposition that God is corporeal.” There is also a statement by Gennadius, *Ecclesiastical Dogmas* I.4: “Let us believe nothing corporeal in the Trinity, as Melito and Tertullian maintain.”

Tertullian, in the seven books that he wrote against the Church on behalf of Montanus, mocks Melito’s elegant and declamatory talent, saying that many of our people considered him a prophet.

[Col. 0644C] In the printed books, an opposite and inept meaning has hitherto prevailed: “Praising his elegant and declamatory talent, Tertullian, in the seven books he wrote against the Church on behalf of Montanus, says that many of our people considered him a prophet.” The ancient manuscripts—the Verona and Vatican manuscripts, one Wolfenbüttel manuscript belonging to Salomon Cyprianus, and those approved by Suffridus Petri, including the Gembloux and Sigeberg manuscripts—correct this by reading “he mocks,” rather than “praising,” and “saying.” We have preferred to follow their authority, since it produces a much more coherent reading. All Melito’s works, except for a few fragments, have perished.

[Col. 0644A] Melito of Asia, bishop of Sardis, presented to the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus, who had been a disciple of the rhetorician Fronto, a book on behalf of the doctrine of the Christians. He also wrote other works, among which are the following: two discourses *On Easter*; one *On the Life of the Prophets*; one *On the Church*; one *On the Lord’s Day*; one *On Thought*; one *On the Faithful*; one *On Creation*; one *On Soul and Body*; one *On Baptism*; one *On Truth*; one *On the Birth of Christ*; one *On His Own Prophecy*; one *On Hospitality*; another discourse entitled *The Key*; one *On the Devil*; one *On the Apocalypse of John*; one *On the Incarnate God*; and six discourses of *Selections*.

Praising his ingenuity, Tertullian, in the seven discourses that he wrote against the Church on behalf of Montanus, says that many of our people considered him a prophet.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Note: [Col. 0643] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0643]

Theophilus, sixth bishop of the Church of Antioch [Col. 0644D]—in Letter 121 to Algasius, question 6, Jerome calls him the seventh bishop of the Church of Antioch, evidently counting Peter there but excluding him here—composed a book against Marcion during the reign of the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus, which still exists today [Col. 0644D]—it is no longer extant, nor are the other works listed below, except for the three books addressed to Autolycus. Some writers mention another book *On Chronology*, likewise addressed to Autolycus, on the basis of Lactantius, Book I, *On False Religion*, but they fail to notice that it is the third of the three earlier books, the one that traces the sequence of times and is therefore the work Lactantius praises.

Three books addressed to Autolycus are also attributed to him, as well as one book against the heresy of Hermogenes and other brief and elegant treatises pertaining to the edification of the Church. I have read, under his name, commentaries on the Gospel and on the Proverbs of Solomon, but they do not seem to me to correspond in elegance and expression with the works mentioned above.

[Col. 0644B] Theophilus, sixth bishop of the Church at Antioch, composed a book against Marcion during the reign of Marcus Antoninus Verus, and it remains to the present day. Three books addressed to Autolycus are also attributed to him, as well as one discourse against the heresy of Hermogenes and other brief books belonging to the edification of the Church. I have read, under his name, commentaries on the Gospel and on the Proverbs of Solomon, but they do not seem to agree with the ingenuity and style of the writings mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Note: [Col. 0645] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0645]

[Col. 0645A] Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, flourished under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus, to whom he also presented a distinguished work on behalf of the Christian faith. Five other books of his against the Gentiles survive, as well as two on the truth [Col. 0645D] a Sigeberg manuscript in the possession of Suffridus Petri counts three books on the truth and two against the Cataphrygians. But these works, as well as those mentioned by Eusebius—two against the Jews and the other writings of Apollinaris—have perished. He also wrote against the Cataphrygians, who first arose at that time with the mad prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla, when Montanus was beginning.

[Col. 0646A] Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, flourished while Marcus Antoninus Verus was reigning. To him he presented a distinguished work on behalf of the faith of the Christians. He also wrote five other discourses against the Gentiles, two on the truth, and works against the Phrygians, who first emerged at that time together with the impious prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla, when Montanus began his movement.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Note: [Col. 0645] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0645]

[Col. 0645A] Dionysius, bishop of the Church of Corinth, was a man of such eloquence and diligence that he instructed by letters not only the peoples of his own city and province, but also the bishops of other [Col. 0645B] cities and provinces.

[Col. 0645D] These words are absent from the Vatican manuscript; the Verona manuscript and the others we consulted have only “bishops.” The Greek translator is also unfamiliar with this wording, and the context itself does not support it. I would therefore prefer to delete it on the authority of so many manuscripts. Eusebius likewise speaks of the islands of other regions and cities; nor were those letters really written separately to bishops, but for the most part to Churches.

Among his works is one letter to the Lacedaemonians, another to the Athenians, a third to the Nicomedians, a fourth to the Cretans, a fifth to the Amastrian Church and to the other Churches of Pontus, a sixth to the Cnossians and to Pinytus, bishop of the same city, a seventh to the Romans, which he wrote to Soter, their bishop, and an eighth to Chrysophora, a holy woman.

[Col. 0645D] The Vatican manuscript, together with the Sigeberg manuscript, reads “to the Amastrian Church.” Of all these letters, only certain fragments survive in Eusebius.

He flourished under the emperors Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

[Col. 0646A] Dionysius, bishop of the Church at Corinth, became so eloquent and diligent that he instructed by his own letters not only the peoples of his own city [Col. 0646B] and province, but also those of other provinces and cities. Among these letters is one to the Lacedaemonians, another to the Athenians, a third to the Nicomedians, a fourth to the Cretans, a fifth to the Amastrian Church and the other Churches of Pontus, a sixth to the Cnossians and to Pinytus, bishop of the same city, a seventh to the Romans, which he wrote to Soter, their bishop, and an eighth to Chrysophora, a devout woman. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

# CHAPTER XXVIII

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0645]

[Col. 0645B] Pinytus of Crete, bishop of the city of Cnossus, wrote to Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, a very elegant letter [Note: This letter, by which he replied to Dionysius’s letter mentioned in the preceding chapter, has perished through the ravages of time. See Eusebius IV, 23.]. In it he teaches that the peoples must not always be nourished with milk, lest, like little children, they be overtaken by the last day; but that they must also feed on solid food, so that they may advance toward spiritual old age. He too flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

[Col. 0646B] Pinytus of Crete, bishop of Cnossus, wrote to Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, a very polished letter, in which he teaches that the peoples must not always be nourished with milk, lest, like infants, they be overtaken on the final day, but also with solid food, so that they may advance into spiritual old age. He too flourished under the same emperors.

# CHAPTER XXIX

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0645]

[Col. 0645C] Tatian, [Note: Miraeus and certain manuscripts have “Tatian the heresiarch,” or “Tatian, a heresiarch.” Compare Jerome, on Joel I, Amos II and III, Hosea VII, and Galatians VI.] who at first taught rhetoric and had acquired no small reputation for himself through the rhetorical art, became a follower of Justin the Martyr and flourished in the Church so long as he did not depart from his side. Later, however, puffed up by the swelling of his eloquence [Note: The Verona manuscript has “puffed up by eloquence and swelling.” See Irenaeus I.1, chapter 32, and from him Eusebius IV, 29. Of Tatian’s innumerable writings, the first place was held by the Diatessaron, which Saint Ephraem illustrated with a commentary; it is said still to exist today in Syriac. See the Catalogue of Ebedjesus, chapter 3.], he founded a new heresy called that of the Encratites, which Severus later enlarged; from him the heretics of the same party have to this day been called Severians. Tatian wrote innumerable volumes, among which one very celebrated book, Against the Nations, is extant and is said to be outstanding among all his works. He too flourished under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

[Col. 0646C] Tatian, who formerly taught rhetoric and acquired no small reputation from the science of rhetoric, became a disciple of Justin the Martyr and flourished in the Church so long as he did not depart from his side. Later, puffed up by the pride of learning, he established a new heresy, namely that of the Encratites, which Severus afterward increased; from him the heretics of this party are called Severianists to the present day. The aforementioned Tatian composed very many books, among which there is one very remarkable discourse Against the Nations, which is distinguished among all his writings. He too flourished when Marcus Antoninus Verus and Aurelius Commodus were emperors.

# CHAPTER XXX

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0647]

[Col. 0647A] Philip, bishop of Crete—that is, of the city of Gortyna [Note: Gortyna was in fact the metropolis of Crete. Recall the letter of Dionysius, chapter 27.]—whom Dionysius 871 mentions in his letter written to the Church of that same city [Note: He did not live to old age.], published an outstanding book against Marcion and flourished in the time of Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

[Col. 0648A] Philip, bishop of the Cretan city of Gortyna, whom Dionysius 872 mentions in his letter written to the Church of the aforementioned city, published a very renowned book against Marcion (perhaps “and”) and flourished in the times of the emperors already mentioned.

# CHAPTER XXXI

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0647]

[Col. 0647A] Musanus, not insignificant among those who wrote on ecclesiastical doctrine [Note: The Vatican manuscript has Mosyanus; the Verona manuscript, Musyanus; Eusebius has Μουσανός. Immediately afterward the same Verona manuscript reads “who wrote ecclesiastical doctrines.”], composed under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus a book for certain brothers who had turned from the Church toward the heresy of the Encratites [Note: Most printed books read “against certain brothers”; our manuscripts and many others, as well as Eusebius himself, disagree, using the preposition πρὸς, “for” or “against.” This work of Musanus, which Eusebius calls Ἐπιτρεπτικώτατον, “most admonitory,” no longer exists.].

[Col. 0648A] Musanus, not without distinction among those who wrote on ecclesiastical doctrine, composed under Marcus Antoninus Verus a book for certain brothers who had inclined from the Church toward the heresy of the Encratites.

# CHAPTER XXXII

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0647]

[Col. 0647B] Modestus too, under the emperor Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, wrote a book against Marcion [Note: Nothing from the writings of this Modestus survives today. Most manuscripts, however, read συγγράμματα, “writings,” and ψευδεπίγραφα, “pseudepigraphical works”; Sophronius also retained these words. There is no necessity, following Martianus, to alter them to συντάγματα, “compositions,” and ψευδόγραφα, “false writings.”], which continues to exist to the present day. Other compositions are also circulated under his name, but learned men reject them as pseudepigraphical works.

[Col. 0648B] Modestus too, under Antoninus and Commodus, composed a book against Marcion, which still exists to this day. Other writings of his are also circulated, but learned men reject them as pseudepigraphical.

# CHAPTER XXXIII

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0647]

[Col. 0647B] Bardesanes [Note: The Verona manuscripts have “in Mesopotamia,” a usage for which the best Latin writers provide examples.] was held in high regard in Mesopotamia. At first a follower of Valentinus, and afterward his refuter, he founded a new heresy [Note: The Verona manuscript and two other codices read, “he himself founded a new heresy.” What the principles of this new heresy were is difficult to say. From Marinus the Bardesanist, in the Dialogue on the Orthodox Faith, one may understand that he admitted two principles, or roots (ῥίζαι), only one of which was good, namely God. He is said to have taught that Christ’s flesh had been brought down from heaven and was not taken from Mary. Finally, he denied the resurrection of the dead. But these same delusions proceeded from the school of Valentinus, from which he had defected. Epiphanius records one distinctive point about him: that he used the Law and the Prophets, the Old and New Testaments, and certain apocryphal writings—something the Valentinians certainly did not accept.]. The Syrians praise his ardent intellect and his force in debate. He wrote innumerable works against nearly all the heretics who had arisen in his time. Among them was that famous and powerful book [Note: Other books read “most celebrated.” Eusebius, book IV, final chapter, from whom Jerome drew this passage, calls it ἱκανώτατον, “very powerful”; Rufinus renders it potentissimum, as did the old translator of Irenaeus concerning the Epistle of Saint Clement to the Corinthians.] which he dedicated to Marcus Antoninus on Fate: 873 [Note: Some learned men maintain that this Antoninus was anything but an emperor and that Jerome incorrectly wrote Marcus Antoninus, whereas Eusebius merely says Antoninus: they suppose that Bardesanes had a companion of that name. In book VI of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 9, after quoting a substantial fragment of this very work On Fate, Eusebius adds that Bardesanes used to philosophize “in the dialogues with his companions” (ἐν τοῖς πρὸς τοὺς ἑταίρους διαλόγοις). Moreover, Valesius considers it highly unlikely that books written in Syriac could have been dedicated to a Roman emperor; this argument once influenced me as well. But if one supposes that Marcus Antoninus Elagabalus is meant—who was a priest of the Sun among the Phoenicians and therefore knew the Syriac language very well—there is no difficulty. As for Eusebius’s testimony, the persons represented as conversing in the dialogues by no means prevent the book itself from being dedicated to someone else. In this work On Fate, however, it is not the supposed Antoninus but a certain Philip who speaks; therefore those who hold the contrary view prove nothing from this point either. Everything else fits Jerome’s opinion very well, especially the chronology, since the author of the Edessene Chronicle reports that Bardesanes was born in the year 465 of the Greeks, that is, A.D. 154. Epiphanius, heresy 66, testifies that he was a friend of Abgar, son of Maʿnu; Eusebius agrees in Preparation for the Gospel V, 10, where he says that the law whose enactment Bardesanes had persuaded the king to establish—prohibiting anyone from emasculating himself thereafter—lasted until the time of Antoninus Caesar, not Antoninus Pius but Verus. Epiphanius further relates that, while holding orthodox opinions, Bardesanes burned with such zeal for God that he refused to listen to Apollonius, a friend of the emperor Antoninus, who urged him to deny that he was a Christian. This Book of His on Fate was published against Abidan, an advocate of Fate.], and many other volumes on persecution, which his followers translated from Syriac into Greek. If there is such power and brilliance in the translation, how much do we suppose there was in his own language?

[Col. 0648B] Bardesanes, who appeared illustrious in Mesopotamia, was first a disciple of Valentinus and later his opponent; he established a new heresy. The Syrians proclaim his natural talent to have been exceedingly ardent and his skill in debate exceedingly forceful. He wrote very many works against nearly all the heresies that arose in his time. Among them is the conspicuous and vigorous discourse which he delivered to Marcus Antoninus on Fate, as well as many other books on persecution, 874 which his followers translated from Syriac into Greek. If there is such strength and brilliance in the translation, how much excellence do we suppose he possessed in his own language? [Note: The Greek translator adds “virtue.”]

# CHAPTER XXXIV

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0649]

[Col. 0649A] Victor, [Note: Namely, the thirteenth if Peter is not counted. The same is stated in the Chronicle.] the thirteenth bishop of the city of Rome, wrote on the question of Easter [Note: That is, letters to the Eastern bishops, forbidding the celebration of the Jewish Passover on the fourteenth day of the moon in March. Nothing from his writings has reached us.] and certain other brief works. He governed the Church for ten years under the emperor Severus [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, “under the emperor Antoninus Verus.” This is incorrect, for from the year 180 Antoninus Verus had ceased both to rule and to live, as Tertullian and Dio testify.].

[Col. 0650A] Victor, the thirteenth bishop of Rome, composed certain works on the question of Easter and governed the Church for ten years during the reign of Severus.

# CHAPTER XXXV

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0649]

[Col. 0649A] Irenaeus, presbyter of Pothinus, the bishop who governed the Church of Lyons in Gaul, was sent to Rome as an envoy by the martyrs of that city concerning certain ecclesiastical questions. He delivered to Eleutherus, bishop of Rome, letters bearing honorable testimony to his name. Later, after Pothinus, nearly ninety years old, had been crowned with martyrdom for Christ, Irenaeus was appointed in his place. It is established that he was a disciple of Polycarp, the priest and martyr whom we mentioned above [Note: Above, chapter 17.].

He wrote five books Against Heresies [Note: An old Latin translation of this work survives, together with a few fragments; all the rest of Irenaeus’s writings have perished.], a short volume Against the Nations [Note: Eusebius knows only one book, the same as the preceding work Against the Nations.], another on discipline, one addressed to the brother Martianus on the Apostolic Preaching, a book of various treatises, one addressed to Blastus on Schism [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, more corruptly than the reader should be asked to tolerate, “on Chrism.” Eusebius V, 20 has πρὸς Βλάστον περὶ Σχίσματος, “to Blastus on Schism.” A little earlier the Wolfenbüttel manuscript reads “to Marcion concerning fraud,” instead of “to the brother Martianus.” Eusebius V, 26 has: “Another work which he dedicated to the brother whose name was Marcianus,” and so forth.], one addressed to Florinus on Monarchy, or that God is not the author of evil, and an excellent commentary on the Ogdoad [Note: Some manuscripts read “on the Eighth,” with Martianus. Eusebius has περὶ Ὀγδοάδος, which the old translator of Irenaeus renders “on the Ogdoad.” Some manuscripts likewise have σύνταγμα, “composition,” while others have commentarium, “commentary.” —And an excellent work on the Ogdoad. The manuscripts here retain no Greek word for “on the Ogdoad”; for “commentary,” several read σύνταγμα, or “composition.” MARTIAN.]. At the end of it, indicating that he had lived near the apostolic age, he appended the following subscription [Note: Eusebius V, 20 gives: “I adjure you who will copy this book, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by his glorious coming, at which he will come to judge the living and the dead, that you compare what you have copied and carefully correct it against this exemplar from which you copied it. You shall likewise copy this oath and place it in your copy.”]:

“I adjure you who 875 copy this book, by the Lord Jesus Christ and by his glorious coming, at which he will judge the living and the dead, that after you have copied it you compare it and correct it against the exemplar from which you wrote it [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, “from which you copied it”; Irenaeus has μετεγράψω, “from which I copied.” The same manuscript reads above, “by our Lord Jesus,” as do the Greek text and the translator.], with the greatest care. You shall likewise transfer this adjuration, just as you found it in the exemplar.”

Other letters of his to Victor, bishop of Rome, on the question of Easter are also circulated. In them he warns Victor that he ought not lightly to sever the unity of the fellowship. For Victor had judged that many bishops of Asia and the East, who celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, ought to be condemned [Note: Recall chapter 34.]. Those who disagreed with them did not yield to Victor on this judgment [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, “had not yielded.”]. Irenaeus flourished especially under the emperor Commodus, who succeeded Marcus Antoninus Verus in the empire.

[Col. 0650A] Irenaeus, presbyter of Pothinus, bishop of the Church of Lyons in Gaul, was sent to Rome as an envoy by the martyrs of that city on certain ecclesiastical matters. Having received letters bearing honor in his own name, he delivered them to Eleutherus, bishop of Rome. Afterward, when Pothinus had suffered martyrdom at nearly ninety years of age, Irenaeus succeeded him. It is acknowledged that he was a disciple of Polycarp, whom we mentioned earlier. He wrote five books Against the Heretics, a short treatise Against the Nations, another on knowledge, one addressed to the brother Marcianus on the Apostolic Preaching, and a book of various homilies; one to Blastus on Schism; one to Florinus on Monarchy and on the proposition that God is not the creator of evils; and an excellent composition on the Ogdoad. At the end of that composition he wrote:

“I adjure you who copy this book, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by his glorious coming, at which he will judge the living and the dead, that after writing it you compare it and carefully correct it against the exemplars from which you copied it, 876 and that you likewise copy this adjuration just as you found it in the exemplars.”

Other letters of his to Victor, bishop of Rome, concerning the question of Easter are also preserved. In them he urges him not rashly to divide the unity of the fellowship. Victor had deposed many bishops of Asia and the East who celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon. Those who disagreed with this judgment did not agree with Victor. Irenaeus flourished especially under King Commodus, who succeeded Verus Antoninus.

# CHAPTER XXXVI

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0651]

[Col. 0651A] Pantaenus [Note: Philip of Side, in the city to which the Christian Academy had migrated, almost abandoning Alexandria, gives an account somewhat different from that of Jerome or Eusebius. He says that Pantaenus was first an Athenian citizen and philosopher, a Pythagorean by sect, and afterward a catechist of the Alexandrian school and a disciple of Clement of Alexandria. See below, chapter 38.], a philosopher of the Stoic sect, was, according to an ancient custom in Alexandria—where there had always been ecclesiastical teachers from the time of Mark the Evangelist—so wise and learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular literature that, when requested by envoys of that nation, he was sent to India by Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria. There he discovered that Bartholomew, one of the twelve Apostles, had preached the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the Gospel of Matthew. He brought this Gospel with him back to Alexandria; it had been written in Hebrew characters [Note: Alternatively, as in the Verona manuscript, “he brought it back.” Eusebius V, 10 teaches that the Gospel remained in India until Pantaenus’s time: “and it is still preserved to the present day.” He does not say that it was brought from there to Alexandria. Nicephorus, book II, chapter 22, agrees. See also the notes above, chapter 2, and elsewhere.].

Many commentaries by him on Holy Scripture are extant [Note: Nothing exists today, and one rarely finds anyone who mentions his works. A fragment seems to be preserved in excerpts of the heretic Theodore at the end of Clement of Alexandria, where it says, “Pantaenus, however, used to say…” He is said to have been the first to teach that the Prophets use the present tense in place of the past and future, a rule afterward followed by interpreters of the Prophets.]; but he benefited the Churches more by his living voice. He taught under the emperor Severus and Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla.

[Col. 0652A] Pantaenus, a philosopher of Stoic doctrine, according to an ancient custom of the Alexandrians, by which ecclesiastical teachers had existed from Mark the Evangelist, possessed such wisdom and learning—both in the divine Scriptures and in secular literature—that, when he was requested by the elders of India, he was sent to India by Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria. There he found Bartholomew, one of the twelve Apostles, who had preached the coming of the Lord Jesus according to the Gospel of Matthew. Having set out again for Alexandria, he brought it with him, written in Hebrew characters. Many commentaries of his on the divine Scriptures are found, but he benefited the Churches more through his living voice. He taught under Severus and Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla.

# CHAPTER XXXVII

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0651]

[Col. 0651B] 877 Rhodon, an Asian by birth, learned in the Scriptures at Rome under Tatian, whom we mentioned above [Note: Above, chapter 29. Compare Eusebius, book V, chapter 13.], published very many works. His chief work was against Marcion, in which he explains how the Marcionites themselves disagree among one another; he also relates that he had once encountered Apelles, an old man and another heretic, and had made him a laughingstock [Note: “Had been confronted.” The Saint-Germain manuscript, with several others, reads “had been convicted.” One manuscript of the Ambrosian Library has “had been defeated” in the margin and “had been confronted” in the text. MARTIAN. I have restored “had met with him” from older manuscripts, since recent editors, thinking to correct the text from other codices, have corrupted it into “had been convicted.” The restored reading agrees with Eusebius’s ἠλέγχθη, “was refuted,” and with Sophronius’s translation, συντετυχηκέναι. Thus Pope Anastasius says in a letter first published by us among Jerome’s letters, no. 104: “I meet your holiness with the writings of the aforementioned Theophilus.”], had been made a laughingstock because he said that he did not know the God whom he worshiped [Note: Apelles did not simply say that he did not know the God whom he worshiped, as though he were ignorant of God, according to Eusebius; rather, he said that he did not know in what manner the one God was unbegotten, though he believed that this was so. For his doctrine, see the author of the Appendix to Tertullian’s book On Prescription, chapter 51. The author of the Catalogue of Heresies under Jerome’s name copied this passage of the holy Doctor.].

In the same book, which he wrote to Callistion, he mentions that he had been Tatian’s pupil at Rome [Note: The Verona manuscript incorrectly reads “assistant.” Recall Eusebius in the cited passage.]. He also composed elegant treatises on the Hexaemeron and a distinguished work against the Phrygians [Note: Elsewhere, and in the oldest manuscripts, “against the Cataphrygians.” Saint Jerome is criticized by Valesius for attributing to Rhodon a book whose author Eusebius, in book V, chapter 16, calls merely “a certain unnamed person.” That book is addressed to Abercius Marcellus; some claim that it was composed by a certain Asterius Urbanus, a conclusion seemingly supported by a note appended to the end of that chapter of Eusebius. Rufinus and Nicephorus, book IV, chapter 23, however, make Apollinaris of Hierapolis its author, on the grounds that Eusebius himself testifies shortly beforehand that Apollinaris wrote against the Cataphrygians. In my view both opinions do violence to the historian’s meaning and to the text, and Jerome’s judgment is preferable. He could easily have learned from other records, or from Rhodon’s own book, the name of an author unknown to Eusebius. Valesius is certainly mistaken when he accuses the holy Doctor of inconsistency, as though he attributed this same book below, in chapter 40, to Apollonius. That is another work, which Eusebius himself records as having been written by Apollonius against the Cataphrygians in book V, chapter 18.]. He flourished in the times of Commodus and Severus.

[Col. 0652B] 878 Rhodon, an Asian, instructed in the Holy Scriptures under the aforementioned Tatian, published many works, including an excellent composition against Marcion. In it he explains how the Marcionites themselves disagree with one another, and how Apelles, the old man and likewise a heretic, had encountered them and become a laughingstock by saying that he did not know the God whom he revered. In the same book, which he wrote to Callistion, he mentions that he had been Tatian’s pupil at Rome. He also composed polished homilies on the Hexaemeron and a distinguished work against the Phrygians. He flourished in the times of Commodus and Severus.

# CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0653]

[Col. 0653A] Clement, presbyter of the Church of Alexandria and a pupil of Pantaenus, whom we mentioned above, took charge of the ecclesiastical school at Alexandria after Pantaenus’s death [Note: It was noted above, in chapter 36, that Philip of Side gives the opposite account: not that Clement succeeded Pantaenus, but that Pantaenus succeeded Clement as head of the Alexandrian school. Most scholars, however, support Eusebius and Jerome. The distinguished Fabricius thinks that both authors can be reconciled if one understands that Clement was placed in charge of the school when Pantaenus went to India, and that Pantaenus took it up again when he returned, leaving it once more to Clement to govern when he died.], and became a teacher of catechesis. His distinguished volumes are circulated, full of learning and eloquence, concerning both the divine Scriptures and the resources of secular literature. Among them are the following: eight books of the Stromata; eight books of the Hypotyposeis; one book Against the Nations; three books of the Paedagogue; one book on Easter; a discussion on fasting [Note: The manuscript of Santa Croce, nearly agreeing with the Sigeberg manuscript, reads “one book on fasting, one on Discussion,” and so forth. Neither this work, nor the preceding Hypotyposeis, nor finally the book on Easter, survives, except for a few fragments. Compare Eusebius, book VI, chapter 13.]; another entitled Who Is the Rich Man Who Shall Be Saved?; one book on Slander; one on the Ecclesiastical Canons [Note: This presumably means a distinct book containing the rules of ecclesiastical faith, directed against Judaizers. Beveregius’s conjecture that Clement is said to have undertaken the collection of the Apostolic Canons is therefore not sufficiently appropriate. Several manuscripts preserved by Martianus, as well as all ours, prefer the printed reading and the Greek verb προσεφώνησεν, which is frequent in Jerome, though they generally omit the adverb “properly.”]; and one book against those who follow the error of the Jews, 879 which he addressed especially to Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem [Note: Προσεφώνησε. The Saint-Germain manuscript, without the Greek word, reads: “which he properly wrote to Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem.” Others retain the Greek verb προσεφώνησεν, commonly used by Jerome in his short prefaces. MARTIAN.].

In his Stromata he mentions the book of Tatian Against the Nations, which we discussed above [Note: This was Julius Cassianus, a disciple of Valentinus and leader of the Docetists, about whom our Clement speaks in books I and III of the Stromata, although he calls his book not a “chronography” but an “exegetical work.” Immediately afterward, Victorius reads “which work I could find in the old books,” as does the Greek translator; but neither our manuscripts nor most others contain “in the old books.” The work of Tatian was discussed above, chapter 29.], and the Chronography of a certain Cassianus, a little work which I was unable to find [Note: “To find the little work.” Marianus Victorius adds “in the old books,” but without justification, since this is found in no manuscript and is unnecessary, as the sense shows. MARTIAN.].

He also mentions among the Jews a certain Aristobulus, Demetrius, and Eupolemus as writers against the nations who, in imitation of Josephus, assert an ancient history of Moses and the Jewish people [Note: Aristobulus was a distinguished Peripatetic who wrote for Ptolemy Philometor books of explanations of the Mosaic Law. Demetrius and Eupolemus published commentaries on the kings of Judea. Clement praises them in the first book of the Stromata.].

There exists a letter of Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, who later governed the Church together with Narcissus, concerning the ordination of Asclepiades the confessor, addressed to the Antiochenes and congratulating them. At the end he says [Note: Eusebius VI, 11: “These letters, my lords and brothers, I have sent to you through the blessed presbyter Clement, an excellent and approved man, whom you also know and will recognize more fully, who, being present here according to the providence and visitation of the Master, strengthened and increased the Church of the Lord.” The manuscript of Santa Croce and two others omit the conjunction in “my lords and brothers.” So too the Greek text has “to you, my lords and brothers.” Below, the Wolfenbüttel manuscript reads “you will know” instead of “you will recognize”; ours reads “you know.”]:

“These writings, my lords and brothers, I have sent to you through Clement, the blessed presbyter, an illustrious and approved man, whom you also know and will now recognize more fully, who, when he came here according to the providence and visitation of God, strengthened and increased the Church of the Lord.”

It is established that Origen was his disciple. He flourished during the reigns of Severus and his son Antoninus.

[Col. 0654A] Clement, presbyter of Alexandria, a pupil of Pantaenus, whom we mentioned earlier, took charge of the school of the Church at Alexandria after Pantaenus’s death and became a teacher of catechesis. He composed distinguished books filled with learning and eloquence, concerning both the divine and the secular disciplines. Among them are these: eight Stromata; eight books of Hypotyposeis; Against the Nations; three Paedagogi; one book on Easter; a discussion on fasting; another entitled Who, Then, Is the Rich Man Who Shall Be Saved?; one discourse on Slander; one on the Ecclesiastical Canons; and a book against those who follow the error of the Jews, which he addressed particularly to Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem. 880

He mentions in his own Stromata the aforementioned book of Tatian Against the Nations, and the Chronography of a certain Cassianus, which we were unable to find in the old books. He also refers to the Jewish writers Aristobulus, Demetrius, and Eupolemus, who wrote against the nations, asserting, in imitation of Josephus, an ancient history of Moses and the Jewish people.

There is also a letter of Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, who later presided over the Church with Narcissus, concerning the ordination of Asclepiades the confessor, addressed to the Antiochenes in congratulation. At its end he says:

“These writings I have sent to you, my lords and brothers, through the most devout Clement, an illustrious and approved man, whom you also know and will now recognize more fully, who, having come here according to the providence and visitation of God, strengthened and increased the Church of the Lord.”

It is acknowledged that Origen became his disciple. He flourished while Severus and Antoninus, his son, were reigning.

# CHAPTER XXXIX

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0653]

Miltiades, whom Rhodon recalls in his work composed against Montanus, Prisca [Note: All our manuscripts, and those used by Erasmus, Suffridus Petri, and Martianus, have this reading. Others, especially the printed editions, have “Priscilla.”], and Maximilla [Note: Recall above, chapter 37, and the notes there concerning Rhodon’s book.], wrote an outstanding volume against the same persons, as well as other books against the nations and the Jews [Note: Namely, two against the nations and two against the Jews, as Eusebius V, 17, records; none of them exists today.]. He also gave an Apology to the rulers of that time. He flourished in the time of Marcus Antoninus and Commodus [Note: The conjunction “and” is supplied by the oldest Verona manuscript, since previously the text incorrectly had only “Commodus”; two emperors must nevertheless be understood. A little earlier, certain manuscripts, with the Greek translator, read “to the ruler” instead of “to the rulers,” incorrectly, whatever Victorius may have thought.].

[Col. 0654C] Miltiades, whom Rhodon mentions in his work composed against Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla, wrote an excellent treatise against them and other discourses against the nations and the Jews. He also delivered an Apology to the emperor of that time and flourished during the reigns of Marcus Antoninus and Commodus.

# CHAPTER XL

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0655]
