[Col. 0655A] 881 Apollonius [Note: This is the Apollonius whom the author of the Predestinarian, heresy 26, which is that of the Cataphrygians, calls bishop of Ephesus: “Saint Soter, pope of the city, wrote a book against them, as did Apollonius, bishop of the Ephesians, against whom Tertullian, presbyter of Carthage, wrote.”], a most eloquent man, wrote a distinguished and lengthy volume against Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. In it he asserts that Montanus and the mad prophetesses [Note: As for this account of the hanging of the insane prophetesses, Eusebius, book IV, chapter 18, does not take it from Apollonius’s book against Montanus, but from another work on the same subject by an uncertain author, whom Jerome, in chapter 37, identifies as Rhodon. Hence Valesius again accuses the holy Doctor of a “memory error,” as we noted there. But since Eusebius lists a separate book by Apollonius against the Cataphrygians, it could easily be that both works—Apollonius’s and Rhodon’s—contained the same story about the hanging of the insane prophetesses, which Jerome here attributes to Apollonius while saying nothing of Rhodon.], had perished by hanging; and he reports many other things concerning Prisca and Maximilla [Note: Eusebius V, 18: “If they deny that their prophets have received gifts, let them acknowledge that, if they are proved to have received them, they are not prophets. We shall provide a thousand proofs of this. It is necessary to test all the fruits of a prophet. Tell me, prophet, does he dye his hair? Does a prophet paint his eyes with stibium? Does a prophet adorn himself with clothes and jewels? Does a prophet play at tables and dice? Does a prophet lend money at interest? Let them acknowledge whether these things are permitted or not; but I shall show that such things have occurred among them.”].

“If they deny that they have received gifts, let them admit that those who receive gifts are not prophets; and I shall prove this with a thousand witnesses. Prophets are also tested by other fruits. Tell me: Does a prophet dye his hair? Does a prophet apply stibium to his eyes? Does a prophet adorn himself with garments and pearls? Does a prophet play at tables and with dice? Does a prophet take interest? Let them answer whether this is permitted or not; my task is to prove that they have done it [Note: The Verona manuscript reads, “my task is to prove that they have done it,” which is the more suitable reading and agrees with the Greek text, ἐγὼ δὲ ὅτι γέγονε παρ’ αὐτοῖς δείξω.].”

In the same book he says that forty years had passed [Note: This should be referred to A.D. 210. Apollonius’s work, except for several fragments in Eusebius, has perished, as have Tertullian’s works mentioned below; seven books have been lost. Pamelius judges from their Greek title that they were once written in Greek, but the manuscripts differ on this point, and two of ours have the Latin title On Ecstasy.] up to the time when he himself was writing the book since the heresy of the Cataphrygians had begun. Tertullian, after publishing six books against the Church, written On Ecstasy, composed a seventh specifically against Apollonius, in which he attempts to defend everything that Apollonius attacks. Apollonius flourished under the emperors Commodus and Severus.

[Col. 0656A] 882 Apollonius, a most learned man, wrote a great and distinguished work against Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla. In it he says that Montanus and the mad prophetesses had hanged themselves, and he reports many other things concerning Priscilla and Maximilla. If they deny having received gifts, they will admit that those who receive gifts are not prophets; and I refute this with a thousand witnesses. Prophets are also tested by other actions. Tell me: Does a prophet dye his hair? Does he paint his eyes with stibium? Does a prophet adorn himself with clothing and pearls? Does a prophet play at tables and with dice? Does a prophet receive interest? Let them answer whether such conduct is permitted or not, and it is my task to prove that they have done these things.

In the same book he says that it was the fortieth year up to the time when he was writing, counting from the beginning received by the Phrygian heresy. Tertullian, having published six discourses against the Church concerning ecstasy, composed the seventh specifically against Apollonius, in which he defends everything that Apollonius attempts to condemn. Apollonius flourished under Commodus and Severus.

# CHAPTER XLI

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0655]

Serapion [Note: Martianus, with several manuscripts, has Sarapion, and the Greek likewise has Σαραπίων. The Vatican manuscript then has “in the tenth” instead of “in the eleventh.”], ordained bishop of Antioch in the eleventh year of the emperor Commodus, wrote a letter to Caricus and Pontius concerning the heresy of Montanus, in which he adds the following [Note: Eusebius V, 19: “But so that you may know that the activity of this false order called the new prophecy is rejected by the whole brotherhood throughout the world, I have sent you writings of the most blessed Claudius Apollinarius, who was bishop of Hierapolis in Asia.” Eusebius has γράμματα, “writings”; these should presumably be Apollinaris’s own writings against Montanus. See Tertullian, On Fasting, at the beginning, and Against Marcion III, near the end, and IV, chapter 22.]:

“But so that you may 883 know that the insanity of this false doctrine, that is, of the new prophecy, is rejected throughout the whole world, I have sent you writings of the most blessed Apollinaris, who was bishop of Hierapolis in Asia [Note: Martianus, with most printed editions, has Domnus; others, especially manuscripts, very often have Dominus; some read Domnion. Eusebius, however, calls him Δομνῖνος, and so do two of our manuscripts, which we follow.].

“He also composed a volume for Domninus, who during the persecution had turned aside toward the Jews; and another book on the Gospel circulated under the name of Peter, which he addressed to the Church of Rhosus in Cilicia, because that Church had turned toward his heresy through reading it [Note: All Serapion’s writings, like the rest, are now lost.]. Short letters of his are also read here and there, corresponding to their author’s ascetic discipline and life.”

[Col. 0656B] Serapion, ordained bishop of the Church of Antioch in the eleventh year of King Commodus, wrote a letter to Carinus and Pontius concerning the heresy of Montanus, adding the following:

“So that you may 884 know that the growth of this doctrine, I mean the new prophecy, and its madness throughout the whole world must be rejected, I have sent you writings of the most blessed Apollinarius, who was bishop of Hierapolis in Asia. He also composed a treatise for Domnus, who during the time of persecution had inclined toward the Jews, and another book concerning the Gospel circulated under the name of Peter, which he addressed to the Church in Rhosus of Cilicia, a Church that had turned toward his heresy and had transferred certain people to the reading of it.”

His very short letters are also read in scattered places, corresponding to his ascetic discipline and his life.

# CHAPTER XLII

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0657]

[Col. 0657A] Apollonius, a senator of the city of Rome [Note: Alternatively, “was ordered to appear,” as in the Vatican manuscript; the Greek translator supports this with ἐπιταγείς, “having been commanded,” and so forth.], was betrayed under the emperor Commodus by a slave named Severus because he was a Christian [Note: Eusebius had included this in the Acts of the Martyrs, which have entirely perished. Concerning the old law that did not permit Christians to be released without a denial, see Pliny, book X, letter 97, to Trajan; and Pagi, under the year A.D. 187.]. When he was granted permission to give an account of his faith, he composed a distinguished volume, which he read in the senate. Nevertheless, by decree of the senate, he was beheaded for Christ, since an ancient law was in force among them that Christians who had once been brought before their tribunal could not be released without denying their faith.

[Col. 0658A] Apollonius, a senator of Rome, was betrayed under the emperor Commodus by a slave before Severus because he was a Christian. Ordered to give an account of his faith, he composed a large work, which he read in the senate. Nevertheless, by decree of the senate, he was beheaded for Christ, since an ancient custom prevailed among them that Christians who had once been dragged before their tribunal could not be released without a denial.

## CHAPTER XLV

[Note: [Col. 0657] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0657]

[Col. 0657C] Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, together with the other bishops of Asia who, according to a certain ancient custom, celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, wrote a synodal letter against Victor, bishop of Rome, in which he teaches that he follows the authority of the apostle John and of the ancients. From it we have excerpted the following few words:

[Note: [Col. 0659C] In Eusebius III.31 and V.24: “We therefore celebrate an unalterable day, neither adding anything nor taking anything away. For in Asia great luminaries have fallen asleep, and they will rise on the day of the Lord, when he comes in glory from heaven and raises all the saints: I mean Philip, one of the Twelve Apostles, who sleeps at Hierapolis, and his two daughters, who grew old as virgins. His other daughter also, who lived her life in the Holy Spirit, rests at Ephesus. And John also, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast, who was a priest bearing the sacred plate, and a martyr and teacher, sleeps at Ephesus. Polycarp also, bishop and martyr, in Smyrna; and Thraseas, both bishop and martyr, from Eumenia, who sleeps at Smyrna. Why need I mention Sagaris, bishop and martyr, who sleeps at Laodicea? And Papirius the blessed, and Melito the eunuch, who lived wholly in the Holy Spirit and lies at Sardis, awaiting the visitation from heaven, at which he will rise from the dead? All these observed the day of the fourteenth of Easter according to the Gospel, deviating in nothing, but following the rule of faith. And I also, Polycrates, the least of all of you, according to the tradition of my relatives, some of whom I followed: seven of my relatives were bishops, and I am the eighth. My relatives always observed the day when the people were removing the leaven. Therefore, brothers, being sixty-five years old in the Lord, having associated with brothers throughout the inhabited world, and having passed through every holy Scripture, I am not alarmed by those who are intimidating us. For those greater than I have said, ‘We must obey God rather than human beings.’”]

“We therefore celebrate an inviolable day, neither adding anything nor taking anything away. For in Asia the greatest luminaries have fallen asleep, and they will rise on the day of the Lord, when he comes from heaven in his majesty to raise all the saints. I mean Philip, one of the Twelve Apostles, who slept at Hierapolis, and his two daughters, who grew old as virgins, and his other daughter, who, filled with the Holy Spirit, died at Ephesus. John also, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast, and who, as his priest, bore a golden plate upon his forehead, a martyr and teacher, slept at Ephesus. Polycarp also, bishop and martyr, lies at Smyrna. 887 Thraseas also, bishop and martyr from Eumenia, rests in that same Smyrna. Why is it necessary to mention Sagaris, bishop and martyr, who sleeps at Laodicea, and the blessed Papirius, and Melito the eunuch in the Holy Spirit, who, always serving the Lord, has been laid to rest at Sardis and awaits the resurrection at his coming? All these observed the day of Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, deviating in no respect from the Gospel tradition and following the ecclesiastical rule. I also, Polycrates, the least of all of you, according to the teaching of my relatives, whom I too followed—for seven of my relatives were bishops, and I am the eighth—have always celebrated Easter when the Jewish people were observing the unleavened bread. Therefore, brothers, being sixty-five years old in the Lord, instructed by many brothers from throughout the whole world, and having traversed all Scripture, I shall not fear those who threaten us. For my elders said: ‘We must obey God rather than human beings.’ I have set these things down for this reason, so that from this brief work I might display the man’s learning and authority. He flourished in the time of the emperor Severus, at the same period as Narcissus of Jerusalem.”

[Note: [Col. 0660C] Some manuscripts read “luminaries” instead of “elements,” which amounts to the same thing: for the ancients called the great luminaries—namely, the sun and moon—the two elements. The Greek has an even more apt expression, στοιχεῖα, “elements,” as Polycrates uses it here also. See Letter 120 to Hedibia, chapter 4, note c.]

[Note: [Col. 0660C] The pronoun “his,” which Valesius strongly favors, is not added by Polycrates, who mentions neither a golden plate nor one customarily worn on the forehead, but only τὸ πέταλον πεφορηκώς, “wearing the sacred plate,” unless πέταλον, as some prefer, signifies a golden plaque. Moreover, it is not really plausible that John actually wore a golden plate upon his forehead, as Valesius and Petavius believe; rather, this is said figuratively, in the sense in which Horace speaks of virtue:

“Nor does it take up or lay down the fasces
according to the judgment of popular favor.”

Thus, among Christians, wearing a golden plate would be equivalent to holding the dignity of high priest, whose insignia it is. In this way Epiphanius’s statements about James, and indeed about Mark, may also be suitably explained, as may the author of his Passion, cited by Valesius.]

[Note: [Col. 0660D] The verb “lies” is absent from the manuscript of the Holy Cross, and the Greek text of Polycrates does not recognize it either.]

[Note: [Col. 0660D] The Greek has Μελίτωνα τὸν εὐνοῦχον, τὸν ἐν ἁγίῳ πνεύματι, etc., “Melito the eunuch, who in the Holy Spirit,” etc.; here in Jerome the words seem to be involved in a faulty transposition.]

[Col. 0658C] Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, together with the remaining bishops of Asia who celebrated the feast of Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, issued a synodal letter against Victor, bishop of Rome, teaching that one ought to follow the apostle John and adhere to the ancient authority. From it I shall relate a few passages:

“We therefore celebrate the undefiled feast, neither adding nor subtracting anything. For in Asia great luminaries have fallen asleep, and they will rise on the day of the Lord, when he comes from heaven in his own glory, raising all the saints. I mean Philip, one of the Twelve Apostles, who slept at Hierapolis, and his two daughters, who grew old as virgins, and another of his daughters, who, filled with the Holy Spirit, attained her perfection at Ephesus. John also, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast, and who became his priest while bearing a golden plate upon his forehead, a martyr and teacher, slept at Ephesus. Polycarp, bishop and martyr, lies at Smyrna; and Thraseas, bishop and martyr from Eumenia, rests in that same Smyrna. There is no need to mention Sagaris, bishop and martyr, who rested at Laodicea, nor the most blessed Papirius, nor Melito, the eunuch in the Holy Spirit, who, always serving the Lord, was buried at Sardis and awaits the resurrection at his coming. All these observed the day of Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, deviating in no respect from the Gospel tradition and following the ecclesiastical rule. And I also, Polycrates, the least of all of you, according to the teaching of my neighbors, whom I too followed—for seven of my relatives became bishops, and I am the eighth—have always celebrated Easter when the Jewish people observed the unleavened bread. Therefore, brothers, being sixty-five years old in the Lord, having been instructed by many brothers from throughout the inhabited world, and having read all Scripture, I shall not fear those who threaten us. For my predecessors said: ‘We must obey God rather than human beings.’”

I have included these details so that I might demonstrate the man’s authority from a very brief work. He flourished in the time of the emperor Severus, when Narcissus also flourished at Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER LIII

[Note: [Col. 0661] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0661]

[Col. 0661C] Tertullian the presbyter, now placed first among the Latins after Victor and Apollonius, was from the province of Africa, the city of Carthage, the son of a proconsular centurion.

[Note: [Col. 0662D] The same author in the Chronicle under the sixteenth year of Severus: “Tertullian the African, son of a proconsular centurion, is celebrated in the name of all the churches.”]

He was a man of keen and forceful intelligence and flourished especially under the emperor Severus and Antoninus Caracalla. He wrote many volumes, which, since they are known to many, we pass over.

I saw an old man, Paul of Concordia—an Italian town—

[Note: [Col. 0662D] The ancient town between Aquileia and Altinum, not, as is commonly supposed, a town near Mirandola. See Letter 10 in our recension.]

who said that, when he himself was a very young man, he had seen at Rome a notary of the blessed Cyprian, then already advanced in age, and had heard him report that Cyprian never let a day pass without reading Tertullian, and frequently said to him, “Give me the master”—meaning Tertullian.

[Note: [Col. 0662D] The Veronese manuscript reads “and he reported”; shortly afterward the Gembloux manuscript has “the master,” without the verb give. It is remarkable that Cyprian never cites Tertullian, although, as our author says again in Letter 84, he used him as a teacher, as his writings demonstrate. Perhaps, while enjoying his talent, he sought to avoid the odium attached to his name.]

When Tertullian had remained a presbyter of the Church until middle age,

[Note: [Col. 0663C] Yet there are those who deny that Tertullian was ever a presbyter and maintain that none of the ancients ever transmitted this information. They consequently argue that the reading here should be “a man of the Church” rather than “a presbyter of the Church,” so that Jerome may remain consistent: otherwise he would seem to say that Tertullian was admitted to the presbyterate in his youth and remained in that rank until middle age, after which he ceased to be a presbyter—something wholly incompatible with the Church’s doctrine concerning the permanence of the sacramental character. Against them may be set the judgment and reliability of all authors who have spoken about Tertullian, whether in ecclesiastical libraries or elsewhere, none of whom doubted Jerome’s text. Moreover, the present wording is perfectly sound: he is said to have been “a presbyter of the Church,” not simply “a presbyter,” so that Tertullian may be understood to have remained attached to the Catholic Church in the rank of presbyter until that time, and afterward to have defected to the Montanists. Even if he did not cease to be a presbyter among them, he was no longer a presbyter of the Church. See Tillemont, Fleury, and others. Among the ancients, the author of the Predestined, who certainly wrote before Hincmar of Rheims, by whom he is cited and regarded by scholars as a fifth-century author, expressly attributes the presbyterate to Tertullian. Finally, Tertullian himself distinguishes himself from the laity in On the Soul, chapter 9. If, in On Monogamy and Exhortation to Chastity, he groups himself with the laity, this is because he composed those books after defecting to the Montanists.]

he later, through envy and insults directed at the clergy of the Roman Church, lapsed into the teaching of Montanus. In many books he referred to the New Prophecy, but he composed works specifically against the Church: On Modesty, On Persecution, On Fasting, On Monogamy, six books On Ecstasy,

[Note: [Col. 0663D] These books On Ecstasy, mentioned above in chapters 24 and 40, have perished.]

and a seventh which he composed against Apollonius. He is said to have lived into extreme old age and to have produced many short works which are no longer extant.

[Note: [Col. 0663D] The Vatican manuscript reads, perhaps with greater truth and in the opposite sense, “which now exist,” instead of “which do not exist.” Jerome says in Letter 64 to Fabiola, On the Priestly Garments, at the end, that he searched in vain for Tertullian’s book On Aaron’s Garments; but there are other volumes of Tertullian’s which Jerome does not mention here, though it is scarcely credible that they had already perished. These include a book On the Submission of the Soul; another On the Superstition of the Age; and On Flesh and Soul, whose titles were copied by Rigaltus from the Agobardine manuscript. Also among them are the works which Jerome himself praises either in this Catalogue, chapters 18 and 70, or elsewhere: On the Hope of the Faithful, a work On the Trinity, On Clean and Unclean Animals, On Circumcision, and On Virginity. I pass over those mentioned by other authors, such as Against the Apellitians, cited by Vincent of Lérins in chapter 24, and On Paradise, cited by Tertullian himself in On the Soul, chapter 55; these same testimonies support the Greek works On Spectacles, On Baptism, On the Veiling of Virgins, and On the Soldier’s Crown. If all these books, which a later age has deprived us of, had not existed even then, Jerome would at least have preserved their titles for posterity.]

[Col. 0662C] Tertullian the presbyter, now reckoned first among the Romans after Victor and Apollonius, came from Carthage in Africa, the son of a proconsular centurion. This man, of formidable and exceptionally gifted intelligence, flourished under Severus and Antoninus surnamed Caracalla. He composed many volumes, which we omit because they are known to many. I met an old man, Paul of Concordia in Italy, who said that, while still young, he had seen in Rome the notary of the most blessed Cyprian—by then an old man—and had heard from him that Cyprian scarcely ever passed a day without reading Tertullian, repeatedly saying, “Hand me the teacher,” clearly referring to Tertullian. Tertullian was a presbyter of our Church until middle age; afterward, through envy and the abuse of the clergy of the Church in Rome, he slipped into the teaching of Montanus. He composed many books in which he mentions the New Prophecy, and wrote specifically against the Church, as well as six treatises on chastity, persecution, fasting, monogamy, and ecstasy, and a seventh against Apollonius, along with many other works. He lived to extreme old age.

[Col. 0663B] Origen, also called Adamantius, when persecution against the Christians broke out in the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, was left poor, at about seventeen years of age, with six brothers and his widowed mother, after his father Leonides had been crowned with the martyrdom of Christ.

Two Vatican manuscripts read: “by his father Leonides, a bishop, crowned with the martyrdom of Christ,” etc. The Cluniac manuscript formerly read: “Origen, also called Amantius the presbyter,” etc. Thus many passages have been corrupted through the errors of ancient scribes, while many others have remained uncorrupted. MARTIAN. In two Vatican manuscripts Martianaeus found “by Leonides, the bishop-father”; in our manuscript even the preposition “by” is absent. Compare Eusebius VI.1–2.]

For the family property had been confiscated because of his confession of Christ.

At Alexandria, when the Church had been dispersed, he undertook the work of catechesis in the eighteenth year of his age. Later Demetrius, bishop of that city, appointed him to the position of the presbyter Clement,

[Note: [Col. 0664D] Clement of Alexandria, mentioned above in chapter 38.]

and he flourished for many years. When he had reached middle age

[Note: [Col. 0664D] He was approximately forty-three years old.]

and, because of the Churches of Achaea, which were being harassed by numerous heresies, was traveling through Palestine toward Athens under the authorization of an ecclesiastical letter,

[Note: [Col. 0664D] Ecclesiastical writers call these letters “formatae.”]

he was ordained presbyter by Theoctistus and Alexander, bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem. This offended Demetrius,

[Col. 0663C] who raged against him with such madness that he wrote throughout the whole world concerning his name. It is established that, before he moved to Caesarea, he had been at Rome under Bishop Zephyrinus. Returning immediately to Alexandria, he made Heraclas the presbyter, who continued to wear the philosopher’s dress, his assistant in catechesis. Heraclas later governed the Church of Alexandria after Demetrius.

[Note: [Col. 0665C] Martianaeus incorrectly inserted the word “again” here; Victorius had removed it long ago.]

His great renown is evident from the fact that Firmilianus, bishop of Caesarea, invited him together with all Cappadocia, kept him there for a long time, and later, when he came to Palestine on the pretext of visiting the holy places, was instructed by him for a long time in the sacred Scriptures at Caesarea.

[Note: [Col. 0665C] The Sigeberg and Guelpherbit manuscripts, as well as the Greek version, incorrectly have Firmianus instead of Firmilianus.]

It is also shown by the fact that, when he was invited to Antioch to visit Mammæa, the mother of the emperor Alexander, a religious woman, he came and was treated with the highest honor; and that he wrote letters to Philip the emperor, who was the first of the Roman emperors to be a Christian, and to his mother, which are still extant.

[Note: [Col. 0665C] This is indeed stated by Eusebius VI.34: “A report holds that he was a Christian,” and is confirmed in the Chronicle under the year 246. Yet scholars, without my saying anything, know well how many difficulties this statement involves. Learned men assert that this Philip has been confused with another Philip, the Christian prefect of Egypt who bore the same name.]

[Note: [Col. 0665D] Oracilla Severa, the mother of the younger Philip and wife of the elder; hence Eusebius says γαμετὴν Σεβήραν, “Severa his wife,” not “his mother.” Vincent of Lérins also cites that letter in the Commonitorium I.23: “How greatly he was revered, not only by private persons but also by imperial authority, the histories show, which relate that he was summoned by the mother of the emperor Alexander because of his heavenly wisdom, with whose grace he burned, while she burned with love for him. The testimony of that same letter also shows that he wrote to Philip the emperor, the first of the Roman rulers to be a Christian, with the authority of a Christian teacher. Understand one letter, not several, written around the year 245.”]

Who does not know how devoted he was to the divine Scriptures, so that, contrary to the nature of his age and nation, he even learned the Hebrew language?

[Note: [Col. 0665D] These statements concerning Origen’s knowledge of Hebrew are also vigorously disputed on both sides; most of the more learned scholars deny him this distinction.]

And, besides the Septuagint translators, he gathered together in one volume other editions as well:

[Note: [Col. 0666C] The word “volume” appears perhaps to be deleted, since neither the Veronese manuscript nor the Greek translator recognizes it. Jerome may have said “in one,” meaning “together in one place,” that Origen gathered these editions; it is not plausible that he contained them in a single volume. The surviving fragments of this labor fill two folio volumes.]

namely, that of Aquila, the Pontic proselyte; that of Theodotion, the Ebionite; and that of Symmachus, who held the same doctrine and also wrote commentaries on the Gospel according to Matthew, by which he attempts to confirm his own doctrine. In addition, he discovered with extraordinary labor the fifth, sixth, and seventh editions, which we too possess from his library, and compared them with the other editions.

[Note: [Col. 0666D] Namely, from the Caesarean library. Concerning Symmachus, see Ebed-Jesu, chapter 10.]

[Note: [Col. 0666D] Some manuscripts, according to Martianaeus, read “joined together.” The Greek translator rendered ὠνήσατο very badly as “bought,” taking it to mean “purchase,” whereas it means “to compare.”]

895 Since I have placed an inventory of his works in the volumes of letters which I wrote to Paula, comparing it with the works of Varro in one letter,

[Note: [Col. 0666D] In one letter. This letter perished through the injury of time, though Rufinus has preserved and reported a substantial portion of it in Book II of his Invectives. See above, at the end of the second class of letters. The modesty and humility of holy Paula deprived posterity of the remaining volumes of her letters, since she did not wish her name to be celebrated through Jerome’s letters. MARTIAN. Rufinus preserved a fragment of this letter in Book II of his Invectives; we present it there, taken from him, in the first volume, Letter 33. Eusebius had drawn up the same inventory in the Life of the holy martyr Pamphilus, which perished together with it.]

I now omit it, saying only this about his immortal natural ability: he learned dialectic, geometry, arithmetic, music, grammar, and rhetoric, as well as the doctrines of all the philosophers, so thoroughly that he had adherents among students of secular literature and interpreted these subjects for them daily, and great crowds came to him. He received them for this reason: under the pretext of secular learning, he instructed them in the faith of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0667C] The Vatican manuscript reads “every student,” instead of “students,” which I would certainly prefer to restore. Since the secular studies enumerated here are geometry, arithmetic, music, and so on, the sense is that Origen had as followers those who studied each of these subjects.]

As for the cruelty of the persecution that arose against the Christians under Decius, because he raged against the religion of Philip, whom he also killed, it is unnecessary to speak of it. Fabianus, bishop of the Roman Church, died in that very persecution, and Alexander and Babylas, bishops of Jerusalem and Antioch, died in prison for their confession of Christ.

If anyone wishes to know what happened concerning Origen’s position, he will be able to learn it clearly first from his letters, which were sent to various people after the persecution; then from Book VI of the ecclesiastical history of Eusebius of Caesarea; and from the six books written in defense of Origen.

[Note: [Col. 0667C] These letters have perished, as has the Apology which he soon mentions in six volumes, of which only one survives in Rufinus’s translation. See Eusebius’s very substantial testimony concerning them in Book VI, chapter 39.]

He lived until Gallus and Volusianus, that is, until the sixty-ninth year of his age, and died at Tyre, where he was also buried.

[Note: [Col. 0667C] Between the words “learn clearly” and “he lived,” the following additional words are found in manuscript 281 of the Ambrosian Library and in Vatican manuscripts 348 and 349: “This praise of Origen is false and deceives many who are attracted to love him, since it is established that, with a poisoned mouth—or perhaps ‘a venomous mouth’—he spoke unheard-of and intolerable blasphemies against our Lord Jesus Christ under a demonic spirit, and that, having been anathematized by holy Fathers, bishops, and monks, even his good works ought not to be read. He lived, etc.” MARTIAN. In Ambrosian manuscript 281 and two Vatican manuscripts Martianaeus found this very foolish scholion: “This praise of Origen is false and deceives many who are attracted to love him, since it is established that, with a poisoned mouth, he spoke unheard-of and intolerable blasphemies against our Lord Jesus Christ under a demonic spirit; and, having been anathematized by holy Fathers, bishops, and monks, even his good works ought not to be read.”]

[Col. 0664B] Origen, also called Adamantius, when persecution against the Christians broke out in the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, was left poor by his father Leonides, who had also suffered martyrdom, together with six brothers and his widowed mother, at about seventeen years of age. For their property was confiscated because they were Christians. When the Church at Alexandria had been scattered, he was eighteen years old and had undertaken the discipline of catechesis. Not long afterward he was appointed by Demetrius, bishop of that city, to the position of the presbyter Clement, and he distinguished himself for many years. Having reached middle age, and because the Churches in Achaea were being troubled by many heresies, he traveled through Palestine to Athens under the authority of an ecclesiastical letter. There, having been ordained presbyter by Theoctistus and Alexander, bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem, he incurred Demetrius’s displeasure. Demetrius displayed such madness against him that he wrote throughout the inhabited world concerning his name.

Before moving to Caesarea, Origen had gone to Rome under Bishop Zephyrinus. Returning immediately to Alexandria, he took as his assistant in catechesis Heraclas the presbyter, who continued to appear in the dress of a philosopher; Heraclas later governed the Church of Alexandria after Demetrius. His great renown is shown by this: Firmilianus, bishop of Caesarea, came with all Cappadocia and received him, kept him for a long time, and later, when he came to Palestine under the pretext of visiting the holy places, was instructed by him in the divine Scriptures at Caesarea.

No one is unaware that, when he was invited to visit Mammæa, the most devout woman and mother of the emperor Alexander, he came to Antioch and was held in the greatest honor; nor that he sent letters to Philip the emperor, the first of the Roman emperors to become a Christian, and to his mother, which remain to the present day. He was so devoted to the divine Scriptures that he even mastered the Hebrew language, despite its opposition to his age and his natural disposition. Besides the Septuagint translators, he gathered together other editions: that of Aquila, the Pontic proselyte; that of Theodotion, the Ebionite; and that of Symmachus, who held the same doctrine and commented on the Gospel according to Matthew, through which he hastened to establish his own doctrine. Likewise, after finding with great labor the fifth, sixth, and seventh editions, which we too possessed from his library, he compared them with the other editions.

Since I have set out an inventory of his works in one of the volumes of letters written by us to Paula, comparing them with the works of Varro, I now pass over it. I will not be silent about his immortal natural ability: he learned dialectic, geometry, arithmetic, music, grammar, rhetoric, and the doctrines of all the philosophers so thoroughly that he had students of secular learning as hearers, interpreted these subjects for them from time to time, and attracted many gatherings. He received them for this reason: under the pretext of teaching, he led them all to the faith of Christ.

As for the severity of the persecution that broke out against the Christians under Decius—for he raged against Philip’s piety, whom he also killed—I consider it superfluous to speak. In that persecution Fabianus, bishop of Rome, also died, and Alexander and Babylas, bishops of Jerusalem and Antioch, died in prison as confessors.

If anyone wishes to learn about Origen, he can learn it clearly first from his letters sent to various people after the persecution, then from the sixth book of the history of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and from the six brilliant books written in defense of Origen. He lived until Gallus and Volusianus, that is, until the sixty-ninth year of his life, and died at Tyre, where he was also buried.

## CHAPTER LV

[Note: [Col. 0667] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0667]

[Col. 0667B] Ammonius, [Note: [Col. 0667D] This Ammonius, the Christian writer of the Monotessaron, has to this day been confused with another Ammonius, surnamed Saccas, Plotinus’s teacher. Porphyry caused the error: having said of Ammonius Saccas, or Saccarius, that he had become a pagan from being a Christian, Eusebius wrongly understood this to have been said of this other Ammonius, a Christian writer who persevered until the end of his life. The decisive difference between them is that Ammonius, Plotinus’s teacher, is known—and Longinus testifies—to have written nothing at all, whereas our Ammonius produced the two works listed here by Jerome.] a man eloquent and highly learned in philosophy, was held in distinction at Alexandria at the same time. Among the many distinguished monuments of his talent, he also composed an elegant work on the harmony of Moses and Jesus and devised the Gospel Canons, which Eusebius of Caesarea later followed.

[Note: [Col. 0668D] This work has long since perished. Eusebius of Caesarea constructed the canons placed before the Gospels from Ammonius’s Harmony, or Diatessaron.]

Porphyry falsely accuses him of having changed from a Christian into a pagan,

[Note: [Col. 0668D] Porphyry, in Book III Against the Christians, is excellently refuted by Eusebius for having lied, both about other matters and especially about Ammonius.]

although it is established that he remained a Christian until the end of his life.

[Note: [Col. 0668D] The Vatican manuscripts omit “in philosophy”; Martianaeus’s edition omits “very.” Porphyry, in Eusebius VI.19, asserts both points, attributing to him “the greatest advancement in philosophy.”]

[Col. 0668B] Ammonius, a most distinguished man educated in philosophy, who appeared illustrious at Alexandria in those same times, composed, among his notable works, a remarkable book on the harmony of Moses and Jesus and devised Gospel Canons, which Eusebius of Caesarea later followed. Porphyry falsely accuses him, saying that he changed from a Christian into a pagan, although he remained a Christian until the end.

## CHAPTER LVI

[Note: [Col. 0667] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0667]

[Col. 0667C] 897 Ambrose, initially a Marcionite,

[Note: [Col. 0668D] Eusebius VI.18 says that he initially adhered to the sect of Valentinus: τὰ τῆς Οὐαλεντίνου φρονοῦντα αἱρέσεως, “holding the opinions of Valentinus’s sect.” Epiphanius, Heresy 64.3, reports that some called him a Marcionite and others a Sabellian; others make him a Noetian. In any case, he was distinguished by nobility of birth, talent, wealth, and the manner of his life after his conversion.]

and afterward corrected by Origen, became a deacon of the Church and was distinguished by the glory of confessing the Lord. To him and to the presbyter Protoctetus Origen’s book On Martyrdom is addressed.

[Note: [Col. 0668D] The common editions and the Greek have “to whom,” in place of “to the presbyter Theoctistus”; the Veronese manuscript, having suffered the hand of a bold copyist, reads “to whom with the presbyter Toctistus,” and shortly afterward “was written.” Before me, the learned Fabricius restored the correct reading from Eusebius and from Origen’s own book, where he addresses Ambrose and Protoctetus: Ἀμβρόσιε θεοπρεπέστατε, Πρωτόκτητε εὐσεβέστατε, “Most godly Ambrose, most devout Protoctetus.” The reading is now supported by the Vatican manuscript: “to him together with Protoctetus the presbyter,” etc. Nicephorus Callistus likewise says in Ecclesiastical History V.19: “He composed a noble exhortation to martyrdom for Ambrose and Protoctetus of the ecclesiastical community at Caesarea, addressing the work to them.”]

With his labor, expense, and persistence Origen, aided by him, dictated innumerable volumes.

[Note: [Col. 0669C] We have emended the text in accordance with the Vatican manuscript cited above, since previously the passage either had no sense or conveyed the opposite meaning. Learned men consequently imagined that Ambrose, as an ἐργοδιώκτης, or “taskmaster,” had commissioned countless volumes from Origen which have perished. Jerome regularly uses the expression “assisted by encouragement, prayers,” and so forth.]

Ambrose himself, being a man of noble birth, also possessed no insignificant talent, as his letters to Origen demonstrate.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] Time has deprived us of these letters. Only a fragment survives, which Jerome attributes to Ambrose in Letter 45 to Marcella; but it seems to be a letter of Origen himself, addressed to Ambrose.]

He died before Origen’s death; and for this reason many criticize him, because, although wealthy, he did not remember his old and poor friend when he was dying.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] The Veronese manuscript reads: “He died before Origen.” Ambrose’s death occurred around the year 351.]

[Col. 0668C] 898 Ambrose, initially a Marcionite and afterward corrected by Origen, became a deacon of the Church and was distinguished by the glory of divine confession. Origen’s book On Martyrdom was written for him, on behalf of the presbyter Theoctistus. Through his zeal, expense, and persistence, Origen sent him innumerable works. Ambrose himself, being a most noble man, was not without talent, as his letters to Origen show. He died before Origen; and for this many condemn him, because, although wealthy, he did not remember his own friend, an old and poor man, when he was dying.

## CHAPTER LVII

[Note: [Col. 0669] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669A] Tryphon, a pupil of Origen, to whom some of Origen’s letters are extant, was highly learned in the Scriptures. This is shown by many of his short works scattered here and there, but especially by the book he composed on the red heifer in Deuteronomy and on the divided offerings which are placed with the dove and the turtledove of Abraham in Genesis.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] I do not know of anyone among the ancients, apart from Jerome, who mentions this Tryphon. I have found his praised works nowhere. In the meantime, the Veronese manuscript calls him Origen’s assistant rather than his pupil, apparently through a faulty transposition of letters.]

[Note: [Col. 0670C] The sacrifice of a red heifer is not commanded in Deuteronomy but in the Book of Numbers, chapter 19. Concerning the “divided offerings”—a term indicating the division into two parts—see the account in Genesis 15 of the victims which Abraham divided. The Vatican manuscript places “in the book” before “to Abraham”; the Guelpherbit manuscript reads more correctly, “from Abraham,” etc.]

[Col. 0670A] Tryphon, Origen’s pupil, to whom many letters exist, was learned in the divine Scriptures, as his works scattered here and there demonstrate, and especially the book on the heifer in Deuteronomy and on the divided offerings, which we read about in Genesis together with Abraham’s dove and turtledove.

## CHAPTER LVIII

[Note: [Col. 0669] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669B] [Note: [Col. 0670C] Minucius Felix. The Sangerman manuscript places Gaius before Minucius Felix, although in the Index and Catalogue it follows the usual order. Certainly they are contemporaries of one another and of Tertullian, if we trust learned writers. MARTIAN.]

Minucius Felix, a distinguished advocate at Rome, wrote a dialogue between a Christian and a pagan disputant, entitled Octavius.

[Note: [Col. 0670D] The Veronese manuscript reads “a disputing pagan.” The Sigeberg manuscript incorrectly reads “heretic.”]

Another work is also circulated under his name, On Fate, or Against the Mathematicians. Although it too appears to be by an eloquent man, it does not seem to me to accord with the style of the former book.

[Note: [Col. 0670D] Whatever this book was, it no longer exists. Minucius himself certainly promised to write something of this sort in Octavius, chapter 36: “And concerning Fate, we shall discuss elsewhere, if only briefly for the time being, both more fully and more completely.”]

Lactantius also mentions this Minucius in his books.

[Note: [Col. 0670D] Lactantius, Divine Institutes I.11.]

[Col. 0670B] Minucius Felix, a distinguished advocate at Rome, wrote a dialogue between a Christian and a pagan, which he entitled Octavius. Another discourse is also circulated under his name, On Fate, or Against the Mathematicians. Although this work too appears to be by a distinguished man, it does not seem to me to correspond in style to the previously mentioned discourse. Lactantius also mentions this Minucius in his own writings.

## CHAPTER LIX

[Note: [Col. 0669] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669B] 899 Gaius, under Zephyrinus, bishop of the city of Rome—that is, under Antoninus, son of Severus—held a very notable disputation against Proculus, a follower of Montanus. He charged him with rashness in defending the New Prophecy. In the same volume he also enumerated only thirteen Epistles of Paul; he says that the fourteenth, which is said to be addressed to the Hebrews, is not his, and that even among the Romans to this day it is not regarded as the work of the apostle Paul.

[Note: [Col. 0670D] Eusebius II.25 and Photius, codex 48, call him Proclus: πρὸς Πρόκλον. Latin writers more often call him Proculus. Gaius’s disputation against him has long since perished. Caracalla, son of Severus, administered the empire from 211 to 217.]

[Note: [Col. 0670D] Eusebius has παρὰ Ῥωμαίων τισίν, “among certain Romans,” not absolutely “among the Romans,” as Jerome interprets it.]

[Col. 0670B] 900 Gaius, under Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome—that is, under Antoninus, son of Severus—held a very extensive disputation against Proculus, a follower of Montanus, charging him with rashness in defending the New Prophecy. In the same volume he counted only thirteen Epistles of Paul; for he says that the Epistle to the Hebrews is not his, and that even among the Romans to the present day it is not considered to be Paul the apostle’s.

## CHAPTER LX

[Note: [Col. 0669] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669C] **Beryllus**, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, [Note: [Col. 0670D] The same author records in the *Chronicle*, under the sixth year of Alexander Severus: “Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, is held in renown.” See Eusebius VI.20.] after having governed the Church gloriously for some time, finally fell into the heresy which denies Christ before the Incarnation, [Note: [Col. 0671B] The Veronese manuscript reads “before the flesh.” The Wolfenbüttel manuscript says “denies that he existed before the Incarnation.” From Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 33, one understands that Beryllus denied Christ’s distinction as a distinct person before he assumed flesh: “nor, indeed, that he possessed a deity of his own,” in accordance with the heresy of Noetus, which later became that of Sabellius.] but was corrected by Origen. He wrote various short works, [Note: [Col. 0671C] Nothing now survives of Beryllus’s writings, whether of his own works or of Origen’s letters to Beryllus.] and especially letters in which he gives thanks to Origen; there are also letters from Origen to him. A dialogue between Origen and Beryllus survives, in which he is convicted of heresy. He flourished under Alexander, son of Mamaea, and under Maximinus and Gordian, who succeeded him in the empire.

[Col. 0670C] **Beryllus**, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, after governing the Church gloriously for a certain time, finally slipping into the heresy that denies Christ before the Incarnation, was turned back by Origen. He composed various works, and especially letters in which he gives thanks to Origen; but there are also letters from Origen to him. There is a dialogue between Origen and Beryllus in which he is convicted of heresy. He flourished under Alexander, son of Mamaea, and under Maximinus and Gordian, who succeeded him in the empire.

## CHAPTER LXI

[Note: [Col. 0671] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0671]

[Col. 0671A] **Hippolytus**, bishop of some Church—for I have not been able to learn the name of the city—wrote a work on the date of Easter and chronological Canons, extending to the first year of the emperor Alexander; and he discovered a sixteen-year cycle, which the Greeks call a *hexakaidekaeterid* (ἑκκαιδεκαετηρίς), [Col. 0671B] and gave Eusebius, who composed a nineteen-year cycle concerning that same Easter, the occasion for doing so. [Note: [Col. 0671C] The Veronese manuscript reads: “He wrote the chronological Canons,” without the word “cycle.” Valesius thinks this was a second section of the book on Easter, something which Scaliger and Bucherius entirely failed to notice. In other words, this chronological canon extended as far as the first year of Alexander; whereas the calculation of Easter itself began from that same year. This remarkable monument survives not only in manuscripts but, engraved in ancient times on the marble chair of Saint Hippolytus—the saint himself seated upon it in marble—still stands in the vestibule of the Vatican Library. Its right side displays the Paschal chronology through cycles of 112 Julian years, arranged proleptically from the sacred writings. The other side displays the expansion of that same Paschal cycle through seven sixteen-year cycles. On the rear side a catalogue of some of his works is displayed, though its inscription has been damaged in its upper portion.] [Note: [Col. 0671D] This nineteen-year cycle is commonly believed to have been lost. But, as the more learned critic above maintains, it was never composed by Eusebius. Jerome drew this information—or rather, misunderstood it—from Eusebius himself, where, in *Life of Constantine* IV.34–35, Eusebius says that he composed a book in which the hidden meaning of the Paschal feast was explained, and that he dedicated it to Constantine. Yet from the whole context, and from Constantine’s own reply to Eusebius, it is quite clear that the book contained the mysteries of Christ and the typological interpretation of his Paschal feast, not a nineteen-year cycle of Paschal lunar years. Jerome does not seem to have consulted Eusebius’s book on Easter itself, since he does not mention it among Eusebius’s writings in its proper place, chapter 81 below. Here, moreover, contrary to Eusebius, he thinks that Hippolytus supplied Eusebius with the opportunity to compose the nineteen-year cycle, although Eusebius himself states in *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.32 that this cycle had been arranged long before, around the beginning of the reign of the emperor Probus, by Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea in Syria. It is also highly probable that the Church of Alexandria had already used this nineteen-year cycle before the Council of Nicaea. In any case, this testimony of Jerome misled Gennadius in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 38; and Gennadius in turn misled Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies* VI.17, who repeat the same claim about Eusebius, to say nothing of the later writers Ceolfrith and Bede, who copied one from another.] He wrote some commentaries on the Scriptures, of which I have found the following: on the *Hexaemeron*, [Note: [Col. 0672C] The words “and on Exodus” are absent from the Veronese manuscript. The manuscripts and printed editions that contain them seem to have adopted them in place of “and after the Hexaemeron.” Thus Eusebius VI.22 joins to his *Commentary on the Hexaemeron* another work, “on the things after the Hexaemeron”; and Rufinus likewise has “on the Hexaemeron and on the things after the Hexaemeron.” Perhaps someone had thought that the same Greek word, *Hexaemeron*, had been repeated corruptly in Jerome’s text and changed it to “and on Exodus.”] and on Exodus, on the *Song of Songs*, on Genesis, and on Zechariah; on the Psalms, on Isaiah, on Daniel, on the Apocalypse, on Proverbs, on Ecclesiastes, on Saul and the Witch, on the Antichrist, on the Resurrection, against Marcion, on Easter, against all heresies, and a *prosomilia* (Προσομιλία), [Note: [Col. 0672D] The Veronese manuscript reads *prosaomelian*. From it, from the Vatican manuscript, and from Jerome’s own text, it is clear that the reading should be *prosomilian* (προσομιλία), as Fabricius restored it. Earlier printed editions incorrectly had *pros homilion* or *peri homilion*, and Erasmus and others similar forms. This was probably a homily on the Epiphany, which survives.] on praise of the Lord and Savior, in which he indicates that he spoke in church in Origen’s presence. [Col. 0673A] Ambrose, whom we have said was corrected from the heresy of Marcion into the true faith, urged Origen to write commentaries on the Scriptures in emulation of this work, providing him with seven or more stenographers, paying their expenses, and an equal number of copyists; and, greater than all this, demanding from him daily work with incredible zeal. Hence in one letter Origen calls him an “exactor of work” (ἐργοδιώκτης).

[Note: [Col. 0673C] The Greek translator and some Latin editions incorrectly join these words, “in emulation of this,” to the preceding sentence.]

[Col. 0672A] **Hippolytus**, I do not know bishop of what Church—or rather, I was unable to learn the name of what city—wrote a work on Easter and the chronological Canons extending to the first year of Alexander the emperor: a sixteen-year cycle, I mean, which those called Greeks call a *hexakaidekaeterid* (ἑκκαιδεκαετηρίς), thereby giving Eusebius, who composed a nineteen-year cycle concerning Easter itself, the occasion. He wrote commentaries on the divine Scriptures, of which I found the following: on the *Hexaemeron*, on Exodus, on the *Song of Songs*, on Genesis, on Zechariah, on the Psalms, on Isaiah, on Daniel, on the Apocalypse, on Proverbs, on Ecclesiastes, on Saul and the Witch, on the Antichrist, on the Resurrection, against Marcion, on Easter, against all heresies, and *prosomilia*—read *prosomilian* (προσομιλία)—on the praises of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which he indicates that, in Origen’s presence, he himself preached in the church in imitation of him. Ambrose, whom we have previously said was turned from Marcion’s error to the true faith, urged Origen to comment on the divine Scriptures, having supplied him with seven or more stenographers, their expenses, and the same number of skilled copyists; and, what is greater, continually demanding work from him with unremitting zeal. Therefore, in one letter, Origen calls him an “exactor of work.”

## CHAPTER LXII

[Note: [Col. 0673] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0673]

[Col. 0673A] **Alexander**, bishop of Cappadocia, [Note: [Col. 0673C] Eusebius and Jerome omit the city. From the fifth book of the Greek-Roman law, concerning the transfer of bishops, it appears to have been Flavia.] when he was traveling to Jerusalem out of devotion to the holy places, and Narcissus, bishop of that city, was already advanced in age [Note: [Col. 0673C] He was 116 years old, as will soon be stated. See Eusebius VI.11.] and governing the Church, it was revealed both to Narcissus and to many of his clergy that on the following morning a bishop would enter who was to become an assistant to the episcopal chair. Accordingly, when the matter had happened just as it had been foretold, all the bishops in Palestine having assembled, and Narcissus himself especially supporting the arrangement, Alexander assumed with him the governance of the Church of Jerusalem. At the end of a letter which he wrote to the people of Antinoe concerning the peace of the Church, he says: [Note: [Col. 0673D] In Eusebius VI.11: “Narcissus, who before me held here the episcopal office, and who now joins me in directing it through his prayers, having completed 116 years, sends you greetings and, together with me, urges you to be of one mind with me.”] “Narcissus greets you, who before me held the episcopal office here, and who now governs the same office with me through his prayers, being about 116 years old, and he asks you, together with me, to hold one and the same opinion.” [Note: [Col. 0673D] The manuscript of Santa Croce adds one year, giving the number as 117.] He also wrote another letter to the Antiochenes, through Clement, presbyter of Alexandria, whom we mentioned above, and likewise to Origen and on Origen’s behalf against Demetrius, because, according to Demetrius’s testimony, he had appointed him presbyter. [Note: [Col. 0674C] He prefers a stronger reply to be written against Demetrius’s testimony. Rather, “according to” must be retained; for, since it is reported above, chapter 34, under the testimony of an ecclesiastical letter, that Alexander kindly received Origen and ordained him presbyter, he ought to have pressed this against Demetrius from Demetrius’s own letters.] Other letters of his to various persons are also reported. During the seventh persecution, under Decius, at the time when Babylas also suffered at Antioch, Alexander was taken to Caesarea and shut up in prison; because of his confession of Christ, he was crowned with martyrdom.

[Col. 0674A] **Alexander**, bishop of Cappadocia, having come to Jerusalem out of longing for the holy places, while Narcissus, bishop of that same city, was already aged and governing the Church, it was revealed both to Narcissus himself and to many of his clergy that on the following morning a bishop would enter who ought to become an assistant to the episcopal chair. When the matter had therefore been fulfilled just as it had been foretold, all the bishops in Palestine having gathered together, and Narcissus agreeing with them, Alexander assumed with him the governance of the Church in Jerusalem. At the end of a letter written by him to the people of Antinoe concerning ecclesiastical peace, he said: “Narcissus greets you, who before me held the episcopal office here, and who now, directing the same office with me, participates in prayer, being in his 116th year; he asks you, together with me, to think the same thing and to be of one mind.” He also wrote another letter to the Antiochenes through Clement, presbyter of Alexandria, whom I mentioned earlier; and also to Origen and on Origen’s behalf against Demetrius, and because, with Demetrius bearing witness, he ordained him presbyter. Other letters of his to various persons are also circulated. In the seventh persecution, under Decius, when Babylas also suffered at Antioch, he was taken to Caesarea and shut up in prison; because of his confession of Christ, he suffered martyrdom.

[Col. 0674C] **Julius Africanus**, whose five books on chronology are extant, undertook, under Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, who succeeded Macrinus, an embassy concerning the restoration of the city of Emmaus, which was renamed Nicopolis. There is also a letter to Origen concerning the question of Susanna; for he says that this story is not found in Hebrew, nor does it agree with the Hebrew etymology, “from *prinos*, to saw, and from *schinos*, to split,” against which Origen writes a carefully reasoned letter. He also has another letter to Aristides, in which he adequately discusses the apparent discrepancy in the genealogy of the Savior in Matthew and Luke.

[Col. 0675B] **Theodore**, who was afterward called Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, being still very young, crossed from Cappadocia to Beirut and from there to Caesarea in Palestine for the study of Greek and Latin literature, together with his brother Athenodorus. When Origen saw their excellent natural abilities, he urged them toward philosophy, [Note: [Col. 0676C] Adamantius did not convert these illustrious brothers to the faith of Christ through the study of philosophy; they had already given their names to the Christian religion. Indeed, Gregory himself, in his *Panegyric of Origen*, professes that he had arrived at the knowledge of truth long before he came to Origen.] and gradually introducing them to the faith of Christ, made them his own followers. The correct reading is probably “to their homeland,” as Lipsius and Gravius had long ago argued from Suidas. — “They are sent back to their father.” Printed books, together with not a few manuscripts, read “to their mother”; others read “to their father.” Perhaps “to their homeland” should be read. MARTIAN.] their mother. Theodore, on departing from them, wrote Origen a *panegyric of thanksgiving* and, after assembling a large audience, recited it in Origen’s presence; it survives to this day. Other letters of his are commonly circulated, [Note: [Col. 0677C] Of these only one survives, the celebrated letter among the canonical letters of the Fathers. After the word “letter,” Suffridus, Miraeus, and others add “and on faith,” and, under Honorius, “other letters on faith.” These words are absent from all our manuscripts and from other very ancient ones, as well as from Freculphus and the Greek translator. See Letter 70, to Magnus, and the commentary on Ecclesiastes, chapter 4.] but especially signs and miracles, which he performed as bishop to the great glory of the Churches.

[Col. 0676B] **Theodore**, who was later called Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, being still very young, crossed from Cappadocia to Beirut, and from there to Caesarea in Palestine, because of his education in Greek and Roman letters, together with his brother Athenodorus. When Origen saw their exceptional natural ability, he urged them toward philosophy and, gradually introducing them to the faith of Christ, made them his own devoted followers. After they had been educated by him for five years, they were sent back to their mother. Theodore, as he was departing, wrote Origen a panegyric of thanksgiving, and, having assembled all the local people, recited this address in Origen’s presence; it still exists. He also wrote a brief but exceedingly remarkable exposition of Ecclesiastes, and many other letters; and he performed signs and wonders when he was bishop.

He governed the Church for two years while Gallus and Volusianus were emperors; Lucius succeeded him after he suffered martyrdom for Christ.

[Col. 0678B] **Cyprian the African**, having first taught rhetoric with distinction, was persuaded by the presbyter Caecilius, from whom he received his surname. Having become a Christian, he distributed all his wealth among the poor; and shortly afterward, having been admitted to the presbyterate, he became bishop of Carthage. I consider it superfluous to compose a catalogue of his natural ability, because his writings are brighter than the sun. He suffered under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, in the eighth persecution, on the very day on which Cornelius suffered at Rome, but not in the same year.

His letter begins as follows: [Note: [Col. 0679D] In Eusebius VI.45: “Dionysius to Novatian his brother, greeting. In the former case he bears witness for the sake of his own soul alone; here, for the sake of the whole Church. And now, if you persuade or compel the brothers to come to unity, your restoration will be greater than your offense, the one will not be reckoned against you, while the other will be praised. The one will not be counted against you; the other will be praised. But if, because they do not obey, you achieve less than you wish, nevertheless do everything possible to preserve your own soul.”] He has another letter to Dionysius and Didymus, and many festal letters on Easter, written in a declamatory style; a letter to the Church of Alexandria concerning exile; a letter to Hieracas, bishop in Egypt; another concerning mortality; one concerning the Sabbath; one concerning exercise; and one to Hermammon, as well as another concerning the persecution of Decius. [Note: [Col. 0681B] The Veronese manuscript more correctly reads “asserted.” These books against Nepos, bishop of Egypt, may perhaps be the ones Jerome notes in the Preface to Book XVIII on Isaiah, where he says that Dionysius of Alexandria mocked the fable of the thousand years in a book against Irenaeus. See Eusebius VII.24.] He wrote against Sabellius, and to Ammon of Berenice, bishop; to Telesphorus; and to Euphranor. He also wrote many letters to Basilides, in one of which he says that he had begun to write commentaries on Ecclesiastes as well. A notable letter of his against Paul of Samosata is also reported to have been written a few days before his death. He died in the twelfth year of Gallienus. [Note: [Col. 0681D] A.D. 265. The Wolfenbüttel manuscript reads “the twelfth year of Gallienus and Valerian.” It is lamentable that, of all the writings of the great Dionysius, only certain fragments survive.]

[Col. 0678C] **Dionysius**, bishop of Alexandria, under Heraclas held the presbyterate of the catechetical school and became Origen’s distinguished assistant. Agreeing with the doctrine of Cyprian and the African synod concerning the rebaptism of heretics, he sent many letters to various people, which remain to this day. He also wrote to Flavian, bishop of Antioch, concerning repentance; another to the Romans through Hippolytus; two letters to Xystus, who succeeded Stephen; two letters to Philemon and Dionysius, presbyters of the Church at Rome; and to that same Dionysius, later bishop of Rome. He also wrote against Novatian, who claimed that he had been unwillingly ordained bishop at Rome. The beginning of that letter is as follows:

“Dionysius of Alexandria to Novatian. If, as you say, you were led into this unwillingly, you will show it by withdrawing willingly. For you ought even to have endured anything whatever rather than divide the Church of God. And the martyrdom undertaken for refusing to practice idolatry was not more glorious than the martyrdom undertaken for refusing to cause division; in my judgment, the latter was even greater. For there one bears witness for the sake of his own soul alone, but here for the sake of the whole Church. And now, if you persuade, or if you compel, the brothers to come to unity, your restoration will be greater than your offense. The one will not be counted against you; the other will be praised. But if, because they disobey, you are unable to achieve your purpose, save your own soul by every means.”

He has another letter to Dionysius and Didymus, many festal letters on Easter written with rhetorical force, a letter to the Church of Alexandria concerning exile, one to Hieracas, bishop of Egypt, another concerning death and the Sabbath, one concerning exercise, one to Hermammon, and another concerning the persecution of Decius. He also wrote two works against Nepos, bishop, who had written in support of a bodily thousand-year reign; in them he carefully discusses the Apocalypse of John. He wrote against Sabellius; to Ammon, bishop of Berenice; to Telesphorus; to Euran; four works to Dionysius, bishop of Rome; and to the Laodiceans concerning repentance; likewise to Conon concerning repentance; to Origen concerning martyrdom; to the Armenians concerning repentance and the canons of sins; concerning nature, to Timothy; concerning temptations, to Euphranor; and many letters to Basilides, in one of which he says that he had begun composing commentaries on Ecclesiastes. A notable letter of his against Paul of Samosata is also reported, written a few days before his death. He died in the tenth year of the emperor Gallienus.

[Note: [Col. 0681] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0681]

[Col. 0681A] **911.** Novatian, a presbyter of the city of Rome, attempting to seize the episcopal see against Cornelius, established the doctrine of the Novatians, called in Greek [Note: [Col. 0682B] Martianaeus, along with the commonly printed editions, reads καθαρόν, “pure,” less correctly and against the better manuscripts. There is no occasion here to discuss the Novatians, who called themselves Cathars, as though on account of purity, and whom, as Saint Augustine says in *On Heresies* 38, they most arrogantly and offensively named.] **Cathars** [Col. 0681B], refusing to receive apostates who were penitent. The originator of this doctrine was Novatus, a presbyter of Cyprian. [Note: [Col. 0682C] The Codex of Santa Croce reads “the author, Novatian,” incorrectly. For Novatus was the originator of the doctrine that those who had lapsed were not to be received; Novatian, a Roman presbyter who became pontiff against Cornelius, joined himself to its propagation.] He wrote *On Easter*, *On the Sabbath*, *On Circumcision*, *On the Priest*, [Note: [Col. 0682C] The Vatican manuscript reads *On Ordination*. Besides this work, and another *On Jewish Foods*, and a third *On the Holy Trinity*, which he cites, the remaining works seem to have perished. It is known that Jerome asked Paul of Concordia, in Letter 10, to send him Novatian’s writings: “So that,” he says, “while we recognize the poisons of a heretical man, we may more willingly drink the antidote of the holy martyr Cyprian.”] *On Prayer*, *On Jewish Foods*, *On Urgent Matters*, *On Attalus*, and many other works; also a substantial volume *On the Trinity*, as though making an abridgment [Note: [Col. 0682C] I am also inclined toward Pamel’s conjecture that ἐπίτασιν, “expansion,” should be restored in place of ἐπιτομήν, “abridgment,” since there is no other work of Tertullian dealing expressly with the Trinity, nor ever was there one, apart from that entitled *Against Praxeas*; and this work of Novatian is much shorter. It therefore could in no way be called an ἐπιτομή, or abridgment, of Tertullian’s work, but rather, on the contrary, an ἐπίτασις, or expansion, of the subject. Jerome not infrequently uses ἐπίτασις in the sense of treating something more fully, or of indicating an addition to a matter. Finally, when writing against Rufinus in Book II, no. 20, he says that Tertullian’s book entitled *On the Trinity* was read at Constantinople under Cyprian’s name by the heretics of the Macedonian party. In this accusation he makes two false statements: the book is neither Tertullian’s nor called Cyprian’s, but Novatian’s, and it bears his title. He does not in any way imply that the work was an abridgment of Tertullian; he ought to have guarded against this lest his opponent make such a reply.] of Tertullian’s work—something which many, through ignorance, believe to be by Cyprian.

[Col. 0682A] **912.** Novatian, a presbyter of the church in Rome, attempting to intrude himself against Cornelius into the episcopal see, established the doctrine of the Novatians, which in the Greek language they call **Cathars**, that is, “the pure,” unwilling to receive those who had apostatized and then repented. Its teacher, or rather its founder, was Novatus, a presbyter of Cyprian. He also composed works *On Easter*, *On the Sabbath*, *On Circumcision*, *On the Priest*, *On Prayer*, *On Jewish Foods*, *On Present Matters*, *On Attalus*, and many others; and a substantial treatise *On the Trinity*, making it, as it were, an abridgment of Tertullian’s work, which many, through ignorance, suppose to be Cyprian’s.

[Note: [Col. 0683D] Carus ruled after Probus, in the year 285.] He was a man of extraordinary learning in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic. [Note: [Col. 0683D] Only an ancient Latin translation of this Paschal Canon survives; of the following work there are only certain fragments. [Col. 0684B] Anatolius, an Alexandrian and bishop of Syrian Laodicea, flourished under the emperors Probus and Carus. He was a man of remarkable education in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic. We can understand the greatness of his talent from the work composed on Easter and from the ten books of his treatment of arithmetic.

[Col. 0684B] Victorinus, bishop of Petavion, did not know Latin as well as Greek; therefore his works, though very great in their ideas, appear poor because of the composition of their words. They are these: commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, the Apocalypse of John, *Against All Heresies*, and very many others. Then, having suffered martyrdom, he was crowned.

[Col. 0683C] Pamphilus the presbyter, a close associate of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, was so inflamed with love for the divine Library [Note: [Col. 0684D] Ecclesiastical authors call Holy Scripture by this name. Alcimus Avitus, Letter 2, called the Old and New Testaments “the two Libraries.” Worth reading is Alcuin’s epigram at the end of the Scripture he corrected:

> Remember to call this sacred body, Reader,  
> By its proper name, the *Pandect* in your speech,  
> Which many now call a Library,  
> Though improperly, as the Pelasgian tongue teaches.]

[Col. 0685A] that he copied out a very large part of Origen’s works in his own hand; these are still preserved in the library at Caesarea. I also found twenty-five volumes of Origen’s commentaries on the Twelve Prophets, written in his hand, and I embrace and preserve them with such joy that I believe myself to possess the wealth of Croesus. For if it is a great joy to possess one letter of a martyr, how much greater is it to possess so many thousands of lines, which seem to me to bear the traces of his own blood! [Note: [Col. 0685C] Alternatively, “through which he seems to me to have marked the traces of his own blood.”] He wrote an *Apology for Origen* before Eusebius of Caesarea wrote his. [Note: [Col. 0685C] He wrote this before the statement that follows. Saint Jerome at one time believed this, but later rejected and retracted it in many places, especially in Book II of his *Apology Against Rufinus*, saying: “Among the other commentators I included this book also, published by Pamphilus; I thought it was as you and your disciples had represented it.” MARTIAN.] [Note: [Col. 0685D] It is well known how eagerly the holy Doctor later retracted this and maintained that Pamphilus had never been the author of any book. See Letter 84, and especially Book II *Against Rufinus*, where recall what we have noted.] He suffered at Caesarea in Palestine during the persecution of Maximinus. [Note: [Col. 0685D] The Verona manuscript reads “of Maximus,” more corruptly than need be pointed out to the reader. Pamphilus suffered in the year 309, on February 15.]

[Col. 0684C] Pamphilus the presbyter, a close friend of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, was so possessed by love for the divine Library that he copied out with his own hand a very large part of Origen’s works, which are still preserved in the library of Caesarea. I found twenty-five volumes of Origen’s commentaries on the Twelve Prophets written in his hand. I embrace and preserve them with such joy that I believe myself to possess the wealth of Croesus. For if it is the greatest joy to possess one letter of a martyr, how much greater is it to possess so many thousands of lines through which, as it seems to me, he has left the traces of his own suffering. He wrote an *Apology for Origen* before Eusebius composed his, and he suffered at Caesarea in Palestine during the persecution of Maximinus.

[Col. 0686B] Pierius, a presbyter of the Church in Alexandria, taught the people with distinction under the emperors Carus and Diocletian, at the time when the bishop Theonas governed that Church. He attained such natural ability in speeches and various homilies, which survive to this day, that he was called the younger Origen. He is acknowledged to have been a lover of ascetic discipline and voluntary poverty, skilled in dialectic and rhetorical learning, and during the persecution to have spent his entire life in Rome. He has a very long homily on the prophet Hosea; that it was suited to the all-night vigil of Easter, for reading, is shown by the discourse itself.

[Col. 0685C] Lucian, a most learned man and presbyter of the Church in Antioch, labored so greatly in the study of the Scriptures that even to the present some copies are called Lucianic. His discourses *On the Faith* are circulated, as are very brief letters to certain persons. He died at Nicomedia for his confession of Christ, during the persecution of Maximinus, and was buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia.

[Col. 0687A] Phileas, from the Egyptian city called [Note: [Col. 0687C] The Codex of Santa Croce reads “called Thebes”; the Guelpherbytan manuscript, “the Thebaid.” Eusebius calls him bishop of Thmuis, “bishop of the Church of the Thmuïtes,” not one born in the city of Thmuis. The place of martyrdom seems to have been none other than the Thebaid, since the *Disputation* that Phileas composed from the Acts was against Culcianus, governor of the Thebaid. From this we are led to prefer the reading of the Codex of Santa Croce, which is also supported by the Guelpherbytan manuscript. Thebes, as is well known, was a city of Egypt and the capital of the region of the Thebaid; Thmuis was near the Mendesian mouth of the Nile, now Damietta.] Thmuis, of noble birth and possessing considerable wealth, composed, after undertaking the episcopate, a most elegant book [Note: [Col. 0687C] Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 10, reports a notable fragment from this book, which he calls a letter to the Thmuïtes.] *On the Praise of the Martyrs*. He was beheaded for Christ while a persecution was taking place in Egypt, under the authority of the same ruler who had directed the persecution of Lucian at Nicomedia.

Damasus notes the character of these letters in Letter 35 among the pseudo-Jeromian letters, no. 2: “I confess to you that I do not read willingly the books of Lactantius that you gave me some time ago, because many of his letters extend to the length of a thousand lines, and they rarely discuss our doctrine. [Col. 0688B] **920.** Firmianus, also called Lactantius, a pupil of Arnobius, was summoned under the emperor Diocletian together with Flavius the Grammarian, whose writings on medicine in verse survive. He taught rhetoric at Nicomedia and, because of the poverty of students, especially because it was a Greek city, devoted himself to writing. We possess his *Symposium*, which he composed as a young man in Africa; a travel account from Africa to Nicomedia composed in hexameters; another book entitled *The Grammarian*; a beautiful work *On the Anger of God*; seven books of the *Divine Institutes Against the Nations*; an incomplete abridgment of the same work; two books addressed to Asclepiades; one book *On the Persecution*; four books of letters to Probus; and one book to the same man *On the Creation of God*. In his extreme old age he became tutor in Gaul to Caesar Crispus, the son of Constantine, who was later killed by his father.
