[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693A] Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, [Note: [Col. 0693C] Under Constantine and Constantius. Thus the manuscript codices read, except the Sangermanensis, which retains “under the emperors Constantine and Constans.” Marianus wished to read “under Constantius and Constans”; Erasmus, “under Constans and Constantine.” MARTIAN. — Only two of our codices have “under the emperor Constantius.” The Sangermanensis, in Martianaeus, has “under Constantius and Constans.” Erasmus, on the contrary, “under Constans and Constantine.” Victorius, “under Constantine and Constans.”] flourished under the emperors Constantine and Constantius. He wrote many volumes on various subjects, and especially 925 against the Arians. There circulate against him books by Asterius and Apollinarius, accusing him of the Sabellian heresy; Hilary also, in the seventh book against the Arians, mentions him by name as though he were a heretic. [Note: [Col. 0693C] Compare what he says at the beginning of Book VII: “Galatia impiously nourished many toward the confession of one God.” For since our author reports that Marcellus was there called a heretic by name, either his memory has misled him, or he read “Marcellus” in his copy instead of “many.” Indeed, in Hilary’s book Against Constantius, Marcellus is joined with the heretics Photinus and Sabellius: “Hence, when Marcellus reads ‘the Word of God,’ he does not understand; hence, when Photinus speaks of the man Jesus, he is ignorant; hence also Sabellius, since he does not understand ‘I and the Father are one,’ is without God the Father and without God the Son.”] But Marcellus defended himself, maintaining that he did not hold the doctrine of which he was accused, and that he was protected by his communion with Julius and Athanasius, bishops of Rome and Alexandria. [Note: [Col. 0693D] This letter on the faith exists; in it he cleared himself before Julius, bishop of Rome. His other writings, apart from certain fragments, have perished, as have also those of Asterius and Apollinarius against Marcellus.]

[Col. 0694A] Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, flourished under Constantine and Constantius. He wrote many books on various subjects, and especially against the Arians. There circulate against him discourses by Asterius 926 and Apollinarius accusing him of the Sabellian heresy; Hilary too, in the seventh discourse against the Arians, mentions him as a heretic. But he replies in his defense that he does not belong to the doctrine of which he is accused, relying upon his communion with Julius and Athanasius, bishops of Rome and Alexandria.

CAPUT LXXXVII.

[Col. 0693] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0693A] Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, [Note: [Col. 0693D] The Veronensis reads “having suffered many plots by the Arians.” Consult Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, Book II, chapter 4.] after suffering many plots by the Arians, fled to Constans, ruler of Gaul. From there he returned with letters; and, driven into exile again after Constans’s death, he remained in hiding until the reign of Jovian. [Note: [Col. 0693D] Martianaeus and other printed books read “Jovinian”; the Vaticanus, “Julian.” The years indicated are 350 to 363. He died in 373.] When the Church was restored to him, he died under Valens. There circulate under his name two books against the Gentiles, one against Valens and Ursacius, works on virginity, many against the persecutions of the Arians, a work on the titles of the Psalms, a history containing the life of the monk Antony, festal letters, and many other writings whose enumeration would be tedious. [Note: [Col. 0694C] This book against Valens and Ursacius no longer exists; the surviving works on virginity are of doubtful authenticity. Likewise lost are the work on the titles of the Psalms and the *festal*, or Paschal, letters. See Ebed-Jesu, chapter 12.]

[Col. 0694A] Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, after enduring many plots by the Arians, fled to Constans, king of the Gauls. From there he departed with letters, and, again driven into exile after Constans’s death, escaped notice until the reign of Jovian. Having recovered the Church, he died under Valens. There circulate under his name two discourses against the Gentiles, one against Valens and Ursacius, a work on virginity, very many against the persecutions of the Arians, a work on the inscription of the Psalms, a History of Antony the recluse containing his life, festal letters, and many other writings, which I hesitate to enumerate.

CAPUT LXXXVIII.

[Col. 0693] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0693B] Antony the monk, whose life Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, presented in a notable volume, sent seven letters in Egyptian to various monasteries, written in an apostolic spirit and style. [Note: [Col. 0694C] Only the Latin translation has seen the light.] They were translated into Greek; the most important of them is addressed to the Arsenoites. He flourished under Constantine and his sons while they were reigning. [Note: [Col. 0694C] That is, while his sons were reigning. The printed books add: “He lived 105 years.” Since this is absent from the manuscript codices, it was right to reject these words as spurious from all editions. MARTIAN.] [Note: [Col. 0694D] This clause—“He lived 105 years”—is absent from our manuscripts and from those consulted by Martianaeus.]

[Col. 0694B] Antony the monk, whose life Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, set forth in a notable book, sent to various monasteries of Egypt seven letters, of an apostolic character and style, translated into the Greek language. One of these is especially important, the one addressed to the Arsenoites. He flourished while Constantine and his sons were reigning.

CAPUT LXXXIX.

[Col. 0693] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0693C] Basil, bishop of Ancyra, [Note: [Col. 0694D] The words “skilled in the art of medicine,” or, as some codices read, “skilled in medical matters,” were not found in the old edition of John of Fuchte nor formerly in the Greek translator, who supplied them from Suidas. All the manuscripts, however, read them, as do Honorius, Freculphus, and others. Suffridus Petrus, followed by Miraeus, found in the Gemblacensis and Sigebergensis codices “of the fortress of Mechea”: incorrectly, as the distinguished Fabricius notes, since it is certain that Basil was bishop of Ancyra. Moreover, the printed reading seems somewhat unsatisfactory; and I, aware of the difficulty, think that something similar should be supplied.] wrote against Marcellus 927 [Note: [Col. 0694D] Martianaeus, omitting the conjunction *and*, makes this one book with the preceding one, contrary to our manuscripts and certain printed editions. Both works of Basil have perished. See Socrates, Book II, chapter 30, toward the end, where he recalls the disputation Basil held with Photinus and which the notaries recorded.] and a book on virginity, as well as some other works. Under King Constantius, he was, together with Eustathius of Sebaste, a leader of the Macedonian party. [Note: [Col. 0695C] Some editions incorrectly read “under King Constantine.”]

[Col. 0694C] Basil, bishop of Ancyra (a physician by profession), wrote against Marcellus 928 and a discourse on virginity, as well as many other works. While Constantius was reigning, he ruled the Macedonian religious party together with Eustathius of Sebaste.

CAPUT XC.

[Col. 0695] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0695A] [The name is absent from the transmitted text.] bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, of elegant and clear expression and especially of historical understanding, published under the emperor Constantius [Note: [Col. 0695C] The Veronensis manuscript reads “under Constantine”; incorrectly.] commentaries on Matthew, John, the Apostle, and the Psalter. [Note: [Col. 0695C] Only the commentary on the Psalms survives in its entirety; excerpts from the other works are preserved in various catenae. Jerome himself quotes a notable fragment from the commentaries on the Apostle in the letter now numbered 119, addressed to Minervius and Alexander. He was deposed in 347 and is believed to have reached the end of his life around 355.]

[Col. 0696A] Theodore, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, of natural talent, excellent expression, and historical understanding, published under the emperor Constantius commentaries on Matthew, John, the Apostle, and the Psalter.

CAPUT XCI.

[Col. 0695] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0695A] Eusebius, of Emesa, [Note: [Col. 0695D] Our codices do not have the word “bishop,” nor do the two codices examined by Victorius; nor does the Greek translator know it. In his *Chronicle*, under the tenth year of Constantius, Eusebius of Emesa, standard-bearer of the Arian faction, writes many and various things. See Tillemont, vol. VI, part II, p. 124; Socrates II.9; Sozomen III.6; and Nicephorus IX.5.] of elegant and rhetorical talent, produced innumerable books, many of them suited to popular applause. Since he followed history more closely, he is read with especial enthusiasm by those who wish to declaim. Among these works are especially ten books against the Jews, the Gentiles, and the Novatians, and one on the Epistle to the Galatians, [Note: [Col. 0695D] Jerome says there were ten books; his Greek translator says one, *heis*. The Wolfenbüttel codex has “ten books of discussions on the Epistle to the Galatians.”] and brief but very numerous homilies on the Gospels. He flourished during the reign of the emperor Constantius, under whom he also died; he was buried at Antioch. [Note: [Col. 0695D] This work against the Jews is said by Lambecius to exist in the Vienna Library; the other works mentioned here by Jerome are lost.]

[Col. 0696A] Eusebius of Emesa, gifted in expression and rhetoric, composed innumerable discourses intended to win the applause of the people. Following history more closely, he is read with particular attention by those who delight in applause. Among these are ten distinguished discourses against the Jews, the Gentiles, and the Novatians, and against the Galatians; and homilies on the Gospels, very brief but numerous. He flourished under the emperor Constantius and, dying at Antioch, was buried there.

CAPUT XCII.

[Col. 0695] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0695B] Triphyllius, bishop of Ledra in Cyprus, or of Leucotheon, [Note: [Col. 0695D] Leucotheon was an episcopal see. At this point the false Greek translator Sophronius, as in many other places, misled Erasmus and Marianus by writing *Leuteon* instead of the genuine name *Leucotheon*, retained in all the manuscript copies. Ledra was a city also called Leutheon, an archiepiscopal city and metropolitan see of the island of Cyprus, on its northern coast; the Greeks call it Leucothon and Leucosia, while Sophronius and others call it Nicosia. Returning, therefore, to Jerome’s Latin original, we correct the very frequently false and corrupt text of Sophronius’s Greek from the manuscript codices. Relying on their fidelity and authority, we disregard the judgment of the ignorant men of our own time and pass over their accusations with deaf ears. MARTIAN. — Two manuscripts, with Freculphus, have *Cypriledensis* as one word. Erasmus and Victorius, following the Greek translator, read *Leuteonis* instead of *Leucotheon*; Honorius and Meursius also follow this reading. But it was Leucotheon, as Martianaeus noted: a metropolitan see of the island of Cyprus on its northern coast, also called Leucosia by the Greeks and, by some, Nicosia.] was the most eloquent man of his age and was highly renowned under King Constantius. I have read his commentaries on the Song of Songs. He is also said to have composed many other works that have by no means come into our hands. [Note: [Col. 0696D] No writings of Triphyllius now survive. See concerning him Sozomen, Book I, chapter 11.]

[Col. 0696B] Triphyllius, bishop of Ledra in Cyprus, or rather of Leucotheon, was eloquent and renowned under Constantius. I have read his commentaries on the Song of Songs. He is said to have written many other works, but these did not come into our hands.

CAPUT XCIII.

[Col. 0695] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0695B] 929 Donatus, from whom the Donatists throughout Africa sprang under the emperors Constantius and Constantine, [Note: [Col. 0696D] Thus all our codices read, as do those examined by others in various places. Martianaeus, following Victorius, incorrectly reads “under Constans and Constantine,” as do other editions, which read “under Constans and Constantius.” Who does not know that the origin of the Donatist schism must be traced back to the age of Constantine?] asserted that the Scriptures had been handed over by our people to the pagans during the persecution, and by his persuasion deceived almost the whole of Africa, especially Numidia. Many short works of his relating to his own heresy survive, as does a book on the Holy Spirit conforming to Arian doctrine. [Note: [Col. 0696D] All Donatus’s writings have long since perished. One should recall the notable passage of Augustine, *Heresy* 69, which Fabricius also quotes: “His writings survive, and from them it appears that he did not hold a Catholic opinion of the Trinity, but, although he considered the Son of the same substance, nevertheless thought the Son inferior to the Father and the Holy Spirit inferior to the Son.” Yet the multitude of Donatists did not concern itself with this error that he held about the Trinity, and scarcely anyone among them can be found who knew that he held such a view.]

[Col. 0696B] Donatus, from whom the Donatists in Africa arose under the emperor Constantius, asserted that the divine Scriptures had been handed over by our people to the pagans during the persecution, and by his persuasion deceived all Africa, especially Numidia. Many writings of his relating to his own heresy exist, as does a discourse on the Holy Spirit agreeing with Arian doctrine.

CAPUT XCIV.

[Col. 0697] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0697A] Asterius, a philosopher of the Arian faction, [Note: [Col. 0697C] It seems to me scarcely doubtful, from Jerome’s judgment, that this is the same Asterius whom he elsewhere calls the Scythopolitan. For in the same order, in the frequently praised letter 70 to Magnus, he lists the names and books of Eusebius of Emesa, Triphyllius of Cyprus, and Asterius of Scythopolis. In letter 112 to Augustine he says: “Especially in the exposition of the Psalms, which among the Greeks were interpreted in many volumes, the first was Origen, the second Eusebius of Caesarea, the third Theodore of Heraclea, the fourth Asterius of Scythopolis, the fifth Apollinarius,” and so forth. From this it is also reasonable to believe that no other Asterius, a namesake who had written on the Psalms, was known to him. Fabricius nevertheless states, both here and in *Bibliotheca Graeca*, Book V, chapter 28, that this man was different from the Scythopolitan: namely, the Cappadocian sophist mentioned by Socrates, Book I, chapter 36, who, after sacrificing to idols, returned to the Christians when the martyr Lucian persuaded him to repent, and afterward became a champion of the Arians.] wrote, during the reign of Constantius, commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans, the Gospels, and the Psalms, [Note: [Col. 0697D] None of this Asterius’s writings now survives.] and many other works, which are read with the greatest eagerness by members of his party. [Note: [Col. 0697D] Recall chapter 86, where books against Marcellus are mentioned, in which Asterius accused him of the Sabellian heresy.]

[Col. 0698A] Asterius, a philosopher of the Arian heresy, wrote during the reign of Constantius commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans, the Gospels, and the Psalms, as well as many other works, which are read with particular diligence by those of the same heresy.

CAPUT XCV.

[Col. 0697] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0697A] Lucifer, bishop of Caralis, together with Pancratius and Hilary, clerics of the Roman Church, was sent by Bishop Liberius as an envoy to the emperor Constantius on behalf of the faith. Since he refused, in the name of Athanasius, to condemn the Nicene faith, he was banished to Palestine. A man of extraordinary steadfastness and a mind prepared for martyrdom, he wrote a book against the emperor Constantius [Note: [Col. 0697D] The words “and sent it to him to read,” together with “and not long afterward,” are absent from the manuscript of the Holy Cross. Moreover, not one but two books of Lucifer against Constantius—or, more accurately, on behalf of Saint Athanasius addressed to Constantius—are now extant. Other writings of his also survive; if God grants me the opportunity, I shall one day undertake to collect and embellish them.] and sent it to him to read. Not long afterward, under the emperor Julian, he returned to Caralis and died during the reign of Valentinian. [Note: [Col. 0698C] That is, in the year 371. We have presented above the book written by Jerome against the followers of this Lucifer.]

[Col. 0698A] Lucifer, bishop of Caralis, together with Pancratius and Hilary, clerics of the Church of Rome, was sent by Bishop Liberius as an embassy to the emperor Constantius on behalf of the faith. Unwilling to destroy the Nicene Council in Athanasius’s name, he was exiled to Palestine. A man of remarkable self-control and a mind prepared for martyrdom, he composed a discourse against Constantius and sent it to him to be read. Not long afterward, while Julian was reigning, he returned to Caralis and died under the emperor Valentinian.

CAPUT XCVI.

[Col. 0697] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0697B] 931 Eusebius, by nationality a Sardinian and formerly a lector of the Roman Church, bishop of Vercellae, was exiled by the emperor Constantius, on account of his confession of the faith, to Scythopolis and thence to Cappadocia. Under the emperor Julian he returned to the Church [Note: [Col. 0698C] “Then,” says Jerome in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, “Italy changed its mourning garments upon the return of Eusebius.”] and published commentaries on the Psalms by Eusebius of Caesarea, which he had translated from Greek into Latin. [Note: [Col. 0698C] This translation, which Jerome also praises in letter 61 to Vigilantius, did not survive. On the other hand, letters of Eusebius written from exile do survive, though Jerome does not mention them here.] He died while Valentinian and Valens were reigning. [Note: [Col. 0698D] In the *Chronicle* he assigns this to the seventh year of Valentinian; there is no doubt, however, that Eusebius died in the year 370.]

[Col. 0698B] 932 Eusebius, a Sardinian by birth and one of the readers of the Church of Rome, bishop of Vercellae, was exiled by the emperor Constantius to Scythopolis and from there to Cappadocia because of his confession of the faith. Under the emperor Julian he returned to the Church and published commentaries on the Psalms by Eusebius of Caesarea, which he had translated from Greek into Latin. He died under Valentinian and Valens.

CAPUT XCVII.

[Col. 0697] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0697B] Fortunatianus, an African by birth and bishop of Aquileia, under the emperor Constantius, [Note: [Col. 0698D] Fabricius reads “under Constantine,” for which he himself wished “Constantius” to be substituted. Thus, however, all our codices read, as does Martianaeus himself.] wrote commentaries on the Gospels, arranged according to headings [Note: [Col. 0698D] That is, according to chapters or sections.], in a brief and rustic style. [Note: [Col. 0698D] The reading of our codices seems preferable: “brief in a rustic style”; perhaps this is what Lipsius intended, when he translates “brief in expression.” Understand “rustic style” as the vernacular, or the style that Jerome calls military and popular at the beginning of Book II *Against Rufinus*. See also the preface to Matthew.] He is detestable for this reason: he was the first to trouble and break Liberius, bishop of Rome, who was going into exile on behalf of the faith, and compelled him to sign the heresy. [Note: [Col. 0698D] The Gemblacensis manuscript incorrectly reads “and compelled him to subscribe to the writing of his heresy,” and so forth. By “heresy” he means the creed formulated at Sirmium, to which Liberius subscribed and which Hilary calls in the Fragments “the perfidy composed at Sirmium”; Liberius called it Catholic after Demophilus had explained it to him. Nevertheless, that it could in fact bear a Catholic interpretation is clear from Hilary himself.]

[Col. 0698B] Fortunatianus, an African by birth and bishop of Aquileia, while Constantius was reigning, drew up canons for the Gospels and composed very brief commentaries in a rustic style. For this reason he is detestable: when Liberius, bishop of Rome, was going into exile on behalf of the faith, he not only undermined and overthrew him, but also compelled him to sign heretical statements.

CAPUT XCVIII.

[Col. 0699] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0699A] Acacius, whom they called “One-Eyed” because he was blind in one eye, bishop of the Church of Caesarea in Palestine, devoted himself to Ecclesiastes in seventeen volumes, and to six books of miscellaneous questions, [Note: [Col. 0699C] As we showed in letter 119 to Minervius and Alexander, no. 6, *symmikton* should be read instead of *syllekton*, on the authority of the Veronensis manuscript. There Jerome quotes a fairly substantial fragment in Latin, translated by himself, from the fourth book of this work. The rest of Acacius’s writings have perished apart from a few excerpts. Jerome also mentions him at the beginning of letter 37 to Marcella.] as well as many additional and varied treatises. He became so distinguished under the emperor Constantius that he appointed Felix bishop of Rome in place of Liberius. [Note: [Col. 0699C] Some editions add “an Arian,” a word unknown to all our manuscripts and to those formerly consulted by Lipsius, Suffridus Petrus, Victorius, and others. Nor does the Greek translator have it. In fact, although Felix communicated with the Arians, he never departed from the orthodox confession, condemned Constantius, and was crowned with martyrdom.]

[Col. 0700A] Acacius, who, because he was blind in one eye, was called “One-Eyed,” bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, composed seventeen books on Ecclesiastes, six books of miscellaneous questions, and many different homilies. He became so distinguished under the emperor Constantius that he ordained Felix bishop of Rome in Liberius’s place.

CAPUT XCIX.

[Col. 0699] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0699A] 933 [Note: [Col. 0699D] The name “Serapion of Thmueos, bishop,” is written variously in the manuscript codices: in the Sangermanensis, “Thimoeus”; in the Cluniacensis, by a second hand, “Thimeus bishop”; in the Tolosanus, “Thumeus bishop.” Others omit the name and read only “Serapion, bishop.” No one retains the form printed by Erasmus and Marianus, “bishop of Thmueos, a city of Egypt.” Thmuis—called Thumuis by Antoninus—was formerly an episcopal city of Egypt under the patriarch of Alexandria, where Pan was worshiped. The people of Thmuis also worshiped a goat, and in the Egyptian language *thmuis* meant “goat.” Hence Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah 46, says: “For many of their towns [the Egyptians] have names from beasts and animals: *Kynon*, from a dog; *Leon*, from a lion; *Thmuis*, in the Egyptian language, from a goat; *Lykon*, from a wolf,” and so forth. MARTIAN. — Thus we read from one Veronensis manuscript and from Fabricius’s edition; the Greek also has *Thmueos*. Other printed books and manuscripts, including those examined by us and by others, give the name variously and corruptly as “Thimeus” or “Thumeus,” the latter being the more frequent reading with Martianaeus. Others omit it altogether; others, as in Erasmus and Victorius, add “Thmueos, a city of Egypt.” There was indeed also *Thmueos Augustanica*, in the Augustan region, as Holstenius notes on Stephanus of Byzantium.]

Serapion, bishop of Thmueos, who earned the surname “the Scholastic” for his elegance of intellect, a friend dear to the monk Antony, published an excellent book against the Manichaean, another on the titles of the Psalms, and useful letters to various people. Under the emperor Constantius he was also illustrious in his confession of faith. [Note: [Col. 0700C] The ancient glossographers interpret this surname as “learned” or “educated.” Apart from his book against the Manichaeans, which Photius also praises in Book I, chapter 11, Against the Manichaeans, all his other writings have perished. He probably died around the year 358.]

[Col. 0700A] 934 Serapion, bishop of Thmueos, called “the Scholastic” because of his natural ability, a true friend of the monk Antony, published an excellent book against the Manichaean, another on the inscription of the Psalms, and useful letters to various people. Under Constantius he was distinguished in his confession of faith.

CAPUT C.

[Col. 0699] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0699B] Hilary, bishop of the city of Poitiers in Aquitaine, [Note: [Col. 0700C] The Veronensis reads “of Poitiers in Aquitaine”; other copies have *Biterensis* and *Biturensis*. This synod was held in the year 356.] was banished from the council of Béziers to Phrygia through the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles. He composed twelve books against the Arians and another book on Synods, which he wrote to the bishops of Gaul; commentaries on the Psalms—namely, on the first and second Psalms, on Psalm 51 through Psalm 62, and on Psalm 118 through the last Psalm. In this work he imitated Origen and also added some material of his own. He also wrote a short book addressed to Constantius, which he delivered to him while he was living at Constantinople, [Note: [Col. 0700D] The Veronensis reads “while he was alive” (that is, “to him”) “at Constantinople,” and so forth. But the other book against Constantius that follows seems to have been written while Constantius was still alive, contrary to Jerome’s view, if one considers the author’s own words in section 2. There he says that he is writing five years after the exiles of Eusebius, Lucifer, and Dionysius—namely, in the year 360—whereas Constantius died in the following year, 361. Perhaps he understood the period of five years somewhat more broadly.] and another against Constantius, which he wrote after Constantius’s death; a book against Valens and Ursacius; a history containing the account of the councils of Rimini and Seleucia [Note: [Col. 0700D] The words “and Seleucia” are absent from the Vaticanus. It reads “against the Prefect,” incorrectly, contrary to the other manuscripts, although some editions agree with it. This book, like the two that follow, no longer exists; only fragments survive today of the preceding work against Valens and Ursacius, as also of the books on Job. Moreover, the Greek translator rather carelessly read *libertinorum* (“of libertines”), *libertinon*, instead of “the book of hymns.”]; a work addressed to the prefect Sallustius, or against Dioscorus; another book of Hymns and Mysteries; commentaries on Matthew; treatises on Job, which he translated from the Greek of Origen according to the sense; [Note: [Col. 0701C] The Vaticanus incorrectly reads “and other selected little books.” Most of the letters to various people have perished. The work that follows on the Song of Songs is entirely unknown.] another elegant short book against Auxentius; and some letters to various people. Some say that he also wrote on the Song of Songs, but this work is unknown to us. He died at Poitiers while Valentinian and Valens were reigning. [Note: [Col. 0701C] That is, in the year 367. Jerome frequently praises this outstanding Father in his letters and other books.]

[Col. 0700B] Hilary, bishop of Poitiers in Aquitaine, having been exiled from the council of Béziers to Phrygia through the machinations of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, composed twelve discourses against the Arians and another on the Synods, which he wrote to the bishops of Gaul. He also composed commentaries on the Psalms—first and second, from Psalm 51 through Psalm 62, and from Psalm 118 through the last. In this work he imitated Origen, adding some things of his own. He has also a short book addressed to Constantius, which he delivered to him while he was alive at Constantinople, and another against Constantius, which he composed after Constantius’s death; books against Valens and Ursacius containing the history of the councils of Rimini and Seleucia; a work addressed to the prefect Sallustius, or against Dioscorus; and a book of the Libertines and another discourse on Mysteries; commentaries on Matthew; homilies on Job, which he translated from the Greek of Origen; another exceptionally elegant short book against Auxentius; and many letters to various people. Some say that he also wrote on the Song of Songs, but that work is unknown to us. He died at Poitiers while Valentinian and Valens were reigning.

CAPUT CI.

[Col. 0701] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0701A] 935 Victorinus, an African by birth, taught rhetoric at Rome under the emperor Constantius. [Note: [Col. 0701C] Some editions, through an obvious error, read “under Constantine.”] In extreme old age, when he had given himself over to the faith of Christ, [Note: [Col. 0701C] Augustine gives a very clear account of his conversion in *Confessions*, Book VIII, chapter 2. Miraeus quotes it: “When I mentioned to Bishop Ambrose that I had read certain books of Plato which Victorinus, formerly a rhetorician of the city of Rome, whom I had heard had died a Christian, had translated into Latin, so that he might encourage me toward the humility of Christ, he told me how that most learned old man, thoroughly skilled in every liberal discipline, who had read, judged, and explained so much of the philosophers, and who had been the teacher of so many noble senators and, because of his distinguished teaching, had deserved and received a statue in the Roman forum, was not ashamed to become a child of your Christ and an infant at your font, submitting his neck to the yoke of humility and bowing his brow to the shame of the cross.”] he wrote books against Arius in a highly obscure dialectical style. [Note: [Col. 0701D] They are understood only by the learned. All the manuscript codices read in this way. Concerning Victorinus’s commentaries on the Apostle, Jerome speaks as follows in the preface to his commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians: “Not that I am unaware that Gaius Marius Victorinus, who taught me rhetoric at Rome when I was a boy, published commentaries on the Apostle,” and so forth. This should be read on the authority of the Cluniacensis manuscript; another manuscript of the Ambrosian Library has, “who taught me rhetoric at Rome from childhood.” On these matters, see what we said in the Addenda to the first part of volume IV of this work. MARTIAN. — Thus all our manuscripts read, as do those consulted by Martianaeus and many others. Victorius also has the same sense: “they are understood only by the learned.” Other editions incorrectly read “they are not understood.” These four books were written specifically against Candidus; Victorinus also answered Candidus’s letters on the divine generation.] They are understood only by the learned, and he also wrote commentaries on the Apostle. [Note: [Col. 0702C] Jerome judges these works as follows in the preface to his commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians: “Not that I am unaware that Gaius Marius Victorinus, who taught rhetoric at Rome when I was a boy—not ‘from childhood’—published commentaries on the Apostle; but because he was occupied with the learning of secular literature and was wholly ignorant of the Holy Scriptures, no one, however eloquent, can discuss well what he does not know.”]

[Col. 0702A] 936 Victorinus, an African by birth, taught rhetoric at Rome while Constantius was reigning. In extreme old age he became a Christian and wrote dialectical works against Arius that were exceedingly obscure and understood only by the educated, as well as commentaries on the Apostle.

CAPUT CII.

[Col. 0701] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0701B] Titus, bishop of Bostra, [Note: [Col. 0702C] Also *Bostrensis*. Of this author’s four books against the Manichaeans, the last two seemed until now to have perished, since in the Hamburg manuscript of Holstenius, where they alone are preserved, the disturbed sequence of the text, caused by a copyist’s error, misled those who examined it only cursorily. Through the diligence of Friedrich Winckler, the first three have now been found intact and restored; they appear in the recent edition of Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*. Ebed-Jesu praises them in chapter 29, as does Photius, codex 232, and Book I, chapter 11, Against the Manichaeans.] under the emperors Julian and Jovian wrote vigorous books against the Manichaeans, as well as several other volumes. He died under Valens. [Note: [Col. 0702D] Valens held imperial power from the year 364 to 378.]

[Col. 0702B] Titus, bishop of Bostra, while Julian and Jovian were reigning, composed vigorous discourses against the Manichaeans and many other works. He died under Valens.

CAPUT CIII.

[Col. 0701] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0701B] Damasus, bishop of Rome, possessed an elegant talent for composing verse. [Note: [Col. 0702D] We would prefer to follow other codices of Victorius—the Mediceus and Fesulanus—as well as all our own and those examined by Martianaeus. They read that he published many brief works in heroic meter, and the Greek translator supports this reading. Jerome also speaks elsewhere of Damasus’s writings, in letter 22 to Eustochium. Ebed-Jesu, chapter 8, says: “Damasus, bishop of Rome, wrote on matters of faith and Canons.” He died at the end of the year 384, after eighteen years in the episcopate.] He published many brief works in meter and died nearly eighty years old under the emperor Theodosius.

[Col. 0702B] Damasus, bishop of Rome, was naturally gifted in epic poetry. He published many short works in heroic meter and died at the age of nearly eighty under the emperor Theodosius.

CAPUT CIV.

[Col. 0701] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0701B] Apollinarius, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, [Note: [Col. 0702D] Certain Brixian copies of Victorius incorrectly read “son of the presbyter Probus.” I would prefer to alter what follows—although it is supported by no manuscript—to “he devoted himself in his youth more to grammar,” so that it may be understood that Apollinarius, whose teacher Jerome had been, gave his attention to the great masters of grammar. Jerome praises this man’s talent in many other places but rejects his doctrines.] the son of a presbyter, devoted himself in his youth chiefly to grammar and afterward, writing innumerable volumes on the Holy Scriptures, [Note: [Col. 0703C] We supply the word “volumes” from our manuscripts and the Greek translator, *having composed books*. Most printed editions either entirely omit this word or put *opuscula* in its place.] died under the emperor Theodosius. 937 Of his works, thirty books against Porphyry survive, [Note: [Col. 0703C] Apart from a paraphrase of the Psalms and brief fragments of his other works, Apollinarius’s writings have disappeared.] and these are considered the most important among his other works.

[Col. 0702B] Apollinarius, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, the son of a presbyter, devoted himself in his youth chiefly to grammar. Later, after composing innumerable books on the divine Scriptures, he died while Theodosius was reigning. 938 He has thirty discourses against Porphyry, which were judged superior among his other writings.

CAPUT CV.

[Col. 0703] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0703A] Gregory, bishop of Eliberis in Baetica, [Note: [Col. 0703C] Some attribute the *Booklet on the Faith* assigned to him by Quesnellius, printed at the end of Saint Leo’s work, to Gregory of Nazianzus; others attribute it to Ambrose.] composed various treatises in an ordinary style until extreme old age, as well as an elegant book on the faith, which is said still to survive today. [Note: [Col. 0703C] The relative pronoun is absent from the Veronensis and Wolfenbüttel codices. Jerome would otherwise have rather needlessly indicated that the most recent book still survived. After removing this little word, understand the sentence to mean that Gregory himself survived.]

[Col. 0704A] Gregory, bishop of Eliberis in Baetica, composed various homilies in ordinary language until extreme old age, as well as an excellent discourse on the faith, which is said to survive to the present day.

CAPUT CVI.

[Col. 0703] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0703]

[Col. 0703A] Pacianus [Note: [Col. 0703D] Other manuscripts call him Pacatianus, among them one of ours; Honorius has Pacatius. Shortly afterward, the Veronese manuscript reads *castitate eloquentiae* (“purity of eloquence”), whereas the Vatican manuscript more correctly has *castigatae eloquentiae* (“refined eloquence”); I would prefer the latter reading. Thus, in chapter 90, Bishop Theodore is called a man of elegant and Latin speech, and in the following chapter Eusebius is called a man of elegant and rhetorical talent, etc. I do not, moreover, wish it to be thought that this Pacianus was the father of Flavius Dexter, to whom Jerome dedicates this book *On Illustrious Men*.], bishop of Barcelona in the Pyrenees, illustrious for purity of life and eloquence, and equally distinguished in life and speech, wrote various short works, among which are *Cervus* [Note: [Col. 0703D] Some have *Cerbus*, and Κέρβος; learned interpreters have explained the name in various ways. The explanation that seems more plausible to the distinguished Fabricius is that Pacianus gave his book the title *Cervus*, or *Cervulus*, because he was attacking the foolish custom of certain [Col. 0704B] Christians in Spain who, on the Kalends of January, disguised themselves as stags or other wild animals. But unless that popular performance was then called *Cervus* from the name of the stag—and this above all would need to be proved by some ancient testimony—why would they take their name from the stag rather than from the lion, goat, and so forth, since they dressed themselves as all kinds [Col. 0704C] of wild animals indiscriminately? It seems more likely to me that the book was entitled *Cervulus*, a name derived from the Greek κερβολεῖν, “to revile” or “to curse,” whence κέρβολος, “a reviler, one who curses.” Certainly Pacianus himself appears to use it in this sense near the beginning of the *Paraeneticus*: “For I think that little *cervulus* recently achieved this much: he became more diligent in proportion as he was more sharply marked out. And he seems not to have suppressed, but to have instructed, his extravagance, by expressing and repeatedly reproving that disgrace. Woe is me, for what a crime I have committed! I think they did not know how to make a *cervulus*, unless I had shown them by reproving them.” Jerome, above, in book I *Against Rufinus*, no. 17, has *cernulus* as a basis for accusing me; we have suspected that *cervulus* should be substituted for that word. See the notes there. This book of Pacianus no longer survives. See the most illustrious Philippus a Turre, *On the Mithra*, p. 208.] and *Against the Novatians*. Under the emperor Theodosius, [Col. 0703B] already in extreme old age, he died. [Note: [Col. 0704C] In the *Chronicle of Dexter*, as the distinguished Fabricius also notes, under the year 391: “Lampius succeeds Pacianus of Barcelona, my father.”]

[Col. 0704A] Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona in the regions of the Pyrenees, illustrious for a temperate life, pleasing speech, and eloquence, composed various works, among which are *Cervus* and *Against the Novatians*. Under the emperor Theodosius he died in extreme old age.

## CHAPTER CVII [Note: [Col. 0703] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0703]

[Col. 0703B] Photinus, from Gallograecia, a disciple of Marcellus, ordained bishop of Sirmium, [Note: [Col. 0704D] The manuscript of the Holy Cross incorrectly has *Smyrnae* for *Sirmii*. See Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* LXXI, 1.] attempted to revive the heresy of the Ebionites. Later, after being expelled from the Church by the emperor Valentinian, [Note: [Col. 0704D] First, in the year 351, under Constantius, he was ordered into exile; Julian recalled him in 362. Jerome therefore records his second exile, during which, after the year 364, Valentinian condemned him as a heretic and persecuted him until his death. In the *Chronicle*, under the year 379: “Photinus died in Galatia, from whom the doctrine of the Photinians was introduced; he lost many good qualities of continence and intellect through a single vice, pride.”] he wrote several volumes, among which the principal are *Against the Pagans* and books addressed to Valentinian.

[Col. 0704B] Photinus, from Gallograecia, a disciple of Marcellus and bishop of Sirmium, attempted to renew the heresy of the Ebionites. Later he was expelled from the Church by the emperor Valentinian. He composed many books, among which are distinguished works *Against the Pagans* and discourses addressed to Valentinian.

## CHAPTER CVIII [Note: [Col. 0703] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0703]

[Col. 0703B] 939 [Note: [Col. 0704D] I have found this name written in manuscripts and printed books in remarkably various forms. The Veronese has *Foedabius*; the Greek translator, together with certain editions, *Saebadius*; the Council of Zaragoza in 380, *Phitadius*; Sulpicius Severus, book II of the *Histories*, *Foegadius*, to omit other forms for the moment.] Phoebadius, bishop of Agen in Gaul, [Col. 0705A] published a book *Against the Arians*. Other short works are also said to be his, which I have not yet read. He is still alive to this day [Note: [Col. 0705C] The year is 392. The manuscript of the Holy Cross has *necdum inveni* (“I have not yet found”) instead of *necdum legi* (“I have not yet read”).], living on in decrepit old age.

[Col. 0704B] 940 Phoebadius, bishop of Agen in Gaul, published a book *Against the Arians*. Other writings of his are also said to exist, which I have not yet encountered. He is still alive to this day, passing his time in extreme old age.

## CHAPTER CIX [Note: [Col. 0705] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0705]

[Col. 0705A] Didymus of Alexandria, having lost his sight in early childhood and therefore also being ignorant of the alphabet, presented so great a marvel to everyone that he learned even dialectic and geometry—which especially require sight—perfectly. [Note: [Col. 0705C] Some exemplars incorrectly have *usu* (“use”) in place of *visu* (“sight”). Next, Martianus has *plurima, nobiliaque opera* (“very many and distinguished works”), a reading shared by all our manuscripts except the Vatican, which does not contain the final word *opera*. See Socrates IV, 25, and Jerome’s *Chronicle* under the year 372.] He wrote many distinguished works: commentaries on all the Psalms; commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew and John; works *On Dogmas*; two books *Against the Arians*; and one book *On the Holy Spirit*, which I translated into Latin. [Note: [Col. 0705C] Didymus’ work *On the Holy Spirit* is divided into three books in Jerome’s Latin translation; but this division is Jerome’s own, or that of his copyists, not Didymus’ as author. MARTIAN.—We printed above Jerome’s Latin translation of this book, the only one extant. Of his remaining works, only fragments occur in various catenae.] He wrote eighteen volumes on Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0705C] The manuscript of the Holy Cross counts nineteen, though incorrectly. Jerome says in his *Prologue on Isaiah*: “Didymus, whose friendship we recently enjoyed, produced eighteen volumes from the passage where it is written, ‘Comfort, comfort my people; priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem,’ to the end of the book.”]; three books of commentaries on Hosea, writing to me; five books on Zechariah, at my request; commentaries on Job; and [Note: [Col. 0705D] The Martianus manuscript and two of ours read *duoque*, “and two,” whereas the sense requires *multaque alia*, “and many other works.”] countless other works, whose enumeration belongs to a separate catalogue. He is still alive today and has passed the eighty-third year of his life. [Note: [Col. 0705D] The Veronese has merely “the eightieth”; another of ours, “the eighty-fourth”; Martianaeus, “the eighty-seventh.” [Col. 0706C] I would prefer the Veronese reading, both because it is more likely that Jerome used a round number and because, in the year 392, when he was writing this, Didymus would scarcely have passed his eighty-first year—not his eighty-third—if he died in 396 at the age of eighty-five, as Palladius testifies in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 4, and Sigebert of Gembloux.]

[Col. 0706A] Didymus of Alexandria, having suffered damage to his eyes from early youth and therefore being unacquainted with the alphabet, displayed such a marvel to everyone that he learned dialectic and geometry—which particularly require sight—to perfection. He composed many distinguished works: commentaries on all the Psalms; commentaries on Matthew and John; works *On Dogmas*; two discourses *Against the Arians*; and one discourse *On the Holy Spirit*, which I translated into Latin; eighteen volumes on Isaiah; three books of commentaries on Hosea, written to me; five books on Zechariah, at my request; commentaries on Job; and countless others, the description of which belongs to a separate catalogue. He survives to this day and has completed his eighty-third year.

## CHAPTER CX [Note: [Col. 0705] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0705]

[Col. 0705B] Optatus the African, bishop of Milevis, belonging to the Catholic party, wrote, under the emperors Valentinian and Valens [Note: [Col. 0706C] This refers to the year of Christ 370.], six books against the slander of the Donatian party, in which he asserts that the crime of the Donatists is falsely turned against us. [Note: [Col. 0706C] The manuscript of the Holy Cross reads seven, and that many books of Optatus are indeed enumerated even in the recent edition prepared by Dupin. Nevertheless, Optatus himself divided the whole work into only six books, as is clear from book I, no. 7: consequently, the seventh book appended to it consists of pieces apparently prepared by the author as additions. Nor do I know of any manuscript of Jerome that reads seven instead of six.]

[Col. 0706B] Optatus, bishop of Milevis, of the Catholic party, wrote under Valentinian and Valens six books against the slanders of the Donatists, in which he says that the accusation has been falsely brought against us by the Donatists.

## CHAPTER CXI [Note: [Col. 0705] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0705]

[Col. 0705B] 941 [Note: [Col. 0706C] The Vatican and our Veronese manuscripts have *Acilius*, as do others consulted by Suffridus Petri. Honorius has *Achilius*.] Aquilius Severus, in Spain, descended from that Severus to whom two books of Lactantius’ letters are said to have been written, [Note: [Col. 0706D] Recall above, chapter 80, concerning Lactantius’ letters. This Severus’ book no longer survives.] composed a volume in the manner of an *odoeiporikon*, containing an account of the whole course of his life, both in prose and in verse. He called it *Catastrophe*, or *Peira*, and died under the emperor Valentinian.

[Col. 0706B] 942 Aquilius Severus, in Spain, a descendant of Severus to whom two books of Lactantius’ letters are said to have been addressed, composed a book in the form of an *odoeiporikon*, containing an account of his entire life, partly in prose and partly in heroic meter. He called it *Catastrophe*, or *Peira*, and died under the emperor Valentinian.

## CHAPTER CXII [Note: [Col. 0705] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0705]

[Col. 0705B] Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, twice expelled from the Church at the command of Constantius and again by Valens, by whom he was finally recalled, held the episcopate securely for eight years under the emperor Theodosius. [Note: [Col. 0706D] He was twice ordered into exile by Constantius and again by Valens, who ultimately recalled him. He governed the church from 379 until 386, when he also died. In our *Chronicle*, under the year 352: “Cyril, after being ordained presbyter by Maximus, was promised the episcopate by Acacius, bishop of Caesarea, and the other Arian bishops, if he would repudiate Maximus’ ordination. He served as a deacon in the Church; for this impiety he was repaid with the priesthood. By various frauds he then harassed Heraclius, whom Maximus, while dying, had appointed as his successor, and degraded him from bishop to presbyter.”] His *catechetical lectures* survive, composed during his youth. [Note: [Col. 0707D] More remarkably, he delivered them extemporaneously.]

[Col. 0706B] Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, repeatedly expelled from the Church, later, while the emperor Theodosius was reigning, held the episcopate securely for eight years. His are the *catechetical lectures* that he composed in his youth.

## CHAPTER CXIII [Note: [Col. 0707] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0707]

[Col. 0707A] Euzoius was educated at Caesarea, while still a young man, together with Gregory of Nazianzus, under the rhetor Thespesius. Later bishop of the same city, he attempted, with great labor, to restore on parchment the already damaged library of Origen and Pamphilus. At last he was expelled from the Church under the emperor Theodosius. Various and numerous treatises are attributed to him, which are very easy to find. [Note: [Col. 0707D] The Veronese adds the word *jam* (“already”), as does the Greek ἤδη. Not even the titles of Euzoius’ writings survive.]

[Col. 0708A] Euzoius, having attended the rhetor Thespesius at Caesarea as a young man together with Gregory of Nazianzus, and later having become bishop of the same city, attempted, with great labor, to restore on parchment the library of Origen and Pamphilus, which had already been damaged. Later, under the emperor Theodosius, he was expelled from the Church. Many and very numerous discourses of his are said to exist, and they are easy to encounter.

## CHAPTER CXIV [Note: [Col. 0707] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0707]

[Col. 0707B] Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, wrote books *Against All Heresies*, and many other works, which the learned read for their content, while the simpler read them [Note: [Col. 0707D] The Veronese and Vatican manuscripts likewise have “also for their words”; at the end they read “he composes short works.”] for their language. He survives to this day and, now in extreme old age, continues to produce various works.

[Col. 0708B] Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, wrote discourses *Against All the Heresies*, and many other works, which the educated read for their subject matter, while ordinary people read them for their words. He survives to this day and, in extreme old age, continues to compose various writings.

## CHAPTER CXV [Note: [Col. 0707] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0707]

[Col. 0707B] 943 Ephraem, deacon of the Church of Edessa, composed many works in the Syriac language and attained such renown that, after the reading of Scripture, his writings are publicly read in certain churches. I read his Greek book *On the Holy Spirit*, which someone had translated from Syriac, and even in the translation I recognized the acumen of his lofty intellect. He died under the emperor Valens. [Note: [Col. 0707D] As far as I know, this no longer survives. Fabricius reports that some read *egregium* (“excellent”) instead of *Graecum* (“Greek”).]

[Col. 0708B] 944 Ephraem, deacon of the church in Edessa, composed many works in the language of the Syrians and attained such brilliance that, after the reading of the divine Scriptures, his writings are publicly read in some churches. I read a Greek book *On the Holy Spirit*, which certain persons translated from the Syriac language, and from the translation I recognized the summit of his lofty intellect. He died while Gratian was reigning. [Note: [Col. 0708D] The Latin version has “under Valens.”]

## CHAPTER CXVI [Note: [Col. 0707] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0707]

[Col. 0707C] Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, formerly called Mazaca, composed excellent books against Eunomius, a book *On the Holy Spirit*, nine homilies on the *Hexaemeron*, [Note: [Col. 0707D] The Veronese omits the conjunction *et*. Saint Basil died in 379.] an *ascetic work*, and various brief treatises. [Note: [Col. 0707D] He died while Gratian was emperor. The chronology is sound here concerning Basil, who was separated by a considerable interval from Photinus, bishop of Sirmium. The fact that Photinus and Basil are placed together in the Eusebian chronicles caused Jerome’s statement about the former to be attributed to the one immediately following, namely these words: “He lost many good qualities of continence and intellect through a single vice, pride.” Jerome said this about the dead Photinus, not about Saint Basil, as the heretics of our own time claim while seeking a knot in a reed. More will be said about this if God grants me years of life [Col. 0708C] until a new edition of the *Chronicles*, which many learned men request from us. MARTIAN.]

He died while Gratian was emperor.

[Col. 0708C] Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, which was formerly called Mazaca, composed distinguished discourses against Eunomius, a book *On the Holy Spirit*, nine homilies on the *Hexaemeron*, an ascetic work, and various brief homilies. He died while Gratian was reigning.

## CHAPTER CXVII [Note: [Col. 0707] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0707]

[Note: [Col. 0708D] Two of our manuscripts and Erasmus read “Gregory of Nazianzus,” omitting the intervening material, first “of Sasima,” and then the words that may not have come from Jerome’s hand. For if he intended to enumerate whatever sees Gregory held, why would he omit Constantinople, which he occupied in 381, when Gregory was his teacher? Gregory was indeed distressed that Basil had appointed him bishop of Sasima. At Nazianzus he properly served as deputy for his aged father, the bishop, although ancient writers also call him bishop of Nazianzus. Some manuscripts preserve the very old reading *Nazanzenus* instead of *Nazianzenus*, which Mabillon also observed in ancient monuments, and which we follow.]

Gregory, first bishop of Sasima and afterward of Nazianzus, a man of the greatest eloquence and my teacher, under whose exposition of the Scriptures I learned, composed all his works in approximately thirty thousand verses. Among them are: *On the Death of His Brother Caesarius* [Note: [Col. 0709C] The manuscript of the Holy Cross incorrectly substitutes Basil’s name for Caesarius. Gregory praised Basil at his funeral, but Basil was his friend, not his brother. Perhaps Jerome wrote “On the death of Caesarius, his brother, and on the death of Basil,” one of which easily fell out through a scribal error. Some pedant confused our Gregory with Gregory of Nyssa and changed Caesarius into Basil. Immediately afterward, our manuscripts, through scribal error, omit *Lauds of Cyprian*.]; *On the Love of the Poor*; *Lauds of the Maccabees*; *Lauds of Cyprian*; *Lauds of Athanasius*; *Lauds of the Philosopher Maximus*, who returned from exile, and whom some incorrectly labeled with the name of Heron [Note: [Col. 0709C] Our manuscripts and those examined by Erasmus have *Herona* or *Jerona*. Gregory did not praise Maximus under the name of Heron; rather, he criticized him, as though it were impossible both to praise and to criticize the same person at different times.]; and a book in hexameter verse in which Virginity and Marriage argue against one another; one book *Against Eunomius*; one book *On the Holy Spirit*; and two books *Against the Emperor Julian*. He followed Polemon in rhetorical style [Note: [Col. 0709C] All our manuscripts, and the Fesulan manuscript together with the Medicean cited by Victorius, incorrectly read “two books against Eunomius and one against Julian.” They also have “the rhetorical character of Polemon,” with the word “rhetorical” deleted, as in the Greek translator. On Polemon of Laodicea, the sophist, see Philostratus, book I, chapter 15.], and, while still alive, appointed a bishop in his own place and lived the life of a monk in the countryside. He died approximately three years before this, under the emperor Theodosius. [Note: [Col. 0709D] I would prefer “two years,” as some earlier editions have. Suidas says that Gregory died in the thirteenth year of the emperor Theodosius. It is well known that Jerome wrote this in the following, fourteenth year. Perhaps, therefore, the beginning [Col. 0710C] of the thirteenth year, in which Gregory died, and the end of the fourteenth, in which Jerome wrote, are indicated.]

[Col. 0708C] Gregory, first bishop of Sasima and afterward of Nazianzus, a most learned man and my teacher, under whose exposition I learned the divine Scriptures, composed all his writings in thirty thousand verses. Among them are these: *On the Death of His Brother Caesarius*; *On the Love of the Poor*; *Lauds of the Maccabees*; *Lauds of Cyprian*; *Lauds of Athanasius*; *Lauds of the Philosopher Maximus*, who returned from exile, whom some falsely titled “of Heron”—for there is also another book containing a condemnation of that same Maximus, as though it were impossible to praise and blame the same person at the appropriate time; and a book in hexameter verse in which Virginity and Marriage debate against each other; one discourse *Against Eunomius*; one discourse *On the Holy Spirit*; and one discourse *Against the Emperor Julian*. He followed the style of Polemon and, while still alive, appointed a bishop in his own place; he led a monastic life in the countryside and died nearly three years before this while Theodosius was reigning.

## CHAPTER CXVIII [Note: [Col. 0709] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0709]

[Col. 0709B] Lucius, bishop of the Arian party after Athanasius, held the church of Alexandria until the emperor Theodosius, [Note: [Col. 0710C] The Veronese and Guelpherbytan manuscripts have “by whom he was expelled.” They assign this to the year 379. Apart from a small fragment, all of this Lucius’ book has perished in the acts of the Roman council under Martin I. See Socrates IV, 37; Sozomen VI, 5, and elsewhere.] by whom he was also expelled. His festal letters concerning Easter survive, together with a few short booklets on various subjects.

[Col. 0710B] Lucius, after Athanasius, bishop of the Arian sect, held the church of Alexandria until the reign of the emperor Theodosius, by whom he was expelled. His letters concerning Easter are preserved, as are a few discourses on various subjects.

## CHAPTER CXIX [Note: [Col. 0709] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0709]

Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, was more distinguished while he was still a presbyter at Antioch. His commentaries on the Apostle survive, along with many other works belonging more to the style of Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0710C] The Veronese manuscript does not recognize the word *Emiseni*, nor does Facundus of Hermiane, who copied this chapter from Jerome word for word. I understand the statement that Diodorus’ writings belonged to his style as meaning that Diodorus especially pursued the historical sense which Eusebius, as he says in chapter 91, set before himself in expounding the Scriptures. [Col. 0710D] It is strange that Jerome adds that Diodorus could not imitate the eloquence of Eusebius of Emesa, since Theodoret, book IV, especially attributes this praise of eloquence to him, comparing him with a crystal-clear stream, and Photius praises him as pure and lucid in speech. His works, however, are now sought in vain apart from certain fragments in chains. Jerome reports a small fragment from his *Commentaries on the Apostle* in letter 119, to Minervius and Alexander. See below, chapter 129.] of Emesa. Although Diodorus followed his meaning, he could not imitate his eloquence because of his ignorance of secular literature.

Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, was more distinguished when he was a presbyter at Antioch. His commentaries on the Apostle survive, together with many other works more suited to the style of Eusebius of Emesa. Although he followed Eusebius’ thought, he could not imitate his literary distinction because of his inexperience in secular letters.

## CHAPTER CXX [Note: [Col. 0709] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0709]

[Col. 0709B] Eunomius, bishop of Cyzicus of the Arian party, advancing into the open blasphemy of his heresy, so that he publicly confessed what they concealed, is said still to be alive in Cappadocia [Note: [Col. 0710D] After being exiled for the third time, he obtained this concession from Theodosius the Great: that he might return to his ancestral estates at Dacora in Cappadocia, as Philostorgius writes, and Nicephorus after him. He is nevertheless said to have died before 396.], and to write much against the Church. [Note: [Col. 0711C] The Guelpherbytan manuscript has “he dared to write.” The distinguished Fabricius recently published an *Exposition* and an *Apology* from his writings.] Apollinarius, Didymus, Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa replied to him. [Note: [Col. 0711C] The writings of Didymus and Apollinarius against Eunomius do not survive. The Cistercian manuscript does not repeat the name of Gregory; it incorrectly reads “of Emesa” for “of Nyssa.”]

[Col. 0710B] Eunomius, bishop of Cyzicus of the Arian sect, advanced so far into the blasphemy of his own heresy that he openly confessed what they concealed. He is said still to survive in Cappadocia and to write much against the Church. Apollinarius, Didymus, Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa wrote against him.

## CHAPTER CXXI [Note: [Col. 0711] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0711]

[Col. 0711A] 947 [Note: [Col. 0711C] Jerome also mentions and attacks this Priscillian of Ávila, bishop in further Spain, in the prologue to his books *Against the Pelagians*. See Sulpicius Severus near the end of book II.] Priscillian, bishop of Ávila, who was executed at Trier by the tyrant Maximus through the faction of Hydatius and Ithacius [Note: [Col. 0711D] Erasmus has *Hythacii* and *Hithatii*; forms *Hydiati* and *Idatii* are also found.], published many short works, of which some have reached us. [Note: [Col. 0711D] None have survived to our time.] To this day he is accused by some of the Gnostic heresy—that is, the heresy of Basilides and Marcus, about whom Irenaeus wrote—while others defend him, saying that he did not understand matters in the sense of which he is accused. [Note: [Col. 0711D] Earlier editions, together with the Greek translator, incorrectly read *Marcionis*. It should be corrected to *Marci*, as we have done on the authority of all our manuscripts; this is also confirmed by the passage in Irenaeus, book I, chapter 8, *Against Heresies*, cited and transcribed by Jerome in the places noted below. The royal manuscripts likewise read this, as the most learned Cotelerius testifies. See letter 65, to Theodora, and the commentary on Isaiah LXIV. Sulpicius Severus, in the book cited above, says: “Marcus, coming from Egypt, first introduced him into Spain,” etc.]

[Col. 0712A] 948 Priscillian, bishop of Ávila, who was put to death at Trier by the tyrant Maximus through the plotting of Hydatius and Ithacius, published many writings, some of which have reached us. To this day some accuse him as a heretic of the Gnostic sect—that is, the sect of Basilides and Marcion, about whom Irenaeus wrote—while others defend him, saying that he did not hold the views of which he is accused.

## CHAPTER CXXII [Note: [Col. 0711] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0711]

[Col. 0711B] Latronianus, [Note: [Col. 0711D] Some read *Matronianus*, but *Latronianus* is found in far more manuscripts and is rightly preferable. The manuscripts of Sulpicius Severus also have this form; consult there the entire history of Priscillian’s teaching. Shortly afterward some of ours and the Guelpherbytan manuscript have “a very learned man.” [Col. 0712C] The Veronese then has “in metrical order” instead of “in verse.”] a man of great learning from the province of Spain and comparable to the ancients in poetic composition, was himself executed at Trier with Priscillian, Felicissimus, Julian, and Euchrotia, leaders of the same faction. Works displaying his talent, composed in various meters, survive. [Note: [Col. 0711D] Nothing of these survives today.]

[Col. 0712B] Matronianus, from the province of Spain, very highly educated and comparable to the ancients in epic poetry, was himself executed at Trier together with Priscillian, Felicissimus, Julian, and Euchrotia, the leaders of the same sect. His writings, published in various meters, survive.

## CHAPTER CXXIII [Note: [Col. 0711] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0711]

[Col. 0711B] Tiberianus of Baetica wrote an apology, in a bombastic and elaborate style, concerning the suspected heresy of which he was accused together with Priscillian. [Note: [Col. 0712C] The printed editions have *postea post*, which we have corrected on the authority and agreement of all our manuscripts. See the passage of Sulpicius Severus just cited. Tiberianus, after his property was confiscated, was sent to the island of Sylina under sentence of the law.] But after the slaughter of his associates, overcome by the weariness of exile, he changed his purpose and, in accordance with Holy Scripture, [Note: [Col. 0712C] Tiberianus’ action seems to be interpreted favorably, as it especially pleased Tillemont. Among Priscillian’s wicked doctrines, with which Tiberianus was suspected of sympathizing, was the condemnation of marriage. After returning to his companions from the island of Sylina, to which he had been deported for having joined one of that sect, he apparently wished to show from his heart how hostile he was to this error: he gave his daughter, although she had already been consecrated to Christ as a virgin, in marriage, or rather compelled her to marry. We do not deny that he acted wrongly, since he demonstrated that he preferred marriage to virginity, and indeed to consecrated virginity; but it does not seem that Jerome’s words mean that he “returned to his vomit.”] like a dog returning to its own vomit (Proverbs XVI, 11; II Peter II, 22), he gave his daughter, a virgin devoted to Christ, [Note: [Col. 0712D] The Guelpherbytan manuscript incorrectly has “he joined her to himself in marriage.” Jerome reproaches Tiberianus only with having given his daughter, a virgin devoted to Christ, to marriage; the Greek translator has “compelled her to marry.”] in marriage.

[Col. 0712B] Tiberianus of Baetica wrote an apology in a lofty and elevated style concerning the suspected heresy for which he was accused together with Priscillian. After the slaughter of his associates, overcome by his distressing life in exile, he departed from his original intention and, in accordance with divine Scripture, returned like a dog to his own vomit; he compelled his daughter, a virgin consecrated to God, to marry.

## CHAPTER CXXIV [Note: [Col. 0711] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0711]

[Col. 0711C] Ambrose, bishop of Milan, continues to write to the present day. [Note: [Col. 0712D] It is commonly thought that Jerome offers this excuse only in the case of Ambrose because Ambrose was still alive, so that Jerome would not have to pass judgment on his works, since he supposedly held a poor opinion of them. But, even if we concede Rufinus’ accusation, that Jerome was attacking the holy bishop’s books *On the Holy Spirit*, he praises many of Ambrose’s other writings very highly, such as *On Widows*, *On Virgins*, *On Duties*, and so forth.] Since he survives, I shall withhold my judgment, lest I be reproached on either side, whether for flattery or for truth.

[Col. 0712C] Ambrose, bishop of Milan, continues to write to this very day; and since he survives, I defer my judgment, lest I be charged with flattery rather than truth.

[Col. 0711]

[Col. 0712C] 950 Evagrius, bishop of Antioch, a man of natural and exceptionally keen intelligence, while still a presbyter, read me discourses on various subjects, which he has not yet published. He also translated the *Life of the Blessed Antony* by Athanasius from Greek into our language.

[Col. 0714A] Ambrose of Alexandria, a student of Didymus, wrote against Apollinarius a book of many verses on dogmas; and, as I recently learned from someone who had just related it, he also wrote commentaries on Job, which survive to the present.

[Col. 0714A] Maximus the Philosopher, originating from Alexandria, became bishop of Constantinople and was deposed. He composed a distinguished book *On the Faith* against the Arians and presented it to the emperor Gratian at Milan.

## CHAPTER CXXIX [Note: [Col. 0713] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0713]

[Col. 0713B] [Note: [Col. 0713C] He was also surnamed Chrysostom (“Golden-Mouthed”) because of his golden elegance in speaking. Certain manuscripts examined by Erasmus and Martianaeus, through the ingenuity of a pedantic interpolator, add the following: “Later he became bishop of the city of Constantinople—a dignity which John obtained six years after this book of Jerome, that is, in the year 398—an extremely skilled interpreter and distinguished extemporaneous speaker. As a follower of Eusebius and Diodorus, he composed many works: *On the Priesthood*; *On Compunction of Heart*; *On the Soul’s Fall*; *On the Mystery of the Cross*; *On the Faith against the Arians*; *Against the Macedonians*; *Against the Anomoeans*; and countless others, which it is not easy to find even with the most diligent search. But throughout the whole world his writings, published both in Greek and translated into Latin, shine like lightning flashing across the sky. He flourished especially under the emperor Arcadius, by whom, through the private indignation of the empress, he was driven into exile and died. Many years later, his bodily remains were brought with great honor by Theodosius, his son, to Constantinople and lie buried in the shrine of the Apostles.” How foolishly and recklessly this material was stitched onto Jerome’s text in favor of Chrysostom is evident from the facts. —“John, presbyter of the church of Antioch,” etc. Some recent writers are distressed that so little was written about Saint John Chrysostom, because they do not know that this work *On Ecclesiastical Writers* was published six years before John was raised to the episcopal throne of Constantinople and before his name had become famous in the churches of the Catholics. But from a manuscript of Cluny we easily learn how old that ignorant question and complaint is. In it some scoundrel and impostor, against Jerome’s will, inserts the following passage in praise of Saint Chrysostom:

> “CXXIX. John, formerly presbyter of the church of Antioch and later bishop of the city of Constantinople, an exceptionally skilled interpreter and distinguished extemporaneous speaker, a follower of Eusebius of Emesa and Diodorus, composed many works: *On the Priesthood*; *On Compunction of Heart*; *On the Soul’s Fall*; *On the Mystery of the Cross*; *On the Faith against the Arians*; *Against the Macedonians*; *Against the Anomoeans*; and countless others, which it is not easy to find even with the most diligent search. But throughout the whole world his writings, published both in Greek and translated into Latin, flash like lightning traveling across the sky. He flourished especially under the emperor Arcadius, by whom, through the private indignation of the empress, he was driven into exile and died. Many years later his bodily remains were brought with great honor by Theodosius, his son, to Constantinople and lie buried in the shrine of the Apostles.”

Let the admirers of Chrysostom now see what a crime an ignorant admirer of John and a foolish corrupter of Jerome committed, not understanding that in the fourteenth year of Theodosius the Elder nothing of this sort could have been written about Saint Chrysostom’s exile, death, or the transfer of his relics to Constantinople. Let the diligent reader remember the cases of Paul the Apostle and the virgin Thecla, and he will admit that ignorant admirers of the saints have often been accustomed to invent and fabricate many things contrary to the truth. MARTIAN.] John, a presbyter of the church of Antioch, a follower of Eusebius of Emesa and Diodorus, is said to have composed many works, of which I have read only *On the Priesthood*. [Note: [Col. 0714D] One of these was mentioned above in chapter 91 and the other in chapter 119. See Sozomen, book VIII, chapter 2, where he also says that Chrysostom was a student of Diodorus. Suidas very truly says: “To enumerate the number of his writings is not the task of a human being, but rather of God, who knows all things.” See Ebed-Jesu, chapter 26.]

[Col. 0714B] John, presbyter of Antioch, a follower of Eusebius of Emesa and Diodorus, is said to have composed many works, of which I have read only *On the Priesthood*.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0715] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0715]

[Col. 0715B] Sophronius, [Note: [Col. 0715D] It can scarcely be believed that this Sophronius, if he was also the translator of this work, would have wished entirely to conceal his own identity here, and, without any intervening indication, heap such praise upon himself, even if speaking from a friend’s perspective.] a man of exceptionally great learning, composed, while still young, a laudatory work on Bethlehem, and recently [Note: [Col. 0715D] The Veronese manuscript omits the name Serapis and reads “composed a book on the overthrow,” as though the reference were to Bethlehem. Christians in Alexandria overthrew the statue of Serapis around A.D. 391, as can be inferred from Theodosius’s law to Evagrius, under the title “On Pagans.” Others, from Marcellinus’s *Chronicle* and likewise from Zosimus, book I, say that it was overthrown two years earlier, that is, in A.D. 389, during the consulship of Timasius and Promotus. In Theophilus’s synodical letter against Origen, numbered 92 among Jerome’s letters and first published by us, section 3: “The Origenists were shouting whatever they thought could bring hatred upon us [Theophilus], stirring up the pagan peoples against us with things that unbelieving ears would gladly hear; among these were the destruction of Serapis and of other idols,” etc. See our notes on that passage, and Rufinus, *History* XI.23 and 27 and following.] composed a notable book on the overthrow of Serapis. [Col. 0716B] Sophronius, a man highly educated, composed the praises of Bethlehem while still young; and recently he composed a distinguished discourse concerning the destruction of the Serapeum. He also translated into Greek with elegant expression *On Virginity*, addressed to Eustochium, and the *Life of the Monk Hilarion*, my writings; likewise the Psalter and the Prophets, which we translated from Hebrew into Roman—that is, Latin.

## CHAPTER CXXXV

[Note: [Col. 0715] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0715]

[Col. 0715B] 953 Jerome, [Note: [Col. 0716D] His full name is Sophronius Eusebius Hieronymus, as we found in one and another Milanese manuscript containing his genuine writings.] born to Eusebius his father in the town of Stridon, [Note: [Col. 0716D] Among the various opinions concerning Jerome’s homeland, we shall show in the *Life of the Holy Doctor*, which we have reserved for the final volume of his works, with supporting arguments, which opinion seems preferable to the others.
