Those who place it near the river Saboria, as Buno does in Cluverius’s *Geography*, or near a similarly named and well-known town in Hungary, do not depart far from them. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXXI, chapter 8, describes the devastation inflicted upon Dalmatia and Pannonia by the Goths.] which, having been destroyed by the Goths, was once on the border of Dalmatia and [Col. 0717A] Pannonia, I have written the following up to the present year, that is, the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodosius: [Note: [Col. 0717B] This corresponds, as we have often said, to A.D. 392.] [Note: [Col. 0717B] From this *Life* we begin this second volume.] the *Life of the Monk Paul*; one book of letters to various persons; [Note: [Col. 0717C] He probably refers to the letters which, while he was at Antioch and in the desert, and during his travels, he wrote to various people up to the year 383. These are the first letters appearing in our edition according to chronological order, although we showed in the general preface that some of them have perished.] the *Exhortation to Heliodorus*; [Note: [Col. 0717C] This may be found in this very second volume, p. 171. In other editions it occupied the place of letter 59.] the *Dialogue between a Luciferian and an Orthodox Christian*; [Note: [Col. 0717C] This *Chronicle*, which Jerome translated from Eusebius into Latin and extended with material of his own from Constantine the Great’s vicennalia to the year 378, will, God willing, make up the eighth volume of our edition.] the *Chronicle of Universal History*; twenty-eight homilies on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which I translated from Origen’s Greek into Latin; [Note: [Col. 0717C–D] We append to the collection of all Jerome’s works these fourteen homilies on Jeremiah and as many on Ezekiel, rendered by the Holy Doctor into Latin from Origen’s Greek; until now they have been published only among Origen’s works.] *On the Seraphim*; *On Hosanna*; *On the Thrifty and Prodigal Sons*; [Note: [Col. 0717D] The Vulgate and some manuscripts read *de Osanna* instead of *de*. These are two letters to Damasus: the first, *On the Seraphim*, written in A.D. 381, is number eighteen in our edition; the second is number twenty, written two years later.] *On Three Questions of the Old Law*; [Note: [Col. 0717D] This now bears number twenty-one, produced in the same year as the preceding work.] two homilies on the *Song of Songs*; [Note: [Col. 0717D–0718B] We presented this little book above in this very volume, p. 205. In other editions it was counted among the letters as no. 35.] against Helvidius, *On the Perpetual Virginity of Mary*; to Eustochium, *On the Preservation of Virginity*; [Note: [Col. 0718B] Letter twenty-two, both in our edition and in the ancient editions.] to Marcella, one book of letters; [Note: [Col. 0718B] By these we mean the sixteen letters which, beginning almost continuously with number twenty-three and with five others interspersed, we present in the first volume; they were written by the Holy Doctor while he was in Rome in A.D. 384.] a consolatory work to Paula on the death of her daughter; [Note: [Col. 0718C] It is entitled *On the Death of Blesilla* and is letter no. 39, sent in the same year.] three books of commentaries on Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, and likewise three books on the Letter to the Ephesians; [Note: [Col. 0718C] We shall discuss these commentaries on Paul’s four letters in their proper places in volume seven. In the Veronese manuscript the title *Commentaries* is repeated also for Ephesians, together with the Greek translator.] one book on the Letter to Titus; one book on the Letter to Philemon; commentaries on Ecclesiastes; one book of *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*; one book *On Places*; [Note: [Col. 0718C] We give the following four books in the third volume. Yet the words “one book *On Places*,” through a scribal error, as I have no doubt, are absent from the Veronese and Vatican codices.] one book of *Hebrew Names* 955; one book *On the Holy Spirit of Didymus*, which I translated into Latin; [Note: [Col. 0718C] It has hitherto been wrongly divided into three parts; we have restored it to its original integrity and present it in this second volume, p. 105. The Greek text of Didymus has perished.] thirty-nine homilies on Luke; [Note: [Col. 0718C–D] We shall include these thirty-nine homilies on Luke among Jerome’s works, in their proper place after the commentaries on Matthew, since Origen’s Greek text has now perished.] seven treatises on the Psalms, from Psalm 10 through Psalm 16; [Note: [Col. 0718D] The punishable hand of an interpolator caused these seven treatises on the Psalms to perish. For the *Breviary on All the Psalms*, which we possess under Jerome’s name, is certainly a spurious offspring; it is altogether reasonable to believe that it contains excerpts from Jerome’s genuine commentaries on certain Psalms, scattered here and there. See our fuller discussion of this matter in the general preface, sections 21 and 22.] the *Life of Malchus, the Captive Monk*, and the *Life of Blessed Hilarion*. [Note: [Col. 0718D–0719B] What this work consisted of is best learned from the author himself, in his dedicatory letter to Damasus prefixed to the Gospels: “The present little preface promises only the four Gospels, whose order is as follows: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, corrected by comparison with Greek manuscripts, though ancient ones. So that they might not differ too greatly from the customary Latin reading, we moderated our pen in such a way that, correcting only those passages which seemed to alter the sense, we allowed the rest to remain as they had been. If he devoted the same labor to the other books of the New Testament—which I certainly do not know well enough to affirm as confidently as learned men do—then at least, something quite foreign to Jerome’s character, he gave the reader no notice of his labor in any such preface.”] I restored the New Testament to the Greek standard; [Col. 0719A] [Note: [Col. 0719B] These words concerning the Old Testament are absent from the Veronese manuscript. Nor, in fact, had he translated the entire Old Testament at this time, but only certain parts of it from Hebrew: for example, the Books of Kings, as is clear from his preface; then the Prophets and the Psalter, as appears from the preceding chapter concerning Sophronius. To these one may add Job, but it must be admitted that he had not yet undertaken the others. Yet just as he had called the Gospels the New Testament, so he called certain parts of it simply the Old Testament, especially since he intended to devote the same labor to the remaining books.] I translated the Old Testament according to the Hebrew. The number of letters to Paula and Eustochium is uncertain, since they are written daily. [Note: [Col. 0719B–C] Only three letters to Paula survive, and no more than a few to Eustochium; many must therefore have perished, if we understand the reference to include those he sent to them separately. It is nevertheless possible that letters which are more numerous, and which he prefixed as prefaces to books dedicated to them, should also be included in this reckoning.] I also wrote two books of expositions on Micah, [Note: [Col. 0719C–0720A] The book on Zephaniah, which is listed after Habakkuk by the Greek translator and placed last after Haggai in the Vatican and Holy Cross manuscripts. Jerome himself explains clearly enough the order in which he treated these books, in the preface to book III on Amos: “For I did not expound them from the first to the last according to the order in which they are read, but as I was able and as I was asked, so I expounded them. First I addressed Nahum, Micah, Zephaniah, and Haggai to the most industrious Paula and her daughter Eustochium. Second, I assigned two books on Habakkuk to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia,” etc.] one book on Zephaniah, one book on Nahum, two books on Habakkuk, and one book on Haggai. And many other works on the prophetic writings, which I now have in hand, are not yet completed. [Note: [Col. 0720A–C] They had not yet been completed. Printed books add: “Two books against Jovinianus, and an *Apology* and *Epitaph* addressed to Pammachius.” In the Cluniac manuscript, however, we read: “Also, after this dedicated book, two books against Jovinianus the heretic, and an *Apology* addressed to Pammachius.” Thus, after publishing the book *On Illustrious Men*, Jerome wrote *Against Jovinianus*, as is firmly established by the preface to his Commentary on Jonah: “About three years passed after I interpreted the five Prophets—Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Haggai—and, being occupied with another work, I could not complete what I had begun. For I wrote a book *On Illustrious Men*, and two volumes *Against Jovinianus*, as well as an *Apology*, etc.” At the end of this book the work of Gennadius of Marseilles was wrongly added as a supplement to Jerome’s little work. We, however, retaining only what is genuine in this volume, relegated the foreign and spurious materials to volume V, where we published Gennadius from the most ancient Corbie manuscript, now Saint-Germain no. 142; consult the volume itself in volume V of our edition. Moreover, I have disregarded the varying additions of different copyists, since I judge them unworthy of being brought to light in print. Martianay.—At the end of this book, the manuscripts we consulted, and those used by Martianay, all end with the words “are not yet completed.” Martianay nevertheless notes that the Cluniac manuscript adds: “Also, after this dedicated book, two books against Jovinianus the heretic,” etc.; these words, enclosed in brackets, we retain from most printed editions and from the Greek translator. We have no doubt, however, that they were inserted by another hand, drawn from these words in Jerome’s preface to the Commentaries on Jonah: “About three years passed after I interpreted the five Prophets—Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Haggai—and, being occupied with another work, I could not complete what I had begun. For I wrote a book *On Illustrious Men*, two volumes *Against Jovinianus*, an *Apology*, and *On the Best Method of Translation*, addressed to Pammachius, and two books to Nepotianus, or *On Nepotianus*—that is, *On the Life of Clerics* and the *Epitaph*—and other works too lengthy to enumerate.”] Two books *Against Jovinianus*, and an *Apology* and *Epitaph* addressed to Pammachius.

[Col. 0716B] 954 Jerome, son of Eusebius, from the small town of Stridon, sacked by the Goths, which bordered Dalmatia and Pannonia, composed the following up to the present year, that is, the fourteenth year of Theodosius: the *Life of Paul the Monk*; one book of letters to various persons; an *Exhortation to Heliodorus*; the *Dialogue of the Luciferian and the Orthodox Christian*; a *Chronicle of Universal Histories*; twenty-eight homilies on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which I translated from the Greek of Origen into Roman; *On the Seraphim*, *On Hosanna*, *On the Thrifty and Prodigal Sons*, *On the Three Questions of the Old Law*, two homilies on the *Song of Songs*, *Against Helvidius, On the Perpetual Virginity of Holy Mary*, *To Eustochium, On the Virginity That Must Be Preserved*, one book of letters to Marcella, a consolatory work to Paula on the death of her daughter, three books of commentaries on the Letter to the Galatians, one book on the Letter to Titus, one book on the Letter to Philemon, commentaries on Ecclesiastes, one book of *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, one book *On Places*, one book of *Hebrew Names*, one book *On the Holy Spirit of Didymus*, which I translated into Roman, twenty-nine homilies on Luke, seven homilies on Psalms 956, from Psalm 10 through Psalm 16, the *Life of the Captive Monk*, the *Life of Blessed Hilarion*, I established the New Testament according to the Greek text, and translated the Old Testament according to the Hebrew. The number of letters to Paula and Eustochium is uncertain, since they are written daily. I also wrote two books on Micah, one on Nahum, two on Habakkuk, one on Zephaniah, one on Haggai, and many other works from the prophetic writings which I now have in hand, and they are not yet completed. Two books *Against Jovinianus*, and an *Apology* and *Epitaph* addressed to Pammachius.

## I. ON THE LIVES OF THE APOSTLES

This was found by Erasmus inserted under the name of Sophronius into the Greek version of the *Book on Illustrious Men* in his manuscript—chapter 1, after chapter 1, and the remainder after chapter 4. [Note: [Col. 0720] The Greek and Latin versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0719D] 957 I. Andrew, his brother [Note: [Col. 0719D] Namely, the brother of Simon Peter; for this Pseudo-Sophronius appended the passage immediately after chapter 1.] as our predecessors have transmitted, preached the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ to the Scythians, Sogdians, and Sacae. [Col. 0721A] He preached also in Sebastopolis the Great, where the camp of Apsarus and the river Phasis are located; there live the inner Ethiopians. [Note: [Col. 0721D] Bochart would prefer *heteroi* (ἕτεροι, “other”). Against him, the distinguished Fabricius more correctly defends the printed reading *esōteroi* (ἐσώτεροι, “inner”).] He was buried at Patras in Achaia, having been crucified by Aegeas, prefect of the Edessenes.

II. James, son of Zebedee, preached the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ to all the twelve tribes that were in the Dispersion. He was killed by the sword by Herod, tetrarch of the Jews.

III. The apostle Philip preached the Gospel of the Lord Jesus in Phrygia. He was honorably buried at Hierapolis with his daughters.

IV. The apostle Bartholomew preached the Gospel of Christ to the Indians called “fortunate,” and delivered to them the Gospel according to Matthew. He died at Albanopolis, a town of Greater Armenia.

V. The apostle Thomas, as tradition has handed down to us, preached the Gospel of the Lord to the Parthians, Medes, Persians, Carmanians, Hyrcanians, Bactrians, and Magi. He died in the Indian city of Calamina.

VI. Simon the Cananaean, surnamed Judas, brother of James the bishop, who also succeeded him in the episcopate after the death of James, surnamed “the Just,” lived 120 years. Having been crucified under the emperor Trajan, when a severe persecution had arisen, he died.

VII. Matthias, one of the Seventy, was enrolled among the eleven apostles in place of Judas Iscariot, who became the betrayer. In the other Ethiopia, where the camp of Apsarus and the harbor of Hyssus are located, he preached the Gospel among people who were uncivilized. 959 He died there and was buried there, even to the present day.

VIII. Timothy, appointed bishop of the Ephesians by blessed Paul, was from the Gentiles, not from the circumcision. Paul bears much witness concerning him, exhorting him to preserve the honorable profession of the gift bestowed upon him; and he also bore glorious witness there.

IX. Titus, bishop of Crete, preached the Gospel of Christ in Crete itself and in the neighboring islands. He also died there and was buried there, namely in Crete.

X. Crescens preached the Gospel in Gaul and was buried there. [Note: [Col. 0721D–0722D] This may be inferred from 2 Timothy 4:10; for where the common text reads “Crescens to Galatia,” some Greek copies have *eis Gallian* (εἰς Γαλλίαν), “to Gaul.” Eusebius, book III, chapter 4, further relates that the very phrase *eis Galatian* (εἰς Γαλατίαν), which other Greeks prefer, is used for *Gallia*. Theodoret says: “They called the Gauls *Galatia* in this way. For this is what they were formerly called; and even now those who have received an education outside [the Greek world] call them by this name.” Epiphanius, *Heresy* LI: “Not in Galatia, as some, being mistaken, suppose, but in Gaul.”] The eunuch of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, preached the Gospel of the Lord in Arabia Felix and on the island of Taprobane in the Red Sea. They say that he also suffered martyrdom there and was honorably buried.

958 Α. Andrew, his brother, as those before us have handed down, preached the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ to the Scythians, Sogdians, and Sacae; and he preached in Sebastopolis the Great, where the camp of Apsarus and the river Phasis are situated, where the inner Ethiopians dwell. [Note: [Col. 0721D] Huet would prefer *esōterā* (ἐσωτέρᾳ, “more inward”), since above, in chapter 1, the expression “the inner Ethiopians” is used.] He was buried at Patras in Achaia, having been handed over to the cross by Aegeas, king of the Edessenes.

Β. James, son of Zebedee, preached the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ to all the twelve tribes in the Dispersion. He was killed by the sword by Herod, tetrarch of the Jews.

Γ. The apostle Philip preached the Gospel of the Lord Jesus in Phrygia. He was gloriously buried at Hierapolis with his daughters.

Δ. The apostle Bartholomew preached the Gospel of Christ to the Indians called “fortunate,” and gave them the Gospel according to Matthew. He died at Albanopolis of Greater Armenia.

Ε. The apostle Thomas, as tradition records, preached the Gospel of the Lord to Parthians, Medes, Persians, Carmanians, Hyrcanians, Bactrians, and Magi. He died in the Indian city of Calamina.

ϛʹ. Simon the Cananaean, called Judas, brother of James the bishop, who received the office of bishop after the death of James the Just, lived 120 years. Having been handed over to crucifixion under the emperor Trajan, when a great persecution had arisen, he died.

Ζ. Matthias, being one of the Seventy, was numbered with the eleven apostles in place of Judas Iscariot, who had become the betrayer. In the second Ethiopia, where the camp of Apsarus and the harbor of Hyssus are located, he preached the Gospel among people who were uncivilized. 960 He died there and was buried there, even to the present day.

Η. Timothy, appointed bishop of Ephesus by blessed Paul, was from the Gentiles, not from the circumcision. Paul bears much witness concerning him, admonishing him to preserve the good confession of the gift bestowed upon him; and he also bore glorious witness there.

Θ. Titus, bishop of Crete, preached the Gospel of Christ in Crete itself and in the surrounding islands. He also died there and was buried there, in Crete.

## II. LETTER

Already published under the name of St. Jerome, [Note: [Col. 0723B] Thus it is entitled in the Florentine manuscripts of the Servites of the Annunciation and of the Friars Minor of Santa Croce, according to Martianay’s testimony, and in the Ambrosian manuscript belonging to the distinguished Lodovico Antonio Muratori.] *On the Twelve Doctors to Desiderius*; already published under the name of Bede, [Note: [Col. 0723B] It is found under this title and Bede’s name in volume III of his works, p. 491.] *On the Lights of the Church*. (G, S)

## CENSURE

He would be wasting his leisure who attempted to prove at length that this is not Jerome’s work but the offspring of an author with too much idle time. So many verbal stumbling-blocks, tasteless circumlocutions, enormous errors of chronology and order, and—to say nothing worse—perverse judgments about writers continually offend those devoted to Jerome’s glory, who cannot bear such babble to be attributed to the name of the greatest Doctor. Yet Erasmus was not therefore justified in accusing it of stupidity because, after the author had announced that he would speak of the luminaries shining throughout the firmament of the world, he inserted Pelagius, Jovinianus, and similar denizens of darkness. For he does not place among the lights of the Church those whose writings he censures, and he does not deny that they are infected with poison and gall. “I shall speak,” he says, “very briefly and plainly about the writers.”

It would have been more justly counted a fault that in chapter two he mentions Hilary, Roman Pontiff, who succeeded St. Leo and became famous long after Jerome’s death. But I do not think that a man so dull and stupid as to be ignorant of this could have been the author; rather, it happened through the fault of copyists, who inserted the title of bishop, which he himself did not write. Certainly, the preceding words, in which Lucifer of Cagliari himself is alluded to, persuade me that the Hilary praised here is Hilary the Roman deacon, a leading defender of the Luciferian sect, whom Jerome also notes in chapter 95 and to whom commentaries on the Letter to the Romans are attributed: “Hilary,” he says, “the Lucifer of the Romans.”

I have said this so that the pseudonymous author might not be harassed by censures beyond what he seems to deserve. For the rest, I append this little work chiefly for this one reason, and I occasionally correct it against the manuscripts, so that the learned or unlearned reader may not lack anything pertaining to Jerome.

961 **Jerome to Desiderius**

[Col. 0723A]

You now earnestly wish, my brother Desiderius, that I should plainly tell you, as though speaking about the luminaries that shine throughout the firmament of the world, a few things about writers who were able to bring forth for us, for the brightness of spiritual contemplation, much concerning those obscurities that impede understanding because of the carnal mind.

But I fear that the judgment concerning Susanna, daughter of Helchias, may be fulfilled against me—the judgment of the presbyters, who said: “Distress surrounds me on every side” [another reading: “everywhere.”] I too am in distress. For if I wish to criticize any one of them, I shall stir up adversaries and hostilities against myself on every side. But if I do not wish to do so, you will never find what you requested. Yet it seems better to condemn the will of only one person than to pass over or despise the counsels of many, because each of them deserved to be praised carefully in the Holy Scriptures. I shall touch upon them all briefly and lightly, with complete affection, so that I may fulfill both obligations peacefully. [Note: [Col. 0724B] The manuscripts read “gently and lightly.”]

[Col. 0724A] I. Augustine, a bishop flying over the peaks of the mountains like an eagle and not considering what takes place at their roots, declares many things in clear language about the spaces of heaven, the regions of earth, and the circuit of the waters. For whoever wishes to climb a fruitful tree hastens gradually toward the higher and greater branches to gather its fruit, while leaving the nearer branches to little ones. But we, who are little, weak, and lesser, shall fare well if we are able to gather the lower fruits.

963 II. Hilary, [Note: [Col. 0724B] The same manuscripts read: “a bishop, Hilary, the Lucifer of the Romans and the lamp of the Churches.” Recall the preceding *Censure*.] bishop of the Romans, the Lucifer and lamp of the Churches, and a precious stone to which mortals scarcely ascend, speaks of everything in beautiful language and with a golden mouth. [Note: [Col. 0724B] The same manuscripts add: “Even if some of his words could have fallen by the wayside,” etc.] For although some things might have fallen by the wayside, nevertheless a great harvest arose from him in the Scriptures.

III. Origen Adamantius, thinking about higher and greater matters, [Note: [Col. 0724B] The manuscripts add: “and not being sufficient in his own genius, he attaches one thing to another,” etc.] and unable to sustain his own genius, while saying one thing entangles himself through another. When he had conceived these matters with excessive ardor of mind, he loaded himself with burdens too great; and when he could not proceed in this way, he was cast down there in a great fall, [Note: [Col. 0725C] The manuscripts read: “so that his fall prepared, through certain seductions, some enticements to his teaching,” etc.] so that his fall prepared doctrines through certain foolish seductions, and he led many from the right road onto another path. His poison, like the tinkling voices and songs of the Sirens, was able to kill many. In good things he was better than all; in evil things, worse. Some things, however, were sown by him beside the way; yet many testify that some of his worst disciples published many poisonous works under his name. [Note: [Col. 0725C] The manuscripts read: “Nevertheless, many of his disciples, the worst of them, published many poisonous works,” etc.]

IV. Eusebius of Caesarea, the key to the Scriptures and guardian of the New Testament, is shown by the Greeks to be greater than many in literary composition. He wrote the Canons of the four Gospels and eleven [another reading: fifteen] books of Ecclesiastical History, which narrate and preserve the New Testament, and the *Chronicon*, that is, a summary of times. These three works are outstanding witnesses to his writings, and we have never found anyone who could imitate all his traces above everything else. [Note: [Col. 0725C] The manuscripts read: “and all his traces, which he could have repeated,” etc.]

V. The presbyter Heliodorus, looking upon a vast house through a small opening, trying its closed doors but possessing no keys, scarcely managed to bring a few things into the light; yet what he could narrate, he narrated faithfully.

VI. The brother Ambrose, carried away on the wing of the depths and flying through the air, seems to pluck fruit from on high for as long as he penetrates into the deep. All his judgments are firm pillars of the faith of the Church and of every virtue.

964 VII. Dardanus, seizing upon many questions through the cunning of his mind, and not breaking the shell around the kernel, confidently speaks many impossible things about the Scriptures.

VIII. Paulinus thought it appropriate to become a teacher, although he had not previously been a disciple, and attempted to make fruit arise and be produced without a root. Therefore his writings require neither a writer nor paper.

IX. Pelagius, concerning whom there is talk among the faithful, and whose words have also been announced throughout almost the whole world as a serious matter of dispute for me, is admired by all the Churches as a wolf from the forest, placing a golden color over black poison; he mixed the sweet spring of the first honey with the bitterness of malice. [Note: [Col. 0726C] The manuscripts read: “a serious dispute over his words,” etc.]

X. Jovinianus, cheerful in face but harsh in heart, gave many drink from a most sweet beverage mixed with gall. Presenting contrary opinions to Christians and composing them through hatred of opportunities, he continually afflicts and torments me—even though I am laborious in all things—with endless questions.

XI. Julius [another reading: Julianus] Africanus, whose trace all the Eastern and Southern peoples diligently and unanimously investigate in the weeks of Daniel, constructed the entire span of times with every skill and in continuous discourse. No contradiction has ever been offered anywhere in the world against anything said by him.

XII. Favonius, blamed by many, attempted to thrust upon them all the most difficult matters with a harsh judgment and great force. Just as one who cannot sail against the waves of the sea or swim against the force of a torrent cannot prevail, so all that he wrote against the Holy Scriptures could not withstand them. Therefore they are like a shadow beside a man.

[Col. 0726C] Hilary, from Jerome’s *Catalogue*, chapter 100.

Damasus, from chapter 103.

Gregory of Nazianzus, from chapter 117.

He wrote to Jubaianus concerning the rebaptism of heretics, 199. Blessed Cyprian, rejecting the baptism of heretics, convened an African synod on this matter, 196. He shed his blood at Carthage, 4. What does he say about the persecution of this period? ibid. What has been said about Saint Cyprian? 891. A saying of the same man, 410. Cyprian’s letters in which Stephen is attacked, 200. His work to Quirinus, 729. The legend of Cyprian the martyr, 513.

D

Demons believe in one God and tremble, 322. [Col. 0735B] The movements of demons, 392. They are deceitful and cunning, 24. They do not wish to wound the wicked but those upright in heart, 766. The voices of demons resounded in the most ancient temple, 38. A demoniac speaks pure Syriac, although he did not know the language, 25. The islands of Dalmatia, 535. Pope Damasus, 415. By what means Danae’s chastity was overcome, 534. Daniel, while still a boy: how was he known to the people? 534. Through fasting he became terrible to lions, 340. What has been said hypothetically about Daniel, Noah, and Job? 276. The churches of Christ read Daniel according to the edition of Theodotion, 527. Darius, the wealthy king of the Medes, 534. David’s virtue of spirit was gentleness, 713. Many kings were preserved through the virtues of David their father, 767. He was abandoned for a while to his frailty, 764. He compensated for his faults with many other good qualities, ibid. In what respect was he a man of blood? 274. We owe ourselves not to the one from whom we are born but to the one from whom we are reborn, 336. See *To be*. Those who deceive themselves, 338. Decius and Valerian, persecutors of Christians, 3. [Col. 0735C] They wished to slaughter souls, not bodies, ibid. Decurions censured, 24. To live amid luxuries and not be held by the vices of luxury is impossible, 338. Those who enjoy the prosperity and luxuries of this age should not be considered blessed, 335. Sins committed through ignorance, 730. For these the Church orders sacrifices to be offered, ibid. and 741. See *Ignorance*, *Sin*, *Crime*. Demetrianus: whose student was he? 919. Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, 875. He was offended by Origen’s ordination, 893. He is attacked by Origen, 509. Demetrius, a Jewish writer against the Gentiles, 879. Demosthenes: how great was his love of study? 473. Demosthenes’ speech on behalf of Ctesiphon, translated by Tullius, 520. Demosthenes and Aeschines hurl thunderbolts against each other, 471. Demotion, chief of the Areopagites, 307. His virgin daughter killed herself, ibid. What does one denarius signify? 374. Some people customarily deny with their eyes closed what they do not wish to believe happened, 193. Kissing as an act of veneration among the Hebrews, 475. [Col. 0735D] The Derbices’ customs regarding elderly parents, 335. What does Desiderius ask of Jerome? 389. We must not despair, even if we sin after baptism, 323. Heretics invented one good God and another just God, 152. The malice of detractors, 524. God alone is immortal, 749. He alone is truthful; every human being is a liar, 799. God alone is without sin, 771. He alone is wise, 750. All things are governed by his will, 698. Everything depends upon the judgment of him who is Creator of all, 751. All things are possible for God, 720. For God, to will is to have done, 427. The power of God is commended, 440. He can do whatever he wills, 783. The mercy of God: by it we are preserved, 752. He is the Creator of all, 697. He is the maker of souls and bodies alike, 497, 559. He is not the craftsman of useless things, 332. God’s works are in truth and justice, 779. All things live to God, 11. God’s foreknowledge, 477. We can hide nothing from God, 777. God’s anger is just, 747. God’s threat sometimes expresses mercy, 714. In comparison with God, no creature can be perfect, 710. No one saw God in this age, 797. God’s will is one thing, indulgence another, 298. God’s will [Col. 0736A] must not be scrutinized but endured with thanksgiving, 766. We cannot know God’s judgments and, by our own decision, prejudge his sentence, 284. Why did he wish victims to be offered to him? 776. He commanded them not by his will but in comparison with idols, ibid. He permits impieties to be committed in order to punish sins, 780. How will God be all in all? 713. When is the likeness of God and true contemplation promised? 796. He does not dwell equally in everyone, 376. He always desires greater things in us, ibid. How are we one in him? 378. God’s words are in themselves exceedingly sweet, 771. Not to comply with them is sin, 770. What does he crown in us? 787. At the fullness of times he recapitulated all things, 267. God judges present things, not future ones, 788. He does not condemn someone in advance because he knows that person will become such as later to displease him, ibid. His goodness is so great that he chooses one whom he knows will become evil, ibid. The substance of the Lord must be guarded, 563. The book of Deuteronomy is an enumeration of past events, 735. Dexter asked Jerome for a catalogue of ecclesiastical authors, 816. Dexter, 825. The devil and his daughters are insatiable, 282. He spoke about some matters from the Scriptures, 242. Nothing is safe with him; his ambushes are indescribable, 44. He never reveals himself openly, 43. [Col. 0736B] He even punishes beasts of burden for the sake of human beings, 25. Christ’s antidote against the poisons of the devil, 242. The snares of dialecticians, 206. Diana remained a virgin, 307. The temple of Diana was burned, 223. What is reported about the authority for this burning? ibid. The priests of Taurian Diana and of Vesta, 307. What does Dicaearchus report in his books of Antiquities? 342. A notable saying of a noble Roman, 317. The history and praises of Dido, 310. Didymus is praised, 106. His book on the Holy Spirit, 107 and following. Jerome’s teacher at Alexandria, 103. He was a defender of Origen, 462, 507. In the Trinity he is Catholic, ibid. He published a book on the Holy Spirit, which Jerome translated, ibid. In it some things are praised and others condemned, 556. In style and doctrine he differs from Apollinarius, 543. Didymus’s three books on Hosea, 558. He explains and expounds the Jewish translation, 528. Didymus’s book to Rufinus, ibid. Didymus, 469. Six days are assigned to the labor of this age, 366. Digamy is subordinate to a first marriage, 262. What has been said about it? ibid. and following. It is rejected by many birds, 285. A digamist cannot be elected to the clergy, 263. [Col. 0736C] The joining and inequality of fingers, 240. The order of dignities among human beings differs according to the variety of labor, 480. Delay is not a loss when victory becomes more certain through delay, 240. A dilemma produced by the executioner’s workshop and by meditation, 535. A framer of dilemmas falling into a great abyss of blasphemies, 787. Those whom we call diligent, 481. Excessive diligence arouses suspicions, 409. Diocletian, 915. Diodorus the Socratic is said to have had daughters of exceptional chastity, 309. The dispute between Diodorus and Chrysippus, 702. In what was Diogenes famous? 344, 345. Why did he trample on Plato’s couches with muddy feet? 338. Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, 867. Dionysius, a presbyter of Rome and later its bishop, 895. Dionysius, bishop of Diospolis, 452. Dionysius’s four volumes against Sabellius, 508. He slips into Arian doctrine, ibid. He is defended, ibid. [Col. 0736D] Dioscorides, 332. No disciple can exist before hearing a teacher preach, 186. It is absurd for a disciple who goes to a teacher to be an expert before being taught, 184. The adversary is defeated, the disciple is taught, 185. Christ had few disciples, the Pharisees many: what is concluded from this? 380. A disciple imitating the vices of his teacher, 556. Some remain uneducated wise men because they refuse to learn what they do not know, 473. The order and method of disputation, 699. In ecclesiastical debate, the ravings of old women’s quarrels should be avoided, 552. No Catholic, in disputing with sectarians, has charged the person against whom he argues with disgrace, 569. Disagreement contains something of human frailty, 763. Things suitable for the dissolute, 338. Where there is the property of individuals, there is difference on the other side, 249. The wretched condition of the rich, 13. Why are riches sought, and what is their use? 341. Christian teachers ought to bark on behalf of Christ, 569. [Col. 0737A] In discussing doctrines and questions, one must seek not the person but the case, 781. The doctrine of the Gentiles, and partly Platonic, 424. In what sense is Christ called the Lordly Man? 157. The emperor Domitian, 280. He banished John the Evangelist, ibid. Domitian’s persecution, 845. He was killed, and his acts were rescinded by the Senate, ibid. What did Domnion indicate to Jerome? 634. Domninus turned toward the Jews, 883. Donatus: what does he accuse Christians of? 929. Africa and Numidia were deceived by his persuasion, ibid. The commentaries of Donatus, Jerome’s teacher, 472. The adverbs “until” and “up to” in Helvidius’ sense, 210. Jerome expounds the same, ibid. Christ’s gifts are diverse, 250. Bodily and spiritual endowments are found in some people in one form and in others in another, 720. Dositheus, leader of the Samaritans, rejected the Prophets, 197. Bishop Dracontius: where was he in exile? 30. Hilarion visited him, ibid. Duilius was the first at Rome to triumph in a naval battle, 312. What is said about him? ibid. [Col. 0737B] Simulated sweetness conceals the worst poison, 463.

E
Ebion, the successor of Cerinthus, rejected the Gospels, 197. He is attacked by ancient writers, 225. Ebion, 200. The doctrine of the Ebionites, 843. Ebiymius, or Ebiymium, an Egyptian or Coptic word, the name of a place, or of the pulpit from which he who led the singing presided, 58. Segments of ivory are used in various remedies, 331. Edessa, 43. The Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh Editions, 893. Where and by whom the Fifth Edition was discovered, ibid. Editions of the Jewish translators were purchased at great expense, 528. The Fathers expounded these, ibid. See Versions. Edom is interpreted either as “earthly” or “bloody,” 442.

The universal Church ought not to be situated in a corner, 186. In the body of the Church, Christ is the head, 713. When certain members resist, the body is not subject to the head, ibid. It was founded upon Peter as upon a solid mass, 707. It is shaken neither by the force of a river nor by any storm, ibid. The differing chambers of Noah’s Ark prefigured the variety of the Church, 267. Just as the Ark contained every kind of animal, so the Church contains people of every nation and character, 195. The Church’s chief elements, 885. Lighter commandments were given to the Church while it was still inexperienced, 290. In the Church of God there are simplicity and pure confession, 192. In the one body of the Church there are different members, 711. The Church became greater in wealth but smaller in virtues, 41. One must remain in that Church which was founded by the Apostles and continues to this day, 201. The orders of the Church, 369. Its grades, 195. The Church of those who believed in Christ was such as monks now strive to be, 847. It is endangered in the world, 195. What adversaries it has, 398. What should one think about the whole Church? 194, 195. The Church has always had very great and learned men, 823. The white garment of ecclesiastics, 727. The Church, consisting of many grades, ends with presbyters and bishops, 195.

Ecclesiastes, the book, supplies much concerning the nature of things, 558. There is no ambiguity concerning it, 731.

Almsgiving. Not everyone who stretches out a hand to the poor immediately lends to God, 188. In almsgiving we seek empty glory, 754. Rare is the person who does not give from such a motive, ibid. The practice of almsgiving among Hebrews and Christians, 399. To whom it should chiefly be given, ibid. No one gives more generously than the person who keeps nothing for himself, 21.

There are four elements from which all things are composed, 431. At Eleusis it was customary to abstain from certain foods, 344. The three commandments in the temple of Eleusis, ibid. Eleutherius, Anicetus’s deacon and later bishop of Rome, 863.

Elias means “strong of the Lord,” 408. Elias’s virtue was zeal, 713. Elias and Elisha are foolishly placed in a catalogue of husbands, 275. Elias was immortal before he died, 348. What did he merit by fasting? 349. He was taken up in the flesh, 437. Elias and Enoch have not yet died, 794. They remain in the same age in which they were taken up, 440. He was not free from fault, 767.

Elisha’s double spirit, 370. Elisabeth and Zacharias are inferior in holiness to blessed Mary, 712.

The most common style of expression, 567. The force and precision of eloquence, 420. He carries his name into eternity, 319. Eloquence varied with Attic refinement, 501.

Elusa, a semi-barbarous city, 26. Emmaus was called Nicopolis, 903.

To buy and to acquire: how they differ, 537. Empedocles, 565, 567. His doctrine, 331. The Encratites: whence they came, 869. Their error, 274.

Enoch: why was he translated? 266. He was translated in the flesh, 437. Enoch and Elias have not yet died, 794. They are also inhabitants of paradise, 437. What food do they eat? ibid. The apocryphal Book of Enoch, 833. The Apostle Judas took testimony from it, ibid.

The writings of Saint Ephraem were read in certain churches, 943. He is praised, ibid.

Epicurus, an advocate of pleasure, turns people away from marriage, 317. What does he teach about foods? 340. Epicurus’s condemned opinion, 333. Luxury, 387. Epicurus, 241, 558. The Epicureans despise logic, 487.

Epidauros, a town of Dalmatia, 35. What does it preach to this day? 36.

Epiphanius, an outstanding priest of the Church, 416. He knew five languages, 537. He is called the father of bishops and a remnant of ancient holiness, 419. The patience of Epiphanius, 420. His prudence, 450. His humility and charity toward John of Jerusalem, 414. In proving the words of John of Jerusalem, Epiphanius clears himself of suspicion of heresy, 418. The people’s veneration for Epiphanius, ibid. He is praised, 411. He came to Jerusalem, 561. Jerome’s letters to him, ibid. Where he received Jerome, 551. Epiphanius, speaking against Origen, is mocked by some, 417. Epiphanius injured by Rufinus, 552. What is he accused of? 504. Letters against Epiphanius, 545. He wrote praises of Hilarion, 13. Some words of Epiphanius are quoted, 553. One of his letters was stolen, ibid. Epiphanius was read both for his subject matter and for his words, 941. Several of his letters: to whom they were written, 434. Epiphanius’s letters to Siricius, 421. Against Origen, 468.

God wishes bishops and presbyters to be such as Paul teaches, 717. They are not therefore to be rejected if in certain respects they are blameworthy, 718 and following. Virtue alone makes bishops and presbyters blessed, not rank, 293. And what is fitting? 718 and following. It belongs to the bishop to lay hands on those who have been baptized, 181. Why is such laying on of hands reserved to him? ibid. It is reserved more for the honor of the priesthood than as a matter of necessity, ibid. The bishop is the light of the Church, 175. He is the seasoning of the whole world and of his own Church, ibid. He is appointed in the Church to restrain the people from error, 176. The zeal and love of peoples for bishops, even to the point of almost killing those who depose them, 192. A bishop should not shine only for himself but benefit everyone, 176. It does not benefit him to enjoy the consciousness of his virtues unless he can instruct the people entrusted to him, 292. What his chastity ought to be, ibid. It is not enough for a bishop to possess chastity of his own unless he adorns the chastity of his sons, companions, and ministers, 718. He should fear incurring the punishment of Heli the priest, ibid. There is no bishop, or scarcely one, who possesses everything he is taught to possess, 719. If one or two items from the catalogue of virtues are lacking in him, he will not therefore lose the title of “just,” ibid. If a bishop falls, he obtains pardon with difficulty, 175. Then he is of no benefit to the people, 176. Bishop, presbyter, and deacon are not names of merits but of offices, 292. What is fitting for them, ibid. What bishop, conscious of his innocence, can bear to be deposed? 192. Jerome does not judge the decisions of bishops, nor does he wish their decrees rescinded, 546. When he is called a disciple of Antichrist, 176. African bishops gathered on ecclesiastical matters, 417. Exiles return to their churches through Julian’s clemency, 191. In receiving a bishop returning from heresy, the entire province over which he presides is joined to the Church, 174. Bishops who do not ordain deacons unless they have first taken wives, 388. Deceived, 189 and following.

The Epistle to the Hebrews: to whom it is believed to belong, 837. It was not held among the Romans, 899. Paul’s Epistle to the Laodiceans, rejected by everyone, 839. The letters of Paul to Seneca and of Seneca to Paul, 851. Biblical letters, 754.

The abundance of banquets breaks the body and the soul, 341. Wars and the destruction of cities are stirred up by the delights of banquets, 340.

The Circus horses were fed in order to celebrate the fortunate rape of the Sabine women, 22. In the Syrian desert: what Jerome saw, 5. The desert of Chalcis, 42. Erichthonius was generated from the mere heat of lust, 247. Eriphyle: why did she betray her husband? 317.

There is no one who is not caught by error, 748. It is human nature to defend one’s error, 191. How great is the error among the people when the person teaching them is himself in error, 176.

Esau degenerated: why? 428. Ezra, restorer of the Pentateuch, 212. An apocryphal book is presented under Ezra’s name, 393.

To be able to be is one thing; to be is another, 701. Everything that is said—whether “to be” or “not to be”—must be reckoned among good or evil things, 699.

The life of the Essenes, 343. How Esther corrected Artaxerxes’ decree, 474.

The Etesian winds, 551. Eubulus wrote a history of Mithras, 344.

The Eucharistic Body of the Lord in the Church, 191. Bishops touched it, 173. It was administered to the people from an elevated place, ibid. Reception of Christ’s body, 800. The pure ought to receive it, 269. We receive it equally, although it is different according to the merits of those who receive it, 364. The first communion of Christ’s Body after baptism, 800. The Lord’s Eucharist must be received with caution, 734.

Eunomius, 508. He is the author of a heresy against relics, 395. His followers do not enter the basilicas of the Apostles and martyrs, and they regard his books as more authoritative than the Gospels, 395. Eunomius’s doctrine concerning Christ, 512. His doctrine, 507. The heresy of the Eunomian “atheist” [ἀθέου], 416. The heresy of the Eunomians and Arians possessed the whole East, 411.

Those eunuchs please him whom not necessity but choice has castrated, 257. Who are the type of voluntary eunuchs? ibid. The eunuch of Queen Candace, because of the strength of his faith, obtained the name of “man,” ibid.

Euphorbus is said to have been born again, 387. Euphranor, 911. What did the Jew Eupolemus write? 879. What does Euripides report? 344. Euripides’ tragedies are curses against women, 317. Europe and Asia fought in a ten-year war, ibid.

Eusebius, the consul, 188. Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, 192. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, 192. He is called their leader, 505. He showed that Origen had belonged to the Arian treachery, ibid. He wrote six books in defense of Origen, 464, 541. He wrote the life of the martyr Pamphilus, 465. He explains and expounds the translation of the Jews, 528. He wrote against Porphyry, 527. Eusebius’s books containing open blasphemy concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit, 418. What did he say in order to approve what he had read? 469. He wrote in defense of Origen, 903. He concedes his opinions, 508. Which codices did Eusebius attribute to Origen? 523. What did Eusebius charge against the martyr Methodius? 466. Where he refutes the disputation of Peter and Apion, 853. Eusebius praised by Jerome, and his works translated, 466. The ten books of Eusebius Pamphilus’s Ecclesiastical History were of assistance to Jerome, 821.

Eusebius of Cremona, 554, 561. He was sent to the West, 554. What the letter of Eusebius contains, 418. A monk stole the letter from Eusebius’s chamber, 534. The same Eusebius is defended, ibid. Eusebius of Vercelli returns from exile to Italy, 191. Eusebius of Vercelli, 194. Eusebius of Emesa, 927.

Children are falsely attributed to Eustathius. 569. Where he was in exile and where he was buried, 923. Eustathius of Sebaste, 927. Eutychius, 411. Euzoius, a deacon and later, under Theodosius, bishop of Antioch, 192.

Eve, a type of the Church, 427. The impious opinion of Evagrius the Iberite, 693.

The Gospel did not exist before Christ’s cross, 277. It was consecrated by his passion and blood, ibid. It is preferred to the Law, 283. And why it ought to be preferred, 729. The grace of the Gospel succeeded because no one could be justified in the Law, 797. To live under the Law is one thing, and under the Gospel another, 274. There is shadow in the Law, truth in the Gospel, 728. In the Law there is the wisdom of the flesh; in the Gospel, the wisdom of the Spirit, 283. We served Adam under the Law; let us serve Christ in the Gospel, 298. If ignorance is condemned under the Law, how much more conscience under the Gospel? 734.

The heretics who tore the Gospels apart, 197. These words of the Gospel are explained: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle,” etc., 703. What is written at the end of the Gospel according to Mark in the Greek codices? 758. What is found in the Greek and Latin texts of Luke? 760.

The Gospel according to the Hebrews, written in the Chaldean-Syriac language but in Hebrew letters, 782. The Nazarenes use it, and some passages from it are quoted, ibid. It is kept in the Caesarean library, ibid. Jerome translated the Hebrew Gospel into Greek and Latin, 831. Origen frequently uses it, ibid. Certain passages from it are cited, ibid.

Why are the four living creatures assigned to the Evangelists? 280. Since each must necessarily excel in certain respects, 714.

To possess complete copies of all the Scriptures requires great expense and infinite difficulty, 524. The whole world contends among itself through a threefold diversity of Scriptural copies, ibid.

The components of armies, 291, 293. The names of interpreters are discreetly omitted, 480.

Hezekiah is called the leader of God, 755. He is accused of unbelief, ibid. From where did he acquire the designation “just”? ibid.

[Col. 0740A]

F

Fabianus, bishop of the city of Rome, fell during the persecution of Decius, 895. Fabiola, 534. Fabius, bishop of the Antiochene Church, 905. The continence of Fabricius, 341. Facidia, a village of the city of Rhinocorura, 20.

To have done once what is good cannot become evil if it is done more often, 396. Everyone acts at his own peril in doing what seems right to him, 546. Whatever is false can never come into being, 721.

Fauns, 7. Felix was appointed bishop of Rome in place of Liberius, 931. The virtue of a captive woman, 45. Festus governed Judaea, 831. He succeeded Felix, 835.

The faith of the Church, 429. It is properly Christian, 254. If it does not have works, it is dead, ibid. What is perfect faith? 189. It is perfect to believe that God is from God, ibid. What zeal faith ought to have, 415. The Roman faith admits no deceptions, 542. It cannot be changed, ibid. It belongs to Catholics, 461. Its truth cannot be overthrown by empty arguments, 752. Pure faith tolerates no delay, 415. Nothing is greater than faith in the sacrament and purity of soul, 187. The house of faith is secure, 436. Perfect faith, and one difficult to find even among those who believe correctly, 187. Undoubting faith toward God is found with difficulty, ibid. If there is little faith in Peter, it is unknown in whom there may be great faith, 188. What does perfect faith do in one who prays? 189. The scrupulousness of faith, 444. Its open confession, 428. The Holy Spirit does not become an inhabitant of this temple when its bishop does not possess the true faith, 181. Faith that has been gnawed away—that is, neither sound nor whole, 415. Under the name of unity and faith, unbelief was written, 188. It is arrogance not to answer those who ask about the faith, 410. When a priest preaches the true faith, darkness is dispelled from everyone’s heart, 175. It is ridiculous to dispute about faith before believing, 184. The faith and devotion of the simple receive their reward, 394. Many things are proposed for belief under penalty of anathema, 190.

How sons and heirs become a cause of grief to their fathers, 315. Firmilianus becomes a disciple of Origen while bishop of Caesarea, 893. He who is still running is less than he who has reached the end, 797.

The letter of Flacius to Florus, 459. A few excerpts are reported from it, ibid. If we cannot endure threats, insults, and poverty, how shall we conquer the flames of Babylon? 696. Flavius the grammarian wrote about medicinal matters, 919. Flavius wrote in verse, 332. Florinus, 873.

The ant has six feet, 557. The labors of ants, 46. What is detestable about Fortunatianus, 931.

In Scripture, “brothers” is used in four ways, 220 and following. We are all brothers in two ways, 222. Nothing should be rejected from oneself so completely as the accusation of fraud and unfaithfulness, 560.

Fronto the orator, tutor of Antoninus Verus, 865. The frugality of many is praised, 342 and following. The skills by which farmers protect grain from birds, 196.

What are we commanded to flee? 255. What did Fulvia do to Cicero? 569. All future things are uncertain, especially those that have never happened, 702. There is one knowledge of future things, 444. For one who predicts the future, it makes no difference whether he announces what will happen after ten years or after a hundred, ibid.

G

Gaas means “disturbance,” 272. What does Galen, the interpreter of Hippocrates, say about athletes? 340. What does ἐν ἁπλοῖς teach? 331.

Galgala means “revelation,” 270. Gallic clothing and Gallicarii, 55. Gallienus, 907. Gaul has always abounded in brave and most eloquent men, 387. The attacks of the Gauls, 308. The river Ganges, 344.

Gaza, a city of the Gentiles where Marnas is worshiped, 19. The Gazans, enemies of God, 24. Gazanus, a disciple of Hilarion, 33. Gazanus Majomites, a paralytic, is cured, 22.

Who are assigned to the fires of Gehenna? 753. Gelasius concealed his works, 951.

A fourfold kind of human generation is assigned, 440. Human nature does not differ within this diversity, ibid. Genesis supplies much concerning the nature of things, 558. A nation between the Saxons and Alemanni, not broad but powerful, 24. The people of the Gentiles earned greatness of rewards through the difficulty of faith, 374. The greatest virtue of the Gentiles was not to seize what belonged to others, 290. The Gentile world is deceived by error concerning those whom it worships, 7. In the genus, what is true is also maintained in the species, 743. Whatever is removed from the parts must necessarily be denied of the whole, 699.

Gorgias the rhetorician: what did he write? 316. What is charged against him? ibid. Germany, now called France, 24. The three-formed Geryon, 387.

Glory. It is rare to find a faithful soul that does nothing from desire for glory, 188. It is difficult to be content with God alone as judge in works of piety, ibid. It is a mark of modesty and prudence to conceal what one hears said gloriously about oneself, 560.

The Gnostics arose from Basilides, 847. Gordian succeeded Alexander in the empire, 899. Why do philosophers and orators tear apart Gorgias of Leontium? 419. He is censured, 559. Gorgunte, 320. Gortyna, a city, 869. Gracchus, 320, 419.

Greece, rejoicing, borrowed something from the Latins through Jerome, 525.

Grace. It is indeed our part to will and to run; but for our will to be fulfilled and our running to succeed belongs to God’s mercy, 700.

Gratian, the emperor, 943. Gregory Thaumaturgus was a disciple of Origen, 905. He performed very many signs and miracles, ibid. Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome’s teacher, 943. Praise of Gregory of Nazianzus, 469. What did he explain in Greek words? 260. Gregory of Nazianzus translated by Rufinus, 486.

Many remedy their inability to restrain their appetite by vomiting, 340. The gymnosophists of India are divided into two doctrines, 344. Their abstinence, ibid. How highly they are honored, ibid. What do the gymnosophists of India teach about their leader Buddha? 309.

H

[Col. 0741C]

Whatever you have must be attributed to God’s beneficence, 700. Hadrian spent the winter at Athens, 861. Hadrian, a disciple of Hilarion, announced to him the death of Julian, 33. He is also called unfortunate: why? ibid.

The heresies of the primitive Church, 197. Two are noted, 482. Heresy is subtle and easily deceives simple souls, 183. In heresy the custom is maintained that the people hear one thing while the priests preach another, 410. There were already innumerable heresies in Jerome’s time, 380. From where had they proceeded? ibid. The Latin language has its own heresy, 381. No one should be tolerant when heresy is suspected, 409. Those who follow the Catholic faith desire and wish that heresy be condemned and people corrected, 687.
