[THE COMPLETE WORKS OF JEROME OF STRIDON.]

[Col. 0765]

PREFACE

At last, in this third volume of Jerome’s works, we undertake the revision of that class of writings whose subject matter is the exposition of the divine Scriptures. Through these writings the most holy interpreter earned for himself his distinctive honor and the title of Doctor Maximus, while the whole world joined in proclaiming his praise. For although in preparing the monuments of his other particular studies he carried off every distinction, in the science of expounding Scripture he excelled so greatly that, whereas the other achievements he shared with many, the whole of this praise, extending as far as possible, seems in a certain sense to belong peculiarly to him.

Of the nearly innumerable qualities required to sustain the full dignity of such a work, he possessed each one in abundance. And—whether anyone before him had achieved this I do not know—he added to the sum of his other attainments a knowledge of the Eastern languages, which are the original and native languages of the book, especially Hebrew and Greek; constant reading and study of the older interpreters from the Synagogue and the Church, as well as of Greek and Latin Fathers who had become distinguished through this pursuit; and the most refined discernment in selecting interpretations and facts. Equipped with so great an apparatus of disciplines, when he turned his mind to explaining the sacred Scriptures he raised this art to a level of dignity and excellence which it had either not previously reached or did not afterward surpass.

For he extracts and investigates three senses of the passage before him. In the first—the historical sense, or what is called the literal sense—he lingers longest, adapting to it various glosses of the ancient interpreters from the Hebrew, together with various opinions and interpretations of commentators. Then he undertakes the other two kinds of explanation and, led into the freer spaces of allegorical interpretation, brings forth with such abundance of material whatever his fortunate genius supplied from the hidden storehouse of his learning for moral and mystical exposition that it is astonishing that stenographers capable of writing it all down ever existed.

Although I do not deny that this study, exceedingly useful as it is, is by no means approved by fastidious men, since the holy Doctor generally conceals the names of those whose opinions he praises, and it is sometimes doubtful which of so many views of the ancient Fathers he himself prefers, yet he often dispelled this stale accusation—already directed against him in his own day—elsewhere, and especially in the Preface to Book XI of his Commentaries on Isaiah, by this outstanding argument:

“I have left it to the reader’s judgment what he should choose from the many opinions. Therefore, what we have done out of modesty in judging, and out of respect for those who would read, may perhaps displease some who desire to know not the opinions of the ancients but our own judgment. To them the answer is easy: I did not wish to accept one in such a way that I might seem to condemn the others.”

And in chapter XXII of Jeremiah:

“Wretched Grunnius, and after many years the disciples of Jovinianus and of that man, have accused and still accuse me of placing my own opinions under the names of others. I do this out of goodwill, so that I may not seem to tear anyone apart by naming him openly.”

Grunnius himself—or Rufinus—and whoever that old accuser from Jovinianus’s faction may have been, since he could not conceal that he was Jerome’s rival, condemned himself more through the charge of envy than he harmed the holy Doctor by his slander. Those more recent heterodox writers who revive that accusation perhaps write less from conviction than to display their cleverness and to indulge some unrestrained desire to criticize the ancient Fathers, from whose faith they have departed.

I say nothing of Catholics, if any of their judgments on this matter exist. They are certainly of such a kind that they detract nothing from Jerome, but rather encourage students to learn, through diligent study of ecclesiastical scholarship, how to assign each author his own opinion. This will surely contribute greatly to the benefit of sacred literature, and especially of the study of Jerome.

Saint Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus, surnamed the Theologian, are said to have devoted nearly the same kind of labor to the writings of Origen: whenever they thought that doctrines peculiar to him and differing from the opinions of others appeared, they marked them with a double X, following the practice of the Platonists, who, when reading their master, marked noteworthy passages with that character, as Laertius reports in his account of Plato. We have striven to do the same with as much diligence as possible, and the volumes that follow this one, consisting entirely of commentaries, will chiefly demonstrate the labor we have devoted to this task. For now, however, we must state what we have done in preparing this third volume, with which we begin the commentaries.

Since it is necessary to arrange and review the individual commentaries according to the order occupied by the sacred books they explain, we have nevertheless placed two short works at the beginning of the entire collection, one entitled *On Names*, the other *On the Places of Scripture*. They do not explain one or another part of Scripture, but embrace the whole of it insofar as it is the subject matter before us, and, as it were, provide an apparatus that clears the way both for understanding Scripture itself and for properly understanding Jerome’s commentaries.

The earlier book was greatly undervalued by the older editors, either because they expected little credit from a subject so unproductive, or because they did not think that their work would be appreciated by the unlearned. More recently, the author of the *Hieronymian Questions* babbled that this book, like most of Jerome’s other labors, was worthless or of very little use. Martianaeus answered this man’s extreme rashness at length in his *Apology*. It could, however, have been refuted by this one outstanding argument: even if, as he claims, some etymologies are forced, others rather absurd, and others contrary to the character of the language, this cannot be charged against Jerome, who disclaims the fault in his Preface and, while faithfully translating the Greek exemplar as he ought, repeatedly warned his reader not to be deceived by any false interpretation of a name.

On the contrary, we owe him great gratitude for translating this book into Latin and frequently correcting it. Almost alone among such works, it was used first by the Greeks and later by nearly all the Latin commentators to derive allegorical meanings from the significance of names; indeed, the whole method of their allegorical interpretation, and so much of the memory of antiquity, is contained in it.

The work that follows, *On the Places of Palestine*, was translated into Latin by Jerome from the Greek of Eusebius, which we reproduce alongside it. I say nothing further about its outstanding quality, which the same reviler rashly diminished. Perhaps our revision of this short work will give him cause to regret having mocked the great Jerome’s statements with such arrogance. In the notes we have omitted no place that he attacked without freeing it from slander. Whenever the opportunity arose, we either restored Jerome’s reading and interpretation where the carelessness of scribes had corrupted them, or defended them against unjust criticism.

I have also enjoyed better fortune than any previous editor of this book. While examining the shelves of the Vatican Library with the greatest diligence I could command, I discovered, among other materials relevant to my purpose, a handwritten exemplar of the Eusebian text that was sufficiently ancient and, above all, of excellent quality—of the sort which learned men had complained did not exist.

Until now, only three manuscript copies of this short work had become known. Bonfrerius published the first from the Royal Library of Paris, and Martianaeus revised it. The second is preserved by the University of Oxford. The third is said to have been transferred from the Vossian Library at Leiden to the public collection of that university by its curators. Rhenferdius laments that no one has yet been granted access to inspect the latter; and those responsible for the Oxford library do not deny that its copy was made from the Paris manuscript a few years ago.

Thus the editions produced until now derive from a single royal exemplar. It is scarcely possible to say how many errors it contains, how badly it has been mutilated and dislocated, and in how many other ways it has been treated most deplorably. By contrast, the copy I was fortunate enough to discover, although not entirely free from every defect, is both much older—dating from before the tenth century—and of far superior quality. With its help, so many previously corrupt readings are restored and so many lacunae supplied that the complete text of Eusebius seems now to be appearing for the first time.

This manuscript once belonged to the celebrated Cardinal Sirleto. It now bears the number 1456 among the Vatican manuscripts, and contains much else relevant to our purpose, which we discuss in its proper place in the *Admonition to the Greek Appendix*.

Next after this universal apparatus come the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, a treasury of Jewish traditions and more deeply hidden learning. The holy Father undertook similar work on the other books of Scripture. But, as we showed in the General Preface, he either never completed what he had drafted for the rough framework of those works, or—what seems more likely—changed his plan and, when later composing his commentaries, made use of those threads which he had hastily collected; or finally, whatever that work may have been, he kept it within the walls of his household and did not permit it to be exposed to the honor of publication.

Certainly, although during the period when he was preparing these *Questions* he often mentions them, especially in the book *On the Places*, when several [Col. 0769] years later he himself listed his works in his *Catalogue*, apart from the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* that survive, he mentions no other *Hebrew Questions*. Thus he clearly indicates that no others were included in the catalogue of his books.

From here, after a great intervening gap, we proceed to the *Commentaries on Ecclesiastes*, which the author himself seems to have valued highly, since he often appeals to them in order to defend his integrity against the accusations of Rufinus. Next come two homilies on the *Song of Songs*, which he rendered into Latin from the Greek of Origen, attracted by the supreme elegance of that work, so that he did not hesitate to say that although Origen had surpassed everyone in his other books, in the *Song of Songs* he had surpassed himself.

These works, then, which occupy what may be called the first part of this volume, are genuine monuments of the holy Doctor. With the help of manuscripts and printed books, I have taken care to cleanse them of countless and exceedingly shameful errors and, insofar as possible, restore them to their former purity.

It remains for me to indicate the year to which each work should be assigned. I shall begin with the homilies on the *Song of Songs*, which are separated from the others by the longest interval. Since they are listed in the *Catalogue* immediately before the book *Against Helvidius* and are addressed to Damasus, bishop of Rome, it is easy to understand that they must be assigned to the year 383. For Jerome came to Rome only toward the end of the preceding year, and, since he wrote against Helvidius relatively late, he did not pass beyond the final part of the year 383, as we have shown in the *Admonition* prefixed to that book.

He lists the remaining four books immediately after his revision of the commentaries on Paul’s Epistles to the Galatians, Ephesians, Titus, and Philemon, in this order and sequence, in the *Catalogue*: “Commentaries on Ecclesiastes. One book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis. One book on the Places. One book of Hebrew Names.”

From this we may first understand from the author himself what chronological relation these works have to one another; for, as I believe, he considered no principle other than chronological order when listing his writings. The particular year to be assigned to each is shown by other testimony of his and by the sequence of events themselves.

It is clear from the Preface to the work itself that the holy Doctor illustrated Ecclesiastes with commentaries almost five years after, while living in Rome, he had read it to Saint Blaesilla in order to urge her to despise this age. That the year 383 is indicated here, when Blaesilla had not yet entirely renounced the world, is evident. If nearly five years are added to that date, one arrives at the year 388, which we assign to these works.

That he composed the *Hebrew Questions*, the books *On the Places*, and *On the Names* at the same time is established by the Prefaces to those books, in which one or another of them is mentioned. That they all belong to the same year, 388, may be clearly understood from another Preface to Origen’s Homilies on Luke. There is no doubt that Jerome translated these homilies into Latin in that very year; there he states that, while devoting himself to their translation, he set aside the book of Hebrew Questions for a short time.

The sequence of the books that follow in the *Catalogue*, and especially the translation of Didymus’s short work, which we assign to the following year, also establishes the matter beyond doubt.

We need not say much in advance about the Appendix that we attach to this volume in two parts, one consisting of Greek, the other of Latin συντάγματα, that is, collections. The critical ἀκρίβεια, or exactness, which rules in all arts and disciplines, and exercises a singular and necessary authority in this kind of ancient monument, will to some extent relieve us of the burden through the *Admonitions* prefixed to those short works.

We must more particularly excuse the length of this Appendix, lest we be accused of burdening Jerome with works belonging to others in order to fill out the size of the volume. For, except for a few pages, we have added nothing new in the case of writings not previously counted among Jerome’s works. Nor was it permissible in any way to diminish the old editions, especially the Benedictine one; a lover of learning would rightly have regretted any such omission.

Finally, these very short works are of a character that brings them as close as possible to the genuine writings of our Jerome, and they could conveniently have been transferred nowhere else. They are also so fruitful that I have been persuaded—partly by my own experience, partly by the judgment and example of other editors—that considerable and varied benefit may come from them to Christian and literary studies.

Now that I have explained what it was necessary to say beforehand to the reader, I would fail in every duty of courtesy unless I openly and eternally acknowledged myself indebted in spirit to so many learned men, both in this Italy and abroad, men of integrity and far removed from every suspicion of flattery, and joined to me by no bond of nationality or favor, who have supported this labor of mine not only with the weightiest testimonies, [Col. 0771] but also with published booklets.

I would name and praise them, and could thereby adorn the front of the book, if that did not seem to savor of vainglory. I would rather have these things done by others than by myself. This is what I wish and request: if any substantial gratitude for my labor is later to come to me, let it be owed to those by whose favor I was encouraged and for whose sake I shall pursue the work, with increasing enthusiasm, to its completion.

For the sake of honor, however, I shall name one man: the most illustrious Francesco Musellius, to whom those devoted to Jerome’s glory owe a very great debt. Just as he formerly encouraged me to undertake this edition, so now he is my most generous assistant in bringing it to completion as quickly as possible.

[Col. 0771]

THE BOOK OF THE HEBREW NAMES OF SAINT EUSEBIUS JEROME, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON. (C)

PREFACE

[Col. 0771A] 1–2 Philo, the most eloquent man among the Jews, is also attested by Origen to have published a book of Hebrew Names and to have placed their etymologies alongside them in alphabetical order. Since it is commonly available among the Greeks and has filled the libraries of the world [Note: [Col. 0771B] Our manuscript, which we keep at home, is of respectable antiquity and quality; here it reads *pro nostri*.], it was my purpose to translate it into Latin.

But I found the copies so discordant among themselves and the order so confused that I judged it better to remain silent than to write something deserving of criticism.

Therefore, at the urging of the brothers Lupulianus and Valerianus [Note: “Of the brothers Lupulianus.” The printed editions read *Lupuli*; several manuscripts have *Lupiniani*. The Colbert manuscript no. 4354 has *Lupiliani*. The Vatican manuscript 341, however, has *Lupuliani*, as we have printed it. Lupulianus and Valerianus were, as far as conjecture permits us to determine, among the brothers in whose community Jerome expounded the Psalms and other sacred books every day. MARTIAN.]—who think that I have made some progress in knowledge of the Hebrew language—and moved by the usefulness of the undertaking [Note: “Moved by usefulness.” Two or three manuscripts read “moved by novelty.” MARTIAN.], I went through the individual books of Scripture in order. Restoring an old building through new care, I believe I have done something that even the Greeks may desire.

Moreover, I give this warning in the Preface: if anything has been omitted here, the reader should know that it has been reserved for another work. For I now have in hand the books of the *Hebrew Questions*, a new work and, up to the present time, unheard of among both Greeks and Latins [Note: I would prefer *temporum* (“of times”) to *locorum* (“of places”), unless a word has fallen out of the context between them; the somewhat impeded wording itself suggests this possibility. Perhaps he had mentioned the book *On the Places*, which he had long ago translated into Latin from Eusebius, and repeats it in the third place after this verse.].

3–4 Not that I am arrogantly exalting my own diligence [Note: Taken from Sallust, *Jugurtha* 4: “Lest anyone think, through arrogance, that I am praising and exalting my own diligence.”], but, conscious of the labor involved, I summon those who are ignorant to read it. If anyone wishes to possess both that work and the present volume, as well as the book *On the Places*, which I shall publish [Note: Our manuscript has the reading printed in the text; we have placed it in the margin of the book.], let him pay little attention to the belching and nausea of the Jews.

And lest, when the building had been completed, the final touch should seem to be lacking, I have interpreted the words and names of the New Testament, wishing in part to imitate Origen [Note: “Whom after the Apostles …” Rufinus uses this praise against Jerome in his *Invective*, where he repeatedly accuses the holy Doctor of inconsistency and vanity. Accordingly, certain ancient writers, wishing to free Jerome from the reputation of this inconsistency, want the passage to be read as follows: “whom, according to the opinion of some, after the Apostles …” As though Jerome had not written this from his own judgment, but had called Origen a teacher of the churches according to the opinion of others. But that this reading is corrupt is clearly demonstrated by Jerome’s own defensive replies, in the Colbert manuscript 2852 and a few others. For he says in his Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus: “It will not harm me if I say: Although Origen surpassed everyone in his other books, in the *Song of Songs* he surpassed himself. Nor will I fear the judgment by which, when I was once a young man, I called him a Teacher of the Churches.” He did not fear this judgment because in Origen he was then praising diligence and study of the Scriptures, not opinions concerning doctrine. See Jerome’s *Apology against Rufinus*. MARTIAN.] whom, after the Apostles, no one but an ignorant man will deny to have been a teacher of the churches. [Note: Our manuscript has *in instanti negat* (“denies immediately”). We learn from the books of the *Invectives* how much envy Rufinus stirred up against the holy Doctor through this testimony.]

Among the other splendid monuments of his genius, he also labored at this task: what Philo had omitted as a Jew, Origen, as a Christian, completed.

THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0773]

[Col. 0773A] Not immediately, whenever names are set down from the letter A—called ALEPH () among the Hebrews—should it be thought that the name begins with that letter alone. For sometimes they begin from the letters AIN (), often from HE (), and sometimes from HETH (), which alter their aspirated sounds and pronunciations.

It must therefore be understood that both in Genesis and in the other books, [Col. 0774A] wherever a name begins with a vowel, among the Hebrews it begins with different letters, as we said above. But because among us there is not such a diversity of sounds [Perhaps: vowel sounds], we are content with a simple pronunciation. Hence it happens that the same names, which are not written alike among them, appear to us to vary in translation.

THE OLD TESTAMENT

ON GENESIS

[Col. 0773]

A.

Aethiopia [Note: [Col. 0773B] “Aethiopia.” Thus it is read in the old codex 4951 of the Colbert Library. Concerning these Greek or Latin names, rather absurdly listed among the Hebrew ones, Saint Jerome himself warned us below, under the word “Puteoli,” occurring in the Acts of the Apostles: “I think it is clear to the reader how violently all these Greek or Latin names have been interpreted according to the Hebrew language.” Earlier, concerning the name “Erastus,” he says: “Erastus, my brother seeing”—a rather absurdly contrived interpretation of the name. Thus, if you attribute such violently derived etymologies and other absurdities to Jerome as their author, you will be an unfair evaluator of the facts and an unjust judge of this outstanding Doctor.

Now, if you wish to interpret the name “Aethiopia” as though it were Hebrew, understand it as a constructed form from two [unprinted Hebrew] elements; for from these two words a form can be made and, according to the custom of the ancients, read as Aethiopa or Aethiopia. Thus contrived, it signifies darkness or gloom. The name “Egypt” should be understood similarly; in the other column it is read with the interpretation “tribulation constricting.” For it seems to have been constructed according to the Hebrew language from similar [unprinted Hebrew] words, from which Egypt, or Αἴγυπτος, may be formed, with the meaning “tribulation crushing and constricting.” Nothing, however, prevents the compiler of such word-formations from having looked to their original Hebrew source, namely the names Cush and Mizraim, according to which we may interpret Cush as “the gloom of burning” and Mizraim as “narrowness” and “tribulation.” Let the reader choose whatever he wishes; and if he proposes something else, we shall readily accept better explanations. MARTIAN.

The reader should be warned at once, at the interpretation of the first word, that some origins of Hebrew names of this sort are obscure, rather absurd, or false; Jerome himself occasionally observes that some have been violently interpreted according to the Hebrew language. Nevertheless, when Latin Fathers eagerly drew etymologies from this book, it is scarcely possible to say how greatly these very forced interpretations assist in properly understanding their allusions and allegories. As for the proposed interpretation of “Aethiopia,” Origen’s lexicon has it otherwise: Αἰθιοπία, ταπείνωσις—“Aethiopia, humility.” Since Jerome perhaps considered this less satisfactory, he substituted the interpretation current among the Latins, deriving the name from Aethiops himself, which means “black-faced.” In our manuscript the words “the Latins interpret” are not added, but only “darkness or gloom.” In any case, understand that we have not undertaken to explain the rationale of every etymology—for that would require enormous books—but only of the somewhat more obscure ones that others had previously passed over.]

MARTIAN. I would rather read “pupil,” from the word from which Dison is here derived; for “nipple” is not called that in Hebrew, nor are nipple and pupil the same in Latin, as Martianus thinks. The Arabs, who borrowed much from Egypt, call the crocodile by this name; scholars show that the king of Egypt also bore the name of this dragon, just as the animal itself was a type and symbol of the Egyptian kingdom. As for the etymology of the name that Jerome explains from Philo and Origen, Homily 2 on Genesis, it comes from an [unprinted Hebrew] word, σκεδαστὴς, “destroyer” or “disperser.” Others, with Josephus, wish it to mean “king” or “lord.”], scattering, or uncovering him.

Javan [Note: [Col. 0780A] “Javan, is and is not.” Javan is written in Hebrew with three letters; therefore, for it to mean “is and is not,” it must be understood as a constructed form from jes, ve, and en. These three, taken together, mean in Latin “is and is not.” But that Javan means “dove” in Syriac seems somewhat difficult because of the interpretation of the name Bar-Jona occurring in Matthew. Concerning this name Jerome says below: “Bar-Jona, son of a dove. It is Syriac and Hebrew alike. For bar means ‘son’ in Syriac, and Jona means ‘dove’ in both languages.” MARTIAN. This interpretation, “is and is not,” which seemed to certain learned men contrary to the rules of analogy, is drawn from Hebrew traditions, as Jerome himself testifies in Book 8 of his Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 27: “The Hebrews say that the Greek word Javan is interpreted ‘is and is not.’” This properly refers to secular wisdom, in which, if they find something correct, it is called “is”; if it tends in the opposite direction, “it is not.” Consult Martianaeus’s commentary at the end of the book.], is and is not, or dove—but the latter is Syriac.

Philo has διανεωγμένον καὶ πλατυσμόν, “opened and expansion”; Ammonius, ἀντίληψιν, “assistance”; Jerome also, in Questions on Genesis 30, interprets it as “conversion” and “comparison.” Josephus appears most correct of all, Antiquities, Book 1, chapter 19: he explains it as Ἀμηχάνητον, “not to be overcome by any schemes.” For Naphtalim signifies stratagems and deceits, as may be gathered from Job 5:13: βουλὴν δὲ πολύπλοκον (in Hebrew, Naphtalim) ἐξέστησεν, “he confounded the intricate counsel.”], he preserved me, or he enlarged me, or certainly he entangled me.

## O
Orech () [Note: [Col. 0782B] Orech means “length.” In place of Orech, which signifies length, the printed editions corruptly read Obeth, a name of which there is no trace in Genesis. Orech is, however, a city of the kingdom of Nimrod in the land of Shinar, called Arach in the Vulgate, from the Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text]. The Septuagint read Ὀρὲχ, Orech, at Genesis 10:10. Therefore we read Orech here in Jerome, who in the present work followed the Greek authority of the Septuagint translators. MARTIAN.], length. Ochozad, holding. Olibama, my tent in something, or the height of the tent. Odollamite, bearing witness to someone, or testimony in water. Ophim (), of the bridal chambers. Up to this point we have read with the short letter O; from here onward let us pronounce the letter long.

Ophir () [Note: [Col. 0783A] Ophir, or Uphir. In the printed books and in several manuscripts, “or Aphir.” But this is plainly an error of the ancient scribes, who, reading that the name was written with Aleph, thought Jerome had written “or Aphir,” whereas, on the authority of the manuscript copies, he wrote “or Uphir.” Aleph is quiescent in this name [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], while the following Vav is heard at the beginning of the name, whether it is read o or u: Ophir or Uphir. MARTIAN. — In our manuscript too the reading is “or Aphir,” as Martianaeus found in others and as the printed books preferred. See what the Benedictine editor himself noted.], or Uphir, which is written with the letter ALEPH, means “vain” or “without vegetation.” Ox [Note: [Col. 0783A] Ox means “willing.” The name is altered in many different ways in Greek and Latin copies, for it is the Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], Hus. The Septuagint translators read ᾧς, Hos, or Os, at Genesis 36:28; and Οὒς, Ous, or Us, at Genesis 22:21. The Latins therefore changed the name Os into Ox, since ancient scribes frequently used x for s, as in the Book of Job according to the Septuagint, where “Auxitide” occurs for “Ausitide.” The Septuagint also retain some Hebrew names written with the letter ξ, such as Βαὺξ, Baux, from the Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], Buz. One difficulty may oppose our observations: namely, the meaning of the word [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], ὧς, Os or Ox, which is translated here as “willing,” although it means “counsellor,” also in Jerome below under the entry Us. But, unless I am mistaken, Jerome had written the Greek word βουλευτήν, just as in the name Chanaan he used the Greek term σάλος, and in Agag, δῶμα, and so forth; this was entirely misunderstood by unskilled scribes, who substituted volentem, “willing,” for βουλευτήν. In Judith 8:1, the Septuagint have Ὤξ for Idex. MARTIAN. — Martianaeus rather ingeniously conjectures that, instead of volentem, “willing,” Jerome had written in Greek letters βουλευτήν, Bouleuten, or “counsellor,” as happens occasionally elsewhere. This, properly speaking, is the interpretation of the name Ox, or rather Hus or Hutz, son of Aram, Genesis 19:23. In Hebrew it is written [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], while the Septuagint rendered it in Greek as Ὧς, Hos.], willing. Omar, people, or bitter. Onan [Note: [Col. 0783B] Origen interprets it in John as “their labor”: Ὠνὰν ἐστι πόνος αὐτῶν, “Onan is their labor.” From [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], with the feminine plural suffix.], their sorrow.

## R

15 Ripheth, seeing a morsel, or seeing good things. Rhodii, which in Hebrew is called RODIM or Rodanim [In Hebrew Dodanim], means “those descending,” or “the uncle judging,” or “vision of judgment.” Raama (Rhegma) [Note: [Col. 0784A] Our manuscript has “Rechema, thundering, or lofty.”], thunder, or lofty. Rhooboth, inclination, or broad streets. Ragau, sick, or feeding. Raphaim, giants. Rebecca [Note: [Col. 0784A] It may be derived from [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], or [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], which means “to be much,” “to multiply,” and “to wait” or “to endure.” Origen agrees in Homily 12 on Numbers: “He found Rebecca, which means patience.” Yet the etymology is drawn from too far away.], much patience, or “she received much,” or patience. Remma, or Ruma (), seeing something, or lofty. Rachel [Note: [Col. 0784A] Rachel means “sheep,” and so forth. Rachel signifies a ewe, since in Hebrew the middle letter is ח, hheth, [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], Rahhel or Rachel. But if it is formed from [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], raa, and [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], el, it means “seeing God.” Again, from [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], raa, and [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], hhalal or Chalal, “seeing the beginning.” Finally, formed from [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], rai, and [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], ra with Ain, it signifies “vision” and “crime,” or “vision of crime.” Jerome therefore understands this diversity of letters, as well as of accents in the words [Hebrew terms omitted in the supplied text]—that is, in ra with Aleph, ra with Heth, or ra with Ain. MARTIAN. — In Hebrew it is written [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], and means “ewe” or “lamb,” from the etymon [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], the millstone of a ram. Martianaeus explains how the remaining, somewhat more forced interpretations might be extracted.], sheep, or seeing the beginning, or vision of crime, or seeing God. This results from the differing accents and letters, so that names may be changed into contrary meanings.

Ruben [Note: [Col. 0784B] Origen gives the nearly more elegant passive interpretation “son who is seen,” that is, “visible.” Homily 17 on Genesis. The evident root is “he saw” and “son.”], seeing a son, or seeing [Col. 0783] in the midst. Raguel, shepherd of God, or his pasture is God. Ros, head. Ramesse (), pasture, [Note: [Col. 0784B] Here too I would prefer “of the moth,” rather than “or moth.” See what we noted concerning this name in Letter 78, On the Stations, to Fabiola, Station 1. Origen says in Homily 1 on Exodus: “Ramesses, which means the agitation of the moth: moth.”], or moth, or wickedness from the moth.

What we said at the beginning should be observed concerning vowel letters: among us there is sometimes one letter, whereas among the Hebrews it is pronounced with various sounds. The same must now be understood concerning the letter S. Among the Hebrews there are three S letters: one called SAMECH (), [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], and read simply as though written with our letter S; another, SIN (), [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], in which a certain hissing sound unlike that of our language is heard; and a third, SADE (), [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], which our ears utterly reject. Therefore, whenever the same names happen to receive different interpretations, the reason is that they have been written with different letters. What we have said here concerning Genesis must likewise be observed in all the books.

Somthonphanech [Note: [Col. 0785A] The excellent Marshall manuscript says Somthofanec, in abbreviated form; for in Hebrew we read Saphineth () phanee (), which means, etc.], is corruptly written. For in Hebrew we read saphneth () phanee (), which means “discoverer of hidden things.”

Moreover, we learned from the Egyptians that in their language it sounds like [Note: [Col. 0785A] “Saviour of the world.” Those who study the Coptic, or ancient Egyptian, language agree with Jerome; they teach that in the Coptic language “Saviour of the age” or “of the world” is called fsotem pane, for which the Septuagint corruptly read ψονθομφανήχ, psontomphanech. More will be said about this name, imposed on Joseph by Pharaoh, in the Hebrew Questions on Genesis. MARTIAN.], “saviour of the world.” Semron, seeing a name, or guardian. Sarad, that he might descend. Sephion, “the mouth of sorrow has gone forth.” Soni, my pupil, or my second. Sare (), malicious, or whistling. Syria (), lofty, or moist. Staulam, rooted.

[Col. 0785] ## T

Tabee, killing, that is, destroying. Tachos (), silent. Talam, dew. Up to this point we have read with the simple letter T; from here onward, with aspiration added, it must be read.

Thobel, or Thubal, led to mourning, or turned, or all things. Thiras, fearing, or returning, or superfluous. Thogorma, some sojourning, or interpreter. Tharsis, explorers of joy, or joy. Thara [Note: [Col. 0785A] See what we note below under Thare in the Book of Numbers. In our manuscript it is read without aspiration, Tara.], explorers of fragrance, or exploration of ascent, or pasture. Thargal (Thadal), knowing the yoke, or explorer. Thamar, palm, or bitterness, or changing. Theman, south wind, or southwest wind. Thamna, forbidding, or failing. Thamath (), a perfected part, or consummation given. Tholae (), worm, or scarlet. 18 Thesbon (Esebon), quick to understand.

Us (), counsellor. Ul (), grieving, or giving birth. Usam (), their haste.

## Z

Zemram, their song, or showing time. Zelphan (), walking mouth: from “mouth,” not from “bone,” or flowing mouth. Zabulon, their dwelling-place, or his oath, or dwelling-place [Note: [Col. 0785A] So too below, in Exodus, “dwelling-place of strength.” Nevertheless, the manuscripts of the Claromontane Glosses, in Rosweid, read “dwelling-place of beauty.”] of strength, or flow of night. # ON EXODUS

## A

Aaron, mountain of strength, or strong mountain. Aser (), blessed. Aheberim (), of the Hebrews, or of those crossing over. Afferezaei (), separated, or without a wall. Anacim, vain humility, or humble vain men, or humble men rising up, or [Note: [Col. 0785A] See Anathoth in Joshua, and Anatha in the Book of Judges.] a vain answer, or a necklace. Aod (), glorious. Amram [Note: [Col. 0785A] Bede gives more fully, in Interpretation of Hebrew Names: Amram [Col. 0785B] “lofty people,” or “the loftiness of a people,” or “exalted people,” or “the exaltation of a people.”], lofty people. Aminadab, my voluntary people. Abiu, “my father is,” or “the father himself.” Asir (), bound. Abiasaph [Note: [Col. 0785B] Previously, in the manuscript as well, it was corruptly written Abiasar. Origen, in Matthew, interprets it as πατρὸς συναγωγήν, “the gathering of the father,” without μοῦ, “my.”], gathering of my father. Amalec [Note: [Col. 0785B] Amalec, “locust people.” The printed editions absurdly read “brute people,” whereas “locust people” should be read. [Col. 0786A] [Hebrew terms omitted in the supplied text]: am means “people,” and jelec or elec means “locust.” Hence Amalec, “locust people.” MARTIAN. — Origen, Homily 19 on Numbers: Amalech means “licking the people” or “turning aside the people.” From ab, “people,” and [Arabic/Hebrew term omitted], “licked” or “licks.” The word is properly Arabic and simple. The Rabbis derive it from “stealing.” But [the other element] means “locust,” as Martian corrects it, in place of the former “brute.” This reading has long been established; for Bede too, who drew his interpretation of names from this Onomasticon of Jerome, interprets Amalec as “brute nation” or “licking people.”], locust people, or licking people. Abiud (), strength of the father, or their father. Accherubim (), “know and understand,” or multitude of knowledge. Achisamech, strengthening my brother.

Yet shortly afterward he gives “ascent of a watchtower,” from “he ascended.” Origen likewise says, Homily 5 on Exodus: “Beelsephon, ascent of a watchtower, or having a watchtower.”], having a watchtower.

Cades, holy. Chanani, merchants, or “this poor man,” or prepared, or humility. ## I

Israel [Note: [Col. 0787B] Israel means “seeing God.” Jerome by no means approves this interpretation of the name Israel, although, following the custom of ancient writers, he did not wish to change it in this book. Concerning the name Israel he discusses the matter as follows in the Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis: “But that which in the Book of Names is interpreted as Israel, ‘a man seeing God,’ worn out by the speech of nearly everyone, seems to me to have been interpreted not so much truly as forcibly. For here Israel is written with these letters: JOD, SIN, RES, ALEPH, LAMED, which means ‘prince of God,’ or ‘upright of God,’ that is, εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ, ‘most upright of God.’ But ‘a man seeing God’ is written with these letters: ALEPH, JOD, SIN, so that ‘man’ is written with three letters and called IS; ‘seeing’ with three others, RES, ALEPH, HE, and called RA. Moreover, EL consists of two letters, ALEPH and LAMED, and means ‘God’ or ‘strong.’ Although, therefore, those who translated Israel as ‘a man seeing God’ possess great authority, and the shadow of their eloquence overwhelms us, we are guided more by the authority of Scripture and of the Angel, or God, who himself called him Israel, than by any worldly eloquence.” From this the reader may see how recklessly certain ignoramuses criticize Jerome as though he were ignorant of the Hebrew language, because he placed foolish and forced etymologies in the books of Hebrew Names and Places. In such interpretations he does not put forward his own opinion, but records the opinions of others, which differ greatly from one another. MARTIAN.], means “seeing God,” or “man,” or “a mind seeing God.” And concerning this we have spoken more fully in the books [Note: [Col. 0788A] It is preferable to hear Jerome himself discussing the matter in this book, at Genesis 32:28: “But that which in the Book of Names is interpreted as Israel, ‘seeing God,’ worn out by the speech of nearly everyone, seems to me to have been interpreted not so much truly as forcibly. For here Israel is written with these letters: JOD, SIN, RES, ALEPH, LAMED, which means ‘prince of God,’ or ‘upright of God,’ that is, εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ. But ‘a man seeing God’ is written with these letters: ALEPH, JOD, SIN, so that ‘man’ is written with three letters and called IS; ‘seeing’ with three others, RES, ALEPH, HE, and called RA. Moreover, El consists of two letters, ALEPH and LAMED, and means ‘God’ or ‘strong.’ Although, therefore, those who translated Israel as ‘a man seeing God’ possess great authority, and the shadow of their eloquence overwhelms us, we are guided more by the authority of Scripture and of the Angel, or God, who himself called him Israel, than by any worldly eloquence. See what we note somewhat more fully on this passage.”] of Hebrew Questions. Jethro, superfluous of this. 21 Jebusi [Note: [Col. 0788B] Jebusi, “trodden down,” and so forth. Some manuscripts wrongly read Jesubi, and the printed editions Jesubaei, although the form is Jesubaei, which occurs in Genesis with the same interpretation: Jebusite, “trodden down,” or “their manger.” MARTIAN. — Our manuscript has Jebusei, formerly Jesubei.], shod, or my manger. Jamuel, his day is God. Jamin, right hand. Jachin, preparing. Jessaar [Note: [Col. 0788B] It seems to be the same as Issaar in Numbers 22:23, which the Vulgate calls Jassa and Jerome also calls it below from Numbers. In Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted], son of Caath, Exodus 6:18. See the Letter to Fabiola on the Stations, and Origen’s Homily 13 on Numbers. Issaar means “fulfilment of a command”: from [Hebrew term omitted], “he commanded,” and [Hebrew term omitted], “he took” or “received.”], it is midday, or southern, or my anointing, or, metaphorically, oil. [Col. 0789] Jochebed [Note: [Col. 0789A] Here the much-praised Bede seems often to exaggerate on his own authority: Jochebed, “the Lord’s germ,” or “the Lord’s preparation,” or “the Lord’s libation,” or “the Lord’s understanding.” It is forced to extract these meanings from the Hebrew word. See the Greek Lexica in the Appendix.], where is glory, or is heavy, or the glory of the Lord. Ithamar, where there is bitterness, or where there is a palm, or is bitter, or palm of the islands. Raphidim, slack hands, or health of judgment, or vision [Note: [Col. 0789B] Jerome himself rejects this interpretation in Letter 78 to Fabiola, Station 11: “Raphidim,” he says, “is the eleventh station, which I find violently interpreted in the Book of Hebrew Names: ‘It saw a sufficient mouth for them,’ or ‘the vision of the mouth of the strong’; it is better translated ‘dissolution of the strong,’ or ‘health of the strong,’ or, according to the proper usage of the Syriac language, ‘release of the hands.’” Shortly afterward he gives the reason for these interpretations from the tropological sense of the history. If, however, one approves “health of judgment,” suppose it is extracted from the words “he healed” and “he judged”; but Origen’s interpretation, “praise of judgment,” is least acceptable of all. Rhabanus also wrongly reads “defect of the mouth of the strong.” See our notes on the cited passage from the Letter to Fabiola.] of a mouth sufficient for them.

Melcho (Moloch), to the king. Salumith, recompense, or peaceful. Fath [Note: [Col. 0790B] Fath, κλίμα, and so forth. There is enormous confusion in the earlier printed books, where the following addition is even stitched into Jerome’s text: “Here end the interpretations of the Hebrew Names in the Book of Exodus, among which you can also find the Questions on Leviticus, except for four, which we have appended.” Then follows the inept name Badrifath, interpreted as κλίμα, that is, “region.” But in the more ancient manuscript copies nothing more is read than what we have published, and rightly so, since the rest is known to have been introduced by unskilled scribes, especially Badrifath, since only the word Fath in the manuscript copies is the Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted], Phath, meaning κλίμα or “region,” sometimes southern and sometimes western. The name Phath is read repeatedly in the Pentateuch. MARTIAN.], κλίμα, that is, region—for example, when we say “the northern region” or “the southern region.”

Deuel, “may they acknowledge God.” Dathan, their gift, or a sufficient gift. Dibon, sufficient for understanding, or understanding abundantly. [Col. 0793] Debongad, understanding temptation sufficiently. 27 Dafeca [Note: [Col. 0793A] “Dafeca, it clung,” etc. What has already been observed in our notes concerning the name Israel must likewise be observed here concerning *Dafeca*, from what is read in Letter 127 to Fabiola: “This name,” says Jerome, “is called among the Hebrews κροῦμα, that is, ‘a striking’ … In the *Book of Hebrew Names*, however, we translated it as ‘clinging’ and ‘release,’ which ought not to trouble the reader; nor should he think that we write inconsistently. There we published it according to the common reading, if the middle letter is written with BET; here, however, I found it written in the Hebrew volume with PH, a letter that denotes striking more than sticking.” For the rest, see the already cited *Letter*, station 9; but the diligent reader must beware of retaining with the printed books this corrupt reading, “we translated it as ‘clinging’ and ‘retention.’” For the genuine reading is that which we have restored, as is clear both from the manuscript copies of the *Letter to Fabiola* and from this very *Book of Hebrew Names*, where *Dafeca* is rendered “it clung,” or “release.” MARTIAN. —Jerome’s own explanation from the *Letter on the Stations*, station 9, should be recalled: “The name *Dephca*,” he says, “is called among the Hebrews κροῦμα, that is, ‘a striking’ … In the *Book of Hebrew Names*, however, we translated it as ‘clinging’ and ‘release,’ which ought not to trouble the reader; nor should he think that we write inconsistently. There we published it according to the common reading, if the middle letter is written with BET; here, however, I found it written in the Hebrew volume with PH, a letter that denotes striking more than sticking.” From this one may readily infer that Jerome formerly read *Dabeca*, not *Dafeca*, in this book, and that it should accordingly be restored if the middle letter is written with the letter Beth. Indeed, the author of this book interpreted this name from a double reading, though both were false: when he rendered it “clinging,” he read *Dabeca* or *Dabca*; but when he rendered it “release,” he read *Raphca*, or, as the Septuagint has it, Ῥαφακὰ. Therefore Jerome adds in the passage just cited: “I am surprised that certain learned and ecclesiastical men wished to translate things not found in the Hebrew, and to seek invented explanations from mistranslations, so that in the present case they read *Rephca* for *Dephca*, substituting letter for letter because Resh and Daleth are distinguished by a small stroke.” Origen likewise read *Raphca* in *Homily 27 on Numbers*.], it clung, or release.

Debelathan, bricks, or lumps that are usually made by compacting fresh figs, which the Hebrews call *debelath* (), and the Greeks call *palathas*. In the present passage, therefore, the name we have proposed is interpreted as “their fig-cakes” [Note: [Col. 0794A] Previously it read *palata*. See what we note concerning this same interpretation in the cited *Letter to Fabiola*, station 40, note a.].

E.

Efraim, increasing, or fruitful. Elaad (Eldad), to the ground, or solitary, or to one. Erma, his anathema. Esebon [Note: [Col. 0794A] Origen also approves the former interpretation, *Homily 15 on Numbers*: “Esebon” is interpreted as “thoughts,” quite plainly from , “he thought.”], thought, or a belt of mourning. Edraim, the descent of shepherds. Elcan, their portion, or their testimony. Esbel, old fire, or vain. Evi [Note: [Col. 0794A] Origen gives a quite different interpretation, *Homily 25 on Numbers*, though I do not know how correctly: “Evin,” he says, is interpreted as “beastlike” or “wild.” Perhaps he read  instead of , as the recent editor properly noted.], I desired. Elale, toward ascent. Ebruna, crossing over, or transgression. Eniel, God is my grace. Ephod, an overgarment, or shoulder-piece. Escol, a cluster, or every fire.

Up to this point, the names are to be read with the short letter E; from here onward, with the letter lengthened. Elisar, my strong father (Elisur, “my God is strong”), or “my father constricting.” Eliab, my God is father, or God the Father. [Col. 0794] Elon, the strength of an army. Elisame, my God has heard. Elisama, my God hearing. Elisaphat (Elisaphan or Eliasaph), God has gathered, or the protection of my God, or concealment. Enan, cloud. Edrai, inundation will feed me. 28 Er, watchful, or rising, or leathery. Elon, oak, or *aulon*. Concerning this we have spoken more fully in the *Book of Places* [Note: [Col. 0794A] “Concerning which in the book of Places,” etc. Consult the *Book of Hebrew Places*, under the letter A and under the headings “Numbers” [Col. 0794B] and “Deuteronomy.” MARTIAN. —We too have collected more material at that place, which you may see below in the *Book of Places*, under A, under “Numbers” and “Deuteronomy.”]. Eran, he emptied. Etthan, strong. Esaon (Asion Gaber), the will of mourning, or of strength. Enon (Enan), fountain of sadness. Elidad, my God is a cousin, or my God is an uncle.

F.

Fodasur, strong redemption, or fortified. Fagiel, God, meet me, or meeting with God. Faran [Note: [Col. 0794B] Origen prefers another explanation, *Homily 27 on Numbers*: “Pharan” is interpreted as “visible mouth,” from “mouth” and “he saw.”], their wildness, or fruitful. Faletti (Phalti), my savior. Feleth, ruin, or downfall. Fesga, cut off, or hewn, or a great mouth—from mouth, not from bone. Fethora [In the Septuagint, XXII, 5], exploration of the mouth, or a morsel of light, or the mouth of a turtledove. Fagur (Phogor) [Note: [Col. 0794B] In Hebrew it is ; the explanation “skin” and “mouth” is therefore derived from it. For Origen it means “sweetness,” or “skin of the mouth.”], skin of the mouth, or he gaped. Finees, the mouth rested; “be silent” [Note: [Col. 0794B] “Finees, the mouth rested, be silent,” etc. Colbert manuscript 4951 does not read the word “be silent,” but only “the mouth rested,” or “he spared the mouth.” Other copies retain the word given above, while earlier editions read “or he is silent.” MARTIAN. —Our manuscript, like the printed editions, reads “or he is silent.” One Colbert manuscript in Martianay’s possession lacks that word.], or he spared the mouth. [Col. 0795] Farez, division. Finoni (), [Note: [Col. 0795A] Origen explains it as “parsimony of the mouth.” In Hebrew it is . The Septuagint has φινώ.], my mouth of nephews. Farnach, a fattened calf, or my departure.

G.

Gedeoni [Note: [Col. 0795A] “Gedeoni, temptation of humility.” The printed editions read: “Gedeon, temptation of iniquity,” or “the temptation of my iniquity.” But *Gedeon* without the final i cannot be rendered with the pronoun “my.” Moreover, all the older manuscript codices have “of my humility,” not “of my iniquity”; and rightly so, since the middle letter is written with Ayin, , *Gedeoni*, Numbers 1:15. MARTIAN. —Our manuscript reads “Gedeoni, temptation of iniquity, or temptation of my iniquity.” The older printed editions agree, though they have *Gedeon* instead of *Gedeoni*.], temptation of iniquity, or temptation of humility. Garizim, division, or cutting off.

I.

Ifanne, he hinted, or hinting. Jegal (), near, or redeeming. Jesu, savior. 29 Jazer, helper. Jarden, their descent, or “see judgment.” Jassa, half, or a deed commanded. Jacob [Note: [Col. 0795A] Nor does Origen disagree, *Homily 13 on Numbers*: “Jacob,” which is interpreted as “struggle.” Apparently from , “he exhausted” or “emptied”; and in wrestling strength is indeed exhausted.], struggle, or dust. Jerio (Jericho), its fragrance, or moon. Jasub, conversion. Jalel, he awaited God. Jamna, sea, or his right hand. Jesevi (), “I desired,” or my equal. Jaasael (Jesiel), God divided in half. Jeser, he formed—that is, fashioned—or formed. Jair, illuminating. Jetebatha (), good things, or he declined in order to come. Isimoth, he will bring death. Jegali, redeeming me, or my kinsman.

L.

Lael, toward God, or for God. [Note: [Col. 0795A] It should be read *Lobna* with the letter B, as the interpretation of the name itself indicates, from , “white” or “to become white.” [Col. 0795B] Origen, *Homily 27 on Numbers*, interprets *Lebna* as “whitening.” Jerome, however, in the *Letter on the Stations*, station 17, prefers that it be translated “brick”: “Although some,” he says, “by transferring *Lebbona*, have wrongly interpreted it as ‘brightness.’” See what we have noted at that place.], Lomna, white, or shining white.

M.

Manasse [Note: [Col. 0795B] The Talmudists likewise think so, from , “he forgot.” Origen too interprets it as ἀπὸ λήθης, “from forgetfulness.”], forgetful, or “because he forgot.” Madiani, contradiction, or answer. Medad, he measured. Michael, who is like God? Machi, what, because? [Col. 0795] Matthana, gift. Medaba, prominent waters. Machir, he will restore, or he sold, or from weakness. Maala, chorus, or weakness. Melcha, his king. Malchiel, my king is God. Maceloth [Note: [Col. 0795B] Origen disagrees, *Homily 27 on Numbers*, interpreting it as “principality,” or “rod.” Certainly  means a staff or rod.], of the assemblies. Mathca [Note: [Col. 0796A] Martianay: “sweetness.” It is derived from , “to be sweet.” Origen explains it as “new death,” which is not convincing.], sweetness, or satiety. Moseroth [Note: [Col. 0796A] Some copies in Origen, *Homily 27 on Numbers*, read *Mesoroth*, others *Mesaloth*; from the latter reading the etymology of “exclusion” would be derived more suitably from , “beyond” or “except.” Perhaps it was once written thus in Jerome’s Latin manuscripts.], exclusions, or bonds, or disciplines, or successions, since our copies read *Maseroth* [In the Septuagint, μασουροὺθ, XXXIII, 30].

N.

30 Nathanael, my God, or gift of God. Naabi, hidden, or “he rested in me.” Nephe, blowing, or [Note: [Col. 0796A] In our manuscript, “or sighing.”] breathing. Namuel, God slept, or [Note: [Col. 0796A] The same manuscript: “or in whom is God”; incorrectly.] “they say, God.” Noa (), movement, which the Greeks more significantly call σάλος, “a tossing.” Neeman, beauty, or their movement. Namra [Note: [Col. 0796A] “Namra, leopard,” etc. From this passage the inept interpretation of the name *Bethanamra* in earlier editions must be corrected, where “house of pack animals” is read instead of “house of leopards.” MARTIAN.], leopard, or bitternesses. Nabau [Note: [Col. 0796A] For Origen, *Nabau* means “departure,” from , “he came” or “went away.”], we shall come, or in confinement. Nobe, barking. Naason, serpentine, or an omen.

O.

Othotam (Etham), their sign. Ozni, my ear. Opham (Hupham), their maritime region, or their bridal chamber. Opher, disgrace (). But among the Hebrews it is written with the letter Heth.

Up to this point, the names are to be read with the short letter O; from here onward, let the letter be read as lengthened. [Col. 0796] Obab, beloved, or embraced, or a hedge. Ori, cooking, or excluding me, or seizing me. Osee, savior, or saving. Onam, pain, or their sadness, or muttering, or murmuring. Or, light. Obath (), a magician, or a ventriloquistic woman, whom the Greeks call ἐγγαστρίμυθον. Og [Note: [Col. 0796A] Adamantius disagrees, *Homily 13 on Numbers*: “Og” is interpreted as “enclosure,” perhaps from the Chaldean or Hebrew , “to describe a circle,” or “to enclose.”], heaping up, or hidden. Oni, my pain.

R.

Raphao (Raphu), healing, or medicating. Roob, streets, or breadth. Recem, variety, or paintings. 31 Rebe, four; but it is written with the letter Ayin. Rathma, completed vision, or juniper, or sound. Remmonpharez, division of pomegranates, or division of lofty things. Reesa [Note: [Col. 0796B] See the *Letter on the Stations*, station 18, and what we noted there. Origen, *Homily 27 on Numbers*: “Ressa,” he says, “may be called among us ‘visible’ or ‘praiseworthy temptation.’” From “he saw,” and in the intensive form “he tempted.”], bridle.

S.

Saddesor (Sedeur), light of their breasts, or light of the breast. Salomiel, God repaying me, or my peace is God. Surisadai, holding my breasts, or my strong one is the Lord. Suriel, God holding me, or my strong one is God. Soar, little. Samoe (Samua), hearing. Saphat, he judged. Sodi, my secret, or he excluded me. Susi, my horse. Sethur, hidden, or turning aside. Sisai, my long-lived one. Soon (), Tanis, a city of Egypt. Seon, a shoot that does not exist, or a useless shoot, or [Note: [Col. 0796B] In our manuscript, “or a useless address, or heat,” etc.] an address, or heat, or an irritating temptation. Seffor, bird. Settim [Note: [Col. 0797A] “Settim, thorns.” The name , *Settim*, is interpreted by Jerome as “thorns” in the present *Book of Hebrew Names*, as also in Book XII of the *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter XLI: “These varieties of trees,” he says, “signify the diversity of spiritual grace. And because their nature is known to everyone, let us explain only the Hebrew *setta* (), which Theodotion translated as ‘thorn.’ It is a kind of tree growing in the wilderness, resembling white thorns; hence all the woodwork of the Ark and the Tabernacle was made from it, and the implements are called *settim*, etc.” Symmachus likewise interprets *Settim* as “thorns.” On this see Jerome’s *Commentary on Joel*, chapter III, and on Micah, chapter VI. MARTIAN.], [In Hebrew, XXII, 32] thorns. Satan, adversary. Seth, placing, or he placed. Seir, hairy, or a he-goat. Salu (), a temptation that looks back [Note: [Col. 0797A] But εὐπαθής, “well-disposed,” is better. In place of εὐπαθής, restored by us on the authority of the manuscript codices, the printed editions read εὐσταθής, “steady”; on what authority, those who defend the old editions so zealously may determine. MARTIAN.]: but better εὐπαθὴς [al. εὐσταθής], which we may render “fortunate” or “vigorous.” Sefion (Sephon), hidden, or “go forth, mouth of sadness,” or their watchtower. Soni, scarlet, or my pupil. Sela, petition, or petitioner. Semron, he saw the name, or its guardian. Sichem, shoulder. Semidae, my name is knowledge. Salphaad [Note: [Col. 0797A] From “shadow” and “mouth,” Origen interprets *Salphaat* in *Homily 21 on Numbers* as “shadow in his mouth.”], shadow of fear, or shadow in itself—that is, equally. Suthale, mixed cup, or green thorn, or moist. Sfufan [Note: [Col. 0797B] “Sfufan, wearing down,” etc. The printed editions read *Suphan*; the Septuagint has σωφὰν. In the Hebrew text it is , *Sephupham* or *Sphupham*, as it is written in the Latin manuscript codices. In the printed editions and some more recent manuscripts we then read *SUPHASIM*; in others, superior in number and antiquity, *SAPHAPHIM*. That *Suphan* or *Sphupham* means “wearing down” and “grinding away” can easily be learned from the words *Saphaph*, *Suph*, and *Saphah*. But what *Suphasim* or *Saphaphim* should mean in Latin—“toward the shelter of snouts” or “of rakes,” as Marianus’s edition has it—I leave to the reader’s judgment. I am weary of having spent good hours badly while vainly pursuing such etymologies despite an ample supply of books. See, however, our conjectures in the Commentary. MARTIAN.], wearing down, or toward the shelter of snouts, which in Hebrew is called *SAPHAPHIM*. Sophar, trumpet. Sarahe (), veil, or prince of a brother. Sicher (σίκερα), drunkenness. Salem (Sellem), restore. Sabama, some kind of conversion, or “raise in them,” or “lift up the height.” Saphan (Saphar), lip, or hedgehog, or hare. Sochoth, booths. Salmona [Note: [Col. 0798A] Namely, from “shadow” and “portion.”], shadow of a portion, or “he counted the shadow,” or its image. [Col. 0797] Sin [Note: [Col. 0798A] In our manuscript, incorrectly, “Sin knowing.” For the Greeks it is also βάτος, “bush,” or δίψα, “thirst.” I think it comes from . Alternatively, Jerome, speaking according to his own sense in the *Letter on the Stations*, station 8, reads  and translates it as “bush” or “hatred.”], thirsting. Senna, will, or his commandment. Sedada, from his side. Sophan, lip, or the upper-lip beard, which the Greeks call μύστακα. Saphatam (Sephtan), judging the people. Samuel, his name is God. Salomi, my peace.

T.

Tholae, worm, or scarlet. Thersa, pleasing itself, more correctly expressed in Greek as εὐδοκοῦσα, “pleasing.” Thena, camps, or given. Theeth (Tehen), beneath. Thare (Thahath), exploration [Note: [Col. 0798A] In the frequently cited *Letter on the Stations*, station 24, Jerome says: “Some translate *Thare* as ‘wickedness’ or ‘pasture,’ and they would not be wrong if it were written with the letter Ayin; but since there is a double aspiration in the final syllable (namely, ), the cause of the error is evident. I find the father of Abraham written with this same word and letters in the aforementioned apocryphal volume of Genesis (the *Little Genesis*); after driving away the ravens that were ravaging human grain, he received the name ‘Driver Away’ or ‘Repeller.’ Origen, *Homily 27 on Numbers*, understands *Thara* as “contemplation of astonishment.” It is derived from “he explored” and from the interjection of one who is astonished.”], or pasture, or wickedness. All the names that we have set down under T are to be read with aspiration at their beginnings.

V.

Vaphsi, and my end.

Z.

Zachur, mindful. Zorad (Zared), foreign, or descent. Zoob [In the Septuagint, XXI, 14], gold. Zemeri (Zambri), this one provoking, or embittering. Zare, he arose. Zeferuna, “this mouth you saw”: from mouth, not from bone. Zamri, psalm, or [Note: [Col. 0798B] Our manuscript: “or my song,” taking the final letter as a masculine suffix.] song.

[Col. 0798] A.

33. ON DEUTERONOMY.

Astaroth, folds, mangers, sheepfolds, or courts. Aza, his strength. Araba (), west, or evening. Argob, accursed height. Avi (Hevaeans), wild. Avothiair [Note: [Col. 0798B] “Avothjair, glory of light,” etc. Some manuscripts and earlier editions have *Avathjair*, which has already been mentioned; for *hhaijuth jair* means “life of light,” and from Jerome one may read *Authjair* or *Avathjair*. MARTIAN. —Our manuscript, together with some others in Martianay’s possession and the earlier printed editions, has *Avathiair*.], glory of light, or life of light; but it is pronounced *Authjair*. Acan, necessity. Aseroth, courts, or vestibules—provided it is written with the letters Heth and Sade (). But if written with Aleph and Sin (), it means “blessings.” Amora (Gomorrha), illumination of the people, or its people. Adama, ground.

B.

Baalfeor, possessing a skin-mouth, or the upper mouth of a skin. Basar, distress, or in distress, or infancy. Bosor, in distress. Beroth, wells. Barne, son of change. [Manuscript: “son of movement.”] Balaam, a futile people [Note: [Col. 0798B] In the same manuscript another gloss, “or gulping,” is missing.], or gulping.

C.

Cademoth, from the beginning of death, or the beginning of death.

The following three names are to be read under C with aspiration. Chorraeus, angry, or from a hole, whom the Greeks call [Note: [Col. 0798B] “Whom the Greeks call τρωγλήτην.” Earlier editions read τρώγλη or τρώγλην instead of τρωγλήτην. But the reading of all the manuscript codices must be retained: τρώγλη means only a cave, or some hole made by gnawing; *troglites*, however, means “full of holes,” namely one who takes his name from a hole. Thus in Hebrew *hhor* means a cave or hole, and *hhori* means “full of holes,” because he enters the caves and holes of the rocks. Τρωγληταὶ are also swallows nesting in caves and holes. MARTIAN. —See what we noted above concerning this name from Genesis, and also Martianay’s note on this passage. *Chori* properly signifies an underground dweller, a troglodyte. Earlier it read τρωγλίτην.], τρωγλήτην. [Col. 0799] Chaphtorim, hands of turtledoves, or of explorers. Chaphtor (Cappadocians), Cappadocia.

E.

Edraim (), inundation of evils, or birth of the worst things, or descent of shepherds. 34 Erma (Horma), anathema. Evim (Hevaeans), wicked. Ermon, anathema of sadness. Esdoth [In the Septuagint, III, 1], outpouring. Emmim, peoples.

The following four names are to be read with the vowel lengthened. Esau, heap of stones, or collection of stones, which in Greek is called λιθολόγιον [Note: [Col. 0799A] Our manuscript incorrectly has “or fragments, or fracture.”], or fragments, or a making—that is, ποίησις, “creation” or “making.” Elath, terebinth, or *aulones*. Emim, terrifying ones. Ebal, ancient abyss.

F.

Fasga, cut off, or hewn, or mouth of transgression. Faran, increased, or growing. Fennador (Dor), conversion [Note: [Col. 0799A] The word “generation” may have dropped out of Origen’s books, *Homily 14 on Joshua*, if only “conversion” is explained. The etymology, however, derives from “he turned” and “generation.”] of generation.

G.

Gaza, strength. But it must be known that among the Hebrews it does not have a consonant at the beginning; rather, it begins with the vowel Ayin (), and is pronounced *Aza*. Gesuri, beside the light, or vicinity of light. Golam, their transmigration, [Note: [Col. 0799A] Our manuscript adds “or their rolling-place.” Certainly *Golan* denotes revolution rather than pleasure.] or their pleasure. Gergesaean, an attached settler. Gaulon, its rolling. Garizim, division, or stranger. Galgal [Note: [Col. 0799A] Theodoret, *Question 7 on Judges*, writes that *Galgal* means “freedom.” See Questions 51, 54, and 59. It could easily be derived from “he freed”; but in Hebrew it is written *Gilgal*, and means “boundary” or “course.”], wheel, or revelation. [Col. 0799] Gai [In the Septuagint, XXXIV, 6], abyss. Gebal, ancient abyss, or λιθολόγιον, “collection of stones.”

We have omitted the letter I and L because the same names are interpreted in the other books, and it is superfluous to repeat what has been said or will be said. H is thought by most people to be an aspiration rather than a letter. It is unnecessary to mention K, since even among the Latins it is judged superfluous except in *kalends*. Therefore it should be observed that the same names omitted here or elsewhere can be found in the other books. 35

M.

Misor [In the Septuagint, III, 10], straight, which in Greek is called εὐθεῖα, or level and flat, and belonging to the plain. Maachathi, they were broken for me, or a struck belly. Mosera, his instruction, or discipline. Mamoazer (Mamzer), from afar, or alienated.

O.

Oraim, conception, or apprehension.

R.

Raphaim, physicians, or giants. Rabath, multitude, or great. Rubeni, vision, my sons, or “see between me.” Ramoth, lofty sign, or “he saw death,” or lofty places.

S.

Sidon, hunting of sadness, or uselessness. Sareon, prince of sorrow. Sanir, raise up newness, or tooth of a lamp. Salacha (Selcha) [Note: [Col. 0799B] The manuscript reads: “Salcha, raising, or lifting, came.” Martianay: “raise up, come.” Concerning the interpretation of the preceding name *Sanir*, Jerome writes in Book VIII of the *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter XXVII: “Sanir is said to mean ‘way of the lamp,’ or, as we more correctly think, ‘tooth of vigils.’”], raise up, come, or lift up, come. [Col. 0800] Settim, thorns. Seboim, wild goats, or fallow deer, or “its station is the sea.” Sames, humble commandment. Sina (), temptation, or bush, provided it is written with the letter Samekh.

T.

Thophel [Note: [Col. 0799B] “Thophel, insipidity.” All the manuscripts incorrectly read *Thebel* instead of *Thophel*. But from the etymology given it is clear [Col. 0800A] that *Thophel* must be read. MARTIAN. —Thus the distinguished Martianay corrects it, although the manuscripts and printed editions wrongly give *Thebel*.], insipidity.

Z.

36 Zozomim, “these thoughts,” or “what is this water?” or “prepared in battle.”

FROM THE BOOK OF JESUS.

A.

Ain, question.

Adonibezec [Note: Adonibezec, “my lord,” etc. That Adonibezec, written at the end with the letter ṣade, signifies “my just lord” would scarcely be accepted by those skilled in the Hebrew language; nor does *bezeq* with ṣade mean “just,” but rather “inflated” and “swollen.” Jerome therefore is not to be understood here in that sense: he merely wished to indicate that the name Adonibezec, written Ἀδωνιβεζὲκ among the Septuagint in Joshua 10:1, is read in Hebrew as Adonisedec and interpreted “my just lord.” Martianus.], “my lord flashing,” or “my lord, contempt of vanity.” If it is written with the letter [Note: That is, if it is written as it appears in Hebrew, Adonisedec. But as it is written among the Septuagint, Adonibezec, Ἀδωνιβεζὲκ, it will more properly be interpreted “lord of Bezech”—the city mentioned in Judges 1:5—or “lord of the stone.” See Martianus’s note above.] ṣade, it may be interpreted “my just lord.”

Azeca, strength, or a snare.

Ailon, which above we called Aulon; but if we wish to read it as *aeglon* (), it means “their cow.”

Asor, arrow of light.

Axaf (), medicine; but if we wish to read it as Axa (), it means “furious.”

Araboth (among the Septuagint, 4:13), low places, level and open country.

Alac (Halchath), my portion, or slipperiness.

Aermon, anathema of grief.

Anaba (Anab), grape, or my humility.

Asdod (Azotus), dissolution, or outpouring, or burning.

Arnon, their light, or their curse.

Aroer [Note: In our manuscript, “Aroer, the pouring out of watchfulness,” etc.], the undermining of watchfulness, or a watch arising; but “tamarisk” is better.

Adar (Eder) [Note: Adar, flock. After these words, “Adar, flock,” the printed books add: “Amanon, a mountain of Cilicia, which is also Taurus. Hence Amana, restless, turbulent, or tooth of watchfulness.” But no trace of those words remains in the manuscript codices, and I think it is obvious to the learned reader—from both the subject matter and the meaning of the words—that this passage is an interpolation and wholly unworthy of Jerome. The book of Joshua does indeed mention Amman or Ammon, a famous city of Arabia called Philadelphia; but I do not know on what occasion the Hebrew book of Joshua could have mentioned the Cilician mountain that is also called Taurus. As for rendering *Amana* in Latin as “tooth of watchfulness,” this is intolerable sloppiness and ignorance, as anyone moderately acquainted with the Hebrew language knows. It should also be observed that the following word, Adaglam in the manuscripts and Adram in the printed editions, is the same as the name called Adollamim below; and that Adullam should be read instead of Adaglam. Martianus.], flock.

[Col. 0801] Adaglam [Note: The old printed editions add: “Amanon, a mountain of Cilicia, which is also Taurus. Hence Amana, restless, turbulent, or tooth of watchfulness.” Consult Martianus.], their assembly.

Apheo, he contained, or containment.

Adraim, inundation of the worst things.

Accaron [Note: I would rather emend *eruditio* to *eradicatio*, “eradication”: I think a careless copyist was deceived by the similarity of the letters. Jerome himself, in his Commentary on Amos, chapter 1, says: “Accaron, στείρωσις, that is, sterility, and ἐκρίζωσις, which means ERADICATION.” Still more clearly, in chapter 2 of Zephaniah: “Accaron, which means ERADICATION, will suffer this, namely, it will be eradicated.” Nevertheless, I alter nothing here against the testimony of the ancient books, especially since this has long been read in this way by the ancients. Rabanus, chapter 6 on the Books of Kings, has: “Accaron, instruction of grief,” and the explanation appended by him agrees with that reading.], instruction of grief, or sterility.

But Afara, with aleph or ayin at the beginning and feminine *he* attached at the end, means “his soil.” Martianus. There are two names of Benjaminite cities mentioned together in Joshua 18:23: one written with [Hebrew term omitted in source], the other with [Hebrew term omitted in source], which the Vulgate renders Aphara and Ophera. The first, [Hebrew term omitted], means “heifer” or “young cow”; the second derives from [Hebrew term omitted], “dust” or “soil.”], his soil; for it is written with different letters.

38. Adame (Adam), bloods or blood: in the plural number.

[Col. 0802] Ammador (Hammothdor), people of generation.

Alal [Note: Alal, breadth, etc. In the printed editions we corruptly read Alax instead of Asal, χαυνότης or χαυνότητα instead of χαύνωσις. Alal, if I am not mistaken, is the name of a city in Joshua 15:58, written *hhalhhul* in Hebrew and αἰλουὰ, Aelua, among the Septuagint; there the lengthening of the first syllable is quite clearly shown by the diphthong αἰ, as though it derived from the Hebrew *hhelulh* or Allua. But after examining the difficulty more carefully and comparing this passage with what is read below under the heading “On the Second Book of Kings,” the letter E seems to require that Alal be read with initial aleph, [Hebrew term omitted]: for Jerome teaches that names beginning with aleph are to be read with a lengthened first syllable, such as Elisue, Elisame, Eliam, and so forth. Finally, since *elil* means “nothing” and “useless,” the name Alal may appropriately signify “lightness.” Yet I do not rest secure in this conclusion, being wearied by excessive inquiry and investigation. The diligent reader should be warned, however, that in all the manuscript codices already cited or to be cited below, Alal is written, not Alax. Martianus. The old printed editions wrongly have Alax; and Martianus has “breadth” instead of “slackness,” although the very word χαύνωσις, which he discusses at length, could have warned him of the corrupt reading.], slackness, which the Greeks call χαύνωσις, or lightness, with the first syllable lengthened.

Balathaba [Note: Balathaba, “having been inhabited.” This name, in Joshua 19:8, appears among the Septuagint as βαλέκ. In some Latin manuscripts of the present book it is Balathala; in earlier printed editions, Belatham; in two older manuscripts—one Colbertine and another from Saint-Cyran—Balathaba. We retain the latter reading because in the Hebrew text at the place cited it is written *Bahalathbeer Ramath*, which the Septuagint or other Jewish Hellenists perhaps read as *Balathaba Ramath*. Hence Balathaba or Balathala remained among the Hebrew names. It should be noted that *Balath*, interpreted above as “having been possessed,” is here feminine, *Balathaba*, because of the penultimate syllable *tha*, which indicates the feminine gender. Martianus. It also seems to Martianus that this name, with the final letter elided, was formed from the two words Joshua 19:8, *Balabath beer*, and pronounced as one word, Balathaba. He reasonably derives it from the etymology of having or possessing. Jerome interprets it in this way, although the complete name *Bahalath beer* should be rendered “mistress of the well.” In the same place Joshua names *Ramathnegeb*, [Hebrew term omitted], “Ramatha of the south”; and there seems no doubt that the whole of these words designated that place in the tribe of Simeon, which held the same towns as the tribe of Judah. Recall Martianus’s note.], inhabited, feminine, from “to have”: it is a participle, not an imperative verb.

40. Caseon (Cesion), hard through strength.

Cabasam [Note: Cabasam, their assembly. In manuscript Regius 3993 it is written Casabam, which the printed editions follow. But in the two oldest Colbertine manuscripts repeatedly cited we read Cabasam, with *b* before *s*. The same reading occurs not only in those manuscripts but in many others from the monasteries of Saint-Evroul, Saint-Martin of Sées, Saint-Cyran, Fécamp, Jumièges, and so forth. And rightly so, for Cebuisa or Cabasa means “assembly,” whereas Casaba means “cutting off” and “cut.” There is no doubt that the name Cabasam is the Hebrew Cabseel, Joshua 15:21. Martianus. Our manuscript, like the commonly printed editions, has Cabasam, which Martianus emends on the authority of the other codices. Nor does he doubt that this name is the Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted], Cabseel, Joshua 15:21. To me it seems more likely to designate Kibtzaim, a city of the Ephraimites, Joshua 21:22, which preserves the ending *-am* in 1 Chronicles 6:53, where it is called Jokmeham.], their assembly.

The printed editions read Jepphonne, “naked,” or “turning.” The Regius manuscript has Jefonne, “naked.” The other older and better manuscripts have Jefonne, “a nod.” Martianus. I restored “naked” on the authority of the manuscripts, instead of “a nod,” which Martianus wrongly read from other copies. In the Pihel stem, the verb means “to empty” or “to free,” to which “to strip naked” is analogous. The word “nod” has an entirely different meaning and is wholly unsuitable to the etymology of Jefonne. The printed editions formerly added “or turning,” which is not found in the manuscript.], naked.

Lachis [Note: I conjecture that *interest*, “it concerns,” should be emended into the two words *iter est*, “it is a journey,” which agrees quite well with the rules of analogy, from the verb “he made a journey.” Origen also interprets Lachis as “journey” in Homily 13 on Joshua. On the other hand, I utterly do not know by what effort *interest* could be extracted from the etymology of Lachis.], it is a journey, or a man for himself.

Luza can finally be interpreted as “and this very one,” because of the initial *vau* of the first syllable and the following *za* or *ze*: for *veza* contains the conjunction “and” together with the demonstrative pronoun “this very one.” Martianus.], ἀμυγδαλόν, “almond”; although some interpret it as κλοιόν, namely the collar of condemned persons, commonly called a *boia*. The old printed editions have Masphat, “observation,” or “contemplation,” or “attention,” or “place of judgment.” It is Masepha in Joshua 15:38, Hebrew *Hammitzpa*; nor is this name assigned to the city without its initial element, since it most truly means “watchtower.”], watchtower, or from the watchtower.

In fact, it belongs not to the Book of Judges but to the First Book of Kings, where the more accurate manuscripts and the printed editions preserve it. The ancient manuscripts add the name Phenenna here, but it should by no means be read in the Book of Judges; nevertheless, in the Book of Samuel they omit it. Regius manuscript 3993 retains the name Phenenna in its proper place and does not add it to the Book of Judges. Martianus.].
