## I
Jezbaam (Jeblaam), “the people flowing away,” or “the people becoming foolish.” Jabin, “understanding,” or “wise.” Jael [Note: Origen interprets it differently as “ascension,” from “he ascended.”], “a doe,” or “a doe’s union,” or “beginning.” Joas [Note: I would prefer “despairing.” For Joasch is from the future Hophal form meaning “he will despair,” “it will be done,” or “he will be deprived of hope”—which is plainly what those who know Hebrew have understood. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, chapter 6, however, reads “breathing” instead of “hoping,” and there are those who would restore that reading here also in Jerome. I myself think it is a common error of pronunciation, substituting *i* for *e*. The Greek *χρονισμός* (“temporal”) agrees very well with the second etymology. But the third requires another explanation: suppose it is derived from [a word] meaning “God” or “Lord,” and from [one meaning] “strong” or “strength.”], “hoping,” or “temporal,” or “the Lord’s strength.” Jerobaal, “let Baal judge,” or “let the one who possesses judge,” or “the superior,” or “having a quarrel.” Jecbaze (in Hebrew VII, 25), “the winepress of a wolf.” Jecba, “winepress.” Jotham, “he is perfect.” Jair, “enlightening.” Jonathan, “the gift of a dove,” or “he gave to a dove,” or “the Lord’s gift.” Jabes, “dried up,” or “dryness.”

## O

Obed [Note: “Obed,” “serving.” Wonder, reader, at the carelessness of the earlier editors, says Jerome: he states that he had placed only three names here under the letter *O*, but they chose to insert five, contrary to the testimony of the oldest manuscripts, which retain only three words. Thus, in the printed books, the following spurious names occur among the genuine ones: Othoniel, “the answer of God,” or “the revelation of God.” And after the word Obab: Othoniel, “the time of my God,” or “the sign of God.” —Martian. —The old printed books insert these two additional names among these three: Othoniel, “the answer of God,” or “the revelation of God”; and again Othoniel, “the time of my God,” or “the sign of God”—contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and Jerome’s own testimony, since he said that he was adding only names to be read with lengthened *O*.], “serving.” Obab (Hobab), “love.” Oreb, “raven,” or “dryness.”

Sasai, “long-lived,” or “senary.” Sepheth (), “watchtower.” Salabbim, “the salvation of hearts.” Syria (), “height.” Sairath, “goat.” Semegar, “the name of a foreigner,” or “a settler there.” Sisara, “the exclusion of joy,” or “taking away the one who is departing,” or “the vision of a horse.” Setta (Bethsetta), “thorns.” Saratha (Saraa), “binding comes,” or “tribulation.” Suroreb (in Hebrew VII, 25), “the rock of a raven.” Salmane, “the shadow of restraining,” or “the shadow of commotion.” Samir, “brambles,” or “untilled ground.” Seon, “a burning temptation,” or “a seed that does not exist.” Semanoth, “a humble name.” Samson, “their sun,” or “the strength of the sun.” Sorec [Note: “Sorec,” “chosen,” “best.” Several old manuscripts have “the best choice”; and below, at the name Ruth, they read “defining” instead of “failing.” —Martian. —Several manuscripts in Martian’s possession have “the best choice.”], “chosen,” “best.” Salma (Salmana), “perceiving,” or “perfect,” or “peaceful.”

## T

Tabath (Tebbath), “good.” Except for this name, the remaining names that follow under this letter are to be read with aspiration. Thalmai, “suspension,” or “furrow.” Thamnathares (Thamnathsare), “numbering of the sun.” Thanach, “humility,” or “he will answer you.” Thebes () [Note: Here refer to the notable passage of Marcus Varro, *On Agriculture*, book II, chapter 1: “Nor does the name of a town indicate any less that the land is older, since its name comes from the kind of land, not from its founder. For in the ancient language, and among the Aeolian Boeotians in Greece, they call hills *Thebae* without aspiration; and among the Sabines, who came from Greece, the Pelasgians still use the same word. A trace of this remains in the Sabine territory, on the Salarian Way not far from Reate, where a hill is called *Tebae*. Plato mentions this in the *Phaedrus*, where he says that the Egyptian Thebes were thus named by the Greeks from the higher site which they occupied: *Βασιλέως δ` αὖ τότε ὄντος Αἰγύπτου ὅλης Θαμοῦ, περὶ τὴν μεγάλην πόλιν τοῦ ἄνω τόπου, ὅν οἱ Ἕλληνες Αἰγυπτίας Θήβας καλοῦσι*—“When Thamus was king of all Egypt, around the great city of the upper region, which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes.” Finally, the Hebrew etymology itself supports the view: *Thebetz*, which occurs twice in Judges IX, 50, is interpreted according to the rules of analogy as “it will shine” or “it will flash,” from the future Cal of the obsolete root [which nevertheless exists in Arabic]. This city was not far from Shechem and seems to have been so called because of its elevated situation. I do not, however, assert that the Egyptian Thebes is mentioned anywhere in Scripture; rather, I have preferred to join those who deny it. I add that Bochart prefers to derive the name from mud, just as *Lutetia* in Latin and *Pelusium* in Greek are so named.], “turning,” or “the production of eggs.”

# Of Ruth

Booz [Note: “Booz,” “in strength.” In the best manuscript of the Colbert library, only three words are written from the book of Ruth, namely Maalon, Orpha, and Ruth. Nothing further is read in one manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Cyran; but in many other manuscript codices we found seven names, as in the earlier printed books, which we have followed here. —Martian. —Of this book, two manuscripts in Martian’s possession display only these three names, Maalon, Orpha, and Ruth.], “in strength.” Elimelech, “my God is king.” Jesse (), “a libation of the islands.” Maalon, “from a window,” or “from the beginning,” or “completion.” Noemi [Note: Jerome himself interprets it differently in Letter 54, to Furia, section 17. See what we have observed there.], “beautiful.” Orpha, “her neck.” Ruth, “seeing,” or “hastening,” or “failing.”

# Of the First Book of Kingdoms

## A

Anna, “his grace.” Aphec, “new anger,” or “continually.” Aminadab (Abinadab) [Note: “Aminadab,” “my father is spontaneous,” etc. The Septuagint reads Aminadab, but corruptly, as is perfectly clear from the etymology itself: for the name Aminadab does not translate into Latin as “my father is spontaneous,” but as “my people is spontaneous.” —Martian. —Abinadab should be read, as is clear both from the interpretation of the name and from the text of Samuel, I Kings III, II.], “my father is spontaneous,” or “courteous.” Abia, “the father is Lord,” or “the father was.” Abiel, “my father is God.” Ammoni, “pressing,” or “constricting me.” Asor, “arrow of light.” Ahias, “another brother,” or “his brother.” Ahitob, “my brother is good.” Ahinaam, “the beauty of a brother.” Abenner, “my father is a lamp,” or “the father of a lamp.” Agag, *δῶμα*, that is, “roof.” Armathaim (Ramathaim), “their height.” Azeca, “strength,” or “snare.” Adreel (), “flocks of God.” Azel, “departing,” “going forward.” Achis, “nevertheless a man,” or “my brother,” or “a brother-man.”

52. Abimelech, “my brother is king.” Avilath (Hevila), “mourning,” or “in labor.” Arth (Haret), “delay.” Abiathar, “an excessive father.” Achela (Hachila), “looking upon her.” Abigal, “father of rejoicing,” or [Note: “Abigal,” “father of dew.” The printed books have “father of error,” but the manuscripts more correctly read “father of dew,” since the author of this work had in mind the name Abital, which can be rendered “father of dew,” not “father of error.” —Martian. —Our manuscript, like the earlier printed books, has “father of error.” Martian conjectures that the author of this work looked to the name Abital, which is rendered “father of dew.” In Origen’s Lexicon, however, *Ἀβιγάην δρόσος*—“Abigaen, dew”—is translated.], “father of dew.” Abisa, “the incense of my father,” or “sacrifice.” Aendor, “eye,” or “fountain of generation.” Abigail, “the rejoicing of my father.” Asan, “smoking.” Athach, “in your time.”

## B

Baalim, “those who possess,” or “those ascending,” or “the higher ones.” Bethahar, “house of recognition,” or “house of a lamb.” [Col. 0813] Bochorach (Bocorath), “your firstborn.” Bezec, “poverty.” Badan, “alone,” or “in judgment.” Boses, “in him it flourished,” or “cutting off.” Bama, “in which.” Baritha [Note: “Baritha,” “a pythoness,” etc. Balitha should be read, because of *baalath ob*, which in the Septuagint, I Samuel XXVIII, 7–8, is called *ἐγγαστρίμυθος* (“ventriloquist”). The ancient scribes, insufficiently acquainted with Hebrew, read Baritha instead of Balitha, just as elsewhere they read Tabitha instead of Talitha. —Martian. —It is called [the pythoness] in Chaldean. Martianaeus teaches that Balitha should be read, from the Hebrew words *baalath ob*, which the Septuagint renders by *ἐγγαστρίμυθον* (“ventriloquist”).], “a pythoness,” whom the Greeks call *ἐγγαστρίμυθος* (“ventriloquist”). ## D

53. David [Note: Thus the ancients commonly interpret it. Origen, at the beginning of his *Commentary on Matthew*, has *Δαβὶδ ὃς ἑρμηνεύεται ἱκανὸς χειρί*—“David, which is interpreted ‘sufficient by hand’”—to say nothing of many others. Yet the explanation is far too inept to deserve discussion, as are the forms [meaning] “to suffice” and “hand,” unless one accepts what others prefer: that it is formed from a word meaning “strength,” “might,” and “hand,” with a change of letters as in related forms. According to the rules of analogy, the correct explanation is that it means “beloved” and “desirable,” from “beloved,” or from a form standing for it.], “strong of hand,” or “desirable.” Damaim (Dommim), “bloody.” Doec [Note: “Doec,” *ἀγωνιῶν* (“being in anguish”). ## H

Hiram, “living in exaltation.” Histob, “good man.” Hiras, “watching.” Hisboseth, “in the confusion.”

We have therefore placed these names with aspiration, because in both Greek and Hebrew they are written with a diphthong [Note: They are written with a diphthong. The four names listed here by Jerome or Philo are written among the Hebrews with a diphthong as follows: Hiram, Histob, Hiras, Hisboseth. The letters *aleph*, *heth*, and *ayin* were not used by the ancient Hebrews as consonants, but as vowels, as Jerome’s present note clearly shows when he states that *aleph*, *heth*, and *ayin* form a diphthong with the following *yod* in the four Hebrew names just mentioned. Thus the opinions of certain modern grammarians disappear—those who thought that diphthongs had been expelled from the Hebrew language and that Hebrew words always began with a consonant rather than a vowel. As for the Greek diphthongs in the four names listed above, this is not readily apparent as Jerome testifies, unless perhaps in Hiram, which the Greeks write *Χειράμ*. For the other names are written in Greek without diphthongs: *Ἰεβοσθὲ*, *Ἰστὼβ*, *Ἴστρα*. Yet careful examination of the Septuagint shows that the name Hisboseth is written with a diphthong in the Alexandrian manuscript at II Kingdoms II, 10: *Εἰεβοσθαὶ*, “Eiebosthai.” From this it is sufficiently clear that the other Hebrew names were likewise formerly written by the Greeks with the diphthong *ει*; this is confirmed still more strongly by the name Jabes, ordinarily written *Ἰαβὶς*, but found in the same Alexandrian manuscript with the diphthong *Εἰαβεῖς*. Finally, it is known to the learned that the vowel *iota* and the diphthong *ei* were used interchangeably by both Greeks and Latins, and that, in accordance with this usage, *Ἰστὼβ* and *Εἰστὼβ*, *Ἴρας* and *Εἴρας* were written indiscriminately. —Martian. —The teachers of Hebrew state that there are no proper diphthongs in the Hebrew language. That is, no vowel is pronounced without a consonant; and those vowels that are commonly heard as [vowels], which seem to be pronounced by themselves, precede a light breathing drawn from the depth of the throat. Jerome, who also says that the four preceding names begin with a diphthong among the Hebrews, nevertheless begins quite learnedly, in accordance with the character of the language, with Latin aspiration, not with a vowel. In Hebrew they are written [the forms cited], in II Kingdoms V, 11; X, 6; XX, 26; and II, 8, with *yod* immediately following the preceding letter. In Greek, as in the printed copies, they are *Χειρὰμ*, *Ἰστὼβ*, *Ἱρὰς*, *Ἰεβοσθέ*.], they are written.

## A

This name, *Abisa*, is corrupt, as its meaning or interpretation clearly shows. It should not be read *Abisa*, but *Aphsiba*, as the Greek manuscripts sufficiently indicate, in which it is written Ἀψιβὰ and Ὀφειβὰ. In Hebrew it is *hhaphsiba*, which in Latin means “my will is in her.” The same word occurs below under the letter E, where the printed editions likewise read *Ebsiba* for *Ephsiba*, owing, I believe, to the pronunciation of the ancient scribes, who, hearing *Ephsiba*, thought they heard *Ebsiba* with *b*, because of the similarity of sound between those consonants. In any case, there is a solecism in the interpretation of this word in both the printed books and the manuscripts: they read the masculine pronoun of the third-person singular, “my will is in him,” whereas, because of the feminine Hebrew suffix at the end, the word *Hapsi-ba* must necessarily be interpreted “my will is in her.” MARTIAN. —Our manuscript and the old editions likewise have “in her,” contrary to Martianay’s false assertion that “in her” is a solecism for “in him.” But that *Aphsiba* must be read instead of *Abisa* is clearly demonstrated by the Hebrew etymology itself, the Greek reading Ἀψιβὰ, and finally the interpretation. ## N

Naboe, prophet, or prophesying. [Col. 0826] Naaman, beauty, or their agitation. 69 Nergal, lamp of the heap. Nabaaz [Note: [Col. 0826A] I read it thus, and have no doubt that this is Nebahaz in IV Kings XVII, 31. Hebrew . It is written *Nibchaz*: in the Septuagint, in the Alexandrian codex, Ναιβάς, and in the Complutensian, Νιβχάξ. It is a divine name of the Hevaeans or Colchians, interpreted “the remote one who sees,” from [] “sun,” which illuminates the spaces of the earth from the height of the heavens. The author’s own interpretation also persuades us that *Nabahaz* should be read: *naba* means “he prophesied,” and [] is then readily derived. Martianay, however, thinks *Nabat* or *Nabaz* should be read. —*Naazab*, “he prophesied then,” and so forth. The corruption of the name *Naazab* is shown by the interpretation itself, which fits the word *Nabat* very well: [] (*Nibba*) means “he prophesied.” It would be better, however, to read *Nabaz*, so that *naba* would mean “he prophesied” and *az* would mean “then.” MARTIAN.], he prophesied then, or beginning of sitting. Sunem, teeth, or scarlet, or variety. Samariam, guarded. Sabath, rest, or interruption. Sir [Note: [Col. 0826B] *Sir*, a cauldron, or hall, and so forth. In Plautus, *Aulularia* 18, one finds “a hall loaded with gold.” MARTIAN. —The grammarians teach that among the ancients *aula* was used for *olla* (“pot”). Hence Plautus’ comedy is entitled *Aulularia*.], a cauldron, or hall, which people commonly call a pot. Read *Sedema*, which is the singular of the name *Sademoth* placed shortly below. *Sedema* means the same as *Sedepha*, *Sedephon*, or *Siddaphon*, which Jerome interprets in III Kings VIII, 37 as “corrupted air,” that is, ἀνεμοφθορία. I cannot determine where *Saesdema* occurs in IV Kings; *Sadepha* is read in chapter XIX, 26. MARTIAN. —The Greeks call what they mean ἀνεμοφθορία “blight” or “corruption of the air.” In Hebrew it is called , *sciddaphon*. *Saesdema*, as Jerome reads it, seems to be [] *scedema*, IV Kings XIX, 26, where it is written in the Hebrew copies [] *scedepha*, with a letter of the same organ substituted. In reality *scedepha* should also be read here, in accordance with the Hebrew text, so that the interpretation “pestilential air” may somehow fit. It should be understood that *scedepha* was written in the cited passage of IV Kings in place of *scedema*, which means “field.” It may once have stood in this very book of Names as follows: “Sedepha, pestilential air,” and so forth. Some diligent reader may have noted *Sedema* in the margin to indicate that this word was written thus in Hebrew; then a copyist, thinking it ought to be substituted for the other, may have erased one and corrupted the other.], pestilential air, which the Greeks more expressively call ἀνεμοφθορία. Jerome retains the name partly translated, “who judged Baal.” The current Hebrew text reads *Arbeel* instead of *Jerobaal*; the Syriac interpreter has neither, but wrote *Beth-il*; the Arabic, following the Septuagint, has *Jeroboam*. I had thought that in Jerome’s time, and before it, *Jerobaal* had been written in the Hebrew text, which differs greatly from the present *Arbeel*. But after examining his *Commentaries on Hosea*, I learned that the holy Doctor always wrote *Arbel*: “He was devastated,” he says, “as it is contained in the Hebrew, by ARBEL; it signifies the same thing as JEROBAAL, but in shorter and clearer language.” MARTIAN.], judgment of God, or judging above.

Anathoth, “answer,” or “an answering sign,” or “obedience.” Amon, “faithful,” or “nourishing,” or “burden.” Achbor, “mouse.” Hananiah, “grace dispersed,” or “grace of God.” Azor, “helped.” Amaziah, “work of God.” Anameel, “to whom God has given.” Asedemoth (in the Septuagint, XXXVIII, 40), “fields,” or “suburbs.” Ananeel, “grace of God.” Azecha [Note: [Col. 0832B] “Azecha,” “closed with a bolt,” etc. These two names, Azeca and Abania, are absent from the editions previously printed. ## ON DANIEL

### A

Ashpenaz, “master of horses.” Hananiah, “grace of God.” Abednego, “serving: I am silent.” Amelsar, [Note: [Col. 0835A] “Amelsar,” “the prince spoke.” In Hebrew, Amelsar, or Hammelsar according to the Masoretic pointing. Amelsar, however, is translated into Latin as “circumcision of tribulation,” not “the prince spoke.” It must be carefully observed that Philo, the first author of this work, takes the letters ṣade and sin indiscriminately and interchangeably, Sar and Sar, and earlier Saphan and Saphat. Moreover, Greek copies read differently: Ἀμελσὰδ, Amelsad, and Ἀμερσὰρ, Amersar; according to the latter pronunciation of the letters, Amersar is correctly interpreted as “the prince spoke.” MARTIAN. —Indeed, as Martianus notes, the Greeks read Ἀμερσὰρ; to this reading the interpretation corresponds, from [Greek root omitted], “to speak,” and [Greek root omitted], “prince.”], “the prince spoke.” Arioch, “reducing to solitude.” Ahasuerus, “his court,” or “blessedness.” Astyages, “will,” or “counsel of festivity.” Ambacum, “embracing them,” or “receiving them.” Artaxerxes, “testing the light in silence.”

## ON MATTHEW

[Col. 0839]

### A

Abraham, “father seeing the people.” Amminadab, “my willing people.” Abijah, “the Lord is father.” Asa, “lifting up,” or “raising.” Aaziah (Uzziah), “apprehending the Lord,” or “the strength of the Lord,” or “his strength.” Ahaz, “apprehend.” Amon ([missing form]), “faithful,” or “nourishing,” if it begins with the letter ALEPH; but if it is written with AYIN, it means “burdened.” Abihu, “my father is this,” or “my father is.” Azur, “helped.” Archelaus, “recognizing a lion.” Amen, “truly,” or “faithfully.” Andrew, “beautiful,” or “answering the fodder.” 89 Alphaeus, “fugitive,” but better “thousandth,” or “learned.” Amora, “a knowing people,” or “illumination of the people.” Abel, “vapor,” or “mourning,” or “vanity.” Akeldama, [Note: [Col. 0839B] “Akeldama,” “field of blood.” So it is: Acel, or hhacal, means “field” in Syriac, not in Hebrew, and dema means “blood.” On Achel-dema, or Hhacel-dama, see our notes on Matthew’s Gospel according to the old Italian version. MARTIAN.] “field of blood.” It is Syriac, not Hebrew.

### B

Boaz, “in whom is strength,” or “in him [Col. 0839] is strength”; but better, “in strength.” Bartholomew, “son of one who suspends waters,” or “son of one who suspends me.” It is Syriac, not Hebrew. Bethsaida, “house of fruits,” or “house of hunters.” Barjona ([missing form]), “son of a dove.” It is both Syriac and Hebrew. For bar means “son” in Syriac, and Jona means “dove” in both languages. Bethphage, “house of the mouth of the valleys,” or “house of the cheek.” It is Syriac, not Hebrew. Some [Note: [Col. 0839B] Not only Origen in Matthew, and in Homily 37 on Luke and in John II, 13, interprets it as οἶκον σιαγόνων, “house of jaws,” but Jerome himself, in Paula’s Epitaph, has “Bethphage, village of priestly jaws”; and in chapter 2 of his Commentary on Matthew, “when he came to Bethphage, to the house of the jaws, which was a village of priests,” etc. See what we have noted on that passage. The derivation is from [Greek or Hebrew form omitted], “house,” and the Syriac [forms omitted], “cheek” or “jaw.” The former explanation, however, seems to derive from [form omitted], “house,” and “mouth,” and [form omitted], “valley,” although this is a Syriac rather than a Hebrew name. Others more plausibly derive it from [form omitted], which in Syriac means “figs,” so that the village is named from that fruit, just as the Macedonian city was called Olynthus.] think it is called “house of jaws.” Bethany, “house of his affliction,” or “house of obedience.” Barachiah, “the Lord is blessed,” or “the blessing of the Lord.” Barabbas, “son of our teacher.” It is Syriac, not Hebrew.

Caiaphas, “investigator,” or “shrewd,” but better “vomiting from the mouth.” Codrantes, [Note: [Col. 0840B] Thus the Syrians pronounced the Latin name. Isidore is mistaken, Book XVI, chapter 25: “Quadrans, likewise the Hebrews call quadrans.”] “mist,” or “darkness.” What we call quadrans with the letter Q. Corban, “offering.” Canaanite ([missing form]), “possessing,” or “possession.” [Col. 0840] Up to this point the names have been written with the simple letter C, which the Greeks pronounce with K; from here onward they are to be read with aspiration added, which they call the 103rd letter. Chanani ([missing form]), “merchant,” or “changeable,” or “a little poor man.” Chorazin, “this mystery of mine.” Canaanites, “merchants.”

Devil, “flowing down”; in Greek, however, it is called “accuser.” David, “desirable,” or “strong in hand.” Daniel, “judgment of God,” or “God judges me.”

### E

Esrom, “he saw an arrow,” or “their court.” Jesse, “libation of islands,” but better “incense.” Up to this point the short letter E is to be read; thereafter the letter is to be read long. Eliakim, “resurrection of God,” or “God raising up,” or “God will raise up.” Elihu, “this is my God,” or “of this my God.” Eliezer, “my God is helper.” Elijah, “God the Lord.” [Col. 0841] Eli, Eli, lama azabthani [Note: [Col. 0841A] Thus the Hebrew has it in Psalm XXII according to the Hebrew reckoning. The current text of Matthew, so that we need not concern ourselves with its Hebrew version, has lamasabactani or sebactani. Moreover, [Syriac form omitted] is the same in Syriac as in Hebrew. Perhaps Matthew presents the passage recited by Christ as it stood in the original form of the Psalm, although the Lord may have pronounced it in the vernacular. —“Eli, Eli, lamazabthani,” etc. In the present Hebrew text of Matthew [Hebrew form omitted], “Eli, Eli, lama sebactani,” and in the margin, as a variant reading for sebactani, we read azabtani. The Latin manuscript codices of this work mostly read lamazabathani. MARTIAN.], “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

### G

Gennesaret, [Note: [Col. 0841A] Origen himself, and likewise Jerome in Matthew, profess not to know the etymology of this name. In the Syriac edition of the New Testament it is written [Syriac form omitted], and it seems to me not implausibly to be explained from [forms omitted], “ten gardens,” or, as Santes Pagninus orders this passage to be corrected, from [form omitted], “garden of princes,” not “rising,” as all Jerome’s books prefer here; for it is known that the region received its name from the abundance of gardens. Yet I change nothing, since I know that Hesychius approves Γενεσαρὲτ πατρὶς ἀρχόντων, “Genesaret, homeland or stock of princes,” from the Chaldean words [forms omitted], as Huetius notes. We shall examine other etymologies devised by learned men in the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 14. Here we have decided to touch scarcely any except those that contribute to correcting or defending the text of this very book.] “origin of princes.” Gehenna, “they are from the valley,” or “free valley.” Gethsemane, “valley of fatness.” Golgotha, “skull.” It is Syriac, not Hebrew.

### I

91 Jesus, “savior,” or “about to save.” To preserve the order of the letter I, we have omitted aspiration in most cases, although grammarians do not think it should be counted as a separate letter. Isaac, “laughter,” or “joy.” Jacob, “supplanter,” or “supplanting.” Judah, “confessing,” or “glorifying.” Jehoshaphat, “he himself judging,” but better, “the Lord will judge.” Joram, “where is the exalted one,” or “he who is exalted,” but better, “he will be exalted.” Jotham, “completed,” or “perfect.” Jezekiah, “strong of the Lord,” or “the Lord will strengthen.” Josiah, “where is the incense of the Lord,” [Col. 0841] or “in whom is the incense of the Lord,” or “salvation of the Lord”; it may also be called “the strength of the Lord.” Jeconiah, “preparing,” or “preparation of the Lord.” Jehoiakim, “where is the preparation?” or “the preparation of the Lord.” Jojakim, “resurrection of the Lord,” or “the Lord raising up.” Joseph, “he added,” or “adding.” Jerusalem, “vision of peace,” or “he will fear perfectly.” Jeremiah, “exalted of the Lord.” Joannan, [Note: [Col. 0841B] Here the distinguished Huetius refers to what Origen, volume V, on John, reports: Εὕρομεν ἐν τῇ ἑρμηνείᾳ τῶν ὀνομάτων … Ἰωάννης, τὸ Ἰωὰ, χωρὶς τοῦ νὴς, μεταλαμβανόμενον, ὅπερ τ` αὐτὸν οἰόμεθα εἶναι τῷ Ἰωάννης, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἀλλὰ ἡ καινὴ Διαθήκη Ἑβραίων ὀνόματα ἐξελλήνισε, χαρακτῆρι αὐτὰ εἰποῦσα Ἑλληνικῷ, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ Ἰακὼβ, Ἰάκωβον, καὶ ἐπὶ Σύμεων, Συμών. “We find in the Interpretation of Names, instead of Joannes, the element Joa taken separately without nes; and we think that this has the same value as Joannes, since the New Testament has also rendered other Hebrew names in Greek, pronouncing them in Greek form, as Jacob for Jacob and Simeon for Simeon.” It is perfectly clear that Joannan, lacking its final syllable, is indicated there, and that he found it interpreted as ἀπὸ Θεοῦ χάρις, “grace from God,” although he unwisely took it for Joannes.] “to whom belongs grace,” or “grace of the Lord.” Isaiah, “salvation of the Lord.” Iscariot, “memorial of the Lord”; but if we choose to read [Note: [Col. 0842A] “Issachariot,” etc. Jerome had in mind the name Issachar, son of Jacob. MARTIAN. —The Greeks do so rather violently. The Origenian Lexicon has Ἰσαχὰρ μισθός, “Issachar, reward,” and Ἰσκαρὼθ μνημόσυνον, σκηνὴν θανάτου, “Iscariot, memorial, tent of death.”] Issachariot, it is interpreted as “his reward.” It may also be said to mean “memory of death.” Jericho, “his fragrance,” or “moon.” We regard the letter K as superfluous and express everything, except the Kalends, with C; accordingly it has been omitted here.

### L

Lebbaeus, a figurative name derived from the heart, which we may render diminutively as “little heart.”

92 Manasseh, “forgetful.” Matthan, “gift,” or “given.” Most people think Mariam means [Col. 0842] “these illuminate me,” or “illuminatrix,” [Note: [Col. 0842A] Or “myrrh of the sea.” Observe, reader, how far from the truth are those who think Jerome the author of all the etymologies in the Book of Hebrew Names. The Hebrew name Miriam, that is, Maria, properly sounds among the Hebrews as “bitter sea”; among the Syrians Maria also means “lady,” according to the note of the holy Doctor. MARTIAN.] or “myrrh of the sea,” but it does not seem so to me at all. It is better to say that it means “star of the sea,” or “bitter sea”; and it should be known that in Syriac Maria is called “lady.” Matthew, “once given.” Magdalah, “its fruits,” or “messenger.” Magdalene, “tower,” but better: just as one says “mountainous” from “mountain,” so “towered” from “tower.”

### N

Naasson: some think it means “rested sound,” but it is better “foretelling,” or “their serpent.” Nazareth ([missing form]), “flower,” or “its shrub,” or “purity,” or “separated,” or “guarded.” It is written not with the letter Z but with the Hebrew ṣade, which represents neither the sound of S nor that of Z. Nazorean, “pure.” Naphtali, “separated,” or “set apart,” or “he turned me,” or “he rolled me up.”

### O
Obed, serving.

Osanna, save, for in Greek it is said, *σῶσον δή* (“save now”). Both names, however, are to be read with the letter O lengthened.

> **Note [Col. 0842B].** Greek: *σῶσον δή*. I cannot pass over the astonishing thoughtlessness of the editors of printed books, as I have already done in six hundred places. Thus they corrupt Jerome’s text in this passage so completely that they have dared to read, against the testimony of manuscript codices, what is said in Greek: *ὡς ἀννά* or *ὡς ἰαννά*. As though *OSANNA*, or the Hebrew word, were said in Greek as *ὡς ἀννά* (*os anna*), and *os* were a word distinct from *anna*, and both were read with a lengthened letter. Good God, what a vast and confused mass of errors! The Hebrew *Osanna* (Matthew 16:9, *Ὡσαννά*) is not said in Greek to be *os anna*, but *σῶσον δή* (*soson de*), as Jerome himself testifies in his Letter to Pope Damasus, where he discussed *Osanna son of David* at length. The two names noted by Jerome should not both be referred to *Osanna*, but to the names *Obed* and *Osanna*, both of which are read with the letter O lengthened. MARTIAN.

> **Note [Col. 0845A].** Jerome himself confirms this reading in his Commentary on Daniel 1:7: “The sons of Zebedee were called sons of thunder, which is read more correctly not *Boanerges*, as most people think, but *Beneraham*.” Yet the common reading prevailed, so that Origen says in his Commentary on Matthew: “The Savior called them *Βοανεργές*, which is ‘sons of thunder,’ or ‘thunder.’” They evidently derived it from Mark 3:17: “for he was tumultuous,” and in Arabic it means “he thundered loudly.”

sons of thunder, although the corrupted form *Boanerges* has become customary. **Barsemia**,

> **Note [Col. 0845A].** “Barsemia, blind son,” etc. The manuscript codices retain the masculine pronoun *quem* (“whom”), and likewise the rest. It should be noted that the name *Barsemia*, or *Bartimaeus*, is not read today in John, but in Mark, chapter 10, verse 46. It had therefore already been transferred from Mark into John in Origen’s time. Unless it is preferable to say that the man born blind in John 9 was called *Barsemia* by certain older writers, and that some later read the name corruptly as *Bartimaeus* because they supposed him to be the son of Timaeus. Certainly, if one attends to the etymology, there is reason to acknowledge a corruption with Jerome, who teaches that *Barsemia* should be read instead of *Bartimaeus*, since in Syriac it means “blind son.” Nor am I unaware that Origen, in his Commentary on Matthew, borrowed the etymology of *Timaeus* from Greek, something like *ἀπὸ τῆς τιμῆς* (“from honor”). But it is better to adhere to Jerome, who assigned the native name of the Syriac man. MARTIAN.

blind son, which some also read corruptly as *Bartimaeus*.

> **Note [Col. 0846A].** I am less reluctant to believe that *Bartimaeus*, because he was blind from birth, was commonly called *Barsamaeus* by a slight alteration of the letters, that is, “son of blindness,” so that the name might fit the fact. But it is most correctly interpreted “son of Timaeus,” *ἀπὸ τῆς τιμῆς* (“from honor”), which also has a similar sound in Chaldean: *time*, honor, price. Origen too called *Timaeus* an eponym derived from *τῆς τιμῆς*. Moreover, it is established that many names passed from the Greeks to the Hebrews, so that there is no reason at all to suspect this reading, *Bartimaeus*, of being corrupt.

> **Note [Col. 0850A].** But Sallustius more correctly says, etc. Sallustius, in *The Jugurthine War*, where he discusses the Leptitans, mentions the word *Syrtis* in this way: “Moreover, the town is situated between two Syrtes, which received their name from their nature; for there are two gulfs near the farthest part of Africa, unequal in size but alike in character. [Note: “Ephesus, my will in her,” etc. It is not sufficiently clear how *Epheso* is rendered “my will in her”; for in that name the attached element, or first-person pronoun *my*, ought to have been expressed by a *yod*: *Ephesi*, “my will.” The letter *beth*, indicating the preposition “in,” is also missing; and the final *o* supplies the place of the masculine pronoun “him” (*eo*) among the Hebrews, not the feminine “her.” Therefore *Ephesum* and elsewhere *Epheso* are better rendered “his will.” Compare these matters with the Epistles to Timothy. MARTIAN. —Martianus rejects the pronoun “my,” as well as the words “in her,” which cannot in any way be derived from the name *Ephesi*. This defect, moreover, occurs above in the Acts and repeatedly elsewhere, almost every third word in Greek and Latin names, if one wished to pursue the matter by annotation. *Ephesus* properly means “end,” although Heraclides reports that the land was called *ἔφεσις* (*ephesis*), that is, “permission,” because Hercules had granted it to the Amazons.]

[Note: “Gaul, transferring.” We very frequently read *Galatia* in Paul’s Epistles; not so *Gaul*. By whom, then, was the name *Gaul* placed here—by Origen, by Jerome, or rather by some Gallic writer? I leave this to the conjecture of readers. MARTIAN. —As to who inserted here the name *Gaul*, which is never read in Paul’s Epistles, in place of *Galatia*, which occurs frequently, Martianus, a Gallic man, leaves the matter to the conjecture of readers. Yet there is no need for conjecture, since ancient writers clearly report that at II Timothy 4:10, where the common text reads *Κρήσκης εἰς Γαλατίαν* (“Crescens into Galatia”), certain Greek copies read *εἰς Γαλλίαν* (“into Gaul”). Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 4: *Κρίσκης μὲν ἐπὶ τὰς Γαλλίας στειλάμενος ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ (Παύλου) μαρτυρεῖται*: “Crescens, having been sent into Gaul, is attested by Paul himself.” Epiphanius likewise insists in *Against the Alogi*: *οὐκ ἐν τῇ Γαλατίᾳ ὥς τινες πλανηθέντες νομίζουσι, ἀλλ’ ἐν τῇ Γαλλίᾳ*: “Not in Galatia, as some, deceived by error, suppose, but in Gaul.” Finally, Theodoret teaches that the name *Galatia* is to be understood as *Gaul*: *Γαλατίαν τὰς Γαλλίας οὕτως ἐκάλεσεν. Οὕτω γὰρ ἐκαλοῦντο πάλαι. Οὕτω δὲ καὶ νῦν αὐτὰς ὀνομάζουσιν οἱ τῆς ἔξω παιδείας μετειληφότες*: “Paul called Gaul ‘Galatia’ in this way; for so they were formerly called, and even now those who have received foreign learning call them so.” See the first Appendix to Jerome’s book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 10: “Crescens preached in Gaul,” etc.]

Lois: *ὠφεληθείσῃ*, that is, “she who has obtained benefit.”

[Note: “Lois, *ὠφεληθείσῃ*,” etc. The Greek word is corruptly printed here and above in the published books as *ὠφεληθεῖσα*, whereas the older manuscript codices write it, in the name *Lydia*, as *ὠφεληθεῖσα*; and here they correctly use *eta* instead of final alpha, that is, *ὠφεληθείσῃ* rather than *ὠφεληθεῖσα*. The manuscript copies are also correct in other respects: in both places, namely in the Acts of the Apostles and here in the Second Epistle to Timothy, they write the name with omega at the beginning, as is proper, whereas the printed books use a short omicron. It is the feminine form of the masculine *ὠφεληθείς*, the first passive aorist from the stem *ὠφελέω*, “I help, benefit, or profit.” MARTIAN.]

Lystra: benefit of distress, or of tribulation. Luke: himself rising, or lifting up. Linus: bright, or flute-player.

### M and P

Moses: touching, or handling. Membranes: opened, or manifest. Miletus: to generate, or “whose is he?” Prisca: recognizing. Pudens: clothed with counsel.

### R and T

117 Rome: lofty, or thunder. Troas: serving. Trophimus: loosening chambers.

## TO TITUS

### A and C

Arteman: cursing, or disturbing. Apollo: wondrous. Crete: completed calling.

### N and Z

Nicopolis: offspring of my protection. Zenas: his disturbance, or disturbing him, or himself resting.

## TO PHILEMON

### A and D

Apphia: containing, or self-control, or free. Archippus: to the length of work. Demas: silent.

### E and F

Epaphras: one whom we may call “growing,” or “increase.” Philemon: wonderfully gifted, or certainly “mouth of their bread.”

### O

Onesimus: answering.

## ON THE APOCALYPSE OF JOHN

[Col. 0857]

### A

Asia: exaltation. Amen: truly, or faithfully. Asher: blessedness, or blessed. Egypt: tribulation. Armageddon ([Hebrew or other original form omitted in source]): raising up of a roof, or raising up toward what lies ahead; but more correctly, “mountain of robbers,” or “rounded mountain.”

[Note: The earlier interpretation, “raising up of a roof,” is not present in our manuscript.]

Alleluia: praise the Lord.

### B

118 Balaam: vain people. Balak: destroying. Benjamin: son of the right hand. Babylon: confusion, or translation.

### D

Devil: flowing downward. David: desirable.

### E and F

Ephesus: my will, or my counsel. Euphrates: fruitful. Philadelphia: saving one who clings to the Lord.

### G

Gad: temptation. Gog: *δῶμα*, that is, roof.

### I

Jezebel: flow of blood, or flowing with blood; but more correctly, “where is the dung heap?” Issachar: “there is a reward.” Joseph: increasing. Jesus: savior.

### L

Laodicea: tribe beloved of the Lord, or “they were in vomit.” Levi: added. Labbadon: destroying, in the sense of killing; but more correctly, “their solitary one.”

[Note: “Abaddon, destroying,” etc. *Abaddon* should be read, from the Hebrew *abad* or *ibbed*, that is, “he caused to perish.” Hence in the Apocalypse the name *Abaddon*, which signifies destruction. MARTIAN. —Martianus teaches that *Abaddon* should be restored.]

### M

Manna: “What is this?” Manasseh: forgetful, or stupefied. Michael: “Who is like God?” Magog: from the roof, that is, from the house, or “which is *δῶμα*?”

[Note: The manuscript and the old printed books read: “or which is the roof?”]

### N

Nicolaitans: pouring out (alternatively, flowing out), or the languishing Church, or the folly of the languishing Church.

[Note: “Nicolaitans, pouring out,” etc. The manuscript copies read “flowing out.” MARTIAN.]

Naphtali: conversing.

### P and R

Paulo (Apollyon): “their mouth,” or “the mouth of the trumpet.”

[Note: “Paul, their mouth,” etc. Above an *l* was corruptly added to the name *Abaddon*, which they read in this work as *Labbaddon*; here, however, they omit the *a* and *n* and change other letters, reading *Paulo* instead of *Apollyon*. MARTIAN.]

Pergamum: dividing their horns, or cutting apart the valley. 119 Reuben: behold a son, or behold in the midst.

### S and Z

Smyrna: their song. Sardis: to the prince of beauty. Satan: to the transgressor, or adversary. Simeon: hearing sorrows. Sodom: to a silent animal. Zebulun: dwelling-place of beauty.

[Note: The glosses of Aquicinctium, cited by Rosweide in his notes on St. Paulinus’s First Epistle: “Zebulun, dwelling-place of strength, or flow of night.” It is also known from the Aeolic dialect that *Zabulus* is used for the devil.]

[Note: On the Epistle of Barnabas. It should be observed that the Epistle of Barnabas was listed here in its proper order because in ancient times it was read in Christian churches for the edification of the people. MARTIAN. —The Bodleian manuscript mentioned above does not recognize the names appended below as coming from the Epistle of Barnabas.]

## ON THE EPISTLE OF BARNABAS

### A and D

Abraham: father seeing a people. Adam: man. 120 Amalek: licking people, or locust people. David: desirable.

### E and M

Eva: calamity, or woe, or certainly life. Ephraim: fruitful, or abundance. Manasseh: forgotten.

### N and R

Nahum: sprout. Rebecca: patience.

[Note: *Nave* appears to be the reading that should be restored, both because Nahum is not mentioned in the Epistle of Barnabas and because, according to Jerome himself, Nahum signifies not “sprout” but “comforter.” On the other hand, *Nave*, or *Nun*, which is the same according to the Hebrew text, is rendered by the holy Doctor as “sprout” in *Names from Exodus*, namely from a verb in the Niphal form. Saint Isidore confuses both meanings, *Etymologies* VII.8: “Nahum, sprout or comforter”; for he rebukes the city of blood and, after its overthrow, comforts Zion.]

### S

Sabbatha: rest. Zion: watchtower. Sinai: measure, commandment, or temptation. Satan: adversary, or transgressor.

[Col. 0859]

# SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, BOOK ON THE SITUATION AND NAMES OF THE HEBREW PLACES

[Note: “Book on the Situation and Names,” etc. In very many manuscript codices this little work is entitled *Book on the Distances of Places*. MARTIAN.]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0859A] 121–122 Eusebius, who received his surname from the blessed martyr Pamphilus, after the ten books of *Ecclesiastical History*; after the *Chronological Canons*, which we published in Latin; after explaining the names of the various nations, showing how they were formerly called among the Hebrews and how they are now called; [Note: After the *Chorography*. One royal codex has “after the Cosmography”; another, most incompetently, “after the Orthography.” The printed editions have “Topography.” MARTIAN. —Alternatively, “Topography.” The old edition of 1496, together with some manuscripts, has “Cosmography”; others have “Orthography.] after the *Chorography* of the land of Judea, and after a brief description of the distinct tribal allotments and of Jerusalem itself and the temple in it, finally undertook in this little work to collect for us from Holy Scripture the names of almost all the cities, mountains, rivers, villages, and various places—names which either remain the same, or were later altered, or have been corrupted in part. Therefore, following the zeal of that admirable man, we translated them according to the alphabetical order in which they are arranged in Greek. [Note: “According to the order in which they are arranged in Greek.” Consult the sense of this passage in our preceding Admonition. MARTIAN.]

We omitted what did not seem worthy of remembrance and changed many things. For I stated once and for all in the preface to the *Book of Chronology* that I am either a translator or the founder of a new work, especially since someone scarcely initiated into the first letters of learning dared to translate this same book into Latin—not in Latin style. A prudent reader will immediately discover his incompetence by comparing it with what we have translated. For just as I do not claim the lofty things for myself, so I believe that I can rise above things attached to the earth.

[Note: “For I do not claim the lofty things for myself.” Some manuscript codices, together with the earlier printed editions, read: “For I do not claim the lofty things for myself; thus I believe I can rise above what clings to the earth.” In the manuscript copies *vendico* (“claim”) is also more frequent than *vindico*. MARTIAN. —Alternatively, “what clings to the earth I can surpass.”]

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK

[Col. 0859]

## ON GENESIS

[Col. 0859B] 126 Ararat: Armenia.

[Note: “Ararat, Armenia.” In accordance with this interpretation of Jerome, the holy Doctor read the Greek as follows: *Ἀραρὰτ, ἡ Ἀρμενία. Ἐν ὄρεσιν δὲ Ἀραρὰτ ἡ κιβωτὸς καθίσαι λέγεται*: “Ararat, Armenia. For the ark is said to have settled in the mountains of Ararat.” Jerome adds “after the Flood,” to indicate more precisely the time when the ark settled in the mountains of Ararat. MARTIAN.]

For the ark is reported to have settled in the mountains of Ararat after the Flood, and traces of it are said to remain there even to this day.

[Note: “Its traces remain.” Here understand *vestigia* as “remains,” for the Greek has *λείψανα*, a plural noun properly signifying “remains,” from *λείπω*, “I leave.” Hence Jerome himself consistently translates *λείψανα* as “monuments.” MARTIAN.]

Jeremiah also mentions these mountains in his vision against Babylon. Josephus too, in the first book of *The Antiquities of the Jews*, bringing forward historians of secular literature, says:

“Observing that the earth had been freed from the Flood, Noah allowed seven further days to pass; and releasing all the animals and beasts through the opened enclosures, he himself went out with his offspring, sacrificing offerings to God and rejoicing with his children. The Armenians call this place the Exit, or Departure. For the inhabitants of those regions testify that the ark first settled there, and that certain remains of its timbers survive.”

[Note: “And rejoicing with his children.” Josephus, *Antiquities* I.3, has *συνευωχεῖτο τοῖς οἰκείοις*, “he feasted together with his household,” that is, with his family. MARTIAN.]

All who have written barbarian histories remember this ark and the Flood. One of them is Berossus the Chaldean, who, recounting the Flood, said:

“It is said that some part of this ship remains in Armenia near the mountain of the Carduchi, and that certain people carry away pieces of bitumen from it, which they use especially when they are purified and perform expiation.”

Jerome the Egyptian also wrote the antiquities of the Phoenicians in elegant language, as did Mnaseas, and many others. Nicolaus of Damascus likewise reports in the 127 ninety-sixth book:

“There is in Armenia, above Myniadem, a mountain called Beris. It is said that many people fled to it during the Flood and were saved there. Others, floating in the hollow of the ark, reached its summit, and for many generations the timbers of the ark were customarily displayed. I think that these people are none other than those whom Moses, the lawgiver of the Jews, recorded in his books.”

Achad: a city of the kingdom of Nimrod in Babylonia.

[Note: Two manuscripts have *Achar*. Eusebius has *Ἀχὰμ*, apparently through a copyist’s error. The Septuagint has *Ἀρχὰδ* in place of *Ἀκχάδ*.]

(The Hebrews say that this is a city of Mesopotamia, now called Nisibis, once besieged and captured by Lucullus, the Roman consul, and a few years ago handed over to the Persians by the emperor Jovian.)

[Note: “By the emperor Jovian.” Gennadius, in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, says the following concerning James of Nisibis: “After many years Julian entered Nisibis and, either envying the glory of the buried man [James], or because of Constantine’s faith, which he was persecuting for that reason, ordered the relics of the saint’s body to be carried out of the city. A few months later, although he was concerned with the administration of the state, the emperor Jovian, who had succeeded Julian, handed the city over to the barbarians; and to this day it remains subject to Persian rule together with its territories.” Consult Ammianus, book XXV. MARTIAN. —One manuscript reads, “which is also today called,” etc. Regarding Jovian, see Ammianus, book XXV, and Gennadius, *Catalogue*, chapter 1.]

Aggai: it lies toward the western side of Bethel, not far from it. Bethel is situated, for those traveling from Neapolis to Aelia, on the left side of the road, approximately twelve miles from Aelia; and to this day a small village, though a modest one, is shown. (A church has also been built where Jacob slept while traveling toward Mesopotamia. Hence he gave that place the name Bethel ([Hebrew form omitted in source]), that is, “house of God.”) Of Aggai, however, scarcely any small ruins remain; only the site is pointed out. It should be known that Hebrew has no letter *g* here, but the name is called *Ai* ([Hebrew form omitted in source]) and written with the letter which they call *ayin* ([Hebrew form omitted in source]).

[Col. 0861C] Astaroth-Carnaim: formerly a land of giants, on the heights of the Sodomites, whom Chedorlaomer killed. Even today there are two fortresses in Batanaea bearing this name, nine miles apart from one another, between the cities of Adara and Abila.

[Col. 0862A] 130 Arboc: in our manuscripts corruptly written *Arboc*, whereas in Hebrew it is read *arbee* ([Hebrew form omitted in source]), that is, “four,” because three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and Adam the greatest were buried there, as is written in the Book of Jesus (Joshua 14:15), although some suppose that he was placed at the site of Calvary.

This is the same place as Hebron, formerly the capital of the Philistines, the dwelling-place of giants, and a kingdom—where there was a royal residence—later belonging to David in the tribe of Judah; it was a priestly and refuge city. It lies approximately twenty-two miles south of Aelia. The oak of Abraham, also called Mamre, was displayed until the reign of King Constantius, and his mausoleum is visible at the present time. (Since a church has now been built there by our people,) all the surrounding nations superstitiously worship the place of the terebinth, because Abraham once received angels as guests beneath it. This place was first called Arbee and afterward received the name Hebron from one of Caleb’s sons. Read the *Books of Chronicles* (1 Chronicles 2:42).

[Note: Rabanus, who almost copies Jerome word for word, adds here: “It was founded seven years before the city of Tanis in Egypt.” He should have said Tanis, the most famous city of Egypt, which this place preceded by seven years.]

Ailath: at the extreme borders of Palestine, adjoining the southern desert and the Red Sea. From there one sails from Egypt to India, and from there back to Egypt. A Roman legion, called the Tenth, is stationed there.

[Note: This and what was said above are wonderfully confirmed by the recently cited *Notitia* in its final entry: “Prefect of the Tenth Legion Fretensis at Aila.” See Panciroli’s commentary on these words. Jerome, commenting on Ezekiel 47, says: “The tongue of the Red Sea, on whose shore Aila is situated, where the Roman legion and garrison now remain.”]

Formerly it was called Ailath by the ancients, but now it is called Aila.

[Note: “It is called Aila.” In several manuscripts it is here and below called *Ala*, where it says, “for those traveling to Aila from Hebron.” MARTIAN.]

There was also once a nation of the Elamites, ruled by Chedorlaomer, who is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2:9) and in the Books of Kings (1 Kings 10:17); a certain city of Palestine is written *Elam*.

131 Adama: one of the five cities of the Sodomites, destroyed together with the others.

Asason-Thamar: the Amorites once lived here, whom Chedorlaomer killed, near the wilderness of Kadesh. There is also another fortress called Thamara, separated by a day’s journey from the town of Mampsis (alternatively, Mamphis), for those traveling from Hebron to Aila; a Roman garrison is now stationed there.

[Note: “One day’s journey from Mampsis.” This passage is extremely obscure in both Greek and Latin. If, with the royal Greek manuscript, we read *διεστῶσα Μάλις ἡμέρας ὁδὸν*, “separated from Malis by a day’s journey,” I have no idea where the town called Malis was situated. But if, with Bonfrerius, we read the adverb *μόλις*, “scarcely,” instead of *μάλις*, the sentence remains suspended, and we do not understand from what place or town the fortress of Thamara is scarcely a day’s journey distant. In the Latin copies the entire disagreement concerns the name of the town from which Thamara is distant. The older and better manuscripts call it Mampsis; some call it Mammephis; others Mansis; the printed books read Memphis. But whether we decide to read Memphis or Mampsis, the same difficulty remains: finding the town which Eusebius or Jerome said was separated by a day’s journey from the fortress of Thamara, where a military garrison was stationed. Until now I have found nothing in geographical writers that might help solve this problem. But when I carefully consult Jerome or Eusebius below under the entry Arad, I have no doubt that *Malathis* should be written in place of *Mampsis*. That is precisely the town which is a day’s journey from the fortress of Thamara, as can easily be gathered from the following: “Arad, a city of the Amorites near the wilderness of Kadesh; even now a village is shown four miles from the town of Malathis and twenty miles from Hebron, in the tribe of Judah.” Therefore in the Greek Eusebius read *Μάλαθις*, not *Μάλις*, nor *μόλις* with Bonfrerius. And lest you desire still greater diligence from me, I inform you, kind reader, that Ptolemy attests the existence of a city called Malialtha in Arabia Petraea. It seems to be the same as the town Malathis, at least on account of the proximity and affinity of the name and region. Compare everything with the geographical maps of Sacred Scripture. Forgive, reader, the difficulty of these places—or, if you can discover something better, teach me; we gladly learn what we do not know. MARTIAN.]

Allus: a region of the Idumeans, now called Gabalene, near the city of Petra.

Aenan: for those traveling toward Thamna, now a deserted place near the large village of Thamna, situated between Aelia and Diospolis. There is also a spring at the aforementioned place Aena; from this it received the name Aenam, that is, “of the spring.” An idol standing there is worshiped with the greatest veneration in that region. (The Hebrews, however, assert that *Aena* does not mean “grove,” but “crossroads,” where, with a fixed gaze, one must choose one of two roads.)

[Note: Bonfrerius says: “All the manuscripts of the Septuagint Interpreters have not *Aena* but *Aenam*, or *Enan*, at Genesis 38:14, where our version has no proper name; for Jerome translates ‘at the crossroads,’ whereas the Septuagint Interpreters said ‘at the gates of Ena.’ In Hebrew it is ‘at the entrance of Henaiim.’ It is disputed to this day whether the final word is a proper or a common noun, just as we stated at that place. Taken as a common noun, it can signify ‘two springs,’ or ‘two eyes,’ or two kinds of sight, as at a crossroads, when someone hesitates and is uncertain which way to go. Whatever the case may be, names are often given to places from their character and circumstances, becoming proper or quasi-proper names; this may have happened here, and it is entirely plausible that this is the same place called Enaim in the tribe of Judah at Joshua 15:34, which later grew into a city.”]

Areaatad: a place beyond the Jordan where Jacob was once mourned, at the third milestone from Jericho and two miles from the Jordan, now called Bethgla.

[Note: “Area-tad, a place beyond the Jordan,” etc. Eusebius omitted this very famous place, although it occurs twice in Genesis 50:10–11 in the Septuagint. MARTIAN.]

[Note: Josephus says that this distance is sixty stadia, that is, seven and a half miles. Procopius of Gaza agrees with Jerome in almost the same words in his commentary on Genesis 50. Learned men suggest that from this passage the gap in the Eusebian text can also conveniently be filled.]

[Note: A manuscript of Regina reads *Bethacla*; shortly afterward, in place of the place-name, I prefer *house*.]

It is interpreted as “place of the circle,” because there, following the custom of mourners, they went around in a circle at Jacob’s funeral.

## ON EXODUS

Aelim: the camp of the children of Israel and a place in the wilderness where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees, which Moses found after departing from the Red Sea.

(Aelus: in the wilderness, where the children of Israel encamped.)

134 ## ON NUMBERS AND DEUTERONOMY

Aseroth: part of the wilderness where Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses. The Avvites once lived in Aseroth as far as the city of Gaza. (The Hebrews, however, think that these places should be called not Aseroth but Aserim.)

Asemona: the camp of the children of Israel in the wilderness.

[Col. 0864A] Ahetharim: Aquila and Symmachus interpreted it as “the way of the spies,” where battle was fought in the wilderness against the Canaanite who had advanced from the south against Israel.

[Note: “Ahetharim,” etc. Here the Greek words differ somewhat from the Latin interpretation. MARTIAN.]

Ahie, also called Achalgai: Symmachus interprets this as “in the hills.” It lies opposite the former Moab, now Areopolis, toward the east.

Arnon: a certain crag rising high in the territory of the Amorites between Moab and the Amorites. Moab is a city of Arabia, now called Areopolis. The inhabitants of that region point out a valley sunk into a very steep and frightening precipice, which many to this day call Arnonas. It extends northward from Areopolis; military garrisons distributed throughout it testify that its entrance was full of bloodshed and terror. This region formerly belonged to the Moabites, and afterward Sihon, king of the Amorites, acquired it by right of war. The land of the children of Israel beyond the Jordan also begins at Arnon and extends as far as the mountains of Hermon and Lebanon.

Ar: a place or town of Arnona, called *Er* by the Septuagint Interpreters with a lengthened vowel.

[Note: “With a lengthened vowel, it is called Er.” An old manuscript of Colbert corruptly reads *Aer*, whereas in the Septuagint at Numbers 21:15 it is written *Ἤρ*, *Er*, with the letter eta; this is what Jerome noted when he said that among the Septuagint it is called *Er* with a lengthened vowel. MARTIAN.]

Aesimon: a desert place; indeed, the word itself signifies uncultivated and deserted land.

[Note: “Abel-shittim, a place in the wilderness,” etc. Eusebius and Jerome do not agree here. The former places Abel-shittim *κατὰ δυσμὰς Μωάβ*, that is, “toward” or “opposite the west of Moab,” whereas the latter places it south of the Moabites. Nor does Bonfrerius remove the difficulty or disagreement by saying that the genitive “of the Moabites” should be joined with “wilderness,” not with the other phrase, “toward the south.” For however we read it, Abel-shittim will be west according to Eusebius and south according to Jerome. But if Jerome’s commentary on Joel 3 is consulted, we find the following written by him concerning Abel-shittim: “It is a place,” he says, “near Livias, across from the Dead Sea, six miles distant from it; where Israel once fornicated with the Midianites,” and so forth. From this we can reconcile Eusebius with Jerome by saying that Abel-shittim, with respect to the wilderness or plains of Moab, lay to the west, but with respect to the city of Livias, faced south toward the Moabites. Consult the geographical maps. Forgive, reader, the difficulty of the places—or, if you can discover something better, teach me; we gladly learn what we do not know. MARTIAN.]

Abel-shittim: a place in the wilderness south of the Moabites.

135 Azor, or Jazer: the boundary of the city of Ammon, now called Philadelphia, separating it from the territory of the Amorites. Approximately eight miles to the west of it, the village of Jazer still exists to the present day.

Aroer, a town of the Moabites situated on the bank of the torrent Arnon, formerly possessed by the very ancient people called Ommim [Note: “The very ancient people Ommim.” The more recent Colbertinus manuscript reads “the most depraved people Ommiim”; some read Ummim. The very ancient Corb. no. 281 has “by the most depraved people Omim.” MARTIAN.], and afterward retained by the sons of Lot, that is, by the Moabites, after they had overthrown the earlier inhabitants. It is shown even today on the summit [Note: Bonfrere denies this point in vain, and in vain argues that Aroer was situated on the riverbank, not on the summit of a mountain. “I do not see,” says Reland, “why a city situated on a mountain could not be said to lie on the bank of a river if the river flows at the foot of that mountain, since the city may extend from the summit all the way to the foot, and may at once rest against the mountain’s side and stand on the bank of the river. See below, under Aruir.”] of that mountain; and the torrent, descending through precipitous ravines, flows into the Dead Sea. Aroer fell by lot to the tribe of Gad, opposite Rabbah.

Astaroth, the ancient city of Og, king of Bashan, where the giants lived; afterward it fell by lot to the tribe of Manasseh, in the region of Batanaea, and is separated from the Arabian city Adra by six miles. Adra, moreover, is twenty-five miles from Bostra. We have also spoken above of Astaroth-Carnaim.

The Lookout of the Fields, a mountain of the Moabites, to which Balak son of Sephor brought Balaam the diviner in order to curse Israel from its summit. Because of its steep precipice it is called “the cut-off,” and it rises above the Dead Sea not far from the Arnon.

Araboth of Moab, where the people were counted for the second time. Aquila interprets it as “the lowlands” or “the level places of Moab”; for he has the practice of interpreting *erēmōs*—that is, “wilderness”—as “level” (*homalēn*, that is, “even” and “plain”), because of its flatness. Symmachus, finally, translated Araboth of Moab as “the plains of Moab.” It is a place still existing beside Mount Phogor, on the road from Liviada to Esebon of Arabia, opposite Jericho, and is so called.

[Col. 0865C] [Note: Araba, as above, etc. In the earlier printed books, and in Bonfrere, this passage has been joined most corruptly to what precedes. MARTIAN.] Araba: Aquila translated it, as above, as “plain”; Symmachus, sometimes “open country,” sometimes “uninhabitable”; Theodotion, “western.”

Altharoth, formerly a city of the Amorites beyond the Jordan, [Col. 0866A] which afterward fell by lot to the tribe of Gad. A son of Salma, or Salmon (another reading: Solamon), was also called Atharoth, as is written in Chronicles.

Ataroth-Sophan, also a city of the tribe of Gad.

Arad, a city of the Amorites near the wilderness of Kadesh, and still shown today as a village [Note: “From the town of Malathis,” etc. The Regius manuscript, the most recent of all, no. 3629, reads Mallatis here. We have discussed this town more fully in our notes under the entry Asasonthamar. MARTIAN.] four miles from the town of Malathis and twenty from Hebron, in the tribe of Judah.

Asemona, a city in the wilderness, south of Judaea, separating Egypt from the allotment of the tribe of Judah, which extends as far as the sea. Above I also listed Asemona, the camp of the children of Israel.

[Note: Another reading: Aorabi, in Bonfrere and Clericus; Adorabi. In Hebrew it is , in Greek Ἀκραββείμ. See Reland under Oreb.] Acrabbi, the eastern boundary of the province of Judaea, facing the tribe of Judah. There is still a large village of this name, nine miles eastward from Neapolis, on the descent toward the Jordan and Jericho, through the district called Acrabittene. It is also a frontier of the Amorites, called Acrabbin; from this place the tribe of Naphtali did not drive out the foreigners, as it is written in the Book of Judges.

Asadada, the northern boundary facing Judah.

Arad, likewise a boundary of Judah, twenty miles south of Hebron; it was mentioned above.

Asarenam, the northern boundary of Judaea.

Asernai, likewise a boundary of Judaea.

[Note: This is the same as Belas; therefore Bonfrere is mistaken, as Martianay himself points out, when he insists that there is no trace of Arbela in the Writer. See Bela.] Arbela, a boundary of Judaea, facing the rising sun. There is still a village called Arbel beyond the Jordan, in the territory of the Palestinian city Pella, and another place of this name in a very extensive plain, nine miles from the town of Legion.

[Note: Aulon is not Greek, etc. Jerome deliberately warns here that Aulon is not a Greek word, as some in his time thought, but Hebrew. It is the same word as Elon, read by the Septuagint as Aulon. Had John Clericus attended to this in his Dissertation on the Salt Statue, he would not have ineptly rebuked Jerome for the learned warning found here. Jerome prefaced his observation because he knew well that *aulōn* is elsewhere a Greek word meaning a long, narrow, hollow place. But in the present Book of Hebrew Places, Aulon is the proper name of a certain region of Judaea in which there are the notable cities expressed here by name. MARTIAN. —Indeed, it is commonly regarded as Greek, not Hebrew; for this reason Clericus eagerly seized the opportunity supplied by this passage to disparage Jerome, whom everyone admires as a master of three languages, and accused him of ignorance. Rhenferd, by contrast, attributes the error to a copyist and proposes that, through the slight transposition of two little words, the text should read: “not Hebrew, as some think, but it is a Greek word.” Jerome’s intention deserves praise, though his example should by no means be followed. I think that Jerome expressly noted that the name was not Greek because, with exactly the same meaning—namely, “valley”—it might at once appear to be derived from the Greek *Aulōn apo tēs aulēs* (“valley from a courtyard”), but was not derived from the Greeks. Rather, among the Hebrews the name, derived from concavity, would have the meaning of a very great valley. Nor is it necessary to insist that the word be used in Scripture in this sense, as Clericus presses so strongly; it is enough if, in ordinary and common speech, especially in a later age, that plain and valley were so called by the inhabitants—not, strictly speaking, by Greeks. Jerome himself clearly testifies to this in Epistle 73, to Evangelus, on Melchizedek, no. 9, in words which critics on both sides ought to have considered, since they stand above the exception of preconceived opinion and belief: “The Valley of the King, or, as the Seventy translated it, the plain, which TODAY THE PALESTINIANS CALL AULON.” Let Clericus now prove that the Palestinians did not give the place its native name, but a Greek one. What does it matter if it also sounds Greek? Nor do I object if he rebukes Martianay for defending a good cause less effectively than he might have done; no one should tolerate Jerome’s being unjustly accused of ignorance.] Aulon (it is not a Greek word, as some think, but a Hebrew one): a great valley and plain extending to an immense length is so called. It is enclosed on both sides by successive and connected mountains, which begin at Lebanon and beyond and extend as far as the wilderness of Paran. In Aulon itself—that is, in the valley plain—there are notable cities: Scythopolis, Tiberias, and the lake beside it; also Jericho, the Dead Sea, and the surrounding regions, through which the Jordan flows midway, rising from the springs of Paneas and emptying into the Dead Sea.

Amalekites, a region in the wilderness south of Judaea, beyond the city of Petra, for those traveling toward Aila. Scripture also recalls it, saying: “Amalek dwells in the land of the South” (Num. XIII, 20). Another Canaanite also lived near it, and fought against the children of Israel in the wilderness. Of these it is written: “But Amalek and the Canaanite dwell in the valley” (Num. XIV, 25).

Araba: Aquila interprets it as “plain,” and Symmachus as “level,” as stated above. There is also another village called Araba in the territory of Diocaesarea, formerly called Saphorine, and another three miles west of Scythopolis.

142 Amman, now Philadelphia [Note: Josephus, *Antiquities*, book I, chapter II; Stephanus of Byzantium, Ptolemy, Pliny, and others refer this city to Coelesyria. The name of the region easily varied according to whether a Syrian or an Arab possessed it.], a distinguished city of Arabia, where the Raphaim formerly lived, an ancient people whom the sons of Lot killed, dwelling in their place in Amman.

Argob, the region of Og, king of Bashan, beyond the Jordan, which fell by lot to half the tribe of Manasseh. There is still a village near the Arabian city Gerasa, fifteen miles west of it, called Arga; Symmachus interprets the name as “measure.”

Asedoth, a city of the Amorites, which fell by lot to the tribe of Reuben. With the additional surname Asedoth-Phasga it is called; in our language this sounds like “the cut-off.”

Abarim, the mountain on which Moses died. It is also said to be Mount Nabau, in the land of Moab opposite Jericho, above the Jordan, on the ridge of Phasga. It is shown to those ascending from Liviada to Esebon, beside Mount Phogor, still retaining its ancient name; the surrounding region is still called Phasga from it.

Avoth-Jair, which is interpreted as ἐπαύλεις ἰαὶρ, “the farmsteads of Jair.” This is Bashan, in which there are villages—sixty in number—on Mount Gilead, which fell by lot to half the tribe of Manasseh. That place is not called Golam, in the land of Batanaea.

## From the Book of Joshua

Antilibanus: the places above Lebanon, [Note: “Facing the eastern region,” etc. The Colbertinus manuscript, of excellent quality, reads “facing the eastern region.” Several other manuscript codices do likewise. MARTIAN.] facing the eastern side, are called Antilibanus, around the region of the city Damascus, which fell by lot to the tribe of Manasseh.

Azeca, a city of the Canaanites in the territory of the tribe of Judah, as far as which Joshua pursued the five kings. It is still called the village Azeca, between Eleutheropolis and Aelia.

Aialon, a valley and precipice over which, when Joshua once prayed, the moon stood still, near the village still called Ailon, east of Bethel, three miles from it, not far from the cities Gabaa and Rama. (The Hebrews, however, assert that Aialon is a village near Nicopolis, two miles distant on the road to Aelia.)

Achor (in Hebrew *emec- achor*, which means “Valley of Tumult” or “of Troubling,” because Israel there made tumult and was troubled), where they once stoned Achan [Note: It was not Achor, and still less Achan, as Jerome prefers, but Achar, as the Greek copies of Scripture, the Latin copies generally, and editions in all languages have it; otherwise the allusion made in Hebrew at Joshua VII, 25, cannot stand. Again, Jerome reads Achor in his commentary on Micah IV according to Eusebius; but there it is not the name of a person, but of a valley.] because of the theft of the ban. It is north of Jericho, and is still so called by the inhabitants of that region. (The prophet Hosea mentions it [Hos. II, 15].)

Asedoth, another city of this name—not the one mentioned above, although it bears the same name—which Joshua once captured after killing its king.

Asor, the city of the kingdom of Jabin, which Joshua alone burned because it was the capital of all the kingdoms of the Philistines. There is still another village called Asor, in the territory of Ascalon, east of it, which fell by lot to the tribe of Judah. Scripture also mentions it (Josh. XIII, 15), distinguishing it from the older city by calling it “the new Asor.”

Aermon, the region of the Hivites, which Joshua conquered. (The Hebrew from whom I learned the Scriptures by reading aloud, however, asserts that Mount Aermon rises above Paneas; the Hivites and Amorites once held it. From there, for the sake of pleasure, summer snows are now brought to Tyre.)

Ahalae, a mountain which Aquila interprets as “the dividing mountain,” and Symmachus as “the smooth mountain,” that is, clear or slippery.

Aermon, the mountain of the Amorites, of which mention has just been made. The Phoenicians call it Sanior [Note: The Phoenicians call it Sanior. So also in the Septuagint at Deut. III, 9. In Hebrew and the other Oriental editions, however, instead of Sanior we read Sarion, and subsequently Sanir. MARTIAN.], while the Amorites called it Sanir. On its summit, it is said, there is a notable temple [Note: Eusebius certainly does not report that a *hierón*, a temple, was built there, but that the mountain itself was honored as sacred, or worshiped by the nations as something sacred. There was an old fable that, when the angels desired the daughters of men and descended from heaven, they gathered especially on this very lofty mountain. See Saint Hilary on Psalm CXXXII. In what follows, Jerome explains the matter according to his own sense rather than that of Eusebius.] regarded by the pagans as a place of worship, facing Paneas and Lebanon. The land of the children of Israel beyond the Jordan, toward the rising sun, also extends from the precipice of the Arnon as far as Mount Aermon.

Anob, a city which Joshua conquered. There is still a village near Diospolis, approximately four miles [Note: “Toward the eastern region.” One manuscript codex of our monastery of Saint Theodoric near Rheims reads “toward the western region.” MARTIAN.] east of it, called Bethoannaba. (Most, however, assert that it lies eight miles away and is called Bethannaba.)

Asdod, in the allotment of the tribe of Judah, now called Azotus. The giants called Anakim were left there, and it is still a notable town of Palestine.

Ader, the city which Joshua conquered after killing its king.

Aphec, also a city which Joshua conquered after slaughtering its king.

Acsaph, against whose king Joshua is also described as having fought. Today it is called the little village Chasalus, eight miles from Diocaesarea, at the foot of Mount Tabor, in the plains.

Accaron, in the tribe of Dan (or, as I think, in the tribe of Judah) [Note: Originally assigned to the tribe of Judah, Josh. XV, 45; afterward assigned to the Danite tribe, Josh. XIX, 43.], on the left of the Canaanites. It was one of the five former satrapies of Palestine. It was indeed assigned to the tribe of Judah, but was not held by it because the tribe could not expel the former inhabitants. Even today there is a large village of Jewish inhabitants called Accaron, between Azotus and Jamnia, facing east. (Some think Accaron was the Tower of Strato, later called Caesarea.)

Azotus, the Asdod mentioned above, still an important municipality of Palestine and one of the five cities of the Philistines. It was assigned to the tribe of Judah but was not retained by it, because it could in no way expel the former inhabitants.

147 Ascalon, a distinguished city of Palestine, which itself was formerly one of the five satrapies of the Philistines. It was indeed separated by lot for the tribe of Judah, but was not retained by it, because the tribe could not overcome its inhabitants.

Apheca, the boundary [Note: Namely, of the Transjordanian region occupied by the Amorite; a large part of it was given to the tribe of Reuben. Thus Bonfrere disagrees with Eusebius and Jerome on slight grounds, although they state that Apheca was the boundary of the Amorites in the tribe of Reuben.] of the Amorites beyond the Jordan, in the allotment of the tribe of Reuben. There is still a large fortress called Apheca near Hippos, a city of Palestine [Note: Near the city of Hippos in Palestine. The printed books present the corrupt reading “near a town of Palestine”; the manuscripts, consistently with the Greek and with the Writer’s meaning, read “near Hippos, a city of Palestine,” as we have published it.], however.

[Note: The complete name appears to be Baalgad, Josh. II, 17, and XIII, 5. The Hieronymian codices certainly less correctly have Agad, of which there is no mention in Scripture.] Agad, situated at the foot of Mount Aermon.

Aemath, a city which fell by lot to Reuben. There is now a village called Amathus beyond the Jordan, twenty-one miles south of Pella. There is also another village near Gadara called Amatha, where hot springs burst forth. In the Books of Kings it is also written: “From the entrance of Aemath even to the sea of Araba” (3 Kings VIII, 65), that is, of the wilderness, which is the Dead Sea. (Investigating the matter, I found that Aemath [Note: Jerome remains consistent with himself below under Emath concerning the Books of Kings, and confirms the point in Epistle 129 to Dardanus, no. 5. When Bonfrere wonders that Jerome calls this city a city of Coelesyria, since all Coelesyria seems to have been outside the boundaries of the Israelites’ land, Reland replies that Jerome does not in fact regard it as lying within the Israelite land; and even if it had been within its boundaries, it could nevertheless have been called a city of Coelesyria, following the example of earlier writers, especially Josephus.] is called a city of Coelesyria, and is now called Epiphania in Greek.)

Ammon, beyond the Jordan, in the tribe of Gad. This is Ammam, of which we spoke above: the distinguished Arabian city Philadelphia.

Addara, in the tribe of Judah, near the wilderness. There is also another village in the territory of Diospolis, around the Thamnitic region, which is still called by this name from the village Thamna.

Accarca, a village situated in the wilderness, in the possession of the tribe of Judah. Symmachus translates it as “pavement.”

Achor, in the tribe of Judah; it was discussed above as well.

Adommim, formerly a small village, now ruins in the allotment of the tribe of Judah. The place is still called Maledomim (in Greek, ἀνάβασις πύῤῥων; in Latin it may be called “the ascent of the red-haired” or “of the reddening,” because of the blood frequently shed there by robbers). It is on the boundary of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, for those descending from Aelia to Jericho; there is also a military fortress there (for the protection of travelers). The Lord also recalls this bloody and murderous place in the parable of the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho.

Amam, in the tribe of Judah.

Aser, in the tribe of Judah. There is still a very large village called Bethasan for those traveling from Azotus to Ascalon.

Asarsual, in the tribe of Judah.

Ain, in the tribe of Judah, a city set apart for the priests. There is still a village called Bethennim, two miles from the Terebinth—that is, from Abraham’s tent—and four miles from Hebron.

Asthaol, in the tribe of Judah. A small village called Astho still remains between Azotus and Ascalon.

Asna, in the tribe of Judah.

Adollam, in the tribe of Judah. There is still a substantial village of this name east of Eleutheropolis, ten miles from it.

Adithaim, in the allotment of the tribe of Judah. There is also a village called Adia near Gaza, and another called Aditha near Diospolis, approximately toward the eastern region.

[Note: Adasa in the tribe of Judah. Adasa is omitted from the Greek codex of Eusebius, although he had included it, as is clear from Jerome’s observation, in which Eusebius is reproved for placing the Gophnite region in the tribe of Judah. MARTIAN.] Adasa, in the tribe of Judah, still a village near Gophna. (But I wonder how he could have placed the Gophnite region in the tribe of Judah, since it is clear from the Book of Joshua that it fell by lot to the tribe [Note: Nevertheless Bonfrere still doubts this, and would rather place Gophna in the tribe of Benjamin—quite wrongly, and contrary to all the ancient records. Consult the map.] of Ephraim.)

Ather, in the tribe of Judah.

Asan, in the tribe of Judah. There is still a village called Bethasan, belonging to Aelia [Note: Eusebius adds πρὸς δυσμὰς, “toward the west,” and “at the sixteenth mile” instead of “at the fifteenth.”], fifteen miles from it.

Asena, in the tribe of Judah.

Agziph, in the tribe of Judah.

Anab, in the tribe of Judah; it is still a village in the territory of Eleutheropolis. There is also another large Jewish village called Anea in the Daroma, south of Hebron, nine miles from it.

Astemoe, a village in the tribe of Judah, itself also inhabited by Jews, in the Daroma, north of the place Anem.
