Anim, in the tribe of Judah. There is a village called Anea, facing east, beside the other one mentioned above; all its inhabitants are Christians.

Apheca, in the tribe of Judah.

Ammata, in the tribe of Judah.

Arebba, in the tribe of Judah.

Atharoth [Note: The old edition reads “against Ramma.”], near Ramma, in the tribe of Joseph.

Atharoth, a city of the tribe of Ephraim. Today a village north of Sebaste, four miles from it, is called Atharus.

Adar, a city of the tribe of Ephraim.

Aser, a city of the tribe of Manasseh. A village is still pointed out to those descending from Neapolis to Scythopolis, fifteen miles along the public road.

Atharoth, a city of the tribe of Benjamin. There are two Atharoth not far from Aelia.

Anathoth, a city in the allotment of Benjamin, set apart for the priests, three miles from Aelia. The prophet Jeremiah was from there.

Addar, a city in the allotment of Benjamin.

Aelmon, a city of the tribe of Benjamin, set apart for the priests.

Amec-Casis—that is, “the valley of Casis”—in the tribe of Benjamin.

[Note: The name Avim, for which Bonfrere has Anim; the Eusebian codices do not recognize it. Instead, a little farther below they have Ἄλφ, which is absent from Jerome.] Avim, in the tribe of Benjamin.

Aphra, in the tribe of Benjamin. There is still a village [Note: Our manuscript and the Queen’s manuscript read Efraim. In the *Notitia Imperii*, the Twelfth Valerian Cohort is called Afro.] called Effrem, five miles east of Bethel.

Amoeniam, in the tribe of Benjamin.

Aphni, in the tribe of Benjamin.

[lacuna]

Arim, in the tribe of Benjamin. There is also a village near Diospolis, still called [Note: It is called Bethariph. The manuscript codex of the Fathers of Saint Dominic at Toulouse retains Bechariph instead of Betariph. MARTIAN. —The printed and manuscript Hieronymian books prefer this reading. Bonfrere, however, wants it rewritten Betharim, so that it may have some affinity with the word Arim. See whether it may be Betaris or Betarus, which is placed between Caesarea and Diospolis in the Antonine Itinerary.] Betariph.

Amsa, in the tribe of Benjamin.

Asar, in the tribe of Simeon.

Asan, in the tribe of Simeon.

154 Amarchabob, in the tribe of Simeon.

Ain, a city in the tribe of Judah or Simeon, set apart for the priests.

Asenna, in the tribe of Simeon.

Amathar, in the tribe of Zebulun.

Anua, in the tribe of Zebulun. There is also another village called Anua, ten miles from Neapolis on the road to Aelia.

Ananthon, in the tribe of Zebulun.

Aschaseluth, a city of the tribe of Issachar. There is also a village called Chasalus near Mount Tabor, in the plains, eight miles east of Diocaesarea, as we stated above.

Aphraim, a city of the tribe of Issachar. Today there is a village called Affarea, six miles north of Legion [Note: “Toward the north.” The earlier printed books contain the greatest confusion here concerning the places and names. We have completely removed it with the help of the manuscripts already mentioned, especially one very ancient Colbertinus; and, like all the other restorations in this edition, this correction has been found most certain and secure by comparing the Latin manuscript codices with the Greek text of Eusebius. MARTIAN.].

Anerith, in the allotment of the tribe of Issachar.

Aemes, in the allotment of the tribe of Issachar.

Acsaph, in the tribe of Asher.

Alimelech, in the allotment of Asher.

[Col. 0873A] Amath, in the tribe of Asher.

Abdon, in the tribe of Asher, a city set apart for the Levites.

Aniel, in the tribe of Asher. [Note: This is a conspicuous error, which Rhenferd thinks entered the text already in Jerome’s own age; the very faulty writing of the Vatican codex itself reveals it and indicates how it may be corrected. It is known from other evidence, and especially from Eusebius’ own testimony under the entry Bethanath, that Eusebius treated the word Anea under a separate heading. There, speaking again of Bethanea, he says: “which above we also listed under the name ANEA.” Indeed, what he says above clearly points to this very passage; nowhere else under the letter A does he mention Bethanea and its situation, or the health-giving waters found there, in separate sections. There should therefore be no doubt that Anaea, which is nowhere listed in this book, originally stood here in its proper place, and that through the carelessness of copyists it easily dropped out because of the occurrence of the same letters in the expression *baito Anaia*, a customary scribal error. Thus what follows after “Anēr, of the allotment of Asher”—“the village Betoanaia,” etc.—has been joined rashly and does not belong to the name Anēr or Aniel. This is indicated first by the Vatican codex, which after “Asēr” places a little line lying apart, marked on both sides with vermilion dots, to show that the heading ends there. It then begins Ἀναιὰ, quite correctly, so that a separate heading begins from that name. But the rest has been scattered and wrongly arranged: after an intervening space the word *kōmē*, “village,” is brought back from the preceding verse, followed by *baito Kaisareias*, etc. Nevertheless we learn from this that Anea had a separate heading, which can readily be restored to its original integrity. Eusebius must have written:

Ἀναιὰ (κλήρου Ἀσὴρ, καὶ ἐστίν ) κώμη βαιτοαναιὰ Καισαρείας etc. (“Anea [of the allotment of Asher, and it is] the village Betoanaea of Caesarea, etc.”)

The first two words, “of the allotment of Asher,” are demanded by the sequence itself, and Rhenferd therefore wrongly supplies “of the tribe of Naphtali,” since it is clear that Eusebius does not interrupt the sequence of the tribes but continually orders the names according to their succession; nearly all those transcribed from Joshua prove this. The words καί ἐστι, “and it is,” are likewise required by the sense. What, then, shall we say of the Hieronymian codices, which it is scarcely credible were corrupted in the same place and by precisely the same error? I say that the word Asher deceived the Latin copyist just as it had deceived the Greek one. I do not deny that this is remarkable, although the lapse could readily have arisen from the greater similarity of the words Aniel and Anea, or Ἀνεὶρ and Ἀναιὰ, than in the other cases. My manuscript omits the whole of Aniel, so that you may understand that the only cause of the hallucination was the occurrence of the word Asher. Surely no one should accept Rhenferd’s claim that this error had entered the Eusebian exemplar already in Jerome’s time: how could Saint Jerome have failed to notice what is immediately apparent to anyone that the text is corrupt? Nor should anyone accept the proposal of this otherwise learned man, and highly skillful in emending several passages of Eusebius, that the passages concerning the Jewish village Anea under the entry Anab and the Christian Anea under Anim should be joined together and read in one continuous sequence.] There is a village called Betoaenea, fifteen miles from Caesarea, situated on a mountain toward the east, where there are also said to be health-giving baths.

Achran, in the tribe of Asher.

Amon, in the tribe of Asher.

155 Accho, now called Ptolemais, in the allotment of Asher; the tribe could not expel its former inhabitants.

Achziph, in the tribe of Asher, where foreigners remained. This is Ecdippa, nine miles from Ptolemais on the road to Tyre.

Amma, in the allotment of Asher.

[Col. 0873B] Aphec, in the allotment of Asher, where the former inhabitants remained.

Addemme, in the tribe of Naphtali.

Assemdim, in the tribe of Naphtali.

Amath, in the tribe of Naphtali.

[Note: Eusebius listed it in this order, and two of our Hieronymian manuscripts omit it. Martianay incorrectly placed Adami after Asor.]

Adami, in the tribe of Naphtali.

Asor, in the tribe of Naphtali, which is said to have been laid waste by the king of the Assyrians.

[Col. 0874A] Azanoth, the boundary of Naphtali. There is still a village belonging to the region of Diocaesarea, in the plains.

Aialon, a city in the allotment of Dan, set apart for the Levites. Today there is a village called Alus [Note: The manuscripts and printed books have hitherto incorrectly read “another village” instead of Alus, as we have also corrected below.], not far from Nicopolis. It should be known that for Aialon the Septuagint translators rendered: “Where the bears were.”

## From the Book of Judges

Arad is the city in which the sons of [Note: The Queen’s manuscript reads “the sons of Jobab,” in agreement with the Greek. Eusebius, however, said: “the sons of Jethor, son of Jobab.” See Judges I, 16.] Obab, Moses’ father-in-law, lived in the midst of Israel.

Areth, the spring beside which Gideon encamped.

Arisoth, the city of Sisera, the commander of Jabin. There is still a very large village called Jabis beyond the Jordan, six miles from the city of Pella, on the road to Gerasa.

[Col. 0874B] Ares, [Note: In one Complutensian manuscript the Septuagint has Ἄρες at Judges I, 35. Aquila translated it as δρυμῶν, “of wooded places.” A Coislinian Hexaplaric codex cited by Montfaucon has δρυμῶνος, “of a wooded place,” without the translator’s name. From this the lacuna in Eusebius can easily be filled.] the ascent of Ares. Aquila interprets it as “of wooded places”; Symmachus, “of mountains.”

[Note: This is not, as Bonfrere thinks, the same place that was called Aroer above in Joshua. That one was the boundary of the Moabites and Amorites at the Arnon; this one belonged to the Ammonites, whose region occupied the other part of Sihon’s kingdom. The former is mentioned in Judges XI, 33, the latter in Joshua XIII, 16; indeed, in that same chapter both Aroers are described. The first is described in verse 16 as “Aroer, which is on the bank of the river Arnon”; ours in verse 25 is called “Aroer, which is before Rabbah.” Again, Bonfrere unjustly blames either Eusebius or Jerome for stating that this place itself, Aruir, where Jephthah fought, was a village north of Aelia, or Jerusalem. After completing the entry on Aruir, they mention another village of the same name situated north of Aelia: Eusebius places it at the sixth mile, Jerome at the twentieth. See above under Aroer.] Aruir, where Jephthah fought. It is still a village situated on a mountain, twenty miles north of Aelia.

158 Arima, where Scripture reports that Abimelech sat.

[Col. 0875A] Ajalim, a city in the land of Zebulun, from which came that Ajalon who judged the people of Israel.

Abel of the Vineyards, where Jephthah fought, in the land of the children of Ammon. Even now, seven miles from Philadelphia, a village called Abela can be seen, planted with vineyards. There is also another city called Abela, rich in wine, twelve miles east of Gadara; and a third Abela in Phoenicia, between Damascus and Paneas.

## From the Books of Kings

Armathem-Sophim, the city of Elkanah and Samuel, in the Thamnitic region, near Diospolis, from which came Joseph, who in the Gospels is said to have been from Arimathea.

Abenezer, which means “stone of help,” or “helping stone.” It is the place from which the Philistines took the ark of the covenant, between Aelia and Ascalon, near the village Bethsamis.

Aphes-Dommim, where Saul fought. Aquila translated it as “in the territory of Dommim.”

Annegeb, which Aquila translated as “the south,” and Symmachus as “the region of the south.”

Arith, where David sat. It is a village called Arath, west of Aelia.

Ahialim, which Aquila translated as “of deer,” and Theodotion as “the stones of deer.”

Aendor, which is in Jezreel, where the children of Israel, preparing themselves for battle, set up camp. There is still a large village called Aendor near Mount Tabor, four miles south of it.

[Col. 0875C] Aphec, near Aendor of Jezreel, where Saul fought.

Arma, to which place David sent a share of the spoil.

Athach, to this place also David sent a portion of the booty.

159 Amma, for those traveling into the wilderness toward Gabaon.

Aethon-Adasai, for which Symmachus gave “the lower road.”

The threshing floor of Orne: this is Jerusalem.

Assur, a city of Judaea which Solomon built.

Abelmaula, the city of one of Solomon’s princes, from which the prophet Elisha also came. It is now a village in Aulon, mentioned above, ten miles from Scythopolis, called Bethaula, toward the south. Abelmea is also now the name of a small village between Neapolis and Scythopolis.

Avoth-Jair, the city of one of Solomon’s commanders.

Ailath, on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom, of which we also spoke above.

Aheloth, which Azariah built.

[Col. 0876A] Aenda, whose conqueror and destroyer was King Asa.

Aziongaber, at this place the fleet of Jehoshaphat was battered by the violence of a storm. It is said to be Essia itself, not far from Aila on the Red Sea.

Alleabar-Gozan, the names of rivers in the land of the Medes, to whose mountains Israel was led captive.

Abana, the river of Damascus.

Aopsithe, or Aphusoth, which Aquila translated as “into liberty.”

Aian, which the king of the Assyrians conquered.

Aia, a place in the region of the Assyrians.

Amech, a region of the Assyrians.

Asyma, a town in the land of Judaea, built by those who had come there from Emath.

[Col. 0876B] Arcem: Josephus reports that this is Petra, the distinguished city of Palestine.

Adramelech, an idol of the Assyrians, which the Samaritans also worshiped.

Aroniim, according to Isaiah (chapter XV), the name of a road in the vision against Moab. Aquila rendered it Oronaim, and Symmachus Orannim.

Agallim, also mentioned by Isaiah in the vision against Moab. There is now a village called Aegalim in the southern part of Areopolis, eight miles from it.

Aelim, the well of Dimon; Isaiah also recalls this place in the same vision.

Ariel: Isaiah also mentions this (XXIX, 1), which Aquila and Symmachus translated as “lion of God.” Some think this is Areopolis, because even now an idol called Ariel is worshiped there, named ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἄρεως—that is, “from Mars”—and hence they suppose the city received its name. (But it seems to me, in accordance with the context and wording of the prophecy, that Ariel there allegorically signifies Jerusalem, or the Temple—that is, “lion of God,” perhaps because it was a kingdom and powerful. This is discussed more fully in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.)

[Note: [Col. 0875D] The *Hebrew Questions* on Isaiah do not survive; if they were ever published by Jerome, they were lost through the injustice of time, to the very great detriment of the republic of letters and of the Church of Christ. MARTIAN. —See what we have said more than once elsewhere, and in the general Preface, concerning these *Hebrew Questions*. [Col. 0876D]]

Adama: in Isaiah; Aquila and Symmachus translate it as “ground,” while Theodotion interprets it as “land.”

Fuller’s Field: this too is written in Isaiah. The place is still shown in the suburbs of Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] Asedech. Let the reader observe that the places of Scripture are here always cited according to the Septuagint interpreters. *Adama* is read in the Septuagint at Isaiah XV, 9; *Asedec* at chapter XIX, 18; and similarly with the other places marked in the margin. MARTIAN.]

Asedech: the prophet Isaiah prophesies that this too will exist in Egypt. It should be known, however, that in Hebrew the name written here is AHARES, which some interpret, from the idea of dryness, as “sun,” while others render it as “potsherd,” wishing either Heliopolis or Ostracine to be signified. You will also find a discussion of this matter in the books of *Hebrew Questions*, since it is too lengthy to include here.

Arphad: a city of Damascus, which the king of the Assyrians conquered, as is written in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the books of Kings.

[Col. 0877A] 163 Aneugava: Isaiah also mentions this (XXXVII, 13), which Aquila translated as *Ane and Gava*—that is, he interpreted the syllable *u*, placed in the middle of the name, as the conjunction “and.” Symmachus, however, translated it as “he troubled and humbled.” We read about this also in the books of Kings (IV Kings XVIII, 34).

Armenia: in Isaiah, this is Ararat.

Asael: the prophet Zechariah mentions this.

Anameel: a tower of Jerusalem, as is written in the book of Zechariah (XIV, 5).

Assameroth: in Jeremiah (XXXI, 40); in Hebrew, SADEMOTH is written instead, which Aquila interprets as “suburban places.”

Aenioth: in Jeremiah (XXXVII, 15), which Aquila translates as “into workshops,” or “shops.”

[Col. 0877B] Alaoth: in Jeremiah (XLVIII, 5); in Hebrew, LUIT is read instead.

Aethan: in Jeremiah (XLIX, 19), which Aquila interprets as “strong,” and Symmachus as “ancient.”

## OF THE GOSPELS

Acheldama: “field of blood,” which is still shown in Aelia, on the southern side of Mount Zion.

[Note: [Col. 0877C] Eusebius said that it lay to the north.]

Aenou, near Salim, where John baptized, as it is written in the Gospel according to John (III, 23). The place is still shown at the eighth milestone from Scythopolis, southward, near Salim and the Jordan.

## OF GENESIS

Babel, also Babylon, means “confusion.” [Col. 0877C] It was the city of the kingdom of Nimrod, in which the languages of those who built the tower were divided; Josephus asserts that Nimrod was their leader. As a witness to this history he also presents the Greek Sibyl: “The place,” she says, “where they built the tower is now called Babylon, because of the confusion of the speech of those who with all their zeal were constructing the very highest tower. For the Hebrews call confusion BABEL.” Concerning this tower and the diversity of languages, the Sibyl also writes as follows: “When all mortals were using one language, some of them built a very high tower, wishing by means of it to climb to heaven. But the gods, sending whirlwinds and winds, overturned the tower and gave each person his own different language. Hence it also happened that the city was called Babylon.”

Bethel: a village twelve miles from Aelia, for those traveling toward Neapolis on the right. It was formerly called Luza—that is, “almond”—and fell by lot to the tribe of Benjamin, near Betham and Gai, which Jesus conquered after killing its king. (As for the view held by some, following the error of the Greek volumes, that it was formerly called Ulammaulas—)

[Note: [Col. 0877C] *Ulammaulas*, and so forth. The older manuscripts and those of the best quality read this way; below, however, in the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, they write the same word *Ulamans*, in agreement with the Alexandrian manuscript in the London Polyglot, where at Genesis XXVIII we read Οὐλαμμαῦς, *Ulammaus*. The Greek books also vary in this name. Consult Nobilius’s edition and notes. MARTIAN.]

—they are greatly mistaken. For they have confused the Hebrew word with the name of the little city itself, although ULAM means “formerly,” that is, πρότερον, while LUZA means “almond.” The meaning is therefore: “Bethel was formerly called Luza.” Moreover, although some suppose Bethaun to be another town, the Hebrews think it is the same as Bethel. But from the time when golden calves were made there by Jeroboam son of Nebat and worshiped by the ten tribes, it was called Bethaun—that is, “house of the idol”—whereas previously it had been called “house of God.” (We have discussed this more fully in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.)

[Note: [Col. 0877C] The following should be answered to John Clericus, who most unjustly accuses Jerome of ignorance. He denies that the word [Hebrew term omitted in source] ever means “formerly”; then, in the passage under discussion, if it is interpreted as “formerly,” he argues that an absurd repetition of a synonymous adverb results. The Hebrew text of Genesis XXVIII, 19, reads [Hebrew text omitted in source]. The sense is: “Previously, or at the beginning, the name of the city was Luz.” Yet he rashly denies what is proved by numerous examples from Scripture. It is clearer than midday that in Job II, 5; V, 8; and XIII, 3, [Hebrew term omitted in source] means “formerly” or “first.” Elsewhere it consistently retains the meaning of beginning, and by transference denotes the vestibule of a house or something principal. The distinguished Rhenferd derives it from the Arabic root *Hol*, meaning “preceded” or “was earlier,” and notes that among the Chaldeans it likewise means “from the beginning.” In Hebrew, “formerly” designates the beginning of time in much the same way that from [Hebrew term omitted in source], “day,” comes the expression for “a long time,” or “the whole day.” As for the second matter, which Clericus calls the fault of an absurd repetition, the same Rhenferd shows that there is no fault at all; rather, it appears to be a most elegant pleonasm, examples of which can also be found among Latin writers. Terence, *Eunuchus*, Act II, Scene II, line 15:

> “Once, long ago, this sort of trade was profitable in the former age.”

And Pliny, Book III, 9: “The town of Formiae, formerly called Hormiae.” Add to this what Reland also observes: Ulam cannot in any way be the name, or part of the name, of the city, since the same form that is used of Luza in Genesis is also used of the city of Laish in Judges XVIII, 19. From all this it may finally be concluded that Jerome corrected the error of the Greeks with sufficient learning, while he himself is falsely and rashly accused of error and ignorance.]

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Yet even before the time of Jeroboam, Bethel and Bethaven are described as two different cities in Joshua VII, 2: “Bethaven was east of Bethel.” Nevertheless, because of its impious worship of idols, Bethel itself is sometimes called Bethaven in Scripture.]

167 Bala, which is Segor, is now called Zoara. It alone of the five cities of Sodom was spared through Lot’s prayers. It overlooks the Dead Sea, and a garrison of Roman soldiers is stationed there.

[Note: [Col. 0878C] It is also inhabited by its own residents.]

Balsam and palm fruit grow there, signs of its former fertility. (No one should be troubled by the fact that Segor is also called Zoara, since both names mean “little” or “smaller.” Segor is called Zoara in Hebrew and Syriac. Bala, however, means “swallowed up”; this is discussed more fully in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.)

[Col. 0879A] Balanus—that is, “oak of mourning”—under which Rebekah’s nurse was buried.

Barad: between Kadesh and Barad; Hagar’s well is still shown there.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] Justinus says that it is thirty-six stades away, that is, nearly seven miles; in contrast, Galliel of Baldensel counts scarcely four. There are also those who assign it not to the tribe of Judah but to Benjamin, as though some right over the descendants had passed to that tribe from Rachel’s burial, which Jacob had established on the road at that place. Finally, what Eusebius and Jerome say—that David’s tomb is there—is confirmed by Brother Anselm, edited by Canisius, in his description of the Holy Land: “One comes to the once-renowned city of Bethlehem, which is in the tribe of Judah, where David himself, king of the Jews, had his origin; now it is like a small town.”]

Bethlehem: the city of David, in the territory of the tribe of Judah, where our Lord and Savior was born, six miles from Aelia toward the south, near the road leading to Hebron. There the tomb of Jesse and David is also shown. About a thousand paces away is the Tower of Eder, which means “tower of the flock,” prefiguring by a certain prophecy the shepherds who were to know of the Lord’s birth. Near the same Bethlehem, the tomb of Archelaus, once king of Judaea, is also shown; it stands at the beginning of the path that turns from the public road toward our cells. Bethlehem was also called the son of Ephrath—that is, of Mary—as we read more fully in the book of Chronicles (I Chronicles II, 19, and following). Read the history carefully.

## OF EXODUS

[Note: [Col. 0879D] Beelsefon, and so forth. In previously printed books all these places are absent, from the word *Beelsefaon* to the word *Bethfaeli*. They are found, however, in all the ancient Roman and Gallican manuscripts, as well as in the Greek Eusebius. The only reason I can infer for their omission from the editions of Erasmus and Marianaeus is the mutilated and corrupt copy they used, which they handed over for publication to incompetent typesetters hastily and carelessly, just as it came into their hands. That great lacuna is found in only a few more recent and very inferior manuscripts, on which the older editions of Jerome were for the most part based. MARTIAN.]

Beelsefon: the encampment of the children of Israel in the desert, beside the Red Sea, as they departed from Egypt.

170 ## OF NUMBERS AND DEUTERONOMY

Banejacan: an encampment of the children of Israel on their desert journey.

Bamoth: a city of the Amorites beyond the Jordan, on the Arnon, which the sons of Reuben possessed.

Basan: concerning which it is written, “And Og, king of Basan” (Psalm CXXXIV, 11). Machaathi called it Avoth Jair—that is, ἐπαύλεις Ἰαίρ, “the farmsteads of Jair.” It fell by lot to half the tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead. This is the Basanitis, now called Batanaea.

Beelphegor: this means “image of disgrace.” It is the idol of Moab, called Baal, on Mount Phogor, which the Latins call Priapus. (This is discussed more fully in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.)

[Note: [Col. 0880D] In the books of *Hebrew Questions*. Jerome’s *Hebrew Questions* on Numbers and Deuteronomy do not survive; there he had discussed at length the extremely shameful Latin Priapus and the Hebrew Beelfegor. MARTIAN.]

Baean: a city of the Amorites, which was likewise held by the sons of Reuben.

Bethamnaram: beyond the Jordan, built by the tribe of Gad. To this day there is a village called Bethnamaris, five miles from Libiada toward the north.

[Note: [Col. 0880D] Betharran, and so forth. Betharran is the same as the preceding Bethanamram, although they are written differently in Scripture. MARTIAN. —A Greek Βηθραμθὰ may have dropped out, as it is called in later Jewish writings; in Hebrew the more correct form is [Hebrew text omitted in source], Joshua XIII, 27.]

Betharran: beyond the Jordan, built by the tribe of Gad.

[Col. 0880A] Beelmeon: beyond the Jordan, built by the sons of Reuben. To this day it is a large village near Baaru (variant: Baara) in Arabia, where the earth naturally produces hot springs, called Beelmans. It is nine miles from Esbus; the prophet Elisha came from there.

Baal: beyond the Jordan, a city of the sons of Reuben.

Buthan: the encampment of the children of Israel in the desert, also called Aetham.

Bela: the eastern-facing boundary of Judaea, concerning which we have also spoken above under the name Arbela.

Bosor: in the desert beyond the Jordan, falling by lot to the tribe of Reuben east of Jericho; a priestly and refuge city. This is Bostra, the metropolis of Arabia. There is also another Bosor, the city of Esau in the mountains of Idumaea, which Isaiah recalls when he says: “Who is this who comes from Edom? His garments are red from Bosor” (Isaiah LXIII, 1, according to the Septuagint).

[Col. 0880B] Beroth of the sons of Jacim: a place in the desert where Aaron died. It is still shown at the tenth milestone from the city of Petra, on the summit of a mountain.

## OF JESUS

Bunos: that is, “hill of the foreskins,” a place at Gilgal, where Jesus circumcised the people of Israel, two miles from Jericho. The stones that were carried there from the Jordan are still shown; Scripture mentions this (Joshua IV, 8).

Bethoron: as far as this place Jesus pursued the enemy kings. It fell by lot to the sons of Joseph, that is, to Ephraim. There are two villages about twelve miles from Aelia for those traveling toward Nicopolis. Because of their position, one is called Upper Bethoron, which Solomon built; the other is Lower Bethoron, given to the Levites as a possession.

Barne: this is the same place as Kadesh-barne in the desert, which extends as far as the city of Petra.

Baalgad: a city in the plain of Lebanon, at the foot of Mount Hermon, which Jesus also captured.

Bethfogor: a city of the sons of Reuben beyond the Jordan, near Mount Phogor, opposite Jericho, six miles above Libiada.

Bethsimuth: that is, “house” or “place of Isimuth.” To this day there is a village called Isimuth opposite Jericho, ten miles from it toward the south, near the Dead Sea.

[Col. 0881A] Beeroth: below the hill of Gabaon.

[Note: [Col. 0881D] As Reland observed, the words “below the hill of Gabaon,” following the Greek text, are to be understood as meaning “under Gabaon,” or under the jurisdiction of Gabaon. Jerome himself renders it in this sense under the entry *Cephira*, and Eusebius shows that Gabaon was a metropolis.]

A village is still shown for those traveling from Aelia—

[Note: [Col. 0881D] “For those traveling to Neapolis.” All the manuscripts read *Neapolis*; Bonfrerius follows the Greek Eusebius, who reads *Nicopolis*. MARTIAN. —The manuscripts of Jerome should now be corrected from Eusebius, and *Nicopolis* should be read instead of *Neapolis*. Beeroth, Gabaon, Chephira, and Cariathiarim were four neighboring cities of the Gabaonites, the last of which, Cariathiarim, even Jerome does not deny stood on the road from Aelia to Diospolis; this was the same road as the one to Neapolis, as Reland observes from the *Itinerary of Jerusalem*. Learned men produce further arguments for this point.]

—toward Neapolis, at the seventh milestone.

Bothnin: beyond the Jordan, a city of the tribe of Gad, still called by the same name.

Betharam: a city of the tribe of Gad near the Jordan, called Bethramta by the Syrians and, after Herod, named Libias in honor of Augustus.

Bethnemra: a city of the tribe of Gad near Libiada, beyond the Jordan.

Bethagla, of the tribe of Judah: a village on the road from Eleutheropolis to Gaza, at the tenth milestone, called Agla. There is also another coastal village called Bethagla, eight miles from Gaza.

Be haraba: in the tribe of Judah.

Baal: this is Cariathiarim, that is, “village of the forests,” or, as some think, the city of Jarib, in the tribe of Judah. To this day there is a village called Cariathiarim, for those descending from Aelia to Diospolis, at the tenth mile.

Balaa: in the tribe of Judah.

Baloth: in the tribe of Judah.

Bethfali: in the tribe of Judah.

Beersheba: in the tribe of Judah, or of Simeon. To this day it is a large village twenty miles from Hebron, toward the south. A garrison of Roman soldiers is stationed there. From this place the boundaries of the land of Judah began and extended as far as Dan, which is visible near Paneas. Beersheba means “well of the oath,” because Abraham and Isaac joined in a covenant with Abimelech there, swearing an oath. No one should be troubled if he sometimes finds the same cities of Judah assigned to the tribe of Simeon or Benjamin. For the tribe of Judah, rich in very warlike men and frequently defeating its adversaries, held the chief place among all the tribes; therefore the territories of other tribes are sometimes also named according to its lot. Otherwise, Scripture very clearly teaches that Simeon lived in the midst of the tribe of Judah.

Balam: in the tribe of Judah.

Bascath: in the tribe of Judah.

Bethdagon: in the tribe of Judah. To this day a large village called Capherdago is shown between Diospolis and Jamnia.

[Col. 0881D] Bethaloth: in the tribe of Judah.

[Col. 0882A] Bethaphu: in the tribe of Judah, a village beyond Raphaim, fourteen miles from those traveling toward Egypt; it is the boundary of Palestine.

Betharaba: for which Symmachus translated, “in places that are near the uninhabitable region,” signifying the desert.

Beesthara: in the tribe of Manasseh, set apart for the Levites in the region of Basanitis.

Bethaun: in the tribe of Benjamin, near Gai and Bethel, opposite Machmas, although many, as stated above, think it is the same as Bethel.

Baliluth: in the tribe of Benjamin.

Bethsur: in the tribe of Judah or Benjamin. Today there is a village called Bethsoron, for those traveling from Aelia to Hebron, at the twentieth milestone. Near it a spring bubbles up at the foot of the mountain and swallows a person at the very place where it rises. The Acts of the Apostles (VIII, 38) report that Philip baptized the eunuch of Queen Candace there. There is also another village called Bethsur in the tribe of Judah, one thousand paces from Eleutheropolis.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] Boon, in the tribe of Benjamin. The order of the places and names in the previously printed books is corrupted as far as the name Bethlehem; but, instructed by the oldest copies and by the Greek text of Eusebius, we restore the genuine sequence here. The Greek text omits several place-names that are nevertheless read in Jerome. MARTIAN.]

Boon: in the tribe of Benjamin.

Bethalon: in the tribe of Benjamin; Symmachus translates it as “in the plains.”

Bethala: in the tribe of Benjamin.

Beroth: in the tribe of Benjamin.

Bola: in the tribe of Simeon.

Bathul: in the tribe of Simeon.

Beth: in the tribe of Simeon.

Baaleth: in the tribe of Simeon.

Barammoth: in the tribe of Simeon.

[Col. 0882C] Bethlabooth: in the tribe of Simeon.

Bethlehem: in the tribe of Zebulun; to distinguish it from this one, the other Bethlehem is called Bethlehem of Judah.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] In our version this is called Bethpheses in Joshua XIX, 21, says Bonfrerius. It is strange that Eusebius places it in the tribe of Judah.]

Bethphases: in the tribe of Issachar.

Bathne: in the tribe of Asher; it is now called the village of Bethbeten, eight miles from Ptolemais toward the east.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] Formerly Bethago. The name is even more corrupt in the Greek. Bonfrerius reads τῷ κλήρῳ Σαβουλὼν καὶ Ἰσσάχαρ, “in the territory of Zebulun and Issachar.”]

Bethdagon: the place where the two tribes of Zebulun and Issachar share a boundary.

Bethemec: Symmachus translates this as “place of the valley.” It belongs to the territory of Asher.

Bethana: in the tribe of Naphtali. There is a village called Batanaea, fifteen miles from Caesarea, in which medicinal baths are said to exist. We also listed it above under the name Anea.

[Col. 0882D] Bane: in the tribe of Dan.

[Col. 0883A] 178 Barac: in the tribe of Dan; to this day a small village near Azotus is called Barecha.

## OF THE BOOK OF JUDGES

Bezec: the city of King Adonibezec. To this day there are two villages called Bezech, near each other, at the seventeenth milestone for those descending from Neapolis toward Scythopolis.

Bethsan: the tribe of Manasseh could not expel its former inhabitants from this town. It is now called Scythopolis, a famous city of Palestine, which Scripture sometimes calls Bethsan, a name that in our language means “enemy.”

Bethsames: a priestly city in the tribe of Benjamin, still shown for those traveling from Eleutheropolis to Nicopolis, ten miles toward the east.

[Col. 0883B] Bethnath: in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. The tribe of Naphtali too was unable to expel its former inhabitants from this place.

The other Bethsames: in the tribe of Naphtali; its former inhabitants likewise remained there.

Baal Hermon: a mountain around Lebanon, on the borders of the Philistines.

Baaleth: in the tribe of Dan.

Bethbera (variant: Bethara): interpreted as “house of water” or “of the well,” which Gideon occupied by military action.

Bethasetta (variant: Bethasepta): where Midian turned its back and fled.

Balanus: that is, “oak of the Shechemites,” where Abimelech reigned. It is still shown in the suburban countryside of Neapolis, near the tomb of Joseph.

Borconni: Aquila translates this as “among thorns”; Symmachus translates it as “among thistles.”

Bera: where Joatham lived after fleeing from Abimelech. The village of Bera is eight miles north of Eleutheropolis.

Baalthamar: near Gabaa, where the Israelites engaged in battle against the tribe of Benjamin. To this day a small village in the places mentioned above is called Bethamari.

179 ## OF THE BOOKS OF KINGS

Bethcur: as far as this place the people of Israel pursued the fleeing foreigners, calling it “Stone of Help.”

Bama: where Saul, about to be anointed king, ate a meal with Samuel. Aquila always translates *Bama* as “High Place.”

Boses: the name of a rock, concerning which we have spoken in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.

[Note: [Col. 0883D] In the books of *Hebrew Questions*. Those books of *Hebrew Questions* on the books of Kings do not survive; they were falsely attributed earlier to Jerome, and we have relegated them to the Appendix of this volume. In the following name there is a persistent and very ancient error: all the manuscripts and the edition of Erasmus consistently read *Besor*, “the tower to which David came.” But the corruption is obvious from I Samuel XXX, 9, where Bosor is called a torrent, not a tower. MARTIAN. —Recall what has been said above in more than six hundred places about these books of *Hebrew Questions*.]

Besor: a torrent to which David came.

[Note: [Col. 0884D] The Jerome manuscripts used by Martianaeus and by us read “the tower to which,” incorrectly.]

[Col. 0884A] Borasan: to this place David sent a portion of the spoil.

Baurim: the place as far as which Michal, Saul’s daughter, was pursued by her weeping husband.

Baalasor: near Ephraim, where Absalom’s sheep were sheared.

Bethmacha: Joab pursued the rebel Sheba as far as this place; later we read that it was captured by the king of the Assyrians. For those ascending from Eleutheropolis to Aelia, it is now a village called Machamim, at the eighth milestone.

Ballath: the city Solomon built.

Bethsarisa: from which a man came with gifts to the prophet Elisha. It is a village in the territory of Diospolis, about fifteen miles from it toward the north, in the region of Thamnitica.

Bethagan: the road by which we read that Ahaziah fled.

Bazechath: an ancient city of Judaea.

Bethacath: a village of Samaria to which Jehu, king of Israel, came. Situated in a very broad plain, it is no more than fifteen miles from the town of Legion. Aquila translated it as “house of those who bend”; Symmachus as “house of individuals,” because its entrance was narrow and low and allowed only one person at a time—and not even those standing—to enter.

Benith: built by the Samaritans who had crossed over from the region of Babylon.

Byblos: a city of Phoenicia, which Ezekiel mentions (XXVII, 9); in Hebrew, GOBEL is written instead.

182 Bubastus: a city of Egypt, according to Ezekiel (XXX, 7).

Boz: in the land of Kedar, as Jeremiah writes (XXV, 23).

Bel: a Babylonian idol.

## OF THE GOSPELS

[Note: [Col. 0884D] Bethsada. The Colbertine manuscript, often praised for its excellent quality, reads *Bethsaida*, in agreement with the Latin Vulgate edition and some Greek copies of the Gospel according to John, rather than *Bethsada*. MARTIAN. —All the manuscripts we use read *Bethsaida*. Bonfrerius says that the opinion of the better authorities, especially Jerome, is that *Bethesda* should be read here instead of *Bethsaida*. Greek codices also have *Bethesda*, as do some Latin manuscripts and the Syriac version. There is no single agreement about what *Bethesda* means, and it cannot be determined with certainty unless the Hebrew spelling is established. The Syriac version writes *Bethehesda* with [Syriac term omitted in source] and means “house of mercy.” Others wish it to be written with [Hebrew term omitted in source] and to mean “house of pouring out,” because the Temple water was poured into it. For *esched* means “pouring out.”]

Bethsaida: a city in Galilee belonging to Andrew, Peter, and Philip the Apostles, near the lake of Gennesareth.

Bethphage: a little village on the Mount of Olives, to which the Lord Jesus came.

Bethany: a village two miles from Aelia, on the side of the Mount of Olives, where the Savior raised Lazarus. His tomb is still shown there, as is a church now constructed on the same spot.

[Col. 0884D] Bethabara: beyond the Jordan, where John baptized for repentance. To this day many of the brethren—that is, from among the number of believers—who desire to be reborn there are baptized in the life-giving waters.

Bethesda: a pool in Jerusalem called προβατικὴ, which we may translate as “sheep-related” or “belonging to the sheep.” It once had five porticoes, and two pools are still shown. One is usually filled by winter rains; the other, extraordinarily red, as though with bloody waters, preserves signs of an ancient function. For it is said that the priests used to wash sacrifices in it, and that it received its name from this practice.

## OF THE PENTATEUCH

Carnaim Astaroth: Carnaim is now a large village in a corner of Batanaea, called Carnaea beyond the streams of the Jordan. They report that Job’s house was there. We also mentioned above the village of Carnaea, nine miles from Aelia.

Cades: where the spring of judgment is. There is also Kadesh-barne in the desert, which is joined to the city of Petra in Arabia. [Col. 0885B] Miriam died there, and Moses, striking the rock, gave water to the thirsty people. Miriam’s tomb is still shown there to the present day; and there the princes of Amalek were struck down by Chedorlaomer.

183 Cene: the region of the princes of Edom.

Cariathaim: a city built by the sons of Reuben. Now it is a village flourishing with many Christians, near the Arabian city of Medaba. It is called Corojatha, ten miles from that city toward the west, near a place called Baare.

Cariatharbee—that is, “village of four”—which is also Hebron, concerning which we have already spoken above.

Canath: an Arabian village now called Canatha. When Nabau captured it, he called it Naboth. It was in the tribe of Manasseh, in the region of Trachonitis, near Bostra.

Cata ta chrysea—that is, “toward the golden places.” These are mountains rich in gold in the desert, eleven stages from Choreb, near which Moses is said to have written Deuteronomy. They estimate that the mountains near the Temple of Bronze, which collapsed in our time, were formerly full of veins of gold.

[Note: [Col. 0885C] Eleven stages from Choreb. Earlier editions read “eleven miles from Choreb,” but this passage is extremely corrupt, as is clear from Deuteronomy I, from which these words were taken by Eusebius; he himself has “eleven days” rather than “eleven miles.” Therefore the place where Moses is said to have written Deuteronomy was eleven stages, or eleven days’ journey, from Horeb or Choreb. The journey is approximately fifty miles, which could be completed in eleven days by proceeding slowly. We have nowhere been able to find among geographers where the Temple of Bronze, which had collapsed in Jerome’s time, was located. See *Dedan* below. MARTIAN. —Formerly the text read “eleven miles,” contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts and the sacred text of Deuteronomy I, where eleven days are counted. Here one day’s journey and one stage are the same, although it can scarcely be determined with certainty how many miles each stage, or day’s journey, contained; according to the nature of the terrain, it must have been longer in some places and shorter in others.]

Cademoth: a desert from which Moses sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites.

Cariath: a village that belonged to the metropolis Gaba.

Cedes: a city conquered by Jesus after killing its king. It is in the territory of the tribe of Judah.

Cademoth: another city of the sons of Reuben.

Cedson: in the tribe of Reuben, a city set apart for the Levites.

## OF THE BOOK OF JESUS

Capseel: in the tribe of Judah.

Cina: in the tribe of Judah.

186 Ceila: in the tribe of Judah, where David once sat. It is now the village of Cela, toward the east for those traveling from Eleutheropolis to Hebron, about eight miles away. The tomb of the prophet Habakkuk is shown there.

Cariathbaal: the city of Jarim, in the tribe of Judah.

Cana: in the tribe of Ephraim.

Campsaim: in the tribe of Ephraim.

Cane: in the tribe of Manasseh.

Cariathiarim: also Cariathbaal, “city of the forests,” one of the cities of the Gabaonites, belonging to the tribe of Judah. For those traveling from Aelia to Diospolis (variant: Heliopolis), it lies at the ninth mile.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] At the ninth mile. Instead of “ninth,” the previously printed books here have “one mile.” MARTIAN. —Formerly it read “one mile.” Elsewhere Eusebius and Jerome place this city not at the ninth but at the tenth mile from Aelia to Diospolis, under the heading *Baal*.]

The prophet Uriah, whom Jehoiakim killed in Jerusalem, came from this place, as Jeremiah writes (XXVI, 20). In the book of Chronicles (I Chronicles II, 50), the son of Shobal is also called Cariathiarim.

[Col. 0886C] Cision: in the tribe of Issachar, a city set apart for the Levites.

Cartha: in the tribe of Zebulun, a city set apart for the Levites.

[Note: [Col. 0886C] Cotta, in the tribe of Zebulun. These entries are also absent from the older editions of Jerome up to *Cana*. MARTIAN.]

Cotta: in the tribe of Zebulun, a city set apart for the Levites.

[Note: [Col. 0886C] Cana as far as Greater Sidon, and so forth. The learned Bonfrerius admits that this passage is obscure and involved, since much seems to be assigned to greater Cana that ought to be assigned to the lesser. For the lesser Cana is the one where Christ changed water into wine and where Nathanael came from. He therefore establishes the following reading to remove the ambiguity: “Cana as far as Greater Sidon.” There was a Cana in the tribe of Asher. There is also another, smaller one—this greater Cana being named in distinction from it—where our Lord, and so forth. MARTIAN. —There is nowhere any mention of Lesser or Smaller Sidon. Jerome appears to have been misled by the epithet τῆς μεγάλης, “the great,” which Joshua II, 2 gives to Sidon without reference to another, smaller city; the Hebrew text is otherwise. Origen believed that under the expression τῆς μεγάλης, which the Greek version has, two Sidons—two “hunters”—were hidden, and understood this allegorically. He writes that although he had stayed several times in the territory of Sidon, he had never discovered two Sidons, one great and one small. How far those who understand these words of Jerome as referring to Cana have gone astray is clear from the text itself. Bonfrerius and Martianaeus are also mistaken when, from their preconceived opinion about two Sidons, they force Saint Doctor’s words.]

Cana: as far as Greater Sidon—for there is also another, Lesser Sidon, in distinction from which this one is called Greater. Cana was in the tribe of Asher, where our Lord and Savior changed water into wine. Hence Nathanael is confirmed by the Savior’s testimony to be a true Israelite. It is now a little town in Galilee of the nations.

Cedes: in the territory of Naphtali, a priestly and refuge city in Galilee, on Mount Naphtali. The king of the Assyrians also captured it. It is now called Cidissus, twenty miles from Tyre, near Paneas.

Chartham: in the tribe of Naphtali, a city set apart for the Levites.

187 ## OF THE BOOK OF JUDGES

Cethron: in the tribe of Zebulun, where the former inhabitants remained.

[Col. 0887B] Carcar: where Zebee and Salmana were, whom Gideon killed. To this day there is a fortress called Carcaria, one day’s journey from the city of Petra.

Camon: the city of Jair, where he was also buried after he had first judged the people of Israel. It is still called the village of Cimona, in a very broad plain, six miles from Legion for those traveling northward toward Ptolemais.

Cison: a torrent near Mount Tabor, where the battle against Sisera was fought.

Cadomi: a torrent near which Deborah waged war.

Coelas of the Titans—that is, “valley of the Giants”—against whom David fought.

[Col. 0887C] Clauthmon: that is, “place of weeping,” receiving its name from lamentation.

## OF THE BOOKS OF KINGS

Ceni: the region of the Philistines.

Carmelus: where Nabal was once a Carmelite. It is now a village called Chermela, ten miles from the town of Hebron toward the east, where a Roman garrison is stationed.

[lacuna]

Cedron: the torrent, or valley, of Cedron, near Jerusalem toward the east, which the Evangelist John also mentions.

Cyrene, in the borders of Egypt: to this place the king of the Assyrians transferred the people of Damascus.

190 Coa: which is near Egypt.

[Col. 0887D] Carchedon—that is, Carthage—which Isaiah and Ezekiel recall in their vision of Tyre. In Hebrew, THARSIS is written instead. We have discussed this more fully in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] In the books of *Hebrew Questions*. No such *Hebrew Questions* survive, nor do those cited below concerning Joshua, Kings, and Job. MARTIAN.]

Coelas: that is, the valley of Jehoshaphat between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. (Read the prophet Joel III, 2.)

Cedem: in Ezekiel, which Aquila and Symmachus interpret as “the east.”

Cedar, in Ezekiel, the princes of Cedar (27:21). Isaiah and Jeremiah also recall this word in their vision of Arabia. It is a region in the wilderness of the Saracens, named after Cedar, the son of Ishmael.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] He seems to be referring to the nomenclature of his own time, for the region was formerly called that of the Ostraceni, not of the Saracens. Saint Hilary, in his Commentary on Psalm 119, indeed attributes it to the Ostraceni, but adds: “These are now called Saracens.”]

Carioth, in the region of the Moabites, as Jeremiah writes.

Capernaum, beside Lake Gennesaret: even today a town situated in Galilee of the Gentiles, within the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali.

Up to this point, through the letter C—that is, the Greek kappa (ΚΑΠΠΑ)—we should read the names. From here onward they should be written and read with the element chi (ΧΙ), which contains an aspiration and is entirely absent from Latin.

## FROM GENESIS

[Note: [Col. 0887D] Chalanne, where the tower was built. These words are found in the Septuagint at Isaiah 10:9. In the Latin Vulgate it is called Calano, but in the Divine Library of Saint Jerome, Chalano is the better reading. MARTIAN.]

Chalanne, a city of the kingdom of Nimrod in Babylonia, which Isaiah also mentions, saying: “And Chalanne, where the tower was built.”

Chalach, a city of the Assyrians, which Assur built after departing from the land of Shinar.

Charran, a city of Mesopotamia, beyond Edessa, which to this day is called Charra; there the Roman army was defeated and the commander Crassus was captured.

Hebron, formerly called Arbe (although the Greek manuscripts incorrectly have Arboc). It was founded seven years before the city of Tanis in Egypt. We have spoken of it above as well. It was the metropolis of the Anakim, whom we must understand as giants and mighty men.

Chobaa, on the left side of Damascus. There is also a village called Chobaa in the same region, whose inhabitants are Hebrews who believe in Christ and observe all the precepts of the Law. And from [a man named] Ebion, the founder of the heresy, they are called Ἐβιωνῖται (Ebionites). The Apostle Paul writes against this kind of doctrine in his letter to the Galatians.

[Note: [Col. 0887D–0888D] Eusebius says nothing of this sort about Ebion, the founder of the heresy. It is in fact closer to the truth that the Ebionites were named from the poverty of their understanding, not from a certain teacher named Ebion. Jerome follows Epiphanius, who thought that this was the man’s proper name; yet it was not without some prophetic significance, since it indicated that he would become a beggar and unfortunate, although he had received the name from his parents. See what we have noted on the first chapter of Isaiah. Now Chobaa, the very seat of the Ebionites, is called Cocabe by Epiphanius: “In a certain village of Cocabe, in the region of the Carnaimites, Arnemi, and the Astharothites, in the district of Basanitis,” and so forth. Nor does the geographical description differ from Jerome’s, since that town was in the vicinity of Damascus, three or four miles away. Edrisi, who is known as the Nubian Geographer, when discussing the villages around Damascus, reports it and calls it Caucaba, or, alternatively, Caucab.]

Chabratha, which Aquila translated καθ’ ὁδόν (kath’ hodon), that is, “beside the road” leading to Ephrata, that is, Bethlehem, where Rachel died after giving birth to Benjamin.

[Col. 0888D–0889A] What we think about this word we have explained in the books of Hebrew Questions.

[Note: [Col. 0889D] In the Books of Hebrew Questions. Jerome discusses Chabratha and Chasbi in his Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis. See below, after the Book of Places. MARTIAN.]

Chazbi, where Tamar gave birth to Judah’s twin sons. The deserted site is still shown near Odollam, in the territory of Eleutheropolis. This too has been discussed more fully in the Books of Hebrew Questions.

## FROM NUMBERS AND DEUTERONOMY

Choreb, the mountain of God in the region of Midian, near Mount Sinai, above Arabia, in the wilderness. Joined to it are the mountain and wilderness of the Saracens called Pharan. It seems to me, however, that the same mountain is called by two names, Sinai at one time and Choreb at another.

Charada, the camp of the children of Israel.

Chennereth, the sea where the boundary of Judea lies in the tribe of Naphtali. There is also a town which, later restored by Herod, king of Judea, in honor of Tiberius Caesar, was called Tiberias; they say that it was first called by this name.

## FROM THE BOOK OF JESUS

Chephira, a village belonging to the city of Gabaon in the tribe of Benjamin.

Chasalon, in the tribe of Judah and within the territory of Aelia, a very large village.

Chisil, in the tribe of Judah.

Chabon, in the tribe of Judah.

Chaphtis, in the tribe of Judah.

Chermel, from which Nabal the Carmelite came; this was mentioned above as well.

[lacuna]

[Col. 0889C] Chilon, in the tribe of Judah.

Chephri, in the tribe of Benjamin.

Chasselath Thabor, in the tribe of Zebulun.

## FROM THE BOOKS OF THE KINGDOMS

Chetthiim, the land of Chetthiim, is called Cyprus; in it Luza founded a city. For even today a city is called Cypricittium.

Charri, to which place Joab pursued Sabee when he was plotting rebellion.

Chomarim, where Josiah burned the idols.

Chalanne, where the tower was built, according to Isaiah, as we said above.

Charran, a city of the Assyrians in the region of Themath, according to Isaiah.

Chaselath, near Tabor, the boundary of Zebulun; we discussed it above under the name Chasalus.

Chabol, the boundary of Asher.

Chalab, whose former inhabitants Asher was unable to expel.

Chorath, a torrent beyond the Jordan, in which Elijah was hidden, opposite the same river.

Chotha, a region of the Assyrians.

[Col. 0890A] Chobar, the Babylonian river, as in Ezekiel.

Charchamis, a city beside the Euphrates River.

Chamoam, a little village near Bethlehem.

Chaelon, also called Ealon, a town of Moab, as it is written in Jeremiah.

Chamos, the idol of Moab.

## FROM THE GOSPELS

Chorozain, a town of Galilee, which Christ lamentably mourns and weeps over because of its unbelief. It is now deserted, two miles from Capernaum.

Chimarrus, that is, the torrent of Cedron, about which we spoke above; it lies between the Mount of Olives and Jerusalem, where the Evangelist John says that the Lord and Savior was betrayed.

## FROM THE BOOK OF GENESIS

[Col. 0890B]

Dasem, a distinguished city of the Assyrians, which Assur built between Nineveh and Chalach.

Drys, that is, the oak of Mamre, near Hebron. Until my childhood and the reign of King Constantius, an extremely ancient terebinth was shown there, indicating its age by its size. Abraham dwelt beneath it. It was held in extraordinary honor by the pagans and consecrated as though to some notable divinity.

Damascus, a distinguished city of Phoenicia. By the same name Masec, Abraham’s maidservant’s son, was also called. I have discussed more fully what Masec signifies in the Books of Hebrew Questions; here I have merely performed the office of translator, not that I approve of calling Abraham’s maidservant Masec.

[Col. 0890C] Dan is a village four miles from Paneas on the road to Tyre. It is still called by this name and forms the northern boundary of the province of Judea; from there the Jordan River also bursts forth. The river takes its name from the place: for the Hebrews call a river—or stream—Jor; ῥεῖθρον (rheithron) means “a flowing stream,” that is, “a river” or “brook.”

[Note: [Col. 0889D–0890D] Thus in the Questions on Genesis, chapter 14: “Dan,” he says, “is one of the sources of the Jordan; for the other is called Jor, which means ῥεῖθρον, that is, ‘a stream.’” See what we have noted in Letter 78 to Fabiola, section 41, and again in the Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 48.]

Dannaba, the city of Balac, son of Beor, king of Edom, after whom Job reigned, although this seems to me quite otherwise. To this day there is a village called Dannaia, eight miles from Areopolis on the road to the Arnon; and another Dannaba lies upon Mount Phogor, seven miles from Esbus.

[Note: [Col. 0890D] Reland prefers Arnon, namely the region that takes its name from the Arnon River. Otherwise Jerome seems quite inconsistent with himself: elsewhere, under the word “Madian,” he says that Arcopolis lies on the Arnon, whereas here he places it eight miles away. MARTIAN.]

Dothaim, where Joseph found his brothers grazing their flocks; it is still shown twelve miles from Sebaste, toward the north.

[Note: [Col. 0890D] “At the twelfth mile,” etc. One Colbert manuscript has “at the tenth.” MARTIAN.]

## FROM NUMBERS AND DEUTERONOMY

[Col. 0890D]

Debon, also called Dibon, the camp of the children of Israel in the wilderness. There is another Dibon, a very large village near the Arnon. It had formerly belonged to the Moabites; afterward Sihon, king of the Amorites, held it by right of war; then it was captured and occupied by the children of Israel and fell to the tribe of Gad. Jeremiah and Isaiah mention it in their vision against Moab.

[Note: [Col. 0891C] “In the vision against Moab.” The numerous “visions” cited in this Book of Places are chapters of prophetic passages, which we have published separately in the Prophets, volume 1 of our edition. Let the reader consult Jerome’s Divine Library. MARTIAN.]

Debongad, a camp of the children of Israel.

Dysmemoab, that is, “to the west of Moab,” near the Jordan opposite Jericho. There Balac, king of Moab, and the elders of Midian deceived Israel by ambush; it was also there that Moses wrote Deuteronomy.

[Note: [Col. 0891C–D] “At which place Moses also,” etc. Above, in *Cata ta Chrysea*, Moses is said to have written Deuteronomy beside mountains rich in gold. MARTIAN. —Recall the word *Cata ta Chrysea* above.]

## FROM THE BOOK OF JESUS

Dabira, a city in the tribe of Dan, whose king Jesus killed. There is also another little Jewish village on Mount Tabor, in the territory belonging to Diocaesarea.

Dornapheth (which Symmachus translated “Dora by the sea”). This is Dora, now deserted, nine miles from Caesarea of Palestine on the road to Tyre. Although it fell by lot to the tribe of Manasseh, Manasseh could not possess it because its former inhabitants remained there.

Dabir, in the tribe of Judah, which was called the City of Letters. Gothoniel, Caleb’s brother, seized it after killing the Anakim there. It too was set apart for the priests. Some, however, think that Gothoniel was Caleb’s nephew.

Dabir, a city of the Amorites on the Jordan.

Dimona, in the tribe of Judah.

Dadan, in the tribe of Judah.

Denna, in the tribe of Judah; it is the same as Dabir, the City of Letters.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] Dahiva, etc. An old Colbert manuscript has Dahuia, or Dahuid. MARTIAN.]

Dahiva, or Dahiud, in the tribe of Judah.

Duma, in the tribe of Judah, a large village in Daroma—that is, toward the southern region—within the territory of Eleutheropolis, seventeen miles from it.

Damna, in the tribe of Zebulun, a city set apart for the Levites.

Dasbath, in the tribe of Zebulun.

Dabrath, in the tribe of Issachar, a city set apart for the Levites.

## FROM THE BOOK OF JUDGES

Drys, that is, “the oak,” in Ephrata, in the tribe of Manasseh, from which Gedeon came. We have explained what we think about it in the Books of Hebrew Questions. For the question is how Ephrata can now be said to be in the tribe of Manasseh.

[Note: [Col. 0891D–0892A] In the Books of Hebrew Questions, etc. Those Books of Hebrew Questions on the Book of Judges have been lost. Jerome was doubtless teaching in them that *Ephra* should be read instead of *Ephrata*, for *Ephra* is read in Jerome’s Latin version and in certain Greek copies. With this reading, every difficulty disappears. MARTIAN.]

## FROM THE BOOKS OF THE KINGDOMS

Dibon, of which we spoke above and which Isaiah mentions in his vision against Moab.

Deseth, which Aquila translated “wall” and Symmachus “rampart.”

Dodanim, of which Isaiah writes in his vision of Arabia. It lies near Areopolis.

Darom, which Ezekiel mentions (20:46 in the Septuagint); Symmachus translated it “toward the southwest.”

Diospolis, a city of Egypt, as Ezekiel writes.

Dadan, in the region of Cedar, about which Jeremiah writes.

Deblataim, in the land of Moab, as Jeremiah writes.

[Col. 0892B] Dedan, in the region of Idumea, concerning which Jeremiah writes. It lies four miles north of Metallophenon.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] “From Metallophenon,” etc. Perhaps *Metallophanon* should be read, as above under *Cata ta Chrysea*. MARTIAN.]

Decapolis, as we read in the Gospel. It is a region of ten cities beyond the Jordan, around Hippos, Pella, and Gadara.

## FROM GENESIS

Eden, the site of the sacred paradise in the East; the name is translated as “pleasure” or “delights.”

Evila, where the purest gold—which in Hebrew is called *zaab*—and the most precious stones, carbuncle and emerald, are produced. It is a region extending toward the East, around which the Pison flows after emerging from paradise; our people, changing the name, call it the Ganges. One of the younger sons of Noah was also called Evila; Josephus reports that he possessed, with his brothers, the territory from the Cephenus River and the region of India as far as the place called Hieria. Ishmael too is said to have dwelt in the wilderness of Evila, which Holy Scripture says lies in the wilderness of Sur, opposite Egypt, and extends as far as the land of the Assyrians.

[Note: [Col. 0891D–0892C] “Which our people, changing the name,” etc. In the Greek we read παρ’ Ἕλλησι, “among the Greeks.” Under the name “Greeks” all nations except the Jewish people are included, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement, “to the Jew first and to the Greek.” MARTIAN.]

Euphrates, the river of Mesopotamia, rising in paradise. Sallustius, a most reliable authority, asserts that the sources of both the Tigris and the Euphrates are found in Armenia. From this we perceive that paradise and its rivers must be understood differently.

[Note: [Col. 0892C–0893D] Sallustius, a most reliable authority, etc. It is uncertain where Sallustius wrote this, for in the Fragments of Sallustius, near the end of page 236, among other uncertain passages, the reader will find this: “Sallustius, a most reliable authority, asserts that the Tigris and Euphrates flow from one source in Armenia; proceeding in different directions, they become separated by a greater distance, leaving between them a space of many miles. Yet the land surrounded by them is called Mesopotamia.” This does not seem to have been taken from the present passage of Jerome, since there are many discrepancies and the Fragment adds several things. Concerning the Euphrates, we also read this in Sallustius, *Histories*, book 4: “He hastened by the longest marches through the kingdom of Ariobarzanes to the Euphrates, where Cappadocia is separated from Armenia,” and so forth. MARTIAN. —In ancient editions this passage is read differently in the fragments of Sallustius. Those who first collected them, it seems to us, took the passage from Isidore of Seville, book 13, chapter 22, rather than from Jerome; yet it is evident that Isidore drew it from here. Sallustius, however, a most reliable authority, asserts that the Tigris and Euphrates flow from one source in Armenia; proceeding in different directions, they become separated, and so forth. It is then added that Jerome consequently observed that the rivers of paradise must be understood otherwise. Martianaeus therefore searches for this passage in Sallustius in vain and attributes the discrepancy between the two texts to differing textual traditions; for the passage was not taken from Sallustius but from Isidore. I do not know whether he read more correctly in ancient copies of Jerome “flow from one source” instead of “their sources are shown,” for the context seems to require the former reading, although Strabo reports separate sources for the two rivers, saying that they are διέχειν ἀλλήλων, στάδιους βφʹ—about 2,500 stades—apart. See also the other Isidore of Charax, Agathemerus, book 1, Plutarch on the Euphrates, and others.]

Ellasar, the city of King Arioch.

Ephratha, the region of Bethlehem, the city of David, where Christ was born. It is in the tribe of Judah, although many incorrectly judge it to be in the tribe of Benjamin. It lies beside the road where Rachel was buried, five miles from Jerusalem, at the place called Hippodrome by the Septuagint. We read *Ephrathan* in the Book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 2:50), as stated above.

[Note: [Col. 0893D–0894D] “Although most judge incorrectly,” etc. Jerome is criticizing Eusebius; he also disagrees with him when he places Ephratha five miles from Jerusalem, for Eusebius placed Ephratha in the tribe of Benjamin, four miles from Jerusalem, in the other column. Above, under the word Bethlehem, they place it six miles away, as most other authorities unanimously report. MARTIAN.]

## FROM NUMBERS AND DEUTERONOMY

Ebrona, a camp of the children of Israel in the wilderness.

Emath, which the scouts sent by Jesus crossed.

[Col. 0893B] Erma, where part of the people of Israel were killed by Amalek and the Canaanite, whom Scripture in Deuteronomy calls an Amorite.

Esebon, the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, in the land of Gilead. Although it had formerly belonged to the Moabites, it was possessed by the Amorites by right of war. Jeremiah mentions it, and Isaiah too in his vision against Moab. It is now called Esbus, a notable city of Arabia in the mountains opposite Jericho, twenty miles from the Jordan. It was in the tribe of Reuben and was set apart for the Levites.

Edrai, where Og, king of Bashan, a giant and mighty man, was killed, together with his entire army. It is now Adra, a notable city of Arabia, twenty-four miles from Bostra.

Eleale, a city of the Amorites in Gilead, which fell by lot to the tribe of Reuben. Isaiah also mentions it in his vision against Moab, as does Jeremiah. To this day a large village is shown one mile from Esbus.

Euna, which is beside the wilderness of Kades.

Ermon, Mount Hermon, which the Phoenicians call Sanior; it was also listed above.

## FROM THE BOOK OF JESUS

Emec Achor, which means “the valley of Achor,” that is, “of tumult and disturbance,” where Achan was crushed by stones because he had taken certain things from the devoted objects. It is a place near Jericho, not far from Galgala.

[Note: [Col. 0894D] Some therefore incorrectly think that the Valley of Achor was named after the man who was stoned, since he was called Achan, not Achor or Achar. Eusebius is being criticized here. MARTIAN.]

Eglom, also called Odollam, in the tribe of Judah; its king, named Dabir, was killed by Jesus. It is now a very large village twelve miles east of Eleutheropolis, about which we spoke above.

[Note: [Col. 0894D] This seems to be a mistake by a Latin copyist; elsewhere Jerome, agreeing with Eusebius, places Odollam ten miles from Eleutheropolis. Recall the entry *Adollam*. MARTIAN.]

Esrom, also called Asor, near the wilderness in the tribe of Judah; it was mentioned above as well.

Enacim; in this region Jesus killed the Anakim, the giants, from the mountainous country around Hebron. It seems to me, however, that Enacim is not the name of a place but of the inhabitants of Hebron.

Ephron, in the tribe of Judah. There is also a very large village called Ephraea toward the north, twenty miles from Aelia.

Edre, in the tribe of Judah.

Ethnam, in the tribe of Judah.

Ebeziuthia, in the tribe of Judah.

[Col. 0894B] Evim, in the tribe of Judah.

Elolath, in the tribe of Judah.

Ereb, in the tribe of Judah. To this day there is a village in Daroma, that is, toward the south, now called Eremiththa.

Esan, in the tribe of Judah.

Elul, in the tribe of Judah. There is also today, in the region belonging to Aelia, a village called Alula, near Hebron.

Elthece (alternatively, Elthei), in the tribe of Judah. Today there is the village of Thecua, nine miles—read twelve—from Aelia toward the south. The prophet Amos came from there, and his tomb is shown there.

Engaddi, in the tribe of Judah, where David was hidden in the wilderness, which lies in the Aulon of Jericho—that is, in the level region about which we spoke above. To this day there is a very large Jewish village called Engadda beside the Dead Sea, from which the balsam also comes; Solomon calls its vineyards “the vineyards of Engaddi” (Song of Songs 1:13).

Esthemo, a priestly city; it is now shown as a very large Jewish village in Daroma, a place belonging to the territory of Eleutheropolis.

Emec Raphaim, that is, the Valley of Raphaim, in the tribe of Benjamin.

Edomia, in the tribe of Benjamin. Today a village called Eduma is shown in Acrabattene, about twelve miles east of Neapolis.

Erma, which Jesus also captured after killing its king. It belonged to the territory of Simeon or Judah.

[Col. 0894D] Ether, belonging to the lot of Simeon; it is now a very large village called Jeththira, in the interior of Daroma near Malatha.

[Col. 0895A] Eththa, in the tribe of Simeon.

Elcath, in the tribe of Asher, a city set apart for the Levites.

Edrai, in the tribe of Naphtali.

Esthaul, in the tribe of Dan, where Samson died. It is still shown ten miles from Eleutheropolis on the road northward to Nicopolis.

Eltheco, in the tribe of Dan, set apart for the Levites.

Elba, from which the tribe of Asher could not expel the former inhabitants.

Eremmon, a very large Jewish village sixteen miles south of Eleutheropolis, in Daroma.

Emathdor, in the tribe of Naphtali, set apart for the Levites.

Emath, the boundary of the Philistines in the region of Damascus.

## FROM THE BOOKS OF THE KINGDOMS

[Col. 0895B]

Ergab, toward which place Jonathan, son of Saul, directed his spear while practicing with military javelins. Aquila and Symmachus translated it “stone,” although elsewhere Symmachus rendered it τὴν περίμετρον, “the circumference” or “perimeter.”

Echela, where David was hidden. It is now called Eccela, a village seven miles from Eleutheropolis; near it the tomb of the prophet Habakkuk is also shown.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] The tomb of Habakkuk. The tomb of Habakkuk was displayed in many different places, just as the head of Saint John the Baptist is today. MARTIAN.]

Elmoni, “some place,” is the interpretation. Aquila and Theodotion translated it τόνδε τινά, “this certain place,” which we may render “this or that.”

[Note: [Col. 0895D] τόνδε τινά. Earlier printed books read τὸν δεῖνα in a very corrupt form, although in the Septuagint interpreters too, at 2 Kings 6:8, from which *Elmoni* is taken, the passage reads: εἰς τὸν τόπον τόνδε τινὰ Ἐλμωνί, “to this certain place, Elmoni.” What *Elmoni*, or *Pheloni Almoni*, means—found in Ruth 4:1, 2 Kings 6:8, and elsewhere—Jerome would have taught us in his Hebrew Questions, had those works not perished to the great detriment of sacred literature. MARTIAN. —Before Martianaeus, the printed editions at least correctly read τὸν δεῖνα; so too does one Regius manuscript cited by Montfaucon in the Hexapla at 2 Kings 6:8: εἰς τὸν δεῖνα τόπον, “to such-and-such a place.”]

The attentive reader should recognize that, as I also touched upon in part at the beginning of this book, I do not approve everything that I translate. I leave certain things according to the Greek authority because I have discussed them more fully in the Books of Hebrew Questions.

[Note: [Col. 0895D–0896D] That is, the etymologies of the names, not necessarily the locations of the cities, are not all approved by Jerome. Whenever Eusebius is mistaken in assigning their distances, Jerome points out the error and declares his disagreement with him. MARTIAN.]

Esthama, to which place David sent.

Eloth, which King Azariah built.

Emath, in Isaiah, a city of Damascus which the king of the Assyrians attacked. Zechariah and Ezekiel mention it. In Amos it is also written “Emath Rabba,” which corresponds in sound to “great Emath.” We spoke of it above, expressing the view that it is Epiphany near Emesa, which to this day is called by that name in the Syrian language.

[Col. 0896A] Eser, a city which Solomon built. Elcese, from which place the prophet Nahum came, for he is called the Elcesaean.

Emacim, which Symmachus and Aquila translated “valleys.”

## FROM THE GOSPELS

Emmaus, from which Cleophas came, whom the Evangelist Luke mentions. It is now the notable city of Nicopolis in Palestine.

[Note: [Col. 0896D] He says the same in Letter 108 to Eustochium, section 8: “Nicopolis, formerly called Emmaus, where the Lord was recognized in the breaking of bread, and the house of Cleophas,” and so forth. Anastasius the Librarian likewise says: “Emmaus, a fortress of Palestine, of which we read in the holy Gospels, was decreed to be honored as Nicopolis by Alexander, later the emperor Severus, when Africanus was carrying out an embassy; Africanus wrote histories in five books.” Reland correctly observes that two places with the same name, Emmaus, are wrongly confused: the *kome*, or village, mentioned by Luke 24:13, was no more than sixty stades from Jerusalem, according to Josephus, whereas the city Emmaus, also called Nicopolis, lay 176 stades away—twenty-two Roman miles. Compare Jerome again with himself in the Commentary on Daniel, chapter 12, Ezekiel, chapter 48, and Obadiah, verse 1.]

Ephraim, near the wilderness, to which the Lord Jesus came with his disciples. We discussed it above under the name Ephon.

Up to this point the beginnings of the names have been read through the short E. From here onward let us read the letter in its extended form, which in Greek is called eta.

## FROM GENESIS

[Col. 0896B]

Elath, the region of the princes of Edom and the city of Esau, ten miles east of Petra.

Eroum (Gesse), a city in Egypt, where Joseph met his father Jacob.

Heliopolis, the City of the Sun, a city in Egypt; in Hebrew *On* is written for it. The priest Petefres lived there. Ezekiel also mentions it.

Etham, the camp of the children of Israel in the wilderness, which is called Ebutham, or perhaps Butham.

## FROM THE BOOK OF JESUS

Engannim, in the tribe of Judah; it is now a village near Bethel.

Enaim, in the tribe of Judah; even today it is a village called Bethenim, near the terebinth.

[Col. 0896C] Endor, in the tribe of Manasseh, where the pythoness was consulted by Saul, king of Judea. We also spoke above of Endor, which lies near the town of Naim, at whose gates the Savior raised the widow’s son. It is near Scythopolis.

Enganni, in the tribe of Issachar, a city set apart for the Levites. There is also another city called Enganna, around Gerasa beyond the Jordan.

Enadda, in the tribe of Issachar. To this day there is a village called Ennadab on the road from Eleutheropolis to Aelia, approximately ten miles away.

Enasor, in the tribe of Naphtali; Asor was also listed above.

[Col. 0897A] Ereccon, the boundary of the tribe of Dan, near Joppa.

## FROM THE BOOK OF JUDGES

Etam, where Samson lived, in the cave of Etam beside the torrent.

## FROM THE BOOKS OF THE KINGDOMS

Ela, we read of the Valley of Ela, which Aquila and Theodotion translate “the valley of the oak.”

Engaddi, the wilderness in which David was hidden. We also listed above Engaddi in the tribe of Judah, beside the Dead Sea, toward the west.

Emath, the region of the Philistines. According to Jeremiah, it is also the city of Damascus.

Enam, the boundary of Damascus, as it is read in Ezekiel, extending eastward from Theman and the palm trees; the other interpreters published “Thamar.”

## FROM GENESIS

[Col. 0897B]

Pison, which means “multitude”: the river which our people, the Greeks, call the Ganges. It flows out of paradise and proceeds toward the regions of India, beyond which it pours into the sea. Scripture says that it surrounds the whole region of Evila, where the finest gold, carbuncle, and green stone are produced.

Pharan, now a town beyond Arabia, adjoining the Saracens, who wander about in the wilderness. The children of Israel passed through it when they moved their camp from Mount Sinai. As we said, it lies beyond Arabia toward the south and is three days’ journey east of Aila. Scripture records that Ishmael lived in the wilderness of Pharan (Genesis 21). Hence the Ishmaelites, who are now the Saracens. We also read that King Chedorlaomer struck those who were in the wilderness of Pharan.

Philistia, now called Ascalon, and the region around it in Palestine.

Phanuel, the place where Jacob wrestled throughout the night and earned the name Israel, beside the torrent Jabbok. Phanuel means “the face of God,” because Jacob saw God there.

Fogo, the city of King Adad, in the region of Gabalitis.

Phinon, a camp of the children of Israel in the wilderness. It was once a city of the princes of Edom; now it is a village in the wilderness where copper is mined by condemned persons as penal labor, between the city of Petra and Zoara. We spoke of it above as well.

## FROM EXODUS

Pithom, a city of Egypt which the children of Israel built.

## FROM NUMBERS AND DEUTERONOMY

Fin, a camp of the children of Israel in the wilderness.

Fathura, a city beyond Mesopotamia, from which Balaam the diviner came. There is also near Eleutheropolis a village called Fathura, on the road to Gaza.

Phagor and Bethphogor, a mountain of the Moabites, to which Balac, king of Moab, brought Balaam the diviner, on the summit of Livias. Another village called Fogor is also visible not far from Bethlehem; it is now called Phaora.

Phasga, a city of the Amorites. There is also a mountain called Phasga toward the east; for this Aquila translates “cut off.” The Septuagint translators likewise translated Phasga as “cut off” in one passage.

[Note: [Col. 0897D] Namely, Deuteronomy 4:49, where they translate ὑπὸ Ἀσηδὼθ τὴν λαξευτήν, “beneath the carved slopes.”]

## FROM THE BOOK OF JUDGES

Phanuel, the city which Jeroboam built.

Phanuel, the tower which Gedeon overturned. One of the sons of Hor was also called Phanuel (1 Chronicles 44).

Phraathon, from which Abdon, judge of the people of Israel, came, on Mount Amalek.

## FROM THE BOOKS OF THE KINGDOMS

[Note: [Col. 0898D] Felmoni Almoni. We have already discussed these names above under Elmoni. MARTIAN.]

Felmoni Almoni, which Aquila translates “that one or this one.” Symmachus, however, translates it “some place,” while Theodotion has “that place, Elmon,” about which we have discussed more fully in the Books of Hebrew Questions.

Fogo, a city of the kingdom of Edom.

Pharphar, a river of Damascus.

Fathore, a region of Egypt, according to Ezekiel and Jeremiah, where the Jewish refugees lived.
