## FROM GENESIS

Geon, the river called the Nile by the Egyptians, rising in paradise and encircling the whole of Ethiopia.

Gomorrah, one of the five cities of the Sodomites, which was overthrown by divine vengeance together with the others.

Gerara, from whose name the region beyond Daroma is now called Geraritica, twenty-five miles south of Eleutheropolis. It was formerly the southern boundary of the Canaanites and the metropolitan city of Palestine. Scripture records that it lay between Kades and Sur—that is, between two wildernesses: one joined to Egypt, to which the people came after crossing the Red Sea; the other, Kades, extending as far as the wilderness of the Saracens.

Galaad, the mountain to which Jacob, fleeing from Charran, came on the seventh day of his journey. It lies behind Phoenicia and Arabia, joined to the hills of Lebanon, and extends through the wilderness as far as the place where Sihon, king of the Amorites, once lived beyond the Jordan. The mountain mentioned above fell to the lot of the sons of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. Jeremiah also says: “Gilead, you are the beginning of Lebanon” (42:6). From this mountain the city founded upon it also took its name; Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, captured it from the Amorites.

Gader, a tower where, while Jacob was living there, Reuben violated his father’s bed. In Hebrew it is written *Ader*, without the letter G.

Getthaim, for which the Hebrew has *Avith*, the city of Adad, who was the fourth king to reign in the land of Idumea, now called Gebalene.

[Col. 0899A] Gesem, a region of Egypt in which Jacob lived with his children.

## FROM NUMBERS AND DEUTERONOMY

Gasiongaber, a camp in the wilderness of the children of Israel, as it is written in the Book of Numbers. According to Deuteronomy, it is a city of Esau, now thought to be called Esiam, near the Red Sea and Aila.

Gai, a camp of the children of Israel in the wilderness. To this day a city of Palestine called Gaia lies near the city of Petra.

Gelmon Deblathaim, a camp, that is, a station of the children of Israel in the wilderness.

Gadgad, a mountain in the wilderness where the children of Israel camped.

Gaza, a city of the Avvim, in which the Cappadocians lived after the former inhabitants had been killed. In ancient times it was the boundary of the Canaanites near Egypt, and it fell by lot to the tribe of Judah. The tribe of Judah could not retain it, however, because the Anakim—that is, the giants, the strongest of the Philistines—resisted. It remains to this day a notable city of Palestine.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] “By lot to the tribe of Judah.” One Colbert manuscript reads “Joseph” instead of “Judah.” MARTIAN.]

Some ask how a prophet can say that Gaza will become an everlasting mound. The answer is that scarcely any traces of foundations remain at the site of the ancient city, whereas the city now visible was built in another place to replace the one that collapsed.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] Namely, Zephaniah, chapter 2. Hence the *Apospasmatia* of an uncertain Greek author, volume 4 of the *Geographi Graeci Minores*, also mentions New Gaza: Μετὰ τὰ Ῥινοκόρουρα ἡ νέα Γάζα κεῖται πόλις οὖσα καὶ αὐτή, “After Rhinocorura lies New Gaza, which is itself also a city.” See also Curtius, book 4, and Arrian, book 2.]

Gargasi, a city beyond the Jordan, adjoining Mount Gilead, which the tribe of Manasseh held. It is now said to be Gerasa, a notable city of Arabia. Some think that it is Gadara itself. The Gospel also mentions the Gergesenes.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] Origen, in his Commentary on Matthew, page 131, distinguishes Gergesa of Palestine from Gerasa of Arabia. From Ptolemy we also learn that there were two cities of the same name: one in Coele-Syria, which Stephen of Byzantium also mentions—Γέρασα πόλις τῆς Κοίλης Συρίας, “Gerasa, a city of Coele-Syria”—and another in Arabia Petraea. Finally, Flaccus, bishop of the province of the Gerasenes in Arabia, subscribed to the Council of Chalcedon. MARTIAN.]

Gaggada, where there are torrents of water. It is a place in the wilderness.

Gaulon, or Golam, in the tribe of Manasseh, a priestly and asylum city in the region of Bashanitis. To this day a very large village is called Gaulon in Batanaea, and from its name the region also received its designation.

Gebal, a mountain in the Promised Land, where an altar was constructed at Moses’ command. There are two neighboring mountains near Jericho, facing one another; one is called Garizim, the other Gebal. The Samaritans, however, believe that these two mountains are beside Neapolis; but they are seriously mistaken, for they are very far apart, and the voices of those blessing or cursing could not be heard by one another—as Scripture records.

Garizin, the mountain upon which those who uttered the curses stood, beside the aforementioned mountain Gebal.

Golgol, also called Galgal, near which the mountains Garizin and Gebal are said to be situated. Galgal, however, is a place near Jericho. (The Samaritans are therefore mistaken when they wish to point out the mountains Garizin and Gebal beside Neapolis, since Scripture testifies that they are near Galgal.)

Gai, in Moab, which is interpreted as “the valley of Moab,” near Phogor, where Moses was buried.

## From the Book of Joshua

Galgala: this is the place we identified above as Golgol, on the eastern side of ancient Jericho, on this side of the Jordan, where Joshua circumcised the people a second time, celebrated Passover, and, when the manna failed, Israel used bread made from grain. At that same place they also set up the stones which they had taken from the bed—or, according to another reading, the channel—of the Jordan; there the tabernacle of the testimony also remained fixed for a long time. It fell within the allotment of the tribe of Judah, and to this day a deserted site is shown at the second milestone from Jericho, held in extraordinary reverence by the inhabitants of that region. Some also suppose that there was another Galgala near Bethel.

Gai, near Bethan and Bethel, which Joshua captured after killing its king. An Amorite once lived there, on this side—or, according to another reading, around—the Jordan; now only a deserted site is shown.

Gabaon, from which the Gabaonites came as suppliants to Joshua. It was formerly the metropolitan and royal city of the Hivites, and it fell within the allotment of the tribe of Benjamin. Even now a village of the same name is shown at the fourth milestone from Bethel, toward the west, near Rama and Remmon. There Solomon, after offering sacrifices, was deemed worthy of a divine oracle. It too was assigned to the Levites.

Gabe, in the allotment of Benjamin; this also was a city assigned to the Levites.

Gazer, in the allotment of the tribe of Ephraim, a city assigned to the Levites. Joshua also captured it, after killing its king. It was later rebuilt by Solomon; it is now called the village of Gazara, at the fourth milestone from Nicopolis, toward the north. It should nevertheless be understood that Ephraim was unable to expel the foreigners from it.

Goson, which Joshua also captured.

Geth: in this place the giants called the Anakim, and the settlers of the Philistines, remained. A village is shown at the fifth milestone for those traveling from Eleutheropolis toward Diospolis.

[Col. 0900D] Gesom, a city of foreigners, situated in Gargasi in the region of Basan, from which the Israelites were unable to expel the Geshurites.

Gader: Joshua also killed its king. We read that Jacob pitched his tent beyond the tower of Gader (Genesis 35:16, according to the Septuagint).

[Col. 0901A] Goim in Gelgel. Aquila and Symmachus interpret this as “nations in Gelgel.”

Gelgel: Joshua also captured this place. Even now a village called Galgulis is shown, six miles north of Antipatris.

Golathmaim, a place whose name is interpreted as “possession of water.”

[Note: For the interpretation of this name, which had dropped out, the scribe of the Vatican manuscript marks, in the intervening space, the note Ζτ. More correctly, Golathmaim, the word found at Joshua 15:19, signifies “the turning of waters”; perhaps Jerome wrote “outpouring” instead of “possession.”]

Gadda, in the tribe of Judah. Even today there is a village at the extreme boundaries of Daroma, toward the east, overlooking the Dead Sea.

Gadera, in the tribe of Judah. It is now called a village belonging to the territory of the city of Aelia, named Gadora, near the terebinth.

Gahedur, in the tribe of Judah. Even today it is called Gedrus, a very large village at the tenth milestone from Diospolis for those traveling toward Eleutheropolis.

[Col. 0901B] Gabli, the land of the Philistines.

Gison, in the tribe of Judah.

Gelon, in the tribe of Judah.

Gaderoth, in the tribe of Judah.

Getremmon, in the tribe of Manasseh, a city assigned to the Levites.

Gai, a valley, or a precipice.

Gehennom, interpreted as “the valley of Hinnom.” Some think that Gehenna was named from this place. It fell within the allotment of the tribe of Benjamin, beside the wall of Jerusalem toward the east. (This has been discussed more fully in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.)

Gethepher, in the tribe of Zebulun.

Gefthael, that is, “the valley of Ephthael,” in the tribe of Zebulun.

[Col. 0901C] Gabathon, in the tribe of Dan, a city assigned to the Levites. There is also a town called Gabe, at the sixteenth milestone from Caesarea; another village, Gabatha, lies in the territory of Diocaesarea, near the great plain of the Legion. There are also Gaba and Gabatha, small villages toward the eastern side of Daroma. There is yet another Gabatha in the tribe of Benjamin, where Saul’s house was; in the Books of Kings a Gabatha of foreigners is also mentioned (and one near Bethlehem in the tribe of Judah).

Getremmon, another city in the tribe of Dan, assigned to the Levites. It is now a very large village at the twelfth milestone from Diospolis for those traveling to it from Eleutheropolis.

[Note: The manuscripts of Jerome are to be corrected from Eusebius, and the reading should be “for those traveling from it to Eleutheropolis” (ἀπιόντων εἰς Ἐλευθερόπολιν).]

[Col. 0902A] Galiloth, a place beside the Jordan in the tribe of Benjamin, where the sons of Reuben erected an altar to the Lord.

Gaas, a mountain in the tribe of Ephraim. On its northern side Joshua son of Nun was buried, and to this day his notable tomb is shown near the village called Thamna.

[Note: This is evidently the Thamnath-sare mentioned at Joshua 24:30, not Thamna without qualification, which belonged to the tribe of Judah. See Book I against Jovinianus, no. 15.]

Gabaath, in the tribe of Benjamin, the city of Phinehas son of Eleazar, where Eleazar was buried. It is now Gabatha, a village at the twelfth milestone from Eleutheropolis, where the tomb of the prophet Habakkuk is also shown.

[Note: The same tomb of Habakkuk is said above, at Ceila and likewise at Echela, to be shown there as well. Clericus, with reckless boldness, ridicules this in the present passage and accuses it of contradiction. Relandus and Rhenferdus, on the contrary, show that neither Eusebius nor Jerome was at fault. They observe very learnedly that these three places—Ceila, Echela, and Gabatha—lay on the Royal or military road between Eleutheropolis and Hebron. This is manifest from what is said at Ceila. For travelers from Eleutheropolis toward Hebron encountered Echela at the seventh milestone, Ceila at the eighth, and Gabatha at the tenth. It is therefore hardly surprising if the same monument was pointed out at three or more places, within a distance of two leagues, on the right or left of the military road—especially if the mound erected over it was somewhat higher, or had been built on a rise, as the character of that people made likely, somewhat removed from the public road. Indeed, neither Eusebius nor Jerome teaches that the prophet was buried in any one of these three places, much less in all three; they say only that his monument was customarily shown near these places to travelers, who could see it equally well from one or another position. Virgil’s verse from *Eclogue* 9 is also brought forward in this connection:

“From here our road runs directly through the middle; for the tomb  
of Bianor begins to appear.”]

Gabaam: as is written in the Book of Judges, war was waged against the tribe of Benjamin as far as this place (Judges 20).

## From the Books of Kings

Geththa, to which place the ark of the covenant was transferred from Azotus. It is now called the large village of Giththam, between Antipatris and Jamnia. Another village is also called Geththim.

Gallim, from which Phalthi came, who, after David’s flight, had taken Michal, his wife. Isaiah also mentions this place. It is said to be a village near Accaron called Gallaa.

Gelamsur, a region of the Philistines.

Gelboe, mountains of foreigners, six miles from Scythopolis, where there is also a large village called Gelbus.

Gedud, to which David descended. Aquila translates it as τὸν εὔζωνον, that is, “the well-equipped” or “the girded”; Symmachus rendered it “a band of brigands.”

Gazera, where David struck the foreigners. We have also placed Gazer above.

Gesur, a region of foreigners in Syria.

Gilon, from which Ahithophel came.

Gob, where the battle took place (2 Samuel 21:18).

Galilee: there are two Galilees. One is called Galilee of the nations, near the borders of the Tyrians, where Solomon also gave Hiram, king of Tyre, twenty cities, within the allotment of the tribe of Naphtali. The other Galilee is around Tiberias and the Lake of Gennesareth, in the tribe of Zebulun.

Gion, where Solomon was anointed king.

Ger, the place where Jehu, king of Israel, struck Ahaziah, king of Judah, near Jibleam.

[Col. 0903A] Gettha-Chopher, from which the prophet Jonah came.

Gaddi, which Hazael, king of Damascus, struck. Gadda has also been placed above.

Gemala, a region of the Idumeans; Aquila and Symmachus interpret it as “the valley of salt.”

Gebin, mentioned by Isaiah. There is a village Geba at the fifth milestone from Gophna for those traveling toward Neapolis.

Gozan, in the region of Hamath; Isaiah also mentions it. It lies in the territory of Damascus.

Gareb, a hill near Jerusalem, as Jeremiah writes.

[Note: “Gebarth,” and so forth. The manuscripts read this way, but the printed books read Gabath. In Jeremiah chapter 40 the word is not Gabarth but Galeroth, meaning “hedges.” MARTIAN.]

Gebarth: Aquila interprets it as “among hedges,” while Symmachus renders it “among colonies.” (Read Jeremiah.)

Gepha, the name of a region, as it is written in Isaiah.

Gamem, or Gamon, a region of the Moabites, according to Isaiah.

## From the Gospels

Gadara, a city beyond the Jordan, situated on a mountain opposite Scythopolis and Tiberias toward the east; at its foot hot springs break forth, with baths built above them.

Gergesa, where the Savior restored to health those who were afflicted by demons. Even today a village is pointed out on the mountain beside the Lake of Tiberias, into which the pigs were driven headlong. We have spoken of this above as well.

Gethsemane, the place where the Savior prayed before the Passion. A church has now been built above it, at the foot of the Mount of Olives.

Golgotha, the place of the Skull, where the Savior was crucified for the salvation of all. To this day it is shown in Aelia, on the northern side of Mount Zion.

## From Genesis

Jaboc, the river which Jacob crossed; afterward he wrestled against the one who had appeared to him, and was called Israel. It flows between Amman, that is, Philadelphia, and Gerasa—at the fourth milestone from the latter—and, continuing beyond, joins the river Jordan.

Idumaea, the region of Esau, which received its name from the fact that he was called Edom. It lies around the city of Petra, now called Gebalene.

Itheth, the region of the princes of Edom, in the same territory of which we spoke above, Gebalene.

## From Exodus

[Col. 0903D] Iroth, a place in the desert to which the children of Israel came after crossing the Red Sea.

[Note: As a compound form, Phihahiroth, which the Septuagint at Numbers 33:5 interprets as στόμα εἰρὼθ, “the mouth of Iroth,” Bonfrerius notes that this name has been torn apart. He also adds after διῆλθον the words οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραήλ, “the children of Israel,” in the Greek.]

## From Numbers and Deuteronomy

Jetabatha, a camp in the wilderness of the children of Israel.

Incendium, that is, ἐμπυρισμός, “burning”: a place in the desert where fire consumed a certain part of the people.

Inthaath, a camp in the desert of the children of Israel.

Janna, which is in the plain of Moab, beneath the summit of Phasga, that is, “the hewn-off place,” facing the desert near the Arnon.

Jassa, where battle was fought against Sihon, king of the Amorites. Isaiah mentions it in his vision against Moab, as does Jeremiah. To this day it is shown between Medaba and Debus.

[Note: “Between Medaba and Debus.” In the previously printed books we corruptly read Deblatham instead of Delus, which misled Bonfrerius. MARTIAN.]

Jazer, a city of the Amorites, at the tenth milestone west of Philadelphia, beyond the Jordan. It was the boundary of the tribe of Gad and extends as far as Aroer, which itself faces Rabbah. Isaiah mentions the city of Jazer in his vision against Moab, as does Jeremiah. It was assigned to the Levites and is fifteen miles from Heshbon. From it a large river emerges and is received by the Jordan.

Jordan, the river dividing Judaea, Arabia, and the Aulon, of which we spoke above. It flows as far as the Dead Sea; after many windings near Jericho, it mingles with the Dead Sea and loses its name.

Jetabatha, a place in the desert where streams of water are shown.

Jericho, the city which Joshua overthrew after crossing the Jordan and killing its king. In its place Oza of Bethel, from the tribe of Ephraim, built another city, which our Lord and Savior honored by his presence. This city too, at the time when Jerusalem was besieged by the Romans because of the treachery of its citizens, was captured and destroyed. A third city was built in its place, which still remains, and the traces of both former cities are shown to the present day.

## From Joshua

[Col. 0904C]

Jerusalem, in which Adonibezek reigned, and which was later held by the Jebusites, from whom it also received its name. Much later David exterminated them and made it the metropolis of the whole province of Judaea, because there he purchased the site of the Temple—and left the expenses of its construction to his son Solomon, as Josephus reports. It is the city called Salem in Genesis, under King Melchizedek. It was in the tribe of Benjamin.

Jebus, the same city as Jerusalem.

Jarim, a city of the Gabaonites.

Jarimuth, the city which Joshua overthrew, in the tribe of Judah, four miles from Eleutheropolis, near the village of Esthaol.

[Note: “Jarimuth,” and so forth. Many Latin manuscripts omit this passage, although it is present in the Greek of Eusebius under the name Ἰαβεῖς. MARTIAN.]

Isimoth, where David hid. We also stated above what seemed to us concerning it, identifying Bethsimuth. In the First Book of Kings, however, Aquila interprets Isimuth as “scattered,” while Symmachus renders it “deserted.”

Jedna, six miles from Eleutheropolis for those traveling toward Hebron.

[Col. 0905A] Jeconam, a city of Carmel which Joshua captured after killing its king.

Jair, a city of the tribe of Manasseh.

Jamnel, in the tribe of Judah. To this day it is the Palestinian town of Jamnia, between Diospolis and Azotus.

Jabir, a city of letters in the tribe of Judah.

Jathur, in the tribe of Judah.

Jermus, in the tribe of Judah. Even today there is a village called Jermucha, ten miles from Eleutheropolis for those ascending toward Aelia.

Jectael, in the tribe of Judah.

Jectan, in the tribe of Judah.

Jether, in the tribe of Judah, a priestly city. Even now there is a very large village called Jethira, twenty miles from Eleutheropolis. All its inhabitants are Christians. It lies in the interior of Daroma, near Malatha. We have spoken of it above as well.

Janum, in the tribe of Judah. There is a village called Janua, three miles south of the Legion. It does not, however, seem to be the place that is mentioned.

Jetan, in the tribe of Judah, a priestly city. Even today it is a very large village of Jews, eighteen miles from Eleutheropolis toward the south, in Daroma.

[Note: Bonfrerius joins this title in the Latin with the following entry as one continuous passage, merely deleting the adverb above: “It is not the same as Jezrael,” and so forth. Eusebius himself could easily have written it in this form: Ἰεσραὲλ, φυλῆς Ἰούδα· μηδὲ αὕτη ἐστὶ Ἰεζραὲλ, “Jesrael, of the tribe of Judah; nor is this the same as Jezrael.” Thus the Greek copyist may have been misled by the occurrence of very similar words. Jerome, however, speaks clearly of the latter city in his Commentary on Hosea, chapter 1: “We have said that Jezrael, which is now near Maximianopolis, was the metropolis of the kingdom of Samaria, near which are very broad plains and a valley of enormous extent, stretching for more than ten thousand paces.” And in his commentary on Zechariah 12: “Adadremmon, for which the Septuagint translated Ῥοῶνος, is a city near Jezrael, formerly called by this name and now called Maximianopolis, in the plain of Maggedon.” See Relandus.]

Jesrael, in the tribe of Judah; but this is not the same place as the one mentioned above.

Jezrael, in the tribe of Manasseh. Even today a very large village is shown in the Great Plain between Scythopolis and the Legion. It was the boundary of Issachar. One of the descendants of Ephrath was also called Jezrael, as we read in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 5:3; supply “in the books”).

Jecdaan, in the tribe of Judah.

Jephlethi, in the tribe of Joseph.

Jano, in the tribe of Ephraim. The king of Assyria also captured it. Even today a village called Jano is shown in the region of Acrabittene, twelve miles east of Neapolis.

Jamin: Aquila and Symmachus interpret this as “the right hand.”

[Note: “Jaseb,” and so forth. Bonfrerius correctly observed that this name is customarily read in different forms in the manuscripts of the Septuagint. For Joshua 17:7 it is read Jaseb, Jassib, and Jasem; the Hebrew has Josebe, meaning “inhabitants,” as Jerome translated it.]

Jaseb (another reading: Jasen): the Hebrews interpret it as “inhabitants.”

Inemec: Aquila and Symmachus translated this as “into the valley.”

[Col. 0905D] Jeblaam, in the tribe of Manasseh, from which it was unable to expel the foreigners.

Jerphel, in the tribe of Benjamin.

[Col. 0906A] Jecnal, in the tribe of Zebulun, a city assigned to the Levites.

Jasthie, in the tribe of Zebulun. It is still called Joppa, the ascent of Japho. There is also a town called Sycaminum, on the sea, for those traveling from Caesarea toward Ptolemais; because of Mount Carmel it is called Epha.

Jephthael, in the tribe of Zebulun.

Jadela, in the tribe of Zebulun.

Jermoth, in the tribe of Issachar, a city assigned to the priests. We have also placed Jerimuth above; the prophet Hosea mentions it as well.

Icoc, in the allotment of Naphtali, at the boundary of three tribes: that is, in the tribe of Zebulun toward the south, in the tribe of Asher toward the west, and in the tribe of Judah toward the sunrise.

[Col. 0906B] Jabnel, in the tribe of Naphtali.

Jeron, in the tribe of Naphtali.

Jethlam, in the tribe of Dan.

Jelon, in the tribe of Dan.

Jud, in the tribe of Dan.

Jerachon, “waters,” in the tribe of Dan.

Inlechi: Aquila interprets this as “in the jawbone.”

Jabis Galaad, which the children of Israel attacked. It is now a village beyond the Jordan, six miles from the city of Pella, above the mountain for those traveling toward Gerasa.

## From the Books of Kings

Joar, a wooded area in which there was a swarm of bees.

Jerameli, a region of the Philistines.

Jether, to which David sent. It is now a village in Daroma called Jetthira, of which we spoke above.

Jecmaam, a city of Solomon’s princes.

Itabyrium: Aquila and Symmachus translated this in the prophet Hosea as “Tabor.” Mount Tabor is in the Great Plain, on the eastern side of the Legion.

[Note: Toward the eastern side. The earlier printed books often read “western” instead of “eastern.” The geographical maps establish that Tabor was situated on the eastern side of the Legion. See below under Tabor.]

Jecthoel, the name of a rock in the Books of Kings.

Jethaba, an ancient city of Judaea.

Inaczeb: Symmachus translated this as “in the valley of Zeb.”

Inachim, or Inbachim: Aquila and Symmachus translated this as “in weeping.” The prophet Micah also mentions it.

Joppe, a maritime town of Palestine in the tribe of Dan.

[Col. 0906D] Inaraba: Aquila translated this as “in a low place” or “on level ground”; Symmachus, “in the plain.”

Ituraea and Trachonitis, the region whose tetrarch was Philip, as we read in the Gospels. Trachonitis is the land beside the Arabian desert, which joins Bostra.

[lacuna]

## From Genesis

Lasa, the boundary of the Canaanites around Sidon.

Luza, in the tribe of Benjamin, which Jacob later renamed Bethel. Even today there is a village on the left side of the road for those traveling from Neapolis to Aelia.

Luza, another place, which fell within the allotment of the sons of Joseph, near Shechem, three miles from Neapolis.

Lotan, a city of the princes of Edom.

## From Numbers and Deuteronomy

[Col. 0907B]

Lebona, in the desert, a camp of the children of Israel.

Lobon, a deserted place beyond the Jordan where Moses read Deuteronomy.

## From the Book of Joshua

Lochis, in the tribe of Judah. Joshua also captured it after killing its king. Isaiah and Jeremiah mention it. It is now a village seven miles from Eleutheropolis for those traveling toward Daroma.

Lebna, in the tribe of Judah, a priestly city which Joshua held after killing its king. It is now a village in the territory of Eleutheropolis called Lobna. Isaiah also writes about it.

Lasaron, which Joshua also captured after killing its king.

[Col. 0907C] The stone of Boen, belonging to the sons of Reuben; it is the boundary of the tribe of Judah.

Laboth, in the tribe of Judah.

Lamas, in the tribe of Judah.

Labaoth, in the tribe of Simeon.

Labanath, in the tribe of Asher.

Lacum, the boundary of Naphtali.

## From the Book of Judges

[Col. 0908A]

Laboemath: Aquila interprets this as “the entrance of Hamath.”

Lesem: after the sons of Dan captured it, they renamed it Dan.

Another Luza, near Bethel, in the land of Ceththim. It was founded by the man who had departed from Bethel, as the history relates.

Lechi: Aquila and Theodotion interpret this as “jawbone”; we have already spoken of it above.

Laisa: after the sons of Dan captured it by force, they possessed it, although it was far from Sidon, and they called it Dan. It was the northern boundary of the land of Judaea, which extends from Dan to Beersheba. Isaiah also mentions it. It is situated near Paneas, from which the river Jordan emerges.

[Col. 0908B]

## From the Books of Kings

Lamatthara, toward which place Jonathan directed his arrows. Aquila interprets this as “toward the mark”; Symmachus, “toward the appointed meeting.”

Ladabar, where Mephibosheth was.

Lodabar, from which Machir came.

Lebanon, the highest mountain of Phoenicia.

Luith, mentioned by Isaiah. Even today there is a village called Luitha between Areopolis and Zoara.

## From Genesis

Messe, a region of India in which the sons of Joktan, son of Eber, lived.

Mambre, which is Hebron, near which Abraham was buried with Isaac and Jacob. We have spoken of it above as well. Mambre was also the name of one of Abraham’s friends.

Madian, a city named after one of Abraham’s sons by Keturah. It lies beyond Arabia, toward the south, in the desert of the Saracens, east of the Red Sea. From it the Madianites and the region of Madian received their names. We also read of the daughters of Jobab, the father-in-law of Moses, as daughters of Madian.

[Note: “The daughters of Jobab,” and so forth. It is not easy to find in Scripture where we should read “daughters of Jobab,” or Obab, as “daughters of Madian.” Bonfrerius is clearly shown to be mistaken here when he says that “daughters of Jethro” should be read instead of “daughters of Jobab” or Hobab. For it is entirely certain to us that Hobab is called Ἰωβάβ by the Septuagint at Judges 4:11. Theodotion, in Question 15 on Numbers, thinks that Jobab was the son of Raguel, who is the same as Jothor or Jethro. The sons of Jobab, Moses’ father-in-law, were called Kenites and at one time lived among the Amalekites and Midianites. Thus the daughters of Jobab could be called daughters of Madian from the city of Madian, which lies near the Arnon and Areopolis.

There is no difficulty in the Greek of Eusebius, since “daughters of Moab” and “daughters of Madian” are used interchangeably in Scripture and in Josephus, *Antiquities* 4.6. Each writes correctly according to his own meaning: Eusebius has Moab, Μωάβ, while Jerome has Jobab. The latter restored the proper name of Moses’ father-in-law, Ἰωβάβ or Ὠβάβ, since there is no doubt that the daughters of Jobab are called Midianite women, whose homeland was Madianitis near the Red Sea. The former had in view Numbers 25:1, where the daughters of Moab are mentioned; throughout that chapter these girls are in fact called Midianite women, and they lived in settlements of Madian adjoining Moab.

Thus they differ only through a different allusion, and neither is at fault, contrary to what Bonfrerius and especially Clericus assert. Clericus falsely claims that Jerome improperly altered Eusebius’s words and substituted the erroneous reading Obab for Moab. They also greatly criticize Jerome for saying that this was the Midianite city near Areopolis and the Arnon. Rhenferdus, with complete truth and learning, clears him of this charge, showing that Jerome’s manuscripts were thoroughly corrupted by the fault of scribes, and that instead of “But this,” one should read “There is also another,” a phrase very familiar to him in hundreds of places.

No one will suppose that the holy Doctor was so foolish, or so ignorant of all geography and history, and so inconsistent with himself, as to establish the region of Madian in the desert of the Saracens, east of the Red Sea, from which he thinks the daughters of Hobab, Moses’ father-in-law, are called daughters of Madian, and then say that this same place is the city near the Arnon and Areopolis. Therefore write, please, “There is also another,” and so forth; nothing is more certain than this correction.

Relandus also supplies the Greek text at this point: Ἔστι δὲ ὄνομα ἑτέρας πόλεως etc., “There is also the name of another city,” and so forth.]

But this is another city of the same name, ὁμώνυμος, near the Arnon and Areopolis, of which now only the ruins are shown.

Moab, a city of Arabia named after one of Lot’s sons, who was called Moab. It is now called Areopolis, and we have mentioned it above. The region too is called Moab from the name of the city. The city itself, however, possesses a name as though it were a proper designation: Rabbath Moab, that is, “Great Moab.”

Masseca, a city of the kingdom of Edom, around Gebalene.

Mabsar, even to the present day a large village in the region of Gebalene, called Mabsara, belonging to the city of Petra.

Magediel, also in the region of Gebalene, once possessed by the princes of Edom.

## From Exodus

Magdolus, to which the children of Israel came after leaving Egypt, before crossing the Red Sea. We also read in Ezekiel of “from Magdolus to Syene.” Jeremiah reports that the Jews who had fled with him to avoid the Babylonian attack lived in this city of Egypt.

Merra, interpreted as “bitterness.” It is the place where Moses changed the bitter waters into sweet-tasting water by throwing in a piece of wood.

## From Numbers and Deuteronomy

Memoriae, that is, “graves of craving,” a camp of the children of Israel in the desert, where, after they had eaten meat, the anger of God rose against them.

[Col. 0909C] Maceloth, a camp of the children of Israel in the desert.

[Note: “Maceloth … in the desert.” The earlier printed books add at this point: “Matheca, a camp of the children of Israel in the desert.” But this is found neither in the Greek nor in the ancient Latin manuscripts of the highest quality.]

Masuruth, a camp of the children of Israel in the desert.

Matthane, now called Masechana. It lies on the Arnon, twelve miles east of Medaba.

Misor, the city of Og, king of Basan. (Misor signifies level and open places.)

Machanarath, the boundary of the city of Amman, also called Philadelphia.

Madobares, which we call a wilderness; the Hebrews call it Madrarim.

Misaida of the sons of Jacim, a place in the desert where Aaron died.

## From the Book of Joshua

Maceda, where Joshua shut five kings in a cave and killed them, together with the king of Maceda. It was in the tribe of Judah and is now eight miles east of Eleutheropolis.

Madon, the city where Jobab was king, against whom Joshua waged war.

Massepha, in the tribe of Judah, near which Jephthah lived, beside Cariathiarim, where the ark of the covenant once was and Samuel judged the people. Jeremiah also mentions it.

Merrom, the waters beside which the camp was established after the army had been prepared. It is now a village called Merrus, twelve miles from the city of Sebaste, near Dothaim.

Massephothmaim: Aquila interpreted this as “Massephoth of the waters”; Symmachus as “Massephoth of the sea.”

Machathi, a city of the Amorites on the Jordan near Mount Aermon, from which the children of Israel were unable to expel the Machathites.

Marom, which Joshua captured after killing its king. Marrus has also been placed above.

Mageddo, which Joshua captured after killing its king. Although it fell within the allotment of the tribe of Manasseh, they did not possess it, because they were unable to expel its former inhabitants.

Misor: Aquila and Symmachus interpreted this as “low.” It is a city of the tribe of Reuben, assigned to the Levites, in the region of Gebalene.

Medaba, to this day a city of Arabia retaining its ancient name, near Heshbon.

Maphaath, in the tribe of Benjamin. There is also another place beyond the Jordan, where a garrison of Roman soldiers is stationed because of the proximity of the desert.

Masapha, in the tribe of Gad, assigned to the Levites. There is also another Maspha today, in the territory of Eleutheropolis, for those traveling toward Aelia in a northerly direction; it belongs to the tribe of Judah.

Maanaim, in the tribe of Gad, assigned to the Levites, in the region of Gilead.

Moladab, in the tribe of Judah or Simeon.

[Note: “Moladab,” and so forth. The printed books place this name after Marala; the Greek of Eusebius and the Latin manuscript copies, however, have the same order in which we restore it.]

Medemena, in the tribe of Judah, mentioned by Isaiah. It is now the town of Menois near the city of Gaza.

Magdala, in the tribe of Judah.

Maresa, in the tribe of Judah. Today only its ruins remain, two miles from Eleutheropolis.

Maon, in the tribe of Judah, east of Daroma.

Maroth, in the tribe of Judah.

Maddi, in the tribe of Judah.

Masfa, in the tribe of Benjamin.

Machoth, in the tribe of Manasseh.

Marala, the ascent of Zebulun.

[Note: Here Jerome again differs from Eusebius, who writes “of the tribe of Manasseh,” φυλῆς Μανασσῆ. Jerome judges more correctly. Josephus too reports that Maralam existed on the borders of Zebulun; certainly it was not far from them, since its boundary is said to have risen toward the sea and Marala. The territory of Zebulun did not extend all the way to the sea itself; otherwise the tribe of Asher and the half-tribe of Manasseh would not have touched one another, as is established by Joshua 17:10. Marala therefore must have been a place on the western boundaries of the allotment of Zebulun. Jerome attributes its ascent to Zebulun, while Eusebius assigns it to Manasseh.]

Masan, in the tribe of Asher, near Carmel by the sea, a city assigned to the Levites.

The Salt Sea, which is called the Dead Sea, or the Asphalt Sea, that is, the sea of bitumen, between Jericho and Zoara.

[Col. 0911A] Meeleb, the boundary of Naphtali.

Magdiel, in the tribe of Naphtali. Even today a small village is shown five miles from Dora for those traveling toward Ptolemais.

Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem, where Jesus taught his disciples.

## From the Book of Judges

Mosphetaim: Aquila interprets this as “of lots”; Symmachus, “of neighboring districts.”

More, the name of a hill. This has been discussed more fully in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.

Mennith, where Jephthah fought. A village called Manith is now shown four miles from Heshbon for those traveling toward Philadelphia.

Machmas, to this day a large village is shown in the territory of Aelia, retaining its ancient name, nine miles from it, near the village of Rama.

## From the Books of Kings

Messab, a hostile town near Gaba.

Magdon, or Magron, where Saul sat.

Massepha, in Moab, to which David came as a fugitive while avoiding Saul’s ambushes.

Masereth, in which David sat; it is now deserted. Aquila interprets it as “fortifications,” Symmachus as “refuges,” and Theodotion as “caves.”

Masbach, the hostile city of King Hadadezer.

Mela, that is, Gemela, which Aquila and Symmachus translate as “the Valley of Salt.” We have spoken of it above as well.

Maacha, the region of the king of Geshur.

[Col. 0911C] Modeim, a village near Diospolis, from which the Maccabees came. Even today their tombs are shown there.

[Note: Jerome may readily have had in mind the descendants of Mattathias, whose definite tombs were at Modin. But those whose remains were displayed at Antioch were the seven celebrated Maccabean brothers, who are quite distinct from the descendants of Mattathias. Martyrologies and ancient authors generally report that they suffered martyrdom at Antioch, although Josephus in *Antiquities* 12, and in the little book on the Maccabees, along with Cedrenus and a few others, say that it happened at Jerusalem. Saint Augustine too, in his sermon on the Maccabees, mentions a church dedicated to them at Antioch.]

I am therefore quite surprised how their relics are displayed at Antioch, or by what reliable authority this has been believed.

Mabsar of Tyre: Aquila and Symmachus interpret this as “fortified Tyre.”

Magau, the city which Solomon built.

Meeber: Aquila translated this as ἀπὸ πέραν, “from beyond”; Symmachus as ἐξ ἐναντίας, that is, “opposite” or “from across.”

Maces, a city of one of Solomon’s princes.

Mello, a city that Solomon built. (Moreover, [Note: [Col. 0911D] You may supplement Symmachus’s interpretation, which was the same as Theodotion’s, from the Regius Hexaplaric manuscript in Montfaucon: Σ. ἀπὸ προσθέματος, “from addition”; for the translation ἀπὸ πληρώματος, “from fullness,” is there attributed to Aquila.] Symmachus and Theodotion translated it as “fulfillment.” And this is discussed more fully in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.)

Maedam, a city that Solomon built.

Memphis, a city of Egypt, which the prophets Hosea, Ezekiel, and Jeremiah mention; and Jews who had fled from Jerusalem with Jeremiah also lived in Memphis.

Machaas, in Hosea; Aquila and Symmachus translate it as “desires.”

Miletus, a city of Asia, about which Ezekiel writes.

Mariboth, which Ezekiel mentions, saying: “As far as the water of Mariboth” (Ezekiel 48:28, according to the Septuagint); Aquila translates it as “quarrels,” and Symmachus as “disputes,” or “contradictions.”

Morasthi, from which the prophet Micah came. It is a village east of Eleutheropolis.

Masagam, a region of the Moabites, as Jeremiah writes.

Misor, a region of Moab, according to Jeremiah.

Mophath, a region of the Moabites, as we read in Jeremiah. It is also situated above Memphrua.

Maon, a region of the Moabites, according to Jeremiah.

Melchom, the idol of the Ammonites, as Jeremiah writes.

[Note: [Col. 0911D] Magedan, etc. Matthew records the name Magedan in chapter 15, verse 39; in the Greek text it is written Magdala. Mark, however, has Dalmanutha instead of Magedan in chapter 8, verse 10. Nevertheless, we must not accuse Eusebius of error, since he used Greek copies in which Magedan was read in Mark, just as it is read today in many manuscript codices, among the Greek variant readings of the New Testament listed in the London Polyglot Bible. MARTIAN.] Magedan, to whose borders the Evangelist Matthew writes that the Lord came; Mark also mentions a place of the same name. It is now called the region of Magedena, around Gerasa.

## Of the Five Books of Moses

[Note: [Col. 0912C] Vatican manuscript: Ναΐν, γῆ, “Nain, land.” Jerome correctly has Naid, Genesis 4:16.] Naid, the land in which Cain lived; it is rendered “the open sea,” that is, “motion” or “wavering.”

Nineveh, a city of the Assyrians, which Asshur built after departing from the land of Shinar. There is also, to this day, another Jewish city called Nineveh in a corner of Arabia (which they now call Nineve with a shortened vowel). [Note: [Col. 0912C] They call it *Nineve* with a shortened vowel. The printed editions read *corrupte* (“incorrectly”); so do the manuscript codices, except for the Colbertine manuscript of excellent quality, no. 4354, and another from the monastery of Saint Cygiranus. We have followed these, since no corruption of the name *Nineve* in relation to *Ninêve* appears: one could have been called *Nineve* with a shortened vowel, while the other was pronounced with a lengthened one. [Col. 0912D] MARTIAN. —The manuscript of the Queen’s Library reads *corrupte Neve*. Our manuscript has the abbreviated writing *corp̄te Nenevem*. Martianus, following two manuscripts, restored *correpte*, without changing the name *Ninive* at all; he supposed that the entire difference in pronunciation lay in the second syllable, which was shortened in this Nineveh and lengthened in the former. Relandus agrees with Martianus, though here he reads *Neneven*, as in our manuscript, and adduces other passages of Jerome in which he discusses the pronunciation of a shortened or lengthened vowel. One such passage is in his commentary on Zephaniah, chapter 1: “Here *pila* must not be read with the first syllable short, lest we take it for σφαῖραν, ‘a sphere,’ but with it lengthened, so that we understand it to mean the *pila* in which grain is pounded.” On the other hand, Clericus thinks that *corrupte*, which had previously appeared in the printed books, should be retained. He much prefers to understand Jerome as meaning that a certain town inhabited by Jews in Arabia was incorrectly—that is, wrongly—called Nineveh, although it ought not to have been so called. Although this reading is not important enough for us to discuss at length, the learned men—and Clericus himself—nevertheless seem to be mistaken in locating the variation of pronunciation in the second syllable. Eusebius, whose meaning Jerome is interpreting, places it in the third. He writes the name of the Assyrian city with a lengthened *e*, or η: Νινευῆ; the other, or Arabian, name with a shortened ε: Νινευέν. Thus Eusebius approves *correpte*, which also appeals more to us. If it should instead be read *corrupte*, suppose that the city meant is the one called Νευή by Carolus a Sancto Paulo in *Notitia*, p. 51, in the province of Arabia. In the Latin *Notitia*, p. 60, it is *Nevi*, where Holstenius observes that *Neve*, *Nevi*, and *Nevis* are read alike in the printed and manuscript *Notitiae*.]

[Col. 0913A] Naaliel, the encampment of the children of Israel beside the Arnon.

Nabau (called Nebo in Hebrew), a mountain above the Jordan opposite Jericho, in the land of Moab, where Moses died. To this day it is shown at the sixth milestone from the city of Esbus, [Note: [Col. 0914D] It is more faithful to suppose that Jerome wrote “toward the western region” than that Eusebius wrote πρὸς ἀνατολάς, “toward the east.” See above under *Abarim*.] toward the eastern region.

Nabo, a city of the children of Reuben in the region of Gilead, which Isaiah mentions in his vision against Moab, as does Jeremiah. There is also the name of a certain man, Nabau, who called Caan (Chanaath) and the other villages surrounding it Naboth (Nobe), after his own name. To this day the deserted site of Naba is also shown, eight miles from the city of Esbus toward the south.

Negeb, “south.” Among the Hebrews it is called *Nageb*, which Symmachus translates as “the south.” (It should be known, however, that among the Hebrews the same direction is called by three names: *Nageb*, *Theman*, and *Darom*. We may translate these as “south,” “southwest,” and “south,” or “east.”)

## From the Book of Joshua

Nepheddor (which Symmachus translates as “maritime”); Dor, however, is now a deserted town at the ninth milestone from Caesarea, on the road toward Ptolemais. [Note: [Col. 0914D] “At the ninth milestone.” The earlier printed books read, most corruptly, “at the eleventh milestone.” MARTIAN.]

Naftho, the name of a spring in the tribe of Benjamin.

Naama, a city of the tribe of Judah.

Neesib, in the tribe of Judah, now called Nasibi, at the seventh milestone from Eleutheropolis on the road toward Hebron.

[Col. 0913C] Nepsam, in the tribe of Judah.

Naaratha, in the tribe of Ephraim; it is now the Jewish village of Naorath, at the fifth milestone from Jericho.

Napheth, in the tribe of Manasseh.

Naalol, in the tribe of Zebulun, a city set apart for the Levites.

Neceb, in the tribe of Naphtali.

## From the Book of Judges

Neela, from which Zebulun was unable to drive out the foreigners. To this day there is a village in the region of Batanea called Neila.

Nabbe, or Nobba, to which Gideon went up; it was a city set apart for the priests, which we later read was destroyed in Saul’s fury.

Nemra, a city of the tribe of Reuben in the land of Gilead; to the present day there is a large village called Namara in the region of Batanea.

## From the Books of the Kingdoms

[Col. 0914A]

Navioth, a place in Ramah where David sat (we discussed this in the books of *Hebrew Questions*).

Nachon, the threshing floor of Nachon; Aquila translates it as “prepared threshing floor.”

Nephath, a city of one of Solomon’s princes.

Nerigel, which the Samaritans who came from Babylonia built in the region of Judaea.

Nezab, which the Hivites founded in the land of Judaea.

Nazareth, an idol of the Assyrians.

Nemerim, which Isaiah mentions in his vision against Moab, as does Jeremiah. It is now a village called Bennamarim, toward the north of Zoara.

Nebeoth, a region about which Isaiah writes.

## From the Gospels

[Col. 0914B]

Nazareth: from it our Lord and Savior was also called a Nazarene. We too were formerly called Nazarenes, as though by way of reproach; now they call us Christians. To this day there is a village in Galilee opposite Legion, at its fifteenth milestone toward the east, near Mount Tabor, called Nazara.

Naim, a small town in which the Lord raised the widow’s son from the dead. To this day it is shown at the second milestone from Mount Tabor, toward the south, near Aendor.

## From Genesis

Orech, a city of Nimrod’s kingdom in Babylonia.

Oolibama, a city of the princes of Edom.

[Col. 0914C] Odollam, we discussed this above; Isaiah also mentions it.

## From Exodus

Oothon, where the children of Israel encamped for the second time when they departed from Succoth, beside the desert, after setting out from Egypt.

## From the Book of Joshua

Opher, which Joshua captured after killing its king.

Ooli, a city in the tribe of Asher.

Ophra, the road of Ophra, leading to the land of Soal.

Up to this point we have read the letter O as short; from here onward let us read the letter as lengthened.

## From the Pentateuch

On, a city in Egypt, called Heliopolis in Greek, that is, “city of the sun,” which the children of Israel built, as the translators of the Septuagint think. Otherwise it is not found in the Hebrew books. And rightly so: for before Jacob entered Egypt, a city had already been built there, and it had a priest named Petefres, the father of Aseneth.

Or, the mountain on which Aaron died, beside the city of Petra. To this day the rock is shown there which Moses struck, giving water to the people.

Oboth, the encampment of the children of Israel in the desert.

## From the Books of Joshua and the Kingdoms

Osa, in the tribe of Asher.

Oram, in the tribe of Naphtali.

Ophir, from which, as we read in the Books of the Kingdoms, gold was brought to Solomon. There was also one of the descendants of Eber named Ophir. Josephus reports that people descended from him lived from the river Cophene as far as the region of India called Hieria; I think the region also took its name from him.

On, a city of Samaria, for which *aun* is written in Hebrew (), a word that Aquila and Symmachus translate as “useless,” while Theodotion translates it as “iniquity.”

Ocho, a priestly city.

Oronaim, a city of the Moabites, as it is written in Jeremiah.

## From Genesis

The Well of the Oath, which Abraham dug—that is, Beersheba—in the region of Gerar. We discussed it above as well.

The Well of the Vision, in the desert, beside which Isaac lived.

The Well of Judgment, still existing today in the region of Gerar. It is called a village named Berdan (which in Latin means “Well of Judgment”).

The Well of the Oath, where Isaac and Abimelech swore an oath; it is called the town of Isaac. There are also many other wells in the Holy Scriptures which are still shown today in the region of Gerar and near Ascalon.

Petra, a city of Arabia in the land of Edom, which was also called Jectael and is called Recem by the Syrians.

[lacuna]

## From the Pentateuch

Rooboth, a city of the Assyrians, which Asshur built after departing from the land of Shinar. (We discussed this more fully in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.) [Note: [Col. 0915D] In the books of *Hebrew Questions*. See the subsequent *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*. MARTIAN.]

Rooboth, another city beside the river where the king of Edom was. To this day there is a fortress in the region of Gabalena, as well as a large village called by this name.

[Col. 0916A] Ramesse, a city that the children of Israel built in Egypt; formerly the entire province in which Jacob lived with his children was also called by this name.

Roob, which the spies crossed, [Note: [Col. 0915D] Those sent by Joshua son of Nun. This appears to be a lapse of memory, unless the Latin copyists wrote “by Joshua” instead of “with Joshua.” For it is certain that Robob, Numbers 13:22, was visited by those spies who had been sent by Moses, and Joshua too was one of the spies. MARTIAN. —The Hieronymian manuscripts should be corrected on the basis of Eusebius, as Victorius and Martianus rightly judge; we should read “who were with Joshua,” οἱ μετὰ Ἰησοῦ. Joshua himself was one of the spies whom Moses sent out. Numbers 13:22.] who were sent by Joshua son of Nun. To this day there is a village called Rooba at the fourth milestone from Scythopolis; it too was set apart for the Levites.

Raphaca, in the desert where the children of Israel encamped.

Raphidim, a place in the desert near Mount Horeb, where water flowed from the rock; it was called “Temptation.” There Joshua also fought against Amalek near Pharan.

Rathma (in the desert), the encampment of the children of Israel.

[Col. 0916B] Remmon Phares, where the children of Israel encamped.

Ressa, the encampment of the children of Israel.

Rammoth, in the tribe of Gad, a priestly and refuge city in the land of Gilead. It is now a village at the fifteenth milestone from Philadelphia toward the east. [Note: [Col. 0916D] Martianus requires Eusebius to conform to the Hieronymian reading, but he is mistaken; the opposite is the case, and Jerome should be corrected according to the Eusebian text: “toward the west,” πρὸς δυσμάς. Otherwise Rammoth would have stood outside the boundaries of the land of Israel, which did not extend beyond Philadelphia toward the east.]

Recem: this is the city of Petra in Arabia, in which Recem reigned, whom the children of Israel killed. He himself is also said to have been the king of Midian. [Note: [Col. 0916D] The Queen’s manuscript has *Roacam*; ours prefers *Rocam*, as do the common Greek books, Ῥοκαν, though the more carefully corrected copies have Ῥοκόμ. Epiphanius, *On the Heresy of the Melchisedecians*: “Some call it in Arabia Petraea both Rocom and Edom.”]

## From the Book of Joshua

Remmon, in the tribe of Simeon or Judah. To this day there is a village called Remmon near Aelia, toward the north, at its fifteenth milestone.

Rogel, the name of a spring in the tribe of Benjamin.

[Col. 0916C] Rama, in the tribe of Benjamin, the city of Saul, at the sixth milestone from Aelia toward the north, opposite Bethel. Jeremiah also mentions it.

Recem, in the tribe of Benjamin.

Remmon, the rock of Remmon, in the tribe of Simeon or Zebulun.

Rabboth, in the tribe of Issachar. To this day there is another village called Rebbo on the borders of Eleutheropolis, toward the rising sun.

Rethom, in the tribe of Issachar.

Roob, in the tribe of Asher, a city set apart for the Levites.

Rama, in the tribe of Asher, as far as the fortified city of the Tyrians.

Rama, in the tribe of Naphtali.

For this reason the same names are assigned to different tribes: although they seem to sound as one name among us, they are written with different letters in Hebrew. Reccath, in the tribe of Naphtali.

[Col. 0917A] Ruma, also called Aria, where Abimelech sat, as it is written in the Book of Judges (Judges 9:41); it is now called Remphis. It is in the territory of Diospolis, and most people now call it Arimathea.

## From the Books of the Kingdoms

Remmath, to which David sent a share of the spoils.

Rachel, to this place also David sent a share of the spoils.

Remmoth-Gilead, a village beyond the Jordan near the river Jabbok. We discussed it above as well.

Rabbath, a city of the kingdom of Ammon, now Philadelphia, which Jeremiah mentions.

Roos, which David passed through; Aquila and Symmachus translate it as “fortress.”

Rogellim, from which Barzillai the Gileadite, David’s friend, came.

[Col. 0917B] Raphaim, the valley of the Philistines toward the north of Jerusalem.

Remmam, a city of the kings of Syria near Damascus.

Reth, which King Asa struck.

Rothem, which Aquila translates as ἄρκευθον, “juniper”; Symmachus translates it as “shelter.”

Remmon, which Isaiah mentions in his vision against Moab.

Raseph, a city of Syria.

Raphet, a city of the Assyrians in the region of Theman, about which it is written in Isaiah.

Rebla, in the land of Hamath; from there Pharaoh, after his victory, brought Jehoahaz to Egypt.

Remma, a mountain in Isaiah; Aquila translates it as “Mount Emmona,” Symmachus as “in Armenia.” There is also a village called Remmus in the Daroma. In the Books of the Kingdoms, however, Remmam is called the house of the idol of Damascus.

Reblatha, a region of the Babylonians (or a city now called Antioch).

[Note: [Col. 0917C] Ramale, etc. I think this word was taken from the Greek Ῥαβεδέ and was corrupted by Latin copyists, who wrote *Ramale* instead of *Ramade*. For in the Septuagint we read Ῥαμὰ δὲ, which Eusebius may perhaps have read as a single word, Ῥαμαδέ. MARTIAN. [Col. 0917D] —There is no doubt that this is the Ramah of which Zechariah speaks in chapter 14, verse 10. In the Septuagint the Greek name Ῥαμά is followed by the particle δέ; thus Martianus’s supposition that Eusebius read it as one word, Ῥαμαδέ, is quite probable. Jerome, commenting on that passage, says: “Ramah, however, will remain in its place; Aquila and the others who rendered it ‘it will be exalted’ translated it better. For *Ramah* means ‘exaltation.’”] Ramale; Aquila translates it as “it will be exalted.” It is written in Zechariah (14:10). There is also another place in the tribe of Benjamin near Bethlehem, of which it is said: “A voice was heard in Ramah” (Matthew 2:18). (This too is discussed more fully in the books of *Hebrew Questions*.)

[Col. 0918A] Rhinocorura, a city of Egypt, which Isaiah mentions. (It should be known, however, that this name is not found in the Hebrew books but was added by the translators of the Septuagint for the sake of identifying the place.)

What we said in the book of *Hebrew Names* should also be prefaced here under the heading of the letter S: among the Hebrews there are three S’s, namely *samekh*, *ṣade*, and *shin*. Although they are pronounced with similar sounds among the Greeks and Latins, they have different sounds in their own language. Hence it happens that the same names seem to sound different among us, and this letter has more variation than the others. For places, cities, and villages are described not by one letter but by three.

## From Genesis

Sidon, a distinguished city of Phoenicia, formerly the northern boundary of the Canaanites and later of the region of Judaea. It fell by lot to the tribe of Asher, but that tribe did not possess it, because it was entirely unable to drive out the inhabitants.

Sennaar, the plain of Babylonia, where the tower was built. From there Asshur departed and built Nineveh. Josephus mentions this place in the first book of the *Antiquities*, writing as follows: “Concerning the plain which in the region of Babylonia is called Sennaar, the historian Hestiaeus relates that certain priests, fugitives from the temple of Enyalius, carrying away the sacred objects of Jupiter, came to the plain of Sennaar in Babylonia.” [Note: [Col. 0917D] Concerning the temple of Enyalius, etc. I am ashamed to say by what authority “Jupiter Gemalius” or “Gemelius” entered Jerome’s text. Nor does the evidence permit us here to accuse the negligence or ignorance of the ancient copyists, since the manuscript codices preserve the true reading *Enyalii*, although the name is written differently in them: *anial*, *enialii*, and *ENYALII*. One of the Regius copies omitted both words, but changed the reading and meaning in this way: “from the temple of Venus, carrying the sacred objects of Jupiter,” etc. Who, then, this fabricated Jupiter Gemalius may be, I simply do not know; but I have read much about Jupiter Enyalius in the best authors. First, the name Ἐνυάλιος signifies Mars and is used by Greek authors for Mars or the war-god. Nevertheless, Enyalius is distinguished from Mars by Sophocles in the *Ajax*: ἢ χαλκοθώραξ, ἢ ἐνυάλιος, “either the bronze-clad one, or Enyalius,” that is, “Mars, or Enyalius.” Likewise, according to Plutarch in the *Life of Romulus*, Quirinus is said by some to have been called ὁ Ἐνυάλιος. Secondly, in Josephus, book 1 of the *Antiquities*, chapter 5, the name is written Ἐνυέλιος; in a Regius manuscript of Eusebius it is ἐννυέλιος, with double ν and ε in the middle, instead of the α that Jerome read, as all copies of the holy Doctor attest, in which the form is *enyalii*, not *enyelii*. As for why the earlier printed books read *Gemalii* instead of *Enyalii*, I can imagine no other cause than Jerome’s *Apology against Jovinian*, book 1, in which Jupiter Gamelius and Genethlius are named. Erasmus and Marianus therefore thought that the same form should always be read in Jerome. Hence *Gamelius*, or *Gemelius*, occurs here instead of *Enyalius*. MARTIAN.]

Sichem and Salem, which was called Sicima in Latin and Greek, the city of Jacob, now deserted. The site is shown in the suburbs of Neapolis, near Joseph’s tomb. Abimelech destroyed it and sowed salt in it, as it is written in the Book of Judges (Judges 9:45). It was later restored by Jeroboam, as the history in the Books of the Kingdoms relates (1 Kings 12:25), and it lies within the borders of the tribe of Ephraim. The son of Hamor was also called Sichem, and the place received its name from him. There was also another Sichem on Mount Ephraim, a city of refuge.

Sennaar, from which came Amraphel, who waged war against the kings of Sodom.

[Col. 0919A] Sodom, a city of the impious, consumed by divine fire, beside the Dead Sea.

Seboim, likewise a city of the impious, reduced to eternal ashes, beside the former city of Sodom.

Sophera, a mountain to the east in India, near which the sons of Joktan, the sons of Eber, lived. Josephus reports that they came from the river Cophene and the regions of India as far as the place called the region of Hieria; Solomon’s fleet also transported certain goods from there over a period of three years.

Soora, a city near Sodom, also called Segor and Zoara (we discussed it above as well).

Save, an ancient city in which the Amorites lived, a powerful people, above the region of Sodom; Chodologomor destroyed it.

Seir, a mountain in the land of Edom, where Esau lived in the region of Gabalena. Because Esau was hairy and shaggy, the place received the name Seir, that is, “hairy.” The Horrite had formerly lived in these places; Chodologomor killed him. Isaiah also mentions Mount Seir in his vision of Idumea.

Salem, a city of the Shechemites, namely Sichem. A different village bearing this name is also shown to the present day: near Aelia, toward the west, and also at the eighth milestone from Scythopolis, in the plain, there is a village called Salumias. Josephus, however, affirms that Salem was the city in which Melchizedek reigned (*Antiquities*, book 1, chapter 11); afterward it was called Solyma and finally received the name Jerusalem.

[Col. 0919C] [Note: [Col. 0919D] As we said, this heading is also absent from the Vatican manuscripts. Along the margin of the book, however, the following glosses on the names Agar, Cades, and Barad are written:

ἌΓαρ· αὐτὴ πάροικος. “Agar: she herself is a sojourner.”

ΚαΔΗϹ. ἁγία αὐτή. “Cades: she herself is holy.”

ΒαΡΑΔ. ἐν κακοῖς ἡ κτίσις. “Barad: creation amid evils”; in Latin, “possession among evils.”

From these it is quite clear that the entry for Sur, concerning which a marginal note remains, had fallen out through that customary carelessness of copyists which we have mentioned.] Sur, where the angel found Agar, Sarah’s maidservant, between Cades and Barad. The desert of Sur extends as far as the Red Sea, reaching the borders of Egypt. Cades, moreover, is a wilderness above the city of Petra; Scripture also says that the desert of Cades extends opposite Egypt, and the Hebrews first came there after crossing the Red Sea.

Segor, also called Bala and Zoara, one of the five cities of Sodom, spared from the conflagration at Lot’s request; it is still shown today. Isaiah mentions it in his vision against Moab; we discussed it above as well.

Sene, that is, “tents,” the place where Jacob lived after returning from Mesopotamia; in Hebrew it is called Succoth.

## From Exodus

[Col. 0920A]

Succoth, the first encampment of the children of Israel in the desert after they had departed from Egypt, before they crossed the Red Sea.

Sin, the desert between the Red Sea and the wilderness of Sinai. From this desert the children of Israel came to Raphidim, and from Raphidim to the desert of Sinai, beside Mount Sinai, where Moses received the tablets of the law. Scripture says that the desert of Sin is the same as Cades; so too do the Hebrews say. It is not found, however, in the translators of the Septuagint.

## From Numbers and Deuteronomy

Selmona, an encampment of the children of Israel in the desert.

Saphar, Mount Saphar in the desert, an encampment of the children of Israel.

[Col. 0920B] Sattim, where the people were defiled by fornication with the daughters of Moab. It is beside Mount Phogor; from there Joshua also sent spies to investigate and learn about Jericho.

Sabama, a city of Moab in the land of Gilead, which fell by lot to the tribe of Reuben. Isaiah also mentions it in his vision against Moab.

[Note: [Col. 0919D] Martianus placed the following heading before this one. Our Latin manuscripts arrange both according to the Greek exemplar. In the Greek, however, the Vatican manuscript incorrectly has οὕτως instead of Ὤγ.] Selcha, the city of King Og, in the region of Basan.

Senna, the boundary of Judaea; to this day, at the seventh milestone from Jericho toward the north, a village called Magdalsena is shown. The name means “the tower of Senna.” [Note: [Col. 0919D] Eusebius said “of Idumea”; nevertheless Jerome is not mistaken in substituting Judaea, since Senna lay within the borders of Idumea. [Col. 0920D] Senna was the boundary of the whole land of Judaea. In almost all copies the Septuagint calls this place Ἐννάκ; one Oxford manuscript has the less erroneous form Σενάχ, Numbers 34:4. Earlier editions are wrong when they immediately read μεγάλη Σεννά, “Great Senna,” instead of Μιγδαλσεννά or Μογδαλσεννά, “Magdal-Senna,” that is, “the tower of Senna,” which we have restored from the Vatican manuscript.]

Sephama, the eastern boundary of Judaea.

Sadada, the boundary of Judaea.

[Col. 0920C] Someron, which Joshua captured after killing its king. They now say that it is called Sebaste, a town of Palestine where the relics of Saint John the Baptist are buried. Seira, which Joshua also captured.

Saorth, in the tribe of Reuben, above the Jordan.

[Col. 0921A] [Note: [Col. 0921D] This heading is absent not only from the Greek but also from the Latin manuscript of the Queen’s Library; in ours it is written in a second hand in the table of contents.] Sochoth, in the tribe of Gad, above the Jordan.

Syphon, in the tribe of Gad, above the Jordan.

Sacharoma, in the tribe of Judah.

Samem, in the tribe of Judah.

Saal, in the tribe of Judah or Simeon.

Selei, in the tribe of Judah.

Saara, a village on the borders of Eleutheropolis, toward the north on the road to Nicopolis, approximately at the tenth milestone; it is in the tribe of Dan or Judah.

Soccho (in the tribe of Judah). To this day there are two small villages on the road from Eleutheropolis to Aelia, at the ninth milestone of the public road: one is situated on a mountain, the other in the plain; they are called Sochoth.

Sarain, in the tribe of Judah.

Senam, in the tribe of Judah.

Saphir, a village situated in the hill country between Eleutheropolis and Ascalon, in the tribe of Judah.

Soccho, which was also mentioned above. The Samaritans who came from Babylon are said to have founded this village.

[Note: [Col. 0921D] Scacha, etc. Earlier editions read *Scatha*, which greatly perplexed the learned Bonfrerius, who did not know that nearly all the names in the old editions of Jerome had been corrupted. MARTIAN.] Sacha, in the tribe of Judah.

Selo, in the tribe of Ephraim. The ark of the covenant remained there, and the tabernacle of the Lord, until the time of Samuel. It is at the tenth milestone from Neapolis, in the region of Acrabatta. We also read that Judah’s son was called Selon.

[Col. 0921C] Sechem, in the tribe of Manasseh, a priestly and refuge city on Mount Ephraim, where Joseph’s bones were buried; we discussed it above as well.

Semri, in the tribe of Benjamin.

Sela, in the tribe of Benjamin.

Sabee, in the tribe of Simeon.

Sams; Theodotion and Symmachus translate it as “of the sun.”

Sunem, in the tribe of Issachar. To this day a village called Sulem is shown at the fifth milestone from Mount Tabor, toward the south.

[Col. 0921D] Seon, or Soen, in the tribe of Issachar; to this day a village is shown near Mount Tabor.

Sirotha, to which the judge Ehud fled. We also discussed Seira above.

Sur Choreb, which means “the rock of Horeb.”

Selmon, the mountain which Abimelech climbed when fighting against Sicima.

Sephina; Aquila and Symmachus translate it as “the north.”

Sorech, the name of a torrent, from which place Delilah, Samson’s woman, came. To this day a village called Capharsorech is shown north of Eleutheropolis, near the village of Saar; Samson also came from there.

## From the Books of the Kingdoms

Sophim, a mountain of Ephraim in the hill country of Armathem.

Salisa, which Saul passed through.

Senna, the name of a rock.

Saalim, a village which Saul passed through on the borders of Eleutheropolis toward the west, seven miles distant from it.

Sim, where Samuel found Saul.

Sabim, where Saul fought.

Sonam, from which came that Shunammite woman. To this day there is a village on the borders of Sebaste, in the region of Acrabatta, called Sanim. [Note: [Col. 0922D] Martianus erroneously reads *ubi*, “where,” in the Latin, instead of *unde*, “from which”; in the Greek he read Ἀκριβαττινῇ and shortly afterward Σωμανίτην instead of Σωανῖτιν, an error he made repeatedly.]

Sophamoth, to which place David sent.

Seira, the name of a well from which Joab made the commander of the army, Abner, turn back.

Suba, whose king David struck.

Sarthan, which is at the foot of Jezreel.

Sophera, also called Sophir, from which Solomon’s ships came; we discussed it above as well. It is a mountain to the east belonging to the region of India.

Saron, which Isaiah also mentions, saying, “Saron has been turned into marshes” (Isaiah 33:9). To the present day the region between Mount Tabor and the Sea of Galilee is called Saronas. The entire land visible from Caesarea of Palestine to the town of Joppa is also called Saronas.

Sephela, as Isaiah writes; Aquila translates it as “the plain,” Symmachus as “the valley.” [Note: [Col. 0923D] Drusius thinks that Isaiah has been substituted here for Obadiah. The term does indeed occur in Isaiah 32:19, but there the Septuagint translates it as ἐν τῇ πεδινῇ, “in the plain,” not as Σεφηλά, as in Obadiah. It is also possible to conjecture that in Eusebius’s time Σεφηλά was once read in the cited passage of Isaiah, at least in some copy, and was later replaced by ἐν τῇ πεδινῇ from Aquila, as learned men observe happened elsewhere.] To this day the entire region near Eleutheropolis that is flat and level, extending toward the north and west, is called Sephela.

Sennaar; Aquila translates it as Sennam, while Symmachus translates it as “fertile.” The prophet Micah also mentions it.

Sedrach, the land of Damascus; we read of it in Zechariah (9:1; see Hadrach).

[Col. 0923B] Sion, the mountain of the city of Jerusalem.

Samaria, the royal city in Israel, now called Sebaste. The entire surrounding region also formerly took its name from the city.

Sor, Tyre, the metropolis of Phoenicia, in the tribe of Naphtali.

Soene, a city of the Thebaid, as Ezekiel writes.

Sais, a city of Egypt, which Ezekiel mentions; from it the district of Saitis also takes its name.

Sadala, the boundary of Judaea, as Ezekiel also writes.

Sabarim, between Damascus and Hamath, as Ezekiel writes.

Salisa; Aquila translates it as “lasting three years.” Jeremiah mentions it.

279. **Sichar**, before Neapolis, near the field that Jacob gave to his son Joseph, where, according to the Gospel of John, our Lord and Savior speaks with the Samaritan woman at the well; a church has now been built there.

## FROM GENESIS

**Tigris**, a river issuing from Paradise, according to the testimony of Scripture, and proceeding toward the Assyrians; after many circuits, flowing, as Josephus holds, into the Red Sea. It is called by this name because of its speed, like a beast running with extraordinary swiftness.

[Note: As Josephus maintains, etc. Consult what was said above concerning the river Tigris and the animal tiger, column 547, in our notes to the Greek Fragments of the Book of Names. MARTIAN.]

**Terebinth**, at Sichem, beneath which Jacob hid the idols, near Neapolis.

## FROM THE BOOK OF JESUS

**Tina**, in the tribe of Judah.

**Talem**, in the tribe of Judah.

**Tesan**, in the tribe of Judah.

**Tyrus**, in the tribe of Naphtali.

## FROM THE BOOK OF JUDGES

**Tabath**, where the battle was fought against Midian.

**Tob**, the land in which Jephthah lived.

**Topheth**, in the valley of the sons of Ennom, where the people of Israel worshiped the images of the nations. It is a place in the outskirts of Jerusalem.

**Tanis**, a city of Egypt, as Isaiah and Ezekiel write.

**Taphnas**, a city of Egypt. Read Hosea, Ezekiel, and Jeremiah. Jews who fled with Jeremiah out of fear of the Babylonians lived there.

## FROM THE GOSPEL

**The region of Trachonitis**, or Ituraea, whose tetrarch was Philip, according to the Gospel of Luke. We also spoke of it above. It lies beyond Bostra, a city of Arabia, in the desert, toward the south, facing roughly toward Damascus.

Thus far we have read names written with the simple letter *t*. But since what follows among the Hebrews is written not with *teth* but with *tau*, that is, with the Greek *theta*, we must read them with aspiration.

## FROM GENESIS

**Theman**, the region of the chiefs of Edom in the land of Gebal, deriving its name from Theman, son of Eliphaz, son of Esau. Even today there is a village called Theman, five miles from the city of Petra, where a garrison of Roman soldiers is stationed; from that place came Eliphaz, king of the Themanites. One of Ishmael’s sons was also called Theman. It should be known that the entire southern region is called *Theman* in Hebrew.

**Thamna**, where Judah sheared his sheep: even today a very large village is shown in the territory of Diospolis, on the road to Aelia, in the tribe of Dan or Judah.

**Thamna**, another city of the chiefs of Edom; the concubine of Eliphaz, son of Esau, was also called Thamna. She bore him Amalek, from whom came the Amalekites.

## FROM DEUTERONOMY

**Thaphol**, a place in the desert beyond the Jordan, where Moses wrote Deuteronomy, opposite Jericho.

**Thaath**, a camp of the children of Israel.

**Thara**, a camp of the children of Israel.

## FROM THE BOOK OF JESUS

**Thaffu**, a city in the tribe of Judah, which Jesus captured after killing its king. Above we also spoke of the boundary of Palestine and Egypt called Bethtaphu.

**Thaanach**, a city that Jesus captured after killing its king. It was in the tribe of Manasseh, assigned to the Levites; today a village of this name is shown at the fourth mile from the town of Legion.

**Thenath**, in the tribe of Joseph. Even today there is a village called Thena, ten miles east of Neapolis, for those descending toward the Jordan.

**Thaffue**, in the tribe of Joseph.

**Thaphuth**, in the tribe of Manasseh.

**Theco**, even today a village is shown near the desert of the city of Aelia; the prophet Amos came from there.

**Thesram**, which Jesus captured together with its king.

**Therama**, in the tribe of Benjamin.

**Tholad**, in the tribe of Judah or Simeon.

**Thabor**, the boundary of Zebulun. It is a mountain in the middle of Galilee, rising with remarkable roundness in the plain, ten miles from Diocaesarea toward the east. It also formed the boundary between the tribe of Issachar and Naphtali.

[Note: The word “plain” is absent from the Regina manuscript.]

**Thalcha**, in the tribe of Simeon. It is now a large Jewish village called Thella, approximately sixteen miles from Eleutheropolis toward the south.

[Note: “Toward the southern region.” In the old editions and in some manuscripts, the western region was incorrectly printed instead of the southern region. For Thalcha is said in Greek to be in the Daroma, an entirely southern region; and Jerome frequently translates *Darom* as “the southern region.” The name Talcha is also read in the Septuagint, Joshua 19:7. MARTIAN. —Our manuscript reads “toward the eastern region”; in others, as also in the old editions, Martianaeus found “toward the western region.” But no one can be unaware that when Eusebius says *ἐν τῷ Δαρωμᾷ* he designates the meridian or southern region.]

[Note: Up to this point the printed books, in a monstrous form, read Θαμνασθαρὰ, while Martianaeus has only Thamnath in the Latin. The Septuagint prefers Θαμνασαρὰχ, Joshua 19:20. The Hebrew reads [Hebrew text]. The Vatican manuscript corrects the Eusebian text; two Latin manuscripts, the Regina and ours, supplement the Hieronymian text.]

**Thamnathsara**, a city of Jesus son of Nave, situated on a mountain. We also spoke of it above under the name Thamna; his tomb is still shown there to the present day, in the tribe of Dan.

[Note: Rather, it is very clearly under the name Gaas, on the northern side of whose mountain, he says, Jesus son of Nave was buried; even today his distinguished tomb is shown near the village of Thamnah.]

[Note: More accurately, Bonfrerius and Clericus say, in the tribe of Ephraim. Certainly, both Eusebius and Jerome place in this tribe the mountain previously mentioned, Gaas, on whose northern side Jesus was buried.]

[lacuna]

## FROM THE BOOK OF JUDGES

**Thaanach**, a city near which Deborah fought against Sisera, in the tribe of Manasseh, assigned to the Levites, but which they were unable to retain because its former inhabitants were not expelled. It is now a very large village three miles from Legion.

**Thebes**, the city whose siege Abimelech was conducting when he died after being struck by a fragment of a millstone. Even today there is a village called Thebes in the territory of Neapolis, on the road to Scythopolis, approximately at its thirteenth milestone.

**Thamnatha**: above we also gave Thamna, in the tribe of Judah.

## FROM THE BOOKS OF THE KINGDOMS

**Thelamuge**, the place where Abenner sent to David.

[Note: It should be understood that for this word Aquila translates “immediately”; Symmachus, “for himself.”]

**Thaad**, near Gilead.

**Thamsa**, the boundary of Solomon’s kingdom.

**Thermoth**, a city that Solomon built in the desert, which we mentioned in the Books of Hebrew Questions.

[Note: In the Books of Hebrew Questions. We said above that, apart from the Questions on Genesis, Jerome’s Hebrew Questions have not survived. MARTIAN.]

**Tharsis**, from which gold was brought to Solomon. Josephus thinks this is the city of Tarsus in Cilicia. According to the prophet Ezekiel, however, Carthage is intended. For where we read “Carthage” in the Septuagint translators, the Hebrew has *Tharsis*. Some have thought it was India; this was discussed more fully both in the Book of Letters (Letter 37), which we wrote to Marcella, and in the Books of Hebrew Questions.

**Thersa**, where Asa, king of Israel, was.

[Note: Perhaps this should be emended on the basis of Eusebius. In the Greek, instead of Ἀσὰφ, I would prefer, following Jerome, Ἀσὰ, Asa: namely, the son of David who reigned at Tharsa. See 1 Kings 15:2 and 2 Chronicles 14:15. Bonfrerius also reads Ἀσὰ, but by conjecture, as with much else; still more objectionably, he never alerts the reader to this. Finally, from the Vatican manuscript we restored Σαμαρέων, instead of the less satisfactory Σαμαρείων formerly printed.]

**Thersila**, from which Manaen came. Even today there is a village of Samaritans in the region of Batanaea called Thersila.

**Therba**, from which the prophet Elijah, the Tishbite, came.

**Theman**, according to Ezekiel, a city of Idumaea. Isaiah, however, places it in Arabia in his vision. Jeremiah also mentions it. Obadiah writes that it is the city of Esau. One of Esau’s sons was likewise called Theman, as we said above.

**Tharac**, which the Hivites founded in the land of Judah.

**Thalassar**, a region of Syria.

**Thogarma**, which we read about in Ezekiel.

**Taphet**, which we read about in Jeremiah (7:32): the altar of Taphet. Even today there is a place in the outskirts of Aelia called by this name, near the Pool of the Fuller and the field of Acheldema.

## FROM GENESIS
