**Ur of the Chaldeans**, where Aram, Abraham’s brother, died. Even today, as Josephus reports, his tomb is shown. We discussed our view of this more fully in the Books of Hebrew Questions.

**Ulammaus**, for which the Hebrew has *Luza*. It is the same as Bethel, as we said above. A village called Ulamma is also shown twelve miles from Diocaesarea toward the sunrise.

**Us**, from which Job came, from the region of Ausitis; one of Esau’s descendants was also called Us. We discussed this in the Books of Hebrew Questions.

[Note: In the Books of Hebrew Questions. See immediately afterward Jerome’s Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis, where he discusses Ur, Ulammaus, and Us. MARTIAN.]

## FROM THE BOOK OF JUDGES

**Xil**, in the tribe of Judah.

## FROM GENESIS

**Zaphoim**, a region of the chiefs of Edom, in the land now called Gebalena.

## FROM NUMBERS AND DEUTERONOMY

**Zoob**, a city of the Amorites situated on the Arnon. Concerning it, it is written: “Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the Lord: Zoob set fire, and the torrents of Arnon” (Numbers 21:14, according to the Septuagint).

**Zephrona**, the northern boundary of Judah.

**Zared**, the valley of Zared in a part of the desert.

[Note: My manuscript corrects “the valley,” where Martianaeus mistakenly has “the village.”]

## FROM THE BOOK OF JESUS

**Zeph**, in the tribe of Judah.

**Zannohua**, in the tribe of Judah. Even today, in the territory of Eleutheropolis on the road to Aelia, it is called the village Zanua.

**Zib**, eight miles east of Hebron. Even now a village is shown there, where David hid. It belonged to the tribe of Judah in the Daroma, in the territory of Eleutheropolis.

## FROM THE BOOKS OF THE KINGDOMS

**Ziph**, a barren, or dark, or misty mountain near Ziph, where David stayed close to Carmel, which is called Carmel in the Holy Scriptures. Today it is a Jewish village, and Nabal the Carmelite came from there. One of Caleb’s descendants was also called Ziph. Read Chronicles (1 Chronicles 2:42).

**Zogora**, a city of the Moabites in Jeremiah. It is the one now called Zoara or Segor, one of the five cities of the Sodomites.

**Zeb**, a city of Ammon. Even today the village Zia is shown fifteen miles west of Philadelphia, concerning which Jeremiah writes.

**Zoeleth**, the name of a stone where Adonijah sacrificed victims beside the spring of Rogel.

[Note: The old editors Erasmus and Victorius append here a booklet entitled *Places from the Acts*, which is also found in various Hieronymian manuscripts. It has been established, however, that Jerome is not its author. In our manuscript it is entitled: “Names of regions and places from the Acts of the Apostles, transcribed not by Jerome but by someone else.” Learned men attribute it to Bede, in whose works it is also found, and consider it worthy of reading. Martianaeus rejected it altogether; we shall review it against the manuscripts in the Appendix to this volume.]

## EXCERPTS CONCERNING CERTAIN PLACES OF PALESTINE

### NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING GEOGRAPHICAL MAP OF PALESTINE

After reading Jerome’s, or Eusebius’s, book on the cities and villages of Palestine, nothing is more useful, or more necessary for retaining their meaning properly and deriving from them the benefit that reading ought to yield, than a geographical map of the whole land they describe, representing at a single glance its situation and the locations in relation to one another. Such a map supplies, as it were, the place of a commentary—or rather, with its help one may obtain, by running the eye over the picture, what one would scarcely achieve through lengthy commentaries.

> Things conveyed through the ears  
> Affect the mind less forcefully  
> Than those placed before faithful eyes,  
> Which the spectator himself hands on to his own understanding.  
> —Horace, *Art of Poetry* 180ff.

But if one had to sketch a map of this kind solely from the testimony of these Fathers and follow only their footsteps, one could scarcely describe many separate maps, one for each region, let alone produce a single map that would display all Palestine simultaneously *ἐν γραφῆς τύπῳ*—“in the form of a map,” as Eusebius puts it.

For, as the distinguished Reland observed long ago, Eusebius and his translator Jerome define, in each region of the land of Israel, the distances of places from the principal city of that region; but they omit stating where the city itself is situated. For example, they measure the locations of more than twenty places from Eleutheropolis, yet nowhere indicate what tract Eleutheropolis itself occupies, since it is not mentioned in Scripture. The same is generally true of the other cities from which they measure places in Judaea—Nicopolis or Diospolis; in Samaria—from Neapolis and Sebaste; in Galilee—from Diocaesarea and Legion; and beyond the Jordan—from Pella and Philadelphia. They evidently regarded it as needless to specify the distances at which these principal cities, already so well known in their own time, were situated. They either pass over them altogether or are content to call them *πόλεις ἐπίσημοι*, “distinguished cities.” Now that they have ceased to be distinguished, however, locating each in relation to the others is not easy if we rely only on their indications.

Another difficulty is added to this defect: even the cities themselves, which the Fathers locate by distances measured from the chief city of each region, are not marked with sufficient precision in relation to the points of the compass. They use only the four common directions—east, west, north, and south—and neglect the intermediate directions. It is scarcely credible that all the cities mentioned by Eusebius faced directly toward the region to which they are referred, or that all lay at the same remove, as though on a single line, from the city from which their distance is measured.

I say nothing now of the other matters that the esteemed Reland finds lacking in this pair of writers and emphasizes at length, perhaps even beyond the truth. In reality they either cause little difficulty or are entirely sound, as we showed in the Preface placed at the beginning of this volume. From the two matters just mentioned it is sufficiently clear that an image of the whole of Palestine cannot be drawn according to the understanding of Eusebius and Jerome solely from these records of theirs, although they are by far the clearest of all. Some features must first be established on the authority of other geographers, especially the ancient ones; only then can the matters left uncertain by Eusebius or Jerome be securely determined.

This, then, is what I had to supply in constructing this map, since it was readily possible to support this description with testimony from other sources. Nor, I think, will anyone devoted to sacred geography be angry that my zeal carried me somewhat beyond the stated purpose. I could not persuade myself to sketch so many separate maps of the regions, and otherwise the benefit of this excellent book could scarcely have been obtained.

I reviewed and arranged the places under their respective names, as they are designated in this book according to the Septuagint edition. I omitted scarcely anything except places whose names are appellative rather than proper, as they say, or which are merely insignificant villages for which no distances are given. It was therefore better to omit them than to deceive readers by mixing certainties with uncertainties.

Jerome himself was available through his other writings, especially his letter to Dardanus, number 129 in our recension. There he measures the length of the entire Jewish possession from Dan to Beersheba, a stretch scarcely more than 160 miles long; its breadth, from Joppa to the village of Bethlehem, is forty-six miles, followed by an immense desert full of savage barbarians. From this it was possible to understand that an equal extent of territory lay eastward in a straight line toward the Jordan, and from the Jordan to Chesbon, a city of Peraea—or, as Eusebius prefers, all the way to Philadelphia, which extended ten miles beyond Chesbon from the Jordan.

Although the breadth of Judaea is somewhat more uncertain, since the authorities do not agree sufficiently on how far it extended beyond the Jordan, I nevertheless felt that I ought to describe the boundaries of Palestine not from the opinions of various and mostly recent travelers—not to mention the Talmud and the fantasies of the Jews—but from the testimony of one exceptionally skilled in such matters: the bishop of Caesarea, distinguished both for his learning and for his proximity to the region, and his great interpreter Jerome, who traveled through those territories with even greater curiosity and lived there for many years.

For this reason I also judged that Jerome’s own excerpts concerning distances between places were worth preserving. I collected them with considerable care after Martianaeus, and they are now for the most part more extensive. I omitted other material that you can recall for yourself from Letter 108, or the Epitaph of Saint Paula, sections 8 through 15, and from the work entitled *On the Stations* addressed to Fabiola, number 78 in our recension. Those works would have had to be copied almost in their entirety if I had wished to present everything they report about the cities of the Holy Land.

## EXCERPTS FROM JEROME’S WORKS CONCERNING CERTAIN PLACES OF PALESTINE

293. **Adadremmon** is a city near Jezreel, which was once called by this name and is now called Maximianopolis, in the plain of Megiddo, where King Josiah was wounded by Pharaoh called Necho (Zechariah 12).

[Note: Martianaeus mistakenly reads “Jerusalem.”]

**Ahila.** The Red Sea, on whose shore Ahila is situated, where a legion and Roman garrison are now stationed (Ezekiel 47).

**Anathoth** is a village situated three miles from the city of Jerusalem, toward the north (Preface to Book 1 of the Commentary on Hosea); three miles north of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 1).

**Apedno.** “He will pitch his tent in Apedno,” near Nicopolis, which was formerly called Emmaus, where the mountains of Judaea begin to rise (Daniel 11).

**Arabia.** “The king of Babylon … will indeed set out by the road of the Chaldeans, but when he comes through the desert and wilderness to the fork of the road in the land of Arabia, which is called the land of the sons of Ammon, one road leads to Jerusalem on the right, while the left leads to Rabbath of the sons of Ammon, which is the capital city and is now called Philadelphia,” and so forth (Ezekiel 21).

**Ar**, the capital city of the region of Moab, which is a province of the Arabs. Today, compounded from the Hebrew and Greek languages, it is called Areopolis—not, as many think, because it is the city of *Ares*, that is, Mars (Isaiah 15).

**Arnon** is the boundary of the Amorites and Moabites (ibid.).

**Azotus.** Understand by “the utmost sea” the sea to the west, which leads to Egypt; on its shore lie Gaza, Ascalon, Azotus, Joppa, Caesarea, and the other maritime cities (Joel 2).

**Beersheba.** Even today there is a town called Beersheba. Not long ago this province, following the division of the governors of Palestine, was called Salutaris (Questions on Genesis 17:30).

**Beth-aven.** Formerly called Bethel, it is a city in the tribe of Ephraim, beyond Benjamin. For where the tribe of Benjamin ends, not far away this city was founded in the tribe of Ephraim (Hosea 5).

**Bethulia.** “With an immense crowd of pursuers she came to Bethulia … on the fifth day she came to Pelusium” (*Life of Saint Hilarion*).

**Cadesbarne.** It is in the desert that extends as far as the city of Petra (Ezekiel 48).

**Carmel.** There are two mountains called by this name. One, where Nabal the Carmelite, Abigail’s husband, lived, lies toward the south; the other is near Ptolemais, on the borders of Phoenicia, formerly called Acho, rising above the sea, where the prophet Elijah obtained rain on bended knees (Amos 1).

**Carmel.** “If they hide themselves on the summit of Carmel,” or near the borders of Phoenicia, in the northern region toward the south, because of the desolation of the wilderness where Nabal the Carmelite once lived (Amos 8).

Mount Carmel lies on the border of Palestine and Phoenicia, overlooking Ptolemais. Scripture also calls another mountain Carmel, where Nabal the Carmelite lived (Isaiah 29).

**Cedar**, formerly uninhabitable, is the region beyond Arabia of the Saracens (Isaiah 42).

**Dan**, on the borders of the Jewish land, where Paneas now is (Amos 8).

**Dan.** “From Dan even to Joppa,” where the towers of Ailon, Selebi, and Emmaus—which is now called Nicopolis—are situated. Yet later we read that, after crossing the territories of the other tribes, they took for themselves the city of Lesem in the tribe of Dan, which is now called Paneas (Ezekiel 48).

**Dimon and Dibon.** No one should think this is a scribal error and, while attempting to correct it, create another mistake. One city is written with both the letter *m* and the letter *b*. Of these names, Dimon means “silence,” while Dibon means “flowing”; both names were given because of the waters that flow silently. Even today this little town is indiscriminately called both Dimon and Dibon (Isaiah 15).

**Duma.** A region of Idumaea that extends southward and lies twenty miles from the Palestinian city now called Eleutheropolis (Isaiah 21).

**Edomia.** One and the same man is therefore called by three names—Esau, Edom, and Seir—and he possessed the region now called Gebalena, in the territory of Eleutheropolis, where the Horites had previously lived. Their name means “free,” and from this the city itself later received its name. What is called Edom in Hebrew and *Idumaea* in Greek is now a village of Palestine, named after its founder (Obadiah 1).

**Lesser Emath**, to distinguish it from Greater Emath, which is now called Antioch, is a city on the borders of the Holy Land facing the sunrise. Later it was called Epiphania after Antiochus, whose surname was Epiphanes (Amos 6).

**Emmaus.** Near Nicopolis, formerly called Emmaus, where the mountains of Judaea begin to rise (Daniel 12).

**Emmaus.** This signifies the period of Judas Maccabaeus, who, coming from the village of Modin with his brothers and relatives supporting him, and with many of the Jewish people, defeated the generals of Antiochus near Emmaus, now called Nicopolis (Daniel 8).

**Engallim** is at the beginning of the Dead Sea, where the Jordan enters it. **Engaddi**, however, is where it ends and is swallowed up (Ezekiel 47).

**Esebon.** Between Esebon and Sabama there are scarcely five hundred paces (ibid., 16).

**Gabaa.** A city in the tribe of Benjamin, near Rama (Hosea 5).

**Galaad**, which half the tribe of Manasseh possessed beyond the Jordan, is mentioned in Scripture. On this mountain Laban overtook Jacob as he fled, and, according to Genesis, the mountain received the name *soros*, that is, “mound of testimony,” because Jacob and Laban swore an oath there over a heap of stones gathered together. It is the head, or beginning, of the lofty mountain of Lebanon, which is entirely planted with cedars (Jerome, on Jeremiah 22).

**Genesareth.** A lake is formed when the Jordan flows into it; on its shore lie Capernaum, Tiberias, Bethsaida, and Chorazin (Isaiah 9).

**Geraris.** It should be noted that from Geraris to Mount Moriah, that is, the site of the Temple, is a three-day journey (Questions on Genesis 22:3).

**Geth**, as the history of the Books of the Kingdoms also testifies, is one of the five cities of Palestine, near the border of Judaea. For those traveling from Eleutheropolis to Gaza, it is even now a very large village. Goliath the Gittite, whom David killed in battle, came from there (in the Commentary on Micah 1, Jerome calls this city the capital of Palestine).

**Geth**, which is in Opher, is a small village two miles from Sephoris, now called Diocaesarea, on the road to Tiberias. “Opher” is added to distinguish it from the other cities called Geth (Jerome, Preface to Jonah).

**Geth** is near and adjacent to Azotus, which is called Esdod in Hebrew (Jeremiah 25).

**Helkesi** is even today a small village in Galilee. It is indeed tiny and barely indicates traces of ancient buildings through its ruins, but it is known to the Jews and was also shown to me by my guide (Preface to Nahum).

**Jasa**, a city overlooking the Dead Sea, where the boundary of the province of the Moabites lies (Isaiah 15).

**Idumaea.** The Idumaeans are separated from Jerusalem toward the south by scarcely seventy-five miles (Letter to Dardanus).

**Idumaea.** Throughout the southern region of the Idumaeans, from Eleutheropolis to Petra and Ahila—for this is the possession of Esau—there are dwellings in caves (Obadiah 1).

No one is unaware that **Jerusalem** lies in the tribe of Benjamin.

We see daily with our own eyes that **Thecua** is also a village situated in the mountains, twelve miles from Jerusalem (Jeremiah 6).

**Jezreel**, now near Maximianopolis, was the capital of the kingdom of Samaria. Near it are very broad fields and a valley of immense desolation extending for more than ten thousand paces. In it, when battle was joined, Israel was struck down by the Assyrians (Hosea 1).

**Joppa.** We read in the Books of the Kingdoms and Chronicles that Joppa is a port of Judaea. King Hiram of Tyre transported timber from Lebanon on rafts to it, so that the timber could be carried by land to Jerusalem … and because of the nature of the region, a prophet coming down from the mountains and highlands to Joppa and the plains is rightly said to have descended (Jonah 1).

**Madian.** No one doubts that the Midianites and the whole desolation of the desert adjoin the land of Arabia (Ezekiel 25).

**Mambre.** From Mambre to Mount Moriah is scarcely a full day’s journey (Questions on Genesis 22:3).

**Morasthi** is even today a small village near the city of Eleutheropolis in Palestine (Preface to the Commentary on Micah).

**Nemrim**, a town above the Dead Sea (Isaiah 15).

**Petra**, which is itself also a city of Palestine (Isaiah 42).

**Pharan.** The place is near Mount Sinai (Habakkuk 3).

**Rabbath.** The capital called Rabbath, which was renamed Philadelphia by Ptolemy, king of Egypt, surnamed Philadelphus, who ruled Arabia (Ezekiel 25).

**Rama** is a city in the tribe of Benjamin, situated seven miles from Jerusalem (Hosea 5).

**Ramoth-Gilead.** A city beyond the Jordan, in the possession of the tribe of Gad. It was itself a city of refuge.

**Rhinocorura** is a town on the border of Egypt and Palestine (Isaiah 27).

**Rhinocorura.** A city beside the torrent of the desert, or of the west, as the Septuagint translated it. Between it and Pelusium, a branch of the Nile, or a torrent coming from the desert, enters the sea (Amos 6).

**Samaria.** There was another city, the capital of the ten tribes, which was later called Augusta by Augustus Caesar, that is, Sebaste. The bones of John the Baptist were also buried there (Hosea 1).

**Saron** is the entire region near Joppa and Lydda, where broad and fertile fields extend (Isaiah 33).

**Segor** lies in the territory of the Moabites and separates the land of the Philistines from them.

**Sochoth.** Even today there is a city beyond the Jordan bearing this name, in the region of Scythopolis (Genesis 33:17).

**The desert.** It bends leftward from Majoma, the port of Gaza, along the shore for those traveling toward Egypt (*Life of Saint Hilarion*).

**Thabatha.** Hilarion was born in the village of Thabatha, situated approximately five miles south of Gaza, a city of Palestine (ibid.).

**Thabor** is a mountain in Galilee, situated in the plains, round and lofty, ending evenly on every side (Hosea 5).

**Tharsis** is either a region of India, as Josephus holds, or else the whole sea is called Tharsis; it resembles the sky (Jeremiah 10).

**Thecue** is a town six miles south of holy Bethlehem, which gave birth to the Savior of the world. Beyond it there is no village, not even a country hut. So vast is the desert that it extends as far as the Red Sea and the boundaries of the Persians, Ethiopians, and Indians (Preface to the Commentary on Amos).

We see daily with our own eyes that **Thecua** is a village situated in the mountains, twelve miles from Jerusalem (Jeremiah 2:7).

**Theman** is the region of the Idumaeans and extends toward the south. This province is called not only Theman but also Darom and Nageb, because it faces the southeast, south, and southwest (ibid.).

**Thophet.** The altar of Thophet, which is in the valley of the son of Ennom, signifies the place watered by the springs of Siloam. It is exceedingly pleasant and wooded and even today offers the delights of gardens. The error of paganism occupied all the provinces, so that victims were sacrificed at the sources of springs and in delightful groves, and every form of depraved superstition was maintained.

In Hebrew, *Thophet* means “broadness.” It is said to be written in the Book of Joshua son of Nun concerning this place, which is in the valley of the son of Ennom and is called *Ge Ennom* in Hebrew. For *ge* means *φάραγγα*, that is, “valley”; and *Ennom* signifies either a man’s name or “grace.” The Hebrews relate that Gehenna was named from this place, because the entire Jewish people perished there by offending God. There they also consecrated their sons to idols in fire, or offered them as holocausts—something he had not commanded them and which no sanction of the Law had ordered (Jeremiah 7).

**Tyre and Sidon** are the principal cities on the Phoenician coast … of which Carthage is a colony (Jeremiah 25).

**The valley**, or **Torrent of Thorns**, is a place near Liviada beyond the Dead Sea, six miles distant from Liviada, where Israel once fornicated with the Midianites (Joel 3).

# SAINT EUSEBIUS, JEROME, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON, BOOK OF HEBREW QUESTIONS ON GENESIS (C)

## PREFACE

[Note: We collated this entire book against five manuscripts: two Vatican manuscripts, formerly belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden, numbered 39 and 215; another very ancient Palatine manuscript, no. 183 in the same Vatican Library; one Milanese manuscript in the Ambrosian Library, under the letter D, no. 88; and finally our own, which we keep at home—not indeed one of the most ancient, but generally of the best quality among the others. In our manuscript it is entitled as follows: “The prologue of Sophronius Eusebius Jerome begins, concerning the Books of Hebrew Questions, previously unknown to all Greeks and Latins.” In the second Regina manuscript: “The brief annotation of Jerome on Genesis begins. Preface.”]

[Note: “If, nevertheless, these things …” This is a poem of Maro from the *Georgics*, which the old editions do not print in full, although it is found written in manuscript copies as we have edited it. MARTIAN. —It is not from the *Georgics*, as Martianaeus thinks, but from Eclogue 6, entitled “Silenus”; these are Virgil’s verses. In most manuscripts, however, a second *si quis* is lacking.]

301–302. I ought, at the beginning of books, to set forth the subject matter of the work that follows; but I am compelled first to answer insults, taking on something of Terence, who placed the prologues of his comedies in the scenes as a defense of himself.

[Note: “Who placed the prologues of his comedies.” Terence answers the slanders of an old poet in the prologue to the *Andria* and sets out the argument of the comedy in its first scene. MARTIAN.]

For Luscius Lanuinus, resembling our Luscius, was pressing him and accusing the poet of theft, as though he were robbing the public treasury.

[Note: Thus all our manuscripts read, as do those in Martianaeus’s possession, the old edition of 1496, and Jerome himself elsewhere, who also calls his rival the “Lanius” in other places. Martianaeus and other editors have *Lavinius*. See Terence’s prologue to the *Andria*. —Luscius Lavinius. In some manuscript copies we read *Lucius Larvinus*, or *Lanuinus*, *Lanuvinus*. Among grammatical writers, the old poet who rivaled Terence is called Lucius, not Luscius. Who Jerome’s rival and Luscius was when he wrote these Hebrew Questions is not yet clear, since at that time the presbyter Rufinus had no disagreement with Jerome over Origen, who is still spoken of favorably in this Preface. Finally, the very ancient Corbie manuscript offers another interpretation, for it reads: “Lucius, resembling our Lavinius Luscius, was pressing him,” and so forth. MARTIAN.]

The Mantuan poet likewise suffered this from his rivals: when he had transferred certain verses of Homer word for word, he was called a plunderer of the ancients. He replied that great strength is required to wrench Hercules’ club from his hand.

Cicero too—who stood at the summit of Roman eloquence, the king of orators and the illuminator of the Latin language—was accused by the Greeks of extortion.

It is therefore no wonder if filthy swine grunt against me, a little man, and trample pearls under their feet, when envy has blazed against the most learned men, and against those who ought by their glory to have overcome envy.

Yet this befell them deservedly, because their eloquence thundered in the theaters, the senate-house, the public assembly, and before the speaker’s platform. Strength always has rivals in the open, and “lightning strikes the highest mountains” (Horace, *Odes* 2.10.10).

But although I am far removed from cities, the forum, lawsuits, and crowds, envy has nevertheless found me, hiding away, as Quintilian says.

Therefore I beg the reader,

[lacuna]

Captivated by love, he will read, [lacuna], so that in the books of *Hebrew Questions*, which I have undertaken to write on all of Holy Scripture, he may not seek eloquence or the charm of orators, but rather may himself answer on our behalf to our adversaries that indulgence ought to be granted to a new work. For just as we are humble and poor, possessing no riches and not deeming ourselves worthy to accept those offered to us, so let them also know that they cannot possess a knowledge of the Scriptures—that is, the riches of Christ—together with the riches of the world. [Note: “Together with the world,” etc. Some manuscript codices read: “to possess them together with their own riches.” MARTIAN. —Our manuscript has “together with the world,” or “together with their own riches.”]

It will therefore be the task of our study—or of those who form various conjectures from the Hebrew books—either to refute errors, or to restore to their proper authority those things that appear to teem with corruption in the Latin and Greek copies; and also to explain, by the method of the vernacular language, the etymologies of things, names, and regions that do not resound in our own speech. And so that the correction may more easily be recognized, we shall first present the testimonies exactly as they exist among us, and by comparing them with what follows we shall indicate what in those copies is lacking, added, or different. [Note: Another manuscript of Regina agrees almost entirely with ours, the Palatine manuscript, and the old edition: “Among our copies are the testimonies”; from a comparison with what follows, we shall indicate [lacuna] whether it is otherwise. (Our manuscript reads *sequentur*.)]

Nor do we criticize the errors of the Seventy Translators, as envious people bark; nor do we consider our labor a condemnation of theirs. [Note: The same manuscript agrees with the old edition. Formerly it read: “Not that we accuse the errors of the Seventy Translators, as the envious tear them to pieces,” etc. The Palatine agrees with Regina 39: “We accuse the Seventy translators of error, as the envious bark.” —In almost all manuscript books the text is corrupt: “as the envious tear them to pieces.” MARTIAN.] For they were unwilling to disclose to King Ptolemy of Alexandria certain mystical matters in the Holy Scriptures, especially those that promised the coming of Christ, lest they should appear to be Jews and to worship another God—for Ptolemy, a follower of Plato, held them in high esteem precisely because they were said to worship one God. But the Evangelists, and our Lord and Savior himself, and also the Apostle Paul, produce many passages as though from the Old Testament that are not found in our copies. On these matters we shall discuss more fully in their proper places. [Note: “On these matters,” etc. Consult the Letter to Pammachius on the best method of translation. These words are likewise absent from many manuscript copies. MARTIAN.]

From this it is evident that those copies are more truly authoritative which agree with the authority of the New Testament. Furthermore, Josephus, who relates [Al. puts forward] the history of the Seventy Translators, reports that only five books of Moses were translated by them—books which we too acknowledge to agree with the Hebrew more than the others. But those who later became translators—I mean Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion—have passages very different from what we read. [Note: We have removed here the word *quoque* (“also”), which the manuscripts more elegantly omit. Josephus’s testimony is found in *Antiquities* XII.2, where he speaks throughout only of the books of the Law, or Pentateuch, translated into Greek by the Seventy at Ptolemy’s command. This view has persuaded most learned men, especially because the style of the remaining books plainly indicates translators altogether different from those commonly called the Seventy, who are said to have rendered Moses into Greek for King Philadelphus.] [Col. 0938A]

Finally, something that may also appease our detractors: let foreign merchandise be conveyed by sea only for those who wish it [Al. is conveyed]; peasants do not buy [Al. buy] balsam, pepper, and dates. [Note: “Foreign merchandise,” etc. This sentence is altogether corrupt in several manuscript copies, which read: “Foreign merchandise alone is carried by ship for those who desire it.” MARTIAN.]

As for Adamantius [Al. Origen], I keep silent. His name, if I may compare small things with great, is more hated than my own, because although in his homilies, which he delivers to the common people, he follows the common edition, in his *tomes*—that is, in his more extensive discussion—he is overcome by the Hebrew truth [Note: “Surrounded by truth.” The constant practice of ancient writers is to alter this reading, substituting “overcome by Hebrew truth,” or “he was overcome,” or “he might be overcome.” MARTIAN. —We have also corrected this passage on the agreement of four manuscripts and the old edition, reading *superatus* (“overcome”), as Rufinus likewise reads in *Invectives* II, and as the context itself requires. Previously it read *stipatus* (“surrounded”). One Vatican manuscript has *superatur* (“is overcome”), and shortly afterward *circumdatur* (“is surrounded”).], and, surrounded by his own forces, sometimes seeks the aid of a foreign tongue. I say only this: I wish that, together with the notoriety of his name, he possessed the knowledge of the Scriptures as well, making little of the images and shadows of phantoms [Note: One other Regina manuscript adds this gloss: “A kind of demons, which peasants call *Oz zellum*.”] whose nature, it is said, is to frighten children and chatter in dark corners.

# THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0937]

## 305 (Chapter I—Verse 1)

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

Many think that, just as it is written in the *Dispute of Jason and Papiscus*, Tertullian likewise argues in his book *Against Praxeas*, and Hilary too, in his exposition of a certain Psalm, asserts that the Hebrew reads, “In the Son God made heaven and earth.” But the truth of the matter proves this false. For the Seventy Translators, Symmachus, and Theodotion all translated it “in the beginning.” [Note: The mystical interpretation of the word “beginning” as referring to the Son was indeed used in the dispute of Jason and Papiscus; it is more likely, however, that although that interpretation has long since disappeared, Clement of Alexandria in Book VI of the *Stromata*, drawing on the *Preaching of Peter*, and other Fathers subsequently explain it in this way. But I do not think that it was ever read that way by anyone in Hebrew.]

[Note: In Tertullian’s book *Against Praxeas* this is nowhere found; rather, one reads something different from Tertullian concerning the followers of Praxeas, chapter 5: “They indeed say that Genesis also begins in Hebrew in this way: ‘In the beginning God made for himself a Son.’ Even if this is not established, other arguments lead me onward.” Saint Hilary, in Psalm II, says: “*Bresith* is a Hebrew word. It contains three meanings, namely, ‘in the beginning,’ ‘in the head,’ and ‘in the Son.’ But the Seventy Translators rendered it ‘in the beginning,’ while others translated it differently.” [Col. 0938C] Immediately afterward, the word *Baben*, which our manuscripts, together with Martianaeus’s, retain, had been conformed by earlier editors to the Masoretic reading, who read *Beben*. —Hilary also has this in his exposition. Saint Hilary, in his treatise on Psalm II, section 2, has the following in our edition: “We shall offer one example of the ambiguity of the Hebrew language, from which it may be understood that other matters of this kind are likewise as they are. *Bresith* is a Hebrew word. It contains three meanings, namely, ‘in the beginning,’ ‘in the head,’ and ‘in the Son.’ But the Seventy Translators rendered it ‘in the beginning,’ while others translated it differently; and according to this ambiguity, confusion has been introduced by them throughout the whole translation.” Hilary does not assert that “in the Son” is found in the Hebrew, but says that the Hebrew word *Bresith* has three meanings, one of which is “in the Son.” [Col. 0939B] Further, Hilary’s interpreters read the word incorrectly in Jerome’s text, writing *Beben* rather than *Baben*, which means “in the Son.” We know that Jerome wrote *Baben*, not *Beben*. Hebrew grammarians teach that it should be read *baben*, and to the present I have seen no manuscript that reads *beben*. We therefore rightly reject this fabricated reading. MARTIAN.]

“And in the Hebrew it is written *BRESITH* (); Aquila interprets it ‘in the chapter,’ and not *BABEN* (), which is called—or interpreted—‘in the Son.’ It may therefore be understood of Christ more according to the sense than according to the translation of the word: for he is shown to be the maker of heaven and earth both at the very front of Genesis, which is the head of all the books, and also at the beginning of John the Evangelist. Hence in the Psalter he says of himself: ‘In the heading [Al. head] of the book it is written of me’ (Psalm 39:9), that is, at the beginning of Genesis. And in the Gospel: ‘All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made’ (John 1:3). It should also be known that among the Hebrews this book is called *BRESITH*, since they have the custom of giving volumes their names from their beginnings.”

[Col. 0938C]

## Verse 2

“And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.”

In place of the word “was borne,” which is written in our copies, the Hebrew has [Note: In Hebrew it has *Merefeth*. The Roman and Gallican manuscripts read this way: one, namely, the Palatine Library manuscript, has *Merefeth*; another, of the Vatican Library, *Merafeth*. Many of our manuscripts also retain this reading, especially the ancient Corbeiensis mentioned above. Others read *Merahefeth* or *Merahaefeth*. MARTIAN. —Nevertheless, some wish “was borne” to be the more accurate rendering from the Hebrew. Against this, Saint Basil, in the *Hexaemeron*, from the Royal Catenae, says: “I shall give you not my own opinion, but that of a Syrian man so far removed from worldly knowledge that he was that much nearer to knowledge of true things. He therefore said that the Syriac expression was more emphatic and, because of its closeness to the Hebrew, came somewhat nearer to the meaning of the Scriptures. Thus, he says, the Syrians interpreted ‘was borne over’ as ‘warmed’ and ‘gave life’ to the nature of the waters, after the likeness of a bird brooding and infusing a certain life-giving power into what it warms.” These words are translated as follows: “I offer you not my own opinion, but that of a certain Syrian who was as far removed from worldly knowledge as he was close to knowledge of true things. This man—commonly thought to have been Saint Ephrem, Basil’s friend—said that the Syriac word meaning ‘incubated’ was clearer and more expressive and, because of its affinity with Hebrew, came somewhat closer to the sense of the Scriptures. The Syrians therefore interpret ‘was borne over’ as ‘warmed,’ in the likeness of a bird brooding and imparting a certain vital force to what it warms.” Diodorus explains it still more clearly: “The expression ‘was borne over,’ he says, is one word among the Hebrews, but among us it could not be represented by a single word. For the Hebrew word corresponding to ‘was borne over’ means that, just as a bird warms eggs with its wings, gently touching them so as to give them life, so the Spirit was borne over the waters, warming them with life.” “Was borne over” is therefore one expression among the Hebrews, but among us it cannot be rendered by a single word. The sense of the Hebrew expression corresponding to “was borne over” is this: just as a bird gently touching eggs with its wings warms them and imprints vital heat upon them, so the Spirit was borne over the waters, warming them and imparting heat. Among Latin writers, see Saint Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* I.8, and Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* I.18. As for Jerome’s having rendered it “was borne” in his own translation, Martianaeus correctly observes that the holy Doctor deliberately retained that word, lest, since it was understood differently by different people, he should seem to restrict it to only one meaning; and whereas many understand it of the wind—that is, of the spirit of this world—he established that the passage should be understood of the Holy Spirit alone, as the creator of all things. The holy Doctor repeatedly acknowledged that he wished to adapt himself to the custom of the ancient translators.]

*MEREFETH* (), which we may call “brooded” or “warmed,” in the likeness of a bird giving life to eggs through heat. From this we understand that the passage does not concern the spirit of the world, as some think, but the Holy Spirit, who from the beginning is likewise called the vivifier of all things. [Note: Another Regina manuscript reads: “But if he is the vivifier, then he is also the creator, and God.” —“But if he is the vivifier.” One manuscript of our monastery of Saint Michael in Periculo Maris, and several other manuscripts in monasteries of Normandy compared with the printed editions, read: “Thus, if he is the vivifier, as creator and God.” MARTIAN.]

But if he is the vivifier, consequently he is also the creator. And if the creator, then God as well. For “Send forth your Spirit,” he says, “and they shall be created” (Psalm 103:30).

## Verse 10

“And he called the gatherings of waters seas.”

It should be noted that every gathering of waters, whether salt or fresh, is called “seas” according to the idiom of the Hebrew language. Porphyry therefore falsely accuses the Evangelists of calling Lake Gennesaret “the sea” in order to create a miracle for the ignorant, because the Lord walked upon the sea, since every lake and every gathering of waters is called “seas.”

## Chapter II—Verse 2

“And God completed on the sixth day his works which he had made.”

In place of “the sixth day,” the Hebrew has “the seventh day.” We shall therefore press the Jews, who boast of the Sabbath’s rest, with the fact that already at the beginning the Sabbath was dissolved, since God works on the Sabbath, completing his works upon it and blessing that day, because on it he completed all things.

## Verse 8

“And the Lord God planted a paradise in Eden, toward the east.”

In place of “paradise,” the Hebrew has “garden,” namely *GAN* (); moreover, *EDEN* () is interpreted as “delights.” For this Symmachus translated “a flowering paradise.” Likewise, where the text continues “toward the east,” the Hebrew writes *MECEDEM* (), which Aquila rendered [Note: The letter-forms in the manuscripts indicate that Aquila wrote ἀπὸ ἀρχῆθεν, which is almost a poetic adverb and reflects the contentious character of that translator. The older Regina manuscript has ΑΠΟ ΑΡΧΗΘΕΝ; another, corruptly, ΑΠΟ ΑΡΧΝΗΗΝ. Finally, the Palatine has ΑΠΟ ΑΡΧΝΕΕΝ, from which I print ἀπὸ ἀρχῆθεν.], “from the beginning,” and which we may also express as “from the origin.” Symmachus, however, translated it “from the first,” and Theodotion “at first,” which likewise signifies not “east” but “beginning.” From this it is most clearly proved [Note: “From this it is most clearly proved.” From this passage some overly immodest critical writers argue, claiming that Jerome indulges in Jewish fables. For these and similar passages, see our fuller *Annotations* and the *Apology for the Holy Doctor* mentioned above. MARTIAN. —That is, according to the Jewish opinion introduced by the author of the Fourth Book of Esdras 3:6: “You brought him [Adam] into the paradise which your right hand had planted before the earth appeared.” Most interpreters, however, hold the contrary view; and the context of Scripture itself clearly shows that the garden was planted for Adam’s benefit.] that, before God made heaven and earth, he had already created paradise, just as it is also read in Hebrew: “The Lord God had planted a paradise in Eden, from the beginning.”

## Verse 11

“The name of the one is Pishon.”

They think this is the Ganges, the river of India.

## 308 Verse 12

“Where [Al. ‘There’] are carbuncle and prase stone.”

In place of “carbuncle” and “prase stone,” others translated *bdellium* and *onyx* [Note: Aquila, however, translated it *sardonyx*, which Jerome perhaps regarded as equivalent to the simple *onyx*.].

## Verse 15

“And the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of pleasure.”

In place of “pleasure,” the Hebrew has *EDEN*. The Seventy therefore have now interpreted *EDEN* as “pleasure.” Symmachus, who shortly before had translated it “a flowering paradise,” here wrote “in the paradise of the [Note: Up to this point *τῆς ἄλσης* (“of the grove”) has falsely prevailed. Drusius rightly suspected this reading, though Montfaucon unjustly criticized him. Yet Drusius did not conjecture quite successfully that *ἀλόσυνης* should be restored. The word *ἄλσης* is certainly wholly spurious and unknown to Greek writers; and if it were taken for *ἄλσος* (“grove”), one would have to write *τοῦ ἄλσους*, while even then it would not be possible to extract from it a translation meaning “pleasantness” or “delights.” By contrast, the word *ἀκτῆς*, which we have substituted, is used by both Greek and Latin authors for a pleasant retreat, especially on the seashore or beside rivers, such as the four mentioned here in Scripture. Countless Greek examples may be found in the lexicons; among Latin authors, the best known are Cicero, *Against Verres* VII.25: “He lay drunk on the shore with little women”; and Virgil, *Aeneid* VI: “Far away, on the solitary shore of secret Troy,” etc. But the chief argument is that *ἀκτῆς* is preferred by the four manuscripts we use; only one, with a corrupt spelling, differs by reading *Ἀκθῆς*.] shore,” which itself signifies pleasantness and delights.

## Verse 17

“But on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die.” [Note: One Regina manuscript has “you shall die” according to the Seventy. Symmachus, in the Royal Catenae cited by Montfaucon, has *θνητὸς ἔσῃ*, “you shall be mortal.”]

Symmachus translated more accurately, saying, “You shall be mortal.”

## Verse 21

“And the Lord God cast a trance upon Adam.”

In place of “trance,” that is, a departure of the mind, the Hebrew has *THARDEMA* (), which Aquila translated *καταφοράν* (“a falling”), Symmachus *κάρον*, that is, a heavy and profound sleep [Note: Compare here the passage from Plutarch’s *Antony* about Cleopatra, cited by Drusius, where he mentions *κάρον* and *καταφοράν* together: “And he found only the mark of the asp’s bite, without convulsion, drawing on a heavy, sleep-like stupor and a profound sleep.”]. Finally, the text continues: “And he slept.” The same word is used in Jonah 1:5 for the sleep of one snoring.

[Col. 0942A]

## Verse 23

“This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, because she was taken from man.”

It does not seem to sound in Greek and Latin why she should be called “woman,” because she was taken from man; but the etymology is preserved in the Hebrew language. A man is called *IS* (), and a woman *ISSA* (). Thus she is rightly called *ISSA* from *IS*. Symmachus therefore beautifully wished to preserve the etymology even in Greek, saying: “She shall be called [Note: *Ἀνδρὶς*, etc. Earlier printed books retained the fabricated Greek reading of Symmachus in this form: *αὕτη κληθήσεται ἀνδρὶς, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτῆς ἐλήφθη*, that is, “She shall be called *vira*, because she was taken from her man.” Erasmus and Marianus accordingly represent a corrupted Greek reading, partly from the translation of the Seventy Translators and partly from the version published by Symmachus. We have restored the genuine reading on the authority of all the manuscript copies of Jerome. MARTIAN. —The earlier editors, whom Martianaeus censures more severely than they deserve, had read *αὕτη κληθήσεται ἀνδρὶς ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτῆς ἐλήφθη*. This translation of Symmachus is found word for word, according to Montfaucon, in manuscript Catenae in a passage attributed to Apollinarius. Our manuscripts agree with the printed reading; only one Regina manuscript has *Ἀνδρηὶς*, which signifies virility, in place of *Ἀνδρὶς*, “woman” or “heroine.”] *ἀνδρὶς*, because she was taken from man,” which we can render in Latin: “She shall be called *virago*, because she was taken from man.”

Theodotion, however, conjectured another etymology, saying: “She shall be called *assumption*, because she was taken from man.” For according to the variation of [Note: “According to the variation of the accent.” See below, in the *Commentary on the Book of Hebrew Names*, what this variation of accents is. There we show that the variation of accent in the names *Damesec* and *Sabee* is nothing other than a different pronunciation of the letter *shin*. From this it is clear that the name *issa* signifies “woman” if written with *shin* or *schin*, but signifies “assumption” if the word *issa* is derived from the verb *nassa*, whose middle letter is read with the left-pointing dot. Thus *ischa* means “woman” with the hissing Hebrew *shin*, whereas with the sound of the Greek sigma—or the Hebrew *samech*—the same word *issa* is interpreted as “assumption.” Compare also what is read in Jerome’s *Commentary on Ecclesiastes* 12, where he discusses the different interpretation of the name *soced* on the basis of variation in accent. MARTIAN. —I do not know what Jerome intends by the word “accent.” Clericus refutes, with many examples drawn from Jerome himself, what is commonly believed and what Martianaeus supposes: namely, that the diacritical point placed on one or the other horn of the letter is meant, as more recent teachers of the language distinguish it. Clericus instead thinks that the term refers to the little strokes placed upon words of different meaning and pronunciation written with the same letters, such as frequently occur in the Samaritan manuscript. In the present passage, however, Jerome seems to intend the differing spelling itself of the two words, for when this word is derived from [lacuna], it is written without a *yod*, although this form nowhere occurs in the sacred text. For the rest, see the commentaries on Ecclesiastes 12 and Jeremiah 1.]

*ISSA* can therefore mean either “woman” or “assumption,” according to the variation of the accent.

## Chapter III—Verse 1

“Now the serpent was wiser than all the beasts of the earth.”

In place of “wise,” the Hebrew has [Note: In Hebrew it has *Arom*. The more ancient manuscript copies read this way; but *arum* and *arom* may be written indifferently, since Latin scribes use *u* and *o* interchangeably. “He is not a servant” and “he is not servants” are frequently found with the same sense in the most ancient copies. MARTIAN.] *AROM* (), which Aquila and Theodotion translated *πανοῦργον*, that is, “wicked” and “crafty.” This word therefore indicates cunning and trickery more than wisdom.

## Verse 8

“And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the paradise toward evening.”

In most Latin copies, in place of “toward evening,” as we have put it here, there is “after midday,” because we cannot translate the Greek *δειλινόν* literally. In Hebrew it is written [Note: Our copies, which usually express Hebrew words in Greek rather than Latin letters, have here ΑΑΡΟΗ ΑΙΩΜ, as in the Hebrew Hexaplaric text.], *LARUE AIOM* (), which Aquila translated “in the wind of the day,” that is, “in the day’s breeze.” Symmachus translated “through the spirit of the day.” Theodotion, more explicitly, wrote “in the spirit toward the cooling of the day,” so as to indicate the refreshing breeze after the midday heat had passed. [Note: The Palatine has *κατάρζιν*; the other Regina manuscript *καταφύζιν*. From these corrupt readings some critic may nevertheless extract something useful.]

## Verse 14

“Upon your breast and your belly you shall walk.”

The Seventy Translators added “belly”; the Hebrew, however, has only “breast,” so as to disclose the cunning and deceitfulness of his thoughts: all his steps would be wickedness and fraud. Likewise, where the text continues, “You shall eat earth,” [Note: The Palatine adds “all the days of your life.”] in place of “earth” it is written *APHAR* (), which we may render “ashes” or “dust.”

## Verse 15

“He shall preserve your head, and you shall preserve his heel.”

The Hebrew has it better: “He shall crush your head, and you shall crush his heel,” because our steps are hindered by the serpent, while the Lord will swiftly crush Satan beneath our feet.

## Verse 16

“Multiplying, I shall multiply your sorrows and your groanings.”

In place of “sorrow” and “groaning,” the Hebrew has “pains” and “conceptions.”

“And your turning shall be toward your husband.”

Aquila translated “association” for “turning”; Symmachus, “desire” or “impulse.”

## Verse 17

[Note: “Cursed is the earth in your works.” Many manuscripts read in the singular, “Cursed is the earth in your work.” Critics attack this passage, but we defend it below in fuller notes. MARTIAN.]

“Cursed is the earth in your works.”

“Works” here signifies not the work of cultivating the soil, as many think, but sins [Note: Previously it read “signifies.” Jerome probably read—and perhaps Aquila and Theodotion likewise—[lacuna], with one letter in place of another, since the two are very easily confused.], as the Hebrew has it. Aquila does not differ, saying: “Cursed is the ground because of you.” Theodotion says: “Cursed is *adama* in your transgression.”

## Verse 20

“And Adam called the name of his wife Life, because she is the mother of all the living.”

Why she was called *EVA* (), that is, “life,” is demonstrated by the fact that she is the mother of all the living. For *EVA* is translated as “life.” [Note: The manuscripts supply the words “that is.”]

## Verse 24

“And he cast out Adam, and made him dwell opposite the paradise of pleasure. And he placed the cherubim and the flaming sword, which turns to guard the way of the tree of life.”

The Hebrew contains a meaning very different from what is understood here [Note: Two manuscripts read “from what is read here.”]. It says: “And he cast out Adam”—there is no doubt that the Lord is meant—“and made the cherubim and the flaming sword dwell before the paradise of pleasure, so that it might turn and guard the way of the tree of life.” It does not mean that God made Adam himself, whom he had cast out, dwell opposite the paradise of pleasure; rather, after expelling him, he placed the cherubim and the flaming sword before the gates of paradise to guard its entrance, so that no one could enter.

## Chapter IV—Verse 1

“And she conceived and bore Cain, and said, ‘I have acquired, or possessed, a man through God.’”

*CAIN* (), “acquisition” or “possession,” is interpreted as *κτῆσις* (“possession”). Hence, expressing his etymology, she says: *CANITHI* (), that is, “I have possessed a man through God.”

## Verse 4

“And God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts; but upon Cain and upon his sacrifices he did not look, and Cain was exceedingly sorrowful.”

How could Cain have known that God had accepted his brother’s gifts and rejected his own, unless the interpretation that Theodotion offered is correct? [Note: This opinion persuaded many other ancient interpreters. Indeed, several pagan writers also appear to have transmitted from Hebrew sources the claim that in ancient times fire was not placed beneath altars, but was obtained from God by prayers. Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII, says: “Among our ancestors altars were not set alight, but they drew forth divine fire by prayers, and this fire kindled the altars.” Solinus, *Polyhistor* 12, and Pausanias in the *Eliac* relate similar things.]

“The Lord kindled a fire over Abel and over his sacrifice; but over Cain and over his sacrifice he did not kindle one.” Fire was accustomed to come from heaven to consume the sacrifice; and we read that this happened at the dedication of the Temple under Solomon and when Elijah built an altar on Mount Carmel (2 Chronicles 7:1; 1 Kings 18:38).

## Verse 6

“And the Lord said to Cain: ‘Why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still; its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it.’”

Necessity compels us to linger longer over individual passages. Here too the sense in the Hebrew is very different from that in the translators of the Seventy. [Col. 0944C] The Lord says to Cain: “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will it not be forgiven you? But if you do not do well, your sin will sit before the doors; and its association is toward you, but you should rule over it.”

What he says means this: “Why are you angry, and why, tormented by the envy and resentment you feel toward your brother, do you cast your face down toward the earth? If you do well, will not all your offense be forgiven you? Or, as Theodotion says, ‘will it not be acceptable?’ That is, I will receive your gift as I received your brother’s. But if you do evil, your sin will immediately sit before your vestibule, and you will have such a doorkeeper accompanying you. Yet because you possess free choice, I warn you that sin should not rule over you, but you over sin.”

The reason the Seventy Translators fell into error is that “sin,” namely *ATTATH* () in Hebrew, is masculine, whereas in Greek it is feminine. [Note: “In Hebrew it is masculine.” I do not know whether anyone before us has explained this passage of Jerome to the reader. The holy Doctor observes that the sense in Hebrew is very different from that in the Seventy Translators and says that the cause of the error among the Seventy lies in the Hebrew word *attath*, or *hhattath*, meaning “sin,” which is masculine in Hebrew, whereas *ἁμαρτία*, meaning “error” and “sin,” is feminine in Greek; nevertheless, the translators attach to it the masculine relative *αὐτοῦ*. This is precisely what Jerome teaches when he says: “Those who translated it rendered it in the masculine gender, as it was in Hebrew.” Although the Seventy Translators may have read the Hebrew verb as the second-person masculine singular perfect, *hhatatha*, that is, *ἥμαρτες* (“you sinned”), they nevertheless proceed to add *πρὸς σὲ ἡ ἀποστροφὴ αὐτοῦ* (“its turning is toward you”), understanding the reference as sin and wishing to attach to it the masculine relative *αὐτοῦ*, in accordance with the masculine Hebrew suffix *o*, which corresponds to the words *hhattath robets*, “sin crouching.” MARTIAN. —In Greek, of course, the word is *ἁμαρτία*, a feminine noun. See Martianaeus’s annotation.]

Those who translated it rendered it in the masculine gender, as it was in Hebrew.

## Verse 8

“And Cain said to Abel his brother.”

The words that the Lord had spoken are to be understood. It is therefore superfluous that the Samaritan and our volume contain “Let us go out into the field.” [Note: An old scholion, commonly attributed to Cyril, says concerning these words: “The words of Cain addressed to Abel are found in none of the other versions, nor among the Hebrews; but they say that they occur in an apocryphal work. They are found among the Seventy and also in the Samaritan.” Another scholion from Origen, preserved by Montfaucon in the *Hexapla*, notes the same thing.]

## Verse 15

“Whoever kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance.”

In place of “sevenfold vengeance,” Aquila translated “sevenfold”; Symmachus, “the seventh”; Theodotion, “through a week.” On this chapter there is our Letter to Bishop Damasus. [Note: Recall Letter 36 in our recension to Damasus, Question 1, and what we annotated there. Procopius, on Genesis, p. 86, says: “Some interpret this passage more precisely, saying that Cain must be punished seven times for the murder he committed. Aquila rendered it ‘sevenfold.’ Symmachus translated it ‘he shall pay the penalty seven times,’ which some understood as: ‘He shall pay the penalty in seven generations.’ But the Hebrew places a period after the word ‘killing.’” And again, on verse 24, p. 90: “But I do not concern myself with whether you understand the seven as gifts of the Holy Spirit or as the persons of the seven Fathers.” Theodotion supports this interpretation, translating the present passage: “He shall take vengeance through the number seven.” Symmachus translates: “The seventh shall pay the penalty.” Perhaps, then, Lamech was the seventh, who inflicted the punishment.]

## Verse 16

“And he dwelt in the land of Nod.”

What the Seventy Translators rendered as *Naid* is called *NOD* () in Hebrew and is interpreted as *σαλευόμενος*, that is, “unstable,” “wavering,” and “uncertain of abode.” Therefore it is not “the land of Naid,” as the common people among us think, but the sentence of God is fulfilled: he wandered here and there, a fugitive and exile. [Note: It nevertheless seems closer to the truth that *Naid*, or *Nod*, is used in Scripture as the name of a definite place. Josephus, *Antiquities* I.2.2: “Cain founded Naida, a place so called, and there established his dwelling.” That is, the name of the place was Naida, and he decided to dwell there, etc.]

## Verse 25

“And he called his name Seth. ‘For God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.’”

*Seth* () properly means *θέσις*, that is, “placing” or “setting.” Since God had placed him in Abel’s place, he was therefore called *Seth*, that is, “placing.” Accordingly Aquila says: “And he called his name Seth, saying: ‘Because God has placed another seed for me.’”

### (Verse 26)

“And he called his name Enosh: he hoped to invoke the name of the Lord God.” Just as ADAM () is interpreted as “man,” so ENOSH (), according to the variation of the Hebrew language, means “man” or “male.” And fittingly, because he bore this name, it is written of him: “Then began the invocation of the name of the Lord,” although most of the Hebrews understand this differently: namely, that at that time idols were first fashioned in the name of the Lord and in his likeness [alternative reading: *fabricati*, “were fashioned”].

[Note: One Regina manuscript reads “the truth of the Hebrew language.”]

[Note: In Hebrew the word is , “then.” The Septuagint, by transposing the letters, reads Οὗτος, “this one.” Whether the passage is to be understood of Enosh himself or of his age, the disagreement is remarkable, both among Jewish opinion and among the ancient Christian Fathers. Among the Jews who interpret it negatively, the chief names are the Chaldean Paraphrast called Rabbi Jonathan ben Uzziel, the Chaldean Onkelos, and Maimonides. Saint Cyril, in Book IX, section 1, Against Julian, writes that Moses indicates that Enosh was called “God” by the men of his time, both as an honorific and because of the piety he displayed. Saint Augustine, however, in Book XV, chapter 18, of The City of God, interprets it thus: “What does ‘He hoped to invoke the name of the Lord God’ mean, unless it is a prophecy that a people would arise who, according to the election of grace, would invoke the name of the Lord God?” I omit the opinions of others, which the commentators on this passage cite.]

### (Chapter V—Verse 2)

“He made them male and female, and blessed them, and called their name Adam,” that is, “man.” The name “man” applies equally to male and female.

### (Verse 3)

“Adam lived two hundred and thirty years, and begot one according to his image and likeness, and called his name Seth.”

It should be understood that, up to the Flood, whenever our books say that someone begot children after two hundred years or more, the Hebrew has one hundred years, followed by the remaining number.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript, agreeing here with one of the two Regina manuscripts, reads “two hundred and twenty.” The reason why the Septuagint added one hundred years to the ages of the patriarchs before stating that they begot children is unknown.]

### (Verse 4)

“And the days of Adam, after he begot Seth, were seven hundred years.”

Because the translator had gone astray by writing two hundred, he consequently wrote seven hundred here, whereas the Hebrew has eight hundred here and one hundred above.

### (Verse 25)

“And Methuselah lived one hundred and sixty-seven years, and begot Lamech. And Methuselah lived, after he begot Lamech, eight hundred and two years, and begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Methuselah, which he lived, were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died.”

This is a famous question, debated throughout all the churches: according to a careful calculation, Methuselah appears to have lived fourteen years after the Flood. For when Methuselah was one hundred and sixty-seven years old, he begot Lamech. Again, when Lamech was one hundred and eighty-eight years old, he begot Noah. Thus, up to the day of Noah’s birth, Methuselah’s years of life total three hundred and fifty-five. The Flood occurred in Noah’s six-hundredth year. Accordingly, when the calculation is made in stages, the Flood is shown to have occurred in Methuselah’s nine-hundred-and-fifty-fifth year. Since he is said above to have lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years, there is no doubt that he lived fourteen years after the Flood. And how is it true that only eight persons were saved in the ark?

It therefore remains that, as in many passages, so also here, there is an error in the number. For in both the Hebrew and Samaritan books I find it written as follows:

“And Methuselah lived one hundred and eighty-seven years, and begot Lamech. And Methuselah lived, after he begot Lamech, seven hundred and eighty-two years, and begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died. And Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years, and begot Noah.”

From the day of Methuselah’s birth to the day of Noah’s birth there are therefore three hundred and sixty-nine years. Add to these Noah’s six hundred years, because the Flood occurred in the six-hundredth year of his life; thus Methuselah died in the nine-hundred-and-sixty-ninth year of his life, in the very year in which the Flood began.

[Note: Saint Augustine also calls this a most famous question in Book XV, chapter 13, of The City of God, and in Book II of On Original Sin he numbers it among matters that may remain unknown without danger to the Christian faith. Yet, as you see, there is no difficulty according to the Hebrew and the Vulgate, since Methuselah is found to have died in the very year of the Flood. Augustine rightly observes in the passage cited from The City of God: “That language should rather be trusted from which the translation into another language was made through interpreters.” Nevertheless, as he reports, in certain manuscripts—three Greek, one Latin, and one Syriac, agreeing with one another—Methuselah was found to have died six years before the Flood.]

[Note: Eusebius lists different years for the ages of Methuselah and Lamech in the Samaritan text. For this reason Selden, in the Preface to the Arundel Marbles, accuses Jerome of a lapse of memory. It is much more probable, however, that the learned saint had obtained a Samaritan copy different from that used by Eusebius. See Bede, On the Six Ages, and Freculph of Lisieux, Chronicle, volume I, book I, chapter 16, who reproduce this passage from Jerome.]

### (Verse 29)

“And he called his name Noah, saying: ‘This one will give us rest from our works.’”

NOAH () is interpreted as “rest.” He was therefore called “rest,” because under him all the works of the earlier world came to rest through the Flood.

### (Chapter VI—Verse 2)

“And when the sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful.”

The Hebrew word ELOIM () is of common number: both “God” and “gods” are expressed alike. For this reason Aquila, boldly using the plural number, translated “sons of gods,” understanding “gods” to mean holy persons or angels.

“For God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes gods” [or: “judges them”] (Psalm 81:1).

Following this interpretation, Symmachus says: “When the sons of the powerful saw the daughters of men,” and so forth.

[Note: In the Greek manuscripts of the Catena preserved by Montfaucon the phrase is τῶν δυναστευόντων, “of those who exercise power.” It is not my purpose here to oppose the opinion of certain ancient writers, according to which angels, who were granted the ability to act well or badly, desired women and entered into marriage with them—a tale that the author of the Book of Enoch is believed to have introduced. The interpretation has long prevailed which belongs to most of the Fathers and which understands by “sons of God” the descendants of Seth, whom Jerome himself shortly below calls “children of the holy,” and by “daughters of men,” those born from the descendants of Cain.]

### (Verse 3)

“And the Lord God said: ‘My spirit will not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh.’”

In Hebrew it is written: “My spirit will not judge these men forever, because they are flesh”; that is, because the human condition is frail, I will not preserve them for everlasting punishments, but here I will repay them what they deserve.

Thus the Hebrew expresses not severity, as our books read, but God’s mercy, since the sinner is punished here for his crime. Hence God also says in anger to certain people: “I will not visit their daughters when they have committed fornication, nor their brides when they have committed adultery” (Hosea 4:14). And elsewhere: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; nevertheless I will not remove my mercy from them” (Psalm 88:33).

Moreover, lest he seem cruel because he had not granted sinners an opportunity for repentance, he added: “But their days shall be one hundred and twenty years”—that is, they would have one hundred and twenty years in which to practice repentance.

Therefore human life was not reduced to one hundred and twenty years, as many wrongly suppose. Rather, that generation was given one hundred and twenty years for repentance. For we find that after the Flood Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years, and others lived more than two hundred and three hundred years. But because they refused to repent, God did not wish to await the appointed time; instead, cutting away twenty-year intervals, he brought on the Flood in the hundredth year assigned for repentance.

[Note: Namely, the Hebrew text has , “he will not contend.”]

### (Verse 4)

“Now there were giants upon the earth in those days, and afterward, when the sons of God went in to the daughters of men, they begot children for them. They were the giants, men renowned from ancient times.”

The Hebrew reads: “The fallen were upon the earth in those days,” that is, ANNAPHILIM (). And afterward: “When the sons of gods went in to the daughters of men and begot children for them, these were the mighty men renowned from the beginning.”

Instead of “fallen,” or “giants,” Symmachus translated “violent men.” The name “fallen” is applicable both to angels and to the children of the holy.

[Note: That is, Annaphilim. The manuscripts read this, and quite correctly; for the Hebrew has the article h, which grammarians call emphatic: hannephilim. As Jerome observes elsewhere, the ancients read the Hebrew letter he as a, and therefore wrote Annaphilim instead of the modern Masoretic Hannephilim. —Martian.]

[Note: Our manuscript has Nifilim without the article. Martian is mistaken in assigning a different pronunciation from the Masoretic text: the difference is not in the first syllable, which does not differ from Jerome’s form, but in the second, namely in the shewa vowel—roughly the distinction between Hanephilim and Anaphilim. Shortly afterward the Palatine manuscript reads “and they begot from them.” —Martian.]

### (Verse 9)

“Noah was a just and perfect man in his generation, and he pleased God.”

He says pointedly, “in his generation,” to show that Noah was not just according to consummate righteousness, but according to the righteousness of his generation.

This is what the Hebrew says: “Noah was a just man; he was perfect in his generations; Noah walked with God”—that is, he followed God’s footsteps [or: “he follows them”].

### (Verse 14)

“Make yourself an ark from squared timbers.”

Instead of “squared timbers,” we read in Hebrew “bituminized timber.”

[Note: The Hebrew has , which may be translated “from pinewood”; for it is one of the four kinds of fir. The rabbis, including Onkelos and Jonathan, believe it to mean cedar: a light wood, especially suitable for floating upon water. Some think that Jerome read , *choper*, which means “bitumen.” Procopius, moreover, states that the Hebrew refers to boards joined together in a quadrangular form.]

### (Verse 16)

“Gathering it together, you shall make the ark, and you shall finish it above at a cubit.”

For “gathering it together, you shall make the ark,” the Hebrew has: “You shall make a south-facing opening in the ark.” Symmachus translated this more clearly, saying διαφανὲς, that is, “you shall make the ark transparent,” intending a window.

[Note: Aquila accordingly translates μεσημβρινὸν ποιήσεις τῇ κιβώτῳ, “you shall make the ark south-facing.” The Hebrew text has , which is translated “window.”]

### (Chapter VIII—Verse 2)

“And the water subsided, and the fountains of the abyss and the cataracts of heaven were revealed.”

Instead of “the fountains were revealed,” all the interpreters translated “were closed and stopped.” And for what follows—“the water ceased upon the earth,” and so forth—the text has: “The waters returned from the earth, going and returning” (Ecclesiastes 1:7).

Observe from Ecclesiastes that all waters and torrents return through hidden channels to the womb of the abyss [alternative reading: “abysses”].

### (Verse 6)

“After forty days Noah opened the door of the ark that he had made, and sent out a raven; and it went out and did not return to him until the waters were dried from the earth.”

Instead of “door,” the Hebrew has “window.” Concerning the raven the text is otherwise expressed: “He sent out the raven, and it went out, going forth and returning until the waters were dried from the earth.”

[Note: “Going forth and returning.” In earlier printed books the negative particle was incorrectly read, giving “going forth and not returning.” Consult this passage in our Notes on Jerome’s Divine Library, or in volume I of our edition. —Martian.]

### (Chapter IX—Verse 18)

“Now the sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth.”

The Septuagint translators frequently, because they could not render the letter HETH () into Greek—a letter producing a double aspiration—added the Greek letter chi (χ), in order to teach us that such names should be aspirated. Thus, in the present passage they translated “Ham” for what is HAM, from whom Egypt is called HAM in the language of the Egyptians even to this day.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript corruptly reads: “from whom, and among the Egyptians to this day,” and so forth. Egypt itself is called from Ham, the father of Mizraim, Hamia or Chemia. In Hebrew it is *Aretz Ham*, “the land of Ham,” and in Coptic Τηρφχημι, “the land of Ham,” and so forth.]

### (Verse 27)

“May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.”

From Shem come the Hebrews; from Japheth comes the people of the nations. Since the multitude of believers has been enlarged, it received its name of enlargement from the breadth called IAPHETH ().

When he says, “And may he dwell in the tents of Shem,” this is prophesied concerning us: after Israel’s expulsion, we occupy ourselves with the instruction and knowledge of the Scriptures.

### (Verse 29)

“And all the days of Noah were nine hundred and fifty years.”

Behold: Noah lived three hundred and fifty years after the Flood. From this it is clear that the one hundred and twenty years were given to that generation for repentance, as we said above, and were not established as the limit of mortal life.

### (Chapter X—Verse 2)

“The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.”

Japheth, the son of Noah, had seven sons. They occupied the land of Asia, beginning at Amanus and Taurus, the mountains of Coele-Syria and Cilicia, as far as the river Tanais. In Europe they extended as far as Gades, leaving their names to places and peoples; later many of these names were changed, while the rest remain as they were.

They are: Gomer, the Galatians; Magog, the Scythians; Madai, the Medes; Javan, the Ionians, who are also the Greeks—hence the Ionian Sea; Tubal, the Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, from whom come the Celtiberians, although some suspect that these were Italians; Meshech, the Cappadocians, whose city is still called Mazaca among them. The Septuagint interpreters, however, consider the Caphthorim to be the Cappadocians. Tiras, the Thracians, whose name has not been greatly altered.

I know that someone has referred Gog and Magog, both from this passage and from Ezekiel, to the history of the Goths, who recently raged through our land. Whether this is true will be shown by the outcome of the battle. Certainly all learned men of earlier times were accustomed to call the Goths Getae rather than Gog and Magog.

These, then, are the seven peoples whom I have said came from the stock of Japheth; they inhabit the northern region.

[Note: Nearly word for word Jerome translated this from Josephus into Latin. The Greek reads:

“Japheth, the son of Noah, had seven sons. Beginning from the mountains of Taurus and Amanus, they inhabited the land and advanced through Asia as far as the river Tanais, and through Europe as far as Gades. They occupied whatever land they happened to reach, since no one had previously settled it, and they called the nations by their own names. The people now called Galatians by the Greeks, but formerly called Gomerites, were founded by Gomer. Magog settled those who were called Magogites after him, but who were called Scythians by the Greeks,” and so forth.

See this in Antiquities, Book I, chapter 6. Compare also Zonaras, Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, the notes of Allatius, Syncellus, and others. Finally, see Jerome himself on Ezekiel, chapter 38, verse 2.]

[Note: I understand “someone” to refer to Saint Ambrose, who in Book II, chapter 16, of On the Faith, applies what is written about Gog to the history of the Goths. Yet the historical agreement with Ambrose’s presumed interpretation was extremely difficult. Hence Jerome modestly rejects it by appealing to the outcome of the battle, saying: “Whether this is true will be shown by the outcome of the battle.” In the Preface to Book XI of his Commentary on Ezekiel he says: “I briefly mention that a man of no small distinction in our age, writing to the emperor about this people, said: ‘This Gog is a Goth.’ How everything written there can be applied to them is not for me, but for those who think this, to explain.” He did not wish to refute the opinion more openly, in order to spare its author embarrassment.

What, then, should we think of the modern writer who declares it credible that, if Jerome had written after Theodosius’s victory, he would have agreed with Ambrose on this matter? That good man does not know that Jerome wrote the Hebrew Questions on Genesis nine years after Theodosius’s victory. Theodosius is recorded as having defeated the Goths in Thrace in the year 379, whereas Jerome published the book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis around the year 388.

For the sake of truth, these brief remarks may suffice for now, lest, if I amassed many more, I might seem to renew the Gothic war. In earlier editions the present word was corruptly printed *futurum monstrabitur*, “will be shown in the future,” instead of *praesenti monstratur*, “is shown by the present [outcome].” Likewise, *vagantium*, “of wanderers,” should read *bacchantium*, “of those raging.” —Martian.]

[Note: This is commonly thought to refer to Saint Ambrose, On the Faith to the Emperor Gratian, Book II, chapter 16. Jerome again censures him in the Preface to Book XI of his Commentaries on Ezekiel: “I briefly mention that a man of no small distinction in our age, writing to the emperor about this people, said: ‘This Gog is a Goth.’ How everything written there can be applied to them is not for me, but for those who think this, to explain.”

Augustine nearly agrees with Jerome in Book II, chapter 12, of The City of God: “These peoples whom he calls Gog and Magog should not be understood as though they were barbarians settled in some particular part of the earth, whether those whom some, because of the first letters of their names, suspect to be Getae and Massagetae, or some other foreign peoples separated from Roman law.”

So also Dorotheus, or the translator of Dorotheus, on Obadiah: “This statement, on its surface, is directed against the Scythians, that is, against Gog and Magog.”

See Martian, who rather sharply criticizes his fellow editor of Saint Ambrose.]

### (Verse 3)

“The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarma.”

The Greeks call Ashkenaz the Rheginians; Riphath, the Paphlagonians; Togarma, the Phrygians.

[Note: The Latin manuscripts retain *Rifan* instead of *Riphath*; similarly, below they read the Greek πέντην instead of πέμπτην. —Martian.]

[Note: I should like the words *he founded the Ascenagites* to be supplied here; otherwise the sense appears incomplete. Josephus, from whom nearly all this material is taken, says: “Ashchanaxus founded the Ashchanaxians, who are now called Rheginians by the Greeks,” and so forth.
