Saint Isidore, citing this very passage of Jerome in Book IX, chapter 2, of the Origins, reads: “Ashkenaz, from whom came the Sarmatians, whom the Greeks call Rheginians.” For *Togarma*, most manuscripts have *Gothorma*.]

### (Verse 4)

“The sons of Javan were Elisa, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. From these the islands of the nations were divided in their lands, each according to his language, his clans, and his nation.”

From the Ionians, that is, the Greeks, came the Elysaeans, who are called Aeolians; hence even today the fifth Greek dialect is called Aeolic, which they call πέμπτην διάλεκτον, “the fifth dialect.”

[Note: Again, this is from Josephus, as are most of these observations: “From Javan, Japheth’s son, who also had three sons, Elisas named the Elysaeans, over whom he ruled; they are now called Aeolians. Tharsus named the Tharsians; for Cilicia was formerly so called. The evidence is that their most notable city, being the metropolis, is called Tarsus, since they changed theta into tau in adapting the name.” Compare Letter 37 to Marcella, section 21, and the notes there.]

Josephus considers TARSHISH to refer to the Cilicians, saying that the aspirated letter theta was later corruptly changed by their descendants into tau. Hence their chief city is called Tarsus, famous for the Apostle Paul.

The Kittim are the Citians, from whom the city of Cyprus is still called Citium. DODANIM means the Rhodians, as the Septuagint translators rendered it.

Let us read the books of Varro On Antiquities, those of Sisinnius Capito, the Greek Phlegon, and the other most learned men. We shall see that almost all the islands, all the shores of the world, and the lands near the sea were occupied by Greek settlers. As we said above, they possessed all the maritime regions from the mountains of Amanus and Taurus as far as the Britannic Ocean.

[Note: Josephus should also be heard here: “Chethimus possessed the island Chethima; this is now called Cyprus.” A little later he adds: “One of the cities in Cyprus happened to preserve the name; it is called Citium by those who changed it into Greek form.” Martian seems to have believed that the city itself was called Cyprus-Citium, for this is how he writes. See above, Jerome’s book On Names. In his Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 23, he says: “From the land of Cethim, which some interpret as Cyprus; for even today there is among them a city called Citium.” And in his Commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 2: “We should understand the islands of Cethim as either Italy or the western regions, because Cyprus, the island near the land of Judah, is called by this name, and the city bearing that name is located there.”]

[Note: The Septuagint appear to have read Rhodanim for Dodanim. Bochart argues that the name “Rhodians” is much more recent. Sisinnius Capito is cited by Servius on the Aeneid, Book I. The books of Phlegon on the Olympic victors, whom Jerome seems to have in mind here, are lost.]

### (Verse 6)

“The sons of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.”

Cush is still called Ethiopia by the Hebrews; Mizraim is Egypt; Put is Libya. From him the river of Mauretania is still called Put, and the whole surrounding region is called Putic. Many Greek and Latin writers bear witness to this.

[Note: He alludes to Josephus’s explanation: “Labimus alone settled Libya and named the country after himself.” See below at verse 13.]

Why the ancient name of Libya remained in only one part of the climate, while the rest of the land was called Africa, is not a matter for this place or time.

Canaan acquired the land that the Jews later possessed after expelling the Canaanites.

### (Verse 7)

“The sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca.”

Seba, from whom came the Sabaeans, concerning whom Virgil writes in Book II of the Georgics:

> The Sabaeans possess a sunlit branch bearing incense.

And elsewhere, in Book I of the Aeneid:

> …and a hundred altars  
> Glow warm with Sabaean incense.

Havilah refers to the Gaetuli, dwelling in the more remote desert of Africa. Sabtah, from whom came the Sabatheni, who are now called Astabari. Raamah and Sabteca gradually lost their ancient names, and it is not known what names they bear today in place of the old ones.

### (Verse 7)

“The sons of Raamah were Sheba and Dedan.”

Here Sheba is written with the letter SIN, whereas above it was written with SAMEKH (), from which we said that the Sabaeans received their name.

Now Sheba is interpreted as Arabia. For in the seventy-first Psalm, where we read, “The kings of Arabia and Sheba shall offer gifts,” the Hebrew has: “The kings of Sheba and Seba.” The first name is written with SIN, the second with SAMEKH.

Dedan is a people of Ethiopia in the western region.

[Note: One Regina manuscript reads “in the seventy-first Psalm, according to the Hebrew order.” The Hebrew is: , *malche sheba usba*, that is, “the kings of Sheba and Seba.”]

[Note: “The king of Sheba and Seba.” In Hebrew we read , “the kings of Sheba and Seba”; the first name is written with sin and the second with samekh, exactly as Jerome observes. —Martian.]

### (Verse 8)

“And Cush begot Nimrod. He began to be mighty on the earth.”

And shortly afterward:

### (Verse 10)

“And the beginning of his kingdom,” he says, “was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.”

Nimrod, the son of Cush, was the first among the people to seize the unfamiliar tyranny of absolute power, and he reigned in Babylon. Because the languages of those building the tower were confused there, it was called BABEL (). Babel is interpreted as “confusion.”

He also reigned in Erech, that is, Edessa; in Accad, which is now called Nisibis; and in Calneh, which afterward, with its name changed by King Seleucus, was called Seleucia, or certainly is now called Κτησιφών, Ctesiphon.

[Note: Ctesiphon was the capital of the Assyrian province of Chalonitis, three miles from Seleucia.]

### (Verse 11)

“From that land Asshur went forth and built Nineveh and Rehoboth-Ir.”

From this land of the Assyrians the empire arose. They founded Ninus, the great city, after the name of Ninus, the son of Bel; the Hebrews call it NINEVEH. The whole prophecy of Jonah concerns either its destruction or its repentance.

When the text says “Nineveh and Rehoboth,” we should not think that these are two cities. Since *Rehoboth* means “broad streets,” it should be read: “He built Nineveh and the broad streets of the city.”

### (Verse 13)

“And Mizraim begot the Ludim, the Anamim, the Lehabim, the Naphtuhim, the Pathrusim, and the Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim.”

Except for the Lehabim, from whom the Libyans were later named, though they had previously been called Putites, and the Casluhim, who afterward became known as the Philistines, whom we incorrectly call Palestinians, the remaining six peoples are unknown to us. They were destroyed in the Ethiopian war, to the point that their former names passed into oblivion [alternative reading: “because they were destroyed”]. They occupied the land from Gaza to the farthest borders of Egypt.

[Note: Josephus, often cited above, says: “Apart from their names, we know nothing of the Nedemites, Pathrusim, Casluhim, and Caphtorim; for the Ethiopian war, which we shall describe later, destroyed their cities.”]

### (Verse 15)

“And Canaan begot Sidon, his firstborn, and the Hittites, the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites.”

The firstborn of Canaan was Sidon, from whom the city in Phoenicia is called Sidon. Then came the Arkite, who founded Arca, a town situated opposite Tripoli at the foot of Lebanon. Not far from it was another city named Sin, which was later destroyed in the changing fortunes of war and preserved only its former name for the place.

The Arvadites are those who occupied the island of Aradus, separated from the Phoenician coast by a narrow strait. The Zemarites were associated with Emesa, a famous city of Coele-Syria.

Hamath is still called by that name by both Syrians and Hebrews, as it was among the ancients. The Macedonians who ruled in the East after Alexander called it Epiphaneia. Some think that Antioch was called by this name. Others, although their view is not correct, attempt to support it with a seemingly plausible name: they suppose that Hamath was the first station from Antioch for travelers going to Edessa, and that it is the same place called Emath by the ancients.

[Note: This too follows Josephus’s opinion and nearly his very words: “The descendants of Canaan were Sidonius, who founded in Phoenicia a city bearing his name, called Sidon by the Greeks. Amathius settled Amathine, which still exists and is called Amathe by the inhabitants; the Macedonians named it Epiphaneia after one of Alexander’s successors’ sons. Arudaeus possessed the island of Aradus, and the Arucaean possessed Arca, a city situated in Lebanon.”]

[Note: Emesa, a famous city of Coele-Syria. Earlier printed books, with a notable error, put “Edessa, a city of Mesopotamia” here instead of Emesa, the city of Coele-Syria. Consult the geographical maps and the description of ancient Syria. —Martian.]

[Note: The two Chaldean Paraphrasts, Jonathan and Onkelos, agree with this, and so does the Arabic interpreter; they call the Zemarites Emesenes. Eusebius considered Simyra, a city near Orthosia on the Phoenician coast, to have been a colony of the Zemarites.]

[Note: Not the famous Antioch, the great metropolis of Syria, but another of smaller size and reputation, which was also called Epiphaneia. Shortly afterward, two Regina manuscripts read *Emmas* instead of *Emath*, and two others, agreeing with them, read *consonantes* instead of *consolantes*. More plausibly, some think that Emath designates Emesa, the renowned city on the Orontes.]

### (Verse 19)

“And the territory of the Canaanites extended from Sidon, as one comes to Gerar, as far as Garam, while traveling toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.”

Since the other cities—Sidon, Gerar, Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim—are known to everyone, only this needs to be noted: Lasha is the place now called Callirrhoe, where hot springs burst forth and flow into the Dead Sea.

[Note: The Regina manuscripts read “as far as Leset” or “Leshe,” both here and shortly below.]

### (Verse 22)

“The sons of Shem were Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram.”

These peoples hold the part of Asia extending from the Euphrates River to the Indian Ocean. Elam was the ancestor of the Elamites, the rulers of Persia. Asshur has already been discussed: he founded the city of Nineveh. Arphaxad was the ancestor of the Chaldeans; Lud, of the Lydians; and Aram, of the Syrians, whose capital is Damascus.

[Note: Rabanus incorrectly has “Nineveh.” Josephus says: “Asshur founded the city of Ninus.” The rest should likewise be taken from Josephus. Shortly afterward, several manuscripts read *Ludim*, “from whom came the Lydians.”]

### (Verse 23)

“The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.”

Uz, the founder of Trachonitis and Damascus, held power between Palestine and Coele-Syria. For this reason the Septuagint translators, in the Book of Job, where the Hebrew reads “the land of Uz,” translated the region as Ausitis, or rather Usitis.

Hul was the ancestor of the Armenians. Gether was the ancestor of the Acarnanians, or Carians. Mash, for whom the Septuagint translators wrote Meshech, is now called the Maeonians.

[Note: Jerome calls these people Acarnanians or Carians, whereas Josephus calls them Bactrians. He then calls the descendants of Mash the Mesanites—Cedrenus and Syncellus have Mesenians—and says that Jerome calls them Maeonians after Mash. Instead of “or Carians,” Jerome’s text seems to require “or Curians,” and below “Curia” instead of “Caria.” Stephanus writes: “Acarnania is a land separated from the Curetes, by the Achelous; therefore the shorn are called Curetes, while the unshorn are called Acarnanians.” Jerome and Isidore, however, confuse the Curetes with the Acarnanians; Strabo reports that others did the same. See Isidore, Book IX, chapter 2.]

### (Verse 24)

“Arphaxad begot Shelah, and Shelah begot Eber. Two sons were born to Eber: the name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided, and the name of his brother was Joktan.”

From Eber came the Hebrews. By a kind of prophetic act, he gave his son the name Peleg, which means “division,” because in his days the languages were divided at Babylon.

### (Verse 26)

“Joktan begot Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab.”

I have been unable to discover the later names of these thirteen peoples. Since they are far from us, either they are still called what they were at first, or else the names that have been changed are unknown.

They occupied, from the river Cophene onward, the whole region of India, which is called Hieria.

[Note: See what we noted above in the Book of Places concerning the names Havilah, Ophir, and Sophira. Jerome consistently retains *Hieria* for Σηεία, “Seria,” here as well.]

## (Chapter XI.—Verse 28)

“And Aran died” [Note: “And Aran died, etc.” The manuscript Royal Codex no. 3994 adds several items in this manner: “Phaleg begot Ragau; Ragau begot Sarach; Sarach begot Nachor; Nachor begot Thare; Thare begot Abram and Nachor and Aran. And he died, etc.” MARTIAN.]

Aran died before his father, in the land where he was born, in the region of the Chaldeans. Instead of what we read, “in the region of the Chaldeans,” the Hebrew has *UR CHESDIM* (), that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.” The Hebrews, on this occasion, relate the following sort of story [Note: This story is told in *Pirke R. Eliezer*, chapter 26, which notes that this was the second of Abraham’s ten trials, following his ten-year imprisonment: [Col. 0956C] it is also related, though in a different order, in *Pirke R. Nathan*, and by R. Eliezer the German in *Mahase aboth*, chapter 2, as well as by many other Hebrews—a people naturally inclined to fabricate stories. R. Maimonides, however, makes no mention of it. For this reason R. Abarbanel, who explains each of Abraham’s trials as related by Maimonides, observes: “See, this Rabbi does not mention the deliverance from the fiery furnace of the Chaldeans, which others have counted among the trials, because Scripture makes no mention of it.” Josephus, moreover, a most reliable author, expressly mentions the revolt raised by the Chaldeans and Mesopotamians against Abraham, because he proclaimed that there is one true God, creator of all things (*Antiquities* I.7). From this Eustathius of Antioch, George Syncellus, and other Greeks embellish the account by saying that Abraham himself burned his father’s idols and house, and that his brother Aran, who was trying to extinguish the fire, was burned with them. See also the following note.]—that Abraham was thrown into the fire because he refused to worship the fire which the Chaldeans worship, and that, by God’s help, he was rescued and escaped from the fire of idolatry. For what is written below, that “Thara went out with his offspring from the region of the Chaldeans,” has in Hebrew, “from the burning of the Chaldeans.” This, they say, is also what is now meant by: “Aran died before the presence of Thare his father in the land of his birth, in the fire of the Chaldeans”—namely, that because he refused to worship the fire, he was consumed by fire [Note: R. Solomon Jarchi refers this interpretation of the present passage in Genesis to an ancient *Midrash*, or Commentary: Tharan, angered before Nimrod against his son Abraham because Abraham had smashed his idols, was ordered to have him thrown into a fiery furnace as punishment for the crime. Then Aram, Abraham’s brother, said to himself: “If Abraham prevails, I will be on his side; but if Nimrod prevails, I will join him.” When Abraham was divinely rescued from danger, Aram was asked whose side he supported. He answered: “Abraham’s.” For this reason he was thrown into the furnace and consumed by the fire.].

Afterward the Lord says to Abraham: “I am the one who brought you out of the fire of the Chaldeans.”

## (Verse 29)

“And Abram and Nachor took wives for themselves. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai; and the name of Nachor’s wife was Melcha, the daughter of Aran. The father of Melcha was also the father of Jesca.”

Aran, the son of Thare and brother of Abraham and Nachor, fathered two daughters, Melcha and Sarai, also called Jesca, *duōnymos* (a person with two names). Of these, Nachor took Melcha as his wife, and Abraham took Sarai. For marriages between uncles and their brothers’ daughters had not yet been prohibited by law; among the earliest human beings, marriages even between brothers and sisters had taken place.

## Chapter XII.—Verse 4

“Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Charra.”

An insoluble question arises. If Thara, Abraham’s father, while still in the region of Chaldea, fathered Abram at the age of seventy, and afterward died in Charra in the two hundred fifth year of his life, how is Abram now said to have been seventy-five years old when he departed from Charra, after Thara’s death? For the years from Abraham’s birth to his father’s death are shown to have numbered one hundred thirty-five.

The Hebrew tradition mentioned above is therefore true: Thara went out with his sons from the fire of the Chaldeans, and Abram, surrounded by the Babylonian conflagration because he refused to worship it, was delivered by God’s help. From that time his days of life and the period of his age are to be reckoned [Note: This nevertheless derives from that Jewish tradition which Jerome himself had called fabulous a little earlier. Saint Augustine also approves this solution of the question in *The City of God* XVI.15: “This question has also been solved in another way, namely, that Abraham’s seventy-five years, when he departed from Charran, should be reckoned from the time when he was delivered from the fire of the Chaldeans, not from the time when he was born, as though he should then rather be regarded as having been born.” The other solution is therefore better, supplied by the Samaritan text, which counts only one hundred forty-five years for Thara: Thara fathered Abram when he was seventy; Abram departed from Charran in the seventy-fifth year of his own age, after his father’s death; thus the total is one hundred forty-five years.].

This is because he confessed the Lord, scorning the idols of the Chaldeans. It is also possible that, since Scripture has left the matter uncertain, Thara departed from Chaldea a few years before his death and came to Charra [Note: One Royal manuscript reads: “and died,” while another has: “because he had died.”], or certainly came to Charra immediately after the persecution and remained there for a longer time. If anyone opposes this interpretation, he will seek another solution; and then he will rightly disprove what we have said.

## (Verse 9)

“And Abram departed and went toward the desert, and famine came upon the land.”

Here and in many other passages, instead of “desert,” the Hebrew has “toward the South.” This should therefore be noted [Note: In Hebrew, , *Negeb*, that is, “the South”; the Vulgate has *ad meridiem*, “toward the south.”].

## (Verses 15–16)

“And Pharaoh’s officials saw her, praised her to Pharaoh, and brought her into Pharaoh’s house. And Abram was treated well on her account, and he had sheep, herds, donkeys, male and female servants, mules, and camels.”

Although the bodies of holy women are not defiled by force but by the will, and Sarai might be excused on the ground that, in a time of famine, alone in a foreign land and with her husband’s connivance, she was unable to resist the king, the shameful necessity can nevertheless be excused in another way. According to the book of Esther, among the ancients any woman whom the king favored [Note: Saint Augustine should be recalled here, *Questions on Genesis* 26: “How should we understand what Abraham wished to conceal upon coming into Egypt—that she was his wife—according to all that has been written about this matter? Was this fitting for so holy a man, or should it be understood as a failure of his faith, as some have thought? I have already argued about this matter against Faustus, and the presbyter Jerome has explained more carefully why it does not follow that, although Sarah stayed several days with the king of Egypt, she should be believed to have been defiled by intercourse with him. For it was the royal custom to admit his women to himself by turns; and unless a woman had first been carefully treated for a long time with lotions and perfumes, none entered the king’s presence. While these things were being done, Pharaoh was struck by God’s hand, so that he might return intact to her husband the woman whom her husband had entrusted to God,” and so forth.] was anointed for six months with myrrh oil, and for six months was treated with various perfumes and women’s preparations; only then did she enter the king’s presence.

Thus it may be that, after Sarai had pleased the king, while her entrance to the king was being prepared over the course of a year, Pharaoh gave many gifts to Abraham, and afterward Pharaoh was struck by the Lord, while she still remained untouched by intercourse with him.

## Chapter XIII.—Verse 4

“And Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that belonged to him, and Lot with him, toward the desert. Abram was very rich in livestock, silver, and gold; and he went from where he had come, through the desert, as far as Bethel.”

He is beautifully said to have gone up after being delivered from Egypt. Yet an objection arises from what follows: how could he have been very rich when he left Egypt? The difficulty is resolved by the Hebrew truth, where it is written: “Abram was exceedingly heavy,” that is, *barýs sphódrа* (“very heavy”), for he was weighed down by the burden of Egypt. Although his wealth appears to consist of livestock, gold, and silver, if these are Egyptian possessions, they are nevertheless a burden to a holy man.

Accordingly, the Hebrew does not read, as the Septuagint does, “He went from where he had come through the desert as far as Bethel,” but: “He went on his journey through the South as far as Bethel.” He therefore departed from Egypt not to enter the desert that he had left along with Egypt, but to come through the South, which is opposite the North, to the house of God, where his tabernacle had been, between Bethel and Ai [or Gai].

## (Verse 13)

“And the men of Sodom were evil and sinners exceedingly in the sight of God” [Note: The Hebrew has , *ladonai*, “to God,” which the Septuagint interprets as *enantion tou Theou*, “in the sight of God”—superfluously, in Jerome’s judgment. It is, as Martianay notes, an idiom of the Hebrew language that serves as a superlative, so that “sinners to God” means “most wicked sinners.” See Martianay’s fuller notes on this passage.].

The words “in the sight of God” have been added unnecessarily here by the Septuagint, since the inhabitants of Sodom were evil and sinners in human estimation [or, “in everyone’s estimation”]. But a person is called a sinner “in the sight of God” when he can appear righteous among human beings, as Zachariah and Elizabeth are commended as having been “both righteous in the sight of God” (Luke 1:6). The Psalter also says: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2).

## (Verses 14–15)

“Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, toward the North, the South, the East, and the Sea; for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring.”

He set out the four regions of the world: East and West, North and South. Since this is read throughout Scripture, it is enough to state it here once: “the sea” is always placed for the West, because the region of Palestine is situated so that the sea lies on its western side.

## Chapter XIV.—Verse 3

“And the king of Bale, that is Segor. All these joined together” [Note: “All these joined together,” etc. One or two manuscript codices read: “Here they encamped by the valley,” etc.; but “these joined together” must necessarily be retained, because the Hebrew has *kol elle hhabberu*, that is, “all these came together.” MARTIAN.] “at the Valley of Salt,” that is, the Salt Sea.

In the Hebrew language, Bale is called *katáposis*, that is, “swallowing” or “devouring.” The Hebrews therefore relate that this same place is called Salisa elsewhere in Scripture [Note: It is called Salisa. In the First Book of Samuel 9:4 we read: “And he passed through the land of , Salisa.” The same name, Salisa, occurs in the Books of Kings. MARTIAN.], and that it is also called *moschon trietízousan*, that is, “a three-year-old heifer” [Note: Two Royal manuscripts read *consternantem*, “terrifying”; this is erroneous. Bale is derived from a word meaning “to swallow,” and from this arose the following Hebrew tradition, which is itself not entirely consistent; for the city Zoara alone is not called *moschos trietízousa* in Scripture. Theodoret thought that the name Segor means “devouring” (*Questions on Genesis*, question 70): “For Segor is interpreted as *katáposis*.” Jerome himself says in Isaiah 15: “It is called Bala, that is, ‘swallowed up,’ the Hebrews reporting that it was destroyed by a third earthquake.” It is the place now called Zoora in Syriac, Segor in Hebrew—“little” in both languages.].

This means “a three-year-old heifer,” namely, one that was swallowed up by a third earthquake (1 Samuel 9:4; Isaiah 15:5). From the time when Sodom and Gomorrah, Adama and Seboim were overturned by divine fire, it has been called “the little one.” For Segor is translated as “little”; in the Syriac language it is called Zoara [Note: Diodorus agrees in the Royal Catena manuscripts preserved by Montfaucon: “Scripture elsewhere calls this place Sogora, while the Syrian calls it Zaari and Bala.”].

The Valley of Salt, as is written in this same book, where there had previously been wells of bitumen, was transformed after God’s anger and the rain of sulfur into the Dead Sea. The Greeks call it *limnē Asphaltítis*, that is, “the bituminous lake.”

## (Verse 5)

“And they laid waste to the giants in Astaroth Carnaim, and the strong peoples with them, and the Ominaeans in Save, before they reached Sodom” [Note: “Before they reached Sodom.” These words are absent from the sacred text and from the Septuagint. MARTIAN.].

The four kings who had come from Babylon killed the giants—that is, the *Raphaim* ()—and all the robust peoples of Arabia [or, “the robust people of Arabia”], as well as the Zozim in Hom and the Emim in the city of Save, which is still so called.

*Zuzim* () and *Emim* () mean “terrible” and “horrible.” Instead of translating the words literally, the Septuagint rendered their sense and put “very powerful peoples.”

Now *Baem*, for which they translated “with them” (*hama autois*) [Note: “With them.” Jerome does not seem entirely consistent here, since in his own Latin translation of the Bible he read *baem* as “in them” or “with them.” More on this below in the fuller notes. MARTIAN.], they thought was written with the letter *he* (), led by the similarity of the characters, although it is written with *heth* [Note: Modern copies have , and thus not only the Septuagint but also the Syriac and Samaritan read it this way. Jerome himself, in his translation from the Hebrew, interprets it as “with them,” presumably so as not to depart from the reading commonly received. His observation that it was read with the middle letter in his own time is intended for the instruction of readers. The Chaldean and the Masoretes, however, confirm the other reading, rendering it as a proper name, Cham or Hom.].

For *baem* (), when written with three letters, has one meaning if its middle letter is *he*: “in them”; but if it has *heth*, as in the present passage, it designates a place, namely, “in Hom” ().

## (Verse 7)

“And returning, they came to the Spring of Judgment, that is Cades.”

This is said by anticipation, since it was called that only later. It denotes the place near Petra called the Spring of Judgment because God judged the people there.

“And they struck the whole region of the Amalekites and the Amorites who dwelt in Asasonthamar.”

This is the town now called Engaddi, fertile in balsam and palms. *Asasonthamar* means in our language “city of palms” [Col. 0960B], for *Thamar* means “palm.”

It should be known that, instead of what follows shortly afterward—“And they drew up their battle line against them in the Valley of Salt”—the Hebrew has “in the Valley of Siddim” (). Aquila translates this as *tōn peripedínōn* [Note: For more than one reason this reading seems suspect to me. I would rather restore, from the Royal manuscript and my own, *tōn peinēōnōn*, although it appears to be written incorrectly for *tōn peinidiōn* or *tōn peinōn*, “of the meadows,” with which the wooded places are generally planted. Likewise, instead of Theodotion’s *tōn alsōn*, it may be possible to restore *tōn aktōn* from the same manuscripts, since Jerome testifies that pleasant places are meant. Recall what we noted above concerning a similar reading of Symmachus in Genesis 2:15.] and Theodotion as *tōn alsōn*, signifying pleasant groves.

## (Verse 11)

“And they took all the cavalry of Sodom and Gomorrah” [Col. 0960A].

Instead of “cavalry,” the Hebrew has *RACHUS* (), that is, “substance.”

## (Verse 13)

“And the one who had escaped announced it to Abram the sojourner.”

He was dwelling beside the oak of Mamre the Amorite, the brother of Escol and the brother of Aunam, who were Abraham’s allies [Note: One Royal manuscript has “of Amorris,” as the Greek reads in the Aldine and Cottonian manuscript: *ho Amorrhis*. Likewise, below it has *Amari* instead of “Amorite.”].

Instead of what we rendered “sojourner,” the Hebrew has *IBRI* (), for this is expressed by “sojourner.”

But where it says “beside the oak of Mamre the Amorite,” it is better read in Hebrew as: “beside the oak of Mamre the Amorite, the brother of Escol”; and not “the brother of Aunam,” as the Septuagint translated, but “the brother of Aner.” Thus it shows that Mamre, Escol, and Aner were Amorites and brothers, Abraham’s allies.

## (Verse 14)

“And he pursued them as far as Dan.”

This was toward the Phoenician town now called Paneas. Dan is one of the sources of the Jordan. The other is called Jor, which means *rheûthron*, that is, “stream” [Note: See what we noted in Letter 78, *On the Stations*, station 41, and in Ezekiel 27, etc.]. Thus, when the two springs—which are not far from each other—join into a single stream, it is thereafter called the Jordan.

## (Verse 18)

“And Melchisedech, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine; and he was priest of the Most High God, and he blessed him.”

Since this little work is a collection either of our *Hebrew Questions* or of *Traditions*, let us report what the Hebrews think about this matter. They say that this was Shem, the son of Noah. By calculating the years of his life, they show that he lived as far as the time of Isaac, and that all Noah’s firstborn sons, until Aaron assumed the priesthood, served as high priests [Note: See Letter 73 to Evangelus, especially section 5, concerning Melchisedech.].

He is said to have been king of Jerusalem, which was formerly called Salem [Note: As is clear from the cited letter, section 2, this was also the opinion of the Greek Fathers concerning the name Jerusalem. They said that Melchisedech was a Canaanite man, king of the city of Jerusalem, which was first called Salem, afterward Jebus, and finally Jerusalem. Josephus (*Antiquities* I.10), Theophilus in his *To Autolycus*, and others among our writers approved this view. Jerome himself, however, shortly afterward refutes it quite learnedly in section 7: “Salem is not Jerusalem, as Josephus and all our writers suppose—a name compounded from Greek and Hebrew, which the mixture of a foreign language shows to be absurd—but a town near Scythopolis, which is still called Salem.”], which had formerly been called Salem.

The blessed Apostle, recalling Melchisedech in the Letter to the Hebrews (7:3) as being “without father and without mother,” refers this to Christ, and through Christ to the Church of the nations. For all the glory of the head is referred to the members [Note: Three manuscripts read: “For all the glory of the body.” We have corrected certain apparent typographical errors below.], since one who bore the foreskin blessed Abraham, who was circumcised; and in Abraham he blessed Levi, and through Levi, Aaron, from whom afterward came the priesthood. From this he wishes it to be inferred that the priesthood of the Church, which possesses the foreskin, blessed the circumcised priesthood of the Synagogue.

As for the statement, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchisedech” (Psalm 109:4), our mystery is signified in the word “order”: not through Aaron, by the sacrifice of irrational victims, but through the offering of bread and wine—that is, the body and blood of the Lord Jesus [Note: “The body and blood of the Lord Jesus.” This is an extremely clear passage, demonstrating most decisively both the sacrifice of the altar and the reality of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus in the sacrament of the Eucharist. MARTIAN.].

## Chapter XV.—Verses 2–3

“Lord God, what will you give me? I am going away without children; and the son of Masec, my servant woman, is this Damascus Eliezer. And Abram said: Behold, you have not given me offspring; and the son of my servant woman will be my heir” [Note: We have removed the words “will be my heir,” which had wrongly entered the printed editions but are absent from our manuscripts and are in fact irrelevant to the matter.].

Where we have “the son of Masec, my servant woman,” the Hebrew has *UBEN MESECH BETHI* [Note: In the present Hebrew text we read *uben mescec bethi*. Jerome nevertheless seems to have read the name Mesec with the article , the emphatic *h*, *amesec*, since several Latin manuscript codices preserve it in this form. MARTIAN.]. Aquila translated this as *ho huios tou potízontos oikian mou* [Note: One Royal manuscript has *oikon mou*, as the Catena manuscripts and Combefis’s papers present it in the recent edition of the *Hexapla*.], that is, “the son of the one who gives drink to my household.”

Theodotion, however, has *kai huios tou epi tēs oikias mou*, that is, “and the son of the one who is over my household.”

What he means is this: “I am dying without children, and the son of my steward or manager, who administers and distributes all the provisions of my household, and is called Damascus Eliezer, will be my heir.” *Eliezer* means “my God is my helper.”

They say that Damascus was founded and named after him [Note: It is more likely that this was his homeland, or the place of his maternal or paternal origin, from which Eliezer himself received the name Damascus.].

## (Verse 7)

“I am God, who brought you out from the region of the Chaldeans.”

This is what we said shortly before: the Hebrew has “who brought you out of *UR CHESDIM*,” that is, “out of the burning of the Chaldeans.”

## (Verses 10–11)

“And he placed them opposite one another, but he did not divide the birds. Birds of prey descended upon the carcasses and their halves, and Abram sat with them.”

An exposition of the sacrament does not belong to the present little work. We say only that, instead of what we have written, the Hebrew has: “And birds of prey descended upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.” By his merit Israel was often delivered from distress.

## (Verse 12)

“At sunset a trance fell upon Abram.”

Instead of “trance,” the Hebrew reads *THARDEMA* (), that is, *kataphorá*, which above we translated as “sleep.”

## (Verse 16)

“But in the fourth generation they will return here.”

There is no doubt that this refers to those who would be descended from Abraham [Note: The Royal manuscript just mentioned reads: “Why then, as in Exodus,” etc.].

The question is how it can be written in Exodus: “But in the fifth generation they went out, the children of Israel, from the land of Egypt” (Exodus 15:18). On this chapter we have published a small volume [Note: This is Letter 36 in our recension, addressed to Damasus; see especially question 2. Consult also Letters 124 and 125 in the previously published books. MARTIAN.].

## Chapter XVI.—Verse 2

“Behold, the Lord has closed me off, so that I may not give birth. Enter, therefore, to my servant woman, so that I may have children by her.”

Note carefully that, in the Hebrew, the procreation of children is written as “building.” For it reads there: “Enter to my servant woman, if somehow I may be built up by her.” See whether this may perhaps be what is said in Exodus: “God blessed the midwives, and they built themselves houses” (Exodus 1:20).

## (Verse 7)

“And the Angel of the Lord found her beside a spring of water in the desert, beside the spring on the road to Sur.”

It follows that the Egyptian woman was hurrying to go to Egypt on the road to Sur, which leads through the wilderness to Egypt [Note: The same Royal manuscript reads: “which leads to Egypt; she was hurrying to go to Egypt.”].

## (Verse 11)

“And he called his name Ishmael, because God heard my humility” [Note: Both the Hebrew and Greek texts of Scripture, speaking in the angel’s person, have “you shall call” and “your humility.” “And he called his name Ishmael” is read differently in Hebrew and in the Septuagint, namely: “And you shall call his name Ishmael, because the Lord has heard your humility.” These words therefore are not Hagar the Egyptian’s, but those of the angel speaking to her. MARTIAN.].

*Ishmael* means “hearing of God.”

## (Verse 12)

“He will be a rustic man. His hand will be against all, and everyone’s hand against him, and he will dwell opposite all his brothers.”

Instead of “rustic,” the Hebrew has *PHARA* (), which means “wild donkey.” It signifies that his descendants will dwell in the wilderness—that is, the wandering Saracens, with no fixed settlements, who raid all the peoples bordering the desert and are themselves attacked by everyone [Note: Two manuscripts read: “who attack and are attacked by everyone”; and one has shortly afterward: “And he will be the father of many nations.”].

## Chapter XVII.—Verses 3 and following

“And the Lord spoke to him, saying: Behold, my covenant is with you, and you will be the father of a multitude of nations. Your name will no longer be called Abram, but your name will be Abraam, because I have appointed you father of many nations.”

It should be noted that wherever we read “testament” in Greek, the Hebrew has “covenant” or “compact,” namely *BERITH* ().

The Hebrews say that God added to Abram’s name the letter *he* from his own name, which among them is the Tetragrammaton [Note: Previously it read “the Tetragrammaton,” though the manuscripts differ. The familiar name is , in which, according to the rabbis, one letter is attributed to Abraham and another to Sarah.]. At first he was called *ABRAM* (), which means “exalted father”; afterward he was called *ABRAAM* (), translated “father of many.” The word “nations” does not occur in the name itself but is understood.

Nor is it surprising that, although among the Greeks and among us an *alpha* appears to have been added, we say that the Hebrew letter *he* was added. For it is an idiom of that language to write with *he* () but read with *alpha* (); conversely, they often pronounce the letter *alpha* as *he*.

## (Verse 15)

“And God said to Abraam: You will not call your wife Sarai; but Sarah will be her name.”

Those are mistaken who think that Sarah was first written with one *r* and that a second *r* was later added [Note: Jerome attacks Philo the Jew and certain of his followers here because Philo, along with some Greek writers, reads the name with double rho, *Sarra*, and supposes that the second letter was added, in his work *On the Change of Names*. Philo may have been led into this error by the translators of the Septuagint, for their Greek version of Genesis 17:15 reads: *ou klēthēsetai to onoma autēs Sara, Sarra estai to onoma autēs*, that is, “Her name shall not be called Sara; Sarra shall be her name.” MARTIAN. —Martianay notes that Jerome reproaches Philo and his followers for reading Sarah’s name with double rho, *Sarra*. Yet Philo first interprets *Sara* as *archē mou*, “my ruler,” showing that he read *Sarai* from the Hebrew; then, although with double rho, *Sarra*, he interprets it as “ruling,” exactly as Jerome does. Moreover, not Philo alone but the Septuagint translators long before him pronounce it *Sarra* again. This was the common Greek opinion, cited by Justin Martyr in his *Dialogue with Trypho*: one alpha was added to Abraham’s name and one rho to Sarah’s—“one alpha in the name of Abraham, and one rho in the name of Sarah.” Even among the Latins, Sulpicius Severus writes in Book I: “Then, by the addition of one letter, the name of Abraham and his wife was changed, so that Abram is now called Abraam and Sara Sarra.”].

Since the name itself is Hebrew, however the name may have been changed, its explanation should be Hebrew, not Greek. No one, when calling someone by a name in one language, derives the etymology of the name from another language.

*SARAI* () was therefore first written with *sin*, *resh*, and *yod*. When the *yod*, that is, the *i* element, was removed, the letter *he* was added, which is read as *a*, and she was called *SARA* ().

The reason for this change of name is as follows. Previously she was called “my ruler,” the mother and mistress of one household only. Later she is called simply “ruler,” that is, *archousa*. For it follows: “I will give you a son by her, and I will bless him, and he will become nations; and kings of peoples will come from him.”

The wording is also significant. Instead of the Greek, “God said to Abraam: Your wife Sarai will not be called Sarai,” the Hebrew has: “You will not call her name Sarai”—that is, “You will not say to her, ‘You are my ruler.’” For she is already destined to be ruler of all nations.

Some absurdly suppose that she had previously been called “leprous” and afterward “ruler.” The word for leprosy is *SARATH* (), which may appear somewhat similar in our language, but in Hebrew is entirely different. It is written with *sade*, *resh*, *ayin*, and *taw*, which clearly differs greatly from the three letters—*sin*, *resh*, and *he*—with which *SARA* is written.

## (Verse 17)

“And Abraam fell upon his face and laughed, and said in his heart: Will a son be born to a hundred-year-old man, and will Sarah, who is ninety, give birth?”

A little later: “And you will call his name Isaac.”

There is a difference of opinion, but one etymology, concerning why he was called Isaac [Note: “Different opinion, but one etymology.” Josephus wants Isaac to have been named from Sarah’s laughter, that is, “laughter”; Philo says the same. See Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities* I.9, and Philo, *On the Change of Names*. MARTIAN.]. *Isaac* means “laughter.”

Some say that he was called “laughter” because Sarah laughed, but that is false [Note: Josephus is among the first to hold this view, *Antiquities* I.12: “He named him Isaac. This signifies laughter. Because Sarah smiled when God said that she would give birth, although she was advanced in age and did not expect to bear a child, he gave this name to the son.”].

Others say that Abraham laughed, and this is the view we approve. After Abraham’s laughter, his son Isaac was named; only afterward do we read that Sarah laughed.

It should nevertheless be known that four persons in the Old Testament were called by their names, without any veil or concealment, before they were born: Ishmael, Isaac, Solomon, and Josiah. Read the Scriptures.

## Chapter XVIII.—Verse 6

“And he said: Hurry; mix three measures of fine flour.”

Since the three measures appear to be stated here without qualification, and the measure is uncertain, I added this [Note: “Therefore I added.” It would be better to read “I add” than “I added,” since he had not previously said enough about the three measures. As for the allegorical interpretation concerning the mystery of the Trinity, Jerome himself taught the following in Book II of his *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 13: “A pious interpretation, certainly; but neither the parable nor the uncertain understanding of riddles can contribute to the authority of dogmas.” MARTIAN. —Martianay would have preferred “I add” here. Jerome may easily have written above “three measures”—or “three seahs”—of fine flour, as he often does when there is only a slight difference between the Hebrew and Greek texts. Three seahs, or three amphorae, make one complete ephah. See the Commentary on Matthew 13.], because the Hebrew has “three seahs,” that is, three amphorae. Thus we may recognize the same mystery both here and in the Gospel, where the woman is said to leaven three measures of flour (Matthew 13:33).

## Verse 10

“And he said: I will return and come to you at this time, and at the hour, and Sarah will have a son.”

Instead of “hour,” we read “life” in the Hebrew. The order or meaning is therefore: “I will return to you at the time of life”—as though he had said, “If I live, if life accompanies me.” This is expressed anthropopathically, as are the other passages.

## (Verse 12)

“And Sarah laughed within herself, saying: It has not yet happened to me until now, and my lord is old.”

The Hebrew reads quite differently: “And Sarah laughed within herself, saying: After I have grown worn out, and has pleasure come to me?” Note also that where we have “pleasure,” the Hebrew has *EDEN* [Note: The Hebrew is . Symmachus, in the Royal manuscript 1888 preserved by Montfaucon, translated it: “After I have grown old through age, has youth come to me?”].

Symmachus translated the passage thus: “After I have grown old through age, has youth come to me?”

## (Verse 32)

“And he said: Surely, Lord, if I speak?”

The Greek has *mēti, Kyrie, ean lalēsō*, “Surely, Lord, if I speak?” Abraham spoke to the Lord for a second time. What this means is not clearly expressed.

The Hebrew therefore states it more plainly: “Please, do not be angry, Lord, if I speak.” Since he appeared to be questioning and pressing the Lord for an answer, he softens what he asks by this introductory phrase.

## Chapter XIX.—Verse 14

“And he spoke to his sons-in-law, who had taken his daughters.”

Since Lot’s two daughters are afterward said to have been virgins—concerning whom he had also previously said to the Sodomites, “Behold, I have two daughters who have not known a man”—and Scripture now mentions that he had sons-in-law, some suppose that the daughters who had husbands remained in Sodom, while those who were virgins went out with their father [Note: This view comes from the schools of the rabbis, though there is no adequate argument for it from Scripture.].

Since Scripture does not say this, the Hebrew truth should be explained. It reads: “Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were going to take his daughters.” His virgin daughters, therefore, had not yet been joined in marriage.

334. **(Verse 21.)** And he said to him: “Behold, I have been impressed by your face.” In Hebrew it has: “Behold, I have accepted your face,” that is, “I yield to your requests.” Interpreting according to the sense, Symmachus says:

> “By your appearance I have been prevailed upon” (ὁράσει ἐδυσωπήθην τὸ πρόσωπόν σου).

[Note: Ὁράσει ἐδυσωπήθην, etc. This means, “By your appearance I have reverenced your face.” MARTIAN. — In the older Regina manuscript it is written: ΩΡΑ ΗΥΔΗ ΗΛΥϹΩΠΗΩΗΝ, which I would read, once corrected, as Ὅρα ἠΰτε (or εὖτε) ἐδυσωπήθην, etc., meaning, “See how I have reverenced,” etc. Certainly Drusius rather ingeniously conjectured that instead of ὁράσει one should read the two words ὅρα σοι, and that the first ὅρα should be understood as “behold” (ἰδού), corresponding to the Hebrew.]

**(Verse 28.)** And behold, a flame was rising from the earth like the vapor of a furnace. In its place we read in Hebrew: “Behold, CITOR () was rising,” like the furnace’s ἀναθυμίασις, “vapor”:

[Note: Until now ἀναπνεύμασις had been printed incorrectly instead of ἀναθυμίασις. I restored and printed the latter from the somewhat corrupt form ΑΝΑΘΥΜΑϹΙϹ found in the manuscripts. Ἀναθυμίασις properly means, as Jerome notes, the heat and vapor of a furnace. On the other hand, ἀναπνεύμασις is not a Greek word, nor do I know of any Greek author who uses it instead of ἀνάπνευσις, which means “breathing.”]

which we may call “vapor,” “smoke,” or “steam.”

**(Verse 30.)** And Lot went up from Segor and settled in the mountain, he and his two daughters with him. For he was afraid to remain in Segor. The question is why, when he had initially preferred the mountain of flight to Segor and wanted Segor to be spared for his dwelling, he now moved again from Segor to the mountain. We shall answer that the Hebrews’ conjecture concerning Segor is true: because it had often been undermined by earthquakes, it was first called Bale and later Salisa [Note: Recall what we noted above in chapter XIV, verse 3.], and Lot was afraid, saying: “If, while the other cities were still standing, this one was repeatedly overthrown, how much less will it now be able to escape in the common ruin?” And on this account of his unbelief he also gave the beginning to intercourse with his daughters. For one who had seen the other cities being overthrown, while this one remained standing, and who had himself been rescued by God’s help, certainly ought not to have doubted what he had heard had been granted to him.

Thus, what is said in defense of the daughters—that they thought the human race had perished and therefore slept with their father—does not excuse the father. Accordingly, the Hebrews, concerning what follows:

**(Verse 35.)** “And he did not know when she slept with him, nor when she rose from him”—

[Note: They place dots above it, etc. I examined more carefully several Hebrew manuscripts, but I could find nothing in them that helped clarify this passage. Erasmus wished to explain it as follows: “They place dots above it; they add above it,” signifying that this was done by divine action, so that Lot would not perceive the intercourse. But this word is not found in our edition either. Erasmus wrote this concerning a very difficult passage, which Marianus entirely omitted. Latin manuscripts read the phrase in various ways instead of “they place dots above it”: “they join above it” or “they place above it.” Whether, then, we understand that dots were placed above the words of Scripture, “And he did not know,” etc., or that the words themselves were added in the upper part of the sacred text, outside the sequence of the other words—in whatever manner one believes this was done—the Hebrews intended to signify, both by the dots and by the position of the words, something incredible. MARTIAN. — There was no reason for Martianus to torment himself so greatly in explaining this passage; even so, he never arrived at the truth. The Hebrew word , meaning “and when he rose from her,” is distinguished by an unusual dot above the middle of the vau, in addition to the dot within it. This may be seen in nearly all Hebrew Bibles supplied with vowel-points, at this passage; and the Masorah also marks it in the margin as unusual:  the dot is above the vau. This, then, is what Jerome reports as “being placed above” as something incredible.]

they “place a dot above it,” as though it were incredible and beyond the capacity of nature that anyone should have intercourse without knowing it.

**(Verses 36 and following.)** And Lot’s two daughters conceived by their father. The elder bore a son and called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to this day. The younger also bore a son and called his name Ammon, that is, “son of my people.” He is the father of the Ammonite peoples.

Moab is interpreted as “from the father,” and the whole name has its etymology. Ammon, however, whose name is explained as “son of my kindred,” or, better, in Hebrew, “son of my people” (), is derived in such a way that the word itself expresses only part of the name’s meaning. For AMMI, from which the Ammonites were named, means “my people.”

[Note: “So that the word itself expresses only part of the name’s meaning.” Ammon, or Amman, was named by the mother from ben-ammi; hence Ammon is derived from ammi in such a way that the sense of the name is present only in part, not its full etymology, and the word itself is present only in part. For ben, which means “son,” is not included in the word Ammon, except according to the etymological sense; while Ammi itself supplies the word, namely, “my people.” MARTIAN. — It is much clearer in Hebrew: “And she called his name Ben-ammi,” which is interpreted as “son of my people.”]

**(Chapter XX. — Verse 12.)** “Indeed, she is truly my sister by my father, but not by my mother.” That is, she is the daughter of his brother Aran, not of his sister. But since the Hebrew has: “She is truly my sister, the daughter of my father, and not the daughter of my mother,” it sounds more as though she was Abraham’s sister. In his defense we say that at that time such marriages had not yet been forbidden by law.

[Note: Many Christian interpreters indeed explain this as meaning that she was Abraham’s niece, not his sister, contrary to what Abraham himself most clearly and unambiguously testifies: “She is truly my sister.” They judged it impious to marry a sister by another parent, which is forbidden in Leviticus 18:9. And, says Jerome in *Against Helvidius*, no. 15, “How is it credible that Abraham, a righteous man, took his father’s daughter as his wife?” See what we have noted on that passage. Only now does the holy Doctor, with complete truthfulness, establish from the Hebrew that Sarah had the same father as Abraham, Terah, but a different mother, whom Saidas Barcides, patriarch of Alexandria, says was called Thevita; he is said to have flourished in the tenth century.]

**(Chapter XXI. — Verse 9.)** And Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, playing. The words that follow, “with Isaac his son,” are not found in the Hebrew. The Hebrews therefore explain this in two ways: either that he played at making idols, in accordance with what is written elsewhere, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exodus 32:6)—

[Note: An older Regina manuscript reads: “he made idols out of clay.”]

—or that, in jest and play, he claimed the birthright against Isaac, as though he were the older. Sarah, hearing this, could not tolerate it; this is confirmed by her own words: “Cast out this maidservant and her son. For the son of the maidservant shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (ibid., 10).

**(Verse 14.)** And he took bread and a skin of water, and gave them to Hagar, placing them on her shoulder, and the child also, and he dismissed her. When Isaac was born, Ishmael was thirteen years old. After Isaac’s weaning, Ishmael was expelled from the house with his mother. Among the Hebrews there is disagreement: some assert that the time of weaning was fixed at five years, while others claim twelve years. We, therefore, choosing the shorter age, calculated that Ishmael was expelled with his mother after eighteen years, and that it was no longer fitting for a young man to sit on his mother’s shoulders.

The idiom of the Hebrew language is therefore true: every son, in comparison with his parents, is called an infant and a little child. Nor should we be surprised that a barbarous language has its own peculiarities, since even today at Rome all sons are called *infantes*. Abraham therefore placed the bread and the skin on Hagar’s shoulder; having done this, he gave the boy to his mother—that is, he entrusted and commended him to her hands—and so sent her out of the house.

But as for what follows:

**(Verses 15–16.)** “And she cast the child beneath a fir tree, and went away and sat opposite him at a distance, about the range of an arrow. For she said: ‘I shall not see the death of my child.’ And she sat opposite him.” Immediately thereafter it says: “The child cried out and wept, and God heard the voice of the child from the place where he was. And the angel of God said to Hagar from heaven,” and so forth. Let no one be troubled by this. In Hebrew, after what is written, “I shall not see the death of my child,” it reads that Hagar herself sat opposite the child, raised her voice, and wept, and that God heard the voice of the child.

While the mother was weeping and pitiably awaiting the death of her son, God heard the child, concerning whom he had promised Abraham, saying: “I shall also make the son of your maidservant into a great nation” (Genesis 17:20). Otherwise, the mother too was lamenting not her own death, but that of her son. God therefore spared the child for whom the weeping had taken place. Accordingly, it is later said: “Arise, take the child, and hold his hand” (Genesis 17:18). From this it is clear that the one who is held was not a burden to his mother, but her companion. The fact that he is held by his parent’s hand reveals the mother’s anxious affection.

**(Verse 22.)** And Abimelech spoke, together with Ochozath, his wedding-attendant (*pronubus*), and Phicol, the commander of his army. Apart from Abimelech and Phicol, the third name found here does not occur in the Hebrew scroll.

[Note: Ochozath was added by the Septuagint from chapter XXVI, verse 26, where it is found joined with the names Abimelech and Phicol. In one Regina manuscript it is written Ocozhac.]

**(Verse 30.)** And he said: “You shall take these seven sheep from me, so that they may be a witness for me that I dug this well.” Therefore he called the name of that place “the well of the oath,” because there the two of them swore an oath. Where the text here reads “well of the oath,” the Hebrew has BERSABEE (). There are two reasons why it was so called: either because Abimelech received seven lambs from Abraham’s hand—for seven is called *sabee*—or because they swore an oath there, since an oath is likewise called *sabee*. If we read this name above, before this event, we should understand it as spoken by prolepsis, just as with Bethel and Galgala, which certainly had other names until the time when they were so called.

It should also be noted from the earlier and present passages that Isaac was not born at the oak of Mambre, or in the valley of Mambre, as the Hebrew has, but in Gerar, where Bersabee is still a town today. This province, not long ago, through the division of the governors’ territories of Palestine, was called Salutaris.

[Note: Salutaris is the name of several provinces or regions: Macedonia, Phrygia, Galatia, Syria, and Palestine. Consult the book of the *Notitia*. MARTIAN. — “Salutaris” was the name by which Palestine Tertia is more frequently known at the beginning of the fifth century after Christ, in the Theodosian Code and in the *Notitia Imperii*. Under the name Salutaris—of which Jerome says that Palestine was endowed not long before through a division of the governors’ territories—the earliest occurrence known to me is book 3 of the Theodosian Code, *De Protostasia*, enacted in 396 for Hygia, governor of Palestine, namely, “Salutaris Palestine.” For what is commonly read as “Phrygia” is, learned men have observed, a scribal error. Bersabee is also mentioned in the aforementioned *Notitia Dignitatum Imperii*, where, under the administration of Palestine, the Dalmatian Illyrian cavalry are listed first at Berosabae.]

Scripture bears witness to this, saying: “And Abraham dwelt in the land of the Philistines” (Genesis 21:34).

[Note: Some manuscripts add the remaining two words of this verse: “for many days.”]

**(Chapter XXII, verse 2.)** And God said to him: “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the high land, and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I shall tell you of.”

It is difficult to transfer the idiom of the Hebrew language into Latin. Where the text now says, “Go into the high land,” the Hebrew has MORIA (), which Aquila translated as τὴν καταφανῆ, that is, “the manifest” or “luminous place”; Symmachus has τῆς ὀπτασίας, that is, “of vision.” The Hebrews therefore say that this is the mountain on which the temple was later built, in the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite, as is also written in Chronicles: “And they began to build the temple in the second month, on the second day of the month, on Mount Moria” (2 Chronicles 3:1).

[Note: Martianus notes that the passage is written differently in the Second Book of Chronicles: “And Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem on Mount Moria.” He therefore thinks that Jerome was quoting this verse from memory. — “And they began to build the temple,” etc. In the Second Book of Chronicles, chapter 3, verse 1, we do not read it in exactly this form. For it is written there: “And Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem on Mount Moria,” etc. Unless I am mistaken, it is therefore clear that Jerome quoted this passage from memory. MARTIAN.]

This mountain is interpreted as “illuminating” and “shining” because there is the DABIR (), that is, the oracle of God, as well as the Law and the Holy Spirit, who teaches human beings the truth and inspires prophecies.

**(Verse 3.)** And he went to the place that God had told him of, on the third day. It should be noted that from Gerar to Mount Moria, that is, the site of the temple, is a three-day journey, and consequently he is said to have arrived there on the third day. Some therefore judge incorrectly that Abraham was living at that time by the oak of Mambre, since from there to Mount Moria is scarcely a full day’s journey.

**(Verse 13.)** And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and behold, a ram was held behind him in a thicket by its horns. Eusebius of Emesa made a ridiculous statement about this passage: “Sabech,” he says, “means a he-goat, which has straight horns and rises high in order to crop the branches of a tree.”

Again, Aquila translated Sabech as συχνεῶνα, which we may call a “thornbush” or “briar,” and, to explain the force of the word, dense, interwoven shrubs. Symmachus, led to the same opinion, says: “And a ram appeared afterward, held by its horns in a net.”

But in this particular passage the Septuagint and Theodotion seem to have translated better, retaining the actual name SABECH (), saying: “In the thicket of sabech, by its horns.” For σύχνεων, or “net,” which Aquila and Symmachus used, is written with the letter SIN (); here, however, the letter SAMECH () is used. It is therefore clear that the word Sabech does not signify an interpretation meaning dense roots or branches interwoven like a net, but the name of a thicket, which is so called in Hebrew.

[Note: Diodorus, in the *Catenae* cited by the same Montfaucon, says: “The Syriac does not have ‘in the thicket’; it has only ‘Sabec.’ I think this is the name of the plant. The Hebrews think that Sabec means ‘release.’”]

I myself, carefully investigating the matter, have frequently found συχνεῶνα written with the letter SAMECH ().

[Note: Martianus gathers many examples from Scripture concerning this matter. — “Inquiring into συχνεῶνα.” What Jerome says is proved to be entirely true: throughout the sacred books, the name Sabech is written with the letter samech, not sin—for example, *sirīm sebukhīm*, “entangled thorns,” Nahum 1:10; *sibkhē ha-ya‘ar*, “the tangled growth of the forest,” Isaiah 10:34. Elsewhere too *sebokh*, meaning “tangled” and “thorny,” occurs frequently, for example, Psalm 74:5 and Jeremiah 4:7. Sometimes it is written with the element sin instead of samech, as in 1 Kings 7:4, *hassebakhot*, “interwoven carvings” or “latticework.” MARTIAN.]

**(Verse 14.)** And Abraham called the name of that place “The Lord sees,” so that they say to this day, “On the mountain the Lord sees.” Instead of “sees,” as the text has here, the Hebrew writes “will be seen.”

[Note: That is, “will appear.” In a Regina manuscript, instead of “sees,” the reading is “saw.”]

This became a proverb among the Hebrews: whenever they are in distress and desire to be lifted up by the Lord’s help, they say, “On the mountain the Lord will be seen,” that is, “As he had mercy on Abraham, so he will have mercy on us.” For this reason they still customarily blow a horn as a sign of the ram that was given.

**(Verse 20.)** And they announced to Abraham, saying: “Behold, Milcah has also borne sons to Nahor your brother: Uz, his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel, the father of the Syrians, and Chesed.”

Uz, the firstborn of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, by his wife Milcah, the daughter of Aran, was born first. From his stock Job descended, as is written at the beginning of his book: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job.”

Some therefore judge incorrectly that Job was of the race of Esau, since what is found at the end of his book—“because he was translated from the Syriac language, and was fourth from Esau,” and the rest of what is written there—is not found in the Hebrew scrolls.

[Note: In his Letter 73 to Evangelus, no. 2, Jerome lists many Greek Fathers who dissent, maintaining that Job was not of the tribe of Levi but descended from Esau. Among them may be added Athanasius in the *Synopsis*, Chrysostom in Homily 2 on patience, Augustine in *City of God* XVIII.47, and many others of a later age, Greek and Latin alike. Jerome sides with the Hebrews, who, as he says below in his note on Genesis 33, assert that Job was descended from Nahor; later interpreters who frequently describe Jerome add their support to this opinion: Isidore—or whoever authored the book *On the Life and Death of the Fathers*—Alcuin, Bede, or whoever wrote on Job, Rupert, and finally Lyra, not to mention other modern authors. What should be established as certain, however, is not sufficiently clear. See what we noted on Letter 73, p. 439, note c (in our edition, column 677, note d). The addition at the end of the Book of Job, which Jerome says is not found in the Hebrew scrolls, is supplied by Theodotion; those who are persuaded of the opposing view draw a major argument from this. Aristeas, Philo, and Polyhistor also mention it, as cited by Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* IX.25. Olympiodorus in the *Catenae* and Origen in his *Letter to Africanus* do likewise.]

Buz, Milcah’s second son, was translated by the Septuagint as Bauz. From his descendants came that diviner Balaam (Numbers 24:3 ff.; Joshua 13:22), as the Hebrews relate. In the Book of Job he is called Elihu: at first a holy man and prophet of God, but later, through disobedience and a desire for gifts, when he wished to curse Israel, he was deprived of the title “divine.” The same book says: “And Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite, became angry” (Job 32:2), since he descended from the root of this Buz.

[Note: In Saint Eucherius, where a substantial excerpt from this book is reproduced, he is deprived of the title “divine.”]

Kemuel was the father of Damascus. The name itself is called Aram, which is written here in place of Syria; the same name is also read in Isaiah. Chesed is likewise the fourth, from whom the Chaldeans, that is, the Chasdim, were later named.

340. **(Chapter XXXII, verse 2.)** And Sarah died in the city of Arboc, which is in the valley; this is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. The words “which is in the valley,” placed here, are not found in the authentic manuscripts. The name of the city, Arboc, was also gradually corrupted by writers and readers. For we should not suppose that the Septuagint translators rendered the name of a Hebrew city barbarously and corruptly, differently from the way it is said in its own language.

[Note: “We should not suppose that the Septuagint translators,” etc. Jerome praises and defends the Septuagint translators wherever the testimony of conscience permits; but he frequently corrects them because of many obvious errors, which, as an investigator and defender of truth, he never passes over in silence. MARTIAN.]

It is called ARBEE (), that is, “four,” because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried there, as well as Adam himself, the first father of the human race, as will be demonstrated more clearly in the Book of Joshua.

[Note: See what we said above in the book of *Places* under the heading Arboc concerning this rabbinic opinion.]

**(Verse 6.)** “Hear us, my lord: you are a prince from God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs.” Instead of “king,” the Hebrew has “prince” or “leader.” For NASI () means not “king” but “leader.”

**(Verse 16.)** And Abraham heard Ephron, and Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver which he had spoken of in the hearing of the sons of Heth. In Hebrew, as we have placed it here, his name is written first EPHRON, and second EPHRAN.

[Note: Namely,  and . Martianus has  and . Jerome himself therefore wrote Ephran in one place. — The second form is Ephran. We now read Ephron and Ephran in the same way, without the letter vau, as it was found in Jerome’s Hebrew manuscripts. MARTIAN.]

After he had been overcome by the price, so that he would sell the tomb for silver, although Abraham compelled him, the letter vau—which among them is read as o—was removed from his name, and instead of EPHRON he was called EPHRAN. Scripture thereby signifies that he was not of consummate and perfect virtue, since he was able to sell the burial place of the dead.

[Note: Our manuscripts read: “so that he would sell the tomb and receive the silver, although,” etc.]

Let those who sell tombs therefore know—and who are not compelled to accept a price, but extort it even from the unwilling—that their name is changed and something of their merit perishes, since even the man who accepted it unwillingly is secretly reproved.

341. **(Chapter XXIV, verse 9.)** And the servant placed his hand beneath the thigh of Abraham his master and swore to him concerning this matter. The Hebrews relate that he swore by its sanctification, that is, by circumcision. We, however, say that he swore by Abraham’s seed, that is, by Christ, who was to be born from him, in accordance with the Evangelist Matthew, who says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1).

**(Verse 22.)** And the man took a golden earring, weighing a didrachm. BACE (), which is written in this passage for “didrachm,” is half an ounce. SECEL (), which in Latin is incorrectly called *siclus*, has the weight of an ounce.

[Note: I would rather restore “half an ounce,” since Jerome himself establishes that the *siclus* is equivalent to four drachmas, while eight drachmas make an ounce. In his Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 4, he says: “The *siclus*, that is, the stater, has four drachmas; eight drachmas make a Latin ounce.” Josephus likewise states in *Antiquities* III.9 that the *siclus* weighs four Attic drachmas, that is, half an ounce. Finally, there is the well-known line of Fannius:

> An ounce is made from twice four drachmas, whence one must suppose  
> That grammata are so called because this number, twenty-four,  
> An ounce contains within itself; in so many forms our word is marked,  
> As the world completes hours through night and day.

Nevertheless, I do not change the text without manuscript support, especially since I think Jerome wrote this through a lapse of memory, or, if it is the fault of copyists, the reading has prevailed for a very long time. For Isidore also reads it this way in his *Etymologies* XVI.24, in Jerome’s manuscripts: “Secel, which in Latin is incorrectly called *siclus*, is a Hebrew name, having among them the weight of an ounce.”]

**(Verse 43.)** “Behold, I stand beside the spring of water, and the daughters of the people of the city will come out to draw water. Let the maiden to whom I say, ‘Give me a little water to drink from your jar,’ be the one,” etc.

In Hebrew it is written: “Behold, I am standing beside the spring of water, and there will be a young woman who comes out to draw; and I shall say to her, ‘Give me a little water to drink from your jar,’” and so forth.

Instead of “young woman,” which is called νεανίς in Greek, we read there ALMA (), which also occurs in Isaiah. For in the passage where our manuscripts read, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear” (Isaiah 7:14), Aquila translated: “Behold, a young woman shall conceive and bear.” In Hebrew it reads: “Behold, alma shall conceive and bear.”

[Note: “That the word alma,” etc. When I made the same assertion against a Hebrew teacher named Moses, he replied that the name Alma is found in Proverbs 30, where it is applied to an adulterous woman. But this error is easily refuted from the Hebrew text itself, where *bealma* is separated by a *silluq* point from the words concerning the adulterous woman. Jerome’s observation is therefore true: in the sacred books the word *alma* is never written except of a virgin. MARTIAN.]

It should therefore be noted that the word *alma* is never written except of a virgin, and that it has the etymology ἀπόκρυφος, that is, “hidden.” For it is written in Job: “Wisdom—where shall it be found? And what is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of every living being” (Job 28:21). Where we have said “it is hidden,” the Hebrew, because of the verb’s inflection, has another form, NAALMA (). Something similar, although inflected in the masculine gender, is written in the Books of Kings, where Elisha says to Gehazi: “And the Lord hid it from me” (2 Kings 4:27).

Thus ALMA, which is interpreted as “hidden,” that is, “virgin,” carefully guarded, seems to me to be a greater praise than “virgin.” For according to the Apostle, a woman may be a virgin in body but not in spirit. But a hidden woman who is a virgin possesses an ἐπίτασις (an intensification) of virginity, so that she is both virgin and hidden. And one who is hidden is, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, consequently also a virgin; whereas of one who is a virgin it does not immediately follow that she is hidden.

We read this same word in Exodus concerning Mary, the virgin sister of Moses (Exodus 2:8).

[Note: One Regina manuscript reads: “concerning Mary, the virgin sister of Moses, still a virgin”; and a little below it has *concedemus* (“we shall grant”) instead of *concedimus* (“we grant”).]

Let the Jews therefore show ALMA used anywhere in Scripture where it means merely “young woman” and not “virgin”; and we shall grant them that what is said in Isaiah in our text—“Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear”—means not a hidden virgin but a young woman already married.

**(Verse 59.)** And they sent away Rebecca their sister, together with her possessions, the servant of Abraham, and the men who were with him. In Hebrew it has: “And they sent away Rebecca their sister, her nurse, Abraham’s servant, and his men.” For it was fitting that a virgin going to her marriage without her parents should be comforted by the support of her nurse.

**(Verses 62 and 63.)** And he was dwelling in the land of the South, and Isaac went out to exercise himself in the field toward evening. The land of the South signifies Gerar, from which he had once been brought by his father for sacrifice. As for “Isaac went out to exercise himself in the field,” the Greek has ἀδολεσχῆσαι.

[Note: The same word, ἀδολεσχῆσαι, meaning “to speak” or “to spend time in conversation,” is found among Greek writers. In Hebrew it is [a word] meaning “to meditate” or “to discuss with much reflection.” Soon afterward one Regina manuscript reads: “And Isaac went out to speak in the field,” etc. In Hebrew it is *la-suahh*, which means “to meditate,” “to speak,” or “to converse.” MARTIAN.]

In Hebrew it reads: “And Isaac went out to speak in the field as evening was falling.” This signifies, in accordance with the passage where the Lord prayed alone on the mountain, that Isaac too—who was a type of the Lord—went out from the house to pray, like a righteous man, and offered spiritual sacrifices to God either at the ninth hour or before sunset.

**(Verse 65.)** And she took her veil and covered herself. A *theristrum* is a cloak, a kind of Arabian garment by which the women of that province still cover themselves.

### Chapter 25

**Verse 1.** “And Abraham continued, and took a wife, and her name was Keturah; and she bore him Zimran, and Joksan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah. And Joksan begot Sheba and Dedan. And the sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim. And the sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Enoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah. And Abraham gave everything that he had to Isaac. But to the sons of the concubines whom he had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he was still alive, toward the east, to the eastern land.”

[Note: The same Regina manuscript has “and Jokshan, and Midian, and Ishbak,” etc.]

Keturah is interpreted in Hebrew as “joined” or “attached” [another reading: “bound”]. For this reason the Jews suspect that, after changing her name, she was the same person as Hagar, who, after Sarah’s death, passed from being a concubine to being a wife. It also seems to excuse the age of the already decrepit Abraham, so that he might not be accused of indulging in new marriages as an old man after the death of his aged wife.

Leaving aside what is uncertain [Note: “Leaving aside what is uncertain,” etc. Would that the learned men of our own time imitated Jerome’s modesty, since he was unwilling to affirm anything concerning uncertain matters, while many presume to teach others what they themselves do not know.], we say this: the sons born to Abraham from Keturah, according to the historians of the Hebrews, occupied Τρωγλοδύτη (*Troglodytis*) and Arabia, which is now called Εὐδαίμων (*Eudaimon*), as far as the boundaries of the Red Sea.

[Note: There is no doubt that he principally means Josephus among the Jewish historians; from him he translated this almost word for word, *Antiquities*, book I, chapter 15:

“Abraham devised means of sending colonies for all these children and grandchildren. They occupied Troglodytis and that part of Happy Arabia which extends as far as the Red Sea. It is said that this Ophren, having undertaken an expedition against Libya, took possession of it; and that his descendants, having settled there, named the land Africa after his name. Alexander Polyhistor also bears witness to my account, speaking as follows:

‘Cleodemus says—the prophet who is also called Malchus, the historian of Jewish affairs, just as Moses, their lawgiver, also recorded them—that many children were born to Abraham from Keturah. He also gives their names, listing three: Apher, Surim, and Japhra. From Surim, he says, Assyria received its name; and from the other two, Apher and Japhra, the city of Aphra and the land of Africa were named.’”]

All these children and grandchildren of Abraham were responsible for sending out colonies. They occupied Troglodytis and the region of Happy Arabia, as far as it stretches toward the Red Sea.
