It is said that Ophren undertook an expedition against Libya and possessed it; and that his descendants, settling there, called the land Africa after his name. Alexander, called Polyhistor, is a witness to this account, as is Cleodemus, surnamed Malchus, who, writing in Greek, reconstructed a barbarian history:

[lacuna]

“Cleodemus the seer, who is also called Malchus, composing a history of Jewish affairs, just as Moses, the legislator of the Jews, had done, relates that several children were born to Abraham from Keturah. He also reports their names, listing three: Apher, Surim, and Japhra. He says that Assyria was called from Surim, and that from Apher and Japhra the city of Aphra and the region of Africa received their names.”

It is said that one of Abraham’s descendants, whose name was Apher, led an army against Libya and, after defeating its inhabitants, settled there; and that his descendants named Africa after the name of their ancestor. Alexander, called Polyhistor, is a witness to this, as is Cleodemus, surnamed Malchus, who recounts barbarian history in Greek.

[Note: Perhaps the reference is to *The Treatise on the Jews*, which, besides Clement of Alexandria, several others mention, as Vossius notes in *On Greek Historians*, chapter 23. You can see how much more plausibly—and in closer conformity with the analogy—the name Africa is derived from Apher [the Hebrew terms are absent from the supplied text] than, as Bochart does, from Africa’s fertile ears of grain.]

As for the statement, “The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim,” they think that *Asshurim* is translated “merchants”; *Letushim*, “those who forge or work the mines of bronze and iron”; and *Leummim*, φύλαρχοι (*phylarchoi*), that is, “chieftains of many tribes and peoples.” Others contend that the Asshurim were called Syrians, and that many of the regions of India were occupied by Abraham’s sons from Keturah.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “and Letushim, and Leummim. And the sons of Midian were Gephar [another reading: Gesara], Apher, Sheba, Neno, and Abida.” The same is found, almost, below.]

**Verse 8.** “And Abraham died in a good old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people.”

The Septuagint has wrongly added, “And Abraham, failing, died” [Note: “And Abraham, failing, died.” Whoever dies truly fails, and in this sense the word “failing,” added by the Septuagint translators, may seem superfluous. The Hebrew has *wayigwa wayyāmoth*, “and he expired and died.” See my fuller annotations below. MARTIAN. Another note: The Hebrew has ויגוע, “and, expiring, he died.” The rabbis think that this denotes a death which comes upon a person without any preceding pain or illness. Martianaeus further observes in his *Additions and Changes* that when Jerome says that “failing” was wrongly added by the Septuagint, he nevertheless more freely pursues this word in allegorical and anagogical interpretations. In his commentary on chapter 1 of Zephaniah, he accepts it in a favorable sense, although here he seems to reject it. “If,” he says, “we wish to understand something more profound because of what is said by the Septuagint, ‘Let failure fail from the face of the earth,’ and to take ‘failure’ in a favorable sense, according to the passage, ‘And Abraham, failing, died in a good old age, an old man and full of days, and was gathered to his people,’ and according to what Scripture relates about Isaac and Jacob, we shall see how they fail with failure from the face of the earth.” Victorius departs even farther from probability when he says that either different Hebrew copies were once in circulation or—which I rather think—the Hebrew text has in many places been altered from the form that was current in Jerome’s time and is now found in use.]

And [the Septuagint adds] “failing, Abraham died,” because it is unfitting for Abraham to fail and be diminished. Likewise, where we have “in a good old age, old and full,” the Greek manuscripts read “full of days.” Although this seems to explain the meaning—that he died full of light and of the works of the day [Note: An older Regina manuscript reads, “and full of light and works,” etc.]—it is more suitable to the anagogical sense if “full” is understood simply.

**Verse 13.** “And these are the names of the sons of Ishmael, by their names and by their generations: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth, and Kedar, and the rest,” down to the passage that says: “And they dwelt from Havilah to Shur, which is before Egypt as one goes toward Assyria; he fell in the presence of all his brothers.”

Twelve sons were born to Ishmael, of whom the firstborn was Nebaioth. From him the whole region extending from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is called Nabataea to this day; it is part of Arabia. Their families, towns, villages, fortified settlements, and tribes are also known by this name. From one of them come Kedar in the desert, Duma, another region, Teman in the south, and Kedemah toward the east.

[Note: We should again recall the source from which Jerome drew: Josephus, *Antiquities*, book I, chapter 12:

“These people inhabit the whole land extending from the Euphrates to the Red Sea, calling the region Nabataea. They are the people who gave their names to the entire nation of the Arabs and to their tribes.”]

As for what we read at the end of this chapter according to the Septuagint, “He dwelt before the face of all his brothers” (Genesis 13:18), the more accurate reading is the one we have given: “He died in the presence of all his brothers,” that is, he died in the hands of all his sons, with his children surviving and none having been taken away by death beforehand.

That brothers may be called sons is also shown by Jacob’s words to Laban: “What is my sin, that you pursued me, and because you searched through all my vessels? What have you found among all the vessels of your house? Let it be placed before my brothers and your brothers, and let them judge between us” (Genesis 31:36). For we cannot believe that, as Scripture relates, Jacob had any brothers with him apart from his children.

[Note: “He died in the presence of all his brothers.” From this passage a certain obscure and contentious man may be refuted—one who repeatedly dared to attack the version of Jerome that we published in the *Canon of Hebrew Truth*, because our edition sometimes differs in wording from what is quoted in the holy Doctor’s *Hebrew Questions*. Let the man therefore be ashamed of his own foolishness, since he sees Jerome expressing the same verse of Genesis in different words: first, “He died in the presence of all his brothers”; then, about twelve lines later, “He died before all his brothers.” These expressions are very different if, like the ignorant, we attend not to the sense of Scripture but to the words of the translator. If Jerome was permitted to interpret the same verse, in the same place and chapter, in such different words, how much more should the holy man be considered to have permitted himself this in different works! Hence it is clear how foolishly those judge who reject the Latin Vulgate as Jerome’s because certain statements are quoted in different words in the present book of *Hebrew Questions* or in the commentaries on the prophets.

Another note: The Regina manuscripts wrongly read, “before the face of all his enemies,” etc.]

**Verse 21.** “And Rebecca his wife conceived, and her children struggled within her.”

For “struggled,” the Septuagint translators used ἐσκίρτων (*eskirtōn*), that is, “played” or “kicked.” Aquila translated it “the children were being crushed in her womb.” Symmachus, however, used διέπλεον (*diepleon*), that is, “they were carried along on the surface like a ship.”

[Note: An older Regina manuscript has διεπάλεον (*diepalēon*), as does the Roman edition; several Greek manuscripts in Montfaucon also give Symmachus’s reading, which easily appears to be the more accurate one, meaning “they were contending.” Jerome must certainly have read διέπλεον in the copy he used, since he explains it as “they were carried along on the surface like a ship.” The more accurate copies, however, may have διεπάλεον.]

**Verse 25.** “And the first came out red, all over like a hairy skin.”

Where we have “hairy,” the Hebrew has *SEIR* (שׂעיר). Hence Esau, as we read elsewhere, was called Seir, that is, “hairy.”

**Verse 30.** “And Esau said to Jacob: Give me some of this red stew, for I am faint; therefore his name was called Edom.”

“Red” or “ruddy” is called *EDOM* (אדום) in Hebrew. Because he sold his birthright for red food, he received the name of the ruddy one, that is, Edom.

### Chapter 26

**Verse 12.** “And Isaac sowed in that land, and found in that year a hundredfold of barley.”

Although Isaac sowed in a foreign land, I do not think that he obtained such an abundance of barley. I therefore consider the Hebrew reading preferable, which Aquila also translated: “And he found in that year a hundredfold, estimated,” that is, ἑκατὸν εἰκασμένον (*hekaton eikasmenon*).

[Note: “A hundredfold, estimated.” See also what is said about this word, “estimated,” in the fuller notes below. MARTIAN. Another note: The manuscripts vary, and many of the errors at this point are to be attributed to the manuscripts themselves: ΕΚΑΤΟΙΚΑϹΝΩΥϹ and ΕΚΑΤΟΝΕΙΔΑϹΜΟΤΕ. Martianaeus noted in his *Additions* that Jerome preferred this interpretation because it served the allegory.]

For the same letters can write both “estimation” and “barley”: estimations are read *SAARIM* (שערים), whereas barley is *SORIM* (שׂערים). Since Scripture does not specify what kind of crop produced the hundredfold increase, it seems to me that it shows the multiplication of all virtues in him. Accordingly, it continues:

**Verse 13.** “And the Lord blessed him, and the man became great, and he went on advancing and growing greater, until he became exceedingly great.”

But I do not know whether the prosperity of increased barley could make anyone glorious.

**Verse 17.** “And Isaac departed from there, and came to the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there.”

Instead of “valley,” the Hebrew has “torrent.” For after Isaac had become great, he could not have dwelt in a valley. He dwelt in a torrent, of which it is written: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Psalm 109:7). Elijah also drank from it in the time of famine. But because Elijah was not perfect like Christ, that torrent dried up for him (3 Kings 17:7). Our Lord, however, was betrayed beside the torrent, dedicating our regeneration and the sacrament of Baptism.

[Note: Saint John, as Martianaeus also notes, says “across the torrent” in chapter 18, verse 1: “He was betrayed across the torrent.” Jerome refers to John 18:1, where the Lord is said to have gone out across the torrent of Kidron, where there was a garden into which he entered with his disciples. Jesus was therefore betrayed beside the torrent; Jerome says “in the torrent” so that he might more easily explain allegorically the dedication of the sacrament.]

**Verse 19.** “And Isaac’s servants dug in the valley of Gerar, and found there a well of living water.”

Here also “torrent” is written instead of “valley”; for a well of living water is never found in a valley.

**Verse 21.** “And they dug another well, and they quarreled also over it; and he called its name Hostility.”

Instead of “hostility,” Aquila and Symmachus translated τὴν ἀντικειμένην (*tēn antikeimenēn*) and ἐναντίωσιν (*enantiosis*), that is, “adverse” and “contrary.” In Hebrew it has *SATANA* (שׂטנה). From this we understand that *satan* means “adversary” or “contrary.”

[Note: One Regina manuscript has τὴν ἀντίωσιν (*tēn antiōsin*).]

**Verse 22.** “And they dug another well, and they did not quarrel with them; and he called its name Broad Place.”

Instead of “broad place,” the Hebrew has *ROOBOTH* (רְחֹבוֹת), confirming what we said above: “He built Nineveh the city, and Rooboth, that is, its streets” (Genesis 10).

**Verse 26.** “And Abimelech went to him from Gerar, and Ochozath his wedding-attendant, and Phicol the commander of his army.”

Instead of “Ochozath his wedding-attendant,” the Hebrew has “the company of his friends,” so that it signifies not so much an individual as the crowd of friends who had come with the king, among whom was Phicol, the commander of his army.

[Note: Earlier books read “Abuzzath,” whereas the Vulgate has “Ochozath,” which the manuscripts of this work retain. MARTIAN. Another note: Above, in chapter 21, verse 22, he showed that the name Ochozath is entirely absent from the Hebrew; here he takes it in an appellative sense, as several interpreters do.]

**Verses 32–33.** “And Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well that they had dug; and they said to him, We have found water. And he called its name Saturity.”

I do not know how the Septuagint has: “And Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well that they had dug; and they said to him, We have not found water; and he called its name Oath.” For what etymology is there in calling it “Oath” because they did not find water?

On the contrary, the Hebrew, with which Aquila and Symmachus agree, signifies that they found water, and therefore the well itself was called “Saturation.” The city was called *BERSABEE*, that is, “well of saturation” (Genesis 21). Although above we maintained that Bersabee was named from the word for an oath, or from the number seven of the sheep—*SABEE* (שבע)—Isaac now, because water had been found, alluded to the name of the city so called, slightly altering the letter. In place of the hissing Hebrew *SIN*, with which *SABEE* begins, he used the Greek sigma, that is, the Hebrew *SAMECH*.

[Note: “In place of the hissing Hebrew sin.” We explained the alteration of the letter *sin* in the *Apology for Jerome*. MARTIAN. Another note: In Hebrew manuscripts the word is written with the same outline of the letter, whether it means “seven,” “oath,” “saturation,” or “fullness.” Grammarians distinguish the meanings by placing the dot on the left horn when it means “seven,” and on the right when it means “saturation.” Isaac himself may have moderated the pronunciation of the word so that it approached *samech* more closely.]

Otherwise, even according to the law of allegory, after so many wells it would hardly be fitting, at the end of his virtues, for Isaac not to have found living water.

[Note: One Regina manuscript has “not found living water at all,” etc. In accordance with the Vulgate below, *lenis* should preferably be read as *laevis*, corresponding to the Hebrew.]

### Chapter 27

**Verse 11.** “Behold, my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man.”

Where we read “hairy,” the Hebrew has *SEIR* (שׂעיר). Hence the mountains of Seir and the region in which he lived were later so called; we have discussed this above.

**Verse 15.** “And Rebecca took the desirable garments of Esau her older son, which she had with her in the house.”

At this point the Jews relate that the firstborn performed the priestly office and possessed priestly clothing, in which, clothed, they offered sacrifices to God before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood.

**Verse 36.** “And Esau said: He is rightly called Jacob, for he has supplanted me these two times.”

Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter.” Because he deceived his brother by craft, Esau alluded to his name. Jacob had first been called this because at birth he had seized his brother’s heel.

**Verse 40.** “And you shall serve your brother; and it shall come to pass when you remove and loose his yoke from your neck.”

This signifies that the Idumeans would serve the Jews, and that a time would come when they would cast off the yoke of servitude from their neck and resist their rule. According to the Septuagint, however, who said, “But it shall be when you have removed and loosed the yoke from your neck,” the sentence appears to hang unfinished and not to be complete.

### Chapter 28

**Verse 19.** “And Jacob called the name of that place Bethel.”

“And Ulammaus was formerly the name of the city.” From what he had said above—“How terrible is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven”—he now gives the place a name and calls it *BETHEL* (בית־אל), that is, “house of God.” The place had previously been called *LUZA* (לוז), which is interpreted as “nut” or “almond.”

[Note: The Roman Greek edition of the Septuagint reads Οὐλαμλοὺζ (*Ulamluz*), which Erasmus retains in this work. The Alexandrian manuscript, together with Jerome’s Latin copies, has Οὐλαμμαῢς (*Ulammaus*). MARTIAN. Our manuscripts likewise retain *Ulammaus*. Earlier editors, following the Roman Septuagint copy, printed *Ulam Luz*, which is somewhat less corrupt, though I do not know how accurate it is. The other Greek manuscripts, although corrupt in various ways, clearly offer Οὐλαμμαὺς, Οὐλαμμαοὺς, or Λαμμαοὺς. I discussed this reading, and Jerome’s interpretation of *ulam* that follows it, at length in the earlier book *On Places*, and showed it to be entirely true and worthy of Jerome’s great learning, against the ridiculous objections of Clericus and others after him—namely, that if *ulam* is taken as “formerly,” the word “formerly” would occur twice unnecessarily in the same text. I now add Theodore’s note from manuscripts held by Montfaucon:

“Know that *Ulam* was rendered ‘formerly’ by Aquila and his followers, and not as part of the city’s name. He expressly calls the city Luza afterward.”

That is, *Ulam* was rendered “formerly” by Aquila, but not as part of the city’s name; for he later plainly calls it Luza.]

The order of the passage is therefore: “And Jacob called the name of that place Bethel, and formerly Luza was the name of the city.” All the ancient Scriptures are full of the word *ulam*, or *elam*, which signifies nothing other than “before” or “formerly,” or else “vestibule,” “threshold,” or “doorposts.”

### Chapter 29

**Verse 27.** “Complete the week of this one, and I will give you this one also.”

After Jacob, deceived by Laban, had taken Leah as his wife instead of Rachel, his father-in-law Laban is said to have told him to complete the seven days after the first sister’s wedding and then to take Rachel, for whom he would serve another seven years.

Therefore, contrary to the mistaken opinion of some, Jacob did not take Rachel as wife after another seven years, but after the seven days of the first wife’s wedding. For it follows: “And he went in to Rachel, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served him another seven years” (Genesis 29:30).

[Note: Josephus held the opinion that Jacob received Rachel after another seven years, *Antiquities*, book I, chapter 19:

“After another seven-year period had passed, he took Rachel as his wife.”]

**Verse 32.** “And she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Reuben.”

For the sake of brevity in reading, I wish to state together the etymologies of the names of all the patriarchs.

[Note: One Regina manuscript supplies the heading: “The names of the patriarchs with their interpretations.”]

“And she called his name Reuben,” it says, “for she said, ‘Because the Lord has seen my humiliation.’” *RUBEN* (ראובן) is interpreted as “son of vision.”

**Verse 33.** “And she conceived again and bore a son, and said: ‘Because the Lord has heard me, since my husband hated me, he has also given me this one’; and she called his name Simeon.”

Because she had been heard, she gave him the name Simeon. *SIMEON* (שמעון) is interpreted as “hearing.”

**Verse 34.** “And she conceived again and bore a son, and said: ‘Now my husband will be with me, because I have borne him three sons’; therefore she called his name Levi.”

Where we read, “My husband will be with me,” Aquila translated, “My husband will be attached to me,” which in Hebrew is *ILLAVE* (ילוה).

[Note: The same manuscript, together with four others in Martianaeus, has *ellave*. Another note: The Hebrew is *illave*. Four manuscripts give *ellave*, but we know that among ancient copyists *i* was frequently changed into *e*. MARTIAN.]

The Hebrew teachers translate it otherwise, saying, “My husband will follow me,” that is: I have no doubt of my husband’s love for me; he will be my companion in this life, and his affection will accompany me and follow me even to death, for I have borne him three sons.

**Verse 35.** “And she conceived and bore a son, and said: ‘Now I will give thanks to the Lord for this’; therefore she called his name Judah.”

*JUDAH* (יהודה) means “confession.” Thus the name of the confessor was derived from confession. Here, however, confession is understood as thanksgiving or praise, as frequently in the Psalms and in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth” (Matthew 11:25), that is, “I give you thanks” or “I glorify you.”

[Note: Josephus, in the passage cited above, likewise says: Ἰούδας, εὐχαριστίαν τοῦτο δηλοῖ—“Judah signifies thanksgiving.”]

### Chapter 30

**Verses 5–6.** “And Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son. And Rachel said: ‘God has judged me, and has heard my voice, and has given me a son’; therefore she called his name Dan.”

She expressed the reason for the name: because she believed that God had judged her, she gave the son of her maidservant the name of judgment. *DAN* (דן) means “judgment.”

**Verses 7–8.** “And Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, conceived again and bore Jacob a second son. And Rachel said: ‘God has made me dwell with my sister, and I have prevailed’; and she called his name Naphtali.”

The reason given here for the name Naphtali differs greatly from the explanation written in the book of Hebrew Names. Hence Aquila says, συνανέστρεψέν με ὁ Θεὸς—“God has caused me to associate with my sister”—καὶ συνανεστράφην, “and I have associated.”

[Note: The conjunction καὶ does not occur in any of our manuscripts and in fact does not correspond to the Hebrew. In the same manuscripts, the Hebrew words that follow are written in Greek letters. One Regina manuscript soon after reads “conversation” instead of “conversion” in both places, as Erasmus also explained it; Victorius corrected him.]

The Hebrew has *NEPHTHULE ELOIM, NEPHTHALETHI*.

[Note: The Hebrew is *naphtule Elohim niphtalti*, or, according to the reading of the ancients, *nephthule eloim nephthalethi*. We discussed the meaning of these words above in our *Apology for Jerome*. MARTIAN.]

Therefore she gave her son the name Naphtali from “conversion” or “comparison,” since both meanings are conveyed by the word.

**Verses 10–11.** “And Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, bore Jacob a son. And Leah said: ‘By fortune’; and she called his name Gad.”

Where we have “by fortune,” the Greek says ἐν τύχῃ (*en tychē*), which may be translated “by chance” or “by event.” The Hebrew has *BAGAD* (בגד), which Aquila interprets as “the coming of the troop.” We may say “in readiness for battle” or “in military array.”

*BA* can function as the preposition “in,” and the remainder means “he comes.”

[Note: This concerns the sound of pronunciation, not the form of the written characters. “He came” is written with the letter *aleph*, which neither usage nor grammatical rules permit to be omitted in that word. We do not dwell on Drusius’s criticism of Jerome’s conjecture because *in* is written with *qamats*; the vowel points of the Masoretes are far too weak a basis for asserting any reading. MARTIAN.]

Thus, from the event or military readiness called *GAD* (גד), Zilpah’s son was named Gad.

**Verses 12–13.** “And Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, bore Jacob a second son. And Leah said: ‘I am blessed, because women call me blessed’; and she called his name Asher—‘wealth.’”

“Wealth,” that is, πλοῦτος (*ploutos*) [another reading: πλουτῶν, “being wealthy”], has been wrongly added, since Scripture itself explains the etymology of the name Asher, saying: “I am blessed, and women call me blessed.” Because she was called blessed by people [another reading: “by all”], she called her son blessed.

*ASHER* (אשר), therefore, does not mean “wealth” but “blessed,” at least in this passage. In other places, according to the ambiguity of the word, it may also signify “wealth.”

[Note: “According to the ambiguity.” The ambiguity of the word *Asher* lies in the change of its middle letter: written with middle *sin*, it signifies “blessed”; but *Asher* with middle *tsade* means “wealth.” Thus Isaiah 23:10 has *ye’aser*, “he will be stored in treasuries.” MARTIAN. Another note: This applies when it is written with the form from which *cimetium*, a repository for stored treasure, derives. One Regina manuscript says that wealthy people may also be called this.]

**Verses 17–18.** “And God heard Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son. And Leah said: ‘God has given me my reward, because I gave my maidservant to my husband’; and she called his name Issachar.”

The Septuagint translators gave the etymology of this name as “there is a reward.” It should not be understood, as many incorrectly read it by adding a pronoun, as though the text said “he is a reward”; rather, the whole name means “there is a reward.” *IS* means “is,” and *SACHAR* (שכר) means “reward.” This was because Leah had bought for herself her husband’s access, which was owed to Rachel, with Reuben’s mandrakes.

**Verses 19–20.** “And Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son. And Leah said: ‘God has endowed me with a good endowment. At this time my husband will dwell with me, because I have borne him six sons’; and she called his name Zebulun.”

[Note: We correct this from the manuscripts, supported by the Greek text, ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ, “at the present time.” Earlier printed books falsely had “in this time.”]

Where we have “he will dwell with me,” the Septuagint translated “he will love me.” The Hebrew has *JEZBULENI* (יזבלני). The sense is: because I have borne Jacob six sons, I am now secure; my husband will dwell with me. Hence my son is also called “dwelling.” It is therefore wrong and forced for the book of Names to interpret Zebulun as “the flow of the night.”

**Verse 21.** “And after this she bore a daughter, and called her name Dinah” (דינה).

This is translated as “cause,” which the Greeks more significantly call δίκη (*dikē*), “judgment” or “lawsuit.” She was the cause of the dispute among the Shechemites.

After the sons, the names of the parents should also be given. *LEAH* (לאה) means “laboring.” *RACHEL* (רחל) means “ewe.” Her son *JOSEPH* (יוסף) is called “increase,” because his mother desired that another child be added to her.

**Verses 32–33.** “I will pass through all your flock today. Remove from it every speckled and variegated animal, and every solid-colored animal among the lambs, and the variegated and speckled among the goats; this shall be my wage. And my righteousness will answer for me tomorrow, when my wage comes before you: whatever is not speckled or variegated among the goats and lambs shall be considered theft in my possession,” and so forth.

[Note: Another Regina manuscript reads: “Remove from it every solid-colored animal among the lambs, and every variegated and speckled one among the goats; and it shall be,” etc.]

The sense is very confused in the Septuagint, and to this day I have been unable to find anyone among our writers who explained clearly what was being said in this passage.

Jacob says: “Do you want me to serve you another seven years? Do what I ask. Separate all the speckled and variegated animals, both sheep and goats, and put them in the hands of your sons. Then from each flock give me the white and black animals—that is, the solid-colored ones. If, therefore, anything variegated is born from the white and black animals that are solid-colored, it will be mine; but if anything solid-colored is born, it will be yours. I am asking for nothing difficult. Nature itself works in your favor, so that white animals are born from white and black from black; while my righteousness will be with me, since God looks upon my humility and labor.”

Laban gladly seized upon the option offered to him. He did as Jacob requested and placed a three-day journey between Jacob and his sons, so that no deception might occur through the proximity of the flocks.

Jacob therefore devised a new stratagem and opposed natural skill to the nature of white and black animals. He took three rods—of poplar, almond, and pomegranate. Although the Septuagint has “storax, walnut, and plane” [Note: Several manuscripts read “storax, nut, and plane”; others, “storax, walnut, and plane,” etc. MARTIAN. Another note: Two manuscripts have “storax, nut, and plane.”], he partly stripped the bark from them and made the rods variegated in color. Wherever he left the bark on the rod, its original color remained; wherever he removed the bark, the white color appeared.

Jacob therefore watched the time when the animals were being mounted and, after the heat of the day, when they went eagerly to drink. He placed the variegated rods in the watering channels and, admitting the rams and he-goats, caused the ewes and she-goats to be mounted while they were in the very act of eagerly drinking. Thus, from the double desire—while they drank eagerly and were mounted by the males—the females conceived offspring such as the shadows of the rams and he-goats mounting above them appeared in the reflection of the water.

The color of the images was also variegated because of the rods placed in the channels.

[Note: We have supplied the word “was” from the manuscripts and Victorius.]

Nor is it surprising that this should be the nature of conception in women: whatever they have seen or conceived in their minds during the final heat of pleasure, they produce offspring of that kind; since this very same thing is also [said] of mares—

[Note: Oppian sang this very elegantly in *Cynegetica*, book I:

“Men have often devised other contrivances with all-wise ingenuity,

to mark the foal while it is still in its mother’s womb,” etc.

“Men have often discovered many things with a sagacious mind …”]

[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence.]

To vary a foal with spots while it is still in its mother’s womb, etc.—in twenty continuous verses, which it will be useful to read. See also Saint Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, 93, and Saint Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XII, chapter 1, where he describes Jerome in almost exactly the same words.]—is said to occur among the herds in Spain; and Quintilian, in the controversy in which a matron who had given birth to an Ethiopian was accused, argues in her defense that this is the nature of conception that we have described above.

[Note: “But after they had been born.” Here the Erasmus edition of the books of Hippocrates falsely inserts a story that the manuscript codices do not preserve. MARTIAN.]

[Note: From Saint Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, 93—not, as Martianaeus thinks, from Hippocrates’ own books—the ancient editors Erasmus and Victorius add a story of this kind and insert it into Jerome’s text: “And it is written in the books of Hippocrates that a certain woman”—supply “woman”—“was liable to punishment on suspicion of adultery, when she had given birth to a most beautiful”—supply “boy”—“child unlike both parents and his entire family, unless the aforementioned physician had resolved the question, advising (in Augustine: ‘after they had been advised’) them to investigate whether perhaps some such picture was in the bedroom. When one was found there, the woman was freed from suspicion.”]

But after the kids and the spotted and variegated lambs had been born from the white and single-colored flocks, Jacob separated them and kept them away from the former flock. But if any single-colored animals were born—that is, white or black ones—he handed them over to Laban’s sons. He placed the rods he had stripped of bark in the channels [Col. 0985B] into which the waters flowed, and the animals came to drink opposite the flocks, so that they might conceive at the time when they came to drink.

**(Verses 41 and 42.)** “And the animals conceived before Jacob’s rods, the rods that he had placed before the flocks [Alternative: flock] in the channels, so that they might conceive by them; but with the late-breeding sheep he did not place them. Thus the late-breeding animals became Laban’s, and the early-breeding Jacob’s.”

This is not found in the Septuagint interpreters; instead of “late-breeding” and “early-breeding,” they translated something else that has no bearing on the sense.

[Note: This does not pertain to the meaning. In the Septuagint we read: “But the unmarked animals became Laban’s, and the marked ones Jacob’s,” which does not seem at all to express the sense of this passage. MARTIAN.]

[Note: Namely: “The unmarked ones became Laban’s, but the marked ones Jacob’s”—*ἐγένετο δὲ τὰ μὲν ἄσημα τοῦ Λάβαν, τὰ δὲ ἐπίσημα τοῦ Ἰακώβ*. “Those that were not marked went to Laban, but those that were marked went to Jacob.” Now, as for Jerome’s interpretation of “late-breeding” and “early-breeding” as offspring of autumn and spring—since, according to the opinion he is about to explain, sheep in Mesopotamia gave birth twice each year—the Eastern interpreters, the Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic, support it. They indicate that Jacob did not place those rods when the autumn offspring were being conceived, since they were weaker and he would freely concede them to Laban. For although Columella says the opposite in Book VIII, chapter 3—“The autumn lamb is better than the spring lamb, as Celsus says most truly,” and so forth—the statement can nevertheless be reconciled with Jerome’s opinion if the holy Doctor is understood to have meant the time of conception, not the time of birth, when he placed the rods under the animals. Accordingly, he called “early-breeding” those animals that were conceived in spring at the sight of the rods but were born in autumn.]

But what Scripture says is this: Jacob, prudent and clever, maintained justice [Note: Several manuscripts read “equality,” etc.] and fairness even in his new method. For if all the lambs and kids had produced spotted offspring, there would have been some suspicion of trickery, and Laban, openly jealous of this, would have resisted it. Therefore he regulated everything in such a way that he himself received the fruit of his labor while Laban was not completely stripped.

Whenever the sheep and goats were first put to the males—for the spring offspring are better—he placed the rods before them, so that variegated offspring might be born. But whenever the sheep and goats sought the male late, he did not place the rods before their eyes, so that single-colored animals might be born. Whatever was born first was his, because it was spotted and variegated; [Note: The same manuscripts add: “but whatever came afterward, both black and white in color.”] whatever came afterward belonged to Laban, for animals of a single color, whether black or white, were born.

Where it is written that they should “conceive by the rods,” the Hebrew has [Note: One manuscript of the Queen’s Library has, in Greek letters, ΥΑΑΜΗΝΑ in both places; another has the form *Iaamena* in Latin.] **JEAMENA** (). I cannot express the force of the Hebrew word except by circumlocution. For *JEAMENA* properly denotes the final heat in sexual intercourse, by which the whole body is shaken and which is near the end of the act of pleasure.

**(Chapter XXXI.—Verses 7 and 8.)** “And your father deceived me and changed my wages ten times, and God did not allow him to harm me. If he said, ‘The spotted animals shall be your wages,’ every animal was born spotted. And if he said, ‘The single-colored animals shall be your wages,’ every animal was born single-colored.”

Instead of what we have rendered, “He changed my wages ten times,” the Septuagint interpreters have “ten lambs,” being led, I do not know by what opinion, to do so, although the Hebrew word **MONI** () denotes a number rather than lambs.

[Note: The Hebrew word is *Moni*. Earlier printed books read the plural *monim*, but we have restored the singular *moni* in accordance with the evidence of the manuscript copies. MARTIAN. See Saint Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, 95. The older editors immediately after this read *MONIM*, as it appears in the Hebrew exemplar.]

Indeed, the following context supports this sense more strongly: Laban continually changed his agreement according to each successive birth. If he saw spotted animals being born, after the birth he would say, “I want spotted ones to be born to me in the future.” Again, when he saw single-colored animals being born—for Jacob, having heard this, did not place the rods in the channels—he would say that future offspring should produce single-colored animals for him.

And why say more? Up to ten times Laban continually changed the agreement concerning his own animals—or Jacob’s. Whatever he had stipulated should be born was turned into the opposite color.

But lest anyone find ten breeding periods in six years incredible, read Virgil (*Georgics* II), where it is said:

> Twice the sheep are pregnant.

It is also reported that the nature of the Italian sheep and that of the Mesopotamian sheep are the same.

**(Verse 19.)** “And Rachel stole her father’s idols.” Where we now read “idols,” the Hebrew has [Note: Two manuscripts consistently read *Tarafi*. See the *Epistle* in our edition, 29 to Marcella, sections 30 and following.] **THERAPHIM** (), which Aquila translates as *μορφώματα*—that is, “figures” or “images.” This is mentioned so that we may know what *THERAPHIM* means in the Book of Judges (XVII, 5).

**(Verse 21.)** “And he crossed the river and came to Mount Gilead.” This does not mean that the mountain was called Gilead at that time, but by anticipation, as we have often said: it is called by the name by which it was afterward named.

**(Verse 41.)** “And you changed my wages ten [Col. 0987B] lambs.” The same error as above: the number must be read instead of “lambs.”

**(Verse 46.)** “And Jacob said to his brothers, ‘Gather stones.’ And when they had gathered stones, they made a heap and ate upon it. And Laban called it the Heap of Testimony, while Jacob called it the Heap of the Witness.”

In the Hebrew language, a heap is called **GAL** (), while **AAD** () means “testimony.” Again, in the Syriac language a heap is called **IGAR**, and testimony **SEDUTHA** (). Jacob therefore called the heap of testimony—that is, *Galaad*—in the Hebrew language. Laban, however, called the same thing, namely, the heap of testimony, *IGAR SEDUTHA* in the language of his people. For he was a Syrian and had exchanged the ancient language of his ancestors for the language of the province in which he lived.

[Col. 0987C] **(Chapter XXXII.—Verses 1 and 2.)** “And the angels of God met him. When Jacob saw them, he said, ‘This is the camp of God,’ and he called the name of that place ‘Camps.’”

Where we have “camps,” the Hebrew has **MANAIM** (), so that, whenever the word is left untranslated elsewhere, we may know what place it signifies. And beautifully, as he goes to his hostile brother, he is received by the choirs of the angels accompanying him.

**(Verses 9 and 10.)** “And Jacob said, ‘God of my father Isaac, Lord, who said to me, “Return to your land, and I will bless you”: I am less than all your mercy and all your faithfulness that you have shown to your servant.’”

Instead of what we have rendered, “I am less than,” something else, which disturbs the sense, is found in the Greek and Latin codices.

[Note: Namely, *ἱκανούσθω μοι*, which may be rendered in Latin “may it suffice for me,” or “I am sufficient.”]

**(Verses 27 and 28.)** “And he said to him, ‘What is your name?’ He answered, ‘Jacob.’ Then he said to him, ‘Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but your name shall be Israel, because you have prevailed with God, and you will prevail with men.’”

Josephus, in the first book of the *Antiquities*, thinks that Israel was given this name because he stood against an angel. But when I examine the matter carefully, I cannot find this at all in the Hebrew.

[Note: You will easily find this if you understand the words of the sacred text as referring not to God, as Jerome does, but to an angel, as Josephus does; so also the prophet Hosea understood it in chapter XII, verse 7: “He fought and contended with the angel.” Josephus’ passage reads as follows in Book I, chapter 20: “The angel commanded him to be called Israel; this means in the Hebrew language ‘one who resists an angel of God.’” Justin likewise says in the *Dialogue with Trypho* that Israel means *ἄνθρωπος νικῶν δύναμιν*, “a man conquering power”: “For *Isra* means ‘a man conquering’; *el* means ‘power.’” He derived it from [the Hebrew term] meaning “man,” and [the term] meaning “to rule” or “to conquer,” and finally [the term meaning] “power” or “angel.”]

And why must I seek the opinions of individuals, when the one who gave the name himself explains its etymology? “Your name shall not be called Jacob,” he says, “but Israel shall be your name.” Why? Aquila translates it, *ὅτι ἤρξας μετὰ Θεοῦ*, “because you ruled with God”; Symmachus, *ὅτι ἤρξω πρὸς Θεὸν*, “because you ruled against God”; the Septuagint and Theodotion, *ὅτι ἐνίσχυσας μετὰ Θεοῦ*, “because you grew strong with God.”

[Note: *Sarith*, etc. Today we read *Saritha*, the second-person masculine singular perfect of the verb *Sara*, which means “to conduct oneself as a prince.” MARTIAN. Some wish to read and supply the passage in this way: “For *Sarith*, or *Sar*, from which the name Israel is derived, means ‘prince.’” Certainly, in Jerome’s final words the expression “to conduct oneself” must be understood, lest anyone suppose that he has taken the second person of the verb as a substantive noun.]

For **SARITH** (), from which the name Israel is derived, means “prince.” The sense, therefore, is: “Your name shall not be called ‘supplanter,’ that is, Jacob; rather, your name shall be ‘prince with God,’ that is, Israel. For just as I am a prince, so you too, who were able to wrestle with me, shall be called a prince. But if you were able to fight with me, who am God—or an angel, since many interpret the passage in different ways—how much more will you prevail with men, that is, with Esau, whom you need not fear?”

But the interpretation found later in the *Book of Names*, “Israel: a man seeing God,” [Note: Among those were Philo, in *On Rewards and Punishments*; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* XI, 6; Olympiodorus on chapter I of Ecclesiastes; Didymus, *On the Holy Spirit*; and many others, whom we mention at that passage of Didymus, section 44. Many others too belong here, for whom Israel is called *ὁρατικὸς ἀνήρ καὶ θεωρητικός*, “a seeing and contemplative man.” Jerome’s preferred explanation is the only sound one: “prince with God.”] seems to me, although worn smooth by almost everyone’s usage, to have been interpreted not so much truthfully as forcibly.

For Israel (), is written with these letters: **IOD, SIN, RES, ALEPH, LAMED**, which means “prince of God,” or “directed by God,” that is, *εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ*, “most direct of God.”

But “a man seeing God” is written with these letters: **ALEPH, IOD, SIN**, so that “man” is written with three letters and is pronounced **IS** (); “seeing” with three letters, **RES, ALEPH, HE**, and is pronounced **RAA** (); and **EL** () consists of two letters, **ALEPH** and **LAMED**, and means “God” or “the mighty one.”

Although therefore men of great authority [Note: This interpretation is found especially in Philo, Eusebius, Olympiodorus, Didymus, and others, as noted above.] and the shadow of their eloquence may weigh upon us—those who translated Israel as “a man” or “a mind seeing God”—we are guided more by the authority of Scripture and of the angel, or God, who himself called him Israel, than by the eloquence of any secular writer.

The following passage also occurs afterward:

**(Verses 29 and 30.)** “And he blessed him there, and Jacob called the name of that place ‘Face of God’: ‘For I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved.’”

In Hebrew it is called [Note: In Hebrew it is called *Phanuel*. In the present Hebrew text we read not *Phanuel* with *vau* in the middle, but *Phaniel* or *Paniel* with *iod*. The interchange of *vau* and *iod* is easy, since they differ only in size, as Jerome often observes. MARTIAN. Here, indeed, it is written with *iod* in the Hebrew manuscripts, but in the following verse with *vau*. In 1 Chronicles VIII, 24, the form with *iod* appears, while the *cheri*, the Masoretic marginal note, has the form with *vau*.] **PHANUEL** (), so that we may know it to be the same place that is read in the other books of Holy Scripture—and in Greek—as *Phanuel*, just as it is written in Hebrew.

**(Chapter XXXIII.—Verses 1 and 2.)** “And he divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two maidservants. He placed the maidservants and their children first, Leah and her children last, and Rachel and Joseph last; and he himself passed before them.”

[Note: Erasmus and Victorius read “second,” contrary to the manuscripts and to the Hebrew text itself. “Leah’s children last.” Older editions placed “second,” but the manuscript codices have “last,” and not without reason: in the Hebrew text Leah’s sons are said to have been placed *abharonim*, that is, later and last, just as Rachel’s sons are also said to have been placed later. This reading is strongly confirmed by Jerome’s annotation, in which the holy Doctor states that Jacob did not make three groups, but only two: one group consisting of the maidservants with their little ones, and another consisting of Leah and Rachel, who were free women, with their children. MARTIAN.]

He did not, as most suppose, make three groups, but two. Indeed, where we have “he divided,” Aquila wrote [Note: The printed editions up to this point have *ἡμίσυσεν* instead of *ἡμίσευσεν*, which the manuscripts prefer.] *ἡμίσευσεν*, that is, “he divided in half,” so that he made one group of the maidservants with their little ones, and another of Leah and Rachel, who were free women, with their children. He made the maidservants go first and the free women second; he himself went before both groups to meet his brother and worship him.

**(Verse 17.)** “And Jacob built a house there, and built shelters for his animals; therefore he called the name of that place ‘Shelters.’”

Where we have “shelters,” the Hebrew reads **SOCHOTH** (). To this day there is a city across the Jordan bearing this name, in the region of Scythopolis, concerning which we wrote in the book *On Places*.

[Note: We discussed it above, column 270.]

[Col. 0989C] **(Verse 18.)** “And Jacob came to Salem, the city of Shechem, in the land of Canaan, when he came from Mesopotamia of Syria.”

A difficulty arises: how can Salem be called the city of Shechem, when Jerusalem, in which Melchizedek reigned, was previously called Salem?

[Note: One manuscript of the Queen’s Library reads: “Or else the interpretation of the two names belongs to one city,” and so forth. Furthermore, the Septuagint translated it as *εἰς πόλιν τοῦ πεδίου*, “to the city of the plain.” See the book *On Places* under the entries *Arboc* and *Chebron*.]

Either both cities have one name—which we can also find with respect to several places in Judea, where the same name belongs to a city and place in different tribes—or else we should say that this Salem, which is now called Shechem, is here interpreted as “completed” and “perfect,” while the one later called Jerusalem is translated in our language as “peaceful.”

For both meanings are conveyed by the word when its accent is slightly altered.

[Note: “With its accent slightly altered,” etc. That accent, slightly inclined on the letter, is now indicated by a small point above it, either to the right or to the left, in this manner. In Hebrew lexicons, however, *Salem* with the point on the right side of the letter means both “completed” and “peaceful.” Hence it is clear that the ancient Hebrews differed somewhat from the modern ones. Compare this with our *Apology for Jerome* and with the entry *Sabee* above, chapter XXVI, verse 33. MARTIAN. See what we said above concerning *Issa* at Genesis II, 23, and concerning *Sabee* in chapter XXVI, verse 33, where the same difficulty recurs. It is certainly clear from Jerome that the letter was formerly distinguished by an accent according to the different meaning of the word in which it occurred. Later grammarians changed that mark into a point, which they place on one or the other horn of the letter; although in the name under discussion, whether it means “completed” or “peaceful,” they now put the point on the right horn.]

The Hebrews relate that Jacob’s dislocated thigh was restored and healed there; for this reason the same city received the name “healed” and “perfect.”

**(Chapter XXXIV.—Verse 20.)** “And Hamor and his son Shechem came to the gate of their city and spoke to the men of the city, saying, ‘These men are peaceful toward us’” [Alternative: “with us”].

Where the Septuagint interpreters have translated “peaceful,” Aquila rendered it *ἀπηρτισμένους*, that is, “completed” and “perfect,” whereas the Hebrew reads **SALAMIM** (). From this it is clear that what we said above about Salem is correct.

**(Verse 25.)** “And they entered the city confidently and killed every male.”

Where the Greek reads *ἀσφαλῶς*, that is, “carefully” or “securely,” the Hebrew has **BETE** (), meaning “boldly and confidently.”

**(Chapter XXXV.—Verse 6.)** “And Jacob came to Luz, in the land of Canaan, which is Bethel.”

Here it is most clearly demonstrated that Bethel is not Ulammaus, as was said above, but Luz, which was formerly called “the almond tree.”

[Note: Two manuscripts of the Queen’s Library read *Ulammaulam*. See what we also annotate above.]

[Col. 0990C] **(Verse 8.)** “And Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died, and she was buried beside Bethel.”

[Note: One manuscript of the Queen’s Library reads, “and she was buried above Bethel”; another, “below Bethel.”]

If Rebekah’s nurse, named Deborah, died, as the Septuagint interpreters also translated here, and if the Hebrew word itself is **MENECETH** (), we cannot know why they rendered it “substance” there [Note: Namely, because there, or in chapter XXIV, verse 59, they read [the Hebrew form] instead of [another form], the transposition of a single little letter. The former word means “substance” or “possessions,” while the latter means “nurse.”] but “nurse” here.

**(Verse 10.)** “And God said to him, ‘Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name’; and he called his name Israel.”

Earlier the name was by no means imposed on him by the angel; rather, it was foretold that it would be imposed by God. What is promised there as future is therefore shown here to have been fulfilled.

**(Verse 16.)** “And it happened, while he was approaching Chabratha in the land of Canaan, so that he might come to Ephratha, that Rachel gave birth.”

The Hebrew word **CHABRATHA** () appears later, where Jacob speaks to Joseph: “But when I was coming from Mesopotamia of Syria, your mother Rachel died in the land of Canaan, on the road to the Hippodrome, as I was coming to Ephrata” (Genesis XLVIII). I do not know what they intended [Note: Two manuscripts read, “speaking to Joseph: ‘But when I was coming,’” etc.] when they translated *Chabratha* as “Hippodrome”:

[Note: The Septuagint did not translate merely “Hippodrome,” but added *Chabratha*: indeed, *κατὰ τὸν ἱππόδρομον Καβραθὰ τῆς γῆς*, corresponding to the Hebrew [form]. In the following passage they render *Ephratha* by itself as “Hippodrome,” namely, *ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ ἱπποδρόμου* for “on the road to Ephratha.” Therefore, if the Greek manuscripts today retain what the Septuagint themselves wrote, they preserved the name *Chabratha*. But it does not appear that Jerome once read it that way; and I think that *Χαβραθὰ* was later inserted from a marginal note.

If it is removed, the difficulty pressed by the holy Doctor immediately disappears, and the passage can easily be explained. Suppose that in this second passage the Septuagint read *Chabratha* instead of *Ephratha*, that is, one form for the other. These names could easily have been confused by the eyes of a copyist, and it might also have seemed more plausible that one should be substituted for the other, so that Rachel was thought to have been buried on the road to the same Chabratha in which she had died.

Nor could they otherwise have translated it as “Hippodrome,” since that etymology, however it may be forced out of *Chabratha*, is entirely unsuitable to *Ephratha*. The word properly denotes a stadium, and differs from “Hippodrome” in only one respect: in a stadium, an imaginary contest and race of horsemen is said to take place, whereas in a hippodrome horses compete in speed without the appearance of battle.

Thus, just as among the Latins *stadium* is generally used for a certain measure of distance, so some of the rabbis teach that this word is composed of *caph* and [a word] meaning “meal,” so that it denotes as much distance as can be traveled from the beginning of the day until mealtime.]

And immediately where the Hebrew says, “They buried her on the road to Ephratha; this is Bethlehem” (Genesis XXXV, 19), the Septuagint again put “Hippodrome” in place of *Ephratha*, although, if *Chabratha* is “Hippodrome,” *Ephratha* cannot be “Hippodrome.”

Aquila translated the passage as follows: “And it happened *καθ’ ὁδὸν τῆς γῆς*”—that is, “on the road of the land”—“as he entered Ephratha.” But it is better translated, [Note: For the holy Doctor to prefer this interpretation, which differs enormously from the present Hebrew archetype—not only here but also in his own Latin translation from the Hebrew Truth, where he twice translates it as “in the spring season” and once as “in the chosen season of the land,” which is the same thing—no better explanation presents itself than that he read in his exemplar [one Hebrew form], *hed chephrath*, instead of [another], *hod chebrath*. These words are almost identical in sound, and the letters in question are easily exchanged in pronunciation. One word means “season,” and the other may be understood as “spring” or “the chosen season of the land.”] “in the chosen season of the land, as he entered Ephratha.”

The spring season is meant, when everything breaks into flower and the season of the year is chosen; or when travelers passing along the road pluck and choose from the neighboring fields whatever comes to hand, attracted by the various flowers.

Ephratha and Bethlehem, moreover, are names of one city, with similar meanings: one is translated “fruitful,” the other “house of bread,” on account of the bread that says it came down from heaven (John VI).

[Col. 0992A] **(Verse 18.)** “And it happened, when her soul was departing—for she was dying—that she called his name ‘Son of my sorrow’; but his father called his name Benjamin.”

[Note: An older manuscript of the Queen’s Library reads: “And it happened, when she was giving up her soul, since she was dying,” etc.]

In Hebrew the similarity of the names can be heard. For “son of my sorrow,” the name given by the dying mother, is called **BENONI** (). But “son of the right hand,” that is, “of strength,” the name Jacob changed it to, is called **BENJAMIM**.

[Note: This interpretation nevertheless seems to be confirmed by Genesis XLIV, 20, where Benjamin is called “the son of old age.” *Jamin* may be taken for *Jamim* in the Syriac dialect, which Jacob, having recently come from Syria, could readily have used. Add that he had been born to Jacob when the latter was nearly one hundred years old.]

Therefore those who think that **BENJAMIM** () means “son of days” are mistaken. For “right hand” is called **JAMIN** (), ending in the letter *n*, whereas “days” is also called **JAMIM** (), but ends in *m*.

**(Verse 21.)** “And Israel departed and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Ader.”

The Hebrews think this was the place where the Temple was later built, and that “the tower of Ader” means “the tower of the flock,” that is, of the congregation and assembly. The prophet Micah also attests this when he says: “And you, tower of the flock, cloudy daughter of Zion” (Micah IV, 8), and so forth. At that time, they say, Jacob pitched his tents beyond the place where the Temple was later built.

But if we follow the order of the road, it is the place of the shepherds near Bethlehem, where either the King of the angels sang at the Lord’s birth, or Jacob pastured his flocks, giving the place its name; or—and this is more truly the case—a future mystery was already being revealed there by a certain prophecy.

**(Verse 7.)** “And Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, the city of Arba”—that is, Hebron.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “This is Hebron,” here and below. The Septuagint, however, translated it as *εἰς πόλιν τοῦ πεδίου*, “to the city of the plain.” See the book *On Places* under the entries *Arboc* and *Chebron*.]

In place of **ARBEE**, the Septuagint has “plain,” although Hebron is situated in the mountains. The same city is also called **MAMBRE**, having been so named in ancient times after Abraham’s friend.

**(Chapter XXXVI.—Verse 4.)** “And Adah bore Eliphaz to Esau.” This is the Eliphaz whom Scripture mentions in the Book of Job.

[Col. 0993A] **(Verse 19.)** “These are the sons of Esau, and these are their chiefs: he is Edom, and these are the sons of Seir.”

Esau, Edom, and Seir are the name of one man, and why he is called by different names has been explained above.

As for what follows:

**(Verse 20.)** [Note: The same manuscripts read, “the Horrites who inhabit,” whereas the Vulgate has, “the Horrites, inhabitants.”]

“And the Horrite who inhabited the land,” and so forth. After enumerating Esau’s sons, he goes back further and explains who had earlier been chiefs in the land of Edom, from the race of the Horrites, who in our language are interpreted as [Note: In the *Book of Names* he interprets them as “angry ones,” “from holes,” and, more correctly, “Troglodytes.”] “free men.”

Let us read Deuteronomy carefully (II, 21), where it is stated more clearly how the sons of Esau came, killed the Horrites, and possessed their land as an inheritance.

**(Verse 22.)** “And the sons of Lotan were Hori and Aeman, and Lotan’s sister was Timna.”

This is the Timna mentioned above. Timna was the concubine of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn son, and Amalek was born from her. He mentioned the Horrites for this reason: Esau’s firstborn son had taken a concubine from among their daughters.

As for the statement that Theman, Kenaz, Amalek, and the others followed, we should know that names were later given to regions of the Idumaeans from these men.

**(Verse 24.)** “This is Anah, who found Jamin in the wilderness while he was pasturing the asses of his father Zibeon.”

Many and varied discussions of this chapter are found among the Hebrews; among the Greeks and our own people there is silence concerning it. Some think that **AJAMIM** () means “seas.”

[Note: In several manuscripts and in Rabanus, *IAMIM* appears without the prefixed *A*, and thus they call them “seas,” as Jerome notes. One manuscript of the Queen’s Library consistently has *Jammim*, and immediately afterward says that “sea” is written with the same letters as this word.]

For “seas” is written with the same letters with which this word is now written. They think that while Anah was pasturing his father’s asses in the wilderness, he discovered gatherings of water, which, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, are called “seas”—that is, he discovered a pool, the finding of which in the desert would be difficult.

Some think that the word denotes hot springs, in keeping with the proximity of the Punic language, which is closely related to Hebrew.

[Note: Jerome himself prefers this interpretation in his Latin translation from the Hebrew source. He is thought to have read in the exemplar he used [the Hebrew word] meaning “baths” or “hot waters” instead of [the form] *Hajemim*. But this explanation does not seem to fit the circumstance added here, namely, that Anah was pasturing the asses of his father Zibeon.]

Others believe [Note: Especially the rabbis whom Kimchi cites. He asserts that those whom they call by another name, namely “mules,” were so called as though the word were compounded from two species, since they are born from a wild ass or horse and a she-ass. They say that Anah discovered or devised this while pasturing asses, by bringing a horse to a she-ass, from which the new species of mules came into the world.

Those who think that he was the first to have mares mounted by asses in the wilderness reach the same conclusion. This opinion may seem more plausible because Anah is said to have guarded asses in the wilderness, but it is refuted by other scriptural arguments—especially because mules are nowhere mentioned by that name, and indeed Scripture indicates that their species became known only under David.]

They think that wild asses were made to mate with she-asses by him, and that he discovered this kind of intercourse, so that extraordinarily swift asses would be born from them, which are called **JAMIM** ().

Most think that he was the first to have herds of mares mounted by asses in the wilderness, so that new animals, mules, contrary to nature, might arise from them.

Aquila translated the passage as follows: “This is Anah, who found *σὺν τοὺς ἐμίμ*.”

[Note: *Σὺν τοὺς ἐμίμ*. The passage is seriously corrupt in the older editions. Erasmus read it in this form: “who found *σὺν τοῖς σιμείμ*.” Symmachus likewise had *τοὺς σιμείμ*. Marianus omitted the particle *σὺν* and read, “he found *τοὺς ἰαμεὶμ*,” etc.

Without exception, the manuscript codices retain the particle *σὺν* in Aquila’s version: “he found *σὺν τοῖς Ἐμίμ*.” Symmachus likewise has *τοὺς Ἐμίμ*. They differ only in that some read *H* for *E*, and *N* for *M* at the end of the word *Ἐμὶμ*.

Diodorus teaches us that the Hebrew word was preserved intact by all the interpreters, namely [the Hebrew form], which the Greeks could read as *emim*, *hmim*, or *jamim*, just as we read both *Esaias* and *Isaias*. Hence it is clear that Erasmus’ *σιμεὶμ* is wholly unacceptable, and that the manifest corruption of Aquila’s text was introduced into Jerome. MARTIAN.

Our manuscripts correct it in this way, but Martianaeus is wrong to read *σὺν τοῖς* against the evidence of the manuscripts. Although he thinks he is restoring the passage, and joins *σὺν*, as a preposition serving the dative, to *τοῖς* according to the rules of grammar, he corrupts it further. For here it does not function as a Greek preposition; rather, it is a word devised by Aquila’s contentious ingenuity to express the Hebrew article. Nothing is more common in that interpreter’s version than for it to be joined with the accusative: in the very first verse of Genesis he renders the Hebrew [form] as *σὺν τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ σὺν τὴν γῆν*.

As for *Ἐμίμ*, some manuscripts prefer *Ἰαμεὶμ*, others *Ἰαμὶμ*. One manuscript of the Queen’s Library has *HAMIN*, another older one *HMHN*, and in Symmachus *HMIN* or *HMYN*.

I have scarcely any doubt that both interpreters translated *Ἐμὶμ* and thereby understood the proper name Emim, the race of giants whose origin and dwelling near the Horrites are described in Deuteronomy II, 10 and following. I am readily persuaded that this interpretation of the passage is more credible than the others: namely, that Anah encountered the giants called Emim.]

And Symmachus likewise translated it as *τοὺς ἐμὶμ*, an interpretation that signifies the plural number. But the Septuagint and Theodotion translated it in the same way, saying *τὸν ἰαμὶμ*, which indicates the singular number.

[Note: Our manuscripts have *YAMYN* or *IAMIN*. See Lambert Bos’s recent edition of the Septuagint.]

**(Verse 33.)** “And Jobab, son of Zerah, from Bozrah, reigned in his place.”

Some suspect that this man was Job, as is added at the end of the book itself.

[Note: Among those who hold this view are Saint Epiphanius, Book I *On Heresies*, and Theodoret, question 93 on Genesis. Recall what we noted above in chapter XXII, verse 20, concerning the addition to Job at the end of the volume, where Job—previously called Jobab, son of Zerah, son of Esau, king of Edom—is identified. MARTIAN. See the end of the Book of Job according to the Septuagint, volume I of the works of Saint Jerome in our edition.]

The Hebrews, on the other hand, assert that he was descended from Nahor’s line, as was already said above.

### Chapter XXXVII

**Verse 3.** Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he was the son of his old age; and he made him a variegated tunic. Instead of “variegated tunic,” Aquila translated a tunic *ἀστραγάλειον* (*astragáleion*), that is, a full-length tunic. Symmachus translated it as a tunic with sleeves,

> [Note: The Greek is *χειριδωτὸν*. Agellius, Book VII, chapter 12: “For a man to wear tunics extending beyond the arms and as far as the hands’ fingertips, or nearly so, was considered unbecoming at Rome and throughout Latium. Our people called such tunics by the Greek term *χειριδωτούς*.”]

either because it descended as far as the ankles and was distinguished by the marvelous variety of the craftsman’s work, or because it had sleeves. For the ancients generally used sleeveless tunics,

> [Note: “Used sleeveless tunics.” A *colobium* is a garment without sleeves, or an undergarment. It is called *κολόβιον* because it is mutilated, that is, *κολοβόν*. Joseph therefore had a distinctive type of garment in his sleeved tunic, as Saint Jerome observes from the usage received among the ancients. MARTIAN.]

**Verse 28.** And they sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty [364] pieces of gold. Instead of “gold,” the Hebrew has “silver.” For the Lord ought not to have been sold for a baser metal than Joseph.

**Verse 36.** The Midianites, however, sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar the eunuch, Pharaoh’s chief cook. In most places Scripture mentions chief cooks—that is, chiefs of the cooks—in place of commanders of the army:

> [Note: Thus Saint Augustine says in *Questions on Genesis*, question 127: “Some do not wish to interpret *chief of the cooks*, who is called in Greek *ἀρχιμάγειρος*, but *commander of the army*, one who had the power to kill. For that is what the man was called whom Nebuchadnezzar sent, in whose case the primacy of military authority is more evident. The Targum, however, rendered both meanings: ‘chief of the executioners,’ or ‘of the slaughterers.’”]

for in Greek *μαγειρεύειν* means “to kill.” Joseph was therefore sold to the commander of the army [Col. 0995B] and of the warriors, not to Petephres,

> [Note: The Greeks too prefer *Πετεφρῆν*. The story of the Hebrews, which Jerome mentions, is exceedingly foolish. Gennadius, however, says quite learnedly: “If Petephres was a eunuch, how is he found to have a wife? But the Syrian, by one designation, calls both a castrated man and a man faithful to his masters; whereas the Hebrew truly calls this man a eunuch as well.” Thus this was the name of an office and rank in Pharaoh’s court.]

as it is written in Latin, but to Potiphar the eunuch. Here the question arises how he is later said to have had a wife. The Hebrews relate that he bought Joseph, because of his extraordinary beauty, for a shameful service; and that, after the Lord had caused his male organs to wither, he was afterward selected, according to the custom

> [Note: “According to the custom of the Hierophants.” The printed Greek reads *ἱεροφαντῶν*. The Hierophants were priests of sacred rites who taught religious ceremonies. See Plutarch, *Numa*; Philo, *On the Life of Moses*, and also his books *On the Number Seven* and *On Festivals*. MARTIAN.]

of the Hierophants, for the priesthood of Heliopolis. They say that Aseneth was his daughter, whom Joseph afterward took as his wife.

> [Note: Origen testifies in the manuscript *Catenae* preserved by Montfaucon, in the *Hexapla*, that the Hebrews derive this from an apocryphal source—*ἐξ ἀποκρύφου*: “Phutirpharem, namely, the very man who was Joseph’s master and father-in-law.” They relate that Aseneth accused her mother before her father of having plotted against Joseph, rather than of having been attacked by him. He gave her to Joseph as a bride, so that he might demonstrate to the Egyptians that Joseph had perpetrated nothing of the sort against his household. See below, Genesis 41:43.]

### Chapter XXXVIII

**Verse 5.** And again she bore a son, and called his name Shelah; and she was in Chazbi when she bore him. The Hebrew word here is used as the name of a place, but Aquila translated it according to its meaning, saying: “And she called his name Shelah.”

> [Note: The Hebrew word itself appears to need to be supplied here, printed in larger letters as CHAZBI, or rather CHAZIB. In Hebrew it is [Hebrew text]. Two manuscripts immediately afterward have it corruptly. Aquila translated it properly.]

“And it came to pass that she was deceptive in childbirth after she had borne Shelah.” For after she had borne Shelah, her childbirth ceased. Therefore Chazbi

> [Note: “Therefore Chazbi is not the name of a place.” Chazbi is produced by a transposition of the letter; in Hebrew it reads Chazib, not Chazbi. MARTIAN. —Most other ancient and modern interpreters disagree; for them it is properly the name of a place, Chasib, not far from Adullam and Mamre. It is also mentioned in Joshua 15:44 and Micah 1:14.]

is not the name of a place, but means “falsehood.” Hence it is also written elsewhere: “The work of the olive tree will lie,” that is, “the olive will produce no fruit” (Habakkuk 3:17).

**Verse 12.** And Judah, having consoled himself, went up to those who were shearing his sheep, he and Hiras his Adullamite shepherd. Instead of “shepherd,” the reading is “friend.” But the word is ambiguous, because both designations are written with the same letters. “Friend” is read *REE* ([Hebrew text]); “shepherd,” *ROE*.

**Verse 14.** And she sat at the gate of Ena, which is on the road to Timnah. The Hebrew word *ENAIM* ([Hebrew text]) is translated “eyes.” It is therefore not the name of a place, but the meaning is this: She sat at a fork in the road, or at a crossroads, where a traveler must look more carefully to determine which path to take.

**Verse 26.** Judah recognized them and said: “She is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah.” The Hebrew has: “She has been justified from me”—not that she had been righteous, but that, in comparison with him, she had done the lesser evil, seeking children rather than wandering into shameful promiscuity.

**Verse 29.** And behold, his brother came out, and he said: “Why has the partition been broken because of you?” And he called his name Perez. Instead of “partition,” Aquila and Symmachus translated “division,” which in Hebrew is called PHARES ([Hebrew text]). Thus he received the name of “division” because he had divided the membrane of the afterbirth [variant: *secundina*]. Hence the Pharisees too, who separated themselves from the people as though they were righteous, were called “the divided.”

> [Note: Yet the Pharisees did not derive their name from [Hebrew root], meaning “to break apart” or “to shatter,” but from [Hebrew root], meaning “to withdraw, separate, divide,” and so forth.]

**Verse 30.** After this his brother came out, on whose hand was the scarlet thread, and he called his name Zerah. This name is interpreted as “rising” or “east.” Therefore, either because he appeared first, or because many righteous men were descended from him, as is contained in the Book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 2 and following), he was called ZERAH ([Hebrew text]), that is, “rising.”

### Chapter XL

**Verse 1.** After these things, the chief cupbearer of the king of Egypt offended. Where we have “chief cupbearer,” the Hebrew has MASEC ([Hebrew text]), the same word that we earlier read in the name of Abraham’s servant, whom we may call, in ordinary language, a cupbearer. His office should not be considered insignificant, since even today among barbarian kings it is a position of the highest rank to present the cup to the king. Poets too write of Catamithus and Jupiter, saying that he devoted his beloved

> [Note: The older Reginensis manuscript reads “of Catamithus,” without “of Jupiter.” It is well known that Ganymede is meant.]

to this office.

> [Note: “His beloved, etc.” That beloved was the exceedingly infamous Ganymede, son of Tros, a youth of extraordinary beauty, who was carried up to heaven and became Jupiter’s cupbearer. Virgil says of him in *Aeneid* 1: “The honors of the ravished Ganymede.” He calls them “honors” because Ganymede was admitted to the service of the cups, after Hebe, Juno’s daughter, who used to serve Jupiter his drink, had been removed. Horace calls him “blond Ganymede” in *Odes* 4.4; Ovid calls him “Phrygian” in *Metamorphoses* 10. Moreover, the office of cupbearer was held in the highest honor not only among barbarian kings but also among the kings of the Franks. See volume 1, *On the State of France*, page 70. MARTIAN.]

**Verse 10.** And behold, a vine was before me, and on the vine were three branches, and it itself was budding with three branches. The Hebrew expression signifies three shoots and three branches, or runners,

> [Note: Previously the wording was very awkward: “in Hebrew.” Our manuscripts read *Sariagim*, as do the Greek letters *ϹΑΡΥΑΓΥΜ*.]

which they call SARIGIM ([Hebrew text]).

**Verse 16.** And it seemed to me that I was carrying three baskets of *chondrites* on my head. Instead of “three baskets of *chondrites*,” the Hebrew has “three baskets of flour.”

### Chapter XLI

**Verse 2.** And behold, seven cows came up from the river, beautiful to look at,

> [Note: Two manuscripts add by hand: “and choice in their horns, and they grazed in *achi*.”]

choice in flesh, and they were grazing in *achi*. The word ACHI (*Ἄχα*) is written twice in Genesis; it is neither Greek nor Latin. Even the Hebrew itself is corrupt. For it is written *AHU* ([Hebrew text]), that is, “in the marsh.”

> [Note: The author of Ecclesiasticus also uses *Ἄχει* for “marsh” in 40:16. See our note on Job.]

But because among the Hebrews the letters *vau* and *yod* are similar, differing only in size, the translators of the Septuagint rendered *AHU* as *ACHI*. According to their custom, to express the double aspiration of the Hebrew letter *heth*, they joined to it the Greek letter chi (χ).

**Verse 16.** Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying: “Without God no answer of well-being will be given to Pharaoh.” The Hebrew has it differently: “Without me, God will answer Pharaoh’s peace.” Finally, Symmachus, translating more plainly in his customary manner, rendered it: “Not I, but God will answer Pharaoh’s peace.”

**Verse 29.** Behold, seven years of great abundance are coming throughout all the land of Egypt. I am surprised that the Hebrew word SABEE ([Hebrew text]), which above we translated as “abundance” or “satiety” in connection with the well dug last by Isaac’s servants, the Septuagint now most correctly translated there as “oath,” since “oath,” “seven,” “satiety,” and “abundance” can all be understood according to the demands of the context and sequence. In the passages that follow as well, wherever “abundance” is read, the same Hebrew word is written.

**Verse 43.** He cried out before him as a herald and appointed him over all the land of Egypt. For this Aquila translated: “And he cried out in his presence, ‘Kneel!’” Symmachus, interpreting the Hebrew expression itself, said: “And he cried before him, ABRECH” ([Hebrew text]). Hence I think that what should be understood is not so much “herald,” or “kneeling”—which may be taken as a gesture of greeting or worship toward Joseph—as what the Hebrews report,

> [Note: The wording seems to have been taken from Origen, who, according to Montfaucon, has the following in the Royal *Catenae*: “The Hebrew has *Abrech*, which properly means ‘tender father,’ and appropriately so. For, being tender in age, he displayed to the Egyptians, as a father, a saving authority. The word signifies nothing else than kneeling, for the herald’s cry is clear.”]

namely, that it means “tender father.” For *AB* ([Hebrew text]) means “father,” and *RECH* ([Hebrew text]) means “delicate” or “very tender.” Scripture thus indicates that, in wisdom, he was the father of all, but in age he was a very tender young man and boy.

**Verse 45.** Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Saphaneth Phanee, and gave him Aseneth, daughter of Potiphar the priest of Heliopolis, as a wife. Although this name in Hebrew means “finder of hidden things,” since it is an Egyptian name, its meaning must be considered according to that language. In Egyptian, therefore, SAPHANETH PHANEE ([Hebrew text]) is interpreted as

> [Note: Jerome cleverly refers these words to an Egyptian origin, although nothing in them is without the flavor of a Hebrew etymology. According to that etymology, the common interpretation among all is that *Psonthom-Phanech* means “interpreter of obscure things,” or one who has clearly explained hidden matters. Bernard, however, in his notes on Josephus, cites two ancient biblical manuscripts supporting Jerome’s explanation: an Arabic Pentateuch copied long ago by an Egyptian hand, whose marginal note interprets *Ψονθομφανέχ* in Arabic as “savior of the world”; and the Greek Octateuch of Oxford College, in which *Ψονθομφανήχ, ὅ ἐστ σωτὴρ τοῦ κόσμου* means “Psonthom-Phanech, that is, savior of the world.” See also Le Moyne, *Varia Sacra*, p. 102. In our manuscripts it is read *Fanech fane*, and in Greek *Spomothon phanech*. —“Saphaneth Phanee.” We have discussed this name at length in our *Apology for Jerome*. See above, the commentary on the book *Hebrew Names*, chapter 2. MARTIAN.]

“Savior of the world,” or, as the Septuagint wished to render it, *Psomthom-Phanech*, because he saved the whole earth from the impending destruction of famine. It should be noted, however, that he once took as his wife the daughter of his former master and purchaser,

> [Note: The older Reginensis manuscript reads: “of his former purchaser,” omitting “master.” Above, in chapter 37, we said that the opinion identifying as one and the same man Joseph’s master and afterward his father-in-law, Potiphar, was derived by the Hebrews from an apocryphal book, according to whose view Jerome speaks; the opinion is of very doubtful reliability. Saint Augustine, in question 136, offers many arguments proving that another, different man existed. These may be consulted there. The letters of the name Potiphar are also different in the Hebrew text from those forming the name of the other, or first, man. Joseph’s master is written [Hebrew text]; this man, whether his father-in-law, is written with two words and with an additional letter at the end, [Hebrew text].]

who at that time was the priest of Heliopolis. For it was not permitted for the priests of that idol to serve without being eunuchs, which confirms the truth of the suspicion of the Hebrews concerning him that we mentioned earlier.

**Verses 50 and following.** Joseph had two sons born to him before the years of famine came, whom Aseneth, daughter of Potiphar the priest of Heliopolis, bore to him.
