Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh, because, he said, “God has made me forget all my labors and all my father’s household.” He called the name of the second Ephraim, because, he said, “God has made me grow in the land of my humiliation.”

Observe, in view of the question that will shortly be raised concerning Joseph’s sons, that before the time of famine, when Jacob entered Egypt, Joseph had only two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. He called Manasseh by a name derived from “forgetting” his labors; for that is how “forgetting” is expressed in Hebrew. Ephraim was so called because God had increased him. From this word too, “increase” is transferred into our language.

### Chapter XLIII

**Verse 11.** Take gifts to the man, something of resin, honey, incense, and *stacte*, pistachios, and nuts—or, as Aquila and Symmachus translated, almonds. We have included this passage so that we may know that wherever our manuscripts have “incense,” the Hebrew has NECOTHA ([Hebrew text]), which Aquila translated as “storax.” Hence the “house of Nechota” mentioned in Isaiah 39:2 is most clearly understood as a storeroom of incense or storax, in which various spices had been stored.

**Verse 32.** And they drank, and became drunk with him. It is an idiom of the Hebrew language to use “drunkenness” for “satiety,” as in the passage: “At its showers it will be drunk as it sprouts” (Psalm 64:11), clearly referring to the earth watered by rains.

> [Note: Our manuscripts read “it will rejoice”; some also read “his” instead of “its.” In fact, “it will be drunk” is found in none of the ancient Latin translations.]

### Chapter XLIV

**Verse 2.** Put the silver of each one into the mouth of his sack, and put my silver cup into the sack of the younger. Instead of “sack,” the Hebrew has “leather bag” or “pouch.” Instead of *condy*, that is, “cup”—which we also read in Isaiah 51:17—Aquila translated “goblet,” and Symmachus “bowl.”

> [Note: “My silver *condy*.” *Condy*, written in Greek as *Κόνδυ*, means a Persian cup among Greek grammarians. Hesychius says it is a barbarian cup; Nicomachus regarded it as Persian; Athenaeus, an Asian cup holding ten *cotylae*. MARTIAN. —Diodorus explains *condy* as *ἁπλοποτήριον*, “a simple cup.” Menander, in *The Flatterer*, says that it is an Asian vessel; Nicomachus, cited by Athenaeus in Book XI, chapter 8, says that it is Persian. Reland, part 1 of *Miscellaneous Dissertations*, explains the Indic origin of the name.]

### Chapter XLV

**Verses 9–10.** Go down to me, then; do not delay, and you shall dwell in the land of Goshen of Arabia. “Of Arabia” has been added here; it is not found in the Hebrew books. Hence the error became widespread that the land of Goshen was in Arabia. Now, if, as it is written in our books, GESEM ([Hebrew text]) is spelled with a final *m*, a reading which I by no means approve,

> [Note: Goshen means “rain.” In the Septuagint we read, with a final *m*, *ἐν γῇ Γεσὲμ*, “in the land of Gesem.” The name Goshen was also written in this form in the Latin copies that Jerome calls “our books,” namely, the Latin copies used by the Western churches in the centuries closer to Christ, before the version derived from the Hebrew source by Jerome. MARTIAN. —It should rather be written “Gesen,” with *n*, corresponding to the Hebrew [Hebrew text]. Nor was it only the Latin books that corruptly pronounced it with *m*; the Greek books too have *Γεσὲμ*. It should be noted that in one Complutensian manuscript the added word *Ἀραβίας* is absent.]

it signifies a land drenched with rain; for GESEM ([Hebrew text]) means “rain.”

**Verse 17.** Pharaoh said to Joseph: “Tell your brothers, ‘Do this: Load your wagons and go to the land of Canaan.’” Instead of “wagons,” which the Septuagint and Theodotion translated as *τὰ φορεῖα*,

> [Note: My manuscript and one of the Reginensis manuscripts read *ΤΑ ΠΟΡΙΑ*, as is also noted in other copies in the recent edition of the Septuagint; another reading is *Πορεῖα*. *Πόρια*, or *πορεῖα*, were carts or vehicles for transporting something; hence *στρατιωτικὰ πόρια* were vessels for transporting soldiers. I think the older Reginensis manuscript should also be read this way, although it has *ΘΑ ΘΥΩΡΥΑ*, since I have discovered that its copyist took the letter Π in the exemplar for the two letters ΤΙ, which he then consistently rendered as Θ and Υ. For a long time now, however, the Septuagint has read *τὰ φορεῖα*.]

the others translated “beasts of burden.”

**Verse 21.** And he gave them provisions for the journey. The word SEDA ([Hebrew text]), which all translators here uniformly rendered *ἐπισιτισμὸν*, that is, “provisions” or “food supplies,” also occurs in the Psalter. Where our copies read, “Blessing his widow, I will bless her” (Psalm 131:15)—although in many manuscripts, instead of “widow,” that is, *χήρα*, some read *θήραν*—the Hebrew has SEDA ([Hebrew text]), that is, “Blessing his provisions, I will bless them.” Now *θήραν* can mean “hunting” more readily than “grain,” although it is customary among the Egyptians also to call meal *θήραν*, which is now corruptly called *atheran*.

> [Note: Jerome himself translated the passage in his version from the Hebrew as: “Blessing his hunting, I will bless it.” The Pseudo-Jerome says concerning this passage: “Instead of *widow*, that is, *χήρα*, both the Hebrew books and the Septuagint themselves have *θήραν*; but because of the novelty of the word and the change of one letter, it gradually prevailed that *χήρα* should be read instead of *θήρα*, especially because the poor followed in the next verse. Symmachus and Aquila translated *θήρα* as ‘provisions.’”]

> [Note: They now corruptly call it *atheran*. In certain manuscripts this word is corrupted to *Catheran*, and in another to *Athertin*; in the very old Colbertinus manuscript it is written in Greek as *ΗΘΗΡΑΝ*. Let the learned in the Egyptian language determine which reading among the variants should be preferred. MARTIAN. —Martianaeus found *Catheran*, *Athertin*, and the Greek *ΗΘΗΡΑΝ* in his manuscripts, leaving to scholars of Egyptian the question of which reading should be preferred. The printed reading, however, is excellent, and all our manuscripts confirm it; one of them equally well has the Greek *ΑΘΗΡΑΝ*. Cassian, once an Egyptian ascetic, uses the same word, *Atheram*, in *Conferences* 15.10, where he understands it as a lentil stew. According to Hesychius, *ἀθήρα* or *ἄθαρα* is a food customarily prepared by Egyptians from wheat and milk. Pliny too, in Book XXII, chapter 25, mentions the Egyptian *athara*.]

### Chapter XLVI

**Verses 26 and following.** Therefore all the persons who entered Egypt with Jacob, who came forth from his loins, excluding the wives of Jacob’s sons, numbered sixty-six persons. The sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, numbered nine persons. Thus all the persons who entered Egypt with Jacob numbered seventy-five.

There is no doubt that, apart from Joseph and his sons, sixty-six persons who came forth from Jacob’s loins entered Egypt. The number is confirmed both by the gradual reckoning of each individual and by the Hebrew books. But where we read in the Septuagint, “The sons of Joseph who were born to him in Egypt numbered nine persons,” we should know that the Hebrew has “two,” not “nine.” Ephraim and Manasseh were born of Aseneth, daughter of Potiphar, in Egypt before Jacob entered Egypt and before the famine began.

Moreover, the passage we read above—“The sons of Manasseh were Machir, whom his Aramaean concubine bore to him, and Machir begot Gilead; and the sons of Ephraim, Manasseh’s brother, were Shuthelah and Tahan;

> [Note: “Shuthelah and Tahan.” Earlier printed books corruptly read *Ethaan* instead of “and Tahan,” and then *Edom* instead of *Edem*. Although the Roman edition of the Septuagint has *Ἐδὼμ* here, the Alexandrian manuscript reads *Ἐδὲμ*, in agreement with the manuscript copies of Saint Jerome. MARTIAN.]

and the sons of Shuthelah were Edem”—was added, since it is described as having occurred later, by anticipation.

> [Note: In certain Greek manuscripts this passage is marked with obeli; Montfaucon mentions one such manuscript, the Coislinian.]

For at the time when Jacob entered Egypt, Ephraim and Manasseh were not of such an age that they could have fathered sons. It is therefore clear that all the persons who entered Egypt from Jacob’s loins numbered seventy: sixty-six entered later and found [variant: “begot”] in Egypt three persons—Joseph, namely, together with his two sons—and Jacob himself was the seventieth.

So that no one may think that we are speaking against the authority of Scripture, the Septuagint translators also rendered the passage in Deuteronomy 10:22 as saying that Jacob entered Egypt with seventy persons.

> [Note: One Roman copy now reads it as Jerome found it in his own copy: “seventy persons.”]

If anyone therefore opposes our view, he will make Scripture contradict itself. For the same Septuagint translators who here said that seventy-five persons entered Egypt with Joseph and his descendants by anticipation (*πρόληψιν*) stated in Deuteronomy that only seventy entered.

If, on the other hand, someone objects that in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 7, Stephen is said in his speech to the people to have declared that seventy-five persons entered Egypt, the answer is easy. Saint Luke, who was the historian of these events, could not, when sending the volume of the Acts of the Apostles to the Gentiles, write anything contrary to the Scripture that had already been circulated among the nations. At that time, the authority of the Septuagint translators was certainly held in greater esteem than that of Luke, who was unknown, insignificant, and regarded among the nations as a man of little authority.

This should be observed generally: whenever the holy Apostles or apostolic men speak to the people, they usually make use of testimonies that had already been circulated among the nations. Some, however, maintain that Luke the Evangelist was ignorant of the Hebrew letters because he was a proselyte.

> [Note: Jerome was so far from holding this opinion himself that, on the contrary, after assigning to Luke from his earliest beginnings a native Hebrew speech, he says in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 7, that Luke was not ignorant of the Greek language, which he had acquired through study. Nor should it be doubted that he had already been a Jew before giving his allegiance to Christ, especially if one accepts the ancient authorities—Origen, or a certain Adamantius, in the *Dialogues against the Marcionites*, and Epiphanius, *Heresies* 51.11—who say that he belonged to the number of the seventy disciples. I pass over the Hebraisms in his writings, which men of considerable learning have observed.]

**Verse 28.** Judah he sent before him to Joseph, to meet him at the city of Heroum in the land of Rameses. In the Hebrew there is neither the city of Heroum nor the land of Rameses, but only Goshen. Some Jews assert

> [Note: He should have said: “They dream”; they are men utterly ignorant of geography. The region of Goshen is the same as the land of Rameses, which derives its name from that city, as is clear from the following chapter, verse 11. The Septuagint rightly has “Heroum” in its own sense. According to Ptolemy, that city was Heropolis, situated at the farthest shore of the Arabian Gulf, which was also called the Gulf of Heropolis.]

that Goshen is now called Thebaid. They also maintain that the passage which follows—“He gave them possession of the best land of Egypt in Rameses”—refers to the district once called Arsinoites.

### Chapter XLVII

**Verse 31.** And he said to him, “Swear to me.” And he swore to him; and Israel worshiped toward the head of his staff. Here some falsely pretend that Jacob worshiped the top of Joseph’s scepter, supposedly honoring his son by worshiping his authority, whereas the Hebrew reads very differently: “Israel worshiped at the head of the bed.” After his son had sworn to him and he was confident that the request he had made would be fulfilled, he worshiped God toward the head of his bed.

For this holy man, devoted to God and beloved by God,

> [Note: The Reginensis manuscripts read “a man devoted to God and beloved by God.” A little later they read: “without any impediment to prayer,” and so forth. Compare Saint Augustine, question 162, on this passage in Genesis.]

weighed down by old age, had his bed positioned in such a way that even while lying down his posture was ready for prayer without any difficulty.

### Chapter XLVIII

**Verse 1.** Joseph was told, “Behold, your father is ill.” And he took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, with him. This demonstrates what we said above: Joseph had only two sons at that time, Ephraim and Manasseh. For if, many years later, when his father Jacob was dying, he brought only two sons to receive the blessing, then certainly, at the entry of his father and brothers, he could not have had grandchildren by them, since his sons, still little children and nursing infants, had not yet been able to beget children.

> [Note: I would prefer to correct the text from an older Reginensis manuscript to read “at that time,” rather than “in those places.” This is Jerome’s meaning, as the entire following context makes clear.]

> [Note: Martianaeus left *quieverant* (“had rested”), perhaps through a printer’s error; we silently correct several such instances above.]

> [Note: Martianaeus also corrects the reading to “at the departure of the father,” against the manuscripts and the more accurate printed books, as well as Jerome’s own text.]

**Verse 2.** Israel strengthened himself and sat upon the bed. I do not know why the Septuagint translators rendered the same word differently in different places. I state this confidently: the very word META, which they translated here as “bed,” they previously used, where we said that Jacob worshiped, to designate a staff rather than a bed.

**Verse 5.** And now, behold, your two sons who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt are mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine like Reuben and Simeon. But those whom you beget after them shall be yours. They shall be called by the name of their brothers.

If anyone was uncertain whether seventy persons of the sons of Israel entered Egypt, and whether Joseph at the time Jacob entered had not nine but only two sons, this chapter confirms it. Jacob himself says that Joseph had two sons, not nine.

When he says, “Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine like Reuben and Simeon,” he means that just as Reuben and Simeon would become two tribes and would be called by their own names, so Ephraim and Manasseh would become two tribes, produce two peoples, and inherit the promised land in the same way as his own sons. “The remaining sons,” he says, whom you beget after my death, “shall be yours,” showing that at that time they had not yet been born.

**Verse 6.** They shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance. “They shall not,” he says, “receive land separately, nor have their own allotments as the other tribes do; rather, within the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh they shall be mingled as appendages of the people.”

**Verse 22.** And I gave you Shechem, a choice portion above your brothers [variant: “I give”],

> [Note: Our manuscripts and many others preserved by Martianaeus read: “above your brothers, more than your brothers, which …”]

which I took from the hands of the Amorites by my sword and my bow. “Shechem” has been declined according to Greek and Latin usage. In Hebrew it is called SICHEM, as the Evangelist John also testifies (4:5), although the corrupt reading “Sychar” has become established.

> [Note: Learned men rather judge that this was deliberately done by the Jews as an insult to the Samaritans. The error did not arise in the Evangelist’s manuscript; instead, the name had already become commonly inflected in this way, with another letter of the same organ maliciously substituted for [Hebrew text], *Secem*, so that it became [Hebrew text], *Sichar*, meaning “lie” or “falsehood.” They did this to reproach the Samaritans for the worship of idols that they had established in that city, the metropolis of their people.]

That city is now the Samaritan city of Neapolis. Since SICHEM ([Hebrew text]) is translated in Hebrew as “shoulder,” he made an elegant allusion to the name by saying, “I will give you one shoulder.” For instead of “a special portion,” that is, *ἐξαιρέτῳ*, the Hebrew has “one.”

> [Note: In an older Reginensis manuscript the word AHID, meaning “one,” is added; I consider this more correct. In Hebrew it is [Hebrew text], pronounced *AHAD* or *ACHAD*.]

When he says that he possessed it by bow and sword, he calls the bow and sword “justice,” by which, though a foreigner and resident alien, he deserved to be delivered from danger after the killing of Shechem and Hamor. For, as we read above, he feared that the neighboring towns and settlements would rise against him because of the destruction of the allied city (Genesis 34), but the Lord did not allow them to harm him.

Or it should certainly be understood in this way: “I will give you Shechem, which I purchased through my strength,” that is, with the money I acquired through great labor and exertion. By saying “above your brothers,” he shows that he gave it to the tribe of Joseph without casting lots. For Joseph was buried in that same place, and his mausoleum is still visible there today.

## (Chapter 49.—Verse 3)

[Note: Here begins the little work entitled *The Blessings of the Sons of Jacob*, composed almost entirely in the same words as the exposition of Jerome that follows, though also assembled from excerpts of other Fathers, Augustine and Gregory; we present it in the Appendix to this volume.]

Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sons, hard to endure and hard in insolence and injury; like water, do not boil over. For you climbed upon your father’s bed. Then you violated the couch when you climbed up.

In Hebrew it is written: “Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the first portion among my children. Greater in bearing, and greater in strength. You poured yourself out like water; do not go further. For you climbed upon your father’s couch and defiled the bed in your ascent.”

The meaning is this: You are my firstborn, the foremost among my children, and according to the order of your birth you ought to have received the inheritance that was due by right to the firstborn, as well as the priesthood and the kingship. This is shown by “bearing” the burden and by very great strength. But because you sinned and, like water that cannot be contained in a vessel, poured yourself out through the impulse of desire, I therefore command you not to sin any further and to remain among the number of your brothers, paying the penalty of your sin because you lost the rank of the firstborn.

[Note: Two manuscripts of the Queen’s collection and three others in Martianaeus, with which the older editions also agree, read “and you sat.” But this passage had previously also suffered from faulty punctuation.]

[Note: The printed editions have “paying the penalty from sin”; certain manuscripts have “mourning” instead of “paying.”]

## (Verses 5 and 6)

Simeon and Levi, brothers, have completed the iniquity of their scheme; may my soul not enter into their counsel, and may my inmost being not join their assembly, because in their fury they killed men, and in their desire they hamstrung an ox.

[Note: “May my inmost being not join.” In the same sense, two manuscripts read: “May my heart not join.”]

Necessity compels us, in accordance with the purpose of this work, to repeat at greater length matters that differ from the Hebrew truth. For there it reads: “Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of iniquity are their arms.” Into their secret counsel, let my soul not enter; and in their assembly, let my glory not be desolate,” because in their fury they killed a man and in their lust they pierced a wall (Genesis 34).

[Note: “May my glory not be desolate.” Several manuscript codices read this way. One Corbeiensis has: “May my glory not be dissolved.” Earlier printed books have “may it be destroyed.” In Hebrew is *tehhad*, from *jahhad*, which means “to unite.” Thus the translators of the Septuagint read *tehhar*, because of the similarity between *resh* and *daleth*; hence their “may it not join,” or “may it not contend.” —Older printed editions have “may it not be dissolved.” The fact that they translated “inmost being” for “glory” arises from the twofold meaning of the Hebrew word, which signifies both “inmost being” and “glory,” although “glory” is always written with a different form. “May it not be desolate” is also not entirely satisfactory; perhaps the negative particle should be removed, so as to agree with the Hebrew, where the opposite sense is found: “may it not be united,” the Vulgate having “may it not be.” Accordingly, under the guise of an assertion, it should read “may it be desolate” or “may it be dissolved.”]

This means that it was not their counsel that they killed Shechem and Hamor, allied men, and that, contrary to the law of peace and friendship, they shed innocent blood; carried away, as though by a kind of fury and cruelty, they overthrew the walls of a foreign city.

[Note: One manuscript of the Queen’s collection reads: “It was not their counsel that they killed Shechem,” and so forth.]

Hence he continues and says:

## (Verse 7)

Cursed be their fury, because it was insolent, and their anger, because it was harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.

Levi did not receive a separate inheritance; rather, throughout all the territories he had only a few cities for habitation. Concerning Simeon, it is written in the Book of Joshua (Joshua 19) that he likewise did not obtain his own allotment, but received a portion from the tribe of Judah. In the Books of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 4), however, it is written more explicitly that, when he had multiplied and had no place of possession, he went out into the wilderness.

[Note: We have supplied the name of the books, which was lacking, from the manuscripts. Or perhaps, as Victorius reads, it should simply be “in Chronicles.”]

Some interpret prophetically the men who were killed as the Apostles, and the hamstrung ox as Christ, hamstrung by the Pharisees.

[Note: Tertullian, above all, gives a sufficiently clear interpretation in *Against the Jews*, chapter 10: “The same will also be found elsewhere, where the ox appears in the same Scripture (Genesis 49:6), when Jacob extends the blessing over Simeon and Levi; he prophesies concerning the scribes and Pharisees, for from them their census is derived. Spiritually it is interpreted in this way: ‘Simeon and Levi completed iniquity according to their sect,’ by which, namely, they persecuted Christ,” and so forth. See also Origen, *Homily 17 on Genesis*.]

## (Verse 8)

Judah, your brothers shall praise you.

Because *Judah* is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” it is consequently written: “Judah, your brothers shall confess to you,” or, “your brothers shall praise you.”

## (Verse 9)

The sons of your father shall worship you.

Judah is a lion’s cub; from the branch, my son, you have risen. He lies down like a lion and like a lion’s cub. Who will rouse him?

Although this contains a great mystery concerning Christ, nevertheless, according to the literal sense, it is prophesied—or interpreted—that kings would be born from Judah through the line of David and that all the tribes would worship him. For he does not say, “the sons of your mother,” but “the sons of your father.”

What follows, “from the branch, my son,” has in Hebrew: “From the captivity, my son, you have risen,” to show that he would lead captive peoples away; and, according to the more sacred understanding, that he ascended on high and led captivity captive (Psalm 67). Or, as I think better, captivity signifies the Passion and ascent signifies the Resurrection.

## (Verse 11)

Binding his foal to the vine, and the foal of his she-ass with a cord.

In Hebrew it reads: “Binding his foal to the vine, and to Sorek, my son, his she-ass.” This evidently means that he joined the foal of the she-ass on which Jesus sat—that is, the Gentile people—to the Apostles’ vine, who are from the Jews. And to Sorek, that is, the choice vine, he bound the she-ass on which he sat, the Church gathered from the nations.

When he says “my son,” he makes an apostrophe to Judah himself, indicating that Christ would accomplish all these things.

[Note: “Apostrophe,” and so forth. Two manuscript codices read the Greek *apostrophēn* (ἀποστροφήν).]

This too must be understood: where we read, “Binding his foal to the vine,” the Hebrew may be read not as “his foal” but as “his city.”

[Note: The same letters are used to write both “foal” and “city,” although the Masoretes call the foal *hair* and the city *hir*.]

[Note: “His city.” The Hebrew has *iro*, which signifies either “his foal” or “his city.”]

According to the same meaning, the Church is indicated in other words, concerning which it is written elsewhere: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:15); and, “The river’s stream makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45:5).

## (Verses 14 and 15)

Issachar desired what is good, resting between the allotted portions, and seeing that rest is good and the land fertile; he placed his shoulder under labor and became a farming man.

In Hebrew it is written: “Issachar, a bony ass, lying between the boundaries and seeing that rest is good and that the land is beautiful; he inclined his shoulder to bear and became a servant paying tribute.”

[Note: The Hebrew has “bony ass.” The Septuagint translators, through a customary change of letters, read “he desired,” and so forth.]

Because he had said above concerning Zebulun that he would possess the shores of the great sea and would touch Sidon and the other cities of Phoenicia, he now returns to the inland province and, since Issachar was going to possess a region adjoining Naphtali, the most beautiful region in Galilee, makes him an inhabitant by his blessing.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “which is adjacent.”]

He calls him a bony ass and one devoted to carrying burdens because he would labor greatly in cultivating the land and transporting to the sea the burdens produced within his borders, while also conveying tribute to the kings.

[Note: In one manuscript of the Queen’s collection: “He labored greatly in cultivating the land and the sea, and in transporting what was produced within his borders.” In another, only the word “burdens” is missing.]

The Hebrews say that, metaphorically, this signifies that, meditating on the holy Scriptures day and night, he devoted himself to labor; therefore all the tribes serve him, as though bringing gifts to a teacher.

[Note: “The holy Scriptures.” The author of the *Commentary on the Song of Deborah* agrees with Jerome, saying: “In the Book of Genesis Issachar is called strong because of the strength of the Law, since he carried the Law upon his shoulder and supplied the other tribes with tribute—that is, with the teaching of the Law.” See the Appendix to this volume.]

## (Verses 16 and following)

Dan shall judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel.

May Dan become a serpent on the road, a horned snake on the path, biting the horse’s hooves so that its rider falls backward. I shall await your salvation, Lord.

Samson, judge in Israel, was from the tribe of Dan. Therefore he says: Now, seeing in the spirit your Nazirite Samson growing his hair and triumphing over his enemies after slaughtering them—so that, in the likeness of a serpent and a horned snake lying in wait along the roads, he permits no one to pass through the land of Israel—but even if some rash man, trusting in his own strength as in the speed of a horse, should wish to escape him and plunder the land like a brigand, he will not be able to do so.

He speaks throughout by the metaphor of the serpent and the horseman. Seeing, therefore, so strong a Nazirite of yours—who himself also died because of a prostitute and, by dying, killed our enemies—I thought, O God, that he was himself your Christ, your Son. But because he died and did not rise again, and because Israel was once more led captive, another Savior of the world and of my race must be awaited: “until he comes to whom it has been reserved,” and he himself will be the expectation of the nations.

## (Verse 19)

Gad, a raiding band, shall raid him, and he shall raid the heel.

We have translated according to the Hebrew. But where we have put “raiding band,” *gedud* is written, so that it alludes to the name Gad, which can be expressed more precisely by the Greek *euzōnos* (εὔζωνος), that is, “well-girded” or “swiftly equipped.”

[Note: It had incorrectly been written *euzonos*. See the preceding book, *On the Names in Genesis and Exodus*.]

The whole passage means that Gad, returning after fourteen years with Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh to the children left beyond the Jordan in their possession, found a great battle against them by the neighboring nations and, after defeating the enemies, fought bravely. Read the Book of Joshua (Joshua 13) and Chronicles (1 Chronicles 5).

[Note: “Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh,” which Alcuin had previously read with greater elegance: “Gad, and so forth, likewise in the nominative; Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh.”]

I do not deny that there are many mysteries in the blessings of the patriarchs, but they do not belong to the present little work.

[Note: “The mysteries of the patriarchs.” He passes over the blessing of Asher because in it there is no disagreement between the Hebrew source and the Greek copies of the Septuagint.]

## (Verse 21)

Naphtali is a loosened shoot, giving beauty in its growth.

In Hebrew it is written: “Naphtali is an irrigated field, giving beautiful words.” This signifies either that the warm waters arise in that tribe or that the region above Lake Gennesaret is irrigated by the flow of the Jordan.

[Note: The older manuscript of the Queen’s collection more correctly has “Naphtali,” corresponding to the Hebrew. But the other manuscript is not equally correct in what follows, where it reads “giving words of beauty.”]

The Hebrews, however, wish this to be prophesied on account of Tiberias, which seemed to possess knowledge of the Law: an irrigated field and beautiful words.

Moreover, where we read “an irrigated field” and the Septuagint translators have *stelechos anemenon* (στέλεχος ἀνειμένον), that is, “a loosened shoot,” the Hebrew reads *AJALA SLUAA* (), which can also be translated “a released hind,” indicating, through seasonal crops, the speed of a more fertile land.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript and the better manuscript of the Queen’s collection more correctly give *sluah*, whereas Martianaeus has *seluah*. Among the ancients, *shewa*, or the very weak *e*, scarcely ever has a sound at the beginning of a word.]

But it is better if we refer everything to the teaching of the Savior, since he taught there above all, as it is also written in the Gospel.

[Note: One manuscript reads “which he taught there to the greatest extent.”]

## (Verses 22 and following)

Joseph is a growing son, a growing son beside a spring; the daughters, walking with measured step, proceed along the wall.

They embittered him, contended with him, and were angry against him, possessing arrows. His bow rested in strength, and the bonds of his hands were broken by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob. From there the stone of Israel shall be nourished by the God of your father—and the rest.

Because the Septuagint translators differ in many places, we have expressed the passage according to the Hebrew rather than according to their interpretation.

The meaning of the chapter is this: O Joseph, who are so called either because God increased you for me or because you were destined to become greater among your brothers—for the tribe of Ephraim was extremely strong, as we read in the Books of Kings and Chronicles—O, I say, my son Joseph, so beautiful that the whole crowd of Egyptian girls looked out at you from the walls, towers, and windows: your brothers envied you and provoked you to anger, bearing arrows of jealousy and wounded by darts of envy.

But you placed your bow and your weapons of war in God, who is a strong defender. Your bonds, with which your brothers bound you, were loosed and broken by him, so that from your seed the tribe of Ephraim might arise, strong, steadfast, and, like a harder stone, unconquerable, also ruling over the ten tribes of Israel.

[Note: Instead of “bonds,” three of our manuscripts have “arms.” The Vulgate retains both: “the bonds of the arms,” and so forth. But the Hebrew has only “arms,” which should also be preferred here.]

## (Verse 27)

Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will still eat, and in the evening he will give food.

[Note: The manuscripts of Metz and the Queen’s collection, although this is an unmistakable prophecy concerning the Apostle Paul—that in his youth, and so forth.]

It is evident to everyone that this is a very clear prophecy concerning the Apostle Paul: in his youth he persecuted the Church, while in his old age he became a preacher of the Gospel.

[Note: Victorius adds “his own.” Among the many Fathers, especially the Latin Fathers, who interpret Jacob’s oracle as referring to Paul the Apostle, born from the tribe of Benjamin, it is best to hear the remarkably clear testimony of Tertullian in Book 5, chapter 1, of *Against Marcion*: “For me, Genesis also formerly promised Paul. Among those figures and prophetic blessings over his sons, when Jacob turned to Benjamin he said: ‘Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning you will still eat, and in the evening he will give food.’ He foresaw that Paul would arise from the tribe of Benjamin: a ravenous wolf eating in the morning, that is, devastating the Lord’s flocks in the first period of his life as a persecutor of the Churches; thereafter giving food in the evening, that is, when his life was already declining, nourishing Christ’s sheep as teacher of the nations.”]

But in Hebrew it reads as follows: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf, or one who captures; in the morning he will eat prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils.”

The Hebrews explain it in this way: The altar on which the sacrifices were offered, and at the base of which the blood of the victims was poured, was in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. This, they say, signifies that the priests sacrifice victims in the morning and in the evening divide what has been conferred upon them by the people according to the Law. They interpret the ravenous, bloodthirsty wolf as the altar, and the division of the spoils as referring to the priests who, serving the altar, live from the altar.

[Note: The words “bloodthirsty wolf” are absent from two of our manuscripts. Shortly afterward, Alcuin seems to have read “divider” more correctly instead of “division.”]

[Col. 1009]

# Commentary of the Holy Presbyter Eusebius Hieronymus of Stridon on Ecclesiastes, to Paula and Eustochium (C)

[Note: “The words of Ecclesiastes,” and so forth. All the manuscripts read *Ecclesiastes* in place of *Ecclesiastae*, as we have already said in the appropriate place in Volume I of our edition. —Martianaeus.]

[Note: In Martianaeus’s edition this is entitled “The Preface of Saint Jerome on Ecclesiastes,” with the following note appended: “Manuscript Codex 4436 of the Colbert Library has this inscription in illuminated letters: ‘Here begins the Prologue of Saint Jerome the Presbyter on Ecclesiastes, addressed to Paula and Eustochium, with good fortune. He first began it at Rome and later completed it at Bethlehem.’” —Editor.]

[Note: We have examined this entire book against four manuscript codices: two Palatine manuscripts marked with the numbers 79 and 175, one Vatican manuscript numbered 318, and finally our own private manuscript, which we keep at home and have already said is of especially good quality. Since Albinus Flaccus Alcuin, as Quercetanus writes, copied almost word for word this Commentary of Jerome and incorporated it into his own work—and since Alcuin was both an ancient author, from the eighth century, and had access to an ancient and sufficiently corrected copy of Jerome—we have also compared his text in its entirety and regularly report better readings from it.]

## Preface

[Col. 1009] 381–382

I remember that nearly five years ago, when I was still at Rome and was reading Ecclesiastes to the holy Blesilla in order to provoke her to despise this present age and to regard as worthless everything she saw in the world, she asked me to explain obscure matters in the manner of a little commentary, so that she could understand what she was reading without me.

Therefore, since she was taken from us by a sudden death while our work was still being prepared, and since we did not deserve, Paula and Eustochium, to have such a companion in our life, I was then struck dumb by so great a wound. Now, situated at Bethlehem, a more august city, and mindful of her, I return to you what I owe.

[Note: “Now, situated at Bethlehem, a more august city,” and so forth. Very many manuscripts and all the printed books read: “Now, situated at Bethlehem, namely in the smaller city.” But “smaller” was inserted through the ignorance of ancient and modern scribes who, unfamiliar with or forgetful of Jerome’s expressions, did not know that the holy teacher called Bethlehem a city more august than Rome. Therefore, so that no doubt may remain about the reading restored by us on the authority of the oldest copies, learned readers should remember that it is written as follows in the Preface to the book of Didymus *On the Holy Spirit*, which Jerome translated into Latin: “The song which I could not sing in a foreign land, here, challenged by you in Judea, I murmur, judging the place much more august which gave birth to the Savior of the world than that which gave birth to the murderer of his brother.” —Martianaeus.]

In briefly reminding you of this, I say that I followed the authority of no one, but that, translating from the Hebrew, I adapted myself more closely to the custom of the Septuagint translators—at least in those matters that did not differ greatly from the Hebrew.

[Note: One Palatine manuscript reads “differed”; shortly afterward it reads “I should deter the zeal.”]

At times I also remembered Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, so that I would neither deter the reader’s zeal by excessive novelty nor, on the other hand, contrary to my conscience, abandon the source of truth and pursue the little streams of human opinions.

[Note: “At times I also remembered Aquila,” and so forth. A recent writer presses his trivial arguments from this passage with excessive incompetence, attempting to prove that Jerome, in his Latin translation of the sacred Scriptures from the Hebrew sources, frequently followed Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion. What Jerome said here by way of preface to the reader concerning his Commentary on Ecclesiastes, that incompetent chronologer attempts to apply to the Latin version of all the books of Scripture. Yet he has not learned what is known among all educated people: namely, that Jerome produced a new translation of the Bible for the Church from the Hebrew source much later than he published his Commentary on Ecclesiastes. —Martianaeus.]

## Commentary

[Col. 1011]

### (Chapter 1)

The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem.

The Scriptures very clearly teach that Solomon was called by three names: “the peaceful one,” that is, *Solomon* (); and *Ididia* (), that is, “beloved of the Lord”; and what is now called *Coeleth* (), that is, “Ecclesiastes.”

[Note: The same manuscripts of ours, along with most of the printed copies and formerly Alcuin, have “Idida,” which properly is the name of Josiah’s mother (2 Kings 22:1), instead of “Ididia” or “Jedidiah,” Solomon’s surname (2 Kings 22:25). More elegantly Alcuin has: “Solomon, that is, the peaceful one, and Jedidiah, that is,” and so forth.]

“Ecclesiastes” is called in Greek one who gathers an assembly, that is, a church; we may call him a public speaker, because he speaks to the people, and his speech is directed not specifically to one person but generally to everyone.

The names “peaceful one” and “beloved of the Lord” were given to him because there was peace in his kingdom and because the Lord loved him. The forty-fourth and seventy-first Psalms are also prefaced with the titles “of the beloved” and “of the peaceful one.”

[Note: “Although they pertain to the prophecy of Christ,” and so forth. Several manuscript copies have: “Although they contain mysteries pertaining to the prophecy of Christ and the Church, nevertheless,” and so forth.]

Although these exceed Solomon’s prosperity and power insofar as they pertain to the prophecy of Christ and the Church, historically they were nevertheless written concerning Solomon.

Accordingly, in keeping with the number of his names, he published three books: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs.

In Proverbs he teaches the child, instructing him, as it were, by maxims concerning his duties. Hence the address to his son is frequently repeated.

In Ecclesiastes he instructs a mature man, so that he will not think anything in the affairs of the world permanent, but will regard everything we see as perishable and brief.

Finally, when the man has been perfected and prepared by trampling upon the world, he joins him to the embraces of the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs. For unless we first abandon our vices, renounce the spectacles and pageantry of the world, and prepare ourselves free and unencumbered for Christ’s coming, we cannot say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss—or kisses—of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1:1).

Not far from this order of instruction, the followers of the philosophers also educate their students: first they teach ethics, then interpret physics; and once they see that someone has advanced in these subjects, they lead him as far as logic.

[Note: “They lead him as far as logic.” Earlier printed books and many manuscripts incorrectly read “they lead him as far as theology.” From the Letter to Paula concerning the Hebrew alphabet, however, we know with certainty that the reading should be the one we have restored here, namely “logic,” not “theology,” which the pagan philosophers did not teach. —Martianaeus.

Most manuscripts, including those examined by us and by Martianaeus, read *theoloicam* or *theologicam*. But in Letter 30 to Paula we said that *theoricen* should be restored, on the testimony of Origen in his *Homilies on the Song of Songs*, which Jerome copies here and elsewhere: “There are three general disciplines by which one reaches knowledge of things; they called them ethics, physics, and theory. We may call them moral, natural, and contemplative.” Shortly afterward he says that this is the faculty by which, having surpassed visible things, we contemplate something divine and heavenly, seeing it with the mind alone. Cassian likewise says in *Conferences* 14.9: “With all zeal, hasten first to grasp completely the practical discipline—that is, ethics—for without it the purity of the theoretical discipline cannot be apprehended,” and so forth. Thus here too in Jerome *theoricen*, or *theorica*, should be restored in place of *theoloicam*, which the manuscripts have, or *theologiam*, which the older printed editions preferred. I think, nevertheless, that “logic” can also be retained without impropriety, since the Origen just cited adds: “Some among the Greeks also placed logic—which we may call rational science—in fourth place.”]

Moreover, this must be observed more carefully: the title differs in the author’s three books.

In Proverbs it reads: “The Proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel.”

In Ecclesiastes, however: “The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem.” The words “king of Israel” are superfluous here, and are found incorrectly in the Greek and Latin codices.

[Note: Namely, βασιλέως Ἰσραὴλ ἐν Ἱερουσαλήμ—“king of Israel in Jerusalem.”]

In the Song of Songs, neither “son of David” nor “king of Israel” or “of Jerusalem” is written in the heading; only: “The Song of Songs of Solomon.”

Just as Proverbs, and elementary instruction, pertain to the twelve tribes and to all Israel, and just as contempt for the world is appropriate only to citizens, that is, to inhabitants of Jerusalem, so the Song of Songs properly pertains to those who desire only heavenly things.

[Note: Until now, the printed books and most manuscripts have falsely and absurdly read “makes mention of them.” We removed this final word with the help of one Palatine manuscript, as the sequence of the argument itself requires. For he says: “Just as Proverbs pertains to all Israel, so the Song of Songs properly pertains to those who desire heavenly things,” that is, “is useful to them.”]

To beginners and to those making progress belong the dignity of ancestry and the authority granted by the merit of their own kingdom.

[Note: Two Palatine manuscripts read “is indicated by merit.” Alcuin reads “is judged by merit.”]

But for the perfect, where the disciple is educated not by fear but by love, his proper name is sufficient; the teacher is his equal, and he does not know himself to be a king.

This is the literal sense for the time being.

According to the spiritual understanding, however, Christ is the peaceful one and the beloved of God the Father, and he is our Ecclesiastes. By destroying the dividing wall and abolishing hostility in the flesh, he made the two one, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

Concerning him the Father said to the disciples: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 3:17). He is the head of the whole Church, speaking not to the synagogue of the Jews but to the multitude of the nations: the king of Jerusalem built from living stones—not of that Jerusalem concerning which he himself says, “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets” (Matthew 23:37), and, “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (ibid., 38), but of that Jerusalem concerning which he forbids us to swear, because it is the city of the great King.

He is the son of David, to whom the blind cried out in the Gospel: “Have mercy on us, Son of David” (Matthew 9:27); and the whole crowd resounded with one voice: “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matthew 21:9).

Finally, the word of God is not addressed to him as it is to Jeremiah and the other prophets. Rather, because he is rich, king, and powerful—for he is the Word himself, Wisdom, and all the other virtues—he speaks words to the men of the Church and communicates his words to the Apostles, concerning whom it is sung in the Psalm: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5).

It is therefore wrong that some think we are invited by this book to pleasure and luxury, when on the contrary it teaches that everything we see in the world is vanity and that we ought not eagerly to pursue those things which, while they are possessed, perish.

Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes; vanity of vanities, and everything is vanity.

If everything that God made is very good, how is everything vanity—and not merely vanity, but vanity of vanities? Just as in the Song of Songs an outstanding song is shown among all songs, so in “vanity of vanities” the greatness of vanity is displayed.

Something similar is also written in the Psalm: “Nevertheless, every living human being is altogether vanity” (Psalm 38:6). If a living human being is vanity, then a dead human being is vanity of vanities.

We read in Exodus that Moses’ face was glorified to such an extent that the sons of Israel could not look upon it. The Apostle Paul says that this glory, in comparison with the glory of the Gospel, is no glory: “For what was glorified,” he says, “was not glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory” (2 Corinthians 3:10).

[Note: “For what was glorified.” Two Corbeian manuscripts, although very old and of excellent quality, omit these words of the Apostle writing to the Corinthians.]

We too can therefore say in this way that the heavens, the earth, the seas, and everything contained within this sphere are indeed good in themselves, but, compared with God, are as nothing.

And just as, if I saw the little flame of a lamp, I would be content with its light, but afterward, when the sun had risen, would not perceive what had been shining, and would see even the lights of the stars hidden by the sun’s radiance, so, when I look upon the elements and the manifold variety of things, I marvel at the greatness of God’s works; but when I consider that everything passes away and that the world grows old toward its end, while God alone always remains what he has been, I am compelled to say not once but twice: “Vanity of vanities, and everything is vanity.”

In Hebrew, instead of “vanity of vanities,” *abal abalim* () is written. Except for the Septuagint translators, all have translated it similarly as *atmos atmídōn* (ἀτμὸς ἀτμίδων), or *atmōn* (ἀτμῶν), which we may call “vapor of smoke” or “a thin breath” that quickly dissipates.

[Note: “Vapor of vapors,” and so forth. The printed editions of Erasmus and Marianus omit the two words *atmídōn*, or “of vapors,” although they are found in all manuscript copies. —Martianaeus. I would prefer *atmis*; the manuscripts, however, consistently write *atmedōn* instead of *atmídōn*.]

This word therefore also shows the transience and worthlessness of the universe.

[Note: Victorius reads: “and something of vanity is shown by this word.”]

For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

[Note: “For the things that are seen,” and so forth. Here some add after “are seen”: “as the Apostle says,” but this is found in no manuscript codex. —Martianaeus.]

Or else, because creation has been subjected to vanity, groans, labors in childbirth, and awaits the revelation of the children of God; and now we know in part and prophesy in part.

[Note: We have supplied the noun “children,” which Martianaeus, following Erasmus, had omitted, from our manuscripts and Victorius.]

Everything is vanity until that which is perfect comes.

What remains for a human being in all his labor with which he labors under the sun?

After the general judgment that everything is vanity, he begins with human beings: they sweat in vain through the labor of this world, gathering riches, educating children, seeking honors, building houses, and, in the midst of their work, suddenly taken away by death, hearing: “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

[Note: Alcuin has: “gathering perishable riches, seeking honors, building houses,” and so forth.]

Especially since they carry nothing away with them from all their labor, but return naked to the earth from which they were taken.

A generation goes, and a generation comes; and the earth stands for an age. [Note: Here, and a little farther on, where Jerome expressly marks this very word, all the manuscripts and printed books have *in saeculum* (“for an age”). Martianaeus says that from the appended observation it is clear that it should be rewritten, as he did, *in saeculo* (“in the age”). [Col. 1015D] “And the earth stands in the ages,” etc. Erasmus and Marianus corruptly printed *terra in saeculum stat* (“the earth stands in the age”), whereas Jerome himself below, in commenting on these same words, has: “And pointedly he does not say, ‘The earth stands in the ages,’ but ‘in the age.’” MARTIAN.] Some die, and others are born; and those whom you had seen, now no longer seeing them, you begin to see those whom you had not seen. [Note: Four manuscripts: “you will begin to see those who did not exist before.” Alcuin: “and you will begin to see those who had not previously existed.”] What is more vain than this vanity: that the earth, which was made for the sake of human beings, should remain, while the human being himself, lord of the earth, is suddenly dissolved into dust?

Alternatively: The first generation, that of the Jews, departs, and a generation gathered from the Gentiles succeeds it; but the earth stands as long as, with the Synagogue having departed, the whole Church enters in. For when the Gospel has been preached throughout the whole world, then the end will come. As the consummation approaches, however, heaven and earth will pass away. And pointedly he does not say, “The earth stands in the ages,” but “in the age.” [Note: Alcuin likewise: “He pointedly said, ‘The earth stands in the age,’ not ‘in the ages.’” See the preceding note.] Yet we praise the Lord not in one age, but in the ages of ages.

The sun rises, and the sun sets, and it leads itself back to its place, and rises there again. [Col. 1015C] [Note: “And it rises there itself.” Both Corbie manuscripts have *et orietur*, “and it will rise,” etc., in accordance with the Hebrew idiom and the shifting of tenses in verbs. Hebrews and other Eastern peoples customarily express by the future what ordinarily happens, or can happen, or is desired, even when the statement concerns an indeterminate present—as here, *et orietur ipse ibi* (“and it will rise there”) for *oritur* (“it rises”), because it habitually rises there. It should nevertheless be noted that in the Hebrew text of this passage a participial noun is written, not a future verb. For this reason I did not hesitate to reject the reading of the Corbie manuscripts. MARTIAN. —In Alcuin: “and it returns to its place, in order to rise again. The sun itself,” etc.] The sun itself, which was given to mortals for light, daily announces destruction by its rising and its setting. After it has dipped its burning wheel into Ocean, it returns by ways unknown to us to the place from which it had emerged; and when the circuit of night has been completed, it bursts forth again in haste from its chamber.

In place of the reading we have adopted by following the Vulgate edition, “it leads itself back to its place,” the Hebrew has *SOEPH*, which Aquila interprets as εἰσπνεῖ, that is, “breathes in” or “draws breath.” [Note: Aquila interprets it as εἰσπνεῖ. For the verb εἰσπνεῖ, which the Greek scholiast also repeats from Aquila in Flaminius Nobilius, Erasmus and Marianus, contrary to the authority of all the manuscript copies, wished to read προσέπνευσε. MARTIAN.] Symmachus and Theodotion, however, have “it returns,” since the sun evidently returns to its place and there, from where it had previously gone forth, breathes in.

All this is intended to teach that, through the changes of the seasons and the rising and setting of the heavenly bodies, human life slips away and perishes without knowing it. [Col. 1016A]

Alternatively: The sun of righteousness, in whose wings there is healing, rises for those who fear God, and sets at noon for the false prophets. When it has risen, it draws us to its place. Where? To the Father, evidently. For this purpose it came: to raise us from earth to heaven and to say, “When the Son of Man has been lifted up, he will draw all things to himself” (John 12). Nor is it surprising that the Son draws believers to himself, since the Father himself also draws them to the Son [Note: “Since the Father himself also draws to the Son.” In this clause too, the sense of the Gospel and Jerome’s statement are overturned by those who read: “Since the Father himself also draws the Son to himself.” MARTIAN.]: “No one comes to me,” he says, “unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

This, then, is the sun which we have said sets for some and rises for others. It set for Jacob the patriarch when he was departing from the Holy Land [Alternative reading: “returning”], and it rose for him again when he entered the promised land from Syria (Genesis 28). Lot likewise, when he had gone out from Sodom and came to the city to which he had been ordered to hasten, went up the mountain, and the sun rose over Zoar (Genesis 19).

It goes toward the south and circles toward the north; circling, the spirit goes on circling, and the spirit returns to its circuits. From this we can suppose that in winter the sun runs toward the southern region, while in summer it is nearer the north, and that it does not begin with the autumnal equinox, but first when the west wind blows, when in spring all things burst forth into fertility. [Note: Previously *quoniam* (“because”) stood here; this is less correct and contradicted by the manuscripts.]

As for the statement, “Circling, the spirit goes on circling, and the spirit returns to its circuits,” either he called the sun itself “spirit,” because it gives life, breathes, and is vigorous, and completes its annual circuits in its course, as the poet says:

> Meanwhile the sun revolves through the great year.  
> (Aeneid 3)

And elsewhere:

> And the year rolls back upon itself along its own tracks.  
> (Georgics 2)

Or, referring also to the moon’s shining orb and the Titanian stars:

> The spirit within nourishes it; and, infused throughout its limbs,  
> Mind stirs the mass and mingles with its great body;

he is speaking not of the sun’s annual course but of its daily paths. [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts: “For the line is obliquely broken.” Understand this as referring to the path of the zodiac.] For it proceeds by an oblique and broken line through the south toward the north, and thus returns toward the east.

Alternatively: When the sun runs through the south, it is nearer the earth; when through the north, it is raised high. Perhaps, therefore, this sun of righteousness is nearer to those who are constricted by the cold of winter and tribulations—for “from the north” evil is kindled against the earth (Jeremiah 1:14)—whereas to those who dwell in the region of the north and are deprived of summer’s warmth, it moves far away and returns through its circuits to the place from which it set out. When it has drawn all things to itself and illumined everyone with its rays, the primordial restoration takes place, and God is all in all.

Symmachus interpreted this passage as follows: “It goes toward the south and circles toward the north; the wind travels onward, and the wind returns by the places through which it had circled.”

All the torrents go into the sea, and the sea is not filled. To the place from which the torrents flow, there they return, in order to depart. [Note: Our manuscripts have “there”; earlier printed editions have “enter” instead of “depart.” —“There they themselves return in order to depart.” The earlier printed books incorrectly read “they return in order to enter.” MARTIAN.]

Some think that the fresh waters flowing into the sea are either consumed by the sun burning above them or serve as nourishment for the sea’s saltiness. [Col. 1017C] Behold our Ecclesiastes, the creator of these very waters, saying that they return through hidden channels to the heads of the springs and from the womb of the abyss continually boil forth at their origins. [Note: Alcuin has: “But our Ecclesiastes, that is, Christ, the creator of these waters,” etc. A little later: “through the hidden veins of the earth,” etc.]

The Hebrews, however, more plausibly think that under the names of “torrents” and “sea” human beings are metaphorically signified: they return to the earth from which they were taken. They are called torrents, not rivers, because they quickly perish, yet the earth is not filled with the multitude of the dead. Moreover, if we rise to higher matters, muddy waters rightly return to the sea from which they had stood. And, unless I am mistaken, apart from an accompanying qualification, “torrent” is nowhere used in a good sense. For “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” is said with the added qualification “of your delight” (Psalm 35:9). Conversely, the Savior is handed over to the torrent of the Kidron (John 18:1). And Elijah, during the time of persecution, hides by the torrent of Cherith [Note: “He hides by the torrent of Cherith.” In the Vulgate *Charith* should be read according to the Hebrew, but in this passage we should read *Chorrath* with the manuscript copies, because the Septuagint has ἐν τῷ χειμάῤῥῳ Χοῤῥὰθ, that is, “in the torrent Chorrath.” Jerome, in the present Commentary, quotes the scriptural testimonies according to the custom of his time—that is, according to the version received in the Latin Church. MARTIAN.], which itself also dries up (1 Kings 17:3).

But the insatiable sea is not filled, just as in Proverbs the daughters of the leech are never satisfied (Proverbs 30:15). [Note: “But the sea is not filled,” etc. Earlier printed books read corruptly: “which itself also dries up, and is not filled; but the sea is insatiable,” etc. Let the diligent reader consult our more extensive Notes placed below on account of the Critical History of Richard Simon. MARTIAN.]

[Col. 1018B] All words are weighty; a man cannot express them. [Note: One Vatican manuscript has: “They are weighty; he will not be able,” etc.] The eye is not satisfied with seeing, and the ear is not filled with hearing.

It is difficult to know not only physical matters but ethical ones as well. Speech cannot explain the causes and natures of things; the eye cannot behold them according to the dignity the matter demands [Note: Martianaeus incorrectly has *posset* (“could”) instead of *poscit* (“demands”). Alcuin: “nor can the eye be satisfied, so that it can behold the dignity of the matter.”]; nor can the ear, even under the instruction of a teacher, attain the summit of knowledge. For if we now see through a mirror in an enigma, and know in part and prophesy in part, then speech likewise cannot explain what it does not know; nor can the eye, in which it is dim-sighted, behold; nor can the ear, concerning which it is uncertain, be filled. [Note: “To behold in that in which it is dim-sighted.” The Sorbonne manuscript has: “in which it is blind, so that it may behold”; the printed editions: “in which it is blind, to behold”; but Corbie manuscript no. 138 has: “in which it may be dim-sighted, to behold.” MARTIAN. —Another Palatine manuscript together with the Vatican has: “in which it is blind, so that, as blind, it may behold.”]

This too should be noted: all words are weighty and are learned with great labor, contrary to those who think that knowledge of the Scriptures comes to the idle and to those who merely offer wishes or prayers for it. [Alternative reading: “to knowledge of the Scriptures.”]

[Col. 1018C] What is that which has been? The very thing that will be. And what is that which has been done? The very thing that will be done. And there is nothing new under the sun. [Note: The Vatican has: “and there is nothing recent.”]

It seems to me that he is now speaking generally about the things he listed above—generation after generation, the mass of the earth, the rising and setting of the sun, the course of the rivers, the greatness of Ocean, and everything we learn either by thought, sight, or hearing: namely, that there is nothing in the order of nature which has not already existed. From the beginning of the world, human beings have been born and have died; the earth has been established, balanced upon the waters; and the sun has risen and set. Not to run through more examples, God the creator has granted birds the ability to fly, fish to swim, land animals to walk, and serpents to crawl.

The Comic poet expresses a similar sentiment:

> Nothing has been said  
> that was not said before.  
> (Terence, Prologue to the *Eunuch*)

[Note: “Nothing has been said.” Terence has the following in the Prologue to the *Eunuch*:

> There is nothing now said that was not said before;  
> Therefore it is fair that you should recognize and pardon  
> What the old poets practiced, if the new do the same.

In the printed commentaries of Donatus the line Jerome repeats is not found. Hence I conjecture that Donatus said, “Let those perish who came before,” etc., while explaining this line of the Comic poet orally in the grammar school. MARTIAN.]

Accordingly, my teacher Donatus, when explaining this line, said: “Let those perish who said our things before us.” [Note: Martianaeus thinks that this was spoken orally by Donatus, since nothing similar can be found in his commentaries. It may, however, be more plausible to derive from this passage a new argument for proving that the commentaries still found in the commonly circulated books are incomplete and mutilated.]

But if nothing new can be said in speech, how much more is this true of the administration of the world, which was perfected from the beginning in such a way that God rested from his works on the seventh day!

I read in a certain book: “If everything that has been done under the sun existed in previous ages before it came to be, and if the human being was made once the sun had already been created, then the human being existed before he was made under the sun.” [Note: “I read in a certain book.” There can be no doubt that Jerome had read Origen’s doctrine in Origen’s *On First Principles*, book 2; for in his letter to Avitus Jerome himself testifies that Origen abused this testimony from Ecclesiastes in order to prove that before the making of this world other worlds had existed in past ages. Consult the letter beginning, “About ten years ago,” etc. MARTIAN. —Although it is readily possible to think that book 3 of Origen’s *On First Principles*, chapter 5, is intended—the passage from which the holy doctor quotes and forcefully argues in Letter 124 to Avitus, section 9—some Jews had long earlier adopted this view as well, among them those whom Rabbi Moses Maimonides mentions in book 2 of the *Moreh Nevukhim*.]

But this is excluded on the ground that, by this reasoning, animals, gnats, tiny creatures of every kind, and large animals would also be said to have existed before heaven. [Note: “But this is excluded,” etc. The older editions read differently: “But by this reasoning it is excluded that animals also,” etc. MARTIAN.] Unless perhaps one should answer that what follows shows that Ecclesiastes is speaking not of the other animals but of the human being. For he says: “There is nothing new under the sun that speaks and says, ‘Behold, this is new.’” Animals, however, do not speak; only the human being does. If animals were to speak, that would be something new, and the proposition that nothing is new under the sun would be dissolved.

Is there anything of which it may be said, “Look, this is new”? It already existed in the ages that were before us. Symmachus translated this more plainly: “Do you think there is anyone who can say, ‘Look, this is new,’ when it has already been done in the age that was before us?” [Note: From this you may infer that the preceding Greek words, which in the Roman edition of the Septuagint are introduced as Symmachus’s—ἄρα ἐστί τι ὃ ἐρεῖ τις, “Is there anything that someone will say?”—belong to another translator, perhaps Aquila, rather than to Symmachus.]

This agrees with what precedes: nothing new happens in the world, nor is there anyone who can arise and say, “Behold, this is new,” since whatever thinks that it can display itself as new already existed in earlier ages.

Nor should we think that signs and wonders, and the many things that occur newly in the world by God’s will, had already occurred in earlier ages, thereby giving Epicurus room to assert that through innumerable cycles the same events occur, in the same places and through the same agents. Otherwise Judas would have betrayed repeatedly, Christ would have suffered for us repeatedly, and all the other things that have happened and are yet to happen would similarly revolve through the same cycles.

Rather, it should be said that, through God’s foreknowledge and predestination, the things that are yet to happen have already happened. For those who were chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world already existed in earlier ages.

There is no remembrance of former things, and even of the latter things that are to come there will be no remembrance among those who will exist afterward in the final age. Just as oblivion hides past things from us, so those who are destined to be born will not be able to know what is happening now or what is going to happen; everything will pass away into silence and will be hidden as though it had never existed. That saying will be fulfilled: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.”

The Seraphim, too, cover their face and feet for this reason: the first and the last things are covered. [Note: They also have the Vatican: “the face of God”; this is erroneous.]

According to the Septuagint translators, who said, “There is no remembrance of former things, and even of the latter things that are to come there will be no remembrance among those who will exist afterward in the final age” (Matthew 20:16), the sense is drawn from the Gospel: those who are first in this age will be last of all. And because God, being kind and merciful, remembers even the least and remembers everyone, he will not give those who deserved to be last because of their vice as much glory as he will give those who, humbling themselves, wished to be last in the world.

Accordingly, it is also said below: “There is no remembrance of the wise man with the fool forever.” [Note: Three manuscripts have “with the wise man.” See below, chapter 2, verse 16.]

[Col. 1021A] I, Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.

Up to this point the preface has discussed everything generally; now he returns to himself and explains who he was and how, through experience, he came to know all things. The Hebrews say that this book belongs to Solomon, who was doing penance because, trusting in his wisdom and riches, he offended God through women. [Note: This is indeed the opinion of most interpreters. Some others, however, oppose it and argue that the work was written by Solomon before the crimes of his more dissolute life, on the ground that the Fathers of the Church, who continually doubt his eternal salvation, make no mention of his repentance.]

And I gave my heart to inquire and consider in wisdom all that is done under the sun. This evil occupation God gave to the children of human beings, that they might be occupied with it.

The word *ANIAN* (ענין) Aquila, the Septuagint, and Theodotion likewise translated as περισπασμόν, which the Latin translator rendered as *distention*, because the human mind, stretched among various anxieties, is torn apart. Symmachus, however, translated it as ἀσχολίαν, that is, “occupation.” Since it is therefore named frequently in this book, whether we call it “occupation,” “distraction,” or something else, everything should be referred back to the sense above.

Ecclesiastes therefore first of all gave his mind to seeking wisdom and, extending himself beyond what was permitted, wished to know the causes and reasons: why little children should be attacked by a demon, why shipwrecks should swallow up the just and the impious alike, and whether these things and similar events happen by chance or by God’s judgment. If by chance, where is providence? If by judgment, where is God’s justice?

“Desiring to know these things,” he says, “I understood that an excessive concern and an anxiety that torments the mind in different directions had been given by God to human beings, so that they might desire to know what they are not permitted to know.”

The cause, however, is beautifully placed beforehand: the distraction is given by God. For how does the Epistle to the Romans say: “Therefore God gave them up to dishonorable passions” (Romans 1:26)? And again: “Therefore God gave them up to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (ibid., 28). And afterward: “For this reason God gave them up to the desires of their heart, to uncleanness” (ibid., 24). And to the Thessalonians: “Therefore God will send them an operation of error” (2 Thessalonians 2:10). [Note: Victorius supplies and connects the following: “And just as the causes are first shown why they are handed over to dishonorable passions, or to a reprobate mind, or to the desires of their heart, or what they have done in order to receive an operation of error, so also in the present passage,” etc.]

The causes are first shown: why they are handed over to dishonorable passions, to a reprobate mind, or to the desires of their heart, and what they have done in order to receive an operation of error. So also here God has given human beings an evil distraction, that they may be distracted by it, because previously, of their own accord and by their own will, they did this or that.

I saw all the works that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a presumption of spirit. [Alternative reading: “all things.”]

We are compelled by necessity to discuss Hebrew words more often than we wish. For we cannot know the meaning unless we learn it through the words. [Note: Several manuscripts have *Ruoth*. Martianaeus here reads *Routh*, and shortly afterward *Rooth*, and νόμην instead of νομὴν, etc. —*ROOTH*: Aquila. The Sorbonne manuscript has *Rooth*; both Corbie manuscripts have *Routh*. But the ancients commonly read the present-day and Masoretic *sheva* according to the sound of the following vowel: *Sodom* for *Sedom*; and here *Rooth* for *Reuth* or *Reoth*. MARTIAN.]

Aquila and Theodotion translated *ROOTH* (רעות) as νομὴν, and Symmachus as βόσκησιν. The Septuagint translators, however, did not render the Hebrew expression but the Syriac one, saying προαίρεσιν. [Note: “But the Syriac,” saying this. Jerome perceptively observes that the Septuagint translators expressed not the Hebrew but the Syriac, because among the Chaldeans and Syrians the word *rea* means “to will” and “to think.” MARTIAN. —Or, “the Chaldaic,” in which language this word means “will”; it occurs in Ezra 5:17 and 7:18. Some rabbis also agreed with the Septuagint, interpreting it as “good pleasure.”]

Whether, then, it is *νομὴ* or *βόσκησις*, the word derives from grazing or feeding; but προαίρεσις means “will” better than “presumption.” The sense is that each person does what he wishes and what seems right to him, and that human beings are carried by free choice in different directions, while all things under the sun are vain because we displease one another in our judgments about the ends of good and evil.

A Hebrew teacher under whose instruction I read the holy Scriptures told me that the word *ROOTH* written above signified in this passage affliction and misery more than grazing and will—not misery as the opposite of good, but in the sense of what is written in the Gospel: “Sufficient for the day is its evil” (Matthew 6:34). The Greeks express this more precisely by calling it κακουχίαν. [Note: Earlier printed books have κάκωσίν, but all the manuscript copies read what we have printed. *Κακουχία* means “evil affliction,” just as *κακοῦμαι* means “I am afflicted, I lose heart.” MARTIAN. —Our manuscripts likewise have this, and Jerome himself, in his Commentary on this passage in Matthew, says that he used “evil” not in opposition to virtue, but for labor, affliction, and the troubles of the age.]

Thus the sense is: “I considered all that happens in the world, and discovered nothing other than vanity and evils—that is, the miseries of the spirit, by which the soul is afflicted through various thoughts.”

The crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be numbered. [Note: “The crooked cannot be made straight.” Here too the printed books have *perversum non poterit* (“the crooked thing will not be able”), etc. See also our more extensive Notes on this word below. MARTIAN.]

Whoever is crooked cannot be adorned unless he is corrected first. Straight things receive adornment; crooked things require correction. A thing is not called crooked unless it has been perverted from what is straight. This is directed against heretics who introduce certain natures that cannot receive healing.

And because what is lacking—that is, what is absent—cannot be numbered, for this reason only the firstborn of Israel were numbered. Females, slaves, children, and the common multitude from Egypt, being not the fullness but the deficiency of the army, were passed over without number.

The passage can also have this sense: So much wickedness is present within the capacity of this world that the world can scarcely return to the complete condition of goodness, nor easily recover the order and perfection in which it was first created.

Alternatively: When all things have been restored to wholeness through repentance, the devil alone will remain in his error. For everything that has been done under the sun has been overturned by his agency and by the spirit of his wickedness, as sins are heaped upon sins at his prompting. Finally, the number of those whom he has deceived and snatched from the Lord’s flock is so great that it cannot be comprehended by calculation.

I spoke with my heart, saying: “Behold, I have been magnified, and I have added wisdom beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem; and my heart has seen much wisdom and knowledge.”

Solomon was wiser not than Abraham, Moses, and the other saints, but than those who had been before him in Jerusalem. We also read in the Books of Kings that Solomon possessed great wisdom and that he had asked this gift from God above all others.

The eye of a pure heart therefore beholds much wisdom and knowledge. For he did not say, “I have spoken much wisdom and knowledge,” but, “My heart has seen much wisdom and knowledge.” We cannot express everything that we perceive.

And I gave my heart to know wisdom and knowledge, errors and folly. I learned that this too is the feeding of wind, or a presumption of spirit.

Contraries are understood through contraries. The first form of wisdom is to be free from folly. But no one can be free from folly unless he has understood it. Hence many harmful things were created in the world, so that, by avoiding them, we might be trained in wisdom.

Solomon’s study, therefore, was equally directed toward knowing wisdom and knowledge and, on the other hand, errors and folly, so that his true wisdom might be tested by pursuing some things and avoiding others. But in this matter also, as in the others, he says that he fed on winds and was unable to grasp perfect truth.

Concerning the presumption of spirit, or feeding on wind, which is frequently mentioned in this book, it is enough to refer to what was discussed above. [Note: Three manuscripts have: “because it is said so often,” etc.]

For in much wisdom there is much anger, and whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow.

The more someone has attained wisdom, the more he is indignant at being subject to vices and far from the virtues he seeks (Wisdom 6:7). Since “the powerful will suffer powerful torments,” and since more is demanded from one to whom more has been entrusted, whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow and is grieved with godly grief and mourns over his sins.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Who is the one who makes me rejoice, except the one who is made sorrowful by me?” (2 Corinthians 2:2).
