Unless perhaps this too should be understood: that the wise person grieves because wisdom lies hidden both in a secret place and in the depths, and does not present itself to minds as light does to sight, but comes forth through certain torments and intolerable labor, through continual meditation and study. [Note: The old printed editions incorrectly had “in the hidden place and in the deep.” —“It lies hidden both in the hidden place and in the depths.” Formerly it read: “wisdom lies hidden both in the hidden place and in the depths.” MARTIAN.]

[Col. 1024A] (Chapter 2.) I said in my heart: “Come now, I will test you with pleasure, and I will see what is good”; and behold, this too is vanity.

After I discovered that in an abundance of wisdom and an increase of knowledge there was labor and sorrow, and nothing other than an empty and endless struggle, I turned myself toward pleasure, so that I might flow in luxury, gather wealth, abound in riches, and seize passing delights before I died. But in this too I perceived my own vanity, since past pleasure does not help the present and what has been exhausted does not satisfy.

Not only bodily pleasure but spiritual pleasure as well is a temptation for the one who possesses it, so that I may need a goad to correct me and an angel of Satan to buffet me, lest I be exalted (2 Corinthians 12:7). Hence Solomon also says: “Give me neither riches nor poverty” (Proverbs 30:8), and immediately adds: “Lest, being satisfied, I become a liar and say, ‘Who sees me?’” (ibid., 9). For the devil too fell through an abundance of good things. Hence it is written in the Apostle: “Lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Timothy 3:6)—that is, into the judgment into which the devil also fell.

We can also say that spiritual pleasure is now declared vanity, like the other things, because we see it through a mirror and in an enigma. But when it has been revealed face to face, then it will by no means be called vanity, but truth.

I said to laughter, “Madness,” and to pleasure, “What are you doing?”

Where we read “madness,” the Hebrew has *MOLAL*, which Aquila translated as πλάνησιν, that is, “error”; Symmachus translated it as θόρυβον, that is, “tumult.” The Septuagint and Theodotion, as in many other passages, agree here also and translated it as περιφορὰν, which we may render literally as “circling about.” [Note: Formerly it was incorrectly written *circumferentur* (“they will be carried around”).]

Just as those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine are unstable and fluctuate in different directions (Ephesians 4:14), so those who laugh with that laughter which the Lord in the Gospel says must be changed into weeping (Luke 6:25) are swept away by the error and whirlwind of the age. They do not understand the ruin of their sins or mourn their past vices, but think that brief goods are perpetual and rejoice in things more deserving of lamentation.

This may also be understood of heretics, who, acquiescing in false doctrines, promise themselves happiness and prosperity.

I considered in my heart [Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript reads: “I considered in my heart”; “I considered within myself, and my heart led me,” etc. It therefore omits “that I might draw my flesh into wine.” It supplies the sense which the printed books overturn, reading consecutively: “that I might attain folly,” instead of “and that I might attain in folly.” For in Hebrew it has *veleehhoz besichluth*, that is, “and to grasp folly,” or “to obtain mastery in folly.”], that I might draw my flesh into wine; and my heart led me toward wisdom, and toward attaining folly, until I should see what was good for the children of men to do beneath the sun during the numbered days of their life. I wished to devote my life to pleasures [Note: The same manuscripts read: “I wished to prolong my life in pleasures, and to free my flesh from every care, as though from wine,” etc.], and to free my flesh from every care, and, as with wine, to lull it to sleep with pleasure. But my thought and natural reason—which God has implanted even in sinners—drew me back and led me to seek wisdom and trample folly underfoot, so that I might see what that good thing was which human beings could accomplish in the course of their life.

He aptly compared pleasure with drunkenness. For drunkenness overturns the vigor of the mind; and whoever can exchange it for wisdom and, as some manuscripts read, attain spiritual joy [Note: “Spiritual joy.” These two words had also been omitted from the printed editions, casting darkness over the sense of Scripture and Jerome’s observation. Now, however, the meaning of the passage remains clear and straightforward, since we know that Jerome read in the Septuagint interpreters: καὶ τοῦ κρατῆσαι ἐπ’ ἀφροσύνην, “and that I might attain folly,” whereas some manuscripts read ἐπ’ εὐφροσύνην, “in joy,” or “above joy.” This is also how it appears in the current edition of the Septuagint translators. MARTIAN. —Now, on the contrary, no Greek manuscripts remain except those which read “joy,” or *euphrosynē*, in place of “folly,” or *aphrosynē*, just as the copies of Jerome’s age, more faithfully following the Hebrew, preferred the latter reading. Below we correct some lesser matters from the manuscripts.], will be able to arrive at knowledge of what ought to be desired and what avoided in this life.

I magnified my works: I built houses for myself; I planted vineyards [Note: The printed reading was “I planted vineyards for myself.” Up to that point, etc.], and so forth, up to the place where he says: “The wise man’s eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness.”

Before discussing each point individually, it seems useful to me to encompass everything briefly in words and, as though gathering the meaning into a single body, to reduce it to a form that can more easily be understood. I possessed everything that is considered good in the world, like a king and a powerful man. I built lofty palaces for myself; I sowed mountains and hills with vines. And, so that nothing might be lacking for luxury, I planted gardens and orchards for myself, establishing various trees, which waters collected in pools [Note: “Which waters collected in pools,” etc. Erasmus and Martianus read: “which pools of water, collected above in one place,” etc. The Sorbonicus manuscript accordingly reads: “so that long vigor”; but the Corbeiensis manuscripts read: “so that they might be continually nourished by their moisture.” This wording gives an excellent sense. MARTIAN.] from above might irrigate, so that the verdure might be nourished for a longer time by perpetual moisture [Note: The manuscripts read: “so that the long-lasting greenery,” etc.].

I also possessed an innumerable multitude of servants, whether purchased or born in the household, and many herds of four-footed animals—cattle and sheep—more than any king before me had possessed in Jerusalem. There were also innumerable treasures of silver and gold, which the gifts of various kings and the tributes of nations had bestowed upon me. Thus it happened that, through excessive wealth, I was prompted to still greater pleasures [Note: Alcuin reads: “so that choirs of musicians might sing to me with the sound of flutes,” etc.], and choirs skilled in music sang to me with flute, lyre, and voice, while both sexes served at banquets. But the more these things increased, the more wisdom was lacking. For whatever pleasure desire drew me toward, I was carried along unrestrained and headlong, and I thought that this was the fruit of my labors: that I should consume myself in lust and luxury.

At last, coming to myself, and awakening as though from a deep sleep, I looked at my hands [Another reading: “and at my hands”] and observed my works: full of vanity, full of filth, full of the spirit of error. For I could find nothing that was considered good in the world [Note: Four manuscripts read “in an instant” in place of “was considered.”]. Having therefore reflected on what belonged to wisdom’s goods and what to folly’s evils, I consequently burst forth in praise of the man who, restraining himself after his vices, can become a follower of virtue.

For there is a great difference between wisdom and folly; and as far as day is separated from night, so far are virtues separated from vices. It seems to me, therefore, that the person who follows wisdom always raises his eyes toward heaven and keeps his face lifted on high, contemplating the things above his head. But the person devoted to folly and vices moves about in darkness and rolls about in ignorance of reality.

“I magnified my works” [Note: Our manuscripts add: “I built houses for myself; I planted vineyards.”], and so forth. He magnifies his works who, according to the image of the Creator, is raised up toward heavenly things. He builds houses so that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit may come and dwell in them. And he plants vineyards for which Jesus may tie up his she-ass.

I made gardens and orchards for myself; I planted in them every fruit-bearing tree. In a rich man’s house there are not only golden and silver vessels, but also wooden and earthen ones (2 Tim. 2:20). Gardens, therefore, are also made for the weaker and more infirm. For “the one who is weak eats vegetables” (Rom. 14:2).

Trees are planted—not all fruit-bearing, as we have it in the Latin manuscripts, but “every fruit,” that is, fruits and produce of various kinds, because there are different graces in the Church: one person is an eye, another a hand, another a foot; and “the parts of our body that seem less honorable, we clothe with greater honor” (1 Cor. 12:23).

Among these fruit-bearing trees I judge the tree of life, which is wisdom, to hold the first place. For unless it is planted in the midst [Note: The Corbeiensis manuscripts, with the same meaning, read: “unless it is planted in the midst of them,” etc. MARTIAN.], the other trees will wither.

I made pools of water for myself, to irrigate from them the forest [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “the forest of budding trees.”] of growing wood. The trees of the forests, the trees of the woods, which do not bear fruit and produce no fruit, are not nourished by heavenly rain or by waters from above, but by those collected in pools from streams.

For Egypt, low-lying and flat, like a vegetable garden, is irrigated by earthly waters coming from Ethiopia. But the land of promise, which is mountainous and elevated, awaits the early and late rain from heaven.

I purchased male and female slaves, and I had household servants; and I possessed a great abundance of cattle and sheep [Note: Our manuscripts add: “more than all who were before me in Jerusalem.”].

If we wish, as we said above, to refer Ecclesiastes also now to the person of Christ, we can call his slaves those who possess the spirit of fear in servitude and desire spiritual things more than they possess them. We can call female slaves those souls which are still devoted to the body and to the earth. We can call household servants those who indeed belong to the Church and surpass the slaves and female slaves whom we have mentioned, but have not yet been granted liberty or nobility by the Lord.

There are also others in the household of Ecclesiastes, like cattle and sheep, because of their works and simplicity. Without reason or knowledge of the Scriptures, they labor indeed in the Church, but have not yet reached the point of deserving to be human beings and return to the image of the Creator.

Observe carefully that no multitude is added in the case of slaves, female slaves, and household servants, whereas in the case of cattle and sheep it says: “I possessed a great abundance of cattle and sheep” [Note: The same manuscripts read: “and I possessed a multitude of sheep.”]. For there are more herds in the Church than human beings, more sheep than slaves, female slaves, and household servants.

As for what is said at the end:

“More than all who were before me in Jerusalem,”

this does not refer to Solomon’s great glory, as though he had been richer than his one father, who was king. Under Saul, kingship had not yet been established in Jerusalem, and the city was held by the Jebusites who occupied it. We must therefore investigate more deeply what Jerusalem is and how Ecclesiastes was richer than all the kings who preceded him in Jerusalem.

I gathered silver and gold, and the wealth of kings and provinces. I made male and female singers for myself, and the delights of the sons of men, male and female wine-servants.

In Holy Scripture, silver and gold always signify speech and meaning. Thus, in the sixty-seventh psalm, the dove—which is interpreted spiritually—has wings “more manifest and exposed to view, silver-plated,” but covers its more hidden inward meaning with the pallor of gold [Note: This passage was corrupted in the old editions, where we read: “It has silver-plated wings because of things more manifest and exposed to view.” MARTIAN.].

He gathered the wealth of kings and provinces, or regions, into the Church of believers: of those kings of whom the Psalmist sings, “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together” (Ps. 2:2); and of those regions toward which the Savior commanded the eyes to be lifted, because they are already white for harvesting (John 4:35).

The wealth of kings and regions may also be understood as the doctrines of philosophers and secular learning, which the ecclesiastical man, carefully understanding them, grasps, “catching the wise in their craftiness” and “destroying the wisdom of the wise and rejecting the understanding of the intelligent” (1 Cor. 1:19).

The male and female singers are those who sing with the spirit and sing also with the mind. The male singer, as a man who is strong and spiritual, sings of higher things. The female singer, however, still turns about near matter, which the Greeks call *hylē* (ὕλη), and cannot raise her voice on high.

Wherever, therefore, Scripture mentions a woman or the weaker sex, let us transfer the meaning to matter. Thus Pharaoh does not wish the males to be kept alive, but only the females, who are close to matter (Exod. 1). Conversely, scarcely any saint is said to have fathered daughters. Only Zelophehad, who died in his sins, fathered all daughters (Num. 27). Jacob, among the twelve patriarchs, was the father of one daughter, and because of her he was placed in danger (Gen. 34).

The delights of the sons of men are also to be understood as wisdom, which, like paradise, has varied orchards and manifold pleasures. Concerning it we are commanded: “Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart” (Ps. 37:4). And elsewhere: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 36:8).

For concerning the male and female wine-pourers—I have deliberately used the feminine form for distinction, although Latin usage does not permit this—Aquila gives an interpretation quite different from what is apparent. He did not name human beings, namely men and women, but kinds of vessels [Note: Two Palatine and Vatican manuscripts read “but kinds of male vessels.” *Kylikion* is a small cup or drinking vessel. —Calling them *kylikion* and *kylikia*. Here the Greek has been corrupted: it reads *kylikian kai kylika*. Then the Hebrew words are added in the context according to the Masoretic vowel points, *schidda* and *schiddoth*, whereas Jerome read *sadda* and *soddoth*, or *sadda* and *saddoth*, as the Sorbonicus manuscript has. MARTIAN.], calling them *kylikion* (κυλίκιον) and *kylikia* (κυλίκια), which in Hebrew are called *sadda* (סַדָּה) and *saddoth* (סַדּוֹת).

Finally, although Symmachus could not reproduce the word word-for-word, he is not far removed from this interpretation when he says: “Kinds of tables and arrangements” [Note: The old reading was “of measures.” Martianus changed this to “a measure in the singular,” and in the collection of the Hexapla it is *metrōn* (“of measures”). In reliance on the Vatican manuscript and another Palatine manuscript in its first hand, I think it better to read “of tables.” If Symmachus said “kinds of tables and settings,” he was not far, as Jerome reports, from Aquila, who named kinds of drinking vessels. But if he translated “kinds of measures,” or, worse still, “measure,” these words neither correspond to one another nor reveal what they mean when joined together. The rest of the context also supports this correction.].

Whether, therefore, pitchers, cups, or mixing bowls were arranged for service, Solomon should be understood to have possessed vessels decorated with gold and gems; and from one *kylikion*, that is, a mixing bowl, wine was drawn into other *kylikia*, namely smaller vessels, and through the hands of the servants the crowd of drinkers received the wine.

Since we interpret Ecclesiastes in relation to Christ, and since in Proverbs Wisdom calls passers-by to herself with wine mixed in a mixing bowl [Note: Martianus omits the preposition “in”; one Palatine manuscript has “mixed” in place of “mixed in.” The passage is Proverbs 9:5: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you.” This is especially noteworthy as an anagogical interpretation of Jerome’s for confessing the truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist.], we must now understand the Lord’s body as a great mixing bowl. In it there is not unmixed divinity, as there was in the heavenly realm, but divinity tempered for our sake by the intervening humanity; and through the Apostles, the smaller *kylikia*, little cups and mixing bowls, this wisdom has been poured out among believers throughout the whole world.

I became great, and I added wisdom above all who were before me in Jerusalem; and indeed my wisdom remained with me [Note: Martianus had wrongly omitted the word “wisdom”; we have supplied it from two Palatine manuscripts and the Victoriana edition. Several Greek books likewise have: καὶ προσέθηκα σοφίαν παρὰ πάντας, “and I added wisdom above all.” Shortly afterward, one Palatine manuscript has “stood by” instead of “stood.” The old editions have “stood by” here and below.].

The statement that Ecclesiastes was made great does not seem to suit the Lord, unless we apply to him the words: “He advanced in wisdom, age, and grace” (Luke 2:52), and: “Therefore God exalted him” (Phil. 2:9).

When he says, “those who were before me in Jerusalem,” he is speaking of those who, before his coming, governed the assembly of the saints and the Church. If we understand the Scriptures spiritually, Christ is richer than all human beings [Another reading: “than all men”]; but if we understand them only carnally, the Synagogue is understood better than the Church. He therefore removed the veil that had been placed over Moses’ face (Exod. 34), and enabled us to see his face in full light (2 Cor. 3).

As for the statement that wisdom remained with him [Note: This wording has been corrupted three times in Erasmus and Martianus. In the text they read “my wisdom stood by me,” and in the Commentary “wisdom stood by him,” followed by “wisdom stands by me.” MARTIAN.], its meaning is that, even while he was situated in the flesh, wisdom remained with him. A person who makes progress in wisdom does not have wisdom standing still within him; but the person who makes no progress and does not increase from moment to moment, but remains always in fullness, can say: “Wisdom stood by me.”

Whatever my eyes desired, I did not withhold from them; I did not restrain my heart from any joy, because my heart rejoiced in all my labor. And this was my portion from all my labor.

The eyes of the soul and the mind’s inward vision desire spiritual contemplation. The sinner, who is ignorant of it, prevents his heart from true joy. Ecclesiastes therefore devoted himself wholly to this, and exchanged the light affliction of the world for eternal glory. For this is our portion and our perpetual reward, if we labor here for the sake of virtue.

I looked again at all the works that my hands had done, and at the labor with which I had labored in doing them.

A person who conducts everything with diligence and caution can say this.

And behold, everything was vanity and desire of the spirit [Note: Three manuscripts read “and pleasure of the spirit.” Much more correctly, however, the second clause is: “and there is no abundance beneath the sun,” which they do not recognize.]. And there is no abundance beneath the sun.

Just as in other passages he judged all things beneath the sun to be worthless and varied according to the diversity of desires, so here he says: “There is no abundance beneath the sun” (Ps. 19:5). Christ placed his tabernacle in the sun. Therefore, whoever has not yet reached the sun’s brightness, order, and constancy cannot have Christ dwelling or abounding in him [Another reading: “whoever has not yet reached it.”].

I looked again, to see wisdom, error, and folly: for who among human beings can follow the king and his Maker? [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts, together with the old editions, have “before” instead of “and”; the Vatican manuscript more correctly omits both words. —“Who can follow the king,” etc. The old editions and a few manuscripts incorrectly read: “Who can follow the king who was made before his Maker?” MARTIAN.].

Since above, up to the place where Scripture says, “The wise man’s eyes are in his head,” I had encompassed everything in a single discourse, wishing briefly to indicate the meaning—and for that reason had again touched upon certain matters according to the *anagogē* [spiritual interpretation]—I must now explain the passage according to the course I had begun.

The meaning at this point differs greatly from the Septuagint interpretation. He says that, after condemning pleasures and delights, he returned to seek wisdom, in which he found more error and folly than true and certain prudence. For human beings cannot know the wisdom of their Creator and King as clearly and purely as the one who is himself the Creator knows it. Thus, even the things we know we rather conjecture than possess, and estimate rather than know as true.

I saw that wisdom has an advantage over folly, as light has an advantage over darkness.

“Although,” he says, “I perceived human wisdom itself to be mixed with error, and although it cannot enter our minds as purely as it exists in our King and Creator, nevertheless I recognized that even in its existing form there is a great difference between it and folly—just as day can be distant from night, and light from darkness.”

The wise man’s eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. And I recognized that one fate would come upon them all.

Whoever reaches mature manhood and deserves to have Christ as his head will always keep his eyes upon Christ; raising them on high, he will never think about things below.

While these things were so, and while there was such a great difference between the wise and the fool—that one was compared with day and the other with darkness, that one raised his eyes toward heaven while the other lowered them toward the earth—a thought suddenly arose in me: Why should the wise and the fool end in a common destruction? Why should the same blows, the same fate, and the same death press upon both equally?

And I said in my heart: As the fate of the fool is, so will mine also be; and what benefit was it that I became wise? [Note: One Palatine manuscript reads: “that I became wise—did I?” corresponding to the Greek ἐσοφίσαμην ἐγώ. —“And what benefit was it that I became wise?” With the same recklessness by which we have seen many complete Greek verses added earlier, the old editions now thrust upon us a Greek chapter of which not a single word appears in the genuine copies of Jerome. MARTIAN.]. And I said in my heart: This also is vanity.

For there will be no eternal remembrance of the wise man together with the fool, since, in the days that are to come, oblivion will cover everything. How then will the wise man die together with the fool?

I said: The wise and the foolish, the just and the impious, will die by an equal lot, and all will endure the evils of this age with a similar outcome. What advantage, then, is it to me that I followed wisdom and labored more than the rest?

But, reflecting again and carefully pondering the matter within myself, I discovered that my judgment was vain. For the wise and the foolish will not have the same remembrance in the future, when the consummation of all things arrives; nor will they be held to an equal end, since one will proceed to refreshment and the other to punishment.

The Septuagint translators rendered the Hebrew meaning more clearly at this point, although they did not follow the order of the words: “And what benefit was it that I became wise?” Then I spoke abundantly in my heart, because the fool speaks from abundance: “For this also is vanity, because there is no eternal remembrance of the wise man with the fool,” and so forth.

In this way, convicting his former opinion of folly, he testified that he had spoken foolishly and had erred because he had previously held such an opinion.

I hated life, because the work that was done beneath the sun was evil to me, because everything is vanity and pursuit of wind.

If the world is placed in evil, and if the Apostle groans in this dwelling, saying, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24), then he rightly hates everything that has been done beneath the sun.

For, in comparison with paradise and that blessed life in which we enjoyed spiritual fruits and the delights of virtues, we are now as though in a workhouse and prison, in a valley of tears, eating our bread in the sweat of our face.

I hated all my labor at which I labored beneath the sun, because I must leave it to the person who will come after me. And who knows whether he will be wise or foolish? He will rule over all my labor at which I labored and in which I became wise beneath the sun. This also is vanity.

He seems to be speaking about riches and possessions: according to the Gospel, when we are taken away by sudden death, we do not know with what kind of heir we shall die—whether the person who will enjoy the fruit of our labor will be foolish or wise. This also happened to Solomon, for he did not have a son like himself in Rehoboam. From this we understand that even a son is not worthy of his father’s inheritance if he is foolish.

But, contemplating more deeply, I think he is speaking of spiritual labor: that a wise man labors day and night in the Scriptures and composes books so that he may leave his memory to posterity, yet those books nevertheless fall into the hands of fools, who frequently take from them the seeds of heresies according to the perversity of their hearts and slander the labors of others.

For if Ecclesiastes is now speaking of bodily riches, why was it necessary to say of labor and possessions: “He will rule over all my labor at which I labored and in which I became wise beneath the sun”? What wisdom is there in gathering earthly riches?

I turned myself to make my heart renounce all my labor at which I had labored beneath the sun: there is a person whose labor is in wisdom, knowledge, and skill, and he will give his portion to a person who has not labored. This also is vanity and great wickedness [Note: The Hebrew has *veraa rabba*, which may be translated either “and great wickedness” or “and a great evil,” because the Hebrew root *rabab* means “much” and “great.” MARTIAN.].

For what does a person receive from all his labor and from the desire of his heart, with which he labors beneath the sun? All his days are days of pain, anger, and anxiety; even at night his heart does not rest. This too is vanity.

Above he spoke of an uncertain heir, because it was unknown whether the person who would become master of another’s labors would be foolish or wise. Now he repeats the same point, but the meaning differs in this respect: even if he leaves his substance and labors to a son, a relative, or some acquaintance, nevertheless everything returns to the same circle, so that one person enjoys another’s labor and the sweat of the dead becomes the pleasure of the living [Note: “And the sweat of the dead.” If it is vanity and great wickedness for one person to enjoy another’s labor, and for the sweat of the dead to become the pleasure of the living, how great a wickedness do you think it is when Bernard’s sweat becomes the honor of the living Nicholas, or John’s labors produce wealth and glory for a cruel master of works? Those who endure this vanity beneath the sun pronounce it, together with Solomon and our Ecclesiastes, most burdensome and most wicked. MARTIAN.].

Let each person examine himself, and he will see with how much labor he composes books, how often, when about to write what is worthy of being read, he turns his stylus again [Note: “He often turns his stylus again.” See above in our notes concerning this Horatian phrase. MARTIAN.] (from Horace, *Satires* 1.10), and gives his portion to a person who has not labored.

For, as I have already said, what do wisdom, knowledge, and virtue—the things in which he testified that he had labored—have to do with earthly riches? Wisdom, knowledge, and virtue consist in trampling earthly things underfoot.

There is nothing good for a person except to eat, drink, and show his soul good in his labor. And indeed I saw that this also comes from the hand of God. For who can eat, and who can spare [Note: The same manuscripts, apparently having undergone the hand of critics, read “and who will feed?” In the Greek it is *pietai*, “he will drink,” or *pheitai*, “he will spare.” —“For who can eat,” etc. The old editions incorrectly read: “Who eats, and who spares, except the one who gives to the good person,” etc. MARTIAN.], without him? For to the person who is good before him he has given wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner [Another reading: “to the sinful person”] he has given anxiety, so that he may increase and gather what is given to the good person before God [Note: Two Vatican and Palatine manuscripts read: “what is given to the good person before the face of God.” The old printed editions corruptly read: “what appears good before the face of God.” —“And gather what is given.” Here too they retain this thoroughly corrupt reading: “and gather what appears good before the face of God.” MARTIAN.].

This too is vanity and presumption of spirit.

After I had considered everything and perceived nothing more unjust than that one person should enjoy another’s labor, it then seemed to me that this was the most just arrangement in the world, and almost a gift from God: that each person should enjoy his own labor, drinking and eating, and sparing the wealth he has gathered for a time [Note: Here too, because of the prejudice created by the preceding reading, three manuscripts have “feeding on his wealth in due season,” etc., instead of “sparing it in due season.”].

For it is God’s gift that a just man should be given such a disposition that he himself consumes what he has acquired through care and wakefulness. Conversely, it is God’s wrath against the sinner that he should gather wealth day and night and, never using it, leave it to those who are just in God’s sight.

But, he says, carefully inspecting and seeing that everything ends in death, I judged this most vain.

These remarks are according to the literal sense, lest we seem entirely to pass over the simple meaning and, while pursuing spiritual riches, despise the poverty of history.

For what good is there, or what kind of gift from God, in longing for one’s own wealth and, as though it were fleeing [Note: Three manuscripts read “and, as though seizing what is fleeing,” whereas the older printed books read: “and, as though knowing the present, to pluck pleasure,” or “and, as though it were fleeing, to seize pleasure.” MARTIAN. —Victorius, from Brixian manuscripts, reads “to seize”; previously it had been “as though knowing the present, to pluck pleasure.” He says that this reading can also be retained, provided that “fleeing” is written in place of “knowing.”], snatching pleasure, or in turning another’s labor into one’s own delights? Is it a gift of God if we enjoy the miseries and labors of others?

It is good, therefore, to take true food and true drink, which we find in the divine books from the flesh and blood of the Lamb.

For who can either eat or, when necessary, spare [Note: Again, all the manuscripts have “feed” in place of “spare,” which here seems more suitable and more consistent with the exposition that follows.] without God? He commanded that what is holy should not be given to dogs (Matt. 7:6), and teaches how food is to be given to fellow servants at the proper time (Matt. 24:45); and, according to another meaning, he teaches that one should eat only as much honey as is sufficient (Prov. 25:16) [Note: Two manuscripts have “he ought to eat only so much.”].

God fittingly gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to the good person. For unless he is good and has first corrected his conduct by his own free choice [Note: The Vatican manuscript lacks the preposition “before,” and once it is deleted, this passage either has no trace of, or at least gives off less of, the Pelagian error, especially if one attends to what follows. Alcuin moderates this sentence according to the sense of Catholic doctrine, which after Jerome was defined more clearly throughout the world, as follows: “Unless he is good and, with the help of God’s grace, has first corrected his conduct by his own free choice,” etc. —“And has corrected his conduct by his own free choice.” This seems somewhat to savor of Pelagius’ error, but the following context easily corrects the passage. MARTIAN.], he does not deserve wisdom, knowledge, and joy, according to what is said elsewhere: “Sow righteousness for yourselves; reap the fruit of life; enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge” (Hos. 10:12, according to the Septuagint).

Righteousness must first be sown, the fruit of life must be reaped, and afterward the light of knowledge can appear.

Thus, just as God gave wisdom and the rest to the good person before him, so, abandoning the sinner to his own free choice, he caused him to gather riches and to sew cushions from the fragments of corrupt doctrines on every side.

When the holy man, pleasing to God, sees these things, he understands [Another reading: “will understand”] that they are vain and composed through presumption of spirit.

Nor is it surprising that he said: “He gave anxiety to the sinner,” and so forth [Note: Alcuin refers these words to the following sense: “For this reason anxiety was given to him,” etc.; he has an exposition that is almost more concise. “He gave” must be understood as “he abandoned.”].

This should be referred to the meaning about which I have often spoken: anxiety, or distraction [Another reading: “affliction”], was given to him because he was a sinner; and the cause of the distraction [Another reading: “affliction”] is not in God, but in the one who had previously sinned of his own will.

### Chapter 3

There is a time for everything, and a time for every matter beneath heaven.

In the preceding passages he taught the uncertain and fluctuating condition of human existence. Now he wishes to show that everything in the world is contrary to itself, and that nothing remains perpetually fixed—at least among those things that are beneath heaven and subject to time—for the other spiritual substances are contained neither by heaven nor by time.

Time to give birth, and time to die. Time to plant, and time to uproot what has been planted.

No one doubts that both the birth and the death of human beings are known to God [Note: From Alcuin we read: “It was previously *et finitus* (‘and concluded’); in the old Vulgate editions, *et agnitus* (‘and recognized’).” — “Is known to God.” Erasmus: “is known and recognized by God.” — “Becomes known to God.” Erasmus: “is known and recognized by God.” MARTIAN.], predetermined by him, and that “to give birth” is the same as “to plant,” while “to die” is the same as “to uproot what has been planted.” But because we read in Isaiah: “From fear of you, Lord, we conceived, and we travailed, and we gave birth,” this must be understood to mean that, for the perfected man, this birth—which was born from fear—dies when he begins to love God. For perfect love casts out fear (I John IV, 18).

The Hebrews understand all that is written here about the opposition of times, up to the place where he says, “A time of war, and a time of peace,” as referring to Israel. Since it is not necessary to state in every verse what they interpret and understand, I shall touch briefly upon the broader discussion, leaving the fuller treatment to the reader’s judgment [Al. “lightly”]. There was a time for generating and planting Israel, and a time for its death and leading into captivity. A time for killing them in Egypt, and a time for liberating them from Egypt. A time for destroying the Temple under Nebuchadnezzar, and a time for building it under Darius. A time for mourning the overthrow of the city, and a time for laughing and dancing under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah. A time for scattering Israel, and a time for gathering it together again. A time for God to surround the Jewish people as though with a girdle and belt [Note: Victorius, on the basis of the Medicean, Fesulan, and Florentine manuscripts of St. Mark, restored *circumdandi* (“to surround”). All our manuscripts support the printed reading.], and a time for leading them into Babylonian captivity, where they would rot beyond the Euphrates. Read Jeremiah’s *perizoma* (περίζωμα, “loincloth”) (Jeremiah XIII, 1 ff.). A time for seeking and preserving them, and a time for destroying and casting them away. A time for tearing Israel apart, and a time for sewing it together again. A time for silencing the Prophets—now, during the Roman captivity—and a time for making them speak, when even in a hostile land they were not deprived of God’s consolation and address. A time of love, with which he formerly loved them under the patriarchs, and a time of hatred, because they laid hands upon Christ. A time of war, while they now refuse to repent, and a time of peace in the future, when, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel will be saved.

[Col. 1035B] A time to kill, and a time to heal.

There is both a time to kill and a time to heal, as he says: “I kill, and I make alive” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 19). He heals by calling people to repentance. He kills, in accordance with the passage: “In the morning I killed all the sinners of the earth” (Psalm C, 8).

A time to destroy, and a time to build.

We cannot build good things unless we have first destroyed evil things. [Note: The Vatican manuscript and the second Palatine manuscript read: “we have first destroyed evil things, just as Jeremiah’s word says,” etc. Previously this passage was impaired by faulty punctuation.] For this reason Jeremiah’s word was given to him by God so that he might first uproot, dig up, and destroy, and afterward build and plant (Jeremiah I).

409 A time to weep, and a time to laugh.

Now is the time to weep, and in the future the time to laugh: “Blessed are you who weep, for you shall laugh” (Luke VI, 21).

A time to mourn, and a time to dance.

For this reason those people are rebuked in the Gospel to whom the Lord says: “We lamented for you, and you did not mourn; we sang, and you did not dance” (Luke VII, 32). We must mourn at present [Note: “So that afterward we may be able to dance,” etc. The Corbie manuscripts read: “so that we may be able to dance that dance which David danced.” *Saltare saltationem* (“to dance a dance”), like *vivere vitam* (“to live a life”). MARTIAN.], so that afterward we may be able to dance with the dance with which David danced before the Ark of the Covenant; and although this displeased Saul’s daughter, it pleased God all the more (II Samuel VI). [Note: The editions of Erasmus and Victorius add this gloss: “because whoever mourns his sins in the present age will laugh rather in the future”; the manuscripts entirely lack it. — “It pleased God all the more.” In the older editions I find an adulterine addition that does not at all fit the passage. Hence I infer that it was inserted by some incompetent copyist who added his glass to Jerome’s most precious pearls, namely: “because whoever mourns his sins in the present age will laugh rather [Col. 1036D] in the future.” MARTIAN.]

A time to scatter stones, and a time to gather stones.

I am surprised that an eloquent man [Note: “I am surprised that an eloquent man,” etc. I have not been able to discover who said this, although I carefully read through a great many volumes of ancient writers for this purpose. I warn the reader, however, that Jerome’s Commentary on this passage of Ecclesiastes has been thoroughly corrupted and overturned in the *Glossa ordinaria*. MARTIAN.] should have said something ridiculous here: “The subject,” he says, “is the destruction and construction of Solomon’s houses, since people now destroy and now build; some gather stones to construct buildings, while others destroy what has been built,” in accordance with that saying of Horace [Note: “In accordance with that saying of Horace.” The order of the verses in Horace himself, *Epistles*, Book I, Epistle 1, to Maecenas, is different:

> He spurns what he sought; he seeks again what he recently abandoned;  
> He is restless and at odds with the whole order of life;  
> He destroys, he builds, he changes squares into circles.

MARTIAN.] (*Epistles*, Book II, Epistle 1):

[Col. 1036A] He destroys, he builds, he changes squares into circles.

[Note: Three manuscripts read *exstruit* (“he builds”). In Horace, the verse cited first here is later than the other one.] He is restless, and disagrees with the whole order of life.

Whether he said this rightly or wrongly I leave to the reader’s judgment. Let us follow the order of the earlier explanation, saying that there is a time for scattering and gathering stones, in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew III, 9). There was a time for scattering the Gentile people, and a time for gathering them again into the Church.

I have read in a certain book—though according to the Septuagint interpreters, who said, “A time for throwing stones, and a time for gathering them”—that the severity of the ancient Law was tempered by the grace of the Gospel. For the Law, rigid, unkind, and unsparing, kills the sinner. The grace of the Gospel has mercy and calls to repentance. This, it says, is the time for throwing stones or gathering them: stones are thrown under the Law and gathered under the Gospel. Whether this has truly been said or not, let its author bear responsibility for it.

A time to embrace, and a time to be far from embracing.

According to the literal understanding, the meaning is clear, and the Apostle agrees with the same words: “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (I Corinthians VII, 5)—that is, to attend to children, and then again to continence. Or there was a time for embracing, when that declaration prevailed: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis I, 28). And a time to be far from embracing, when this followed: “The time is constrained.” [Note: Victorius reads: “The time is now constrained”; formerly the reading was: “The time which is constrained,” etc.] “It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” [Col. 1036C] (I Corinthians VII, 29).

But if we wish to ascend to higher things, we shall see Wisdom embracing her lovers: “Honor her,” she says, “and she will embrace you” (Proverbs IV, 8), and she will hold you tightly within her arms and bosom [Note: Martianaeus reads incorrectly: “to hold with a tighter embrace.” Two manuscripts read: “to bind more tightly.”]. Since the human mind cannot always strive toward the heights and think about divine and higher things, nor remain continually in contemplation of heavenly matters, but must sometimes indulge the needs of the body, there is therefore a time for embracing Wisdom and holding her more tightly, and a time for loosening the mind from the sight and embrace of Wisdom, so that we may serve the needs of the body and those things without which our life cannot proceed without sin.

[Col. 1037A] A time to acquire, and a time to lose. A time to preserve, and a time to cast away.

Under different expressions, the sense here is the same as above and below, in the statement: “A time to destroy, and a time to build.” And then: “A time to tear apart, and a time to sew together.” For just as the Synagogue is destroyed so that the Church may be built, and there is a rending from the Law so that the Gospels may be sewn together—something each Evangelist accomplished by sewing together testimonies concerning the Lord’s coming from the Law and the Prophets [Note: In Alcuin: “and they bind together the legal rifts, so that the glory of the Gospel may be sewn together.”]—so there was a time for seeking and preserving Israel, and a time for destroying and casting it away. Or certainly, a time for seeking a people from the Gentiles, and a time for destroying the Jewish people. A time for preserving believers from the nations, and a time for rejecting unbelievers from Israel.

[Col. 1037B] A time to be silent, and a time to speak.

I think that the Pythagoreans, whose discipline requires them to remain silent for five years and afterward to speak once they have been instructed, derived the origin of their rule from this. Let us therefore learn also to refrain from speaking at first, so that afterward we may open our mouths to speak. Let us be silent for a definite period and depend upon the words of our teacher. Let nothing seem right to us except what we are learning, so that after prolonged silence we may become teachers from being disciples.

But now, through the fault of the ages, which daily decline for the worse [Note: The Corbie manuscripts read: “through the fault of the schools, which daily decline for the worse”; and below: “who is the promoter of errors.” MARTIAN.], we teach in the churches what we do not know. And if, through the arrangement of our words or through the instigation of the devil, who promotes error, we stir up the applause of the people, we imagine against our conscience that we know what we have been able to persuade others of. [Note: Recall Letter 53 to Paulinus, sections 6 through 8. — “All the arts without a teacher.” He makes the same complaint in his Letter to Paulinus concerning the study of the divine Scriptures, whose opening is: “Brother Ambrose,” etc. MARTIAN.] We do not learn any art without a teacher; only this one is considered so worthless and easy that it does not need an instructor.

A time to love, and a time to hate.

There is a time to love, after God, children, wife, and relatives; and a time to hate them in martyrdom, when, for Christ’s confession, hostile natural affection assails those who stand firm. Or certainly, there is a time to love the Law and the things commanded by the Law—circumcision, sacrifices, Sabbaths, and new moons—and a time to hate them when the grace of the Gospel has succeeded them.

This too can be said: since “now we see through a mirror, in an enigma” (I Corinthians XIII, 12), there is a time to love present things, and a future time will come when, seeing face to face [Note: The Vatican manuscript adds *intuebimur* (“we shall behold”), for which the second Palatine manuscript has *intuemur* (“we behold”). Shortly afterward, instead of *incipiemus* (“we shall begin”), and “what we loved,” as all the manuscripts prefer—and Victorius also restored from the Florentine copies—Martianaeus retained *incipimus* (“we begin”) and “what we now love.”], and progressing toward better things, we shall begin to hate and despise what we loved.

[Col. 1037D] A time of war, and a time of peace.

As long as we are in the present age, it is a time of war; but when we have departed from this age, the time of peace will come. For God has his dwelling in peace, and our city, Jerusalem, received its name from peace (Psalm LXXV, 3). [Col. 1038A] Let no one therefore think himself secure now: in a time of war [Note: The second Palatine manuscript reads: “in a time of war you must fight.” Alcuin has: “where one must fight.” Then, together with the same Palatine manuscript, the Vatican reads: “and spiritual weapons must be taken up.”], one must gird oneself and take up weapons, so that afterward, once victorious, we may rest in peace.

What advantage does the worker have from that in which he labors?

I saw the occupation that God has given to the children of men, so that they may be occupied with it. He has made everything good in its time, and indeed has placed the age in their hearts, so that a human being cannot discover the work that God has done from beginning to end.

I am not unaware of what many have said about this passage: that God has therefore granted occupation in the present age even to teachers of perverse doctrines, lest the human mind, left idle, should grow numb; and that this is the good which God made in its time, although he has nevertheless prevented them from comprehending the nature and knowledge of things.

But this is how it was explained to me by the Hebrew who instructed me in the Scriptures: Since everything passes according to its own time, and there is a time for destroying and building, for weeping and laughing, for silence and speech, and all the other things that have been said about time, why do we strive and exert ourselves in vain, and think that the labors of a short life are perpetual? Nor are we content, according to the Gospel, with “the evil of the day,” and think nothing about tomorrow (Matthew). What more can we have in this age by laboring, when God has granted human beings only this: that one person, pursuing one thing and another person another, may have matters in which to be instructed and exercise himself?

For everything that God made is good, but good in its own time. It is good to stay awake and to sleep; yet it is not always good either to stay awake or to sleep, because in turn, according to God’s arrangement, each is good when it is necessary. God also gave the world to human beings for habitation, so that they might enjoy the variations of the seasons and not investigate, concerning the causes of natural things, how everything was created, or why he caused this or that to grow, remain, and change from the beginning of the world to its consummation.

I have learned that there is nothing good except to rejoice and to do good during one’s life.

Indeed, whenever anyone eats and drinks and displays what is good in all his labor, this is from the gift of God [Note: The same Palatine manuscript reads: “will eat, and drink, and show his soul what is good,” etc.]. Therefore the human being was given as a tenant and guest of the world, so that he might enjoy the brief span of his life; and, with the hope of a longer life cut short, might regard everything he possesses as though he were about to depart for other things, and do what good he can during his life [Al. “as much as he can”]. He should not torment himself with thoughts for the sake of accumulating wealth.

Nor should he think that he can gain more from his labor than food and drink; and if he spends any of his wealth on good works, this alone is the gift of God. From these things we are not, as some think, driven toward luxury and pleasures and despair, in accordance with Isaiah: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isaiah XXII, 31), like animals [Al. “may be driven”]; rather, in accordance with the Apostle: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (I Timothy VI, 8), so that [Al. “and”] whatever more we can possess, we may spend on nourishing the poor and giving generously to the needy.

Moreover, since the Lord’s flesh is true food and his blood true drink, according to the *anagoge* (spiritual interpretation), the only good we have in the present age is to feed upon his flesh and drink his blood—not only in the mystery of the Eucharist, but also in the reading of the Scriptures. For the true food and drink taken from the word of God is knowledge of the Scriptures.

No one should think that what was prophesied by Balaam—“There will be no labor for Jacob, nor pain in Israel” (Numbers XXIII, 23)—contradicts the statement that it is a gift of God if anyone eats and drinks and displays what is good in all his labor. “Many are the tribulations of the righteous.” The Apostle also complains of these things, saying that he sweated in labor and pain (II Corinthians II) [Note: Instead of “in pain,” the second Palatine manuscript reads “in abstinence.”]. But when the Lord has freed us from these things in the future, “There will be no labor in Jacob, nor pain in Israel.”

And just as we read, “Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh” (Luke VI, 21), so our laughter will follow the words of the prophet Job: “The mouth of the truthful will be filled with joy” (Job VIII, 21) [Note: Victorius wishes *risu* (“with laughter”) to be restored in place of *gaudio* (“with joy”), both because the Greek text has γέλωτος (“of laughter”) and because Jerome is speaking of laughter, not joy. Nothing, however, should be changed against the authority of the manuscripts.]. In the same way, we now enjoy our labor in good works, by which we are confined and oppressed, so that afterward we may cease to labor.

I have learned that everything God has made will endure forever; nothing can be added to it, and nothing can be taken away from it. God has made it so that they fear before him.

There is nothing new in the world. The course of the sun, the phases of the moon, and the dryness or greenness of the earth and trees came into being and were created together with the world itself [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “and were created together,” almost as Alcuin has it.]. Therefore God has governed everything according to a fixed order and commanded the elements to serve human uses, so that people, seeing these things, may understand that there is providence [Al. “wisdom”] and fear before God, while from the equality, course, order, and constancy of things they understand the Creator [Note: The same Vatican manuscript reads: “from the quality, course, order, equality, and constancy of things”; the second Palatine manuscript partly agrees.].

“For the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made; his eternal power also and divinity” (Romans I, 20). [Note: “For the invisible things of God.” The Corbie manuscripts read: “For the invisible things of God are perceived and understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made.” MARTIAN.]

If we wish, having finished the earlier sense, to read as though beginning again: “And God made it so that they fear before him,” the meaning is this: God made everything so that people would fear him and would not turn aside into another direction from what God once ordained [Note: Together with Erasmus and Victorius, the Vatican manuscript reads: “and not turn aside into another direction.” — “Into another direction.” Erasmus and Martianus falsely read: “and not turn aside into another direction.” MARTIAN.]. He has beautifully moderated the statement by saying, “so that they fear before him” (Psalm XXXIII, 17). For the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.

What is that which has been? The same thing that is, and what is going to be has already been; and God will seek out the one who suffers persecution.

Whether past, present, or future, all the things that we see both have been, are, and will be. The sun that now rises existed before we were in the world, and after we have died it will rise again. We have named the sun so that from it we may understand that the other things also are the same as those that existed before.

Although they may seem to perish through the condition of death, they do not perish, because they grow again in renewed life. Nothing perishes forever; rather, it is reborn and, as though with interest, comes back to life.

This is what he means when he says: “And God will seek out the one who suffers persecution,” which is better expressed in Greek as καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ζητήσει τὸν διωκόμενον—that is, “and God will seek out the persecuted one,” meaning what has passed away, what has been expelled, what has ceased to exist [Note: The second Palatine manuscript has the neuter form τὸ διωκόμενον (“the thing persecuted”).].

If this is said of all the things that exist in the world, there can be no doubt that it is said of the human being: the dead person will be reborn. But if anyone prefers to read it as though it were the proper beginning: “And God will seek out the one who suffers persecution,” let him use this testimony during the persecution of the Gentiles, to console the one who perseveres in martyrdom.

And since, according to the Apostle, “all who desire to live piously in this age suffer persecution” (II Timothy III) [Note: Up to this point the printed editions read differently from the manuscripts; they formerly had “in Christ” instead of “in this age.”], they should have consolation because God seeks the one who suffers persecution, just as he requires the blood of the slain; and he comes to seek what was lost, and carried the wandering sheep back to the flock on his shoulders (Luke XIX, XV) [Note: “And the wandering sheep.” We followed the Sorbonne manuscript; others read *erratam ovem* (“the sheep that had gone astray”); the editions of Erasmus and Martianus, *erroneam ovem* (“the erring sheep”). MARTIAN.].

[Col. 1040C] And again I saw under the sun the place of judgment: there was impiety; and the place of justice: there was iniquity.

415 I said [Al. “therefore”] in my heart: God will judge the righteous and the impious, because there is a time for every purpose and for every deed there.

The meaning is clear, but it is enveloped in a cloud of interpretation. “Under this sun,” he says, “I sought truth and judgment, and I saw that even among the very benches of the judges, it was not truth that prevailed but bribes.” Or otherwise: “I thought that some justice was being carried out in the present age, and that either the godly person was receiving what was due to him or the impious was being punished for his crime; but I found the opposite of what I had thought. For I saw the righteous suffering many evils here, and the impious reigning because of his crime.”

Afterward, conversing with my heart and reflecting, I understood that God does not judge partially and individually now [Note: Our manuscripts lack the adverb “now”; Alcuin reads “always” in its place.], but reserves judgment for the future, so that all may be judged together and there receive according to their will and their works.

This is what he means when he says: “There is a time for every purpose and for every deed there”—that is, in the judgment, when the Lord begins to judge. Then truth will exist; now injustice rules in the world.

We read something similar in the book called the Wisdom of Sirach [Note: We restore the word “son” from our manuscripts and editions before Martianaeus, who omitted it. — “Which is entitled Sirach.” The printed books read “which is entitled the Wisdom of the son of Sirach,” but the manuscripts more correctly read “which is entitled Sirach”; among the Septuagint the book of Ecclesiasticus is called Σοφία Σείραχ, “Wisdom of Sirach.” The Syriac interpreter, however, has: “The book of Jesus, son of Simeon Asiro,” and the same book is called “Wisdom of the son of Asiro.” MARTIAN.]: “Do not say, ‘What is this?’ or, ‘What is that?’ For everything will be sought out in its own time.”

I said in my heart concerning the speech of the children of men, that God separates them, in order to show that they are themselves beasts [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “they are beasts” twice. Formerly the text read: “in order to show that they themselves are beasts, or that the outcome,” etc. In editions before Martianaeus the text was most corruptly printed: “that God separates them, in order to show that they themselves are beasts; or that the outcome,” etc. MARTIAN.].

The outcome of human beings and the outcome of cattle is one and the same [Note: The same Vatican manuscript, with the second hand of the Palatine, reads: “the outcome is one and the same for them all.”]. The death of the one is like the death of the other; there is one breath for all, and a human being has nothing more than cattle, because everything is vanity. All go to one place; all are made from the earth, and all return to the earth. [Note: The manuscripts agree with the Greek Καὶ τίς (“And who?”). Previously the conjunction *et* was missing.]

And who knows whether the spirit of the children of men goes upward, and whether the spirit of cattle goes downward into the earth?

It is not surprising that in the present life there is no distinction between the righteous and the impious, nor that virtues have no effect and everything is tossed about by uncertain chance, when even between cattle and the human being, according to the body’s lowliness [Note: They likewise read corruptly, “according to the body’s quality,” whereas the following words show that Jerome wrote “lowliness,” not “quality.” MARTIAN.], there seems to be no difference. Their condition of birth is the same, and their lot in dying is one: we proceed alike into the light, and are equally dissolved into dust.

But if there appears to be this difference—that the human spirit ascends into heaven while the spirit of cattle descends into the earth—by what certain authority have we learned this? Who can know whether what is hoped for is true or false?

He does not say this because he thinks that the soul perishes with the body, or that one place is prepared for beasts and human beings alike, but because, before the coming of Christ, all were led together to the underworld [Note: Compare the Commentaries on Hosea, chapter 13; also Saint Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book 8, chapter 4. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 31, says: “We believe that the underworld is not a bare emptiness, nor some subterranean sewer of the world, but a hollow in the earth, a vast region below, and a hidden depth in its very bowels.”].

Thus Jacob says that he will descend to the underworld (Genesis XXXVII and XLIV). Job complains that the pious and the impious are held in the underworld (Job VII and XVII). The Gospel testifies that there is a great chasm in the underworld, and that Abraham is there with Lazarus while the rich man is in torments (Luke XVI). Indeed, before Christ opened the heavenly places with that fiery wheel, that flaming sword, and the gates of Paradise for the thief, heaven was closed, and the same lowliness of human and animal spirits confined them alike.

Although one seemed to be dissolved and the other reserved, it made little difference whether one perished with the body or was detained in the darkness of the underworld.

Let us return to each point and discuss it briefly, in a concise manner of speech, according to its order [Al. “let us unfold it”].

“I said in my heart concerning the speech of the children of men, that God might distinguish them.” He means this alone, he says, as the difference God willed between human beings and beasts: we speak, whereas they are mute; we express our will in speech, whereas they are numbed in silence.

And although we differ from beasts so greatly through speech, it is nevertheless shown to us that, according to the fragility of the body, we are cattle. As the animal dies, so the human being dies; there is one breath for all, and this air by which we are nourished. For this is what he says: “There is one spirit for all, and the human being has nothing more than cattle.”

Lest we think that this is also said of the soul, he added: “All things are made from the earth, and return to the earth.” Nothing except the body was made from the earth. It is specifically of the body that it is said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis III, 11).

But when he appears to say something blasphemous—“Who knows whether the spirit of the children of men goes upward, and whether the spirit of cattle goes downward into the earth?”—he is not claiming that, according to the dignity of the soul, there is no difference between cattle and the human being. Rather, by adding “who,” he wished to demonstrate the difficulty of the matter.

For in the holy Scriptures the pronoun “who” is always understood not of what is impossible, but of what is difficult. As in the passage: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah LIII, 8); and in the fourteenth Psalm: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, and who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Psalm XIV, 1), and the rest that follows.

And in Jeremiah, although the Hebrew is different: “And he is a man, and who shall know him?” (Jeremiah XVII, 9). [Note: Although the Hebrew is different. The Hebrew has *ve’anush hu*, “and incurable is it,” or “and afflicted is it”—that is, “the heart of all.” The Septuagint, however, read *enos* for *anush*, which signifies “man,” hence: “and he is man.” MARTIAN. The same Hebrew letters misled the Septuagint translators, since they can denote both “man” and “something incurable.”]

Therefore, the sole difference between human beings and beasts is that the human spirit ascends into heaven, while the spirit of cattle descends into the earth and is dissolved with the flesh—provided that some ecclesiastical man, instructed in heavenly disciplines and a certain assertor of a doubtful matter, establishes this.

This is the literal meaning for now.

As for the spiritual understanding: “The Lord will save both human beings and beasts” (Psalm XXXV, 7); and in another place: “I have become like a beast before you, yet I am always with you” (Psalm LXXII, 23). In all the Prophets, human beings and cattle are said to be saved [Al. “to have been saved”] in Jerusalem, and the land of promise is said to be filled with cattle and herds [Note: The second Palatine manuscript, omitting the word “promise,” substitutes, in a second hand, “for human beings.”].

Who knows whether the saint who is worthy to be called a human being ascends into heaven, and whether the sinner who is called a beast descends into the earth? For, given the uncertainty and slippery condition of this life, it can happen that the righteous falls and the sinner rises. Sometimes it happens that someone more rational and learned in the Scriptures—that is, a human being—does not live prudently or as his knowledge requires, and is led down to the underworld; while someone simpler and more rustic, who in comparison with a human being might be called a beast, lives better, is crowned by martyrdom, and becomes a citizen of Paradise.

And I saw that there is nothing good except that a person should rejoice in his work, for that is his portion.

Who, then, can bring him to see what will happen after him?

418 Instead of what we have placed—“to see what will happen after him”—Symmachus interpreted it more clearly, saying: “to see what will happen after these things” [Note: The same manuscript again reads: “to see what was previously going to happen”; incorrectly.].

There is therefore nothing good in this life except that a person rejoice in his work, giving alms and preparing treasures for himself in the kingdom of heaven. This is the only portion we possess, which neither thief nor robber nor tyrant can take away, and which follows us after death.

For when this life has been dissolved, we cannot again enjoy our labors, nor know what will happen afterward in the world.

Alternatively: Troubled by the preceding error, because I thought there was no difference between human beings and beasts, I was led by a perverse opinion [Note: In Alcuin: “I was led astray by a perverse opinion.”] to say that nothing else was good except to seize present pleasure. For once destruction had dissolved us, we could not enjoy those things from which we would depart ungratefully.

Others referred the statement, “Who can bring him to see what will happen after him?” to this interpretation: that it is better for a person to enjoy his own labors, because this alone he can carry away from his substance. When death comes, he does not know what kind of heir he will die leaving—whether a worthy or an unworthy one will enjoy his wealth.

[Col. 1044A] (Chapter IV.) And I turned [Note: Martianaeus: “And I turned myself,” although both our manuscripts and those used by him, as well as the Florentine manuscripts praised by Victorius, reject this. — “And I turned myself.” In the books previously published we read corruptly: “And I turned,” instead of “I turned myself,” as all the manuscripts read. MARTIAN.], and I saw all the oppressions that are committed under the sun. And behold, the tears of those who suffer oppression, and there is no one to comfort them; and power is in the hands of those who oppress them, and there is no comforter for them.

After this reflection I turned my mind and eyes there [Note: The adverb “there,” which Martianaeus had omitted, has been supplied from our manuscripts and Victorius’s edition.], so that I might see both the oppressors and those who suffer oppression. And behold, those who are unjustly oppressed by the powerful have only tears, which alone are permitted to them in their misfortunes, as witnesses to the resentment caused by their suffering; they cannot find a comforter.

And so that their misery and inconsolable grief might be the greater, the oppressors see themselves as stronger in their own iniquities [Note: “The oppressors appear stronger in their own.” The Corbie manuscripts read: “The oppressors seem stronger in their iniquities. And this is the reason why I cannot be consoled.” As though Jerome himself were saying these things about inconsolable grief on account of the power of the wicked. MARTIAN.]. And this is why they cannot be consoled.

David treats this passage more fully in Psalm 72, and Jeremiah in his own book [Note: The two Palatine manuscripts read: “they investigate.”].

[Col. 1044B] 419 And I praised the dead who are already dead above the living, whoever they may be who are still alive. And better than both of them is the one who has not yet been born, who has not yet seen the evil deed that is done under the sun.

[Note: Three of our manuscripts read: “who has not seen the work,” more closely following the Greek *ouk eide*.]

In comparison with the miseries that oppress mortals in this age, I judged the dead happier than the living, in accordance with what Job says when he discusses the underworld: “There the weary in body rest, with those who were once bound, now secure, no longer hearing the voice of the taskmaster” (Job 3:17–18). Better than these two—the living, that is, and the dead—is the one who has not yet been born. For one is still suffering evils, while the other has escaped naked, as it were, from a shipwreck. But the one who has not yet been born is happier in this respect: he has not yet experienced the evils of the world.

[Col. 1044C] [Note: Alcuin presents or explains this passage as follows: “But he says this not because the souls of human beings exist, according to the error of some, before a person is born into the world, but because it is better not to exist at all.” As for what Martianaeus thinks—that Jerome’s judgment here demolishes the foolish opinions of the Scholastics, who teach that for the most wretched human being it is preferable to exist rather than not to exist at all—this is disapproved not only by most philosophers but by Augustine himself, in Book III of *On Free Choice of the Will*, and after him by Thomas, Book II, Question 8, Article 1, reply to objection 3.]

But he says this not because the one who has not yet been born exists before he is born, and is happier because he has not yet been weighed down by the body, but because it is better not to exist at all, and not to possess the perception of existence, than either to exist or to live unhappily.

[Note: “But because it is better.” This passage demolishes the foolish Scholastic opinions and quibbles by which they try, before the unlearned, to prove that it is better for a person to exist and live in the greatest misery than not to exist at all. MARTIAN.]

So also the Lord speaks concerning Judas, indicating his future torments: “It would have been better for that man not to have been born” (Matthew 26:24)—that it would have been better for him not to exist at all than to endure eternal torments.

Others, however, understand this passage as follows: they say that those who are dead are better off than those who are living, even though they may previously have been sinners. For the living are still in battle and are, as it were, held confined in the prison of the body; but those who have suffered death are already secure and have ceased to sin. Thus John also, than whom no one was greater among those born of women (Matthew 2), “is less than the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven”; freed from the burden of the body, he does not have to say with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:14).

[Col. 1045A] Better than these two is the one who has not yet been born and has not seen the evils by which human beings are weighed down in the world. For our souls, before they descend into these bodies, dwell among the heavenly beings and remain blessed for as long as they are held in the heavenly Jerusalem and in the angelic choir.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript and the second Palatine manuscript have: “is least than he who is least in the kingdom,” and so forth.]

[Note: Whoever uttered this was Origen, whose error Jerome often refutes. See especially Letter 124 to Avitus, and the Paschal Letters of Theophilus, which the holy Doctor translated into Latin. In any case, three of our manuscripts lack the word “our.” These words—“our souls before they”—must not be attributed to Jerome, who vigorously refuted this error in his letter to Avitus. This Commentary is therefore Origenian, as is made entirely clear by the preceding words: “Others, however, understand this passage as follows,” and so forth. MARTIAN.]

420 And I saw all the labor and likewise all the excellence of work: for the rivalry of a man is with his companion; and this too is vanity and presumption of spirit.

[Note: Martianaeus reads *aemulatio viro*, contrary to the manuscripts, the printed books, and the text itself.]

I turned again to other things, and I saw all the strength and glory of those who labor; and I discovered that what is good for one person is evil for another, while the envious person is tormented by another’s happiness and the illustrious person is exposed to ambushes. For what is more vain, what more unstable and worthless, than people who do not weep over their own miseries or mourn their own sins, but envy those who are better?

[Note: Two manuscripts read *quid instar spiritus*—“what is like spirit”—and so forth.]

“The fool folds his hands together and eats his own flesh” (Proverbs 24).

This is the person who is also described in Proverbs as lazy, holding his chest in his hands. Poverty comes upon him like a swift runner, and because of extreme hunger—though this is said hyperbolically—he eats his own flesh. He thinks it better to have one handful of grain and live idle and sluggish than, while laboring, to fill both hands.

But the whole point of the discussion is to show that both the person who labors and possesses something is exposed to envy in the world, and again that the person who wishes to live peacefully is oppressed by poverty; and that both are miserable, since one is endangered because of his wealth while the other is worn down by want because of his poverty.

Or certainly this:

[Note: “Or certainly this: He who envies another’s…” I read the passage differently in the Corbie manuscripts, which have: “or certainly, if one envies another’s happiness,” and so forth. But the ancient reading of the printed books and of the other manuscript copies should be retained: “Or certainly this: He who…” MARTIAN.]

He who envies another’s happiness, and is carried away as though by the fury of a spirit, and has received envy into his bosom and nourished it in his heart—this person eats his own soul and his own flesh. For the happier he sees the person whom he envies, the more he himself withers and wastes away, gradually dripping away through jealousy and resentment.

Alternatively: hands are often understood as works, as in the passage: “The word of the Lord that came by the hand of Haggai” (Haggai 1:1)—whether referring to that prophet or to this one, because he performed such works that he was worthy for the word of the Lord to come through his work. David’s statement also agrees with this: “He trains my hands for battle” (Psalm 143:1).

[Col. 1045D] The fool, then, has folded his hands together—that is, he has contracted them and refused to extend them. Therefore he does not eat the labor of his hands, which he does not possess, but his own flesh, living according to the wisdom of the flesh and feeding upon the works of the flesh.

421 Better is one handful full with rest than both hands full of labor and presumption of spirit.

It is better to possess a little with righteousness than many riches belonging to sinners. And in Proverbs: “Better is a small possession with righteousness than abundant produce with iniquity” (Proverbs 16:8). Elegantly, righteousness has rest, while iniquity has labor. And because the singular number is always taken in a good sense, but the dual in an evil one, therefore one handful has rest, while two hands are full of labor.

And I turned, and I saw vanity under the sun. There is one, and there is not a second; indeed, he has neither son nor brother, and there is no end to all his labor. His eye is not satisfied [Alternatively: will be satisfied] with riches; and for whom do I labor and defraud [Alternatively: will defraud] my soul of goodness? But this too is vanity and a most grievous affliction.

I turned to others, and I saw them laboring more than necessary, gathering riches by lawful and unlawful means, yet not using what they had gathered; possessing everything, lying upon their riches, preserving them for another, and not enjoying the fruit of their own labor—especially when they had neither son nor brother nor relative for whom the labor of reserving necessities might appear dutiful.

[Note: “So that the labor of the one who reserves may appear dutiful,” and so forth. The printed editions have: “so that the labor of the one who reserves may appear necessary.” MARTIAN. One Vatican manuscript, together with the older printed editions, reads: “necessary labor for the one who reserves.” We have corrected some minor matters above and below.]

I therefore discovered that nothing is more vain than a person who gathers riches while not knowing to whom he will leave them.

This may also be understood, according to the preceding interpretation, of those who write books and leave them to fastidious readers.
