Some interpret the passage beginning, “There is one, and there is not a second,” as referring to the Savior: that he descended alone and without any companion to save the world. And although there are many sons of God and they are called his brothers by adoption, nevertheless no one proved worthy to be joined with him in this work. His labor has no end, since he bears our vices and sins and grieves for us; and his eye will not be satisfied with riches, since he continually desires our salvation and, the more he sees someone sin, the more he urges that person to repentance.

[Col. 1046D] [Note: The Vatican manuscript has: “Better are two than one,” and so forth. “Two are better than one.” One Corbie manuscript placed *meliores sunt duo*—“two are better”—in the margin, while the Colbert manuscript has it in the body of the translation. MARTIAN.]

Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if one falls, he will raise up his companion. But woe to the one who falls when there is no second person to raise him up. And if two sleep [Alternatively: have slept], they will also have warmth; but how will one person keep warm? And if one prevails against him, two will stand against him, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken [Alternatively: will be broken].

[Note: “After the anxieties and miseries…” Many manuscripts have: “After the miseries of solitude,” and so forth. MARTIAN.]

[Note: Together with the Vatican manuscripts, Alcuin, and the older printed editions: “the one who has been afflicted,” and so forth. MARTIAN.]

After the anxieties and miseries in which the man who torments himself by gathering wealth without a definite heir has been caught, the discussion now turns to companionship. It explains what good there is in the fellowship of friends and in mutual consolation: one person’s fall is lifted by another’s help, and even the household cares and the repose of the night are better managed by the person who has a faithful friend than by the one who lies upon his accumulated wealth.

[Note: All our manuscripts, Alcuin, and Victorius prefer this reading; Martianaeus, however, has: “But if a stronger person…” and shortly afterward omitted the word “one.”]

Even if a stronger enemy rises against one person, the weakness of the other is supported by the friend’s consolation. And just as two, if joined by love, differ from one, so the companionship of three is also more powerful. For true charity, violated by no envy, grows in strength as it increases in number. Let this suffice for now as a simple explanation.

Since in the preceding passage we presented the interpretation of some concerning Christ, the remaining points must also be discussed in the same order.

It is better for two to be together than for one. For it is better to have Christ dwelling within oneself than to dwell alone and be exposed to the ambushes of the adversary.

[Note: We supplied from three manuscripts—the Vatican and Palatine copies—the word “dwelling” and the particle “also,” which had been lacking until now.]

The reward of companionship is immediately shown in the benefit of the fellowship itself. For if one falls, Christ raises [Alternatively: will raise] his companion.

[Note: “He will raise his companion.” The printed editions corruptly have: “The companion will raise his associate,” since the Commentary clearly shows that Jerome read: “He will raise his companion.” See the allegorical exposition of Christ’s companionship. MARTIAN.]

Woe, then, to the person who, when he has fallen, does not have Christ within him to raise him.

[Note: Instead of *ei*—“to him”—the manuscripts have *uni*—“to the one.”]

And if one also sleeps—that is, if he has been released by death—and has Christ with him,

[Note: Two Corbie manuscripts read with the same meaning: “and has Christ as his second.” MARTIAN.]

then, having been warmed and given life,

[Note: Alcuin did not know the words “and is given life.” The manuscripts read “he will live again” in the future tense.]

he rises again more quickly. And if the devil, stronger in battle, stands against a human being, the human being will stand, and Christ also will stand for his human being, for his companion.

[Col. 1048A] 423 Not that the power of Christ alone is weak against the devil, but that human free will is left intact, and that, when we exert ourselves, he himself becomes stronger in battle.

And if the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit also come, this companionship is not quickly broken [Alternatively: will be broken].

[Note: “And a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” The four manuscript copies I use consistently retain *non facile rumpitur* or *rumpetur*—“is not easily broken” or “will not be easily broken.” Nevertheless, there is no doubt that *cito*, “quickly,” should be read, and not *facile*, “easily,” since Jerome himself twice reads “is not quickly broken” in his Commentary. In the Colbert manuscript I also found the following two verses, in which the monk who copied the book appears to complain about companionship:

“Superiors have wine; we taste vinegar.

For superiors, a threefold portion; for us, a single share.” MARTIAN.]

What is not quickly broken will nevertheless at some time be broken. Judas the Apostle also possessed this threefold cord; but because Satan entered him after the morsel, this cord was broken.

As for what he says above—“And if two sleep, they will also have warmth; but how will one keep warm?”—let us take the example of Elisha, who drew himself together with the boy, slept, warmed his little body, and thus gave life to the one who was rising again (4 Kings 4). Unless Christ therefore sleeps with us and rests in death, we cannot receive the warmth of eternal life.

A poor and wise child is better than an old and foolish king who does not know how to provide for the future.

[Note: The manuscripts have *qui nescivit*—“who did not know”—here and below, following Symmachus, and more correctly in relation to the Hebrew and Greek text. Shortly afterward, the Vatican and one Palatine manuscript have *in regem, ut regnet*—“into a king, so that he may reign”—whereas the older printed editions have only *ut regnet*—“so that he may reign”—instead of *in regem*. In Hebrew there is only the latter idea; in Greek, *tou basileusai*—“to reign.” Thus one reading is a gloss on the other.]

For he comes out of the house of prisoners to become king,

[Note: “He comes out to become king.” This is how the manuscript copies read; the printed editions have: “so that he may reign.” MARTIAN.]

because even in his kingdom he was born poor.

I saw all the living who walk under the sun with the second youth, who will rise in his place. There is no end to all the people, to all who were before them. And indeed those who come last will not rejoice in him; but this too is vanity and presumption of spirit.

Symmachus translated this passage as follows: “Better is a poor man with wisdom than an old and foolish king who does not know how to guard against change. For one comes out [Alternatively: came out] of prison to reign; the other, although born a king, has been oppressed by poverty. I saw all the living who walk under the sun with the second youth, who rose up in his place. All the people who existed before both of them were innumerable; and those who came afterward did not rejoice in him. But this too is breath and pursuit of wind.”

[Note: The Vatican has: “who will rise up in his place.” Then: “An innumerable people who…” without *omnis*, “all,” a word also deleted by a second hand in the second Palatine manuscript.]

My Hebrew teacher, whom I often mention, testified that when he was reading Ecclesiastes with me, Baracibam—whom the Hebrews especially admire—had handed down this interpretation of the present passage.

[Note: “These words, Baracibam.” This is a notable passage because of the name Baracciba, or Barachiba, the name of a certain celebrated teacher of the Hebrews, of whom no record has been preserved among the Talmudists or other Jewish writers. Therefore we should advise the prudent and diligent reader that there is no manuscript copy in which the name is read, according to Erasmus and Marianus, as *Barucheam*; rather, in all of them I have found it written either *Barachiam*, *Barachivam*, or *Baracchibam*. The oldest of all, the first hand of the Corbie manuscript, retained *Barachibam*, which an incompetent corrector changed to *Barachiam*. The Sorbonne manuscript reads *Barachivam*, but the Colbert manuscript more correctly has *Baracchibam*. Who this Baracciba was, whom the Hebrews in Jerome’s time most admired, I do not wish to guess, lest I propose about the son as many foolish things as a recent champion of ancient chronology proposed about his father Akiba. MARTIAN.]

In the manuscripts the name appears as *Baracchiban* or *Baracubivan*. This is the very famous Akibas, or Barakibas, about whom Jewish writers invented so many grand and numerous stories that it is astonishing that Martianaeus knew nothing about him, although he says he refrains from guessing lest he rashly impose anything upon his readers. So great was the fame of his name that the Hebrews claimed that Moses himself descended to hear Akiba and answered him when questioned. Rabbi Abraham Zacut, in the book *Succhasin*, says that just as the earlier law was received from Moses, so the whole Oral Law is attributed to Akiba.

Christian authors also mention him clearly and at length. Saint Epiphanius, in *Heresy* 15, counts him among the four fathers of Jewish traditions and calls him “their teacher, Akiban, so named, or Barakiban” (*didaskalon auton Akiban houto kaloumenon ē Barakiban*). In *Heresy* 33 he likewise calls him *Rabbi Akiba*, Rabbi Akiba. Jerome himself often praises him; in Letter 121 to Algasiam, Question 10, he says: “Barakibas, according to the understanding of the Hebrews, and Simeon and Hillel, our teachers…” In his Commentary on Isaiah, Book III, chapter 8, he simply calls him Akiba and says that from Shemaiah and Hillel arose the scribes and Pharisees, whose school Akiba took over; Aquila the proselyte is said to have been his student, and so forth. From this it may also be inferred that he flourished around the time of Hadrian. See our notes on the cited passage in the Letter to Algasiam and in the Commentary on Isaiah.

The better inner person, who arises in us after the fourteenth year of puberty, is better than the outer person who was born from his mother’s womb: the latter does not know how to withdraw from vice, and he came out of the house of prisoners—that is, from his mother’s womb—in order to reign [Alternatively: reigns] in vices.

[Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, has “in posterity.” Our manuscripts, however, have *potestate*—“in power”—and Victorius says that the Brixian copies likewise preserve this as the true reading. He explains the words “because even in his kingdom he was born poor.” The word *potestas*, “power,” suits the passage better than *posteritas*, “posterity.” The context of the later exposition by Saint Gregory of Neocaesarea also proves that this should be restored. Alcuin formerly read or altered it by conjecture as: “who was made poor in his nature, possessing no wisdom and carrying out all evils.” Then: “I saw,” and so forth.]

I saw those who lived in the former person and afterward dwelt with the second person, namely, the one who was generated in place of the former predecessor. And I understood that all had sinned in the former person before, when, with the second being born, two persons came to exist.

But because they turned toward better things and, after the philosophers’ letter Y, abandoned the left-hand path and pressed toward the right-hand summit,

[Note: “And after the letter Y.” The manuscripts omit the words “the letter Y,” although the letter may at times have been written, as can easily be shown from the reading of the Corbie copies: “and they, after the letter of the philosophers…” Ancient copyists, not understanding the mystery of this element, changed Y into *hi*. Hence in the manuscripts mentioned above we find “and they, after the letter,” instead of “and after the letter Y.” MARTIAN.]

and followed the second—that is, the later—person, they will not rejoice in him, that is, in the former person.

The Apostle also bears witness to these two persons (2 Thessalonians 2), and Leviticus does not remain silent: “If a person, a person, wishes this or that” (Leviticus 17).

[Note: “If a person, a person, wishes.” Elsewhere we read: “if he wishes this or that.” Shortly afterward appears the expression “Origen’s assistant,” but this is clearly an error. For who does not know that Gregory, bishop of Pontus, was Origen’s auditor—that is, his disciple? MARTIAN.

Two Palatine manuscripts and the Vatican read: “if he vows this or that.”]

The holy man Gregory, bishop of Pontus, a disciple of Origen, understood this passage in his paraphrase of Ecclesiastes as follows:

“I, however, prefer a poor and wise youth to an old and foolish king, to whom it has never occurred that it is possible for anyone whom he had bound to come out of prison into kingship, and for him himself afterward to fall from his unjust authority.

For it sometimes happens that those who were under the wise youth are without sorrow, although they had previously been under an old king. But those who were born afterward, because they did not know the earlier evils, can neither praise the youth who later rose up, having been carried away by a perverse opinion and the impulse of the opposing spirit.”

[Note: “I, however, prefer a youth,” and so forth. Erasmus and Marianus printed this passage in a thoroughly corrupted form, reading: “I, however, understand a poor and wise youth to be better than an old and foolish king.” These words were not spoken by Gregory Thaumaturgus. I restored the text with the aid of the Greek context of the holy man and manuscripts of excellent quality. The Greek has *ego de prokrino*, that is, “I prefer” or “I place first.” MARTIAN.

One Palatine manuscript has: “and wise, better than an old king and a fool.”]

[Note: “The Laodicean Interpreter,” and so forth. This is Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, who wrote innumerable volumes on the Holy Scriptures. Consult the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. MARTIAN.]

The Laodicean Interpreter, striving to express great matters in a brief discourse, spoke here also in his customary manner:

“Ecclesiastes is now speaking of the transformation of good things into evils, attempting to portray the foolish person who, giving no thought to the future, delights in present and fleeting things as though they were great and everlasting.

And after the various things that commonly happen to human beings in their life and undergo change, he introduces a general judgment concerning death: an innumerable multitude perishes, is gradually brought to an end, and passes away, each person leaving another in his place, and again another successor dying.”

[Note: “And after various things,” and so forth. The Corbie manuscripts have: “And through the various things that…,” and so forth. MARTIAN.]

Origen and Victorinus did not think very differently from one another. After that general judgment, which is evident to everyone—that a poor and wise youth is better than an old and foolish king, and that it frequently happens that the youth, through his wisdom, even comes out of the king’s prison and rules in place of the perverse ruler, while the foolish king loses the authority he held—they interpreted this passage concerning Christ and the devil, intending the poor and wise youth to be Christ.

He is called a youth in accordance with the words: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isaiah 49:6). He is called poor because, although he was rich, he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). He is called wise because he “increased in age and wisdom and grace with God and human beings” (Luke 2:52).

He was born in the kingdom of the old man. Therefore he says: “If my kingdom were of this world, my ministers would certainly fight for me, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from this world” (John 18:36).

Thus, in the kingdom of that foolish old man who showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, the excellent child was born. He came forth from the house of prisoners, concerning whom Jeremiah speaks in the Lamentations: “To humble beneath his feet all the prisoners of the earth” (Lamentations 3:34). He advanced to kingship, went away into a distant country, and after some time returned as king against those who did not want him to reign over them.

Therefore Ecclesiastes, with prophetic spirit, saw all the living who could become companions of the youth who says: “I am the life” (John 14:6), leaving behind the old foolish king and following Christ.

At the same time, two peoples of Israel are signified: the first, which existed before the Lord’s coming, and the later one, which will receive the Antichrist in place of Christ. The former is not utterly rejected—for the first Church was gathered from Jews and Apostles—and at the end the Jews who will receive the Antichrist in place of Christ will not rejoice in Christ.

“Guard your foot when you go into the house of God, and draw near in order to hear. For the sacrifice of fools is a gift,” because they do not know that they are doing evil.

[Note: “For the sacrifice of fools is a gift.” The older editions now overturn the context, in which we read with the opposite meaning: “For above the gift of fools is your sacrifice,” and so forth. MARTIAN.]

He gives commands for life and does not want us to offend when we go to church. It is not entering the house of God itself that is praiseworthy, but entering without offense. And if everyone who is in the Church of God were to hear, he would never have added: “Draw near in order to hear” (Exodus 24:2 and following).

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “and if it were for all who are in the Church to hear the word and the divine mysteries, he would never….” Alcuin has: “and if it were for all to hear the word and the divine mysteries, he would never….”]

Finally, Moses alone drew near to hear God; the others were unable to approach. Fools, not knowing that this is a remedy for sin, think that they can satisfy God by offering gifts, and they do not understand that this too is evil and sin: to wish to correct what they have done not through obedience and good works but through gifts and sacrifices.

This agrees with the statement found elsewhere: “Obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:21). And: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).

(Chapter V.) “Do not be hasty with your mouth, and do not let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, because God is in heaven and you are upon the earth. Therefore let your words be few, because a dream comes through an abundance of anxiety, and the voice of a fool through a multiplication of words.”

[Note: I restore *ad proferendum sermonem*—“to utter a word”—from the Vatican and one Palatine manuscript, as Jerome himself translated it from the Hebrew. Martianaeus, apparently following the Greek *tou exenegkai*, had *ad perferendum*—“to bring forth.”]

Most people think that this passage commands us not to promise anything rashly before God and not to vow, without considering our strength, what we cannot fulfill. God is present, they say, and although he seems to be in heaven while we are on earth, he nevertheless hears what we say, and our foolishness is exposed by the multiplication of our words.

Others, understanding the passage better, assert that it commands us not to think or speak more about God than we are able to do, but to recognize our weakness: just as far as heaven is from earth, so far is our understanding separated from his nature. Therefore our words ought to be measured.

For just as the person occupied with many thoughts frequently dreams about the things he is thinking of, so the person who wishes to say too much about divinity falls into foolishness.

Or certainly it may be understood in this way: our words ought to be few because even what we think we know we see “through a mirror and in an enigma,” and grasp as though it were a dream—something we imagine we hold firmly. And when we have said more than seemed proper to us, the end of our discussion is foolishness. For through much speaking we do not escape sin.

When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because there is no will among fools. Whatever you vow, fulfill. It is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill.

[Note: The printed editions have: “When you have vowed a vow.” But the difference is slight, and there is no change in meaning. MARTIAN.]

The straightforward meaning requires no interpretation. It is better not to promise than not to do what one has promised, because those who do not fulfill their vows displease God and are counted among fools.

When he says, “There is no will among fools,” “of God” is understood, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “And certainly it was not my will to come to you now” (1 Corinthians 16:22).

But if we wish to say something more searching, the Christian is commanded to complete faith through works and not to resemble the Jews, who promised and said: “Everything that the Lord has commanded, we will do” (Exodus 24:3), yet worshiped idols. After beating the servants and stoning them, they finally killed the son of the householder himself.

It is therefore better to weigh an uncertain judgment for a long time than to be facile in words and difficult in deeds.

[Note: “To weigh an uncertain judgment for a long time,” and so forth. Previously the reading was: “to deliberate for a long time over an uncertain judgment.” We have followed the manuscript copies, which consistently retain “to weigh the judgment,” not “to deliberate over the judgment.” MARTIAN.]

For the servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten with many blows (Luke 12:47).

[Note: One Vatican manuscript has: “and does not do it, will be beaten with many blows.”]

Do not give your mouth the power to make your flesh sin. And do not say before the angel, “It was ignorance”; lest God become angry at your voice and destroy the works of your hands.

[Note: Two Palatine manuscripts and the Vatican manuscript read “so that it may make [your flesh] sin,” here and below; and shortly afterward, “lest he scatter,” in place of “lest he destroy.”]

The Hebrew understood it as follows: “What you cannot do, do not promise.” For words do not pass away into the wind; rather, they are immediately carried by the present angel, who accompanies each person, to the Lord. And you, who think that God does not know what you promised, provoke him to anger, so that all your works may be destroyed.

But in the words, “So that you do not cause your flesh to sin,” he understood the passage without close examination, as though Ecclesiastes had said: “Do not give your mouth so that you do not sin.”

[Note: “Do not give your mouth the power not to sin.” In the earlier printed books this passage cannot be understood because of the absence of the negative particle. Nor could Jerome have said that his Hebrew teacher had not carefully examined the statement if he understood it as though Ecclesiastes had said: “Do not give your mouth the power to sin.” For “to sin” means the same as “to make your flesh sin.” The Hebrew therefore examined the sacred text with less care at the point where he thought that the negative particle *lo*, “not,” was expressed or understood in the words “so that you do not sin.” This reading agrees perfectly with the preceding interpretation of the same Hebrew teacher: “What you cannot do, do not promise.” That is, “Do not give your mouth to making promises rashly, so that you promise what you cannot do and sin by failing to fulfill what you promised.” Let us therefore read with the manuscript copies: “so that you do not sin,” because in this way the Hebrew’s meaning becomes clear. MARTIAN.]

But to us the meaning seems different: those are being reproved who complain about the vice of the flesh and say that they are compelled by bodily necessity to do what they do not wish to do, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “For I do not do what I want, but what I do not want,” and so forth (Romans 7:15).

[Note: “Those who complain about the vice of the flesh.” The Colbert manuscript has: “those who complain about the God of the flesh.” The Corbie manuscripts have: “those who complain about the force of the flesh.” MARTIAN.]

“Do not seek,” he says, “vain excuses or give your flesh an occasion for sin, saying: ‘It is not I who sin, but sin that dwells in my flesh.’”

Finally, where he says, “Do not say before the angel, ‘It was ignorance,’” Aquila, translating the Hebrew word *segaga*—“ignorance”—rendered it as *akousion* (ἀκούσιον), that is, “involuntary.”

[Note: “The Hebrew word *segaga*.” In Erasmus the Hebrew name is completely corrupted and altered: instead of *segaga* he reads *senana*, with a double nun in place of the double gimel. This is undoubtedly a typographical error. The Corbie manuscripts read *segoga*. MARTIAN.]

“For if,” he says, “you say this, you provoke God as though he were the author of evil and sin, so that, angered, he may take away from your hands whatever good you appear to possess.”

Or, if you hold such a view, he may hand you over to a depraved mind, so that you do the things that are improper.

Because of the multitude of dreams and vanities, there are also many words. But fear God.

The Hebrews explain this passage as follows: “Do not do what was said above, namely, do not readily believe dreams. For when you see various things during the repose of night, and your soul has been shaken by various terrors or stirred by promises, disregard what belongs to dreams. Fear God alone.” For whoever believes dreams gives himself over to vanities and foolishness.

Alternatively: “Because I said and commanded, ‘Do not give your mouth occasion to make your flesh sin, and do not seek various excuses,’ I now add that, in the sleep of this life and in the image of the shadow of a cloud[2] in which we live, we can find many things that seem plausible to us and that excuse our sins. Therefore I warn you to take care only that you do not think God absent, but fear him and know that he is present with all your actions; and that, having been created with free will, you are not compelled, but willingly do what you do.”

[2] [Col. 1054C] “And in the image of the shadow of a cloud.” The same copies preserve here another reading, namely the following: [Col. 1054D] “Because in the sleep of this life, and in image, shadow, and cloud, we live, we can find many things …” —Martian.

If you see the oppression of the poor, and the robbery of justice, and injustices in the province, do not be amazed at the matter, because one who is exalted watches over one who is exalted, and one higher than they watches over them, and over all there is the king in the cultivated field.[3]

[3] [Col. 1054D] “And the robbery of justice.” Earlier printed books had “and the ruin of justice,” but wrongly; for in Hebrew we read *wenezel misphat*, “and the robbery of justice,” in agreement with all the manuscripts of Jerome and with the Septuagint translators, who rendered it, “and the seizure of judgment” (*καὶ ἁρπαγὴν κρίματος*). —Martian.

The Vatican manuscript reads: “and the robbery of justice, and you see injustice in the province”; and shortly afterward, together with two Palatine manuscripts: “the exalted watches over the exalted, and those higher than them.”

[Col. 1054D] “Because one who is exalted watches over one who is exalted.” The Corbie manuscripts read: “Because the exalted is over the exalted, and the one higher is over them, and above all the earth there is a king in the cultivated field.” —Martian.

The seamless tunic of Christ, woven from above (John 19; Luke 8), could not be torn by those crucifying him; and he commanded the man from whom the Savior had driven out demons to depart clothed in the garments of the apostles. Let us therefore strive not to tear the clothing of our Ecclesiastes, nor, according to our own preference, sew together patches of opinions from here and there, but preserve one continuous texture of argument, following the same meaning and order.

Above he had said: “Do not say in the presence of the angel, ‘It was ignorance,’ lest God become angry at your words,” and the rest. He had been speaking against those who denied that human affairs are governed by providence. Since, then, a question arose against this command—why the righteous should suffer oppression, why unjust judgments should be made throughout the world, and why God should not avenge them—he now introduces and resolves what could be objected, saying:[4]

“If you see the oppression of the poor”—the poor man who is proclaimed blessed in the Gospel—and property being violently carried off rather than administered by justice, do not be amazed or think that something strange is happening.[5] For God, the one exalted above the exalted, observes these things; he has placed his angels over the judges and kings of the earth,[6] and they can indeed prevent injustice and have greater power on earth than any human authorities.

[4] [Col. 1054D] The same three manuscripts read: “Since, then, this question arose against this command,” some adding “those”; “and why the righteous,” and so forth.

[5] [Col. 1054D] Thus we emend with the aid of three manuscripts, in which *vigeri* is written as one word; we have made it two words, *vi geri*. Until now it had been read as the single word *vigere*, in a useless and erroneous sense.

[6] [Col. 1055C] “He placed them over the judges and kings of the earth.” This preposition was missing in the text, though it produces a different meaning. There is a great difference between “angels, whom he placed above the kings of the earth” and “angels, whom he placed over the kings of the earth.” —Martian.

But because he reserves judgment for the end and for the consummation of the world, when the ripe harvest has come and the reapers arrive, and he will command that the wheat be separated and the weeds be handed over to the fire, he now waits and postpones the sentence until the field of this world has been fully cultivated.[5] That “field” means “the world” the Lord explained in the parable of the weeds and the wheat (Matthew 13).

[5] [Col. 1055C] Three manuscripts read: “until the field of this world has been more fully cultivated.”

Whoever loves silver will not be satisfied with silver, and whoever loves wealth will not enjoy it. This too is vanity. For when goods are multiplied, many consume them,[6] and what advantage is there for their possessor except to see them with his own eyes?

[6] [Col. 1055C] One Vatican manuscript reads: “who eat of them.”

Wherever we have “silver,” because of the ambiguity of the Greek expression, it may also be translated “money”; for *ἀργύριον* signifies both. Cicero, moreover, reports that those who possessed more *peculia* were originally called “wealthy,” that is, “owners of livestock.”[7] In ancient times they called them this. Gradually, through misuse, the word came to be applied to something else.

[7] [Col. 1055C] Until this point the text had read: “who are designated as having possessed more *peculiae*, that is, cattle,” but our manuscripts contradict this; none of them contains the final word. When it was deleted and *habuissent* was substituted for *habuisse*, the construction became smoother. These manuscripts read *pecuia* rather than *peculia*. See also Nonius, cited by Martian.

[Col. 1055D] “Moreover, Cicero on this subject …” Nonius says that M. Tullius Cicero explained the distinction between the wealthy and the rich in *On Old Age*: he asserted that people were called wealthy (*pecuniosi*) from livestock (*pecus*), and rich (*locupletes*) from possessions of land; at that time wealth consisted in sheep, cattle, and possession of land, from which they were called *pecuniosi* and *locupletes*. —Martian.

Thus the miser is described as never being filled with riches; the more he possesses, the more he desires. Flaccus likewise agrees with this judgment when he says (Horace, Book 1 of the *Epistles*, Epistle 2 to Lollius): “The miser is always in need.”[8]

[8] [Col. 1055D] “Flaccus likewise on this matter …” Flaccus, that is, Horace, *Epistles* 1.2:

> Spurn pleasures; pleasure purchased by pain is harmful.  
> The miser is always in need. Set a definite limit to your desires.  
> The envious man wastes away at another’s prosperous fortunes.

And the noble historian says that avarice is diminished neither by poverty nor by abundance.[9]

[9] [Col. 1055D] “And the noble historian.” Sallust, *Catiline* 11. See what we noted in Epistle 108, section 19.

[Col. 1056C] He repeats the same point in the *Epitaph for Mother Paula*, saying: “He would not, through the habit of possessing more, make room for avarice, which is satisfied by no riches, and the more it has, the more it demands; neither abundance nor poverty diminishes it.” These are the words of Sallust in *The Conspiracy of Catiline*, pages 8–9, where the noble historian says: “Since he lacks good qualities, he strives by deceit and treachery. Avarice is a desire for money, which no wise person has coveted. As though steeped in evil poisons, it effeminates body and manly soul; it is always boundless and insatiable, and is diminished neither by abundance nor by poverty.” —Martian.

Therefore, Ecclesiastes says, riches benefit their possessor in no way except that he sees what he possesses. For the greater his substance, the more servants he will have to consume the wealth he has amassed. He himself, however, merely sees what he has and cannot take in more than one person’s food.

Sweet is the sleep of the laborer, whether he has eaten little or more. But the abundance of the rich does not allow him to sleep.

The subject is still the rich and the miser. He is compared with the laborer who sleeps without anxiety, whether he has eaten little or much, because the laborer, through the toil and sweat of his work, digests whatever food he has and enjoys sweet sleep. The rich man, however, distended by banquets and torn by thoughts in different directions, cannot sleep, as his excess of food surges within him,[10] and undigested food burns in the narrow confines of his stomach.

[10] [Col. 1056C] One Vatican and two Palatine manuscripts read: “and the undigested food burns in the narrow confines of the stomach.”

Since sleep is also a name for the common departure from this life, the rest of the one who works in the present and conducts himself according to his strength in good works will be better than the riches of those of whom it is written: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation” (Luke 6:24).[11]

[11] [Col. 1056D] The same manuscripts read: “Woe to you who are rich, because …”

There is a most grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches guarded by their owner to his own harm.[12] And those riches perished in a most grievous misfortune. He fathered a son, and he has nothing in his hands.[13]

[12] [Col. 1056D] The words “and those riches perished” are absent from the Vatican manuscript. A few minor corrections are made below.

[13] [Col. 1056D] The Vatican adds: “And what advantage is there for their possessor except to see them with his own eyes.” It then reads *egressus* (“having gone out”) instead of *exivit* (“he went out”), as does one of the Palatine manuscripts in the margin.

As he came forth from his mother’s womb, naked he will return as he came,[14] and he will take nothing from his labor to carry away in his hands. This too is a most grievous evil: as he came, so he goes. What more will he have, since he labored for the wind? And throughout all his days he will eat in darkness, in great indignation, sickness, and anger.

[14] [Col. 1056D] “Naked he will return as he came.” You can easily see how numerous and frequent are the corruptions of both the sacred text and Jerome’s commentaries in earlier printed books from the notes that follow. At this point they first read: “Naked he will return, to take them as he came, and he takes nothing from his labor to hold in his hand. This too is vanity and a most grievous evil; for as he came, so he departed. What abundance belongs to him who labors for the wind? And throughout all his days he eats in darkness, in grief, much anger, sickness, and madness.” —Martian.

Join to the preceding what follows: Ecclesiastes is describing the rich man who cannot himself enjoy his riches and frequently comes into danger because of them, nor leave to his heir what he has gathered; both he and his son, just as they came naked, so return naked to the earth, and none of the results of their labors accompanies them.

Is it not a most grievous evil to be tormented by anxious thoughts on account of riches, and to seek with sadness, groaning, indignation, quarrels, and fruitless labor wealth that will perish and that we cannot take away with us when we die? This is according to the literal sense.

But, to rise to a higher interpretation, it seems to me that he is speaking of philosophers or heretics who gather the riches of doctrines to their own harm and can obtain no benefit themselves, nor leave their followers any lasting fruit. They and their disciples return to the earth and lose their riches from the one who said: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the understanding” (1 Corinthians 1:19).[15]

[15] [Col. 1057D] “I will reject the understanding of the understanding.” Here some copies add: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age? Has not God made the wisdom of this world foolish?” and the rest. —Martian.

For truly, just as they came forth from their mother’s womb—namely, from the perverse Church[16] and its contrary, of which it is written: “But the Jerusalem above is free; she is the mother of us all” (Galatians 4:26)[17]—so they will go naked into the wind and labor for nothing. They have failed while searching with investigation, are carried about by every wind of doctrine, have no light, but eat their mysteries in darkness. They are always in sickness and always in anger, storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, and they do not have God’s favor.

[16] [Col. 1057D] The same Vatican manuscript reads: “which has been crushed by her from whom …”

[17] [Col. 1057D] “She is the mother of us all.” With similar boldness they added after *nostrum* the following text: “And of her it is written: ‘Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband.’ Thus naked they go …” —Martian.

Behold what I myself have seen to be good—indeed, what is most excellent: to eat and drink and experience enjoyment in all one’s labor with which one labors under the sun during the number of the days of one’s life that God has given; for this is his portion.

And every person to whom God has given riches and possessions, and has granted the ability to eat from them, take his portion, and rejoice in his labor—this is God’s gift. For he will not remember the days of his life for long, because God occupies his heart with joy.

In comparison with the man who consumes his wealth amid the darkness of anxieties and carries perishable things with great weariness of life, he declares better the one who enjoys present goods. For the latter has at least a small pleasure in enjoyment; the former has only anxiety from the magnitude of his possessions. He gives the reason why it is God’s gift to be able to enjoy riches:[18] “Because he will not remember the days of his life for long.” God draws him away into the joy of his heart; he will not be in sadness or tormented by thoughts, being carried away by present joy and pleasure.

[18] [Col. 1058D] The word *frui* (“to enjoy”) is supported by four manuscripts, which we follow.

But it is better, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 10:3), to understand this as the spiritual food and spiritual drink given by God, and to see goodness in all one’s labor, because through great labor and study we can contemplate true goods. This is our portion: to rejoice in our study and labor. Although this is good, it is not yet fully good until Christ, our life, is manifested. Therefore he will not remember the days of our life for long. It should also be noted that here *περισπασμός* (“distraction” or “occupation”) is taken in the better sense, as occupation with spiritual and true joy.

## Chapter 6

There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it is common among human beings: a man to whom God has given riches, possessions, and glory, and whose soul lacks nothing of all that it desired, yet God has not given him the power to eat from it; instead, a stranger consumes it. This is vanity and a most grievous evil.

If a man fathers a hundred children[19] and lives many years, and the days of his years are numerous, but his soul is not satisfied with good things and he has no burial, I said that an untimely birth is better than he. For it comes in vanity and departs in darkness, and its name is hidden in darkness. Indeed, it has not seen the sun or known it; its rest is greater than his. And if he lives a thousand years twice over, but sees no goodness, do not all go to one place?

[19] [Col. 1058D] Two Palatine manuscripts add “children”; the Vatican has “sons.”

He describes the miserly rich man and asserts that this evil is common among people: nothing that is considered good in the world is lacking to him, yet through the most foolish frugality he torments himself, preserving things for others to devour. He adds hyperbolically that even if he fathers a hundred children and lives not, like Adam, nearly a thousand years, but two thousand years, while his soul wastes away through desire and avarice, he is in a far worse condition than an untimely birth, which, as soon as it seems to have been born, perishes.

The latter sees neither evils nor goods; the former, although he possesses goods, is always tormented by sorrows and anxious thoughts. The untimely birth therefore has greater rest than that long-lived miser. Yet both are carried away to the same end,[21] since both are removed by a similar death.

[21] [Col. 1058D] Four manuscripts have this reading. Earlier the text had *rapiuntur* (“are seized”).

This may also be understood of Israel: God gave it the Law, the Prophets, the Testament, and the promise, while the Savior says: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21:43).[22] All these things have been transferred to another and foreign people from the nations, and they see their goods without enjoying them.

[22] [Col. 1058D] Victor adds: “And whoever falls upon this stone will be shattered; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.”

We are in a much better condition, we who were regarded by them as untimely births and newborns, while they applauded themselves in their antiquity, boasting of their fathers and saying: “Our father is Abraham” (John 8:39). Yet both they and we hasten to one place, that is, to the judgment of God.

As for the statement in the middle, “And he had no burial,” it may mean that the rich man does not think about his death and, although he possesses everything, is miserly even in constructing a tomb; or that, often murdered because of these riches by ambushes, he is cast away unburied; or—what I think better—that he has performed no good deed[23] by which he might acquire a memorial among later generations and not pass through life in silence like the animals, although he had the means by which it could become evident that he had lived.

[23] [Col. 1059D] Alcuin has: “that he has done nothing good or honorable,” and so forth. Victor has: “that he has done nothing and acquired no honor,” and so forth.

All the labor of a person is for his mouth, yet his soul is not satisfied.[24] For what advantage does the wise man have over the fool, or the poor man, except knowing how to go against life?

[24] [Col. 1059D] The manuscripts read: “his soul will not be satisfied,” and so forth.

Everything people labor for in this world is consumed by the mouth, worn down by the teeth and handed over to the belly for digestion. When it has pleased the throat for a little while, it seems to provide pleasure only as long as it is held there. But when it has passed into the intestines, there is no longer any distinction among foods.

After all this, the soul of the eater is not satisfied—either because it again desires what it has eaten, and both wise and foolish cannot live without food, while the poor man seeks nothing except how he can sustain the organ of his little body and not perish from hunger; or because the soul gains no benefit from the nourishment of the body, food is common to wise and foolish alike, and the poor man goes where he sees that wealth exists.

It is better, however, to understand this of the ecclesiastical man who, instructed in the heavenly Scriptures, has all his labor in his mouth, and whose soul is not satisfied because he always desires to learn. In this respect the wise man has more than the foolish: because, realizing that he is poor—for the poor man is the one called blessed in the Gospel—he hastens to grasp the things that belong to life. He walks on the narrow and constricted way that leads to life, is poor in evil works, and knows where Christ, who is life, dwells.

Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the soul. This too is vanity and presumption of spirit.

Symmachus interpreted this clearly, saying: “It is better to foresee than to walk as one pleases”;[26] that is, it is better to do everything according to understanding, which is the eye of the soul, than to follow the desire of the heart.[27]

[26] [Col. 1059D] The Vatican reads: “than to follow the desire of his own heart.”

[27] [Col. 1059D] “To walk in the soul” means what Ezekiel says: “Those who walk in the desire of their heart” (Ezekiel 2:21).

Alternatively, he rebukes the proud person who pleases himself and says that the one who foresees everything is better than the person who approves nothing unless he himself has done it. Nothing is worse than such a person, and nothing is emptier than every wind.

Again, here Aquila and Theodotion interpreted “presumption of spirit” as “feeding on wind”; Symmachus, however, rendered it “affliction of spirit.” It should be known that among the Hebrews “spirit” and “wind” are called by the same word, namely *RUHA*.[28]

[28] [Col. 1059D] “Namely, *RUHA*.” In all the manuscript copies I found *Ruha* written with an *h* in the middle, although elsewhere the Hebrew name is written without aspiration, *rua*, rather than *ruha*. Yet no learned person denies that both forms may be read and written. —Martian.

What is to happen has already been named, and its name has been recognized, because it is human, and it cannot contend in judgment with one stronger than itself.

This is plainly proclaimed concerning the coming of the Savior: he who was to come, before he was seen in the body, already had his name called in the Scriptures and was known to the prophets and saints of God; for he is human, and, insofar as he is human, he cannot compare himself with the Father, and in the Gospel he says: “The Father who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28).

Therefore, in what follows, we are commanded not to inquire beyond what has been written about him, lest a human being wish to know more than Scripture has testified. Since we do not know our own condition, since our life passes like a shadow, and since the future is uncertain, it is not useful for us to inquire into things greater than we can comprehend.

Some think that this passage means that God already knows the name of all who are to come and are to be enclosed in human bodies,[29] and that a human being cannot answer against his Maker, asking why he was made this way or that.

[29] [Col. 1059D] The Vatican reading is preferable: “and of the human being enclosed in a body, God already knows …”

For the more we inquire, the more our vanity and superfluous words are revealed. Free will is not taken away by God’s foreknowledge; rather, causes precede, explaining why each thing was made as it was.

Because there are many words multiplying vanity, what more is there for a person?[30] For who knows what is good for a person in life, during the number of the days of the life of his vanity? And he makes them like a shadow, for who will announce to a person what will happen after him under the sun?

[30] [Col. 1060D] Three of our manuscripts lack the word *multa* (“many”).

[Col. 1060D] “What more is there for a person?” This is the beginning of chapter 7 in the Vulgate Latin, but the ancients followed other divisions of the sacred text, as this passage most clearly proves. Consult the Prolegomena that we published in Jerome’s *Divine Library*, where this matter is discussed at length. —Martian.

Since, he says, a person is ignorant of his own condition, and since whatever he seems to know and see he sees not as the truth of the matter actually is, but through a mirror, a shadow, and an image; since he does not know the future and does not escape sin through much speaking, let him place silence upon his mouth and believe that the one who was written of has come, without asking how, how great, or what kind of person he came.

## Chapter 7

A good name is better than good oil, and the day of death than the day of his birth.

Consider, he says, O human being, that your days are brief and that soon, once the flesh has been dissolved, you will cease to exist. Make a reputation for yourself that will last longer, so that, just as ointment delights the nostrils with its fragrance, all posterity may be delighted by your name.[31]

[31] [Col. 1060D] Alcuin reads: “so that all posterity may be delighted by your name.”

Symmachus interpreted this plainly, saying: “A good name is better than fragrant ointment.” It is customary among the Hebrews to call good ointment “oil.”

As for the statement, “and the day of death than the day of his birth,” it may show that it is better to depart from the world and be free from tribulations and the uncertainty of life than to enter the world and endure all these things. Or it may mean that at death what we are is known, whereas at the beginning of birth it is unknown what we will become. Or it may mean that birth binds the freedom of the soul to the body, while death releases it.

It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, for that is the end of every person; and the living person will take it to heart.

It is more useful to go to a funeral than to a banquet, because there we are reminded, by the corpse before us, of our condition and human frailty. In the joy of a banquet, however, even if we seemed to have some fear, we lose it.[32]

[32] [Col. 1061D] Alcuin, along with the books printed before Martian, reads: “because there, through remembrance of our condition …”; shortly afterward: “but in banquets and joy.” “Because there, through remembrance of our condition.” The printed editions add this superfluously. —Martian.

Symmachus interpreted the final verse more clearly, saying: “And the living person will look back toward the mind.”

From this it is shown that when, above, he seemed to approve food and drink, he did not place pleasure in all things, as many wrongly think; rather, in comparison with avarice and excessive frugality, even brief enjoyment is preferable, if someone enjoys his possessions even for a moment. For he would never have preferred the sadness of mourning to the festivity of a banquet if he had thought that drinking and eating were of no importance.[33]

[33] [Col. 1061D] The Vatican reads: “He would never have preferred sadness to mourning, but a banquet to festivity.”

Better is anger than laughter, because through the sorrow of the face the heart is corrected.

Laughter dissolves the one who laughs; anger seizes and corrects him. Let us be angry with ourselves when we sin, and angry also with others. Through sadness of countenance the mind will become better, as Symmachus interpreted it. Hence: “Woe to you who laugh now, because you will mourn” (Luke 6:25).

The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of fools is in the house of joy.

“Blessed,” says the Savior, “are those who mourn, because they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:5). Samuel also mourned King Saul all the days of his life (2 Samuel 16). Paul says that he mourned over those who, after various sins, had refused to repent (2 Corinthians 12).

Let the heart of the wise therefore go to the house of such a man as rebukes himself when he sins, so that he may be brought to tears and prompted to weep over his own sins. Let him not go to the house of joy, where the teacher flatters and deceives, where he seeks not the conversion of his hearers but applause and praise.

Such a teacher is to be mourned: rich in speech and rich in words, but not rich in deeds.[34] Since he has been filled, he therefore receives his consolation.

[34] [Col. 1061D] Alcuin and the earlier printed books again read: “not rich in deeds.”

The following verses also agree with this interpretation. For he says:

It is better to hear the correction of a wise man than a man hearing the song of fools. For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of a fool. This too is vanity.

It is better to be corrected by a wise man than to be deceived by flattering praise. Similar is the saying: “Better are the wounds of a friend than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6).

Just as burning thorns beneath a pot produce an unpleasant noise, so the words of a teacher who merely pats his hearer will not benefit him—whether the teacher is exhorting his hearers concerning worldly cares, which are interpreted as thorns, or preparing them for the fire to come.[35]

[35] [Col. 1061D] The Vatican reads: “concerning the cares of the world.”

For what we have rendered, “For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of a fool,” Symmachus, interpreting the meaning discussed above, says: “Through the voice of the ignorant a person is bound in chains”; that is, by the voice of such teachers the hearer is more tightly entangled, as each person is bound by the chains of his sins.

Slander troubles the wise man and destroys the heart of his strength (Proverbs 9:8).

Here understand “wise man” as one who is advancing, according to the saying: “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you.” For the perfect wise man needs no reproof and is troubled by no slander.

Let us use this verse whenever we see a just and wise man enduring slander and being troubled by the injustice of judgment, while God does not immediately come to his aid.

For what the Septuagint, Aquila, and Theodotion translated as “he destroys the heart of his strength” (*εὐτονίας αὐτοῦ*),[36] Symmachus says: “And he destroys the heart of *MATTHANA*, that is, ‘gift,’” joining the Hebrew word with its interpretation and producing the sense expressed elsewhere: “Gifts blind even the eyes of the wise” (Deuteronomy 16:19).

[36] [Col. 1062D] Earlier editors, both ancient and recent, do not seem to have taken the Greek words *εὐγενείας αὐτοῦ* from Jerome’s manuscripts, but from the widely circulated edition of the Septuagint. The manuscripts, as I correct them, prefer *εὐτονίας*; and if, through scribal carelessness, some replace tau with gamma and read *εὐγονίας* or *ἐκγονίας*, the evident error of that letter supports the reading restored here. I would argue that *εὐτονίας* should likewise be restored in the Septuagint, for in the Roman edition Flaminius noted that it was read in certain Greek manuscripts. The decisive argument is Jerome’s translation of the word as “strength” or “vigor,” which corresponds well to *εὐτονίας*, a term interpreted as vigor, force, energy, and the like, but not to *εὐγενείας*, which signifies nobility of birth or rank. I add that Victorius reads *prodit* (“brings forth”) where the text has *perdit* (“destroys”); I find *perdet* (“he will destroy”) more convincing. —Martian.

Better is the end of a speech than its beginning. The conclusions of a discourse are better than its opening. In the former the speaker’s anxiety comes to an end; in the latter it begins.

Or it may be understood as follows: the person who begins to hear a speech and goes to the teacher is at the beginning; the one who hears its conclusion has been completed and perfected.

It may also be understood in this way: while we are in this world, whatever we know is all beginning; when what is perfect has come, we will be among those who are at the end and have been completed.

The Hebrew explains this passage together with the following verse: “It is better for you to consider the end of a matter than its beginning, and to be patient rather than carried away by the fury of impatience.”[37]

[37] [Col. 1063D] “Than its beginning, and to be patient.” The Corbie manuscripts read: “And to be wise rather than carried away by the fury of foolishness.” Shortly afterward: “There is no patience among human beings.” Both readings are certainly correct, for among human beings there is neither patience nor wisdom. —Martian.

From this little sentence we also learn that there is no wisdom among human beings, since it is better to remain silent than to speak. When the speech has been completed, the hearer reflects within himself on what was said; but when we begin to speak, he has not yet received any benefit.

Better is the patient person than one exalted in spirit.

Because above he had allowed anger when he said, “Better is anger than laughter,” lest we think that anger in a state of passion was being praised, he now commands that anger be entirely removed.[38] There he used anger for correcting sinners and educating those who are inferior; here he restrains impatience.

[38] [Col. 1063D] In Alcuin: “Anger is to be removed by patience.”

Patience is necessary not only in hardships but also in more pleasant circumstances, lest we become more exalted than is fitting. It seems to me that the person now called “exalted in spirit” is also opposed in the Gospel to the poor in spirit, who is placed among the blessed.[39]

[39] [Col. 1063D] Two Palatine manuscripts and the Vatican read: “It seems to me that the person who is now called …”

Do not be quick in your spirit to become angry, because anger rests in the bosom of fools.

He does not mean that anger should be delayed and therefore says, “Do not be quick in your spirit to become angry.” Rather, when anger is raging and still fresh, postponing it makes it easier for it to subside and be removed.[40]

[40] [Col. 1063D] Two manuscripts read: “when you are raging”; shortly afterward the Palatine manuscript, together with the old printed editions, reads: “so that once calmed it can more easily be removed.” The Vatican reads: “so that, once calmer, it may …”

Since anger is always joined with pride and desires vengeance, he said above that the patient person is better than the one who is exalted in spirit. Here he gives the sign of foolishness: however powerful and wise someone may be thought, if he is irascible, he is judged foolish. For anger rests in the bosom of fools.

Do not say, “Why were former days better than these?” For you have not asked wisely about this.

Do not prefer the ancient age to the present, since one God is the creator of both. Virtues make days good for the person who lives them; vices make them bad.

Therefore do not say that the days under Moses and under Christ were better than those of the present. In that former time there were also many unbelievers, and their days were made evil; now many believers are found, concerning whom the Savior said: “More blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29).

Alternatively: You should live in such a way that the present days are always better for you than the past, lest, when you gradually begin to decline, it be said to you: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Galatians 5:7). And again: “Having begun with the Spirit, are you now being completed in the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3).

Alternatively: Do not say that the times of Moses were formerly better than the times of Christ now, or that the time of the Law was better than that of Grace. If you wish to ask this, you act imprudently, failing to see how greatly the Gospel differs from the Old Testament.[41]

[41] [Col. 1064D] The Vatican reads: “Do not say that the former times, those of Moses, were better than the present times, those of Christ, and so forth.” The Palatine reads: “formerly under Moses rather than …”

### [Column 1064A]

Wisdom is good together with an inheritance, and it is an advantage to those who see the sun, because, just as there is a shadow of wisdom, so there is a shadow of silver; and what is more, the knowledge of wisdom will give life to the one who possesses it. A wise man with riches has greater glory than one who is merely wise. Some people need wisdom, others resources; and one who is wise but not rich can indeed teach what is good, but sometimes cannot provide what is requested. Therefore he says: “For just as there is a shadow of wisdom, so there is a shadow of money”—that is, just as wisdom protects, so sometimes money also protects.

And lest he seem to have disparaged wisdom by subjecting it to a chance advantage—for riches are not in our power, and the unjust often possess them in greater abundance—he therefore demonstrates that wisdom is greater, saying: “And the knowledge of wisdom will give life to the one who possesses it.” In this, he says, wisdom is greater than riches: it gives life, without any resources at all, to the one who possesses it.

Some interpret this passage as follows: “Inheritance,” they say, he used for a good way of life, through which we are heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ. Ecclesiastes therefore wishes to teach how greatly those differ who deserve to see the sun of righteousness and possess wisdom together with a good way of life from those who, without wisdom, have devoted themselves only to life and conduct. Daniel also shows this when he says: “Those who understand my words will shine like the lights of heaven” (Dan. XII, 3). Or, as Theodotion translated it: “Like the brightness of the firmament.” “Those who have performed my words will be like the stars of heaven.”

As for the shadow of silver [Note: Palatinus has “and all the [silver] in the parables.” — “And the minas in the parables of the Gospel are gathered.” The reading in earlier editions, “are read in the parables of the Gospel,” is less satisfactory. MARTIAN.], or money, we should understand it according to the *anagoge* (ἀναγωγή), as that of which the talents and minas are gathered in the parables of the Gospel (Matt. XXV; Luke XIX), so that, when we are under the shadow of wisdom and under the shadow of such silver, “the sun will not strike us by day, nor the moon by night” (Ps. CXX).

It can also be said that our life upon earth is a shadow: “And the breath of our nostrils, the Christ of the Lord,” to whom we said: “We shall live in his shadow among the nations” (Lam. IV, 20). All our protection in this earth is like a shadow, whether of wisdom or of the silver mentioned above, until the day dawns and the shadows are removed.

Symmachus, as is his custom, translated this passage more plainly, saying: “As wisdom protects, so money likewise protects.” The following verse clearly exhorts us to the pursuit of knowledge.

### [Column 1064D]

“Consider the works of God, for who can adorn what God has made crooked?” [Note: So also the manuscripts and printed editions; Martianæus himself restored this reading in his second revision, since earlier he had read “whom he strikes.”]

Symmachus translated the passage as follows: “Learn the works of God, for no one can correct what he has diminished”—that is, let it be enough for you, from the holy Scriptures or from contemplation of the elements themselves, to know and understand what has been made; but do not investigate the causes and reasons why each thing was made as it was, or why it ought to have been made otherwise.

For example, if someone wishes to ask why God speaks to Moses in this way: “Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?” (Exod. IV, 12), and says, “Why were the blind, deaf, and mute created in this way?” and similar questions, one should take in this passage the testimony from the seventeenth Psalm, where it is said to the Lord: “With the holy man you will be holy, and with the perverse you will act perversely” [Note: “And with the perverse you will act perversely.” From this passage we understand that the interpretation commonly received among the people is false, by which they apply the present passage of Psalm XVII to companionship with the wicked, among whom the good are often perverted and become like them. MARTIAN.].

It must be said that the holy Lord is holy with the one who is holy, and that he is perverted with the one who, by his own will, was previously perverse. This also accords with what is written in Leviticus: “If they walk perversely against me, I too will walk against them in my wrath perversely” (Lev. 26, 27).

This can also explain why the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart. For just as one and the same action of the sun melts wax and dries clay [Note: In the Vatican and Palatine manuscripts these words—“and according to its substance wax melts and clay dries”—are absent], so one and the same action of God’s signs in Egypt softened the hearts of believers and hardened unbelievers. In accordance with their hardness and impenitent heart, they were storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, because, although they saw these wonders being performed, they did not believe.

### [Column 1065B]

“On the day of prosperity, be prosperous; and on the day of adversity, consider. God has made the one corresponding to the other, so that a human being may find nothing to complain of against him.”

This statement is indeed fittingly connected with the preceding one. I remember hearing in church from someone thought to possess knowledge of the Scriptures an exposition of these verses as follows:

> “While you are in the present age, and are able to perform some good work, labor so that afterward, secure yourself on the day of adversity—that is, on the day of judgment—you may watch others being tormented. For just as God made the present age, in which we can prepare for ourselves the fruit of good works, so he also made the age to come, in which no opportunity for a good work is granted.”

He seemed to persuade his hearers when he said this [Note: Three manuscripts read “hearing,” namely, “hearing them persuade”]. But it seems to me that the sense is different, and Symmachus also translated it in this way: “On the good day, be good; but look upon the evil day. For God has made the one like the other, so that a human being might find nothing to complain of against him.”

“Bear,” he says, “both good and evil, according to what happens to you.” Do not think that the world contains only the nature of good things or only that of evil things, since this world consists of diverse opposites: hot and cold, dry and moist, hard and soft, dark and bright, evil and good [Note: The Palatine and Vatican manuscripts are somewhat more coherent: “since the world itself subsists from opposites.”].

God made this so that wisdom might have a place in choosing the good [Note: “Wisdom in choosing the good.” Some manuscripts have: “And in understanding good things and avoiding evil things.” Others: “And in choosing the good and avoiding the evil.” MARTIAN.] and avoiding evil, and so that free choice might be left to human beings. Thus no one can say that he was created by God without understanding or foolish, but that God made diverse things so that human beings could not complain about their condition.

This testimony can also be joined appropriately to what was said above: “Who can adorn what God has made crooked?”

### [Column 1066A]

“I have seen everything in the days of my vanity. There is a righteous person who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked person who is long-lived in his wickedness.”

The Savior says something similar in the Gospel: “Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matt. X, 59).

The Maccabees seemed to perish in their righteousness for the sake of God’s law and righteousness, as did the martyrs who shed their blood for Christ. Conversely, those who, both at that time, ate pork and, after the Lord’s coming, sacrificed to idols seemed to live in this world and to persist for a long time because of their wickedness [Note: “Conversely, those who also at that time…” A change of a single letter in Erasmus and Martianæus, who read “from that time,” produces a different meaning, and one insufficiently consistent with Jerome’s statement, which concerns the time of Antiochus and the Maccabees, when apostates from the Mosaic Law ate swine’s flesh. MARTIAN.].

But God’s patience is hidden. He now allows the saints to suffer, so that they may receive evil things in their lifetime, while he does not punish sinners for their crimes and, as it were, reserves them for sacrifice, so that he may restore eternal good things to the former and inflict perpetual evils upon the latter.

The Hebrews suppose that the righteous who perish in their righteousness are the sons of Aaron, because, while thinking that they were acting justly, they offered alien fire. They say that the wicked person long-lived in his wickedness is Manasseh, who, after being restored from captivity to the kingdom [Al. “in the kingdom”], lived for a long time thereafter.

### [Column 1066C]

“Do not be excessively righteous, and do not seek beyond measure, lest you become dismayed.”

If you see someone rigid and harsh toward all the sins of his brothers, so that he forgives neither one who sins in speech nor one who delays because of ordinary human sluggishness, know that this person is more righteous than he ought to be. For since the Savior commands, saying, “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Luke VI, 37), and since no one is without sin—not even if his life were only one day long—it is inhuman righteousness that does not forgive the frailty of human condition.

Therefore do not be excessively righteous, because a large weight and a small weight are both an abomination before the Lord. Hence among philosophers [Note: See what we noted in Letter 130, no. 11. — “Hence among philosophers.” The same point is taught more explicitly in the letter to the virgin Demetrias: “It is also the opinion of philosophers,” he says, “that moderate qualities are virtues, but excesses are vices” (μεσότητας ἀρετὰς, ὑπερβολὰς κακίας εἶναι). In Latin this may be rendered: “That virtues are moderate, while what exceeds measure and proportion is counted among vices.” Hence one of the Seven Sages said: “Nothing in excess” (Μηδὲν ἄγαν). This became so famous that it was also expressed in a comic verse. The same sentiment is repeated frequently in several of his works, such as the *Epitaph of Saint Paula*, the *Commentary on Isaiah LXI*, the *Commentary on Zechariah XII*, and elsewhere. Diogenes Laertius ascribes a similar saying to Pythagoras; Aristotle, in the third book of the *Rhetoric*, attributes it to Bias. Some assign it to Thales or Solon, as Laertius testifies. Finally, Pindar, according to Plutarch, says: “The wise praised excessively the saying, ‘Nothing in excess’” (Σοφοὶ δὲ καὶ τὸ Μηδὲν ἄγαν, ἔπος αἴνησαν περισσῶς). Terence expressed the same saying in the *Andria*, Act I, Scene 1, near the beginning:

> He excelled in none of these things, among all the rest  
> He pursued them, and yet all moderately.  
> I was glad. Not without reason; for I think  
> That in life it is especially useful to have nothing in excess. MARTIAN.]

virtues are placed in the middle, and everything excessive, whether above or below, is reckoned as a fault.

When he says, “Do not seek beyond measure, lest you be disturbed,” or “lest you become dismayed,” he knows that our mind cannot grasp perfect wisdom, and he commands us to recognize the measure of our frailty.

Finally, Paul also responded to the one who wished to know more than a human being could know [Note: “More than a human being could know.” Earlier editions falsely read: “who wished to know more than a human being, he asked,” and so forth. MARTIAN.], saying: “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” He answered: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. IX, 19), and so on.

If the one introduced as asking had heard the reasons for the question from the Apostle, perhaps he would have been paralyzed with astonishment and would have perceived grace to be useless. For, according to the same Apostle, there is also a gift that does not benefit the one to whom it is given.

The Hebrews interpret this command—“Do not be excessively righteous”—with reference to Saul, who pitied Agag, whom the Lord had commanded to be killed (I Sam. XV). The servant in the Gospel, too, whom the Lord had forgiven but who himself refused to forgive his fellow servant (Matt. XVIII), can be fitted to this verse, since he was excessively righteous.

### [Column 1067B]

“Do not act excessively wickedly, and do not be foolish; why should you die before your time?”

[Note: “Why should you die before your time?” The manuscripts of better quality read this, in agreement with the Hebrew source, *lammah thamuth*, “Why should you die?” Older editions and some manuscripts instead have “lest you die,” according to the Latin Vulgate. MARTIAN. Two manuscripts, together with the older editions and the Vulgate translator, read “lest you die,” as is found below. Another Palatine manuscript deletes *cur* (“why”) and substitutes *ne* (“lest”) in a later hand.]

Since the Lord says, “I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but only that he should turn back and live” (Ezek. XVIII, 32) [Note: The same manuscripts have “but only that he should turn back.” Alcuin and the older editors have: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he should turn back,” and so forth. Martianæus notes that Jerome cites the passage from chapter XVIII of Ecclesiasticus. — “I do not desire the death of the one who dies.” Erasmus and Martianæus think that what Jerome quotes from chapter XVIII of Ecclesiasticus was taken from chapter XXXIII, and they accordingly corrupt the present passage: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he should turn back and live.” MARTIAN.], it is enough to have sinned once; we ought to raise ourselves up after a fall.

For if, according to those who discuss natural science, the swallow knows how to restore the eyes of its young with its own celandine, and wounded she-goats seek dittany [Note: “The swallow knows how to restore the eyes of its young with its own…” All the manuscripts retain this reading, while the printed editions have: “The swallow knows how to restore its young with the juice of celandine.” But, unless I am mistaken, “from the juice” was taken from the pronoun *suos*, which appears in some manuscript copies: “the swallow knows its young,” and so forth. The reading of all the manuscripts, “to restore the eyes with its own celandine,” should therefore be retained. It is elegantly said “with its own celandine,” either because swallows discovered this herb to be highly beneficial to the eyes, or because it blossoms at the coming of the swallows. See Dioscorides, Book II, chapters 211–212, and Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 27. “Swallows showed celandine, highly beneficial to sight, healing their young with it when their eyes were afflicted.” Consult also the same Pliny, Book XXV, chapter 8. Regarding the dittany that follows immediately, it should be noted that in Virgil’s verse, *Aeneid* XII,

> The Cretan mother plucks dittany from Ida,

Hermolaus and all learned men think that *dictamnum* should be read, with the letter *n* inserted; otherwise the verse would not scan. All our manuscripts also read *dictamnum*, and Theophrastus and Galen seem to support them, since one always reads δίκταμνος in their works. See Theophrastus, *History of Plants*, Book IX, chapter 16; Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 27, cited above; Dioscorides, Book III, chapter 37; and Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*: “It is said that wild goats in Crete, when pierced by poisoned arrows, seek a plant called dittany, and, when they have tasted it, the arrows are said to fall from their bodies.” Pliny says the same in Book XXVI, chapter 14. I omit the rest as irrelevant to the exposition of this passage. MARTIAN. — The Vatican and Palatine manuscripts have “the young with their own celandine for the eyes,” incorrectly using *oculare* as a noun, although its opposite, *exoculare*, occurs frequently. Martianæus needlessly discusses the herb celandine from Dioscorides and Pliny. It is worth noting that Jerome copied this passage almost word for word from Tertullian, *On Repentance*, chapter 12: “If the swallow blinds its young, it knows how to restore their eyes with its own celandine”—which is so called because of the swallow itself, which in Greek is called χελιδών, *chelidon*. The remainder is also taken from the same source: “The deer pierced by an arrow knows that it must be healed with dittany, so that it may expel the iron and its unalterable delay from the wound. Will the sinner pass by the repentance instituted by the Lord for his restoration?”]

why should we be ignorant that the medicine of repentance has been appointed for sinners?

As for the statement, “Do not die before your time” (Num. XVI), we know that Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, because of their rebellion against Moses and Aaron, were suddenly swallowed up by the opening of the earth. Many others also have been judged in this life, before the day of judgment, as a correction for others.

The meaning, therefore, is this: Do not add sins to sins, lest you provoke God to inflict punishment upon you even here.

### [Column 1068B]

“It is good for you to hold on to this” [Note: “It is good for you to hold on to this.” The earlier editions incorrectly read “to hold on to the righteous person,” instead of “to hold on to this.” MARTIAN.]. “And indeed, do not withdraw your hand from it; for whoever fears God will go forth toward all things.”

It is good to do good to the righteous, but it is not unjust to do good to sinners as well. It is good to support members of the household of faith, but it is also commanded to give to everyone who asks. For the one who fears God and imitates his Creator, who sends rain upon the just and the unjust, hastens to do good to all without respect of persons.
