Alternatively: Since this miserable life is daily changed by various events, both adverse and prosperous, let the mind of the righteous be prepared, and let it ask the Lord’s mercy, so that whatever happens it may endure with a balanced mind [Note: Alcuin has: “whatever happens, with a free mind,” and so forth.]. For the one who fears God is neither lifted up by prosperity nor crushed by adversity.

### [Column 1069A]

“Wisdom will strengthen the wise man more than ten rulers who are in the city, because there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” [Note: Some manuscripts have “Wisdom strengthened the wise man,” in the past tense. But the future reading, “will strengthen,” should be retained, because it is so found in the Hebrew source. MARTIAN.].

Therefore wisdom strengthens the righteous, and the assistance of all the rulers of the city is surpassed by it, because, although someone may be righteous, nevertheless, as long as he is established in this flesh, he is subject to vices and sins and needs greater protection.

Alternatively: The ten who possess authority and reside in the city are angels who have reached the perfect number, ten, and who assist the human race. But if someone considers all forms of assistance, the greater assistance is that of wisdom—that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ.

For after the angels said, “We have healed Babylon, and she was not healed; let us leave her, and let each one go to his own land” (Jer. LI, 8), the Master of physicians himself descended. We had been sprinkled with blood and drenched in the gore of sins, and had spent all our substance on physicians; but he healed us by the touch of his fringe (Luke VIII).

He healed us in the city—that is, in this world—and “strengthened” the wise man, or, as the Septuagint translated it, “helped” him [Note: The Vatican has “will strengthen”; immediately afterward, together with the Palatine, it has *adjuvat*, “helps,” instead of *adjuvit*, “helped.” The Septuagint has βοηθήσει, “he will help,” at least in the current copies.]. “For to everyone who has, it will be given, and it will be added to him.”

Because the human being, placed in sins and fixed in the mud of the deep, needed greater assistance, Wisdom itself therefore came.

Alternatively: Above he had said that good should be done both to members of the household of faith and to outsiders. Someone could therefore reply: “If I wish to do good to everyone, I have no means by which to do it.” Nor can a righteous person possess such great riches as usually abound more among sinners. Therefore he now says: “Those whom you cannot help by material means, assist by counsel and encourage with consolation” [Note: The same Vatican manuscript has: “Those whom you cannot govern by counsel, assist with consolation.” Another Palatine has: “Those whom you cannot assist by counsel, cherish with consolation,” and so forth. — “Those whom you cannot help materially…” Earlier editions have: “Those whom you cannot help with resources, assist by counsel,” and so forth. The same editions below have: “Do not give your mouth so that you may not hear what the wicked will say.” All these readings are corrupt. MARTIAN.].

Wisdom can provide more to one who is in distress than any of the greatest powers. And do this with prudence. The scale of justice is indeed a large one: to whom, how much, for how long, and what kind of assistance one should give, whether materially or by counsel.

### [Column 1069C]

“And do not give your heart to all the words that people will speak, lest you hear your servant cursing you” [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts and the Vatican have: “to all the words that the wicked will speak, do not give…” The Roman Septuagint manuscript has ἀσεβεῖς, “wicked.”].

For your heart often knows that you too have cursed others. Do what has been commanded, and, strengthened by the help of wisdom, prepare your heart for good or evil; do not care what your enemies say about you or what public opinion outside may be.

For just as it is characteristic of a prudent man not to listen to a servant who is grumbling, nor to lend a curious ear to what he says about him in his absence—for if he did this, he would always be in distress, and the servant’s murmuring would provoke his anger—so it is characteristic of a wise person to follow wisdom as his guide and not pay attention to empty rumors.

He also teaches by another example that a righteous person should give no attention at all to what people say, when he says: “Your conscience knows how you have spoken about many people and often slandered others; therefore you too ought to forgive those who slander.” At the same time he teaches that judgment should not be made hastily, and that one who has a beam in his eye should not speak about another’s speck [Note: Victor restored this reading. Martianæus, however, together with Erasmus, retained “the one possessing” the beam.].

### [Column 1070B]

“I tested all this through wisdom, and I said: ‘I will become wise’; but it remained far from me, farther than it had been: a deep profundity—who can find it?”

He says that, as the Books of Kings also testify (III Kings III; IV Kings), he sought wisdom beyond all human beings and tried to reach its end. Yet the more he sought it, the less he found, and he was plunged into the midst of darkness and surrounded by the darkness of ignorance.

Alternatively [Note: Alcuin has “But one who has been instructed,” from which our manuscripts differ only in having *Alias* or *Alius* instead of *Aliter*.]: A person learned in the Scriptures, the more he begins to know, the greater the obscurity that arises in them for him each day.

Alternatively: In this life, contemplation of wisdom is seen in a mirror and in an image. When, therefore, I shall consider that in the future its knowledge will be revealed face to face, then I shall clearly recognize how far I now differ from knowledge of it.

### [Column 1070C]

“I went around, I and my heart, to know, to examine, and to seek wisdom and reason, and to know the wickedness of the foolish and the error of the senseless.”

And I find a woman more bitter than death, whose heart is a snare and a net, and whose hands are bonds. The one who is good before God will be delivered from her, but the sinner will be captured by her.

Instead of the Septuagint’s “I went around, I and my heart, to know,” Symmachus translated: “I passed through everything with my understanding, to know, learn, and investigate” [Note: Another Palatine manuscript, together with the Vatican, has “and discuss.”].

Since Ecclesiastes had said above that he had tested everything through wisdom, and that the more he sought it, the farther it withdrew from him, he now says that he also discovered in his wisdom what evil surpasses every evil in human affairs, and what thing holds first place in wickedness, folly, error, and stupidity.

He says that he found woman to be the head of all evils, because through her death entered the world and captures the precious souls of men. “For all who commit adultery are like an oven: their hearts,” which she has made the hearts of young men fly away. When she enters the mind of the wretched lover, she drags him headlong; she does not allow him to look at his feet, but, like a snare and a net, entangles the young man’s heart.

“For her hands are bonds.” In place of this, Aquila translated: “Her hands are bound,” which in the Hebrew language is called *ASSURIM* [Note: “Which in the Hebrew language is called…” Erasmus and Martianæus add the word *jadeab*, but falsely and unnecessarily. The name *assurim* is sufficient to explain Jerome’s statement and Aquila’s variant reading. MARTIAN.].

She can persuade, but she cannot use force, nor can she draw to herself those who are unwilling. The righteous and good person before God will be delivered from her [Note: The Vatican has “will be preserved by him,” namely, by God’s help]; but the sinner, once captured, will be led to death.

Let us not think that Solomon uttered this judgment rashly concerning the female sex: he speaks from experience. For this is why he offended God—because he was captured by women. This is the literal interpretation.

But according to the spiritual understanding, we either call every sin in general “woman,” and wickedness, which in the form of a woman sits upon the talent of lead in Zechariah (Zech. V, 7); or we take the devil tropologically (τροπικῶς) as “woman,” because of his effeminate strength; or certainly idolatry; and, to come closer to the point, the assembly of heretics, which calls the foolish-minded to itself so that, having been led astray, he may receive stolen bread and stolen water—that is, a false sacrament and a polluted baptism.

### [Column 1071A]

“Behold, this I found,” says Ecclesiastes, “adding one to one, in order to find the number that my soul still sought, and I did not find it. I found one man among a thousand, but among all these I did not find one woman.”

“This alone I found: that God made human beings upright, but they themselves sought many devices.”

“This,” he says, “I discovered after carefully examining everything: by sinning little by little and adding one offense to another, we make for ourselves a great total of sins. For *hesbon* (חשבון), which everyone with one voice translated as λογισμός (reasoning or thought) [Note: Earlier editions had λογισμούς in the plural, contrary to the better manuscripts, the Greek Scholiast on Aquila preserved by Flaminius, and Flaminius’s Roman edition], can, because of the ambiguity of the Hebrew word and its number, mean ‘number,’ ‘sum,’ ‘account,’ or ‘thought.’”

But this too, he says, my soul sought: whether a righteous woman could be found. And although I scarcely found a few good men, so that one among a thousand could be found [Note: The Vatican is slightly more accurate: “one whom I could find among a thousand”], I could not find a good woman at all. For they all led me not to virtue but to indulgence.

And because “the heart of man is diligently set upon evil from his youth” (Gen. VIII, 21), and almost all have offended God, in this ruin of the human race woman is more prone to fall. Concerning her, the pagan poet also says:

> …changeable and ever mutable,  
> Woman…

(Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, V. 35.)

And the Apostle says: “Always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth” (II Tim. III, 7).

And lest he seem to condemn the common nature of human beings and make God the author of evil, since he is the creator of those who cannot avoid evil, he wisely took precautions and said that God created us good; but because we have been left to free choice, through our own fault we slip toward worse things while seeking greater ones and thinking various thoughts beyond our strength.

Alternatively: Each day, as I set an account beside myself for every matter, I could find no thought that was not disturbed externally by a perverse thought. Among a thousand men I found one human being created according to the image of the Creator—and among a thousand not simply people, but among a thousand men: a number that woman could not complete. And among a thousand who had not approached a woman, and therefore remained most pure.

All these things, however, must be understood tropologically. Among many diligent students [Al. “studies”] who labor in daily meditation, a pure thought, worthy of the name of man, is scarcely found. We can also take thoughts as men and works as women, and say that it is difficult for anyone’s thought to be found pure, while works, because they are carried out through the body, are always mixed with some error.

As for what we said above when interpreting the Hebrew expression—“adding one to one, so that a number, or sum, or account, or thought might be found”—Symmachus translated it more clearly [Note: “To find an account by adding one to one.” Earlier editions falsely read “to find an account by adding one to one” in the feminine form. If we retain the feminine form, Symmachus has nothing different, nor does he interpret the Hebrew expression more clearly, since Jerome too rendered it in the feminine. It must therefore be read in the absolute and neuter form, “one to one.” MARTIAN.]: “To find an account by adding one to one.”

What we ordinarily express in the absolute and neuter form—“I sought this; I wished to find that”—the Hebrews pronounce in the feminine gender, as in the Psalm: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Ps. XXVI, 4), instead of “one thing” [Note: Another Palatine manuscript adds, “and this I will seek.”].

### [Chapter VIII; Column 1072D]

“Who is like the wise man, and who knows the interpretation of a word? The wisdom of a man will illuminate his face, and a strong man will change his face” [Note: The same manuscript has “illuminated,” and shortly afterward “changed,” also below where this passage is repeated. — “Who is like the wise man,” and so forth. From this passage and another above, we learn with certainty that among the ancients the divisions of chapters differed from those now customary in sacred volumes. MARTIAN.].

Above he had taught that it is difficult to find a good person, and, in answering the question that had been brought forward, had shown that God created human beings good but that they voluntarily fell into sins.

Now, as though boasting, he enumerates what good God gave to human beings: wisdom, reason, and foresight; the knowledge of God’s hidden mysteries; and entry, through the understanding of the heart, into his secrets.

He speaks indirectly about himself, saying that no one was as wise as he was and that no one knew the solutions of problems in the same way [Note: “And no one knew in the same way.” Earlier editions read *fecerit*, “had done,” instead of *scierit*, “had known,” which does not suit the present passage, as I think is clear to the reader. MARTIAN.]. His wisdom was praised by all the people, and it did not lie hidden only within him; it also shone upon the surface of his body and in the mirror of his face, and he displayed the prudence of his mind in his countenance beyond all other people.

Instead of our reading, “Who is like the wise man,” the Septuagint translated: “Who knows the wise?” [Note: “Who knows the wise?” Erasmus and Martianæus unnecessarily add many Greek words and entire verses of the Septuagint to this Commentary. It is enough to have warned of these additions here. MARTIAN.]. And instead of what we said, “And a strong man will change his face,” they have: “And the shameless person will be hated in his face.”

Indeed, although many promise wisdom, it is difficult to find someone able to distinguish the true wise man from those who merely seem wise. And although many claim that they can solve the hidden things of Scripture, one who finds the true solution is rare.

The statement that follows—“The wisdom of a man will illuminate his face, and the wicked person will be hated in his face”—can be explained by using Paul’s words: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord” (II Cor. III, 18), and the Psalmist’s song: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV, 7).

Here he speaks of no wisdom of man other than the wisdom of God. Since it is the wisdom of God, it begins to belong to the human being according to the capacity of the one who has deserved to possess it.

Every heretic and defender of a false doctrine has a shameless face. Thus Marcion and Valentinus say that they are of a better nature than the Creator [Note: “Marcion and Valentinus,” and so forth. Marcion called the Creator of the universe an evil principle and said that God was evil, while with the most shameless blasphemy he proclaimed himself just and holy. He denied the reality of Christ’s flesh and the resurrection of bodies, as Valentinus also did. See Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Epiphanius concerning them. MARTIAN.].

This could be tolerated to some extent if they claimed to have hope for such a thing, and not already to possess that nature.

I keep the king’s command, and the word of God’s oath. Do not hasten to depart from his presence, and do not persist in an evil matter, [Col. 1074A] for he will do whatever he wishes. As the king says (or: will say), having authority—and who will say to him, “What are you doing?”

He seems indeed, in accordance with the Apostle, to command obedience to kings and authorities (Titus III, 1), especially since the Septuagint translators express it in the imperative: “Keep the king’s mouth.” But I think that this is now spoken of that king of whom David says: “The king will rejoice in your strength, O Lord” (Ps. XX, 1). And elsewhere, to signify the one kingdom of the Father and the Son, Scripture says: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. LXXI, 1). For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John V, 22).

The Son of God, who is king [Note: [Col. 1074C] “The Son of God, who is king,” etc. In the earlier editions we read as follows: “The king, the Son of God, is the Son of the king, the Father.” Therefore the commands of this Son must be kept, his will must be obeyed, etc. MARTIAN.], is the Son of the king, the Father. His commands, therefore, must be kept, and his will carried out. [Col. 1074B] This is also what is written in the Book of Tobit: “It is good to conceal the mystery of a king” (Tobit XII, 7). And he especially warns us not to inquire why God has commanded each thing, but whatever he sees to have been commanded, let the human mind hasten to fulfill with reverence [Note: [Col. 1074C] Two manuscripts read: “Let him hasten to fulfill it, and let his will be in the law of the Lord.”]. And his will shall be in the law of the Lord.

But because the Septuagint translated differently, saying, “And concerning the oath and the word of God, do not hasten from his presence” [Note: [Col. 1074D] “And concerning the oath,” etc. Here too, besides the superfluous addition of the Greek verse, they alter the sacred context of the Septuagint translators, reading: “Concerning the word of God’s oath, do not hasten,” etc. It is most clearly established from Jerome’s Commentary that the words in the divine books were written differently from the Septuagint reading—namely, “concerning God’s oath,” or “concerning the word of God’s oath,” not “concerning the oath and the word of God,” as it was read in the edition of the Septuagint translators. Whoever attends to this passage will therefore acknowledge with us that the reading of all the manuscript codices is the true one. MARTIAN.  
—All the manuscripts we use read: “to walk from the presence of God.”], we should know that God’s oath has been written in the divine books. This oath, sacred and mysterious because it is the word of God, we ought not to relate to everyone, bring it out into the open, or promptly pronounce judgment upon it [Note: [Col. 1074D] “To pronounce judgment upon it.” Several manuscript copies read “to refer the law”; Erasmus and Marianus read “to bring forth judgment.” MARTIAN.].

Nor, like Moses, should you hasten to see the face of God; rather, wait until he himself has passed by, so that you may see only his back. [Col. 1074C] We should likewise understand the following statement—“Do not persist in an evil matter,” and so forth—as referring to one who has been overtaken by the error of heresy, or to one who, although he holds the faith of the Church, is nevertheless overcome by sins and thereby becomes faithless. Do not persist in slander, filthy speech, luxury [or: wantonness], avarice, or lust. If you persist, the king of vices and sin, the devil, will bring destruction upon you and do whatever he wishes.

Whoever keeps the commandment will not know an evil word; and the wise heart knows the time and the judgment. [Col. 1075A] It should be noted that “he will not know an evil word” is put for “he will not suffer it” or “it will not be in him.” For it is likewise written of the Savior: “He who knew no sin [Note: [Col. 1075C] Martianus adds “God,” a word found neither in our manuscripts nor in the other printed books; nor, finally, does he himself acknowledge it in the scriptural text.  
—“He who knew no sin.” The Corbie manuscript codices read: “He who, having known no sin, made sin for us.” MARTIAN.], he made sin for us” (II Corinthians V, 21).

Symmachus also interpreted the word in this sense, saying: “Whoever [Note: [Col. 1075C] The manuscripts read: “Whoever keeps the commandment,” etc.] keeps the commandment will not experience an evil thing.” He commands that the king’s order be preserved, and that one should know what he commands, why he commands it, and at what time.

For there is a time and a judgment for every matter. Indeed, the affliction of humanity is great upon it, because it does not know what will happen; for, as it will be, who will announce it?

Although different things occur, and although the righteous person cannot know what will happen to him or understand the causes and reasons of individual events—for no one is aware of the future—[Col. 1075B] nevertheless he knows that everything is brought about by God for the benefit of human beings and is ordered not apart from God’s will. For the affliction of the human race is great, because, as the Poet says (Aeneid X, 501):

> The mind of humankind, ignorant of fate  
> and of the future lot,

[Note: [Col. 1075C–D] “The mind of humankind, ignorant,” etc. Ambrosius Calepinus falsely cites this verse from Book I of the *Aeneid*, which caused me to read the entire first book of the *Aeneid* twice to no purpose. Other writers do cite the same verse, but do not indicate its source. But I, having been kindly informed by the Reverend Father Commire, S.J., found that Jerome cited a verse of Vergil, and read it in Book X of the *Aeneid*, line 501:

> In the spoil over which Turnus now exults and rejoices to have gained;
> the mind of humankind, ignorant of fate and of the future lot,
> and unable to keep moderation when lifted up by prosperity.
> A time will come for Turnus when he will wish, at great cost,
> that Pallas had remained untouched, etc. MARTIAN.]

hopes for one thing, and something else occurs: in one place it expects the enemy, and it is wounded by another’s spear. Instead of what the Septuagint translators and Theodotion said, “For the knowledge of a human being is a great burden upon him,” the Hebrew has “evil,” not “knowledge.” But because the Hebrew letters RES and DALETH, apart from a small stroke, are alike, they read DAATH [Note: [Col. 1075D] Martianus reads *Dath* for *Daath*, which all the manuscripts prefer. MARTIAN.], that is, “knowledge,” instead of RAATH [Note: [Col. 1075D] In the manuscripts, as we observe frequently elsewhere, it is *Deleth*.], “evil.” This will be better understood by someone who possesses knowledge of that language.

[Col. 1075C] The statement written at the end of these verses, “For he does not know” [Note: [Col. 1075D] “For he does not know what has happened.” The Septuagint translators make no mention of past events, nor does the present Hebrew text, where we read *ki enennu jodea ma schejihje*, that is, “because he himself does not know what will be.” Jerome’s present observation therefore compels us to say that he read in the past what is now read in the future—that is, *schehaja*, “what was” or “what has happened,” instead of the present Hebrew *schejihje*, “what will be” or “what is to come.” The Syriac interpreter likewise agrees with Jerome, saying: “Because he does not know what has happened, and what will happen to him afterward, who can tell him?” The Syriac therefore read *dahuo*, “what was,” in the past tense, and not *dinehue*, “what will be.” From this it is clear that Jerome conformed himself to the custom of the Septuagint translators in the sacred context, but in the Commentary translated word for word from the Hebrew language what he read in his own copies or in Origen’s Hexapla. Nor did he read it differently when he later produced our Vulgate from the purest sources of the Hebrew language; for he says: “Because he does not know the past, and no messenger can know the future.” MARTIAN.  
—Martianus correctly notes that the Hebrew has [the form] “what will be,” whereas Jerome read in his copy [the form] “what has happened.”], “what has happened, and what will happen after him—who will announce it to him?” We have now translated this word for word from the Hebrew language, so that we may recognize another sense: namely, that we can know neither what has passed nor what is to come, as it will actually come to pass.

A human being has no power over the spirit, so as to restrain the spirit; and he has no power on the day of death; there is no discharge in war; and wickedness will not save the one who possesses it. Our soul is not within our power, so that it cannot be taken from us; and when the spirit of the Lord goes forth at his command [Note: [Col. 1076D] “And when it goes forth at the command.” According to the books printed before ours, one should read here: “and to restrain the spirit that goes forth at the command of the Lord.” Nothing is gained, etc. MARTIAN.], it is useless to close one’s mouth and retain the life that is fleeing.

When destruction, the enemy and adversary of our life, arrives, we cannot obtain a reprieve. Nor can kings once powerful in the world, who have laid waste to everything through their wickedness, raise their hands against death; we shall be dissolved into ash and earth. There is therefore no need to grieve because we cannot know the future and are often oppressed by more powerful wicked people [Note: [Col. 1076D] Previously it incorrectly read “is oppressed.”], since death brings everything to an end, and the proud and powerful person who has plundered everything cannot retain his soul when it is seized.

Alternatively: The spirit that disposes all things cannot be restrained by any human being or be given laws governing its breathing. Concerning this it was said above: “The spirit goes, turning and turning.” On the day of death we have no power; for during the day of life the enemy can easily be avoided. Likewise, whoever is in warfare and does not possess the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will have no discharge—the discharge of which it is said to the bride: “Your emissions are a paradise with the fruit of trees” (Song IV). And because wickedness will not save the one who possesses it, piety, by contrast, will save him. Wickedness may be called the devil, and piety our Lord Jesus Christ.

I saw all these things and gave my heart to every work that is done under the sun, and man exercised power over man to afflict him. Then I saw the wicked buried; they came and went out from the holy place, and they were praised in the city because they had acted in this way. This also is vanity [Note: [Col. 1076D] The Vatican manuscript adds “and presumption of spirit,” incorrectly.].

Because there is no immediate contradiction of those who do evil [Col. 1077A] [Note: [Col. 1077D] Two Vatican and Palatine manuscripts omit the adverb “quickly” and the words “in them.”], therefore the hearts of human beings are filled within them so that they do evil. “I gave my heart,” he says, “to observe everything that happens under the sun,” and especially this: that a human being has received power over another human being, so that he may afflict and condemn whomever he wishes.

When, therefore, I directed my mind to observe these things, I saw the wicked dead with such an opinion of them and buried in such a way that they were regarded as saints on earth. While they were alive, they were thought [Note: [Col. 1077D] Two Palatine manuscripts, together with the books printed before Martianus—and Alcuin himself—read: “who, while they were alive, were thought worthy to be leaders of the Church and of the temple of God.”] worthy of the Church and of the temple of God. Moreover, as they walked about swollen with pride, they were praised for their evil deeds [Note: [Col. 1077D] The words “as it is written” are absent from the Vatican and one Palatine manuscript.], as it is written: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who acts unjustly is blessed” (Ps. IX, 24).

This happened because no one dares to contradict sinners [Note: [Col. 1077D] Erasmus and Victorius, with Alcuin, read: “because no one dares to contradict sinful bishops.”  
—“Because no one dares.” The same printed editions of Erasmus and Marianus incorrectly add the name “bishops”: “because no one dares to contradict sinful bishops.” But here they falsely added the name of bishops, just as above they added the name of the leaders of the Church.], nor does God immediately punish the crime; rather, he postpones the penalty while waiting for repentance. But sinners, because they have not immediately been rebuked and corrected, suppose that there will be no judgment and persist in their crime.

We can use this testimony against bishops who have received power in the Church and scandalize those whom they ought to teach and encourage toward better things. They are frequently praised in the Church after death, and are publicly proclaimed blessed in those things that they had not done commendably, either by their successors or by the people. This too is vanity, because they are not judged according to what they did, nor are they immediately rebuked for their sin—for no one dares to accuse a superior. Therefore, as though they were saints and blessed and walking in the commandments of the Lord, they add sins to sins.

The accusation of a bishop is difficult. Even if he has sinned, he is not believed; and even if he has been convicted, he is not punished.

Because the sinner does evil a hundred times and God prolongs for him [Note: [Col. 1077D] Three manuscripts read: “and God prolongs it for him. From this,” etc. MARTIAN.], I know from this that it will be well with those who fear God, who will fear before his face. Because God gives the one who sins repeatedly—for this is what “a hundred times” signifies—a place for repentance, and does not immediately punish him for his crime but waits for him to turn from his wickedness, I understand how kind and merciful God will be toward those who fear him and tremble at his word.

Symmachus translated this passage as follows: “For the wicked sinner has died” [Note: [Col. 1077D] “With longevity granted to him.” In several manuscript copies we read “with patience” instead of “with longevity”; and in the printed editions, “with a long age granted to him.” MARTIAN.  
—The earlier printed editions incorrectly read “with a long age,” and Martianus substituted “with longevity.” We correct it to “with patience” from four of our manuscripts, supported by several others in Martianus’s possession. For Symmachus translated *μακροθυμίας* [*makrothymias*], which means precisely “patience,” as is also clear from an old scholion in Flaminius’s Greek edition; that word conveys only “patience” in Latin.], with patience granted to him. “But I know that it will be well with those who fear God, who have feared before his face.”

But it will not be well with the wicked, nor will he long survive, because he did not fear before the face of God. Since it is clear what this translator rendered, we should say that the Hebrew word MAATH [מעת], which the Septuagint translated as “from that time” and which we rendered as “a hundred times,” was interpreted by Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion as “he has died.” Thus the sense is that the one who sinned and did evil has died: in the very act of sinning, he died.

But if, according to the Septuagint translators, instead of “he has died” we read “from that time,” the sense, according to some, may be as follows: A sinner does not first sin at the moment when he appears to commit sin, but had already sinned previously: “The sinners were estranged from the womb; they went astray from the belly” (Ps. LVII, 4). And they ask how what follows can be explained: “They spoke falsehood.” For a simple understanding does not seem to make the statement coherent if infants are sinners and speak lies as soon as they have been expelled from the womb.

And it will not be well with the wicked, nor will he prolong his days like a shadow—he who does not fear before the face of God. He invokes evil upon those who do not possess the fear of God, and wishes that punishment not be delayed for long [Note: [Col. 1078D] Previously it read: “that they be delayed from punishment.” The translators praised above apparently read [one form] instead of [another].], but that they be immediately taken away by death and receive the torments they deserve.

The Apostle says something similar: “Would that those who are troubling you would cut themselves off” (Galatians V, 12). And elsewhere: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; may the Lord repay him according to his works” (II Timothy IV, 14). We must inquire how such statements were spoken mercifully.

This is according to the truth of the Hebrew sense. But if someone follows the Septuagint translators, who, as though beginning from another meaning, said: “And I recognize that it will be well with those who fear God, so that they fear before his face; and it will not be well with the wicked, and he will not prolong his days in the shadow, because he does not fear before the face of God,” he may say this:

Those things of which I spoke a little earlier will indeed occur; nevertheless, I recognize most clearly that it will be well with those who fear before the face of God: “For the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. XXXIII, 17). And it will not be well with the wicked, for he does not fear before the face of God, and he will not prolong his days in the shadow—that is, the days of his life, which are like a shadow to those who live.

[Note: [Col. 1078D] Martianus: “Not that those who live for a long time prolong their days.”] For it is not those who live for a long time who prolong their days, but those who make their days great through the magnitude of their good works. Hence Jacob, confessing himself to be a sinner, says: “Few and evil are the days of my years” (Genesis XLVII, 9). And in the psalm he confesses: “My days have declined like a shadow” [Note: [Col. 1078D] “They have declined like a shadow.” Thus the manuscripts read it; the earlier printed books, however, read: “They have passed away like a shadow.” MARTIAN.] (Ps. CI, 12), “and I have withered like grass.”

He did not seek a long life in the present, in which everything we live is brief, a shadow, and an image: “For man walks about in an image” (Ps. XXXVIII, 7). Rather, he feared concerning the future, lest the length of his life—where true life exists—be shortened.

There is a vanity that takes place upon the earth: there are righteous people to whom things happen as though they were the deeds of the wicked, and there are wicked people to whom things happen as though they were the deeds of the righteous. I said that this too is vanity.

Among the other vanities that occur in the world with varied outcomes, I also discovered this: that things frequently happen to the righteous which ought to happen to the wicked, while the wicked live so prosperously in this world that you would think them perfectly righteous. The Gospel provides the example of the rich man clothed in purple and the poor Lazarus (Luke XVI). The seventy-second psalm likewise discusses this matter: why evils sometimes happen to the righteous and good things to the wicked.

Instead of what we rendered, “There is a vanity that takes place upon the earth,” Symmachus translated plainly, saying: “There is something difficult to understand that takes place upon the earth.” The Hebrews interpret the righteous to whom evils happen and the wicked to whom the works of the righteous accrue as the sons of Aaron and Manasseh: the former perished while offering sacrifice, whereas the latter, after such great evils and captivity, was restored to rule.

And I praised gladness, because there is no good for a human being under the sun except to eat, drink, and be glad. And it will accompany him in his labor during the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.

We interpreted this more fully above, and now we speak briefly: one may prefer the pleasure of eating and drinking, though brief and soon to end, to the troubles of the world and to the things that appear to be done unjustly in the world, since a human being seems to possess from his labor only this, if he enjoys even a little relief.

Yet if this interpretation is accepted as it is written, it will pronounce miserable those who fast, hunger, thirst, and mourn, whom the Lord calls blessed in the Gospel (Matthew V). Let us therefore understand food and drink spiritually, and likewise the gladness that we can scarcely find amid the labor of our life.

That these things should be understood as we have said is demonstrated by the following verse, in which he says: “I gave my heart to see wisdom and occupation”—that is, to see that human beings are occupied upon the earth and devote themselves day and night to meditation upon the Scriptures, so that often, in searching for the truth [Note: [Col. 1079D] The Vatican and Palatine manuscripts read: “in searching for the word.”], sleep flees from their eyes.

Therefore I gave my heart to know wisdom and to see the occupation that has been made upon the earth. For he who does not see sleep [or: a dream] in his eyes, day and night. And I saw all the works of God, because a human being cannot discover the work that has been done under the sun, at which he labored [Col. 1080A] to seek, and will not find it. [Note: [Col. 1079D] One Palatine manuscript reads: “and will not find it”; a little farther below, together with the Vatican, it reads “being able” instead of “seeing.”]

Even if the wise person says that he understands, he will not be able to discover it. Whoever seeks the causes and reasons of things—why this or that has happened, and why the world is governed by varying outcomes; why one person is born blind and weak, another seeing and healthy; one poor, another rich; one noble, another without distinction—gains nothing except to be tormented in his own inquiry, to have argument as his torture, and nevertheless not to discover what he seeks . . .

And when he says that he has understood these things, he then begins his ignorance and dwells in profound error. Yet he hints that there are causes and a justice behind all things, explaining why each thing happens as it does; but they lie hidden and cannot be grasped by human beings.

(Cap. IX.) I placed all this in my heart, to consider everything: that the righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God. There is both love and hatred; no human being knows everything from their outward appearance.

Symmachus also interpreted this passage more clearly, saying: “I set all this in my heart in order to sift everything: for the righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God. Moreover, no human being knows either friendships or enmities; everything before them is uncertain, because similar things happen to everyone, to the righteous and to the unrighteous.”

The sense here is as follows: I also gave my heart to this matter and wanted to know whom God loved and whom he hated. I found that the works of the righteous are indeed in God’s hand, and yet that they cannot now know whether they are loved by God or not, and waver in uncertainty as to whether they endure what they endure for testing or for punishment [Note: [Col. 1080D] The Corbie manuscripts read: “or for judgment.” MARTIAN.].

In the future, therefore, they will know, and all things are before them—that is, knowledge of this matter goes before them when they depart from this life, because then there is judgment, whereas now there is struggle. And in the case of everyone who endures adversity, it is now uncertain whether he endures it through God’s love, like Job, or through hatred, like very many sinners.

There is one outcome for all things: for the righteous and the wicked, the good and the bad, the clean and the polluted, the one who sacrifices and the one who does not sacrifice. The good person is like the sinner, the one who swears like the one who fears an oath [Note: [Col. 1080D] These same manuscripts read: “the perjurer like the one who fears an oath.” MARTIAN.].

Things that in themselves are neither good nor evil, but are called indifferent by the wise of this world—for they happen equally to the righteous and the unrighteous—disturb the simple-minded, who ask why they happen in this way. For this reason they do not believe that there is a judgment, although there will be a distinction among all things in the future, while here everything is confused.

When he says, “There is one outcome for all, for the righteous and the wicked,” he signifies the outcome either of distress or of death; and therefore they cannot know in themselves either God’s love or his hatred. The one who sacrifices and the one who does not sacrifice, and the other contrasting pairs that are listed [Note: [Col. 1080D] Three manuscripts read: “which are listed in contrast,” etc.], should likewise be understood spiritually, according to the statement: “The sacrifice of God is a broken spirit” (Ps. L, 19).

This is the worst thing in all that is done under the sun: that there is one outcome for everyone. Yet the hearts of the sons of men are filled with evil, and there are errors [or: error] in their hearts throughout their life, and after this they go to the dead.

For who is there that shares fellowship with all the living? Symmachus, in his customary clearer manner, interpreted this as follows: “The hearts of the sons of men are also filled with evil and insolence according to their hearts during their life. But at the end they go to the dead.”

Scripture repeats the same sense that we discussed a little earlier: since all things happen equally to everyone, and there is no distinction either in enduring good things or in suffering evils, or since we are certainly all removed from this world by an equal death, nevertheless we are filled with errors, insolence, and wickedness, and after all these things are suddenly snatched away by destruction [Col. 1081B] [Note: [Col. 1081D] “We are suddenly snatched away by destruction.” This passage too is retained by them as: “we are suddenly snatched away into destruction.” MARTIAN.] [or: into destruction], nor can we thereafter have fellowship with the living.

Or certainly it may be understood in this way: Since common distresses press upon both the righteous and the unrighteous, human beings are therefore provoked to sins; nevertheless, after all their efforts, in which they have striven in vain while ignorant, they descend to the lower regions.

There is confidence in this saying: a living dog is better than a dead lion [Note: [Col. 1081D] These same manuscripts omit the preposition *a*: “better than a dead lion,” etc. One Palatine manuscript reads: “it is better than a lion,” etc.]. For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and there is no further reward for them. For the memory of them has come into oblivion.

Their love, their hatred, and their jealousy have already perished, and they have no further share in the world, in anything that is done under the sun.

Since he had said above that the hearts of human beings are filled with evil and insolence, and that all these things end in death, he now completes and repeats the same point: while human beings live, they can become righteous; after death, no opportunity for a good work is granted.

A living sinner can be better than a dead righteous person, if he wishes to pass over to the latter’s virtues. Or certainly a poor and utterly insignificant person can be better than one who gloried in his wickedness, power, and insolence and has died [Note: [Col. 1081D] The Vatican and one Palatine manuscript read: “who, though you wish to be poor, is utterly insignificant.”].

Why? Because the living, through fear of death, can perform good works; but the dead can add nothing to what they once carried away with them from life. Everything is wrapped in oblivion, according to what is written in the psalm: “I have been forgotten as one dead from the heart” (Ps. XXX, 13).

Their love, hatred, rivalry, and everything they could possess in the world also end with the arrival of death. They can no longer do anything justly [Note: [Col. 1081D] In the manuscripts there is *jam*, “now,” instead of the single word *quippiam*, “anything.”], nor sin, nor add virtues, nor vices.

Although some contradict this interpretation, asserting that even after death we can increase and decrease, they understand the statement “They shall have no further share in the world, in anything that is done under the sun” to mean that they have no fellowship in this world and under this sun, which we see, but do have fellowship under another world, of which the Savior says: “I am not of this world” (John VIII, 23), and under the sun of righteousness. They do not exclude the opinion that maintains that after we have departed from this world we can still offend rational creatures and merit [further recompense].

The Hebrew, however, reported the verse differently [Note: [Col. 1082D] Victorius reports: “A Hebrew explained the verse to me.”], in which it says, “For a living dog is better than a dead lion.” Among his people, he said, it is explained in this way: A living person, even if unlearned, who still lives and teaches, is more useful than a perfect teacher who has already died. For example, one should understand the dog as any one of several teachers, and the lion as Moses or any other of the prophets.

But because this interpretation does not please us, let us reach for greater things. Let us say that the Canaanite woman to whom it was said, “Your faith has saved you” (Matthew IX, 23), is a dog according to the Gospel, while the dead lion is the people of the circumcision, as the prophet Balaam says: “Behold, the people shall rise like a lion’s cub and like a lion exulting” (Numbers XXIII, 24).

Therefore the living dog is us, from the nations; the dead lion is the Jewish people, abandoned by the Lord. And this living dog is better in the Lord’s sight than that dead lion. For we, being alive, know the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; but they, being dead, know nothing and expect no promise or reward. Their memory has been completed.

Nor do they themselves remember what they ought to have known, nor does their Lord any longer remember them. Their love, too, by which they once loved God, has perished, as has the hatred of which they spoke boldly: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and did I not waste away because of your enemies?” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 21). Their zeal has likewise perished—the zeal by which Phinehas was zealous and Mattathias’s knees trembled [in Greek: νεφροί, “kidneys”].

It is evident also that they have no share in the world. For they cannot say: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. LXXII, 26).

Go, eat your bread with gladness, and drink your wine with a good heart, for your works have now pleased God. Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not fail from your head (Ecclesiastes IX, 7)—up to the passage where he says: “Like fish caught in the worst of nets, and like birds caught in a snare, so the sons of men are caught at the worst time, when it suddenly falls upon them.”

Before we discuss each point, everything should be briefly gathered together, so that the single sense in which all these things are spoken may become apparent. Since in the preceding chapter he had stated beforehand that after human beings died they would fall from the hearts of the living, and that no one would have either love or hatred for them, according to the Poet (Aeneid II):

> No contest remains with the vanquished [Note: [Col. 1082D] “No contest remains with the vanquished.” These are the words of the Latin envoys to Aeneas, in Book XI of the *Aeneid*, verse 104:
>
> “Let him return them, and allow the earth to receive them in a tomb:
>
> No contest remains with the vanquished, and those deprived of heaven;
>
> Let him spare the guests once called fathers-in-law.” MARTIAN.],

and since they could do nothing further under the sun, he now introduces human error and the custom by which people encourage one another to enjoy the goods of this age. He employs προσωποποιΐαν (*prosopopaeian*) [Note: [Col. 1083C] *Prosopopoiïa.* Some grammarians write it without the double iota, *prosopopoeia*. It is the introduction of fictitious persons; hence Cicero, *On the Orator* III, calls this figure “the introduction of fictitious persons.” See also Quintilian, Book IX, chapter 2. MARTIAN.] in the manner of rhetoricians and poets, saying:

“O human being, since after death you are nothing, and death itself is nothing, listen to my advice. While you live this brief life, enjoy pleasure; make use of food; suppress your cares with wine; and understand that these things have been given to you by God for your use. Walk adorned in white garments; let your head breathe forth perfumes; rejoice in the embrace of whichever woman pleases you; and pass through this vain and brief life with vain and brief pleasure.

“For you will have nothing more beyond these things in which to take pleasure. Seize quickly whatever can delight you, lest it perish. Nor should you fear the frivolous notions that an account of every deed, whether good or evil, will have to be rendered to you among the dead. For there is no wisdom in death; after the dissolution of this life no consciousness remains [Note: [Col. 1083C] The manuscripts omit the word “remains”: “of this life,” a complete sense. See Cicero, if desired, *Tusculan Disputations* III.].

“And, he says, let some Epicurean say these things—Epicurus [Note: [Col. 1083C] “Let someone say Epicurus.” In Book II *Against Jovinianus* and Book VII of the *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter XXII [Col. 1083D], he says: “With Epicurus, who says, ‘After death there is nothing; death itself is nothing.’” Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “That there is nothing after death is the doctrine of Epicurus’s school.” Lucan expresses Epicurus’s opinion in Book III in these words:

> “What? Are we frightened,” he says, “by the image of a vain dream?
>
> Or is there no consciousness left to our minds after death? [The supplied source breaks off here.]

Or death itself is nothing, and so forth. Moreover, who those beasts of the philosophers were, Cicero clearly teaches in *Tusculan Disputations*, Book III:

“But Aristippus and the Cyrenaic philosophers, who were named after him, placed every good in pleasure and judged that virtue ought to be praised for this reason, that it produced pleasure.”

See the same Cicero, Book III *On the Orator* and Book III *On Duties*, and Diogenes Laertius, Book II, in the life of Aristippus of Cyrene. Concerning Epicurus, however, this should be known: according to Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book III, chapter 7, he placed the highest good not, like Aristippus, in bodily pleasure, but in pleasure of the mind. Yet Jerome and other ecclesiastical writers call him an advocate of pleasure. [Martianus]

—and Aristippus and the Cyrenaics, and the other beasts of the philosophers.

But I, carefully reconsidering the matter with myself, find that everything is not, as some wrongly suppose, done by chance, nor that Fortune plays with human affairs in a variable fashion; rather, all things happen by the judgment of God. For the swift-footed man ought not think that his course belongs to him merely because he runs. Nor should the strong man trust in his own strength, nor the wise man suppose that riches and wealth are gathered by prudence; nor should the eloquent and learned man think that through eloquence and learning he can find favor with the people. Rather, all things are done as God disposes them.

And unless he governs all things by his own decision and builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain. Unless he guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain (Psalm 126:1).

It is not therefore, as they suppose, that there is one single outcome and an uncertain condition to this life, since, when they least expect it, they will be carried away by sudden death and come to judgment. And just as fish are caught by hooks and nets, and birds, though free in the air, are bound by a snare while they are unaware, so human beings, according to their deserts, will be led to eternal punishments when death suddenly comes and judgment falls upon those who supposed that everything was tossed about in an uncertain condition.

These remarks have been made according to the sense in which we wished briefly to encompass everything. Now, as though he were speaking not in another’s person but in his own, the individual statements must be interpreted:

“Go, eat your bread with gladness, and drink your wine with a good heart” [462] [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts omit the pronoun “your.”] “because your works have pleased God.”

Since you have learned that all things end in death and that there is no repentance in the underworld, nor any return to virtue, while you are in this age hasten and strive to do penance [Note: Three manuscripts read: “Strive, do penance.” Below we correct less significant faults.]. While you have time, labor. For God willingly receives the penitent.

Alternatively, the passage is beneficial when understood simply, in accordance with the statement: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything in the name of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 10:31) [Note: The Vatican manuscript, following the Vulgate translator, reads: “or whatever else you do.” Martianus noted that the following Scriptural text is drawn from Proverbs, Book 24, where a fragment of chapter 31 is inserted in Greek at verse 4: μετὰ βουλῆς οἰνοπότει, “drink wine with counsel.”]. And elsewhere: “Drink wine with counsel” [Note: “Drink wine with counsel.” It is scarcely possible to believe how much this passage tormented me. For a long time it was full of difficulties because of the incompetence of Erasmus’s edition, on whose authority I was seeking in Paul, First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 5, what is found near the end of the Greek edition of Solomon’s Proverbs, chapter 24, where these words are inserted: Μετὰ βουλῆς πάντα ποίει, μετὰ βουλῆς οἰνοπότει, that is, “Do everything with counsel; drink wine with counsel.” Martianus].

For he does not possess true gladness and a good heart who abuses created things beyond measure.

It is better, however, to understand it in this way: whoever’s works have pleased God will in no way be able to lack the true bread and wine, that which was pressed from the vine of Sorek. Since, therefore, the commandment has been given to us which says, “You desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord will supply it to you” (Sirach 1:33), let us keep the commandments, and we shall be able to find spiritual bread and wine.

But to the one who does not keep the commandments and boasts in an abundance of bread and wine, Isaiah says: “Do not say, ‘I know it’; for you neither knew nor understood, nor from the beginning did I open your ears. For I know that, in despising, you will despise” (Isaiah 48:8, according to the Septuagint) [Note: Formerly the reading was “he opened,” against the manuscripts and the Greek, which have ἤνοιξα, “I opened.”].

Moreover, where the Septuagint interpreters say, “Come, eat your bread with gladness” [Note: Victor adds, “and drink your wine with a good heart.” —“Come, eat your bread with gladness.” In the previously printed books of Erasmus and Marianus, many Greek and Latin words have been wrongly added here. Martianus], it is the voice of that Ecclesiastes who speaks in the Gospel: “Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). And in Proverbs: “Come, eat my breads and drink my wine” (Proverbs 9:5).

“Let your garments always be white, and let oil not be lacking from your head.”

“Have,” he says, “a clean body and be merciful.”

Or thus: Let there be no time when you do not have white garments; take care that you are never clothed in soiled garments. For the sinful people are described as having mourned in dark garments. But you should put on light, and not the curse that was written against Judas: “Let him be clothed with cursing as with a garment” (Psalm 108:18). Put on “the bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience” [Note: Some manuscripts read “wisdom”] (Colossians 3). And when you have stripped off the old man with his works, put on the new man, who is renewed from day [463] to day.

As for what he says, “Let oil not be lacking from your head,” one should know that the nature of oil is such that it both feeds a flame and relieves the labor of the weary. There is spiritual oil, the oil of gladness, of which it is written: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:8). With this oil our face must be made joyful.

This is the oil with which the head of the fasting person is to be anointed [Note: Alcuin, and another Palatine manuscript agreeing with him, read: “Let those who fast have this ointment on their head”; the sinners cannot possess it. The older printed editions differ in these words, reading: “have it for anointing the head.”], which sinners cannot possess, to whom it is said: “There is no poultice to put on, nor oil, nor bandages” (Isaiah 1:6). For they possess the contrary oil, which the righteous man detests, saying: “Let the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” (Psalm 104:5). Heretics possess this oil, and they desire to pour it over the heads of the deceived.

[Col. 1085C] [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts read: “Live life with the woman whom you loved all the days of your vanity. For this is …” The Vatican manuscript reads: “Live life with the woman whom you took in marriage all the days of your vanity, which were given to you under the sun, all the days of your vanity, or instability. For this is your portion in your life and in your labor,” and so forth.]

“See life with the woman whom you loved all the days of the life of your vanity, which were given to you under the sun; for this is your portion in life and in the labor with which you labor under the sun.”

Follow wisdom and knowledge of the Scriptures, and join this woman to yourself in marriage, of whom it is said in Proverbs: “Love her, and she will preserve you; embrace her, and she will surround you” (Proverbs 4:8).

The days of vanity signify the days of this wicked age [Note: Some manuscripts read “signify,” singular]. The Apostle, too, does not remain silent about it.

As for what he says, “See life with the woman whom you loved” [Note: Here again three of the manuscripts mentioned above prefer *vive* (“live”) to *vide* (“see”), and below consistently read *vivere vitam* (“to live life”) instead of *videre* (“to see”). Moreover, for *dilexisti* (“you loved”), the Vatican retains, as above, *duxisti* (“you took in marriage”).], it is ambiguously expressed: either, “See and contemplate life, both you and your wife with you”—for you will not be able to see life alone without such a wife—or, “Consider both things, and see life and the woman during the days of your vanity.”

Beautifully he commands that, during the days of our vanity, we seek true life with wisdom as our wife. For this is our portion, and this is the fruit of labor, if in this shadowy life we are able to find true life.

“Whatever your hand finds to do, do with your strength, because there is neither work, nor thought, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld to which you are going.”

Do now whatever you can, and labor, because when you descend to the underworld [Note: The manuscripts read “to the underworlds.”] there will be no place for repentance. Something similar is commanded by the Savior: “Work while it is day; night will come, when no one can work” (John 9:4).

As for what he says, “In the underworld to which you are going,” note that this makes it possible to believe that Samuel too truly was in the underworld, and that before Christ’s coming all, even the saints, were held under the law of the underworld. But that after the Lord’s resurrection the saints are by no means held in the underworld, the Apostle testifies when he says: “It is better to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23) [Col. 1086B]. Whoever is with Christ is certainly not held in the underworld.

I turned and saw under the sun that the race is not of the swift, nor the battle of the strong, nor bread of the wise, nor riches of the prudent, nor favor of the learned, because time and chance will overtake them all.

The person who is bound in iron fetters and weighed down by heavy chains of lead—for “Iniquity sits upon the leaden talent” (Zechariah 5:7)—and who says in the Psalm, “They have been made heavy upon me like a heavy burden” (Psalm 37:5), is not suited to that race of which it is said: “I have finished the race; I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7).

But even the person who is light and whose soul is not weighed down cannot reach the goal without God as helper [Note: Alcuin reads: “Without the Lord’s help, he cannot reach heaven.”].

And when there is battle against hostile powers, concerning which it is written, “Sanctify war” (Jeremiah 6:4), even though a person is strong, he will not be able to conquer by his own powers. Nor will the man who is perfect and wise among the children of men be able to possess living and heavenly bread except through Wisdom, who calls out: “Come, eat my breads” [Note: Another Palatine manuscript adds: “and because riches are not lacking.”].

And since there are riches concerning which the Apostle says, “To become rich in good works” (1 Timothy 6:18), and elsewhere, “You have been enriched in every utterance and in all knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1:5), one should know that the prudent man cannot gather these riches unless he has received them from the Lord, whose riches they are. Concerning these it is also said elsewhere: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Proverbs 15:8).

Favor, too, unless it is accompanied by knowledge and granted by God, an educated man will not be able to find, however learned he may be. Paul, knowing this, says: “I labored more than all of them” [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads, “I labored more than all”; the Vatican adds, “and yet grace,” and so forth.] [Col. 1087A] “yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me” [Note: “But the grace of God which …” In many manuscripts: “but the grace which is with me.” Martianus] (1 Corinthians 15:10). And again: “His grace toward me was not empty.”

Finally, a person does not know when the time will come in which varied fortune and the end of all things will follow.

This is according to the *anagogy* (ἀναγωγήν), the higher spiritual interpretation.

But, to speak more simply [Note: Some manuscripts read “to speak simply”], the Epistle to the Romans corresponds to this passage: “It is not of him that wills or of him that runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16).

As for what he says, “There is no bread for the wise,” this is proved daily by the example of many who, although exceedingly wise, lack necessities. And, “There is no favor for the learned.” For you may see the most ignorant people in the Church flourishing; because they have cultivated boldness of face and acquired fluency of tongue, while they do not consider what they are saying, they think themselves prudent and learned—especially if they have the favor of the crowd, which is more pleased and moved by frivolous words.

Conversely, you may see an educated man hidden in obscurity and suffering persecutions; not only does he fail to find favor among the people, but he wastes away in poverty and want. These things happen because everything is carried along in an uncertain condition, and merit is not repaid in the present but in the future.

And indeed a person does not know his time, like fish that are held in a disastrous catch [Note: “Are held in a disastrous catch.” The books previously printed by us read *retinent, in retinculo malo* (“are held in an evil net”), but this is an obvious error and contrary to the testimony of all the manuscript codices, which read *in captione pessima* (“in a disastrous catch”). Jerome himself has the same reading above in his Commentary, saying: “Up to the place where he says: like fish that are held in a disastrous catch,” and so forth. This proves that the authors of the old editions never used Jerome himself in restoring Jerome; yet he is often our sole authority for the true and complete restoration of his works. Martianus], like birds that are caught in a snare. Thus the children of men will fall in an evil time, when it suddenly falls upon them.

We have already said above [Note: Three manuscripts read *unde habent* (“from which they have”) instead of *ita* (“thus”), a reading that would be more agreeable if the little word were deleted.], that, while people are unaware, either distress or destruction comes upon them.

But, according to the allegory, one must know that the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea (Matthew 13). Conversely, heretics possess a net by which they catch fish for destruction. Their net is agreeable speech, flattering eloquence, simulated or forced fasts, humble clothing, and imitation of virtues.

If they begin to discuss higher matters, to raise their mouths on high, and to seek the heights of God, they set a snare in lofty places. Therefore, just as fish and birds are quickly caught by such a net and such a snare, so, when iniquity has multiplied, the love of many has grown cold, and signs and wonders have occurred, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led astray (Matthew 24), it must be understood that ecclesiastical men also—those who are called children of men and are of weak faith—can quickly fall.

It should also be noted that throughout the book, wherever “children of men” is said, the Hebrew has () “sons of man,” that is, “sons of Adam” [Hebrew term not supplied in the text]. Nearly all Scripture is filled with this idiom, calling the whole human race the children of Adam.

But I also saw this wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me. There was a small city and few men in it; and a great king came against it, surrounded it, and built a great siegework against it. And there was found in it a poor and wise man, and he saved the city by his wisdom; but no one remembered that poor man.

While others say that everything is uncertain and that the just man has nothing more than the unjust, I proved that wisdom is also very great in this respect: it frequently happens that a city is small, its inhabitants few, and it is surrounded by an army of innumerable enemies; the people inside are killed by siege and famine; and suddenly, contrary to everyone’s expectation, a humble and poor man is found [Note: Alcuin reads: “a poor man who possessed greater wisdom,” and so forth]. Because he has greater wisdom than all the rich, great, powerful, and proud men who are in danger and trembling before the siege, he considers and investigates and finds a way to rescue the city from its evils.

And what thankless forgetfulness there is among human beings! After they have been freed, the captivity dissolved, and liberty restored to their homeland, no one remembers that wise poor man; no one gives thanks for their safety. Instead, everyone honors the rich, who were able to provide no help in the danger.

Alternatively, the Hebrew interpreted this passage as follows: The small city is the human being, who is also called by the philosophers the “smaller world.” The few men in it are the members from which the human being himself is composed.

When the great king, the devil, comes against it [Note: “And seeks a place,” and so forth. The old editions of Erasmus and Marianus insert many inept words into Jerome’s text here, enclosing them in parentheses as follows: “The devil is a slippery serpent; if one does not resist his head, that is, his first suggestion, the whole interior of the heart slips in unnoticed. The beginnings of diabolical temptations are crimes; he is not the one who casts in, but the one who kindles vices. Hence David: ‘You have crushed the head of the dragon.’” Martianus] and seeks a place through which he may break in, there is found in it a humble and wise man, and a quiet thought of the inner man, and it preserves [Note: Some read “rescues”] the city that was surrounded by enemies [Note: The Vatican reads: “And because this thought is that of the inner man, it preserves,” and so forth. Others: “The sense of the inner man, and it preserves,” and so forth. —For “a quiet thought,” the printed books read “a quiet sense”; they read: “and the wise and quiet sense of the inner man will rescue the city, which was besieged,” and so forth. Martianus].

And when the human being has been rescued from danger—whether persecution, distress, or any other adversity and sin—that outer man, who is the enemy of the poor and wise man, does not remember the inner man, nor submit himself to his counsels. Instead, he again enjoys his freedom [Note: Here, for “freedom,” some retain “free will.” Martianus].

Alternatively: The small city, with few men in it in comparison with the whole world, is the Church. Against it the great king, the devil, often rises—not because he is great, but because he boasts that he is great—and surrounds it with a siege, whether through persecution or through some other kind of distress.

And he finds in it a poor and wise man, the Lord Jesus Christ, who became poor for us (2 Corinthians 8:9) and is wisdom itself. That poor man frees the city by his wisdom.

How often have we seen the lion sitting in ambush with the rich—that is, with the senators and rulers of this age—and plotting against the Church, only to have his plans collapse before the wisdom of this poor man? And when this poor man has conquered and the city has been restored to peace, scarcely anyone remembers him; scarcely anyone considers his commandments. Instead, surrendering themselves entirely to luxury and pleasures, they seek riches, which do not rescue anyone in time of need.

And I said, “Wisdom is better [Note: Many manuscripts read “I said that wisdom is better”; a few agree with the printed editions. Whether we read one way or the other, there is no difference in meaning. Martianus] than strength; and the wisdom of the poor man, which is despised, and his words, which are not heard.”

Although no one remembers that wise poor man when everything is prosperous, but everyone admires power and riches, I nevertheless, according to all the interpretations given above, honor more highly despised wisdom and the words that no one considers worthy of hearing.

The words of the wise are heard in quiet, more than the shouting of a ruler among fools.

Whenever you see in the Church a declaimer [Note: Both Corbie manuscripts and the Colbertinus read: “Whenever you see a shouter in the Church.” Martianus] who, with a certain seductive charm and verbal elegance, stirs up applause, provokes laughter, and excites his listeners into joyful emotions, know that this is a sign of foolishness, both in the speaker and in those who listen.

For the words of the wise are heard in quiet and moderate silence. But the foolish person, even if he is powerful and possesses either the shouting of his own voice or the acclamation of a crowd, will be counted among fools [Note: Alcuin reads *computatur* (“is counted”); other printed editions read *loquitur* (“speaks”).] [468].

Wisdom is better than weapons of war, and one sinner destroys much goodness.

Here too he sets wisdom above strength, and says that in battles it is worth more than the weapons of combatants. But if one person is foolish, even though he is small and insignificant, nevertheless by that person’s folly great resources and riches are often overthrown.

Since in Hebrew it can also be read, “And one who sins destroys much goodness,” it should likewise be understood in this way: because of one sin, many previous acts of righteousness perish; virtues follow one another in turn, and whoever possesses one possesses them all. And whoever sins in one matter is subject to all vices (James 2:10).

### Chapter 10

Flies of death [Note: “Flies of death pollute,” and so forth. The Colbertinus manuscript reads this according to the Hebrew idiom *zebube maveth*, “flies of death,” or, in the manner of the Latins, “dying flies,” as other manuscript copies have it. It is therefore wrongly read in the previously printed editions: “Dying flies destroy the oil,” and so forth. Martianus. —The Vatican reads “dying flies”; the two Palatine manuscripts read “flies destined to die.”] pollute the oil of the perfume; a little foolishness is more precious than wisdom and glory.

He gives an example of the preceding meaning, in which he said that one fool can overturn many good things: so a bad element mixed with good contaminates many, just as flies, if they die in perfume, destroy both its fragrance [Note: “Its fragrance and its color.” Instead of “color,” the printed editions retain “flavor,” but this does not suit the meaning, since perfume requires fragrance and color, not flavor. The Corbie manuscripts accordingly read: “And since cunning is always …” Martianus. —Martianus reads “and color,” contrary to all our manuscripts, as well as Alcuin and the earlier printed books. Nor do I see why he says that “flavor” is unsuitable for oil or perfume.], and its color.

And since wisdom is often mixed with cunning, and prudence possesses wickedness, he commands us to seek simple wisdom, mixed with the innocence of doves: to be prudent for what is good, but simple with regard to evil.

The meaning is this: It is fitting for a righteous person to possess a little simplicity and, because of excessive patience, to seem foolish while reserving vengeance for God, rather than immediately taking revenge and practicing wickedness under the cover of prudence.

Alternatively: The flies which, according to Isaiah (chapter 7:18), rule over the part of the river of Egypt [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads “the gates of the river”; others “the part,” and so forth.] destroy the sweetness of the oil, leaving in each believer the odor and traces of their uncleanness.

The prince of demons, Beelzebub, was named after these flies (Matthew 12:24). The name is interpreted either as “idol of flies,” or “man of flies,” or “one who has flies” [Note: The same is found in the book *On Hebrew Names*, following Jerome’s account, although it seems more probable—especially in Matthew—that Beelzebub was so called because a dwelling, once inhabited, is abandoned only with difficulty and reluctance. In any case, the Jews commonly called him the prince of demons.].

The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool at his left. But even on the road, when the fool walks, his heart diminishes; and he says, “Everyone is a fool.”

In the Gospel, too, it is commanded that the wise man’s left hand should not know what his right hand does (Matthew 6:3; 5:39). And when we are struck on the right cheek, we are not commanded to offer the left cheek to the one striking us, but the other right cheek [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads simply “but the other,” without the addition “right”; as I think, this is the better reading.] (Matthew 5:39). For the righteous person has nothing left-handed in himself; everything in him is right-handed.

And when the Savior comes to judge, the lambs will stand at his right, while the goats will be at his left (Matthew 25:33). And it is written in Proverbs [Note: Three manuscript codices read “And it is written in the Prophet.” Martianus]: “The Lord knows the right-hand ways; but the crooked ways are on the left” [Note: The Vatican reads “on his left” instead of “are on the left.”] (Proverbs 4:27).

Therefore, the person who is wise always thinks about the future age, which leads to the right. But the fool thinks about the present, which is placed on the left.

Following the same thought, that philosopher and poet [Note: “The philosopher and poet says.” These verses are Virgil’s, from the middle of Book VI of the *Aeneid*:

“Here is the place where the road divides into two parts:

The right-hand path, which leads beneath the walls of mighty Dis;

By this path lies our way to Elysium; but the left

Inflicts punishments upon the wicked and sends them to impious Tartarus.”

Lactantius Firmianus repeats the same passage in Book VI, chapters 3 and 4, of the *Divine Institutes*, where he discusses virtues and vices at length and mentions the letter Y, which others call the Pythagorean letter, or the letter of Pythagoras, as Jerome himself does in his letter to Laeta on the education of her daughter and in his letter to Pammachius on the death of Paulina. Consult also the commentaries of Sixtus Betuleius of Augsburg on the passages cited from Lactantius. Martianus], says (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6):

> The right-hand path, which leads beneath the walls of mighty Dis [or: stretches beneath them].
>
> By this path lies our way to Elysium; but the left
>
> Inflicts punishments upon the wicked and sends them to impious Tartarus [or: leads them there].

Our own Firmianus, too, in his celebrated work of the *Institutes* [Note: Specifically, Book IV, chapter 3: “For they say that the course of human life resembles the letter Y: when each person first reaches the threshold of adolescence and comes to the place where the road divides into two parts, he remains hesitating and wavering and does not know toward which side he should incline. If he finds a guide who directs him toward better things,” and so forth. The entire chapter discusses these matters with great elegance.], mentioned the letter Y and discussed at great length the right and left sides—that is, virtues and vices.

Nor should we think that the statement, “Do not decline to the right or to the left” (Proverbs 4:27), contradicts this little sentence. Here the right side is understood as good [Note: Two Palatine manuscripts read: “The right side of the Y is for good,” and so forth]; there, it is not so much the right side as the deviation toward the right that is condemned: we must not be wiser than it is necessary for us to be, because virtues lie in the middle [Note: “Because virtues lie in the middle.” You will find much on this moderation of the virtues in our notes above, column 443 (see column 1066 of our edition, note g). Martianus], and every excess is a vice.

As for the following verse, where he says, “But even on the road, when the fool walks, his heart is deficient, and he says, ‘Every foolishness is,’” or “he is foolish,” the meaning is this: The fool, just as he himself sins, expects everyone else to sin in the same way and judges all people according to his own character.

Accordingly, Symmachus translated it as follows: “But even on the road, when the fool walks, he himself, being foolish, suspects of everyone that they are fools.” The Septuagint, however, made another sense, saying that everything the fool thinks is utterly vain.

If the spirit of one who has authority rises against you, do not leave your place, because healing makes great sins rest.
