The Scripture now signifies the prince of this world, the ruler of this darkness, who works in the children of unbelief, whom the Apostle also mentions (Ephesians 2:2; 6:12).

If he rises into our heart and the mind receives the wound of an evil thought, we must not give it further ground [Note: Alcuin and the old printed books read *ultro* (“willingly”); soon afterward four manuscripts read “and to be freed from the greatest sin.” He calls it the greatest sin, as has been observed by us elsewhere, including in the Letter to Demetrias: namely, completing the perverse thought by an act. —For “to give further ground,” the older editions read *ultro*, which produces an entirely different meaning. They also read, consistently with many manuscript copies, “and to be freed from the greatest sin.” Martianus], but fight against the worst thought [Col. 1092A] and free ourselves from the greatest sin, so that we do not complete the thought by an act. For it is one thing to sin in thought and another to sin in deed.

Concerning this great sin it is also written in the Psalm: “If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless and cleansed from the greatest offense” (Psalm 18:4).

Symmachus interpreted the Hebrew word () *MARPHE* [Hebrew term not supplied in the text], which all the others translated similarly as ἴαμα, that is, “healing” or “remedy,” according to its meaning, and said: “If the spirit of the ruler rushes upon you, do not leave your place, because chastity restrains great sins.”

That is: if the devil tickles your mind and stirs you toward lust, do not follow the worst thought that flatters pleasure. Stand firm and resolute, and extinguish the flame of pleasure with the coldness of chastity [Note: “And with the coldness of chastity.” A considerable number of manuscripts read: “And with the coldness of charity, extinguish the flame of pleasure.” Martianus].

The Hebrew suspected something of this kind in the passage: If you have received some dignity in the world and have been appointed great among the peoples, do not abandon your former works, and do not begin to forget your ancient virtues or cease from your former labor; for the remedy of sins arises from a good manner of life, not from swollen and excessive dignity [Note: The printed editions add “your,” although the manuscripts are silent; they also read *conversione* (“conversion”) where the manuscripts read *conversatione* (“conduct” or “manner of life”).].

There is an evil that I saw under the sun, like ignorance proceeding from the face of the powerful: a fool placed in great dignities, and the rich sitting in a lowly place. I saw servants on horses and princes walking like servants upon the earth.

In place of what we have rendered, “Like ignorance proceeding from the face of the powerful,” Aquila, Theodotion, and the Septuagint translated: “Like something not voluntary” [Note: “Like something not voluntary.” As is their custom, the old editions add many Greek words here, although the evidence of all the manuscript codices shows that Jerome placed only these two words. Martianus], that is, ὡς ἀκούσιον, “as something involuntary,” from the face of the ruler.

Symmachus, adding to this, said: “A fool placed in great eminence; but the rich sit in lowliness.”

He therefore recalls that he saw this injustice in the world: that God’s judgment appears unjust, and that, whether through ignorance or without God’s will, in the powers of the world or in the leadership of the Church, those who are rich in speech and wisdom, rich also in good works, sit in ignoble positions, while an imprudent person holds the chief place in the Church.

The Apostle does not leave unsaid that this is done by the devil, who possesses power in the world, so that he oppresses powerful and learned men and does not allow them to appear among the peoples. But those whom he knows to be imprudent in the churches he makes greater, so that the blind may be led by the blind into the pit.

The same sense applies to what follows: “I saw servants on horses and princes walking like servants upon the earth.” Those who are servants of vices and sin, or so humble that they are counted servants by human beings, puffed up by the devil with sudden dignity, trample the public roads with ponies [Note: “Puffed up by the devil with dignity.” This is a very famous passage, both because of the variant readings in the manuscripts and because many words were falsely added and corrupted in the Erasmian edition and in several manuscript codices. There we read the passage in a corrupted form as follows: “Suddenly raised up by the devil through public crimes, let them be elevated; those whom people commonly call slippery; but every noble master …” The Sorbonne manuscript has the same reading, though it omits *sublimentur* (“let them be elevated”) and reads *luridos* (“squalid”) instead of *lubricos* (“slippery”). In the margin, however, the copyist adds: “Another book: let them trample the public roads with ponies.” Thus we know with certainty that the genuine reading which we have restored existed in some books. It remains slightly corrupt today in the Colbertinus manuscript, where I find written: “Puffed up by sudden dignity from the devil, they were serving the public roads.” The copyist wrote what he understood, not what he found; hence, instead of *mannis terant* (“trample with ponies”), he wrote *ministrarent* (“they were serving”). The Corbie manuscripts retain an interpolation in the text, for after *publicas* (“public roads”) they add: “whom they commonly call *lorichos*.” Apart from these words, everything is genuine in those copies.

For the present sentence Jerome borrowed his thought, and indeed elegantly, from Horace Flaccus, *Epodes*, poem 4, concerning Mena, the freedman of Pompey the Great:

> Cut by the triumviral scourges,
>
> To the disgust of the herald,
>
> He plows a thousand acres of Falernian land,
>
> And tramples the Appian Way with ponies,
>
> And, foremost among the seats, is a great knight …]

[The supplied text ends here.]

Otho, having been despised, sits. Horace’s verses have the same meaning as Ecclesiastes when he says: “I saw servants upon horses,” and so forth. Now *manni* were small horses, so called because, on account of their tameness, they followed the hand (*manus*) more familiarly. Jerome, in his Letter to Pammachius on the death of Paulina, calls swift little horses *burici*, or *burdi manni*.

**MARTIAN.** One of the seven manuscripts that we consulted at this passage proved to be the Vatican manuscript, which correctly reads, as we have printed it. It has only *equis* (“horses”) instead of *mannis* (“ponies”), though this is somewhat less satisfactory, since Jerome is plainly alluding to that Horatian passage in *Epodes*, Book I, Ode 4, concerning the freedman Menas: “And he wears down the Appian Way with ponies” [Col. 1094B]. Most of the other manuscripts likewise have the same erroneous reading: “inflated by rank through public crimes” (some add *sublimentur*), “whom people commonly call *lyzichos*” (others have *lurichos*, *luridos*, or some other monstrous form of the name), “and every noble man, etc.” We omitted the gloss “whom people commonly call *Luricos*,” since it did not seem to have proceeded from the holy Doctor’s pen. If, however, you wish to retain it in accordance with the books published before Martianaeus, read *Burichos*: for *manni*, as the ancient scholiasts on Horace teach, are horses whom we commonly call *burdones* or *buricos*. The ancient Glosses likewise have: *Mannis*, Βουρίχοις (*bourichoïs*). See what we observe in Letter 66 to Pammachius, §8, where we deleted this same passage.

“Suddenly puffed up by dignity bestowed by the devil, they wear down the public roads on ponies; and every noble and prudent man, oppressed by poverty, walks along as though he were a servant, and performs a servant’s duty” [Col. 1093B]. The Hebrew interpreted “the powerful and the prince, from whose face ignorance seems to proceed,” as God, because people think that amid the inequality of worldly affairs he does not judge justly and as is right.

[Note: Two Palatine manuscripts read: “amid this inequality of worldly affairs,” etc.]

Others, however, think this should be joined with what precedes: “Let him himself be the powerful one of whom it is said before these verses: ‘If the spirit of one who has authority rises against you, do not leave your place’” [Col. 1094A]. Let us therefore not be sad if in this world we seem to be humble, knowing that before the face of the devil both fools are raised up and the rich cast down; that servants bear the insignia of their masters, and princes enter upon the lowliness of servants. It should also be noted that here too the horse is understood in a good sense, as in: “And your riding is salvation.”

“He who digs a pit will fall into it, and he who tears down a hedge will be bitten by a serpent” [472]. The meaning is partly literal and partly mystical. Elsewhere also Solomon himself says: “He who sets a snare will be caught in it” (Ecclesiasticus 27:29). And in the seventh Psalm: “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the pit that he made.”

[Note: He seems to think that the author of Ecclesiasticus himself was Solomon, an opinion that was indeed held by many Fathers, both Greek and Latin; according to their understanding Jerome is likely speaking here. Yet when he examined the matter more carefully in the Preface to the Books of Solomon, he clearly excludes Ecclesiasticus from them. Victorius long ago made this observation, and Martianaeus follows him.—“For Solomon himself also says elsewhere.” Jesus, the author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus, is called by Athanasius, in the *Synopsis* attributed to him, ὀπαδὸς τοῦ Σαλομῶντος, that is, “a follower of Solomon,” because in composing proverbs he maintained Solomon’s method and reasoning and described many of his sayings and parables. Learned men consequently suppose that this led many of the ancient Fathers to proclaim Solomon as the author of Ecclesiasticus, and that it is therefore not uncommon for the book to be cited in their writings under Solomon’s name—as here by Jerome, who, following the custom of his age, counted Ecclesiasticus among Solomon’s works. For we read in Origen, *Homily 22 on the Book of Numbers*: “In the book which among us is usually reckoned among Solomon’s volumes and is called Ecclesiasticus, but among the Greeks is called the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach.” These words are attributed not to Origen but to his translator Rufinus. It is therefore clear that among the Latins Ecclesiasticus was counted among Solomon’s volumes; yet Jerome most plainly separates it from them in his Preface to the Books of Solomon, which are distinguished by asterisks and obeli. We have discussed this fully at the end of Part I of St. Jerome’s *Divine Library*. **MARTIAN.**]

[Note: In Alcuin: “The strengthening of the hedge, ecclesiastical …”; in the Palatine manuscript: “the tearing out …,” etc.]

The hedge and the stone walls signify ecclesiastical doctrines and the institution founded upon the Apostles and the Prophets. Whoever dismantles them and wishes to pass beyond them is struck by the serpent in the very act of neglecting them. Concerning this serpent it is also written in Amos: “If he descends into hell, I will command the serpent, and it will bite them” [or, “him”] (Amos 9:3).

“He who removes stones will suffer because of them; and he who splits wood will be endangered by it” (Zechariah 9:16) [Col. 1095A]. In Zechariah too the holy stones roll upon the earth. They do not remain firmly fixed in that position; rather, they pass onward and, always striving toward higher things, hasten to depart from it. From these living stones the city of the Savior is constructed in Revelation (chapter 21:18 ff.), and the Apostle does not fail to say that the Church is built from them.

If, therefore, someone perverted by heretical art removes these stones from the building of the Church—for this reason Aquila and Symmachus significantly said, instead of our reading “he who removes stones will suffer because of them,” “he who transfers stones will be torn apart by them”—he will afterward endure torments.

But since Scripture says simply, “He who removes stones,” or “he who transfers stones,” and does not add “good” or “bad,” the contrary meaning must also be understood: if an ecclesiastical man, namely a bishop or presbyter, removes a stone from a leprous house, in accordance with the command of Leviticus 14:45, so that it may be crushed into ash and dust, he will suffer precisely because he is compelled [or “is compelled”] to remove a stone from the Church of Christ, saying with the Apostle: “To weep with those who weep, to mourn with those who mourn” (Romans 12:15), and, “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Corinthians 11:29) [473].

[Note: “Who is weak, and I am not.” Many manuscripts omit the middle part of this verse because the words “and I am not” occur twice. **MARTIAN.**]

Likewise, he who splits wood will be endangered by it. Heretics are fruitless wood, a thicket without useful fruit. Hence the planting of a grove is forbidden in the temple of God, and the useless shelters of leaves—that is, of words that merely make a sound—are despised.

Although, therefore, the man who cuts up this wood with the sword of his speech may be prudent and learned [Col. 1095C], he will be endangered by it unless he is very careful, especially if what follows should happen to him: “If the iron is blunted and its face has become distorted”—that is, if his disputation is found to be weak and lacks the sharpness with which to cut down every opposing argument, and if the governing principle of his heart becomes dull—he will pass over to the opposing side, and perverse strength will confirm him.

This is what the Septuagint translated: “And he will be strengthened by strength.” Strengthened by superfluous knowledge, he will begin, as it were, to possess strength and a wisdom that is superfluous and does not help its possessor.

[Note: Three manuscripts read: “If he cuts up the wood, he will be endangered by it,” and so forth.]

“If the iron is blunted—and this not as before, but has become disturbed—it will be strengthened by powers, and the remainder of strength is wisdom.”

If someone, he says, has through negligence seen himself lose knowledge of the Scriptures, and the sharpness of his intellect has become dull, and, being disturbed, he has by no means remained what he had begun to be, the following may happen. Sometimes, when a person possesses a small amount of knowledge, he is lifted up into pride and ceases to learn and read. Gradually, because nothing is added to him, something is taken away, and his breast remains empty of learning; the iron that had been sharp becomes blunt. Idleness and sloth are, as it were, a kind of rust upon wisdom.

If someone has suffered this, let him not despair of the remedy of healing. Let him go to a teacher, be instructed by him again, and, after labor, diligence, and excessive sweating, he will be able to recover the wisdom he had lost. This is expressed more significantly in the Hebrew: “And he will be strengthened with strengths”—that is, through labor, sweat, diligence, and daily reading he will acquire wisdom, and the end of his strength will be that he receives wisdom.

“If a serpent bites in silence, there is no advantage to the one who has a tongue” [474].

The literal meaning is this: the serpent and the slanderer are alike. For just as the serpent, biting secretly, injects poison, so the slanderer, secretly disparaging, pours the venom of his heart into his brother; and he has no more benefit from his tongue than a serpent does.

[Note: Alcuin has: “and he has no less from the serpent.” Immediately afterward the ancient printed editions have “to bless God,” etc.—“To bless.” The printed editions add “God,” but, unless I am mistaken, unnecessarily, since here “to bless” means to wish good for one’s neighbor. **MARTIAN.**]

Since the human tongue was created for blessing and for the edification of one’s neighbor, the slanderer makes it equal to a serpent by perversely abusing its powers.

Alternatively: if the serpent, the devil, secretly bites someone and infects him with the poison of sin without anyone knowing, and if the one who has been struck remains silent and does not repent, and does not wish to confess his wound to his brother and teacher, the teacher and brother, who have tongues for healing, will not easily be able to help him.

[Note: Alcuin has: “and does not wish to confess his wound to the teacher”; “the teacher, who has a tongue, and correspondingly, will not be able to …”]

For if the sick person is ashamed to confess his wound to the physician, medicine does not heal what it does not know.

“The words of the mouth of the wise are grace, but the lips of the fool will bring him down” [Col. 1096C].

Foolishness, if it were content with its own rusticity, would have somewhat less evil in it. But now it wages war against wisdom, and whatever prudence it sees in a learned man, it does not accept, goaded by jealousy.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “whatever it sees in a learned man,” without *viro* (“man”).]

The wise man speaks words of knowledge and words of grace, which can benefit those who hear them. The fool’s ears, however, do not receive what is said as it is said; rather, they try to trip up the prudent man and make him like themselves.

And indeed the wise man is brought down when he speaks into the ear of the imprudent, and his words perish, so to speak, in a deep whirlpool. Hence blessed is the man who speaks into the ear of one who listens.

[Note: Our manuscripts and the old editions of Alcuin have: “Hence blessed is that man,” and shortly afterward *audientem* (“the hearer”) instead of *audientis* (“of the hearer”); the ancient editions have *sapientium* (“of the wise”).]

“The beginning of his words is foolishness, and the end of his mouth is the worst error” [Col. 1096D].

[Note: A second Palatine manuscript, deleting *ejus* (“his”), substitutes *stulti* (“of the fool”).]

And the fool multiplies words. A man does not know what has happened; and what will happen after him, who will declare to him?

He is still discussing the fool, whose lips bring down the wise man—or, according to another interpretation, make the fool himself collapse. The beginning and end of his speech are foolishness and the worst error; or, as Symmachus translated, tumult and a kind of instability of words: he does not remain in his position, but thinks that by multiplying his speeches he can escape sin.

Since he remembers neither past things nor knows future things, and rolls about in ignorance and darkness, promising himself a false knowledge, he thinks that he is learned and wise if he multiplies words.

[Note: In Alcuin: “wrapped in darkness, promising knowledge to himself alone.”]

This may also be understood of heretics, who do not grasp the statements of prudent men. Preparing themselves for contrary disputes, they wrap both the beginning and the end of their speech in vanity, tumult, and error, and, knowing nothing, speak more than they understand.

[Note: With Erasmus and Victorius, two Palatine manuscripts have: “with much error,” etc. Alcuin has: “they heap up with much error,” and “with …”—“In vanity, tumult, etc.” The very ancient Corbeiensis manuscript has: “they wrap the beginning and end of their speech in tumultuous vanity and shamelessness and error”; another Corbeiensis: “they wrap them in shameless error”; the editions of Erasmus and Martianaeus: “they wrap them in vanity with much error.” **MARTIAN.**]

“The labor of fools will afflict them, because they do not know how to go to the city” [Col. 1097B].

Join these verses also with what precedes. Or he is speaking generally of all fools who do not know God, or specifically of heretics disputing [476].

[Note: With the same printed editions, the Palatine manuscripts read: “he discusses heretical disputations”; the Vatican: “heretics disputing”; Alcuin: “heretics who dispute.”]

Read Plato; turn over Aristotle’s sophistries; examine Zeno and Carneades more carefully, and you will prove true what is said: “The labor of fools will afflict them.”

They indeed sought the truth with every effort, but because they had no guide or one to lead them on the way, and thought they could grasp wisdom by human senses, they did not reach the city, of which the Psalm says: “Lord, in your city you will destroy their image” (Psalm 72:20).

For all the shadows, various images, and masks that they assumed for themselves in their different doctrines, the Lord will destroy in his city. Concerning it, it is also written: “The river’s rushing stream gladdens the city of God” (Psalm 46:5). And in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14). And in Isaiah: “I am a fortified city, a city that is besieged” (Isaiah 27:30, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: This should be retained with the manuscripts and the printed editions. Elsewhere, however, Jerome himself reads: “a city that is not besieged.” See Letter 30 to Paula, §14.—“A city that is besieged.” At the end of Letter 30 to Paula, concerning the Hebrew alphabet, the reading includes the negative particle, “a city that is not besieged,” because the context requires a negation, as does the Letter to Algasius, Question 2. Unless perhaps *non expugnatur* (“is not conquered”) should be read there instead of *oppugnatur* (“is besieged”). **MARTIAN.**]

Since this city of truth and wisdom is firm and strong, all the wise men of the world and the heretics try to attack it. What we have said about philosophers must also be understood of heretics: they labor and are afflicted in their study of the Scriptures to no purpose, since they walk in the desert and cannot find the city.

The Psalmist also recalls their error, saying: “They wandered in the desert, in a waterless place; they did not find the way to a city of habitation” (Psalm 106:4).

“Woe to you, land whose king is a boy, and whose princes eat in the morning” [476].

“Blessed are you, land whose king is the son of noblemen, and whose princes eat at the proper time, in strength and not in shame.”

[Note: The Vatican and Palatine manuscripts have: “Blessed are you, land …”]

The passage seems to condemn the rule of young men and to censure luxurious judges: in the one, wisdom is weakened by age; in the others, mature age is enervated by pleasures. Conversely, it seems to approve a ruler well formed in good morals and liberally educated, and to praise those judges who by no means place pleasure before the affairs of citizens but, after much labor and the administration of the state, take food as though compelled by necessity.

Yet I think something more sacred lies hidden in the literal wording: in Scripture those are called young who depart from the ancient authority and despise the gray-haired precepts of their parents, who, neglecting God’s commandment, wish to establish human traditions.

Concerning them, in Isaiah chapter 8, the Lord threatens Israel because it refused the waters of Shiloah, which flow quietly, and turned away from the ancient pool, choosing for itself the streams of Samaria and the torrents of Damascus. “And I will give,” he says, “their young men as rulers, and mockers will dominate them” (Isaiah 3:4).

Read Daniel, and you will find God as the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7). Read the Apocalypse of John, and you will find the Savior’s head white as snow and like white wool (Revelation 1). Jeremiah also, because he was wise and his gray hairs were counted as wisdom, is forbidden to say that he is young (Jeremiah 1).

Woe, therefore, to the land whose king is the devil, who is always eager for novelties and even rebels against his parent in Absalom. It has as judges and rulers those who love the pleasures of this world, who, before the day of death arrives, say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isaiah 22:13).

Conversely, blessed is the land of the Church, whose king is Christ, the son of noblemen, descended from the stock of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and also of all the prophets and saints, over whom sin did not rule; and for that reason they were truly free.

From them was born the freer Virgin, holy Mary, who had no branch and no shoot on her side, but whose entire fruit burst forth into a flower speaking in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1) [477].

Its princes are also the Apostles and all the saints, who have as king the son of noblemen, the son of a free woman—not born of the slave-woman Hagar, but generated from the freedom of Sarah.

They do not eat in the morning, nor do they eat hastily. For they do not seek pleasure in the present age; rather, they will eat at the proper time, when the time of recompense has arrived, and they will eat in strength and not in shame. Every good of the present world is shame; that of the future is everlasting strength.

Something similar is said in Isaiah: “Behold, those who serve me shall eat; but you shall hunger. And again: Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice; but you shall be ashamed” (Isaiah 65:13–14).

[Note: All our manuscripts omit this first passage from Isaiah. Victorius adds: “They shall eat good things.”]

“In laziness the beams will be brought low, and through the weakness of the hands the house will drip.”

Our house, which was made upright along with the stature of man, and the dwelling that we have in the heavens, will be brought low if we are lazy and slow to perform good works. Every framework that ought to carry the roof upward will collapse to the ground and crush its inhabitant. When the help of our hands and virtues has grown sluggish, every storm from above and every whirlwind of clouds bursts upon us.

What we have interpreted concerning one human being can better be understood of the Church: through the negligence of its rulers all its height collapses, and there are the enticements of vices where the covering of virtues was thought to be.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript has *ubi regimen* (“where governance”); the Vatican, *tegimen* (“covering”).]

“They make bread and wine amid laughter, so that the living may feast. And everything obeys silver” [Col. 1099C].

[Note: “They make bread and wine amid laughter.” All the manuscripts read this way, and the words that follow in the Commentary on this chapter teach that it should be read so, although Jerome later interpreted the Hebrew as: “They make bread for laughter,” etc. **MARTIAN.**]

I think what follows depends upon what has preceded. For we have explained that through the laziness and negligence of teachers the Church is humbled, its summit falls, and its beams drip.

[Note: Martianaeus reads *perplui* (“to be rained through”), rather badly and contrary to our manuscripts and earlier printed books. Alcuin read more elegantly *perfluere* (“to flow through”).—“And the beams to be rained through.” The Corbeiensis manuscripts read: “and the coverings to be rained through”; Erasmus: “the beams to flow through.” **MARTIAN.**]

Now, therefore, he speaks about the same teachers. Since he seemed to have accused them because they were silent and did not perform the office of teachers, and because bishops and presbyters established in the Church did not labor in speech and doctrine—as Titus is also admonished to do (Titus 1:5), and Timothy is commanded not to neglect the grace he had received through the laying on of hands—but thought themselves presbyters and bishops merely so that they might receive benefits [or “salaries”] and, as teachers, seek the double honor owed to those who labor in teaching and preaching (1 Timothy 4:14), he now, conversely, accuses those who do indeed speak in the Church and teach the people, but teach what the people enjoy hearing: who flatter sinners in their vice and stir up the applause of their hearers.

[Note: “So that they might receive benefits.” Three manuscript copies have *salaria* (“salaries”). The Sorbonicus manuscript has *salutatoria* (“gifts of greeting”). Among these variant readings we have retained the ancient reading of the printed books, as also the following reading, *et uti praeceptores* (“and, as teachers”), whereas three manuscripts have *et muti praeceptores* (“and silent teachers”). **MARTIAN.**]

When a speech becomes wanton in the Church, and promises the multitude blessedness and the kingdoms of heaven, does it not seem to you to be making bread amid laughter and mixing wine for the joy of the living?

[Note: “When speech becomes wanton in the Church.” The printed editions have *lascivit orator* (“the speaker becomes wanton”), but I have found no manuscript that does not read *lascivit oratio* (“the speech becomes wanton”). **MARTIAN.**]

Or is it because the teachers themselves seek riches, food, and wealth through attractive promises; or because they prepare the Church’s bread—which is the bread of mourners, not of those who laugh (for “blessed are those who mourn, because they shall laugh”)—amid joy and gladness?

As for what follows, “Everything obeys money,” or “silver,” it should be understood in two ways. Either the teachers themselves, after being enriched by flattery, exercise dominion over the people; or else because silver always signifies speech:

“For the words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proven upon the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm 12:7).

He asserts that the common crowd readily yields to eloquence and speech composed with a leafy display of words.

[Note: Victorius, with the Vulgate, has: “silver tested by fire, proven upon the earth,” etc.]

Alternatively: those who have the bridegroom with them, and therefore are forbidden to mourn and fast, “make bread amid laughter.” From this laughter Isaac also received his name, and they prepare wine in the joy of those who drink.

[Note: The Vatican corrects the reading to *bibentium* (“of those who drink”), which the second hand of the Palatine manuscript also supports; previously the incongruous reading was *viventium* (“of the living”).]

Every holy man, therefore, who, as Christ commanded, is a teacher of the Church makes bread amid laughter and gladness, and serves cups of wine in joy.

The silver also, which everything obeys, consists of the five talents from the Gospel, and the two, and the one entrusted by the master of the house to his servants for trading, as well as the ten minas (Matthew 25:15 ff.).

“In your mind do not curse the king, and in the secrecy of your bedchamber do not curse the rich man, because a bird of the sky will carry away the voice, and the winged creature will announce the word” [479].

[Note: The second Palatine manuscript has: “because birds will carry away the voice”; the ancient editions have: “the birds of heaven will carry it,” etc.—“Because a bird of the sky will carry away the voice.” Some manuscripts retain this genuine reading; in others it is incorrectly written: “the birds of heaven will carry the voice.” **MARTIAN.**]

The simple commandment edifies those who hear it: let us not, overcome by anger and fury, break out into cursing and slander against kings and rulers. For contrary to expectation it sometimes happens that what we have said in cursing is reported to those whom we cursed, and we incur danger through the immoderation of our tongue.

What he says—“A bird of the sky will carry away the voice, and the winged creature will announce the word”—should be understood hyperbolically, as when we are accustomed to say that even the walls, to which we speak as witnesses, will not conceal what they have heard.

But it is better to understand the command in this way: we should know that we are commanded not only to say nothing rashly against Christ, but also, in the secrets of our heart, even when we are hemmed in by various tribulations, to think nothing blasphemous or impious.

And because the love we show to Christ must also be shown to our neighbor—“You shall love the Lord your God,” but also “your neighbor as yourself”—we are now likewise commanded not easily to disparage the saints after the king, nor to gnaw with the bite of our tongue at those whom we see enriched with wisdom, knowledge, and virtues.

For the angels who travel around the earth and are ministering spirits, and who speak in Zechariah—“We have traveled around the earth, and behold, the whole earth is inhabited and is quiet” (Zechariah 1:11)—may, like birds, carry our words and thoughts to heaven, so that what we secretly think is not hidden from the knowledge of God.

### Chapter XI

“Cast your bread upon the face of the waters, for after many days you will find it.”

He exhorts us to almsgiving: everything should be given to the one who asks, and good should be done without discrimination. For just as someone who sows upon irrigated ground expects the fruit of his seed, so one who gives generously to the needy sows not a grain of seed but bread itself, awaiting its multiplication as though at interest. When the day of judgment arrives, he will receive much more than he had given.

[Note: “You will find it again after what you have given.” The Sorbonicus manuscript and the earlier printed books read, in the same sense, “you will receive it again.” **MARTIAN.**]

Alternatively: in whatever person you see that water of which it is said, “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38), do not be reluctant to provide the bread of wisdom, the rational bread, the bread of speech. For if you do this frequently, you will find that you have not sown the seed of learning in vain [480].

I think something similar is said in Isaiah: “Blessed is the one who sows beside the water, where the ox and the donkey tread” (Isaiah 32:20). That teacher is judged worthy of blessedness who sows upon the irrigated heart of his hearers, gathered both from the Jews and from the people of the nations.

[Note: Three manuscripts read: “gathered both from the Jews and from the people of the nations.”]

“Give a portion to seven, and indeed to eight, because you do not know what evil will come upon the earth.”

In Ezekiel also seven and eight steps are read as an ascent to the temple (Ezekiel 40:26, 31). And after that ethical Psalm—that is, Psalm 118—there are fifteen Psalms of Ascents, through which we are first instructed in the Law; and, when the number seven has been completed, we ascend through the octave to the Gospel.

The command, therefore, is that we believe with equal reverence in both instruments, namely, the Old and the New. The Jews gave a portion to seven, believing in the Sabbath, but did not give to eight, denying the resurrection on the Lord’s Day. Conversely, the heretics—Marcion, Manichaeus, and all who tear the Old Law apart with savage mouths—give portions to eight, accepting the Gospel, but do not assign the same value to the number seven, rejecting the Old Law.

[Note: “Rejecting the Old Law.” Both Corbeiensis manuscripts have: “rejecting the instruments of the old things.” **MARTIAN.**]

Let us therefore believe in both instruments. We cannot even now comprehend in our minds the fitting torments and fitting punishment reserved for those who dwell upon the earth—Jews and heretics—who deny one of the two.

The Hebrews understand this passage in the following way: “Keep both the Sabbath and circumcision, lest, if you happen not to do this, unexpected evil overtake you.”

“If the clouds are filled, they will pour rain upon the earth. And if a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will be.”

[Note: The Palatine manuscript has: “or toward the place of the north, where …”]

Keep the commandments that were given to you above, so that the clouds may pour out their rain upon you. For wherever you prepare a place for yourself, and a future dwelling, whether toward the south or toward the north, there you will remain when you have died.

Alternatively: for this reason we said above, “Cast your bread upon the face of the waters, and give to everyone who asks you,” because when the clouds are full they lavish their riches upon mortals. You, like a tree, although you may be long-lived, will not be forever; rather, suddenly, like the winds, overturned by the storm of death, wherever you fall, there you will remain forever—whether the final hour finds you harsh and savage, or gentle and merciful [481].

[Note: Erasmus and Marianus read incongruously: “but suddenly by the force of the winds, so in the storm of death …” **MARTIAN.**]

Alternatively: in the Psalms it is said to God, “Your truth reaches to the clouds” (Psalm 36:6). And in Isaiah God threatens the sinful vineyard: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isaiah 5:6).

The clouds, therefore, are the Prophets and every holy man who, when he has gathered many disciplines in his heart, is then able to rain down the commandments of learning and to say: “Let my speech be expected like rain,” and, “They shall pour rain upon the earth” (Deuteronomy 32:2), to which it was said: “Let the earth hear the words of my mouth.”

As for what follows—“And if a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will be”—let us take as an example the passage from Habakkuk where it is written: “God will come from Teman” (Habakkuk 3:3), which other interpreters rendered, “God will come from the south.”

[Note: The same Palatine manuscript omits the word “south.” —“God will come from the south.” From this passage it may be inferred that Jerome completed his Commentary on Ecclesiastes before he had published his Latin translation of the Prophets from the Hebrew source. **MARTIAN.**]

As I judge, the south is always understood in a good sense. Hence in the Song of Songs it is said: “Rise up, O north wind” (Song of Songs 4:16)—that is, depart, go away, and come, O south wind.

The tree, therefore, that falls in this life and is cut down by the condition of mortality either sinned before it fell, and is afterward placed in the region of the north; or, if it produced fruits worthy of the south, it will lie in the southern quarter.

There is no tree that is not either toward the north or toward the south.

[Note: Alcuin has, almost as Erasmus and Victorius: “which is not either toward the north or toward the south,” etc.—“Either toward the north or toward the south.” Take care not to read: “which is not toward the north or toward the south,” nor rashly reject the authority of all the manuscript copies. The printed books altered the text to: “which is either not toward the north or toward the south.” **MARTIAN.**]

The same meaning is conveyed by what is written in Isaiah: “I will say to the north: Give them up; and to the south: Do not withhold” (Isaiah 43:6).

For the south and the eastern wind are never commanded to bring them, because those who are to be led afterward toward the east and south must first be in other regions. Thus the north wind leads its inhabitants toward the south, and the southwest wind leads its inhabitants toward the east. They cannot advance if they remain in their former dwellings.

“He who watches the wind will not sow, and he who looks at the clouds will not reap.”

The person who considers to whom he should do good and does not give to everyone who asks him often passes by the one who deserves to receive (Luke 6:30).

Alternatively: the person who preaches the word of God only at the time when the people willingly listen, and when a favorable breeze of popular approval is blowing, is a negligent sower and a lazy farmer. For amid prosperity, while we are unaware, adversity rises up.

But the word of God must be preached in season and out of season, at its proper time and at an inconvenient time (2 Timothy 4:2); nor, in the time of faith, should one watch the storm of threatening clouds.

[Note: The Vatican reads *suo tempore* (“at its proper time”). Alcuin: “For this reason the word of God must be preached at a suitable or unsuitable time.”]

Concerning this it is said in Proverbs: “As a violent and useless rain, so is one who abandons wisdom and praises ungodliness” (Proverbs 28:3–4).

Therefore, without watching the clouds or fearing the winds, we must sow in the midst of storms. We must not say, “That time is suitable, this one useless,” since we do not know what way or what will belongs to the Spirit who orders all things.

“How do you not know what the way of the spirit is, or how bones are formed in the womb of a pregnant woman? So you do not know the works of God, who makes all things.”

Just as you do not know the way of the spirit and soul entering into the infant, and do not understand the variety of bones and veins in the womb of a pregnant woman—how the body of a human being is varied from a worthless element into different forms and limbs, and how from the same seed one part becomes soft in the flesh, another hard in the bones, another pulses in the veins, and another is bound in the sinews—so you will not be able to know the works of God, who is the maker of all things.

From this he teaches that adversities should not be feared, and that we should not rashly judge concerning the winds and clouds mentioned above, since the sower ought to proceed according to his appointed course and leave the outcome to the judgment of the Lord.

[Note: Alcuin appears more correctly to have read: “the sower ought to scatter [seed] and reserve the outcome …”]

“For it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16).

In the morning sow your seed, and at evening do not let your hand rest; for you do not know [Note: [Col. 1103D] Another Palatine manuscript: “what pleases more.”] what will please, this [Al. or this] or that. Or whether both, as though one good thing. The light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun; for if a person lives many years, let him rejoice in them all, and let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. Everything that is to come is vanity.

Do not choose whom you should benefit; but even when you have done good, never desist from the good work. Let evening find the justice begun in the morning. And let the rising sun [Al. of the sun] increase the mercy shown at evening. For it is uncertain which work will please God more, and from which one the fruit of righteousness will be prepared for you. It may happen, however, that not one but both will please God. Alternatively: Let your labor be equally constant both in youth and in old age. Do not say, “While I was able, I labored; in old age I ought to rest.” For you do not know whether you will please God in youth or in advanced age. Nor does frugality in youth profit if old age is spent in luxury. For on whatever day the righteous person goes astray, his former righteousness will not be able to deliver him from death.

But if, according to either interpretation, you have always done good and maintained an equal course throughout every age, you will see God the Father, the sweetest light; you will see Christ, the sun of righteousness. Moreover, if you have lived many years, possessed all good things, or performed good works, and have known that you will always be dying, while the coming of darkness is continually before your eyes, you will despise present things as fleeting, fragile, and perishable. [Col. 1104B]

Symmachus interpreted the conclusion of this sentence as follows: “If a person lives many years and rejoices in all of them” [Note: [Col. 1103D] Martianus has “will have rejoiced,” contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts and of the earlier printed books.], “he ought also to remember the days [Al. of the days] of darkness, for they will be many, and in all of them he will come to cease to be.”

Alternatively: In another passage of Scripture God promises, saying, “I will give you the early rain and the late rain” (Deut. 11:14)—that is, the Old Testament and the New—and “I will water you with both rains.” Therefore we are now also admonished to read the ancient Law in such a way that we do not despise the Gospel, and to seek spiritual understanding in the ancient Instrument [i.e. Testament], so that in the Gospels and the Apostles we do not suppose that only what is read aloud is expressed. For we do not know in which of the two God will grant us greater knowledge and grace; and blessed is the person who has joined both together in one, [Col. 1104C] and made them, as it were, one body.

Whoever has attained this will see the light; he will see Christ, the sun of righteousness. And if he lives many years, he will remain in complete joy and delight, possessing knowledge of the Scriptures, and will be compelled still more [Note: [Col. 1103D] Palatinus adds: “and still more, by remembrance of this labor, etc.”] to this labor by remembrance of the future judgment: for the everlasting time of darkness will come, and eternal punishments will be prepared for those who have not sown in the morning and at evening, and have in no way joined both together. They have neither seen the light nor the sun, from which the light itself proceeds [Al. will proceed].

## Chapter XII

“Rejoice, young man” [Note: [Col. 1103D] “Rejoice, young man, etc.” In the most ancient manuscript of Corbie this chapter is numbered XXXVIII; [Col. 1104D] for there is an enormous difference between the ancient divisions of the sacred books and those of today, as may be seen in our Prolegomena, Volume I. MARTIANUS. —Two more accurate manuscripts read: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth.” This is also how Jerome quotes the passage below.] “in your youth, and let your heart be good in the days of your youth, and walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes” [Note: [Col. 1104D] Two Palatine manuscripts add, without criticism, “without blame,” which is derived from the Greek ἄμωμος (*amōmos*, “blameless”).]. “And know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment. And remove anger from your heart, and take wickedness away from your flesh, for youth and folly are vanity. And remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of evil come and the years approach in which you will say, ‘I have no desire in them’” [Note: [Col. 1104D] “I have no desire in them.” Erasmus read *voluptas* (“pleasure”), and this reading has been retained in very many manuscripts. The Hebrew has *hhephets*, which the Greek translators also interpret as “will” or “desire.” MARTIANUS.] [Al. “pleasure”].

In this chapter there has been a diversity of interpretation among all commentators, and almost as many opinions as people. Since it would be a task nearly the size of a single volume to list everyone’s views and explain the arguments by which they wished to support them, it will be enough for sensible readers that we indicate what they thought and, as on a small tablet, sketch the situation of the lands and show, in narrow summary, the vastness and circumference of the entire world and of the Ocean.

The Hebrews believe that the command pertains to Israel: he is instructed to enjoy his riches before the time of captivity arrives and exchanges his youth for old age. Whatever appears delightful or pleasant, whether to the heart or to the eyes, he should enjoy while it is available; yet in such a way that he knows he will be judged in all things. He must flee both evil thoughts and lusts, knowing that folly is joined to youth; and he must always remember his Creator before the days of Babylonian and Roman captivity arrive, in which he will not be able [Note: [Col. 1105D] Most manuscripts prefer “pleasure” here instead of “desire.” —“To have desire.” Here I have corrected the same error, because from the sacred context it is sufficiently clear that Jerome wrote “desire,” not “pleasure.” MARTIANUS.] to have desire.

They explain the entire passage beginning with “before the sun, the moon, and the stars grow dark” and extending to the place where Scripture says, “And the dust will return to its earth as it was, and the spirit will return to God who gave it,” as referring to the condition of Israel’s state. Since these matters are, as we said above, [Note: [Col. 1105D] Vaticanus has “more extensive,” instead of “more fragmentary.”] fragmentary and lengthy, we shall touch on them briefly and concisely.

“Rejoice, therefore, in your youth, O Israel, and do this or that”—of the things already mentioned—“before captivity comes and your honor and glory depart from you”; before your judges and saints (whom they wish to be understood by the sun, moon, and stars) are taken away. This will be before Nebuchadnezzar comes, or Titus, son of Vespasian, summoned by the prophets, and their prophecies are fulfilled.

On the day when the angels who preside over the Temple depart, all the strongest men in your army will be terrified, the teachers’ idle words will cease, and the prophets, who used to receive the light of their visions from heaven, will grow dark. This will be when the Temple doors are shut and Jerusalem is humbled, and the Chaldean comes like the song of a bird, summoned by Jeremiah’s words [Note: [Col. 1105D] Two manuscripts, Alcuin, and the old printed editions read “prophesied,” rather than “summoned.”] (Jer. 9), while the daughters of song—the choirs singing psalms in the Temple—fall silent.

At that time, when they come to Jerusalem, even the enemies of God will fear his greatness; and, uncertain on the road, they will dread the destruction of Sennacherib. For they think this is what is meant: “They will fear what is lofty, and they will be afraid on the way” (Isa. 37).

In those days the almond tree will blossom [Al. the almond tree], that staff and rod which Jeremiah saw at the beginning of his prophecy; the locust will be fattened—Nebuchadnezzar with his army—and the caper plant will be scattered [i.e. destroyed] (Jer. 1), meaning God’s friendship with Israel. What the caper plant signifies will be explained more fully when we begin to discuss each item.

All this will happen to Israel, because “the human being will go to his eternal house” [Note: [Col. 1105D] Martianus has “and from God’s estate.” All our manuscripts, as well as Alcuin and Victorinus, have “from God’s protection,” which reading we restore on their authority. Shortly afterward Alcuin again reads “while he dwells in his tabernacle,” instead of “when he departs,” [Col. 1106D] etc. —“From God’s estate to heavenly things,” etc. The Corbie manuscripts preserve another reading: “and God, his protector, will return to heavenly things.” The same manuscripts also read “a golden fillet” where others read “a golden cord.” MARTIANUS.] and will return from God’s protection to the heavenly places. When he departs to his tabernacle, they will go around the street, weeping and lamenting, surrounded by the siege of their enemies.

Rejoice, therefore, O Israel, in your youth, before the silver cord is broken—that is, while your glory remains with you; before the golden fillet [Note: [Col. 1106D] The Palatine manuscripts read “before the golden moth returns.”] returns—that is, before the ark of the covenant is taken away; before the pitcher is broken at the fountain and the wheel is rolled over the cistern [Col. 1106B]—that is, while the precepts of the Law and the grace of the Holy Spirit remain within the Holy of Holies—and before you return to Babylon, from which you came forth in the loins of Abraham, and begin to be crushed in Mesopotamia, from which you once departed. Then all the grace of prophecy with which you were once inspired will return to its giver.

This is how the Jews explain the passage to this day, drawing its interpretation toward their own person.

We, however, returning to the order of the preceding discussion, shall attempt to explain each point. “Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart be good” [Note: [Col. 1106D] The text was corrupt in this form. Alcuin also quotes the passage as follows: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let it be good,” etc. —“And let your heart be good,” etc. I think it is clear to the reader from this passage and the three that follow how many passages of Scripture are omitted in the ancient editions. MARTIANUS.] “in the days of your youth, and walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes. And know concerning all these things that God will bring you into judgment.”

He had said that the light of this world is exceedingly sweet, and that a person ought to rejoice in the days of his life and seize pleasure with every effort; for the eternal night of death is approaching, when it will not be possible to enjoy what has been gathered, and everything we possessed will pass away like a shadow.

Now, therefore, he exhorts the human being and says: “O young man, before old age and death overtake you, rejoice in your youth, and whatever seems good to you in your heart and pleasant to your eyes, take it up and enjoy the things of the world as you wish.” Again, lest he be thought by saying this to be urging a person toward luxury and causing him to fall into the doctrine of Epicurus, he removes this suspicion by adding: “And know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.” In other words: Enjoy the things of the world in such a way that you know you will be judged at the end.

“And remove anger from your heart, and take wickedness away from your flesh, for youth and folly are vanity.” By “anger” he includes all the disturbances of the mind. By “wickedness of the flesh” he signifies all bodily pleasures. Thus he says: Enjoy the good things of this age, but do not sin either through desire or through the flesh. Abandon the ancient vices by which in your youth you served vanity and folly, for youth is joined to ignorance.

“And remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of evil come and the years approach in which you will say, ‘I have no desire in them.’” Always remember your Maker, and walk the path of your youth in such a way that you remember the final death, before the time comes upon you when all sad things will follow.

“Before the sun and the light” [Note: [Col. 1107D] The words “and the moon” are absent from the Palatine and Vatican manuscripts.] “and the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain.”

If we understand this as referring to the general consummation of the world, this chapter agrees with the Lord’s words, in which he says: “There will be tribulation and distress such as has not been from the beginning of creation, nor will there be” [Col. 1107B] (Matt. 24). “For the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken” (Matt. 24). These are the guardians of the house, so that the house is understood here as the world, while the strong men are those deceived by error, and the opposing powers that are to be dispersed. [Note: [Col. 1107D] Martianus had wrongly omitted the word “house” in this second occurrence; we have supplied it from the manuscripts and other printed books.] [Note: [Col. 1107D] The Vatican reads “great tribulation and distress,” etc.]

But if the conclusion of each individual person is referred to the end of this life, then the sun, moon, stars, clouds, and rains will cease to exist for the person who has died.

Alternatively: “Rejoice, young man, O Christian people, and enjoy the good things granted to you by God; and know in all these things that you will be judged by the Lord.” Do not think that because the former branches were broken off and you were grafted into the root of the good olive tree you are therefore secure. Rather, remove anger from your heart and pleasures from your body; after abandoning the remaining vices, remember your Creator before the evil and incurable day comes upon you [Note: [Col. 1107D] One Palatine manuscript reads: “before the day of evil comes upon you in your youth, incurable.” I readily prefer the reading of the Vatican and another Palatine manuscript: “before the day of evil, the incurable day, comes.”], in which punishments are prepared for sinners, lest, when you have sinned, the sun of righteousness may set for you at midday, the light of knowledge may perish, and the splendor of the moon—that is, of the Church—may be taken away. The stars may fall, of which it is written: “Among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” [Al. “having the way of life”] (Phil. 2:15). And elsewhere: “Star differs from star in glory” [Al. “brightness”]. [Note: [Col. 1107D] “Star differs from star in glory.” All the manuscripts read this way, according to the ancient Vulgate, in which it was written: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon,” etc., as the manuscript Greek-Latin copy of St. Paul’s Epistles now preserved in our library at Saint-Germain confirms. MARTIANUS.]

“Before the clouds return after the rain” (1 Cor. 15:1): lest the prophets who water the hearts of believers with their speech and rains, after they have seen that you are unworthy of their rain, return to their own dwelling—that is, to the one from whom they were sent.

[Col. 1107D] “On the day when the guardians of the house are shaken and the men of strength perish.”

By the guardians of the house we may understand either the sun and moon and the remaining choir of the stars, or the angels who preside over this world. By the men of strength, or “the strong men,” as Symmachus interpreted it, [Col. 1108A] who will perish—or, as Aquila translated it, “will wander”—the demons are understood. They received the name of strong men from the strong devil himself. When the Lord conquers and binds him, according to the Gospel parable, he plunders his house (Luke 11). [Note: [Col. 1108D] “According to the Gospel parable.” Erasmus and Marianus have “according to the Gospel saying.” MARTIANUS.] [Al. “saying.”]

Alternatively: Those who refer all the written material to the human body think that by the guardians of the house the ribs are signified, because the intestines are enclosed by them and the entire softness of the belly is protected. They consider the strong men to be the legs; and they relate the sun, moon, and stars to the eyes, ears, nostrils, and the senses of the entire head. This is because, as the discussion proceeds, they are compelled by necessity to understand not angels and demons, nor sun, moon, and stars, but parts of the human body.

“And the grinders will cease, because they have become few; and those who see through the openings will grow dark.” At the consummation of the world, when the love of many has grown cold, and the souls of teachers who are able to provide heavenly food for believers have become few and have been transferred to heavenly things, then those who in this world saw the light of knowledge only partially will begin to be wrapped in darkness.

For if Moses is told, “I will place you in the cleft of the rock, and you will see my back” (Exod. 33:22), how much more does each soul behold the truth through a cleft and through certain dark caverns!

Alternatively: The Gospel does not conceal that there are two women grinding, one of whom is received and the other left behind (Matt. 24:41). [Note: [Col. 1108D] The manuscripts read: “one is snatched away and the other left.”] When these have become few and have ceased, it is necessary that all the light of knowledge be taken away from the eyes. [Col. 1108C]

Alternatively: Some think that “the grinders will cease because they have become few” is said of the teeth. When extreme old age arrives, the teeth are also either worn down or fall out; with them food is ground and sent into the stomach. They understand “those who see through the openings will grow dark” as the eyes, because in those worn out by age the sharpness of vision becomes dim and their sight is obscured.

“And they will shut the doors in the street, when the sound of the grinding is low; and they will rise at the voice of the bird; and all the daughters of song will become silent.”

When the voice of the grinder has grown weak and the teaching of the teachers has ceased, everything will consequently cease. Among these things, the doors in the street will also be shut, so that, in accordance with the foolish virgins of the Gospel (Matt. 25), each person will have the doors of his street closed and they will not be able to buy oil. Or certainly, while the foolish virgins wander about in the street, those who have entered with the bridegroom will shut the bridegroom’s chamber.

For if the way that leads to life is narrow and constricted, while the way that leads to death is broad and spacious (Matt. 7), then, when the love of many has grown cold, the door of instruction is rightly shut in the streets. [Col. 1109A]

In the following verse, where it says, “And he will rise at the voice of the bird,” or “sparrow,” we shall use [Al. “we use”] the passage at the appropriate time, whenever we see a sinner rise through repentance at the voice of a bishop or presbyter. It may also be understood, in an exceptional way, even though we do not follow the context of the chapter, as referring to the final resurrection [Note: [Col. 1109C] The same manuscripts read “legitimate” for “final.”], when the dead will rise at the voice of the archangel. Nor is it surprising if we compare the angels’ trumpet with a sparrow, since every voice is faint when compared with Christ.

And as far as I can remember, I do not know that I have ever read “sparrow” in a negative sense. In the tenth psalm the righteous person says: “In the Lord I trust; how can you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” And elsewhere: “I watched, and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. 101:8). Also in another place: “For even the sparrow has found a house for itself” (Ps. 83:4).

Alternatively: They wish the doors shut in the street to be understood as the feeble steps of an old man, because he is always sitting and cannot walk. They interpret the lowering of the sound of the grinder as referring to the jaws, because he cannot grind food and, with his breath constricted, his voice is scarcely audible.

Moreover, the fact that he rises at the voice of the bird shows that, when his blood has grown cold and his moisture has dried up—the substances by which sleep is nourished—he wakes at a slight sound and rises quickly in the middle of the night when the rooster has crowed, being wholly unable to turn his limbs repeatedly on his bed.

“Becoming silent,” or, as the Hebrew more accurately has it, “becoming deaf,” “the daughters of song” signifies the ears: the hearing of old people becomes heavier, they can no longer distinguish among voices, nor take pleasure in songs. Barzillai also says this to David when he refuses to cross the Jordan.

“But they will fear what is lofty and be afraid on the way.” That is, they will not be able to enter difficult places; and, with exhausted knees and trembling steps, they will fear stumbling even on level ground.

“And the almond tree will blossom, and the locust will be fattened, and the caper plant will be scattered, because the human being will go to his eternal house, and they will go around in the street mourning.”

Even now Ecclesiastes is speaking metaphorically about the limbs of the human being: when old age has arrived, the hair has become white, the feet have swollen, desire has grown cold, and the person has been dissolved by death, then he will return [Col. 1110B] to his own earth [Note: [Col. 1109C] “And to his eternal house.” Erasmus and Marianus have another sense, changing Jerome’s text as follows: “and to his eternal house: let him seek the tomb after the funeral rites have been celebrated, and let a crowd of mourners precede the funeral procession.” This is because they do not understand the scriptural idiom by which the tomb is called an eternal house, according to Psalm 48:12: “Their tombs are their houses forever.” MARTIANUS. —Alcuin has “to his eternal house, to the tomb.” The old printed editions have: “to his eternal house: let him seek the tomb after the funeral rites have been celebrated,” etc.].

After the funeral rites have been properly celebrated, a crowd of mourners will precede the funeral procession. As for the blossom of the almond tree, which we have taken to mean gray hair, some interpret it as the sacred thorn [Note: [Col. 1109C] Three manuscripts read “the thornbush.”], because, as the flesh of the buttocks diminishes, the spine grows and blossoms.

Regarding the statement, “The locust will be fattened,” it should be known that where our manuscripts read “locust,” the Hebrew has written AAGAB (): a word that is ambiguous among them. For it can be translated both as “locust” and as “ankle.” [Note: [Col. 1109C] Erasmus, instead of “and ankle,” had read the Greek ἀττάλαβος (*attalabos*), and Martianus says that he does not know why he did so. Victorinus, however, had already explained the matter, being the first to restore this passage; it is greatly in the reader’s interest that his sufficiently learned observation be reproduced here word for word. He says: “Those who substituted *attalabos* for ‘ankle’ here fell into a shameful error; otherwise there would be no ambiguity in the word if it meant the same thing. For what else is *attalabos*, or *attelabus*, except a locust, or, if something more specific is intended, a grasshopper, a kind of locust? Thus Theodorus explicitly interprets it in Aristotle: or, as Jerome himself explains it in Nahum 3, a small locust, between a locust and a grasshopper, crawling rather than flying on small wings and continually leaping. But Jerome understands the word to signify both locust and ankle at once; and, to leave no room for evasion, he immediately interprets himself by revealing that to fatten the locust under the same word means precisely that the ankles and legs of old people become swollen. Thus here too the ambiguity of the word, through its etymology, indicates the swollen legs of the elderly, burdened by the swellings or fluids of gout. The example of the word in Jeremiah wonderfully confirms this interpretation: there the word means both ‘almond’ and ‘to watch.’ Just as there he derived the idea of watchfulness from the word for the nut, so here he understands the fatness of the locust as the swelling of the ankle. Rabbi Jonathan confirms that Jerome’s opinion is correct; he is said to agree with Theodotion, as does Aben Ezra. The former rendered it ‘ankle’ in Chaldean when he interpreted these words; the latter translated the word as ‘ankle.’ David Kimhi also hints at the same thing: when explaining what [the Hebrew term] means, namely ‘ankle,’ he gives an example in [another Hebrew form]. We have therefore rescued this passage from a serious error. We owe this emendation to two manuscripts from Brescia. Ignorance of the word introduced the error: those who professed knowledge of Hebrew did not easily discover that the word also meant ‘ankle,’ and rashly changed ‘ankle’ into *attalabos*.”]

How, then, at the beginning of Jeremiah, does the word SOCED (), when the accent is changed, signify both “almond” and “watchfulness”? The Lord says to him: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” And he answered: “A staff of almond wood” [Note: [Col. 1110D] Three manuscripts retain only “an almond” instead of “a staff of almond wood.” Regarding the varying accent of the Hebrew letters, I have spoken in the earlier Commentary on the Apology of St. Jerome. MARTIANUS.]. And the Lord said to him: “You have seen well, because I will watch over my word” [Col. 1111A] “to carry it out” (Jer. 1:11), or “over my people,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 1110D] The Vatican and Palatine manuscripts read “over my people, in order to,” etc.]. The word therefore has the etymology of “almond,” because God is going to watch and repay the people what they deserve [Al. “what is owed”], and this is the occasion for the expression.

So also now the ambiguity of the word, through its etymology, indicates the swollen legs of the elderly, burdened by the fluids of gout [Note: [Col. 1111C] Four manuscripts read: “burdened by the swellings of gout.”]. This is not because this happens to every old person, but because it often occurs; by a *synecdoche*—from the part, the whole is named.

Where we have “caper plant,” the Hebrew has ABIONA [אֲבִיּוֹנָה] (): this too is ambiguous and is interpreted as “love,” “desire,” “lust,” or “caper plant.” As we said above, it signifies that the desire of the elderly grows cold and the organs of intercourse are destroyed.

This is because these ambiguous words, while in their own terms they sound like “almond,” “locust,” and “caper plant,” signify something else when derived [Note: [Col. 1111C] Martianus has “derived toward another meaning,” less correctly.] and, through figurative speech, are transferred to meanings appropriate to old age.

It should also be known that where the Seventy Translators have now placed “almond,” the word itself is SOCED (), the same word that occurs at the beginning of Jeremiah; but there it is rendered as “nut,” while here it is rendered as “almond.”

Symmachus, evidently understanding something different in this passage, translated it very differently. For he says: “Moreover, concerning these things they will look from on high, and terror will be on the road, and the watchful man will sleep, and the strength of the laborious spirit will be dissolved.” [Note: [Col. 1111C] Martianus restores “and” on the basis of the manuscripts, to which our manuscripts also agree, lest we conceal anything. Yet nothing is more common in these manuscripts than the omission of one of two identical letters when they occur together, and I have no doubt that this happened here. I am not deterred by his insistence that the printed reading, “and terror,” agrees with the Hebrew text, since Jerome testifies that Symmachus was far from that text in his interpretation of this sentence. He has indeed departed from it in other respects, and we should judge that this word too—which could easily have been corrupted in Latin but could never have been extracted from the Hebrew—was written by him. He therefore translated καὶ τρόμος ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ (*kai tromos en tē hodō*) as “and terror on the road.” Aquila translated ἐν τρόμῳ τρομήσουσιν ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ (*en tremō tremēsousin en tē hodō*) as “they will tremble with trembling on the road.” Shortly afterward, instead of “the watchful man will fall asleep,” a Palatine manuscript, together with the old printed editions, has the plural “the watchful men will fall asleep.” Finally, it should be observed that only two words of Symmachus remain in the Greek: καὶ διαλυθῇ ἡ ἐπίπονος (*kai dialythē hē epiponos*), that is, “and the laborious one will be dissolved.” These do not seem to correspond suitably to Jerome’s “and the strength of the spirit will be dissolved.” —“And terror will be on the road.” In the earlier printed books, instead of “error,” we read “and terror will be.” This reading agrees with the Hebrew context, “and they will fear on the road.” But since St. Jerome asserts that Symmachus rendered this passage in Greek very differently from the Hebrew or the Seventy Translators, it appears clear that Jerome’s genuine reading is the one we have restored on the authority of all the manuscripts. MARTIANUS.]

“For the human being will go to his eternal house, and they will go around in the street mourning.” Laodicean followed this interpretation, but it can please neither Jews nor Christians: it is far from the Hebrews, and it disdains to follow the Seventy Translators.

[Col. 1111C] “Before the silver cord is broken, and the golden fillet returns, and the pitcher is shattered at the fountain, and the wheel is broken over the cistern.” [Note: [Col. 1112C] Two manuscripts read: “and the wheel is shattered,” etc.] “And the dust returns to its earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes; all is vanity.”

He returns to what came before and, after a great hyperbaton—having inserted material after the place where he had said, “And remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of evil come and before the sun and moon grow dark,” and so forth, “on the day when the guardians of the house are shaken”—now concludes the sentence he had begun with a similar ending, saying: “Before the silver cord is broken, and this or that happens.”

The silver cord indicates this bright life and the breath that is granted to us from heaven. The return of the golden fillet signifies the soul, which returns to the place from which it descended. The two things that follow—the shattering of the pitcher at the fountain and the breaking of the wheel over the cistern—are, metaphorically, riddles of death.

For just as a pitcher that is shattered ceases to draw water, and a wheel by which water is raised from a cistern or well ceases to function if it is broken—[Note: [Col. 1112C] Or, as the Seventy Translators have it, etc. Erasmus and Marianus have wrongly placed here as well: “Or, as the other interpreters wished.” For the interpretation that follows immediately, “rolled up in its cord,” is found in the Seventy Translators: καὶ συντροχάσῃ ὁ τροχὸς ἐπὶ τὸν λάκκον (*kai syntrochasei ho trochos epi ton lakkon*), that is, “and the wheel rolls toward the cistern.” MARTIANUS.] or, as the Seventy Translators wished, when the wheel is rolled up in its cord, the use of the water is cut off—so also, when the silver cord is broken and the stream of the soul returns to its source, the human being will perish. [Note: [Col. 1112D] The printed editions up to this point have: “when the silver cord has been broken,” etc. We have removed the conditional conjunction *if*, which is superfluous and makes the sense awkward, with the help of our manuscripts.]

And, as the text more clearly continues: “The dust will return to its earth, from which it was taken, and the spirit will return to the Lord who gave it.” From this it is quite evident how laughable are those who think that souls are sown together with bodies and generated not by God but by the parents of bodies. [Note: [Col. 1112D] “By the parents of bodies.” Since the present passage concerns the origin of souls, I shall omit nothing regarding the variant readings of the manuscripts. Many therefore read in the singular, “by the parent of the body”; but below they all consistently retain “the parent of souls,” and not “the father of souls,” as the old editions read. MARTIANUS. —See the exchange of letters between Jerome and Augustine concerning the origin of the soul.] For since the flesh returns to the earth and the spirit returns to God who gave it, it is evident that God is the parent [Al. “father”] of souls, not human beings.

After describing human destruction, beautifully returning to the beginning of his book, he says: “Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes; all is vanity.” Since all human labor, about which he has argued throughout the entire volume, comes to this—that the dust returns to its earth and the soul returns to the place from which it was taken—it is a great vanity to labor in this age and accumulate things that will profit nothing.

And further, because Ecclesiastes had become wise, he continued to teach the people knowledge and caused them to listen; and, searching, he composed proverbs. [Note: Ecclesiastes sought much. Some manuscript copies read differently, where we find written: “searching, he composed many proverbs.” “Ecclesiastes sought much.” MARTIAN.] Ecclesiastes sought much in order to find words of delight and to write words of truth correctly. The wisdom by which Solomon surpassed the whole human race [Note: “By which Solomon surpassed.” The Sorbonne codex reads, “by which Solomon is preferred above the whole human race”; the printed books, “by which Solomon went before the whole human race.” MARTIAN.] he now also declares at the end of his little work that he was not content with the instruction of the ancient Law, but voluntarily plunged into profound questions and, in order to teach the people, composed proverbs and parables [Note: It is therefore more probable that, as Jerome observed at the beginning of this work, the book of Ecclesiastes, being the last of all those Solomon composed, is a memorial of his repentance and conversion to God.], presenting one thing in their inner meaning and promising another on the surface. For we are taught even in the Gospels (Matthew XIII and XV) that proverbs do not signify merely what is written: the Lord spoke to the people in parables and proverbs, but privately explained them to the apostles. From this it is clear that the Book of Proverbs, contrary to the opinion of the simple, does not contain plain precepts, but that, just as gold is sought in earth, a kernel in a nut, and a hidden fruit beneath the rough husks of chestnuts, so the divine meaning must be searched out more deeply in them. In addition, he said that he had wished to understand the causes and natures of things, and God’s [Note: Alcuin also once read it this way, and the manuscripts prefer it. But the old printed editions have “providence.” “Disposition and prudence.” It would be better to read “and providence,” which the printed editions also read; nevertheless, I restored “prudence,” because this is written in all the manuscript copies. MARTIAN.] disposition and prudence: he wished to know why each thing, or how it had been made, so that what David hoped he would see after the dissolution of body and soul, when he expected to return to the heavens, saying, “I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Psalm VIII, 4), Solomon might now strive to discover: [Note: Another Palatine manuscript, as Erasmus also read it: “and the truth known to God alone, the human mind, enclosed within the barrier of the body, cannot comprehend.” Victor places “which” before “the body.” — “The truth known to God alone.” The Erasmian edition acknowledges this reading and places it in the margin, while it has the following, false reading in the text: “And the truth known to God alone, the human mind, enclosed within the barrier of the body, cannot comprehend.” Marianus also followed this reading, adding only the relative pronoun “which,” that is, “which the body …” MARTIAN.] so that the human mind, enclosed within the barrier of the body, might comprehend the truth known to God alone.

The words of the wise, like goads and like nails driven deep, are given to assemblies by one shepherd. Lest he appear suddenly, after the Law of God, as a rash teacher bursting forth and claiming for himself a doctrine which Moses had received not so much of his own accord as first when God was angry and afterward when God inspired him [Note: The Vatican manuscript, with the Palatine in a second hand and finally Alcuin, reads: “as first at God's command,” and so forth.], he says that his words are the words of the wise. These words, like goads, correct those who do wrong and rouse the sluggish steps of mortals by pricking them with their sting; and thus they are firm, like nails driven deeply into solid and stable material. Nor are they brought forth on the authority of one person, but through the counsel and agreement of all the teachers.
