[Note: Three manuscripts, here and below, read “but by counsel.”] [Note: The old editions read, “and lest the wisdom of all should be despised.” Alcuin then has, “yet the Lord is the author of this doctrine”; the old editions, “one author is …,” and so forth.] And lest human wisdom be despised, he says that it was granted by one shepherd: that is, although many teach, nevertheless [Note: “One is the author, the Lord.” In the printed editions: “Yet the author of this doctrine is one, the Lord.” But the manuscript codices indicate that “of this” should be read absolutely, so that not only is the Lord the one author of this doctrine, but of every kind of knowledge and true teaching, although there are many who teach. MARTIAN.] the Lord is the one author of doctrine.

This passage stands against those who consider the God of the Old Law one and the God of the Gospel another, since one shepherd instructed an assembly of the prudent. The prudent are both the prophets and the apostles. At the same time, we must observe that the words of the wise are said to prick, not to flatter, nor to caress wantonness with a gentle hand [Note: The same manuscript has “to draw out wantonness,” and shortly afterward, “to inflict a wound.”]; rather, they inflict upon those who err and, as we said above, upon those who are slow the pains and wound of repentance. If, therefore, someone’s speech does not prick but exists only to delight its hearers, that is not the speech of a wise man. For the words of the wise are like goads. Since they summon the transgressor to conversion, they are firm, given by the council of the saints, granted by one shepherd, and founded upon a solid root.

By this goad I suppose that Saul—he was not yet Paul—heard, while pierced on the road of his error: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts IX, 5). [Note: In the old editions: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad of God.” MARTIAN.]

And further, my son, beware of these things. [Note: Victorius reads: “There is no end to making many books,” and so forth.] “Of making many books there is no end, and much meditation is a weariness of the flesh.” Except for these words, which were given by one shepherd and approved by the council and [Note: “Approved by the agreement of the wise.” The Corbie manuscripts read this way; others, together with the printed editions, have “uttered by the wise.” MARTIAN.] agreement of the wise, do nothing and claim nothing for yourself: follow the footsteps of your elders and do not depart from their authority. Otherwise, when you seek many things, an endless number of books will confront you; they will drag you into error and make you labor uselessly as you read. Or certainly he teaches that one must pursue brevity and follow meanings rather than words, in opposition to the philosophers and teachers of this age, who try to assert the falsehoods of their doctrines through the vanity and multiplication [Al. multitude] of their words. By contrast, divine Scripture is compressed within a brief compass, and as much as it expands in meaning, so much is it contracted in expression. [Note: “It expands in meanings.” Very many manuscript copies read “it expands in senses.” In Tertullian's *On the Lord's Prayer*, if I remember correctly, it is said: “As much as it is compressed in words, so much is it expanded in meanings.” MARTIAN.] For “God made a brief and concise word upon the earth,” and “his word is near us, in our mouth and in our heart” (Romans X, 8; Deuteronomy XXX, 14).

Alternatively: frequent reading and daily meditation are usually more a labor of the soul than of the flesh. For just as whatever is done with the hand and body is completed through the labor of the hand and body, so what belongs to reading is more the labor of the mind. From this it seems to me that the preceding statements about the multitude of books should be understood differently from the way most people judge them. It is customary in Scripture, even when there are several books, provided they do not disagree with one another and are written about the same matter, to call them one volume. Thus both the Gospel and the Law of the Lord, which is without blemish and converts souls (Psalm XVIII, 8), are called in the singular, although there are several Gospels and many commandments of the Law. Likewise, the volume sealed in Isaiah’s prophecy signifies all divine Scripture (Isaiah XXIX), and Ezekiel and John feed upon one chapter of the book (Ezekiel VIII; Revelation X). The Savior also, foretold by the voices of all the saints of former times, says: “In the chapter of the book it is written concerning me” (Psalm XXXIX, 9).

According to this meaning, therefore, I think the command now is that many books should not be made. Whatever you say, if it is referred to him who “in the beginning was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 2), is one volume; and countless books are called one Law, one Gospel. But if you discuss things that are diverse and contradictory, and by excessive curiosity lead your mind here and there [Al. draw it away], then even in one book there are many books. Hence it is said: “You will not escape sin through much speaking” (Proverbs X, 19).

There is therefore no end to such books. [Note: Alcuin has “For every good thing …”; and “all truth is enclosed within a fixed …,” and so forth.] For every good thing and truth are enclosed within a definite limit, whereas wickedness and falsehood are without end. The more they are sought, the greater their succession is born. [Note: On this matter. In the printed editions and several manuscripts: “In this matter, study …,” and so forth. MARTIAN.] On this matter, study and meditation are a labor of the flesh—the flesh, I say, not the spirit. The spirit, too, has its own labor, according to the Apostle’s statement: “I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians XV, 10). And the Savior says: “I labored, crying out” (Psalm LXVIII, 4).

The conclusion of the entire discourse, very easy to hear, is this: “Fear God and keep his commandments.” For this is the whole of man, because God will bring every deed into judgment, including everything hidden, whether it is good or evil.

The Hebrews say that, although among Solomon’s other writings—writings that have become obsolete and have not endured in memory—this book also seemed destined to be forgotten [Note: Testimony concerning this matter can be found among ancient Jewish writers. In the book of Shabbat it is said: “The sages sought to hide the book of Qoheleth, because its words overturn one another.” And in the Midrash Qoheleth, because they found in it words inclining toward heresy. Yet it did not subsequently earn authority among them from this one chapter alone, but also from the first chapter, verse 3: “For,” they say, “at its beginning and at its end the words of the Law are encountered.”], because it asserted that God’s creatures were vain, considered everything to be nothing, and preferred food, drink, and passing pleasures to all else, nevertheless it gained authority from this one chapter, so that it might be placed among the divine Books, because it compressed his entire discussion and his whole catalogue in this kind of ἀνακεφαλαίωσις (recapitulation), and declared that the end of his discourse was most readily understood and contained nothing difficult: namely, that we should fear God and do his commandments. For man was born for this purpose: that, recognizing his Creator, he might revere him with fear, honor, and obedience to his commandments.

For when the time of judgment comes, whatever we have done will stand before the judge and will long await an uncertain verdict, and each person will receive according to his work, whether he has done evil or good. [Note: Alcuin had read: “and await the Lord’s uncertain judgment.”]

Instead of what we have written, “concerning everything hidden, whether it is good or evil,” Symmachus and the Septuagint translated “concerning everything despised,” or certainly “concerning everything unknown,” so that we shall also have to give an account on the day of judgment even for an idle word, one uttered not intentionally but through ignorance. [Note: Previously, “contempt” was incorrectly found. The Septuagint translated the adjective as ἐν παντὶ παρεωραμένῳ, “concerning every thing that is despised,” and Symmachus as περὶ παντὸς παροραθέντος, “concerning everything that has been neglected.”]

Alternatively: since “fear belongs to servants,” and “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John IV, 18), and in divine Scripture a twofold fear is attributed both to beginners [Note: “Both of beginners …” Through an inept error, the edition of Erasmus and Marianus has “both of the foolish and of the perfect,” as though there were some divine fear in foolish or impious people, whom Holy Scripture calls foolish. MARTIAN.] and to the perfect, I think that the present passage speaks of fear perfected in the virtues, according to the saying: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear him” (Psalm XXXIII, 10). Or certainly, because he is still a human being and has not yet received the name of God, this is proper to his condition: that, placed in the body, he should fear God. For God will bring every deed—that is, all human beings—into judgment concerning everything they have understood in a way different from what he arranged and said, whether in this direction or in that. Woe, indeed, to those who call evil good and good evil (Isaiah V, 20).

[Col. 1117]

## The Translation of Two Homilies of Origen on the Song of Songs by Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon

### Preface: Jerome to the Most Blessed Pope Damasus

Origen, although he surpassed everyone in his other books, surpassed himself in the Song [Al. Songs] of Songs. For after completing ten volumes, which extend almost to twenty thousand lines of verse, he discusses first the Septuagint translators, then Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, and finally the fifth edition, which he writes that he found on the shore at Actium. [Note: Jerome seems commonly to be mistaken in calling this the fifth edition; it ought to have been called the sixth, since Epiphanius (*On Weights and Measures*, ch. 18), and the author of the *Synopsis* among the works of Athanasius, testify that it was found at Nicopolis near Actium by a devotee of Origen. The edition which Origen himself reported finding, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.16, they maintain was the fifth, concealed in jars (*en pithois*, ἐν πίθοις) at Jericho. I think Jerome had this testimony of Eusebius before his eyes; but I maintain that Eusebius's words leave it open whether one wishes to call either of the two editions he mentions fifth or sixth. Rather, from the order in which each is listed, I think this Nicopolitan edition near Actium is more correctly called the fifth by the holy doctor. The words of the bishop of Caesarea are as follows, where he relates that Origen discovered other translations distinct from those of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion: “He first brought to light these versions, drawn from I know not what corners, in which they had long lain hidden; and, as he had no clear or certain knowledge whose works they were, he noted only this concerning them: that he had found one at Nicopolis near Actium, and the other in another such place” (*hōs ara tēn men heuroi en tē pros Aktiōi Nikopolei, tēn de en heterōi topōi toiōide*, ὡς ἄρα τὴν μὲν εὗροι ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ἀκτίῳ Νικοπόλει, τὴν δὲ ἐν ἑτέρῳ τόπῳ τοιῷδε). That is, he found one—the fifth, which precedes the sixth in order—at Nicopolis near Actium, and the other, the sixth, elsewhere. — “On the Actian shore,” etc. Erasmus and Marianus corruptly read “at Actaeum.” Athanasius, in the *Synopsis*, teaches that the fifth edition was found in jars at Jericho by a devotee among those in Jerusalem, but the sixth at Nicopolis near Actium by a disciple of Origen. Thus the author of the *Synopsis* seems to refer to the sixth what Jerome here asserts about the fifth. Consult Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*. MARTIAN.] He speaks so magnificently and openly that from this alone I seem to see fulfilled in him what is said: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song I, 3). [Note: I compared this work with two manuscript copies, one belonging to the Library of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, the other to the Vatican, formerly marked with the number 66 as belonging to the Queen of the Swedes. I also continually consulted the old edition of 1496, which experience itself taught me, despite its abundance of errors, to be richer in sound material than the other printed books.]

Therefore, setting aside that work, since it would require immense leisure, labor, and expense to transfer such great matters and so worthy a work into Latin, I have faithfully rather than ornamentally translated these two treatises, which he composed in the manner of ordinary speech for little ones still at the breast [Al. and still suckling]. I offer you a taste of his meanings, not the meal, so that you may recognize how highly those greater things must be esteemed when even these lesser things can give such pleasure. [Note: Vallarsius prefixes the following to the First Homily: “The First Treatise of Origen on the Song of Songs Begins.” He then adds this note: “In the ancient edition it is entitled: ‘Origen’s Preface to the Song of Songs,’ which extends through the exposition of the first verse, ‘Let him kiss me with a kiss,’ and so forth; after this another heading follows: ‘The First Homily.’ Then: ‘Let him kiss me,’ and so forth.” He likewise later places “The Second Treatise.” EDITOR.]

### First Homily

[Col. 1117]

As we have learned through Moses that some things are not only holy but also holy of holies, and that some days are not merely sabbaths but sabbaths of sabbaths, so now we are taught, through Solomon’s writing, that there are some songs that are not merely songs but the Song of Songs.

Blessed indeed is the one who enters the holy places, but more blessed is the one who enters the holy of holies. Blessed is the one who keeps a sabbath, but more blessed is the one who keeps the sabbaths of sabbaths. Likewise blessed is the one who understands songs and sings them. For no one sings except on solemn occasions; but much more blessed is the one who sings the Song of Songs.

And just as the one who enters the holy places still needs many things in order to be able to enter the holy of holies, and the one who celebrates the sabbath established by the Lord for the people still needs many things to perform the sabbaths of sabbaths, so it is difficult to find someone who, traversing everything contained in Scripture [Note: The manuscript of the Queen of Sweden reads: “traversing the songs, may be able …”], can ascend to the Song of Songs.

You must go out from Egypt and, having gone out from the land of Egypt, cross the Red Sea, so that you may first sing the song, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored” (Exodus XV, 1). Although you have sung the first song, you are still far from the Song of Songs.

Travel spiritually through the desert until you come to the well that the kings dug (Numbers XXI), so that there you may sing the second song. After this, come near to the Holy Land, so that, standing on the bank of the Jordan, you may sing the song of Moses, saying: “Attend, O heaven, and I shall speak, and let the earth hear the words of my mouth” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 1). [Note: The manuscript of the Queen of Sweden reads: “Attend, O heaven, to what I shall say,” and so forth.]

Again, you must serve as a soldier under Jesus, possess the Holy Land as an inheritance, and have the bee prophesy to you and judge you—Deborah means “bee”—so that you may also learn by heart the song contained in the Book of Judges (Judges V).

Then, ascending to the Book of Kings (2 Samuel XXII), come to the song [Note: The manuscript of the Queen of Sweden reads: “when David was delivered from the hand …” It omits what follows, “and my strength.”] sung when David was delivered from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and he said: “The Lord is my firmament, my strength, my refuge, and my deliverer” (Psalm XVII, 1).

You must reach Isaiah, so that with him you may say: “I shall sing a song to the beloved of my vineyard” (Isaiah V, 1). And when you have passed through all these stages, climb to higher things, so that you, a beautiful soul, may sing this Song of Songs with the bridegroom.

I am uncertain of how many persons the song consists. But as you prayed and the Lord revealed it, I seem to have discovered four persons in it: the bridegroom and the bride, the young women with the bride, and the companies of companions with the bridegroom. Some things are spoken by the bride, others by the bridegroom, some by the young women, and others by the bridegroom’s companions. For it is fitting that at a wedding there should be a multitude of young women with the bride and a crowd of young men with the bridegroom.

Do not seek all these things outside; do not look beyond those who have been saved through the preaching of the Gospel. Understand Christ as the bridegroom and the Church as the bride, without spot or wrinkle, concerning whom it is written: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but that she might be holy and immaculate” (Ephesians V, 27). [Note: Two manuscripts read “or anything of that kind, but that she …” We correct minor matters below from the same manuscripts.]

But those who, although they are believers, are not of this kind—who do not possess the qualities described in the preceding passage, but seem to have attained salvation in some measure—understand as the souls of believers, and as the young women with the bride. Understand the angels and those who have attained mature manhood as the men with the bridegroom.

Thus there seem to me to be four orders: one man and one woman, and two choirs singing antiphonally, the bride singing with the young women and the bridegroom singing with his companions. Once you have understood this, listen to the Song of Songs, hasten to understand it, and say with the bride what the bride says, so that you may hear what the bride heard.

But if you cannot say with the bride what she said, so as to hear what was said to the bride, hasten at least to become one of the bridegroom’s companions. If you are inferior even to them, remain with the young women who dwell amid the bride’s delights. For these are simultaneously characters in the drama and the epithalamium of this book, from which the Gentiles also claimed the epithalamium for themselves, and this kind of song was adopted. Indeed, the Song of Songs is an epithalamium. [Note: In almost these words begins the prologue to the two homilies on the Song of Songs, as they are commonly received, which Rufinus translated into Latin: “This little book, an epithalamium—that is, a nuptial song—seems to me to have been composed by Solomon in the form of a drama, which he sang as though he were a bride being married and addressing her bridegroom,” and so forth.]

First the bride prays, and immediately, in the midst of her prayers, she hears and sees the bridegroom present, and the young women joined to her company. Then the bridegroom answers her, and after the bridegroom’s words, while he suffers for her salvation, the companions respond, until the bridegroom is at rest and rises from his passion, and they declare that they will make certain ornaments for the bride. But now the actual words must be set forth, in which the voice of the supplicating bride is heard first.

[Note: With the commonly received version, the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden reads “Let him kiss me with a kiss,” here and below.]

“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” (Song I, 1).

The meaning is this: How long will my bridegroom send me kisses through Moses? How long will he send kisses through the prophets? Now I desire to touch his very lips. Let him come himself; let him descend himself.

Therefore she prays to the bridegroom’s Father and says to him: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.” And because she is such that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled in her—“While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Behold, here I am’” (Isaiah LVIII, 9)—the Father of the bridegroom hears the bride and sends his Son.

When she sees him whose coming she had entreated, she ceases to pray and speaks to him face to face: “For your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes is above all spices.”

The bridegroom, therefore, Christ, sent by the Father, comes anointed to the bride, and it is said to him: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm XLIV, 8).

If the bridegroom touches me, I too shall become a fragrance; I too shall be smeared with perfumes, and his perfumes will reach me [Al. will reach me in the future], so that I may say with the apostles: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Corinthians II, 15).

But when we hear these words, we still stink with sins and vices, concerning which the repentant prophet says: “My wounds have putrefied and festered because of my foolishness” (Psalm XXXVII, 4). Sin has the odor of what is foul [Al. putrid]; virtue breathes perfumes, whose types you may read again in Exodus. There you will find storax, onycha, galbanum, and the rest. [Note: The same manuscript of the Queen of Sweden reads: “These things are for incense. Then …”]

These are used for incense. Then, for the work of the perfumer, various perfumes are taken, among which are nard and storax. And God, who made heaven and earth, speaks to Moses, saying: “I have filled them with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, to make works of the perfumer’s art” (Exodus XXXV and XXXVI). God also teaches the perfumers.

If these things are not understood spiritually, are they not merely stories? [Note: The words, “Unless these things contain some secret meaning, are they not unworthy of God?” are missing from the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden.] Unless they contain some secret meaning, are they not unworthy of God?

It is therefore necessary for the one who knows how to hear Scripture spiritually—or who does not yet know how but desires to know—to strive with every effort not to live according to flesh and blood, so that he may become worthy of spiritual secrets and, to say something bolder, of spiritual desire or love. For there is also a spiritual love. [Note: The manuscript of the Holy Cross adds “and a carnal one.”]

Just as there is one kind of carnal food and another spiritual, and one kind of drink of the flesh [Al. carnal] and another of the spirit, so there is a carnal love that comes from Satan and another love of the spirit that has its beginning from God. No one can be possessed by two loves. If you are a lover of the flesh, you do not grasp the love of the spirit.

If you have despised all bodily things—not merely flesh or blood, but also silver and possessions, and the earth itself and heaven itself, for these things will pass away—if you have despised all these things and your soul is attached to none of them, nor held captive anywhere by love of vices, you can receive spiritual love.

We have said these things because the occasion arose to speak about spiritual love. [Note: The old edition has: “We have said these things because the occasion arose”; the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden instead reads: “And so the occasion arose.”]

It is beneficial for us to keep Solomon’s command, and especially the command of the one who spoke through Solomon concerning wisdom, saying: “Love her, and she will preserve you; surround her, and she will exalt you; honor her, that she may embrace you” [Al. may embrace you] (Proverbs IV, 8).

There is a spiritual embrace. Would that it might happen that the higher embrace of the bridegroom should enfold my bride, so that I too might say what is written in the same book: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song II, 6).

Therefore: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.” It is customary for the Scriptures to use the imperative mood in place of the optative, as in: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name,” instead of “May thy name be hallowed”; and here too: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth,” meaning “May he kiss me.” Then she beholds the bridegroom: he comes drenched in perfumes. He could not come to the bride in any other way, nor was it fitting for the Father to send the Son to the wedding in any other manner. He anointed him with various perfumes and made him Christ; he came breathing forth diverse fragrances, and she hears: “For your breasts are better than wine.”

The divine word appropriately calls one and the same thing by different names according to the circumstances. When a sacrificial victim is offered under the Law and he wishes to indicate its meaning, he addresses the breast of separation. But when someone reclines with Jesus and enjoys communion with his understanding, he addresses not the breast of separation, as above, but the breast. When, moreover, the bride speaks to the bridegroom—since a nuptial song is being introduced—she names neither the breast of separation, as in the sacrifice, nor the breast, as in the case of John the disciple, but the breasts, saying: “For your breasts are better than wine.”

[Note: One word was missing; the manuscripts supply it. For the sake of borrowing light from them, the following should also be referred here: in the earlier homily among those which Rufinus translated from the Greek, Origen discusses the ἡγεμονικόν, that is, the ruling principle, which he says is designated in Holy Scripture by various names—sometimes as the breast and bosom, as when John is said to have reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper; sometimes as the breast-piece or arm, which is set apart for the priests, as in Leviticus; and finally as the breasts, as here in the Song. “Your heart,” he says, “O my bridegroom,” that is, the teachings within you, or your teaching, “is better than all wine,” which ordinarily makes the human heart glad. For just as, in the passages where it says, “for they shall see God,” the heart seems appropriately mentioned; and among those reclining, the bosom and breast undoubtedly signify the posture of those reclining and the form of the banquet; and again, among the priests, the breast-piece and arm are designated in mystical expressions—so also, I think, in the present passage of the Song, where the conduct and conversations of lovers are described, this same ruling principle has most graciously been called the heart.]

Share, as the bride, in the bridegroom’s understanding, and you will know that thoughts of this kind intoxicate and gladden. Just as the Lord’s cup, which intoxicates, is exceedingly excellent (Ps. XXII), so the bridegroom’s breasts are better than all wine: “For your breasts are better than wine.”

[Note: The Cistercian, or Holy Cross, manuscript reads: “better than all.”]

In the midst of her prayers she turns her words toward the bridegroom: “And the fragrance of your perfumes is better than all spices.” The bridegroom comes anointed not with one perfume but with all perfumes. But if he also deigns to come to my soul, which has been made his bride, how beautiful it must be—so that it may draw him from heaven to itself, make him descend to earth, and cause him to come to his beloved! With what beauty must it be adorned, with what love must it burn, so that she may say to it what was said to the perfect bride: “For your neck, your eyes, your cheeks, your hands, your belly, your shoulders, your feet” (Song IV and following)! If the Lord grants it, we shall discuss these things: how the bride’s members vary and the praise of each part is differently expressed, so that after the discussion we may likewise strive to apply it to our own soul.

“Your breasts, therefore, are better than wine.” If you behold the bridegroom, then you will understand the truth of what is said: “For your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes is better than all spices.” Many have possessed spices. The queen of the South brought spices to Solomon, and many others possessed spices; but however great the quantity anyone may have had, they cannot be compared with Christ’s fragrances, of which the bride now says: “The fragrance of your perfumes is better than all spices.” I think that Moses also had spices, and Aaron, and each of the prophets. But if I see Christ and perceive the sweetness and fragrance of his perfumes, I immediately pronounce judgment, saying: “The fragrance of your perfumes is better than all spices.”

[Note: The manuscripts read “your perfume poured out,” which is also confirmed by the interpretation that follows.]

“Your name is poured-out oil.” This is a prophetic mystery. The name of Jesus alone comes into the world, and the perfume is proclaimed as poured out. In the Gospel also, a woman took an alabaster flask of costly genuine nard, and poured it over Jesus’ head and feet (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV).

Observe carefully what is written concerning the two women who poured perfume over the Savior’s head.

[Note: Origen held the view that the woman who anointed Christ at the house of Simon the Pharisee was different from the woman who anointed him at the house of Simon the Leper; and that the one called a sinner anointed his feet, while the holy woman anointed his head. He explains this more clearly near the beginning of the following homily: “The Gospel says that a woman came with an alabaster flask of costly genuine nard—not that sinful woman, but the holy woman about whom I am now speaking. I know that Luke speaks of the sinful woman, whereas Matthew, John, and Mark do not speak of a sinful woman. Thus it was not that sinful woman who came, but the holy one, whose name John also inserted.” Indeed, he introduces a third anointing woman, different from both of these, in his commentary on Matthew XXVI: “I rather agree that there were three: one of whom Matthew and Mark wrote, making no distinction in their exposition within the same chapter; another of whom Luke wrote; and another of whom John wrote.” It is enough for us to have noted these matters according to Origen’s view; for it is not the purpose of our work to undertake the very famous question on both sides or to support the position we approve with arguments.]

For the sinful woman is shown to have poured it over his feet, while the woman who is not called sinful is shown to have poured it over his head (Luke VII; John XII).

[Note: We read with the Reginensis manuscript: “and the woman who is said not to have been sinful.” The earlier reading had an awkward sense.] Observe, I say, and you will find that the Evangelists recorded not fables and narratives but mysteries.

Thus [Al.: indeed] the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume: if what the sinful woman possessed is to be referred to the feet, and what the woman who was not sinful possessed to the head (ibid.). Nor is it surprising that the house was filled with fragrance, since the world has been filled with it. In the same passage there is mention of Simon the Leper and his house (Mark XIV; Luke VII). I think that the leper signifies [Al.: is the ruler] of this world, and that this leper was called Simon, whose house was filled with a sweet fragrance at Christ’s coming: the sinful woman performing repentance, and the holy woman pouring the fragrances of perfume over Jesus’ head.

“Your name is poured-out oil.” Just as perfume, by being poured out, disperses its fragrance far and wide, so Christ’s name has been poured out. Christ is named throughout the whole earth; the Lord is preached throughout the entire world. His name, then, is poured-out perfume.

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “The name of Moses is not heard.”]

Now the name of Moses is heard, whereas previously it was confined within the narrow limits of Judea. No Greek, after all, remembers him, nor do we find anything written about him or the others in any history of the literature of the gentiles. As soon as Jesus shone forth in the world, he brought the Law and the Prophets with him, and the statement was truly fulfilled: “Your name is poured-out oil.”

Therefore the maidens loved you.

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads: “Therefore the maidens loved you,” etc.]

Because through the Holy Spirit the love of God has been poured out in our hearts (Rom. V), the name of pouring is appropriately introduced: “Your name is poured-out oil.”

As she says this, the bride sees [Al.: desires] the maidens.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “desires” instead of “sees.”]

When she was asking the Father of the bridegroom and speaking face to face with the bridegroom himself, the maidens were not yet present. But in the midst of her prayers the chorus of maidens enters, and they are praised in the bride’s words: “Therefore the maidens loved you, and they drew you.” The maidens reply: “After you, we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes.”

How beautifully the bridegroom’s attendants, who do not yet possess the bride’s confidence, behave! The bride does not follow behind him but enters at his side, joined to him. She grasps the bridegroom’s right hand, and her hand is held by the bridegroom’s right hand. The servants, however, enter after him [Al.: after her].

[Note: The older edition and the Reginensis manuscript read “after her.”]

“There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. One is my dove, my perfect one; one is her mother’s, one is hers who conceived her” (Song VI, 7–8).

“After you, therefore, we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes.” This is said to those walking with all dignity: “After you, we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes,” according to: “I have finished the course” (II Tim. IV, 7), and: “Those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize” (I Cor. IX, 24). Christ is the prize. These maidens, whom we understand to remain outside because their love is only beginning, endure something like the following example: “But the friend of the bridegroom, standing and hearing him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John IX, 24).

[Note: The same books read: “and the maidens endure something of this kind.”]

When the bridegroom enters, they remain outside. But the beautiful, perfect, spotless bride, without blemish or wrinkle, enters the bridegroom’s chamber, the royal bedchamber; then she returns to the maidens and announces to them what she alone has seen, saying:

“The king brought me into his chamber.” She does not say, “He brought us, many, into his chamber.” Many remain outside; the bride alone enters the chamber, so that she may see treasures dark and hidden and report to the maidens: “The king brought me into his chamber.”

Again the maidens—that is, the very numerous multitude of brides who are just beginning—after the bride has entered the bridegroom’s chamber and seen the riches of her husband, while they await his coming, sing joyfully: “We shall exult and rejoice in you.”

[Al.: “We exult and rejoice.”]

They rejoice [Al.: we rejoice] over the bride’s perfection. There is no jealousy in virtue. This love is pure; this love is without fault.

“We shall exult and rejoice in you; we shall love your breasts.”

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript adds: “better than wine.”]

The one who is greater already enjoys the milk of your breasts and speaks exultantly: “Your breasts are better than wine.” But these who bring exultation and joy—since they are maidens, they bring love—and say: “We shall exult and rejoice in you.”

[Note: It seems that “they differ” should be emended here and shortly below from Victor’s edition, as its Brescian codices attest and as the following words show: they say “we shall love,” not “we love.”]

[Note: The older edition more harmoniously reads: “We shall love your breasts better than wine.” It says “we shall love,” not “we love.” Then follows, etc.]

“We shall love,” not “we love,” your breasts better than wine.

Then they speak to the bride: “Righteousness has loved you.” They praise the bride, giving her the name of righteousness on account of her own virtues: “Righteousness has loved you.”

Again the bride responds to the maidens:

“I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Cedar, like the skins of Solomon. Do not look at me, because I am darkened, for the sun has looked upon me.”

She is certainly beautiful, and I can discover how the bride is beautiful. But we ask how she is black and, without fairness, beautiful. She repented of her sins; conversion [Al.: manner of life] granted her beauty, and therefore she is sung as beautiful. But because she has not yet been cleansed of every stain of sin, because she has not yet been washed unto salvation, she is called black; yet she does not remain in blackness.

Thus she becomes white when she rises to greater things and begins to climb from lowly matters to lofty ones, and it is said of her: “Who is this who ascends, made white?” (Song VIII, 5).

And so that the mystery might be described more clearly and perfectly, he does not say, as is read in many manuscripts, “leaning upon her beloved,” that is, ἐπιστηριζομένη; rather, he says ἐπιστηθιζομένη, that is, “reclining upon his breast.”

[Note: The word was previously lacking in the manuscripts. Not merely most, but all the surviving Greek books prefer ἐπιστηριζομένη over ἐπιστηθιζομένη; Martianus reads ἐπιστηθισομένη.]

Significantly it is said of the bride’s soul and of the word, “reclining upon his breast,” because the ruling principle—ἡγεμονικόν—is there, namely, our heart.

[Note: Greek: ἡγεμονικόν. See the note above.]

Therefore, departing from carnal things, we ought to perceive spiritual things and understand that it is much better to love in this way than to cease loving.

She ascended, then, reclining upon the breast of her beloved; and she who is now placed at the beginning of the Song as black is sung at the end of the nuptial song: “Who is this who ascends, made white?”

We have understood how the bride is both black and beautiful. But if you do not repent, beware lest your soul be called black and ugly, and you be made ugly by a double deformity: black because of past sins, ugly because you persist in those same vices. But if you repent, your soul will be black because of its ancient offenses; yet because of repentance it will possess, so to speak, something of Ethiopian beauty.

And since I have once mentioned an Ethiopian, I wish to summon Scripture as a witness for this discourse. Aaron and Miriam murmured because Moses had an Ethiopian wife (Num. XXI).

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads: “because Moses had taken an Ethiopian woman as his wife.” Compare the other homily of Origen in Rufinus’ translation near the beginning.]

And now Moses takes an Ethiopian woman as his wife. For his Law has migrated to this Ethiopian woman of ours. Let Aaron—the Jewish priesthood—murmur; let Miriam—their synagogue—also murmur. Moses does not care about their murmuring; he loves his Ethiopian woman, of whom it is also said elsewhere through the Prophet: “From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia they shall bring sacrifices” (Zeph. III, 10);

[Note: We supply the word “Ethiopia,” previously lacking here, from the manuscripts, in accordance with Origen’s meaning and the text of Scripture.] and again: “Ethiopia shall stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. LXVII, 32).

Beautifully it says, “shall stretch out her hands.” For just as in the Gospel the woman who suffered from an issue of blood anticipated the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter by receiving healing (Matt. IX; Mark V; Luke VIII), so Ethiopia, while Israel was sick, was healed. Their offense became salvation for the gentiles, so as to provoke them to emulation.

“I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” And you, ecclesiastical soul, turn your speech toward the daughters of Jerusalem and say: “The bridegroom loves me more; he loves me more than you,” who are the many daughters of Israel. You remain outside and watch the bride enter the chamber.

Let no one doubt that she who is called black is also beautiful.

Who are we, that we should know God, proclaim the Song of Songs, and come from the ends of Ethiopia, from the farthest limits of the earth, to hear the wisdom of the true Solomon?

And when the voice of the Savior thunders: “The queen of the South will rise in judgment and condemn the people of this generation, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (Matt. XII; Luke XI), listen to the mystical meaning of these words.

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads “to hear Solomon”; the Cistercian manuscript, “hear the mysteries that are spoken.”]

The queen of the South comes from the ends of the earth: she is the Church. And she condemns the people of this generation, that is, the Jews devoted to flesh and blood. She comes from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon—not of the Solomon proclaimed in the Old Testament, but of this one who is greater than Solomon in the Gospel.

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “Black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.”]

“I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem”: black like the tents of Cedar, beautiful like the skins of Solomon. For she answers both descriptions: “I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” [Al.: Israel], “like the tents of Cedar, like the skins of Solomon.”

The names themselves also correspond to the bride’s beauty. The Hebrews say that Cedar is interpreted as “darkness.” I am therefore black like the tents of Cedar, like Ethiopians; beautiful like the skins of Solomon, which he arranged as an ornament for the tabernacle when he built the temple with the greatest care and labor. Solomon was rich, and no one surpassed him in all his wisdom.

[Note: Victorius, together with the older edition, does not recognize the words “like one of these.”]

“Like one of these, I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Cedar, like the skins of Solomon. Do not look at me, because I am darkened.”

She has made satisfaction concerning her blackness, and, turned toward better things through repentance, she announces to the daughters of Jerusalem [Al.: Israel] that she is indeed black but beautiful, according to what we explained above, and says: “Do not look at me, because I am darkened.”

“Do not,” she says, “be amazed that my color is so gloomy. The sun looked upon me: the brilliance of its full ray shone upon me, and I was darkened by its heat. For I did not receive its light within me as was fitting, as the dignity of the sun required.”

[Al.: “and” for “and I was”; “I may be” for “I was.”] Their offense became salvation for the gentiles, and again, through the unbelief of the gentiles, knowledge came to Israel. You have both points in the Apostle.

“My mother’s sons fought against me.” We must consider how the bride says: “My mother’s sons fought against me,” and when the battle of brothers arose against her. Look at Paul, the persecutor of the Church, and you will understand how her son fought against her. The persecutors of the Church repented, and her former adversaries, turning again to the signs of their sister, preached the faith which they had previously destroyed.

The bride now sings in a prophetic spirit: “They fought against me; they made me keeper of the vineyards. My own vineyard I did not keep.”

I, the Church, I, the bride, spotless, was appointed keeper of many vineyards by the sons of my mother, who had once fought against me. While I was occupied with such concern and care in guarding many vineyards, I did not preserve my own vineyard.

Understand this to refer to Paul and to any other saint who is concerned for the salvation of all, and you will see how, while not guarding his own vineyard, he guards the vineyards of others; how, in order to win others, he himself suffers loss in certain matters.

And when he was free from all, he made himself a servant of all, in order to win them all: “To the weak I became weak; to the Jews, a Jew; to those under the Law, as one under the Law” (I Cor. IX), and so forth. Let him say: “My own vineyard I did not keep.”

Then she sees the bridegroom, who, after being seen, has departed. She does this frequently throughout the entire song; and unless someone experiences it himself, he cannot understand it. Often, God is my witness, I have seen the bridegroom coming to me and being with me at great length; then, when he suddenly departed, I could not find what I was seeking. Again I desire his coming, and sometimes he comes once more; and when he has appeared and has been grasped by my hands, again he slips away; and when he has slipped away, I seek him again. I do this repeatedly until I truly hold him and ascend, leaning upon my beloved.

[Note: From the Reginensis manuscript we read “I do this,” instead of the earlier “he does this”; shortly afterward, “leaning,” instead of “leaning,” masculine.]

“Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.” I do not seek other times—when you pasture in the evening, at dawn, or at the setting of the sun. I seek that time when the day is flourishing, when you move in full daylight, in the splendor of your majesty.

“Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday” (Gen. III). Carefully observe where you read of midday. In Joseph, the brothers take their meal at midday. At midday the angels are received as guests by Abraham (Gen. XVIII), and there are other examples of this kind. Search, and you will find that the divine Scripture does not use each expression pointlessly, accidentally, or by chance.

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads: “not pointlessly, nor accidentally, nor by chance.”]

Who, do you think, among us is worthy to reach midday and see where the bridegroom pastures and where he lies down?

“Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.” For unless you tell me, I begin to wander about aimlessly; and while I seek you, I rush into the flocks of others.

[Note: The older edition reads: “and because I am ashamed to approach the face and mouths of others, I immediately cover my own face and mouth.” The Cistercian manuscript likewise reads “I cover,” instead of “I begin to cover.”]

And because I am ashamed before others, I begin to cover my face and mouth. For I am a beautiful bride, and I do not show my uncovered face to others, but only to you, whom I kissed long ago.

“Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday, lest I become like one who is covered among the flocks of your companions.” To prevent this from happening to me—to prevent me from becoming covered, from hiding my face, and from reaching others, where I might perhaps begin to love those whom I do not know—tell me, therefore, where I should seek you and find you at midday, lest I become like one covered among the flocks of your companions.

After these words the bridegroom warns her and says: Either recognize yourself, since you are the bride of the king, beautiful and made beautiful by me—for I have presented to myself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle (Eph. V)—or know that if you do not recognize yourself and understand your dignity, you will suffer what follows.

What is that? If you do not recognize yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out in the tracks of the flocks and pasture not flocks of sheep, not flocks of lambs, but your own goats. For he will set the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left (Matt. XXI).

“If you do not recognize yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out in the tracks of the flocks and pasture your goats in the tents of the shepherds.” In the tracks, he says, you will become the last of the shepherds—not among the sheep but among your goats. Dwelling with them, you will not be able to be with me, that is, with the good shepherd.

“I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.” If you wish to understand, O bride, how you ought to know yourself, recognize with whom I have compared you, and now you will see that you are such a one as should not be humiliated once you have understood your appearance.

What, then, does this mean? “I have compared you to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.” I know that the bridegroom is a horseman, as the Prophet says: “His riding is salvation” (Hab. III, 8). You have therefore been compared to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots.

How much does my cavalry differ from Pharaoh’s horses—my cavalry, since I am the Lord, who plunge Pharaoh, his crested warriors, his riders, his horses, and his chariots into the waves (Exod. XIV)—so much better are you, O bride, O ecclesiastical soul, than all daughters and all souls that are not ecclesiastical. Therefore, if you are an ecclesiastical soul, you are better than all souls; if you are not better, you are not ecclesiastical.

“I have compared you to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots, my companion.”

Then he describes the bride’s beauty in spiritual love.

“Your cheeks are like a turtledove’s.” He praises her face and is inflamed by the redness of her cheeks. The greatest beauty of women is said to be in the cheeks. So let us understand the soul’s beauty in its cheeks as well.

Let us proclaim her lips and tongue as the understanding of preaching.

[Note: It may be more accurate in the Cistercian manuscript: “the understanding of preaching.”]

“Your neck is like a necklace.” Like an ornament that customarily hangs from a virgin’s neck and is called ὄρμισκος, “a small necklace,” so your neck itself is an ornament without this adornment.

After this the bridegroom lies down; he rested like a lion and slept like a lion’s cub (Gen. XLIX, 9), so that he might later hear: “Who will rouse him?”

While he sleeps, the bridegroom’s companions, the angels, appear to the bride and console her with these words:

“We cannot make golden ornaments for you, for we are not as rich as your bridegroom, who can give you a golden necklace. We shall make the likeness of gold; we do not possess gold. And even in this there is reason for joy, if we make likenesses of gold and marks of silver. We shall make likenesses of gold for you, with marks of silver.”

But not for all time—only until your bridegroom rises from his resting place. For when he rises, he himself will make gold for you, he himself will make silver; he himself will adorn your mind and understanding, and you will truly be a rich and beautiful bride in the bridegroom’s house. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SECOND HOMILY

From the passage where it is written: “My nard gave forth its fragrance,” to the passage where he says: “For your voice is sweet, and your appearance beautiful” [Al.: comely].

[Col. 1129]

All the movements of the soul were created by God, the Creator of the universe, for good.

[Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads: “He created and made them for good.”]

But because of our use, it often happens that things which are good by nature, when we misuse them, lead us into sins. One of the soul’s movements is love, which we use well when we love wisdom and truth. But when our love falls toward worse things, we love flesh and blood.

You, therefore, as a spiritual person, hear spiritual meanings in the singing of these love words, and learn to transfer the movement of your soul and the fire of natural [Al.: carnal] love toward better things,

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “and the fire of carnal love.”] according to: “Love her, and she will preserve you; surround her, and she will exalt you” (Prov. IV, 8).

“Husbands, love your wives,” the Apostle says (Eph. V; Col. III). But he did not stop at what he had said: “Husbands, love your wives.” Rather, knowing that the love of husbands even for their own wives can be dishonorable, and knowing that there is a form of love pleasing to God,

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript has the opposite sense: “knowing that there is a form of love that is not pleasing to God,” namely, dishonorable love.]

he taught how husbands ought to love their wives, adding: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church.” These things we have said in the preface to what is to be discussed later.

Since the friends of the bridegroom had promised the bride that, while the king was resting in his reclining place—for, while resting, he slept like a lion and a lion’s cub (Gen. XLIX, 9)—they would make likenesses of gold and silver until he rose, although they did not possess gold as the bridegroom did, the bride responds to this, and, in a certain sense, understanding the dispensation of the Passion, answers what she had heard: “We shall make likenesses of gold for you, with marks of silver, while the king is resting in his reclining place.” She says:

“My nard gave forth its fragrance. A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; he will dwell between my breasts” (Song I, 11–12).

How, then, shall we fit to it [Al.: to it, that which precedes] what precedes—“while the king is resting in his reclining place”—with what follows: “My nard gave forth its fragrance”?

The Gospel says that a woman came with an alabaster flask of costly genuine nard—not that sinful woman, but the holy woman about whom I am now speaking.

[Note: Recall what we noted above in the middle of the first homily; to this may be added Victor of Antioch’s testimony concerning Origen’s view on this matter in his Commentary on Mark XIV: “Origen says that the woman who poured perfume over Jesus’ head in Matthew and Mark, at the house of Simon the leper, was one woman; and that another was the woman who, when she was a sinner in the city, entered the Pharisee’s house, washed his feet with her tears, and anointed them with perfume.”]

For I know that Luke speaks of a sinful woman, whereas Matthew, John, and Mark do not speak of a sinful woman (Luke VII; Matt. XXVIII; John XI and XII; Mark). Thus it was not that sinful woman who came, but the holy one, whose name John also inserted. For it was Mary who had an alabaster flask of costly genuine nard, and she poured it over Jesus’ head.

Then, when they were indignant about this—not all the disciples, but Judas alone—saying, “This could have been sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor” (Matt. XXVI, 9; Mark XIV, 5 and following), the Teacher and Savior replied:

“You always have [Al.: will have] the poor with you, but me you will not always have. For she has anticipated the day of my burial by doing this. Therefore, wherever this Gospel is preached, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

In the figure of this woman, who is now speaking—“My nard gave forth its fragrance”—she poured perfume over the Lord’s head. You too, therefore, take up nard, so that, after you have perfumed Jesus’ head with its sweet fragrance, you may boldly [Al.: boldly utter] say: “My nard gave forth its fragrance,” and hear Jesus answer in return: “Wherever this Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.”

[Note: We read this from the Cistercian manuscript. In Martianus the earlier reading had an awkward sense: “You too, make it known among all nations as it is preached.” In the Reginensis manuscript the wording is somewhat more harmonious: “in memory of her, your deed also being preached among all nations.”]

Your deed also will be proclaimed among all nations.

When will you do this? If you become like the Apostle and say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (II Cor. II, 15). Your good works are nard. But if you sin, your sins will exhale a foul odor. For the penitent says: “My wounds have become foul and corrupt because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII, 6).

The Holy Spirit is not now proposing to speak about the nard that is visible to our eyes, nor does the Evangelist write about such perfume; rather, the subject is spiritual nard—the nard that gave forth its fragrance.

A bundle of stacte—that is, drops, or 518 droplets—my cousin is to me. We read of a drop of perfume, cassia, and galbanum [Al. galbani, “of galbanum”] in Exodus (chapter 30), made at the Lord’s command into incense, that is, into priestly chrism. If, then, you see my Savior descending to earthly or humble things, you will see how, by great power and divine majesty, a small drop has flowed down to us. Of this drop the Prophet also sang, saying: “And from the drop of this people Jacob shall be gathered, he shall surely be gathered” (Micah 2:11–12).

And just as, according to another interpretation, the stone was cut from the mountain without hands (Daniel 2), so too was our Savior’s coming in the flesh [Note: From this Origenian opinion Vigilantius produced a monstrous blasphemy, for which Jerome reproached him in Letter 62 of our recension, no. 4: “Among the other blasphemies which you uttered with sacrilegious mouth, you dared to say that the mountain from which, in Daniel, the stone was cut without hands was the devil, and the stone Christ—who, because he assumed a body from Adam, who had previously been joined to the devil through vices, was born of a Virgin so that he might separate man from the mountain, that is, from the devil.”] For the whole mountain did not descend to the earth, nor could human frailty contain the magnitude of the entire mountain; rather, the stone from the mountain—the stone of stumbling and rock of offense—descended into the world (Isaiah 8 and 28; 1 Peter 2). Thus, according to another interpretation, it is called a drop.

For it was necessary that, since all the nations are reckoned as a drop from a bucket (Isaiah 40:15) [Note: Read *is* in the text in place of *his*, as Victorius had previously observed.], he who was made all things for the salvation of all should also become a drop in order to free them. For what did he not become for our salvation? We are empty, and he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2; 1 Corinthians 1). We are a foolish and senseless people, and he became “the foolishness of preaching,” so that what is foolish of God might become wiser than men. We are weak (ibid.), and what is weak of God became stronger than men.

Since, therefore, all the nations have been reckoned as a drop from a bucket and as a moment [Note: Martianaeus corruptly reads *ut monumentum staterae*, “as a monument of a balance.”] of a balance, for this reason he became a drop, so that through him fragrance might proceed from our garments, according to the words: “Myrrh, and drop, and cassia are from your garments, from ivory houses, by which the daughters of kings have made you glad in your honor” (Psalm 44), which in the forty-fourth psalm are spoken to the bride.

A bundle of stacte, my cousin is to me. Let us consider what the Church means by the name “cousin,” for she speaks thus of her cousin; we are gathered from the nations. Our Savior is the son of her sister, that is, of the Synagogue. For there are two sisters, the Church and the Synagogue; therefore the Savior, as we have said, the son of his sister the Synagogue, the husband of the Church, the bridegroom of the Church, is the cousin of his bride:

“A bundle of stacte, my cousin is to me; he shall dwell in the midst of my breasts.”

Who is so blessed as to have a guest in the ruling faculty [ἡγεμονικῷ] of the heart, in the midst of his breasts, in his bosom—the word of God? Such is what is sung: “He shall dwell in the midst of my breasts.” If your breasts have not been broken, the divine word will dwell in their midst. It was fitting in a nuptial song that breasts should be named rather than the chest. And it is clear why, in explaining the words “He shall dwell in the midst of my breasts,” the phrase was adopted: “If your breasts have not been broken, the divine word shall dwell in the midst of your breasts.”

Why did I say, “If your breasts have not been broken”? From Ezekiel. In the passage where Jerusalem is rebuked by the Lord’s voice, among other things he says to her: “Your breasts were broken in Egypt” (Ezekiel 25). The breasts of chaste women are not broken; rather, the breasts of prostitutes are wrinkled with hanging flesh. The breasts of modest women are erect and swollen with virginal strength [Al. rubore, “redness”]. They receive the bridegroom’s word and say: “He shall dwell in the midst of my breasts.”

## “A cluster of Cyprus, my cousin is to me”

The beginning of the utterance is in the word, and the beginning of Cyprus—that is, of flowering—is in the bud; hence he says: “A cluster of Cyprus,” that is, of flowering, “my cousin is to me.”

The cluster of Cyprus is not for everyone, but for those who are worthy of its flower. For others the grape is variegated; but to this one alone—she who is black and beautiful—it displays itself in the loveliness of its flower.

“A cluster of Cyprus, my cousin is to me.” He does not simply say, “A cluster of Cyprus is my cousin,” but adds “to me,” to show that he is not a cluster of Cyprus for everyone.

Let us see, then, in what regions this cluster belongs to the bride. “In the vineyards of Engaddi,” which is interpreted as “the eye of temptation.” In the vineyards, therefore, of the eye of temptation: “A cluster of Cyprus, my cousin is to me.”

The eye of temptation belongs to the present. For we remain in temptation in this world, and “human life upon earth is temptation” (Job 7). While we are in this light, we are in the vineyards of Engaddi. But if afterward we should deserve to be transplanted, our husbandman will transfer us. Do not doubt that you can be transferred from the vineyards of Engaddi to better places. Our husbandman has already become practiced through continual meditation in transplanting the vineyard. For you transplanted a vineyard from Egypt, drove out the nations, and planted it. “Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God” [Al. Libani, “of Lebanon”].

These things which we have expounded the bride has spoken of the bridegroom, signifying her love and the lodging of the coming bridegroom—how the coming bridegroom dwells in the midst of her breasts and in the secret place of her heart [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “and the bridegroom coming dwells in the secret place of her heart,” without the hidden clause].

Again the bridegroom’s speech is directed to her, and he says:

“Behold, you are beautiful, my companion; behold, you are beautiful, your eyes are like doves” [Note: The old edition reads: “your eyes are like doves,” etc. Together with the Cistercian manuscript: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved.”]

She says this to the bridegroom: “Behold, my cousin is beautiful”; she does not add, “and my companion.” But when he speaks to her, he says: “Behold, you are beautiful,” and adds, “my companion.”

Why does she not say, “Behold, he is beautiful, my companion to me,” but only, “Behold, he is beautiful”? Why does he not say merely, “You are beautiful,” but “You are beautiful, my companion”?

If the bride is far from the bridegroom, she is not beautiful; she becomes beautiful when she is joined to the word of God. And rightly she is now taught by the bridegroom to be near and not to withdraw from his side.

“Behold, you are beautiful, my companion; behold, you are beautiful.” You begin to be beautiful because you are near me. But after you have begun to be beautiful, even without the addition “my companion,” you are simply beautiful.

“Behold, you are beautiful, my companion; behold, you are beautiful.”

Let us examine another praise of the beautiful one [Note: Victorius maintains that, on the evidence of the Brescia manuscripts, *of the bride* should be restored in place of *of the beautiful one*], so that we too may strive to become brides:

“Your eyes are like doves.”

Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matthew 5); he does not have dove’s eyes. If someone does not have dove’s eyes, he enters the house of his brother in misery, not observing what is commanded in Proverbs: “Do not enter the house of your brother in misery” (Proverbs 27:10).

(In place of the Septuagint’s “in misery,” Aquila, expressing the Hebrew truth, used ἄγροικον [*agroikon*]. [Note: Our manuscripts and the old edition add “that is, foolish,” though the word ἄγροικος does not sound at all similar to it; it means “rustic” or “uncivilized.” I have considerable doubt about the Greek word itself being correct: it seems to depart farther from the Hebrew truth than to adhere closely to it.])

But whoever has dove’s eyes sees what is right and obtains mercy. For whoever sees what is right will receive mercy. And who sees what is right except one who looks with chaste vision and pure eyes?

Do not therefore understand these words only of the eyes of the flesh, although it is not unprofitable to understand them also of these. Rather, enter into the inner regions of your heart and seek with your mind other eyes, which are also enlightened by God’s commandment: “The commandment of God enlightens the eyes.” Strive, labor, contend to understand spiritually all that has been said, and similar things from the Spirit—who descended in the form of a dove—and to hear: “Your eyes are like doves.” [Note: From the same manuscripts we read, with a more fitting sense, “and similar things from the Spirit, who …” in place of the hitherto printed “and things similar to the Spirit, who …”.]

If you understand the Law spiritually, your eyes are like doves. If you understand the Gospel as the Gospel wishes to be understood and preached, you see Jesus healing every sickness and infirmity—not only at the time when these things took place bodily, but healing them even today [Al. *meditatum et meditantem*, “having reflected and reflecting”]; and not merely descending then to human beings, but descending even today and being present. For he says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Your eyes are like doves:

“Behold, you are beautiful, my companion; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are like doves.”

Hearing these praises of herself, the bride in turn gives praise to the bridegroom—not as though by her proclamation she were giving him something he does not possess, but, understanding his beauty and contemplating it, she says:

“Behold, my cousin is beautiful”—indeed, beautiful [Al. pulchre, “beautifully”].

“Our bed is shady.”

I seek the bed on which the bridegroom rests with the bride, and, unless I am mistaken, it is the human body. For that paralytic in the Gospel who lay on a bed and was ordered by the Savior’s voice, before he was healed, to rise, take up his pallet, and go to his house (Mark 2), lay upon the weak body of his limbs, which afterward was strengthened by the power of God.

Thus I understand: “Take up your pallet and go to your house.” For the Son of God had not descended from the heavens to earthly things for this purpose, that he might give orders about beds and not permit the one rising from his sickness to depart without a bed. “Take up,” he says, “your pallet and go to your house.”

And you, therefore, healed by the Savior, take up your pallet and go to your house [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “and when the bridegroom comes to you with the bride.” The old edition reads: “to you as a bride,” etc.], so that, when the bridegroom comes to you as a bride and reclines with you in it, you may say:

“Behold, my cousin is beautiful” [Note: I suspect that “bridegroom” resulted from a scriptural abbreviation for “beautiful,” which I would prefer to restore.], indeed beautiful.

“Our reclining place is shady.”

Behold, my cousin is beautiful; he is both beautiful and shady. “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Psalm 120).

## “The beams of our houses are cedars”

These are the words of a multitude. It seems to me that the men who are with the bridegroom say these things; of them the preceding discussion spoke. Their houses are woven with cedar beams [Note: The manuscripts read this way. Previously the text had: “houses with cedar beams,” etc.] and roofed with cypresses.

For in place of stybe [Note: Victorius corrects this to *stoebe*. The passage alludes to Isaiah 55: in the Greek, “and instead of the stoebe shall rise the cypress, and instead of the conyza shall rise the myrtle.” Our text reads: “Instead of the reed shall rise the fir, and instead of the nettle the myrtle shall grow.” Stoebe is a plant also called *phleos*, discussed by Pliny and Dioscorides, whom Victorius cites.] the cypress rises, and in place of conyza the myrtle rises.

Therefore, investigating the nature of these woods, discovering both the incorruptible cedar and the cypress of most excellent fragrance, labor also to roof your house in such a way that it may likewise be said of you:

“The beams of our houses are cedars, and our rafters are cypresses.”

After this the bridegroom speaks:

## “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys”

For my sake, who was in the valley, he descended into the valley; and, coming into the valley, he becomes a lily. In place of the tree of life planted in the paradise of God, he became the flower of the whole field—that is, of the whole world and of the entire earth. For what can be the flower of the world in such a way as the name of Christ? “Your name is perfume poured out.”

Alternatively [Note: The editions print: “Alternatively, the same thing is said,” contrary to the manuscripts.] these words are spoken by him:

“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.”

These things he has said about himself. Then, praising the bride, he says:

“As a lily among thorns, so is my companion among the daughters.”

Just as a lily cannot be compared with the thorns among which it continually arises, so my companion, above all the daughters, is a lily among thorns.

Hearing this, the bride returns praise to the bridegroom; and, sensing his sweetness as well, she bursts into a voice of praise. For although the fragrance of perfumes breathes sweetly and caresses the sense with its scent, it is not of such a kind as to be pleasant to eat. There is something, however, which is excellent both in taste and in fragrance: it delights the throat with sweetness and soothes the breath with its scent. Such is the apple; its nature is such that it possesses both qualities in itself.

Therefore, wishing to praise not only the goodwill of his speech but also its sweetness, the bride says:

## “As an apple among the trees of the forest, so is my cousin among the sons”

All woods, all trees [Note: The old edition reads: “All the trees of the forests”], are considered unfruitful in comparison with the word of God. Compared with Christ, everything you might name is a woodland, and all things are fruitless. For what can be called fruitful in comparison with him? Even the trees that seemed to bend beneath their fruits have been shown to be fruitless in comparison with his coming.

Therefore: “As an apple among the trees of the forest, so is my cousin among the sons.”

“Under his shadow I desired and sat.”

How beautifully she does not say, “Under his shadow I desire,” but “I desired”; and not “I sit,” but “I sat.” For at the beginning we cannot compare with him a word proper to ourselves; rather, at the beginning, so to speak, we enjoy a certain shadow of his majesty.

Hence it is also read in the Prophets: “The breath of our face is Christ the Lord, to whom we said: Under his shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lamentations 4:20); and we pass from shadow to another shadow [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “we migrate to his shadow.”]

“For those who sat in the region and shadow of death, light has risen” (Isaiah 9:2).

And we pass from the shadow of death to the shadow of life. Progresses of this kind are always such that, at the beginning, a person desires at least to stand in the shadow of the virtues.

I think that for this reason Jesus’ birth also began from a shadow and ended not in a shadow but in truth. “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

Christ’s birth took its beginning from a shadow. But not only in Mary did his birth begin from his shadow; in you also, if you are worthy, the word of God is born [Note: Again, the old edition reads, “if he has deigned”; and the Cistercian manuscript immediately adds, “that you may be able to receive his shadow.”]. Make yourself capable of receiving his shadow, and, when you have become worthy of the shadow, let his body, so to speak, from which the shadow arises, come to you. For “whoever is faithful in a very little will also be faithful in much” (Luke 16:10).

“Under his shadow I desired and sat.”

You see that she did not always remain in the shadow, but passed from it to better things, saying:

“And his fruit is sweet in my throat.”

“I desired,” she says, “to rest under his shadow; but after his shadow protected me, I was also filled with his fruit [Al. saturatus sum, ‘I was filled,’ masculine], and I say: ‘His fruit is sweet to my throat’” [Note: Victorius reads “to my throat,” following the Greek ἐν λάρυγγί μου, *en laryngī mou*.]

## “Bring me into the house of wine”

The bridegroom stood outside and was received by the bride; for he rested in the midst of her breasts. The young companions are not such as to deserve to have the bridegroom as their guest. He speaks to the multitude outside in parables. I fear that perhaps we are many of these young women.

“Bring me into the house of wine.” Why do I remain outside so long? “Behold, I stand before the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I will enter to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me.”

“Bring me in.”

And now the divine word says the same thing: Behold, Christ speaks: “Bring me in.” He speaks also to you catechumens: “Bring me in,” not simply into a house, but into a house of wine. Let your soul be filled with the wine of joy, with the wine of the Holy Spirit. And thus bring the bridegroom, the Word, Wisdom, and Truth, into your house.

This can also be said to those who are not yet perfect: “Bring me into the house of wine.” “Set love in order within me.”

He spoke elegantly: “Set in order.” For the love of many is disordered. What they ought to love in first place, they love in second; what in second place, they love in first; what ought to be loved in fourth place, they love in third; and again they place the third in the fourth. In many people the order of love is perverse.

But the love of the saints is ordered.

To understand what has been said—“Set love in order within me”—I wish to review some examples. The divine word wants you to love father, son, and daughter; the divine word wants you to love Christ. It does not say to you, “Do not love your children” or “Do not be joined to your parents in affection.” What does it say? Do not have disordered love. Do not love your father or mother first and me afterward; do not be held by love for your sons and daughters more than by love for me.

“Whoever loves father or mother above me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37).

Review your conscience concerning your affection for father, mother, or brother, and consider what kind of love you have for the word of God and for Jesus. Immediately you will discover that you love son and daughter more than the Word, and love your parents more than Christ [Note: The same authority says that “Jesus” should be read; the words that follow show this: “You will discover that you love son and daughter more than the Word, and love your parents more than Christ.”]

Who among us, do you think, makes such progress as to have a foremost and primary love among all the words of God, placing children in second position?

In the same way, love your wife. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but loves it as flesh. “And the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), not one spirit.

Love God also, but love him not as flesh and blood, but as spirit. For “whoever clings to God is one spirit.”

Therefore, love is ordered in the perfect. But so that an order may also be established among us after God, the first commandment is that we love our parents; the second, that we love our children; the third, that we love our household members. But if a son is bad and a household member good, let the household member be placed in the love due to a son. And thus the love of the saints will be ordered.

Our Teacher and Lord, too, when establishing commands about love in the Gospel, attached something proper to the love of each person and gave an understanding of order to those who can hear Scripture saying: “Set love in order within me.”

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, with all your soul, and with all your strength. You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Deuteronomy 6; Matthew 22; Mark 12; Luke 10).

It does not say “your neighbor with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind.”

Again he says: “Love your enemies” (Luke 6:35); he does not add “with all your heart.” The divine word is not disordered. It does not command impossible things, nor does it say, “Love your enemies as yourselves,” but only, “Love your enemies.” It is enough for them that we love them and do not hate them. Your neighbor, however, is to be loved as yourself. God is to be loved with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength.

If you understand these things and fulfill what you have understood, you have done what the bridegroom’s word commands:

“Bring me into the house of wine; set love in order within me.”

Who among us, do you think, possesses ordered love [Al. ordinator, “is an arranger of love”]?

## “Strengthen me with unguents”

One of the interpreters rendered this as οἰνανθῶν [*oinanthōn*] [Note: The old editions have οἰνανθίνων, which is by no means an objectionable reading. The Reginensis manuscript has *onesiaston* in Latin letters; Martianaeus found various forms in other manuscripts. Yet the printed reading οἰνάνθων [*oinanthōn*] is certainly preferable, as Symmachus’s version persuades us; he translated it as οἰνάνθη [*oinanthē*], although it is by no means easy to determine which interpreter Jerome means, since he does not name him. He wrote οἰνανθῶν. The oldest Corbie manuscripts read: “he placed me in the wine room.” The copy of Saint-Thierry near Reims reads: “he placed me in οἰνάον, that is, the wine cellar,” etc. Another manuscript of the Paris Navarre College, as well as the Royal manuscript, reads ΟΙΝΑΝΩΝ. In the margin the Navarre manuscript adds: οἰνέων, that is, “wine cellar,” from οἶνος, “wine.” We read οἰνανθνων in the old editions, but οἰνάνθιων is better, since οἰνάνθη is a flowering vine. Unless perhaps οἰνῶνων should be read, in accordance with the Latin interpretation of the old manuscript books. MARTIAN.]

But this is the bride who speaks:

“Support me with apples.”
