With what apples? “As an apple among the trees of the forest, so is my cousin among the sons.”

Therefore support me with his apples, because I am wounded by love. How beautiful and fitting it is to receive a wound from love!

One person has received the dart of carnal love; another has been wounded by earthly desire. But you, bare your limbs and offer yourself to a chosen dart, a beautiful dart—for God is an archer.

Hear Scripture speaking of this same dart; indeed, so that you may marvel more greatly, hear the dart itself speaking. “He made me like a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he hid me, and he said to me: It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isaiah 49:2) [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads: “he hid me in his quiver.”]

Understand what the arrow says and how it was chosen by God.

How blessed it is to be wounded by this dart! Those who were wounded by this arrow were the men who spoke with one another, saying: “Was not our heart burning within us on the way, while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

If someone is wounded by our word, if someone is wounded by the teaching of divine Scripture and can say, “I am wounded by love,” perhaps what follows also belongs to him. Why do I say “perhaps”? I bring forward a manifest statement:

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.”

The word of God possesses wisdom both in its left and in its right hand. Although it is multiple according to the variety of understanding, it is one in its underlying reality. Solomon himself taught about the left and right of wisdom, saying:

“For length of days and years of life are in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and glory” (Proverbs 3:16).

Therefore, “his left hand is under my head,” so that he may make me rest, and the bridegroom’s arm may become my pillow; let the ruling faculty [ἡγεμονικόν] of the soul recline upon the word of God.

“His left hand is under my head.”

It is not beneficial for you to have pillows followed by lamentation. It is written in Ezekiel: “Woe to those who sew pillows under every elbow” (Ezekiel 43:18). Do not sew pillows; do not seek rest for your head elsewhere. You have the bridegroom’s left hand; let it be under your head, and say:

“His left hand is under my head.”

When you have it, everything that is in the left hand is attributed to you. For you say: “In his left hand are riches and glory,” and “his right hand will embrace me.”

Let the bridegroom’s right hand embrace you entirely. For “length of days and years of life are in his right hand”; and therefore you will be of long life and many days upon the good land which the Lord your God gives you (Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 4) [Note: The same authority reads: “and many years of his days.” I think that this also alludes to the custom of the ancients of counting years on the fingers of their hands, with the right hand representing numbers exceeding one hundred. Hence Juvenal’s line: “Happy is he who counts your years on his right hand.” See what we have noted in Book 1 Against Jovinianus, no. 3.]

## “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem”

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field.”

What does the bride adjure the daughters of Jerusalem to do?

“If you raise up and awaken love.”

As long as love sleeps [Al. *dormivit*, “has slept”] in you, O daughters of Jerusalem, O young women—love which does not sleep in me, because I am wounded by love—what will you do? In you, who are many, young women and daughters of Jerusalem, the love of the bridegroom sleeps.

Therefore I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you raise up, and not only raise up but also awaken, the love that is in you.

When the Creator of the universe formed you, he implanted seeds of love in your hearts. But now, just as it is said elsewhere, “Justice slept in her” (Isaiah 1:21), so love sleeps in you. In accordance with what is also said elsewhere: “The bridegroom rested like a lion and like a lion’s cub” (Genesis 49).

The divine word still sleeps in unbelievers and in those who are doubtful in heart; it keeps watch in the saints. It sleeps in those tossed by storms, but is awakened by the voices of those who desire to be saved while the bridegroom keeps watch (Maccabees 4). As soon as he keeps watch, calm arises; immediately the masses of waves become still, the opposing spirits are rebuked, and the fury of the waves falls silent. When he sleeps, there is storm, death, and despair.

Therefore I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field. Of what field? Of that whose fragrance is like a full field, which the Lord blessed (Genesis 27:27) [Note: The words “whose fragrance” are absent from the old edition. The Reginensis manuscript reads: “which he blessed.” Some less important matters above have been corrected from the same manuscript.]

“If you raise up and awaken love, until the voice of my cousin desires it.”

Behold, he comes here, leaping over the mountains.

The Church is still speaking, exhorting the young women to prepare for the bridegroom’s coming—if he should wish to come and grant them his conversation.

While she is still speaking, the bridegroom comes. She points him out with her finger and says:

“Behold, he comes here, leaping over the mountains.”

Understand the bride—or the blessed and perfect soul [Al. *sponsae*, “of the bride”]—which sees more quickly, which more quickly contemplates the coming of the word, which perceives that wisdom and love have come to it, and says to those who do not see:

“Behold, he comes here.”

Pray that I too may be able to say: “Behold, he comes here.” For if I am able to explain the word of God, I too, in a sense, say [Al. “will say”]: “Behold, he comes here.”

Where does he come? Certainly not where there is a valley, nor where there are low places.

Where does he come? “Leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.”

If you are a mountain, the word of God leaps upon you. If you have not been able to be a mountain but are a hill, second only to a mountain, he will bound over you.

How beautiful and appropriate the words are! He leaps over the mountains because they are greater; he bounds over the hills because they are smaller. He does not bound over the mountains, nor leap over the hills.

“Behold, he comes here, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.”

## “My cousin is like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bethel”

These two animals are frequently named in Scripture, and, what is more remarkable, they are often placed together. “These are the things you shall eat,” he says, shortly afterward introducing the gazelle and the deer. In the present book also the deer and the gazelle are named together. In a certain sense these animals are related and close to one another.

The gazelle, that is, the *dorcas*, sees with extraordinary sharpness. The deer is a killer of serpents.

Who among us, do you think, is worthy and capable of fully explaining the meaning according to the dignity of the passage and its mystery? Let us pray to the Lord that he grant us understanding for opening the Scriptures [Note: The old edition, together with the Cistercian manuscript, reads: “understanding for perceiving the Scriptures”], so that we may be able to say: “How Jesus opened the Scriptures to us” (Luke 24:32).

What, then, shall we say? The *dorcas*, that is, the gazelle, according to those who discuss the nature of all animals, received its name from an innate power. Because it sees more sharply—that is, ὀξυδερκέστερον [*oxyderkesteron*, “seeing most sharply”]—it was called *dorcas*.

[Note: Before Martianaeus, the printed editions had ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀξέως δέρκειν, “from seeing sharply.” I would prefer simply ὀξυδέρκειν, “to see sharply,” as one word. Our Zeno, very elegantly, says near the beginning of his sermon *On the Commandment, Attend to Yourself*: “The doe does not run into a snare,” in place of the expression “possessing extremely sharp sight.” Thus the etymology of its name is preserved in Greek. Scaliger, however, opposes the received opinion in Book 2 of Aristotle’s *On Animals*, commentary 130, where he thinks that *dama* should be called πρόκα, as the Stagirite calls it, with Theodore agreeing in his translation. That is, ὀξυδερκέστερον. In the books previously printed, Erasmus and Marianus disastrously fabricate this Greek phrase, παρὰ τὸ ὀξέως δέρκειν. We have restored the genuine reading with the help of the oldest manuscript copies, which consistently preserve the Greek name ὀξυδερκέστερον, derived from the primitive ὀξυδερκής, “seeing sharply,” “endowed with keen eyesight,” “far-sighted.” Hence ὀξυδερκέστατος in Herodotus. MARTIAN.]

The deer, however, is the enemy and conqueror of serpents. It draws them from their caves with the breath of its nostrils; and, after overcoming the danger of their poison, it delights in feeding upon them.

Perhaps my Savior is a gazelle according to contemplation, and a deer according to works. What works are these? He himself kills serpents when he slaughters hostile powers. Therefore I shall say to him:

“You crushed the heads of dragons upon the water” (Psalm 73:13) [Note: The Reginensis manuscript and the old edition add: “You crushed [Al. broke] the heads of dragons.” We correct some minor matters above and below from the manuscripts.]

“My cousin is like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of the house of God.”

For Bethel is interpreted as “house of God.” Not all mountains are mountains of the house of God, but those which are the mountains of the Church. Other mountains are also found, raised up and rising against the knowledge of God: the mountains of the Egyptians and of the Philistines.

Do you wish to know that my cousin is like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bethel? Be an ecclesiastical mountain, a mountain of the house of God, and the bridegroom will come to you like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bethel.

She sees that the bridegroom has drawn nearer. Previously he was upon the mountains and hills; she compares him to one bounding and leaping, and, recognizing that he has afterward come to her and to the other young women, she says:

## “Behold, he is here behind our wall”

If you build a wall and make a building of God, he will come behind your wall, looking through the windows [Note: The same authority reads: “behind our wall, looking through the windows,” and shortly afterward: “through this one the bridegroom looks,” omitting the words “the bridegroom is unaware.”]

One window is one sense; through it the bridegroom looks. Another window is another sense; and through it the bridegroom gazes attentively. For through which senses does the word of God not look?

What it means to look through the windows, and how the bridegroom looks through them, the following example will teach.

Where the bridegroom does not look, there death is found ascending, as we read in Jeremiah:

“Behold, death has ascended through your windows” [Note: The same authority reads: “through our windows.”] (Jeremiah 9:21).

When you look at a woman in order to desire her, death has already ascended through your windows.

“Appearing through the lattices.”

Understand that you walk in the midst of snares and pass beneath threatening devices. Everything is full of nets; the devil has filled all things with snares.

But if the word of God comes to you and begins to appear through the lattices, saying:

“Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been set free” (Psalm 123:7). “Blessed are we [Al. you] by the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 113:15).

The bridegroom therefore appears through the lattices, making a way for you.

Jesus descended to the earth and subjected himself to the nets of the world. Seeing the great flock of human beings entangled in nets, and knowing that they could be cut through by no one other than himself, he came to the nets, assuming a human body that was held by the snares of hostile powers. He tore them apart for you [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “he tore them apart so that you might speak.”], and you will say:

“Behold, he is here behind our wall, looking through the windows, appearing through the lattices.”

When he has risen above them, he says to you:

“My cousin answers and says: ‘Rise, come, my companion. I have made a way for you; I have cut through the nets. Come thus to me, my companion.’”

Rise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove. Why does he say, “Rise”? Why, “Hasten”? I endured the fury of storms for you; I received the waves that were owed to you. “My soul became sorrowful for you, even unto death” (Matt. XVI; Mark XIV). I rose from the dead, having broken the stings of death and dissolved the bonds of hell; therefore I say to you: “Rise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove,” because, behold, winter has passed, the rain has gone away, and flowers have appeared on the earth. Rising from the dead, with the storm subdued, I restored tranquility. And because, according to the dispensation of the flesh, I grew from the Virgin by the Father’s will, and advanced in wisdom and age, flowers have appeared on the earth; the time of pruning has arrived.

[Note: Regin. manuscript: “the time of pruning is at hand.”]

Pruning is the remission of sins. For he says: “Every branch in me that remains and bears fruit, my Father cleanses, so that it may bear greater fruit” (John XV). Have fruits; and the former things in you that are fruitless [Al.: fruitful] will be removed. For the time of pruning has arrived.

The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land. It is not without reason that a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons is offered in sacrifices; for they have the same value, and it is never said separately, “only a pair of pigeons,” but “a pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons” (Lev. I, V, XII, and XIV, and Luke II). The dove is the Holy Spirit. But when the Holy Spirit speaks of great and hidden mysteries, which many cannot grasp, he is signified under the name of the turtledove—that is, under the name of the bird that always dwells on mountain ridges and the tops of trees. In valleys, however, and in matters that reach down to human beings, the dove is employed.

Finally, because the Savior deigned to assume a human being and came to the earth, and because at that time many sinners were gathered around the Jordan, the Holy Spirit does not become a turtledove but a dove.

[Note: Victor restores the reading “among us” with the help of manuscript copies.]

Among us, because of the multitude of human beings, the gentler bird dwells. The turtledove, for example, may be understood as Moses and each of the prophets who withdraw into the mountains and deserts and there receive the words of God.

[Note: In another sense, the old edition reads: “But the turtledove is understood, for example, as Moses and each of the prophets,” etc. Martianay notes that other exemplars read: “Moses and each of the prophets are to be understood.” — “But the turtledove is understood, for example,” etc. In other exemplars: “But the turtledove is understood, for example. Moses and each of the prophets are to be understood.” MARTIANAY.] Therefore, “the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.”

“The fig tree has produced its early figs.” “From the fig tree learn the parable. When its branch becomes tender and puts forth leaves, know that summer is near.” The word of God wishes to announce to us that, after winter and after storms, the harvest of souls has drawn near, and says:

“The fig tree has produced its early figs; the vines are flowering and have given their fragrance.” If the vines are already bursting into flower, the time will come and there will be grapes. “Rise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove.” These matters that we have explained above are spoken by the bridegroom—not while the young women are listening, but while the bride alone is listening.

[Note: The Regin. manuscript wrongly reads: “The bride, while the young women are not listening and the bride alone is hearing, speaks.”]

But we also wish now to hear the speech of the one who is speaking to the bride.

“Rise, come, my near one, my dove, and come, my dove, into the shelter of the rock.” Moses too is placed under the shelter of the rock, so that he may see the back parts of God under the shelter of the wall or rampart (Exod. XXXIII). First come to what is in front of the wall; afterward you will be able to enter where the wall of the rock is.

“Show me your face.” Similar words are spoken to the bride down to the present day. For she did not yet have the confidence to contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face. But because she is now adorned and prepared, it is said to her: “Show me your face.” For her voice was not yet so sweet that she deserved to be told: “Make me hear your voice.” When, then, did she learn to speak? “Be silent and hear, Israel”; and you will know [Al.: know] what the Lord says. And her voice became sweet to the bridegroom, according to the prophetic saying: “May my petition be sweet to him.” Then the bridegroom says to her: “Make me hear your voice, because your voice is sweet” (Song II, 14).

If you open your mouth to the Word of God, the bridegroom will say to you: “Your voice is sweet; your appearance is beautiful.” Therefore, rising together, let us beseech the Lord that we may be made worthy of the speech of the bridegroom, the wisdom of Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: Vallarsius adds from other editions: “Here ends Origen’s Exposition of the Song of Songs, which Blessed Jerome translated from Greek into Latin. Amen.” EDIT.]

# APPENDIX TO VOLUME III OF THE WORKS OF SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS IN THE VALLARSIAN EDITION

Part One.

In which the Greek interpretations of the Book of Hebrew Names are reviewed.

[Col. 1143]

## NOTICE

Martianay found in the Royal Library at Paris a manuscript copy of the following miscellany of Greek words, Λέξεις, and was the first to publish it; he also discussed at length its rarity and excellence. Indeed, he performed a worthwhile service by appending these fragments of the ancient Greeks to Jerome’s book on the interpretation of Hebrew names, especially the two complete lexica of Origen. For if one may now examine the meanings of the words according to the understanding of those authors, Jerome, when preparing his translation of that book, often tested his own fidelity against their judgment.

Yet so many serious defects had settled into that little Greek copyist’s exemplar—transpositions, lacunae, and other errors—that they often caused difficulty for the Benedictine editor, who was forced to supply slight conjectures from the proximity of the letters. In fact, unless they could be corrected with the help of another manuscript, the fragments seemed to possess little usefulness for explaining those etymologies and comparing them with Jerome’s interpretation.

It was granted to me, while diligently examining the Vatican shelves, to make use of better fortune, which had been my earnest wish: I encountered a parchment exemplar not merely older, or only somewhat more accurate, but far superior. It presents these very glosses much more correctly and appends many other sacred names that had not yet appeared in print. Finally, many indications reveal it to be the archetype from which the Royal manuscript was copied, although the latter reproduces it badly in many places, as commonly happens through a copyist’s ignorance.

This is also the very codex that contains Eusebius’ book Περὶ τῶν Τοπικῶν ὀνομάτων, that is, *On the Names of Places in Palestine*, whose extraordinary rarity we discussed in the Preface. It once belonged to the celebrated Cardinal Sirlet, as he himself testified in his own hand on the blank page at the beginning. It is now designated in the Vatican Library as no. 1450.

From this new sort of autograph, therefore, I reproduce these little books in their entirety, and I repeatedly bring and correct the Latin interpretation that Martianay had prepared against this standard. I immediately append his annotations—not, as was done in the other books and will continually be done hereafter, by relegating them to the end of the volume—for, since they are exceedingly numerous and at times more thorough than the others, I have learned through experience that, if they were sent farther away, their encounter with those written on Jerome’s similarly titled book could confuse good readers.

I add my own notes, marked with Saracen characters. If these should perhaps seem fewer than the character and obscurity of these names require, know that I attempt nothing beyond the testimony of the manuscripts and that I do not devote equal labor to spurious books and genuine ones. Finally, let the slenderness of our labor deprive no diligence of the opportunity to restore what is lacking or to replace readings with better ones, should they be discovered.

[Col. 1145]

From Royal manuscripts 772, or 2282, first edited by Martianay; much more accurately from Vatican manuscript 1450; rendered into Latin and compared with Jerome’s interpretation. (C)

## Vatican Codex

Interpretation of the Hebrew Names contained in divinely inspired Scripture.

[Col. 1145]

Adam: testimony, or earth-born, or human being, or dust, or blood, or fleshly earth, or red.

[Note: The words “or dust,” namely, “or ground,” were absent from the Royal manuscript, and we supplied them from the Vatican. See the Third Fragment below. Moreover, the interpretation of αἷμα, “blood,” is also supported by Paula and Eustochium, *Letter* among Jerome’s works 46: “The second Adam, that is, the Blood of Christ dripping from the cross,” etc.]

Abel: from God.

[Note: We warn the attentive reader that the Greek manuscript contains many errors and omissions, frequently erring in accents and breathings, in the separation of words, or in the spelling of syllables. For example, it wrote the name Abel with an acute accent on the first syllable, Ἄβελ; and, worse, it so confused its etymology with the name Cain: “Ἄβελ: ἀπὸ Θεοῦ Καΐν κτῆμα ἢ ξυλοπία.” The reading and the interpretation of Cain’s name are here corrupted in more than one way. I did not hesitate to supply the interpretation from another Fragment, because there we clearly read ζηλοτυπία.

As for why the Greeks interpret Abel as ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ, “from God” or “by God,” I can suggest no other reason than the writings of Philo the Jew. From him they learned that Abel represents the pious doctrine descending from God, the giver of all good things, and hence he was called ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ. The same writers also interpret him as one who refers everything to God; they learned such etymologies—or rather, symbolic meanings—from Philo.

This conjecture is especially supported by two passages of the same author. In *On the Sacrifices of Abel and Cain*, p. 137, we read expressly: ὁ τὰ ἄριστα ἐπὶ τὸν θεὸν ἀναφέρων Ἄβελ, ποιμὴν κέκληται: “Abel, who refers whatever is best to God, is called a shepherd.” The same may be read in *That the Worse Is Wont to Attack the Better*, p. 161: ὁ μὲν γὰρ Ἄβελ ἀναφέρων ἐπὶ θεὸν πάντα, φιλόθεον δόγμα: “For Abel, who refers everything to God, is a pious doctrine.”

Supported by the same authority, they commonly write Abel’s name before Cain’s, although Cain was the elder, because Philo taught that virtue and piety precede vices in *On the Sacrifices of Abel and Cain*, p. 132.]

Cain: possession, or jealousy.

### FROM SHEM

Abraham: father of mercies.

Abram: passer-by.

[Note: I would prefer to restore Ἔβερ, Eber, which properly means “passer-by,” in place of Ἀβράμ, to which this etymology scarcely fits. Jerome: “Eber, passer-by.”]

Reuben: Spirit of God.

[Note: Do not be surprised that the Greeks interpret Reuben as “Spirit of God,” since they wrote the name corruptly as Ῥουβήλ, Rubel, as is established below from Origen’s Lexicon.]

Simeon: obeying.

Levi: “he will remember me.”

[Note: Levi does not mean “he will remember me,” but “he will adhere to me,” from the root *lava*, “he adhered.” I think the manuscript is corrupt and that, in place of μνησθήσει, one should read μνηστεύσει, from the verb μνηστεύω, “I seek marriage,” which fits Leah’s words very well after she had brought forth her son Levi. For, as Jerome testifies, the ancient interpreters and teachers of the Hebrews drew this meaning from the Hebrew. Consult the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.]

[Note: The Vatican has μισθός, “reward,” or “a reward for me.”]

Judah: confessor.

Issachar: reward.

Zebulun: gift.

Dan: judgment.

Naphtali: breadth.

Gad: place of testing.

Asher: riches, or blessed.

[Note: Concerning this etymology of the name Asher, Jerome warned us as follows: “Riches,” that is, πλοῦτος, was wrongly added, since the etymology of the name Asher is revealed by the authority of Scripture, etc. Asher therefore means not “riches” but “blessed,” etc.]

Joseph: removal of reproach.

Benjamin: child of sorrow.

Rebecca: joy.

Rachel: sheep.

Climax: word of God.

[Note: The name Κλίμαξ, together with the following three—Μαρσίππιον, Ὀπηλός, and Πλίνθω—does not belong at all to the Hebrew language. They are purely Greek expressions, which may have been used proverbially among ordinary Greeks according to the sense attached to each word. Thus the word of God is metaphorically Κλίμαξ, that is, “ladder,” Genesis XXVIII, 12, by which human beings ascend to God.

Μαρσίππιον, or *marsupium*, “purse,” signifies agreement in Proverbs I, 14, according to the proverb “all things obey money.” Finally, the other two words condemn vices of intemperance, which were typologically prefigured in the works of clay and brick by which the Egyptians once oppressed the Hebrews in servitude, Exodus I, 14.

I should not omit that Μαρσίππιον is interpreted differently on folio 41 of the Royal manuscript: Μαρσίππιον, βαλάντιον, that is, “marsupium,” a purse or money-bag.]

Sepphora: joy and beauty.

Marsippion: obedience.

Opelos: gluttony.

Plintho: fornication.

Bethlehem: house of life, or house of the holy one, or house of bread.

[Note: Bethlehem, according to the proper character of the Hebrew language, means “house of bread.” The other etymologies were joined by the Greeks because the Lord Christ was born at Bethlehem.

It is nevertheless a matter of considerable wonder why Jerome omitted the name Bethlehem from his book on Hebrew Names, although it is read in nearly all the volumes of the Old and New Testaments. Perhaps the reason is what he himself indicates in *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*: “Ephrathah and Bethlehem,” he says, “are names of one city, with a similar interpretation.” For it is translated as “fruitful” and as “house of bread,” because of that bread which he says descended from heaven.

He therefore does not list the name Bethlehem because he interprets Ephrathah more frequently.]

Bethphage: house of encounter.

Bethany: house of glory.

Beersheba: daughter of the strong one.

Sarah: one who is ruled.

Sarra: ruling.

[Note: Thus, with the double ρ, the Vatican reads Σάρρα. See what we noted in the *Questions on Genesis*, p. 331.]

Deborah: bee.

[Note: The Royal manuscript corruptly reads ἔλισσα, from which Martianay translated “gathering” or “constricting.” The Vatican corrects this to μέλισσα, “bee.”]

[Note: Opposite the name Moses, in larger letters, the Vatican contains the following words from Hebrews XI, 23: γεννηθεὶς ἐκρύβη τρίμηνον, that is, “having been born, he was hidden for three months.” Martianay placed these words from the Royal manuscript before the subsequent heading “Names of the Prophets,” and complains in the following annotation that they have been confused and removed from their proper place.]

Moses: mind, or pious, or inquiry of the Lord.

[Note: The Greeks borrowed the etymologies or interpretations of Moses’ name from Philo’s works; they do not fit the name according to the actual letters or the character of the Hebrew language.

Thus Moses is called “mind” by Philo in *On the Change of Names*, p. 1077: Μωσὴς μέν ἐστι νοῦς ὁ καθαρώτατος, Ἀαρὼν δὲ λόγος αὐτοῦ: “Moses is the purest mind, while Aaron is his word.” He is likewise often called “pious” by the same Philo, and “one who beholds God” in the work just cited, p. 1045, since he searched through everything in all things: πάντα διὰ πάντων ἐρευνήσας.

The same judgment applies to many other names that are known to have been interpreted not according to the proper character of the language but according to symbolic meanings.]

Aaron: seeing a vision.

Gideon: testing injustice.

[Note: Vatican: “injustice.”]

[Col. 1149]

[Note: This passage has been especially corrupted by the copyist, who completely confused the words of Hebrews XI, 23, γεννηθεὶς ἐκρύβη τρίμηνον, that is, “having been born, he was hidden for three months,” with the heading attached to the names of the prophets, and wrote them corruptly as follows: γεννηθῆς ἐκρύβη τρίμηνον, ὄνομα προφητῶν, “having been born, he was hidden for three months, name of the prophets.” As written, this cannot be explained by any method or in any meaningful sense.

As a result, another more recent and equally ignorant copyist was led into the error of supposing that the genealogy of the prophet Hosea and the others had been recorded. Accordingly, the following words were written by him in the margin, with a transverse line between the words Hosea and Amos:

“Who is the prophet, son of Barachiah, and the son of the forerunner, son of Barach, of the tribe of Levi; and again Ezra, also Salathiel, the priest, father of Zerubbabel, who was the son of Jeconiah. Nebuchadnezzar the king sent him after the law to those settled in Samaria, the nations; and they also hid their idols. There is also another Ezra.”

I consider this scholion so absurd and false that it is unworthy of Latin translation. But I wish to warn the reader that the words of the Epistle to the Hebrews should be written with the name of Moses, or opposite it; for it was written concerning Moses that, after being born, he was hidden for three months.]

## NAMES OF THE PROPHETS

Hosea: overshadowing, or guardian.

Amos: strong, or faithful, or one who tears away the people.

[Note: The names corrupted in the Greek manuscript can easily be recognized by comparison with those read in Jerome in the opposite column—for example, Ὠμῶς, “Omos,” here for Amos, and Ambacum for Habakkuk. We would therefore needlessly recall similar corruptions from this point onward, since, as we have said, they are clear from comparison with Jerome.]

[Note: Martianay, from the Royal manuscript, wrongly reads Ὠμώς, “Omos.” In the Vatican, the same gloss is added in the margin and is also reproduced by Martianay. Correct his errors in transcription as follows: read ὅτι καὶ ὁ προφήτης instead of ὅ τις ὁ; Ἰεχονίου instead of Ἰχονίου; and μετὰ τοῦ νόμου instead of τὸν νόμον.]

Micah: “Who is this king?”

Joel: beloved of God, and firstfruits of God.

[Note: We supplied from the Vatican the words καὶ ἀπαρχὴ Θεοῦ, “and firstfruits of God,” and accordingly added them to the Latin.]

Obadiah: serving the Lord.

Jonah: dove.

Nahum: consolation.

[Note: The manuscript had Ναόμ, and “Naom,” incorrectly.]

Habakkuk: father who raises up.

Zephaniah: understanding him.

Haggai: celebrating a feast.

Zechariah: victorious lion.

Malachi: angel, or salvation of the Lord.

Isaiah: salvation of the Lord.

Jeremiah: exalted of the Lord.

Baruch: blessing, or “bless.”

Ezekiel: strength of God.

Daniel: his strong judgment.

Seraphim: spirit of resurrection, or it represents those who set on fire, that is, those who warm.

[Note: Seraphim properly means “those who set on fire” or “burning ones,” from the verb *saraph*, “he burned” and “set on fire.” Therefore, when they are called spirits of station or resurrection, this refers more to their function. The Seraphim stood above the one mentioned in Isaiah VI, 2, rather than this being the etymology of the name.]

Cherubim: multiplied knowledge, or wings, or outpouring of wisdom.

[Note: Because Cherubim are customarily represented as entirely winged, with patterned or variegated painting, they are called “wings” by the Greeks, while among Latins they are associated with variegated painting.]

Amen: “I have believed that it is truly so.”

[Note: Both manuscripts read this way; therefore I do not agree with Clericus, who conjectures that one should read πεπιστευμένως ἀληθῶς, “believed truly,” as Suidas reads it. Below we correct some minor matters according to the Vatican exemplar.]

Alleluia: “Praise the one who is,” or the Lord.

Michael: commander of the army from God.

Gabriel: young man of God.

Uriel: fire of God.

Raphael: Spirit of God.

[Note: The name of the angel Raphael was added by Greek writers, taken from the Book of Tobit; neither Philo nor Jerome lists its name in the little work on Hebrew Names. Concerning the preceding name, Uriel, it should also be noted that it is the name of an angel among the rabbis and ancient heretics. For this reason Jerome does not interpret it as an angel’s name, but because several human beings in sacred Scripture bore that name.]

[Col. 1151]

Eliezer: help of God.

Galilee: revelation.

Jeconiah: pure.

## NAMES OF THE TWELVE APOSTLES
Πέτρος: one who explains, or one who recognizes. Paul: marvelous, or an elect counselor. Matthew: granted. Matthias: gift of God. Mark: exalted by command. Luke: himself raising up. John: “he has shown favor to Io,” that is, “the grace of God.” [Note: [Col. 1151B] In the Vatican manuscript, immediately after the word Ἰῶ, the name Ἰωάννης is repeated, so that one understands it not to be an abbreviated writing of the same name, but rather a word belonging to the preceding interpretation: ἐχαρίσατο Ἰῶ, “he has shown favor to Io.” For I think that Ἰῶ itself is Ἰαῶ, “God,” a name very frequently used by the Greeks, especially by Origen. It is the Hebrew [unreadable term] which the Samaritans pronounce Ἰαβαὶ, Eusebius Ἰευνὼ, and Theodoret ἀϊὰ (perhaps ἰαϊὰ). It was customary for Adamantius to interpret Hebrew names composed of letters through Ιαὼ. Thus, for example, he translates μετεωρισμὸν Ἰαὼ as “the exaltation of Iao”; and nothing is therefore more likely here than that Ἰῶ, or Ἰαῶ, is intended. See what we noted concerning the name Joanna in Jerome, p. 91.] Andrew: a beautiful strength, or one who answers. James son of Alphaeus: the supplanting of the learning of life. James: one who supplants labor. Philip: mouth of hands, or mouth of a lamp. Bartholomew: son of one who hangs waters. Thomas: abyss, or twin. Ananias: glorifying. Azariah: seeing a lion. Mishael: how [Note: [Col. 1151A] I think that ἀνιστᾷ, “may he rise again,” or something similar, should preferably be read in the Greek. We have restored Jerome’s Latin according to the evidence of the manuscripts of the monasteries of Gemeticum, Fécamp, Saint-Evroul of Ouche, and Saint-Martin of Sées; all preserve the genuine reading, “which is the salvation of God.” The printed editions, however, together with the manuscripts of the Royal Library, two Colbertine manuscripts, and several others, corruptly read “which is the marsh of the Lord.” Nor can the meaning “marsh” be derived from the name Misael, but rather that of “salvation”; yet the name is to be understood figuratively, as formed from , mi, that is, “which,” , jes, “is,” jasa, “he saved,” and , el, “God.”] does God raise up? [Note: [Col. 1152B] The Vatican manuscript corrects it in this way, just as Martianay had conjectured, though he retained ἀνιστὰ from the Royal manuscript and translated it into Latin as “he rose again,” incorrectly. See our notes on this name in Jerome.] Ephod: manifestation and truth. [Note: [Col. 1151A] There is no etymology of the name Ephod in the Greek or in our Latin interpretation. For Ephod does not mean “manifestation” or “truth”; rather, on the Breastpiece of Judgment it was placed, or written: haurim vehattumim, that is, “doctrine and truth,” Exodus 28:30. Hence the Greeks, who were inexperienced in the Hebrew language, thought that Ephod meant “manifestation and truth.”] Jesus: savior. [Note: [Col. 1152A] Read ἀνυόμενος, from ἀνύομαι, that is, “I am brought to completion.” Jesus is therefore called in Latin “Savior”; the word “perfect” has been added by the Greeks.] being perfected. Elihu: of the mighty, authoritative one. [Note: [Col. 1152A] Αὐθέντης is one who possesses the power to do anything according to his own will and authority. In this sense the Lord, God of all, is truly called αὐθέντης, or ἰσχυρὸς αὐθέντης, as if one were to say “the unconquerable and omnipotent one.”] Elisha: strength of God. [Note: [Col. 1152A] The name Zacchaeus, according to Syriac usage, means “just,” that is, “pure,” and “victorious.” Thus tizke in Psalm 50 is understood as “may you be pure,” or “may you conquer.”] Zacchaeus: victor. Kadesh: sanctification. Kaddōn: holy. Zoar: humiliation. [Note: [Col. 1152A] According to the proper meaning of the Hebrew language, we cannot interpret Sion as “house of the spirit.” These things must therefore be understood symbolically, because Mount Sion is a type of the Church of Christ, which has the Holy Spirit dwelling in it and presiding over it.] Zion: watchtower, or house of the spirit. [Col. 1153] Aaron: mountain of strength. Jerusalem: vision of peace. Babylon: confusion. Bashan: shame. Og [Note: [Col. 1153B] Martianay wrongly substituted the name Ὢν, “On,” for Ὤγ, “Og”; and in Jerome’s corresponding list he likewise printed On, “labor” or “pain.” Yet not only the authority of the Vatican manuscript, but also the interpretation of this name, διάφραξις, “barrier” or “enclosure,” proves that the name of King Og is intended here. The etymology of interruption or enclosure fits him readily according to the Greek sense, but not at all the word On, from which nothing similar can be extracted. Origen says in Homily 13 on Numbers: “Og is interpreted as ‘enclosure.’”] enclosure. Adonibezek [Note: [Col. 1153A] The Greeks interpret this name as though it were read Adoniezer; they would rightly translate that as “the Lord’s help,” from adon and ezer. But concerning the word Adonibezek, consult our notes above on the names in the Book of Judges.] the Lord’s help. David: beloved son. Solomon: merciful, [Note: [Col. 1153A] What properly belongs to David, the Greek copyists ignorantly ascribe to his son Solomon. For it is not Solomon but David who is interpreted as ἱκανὸς χειρί, “strong of hand,” from , dai, and , yad. Conversely, “beloved son” would more appropriately be said of Solomon than of David, since Solomon was also called Jedidiah, which means “beloved of the Lord.” Yet neither David nor Solomon can have these meanings according to the proper character of the Hebrew language or the evidence of the letters, except insofar as they are images and symbols of the true David and the peaceful Solomon, that is, Christ the Lord, whom God the Father called his most beloved Son. The same judgment should be applied to the remaining words that follow; almost all are set down according to typological and symbolic explanations, not according to the etymology of the Hebrew language.] or strong of hand, or peaceful. Rachel: a strong breath from above. Rebekah: a breath from above. Canaanites: those who worship lawlessness. Hittites [Note: [Col. 1153B] Jerome took the name hhiththim, or Chetthim, passively, from the root hhathath, which has a passive sense in the Qal and means “he was terrified and dismayed.” In the Hiphil, however, it has an active sense, which the Greeks follow, adding the word ἀνόμων, “of the lawless,” to the etymology of the name Chettim.] those who cause the lawless to be astonished. Amorites: those who make bitter. Perizzites: those who are scattered. Hivites [Note: [Col. 1153C] Through a notable corruption, this explanation of the name Hivites was missing: σκολιοὶ ὡς ἐπὶ ὄφεις, “malignant,” or “twisted,” “like serpents.” In its place, under the following word Γεργεσαῖοι, there had been most wrongly substituted Εὐαῖοι κατοίκησις, etc.; and what belonged to the etymology of the Girgashites had been attributed to the Hivites. Martianay, failing to notice the lacuna in the Royal manuscript, discoursed conjecturally as follows: “The Hivites, called Evim, are wicked and savage, from ava, that is, ‘he acted unjustly.’ They may interpret ‘dwelling’ as vanity if the name is violently derived from aun, whence maon, that is, dwelling and habitation, and also from aven with aleph at the beginning, which signifies vanity.” We have supplied and restored the passage from the Vatican archetype. See also this name in Fragment IV.] twisted like serpents. Girgashites: a vain dwelling. Jebusites: those who are put to shame. Pishon [Note: [Col. 1154A] I am astonished at the Greeks’ ingenuity in fabricating etymologies of Hebrew names, since Pishon and Gihon, however they are understood, ought certainly to be explained not according to Greek but according to Hebrew principles, because the names themselves are Hebrew. No one, when giving a name in one language, derives the etymology of the word from another. But let us pardon the Greeks, who are known to have received such etymologies from Philo, a very eloquent Jewish writer. In his book On the Allegories of the Law, discussing the four rivers of Paradise, he makes the following observation concerning the name Pishon, p. 52: “One species of the four virtues is prudence, which he called Physon, from sparing and guarding the soul from injuries.” That is: “Of the four virtues, one species is prudence, which he called Physon, because it spares and preserves the soul from harm and injury.” The Greeks therefore agree with Philo in the allegorical interpretation of the name Pishon, which they derive from φείδεσθαι, “to spare,” and φυλάττειν, “to preserve.” God especially spares human nature and weakness when he preserves the soul from the harm and injury of sin. But these are moral interpretations, and they are not written with sufficient precision in the interpretation of Hebrew names, which requires attention to the significance of the letters, not a foreign diffusion of allegories. Let us therefore leave the Greeks aside and adhere wholly to our Jerome, who sets forth the etymologies of Hebrew words no less accurately than learnedly.] because God spared humanity. [Col. 1155] Gihon: because God formed the human being from the earth. [Note: [Col. 1155A] Jerome does not mention the name Tigris because it is Greek and unknown to the Hebrews. The third river is called in Hebrew hhiddecel, or adacel, which may be interpreted as “sharp” and “swift.” Its waters are called haddim, that is, “sharp,” and Calim, “smooth” or “swift.” In corrupt form it is called diglath by the Chaldeans. Hence Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, chapter 2: “The Tigris is called Diglath, which means narrow and swift.” Among the Greeks, Tigris is the same word as among the Persians and Chaldeans, , gir, “arrow,” whose speed this river seems in some measure to imitate. Concerning the same river we read in Hesychius: “Tigris: a river of the Persians; also the roar of this river, and an animal, called by the Jews Phoradei, but by the Greeks Tigris.” This is an obscure passage, and, unless I am mistaken, corrupt in more than one way. For the Greeks, Tigris is an animal called Phoradei by the Jews. This seems to be what Hesychius’s Greek words mean. But among the Jews Phiradim, or Phoradeim, are mules, not tigers. Let us therefore say that Hesychius confuses the river Tigris with the Euphrates, just as above he confused the Seraphim with the Cherubim; and that φοράδει should be read φοράθει or φοράτης, which would be the Jewish Pherath or Phorathe.] Tigris: a pledge, a spirit of swiftness. [Note: [Col. 1155B] Clericus learnedly argues that ῥεῦμα, “flowing,” should be restored in place of πνεῦμα, “spirit.” Likewise, ὀξύτητος should be translated “of swiftness,” not “of sharpness.” Through the carelessness of the printers, this note has fallen from its proper place.] Euphrates: an authoritative one, the spirit of the one who gives light. [Note: [Col. 1156A] From this passage the error of the old editions may again be refuted. There we read that the Greek interpretation of Hosanna is ὡσαννὰ, which is as though one said that a book means “book.” Hosanna is therefore translated into Greek as σῶσον δὴ, which in Latin is “save, I pray.”] Hosanna: save, I pray, or “of the one who saved.” Enoch: dedication. Jesse: refreshment. Egypt [Note: [Col. 1156A] Since Egypt had been a place of affliction for the Hebrews, who there were oppressed by many and various tribulations and injuries, the Greeks interpret it as “distress” or “tribulation.” Likewise, because of the dreadful darkness with which the land of Egypt was covered in the time of Moses, Egypt is called “darkness.”] tribulation, or darkness. Devil [Note: [Col. 1156A] Jerome interprets Diabolus as “flowing down,” because among the Hebrews zub means “to flow”; among the Aeolians, however, διάβολος is written ζάβουλος. Hence diabolus, or rather zaboulos, can readily be interpreted as “flowing down.” The Greeks call him “afflicting” and “temporary,” not according to the evidence of the letters, but because of the maliciousness of his temptations, which God does not permit to continue forever. Hence we read concerning him in Luke 4:13: “When the devil had finished every temptation, he departed from him until the time,” ἄχρι καιροῦ; hence he is called πρόσκαιρος, that is, “temporary.”] afflicting, or temporary. Abba: the Father.

Peter: recognizing, or loosening. Paul: marvelous, or chosen. Matthew: once given. Matthias: gift of God. Mark: exalted by command. Luke: himself rising, or himself lifting up. Perizzites: separating, or scattered, or bearing fruit. Hivites: wild, or exceedingly wicked. Girgashite: driving out a settler, or one approaching as a stranger. Jebusites: trampled, or their manger. Pishon: mouth of the pupil, or change of mouth. [Col. 1156] Gihon: breast, or precipice. Tigris. Euphrates: fruitful, or growing. Hosanna: save. Enoch: dedication. Jesse: island libation, or incense. Egypt: tribulation that constricts. Devil: flowing down; in Greek, accuser. Abba: father. It is Syriac.

## IN THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK
Ἀριμαθαῖος (Arimathea), “of their height.” [Note: [Col. 1160A] “His height” is the better interpretation than “their height”; hence αὐτῶν seems to have been written in Greek instead of αὐτοῦ.] [Note: [Col. 1160C] The Regius manuscript had Ἀριματθαῖος, *Arimatthaeus*, less correctly. The Colbertine adds another etymology, ἀρῶν ἐκεῖνο, ἑτοιμότης, which Martianay translates “ploughing that thing, disposition”; but he admits that he does not know what it means or whence the Greeks derived it. Yet there is no difficulty if ἀρῶν is understood to be derived from αἴρω and translated “bearing up,” or “lifting up that thing.” Jerome also says: “Arimatthaeus, his height, or he himself has been exalted.”] [Col. 1161] Ἀββᾶ (Abba), “father,” or “of a father.” Βαρτιμαῖος (Bartimaeus), “blind son.” [Note: [Col. 1161A] Among the Greeks, Bartimaeus is corruptly written for Barsemia, as Saint Jerome taught us above in the Names from John. But this fragment of Origen’s Lexicon most clearly confirms that the name Bartimaeus, or Barsemia, is to be read in Mark, not in John. Consult our earlier notes on this word.] Βοανηργὲς (Boanerges), “son of thunder.” Βεελζεβοὺλ (Beelzebul), “swallowing flies.” Ἰσραὴλ (Israel), “a man seeing God,” or “a mind seeing God.” [Note: [Col. 1161A] Here retain the etymology of the name Israel, which Saint Jerome learnedly refutes in his *Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, and frequently elsewhere.] [Note: [Col. 1161B] The Colbertine manuscript places the name Ἑφφαθὰ before the name Ἰσραὴλ in the more orderly sequence.] Ἑφφαθὰ (Ephphatha), “be opened.” [Note: [Col. 1161A] Although the sequence of the alphabet’s elements is preserved in this Fragment of the *Book of Names*, we nevertheless find Ephphetha placed after the letter I, because the first syllable of this word is a servile element in Syriac and Hebrew, characteristic of the Ethpael conjugation. It is therefore just as though the verb began with the root *pha*, or *phe*. Hence, in the already published text of Saint Jerome, the final word in Mark is *Phata* itself, without any servile particle. The earlier editors failed to understand this and consequently disturbed both the word and its order, as we noted above.]

That word cannot mean “redeemed” according to the character of the Hebrew language; but Lot may be understood in the sense that he was delivered by Abraham from the hands of those who had conquered the possessions of Sodom.] Λὼτ (Lot), “delivered,” or “shutting out.” [Note: [Col. 1162B] Martianay had read Λώλ, quite erroneously, from the Regius manuscript; the Vatican corrects it.] [Col. 1163] Μαρία (Mary), “ruling.” Μάρθα (Martha), “provoking.” Ναοὺμ (Nahum), “consolation.” Νάθαν (Nathan), “he gave,” or “a gift,” or “of one giving.” Νῶε (Noah), “rest.” Νινευῆ (Nineveh), “beauty of offspring.” [Note: [Col. 1163B] The Colbertine manuscript more correctly has γονῆς ὡραιότητος, “offspring of beauty.” It also has Νηνευΐ instead of Νινευῆ.] Ῥαμα (Ramah), “the lofty one.” Σαρεφθὰ (Zarephath), “fiery,” or “affliction of bread.” [Note: [Col. 1163B] The Vatican manuscript has πυρωτή, “burnt.”] Σίμων (Simon), “hearing grief.” Σόδομα (Sodom), “pasture,” or “hardening.” [Note: [Col. 1163A] Sodom is likewise called πύρωσις, “burning,” because it was consumed by heavenly fire and avenging flames; πύρωσις also means “conflagration.”] Σατᾶν (Satan), “opposing,” or “apostate.” Σαβὰ (Saba), “captivity.” [Note: [Col. 1163A] Tiberius is better translated “his vision” than “the vision of them”; the final *u* is a suffix of the third-person singular pronoun in Hebrew, not of the plural. ## In the Gospel according to John

[Note: [Col. 1163A] Ainon is correctly said to mean “fountain of strength”; *ain* means “fountain,” and *on*, “strength” and “power.”] Αἰνῶη (Ainon), “fountain of strength.” [Note: [Col. 1163A] In the Origenian Lexicon that follows, Galilee is interpreted not as ἀπόκαμψις, “deflection,” but as ἀποκάλυψις, that is, “revelation.” This is entirely justified, since the Hebrew *gala* means not only “he migrated” and “was carried into captivity,” but also “he revealed” and “uncovered.” The word ἀποκάλυψις therefore seems to have been changed by scribal incompetence into ἀπόκαμψις. The manuscript’s accent makes the error sufficiently clear.] Γαλιλαία (Galilee), “revelation,” or “rolling,” or “migration.” [Note: [Col. 1163B] As you can see from his annotation, Martianay had read ἀπόκαμψις and translated it “deflection.” He later corrected it to ἀποκάλυψις from a Colbertine manuscript, and we have restored it from the Vatican manuscript.] Ἐφραῒμ (Ephraim), “increased,” or “bearing fruit.” Κανὰ (Cana), “possession,” or “he possessed.” [Note: [Col. 1163B] Martianay formerly read Ναζαρέθ ἠλεημένος, “Nazareth, having obtained mercy,” in place of Μεσσίας, ἠλειμμένος, “Messiah, anointed,” and had inserted the corresponding heading on Nazareth from Jerome. Since another Nazareth immediately follows, he conjectured in his Notes concerning the first: “The repetition of the word Nazareth and its different interpretation plainly show that Ναζοραῖος should be read in the first place. Christ was called Nazarene, and, having obtained mercy from God beyond his fellows, bestowed on us a more abundant grace and power.” In Jerome’s Matthew, Nazareth has all the meanings listed here in the proper column; Nazaraeus, however, is expressed there only as “pure.” Later, after being alerted by the Colbertine manuscript, he ordered Μεσσίας ἠλημένος (instead of ἠλειμμένος) to be restored, as we correct it from the Vatican manuscript.] Μεσσίας (Messiah), “anointed,” or “Christ.” Ναζαρὲθ (Nazareth), “purity.” [Note: [Col. 1163B] The word *Salim* makes it perfectly clear that the Greek Fragment of the *Book of Names* is precisely the text that Jerome translated into Latin. Concerning Salim he said: “Saalim, of the fist, or of the hollow of the hand, or arising of waters,” which is expressed more briefly in Greek as βρύοντα, “springing.” Moreover, the genuinely Origenian character of this entire second Fragment can be demonstrated by many other arguments: first, by the sequence of the words, which is frequently the same in the Greek and in Jerome’s Latin text; then by the exactly corresponding etymologies and similar interpretations, which the careful reader can now easily compare with one another with the assistance of our edition.] Σαλεὶμ (Salim), “springing.” Συχὰρ (Sychar), “shading.” Σιλωὰμ (Siloam), “sent.” [Note: [Col. 1164A] We do not find the etymology of θεὸν in Jerome’s *Book of Names*. It is therefore a reasonable judgment that this name was added by the recklessness of Greek copyists, who earlier inserted several other Greek words as well. Besides what is stated here concerning the name θεὸν, it will be useful to add something. Some hold that Θεὸν comes from *θεᾶσθαι*, “to behold,” because he sees and observes all things. Others derive it from the noun δέος, “fear,” because he is fearsome. Most, together with our Regius manuscript, derive it from Θέειν, “to run.” For many in ancient times believed that the heavenly bodies and stars, which are borne along in perpetual motion, were gods. Consult the mythological writers.] Θεὸν (God), “from running and moving about, never standing still, but filling all things.”

## Vatican Manuscript

Interpretation of the names and words occurring in the divine Scriptures in the Hebrew language.

[Col. 1165]

Ἀδὰμ (Adam), “earth becoming flesh,” or “testimony,” or “earth-born,” or “man,” or “dust,” or “red earth,” or “blood,” or “likeness.” [Note: [Col. 1165A] The name Adam is dispersed among the Greeks into many different etymologies because they confuse it with *Adama*, *Dam*, and *Ada*. The first signifies dust and red earth; *Dam*, blood; and *Ada*, testimony. It signifies flesh only by an abuse of language, by which Philo and Origen often express not the meanings of names, but events or the virtues of the patriarchs. Thus they say that Adam means “horned earth,” because Adam’s body was formed from earth. Elsewhere they also interpret Noah as “just,” because Scripture says that he was found to be just. What we have noted here concerning the names Adam and Noah should likewise be observed by the careful reader in many other cases, for allegorical and symbolic interpretations of this kind are frequent among the Greek writers mentioned above. Consult also what has already been observed concerning the name Abel in the First Fragment.] Ἀββὰ (Abba), “father,” or “elder.” Ἀβὲλ (Abel), “vapor,” or “mourning,” or “one who brings up,” or “measured strip of land.” Κάϊν (Cain), “possession,” or “jealousy.” [Note: [Col. 1165A] The Greek manuscript contains no shortage of scribal errors, [Col. 1166A] nor of corruptions of names. I would have him consulted in the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, where he discusses the etymologies of all the patriarchs’ names together.] Ζαβουλὸν (Zebulun), “gift.” Δὰν (Dan), “judgment.” Νεφθαλεὶμ (Naphtali), “help.” Γὰδ (Gad), “achievement.” Ἀσὴρ (Asher), “blessedness.” Ἰωσὴφ (Joseph), “addition,” or “reproach,” or “removal.” [Note: [Col. 1168A] Here ὄνειδα is written incorrectly for ὀνειδεία or ὀνειδία. The fact that the name Joseph is changed among the Greeks into such opposite meanings arises from a different stem, or different Hebrew root: *jasaph* means “he added” among the Hebrews, while *suph* means “he ended” and “consumed.” Hence among the Arabs there remains *sajaph*, which means “he cut off the head.”] [Note: [Col. 1168A] Martianay had read ἤ ὄνειδα instead of ὄνειδος.] Βενιαμὶν (Benjamin), “child of sorrow,” or “son of the right hand.” [Note: [Col. 1168A] Because Benjamin was called by his mother Benoni, that is, “son of sorrow,” Greeks ignorant of the Hebrew language thought that Benjamin meant “son of sorrow.”] Μελχισεδὲκ (Melchizedek), “righteous apostle,” or “righteous king,” or “one making peace.” [Note: [Col. 1168A] The same manuscript printed βασιλικὸς, “royal,” instead of βασιλεὺς, “king.”]

[Col. 1169] ## Sons of Reuben

Ῥουβὶμ (Reuben), “wonderful.” [Note: [Col. 1169A] The corruption of the names and the confusion of the interpretations continue here. The etymology θαυμαστὸς, “wonderful,” belongs to the following name Φελὸχ, which is written in Hebrew as Phallu and means “wonderful.” Moreover, τόξον αἰώνιον, “everlasting bow,” belongs to the name Hesron, omitted by the copyist while listing the sons of Reuben. I pass over the rest, since they are clear to the reader by comparison with Jerome’s text. The name Esrom below in this Fragment should nevertheless be consulted.] Φελὸχ (Pheloc), “everlasting bow.” [Note: [Col. 1169B] Again he had read Χαρμὲν instead of Χάρμιν; the Vatican corrects it.] Χάρμιν (Charmin), “my vine.”

## Sons of Simeon

Ἰεμουὴλ (Jemuel), “right hand of the strong one.” Ἰεμὶν (Jemin), “right hand.” [Note: [Col. 1169A] No one among Simeon’s sons is listed in Genesis under the name Oli or Bana, nor do such names occur in this form under Jerome. It is easy to believe that the names Oli and Bana arose through an error of ancient copyists from the name Oolibama. Oolibama, however, is not the name of a man but of a woman, Esau’s wife.] Ὠλὶ (Oli), “tabernacle.” [Note: [Col. 1169B] The Vatican gives the names that follow in this order: Ὠὲλ, σκήνωμα, “Oel, tabernacle”; Ἰαχὴλ, ἕτοιμος, “Jachel, ready”; Βανὰ, λευκόν, “Bana, white.”] Βανὰ (Bana), “white.” Ἰαχὴλ (Jachel), “ready.”

[Note: [Col. 1169B] We have supplied from the Vatican manuscript the heading ΥΙΟΙ ΛΕΥΕΙ, “Sons of Levi,” which was absent from the Regius manuscript through the carelessness of a Greek copyist and which Martianay failed to notice.]

At least the Hebrew, which contains the particle *lo*, rendered in Greek as αὐτῷ, “to him,” indicates that αὐτῷ, “to him,” not αὐτός, “he himself,” should be read.] Γηρσὰν (Gershan), “sojourner.” Καὰθ (Caath), “assembly-leader.” Μεραρὶ (Merari), “being embittered.”

But read τόπου θηριώδους, “of a place left to wild beasts,” and both the meaning and the construction will stand.] Αὐνᾶν (Aunan), “fountain.” Σηλὼμ (Shelom), “lawlessness.” Φαρὲς (Phares), “fence.” Ζαζὰ (Zaza), “illustrious.”

## Sons of Issachar

Θωδὰ (Thoda), “worm.” Φουὰ (Phua), “here I am.” Ἰὼβ (Job), “beloved.” Σωλομὼν (Solomon), “being kept.”

## Sons of Zebulun

Ζαβουλὼν (Zebulun), “fragrant.” [Note: [Col. 1169B] Perhaps εὐοδῶν should be read, meaning “providing a prosperous journey,” or deriving from εὐοδέω, “having an easy journey.” This etymology suits the name Zebulun well, since elsewhere it is interpreted as “flowing.” Certainly εὐώδωμ is a corrupt word, whatever sense is assigned to it.] [Note: [Col. 1170B] I would prefer to restore εὐοδμὸς, meaning “fragrant,” or “scented.” In the Vatican exemplar, εὐόδωμος appears to be written; the final stroke of the letters, obscured by age, seems to have caused the copyist of the Regius manuscript to represent only Εὐώδωμ.] Σεὲρ (Seer), “instructed.” [Note: [Col. 1170A] The Greeks confuse Elon with *elom*, which signifies “age” or “everlasting.”] Ἐλὼμ (Elom), “everlasting.” [Note: [Col. 1170A] No clearer or more effective proof could be given of the corruption of proper names, about which Origen and Jerome so often complain, than this defective series of names. It surpasses all the other corruptions of names found in the printed Greek copies. Who would believe that the name Joalel, or Jahelel, could through the recklessness or negligence of ancient copyists fall into such corruption that Geel would be read for it; Sedon for Sephion; Varilei for Arodi; and likewise for the rest? The reader can easily detect their deformity by comparing them with Jerome’s table. But besides this kind of corruption, there are other errors in the manuscript, such as reading υἱοὶ Δὰν, “sons of Dan,” for υἱοὶ Γὰδ, “sons of Gad,” and conversely, “sons of Gad” for “sons of Dan.” Usim alone is Dan’s son; Sephion and the others were sons of the patriarch Gad. The name Gad is written before Usim in Jerome’s column solely for comparison with a different etymology; I am not so dull as to list Gad among the sons of Dan.] Γεὴλ (Geel), “mercy of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 1170B] In the Vatican manuscript this is listed among the sons of Dan.]

[Col. 1171] ## Sons of Dan

Σεδὸν (Sedon), “bishop.” Ἀγγεὶ (Aggi), “celebration.” Σωμίειν (Somiein), “my second.” Ἱεσβὰ (Hiesba), “my strength.” [Note: [Col. 1171B] The Vatican writes Μήρε, and a little later, as though it were one word and a single alternative name, Θουαριλεῖ instead of θωῦ Ἀριλεῖ.] Μέρε (Mere), “my witness.” Οὐαριλεῖ (Varilei), “my descent.” Θοῦ Ἀριλεῖ (Arilei), “my nature.”

## Sons of Naphtali

Νεφθαλεὶμ (Naphtali), “prayer.” Ἀσαὴλ (Asael), “strength of a strong father.” Γωνίει (Goniei), “everlasting from me.” Ἰεσσαὰρ (Jessaar), “strong.” Θυσιλὴμ (Thusilem), “perfect.”

## Sons of Gad

[Note: [Col. 1171A] So as not to repeat what has already been said and continually reproduce the same material, the reader should remember our earlier notes, in which it was shown that the Greeks did not everywhere interpret Hebrew words according to the character of the language or the evidence of the letters. This is also perfectly clear from the name Gad, which they interpret as “coming.” But on this subject we should hear Jerome: “Where we have written *in fortune*, and in Greek it is ἐν τύχῃ, which may be called an event, the Hebrew has BAGAD, which Aquila interprets as ‘the binding came.’ We may say, ‘in readiness for battle.’ For *ba* can signify the preposition ‘in,’ and ‘he came.’ Thus from the event, or readiness for battle, Gad is named. Zilpah’s son was called Gad. Gad therefore means ‘binding,’ and *ba*, ‘he came.’ The inexperience of the Greeks escaped this, for when they happened to read in Aquila ‘the binding came,’ they supposed that Gad in Hebrew meant the same as ‘to come.’ Jerome corrects the ignorance of this opinion in the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* cited by us above. Similar etymologies of the Greek names soon occur in the other names. I have not undertaken to illustrate them individually in Notes, lest, while spending effort on these grammatical subtleties, I should be drawn away from more important matters and cause delay in the diligence owed to serious subjects.”] Γὰδ (Gad), “coming.” Θυεὶμ (Thuim), “likeness.”

## Sons of Asher
Ἀσὴρ (Asher), blessed. Ἐμμὰ (Emma), numbered.

[Note: [Col. 1172A] In the Greek etymology of this name, one should apparently read not ἐξιούμενος but ἐξιώμενος, from ἐξιῶμαι, which means “to heal” and “to sanction.” In this sense Jasua, or Jesua, is not inappropriately called “healing,” since he went about doing good, καὶ ἰώμενος, “and healing” all who were oppressed by the devil (Acts 10:38). In the Latin translation of Jerome, it should likewise be observed that the second etymology of the name Jesua, “my desire,” belongs more properly to the following name, since in Jessui the pronoun “my” is found, whereas we do not read it in Jesua.]

Ἰάσουα (Jasua), [Note: [Col. 1171B] The Vatican manuscript has the plural ἐξιούμενοι.] ἐξιούμενος, healing. Ἰασούη (Jasue), ἀξίωμά μου, my dignity. Οὐκρία (Ucria), δυνατός, strong. Οὐσεὴλ (Useel), περισσευομένη, abounding.

## Sons of Joseph

Ἰωσὴφ (Joseph), addition. Ἐφραῒμ (Ephraim), broad. Μανασσῆς (Manasses), sold. Ἀσσενὲθ (Aseneth), hated.

## Sons of Benjamin

Βενιαμὶν (Benjamin), son of the right hand. Σαλαὶ (Salai), being famished.

Σαβαχὰρ (Sabachar), firstborn. Σεβὴρ (Seber), coming fire. Περὰ (Pera), to dwell as a resident alien. Ναβαῦ (Nabau), singing pleasantly.

[Note: [Col. 1172B] We can identify the corruptions in these names in the Greek from the interpretation itself. For example, since Leis is interpreted as ἀδελφός μου, “my brother,” it is perfectly clear that Echi should be read and written in place of Leis. This is written in Hebrew as אֶחִי, Echi, or Ahhi, and means “my brother.”]

Λεὶς (Leis), ἀδελφός μου, my brother.

[Col. 1173] Οὔαρος (Uaros), ἀοχηγός, leader.

[Note: [Col. 1173A] The etymology of Momphin among the Greeks appears to have been made from Greek and Hebrew. Μορφὴ in Greek means the appearance of the face, while the suffix i in Hebrew is the first-person singular masculine pronoun “my.” Hence Momphi, or Morphi, may be called among Greeks unfamiliar with the Hebrew language “my likeness.”]

Μομφὶν (Momphin), ὁμοιότης μου, my likeness. Θουαρὰ (Thouara), κατάβασίς μου, my descent.

[Note: [Col. 1173A] The Vatican manuscript adds here the word ἐξόδου, “of Exodus”; then it reads Πίθων in place of Πίθωμ.]

Πίθωμ (Pithom), στόμα αἰώνιον, eternal mouth. Ῥαμεσσὴ (Ramesse), ἁρπαγή, seizure. Σεμφόρα (Sephora), ἐπίσκεψις ὡραία, beautiful visitation. Φουὰ (Phua), προφήτης, prophet. Λευεὶδ (Leueid), ὑπουργός, minister.

Μωϋσὴς (Moses), ὕδατος ἀναίρεσις, taking away from water; or νοὺς εὐσεβής, pious mind; or ἔρευνα κυρίου, inquiry of the Lord.

Ῥαγουὴλ (Raguel),

[Note: [Col. 1173A] Martianus had read ἴλλος instead of φίλος; this is an Ionic word meaning “eye.” Accordingly, he translated it in that sense and offered the following explanation of the etymology: Because of the first syllable Ra, the Greeks extract from the name Raguel the meaning “eye” or “sight,” not understanding that the word is written with the letter ʿayin, [letter not reproduced], and not [letter not reproduced].]

[Col. 1173B] [Col. 1174A] But I think it is clearer than daylight that it should be emended, as we have done, from the Vatican manuscript: φίλος, “friend.” This agrees with Hebrew analogy and with Jerome’s interpretation, who translates it “pasture” and “friend,” and so often teaches elsewhere that the same letters רעה denote both “shepherd” and “friend.”]

φίλος ἰσχυρός, strong friend. Ἰωθὼρ (Jethor), περισσεία, abundance. Ζωφὴθ (Zopheth), ζωὴ πλατεῖα, broad life.

[Note: [Col. 1174A] The Greeks seem here to attach the etymology of Methuselah to the word Melchiel, although Melchiel can in some way be interpreted as “sent,” if we regard it as a figurative or formed word from the Chaldean verb malach, which among Eastern peoples means “to announce” and “to send.” Hence the Targumists render the verb malach in Proverbs 13:17 by שליחא, scelihha, derived from שלח, salahh, which means “to send.”]

Μελχιὴλ (Melchiel), ἀπεσταλμένος ἀπὸ ἰσχυροῦ, sent by the strong one.

## Vatican Codex

[Col. 1173]

### Interpretation of the Female Names in the Hebrew Dialect

Εὖα (Eua), ζωή, life.

[Note: [Col. 1173A] The name Sarah is not interpreted as “barren” according to the literal meaning of the letters, but according to the preference of the Greeks, who often use statements from Sacred Scripture as etymologies. For it is said of Sarah in Genesis 11:30, “But Sarai was barren.” I am nevertheless not unaware that בשרות, basoreth, signifies dryness and barrenness; hence the Greeks, following their custom, perhaps violently understand the name Sarai as formed from it.]

Σάῤῥα (Sarah), δέσμη βλεπομένη, ἢ στεῖρα, ἢ ἄρχουσα, a visible bundle, or barren, or ruling.

[Col. 1175] Ἄγαρ (Hagar), αὔτη προσήλυτος, ἢ συντρέφουσα, ἢ προσηλυτεύουσα, she herself a proselyte, or nourishing together, or making a proselyte. Ῥεβέκκα (Rebecca), πολλὴ ὑπομονὴ, ἢ ποικίλη, ἢ πνοὴ ἄνωθεν, ἢ χαρά, great patience, or varied, or breath from above, or joy. Δεβόῤῥα (Deborah), μέλισσα, bee. Σεπφόρα (Sephora), χάρις καὶ κάλλος, grace and beauty. Ῥαχὴλ (Rachel), πρόβατον, ἢ πνοὴ ἰσχυροῦ, sheep, or breath of the strong one.

[Note: [Col. 1175A] In Philo, Leah is interpreted as κοπιῶσα and ἀνανευομένη, that is, “laboring” and “rejecting,” or rather “rejected,” as we rendered it in Latin. This agreement of interpretation clearly proves that the etymologies of this Fragment were, if not all, at least many of them borrowed from Philo.]

Λεία (Leah), κοπιῶσα, ἢ ἐμόχθησεν, ἢ ἀνανευομένη, laboring, or she labored, or rejecting. Βηρσαβεὲ (Bathsheba), θυγάτηρ δυνατοῦ, daughter of the mighty one.

Σαραὰ (Saraa),

[Note: [Col. 1175A] Earlier, among the Greek Fragments, we are taught that this word should be read with alpha as ἀρχομένη, that is, “subject,” or “one who obeys another’s command,” and not ἐρχομένη, which means “coming.” Nor does the etymology “coming” suit the name Sarai if we interpret it according to the proper character of the Hebrew language. We, however, have preferred to leave ἐρχομένη written here in error rather than ἀρχομένη, because of certain overly exacting critics who revere scribal mistakes in manuscripts.]

ἐρχομένη, coming.

Θάμαρ (Thamar), ἀλλαξάσης,

[Note: [Col. 1175A] Martianus has ἢ ἄλλαξεν.]

or ἤλλαξεν, ἢ φοίνιξ, ἢ πικρασμός, of one who changed, or changed, or palm tree, or bitterness.

Μαρία (Maria), κυριεύουσα, ἤ πικρὰ θάλασσα, ruling, or bitter sea. Μαριὰμ (Mariam), φωτιζωμένη, ἢ φωτίζουσα αὐτούς, ἢ κύριος ἐκ γένους μου, ἢ σμύρνα θαλασσία, illuminated, or illuminating them, or “the Lord from my lineage,” or maritime myrrh. Ῥοὺθ (Ruth), πνοὴ, ἢ σπεύδουσα, breath, or hurrying.

[Note: [Col. 1175A] Jerome recalls the name Susanna in his commentary on Luke, not in the Old Testament.]

[Note: [Col. 1175A] The Vatican manuscript has ΑΡΣΕΝΙΚΑ.]

### Masculine Names

Φαρὲς (Phares), φραγμός, enclosure.

[Note: [Col. 1176A] It is not sufficiently clear why the Greeks interpret Esron as ὕλη, that is, “material,” unless they understand “material” as earth, which is sometimes called arha or ero. Jerome’s interpretation is better and more accurate: Esron means “he saw an arrow,” or “their court.” For es, or hhets, is “arrow”; raa, “he saw”; and hhaser, “court.”]

Εσρὼμ (Esrom),

[Note: [Col. 1175A] Martianus, from the Regius manuscript, incorrectly has Ὠσρῶμ, Osrom.]

Ἀθὰμ (Atham), ὑψηλός, exalted. Ἀμιναδὰβ (Aminadab), ἔθνος ἐπιθυμητόν, desirable nation.

[Note: [Col. 1176A] The Vatican manuscript has ἐπιθυμητικὸν, which properly means “desiring” or “eager.”]

Ναασσῶν (Naasson),

[Note: [Col. 1176A] The form Νασσῶν, Nasson, had been written incorrectly from the Regius manuscript.]

ἀνάπαυσις αἰωνία, everlasting rest. Σαλμὼν (Salmon), λάβε σκεῦος ἐκλεκτόν, receive the chosen vessel. Βοὸζ (Booz), ἔλευσις δυνατή, powerful coming. Ἰωβὲδ (Jobed), ὑποτασσόμενος, subordinated. Ἰεσσαὶ (Jesse), ἀνάψυξις, refreshment.

[Note: [Col. 1176A] It is written of David in Psalm 118: “You have revealed to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” Therefore the Greeks attach this etymology to his name: “for whom hidden things were prepared.” The highly learned Jerome nowhere attends to such allegories, but wished to express the etymologies of all the words according to the proper character of the Hebrew language. Thus, in place of David, he interprets it as “strong in hand,” from dai and yad; but “desirable” from ava, or from amad, that is, “he desired” and “he longed for.”]

Δαβὶδ (David), πεποθημένος, ἢ ἠλεημένος, ἢ ἱκανὸς χειρὶ, ἢ ᾧ ἡτοίμασται τὰ ἀπόκρυφα, desired, or pitied, or sufficient in hand, or for whom hidden things have been prepared.

[Col. 1177] Σολομῶν (Solomon), εἰρηνικός, peaceful. Ῥοβοὰμ (Rehoboam), ἐν πλήθει λαοῦ, in the multitude of the people. Ἀβιοὺδ (Abiud), πατὴρ ἐρχόμενος, father coming.

[Note: [Col. 1177A] This notable corruption of names entered the Latin manuscripts of the old Vulgate Gospel according to Matthew. In a very ancient manuscript of this monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés I found the passage written as follows: “Rehoboam fathered Abiud; Abiud fathered Asaph; Asaph fathered Jehoshaphat.” Thus Asa is corruptly written as Asaph, whom the Greeks compare to a flourishing myrtle because of the exceptional virtue and piety for which he is remembered as the most distinguished among the kings of Judah.]

Ἀσὰφ (Asaph), μύρτον· ὥσπερ γὰρ τὸ μύρτον θεωρεῖται καὶ χειμῶνος εὐθαλὲς, καὶ εὐῶδες, οὕτω καὶ ἡ ἱστορία τῶν δικαίων, myrtle; for just as the myrtle is seen flourishing and fragrant even in winter, so also is the history of the righteous.

Ἰωσαφὰτ (Jehoshaphat), κύριος κριτής, the Lord is judge. Ἰωρὰμ (Joram), κύριος ὕψους, the Lord of height.

[Note: [Col. 1177A] The name Ozias is interpreted by the Greeks with extreme violence as “illustrious sisters.” Nor could the Hebrew Ozihau ever have the meaning “sister,” even if the word “above” is taken in various directions. Read therefore Ochozias, both because of the sequence of the genealogies in 2 Kings 8:24, where it is not Ozias but Ochozias who is the son of Joram, and because of the etymology ἀδελφῆς, “of a sister,” which is contained in some form in Achasiahu, or Ochosiau. For ahhoth, or achoth, means “sister” in Latin. Moreover, aze, or achze, in Chaldean means “seen” or “conspicuous,” which corresponds especially well with the Greek ἐπιφανής, “illustrious.”]

Here the reader should also remember that, through the error of Greek scribes, Enos was written above in place of Noah; so it is not surprising if we read Madiam for Manasse and Jesba for Josiah.]

The same is true of πᾶσαι φυλαί, “all tribes,” in place of the single word παμφιλί, or, less incorrectly in the Vatican manuscript, παμφιλία. The error of the copyist is made clear both by the sense and especially by the Origenian Lexicon to be appended shortly: Μαγὼγ, τῆξις, ἢ πᾶν ἔθνος, ἢ πᾶσαι φυλαί—“Magog, liquefaction, or every nation, or all tribes.”]

[Note: [Col. 1180A] The Vatican manuscript has ἀνθηρῶν.]

ἀνθηρῶν, flowering.

[Note: [Col. 1180B] The Vatican manuscript likewise has Χανουὰν, Chanuan.]

Χαναὰν δὲ ἐγέννησε τὸν Σιδῶνα, and Canaan fathered Sidon.

Σιδὼν (Sidon), ἔξελθε ἐν κρίσει, go forth into judgment. Χεθαθὰ (Chethatha), ἁμαρτάνων, sinning.

[Col. 1181] Αἰλὰμ (Elam), οἰκουμένην, the inhabited world. Ἀρφαξὰδ (Arphaxad), ὁρώμενος ἐκ παντός, seen from every side. Ἀρὰμ (Aram), ὑψηλός, exalted. Ἰὼβ (Job), ἀγαπητὸς κυρίου, beloved of the Lord. Γαμὲρ (Gamer), ληνος, winepress. Μοσὸχ (Mosoch), τοξευτής, archer. Ἔβερ (Eber), διαπερῶν, passing over. Ἰεκτὰν (Joktan), μικροφυής, small by nature. Ἐλμωδὰδ (Elmodad), κινούμενος, moved.

[Note: [Col. 1181A] Here there are notable corruptions of names among the Septuagint and in the Regius manuscript. Nothing could be more corrupt than writing Aithiai for Jaree, Atharoudam for Aduram, and especially Ethecmal for Decla and Ebal. Let the diligent reader consult Genesis 10:26–30; he will immediately see that the Hebrew accusative article את, joined with the name, has through the ignorance of the Greeks been treated as part of the name. For example, Atharoudam is the name Adouram with the preceding article את, or ath: אתאדורם, athadouram. We should also observe that the Greeks read daleth for resh and resh for daleth. The same judgment applies to the preceding Aithiai, which was formed from ath and jare, with r changed into i at the end of the word, so that Aithiai stands for Athiare. The other two, Ethecmal and Ethemmimael, have the same cause and origin of corruption.]

Αἰθίαι (Aithiai), καταβαίνοντες, descending. Ἀθαρουδὰμ (Atharoudam), ὅρατον ὑψηλόν, visibly exalted.

[Note: [Col. 1181A] The Vatican manuscript has the less corrupt Ὀζὰλ, Ozal, and immediately afterward Ἐθεκβὰλ, Ethecbal. I am weary of pursuing these monstrosities of words.]

Ὀζὰν (Ozan), ἐλαφρούς, light. Ἐθεκμὰλ (Ethecmal), νεφελώδης, cloudy. Ἐθεμμιμαὴλ (Ethemmimael), πατήρ μου ἰσχυρός, my father is strong. Ὠφὲδ (Ophed), φῶς θεραπείας, light of healing. Εὐειλὰτ (Evilath), δεῖξον ὧδε, show here. Ἀρὰμ (Aram), ἐσχάτη, last.

[Note: [Col. 1182A] Jerome rendered Jobab in Latin as “magician, father,” because ob in Hebrew means “magician” and ab means “father.” The Greeks derive the etymology from jaab, “he desired,” or ahab, “he loved.” They also hold that the first syllable Jo is an abbreviated form of the name Jao, or Jehovah, that is, “Lord.”]

Ἰωβὰβ (Jobab), ἀγαπῶν κύριον, loving the Lord. Ναχὼρ (Nahor), δέησις ἐσχάτη, final supplication. Αὼτ (Lot), λελυτρωμένος, redeemed.

[Note: [Col. 1182A] So that it may be clear to every reader why the Chaldeans are called magicians and diviners, or almost demons, I thought it worthwhile to record the following observations with the learned. Jerome interpreted Chasdim as “demons,” taking cha as “as” and sin as “demons,” and changing sin into lamed, so that it becomes Chaldim instead of Chasdim. Again, because the Chaldeans discovered judicial astrology, all mathematicians, astrologers, magicians, diviners, and others practicing the same art were called Chaldeans. Hence among the Greeks they are interpreted as μάντεις and μάγοι, “diviners” and “magicians.”]

Χαλδαῖοι (Chaldeans), μάντεις, μάγοι, diviners, magicians. Συχὲμ (Shechem), ὦμος, shoulder. Βηθήλ (Bethel), οἶκος ἰσχυρός, strong house. Ἀγγαὶ (Aggai), ἑορτή, festival. Ἀμαρφὰ (Amarpha), συμβολία πονηρά, evil encounter. Ἀριὼλ (Ariol), λέων, ἢ ὄνομα βασιλέως, lion, or the name of a king.

[Note: [Col. 1181A] The Regius manuscript had the more corrupt Ἐσχέοδ, Escheod.]

Ἐσχὼδ (Eschod), βότρυς, cluster.

[Note: [Col. 1181A] We restored this somewhat more correctly from the Vatican manuscript. Martianus had read Ἀναὰν, Anaan, and had added in the Jerome section the syllable Ana, “answer,” etc.]

Ὠναὰν (Onaan), ἀνομία, iniquity. Χωβὰλ (Chobal), ἀρκεῖ, it is sufficient. Δαμασκὸς (Damascus), ἀνάβασις σιωπηρά, silent ascent. Βάτος (Batus), μῖσος, hatred. Χαναναίων (Canaanites),

[Note: [Col. 1182A] The Regius manuscript had προσκυνούντων ἀνομίαν, “worshiping iniquity.”]

προσκυνούντων ἀνομίᾳ, worshiping iniquity.

Ἀμοῤῥαίων (Amorites), μικρῶν, small. Φερεζαίων (Perizzites),

[Note: [Col. 1182A] Martianus, from the Regius manuscript, had read the single word σκολιῶνος and translated it “making crooked.” See this same name above in the other Fragment.]

[Col. 1183] Γεργεσαίων (Girgashites), κατοίκησις ματαία, vain dwelling.

[Note: [Col. 1183] The Vatican manuscript has ματαίου, “of the vain.”]

Ἰεβουσαίων (Jebusites), καταισχυνομένων, those who are put to shame. Δαρῶν (Daron), κιβωτός, ark.

[Note: [Col. 1183] Sinai is allegorically called “everlasting vision” because of the events that took place there and Moses’ frequent conversations with God. Do not therefore take this as the etymology of the name, but as the mystical or typological interpretation of Mount Sinai, on which God appeared and established the law for the Hebrews. We should think the same about the name Israel that follows, when it is interpreted as “strong people.”]

Σινὰ (Sinai),
