# Jerome: Book of Hebrew Names

[Col. 1174]

Eve, life, or woe, or calamity. Sarah, princess.

[Col. 1176] Hagar, resident alien, or converted. Rebecca, great patience, or she received much, or patience. Deborah, bee, or talkative. Sephora, her bird, or her beauty, or pleasing. Rachel, sheep, or seeing the beginning, or vision of wickedness, etc. Leah, laborious. Bathsheba, daughter of the oath. Sarai, my princess. Tamar, palm tree, or bitter. Maria is called “lady” in the Syriac language. Miriam, most people think should be interpreted as “these illuminate me,” or “illuminatrix,” or “myrrh of the sea,” but this does not seem so to me at all. It is better to say that it means “star of the sea,” or “bitter sea.” Ruth, hurrying, or seeing, etc. Susanna, lily, or her grace; but better if the feminine name is formed from “lily.”

## Masculine Names
Phares, division, or he divided. Esrom, he saw an arrow, or their courtyard. Aram, exalted. Aminadab, my willing people. Naasson: some think “rested sound,” but “divining,” or “their serpent,” is better. Salmon, perceptive, or perception. Booz, in whom there is strength, or in him is fortitude; but better, “in strength.” Obed, serving. Jessai, libation of the islands, but better, incense. David, desirable, or strong of hand. [Col. 1178] Salomon, peaceful, or he will be pacified. Roboam, the people’s assault. Abia, the father is lord. Asa, taking away, or lifting up. Josaphat, he himself judging; but better, “the Lord will judge.” Joram, where is he exalted? or who is exalted? but better, “he will be exalted.” Ozia, the strength of the Lord. Joatham, completed, or perfect. Achaz, take hold. Sedecias, the Lord is just. Manasse, forgetful. Josias, where is the incense of the Lord? or the salvation of the Lord, etc. Samaria, guarded. Raason, course, or favor, or graciousness, which the Greeks more significantly call εὐδοκίαν, “good pleasure.” Romelias, exalted of the Lord. Pharao, destroyer, or “he uncovered him.” Bathuel, virgin of God. Chettura, offering incense, or joined, or united. Cheth, striking. Gersan, a stranger there. Chaleb, like a heart, or the whole heart, or dog. Jefanne, he hinted, or hinting. Elia, God the Lord. Elisaeus, the salvation of my God. Chebron, marriage, or eternal vision, etc. Asaph, gathering. Gelhoe, rolling, or descent, or a heap raining. Melcha, his queen. Eden, pleasure, or delights, or adornment. Gedera, a wall, or hedge. Maviael, he who is lord, or God from life. Ada, testimony. Sella, his shadow. [Col. 1180] Thobel, led to mourning, or turned, or everything. Noema, beauty, or pleasure, or faith. Jared, descending, or strengthening. Chanaan, σάλος, that is, “their movement,” etc. Gomer, reception, or completion, etc. Magog, δῶμα, that is, roof, or “from the roof.” Madai, measure, or “as much as is sufficient.” Mesech, prolongation, or certainly compressed. Thiras, fearing, or redeeming, or superfluous. Aschenez, fire thus sprinkled. Elisa, my God, or his salvation, or “to the island,” or the salvation of my God. Tharsis, scouts of joy, or of gladness. Chetim, broken. Chus, an Ethiopian. Mesraim, their enemies, or Egypt. Egypt, tribulation that constricts. Phut, Libya, or a bending of the shore. Seba, captured, or captivity, or certainly converting. Dedan, judging. Chus, an Ethiopian. Nemrod, tyrant, or fugitive, or transgressor. Babylon, confusion. Orech, length. Sennaar, shaking off of teeth, or their stench. Assur, directing, or blessed, or walking. Nineve, beautiful, or a shoot of beauty. Chanaan, their movement, or merchant, or humble. Sidona, the hunting of sorrow. Chethaeus, ecstasy of mind, or fixed, or cut off. [Col. 1182] Elam, of the age, or of the world. Arphaxad, healing devastation. Aram, exalted. Job, a magus. Gomer, reception or completion, or perfection. Mesech, prolongation, or failure, or certainly compressed. Eber, one who crosses over. Jectan, little. Elmodad, “to his principal mother,” or “the measure of God.” Jaree, moon. Aduram, exalted generation. Aizel, proceeding. Decla, subtle, or palm-bearing. Ebal, an ancient valley, or heap of stones. Abimael, my father from God. Ophir, useless, or “into the grassy place.” Aevila, grieving, or in labor. Aran, angrily, or beauty. Jobab, “with a magus as father,” or dripping. Nachor, rest of light, or final supplication. Lot, bound, or declination. Chaldaei, as it were demons, or as it were breasts, or fierce. Sychem, shoulders. Bethel, house of God. Aggai, question, or festival. Amaraphal, he said that he should fall. Arioch, drunk, or drunkenness. Eschol, a cluster, or all fire. Onam, pain, or their sorrow, etc. And On, iniquity. Chobal, condemnation. Damascus, drink of blood, or kiss of blood, or blood of a sack. Batus, the name of a measure. Chananaei, merchants, or “this poor man,” or prepared, or humility. Amorrhaei, bitter, or speaking. Pherezaei, separated, or without a wall, or separating, or scattered, or bearing fruit. [Col. 1184] Gergesaei, driving out a settler, or strangers drawing near. Jebusaei, trodden down, or manger. Aaron, mountain of strength, or strong mountain. Sinai, my amphora, or my measure, or commandment. Israel means “to see God,” or “a man,” or “a mind seeing God”; but better, “upright of God.”

### Latin Interpretation

## WORDS ACCORDING TO THE LETTERS OF THE HEBREW LANGUAGE

[Col. 1183]

### A

Asara, ungrateful. Adonai, Lord. Adon, prophet; it is said in two ways. Abenezer, stone of help. Ano, glory. Abael, from God. Ada and Seila, earth and hope. Abigaea, exalted of the father. Ammonites, curvature. Abba, father. Azael, sending away. Adamatha, red earth. Ariel, lion of the strong. Aaron, behold the work, behold. Adonibezec, the Lord’s help. Abiel, praise. Aenos, man. Aria, lion. Ammon and Moab, from my kindred and from my father. [Col. 1185] Alleluia, praise and celebrate the Lord with hymns.

Elisaeus, strength of God. In the plantation of Sabec, in a strong plantation, or a golden herb. From Agge, from rest. In the land of Naim, in the land of those praising. Zacchaeus, victor. Zorobabel, who was Salathiel, from confusion.

A psalm concerning Idithum, a psalm concerning one judge. Anathom, of my coming one. From the land of Benjamin, from the land of the son of sorrow. From Babylon, from confusion. Jessias, who belonged to Sophonias, “overshadowing,” belonging to the one who makes the earth stand. Ephud, manifestation and truth. Pharia, daughter of Pharaoh. “She came to be washed, and she found Moses still an infant.” And when she had looked up into heaven, she said: “O one God, having infinite names!” Hence the Gentiles call her Eisitan, 666. It is the name of the man bearing this number in the Apocalypse of John. That is, “he will come from the Medes to destroy the faithful.” Isaiah also says of him: “Behold, I will raise up the Medes against you,” and the rest. Baruch, blessed. Eloai, God. Adonai, Lord. Jao, invisible. Sabaoth, of hosts. Elimaz, word of God. Marsippion, assent. Opelos, gluttony of the belly. Τῇ πλίνθῳ, “for prostitution.” Cherubim, multiplied knowledge, or wings. Amen, confirmation that it is truly so.

### WORDS IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER OF THE HEBREW DIALECT

Bethel, house of God. Bethlehem, house of bread. Bethania, house of glory. Bethphage, house of success. Bersabee, daughter of the powerful one. Bathuel, he who belongs to the one coming. Bosor, flesh. Beliar, seeker. [Note: [Col. 1185B] Martianus incorrectly read ἐκζητής from the Regius manuscript instead of ἐκζητητής, which we restore from the Vatican.] Beelzebul, [Note: [Col. 1185A] On the authority of Scripture we are certain that Beelzebub was the god of the Ekronites. Ahaziah, lying sick after falling, sent men in 2 Kings 1:2 to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, about his health; the Septuagint has Βαὰλ μυίας, “Baal of flies.” Thus the idol was called, because the inhabitants of the city of Ekron in Palestine worshiped it and believed that the demon had power over harmful flies and could drive them from its territory. I also know that among the Gentiles Zeus was called μυαῖος and ἀπομυαῖος, “fly-god” and “fly-driver,” and that he was called ἀχώρ. Hence Pliny, Book X: “The Cyrenaeans invoke Achor as a god; when an abundance of flies brings pestilence, they immediately perish once sacrifice has been offered to that god.” Cyrenaica, a region of Africa, includes the kingdom of Barca, a word that somewhat resembles *Baceloseon* in the Greek manuscript, by which we are told that Beelzebub was a demon of the Βακηλωσέων. But perhaps the copyist should have written βακήλων, meaning that Beelzebub was the god of prostitutes; for among the Greeks βάκηλος is a man of great stature but foolish and womanizing, indeed effeminate and castrated. These characteristics fit extremely well those effeminates consecrated to the Mother of the Gods or to Priapus, about whom Jerome discusses at length in Book I of his Commentary on Hosea, chapter 4. Compare this with what is read below in the Origenian Lexicon under Beelzebul.] a demon of the Baceloseans. [Note: [Col. 1185B] The Vatican has βακηλώσεως. **Pasek**, redemption. **Pathoura**, table. [Note: I have not yet discovered where the Greeks obtained this statement; but there is no doubt that it concerns the name Βῆ (*Bē*), by which they intend to indicate a demon—whether it is Bel, Belial, or Baal, all of whom are frequently mentioned in the sacred books. In Hesychius there are clear indications of this Βῆ: “Βῆλος,” he says, “οὐρανὸς, καὶ Ζεὺς Ποσειδῶνος υἱός,” that is, “Belus: heaven, or Zeus, son of Poseidon.” Βῆλος could have been contracted to Βῆ, so as to signify the idols and demons of the pagans.] **They set before [him] in** [Note: Everyone readily understands that this was badly transmitted by a Greek copyist and that βὴλ should be restored to βῆ; nevertheless, the Vatican manuscript also prefers this reading. “It seems,” says Clericus, “that in the source from which this was taken there was mention of what is related in the history of Bel or Belus: for daily food was set before him in the temple of Bel (παρέθεντο τροφαὶ ἐν τῷ Βῆλ ἱερῷ), and he was believed to consume it.” What Martianaeus has in his notes is absurd: “Βῆλος could have been contracted to Βῆ, so as to signify the demons and idols of the pagans.” For such a contraction does not occur in Greek, much less in Hebrew. We have rendered only the Latin, using “were set before” for what Martianaeus translated. He approved this.] βῇ, τῷ διαβόλῳ, τῷ λεγομένῳ, **in Bē, the devil, the one called [so].**

[Note: Samuel is called “petition from God” not so much from the proper meaning of the Hebrew language as from his mother’s vows and prayers, by which the barren Hannah obtained a son from God.] **Samuel**, a petition from God. [Note: The Greeks do not express the etymology of the name Samuel, but his office and virtue, by which he was always ready to obey the voice of the Lord.] **Samuel**, servant, [Note: See below in the second Origenian Lexicon. Cyril of Jerusalem and others commonly interpret it from the Greeks as σωτηρίαν θεοῦ ἐπακούσαντος, “salvation of the God who hears.”] **hearing God.** **Sikima**, ascending. **Saul**, [Note: We emend this from the Vatican manuscript to ἡττημένος, “defeated,” which means “set free,” with Jerome himself supporting the reading. [Note: An unskilled copyist read *Saphecka* for *Baphecka*, that is, “in Apheca.” For *be* is a Hebrew preposition translated in Latin as “in.”] **Saphecka**, in darkness. **Senaaar**, [Note: Martianaeus has *sapria*, which he interprets as “wine seasoned from rotting herbs.”] **rottenness.** **Sabbaths**, sanctifications. [Note: These expressions are interpretations of sentences in sacred Scripture, not etymologies of Hebrew names, as the present passage clearly demonstrates in the names Seraphim, Salathiel, and Saba, etc. Concerning the word Salathiel, two points especially deserve notice: first, Salathiel is interpreted as “grace” with the same freedom with which the name Salem was interpreted above; second, some word has been omitted in the Greek. To prevent an entirely false and absurd sense in the interpretation of this word, it should be read in this manner: “Salathiel, grace of the coming God”—the Salathiel who lived in the time of Daniel.] **Seraphim**, they stood, spirits rising, a plant stood. [Note: The Royal manuscript corruptly had Σαλαθεήλ, *Salatheel*.] **Salathiel**, grace of the one coming, of Daniel. **Saba**, the queen of Ethiopia, whom the nations call [Note: Cedrenus also bears witness to this Greek fiction in his *Annals*: “And Queen Saba, who was called Sibyl by the Greeks” (καὶ βασίλισσα Σαβὰ, ἥτις ἐλέγετο Σίβυλλα παρ’ Ἕλλησι). Petitus notes that the story was invented from the similarity of the names and from the fame for wisdom by which that queen became renowned. Moreover, Martianaeus had incorrectly read Σεβύλλην, *Sebyllen*, from the Royal manuscript instead of Σίβυλλαν, *Sibyllan*.] **Sibyl.**

**A psalm concerning Idithum**, a psalm concerning one judge. **Anathom**, of my coming. **From the land of Benjamin**, from the land of the child of sorrow. **From Babylon**, from confusion. **Josiah**, the son of [Note: Martianaeus wrongly inserts the name Σοφρονίου, Latin *Sophronii*, “of Sophronius,” from the Royal manuscript in place of Sophoniah. The Greek author alludes to Zechariah 6:10, οἶκον Ἰωσίου τοῦ Σοφονίου, “the house of Josiah son of Sophoniah,” etc. See above under Issecias.] **Sophoniah**, overshadowing, the son of the one who raises up the earth. [Note: Consult above, col. 545 (in this edition col. 1151, note [2]), our observations on this etymology of the name Ephod.] **Ephod**, declaration and truth. **Pharia**, the daughter of Pharaoh. **She came to bathe and found Moses while he was still an infant. And, looking up toward heaven, she said: “O one God of countless names.” From this the nations call her [Note: The Greeks said *Eisitan* instead of *Isis*, so that in the word Εἰσιτὰν the number would be 666; enough has already been discussed above under the entry Evinas. What follows is otherwise merely a futile Greek fabrication.] **Eisitan**, 3 [Note: The Vatican manuscript prefers Εἰσίτειταν (thus written) instead of Εἰσιτάν. This daughter of Pharaoh, whom Josephus calls Thermuthis, is called Pharia by later Greek writers. George Syncellus, p. 120 of the Paris edition, writes: “The infant himself was adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter Thermuthis, who was also called Pharia and was queen” (Ὁ δὲ αὐτὸς υἱὸς τῇ θυγατρὶ Φαραῶ Θερμούθιδι, τῇ καὶ Φαρίῃ βασίλιδι οὔσῃ εἰσποιηθείς). And Cedrenus, p. 42: “Thermuthis, who was also Pharia, daughter of Pharaoh,” etc. See below in the Origenian Lexicon.] 666, **of the man who has the number in the Apocalypse of John.** **This is the one coming from the Medes to wage war against the faithful, concerning whom Isaiah also says: “Behold, I shall rouse the Medes against us,” and the rest.** **Baruch**, blessed. **Eloai**, God. **Adonai**, Lord. **Jao**, invisible. **Sabaoth**, of the powers. [Note: You will find these four Greek names in the preceding Fragments.] **Elimax**, [Note: We read Ἐλίμαξ, *Elimaz*, from the Vatican manuscript; this is the name of a magus. Martianaeus read Κλίμαξ, *Klimax*, here and above in the other Fragment from the Royal manuscript.] **the word of God.** **Marsippion**, obedience. **Hopelos**, gluttony. **To the brick**, to fornication. **Cherubim**, multiplied knowledge, or wings. **Amen**, [Note: Martianaeus did not read this correctly. He read πίστωσιν and translated it as *fidem faciunt*, “they make faith.” The Vatican manuscript supplies the correction. The excerpts of Hebrew Names from Philo and Josephus—one of which Martianaeus placed before these Fragments and the other after them—we shall review in a more suitable place, after the two complete Lexicons that follow, and again more accurately.] **confirmation, truly.** [Note: Here the Greek Fragments of the Book of Hebrew Names end; they prepare an easier route for us to understand what is attributed to Philo the Jew. Among these Fragments, however, there is one complete work that acknowledges Origen as its author, since it consists entirely of names from the New Testament, whose terms had been omitted in the Lexicon of the Jewish writer. Since nearly all the rest derive from the books of the Old Testament, they seem attributable to Philo, or also to Josephus, Jewish authors. I have called Josephus the author here of the etymologies in the Greek Fragments—not of all of them, certainly, but only of those that are found written in his works. Such, if it is useful to establish the matter by examples, is the etymology of the name Adam, concerning which he argues as follows in book I, chapter 2, of the *Jewish Antiquities*: “This man was called Adam; and in the language of the Hebrews this means ‘red,’ since he had been formed from red earth that had been kneaded. For such is the true virgin earth.” If you compare this with our Commentary at the end of the book, you will clearly see that Josephus is in agreement with Hesychius and especially with the Royal manuscript.]

# PREFACE OF D. JOANNES MARTIANAEUS TO THE ORIGENIAN LEXICON OF HEBREW NAMES

To make it known to all students that Origen composed a book of *Hebrew Names*, and that he frequently proposed forced and unlearned etymologies in it, I shall produce as a witness a very learned man who certainly deserved well of Origen, but was by no means indulgent toward his errors. By this author’s prior testimony, I shall more easily obtain pardon if, compelled at times by the necessity of truth and by judgment, I refute Origen’s etymologies and do not hesitate to make his manifest ignorance of the Hebrew language clear to readers.

Accordingly, in book 3, chapter 3, section 7 of the *Origeniana*, Daniel Huetius discusses this present compilation as follows:

> “I find among the ancients mention also of certain other writings of Origen. Philo the Jew had published a book of the Hebrew Names of the Old Testament and had added their etymologies and interpretations; Jerome rendered this book in Latin. What Philo had done in the Old Testament, Origen likewise did in the New, and he appended his work to Philo’s work, having Jerome as his imitator. Jerome’s words are these in the Preface to the Book of Hebrew Names: ‘And lest, when the building had been completed, the finishing touch should seem to be lacking, I have interpreted the words and names of the New Testament, wishing in part to imitate Origen, whom no one except an ignorant person denies to have been the teacher of the churches after the apostles. Among the other distinguished monuments of his genius, he also labored at this: what Philo, as a Jew, had omitted, he, as a Christian, completed.’ The same book is mentioned by the author of the *Questions to the Orthodox*, falsely attributed to Justin, in Questions 82 and 86; he says that in it, besides the Hebrew names, Origen also interpreted measures. Let Rufinus therefore consider with what fidelity he wrote in *Invective* 2 against Jerome that Origen did not translate even a single word of Scripture.”

You now know from the testimony of a man celebrated for his learning that Origen was the author of the Book of Hebrew Names in the New Testament. Let the same Peter Daniel Huetius now teach you briefly what Origen’s knowledge of the Hebrew language was. In book 2, chapter 1, section 11 of the *Origeniana*, he writes:

> “If he [Origen] had devoted himself more to Hebrew and had acquired greater proficiency in that language, nothing would have been lacking to him for a perfect knowledge of the Sacred Law. But he lost as much of that glory as he withdrew from the study of this language. For I shall speak truthfully: either those who know little of Hebrew, or those who have read Origen’s works only superficially, attribute to him something exceptional in his knowledge either of the sacred language or of the dialects that arose from this source. Nor does Jerome contradict our opinion [Letter 25 to Paula], even though he seems to contradict it when he says that all Greece marveled at Origen’s singular knowledge of this language. That could indeed have seemed remarkable to Greeks inexperienced in Hebrew and ignorant of how far Origen had advanced in it. Yet Origen himself by no means conceals his ignorance of the language, in Homily 14 on Numbers: ‘They say,’ he writes, ‘who read the Hebrew letters, that in this passage “God” is not written under the sign of the Tetragrammaton; concerning this, let whoever can inquire.’
>
> “We have noted many things in our observations that demonstrate his ignorance of Hebrew. One example is the frivolous distinction he invents between οὐρανόν and οὐρανούς in his Commentary on Matthew 18:18, claiming that Christ referred to this distinction, as though the Syriac dialect used by Christ supported it. Another is the false interpretation of the name Asher found in the Commentary on Matthew 18:19, as though it were derived from ‘he instructed,’ whereas it comes from ‘he bound.’ This may perhaps be excused by the authority of the elders of the Seventy, who sometimes rendered it as though it meant the same thing. Thus, in Psalm 104 [Hebrew 105]:22, instead of the Hebrew [text], they have τοῦ παιδεῦσαι τοὺς ἄρχοντας αὐτοῦ, ‘to instruct his princes.’ The Vulgate has, ‘To instruct his princes.’ And in Hosea 10:10, [the Hebrew text]; the Septuagint has παιδεῦσαι αὐτούς, ‘to instruct them’; the Vulgate, ‘Let them correct them.’
>
> “Another example is the corrupted reading of the passage in the Septuagint interpreters at 2 Esdras 1:11, εὐνοῦχος τῷ βασιλεῖ, ‘a eunuch to the king.’ If he had been at all conversant with Hebrew, he would have corrected what reads [in Hebrew], restoring it in the Septuagint to οἰνοχόος τῷ βασιλεῖ, ‘cupbearer to the king,’ provided, of course, that he himself did not introduce this error; for it is found nowhere in the manuscripts of the ancient Septuagint translators. Another example is the foolish explanation of the word John, which he thought was formed from a prefixed name and [another element], although it is derived solely from [the Hebrew form], with servile letters prefixed.
>
> “He is likewise often mistaken in investigating the origins of Hebrew names. It was easy for a man who was borrowing light to guide his footsteps through unknown places to go astray; Philo the Jew, however, provided the light, having interpreted the Hebrew names of the Old Testament in a special book. Origen appended a corresponding work, comprising an exposition of the Hebrew names of the New Testament. Yet how could Origen, following Philo as his guide, have avoided stumbling, when Philo, although a Jew and descended from Jews, had not been endowed even with a moderate breeze of knowledge of the Hebrew letters, any more than nearly all the other Hellenists? If this is not surprising in men born and raised in Alexandria—of whom Jerome writes that it is contrary to their nature to learn the Hebrew language, following the custom of all Greeks, who are accustomed to disdain the study of foreign languages—it must seem entirely astonishing in that Hebrew Josephus, son of Matthias. For it is easy to detect from his writings that, despite his great and exceptional knowledge of Jewish origins, he did not possess a corresponding command of his native language, although he says that he wrote certain works in Hebrew which were lost through the passage of time.”

[Col. 1201] What answer can the unlearned defenders of Josephus give to this? They scarcely catch even a little breath of Hebrew learning, yet do not hesitate to judge the innermost meanings of the Sacred Law and to ascribe to this writer a knowledge of Hebrew speech which they themselves have not even glimpsed from afar. But it is enough for them to gain popular applause if on this occasion they enter upon a lengthy disputation and use as much labor to persuade people of what they want understood as falsehood always requires in order to appear true.

For our part, adhering to the judgments of sensible and learned men, we do not fear to criticize Philo, Josephus, or Origen wherever the demands of truth require it. But lest we too should seem liable to criticism in presenting the Origenian Lexicon, we shall here make several general observations about it.

The first point to be noted is the order of the Hebrew Names. Throughout the entire Dictionary mentioned above, they are arranged according to the sequence of the letters of the Greek alphabet, without any distinction or mention of the sacred books. Whether Origen himself followed this order is not sufficiently clear. Indeed, the contrary opinion appears more probable, both from Jerome, who repeatedly follows Origen’s footsteps, and from the Greek Origenian Fragment published above by us. That Fragment places the Hebrew names of each Evangelist separately according to the sequence of the letters of the Greek alphabet: the terms found in Matthew are written first, then those belonging to Mark, and so successively down to John.

I can scarcely persuade myself that Origen observed an order distinguished according to the sacred books in the Fragment of the Book of Names, but adopted another method in the Lexicon that survives complete, placing confusedly and indiscriminately under each letter the Names of all the books of the Old and New Testaments. I would therefore more readily believe that this Lexicon was compiled through the ill-advised diligence of some Greek, but was entirely borrowed from Origen’s Book of Hebrew Names, which he himself had published with distinctions both of the volumes of Scripture and of the terms.

I am all the more inclined to this view because I have learned that some Latins did the same thing with Jerome’s Book of Hebrew Names. At Venice, through the brothers Giovanni and Gregorio de Gregori, on 25 August in the year of the Lord 1498, Jerome’s Book of Hebrew Names appeared among his works with this confusion and overturning: all distinction and mention of the books of Scripture had been removed, and absolutely all the terms of both the Old and New Testaments were placed under the letter with which they begin.

The sequence of names in the Origenian Lexicon is therefore extraneous, and belongs to some Greek subverter who, following a perverse rather than an original order, removed the notes and citations of the books from the middle, permitting himself—indulging his own saliva, so to speak—to join together what had been written separately and in parts by Philo and Origen, and to confuse what had been distinguished.

Yet although the order of the Names is defective in the Lexicon, the facts and interpretations of the words are entirely genuine, like pure water drawn from its own spring. I establish this clearly and decisively from two passages in the *Questions and Answers to the Orthodox*, falsely attributed to Justin Martyr.

To Question 82, “What is the explanation of the name Beelzebub?” the Greek author gives the following response:

> τοῦ τε Βεελζεβοὺλ, καὶ τοῦ Βελίαρ, λέγει τὰ ὀνόματα . . . . . εἴρηται δὲ τῷ Ὠριγένει τούτων τῶν ὀνομάτων ἡ ἑρμηνεία ἐν τῇ Ἑρμηνείᾳ τῶν Ἑβραϊκῶν ὀνομάτων

That is:

> “He expresses the names Beelzebul and Beliar . . . . . The interpretation of these names is said by Origen to be found in the Interpretation of the Hebrew Names.”

This response of the Greek writer, whoever he may have been, is entirely confirmed as true by the Origenian Lexicon that follows shortly, where the names Beelzebul and Beliar are read corruptly in exactly the same form as in the quoted Response, and where they have different interpretations appended by Origen.

Question 86: “What is the interpretation of these terms: Mna, Ephi, Nehel, Gomor, Siclus, Basilicon, Sanctum, Stater, Drachma, Quadrans, Hormiscus, Didrachma, Talent, Ass, Seraphim, Bezel, Sabaoth, Adonai, Ephud? For knowledge of both is extremely necessary to us, since both are contained in the Scriptures.”

Response:

> Εἴρηται τῷ Ὠριγένει, ἀνδρὶ ἐπισταμένῳ τὴν τῶν Ἑβραίων διάλεκτον, πάντων τῶν ἐν ταῖς θείαις γραφαῖς φερομένων Ἑβραϊκῶν ὀνομάτων ἢ μέτρων ἡ ἑρμηνεία· ἐκείνην ζητήσας, εὑρήσεις ἐν αὐτῇ τὴν πάντων ἑρμηνείαν ὧν ἐζήτησας.

That is:

> “The interpretation of all the Hebrew names or measures occurring in the divine Scriptures has been set forth by Origen, a man skilled in the Hebrew dialect. If you seek that work, you will find in it the explanation of all the things about which you have inquired.”

The Lexicon that I have called Origenian certainly includes not only the etymologies of Hebrew Names but also interpretations of measures. It therefore appears to be the very work of Adamantius, although, as I observed earlier, the order of the names is confused and altered. If one adds that the Hebrew Names of the New Testament are written and interpreted in the same Lexicon, no room for doubt remains that Origen was its author: as a Christian, he supplied the Names omitted by the Jew Philo.

With these general proofs set forth in advance, let us now turn our hand to the Lexicon itself, which we shall illuminate below with many other particular annotations according to our ability.

[Col. 1203]

# ORIGENIAN LEXICON OF HEBREW NAMES

First published from Codex Royal 772, or 2282; rendered into Latin much more accurately from Vatican 1456; and compared with Jerome’s interpretation. [Note: In Migne, the sections of text headed “Latin Interpretation,” “Vatican Manuscript,” and “Jerome” are printed in parallel.]
