# A

**Adam**, earth-born, human being, or [Note: The word γῆ (“earth”) has been omitted in the manuscript; it is supplied by the earlier Greek Fragment of the *Book of Hebrew Names*. Moreover, Philo, or Origen, confuses the Hebrew *Adam* with *Ada* and *Ud*, and consequently derives the etymologies “of things coming” or “of those who come,” and “testimony.” The learned Jerome does not do this: he interprets the name *Ada* from the Hebrew *Ud* as “testimony,” but *Adam* as “red earth,” from the root *adam* with aleph, meaning “to redden” and “to be red.”] red, or earth clothed with flesh, or coming earth, or testimony.

**Adama**, virgin earth, or blood-colored earth. [Note: I have no doubt that Ἀδάμα should be restored here. Josephus (*Antiquities*, book I) agrees, as does Hesychius, who interprets it as “virginal.” Pliny relates that virgin soil was discovered by Esubope (*Natural History* XXXIII.3); and the scholiast on Apollonius, at II.874, calls the island of Samos Παρθενία, “Virgin.”]

**Abel**, from God, or bringing toward God, or vapor, or mourning. [Note: We have said more about this Greek interpretation of the name Abel in the first preceding Fragment. Consult our scholia.]

**Abraham**, father of the Most High, or father of a son. [Note: The Greeks interpret the name Aaron with complete violence: properly, it means “mountainous,” or “mountain of strength.”]

**Aaron**, ark, or seeing visions, or word, or height, or mighty, or spirit.

**Abdiou**, my servant, [Note: Jerome seems to have read Θεοῦ, “of God” or “of the Lord”; certainly this is much more correct.] confessor. [Note: In the name Abdiou, interpreters find an etymology meaning “confessing,” because among the Greeks Ἀβιοὺδ was often corruptly read for Abia, and Ἀβδιοὺδ for Abdia. Hence they supposed that the name was formed [Note: The Greek interpreters derived this from *jada*, “he confessed.”] from *jada*, “he confessed.”]

**Ebenezer**, a helping people, or stone of the helper.

**Absalom**, the father’s peace upon them.

**Aminadab**, [Note: The first exposition of this name itself suggests that Ἀβιναδὰβ should be restored; moreover, β and μ are frequently confused in Greek manuscripts. The Vatican manuscript also errs in the final β, reading Ἀμιναδὰμ, and places this after the following Ἀβιγάην.] my father’s good pleasure, or a desirable nation. [Note: We discussed the name Aminadab, in place of Abinadab, in our scholia. Here it should be observed that the Greeks interpret the word in both its corrupt and its correct forms: Aminadab means “desirable people,” whereas Abinadab means “the good pleasure of my father,” that is, “inclination of will.”]

**Abigaen**, the revelation of my father, or dew. [Note: The following etymology makes it easy to understand that the Greek writer read Abigael, or Abigail, as Abigaen.]

**Appho**, [Note: In the Vatican manuscript, τὰ νῦν (“the present things”). Some read Ἀπφοὺς from the Hebrew epithet by which Jonathan, brother of Judas Maccabaeus, is called in 1 Maccabees 2:5.] now, just now; thus I found it. [Note: This name is read in the Septuagint at 2 Kings 2:14: Ποῦ ὁ Θεὸς Ἠλιοὺ Ἀφφὼ, “Where is the God of Elijah, Appho?” Jerome rendered it in Latin from the Hebrew *aph-hu*, or *aph-o*, “even now?”—or perhaps from *aphpho*, which the Septuagint and Jerome seem to have read in Hebrew copies. That adverb also occurs with a final ο, as in Genesis 27:33, *mi appho hu*, “who, then, is he?”, in place of the modern *aph-hu*. We may therefore suspect that in ancient times, at least in some manuscripts, the name *aphpho*, or ἀπφὼ, was read; it survives in the Greek Origenian Lexicon. To whom the following brief note, οὕτως εὗρον (“thus I found it”), should be attributed—whether to Origen, reporting that he found ἀπφὼ written in Hebrew, or to the Greek writer, indicating that he had not invented the name’s etymology but had received and transcribed it from another—is left to the reader’s judgment.]

**Abraham**, chosen father, father of sons, or one who crosses over, or father of the Most High, or conspicuous father. [Note: Suidas calls ἀπόβλεπτος a conspicuous and celebrated man, which fits Abraham especially well, distinguished as he was in fame and virtue. I therefore render βλεπτὸς as “conspicuous,” without changing the Greek word in the manuscript.]

**Abeiron**, lofty father.

**Haggai**, festivals, or those celebrating festivals.

**Agrippas**, suddenly turning around.

**Anchous**, washing-off [Note: In the Vatican manuscript, ἐπικάλυμμα, “covering,” “lid,” or “veil,” which has the opposite sense.] or uncovering. [Note: I have not yet been able to discover from where the corrupt name Agchus was taken here, nor to determine it by conjecture.]

**Aermon**, heavenly light, or spirit.

**Azael**, conspicuous, vision, or strength, or might of God.

**Azeka**, strengthening.

**Athens**, [Note: This etymology is very corrupt in the Royal Greek manuscript, which reads καὶ ρῶ διασκεζόμεναι, a phrase meaning nothing. I have joined what was separated, supplied what was omitted, and removed the faulty accent, guided by Jerome’s interpretation, which he declared above, in his collection of names from Acts, to be forced and foreign to him. For the following two names, consult what we said there in the Notes.] scattered in season. [Note: The Vatican manuscript likewise has διασκεζόμεναι.]

**Egypt**, darkness, or affliction, or foreign residence.

**Ethiopia**, humiliation.

**Elamites**, looking aside.

**Abba**, father.

**Ebed-melech**, serving a king.

**Achar**, distortion, firstborn. [Note: The Greeks confuse Achar with Bechar, or Bechor, which means “firstborn.”]

**Ahikam**, the resurrection of my brother.

**Ahimelech**, my brother is the king.

**Achor**, distortion.

**Aoth**, confessor, praise.

**Abner**, lamp of the father, or lamp of the son.

**Abijah**, of the father, or father of a son, or my father. [Note: For Abia, the Greeks may have had Abiar written somewhere; hence they wished to derive it from *ab*, “father,” and *bar*, “son.”]

**Abiathar**, empty. [Note: In the Vatican manuscript, ῆν is written in place of κενόν.]

**Abiazer**, O calculator of the father. [Note: In the Hieronymian context above, we read Abiezri for Abiezer, which we said was wrongly interpreted as “the help of my God,” since *abi* means “of my father.” The Greek etymology is expressed in the vocative case. ἐκλόγιστος is one who calculates, weighs, and estimates after making an account, or who gives something counted out; compare ἐκλογίζομαι. But how the Hebrew *abiezer* corresponds to the Greek ἐκλόγιστε, I do not yet understand. Perhaps the Greeks looked to *aza*, which is certainly closer to the Greek word than *azar*.]

**Abimelech**, kingdom of the father, or father is king.

**Abiud**, the approaching father.

**Agabus**, angel, evangelization. [Note: Perhaps εὐάγγελος, “evangelist” or “bringer of good news,” should be read in Greek instead of εὐαγγελισμός, “evangelization.” Jerome’s interpretation, which he rejects as forced, seems at least to indicate this.]

**Agag**, roof, or calf.

**Hagar**, dwelling as a foreigner, or gathering, or proselyte. [Note: The Hebrew verb *agar*, meaning “to collect and heap together,” corresponds well to the Greek συστρέφω, “to roll together into a bundle,” or “to gather.” Thus Hagar, interpreted in Greek as συστρέφουσα, should be rendered in Latin as “gathering” or “collecting.”]

**Angel**, work, or circumcision, or word. [Note: The Greek name is not interpreted by Jerome. I cannot at all determine by conjecture why it should mean “work” or “office,” unless the Greeks derived it figuratively from *hhag*, meaning the sacrifice of a feast. It may also be said to mean “word,” as though derived from *aga* or *hegeh*, that is, speech, meditation, or groaning. Finally, the Hebrew *namal* approaches the Greek word ἄγγελος by force: through the affinity of γ and נ, and by means of ל, it conveys the meaning of circumcision.]

**Ader**, beauty.

**Adrias**, restraint of evils.

**Adonai**, Lord.

**Aza**, her strength, or brother. [Note: I think that the Greeks should read not Aza here but Achaz, or at least Oza, because those words contain *ahh*, meaning “brother”; and Uza or Oza means “his strength.”]

**Azariah**, help of the Lord, or turning back of the Lord.

**Azotus**, strength, or tower-fire. [Note: Jerome advises the reader as follows: “Azolus is called ESDOD in Hebrew, and according to its former name its etymology is ‘fire of the uncle.’” This is, unless I am mistaken, expressed in Greek by πυργένεια, which I leave written as it stands, lest I provoke certain critics to quarrels. I am aware, however, that γένεια, plural, is often used for γένειον, “chin” or “beard.” But if “fire of the uncle” is to be understood according to Jerome, it should be written πῦρ γέννας, that is, “fire of the uncle.”]

**Aidem**, bloodshed, or delight.

**Ailam**, road, or vestibule, or colonnade.

**Akeldama**, field of blood.

**Akarim**, cattle enclosure.

**Akrabbin**, scorpion.

**Alexander**, restraint of nations.

**Allophyles**, those falling upon a corpse. [Note: The Allophyles are the Philistines, whom Saint Jerome interprets as “falling by the cup,” from the Hebrew *naphal* and *sethi*. The Greeks derive the interpretation from *naphal* and *nephesh*, that is, “corpse.”] [Note: Nevertheless, since Jerome immediately translates it “falling by the cup,” I think that πτώματι, “by a corpse,” was read by him as πόματι, “by a cup” or “drink,” and that the Greeks once wrote it more correctly in this form.]

**Alphaeus**, departing, or χίλος of the same. [Note: χιλὸς with the grave accent means “fodder”; in the manuscript it is accented χίλος. It seems to have been placed here for χιλίοι or χιλιοστὸς, meaning “thousandth.” Jerome’s interpretation supports this conjecture, as does the Hebrew *alaph* or *elaph*, “thousand,” or also “he taught.”]

**Amalek**, a people licking up, or turning aside.

**Habakkuk**, reception.

**Aminadab**, desirable nation, or well-regarded people.

**Amyon**, faith, or our people.

**Amplias**, a people working in bronze. [Note: Martianay had read the somewhat more corrupt Ἀπλὴν, Aplen, from the Royal manuscript. The Greek text of Romans 16:8 has Ἀμπλίαν; other books have Ἀμπλιάτον.]

**Amphipolis**, a people fallen by the mouth.

**Ana-meel**, grace of God, or grace of death, circumcision. [Note: Since *mul* means “to circumcise” and *muth* in Hebrew means “death,” the Greeks attach these different etymologies to the word Anameel.]

**Andronicus**, distinguished.

**Hannah**, her grace, or glory.

**Annas**, gracious. [Note: The Vatican manuscript has χαριστάμενος.]

**Antipatris**, grace of relaxation. [Note: From Jerome’s interpretation, the Greek should apparently read αἰνέσεως, “of praise,” rather than ἀνέσεως. Jerome rejects this etymology as forced and foreign to him, plainly indicating that it belonged to the Greeks. He therefore read αἰνέσεως in his Greek copies, not ἀνέσεως.]

**Apollos**, gathering them.

**Apphius Phoro**, fruitfulness of freedom.

**Aradus**, descent.

**Ararat**, testimony, or plucked out. [Note: In place of τεπιλυμένη in the manuscript, τετιλλομένη, “plucked” or “tweaked,” should be read, as we have printed it. Moreover, according to the evidence of the letters, the name Ararat cannot mean “testimony.” We should therefore follow Jerome, who interprets Ararat as Armenia, or “plucked-up mountain,” from the Hebrew *ara*, “he plucked and tore away,” and *erer*, which means “mountain” in Latin.] [Note: The same manuscript has τετιλμένη.]

**Areopagus**, a feast being gnawed around, or being scattered.

**Ekron**, barrenness, or uprooting.

**Aquila**, pain, elevation.

**Hallelujah**, praise to the living God. [Note: Martianay has Ἀλλελούια.]

**Hamath**, my faith, or an arriving race.

**Amman**, race from someone.  
**Ammon**, from my race. [Note: The same manuscript has Ἀμανίτις, Ammanitis. If the word denotes the territory of the Ammonites, it should be written Ἀμανίτης; if an inhabitant, Ἀμανῖτις.]

**Amasa**, elevation of my people.

**Amen**, let it be.

**Amorite**, spoken of, or making bitter, or a people being torn away. [Note: The same manuscript has ἀποσπάσμενος.]

**Anathoth**, empty answer, or conception of death. [Note: To give Anathoth the meaning of death, the middle letter mem must be supplied, producing *Anathmoth*; for *moth*, or *muth*, means “death.”]

**Ananias**, gift of the Lord.

**Andrew**, beautiful strength, or constitution, or answering. [Note: Jerome’s Latin translation indicates that the Greek νόμον, accented on the penultimate syllable, was written by scribal error for the barytone νομὸν, “pasture” or “fodder.” νόμος means “law.” Jerome also rightly adds that this is forced, and that according to the Greek etymology Andrew should better be called ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς, “from the man,” that is, “manly.”]

**Antiochia**, poverty, or having become silent. [Note: Martianay has σεγήσασα; the Vatican manuscript, as above, gives the corrected reading.]

**Apelles**, gathering them.

**Apollo**, gathering, their instruction.

**Arabia**, sunset, or evening.

**Aram**, vision, or light, or word.

**Arioch**, lion, or the king. [Note: Arioch does not mean “king”; it is the name of the king of Pontus, Genesis 14:1 and 9.] [Note: The Vatican has ὁ βασιλέως. I would therefore prefer to regard ὁ as an article, or as the abbreviated form of the letter used for the word “name.”]

**Armathém**, numbered mountains, or conception, or attack. [Note: It has already been observed in many places how freely the Greeks invent etymologies; this is especially evident in the present word Armathém, which has partly a Hebrew and partly a Greek etymology. *Ararim* means “mountains,” while ἀριθμητική means “the art of counting.”] [Note: The same manuscript has προβολὴ, “advance” or “array.”]

**Artemas**, cursing.

**Arodi**, ruling. [Note: The shorthand of the Royal manuscript requires this reading; but the genuine etymology of Arodi is not κατάρχων, “ruling,” but κατάρατον, “accursed,” or “worthy of execration.”]

**Assa**, delighting, or strengthened.

**Asaph**, gathering, or of ointments.

**Asedek**, righteousness of the sun. [Note: For the Hebrew term meaning Heliopolis, or, as Jerome has it, “city of the sun,” the Septuagint interpreted the word as πόλις Ἀσεδὲκ in Isaiah 19:18. In that passage the holy Doctor says: “In place of ‘city of the sun,’ the Septuagint, wishing I knew what, interpreted ‘Asedek.’”]

**Asher**, wealth, or blessedness.

**Asida**, the appearance of her mercy, or the heron, which is called the stork. [Note: Jerome discusses Asida in his letter to Sunia and Fretela.]

**Assyrians**, directing straight.

**Asynkritus**, directing incense.

**Aunan**, spring, or wounded in heart.

**Appho**, fathers. [Note: Consult what was said above about the word Appho. Do not be surprised that it is interpreted here as “fathers”: the Greeks frequently interchange π and β, and conversely β and π. Thus they understand Aphpho as though it were *abboth*, “fathers.”]

**Ahaz**, strength.

**Arab**, of strength.

**Arinath**, her height. [Note: Martianay had read ὅσον from the Royal manuscript; with the support of the Vatican manuscript, we correct it to νόσον.]

**Aristarchus**, raising up a crown of humiliation.

**Arioth**, wild vegetables.

**Armageddon**, an uprising toward what lies ahead.

**Aroer**, their newness.

**Artemis**, raising up illness. [Note: Jerome advises that νόσους, “illnesses,” should be read in Greek instead of the corrupt ὅσον, since νόσους means “diseases.” Thus Artemis is understood as “she who raises up illnesses” or “sicknesses.”] [Note: Martianay had read ὅσον from the Royal manuscript; with the support of the Vatican manuscript, we correct it to νόσον.]

**Arphaxad**, visible prophecy, or troubled misery. [Note: This kind of etymology is not foreign to Philo. See below.]

**Asael**, work of God, or shadow.

**Asemoth**, bones.

**Aseneth**, accident. [Note: The following two headings, Aseroth and Assur, were missing from the Royal manuscript and consequently also from Martianay’s edition. The word σύμπτωμα, which is the etymology of the name Aseneth, was also missing. Consequently, the words belonging to Assur, εὔθυμος ἢ Μεσοποταμία, were grievously distorted and joined to Aseneth, as though they were its own interpretation, although nothing corresponds to it less. We have supplied the lacuna from the Vatican archetype and restored the proper interpretation of each word in the Latin section as well.]

**Aseroth**, blessings.

**Assur**, cheerful, or Mesopotamia.

**Assarion**, a tenth of a coin. [Note: The Greek word *assarion* occurs at Matthew 10:29 and derives from the Latin *as*, *assis*. An obolus is an Italian coin. According to the Greek etymology, it is a tenth part of a coin, or our copper denarius. I assert nothing, however, in a matter that remains sufficiently uncertain and doubtful.]

**Astarte**, Aphrodite, or also Ashtaroth.

**Augustus**, celebrating, or creation, an added festival.

**Ausitis**, race of counsel, or of one deliberating.

**Ahab**, brother of my father.

**Achaia**, their brotherhood.

**Ahiezer**, my brother’s help. [Note: We emend according to the Vatican manuscript, which has βοήθεια, “help,” where Martianay, from the Royal manuscript, read βοηθὶ. Although he says that βοηθὶ seems corruptly written for βοήθει or βοήθεια, I nevertheless did not wish to alter the manuscript reading, because of the prejudices of certain critics, which I mentioned briefly above.]

**Ahimaas**, the counsel of my brother.

**Ahitub**, my brother is good.

**Ahithophel**, my brother’s [Note: The Vatican also has τρῶσις, but, so far as I know, πτῶσις—“fall,” “ruin,” “precipitation,” and similar meanings—should easily be restored. These agree with Jerome’s interpretation.] eating; in Latin, *akétou edphelle*, that is, vinegar and gall. [Note: The Greek interpretation of the name Ahitophel is a charming invention produced by the Greeks for Latin readers. But it is spurious and must therefore be rejected; we should send it back to Greece.]

# B

**Baal**, [Note: From the name Baalim, given a little below, we are warned that δαιμόνια should be understood here—that is, “demons,” or the powers and rulers of these darknesses whom the Apostle calls, in Ephesians 6:12, τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις, “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.”] those who have gone up, or higher, or lower.

**Babylon**, confusion of change, or captivity.

**Bethuel**, of the one who is coming, or virgin, or powerless daughter of God.

**Bethel**, house of God.

**Bethsamos**, house of salvation.

**Ammon**, son of my race; he is the father. [Note: The Royal Greek manuscript places here the names Ammon and Moab, whose interpretation it borrowed in full, with a few alterations, from Genesis 19:37–38.] He became the father of the Ammonites from the younger daughter, and from the elder, Moab, from my father; he is the father of the Moabites. [Note: The Vatican manuscript has γεννᾶται, “is born.”]

**Baal**, demon, or one who rejoices.

**Belshazzar**, vanity joined with blessedness.

**Barak**, house of labor, or spirit. [Note: The Greeks interpret Beth-horon here rather than the name Barak, which is in no way suited to the meaning “house of labor.”]

**Bartholomew**, son of the one who suspended the waters. [Note: Martianay, from the Royal manuscript, had κρεμάσας in the nominative, “suspending.” The reading is corrected from the Vatican manuscript.]

**Barne**, a shaken son, or of Salo.

**Bashan**, shame of dryness, or of what has been broken.

**Beelzebul**, demon, a tavern-keeper, or one swallowing in the repose of the mouth; it is also the name of a certain Priapus of obscene, oversized member. [Note: This material belongs here. In the Royal manuscript the word κακελὺς is written; we changed it to καπελεὺς because it better suits the sense of the passage. Since Martianay had already taken such liberty as to emend it conjecturally to καπελεὺς, we may, following Clericus, restore the word more correctly as καπηλεὺς, which properly means “tavern-keeper”; and *zabul*, as Clericus himself notes, means “inn” or “tavern.” See what we noted above in the fifth Fragment under the word Beelzebul. The Vatican manuscript shortly afterward also reads πριάμου instead of πριάπου.]

**Barzillai**, knowledge of a journey, or of iron.

**Belial**, apostate, or transgressor, or seeker, or light of the blind.

**Benjamin**, child of sorrow, or son of days. [Note: For this etymology of Benjamin, see our notes below under Philo and in the Greek Fragments.]

**Baalim**, higher demons: the sun, moon, and air.

**Baddai**, distinguished garment, or linen, or variegated garment.

**Bernice**, chosen, shaken.

**Bezalel**, in the shadow of God.

**Beor**, in the skin. [Note: We restore βεὼρ according to the Vatican archetype, compelled by the etymology itself: ἐν δέρματι, “in the skin.” Martianay, from the Royal manuscript, had inserted βεελφεὼρ, Beelpheor, and likewise placed that name in the Latin columns. But it is another name, with another etymology; Jerome explains it as “the leathern mouth.”]

**Bethany**, house of glory, or house of affliction, or house of obedience.

**Bethsaida**, house of hunters, or of provisions.

**Bethphage**, house of success, or house of jaws, where the priests lived near the Mount of Olives.

**Boanerges**, sons of thunder, or of the Most High.

**Boaz**, in strength, powerful coming.

**Bosor**, flesh.

**Bethlehem**, house of bread, or of life.

**Beth-horon**, house of spies.

**Balaam**, accursed, or frustration of the people, or word, or agreement.

**Baneas**, building materials.

**Barabbas**, son of the father, or son of our teacher.

**Bar Jonah**, son of a dove.

**Bar Jonah**, son of Jonah.

**Barnabas**, son of consolation.

**Baruch**, blessed.

**Barsabbas**, son of one who turns back, or son of one who rests.

**Batos**, worship, or hatred.

**Beersheba**, daughter was given, or daughter filled. [Note: The Greeks, according to their custom, confuse Bersabee with Bethsabee; that name means “daughter who has been filled,” or “daughter of satiety.”]

**Bel**, antiquity, or Cronus.

**Bosora**, this restraint, or body.

**Buzite**, despised.

# G

**Gabaathon**, lofty things.

**Gabbatha**, paved with stones.

**Gaber**, a foreign resident among many, or man. [Note: Here the Greeks—or Origen or Philo himself—state that the name Gaber means “man.” This is consistently affirmed by the lexicons of the Oriental languages, Hebrew, Chaldean, and Syriac, where *gebar* or *gaber* means the same as “man.” Hence Gabriel below is not badly rendered νεανίσκος θεοῦ, “young man of God,” since *gebor* means “strong” and “robust,” as young men and adolescents are.]

**Gabriel**, young man of God, or mighty, or strong, or mountainous of God, or man of God. [Note: The Vatican manuscript has ὄριος, “border” or “terminal,” and does not contain the second θεοῦ after ἄνθρωπος.]

**Gadara**, this is the sojourn of a generation.

**Geder**, flock.

**Gaza**, her strength, or of strength, always wealth.

**Gazerin**, dwelling of Gebal, clefts of ancient things.

**Gilead**, habitation, testimony of Jason. [Note: The Vatican also gives this corrupt reading. It should be restored, as Clericus teaches, to μαρτυρίας σωρὸς, “heap of testimony,” which Jerome likewise translated.] [Note: Perhaps the Greek copyist intended to write Ἰάκωβος, or Ἰακώβου, “Jacob” or “of Jacob”; for Gilead was the testimony of Laban and Jacob, not of some Jason. See Genesis 31:48.]

**Gilgal**, place of testing, or those being held together, or those being gathered. [Note: The Vatican has συνεχόμενοι, “held together,” or “adhering.”]

**Gamaliel**, recompense of God, or spoken by God.

**Geth**, mountain, or cleft, or ravine, or winepress.

**Gilboa**, revelation of the heart.

**Galgal**, rolling, rolling around, or wheel in a four-faced wheel. [Note: The Vatican has ἐν τρίγχῳ, “in a wall.” The Greek writer was referring to the wheels of Ezekiel 1:16.]

**Gerasinon**, suburb.

**Gephar**, surrounding inhabitants.

**Gera**, settlement of those seeing, or rumination.

**Gershom**, a foreign resident there.

**Gihon**, breast, or cleft, or incision of grace, or because God fashioned the human being from earth. [Note: See what was said somewhat above concerning the source of such Greek etymologies.]

**Gaesus**, weapon of war. [Note: The manuscript corruptly reads γησσὸς for γαισός. A *gaesus*—which the Latins call *gasum* or *gesum* in the neuter—is a type of weapon, in both sacred and profane writers. The Hebrew is *chidon*, Joshua 8:18 and elsewhere; Judith 9 has καὶ γαισῷ, “and with a gaesus.” Consult Hesychius, Suidas, and Pollux, lest we confuse a shield or buckler with a weapon.]

**Gedaliah**, greatness of peoples.

**Gideon**, judgment beside, or judgment against.

**Gothoniel**, answer of God, or my time of God.

**Golgotha**, skull.

**Gomor**, a *corus*, ξςλ., or ten cotylae. [Note: Gomor, or Corus, contained sixty—if I read ξ. ς. λ. correctly—or held ten cotylae. There is no difficulty concerning the cotylae, since Ezekiel 45:14 expressly says that ten cotylae are a Gomor. On this measure, Gomor or Corus, consult Epiphanius, *On Measures and Weights*, Jerome on Ezekiel 45, Theodoret, Isidore, and others.]

**Gad**, houses.

**Goliath**, uncovered.

**Gabeth**, lofty and elevated things.

**Gabriel**, God is the same and man; *Gabri*, man; and *El*, God. [Note: This heading has been restored almost in full according to the Vatican manuscript. Martianay had read only Γαυριὴλ, θεὸς, “Gabriel, God,” from the Royal manuscript, and that somewhat corruptly.]

**Gaddi**, trial, or my place of testing.

**Galatia**, being magnified, or being transferred.

**Galilee**, rolling place, or migration, or revelation.

**Gebal**, ancient ravine.

**Gideon**, judgment beside.

**Gethsemane**, ravine of rich things, or some obedience of rest, or “the Lord himself judged.”

**Gennesaret**, garden of rulers.

**Gerar**, enclosure.

**Gergesenes**, expelling a settlement, or bringing in settlers. [Note: Martianay, from the Royal manuscript, had falsely and absurdly read πάροικοι ἐκκεκληκότες, “foreign residents who summoned,” instead of παροικίαν ἐκβεβληκότες, “expelling a habitation,” which we restore from the Vatican manuscript. Jerome’s translation, “expelling a settler,” confirms the restored reading; so does Adamantius, who elsewhere, and especially in volume X on John, page 160, says that when the inhabitants of the city of Gergesa asked Jesus to depart from their borders, the city thereby, as though it had then first received its name, was called Γέργεσα, ἑρμηνεύεται παροικία ἐκβεβληκότων, “Gergesa is interpreted as the habitation of those who expel.” The learned Huetius likewise notes in this passage that Origen derives the word from [Hebrew omitted in the supplied text], whence [Hebrew omitted], “habitation,” and [Hebrew omitted], “he expelled.”]

**Gehor**, the foreign resident.

**Glossocomon**, their light. [Note: We read the Greek word γλωσσόκομον at John 13:29; Jerome interprets it as “money-box,” while the Greeks explain it as “their light,” because they are looking not to the Greek word *glossocomon* but to the Hebrew *aron*. *Aron* means a small chest or box, called in Greek γλωσσόκομον. Hence, in place of *baaron* at Genesis 50:26, the Jerusalem Targum has *biglusecema*, which is the Greek γλωσσόκομον.]

**Gotholia**, this is my time.

**Gomorrah**, fear of the people, or blindness, or barrenness.

# D

**Daber**, ark, or oracle, or speech, or power.

**Dagon**, a kind of fish, or grief; it is also said to be a gift, holy things, or Zeus of the fields. [Note: The Greek interpretation of the name Dagon is composed partly from the sacred text and partly from mythological accounts. Dagon was worshiped by the Philistines at Ashdod, where there was both a temple of Dagon and an idol with a human form, 1 Samuel 5:1–2 and following. Dagon was also the god of grain and inventor of the plow, called ἀρουραῖος—“of the fields”—as a grain god and guardian of cultivated land. Hence Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.7, says that Janus was taught knowledge of agriculture by Saturn. Saturn, therefore, with his sickle, and rural Jupiter are to be regarded as the same.]

**Dathan**, judgment, given, sufficient gift.

**Delilah**, drawing out, or bucket, or judgment for me.

**Dedan**, beautiful, judged. [Note: The Vatican manuscript adds the letters Ἐθ`, and at the margin of the book the sign Ζτ., indicating that something should be sought and examined more carefully.]

**Damaris**, silent head.

**Dan**, strong judgment.

**Daniel**, judgment of God.

**Deblatha**, or Daphne of Antioch. [Note: The Greek writer omitted the etymology of the word Deblatha, as is clear from the particle ἢ, “or,” which presupposes an earlier interpretation. Daphne was a suburb of Antioch, enclosed within a circuit of eighty stadia according to Strabo. It contained a very pleasant grove and a temple of Apollo together with a shrine of Diana, as Julius Capitolinus relates; he calls it Epidaphne.] [Note: The word παλάθην, *palatham*, must clearly be supplied here. This was the name for masses of fat dried figs, shaped like bricks. See what we said about this name from Jerome. A new heading must then begin: “Daphne of Antioch.” Martianay had read Ἀντιοχίας.]

**Deborah**, wise, learning, or bee.

**Demas**, being silent.

**Denarius**, a gold coin. [Note: We restored this heading from the Vatican manuscript. Previously, with the name Δηνάριον omitted, the words νόμισμα χρυσοῦν, “gold coin,” were joined in a single sequence, through a gross error, to Δῆμας, as though they were another etymology of Demas.]

**Devil**, a heavy pouring-down, and greatly.

**Dionysius**, distinguished, being distinguished.

**Dew of Aermon**, dew being glorified.

**Damascus**, kiss of blood, or watering with blood.

**David**, sufficient by hand, or uniquely desired, or beloved, pitied, or contemptible. [Note: Jerome’s column teaches us the true etymology of the name David. The other interpretations found among the Greeks may indeed suit David if one considers his life and deeds, but they are very far from the point if one seeks the etymology of the name.]

**Dekdera**, she kept watch here, or level, broad, and fertile. [Note: The Vatican has Δεκρὰ, “Decra,” and shortly afterward πλατῶ instead of πλατεῖ.]

**Demetrius**, sufficient to avenge.

**Deina**, her judgment.

**Diapsalma**, always, or change of rhythm, or temporary, or of a season. [Note: The same manuscript leaves an empty space as large as would be needed for entering this word; nevertheless, it represents πρὸς, “toward,” before the preceding syllable, and places the marginal sign Ζτ., meaning “seek.”]

**Diospolis**, by nodding assent.

**Doke**, shaking.

**Dothan**, sufficient eclipse.

## E

**Ἔβερ** — crossing, or crossing over.  
**[Note: [Col. 1220A]** Here the Greeks interpret the word *Hebrew* as though it were written with a *daleth* at the beginning, *Dabereth*, that is, “sentence” or “word.”**]**

**Ἑβραῖος** — understanding.  
**Ἔγλων** — a wheel-track.  
**Ἐδὲμ** — delight, or the highest point, or a desirable land, or bloodletting.  
**Ἐζεκίας** — strength.  
**Ἐλεηλὰ** — knowledge of God.  
**Ἐλεσσὰ** — the work of God.  
**Ἐλιακεὶμ** — the resurrection of God.  
**Ἐλὴμ** — the place of God.  

**[Note: [Col. 1220A]** The same must be thought and said of the exceedingly corrupt word *Eexe* as of the preceding *Decdera*.**]**

**Ἐέξη** — the grace of God.  
**[Note: [Col. 1220B]** Again the Vatican manuscript has *Ἔαξη* instead of *Ἔεξη*.**]**

[Col. 1221]

**Ἑβραῖος** — one who crosses over, or one who has crossed through.  
**Ἐγκρυφίας** — one hidden in the ember-bed.  
**Ἐδὼμ** — earthly, or red, or one who is failing away.  
**Ἔλαιον** — divinity, or those who labor.  
**[Note: [Col. 1221A]** Martianus had read *προστονοῦνδε* from the Royal manuscript, quite corruptly and with scarcely any sense, and translated it “to whom, then?” From Jerome’s interpretation, which we present in full in its own column, it is easily established that the true reading is that of the Vatican manuscript, which we have restored: *προσπονοῦντες*, meaning “those who labor.”**]**

**Ἐλέει** — knowledge of God.  
**Ἐλεάζερ** — the calling of God.  
**[Note: [Col. 1221A]** “Elaeonis,” that is, “of the Mount of Olives,” which is interpreted as “divinity” or “those who labor.” Thus Saint Jerome a little above.**]**

**Ἔλαινος** — divinity.  
**Ἐλιὰμ** — my God, my father.  
**[Note: [Col. 1221A]** Martianus has *Ἐλιάζερ* (*Eliazer*), and immediately afterward *Ἐλισαβὲ*, instead of the Vatican manuscript’s *Ἐλισάβετ*.**]**

**Ἐλίεζερ** — the help of my God.  
**Ἐλιμέλεχ** — the kingdom of God.  
**Ἐλισάβετ** — the rest of the Lord, or fullness.  
**Ἐλισοὺρ** — the salvation of God, or “God is my strength.”  
**Ἐλισσαιὲ** — the salvation of God, or shade.  
**Ἐλκανὰ** — the possession of God, or glory.  

**[Note: [Col. 1221A]** In Numbers 33:47 the name *Helmon-Deblathaim* is read; but *Helmon*, or *Elmune*, does not mean “the portion of God.” It is therefore better that the name *Helcia*, or *Helcath*, be set against the word *Elmune*.**]**

**Ἐλμουνὴ** — the portion of God.  
**Ἐλοὶμ** — the perfection of God.  
**Ἔλσαμους** — the sun of God.  
**Ἔλωε** — God.  
**[Note: [Col. 1222A]** The Vatican manuscript has *Ἐλωέν*. Immediately afterward it has *Σαπφαρεὶμ*; among the Septuagint manuscripts, *Σεπφαρουαῒμ* or *Σεφφαρουαΐμ*.**]**

**Ἐλοὶν** — God has come.  
**Ἔμαο καὶ Ἀρφὰθ, καὶ Σαπαφαρεὶμ** — Chaldean idols.  
**Ἐμμὸρ** — word, or a speaking ass.  
**Ἐννὰ** — of living creatures.  
**[Note: [Col. 1222A]** The same manuscript has *ζωὴ* (“life”) instead of *ζώων* (“of living creatures”).**]**  
**ἔνυστρον** — belly.  
**[Note: [Col. 1222A]** The Royal manuscript itself, folio 46, has explained what *ἔνυστρον* means: *ἔνυστρον, τὸ ἔσωθεν τῆς κοιλίας, ἐν ᾧ ἡ κόπρος*, that is, “enustron, the interior of the belly, in which the dung is.”**]**

**Ἐνὼχ** — renewal.  
**Ἐρμωνὴ** — accursed, or an elevated light.  
**[Note: [Col. 1222A]** The Vatican manuscript likewise prefers this reading. But Clericus says that one must certainly read *ὄρος μετέωρον*, “a high mountain”; for it was well known that the inhabitants called a part of Mount Anti-Libanus by this name, and this is the Arabic meaning of the word.**]**

**Ἐσρὼμ** — the final supplication, or an arrow, or an everlasting bow.  
**Εὐηλὰτ** — “show here,” and “the inhabited world.”  
**Εὐφράτης** — dispersion, or fruitfulness, or salvation.  
**Ἐφοὺδ** — declaration and truth; in it are the oracle, redemption, or the censer.  
**Ἐφραΐμ** — enlargement, or consolation, or dispersion.  
**[Note: [Col. 1222A]** The same manuscript has *πλατὺς*, “broad.”**]**

**Ἐλισὰ** — the sheep of my God.  
**Ἐλισαμὰ** — the hearing of God.  
**Ἐλησὰφ** — the quiet of God.  
**Ἐλισαφὰν** — the watchtower of God.  
**Ἐλιφὰζ** — the dispersion of God.  
**Ἔλλην** — one who prays, or their god.  
**Ἐλμοδὰδ** — the measuring-out of God, or one who is moved.  
**Ἐλύμας** — one who causes to depart.  
**Ἐμὰθ** — anger, or provocation.  

[Col. 1223]

**[Note: [Col. 1223A]** This word is compounded from the Greek preposition *ἐν*, “in,” and the Hebrew word *negeb*, which means “south” and “noon”; hence among the Greeks: *Enageb*, “in the south.” Jerome did not read this word in this form.**]**

**Ἐναγὲβ** — in the south.  
**Ἐνὰχ** — brother of God, or humility, or eternal.  
**[Note: [Col. 1223A]** Instead of *ἀνέοια*, one should perhaps read *αἰωνία*, that is, “eternal.”**]**

**Ἐνὼς** — one who has forgotten.  
**Ἔραστος** — my brother.  
**Ἐσσεβῶν** — a thought of sorrow, or an increase of fruitfulness.  
**Εὐὰ** — life.  
**Εὔτυχος** — one who is astonished.  
**Εὐφραθὰ** — consolation, or fruitfulness.  

## Z

**Ζαβουλὼν** — age, or *idam*.  
**[Note: [Col. 1223A]** The Vatican manuscript has *ἐδὰμ*.**]**  
**[Note: [Col. 1223A]** I could extract nothing beyond what I have printed here. But I openly confess that I do not know what *idam* is, unless *ἴδιον* should be read instead of *ἰδὰμ*. In Hesychius, *ἲδιον* itself means *οἰκεῖον*, “belonging to the household,” or “dwelling,” which plainly suits the etymology of Zebulun.**]**  
**Ζαβουλὼν** — or a gift, or their flow.  

**Ζαχαρίας** — honor of the Lord, or the victor who alone receives.  
**[Note: [Col. 1223A–B; 1224A]** We have corrected by conjecture an obvious error of the little Greek copyist. Instead of *ἢ νικητὴς*, Martianus had read from the Royal manuscript *ἤνικά τις*, which he translated “when someone.” The Vatican has the single word *ἠνίκκυτις*, which is no word at all. But we had no doubt that the scribe of both manuscripts had been deceived by the similarity of the letters: the Greeks are known to have interpreted Zachariah as *νικητής*, “victor,” both in the preceding first Fragment and in the lexicon printed below, where *Ζαχαρίας, νικητής* means “Zacharias, victor.” The following name, Zacchaeus, is likewise interpreted as “victor” because of the similarity of the letters. I add that the earlier etymology itself, “honor of the Lord,” is less credible. *Τιμή* should easily be corrected to *μνήμη*, “memory,” which is obvious and true both in Origen at many places and in Jerome’s explanatory column for this name.**]**

**Ζακχαῖος** — victor, or strengthened, or called.  
**Ζωὸβ** — gold.  
**[Note: [Col. 1224A]** Martianus corruptly has *Ζωοὺς* (*Zous*) from the Royal manuscript, and *Ζαβεὲ* (*Zabee*).**]**

**Ζεβεὲ** — sacrifice.  
**Ζελφὰ** — a moving mouth.  
**Ζωρομβαβὲλ** — “this is rest after confusion,” or a stranger of transposition, or “he himself is the teacher of Babylon.”  
**[Note: [Col. 1224B]** Martianus has *συγκύσεως*.**]**

## H

**Ἡλίας** — a strong God, my Lord.  
**Ἡρώδης** — glory of the skin.  
**Ἡσαῦ** — making, or a work; exaltation of the Lord, or oak-like.  
**[Note: [Col. 1224B]** The Vatican manuscript incorrectly has *ἢ πότιμα*, “or a drink.”**]**

**Ἡλεὶμ** — our God.  
**[Note: [Col. 1224B]** Martianus read *Ἡλύμ*, Latin *Helym*, and opposed to it in Jerome’s explanatory column *Eliana*, “with the Lord giving,” on account of the Greek etymology, as he says, which comes closer to *Eliana* than to *Elim*. We have restored the passage according to the Vatican manuscript.**]**  
**[Note: [Col. 1223A; 1224A]** To the Greek *Ἡλὺμ* I opposed *Eliana* because the Greek etymology comes closer to *Eliana* than to the *Elim* placed above.**]**

**Ἡσαΐας** — the shade of God, or the salvation of the Lord.  

## Th

**Θαβὼρ** — a chosen pit.  
**[Note: [Col. 1224A]** Jerome recognizes the etymologies of the name Thabor in Book I of his Commentary on Hosea, chapter 5: “And on Mount Thabor,” he says, “a lofty and most beautiful mountain, which is interpreted as ‘coming light,’ they set an ambush . . . . Some think Thabor is interpreted as ‘lake,’ etc.”**]**

**Θέμαθα** — the completion of the same things.  
**Θάμαρ** — tested, palm tree, or the words of God, or “come here, words.”  
**Θεκὲλ** — measure, or weight.  
**[Note: [Col. 1224A]** The Greek etymologist looked to Daniel 5:26–27, where the Septuagint uses the words *ἐμέτρησεν* and *ἐστάθη*; hence here “measure” and “weight.”**]**

**Θέκειε** — a blow, or a trumpet-blast.  
**Θελισταὶ, καὶ γνωσταὶ** — ventriloquists.  
**[Note: [Col. 1224A–1225A]** In 2 Kings 23:24 we read that Josiah removed *τοὺς θελητὰς, καὶ τοὺς γνωριστὰς*, that is, “the Theletas, or ventriloquists, and the cognizers.” In Hebrew it is *eth-haoboth veth-haijideonim*, that is, “the pythons and the knowing ones,” or “soothsayers,” as Jerome interprets it. It is therefore sufficiently clear that the Septuagint translators wished to express the word *oboth*, or *avoth*, in Greek by *θελητὰς*, and *jideonim* by *γνωριστὰς*, or *γνωστὰς*, according to some Greek manuscripts. *Θελητής*, from the verb *θέλω*, means “one who wills” or “desires”; hence the same Septuagint translators, in 2 Kings 21:27, call *ob* a *θελητής*, “a willing one,” because they took *ob* for *ab*, derived from *aba*, “he willed,” “he desired,” and so forth, as all Hebraists know. The same must be said of *jedonim*, or *ideonim*: for among the Hebrews *jada* is the same as *γνωρίζω* among the Greeks. Moreover, in the Royal manuscript we corruptly read *θελισταὶ* instead of *θεληταὶ*, and *γνῶσται* instead of *γνωσταὶ*.**]**

**Θεμανίτης** — completion of peace.  
**Θερσὰμ** — pity.  
**[Note: [Col. 1225A]** Jerome adds, “In Thersa,” which is more significantly said in Greek as *εὐδοκία*. Thus the word *εὐδοκία* in Luke 2:13 seems to be the same as *οἰκτιρμός* in the Greek manuscript, signifying divine mercy and compassion.**]**

**Θέριστρον** — a transparent veil.  
**[Note: [Col. 1225B–1226A]** Jerome says the following about *theristrum* in Book II of his Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 3: “They also have *theristra*, which we can call cloaks; Rebecca was wrapped in one, and even today the women of Arabia and Mesopotamia cover themselves with them. In Hebrew they are called *ARDIDIM*, in Greek *θέριστρα*, because they protect women’s bodies in *θέρος*, that is, in summer and heat.”**]**

**Θεύδας** — one who takes captive, or a sign of blood.  
**[Note: [Col. 1226A]** For Theudas to have the meaning “blood,” it must be written with *m* at the end, *Theudam*, since *dam* means “blood.” We shall not henceforth attend to such grammatical intricacies, lest our attention be divided from matters of greater importance.**]**

**Θουβὰλ** — one who turns to God.  
**Θωμᾶς** — abyss, or twin, or incomprehensible depth.  
**Θαιμὰν** — eclipse for him, or a countable insignificance, or south.  
**Θαῤῥὰ** — slow fragrance, or extraordinary fragrance, or the light of fire.  
**Θαρσεὶς** — an observation-post of joy, or the lightning of completion and gladness, or chrysolite, or settlers, Ethiopians.  
**[Note: [Col. 1226A]** The Greeks do not agree with Josephus and Jerome, who think that Tarshish means Cilicians; hence their metropolis is called Tarsus. Consult the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* and Book I of the *Jewish Antiquities*, chapter 6.**]**  
**[Note: [Col. 1225B]** The Vatican has *οἰκιστιοὶ*, which, however one interprets it, means “founders of colonies.”**]**

**Θέοφιλος** — one who brings up, or one who turns back.  
**Θεραφὶμ** — figures, images of idols.  
**[Note: [Col. 1225B]** The Vatican supplies the missing word *εἰκόνες*.**]**

**Θεσβήτης** — turning back.  
**Θειμὰρ** — temptation.  
**Θωβὲλ** — assembly, or purpose, or Athenians, or Thessalians, or Iberians, or Alans.  
**[Note: [Col. 1226A]** Jerome admits that the Iberians, or Spaniards, descended from Thobel, or Tubal; but certainly not the Athenians or Thessalians. See the passage cited above.**]**

## I

**Ἰαφὲθ** — enlargement of beauty, or one who is gathered.  
**Ἰὼκ** — father of the Lord.  
**[Note: [Col. 1225B]** The Vatican has *Ἰαὼμ*. To make the explanation “father,” etc., fit, it should be corrected to *Ἰαὼβ*, especially since confusion between *β* and *μ* is a common fault in Greek manuscripts. See below, *Ἰωάβ*.**]**

**Ἰάω** — Lord, or God, or invisible.  
**Ἰωακεὶμ** — the presence of the Lord.  
**Ἰασὰ** — a command that has come to pass.  
**Ἰάβις** — dryness, or shame, or extreme enlargement.  
**Ἰαθὴλ** — a pair of deer.  
**Ἰάειρος** — enlightened, or the Lord’s watchfulness.  
**Ἰάκωβος** — a supplanter through toil.  
**[Note: [Col. 1226B]** The Vatican has *πτέρνησις*, which in Latin should be rendered “supplantation.”**]**

**Ἰαννὴς** — a fisherman.  
**[Note: [Col. 1226B]** Martianus incorrectly read *θαλασσὴν* and translated it “sea.” The Vatican had *θαλασσεῦ*, which the corrector rightly indicated should be *θαλασσεὺς*; this means “fisherman” more properly than “mariner.”**]**

**Ἰασσῶν** — desiring, or of a begetting command.  
**[Note: [Col. 1226A–1227A]** Unless I am mistaken, *γεννώσης* is badly read in the Greek; for what suitable meaning does *gennoses* have? *Γενέτης* would be better, and it is reasonable to believe that Jerome also read it because of the later etymology, “one who makes a command.”**]**

**Ἰδουμαία** — failing away, or red, or ancient sin, or earthly.  
**Ἰεναὴλ** — the building of God.  
**Ἰεζαύελ** — the flow of blood.  
**Ἰεζεκιὴλ** — the strength of God.  
**Ἰεσιὴλ** — the life of God.  
**Ἰεμονιὴλ** — the right hand of the strong one, or portion, circumcision.  
**Ἰερεμεὴλ** — the pity of God.  
**Ἰεριχῶ** — the descent of a field, or humility.  
**Ἰεροβοὰλ** — a completed judgment.  

**Ἰερουσαλὴμ** — vision, watchfulness, or their spirit of grace.  
**[Note: [Col. 1227A–1228A]** Understand the many changes in the interpretation of the name Jerusalem as follows: *rei* means “vision,” and *salom*, or *salem*, means “peace”; hence Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” Again, *jara* means “he fears,” and *salem* is expressed as “perfectly,” producing “he will fear perfectly.” As for the interpretation “their spirit of grace” among the Greeks, this arises from their errors already noted above: they think the name is formed from the verb *ruahh* and *salem*, with *mem* attached as the third-person masculine plural. They also interpret *salem* as “grace.” But the name Jerusalem is dragged most violently into these meanings.**]**

**Ἰεχονίας** — pure, or a preparation taking place.  
**Ἰερεμίας** — an exaltation being raised aloft.  
**Ἰθάμαρ** — completion of bitterness, or pity, or palm tree.  
**Ἴαρεθ** — descent, or the Lord’s looking upon, or dominion.  
**[Note: [Col. 1227A]** Martianus read *Ἰόρεθα*, *Jaretha*, from the Royal manuscript.**]**

**Ἰακωὴ** — again, or release, or one newly seated.  
**Ἰακὼβ** — one who trips at the heel, or one who holds the last place, father.  
**Ἰαμβρὶς** — leather sea.  
**Ἰαρὲτ** — enlargement.  
**Ἰὲ Βαραχίου** — blessing of the Lord.  
**[Note: [Col. 1228A]** Thus the Greeks often quote the words of Scripture in the *Book of Names*: *υἱοῦ Βαραχίου*, “son of Barachiah,” or *υἱὲ*, “son.” This contributes nothing to the etymology, except that they place the name Barachiah among those beginning with I.**]**

**Ἰεβουσαῖος** — one who has gone astray, or one who is put to shame.  
**[Note: [Col. 1227A]** The Vatican has *καταισχύμμενος*.**]**

**Ἰεζραὴλ** — sowing of God.  
**Ἰεκτὰν** — a small plant.  
**Ἰεμενὶ** — the right hand of the Lord, or my right hand.  
**Ἰεναὴλ** — answer of God.  
**Ἱερεὺς** — he himself [does] these things, or according to the same.  
**Ἰεροβοὰμ** — judgment of the people.  
**Ἰεσσαὶ** — refreshment, or strong, or fruitfulness.  
**Ἰεφωνῆς** — turning back, or my appearance.  
**Ἰησοῦς** — salvation of the Lord.  

**Ἱλαστήριον** — the cover of the ark, or a plate.  
**[Note: [Col. 1228A]** In Exodus 31:7, *Ἱλαστήριον τὸ ἐπ’ αὐτῆς* means “the propitiatory which is upon it,” namely, the ark. *Hilasterion* is therefore the cover, or golden plate, by which the ark of the testimony was covered, or which was upon it. The Greek manuscript reads *πόμα*, “the drink of the ark.” *Hilasterion* means “propitiation” in Romans 3:25.**]**

**Ἰλλύριος** — proselyte.  
**Ἰόδωρ** — excessive.  
**Ἰορδάνη** — their descent, or dominion that does not exist.  
**Ἰούδας** — confession, or sufficiency of the Lord.  
**Ἰούστος** — one who spares them.  
**Ἰσαὰκ** — laughter and joy, a report.  
**[Note: [Col. 1227A; 1228A]** We correct this from the Vatican, which has *γέλως*, “laughter,” whereas Martianus printed *γέβωη* from the Royal manuscript, which is meaningless.**]**

**Ἰσμαὴλ** — hearing of the Lord, or observation.  
**[Note: [Col. 1228A]** The Vatican has *ἐφόππευσις*.**]**

[Col. 1229]

**Ἰταβύριον** — Mount Katalson [an unintelligible reading; read *κατάλληλον*, “suitable”], in Galilee.  
**[Note: [Col. 1229A]** Jerome clarified the present passage in his *Book of Hebrew Places*, and even more clearly in Book I of his Commentary on Hosea, chapter 5. He says: “Thabor, which the Septuagint translated *Ἰταβύριον*, following their custom of declining Hebrew names in Greek, just as they always interpret Edom—that is, Esau and Seir—as Idumaea. Thabor is a mountain situated in Galilee, in the plain, rounded and lofty, and equally bounded on every side . . . . The Septuagint also translated this mountain as Itabyrium in Jeremiah, etc.” From these words it is easily concluded that the Greek should read *κατάλληλον*, not *κάταλσον*, which means nothing.**]**

**Ἰταλία** — one who is astonished.  
**Ἰωάθαμ** — blameless of the Lord, or perfect.  
**Ἰωάννης** — baptist, or grace.  
**[Note: [Col. 1229A]** Josephus places these two words in the same order: “John, Baptist.” Hence the Greeks rather ineptly suppose that *Baptist* is an etymology of the name John.**]**

**Ἰωάχας** — strength of the Lord.  
**Ἰωβὴθ** — one who is subjected.  
**Ἰωὴλ** — beloved of the Lord.  
**Ἰωνάθαν** — dove, a gift that comes.  
**Ἰωσὴφ** — addition of the Lord, or removal of reproach.  
**Ἶν** — it is a measure, namely six measures, or the eighth part of a *xestes*.  
**[Note: [Col. 1229A]** The Vatican has *ξεστῶν* instead of *μέτρων*.**]**

**Ἰώππη** — beauty, observation-post.  
**[Note: [Col. 1229A–1230A]** Saint Gregory Nazianzen, *Apologetic Oration* 1: “Among the Hebrews, Joppa can mean the observation-post of joy.” *Ioppe* means “observation-post of joy” among the Hebrews.**]**

**Ἰοῦ** — it is, or it was.  
**Ἰουδαία** — one who confesses.  
**Ἰουδὴθ** — praising, or Judaea.  
**Ἰουλία** — one who has begun.  
**Ἵρ** — of watchful powers.  
**Ἰσκαρὼθ** — a memorial, a tent of death.  
**Ἰσραὴλ** — a mind seeing God.  
**Ἰσάχαρ** — it is a reward, or pure strength.  
**Ἰτουραία** — mountainous.  
**Ἰωὰβ** — father of the Lord, or beloved.  
**[Note: [Col. 1230A]** The etymologies of the name Joab are opposed: “enemy” and “beloved.” Jerome derives his from *ajab*, or *ojeb*, “he was hostile.” The Greeks derive theirs from *ahab*, “he loved,” “he cherished,” and so forth.**]**

**Ἰωακεὶμ** — resurrection, or preparation of the Lord.  
**Ἰὼας** — delay of the Lord, or knowledge.  
**Ἰωάχαρ** — possession of the Lord.  
**Ἰὼβ** — beloved of the Lord, or father of times.  
**[Note: [Col. 1230A]** To the Greeks Job means “father of times,” because of the number of days added by God to his life, not according to the proper character of the Hebrew language, which Jerome follows with the greatest fidelity; for *ob* means “magician” in Hebrew.**]**

**Ἰωβὴλ** — being changed, or having departed.  
**Ἰωσαφὰθ** — judgment of the Lord.  
**Ἰωσεδὲκ** — righteousness.  
**Ἰωσίας** — salvation of the Lord, or one being saved.  
**Ἰωχάβεδ** — glory of the Lord.  

## K

**Κάδις** — holy, or an extending stone.  
**[Note: [Col. 1230A]** Martianus has *παρατεῖνε* from the Royal manuscript and translates it “extend.”**]**

**Καὰθ** — molar, or preacher.  
**Κάδις** — an ear, or her vessel, exchanged.  
**Καδμαῖος** — before the Lord.  
**Καῒν** — jealousy.  
**Καϊνὰν** — their possession.  
**[Note: [Col. 1230A]** The Greek manuscript corruptly writes *κτίσις* here and in the following word instead of *κτῆσις*, thereby offering the false etymology “creature” instead of “possession.”**]**

**Κανὰ** — possession.  
**Κανδάκη** — exchanged.  
**Κάρμηλ** — knowledge of circumcision.  
**[Note: [Col. 1231B]** The Vatican has *Κάρμηλος*, which is the same.**]**

**Κάρπω** — to one who has recognized an appearance.  
**Καρφαναούμ, Καρφανδοὺμ** — village of consolation.  
**[Note: [Col. 1231A]** The name Capernaum is written in two ways in the Greek manuscript, but the second spelling is more corrupt than the first.**]**

**Καμψαὴλ** — assembly of God.  
**Κυδὰρ** — deep darkness, or darkness.  
**Κηφᾶς** — Peter.  
**Κιναῖος** — one who has acquired.  
**Κινύρα** — lyre, or knowledge of light.  
**Κλαύδιος** — hope of fair weather.  
**Κλεόπας** — greatly laboring.  
**[Note: [Col. 1231A]** Saint Jerome omitted the name Cleopas in his *Book of Hebrew Names*.**]**

**Κοδράντης** — one small coin, the so-called *nummion*.  
**Κολασαεῖς** — of a voice that has come to be.  
**[Note: [Col. 1231B]** It should certainly be read *γενομένης*.**]**

**Κωλωνία** — uncovered.  
**Κωρὲ** — bald.  
**Κορνήλιος** — knowledge of circumcision.  
**Κούαρτος** — sounding the trumpet loudly.  
**[Note: [Col. 1231A]** The Greek etymology warns us that an error has entered the Latin manuscripts of Jerome: they read *plangens*, “weeping,” instead of *clangens*, “sounding.”**]**

**Κρίσκη** — darkness.  
**Καθαμὰ** — loosened, or woven.  
**[Note: [Col. 1231A–B]** In Greek, *κάθαμμα* means a bond and a knot; this word was as tangled and almost Herculean for me until the edition of the Septuagint translators came to my aid. In Isaiah 3 and Ezekiel 16:11 I found *κάθεμα* written. *Κάθεμα* is a necklace made from various gems descending onto a woman’s breast, from *καθίημι*, “I lower” and “I submit.” Hesychius says of the same word: *Κάθεμα, ὁ κατὰ στήθους ὅρμος*, that is, “Kathema is a necklace or collar reaching to the breast.” In addition to this interpretation, the Greek manuscript adds another, namely *κροκύφαντα*. *Κροκύφαντον* means “that which is woven through the weft,” with “veil” or another kind of garment worn by women understood.**]**  
**[Note: [Col. 1231B]** The Vatican more correctly has *Κάθαιμα* [perhaps to be read *Κάθαμμα*].**]**

**Καίσαρ** — princely possession.  
**[Note: [Col. 1231B–1232A]** Jerome’s interpretation informs us that *κρίσις* should be read as *κτῆσις*. For the Greeks figuratively derive the name Caesar from *cana* and *sar*, in which lies the etymology “princely possession.”**]**

**Καμουὴλ** — resurrection of God.  
**Καριαθειαρὴμ** — city of the forest.  
**Καρπόσινον** — undefiled.  
**Κασία** — a family gathering.  
**Κενεὶ** — those who have acquired.  

**Κίνσος** — census.  
**[Note: [Col. 1232A]** There is no name *Cinsus* in Scripture, and its interpretation sufficiently suggests that *Κίνσος* has been written instead of *Κυρήνιος*. Since Luke 2:2 says that the first registration was made when Quirinius was governor of Syria, perhaps the Greek copyist thought that *ἀπογραφή*, “registration,” interpreted his name. I would not, however, insist on this in doubtful and uncertain matters.**]**  
**[Note: [Col. 1231B; 1232B]** The Latin word is *Census*, which the Greeks write *Κήνσον* in Matthew 17:25 and 22:17, 19; this has been noted very accurately by Clericus.**]**

**Κίδαρις** — a fraying fabric.  
**Κὶς** — one wearing a hard helmet.  
**[Note: [Col. 1232B]** Martianus had incorrectly read *περιφαλλὶν* instead of *περικεφαλήν*, which the Vatican restores.**]**

**Κιτιεῖς** — a blow, or islands, or, by transference, from Citium, a city of Cyprus.  
**Κλήμης** — preacher.  
**Κυλὰς** — sea.  
**Κόλυβος** — a type of coin, whence also the money-changers.  
**[Note: [Col. 1232A–B]** Hesychius mentions this expression but interprets it as a dwelling or villa: *Κόλυβος, ἔπαυλις*. We should therefore not follow the Greek writer’s traces by reading *Κόλυβος* and *κολυβισταί*, but should read with Hesychius *Κόλλυβος* and *κολλυβισταί*. According to that same Hesychius, *κόλλυβος* is “a type of coin, and one on which the image of an ox was stamped on bronze.” The *κολλυβισταί*, frequently mentioned in the holy Gospel, were bankers and money-changers who exchanged silver or gold coins for small coins, such as obols, and so forth.**]**

**Κορβὰν** — offering, gift.  
**Κορίνθος** — citizenship.  
**Κόσυμβοι** — carrying-straps, or knot-fasteners, tight, or gilded, like a crescent ornament having [corrupt text] curved pieces on both sides.  
**[Note: [Col. 1233A–1234A]** *Cosymbi* are understood as knots in Exodus 28, where there are knots in the linen garments and a tunic fastened with knots. The following words in the Greek manuscript suit this meaning, for they signify knots that bind garments tightly. Hesychius says of *Cosymbos*: *Κοσσύμβη, καὶ κόσσυμβος, ἐγκόμβωμα καὶ περίζωμα αἰγύπτιον, καὶ ἐγκομβοῦται*, teaching that *cosymbon* is Egyptian clothing and an ornament, as though knotted and tied. Others think *ἐγκόμβωμα* was a kind of garment tied into a knot and worn by servants. But what the Greeks add conflicts with this opinion: namely, that *cosymboi* were also certain gilded ornaments, like the *meniskos*, which is said to be an ornament, a collar, necklace, or torc. Since the remaining words are utterly corrupt and disfigured in the Greek manuscript, we do not interpret them. One of our experts in Greek thought that it might be read *ἄλλον ἄσσους ἔχων, ἀμφίκυρτα*, so that the sense would be that another interpretation calls *kosymbos* a garment having “eyes,” that is, spotted; or that *kosymboi* would be pieces of wood for carrying burdens, namely *ἀμφίκυρτα*, “curved on both sides.” We do not omit the tunic called *κοσυμβωτὸν* in Exodus 28:4, a tunic with curls, which, when properly arranged, serve as an ornament for garments. Consult Augustine, *Questions on Exodus* 114.**]**

**Κρίσος** — powerful knowledge.  
**Κύπρος** — gloom.  
**Κυριναῖος** — a man who inherits.  
**Κῶλα** — their voice.  
**Κρίτη** — of calling, or of creations, completion.  
**Κύψαλιν** — a beaten vessel.  
**[Note: [Col. 1233A–1234A]** Through the Greek etymology we have been warned of an error that entered the Latin manuscripts of Jerome. They read *Κάλυψιν*, and he noted that *Keli* in Hebrew means a vessel and instrument, but that he entirely failed to understand where the Greeks derived the word *Κάλυψιν*. We correct it from the Vatican to *Κύψαλιν*, and have no doubt that the word’s origin is Greek rather than Hebrew. Pollux, Book 10, chapter 23, section 92: *τὰ μὲν τῶν ἡδυσμάτων ἀγγεῖα ἐρεῖς Κυψέλας*—“you will call the vessels of seasonings *Kypselas*,” that is, small dishes. Martianus also read *πληκτόν* from the Royal manuscript and translated it “struck,” instead of *πλεκτόν*, which means “woven.” See the cited passage of Pollux.**]**

**Λαβᾶν** — whitening.  
**Λάζαοος** — one who is assisted.  
**Λεββαῖος** — heart.

**[Note: [Col. 1234A]** Instead of *αὐτῷ δῶρον*, “a gift to him,” the Greek writer perhaps inserted the meaningless word *αὐτόδωρ*. Unless he thought that *autodor* referred to Leviathan as the king of *ὕδωρ*, “water.”**]**

**Λΐα** — laboring, or turning back.

Hence in Jerome we read *ἀμυγδαλόν*, although some interpret it as *κλοιόν*, namely the collar of the condemned, commonly called a *boia*.**]**

**Λουζακάριον** — without wings.  
**Λύδδα** — benefit.  
**Λυκαονία** — rising up.

**Λῖνος** — whitened.  
**Λῶμνα** — whitening.  
**Λύκιος** — he himself, rising.  
**Λυδιὰ** — one who has been helped.  
**Λυσανίας** — the temptation of Gehenna.  
**[Col. 1235]**  
**[Note: [Col. 1235A]** Saint Jerome read in his Greek copy *γενεὰ*, or *γενετή*, that is, “origin” or “birth,” not *γεέννης*, “of Gehenna.”**]**

**Λύστρα** — beautiful birth.

# Μ

Μαλαὰδ, “God alone.”

Μαγδαλινὴ, “guarded.”

Μαγώγ, “melting,” or “every nation,” or “all tribes.”

[Note: Πλειάς is a constellation in the tail or back of Taurus, also called πλείονες because of the number and multitude of stars clustered together. Pliny assigns seven stars to it; hence a Greek writer called it κοινάστρον, or rather, as I restored it, κύναστρον, that is, “the Little Dog.” Ἄστρον is also understood as a sign, or ζῴδιον, containing many stars. More particularly, ζῴδια are the twelve heavenly signs seen in the circle of the Zodiac. Hence Saint Jerome above, col. 68: “Mazaroth, among the zodiacal signs,” which mathematicians assert are the twelve signs. In the Royal Greek manuscript, fol. 38: Μαζουρώθ, ἀστὴρ οὕτω καλούμενος, that is, “Mazuroth, a star so called.”]

Μαζουρώθ, “the Pleiades,” or “the Little Dog,” or “the twelve.”

[Note: In the Royal manuscript also, as in the Vatican, the reading was κοινάστρον. In the margin of this book the note ZT is added, indicating that the text is corrupt.]

Μαλαχίας, “angel.”

Μαμβρί, “of the son,” or “from a vision.”

[Note: Martianay had omitted the preposition ἀπό, although it is echoed by the first syllable of this name and Jerome himself expresses it. We have supplied it from the Vatican: “from.”]

Μαμωνᾶς, “wealth,” or “reproach,” “gifts,” or “dainties.”

Μάνη, “measure.”

Μαγδά, “from a tower,” *pyrra* [a corrupt reading; perhaps “tower-dweller”].

[Note: I would read πυργάτης, that is, “of the tower,” in place of the corrupt πυρρά, *pyrra*, which I nevertheless retain on the authority of both manuscripts. Recall the name Magdalene above.]

Μαγεδών, “from his promise.”

Μάγοι, “deceivers.”

Μαδιὰμ, “bringing,” or “answer.”

Μαθεία, “of one suffering.”

Μαθουσάλα, “sending of death,” or “sent one.”

Μανασσής, “cast off,” or “sold.”

[Note: The Vatican has πεπραμένος, “sold,” with the same meaning.]

[Note: Hesychius explains this word as follows: Μανδύας, εἶδος ἱματίου Περσῶν πολεμικοῦ, ἢ μαντείας, that is, “Mandyas, a kind of Persian military garment, or of divination.”]

Μανδύας, “a divining cloak.”

Μανωέ, “rest.”

[Note: We discussed Mamzer and ἐπίμηκτος, or ἐπίμηκος, above, col. 594, in the Notes (in our edition col. 1192, note 6).]

Μαμζήρ, “elongated.”

Μαραναθά, “the Lord is coming.”

Μαριά, “our lady,” or “from invisible things.”

Μαριάμ, “she who gives light.”

Μάρκος, “high,” “by command.”

Μαρτύριον, “a royal crown.”

Μαχεὶρ, “departure of a father,” or “the father’s watchfulness.”

[Note: The Greeks interpret Medath, like Malaad, as “God alone.” They may perhaps intend to emend Elmodad, since that name sounds more clearly like “God alone” than Medath or Malaad.]

Μεδάθ, “God alone.”

Μελελεήλ, “praising God.”

[Note: The same as Melchίου. In Jerome’s list, Malchus, “his king,” stood in place of Melchia.]

Μαλχίου, “of the king of the Lord.”

Μελχάλ, “from all.”

Μέμβρανος, “highly conspicuous.”

[Note: Because of the etymology, I set Memphiboste against the name Memphibaal.]

Μεμφιβαάλ, “shame from the mouth.”

Μέρρα, “bitterness.”

Μεστραΐμ, “Egypt.”

Μηνίσκους, “crescent-shaped necklets.”

Μιχαήλ, “Who is like the mighty God?” or “a brave God.”

[Col. 1237]

Μωάβ, “from a father,” or “a locust.”

Μωράθ, “heir.”

Μάρθα, “provoking,” or “lady.”

Μαριάμ, “the Lord from my birth,” or “ruling,” or “myrrh of the sea.”

Μασιφφά, “watchtower.”

Μαχμά, “humiliation.”

Μαγεδεήλ, “from God’s promise.”

Μετανίου, “gift of the Lord.”

Μελχήλ, “kingdom of God.”

Μελχισεδέκ, “king of righteousness,” or “a righteous apostle.”

Μεμφής, “mouth of confession.”

Μεσοποταμία, “being lifted up.”

Μεσίας, “Christ.”

[Note: In place of the corrupt εἰλημμένος, ἱλασμένος should preferably be read: “atoned for.” For Christ is typologically the ram in Numbers 5, offered for expiation, or to propitiate God, according to what is written in 1 John 2:2: “And he himself is ἱλασμός, a propitiation for our sins,” and so forth.]

εἰλημμένος, “taken.”

[Note: Write ἠλειμμένος, which means “anointed.” Martianay omitted this word from the Latin; as can be gathered from his annotation—which no one is unaware of—he did not understand the etymology.]

Μίδα, “measuring out.”

Μισαήλ, “touching of God,” or “visitation of God.”

Μιχά, “humble.”

[Note: The corrupt reading Μιχαῖος, *Michaeos*, stood in Martianay’s text.]

Μωσῆς, “taking up from water.”

Μωϋσῆς, “inquiry of the Lord,” or “from salvation.”

# Ν

Νάας, “serpent.”

Ναβαῦ, “a sitting-place,” or “their pasture.”

Ναβλέαι, “psalteries,” as a kind of lyre.

Ναβουθέ, “coming,” or “daughters.”

[Note: Martianay printed Ναυοχοδονόσωρ, *Navochodonosor*.]

Ναβοχοδονόσωρ, “sitting down,” or “knowledge of confinement.”

Ναγέβ, “midday,” that is, “the south.”

[Note: Martianay again corruptly printed Ναγέκ, *Nagec*, for the correct name Ναγέβ, which the Vatican restored.]

Ναζαρέθ, “a pure flower,” or “purity.”

Ναάσσων, “serpent-like.”

Ναβέλ, “folly,” or “of a measure.”

[Note: By conjecture we correct the text to ἀφροσύνη, “folly,” in place of the erroneous εὐφροσύνη, “joy.”]

Ναβεώδ, “the prudent,” or “prophets.”

Ναβουζαρδάν, “contempt of another’s judgment.”

Ναζωραῖος, “holy,” or “pure.”

[Note: The Vatican more correctly has καί, “and,” in place of ἤ, “or.”]

Ναζειραῖος, “holy,” or “most pure,” or “set apart for God from the mother’s womb” (the Vatican has θεῷ, “for God”).

Νάθαν, “gift.”

Ναθανίου, “gift of the Lord.”

Νάρκισος, “ascent of joy.”

Ναβή, “beauty to him,” or “my labor” (the Vatican has Ναβεΐ).

[Note: *Naphtha* is a Greek word. According to Dioscorides, book 1, chapter 2, naphtha is “a white-colored filtration of Babylonian bitumen, possessing the power of attracting fire, so that it draws it to itself even from a distance.” The Greek manuscript further adds that naphtha is also called the dregs from the produce of the earth, or olive pits that are discarded. But Jerome must be heard especially here; in book 1 of his Commentary on Daniel, chapter 3, he discusses naphtha as follows: “Sallust writes in his Histories that naphtha is a kind of fuel among the Persians, by which fires are especially fed. Others think that the olive pits discarded with the dried dregs are called naphtha. Hence in Greek it is called πυρρίνη, from πῦρ, ‘fire,’ because it feeds fire.” Thus, instructed by Jerome, I freely corrected the corrupt reading of the Greek manuscript, writing ἐλαιῶν, “of olives,” in place of the corrupt ἐξαιῶν.]

Νάφθα, “a certain Persian substance which, as they say, draws fire to itself,” or “the pressed residue, the pits of olives.”

Ναχώρ, “rest of light,” or “stalk.”

Νεσσα, “the heron, called a stork.”

Νεχοθά, “of spices.”

Νηγάρ, “ascending.”

Νικόλαος, “folly of the sick.”

[Note: Martianay falsely printed εὐφροσύνη, “joy,” from the Royal manuscript, in place of ἀφροσύνη, “folly,” which the Greeks commonly extracted as the etymology of Nicholas, with Jerome’s agreement. We correct the passage with the aid of the Vatican.]

Νινευή, “beautified.”

Ναθαναήλ, “gift of God,” or “I, God, am coming.”

Ναούμ, “consolation,” or “I am merciful to all.”

Νεβρώδ, “desertion,” or “rebellion.”

Ναχαώ, “their blow,” or “he himself is ready.”

Νηρεύς, “lamp of God.”

Νικόπολις, “offspring of protection.”

Νῶε, “rest.”

# Ο

Ὀβίδ, “being subjected.”

Ὀζία, “strength.”

Ὀζιήλ, “strength of God.”

Ὀνήσιμος, “answering most appropriately.”

Ὀρίου, “light of the Lord.”

[Note: In Song of Songs 1:9, *hormisci* among the Septuagint are the same as the necklaces in Jerome’s version. In Hebrew they are called *hharuzim*. Properly, among the Hebrews this denotes pearls and similar necklaces threaded on a string, a meaning that comes close to the interpretation of the Greek manuscript, δεσμὸς κυκλοφερής, “a circular necklace.”]

Ὁρμισκός, “a necklace,” or “a circular necklace.”

Ὀρνά, “light of rest.”

Οὐρίας, “powerful,” or “illumination of God.”

Ὀφαραθονίτης, “our scattering.”

Ὀδολάμ, “his testimony in water.”

[Note: In place of ἐν ὕδατι, which I consider entirely correct, the Vatican has εὐόδοτος, “prosperous,” which, however one interprets it, means “one who prospers.”]

Ὀζίας, “illustrious brother,” or “strength of the Lord.”

Ὀνησιφόρος, “answering,” “explaining.”

Ὀρνιάς, “curse of the Lord,” or “that which is a beginning.”

Οὐριήλ, “fire of God.”

Ὀχοζίας, “his brother,” or “light.”

# Π

Πάζω,

[Note: *Pazo* seems to be written here for *Pazion*, or *Topazion*, concerning which Hesychius says: Πάζιον, ἢ τοπάζιον λίθος πολύτιμος, “Pazion, or topaz, a very precious stone.”]

“morning-bearer.”

Πάρθοι,

[Note: With the aid of the Vatican archetype we have wonderfully restored this very corrupt passage. In place of διακοπὴ τελεία, “complete division,” Martianay had read the single word διακαπηλεία, which he translated as “trade” or “huckstering.” The restored reading is supported by Jerome’s own explanation, although there is no reason either to establish it by the testimony of others or to reject Martianay’s manifest error.]

“complete division.”

[Col. 1241]

Παριστρῶσα, “being aroused.”

Παστοφόρια, “of houses,” or “minister of trials.”

Πατρωβᾶς, “dissolving smoothly.”

Παῦλος, “mouth of agitation,” or “wonderful,” or “chosen.”

[Note: Hesychius likewise has: Πέλθη, εἶδος ὅπλου, δόρυ, ἢ μικρὰ ὅπλα, “Peltha, a kind of weapon, a spear, or small arms.” The Greek writer in the Royal manuscript is wrong to say that among the Romans small weapons with attached cymbals were called *armatura*. For among the Latins, as everyone knows, *armatura* is called ὁπλισμός or πανοπλία in Greek; this signifies not only weapons of every kind, but also cohorts and armed men.]

Πέλται, “small arms having cymbals attached, which the Romans call *armatoria*.”

[Note: Martianay has ἁρματύρωα, *harmaturoa*.]

[Note: The word περικνημίδες occurs in the Septuagint, Daniel 3:21, and means trousers, which Symmachus calls ἀναξυρίδες, garments covering the legs and shins. In Chaldee, Daniel has *besarbalchun*, that is, “with their sarabals.” Consult Jerome’s Commentary on this passage.]

Περικνημίδες, “breeches” [perhaps βράκεα rather than βράκη].

[Note: Hesychius explains this word as follows: Περὶπτερον, ὑψηλὸν πανταχόθεν διέχων, ἢ στέγην ἔχουσαν ἐξοχήν, “Peripteron, something high projecting on every side, or a roof having a projection.” It therefore seems to be the same as δῶμα, or an upper summer chamber, Judges 3:20 and 24.]

Περίπτερον, “a lofty summer chamber.”

Πέρσις, “loosening the sides.”

[Note: Martianay had falsely and senselessly read ἐπιλεγομένη, adding a comma, and accordingly translated it “which is called this oblique thing.” The matter itself shows that ἐπιλυομένη, “loosening,” should be restored, as we have done from the Vatican. Jerome himself has “unsewing.” We likewise correctly interpret τὰ πλάγια as “the sides,” with the holy Doctor. In Greek, κατὰ πλάγια means “along the sides.”]

Παραξιφίς, “a small knife,” or “sheath.”

[Note: *Pugio* occurs in Hesychius.]

Παρμενάν, “dividing fullness.”

Πάσχα, “passage,” or “above,” or “ransom” [perhaps ὑπερβατήριον, “that which passes over”].

Πέτρος, “knowing,” or “loosening,” or “obeying.”

[Note: Martianay again incorrectly read ἐπιγνώμονος, “of one knowing,” from the Royal manuscript, in place of ἐπίγνωμων, “knowing,” as Jerome also reads it.]

[Note: In the Apocalypse of John 1:13, and frequently elsewhere in the Old Testament, ποδήρης is found. The noun ἐσθής, “garment,” is understood, since *poderes* is an adjective meaning “reaching to the ankles,” derived from πούς, “foot,” and ἄρω, “to fit.” *Poderes*, therefore, is a garment hanging down to the feet, according to the explanation of the Greek manuscript.]

Ποδήρης, “the garment reaching to the feet, a more honorable priestly garment.”

[Note: Σπουδή should have been read; it signifies earnestness of mind and desire.]

Πουδής, “putting on,” “will.”

[Note: I do not know what Πουδής means. I do know, however, that Martianay’s conjecture, that σπουδήν should be read, is entirely irrelevant. In the Vatican, βουλὴν, “will,” occurs in place of βούλημα. From this the meaning should more correctly be “clothing himself with the will.”]

Πτωχώρ, “gathering fruit.”

Πύθουν, “mouth of the abyss.”

Περάτης, “sojourner,” or “eastern.”

[Note: Jerome discusses the word *periousion* as follows in book 1 of his Commentary on Matthew, chapter 6: “What we have rendered *supersubstantial* is found in Greek as ἐπιούσιον, a word which the Septuagint translators very frequently render as περιούσιον. We therefore examined the Hebrew, and wherever they rendered it περιούσιον, we found *sogola*, which Symmachus translated as ἐξαίρετον, that is, ‘special’ or ‘excellent,’ although in one place he translated it ‘peculiar.’ … In the Gospel called according to the Hebrews, instead of ‘supersubstantial bread’ I found *moar*, which is said to mean ‘tomorrow,’ so that the sense is: ‘Give us today our bread for tomorrow,’ that is, our future bread.”]

Περιούσιον, “made abundant.”

Περιοπή, “summit.”

Πέρσαι, “being tempted,” or “being scattered.”

Πίθον, “eternal mouth.”

Πιλάτος, “mouth of a hammer-smith.”

Πόντιος, “inclining the will.”

Πόρκιος, “dividing their harshness.”

Πτώκα, “recognizing.”

[Note: Martianay has ἐπιγινώσκουσα, “recognizing.”]

Πτολεμαΐς, “being led to measurement.”

Πυρσός, “being loosened.”

# Ρ

Ῥαάβ, “broadness.”

[Note: Martianay corruptly printed Ραάμ, *Raam*, because of the customary erroneous transposition of β into μ in the Royal manuscript.]

Ῥαββί, “teacher.”

Ῥαββίν, “many,” or “the multitude of a teacher.”

Ῥαάν, “being afflicted.”

Ῥαμέσι, “shepherding from a moth.”

[Note: The reading was ἐκ σίτου, “from grain,” a foolish error by a Greek scribe, in place of ἐκ σητός, “from a moth”; we have restored it. Martianay himself perceived in the Commentary appended to this book that it should be corrected. You could never extract an etymology of grain from the name Ramesses; by contrast, the moth, called in Hebrew and in Greek σής, is entirely familiar among such lexicographers and agrees with Jerome’s interpretation. Philo likewise says: Ῥαμεσή ἑρμηνεύεται σεῖσμος σητός, “Ramesse means the shaking of a moth.”]

Ῥαφαήλ, “healing of the mighty,” or “spirit of God.”

[Note: We said above that the name Raphael was added by the Greeks and is not listed by Jerome.]

Ῥαχήλ, “sheep of God,” or “mighty breath.”

Ῥεβέκκα, “great perseverance,” or “having taken the first husband.”

[Note: The Vatican has πρῴην, “recently,” in place of πρῶτον, “first.”]

Ῥοβοάμ, “broadness,” or “in the multitude of the people.”

Ῥοώδι, “seeing.”

Ῥοῦφος, “healing,” or “rest.”

Ῥώμη, “high thunder.”

Ῥαάσσων, “light of God,” or “good pleasure.”

Ῥάβος, “filled,” or “teacher.”

[Note: In the same manuscript, and indeed more correctly, πεπληθυμμένος occurs: “filled,” “overflowing.”]

Ῥαγαβίν, “vision of height.”

Ῥαγουήλ, “shepherding,” or “a strong friend.”

[Note: Martianay himself corrected this on his second revision. In both the Royal and Vatican manuscripts it was corruptly written ἑτοιμασία.]

Ῥαφαήν, “healing,” or “the mother’s flowering.”

Ῥαψάκις, “breadth of the people,” or “great in affection.”

[Note: The customary error of the Royal manuscript gave Ῥιχάμ, *Richam*.]

Ῥιχάβ, “ascent.”

[Note: We also read *Rubil* for *Ruben* in the Greek text of Flavius Josephus’s *Jewish Antiquities*.]

Ῥουβίλ, “spirit of God.”

Ῥομελλίας, “being raised up,” or “circumcision.”

[Note: The Vatican adds only the words ἢ ἀνά, leaving the sense incomplete; there is also a ZT mark in the margin.]

Ῥοὺθ, “having increased.”

Ῥωβώθ, “by thunder,” “broken.”

[Note: It seems that not *Roboth* but *Ramoth* should be read, so that the name may have the meaning of thunder. Learned colleagues and I derive ῥωγίλους from the abbreviated Greek writing of the manuscript, which I interpret as “broken,” since ῥωγαλέος in Homer means “cracked” and “broken.”]

Σαβαί, “Ethiopians.”

[Note: The Greeks confuse Sahachar with the name Bochor, meaning “firstborn.”]

Σαβάχαρ, “firstborn.”

Σάββατα, “rest,” or “return of sanctification.”

Σαβέκ, “release,” or “atonement.”

Σαδώκ, “righteous.”

Σαλαθιήλ, “request of God,” or “of the one who is coming.”
