Σαλών, “making peace.”

Σαμάρεια, “their despised guard.”

Σαμψών, “their sun.”

[Col. 1245]

[Note: Jerome teaches in book 1 of his Commentary on Daniel, chapter 3, that *Sarabara* is corruptly written in place of *Saraballa*.]

Σαράβαρα, “a kind of Persian footwear.”

Σαρέθα, “distress of bread.”

[Note: The Greeks interpret the name Satan as τριμόδιον, “three measures,” because of the three *sata* of flour mentioned by Christ in Matthew 13:33 and Luke 13:21, and by Moses in Genesis 18:6.]

Σατάν, “temptation of pride,” or “three measures.”

[Note: In the Vatican there is a space for one word between ἤ and καὶ. Perhaps the omitted name was Σάτουμ, which is Latin but could easily have been explained by the Greeks as τριμόδιον; the copyist may have omitted it because of the similarity of its letters to those above. There is also a ZT mark in the margin.]

Σαούλ, “asked for,” or “needed.”

Σέβεαι, “swift,” or “full.”

Σεδεκίας, “righteousness of the Lord.”

Σεκλά, “hope.”

[Note: The Vatican restored this name in full. In place of Σεκοῦνδος, Martianay had read ἐκοῦνδος from the Royal manuscript, and appended that word in the same sequence as a second etymology of the name Secla, translating it “voluntary.” In the Notes, however, he struggles without reaching a conclusion. “I read,” he says, “ἑκόντος, so that the sense may be ‘the hope of one who is willing,’ or perhaps ἐκουσίως ἐπαίρων, ‘raising voluntarily.’” Now, as you see, once Jerome’s own explanation has been restored by us, everything is clear and straightforward.]

Σεκοῦνδος, “raising.”

Σελμῶν, “requital of peace.”

Σεφφαρίμ, “books.”

Σεφφόρα, “beautiful visitation.”

Σεροὺχ, “departure.”

[Note: In the Vatican, here and below, ἀπάρτιμα occurs, a word that in some sense conveys completion. But what Martianay writes from the Royal manuscript, ἀπάρτημα, more properly means “departure”; hence in Jerome’s list we conjectured that *departure* should be read in place of *completion*. The word derives from ἀπαρτάομαι, “to withdraw farther away.” See what we noted at col. 16.]

Σήθ, “beautiful resurrection.”

Σεροὺχ, “completions.”

[Note: *Zaram* or *Zeruch* would be a better reading, since *zerua* means “sown,” and *zara*, “seed.”]

[Note: With the aid of the Vatican manuscript we have also restored this separate heading and assigned its proper etymology to the preceding entry. Martianay, from the Royal manuscript, had joined ἀπάρτιμα and Σηών—truncated words—as one explanation of this name, in an obvious error: Σεροὺχ, σπειρασμός. He had then read σπειρασμός quite incorrectly and translated it “sowing,” in place of πειρασμός, “temptation,” which is the true etymology of the name. Our correction is confirmed by Jerome’s own interpretation, which we restored in his list.]

Σηών, “hot temptation.”

Σικαρίοι, “drunkards.”

Σίκεμα, “rest,” or “likeness.”

Σαβά, “rod.”

Σαβαώθ, “of the powers.”

[Note: Because the oracle was in the Holy of Holies, the Greeks took this as an occasion for error, interpreting Caber, or rather Daber, as “Holy of Holies.”]

Σαβὴρ, “Holy of Holies.”

[Note: I think Σαήλ is used in place of Ἰασαήλ, *Jasael*. Martianay had inserted “Sava, of the savior” in Jerome’s list. In the Greek text, the Vatican has κυρίου, “of the Lord,” in place of θεοῦ, “of God.”]

Σαὴλ, “salvation of God.”

Σαλὴμ, “peace,” “gracious.”

[Note: Martianay has ἐπιχαρής, “joyful.”]

Σαλμῶν, “take a vessel.”

Σολομών, “peace,” or “grace.”

Σαμαήλ, “a minister hearing God.”

[Note: As we noted earlier, the Greek interpretation expresses not the etymology of the name Samuel but his virtue and obedience.]

Σαμουήλ, “their law of God,” or “there he himself is God.”

[Note: Martianay likewise had Σαμοήλ. The Vatican corrects it.]

Σαρόα, “my beginning.”

Σαραφίμ, “burning,” or “the beginning of a fiery mouth.”

Σατανᾶς, “afflicting,” or “opposing.”

Σαυχιτής, “talkative.”

Σεβαστή, “circling.”

Σεβοΐμ, “standing.”

Σέδρα, “confinement.”

Σηρεῖναι, “the ἀκίδονες” [an unintelligible reading].

[Note: The word ἀκίδονες has no meaning at all. Jerome indicates that κακοδαίμονες, “evil spirits,” should be read; he himself teaches this in book 5 of his Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 13: “The Sirens are called *thannim*, which we have interpreted as either demons, or certain monsters, or, at any rate, great dragons, crested and flying.”]

[Note: What Martianay conjectures should be read here, κακοδαίμονες, is, says Clericus, too far from the manuscript’s reading; both the Royal and Vatican manuscripts agree. He thinks that two errors are present: first, Σειρῆνες should be read, as required by the constant usage of the Greek language and of the Septuagint translators; second, ἀκιδόνες should be changed to ἁλκυόνες, “halcyons,” or ἁλκηδόνες, for the ancient Greeks seem to have used both forms, from which the Latins made *halcedones*. Chrysostom and Cyril of Alexandria interpreted the word *siren* in this way, as Samuel Bochart shows in *Hierozoicon*, part 2, book 2, chapter 14. He likewise observes that in the writings of the ancients ἁλκυόνες and ἀηδόνες were often confused by copyists, apparently because ἁλκηδόνες and ἀηδόνες were similar in sound and because ἁλκηδόνες was less common.]

[Col. 1247]

Σελλὰ, “shadow,” or “its own shelter.”

Σεμεΐ, “my hearing,” “my being heard.”

[Note: The Royal manuscript had the more corrupt Σειρναχειρίμ, *Sirnachirim*.]

Σενναχειρίμ, “temptation,” or “dryness.”

Σεραφίμ, “spirit of resurrection.”

Σιγώρ, “rising.”

Σιλώμ, “this release.”

Σιβά, “army,” or “joy.”

Σίκερα, “drunkenness.”

Σιλᾶς, “mediator.”

[Note: The place is obscure and especially suited to encouraging contrary opinions among scholars concerning the weight and value of the sacred or common shekel. It should be noted that the Septuagint translators in Ezekiel 25:12 used στάθμιον, “a weight,” for *shekel*, while elsewhere they translated it as δίδραχμον, “double drachma.” I therefore think that the abbreviated sign of the name γο γο is corrupt, and that διδον, or something similar, should be written in its place, signifying δίδραχμον according to the edition of the Septuagint followed by the Greeks. Consult Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*, p. 183.]

Σίκλος, “a weight: three [units] make one priestly [shekel],” or “γο γο,” or “twenty obols.”

Σιλωάμ, “sending.”

Σινά, “eternal lifting up,” or “thirst,” “commandment.”

Σιφά, “illumination.”

Σιών, “watchtower,” or “thirsting,” or “command of a watchtower.”

Σόδομα, “burning to ashes,” or “burning,” or “trial.”

Σώρ, “rock,” or “the city of the Tyrians.”

Σοφονίας, “watchtower of the Lord.”

Σουλαμίτης, “making peace,” or “for spoil.”

Σουσάννα, “resurrection of glory,” or “grace.”

Στέφανος, “rule,” or “aim.”

Συήνη, “temptation,” or “circle.”

Συρία, “lofty,” “accusation.”

Συχέμ, “back,” or “shoulders.”

[Note: The words ἤ ὤμοι, “or shoulders,” which were previously missing, have been supplied from the Vatican.]

Σώπατρος, “saving the scattered.”

Σωσθένης, “saving time.”

Σιλουανός, “sent.”

[Note: In Acts 19:12 we read the name *Simicinthia*: “sweat-cloths and semicinctia.” According to Suidas, φακιόλιον is a kind of head-covering, also called φάκελλος. In this sense, the *semicinctia*, which the Greek manuscript interprets as φακιόλια, *faciolia*, would be head-coverings. Others, however, hold that *semicinctia* are strips that form the outermost parts of a garment; because they were split to the middle of the body and girded there, they are appropriately called *semicinctia*. Hesychius seems to support this view: Σιμικίνθια, φακιόλια, ζωνάρια ὠράρια τῶν ἱερέων, “Simicinthia, faciolia, sashes, priestly oraria.”]

Σιμικίνθια, “faciolia.”

Σὶν, “bush,” or “temptation.”

Σισαρά, “as a vision of a horse,” or “removals of rebellion.”

Σκεῦος, “fox,” or “speaking.”

Σκυτάλη, “rod,” or “multitude.”

Σμύρνη, “their melody.”

Σοῦβα, “this commandment.”

Σουμανίτης, “water,” or “bearing witness.”

[Note: The following two names are given in the Vatican in this form:

Σπεῖρα, “higher.”

Σπωρία, “uncountable suburbs.”]

Σεῖρα, “higher,” “journey.”

Σαριθμός, “suburbs.”

Συμεών, “labor of obedience,” or “image.”

Συχάρ, “dense shade of branches.”

Σχιζαί, “arrows.”

# Τ

Τωφάρ,

[Note: The Greek writer placed the name Sophar under the letter T, although it belongs to the preceding series under S. Unless it is *Tasoph*, which in Ezekiel means “watchtower.”]

“watch,” or “hope.”

Ταβιθά, “gazelle.”

Ταλιθὰ κουμί, “girl, arise.”

[Note: *Talitha* is a Syriac word meaning “girl,” but the verb *cumi*, that is, “arise,” is Hebrew as well as Syriac. In the masculine it has the form indicated in the annotation of the Greek manuscript.]

Κοῦμ, addressed to a man; Κοῦμι, addressed to a woman.

Ταβεήλ, “these are the good things of God.”

[Note: Epiphanius says that a talent, ρκέ, consists of 125 pounds. The manuscript adds, “or 126.”]

Τάλαντα, “125,” or “126.”

[Note: In place of the corrupt *Tamias*, the etymology shows that *Samer*, *Somer*, or *Samarites* should be read, since these words mean “guardian.”]

Ταμίας, “guardian.”

Τανίης, “humble command,” or “being moistened with dew.”

Τάφνος, “the mouth of a serpent rising up.”

[Note: *Tiara* is a Greek word that has entered Latin usage. Virgil says: “And the scepter and sacred tiaras.” It is a kind of small cap used by the Persians and Chaldeans. Thus Saint Jerome on Daniel, chapter 3.]

Τιάραι, “head-coverings made from felt.”

Τίγρις, “fruitfulness,” or “increase,” or “sharpness.”

Τέρτιος, “drawing near.”

Τέρτιλλος, “being well pleased,” or “their dung.”

Τιβερίας, “beautiful,” or “frugality” [perhaps φειδώ].

Τιμόθεος, “doing good.”

[Note: The reading in Jerome’s Latin interpretation should apparently be corrected in conformity with the Greek, “seeking good things.”]

Τίτος, “seeking good things.”

[Note: The Vatican adds ἤ ζητῶν ἀπό, “or seeking from,” leaving the sense incomplete; it also places a ZT mark in the margin.]

Τραχωνίτης, “commerce of sorrow,” or “friendliness.”

[For ἐμπορεία, read ἐμπορία, “commerce.”]

[Note: Concerning this expression, *trochos en trocho*, see what was said above.]

Τρόχος ἐν τροχῷ, “four-faced.”

[Note: We have also followed the Vatican here, but Clericus notes that in place of τρύφαινα, Romans 16:12, this form was written.]

Τρύφενα, “turning away.”

Τρωάς, “relief.”

Τύμπανον, “enclosure.”

Τύραννος, “holding together,” or “ruling.”

Τίμων, “counting.”

Τοβίας, “the good things of the Lord.”

Τρισσός, “bow.”

[Note: *Trichaptum* occurs in the Septuagint, Ezekiel 16:10. According to Hesychius, it is a certain fine, silken, very costly textile placed over the hair.]

Τρίχαπτα, “gold thread,” or “entire silk.”

Τρόφιμος, “loosening the breasts.”

Τρυφῶσα, “manifest.”

Τρῶγλοι, “feeding.”

Τύρος, “confinement,” “distress.”

Τυχικός, “being silent.”

# Υ

Υἱοῦ ἱεμένει, “son of the right hand.”

Ὑμένεως, “dozing.”

## Φ

Φαὰμ [Note: The name is thoroughly corrupt; the etymology indicates that Atham should be read instead of Phaam], “season.” Φανουὴλ, “face.” [Col. 1251] Φαρὰν, “mouth of vision.” [Note: This name is not found in Holy Scripture, and was plainly fabricated by the Greeks, who, because of the name of the king of Egypt, Pharaoh, wish his daughter to be called Pharia.] Φαρία, “daughter of Pharaoh.” Φασὲκ, “crossing over,” or “release.” [Note: In Daniel, chapter eight: “And one holy one said to Laphelmon, to someone”; for this the Septuagint has τῷ φελμούνι. Among the Hebrews, Pheloni, when the name of a thing is not expressed, denotes a certain man, angel, or place whose name the speaker conceals, mentioning the same even though he does not fail to know it. Moreover, the name Phelmoni is composed of Pheloni, already mentioned, and almoni; concerning the latter, consult the Hebrew lexicons.] φελμωνὶ, “angel,” or “form of power.” Φεννανὰ, “turning away.” [Note: The Vatican has φίστος, Fistus.] Φέστος, “many-mouthed.” Φιλήμων, “wonderfully endowed.” Φίληξ, “fall,” or “fracture.” Φιλόλογος, “mouth lifting up.” Φλέγων, “cutting apart.” Φογὼρ, “mouth.” Φοιβὴ, “building with her mouth.” Φουὰ, “red,” or “fall.” Φοὺδ, [Note: Martianus had corruptly read Δίυνες instead of Λίβυες.] Λίβυες, or “Africans.” [Note: Martianus has Φυλυστείμ, Fylystim, instead of Φυλιστιείμ, which the Vatican has.] Φυλιστιεὶμ, “foreigners,” “wonderful.” Φωνὴ ἐν ῥαμὰ, “a voice in Ramah, a cry in a high land.” Φαθουὴλ, “breadth of God,” or “meeting” [Note: The same Martianus read κυρίου, “of the Lord,” instead of θεοῦ, “of God.”] “of God.” Φαρὲς, “fence,” or “division.” Φαρισσαῖος, “separated.” Φελεθθὶ, “struck with a sling.” Φελώνης, “face of God.” Φερεζαῖοι, “scattering,” or “fruits.” Φιλητὸς, [Note: We correct this from the Vatican to ἀποκεκλικώς, “turning aside,” or “turned aside,” a participle derived from the verb ἀποκλίνω. Jerome’s own interpretation indicated that the reading should be restored. The obvious error that Martianus had printed from the Regius manuscript was ἀποκλείας, which he translated “of exclusion.”] ἀποκεκλικώς, “turning aside.” Φίλιππος, “mouth of lamps.” Φινεὲς, “muzzle of the mouth,” or “turning away.” Φορθομμὴν, “opposed,” or “from all.” Φύγελλος, [Note: From the common Latin meaning, Fygellus seems to be explained as though it meant “son”—Italian Figliuolo—namely, πάρθον, “born,” a young man, or a virgin.] πάρθοι, “Parthians,” or “virgins,” or “young men.” Φῶκα, “taking of the mouth.”

## Χ

Χαβὼρ, “joining together.” Χαλάνη, “all of us.” Χαλὲβ, “as a heart,” or “every heart.” Χαμὸς, “as a touch,” or “Cronus,” the idol of the Moabites. [Note: Martianus corruptly has Χανάν from the Regius manuscript.] Χαναὰν, “as an answer.” Χαναναία, “changing.” Χαηλὰ, [Note: In the Vatican, in the singular, παρεμβολὴ, which is more correctly translated “interposition.”] “of encampments.” Χαλδαῖοι, “seers,” or “magicians,” or “as demons.” Χὰμ, [Note: Martianus has θέρμοι, “hot things,” in the plural, with the Latin calores, “heats”; he should have said calidi, “hot.”] θέρμη, “heat.” [Col. 1253] Χαναναῖος, “of change,” or “poor,” or “interpreting,” or “answering.”

# Hieronymus. BOOK OF NAMES.

[Col. 1204]

## A

Adam, man, or earthly, or native, or red earth. Ada, testimony. Adama, soil, or earth, or earthly. Abel, mourning, or vanity, or vapor, or miserable. Abram, lofty father. Aaron, mountain of strength, or strong mountain, or their mountain. Abdias, servant of the Lord. Abenezer, stone of help. Abessalom, father of peace. Abinadab, my spontaneous father, or courteous. Abigal, father of exultation, or father of dew, or my father is dew. Appho, “even now?” [Col. 1206] Abraam, father seeing the people. Abiram, my lofty father. Aggaeus, solemnity, or festive. Agrippa, suddenly gathering. Aermon, anathema of grief. Azael, seen by God. Azeca, strength, or a snare. Athens, dissipated in time. Egypt, darkness, or tribulations. Ethiopia, mist, or darkness. Elamites, cast down, placed beside, or despised, etc. Abba, father. It is Syriac. Abdemelech, servant of the king. Achor, disturbance, or tumult. Ahicam, my rising brother. Achimelech, my brother is king. Achor, tumult, or perversity. Aod, glorious. Abenner, my father is a lamp, or father of a lamp. Abia, father the Lord, or “the father was.” Abiathar, superfluous father. Abiezer, my father’s help. Abimelech, my father is king. Abiu, “my father is this,” or “my father is.” Agabus, messenger, or messenger of tribulation. But this is forced. Agag, δῶμα, that is, “roof.” Agar, stranger, or converting. Angel. [Col. 1208] Addar, magnificent, or cloak. Adrias, containing evils, or place of evils. Forced. Adonai, Lord. Aza, strength. Azaria, the Lord is helper, or help of the Lord. Azotus, fire of a paternal uncle, etc. Eden, pleasure, or adornment, etc. Elam, before the doors, or vestibule. Aceldama, field of blood. Accaron, pasture of the flock, etc. Acrabim, scorpions. Alexander, removing the distress of darkness. But this too is forced. Allophyles, falling, or the fall of a cup, etc. Alphaeus, fugitive, but better “thousandth,” or “learned.” Amalec, locust people, or licking people, etc. Abacuc, embracing. Aminadab, my willing people. Amon, faithful, or nourishing, etc. Ampliatus, hammering people. Amphipolis, people falling by the mouth. Anameel, to whom God gave. Ananeel, grace of God. Andronicus, handsome for the contest, etc. Anna, his grace. Annas, giving. Antipatris, giving praise. Forced. Apollo, miracle, or gathering them. Forum of Appius, free, or strong abundance. Forced. Aradii, laying down, etc. [Col. 1210] Ararat, Armenia, or a shaken-up or plucked mountain. Areopagus, primitive solemnity. But this too is forced, etc. Accaron, instruction of grief, or barrenness. Aquila, grieving, or in labor. Alleluia, praise the Lord. Amathi, my truth, or my faithful one. Ammon, people of grief. Ammon, son of my people, etc. Ammoni, compressing, or narrowing me. Amasa, lifting up or raising the people. Amen, truly, faithfully. Amorite, bitter, or speaking, etc. Anathoth, answer, or answering sign, or obedience. Ananias, grace of the Lord. Andreas, beauty in standing, or answering the food. But this is forced, etc. Antioch, silence of poverty. Apelles, gathering them. Forced. Apollonia, discipline, or their synagogue. Arabia, humble, or western. Araba, west, or evening. Aram, lofty. Arioch, drunk, or drunkenness. Armathaim, their height. Artemas, cursing, etc. Arodi, sufficient curse. Asa, taking away, or lifting up. Asaph, gathering. Asedec, city of the sun. Aser, blessed, or blessedness. Asida, kite. Assyrians, directing. Asyncritus, directing the censer. Aunan, their grief, or labors. [Col. 1212] Appho, “even now?” Achaz, grasping, etc. Arabs, ambushes. Aramathi, casting him down. Aristarchus, raising up a crown. Arioch, reducing to solitude. Armageddon, rising toward the former things, but better, “mountain of robbers,” etc. Aroer, dug up, but better “tamarisk.” Artemis, Diana, raising up illnesses. Arphaxad, healing devastation. Asael, work of God, that is, ποίημα. Asemona, his bone, from “bone,” not from “mouth.” Aseneth, ruin. Aseroth, court of distress, or blessednesses. Assur, directing, or blessed, etc. Assarion, an as. ## B

Baal, possessing, or devouring. Babylon, confusion, or translation. Bathuel, virgin of God. Bethel, house of God. [Col. 1214] Bethsemus, house of the sun. Ammon, son of my people, or people of grief. Moab, from the father. Baal, possessing, or man. Balthasar, hair of the head. Barac, flashing. Bartholomaeus, son of the one who suspends the waters, etc. Barnee, chosen disturbance. Basan, locust, or fatness—for what is usually interpreted as disgrace or confusion is called BUSA. Beelzebub, one who has flies, or devours flies, or man of flies. Bethphage, house of the mouth of the valleys, or house of the cheek, etc. Some think it is called “house of jaws.” Banereem, sons of thunder; what usage has corruptly established as Boanerges. Booz, in strength. Bosor, in distress, or flesh, etc. Bethlehem, house of bread, as above. Bethoron, house of wrath. Balaam, vain people, or bringing them headlong, or without a people. # Codex Colbertinus. From the Old [Testament].

[Col. 1253]

## A

Adam, earthly, or reddish earth. Abraham, father [Note: According to Jerome, Abraham is translated “father of many,” for what follows—“of nations”—is not contained in the name but is understood. Consult above, the Hebrew Questions on Genesis.] of nations. Alleluia [Note: The Greeks unnecessarily add the words “God is present” to the etymology of the word Alleluia, for its true interpretation appears in Jerome’s column: namely, “Praise the Lord.” In Hebrew this is said hallelu-ja.], “God is present,” “praise.” Ambacum, father of rising. Armathem, projection. Anna, glory, or grace. Aermon, discovery. Abiglae, joy of the father. Ananias [Note: This is a mystical etymology of the word Ananias. It is therefore interpreted as “winepress,” because *ani* signifies affliction and poverty, which can indeed be called the winepress of human weakness. The same word Ananias is expressed in Latin as “scattered grace,” from *hhen*, or *an*, that is, grace, and *nua*, which means “he was shaken” or “scattered.”], winepress and graced. Azarias, seeing, or strength. Aermonam, of discovery. [Note: Read *Amen*.] Amen, let it be done. Aser [Note: We have already noted, on Jerome’s authority in the book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis, that the word “wealth” was wrongly added, since the etymology of the name Aser is disclosed by Scripture’s testimony, which says: “I am blessed, and women call me blessed.” Because she was called blessed by human beings, she called her son blessed, and so forth.], wealth. Andreas, noble. Asech, freedom. [Note: The name Enos, as though Greek, is interpreted and written in Greek here: for among the Greeks *ainos* means praise.] Ainos, hymn. Ariel, mighty lion. Aggaeus, feast. Anathema, of my coming. [Note: Ephod was discussed above, col. 543.] Ephod, declaration and truth. Arimathem, from a projection. Arsaph, gathering. Arab, ambush. Adonai, Lord. Aron, ark. Arra, provocation. [Note: In the series of names from Deuteronomy, Jerome discusses the matter as follows: Aseroth means courts or vestibules, if it is written with the letters HETH and SADE. But if it is written with ALEPH and SIN, it means blessednesses.] Asiroth, blessednesses. Aitam, bird. Azotus, strength of the living one. Anath, answer. [Col. 1255] Amorrhaeus, spoken, or bitter. [Note: Because of the plague of darkness by which the Egyptians were afflicted, and because of the persecution by which they oppressed the Hebrews, the Greeks fabricate etymologies of this sort. They suppose the word *skotige* to be formed from *skotia*, darkness, and *ge*, that is, earth. See our annotations on the name Egypt, col. 3.] Egypt, “dark earth,” persecutress. [Note: It should be emended, as Clericus observes, to *skotia ge*. Then *dioktria* does not mean “persecution,” as Martianus translates it, but “she who pursues,” or “persecutress” in Latin.] Aitias, good things. Arnon, their light. [Note: Jerome notes that Elon signifies “oak,” and is often written Ailon and Aulon. If we choose to read Aeglon, it is interpreted “their calf.” In the etymology of the name Aeglon, the Greeks omit the letter Ghimel and interpret it as “their God,” as though it were *elom*.] Aglaon, their God. Ada, testimony. Aaron, having conceived. Abimelech, advising the king. Asael, work of God. Amisa, rejected people. Akkaro, barrenness. Agla, feast. [Note: The name Adino, for which the Greek copyist wrote Asao, is read in II Samuel 22:8 among the Septuagint translators, for whom it is a man’s proper name. For others it is a common noun meaning “his delight,” on account of the attached Vau at the end: *adino*.] Asao, luxuriating. [Note: These two names, Hasadias and Asel, are not found interpreted in Jerome, from whom they were taken in the First Book of Chronicles, chapters 1 and 8. It has already been observed above that the Book of Hebrew Names was not compiled from Ezra or from Chronicles.] Asedou, mercy of the Lord. Asel, shadow. Apher, dust. Amal, toil. Azoth, of the fruitful one. Asael, strength of God. Ariel, light of God. Armatham, conception of death. Abenezer, helpful stone. Amorrhaeans, spoken of. Asor, court. Abenner, father of the lamp. Azeca, empty strength. Artob, sunset. Arabia, evening. Aggith, work. Agal, calf. Adraazar, comely help. Apheci, new anger. Amathe, my faith. Asur, he who is good-humored—read “directing.” Assyrians, directing. Ametran, heat of dew. Amos, strong [Note: Here too I read *pursuer* for the corrupt manuscript reading *diractes*; and consequently *held fast* for another word slightly corrupted in the Colbertine copy.] or pursuer. Achaz, held fast. Anathoth, hearing. Ano, answer. [Note: The Hebrew word Asida, which immediately follows, means “stork,” a pious and beneficent bird, which Petronius Arbiter calls a cultivator of piety. The name Asida occurs in the Septuagint at Jeremiah 8:7. Jerome translated it here as “kite,” and in his letter to Sunia and Fretela likewise indicates that he translated it as “kite” in Psalm 103.] Asid, mercy.

[Col. 1257] Ethiopia, humility. Achor [Note: I make no change in the Greek reading, although Jerome’s interpretation plainly shows it to be corrupt, and that *diatrope*, meaning “disturbance,” should be read instead of *diatrophē*.], nourishment. Azeca, strengthening. [Note: In Joshua 18:28, Eleph is the name of a city, which the Greeks corruptly read as Adepha; above, in the Book of Names, it is Aaleph.] Adepha, instruction. Ain, eye. Azere, east. Ausitis, counsel. Asida, mercy. Asouph, oracle. [Note: In Hebrew, Asaph, with Samech in the middle, means “gathering”; but if Asaph has Sin, in Chaldean it means “astrologer.” Thus Asouph, which Jerome translated “gathering,” the Greeks rendered *chresmos*. Among the Greeks, *chresmos* means an oracle and prophecy, or divination, or what has been answered by an oracle. Hence Asaph, or Asouph of the Chaldeans, seems to correspond to the Greek *chresmos*. Asaph is also especially renowned for prophecy.] Aod, praise. Abelmaula, mourning of firstfruits. [Note: Ebion means poor and needy. The Greeks therefore confuse the name Abiud with the name Ebion, which was especially widespread among Christians.] Abiud, poverty. [Note: Against the corrupt Asarom I have supplied Esrom, because Asarom, according to the sound of the letters, can signify height: for *rom* expresses height.] Asarom, height of counsel. Aeaba, fullness. Araph, ambush. Ari, my light. Abiel, my father is God. Abieza, my father is strength. Amalec, a people turning aside. Ammon, a people of nations, or of toil. Amesa, people, exaltation. [Note: The opposite column of Jerome’s text shows these names to be corrupt; therefore nothing further will be said about them.] Amenalab, goodwill of the people. Abdiu, my people is. Abdias, pillar. [Note: Let those skilled in the Greek language judge what *anasystes* is to be understood as meaning. I do not know whether *anastes*, or rather *anaseistes*, should be read.] Annas, *anasystes* [meaning uncertain].

## B

Barne [Note: The Greeks commit solecisms in the names Barne and Bersabee. In the first, they use the feminine gender instead of the masculine—“daughter” instead of “son,” that is, Hebrew *bar* instead of *bath*. In the second, they use the masculine instead of the feminine, namely *thygater hebdomos* instead of *hebdomē*.], chosen daughter. Basanites, being ashamed. Bersabee, seventh daughter. Beelphegor, demon of Phegor. Bosor, flesh. Bartholomaeus, blessed son. Boanerges, son of thunder. Bethania, house of obedience, [or] of glory. [Note: The particle *ē*, “or,” is absent here, as is readily proved from the earlier Greek copies.] Bethphage, house of success. Besania, house of the bramble. Belial, inquiry. Balin, demon. Bar-Jona, son of a dove. Babylon, confusion. Benjamin, right-handed son, or son of grief. [Col. 1259] Bethel, house of God. Bara, creation. [Note: The Greek etymology of this name Barsac warns us that Bara should again be read.] Barsac, in impiety. Balla, drowning, or kneaded dough. Beeri, wells. Bathuel, daughter of God. Bethlehem, house of bread. Betheberra, house of construction. Bith, house. [Note: Origen seems to have taken this name from the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew, because there it was written in chapter 21:9, *baruch abba*, with emphatic He, so that the sense is “Blessed is he who comes,” and so forth.] Baruchabe, the father is blessed. Baruch, blessed. Beelamon, detention of the crowd.

## G

Gebuel [Note: Gelboe is not called “a mountain made vain” according to the etymology and the force of the letters, but because of David’s words, “Mountains of Gelboe, let neither dew nor rain come upon you.” For that reason the mountains become vain and useless for fostering the seeds of crops. We say something similar about Mount Garizim, which according to the allegorical interpretations of the Greeks may be called “a redeemed mountain,” because the blessings are said to have been placed upon Mount Garizim, while the curses were placed upon Mount Hebal.], a mountain made futile. Garisin, a redeemed mountain. Gabriel, man and God. Gomorrha, standing. Geon, the Nile. Gad, occupation, or fortune. Gamel, higher fullness. [Note: The particle *en* was omitted in the name Engaddi, which means “eye of temptation”: for *en* means eye, and *gad*, temptation.] Gaddi, eye [Note: Above, in the First Fragment, Martianus himself interpreted this as *peiratērion*, “a refuge of robbers,” instead of “temptation,” from *peirazein*, an etymology rejected by Clericus, who notes the Hebrew meaning of the word Gad.] of a refuge for robbers. Gallad, migration of testimony. Galilee, rolling of the Lord. Gergesa, dwelling of the expelled [read: dwelling of the expelled woman]. Gabbatha, paved with stones. Golgotha, skull. Gamiel, talkative of God. Gersam, resident alien, stranger.

## D

David, mighty in hand. Daniel, judgment of God. Dan, judgment. Damascus, kiss of blood.

## E

Elissaee, power of God. Elimelech, kingdom of God. [Note: In this Greek copy we read Elilatous in a most corrupt form instead of Evilat, as is proved by the etymology of the name and by Origen’s Lexicon above, col. 627, under the word Evelat.] Elillatous, inhabited world. Elcana, possession of God. Edom, failing. Ephrath, consolation. [Note: The Greek interprets this name as though it were written Eldan, for El means God and Dan means judgment. Thus Edad was substituted for Elmodad or Elmodan.] Edad, judgment of God. Eli, of God. Euphrates, humility of spirit. Ephraim, fruitfulness, or consoler. Elisabeth, forgiveness of God. Ezecias, divine strength. [Note: Just as Emimyr is corrupt for Emor, so the copyist may have written *ponos* instead of *onos*.] Emimur, toil. [Col. 1261] Eliezer, my God, my helper. Emmen, mothers. Engadi, eye of a kid. Enagallim, eye of heifers. [Note: Perhaps not Enagallim but Engannim should be read, unless the etymology of Engannim—“fountain of gardens,” or “eye of gardens”—stands in the way.] Enagallim, eye of heifers. Enoch, renewal. Esebon, thoughts. Endendor, pure eye. Eloi, God. Ermon, cursing. Eden [Note: Because Cain is said in the Septuagint to have dwelt in the land of Eden, the Greeks, poorly acquainted with the Hebrew language, thought that Eden meant “land.”], land. Eliacim, my God has risen. [Note: This etymology belongs to Josephus the Jew, as was observed above in Origen’s Lexicon.] Eve, mother of the living, beauty.

## Z

Zara, illustrious, rising. Zacharias, victor, or [Note: Here the name Zacharias is confused with the name Iscariot, which is interpreted “memory of death.”] memory of death. Zorobabel, little one from confusion. Zebedaeus, that very sacrifice of mine. Zacchaeus, chosen by lot. Zabulon, gift. [Note: The name Zelpha is interpreted as “walking mouth”; the ancients derive it from *azal*, “he went away,” and *phe*, that is, “mouth,” from the mouth, not from bone.] Zelpha, drawing out. [Note: I have supplied the name Zanoe for Zan, because it contains the syllable Zan. Perhaps Zenam could have been read. In any case, Zan is a Greek verb, not a Hebrew name.] Zan, he lives.

## H

Hesaias [Note: Saint Jerome, in the Names from the Epistle to the Romans, warned us that the following three names are to be read with H: Hesaias, Helias, and Herodion. Therefore do not be surprised that we read them with aspiration, according to the rough breathing marked in Greek.], shadowing, or exaltation of God. Heliu, God of the mighty, the sovereign. Hesau, forest, or oak. El, God. Eth, living. [Note: “Divine fire” is not the interpretation of the name Elijah, but an indication of his power or of the divine zeal with which he burned.] Helias, divine fire.

## TH

Thamar [Note: The etymology given here is wholly corrupt, as the Greek copy above, col. 631, has shown, where the name Thamar is interpreted as *Theou logoi*, “words of God,” or *deuro logoi*, “hither, words.” Therefore read *deuro logoi* and *kyrios*.], “hither, words,” or “Lord.” Thema, rising. Thecel, measure. [Note: I am not sufficiently certain whether Thartan should be read instead of Tabrathen; I supplied Chabrath because of the similarity of the letters.] Thabrathen, shattered. Thala, “they will roll”; read “they resound.” Thomas, incomprehensible, or twin. [Note: Jerome does not list the name Thaddaeus, but does list Theudas, which has the same meaning.] Thaddaeus, praised. [Note: This is the interpretation of Thecel in Daniel 5:27. The Greek copyist, however, placed the letter B before the verb *estathē*, producing great confusion. The element B, which occurs twice in the name Thecel, signifies that it has been weighed, whether in Daniel or in the present Vocabulary.] Thecel, it has been weighed. [Col. 1263] [Note: These are words from Joshua 6:19, sufficiently corrupt: “See the roads of the Themanites.”] Thaemanon, to have forbidden the ways by a sign, or apocryphal. [Read: African.] [Note: The Septuagint gives the Hebrew Thalpioth without interpretation in Song of Songs 4:4. Jerome translated it “fortifications,” according to the first Greek etymology.] Thalpioth, battlement, or lofty things. Thabor, of mockery. [Possibly: of jesting.] Thera, spirit of light. Thuer, sign, or calling. [Note: The Greek corruptly writes *notos*, “back,” instead of *notos*, “the southern region.” It is therefore the name of a wind blowing from the south.] Thanaam, south wind. Theman, from there.

## I

Jesus, salvation, savior, deliverer. Josias, saving. Jeremias, provision of water. Jezeciel, strength of God. Jonathan, dove coming. Jonas, dove. Joannes, expiation, rest, gift of God, healing of God, the grace of God, labor of God, flight from beauty, labor of God. Josedec, righteousness. Jacob, supplanter. Israel, a mind seeing God. Joppe [Note: This is a hallucination, or rather a deception, of the Greek copyist, who here suppresses the name Tharsis, interpreted as “exploration of joy,” and attaches this etymology to the name Joppe, because the two occur together in the same verse of Jonah 1:3.], observation of joy, wondrous beauty. Joac, brotherhood of God. Jezrael, not seeing God. Japheth, breadth. Jothor, blind, or superfluous. Jacobus, son of the heel. Isaac, exultation [Note: Isaac in no way means “angel.” Therefore, for the corrupt Greek word *angelos*, read—as in all the other earlier Fragments—*gelos*, that is, “laughter.”], angel. Judas, confession. Joseph, addition. Isachar, reward. Job [Note: *Eratοs*, “lovable,” should be read instead of *horatos*, “visible.” The ancients everywhere interpret Job’s name as “beloved of the Lord,” or “lovable of the Lord.” See above in the Fourth Fragment.], visible. Idumaea, failing. Jericho, rolled downward, or hollow and low-lying, or moon. Jael, ear of God. Jordan, descent of arrogance. Judaea, confessing. Jerusalem, vision of peace, sanctuary of peace. Joel, he has the spirit of God. Jaerus, watchfulness of the Lord. Jasuph, return. Jechonias, pure. Jao, Lord, or invisible. Jebus, Jerusalem. Joacim [Note: The Greeks confuse Joacim with the name Jechonias, which is expressed in Latin as “preparation of the Lord.” Joacim, however, means “resurrection of the Lord.”], preparation of the Lord.

## K

Cain, zeal, or possession. Kades, holy. Cephas, rock. Kedar, darkness. Capernaum, field, or house of consolation. [Col. 1265] Caiaphas, inquisitive. Carmel, knowledge of circumcision. Cana, possession. Konachol, almighty. Keph, calling. [Note: In Luke 1:28 we read the word *kecharitomene*, “full of grace,” as though the Virgin Mary were a receptacle of grace and virtues according to the Greek interpretation.] Kecharitomene, she who has received.

## L

Lamech, of election. Lia, laboring, having weak eyes. [Note: The Greek copyist again gives the name Lia and interprets it according to the character of the Greek language, for *leia* means “flat” among the Greeks; among the Hebrews it does not, since *laa* properly means “to suffer vexation,” “to labor,” and so forth.] Lia, flat. Levi, joining. Lazarus, turning back and being helped. Lebanon, whitening. Lot, exclusion.

## M

Messiah, Christ. Michael, general of God. Moses, removal of water. Mathusala [Note: The meaning of these Greek words is wholly uncertain. Certainly they do not express the etymology of Mathusala’s name. I do not know whether they can be understood in this way, according to the surface of the letters: “speaking because of the face,” “sent.”], speaking because of the face, sent. [Note: The etymology of Manasses among the Greeks is false and contrary to the truth, since *nasa*, from which the name Manasse is formed, means “he forgot,” not “he remembered.”] Manasses, remembrance. Melchi, king. Melchisedech, peaceful king. Mane, he measured. Moldan, judgment of water. Misael, mercy of God. Martha, the Lord came. Mariama, bitter sea. Michtheel, incomparable strength. Magdalene [Note: The same name Magdalene is interpreted above as *pephylagmenē*, that is, “guarded”; unless I am mistaken, it should likewise be read here, not *pephyteumenē*, “planted.”], planted. Matthew, glory of life. Malachi, angel. Michaeas, who is like the Lord? Mariam, seal of the Lord; “the Lord from my lineage”; illumination.

## N

Nephthalem, breadth, or assistance. Noemen, sweet. Nadam, goodwill. Natham, he gave. Naoum, consolation. Noema, faith. Naba, raven. Noah, rest. Nathanael, God gave. Nae, shaken. Nazareth, flower. [Note: We have discussed Naphtha at length in the preceding copy of Origen’s Lexicon. Compare the two passages.] Naphtha, oil poured out among the Persians. Noah, righteousness.

[Col. 1267]

## O

Hoon [Read: *hōon*.] [Note: Hoon may be thought to stand for Heroon, *hyperōon*, “upper chamber,” or for *rom*, that is, Ram, which means “lofty.”], the Most High. Urias, the spirit. [Note: The Greeks interpret the names of the two women Oola and Ooliba in this way, without attending to the force of the letters or the character of the Hebrew language, but according to what is written about them in Ezekiel 23, where the divine prophet attacks the idolatry of Samaria and Jerusalem, represented under the type of two prostitutes.] Ooliba, adulteress. Hodolla, prostitute. Ozias, strength of God.

## P

Passover [Note: Passover, or Phase, means “redemption” and “freedom,” not according to the proper meaning of the word, which signifies “crossing,” but because at the time of Passover, or the sacrifice of Phase, the Hebrews departed freely from Egypt and were redeemed from the harshest captivity by which they were oppressed.], crossing, redemption. Pessech, freedom. [Note: This name is written in Hebrew with Heth in the middle, which the Septuagint often renders with Chi; hence Paschor here stands for Phashur or Phasor.] Paschor, free. Paul, rest, least.

## R

Rubel [Note: This same word, by which Jacob’s firstborn was named, is corruptly written with an *l* at the end and interpreted here as “spirit of God.” The Greeks restore it with the correct reading and genuine etymology, namely Ruben, “seeing son.”], spirit of God. Ruben, seeing son. Rabbi, teacher. Ramma, lofty. Racca, empty. Raguel, shepherding of God. Raphael, spirit of God, or physician of God. Rachel, flock of God, or sheep of God. Rebecca, daughter of a shepherd. Ruth, flock. Rachel, ruler, knowledge.

## Σ

**Samuel** [Note: This false Greek etymology of the name Samuel has already been discussed above], “a request,” or “obedience to God.” **Symeon**, “hearing,” or “one who hears.” **Solomon**, “peaceful.” [Note: The Greeks always falsely interpret the name *Sedec* as “peace,” as earlier in the name *Melchisedec*, whereas its true interpretation is “just.”] **Sedec**, “of peace.” **Salim**, “peace.” **Seraphim** [Note: This alludes to the passage in Isaiah, where two Seraphim are described as standing; it does not explain the etymology of the word, which is very familiar in these books also. Thus Dionysius calls them *ἐμπρησταί*, “kindlers”; Cyril of Alexandria, *θερμαίνοντες*, “those who warm”; Chrysostom, *ἔμπυρα στόματα*, “fiery mouths,” to which the Latin *incendentes*, “those who set on fire,” corresponds], “spirits that rise.” **Satan**, “afflicting” (perhaps *θλίβων*, “causing distress”). **Sonam**, “hearing.” **Sidon**, “prey.” **Sin**, “thirst.” **Zion**, “thirsting.” **Samaria**, “it is called obedience.” **Sodom**, “assembly.” **Shephelah**, “a narrow basin.” **Sebna**, “returns.” **Senaiah**, “bush.” **Sabbath**, “rest, sanctification, cessation from work.” **Segor**, “rising.” **Siphah**, “rising.” **Sabai**, “Ethiopians.” **Sabaoth**, “power.” **Susanna**, “walled in.” **Zephaniah**, “understanding hidden things.” **Simon**, “humiliation.” **Seth**, “forgetfulness of evils” [Note: The Greek codex has *τημενός* instead of *θετός*, that is, “placed,” according to the etymology of the name *Seth*, which means “he placed,” and according to Jerome’s interpretation. I preferred, however, to substitute *θέμενος*, “having placed,” rather than *θετός* or *θέσις*, since fewer changes are made in the restored name]. **Sim**, “rest,” a name. **Solem**, “the perfect one.” **Saul**, “a request.” **Sanir** [Note: Martianay himself later emended this in the Addenda and Changes to *ὁδός*, “road,” instead of *ὀδούς*, “tooth,” and “road” instead of “tooth”], “the road of a lamp.” **Shulammite**, “she who makes peace.” [Note: The Greeks thought that Abraham’s wife’s name was originally Sarah, but was changed to Sarra by adding the element *r*; and because *r* is the number one hundred among the Greeks, they have imagined many foolish things about her name. Hence in the Greek manuscript Sarah is called “little” or “with few,” whereas Sarra is called “multiplied.”] **Sarah**, “very little.” **Sarra**, “having been multiplied” (perhaps “having been made numerous”). **Seir**, “a wheel.” **Shinar**, “a shaking off.” **Shechem**, “labor,” or “exercise.” **Saul**, “a pursuer.” **Shen**, “teeth.” **Zipporah**, “visitation,” or “beauty.”

## Τ

**Tigris** [Note: Clericus learnedly argues that *ὀξύτατον ῥεῦμα*, “the swiftest current,” should be read], “the sharpest spirit.” **Titus**, “discrimination.”

## Φ

**Perez**, “a cutting-off” [Note: Perhaps *διαίρεσις*, “division,” should be restored]; “it is divided.” **Phit**, “mouth.” **Pishon**, “mouth of fire.” **Philip**, “a life that has fled.” **Phanuel**, “redemption of God.” **Peninnah**, “repentance” (perhaps *μετάνοια*, “repentance”). **Paran**, “a heifer.” **Pharisees**, “divided,” “being cut apart.”

## Χ

**Ham**, “a sheaf of grain.” **Horeb**, “a new growth.” **Chelkiah**, “of the God who raises up.” **Cherub**, “a multitude.” [Note: I have no doubt that *γνώσεως*, “of knowledge,” has dropped out, as Philo himself interpreted it: “a multitude of knowledge,” or elsewhere, “much recognition and knowledge.” Anastasius of Sinai makes the same point in the twelfth *Anagogical Contemplation on the Hexaemeron*, as does Dionysius in *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, where the expression is “an outpouring of wisdom”; Chrysostom, in Homily 3 against the Anomoeans, has “knowledge made abundant.” Among Latin writers see Philastrius and Augustine, to omit the many others by whom “a multitude of knowledge” is confirmed.]

## Ω

**Hosanna**, “glory; save now.” **Hosea**, “shading,” or “guardian.”
