# [Col. 1269]

# On the Ten Names of God

## Preliminary Explanation

I do not deny that I derive the greatest intellectual pleasure from this final part of the Colbertine Greek codex, which opened the way for us to attain a complete understanding of Saint Jerome’s letter to Marcella. Although its words are in themselves perfectly clear, different people might nevertheless interpret them differently, especially where he says that the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, because of the similarity of its letters, was customarily read by some as *Pipi* when it was found in Greek books.

For who knew with certainty in what books that ineffable name was found? Was it in the text of the divine Scriptures, in the commentaries of Greek writers, or was it customary to read it in both? We know indeed that the Tetragrammaton, the Lord’s name, was found in certain Greek volumes—even down to Jerome’s own time—written in ancient letters, that is, Samaritan letters, as the same holy Doctor has left on record in the great Prologue to Scripture, or Preface to the Books of Kings.

It is undoubtedly reasonable to believe that these Samaritan letters, or those ancient Hebrew characters, distinguished from the modern ones by their shapes and strokes, were read and written only in certain Greek volumes of the Bible, and not expressed in other books. From this it was easy to conjecture, and there was sufficient basis for thinking, that the form which some read as *Pipi* was written only in those copies called the Holy Scriptures.

But from the Colbertine Greek manuscript, although it is extremely corrupt, we have learned clearly that the Tetragrammaton was written in Hebrew letters in Greek commentaries and, because the four letters resembled the Greek characters ΠΙΠΙ, was accustomed by some to be read as *Pipi*. I have called the Greek manuscript an utterly corrupted copy because, through the ignorance of its scribes, several of the names of God—and especially the Tetragrammaton—are read in it in a most corrupt form. To make this clearer, let us proceed in order to explain such corruptions.

The first lapse of the copyist, or of the writer—if indeed it was a lapse—appears in the quotation from the Law, that is, Exodus 28:36–37, where we read concerning the Tetragrammaton: “And you shall make a pure golden plate, and you shall engrave upon it an engraving like the engraving of a seal, holiness of the Lord.” Several words of this passage have been omitted, as you can see by comparing it with the same passage in the Colbertine manuscript, where instead of *ἁγίασμα κυρίου* it also reads *ἁγίασμα κυρίῳ*, and indeed equally or perhaps better, for the Hebrew reading is absent in the supplied text, which some read *Codes Laihova*, others *Codes Ladonai*, and interpret as “holiness of the Lord,” or, according to Jerome, “holy to the Lord.”

Immediately after the words just mentioned, *ἁγίασμα κυρίῳ*, the name [the name is absent in the supplied text] was written in the Greek books and was read as *ἴαω*. The person who copied the Colbertine codex, understanding this not at all, supposed that it was a Greek name and should be read *τε αρ*. Yet, however corruptly he wrote it, Greek letters still survive in the manuscript in a peculiar form that comes very close to the Hebrew, whose more usual reading was *ἴαω*, plainly visible in the manuscript.

Thus the first syllable of the word *tetarlon* was actually the Hebrew *he*; the form of the next letter indicates *vau*; then *α* joined with *ρ* represents the form of the second [letter], or the first if we read from right to left in the Hebrew manner; finally, the last place is occupied by *yod*. From these elements, written together, emerges the frequently mentioned and ever-adorable name [the name is absent in the supplied text], which the more learned Greeks read as *ἴαω*. Others, wholly ignorant and unskilled in the Hebrew language, accustomed themselves to read ΠΙΠΙ as though it were Greek when they encountered it in Greek books.

There is such confusion among the names of God in the manuscript after the word *τε αρ* that, without any ordinal number being assigned thereafter, they are set down indiscriminately in this way: *Ἴαω, ἐλωὶ, ἀδωναῒ, σαββαὼθ, σαδαῒ, ἰέαι, έκχέαι*. But from Jerome’s letter I would point out that three names of God have been omitted here: *El*, meaning “Strong”; *Elion*, meaning “Most High”; and *Eloe*, meaning “God,” the third and last.

The name *Adonai* is also read among the others, although the same Greek codex listed it earlier as the first of all. Thus we have no more than six names of God assigned by the Greeks, namely Adonai, Ia, Jao or Jehovah, Eloim, Sabaoth, and Saddai. For the last name, which the ignorance of the Greeks split into two by writing *ἰέαι, ἐκχέαι*, is one name among the Hebrews and the sixth in Jerome’s order: *ESER JEJE*. In Hebrew it is *ehje ascher ehje*, and in Latin it is expressed, “I shall be who I shall be.”

This name consists of these three words. Its reading has been entirely corrupted among the Greeks and must be restored from the traces of the Greek letters themselves as *ἰέαι ἔσερ ἰέαι*, unless someone prefers to borrow from Jerome this genuine and anciently accepted reading: *Ἰέιε ἔσερ Ἰέιε*. From this we understand that the ancients were not accustomed to read the vowel *e* under the characteristic of the future, but the vowel *i*; hence *Jeje* instead of the modern *ehje*.

Yet while we correct the errors of the Greeks, let us also imitate their commendable diligence by setting out the names of God at the end of these observations in their proper order and in an uncorrupted form:

1. **El**, Strong, or God.  
2. **Eloim**, God.  
3. **Eloe**, God.  
4. **Sabaoth**, of hosts.  
5. **Elion**, Most High.  
6. **Jeje eser Jeje**, I am who I am.  
7. **Adonai**, Lord.  
8. **Ia**, Lord.  
9. **Jao**, Lord.  
10. **Saddai**, Almighty.

Here we have followed the practice of the ancient writers. Although the matter itself called for this statement, I thought it not superfluous to make it because of certain modern Hebraists, whom I see becoming more readily irritated if something is read differently in Hebrew volumes from the way they themselves are accustomed to read it.

Moreover, the word *τετράγραμμον*, “tetragrammon,” in Theodoret, *Questions on Exodus*, question 15, was thought by J. Drusius to be corrupt and was restored by him in his *Tetragrammaton*. But from the Colbertine Greek manuscript and from the Latin copies of Saint Jerome it is abundantly clear that the ancients, with Theodoret, read *τετράγραμμον*. Therefore Drusius’s restoration or correction in chapter 23 of the work mentioned is a mere corruption if *τετραγράμματον* is read in the passage cited from Theodoret.

# Chapter

[Note: In Migne, the sections of text headed “Latin Translation,” “Colbertine Codex,” and “Jerome” are printed in parallel.]

## [Col. 1271] Latin Translation

Because of the Hebrew designation concerning the Lord, the following must be said. Among the Hebrews God is called by ten names. One is **Adonai**, which means “Lord.” Another is **Ia**, which is likewise translated into Greek as “Lord.” A third, besides these, is the name **Tetragrammaton**, existing as ineffable, which among the Hebrews is called **Adonai**, but among us **Lord**.

They say that this was written on the golden plate placed upon the forehead of the high priest, in accordance with what is said in the Law: “An engraving like the engraving of a seal, holiness to the Lord.” The fourth is **Jao**, **Eloi**, **Adonai**, **Sabaoth**, **Sedai**, **Jeai-eccheai**.

## Colbertine Codex

[Note: Martianay had read *περασμίως*, a corrupt word which he later corrected; below we in turn correct the Latin translation and Jerome’s text.]

Because of the Hebrew designation concerning the Lord, the following must be said. Among the Hebrews God is called by ten names. One is called **Adonai**, which means “Lord.” Another is **Ia**, which is likewise rendered in Greek as “Lord.” Another, besides these, is the **Tetragrammaton**, which is unutterable; among the Hebrews it is called **Adonai**, but among us **Lord**.

They say that this was written on the golden plate worn on the forehead of the high priest, in accordance with what is said in the Law: “An engraving like the engraving of a seal, holiness to the Lord.” … *τε αρ ἴαω. ἐλωῒ. ἀδωναῒ. σαβαὼθ. σαδαῒ. ἰέαι. ἐκχέαι.*

## Jerome

The first name of God is **El**, which the Septuagint translates as “God,” while Aquila, expressing its etymology, translates it as *ἰσχυρόν*, that is, “strong.” Next come **Eloim** and **Eloe**, which likewise mean “God.”

The fourth is **Sabaoth**, which the Septuagint translated as “of hosts” and Aquila as “of armies.” The fifth is **Elion**, which we call “Most High.” The sixth is **Eserieie**, which is read in Exodus as, “He who is has sent me” (Exodus 3:14).

The seventh is **Adonai**, whom we generally call “Lord.” The eighth is **Ia**, which is used only of God and is also heard as the final syllable of *Alleluia*. The ninth is the **Tetragrammaton**, which they considered *ἀνεκφώνητον*, that is, “ineffable,” and which is written with these letters: **Jod, E, Vau, E**. Some, not understanding it, became accustomed to reading it as **III III** because of the similarity of the letters when they encountered it in Greek books. The tenth is **Saddai**, which is left untranslated in Ezekiel, and so forth.

# [Col. 1273] Another and Better Copy of the Greek Chapter on the Ten Names of God

## Preliminary Explanation

I had been taking some pride in having first published these materials on the names of God and the Tetragrammaton from a Greek manuscript, when suddenly, during my daily reading, I came upon a fragment of Evagrius which the distinguished Joannes Baptista Cotelier had long ago published from four royal manuscripts in the third volume of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*.

My conscience bears witness both to the exultation and astonishment that then seized my mind—mine, because I rejoiced, and that of my companions, who shared my life—and I give thanks to the Lord that from this fragment, or chapter of Evagrius, I have discovered that my conjectures concerning the corrupted name ΠΙΠΙ in the Colbertine manuscript were entirely correct.

Where the Greek copyist who transcribed the manuscript in question had corruptly and incompetently written *τε τ αρ τ*, that is, *τέταρτον*, the royal manuscript copies retain the name ΠΙΠΙ, or *πι πι*, distinctly and without corruption. They do not, however, immediately add *Ἴαω*, which is nevertheless retained in the Colbertine codex, as I noted earlier when discussing the reading used among the Greeks.

Everyone should therefore recognize how greatly useful a large supply of manuscript books always proves: they support one another in restoring genuine readings, and what seemed missing from one is immediately supplied from others. Thus the royal copies in the Greek fragment under discussion display the name ΠΙΠΙ, which other copies either corrupt or omit; conversely, the Colbertine codex, although corrupted in many places through the ignorance of its scribe, nevertheless supplies the reading of the Tetragrammaton, namely *Ἴαω*, which is omitted in the other manuscripts.

Moreover, many things in the royal codices seem to require correction and supplementation in the Colbertine manuscript as I published it. Since I had found that one manuscript alone in the chapter on the Ten Names of God, I did not then wish to indulge correction too freely, and left untouched several things that I now recognize must be changed. I wish them to be restored in the following manner.

I interpreted the word *περασμίως* at the end because *πέρας* means “end” or “limit,” and *πεπερασμένος* in Aristotle means “bounded” or “terminated.” Since that is how I found it written in the Colbertine codex, I published it as though it were an adverb. Taking *περασμίως* adverbially, I necessarily thought that the noun *γλῶτταν*, “tongue” or “language,” had to be understood, so that the Greek phrase would have a complete sense: *Διὰ τὴν Ἑβραϊκὴν γλῶσσαν*, that is, “for the sake of the Hebrew language.” Otherwise even the more learned could have extracted no meaning that was not false or inconsistent with the force of the Greek words.

But from the four royal codices cited and explained by the distinguished and learned Cotelier, an obvious error appears in the Colbertine copy, which reads *περασμίως* instead of *παρασημείωσιν*. Hence a meaning emerges that is entirely different from the one I gave in Latin from the thoroughly corrupted Greek.

The expression *παρασημείωσις Ἑβραϊκή*, “Hebrew designation,” is particularly appropriate for the name of the Tetragrammaton, because it always designates the omnipotent God in Hebrew books, as though it were the sign of divinity and unchangeable essence. It is therefore this name, which the Hebrews were accustomed to use for God alone, that is meant by *παρασημείωσις Ἑβραϊκή*, “Hebrew designation,” for whose sake Evagrius—or whoever else was responsible—explained the other matters set out in the following chapter.

There is another sufficiently notable difference between the manuscript copies in these words concerning the Tetragrammaton. The Colbertine reads: “The Tetragrammaton, being ineffable, is called among the Hebrews Adonai.” The royal copies read instead: “The Tetragrammaton—being ineffable among the Hebrews—is, by an abuse of language, called among them Adonai.”

Here you see many details expressed that are omitted in the Colbertine, especially *καταχρηστικῶς*, “abusively” or “by an improper usage,” which means that among the Hebrews the name Tetragrammaton, although ineffable, is called and read as Adonai.

Modern Jews and Hebrew grammarians do not agree with this note. They teach that the proper, self-existent name of God is never read by the Jews as it is written, out of the greatest reverence with which they regard that name. Instead, they attach to it vowel points belonging to another word—almost always the vowel points of *Adonai*, that is, “Lord.” If, then, there is an abuse in the designation of the Tetragrammaton among the Hebrews, it is no other than an abuse—or rather a sign—of reverence and religious devotion.

Besides the differences between the manuscript copies already mentioned, many others, both numerous and serious, remain. For example, the final name recorded in the Colbertine codex, *Ἰέαι, ἐκχέαι*, is extremely corrupt. The royal copies read *Ἰαιὲ, Ἐσεριὲ*, and do so better, though not without a very significant corruption.

As I said in the preceding observations, this name is one of the ten Names of God, placed in Exodus 3:14: *ehje ascher ehje*, or, according to Jerome’s reading, *Jeje eser Jeje*. Since it is one name of God composed of three words, the Greek codices wrongly divide it into two names, and all of them make this mistake.

The royal copies rightly give *Jaje* and *Eser*. But for the complete restoration of the genuine reading, *Eser* must be separated from the final syllable *je*, and the other syllable must be placed before it in conjunction, namely *Ja*, so that the Greeks may read, in conformity with the Hebrew, *Ἰαιὲ Ἐσὲρ Ἰαιὲ*, that is, “I shall be who I shall be.” Following the pattern of this restored reading, the Colbertine codex can be corrected from the royal copies.

The same Colbertine copy also omitted these necessary words, which are found in the royal copies: *Τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ ὀνόματά ἐστιν ταῦτα. Ἤλ*, and so forth; that is, “The remaining names are these: El,” and so forth.

I noted above that in the Colbertine codex the name of God **El**, together with two others, **Elion** and **Eloe**, had been omitted, and that only six or seven names by which God is called among the Hebrews had been listed. The same point must now be observed concerning the royal Greek codices, because they contain no mention of Elion or Eloe.

To make the matter more exact, we now place the entire Greek chapter of Evagrius on the Ten Names of God before the press, together with the notes of the distinguished Joannes Baptista Cotelier. I am eager to congratulate him fully on his work, although I have decided to supply some things that seem to have escaped the diligence of this most learned writer.

The notable fragment of Evagrius was therefore published for us by that man, now deservedly remembered, in volume 3 of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, pages 116 and 554–555.

# [Another Copy on the Ten Names of God]

[Note: In Migne, the Greek and Latin versions of the following text are printed in parallel.]

## EVAGRIUS: On ΠΙ ΠΙ

### [Col. 1275A]

Because of the Hebrew designation concerning the Lord, the following must be said. God is called by ten names among the Hebrews. One of them is pronounced **Adonai**, that is, “Lord.” Another is **Ia**, which has likewise been rendered in our language as “Lord.” Another besides these is the **Tetragrammaton**, or “four-letter name,” ineffable among the Hebrews, which, by a misuse of language, is called by them **Adonai**, but by us **Lord**.

They say that this was written on the golden plate worn on the forehead by the high priest, in accordance with what is said in the Law: “An engraving like the engraving of a seal, holiness to the Lord” (Exodus 28:36).

**ΠΙΠΙ.** The remaining names are these: **El, Eloim, Adon, Sabaoth, Saddai, Iaie, Eserie**. And the three written above, among which is the Tetragrammaton, are written with these letters: **Joth, Hep, Vau, Hiep**. **III III. God.**

### [Col. 1275C]

The ineffable name used for the Lord is written with four letters, namely **Joth, Hep, Vau, and Heth**, with a letter inserted in the middle, or after the first two, which the Hebrews call **Sen** and which means “teeth.”

Thus the five letters, when transliterated, form this sequence or sentence: “This beginning, teeth in it, the one who lives.” For the four letters have these interpretations: **Joth**, “beginning”; **Hep**, “this”; **Vau**, “in it”; **Heth**, “the one who lives.”

[Note: I think he is hinting at the name Jesus, although he draws it forcibly into his own argument, writing [Hebrew form absent in the supplied text], or *Jehoshuah*, instead of [name absent in the supplied text].]

[Note: [Col. 1275C] Evagrius on ΠΙΠΙ. Although this fragment, or chapter and scholion, had already been published without its author’s name by John Croy in *Specimen of Conjectures on Certain Passages of Origen, Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Epiphanius*, p. 50, nevertheless, because of the name of Evagrius and because the piece is notable and brief, we have arranged for it to be printed again here in a more correct form, chiefly for comparison with Jerome’s Letter 136 to Marcella on the same subject. Peter Lambecius, *Bibliotheca Caesarea*, book 3, codex 3, says that it is part of the Athanasian synopsis.]

## Evagrius: On ΠΙΠΙ

[Col. 1276A]

Concerning the Hebrew notation used for the Lord, the following must be said. Among the Hebrews God is called by ten names, [Col. 1276B] one of which is called Adonai, that is, “Lord”; another is Ia, which likewise in Greek has been rendered “Lord.” Another name besides these is the Tetragrammaton, which is unutterable among the Hebrews. By an abuse of language it is called Adonai by them, but by us “Lord.” They say that it was written on the golden plate worn on the forehead of the high priest, in accordance with what is said in the Law: “The representation of a seal: holiness to the Lord” (Exodus 28:36) ΠΙ ΠΙ [variant: πι πι; absent in another reading].

[Note: [Col. 1275D] Ia. At the end of Letter 63 among the letters attributed to Boniface there is a very corrupt rhythm concerning the names of God: “Elon and the illustrious Acaddai. Allevatia.” It seems that it ought to be restored approximately as follows:

“Farewell, living one, in happiness,

that you may be holy in simplicity.

May salvation be granted to you

through the ages, from the heights.

Let us live for the Lord alone,

always alive throughout the age.

Indeed, with abundant prayers

and very frequent tears,

I ask him alone

to furnish us with most frequent aid,

that we may be worthy of glory,

where the most joyful songs

of the angels resound,

and heavenly gladness,

the radiant mercy of Christ,

and lofty praise through the ages.

May we fare well; join us to

the victorious angelic hosts;

may we endure forever

in the joys of Paradise.

And Eloim, El,

and Michael,

and Saddai,

Adonai,

raise up Ia;

Alleluia.”]

[Note: [Col. 1275D] Ia. A passage from a Catena on John, at the end of chapter 8, presents itself here: “For Jobel is Hosanna doubled, ‘God, God.’ For Joah and El among the Hebrews are called God.” That is, if we trust the translator: “Jubil is Hosanna doubled, that is, ‘God, God.’ Jehovah and El among the Hebrews are called God.”]

[Note: [Col. 1276C] “Holiness to the Lord.” Thus Origen in his commentary on the first Psalm, together with Cyril of Alexandria, book 11 of *On Worship in Spirit and Truth*, p. 388; likewise Royal codex 24.16 and the Colbertine codex. The common reading is “of the Lord.” From chapter 28:36.]

The remaining names are these: El, Eloim [variant: Eloi], Adon [variant: Adonai], Sabaoth, Saddai, Iaie [variant: Iaith], Eserie, together with the three written above, one of which is the Tetragrammaton, written with these letters:

[Note: [Col. 1276D] “Written with these letters.” For Photius has been corrupted here, when he writes in Letter 162: “It is also written with these letters: ioth, alpha, vau, eth.”]

Ioth, Hep, Vau, Hethi [variant: Hep]. ΠΙΠΙ [variant: πι πι], “God.”

[Col. 1276C] The name assigned to the Lord, which is unutterable, is written with four letters: with Ioth, with Hep, with Vab, and with Hethi. Between these, after the first two, there is inserted a letter called by the Hebrews Sen, that is, “teeth.” Thus the sequence of the five letters is as follows: “Beginning, this, teeth in it, the living one.”

[Note: [Col. 1275] I think he is hinting at the name Jesus, although he draws it violently into his own argument, writing [uncertain or omitted form], or *Jehoshuah*, instead of [uncertain or omitted form].]

The four letters have these interpretations: Ioth, “beginning”; Hep, “this”; Vau, “in it”; Heth, “the living one.”

[Note: [Col. 1276D] “On the Lord,” etc. I refer you to Drusius at the end of his book *On the Tetragrammaton*, and to Vossius in the *Etymologicum*, under the word *juvo*, as well as to Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book 10, chapter 5; Jerome, Letter 155; and Alcuin, *On Divine Offices*, chapter 39. To the learned notes of J. B. Cotelerius on Evagrius’s fragment we add our own observations for a fuller understanding of the name Tetragrammaton and of the letters with which it is said to have been written among the Hebrews.

In the Royal codices it is called *τετράγραμμα*, not *τετραγράμματον*; in the Colbertine manuscript, however, it is *τετράγραμμον*, in accordance with the reading of Theodoret quoted above and with this observation of Eusebius of Caesarea, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, book 9, chapter 7:

“‘Lord’ is rendered in Hebrew by means of the name consisting of four letters; and since the children of the Hebrews say that it is unutterable, they customarily use it of God alone.”

Although *τετράγραμμον* is understood more properly as “of four lines” than “of four letters,” usage nevertheless prevailed among the most distinguished ancient writers, so that this unutterable name was called *τετράγραμμον*, not *τετραγράμματον*. This seems to have escaped Cotelerius, who printed *τετραγράμματον* from the Royal codices.

Saint Jerome also testified that the proper and ineffable name of God was written on the golden plate worn on the forehead by the high priest. In his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 6, he writes:

“What is often called ADONAI in this Prophet, meaning ‘Lord,’ ought, for Greeks and Latins who do not know the Hebrew language, to be explained briefly. ADONAI is one of the ten names of God and signifies ‘Lord’; we often use it of human beings as well. Thus Sarah, calling Abraham her lord, called him by this name. And where it says, ‘Lord, my king,’ ADONAI is written. Whenever, therefore, the two names ‘Lord’ and ‘Lord’ are joined together, the first is the common name, while the second is properly God’s, and is called *ἄρρητον*, that is, ‘ineffable’; it was written on the golden plate that was on the forehead of the high priest.”

Few people, unless I am mistaken, clearly perceive the meaning of this passage, because it is not evident either from our Latin Vulgate or from the Greek Roman version of the Seventy that, in the Prophet Ezekiel, chapter 6 and often elsewhere, ADONAI, “Lord,” is written. For in Greek one reads: “Hear the word of the Lord: Thus says the Lord to the mountains” (Ezekiel 6:3). In the Vulgate, however: “Hear the word of the Lord God: Thus says the Lord God to the mountains.”

From this it may readily be conjectured that ADONAI, “Lord,” is written only in the Hebrew text, where *Adonai Eloim* occurs very frequently; this is interpreted as “Lord Lord,” or as “Adonai Lord,” according to Jerome’s annotation. But whoever compares the Alexandrian manuscript with Jerome’s commentaries at this point will immediately understand that Jerome read in his Greek copies of the Septuagint translators what he was reminding Greeks and Latins ignorant of Hebrew.

For in the Alexandrian manuscript at Ezekiel 6:3 one finds written: “Hear the word of Adonai Lord: Thus says Adonai Lord to the mountains”—“Hear the word of Adonai Lord: Thus says Adonai Lord to the mountains.” The observation of the holy Doctor is therefore proved correct: of the two joined names “Lord” and “Lord,” the first is the common name, Adonai, which we often use of human beings; the second is God’s proper name, that is, the unutterable Tetragrammaton, which was written on the golden plate that was on the forehead of the high priest.

Jerome likewise left this testimony in book 5 of his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 16:

“We wish to know what the crown of beauty on Jerusalem’s head is. Let us turn to Exodus, where it is written: ‘And he made a golden plate and wrote upon it letters formed like a seal of the holiness of the Lord, and placed it upon Aaron’s head.’ The sign of the Lord’s holiness is the name of almighty God, which is written with four Hebrew letters and is called by them ineffable, since his name cannot be spoken. Even the Gentiles were not ignorant of its majesty, as the altar of the Athenians testifies: ‘To the unknown God.’ Hence the Apostle also says: ‘The one whom you worship as unknown, I proclaim to you.’ I think this is the crown,” and so forth.

If only the recent writer named Gravisset had read this passage when discussing the Urim and Thummim! In a novel conjecture he persuaded himself that the Hebrew high priest, crowned or adorned with a tiara, was called “Holiness to the Lord.” As though it had ever been permissible to say that the ineffable and incommunicable name Jao was shared by a corruptible human being and almighty God. How much less could he be called “Holiness to the Lord,” whose sign was that name written with four letters? The name, therefore, was called “Holiness to the Lord,” not the high priest who wore the crown of beauty on his head.

We have spoken briefly above of several names of God that are corrupt or omitted. Here, too, it must be observed that the name Adon or Adonai, which Cotelerius wished to have in the Royal codices, perhaps in place of Adoni, however it is understood, is corruptly read for Elion. Nor can there be a threefold name Adonai among the ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews; yet it would be counted as a third name of God if, after the word ΠΙΠΙ, we counted another Adonai.

Furthermore, in the Royal copies Iaie [variant: Iaith] is incorrectly listed as though it were a name distinct from Eserie. For the three words Iese, Eser, and Ieje, as I said earlier, constitute one of the ten names of God. It follows that two names of God have been omitted, and that only eight are read in the codices of the Royal Library, namely: common Adonai; proper Adonai, that is, ΠΙΠΙ; Ia; El; Eloim; Sabaoth; Saddai; Iaje; Eser; Iaje. The number ten will be complete if Elion and Eloe are added.

As for the letters with which the ineffable name of God is read as written among the Hebrews, the Greeks designate them in Evagrius’s chapter as follows: Ioth, Hep, Vau, Hiep [variant: Hep], ΠΙΠΙ [variant: πι πι]. But they write Ioth corruptly for Iod. For Hebrew grammarians read the name of this element at the end with Daleth, not with Tau: Jod, not Joth.

Next, the Greek Hep encompasses two ways of reading the Hebrew element, for among the ancients we commonly read it as He or E. The Greeks seem to assign to it the name πι; and with the same ignorance by which they read ΠΙΠΙ, they read Hep in it instead of E, the fifth letter of the Greek alphabet.

Vau, or Vab, differs in no way from the custom of the Greeks, who read consonantal v by *ou* and substitute b for υ: *Seoueros* and *Sebēros* for Severus, *Ouespasianos* for Vespasianus, and so forth. Thus, according to their custom, they read the Hebrew Vau as Ouau. The Easterners also want it to be soft, like the monosyllable *oua*, whereas many rabbis would pronounce it more harshly, as *va*.

Finally, the meaning of these four elements sufficiently indicates that Jerome followed the opinion of the Greeks in the interpretation he attached to them. Among the Greeks, Jod is interpreted as *ἀρχή*, that is, “beginning”; He is expressed as *αὕτη* or *αὐτή*, “this” or “itself.” Likewise, in Jerome’s present Letter 30, Jod sounds as “beginning,” while He is rendered in Latin as “this.”

But Vau, which the Greeks falsely and forcibly interpret as *ἐν αὐτῇ*, “in it,” Jerome took as the coordinating conjunction “and,” and avoided the Greeks’ error by which they assert that the second He of the Tetragrammaton signifies “the living one”: “and through Heth, the one who lives.” I admit that Hheth, which has a double aspiration among the Hebrews and occupies the eighth place in the sequence of the alphabet, signifies “life,” as Jerome also testifies. But here the Greeks’ error is manifest: they confuse He, the fifth element, with Hheth, which is counted eighth in the Hebrew alphabet.

It will readily be understood that Hheth is interpreted as “life” if we remember that *Hhaja* means “he lived,” “he came to life again,” and so forth. But if we read *Haja* with He, with a simple aspiration, it is the substantive verb “was.”]

Having considered the Greeks’ faulty understanding of the elements of the ineffable divine name, I might think that my curiosity had reached its end. Yet a greater eagerness to inquire and discuss arises, for I am utterly distressed and cannot endure what Jerome wrote concerning the Tetragrammaton to Pope Damasus:

“It must be known that wherever the Seventy Translators expressed ‘Lord of hosts’ and ‘Lord almighty,’ the Hebrew has ‘Lord SABAOTH,’ which Aquila translates as ‘Lord of armies.’ The Lord himself also is the Lord of four letters. This is properly applied to God: JOD, HE, JOD, HE, that is, two IAs, which, being doubled, produce that ineffable and glorious name of God.”

If Jerome is set against Jerome, it is necessary to admit that he is not entirely consistent with himself, since above he said that the ineffable name of God was composed of JOD, HE, VAU, JOD, whereas here he teaches that it was formed from two IAs, that is, JOD, HE, JOD, HE. But, as we noted elsewhere, that error is corrected in two manuscript copies of the letter to Pope Damasus. For in the oldest Colbertine codex the following annotation is written in the margin beside Jerome’s text: “Jod, He, Jod, He.” In place of the second JOD, VAU is more correctly read, giving JAO. The manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Cygirannus also exhibits this correction, though it was clumsily transferred into the body of the letter.

Jerome, or whoever else it was, therefore intended a double HE to be written in the Tetragrammaton, but not a double JOD, and consequently not a double IA. The learned reader will find another answer to this difficulty in *Prolegomena* 3 to Jerome’s *Divine Library*, no. 6, where we said that the holy Doctor was referring to Greek codices when he taught that the ineffable name of God was composed of two IAs. For since that name was written in this form among the Greeks, ΠΙΠΙ, it was easy, given the complete equality of the elements and syllables, for Jerome to say to Damasus that the divine Tetragrammaton consisted of two IAs, that is, of two ΠΙs.

This answer gains strength from the time at which he sent his letter to Damasus, bishop of Rome. At that time Jerome was a student of Gregory of Nazianzus at Constantinople, and during those three years he seems to have been occupied more with reading Greek books than with the Hebrew sources, to which he later devoted himself entirely when he had grown older.

It may not be irrelevant to add that Jerome perhaps indicated the Chaldean rather than the Hebrew manner of writing the ineffable name. For the Chaldeans write that glorious name of God with two Jods and a single Qames, in this form [form omitted]. These signs, when divided, can produce two IAs; hence there is nothing to prevent us from saying that the Tetragrammaton was formed from two syllables, or from one and the same syllable doubled.

Nevertheless, I am not unaware that, against this last explanation of Jerome’s words, there are certain matters difficult to explain, which seem to be raised against our answer and to call for a better one. I therefore think that the earlier explanation should be preferred.

To this discussion also belong the observations made by John Drusius in book 1 of *Hebrew Questions*, question 56.

But after weighing the Greeks’ errors concerning the Tetragrammaton, and weary of their ignorance, let us turn to the Hebrews, so that we may disclose to the learned reader here the tradition concerning the ineffable name of God that they themselves have received from the Fathers and preserve. In this way the curiosity of study will lack nothing, and no one will demand greater diligence from us.

I therefore set down what I found among Hebrew grammarians that was more learned concerning that most glorious name which we call the Tetragrammaton:

*ὁ ὢν*, “the being,” “the one who is,” and who truly subsists or exists, and through whom all things that are and exist were made. It is God’s proper name, by which he is distinguished from idols, which are not and do not exist but are fabricated.

John expressed it thus in Revelation 1:4: *ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος*, “the one who is, who was, and who is to come,” as though *Jeheve*, “he will be”; *hove*, “being”; and *hava*, “he was,” constituted the three tenses, and as though he were judging God’s eternity, since he alone exists of himself from eternity.

But it is simply formed through Jod from *heemanthi*, “I believed,” just as it may be formed from *hava*, “he was”; or also from *haja*, “he was,” with the letter He changed, so that it differs from *jihje*, “he will be.”

The author of this name is God himself, Exodus 3:14: “And they will say to me, ‘What is his name?’ What shall I say to them?” And God said to Moses: *ehje ascher ehje*, “I shall be who I shall be.” The Seventy: *ἐγὼ εἰμὶ ὁ ὤν*, “I am the one who is.” And he said: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: *ehje*, ‘I shall be,’ *ὁ ὤν*, ‘the one who is,’ has sent me to you.”

And God said further to Moses: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: Jehova, *κύριος*, the Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you. This is my name forever, and this is my memorial throughout every generation.”

Thus *ehje ascher ehje*, “I shall be who I shall be,” and simply *ehje*, “I shall be,” and Jehova, “the one who is,” are the same.

The Jews call it *schem schel arba othijoth*, “the name of four letters”; the Greeks call it *τετραγράμματον*, from the number of letters with which it is written. They neither use it in reading nor employ it in writing, out of a certain religious scruple. Rather, wherever it occurs in the Holy Scriptures, they read Adonai in its place, which means “Lord” and is rendered *κύριος* by the Seventy and by the Apostles.

It has the same vowel-points, except when Adonai precedes or follows it. Then they read Elohim, which means “God,” so that they will not be compelled to say Adonai twice, which they consider improper. Concerning these added points—a chirek beneath [form omitted] and a hateph-segol beneath [form omitted]—they give instruction, as in 2 Samuel 7: “You have known your servant, Adonai Eloim,” whereas in 1 Chronicles 17 one finds “Jehova Elohim,” “Lord God.”

When it must be written, they put [form omitted] in its place, that is, *hassem*, “that name”; and *κατ’ ἐξοχήν* they understand this to mean the name of God, taken from Leviticus 14. They subsequently call it by various names.

First, they call it “the name of four letters,” because it is written with four letters. Next, they call it *schem hamphorasch*, “the explained name,” when, as it is written, it is expressed, spoken, or pronounced. Thus the son of an Israelite woman in Leviticus 24 “pronounced,” *eth-hassem*, “that name,” and cursed.

He pronounced the name Jehova, which he had heard on Mount Sinai, *bichthiva*, “with its written letters,” and cursed. The Jews falsely claim that Christ performed miracles *al schem hamphorasch*, “through the expressed name,” which, they say, Jehova pronounced over the sick who were healed and over the dead who came back to life, just as the Apostles performed miracles through the name of Jesus Christ.

Benjamin the Jew, in his *Itinerary*, writes that David the magician completed in one day a journey of ten days *per Schem amphoras*, that is, through the power of the pronounced name Jehova.

Third, they call it *Schem amphoras*, “the name of twelve letters,” the name Jehova in the blessing of Numbers 6: “May the Lord bless you and keep you.” For, being placed there three times, it makes twelve letters, and it was pronounced by the priests when they recited this blessing in the Temple.

Fourth, they call it “the explained name of seventy-two letters,” *schem haggadol*, “the great name,” which occurs in Exodus 14: “And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the Lord drove back the sea by an east wind.” For that verse consists of seventy-two letters, as do the two preceding verses, with which it is connected in continuous discourse.

From those three verses they make seventy-two words and names; hence they call it the name of seventy-two words or names. Thus in the Song of Songs 3, “Until the day breaks,” the Targum calls it the great name explained through seventy names. They invent the story that this name of seventy-two letters was engraved on the staff with which Moses divided the sea and struck the rock that poured forth water.

Fifth, they call it “the explained name of forty-two letters,” which the high priest pronounced on the Day of Atonement. This is from Leviticus 16: “For on that day he shall make atonement for you, to cleanse you from all your sins; before the Lord you shall be clean.”

The priests blessed Israel: first, in the holy language; second, standing; third, with hands raised; fourth, in a loud voice; fifth, face to face; sixth, *besem hamphoras*, “in the expressed name”; seventh, in the sanctuary.]

Adam, “earth.” Abel is the name of one who mourns. Abraham, “exalted father.” Abram, “father chosen for sound.” Abiud, “my father.” Aelim is interpreted as “gates.” Ethiopia, “humility.” Agar, “resident alien.” Amalec, “a people who lick.” Anna, “grace.” Aaron, “mountainous.” Arphaxat, “he troubled misery.” Aunam is interpreted as “eyes.” The Amorites, “speaking.”

Babylon, “confusion.” Babylon, “transposition.” Balac, “mad.” Bathuel, “daughter of God.” Balaam, “vain people.” Balla, “swallowing.” Benjamin, “son of days.” Beseleel, “in the shadow of God.” Beelphegor, “the upper mouth of skin.”

Cades, “holy.” Cain, “possession.” Chaldim is interpreted as “equality.” Chaleb, “whole heart.” Cham is interpreted as “heat.” Chamos, “as if touching.” Chanaan, “commotion.” Charran, “pit or cavern.” Cherubim, “great knowledge.”

Damascus, “blood of a sack.” Dan, “judgment.” Debon, “judgment.” Dina, “judgment.” Dothaim, “sufficient abandonment.” Dothain, “not insignificant failure.”

Edem, “delights.” Edom, “earthly.” Eliezer, “my God is my helper.” Eliphas, “God scattered me.” Emor, “ass.” Enoch, “your grace.” Enoch, “gracious.” Enos, “hope.” [Col. 1285] Enos is called “man” by the Latins.

Ephraim, “fruitfulness of memory.” Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitfulness.” Ephron, “dust.” Esau, interpreted sometimes as “work” and sometimes as “oak.” Eschol derives its name from “fire.” Esebon is interpreted as “thoughts.” Eva, “life.” Evilat, “giving birth.”

Galaad, “migration of testimony.” Gedeon is interpreted as “a pirates’ station.” Geon, “breast” or “horned one.”

Jacob, “one who attacks with his heels,” “supplanter.” Israel, “seeing God.” Japheth, “breadth.” Jordan is interpreted as “descent.” Joseph, “addition of the Lord.” Joseph is interpreted as “addition.” Jothor is interpreted as “superfluous.” Ir is interpreted as “leathery.” Isaac, “laughter and joy.” Ismael, “hearing of God.” Issachar, “reward.” Judas, interpreted as “confession to the Lord.” Joshua, “salvation of the Lord.”

Laban, “white.” Lia, “weariness,” “refusing and laboring.” Lot is interpreted as “declination.”

Madian is called “from judgment.” Mambre is named from “vision.” Manasses, “from forgetfulness.” Melcha, “queen.” Melchisedec, likewise “king of peace,” that is, Salem—for that is how it is interpreted. [Col. 1287] Moab, “from the father.” Moses, “taken from the water.” *Mos*, in the language of the Egyptians, means “water.” Moses is called “taking” by translation; it can also mean “touching.”

Nadab is interpreted as “willing.” Nachor means “rest of light.” Naid, “commotion.” Nebrod, “desertion.” Nephthalim, “he opens and enlarges.” Noe is interpreted as “rest” or “just.” Noe, “solid.”

### O

Osee is interpreted as “what sort of person is this?” Or, “light.”

### P

Pharaoh, “destroyer.” Phison is interpreted as “change of mouth.” Phua is interpreted as “redness.” Pitho, “persuasive speech.” Psontomphanech, “in the answer, a judging mouth.”

### R

Rachel, “vision of profanation.” Raguel, “the art of God’s shepherding.” Ramese is interpreted as “the moth’s shaking,” or “one who exalts the mind.” Rebecca, “patience.” Ruben, “seeing a son.” Ruma, “seeing something.”

[Col. 1289]

Samuel is interpreted as “appointed to God.” Sara, “my principate.” Sarra, “princess.” Sepphora, “little bird.” Sychem, “shoulder.” Syria is interpreted as “exalted.” Sicima, whose name means “support.” Settin, “thorns.” Sur, “fortification” or “direction.” Symeon, “being heard.” Sennaar, “shaking off.”

### T

Thamar is interpreted as “palm tree.” Thamna, “wavering deficiency.” Tharra is interpreted as “investigation of odor.”

### Z

Zabulon is called “nightly nature.” Zelpha, “journey of the mouth.”

[Note: [Col. 1281A] Philo interprets the name Abraham rather violently. From the Hebrew, *Abraham* can scarcely be extracted as “father chosen for sound,” unless he assumes that *ab* means “father,” *bar* “chosen,” and *hama* “sound.” Jerome’s interpretation likewise proves more accurate according to the sound of the letters than according to their actual elements: the word *Abraham* is written with only five letters, whereas “father seeing a people” has seven elements, [Hebrew forms omitted], so that *ab* means “father,” *ra* “seeing,” and *am* “people.” See another interpretation of the name Abraham in the book of *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.]

Abiud, “my father,” p. 414.

[Note: [Col. 1281A] In the explanation of many names, Philo supplies or assumes elements that are not expressed. Here, in Abiud, he drops the final syllable *ud*, since only *Abi* means “my father.” Jerome does not do this: he expresses the whole name, saying “strength of the father”; but he nevertheless takes the name as though it were corruptly written *Abiam* or *Abium*, with *m* at the end, as I have found *Eliam* and *Elium* written in some copies of the Old Latin version of Matthew. [Col. 1282A] *Abiam* means “their father,” because of the final letter *m*, which among the Hebrews is the suffix, or third-person masculine plural pronoun.]

> **Note [Col. 1293A].** Jerome discussed this etymology as follows in the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*: “The cause of the name Naphtali is explained here quite differently from the way it is written in the *Book of Hebrew Names*. Thus Aquila says, *synanestrepsen me ho theos kai synanestraphēn*, ‘God turned me about, and I was turned about,’ whereas in Hebrew it is written *Nephtule Eloim Nephtalethi*. Therefore he gave the name Naphtali to his son from ‘turning’ or ‘comparison,’ since both words have the sound of turning or comparison. The grammarians of our own time do not interpret Rachel’s words, *naphthule Eloim niphthalti*, in this way, but as ‘I have wrestled with God.’ Nevertheless, they admit that the word is metaphorically transferred to the mind, and that the Hebrew name *niphthal* denotes cunning and craft, as in Proverbs 8 and Job 5. [Col. 1295] ## Ζ

**Zoor** —

> **Note [Col. 1295A].** If the reading of the name *Zoor* in Josephus is genuine, it plainly appears that he read the letter *tsade* as the Greek zeta, or the Latin *z*, for the word has *tsade* as its initial element. Jerome did not do this; he counted the letter *tsade* among the three Hebrew *s* letters. Concerning this same name *Zoor*, Jerome wrote above, col. 16: “Segor means ‘small’; it is the same place that is also called Soor above. But it must be known that it does not have the letter *g* in the middle; among the Hebrews it is written with the vowel *ayin*. Finally, the sound of the Hebrew letter *sade* is one that Latin ears recoil from,” as col. 15 testifies. I would have the learned and inquisitive reader consult that passage.

“the small” (p. 20).

> **Note [Col. 1295].** The Septuagint translated the Hebrew word as *Sēnōr* in Genesis 19:22–23. Martianus immediately reads *oligos*, “small.”

**Zebulun** —

> **Note [Col. 1295B].** Josephus interprets the name Zebulun wrongly and violently, because the Hebrew *Zebul* or *Zabal* is not correctly translated by the Greek *enechurazomai*, “I am pledged,” whence *ēnechurazmenos*, “pledged” or “taken as a pledge.” Jerome’s etymology must therefore be followed, since it is known to have been established according to the evidence of the Hebrew letters. [Col. 1296A] If we now compare Josephus with Philo, and both of them with Jerome, we shall acknowledge that Jerome sometimes disagrees with Josephus, sometimes with Philo, sometimes with both; and more rarely we shall find him agreeing with both. For example, Jerome agrees with the Jewish writers in the etymology of the name Abel, which means “mourning” for Philo as well as for Josephus. Likewise with the name Babel, or Babylon, which they interpret as “confusion,” according to the proper character of the Hebrew language. But in the famous name Israel Jerome disagrees with both and corrects their errors in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*: he refutes Philo’s etymology, by which he translated it as “seeing God,” and Josephus’s claim that it means “resisting the angel of God.” He does not do so in the case of Eve, for here he agrees with Philo and disagrees with Josephus, who wanted Eve to mean “mother of all living,” whereas according to the evidence of the letters it means “life,” with nothing added from Josephus’s other words. [Col. 1296B] But lest I repeat things already said or about to be said unnecessarily, I leave such comparisons of authors to the reader’s diligence. Having repeated the same matters once and again, I shall be satisfied and shall find it easier and more convenient to discuss other matters not yet explained.”

“pledged” (p. 31).

**Israel** — mind, or a man seeing God; but better, upright of God.  
**Jubilee** — releasing, or changed, or “it will flow down.”

## L

**Levi** — added, or taken up.

[Col. 1294] ## M

**Melchisedec** — righteous king.  
**Man** — “what?”  
**Moab** — from the father.  
**Moses** — touching, or feeling, or taken from the water, or taking up.  
**Mara** — bitterness, or bitter.  
**Manasseh** — forgotten, or necessity.  
**Mesraim** — Egypt.

## N

**Naomi** — beautiful.  
**Naphtali** — he preserved me, or enlarged me, or certainly entangled me.

## O

**Obed** — serving.

## P

**Phasee** — crossing over, or passage.  
**Psonthomphanech** — corruptly written; for in Hebrew we read *Saphneth phanee*, which is interpreted “finder of hidden things,” etc.  
**Peleg** — dividing.  
**Pharaoh** — destroying, or uncovering him.  
**Phison** — mouth of the pupil, or change of mouth.  
**Euphrates** — fruitful, or growing.

## R

**Reuben** — seeing a son, or seeing in the midst.  
**Rooboth** — inclination, or streets.

## S

**Sabbatha** — rest.  
**Simeon** — hearing, or the name of a dwelling-place.  
**Satan** — hostilities, or adversary.  
**Samson** — their sun, or strength of the sun.  
**Samuel** — his name is God.  
**Seir** — hairy, or bristling.

[Col. 1296] ## Z

**Soor** — small, or southern.  
**Zebulun** — dwelling-place of strength, or oath, etc.

# APPENDIX

## Second Part, Containing Certain Latin Minor Works Once Falsely Attributed to St. Jerome, Both in Printed and Manuscript Books

## [Book of the Names of Places]

[Col. 1295]

## Notice Concerning the Book Immediately Following

The earlier editors consistently placed this diligent and learned little book immediately after Jerome’s *Book of Places*, since, although they could establish by sound arguments that it was not the work of the holy Doctor, they nevertheless knew that it belonged to the collection of his works and did not dare to reject it entirely in opposition to the testimony of earlier writers. Everyone must disapprove of Martianay’s rash action in ordering it to be banished from that collection.

Indeed, certain features seem to assert the authenticity of the work, especially these: the author appears to know Syriac; and what he reports about Shechem and Saron identifies him as sufficiently knowledgeable about Jewish geography. No one is unaware how especially well these matters suit Jerome. For the fact that, when speaking of the Lycian city of Smyrna, he praises Jerome by name—an argument highly valued by learned men when they deny that this book is Jerome’s—did not seem sufficiently firm to Erasmus, since an annotation by some diligent reader could have passed from the margin into the text. This becomes more plausible because the passage is not quoted here in the same words as in the holy Doctor:

“Moreover, Jerome, in the books of the *Hebrew Names*, gives *myrrh* and interprets it as ‘bitter.’”

Finally, there are testimonies from learned men, especially those who bore the reputation of critical scholarship, Casaubon and Scaliger. One of them brings the account of the miracle here narrated to an end as though on Jerome’s authority; the other praises the author very highly.

Nevertheless, the considerations that persuade us that Jerome was not its author are stronger. In fact, it is much more truly attributed to Bede, in whose works it is also found and has been published; for the entire sequence and style of the writing reflect both that period and that author’s character.

Conversely, who would think that this belongs to Jerome’s age, when, speaking of Damascus, the author says: “Now it is said to be the metropolis of the Saracens. Their king, Navvias, therefore dedicated in it a famous basilica to himself and his people, while the Christian inhabitants in the surrounding area frequented the church of John the Baptist”? The Saracens did not seize Damascus until the seventh century, long after the death of the holy Doctor.

Nor would Jerome have written, “Arabia is said to be interpreted as sacred, because it is an incense-bearing region producing fragrances,” since these are the exact words of Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, book 14, chapter 3. The same is true of the following: “The island of Chios, whose name in the Syrian language denotes mastic, because mastic grows there,” along with many other passages copied from that same book with only slight changes of wording.

Some things are also drawn from Jerome’s own commentaries, as will be entirely clear from the heading on Joppa and from other passages here and there, which we leave the reader to compare. For this reason, we do not see anyone to whom it can more truly be ascribed than Bede, who was also accustomed to patch together his works from the writings of others.

In our manuscript, which we keep at home and against which we collated the published text, the inscription itself guards against error: “Names of Regions and Places from the Acts of the Apostles, transcribed not by Jerome but by someone else.”

[Col. 1297]

# Book of the Names of Places from the Acts [G, S]

[Col. 1297A] ## A

**Acheldema** (Acts 1) — the field of blood, which is still shown today at Aelia, on the southern side of Mount Zion. To this day, following the Jewish practice, it covers the ignoble dead: some with earth, while others it leaves to decay in the open air.

> **Note [Col. 1297C].** My manuscript reads *Acheldemach*; immediately afterward the reading now current is more correctly displayed.

> **Note [Col. 1297C].** The earlier editions read corruptly *tetigit*; [the manuscript reading] follows.

**The region of Asia** (Acts 16, 19), which is called Asia Minor, except on its eastern side, where it extends toward Cappadocia and Syria, is surrounded on every side by sea. Its provinces are Phrygia, Pamphylia, Cilicia, Lycaonia, Galatia, and many others; but specifically the area in which the city of Ephesus lies is called Asia.

**The region of Egypt** (Acts 7) has the Great Sea and the Arabian Gulf to the north, the Red Sea to the east, the Ocean to the south, and Libya to the west. The lower part of Egypt is bounded by the Nile, which divides to the right and left and encloses it in its embrace: by the Canopic mouth toward Africa and the Pelusiac mouth toward Asia, with an interval of one hundred and sixty paces. For this reason some have counted Egypt among the islands, since the Nile divides it on both sides so as to form the shape of the Greek letter Δ. Hence many called it by the name *Delta*, because it produces the shape of the Greek letter.

The measurement of Egypt, from the point where the river first divides [variant: “pours forth”] from its channel toward the sides, is one hundred and sixty-six paces to the Canopic mouth and two hundred and fifty-six to the Pelusiac mouth.

> **Note [Col. 1297C].** Earlier editions read *fundente Nilo*, “with the Nile pouring forth.” My manuscript has the shorter and more correct reading. [Col. 1298C]

**The region of Arabia** (Acts 2:11), between the gulf of the Red Sea called the Persian Gulf and the one called the Arabian Gulf, contains many peoples: Moabites, Ammonites, Idumaeans, Saracens, and very many others.

Arabia is said to be interpreted as “sacred,” because it is an incense-bearing region that produces fragrances. Hence the Greeks called it *eudaimona*, and our people called it *beata* [“blessed,” or “fortunate”].

[Col. 1298A] **The region of the Ethiopians** (Acts 8:27) rises beside the river Indus, lies near Egypt between the Nile and the Ocean, and extends southward beneath the immediate vicinity of the sun. Its peoples are three: those of Egypt, Hesperia, and the West.

**Antioch** (Acts 11, 14, 15) — a city of Coele-Syria, in which the apostles Barnabas and Paul were ordained. There is also another Antioch in the province of Pisidia. While preaching there, the same apostles said to the Jews: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you rejected it,” and so forth (Acts 13).

**Alexandria** (Acts 6) — a city of Egypt, formerly called No, situated between Egypt, Africa, and the sea, as though a barrier. The tomb of the blessed evangelist Mark is still venerated there.

> **Note [Col. 1298C].** My manuscript adds: “in the church.”

[Col. 1298B] **Azotus** (Acts 8) — a notable town of Palestine, called *Esdod* in Hebrew, and one of the five cities formerly belonging to the Philistines.

**Attalia** (Acts 14) — a coastal city of Pamphylia.

**Amphipolis** (Acts 17) — itself a city of Macedonia; there is another of the same name in Syria.

**Apollonia** — likewise a city of Macedonia; there is another in the province of Africa, called Pentapolis.

**Athens** — a city in Achaea, devoted to philosophical studies. Although it is one city, it is always called in the plural. Its harbor, the Piraeus,

> **Variant:** *Phircus*.

is said once to have been fortified with a sevenfold wall.

**Areopagus** — the court of Athens, interpreted as “the village of Mars,” because Mars was once consecrated there together with two hundred and twelve gods.

**Assos** (Acts 20, 27) — a coastal city of Asia, also called Apollonia.

[Col. 1299A] **Antipatris** (Acts 23) — a city of Palestine, now ruined, which Herod, king of Judaea, named after his father.

**Forum of Appius** (Acts 28) — the name of a forum at Rome, derived from Appius, once consul; from him the Appian Way also received its name.

## B
Babylon, the metropolis of the Chaldean kingdom, where the languages of those who were building the tower were divided; from it the surrounding region too is called Babylonia. [Note: [Col. 1299D] These statements about the tower of Babylon are described in exactly the same words from Jerome’s Commentaries on Isaiah, Book V, chapter 14; see in that passage what we have observed from Herodotus and other authors.] Herodotus and many others who wrote Greek histories report that it was exceedingly powerful and situated on a square plain, extending sixteen thousand paces from corner to corner of its walls—that is, sixty-four thousand paces in circumference altogether. [Col. 1299B] Its citadel, that is, the Capitol of that city, is a tower which is said to have occupied four thousand paces and to have been built after the Flood (Gen. XI). After its collapse, only the brick walls are said to have remained; these were recovered for the purpose of capturing the wild beasts that abound there.

Bithynia (Acts XVI), a province of Asia Minor, once also called Bibraja and later Mygdonia. Greater Phrygia too, separated from Galatia by the river Jera, contains a city of the same name.

Beroea (Acts XVII), a city in Macedonia, which nobly received the word of the Lord.

## C

Cappadocia (Acts II), a region at the head of Syria, that is, toward the north. [Col. 1299C]

Cyrene, a city in Libya, whose region is also called Pentapolis because it is especially distinguished by five cities: Berenice, Arsinoe, Ptolemais, Apollonia, and Cyrene itself.

Crete (Acts XXVII), an island of Greece [Al. Galatia], once famous for its hundred cities and renowned for its wealth, especially in bronze; for the discovery and use of this metal first took place there. Near it, within the borders of Cilicia, is a promontory and the town of Venus.

Cilicia (Acts XXIII), a province of Asia, through which the river Cydnus flows, and which Mount Amanus—mentioned by Solomon (Song IV)—separates from Coele-Syria.

Carrhae (Acts VII), a city of Mesopotamia, famous among the Romans for the disaster of Crassus, and among us for the hospitality shown to the patriarch Abraham and for the death of his father (Gen. [Col. 1299D] XI, 12).

The region of the Chaldeans (Acts VII), between Babylonia and Arabia, the Tigris and the Euphrates.

Canaan, the son of Ham, possessed the land from Sidon to Gaza, which the Jews subsequently occupied after expelling the Canaanites.

There are two Caesareas (Acts VIII) in the Promised Land. One is Caesarea of Palestine, situated on the shore of the Great Sea. Once called Pyrgos, that is, “the Tower of Straton,” it was made more distinguished and beautiful by Herod, king of Judaea, and much better equipped to withstand the force of the sea; in honor of Caesar Augustus it was given the name Caesarea. He also built a temple of white marble there. In this city Herod, his grandson, was struck by an angel (Acts XII, 10–11), the centurion Cornelius was baptized, and the prophet Agabus was bound with Paul’s belt.

The other is Caesarea Philippi (Matt. XVI; Mark VIII), which Scripture mentions in the Gospel. It was built by Philip the tetrarch of that region at the foot of Mount Lebanon, where the sources of the Jordan are, and was named in honor of Tiberius Caesar.

There is also a third Caesarea, the metropolis of Cappadocia, which Luke mentions as follows: “Departing from Ephesus and going down to Caesarea, he went up and greeted the Church” (Acts XVIII).

Corinth (Acts XIX, 18), a maritime city of Achaia. [Col. 1300B]

Cenchreae (Acts XX), the harbor of the city of Corinth.

Chios (Acts XXVII), an island before Bithynia whose name in the Syrian language designates mastic, because mastic is produced there. Some have called it Chia, after the nymph Chione of Choos.

Cnidus, the most renowned island lying opposite Asia and adjoining the province of Caria; there is also a town of the same name on the island of Calymna.

## D

Damascus (Acts IX), a famous city of Phoenicia, which once held supremacy throughout Syria and is now said to be the capital of the Saracens. Hence their king Navvias dedicated there a famous basilica to himself and his people, while Christian citizens in the surrounding area regularly attend the church of John the Baptist. [Col. 1300C]

Derbe (Acts XIV), a city of the province of Lycaonia.

## E

The Elamites (Acts II), the leaders of Persia, named after Elam, the son of Shem.

Ephesus (Acts XVIII, XIX), the work of the Amazons, a city in Asia where the blessed Evangelist John rests.

## F

Phrygia (Acts XVIII), a province of Asia, lying above the Troad, bordering Galatia on its northern side, Lycaonia and Pisidia on the south, and reaching Cappadocia on the east. There are two Phrygias: Greater Phrygia contains Smyrna, while Lesser Phrygia contains Ilium. [Col. 1300D]

Phoenicia (Acts XI), a province of Syria, whose regions include Samaria and Galilee, as well as many others.

## G

There are two Galilees (Acts XIII). One, near the borders of Tyre, lies among the nations in the tribe of Naphtali (Josh. XIX). The other lies around Tiberias and the Lake of Gennesaret in the tribe of Zebulun.

Galatia (Acts XVIII), a province of Asia, deriving its name from the Gauls. These had been summoned by the king of Bithynia as auxiliaries; after achieving victory with him, they divided the kingdom with him. [Col. 1301A] Thereafter, mingling with the Greeks, they were first called Gallo-Greeks and later Galatians.

Greece (Acts XX), a certain province of Achaia, which Greek writers called Hellas. Athens is situated in it; the region was once called Attica. [Note: [Col. 1301D] The same author, though not correctly, once called it “ancient.”]

## H

Hadrumetum (Acts XXVII), a city in the Bazacian region of Africa.

The Adriatic, the name of the sea opposite Ravenna, entered through the mouths of the river Po; it takes its name from the nearby city of Adria, which also gave the sea its name, Adriatic.

Jerusalem (Acts II, IV, V, XXI), once the metropolis of all Judaea, is now called Aelia after the emperor Aelius Hadrian, because he restored it on a broader site after it had been destroyed by Titus. [Col. 1301B] Through his work it came about that the Holy Places—that is, the sites of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, as well as of the Finding of the Holy Cross—which once lay outside the city, are now enclosed by the northern wall of the same city.

## I

Judaea (Acts I, II, IX, X) sometimes denotes the entire land of the twelve tribes; at other times it denotes only the two tribes once called Judah, to distinguish them from Galilee and Samaria and the other regions of the Promised Land. It should also be noted among historians that Judaea (Acts IX) belongs to Palestine, whereas Galilee and Samaria belong to Phoenicia.

Joppa, a maritime town of Palestine in the tribe of Dan. On the shore there are still shown the rocks on which Andromeda, after being exposed there, is said to have been rescued through the protection of Perseus, once her husband. [Col. 1301C]

Iconium (Acts XIII, XVI), a very famous city of Lycaonia; there is another of the same name in Cilicia.

Italy (Acts XXVII), the region and homeland of the Romans, deriving its name from King Italus. It is enclosed on one side by the Great Sea, from the southwest and the north, while the remainder is shut in by the barriers of the Alps.

## L

There are two provinces called Libya. One is Libya Cyrenaica, of which we have spoken. “And the regions of Libya that are around Cyrene” (Acts II). This is the first gateway of Egypt on the African side and gave its name to the Libyan Sea. Beyond it lies the Libya of the Ethiopians, extending as far as the southern Ocean. [Col. 1301D]

Lydda (Acts IX), a city of Palestine situated on the shore of the Great Sea; it is called Diospolis. [Note: [Col. 1301D] Again the same source: “which is now Diospolis,” and so forth.]

Lycaonia (Acts XIV), a province of Asia; there is also a city of the same name in Lesser Phrygia.

Lystra, a city of Lycaonia.

Lycia (Acts XXVII), a province of Asia.

Lasaea, a coastal city of the island of Crete near the place called Fair Havens, as Luke himself explains. In its place some corruptly read Thalassa.

## M

The Mount of Olives lies east of Jerusalem, with the torrent Kidron flowing between them; there the final footprints of the Lord, impressed upon the ground, are still shown today (Acts I). Although the same earth is daily taken away by believers, nevertheless those same holy footprints continually return to their original form. Finally, when the church in whose center they are was built in a circular design and with exceedingly beautiful workmanship, only the very summit, as they say, could not in any way be covered or vaulted, because of the passage of the Lord’s body; rather, its passage from earth to heaven remains open all the way.

The Medes (Acts II), named after Madai, the son of Japheth, are the regions between the river Indus and the river Tigris, extending from Mount Caucasus to the Red Sea: Arachosia, Parthia, Assyria, [Col. 1302B] [Note: [Col. 1301D] In my manuscript, Persia, as it is also written by Isidore of Seville [Col. 1302D] in the proper order.] Persia, and Media. Sacred Scripture often calls all of these collectively by the name Media.

Mesopotamia, the region between the Tigris and the Euphrates, which is shown by the Greek word itself to lie “in the midst of the rivers.” South of it lie Babylonia, then Kedar, and finally Arabia Felix.

Madian (Acts VII), a city near the Arnon and Areopolis, of which only ruins are now displayed; there Moses lived in exile with his father-in-law Jethro (Exod. II).

Moesia, a province of Asia, now called Aeolis. There is also another of the same name near the river Danube. Some authorities say that the Mysians, Phrygians, and Huns crossed over from Europe; from them the peoples in Asia are called Mysians, Phrygians, and Bithynians. [Col. 1302C]

Macedonia (Acts XX), the most renowned province of the Greeks, made still more renowned by the virtues of Alexander the Great.

Mytilene, an island opposite Asia, five hundred and seven thousand paces distant from the neighboring mainland.

Miletus (Acts XX), a maritime city in Asia, separated by ten stadia from the mouth of the river Maeander. There Paul addresses the elders of the Ephesians. There is also an island of the same name in the Aegean or Ionian Sea, not without distinction. [Note: [Col. 1302D] My manuscript lacks the negative particle, but the sense is the opposite: “an island of no little renown,” and so forth.]

## N

Nazareth (Acts II, X), a village in Galilee near Mount Tabor, from which our Lord Jesus Christ was also called Nazarene. It has a church at the place where the angel entered to announce the Gospel to blessed Mary, and another where the Lord was brought up.

Neapolis (Acts XVI), a city of Caria, which is a province [Al. “of the province”] of Asia.

## P

The Parthians (Acts II) are situated between the river Indus, which is to the east, and the river Tigris, which is to the west, as stated above.

Pontus (Acts XIII), a region of many peoples beside the Pontic Sea, which divides Asia and Europe. Because of the immense inflow of the Danube through its mouths, this sea is recognized as sweeter than the others. [Col. 1303A]

Pamphylia, a province of Asia.

Paphos, a maritime city on the island of Cyprus, once famous for the sacred rites of Venus and the songs of poets. Having collapsed through frequent earthquakes, it now displays what it once was only through the traces of its ruins.

Perge, a city of the province of Pamphylia.

Philippi [Al. Philippis], a city in the first part of Macedonia.

Pisidia (Acts XVI, XX), a province of Asia.

Patara (Acts XXI), a city of the province of Lycia in Asia.

Ptolemais (Acts XXI), a maritime city in Judaea near Mount Carmel, once named after a certain Ptolemy. [Note: [Col. 1303D] My manuscript does not contain the word “once.”] There is also another Ptolemais in the African province of Pentapolis, mentioned above.

Puteoli, a city and colony of Campania, also called Ceadicta.

## R

Rome (Acts XXVIII), once the mistress of the entire world, so called from the name of its founder Romulus. [Note: [Col. 1303D] My manuscript, adding the word “city,” reads somewhat more elegantly: “Rome, the city once of the whole world,” and so forth. Learned men have noted—and the matter itself makes clear—that neither this statement about Rome nor what follows could in any way have been written by Jerome.] Because of its extraordinary virtue, most writers preferred to call it “the City,” as though it alone existed.

Rhodes (Acts XXI), the most renowned of the Cyclades and the first toward the east, once called Ophiussa. It contained a city of the same name, famous for its bronze Colossus, seventy cubits high. It lies twenty miles from the harbor of Asia. [Col. 1303C]

Rhegium (Acts XXVIII), a maritime city of Sicily, twenty miles distant from the promontory of Pelorus. Its Greek name means “separation,” because this part of Sicily, once joined to the Bruttian territory of Italy, was later torn away by the intervening sea. The strait is fifteen paces long and, in width, only as broad as the area near the Rhegian column [Al. Regio]. In this strait are the rock Scylla and Charybdis, a swirling sea [Note: [Col. 1303D] I would certainly prefer “vorticosum” to be restored in place of “verticosum”], both famous for their savagery.

## S

Samaria (Acts VIII), a royal city in Israel situated on the summit of Mount Shomer. The entire region surrounding it also once received its name from the city. It lies between Judaea and Galilee. Herod, son of Antipater, called it Sebaste by the Greek name, that is, “Augusta,” in honor of Augustus Caesar. [Col. 1303D]

Shechem (Acts VII), the city of Jacob, now called Neapolis, near the tomb of Joseph. It took its name from the son of Hamor, its king. Near it the Lord speaks to the Samaritan woman at a well. [Note: [Col. 1303D] Earlier editions of the Vulgate read “at the spring.” The reading of my manuscript is closer to historical truth.] A church has now been built there on the slope of Mount Gerizim. [Col. 1304A]

Sinai (Acts VII), a mountain in the region of Midian, above Arabia in the desert, also called Horeb. Hence it is said, “And they made a calf in Horeb” (Ps. CV, 19), although Moses wrote that this was done at Sinai.

Saronas (Acts IX), which means “plain,” is a region of Caesarea of Palestine extending as far as the town of Joppa. Today it is a place suitable for grazing flocks; according to the quality of its soil, while Peter preached, it immediately produced the fruits of faith. The region between Mount Tabor and the Lake of Tiberias is also called Saronas.

Sidon (Acts XXVII), a distinguished city of Phoenicia, once the northern boundary of the Canaanites, situated near the rising of Mount Lebanon, and itself a maker of glass. [Note: [Col. 1304D] My manuscript does not recognize this addition, including the words “itself a maker of glass.”] [Col. 1304B]

Seleucia (Acts XIII), a famous city of Syria, situated on the promontory of Syrian Antioch.

Salamis (Acts XIII), a city on the island of Cyprus, now called Constantia. In the time of the emperor Trajan, the Jews destroyed it after killing all its inhabitants.

Samothrace (Acts XVI), an island in the Gulf of Pacaia.

Syria (Acts XX), called Aram in Hebrew, is the region extending between the river Euphrates and the Great Sea as far as Egypt. It contains the major provinces of Commagene, Phoenicia, and Palestine, excluding the Saracens and Nabataeans, whose peoples number twelve.

Samos (Acts XX), an island in the Aegean Sea where earthen vessels are said to have been discovered first; hence such vessels were called Samian.

Smyrna (Acts I, II), a city in the province of Lycia in Asia, which Luke mentions as follows: “And sailing across the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Smyrna of Lycia.” [Col. 1304C] [Note: In place of Smyrna my manuscript has Smira, closer to the reading preferred by the Greek manuscripts noted by the author, εἰς Μύρα, “to Myra”; accordingly, below it reads Myrram in place of Smyrnam.] Some manuscripts instead read: “We came to Lystra, which is in Cilicia.” Jerome, however, in his books of Hebrew Names, gives Smyrna and interprets it as “bitter.”

Salmon (Acts XXVII), a maritime city of the island of Crete.

The Syrtes (Acts XXVII), sandy places in the Great Sea, exceedingly terrifying and fearsome because they habitually drag everything toward themselves, and those who approach become stuck in their shallow waters [Al. “the one who approaches”]. They lie near the Egyptian Sea and merge with it.

Syracuse (Acts XXVIII), the metropolis of Sicily, beneath the promontory of Pachynus. Sicily itself is divided by three promontories; hence, from its triangular shape, it was once called Trinacria, and later, after the Sicilian king, Sicily. The first promontory is called Pelorus and faces north; the city of Messana lies nearby, and opposite it, on the Italian side, is the promontory called Caenys, twelve stadia away. The second is called Pachynus and faces the southeast wind. The third is called Lilybaeum; it contains a city of the same name and extends toward the west.

## T

Tarsus (Acts XXII), the metropolitan city of the province of Cilicia, made famous by the Apostle Paul.

Tyre (Acts XXI), the metropolis of Phoenicia in the tribe of Naphtali, almost twenty miles from Caesarea Philippi. Once it was an island in the deep sea, separated from the mainland by seven hundred paces. Alexander later made it part of the mainland for the purpose of conquering it, bringing many embankments into the narrow strait. Its chief fame rests upon its shellfish dye and purple. [Col. 1306A]

Troas (Acts XX), a maritime city of Asia, also called Antigonia.

Thyatira (Acts XVI), a city of Libya, which is a province of Asia, once famous for its temple of Aesculapius. Its citizen was that Lydia, πορφυρόπωλις, that is, “a seller of purple,” who received the faith of Christ at Philippi.

Thessalonica (Acts XVI), a city of Macedonia.

The theater (Acts XIX), a place taking its name from the spectacle, because there the people stood above and watched as they contemplated theatrical games.

[Col. 1305] In my manuscript the following material is appended; it is not unworthy of being read and is taken for the most part from Jerome. It is an interpretation of the Hebrew alphabet, followed by an exposition by a certain Jewish Simeon of the ten names of God. I thought it not unreasonable to add it here, especially since both this exposition and another, somewhat longer exposition of the same Names, carelessly edited by Martianus in volume V, ought to be transferred here so that nothing might be missing; both the character of the writing and the order established by us in arranging this collection require it.

## Interpretation of the Hebrew Alphabet

[Col. 1305]

[Col. 1305B] [Note: [Col. 1305C] The terms which we have printed in italics agree with Jerome’s interpretation.] Alef, “thousand,” or “doctrine.” Beth, “house.” Gimel [Al. Gemel], “retribution,” or “fullness.” Daleth [Al. Deled], “poor,” or “tablets,” or “door.” He, “she herself,” or “this,” or “receiving.” Vau, “and,” “he himself,” or “this.” Zayin [Al. Zai], “olive,” or “fornication,” “this.” Heth, “life,” or “vitality.” Teth, “good.” Yod [Al. Joth], “knowledge,” or “beginning,” or “ruler.” Kaph [Al. Caph], “hand,” “palm,” or “hollow of the hand.” [Note: [Col. 1305C] Martianus reads palpa corruptly.] [Col. 1306B] [Note: [Col. 1305C] Again corruptly, “Lab” in place of Lamed.] Lamed, “doctrine,” or “discipline.” Mem, “from which,” or “from them,” or “water.” Nun, [Note: [Col. 1305C] The same author has “Feta,” and then “serpentine,” in place of “everlasting.”] “offspring,” or “fish,” or “everlasting.” Samekh, “firmament,” although some think it means “raising,” or “help,” or “support.” Ayin, “fountain,” or “eye.” Pe, or rather Fe, “mouth,” from the mouth and not from the bone, or “snare” or “trap.” Tsadi [Al. Sade], “region,” or “justice.” Qoph, “calling.” Resh, “head.” Shin, “teeth.” Tav, “sign,” or [Note: [Col. 1306C] In my manuscript the letters expressing the other etymology have disappeared, and “but” is scarcely legible. Martianus had read in his copies “subter.”] . . .

## Simeon the Jew’s Exposition of the Ten Names of God

[Col. 1305]

[Col. 1305C] Sabaoth, that is, “Lord of hosts,” “Lord of armies,” “Lord who holds all things.” Eloi, “God.” Saddech, “Just.” Adonai, “Lord.” El, “Strong.” [Col. 1306C] Elyon, “Most High.” Coneacol, “Almighty.” [Note: [Col. 1306C] Martianus has Aio; and shortly afterward he reads Barucae, for which he would prefer Baruca, with an Arabic ending; and above, more correctly, “possessor of all” instead of “almighty.”] Aia, “He who was and who will be.” Barucabba, “Blessed Father.” Baruc, “Blessed.”

## Concerning God and His Names (G, S)

[Col. 1305C] The most blessed Jerome, a very learned man skilled in many languages, was the first to translate the interpretation of the Hebrew Names into Latin. Omitting many of them for the sake of brevity, I have endeavored to insert some into this work together with their interpretations, since the explanation of the words sufficiently indicates what they are intended to mean. At the beginning, however, we set down ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews.

The first name of God among the Hebrews is El. Some interpret it as “God”; others, expressing its etymology, have rendered it Schiros [read Ἰσχυρός, *ischyros*], that is, “strong,” because He is oppressed by no weakness but is strong and sufficient to accomplish all things.

The second name is Eloim. The third is Eloe.
