Both are translated into Latin as “God.” This word itself has been transferred into Latin from a Greek designation, for in Greek God is called *Theos*, and *phobos* [read φόβος, *phobos*], that is, “fear.” Hence the word “God” is derived, because He is feared by those who worship Him. “God,” properly speaking, is the name belonging to the Trinity, referring to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The remaining names placed within the Lord also refer to this Trinity.

The fourth name is Sabaoth, which is translated into Latin as “of hosts.” There are many powers in such an order: Angels, Archangels, Principalities, and Powers, together with all the orders of the heavenly army; yet He is their Lord. [Col. 1307B] For they are all subject to Him and subordinate to His dominion.

The fifth is Elyon, which is interpreted as “Most High,” because He is above the heavens, as it is written of Him: “The Lord is exalted; His glory is above the heavens.” He is called “exalted” in the sense of “very high,” just as *eximius* means “highly eminent.”

The sixth is Eheie, that is, “He who is.” Because God alone is eternal—that is, because He has no beginning—He truly bears the name of being. This name was delivered to holy Moses through an angel. When Moses asked what was the name of the one who was commanding him to go to the people to free them from Egypt, he replied: “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III). This is as though, in comparison with the one who truly is because He is unchangeable, those things that were made changeable were as though they did not exist. For what is said to have been is not; and what is said to be will be is not yet. God, however, knows only being; He does not know having been or being destined to be. The Father alone, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, truly is; compared with His essence, our being is non-being. Hence in conversation we say, “God lives,” because life lives through essence, which death does not possess.

The seventh is Adonai, which is generally interpreted as “Lord,” either because He rules over the whole creation or because every creature serves His dominion. He is therefore called both Lord and God, either because He rules over all or because He is feared by all.

[Col. 1308B] The eighth is Ia, which is used only of God and which also sounds in the final syllable of *alleluia*.

The ninth is Tetragrammaton, that is, “of four letters,” which is used properly among the Hebrews of God. It consists of two Ias, which, doubled, produce that ineffable and glorious name of God. It is called ineffable not because it cannot be spoken, but because it cannot in any way be bounded by human sense and understanding. Therefore nothing worthy of Him can be said about Him, because He is ineffable.

The tenth is Saddai, that is, “Almighty.” He is called Almighty because He can do all things—not by suffering what He does not will, but by doing what He wills.

[Col. 1307]

## Concerning the Blessings of the Patriarch Jacob (G, S)

[Col. 1307]

## Notice Concerning the Following Short Work

This little book concerning the Blessings of Jacob is attributed not only to Jerome but also to Augustine, both in manuscripts and frequently in printed books. It was evidently transcribed from the Questions on Genesis of both Fathers. The first exposition, which is historical, is taken almost word for word from Jerome, with certain passages from Augustine interspersed. The second, or Allegorical, exposition, as the learned Benedictine editors of Augustine’s works point out, is found in Gregory’s books of the *Moralia on Job*. The work itself, however, stitched together in this manner by Alcuin, is unquestionably his; it was also published under his name in the collection of his works.

Nevertheless, as the aforementioned Benedictines note, both expositions in their entirety, though in a somewhat different order and with certain words altered, are found in the third book of the Commentaries on Genesis, formerly and falsely attributed to Eucherius of Lyon and published in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. There is moreover another copy of the same exposition, presented by Martianus in volume V of Jerome’s works, which contains spurious writings. It is entitled *The Blessings of the Sons of Jacob*, preceded by a brief preface, and in its final portion is reproduced word for word from the holy Doctor.

Since we first transcribe the former copy from the edition of Augustine prepared by the Benedictines and assign it among Jerome’s spurious writings, we have also transferred the other one here, so that nothing might remain which a learned or unlearned reader could justly miss.

## Concerning the Blessings of the Patriarch Jacob

[Col. 1307]

What are we to understand concerning the blessings with which the patriarch Jacob blessed his sons? Are they to be understood historically or allegorically when he says, “Gather yourselves together, sons of Jacob, that I may announce to you what will happen in the last days” (Gen. XLIV, 2)? And does it seem that these words sound more allegorical than historical?

Both are intended: history and allegory—history concerning the division of the Promised Land, which was to be divided among their descendants, and allegory concerning Christ and the Church, which would come into being in the last times. But first the foundations of the historical account must be laid, so that the summit of the allegory may more suitably be placed upon the earlier structure.

Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my grief, foremost in gifts, greatest in authority. [Col. 1309A] You have poured yourself out like water; you shall not increase, because you climbed onto your father’s bed and defiled his couch (Gen. 49:3).

[Note: [Col. 1309D] From Jerome, *Book of Questions on Genesis*.]

The sense here is: You are my firstborn, greater in children, and according to the order of your birth you ought to receive the inheritance that was due by right to the firstborn, as well as the priesthood and the kingdom. This is demonstrated by the honor [read: burden] borne and by his powerful strength. But because you sinned and, like water that is contained by no vessel, poured yourself out in the impulse of lust, I therefore command you not to sin any further, but to remain among your brothers, paying the penalty for your sin because you have lost the rank of the firstborn.

[Note: [Col. 1309D] The words enclosed in brackets are not Jerome’s.]

“Beginning of grief” applies to every firstborn, because the parents’ hearts are moved on his behalf.

Simeon and Levi are brothers, weapons of battling iniquity. [Col. 1309B] Let my soul not enter their council, and let my glory not be in their assembly, because in their fury they killed a man, and in their determination they undermined a wall. Cursed be their fury, because it is stubborn, and their indignation, because it is harsh. I shall divide them in Jacob and disperse them in Israel (Gen. 49:5–7).

This signifies that it was not with his approval that they killed Shechem and Hamor, men bound by treaty, and that against what was lawful, during a time of peace and friendship, they shed innocent blood; and that, as if carried away by a kind of fury and savage cruelty, they destroyed the walls of the hospitable city (Gen. 34). Hence he says: “Cursed be their fury, because it is stubborn” (Josh. 21:20), and so forth. “And I shall disperse them in Israel.” For Levi did not receive a distinct inheritance, but had a few [Col. 1309C] cities in all the tribal territories for habitation. Concerning Simeon, it is written in the Book of Joshua (Josh. 19:1) that he too did not receive his own allotment, but received something from the tribe of Judah.

Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be on the necks of your enemies; your father’s sons shall bow down to you. Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to seize prey, my son; reclining, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness. Who shall rouse him? (Gen. 49:8–9)

Since Judah is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” it is rightly written concerning Judah, “Your brothers shall confess to you,” or “shall praise you.” And although this contains a great mystery concerning Christ, according to the literal sense it signifies that kings would be born from David’s line, and that all the tribes would bow down to him. For he does not say, “your mother’s sons,” but “your father’s sons.” What follows, “You have gone up to seize prey, my son” [Col. 1309D] (Ps. 67:19), shows that he would lead captive peoples, and, according to the more sacred understanding, would ascend on high and lead captivity captive (Eph. 4:8). Or, as I think better, captivity signifies the Passion and ascent the resurrection.

Binding his young donkey to the vine, and his female donkey to the vine (John 12:14).

That is, he joined the colt of the donkey upon which Jesus sat—that is, the people of the Gentiles—to the vineyard of the Apostles, who are from the Jews; and to the vine—or, as it is found in Hebrew, *Sorech*, that is, “the choice vine”—he bound the female donkey, upon which the Church gathered from the nations sat. [Col. 1310A]

When he says, “My son,”

[Note: [Col. 1309D] Jerome and the Corbie manuscript address the apostrophe to Judah himself.]

he turns to Christ from Judah himself, because Christ would accomplish everything.

[Note: [Col. 1310D] These words are not Jerome’s.]

When it is said, “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations,” it signifies that rulers would not fail from the tribe of Judah until the time when Christ was born. Sent by the Father, he is the expectation of the nations.

Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, reaching as far as Sidon. Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the boundaries; he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he placed his shoulder under the burden and became subject to tribute (Gen. 49:13–15).

Since he had said above concerning Zebulun that it would possess the shores of the Great Sea and would also touch Sidon and the other Phoenician cities, he now returns to the inland province and, by his blessing, makes Issachar—who was to possess the beautiful region of Galilee beside Naphtali—its inhabitant. He calls him a bony or strong donkey and says that he placed his shoulder under the burden, because he would labor greatly in cultivating the land and transporting to the sea what was produced in his territory, also conveying tribute to kings.

The Hebrews say that this is signified metaphorically: meditating on the Holy Scriptures day and night, he devoted himself to labor; and therefore everyone serves him, as though carrying gifts to a teacher.

Dan shall judge his people, as also the other tribes in Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a horned serpent [Col. 1310C] on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, so that its rider falls backward. I shall await your salvation, Lord (ibid. 16 ff.).

Samson, a judge in Israel, was from the tribe of Dan (Judg. 13:2). He therefore says this: Now, seeing in the spirit that your Nazirite Samson is growing his hair and, after striking down his enemies, triumphing—so that, in the likeness of a serpent and a horned snake, he may lie in wait along the roads and allow no one to pass through the land of Israel—but even if some reckless man, trusting in his own strength as in the speed of a horse, wishes to ravage it like a brigand, he will not be able to escape.

He speaks throughout by the metaphor of the serpent and the horseman. Seeing, then, that your Nazirite is so strong, and that he himself died because of a prostitute and, in dying, killed our enemies (Judg. 16:29), I thought, O God, that he was himself your Christ, your Son. [Col. 1310D] But because he died and did not rise again, and because Israel was once more led into captivity, another Savior of the world and of my race must be awaited, so that he may come for whom this has been reserved, and he himself may be the expectation of the nations.

Gad, armed, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be armed behind (Gen. 49:19).

This signifies that Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh, returning after fourteen years to the sons whom he had left in possession beyond the Jordan, found a great battle awaiting them against the neighboring nations and fought bravely after defeating their enemies. Read Joshua son of Nun [Col. 1311A] (Josh. 13:7) and Chronicles (1 Chron. 5:1).

Naphtali is a released hind, giving words of beauty; or, Naphtali is an irrigated field (Gen. 49:21).

The Hebrew expression *AIALA SELUHA* signifies both meanings (1 Chron. 5:11). It signifies that hot springs arise from that tribe, or that it was watered by the course of the Jordan above Lake Gennesaret [alternative: “irrigated,” masculine]. The Hebrews, however, wish “irrigated field” and “words of beauty” to be prophesied on account of Tiberias, which seemed to possess knowledge of the Law.

The released hind indicates seasonal crops and the speed of a more fertile land. But it is better if we refer everything to the teaching of the Savior, because the Savior taught there especially, as is also written in the Gospel (Matt. 4:15).

My son Joseph is growing; my son is growing and beautiful in appearance; daughters ran along the wall, but they embittered him, quarreled with him, and envied him, having arrows. His bow sat firmly, and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosed by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob. From there the shepherd, the stone of Israel, went forth (Gen. 49:22–24).

O son Joseph, who are so beautiful that a whole crowd of the girls of Egypt looks out at you from walls, towers, and windows: they envied you, and your brothers provoked you to anger, carrying the arrows of envy and wounded by darts of jealousy. But you placed your bow and weapons of warfare in God, who is a strong warrior; and your bonds, with which your brothers had bound you, were loosed and broken by him, so that from your seed the tribe of Ephraim might arise, [Col. 1311C] strong and stable, harder and unconquerable like a stone, and also ruling the ten tribes of Israel.

Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoil (Gen. 49:27).

That these words are a most evident prophecy concerning the apostle Paul (Acts 8:3; Gal. 1:13) is clear to everyone: in his youth he persecuted the Church, and in his old age he became a preacher of the Gospel.

The Hebrews, however, said the following: The altar on which the sacrifices were offered, and at whose base the blood of the victims was poured, was in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. This, they say, signifies that the priests sacrifice victims in the morning and in the evening divide among themselves what has been granted to them from the Law. They interpret the bloodthirsty, ravenous wolf as the altar, and the divider of spoils as the priests, who, serving the altar, live from the altar. [Col. 1311D]

[Note: [Col. 1311D] Thus far is from Jerome.]

These matters, then, are historical.

Spiritually, however, in Reuben he shows the person of the earlier Jewish people, to whom the Lord says, “Israel is my firstborn” (Gen. 49:3). For, in accordance with what was due to the firstborn, it belonged to that people to receive the priesthood and the kingdom. The words are added, “You are my strength” (Exod. 4:22). Certainly, from that people came the foundation of faith, and from it came the power of God, who is Christ (1 Cor. 1:24).

But how is that people itself “the beginning of grief,” unless because it continually inflicted injury upon God the Father, turning its back toward him and not its face? It is “foremost in gifts,” because the oracles of God were first entrusted to them (Rom. 3:2), together with the legislation and the Testament, or promise. It is “greatest in authority,” certainly on account of the greatness of its strength, because that same people reigned more abundantly than the others in this world.

It poured itself out like water by sinning against Christ, like water that cannot be held by a vessel. It poured itself out in the impulse of lust, and therefore he added, “It shall not increase,” because after that people was dispersed throughout the whole world, it was greatly diminished.

But why did it deserve such things? He explains as follows: “Because you climbed onto your father’s bed.” He proclaims the audacity of the firstborn of the people, who climbed onto his father’s bed and defiled his couch when he seized and hung upon the cross the Lord’s body, in which the fullness of divinity rested (Col. 2:9), and stained it with iron.

Simeon and Levi are brothers, weapons of battling iniquity [Col. 1312B] (Gen. 49:5). By Simeon and Levi are understood the scribes, Pharisees, and priests of the Jewish people. The scribes of the Jews were associated with Simeon, while the chief priests were from the tribe of Levi; they formed a plan to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. Concerning this plan he says, “Let my soul not enter their council.” He recoiled from such great crimes, which the Jews were to commit in the last times.

“For in their fury they killed a man”—that is, Christ, of whom it is said, “Behold, a man whose name is Rising” (Zech. 6:12). And elsewhere: “A woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). “They undermined a wall”—that is, they pierced with a lance that very strong spiritual wall which guards Israel.

“Cursed be their fury, because it is stubborn”—certainly when, inflamed by fury and anger, they handed Christ over to Pontius Pilate, saying, “Crucify, crucify” (John 19:6). “And their indignation, because it is harsh”—when they asked for the robber Barabbas and demanded that the Prince of Life be crucified (Matt. 27:21).

“I shall divide them in Jacob and disperse them in Israel,” because some of them believed, while others remained in unbelief. Those who separate themselves from them and come to faith are said to be divided; those whose homeland and temple were overthrown, and whose unbelieving race was scattered throughout the world, are said to be dispersed.

Judah, your brothers shall praise you (Gen. 49:8). Through this Judah the true confessor, Christ, is expressed, who was born from his tribe according to the flesh. His brothers shall praise him: namely, the Apostles and all his fellow heirs, who through adoption by the Father have become children of God and, by grace, brothers of Christ, while he himself is their Lord by nature. [Col. 1312D]

Your hands shall be on the necks of your enemies. By these same hands and by the same trophy of the cross he both sheltered his own and bowed down his enemies and the opposing powers. Accordingly, the Father also promises him, saying, “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1).

Your father’s sons shall bow down to you: when many of Jacob’s sons bow down to him, having been saved through the election of grace.

Judah is a lion’s cub. When, by being born, he became little, as it is written, “A little one has been born for us” (Rom. 11:5).

“You have gone up to seize prey, my son” (Isa. 9:6): that is, ascending the cross, you redeemed captive peoples; and those whom the adversary had seized, you rescued by dying. Finally, returning from the underworld, you ascended on high and led captivity captive.

“You have lain down at rest like a lion” (Ps. 67:19). Christ most plainly lay down in his Passion when, bowing his head, he handed over his spirit (John 19:30), and when, secure in the tomb, he rested as though in a kind of sleep of the body.

But why “like a lion,” and “like a lion’s cub”? In his sleep he was a lion, because he fulfilled this not from necessity but by power, as he himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down” (John 10:18). What he adds, “and like a lion’s cub,” means that he died from whence he was born. Christ therefore rested like a lion, who not only did not fear the bitterness of death, but also conquered the dominion of death in death itself.

When he says, “Who shall rouse him?” he means that no one shall do so except himself, in accordance with his own words: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up” (John 2:19).

“The ruler shall not fail from Judah,” and so forth. This most clearly refers to Judah. For a long time an unbroken succession of royal rule among the Jews existed from his seed, until Christ was born, as we said above.

Binding his young donkey to the vine. His young donkey is the people from the Gentiles, upon whom the burden of the Law had never yet been imposed. He joined it to the vine—that is, to the Apostles, who are from the Jews. For “the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7).

And his female donkey to the vine. He himself says, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). To this vine, therefore, he binds his female donkey—that is, the sluggish Synagogue, weighed down by the heavy burden of the Law.

He washed his robe in wine (Matt. 26:28), or his flesh in the blood of the Passion, or the holy Church in that wine which “will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.” And in the blood of the grape, his cloak. The nations are the cloak, which he joined to his body, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe all these as a garment.”

His eyes are more beautiful than wine (Gen. 49:12). The eyes of Christ are the Apostles and Evangelists, who provide the Church with the light of knowledge. Their precepts surpass the austerity of the wine of the ancient Law, because they are far lighter.

And his teeth are whiter than milk. The teeth are the holy teachers, who cut people away from errors and, as though chewing them, pass them over into the body of Christ. The teachers of the Church have become whiter than the milk of the old [Col. 1313D] Law.

Zebulun dwelled on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships (Gen. 49:13). Zebulun is interpreted as “dwelling of strength,” and it signifies the Church. It dwells on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, so that it may be a refuge for believers and show the harbor of faith to those in danger.

With unshaken firmness it looks upon the shipwreck of the Jews and the storms of the heretics, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine. Although it is battered by the waves, it is not broken. It extends as far as Sidon—that is, as far as the Gentiles.

It is also read in the Gospel that some Apostles were taken from that region, and that the Lord often taught in those places, as it is written: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali; the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light” (Matt. 4:15–16, from Isa. 9:1).

Sidon is interpreted as “hunter” or “huntress.” Who are the hunters except the Apostles? As we said above, they were taken from those regions, concerning which it is said: “I shall send many hunters, and they shall hunt you on every mountain” (Jer. 16:16).

Issachar is a strong donkey (Jer. 16:16). Issachar, which is interpreted as “reward,” refers to the people of the Gentiles, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his blood. This Issachar is written to be a strong donkey (Gen. 49:14), because formerly the Gentile people, like a brutish and lustful animal, stood firm by no reason; but afterward it willingly bore the yoke of evangelical discipline.

Lying down between the boundaries, it saw that rest was good [Col. 1314B] and that the land was excellent.

[Note: [Col. 1313D] From Gregory, *Book I of the Moralia*, chapter 6.]

To lie between the boundaries means to rest while awaiting the end of the world, seeking nothing of the things now occurring in between, but desiring the final things. The strong donkey sees rest and the excellent land when the simple Gentile people raise themselves to the strength of good works precisely because they are heading toward the homeland of eternal life.

Therefore it also places its shoulder under the burden, because, desiring to reach the promised rest, it willingly bears all the burdens of the commandments. Thus it becomes subject to tribute: that is, it offers gifts to Christ its king, consisting of the good things of its faith and its good works.

Dan shall judge his people, as the other tribes in Israel do. Let Dan be a serpent on the road, a horned serpent on the path (Gen. 49:16), and so forth.

Some say that these words prophesy that the Antichrist will arise from this tribe,

[Note: [Col. 1314D] From Gregory, *Book XXXI of the Moralia*, chapter 10.]

because in this passage Dan is called both a serpent and one who bites; and because Dan was the first among the tribes of Israel to camp in the north, signifying the one who says that he will sit on the sides of the north (Num. 2:25). Concerning him the Prophet says figuratively, “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard” (Jer. 8:16).

He is called not only a serpent but also a *cerastes*. In Greek, κέρατα (*kerata*) means “horns.” That serpent, therefore, is said to be horned, through whom the Antichrist is rightly indicated, because against the life of the faithful he will be armed not only with the poisonous bite of his preaching but also with the horns of power.

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Dan therefore becomes a serpent on the road because he urges those to walk in the broadness of the present life whom he flatters as though sparing them. But he bites on the road because he destroys with the poison of his error those to whom he grants freedom.

He becomes a horned serpent on the path because those whom he finds faithful, constraining themselves amid the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment, he attacks not only with the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also presses with the terror of power; and, during the exhaustion of persecution, after the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of his power.

This horse whose hooves the horned serpent is said to bite signifies the present world, which, through its arrogance, foams along in the course of passing time. And because the Antichrist strives to seize the final parts of this world, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s hooves. [Col. 1315A] To bite the horse’s hooves means to reach the extremities of the age by striking them.

[Note: [Col. 1315A] In the Corbie manuscript the passage ends as follows: “The rider is whoever is exalted by the iniquities of this world; he is said to fall backward.” [Col. 1316A]]

So that its rider may fall backward. The unbelieving Jewish people, caught in the snares of its error, awaits the Antichrist in place of Christ.

Jacob rightly, in the same passage, suddenly turns into the voice of the elect, saying, [Col. 1316A] “I shall await your salvation, Lord”: that is, I do not believe faithfully in the Antichrist, as unbelievers do, but in the true Christ, who will come for our redemption. Amen.

## ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCH JACOB: ANOTHER [Note: [Col. 1315D] We have collated this fragment with the manuscript codex of the Library of Saint Savior at Bologna; for it is not our purpose to transcribe the entire little work, which the distinguished Father Mingarelli recently completed in *Anecdota*, volume II. Moreover, we have reserved whatever work this may be for a second edition. For when its manuscript exemplar was sent to us by the distinguished Abbot Father Trombellius, our earlier edition had already been completed, and it was no longer possible.]

EXEMPLAR

[Col. 1315]

[Col. 1315B] The most holy and prophetic blessing of the holy Patriarchs, which was distributed to each according to his appropriate condition through the Holy Spirit and the mouth of blessed Jacob, cannot be understood wholly in the literal sense—especially since the same blessed Patriarch says, “so that I may announce to you what is going to happen in the last days.” Nor should it be so weakened through the allegorical sense that the historical sense must be entirely emptied of meaning, because certain things, as we shall see later, were prophesied for them in such a way that some came soon and others much later; nevertheless, many of them were reserved for the end.

[Note: [Col. 1315D] We supplied from the manuscript the words “some [things] soon,” which had fallen out through repetition of the same word. The same manuscript then adds [Col. 1316D]: “things to come, namely, things reserved to come at the end.”]

Therefore, whatever we can understand historically in these words, let us first disclose briefly, as though laying foundations, with the Lord’s help. But whatever in every respect avoids the literal sense, let us examine through spiritual understanding, since it must also be grasped spiritually.

[Note: [Col. 1316D] From the manuscript codex we read: “but whatever altogether eludes the letter, let us examine them through …,” whereas the former reading was: “but whatever eludes the letter ….”]

## ON REUBEN

Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my grief, foremost in gifts, greatest in authority.

[Note: [Col. 1316D] Earlier the text read *Latet*, with the opposite sense. We correct lesser matters below.]

The literal sense is clear, because blessed Jacob received his first son Reuben from his wife Leah; and if Reuben had conducted himself worthily toward so great a father, the firstborn right and the kingdom would have belonged to him. Hence Jacob calls him his firstborn, as one to whom the gifts of the firstborn ought to belong. He also calls him his strength, because the power of rule ought to have passed to him.

He did not utter these things declaratively because he had foreseen or desired that they would come to pass in this way, but in order through these words to exhort him to repentance, as he recalled from how great a dignity he had fallen through sinning.

Hence he says, “and the beginning of my grief.” For he was the beginning of that grief when, after breaking the reins of chastity, he rushed without restraint [Note: [Col. 1316D] Here we read from the manuscript “and then rushed in,” instead of the former reading “withered”] to violate his father’s wife. This must be believed to have afflicted him with no ordinary grief.

He is rightly called “the beginning of grief,” because the other brothers too were accused by blessed Joseph before their father of a very serious crime.

When he says, “foremost in gifts,” this refers to the rights of the firstborn that were due to him as firstborn. When he adds, “greatest in authority,” it is plainly declared that it belonged to him for kings to be created from his descendants over the remaining brothers.

When he says, “You have poured yourself out like water,” the meaning is this: Just as water that is not contained by a vessel flows in every direction, and wherever it finds a steeper place it descends to a lower level with its whole force, so you restrained your conjugal lust by no measure. Wherever the impulse of pleasure attracted you [alternative: “attracted them”], there you poured out the flood of your desire.

When he adds, “You shall not increase,” he forbids him to continue in such or similar disgrace. [Col. 1316C] Thus the Lord also says to Cain, “You have sinned; be still.”

Where these words are leading is testified by what follows: “Because you climbed onto your father’s bed and defiled his couch.” These words plainly amplify the crime of incest that he committed with Bilhah, his father’s concubine—although this may perhaps seem forced to someone because what was stated above [alternative: “what has been stated above”] precedes it.

“I shall announce to you what is going to happen in the last days.” Let the Book of Chronicles say what it has to say about this matter:

“The sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel”—he himself was indeed his firstborn; but when he violated his father’s bed, his firstborn rights were given to the sons of Joseph, the sons of Israel, and he was not reckoned as firstborn.

Typologically, however, this Reuben, the firstborn, designates the Jewish people, which was God’s firstborn, in accordance with what the Lord says concerning it to Moses: “Israel is my firstborn son.” And blessed Jeremiah says, “Israel is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest.”

He was his strength when, formerly, in the Patriarchs, Prophets, and all the other strong men, he fought bravely against idolatry and the impure host of all vices. Yet he was the beginning of his grief [Note: [Col. 1317C] We supplied from the manuscript the missing clause containing the phrase “was previously present,” which had been absent; shortly afterward we also supplied the word “to receive”], when, at the coming of the Savior, he remained in unbelief and refused with a proud mind to receive his teaching.

Hence the Lord is said to have wept when he saw the city of Jerusalem; and at the raising of Lazarus he is reported to have shed tears over the blindness of that people.

When it is said, “foremost in gifts,” it is shown that this people preceded the Church of the Gentiles in the gifts bestowed by God, while the latter was destined to receive the same and far greater spiritual gifts.

When he adds, “greatest in authority,” it is not surprising if that people is honored, since it was the first to believe through the prerogative of the patriarchs, when the blessed apostle Paul says that the Jew is superior in every way.

He then adds, “You have poured yourself out like water,” considering in his mind the unrestrained character of that people, which was not controlled by the measure of the vessel of the Law and divine commandments [Note: [Col. 1317C] We supplied from the manuscript the words “It was not restrained by the measure of the divine commandments,” which had fallen out through the customary scribal omission caused by the repetition of the final phrase], but, casting aside all the bonds of God’s commandments, poured out the streams of its speech with all its strength toward the killing of the Savior.

That speech may signify good or evil through water is testified by divine Scripture. In the good sense it says, “Deep water is the word from the mouth of a man”; and in the evil sense, “Whoever releases water is the beginning of quarrels.”

When he adds, “You shall not increase,” he shows that this same people, as we can see with our own eyes, has been reduced to a very small number among all the nations.

Why it suffered these things is testified by the words that follow: “Because you climbed onto your father’s bed and defiled his couch.” Through “your father’s bed” he indicates the flesh of the Savior. Nor is it surprising that his father’s bed should be understood as the nations and the Lord’s body, because that people was created by him. For it is written concerning him, “All things were made through him.”

By “the couch” the same body is understood: it was defiled by the Jews when, at their outcry, the Lord was hung on the cross, pierced through with a lance, and drenched with his own blood.

## THE SECOND PATRIARCH, SIMEON

Simeon and Levi, weapons of battling iniquity.

[Note: [Col. 1318C] We continue from the same manuscript this other passage on Simeon through to the end. In Martianay’s edition only a few verses from the genuine Jerome were transcribed in its place; the editor himself noted that the remainder is found in the same number of verses in the Holy Father’s *Hebrew Questions*, edited above.]

The literal sense is clear, because these two brothers, in order to avenge the violation of their sister, deceived Shechem and Hamor, her father, by arranging a false peace and feigned friendships. He calls them “weapons of battling iniquity,” because it was exceedingly wrong to pretend friendship and afterward betray it.

“Let my soul not enter their council,” that is, he curses every simulated peace. Thus blessed David also calls down curses upon such counterfeiters, who speak peace with their neighbor while evil is in their hearts: “Give them according to their deeds.”

When he adds, “and let my glory not be in their assembly,” he certainly did not wish to glory in such a victory—or rather, in such slaughter—in which the warrior’s courage could not be praised, but the deceiver’s falsehood had instead to be exposed.

“For in their fury they killed a man, and in their determination they undermined a wall.” Shechem is to be understood by “the man,” and through him all those who were killed on his account.

The undermining of the wall, however, is not in fact read as having been carried out in that place in the Book of Genesis.

[TWO TREATISES.]

[Col. 1317]

## INTRODUCTORY NOTE ON THE TWO FOLLOWING TREATISES

Most manuscript books, including my own, which I use very frequently in this volume, append these two apocryphal treatises immediately after the genuine work of Jerome, the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, which we reviewed above.

The first, which is there entitled *Explanation of the Ten Temptations from Deuteronomy*, had long before held a place among the works falsely attributed to the holy Doctor. The second, whose title in that manuscript is likewise *Explanation of the Song of Deborah and Barak from the Book of Judges*, was first added and published among the spurious works by Martianay.

There is no doubt that the author of both is one and the same, on account of the similarity of style and ideas. The Benedictine editor thinks that he was some Hebrew praised by Rabanus in the prefaces to his commentaries on the Books of Kings and Chronicles, and again identifies him with the author who composed the *Hebrew Questions* on the Books of Kings and Chronicles—also falsely inscribed with Jerome’s name—which we shall shortly revise.

I would not unwillingly accept this opinion, since there is a very great similarity of intellect between the two in their writing. Yet I should not fail to observe that these treatises, and their author, do not seem to have been known to Rabanus when he interpreted the Books of Deuteronomy and Judges.

Finally, Erasmus judged the first treatise—and plainly the second as well—in the following way:

“The style is not that of some recent author. It appears to be a fragment excerpted from someone’s commentaries, for its beginning is abrupt and it ends in a similar way, just as it begins. Nor do I see why anyone should have thought it ought to be attributed to Jerome, unless perhaps he was deceived by the conjecture that it interprets several Hebrew words.”

[Col. 1319]

## THE TEN TEMPTATIONS OF THE PEOPLE OF ISRAEL IN THE DESERT (G)

[Col. 1319A] These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel on the other side of the Jordan, in the wilderness, in the Arabah, opposite the Red Sea, between Paran and Tophel, and Laban and Hazeroth and the abundance of gold. It is an eleven-day journey from Horeb to Mount Seir, as far as Kadesh-barnea (Deut. 1:1–2). These are the words with which Moses rebuked the children of Israel for the ten temptations by which they tested the Lord. Hence the Lord says in the Book of Numbers: “But all the men who saw my majesty and the signs that I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness, and who tested me now ten times, and did not obey my voice, shall not see the land concerning which I swore to their fathers” (Num. 14:22).

Moses briefly and obscurely enumerates these temptations here, saying: “In the wilderness,” by which he shows that they tested the Lord twice because of a shortage of water. Concerning the first temptation, it is written in Exodus: “The people quarreled with Moses and said, ‘Give us water, that we may drink’” (Exod. 17:5). Moses answered them: “Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the Lord?”

Concerning the second temptation, the Book of Numbers says: “And when the people lacked water, etc.” (Num. 20:2), up to the place where it says: “This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarreled with the Lord, and he was sanctified among them” (ibid., 13).

The third temptation is contained in the words: “In the Arabah, opposite the Red Sea.” At that place they are said to have murmured against the Lord, because they did not believe Moses when he said, on the basis of the Lord’s word, that the Egyptians had been destroyed, but instead feared that they were following them.

[Note: [Col. 1319D] The printed books have altered this passage, for they read: “Because they did not believe Moses that the Egyptians had to be destroyed, but were concerned for themselves, etc.” All the manuscripts retain the reading that we have published.]

Hence it is said: “Our fathers did not understand your wonders, etc.” (Ps. 105:7).

[Note: [Col. 1319D] In my manuscript it reads: “Hence it is said in the psalm: ‘Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders; they did not remember the multitude of your mercies, and they provoked you to anger at the sea, at the Red Sea.’” [Col. 1320D]]

The fourth and fifth temptations are contained in the words: “Between Paran and Tophel, and Laban.” Paran means “wild ass”; Tophel, “folly”; Laban, “white.” This is understood as follows: the children of Israel became like a wild ass and acted foolishly, testing the Lord twice concerning the white thing—that is, concerning manna. Manna is called white, as in Exodus: “And the house of Israel called its name Man, which was like white coriander seed” (Exod. 16:31).

One temptation concerned that same manna, as Exodus says: “This is the word that the Lord has commanded: Let each person gather as much of it as is sufficient for eating.” And shortly afterward: “Moses said to them, [Note: [Col. 1320D] The same manuscript reads: “Let none of it be left until morning.”] ‘Let none of it be kept until morning.’” But they did not obey him; some left part of it until morning [Col. 1320A] (ibid., 16 ff.).

The other temptation is described shortly afterward in the same book: “Gather it for six days, but on the seventh day it is the Sabbath of the Lord; therefore it will not be found.” When the seventh day came, some of the people went out to gather it but did not find any. Then the Lord said to Moses: “How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my law? etc.” (ibid., 26 ff.).

The sixth temptation is contained in the words: “And Hazeroth.” Hazeroth is a city near the wilderness, and its name means “Village.” In its territory—that is, at Kibroth-hattaavah, “the graves of craving”—the second temptation concerning meat is said to have occurred; this also includes the first temptation concerning meat.

Concerning the first, the Book of Exodus says: “Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, ‘In the evening you shall know that the Lord brought you out from the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord; for he has heard your murmuring. Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord’” (ibid., 6 ff.). And shortly afterward: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel. Speak to them: In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread, and you shall know that I am the Lord your God.’ And it came to pass in the evening that quail came up and covered the camp” (ibid., 11 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 1319D] The printed books correct this reading, putting “seventh” in place of “second,” “eighth” in place of “seventh,” and “ninth” in place of “eighth.” They thought this should be corrected so that the number of the ten temptations would appear more clearly in the exposition. But the author of this little work has informed us that there were two temptations concerning meat, and that the second is included in the first. Thus the number “seventh” may here be understood also as the eighth number. [Col. 1320D]]

The second is described in Numbers: “Meanwhile there arose a murmuring of the people, as of those grieving over their hardship, against the Lord. When he heard it, he was angry, [Note: [Col. 1320D] Again, the same manuscript reads: “And the fire of the Lord was kindled among them.”] and the fire of the Lord, having been kindled, devoured the outermost part of the camp” (Num. 11:1). And shortly afterward: “Sanctify yourselves, for tomorrow you shall eat meat. For I have heard you saying, ‘Who will give us meat to eat? It was better for us in Egypt.’ The Lord will give you meat, and you shall eat—not for one day, nor two, nor five, nor ten, nor indeed twenty, but for a whole month, until it comes out through your nostrils and turns into nausea, because you rejected the Lord who is in your midst and wept before him, saying, ‘Why did we come out of Egypt?’” (ibid., 18 ff.). Again, a little later: “The meat was still between their teeth, nor had such food ceased, when behold, the anger of the Lord was aroused against the people, and the Lord struck the people with an exceedingly great plague” (ibid., 33 ff.).

The seventh temptation is contained in the words: “Where there is a great abundance of gold.” It must be noted that in Hebrew the text has “an abundance of gold.” The abundance of gold is understood as the golden calf, which the children of Israel fashioned for themselves as gods while Moses remained with the Lord on Mount Sinai. It is called an abundance of gold because the mass of all sins is concentrated in the idol, and the idol abounds in place of all sins.

[Note: [Col. 1321C] My manuscript adds: “And the ninth temptation,” etc.]

The eighth temptation is contained in the words: “Eleven days from Horeb by the road to Mount Seir.” In Hebrew it reads: “An eleven-day journey from Horeb to Mount Seir.” After they had fashioned the idol at Horeb, on the eleventh day they came to Mount Seir, which is in the vicinity of the city of Kadesh-barnea. There the children of Israel tested the Lord, as it is written in the Book of Numbers: “How long will this most wicked multitude murmur against me? I have heard the complaints of the children of Israel. Say to them: ‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘just as you have spoken in my hearing, so I will do to you. In this wilderness your corpses shall lie’” (Num. 14:27 ff.).

[Col. 1321B] And shortly afterward: “According to the number of the forty days during which you inspected the land, a year shall be reckoned for each day. For forty years you shall bear your iniquities, and you shall know my vengeance; for just as I have spoken, so I will do to this most wicked multitude that has risen up against me. In this wilderness it shall fail and die” [Note: [Col. 1321C] The same manuscript reads: “To this whole multitude, etc.”] (ibid., 34 ff.).

Again: “Moses spoke all these words to the children of Israel, and the people mourned greatly. And behold, rising early in the morning, they went up to the summit of the mountain and said: ‘We are ready to go up to the place of which the Lord spoke, for we have sinned.’ Moses said to them: ‘Why do you transgress the word of the Lord, which will not prosper for you? Do not go up, for the Lord is not in your midst, lest you fall before your enemies’” (ibid., 39 ff.).

Again: “But they, blinded, went up to the summit of the mountain; while the ark of the covenant of the Lord and Moses did not leave the camp. The Amalekite and the Canaanite who lived in the mountain came down, struck them, cut them to pieces, and pursued them as far as Hormah” (ibid., 44 ff.). The mountain where the Amalekite and Canaanite are said to have lived is understood as Mount Seir, as it is written in Deuteronomy: “Then the Amorite who lived in the mountains came out and, meeting you, pursued you, as bees are accustomed to pursue; and he struck you from Seir as far as Hormah” (Deut. 1:44).

The tenth temptation is contained in the words: “As far as Kadesh-barnea.” From there Moses sent scouts to inspect the land of Canaan, as the Book of Numbers says: “The Lord spoke to Moses: ‘Send men to inspect the land of Canaan, which I am about to give to the children of Israel’” (Num. 13:3).

[Note: [Col. 1321C] I supplied from my manuscript the whole of this passage, approximately twelve verses, from here through the words “he will see it.” [Col. 1322C]]

And shortly afterward: “The Lord said to Moses: ‘How long will this people despise me? How long will they refuse to believe me, despite all the signs that I have performed before them? I will strike them with pestilence and consume them. But you I will make into a great nation’” (Num. 14:11). Again, a little later: “Nevertheless, all the men who saw my majesty and the things I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness, and who tested me now ten times and did not obey my voice, shall not see the land concerning which I swore to their fathers; nor shall any of those who despised me see it” (Num. 14:22–23).

No one should be troubled by the fact that Moses sent the scouts from the wilderness of Paran, not from Kadesh-barnea. For Kadesh-barnea itself is Paran, as it is written in the Book of Joshua: “Caleb spoke to Joshua: ‘You know what the Lord spoke to Moses concerning me and you at Kadesh-barnea. I was forty years old when Moses sent me to inspect the land’” (Josh. 14:6–7).

[Col. 1321]

[Note: [Col. 1321D] The same manuscript, as can easily be observed from the Book of Joshua. For in that same book it is written: “He spoke, etc.”]

## A Concise Recapitulation of the Ten Temptations (G)

[Note: [Col. 1322D] I append this recapitulation of the preceding little work—ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν, that is, a summary—from the same manuscript of mine.]

[Col. 1321D] The first temptation was at the Red Sea; hence it is written in the psalm: “And they provoked him who ascended in the sea, in the Red Sea.” The second concerned the making of the calf. The third was that they murmured, saying: “Why did you bring us out of Egypt? Our souls are nauseated by this very light food.” And he sent them fiery serpents. The fourth and fifth were at the waters of contradiction: one before Miriam’s death, the other after Miriam’s death. The sixth was when the manna putrefied for them and boiled with worms. The seventh and eighth concerned the quail. The ninth concerned Korah. The tenth concerned the scouts.

[Col. 1321]

## Commentary on the Song of Deborah (G)

[Col. 1321D] (Judges 5:1.) “Deborah and Barak, son of Abinoam, sang.” Barak is reported to have been the husband of Deborah the prophetess. The same Barak is also called Lapidoth in the preceding passage. Lapidoth means “lightning”; Barak likewise means “thunderbolt.” He is called “lightning” because, before he avenged Israel against the Canaanites, he shone among the people like lightning—namely, through the merits and precedence of his works. But after he had avenged Israel against the Canaanites, he was called “thunderbolt,” that is, “one who strikes.”

(Verses 4–5.) “Lord, when you went out from Seir and passed through the regions of Edom, the earth was moved, the heavens and the clouds dripped with water.” The Lord is said to have gone out from Seir and passed through Edom because, when the Idumaeans refused to receive his law, he gave the law to Israel on Mount Sinai. “The earth was moved, and the heavens and the clouds dripped with water.” The earthquake of Mount Sinai is described. When he says, “The heavens and the clouds dripped with water,” this refers to the Lord’s presence: the heavens, as though sweating from fear, are said to have sent forth drops of water.

Likewise, the mountains melted before the face of the Lord. What follows—“Sinai before the face of the Lord God of Israel”—should be understood to mean that Sinai trembled and smoked.

[Note: [Col. 1323D] Martianaeus incorrectly printed, and without any intelligible sense, “are mixed together,” in place of “sending forth.” I restored the reading from my manuscript.]

(Vers. 6.) “In the days of Shamgar, son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the paths rested, and those who traveled them walked along crooked byways.” The paths are said to have rested because, in the time of Shamgar, Israel’s judge, the paths had been seized by Israel’s enemies, and the people did not dare to go up freely to the house of the Lord for the sake of prayer. Those who traveled them went secretly, out of fear of the enemies, and ascended by crooked byways. It is written that Shamgar did not completely free them from these enemies (Judg. 3:31).

The phrase inserted somewhat earlier, “in the days of Jael,” is to be understood as follows: after Sisera had been killed by Jael, the roads were opened, and they went without any fear to the house of the Lord—those who had previously made their way there by crooked byways. The fact that Jael is placed here before Deborah is said to have been done by Deborah out of humility, since Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, killed Sisera.

(Vers. 7.) “The strong ceased; they rested in Israel, until Deborah arose, a mother in Israel.” Here “the strong” means the teachers and preachers of the law. They are said to have rested—that is, not to have existed—until she arose who would teach Israel through preaching and exhortation and would free it from its enemies by her counsel.

The same Deborah also calls upon these strong men above to bless the Lord with her, in these words: “You who willingly offered your lives from Israel to danger, bless the Lord” (vers. 2). These strong men—that is, teachers—are said to have offered their lives to danger, that is, to have subjected themselves to the law of God and to his service, and to have worn out body and soul day and night in meditation upon the law.

[Note: [Col. 1323D] In other copies: “to mortify.”]

(Vers. 8.) “The Lord chose new wars, and he himself overturned the gates of the enemies. Neither shield nor spear appeared among forty thousand of Israel.” By “shield and spear” we should understand that she spoke as if under oath: among the forty thousand of Israel neither shield nor spear could be found. Therefore the Lord is said to have chosen new wars and overturned the gates of the enemies because he made the unarmed strong and victorious.

The fact that the Israelites had been stripped of their weapons by Jabin, king of Canaan, is explained above, where it is said: “The children of Israel cried out to the Lord. He had nine hundred iron chariots and oppressed them severely for twenty years” (Judg. 4:5). He oppressed them severely and forcefully because he is said to have stripped them of their weapons, as it is written in the Book of Samuel: “When the day of battle came, neither sword nor spear was found in the hand of all the people who were with Saul and Jonathan, except Saul and Jonathan his son” (1 Sam. 13:22).

(Verses 9–10.) “My heart loves the princes of Israel.” It should be noted that in Hebrew it does not read “princes,” but “teachers.”

[Note: [Col. 1324D] The Hebrew has *lehhocece Israel*, “for the scribes of Israel.”]

[Note: [Col. 1323D] Rabanus says: “The princes of Israel are the holy teachers,” and so forth. [Col. 1324D]]

Deborah speaks this in the person of God: God loves the teachers who devote themselves to the law of God. Concerning them it follows: “You who willingly offered yourselves to danger among the people, bless the Lord.” The same has already been said above, where it says: “You who willingly offered your lives from Israel, etc.”

“You who have mounted shining she-asses.” In Hebrew, “she-asses.”

[Note: [Col. 1324D] The same source says: “Another edition reads: ‘Bless the Lord, you who have mounted beasts, sitting upon chariots, and upon shining asses.’”]

“And you sit in judgment.” In Hebrew: “sitting upon judgment.”

“And you walk on the road; speak where the chariots were shattered and the army of the enemies was suffocated; there let the righteous acts of the Lord be recounted, the mercies of the strong one of Israel.”

The people of Israel are called riders of she-asses; the she-asses on which they ride are called the teachers of the tribes of Israel. The rest of the people are said to mount upon these she-asses—that is, to rest upon the teaching of the teachers. The she-asses themselves are so called because they proceed like an ass in the law, sitting upon judgment—that is, upon the law.

They are also said to sit upon judgment, that is, upon the law, and to walk on the road under the law, because they never departed from the way of the law. Deborah therefore urges the people who rested upon these she-asses—that is, upon these teachers—to bless the Lord, and says: “Speak,” that is, “praise.”

And as if they had asked, “Where and when shall we praise the Lord?” she answers: “Where the chariots were shattered and the army of the enemies was suffocated, there let the righteous acts of the Lord be recounted, the mercies of the strong one of Israel.” It is as though she said: Although God is always and everywhere to be praised, nevertheless he should now be praised and blessed by us especially, because he has overthrown our enemies, just as he overthrew the Egyptians in the Red Sea.

[Col. 1324D] (Vers. 11.) “Then the people of the Lord went down to the gates and obtained dominion.” The people of the Lord went down to the gates—that is, to the gates of the house of the Lord—for, after blessing and praising the Lord at the site of the victory, they went down into the house of the Lord so that there too they might praise him, offering prayers and sacrifices to him.

That the teachers of the foreign tribes were from the tribe of Issachar is shown in the Book of Chronicles, where it says: “From the sons of Issachar also, men skilled in understanding the times, so that they knew what Israel ought to do, two hundred chiefs; and all their brothers followed their counsel” (1 Chron. 12:32).

That these same teachers are called asses is shown in Genesis, where it follows: “Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries; he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he bent his shoulder to bear, and became a servant paying tribute” (Gen. 49:14–15).

In the Book of Genesis the ass is called strong because of the strength of the law: he bore the law upon his shoulder and supplied the other tribes with tribute—that is, with the teaching of the law. In the Book of Judges, however, they are called she-asses because, broken and humbled in their strength and remaining weak, they were oppressed and humbled under the yoke of the nations and were content with the law of God alone.

(Vers. 12.) [Note: [Col. 1325D] In Hebrew it is *uri*, that is, “arise,” etc.] “Arise, arise, Deborah; arise, speak a song.” It should be noted that in Hebrew the word *exspergisce* is read, that is, “rouse yourself in the spirit of prophecy.” Deborah is therefore urged by the voices of the aforementioned teachers to rouse herself in the spirit of prophecy and praise and not to cease praising God.

Hence it also follows: “Speak a song.”

“Arise, Barak, and seize your captives, son of Abinoam.” In Hebrew it says: [Note: [Col. 1325D] *usabe sebjecha*, “And take captive your captivity.”] “Plunder the spoil that is yours, son of Abinoam.”

This statement, too, admonishes Barak through the voices of the same teachers to plunder the remnants of his enemies, to bring them all the way to destruction, and to acquire for himself a praiseworthy name through victory.

[Col. 1325C] (Vers. 13.) “Then the remnants of the people were saved.” This sentence must be joined for interpretation to the preceding sentence, where it says: “There let the righteous acts of the Lord be recounted, the mercies of the strong one of Israel,” because then the remnants of the people were saved.

“The Lord fought among the strong.” In Hebrew it reads: “The Lord fought for me among the strong.” These are the words of the whole people of Israel. For he fought for them against the Egyptians and against Israel’s other enemies. Hence it follows:

(Vers. 14.) “From Ephraim he destroyed them in Amalek”—that is, Joshua, being from the tribe of Ephraim, destroyed the strong, that is, the enemies of Israel, in Amalek, as it is written in Exodus: “Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword, etc.” (Exod. 17:13).

That Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim is shown in the Book of Numbers, [Note: [Col. 1325D] where it says: “From the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Nun” (Num. 13:9), whom Moses later calls Joshua, saying: “Moses called Hoshea son of Nun, Joshua.”] And after him, “among your peoples, Amalek”—that is, after Joshua, Saul, who was from the tribe of Benjamin, destroyed the people of Amalek at the Lord’s command. Deborah prophetically foretold that this would happen through Saul.

This is said according to the figure called prolepsis, since he was to destroy Amalek, as you find in the Book of Samuel (1 Sam. 14:48). But when it says “O Amalek,” this is not found in Hebrew; the Latin translator added it for the sake of the sense.

(Vers. 14.) “From Machir princes descended, and from Zebulun those who would lead the army to battle.” In Hebrew it reads: “From Machir [Note: [Col. 1325D] Read “teachers,” in accordance with the observation above: in Hebrew *mehhocecim*, which our Hebrew scribe interprets as “teachers.”] [Note: [Col. 1325D] Rabanus accordingly interprets it as “princes,” that is, “the apostles and teachers of the primitive Church.”] princes descended,” with “to battle,” that is, to overthrow Sisera the prince, understood.

“And from Zebulun”—“descended” is understood—“those who would lead the army.” And from the tribe of Levi and from the tribe of Issachar, “to battle” is understood, that is, [Col. 1326B] to praise the Lord and entreat him. Concerning them it also follows:

(Vers. 15.) “The leaders of Issachar were with Deborah.” In Hebrew: “The princes,” that is, the teachers of the law, “were with Deborah” to praise the Lord, “and they followed the footsteps of Barak.”

This must be understood as follows: part of them remained with Deborah to praise the Lord, while another part followed the footsteps of Barak in exhorting the people and waging war against Sisera. Barak, as though rushing headlong into an abyss, gave himself over to danger. Trusting the words of the Lord, Barak exposed himself to danger, plunging into the torrent of Kishon, pursuing and defeating Sisera’s army. The abyss is understood in this passage as the torrent of Kishon.

“Among the divisions of Reuben there was found a dispute among the great-hearted.” In Hebrew [Col. 1326C] “against himself” is not read. These are Deborah’s words, rebuking the tribe of Ephraim because, failing to obey the Lord’s command, it did not go with its brothers to fight the Lord’s enemies. Instead, terrified by fear and distrustful of the Lord’s words, it separated itself from them and thereby proved to be great-hearted—that is, proud.

Hence their rebuke follows in the spirit of prophecy:

(Vers. 16.) “Why do you dwell between two boundaries, to hear the whistling of the flocks?” In Hebrew it does not read “two,” but “between your boundaries.”

[Note: [Col. 1326D] The Hebrew scribe is mistaken here, because in the Hebrew text we read *hammiscphethaim* in the dual form, that is, “two boundaries.” But he may have been reading *hammiscphetheka* in his copy, with a final *kaph* attached, instead of the present-day *hammiscphethaim*.]

[Note: [Col. 1325D] From this, I think, it may be inferred conversely that when he praises the Hebrew, the author of this little commentary is not appealing to the Hebrew text itself, but calls the Latin notes placed in the margin of the Bible from the Hebrew “Hebrew” notes. These were also called Correctoria. [Col. 1326D]]

“Your boundaries,” namely, those of your neighboring tribes, “to hear the whistling of the flocks.” It is as though she said: You wish to protect the flocks in which you abound and fear to lose them, and you prefer to listen to their whistling rather than to go forth with your brothers to defeat Israel’s enemies.

Because you do this, you proudly resist the Lord’s command. Hence the same statement as above follows: “Among the divisions of Reuben there was found a dispute among the great-hearted,” because he acted wrongly, disregarding the Lord’s command and behaving proudly.

(Vers. 17.) “Gad rested beyond the Jordan.” This too is said as a rebuke, because when Reuben remained behind, Gad remained with him by the same decision.

“And Dan was occupied with ships.” When he saw that the tribe of Reuben and the tribe of Gad were not going with their brothers to battle, he was terrified by fear and, occupying himself with ships, took flight.

“Asher dwelt on the seashore and lingered in the harbors.” This too is said as a rebuke, because Asher, dwelling on the seashore, likewise lingered in the harbors, intending to take flight rather than fight alongside his brothers.

(Vers. 18.) “Zebulun and Naphtali offered their lives to death in the region of Merom.” In Hebrew: “Above the region of Merom.”

The sense is that, while the other tribes were unwilling to go, these two tribes gave their lives over to death. “Above the region of Merom.” Merom means “high.” They are said to have offered their lives on behalf of the region of the Most High—that is, of God—and therefore they are lifted up in praise, while the other tribes are reproved.

(Vers. 19.) “Kings came and fought.” He means the kings of the land of Canaan who were subject to King Jabin.

“The kings of Canaan fought.” He repeats the same thing: “At Taanach.” Taanach is a province where the torrent of Kishon is located.

“By the waters of Megiddo.” Megiddo is a city situated on the torrent of Kishon. When it says “by the waters of Megiddo,” this is understood as meaning “by the torrent of Kishon, at the city of Megiddo.”

“Yet they took no spoil.” This is said mockingly, since they not only took no spoil, but were unable even to save their own lives.

(Vers. 20.) “From heaven the battle was fought against them.” Because no shield or spear could be found among the forty thousand of Israel, the Lord fought from heaven on their behalf against their enemies with hailstones and fire.

The same is found in the Book of Joshua: “The stars, remaining in their order and course, fought against Sisera” (Josh. 10:11). The stars are understood as angels, who fought from heaven against Sisera.

(Vers. 21.) “The torrent of Kishon dragged their corpses.” There is an ellipsis here, as though one asked, “Where?” and the answer were given: “Into the torrent of Kedumim,” that is, into the Red Sea. Hence it follows: “The torrent of Kedumim, the torrent of Kishon.”

He calls the Red Sea the torrent of Kedumim. Kedumim means “of ancient things,” because ancient miracles took place in it when the children of Israel crossed over and the Egyptians perished.

And because the Red Sea cast out the dead Egyptians, so that the Israelites saw their corpses lying upon the shore, and because those corpses were carried away by the fish and beasts of the sea, the torrent of Kishon is therefore said to have dragged their corpses, so that, in place of the corpses of the Egyptians taken away by it, the fish and beasts of that same Red Sea might consume the corpses of the Canaanites.

“Trample down, my soul, the mighty.” Deborah says this in the person of all Israel, so that all, united in spirit, might trample the necks of their mighty—that is, their exceedingly strong—enemies, as is also found in the Book of Joshua concerning the five kings of the Canaanites (Josh. 10:24).

(Vers. 22.) “Then the hooves of the horses fell from the fleeing in their rush, and the strongest of the enemies rushed headlong.”

[Col. 1328B] “Their hooves.” [Note: [Col. 1327D] Here too the Hebrew scribe is mistaken, because in Hebrew it is written *iche sus*, “the heels of a horse,” or “the hoof of horses,” unless he used another copy. [Col. 1328D]]

[Note: [Col. 1327D] In my manuscript, however, which I believe was written most faithfully by the author himself, the entire passage is read with the opposite sense, as follows: “Their hooves. In Hebrew it is read: ‘Then the hooves of the horses fell from the fleeing in their rush, and the strongest of the enemies rushed headlong’; for hailstones from heaven, etc.” [Col. 1328D]]

In Hebrew it is read: “Their hooves.” For it is said that, by the stones of hail from heaven—that is, from their angels—the hooves of their horses fell, so that the sense is: If the hooves of the horses fell when struck by stones, what do you think happened to the riders?

(Vers. 23.) “Cursed be the land of Meroz, said the angel of the Lord.” In Hebrew it reads: “Curse Meroz, said the angel of the Lord.”

The angel of the Lord is understood by the Hebrews as Michael, who orders the people of Israel through Deborah to curse Meroz—that is, the angelic power presiding over the Canaanites. For Meroz means “secret.” It is therefore ordered to be cursed, that is, anathematized, because, while the other angels fought on Israel’s behalf, it not only did not fight but also persisted in their adversity.

“Curse its inhabitants,” that is, the inhabitants of Meroz, “and its people.” The reason why they are cursed is given: namely, that they did not come to the aid of the Lord and to the assistance of his strongest ones.

(Vers. 24.) “Blessed among women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite.” “Among women” means Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Leah, and nearly all the other women.

“Let her be blessed in the temple”—the temple of the Lord is understood—so that her memorial may be there, as was also that of Judith.

The reason why she is blessed is given: she acted wisely and prudently, because when her enemy asked for water, she gave him milk. She gave him milk so that the fleeing enemy would place greater trust in her. If someone asks why she did not give him wine, the answer is that the house of Rechab does not drink wine, as you find in the prophet Jeremiah (Jer. 35:14).

[Col. 1327]

## Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings and Chronicles (G)

## Notice on the Following Little Works

We give this praise to Martianaeus: he identified, on the testimony of Rabanus Maurus, the genuine author of the following Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings and Chronicles, concerning whom learned men had previously debated so extensively on both sides.

“Until the present time,” he says in the notice prefixed to these books, which we reproduce, “it was not sufficiently clear by what author questions of this kind had been published; and it was falsely thought plausible that certain passages in them had been excerpted from Jerome’s Commentaries.

“But now it is most plainly evident that these compilations had as their author a certain Hebrew, flourishing in knowledge of the Law, who is reported to have lived somewhat before Rabanus Maurus. For Maurus himself expressly testifies that this anonymous Hebrew published commentaries on the volumes of Kings and Chronicles. Rabanus wished to insert certain chapters and observations from those commentaries together with the expositions of the more celebrated writers of the Church of Christ, so that nothing would be lacking to the study and diligence with which he had undertaken to illuminate the books already mentioned.

“Moreover,” he says in the preface to his Commentaries on the Books of Kings, “I have inserted in many places, together with the notes bearing his name, chapters containing the traditions of the Hebrews, from a certain HEBREW flourishing in knowledge of the Law in our own times—not as though I were imposing his authority upon anyone, but rather simply because I found it written thus, leaving its proof to the judgment of the reader.”

He repeats the same point in the preface to his Commentary on Chronicles: “I have published four books of Commentaries, which I also personally delivered in our monastery to your most sacred father, the Emperor Louis. In them, as I have done in the present work, I have inserted in many places the account of Josephus, the historian of the Jews, as well as the opinions of a certain HEBREW flourishing in knowledge of the Law in our own times—not in such a way as to compel an unwilling reader to assent to their teaching, but rather leaving those matters to the reader’s judgment and examination.”

Now, if you compare those chapters of the Hebrew writer inserted in the Commentaries of Rabanus Maurus with the Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings and Chronicles, you will find everywhere the same words, neither more nor fewer. From this there arises the clearest possible argument that that Hebrew, known to Maurus as flourishing in knowledge of the Law, is himself the author of these subsequent Hebrew Questions.

Certainly this Hebrew differs from Jerome as much as glass or brass differs from the most precious pearl. And I am astonished that learned men thought it plausible that much had passed from Jerome’s Commentaries into the Questions of the aforesaid Hebrew, when many statements in them are unlike and contrary to those of Jerome, and when absolutely none, or very few, of their Hebrew traditions are found to be worthy of Jerome’s Latin, learning, and diligence.

To this we add only that it sometimes seems that more material than is found here is presented under the name of this Hebrew, marked beforehand in the margin of the book, contrary to Martianaeus’s view, in the works of Rabanus. But the material cited there from Jerome is drawn not from some lost book of Hebrew Questions, but from the Commentaries on the Prophets and from other works of the holy teacher, especially from the work On the Names of Places.

For the rest, see what we observe in the general preface concerning such Questions of Jerome on the remaining books of Scripture—whether lost, or, more accurately, never actually composed. We have collated these works against the evidence of a domestic manuscript codex, which we have often used, both because it preserves Rabanus’s reading, which is sometimes of better quality, and because we also used another Milanese manuscript codex, in the Ambrosian Library under the letter D, number 88. Its variant readings we have examined in this edition in their respective places, something that the typesetters did not sufficiently permit in the previous edition.

## On Book I of Kings

[Col. 1329]

[Col. 1329A] **(Chapter I.—Verse 1.)** There was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim, from the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Elkanah, son of [Note: [Col. 1329A] The Ambrosian manuscript reads “his son Jeroboam.”] Jeroam, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite. Ramathaim is interpreted as “two heights.” These two heights are understood as the two tribes, namely the royal and the priestly. That Elkanah’s father was of the tribe of Levi is taught most fully by the book of Chronicles, in which his genealogy is traced all the way to Levi [Col. 1330A] (1 Chronicles 6). His mother too is shown to have belonged to the tribe of Judah, in that he is called an Ephraimite. He is called an Ephraimite from Ephrath, Caleb’s wife, who is known to have belonged to the tribe of Judah. If anyone is troubled by the fact that [Note: [Col. 1329A] Thus reads our manuscript of the monastery of Gemmeticum. Other copies, in the opposite sense and together with the printed books, read that he is called an Ephraimite from Ephraim, not from Ephrath. [Col. 1330A] Rabanus Maurus has the same reading in chapter 1 of book 1 of Kings.] [Note: [Col. 1329A] The manuscript agrees with the earlier printed books: “that he is called an Ephraimite from Ephraim, [Col. 1330A] not from Ephrath,” and so forth. The Ambrosian manuscript likewise.] he is called an Ephraimite not from Ephraim but from Ephrath, let him consider in what follows how David is called the son of an Ephraimite, although it is perfectly clear that the same Jesse belonged not to Ephraim but to the tribe of [Col. 1331A] Judah; this proves that Elkanah too is called an Ephraimite from Ephrath, not from Ephraim. Zophim is interpreted as “watchers.” Here “watchers” means the prophets, whose son Elkanah was. “From the hill country of Ephraim.” He is said to have been from the hill country of Ephraim because his dwelling was there. For there is no doubt that the Levites had dwellings among all the tribes.

**(Verses 3–4.)** “That man went up from his city on the appointed days.” He went up to the house of the Lord on the three festivals, namely Passover, Pentecost, and the feast of Tabernacles. “And he gave portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters.” These portions are understood as garments, which according to the custom of that people were distributed at those three festivals to wives, [Col. 1331B] children, and servants.

**(Verse 5.)** “But to Hannah he gave one portion, sorrowful.” In Hebrew it reads: “But to Hannah he gave one double portion, because he loved Hannah.”

**(Verse 16.)** “Do not regard your maidservant as one of the daughters of Belial, for out of the abundance of my grief and sorrow I have spoken until now.” Belial is interpreted as “without a yoke.” It should be noted that all who pursue drunkenness are called sons of Belial.

**(Verse 24.)** “And she brought him with her, after she had weaned him, with three calves, three measures of flour, and a jar of wine; and she brought him to the house of the Lord at Shiloh.” [Note: [Col. 1331D] There is no error in the Latin translation where we read “three measures of flour,” since, as has been abundantly demonstrated elsewhere from Jerome, the ephah, a Hebrew measure, is three modii. Let the reader consult our scholia on the first chapter of the first book of Samuel.] In Hebrew it does not read “three measures of flour,” but “a measure of flour”; the passage is known to have been corrupted among Latin writers through scribal error. For if [Col. 1331C] she offered three measures of flour along with three calves, she acted contrary to the precept of the Law. For the Law prescribes as follows: “The first day of the seventh month shall be venerable and holy for you. You shall do no servile work; it is a day of the sound of the trumpet. And you shall offer a burnt offering as a pleasing fragrance to the Lord: one bull from the herd, one ram, seven unblemished yearling lambs, and, with their offerings, fine flour mixed with oil—three-tenths for each bull, two-tenths for the ram, and one-tenth for each lamb” (Leviticus 23:34 and Numbers 29:1ff.). This tenth was a tenth part of an ephah. Hence it is understood that Elkanah did not offer three measures of flour with three calves, but nine-tenths, which according to Hebrew measure make one ephah.

[Col. 1331D] **(Chapter II.—Verse 1.)** “My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in the Lord.” By “horn” she calls her son, because when she was without a son she seemed to herself to be without a horn.

**(Verse 3.)** “Let old things depart from your mouth.” In Hebrew it reads: “Let old things go forth,” and so forth. The sense is: Let lowly things go forth from your mouth, from which previously great and arrogant things came forth. By these words she rebukes Peninnah [Col. 1332A] and her sons; because fertility had been granted to her, Peninnah exalted herself against Hannah.

**(Verse 4.)** “The bow of the mighty has been overcome, and the weak have been girded with strength.” The bow of the Egyptians—that is, their strength and power—has been overcome, and the weak, namely the Israelites, have been strengthened. Alternatively: the bow, that is, the pride and strength of Peninnah, in which she gloried because of her children, has been overcome; and Hannah, who was weak because of her barrenness, has been girded with the strength of children.
