**(Verse 5.)** “Until the barren woman bore many, and she who had many sons grew weak.” In Hebrew and in the Septuagint translation, not “many” but “seven” is read. The Jews understand this passage as follows: when Samuel was born, Peninnah’s firstborn son died, [Note: [Col. 1331D] Rabanus also reads this, following the Gemmeticum manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 1332D] The same Gemmeticum manuscript reads here: “and as each of Hannah’s children was born, one of Peninnah’s sons died.” Erasmus has: “Peninnah’s firstborn died, and her other sons also died.”] and thus, as Hannah’s children were born, Peninnah’s sons died. But one must ask how this can stand, since Peninnah had seven sons, whereas Hannah had no more than five. The Hebrews resolve the question by counting Samuel’s two sons among Hannah’s children.

**(Verse 8.)** “For the pillars of the earth are the Lord’s, and he has set the world upon them.” In Hebrew it reads: “For the afflicted of the earth are the Lord’s.” By “the afflicted of the earth,” the Hebrews understand those who are poor in spirit and humble in heart; they say that the Lord has set the world upon them, because they believe that the earth stands through their merits.

**(Verse 10.)** “The Lord’s adversaries shall fear him, and he will thunder over them in the heavens.” The Lord will thunder from heaven over his adversaries, as in the book of Joshua: “As they fled from the face of Israel and were on the descent of Beth-horon, the Lord cast down upon them great stones from heaven as far as Azekah; and many more died from the hailstones than the sons of Israel had struck down with the sword” (Joshua 10:11).

**(Verse 22.)** “Eli was very old, and he heard all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they slept with the women who attended at the door of the tabernacle.” The Hebrews say that they slept with the women because, after menstruation or childbirth, before the prescribed sacrifice had been completed according to the Law, they persuaded the women to return to their husbands [Note: [Col. 1332D] In my manuscript the words “and to have intercourse with them” are absent.] and have intercourse with them. They are therefore said to make them sleep because they caused the women to sleep with their husbands contrary to the precept of the Law. Hence the same Eli says shortly afterward:

**(Verse 24.)** “For it is not a good report that I hear, that you make the people of the Lord transgress.” The people therefore transgressed because they joined themselves to their wives without the sacrifice having been properly performed. Just as the sons forcibly took flesh from the sacrificer, so they also extorted the sacrifice from the offerer. And therefore, just as in taking the flesh they made men diminish the Lord’s sacrifice, so likewise in joining them to their wives they made the people of the Lord transgress.

[Col. 1333A] **(Verse 25.)** “If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased on his behalf.” When the man against whom he has sinned has been appeased, he makes God, against whom he sinned through that man, favorable to himself. “But if a man sins against God, who will pray for him?” Sin against a man is therefore not of the same kind as sin against God. To sin against a man, although it is still sin, is lighter and more readily forgiven. But to sin against God—that is, to depart from his worship—is the sin of impiety, and its forgiveness is more difficult. Since, when someone sins against a man, he makes God favorable to himself by appeasing the man, when someone sins against God, who will pray for him? It is as though he were saying: Through whom will he be able to make God, against whom he has sinned, propitious to him?

**(Verse 27.)** “A man of God came to Eli and said to him: Thus says the Lord: Did I not openly reveal myself to the house of your father when he was in Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh? And I chose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest,” and so forth. The Jews say that this man of God was Phinehas, whom they also believe to have been Elijah. [Note: [Col. 1333D] For this is their view: that between Aaron and Eli only two men, Eleazar and Phinehas, intervened as high priests; accordingly, to fill the interval, they have invented several centuries of Phinehas’s life. Some rabbis even say that he was not a man, but an angel clothed in a mortal body, who repeatedly came into this world and departed; they imagine that he came to Eli bearing God’s message of vengeance, appeared again under Solomon as Phinehas son of Eleazar, and will come on the last day of the ages under the person and name of Elijah.] The Lord is said to have been revealed to the house of his father, that is, to Aaron, at the place where he says: “For the Lord said to Aaron, ‘Go to meet Moses in the wilderness’” (Exodus 4:27), and so forth. At this place the Lord is said to have first revealed himself to him. He was chosen to be priest from all the tribes of Israel, as you find in *Elleh Shemoth* and in *Vayyiqra*. [Note: [Col. 1333D] Among the Hebrews this is called *Elleh Shemoth*, “These are the names,” because it begins with those words, “These are the names,” and so forth. Likewise Leviticus is called *Vayyiqra*, “And he called,” according to the custom of the Hebrews of assigning names to books from their openings.] As for the statement, “A man of God came to Eli,” and the rest that follows, they believe that these words were spoken before the time of Elkanah; they have been inserted here for the glory of Samuel.

**(Verses 31–32.)** “Behold, days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house.” By “arm” he calls the ark and the dignity of the priesthood. [Note: [Col. 1334D] In Rabanus: “Arm expresses the dignity and strength of the high priest,” and so forth.] “So that there will be no old man in your house.” By “old man” he means the high priest. “And you shall see your rival in the temple, amid all the prosperity of Israel.” Eli’s rival was Zadok the priest, who, after Solomon expelled Abiathar, assumed the priesthood, as it is read in Kings: “And Solomon expelled Abiathar, so that he would not be priest of the Lord, in order to fulfill the word of the Lord which he had spoken concerning the house of Eli” (1 Kings 2:27).

**(Verses 33, 36.)** “Nevertheless I will not utterly cut off every man of yours from my altar, so that your eyes may fail and your soul may waste away.” The Lord therefore says that he will not entirely remove a man from Eli’s house from his altar, so that there would always be a man from Eli’s house in the house of the Lord who would see another installed in the dignity of the priesthood; and, seeing himself deprived of that same dignity, his eyes would fail and his soul waste away. Hence it is also said in what follows: “Let him come to [Note: [Col. 1333D] In Jerome’s version, or in the canon of Hebrew truth that we have published, we read, “Let him come to be prayed for and offer a coin,” and so forth. But in the margin opposite this passage there is a scholion by the Hebrew scribe of this work, indicating that the Hebrew reads, “Let him come to bow down to him and receive a coin from him,” and so forth. This argument most clearly proves that the author of the scholia on the canon of Hebrew truth and of the Hebrew Questions on the books of Kings is one and the same.] bow down to him,” that is, to the high priest, “and receive from him a silver coin and a round loaf of bread, and say: ‘Dismiss me, I beg you, to one priestly portion, that I may eat a morsel of bread.’”

**(Chapter III.—Verse 1.)** “The word of the Lord was precious in those days.” [Note: [Col. 1334D] The true Jerome, in his Commentary on Isaiah, book 5, chapter 13, commenting on the words “More precious than gold,” says: “Everything that is rare is called precious . . . And in the book of Samuel it is contained: ‘The word of the Lord was precious in those days,’ that is, rare.”] It is called precious because it was exceedingly rare. Everything that is rare is precious. “There was no manifest vision,” because prophecy was not yet fully disclosed.

[Col. 1334B] **(Verse 2.)** “It came to pass one day that Eli was lying in his place, and his eyes had grown dim so that he could not see.” Here the sentence must be divided, and what follows added: “And before the lamp of God was extinguished.” Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was. It should be understood in this way: before the lamp of God was extinguished, Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was. The statement “before the lamp of God was extinguished” must be understood to mean before daylight came, when that lamp was to be extinguished. For the Lord had commanded through Moses that it should burn until morning, as in Exodus: “Command,” says the Lord, “the sons of Israel to bring you pure oil from olive trees, beaten with a pestle, so that the lamp may burn continually in the tabernacle [Col. 1334C] of the Lord. Aaron and his sons shall arrange it so that it may give light until morning before the Lord” (Exodus 27:20–21). [Note: [Col. 1334D] We have emended this on the basis of Rabanus, reading “that passage from Exodus,” or “in Exodus,” instead of the incongruous reading in the earlier printed editions, “that passage in Hebrew.” My manuscript reads “that passage in the book,” with “of Exodus” understood; for the author often uses this expression, as in “that passage in the book of Genesis,” “of Exodus,” and similar phrases. My Ambrosian manuscript agrees.]

**(Verse 7.)** “Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord.” He is said not to know the Lord because, through the mystery of prophecy, the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him.

**(Verse 11.)** “The Lord said to Samuel: Behold, I am doing a deed in Israel, which whoever hears will have both ears ringing.” Here the Lord’s threat is directed against Eli and his house, because through the sin of Eli’s sons the ark of God would be captured, Israel would fall, his sons would perish, and Eli’s house would be deprived of the priesthood of the house of the Lord. For this reason the ears of those who heard would ring with intense astonishment.

**(Verse 15.)** “He opened the doors of the house of the Lord, and Samuel was afraid to report the vision to Eli.” It should not be understood that Samuel opened the doors of the house of the Lord, but rather the priest did so.

**(Verses 19, 21.)** “Not one of all Samuel’s words fell to the ground.” It is said that none of his words fell to the ground because whatever he prophesied was demonstrated by events. “And the word of Samuel came to all Israel.” His word concerned all Israel: they were to be struck by the Philistines because of the sins of Eli’s sons. The subsequent outcome of events confirmed that word.

**(Chapter VI.—Verse 14.)** “There was there a great stone, and they split the wood of the cart.” The Hebrews understand this stone as the altar built by Abraham.

**(Verses 17–18.)** “These are the golden tumors which the Philistines returned to the Lord as a guilt offering: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, and one for Ekron.” These five cities gave five tumors and five mice. The remaining cities of the provinces, and the villages that were without walls, gave only mice. Hence it says, “from the fortified city to the village that was without walls.” What follows—“and as far as Abel the Great, upon which they set down the ark of the Lord”—means that Abel the Great was a city on the border of Israel. It is called Abel the Great, although previously it was called Beth-shemesh, either because of the mourning that took place there over the men of Beth-shemesh, or to distinguish it from the city of Abel-beth-maacah, concerning which the wise woman cried out to Joab, saying: “Let them inquire at Abel.” Thus the passage should be understood to mean that from the fortified city to the village without walls, and as far as Abel the Great, they gave mice. “Upon which”—that is, upon the mourning—they set down the ark of the Lord, which until that day had been in the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite. It therefore remained in his field until it was taken to Kiriath-jearim.

**(Verse 19.)** “And he struck down among the people seventy men and fifty thousand of the common people.” In Hebrew it reads: “And he struck down among the people seventy men and fifty thousand men.” The Hebrews understand these seventy men as the seventy judges, whose merit and glory were matched by the fifty thousand men, just as it is said of David: “You are worth ten thousand.”

**(Chapter VII.—Verse 2.)** “And from the day when the ark of the Lord remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days were multiplied,” that is, twenty years. [Note: [Col. 1335] This entire passage, from the words “From the time” through “to be referred,” is missing from my manuscript.] From the time when Eli’s priesthood was rejected until Samuel’s leadership, there were twenty years filled with misery. At the completion of the twentieth year, Samuel transferred the ark to Mizpah; from Mizpah Samuel and Saul transferred it to Gilgal. From there Saul transferred it to Nob; from Nob to Gibeah; from Gibeah David transferred it to the house of Obed-edom; from the house of Obed-edom David transferred it to Zion; and from Zion Solomon transferred it to the Holy of Holies.

[Col. 1336A] **(The same passage.)** “And all Israel rested after the Lord.” They are said to have rested after the Lord because, having rejected the filth of idols, they devoted themselves to serving the Lord with their whole heart. The same is stated in what follows:

**(Verse 4.)** “The sons of Israel removed the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and served the Lord alone. And they gathered at Mizpah, drew water, and poured it out before the Lord.” The Hebrews relate that curses were placed into that same water before the Lord; and just as the adulterous woman is tested in the Law by drinking water, so idolaters were tested here by this water. These were those who completely denied having worshiped idols. They also relate that whenever an idolater tasted this water, his lips clung together so tightly that he could never separate them from one another. By this sign the idolater was detected and killed. The following also demonstrates this, where it says:

**(Verse 6.)** “And Samuel judged the sons of Israel at Mizpah.” Here “to judge” idolaters must be understood as handing them over to death according to the Law. They also say that Moses tested the idolaters who had made the calf in this way, when he seized the calf, burned it, ground it to powder, scattered it into water, and gave the sons of Israel drink of it.

**(Chapter IX.—Verse 7.)** “Saul said to his servant: Behold, we shall go; what shall we bring to the man? For Saul did not think that Samuel could indicate the donkeys to him in any other way than by the price of divination. Hence he says: ‘What shall we bring to the man?’”

[Col. 1336C] **(Verse 12.)** “Hurry now, for today he will come into the city, because today there is a sacrifice for the people on the high place.” Here “sacrifice” means the meal that Samuel had prepared for the people on the new moons.

**(Verses 19–20.)** “I will dismiss you in the morning, and I will tell you everything that is in your heart. As for the donkeys that you lost three days ago, do not be anxious, for they have been found.” According to the Hebrews, it was in Saul’s heart that he would become king, because he had seen in a vision that he was placed at the top of a palm tree. This vision was a royal sign.

**(Chapter X.—Verse 3.)** “When you leave there, go farther and come to the oak of Tabor; there three men will meet you going up to God at Bethel.” These men were going to Bethel for prayer, where Jacob had erected a stone.

**(Verse 5.)** “After this you will come to the hill of God.” The hill of God was the place where the prophets lived. “And the Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them.” The Jews say that he prophesied there about the future age, Gog and Magog, the rewards of the righteous, and the punishment of the wicked.

**(Verse 7.)** “When all these signs have come upon you, do whatever your hand finds to do, for God is with you.” It is as though he were saying: By these signs you will know that God has willed you to be king. Therefore act royally in everything that you must do, because God is with you.

[Col. 1337A] **(Verse 8.)** “You shall go down before me to Gilgal. For I shall surely come down to you, so that you may offer an oblation and sacrifice peace offerings. You shall wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.” Some think that Saul offered the burnt offering without blame, since Samuel, whom he had awaited, did not come according to the appointed seven days. But if anyone carefully distinguishes this passage, he will find that Saul was rightly blamed and reproved as disobedient. Among the Hebrews the passage is divided as follows: “You shall go down before me to Gilgal; for I shall surely come down to you.” Then follows: “To offer oblations and sacrifice peace offerings, you shall wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.” Samuel did not command Saul to await his arrival for seven days; rather, he wished Saul to await him for those seven days in order to offer oblations and sacrifice peace offerings. Saul did not do this at all, and therefore is rightly blamed and marked with the charge of folly.

**(Verse 12.)** “The other answered the other, saying: And who is their father?” [Note: [Col. 1337D] In my manuscript: “And who is greater than he among them in dignity,” and so forth.] It is as though he were saying: “And who is greater than he in dignity and wisdom?” For one who is so learned and wise can very well be numbered among the prophets and be called their father, that is, their teacher. A teacher is called “father,” as Elisha calls Elijah “father,” that is, teacher: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer” (2 Kings 2:12). In the book of Job, Elihu likewise calls Eliphaz “father,” that is, teacher, in this way: “My father, let Job be tested to the end” (Job 34:36).

[Col. 1337C] **(Chapter XIII.—Verse 1.)** [Note: [Col. 1337D] The order of the chapters is reversed at this point, for these words occur at the beginning of chapter 13, although other material follows that is known to belong to chapters 10 and 12.] [Note: [Col. 1337D] Nevertheless, Rabanus recites these words in their proper, not reversed, order.] “Saul was a son of one year when he began to reign. He reigned over Israel for two years.” This is not said of Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, but of Saul himself. For he was as innocent when he began to reign as a one-year-old son, and he is said to have reigned for two years in that same innocence.

**(Chapter X.—Verse 25.)** “Samuel spoke to the people the law of the kingdom.” The Hebrew has: “The judgment of the kingdom.” “And he placed it before the Lord.” “Before the Lord” means before the ark of the Lord, which was at Mizpah.

**(Chapter XII.—Verse 11.)** “The Lord sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel, and rescued you from the hand of your enemies all around.” Jerubbaal is Gideon, and Bedan is Samson.

[Col. 1337D] **(Verse 14.)** “If you fear the Lord, serve him, listen to his voice, and do not provoke the mouth of the Lord.” By “the mouth of the Lord” he means the mouth of the prophets, who spoke from the mouth of the Lord.

**(Chapter XIII.—Verses 3–4.)** “When the Philistines heard this, Saul sounded the trumpet throughout all the land, saying: ‘Let the Hebrews hear.’ And all Israel heard this report: ‘Saul has struck the garrison of the Philistines.’” It should be understood that when the Philistines heard this, the implied meaning is that they were thrown into confusion. Saul sounded the trumpet. This trumpet was a sign of victory and exhortation, so that the Hebrews might hear and know that the Philistines had been thrown into confusion and defeated. Therefore it follows: “And all Israel heard this report: ‘Saul has struck the garrison of the Philistines.’” When Israel learned these things, it was encouraged because of them. And it follows: “And Israel rose up against the Philistines,” that is, it began to act courageously against the Philistines.

**(Verse 6.)** “When the sons of Israel saw [Note: [Col. 1337D] My manuscript, together with the Vulgate translator, reads “when the men of Israel saw.”] that they were in a difficult position—for the people were hard pressed—they hid themselves in caves and hiding places, and also among rocks, in pits, and in cisterns.” But the Hebrews crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. [Note: [Col. 1338D] In Rabanus: “A question not unworthy of consideration arises: if Israel hid itself,” and afterward, “This is resolved as follows: with some in hiding,” and so forth.] If Israel hid itself in the places mentioned above, what is meant by the statement: “But the Hebrews crossed the Jordan”? The explanation is that, while some Israelites hid themselves—those who had abandoned Saul and the people who were with him—a certain part of those who are here called Hebrews, terrified by fear, deserted Saul and the men who were with him and went down into the camp of the Philistines. The following passage makes this place clearer and more evident, where it says:

**(Chapter XIV.—Verses 21–22.)** “Moreover, the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines yesterday and the day before, and had gone up with them in the camp, returned to be with Israel, who were with Saul and Jonathan. Likewise all the Israelites who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim, when they heard that the Philistines had fled, joined their own people in the battle. And turning to the spoil, he took sheep, oxen, and calves; they slaughtered them on the ground, and the people ate with the blood.” The people did not invalidate the oath by which Saul had adjured them, saying: “Cursed be the man who eats bread until evening, until I have avenged myself on my enemies,” because they had already gained the victory. But they are said to have sinned against the Lord and eaten with the blood because they ate before the evening sacrifice had been performed, contrary to the precept of the Law. The practice was that whenever a homicide had occurred among them, whether of their own people or of foreigners, they were not to eat until the evening sacrifice had been offered for it. Alternatively, they are said to have sinned against the Lord and eaten with the blood because, after slaughtering the victims, they did not offer the fat and blood to the priests at the sanctuary according to the precept of the Law, even though they had the sanctuary with them. When the sanctuary was far away, the blood of the victims was commanded to be poured out on the ground—namely, of those victims that they prepared for their own consumption. But when the sanctuary was present, the blood of the sacrifices was commanded to be poured out upon the altar of the Lord, as in the book of Deuteronomy: “You shall pour out the blood of your sacrifices upon the altar; but you yourself shall eat the flesh.” The people mentioned above did not do this; therefore they are said to have sinned against the Lord and eaten with the blood.

**(Verse 35.)** “Saul built an altar to the Lord.” This was the first time he began to build an altar to the Lord. The Hebrew does not have “first.” It must therefore be asked: since he is previously said to have built an altar when he was rebuked by Samuel, why is it said here that he then began to build an altar to the Lord? He is indeed previously said to have built an altar, but because he built it disobediently, it is not understood that he built it to the Lord. Here, however, because he built it obediently and correctly, he is said to have built it to the Lord.

[Col. 1339B] **(Verse 38.)** “Saul said: Bring here all the corners of the people.” By “the corners of the people” he calls the leaders of the people, to whom the people clung.

**(Chapter XV.—Verse 3.)** “Now go and strike Amalek, and destroy everything that belongs to him. Do not spare him, but kill man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey, and every beast of burden.” The Lord commanded that Amalek’s animals also be destroyed so that no memory of him might remain even in his animals. For the Lord had said that he would blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. Therefore Saul was commanded to destroy him completely, from man to beast. But because his memory—that is, Amalek himself—was not completely destroyed, Saul’s sin and disobedience were responsible. Concerning Amalek it is said in the book of Deuteronomy: “Remember what Amalek did to you on the way when you came out of Egypt: how he met you and struck down the rear of your army, those who were weary and lagging behind.” Here the Hebrews understand “the weary” as those who, according to the Law, were unclean and remained outside the camp. The Amalekites are said to have struck them down because, as they relate, they cut off their circumcisions and, as an insult to God, threw them toward heaven.

**(Verse 6.)** “Saul said to the Kenite: Go, withdraw and depart, lest I involve you with him. For you showed kindness to all the sons of Israel when they came up from Egypt.” The Kenite is Jethro, Moses’ kinsman. The Kenites who had gone down to Amalek and lived with him were of his family and therefore his relatives; he also held an inheritance in his land. The Kenite is said to have shown kindness to the sons of Israel either because he supported Moses in the land of Midian, or because he gave Moses advice on how to govern the multitude of the people.

**(Verse 12.)** “It was reported to Samuel that Saul had come to Carmel and had erected there [Note: [Col. 1339D] The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “and had erected for himself a triumphal arch,” and so forth.] a triumphal arch.” When they gained a victory, they made an arch from myrtle, palm, and olive branches as a sign of victory.

**(Verse 21.)** “The people took sheep and oxen, the firstfruits of what had been slaughtered.” Here “firstfruits” means those things that were more valuable and better.

**(Verse 29.)** “Moreover, the Triumph of Israel will not spare, nor will he be swayed by repentance; for he is not a man, that he should repent.” In Hebrew it reads: “Moreover, the Triumph of Israel will not lie.” This “Triumph” is God. He will not lie, because he grants what he promises to those who serve him. He will not be swayed by repentance, because he does not repent of the good things he has bestowed.

**(Verse 30.)** “But now honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel.” Honor me as king, so that I may go before them as king and you may follow, and that I may worship the Lord your God. By “the elders of his people” he means his own tribe; by “before Israel,” the other tribes of Israel.

[Col. 1340B] **(Chapter XVI.—Verse 18.)** “One of the young men answered and said: Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite,” and so forth. This young man is said to have been Doeg the Edomite, David’s enemy. Everything he appears to have said in praise of David is said to have been spoken out of hatred, because, motivated by enmity and the rancor of envy, he wanted David to come to Saul, so that he might be killed there on some pretext.

**(Verse 13.)** “And the Spirit of the Lord was directed into David from that day and thereafter.” The Spirit of the Lord is said to have been directed into him because at that time he began to sing psalms.

**(Chapter XVII.—Verse 4.)** “A bastard went out from the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath.” He is called a bastard because he was born of a giant father and a woman of Gath.

[Col. 1340C] **(Verse 12.)** “David was the son of an Ephraimite from Bethlehem of Judah, whose name was Jesse, who had eight sons.” It is asked why he is here said to have had eight sons, since in Chronicles no more than seven are read. The matter is resolved as follows. He counts Nathan, the prophet, the son of his son Shammah, whom he had raised and nurtured in the place of a son, among his sons. For seven of his sons are also read as having been brought before Samuel, while the eighth was in the pasture (verse 10). It is clear that Nathan was among those brought forward, and that he is also called Jonathan. Concerning him it is said in the final part of Samuel: “Jonathan, the son of Shammah, David’s brother, struck him down” (2 Samuel 21:21). It should be noted that wherever he is called a prophet, he is written as Nathan, not Jonathan.

[Col. 1340D] **(Verse 18.)** “And visit your brothers to see whether they are well, and learn from whom they have been assigned.” In Hebrew it reads: “And visit your brothers to see whether they are well, and take their pledges.” Here the Hebrews understand “pledges” as bills of divorce. They report that it was the custom of that people, when they went into battle, to give their wives bills of divorce, so that if it happened that a husband was captured in battle and led away into captivity, his wife, after waiting three years and if her husband had not returned, could marry another man. [Note: [Col. 1339D] It is strange that a man of Hebrew descent, although he later wished to take the name of the Christian faith, should have spoken in this way about the customs of his own people as though from the mouth of others.]

[Col. 1341A] **(Verse 28.)** “Why have you come, and why did you leave those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride and the wickedness of your heart.” He says that he knows his pride and the wickedness of his heart because he thought that David was being puffed up in his heart, since Samuel had anointed him king.

**(Verse 54.)** “David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem; but he put his weapons in his tent.” The statement that David brought the Philistine’s head to Jerusalem is an anticipation of what he did later. As for his weapons—that is, the Philistine’s weapons—it should not be understood that he put them in his own tent, but in the tent of the Lord, from which tent he later received them from Abimelech the priest.

**(Verse 55.)** “Abner said: As your soul lives, O king, if I know.” This was spoken according to the type of expression found in the statement: “Naboth blessed God and the king” (1 Kings 21:13), as though he were saying: “May your soul not live, O king, if I know.” Alternatively: “May I see your death, if I know.”

**(Chapter XVIII.—Verse 10.)** “On the following day the evil spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of his house.” He prophesied in the manner of those seized by a spirit. His prophesying here should be understood as nothing other than his uttering things belonging to another.

**(Verse 13.)** “David went out and came in before the people.” When they went out to battle, he went before them first in royal fashion, and returned likewise.

(Vers. 21.) And Saul said, “I will give her to him, so that she may become a snare to him, and the hand of the Philistines may be against him.” Saul thought that David could be destroyed by these two dangers: either by the schemes of his daughter, by whom he saw himself to be greatly loved, or because of the foreskins of the Philistines, for the sake of acquiring which he would attack the Philistines in war. Therefore Saul said to David: “Today you shall be my son-in-law in two ways.” He says that David would become his son-in-law in two ways, because he had already brought him the foreskins of the Philistines in place of Merab, whom Saul gave to Adriel the Meholathite, and afterward two hundred for Michal. Although it is not stated openly that Saul gave David the foreskins of the Philistines for Merab, nevertheless anyone who reads through and carefully examines what precedes and follows will find that he gave Saul the foreskins of the Philistines twice. It may also be understood in another way: “Today you shall be my son-in-law in two ways,” because I asked you for one hundred foreskins of the Philistines, and you presented two hundred.

(Cap. XIX.—Vers. 3.) “But as for me, going out, I shall stand beside my father in the field where you will be; I shall speak about you to my father, and whatever I see I shall report to you.” Jonathan had told David that Saul would come down into that same field, and they had arranged that David should hide in that field. Saul frequently used to meet in that field for the purpose of deliberation; it had also been decided there that David should be killed, which Jonathan had disclosed to David.

(Vers. 24.) “And Saul also stripped off his garments and prophesied before Samuel.” A serious question arises here, since earlier we read: “And Samuel did not see Saul until the day of his death” [Note: More correctly in Rabanus: “how he prophesied here.”]; and here Saul is said to have prophesied before Samuel. The Hebrews resolve this question in two ways. Either Samuel did not see him because, when Saul joined the band of prophets, Samuel hid himself so that Saul would not see him; or he did not see him wearing royal attire, in which he had been dressed when it was said, “He did not see him until the day of his death”—with “wearing royal attire” understood. His stripping himself, however, must be understood as referring not to all his garments but only to his royal garments.

(Cap. XX.—Vers. 1, 2.) “And may the Lord be with you, as he was with my father. And if I live, you shall show me the mercy of the Lord.” “May the Lord be with you as he was with my father”—that is, may he make your kingdom exalted, as he made my father’s kingdom exalted. “And if I live, you shall show me the mercy of the Lord”—namely, that I may be second in your kingdom; and if I die, you shall not remove your mercy from my house forever.

(Cap. XXI.—Vers. 1.) “David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest.” This Ahimelech is Aja, son of Ahitub, son of Phinehas, son of Eli.

[Col. 1342C] (Vers. 5.) “And the vessels of the young men were holy.” Ahimelech asks whether David and his young men, whom he had said he had brought to such-and-such a place, were clean. David answered enigmatically, in the plural, speaking of himself: “And the vessels of the young men were holy,” that is, free from marital intercourse. But when he says, “Moreover, this way is profane,” and the Hebrew reads, “Moreover, this way is common”—that is, secular—it must be understood in this way: “This way is common,” as if he were saying, “The Law commands that an outsider must not eat of these things; yet you are asking whether the young men are clean, although, even if they were clean, they ought by no means to eat them. Therefore this way is common, because you are asking a secular question.” What follows—“But it shall also be sanctified today in the vessels” [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript adds “mine,” which it joins to the following verse.]—is understood to mean that it is sanctified in the vessels, that is, in his own mind, because he would not eat them unless bodily necessity and danger to life compelled him. Nevertheless, David is not explicitly said to have eaten those loaves. The Hebrews maintain that David did not eat those loaves at all; but otherwise [Note: Rabanus does not recognize this passage at all, from which it is again possible to argue that the Hebrew author of the work gave his name to the Christian religion.] [Note: The author of this work set the Lord Jesus and his Gospel against the tradition of the Hebrews; therefore it seems easy to believe that he himself believed in Christ, as we have observed elsewhere.] the Lord in the Gospel (Matt. 12:4).

(Vers. 7.) “Now a certain man was there on that day, one of Saul’s servants, inside the tabernacle, and his name was Doeg [or Dog], the Idumean.” In Hebrew it says, “bound in the presence of the Lord.” The same Doeg the Idumean was bound by a vow by which he had obligated himself to remain for several days in the tabernacle of the Lord and devote himself to prayer.

(Cap. XXII.—Vers. 5.) “And Gad the prophet said to David: Do not remain in the stronghold. Depart and go into the land of Judah.” Gad the prophet is introduced here in a remarkable manner, since no mention of him had been made earlier. He is introduced here in the same way as Elijah the prophet in the passage that says, “And Elijah the Tishbite, from the inhabitants of Gilead” (III Kings 17:1). Thus, from the mouth of the Lord, the prophet Gad told David not to remain among the nations and in a polluted land, but to return to the land of Judah and there, according to the Lord’s will, endure the persecution of his enemies.

[Col. 1343B] (Vers. 18.) “And Doeg the Idumean slaughtered on that day eighty-five men wearing the linen ephod.” In Hebrew it reads, “carrying the linen ephod.” The Hebrews say that not all of them wore the linen ephod, but that they were men who were worthy and qualified to carry the ephod.

(Cap. XXIII.—Vers. 11.) “If the men of Keilah will hand me over into his hands, and if Saul will come down, as your servant has heard, O Lord God of Israel, reveal it to your servant.” And the Lord said, “He will come down.” It is as though he had said, “If you remain here, he will come down.” And when David says, “If the men of Keilah will hand me over,” and the Lord says, “They will hand you over,” the meaning is this: “If Saul comes down and finds you here, they will hand you over.” Now, at the time when Abiathar, son of Ahimelech, had fled to David at Keilah, he had come down carrying the ephod with him. That was the ephod which Moses had made at the Lord’s command. In it were instruction and truth, and in it the priest consulted the Lord. [Col. 1343C] [Note: “David” is supplied in place of “the priest.”]

(Vers. 18.) “Then Jonathan and David made a covenant before the Lord.” “Before the Lord,” that is, before Gad the prophet and Abiathar the priest, who was carrying the ephod.

(Vers. 25.) “So Saul and his companions went to seek him. And it was reported to David, and he immediately went down to the rock and remained in the wilderness of Maon.” He is said to have gone down to the rock, that is, to a very secure place, where he deposited the things that were burdensome and heavy for him. He himself remained in the wilderness of Maon, where refuge was available to him.

(Cap. XXV.—Vers. 2.) “Now there was a certain man in the wilderness of Maon.” The Hebrew does not have “in the wilderness” at this point. He lived in the city of Maon, not in the wilderness.

(Vers. 21.) “Truly, I have kept everything that belonged to this man in vain, and nothing of all that belonged to him has perished, and he has repaid me evil for good.” He repaid him evil for good at the time when he reviled him with insults and said: “Who is David, and who is the son of Jesse? Today servants are increasing who flee from their masters” (verse 10).

(Vers. 26.) “And now, let your enemies and those who seek evil for my lord become like Nabal.” “Let them become,” she says, “like Nabal, so that they may perish like Nabal in their folly.”

(Vers. 30.) “Therefore, when the Lord has done for my lord all the good things that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you ruler over Israel, this will not be a cause of trembling for you.” “It will not,” she says, “be a cause of groaning for you”—that you should now shed Nabal’s blood and, on that account, have cause to mourn and repent.

(Vers. 44.) “But Saul gave his daughter Michal, David’s wife, to Phalti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.” As the Hebrews relate, he did not have intercourse with her [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has “the same one” instead of “that is,” namely Phalti], because, if he had had intercourse with her, David would never afterward have taken her back, since such intercourse is utterly forbidden by the Law. That same Phalti was from Gallim, that is, from “inundation.” “Inundation,” namely Gallim, is understood as the Law. For he was a teacher of the Law, from Bahurim, that is, “from the chosen.” When Michal is given to him by Saul, Phalti, that is, “one escaping,” is the interpretation. But when the same Michal is taken away from him, he is called Phaltiel, that is, “one escaping from God.” He is called “one escaping from God” because God protected him so that he did not touch her and become a transgressor of the Law.

“And her husband followed her, weeping as far as Bahurim” (II Kings 3:16). He is said to have wept from joy, because the Lord had protected him from touching her.

(Cap. XXVI.—Vers. 6.) “David said to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai, son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother: Who will go down with me?” This Ahimelech is Uriah. Uriah therefore means “my light is God.” [Col. 1344C] Ahimelech means “my brother is king.”

(Cap. XXVII.—Vers. 8.) “David and his men went up, and they raided Geshur, and Gethri, and the Amalekites.” These villages had been inhabited in the land from ancient times. These villages were not under the power of Achish. They are said to have been inhabited in the land from ancient times because they had been inhabited peacefully and securely and had suffered the depredations of no enemy.

(Cap. XXVIII.—Vers. 3.) “Now Samuel had died, and all Israel mourned him. And they buried him in Ramah, his own city.” Earlier (at chapter 25:1) it is said that he had been buried in his house in Ramah. “In his house,” that is, in his family and kindred. A question arises: since he is already said above to have died, why is his death mentioned again here? According to the Hebrews, his death is repeated here because he was to be raised again [Note: Rabanus had also read: “provided that it was not enough from his own account”; and “it is repeated so that the condemnation of Saul might be shown to be just, since he was dead in his sins and, having abandoned God, consulted the Python contrary to the Law.”].

(Vers. 6.) “And he consulted the Lord, but he did not answer him, neither by dreams nor by priests.” The Hebrew has, “neither by instruction nor by prophets.” The Lord answered by dreams, as those same Hebrews assert, because they sought a divine oracle by praying and fasting, and God revealed through dreams the things that were going to happen. Saul, however, is not at all said to have done this here. “By instruction,” namely, through the ephod, which the priest wore upon his chest. [Col. 1345A] “Nor by prophets,” because when they consulted him, the Lord did not answer them at all. These prophets are said to have been Samuel’s disciples, and when they were prophesying Saul joined himself to them and prophesied.

(Vers. 7.) “Seek for me a woman who has a Python, and I will go to her, and I will be raised up through her.” Having received no answer from God, Saul turns to the Pythons. Although Saul is said to have wiped out the magicians and diviners from the land, the Hebrews maintain that this woman was the mother of Abner, son of Ner, and that, because of that same Abner, she was hidden and spared so that she would not be killed with the other Pythonesses.

(Cap. XXX.—Vers. 24.) “And no one will hear you concerning this matter. For the portion of the one who goes down to battle and of the one who remains with the baggage will be equal.” Although the Latin manuscripts read that certain exhausted men remained with the baggage, while the Hebrew has [Note: I have refuted this passage at length in my notes on the Divine Library of St. Jerome, showing that the Latin version—“those who had remained because they were exhausted”—is excellent and agrees entirely with the Hebrew source, *piggeru*. Whoever wishes may consult our observations.], that they had been ordered to remain with the baggage, this passage shows that one ought here to follow the Hebrew truth, which says that it was not the exhausted who remained with the baggage, but those who had been ordered to remain. For it says as follows: “The portion of the one who goes down to battle and of the one who remains with the baggage will be equal.” It does not say, “of those who remained with the baggage because they were exhausted,” but simply, “of the one who remains with the baggage”; [Col. 1346A] for if they had remained because they were exhausted, no share of the spoils would have been owed to them.

(Cap. XXXI.—Vers. 5.) “When his armor-bearer saw this—namely, that Saul was dead—he too threw himself upon his sword and died with him.” The Hebrews say that this armor-bearer was Doeg the Idumean, who, seeing Saul dead, killed himself through fear of David.

(Vers. 6.) “So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men.” These men are to be understood as his household servants. The three sons of Saul who were killed with him were Jonathan, Abinadab, who was also called Jesui, and Melchishua. Ish-bosheth, however, was at home. He is said to have been born in the year in which Saul was established as king, and he is also read to have been forty years old when he began to reign; [Col. 1346B] from this it is inferred that Saul reigned forty years. It must be asked why he is called Jesui in one place and Abinadab in another. Jesui means “equal.” He is called “equal” because the sons are said [or: the son is said] to have been of equal merit with their father. Abinadab means “my father is spontaneous.” For his father Saul acquired this spontaneously by doing evil, so that he might be killed together with his sons in such a manner [Note: In the Ambrosian manuscript: “Here end the Hebrew Questions on the books of Kings.”].

[Note: My manuscript supplies this heading.] ON THE SECOND BOOK OF KINGS.

[Col. 1345]

[Col. 1345C] (Cap. I.—Vers. 2.) “On the third day, a man appeared, coming from Saul’s camp, and the rest.” The Hebrews say that this Amalekite was the son of Doeg. For an Amalekite and an Idumean are the same, since Esau’s firstborn was Eliphaz, and his son was Amalek. The Hebrews maintain that the diadem and the armlet that he brought to David had been entrusted to him by his father Doeg.

[Note: In almost all manuscript copies these words are read continuously, and there is no division of the Hebrew Questions into the first and second books of Kings. Nevertheless, there is one manuscript, the Colbertinus, no. 2852, [Col. 1346D] that uses this division after the word “killed”: “THE BOOK OF KINGS ENDS. ALSO JEROME ON THE SECOND BOOK OF KINGS, CHAPTER I.” All of this is written in red letters.]

(Vers. 12.) “And they mourned, and wept, and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of the Lord, and for the house of Israel.” By “the people of the Lord” he means the priests, and by “the house of Israel” he means the whole people of Israel generally.

(Vers. 18.) “And he said that he should teach the sons of Judah the bow: Behold, it is written in the Book of the Just.” “And he said”—“David” is understood—“that he should teach,” with “God” understood, “the sons of Judah the bow”: that is, he should teach the kings of Judah strength, so that they would be strong and attentive in the fear of the Lord and in the commandments of God, lest, through disobedience, the kings of Judah depart from the strength and fear of the Lord, like Saul, and perish in the manner in which he perished. But when he says, “Behold, it is written in the Book of the Just,” the Book of the Just is the book of Samuel [Note: The true Jerome, at the beginning of his commentary on Isaiah 44 and in his commentary on Ezekiel 8, does not attribute this book, which he calls the Book of the Upright, to Samuel, but thinks that it is the book of Genesis itself, following the opinion of the Hebrews.], in which the just prophets are contained—namely Samuel, Gad, and Mathan. In their book it is said to be written how Saul, departing from the fear of the Lord, perished through his disobedience.

(Vers. 19.) “Your illustrious ones, O Israel, have been slain upon your mountains.” The Hebrew has, “upon your heights.” The meaning is: “O Saul, the glorious ones of Israel have been slain upon your heights, because they perished together with you in the sin of your disobedience.” Your disobedience was reckoned as idolatry, that is, as “high places,” as in the Book of Samuel: “For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams; for rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is like the crime of idolatry” (I Kings 15:22–23).

(Vers. 24.) “Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet amid delights, who supplied golden ornaments for your adornment.” He clothed them in scarlet and supplied golden ornaments for their adornment from the spoils of the enemies whom he defeated.

(Vers. 25.) “How have the mighty fallen in battle?” “Through your sin” is understood. “Jonathan is slain upon your heights.” The Hebrew does not have “is.” The sense is: “O Saul, Jonathan [is] slain upon your heights”—that is, in the sin of your disobedience.

(Cap. II.—Vers. 6.) “And now may the Lord indeed repay you with mercy and truth.” “Mercy” refers to the present age, and “truth” to the future; for the mercy granted in the present age is, by comparison with eternal mercy, a lie.

(Vers. 8.) “But Abner son of Ner, commander of Saul’s army, took Ish-bosheth son of Saul and brought him through the camp.” The Hebrew has, “he brought him across to Mahanaim,” which is interpreted as “camps.” “He brought him across” is understood to mean beyond the Jordan, and there he established him as king.

“Over Gilead and over Jessuri.” The Hebrew has “Assuri,” that is, “over the tribe of Asher.”

(Vers. 26.) “Abner called to Joab and said: Will your sword rage forever unto destruction?” The Hebrew does not have “your.” “Do you not know that despair is dangerous?” The Hebrew reads: “Do you not know that the end will be bitter?” The meaning is: “Do you not know that this will turn out bitterly for you, because you are trying to destroy this people?”

(Cap. III.—Vers. 5.) “And the sixth was Jethraam, from Eglah, David’s wife.” It must be asked why David’s other wives are listed above without being called David’s wives, whereas here Eglah alone is called David’s wife. Eglah is Michal herself, who is here called his wife alone because he first took her as his wife in his youth; she is also said to have died in childbirth. Eglah therefore means “heifer.”

(Vers. 8.) “Am I a dog’s head against Judah?” It is as though he were saying: “Because of you and because of your father’s house I am said to be a dog’s head against Judah, since I do not bring the house of Israel back to David, whom I know to have been anointed king and to be destined to reign over all Israel.” He says that he is a dog’s head, that is, contemptible, because he was regarded by the house of Judah as a dog’s barking, and because he was the leader of dogs, that is, of foolish men.

(Vers. 13.) “But I ask one thing of you: You shall not see my face before you bring Michal, the daughter of Saul; then you shall come and see me.” There is an omission here, and a necessary implied statement: Abner is reported to have answered David that he could not do this at all, namely, restore Michal to him, because her brother the king held her under his authority. After receiving from him an answer full of this excuse, David is recorded to have sent to her brother Ish-bosheth for her, as what follows makes clear.

(Vers. 14.) “David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, saying: Restore to me my wife Michal, whom I betrothed to myself for one hundred foreskins of the Philistines.”

[Col. 1348A] (Vers. 33.) “And the king mourned for Abner and said: You did not die as ignoble men usually die, Abner.” That is, you did not perish in your folly, as ignoble men usually perish, because you were deceived by treachery.

(Vers. 34.) “Your hands were not bound, and your feet were not weighed down with fetters.” You were not captured according to the law of war; your hands were not bound and your feet weighed down with fetters, as the hands and feet of those who are usually captured in battle are bound. Therefore you were killed by deceit, not by force.

(Cap. IV.—Vers. 2.) “Now there were two men, commanders of raiding bands, belonging to Saul’s son; the name of one was Baana, and the name of the other Rechab, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, from the sons of Benjamin.” These two men were commanders over Ish-bosheth’s expeditions. After Abner’s death, as the Hebrews relate, they made an agreement with Mephibosheth to kill Ish-bosheth together, and they established that same Mephibosheth as king; and Mephibosheth became the informer of this very plot. Therefore this same Mephibosheth is introduced here in this way.

(Vers. 4.) “Now Jonathan, son of Saul, had a son disabled in his feet; for he was five years old when the report came from Saul and Jonathan from Jezreel, and the rest that follows.” When Baana and Rechab saw that their plot had been betrayed by Mephibosheth, they were terrified by fear and fled to Gittaim; and they remained there as resident foreigners until that time. “That time” is understood to be when they returned from there and entered Ish-bosheth’s house in the heat of the day, carrying sheaves of wheat and striking him in the groin. They brought sheaves of wheat as if for the sake of firstfruits, so that they might appear to be paying honor to the king and their deceit might not be detected at all.

(Cap. V.—Vers. 4.) “David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years. In Hebron he reigned over Judah for seven years and six months. In Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.” It must be asked why, in the total, forty years and six months are not counted. The Hebrews resolve this in two ways. They say that David fled from his son Absalom for six months, and therefore those same six months were rightly excluded from the total of his reign. They also say that David suffered from a bodily illness in Hebron for six months, and therefore those same six months were not counted in his reign. For they say that he began to reign in Hebron from the time when, after defeating the Amalekites, he sent gifts from their spoils to the elders of Judah—to those who were in Hebron, to those who were in Bethel, and to the others who were in the places where David himself and his men had stayed.

(Vers. 6, 8.) “And they said to David: You shall not enter here unless you remove the blind and the lame, who say: David shall not enter here.” It is as though they were saying to him: “David shall not enter here until he removes us from here—we who are unarmed and weak, whom he considers to be like the blind and the lame, and whom he thinks he will defeat in war as though they were blind and lame.” Hence it is said in the proverb: “The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple.” The Hebrew has: “The blind and the lame shall not enter the house”—that is, “the blind and the lame,” with “say” understood: “No one shall enter the house of the blind and the lame so long as the blind and the lame are inside.”

(Ibid.) “For on that day David had promised a reward to anyone who struck the Jebusite, touched the water conduit, and removed the lame and the blind who hated David’s life.” The Hebrew reads: “And David said on that day: Whoever strikes the Jebusite and touches the water conduit, and the lame and the blind who hate David’s life”—“shall be prince and commander” is understood, as the Book of Chronicles explains in these words: “Whoever strikes the Jebusite first shall be prince and commander.” Joab son of Zeruiah went up first and became prince (I Chron. 11:6). What he says, “Whoever touches the water conduit,” must be understood as follows: Whoever is so bold and courageous that he comes right up to the city wall and touches with his spear the water conduit that is in the wall—he shall be prince.

(Vers. 21.) “And they left their idols there, which David and his men carried away.” David carried them away and ordered them to be burned with fire, as the Book of Chronicles explains, saying: “They left their gods there, which David ordered to be burned” (I Chron. 14:12).

(Vers. 23.) “David consulted the Lord, who answered: Do not go up; circle around behind them, and come upon them opposite the pear trees.” The Hebrew does not read “pear trees,” but “weeping ones.” Therefore he commands him to come upon them opposite the weeping ones—that is, opposite their idols, where their idols were, in which they trusted. These idols are called “weeping ones” because they are worthy of weeping and bring those who worship them to weep over their miseries. Thus, on account of their blasphemy, the divine word here calls their idols “weeping ones,” just as elsewhere the idol of Moab is called “the pollution of Moab.”

(Vers. 24.) “And when you hear the sound of marching on the summit of the weeping ones”—that is, when you hear that, through angelic powers, their idols, in which all their strength lies, are being crushed and trampled down—then you shall enter the battle, because the Lord will go out before your face to strike the camp of the Philistines. For the Lord executed his judgments upon their idols, just as he did upon the gods of the Egyptians.

[Col. 1349D] (Cap. VI.—Vers. 8.) “David was distressed because the Lord had struck Uzzah.” The Hebrew has, “because the Lord had divided.” The Lord is said to have divided him because the place where Uzzah had been appeared empty. David did not wish to bring the ark of the Lord to himself, into the city of David; instead, he turned it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. He is called a Gittite because his father had lived in Gath.

(Vers. 11.) “And the Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his house.” The Hebrews say that the Lord blessed his house because all his wives, concubines, daughters-in-law, and maidservants gave birth to male children, and the female quadrupeds also produced twin offspring for him. Concerning this it is written in the Book of Chronicles: “So the ark of God remained in the house of Obed-edom for three months, and the Lord blessed his house and all that he had” (I Chron. 13:14). Elsewhere in the same Book of Chronicles it is said: “The sons of Obed-edom were Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sachar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth, Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, and Peullethai the eighth, because God blessed him” (I Chron. 26:4).

(Vers. 23.) “Therefore Michal, daughter of Saul, had no son until the day of her death.” Michal is Eglah herself; she bore Jethraam to David and died in childbirth.

(Cap. VII.—Vers. 3.) “And Nathan said to the king: Go and do everything that is in your heart, for the Lord is with you.” Nathan said this to David from himself, not from the word of the Lord. But what follows he said from the word of the Lord: “Thus says the Lord: Will you build me a house in which to dwell?” It is as though he were saying: “You cannot build me a house, because you are a man of blood and have shed much blood.”

(Vers. 6.) “For I have not dwelt in a house from the day when I brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt until this day, but I walked in a tabernacle and in a tent.” The Lord says that he walked in a tabernacle and in a tent because neither Moses nor Joshua could build him a house, since they were men of blood, as David also was.

(Vers. 7.) “Through all the places where I passed with all the children of Israel, did I ever speak a word to one of the tribes of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying: Why have you not built me a house of cedar?” The places through which the Lord says that he passed are understood to be Shiloh, Gilgal, Nob, and the other places where the tabernacle and the ark of the Lord were established. “Did I ever speak to any judge of the tribes of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel: Why have you not built me a house of cedar?” He did not command any of the Judges to build him a house of cedar because all of them fought against enemies and all were shedders of blood. But your son, against whom the wars of the enemies will not press and who will not be a man of blood, will build me a house.

(Vers. 8.) “And now say this to my servant David: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I took you from the pasture, from following the flock.” And a little later: “And I made your name great, like the name of the great ones who are on the earth.” “I made,” says the Lord, “your name great, as I made the names of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and Joshua great—their names are very famous throughout the earth.”

(Vers. 10.) “And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant it, and it shall dwell beneath it.” In this passage the divine speech describes the time of Solomon, when the children of Israel would have peace all around and would not be afflicted and oppressed as they had been afflicted and oppressed in the time of the Judges.

(Vers. 14.) “If he commits any iniquity, I will rebuke him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men.” By “the rod of men” he means the sword of enemies. The “blows of the sons of men” are bodily afflictions, by which human beings are deservedly chastised by the Lord for their sins.

(Vers. 19.) “For this is the law of Adam, Lord God.” That is: “It is the law of man, Lord God, that he serve you with simplicity of heart and purity.”

(Vers. 21.) “And you will act toward him according to your mercy, as you have deigned to act toward your servant because of your word; and according to your heart you have done all these great things.” Because of your word, which you promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, you have done all these things for me, your servant. When he says “according to your heart,” this is understood as “according to your mercy.”

(Vers. 22.) “For there is none like you. Nor is there a God besides you, in all that we have heard with our ears.” “There is no God,” he says, “like you who has done these great things that we have heard with our ears.”

(Vers. 23.) “From before your people, whom you redeemed from Egypt, a nation and its god.” The Hebrew has, “from the nations and their gods.” The meaning is: “From before your people, whom you redeemed from Egypt”—that is, from the hand of the Egyptians, whom you killed in the Red Sea—and from their gods, upon whom you executed judgments.

(Vers. 27.) “For you, Lord of hosts, God of Israel, have revealed the ear of your servant, saying: I will build you a house. Therefore your servant has found his heart, so that he might pray this prayer to you.” The Lord had revealed through the prophet that he would build him a house. Therefore David says that he found his heart—that is, he found courage in his heart—to pray to him with this prayer.

(Cap. VIII.—Vers. 15.) “After these things David struck the Philistines and humbled them, and David took the bridle of tribute from the hand of the Philistines.” The “bridle of tribute” refers to the five cities of the Philistines, which frequently made Israel tributary to themselves. David took them from their hand, humbled them, and made them tributary to himself. Hence it is also read in Chronicles: “David struck the Philistines and humbled them, and took Gath and its villages from their hand” (I Chron. 10:1).

(Vers. 19.) “And David made a name for himself when he returned, after Syria had been conquered.” He is said to have made a name for himself because, after killing eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt, he erected a triumphal arch for himself. He also made a name for himself because, after conquering Syria of Damascus and Syria of Zobah, he is said to have erected another triumphal arch. If anyone is troubled by the fact that in many Latin manuscripts David is found to have killed not eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt but twelve thousand, let him know that this was inserted in those manuscripts through the fault [Note: We discussed this sort of variant reading in our notes on the Divine Library of St. Jerome. Whoever wishes may consult that passage.] of the scribes [Note: This sort of error, which is an indication of the most remote antiquity, is also found in the Verona manuscript. Moreover, for *inditum* one should read *inolitum*, as may be inferred from Rabanus, who has the erroneous *molitum*.]. Nevertheless, David truly killed eighteen thousand in that same Valley of Salt. Joab, however, killed twelve thousand, as is written in the title of Psalm 58.

[Col. 1352A] (Cap. IX.—Vers. 11.) “And Ziba said to the king: As you have commanded, my lord the king, your servant, so your servant will do; and Mephibosheth shall eat at your table.” It should be noted that the Hebrew reads, “at my table,” because there is an omission here and a necessary implied statement. When Ziba said, “As you have commanded, my lord the king, your servant, so your servant will do,” it must be understood that David said, “And Mephibosheth shall eat at my table,” as one of the king’s sons.

(Cap. X.—Vers. 2.) “And David said: I will show mercy to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed mercy to me.” When David fled from the presence of Achish, king of Gath, he came to Nahash, king of the Ammonites, who showed him mercy and bestowed many benefits upon him. From Nahash he therefore came to the cave of Adullam, where his father, mother, and entire household came to him. From there he went to Moab and left his father, mother, and entire household with him. But when Achish, king of Gath, said, “Will this man enter my house?” David departed from there and fled to the cave of Adullam. “He departed from there” must be understood as meaning “from the house of Nahash,” and that he fled from there to the cave of Adullam. If it is asked why David returned to him—that is, to Achish—before whose presence he had fled, it must be understood that this Achish was the son of that Achish from whom David fled. Hence, in what follows, Achish, with whom David went down to battle against Saul, is said to have been the son of Maoch. He did not take this patronymic name from his father, but from his mother, who was called Maacah. He did not therefore take this name from his father because David had rejected him.

(Vers. 10.) “But he entrusted the rest of the people to Abishai his brother.” It should be noted that only here the Hebrew reads *Abisa*, whereas in all the other passages it reads *Abishai*. Abisa therefore means “father of sacrifice,” and Abishai means “my father is sacrifice.” The Hebrews say that one letter was removed from his name because he was an accomplice in the killing of Abner.

## (Chapter XI—Verse 1)

It came to pass, therefore, [Note: [Col. 1352D] The Ambrosian manuscript reads “when the year turned”; and a little later, “or in the sixth [verse] from this verse,” omitting Istob and Maacha and retaining the name Soba.] when the year had come around again, at the time when kings customarily go forth to war, that David sent Joab and his servants with him, and so forth. In Hebrew it is read as follows: “At the time when kings had gone forth to war, David sent Joab,” and so forth. By “these kings” he means those who went forth against David to battle, namely [Col. 1352D] the king of Roob, Istob, Soba, and Maadia, who were in fact kings of Syria and wished to fight, hired for pay by the king of Moab against David, by whom they are recorded to have been defeated.

### (Verse 3)

And David said: “Is this not Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?” Eliam was the son of Ahithophel.

### (Verse 13)

And David summoned Uriah, so that he might eat before him and drink, and he made him drunk. He is said to have made him drunk for this reason: so that, at least when intoxicated, he would go down to his own house.

## (Chapter XII—Verse 14)

Nevertheless, because you have caused the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, on account of this word the son who has been born to you shall surely die. In Hebrew it is read as follows: “Nevertheless, because by blaspheming you have blasphemed the enemies of the Lord, on account of this word the son also who has been born to you shall surely die.” This is said by antiphrasis, and the meaning is: “You have granted salvation to the enemies of the Lord; when they rise up against the Lord’s people, because of this sin of yours the Lord’s people will not be able to resist them. Moreover, those enemies themselves will prevail over the Lord’s people because of your sin.”

### (Verse 25)

And he called his name Beloved of the Lord, [Col. 1353B] because the Lord loved him. In Hebrew it is read as follows: “And he called his name” [Note: [Col. 1353] The manuscript codices read this way; the printed editions, however, read Jedidiah. For the meaning of *mamzer*, see Deuteronomy 23:2.] [Note: [Col. 1353D] In my manuscript, as also in Ambrose, *Ididiam*; Rabanus has *Ididam*.] **IDDIDIA**, that is, “beloved of the Lord,” because of the Lord. He is called “beloved of the Lord because of the Lord” on account of His gratuitous mercy, by which He deigned to love him, although he was plainly unworthy of that love and mercy, since he was known to be a *mamzer*—that is, one born of an illicit union.

### (Verse 27)

I have fought against Rabbah, and the city of waters is to be captured. It should be noted that in Hebrew, when *Rabbath* is used with an accompanying name, as in “Rabbath of the sons of Ammon,” [Note: [Col. 1353D] Rabanus writes *Rabbat* at this point.] it is written *Rabbath*. But when it is used without an accompanying name, it is written not *Rabbath* but *Rabba*.

### (Verse 30)

And when he had fought against it, he captured it and took the crown of Milcom from its head. *Milcom* means “their king.” Their idol is called “their king.” Here it is called Milcom; David is said, according to the law, to have melted down and purified the gold and gems of its crown and made a crown for himself from them, which is here said to have been placed upon his head.

### (Verse 31)

And he brought out its people, sawed them apart, and drove iron chariots over them; he divided them with knives and passed them through the brick mold. For he sawed them apart with iron chariots and divided them with knives, just as bricks are customarily divided—bricks made from straw and clay.

## (Chapter XIII—Verse 37)

But Absalom, fleeing, went to Talmai, son of Amibur [Ms. *Amui*], king of Geshur. Talmai was the father of Maacah, the mother of Absalom. The Hebrews say that David captured her in battle (Deut. 21) and, after cutting her hair and trimming her nails according to the law, took her as his wife; by her he fathered Tamar and Absalom.

### (Verse 39)

King David ceased pursuing Absalom. In Hebrew it is read: “King David ceased going out after Absalom.” [Note: [Col. 1353D] My manuscript and Rabanus say that the name David itself is not present in the Hebrew; this is nevertheless false.] The same David is said to have wished to go out in order to bring Absalom back. But when he considered in his heart that every time he saw him, he would recall the pain of Amnon’s death, he is therefore said to have ceased going out after Absalom—that is to be understood, in order to bring him back to his own place.

But when it says that he had been comforted concerning Amnon’s death, this is to be understood as follows: after he did not wish to go out after Absalom in order to bring him back and see him, he began to be comforted concerning Amnon’s death. For as long as Absalom was thought to be brought back so that David might see him, the death of his son Amnon continually came before his mind. Alternatively, he is said to have been comforted concerning Amnon’s death because he knew that Amnon was disgraceful, deserved death, and had perished deservedly.

## (Chapter XIV—Verse 1)

Now Joab, son of Zeruiah, understanding that the king’s heart had turned toward Absalom, is said to have seen that the king’s heart had turned toward Absalom because Joab saw him sighing for Absalom [Note: [Col. 1354D] Martianus reads “through Absalom.”]; from this he understood that his heart had turned toward Absalom.

### (Verse 2)

He sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman. Tekoa is the city from which the prophet Amos came. It is thought [Note: [Col. 1354D] Rabanus has: “It is thought by the Hebrews that she was a widow,” etc.] that this same woman was the grandmother of the prophet Amos.

### (Verses 5 and following)

She answered him: “Alas, I am a widow. My husband has died, and your handmaid had two sons who quarreled with one another in the field, and there was no one who could restrain them. One struck the other and killed him. And behold, the whole family has risen against your handmaid and says: ‘Hand over the one who struck his brother.’”

In truth, as the Hebrews relate, this widow had two sons who quarreled in the field over their father’s inheritance, and one was killed by the other. Yet this same widow represented herself in the person of David, her two sons in the persons of Amnon and Absalom, and the family that rose against her son in the persons of David’s remaining sons.

### (Verse 9)

“Upon me, my lord the king, be the iniquity, and upon my father’s house; but let the king and his throne be innocent.” As though she were saying: “Because one of my sons rose against the other, let the iniquity be upon me, if there must be any. But upon you, O King David, let there be no iniquity, because you are without fault, since Absalom killed Amnon, who deserved death. And just as I am without fault because my two sons rose against one another and one was killed by the other, so you also are without fault because Absalom killed Amnon, who deserved death.”

[Note: [Col. 1354D] Rabanus reads: “because those two brothers fought with one another.”]

### (Verse 11)

She said: “Let the king remember the Lord his God, so that the avengers of blood may not multiply to take vengeance, and so that they may not kill my son.” Here “remember” is used in place of an oath. As though she were saying: “Let the king remember the promise—indeed, his oath—which he made to me by the Lord his God, that the avengers of blood should not multiply to take vengeance.”

### (Verse 13)

And the woman said: “Why have you devised such a thing against the people of God? By speaking this word, has not the king acted so as to sin and not bring back his banished one?”

From this passage what was said a little earlier is demonstrated: “King David ceased to go after Absalom”—that is, he ceased so that no one might go out and bring Absalom back. Hence the woman says: “By speaking this word, has the king acted so as to sin and not bring back his banished one?”

But when she says: “Why have you devised such a thing against the people of God?” she calls Absalom himself, or those who had gone with him [Al. “were with him”], “the people of God”; they were like captives and outcasts because they were not brought back to the inheritance of God, lest perhaps, compelled by circumstances, they should serve foreign gods in a foreign land.

### (Verse 14)

“God does not desire that a soul should perish, but, thinking it over, He delays, lest the one who has been cast away should perish utterly.” As though she were saying: “God calls sinners, who are held captive by the devil, so that they may turn back to Him; and you, who ought to imitate Him, why do you not act in the same way?” [Note: [Col. 1354D] Another reading, with the Ambrosian manuscript, has: “Why do you not act all the more in that way?”]

### (Verse 26)

And when his hair was cut—for it was cut once a year. In Hebrew it is read: “And when the hair of his head was cut.” It was cut at a fixed time, because its thickness burdened him. He weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels by the public standard. His head was not cut once a year, as the Latin manuscripts have, but at a fixed time—that is, every thirty days.

## (Chapter XV—Verse 7)

After forty years Absalom said to the king: “I will go and pay my vows which I vowed to the Lord in Hebron.” The fortieth year was being reckoned from the time when Saul killed the inhabitants of Nob, together with eighty-five priests, because of David. Therefore this fortieth year is placed here to show that divine vengeance was being stirred up against David because he had deceived Ahimelech [Note: [Col. 1355D] From the older reading, my manuscript and Rabanus have “Abimelech”], and because so many priests had been slaughtered on his account.

Beware, reader, of the many corrupt manuscripts [Note: [Col. 1355] We have thoroughly refuted these errors in the Notes on the Divine Library.] in which one finds written “after four years,” not “after forty years.” In the more accurate manuscripts, and in the Hebrew original, not four but forty years are written.

If, however, someone should obstinately insist on those same four years, reckoning them from the time when Absalom killed his brother Amnon to the time when he said to his father, “I will go and pay my vows which I vowed to the Lord in Hebron,” he will plainly discover that he is mistaken if he investigates carefully. For after killing Amnon, Absalom remained three years in Geshur with King Talmai; after he was recalled to Jerusalem, he remained there two years without seeing his father; and in the sixth year he saw his father’s face and prepared rebellion against him.

He falsely said that he had vowed a vow—that is, that he would pray in the place where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob rest.

### (Verse 24)

And they set down the ark of God. And Abiathar went up until all the people who had gone out from the city had been completed. They are said to have set down the ark of God so that the Lord might be consulted through Abiathar the priest concerning the direction David ought to take. Abiathar is said to have gone up—that is, to have prayed. And because he received no answer from the divine oracle, David consequently says that the ark of God should be carried back into the city.

## (Chapter XVI—Verse 10)

“What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse.” The Hebrew does not have “let him curse” in this form, but only “he curses” [Ms. “he cursed”].

[Col. 1356B] Abishai alone had said: “I will go and cut off his head.” David answered Abishai and Joab, saying: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?” As though he were saying: “Do you perhaps wish to kill this man, as you killed Abner? For the Lord has commanded him to curse David. And who is there to say, ‘Why has he done this?’” This is to be understood as: “Why has he done this—not the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1356D] Rabanus adds: “as the Hebrews say”], “but Shimei?”

The Shimei who was cursing David is Nabat, the father of Jeroboam, who is called the son of Gemini; in his zeal for the house of Saul he cursed David. His grandfather’s name, however, was Gemini, and this Shimei was from the tribe of Ephraim, the son of Joseph. Hence this same Shimei says to David: “I also came first today from the whole tribe of Joseph.”

### (Verse 17)

And Absalom said to him: “Is this your kindness toward your friend?” In Hebrew it is read: “Is this your mercy toward your friend?” [Col. 1356C] This should be spoken not affirmatively but negatively. The meaning is: “Is it mercy, or should it be called mercy, that you have let David, your friend, go and have not gone with him?”

## (Chapter XVII—Verse 2)
