“When all the people who are with him have fled, I will strike the king when he is isolated, and I will bring back all the people, just as everyone ordinarily returns.” That is, just as those who return after losing their king in battle customarily return, so the whole people of Israel will return to you.

### (Verse 19)

“When any one of them falls at the beginning, he will hear whatever he hears and say: ‘A slaughter has taken place among the people who followed Absalom’; and every brave man, whose heart is like a lion’s, will melt with fear.” [Col. 1356D] In Hebrew it is written: “And the bravest man, whose heart is like a lion’s, will melt with fear?” This too should be pronounced not affirmatively but negatively. This bravest man is to be understood as David, as the following also makes clear.

### (Verse 20)

For all Israel knows that your father is strong, and that all who are with him are mighty. The handmaid went and told them, and they departed.

This handmaid had gone to the spring of Rogel with clothes, supposedly for washing, so that the matter might not be discovered at all. The boy who reported the affair to Absalom is said to have been the young son of this same handmaid.

### (Verse 21)

“Arise and cross the river quickly.” At this point the Hebrews have not “river” but “water,” which is understood to mean the river Jordan.

### (Verse 24)

David came to the camp, which in Hebrew is called *Mahanaim*. At this place the angels of God met Jacob, as it is written in Genesis: “And Jacob called the name of the place Mahanaim,” that is, “camps” (Gen. 32:2).

### (Verse 25)

Amasa was the son of a man who was called Jether of Jezreel. In Hebrew it is read: “Jether the Ishmaelite.” Hence it is also written in Chronicles: “Abigail bore Amasa, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite.”

[Col. 1357B] He is called an Ishmaelite because the son born to him, Amasa, imitated the conduct of Ishmael and did not at all accompany David when he was fleeing, although David had said: “You are ours, O David, and we are with you, sons of Jesse.” In the Book of Samuel he is called Jether the Jezreelite for this reason: the sin that his son Amasa had committed against David was erased when Joab struck him—that is, Amasa.

### (The same passage)

He entered in to Abigail, the daughter of Nahash, the sister of Zeruiah. *Nahash* means “serpent.” He is called “serpent” because he is said to have committed no deadly sin except that which he originally contracted from the ancient serpent.

There is also a Nahash who is Jesse, David’s father, as is shown in Chronicles, where, after the sons of Jesse have been listed, it is written that their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail.

### (Verse 27)

When David came to the camp—that is, to Mahanaim—Shobi, son of Nahash, from Rabbah of the sons of Ammon, and so forth.

This Shobi was the son of Nahash the king, against whom Saul fought. That same Nahash also showed kindness to David when he fled from Saul. After Nahash died, David said: “I will show kindness to Hanun, as his father Nahash showed kindness to me.” After Hanun was killed by David because he had insulted him by shaving his servants, this Shobi was appointed by David in his brother’s place. He is recorded as having come to David with the others and brought him beds, carpets, earthen vessels, and the other things that follow.

## (Chapter XVIII—Verse 8)

The battle there was scattered over the face of the whole land. And far more were those whom the forest consumed from among the people than those whom the sword devoured in battle.

The Hebrews think that this forest, which is said to have consumed more than the sword devoured, contained extremely fierce beasts, by which more were consumed than were devoured by the sword.

### (Verse 18)

Now Absalom, while he was still alive, had erected for himself a monument in the king’s valley. For he had said: “I have no son, and this will be a memorial of my name.” He called the monument by his own name, and it is called Absalom’s Hand to this day.

This passage must be joined to the preceding one, where it is said (verse 14): “Joab took three spears in his hand and thrust them into Absalom’s heart while he was still hanging, quivering, from the oak.” The Hebrew has: “While he was still alive, hanging from the oak.” Here, too, the following should be joined: “Now Absalom, while he was still alive, had erected for himself a monument in the king’s valley,” and the rest that follows.

The Hebrews relate that, after being taken down from the oak, he asked for a delay before being killed, so that he might make a monument for himself in remembrance of him, since he had no son worthy of the kingdom. For he thought that his sons were not only unworthy of the kingdom but also, because of the sin he had committed against his father, unworthy of the present life.

In this monument he is said to have fixed a hand and impressed the shape of his own hand; for this reason the monument was called in this manner: “He called the monument by his own name, and it is called Absalom’s Hand to this day” (verse 17).

But where it is read: “And they threw him into the forest, into a great pit, and heaped over him a very great mound of stones,” the Hebrews say that he was thrown into the forest so that, after being killed by the sword, he might be covered with stones, since he was utterly wicked and liable to a double death: he had both gravely dishonored his father contrary to the commandment of the law and exposed his father’s shame.

### (Verse 20)

Joab—that is, Ahimaaz—said to him: “You shall not be a messenger on this day, but you shall carry the message on another day. Today I do not want you to report it. For the king’s son is dead.” As though he were saying: “I do not want a man such as you are to carry to the king the news that his son is dead. It is not fitting for you to bear such a message.”

Therefore he said to Cushite: “Go and report to the king what you have seen.” It should be noted that here *Cushite* is not a proper name but a common noun. As though he were saying: “You are worthy to carry the mournful message—not Ahimaaz.”

## (Chapter XIX—Verse 8)

And all the people came before the king; but Israel fled to its tents. The whole people who are recorded as having come before the king are those who had remained with David. But when it says, “Israel fled to its tents,” those are to be understood who had become rebels with Absalom.

### (Verse 24)

Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, also came down to meet the king with unwashed feet. It should be noted that the Hebrew does not say “with unwashed feet,” but “with artificial feet.” [Note: [Col. 1357] Rabanus has “with bent feet”; then he adds that, according to the Hebrews, Mephibosheth had wooden feet, etc.]

For this same Mephibosheth had made himself wooden feet, which he used as though they were natural ones, as the lame customarily do, and as he himself was.

### (Verse 29)

“Why do you speak any further? What I have said is fixed. You and Ziba shall divide the possessions.” In Hebrew it is read: “I have said: You and Ziba shall divide the field.”

Because David was forgetful in this matter of the friendship and covenant—or rather, the oath—that he had with Jonathan, and gave so cruel a judgment, saying, “You and Ziba shall divide the field,” Rehoboam and Jeroboam therefore divided his kingdom.

In the Book of Samuel, Mephibosheth is read as meaning “mouth of shame” [Al. “shameful mouth”]. In Chronicles the same Mephibosheth is called Meribaal, meaning [Note: [Col. 1359D] My manuscript has “one who litigates with the Most High.” “Litigated,” etc.] “one who litigates with the Most High.” He is said to have litigated with the Most High—that is, with God—because David brought him back in peace.

And when this same Mephibosheth says to the king, “Let him also take everything, after my lord the king has returned peacefully to his house” [Al. “my house”], this should not be understood as having been said in a spirit of gratitude, but of mockery and as though he were murmuring against God, because the Lord David had brought him back in peace.

### (Verse 37)

Your servant is Chamaam. In Hebrew: “Behold, your servant Chamaam; let him go with you, my lord the king.” *Chamaam* means “sighing.” As long as he remained with his father, he was called “Sighing.” After he entered the teaching of King David, he was called not Chamaam but Chamaan, which means [Col. 1359B] “faithful.”

### (Verse 41)

Then all the men of Israel came running to the king and said to him: “Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan, together with all David’s men?” Every man of Judah answered the men of Israel: “Because the king is nearer to me.”

There is an omission here, with the following understood: “and I love the king more than you.” A little later:

### (Verse 43)

The man of Israel answered the men of Judah and said: “I am greater by ten parts with the king, and David pertains more to me than to you.” In Hebrew it is read: “I have ten parts with the king, and I am more in David than you.”

The ten parts belonged to Israel—that is, the ten tribes. Therefore they say that they have more in David than the men of Judah.

“Why have you done me an injury?” The men of Israel complain that he injured them because the tribe of Judah did not wait for them to bring back the king.

“Was not my word first, that I should bring back my king?” His word was first concerning bringing back the king, as is shown earlier in the passage where it says: “The word of all Israel came to the king in his house,” with the following understood: “so that they might bring him back.”

David is also recorded to have given this command to the elders of Judah through Zadok and Abiathar the priests, saying: “Speak to the elders of Judah, saying: ‘Why are you the last?’” The Hebrew has: “Why are you the last in bringing back the king to his house?” And here the following should be added: “You are my brothers, you are my bone and my flesh; why are you the last to bring back the king?”

By these words it is to be understood that he commanded them because the word of all Israel had already reached him, saying: “The word of all Israel came to the king in his house.”

### (The same passage)

The men of Judah answered the men of Israel rather harshly. Here too there is an omission. The men of Judah are said to have answered the men of Israel because they were lying and had not done this out of love for the king, as they claimed.

## (Chapter XX—Verse 8)

Because of these words, Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite, blew the trumpet and said: “We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse.” He blew the trumpet so that they would be stunned by its sound and fall silent. When they were silent, he said: “We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse.”

### (Verse 18)

A saying is found in an ancient proverb: “Those who inquire should inquire in Abel, and thus they will complete [Al. ‘advance’].” In Hebrew the word “proverb” is not present.

This saying is a saying of the law, in which the Lord commands through Moses (Deut. 20) that, when they were about to enter the land of Canaan and destroy the nations, they should first offer peace. If peace were accepted by them, those who accepted it would become tributaries; if they did not accept peace, then they would be destroyed by the children of Israel. For this reason the wise woman from the city is said to have cried out.

[Col. 1360B] ### (Verse 19)

“Am I not one who answers truthfully in Israel? And you seek to overthrow the city? Why do you throw down the inheritance of the Lord?” As though she were saying: “Why do you wish to destroy this city before offering peace by questioning it, as the law commands? Why also do you not observe among us Israelites the same law that was once observed among foreigners?”

The Jews understand this woman to be Zarah, the daughter of Asher, son of Jacob. When she says that she is a mother, saying, “You seek to overthrow a mother in Israel,” she is called a mother because she was advanced in years.

### (Verse 26)

Ira the Jairite was David’s priest—that is, his teacher—just as it is written elsewhere: “The sons of David were priests,” that is, teachers of their brothers.

## (Chapter XXI—Verse 1)

And the Lord said: “Because of Saul and the house of blood, because he killed the Gibeonites.” The “house of blood” means Saul’s sons, who, together with Doeg the Edomite, while they were still boys, killed the priests and the Gibeonites at Nob.

### (Verse 8)

These are Armon and Mephibosheth, whom Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, bore to him, and the five sons of Michal, the daughter of Saul, whom she had borne to Adriel, the son of Barzillai, who was from Meholah.

It is asked why they are called the sons of Michal, when it was not Michal but her sister Merab who was the wife of Adriel, son of Barzillai. The matter is resolved as follows: Merab naturally gave birth to them, but Michal, David’s wife, who is also called Eglah, raised them in the place of sons and adopted them as her own sons. For this reason they are called her sons.

### (Verse 2)

For the children of Israel had sworn to them. And Saul wished to strike them out of zeal. He acted as though on behalf of the children of Israel and Judah, saying that Joshua had gratuitously allowed those same Gibeonites to live (Josh. 9 and 10), and that they had unjustly taken away their spoil from the children of Israel and Judah. Therefore he ordered them to be killed, ostensibly out of zeal for Israel and Judah.

The cause of this vengeance against the Gibeonites was the priest Ahimelech.

### (Verse 21)

Jonathan, son of Shimea, the brother of David, struck him. This Jonathan is the prophet Nathan.

### (Verse 19)

There was also a third battle at Gob against the Philistines. In it Adeodatus, son of the Forest, the Polymitarius, a Bethlehemite, struck Goliath the Gittite.

*Gob* means “pool.” It is called “pool” because, just as someone is thrown into a lions’ den, so David sent himself against Goliath.

Adeodatus is David himself. He is called Adeodatus—“given by God”—because he was chosen by God for the kingdom. “Son of the pasture” means that he was brought out of the pasture where he pastured sheep. “Polymitarius” means that his mother was descended from Bezalel. “Bethlehemite” refers to the fact that Naomi and Ruth returned to Bethlehem during the time of abundance. And because Ruth obtained bread from Boaz, that place was called “house of bread.”

That Adeodatus himself is David is made clear by what follows, where it says: “These four were born to Harapha in Gath, and they fell into the hands of David and his servants.”

## (Chapter XXIII—Verse 1)

The man to whom it was appointed concerning the Anointed One of the God of Jacob. In Hebrew: “To whom the ladder was appointed, to the Anointed One of the God of Jacob.”

A ladder was appointed for that same Anointed One of the God of Jacob—that is, David—by which he might ascend to God, because he confessed that he had sinned against the Lord in the matter of Uriah the Hittite and, doing penance, ascended to God by this ladder.

### (The same passage)

These are the last words of David. They are called “last” because, after the Psalter and the other meters, he is said to have composed this meter, in which he says: “David the son of Jesse said. The man to whom the ladder was appointed, to the Anointed One of the God of Jacob.”

### (Verse 13)

And three who were commanders among the thirty went down and came at harvest time to David in the cave of Adullam. [Note: [Col. 1361D] My manuscript has: “Three men went down, who,” etc.]

These three were Abishai, son of Zeruiah; Sibbecai the Hushathite; and Jonathan, son of Shimea, the brother of David. These three also broke into the camp of the Philistines and drew water from the well of Bethlehem. Of these three, Abishai was the first, as is made clear below.

### (Verse 18)

Abishai, the brother of Joab and son of Zeruiah, was also commander of these three, being named among those three; he was more distinguished than the three and their commander, but he did not attain to “the Three”—that is, to David’s three virtues: wisdom, humility, and strength.

As it says earlier (verse 8):

“Seated in the chair, most wise”—behold, wisdom.

“He is like the most tender worm of wood”—behold, humility.

“He killed eight hundred in a single charge”—behold, strength.

None of David’s mighty men attained to these three virtues.

Eleazar is therefore said to have been among the three mighty men who were with David because, in the battle in which David killed eight hundred in a single charge and Jonathan, son of Shammah, killed a man who had twenty-four fingers and toes, that same Eleazar struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary and stiffened around the sword.

### (Verse 20)

And Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, son of a very valiant man of great deeds, from Kabzeel. It should be noted that the Hebrew does not have “of great deeds,” but “master of deeds.” [Col. 1362A]

*Kabzeel* means “assembly of God.” He was the master of the assembly of God—that is, of the Cherethites and Pelethites, whose names mean “killing” and “giving life.”

He struck the two lions of Moab—that is, two exceedingly mighty men of Moab. When David attacked those same Moabites in battle and made three measuring lines, two for putting to death and one for preserving alive, these powerful men were defending the Moabites.

He also went down and struck the lion in the middle of the cistern, on a snowy day. This lion was Joab. “In the middle of the cistern” means in the house of the Lord, where he was holding the altar’s horn. It is called a cistern because, just as the water of a cistern brings cleansing, so also this cistern—that is, the sanctuary of the Lord—expiated sins.

“On a snowy day” means that he expiated sin through death, according to the Psalmist: “You shall wash me” (Ps. 50), which was fulfilled by “in the middle of the cistern”; and “I shall be made whiter than snow,” which was fulfilled in the words “on a snowy day.”

### (Verse 21)

He also killed an Egyptian man, [Note: [Col. 1361D] My manuscript repeats “man” in agreement with the Vulgate translator.] a man worthy of spectacle.

This Egyptian man was Shimei, son of Gera, who cursed David. It should be known that this same Shimei was from Bahurim, that is, from “the chosen.” He is called an Egyptian because he imitated the deeds of that Egyptian who blasphemed God and whom Moses killed in the wilderness at the Lord’s command (Lev. 24). The Egyptian blasphemed God, while this man cursed the prophet and king.

“Worthy of spectacle” means “worthy of death.” It was expected that, if he went out from Jerusalem, he would be killed.

He had a spear in his hand—that is, the law of God. If he had meditated upon it by remaining in Jerusalem, he would not have been killed. Because, by going outside Jerusalem, he made void the king’s command [Note: [Col. 1362D] My manuscript has “the command of King Abagana,” that is, “made void,” etc.], Benaiah therefore descended upon him with a staff—that is, with the uprightness of justice—and the spear that he was not holding upright was forcibly wrested from him.

“And he killed him with his own spear.” He was killed by his own spear because, by failing to keep the law, he was killed by the law’s judgment. For in the law it is written: “You shall not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of your people” (Exod. 22:28).

### (Verse 21)

Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, did these things. He was also named among the three mighty men who were more distinguished than the thirty.

It is understood that he deserved to be named among the three mighty men—Abishai, Sibbecai, and Jonathan—since he could equal them in strength. These three were also above the thirty.

And no one should be troubled by the fact that in the total they are read as thirty-seven, not thirty. There are thirty-seven in this way: seven who were stronger, namely David, who is called Adeodatus; Abishai; Sibbecai; Jonathan; Eleazar; Shammah, son of Agee the Hararite; and Benaiah—there are the seven.

The thirty are: Asahel, Elhanan, Shammah of Harod, Elika, Helez, Ira, Abiezer, Mebunnai, Zalmon, Maharai, Heleb, Benaiah the Pirathonite, Iddai, Hidai, Abi-albon, [Col. 1363A] Azmaveth, Eliahba, Shammah of Harar, Eliah, Eliphelet, Eliam, Hezrai, Paarai, Igal, Bani, Zelek, Naharai, Ira, Gareb, and Uriah the Hittite.

Uriah the Hittite is placed last because of what follows.

## (Chapter XXIV—Verse 1)

And the anger of the Lord continued to burn against Israel. Vengeance had already been carried out against David and his house. But against the people [Al. “in the battle,” here and below], who had not resisted David when he killed Uriah the Hittite, divine vengeance had not yet been carried out. Therefore Uriah is placed last here, so that the vengeance for his death might be shown in the people. Concerning this people David is recorded to say later: “Let your hand, I pray, be against me and against my father’s house.”

### (Verse 9)

And there were found in Israel eight hundred thousand fighting men who drew the sword, and in Judah five hundred thousand warriors. In Hebrew it reads: “Men.” [Col. 1364A] In Chronicles, however, it reads: “A thousand thousand and one hundred thousand from Israel, and from Judah four hundred seventy thousand” (1 Chron. 21:5).

It should be understood that Joab counted them, but that David did not wish to disclose their total except to the extent that it is written in the Book of Samuel.

### (Verse 15)

And the Lord sent a pestilence upon Israel from morning until the appointed time. The “appointed time” is said to be the time when the evening sacrifice was offered.

### (Verse 24)

So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty silver shekels. The same is read in Chronicles: “David gave Ornan six hundred shekels of gold of the purest weight for the place” (1 Chron. 21:25).

It should be understood that he bought the oxen for fifty silver shekels, [Col. 1364B] but the threshing floor for six hundred gold pieces.

[Note: [Col. 1363D] My manuscript supplies the heading.]

# On the Third Book of Kings

[Col. 1363]

[Col. 1363B] ## (Chapter I—Verse 6)

Now Adonijah was very handsome, second in age after Absalom. It should be noted that in Hebrew it is read as follows: “And she bore him after Absalom,” with “sin” understood.

### (Verse 8)

But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David’s very mighty men were not with Adonijah.

Shimei is the same as Nabat, the father of Jeroboam, who was Solomon’s teacher and was from Bahurim, that is, from “the chosen.”

Rei, however, is Hiram the Zairite, the priest—that is, the teacher—of David. David’s “very mighty men,” mentioned above, are understood to mean his strongest men.

### (Verse 17)

“Was it not you, my lord the king, who swore to your servant-girl, saying: ‘Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne’?” David is said to have sworn this when he comforted her after the death of her son, as it is written in the Book of Samuel: “And David comforted Bathsheba his wife.”

### (Verse 21)

“And it shall be, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, that I and Solomon my son shall be sinners”—that is, *mamzerim*, illegitimate children.

[Note: [Col. 1363D–1364D] Previously, *ergo* (“therefore”) stood incorrectly, and contrary to the authority of the sacred text, in place of *ego* (“I”). The Ambrosian manuscript also prefixes the particle *quoque*: “and I too.”]

Solomon subsequently says that God showed mercy to David on this account: namely, because he made the son who, according to the Law, was a *mamzer* his successor. For he says:

“You have shown great mercy to your servant David, my father, and have given him a son sitting upon his throne, as it is today.”

[Col. 1363D: My manuscript inserts “my father”; Ambrosianus does likewise.]

### (Verse 33)

“Take with you the servants of your lord, and set my son Solomon upon my mule.”

Here he calls the Cherethites and Pelethites “servants”: that is, the seventy elders who were judges.

## Into the Second Book of Kings

### (Chapter II, verse 8)

“You also have with you Shimei the son of Gera, the son of Jemini, from Bahurim, who cursed me with a very evil curse.”

“Very evil” is called in Hebrew *NIMREZETH* [Hebrew term omitted in the manuscript], a word pronounced with five letters: *nun, mem, resh, sade,* and *taw*. With *nun*: *NOEPH*, that is, “adulterer”; with *mem*: “Moabite”; with *resh*: *RASA*, that is, “impious”; with *sade*: *ZARUA*, that is, “leprous”; with *taw*: *THEEBA*, that is, “abominable.”

“And I swore to him by God, saying: ‘I shall not kill you with the sword—but with the tongue.’”

### (Verse 22)

“Ask the kingdom for him. For he is my elder brother, and he has Abiathar the priest and Joab the son of Zeruiah.”

In Hebrew it reads: “And to Abiathar the priest, and to Joab the son of Zeruiah.” This is to be understood as follows: “Ask for him”—that is, for Adonijah—the kingdom, and also for Abiathar the priest and Joab the son of Zeruiah.

[Col. 1364D: The word *habet* (“has”) is absent from the Ambrosian manuscript, nor does the Hebrew read in that way; rather, it has “and to him,” with “is” to be supplied.]

### (Verse 24)

“ As the Lord lives, who established a house for me, as he spoke”—that is, as David promised, he made me king of the house of David.

## Second Chapter, verse 5

[Note: Martianus had postponed the explanations of this verse and the following one from corrupt manuscripts to the end of the book; he himself complains about this displacement. My manuscript restores both to their proper places, although in it the final section, beginning with the words “namely, before,” and so forth, is missing. The Ambrosian manuscript differs from mine in this one respect: it places the explanation from “A messenger came to Joab” through “after Adonijah” before the explanation “whom he killed and shed blood.” In the former verse the words “namely, before Adonijah had sought the kingdom” and everything through the end are likewise absent.]

“Whom he killed, and shed the blood of war in peace; and he placed the blood upon his belt,” and so forth.

He is said to have shed the blood of war because, while there was peace, he stirred up war.

### (Verse 28)

“And a messenger came to Joab that he had turned after Adonijah and had not turned after Solomon.”

That is, report came to him that it was being said in Solomon’s household that Joab had not followed Solomon but had turned after Adonijah: namely, that before Adonijah sought the kingdom, Joab had not loved Solomon or favored him, but was said to have turned away from him. The outcome of the matter proved all this.

### (Verse 34)

“And Joab was buried in his house in the wilderness.”

Here “wilderness” is used for purity. For his house had been clean, like the wilderness, from every pollution and bloodshed, except for the blood of Abner and Amasa.

## Third Chapter, verse 3

“Solomon loved the Lord, walking in the commandments of David his father, except that he sacrificed in the high places.”

This makes clear that Solomon delayed four years in building the house of the Lord, because when it says that he sacrificed in the high places, that highest place is meant—namely, the altar that Moses had made.

## Fourth Chapter, verse 5

“And there was one prefect over the land.”

This prefect was Azariah the son of Nathan, concerning whom it is written above: “And Azariah the son of Nathan was over the prefects”—not “over the works,” but simply “over the prefects.”

[Col. 1365D: My manuscript does not recognize the words “not over the works, but simply.”]

### (Verse 31)

“And he was wiser than all men: wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol.”

For Ethan is interpreted as “very hard.” *Ezrahite* means “eastern.” This Ethan is Abraham the eastern. Heman, interpreted as “faithful,” is Moses. Chalcol, interpreted as “governing,” is Joseph. Darda is interpreted as “generation of knowledge.” *Mahol* means “indulgence.” The “generation of knowledge” is understood as the twelve tribes: the sons of Mahol, that is, the sons of Jacob.

### (Verse 32)

“Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs.”

For in Proverbs there are nine hundred and fifteen verses, within which the three thousand proverbs are also contained.

“And his songs were five thousand. And he discoursed about trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He also discussed beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish.”

He discussed the properties of trees, animals, reptiles, and fish—namely, their powers and natures, the season in which they are born, and why not all of them are born in every land.

[Note: From this passage it is most clearly proved that the author of the *Hebrew Questions on the Books of Kings* wrote after the Masoretes. For the Masoretes wished Solomon’s Proverbs to be divided into nine hundred and fifteen verses.]

## Sixth Chapter, verse 37

“In the fourth year the house of the Lord was founded, in the month of Ziv.”

This month is April, which is also called Var.

[Note: In Ambrosianus it is also called Jajar and Jiar.]

For *Ziv* is interpreted as “face.” It is called “face” because, at the dedication of the Temple, the cloud of the glory of the Lord’s face covered the Temple.

*Var* is interpreted as “fear.” It is called “fear” because there is apprehension that, in this month, the unseasonable condition of the air may render unfruitful the crops that the earth ought to produce.

## Seventh Chapter, verse 13

“King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre, the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, whose father was a Tyrian, a craftsman in bronze.”

Accordingly, it is also written in Chronicles:

“I have therefore sent you a wise and most learned man, Huram my father, the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan, whose father was a Tyrian” (II Chronicles 2:13).

It should be noted that in *Malachim* he is called Hiram, whereas in Chronicles he is called Huram. Hiram is interpreted as “the exalted one lives”; Huram as “God is exalted.”

In *Malachim* Hiram is said to have been from Tyre, the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, with a Tyrian father. It must be understood that his father was from the tribe of Naphtali and that, after his death, his wife—who is here called a widow—sent this same Hiram to Tyre to be taught. The man by whom he was taught at Tyre is called his Tyrian father. Thus he is said to have had a Tyrian father, even though his actual father was from the tribe of Naphtali.

But when in Chronicles King Huram is said to have stated, “I have sent you the wisest and most learned man, Huram my father,” he calls him “father” as a title of honor, as is read in many passages.

He calls him “the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan” because his mother was from the tribe of Dan, from the family of Shelomith, the sister of Oholiab the son of Ahisamach. Her Egyptian son was stoned in the wilderness. For that Shelomith did not willingly unite herself with the Egyptian, but suffered violence at his hands.

Therefore it is said to have happened through her merits that such a man was born from her daughters, one who would work in the house of the Lord. They likewise hold that through the merits of Bilhah, Jacob’s concubine, it once came about that, after Rachel’s death, she not only raised Joseph in the place of a son but also interceded for his brothers, so that he might forget the injury done by his brothers.

For this reason the Lord granted her that from one of her sons, Dan, Oholiab should be born, the companion of Bezalel, who would build the house of the Lord; and from her other son, Naphtali, Hiram should be born, who would construct the house of the Lord in Jerusalem.

[Note: Martianus has: “Here begin the Hebrew Questions on the first part of the Book of Dabrejamin, or Chronicles.” To this title he appends the following note: “I copy this title of the book from my manuscript, which further adds the following in red: ‘If you wish, hold to the order of the history; I attach the alphabet opposite it; rely naturally upon the rubric.’ Previously the printed editions had: ‘Hebrew Questions on the Books of Chronicles.’ But Jerome himself stated in the Preface to this book, addressed to Domnio and Rogatianus, according to the Septuagint: ‘This must first be known: among the Hebrews the book of Chronicles is one book, and among them it is called *Dabre jamin*, that is, “words of days.” Because of its size it has been divided among us—just as some also do with Cicero’s dialogue *Brutus*, cutting it into three parts, although it was published as one work by its author.’ Thus the author of these Questions divides it into two parts—not books.” EDITOR.]

# Into the First Book of Chronicles

## First Chapter, verse 19

“Two sons were born to Eber; the name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided.”

For in his days the tower was made, at which the confusion of languages took place.

[Col. 1365: My manuscript begins thus: “In the days of Eber the earth was divided, because in his days…”]

### (Verse 30)

“Nimrod began to be on the earth”—that is, he began to be powerful.

### (Verse 32)

Keturah is Hagar. This is made clear in the Psalm, where it says: “The tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites” (Psalm 82:7).

It calls the sons of Ishmael “Ishmaelites,” since Ishmael was certainly the son of Hagar; and it calls the Midianites and the other tribes “Hagrites,” since Scripture records that they were descended from Keturah.

### (Verse 36)

Zephi, the son of Eliphaz, is called in Genesis Zepho, that is, “watcher”; in Chronicles, Zephi, that is, “watched.” Both are written with the letter *sade*.

Sephi, the son of Shobal, means in Chronicles “one-footed.” Sepho in Genesis means “two-footed”; both, however, are written with the letter *sin*.

Thamna, the concubine of Eliphaz (Genesis 36:12), the mother of Amalek, was of the race of the Horites, who lived in the land of Seir before the Edomites. But in Chronicles she is counted among the sons of Eliphaz. Although she was his concubine and bore Amalek by him, he raised her as a daughter.

### (Verse 39)

Heman, the son of Lotan, means in Genesis “one who troubles”; in Chronicles he is written as Homam, that is, “troubled.”

### (Verse 40)

The son of Shobal was Alian, of the race of the Horites. In Genesis he is written as Alvan, that is, “exalted”; in Chronicles, Alian, that is, “cast out” [manuscript: “thrown down”]. The Horites were exalted before Edom took possession of that land; after they were defeated by him, they were cast out and lost their homeland.

### (Verse 41)

“Hemran, the son of Dishon, the son of Anah.”

In Chronicles, Hemran means “reddened,” “filthy,” or “drunken”; in Genesis, Amdan means “desirable.” Hemran and Amdan are the name of one man [variant: “are the names of one man”].

### (Verse 42)

Alchan, the son of Ezer, was of the race of the Horites. In Genesis he is “one who troubles”; in Chronicles, Jachan, that is, “troubled.”

### (Verse 5)

Phou, that is, “one who belches,” is written in Genesis as Phau, that is, “those who belch”; in Chronicles, Phou, “one who belches.”

His wife was called Mehetabel, which is interpreted as “the Lord’s kindness”; she was the daughter of Matred, that is, “of the steward” [variant: “of the stewardess”], and of Mezaab [manuscripts: Emazaab], the daughter of an engraver of gold. She is described as having two fathers in order to signify a mystery through the single interpretation of the names: so that the goldsmith might beget the steward, and the steward might beget the kindness of the Lord.

### (Verse 52)

Alvah in Genesis is interpreted as “elevation”; in Chronicles, Aleiah, “upon her.”

It should be noted that he first speaks of kings from Edom and afterward of chiefs, although they were chiefs first and kings afterward. Here he names some of the mothers of those chiefs—that is, the wives of Esau—including Oholibamah, Esau’s wife, and Thamna, the concubine of Eliphaz.

## Second Chapter, verse 7

Achan the son of Carmi is called in Joshua Achan, that is, “a serpent lying in wait”; in Chronicles, Achar, that is, “troubler.”

### (Verse 8)

[Note: There are many disturbances of the text and corruptions of names in the previously printed books, and it would be too long and laborious to list them individually. Whoever wishes may compare our edition with the older ones and will confirm that I speak the truth.]

Calebai, or Chalubi, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, is the same as Caleb the son of Jephunneh.

Caleb was a Kenizzite, from the place called Kenaz. He took Azubah as his wife, and by her Gerioth was born. He also took another wife named Ephrath, by whom he fathered Hur, the husband of Miriam, the sister of Moses, and the father of Uri, the grandfather of Bezalel.

In Chronicles he is called Chlubai, “my dog.”

[Note: The words “a Kenizzite, from the place called Kenaz,” which had been dislocated in the Vulgate and placed after Bezalel, have here been restored in accordance with the manuscript.]

In Joshua and in the Pentateuch [perhaps: “Hexateuch”], Caleb means “dog.” Hezron and Jephunneh are one person.

When Hezron had died, Caleb went in to Ephrath. Therefore Caleb is called Ephrath, because Caleb was Ephrath’s husband.

Hezron is said to have been sixty years old when he took as wife the daughter of Machir, in order to show by the number of years both that he had come out of Egypt and that he had entered the promised land. For those from twenty years of age onward were reckoned for war up to their sixtieth year. From the age of sixty, both the Levites ceased to minister and the soldiers ceased to fight. Hence the Romans also call those *emeriti* who have ceased to serve as soldiers.

### (Verse 11)

“Naashon begot Salma.”

In Chronicles: Salma, that is, “peace.” In Ruth: Salmon, that is, “peaceful.”

### (Verse 12)

In Chronicles: “Jesse, the son of Obed,” that is, “my sacrifice.”

In Kings: Jesse, that is, “sacrifice”; “the son of Jesse, Abinadab; the son of Ram, Amminadab.”

### (Verse 13)

In Chronicles: Simmaa. In Kings: Shammah.

Shammah means “hear”; Simmaa, “one who is heard.”

### (Verse 16)

In Chronicles: Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, that is, “father of sacrifice.”

In Kings: Abishai, “my father is sacrifice.”

### (Verse 32)

In Chronicles: “The son of Jether the Ishmaelite.”

In Kings: “The son of Jethra the Ishmaelite.”

Jethra means “remainder”; Jether, “a small remainder.” He is called “the son of the Ishmaelite” because of the quality of his merits.

### (Verse 34)

Aalai, the son of Sheshan, is the same as Elimelech, the father of Mahlon and Chilion.

Sheshan is said not to have had sons because these men died without children.

### (Verse 41)

“Ichamiah begot Elishama.”

In Jeremiah: “Ishmael, the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of royal descent.”

[Note: My manuscript has “of the family of Jeraa the Egyptian” instead of “of royal descent.”]

When it says that he was of royal seed, it wishes Moloch, the idol of Moab, to be understood; for in Hebrew *melech* means “king.”

### (Verse 42)

Ziph is the name of a place from which the Ziphites came, who went to Saul.

### (Verse 46)

Gazez, that is, “shearer,” was the son of Haran, the son of Caleb. He is the same as Nabal the Carmelite.

### (Verse 50)

Ephrath: because he was from Ephraim. Bethlehem is called Ephrath after his name.

### (Verse 22)

[Note: The writer frequently moves backward in these *Hebrew Questions*, resuming earlier verses after the lower verses in his explanation, as here with verse 22 and the following verses after verse 50.]

Jair, the judge who is mentioned in Judges, was the son of Segub, the son of Hezron.

He is considered a Gileadite because Hezron took as wife the daughter of Machir, the father of Gilead.

Jair received sixty villages and cities as an inheritance because his grandmother was the daughter of Machir, the son of Manasseh.

### (Verse 24)

Ashhur, the son of Hezron, was the father of Tekoa.

Tekoa is the city from which Joab obtained the wise woman.

### (Verse 26)

Onam, the son of Jerahmeel, the son of Hezron, received the name of Onam, the son of Judah, who died.

They differ in this respect: the son of Judah is written in Hebrew with *nun*, whereas the son of Jerahmeel is written with *mem*.

### (Verse 42)

Maresha was the father of Hebron.

Hebron is the place where David reigned for seven years.

### (Verse 43)

The sons of Hebron were Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema. They were the sons of Mareshah.

### (Verse 44)

Shema begot Raham, the father of Jorkeam.

Jorkeam is the name of a place.

### (Verse 45)

Maon, the son of Shammai, was the father of Beth-zur.

Beth-zur is the name of a place, and from the same Maon the place received its name. In Kings it is written Maon.

### (Verse 49)

Saab, the son of Jaddai, was the father of Madmannah.

Madmannah is the name of a place.

Shuah was the father of Machbenah. Machbenah is the name of a place, and these were the sons of Caleb.

He was also the father of Gibeah, that is, the place from which Saul came.

[Note: My manuscript reads Machbenah first and Madmannah second, in the reverse order; it has Dai instead of Shuah.]

### (Verses 50–51)

“The sons of Hur: Shobal, the father of Kiriath-jearim, and Salma, the father of Bethlehem. Hariph, the father of Beth-gader.”

Kiriath-jearim, Bethlehem, and Beth-gader are names of places.

Kiriath-jearim is the same as Kiriath-arba, Kiriath-baal, and Hebron, which is called Kiriath-jearim, that is, “city of forests.”

Kiriath-baal means “city of the husband”; Kiriath-arba, “city of four.” All these names can be interpreted in relation to the Patriarchs who were buried there.

[Note: The manuscript adds: “From this point through the following letter the correct order proceeds.” No such letters, however, are written in the margin of the book.]

### (Verses 52–53)

Shobal, the father of Kiriath-jearim, saw half of the resting-places because of the proximity of the Patriarchs’ tomb.

His sons were the Jetherites, the Puthites, the Shemathites, and the Maserites. From these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites, who took their names from places—namely, Zorah and Eshtaol, where Samson was buried.

“Resting-place” is understood to mean a tomb.

### (Verse 54)

The sons of Salma, the sons of Hur, were Bethlehem and the Netophathites, who are written in the Books of Kings as Elhanan, the son of his paternal uncle, from Bethlehem, and Eleb, the son of Baana, the Netophathite.

They are called the “crowns of the house of Jacob” because of the association by which Sarai—that is, the Zorathites—used to fight alongside one another. This has been discussed above.

### (Verse 55)

Jabez, the son of Shobab, concerning whom it is written later that the Lord heard him, was a teacher. The sons of the Kenite, who was also Hobab, a kinsman of Moses, sat in his presence; in this book they are called scribes.

They are called “singing and resounding” because they were continually occupied with the Law of God and the Prophets.

The history of Kings also records that they lived in tents. “These came from the heat of the father of the house of Rechab” (I Chronicles 3:1), that is, from the stock of Rechab.

### (Same passage)

“Ahinoam, David’s wife, the Jezreelitess.”

Jezreel is the place in which Naboth lived.

In Chronicles: Daniel. In Kings: Chileab, that is, “vindicating his father.” For, when disputing with Mephibosheth on questions of the Law, he appeared victorious and seemed to avenge his father.

### (Verse 3)

“Jetheram, the son of David by his wife Eglah.”

Eglah is interpreted as “heifer.” Some think that she was Michal, the daughter of Saul.

### (Verse 5)

In Chronicles: Simmaa, the son of David, who in Kings is called Shammah.

Simmaa means “hear”; Shammah, “heard.”

Bathshua was the mother of Solomon. In Chronicles she is said to be the daughter of Ammiel, and her name is interpreted as “her name”; Bathshua means “daughter of supplication.”

In Kings she is Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the son of Ahithophel. Her name is interpreted as “daughter of seven,” “daughter of satiety,” or “daughter of an oath.”

Eliam means “my God is the people”; Ammiel, “my people is God.”

### (Verse 6)

In Chronicles two sons of David are recorded, Nogah and Eliphelet, who are not found in Kings.

### (Verse 15)

“The sons of Josiah were Shallum, Joanan, and Jehoiakim.”

Shallum is the one whom Necho, king of Egypt, took captive to Egypt. Hence Jeremiah makes mention of him:

“For thus says the Lord concerning Shallum, the son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father: ‘He shall not return here again, having departed from this place’” (Jeremiah 22).

[Note: According to the manuscript, Joanan and Joahaz are one person, whom King Necho…]

### (Verse 26)

Jehoiakim, who is also Eliakim, is the same Jehoiakim who was led to Babylon with the vessels of the Lord’s Temple, together with Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael.

His son Jehoiachin, who is also Jeconiah, was taken captive to Babylon with the remaining vessels of the Lord’s house, together with Ezekiel and Mordecai. In his place Mattaniah, who is also Zedekiah, was installed.

[Note: The manuscript does not have the word “captive”; instead it adds: “who was also taken, Hananiah…”]

### (Verse 17)

“The sons of Jeconiah: Assir, Salathiel”—one name.

He is Phadaiah, the father of Zerubbabel.

Phadaiah is interpreted as “redeemed by the Lord”; Assir, “imprisoned”; Salathiel, “the Lord’s shrub.”

Shenazzar, the son of Jeconiah, is called Sheshbazzar in Ezra.

Shenazzar means “blasphemed”; Sheshbazzar means “troubled.”

Sheshbazzar is the one to whom Cyrus entrusted the vessels of the Lord’s house.

### (Verse 22)

Shecaniah had one son, Shemaiah, who had five sons: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat.

Together with his father Shemaiah, who was his father’s only son, they are counted as six.

## Fourth Chapter, verse 1

The five sons of Judah have already been named above under other names. Here, however, the names are changed when they are repeated for the sake of interpretation.

Perez is interpreted as “division”; Hezron as “courtyard”; Zerah as “rising.”

Carmi is the same as Er. Carmi means “my vineyard”; Er, “watchful.”

Hur is also Onan. Hur means “window”; Onan, “murmuring.”

Shobal is the same as Shelah.

### (Verse 2)

Shobal begot Reaiah, and Reaiah begot Jahath; Jahath begot Ahumai and Lahad; Lahad begot Etham; Etham begot Jezreel, from whom the city where Naboth lived received its name.

Shobal himself begot Reaiah, who is also called Er under another name, because Er and Onan died in their sin.

Shobal means “ear of grain”; Shelah, “sent.”

The fact that they are first named by one set of names and afterward by another belongs to the mystery.

### (Verse 4)

Penuel, the father of Gedor, and Ezer, the father of Hushah, were sons of Hur, the brothers of Hur, the son of Miriam.

Gedor and Hushah are names of places.

### (Verses 7–8)

Ashhur begot Ethan, and the name of his mother was Halah. Ethan begot Koz; Koz begot Shobebah; Shobebah begot Jabez, who was a teacher, as was stated above.

The reason that between Koz and Jabez the kindred of Aharhel, the son of Harum, are introduced is this: Aharhel is the same as Hobab, who is interpreted as “after the army.” The son of Harum is Jethro. Harum means “exalted.”

Since Jabez taught those who lived in tents, as was stated above, they are therefore introduced into his genealogy, as though they had been begotten by his ancestors.

Some maintain that this Jabez is still alive, because of the statement: “God granted him what he had asked” (verse 10).

### (Verse 11)

Caleb, the brother of Shuah, is the same as Ram.

Ram means “exalted”; Shuah, “lofty” [variant: “humble”].

Caleb begot Machir; Machir begot Eshton; Eshton begot Tehinnah.

When it says that he was the father of the city of Naash, this may be understood either as Bethlehem or as the mother of Jesse, because Jesse is called Naash elsewhere—that is, “serpent.”

Abigail was David’s sister, the daughter of Naash, that is, Jesse, who was called by both names.

Jether the Ishmaelite had as wife Abigail, the daughter of Naash.

When it says, “These are the sons of Rechah” (verse 12), Rechah means “tender.” Some wish David to be understood here. For he himself says: “I am tender and anointed king” (II Samuel 3:39), and elsewhere: “Like a tender little worm of wood.”

Therefore they are called “the men of Rechah,” that is, of David, because they are noted in this statement in order to set forth David’s genealogy.

[Manuscript: “These are the men of Rechah.”]

### (Verse 13)

Kenaz begot Othniel and Seraiah.

Joab is said to have come from Seraiah. He is therefore called “the father of the valley of craftsmen,” because architects who built the house of the Lord came from his sons.

### (Verse 17)

The sons of Ezra were Jether and Mered, Epher and Jalon.

Ezra means “help.” They say that this is Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron.

Jether means “remainder”; he is Aaron.

Mered means “rebelling”; he is Moses.

Epher means “dust”; he is Eldad.

Jalon means “law”; he is Medad—the same two men who prophesied.

For it is handed down that after Moses received the Law in the wilderness, he ordered his father to send away his mother because she was his aunt, since she was the daughter of Levi. After this separation, Amram took another wife, by whom he fathered these two sons, Eldad and Medad.

The text continues: “And he begot Miriam and Samai, and Jesba, the father of Eshtemoa.”

They wish Samai to be understood as Moses, whose name means “heavenly”; Jesba as Aaron, whose name means “praise”;” and the father of Eshtemoa—that is, “remaining fire”—because Aaron’s sons used fire in their continual sacrifices.

The text then says: “His wife Indaia begot Jared.”

Indaia is the same as Jochebed, the mother of Moses.

[Note: The ancient Hebrews, including the author of *Vaikra* and, following him, Rabbi Gedaliah in the *Shalshelet*, state that Moses had ten names. They differ somewhat from these accounts both in the writing of the names themselves and in the presentation of their etymologies. They write Schemaiah instead of Shammai; Jether instead of Jedor; Chaber instead of Heber; Jekuthiel instead of Icuthiel; Abi Zannach and Abi Socho instead of “father of Sanoha” and “father of Socho.” They also add Ben Nathanael, that is, “son of Nathanael,” and Tobiah, and [Hebrew term omitted], which means “scribe.”]

They wish nearly all the names that follow to be understood as names of Moses, because he is called Jared, that is, “descending,” since he descended from the mountain.

He is called the father of Jedor, that is, “of fences,” because he enclosed the people with the Law as with a fence.

He is called Heber, “one who joins,” because he joined the people to the service of God.

He is called the father of Socho, that is, “of prophecy,” because he was the teacher of the prophets.

He is called Icuthiel, that is, “hoping in God,” because he hoped to free the people from Egypt, or because, through the hope of his parents, he was rescued from the danger of the water.

He is called the father of Sanoha, which means “governor,” because he provided great governance for the people in the wilderness, or because by his teaching he governed them daily.

### (Verse 18)

The text continues:

“These were the sons of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took.”

Here it calls Pharaoh’s daughter the mother of Moses and interprets her name as “daughter of the Lord,” because of the good will she showed in raising the child. She is said to have been taken by Mered, that is, by Moses, because, abandoning the worship of idols, she turned to the worship of God.

### (Verse 19)

Carmi was the father of Keilah and Eshtemoa, who was from Machathi.

Keilah is the name of a place, and Machathi likewise.

### (Verse 20)

Simon was the father of Amnon and Rinnah; he was the son of Eshtemoa, the son of Hodai, the son of Asriel, the son of Jehallelel, the son of Kenaz, the son of Shelah, the son of Judah.

### (Verses 21–23)

“And the father of Lecha.”

This is placed here to preserve the memory of the former name.

The clans of the house of those who worked in fine linen in the House of the Oath are those who lived with Bezalel to complete the work of the Tabernacle.

It is called the House of the Oath, just as it is called the Tabernacle of the Covenant, because in it was the covenant of God that he made with human beings, and the oath that he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

The text that follows—“who caused the sun to stand still”—returns to the genealogy of Perez, from whom David arose, since it judged it fitting to bring the genealogy of Judah, from which the royal tribe arose, to an end in David.

The Hebrews transmit that this man was Elimelech, the husband of Naomi and the father of Mahlon and Chilion. In his time the sun stood still because of the transgressors of the Law [manuscript: “transgressions of the Law”], so that, after witnessing so great a miracle, they might be converted to the Lord their God.

But because they refused to do this, famine prevailed, so that the man who seemed foremost in the tribe of Judah was driven not only from his homeland by the scarcity of food, together with his wife and sons, but also died with his sons during that same exile.

Mahlon and Chilion are called men of falsehood. Here they are called “the secure one” and “the one who walks” [manuscript: “the one who intercedes”], and it is said that they were princes in Moab because they took Moabite wives.

In Hebrew the expression is set forth more clearly, and we learned it from the learned men of that language: they are called not “princes” but “husbands.”

[Note: From this passage Erasmus incorrectly infers that the author of this little work almost admits that he did not know Hebrew. In obscure Scriptural expressions, experts deliberately consult those more expert; this is not attributable to ignorance but to prudence and more mature judgment.]

[Note: A prudent reader may instead concede the point to Erasmus. See what we have said about this in the Preface.]

The phrase that follows, “who returned to Lehem,” refers to Naomi and Ruth. After the famine, when they heard of the abundance of bread, they returned to Lehem—that is, “bread”—in Bethlehem.

Because this history is written in the Book of Ruth (Ruth 1:4), the text continues: “These are ancient words.”

He calls potters those dwelling in plantations and hedges—the descendants who came from Ruth. They are said to have lived in hedges and plantations when this planting reached royal dignity.

“They lived there,” that is, in Bethlehem, with the king and in his works, because King David arose from them, whose deeds are celebrated with wondrous praises.

### (Verses 24, 31, and 32)

Six sons of Simeon are described in Genesis. Here the sixth is removed because no descendants proceeded from him.

Some names are changed according to their meanings.

In Genesis it is written Jemuel: Jemuel, “sea of God.” In Chronicles, Namuel: Namuel, “speaking with God.”

Another is called Ohad in Genesis; in Chronicles, Jarib.

Ohad means “praise”; Jarib, “quarreling.” From his descendants came Zimri, who sinned with the Midianite prostitute and was killed by Phinehas.

Jachin in Genesis means “preparation”; in Chronicles, Zerah, “rising.”

Saul, whom both books mention by the same name, is here not said to be the son of a Canaanite woman; rather, through the proximity of his brother’s name, Zerah, which means “rising,” he is adorned.

When it says, “These were their cities until the reign of David,” it wishes this to be understood: Ziklag and Beersheba, which belonged to the tribe of Judah and had been seized by the tribe of Simeon, were restored by David to their former inheritance in Judah.

Ain-rimmon is the name of a single village, interpreted as “fountain of pomegranates.”

### (Verse 33)

“And all their villages surrounding these cities as far as Baal.”

In this passage Baal is the same place that elsewhere is written Kiriath-baal, concerning which we have spoken above.

It should be noted concerning the remnant of Amalek: Beera, the son of Baal, was from the tribe of Reuben; he is the father of Hosea the prophet.

It should also be noted that Keturah is the same as Hagar.

## Fifth Chapter, verse 19

When it says that the Reubenites, Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh fought against the Hagrites, it goes on to say that they were given assistance:

“The Ituraeans, the Naphishites, and Nodab,” who were certainly sons of Ishmael.

In Chronicles the same man is called Nodab; in Genesis, Kedemah.

Kedemah means “of ancient things”; Nodab, “womb.”

For it was the Lord’s war, because the Lord fought with them.

### (Verse 26)

Tiglath-pileser carried away Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh and brought them to Halah, Habor, and Hara. Hara is the same as Rages.

In *Malachim*, Hara is omitted.

## Sixth Chapter, verse 15

Jehozadak the priest is the same as Ezra.

The Book of Ezra itself demonstrates this, where it says: “After these words, during the reign of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians: Ezra, the son of Seraiah, the son of Azariah.”

But in his own book he omits himself out of humility.

When it says that Johanan begot Azariah, this is the Azariah who served as priest in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem. It shows that this same Azariah resisted King Uzziah when he entered the Temple of the Lord with a censer and a great earthquake occurred.

They also transmit that this same Ezra was the prophet Malachi, who is the last of the Twelve Prophets.

His son was Jesus the high priest, whom the prophet Zechariah mentions.

It should certainly be understood that the frequent appellations of persons, changes of names, and repetitions belong to a great mystery.

[Note: The words “of names and repetitions” are absent from my manuscript.]

### (Verse 21)

“The sons of Kohath: Amminadab his son.”

This Amminadab is the same person who is written in Numbers as Izhar, the father of Korah.

“The son of Samuel,” who in Kings is called Joel, is written in Chronicles as Vashni, because Abijah, the son of Samuel, when appointed judge, was a taker of gifts.

And because this Joel, who is also Vashni, knew this and did not correct him, both are said to have acted wrongly.

In this passage, however, he shows him separated from his brother, because he was the taker of gifts.

(Vers. 34.) Eliel, father of Jeroam, son of Thou; in the Books of Kings it is written Eliu. For there you read: “and his name was Elkanah, son of Jeroam, son of Eliu, son of Thou.” Eliel is interpreted as “My God is God.” Eliu means “My God is he himself.” Here too Eliel is said—that is, “My God is God”; but in the Books of Kings, where he has not yet been appointed to the ministry of the Temple, and only the genealogical sequence is set out, he is called Eliu, that is, “My God is he himself.”

As for the statement that Heman the singer was the son of Joel, and that, after completing the genealogy, it calls Asaph his brother: “brother” here does not mean the son of the same father or mother, but is used in the way in which we customarily call relatives brothers. [Col. 1375D] The Hebrew author’s usage is recognized here, since it is customary among the Hebrews to call relatives brothers.

The reason Aaron’s genealogy is repeated and extended as far as Achimaas is thought to be that this was done for the praise and remembrance of Achimaas, because he acted faithfully toward David in all things. [Col. 1375B]

(Vers. 68.) “Jecmaam with its surrounding villages.” In Chronicles, Jecmaam is written with Mem, which is interpreted as “vengeance of the people”; in Joshua it is written Jecnaan. [Col. 1375D] In the previously published books it is incompetently written Jecmaan instead of Jecnaam. For Nun—the letter of which this Hebrew author speaks—ought to be in the middle of the word, not at the end, as those skilled in the Hebrew language know. [Col. 1376D] Jecnaan is interpreted as “acquisition of the people.” The reason is this: those who were originally occupied with keeping the Law were an acquisition of the people; because of their sins they were turned into vengeance upon the people.

(Vers. 70.) “From the half-tribe of Manasseh, Aner and its surrounding villages.” Aner took its name from one of Abraham’s servants, who was called Aner, because he lived there and was buried there. In Joshua it is called Thaanath. Aner is interpreted as “light”; Thaanach as “he answered.”

In Chronicles: “Balaam and its surrounding villages”; in Joshua it is written Giblaam. Giblaam means “the people’s old age”; Balaam means “the people’s disturbance.” [Col. 1375C]

(Vers. 73.) In Chronicles it is written Ramoth. Hence the text says: “Ramoth also and its surrounding villages,” and places it in the tribe of Issachar. But Ramoth-gilead, which is written in the Books of Kings, is in the tribe of Ephraim.

(Vers. 74.) In Chronicles, from the tribe of Asher: “Masal with its surrounding villages.” Masal is interpreted as “parable.” In the Book of Joshua it is written Misaal, which is interpreted as “question of God.” [Col. 1375D]

(Vers. 75.) In Chronicles: “Hucac and its surrounding villages”; in Joshua it is written Helcath. Hucac is interpreted as “he carved”; Helcath as “portion.”

(Vers. 76.) There are two places called Cedes: one in the tribe of Issachar, and the other in the tribe of Naphtali in Galilee, where Barak son of Achinoem lived.

In Chronicles: “Hamon with its surrounding villages”; in Joshua, Hamath-dor. Hamon is interpreted as “heating”; Hamath-dor as “heating of the generation.”

In Chronicles: “Cariathaim and its surrounding villages”; in Joshua it is written Carthan. Cariathaim is interpreted as “city of the sea”; Carthan as “city.”

In Chronicles, from the tribe of Gad: “Ramoth in Gilead and its surrounding villages.” Ramoth-gilead is one name in the Books of Kings, and it is in the tribe of Ephraim.

(Cap. VII.—Vers. 6.) In Chronicles, moreover, the sons of Issachar are Thola and Sua, Jasub and Simeron. Jasub is called Job in Genesis. Job is interpreted as “howling”; Jasub as “recalling.” Simeron is the name of a man, and Samaron the name of a city. Simeron, when it is the name of a man, is written with *i*; when it is the name of a city, with *a*.

(Vers. 3.) In Chronicles the sons of Jezraia are said to be five, although there are only four. Their father Jezraia is counted with them; he was the only son of his father Ozi, and thus they become five.

(Vers. 6.) In Chronicles: “The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Jadiel.” In Genesis, Asbel is written instead of Jadiel. Jadiel is interpreted as “knowing God”; Asbel as “captive of God.” [Col. 1376B]

(Vers. 8.) “All these are the sons of Becher.” Wherever the Law says “all these are the sons of” someone, the expression is used either because of the excellence of their merits or because of the deterioration of their merits.

(Vers. 9.) “The sons of Belan were Jehus, Benjamin, Aoth, and Canana.” Aoth was the ancestor of the judge Aoth, who is recorded in the Book of Judges. Canana is the man from whom came the Benjamites who committed the abomination on account of which great slaughter took place in Israel in the time of the Judges.

(Vers. 18.) In Chronicles: “The sons of Naphtali: Jasiel, Guni, Jezer, and Sellum.” In Genesis this Sellum is written Sillem. Sellum is interpreted as “peace”; Silem as “new.”

[Col. 1376C] As for what follows, “the sons of Balaa,” who was Jacob’s concubine: some think that Ezra named her here for this reason—that after Jacob’s death she acted as an intermediary between Joseph and the other Patriarchs, who begged him not to remember their sin.

(Vers. 14.) In Chronicles: “Now the sons of Manasseh were Asriel, and his concubine Syra.” This same Manasseh fathered Machir, the father of Gilead. They relate that this Syra was the daughter of a son of Laban. Her father brought her into Egypt during the famine in order to sell her. Manasseh, who was in charge of the storehouses, received her mercifully; after giving her father provisions, he took her in marriage. She bore him Machir, the father of Gilead.

(Vers. 15.) “The sons of Machir were Huphim and Suphim.” Huphim and Suphim are one name. Their sister was Maacha, whom Esrom took when he was sixty years old; by her he fathered Segub. Huphim is interpreted as “bridal chamber”; Suphim as “anointed.” [Col. 1376D]

(Ibid.) “The name of the second was Zalphaad.” He is therefore called the second because these two were princes in the tribe of Manasseh: Huphim, who is also Suphim, and Zalphaad.

[Col. 1377A] (Vers. 18.) “His sister was Regina,” that is, Bedan, son of Ulam. This Bedan is a different man from the Bedan in the Books of Kings, namely Samson. Bedan is interpreted as “in Dan.”

This sister Regina is Deborah, the wife of Barak, who is also called Laphidoth. [Col. 1377D] Martianaeus and others add a lengthy passage of this kind from the Vulgate, but he omits it in his own book out of humility. As for the statement, “Johannas fathered Azariah,” and “he is the same Azariah who served as priest in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem,” it shows that this same Azariah resisted King Ozias when he entered the Temple of the Lord with a censer and a great earthquake occurred. [Col. 1378D] These matters are also read above, and Martian himself complained that they had been wrongly repeated here. We have removed them from this place in accordance with the evidence of our manuscript.

(Vers. 20.) “Suthala, son of Ephraim, fathered Ezer and Elaad.” They attempted to go up to the land of promise with a multitude gathered from Israel, but they were killed at Gath of the Philistines. As for the brothers who came to console Ephraim, we may understand either those who remained of the Patriarchs or the kinship whom we have often designated by the fraternal name “brothers.” [Read “brothers” as above.]

(Vers. 24.) “His daughter was Beria,” that is, Sara, who built Lower Bethoron and Ozen-Sara. The virtue of this woman is being described. Ozen-Sara is the name of a place. [Col. 1377B]

(Vers. 26.) Elisama, son of Amiud, is the Patriarch from the tribe of Ephraim who is recorded in the Book of Numbers.

(Vers. 28.) “This is Shechem,” which Simeon and Levi struck down. [Col. 1378D] My manuscript says that Bera, son of Asher, was a prophet. Sara, daughter of Asher, is said to have been a prophetess and to have abounded in the prerogatives of merit.

(Vers. 31.) Berzaith, of the lineage of Melchiel and among the sons of Asher, was exceedingly rich in oil and other possessions, and he brought the firstfruits to the prophet Elisha. They say that in him was fulfilled what Moses said concerning Asher: “Let him dip his foot in oil.”

(Cap. VIII.—Vers. 1.) “Aara, son of Benjamin.” In Genesis Gera is written, which is interpreted as “stranger.” In Chronicles, Aara means “brother of fragrance.” It should be noted that here he omitted five of the sons of Benjamin, whose descendants had not yet increased.

(Vers. 2.) Nohaba in Chronicles is the same person who is called Naaman in Genesis. Nohaba means “rest”; Naaman, “most beautiful.”

In Chronicles, Rapha; in Genesis it is written Ahi, which is interpreted as “my brother.” Rapha means “healing.”

(Vers. 6.) “These are the sons of Ahod, princes of the clans dwelling in Gabaa, who were transferred to Manahath.” Manahath is interpreted as “tomb.” They were transferred to Manahath when they fell by the sword because of the crime committed against the Levite’s wife.

As for what follows—“Naaman, Ahia, and Gera himself transferred them”—it indicates that they were princes and that Gera stood out among them. Hence he is described in the singular: “he himself transferred them.” From this Gera came the descendants of Gera, who was the father of Semei.

(Vers. 8.) “Serachim dismissed his wives Usim and Bara, fled to the land of Moab, and took Odes as his wife.” By her he fathered the sons who are listed here.

[Col. 1378A] (Vers. 13.) “These men drove out the inhabitants of Gath and avenged their brothers, the sons of Ephraim, who had fallen by their sword.”

(Vers. 40.) “The sons of Ulam were mighty men of great strength, drawing the bow, and having many sons and grandsons—one hundred and fifty.” The one hundred and fifty are referred to the sons of Ulam, so that the meaning is: “the sons of Ulam were one hundred and fifty,” by the rhetorical figure called hyperbaton.

(Cap. IX.—Vers. 2.) Nathinnei, that is, “the given ones.” These are the Gibeonites, because they were given by Joshua to serve at the Temple of the Lord.

(Vers. 11.) Azariah also, son of Helchias. This is Helchias the high priest, who found the book of the Law in the time of Josiah; he is said to have been the father of the prophet Jeremiah.

[Col. 1378B] Bachbachar is described as a carpenter because he practiced his craft in the house of the Lord and belonged to the tribe of Levi.

(Vers. 15, 16.) “And Barachiah, son of Asaph, son of Elcanah, who dwelt in the courts of Netophath.” Netophath is the name of a place where Heleel, son of Bana, dwelt, concerning whom it was said above. These were the crowns of the house of Jacob.

“Abdiah, son of Semeiah, son of Galal, son of Idithun.” This is Idithun, David’s singer. They kept watch at the king’s gate, toward the east, from among the sons of Levi, according to their divisions; they were singers, and in their divisions they came to sing psalms with David.

(Vers. 19, 20.) “Sellum, son of Core, son of Abiasaph, son of Core.” The first Core is written with Aleph [Col. 1378C] and sounds like *Core*; the second is written with Heth and sounds like *Corach*. Core means “crying out”; Corach, “bald.” This is the man recorded in Numbers (Chapters XVI and XXVI).

These are the Korahites, keepers over the work of the ministry and the vestibules of the tabernacle. They guarded the outer entrance of the tabernacle. Their fathers, who are listed below and whose names appear in the headings of the Psalter, guarded the inner entrance of the tabernacle of the Lord and were singers of the camps of the Lord.

“Tabernacle” refers to the place where the Lord rested. The entire number of gatekeepers was entrusted to these four watches, and the four divisions in which the guardians of the house of the Lord served are described in the Book of Numbers (Chapter III). In each division there were fifty-three, making two hundred and twelve. Phinehas, son of Eleazar, was their leader before the Lord. This shows that Phinehas was still alive at that time and was keeping watch in the tabernacle according to his divisions.

These are the twenty-four divisions that are described below, [Col. 1378D] and which are mentioned in the Gospel (Luke I) in connection with the division of Abia. [Col. 1377] Our Hebrew author knew the volumes of the Gospels: previously that of Matthew, and here that of Luke.

(Vers. 35.) “In Gabaon dwelt Jaiel, the father of Gabaon, and the name of his wife was Maacha.” [Col. 1378D] My manuscript has “mother” instead of “wife.” Jaiel is the same person who is called Abiel in the Books of Kings, father of Chis, father of Saul. Abiel is interpreted as “my father is God”; Jaiel as “abandoned of God,” because of the difference in their merits.

It should be noted that among the sons of Jaiel, Ner and Chis are called brothers, as they truly are, and this is how it is found in the Books of Kings. Later, however, it says that Ner fathered Chis—not that he begot him, but because the one who raised him is said to have fathered him.

(Vers. 38.) “These dwelt opposite their brothers in Jerusalem, with their brothers.” Although they lived outside the walls of Jerusalem, they are nevertheless said to have lived in Jerusalem because of the proximity and the gathering of the place.

(Vers. 39.) “Aminadab, son of Saul.” In Chronicles; but in the Books of Kings, where he was killed with his father, he is called Abinadab, that is, “my father is a vow.” In other places he is called Jesbi, that is, “made equal.”

(Ibid.) “Asbaal, son of Saul.” He is the same person as Isboseth. Esbaal is interpreted as “the husband of fire”; Isboseth as “man of confusion.”

(Vers. 40.) “The son of Jonathan was Meribaal, also called Meribabaal.” He is the same person as Miphiboseth. Meribaal means “contending with a husband”; Meribabaal, “contending against a husband.”

(Vers. 43.) Raphaia and Rapha are one name: the son of Binaa, son of Mosa. Rapha is interpreted as “flowing away.” [Col. 1379D] My manuscript has “weeping” instead of “flowing away.” Raphaia means “healing of God.”

(Vers. 44.) Azaricham Bocru is the name of one man. Bocru is interpreted as “firstborn.” For they relate that he was the armor-bearer of Saul’s Doeg the Idumean, and that the boy who brought Saul’s diadem and bracelet to David was the son of Doeg the Idumean. They also say that Doeg himself was a boy of Saul’s who had gone with him to search for his father’s asses.

(Cap. X.—Vers. 6.) “So Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house fell together.” By saying that his house fell together, he does not mean that it ceased to exist—for Mordecai was among them—but that it ceased to reign.

(Vers. 10.) “And they fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.” In Hebrew it has not “head” but “body,” because they had already sent the head around for display.

In the Books of Kings it is written “in Bethshan.” They relate that Bethshan was called “the house of Dagon,” which is interpreted as “house of the sleeping one.” There is another Bethshan in Judges and Joshua, which is interpreted as “house of security.”

[Col. 1379D] (I Chron. XI, 8.) “Joab rebuilt the rest of the city,” that is, when the Jebusites were slain by the sword, any Israelites found among them were saved by him.

(Cap. XI.—Vers. 11.) “Jesbaam, son of Achamoni, was chief among the thirty.” [Variant: “is placed among the thirty.”] Jesbaam is interpreted as “sitting among the people.” “Son of Achamoni,” that is, “the wisest”—this is David.

This is what is written in the Books of Kings: “He sits in the chair, the wisest, and is diminished in wisdom, like the most tender little worm of wood,” because of the sin he committed against Uriah. Although in the Books of Kings it says that he killed eight hundred in one assault, here in Chronicles it says that he killed three hundred [Col. 1379D] because of that same sin.

“By one assault” is understood as “in one charge,” and he killed eight hundred. Hence in the Books of Kings also it is written “in one assault.” [Col. 1380D] The words that follow here up to “killed another” had previously been missing, except for the words “because of that very sin,” which, joined to the preceding isocolon, could nevertheless appear dislocated. My manuscript supplies the passage in some fashion, as does an Ambrosian manuscript, marked D, number 88, which has only now come to our aid. The variant readings formerly extracted from it had long lain hidden among my notes, not only concerning these matters but also concerning the Questions on the Books of Kings printed above. Otherwise, you should know that it scarcely ever, or only very rarely, differs from my manuscript.

(Vers. 12.) Ahohi was the brother of Jesse, David’s father. His son was Eleazar, who was one of the three most powerful men [Col. 1380D]—namely, Baanaiah son of Joiada and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother. [Thus read my manuscript and the Ambrosian manuscript. Previously “the most powerful” stood here, referring to Eleazar.]

(Vers. 14.) “They stood in the middle of the field and defended it”—namely, David and Eleazar. In Chronicles this is stated in the plural; in the Books of Kings it is expressed in the singular, so that the king’s strength may be displayed. [Col. 1380B]

(Vers. 15.) “Three of the thirty chiefs went down to the rock where David was, to the cave of Odollam.” These three are the men whom we mentioned above.

(Ibid.) “David desired water.” He did not do this out of thirst for water, but to test whether men so brave could be found as to attempt such a deed. He poured it out as a sacrifice to the Lord, giving thanks because He had given such strong men to Israel. It should be noted that the wine offered to God as a sacrifice was mixed with water.

(Vers. 22.) “Baanaiah, son of Joiada, struck down two *ariel* of Moab.” In the Books of Kings it is written “two lions of Moab.” He struck down, that is, two strong men of Moab.

This same Baanaiah performed many deeds at Cabseel. Cabseel is the name of a place. Here his deeds—that is, his wisdom—are praised, because he was one of the seventy elders of Israel. Cabseel means “assembly of God.” [Col. 1380C]

(Vers. 27.) In Chronicles, Sammoth the Harodite; he is the one called Samma in the Books of Kings. Samma means “there”; Samoth means “names.”

“Elles, son of Phalti, from Jaito,” as it is written in the Books of Kings. In Chronicles Elles is called the Plonite. Here the lineage of his mother is indicated. For Ploni was the relative of Boaz concerning whom it is said in Ruth: “There is a nearer relative.”

(Vers. 29.) In Chronicles, Sibbochai the Hushathite; he is the one called Mebunnai in the Books of Kings. Mebunnai is interpreted as “my building”; Sibbochai as “entangled.”

In Chronicles, Illai the Ahohite; he is the one called Zalmon in the Books of Kings. Zalmon means “under the shadow”; Illai, “exalted.” [Col. 1380D] The manuscripts of Corbie and Colbert read otherwise: “Hilai, exalted. Banaiah the Pirathonite, son of Ahod, brother of Jesse, Hurai, and so forth.”

Ahohite means “son of Ahohi, brother of Jesse.”

[Col. 1381A] (Vers. 30.) In Chronicles, Heleb; in the Books of Kings, Heled. Heleb means “fat”; Heled, “earth.”

(Vers. 32.) In Chronicles, Hurai; in the Books of Kings, Hedai. Hurai means “my window”; Hedai, “my sharpness.”

In Chronicles, Abiel; in the Books of Kings, Abialbon. Abiel means “my father is God”; Abialbon, “my father is sorrow.”

(Vers. 33.) In the Books of Kings: “The sons of Jasen, Jonathan.” It should not be thought that Jonathan was his son. Jonathan is listed separately, and his son is Sagie in Chronicles. “The sons of Asem the Gizonite.” Jasen is interpreted as “sleeper”; Asem as “renowned.”

(Vers. 34.) “Aiham, son of Sachar.” In Chronicles this name is interpreted as “reward”; in the Books of Kings it is written Saar and interpreted as “singer.”

[Col. 1381B] (Vers. 35.) In Chronicles, “Eliphal, son of Ur”; in the Books of Kings, “Eliphelet, son of Asbai.” Eliphal means “my God is wondrous”; Ur, “fire.” Eliphelet means “my God will deliver”; Asbai, “he spared me.”

(Vers. 36.) In Chronicles, “Epher the Mecherathite.” Fiepher is the same person as Eliam, the father of Bathsheba and son of Ahithophel. Mechorati means “sold”; Epher, “a pit”; Eliam, “my God is wondrous”; Achitophel, “my brother is ruin,” or “my brother is wondrous.”

(Vers. 37.) In Chronicles, Esro, interpreted as “his court”; in the Books of Kings, Esrai, interpreted as “my court.”

In Chronicles, Noorai son of Esbai; in the Books of Kings, Pharai of Arbi. Noorai means “my boy”; Esbai, “my hyssop.” Pharai is interpreted as “glutton”; Arbi, “locust.”
