[Col. 1381C] (Vers. 37.) In Chronicles, “Joel, brother of Nathan”; in the Books of Kings, “Igal, son of Nathan.” Joel is interpreted as “the Lord God.”

Joel, Jonathan, and the prophet Nathan were brothers, sons of Sammaa, David’s brother. Igal means “redeemed.” The reason that Chronicles calls Joel “brother of Nathan,” while the Books of Kings call him “son of Nathan,” is this: in the former, “father” is used with reference to upbringing; in the latter, “brother” with reference to nature.

“Mibahar, son of Agari,” in Chronicles; in the Books of Kings, “Bani of Gad.” Mibahar means “from the chosen”; Agari, “my stranger.” Bani means “my son”; “of Gad” means “of the tribe of Gad.”

(Vers. 41.) Hira the Jethraite, son of Jether, the father of Amasa. Uriah the Hittite, Bathsheba’s husband, was called a Hittite from the place called Eth. These thirty-seven were with David when he fled before Saul. [Variant: “fled.”]

(Vers. 43.) Maacha is the name of an office held by women in matters concerning women. Maacha means “resourceful.”

Selec the Ammonite is so called because he held an office in Ammon. Githma the Moabite is so called because he held an office in Moab.

Up to this point there are the Benjamites, Elcanah, Jesia, and Azrael. The Levites now begin.

[Col. 1382A] (Cap. XII.—Vers. 8.) “From Gad also some defected to David”—that is, from the tribe of Gad.

(Vers. 21.) “These men gave David assistance against the raiders,” namely the Amalekites, who had plundered the wives of David and of those who were with him.

(Vers. 22.) “Until a great number was formed, like the army of God”—the number of the six hundred thousand who came out of Egypt.

Joiada, a prince of the line of Aaron, is reported to have been Phinehas himself, in comparison with whom Zadok is called a boy.

When it says that princes came with them, it means priests. “From the sons of Issachar, men learned in understanding, who knew the individual times.” They were teachers, calculators, and instructors, whether for celebrating the feasts or for other matters. Therefore it was said in the blessing of Issachar: “He bent his shoulders and became a servant under tribute” (Gen. XLIX, 15). [Col. 1382B]

(Cap. XIII.—Vers. 5.) “David therefore gathered all Israel, from Sihor of Egypt.” Sihor of Egypt is a river derived from the Nile. In Jeremiah: “What have you to do with the road to Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor?” In Joshua: “From Sihor, which is before Egypt, as far as the borders of Accaron.”

(Vers. 9.) “When they reached the threshing-floor of Chidon.” Chidon is interpreted as “shield.” This place is said to be where Joshua stood when he was told: “Raise the shield against the city of Ai.”

(Cap. XI.—Vers. 32.) Eliada, son of David, is named in the first place in both the Books of Kings and Chronicles in the same form; in the second place, however, it is written Baliada. Eliada means “my God has known”; Baliada, “the husband has known.” They relate that the name was changed because of David’s transgression.

(Cap. XIII.—Vers. 7.) Abinadab is interpreted as “my father is a vow”; [Col. 1381D] Aminadab as “my people is a vow.” Until now, “my God is” had wrongly prevailed instead of “my father is,” for everyone knows that *Abi* means “my father”; and unless one interprets it tropologically—which we know has nevertheless been done elsewhere—the name of God cannot at all be extracted from that word. My manuscript and the Ambrosian manuscript restore the reading. [Col. 1382D]

The same Aminadab ordered his two sons, Uza and Ahio, to carry the ark of the Lord on their shoulders. Since neither did they themselves carry it nor did they hand it over to the Kohathites for carrying, Uza was punished with death. The sin consisted in not carrying it; in supporting the ark there was already the punishment of the sin.

The division of Uza is related—that his arm and shoulder withered, where the ark of the Lord was to be carried, and that a certain division was made in its place. [Col. 1382D] But the tradition is not so consistent: the author of the *Miracles* says that he was suffocated; others maintain that he was struck by lightning; still others that he wasted away.

(Vers. 13.) “He turned aside the ark of God into the house of Obed-Edom.” [Col. 1382D] Obed-Edom was a Levite, and David did not know for what reason God’s anger had come upon Uza. After he learned the reason for which Uza had been struck, he ordered the ark to be carried on the shoulders, as the following passage shows.

(Cap. XIV.—Vers. 8.) “He came against them opposite the weeping ones.” They relate that the Philistines had an idol to which sacrifices were prepared in human tears. In accordance with their custom they sacrificed to it with tears. David came against them while the fury of the Lord was already raging over their heads when he approached them. Therefore the nations feared David because the idol to which sacrifice had been offered with human tears had been destroyed.

(Cap. XV.—Vers. 1.) “And he stretched out a tabernacle for it,” and so forth. He made another new tabernacle, by which he might cover the one that had been made by Moses in the wilderness. [Variant: “that.”]

(Vers. 19.) “Sounding with bronze cymbals.” In Hebrew it has “with bronze cymbals, for hearing,” because they began with the psalm that has at its head, “Hear, O Lord, my justice,” which is the sixteenth.

(Vers. 20.) “They sang hidden things on nabli.” In Hebrew it has “for the maidens,” because they began with the forty-fifth psalm, which has this in its title. [Col. 1383B]

(Vers. 21.) “On lyres they sang for the octave,” because they began with the sixth psalm, which has this in its title. Some think that “for the octave” means “for circumcision.” [Col. 1383D] This is understood because the firstborn are circumcised on the eighth day and cease to be unclean, as Pseudo-Hieronymus notes in his commentary on that psalm.

(Vers. 22.) Chonenias, the leader of the Levites, presided over prophecy for leading the melody, because by the spirit of prophecy he recalled to their memory melodies and words.

(Vers. 23.) “Barachiah and Elcanah were gatekeepers of the ark.” Here he calls them gatekeepers, meaning bearers. [Col. 1384D] Martianaeus had incorrectly read “sinners”; both manuscripts correct it.

(Vers. 26.) “When God had helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant,” fearing the fall of Uza.

(Cap. XVI.—Vers. 5.) “Obed-Edom and Jeihel over the instruments.” This Jeihel is the ancestor of Ahiel the prophet, who prophesied in the days of Jehoshaphat. [Col. 1383C]

(Vers. 21.) “But he rebuked kings for their sake, Pharaoh and Abimelech.”

(Vers. 39.) “Zadok the priest and his brothers, the priests, before the tabernacle of the Lord at the high place that was in Gabaon.” Some think that this Gabaon was a certain place in Jerusalem, where David placed the tabernacle of the covenant and the ark of the testimony of the Lord. Gabaon is interpreted as “valley.” They think that “high place” refers to the elevation of divine worship.

(Vers. 43.) “David returned to bless his household.” Some think that “blessing” is used here by antiphrasis. The household was that of Michol, Saul’s daughter, whom David rebuked because she had been indignant when she saw him leaping before the Lord in front of the ark of the covenant.

(Cap. XVII.—Vers. 8.) [Col. 1384D] Victorius rewrote: “And I made you a name,” and so forth. “And he made for himself a name like that of one of the great men who are celebrated in the earth.” One of the great men means either Abraham, Isaac, or Jacob.

(Cap. XVIII.—Vers. 1.) “That David might take Geth and its daughters from the hand of the Philistines.” In the Books of Kings it is written: “He took the bridle of tribute,” in order to extend his dominion as far as the Euphrates River. Some think that this refers to Adadezer, and likewise to Thibahath and Chun. [Col. 1384A] In the Books of Kings: Betha and Berothai. Betha means “rest”; Berothai, “my wells.” Thibahath means “slaughterhouse”; Chun, “struck down” [variant: “struck together”]. The names were changed here because of mockery.

(Vers. 9.) “Thou, king of Emath,” in Chronicles; in the Books of Kings, Thoi. Thoi means “my error”; Thou, “their error,” because he was sending his son deceitfully to David. For this reason the name was changed.

(Vers. 10.) “He sent Aduram his son”; in the Books of Kings, Joram. Joram means “exalted God”; Aduram, “exalted beauty.”

(Vers. 12.) “David made a name for himself when he returned after Syria had been captured, with eighteen thousand slain in the Valley of Salt.” The same is written in the Books of Kings. [Col. 1384B] Many manuscripts have twelve thousand, led into error by the fact that the psalm says twelve thousand. But there it is reported that Joab killed twelve thousand, whereas here Abishai killed eighteen thousand; and because of the dignity of the royal name, the victory is attributed to David. For Chronicles clearly states that Abishai killed these eighteen thousand.

(Vers. 15.) *Commentarii*, “commentators”: those who, after recording matters and reasons, reported them to the king for remembrance.

(Vers. 16.) Abimelech, son of Abiathar, in Chronicles; in the Books of Kings it is written Achimelech. Abimelech means “my father is king”; Achimelech, “my brother is king.”

Susa is written in Chronicles; in the Books of Kings, Saraia. Susa means “joy”; Saraia, “prince of the Lord.”

Bahurim is interpreted as “of the chosen.” Phalti means “liberated”; Lais, “son of a lion.” [Col. 1384C]

(Vers. 17.) “He came as far as Bahurim,” as far as the place of teachers and chosen men, one of whom he was.

Cerethi means “exterminators”; Phelethi, “wonderful.” They are said to have been seventy judges substituted in the place of those whom Moses had chosen in the wilderness at the Lord’s command.

In the Books of Kings, “the sons of David, priests”; in Chronicles, “first at the king’s hand.” Both expressions have the same meaning: here they are called first, and there priests, because of their nobility and precedence. These are the sons who were born to him in Hebron.

(Cap. XIX.—Vers. 2.) “I will show mercy to Anon, son of Naas, for his father showed me kindness.” [Col. 1384D] Naas was king of Ammon, who is mentioned in the Books of Kings as the man against whom Saul first fought in defense of Jabesh-gilead and whom he defeated. Since he was therefore Saul’s enemy, he showed kindness to David whenever David came to him.

In the Books of Kings: “He cut off half of their beards and their garments halfway, as far as their buttocks.” In Chronicles: “He shaved them and cut their tunics halfway, as far as their groins.” What is absent in one place is present in the other. Thus it may be inferred that they were shaved, that their beards were cut off, and that their garments were cut in front and behind.

[Col. 1385A] (Vers. 16.) “Sophach was the commander of the army of Adadezer.” Sophach is interpreted as “disemboweled”; in the Books of Kings it is written Sobach and interpreted as “dovecote.”

(Cap. XX.—Vers. 2.) “David took Melchom’s crown from his head.” Melchom was the idol of the Ammonites, concerning which there is writing in the Books of Kings, in Chronicles, and in Zephaniah. Melchom means “their king.” David took the diadem from the image of that idol.

Under the Law it was forbidden to the Jews to desire anything of gold or silver from idols. But, as they themselves relate, Ethai the Jethaean, who had come to David from the nation of the Philistines, tore the diadem from Melchom’s head, so that it would be permissible for a Hebrew to take from the hand of a man what he was not permitted to take from the head of an idol.

(Vers. 4.) “After this war began at Gezer.” In the Books of Kings, at Gob. Gob means “locust.” Gezer is the name of a place and is interpreted as “arrangement.” As locusts do, the sons of Rapha were destroying Israel. Arapha was Naomi’s daughter-in-law, from whose descendants came the giants, Goliath and his brothers.

(Ibid.) “At which Sobochai the Hushathite struck Saphai.” In the Books of Kings, Saph. Saph means “threshold”; Saphai, “my threshold.”

In Chronicles, “of the family of the Rephaim”; in the Books of Kings, “of the stock of Rapha,” because they were sons of Orpha and belonged to the race of giants.

(Vers. 5.) “At which Adeodatus struck.” In Hebrew it reads: “Elhanan, son of Jair, brother of the Lehemite.” [Col. 1385D] Martian had here read “the Bethlehemite,” as it is written not in Chronicles but in the Books of Kings.

Jair means “watchful.” In the Books of Kings it is written, “Hur, son of Jaare,” which is interpreted as “forest”; in the Books of Kings, “the Bethlehemite”; in Chronicles, “the Lehemite’s brother.”

Thus he killed Goliath the Gittite, the brother of Goliath the Philistine, whom David killed. For there were five of the stock of Orpha, concerning whom he speaks below.

(Vers. 7.) “Jonathan, son of Sammaa, David’s brother, struck him.” This Jonathan is the prophet Nathan himself, who had two brothers, Joel and Jonadab. His father’s name is given here because he is being described among the warriors. But where his prophecy is recorded, his father is not mentioned, since his father was not a prophet.

(Cap. XXI.—Vers. 3.) “That it may be counted as a sin against Israel,” that is, as death, which comes on account of sin.

(Vers. 5.) In Chronicles, “one thousand thousand and one hundred thousand”; in the Books of Kings, “one thousand three hundred thousand.” In Chronicles both those who remained and those who were killed are recorded. In the Books of Kings only the living are counted.

As for the statement that seventy thousand were killed: here only the heads of the elders are counted. In addition, so many thousands of the common people were killed as exceed the number of three hundred thousand. [Col. 1386A]

Those from the tribe of Levi and Benjamin were not counted and were not killed. Benjamin escaped because, in recent times, it had nearly been destroyed by the sword of its brother. Levi was not counted because it excelled in the dignity of the priesthood.

(Ibid.) “The sword of the Lord, and death, and the angel of the Lord.” It is said that the Lord descended into Egypt, struck Egypt with plagues, and killed the firstborn of the Egyptians (Exod. XI).

Here, however, what is first stated terrifyingly as “the sword of the Lord” is moderated when it says “and the angel of the Lord”: it was not in the hand of a man, so that His scourge would not be in human hands but in the hand of God, for He is rich in mercy.

The scourge of man consists both in the sword and in famine, because those who possess grain can prevent its sale. [Col. 1386B]

(Vers. 15.) “The Lord saw and had pity.” They say that the priest Zadok, wearing the priestly fillet, prayed to the Lord and imitated his father Aaron; the Lord saw his prayers and devotion and had pity.

(Vers. 18 and following.) In Chronicles, Ornan, interpreted as “light for us”; in the Books of Kings, Arauna, that is, “ark.”

It is clear that Ornan was a Jebusite, because David did not wish to offer anything belonging to him to the Lord without payment. For this is prohibited in the Law.

Some say that David twice shed blood: once for the blood of the enemy that he had shed, and once for the blood of Uriah, which had been shed.

### Chapter XXIII — Verse 1

The sons of Gershon, the sons of Moses: Shebuel, the first. They say that this is the man who is called Jonathan in Judges, who was priest in the tribe of Dan. Jonathan means “gift of the Lord.” Shebuel means “returning to the Lord”; concerning him it is written: “He and his sons were priests in the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land,” that is, until the day when the ark of the Lord was captured by the Philistines. Shebuel means “God returns,” in accordance with what is found in the Prophet: “Return to me, and I shall return to you” (Zech. 1:3).

### Verse 17

Moreover, the sons of Rehabiah were multiplied exceedingly [variant: “above the house”]. Here too was fulfilled what the Lord said to Moses: “Leave me, so that I may destroy this people and make you into a nation greater than this one” (Exod. 32:10).

### Verses 27–29

[Note: We have restored this passage in accordance with the evidence of the manuscript copies. In the editions published by Erasmus we read: “Which is greater than this one. The last census of the sons of Levi shall be reckoned: while the tabernacle of the Lord was moved from place to place, they were chosen from the age of twenty years. But after the temple of the Lord had been built, from the age of thirty years.” This is altogether mutilated and corrupt, as the sacred context of 1 Chronicles 23:27 proves.]

According to David’s command, the final census of the sons of Levi was to be reckoned from twenty years of age and upward. When the tabernacle of the Lord was moved from place to place, they were chosen from thirty years of age; but after the temple of the Lord had been built, from twenty years of age.

[Note: My manuscript, together with the Ambrosian manuscript and the books circulated before Martianay, agrees on this point: here they prefer twenty years for thirty, and shortly afterward thirty years for twenty.]

But what is found in some copies—“for roasting fine flour”—and in others merely “for roasting” is an error. The Hebrew does not have “fine flour” in this place, since fine flour was already mentioned a little earlier; rather, the Hebrew has “for roasting,” with ears of grain understood. For when the firstfruits of the ears were brought, they were roasted and the grains were eaten. This kind of food is commonly called *graneae*.

### Verses 27–29

Some copies read: “above every weight and measure.” But in the Hebrew this passage does not have “weight”; it has only “measure,” with the noun repeated—whether referring to what is measured with arms, hands, or ropes, or to what is measured with vessels.

## Chapter XXIV — Verse 5

The leaders of the sanctuary were the sons of Ithamar; the leaders of God were from the sons of Eleazar; the leaders of the priests were from Eleazar. For this reason the leaders of the sanctuary from Ithamar are called “leaders of God,” because they ministered there.

### Verse 16

The twentieth was Ezekiel, from whom the Prophet Ezekiel received his name.

### Verse 22

Shelomith, of the sons of Issachar. Above, the name is feminine; but in what follows, Shelomoth is masculine.

### Verse 26

The sons of Merari: Jaaziah. This Jaaziah is written as Maaziah in the twenty-fourth division. Maaziah means “from the help of God”; Jaaziah, “the help of the Lord.”

## Chapter XXV — Verse 5

To exalt the horn—that is, the horn of Israel, or the horn that is King David.

### Verse 27

In the twentieth lot was Elibah, who a little earlier was called Eliathah. Eliathah means “You are my God”; Elibah, “My God, come.”

## Chapter XXVI — Verse 15

Obed-edom: the southern quarter, and for his sons the house of counsel. Most people understand “the house of counsel” to mean the Holy of Holies, in which the secret of counsel was located.

## Chapter XXVII — Verse 18

Elihu, David’s brother, was leader of Judah; in Kings he is called Eliab. Eliab means “My God is father”; Elihu, “My God is the Lord.”

### Verse 23

David did not wish to count them from twenty years [Note: The manuscript books read, “from twenty years of age and upward.”] downward. The custom was that whenever a census began at twenty years and upward, those who could go out to war or perform some ministry were counted. But because David ordered everyone to be counted, both those above twenty and those below twenty years, he therefore experienced the Lord’s indignation.

[Col. 1388A] ### Verse 24

In the chronicles of King David: for when God’s indignation came upon them, this entire number was thrown into confusion, and they were not distributed according to ministries or assigned to any offices.

### Verse 25

These treasuries that were in the cities. In this passage he calls treasuries not only money, but every kind of substance.

### Verse 32

Jonathan, David’s uncle, was his counselor; he is the prophet Nathan. He is called “uncle” on account of honor and kinship.

### Same passage

Jahiel, the son of Hachmoni, was with the king’s sons. This Jahiel is David’s son, who is called Chileab in Kings. Hachmoni means “most wise”; he himself is David.

## Chapter XXIX — Verse 21

A thousand bulls with their libations—that is, with wine.

### Verse 22

They anointed Solomon, the son of David, a second time. They anointed him as prince, saying: “Whoever reigns, may you, our God, always be our God.”

## Chapter XXVIII — Verse 1

Those who were in charge of the king’s property, together with eunuchs. It may be asked why eunuchs are said to have been summoned to so great a council, since the Law prohibited Israelites from being castrated, and foreigners could not easily be admitted to so great a council (Deut. 23). The Hebrews say that in this passage those are called eunuchs who, being alienated from all worldly activities, devoted themselves solely to prayer and reading; and that they had wives not for the sake of lust, but for the purpose of having children. Josephus calls them Essenes according to their [Col. 1388C] sect.

[Note: Josephus is speaking of the Essenes in *The Jewish War*, book 2, chapter 8. But the true reading in Jerome’s *Letter 22 to Eustochium*, no. 35, is: “Such men—namely, the continent—Josephus, in the second history of the Jewish captivity, calls Essenes.”]

### Verse 2

“Listen to me, my brothers and my people.” In this passage he demonstrates both his brotherhood and his precedence.

## Chapter XXIX — Verse 23

Solomon sat upon the throne of the Lord, because of the likeness to the lions that are also described among the cherubim.

### Verse 29

The earlier and later deeds of David. The earlier deeds were those performed when he reigned in Hebron; the later, those performed when he reigned in Jerusalem. It should be noted that he is said to have reigned for forty years, while in the Second Book of Samuel it is written that he reigned seven years and six months in Hebron, and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.

[Note: In the manuscript copies these Questions are read continuously, and there is no distinction in them between the First and Second Books. But the Colbertinus manuscript mentioned above retains the following title in illuminated letters: “Here end the Questions on the First Book of Chronicles. Here begin those on the Second.”]

[Note: Here, as above, Martianay gives: “Here begin the Hebrew Questions on the second part of the book of *Dabrejamin*”; and he appends the following note: “Thus reads only my Ambrosian manuscript: ‘It begins with the second part.’ Previously it read, ‘On the Second Book of Chronicles.’ See what we have noted concerning the title of the first part.” — Editor.]

# On the Second Book of Chronicles

[Col. 1387]

## Chapter I — Verse 8

You showed great mercy to my father and appointed me king in his place. For according to the Law it was forbidden for anyone born of another man’s wife to presume to enter the Church of God.

### Verse 14

He made them be in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. By “chariot cities” he means the enclosures that had been built in Jerusalem for the stationing of chariots, as the following words also show: “and with the king in Jerusalem.”

[Note: He signifies places enclosed by walls in which animals are kept; in this sense Vitruvius, book 6, also calls them *boum cortes* (“cattle enclosures”). In Italian as well, *corti*. This explanation appears preferable to the one that says the cities Beth-marcaboth—that is, “house of chariots”—and Hazer-susa, meaning “dwelling of horses,” are intended.]

### Verse 16

Horses from Egypt and from Kue. Some say that Kue was one of the Cyclades, on which Aesculapius lived. The Hebrews say that this name also signifies “assembly.”

## Chapter II — Verse 13

In Chronicles, Huram, which means “exalted God”; in Kings, Hiram, which means “the exalted one lives.” “And I have sent you Huram, my father.” This Huram was the son of the woman descended from Shelomith of the tribe of Dan, who is mentioned in the Book of Numbers. The Hebrews say that his father was a Hebrew descended from Oholiab of the tribe of Dan, who worked with Bezalel in the wilderness.

But when this passage calls him a Tyrian, they say that this was done by way of translation. For in their language *zoori* means “craftsman.” Tyre, which they call *Sor*, can in some places mean “narrowness,” and in others “craftsmanship.” He therefore calls him his father because, having gone from the land of Israel to him as a sojourner, he taught him the fear of the Lord and brought him to the knowledge [manuscript: “assembly”] of God.

## Chapter III — Verse 1

Moriah means “vision.” It is the place concerning which God said to Abraham: “Go to the land of vision” (Gen. 22).

### Verse 3

In the first measure—that is, the measure with which Moses measured the tabernacle in the wilderness.

### Verse 17

Jachin means “preparer”; they wish David to be understood by this name. Boaz refers to the strength of chastity.

## Chapter IV — Verse 7

According to the pattern which he had commanded to be made; “God” is understood. The oxen were made in remembrance of the calf fashioned in the wilderness. A great basilica in which the kings prayed.

## Chapter VI — Verse 1

The Lord said that he would dwell in darkness, when he said to Moses: “Behold, I am coming to you in a pillar of cloud.”

### Verse 25

“And when they pray in this place, hear from heaven, and be gracious to their sins, and bring them back to the land that you gave to their fathers.” Since he says that they will pray in that very place, why does he say, “Bring them back to the land that you gave to their fathers,” unless perhaps those who come there to pray are able to obtain that those who have been led into captivity may be brought back?

### Verse 26

“And when they turn from their sins, hear them.” It should be noted that when one goes to pray, one must turn away from sins.

Solomon sanctified the middle of the court before the temple of the Lord. Since, because of the multitude of sacrifices, all the victims could not be offered on the altar, he dedicated half of the court, so that sacrifices might also be offered there in the same way as on the altar.

## Chapter VII — Verse 9

He held the assembly on the eighth day. This is the assembly that is written about in the Book of Numbers [variant: Leviticus]: “The eighth day shall be for you most solemn and most holy.” It is both a gathering and an assembly. For these assemblies were held twice a year: on the eighth day of Passover and on the eighth day of Tabernacles.

It should be noted that concerning the assembly celebrated at Passover it is said: “You shall celebrate an assembly for the Lord your God” (Deut. 16); but concerning the one celebrated at the festival of Tabernacles: “You shall celebrate an assembly for yourselves.”

[Col. 1390B] ## Chapter VI — Verse 42

Do not reject the face of your anointed one—that is, do not reject my prayer. Hence it is also said: “He has received your face.”

## Chapter VII — Verse 10

They rejoiced and were glad over the blessings that the Lord had bestowed upon David, Solomon, and his people Israel. For David, after the sin of Uriah the Hittite had been forgiven, was granted an everlasting kingdom. And Solomon, whom the Law prohibited from entering the Church of God, received not only pardon but also a kingdom. Israel, after its many transgressions, deserved a temple in which to invoke the Lord, as well as rest and God’s favor.

## Chapter VIII — Verse 2

He rebuilt the cities that Hiram had given to Solomon. He means those cities that Solomon had given to Hiram, which Hiram refused to accept and called the land of Cabul; these, he says, Hiram gave to Solomon.

[Col. 1390C] ### Verse 6

Everything that Solomon desired and planned, he built in Jerusalem and in Lebanon. Here “Lebanon” signifies the temple, in accordance with the saying of Ezekiel: “Open your doors, Lebanon.” This was during the festival of Weeks, that is, Pentecost.

## Chapter IX — Verse 29

The rest of Solomon’s deeds, earlier and later. The earlier deeds were those performed before he transgressed; the later, those performed after he transgressed.

## Chapter X — Verse 4

Also in the vision of Jaddo the seer. Jaddo is the prophet who was sent by God to Samaria to rebuke Jeroboam concerning the altar that he had made.

Your father oppressed us with an exceedingly harsh yoke, because twenty-four thousand men, in rotating groups, remained with the king in Jerusalem each month.

### Verse 6

He took counsel with the elders who had stood before his father Solomon—that is, with Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and Jahiel the son of Hachmoni, who is also called by another name, Chileab.

### Verse 8

Abandoning the counsel of the elders, he began to consult with the young men—that is, with Aduram, who is later described as having been stoned.

### Verse 16

“Now look to your own house, David.” Now let God see that our withdrawal from the house of David is the sin of his sons, who reject us.

### Verse 18

In Kings, Huram; in Chronicles, Aduram. Huram means “exalted river”; Aduram, “exalted ruin.”

## Chapter XI — Verse 5

He built fortified cities. He built the cities because of the war.

### Verse 15

The priests of the high places and of the demons. Whenever an image was made somewhere, demons gave responses, and priests were appointed for them.

### Verse 18

Rehoboam took as his wife Mahalath, the daughter of Jerimoth, the son of David. This Jerimoth is recorded neither in Kings nor in Chronicles, because he was one of the sons of the concubines.

[Col. 1391B] ### Verse 20

He took Maacah, the daughter of Absalom. This is not Absalom the son of David, but another man, as is shown in the Book of Kings.

## Chapter XII — Verse 15

They are written in the book of Shemaiah the Prophet and of Iddo the seer. This Iddo is the man whom he earlier called Jaddo.

## Chapter XIII — Verse 4

Abijah stood on Mount Zemaraim. Many think that this refers to Samaria, which cannot be the case. There was a mountain in Ephraim, not far from Carmel, where Elijah lived.

### Verse 5

A covenant of salt with him and his sons. In some passages “covenant of salt” is used for the Law, which is the seasoning of all things; in this passage it refers to the house of David, which was the seasoning of all Israel.

### Verse 7

Rehoboam was inexperienced and fearful in heart. [Col. 1391C] For he feared the words of the Prophet Shemaiah.

### Verse 9

His hands were consecrated with a bull and seven rams, as those of a man who was to become a priest. Jeroboam had adopted this custom for consecrating the priests of the idols.

### Verse 17

Fifty thousand valiant men fell wounded from Israel. These were evidently the men who had bent their knees before the idol. For the Law commanded that if anyone worshiped an idol, he should die.

### Verse 19

He captured Bethel and its villages. Bethel itself is the place where Jeroboam had set up the calf. Also Ephron and its villages. Ephron itself is Shechem.

## Chapter XV — Verse 1

Azariah, the son of Oded. Oded himself is Jaddo, who was sent to Jeroboam.

### Verse 5

“At that time there shall be no peace for one going out or coming in.” They report that this was fulfilled fifty-two years after the destruction of the temple, so that during those fifty-two years neither bird flew nor beast passed through Jerusalem, and Israel was without hope, while all the nations were in confusion.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “was without it” [or “was without that very thing”]. Shortly afterward it reads “and he dedicated” instead of “and he built.”]

### Verse 8

He built the altar of the Lord that was before the portico. That is, he restored the altar that had been constructed by Solomon.

### Verse 15

For they swore with all their heart. With their heart, in fasting and affliction, in willingness, and in almsgiving.

### Verse 16

And Maacah, the mother of Asa the king. [Col. 1392A] He did not say “his mother,” because she did not walk in the right way as her son did. He removed her from her exalted position—that is, from the priesthood. He crushed the image of Priapus and burned it in the torrent of Kidron.

They say that he crushed it and secretly intended to throw it away; but, so that the Lord might disclose the matter, fire came forth from the water in the torrent of Kidron.

## Chapter XVI — Verse 10

He ordered him to be put in the stocks, because he had publicly rebuked him.

### Verse 12

Asa’s feet became diseased, because he was afflicted with gout. It should be noted that, as a mark of reverence for kings, their garments and spices were burned. Hence it is said: “And according to the burnings of your fathers they shall make one for you.”

## Chapter XVII — Verse 3

He walked in the first ways of David—that is, before David had sinned.

### Verse 16

After him, Amaziah the son of Zichri was also consecrated to the Lord, because he was from the tribe of Issachar and was a teacher.

## Chapter XVIII — Verse 38

The king of Israel stood in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening, and he died when the sun was setting. After receiving a mortal wound, he ordered himself to be held up, lest the enemies discover that he was wounded and his fall should bring victory to the enemies and the danger of flight upon the people. He died at sunset, so that the people would have the protection of night for their escape.

## Chapter XIX — Verse 2

Jehu the son of Hanani—that is, the son of the prophet whom Asa, king of Judah, had sent to prison.

## Chapter XX — Verse 1

The sons of Moab, the sons of Ammon, and with them some of the Ammonites. By “Ammonites” he wishes Edomites to be understood. Out of reverence for the name of their brother, they did not wish to take up arms against Israel in their former appearance, but disguised themselves in the appearance of Ammonites.

### Verse 2

From the regions that are across the sea. The sea is the Salt Sea, where the Jordan flows in.

### Verse 5

Before the new court. He calls it the new court because they had made the court old through sinning and had restored it to its former newness through repentance.

### Verse 9

“For your name is in this house.” This was written on the forehead of the High Priest, or on the garment of the ephod, as is shown below. That same place was called Jeruel from that day onward—that is, “fear of God.”

[Col. 1392D] ### Verse 20

They went out through the wilderness of Tekoa. The Tekoite woman was from there.

### Verse 21

“Give thanks to the Lord, for his mercy is everlasting.” The word “good” is absent because in this matter he did not exercise his gentleness, by which he tolerates everyone, but his judgment.

### Verse 26

They called that place the Valley of Blessing. The Valley of Blessing is Jeruel itself, of which it was said above.

### Verse 31

His mother’s name was Azubah, the daughter of Shilhi. Shilhi means “sent”; he himself is the Prophet Hanani, the son of Jaddo, mentioned above. He was called “sent” because he was sent to prophesy to the father of Jehoshaphat, his son-in-law.

### Verse 37

Eliezer the son of Dodavahu prophesied. Dodavahu is understood to have been the son of Jehoshaphat’s uncle.

## Chapter XXI — Verse 2

All these were the sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Because they imitated the deeds of King Jehoshaphat, the phrase “all these were the sons of Jehoshaphat” is repeated.

### Verse 6

Joram walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done. For his wife was the daughter of Ahab. Athaliah was his wife, and she was not the daughter of Ahab but of Omri; nevertheless, because she imitated him, she was called his daughter. Hence in Kings it is also said of Joram: “For he was the son-in-law of the house of Ahab.”

[Col. 1393B] ### Verse 11

Moreover, he built high places. Many think that he built high places in the house of the Lord, which is situated on Mount Moriah; this is shown more clearly in the deeds of King Manasseh.

### Verse 17

No son remained to him except Jehoahaz. Jehoahaz is the same as Ahaziah, the father of Joash, the son of Joram, whose sister was Jehoshabeath. Jehoshabeath was not the daughter of Athaliah; Joram had her by another wife.

A very perplexing question arises. It says that Joram reigned for eight years and lived forty years; and it says that his son Ahaziah, when he began to reign, was forty-two years old. If this is so, he fathered him two years before he himself was born. Anyone can see how absurd this is if it is not resolved.

That same Joram, who is here described as having lived forty years and reigned eight years, lived forty years and reigned twenty-eight. The eight years assigned to him in his reign are those before he killed his brothers, while he was still living innocently. The twenty years during which he reigned are subtracted from his number because he spent them in illness and tribulation; they are therefore assigned to his son, who is said to have reigned when he was no more than twenty-two years old, so that the years remaining from the total would not create an error in the investigation of the chronology.

Ahaziah lived twenty-three years but reigned only one year. A comparison with the text of the Book of Kings provides great assistance in resolving this question.

## Chapter XXII — Verse 4

Therefore Azariah, the son of Joram, king of Judah. This Azariah was called Ahaziah a little earlier. Ahaziah means “one who grasps the Lord”; Azariah, “the help of the Lord.” His name is changed here to a better one because, in obedience to the Lord’s command, he had gone down to visit a sick man.

### Verse 8

And the sons of Ahaziah’s brothers who ministered to him. By “the sons of his brothers” he means cousins and relatives.

## Chapter XXIII — Verse 5

A third part was at the gate called the Foundation Gate. The Foundation Gate was the gate of the sanctuary. “Let all the rest of the people keep the watches of the Lord”—that is, although they were necessary to complete the work, namely, to establish the king, nevertheless they were to keep the watches of the Lord, so that no outsider should enter a place that only priests and Levites were permitted to enter.

### Verse 11

They placed the diadem and the testimony upon him. The testimony was the phylacteries, because they contained the Ten Words of the Law. Jehoiada the high priest and his sons anointed him. By “his sons” he means Zechariah the prophet, whom Joash himself later killed, thereby greatly increasing his condemnation: he killed the man who had anointed him king.

[Note: My manuscript, together with the Ambrosian manuscript, rightly prefers “detriment” to “increase.”]

### Verse 13

He saw the king standing on his platform—that is, upon the column that Solomon had prepared for the kings in the basilica.

[Col. 1394B] ### Verse 16

Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, the whole people, and the king. He placed himself in the position of the Law and of God, since he was God’s minister and his name means “knowing the Lord.” He made the covenant with both the people and the king so that the people and the king would obey God and his Law, the people would act faithfully toward the king, and the king would rule the people with justice.

### Verse 18

Under the hands of the priests and Levites. This was so that priests might not be made from any tribe except Levi.

### Verse 19

He also appointed doorkeepers at the gates of the house of the Lord, so that no unclean person might enter in any matter—that is, so that none of the priests of Baal might enter the house of the Lord under any pretext whatsoever.

### Verse 21

The city rested. This was either because until then it had been troubled by the worship of idols during Athaliah’s time, or because, after the tumult in which the king was anointed and Athaliah was killed, everyone returned to his own house and all the disturbance subsided.

## Chapter XXIV — Verse 1

His mother’s name was Zibiah, from Beersheba. The name of her father is not written because he was not sufficiently renowned to be recorded. When people’s names are written, this is done because of their renown, power, or nobility.

### Verse 5

Go out to the cities of Judah and collect from all Israel, each year, money for repairing the temple of your God. This is the money that the Law commanded to be given and that they customarily paid annually when the census was taken—namely, each person half a shekel—which they had not paid from the day Athaliah began to reign.

### Verse 7

For the utterly wicked Athaliah and her sons destroyed the house of the Lord. By “her sons” he means the priests of the idols; for in sacred language people are often called sons not by birth but by imitation.

They had destroyed the house of God either by stripping it of its ornaments, or, as some report, by an earthquake, as in the time of Uzziah. Just as an earthquake occurred when Uzziah entered with a censer, so too one occurred when Athaliah attempted to bring idols into the house of the Lord.

### Verse 16

Because he had done good in Israel, both toward God and toward his house. He did good toward God because he overthrew the idols that had been made in contempt of God. He did good toward God’s house because he restored the ruins and breaches in Israel, restoring the kingdom of the house of David and removing from it the idolatry that had ruled over them because of their sins.

### Verse 17

After Jehoiada died, the leaders of Judah entered and worshiped the king. They worshiped him as God. He, charmed by their service, yielded to them and allowed himself to be worshiped as God.

### Verse 20

Thus says God [variant: “the Lord”]: “Why are you transgressing the commandment of the Lord?” It is as though he were saying openly: “You have abandoned the one whom you ought to have as God, to such an extent that you have committed a crime such as had never before been found among you.”

It should be noted that the phrase “Thus says God” is found nowhere else except here. The sons of Zechariah were killed with him; therefore it says “the sons of Jehoiada the priest.”

[Col. 1395B] ### Verse 26

Zabad the son of Shimeath the Ammonitess and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith the Moabitess conspired against him. He calls them sons of Ammonitesses and Moabitesses in order to magnify the wickedness of the Israelites, who did not wish to avenge the priest of God, whereas men who were sons of foreigners did so.

### Verse 27

Moreover, his sons [Note: In place of the words of the sacred text, “and the sum of the money,” the earlier printed books inserted the absurd phrase “and the multitude of prophecy.” In the same way they retain six hundred other corruptions that make the learned reader laugh while pleasing the uneducated.] and the sum of the money [Note: My manuscript, together with the Ambrosian manuscript, also has “and the multitude of prophecy” instead of “and the sum of the money.”]

“His sons,” whom the Syrians killed before him, inflicting shameful judgments upon him—either because they did shameful things to him, or because, while killing his sons, they reproached him for the crime he had committed against Zechariah.

In Hebrew: “And the foundation of the house of God,” because the blood of Zechariah had reached the foundation of the temple and the altar.

## Chapter XXV — Verse 2

He did what was good in the sight of the Lord, but not with a perfect heart. For he labored for the dignity of the present age, not for the future homeland.

### Verse 3

He slaughtered the servants who had killed his father, the king. Although they had killed him out of fear of God and in vengeance for Zechariah, nevertheless they were judicially killed by him, because they had killed him not at the word of a prophet or on the Lord’s counsel, but on their own presumption.

### Verse 7

God is not with Israel and all the sons of Ephraim. He was with the other tribes, but not with the tribe of Ephraim, from which the kings came, because of the transgression of Jeroboam and the other kings.

[Col. 1395D] ### Verse 10

Amaziah therefore separated the army that had come to him from Ephraim, because they had idols with them. After the slaughter of the Edomites and the seizure of the gods of the sons of Seir, Amaziah established those gods for himself.

When the ten thousand were thrown down, the idols that they had with them gave an answer: they had been killed because they had been negligent in their worship. Seeing, therefore, that the idols gave answers and had been rescued from the fall, he was deceived by this error and worshiped them.

### Verse 15

He sent a prophet to him. This prophet is Eliezer, the son of Dodavahu—that is, of his uncle—of whom it was said above.

“And the prophet ceased and said.” He ceased because of the king’s threats, and he spoke at the Lord’s command.

### Verse 16

Because you have done this evil and, moreover, have not listened to my counsel. He would have listened to his counsel if he had burned them with fire, torn his garments, scattered ashes over his head, and devoted himself entirely to repentance. For this was the counsel the prophet had given him.

### Verse 18

The thornbush of Lebanon, which is in Lebanon. He calls him the thornbush of Lebanon because of his nobility: although he acted carelessly, he was born of great ancestors, since he was descended from the seed of Israel.

### Verse 20

All the gold and silver and everything found in the house of the Lord with Obed-edom. They were with Obed-edom because his sons guarded them, and they remained assigned to him by record.

### Verse 25

Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Joash the son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel. At that time Uzziah was still in the womb; he later reigned in Jerusalem. Hence it is also written that Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign.

From the time Amaziah departed from the Lord, a conspiracy arose against him in Jerusalem. For from the time when he refused to listen to the prophet’s counsel and would not turn to the Lord, preparations for his conspiracy were made; they were delayed until the matter reached its completion.

### Verse 28

They carried him on horses and buried him. Scripture does not say without reason that he was carried on horses. It may be inferred that he was carried on horses because he had worshiped the gods of Edom, which were carried on horses.

For this reason he was not carried on shoulders: he had neglected to serve the God of Israel, whose mysteries he had commanded to be carried on the shoulders of the Kohathites.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “whose ministries were commanded to be carried on the shoulders of the Kohathites”; only in its final words does my manuscript agree with it.]

## Chapter XXVI — Verse 1

In Chronicles he is called Uzziah; in Kings, Azariah, the son of Amaziah. Uzziah means “the strength of God”; Azariah, “the help of the Lord.” He is called the Lord’s strength because the Lord’s great power was manifested in him through the plague of leprosy and the occurrence of an earthquake.

### Verse 5

He sought God in the days of Zechariah, who understood and saw God. This was Zechariah the son of Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada, who was born after his father’s death and received his father’s name as a posthumous child. He was called “understanding” and “seeing”: understanding because of the priesthood, seeing because of prophecy.

[Col. 1397A] ### Verse 7

Against the Arabs who lived in Gurbaal. This is Gerar, where Abraham sojourned.

### Verse 8

Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem over the Corner Gate and over the Valley Gate, the city gate, from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate. Joash, king of Israel, had destroyed it; Uzziah restored it.

He calls the Gate of Ephraim the Valley Gate. In rebuilding it, he did not wish to give it the name that it had borne when it was destroyed. Nor was this without reason: because the man who sacrificed to idols and had shared in its destruction did not deserve to have his own name attached to its rebuilding. Instead, it is designated by the name “valley,” because of humility.

### Verse 21

In a separate house, as is written in Leviticus.

[Col. 1397B] ### Verse 22

The rest of the earlier and later deeds of Uzziah were written by the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah the prophet also wrote: “In the year when King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated.” He describes him as having died in the year in which he was struck with leprosy.

## Chapter XXVII — Verse 3

He built many structures on the wall of Ophel. On the wall of Ophel—that is, on the wall of the cloud—which is understood as the Holy of Holies. For the Lord said that he would dwell in the cloud.

### Verse 8

Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign. Here both the beginning of his reign and his innocence are described, to show that he persevered in the innocence with which he began.

## Chapter XXVIII — Verse 7

Maaseiah, the son of Molech—that is, the son of the idols of Ammon, which was called Molech, meaning “king.” He is called its son because he instituted its sacrifices and worship.

You also find this in Jeremiah concerning Ishmael, who is described as being of royal descent, although he was not of royal descent but descended from Gera, an Egyptian servant (Jer. 41).

### Verses 9, 19

At that time there was there a prophet named Obed.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads “named Eded”; shortly afterward it reads “from Judea” rather than “from Judah.”]

He is the father of Azariah, who prophesied to King Asa. He had come to Samaria to prophesy because he was from Judah.

For this reason he did not say, “Thus says the Lord,” because they were not worthy of the word of a prophet. God was angry with them.

In this one passage alone Ahaz is called “king of Israel”—not because he ruled over all Israel, but because he followed the deeds of the kings of Israel, to such an extent that no king before him had been more wicked.

Hence it is also said of him that he stripped Judah of the commandments and help of God, just as it is written concerning Aaron that he stripped the people. King Ahaz himself increased the contempt.

[Note: Martianay and other printed editions add “sin,” but the manuscripts resist this reading. The Ambrosian manuscript has *duxit praeterea* (“he furthermore led”), instead of *auxit* (“he increased”).]

This may appear superfluous. But when it says “he himself,” it does so in order to mark him out. For the pronoun is often placed in praise as well.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript adds the pronoun in this way.]

### Verse 27

They buried him in the city of Jerusalem, because they did not bury him in the tomb of the kings, but in another place in the city of Jerusalem.

But when it says, “They did not receive him into the tomb of the kings of Israel,” the Hebrew sounds as though those who had been buried there themselves did not receive him. Since this should be understood more suitably, either the custodians who guarded those same tombs prevented him, or it occurred in some other way—but nevertheless by the will of God.

## Chapter XXIX — Verse 2

His mother’s name was Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah the posthumous child: Zechariah the prophet and priest, who had been killed by King Joash.

(Vers. 3.) In the first year and first month of his reign. In the idiom of the Hebrew language, “the first day of his reign” is also understood in this description.

(Vers. 5.) Remove every impurity from the sanctuary—that is, the idols which Ahaz had set up, which were like a menstruating and polluted woman and which polluted others.

(Vers. 6.) They turned their faces away from the tabernacle of the Lord and presented their backs. This is described fully in Ezekiel, where it is said that twenty-five men had their backs toward the temple and were worshiping toward the rising sun.

(Vers. 21.) Seven male goats for sin. Something contrary to the usual practice was done here. In all other passages a single male goat was customarily offered for sin (Leviticus 4, 9, 23). But because the sins were many, seven male goats had to be offered. For this reason he calls Gad a seer, because prophecy came to him through a vision. It was the custom of the Levites to remove the skins of burnt offerings, and of the priests to remove them when a sacrifice was made for sin. Therefore the priests removed the skins here, because it was a sacrifice for sin. And because the number of priests was not [the manuscript reads: less] sufficient for carrying this out—for in the time of King Ahaz those who had been scattered had not yet returned—their fellow Levites assisted them, since it was more appropriate to use Levites for the sacrifice than priests: for in the time of Ahaz they too had consented, especially since the model of the altar at Damascus had been sent to Uriah the high priest.

(Cap. XXX.—Vers. 1.) He also wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh. Although he had publicly sent messengers throughout all Israel, he secretly sent to Manasseh and Ephraim those whom he knew could be brought back by letters. They were more arrogant because of the royal dignity that belonged to the house of Ephraim.

(Vers. 18.) For a great part of the people ate the Passover contrary to what had been written. It had been written that those who could not eat in the first month should eat in the second. A very large multitude came, however, and had not been purified in the second month; and because it was unlawful to perform this rite in the third month, they performed it in the second. Hezekiah prayed for them, and the Lord heard him and was reconciled to his people. They say that no impure person could eat the Passover without immediately dying, and they recognized that the Lord had been appeased in this matter because those who ate were not struck dead.

(Cap. XXXII.—Vers. 21.) And he returned with disgrace to his own land. The Hebrews relate that the Angel shaved his head and beard as a disgrace, and that this was what was said through the prophet Isaiah: “On that day the Lord will shave with a hired sharp razor, by the king of Assyria, the head and the beard,” and so forth (Isaiah 7). They say that, in this same disgrace, he reached the temple of his god Nesrath, whose worship, they claim, was located among the remains of Noah’s ark. When he asked, in supplication, why the god had not helped him—and even offered to sacrifice his sons Adrammelech and Sarasar to him, if the god approved—his sons, hearing this after so many disasters, ruins, and disgraces, feared that he would kill them and killed him instead.

(Vers. 31.) Concerning the portent that had occurred over the land, namely, the return of the sun along ten lines.

The Babylonian king’s envoys came to investigate this one mystery. God left him to be tested because he did not prevent him, through the prophet, from displaying his treasures—not merely the treasures of his own house, but the treasures of the house of the Lord. For this he was later rebuked by the same prophet.

(Vers. 33.) And they buried him above the tombs of the sons of David. This too should be noted: by the privilege of his merit he had a tomb higher than those of the other sons of David.

(Cap. XXXIII.—Vers. 3.) And he worshiped the whole host of heaven. According to what they relate, the twelve signs that are in the zodiac.

(Vers. 3.) He built them for the entire host of heaven—that is, for demons under the name of stars—in the valley of Ben-enon, which elsewhere is called Gehennon, that is, “the valley of the sons of Ennon.” It is not far from Jerusalem; it is described fully in Jeremiah and in the Book of Kings. Gehenna received its name from this place.

(Vers. 10.) And the Lord spoke to him and to his people, but they were unwilling to heed the hand of Isaiah the prophet. The Hebrews relate that this same Manasseh was the son of Isaiah’s daughter; and therefore, although his mother’s name is written here, his father’s name is not written, because the impious king was unworthy of so great a grandfather.

[Note: The word “daughter” is absent from my manuscript; but both the text itself and the Ambrosian manuscript, as well as the commonly printed books, seem to err much more seriously afterward in the words “father” and “mother,” which I would suppose have been transposed here, so that the passage should be read in the opposite order. Although the father’s name is written, his mother’s name is not. Manasseh’s mother is not named; she is said to have been Isaiah’s daughter because the profane king was unworthy of such a grandfather, namely Isaiah. His father, however, Hezekiah, is named both here and in 4 Kings 21.]

The Hebrews relate that Isaiah was killed because he had called them “princes of Sodom and Gomorrah.” Also because he said, “I saw the Lord sitting” (Isaiah 6:1), whereas through Moses it had been said, “For man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20). And because he said, “God will add fifteen years to your days” (4 Kings 20:6), whereas through Moses it had been said, “You shall fulfill the number of your days” (Exodus 23:26). And because he had said, “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6), whereas it is said: “Who is so near as the Lord our God whenever we call upon him?”

[Note: Compare the Author of the Book of the Prophets cited by Epiphanius, as well as Saint Augustine and Theodoret.]

(Vers. 13.) And Manasseh knew that the Lord himself is God. For when he had been led away to Babylon and placed in a perforated bronze vessel with a fire applied to it, he invoked all the names of the idols whom he worshiped. When he was neither heard nor delivered by them, he remembered what he had often heard from his father: “When you call upon me in your tribulation, and turn back, I will hear you,” as it is written in Deuteronomy. He was heard by the Lord, delivered, and restored to his kingdom, and he was brought back in the manner of Habakkuk, just as Habakkuk had been led away to Babylon.

[Note: The Hebrew writer acknowledges the account of Habakkuk as genuine, just as Catholics also receive it among the authentic Scriptures.]

He surrounded Ophel—that is, he restored the building of the Holy of Holies which he had constructed for the idols. To the west of Gihon—that is, from the torrent of Gihon—he began to build as far as the Fish Gate, which is the gate on the side of Joppa.

(Vers. 19.) The rest of his acts were written in the words of Ozai. Some wish to understand Ozai here as Isaiah. For Ozai means “my vision.” Thus, with the name changed, he is introduced in order to show that the merits of this man were far removed from those of the one whom he killed.

(Cap. XXXIV.—Vers. 9.) From all Judah and Benjamin and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. By “the inhabitants of Jerusalem” he means half the tribe of Manasseh, who are often counted as belonging to the tribe of Benjamin.

(Vers. 22.) To Huldah, who lived in the Second Quarter. Huldah was the wife of Shallum, the maternal uncle of Jeremiah’s father and the father of Hananel. “Who lived in the Second Quarter.” There was a place in Jerusalem outside the wall—that is, between the city wall and the outer rampart—which was called the Second Quarter; it is mentioned by the prophet Zephaniah. In Chronicles: “the sons of Tekoah, the son of Hasrah”; in Kings: “Tikvah, the daughter of Araaz.” Tekoah means “a cry.” Hasrah means “diminution.” Tikvah means “hope.” Araaz means “merchant.” “Of the keeper of the garments,” because he guarded the temple of the Lord.

[Note: In place of “of the garments,” my manuscript restores this word according to the actual text of Scripture; previously it read “of the temple.”]

(Cap. XXXV.—Vers. 3.) Put the ark in the sanctuary of the temple which Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, built. It should be noted that the ark of the Lord had been removed from the temple and that Josiah now ordered it to be brought back into the temple. For in the time of Ahaz, when images had been brought into the temple, it was removed from there and taken to the house of Shallum, Huldah’s husband and Jeremiah’s maternal uncle, where it remained until the time of Josiah. The ark of God could not be in a place where images had been introduced and pagan practice and the most abominable rites were being observed.

(Vers. 15.) They stood in order according to the command of David and Asaph and Heman and Jeduthun, the king’s prophets. They were called the king’s prophets because they sang with King David.

(Vers. 18.) There was no Passover like this in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet, because all who were found at that festival remained there for seven days, and all feasted sufficiently from the king’s resources and from the things mentioned above.

(Vers. 21.) “I am fighting against another house”—that is, against Hadad-remmon, son of King Tabrimmon, who ruled at Carchemish; whom, at that time when King Neco killed Josiah, [the surviving fragment is syntactically incomplete]. There was great mourning at Megiddo, which the prophet Zechariah mentions.

(Vers. 22.) He was unwilling to heed the words of Neco from the mouth of God, because he had prophesied through the prophet Jeremiah that Neco would go up to Carchemish and obtain victory; this prophecy was not unknown to King Neco. Hence the Rabshakeh also says concerning Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians: “The Lord commanded me to go up against this land.” For the prophets of Israel had already prophesied that he would go up, and this was not unknown to him.

(Vers. 25.) All the male and female singers, to the present day, because it is written in the Lamentation of Jeremiah: “The breath of the mouth of the Lord, the Lord Christ” (Lamentations 4:20).

(Vers. 27.) His first and last acts. Here he calls “last” those acts in which he did not consult the Lord about whether he ought to proceed against Neco.

(Cap. XXXVI.—Vers. 8.) The rest of the words of Jehoiakim and his abominations which he committed, and which were found in him. Among the other evils he committed, he also did this to his own body, which the Lord had forbidden when he said: “You shall not round off your heads for the dead, nor make tattoo marks upon your bodies.”

[Note: The printed editions read: “You shall not cut your hair … over the dead, nor make tattoo marks, and so forth.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “your head.” In addition, the error which Martianay notes in his copies is not found in ours.]

After he died, these things were found on his body.

[Note: The manuscript copies read this way after “were found”: There is the name of the idol whom Jehoiakim also worshiped, Chodonazer, which means “a form that captures wine.” It should be noted, however, that the Hebrew writer here gives the etymology of the name Nebuchadnezzar, separating Nabo from Chodonazer; consequently, the manuscripts contain an error.]

(Vers. 10.) Nabo: a prophecy. For it is the name of the idol whom this same Nabo served. Chodonasar: “capturing a form of wine.”

[Note: Jerome held the opposite view: Nabo was not the name of an idol but of a city, although his opinion seems to depart rather far from the truth. In Book 5, chapter 15, of his Commentaries on Isaiah, at verse 2, he says: “The royal house and the city of Dibon have gone up to the idols that are set in the printed editions, and the whole province will howl over Nabo and Medaba, noble cities. For in Nabo the idol Chemosh had been consecrated, which is called by another name, Beelphogor. See what we note on this passage.”]

(Vers. 22.) [Note: This entire section of the sacred text, nearly seven verses long, extending to the words “and he himself commanded me,” is absent from my manuscript and from the Ambrosian manuscript. It is more properly absent, and can be omitted without any loss to the exposition that follows.]

In the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, to fulfill the word of the Lord which he had spoken through the mouth of Jeremiah, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, king of the Persians, who ordered it to be proclaimed throughout his entire kingdom, even in writing, saying: “Thus says Cyrus, king of the Persians: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he himself commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem.”

For he had heard the prophecy of Isaiah, in which he had said: “Thus says the Lord to my anointed Cyrus, whose hand I have grasped” (1 Esdras 1). Ezra the scribe read these words to him, and therefore he said that this command concerning all the kings of the earth had been given to him by the Lord. These two men were called by their proper names through prophecy before they were born, namely Josiah and Cyrus: Josiah, to destroy the idols and renew the worship of God; Cyrus, to restore the ruins of the temple.

[Note: Here the following is added: “The Questions on the Book of Chronicles are concluded.” Vallarsius appends the following note.]

This is how my manuscript and the Ambrosian manuscript read. In mine, however, there follows a set of Questions on the prophet Habakkuk attributed to Jerome, beginning as follows: “Wherever the burden of the word of the Lord is placed, heaviness is signified in that prophecy.” But there is no doubt that the name of Jerome falsely identifies him as their author.

# Interlinear Exposition of the Book of Job

## Notice concerning the following interlinear exposition of Job

Jerome composed no Commentary on Job—unless, perhaps, while reflecting on the Hebrew Questions concerning the whole of Scripture, which, except for those on Genesis, he either abandoned entirely after changing his plan or preferred to let perish within the walls of his own house, he also prepared certain threads and woof for a work on Job. In order that this may be established as certain and indisputable, let all lengthy arguments on either side be dismissed, and let this single consideration prevail.

No such Commentary is ever mentioned by Jerome, even in passing; nor is there any testimony from later generations of people who read or saw it, except for Bede; nor do any fragments or remnants survive that are genuine and truly Jerome’s. Learned critics of great reputation, however, were misled by a false reading in a certain passage of the Commentary of the holy Doctor on Amos, chapter 5. The reading long circulated was: “Nahas in Job is called Leviathan; concerning whose nature and manifold terror we have spoken more fully in this volume.” Yet we learn that the sense was entirely different: the holy Father wrote “we learn” there, not “we have spoken,” just as Martianay restored it from two manuscripts, and as we establish and confirm it from several others, especially very ancient ones—one from the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, written around the year seven hundred, two Palatine-Vatican manuscripts of somewhat later date, and others which we shall cite at that passage.

The true sense of the passage is this: from the Book of Job itself—that is, from chapters forty and following—we can learn something more fully about the nature and manifold terror of Leviathan and Behemoth; but there is no Commentary on Job published or composed by Jerome.

Since this is so, the only remaining question is to investigate the author of the Commentaries on that book circulated under Jerome’s name. In this matter, one point must be observed above all: there are nearly four copies of what, in my opinion, is a single composition, although people generally regard them as different works.

The first, which is listed among the spurious works in the final volume of Jerome’s works—each item must indeed be identified by its own notes—was retrieved by Johannes Sichardus from the library at Fulda and published at Basel in 1527. It is attributed, not entirely without reason, to Philip, who was a distinguished pupil of Saint Jerome, although it is plainly interpolated at times with additions by another hand.

The second, if indeed it is so different from the first, is found in volume 4 of the collection of Bede’s works. It is addressed to a certain Nectarius or Vecterius, whether abbot or bishop, enlarged by a Preface and by several additions within the work deriving from Bede’s own ingenuity.

We call the third the Martianay version. It is this very Interlinear Exposition which follows, first published by him from a certain manuscript of Corbie. He most certainly reports that he received it from the aforementioned Philip, a disciple of our holy Doctor, on the basis of the following testimony appended to the codex by the copyist: “This interpretation is excerpted from Philip’s Exposition.”

The fourth, finally, is the Meibomian version, named after Marcus Meibomius, in whose library at Utrecht it was found. He represented it as a genuine work of Jerome; and before a specimen of it was published, it was regarded as authentic.

I have said that these do not seem to us to be commentaries by various authors, but excerpts compiled from a single work by people who, according to their preference, either abridged passages written at greater length or expanded what had seemed to have been expressed concisely. Concerning the two which we named first, there is no doubt if one compares them with each other: not only are the ideas the same in both, but nearly the very words. From chapter 30 to the end, the words are identical in both, with not even the concluding portion of the work, as Valesius says, omitted.

If more extensive additions sometimes occur in one version, this must clearly be attributed to Bede’s ingenuity, for it was his custom to append many things of his own to the writings of earlier authors. Thus Victorius is quite spectacularly mistaken when he prefers to attribute to Bede what is assigned to Philip and, conversely, attributes to Philip what Bede compiled.

The third version itself, as the attentive reader will observe, would persuade us—even if the other arguments were absent—that it derives from Philip’s commentaries. I believe I have detected the same thing in the fourth, although in that version the compiler took every care to conceal it by slightly altering the wording.

Heumantius, who published some excerpts from it in the *Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensia* in 1711, thought that he had detected the genius of Rabanus Maurus in it, especially because of the striking similarity of style and method, which he tries to demonstrate by adducing many passages. He does not deny the meagerness of the composition, however, and says that the person who publishes it in full will not have rendered any great service to the republic of letters, since it is full of unlearned and even ridiculous interpretations. He would do much better—and this also suited our judgment—to gather from that dunghill whatever seemed useful and publish it separately, namely, what could be contained in one or two pages.

There are, moreover, two manuscript codices that claim for themselves the distinction of Jerome’s name. Since they are not different from each other, I would maintain that they are one and the same as the Meibomian version. I call one the Roman copy and the other the Duboisian copy. The latter was brought into the Dubois library by the distinguished Bignon and, about ten years ago, was sold at auction at The Hague.

Those who prepared the catalogue appended certain arguments there, apparently to commend its excellence to bidders, by which they claimed that the work could rightly be attributed to Jerome. These arguments were drawn from the contents of the book itself, so that, although it was not possible to inspect it with one’s own eyes, it could nevertheless be gathered from them, as from certain identifying marks, that it was exactly the same as the other copy, namely the Roman one, which I was permitted, at my discretion, to inspect and examine thoroughly in Rome.

A brief description must therefore be given of this Roman manuscript, which the distinguished custodian of the Vatican Library, Assemanius, very kindly made available to us, so that it may become public by what arguments—or, more truly, by what disguises—it has so far acquired its reputation.

This book is in the square format, bound in approximately 130 parchment leaves. I believe it was written only a few years before the invention of the art of printing, as its rather elegant formation of letters shows. At the beginning it copies Jerome’s earlier Preface to Job, translated from the Hebrew truth, beginning with the words, “I am compelled to answer, book by book, the curses of my opponents in Holy Scripture,” and continuing to: “Let each person choose what he wishes, and let him prove me diligent rather than malicious.”

It then appends, in continuous sequence, another complete Preface by Jerome to the same Book of Job, based on the Septuagint, restored by the addition of obeli and asterisks: “But if I were weaving a basket from rushes, I would judge that something more useful would come from my leisure for the churches of Christ, even to the end, than from the business of others.”

Thus, from Jerome’s genuine Prefaces—of which there are two to the Book of Job itself, not to a Commentary illuminating it, since we have said that no such Commentary exists, but first to the version translated from the Hebrew truth and then corrected according to the Greek exemplar—the compiler copied nearly everything word for word and adapted it to his own purpose.

It is clear that the Duboisian codex perpetrates exactly the same fraud. For those who try to pass it off as the genuine offspring of the holy Doctor say that it reflects Jerome’s character because the author now complains about rivals secretly detracting from his work, now praises the ancient translators Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion by name, and finally introduces certain remarks about translation from the Hebrew.

These are indeed Jerome’s own words:

“I am compelled to answer, book by book, the curses of my opponents, who accuse my translation of censuring the Septuagint translators, as though among the Greeks also Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion had not expressed either a word-for-word translation, or a sense-for-sense translation, or a mixed translation composed from both and balanced between them.”

Shortly afterward, when Bede cited this passage, it led many into the error of thinking that it had been taken from Jerome’s Commentary.

Finally, the Duboisian manuscript also contains what, for those who rely on their preconceived opinion, supplies a conspicuous argument for the authenticity of the work:

“For among the Hebrews also the whole Book of Job is said to be oblique and slippery, and what the Greek rhetors call *eschematismenos* (ἐσχηματισμένος), ‘figured’ or ‘expressed indirectly’: while it says one thing, it does another. Thus, if you wished to hold an eel or lamprey in tightly closed hands, the more firmly you pressed it, the more quickly it would slip away.”

The pseudonymous author repeats these words exactly and thus attempts to impose upon the faith of his readers.

The subsequent text of the Roman codex is also the same as the Meibomian version. Eleven headings follow. The first begins with the method of exposition: “Certain things are said here historically, allegorically, and morally,” and so forth. The last, concerning moral exposition, begins: “An innumerable crowd of thoughts, like maidservants, abandons its work, its mistress, when reason is absent,” and so forth. We present these in the excerpts below.

Finally, the Commentary itself is threefold and likewise divided into three columns, and it begins as follows.

[Note: In Migne, the following four paragraphs are printed in parallel. The two central paragraphs contain interlinear text.]

They fear God. Solomon: “Whoever fears God neglects nothing.” Departing from evil. Again Solomon: “Whoever offends in one matter will lose many good things.” First the suitable character is described, and only afterward his struggle is related, so that it may appear that such a man is capable of fulfilling his role. It is necessary that the dove’s simplicity be equipped with the serpent’s good kind of prudence, and that prudence be tempered by simplicity.

In the land of Uz, named Job, there was a man who was simple and upright and who feared God and departed from evil, and so forth.

That is, the land of the Gentiles, to the praise of Job, who was good among the wicked, like Lot in Sodom; like a lily among thorns, and so forth. Meekness is the principal form of righteousness. To fear God is to omit none of the things that ought to be done. For good things mixed with evil are not acceptable to the Lord.

Allegorically, Job is interpreted as “the suffering one,” Jesus Christ, who bore our sufferings. Uz: “counselor.” Therefore he inhabits the land of Uz, and hearts rightly devoted to counsel. Hence Wisdom says: “I dwell in counsel.” Simple and upright. We abandon righteousness through gentleness and gentleness through righteousness; God, as man, preserved both completely. Fearing God. Hence he filled him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord. He also departed from evil—not evil that occurs through doing, but evil that he found in the world and rejected.

It ends with these words:

[Note: In Migne, the following four paragraphs are printed in parallel. The two central paragraphs contain interlinear text.]

Can you bind together the shining stars? It is clear that no human being can do this; but when Job is questioned about them, the point is to make him take refuge humbly in the one who alone can demonstrate this.

Can you bind together the shining stars, the Pleiades, or can you disperse the circle of Orion? Can you bring out Lucifer at its appointed time, and make the evening star rise over the children of the earth? Do you know the ordinances of heaven, and can you establish its rule upon the earth? Can you raise your voice in the cloud?

Clearly, I can. Morally: Every day Lucifer shines for the good, and evening comes for the reprobate, as the word of the Lord testifies, and so forth. “In the cloud” he filled the house of the Lord—that is, the prophets and priests, and so forth.

Can you bind together the shining stars, and so forth. They are called by a plural name because they are both near one another and separate. He signifies all the saints, whom the sevenfold grace of the Spirit illumines amid the darkness of the present life. Sent at different times from the beginning of the world to its end, they are separated from one another yet united in the intention of their minds, and together proclaim one Lord, and so forth. Can you raise your voice in the cloud?

From the entire work we present excerpts after the Interlinear Exposition, somewhat fuller than the Leipzig edition. Since we have established that these glosses were originally derived from Philip’s Commentaries, but it is not easy to say which part should be regarded as wholly genuine offspring of that author, we shall append a few fragments of his work. We have copied them from a very ancient Catena on Genesis in an Ambrosian manuscript, dating from approximately the seventh century and marked beforehand with the letter F and number 60, so that they may serve as a test.

“And God said, ‘Let there be light.’” PHILIP.
