[Col. 1448B] on the poor. I expected good things, and evils came upon me; I awaited light, and darkness burst forth. My inward parts seethed without any rest. The days of affliction overtook me. Mourning, I walked about, without anger; rising, I cried out in the assembly. I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches. My skin has grown black upon me, and my bones have dried up

[Col. 1448C] because of the burning heat. My lyre has been turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep.”

[Col. 1446D] He did not do this boastfully because of his riches, but because of the baseness of the wicked, so that the fathers of those mocking him had not once been worthy even to be compared with his dogs. That is, they were despised for their laziness and baseness.

[Col. 1447A] Through misery and hunger they attacked even those things that were outside the human or animal diet, as though they were banquets and delicacies, searching through damp valleys in their extreme poverty. He spoke of this above, saying: “The rains of the mountains water them.” That is, if in their heat they covered themselves with the leaves of the most worthless thorn bushes.

[Col. 1447B] Obscure and utterly unworthy of remembrance. These matters are clear and require no historical interpretation. Because of the multitude of blows with which the devil afflicted him. Because, on account of the pain, he could speak only with difficulty. That is, these things were inflicted by permission of the divine power. For he is the one rising from on high; he is the right hand, that is, the strength of the Most High. Calamities, afflicting me through frequent repetition, overturned all the straight paths of my conduct as though with waves. They disturbed the way of my righteousness,

[Col. 1447C] lying in wait for me. By refusing to offer consolation, my neighbors. The evils mentioned above rushed upon me, he says, with such a swift assault that no one resisted. You snatched away the desire for your reward, together with salvation, as with the force of wind and the speed of a passing cloud, because you permitted it to be snatched away. That is, it is dissolved from the intensity of its strength.

[Col. 1447D] This can be understood of worms and demons, because the worms that were eating his flesh kept watch through the nights. The multitude of swarming worms, always in motion as it continued to crawl through me, wore away my clothing. For, since the whole body had been reduced to a single wound, it tortured him through unceasing eating and drinking. He says that he had been reduced to the greatest degradation, since through wounds and corruption he rotted like mud. He displays the intention of one praying to God. He says that he possessed unwavering perseverance toward God.

[Col. 1448A] He says that God had been pious and merciful toward him in prosperity but had suddenly changed in adversity. You inflict punishment by your power, because you permitted it. You raised me up through the glory of earthly honor; once this was taken away from me, I was struck down as though you had placed me upon the wind. After the sin of the first parent, hell was appointed as the house of human beings; you wished me to go there. He prophesied that the reconciliation of the world would take place in Christ. After the redemption through which we are saved by faith in Christ, if people should fall again through sin, you yourself will save them by the hand of mercy raising them through repentance. He says that he wept for the afflicted. Certainly, he suffered with the wretched.

[Col. 1448B] Divine benefits. The misery of his wounds. It happened that, instead of the light of prosperity, I encountered the darkness of torments. He expresses his sufferings, by which his inward parts were cooked with internal heat. Because I did not know the reason for the punishment, and yet I was without anger. By strength of spirit, I prayed for hope through public satisfaction. Abandoned by human beings, I was made like those birds. This contributed to the accumulation of his sufferings: while lying in filth, he endured the sun’s most burning rays penetrating to his bones for a long time.

[Col. 1448C] He says that the happiness of his days, and his joy and delight, had been turned into mourning.

## CHAPTER XXXI

“I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin. For what portion would God have in me from above, and what inheritance would the Almighty have from the heights? Is not destruction for the unjust, and alienation for those who practice injustice? Does he himself not consider my ways and count all my steps?

[Col. 1448D] And if I walked in vanity, and my foot hastened in deceit, let him weigh me in a just balance, and let God know my simplicity. And if my step turned aside from his way; and if my eye followed my heart, and a stain clung to my hands: let me sow, and let another eat, and let my offspring be uprooted. If my heart was deceived concerning a woman, and if I lay in wait at the door of my enemy,

[Col. 1449A] let my wife be another man’s prostitute, and let others bow over her. For this is a crime, and a very great iniquity. It is a fire that devours even to destruction and eradicates every growth. If I refused to enter into judgment with my servant and my maidservant when they disputed against me, what then shall I do when God rises to judge? And when he investigates, what shall I answer him? Did not the one who made me in the womb also make him, and did not one and the same creator form us in the womb?

[Col. 1449B] And if I denied the poor what they wanted, and caused the eyes of the widow to wait. If I ate my morsel of bread alone, and the orphan did not eat from it [Vulgate omits “of bread”], because compassion grew up with me from my infancy and came forth with me from my mother’s womb. If I looked down upon one who was perishing because he had no clothing, and upon the poor man without a covering,

[Col. 1449C] if his sides did not bless me, and he was warmed by the fleeces of my sheep. If I raised my hand against the orphan, even when I saw myself superior in the gate, may my shoulder fall from its joint, and may my arm be broken with its bones. For I always feared God as though waves were swelling over me,

[Col. 1449D] and I was unable to bear his weight. If I thought gold was my strength, and said that fine gold was my confidence [Vulgate: ‘my confidence’]. If I rejoiced over my many riches, and if my hand had found very much. If I saw the sun when it shone and the moon moving

[Col. 1450A] brightly, and my heart rejoiced in secret, and I kissed my hand with my mouth. This is a very great iniquity and a denial against the Most High God. If I rejoiced at the ruin of one who hated me, and exulted because evil had found him, so that I might seek his soul with a curse. If the men of my tent did not say: ‘Who will give us some of his flesh, that we may be satisfied?’ No stranger remained outside;

[Col. 1450B] my door was open to the traveler. If, like a human being, I concealed my sin and hid my iniquity in my bosom. If I was afraid of the excessive multitude, and the contempt of relatives terrified me, and I did not remain silent, nor go out of the door. Who will grant me a hearer, so that the Almighty may hear my desire? Let him himself who judges write a book, so that I may carry it on my shoulder

[Col. 1450C] and place it around me like a crown. At each of my steps I shall proclaim it, and offer it as to a prince. If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it. If I ate its produce without payment, and afflicted the souls of its farmers, may thistles spring up for me instead of wheat, and thorns instead of barley.” The words of Job are ended.

[Col. 1448C] “I,” he says, “determined and resolved with the eyes of my flesh that they should report to me nothing shameful or obscene, which I might inwardly turn over in wicked thoughts through the pleasure of desire.” And therefore he had girded himself with the virtue of continence, fearing the eye of God, since he is the searcher of the heart and knows all the ways of human conduct and all the steps of human actions. Here “vanity” is used in place of arrogance.

[Col. 1448D] Holy Job, certain of the equity of God’s justice, desires that he be made manifest to human beings. Let him make my deeds known to others—the works of my life in relation to the way of God’s commandments. In my heart I did not consent to the desire that my eyes presented. No stain of sin could cling to my works. He confirms this with a kind of oath and imprecation. He speaks according to the good of nature, as it is written in Tobit: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV, 16).

[Col. 1449A] To think or do such mournful and detestable things. It is the fire of lust, consuming all the good works of the virtues. The holy man displays great humility. Great is the thought of future judgment, which continually presses the heart into humility, so that he does not consider in those same servants the inequality of their status, but the commonality of their nature. Why should we not likewise be examined in the judgment of every matter, since by the power of the Creator we have been made equal? Through these words

[Col. 1449B] the holy man is shown to have served not only the poor in their need but also the desire to provide assistance to them. He speaks of every kind of food, fulfilling the command: “Break your bread for the hungry.” In praise of the Creator he says that he received from him the fact that he was compassionate, from the one from whom he received the fact that he existed; for just as he was not formed in the womb by his own work, so neither was he compassionate from the womb by his own virtue. In accordance with: “If you see a naked person, cover him.”

[Col. 1449C] He indicates that he also took pity on an unknown neighbor, whom he calls someone passing by. He said all these things to signify how the work of mercy ought to be done: namely, that you should not take from one person what you imagine you are giving to another, as Solomon says: “Honor the Lord from your righteous labors.” I did not wish to exercise my power against the orphan when I saw myself, even in accordance with justice, superior in judgment. The shoulder signifies works. “Unless it is as I say,” he says, “all my labors will come before God in vain.” The virtue of perseverance in good works.

[Col. 1449D] Thus the person who desires the true life fears God as though waves were swelling over him, while he despises everything else. How will one who despises all things be able to bear God’s weight, if he too endured in punishment what he had foreseen through fear? He also testifies that he regarded gold as nothing. As a man of true philosophy, he was held by no vice, just as he is now a most courageous despiser of greed and arrogance. “Not only,” he says, “did I not delight in the worship of idols, but I was not even delighted by the beauty and appearance of these great lights;

[Col. 1450A] nor, as though worshiping them, did I kiss my hand in reverence for them; nor did I venerate the creature in place of the Creator.” It is a great thing if someone does not wish to avenge himself upon his enemies when he is able to do so; how much more beautiful before God not even to rejoice in their ruin in one’s heart? The servants, overcome by weariness from their labor, cursed their master, because through the hospitality by which the other saints pleased God, he had incurred the hatred of his servants. He would willingly receive everyone.

[Col. 1450B] He speaks only of those sins that are committed in thought, because he himself did not wish to conceal them. This depends upon what precedes, as though he were saying: “I was not ashamed to confess before the multitude of the people.” Because, while he was placed in misery, they continually inflicted insults upon him out of contempt. He observed the saying: “I set a guard over my mouth” (Ps. XXXVIII, 2), and what follows. He implores God as a hearer for the many virtues of his righteousness, knowing that he is the most just judge.

[Col. 1450C] For this reason he desired, on account of the merit of his just recompense, a book written by him; he would display it to others on his shoulder, in a place visible to all, and would be crowned with a crown of glory for the merits of his labor. A book for the author of all good things, so that by it he might judge me more gloriously. If he should not obtain the measure of his possibility. If it were alive and possessed reason, it could cry out and lament wrongs committed. He indicates that he did not take its produce without the corresponding expense of labor, nor while the laborers were crushed by harsh work. In accordance with: “I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes” (Isa. V, 2). The divine words are most firmly established and cannot be made void.

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 1450D]

These three men ceased to answer Job because he seemed righteous to himself. And Eliu, son of Barachiel [Vulgate: Barachel] the Buzite, of the family of Ram, became angry

[Col. 1451A] and indignant. He was angry with Job because he said that he was righteous before God. But he was angry with his friends because they had not found a reasonable answer, but had merely condemned Job. Therefore Eliu had waited for Job to speak, because those who were speaking were older.

[Col. 1451B] But when he saw that the three could not answer, he became exceedingly angry. And Eliu, son of Barachiel [Vulgate: Barachel] the Buzite, answered and said:

“I am younger in age, but you are older; therefore, lowering my head, I was afraid to declare my opinion to you. For I hoped that greater age would speak, and that the multitude of years would teach wisdom. But, as I see, there is a spirit in human beings, and the breath [Vulgate: inspiration] of the Almighty gives

[Col. 1451C] understanding. The long-lived are not necessarily wise, nor do the aged understand judgment. Therefore I say: Hear me; I too shall show you my opinion. For I waited for your speeches; I heard your prudence. While you disputed in words, and while I thought you were saying something, I paid attention. But as I see, there is no one who can convict Job and answer his words among you. Lest you perhaps say: ‘We have found wisdom; God has cast him away, not man.’ He has spoken nothing to me, and I shall not answer him according to your speeches.

[Col. 1451D] And they were afraid, and answered no more; they withdrew their words. Since, therefore, I waited and they did not speak, they stood and answered no further. I too shall answer my part and display my knowledge. For I am full of words, and the spirit of my womb constrains me.

[Col. 1452A] Behold, my belly is like wine without a vent, which bursts new wineskins. I shall speak and answer briefly; I shall open my lips and answer. I shall not show partiality to a man, nor equate God with a human being. For I do not know how long I shall remain, or whether my Maker will take me away after a short time.”

[Col. 1450D] The writer of this history spoke from the perspective of the respondents, saying that Job seemed righteous to himself, not expressing his own judgment. Chus and Buz were sons of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. From the line of Chus Job was born, and from the line of Buz

[Note: [Col. 1449D] Here the statement of the genuine Jerome in the Hebrew Questions on Genesis, chapter XXII, 20, must be referred: “The second,” he says, “was born to Milcah: Buz, whom the Seventy wished to translate as Bauz. And from his line came that diviner Balaam, as the Hebrews report, who in the Book of Job is called Eliu: first a holy man and prophet of God,

[Col. 1450D] later, through disobedience and desire for gifts, while he wished to curse Israel, he is called by the name of a diviner. And in the same book it is said: ‘And Eliu, son of Barachiel, the Buzite,’ descending, that is, from the root of this Buz. See what we annotate concerning him at that place, col. 339, note d.]

[Col. 1450D] Eliu was born, and hence he is called a Buzite. He is also Balaam under another name, the son of Beor, whom, as we read in Numbers (Num. XXXII), Balak

[Col. 1451A] king of the Moabites hired to curse Israel. He also possessed the spirit of prophecy, but not in the manner or by the grace of the holy prophets. That is, Abraham. As is demonstrated by the content of the words, it seems to me that the events we read here took place before those which we read in Numbers concerning this Eliu, or Balaam; and that he was closer in time to Abraham and Nahor than to Moses. When he rebuked holy Job in words, he was a young man, and he lived into old age until the time of Moses.

[Col. 1451B] Clearly, blessed Job preserved patience not for his own sake but out of respect for his friends. I think that this alone should briefly be made clear: as long as Eliu kept silent out of regard for his age, he was wiser; but when, in other matters, he preferred himself on account of the multitude of his years and despised others, he showed how childishly foolish he was. He says that it seems more likely to him that human beings are moved by the spirit when God has granted them the inspiration of his wisdom; he says this obliquely, as a reproach to those mentioned above,

[Col. 1451C] as though this good of wisdom had been granted to him alone. In these speeches he shows that he kept silent because of his pride, judging the words of the elders with a desire to speak rather than to learn. As though he were saying: “Do not suppose that God cast away an innocent man, but rather that, according to his deserts, he most deservedly endured all those evils of punishment; for the divine will is justice.” He says: “Job held no disputation against me; nor do I, as you do, attack him with curses and insults.”

[Col. 1451D] This Eliu says that the friends of blessed Job were defeated by him, since they stood fast in their disputes, unable to proceed any further or answer. Therefore I too, Eliu says, shall attempt to answer according to my strength, and shall display both my knowledge and Job’s knowledge to you. That he says this from the boastfulness of vanity is sufficiently evident in what follows.

[Col. 1452A] He called his belly, or womb, his memory, because he had gathered almost all the speeches of Job and his friends, who had disagreed for some time, like food within the capacity of his memory. It is the judgment of my just decision that I should neither spare a human being by withholding the truth nor wrong God by claiming that he acted unjustly. And therefore I cannot remain silent about what is true, especially since I do not know how long I shall remain in this life, since perhaps, while I am speaking these very words, my Maker and Creator will take me away.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

“Hear now, Job, and listen to all my speeches:

[Col. 1452B] Behold, I have opened my mouth; let my tongue speak in my throat. My words will be spoken with a simple heart, and my lips, pure, will speak my judgment. The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life. If you can, answer me and stand against my face. Behold, God made me as he made you, and I too was formed from the same clay. Nevertheless, let not my miracle terrify you;

[Col. 1452C] my eloquence shall not be burdensome to you. You have spoken in my ears, and I heard the sound of your words: ‘I am clean, without fault, blameless, and there is no iniquity in me, because he found no complaints against me. Therefore he considered me his enemy; he placed my feet in the stocks and guarded all my paths.’ This, then, is the matter in which you are not justified. I shall answer you that God is greater than man; you contend against him because he has not answered you concerning every word of your complaints.

[Col. 1452D] God speaks once, and he does not repeat the same thing a second time. In a dream, in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon human beings and they sleep in their bed. Then he opens the ears of men and, instructing them, teaches them discipline. To turn a person away from the things he does and deliver him from pride. Delivering his soul from corruption

[Col. 1453A] and his life from passing to the sword. He also rebukes him through pain in bed and makes all his bones wither. Bread becomes detestable to him in his life, and the food formerly desired by his soul. His flesh wastes away, and the bones that had been covered are exposed. His soul draws near to corruption, and his life to things that bring death.

[Col. 1453B] If there should be for him an angel speaking, one among a thousand, to announce the righteousness of the man, he will have mercy on him and say: ‘Deliver him, and let him not descend into corruption. I have found a means by which I may be gracious to him; his flesh has been consumed by punishments. Let him return to the days of his youth.’ He will entreat God, and God will be gracious to him; he will see his face with rejoicing. And he will restore to the man his righteousness; and the man will look

[Col. 1453C] and say: ‘I have sinned, and truly I have transgressed, and I have not received what I deserved.’ He will deliver his soul so that it does not proceed into destruction, but, while living, sees the light. Behold, God does all these things three times for each person, to recall their souls from corruption and illumine them with the light of the living.

[Col. 1453D] Pay attention, Job, and hear me, and be silent while I speak. But if you have something to say, answer me; speak. For I wish you to appear righteous. If you do not, hear me, be silent, and I shall teach you my wisdom.”

[Col. 1452A] “As though he already had an open mouth, which he had long kept covered in silence.” With these words prefaced, he prepares the hearer’s mind: without deceit—that is, in simplicity of heart and with pure lips—he is about to speak a settled discourse as though it were an authoritative judgment. To establish his authority to be heard, he began to speak in such a way as to suggest that one made by God’s Spirit and animated by the breath of the Almighty cannot speak anything but truth and rectitude.

Perhaps Elihu said this concerning the creation of the first human being, in which he declares himself formed, as it were, at the source from which he flowed. As he is about to utter his words, he demands attention, so that under a certain blandishment and feigned consolation he may instill the terror of threats, and Job, disturbed by it, may readily yield to his verbosity.

[Col. 1452C] What then are we to say of his making holy Job say of God: “Because he found no complaints in me, he therefore considered me his enemy”? We do not read that Job said this. He has here composed it in his own words, as though it expressed the sentiment of that same holy Job. That is: you ought to have accused yourself, not praised yourself. “Why then,” he says, “do you try to contend against him because he does not answer you, as though satisfying you, on every word of your complaints?”

[Col. 1452D] For he does not alter what he speaks, unless the very change of our life requires it. God sometimes sends a heavier sleep upon a person with rebuke, so that, when the bodily senses are lulled, the mind may be bound to receive the words of the Lord’s discipline; this is called the Lord’s sleep. Of these ears the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8)—that is, ears turned away from sins. For just as this bodily death is inflicted by the sword, so the second death is incurred through sin; from it he rightly declares that those who have been chastised and corrected will be delivered.

[Col. 1453A] Elihu says: “God not only terrifies human souls by dreadful visions in order to correct offenders, but also torments them with bodily infirmities in order to amend them. Therefore, when a person has been worn out and consumed by these things and has drawn near to death and the ministers of hell, if there is some saint who deserves to bear the name of Angel, he will be able to obtain mercy for one thus rebuked by God for his sins, if he can find at least one good work—which he ought to have performed among many good works—to offer for him as an acceptable sacrifice.”

[Col. 1453B] Or any angel standing from heaven before God’s face may intercede for any sinner placed under scourges; for God has imposed upon them the charge of bringing help to the people committed to their guardianship. “He has received evils according to his merits; now, by the pardon of divine mercy, let him return to the days of youth”—that is, let him again be sound and unharmed. He will see God’s face, sensing his countenance to be favorable to him, and will render him justice by worthy satisfaction. It is a great thing, and exceedingly acceptable to God, for a person not to be ashamed to confess his errors and to say that he has suffered too little for his deserts.

[Col. 1453C] Enlightened, he will recognize the light of the knowledge of God and his immeasurable benefits. He is crushed, and, purified by that very crushing, is delivered—that is, either by the labor of conversion, or by the trial of temptation, or by fear of dissolution. Of this light the Prophet says: “That I may please God in the light of the living” (Ps. 55:13). “Be obedient when I teach you, and give assent.” He commands him, as unlearned or impatient, to be silent. Here he wishes to show that holy Job had been corrected and convicted by his words and by the truth, and that he would speak no more against his friends.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Elihu therefore also spoke these things: “Hear my words, you wise men; and you learned, listen to me. For the ear tests words, and the throat judges foods by taste. Let us choose judgment for ourselves, and let us see among ourselves what is better. For Job said: ‘I am just, and God has overthrown my judgment. In judging me there is falsehood; my violent arrow is without sin.’

“Who is the man like Job, who drinks mockery like water, who goes with workers of iniquity and walks with impious men? For he said: ‘A man will not please God, even if he runs with him.’ Therefore, men of understanding, hear me: far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty. For he will render to a person his work and repay each according to his ways. Truly God does not condemn without cause, and the Almighty does not overthrow judgment.

[Col. 1454B] “Whom has he appointed over the earth besides himself? Or whom has he set over the world which he made? If he should direct his heart toward him, he would draw his spirit and breath back to himself. All flesh would fail together, and man would return to ashes. If therefore you have understanding, hear what is said, and listen to the voice of my discourse. Can one who does not love judgment be healed? And how do you condemn so greatly him who is just?

[Col. 1454C] “He says to a king, ‘Apostate,’ and calls judges impious; he does not accept the person of princes, nor recognize a tyrant when he pleads against a poor man. For all are the work of his hands; they will die suddenly, and at midnight peoples will be troubled; they will pass away, and the violent man will be removed without a hand. For his eyes are upon the ways of men, and he considers all their steps. There are no darknesses and no shadow of death in which those who work iniquity may hide themselves.

[Col. 1455A] “For it is no longer in a person’s power to come before the Lord in judgment. He will crush many, even numberless persons, and set others in their place. For he knows their works, and therefore he will bring on night, and they will be crushed. He struck them as impious persons in a place where people see, because they deliberately withdrew from him and would not understand any of his ways, so as to bring before him the cry of the needy, that he might hear the voice of the poor.

[Col. 1455B] “But when he grants peace, who is there to condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him? This applies alike over nations and over all human beings: he makes a hypocritical man reign because of the sins of the people. Since therefore I have spoken to the Lord, I will not forbid you also to speak: ‘If I have erred, teach me; if I have spoken iniquity, I will add no more.’ Will God demand it of you, though it displeased you? For you began to speak, not I; if you know anything better, speak.

[Col. 1455C] “Let intelligent men speak to me, and let a wise man hear me. But Job has spoken foolishly, and his words do not convey instruction. My father, let Job be tested to the end; do not cease from the man of iniquity. For he adds blasphemy to his sins; meanwhile let him be bound among us, and then let him summon God to judgment by his words.”

[Col. 1453D] He is said to pronounce this as though giving a judgment, and, while blessed Job disputes generally against the impious, he wishes him to be understood as their associate. Just as the taste of foods is discerned by the palate, so words are tested by the judgment of the ears. That is: let us examine matters before we condemn a man. Job did not utter this speech.

[Col. 1454A] Likewise, we do not read this either. “No one” is understood: no one who, being iniquitous and impious, is not afraid to mock and deride God. His inward parts are filled, like an abundance of water, with the poison of this passion. Again, he falsely alleges that holy Job spoke of God enviously. “If anyone were so great that he met God in fulfilling all his commands”—we do not remember holy Job saying this. Having thus laid out holy Job’s alleged impiety and brought it before the hearers to make Job odious, as though he had spoken impiously, he disputes concerning God’s equity and justice.

[Col. 1454B] These things are plain and need no historical interpretation, because affliction increases the merits of the innocent. “No one else” is understood, because he who is so mighty a Creator is also so merciful a Governor: he knows and loves his work. The heart is directed if it is lifted up to heavenly things. By “spirit” he means the soul, which gives life to a human being; by “breath,” the present life supplied to our bodies by inhalation from this air, when he takes it away from people.

[Col. 1454C] After Elihu had spoken above about God’s power and justice, he again turns to Job. “It is plain,” he says, “that one who does not love to judge justly and rightly can neither heal a soul of vices nor correct anyone; and how do you presume to mark God, the healer of our infirmities, with iniquity?” God does not accept the person of a king if he is iniquitous and rebellious against him, nor of leaders if they are impious; rather, according to his singular justice, he says to an iniquitous king: “Apostate.” The scribes, Pharisees, and priests, because of their sins—the Jewish people were disputing against Christ, who, though rich, became poor for us.

[Col. 1454D] However fiercely the wicked are removed from this life, they are removed suddenly and unexpectedly, in a sudden tempest, because they do not know how to foresee their end by reflection. The violent man will have no helper by whom he may be rescued from the punishment of death. “Without a hand” means that the violent enemy will be led to punishment without protection. This is plain. Of this the Psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” and the rest (Ps. 138).

[Col. 1455A] We are reminded of this because, when we then cannot act, we should not neglect what we can do now. We have already said this, as occurred with Eli and Samuel, David and Saul, and the peoples of Jews and Gentiles. It may be understood of the Jews, who were blinded in the night of unbelief and are punished by vengeance. All sinners and impious persons act against the natural good placed in them; they refused to know and understand, in order to fulfill in deed, all the ways of God’s commandments which they had inborn in their hearts. They also acted impiously against people, so that the voice of the poor and needy rose to God.

[Col. 1455B] When God grants peace, no human being can examine matters in order to condemn—that is, revoke his act as void. Unless he himself deigns to reveal himself to a person, no one will be able to behold him by his own powers. God will do what he wills. The devil is called a hypocrite because he transforms himself into an angel of light, when he is rather the author of darkness. Thus, by God’s judgment, he rules over the impious. Elihu permits him to speak as though set before a court. For he would not ask if he believed that he had erred.

[Col. 1455C] That is: “I will not speak.” That is: blasphemy. You said that he was unjust, that by the force of an unjust correction he exacted from you that you must, being unjustly afflicted, speak blasphemy against him; and therefore he displeased you. In his pride he doubted the knowledge of one better informed. Despising holy Job, Elihu turned to those standing nearby and spoke. He believed that blessed Job had spoken without instruction because he recalled that he had been just in his works. This is plain. For man was created by him. Let the blow of this scourge remain continually upon him. Let a blow be inflicted upon him. He adds to the heap of sins so as to incur the crime of blasphemy.

[Col. 1455D] “Meanwhile let him be condemned among us, lest injustice be imputed to us also. It will be without our fault if afterward he tries to summon God; if through our assertion he learns that he is in no way adequate for divine examination.”

## CHAPTER XXXV

Elihu again spoke these things: “Do you think your thought just, when you say, ‘I am more just than God’? You said: ‘What is right will not please you’; or, ‘What benefit will there be to me if I sin?’ Therefore I too will answer your words, and your friends with you. Look up to heaven and see; contemplate the sky, which is higher than you.

[Col. 1456A] “If you sin, what harm will you do him? If your iniquities are multiplied, what will you do against him? But if you act justly, what will you give him, or what will he receive from your hand? Your impiety will harm a person like yourself, and your justice will help a son of man. Because of the multitude of oppressors they will cry out and howl because of the violence of tyrants’ arm. Yet they did not say: ‘Where is God, who made me, who gives songs in the night, who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and teaches us wisdom beyond the birds of heaven?’

“They will cry out, but he will not answer, because of the pride of evil men. Therefore God will not hear in vain, and the Almighty will regard the causes of individuals. Even when you say, ‘He does not consider it,’ judge before him and wait for him; for now he does not bring on his fury, nor does he exact punishment for crime to the full. Thus Job opened his mouth in vain and multiplied words without knowledge.”

[Col. 1455D] Throughout all those nine replies of blessed Job, in which he answered his friends’ individual speeches, we do not find that holy Job said any of these things. But it is characteristic of the arrogant that, when they cannot rightly criticize what exists, they criticize by lying about what does not exist. Since they could not answer him rationally, Elihu says this. He imagined that God was bodily confined to places and dwelt only in the heights. It is as though he said: “When you sin, no harm is inflicted upon God.”

Nevertheless, what is said is true: our sins do not harm God, nor do our good deeds contribute anything to him. If he wishes to avenge himself upon you, can you resist him? Yet these things ought by no means to have been said to blessed Job, who knew greater matters. As David says to God: “You have no need of my goods.”

[Col. 1456A] Whoever imitates your impiety will be harmed by it. Likewise, whoever follows justice will be helped by justice. In this plural form of his argument Elihu associates holy Job with such people and declares him like them. He calls the wicked men oppressors and tyrants. The multitude may mean the impious, or demons. Consolation in tribulation. God gave human beings reason and wisdom above all living creatures, not only through the good of nature but also through the gifts of grace. He makes clear why sinners are not heard. God does not hear those who persist in evil, and those who do not deserve to be heard cry out in vain. Bear it patiently, and do not say that God’s providence is absent from the world. He urges him to consent to God’s judgments, because God has appointed a day of judgment.

He says all this as a reproach to holy Job, whom he declares to be guilty and destined to suffer punishments here and greater ones in the future. Elihu considers holy Job convicted and enclosed, as it were, by a certain verbal argument. For the more arrogantly learned people wish to show themselves, the more fully they expose themselves through their abundance of talk.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

[Col. 1456D] Moreover, Elihu continued and said:

“Bear with me a little, and I will show you; for I still have something to say on God’s behalf. I will repeat my knowledge from the beginning and prove my Maker to be just. Truly my words are without falsehood, and perfect knowledge will be demonstrated to you.

“God does not reject the mighty, since he himself is mighty. But he does not save the impious; he grants judgment to the poor and does not remove his eyes from the just. He establishes kings upon the throne forever; they are raised up, even if they have been in chains and bound with the cords of poverty. He declares to them their works and their crimes, because they have acted violently. He also opens their ears to correct them and speaks so that they may turn back from their iniquity.

“If they listen and obey, they will complete their days in goodness and their years in glory. But if they do not listen, they will pass away by the sword and be consumed in folly. Hypocrites and crafty men provoke God’s wrath, and they will not cry out when they are bound. Their soul will die in the storm, and their life will be among the effeminate.

“He will rescue the poor from his distress and open his ear in tribulation. Therefore he will save you from the narrow mouth, broadening it greatly, where there is no foundation beneath it. Your table’s rest will be full of fatness. Your cause has been judged as that of an impious man; you will receive a cause and a judgment.

“Therefore let anger not overcome you so that you oppress anyone, nor let the multitude of gifts incline you. Lay aside your greatness without distress, and all the strong in power. Do not prolong the night so that peoples may rise up on their behalf. Beware lest you turn toward iniquity; for after your misery you have begun to follow this.

“Behold, God is exalted in his strength, and none is like him among lawgivers. Who can search out his ways, or who can say to him, ‘You have acted unjustly’? Remember that you do not know his work, concerning which men have sung. All human beings have seen him; each one beholds him from afar.

“Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge; the number of his years is beyond calculation. He draws away the drops of rain and pours down showers like torrents. For waters flow from the clouds, and from above they cover everything. If he wishes to spread the clouds like his tent and flash with his light from above, he covers also the hinges of the sea. Through these things he judges peoples and gives food to many mortals.

“In his hands he hides the light and commands it to return. He announces concerning it to his friend that it is his possession and that he may ascend to it.”

[Col. 1456D] That is, on behalf of God’s justice and cause. In the knowledge he claims, the swelling of his heart is revealed. While he seems to speak on behalf of God’s justice, he excuses whatever flows arrogantly from him before human judgments.

In this, his fourth speech, he pursues at excessive length and with abundant discourse the singular justice of God. By the goodness of his nature, God is willing to envy no one, since no one, however powerful, can equal him. He destroys the exalted but makes the humble free according to the rule of his justice, as David says: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the just,” and so forth.

[Col. 1457A] Here “kings” means not only the kings of this world but also the kings and leaders of the Church. Those who have been humbled here are raised up there. This is still the restraint of pilgrimage: they are bound by the strong judgments of God and by the cords of poverty, having no assistance from divine help and having become needy in every good thing.

“According to the quality of their merits.” Or: the saints, loving heavenly glory, condemn their evils through repentance. Through chastisements and secret inspirations God will open the ears of their hearts to obey him, so that they may perceive desire for eternal goods and recognize the evils they committed outwardly. As Solomon says: “The memory of the righteous is with praises,” and so forth (Ps. 33).

[Col. 1457B] If, while God teaches them, they despise him, they will pass from this world through this mortality and will be assigned to the place where fools have been established. In this passage Elihu seems to strike holy Job more openly, though indirectly, alleging that he acted craftily and wickedly and took no care to invoke God so that he might rescue him from the scourge of his affliction.

The soul of the wicked will always be amid the storm of vices. We should understand “vicious people,” or “vices,” as those that possess no virtue of soul. The saints receive consolation from every tribulation in the ear of the heart, hearing God there.

Here Elihu describes the dwellings of hell as spacious for receiving but narrow for release, because of their immense capacity. He signifies the pleasantness of paradise, abounding in every good. According to your merit, you have received a most severe judgment. The holy man was overcome by anger and desire, by which he had not previously been held. For if you are exalted by universal veneration, you will fall away from inward attentiveness.

[Col. 1457C] Here he marks holy Job as proud and arrogant: the swelling and elation of your mind. Let neither the ordinary nor the powerful be unjustly crushed by your strength. It is enough to have lived until now in this blindness; now strive to come to the light of prudence, lest peoples testify before God against your crimes. I ask you not to fall into despair, and now to beware of the iniquity of blasphemy.

“Recognize,” he says, “that no one can be unjustly condemned by God, who alone is strong and wise. Who, unless he is impious and proud, thinks that he can comprehend the Lord’s judgments? Who, then, is so rash as to dare say this?” All these things are said as an insult to Job.

[Col. 1457D] Since his miracles surpass human understanding—that is, the prophets. Through the good of nature there is knowledge of the Creator in human hearts. Although he is far away, a person nevertheless senses and understands God. By the greatness of his wisdom and the depth of his judgments. Through this, the enduring nature of God is shown and he is demonstrated to be infinite and incomprehensible.

The Jews, because of their unbelief, rejected the precepts of Moses’ law. He poured out the grace of the Holy Spirit abundantly upon believers. The apostles and apostolic preachers cover the hearts of carnal people with the hidden mysteries of God. For the voice of the preachers has gone out into all the earth.

[Col. 1458B] Through the preachers of Christ’s name, fame shone forth like a light and occupied the ends of the world. “Of the world,” that is, through the preachers. He gives all mortals the teaching of his word, or of the mysteries. That is, he rightly hides the preaching of the Gospel in evil works. To those who deserve it, God sends the light of his manifestation into the heart, choosing them as his friends so that they may possess the kingdom, advancing through good works.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

[Col. 1458B] “Over this my heart trembles, and it is moved from its place. Hear the hearing of his voice in terror and the sound proceeding from his mouth. He looks upon everything beneath the heavens, and his light is over the ends of the earth. After him a roar resounds; he thunders with the voice of his greatness.

“When his voice is heard, it cannot be investigated. God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great and inscrutable things. He commands snow to descend upon the earth, and the rains of winter and the storm of his strength. He marks the hand of every human being, so that each may know his works.

“The beast enters its hiding place and remains in its den. From within comes the storm, and cold from the Bear. When God blows, frost congeals, and again the waters are poured out over a vast expanse. The cloud desires grain, and the clouds scatter their light; they illuminate all around. Wherever their will leads them, they go to everything he has commanded them, upon the face of the inhabited world: whether over one tribe, or over his own land, or wherever he has ordered them to be found by his mercy.

“Listen to this, Job; stand and consider the wonders of God. Do you know when God commanded the rains so that they might display the light of his clouds? Do you know the paths of the clouds, their great and perfect knowledge? Are your garments warm when the earth is fanned by the South wind?

“Did you perhaps build the heavens with him, which are as solid as bronze poured out? Show us what we should say to him; for we are wrapped in darkness. Who will suddenly tell him what I say? Even if a man speaks, he will be swallowed up.

“But now they do not see the light; suddenly the air will be compressed into clouds, and the passing wind will drive them away. From the North gold will come, and a fearful praise to God. We cannot find him worthily. He is great in strength, judgment, and justice, and he cannot be described. Therefore they will fear him, and all who seem wise in their own eyes will not dare to behold him.”

[Col. 1458B] I marvel at how he is near to the faithful: from worse things to better, or from ignorance to knowledge of secrets.

[Col. 1458C] The teaching of divine law, because they resound with the word of God strongly and terribly. He searches into his saints while he examines what is hidden within them. They are the saints who put an end to earthly desires. Human beings roar in repentance when God has been recognized, proclaiming the kingdom of heaven.

For before God comes to anyone, who could investigate him? “No one” is understood. Through thunder, or through preachers, when he makes knowledge of his name resound in the ear of the mind.

[Col. 1458D] The grace of the Holy Spirit, by the command of the Godhead, through Christ, by whom our old condition is restored to something better. The heavy persecutions of the Church were overcome by the rain of the strength of the Holy Spirit. He shows that free choice is present in each person.

The first enemy is the sinner’s heart, which is called a solitary beast, in the hidden place of the ruined mind, in the hearts where the beast dwells. The pursuit of persecutions; from the North, the distrust of unbelief. By God’s command, or by his permission, unbelievers are hardened. In the love of charity, an abundance of teaching.

[Col. 1459A] The preachers pour out teaching. Concerning this grain it is said: “Gather the wheat into the barn” (Matt. 13:30). The teachers’ brightness of speech, because by teaching they fortify their hearers on every side. As the Psalmist says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18:15), and so forth—that is, the sound of God, who through them sends his word into the earth. As he himself says: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria” (Acts 1).

Through the grace and mercy of Christ he signifies those who are to be called to the faith. Elihu admonishes Job to attend carefully with the ear of his heart to the sacraments that are to be fulfilled in Christ and the Church. He recalls future things on the basis of what has happened.

[Col. 1459B] Therefore God commanded the evangelical rains, so that the holy works of teachers might be displayed through the infusion of faith. He clearly shows that he is speaking of rational clouds: the paths of the preachers and the tracks of subtle meanings. The virtues of souls burning with love of God through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

These things are said by Elihu according to the literal sense, ironically and as an insult to Job. The saints are compared to solid bronze, because they sounded forth the evangelical trumpet and remained exceedingly strong in Christ. “While you were accustomed to speak with him”—that is, in the darkness of ignorance.

Does he himself not know, since he does not need a witness? Whoever thinks that anything is hidden from him will be overwhelmed by his knowledge.

[Col. 1459C] In this world. Spiritual knowledge. “Yes,” he says, “they have been stirred up in such unbelief that they become like air and, by God’s judgment, will be carried away like a gust of wind.”

The saints are redeemed from the devil by the blood of the Lord, praising God with trembling. As he is, he cannot be found by his creature. Just as he is great and powerful in strength, so he is true in judgment and justice, and cannot be described. They will not presume to search out the incomprehensible or behold the invisible.

All this is said as a reproach to holy Job, who complained that he was scourged by God without any merit of iniquity.

(By contrast, the Lord, answering Job from the whirlwind, said: “By my angels and by the throne of my kingdom, [I swear—the wording is corrupt] that if for the space of one year you had made amendments in the world, I would never have recalled your former deeds to you.”)

This statement is said to have been taken from the Book of the Shepherd.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 1459D] But the Lord answered Job from the whirlwind and said:

“Who is this who entangles counsels with unlearned words? Gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and you answer me. Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding.

“Who determined its measurements, if you know? Or who stretched the measuring line over it? Upon what were its bases made firm? Or who laid its cornerstone? When the morning stars praised me together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?

“Who enclosed the sea with doors when it burst forth as though proceeding from the womb? When I made the cloud its garment and wrapped it in darkness as in the swaddling clothes of infancy? I surrounded it with my boundaries, set a bar and doors, and said: ‘This far you shall come, and you shall go no farther; here your swelling waves shall be broken.’

“Have you, since your birth, commanded the dawn and shown the morning its place? Have you taken hold of the ends of the earth, shaking them, and shaken the wicked out of it? It is turned like clay under a seal and takes its stand like a garment; the light will be taken away from the wicked, and the uplifted arm will be broken.

“Have you entered into the depths of the sea and walked in the farthest parts of the abyss? Have the gates of death been opened to you, and have you seen the dark doors? Have you considered the breadths of the earth? Tell me, if you know all things: by what way does the light dwell, and where is the place of darkness, so that you may lead each to its boundaries and understand the paths of its house?

“Did you know then that you would be born, and did you know the number of your days? Have you entered the treasuries of snow, or looked upon the treasuries of hail, which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?

“By what way is the light dispersed, and the heat divided over the earth? Who gave a course to the most violent rain and a way to the thunder of the crashing storm, so that it might rain upon the earth without a human being, in the desert where no mortal dwells? So that it might fill the trackless and desolate place and bring forth green herbs?

“Who is the father of rain, or who begot the drops of dew? From whose womb did ice come forth, and who begot the frost from heaven? The waters harden like stone, and the face of the abyss is bound fast.

“Can you join together the shining stars of the Pleiades, or can you break apart the circle of Arcturus? Can you bring out the morning star in its time and cause evening to rise over the sons of earth? Do you know the order of heaven and establish its reasoning upon the earth?

“Can you lift up your voice to the clouds, and will the force of the waters cover you? Can you send forth lightning, and will they go, and on returning say to you, ‘Here we are’? Who placed wisdom in the inward parts of man, or who gave the rooster understanding?

“Who has recounted the ordering of the heavens, and who causes the harmony of heaven to sleep? When dust was poured upon the earth and clods were joined together, can you seize prey for the lioness and fill the souls of her cubs when they lie in their dens and lie in wait in their caves?

“Who prepares food for the raven when its young cry out to God, wandering because they have no food?”

[Col. 1459D] This belongs to the terror of the one rebuking. By these words Elihu is removed, confounded together with his speeches. After Elihu has been removed with his foolish speeches, [Col. 1460A] the Lord turns to Job. Just as we gird clothing around the loins, so let us fortify the course of the soul with good works. That is, I would establish the Church, gathered from the earth of the human race, in the strength of faith. God describes his strength and power, and the dimensions of the world, in its creation—over it he has stretched the line of his good and righteous work. The powerful and strong: those who sustain the Church of God. He is the cornerstone, appointed by God as the foundation of the Lord’s earth. For a cornerstone is quadrangular and made stable on every side. It signifies Christ, in whom the peoples are contained. That is, the angels before they fell. Those who always stood in goodness. Or, the sons of Seth. This age is enclosed by the Lord’s commandments, lest that man bring the enticements of thought forth into action.

I think the womb of the sea means the bosom of the earth, so that we may understand that the sea was produced from the same source. This is the garment which, through the ministers of my Gospel, I spread over the sea of the peoples, lest it be scorched by the heat of unbelief. I enclosed the age within the limits of my commandments, set up the bar of charity, and destroyed the doors of unbelief, so that if any waves of evil thoughts should agitate, they might not proceed into action. That is, after you were born, at your birth you could not produce the dawn of faith, nor, after the setting of your death, the sunrise of resurrection.

The sinners of the Church’s earth are to be shaken at the last time. Just as the clay of the human body will be separated, so the soul also will at the same time be clothed with the garment of immortality. The glory and transient prosperity of the world. The strength and secular power of the age. The sea means the age; its depths signify all sinners and unrighteous people; the lowest parts of the abyss mean all the ungodly and sacrilegious, deeper still in sins. The gate of death is the devil, through whom the death of perdition entered. [Col. 1460D] The interior recesses of the punitive cavern.

Who will be able to contemplate the breadth of the earth, except the one who founded it? Likewise, the doctrine of the Church: a person of holy conduct is the light of virtues, while the sinful person is the dwelling-place of vices. Toward the predetermined rewards, whether to the right or to the left. The thoughts of hearts. What human being knows, before he exists, what he will do, or knows the days and years of his life?

Under the name of snow and hail, the hostile powers are understood here; they have withdrawn far from the warmth of God’s charity. God wished certain secret mechanisms of thoughts to be called treasures. Those who, with unrepentant hearts, would never turn to the Lord were made, by divine dispensation, ministers of punishment; others, however, were corrected through God’s chastisement.

The way is the preaching of the Gospel, through which the light of faith is scattered over the hearts of believers. The gifts of the fervent Holy Spirit. The most violent rain is the Gospel of the Savior, who by signs and powers made a way for himself among the nations through faith, by the terror of God’s name and the thunder of miracles. The abundant richness of preaching among the nations, to whom no prophet had been sent. The evangelical rain filled the earth of the Church, [Col. 1461B] which had been desolated by God, with the richness of God’s charity, so that from the abundance of heavenly gifts the seed of life might arise.

Who is the author and creator of this rain and this shower of the Lord, of which we spoke above, except God? A strict judgment issuing from the secret of the heart. For the hearts of some are bound by an unbreakable frost, so that they do not feel the warmth of God’s charity. Ungodly people have been made solid and exceedingly hard, like stones, and are plunged into the deepest darkness of the mind.

The seven stars that shine brilliantly signify all the saints, radiant with the sevenfold power of the Spirit. Arcturus [Col. 1461C] consists of seven stars; likewise, the Church is perfected by faith in the Trinity and by the works of the four principal virtues. Christ, coming from the heights, displays to us the light of faith; he is also called the evening star, because at the time of his Passion he set upon the cross. So that they may not be children of darkness, but children of the morning star and children of God.

Job, do you, as though you knew the future, already know in what order the Church is arranged in heaven, and how the diverse graces of my Spirit shine like stars? In secret, where you are seen by no one. The hostile synagogue of the peoples will surround you. The saints are called lightning-flashes; they are sent by God to illuminate the world through the preaching of the Gospel. [Col. 1461D] They show themselves present to God with thanksgiving and praise. For Christ, the Wisdom of God, came into the Virgin’s womb.

It signifies all the saints who, in the night of this age, cry out to the Lord through faith. The faith of the Church, which is called heaven, where the angelic powers cry out the praise of God with tireless voice. The dry dust of unbelief is mixed, through apostolic labor, into the fruitful faith of the Church. The soul deceived by the devil’s fraud. [Col. 1462A] That is, those who had formerly belonged to him but have now turned to God. In the hearts of ungodly people. In these hiding-places the demons sit, concealed among sinners. The raven signifies the devil, his companions, and all the fathers whom we had in error. And, leaving them, all believers cry out to God in prayer, asking for their daily bread, because they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Do you know the time when the mountain goats give birth among the rocks, or have you watched the does in labor? Have you counted the months of their conception and learned the time of their delivery? They crouch down for the young and give birth, and they utter cries. Their young separate from them, go out to pasture, and depart without returning to them. Who released the wild ass, and who loosed its bonds? To which I gave a house in the wilderness and its dwellings in the land of salt, [Col. 1462C] and it despises the multitude of the city. It does not hear the cry of the tax collector; it surveys the mountains of its pasture and searches out every green thing.

Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you, or will it remain at your manger? Will you bind the rhinoceros to plow with your rope, or will it break up the clods of the valleys behind you? Will you trust in [Col. 1462D] its great strength and leave your labors to it? Will you believe that it will return your seed to you and gather your threshing-floor?

The wing of the ostriches is like the wings of the heron and the hawk. When it leaves its eggs on the ground, perhaps you will warm them in the dust. It forgets that a foot may trample them or that the beasts of the field may crush them. It is hardened toward [Col. 1463A] its young as though they were not its own; its labor is in vain, with no fear compelling it. For God deprived it of wisdom and did not give it understanding. When the time comes, it raises its wings on high; it mocks the horse and its rider.

Will you give strength to the horse, or clothe its neck with a neighing? Will you [Col. 1463B] make it leap like locusts? The glory of its nostrils is terror. It digs the earth with its hoof and exults; boldly it goes to meet the armed enemy. It scorns fear and does not yield to the sword. Over it the quiver will resound; the spear and shield will flash. Seething and snorting, it swallows the ground and does not reckon the sound of the trumpet’s blast. [Col. 1463C] When it hears the bugle, it says, “Ha!” From far off it scents war, the exhortation of commanders, and the howling of the army.

Does the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom, spreading its wings toward the south? Or does the eagle rise at your command and place its nest in high places? It dwells among rocks, remains among steep crags and inaccessible cliffs. From there it watches for prey, and [Col. 1463D] its eyes see from far away. Its young lap up blood, and wherever a corpse is, it is immediately present.

And the Lord continued and said to Job: Will the one who contends with God so easily come to rest? Surely the one who argues with God must answer him.

Job answered the Lord and said: Since I have spoken lightly, what can I answer? I will put my hand over my mouth. I have spoken once—would that I had not said it—and a second time; I will add nothing further.

[Col. 1462A] It signifies the apostles and all preachers of the truth, who—that is, the doe—in the strength of faith, as though among rocks, give birth to the word of the Gospel through the Spirit who imbues them. [Col. 1462B] The living word of God, penetrating in this spiritual conception, produces in the bosoms of hearts a certain progress of growth, as though through the months of time. By accommodating itself to the weaker. Compelled by persecutions or by the affection of charity, the saints cry out to God. From their carnal and former desires. They advance toward the blessedness of eternal life in virtues, toward the empty thoughts of this age.

The Jewish people. In desires. The precepts of the Law, of which they are now stripped. For they have been expelled from the kingdom. In a barren life and unproductive land. The Church of common life. Every Jew despises this multitude. [Col. 1462C] The word of any evangelist who proclaims the word of God and the faith of the Church. The proud scribes and Pharisees. Their traditions, which pertain to the delights of the flesh.

The same applies to the unicorn. Pride is represented by the horn. It signifies the Gentile people. For the pasture of your doctrine in the Church. The formerly uncircumcised people, bound by faith to the strongest cord of Christ’s charity, will break the hardness of sins and cultivate the Lord’s earth of humility.

I, God, know the strength of its charity and patience; therefore I left to it, for imitation of me, all [Col. 1462D] the labors of my dispensation. So that it might bring forth the Church’s fruit for me.

There are three kinds of them: white, black, and variegated. These three birds signify people of different conduct, but they enter the Church through similarity of behavior. The children of the Church whom it bears here through doctrine. It is said to leave them when it does not resist those who oppose it. By nourishing them with doctrine. The Church does not care. The condemnation of persecution. The ancient serpents, persuading to unlawful things. That is, the Church, [Col. 1463A] because it does not attend to earthly generation but denies it, so that it may not find it there. “Not in vain” is understood. Willingly, not from fear of the ancient Law, the Church left its children amid persecution. For it chose the foolish things of the world. Therefore he deprived the Church of carnal wisdom.

To flee earthly losses. To give back a reward. To the sublimity of merit. The devil and his satellites, since they will fail at the end. The hostile power against the devil. Because of the pride with which it perversely speaks against God. For just as the locust desires to harm the earth, so the devil desires to harm Christ’s field.

The boldness of its strength, by which it puts its enemies to flight—namely, the enemies of Christ. It tramples earthly people, sinking them into earthly things. Because at times it trusts against those who are clothed in spiritual armor. For, often terrified for a time by the sword of the word of God, it turns back. The place of the wicked, in which faithlessness is hidden, like arrows in a quiver. He refers to the various wickednesses of its satellites, by which it sometimes attacks Christ’s army.

The earthly in their activity. It does not fear hearing the preaching. When the adversary hears the one exhorting his fellow soldiers—the Teacher of the Church—he says, “Ha! Who can rise against me?” That is, who would dare to fight against me? From afar [Col. 1463C] he senses those who, through various exhortations, sharpen one another against the devil; this signifies the howling of the army.

He will be adorned with the good things of baptism, because now he signifies the Christian people. Spiritual ascent into the fervor of charity. From the lowly enticements of the world, then strong in spiritual flight. His dwelling in good merits. Strong foundations signify the blasphemers, who are exceedingly hard of heart. In the hearts of sinful people. Through other sinners he deceives. The adversary’s gaze of the mind looks far ahead with subtle attention. The devil’s companions [Col. 1463D] lap up the blood of human beings, thirsting with the envy of hatred. The devil and his companions know the stench of the soul wherever they recognize sin.

Here it appears that he spoke against God with a certain presumptuous boldness, relying on a good conscience; nevertheless, he did not blaspheme God, as some think. He answered the questions, and the writer of this book said: Blessed Job, recognizing that he had spoken lightly and without bringing his speech to completion, says that he cannot answer God at all. [Col. 1464A] To cover the fault of careless speech with a good work. Those two statements. As though he were saying: “I consider it right what he said: ‘My soul chose hanging, and my bones chose death’; and: ‘If he scourges, let him kill once for all, and let him not laugh at the punishments of the innocent.’ I believed myself to be just among human beings; but when you spoke, I found myself perverse before the scourges and harsh after the scourges. I will add nothing further.” For now, the more subtly I understand you speaking, the more humbly I examine myself.

## CHAPTER XL

The Lord answered Job from the whirlwind and said: Gird your loins like a man; I will question you, and you shall answer me. Will you annul my judgment and condemn me, so that you may be justified? And do you have an arm like God, and can you thunder with a voice like his? Surround yourself with beauty and raise yourself on high. And be glorious, and clothe yourself in splendid garments. Scatter the proud in your fury, and, looking upon every arrogant person, humble him. Look upon all the proud and confound them. Crush the wicked in their place, hide them together in the dust, and plunge their faces into the pit. Then I too will confess that your right hand can save you.

Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you; he eats grass like an ox. [Col. 1464D] His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel of his belly. He tightens his tail like a cedar. The sinews of his testicles are intertwined. His bones are like pipes of bronze; his cartilage is like plates of iron. He is the beginning of God’s ways; the one who made him will apply his sword. [Col. 1465A] The mountains bring him herbs; all the beasts of the field play there. He sleeps under the shade, in the secret places of reeds and in moist regions. The shades of the trees protect him. The willows of the torrent surround him. Behold, he will swallow a river and not be amazed; he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth. [Col. 1465B] With his eyes he will catch him as with a hook, and with stakes he will pierce his nostrils.

Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook and bind his tongue with a rope? Will you put a ring in his nostrils and pierce his jaw with a bracelet? Will he multiply [Col. 1465C] entreaties to you, or speak soft words to you? Will he make a covenant with you, and will you take him as a perpetual servant? Will you mock him as a bird, or bind him with your maidservants? Will friends cut him up? Will merchants divide him? Will you fill nets with his skin and a fish-basket with his head? Will you place your hand upon him? Remember the battle, [Col. 1465D] and do not speak further. Behold, his hope will deceive him, and before all who see him he will be cast down.

[Col. 1464B] From the force of the rebuke. Everyone who speaks with God is first commanded to gird his loins with charity. How God speaks to human beings, the divine Scriptures indicate to us through many signs. Whoever tries to defend himself against the scourges attempts to nullify the judgment of the one who scourges. Or understand it this way: “You consider your own good deeds, but you do not know my hidden judgments. If you argue from your merits against my scourges, what else are you doing but hastening to charge me with injustice by justifying yourself?” As though he were saying: “If you can, attack and scatter the very demons by whose afflictions you are crushed.”

The arm signifies divine power; in the voice, God signifies the terror of his majesty—not that blessed Job was so exalted that he conceived, even in thought, of raising himself [Col. 1464C] against God, but the words of the rebuking God are these: “You ought not therefore to contend against God as though on equal terms, even if you had strength like God.”

Plunge the souls of the proud and arrogant, together with their understandings, into the pit of hell. Since it is impossible for a human being to possess these things, it is foolish for him to speak against God as though from a position of equality. From him you ought humbly to hope for mercy, so that by his right hand—that is, by his power—you may be saved from those proud, arrogant, and ungodly people whom I have mentioned.

The devil was made condemned in such a way that he who had formerly rejoiced in the destruction of many now, unwillingly and gently, lives with you like an ox. Hence the devil’s power in the human race prevails chiefly through lust over men, [Col. 1464D] and over women. At the end he will enclose it in the hardness of pride and despair. The bonds signify the many-sided tenacity of unlawful desires and lusts. The hardness and inflexible wickedness of him. Here it is understood that the devil will never humble himself to God through repentance.

He was regarded as first among God’s other creatures in his commands. That is, so that he may be punished by the judgment of the judge for the evil by which he destroyed others: that is, Behemoth. [Col. 1465A] Carnal people offer him the pleasure of temporal delights. His companions, delighted by the enticements of the world. In the sweetness of bodily thoughts, and therefore unfruitful. People smeared with every kind of pleasure. This means that by his own sins he defends the sins of others. The devil means people full of the thorns of sins, who also, by words like leaves, falsely claim the fruits of good works.

He called it Gentility, and rightly so, because they are without baptism. He also has confidence in those who have been washed in the bath of renewal. [Col. 1465B] Now God has spoken of the Son, because Christ appeared to the devil in his eyes as a human being. In the saints, who continually carry the Cross by which the enemy was conquered, he lost the discernment of his cunning.

This means: Just as the fish Leviathan, which is said to be in the waters, cannot be drawn out, so the devil cannot be uprooted from the sea of the human race by your power. Will you restrain his doctrine by the strictness of divine rebuke? By the names of rings, bridles, pincers, and bracelets are understood the words of divine power, by which the proud one has been humbled and bound. For he is subject only to God, whose creature he acknowledges himself to be; and before him alone the proud spirit, fearing in its very conscience, is condemned. [Col. 1465C] It does this by no will of its own, but by the command of divine power.

That he will never recover angelic dignity. The strength of this dragon will be so humbled before God that it will become altogether nothing and will be mocked by the holy souls who are Christ’s maidservants. The apostles and all preachers of the truth, because they divide many from the devil. That is: His ministers, who cling to him like skin to flesh, are not easily separated from him by their doctrine. The head of the devil means the rulers of the world, who will be enclosed within the enclosure of the Church, as within a receptacle for fish. You do not subdue him by your power, because the dragon is great and powerful. This is the tribulation [Col. 1465D] that comes to you from him; it must not now disturb you for the worse. While he promises himself more than he is able to accomplish, he will be thrust into punishments while all the angels and saints look on.

## CHAPTER XLI

Will I not raise him up as though he were cruel? Who can resist my face? Who has given to me first, that I should repay him? Everything beneath heaven is mine. I will not spare him for powerful words composed for entreaty. Who will uncover the face of his garment? And who will enter the midst of his mouth? Who will open the doors of his face? Terror is around his teeth. His body is like cast shields, compacted with scales pressing against one another. One is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them. One adheres to another, and, holding one another, they will by no means be separated.

His sneezing is the splendor of fire, and his eyes are like the eyelids of dawn. From his mouth proceed torches, like burning brands of fire. From his nostrils comes smoke, like a pot kindled and boiling. His breath makes coals burn, and flame goes out from his mouth. In his neck strength resides, and want goes before his face. The parts of his flesh cling together. He will send lightning against him, and it will not be carried elsewhere. His heart will be hardened like a stone and compressed like a smith’s anvil.

When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, will purify themselves. When the sword has seized him, he will not be able to stand; neither will the spear nor the breastplate. For he will regard iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood. The archer will not put him to flight; slingstones have become straw to him. He will regard the hammer as straw and mock the one brandishing the spear. [Col. 1467A] Beneath him are the rays of the sun; he spreads gold beneath himself like mud. He makes the depth of the sea boil like a pot and makes it as when ointments boil. Behind him a path shines; he regards the abyss as though it were growing old. There is no power upon earth comparable to him, who was made so that he might fear no one. He sees every lofty thing, and he himself is king over all the sons of pride.

[Col. 1465D] God did not raise up the enemy as a cruel being who desired to punish him. Let every creature yield to the mere sight of God’s majesty. In these words God alone is shown always to have existed. It is clear. For although the devil is a wicked servant, nevertheless, trembling, he feels his Creator. The cunning devices of his craft, because at times he presents himself as an angel. Who entered hell to lead captives out from there, except Christ? He wishes the hidden strength of his hypocrisy to be understood. Therefore there is fear and trembling all around, since he is always prepared to devour.

The heretics, who are his body, are therefore like molten metal, because they love themselves more than the body of Christ and are joined to the devil by an unbreakable connection. He also called them, allegorically, by the name of scales; they are so thickened and cling to one another that, through their unceasing wickedness, they have no room to breathe toward God. [Col. 1466B]

That which cleanses the filth of the brain signifies that he, dwelling in filth, displays from it the splendor of a counterfeit light. The false prophets, as though endowed with the light of knowledge, pretend to be righteous and enlightened. All the ungodly and blasphemers present themselves as torches of true light, but, turned toward severity, they burn emptily.

Concerning the discernment of his understanding. The darkness of understanding. That is: In such cunning they prepare eternal punishment for themselves. Smoke from his nostrils, from his breath, so that he may provide eternal fire and smoke for himself and his ministers. The malicious anger of his preachers. [Col. 1466C] In the unconquerable noise of his arrogance. For wherever the ancient enemy comes, he brings want of eternal life.

His followers, because they follow him in the flesh. God’s tribulations against the devil. Except toward the place appointed for him, nor does the devil boast of being unpunished by them. The anvil is struck, but is not lengthened; it overcomes what is thrown upon it and itself remains immovable. So the devil is beaten by the rebukes of the faithful, but, remaining rigid and hard, is condemned to eternal punishments.

This may be understood of the first beginning of the age, because when the evil fell, the good remained steadfast, strengthened and never fearing a fall. Others have said more plainly: If spears encountered him, they would do nothing to him; that is, no one can be corrected by errors and rebukes.

He will regard the strength of the saints as refuse of straw, so that, because of his pride, he may count all these things as nothing. He will regard the power of the elect as rotten wood. The devil is not pierced to repentance by the words of the saints. He turns the arrows of the saints into straw for himself when he considers their words worthless, so erect is he in pride. God says all this about the devil in various ways and images in order to show human beings how evil he is and how powerful. [Col. 1467A] For he dragged a portion of the angels down with him.

He spreads the saints beneath himself like mud when he makes them subject to him in the filth of sins. He makes this age, which is compared with the depth of the sea, boil toward iniquity.
