The devil inflames his followers with carnal desire, so that they burn with love of earthly things. For at the end he will understand that he needs repentance, which he will never obtain.

He believes that the world will always remain in sins, not considering that it has been converted after Christ. For no creature is such in power, nor in malice and wickedness. Thus his heart is in hardness, since at first he surpassed all others. He raises himself on high and into the heights. The head and prince of all the proud. His angels and ungodly human beings became the sons of his pride, imitating him. [Col. 1467B]

## CHAPTER XLII

Job answered the Lord and said: I know that you can do all things, and that no thought is hidden from you. Who is this who hides counsel without knowledge? Therefore I have spoken foolishly, and of things exceeding my knowledge beyond measure. Hear, and I will speak; I will question you, and you will show me. I heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. Therefore I rebuke myself and repent in dust and ashes.

After the Lord had spoken these words to Job, he said to Eliphaz the Temanite: My wrath is kindled against you and against your two friends, because you have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job did. Therefore take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job and offer a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job will pray for you. I will accept his face, so that your foolishness may not be charged against you; for you did not speak rightly to me, as my servant Job did.

Then Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite went and did as the Lord had spoken to them. And the Lord accepted Job’s face. The Lord also turned toward Job’s repentance when he prayed for his friends. And the Lord added all that Job had possessed, twofold. All his brothers and all his sisters and all who had known him before came to him. They ate bread with him in his house. And they shook their heads over him [Col. 1468B] and comforted him concerning all the evil that the Lord had brought upon him. And each one gave him one sheep and one gold earring.

The Lord blessed the latter days of Job more than his beginning. He came to possess fourteen thousand sheep, six [Col. 1468C] thousand camels, a thousand she-asses, seven sons, and three daughters. He called the name of one Day, the name of the second Cassia, and the name of the third Horn-of-Stibium. No women as beautiful as Job’s daughters were found in all the land. Their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers. Job lived after these events one hundred and forty years, and saw his sons and his sons’ sons to the fourth generation. And he died old and full of days.

[Col. 1467B] You humble the devil as you wish and as much as you wish. Blessed Job, repenting, confesses his thoughts to God. No one can hide counsel from your conscience. In what follows he has now made his error plain and confesses his foolishness, by which, in ignorance, he exceeded the proper manner of speaking to God; and through knowledge of the divine rebuke he has been raised up for correction.

After the Lord’s rebuke, having laid aside his foolishness, [Col. 1467C] he dares to question. After the testing of temptation, having been brought nearer to knowledge of the divine, he now says that he sees God, whom he had previously heard before he was examined. That is, of the heart. That is, of the mind. He said of himself. For the more closely anyone understands God, the more humble he becomes.

Or, as others have said: “Therefore I despised myself and considered myself earth and ashes.” Here it is shown that Job’s friends did not speak rightly when they insulted him. He strictly reproved his friends by justice and kindly converted them through mercy. Here we understand that no one benefits from rebuking with insult one who has been placed under God’s chastisement.

By calling him his servant, he shows that everything he had said in his defense he had said not with rebellious pride but with humility. Here it is shown that their sin of reproach could not be forgiven them unless blessed Job himself prayed to the Lord for them and offered a propitiatory burnt offering.

Job is said to have had his face accepted, because whoever attempts to intercede for others benefits himself even more through that very charity. [Col. 1468A] It is shown that, although he repented for himself, he deserved to be heard all the sooner because he had devoutly interceded for others.

But his possessions were doubled both in what was transferred to him by God and in what he begot again after his calamity; yet this doubling increased little by little and was not heaped up all at once. His entire kinship and family of that kind are to be understood, as are his acquaintances and friends who had previously known his royal power.

The reverence of his honor is shown in the banquet, because all the squalor of his filth had been wiped away from him. From the movement of their heads we recognize the joy of those who came together around him. It is shown that the more a person is seen rejoicing at the restoration of his neighbor’s well-being, the more he indicates that he had grieved over its loss.

They gave him gifts as though he were poor and possessed absolutely nothing. And if his wealth was doubled through this small collection, there was a great multitude of those who came to him, because he received a small gift from each person and suddenly became master of such great riches.

The writer of this book may have said this by anticipation, so that after that temptation, with the Lord’s blessing, he would possess the wealth of his life—one hundred and forty years—multiplied twofold; but we do not read that the number of his children was doubled. For the building up of our faith, therefore, we should understand that God returned to him as many children as he had lost, so that, with the substance of all his goods returned to him twofold by God, he might also believe that he had his children twofold—for, as God’s most faithful servant, he ought not in the least to doubt that those whom he had sent ahead to God had not perished.

## CONCLUSION

Glory to you, Father; glory to the Only-Begotten, with the Holy Spirit, for everlasting ages.

[Col. 1468D] Blessed Job, in his words and sufferings, expressed an image of Christ. His wife represents the type of carnal people who, placed within the Church, scandalize those who live spiritually by their conduct. His friends represent the figure of heretics. Elihu, however, bore the image of paganism. But now that paganism has been extinguished and abolished, heretics are sent on ahead to Christ by God and reconciled to God through the Mediator.

In the burnt offering of seven bulls and rams, repentance is shown through the satisfaction of prayers and almsgiving. As for the statement, “The Lord accepted Job’s face,” and what follows: as John says, “He is the propitiation with the Father.” Thus the face of the Savior is accepted by the Father, while he both hears and is heard on our behalf [Col. 1469A]. “And the Lord added,” and what follows. Those things were added to Christ the Lord when the multitude of the Gentiles was added to the Jewish people.

“All his brothers and sisters”: the whole kindred of the Jewish people, from whose family Christ was born. Or we may understand it generally as the multitude of all the Gentiles.

“Those who had previously known him”: all the saints and prophets who saw him in the Spirit and announced that he would also come in the flesh.

“They ate with him”: now, in the house of the Savior’s Church, all the faithful are refreshed by the exhortations of the Scriptures.

“And they moved their heads over him”: all the saints rejoicing that they have become participants in Christ’s spiritual and sacred banquet.

“And they consoled him”: nothing consoles our Savior moderately; rather, he is greatly consoled because the world has been redeemed through his passion.

But he says that God the Father inflicted upon his Son the evil of suffering and death, as the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son.”

“And each of them gave him one sheep”: each person who comes to Christ through faith offers him his innocence and the obedience of his mind.

“But the Lord blessed Job’s latter days more than his beginning.” The beginning of Christ, God and our Lord, signifies the beginnings of the law of Moses; his latter days signify the Gospel. The manifestation of truth in the Gospel is better than the shadow of allegories in the Old Testament.

As for the meaning contained in the names of the animals, I remember saying it at the beginning of this work. The seven sons signify the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit; the three daughters signify the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel.

The names of his daughters were Day, Cassia, and Horn-of-Antimony. Day, therefore, is the law of God, which illuminates the night of human ignorance for the recognition of truth. Cassia is the gift of holy anointing. Horn-of-Antimony is most appropriately fitted to the resources of the Gospel. The horn pertains to the dignity of the Church.

Just as blessed Job was enriched in children after his loss, so the Savior, after the loss of the unbelieving Jews, was enriched among the Gentiles. No women more beautiful were found, because the souls of the elect surpass everything that lives upon earth by the splendor of their beauty.

“And their father gave them,” and what follows. The sisters enter into the inheritance with their brothers, because the weak are admitted into the kingdom of God together with the strong [Col. 1470B].

“And he saw his sons.” Holy Church sees her sons when she beholds the first offspring of the faithful; she sees her sons’ sons when she generates other faithful persons through those same faithful people.

“And he died full of days,” because through these transitory times she performs what cannot pass away: the faithful of the Church and their good works remain with Christ forever.

[Col. 1469]

# EXCERPTS FROM THE COMMENTARY ON JOB

Which manuscript was preserved at Amsterdam in the library of the distinguished man Marcus Meibomius and is thought to be by St. Jerome; here included for the first time—as Vallarsi says—and also expanded and corrected in several places from another Roman manuscript. (C, G)*

## FROM THE PREFACE TO THIS COMMENTARY

[Col. 1469C] [Note: The Roman manuscript places this epigraph first; it also divides the entire preface into approximately eleven titles or chapters.]

### On the Method of Interpretation

Some things are said here historically, allegorically, and morally. Some cannot be taken literally, because they would be erroneous, impossible, or mutually inconsistent; for example: “Under which those who carry the world are bent,” as though giants were carrying the world; and, “My soul chose hanging,” as though someone so patient wished to end his life by hanging; and, “Let the day perish on which I was born,” and so forth.

[Note: The Roman manuscript reads more elegantly: “because they would be erroneous, or impossible, or inconsistent with one another,” etc.]

Sometimes the person who neglects the literal sense hides the light of truth from himself: while seeking something inward, he loses what is outward. Thus, speaking of works of mercy: “If I denied the poor what they wanted.”

[Col. 1470C] The divine word exercises the discerning through its mysteries, while by its surface it refreshes the simple, because it is like a river both level and deep, in which a horse may walk and an elephant swim.

[Note: The Meibomian manuscript reads *ministeriis* (“services”); the Roman manuscript corrects this, and the editor of these excerpts himself corrected it in the *Acta Eruditorum* of Leipzig for the year 1711. It is clear that the author of this work is referring to the mystical sense of Scripture.]

The law was given to the erring human being; the person disobedient to the law is confounded—by the example of the greatest human being, who lived lawfully without the law. Hence: “Be ashamed, Sidon,” that is, the stability of those established in the law. The sea, that is, paganism, says this: while keeping the law, it rebukes the hearers of the law.

Moses is said to have written these things about Jacob, as though about a predecessor, because in Genesis we read that Jobab descended from Esau and that Bela, son of Beor, succeeded him in the kingdom. But it is the custom of sacred speech to touch briefly, in the accounts of earlier fathers, upon events that would occur much later, while it hastens on to other matters. Job therefore did not live before the law, but in the time of the Judges.

He himself is more plausibly believed to have written the account of his victory.

[Note: Read “the history of his victory.”]

Nor is it a problem that it says, “Job said” or “Job did this,” because it is the custom of a holy person to speak about himself as though about someone else. For it is the Spirit who speaks in them about themselves as about others. Thus the angel of Moses is at one time called an angel, as the one who serves outwardly, and at another time the Lord, who presides inwardly. Hence David also says: “Attend, my people, to my law.” David was not the people or the law; rather, he spoke of the one who speaks in him.

And he wished prophecy to be spoken by a Gentile as well as by a Jew, since he had come for both peoples.

Fruitless loquacity, like leaves of words, is cut away from divine discourse, since the planting of a grove is forbidden in the temple of God. It is unworthy that the words of the heavenly oracle should be confined beneath the rules of Donatus.

Job’s virtue was known to himself and to God in great repose, but when shaken by scourges it gives off its fragrance to us, like spices. Hence faith is compared to a mustard seed: while uncrushed it is mild, but when crushed it burns, and brings forth what had been hidden within it. Thus in the Psalm: “In the day the Lord commanded his mercy, and in the night he declared it.” The gift of mercy that is prescribed in the quiet of day is said to be revealed in the night of adversity.

He is scourged so that he might learn to give thanks even amid evils; this was surely the one thing he lacked.

[Note: Perhaps *perfecto* should be read.]

What the enemy requested for evil, God permitted for good. Let no one therefore think that Job’s words should at some point be condemned, when God commends him so highly—Job, in whom, as in a middle ground, the devil contends against the Lord.

But when he recounts his good deeds, this is not arrogance; rather, through them he strengthens himself lest he despair, since he was being driven to despair of his life by so many evils and by the reproaches of his friends.

[Note: The Meibomian manuscript again has the erroneous *vera* instead of *vero* (“but in truth”).]

[Col. 1472A] Job is struck by every kind of temptation: by the loss of his possessions, through which he was thought capable of being shaken as a powerful man in the world—but he despises these; by the bereavement of his children, which he mourns with equanimity; and by the striking of his flesh, which he endures patiently.

These were like the outward assault of a war, like enemies fighting from the front. Within, however, through his wife as through a fellow citizen, his mind endured the poison of counsel; yet he taught her wisely as well.

His friends come to offer consolation, but rush forward to rebuke him. Among them is also the last, the younger one.

[Note: Read “the last and the younger,” because he is unworthy.]

He rebukes him more sharply, because words sometimes disturb more than wounds. Behold, they are like enemies attacking from the side. Through wounds patience is tested; he overcame the former by strength and the latter by reason.

Job’s friends sinned more through ignorance than through malice. For such a great man did not have wicked friends; rather, because they could not discern the cause of his afflictions, they fell into guilt.

There are different kinds of affliction: one by which the wicked person is oppressed so that he may be punished; another, so that he may be corrected; another, so that he may not commit future offenses; and another, so that when salvation follows, the Savior may be loved more greatly.

When a good person is struck, his merits increase. Because Job’s friends did not know how to distinguish these things, they believed that the afflicted man was being punished for guilt. Hence they return more quickly to pardon. God humbles them in such a way that he receives them back into grace only through the one whom they had despised.

[Note: We supplied this final chapter, in which the third sense of Scripture is explained according to the author’s mind, from the Roman archetype.]

### Morally

Many things … [lacuna]. An innumerable crowd of thoughts, which, like servants without their mistress and in the absence of reason, make a din and abandon their work, while when she returns they work in silence.

These are evidently the things by which the mind overcomes its mistress amid their multitude. We are great companions of the eastern peoples and of the angels who cling to the eastern light, and so forth.

# FROM THE COMMENTARY ITSELF

[Col. 1471]

## On Chapter I, 1

[Col. 1471D]

It is necessary that the serpent’s cunning train the dove’s simplicity, and that simplicity moderate cunning. Hence Christ appeared in the dove and in fire, because those who are filled with him serve the gentleness of simplicity in such a way that they are inflamed against evils by zeal for righteousness.

[Note: It seemed fitting to append this passage also from the Roman manuscript.]

“Fearing God.” Solomon: “Whoever fears God neglects nothing.”

“Turning away from evil.” Again Solomon: “Whoever offends in one thing loses many good things.”

First the suitable person is described, and only afterward his struggle is mentioned, so that such a person may be seen as capable of answering in kind.

## On Chapter III, 8

“Let those who curse the day curse it.”

### Morally

In the old translation: “Let him who curses the day curse it, he who is ready to capture the great sea-monster.”

The devil, who is now night, will at the end be seen as day, when he exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped as God. But now the one who destroys his wickedness destroys his power by his final coming; he extinguishes the great sea-monster in the waters of holy baptism—that is, his strength.

Or: “Let them curse it,” that is, the night, namely, the elect angels who announce it while condemning the darkness. “Those who curse the day,” that is, those who show that his feigned brightness, by which he presumed to become equal to God, is to be despised.

“Those who are ready to raise him,” that is, to release him, so that he may act against the Church with all his strength. Now he is held bound and pressed down in the abyss; and he who exalted himself proudly above others has been subjected beneath their dominion, so that now he lies hidden, bound by their ministry, even though at the end, once released, he will wage open warfare.

## On Chapters IV, 10–11

[Col. 1473A]

After offering a merciful warning, he rebukes him openly.

“The roaring of the lion”: that is, the severity and terror of Job himself.

“The voice of the lioness”: the loquacity of his wife.

“The teeth of the lion’s cubs”: the greed of his children.

“It has been destroyed.” He attacks these harshly, as though dealing with something condemned.

He also compares Job to a tiger, on account of the spots of pretense. For the hypocrite, who appears upright, has hidden vices that, when they eventually break out, alter his color.

The glory of the righteous is prey, which he seizes for himself. Therefore, supposing that holy Job had retained by hypocrisy the good qualities he recognized in him, he says: “The tiger has perished”—that is, “the variety of your pretense has been extinguished, because the flattery of praise has been removed.”

In place of “tiger,” the Septuagint reads *mirmicoleon*, which in Latin is called “the lion of ants,” or more explicitly, “ant and lion.” It is a small animal that lies hidden in the dust and ambushes ants, eating them; but to birds and other animals it is itself an ant, since it is eaten by them.

By this he indicates that Job was timid toward those who were exalted and bold toward those who were subject to him. But now exaltation has no prey in him, because, struck by another’s injury, he is prevented from attacking.

The same things are understood typologically of heretics. The lion is the devil, on account of his savagery. The lioness is the city of the world. Babylon, associated with the lion, is the lion’s cub. Those generated by them are reprobate, while the saints guard themselves against them.

Heretics, however, secure in themselves, think they have overcome everything, as though saying: “We are not scourged because we overcome the devil’s power, his voice—that is, the glory of the world—and his teeth—that is, the persuasion of the reprobate.”

Again, the tiger is the devil because of his many-sided cunning; or *mirmicoleon*, weak against those who resist but strong against those who consent. They say that he has perished because he has no prey among them.

They repeat this for joy, because what is said with joy is often repeated.

[Note: Perhaps *prae* should be read.]

## On Chapter XIX, 24

What is written in lead is erased more quickly. It is difficult to write on flint, but what is written remains. Thus Judea quickly receives the words of God and abandons them; the Gentiles receive them with difficulty but preserve them firmly.

## On Chapters XIX, 25–27

“For I know that my redeemer lives.” He does not say “creator,” but “redeemer,” clearly announcing the one who, after creating all things, redeemed us from captivity through his passion.

“He lives,” even though he fell among the hands of the impious.

“Whom I shall see”: that is, our flesh after the resurrection will be the same and different— the same in nature, different in glory. It will be spiritual because incorruptible, and tangible because the substance of true nature is not lost.

“This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom.” We believe that we possess nothing more securely than what we hold in our bosom. He therefore kept hope stored in his bosom because he anticipated the hope of resurrection with true certainty.

He expressly indicates the truth of the resurrection. It is not one person who dies and another who rises, as those say who claim that the body will be invisible; it is the very same person.

“My redeemer lives, and through the resurrection I hope for one like myself.” Thus other rods remained dry, but Aaron’s rod—that is, the body of our priest—burst into the flower of resurrection. By that flower the priest who intercedes for us is revealed.

## On Chapter XXII, 11

“And that you will not be overwhelmed by the rush of flooding waters.”

Tribulations are compared to flooding waters because they rush one upon another, like wave upon wave. You therefore did not think that you would be overwhelmed, because you imagined that God did not see these lower things.

“And do you still think so?” Heretics consider themselves wise and ridicule Catholics because they do not fear God, since they do not see him bodily. Nor do they think that he sees earthly things from afar; rather, they imagine that, because he is higher than heaven and, as though hidden in a cloud, judges through darkness—

[Col. 1474B] since the airy regions lie between us and heaven, and, intent upon higher things, he sees the lower less clearly, or, encircling the pivots of heaven, does not look upon the things below.

[Note: The Leipzig editor thinks the passage should be rewritten as follows: “And even now heretics think this, considering themselves wise,” etc.]

## On Chapters XXII, 15–16

“Do you wish to keep to the path of the ages?”

Just as the path of the redeemer is humility, so the path of the ages is pride. Wicked men therefore tread the path of the ages, because they walk in exaltation through the desires of this life.

“Those who were taken away before their time”: those who love the present life promise themselves longer stretches of that same life. But when death suddenly removes them, it cuts short the span of their life that they had extended in their thoughts.

“And a river overturned their foundation.” The wicked, failing to perceive that present things are fleeting, fix their minds in love of the present life and build for themselves in it, as though for a long dwelling, a foundation.

But the river overturns their foundation, because the very course of mutability undermines the state of their wicked construction.

[Note: The sense can be maintained more or less if *subruit* (“undermines”) is read.]

[Col. 1474D] [Note: Perhaps, however, the author wrote this way, indicating even the wickedness of the construction. The Leipzig editor wishes to read *fundamenta* (“foundations”) instead of *statum ejus* (“its state”).]

## On Chapter XXII, 16

“Those who were taken away before their time.”

It should be understood that God orders the years according to the merits of individuals and also determines the limit: so that the wicked may live briefly, lest they harm more people; or so that the good may live longer, in order to benefit more people; or again, so that the wicked may live longer, in order to increase the evils by which the good are tested; and so that the good person may be removed sooner, lest, if he lived longer, he be corrupted by wickedness.

God’s sentence is changed, but not his eternal purpose.

[Note: The Leipzig editor prefers: “when he orders.”]

## On Chapter XXIV, 5–11

[Col. 1474D]

“Others, like wild asses in the desert, go out to their work.”

These are heretics, who refuse to mingle with the peoples but seek the retreat of a more secluded life; and they infect others with the plague of their persuasion all the more because they appear, as though on account of the merits of their life, more worthy of reverence.

They are compared to wild asses because, given over to their own desires, they are estranged from the bond of faith and reason.

“They go out to their work.” They perform not God’s work but their own, since they follow not sound doctrines but their own desires.

“Keeping watch for prey, they prepare bread for their children.” They keep watch for prey who always try to snatch the words of the righteous for their own interpretation, so that through them they may prepare the bread of error for perverse children.

“They reap a field that is not theirs.” By the name of field or vineyard the Church is signified. Perverse preachers reap it and vintage its author by oppressing him in his members. While persecuting the grace of the Creator, when they seize from it certain people who seemed upright, what else do they take away but ears of grain or clusters of souls?

“They leave men naked, taking away their clothing, for whom there is no covering in the cold.” Just as clothing protects the body, so good works protect the soul. Heretics therefore take away clothing when they destroy the good works of certain people.

“For whom there is no covering in the cold.” The covering pertains to righteousness; the cold to guilt. Therefore the person both grows cold and is covered who, by one work, grows warm toward righteousness and, by another, grows cold toward guilt. But when heretics take good works away from such people, they ensure that, in the cold, they have nothing with which to clothe themselves.

“Whom the rains of the mountains water”: that is, whom the streams of preachers sanctify.

“And having no covering, they embrace stones.” He calls the strong men in the Church “stones,” such as martyrs.

Those, therefore, who trust in none of their own works but run in prayer to the protection of the holy martyrs—what do they do except embrace stones, having no covering of good action?

[Note: He restores the passage in the following way: “having no covering of good action.” Nevertheless, the sense remains very obscure and strongly suggests, contrary to the writer’s intention, the teaching of Vigilantius.]

“They used violence, plundering orphans, and stripped the common people of the poor.” Heretics use violence while plundering, because they assault the weak minds of the faithful with the force of their words and deeds.

They strip the common people who are poor because, being unable to prevail against the learned, they deprive the uneducated of the covering of faith.

“They took ears of grain from the naked, from those walking without clothing, and from the hungry.”

Whoever does neither good nor evil is naked and idle. Whoever does evil walks naked, because he proceeds along the path of wickedness without the covering of good works.

[Note: The Leipzig editor restores this passage, which suffers from faulty punctuation.]

From the hungry, who desire the nourishment of the word through repentance, heretics take ears of grain, because they destroy in their minds the judgments of the Fathers, which are signified by ears of grain.

For when the words are brought forth figuratively, we remove from them the covering of the letter, like the chaff of ears of grain, so that we may refresh ourselves with the marrow of the spirit.

“Among their heaps they rested at midday, those who thirst after having trodden the winepresses.”

Those who persecute the Church tread the winepress. For when the unjust oppress the just, they cast the clusters beneath their feet; the just, stripped of the flesh, hasten heavenward as though into a storehouse.

They tread and thirst because, by committing cruel acts, they become all the more cruel and strive to commit worse ones. When heretics see them committing cruel acts against Catholics, they rest at midday among their heaps.

They thirst after having trodden the winepresses because they join themselves to the multitude of those whom they see committing grave acts and thirsting for still graver ones. And when they cannot raise persecution by themselves, they stir up the powerful of the world to do so. While the fervor of these powerful people satisfies their desires, the heretics rest in their actions as though at midday.

## On Chapters XXVI, 2–4

“Whose helper are you? Is it perhaps the helper of the weak?” and so forth.

To help the weak is charity; to wish to help the powerful is pride. The meaning is: while you intend to help the one beneath whose greatness you collapse, the consolation you offer proceeds from ostentation, not piety.

“Whom did you advise?” To give advice to a fool is charity; to give advice to a wise person is ostentation; to give advice to Wisdom itself is perversity.

Hence it continues, “and understanding.” Every understanding that one possesses is right. It is not excessive, because it does not desire to know more than it should.

“Was it not the one who made the breath?” Bildad, because he believed that Job had been scourged for guilt, tried through proud rashness to penetrate the hidden judgment of God, which he ought humbly to have revered.

Therefore he set himself above God through his understanding, passing judgment on God’s judgment because he did not understand it.

But because Job, bearing the figure of the Church, had said little in correcting the proud, he suddenly expanded into instruction through a series of statements, saying:

[Verse 5:] “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters.”

The giants are the proud; the waters are the peoples. The exalted, while desiring to attain the honor of eminence in this world, groan beneath the burdens of the peoples.

A person is subjected to those peoples in mind to whom he is subjected in dignity. These words therefore indicate that all pride lies in the depths precisely by raising itself on high.

## On Chapters XXIX, 19–20

“My root was opened beside the waters.”

By the name of root a hidden thought is signified. The root is opened beside the waters because the mind’s thought is secretly opened to receive the flowing streams of truth.

[Note: Read “streams.”]

“And the dew will remain on my harvest.” Supply: “I said.”

[Note: Read “supply,” namely from the beginning of verse 18.]

The harvest signifies the Church, when perfected souls, withdrawn from their bodies like ripe grain cut from the earth, descend into the heavenly storehouses.

The dew remains on the harvest because grace coming from above brings it about that we are worthy to be gathered from below.

“My glory will always be renewed,” because he laments the glory he has lost: he recognizes that those whom he himself had believed to be serving the new life are serving ancient desires.

[Note: The preposition should more correctly be deleted.]

## On Chapters XXXI, 25–28

Understanding either grows sluggish through idleness or vanishes through pride. Therefore he says: “If I rejoiced.”

When someone acts upon what he understands, he often slips because of what is displayed outwardly. But blessed Job, just as he was not exalted by the gold of understanding, so neither did he exalt himself by the light of action.

This is the meaning of: “If I saw the sun.” It is fitting that the righteous do not see their own good deeds, which they offer for others to see, nor the moon—that is, the reputation of good work—which shines for those who walk in darkness.

Job did not exalt these things, which are more to be feared.

[Note: Read “fame.”]

For then, like a tall tree, he is shaken more violently by the winds—the tree that, through understanding, had been as though dead in the seed of action.

In matters of praise he was not only not made arrogant in his words, but not even in so great a thought. This is the meaning of: “My heart rejoiced in secret.”

And because an unreflective mind, raised up by approval, sometimes praises what it has done, he adds: “And I kissed my hand with my mouth.” This is the greatest iniquity.

Every sin that arises from weakness does not destroy the spirit, because the sinner seeks pardon from God. Presumption, however, the farther it is from humility, the more grievous it is in desperation; while attributing strength to itself, it does not seek it from God.

While the wicked admire good things, a lamp burns in the night. If the good also admire the best things, the sun shines.

[Note: The Leipzig editor prefers *inde* (“hence”).]

In the day, when the good shines through bodily action, it is a lamp—that is, a light in a vessel; when it shines through contemplation of the mind, it is the sun from heaven.

## On Chapter XXXVIII, 7

“When the morning stars praised me together.”

Even the elect angels marveled at the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, because they were created first in time, not at the beginning.

They are called morning stars either because they are often sent to exhort human beings, announcing the coming morning and driving away from human hearts the darkness of the present life; or because these morning stars, together with the evening stars, praise the Redeemer’s power, glorifying the abundance of heavenly grace bestowed upon people redeemed at the end of the world.

“And all the sons of God shouted for joy.”

Shouting for joy is said to occur when the joy of the heart cannot be fully expressed by the effectiveness of the mouth. The angels therefore praise, because they already behold in the heights the breadth of such great brightness. Human beings, however, shout for joy because, while still below, they endure the narrowness of their mouths.

Since the Lord knew that these things would happen, he narrates them as already done. But because when the good rejoice, envy inflames the wicked, whom the Lord nevertheless restrains, he immediately adds concerning them:

## On Chapter XXXVIII, 31

[Note: Here the Roman manuscript ends; from it this entire passage of chapter 38 is now supplied for the first time. The remainder is missing.]

“Will you be able to join the shining stars?” and so forth.

It is clear that no human being can do this. But when Job is questioned about these things, he is shown to be humble and to take refuge in the one who alone could do it.

## On the Beginning of Chapter XXXIX

[Note: These excerpts are taken from Isidore, whom the distinguished Reland also praises, *Etymologies*, book XII, chapter 1, around the middle: “Ibices, as though *avites* … these animals live among the highest rocks, so that whenever they sense the hostility of wild beasts or human beings, they hurl themselves from the highest rocky peaks and catch themselves unharmed upon their horns.” Some material from the same source is described below in nearly identical words.]

Ibices are said to be small four-footed animals that live among the rocks and give birth there; when falling, they catch themselves unharmed upon their horns.

In them the person of spiritual teachers is signified. Like ibices, they give birth among the rocks, because in the teaching of the Fathers—who are called rocks on account of their solidity—they beget souls for conversion.

They, like ibices, suffer no harm from any fall when they are caught upon their horns, because whatever ruin temporal adversity brings, they receive themselves into the testimonies of sacred Scripture and are saved, as though by the support of horns.

They are also called deer, because, after killing their vices as though extinguishing serpents, they live, and from that very extinguishing of vices they burn more intensely for the fountain of life.

## On Chapter XLII, 15

“And their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.”

Therefore the beautiful women are mentioned among the number of the perfect. They also receive an inheritance as figures of the imperfect, like weak minds.

The sisters therefore come into the inheritance with their brothers, because the weak are admitted to heavenly things together with the strong.

[The manuscript reads *ad mittuatur*; the sense requires “are admitted.”]

“Job lived after this.”

A person is empty of days who, however long he may have lived, has spent the time of his life in vanity. In contrast, the person is called full of days whose days do not pass away in vain, but are preserved—both after they have passed and while they will pass—through the daily reward of good works with the righteous Judge.

As a figure of the Church, if we multiply fourteen by ten, we arrive at the number one hundred forty. It is rightly counted as ten multiplied by fourteen, because the Church, guarding both Testaments and living both according to the Decalogue of the Law and according to the four books of the Gospel, extends to the summit of perfection.

Job is rightly said to live after his scourging, because the Church is first struck by the scourge of discipline and afterward strengthened by the perfection of life.

She also sees her sons and her sons’ sons to the fourth generation, because during this age, which revolves through four annual seasons to the end of the world, she beholds through the mouths of preachers offspring being born to her. She sees her sons’ sons when she recognizes that others are begotten by them, even to the end.

She dies old and full of days because, when the following light comes, she is changed from the burden of corruption into the incorruption of the spiritual homeland through the reward of her daily works.

She dies full of days because her passing years do not pass away, but are made firm by the recompense of enduring actions.

She dies full of days because through these transitory times she works what does not pass away.

In the practice of ancient life women did not possess an inheritance among men, because the severity of the law, choosing the strong and despising the weak, preferred to enact strict measures rather than benevolent ones. But when the merciful Redeemer came, the weak too were taken into the kingdom together with the perfect.

# MISCELLANY

Excerpts from various pages of the same manuscript codex.

[Col. 1479]

[Col. 1479A] Page 3. Like all the righteous, Job foreshadowed Christ not only in words but also in deeds, so that through his suffering he might show Christ who was to suffer—that is, the head together with the body, which is the Church.

[Note: In the Interlinear Exposition printed immediately above, at the end: “Blessed Job, in words and sufferings, expressed an image of Christ.”]

His wife signifies carnal people who, within the Church and therefore closer through faith, are oppressed more harshly in life.

Job’s friends signify heretics who wish to deceive under the appearance of giving advice and who, while speaking as though on behalf of the Lord, oppose the truth.

Job is called sorrowful, by which the passion of Christ or the labor of the Church is expressed.

Eliphaz: “contempt of the Lord”—that is, heretics who, while holding false opinions about God, contemptuously despise him in their pride.

Baldad: “ancientness,” that is, “alone,” because they speak not with good intention but from a desire for glory; that is, not from zeal for the new human being but from the wickedness of the old life.

Sophar: “the dispersal of the watchtower,” or “the one who disperses the watchman,” because heretics seek to corrupt by their words minds that contemplate heavenly things.

[Note: And so indeed Jerome in the *Onomasticon*, above, col. 87: “Eliphaz, contempt of God; Bildad, antiquity alone; Zophar, dispersal of the watchtower,” etc.]

By despising God, therefore, they remain in ancientness; remaining there, they harm those who watch through their evil speech.

But because they themselves sometimes return to the Church, this reconciliation of the years shows the matter for which Job prays: the sacrifices of heretics are not acceptable to God unless they are offered by the hands of the Church.

[Note: The Leipzig editor rewrites this as *amicorum* (“of the friends”).]

“Seven sacrifices are offered for them,” because, when they receive the sevenfold Spirit, they are purified as though by seven offerings.

[Note: I have no doubt that the seven sons of Job are indicated here, through whom, also according to the Interlinear Exposition, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is explained. The word *procis* is so suspect to me that I think it is a corrupt reading. The author easily wrote *pro eis* (“for them”), and the word *filii* (“sons”) should be supplied as follows: “Seven sons; sacrifices are offered for them,” etc.]

Bulls and rams were offered for them. In the bull the neck of pride is signified; in the ram, the leadership of the flock, because those who recoiled from the Church through pride dragged weak flocks after them.

[Col. 1479]

Page 147. Sardonyx takes its likeness from red earth; sapphire possesses an aerial appearance.

Page 148. “And topaz from Ethiopia”: because it shines with every color, topaz is called *topadion*.

[Note: From St. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVI, chapter 6: “Topaz belongs to the green variety and shines with every color.”]

Page 150. It was the custom of the ancients for elders to stand at the city gate and judge the cases of the innocent, provided the city’s people were peaceful and discordant persons were not permitted to enter it. The divine Job did this as well.

Page 158. The path of adversaries is compared to waves because, through the insolent restlessness of the wicked, it is troublesome and, so to speak, pours in like a storm to overwhelm the ship of the heart.

Page 169. To carry the book upon one’s shoulder is to complete sacred Scripture by putting it into practice.

# COMMENTARIES OF DOM JEAN MARTIANAY

Benedictine monk of the Congregation of St. Maur, on the books of St. Jerome contained in this third volume.

[Col. 1479]

## PREFACE ON THE EMINENCE OF LEARNING AND THE PIETY OF THE LITTLE WORKS OF ST. JEROME

[Col. 1479C] § I. Jerome is far superior in learning to all ecclesiastical writers.

No one denies that Jerome was polished by the liberal arts and scholarly studies; indeed, even had he himself kept silent about it, every syllable and letter of his little works would plainly testify that, in Latin especially, he had been worn smooth and thoroughly exercised from almost the very beginnings of his education among grammarians, rhetoricians, and philosophers. Yet that was only the smallest portion of his youthful proficiency compared with his striving toward the summit of understanding the sacred Volumes—a summit attained only through the greatest labors, enabling him to say with the most holy and unconquered king: “I have more understanding than all my teachers.”

Such is the unanimous fame of Jerome’s learning that the following unique eulogy applies to him most appropriately: “With one voice many nations agree that he was the foremost man among peoples.” I certainly do not hold this opinion alone, since I have the most learned men agreeing with me, above all Desiderius Erasmus, the most illustrious and cultivated man of the preceding age in the humanities. Accordingly, we shall cite his words, which are particularly apt for establishing the point.

> “And indeed,” he says, “although this seemed to me exceedingly unworthy in all learned men, it seemed far more unworthy in Jerome, whose many and extraordinary gifts deserved that he alone, entire and uncorrupted, should be preserved. For in the case of others, different gifts recommend different men; in this one man, as they say, everything was joined together *συλλήβδην*—‘all together.’ Whatever we admire in others in separate parts was outstandingly united in him. And although it is a great and rare achievement to excel in individual fields, he surpassed everyone in every field, so that, if you compare him with others, he far outstrips them in each particular; but if you compare him with himself, no single quality predominates. Such is the balance of all his highest qualities!
>
> “For if you consider the happiness of his nature, whose intellect was more ardent in learning, keener in judgment, or more fertile in invention? Finally, who was more dexterous or more engaging, whenever the subject called for entertainment? If you seek the praise of eloquence, in this respect he left all Christian writers so far behind that even those who spent their whole lives in the single pursuit of speaking well cannot be compared with Jerome. Indeed, it is wholly beside the point to ask whether there is any writer of our religion whom one could set beside him: in my judgment, he surpassed Cicero himself—the acknowledged prince of Roman eloquence—in certain virtues of expression, as we shall demonstrate more fully in his Life. This regularly happens to me with Jerome, as once it did with Marcus Tullius: whenever I compare anyone with him, however eloquent that person may be in himself, he suddenly seems almost struck dumb; and a tongue which, considered on its own, I greatly admire without qualification, appears, when set beside and brought near to Jerome, speechless and stammering.
>
> “If you require learning, I ask you: whom does even the most learned Greece possess so complete in every kind of knowledge that he could be matched with Jerome? Who ever combined and perfected all the branches of learning with equal success? Who ever excelled alone in so many languages? To whom was granted such extensive knowledge of history, geography, and antiquity? Who ever attained an equal and complete knowledge of all sacred and profane literature? If you examine his memory, what author, ancient or modern, did he not have readily at hand? What corner of divine Scripture, what matter so obscure or so varied, did he not possess as though it were counted out before him? If you consider his industry, who ever read through or wrote so many volumes? Who so thoroughly learned, absorbed, digested, handled, and meditated upon all divine Scripture? Who labored equally in every branch of learning?
>
> “And if you consider the holiness of his character, who breathed Christ more vividly? Who taught more fervently? In short, who expressed Christ more fully in his life? This one man could have sufficed for all Latin writers, whether for the piety of life or for knowledge of theology, if only he had survived entire and unharmed. But now I scarcely know whether anyone has been treated more shamefully. A good part of his vigils has perished. What remains was not merely corrupted, but utterly extinguished and obliterated—partly through the fault of illiterate scribes, who habitually copy the uncorrected from the corrected, make worse errors out of faulty exemplars, omit what they do not read, and corrupt what they do not understand, such as the Hebrew and Greek words which Jerome frequently intersperses; but far more wickedly through the deliberate mutilation by sacrilegious persons—I do not know whom—of very many passages, the addition of some, the alteration of most, and the corruption, degradation, and confusion of nearly everything, so that scarcely any sentence can be read without difficulty even by a learned man.
>
> “Indeed, as though it were not enough to have attached so many utterly foolish trifles, childish and unlearned, to the name and title of a man at once most eloquent and most learned, they have everywhere inserted their own nonsense into the middle of his Commentaries, so that no one could object. For there are many things that expose a book falsely attributed to him. But as for the fragments scattered and mixed throughout, like darnel confused with wheat, by what sieve can anyone at last cleanse them? We shall shortly show that all these things have occurred here, in our catalogue of his works, and so forth.”

All these and so many praises woven together by Erasmus can certainly contribute nothing to Jerome’s honor that is not his due, since he has always been called and regarded by the most distinguished men, both ancient and modern, as well as by the supreme pontiffs and the synods of the Catholic Church, as a most learned man, most skilled in every language, pre-eminent in every branch of knowledge, the most diligent investigator of the divine law, and, finally, the teacher of the world and the greatest interpreter of the sacred books. In order to establish this with approval, I present the precedents and arguments for this praise—precisely the matters which the learned men of our own time always most desire to have established for themselves.

## § II. Precedents and arguments for this highest learning

It would scarcely be proper for me to anticipate the supreme pontiff in these arguments. I shall therefore begin with the words of Sixtus V, who partly anticipated our eulogy when he said in the preface prefixed to his Bible:

> “The authority of the Vulgate edition is in itself so great, and its excellence so outstanding, that it seems wholly pointless to desire anything greater. For the books contained in it—as our ancestors have handed them down to us, as it were from hand to hand—were retained partly from a certain common and most ancient Latin edition, which Saint Jerome calls the Vulgate edition, Blessed Augustine the Italic, and Saint Gregory the old translation; Blessed Augustine likewise judged it preferable to the others that were then widely in use, because it was more faithful to the words while preserving clarity of meaning. Partly, they were taken from the translation of Saint Jerome; and anyone who recognizes the dignity of that interpreter readily understands how much honor should therefore be paid to them.
>
> “For Saint Jerome—as the same Blessed Augustine testifies among others—was learned in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew eloquence. Passing from the Western Church to the Eastern, he lived in the holy places and among the sacred writings almost to extreme old age. He saw or read nearly all who had written on ecclesiastical doctrine before him in either part of the world; and not only Augustine, Chromatius, Paulinus, and the other most holy bishops, but even Damasus, bishop of Rome, consulted him concerning passages of Scripture.
>
> “Nor had he undeservedly acquired such renown among all people, especially in knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, since he spared no vigils or journeys in attaining it. He visited the most learned men in Gaul; at Constantinople, Gregory of Nazianzus; at Alexandria, Didymus; and elsewhere he sought out others, finally making use of the most distinguished teachers of the Hebrew language. He was not content with one teacher, but employed many, and those most learned—a diligent investigator not only of matters but also of names.
>
> “Moreover, he inspected the very places often mentioned in Scripture, and testifies that this greatly assisted him in understanding the Scriptures. Whoever carefully considers the holiness, intellect, learning, skill, teachers, and labors of so great an interpreter, together with the age in which he lived, when the study of all languages—especially Hebrew—was flourishing, will readily condemn the judgment of those who either are not satisfied with the labors of so eminent a teacher or presume that they themselves can provide something better or equal.”

Thus Sixtus V commends the Vulgate Edition on the authority of Jerome’s name.

The learned Serarius likewise agrees with him in *Prolegomena Biblica*, chapter 19, question 7. In opposition to Jerome’s detractors and the innovating heretics, he demonstrates Jerome’s diligence in translating and correcting the sacred books, saying:

> “Jerome’s diligence in translating or correcting the sacred books of the Bible is first demonstrated by his diligence in other matters, since this task was in reality of the greatest importance and was also so understood by him. Second, it is demonstrated by the number and impudence of his rivals. For, even if they are of no other benefit, such men generally drive a person to attend more closely and carefully to what he is doing, just as fleas and flies drive horses to shake and move themselves.
>
> “Third, it is demonstrated by the agreement of everyone. For I have not seen anyone who found anything wanting in Saint Jerome on this point, apart from a very few Catholics mentioned by Andradius in book 4, page 92, where he says that he does not oppose those who sometimes find in Jerome a lack of diligence and clarity; and apart from one of the Innovators, Junius, who in book II, chapter 13, number 19, page 144, not openly but secretly mutters something or other when he writes: ‘Jerome was so occupied with other matters that he had time only to skim and pluck at most things.’
>
> “Saint Jerome was certainly very greatly occupied. Yet his prudence—which Saint Augustine calls in Letter 19 ‘learned, leisurely, seasoned by years, studious, ingenious, and diligent’—itself advised him to devote greater attention and effort to matters of greater weight. And in these matters Saint Jerome, standing on one foot, could accomplish more than Junius, superficial scholars like him, and other petty Hebraists, even when they bent to them with their whole chests for many hours and days.”

Thus far Serarius.

The scribes would not suffice if I were to repeat here everything that I have found written in the books of the learned in praise of Jerome’s intellect and learning. Therefore, so that the discussion may not extend too far, I now return to certain chief precedents and arguments by which we can confidently ascribe to Saint Jerome the outstanding skill and sacred learning of which we are speaking.

You will find nothing in him that is not pre-eminent and exceptional, once you consider the nature and formation of his intellect; the distinction of his teachers; the company of noble boys; the renown of the places and the populous cities of which he was an inhabitant; the abundance of books and volumes; his own industry, skill, and diligence; his constant and unconquered labor in study; and, finally, the years spent and completed in the sacred Letters. Whoever directs his attention to these and similar precedents of Jerome’s learning will immediately agree with me about the foolish confidence of superficial scholars, Critics, and Hebraists who claim to be Jerome’s equals in knowledge of the divine Scriptures—or, worse still, boast openly that they surpass him in Hebrew learning.

But after briefly enumerating the arguments for Jerome’s learning, which he possessed beyond all other writers, I shall proceed to shake such arrogance.

### 1.

From his earliest childhood he was carefully instructed at home by Christian and devout parents. He immediately imbibed Christ and, at the same time, was trained under Orbilius in the liberal arts, insofar as his age was then capable of receiving them. [Note: This was not, however, a designation peculiar to the master who taught Jerome, but a celebrated name for a schoolmaster; Jerome therefore applied it to his own teacher *κατ᾽ αὐτονομασίαν* (“by antonomasia”).] While still a boy he was sent to Rome, as though to the foremost teacher both of religion and of learning, to attend grammarians, rhetoricians, and philosophers who were then most renowned for prudence and eloquence.

Thus, having been worn smooth from childhood among the most distinguished teachers, he learned Greek and Latin literature all the more successfully because he learned them earlier. For literature possesses, I know not what, a somewhat hard and acrid quality in those who come late to learning. In grammar he had Donatus as his teacher, whose Commentaries on Virgil and Terence survive; Jerome also mentions him in his first *Apology against Rufinus*, in these words:

> “I suppose that, when you were a boy, you read the Commentaries of Asper on Virgil and Sallust; those of Vulcatius on Cicero’s Orations; those of Victorinus on his Dialogues; and my teacher Donatus on the comedies of Terence, likewise on Virgil, and others on other authors.”

Under such teachers and others like them, Jerome, having now grown older in the liberal arts, left no branch of learning untouched. For he wished to read Porphyry’s *Isagoge*, as well as Platonic, Academic, Stoic, and every other philosophy. In rhetoric, however, he exercised himself with particular zeal and did not refuse to enter the arena of declamation. Nor does he anywhere reproach himself for having, as a boy, played at times with fictitious controversies and the oblique tricks of rhetoricians.

Among his companions in these studies were Pammachius, born in the highest rank; earlier, the noble boy Bonosus, who possessed abundant wealth; and also Heliodorus, whom the integrity and virtue of his character later led to the office of bishop.

Therefore, if the first stimulus to learning, according to Saint Ambrose, is the distinction of one’s teacher; if it is a great thing to have the most honorable boys as rivals in virtue and literary study; and if Rome’s recognition as one’s educator appears to everyone a most outstanding commendation, who, I ask, could surpass our Jerome—that is, a man of the happiest disposition, a ready and capable intellect, a passionate and tireless spirit, cultivated and polished in every liberal discipline?

### 2.

Having therefore been fully educated in secular literature at Rome, and now turning his mind toward more serious studies, he also imitated in this respect men of the highest renown—Pythagoras, Plato, and Apollonius—so that by visiting different regions he might enlarge his store of wisdom and knowledge.

Accordingly, he traveled through Gaul with his companion on that journey, Bonosus, and diligently visited all the libraries in the various places. He also met with those whom either learning or integrity of character had made more distinguished than others. Finally, at Trier, he copied with his own hand Hilary’s large volume on the synods.

Afterward, when he had revisited both his homelands—the one in which he had been born and the one in which he had been reborn—he went east with the very rich library that he had acquired through the greatest effort; for he could not do without it.

It is useful to learn from Jerome himself what teachers he subsequently made use of, so that nothing may be misunderstood. From the letter addressed to Pammachius and Oceanus I shall first make the matter especially clear.

> “When I was young,” he says, “I was carried along by an extraordinary passion for learning, and I did not teach myself, as certain people presume. I frequently heard and honored Apollinarius of Laodicea at Antioch; and although he instructed me in the sacred Scriptures, I never adopted his contentious doctrine concerning their meaning.
>
> “My head was already being sprinkled with gray hairs, and it was more fitting for me to be a teacher than a pupil; nevertheless, I went to Alexandria and heard Didymus. I thank him for many things: I learned what I did not know, and under his instruction I did not lose what I knew.
>
> “I came again to Jerusalem and Bethlehem. With what labor and at what price did I obtain Bar-Anina as a teacher by night? For he feared the Jews and presented himself to me as another Nicodemus . . . .
>
> “As for their objection that I gathered Origen’s books more than any other man, would that I possessed the volumes of all interpreters, so that I might compensate for the slowness of my intellect by the diligence of reading! I gathered his books, I confess; and for that very reason I do not follow his errors, because I know everything he wrote. Believe one who has experience: I speak as a Christian to Christians. His doctrines are poisoned, alien to the holy Scriptures, and do violence to the Scriptures. I read Origen—I read him, I say—and if there is guilt in reading, I confess it. And they emptied our purse for Alexandrian paper.”

In his *Apology to Domnio* as well, while mocking an ignorant monk, he taught us much about his teachers, saying:

> “For you write that a monk—or rather, I do not know what man from the crossroads, alleys, and streets, a marketplace wanderer, gossip, and trickster, skilled only in slander, who tries to pull the speck from another’s eye while the beam remains in his own—has been preaching against me and gnawing, tearing, and ripping apart with a dog’s tooth the books I wrote against Jovinianus.
>
> “This dialectician of your city, the pillar of the Plantina family, has certainly not read Aristotle’s *Categories* (*Κατηγορίαι*), nor *On Interpretation* (*περὶ Ἑρμηνείας*), nor the *Topics* (*Τοπικά*), nor even Cicero’s *Topics* (*Τόποι*); yet among the circles of the ignorant and the banquets of little women he weaves syllogisms and, as though they were sophisms, dissolves our arguments by clever reasoning.
>
> “How foolish I was to think that I could not know these things without philosophers; I who read the better part of a stylus—that which erases—rather than that which writes. In vain, then, did I translate Alexander’s Commentaries; uselessly did a learned teacher introduce me to logic through an *introduction* (*εἰσαγωγή*). And, to leave human matters aside, I had Gregory of Nazianzus and Didymus as catechists in the sacred Scriptures for no purpose.
>
> “The learning of the Hebrews was of no benefit to me, nor my daily meditation, from adolescence to this age, upon the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, and the Apostles. A man has been found who, without a teacher, is perfect, ‘spirit-bearing’ (*πνευματοφόρος*), ‘inspired by God’ (*ἔνθεος*), and ‘self-taught’ (*αὐτοδίδακτος*); who surpasses Cicero in eloquence, Aristotle in argument, Plato in prudence, Aristarchus in learning, Chalcenterus in the number of his books, Didymus in knowledge of the Scriptures, and all the interpreters of his own age.”

Finally, in his *Apology against Rufinus* he addresses the same man as follows:

> “I also hear that you criticize certain things in my letter philosophically, and that, like a man with a wrinkled brow and raised eyebrow, you play upon me with Plautine wit, because I said that Barabbas the Jew was my teacher. Nor is it surprising that, where there is some similarity of names, you wrote ‘Barabbas’ instead of ‘Bar-Anina,’ since you have such license in changing names that you have turned Eusebius Pamphilus into a martyr from a heretic . . . .
>
> “Hear, then, O pillar of wisdom and standard of Cato-like severity. I did not call that man my teacher; I wished to demonstrate my devotion to the sacred Scriptures, showing that I had read Origen as I had heard him. For I ought not to have learned the Hebrew letters from you.
>
> “Has an injury been done to you because I followed Apollinarius and Didymus? Could I not, in that letter, have named Gregory, a most eloquent man, who has no equal among the Latins, and in whose instruction I glory and rejoice? And so forth.”

From these testimonies already cited, together with many similar ones omitted for the sake of brevity, it is perfectly clear that Jerome gathered the books of learned men more extensively than anyone else; that in secular and sacred Letters he had as teachers the most learned men of his age, whether Greek or Hebrew; and that he never ceased learning in Rome, Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople, and Jerusalem—places where, at that time, the schools of the Latins, Greeks, and Hebrews, and the studies of secular and divine Letters, were undoubtedly flourishing.

### 3.

These are indeed the principal arguments for Jerome’s learning, but the summit of his scholarship was his manner of study, which Erasmus elegantly expressed in these words:

> “He divided all his time between study and prayer, adding a good part of the nights to these labors. The smallest portion was given to sleep, less to food, and none to leisure. He refreshed the weariness of study with supplication or a hymn; then, as though renewed, he returned to the reading he had interrupted.
>
> “He reread his entire library, renewing in himself the memory of his earlier studies; he learned the sacred Letters word for word. He meditated upon the Prophets, watching most attentively to discover the mysteries of the oracles. From the evangelical and apostolic writings, as from the purest springs, he drew the philosophy of Christ. For the first step toward piety is to know the teachings of one’s author.
>
> “He read the other interpreters with selectivity and judgment, omitting no writer whatever from whom he could gather something—not pagans, not heretics. For that wisest of men knew how to extract gold from a dunghill; he knew how to draw honeyed juice from thorns while leaving the spider its poisons. Even then he was gathering together from the Egyptians whatever he could, intending to enrich the Lord’s temple with the resources of its enemies.
>
> “And so that his memory might be more certain and his use of what he had learned more ready, he arranged everything he had read under topics, composing each item according to the demands of affinity or opposition . . . . What more need be said? Nothing at all was omitted that could contribute to forming the renowned teacher of the Church and truly great theologian, so that his learning might nowhere be deficient, nor a life insufficiently corrected diminish or weaken the authority of his teaching.”

To these things must also be added the frequency of his supplications and fasts, by which the holy man sought more often to obtain from God the Father of lights a pure mind and the perfect gift of understanding, so that he might interpret the sacred volumes with the same Spirit by whom they were first believed to have been written.

Thus, in the prefaces to his little works and in his letters, you often hear him say: “Supported by the help of your prayers, I shall undertake a most difficult work”; or: “Pray, therefore, brother, to the Lord Jesus Christ that, by the same labor and grace of the Spirit by which we have interpreted the other Prophets, we may also be able to explain this one”; or: “While you were praying, I brought the work through to its conclusion.”

Thus nothing was more sacred or more important to Jerome than that his treatises and little works should be consecrated to the Lord through the prayers of devout friends, his own prayers, and the austerity of fasts.

Now, after the divine helps, let us consider the remaining human aids in the fourth argument and final precedent of Jerome’s highest learning. The great man did not regard himself as *ἔνθεος*, *πνευματοφόρος*, or *αὐτοδίδακτος*—that is, “full of God,” “inspired by the Spirit,” or “self-taught”—but, applying every diligence, he eagerly sought, at suitable and unsuitable times alike, to learn what he did not know.

Because he understood that matters concerning the Hebrews must be sought from Hebrews, those concerning the Chaldeans from Chaldeans, those concerning the Egyptians from Egyptians, and those concerning the Syrians and Greeks from Syrians and Greeks, he frequently made use of all their company in order to gain a clear understanding of the language of each people in the sacred books.

Moreover, he wished to be an eyewitness of the places where the sacred books had been written or interpreted, so that he might contemplate the innermost meanings of Scripture more clearly.

> “For just as,” he himself says, “those who have seen Athens understand Greek histories more fully, and those who have sailed from Troy through Leucate and the Acroceraunian mountains to Sicily and from there to the mouths of the Tiber understand the third book of Virgil more fully, so the holy Scripture will be contemplated more clearly by one who has seen Judea with his own eyes and has learned the memories of ancient cities and the names of places, whether unchanged or altered.
>
> “For this reason, too, we took care, together with the most learned Hebrews, to undertake this labor, so that we might travel around the province which is proclaimed by the whole Church of Christ.
>
> “I confess, my dearest Domnio and Rogatianus, that I have never trusted my own strength in the divine volumes, nor taken my own opinion as a teacher. Rather, I have been accustomed to ask even about matters which I thought I knew—how much more, then, about those concerning which I was uncertain!
>
> “Finally, when you recently demanded by letter that I translate the *Paralipomena* for you into Latin, I took on a certain teacher of the Law from Tiberias, who was held in admiration among the Hebrews. I compared it with him, as they say, from the crown of the head to the tip of the nail; and thus, having been assured, I dared to do what you commanded.”

The preceding four precedents and arguments therefore demonstrate Jerome’s learning, amassed in every kind of subject. For what perfection of letters could we desire in one who, endowed with a good disposition and ardent intellect, was a constant pupil of the leading teachers of his age in grammar, philosophy, and theology; who was instructed by Hebrews, Syrians, Chaldeans, Egyptians, and Greeks, both orally and through books; who absorbed the whole of sacred Scripture so deeply into his mind that he made his own breast a library of Christ; and who became the oracle of the Church and of the supreme pontiffs, who considered no conversation in life more worthy than speaking about the Scriptures with Jerome—yet in such a way that they asked the questions and he gave the answers?

These were the exercises of the holy Doctor’s intellect; these were the courses along which his mind ran. Laboring and toiling in them, he could at last become old in body, but never in spirit.

## § III. Certain superficial scholars, rivals, and recent Critics refuted

Some superficial scholars, rivals, and Critics may perhaps be ashamed to look up to Jerome, adorned with so many gifts, complete in every respect, and pre-eminent in every kind of learning, while they boast of picking him apart with a dog’s tooth amid crowds of ignorant people or among little women, and of showing that he was insufficiently learned.

But what do those rivals of Jerome’s virtue and learning say? Above all, they bring against us one objection which seems to diminish the praises due to so great a man’s skill. “Jerome,” they say, “was often mistaken in his translation of the Bible and in his Commentaries on the same books, because he allowed himself to be credulous toward the Jews and often indulged Jewish fables and traditions.”

Thus David Clericus, in *Sacred Questions*, page 245:

> “But deceived by a rabbinical teacher, as others have observed, the great man hallucinated.”

And Jacobus Capellus, in his *Observations on chapter IV of the Song of Songs*:

> “Jerome consistently translates this . . . . But the Jew whom that great man was then using completely deceived him.”

Another Jacobus Capellus, in the *Index of Matters and Words* of his father Ludovicus Capellus’s *Sacred Criticism*, under “Jerome”:

> “He translates certain passages badly in the Hebrew text . . . and elsewhere he was repeatedly deceived by a Jewish teacher.”

R. Simonius and several others bring forward similar hallucinations and errors; but these men have already been refuted below in the longer Notes or in my Commentary on the book of Hebrew Names.

To all the Critics collectively, however, I first make this response, and then I shall engage directly with Clericus and the Capelli, whom no ordinary learning and knowledge of the Hebrew language permit me not to hold in honor.

What Jerome’s attitude truly was concerning this matter—and how profoundly unjust is that refrain which both ignorant Catholics and heterodox Critics repeatedly whisper to us—will be made most clearly evident by the words that follow. In them Jerome offers many arguments demonstrating that he never inclined toward the Jews, much less indulged their foolish traditions and fables.

Let everyone therefore listen and recognize the justice of my complaint against the detractors of so great a man, who spoke according to the conviction of his own mind in his little works.

**Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus:**

> “If it is expedient to hate men and to detest some nation, I turn away from the circumcised with extraordinary hatred. For to this day they persecute our Lord Jesus Christ in the synagogues of Satan.
>
> “Let someone object to me why I had a Jewish man as my teacher. And someone dares to produce my letters to Didymus as though they were addressed to a teacher. It is a great crime for a pupil to have called an educated and elderly man a teacher . . . . These are foolish and trivial matters.”

**Preface to the Book of Joshua:**

> “Therefore let the scorpion cease to rise against us with its arched wound, and let it desist from attacking the holy work with its poisoned tongue—either accepting it, if it pleases, or despising it, if it displeases. Let it remember those verses: ‘Your mouth has overflowed with wickedness, and your tongue was fashioning deceit. You sat and spoke against your brother,’ and so forth.
>
> “For what benefit is there to the hearer or reader when we sweat through labor while others labor through slander? Let the Jews grieve that the opportunity to slander and ridicule Christians has been taken away from them, and let the men of the Church despise—or rather, tear apart—what torments their adversaries.”

**Preface to the Book of Chronicles:**

> “But now, since different copies are circulated according to the diversity of regions, and that genuine and ancient translation has been corrupted and violated, do you think it is a matter of our choosing either to judge from several copies what is true or to forge a new work within an old work, and thereby, as the saying goes, put out the eyes of the crows while the Jews mock?”

**Preface to the Book of Tobit:**

> “I never cease to marvel at the urgency of your demand. For you insist that I bring into Latin style a book written in the Chaldean language—the book, namely, of Tobit—which the Hebrews, cutting it away from the catalogue of the divine Scriptures, assigned to those writings that they call Apocrypha.
>
> “I have satisfied your desire, though not my own inclination. For the studies of the Hebrews accuse us and charge us with transferring these things into Latin ears against their Canon. But judging it better to displease the Pharisees’ judgment and to serve the commands of the bishops, I persisted as best I could, and so forth.”

**Book III of the *Apology against Rufinus*:**

> “You will correct the Latin Scriptures from the Greek and give the Churches something different to read from what they once received from the Apostles; but I shall not be permitted, after the Septuagint edition which I carefully corrected many years ago and gave to the people of my language, to translate even those copies which the Jews themselves acknowledge to be most true, in order to refute the Jews? Thus, whenever there is a dispute with them among Christians, they will have no side paths by which to escape, but will be struck by their own sword above all.”

**Letter to Marcella, “That so small a thing,” etc.:**

> “You ask what it is that has excluded the duty of letter-writing and conversation. For a long time now I have been comparing the edition of Aquila with the Hebrew volumes, lest perhaps the synagogue, out of hatred for Christ, has altered something. And, to speak frankly to a friendly mind, I find more things that strengthen our faith.
>
> “Now, having carefully reviewed the Prophets, Solomon, the Psalter, and the Books of Kings, I have in hand Exodus, which they call *EELLE SMOTH*, and am about to proceed to Leviticus. You see, therefore, that no duty ought to be placed before this work.”

**Letter to Damasus, “The Seventy,” etc.:**

> “But lest we seem to have passed over something important—the matters which the Jews call *δευτερώσεις* (‘second traditions’) and in which they place their entire knowledge—we shall now briefly touch upon why the Hebrew has: ‘And who will go for us?’
>
> “For just as it is said in Genesis, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness,’ so here too, I think, it says, ‘And who will go for us?’ But whom else should we understand by ‘us’ except the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, to whom goes whoever obeys their will?
>
> “In the fact that the speech is presented as coming from one speaker, the unity of the Godhead is indicated; in the fact that it says ‘us,’ the distinction of the persons is indicated.”

**Letter to Hedibia, Question II:**

> “If, therefore, the bread that came down from heaven is the body of the Lord, and the wine which he gave to the disciples is his blood, the blood of the New Testament, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins, let us reject Jewish fables and ascend with the Lord to the large upper room, furnished and cleansed; let us receive from him above the cup of the New Testament, and there, celebrating the Passover with him, let us be made drunk with the wine of sobriety.”

**Book III of the Commentary on Isaiah, chapter VIII:**

> “The Nazarenes—who receive Christ in such a way that they do not abandon observance of the ancient Law—interpret the two houses as the two families of Shammai and Hillel. From these arose the scribes and Pharisees, whose school Akiba assumed; they say that Akiba was the teacher of Aquila the proselyte. After him came Meir, followed by Johanan son of Zachai; after him Eliezer, and in due order Delphon. Then again Joseph the Galilean; and up to the captivity of Jerusalem, Joshua . . . .
>
> “Shammai and Hillel therefore arose in Judea not long before the Lord’s birth. The former is interpreted as ‘destroyer,’ the latter as ‘profane,’ because through their traditions and *δευτερώσεις* (‘second traditions’) they destroyed and defiled the precepts of the Law.
>
