> “These, then, are the two houses that did not receive the Savior, because he became for them a ruin and a stumbling block.”

**Commentary on Ecclesiastes, chapter V:**

> “His Hebrew teacher understands it as follows: ‘What you cannot do, do not promise’ . . . . But in his interpretation of the words, ‘so that you cause your flesh to sin,’ he did not examine the matter carefully, understanding it as though it said: ‘Do not give your mouth an opportunity to sin.’
>
> “To us, however, another meaning seems preferable: that those are being reproved who complain about the fault of the flesh and say that, compelled by bodily necessity, they do things they do not wish to do.”

In the same Commentary on chapter IX of Ecclesiastes:

> “The Hebrew [teacher] explained this verse differently, in which it is said: ‘For a living dog is better than a dead lion.’ Among his own people he explained it in this way: that any unlearned person, and one who is still alive and teaching, is more useful than a perfected teacher who has already died [Col. 1489C] . . . . . But since this explanation does not please us, let us aim at greater things . . . Therefore the living dog is us, from the nations; the dead lion is the people of the Jews, abandoned by the Lord. And this living dog is better before the Lord than that dead lion. For we, being alive, know the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but they, being dead, know nothing and await no promise, and so forth.”

I wished to bring a few such testimonies, out of many, into view and the light, so that the diligent reader might be astonished by them at the futility of the opinion—held both by such superficial writers and by the Critics—who continually repeat to us, in speeches and books, that Jerome was deceived by the Jews and placed more than sufficient trust in their fables and traditions. Indeed, who was more difficult to persuade and deceive than Jerome [Col. 1489D] in matters concerning the practice and customs of the Hebrews? He was the man who turned away from the Circumcised with extraordinary hatred, and by whose translation the Jews—adversaries of the Church of Christ—were distressed and tormented; the man who daily pierced the eyes of those crows; who removed from unbelievers the hiding places of evasion and stabbed them with their own sword; who compared the edition of Aquila minutely with the Hebrew volumes, lest the synagogue might perhaps have altered anything out of hatred for Christ; who drew the Jewish *deuterōseis* (δευτερώσεις) captive to his own interpretations, or taught that they should be altogether rejected and cast away; who calls the Jewish *Deuterotae*, and their leaders, dissipators and contaminators of the divine Law, for whom our Savior had become a ruin and a stumbling block. Finally, he is the man who, in his Commentaries, refutes with learned freedom and prudence his Jewish teachers, although some of them had believed in Christ. Let the Critics, therefore, cease inventing Jewish frauds, traps, and hallucinations in Jerome, when [Col. 1490A] the man of God and most diligent Doctor’s learning, prudence, zeal, and piety cry out against suspicions of this kind.

But now let us come to the hallucinations attributed to Jerome by the Clerics and Capelli. The first weapon, then, which David Clericus wields, is forged in this manner:

> “Question XXVI. On the word *αἰών*. When I read Jerome, not so much to learn the rites and opinions of the ancient Church as to obtain from him whatever assistance I can toward a genuine knowledge of the Hebrew language, I encounter a passage in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter I, which I should like you to examine. These are his words:
>
> ‘In Hebrew, *saeculum*, that is, where it has the letter [Vau] written, signifies eternity; but where it is written without [Vau], it signifies the fiftieth year, which they call the Jubilee. For this reason that Hebrew man also who, out of love for his master, because of his wife and children, has his ear pierced and is subjected to slavery, is commanded to serve forever, that is, until the fiftieth year. And the Moabites and Ammonites do not enter the assembly of the Lord until the tenth and fifteenth generation, and forever, because every harsh condition of the Jubilee was dissolved at its arrival.’”

> “Response. The first passage to which Jerome refers is found at Exodus XXI, 6; the second at Deuteronomy XXIII, 3. In the first, Vau is in fact absent, whereas in the second it is seen; but, deceived by his rabbinic teacher, as others have observed, the great man fell into error . . . At Ezekiel XXVI, 20, [the Hebrew expression], ‘the people of the age,’ refers to those who have long been dead. In commenting on this passage Jerome interprets the word differently:
>
> ‘You shall not be forever—or, as it is written in Hebrew [the Hebrew expression], and in Greek *αἰών*, it signifies one age—according to Isaiah, who says that Tyre will be restored after seventy years.’”

> “You may perhaps be astonished that Jerome is so inconsistent [Col. 1490C] that elsewhere he denies the very thing he affirmed elsewhere. But listen to the great haste with which he wrote his Commentaries:
>
> ‘It is one thing,’ he says at the end of his Commentary on Obadiah, ‘to turn one’s style often and to write what deserves to be remembered; it is another to dictate, with the shorthand writers’ tablets prepared, whatever happens to come into one’s mouth, out of embarrassment at remaining silent.’
>
> In the preface to his Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians he testifies that, in dictating his Commentaries, he reached as many as a thousand verses each day. Long ago Rufinus had also reproached him for inconsistency in his Commentaries, and in his Apology he excuses the matter as follows:
>
> ‘I,’ he says, ‘in my Commentaries on Ephesians, and so forth.’”

Thus far David Clericus, and also John Clericus, David’s nephew on his brother’s side.

I do not doubt that our uninformed Catholics, and all the heretics of the present time, make much of the foregoing annotations of the Clerics against Jerome, which, as they claim, refute him on their merits. But if they had known the errors and ignorance of this sort of refutation, they would altogether repent of their hallucinations [Col. 1490D]. Therefore, if they are capable of repentance, let them not be angry with me or wish to take offense when they see their arguments refuted and their own manifest ignorance exposed.

The Clerics therefore accuse Jerome because the holy man said that the Hebrew word *OLAM* signifies eternity if it is written with Vau, in this form [Hebrew form]; but if written without Vau, [Hebrew form], it means an age, or the fiftieth year and Jubilee. And because in Hebrew volumes and in the older editions of St. Jerome’s Commentaries they now find the word *OLAM* written with Vau in the middle, [Hebrew form], although there the same Hebrew word is interpreted by Jerome as *saeculum*, they think they have cleverly identified an inconsistency in the holy Doctor, who elsewhere denies the same thing that he affirmed elsewhere. They claim that the cause of this inconsistency was Jerome’s haste in [Col. 1491A] writing his Commentaries, and his Hebrew teacher, from whom he learned the Scriptures by listening to him, and by whom he was repeatedly deceived.

But who would not be astonished that writers themselves deceived and misled by Rabbis and Masoretes should accuse others of Rabbinic hallucination and error? The Clerics themselves were deceived by the Masoretic text and by modern Hebrew, supposing that the name *OLAM* had been written with Vau—the so-called full form—in the Hebrew copies of St. Jerome, just as it is now seen written at Deuteronomy XXIII, 3. Then, deceived by the Erasmian edition of Jerome, they hallucinated again, believing that he had written in his Commentary on Ezekiel XXVI, 20: “Or, as it is written in Hebrew [Hebrew expression], and in Greek *αἰών*.” Jerome did not write this at all; rather, in accordance with the testimony of all manuscript copies, he wrote: “Or, as it is written in Hebrew *LOLAM*, and in Greek *ΑΙΩΝ*.”

*Lolam* can be written in Hebrew either with defective Vau, [Hebrew form], or with full Vau, [Hebrew form], as it is written even today and read *leolam*. [Col. 1491B] The third error, and one peculiar to the Clerics, is that they assert that Jerome was deceived by his rabbinic teacher in reading the Hebrew volumes—as though the holy Doctor had studied only through language and hearing, asking his teacher what was being read and hearing from him what was written in the Hebrew copies. It was certainly foolish even to imagine this, because we know with certainty and complete clarity that St. Jerome, being occupied with daily reading of the Hebrew sources, contracted, as he himself says, some rust in the Latin language; that he compared the Greek editions minutely with the Hebrew volumes; and that the Hebrew letters themselves, because of their smallness, were invisible to him by lamplight.

St. Jerome is therefore consistent with himself. He would not have given occasion for so many and such great hallucinations of the Clerics had he not been most corruptly edited by Erasmus and Marianus, who, as I have already warned many times, impose upon Jerome the Masoretic readings with their points and Hebrew letters [Col. 1491C], although he nowhere reproduced Hebrew words except expressed in Latin letters. Nor should a learned man be accused by the Clerics of being almost excessively hasty in his little works. In one day, writing or dictating rapidly, he could accomplish more than the Clerics could in twelve months, applying their whole minds to the composition of books.

We have the clearest evidence of this learned haste in his Commentaries on the Prophets, and especially in the letter to Fabiola on the priestly vestment, where the following are signs of the greatest haste:

> “These matters,” he says, “I dictated in a single brief night’s work, when the rope was already being cast off from the shore and the sailors were calling out more and more frequently. In hurried speech I set down what I could retain in memory and what I had gathered through long reading in the reasoning chamber of my heart. I understood well enough that I was flowing more through the impetus of speaking than through the judgment of a writer, and that, like a torrent, I was bringing forth turbid speech.”

What the three Capelli now object to us as a reproach against Jerome [Col. 1491D] chiefly concerns certain passages in his Commentaries on the Prophets. Their difficulties will have to be discussed in the third volume of the following edition of our work. For that reason I shall add a few remarks here in Jerome’s defense, so that from them the prudent reader may understand that none of the Critics has rightly censured the most learned man.

In Capellus’s *Index of Matters and Words of Sacred Criticism*, I found the following remarks concerning Jerome:

> “He translated certain passages in the Hebrew text badly, p. 82b; . . . and elsewhere he was often deceived by his Jewish teacher, p. 113, etc.”

On page 113a we read the following in his Commentary on the Prophet Habakkuk, chapter III, 5:

> “Before his face death shall go. And the devil shall go out before his feet.”

Jerome, says Ludovicus Capellus, here renders *reseph* as “devil.” That is, he thought that the devil was allegorically designated in this passage as the author and almost the prince of pestilence and death. But it seems that some Jew imposed upon him [Col. 1492A] and pulled the wool over his eyes when he interpreted it as “crawling on the belly” (for it signifies nothing similar). Hence Capellus supposes that the devil was so named because of the curse which God pronounced against him in the person of the serpent in Genesis III, and that he is the one who deceived Eve in the form of a serpent.

Our response to these remarks of Capellus will be very easy and straightforward once I have transcribed the passage in full from manuscript codices that preserve the genuine Jerome in his Commentary on Habakkuk:

> “Before his face death shall go: and the devil shall go out before his feet. In place of what we have translated ‘death,’ says Jerome, three letters are written in Hebrew [Hebrew letters], *DALETH, BETH, RES*, without a vowel. If they are read *DABAR*, they signify ‘word’; if *DEBER*, ‘pestilence,’ which in Greek is called *λοιμός*. Finally, Aquila also interpreted it in this way: ‘Before his face pestilence shall go.’ Symmachus: ‘Before his face death shall precede.’ The Fifth Edition: ‘Before his face death shall walk.’ Only the Septuagint and Theodotion interpreted the word as ‘death.’
>
> “Likewise, in the following verse, where we said, ‘The devil shall go out before his feet,’ the Septuagint translated it differently; we shall discuss them later. Aquila translated ‘devil’ as ‘flying creature’; Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Sixth Edition as ‘winged creature,’ which in Hebrew is called *RESEPH* [Hebrew form].
>
> “The Hebrews relate that, just as Beelzebub is called the prince of demons in the Gospel, so *Reseph* is the name of a demon who holds authority among the others; and because of his great speed and movement in different directions, he is called a bird and a flying creature. They say that he is the one who spoke to the woman in paradise under the figure of a serpent, and that he received his name from the curse by which he was condemned by God. For *RESEPH* is interpreted as ‘crawling on the belly.’
>
> “This, then, is what is meant: As soon as the Lord comes, is baptized in the Jordan, and the Father’s voice thunders at the descent of the dove—‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’—the devil will meet him as he comes out of the waters, and before his feet will stand death and the ancient serpent, who tempted him for forty days in the wilderness.”

It is truly astonishing to me to see any Critic opposed to this most learned exposition. But Capellus says that a Jew pulled the wool over Jerome’s eyes and imposed upon him when he interpreted *Reseph* as “crawling on the belly,” because it signifies nothing of the kind.

Who, then, imposed upon Capellus himself, and which of the modern Jews pulled the wool over his eyes so that he did not know that the word *reseph* signifies “he crawled,” or “the serpent crawled on its belly”? Let diligent readers hear, therefore, that the word *Reseph*, or *Resaph*, in the Syriac language—which is related and adjacent to Hebrew—means the same as “he crawled” and “he crawled on his belly.” For I have consulted no polyglot lexicon that did not immediately report this same meaning under the root *reseph*. See especially Edmund Castell’s *Heptaglot Lexicon*, column 3654, where under the aforesaid word *Reseph* you will find Jerome’s very statement about the devil and the other infernal flying creatures, and about the serpent’s crawling [Col. 1492D].

This is what I had to say about Jerome’s learning. Would that we might approach it, however slightly, so that the prudent reader may prove by experience the things he has heard from me in defense of the holy Doctor. For whoever wishes to acknowledge his little works and his learning will grant me calmly that Jerome surpasses all modern Critics in erudition, and will laugh at certain obscure followers of the later Rabbis, who, together with their masters, are altogether unworthy to be compared in any respect with the prince of all learned men and the phoenix of interpreters.

## § IV. Jerome’s supreme piety and religious devotion even in his critical Commentaries and little works

I have undertaken briefly to demonstrate Jerome’s supreme piety even in his critical little works [Col. 1493A]. I shall complete the whole matter by examples, since on this subject examples alone are sufficient.

**1.** The first example is taken from the letter to Fabiola on the priestly vestment:

> “He shall not be defiled over his father or his mother. Affection compels us to do many things; and, while we regard the kinship of bodies, we offend the Creator both of body and soul. Whoever loves father or mother more than Christ is not worthy of him. The disciple who desired to go to his father’s burial is forbidden by the Savior’s command. How many monks, while they pity their father and mother, have lost their souls? We may not be defiled over father or mother; how much less over a brother, sisters, cousins, household members, or servants? We are a royal and priestly race. Let us attend to that Father who never dies, or who dies for us—and who, living, died for this reason, that he might give life to us who were dead. If we possess anything from Egypt that the prince of this world can recognize as his own, let us leave it with the Egyptian woman who holds the cloak. The young man covered with a linen cloth followed the bound Lord; only by slipping away naked and unencumbered could he escape the attack of those pursuing him. Let us return to our parents what belongs to our parents—if they are still alive; if, while serving the Lord, they glory in having their children preferred to themselves.
>
> “He shall not go out from the sanctuary, and he shall not profane the sanctification of his God. We shall have to give an account even for an idle word; and everything that does not edify those who hear is turned into danger for those who speak. If I do or say anything deserving of blame, I go out from the sanctuary and pollute the name of Christ, in which I take pleasure. How much more does this apply to a high priest and bishop, who ought to be blameless and endowed with such virtues that he always dwells in the sanctuary and is prepared to offer sacrifices for the people—an intermediary between human beings and God, consecrating the Lamb’s flesh with his sacred mouth—for the holy oil of Christ his God is upon him. He shall not go out from the sanctuary, lest he pollute the garment with which he is clothed. For all of us who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ. That inhabitant of the hills who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho was not wounded until he had been stripped. Oil, a gentle medicine tempered with mercy, is poured into his wounds; and because he ought to feel the torment of negligence, he is bitten by the harshness of wine, so that through the oil he may be summoned to repentance and through the wine may experience the severity of the judge.
>
> “I realize that I have already exceeded the proper length of the letter, and I see that the wax tablets of the person receiving it are full. Therefore I pass on to the remaining matters, so that the speech may finally come to an end. The golden plate gleams on the forehead; for all our learning in every subject benefits us nothing unless we are crowned with the knowledge of God. We are clothed in linen, adorned with hyacinth-colored garments, girded with the sacred belt; works are given to us, and the breastpiece is placed upon us. We receive truth; speech brings forth doctrine. Everything is incomplete unless a driver worthy of so beautiful a chariot is sought, and the Creator, seated above his creatures, himself governs what he has made.
>
> “What was formerly displayed on the plate is now shown in the sign of the cross. Gold is less precious than the blood of the Gospel. Formerly, according to Ezekiel’s word, a sign was placed on the forehead of those who groaned; now, bearing the cross, we say: ‘The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us.’
>
> “Twice in Exodus we read that, at the Lord’s command and Moses’ execution of the command, there were eight kinds of garments for the high priest. In Leviticus only seven are mentioned, and it is related how Moses clothed his brother Aaron in them. Nothing is said of the undergarments; for this reason, I think, that the Law does not extend its hand to our genitals and private parts. We ourselves must cover and veil what is most secret and worthy of shame, reserving the consciousness of purity and of our seed for God the judge.
>
> “Others may judge of the remaining virtues—for example, wisdom, courage, justice, temperance, humility, gentleness, and generosity. Only conscience knows chastity, and human eyes cannot be reliable judges of it—apart from those who everywhere surrender themselves to lust like brute animals. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord,’ as though Moses were saying: ‘I do not clothe anyone in undergarments, nor impose a necessity upon anyone. Whoever wishes to be a priest must clothe himself.’
>
> “Oh, how many virgins, and the hoped-for chastity of how many people, will be disgraced on the day of judgment; and the defamed chastity of how many will be crowned by God the judge! Let us therefore ourselves put on the undergarments; let us ourselves cover our private parts; let us not seek the eyes of others. Let the genitals be so covered that they are exposed to no one’s eyes, lest, when we enter the Holy of Holies, any indecency should appear and we die.
>
> “Now the speech is ending, and I am drawn back to what preceded [Col. 1494B]. Such must be the knowledge and learning of God’s high priest that his steps, movements, and every utterance may be eloquent. Let him conceive truth in his mind and resound with it in his entire bearing and adornment, so that whatever he does and whatever he says may be the teaching of the peoples. Without bells, varied colors, and the gems and flowers of virtues, he can neither enter the sanctuary nor possess the name of bishop.
>
> “These matters I dictated in a single brief night’s work, when the rope was already being cast off from the shore and the sailors were calling out more and more frequently. In hurried speech I set down what I could retain in memory and what I had gathered through long reading in the reasoning chamber of my heart. I understood well enough that I was flowing more through the impetus of speaking than through the judgment of a writer, and that, like a torrent, I was bringing forth turbid speech.
>
> “It is reported in the index of Septimius Tertullian that there is a book on Aaron’s vestments, which I have not yet found to this day. If, because of the fame of the City, it should be found by you, I ask you not to compare my little stream with that river. For I should be judged not by the talents of great men, but by my own strength.”

**2.** From the letter to the same Fabiola on Israel’s forty-two encampments in the wilderness, you also have these examples of virtue:

> “From this we observe that the High Priest did not die simply on a mountain, but on the mountain of a mountain, so that a place worthy of his merits might be shown. He died in the year when the new people was about to enter the promised land, at the farthest borders of the land of Edom. Although he left the priesthood on the mountain to Eleazar his son, and although the Law brings those who fulfill it to the highest point, that elevation is nevertheless not beyond the waters of the Jordan, but at the farthest boundaries of earthly works; and the people mourned him for thirty days. Aaron is mourned; Jesus is not mourned. In the Law there is descent into hell; in the Gospel there is a passage into paradise.
>
> “The Canaanite also heard that Israel had arrived. At the place of the spies, where they knew that the people had once offended, they entered battle and took Israel captive. Again battle was waged in the same place; the victor was defeated by a vow, and the defeated prevailed. The place was called Hormah, that is, ‘anathema.’
>
> “I am not reluctant to repeat what is necessary for readers: the human condition always fluctuates along the road of this age. One person dies in the valley, another in the plains, another on a mountain—that is, at an elevated summit. When the enemy attacks us, deprived of God’s help, and leads us captive, let us not despair of salvation; let us arm ourselves again for battle. It may happen that we conquer where we were defeated and triumph in the same place where previously we were captives.”

**3.** From the letter to the virgin Principia:

> “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one. I think you understand this passage very well and that, girded with the sword of Christ, you serve as a soldier. But so that you may know that virginity always possesses the sword of chastity, by which it cuts off the works of the flesh and overcomes pleasures, even pagan error invented armed virgin goddesses.
>
> “Peter also girded his loins and held a burning lamp in his hands. . . . Therefore, by his glory and beauty—or by the splendor and loveliness of his divinity—mortifying the works of the flesh, and born of a Virgin, he became the prince of virginity for future virgins.”

**4.** From the letter to the presbyter Cyprian:

> “‘Lord, you have become our dwelling place from generation to generation.’ The Septuagint: ‘Lord, you have become our refuge in every generation and generation.’ In place of ‘dwelling’ and ‘refuge,’ *MAON* is used in Hebrew, which denotes a dwelling more than a refuge.
>
> “When he is about to relate sad events and lament the human race, he begins with praises of God, so that whatever adversity later befalls human beings may seem to have happened not through the Creator’s harshness but through the fault of the creature. Whoever endures a storm seeks refuge either in a rock or beneath a roof. Whoever is pursued by an enemy flees to the walls of cities. A weary traveler, worn by both sun and dust, seeks the comfort of shade. If a savage beast thirsts for human blood, a person desires and strives by every possible means to avoid the present danger.
>
> “So too, from the beginning of his creation, human beings have used God as their helper. Since it is by his grace that a person was created, and by his mercy that he continues and lives, no one can perform any good work without him—he who granted free will in such a way that he did not withhold his grace in each individual work. Otherwise the freedom of the will would overflow into an injury to the Creator and into an insult against him who was created free for this reason: that he might know himself to be nothing without God.
>
> “By saying ‘from generation to generation,’ he signifies all times: before the Law, under the Law, and in the grace of the Gospel. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves but the gift of God.’ And all his letters, at the beginning of their salutations, do not first have peace and then grace, but grace before peace, so that, after our sins have been forgiven, we may obtain the peace of the Lord.”

**5.** From the Commentary on chapter X of Ecclesiastes:

> “‘Woe to you, land whose king is a boy and whose princes eat in the morning. Blessed are you, land whose king is the son of freeborn men and whose princes eat at the proper time, in strength and not in confusion.’
>
> “He appears to reject the rule of young men and condemn luxurious judges, because in the one case wisdom is weakened by age, while in the others even mature age is enervated by pleasures. Conversely, he appears to approve a ruler of good character and liberally educated, and to praise those judges who in no way place pleasure above the affairs of their citizens but, after much labor and administration of the state, take food as though compelled by necessity.
>
> “Yet I think something more sacred lies hidden in the letter: those are called ‘young’ in Scripture who depart from ancient authority and despise the gray-haired precepts of their parents; who, neglecting God’s commandment, desire to establish human traditions. Against such people the Lord also threatens Israel in Isaiah, because it did not wish for the water of Shiloah, which flows quietly, and turned away from the ancient pool, choosing for itself the streams of Samaria and the torrents of Damascus. ‘And I will give them young men as princes,’ he says, ‘and mockers will rule over them.’
>
> “Read Daniel, and you will find God as the Ancient of Days. Read the Apocalypse of John, and you will find the Savior’s head white as snow and like white wool. Jeremiah too, because he was wise and his gray hair was reckoned as wisdom, is forbidden to call himself young.
>
> “Woe, therefore, to the land whose king is the devil, who is always eager for novelty and even rebels against his parent in Absalom; a land whose judges and princes are those who love the pleasures of this age, who, before the day of death arrives, say: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.’
>
> “By contrast, blessed is the land of the Church, whose king is Christ, the son of freeborn men, descended from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and also from the stock of all the Prophets and Saints, over whom sin did not rule and who therefore were truly free. From these was born the freer Virgin, holy Mary, having no branch and no shoot at her side; all her fruit burst forth into a flower speaking in the Song of Songs: ‘I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.’
>
> “Her princes also are the Apostles and all the saints, who have as their king the son of freeborn men—the son born of a free woman, not of the slave-woman Hagar, but of Sarah’s freedom. They do not eat in the morning or hastily. For they do not seek pleasure in the present age; they will eat at their proper time, when the time of recompense has arrived, and they will eat in strength and not in confusion. Everything good in the present age is confusion; everything good in the future age is everlasting strength.
>
> “Something similar is also said in Isaiah: ‘Behold, those who serve me shall eat; but you shall be hungry.’ And again: ‘Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice; but you shall be ashamed.’
>
> “‘Through sloth the framework will be brought low, and through weakness of the hands the house will drip.’
>
> “Our house, which has been erected together with the upright stature of a human being, and the dwelling that we have in heaven, will be brought low if we are slothful and slow to good works. Every framework that ought to carry the roof upward, when it collapses to the ground, crushes its inhabitant. And when the help of the hands and of the virtues grows numb, all the storms above and the whirlwind of the rains burst upon us.
>
> “What we have interpreted in the case of one human being can more suitably be understood of the Church: through the negligence of its rulers, all its height collapses, and there the allurements of vices are found where the covering of virtues was thought to be.”

These are the examples by which I wished to encourage you, diligent reader, to read Jerome’s little works, believing that in them you would find not Rabbinic and bloodless learning but the richest fruits of Christian piety and religion. Finally, let no one be surprised if something has escaped me in so extensive and difficult an edition of the works of St. Jerome; for alone and refreshed by the help of no one, I have been compelled to undertake this labor, greater than that of Hercules.

[Col. 1495]

# COMMENTARY ON THE BOOK OF HEBREW NAMES

[Col. 1495D] In publishing today the little works and compendia of the holy Fathers and other writers, our practice has been that, after a complete and finished edition of the texts, the prefaces to the whole work, or universal prolegomena, are submitted to the press last; and the final touch is, as it were, placed upon the head of the volume being assembled.

From this custom, now established among book editors, the following disadvantage may often arise: while an author carries through the labor begun for a new edition, he may die before undertaking to fortify that edition with a general preface and before informing the diligent reader of many things he has diligently accomplished, knowledge of which another writer afterward cannot disclose to us.

Desiring to meet this danger to commendable scholarship, I have undertaken here to illuminate with a Commentary the book of Hebrew Names, whose preface I may perhaps not publish before the end of my life. Thus the kindly reader might know into what rugged places I first stumbled while performing the office of corrector, everywhere restoring corrupted names, repeating many things that had been omitted, and cutting down everything superfluous in Jerome’s volume—one often published before, but badly edited and neglected both in its first and in its later revisions.

For, speaking boldly, no little work by learned men has appeared in our age with such a mass of errors, nor any with less benefit to its readers. What else, indeed, is the previously published Book of Hebrew Names than Jerome’s foul corpse, intended to frighten simpler people away from the study of the divine Scriptures and to provoke the laughter of the learned because of the absurdities with which it everywhere teems?

This work, therefore, so neglected before us and covered in every kind of dreadful squalor, but now wholly complete, spotless, and splendid, I wished to explain in this little Commentary—so that certain fastidious evaluators of matters would not think it had arisen of itself—the causes and origins both of its former corruption and of the labor I expended. In this way, learned people might finally understand how much is lacking in books previously published and what I have endured while struggling daily with monsters of error and prodigies of wording.

For at least ten months I pursued these matters, until I could erase and extinguish, to the best of my ability, everything badly written or edited—not only in the Latin copies of Jerome, but also in the Greek Fragments of Philo and throughout Origen’s Greek Lexicon of Hebrew Names—which I have copied out and interpreted here with great labor.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Authors of the Book of Hebrew Names

The last of the three writers of this work, Jerome himself, taught us in the preface he placed at the beginning of the book that there were three authors of it.

Philo, a man of great eloquence, was the first of the Jews to interpret the Hebrew Names of the Old Testament in Greek and to append their etymologies according to the order of the letters. Origen followed him, who, among the other splendid monuments of his genius, also labored at this task so that what Philo, as a Jew, had omitted, he, as a Christian, might complete—namely, by adding the Hebrew Names of the New Testament, which were nowhere found in Philo.

The third and later founder of this work was Jerome. Restoring the whole old structure with new care, he says that he had done something desirable not only to the Latins but also to the Greeks. For he corrected very many things according to the Hebrew sources, which lay corrupted in the Greek copies of Philo or Origen.

Yet it is not easy to say which things in the Book of Hebrew Names belong to the Jew Philo or to Origen, and which belong to our Jerome. Jerome did not wish to identify the names or words he had corrected and restored to better form, preferring to remain silent about them rather than write anything deserving criticism [Col. 1497D].

Because of that modesty of the holy Doctor, many things remain hidden from us, although knowledge of them would be of no small help in avoiding the blind prejudices by which more than a few people are entangled today. To avoid becoming involved in errors of this kind myself, I sought with much labor what no one before us had taught, so that I might discover at least in part which things properly belonged to Philo or to Adamantius [Origen], and which ought to be attributed to Jerome. We must therefore discuss this subject in the following sections.

## § I. Which names in the Book of Hebrew Names should be attributed to Philo the Jew

If some complete Greek copies of Philo survived and had been made available to us for use, every ambiguity would be removed, and his genuine offspring would immediately become known, just as Jerome’s restoration in the Hebrew Names would be known. But since the Greek book of the Jewish writer has not come down to our age—although in Jerome’s time it was commonly possessed by the Greeks and filled the libraries of the world—judgment concerning the matters proposed for examination must be reached by another method.

I therefore think that the distinction between Jerome’s corrections in the Book of Hebrew Names and the things written by its first author should be sought above all in the edition of the Seventy Translators, which alone the Jewish Hellenist Philo certainly knew and to which he adhered throughout his composition of the Book of Hebrew Names. For from this source the names that still remain intact will first become clear to us: names borrowed by Philo from the translation of the Septuagint Interpreters and left unchanged by Jerome.

Such, first, are the Hebrew words set down without interpretation by the Septuagint Translators themselves, which we either have read differently or possess in Latin translation from Saint Jerome. For example, in the book of Genesis the Septuagint Interpreters read *Achi*, *Chazib*, *Naid*, and several similar forms, which Jerome decided should be read or interpreted differently. Thus, while censuring all these in his book *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, he made the following apt observation concerning *Naid* (Gen. 4:16):

> “What the Septuagint translated as *Naid* is called *Nod* in Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], and it is interpreted as σαλευόμενος, that is, unstable and wavering, and of uncertain dwelling. It is therefore not ‘the land of Naid,’ as our common people think; rather, God’s sentence is fulfilled, namely, that he wandered here and there as a fugitive and exile (Gen. 38:5).”

He also discusses the name *Chazib* immediately afterward, and, following the Scriptural testimony according to the Septuagint, says:

> “Now this occurred at Chazbi, when she gave birth to him.” Here he says: “A Hebrew word has been placed in this passage in place of a place-name, which Aquila translated as a matter or event, saying: ‘And it happened that she was false in childbirth after she had borne Shelah.’ For after she had borne Shelah, her childbirth ceased. *Chazbi*, therefore, is not the name of a place but means ‘falsehood.’ Hence it is also written elsewhere: ‘The work of the olive will lie,’ that is, it will not produce the fruit of the olive.”

Let the discerning reader note that the name *Casbi* was written by Philo in the book *Hebrew Names* according to the Greek Χασβί, which we read in the Septuagint, but that Jerome restored it in conformity with the Hebrew source, where it is written [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text]—*Chazib*, with *zayin* in the middle and *beth* at the end of the word. Thus *Chazib* belongs partly to Philo the Jew and partly to our Jerome in the book just mentioned, *Hebrew Names*.

It would be wrong to omit what the same Jerome discussed concerning the name *Achi* in the already mentioned book *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*. For he wished to make the following observation concerning that word:

> “*Achi* is written twice in Genesis, and it is neither Greek nor Latin. Even the Hebrew itself is corrupt; for it is written *Ahu* [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], that is, ‘in the marsh.’ But because among the Hebrews the letters *vav* and *yod* are similar, differing only in size, the Septuagint Interpreters translated *Ahi* for *Ahu*; and, according to their custom, to express the double aspiration of the Hebrew letter *heth*, they joined to it the Greek letter *chi*.”

So it is: twice in Genesis we read *Achi*, or *Achei*, in the Septuagint, because twice it is written *Ahhu* in Hebrew—namely, in chapter 41, verses 2 and 18. For in these passages the Septuagint translated the Hebrew *baahhu* as ἐν τῷ Ἄχει, that is, “in Achi.” What we have said here concerning Genesis, namely, the Hebrew names set down without interpretation by the Septuagint and subsequently carried over through Philo’s work into the book *Hebrew Names*, we likewise recommend observing in the other books of the Old Testament, where readers will encounter very many names of this kind requiring attention.

Second, there can be no doubt that the Greek names substituted for Hebrew names should be attributed to Philo the Jew, who borrowed all these from the Septuagint Translation and interpreted Greek forms as though they were Hebrew. A striking example of this liberty is provided by the word *Eroon*, or *Eroum*, together with its etymology placed alongside it. For it is plainly the word of a Hellenistic Jewish writer who read in Genesis 46:28, according to the Septuagint Interpreters, that Judah had been sent by Jacob to Joseph to meet him at the city of Heroum, καθ’ Ἡρώων πόλιν, “in the land of Ramesse.” Yet, as Jerome testifies, and as the Hebrew codices contradict, Scripture contains neither the city of Heroum nor the land of Ramesse, but only Goshen.

Philo therefore derives the rationale and origin of the name Ἡρώων, *Eroon*, fabricated by the Septuagint Interpreters, in the book *Hebrew Names* as though we were reading *Eroon* somewhere in the Hebrew text of Genesis. He supposes that it could appropriately be translated “the vigilance of sorrows,” because *Er*, or *ir*, means “watchful” or “vigilant,” while *on* is also said to mean “sorrow” and “trouble.” Jerome, however, very frequently warned his readers about these Greek words, so absurdly shaped and interpreted according to the Hebrew language. It is therefore evident that this most learned man had no share in the ignorant interpretations with which the book *Hebrew Names* is filled. This is especially clear from the present word *Eroon*, which Philo interprets as “in their face.” For no Hebrew scholar, however acute, will ever persuade me that the elements of the word Ἡρώων contain Hebrew elements which, according to their proper idiom, mean “in their face.” The letter *beth* [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], the necessary preposition translated in Latin as “in,” is lacking.

Moreover, it is excessively arbitrary to say that *Eroon* signifies “face” because of the single letter *resh* in its middle, which by itself cannot take the place of the noun *mare*, sometimes meaning “countenance” or “face.” Let that immoderate liberty of inventing names and their interpretations therefore be far removed from our Jerome, since it is suited to deceive the ignorant but to offend the learned.

Third, not only are Hebrew names, and Greek names fabricated after their form together with their etymologies, attributed here to Philo the Jew; so too are those words which consist both of Hebrew words and of Hebrew articles. For example, the names *Aeberim*, *Afferezaei*, and *Accherubim*, which are read in this form in Exodus, are found to be composed with the prefixed article *he*, which they call emphatic. *Aeberim* is the name *Eberim*, that is, “Hebrews”; *Afferezaei* is *Pherezaei* itself; and *Accherubim* is the same as *Cherubim*.

But since Hellenistic Jews preferred to read such names, and many others, with *he*, which they pronounce *a*, it should cause no surprise if they wrote *Accherubim* for *Cherubim*, *Afferezaei* for *Pherezaei*, and so forth. For these names are sometimes read in the Hebrew text with the initial article, which doubles the following letter: *Aeberim*, *Afferezi*, *Accherubim*. Jerome therefore left these names unchanged in the book *Hebrew Names*, since they are read differently in Hebrew—sometimes with the emphatic *he*, and more often without that article.

A fourth class of Philo’s words and interpretations remains, unless I am mistaken, in the Greek Lexicon of Hesychius, the Alexandrian grammarian. He could have borrowed many names from no other source than the Greek book of that most eloquent Hellenistic Jew, namely, from the book *Hebrew Names*, and he himself interprets them according to the proper character of the Hebrew language. For whence did such a wealth of names come to Hesychius—names whose explanation was unknown to all the profane Greek writers—unless from that first author of the book of Hebrew words, or sacred Lexicon, whose work the Alexandrian could easily have used?

Accordingly, whatever Hebrew names are read in the Lexicon of Hesychius with interpretations according to their proper idiom undoubtedly acknowledge Philo the Jew as their first parent. I have therefore set down the following names, since I consider them neither superfluous to my work nor likely to be unwelcome to the curious reader:

- Ἄβελ, πένθος—that is, “Abel, mourning.”
- Ἀβράμ, περάτης, ἢ πατὴρ μετέωρος—“Abram, passer-by, or lofty father.”
- Ἀβράμ, δὲ, πατὴρ πολλῶν ἐθνῶν—“Abraham, father of many nations.”

Whence did the Greek grammarian Hesychius know that *Abel* signifies “mourning,” that *Abram* means “passer-by” or “lofty father,” and that *Abraham* means “father of many nations”? Certainly Aristarchus did not teach him such interpretations, nor Apion, nor Diogenianus; rather, it was Philo the Jew, who published the book *Hebrew Names* and placed their etymologies alongside them.

This is proved above all by an established error found in Philo and in the Greeks who followed this writer, namely, their teaching that *Abram* signifies περάτης, “passer-by,” although *perates* is a surname of Abraham, who is called *Ibri*, that is, “Hebrew,” in Genesis 14:13. *Ivri*, or *Ibri*, is translated “passer-by,” whereas the name *Abram*, according to the proper character of its elements and of the Hebrew language, means “lofty father.”

I have said that the error by which the Greeks interpret *Abram* as περάτης had become deeply rooted. This is perfectly clear from Royal Manuscript Codex 2282, where, on folio 67, we read:

> Ἄβραμ, πῆρ ὑψηλὸς, ἢ περάτης

That is: “Abram, lofty father, or passer-by.”

Other words with their interpretations prove the same point, such as Ἀδάμα, παρθενικὴ γῆ—“Adama, virgin earth.” In the Royal Manuscript, folio 84, we read: Ἀδάμα, γῆ παρθένος—“Adama, virgin earth.” These agree perfectly with the interpretation of Hesychius, because both readings derive from one source.

But lest anyone be able to find me lacking in either accuracy or diligence in reporting the readings of the manuscripts, I warn the attentive reader that several things in them are written corruptly. For in the aforementioned Royal Codex we read:

> Ἀδὰμ, γῆ παρθένος, ἢ γῆ αἱματώδης

That is: “Adam, virgin earth, or blood-colored earth.”

The Greek writer therefore substituted the name Ἀδάμα for Ἀδάμ, as is readily proved by the manuscript itself, which in the same place gives the name Ἀδάμ twice with different interpretations. The first interpretations correspond to the name *Adam*, while the latter two correspond to the name *Adama*.

Now, if anyone wishes to know why *Adama*, from which man is said to have been formed, is expressed as “virginal earth,” he should remember that *Adama* among the Hebrews is the same as “red earth.” True, pure, and untouched earth is red; hence γῆ παρθένος, “virgin earth,” signifies a red portion of the earth which has not yet been handled by human hands or trodden by human feet—such as, without doubt, was the earth from which the first man is read to have been formed, earthly from the earth.

For this reason Philo, in his book *On the Creation of the World*, page 52, while explaining the various causes of the perfection of Adam’s body, taught that a purer and more genuine material had been used in his formation:

> “The second reason,” he says, “is that God appears to have wished to fashion this statue in human form with the greatest care, not by taking soil from just any part of the earth, but by selecting from every quarter what was best, and cultivating with precision, from pure material, ἐκ καθαρᾶς ὕλης, that which was most pure and especially suitable for this work.”

Nor is the expression “virgin earth” unusual in Philo himself. For in his book *On the Cherubim*, page 116, discussing virtues allegorically, he honors the mind of the wise man by this name, saying:

> “And the wise man, sowing the seed of happiness for the use of mortals, into good and virgin earth, εἰς ἀγαθὴν καὶ παρθένον γῆν. For it is fitting that the undefiled, untouched, pure, and truly virgin nature, τῇ πρὸς ἀλήθειαν παρθένῳ, converse with God, etc.”

“Virgin,” or “virginal,” earth is therefore said to be the same as untouched and pure nature and material. Both the learned and the unlearned will readily grant, if they follow Philo’s discussion, that Adam’s body was composed from such a substance. The soil from which Adama, the first-created human being, was taken was entirely untouched and pure; hence the Greek writers not unreasonably interpret it as “virgin earth.”

But if our discussion returns to the Hebrew names mentioned in the Lexicon of Hesychius and in the Royal Manuscript, the name of Obadiah appears first, with an obscure and excessively intricate etymology, since the words and the meanings differ between them.

In Hesychius it is written:

Ἀβδιοῦ, Ἑρμοῦ δοῦλος ἐξομολογητός

That is: “Abdia, Mercury’s confessing servant.”

[Note: Martianaeus tortures himself miserably throughout this entire chapter, failing entirely to notice that the words of Hesychius are corrupt. The matter is nevertheless straightforward if, instead of Ἀβδιοῦ ἑρμοῦ, one reads and corrects it to Ἀβδιοὺδ ἑρμηνεύεται, or translates it as “Abdiud is interpreted as a confessing servant,” rather than “Abdiou, the confessing servant of Hermes.” It is especially clear—and Martianaeus himself noted this in his remarks on the Origenian Lexicon—that the Greeks habitually pronounce the name of Obadiah as Ἀβδιὺδ, just as Ἀβιοὺδ for *Abia*, and similarly in other cases, presenting forms in the genitive rather than the nominative. Indeed, no one acquainted with Hebrew letters denies that *Abdiud* is best rendered “confessing servant,” or “servant who has confessed,” from the verbs [Hebrew terms omitted in the supplied text]. Further, in place of ἑρμοῦ one should restore ἑρμηνεύεται, as the matter itself makes clear. *Abdiud* is interpreted as “servant,” not “Abdiud, Mercury’s servant”; for what place would Mercury have here? A Greek copyist could easily have been misled by the abbreviated writing of the verb ἑρμηνεύεται, so that he took the abbreviation for a circumflex accent and rashly rewrote it as ἑρμοῦ according to his own conjecture.]

In the manuscript, however, the words are clearly distinguished in this way:

> Ἀδιοῦ, δοῦλός μου, ἐξομολογητός

That is: “Abdia, my servant, confessing.”

How far “the servant of Hermes” differs from the other interpretation, “my servant,” is evident to every attentive reader. Nevertheless, Greek writers could have extracted both interpretations, however different, from the Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], *Abdia*. For if we take the final letter *he* as quiescent, *Abdi* will be read, which we may correctly interpret as “my servant,” in accordance with the manuscript. Moreover, since [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], *Abdia*, is a compound word formed from *Abad* and *Ia*, it is translated into Latin as “servant of God” or “servant of the Lord.” This name could be applied to Mercury, who among the Gentiles, worshipers of false gods, was both called and believed to be the servant or minister—that is, the messenger—of God.

I cannot easily say how the differing interpretation arose in Hesychius and in the Royal Manuscript, unless perhaps we should say that μοῦ was made from Ἑρμοῦ, or conversely that ἑρμοῦ arose from μοῦ. Whatever happened in that matter, the greater difficulty remains in the following word, ἐξομολογητός, which can in no way explain the Hebrew word *Obadia*, or *Abdia*. For Ἀβδιοῦ will have been interpreted with excessive violence as ἐξομολογητός, “confessing,” because of the first syllable Ἰοῦ of the name Ἰούδα, which signifies that meaning. For this reason, it seems to me that the interpretation of the name ἐξομολογητός belongs not to the Hebrew *Abdiou* but to the Greek *Hermou*, which in Hesychius himself is interpreted as “herald”: Ἑρμῆς, κῆρυξ. But let learned men judge these matters.

There are very many other Hebrew names in the readings of Hesychius, of which I shall present only four or five more, interpreted according to the proper character of the Hebrew language and therefore borrowed from Philo the Jew:

- Ἰωαθάμ, ἰαὼ συντέλεια—that is, “Joatham, perfection of God,” or “Jao, completion.”
- Ἰωήλ, ἀγαπητὸς Κυρίου: ἀρχή—“Joel, beloved of the Lord, beginning.”
- Ἰωνᾶς, ἑρμηνεύεται ὑψίστου πονοῦντος, ἢ περιστερά, προφήτης παρ’ Ἑβραίοις—that is, “Jonas is interpreted as ‘the Most High who suffers,’ or ‘dove’; a prophet among the Hebrews.”
- Σαράβαρα, τὰ περὶ τὰς κνημῖδας ἐνδύματα—“Sarabara, garments that surround the shins.”
- Σαραφὶν, γνώσεως πληθυσμός, ἢ σοφίας χύσις—“Seraphim, an abundance of knowledge, or an outpouring of wisdom.”

If we examine each of these carefully, we shall be compelled to admit that they were taken from Philo, unless Hesychius himself was responsible for the particular hallucination in the etymology of *Seraphin*. That interpretation is demonstrably false and belongs to another name, as I shall show shortly.

Concerning *Joatham*, which is understood as *Jao*, that is, “perfection of God,” only this should be observed: Jerome took the name as a single unit and interpreted it as “completed” or “perfect,” whereas, by contrast, the Greek writers regard the name as composed of *Jao*, or *Jehovah*, according to modern grammarians, and *tham*, which in Latin means “perfect” or “perfection.”

Thus, in the Greek Royal Manuscript, folio 88, we read:

> Ἰωάθαμ, ἄμωμος κυρίου, ἢ τέλειος

That is: “Joatham, blameless of the Lord, or perfect.”

A little farther on we read:

> Ἰωήλ, ἀγαπητὸς κυρίου

That is: “Joel, beloved of God.”

The Royal Codex does not add, with Hesychius, ἀρχή, or rather ἢ ἀρχή, “or beginning.” Nevertheless, the name *Joel* does have this sound, since it is taken from the Hebrew verb *jaal*, or from the Chaldean *evil* and *aval*, which signify “beginning” and “origin.” [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], *jaal*, is also used among the Hebrews for “he desired” and “he willed”; hence [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], *Joel*, “beloved of God.”

In the book *Hebrew Names*, Jerome interprets *Jonas* as “dove,” or “where he has been given,” or “suffering.” Nothing in this etymology appears to agree with the interpretation of Hesychius, ὑψίστου, “of the Most High”; nor do I understand how the Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], *Jona*, can be suited to produce the meaning “sublime” or “lofty.”

Nor am I influenced by the Latin translation of the second volume of Origen’s *Commentaries on John*, where the following words are written:

> “In the same way he was raised up toward Jeremiah by divine exaltation—for ἰαὼ is interpreted as ‘exaltation’—but toward human beings, etc.”

If this explanation or interpretation were correct, the name *Jehovah*, which the ancients read as ἰαὼ, would signify “the sublime and lofty,” or rather “exaltation itself” and “height.” This would provide considerable support for the etymology of the name *Jona*, which, being composed of *Jo*, or *Jao*, could be expressed as ὑψίστου, “sublime” or “lofty,” according to Hesychius.

But the error plainly belongs to the Latin translator of Origen. “Exaltation” does not refer to the Greek name Ἰαὼ, or to the Hebrew *Jehovah*, but to the whole name *Jeremiah*, which is composed from *rum*, from which it receives the meaning “lofty,” and *Ia*, or *Jehovah*, which are counted among the names of God.

The matter is evident from the Greek context of Origen Adamantius himself:

> Ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ πρὸς Ἱερεμίαν θείῳ μετεωρισμῷ ἐπαρθέντα, ἑρμηνεύεται γὰρ, μετεωρισμὸς ἰάω

That is:

> “In the same way, raised up toward Jeremiah by divine exaltation; for it is interpreted as ‘the exaltation of Jao.’”

*Jeremiah*, therefore, means “the exaltation of Jao,” or “the sublimity of Jehovah,” or rather, according to Jerome, “the lofty one of the Lord.” For ἰαὼ is an indeclinable name and must be understood in the genitive case—something that escaped the Latin translator of Origen.

[Col. 1502C]

Concerning the name Σαράβαρα, there is nothing that should greatly trouble us, since Jerome discussed this word sufficiently in Book 1 of his *Commentary on Daniel*, chapter 3:

> “In place of the trousers,” he says, “which Symmachus translated as ἀναξυρίδες, Aquila and Theodotion used *Saraballa*, and not, as it is read corruptly, *Sarabara*. In the language of the Chaldeans, *Saraballa* means the legs and shins of human beings, and, by homonymy, their trousers as well, by which their legs and shins are covered—garments called, as it were, ‘leg-coverings’ and ‘shin-coverings.’”

Jerome and Hesychius therefore agree: Hesychius interpreted *Sarabara* above as garments that surround the shins, or by which the shins are covered. Hesychius could not have read *Sarabara* except in corrupt form, since he borrowed that Chaldean name from Philo, while Philo had borrowed it from the Septuagint.

Very few things in the readings of Hesychius fail to support our opinion that the etymologies of the *Hebrew Names* were transferred from Philo the Jew’s book into the Lexicon of Hesychius. But even if the other evidence were contradictory, the interpretation of the name *Seraphim* that we cited above would establish the point most clearly.

According to Hesychius, *Seraphim* means “an abundance of knowledge” or “a store of wisdom.” A Greek writer could not have asserted this unless he was entirely ignorant of the Hebrew language and interpreted the name *Seraphim* as the word *Cherubim*. For *Seraphim*, according to the proper character of the Hebrew language, are translated into Latin as “those who inflame” or “those who burn,” from the verb *saraph*, which means “he burned” or “he set on fire.”

*Cherubim*, however, is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge,” from *nachar*, that is, “he knew,” and from *raba*, “to be many” or “to multiply.” Hesychius therefore confuses *Seraphim* with the name *Cherubim*, whose etymology he wrongly joined to the Hebrew *Seraphim*.

It is difficult to explain what led Hesychius into this error: whether a corrupt Greek copy of Philo the Jew, or a collection of prayers that had become customary among Christians, perhaps even among Jews. It is especially noteworthy that Jerome reports this pious and widespread error in his Letter 143, now addressed to Pope Damasus:

> “Their error also, although pious, must nevertheless be censured: they dare to say in their prayers and offerings, ‘He who sits upon the Cherubim and Seraphim.’ For it is written that God sits upon the Cherubim, as in the passage: ‘You who sit upon the Cherubim’ (Ps. 79). But no Scripture mentions God sitting upon the Seraphim; nor do we find the Seraphim themselves, who stand around God, anywhere in all the holy Scriptures except in the present passage (Isa. 6).”

The error of those who pray, a pious error in which *Cherubim* and *Seraphim* are confusedly named together, could have flowed into the error of Philo and afterward of Hesychius. In this conjecture, however, I do not wish to be contentious.

Besides the Lexicon of Hesychius, some Greek manuscripts also preserve a large part of the book *Hebrew Names*. I obtained one in the extensive library of the Most Christian King. I decided to copy it out entirely in my own hand, correct it, and translate it into Latin, drawn into this arduous undertaking by the hope of public benefit. For although there are people who despise Hebrew matters because they are entirely ignorant of the language, I do not despair of finding many learned men who will consider neither my study superfluous nor my diligence unwelcome to a discerning reader.

To please such kindly readers, therefore, I describe the manuscript and perform the office of translator. First, however, after reviewing all the Hebrew names that I was able to find in Philo himself, together with Jerome’s Latin interpretation and also the new explanation, I found that very many words required comparison with other sources.

If we now compare Josephus with Philo and with both of them with Jerome, we shall admit that at times Jerome disagrees with Josephus, at times with Philo; at times he agrees with both, though more rarely. For example, Jerome agrees with the Jewish writers in the etymology of the name *Abel*, which signifies “mourning” in Philo just as it does in Josephus. Likewise with the name *Babel*, or *Babylon*, which they interpret as “confusion” according to the character of the Hebrew language.

But in the famous name *Israel*, Jerome disagrees with both of them; indeed, he corrects their errors in his book *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*. He refutes Philo’s etymology of the word *Israel*, because Philo translated it as “seeing God”; and he refutes Josephus, who said that it means “resisting the angel of God.”

The case is different with the word *Eve*. Here Jerome agrees with Philo and disagrees with Josephus, who wished *Eve* to mean “mother of all living things,” whereas, according to the character of its elements, it means “life,” with nothing added from Josephus’s other words.

But lest we repeat unnecessarily what has already been said or what remains to be said, I leave such comparisons of the authors to the reader’s study. Once I have repeated the same matters once or twice, I shall be content to proceed more readily and easily to discuss others not yet explained.

Having therefore illustrated the collection of Hebrew names from Philo’s works, from various Greek fragments, and from the little works of Josephus, let us proceed to Origen—among Christian writers, I do not know whether there is a greater name.

## § II. On the Origenian Lexicon of Hebrew Names

[Col. 1504A]

To make it clear to all students that Origen composed a book of *Hebrew Names* and that he frequently proposed violent and unlearned etymologies in it, I shall produce as a witness a most learned man who rendered excellent service to Origen but by no means flattered his errors. With this author’s testimony placed in advance, I shall more readily be granted pardon if, compelled by the necessity of truth and sound judgment, I criticize Origen’s etymologies and do not shrink from exposing to readers his manifest ignorance of the Hebrew language.

Thus, in Book 3, chapter 3, section 7 of his *Origeniana*, Daniel Huet discusses the present work as follows:

> “I find among the ancients mention also of certain other writings of Origen. Philo the Jew had published a book of the Hebrew Names of the Old Testament and had added their etymologies and interpretations; Jerome rendered this book in Latin. What Philo had done for the Old Testament, Origen did in the same way for the New, adding his own work to Philo’s and taking Jerome as his imitator. Jerome’s words are these in the Preface to the book *Hebrew Names*: ‘And lest, when the building was completed, the finishing hand should seem to be lacking, I have interpreted the words and names of the New Testament, wishing in part to imitate Origen, whom no one but an ignorant person denies to have been the teacher of the Churches after the Apostles. Among the other splendid monuments of his genius, he also labored at this task, so that what Philo, as a Jew, had omitted, he, as a Christian, might complete.’”

> “The author of the *Questions to the Orthodox*, falsely attributed to Justin, mentions the same book in Questions 82 and 86, and teaches that in it, besides Hebrew names, measures were also interpreted. Let Rufinus therefore consider in what spirit he wrote in the second *Invective against Jerome*, where he says that Origen did not translate even one word of Scripture.”

You now know, on the testimony of a man renowned for his learning, that Origen was the author of the book *Hebrew Names* in the New Testament. The same Peter Daniel Huet, in Book 2, chapter 1, section 2 of his *Origeniana*, will now briefly teach you what Origen’s expertise in the Hebrew language was:

> “If he [Origen] had devoted himself more to Hebrew matters and had acquired greater proficiency in that language, nothing would have been lacking for his perfect knowledge of the sacred Law (Jerome, Letter 25, to Paula). But he lost as much of that glory as he withdrew from the study of the language. I will speak truthfully: either those who know little of Hebrew, or those who have read Origen’s works only superficially, attribute to him an exceptional proficiency in the Holy Language or in the dialects derived from it. Nor does Jerome contradict our opinion, although he appears to do so, when he says that all Greece admired in him his singular knowledge of the language. This could indeed have seemed remarkable to Greeks who were ignorant and inexperienced in Hebrew and unable to judge how far Origen had advanced in it.”

> “He himself certainly does not conceal his ignorance of this language in Homily 14 on Numbers: ‘Those who read the Hebrew letters,’ he says, ‘say that in this passage the word “God” is not written under the sign of the tetragrammaton; concerning this, let anyone who can inquire.’”

> “In our Observations we have noted many things that demonstrate his ignorance of Hebrew. One such example is the frivolous distinction between οὐρανόν and οὐρανοῖς, which he invents in commenting on Matthew 18:18 and to which he says Christ referred—as though the Syriac dialect used by Christ supported this distinction. Another is the false interpretation of the name *Aser* found in the Commentary on Matthew 18:19, as though it were derived from [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], ‘he instructed,’ and [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], ‘he bound,’ whereas it is formed from [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], ‘he bound.’”

> “This may perhaps be excused by the authority of the Seventy Elders, who sometimes translated it as though it were identical with [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text]. Thus, in Psalm 104 [Hebrew 105]:22, for the Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], they have τοῦ παιδεῦσαι τοὺς ἄρχοντας αὐτοῦ, ‘to instruct his princes.’ And in Hosea 10:10 the Septuagint has παιδεῦσαι αὐτούς, ‘to chastise them,’ whereas the Vulgate reads, ‘I shall correct them.’”

> “Another example is the corrupt reading of the Septuagint Interpreters’ passage in 2 Esdras 1:11: εὐνοῦχος τῷ βασιλεῖ, ‘a eunuch for the king’ (Origen, on Matthew 19:12). If he had had even some acquaintance with Hebrew, he would certainly have corrected the reading of the manuscripts, which contain [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], to τοῖς ὁ οἰνοχόος τῷ βασιλεῖ, if indeed he himself did not introduce this error—for it is nowhere found in the manuscripts of the Seventy Elders.”

> “Another example is the foolish explanation of the word *John*, which he thought was formed from the name [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], with the prefix [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], although it is derived solely from the prefixed servile letters.”

> “He is likewise frequently mistaken in investigating the origins of Hebrew names. It was easy for a man following borrowed light to guide his steps through unknown places; but Philo the Jew provided that light, having interpreted the Hebrew names of the Old Testament in a special book. Origen appended to that work an equivalent volume containing the explanation of the Hebrew names of the New Testament.”

> “Who, following Philo as his guide, could have failed to stumble, although Philo, a Jew and descended from Jews, had received not even an average breath of Hebrew learning, as was also true of almost all the other Hellenists? If this is not surprising in men born and raised in Alexandria—of whom Jerome writes that it is contrary to their nature to learn the Hebrew language, in accordance with the custom of all Greeks, who habitually disdain the study of foreign languages—it should seem entirely astonishing in that Hebrew Josephus, son of Mattathias. For it is easy to discern from his writings that, although he possessed that great and singular knowledge of Jewish origins, he did not bring to it an equal proficiency in his native language, even though he says that he wrote certain works in Hebrew which were subsequently lost.”

What answer can be made to these statements by the ignorant defenders of Josephus, who, having barely caught some slight breath of Hebrew learning, do not hesitate to pass judgment on the innermost meanings of the sacred Law, and to attribute to this writer an expertise in Hebrew which they themselves have not even glimpsed from afar?

For their popular applause, however, it is enough if they use this occasion to enter into a lengthy dispute and employ as much labor to persuade people of what they wish them to understand as falsehood always requires in order to appear true.

We, however, adhering to the judgments of sensible and learned men, do not fear to criticize Philo, Josephus, or Origen wherever the demands of truth require it. But lest we too appear liable to criticism in presenting the Origenian Lexicon, we shall make a few general observations about it here.

The first point to be noted is the order of the Hebrew names, which are placed according to the sequence of the letters of the Greek alphabet throughout the entire dictionary mentioned above, without any distinction or reference to the sacred books. Whether Origen himself followed this order is not sufficiently clear. Indeed, the contrary opinion appears more probable, both from Jerome, who frequently follows in Origen’s footsteps, and from the Greek Origenian Fragment published above, which places the Hebrew names of each Evangelist separately according to the sequence of the elements of the Greek alphabet.

Thus the words found in Matthew are written before the others, followed by those belonging to Mark, and so consecutively through John. I can scarcely persuade myself that Origen observed one order organized by the sacred books in the Fragment of the book *Names*, but entered upon another path in the Lexicon that survives intact, placing confusedly and indiscriminately under each letter the names of all the books of the Old and New Testaments.

I would therefore more readily believe that this Lexicon was arranged through the ill-advised diligence of some Greek, though borrowed entirely from Origen’s book *Hebrew Names*, which Origen himself had published with distinctions both of the Scriptural books and of the words. I am all the more inclined to this view because I have become certain that some Latins did the same thing in Jerome’s book of Hebrew names.

For at Venice, through the brothers Giovanni and Gregorio de’ Gregori, in the year of the Lord 1498, on 25 August, the book *Hebrew Names* appeared among Jerome’s works in this disorder and reversal. In it, every distinction and reference to the books of Scripture had been removed, and all the words of both the Old and New Testaments were placed under the letter with which they begin.

The sequence of names in the Origenian Lexicon is therefore secondary and belongs to some little Greek who overturned the original order. He removed the annotations and citations of the books, so that what had been written distinctly and separately by Philo and Origen, indulging his own saliva, he allowed himself to join when separate and to confuse when distinct.

Even if the order of the names in the Lexicon is defective, however, the matters themselves and the interpretations of the words are entirely genuine, drawn as living water from their own native source. I establish and confirm this from two passages in the *Questions and Responses to the Orthodox*, falsely attributed to Justin Martyr.

Regarding QUESTION 82, “What is the explanation of the name Beelzebub?” the following RESPONSE was given by the Greek Author:

> “Of Beelzebul and Beliar he says the names …; and the interpretation of these names is said by Origen to be found in the Interpretation of the Hebrew Names.”

That is: “I set forth the names Beelzebul and Beliar …; and Origen is said to have given the interpretation of these names in the Interpretation of the Hebrew Names.”

This response of the Greek Writer, whoever he may have been, is entirely confirmed as true by the Origenian Lexicon that follows shortly afterward, where the names Beelzebul and Beliar are read in a corrupt form, precisely as they are quoted in the Response, and where they have different interpretations appended by Origen.

## QUESTION 86. What is the interpretation of these terms?

Mna, ephah, nebel, homer, shekel, basilicon, holy thing, stater, drachma, quadrans, hormiscus, didrachma, talent, as, seraphim, bezel, Sabaoth, Adonai, ephod? For knowledge of both kinds is exceedingly necessary to us, since both are contained in the Scriptures.

### RESPONSE

> “The interpretation of all the Hebrew names or measures occurring in the divine Scriptures has been given by Origen, a man skilled in the Hebrew language. If you seek that work, you will find in it the interpretation of everything you have asked about.”

That is: “The interpretation of all the Hebrew names and measures found in the sacred Scriptures was given by Origen, a man skilled in the Hebrew language. If you look for it, you will find in it the explanation of all the names about which you have inquired.”

The Lexicon that I have called Origenian certainly contains not only the etymologies of Hebrew names but also interpretations of measures. It therefore appears to be the very work of Adamantius, although, as I observed earlier, the order of the names is confused and altered. If one adds that the Hebrew names of the New Testament are written and interpreted in the same Lexicon, no room for doubt remains that Origen was its author. As a Christian, he supplied the names omitted by the Jewish Philo. Having therefore established these general points in advance, let us now turn to the Lexicon itself, which will be illustrated below, according to our ability, by many other particular annotations.

# CHAPTER II. Jerome’s Learning in Hebrew Matters and the Usefulness of the Book of Names

In the preceding chapter we discussed at length the earlier Greek writers of the Book of Hebrew Names, namely Philo and Origen. To complete this little Commentary, it remains to present what concerns Jerome, the Latin translator of the same Book of Names, in order to make evident to all the great Doctor’s learning in Hebrew matters and the supreme usefulness of his labors.

For I often hear learned and unlearned alike complaining that they stamp upon this illustrious man, so highly skilled in divine Scripture and the Hebrew language, sometimes the suspicion of ignorance, sometimes the reputation of an unstable mind—as though Jerome either did not know that the etymologies in the Book of Hebrew Names were generally forced, or elsewhere had not remembered that here he had rendered something in Latin which he later acknowledged to have been interpreted forcibly.

Against such blind and hasty prejudices of certain men of letters, and against the foolish, talkative learning of many people in our own age, I have thought it worthwhile here to undertake an Apology for the most holy Doctor. My purpose is that henceforth they may not dare to disparage the greatest interpreter of the Scriptures and the most skilled man in the Hebrew language, nor imagine that they may safely attack with a malicious tooth the highly learned man whom perfect erudition joined to integrity of character raised to the highest summit of glory.

## § I. Jerome possessed exceptional knowledge of the Hebrew language

There is certainly no reason why certain writers should begrudge Jerome a complete knowledge of the Hebrew language, although this opinion may seem to arise, first, from the fact that he interprets as Hebrew a great many Greek and Latin names which no learned man ever proposed to explain according to the proper character of the Hebrew language.

Second, frequent etymologies occur in the Book of Names in which words are forcibly derived from a Hebrew origin and which show little savor of learning in the Hebrew idiom.

Third and finally, the holy Doctor often wished a term to be ambiguous and capable of several interpretations when in fact it has only one etymology and admits only one interpretation.

These are the principal charges brought against Jerome, and which some people raised with me when we were discussing his learning in Hebrew matters.

But the answer to these difficulties is easy and straightforward; it is not difficult to remove each of them, provided they are dissolved in the same order in which they were brought against us.

Erasmus, and after him not a few readers of the Book of Names, are amazed that Jerome interprets Greek and Latin words such as Ethiopia and Egypt as though they had once been Hebrew names, even though it is established for everyone that these names have always had a Greek or Latin origin and etymology.

I, however, am most amazed if Jerome could have had any editor or reader who suspected such things of him. For all who have read the Book of Hebrew Names even cursorily and in haste admit that Saint Jerome was wrongly censured and doubted by Erasmus, because it is perfectly clear that Jerome disapproved and rejected such a forced and absurd method of interpreting names that are not purely Hebrew.

This is proved above all by Jerome’s own brief note written after the word *Puteoli* from the Acts of the Apostles, column 103:

> “All these names,” he says, “are Greek or Latin; I think it is clear to the reader how forcibly they have been interpreted according to the Hebrew language.”

Nothing could be clearer to the reader. From this I infer that Desiderius Erasmus did not read the complete Book of Hebrew Names, but handed it over to the printers for publication with the same negligence with which it had been written in some corrupt copy.

For Erasmus was not so foolish—a man celebrated for nobility of intellect and learning—that he would have attributed to Jerome, even hesitantly, the etymologies of Greek and Latin names which he had read rejected and condemned in Jerome himself.

That single note already cited would have sufficed for the holy Doctor’s defense. But there is such an abundance of admonitions of this kind in the alphabet of names from the Acts of the Apostles, where both Greek and Latin words frequently occur, that under the single letter A he declares twelve times that the interpretations of words are forced.

At the end of the names beginning with C he also added this conclusion:

> “With a few names excepted, almost all those beginning with the letter C have been interpreted forcibly.”

A similar statement is found under L:

> “Almost all the names beginning with the letter L have been used forcibly.”

Let the learned reader now observe how great is the imprudence and ignorance of certain critics who customarily attack Jerome as though he were the author of all the etymologies in the Book of Hebrew Names.

What the examples just cited teach in general, or what common observations concerning the sequence of many names taken together demonstrate, is shown equally clearly and decisively by not a few individual names, Greek or Latin, to which Jerome’s censure was specifically applied.
