These include Andreas, Areopagus, Erastus, Eutychus, Festum, Mesopotamia, and Syrtis. It will not be irrelevant to our purpose to repeat their interpretations individually:

> “Andreas: ‘glory in his station,’ or ‘answering the pasture’; but this is forced. It is better that, according to the Greek etymology, *ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνδρός* (*apo tou andros*)—that is, ‘from man’—it should be called ‘manly.’
>
> “Areopagus: ‘primitive solemnity’; but this too is forced, since it is the name of an Athenian court, which received its name from Mars.
>
> “Erastus: ‘my brother seeing’; a sufficiently absurd figurative meaning.
>
> “Eutychus: ‘mad’; whereas in Greek it means ‘fortunate.’
>
> “Festum: ‘from the mouth of many’; this too is a Latin name, and is forcibly given a Hebrew form.
>
> “Mesopotamia: ‘raised by a certain calling’; but it possesses a better etymology from Greek, since it is surrounded by two rivers, the Euphrates and the Tigris.
>
> “Syrtis: ‘distress’ or ‘tribulation’; but Sallustius gives a better account when he says that it received its name from its dragging movement.”

Are these the words of an ignorant writer who received Greek and Latin names as though they were Hebrew, or interpreted them according to the character of the Hebrew language?

Let those critics therefore admit, whether they wish to or not—those among whom Jerome’s Hebrew learning has been ill spoken of—that our Jerome merely translated into Latin what had been collected in the Book of Names by Origen, its first author, or by other Greek writers. For Jerome expressly rejected such a forced and absurd method of interpreting Greek and Latin words, preserving everywhere the Greek etymology for Greek names, the Latin for Latin names, and the Hebrew for Hebrew names.

Some of the Hebraizers raise another objection, refusing to admit that Jerome knew the Hebrew language. “If,” they say, “he had possessed knowledge of this idiom, we would not read so many words forcibly interpreted in the Book of Names, nor would the volume abound in such absurd etymologies.”

But what could be more forced, they ask, than the interpretation of the name Israel as “seeing God,” or “man,” or “a mind seeing God”? What greater absurdity could there be than this etymology of Ramesses: “he thundered joyfully,” or “malice from a moth”?

The entire Book of Names, whose author they suppose Jerome to have been, teems with interpretations of both kinds. Let the praise of Hebrew learning therefore cease—the learning that the common crowd imagined was not ordinary in him.

Those who perpetually complain in this fashion fail to understand that Jerome himself, whom they rashly presume to criticize, repeatedly complained of the same wrongly interpreted names in the Book of Names, and declared war more than a thousand years before his detractors against the forced and false etymologies of Hebrew names.

Since the unjust complaints of certain critics have given us such a broad field for discussion, let us indulge here and heap upon Jerome many ornaments, but upon his adversaries testimonies like enormous stones, so that their tongue may remain forever silenced.

To begin our replies with the name Israel, let the reader remember that the etymology of this word belongs properly to Philo and Origen, and was never approved by Jerome, although he at times translated it from Greek into Latin.

Let our carping critics therefore hear Jerome discussing the change of Jacob’s name in his *Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis*:

> “Josephus,” he says, “in the first book of the *Antiquities*, thinks that he was called Israel because he stood against the Angel. But when I examined this carefully, I could not find it at all in the Hebrew. And why must I seek the opinions of individuals, when the one who gave the name himself explains its etymology? ‘Your name shall not be called Jacob,’ he says, ‘but your name shall be Israel.’
>
> “Why? Aquila translates: *ὅτι ἤρξας μετὰ Θεοῦ* (*hoti ērxas meta Theou*)—‘because you have ruled with God’; Symmachus: *ὅτι ἤρξω πρὸς Θεόν* (*hoti ērxō pros Theon*)—‘because you have ruled toward God’; the Septuagint and Theodotion: *ὅτι ἐνίσχυσας μετὰ Θεοῦ* (*hoti enischysas meta Theou*)—‘because you have prevailed with God.’
>
> “For *sarith*, from which the word Israel is derived, means ‘a prince.’ The meaning therefore is: ‘Your name shall not be called Supplanter,’ that is, Jacob; ‘but your name shall be called Prince with God,’ that is, Israel. For just as I am a prince, so you too, who were able to wrestle with me, shall be called a prince. But if you were able to fight with me, who am God—or an Angel, since many interpret the matter differently—how much more with human beings, that is, with Esau, whom you need not fear?
>
> “But the interpretation of Israel in the Book of Names as ‘a man seeing God,’ worn out by nearly everyone’s repetition, seems to me to have been interpreted not so much truly as forcibly.
>
> “For here Israel is written with these letters: *yod, sin, resh, aleph, lamed* (), which is interpreted as ‘prince of God,’ or ‘the upright one of God,’ that is, *εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ* (*euthutatos Theou*), ‘the most upright of God.’
>
> “‘A man seeing God,’ however, is written with these letters: *aleph, yod, sin* (), so that ‘man’ is written with three letters and pronounced *ish*. ‘Seeing’ is likewise written with three letters: *resh, aleph, he* (), and pronounced *ra*. Finally, *El* is written with two letters, *aleph* and *lamed* (), and means ‘God’ or ‘the strong one.’
>
> “Although therefore the great authority of those men is imposing, and the shadow of their eloquence overwhelms us—those who translated Israel as ‘a man’ or ‘a mind seeing God’—we are guided more by the authority of Scripture and of the Angel or God who called him Israel than by the eloquence of any worldly speaker.”

I wished to reproduce this entire passage in order to make Jerome’s diligence, the splendor of his eloquence, and the unshakable foundations of his teaching plainly evident. Nothing is more splendid than that exposition of the name Israel; nothing is more suitable for commending Jerome’s learning and diligence; and nothing is more effective for refuting his accusers, who, content with having read a single passage in the immense multitude of Jerome’s books, think themselves qualified to judge the perfect learning of the greatest Doctor.

If anyone wishes to know the names of the Greek writers whose authority was so great, and whose shadow of eloquence overwhelmed Jerome’s modesty, let him read Philo, Greek and Latin, p. 480; the Origenian Lexicon above, column 637; Eusebius of Caesarea, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, book V, chapter 11; and Didymus of Alexandria, book II, *On the Holy Spirit*. At the end of that volume these words are found:

> “They say that he remembers his mercy and his virtues in all that he repays them—not according to his own justice, but according to the mercy and goodness of him who is judge of the house that sees, and of the pure mind that perceives the Lord. This, translated from the Hebrew language into ours, is Israel, that is, ‘a mind seeing the Lord.’”

Philo, Origen, Eusebius, and Didymus, all highly celebrated among Greeks and Latins, therefore interpreted the name Israel as “a mind,” or “a man,” seeing God. So too did an apocryphal author cited by Origen in his *Commentary on John*, volume V, p. 72:

> “But my name is Israel, he who was called Israel by God: a man seeing God.”

So that Jerome might not stand alone in opposing these authorities in the Book of Hebrew Names, he too, at times amid the variety of allegorical explanations, says that the word Israel signifies “a man” and “a mind seeing God.”

Elsewhere, however, proceeding as though midway between his own opinion and that of others, and making a distinction, he teaches us to interpret Israel as “a man seeing God,” more according to the sound of the letters than according to the exact identity of the elements.

No prudent person will deny that this is so. For *ish* plainly means “man,” *ra* means “he saw” or “seeing,” and *El* likewise means “God”; hence Israel means “a man seeing God.”

But if the matter is tested according to the exact identity of the letters, three elements essential to the truth of this word’s etymology are absent from the name Israel, according to Jerome’s exposition given a little earlier. There he taught that the name *ish*, meaning “man,” is written with these three letters (); that *ra*, meaning “seeing,” is written with the same number (); and that *El*, meaning “God,” is written with two letters ().

From this it is clear that the critics of Jerome’s learning are unjust when, because of the etymology of the name Israel, they deprive the holy man of knowledge of the Hebrew language.

[Col. 1510B] Those who mock Jerome’s learning with the great amusement of the ignorant likewise act beyond all fairness and reason in connection with the etymology of the name Ramesses, which he interprets above, in the Book of Genesis, as “pasture,” or “a moth,” or “malice from a moth.”

For even if we grant that this interpretation belonged to Jerome, what is futile or ridiculous about it? Indeed, it is excellent if we examine it according to the character of the Hebrew language. For *Ramesses* contains all the elements necessary for the proposed etymology, “pasture from a moth,” or “malice from a moth.” *Ra* signifies “malice” or “pasture”; *me* conveys the Latin preposition *de*, “from”; and *sas*, or Hebrew *ses*, written like the Greek *σής* (*sēs*), means “moth.”

I do not, however, wish to attribute to Jerome the interpretation which I know to belong properly to Philo and Origen, and which was not sufficiently approved by Jerome the Latin translator.

Philo’s interpretation of the name Ramesses, above, column 709, is therefore this:

> “Ramesse is interpreted as ‘the shaking of a moth,’ or ‘stirring the mind.’”

In the Origenian Lexicon, column 633, we read the following concerning the same word:

> “Ramesi: shepherding from grain.”

This etymology is certainly shown to be extremely corrupt both by Philo’s Greek and by Jerome’s Latin. For Philo’s *σεισμὸς σητός* (*seismos sētos*), “the movement of a moth,” teaches us that the Greek scribes’ ignorance introduced into Origen’s Lexicon *ἐκ σίτου* (*ek sitou*) instead of *ἐκ σητός* (*ek sētos*): “from grain” instead of “from a moth.”

Moreover, Jerome’s interpretation, “pasture from a moth,” means in Latin the same as Origen’s Greek words *ποιμανσία ἐκ σητός* (*poimansia ek sētos*), “pasture or fodder from a moth.”

The proof is therefore unmistakable that Jerome was Origen’s translator in the etymology of the name Ramesses, not its first author or originator. Great strength is added to this conclusion by what Jerome wrote in his letter to Fabiola concerning the forty-two Stations of the Israelites in the wilderness. Concerning the first station he said:

> “Ramesse,” he says, “is interpreted by some as ‘a turbulent commotion,’ or ‘bitterness,’ or ‘the commotion of a moth.’ We, however, judge that it more truly expresses ‘the thunder of joy.’
>
> “To this city, which lay at the farthest boundaries of Egypt, the people assembled who desired to go out into the wilderness. For, abandoning the turmoil of the world, they were being moved away from their former vices and from the moth of sins that had previously consumed them, so that, turning all bitterness into sweetness, they might hear the voice of God thundering from above on Mount Sinai, and so forth.”

Observe now, kind reader, how great is the difference and disparity between Jerome the etymologist in his Commentaries and Jerome himself as interpreter in the Book of Hebrew Names.

“By some,” he says, “Ramesse is interpreted as ‘the commotion of a moth’”—that is, by Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, who expressly wished to interpret Ramesses as *σεισμὸν σητός* (*seismon sētos*), “the movement” or “commotion of a moth”; and then by Origen, “turbulent commotion” or “the commotion of a moth,” volume I, *Homilies on Numbers* 33, p. 175e.

Nor should one think that Origen’s other aforementioned etymology, “pasture from a moth,” has been omitted here. Jerome pursues it most clearly in the present allegorical exposition when he says, “and from the moth of sins that had previously consumed them.” He would certainly not have added this had not such an Origenian etymology of the name Ramesses already been conceived and impressed upon everyone’s mind.

Philo himself also indicated this interpretation sufficiently in his book *On Dreams*, p. 577b, when he allegorically discussed the fortified cities Pithom and Ramesses built for Pharaoh in these words:

> “They built Ramesse, the sense, by which the soul is consumed as though by moths.”

Hence it is demonstrated more clearly than daylight that in the etymology and allegory of Ramesses Jerome presented himself as an imitator of Philo and Origen. In what follows, however, he expressed his own opinion, for he says:

> “But we judge that it more truly expresses”—namely, Ramesses—“the thunder of joy.”

There would be no room for doubt concerning this interpretation if the name Ramesses were written at the end with a doubled *sin*. But since it has two *samekh* letters, this final etymology of Jerome’s does not seem sufficiently exact.

Yet it contributes greatly to demonstrating Jerome’s learning, although it might seem considerably to count against him. For the holy Doctor knew, from his extremely familiar use of the Hebrew language, that among the Chaldeans, Syrians, and Arabs *sin* is often exchanged with *samekh*, and that in the etymology of names the word *saal*, written with *sin*, has among the Hebrews the same meaning as *saal* with *samekh* among the Arabs and Chaldeans.

Thus Jerome interpreted Ramesses as “the thunder of joy” not through any carelessness or plausible ignorance, but through a perfect knowledge of the Hebrew language. For *raam* expresses “thunder,” and *ses*, or *sas*, means “joy.”

Rabbi Bechai, cited by Buxtorf, especially supports this etymology. He teaches that a horse is called *sus* and is so named from cheerfulness, since it is naturally cheerful and by its liveliness cheers the sad rider.

He further demonstrates the interchange and equivalence of *samekh* and *sin* in these words:

> “For this reason it is called *SUS*, because it is the same as *SAS*.”

That is: “For this reason it is called *sus*, because it is equivalent to *sas*.”

Jerome could therefore interpret Ramesses as “the thunder of joy” through the interchange of *samekh* and *sin*. So far from being called ignorant of Hebrew matters on account of this etymology, he must be regarded as highly learned, since in it he followed the practice of the Hebrew teachers.

I will offer one further example in this apologetic composition concerning Jerome’s Hebrew learning. It is taken, like the preceding examples, from the Book of Exodus, and in the word Raphidim it demonstrates with complete clarity that most of the etymologies in the Book of Hebrew Names had not Jerome himself but Philo or Origen as their author. Consequently, no critic can bring such interpretations against the holy Doctor without being marked by rashness and ignorance, unless he has certain evidence from elsewhere that they were derived from Jerome.

Raphidim, above, column 22, is interpreted as “relaxed hands,” or “soundness of judgment,” or “a sufficient vision of the mouth for them.”

Those who have dealt only superficially with the reading of Saint Jerome’s works would not hesitate stubbornly to ascribe this threefold etymology to him as its author, since nothing in the Book of Names indicates whose interpretations of the Hebrew word Raphidim these originally were.

But that judgment would be hasty and false, as we can learn from the letter cited above. At the eleventh Station Jerome discusses Raphidim in this way:

> “They departed from Alus,” he says, “and encamped at Raphidim; and there was no water for the people. It is the eleventh Station, which I found interpreted forcibly in the Book of Hebrew Names: ‘he saw a sufficient mouth for them,’ or certainly ‘the vision of a mouth of the strong’; but it is better translated as ‘the dissolution of the strong,’ or ‘the health of the strong,’ or, according to the character of the Syriac language, ‘the relaxation of the hands.’
>
> “This is also read in Exodus after the departure from the wilderness of Sin … It is fittingly called ‘the dissolution’ or ‘health of the strong,’ either because Amalek was scattered or because Israel was healed. But if among the Syrians Raphidim signifies ‘the relaxation of the hands,’ let us say that this name was given to the place because of the offense of the people, since they murmured against the Lord.”

Jerome had therefore found in the Book of Hebrew Names the forced etymology of the name Raphidim. In expressing it himself in his letter to Fabiola according to the proper character of both the Hebrew and the Syriac languages, he shows himself exceedingly learned and skilled in both Hebrew and Syriac.

The present-day Hebraizing critics, who judge Jerome’s learning in Hebrew matters from the one Book of Names, would scarcely—or not even scarcely—have granted us this, unless Jerome’s own testimony had also confirmed that he was merely the translator of many etymologies which he indicates must be attributed to Philo or Origen, the earlier authors of the Book of Names.

Nor is this the only passage in which Jerome left a testimony that he had found in the Book of Hebrew Names etymologies which even learned men claimed had originated with him.

In the sixth book of his *Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter 15, he expressly warns us that the following interpretation of the name Philistines, “falling by the cup,” had been current before his Latin translation of the Book of Names:

> “In the Book of Hebrew Names,” he says, “I found Philistines interpreted as ‘falling by the cup.’”

Let the diligent reader therefore beware of attributing henceforth to Jerome the forest of Hebrew names that are interpreted forcibly or absurdly. For they have Greek authors, whose names we have already listed sufficiently and more than sufficiently.

I also point out that Jerome, in his allegorical exposition of the Prophets, often makes use of forced etymologies of names which elsewhere he wished to reject and disdain. Conversely, he sometimes neglects true and proper etymologies when they do not suit the passage of Scripture under discussion.

Hence in his eighth book of the *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter 27, we read the following concerning Damascus:

> “But if Damascus is interpreted as ‘drinking blood,’ and if there is a true Hebrew tradition that the field in which Abel was killed by his fratricidal brother Cain was in Damascus, and that the place was therefore marked by this name, then Paul rightly proceeded to Damascus after the killing of Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, in order to lead bound to Jerusalem those who believed in Christ.
>
> “By God’s mercy—he who made him seeing and blind—he lost the eyes of the flesh so that he might receive those of the mind; and the dragon’s scales fell from his eyes, by which he had lost the light of truth. He went to the village called Straight and found Ananias, who in our language is interpreted as ‘obedient.’”

A little later he adds:

> “But the interpretation of Damascus as ‘the blood of sackcloth’ and ‘the blood of a kiss’ does not suit the present passage. Hebrew names are frequently interpreted in different ways according to differences of accent and changes of letters, and especially of vowels, which among them possess their own particular properties.”

Since the interpretation of the name *Damesec*, which according to the character of the Hebrew language means “the blood of a sack,” did not suit the present passage, Jerome employed another sufficiently forced etymology, namely “drinking blood,” in order to indulge the richness of the allegory and the Hebrew tradition commonly received.

What that difference of accents is—which Jerome mentions frequently here and elsewhere, and which changes the meanings and interpretations of names—may be learned briefly from Jerome himself in his *Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, chapter 26, verses 32–33:

> “I do not know,” he says, “how the matter is found in the Septuagint Translators: ‘And Isaac’s servants came and reported to him concerning the well which they had dug, and they said to him, We found no water; and he called its name Oath.’ What etymology is there for calling it ‘Oath’ because they found no water?
>
> “On the contrary, in the Hebrew text, with which Aquila’s and Symmachus’s interpretation agrees, the meaning is that they found water, and that for this reason the well itself was called ‘abundance’; and the city was called Beersheba, that is, ‘the well of abundance.’
>
> “Although above we asserted that Beersheba was named either from the word for oath or from the number seven of the sheep, which is called *Sabee*, nevertheless Isaac now, because water had been found, alluding to the name of the city that already bore that name, altered the letter slightly. Instead of the hissing Hebrew *sin*, with which *Sabee* begins, he put the Greek sigma—that is, the Hebrew *samekh*.
>
> “Otherwise, according to the rule of allegory, after so many wells, at the end of the virtues, it is wholly unsuitable that Isaac should have found no water at all.”

Those who have not learned the Hebrew language will readily allow themselves to be persuaded by this passage from Saint Jerome’s *Hebrew Questions* that Isaac changed *sin* into *samekh* in the name *Sabee*, and that he wrote one form instead of the other.

But the Hebrew text of the present Book of Genesis removes this suspicion. In it the name *Sabee* is always written with *sin*, which Jerome calls hissing, whether it means “seven” and “oath” or “abundance” and “satiety.”

For *Sabee* in Genesis 26:33 differs in no respect from the same *Sabee* in chapter 21:30 and following. Isaac therefore placed *samekh* for *sin* only in the sound and pronunciation of the word; that is, he slightly altered the letter in its accent when calling *Sabee* the well which his servants had dug in order to draw water for him.

This native inflection of the sound, and the different pronunciation of the letter *sin* among the ancient Hebrews, is represented by the later school of the Masoretes and grammarians through the right-hand and left-hand dot placed above the same letter *sin*.

For if it is written with the right-hand dot, it sounds like a soft *ch*, or, according to some, like *sh*. But when written with the left-hand dot, it sounds like a hard *s*.

Thus, in modern Hebrew lexica, *Saba* with the right-hand dot expresses “seven” or “oath.” But if it has the left-hand dot, it signifies “satiety” or “abundance.”

With these observations concerning the varying accent of the Hebrew letter *sin*, it is clear to everyone that Jerome deliberately said above, in connection with the etymology of the name Damascus, that Hebrew names are frequently interpreted in different ways according to differences of accent.

He was referring to the middle *sin* in the word *Damesec*, from which the Greek and Latin ending produces *Damascus*. *Dam* means “blood”; but *sac*, with the left-hand dot on the initial letter, means “sackcloth” or “sack.” If the same letter *sin* at the beginning has the right-hand dot above it, however, the word changes into “drinking” or “giving to drink,” because the Hebrew root *shaqah* means “gave to drink” and “watered.” Likewise *nashaq* means “he kissed.”

Hence the name Damascus is interpreted both as “drinking blood” and as “the blood of sackcloth” and “the blood of a kiss.”

Having disposed, by so many examples, of every preconceived opinion of those critics who begrudge Jerome his knowledge of the Hebrew language, let us now come to the same or similar critics in order to vindicate for the holy Doctor the praise of consistency.

As we said earlier, there were also people who accused Jerome of inconstancy in his exposition of the divine Scriptures and complained that he frequently wrote contradictory things.

Rufinus once devoted himself to constructing this accusation against him. But Jerome did not wish to be held guilty of differing interpretations and mutually contradictory meanings, since he customarily sets forth not so much his own opinion as the expositions of many others.

He therefore vigorously and elegantly defended the abundance of differing interpretations and the freedom of discussion in these words:

> “What purpose do Commentaries serve? They explain the statements of another; they make obscure matters clear in plain speech; they repeat the opinions of many and say: ‘Some explain this passage in this way; others interpret it in that way.’ They strive to support their own meaning and understanding with these testimonies and by this reasoning, so that a prudent reader, when he has read differing explanations and learned what in the opinions of many should be approved or rejected, may judge what is more true and, like a good money-changer, reject counterfeit coin.
>
> “Is a person to be held guilty of differing interpretations and mutually contradictory meanings if, in one work in which he is explaining a passage, he has set forth the expositions of many?”

Explaining his own case still more clearly, he refutes Rufinus’s ignorant objection concerning the differing interpretation of the words *Nescu Bar* () with this illuminating response:

> “He is also said to criticize me because, when interpreting the Psalm, instead of what we read in Latin, ‘Embrace discipline,’ while in the Hebrew volume it is written *Nescu Bar*, I said in my little Commentaries, ‘Worship the Son.’
>
> “And again, when translating the entire Psalter into Roman speech, as though forgetful of my earlier explanation, I wrote, ‘Worship purely.’ Everyone can see that these are contradictory.
>
> “Indeed, he should be forgiven if he does not know the truth of the Hebrew language, since at times he even stumbles over Latin. *Nescu Bar*, if I translate word for word, is said to mean *καταφιλήσατε* (*kataphilēsate*), that is, ‘kiss’ or ‘kiss fervently.’ Since I did not wish to translate this inelegantly, I followed the meaning more closely and said, ‘Worship.’
>
> “For those who worship customarily kiss the hand and bow their heads. Blessed Job denies that he did this to the elements and idols when he says: ‘If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon proceeding brightly; and my heart rejoiced secretly, and I kissed my hand with my mouth—this too would be a very great iniquity and a denial against the most high God.’
>
> “The Hebrews, according to the character of their language, use kissing in the sense of veneration. I translated what they themselves understand, whose word it is.
>
> “But *bar* has different meanings among them. It means ‘son,’ as in *Bar-Jona*, ‘son of the dove’; *Bartholomew*, ‘son of Ptolemy’; *Bartimaeus*, *Barieu*, and *Barabbas*. It also means ‘wheat,’ ‘a bundle of ears,’ and ‘chosen’ or ‘pure.’
>
> “What fault did I commit, then, if I translated an ambiguous word in different ways? In my little Commentaries, where there is freedom of discussion, I had said, ‘Worship the Son.’ But in the text itself, so that I would not appear a violent translator and give occasion for Jewish slander, I said, ‘Worship purely,’ or ‘worship as the chosen’—which Aquila and Symmachus likewise translated.
>
> “What harm, then, is done to ecclesiastical faith if the reader is taught in how many ways a single verse may be explained among the Hebrews?”

Thus Jerome writes in the first book of his *Apology against Rufinus*. Although he acknowledged that he himself had worked out differing interpretations of the same words, he nevertheless refused to admit that his explanations contained either a lapse of memory or an unstable or contradictory intention.

What his accuser attributed to him as a fault, Jerome very clearly taught should instead be attributed to learning and knowledge of the Hebrew language.

The letter to the matron Fabiola, cited above, clears Jerome of any suspicion of the same inconsistency and contradictory interpretation. Indeed, it anticipates so explicitly, in its own wording, the arguments I had undertaken in the *Apology*, that it is unnecessary to say anything else or anything different, beyond what he wrote in his own defense in station IX of the already-mentioned letter:

> “Dephca,” he says, “the ninth station is called by the Hebrews κροῦμα, that is, ‘a knocking,’ in accordance with what the Lord also says: ‘Knock, and it shall be opened to you.’ In the *Book of Hebrew Names*, however, we translated it as ‘adhesion’ and ‘remission’; this ought not to disturb the reader, nor should he suppose that we write contradictory things. There we published the reading according to what is commonly found, if the middle letter of the word is written with *beth*; here, however, I found it written with *phe* in the Hebrew volume, and that letter denotes a knocking rather than a gluing. The meaning is clear: after the Lord’s responses, after the eighth number, which signifies the resurrection, we begin to knock upon the mysteries of Christ. I ask the prudent and diligent reader to understand that I translate the names according to the Hebrew truth. Otherwise, in the Greek and Latin manuscripts, apart from a few passages, we find everything corrupted; and I am astonished that certain learned and ecclesiastical men have wished to translate things that are not found in the Hebrew, and to seek fabricated explanations for badly interpreted words, so that in the present case they read *Raphca* instead of *Dephca*, putting one letter in place of another because *res* and *daleth* are distinguished by a small mark, and they interpret it as ‘healing,’ proceeding from this to develop a similar tropological interpretation.”

Jerome could not have removed more clearly from himself the charge of inconsistency in interpretation. Whoever wishes to read this testimony through, unless he is obstinate and burdened by insuperable prejudices against the holy man, will never allow himself to doubt Jerome’s Hebrew learning. No prudent person will deny that, even amid the greatest diversity of interpretations, it remained consistent and perfect.

Jerome’s treatment of the etymologies of names often seems slippery to me, because it scarcely permits the meaning to be known or retained—especially in the *Book of Hebrew Names*, of which he was an interpreter rather than an author. To demonstrate the matter and its difficulty with one or two examples, it is useful to present the name *Cades* with its etymology as found in the *Book of Names*. Throughout the books of the Pentateuch, *Cades* is always interpreted as “holy” or “holy woman,” or “changed” or “changed woman”; but in the book of the prophet Ezekiel, *Cades* is rendered only as “changed.” Nowhere in the entire *Book of Hebrew Names* does Jerome indicate which etymology of the word *Cades* is preferable: “holy woman,” “holy man,” or “changed.” Hence it comes about that both interpretations are attributed to Jerome as his own by everyone who does not read through the individual works of Jerome, although the former is the interpretation of the Jew Philo, namely, *Cades*, “holy,” while the latter is Jerome’s own: *Cades*, “changed” or “transferred.”

We have the clearest evidence of this in the same letter to Fabiola, station XXXIII, where *Cades* is discussed as follows:

> “And setting out from Asiongaber, they encamped in the desert of Sin; this is Cades. It is asked why the eighth station is now said to be the thirty-third. But it must be understood that the former is written with the letter *samech* (ס), and is interpreted as ‘bush’ or ‘hatred’; whereas this one is written with *sade* (צ), and is translated as ‘commandment.’ And the name joined to it, *Cades*, does not, as most suppose, mean ‘holy,’ but ‘changed’ or ‘transferred.’ We read in Genesis, according to the Hebrew truth, that Judah, supposing Tamar to be a prostitute, sent gifts; and the intermediary of the gifts asks, ‘Where is the *Cadesa*?’—that is, ‘the prostitute,’ whose appearance was changed from that of the other women. We find the same thing in many places. But if it is interpreted as ‘holy,’ it must be understood κατ’ ἀντίφρασιν, that is, by antiphrasis—as ‘sparing’ is said of one who does not spare at all, and ‘war’ of what is in no way warlike, and ‘grove’ of what gives no light.”

The name *Zabulon* supplies another example of this ambiguity or difficulty. In the book of Genesis it is interpreted above as “dwelling of strength” or “flow of the night.” From the *Book of Names* alone, who can distinguish whether this latter etymology, “flow of the night,” was approved by Jerome as his own, or whether it is to be regarded as someone else’s and rejected by him? But when I turn to the *Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, every shadow of ambiguity and cloud of obscurity immediately disappears, and Jerome’s meaning concerning the proposed etymology of *Zabulon* shines forth clearly:

> “And she called his name Zabulon. Where we have placed,” he says, “‘He dwelt with me,’ and the Seventy translated, ‘He will love me,’ the Hebrew has *Jezbuleni*; and the meaning is: ‘Because I have borne Jacob six sons, I am now secure, for my husband will dwell with me.’ Hence my son is also called ‘dwelling.’ Therefore, in the *Book of Names*, *Zabulon*, ‘flow of the night,’ is interpreted badly and violently.”

Here he teaches that it was interpreted badly and violently. Yet the learned and the unlearned alike commonly attribute this interpretation to Jerome as the author of all the etymologies found in the *Book of Hebrew Names*. Nevertheless, anyone who has spent some time reading through the records of his studies knows that Jerome rejected the greater part of them.

It would be easy to collect six hundred similar examples, and it is always honorable to defend the rights of Jerome’s learning. But since enough has now been brought forward and explained for the diligent and kindly reader to refute every preconceived opinion of those critics who delight in blaming Jerome for the etymologies of names, we proceed to another heading of criticism and accusation, which we previously said was the third cause. Some writers’ complaint remains to be overturned at the end, lest the great names of this age rob the supreme interpreter of Scripture of the palm of Hebrew learning. I mean learned men who, when occasion requires, either attack Jerome or defend those who attack him badly and ignorantly.

In this company, the most learned Samuel Bochart first comes to mind, and Richard Simon, who unsuccessfully attempted to remove his scruple. It is now my concern to tear from the minds of students both men’s opinions, which are by no means favorable to Jerome, by means of true answers; for I often see students become entangled in similar errors through reading the *Critical History of the Old Testament*.

In the second book of *Sacred Scripture’s Animals*, chapter 10, while discussing the raven, Bochart wished to censure Jerome modestly in these words:

> “There is also the passage from Zephaniah 2:14, where, concerning the devastation of Nineveh, we read: ‘the voice of one singing in the window, a raven upon the threshold.’ Thus Jerome has it. The Greek version reads: Θηρία φωνήσει ἐν τοῖς διορύγμασιν αὐτῶν, καὶ κόρακες ἐν τοῖς πυλῶσιν αὐτῆς—‘Beasts shall cry out in their openings, and ravens in its gates.’  
>   
> “But the Hebrew word [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], *choreb*, which they explain as ‘raven,’ signifies dryness and desolation; or, if one reads *chereb*, ‘sword.’ Accordingly, the Syriac translator renders it ‘sword,’ as does Aquila. Other Greek translators render it ‘dryness,’ as Jerome testifies, and I cannot understand why he preferred to render it ‘raven.’ ‘In the Hebrew,’ he says, ‘[Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text] is written, which, according to the diversity of reading, may be understood as dryness, sword, or raven.’ As though the forms with *cheth* and with *ayin* were the same. Jerome could not have been granted this. With *ayin* and *holem* it denotes ‘raven’; but with *cheth* and *holem* it denotes ‘dryness’ and ‘desolation,’ or ‘sword’ if it has *segol*. Since the Hebrews write it with *cheth* and *holem*, the words of Zephaniah should therefore be rendered: ‘A voice will resound from the window; desolation will be on the threshold, when the cedar has been stripped bare,’ that is, the cedar paneling. Here I understand ‘voice’ in the sense found in Isaiah 13:21.”

The author of the recent *Critical History*, book I, chapter 16, pages 95–96, repeats Bochart’s difficulty and attempts to solve it. I shall quote his words in French, exactly as he wrote them, so that in translating them into Latin I might not appear to have altered or added anything:

> “The same Saint Jerome,” says Simon, “in his commentary on Zephaniah, testifies that the word which he translated ‘raven’ with the Septuagint was written differently in the Hebrew copy of his time; but that, according to the diversity of reading, it could be translated ‘dryness,’ ‘knife,’ or ‘raven.’ Bochart says that he cannot understand this observation of Saint Jerome, since there is a great difference between *oreb*, written with *ayin* and *holem*, which means ‘raven,’ and *hereb*, with *heth*, which means ‘knife.’  
>   
> “To answer this difficulty, it is enough to observe that Saint Jerome was not always so closely attached to following his Hebrew copy that he did not sometimes follow other readings, which were based either on the ancient versions or on the nature of the Hebrew language. He regarded the Hebrew text as a very changeable writing, and took the liberty of changing one letter into another whenever he believed that he was producing a better sense. In his translation he prescribed no fixed rule for himself, and he is not even always consistent in his observations.”

To put it most mildly, Simon would have had an easy and straightforward answer to Bochart’s objection if he had examined even one manuscript copy of Jerome’s commentaries on Zephaniah. But, neglecting all reliance on the ancient books, he indulges his own ingenuity so freely that he would have acted more excusably by simply conceding to Bochart that Jerome had blundered.

For if what Richard Simon proposed while considering the difficulty raised by the already-mentioned writer were true of the holy Doctor, Jerome would not merely have been wrong in his interpretation of *oreb*, as Bochart thought; he would in fact have been inconsistent with himself in everything, since he would neither have adhered firmly to the Hebrew context nor allowed himself to be bound by any fixed rules of interpretation in his translations or etymologies of names, but would have changed the letters of the Hebrew language indiscriminately and promiscuously in order to adapt the meaning to his own statements. Even the most ignorant interpreter and etymologist ought surely to have been free from such faults.

To reject this poorly digested response of the recent critic, which is utterly destructive of Jerome, I appeal to the evidence of the Tables—that is, to the authority of ancient records. By this means I shall remove the scruple from the learned Bochart and bring to light the insulting falsehood of the *Critical History*.

Deceived by the corrupt modern editions of Jerome, Bochart thought that the holy Doctor had written in the second chapter of his commentary on the prophet Zephaniah:

> “Moreover, what both we and the Seventy likewise translated: ‘A raven upon the threshold’; in the Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text] is written, which, according to the diversity of reading, may be understood as dryness, sword, or raven. Hence Aquila interpreted it as ‘sword,’ and others as ‘dryness.’”

Seeing the Hebrew letters written with *heth* at the beginning, he more easily persuaded himself that Jerome had taught that the Hebrew name [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], according to the diversity of reading, could mean “sword,” “dryness,” and “raven.” This would indeed be proved entirely true if the passage in Jerome’s book retained the aforementioned word written with all three sets of elements. But since there is no manuscript copy of Jerome’s commentary on Zephaniah or on the other prophets that does not clearly show that Jerome himself wrote Hebrew names in Latin characters—*HAREB*, *OREB*, *EREB*, and similar forms—the corruption of Jerome’s text is perfectly evident. It gave rise to the error both of Bochart and of the other critical writers who wish the words [Hebrew terms omitted in the supplied text], that is, *choreb* and *oreb*, to have been accepted confusedly and indiscriminately in Jerome’s commentary.

The true reading of the holy Doctor is therefore the following, which I have recovered after carefully consulting five manuscript codices for this purpose:

> “In the Hebrew *HAREB* is written, which, according to the diversity of reading, may be understood either as dryness or sword, or as raven, etc.”

Who, then, I ask, will deny that Jerome meant the Hebrew name *hareb*, according to the diversity of reading, sometimes to signify dryness or sword, and sometimes raven? For if it is written in Hebrew beginning with *kheth* [Hebrew character omitted in the supplied text], it denotes sword or dryness, as Bochart concedes. But if it begins with *ayin* [Hebrew character omitted in the supplied text], no one will deny that it expresses “raven.” The observation that modern critics had considered an error and a blunder is therefore most true and entirely worthy of Jerome, whereas they themselves, on the contrary, had become entangled in errors introduced by the editors of the books and were subject to perpetual blunders.

And indeed, why should Jerome have been accused of error concerning the word *hareb* or *oreb*, when he himself rebuked the error of others arising from the confusion of *choreb* with *oreb*?

> “The history of the Midianites,” he says, “is written in the book of Judges, and we read it also in the Psalm: ‘Make their princes like Oreb and Zeeb and Zebah and Zalmunna.’ Therefore they are mistaken who think that this refers to the time when, in the book of Numbers, the Midianites are reported to have been slain by Israel; and to the desert of Shur; and to Mount Horeb, which among the Hebrews are written with other letters, since at that time they were not on Mount Horeb but in the wilderness of Shittim.”

This statement’s truth is revealed by the authority of sacred Scripture. In the book of Judges, chapter 7, verse 25, *the rock of Oreb* is written with *ayin*, *sur Oreb*; but in the Third Book of Kings, chapter 19, verse 8, *the mountain of God, Horeb*, is written with *heth*: *ar aeloim, hhoreb*, or *choreb*. The most learned Jerome therefore knew that there was a great difference between *choreb* with *heth* and *oreb* with *ayin*. Bochart would not have been permitted, had he used an authentic edition of Jerome’s works, to accuse him of the very error that the incomparable man’s diligence had rejected in the fourth book of his commentaries on Isaiah.

Much less would he have done so if, beyond the passage just cited, he had read Jerome’s commentary on chapter 15, where Jerome discusses the same name in the plural:

> “For ‘willows,’” he says, “we read in the Hebrew *ARABIM* (ערבים), which can also be understood as ‘Arabians,’ or read as *ORBIM*, that is, ‘a village situated on their borders,’ whose inhabitants, according to many, are said to have supplied food to Elijah on Mount Horeb. Because of its ambiguity, this name is also translated as ‘ravens,’ and as ‘the west,’ and ‘level places.’”

Let the critics of our own time therefore admit that nothing escaped Jerome in the etymology of the name *hareb* or *oreb*, and that he correctly wrote that this word, according to the diversity of reading, could be interpreted as sword, dryness, or raven.

If we now briefly examine the errors of the *Critical History of the Old Testament*, in order to repel the injuries inflicted on Jerome, the diligent reader should especially observe three things.

First, the suspicion of inconsistent interpretation was removed above by Jerome himself; in response to the critics’ second objection, we showed that he was entirely free from this defect.

Second, there would be no credibility in the words of the most holy Doctor if the recent critic’s observation were true—namely, that Jerome changed the letters of the Hebrew context at will, frequently reading *ayin* for *aleph* or for *heth*, and in the same way confusing all the elements in interpretation. For if this were believed, with what confidence could Jerome have said in his preface to the book of Psalms according to the Hebrew truth:

> “I shall certainly say this with confidence, and shall cite many witnesses to this work: that I have changed nothing whatsoever while knowing the Hebrew truth. Therefore, if my edition differs anywhere from the ancient ones, ask any Hebrew, and you will clearly see that I am being torn apart by my rivals in vain.”

Certainly he would not have written this so confidently if he had been conscious of such a thing and knowledgeable in the Hebrew language, unless he had been entirely certain that he had changed nothing whatsoever of the Hebrew truth. If he changed nothing whatsoever, then surely he changed neither the letters of his copies, on which the entire meaning of Hebrew words and the whole sense of the sacred books depends.

Moreover, a man who is accustomed to criticize others for this kind of confusion or alteration of Hebrew letters cannot prudently permit himself what he declares unlawful in other writers. Yet frequent criticisms of this kind are found in Jerome’s works, as in the much-repeated letter to Fabiola, station IV:

> “The fourth station is Phiairoth, which is interpreted as ‘the mouth of nobles,’ and is written with the letter *heth*. Some wrongly suppose it to be *Iroth*, meaning ‘villages’; and the error is obvious, since they read the letter *ayin* in place of the element mentioned above.”

He rebukes the same alteration of elements still more clearly and fully in station XXXIV, where he says:

> “The thirty-fourth station is interpreted by most as ‘light’; and they would not be mistaken if it were written with the letter *aleph*. Others interpret it as ‘skin’; and they too would be correct if *ayin* were present. Some interpret it as ‘hole’; this could be accepted if the element were *heth*. But since it is read with *he*, it more properly means ‘mountain,’ and it can be read: ‘Aaron the priest ascended the mountain of the mountain,’ that is, its summit.”

Finally, he sharply rebukes the Seventy Translators for changing Hebrew words. Thus, in book XII of his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 11, he teaches:

> “As for *Talami*, or as the Seventy rendered it, *thau* or *thee*—changing and altering the Hebrew names in each place as they wished—it is six cubits, etc.”

Since Jerome was so tireless in rebuking such practices, it could not be believed without doing him an injustice that he had, as the author of the *Critical History* recklessly claims, indiscriminately changed the Hebrew elements and led them captive into his own meanings as though by a conqueror’s right.

But, in order to restore good relations with that recent critic, let us concede that variant readings sometimes occurred in the Hebrew manuscripts used by Jerome. Among these variant readings, the holy Doctor chose those that he considered more suitable and more accurate for his interpretations, without changing anything in the archetypal copy whose reading he had followed. For if he had acted otherwise, he would not have been translating the books of the Hebrews but overthrowing them, and treating the Hebrew truth with contempt. May God keep this far from Jerome, the outstanding and greatest interpreter of Scripture, lest the entire credibility of his translations collapse, unsupported by any foundation in the Hebrew truth.

Third and finally, the reader must especially note and guard against what Jerome himself warned in these words, in book V of his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 15:

> “Let no one suppose that this is a scribal error and, in wishing to correct it, create an error. One city is written with both the letters *mem* and *beth*: *Dimon* with one means ‘silence’; *Dibon* with the other, ‘flowing.’ Both names are given because of the waters that flow silently. To this day the town is indiscriminately called both *Dimon* and *Dibon*.”

The present Hebrew text agrees with this observation of Jerome. In Isaiah 15:2 it reads *Dibon*, and afterward, in verse 9, [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], *Dimon*. The Chaldean likewise agrees, as do the Greek manuscripts of the Roman edition, where the forms are Δηβὼν and Δειμὼν. But the Alexandrian manuscript of the Septuagint has a different reading, namely Δαιβηδὸν and Ῥεμμώμ. The Syriac everywhere retains *res* at the beginning and *beth* in the middle: *Ribon*. The Arabic, following the Alexandrian Greek manuscript, reads *Dibon* and *Remmon*.

Amid so many variant readings of the same name, what Hebraist, unaware of Jerome’s observation, would not criticize him for writing *Dibon* instead of *Dimon*, or instead of *Remmon*, in Isaiah 15:9? The author of the recent *Critical History* would undoubtedly have said that Jerome had, in his customary manner, accepted the Hebrew elements indiscriminately and read *beth* for *mem* arbitrarily. But he would have fabricated that opinion at will, just as he fabricated the preceding ones, as is proved by the diversity of the translations mentioned above. By these we have demonstrated beyond contradiction that different Hebrew manuscripts of sacred Scripture existed among different people.

Let that recent critic therefore restrain his excessive freedom of argument, and he will immediately join us in acknowledging Jerome’s faithfulness and learning, both in the text of his translations and in the etymologies of the Hebrew Names.

If he refuses our admonition, let him at least listen to the most learned John Drusius, who discusses the name *Oreb* in *Hebrew Questions*, book III, question 75:

> “The recent correctors have erred concerning Jerome in two ways. First, they have written in Hebrew characters what Jerome had written in Latin; second, they have replaced the old reading with a new one unknown to Jerome. As for the reading, I shall show that what I say is sometimes true, if life, health, and leisure permit. Concerning the characters, I shall now cite a passage by which I can easily prove that an injury was done to the most holy man, unless we wish to accuse him of the greatest ignorance. The passage is in the commentary on Zephaniah, chapter 2, where all printed books read as follows:  
>   
> “‘Moreover, what both we and the Seventy likewise translated, “a raven upon the threshold”; in the Hebrew [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text] is written, which, according to the diversity of reading, may mean dryness, sword, or body; hence Aquila translated it as “sword,” and others as “dryness.”’  
>   
> “Do not doubt that Jerome wrote: ‘In the Hebrew *Oreb* is written, which, according to the diversity of reading,’ and so forth.”

Those who altered this and wrote *Oreb* in Hebrew letters from the Hebrew text should consider how they will excuse Jerome here.

> [Note: A similar passage occurs in the Commentary on Micah 2: “*Zara* in our language means ‘seed’ or ‘rising,’ whereas [the Hebrew term is omitted in the supplied text] is called ‘seed’ or ‘rising’; thus Hebrew characters cannot possibly be used here.”]

For however one reads it, it never has the meaning “raven”; nor, if one reads it [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], does it ever denote dryness or sword. But since the roots are different and are distinguished even by their first letters, one of them, which has *ayin* at its beginning, always signifies “raven”; the other, which has *heth*, means sometimes “dryness” and sometimes “sword.”

> [Note: Jerome, *Commentary on Haggai* 1: “For ‘dryness’ the Seventy translated Ῥομφαίαν, ‘sword’; but in the Hebrew I find it written with three letters: *heth*, *res*, *beth*. If we read *Hereb*, it means ‘sword’; if *Horeb*, καῦμα, ‘burning heat,’ which we translated ‘dryness,’ although it could better be rendered ‘a scorching wind.’”]

It signifies “dryness” when the first vowel is *holem* followed by *segol*, namely *Horeb*, as it is read today; and “sword” when the same letter has *segol* and is followed by another *segol*, in this form: *Hereb*. Therefore Aquila, who translates it as “sword,” undoubtedly read it thus—unless, indeed, he thought that *Horeb* also signifies “sword,” which does not seem implausible. For as far as the meaning is concerned, it makes little difference whether one explains the word here as “sword” or “dryness.”

In the meantime, Jerome’s statement is true: the word *Oreb*, according to the diversity of reading, means dryness, sword, and raven. What the correctors have added is false: that [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], κόρακα, that is, “raven,” is denoted.”

Modern Hebrew critics and their fellow critics bring many other objections against Jerome, although they are entirely ignorant and unskilled in the Hebrew language. The distinguished Ludovicus Ferrandus, a man who rendered excellent service both to sacred letters and to Jerome, collected their arguments. Having undertaken the task of defending Jerome’s Hebrew learning, he set himself the praiseworthy goal of answering, after gathering arguments from every side, the objections by which the holy Doctor’s expertise is attacked. In chapter 3 of section IV of the *Prolegomena* to his *Biblical Summary*, he began to fight against those who always find something to criticize in Jerome’s etymologies or interpretations.

Yet many do not wish the reputation of the greatest interpreter of Scripture to depend upon the answers of this highly esteemed man, because they scarcely accept even half of his response. For who, several ask, can patiently endure such vague and futile answers in defense of Jerome as these, found on page 146 of the *Biblical Summary*?

> “The interpretations involved in the remaining part of the sixth objection can easily be defended or excused by resorting to unknown meanings, or by blaming careless writers; and one might perhaps also add the diversity of readings that caused the ancients to produce interpretations foreign to our usage.
>
> “The sound of the word, which is almost the same in the names *Hereb* [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text] and [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], *Cades* [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text] and [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], may have deceived Jerome, who was intent on higher matters and perhaps in a hurry—just as even the most learned men make daily mistakes in such matters.”

Certainly the matter is settled if we bring forward nothing else in defense of Jerome’s Hebrew learning. For whether the holy Doctor was mistaken because he was hurrying or because he was intent on higher matters, the judgment among the learned will remain that Jerome frequently blundered in his interpretations and in the etymologies of names.

Moreover, there is no error so obvious, no form of corruption so manifest, that it cannot be defended, provided that we take refuge in these unlearned evasions—namely, unknown meanings of Hebrew names or the careless ignorance of ancient writers. It is therefore better to supply new and particular answers than to cling to these general assertions, with which even moderately learned men, in my view, have not been sufficiently satisfied.

I shall undertake this all the more willingly because Jerome himself provides us with a greater abundance of answers and solutions. But we have decided to assign the proper explanation to each difficulty in its due order, and, together with the learned Ferrandus, we present the first objection in the following manner:

> “It is wrongly said that Jerome had an excellent command of the Hebrew language, since he himself testifies that he learned Hebrew only in part and that, when he intended to interpret the Scriptures, he repeatedly summoned Hebrew teachers—something that reveals a man dependent on another’s assistance and not sufficiently learned. He says that he learned the Hebrew language in part in book II *Against Rufinus*. He likewise admits this in Paula’s epitaph and in the preface to Ezra and Nehemiah.”

As though it were not permissible for a man of the greatest diligence and learning to practice modesty in his works. Indeed, it would smell strongly of empty glory and would be unworthy of a wise man if he arrogantly acknowledged in himself the highest mastery of the Hebrew language.

It is not the behavior of a man professing Christian piety to boast of his virtues, knowledge, or achievements. Such boasting belongs rather to the Jewish historian Josephus, who in book III, chapter 14, of *The Jewish War* and elsewhere repeatedly sings the praises of his own merits and sometimes indicates that he is the wisest of the Jews and the most knowledgeable in the sacred laws.

All such boasting was far from Jerome. In book I of his *Apology against Rufinus*, he plainly shows that he guarded himself against this fault, saying:

> “For unless it were lengthy and smelled of empty glory, I would now show you the value of wearing out the thresholds of teachers and learning an art from its practitioners; and you would see how great a forest of ambiguous names and words there is among the Hebrews. This circumstance provided material for differing interpretations, since each person translates amid uncertainties whatever seems more suitable to him.”

Thus, so that Jerome might not present himself as a demonstrator of his own Hebrew learning, he said that he had learned the Hebrew language only in part. And if at times he employed Jewish teachers as assistants in interpreting the divine books, this must be attributed to the diligence and zeal of a most wise man, who devoted everything he possessed of mature judgment, knowledge, and even knowledge acquired from others to producing a perfect translation of the sacred Scriptures, which the Church of Christ afterward adopted for use.

> “I confess,” he says in the preface to the book of Chronicles, “that I have never trusted my own strength in the divine volumes . . . but that I have been accustomed to ask even about matters I thought I knew, etc.”

The critics derive their second argument against Jerome’s Hebrew learning from his letter to Pope Damasus, and formulate it as follows:

> “Discussing the word *Osanna*, Jerome first says: ‘*Osanna*, or, as he thinks it should be read, *Osianna*, is translated “save,” or “save, I pray.”’ But that word means: ‘Save, I beseech you.’ Then the holy Doctor says that, if *Anna* is written with *heth*, it is a conjunction or interjection used by the Greeks in an indignant sense (σχετλιαστικῶς), whose meaning the Latin language does not express. Yet Latin expresses the meaning of this word perfectly, since it means ‘grace,’ corresponding to the Hebrew word from which the name *Anna*, given to the mother of the most blessed Virgin, is derived and which signifies ‘grace,’ as everyone knows. From it also came the true expression ‘have mercy on me,’ with which the most celebrated fiftieth Psalm begins.
>
> “Finally, Jerome says that the third *Anna*, which is read in Psalm 117, is written with three letters, *heth*, *nun*, and *he*, and that it is the same conjunction or interjection whose meaning the Latin language does not express. But the letter *heth* has no connection whatsoever with the conjunction or interjection mentioned above; it properly belongs to the Hebrew verb [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], ‘to prosper,’ of which it is the third radical. It cannot be separated from that verb so as to constitute an interjection by itself, as Jerome assumes, contrary to the rules of the Hebrew language.”

I would have wasted oil and effort copying out this argument of no importance, if it had not provided an opportunity to restore the context of Jerome’s letter to Pope Damasus, which has suffered the greatest mutilation in previously published books. I call the argument superfluous and of no importance because it receives its answer in the very words of the letter. For from those words it most clearly appears that Jerome interpreted *Osanna* as “save, I beseech you,” and that the holy Doctor never failed to know that the word *Anna*, beginning with *heth*, signifies “grace”; still less did he suppose, contrary to the rules of the Hebrew language, that the third radical was to be torn away from the verb [the Hebrew verb is not legible in the supplied text], so that, together with the following elements in the word *ASLIANA*, it might constitute a separate interjection:

“Some,” says Jerome, “have thought that *Osanna* means ‘glory.’ But glory is called *Chabod*. Others [have thought it means] ‘grace,’ since grace is called *Thoda*, or *Anna*.”

And afterward:

“And because *Osianna*, which through ignorance we corruptly call *Osanna*, is rendered ‘save,’ or ‘save [for us],’ this has been established by the interpretation of all. Now the question is what the word *Anna* by itself signifies, without the addition of ‘saving.’”

He explained this at the end of the letter:

“Thus *Osia* is interpreted ‘save’; *Anna* is the interjection of one pleading. If you wish to make a compound word from these two, you will say *Osianna*, or, as we pronounce it, *Osanna*, with the middle vowel elided, etc.”

That discussion must therefore be regarded as idle, and its argument cold; for the words of the letter itself explain its difficulties more clearly. Whatever could be objected in it against Jerome’s Hebrew learning, we already find anticipated and answered in the very context of the letter from which the critics construct this argument.

The passage, as I have already remarked, is of great value because it gives an opportunity to restore the context of the letter even in matters of the greatest importance. For it is not permissible to read it as in the previously printed books:

“Which among the Greeks is placed *σχετλιαστικῶς* [as an expression of lament or protest]; its interpretation the Latin language does not express.”

Rather, with the oldest manuscript copies, we must read:

“Which among the Greeks is placed *δὴ*, and is found in *σῶσον δὴ*; its interpretation the Latin language does not express.”

That is, the Greeks express the Hebrew interjection *Anna* by *δὴ*, as in the preceding *σῶσον δὴ*; but the Latin language does not express that interjection in *Osianna* and *Aslianna*, because for these compound words it renders merely “save” and “prosper well,” although in Latin one ought to translate *Osanna* as “save, I beseech you,” and *Aslianna* as “prosper well, I beseech you.” In Greek this is expressed by *σῶσον δὴ* and *εὐόδωσον δὴ*.

I ask you, reader, what could make Jerome easier to understand, if only a pure text of his works had previously been published on the basis of the testimony of so many ancient manuscripts of the highest quality? Yet I do not wish to deny that in a very large number of manuscripts the Greek words are read so corruptly that they leave room for the conjectures of highly learned men to restore the text. Hence the learned Erasmus has the following annotation on the present word:

“Which among the Greeks is placed. This passage is so corrupt in all copies that I cannot conjecture with certainty. Nevertheless, from the traces of the letters I think it should be read *δεήσεως ὡς ἄνα*, that is, ‘of supplication,’ since *ἄνα* is sometimes among the Greeks the word of one beseeching, especially among poets. But let whoever finds something more probable immediately reject this conjecture of mine, etc.”

We do not immediately reject Erasmus’s conjecture because of some more probable conjecture; rather, we reject it on the established authority and testimony of two manuscript codices, the first belonging to the monastery of Saint Cygirannus, the second to the celebrated Abbey of Cluny.

In the Saint-Cygirannus manuscript we read:

“Which among the Greeks is placed *αΗ* and is *IN SOSONAN*.”

According to the practice of that copy, these words are to be read in Greek as follows:

“*ΔΗ* and is in *ϹωϹΟΝ ΔΗ*.”

For in that same manuscript *a* is written for Greek *Δ*, and *Ν* or *n* for Greek *Η* (*eta*). It also frequently changes small *ο* into large *ω*, and conversely *ω* into *ο*. Through this use—or misuse—of the letters, the inexperienced scribe wrote *a Η* for *δὴ*, and *sosonan* for *σῶσον δὴ*.

The copyist of the Cluniacensis manuscript intended to write the same thing, but, equally ignorant of Greek and not knowing what he was writing, copied the following by chance:

“Which among the Greeks is placed *ΚΗ* and is *ϹωΝan*.”

Above it he added a representation of the Greek words in this form: *apesesinos anay*. Although this is held to be extremely corrupt, certain traces of letters nevertheless remain in the corrupted reading that allow the genuine reading to be restored:

“*ΔΗ* and is in *ϹωϹΟΝ ΔΗ*.”

We have learned from the Saint-Cygirannus copy that this should be written out in full. In that manuscript no element is missing and none is superfluous; and, apart from the form of the letters—which does not correspond to the modern form, though it is very commonly found in manuscript copies—it preserves the genuine reading. Among all the copies, that single ancient Saint-Cygirannus codex retains it.

The other copies, apart from the Cluniacensis, commonly read *anesesin sosannan*, *anesesin, nosanai*, or *anesesin*, that is, “with praises.” These readings seem in some way to approach the Erasmian conjecture cited shortly before.

Nor should you think that this is the only passage of Saint Jerome’s letter requiring restoration in the present edition. There are two other restorations of no less importance, which it will be enough to indicate here until we reach the volume devoted specifically to this letter and its various annotations.

The printed books read as follows concerning the Latin interjection by which we command silence:

“And when we wish to command silence, we contract and force the breath through clenched teeth, producing, that is, a hissing sound; so also the Hebrews, etc.”

The Saint-Cygirannus manuscript reads differently:

“And when we wish to command silence, we contract the breath through clenched teeth and force it to sound *sith*. So the Hebrews, etc.”

The Cluniacensis codex reads differently again:

“And when we wish to impose silence, we contract the breath through clenched teeth and force it to sound *sith*. So the Hebrews, etc.”

And again the older Cluniacensis codex has:

“And when we wish to impose silence, we contract the breath through clenched teeth; and, by hissing, we produce only the sound *si*. So also the Hebrews, etc.”

Which of these variant readings is to be preferred above the others, you will easily discover for yourself if, as nature requires, you attempt to command silence.

Another variant reading occurs in the elision of the middle vowel of the word *Osianna*. In the previously published books we read:

“For the first letter of the following word, *Aleph*, encountering the final letter of the preceding word, *Jod*, excluded it.”

But the manuscript codices customarily read this passage in different ways. The Saint-Cygirannus manuscript mentioned above and another belonging to the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs read:

“For the first letter of the following word, *Aleph*, coming upon the final letter of the preceding word, *Ain*, excluded it.”

The Cluniacensis manuscript, however, reads:

“For *Aleph*, the first letter of the following word, coming upon the final letter of the preceding word, *Ain*, excluded it.”

This reading depends upon another earlier reading, namely:

“Thus *Osia* is interpreted ‘save’; *Anna* is the interjection of one pleading.”

But these readings will be discussed fully elsewhere.

The third argument against Jerome’s learning is supplied by Jerome’s letter to Paula of Rome on the Hebrew alphabet. In that letter he “teaches that the name *Daleth* signifies tablets or books; the word *Zain*, ‘this’; the term *Jod*, ‘beginning’; *Mem*, ‘from themselves’; *Nun*, ‘everlasting’; and *Coph*, ‘calling.’”

But none of these meanings lies beneath the words in question—not even in *Zain* and *Mem*, which could more easily be defended. For *ze*, or *za*, does indeed signify “this”; but if *in* is added to it so that *Zain* is formed, it loses that meaning. *Mem*, moreover, if it is to signify “from themselves,” requires the letter [the Hebrew form is missing in the supplied text] in this manner. Since it does not have that form in the word *Mem*, it cannot acquire the meaning Jerome assigns to it. Jerome would have interpreted *Samech* more accurately as “support” than as “assistance,” and he would have spoken more learnedly if he had said that the letter *Tau* had been used as a sign, rather than interpreting the word “signs.” For the Hebrews call signs *Othoth*, as is clear from Genesis 1:14.

Those who bring these objections against Jerome certainly deserve no pardon; they must be pierced with their own sword—that is, refuted by their own words. They would speak more learnedly if, under Jerome’s instruction, they had learned the interpretation of *Samech* from the book of the Hebrew Names.

“*Samech*,” says Jerome above, column 72, “means ‘firmament,’ although some think it means ‘erection,’ or ‘assistance,’ or ‘support.’”

Thus, according to the opinion of some, Jerome interprets *Samech* as “assistance” in his letter to Paula; here, however, he more correctly explains it as “firmament,” according to the proper meaning of the Hebrew word *samach*, which signifies “he laid a hand upon” or “he confirmed.” Hence in the New Testament the laying on of hands was used for the imparting of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, for the designation of Christ’s disciples, and for imposing the apostolic office or the public function of ecclesiastical ministry. From this laying on of hands the sacrament of confirmation received its name. For the same verb *samach* signifies both “to lay on hands” and “to confirm.” Properly, therefore, *Samech* is called in Greek *στήριγμα* (*stērigma*), in Latin “firmament”; metaphorically, “assistance” and “help.”

The same judgment applies to the letter *Tau*, which Jerome interprets as “sign” or “below”; and to the word *Coph*, which is interpreted above, column 50, as follows:

“Calling or bird; but more accurately ‘a striking away,’ which the Greeks call *ἔκκρουμα* (*ekkrouma*).”

* Coph* is most accurately interpreted as “a striking away,” from the root *nacaph*, that is, “he struck off” or “he fell down.” Hence *noceph*, “a cutting off,” that is, the final stripping away and virtual cutting off of olives, Isaiah 17:6.

In short, whenever you find anything forced in Jerome’s interpretation of the Hebrew letters, you should know without hesitation that it must be attributed to the Greeks. Do not rashly and ignorantly charge Jerome with six hundred errors when he himself decrees that what he rejects should be discarded. And, so that you may not be unaware from what source Jerome drew both his interpretation of the Hebrew alphabet and his combinations of the letters, I urge you to return quickly to the preceding chapter of Evagrius under the name *IIIIII*.

Many similar arguments are read in abundance on page 139 of the *Biblical Summary*. Although they are invalid and trivial, I will not disdain any of them until the defenders of Jerome’s learning, who are zealous to vindicate it, have weakened them by a true answer.

“They say: ‘Jerome offers many interpretations that are unworthy of a man learned in Hebrew. Examples are these: *David*, “strong in hand”; *Cherubim*, “multitude of knowledge”; *Moab*, “paternal water”; *Carmel*, “knowledge of circumcision”; *Ammon*, “son of my people” or “our people”; *Beelsephon*, “ascent of a lookout”; *Sin*, “hatred”; *Alus*, “leaven”; *Pharan*, “wild ass” or “wildness”; *Ressa*, “bridles”; *Harada*, “miracle”; *Thare* with *Ain*, “wickedness” or “pasture,” and with *Heth*, “one who drives away” or “repeller”; *Asmona*, “haste”; *Bene-jaakan*, “sons of necessity” or “of gnashing”; *lotbatha*, “goodness”; *Asiongaber*, “wood of a man” or “workings of a man”; *Phasga*, “hewn”; *Zin*, “commandment”; *Jeabarim*, “heaps of stones of those crossing over”; *Dibongad*, “a temptation understood strongly”; *Aaron*, “mountainous”; *Arnon*, “curse”; *Almon Diblathaiema*, “contempt of blows” [read: “cakes”] or “of reproaches”; *Nabo*, “conclusion”; *Abel Asitim*, “mourning of thorns”; *Ulam*, “before.”’”

Those who bring forward such trifles against Jerome must either be considered ignorant of the Hebrew language or extraordinarily devoted to contentious disputation. For who, with even a moderate education in Hebrew speech and learning, could fail to know that the word *David* is interpreted not only as “beloved” but also as “strong in hand”?

The Greeks interpret that name in both ways above, in the fragments of the Book of Names and in the Origenian Lexicon, column 626:

“*Δαυίδ, ἱκανὸς χειρί, ἢ μόνος πεποθημένος, ἢ ἀγαπημένος*, etc.”—“David, strong in hand, or desired alone, or beloved, etc.”

Jerome likewise gives both meanings in column 53: “David, strong in hand, or desirable.” In column 107, however, he gives “David, desirable,” adding nothing further.

It is therefore sufficiently clear that Jerome, in his Commentary on Ezekiel, explained *David* as “strong in hand” as the Greeks do; elsewhere, according to the proper character of the Hebrew language and the root *dud* or *dod*, he interprets the same name as “desirable” or “lovable.”

David could be called “strong in hand” from the verb *jada*, from which the name *Juda* was taken, as is clear even to the unlearned. But I am convinced that among the Greeks this kind of etymology is derived from the Hebrew word *dai*, because the Greeks express it as *ἱκανὸς χειρί* (“sufficient in hand”), not *δυνάτος χειρί* (“powerful in hand”). For the Hebrew *dai* means precisely what the Greek *ἱκανός* means, namely “sufficient.”

The explanation which I find in the Hebraizing writer is therefore foolish and unworthy of its author. Nor were the ancients wrong to add the letter *Vau*, so that it might be the pronoun “his,” as though the aforesaid word *David* meant “one who is sufficient for himself in hand,” that is, “one who is powerful and strong in hand.” That the word “hand” is expressed by it is unknown to no beginner in Hebrew.

“It was forbidden among the ancient Hebrews to assign the proper name of God to any mortal. Above all, what is proper to God is that he is sufficient for himself in hand, that is, that he needs no assistance, that he can do all things by his own power, and that he is truly *Saddai*, self-sufficient. Therefore the ancients did not add the letter *Vau* in the name *David*; perhaps they did not read [the Hebrew form is absent in the supplied text], and they formed the name from the first three letters, which even now, with two letters, means ‘sufficient.’ These claims are fictitious and almost playful. But they took the *Vau* written in the word *David* for *Jod*, so that it contained *dai* and *jad*, that is, ‘strong’ and ‘hand.’ For among the Hebrews it makes no difference whether words are written in the middle with *Vau* or with *Jod*. Thus the substantive verb *hava* or *haja* is written in either way, and however one writes it, it means the same thing. Hebrew grammarians also call verbs that have *Jod* as their second radical ‘quiescent in *Ain Vau*.’”

For the present I have answered these matters briefly and concisely, according to the modest measure of my understanding. The reader should nevertheless know that in such disputes he must not allow weariness in reading to creep over him. We too could easily have invented something that would settle the question by means of a single word, just as we have shown others to have done. But it is more fitting to labor for a little while on behalf of the truth and lend one’s ear to an unfamiliar language than to report a fabricated and false judgment about another tongue.

In the explanation of the words *Cherubim* and *Carmel*, the Hebraizing writer’s answer is no more successful than the preceding one. I am astonished that a writer celebrated by many for his reputation in Hebrew learning could have been so ignorant of the common roots of the sacred language that, while criticizing Jerome’s errors, he displays his own:

“The interpretations of *Cherubim* and *Carmel* are free from fault if we assume that *Kara* among the ancients signified ‘knowledge.’ This follows with complete plausibility from the usage of the rabbis, for with them *Kara* means ‘to read,’ whence *mikra*, ‘reading,’ specifically sacred reading—that is, Holy Scripture, which is the source of all knowledge.”

It would be most absurd to decide that the names *Cherubim* and *Carmel* signify “multitude of knowledge” and “knowledge of circumcision,” even if *Kara* had possessed the meaning “knowledge” among the ancients. For who does not know that the words *Cherubim* and *Karmel* arise from the root *nachar*, which is rendered in Latin “he knew,” and in the *Hiphil*, *hikkir*, “he recognized” or “acknowledged”? *Hakkara* likewise expresses “recognition.”

Understand, therefore, the name *Cherubim* as compounded from *nachar* and *rabab*. Since these are defective verbs among the Hebrews, the names derived from them must undoubtedly lose certain radical letters in composition. *Rab* signifies “multitude,” and *hakkara*, “knowledge”; hence the word *Cherubim* is readily interpreted as “multitude of knowledge.”

Similarly, the name *Carmel* is derived from *nachar* and *mul*, and according to the proper character of the Hebrew language signifies “knowledge of circumcision,” since *mul* is rendered in Latin “he circumcised.”

We present these etymologies of the Hebrew Names without childish embellishment, so that the diligent reader may know how much deception has been practiced in many books of modern critics, in which Jerome’s Hebrew learning is rashly attacked or defended ignorantly. But let us proceed to the remaining matters.

The name *Bene-jaakan* has likewise been badly handled, corrupted, and violently interpreted by critical writers, as the following explanation of the same name proves:

“For *Benejaakan*, perhaps the great Doctor’s copy read *Benejaracan*; and in that form the interpretation ‘sons of gnashing’ will be correct, from the root [Hebrew root absent in the supplied text], ‘he gnashed.’”

I say nothing about *bene* or *benei*, since no one is unaware that this word denotes “sons.”

If it is permissible to change square things into round ones, and to replace *Bene-jaakan* with the fictitious *Benejaracan*, then no interpretation of the Hebrew Names will be ambiguous or difficult to explain.
