But no one allows an inexperienced beginner in the Hebrew language so many corruptions in a single word: that *Heth* should be read for *Ain*, and that *Res* should be added to force an etymology of Jerome which flows in conformity with the Hebrew language from the verb *uc* or *ac*, that is, “he constrained,” “he was troublesome,” or “he harassed”; or absolutely, “he was confined, pressed, or afflicted.” Hence *aca*, “constraint, trouble, poverty”; in the plural *acethin* and *acan*, “constraints,” and so forth. Among Jewish teachers also, *avac* signifies “he twisted.”

Let such entirely distorted and alien etymologies of names—or explanations of etymologies—therefore withdraw and be permanently banished from this Apology for Jerome. Certain critics have hitherto taught them to the ignorant.

Yet I do not wish to conceal that in Jerome’s allegorical interpretation of the name *Benejaakan*, his meaning seems more readily directed toward the root *acad* than toward the preceding *uc* or *ac*. For in the twenty-eighth station, in his letter to Fabiola, we read:

“The twenty-eighth station is translated ‘sons of necessity’ or ‘sons of gnashing’ [the supplied text contains a lacuna]. Who these sons of necessity are, the Psalm itself teaches us: ‘Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord sons of rams.’ What necessity is so great that it is imposed upon the unwilling? When you have been instructed in the divine Scriptures, and have learned their laws and testimonies as the bonds of truth, by contending with your adversaries you will bind them and lead them captive, etc.”

He therefore understands “sons of necessity” as those who are bound and captive, like the rams and sheep that are offered to the Lord as sacrifices. The Hebrew verb *acad* is rendered in Latin by grammarians as “he bound” or “he tied together,” specifically binding the limbs, as sheep are accustomed to be bound by all four feet for slaughter.

Of Isaac, too, when he had been prepared for sacrifice, it is said in Genesis 22:9, *vaijaacod*, “and he bound,” namely his son Isaac; that is, he tied him with his hands and feet behind his back, just as sheep are bound for shearing or slaughter.

Because Jerome said that *Alus*, the tenth station of the Hebrews in the desert, was interpreted as “leaven,” the critics and Hebraizing writers take the opportunity to tamper with the true reading *Alus*, thinking that *Amus* should be substituted. If we believe them, there is nothing to prevent Jerome from having read *Amus* instead of *Alus*, and his interpretation will thus be free from blame.

It is false that Jerome read *Amus* instead of *Alus* against the authority of Scripture. Nor do we call the holy Doctor’s interpretation free from blame on the basis of false conjectures. Rather, his exceptional knowledge of the Hebrew language was such that he could not have been unaware that the verb *lus* signifies “he mixed,” “he mingled,” and “he imbued with leaven.” Therefore, in the Book of the Hebrew Names, above, column 24, he wrote of *Alus*:

“*Alus*: ‘leaven’ or ‘mix’; in Greek, *φύρασον* [“knead” or “mix thoroughly”].”

These facts certainly ought not to have escaped the defenders of Jerome’s learning, which must be regarded as entirely free from blame when he says:

“*Alus* is interpreted as ‘leaven’: for the woman took it and mixed it with three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.”

The following observation from the *Biblical Summary*, page 146, opens before us a very broad field of discussion:

“*Abel Asitim*, in my judgment, must be attributed to the copyist, not to the author. It is probable that he read *Abel Asirim* with *Samech*, which Jerome correctly translated ‘mourning of thorns.’”

Jerome’s own contrary observations in the third chapter of the prophet Joel openly prove that this conjecture is far removed from the truth. There, discussing the torrent of thorns, he writes:

“For ‘torrent of thorns,’ the Seventy translated ‘torrent of cords,’ that is, *χοίνων*. This word either signifies ‘cords’ or, according to the Egyptians, a measure of a fixed journey, as the Psalmist says: ‘You have investigated my path and my cord.’ For on the river Nile, or on its branches, they commonly draw ships with ropes, having fixed distances that they call ‘cords,’ so that the fresh necks of those who draw may take the place of the labor of the exhausted. Nor is it surprising if each nation calls fixed distances on roads by different names, since the Latins call them miles, the Gauls leagues, the Persians parasangs, and all Germany rastas, while each name denotes a different measure.

“This is why the Hebrew word *Sattim* was translated by the Seventy as ‘cords.’ Yet there is no doubt that everything we read in the Tabernacle of God was made of the wood of *Settim*, which the Seventy translated as ‘incorruptible wood.’ It is a kind of tree in the desert, resembling the white thorn in color and leaves, though not in size. Otherwise the trees are so large that boards of great breadth are cut from them. The wood is extremely strong and of incredible lightness and beauty, so that even the wealthiest and most diligent people make from it the vessels of winepresses, which they call *ἄρσενας* and *θηλύας*. Such wood is not found in cultivated regions or on Roman soil, except in the wilderness of Arabia.

“For ‘torrent of cords’ or ‘of thorns,’ Symmachus translated ‘valley of thorns.’ There is a place near Libias, across the Dead Sea and six miles distant from it, where Israel once fornicated with the Midianites. The prophet Micah mentions this place in the person of God, saying: ‘My people, remember, I beseech you, what Balak king of Moab devised, and what Balaam son of Beor answered, from Settim to Galgal.’ For this the Seventy also translated there, *ἀπὸ τῶν χοίνων*, that is, ‘from the cords to Galgal,’ etc.”

The holy Doctor could not have presented his opinion of the name *Sittim* or *Sattim* more plainly, nor could he more forcefully have rejected the false conjecture that a copyist had erred in the reading *Abel Asirim* instead of *Abel Asitim*. The opinion must therefore be constant among all students and learned men of the Hebrew language: the word *Sittim* was translated “thorns” by the ancient Greek and Latin interpreters. Consequently, the reading *Abel Asitim* in the forty-second station of the letter to Fabiola is genuine and Jerome’s own, not the error of some unknown and ignorant copyist.

To the other violent interpretations of the Hebrew Names proposed by the critics, the defenders of Jerome’s learning offer no answer beyond what we call in French *Le pont aux Ânes* [“the bridge of asses,” an obvious or facile answer]. They say:

“These difficulties seem insoluble to us; but they can be excused by resorting to unknown meanings or by blaming negligent copyists.”

This is how we answer etymologies such as these: *Abraham*, “father of many”; *Dibongad*, “a temptation understood strongly”; *Nabo*, “conclusion”; *Oreb*, “raven” or “dryness”; *Aser*, “riches” or “blessed”; *Cades*, “holy” or “changed”; *Nephthali*, “he converted me” or “he compared me.”

Thus Jerome remains ignorant of the Hebrew language unless we accept unknown meanings of the Hebrew Names, or accuse all the ancient copyists of Saint Jerome’s works everywhere of perpetual corruption.

It will not be so that either suspicion of ignorance should cling to Jerome or all who ever copied Jerome’s works anywhere in the world should be charged with corruption. Nor do I consider it equal to affirm one or the other absolutely. I would rather say that those who, overcome by these difficulties, show themselves unequal to the defense they have undertaken on behalf of Saint Jerome are only lightly tinctured with knowledge of the Hebrew language.

For what is so difficult in the interpretations just cited that it is necessary either to invent charges against copyists or to resort to unknown meanings of Hebrew words? The simple reading of Genesis 17:5 is enough to show that the objection concerning the etymology of the name *Abraham* is wholly futile and ignorant. Nor will the remaining interpretations fare better if the matters are examined clearly and in their proper order. I therefore defend the disputed interpretations as follows.

The holy Jerome explained this verse of Genesis according to the Septuagint:

“Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, because I have made you the father of many nations” [the supplied Greek/Hebrew text is partially corrupt or incomplete], that is: “And your name shall be Abraham, because I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.”

To make the rationale of the name clear to the reader, he seeks the assistance of a foreign language:

“The Hebrews say that God added the letter *He* to Abraham and Sarah from his own name, which among them is the Tetragrammaton. For he was first called *Abram*, which is interpreted ‘exalted father’; afterward he was called *Abraham*, which is rendered ‘father of many.’ For the word that follows, ‘nations,’ is not contained in the name but is understood. Nor should it be surprising that, although among the Greeks and among us an *A* appears to have been added, we say that the Hebrew letter *He* was added. For it is a characteristic of that language to write with *He* but pronounce with *Aleph*, just as, conversely, they often pronounce the letter *A* as *He*.”

Among the Greeks and Latins, the letter *A* was added to the name *Abraham*, because he was first called *Ἄβραμ* (*Abram*) and afterward, when the letter was added, *Ἀβραάμ* (*Abraham*). Among the Hebrews, however, it was not *Aleph* that was added but *He*. Hence he was first *Abram* and afterward *Abraham*, because they pronounced *He* as *A*, as Jerome testifies.

The addition of the letter *He* was made so that the man who had first been called “exalted father” might afterward, in his name, be called “father of a multitude.” For in Hebrew *amon* means the same as the Latin “multitude” and “crowd.” In the name *Abraham*, the final syllable is the first part of the word *amon*, namely *am*, from which the name Abraham receives its meaning of “multitude.” From *ab* it receives the meaning “father,” while the middle letter *Res* remains inactive, carried over from the earlier name *Abram*, which expresses “exalted father.”

When these points have been observed, it is most clearly demonstrated that Jerome’s interpretation—or rather, his explanation—was excellent and extremely careful. Nor could our critics have been entirely unaware that when Jerome said Abraham was interpreted “father of many,” he had in mind the Hebrew Scripture and the Greek text:

“*Ἀλλ’ ἔσται τὸ ὄνομά σου Ἀβραὰμ, ὅτι πατέρα πολλῶν ἐθνῶν τέθεικά σε*,” that is, “But your name shall be Abraham, because I have made you the father of many nations.”

What follows after “father of many,” namely “nations,” is not contained in the name *Abraham* but is understood, as Saint Jerome correctly observes—though he is rashly and ignorantly attacked by uninformed critics.

I do not omit that Jerome elsewhere, in the Book of the Names, interprets the name *Abraham* as “father seeing the people” or “father seeing the multitude.” In that interpretation the letter *Res* is expressed, although I called it inactive for the etymology “father of many.” No one is unaware that the verb *raa*, which begins with *Res*, signifies “he saw” or “seeing.” Hence Abraham means “father seeing the multitude.”

But, to free ourselves briefly from these critical entanglements, I say that *Dibongad* signifies “a temptation understood strongly,” because in Hebrew *dai* means “sufficiently” or “strongly,” *bon* means “understanding,” and *gad* means “temptation.” The Greeks retain these syllables in *δαιβὼν γὰδ*, and Jerome is their interpreter in such etymologies of names.

In the letter to Fabiola, *Nabo* is interpreted “conclusion.” But in the Book of the Hebrew Names, *Nabau* is rendered “we shall come” or “in conclusion”; *Nabao*, “prophecy” or “those coming”; *Nabo*, “sitting” or “one who comes upon.” The Hebrew roots *bo*, *nub*, and *nibba* can supply the grounds and interpretations of all these meanings.

The name *Oreb* has been discussed at length against the learned Bochart. See above in this Apologetic Treatise the critics’ hallucinations. For it is false that someone said:

“The sound of the word, which is almost the same in the names *Hereb* [Hebrew form supplied in the source], *Cades*, and [another Hebrew form], could have deceived Jerome, intent upon higher matters and perhaps in haste, etc.”

“Aser,” says Saint Jerome in the *Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, “does not mean ‘riches’ but ‘blessed,’ at least in the present passage; in other places, according to the ambiguity of the verb, riches may also be called by that name.”

These words can be understood in two ways.

First, Jerome seems to be understood as saying that *Aser*, written with *Aleph* as it is written in the present passage of Genesis, is interpreted “blessed”; but in other passages—for example, 1 Samuel 17:25 and Psalm 52:9—the name *Aser*, which because of the ambiguity of the word can be written with *Ain*, signifies “riches.” The ambiguity of this word *Aser*, written among us with *A*, therefore causes it sometimes to mean “blessed” and sometimes “riches.”

Second, the ambiguity of the word may arise from its second radical. For if the word *Aser* is written with *Sin*, as in Genesis [Hebrew form supplied in the source], then it means “blessed”; but if it is written in the middle with *Sade* [Hebrew form supplied in the source], then it means “riches.” For *Osar* is rendered in Latin as “treasure.”

Although some difficulty arises in the interpretation of *Cades*, little will remain of the critics’ objection after this explanation of Jerome’s, which is read in the thirty-third station of his letter to Fabiola:

“And the word that is joined to it, *Cades*, is not called ‘holy,’ as most people think, but ‘changed’ or ‘transferred.’ We read in Genesis, according to the Hebrew truth, where Judah, thinking Tamar to be a prostitute, sent gifts and the intermediary of the gifts asked: ‘Where is *Cadesta*?’—that is, the prostitute whose clothing had been changed from that of the other women. We find the same thing in many places. But if *Cades* is interpreted ‘holy,’ it must be understood *κατ’ ἀντίφρασιν* [ironically, by antiphrasis], just as women are called ‘sparing’ from the fact that they spare nothing, etc.”

He does not deny that *Cades* can be called “holy” by antiphrasis, or irony; but he intended the proper meaning of this name in the preceding etymology to be “changed” or “transferred.”

This can be strongly confirmed by the primary meaning of the root *Cadas* in the Hebrew lexicons, where that verb is interpreted in many places in the biblical books as “separated from common use for divine use.” Whatever passes from common use into sacred use is truly called “changed” and “transferred.” From this meaning, therefore, Jerome derived the etymology of the name *Cades*, not from the invented *Chades* or *Hhades*, which means “new,” not “transferred.”

In the *Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, Jerome warns us of something that by no means pleased the Critics; for they do not wish the name Nephthali to have been given from Rachel’s conversion, or comparison, with her sister Leah. “The reason for the name Nephthalim,” says the holy Doctor, “is explained here quite differently from the way it is written in the *Book of Hebrew Names*. Hence Aquila also says, συνανέστρεψέν με ὁ Θεὸς, καὶ συνανεστράφην [“God turned me about, and I was turned about”]. In Hebrew, in its place, is written *Nephthule Eloim Niphthalthi*. Hence he gave the son the name Nephthali from conversion or comparison, since both words signify conversion or comparison.” From the Hebrew words [Col. 1530A], if the Critics are to be believed, the opposite of Jerome’s opinion is demonstrated: for *nephthule eloim niphthalthi* conveys no notion of conversion or comparison, but literally means, “I have wrestled with the wrestlings of God,” that is, “I have prevailed.”

But, with due regard for these Critics, let us be permitted to say that among the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin interpreters, as well as among the French and Basques, “I have wrestled with the wrestlings of God” means the same as Aquila’s translation, “God turned me about, and I was turned about.” This is perfectly clear if we remember that Rachel, before she bore Jacob children of her own or adopted ones through her maidservant, had been unequal and inferior to her sister in the eyes of her husband Jacob. But after she rejoiced in the honor of a mother of a household at the birth of the children of her maid Bilhah, she presented herself as equal to her sister before her husband. Hence she said: “God has compared me with my sister, and I have prevailed.”

The sisters were therefore wrestling with one another in their rivalry over offspring; in this contest Rachel for some time remained inferior [Col. 1530B]. But Rachel, seeing that she was barren, envied her sister and said to her husband: “Give me children, or else I shall die.” Yet when first Dan and then Nephthali had been born, she who had previously remained unequal and inferior through envy and barrenness became equal to her sister Leah in the production of children. God had opened Leah’s womb, so that she would not be despised by Jacob because of the weakness of her eyes. God had therefore compared Rachel with Leah when he made the younger equal to the elder in the equal glory of bearing children. For among the Latins, to contend with something is equivalent to comparing oneself with it; and, again, to contend and to wrestle are taken in the same sense.

From this it follows that the etymology of the name Nephthali appears excellent: it signifies comparison or conversion, in the sense in which ordinary French says *retournez-vous* [“turn yourselves about”], and the Basques *tourne-te* [“turn yourself”]; in Latin we would say: “Contend, wrestle, fight, make equal to an equal.” Whoever seeks other interpretations of the word Nephthali should consult the *Book of Hebrew Names* above, or the Greek Fragments.

[Col. 1530C] Having refuted the difficulties ignorantly raised by the Critics against Jerome’s Hebrew learning, I thought nothing needed to be added except the words of the distinguished Ferrandus, with which he concludes his *Prolegomenal Disputation on St. Jerome*, p. 147 of his *Biblical Summary*:

“From these things,” he says, “it is evident that Jerome can easily be cleared, and that the accusations brought against him by wicked or ignorant men can readily be washed away, if judgment is rendered according to true rules and the dispute is weighed by a just examination, rather than directed according to the standard of ignorance or hatred. Some Critics of our age measure our controversy by this ruler; nor is it surprising that, using such an unjust balance, they should charge ancient Writers—toward whom they ought to show reverence—with ignorance, and treat as crimes interpretations that deserve praise or at least can be covered by a just defense.

“That Jerome’s interpretations are of this kind, I believe I have demonstrated sufficiently and more than sufficiently; and I hope that this holy Doctor will henceforth be an object of admiration to those who had sunk to such a degree of unhappiness and blindness that they held him in contempt. No one, I trust, will hereafter be found who does not attribute to him outstanding expertise in the Hebrew language.”

Thus far I too have discharged the office of advocate in this *Apology for Jerome*. Now it is my task to act as herald of that same Hebrew learning, which I have sufficiently defended against the falsely alleged faults in those matters that appeared to possess some weight. But from which books the arguments for this praise should first be drawn, I did not immediately settle upon, because of the more abundant wealth of Jerome’s knowledge, which shines throughout all his little works. As far as I have been able to grasp from frequent reading of his Commentaries and other writings, there is no page in them where the most manifest indications of his outstanding [Col. 1531A] learning do not appear. Yet, for a concise demonstration of his praise, it is better to prove his exceptional learning from the *Book of Hebrew Names*—the very work on whose authority Jerome was regarded as ignorant of Hebrew—than to heap up an infinite multitude of testimonies from every side. The observations and brief annotations in the *Book of Names* will therefore make Jerome’s complete expertise in Hebrew matters manifest.

In the *Book of Hebrew Names* published earlier by us, a thorough and exact knowledge of the Hebrew language shines forth in more than one way, provided that we consider only those features that can be recognized as Jerome’s own. Whether one seeks a deeper understanding of the elements of the language, an explanation of the meanings of words, or a precise distinction among sounds and the particular properties of ambiguous names, the single *Book of Hebrew Names* plainly demonstrates that all these things are found in Jerome through innumerable examples. And, so that Jerome’s exact knowledge of the elements of the Hebrew language may first be established for us, it is useful to quote some of his annotations [Col. 1531B]. He himself placed the following warning at the beginning of the *Book of Names*, so that the reader would not be misled by the ambiguity of the Latin letter A, which among the Hebrews corresponds to several different consonantal letters:

“Whenever names are written with the letter A, which among the Hebrews is called *Aleph*, one must not immediately suppose that Aleph alone is being used. For sometimes they begin with *Ain*, often with *He*, and occasionally with *Heth*, letters that alter their aspirations and sounds. It must therefore be understood that both in Genesis and in the other books, wherever a name begins with a vowel-letter, among the Hebrews it begins with different elements, as we have said above. But because among us there is not such a diversity of sounds, we are content with a simple pronunciation. Hence it happens that the same words, which among them are not written alike, appear to us to vary in translation.”

He wished the same point to be observed concerning the letter S, which is multiple among the Hebrews [Col. 1531C]:

“What we said at the beginning should be observed concerning vowel-letters: among us there is sometimes one letter, while among the Hebrews it is pronounced with various sounds. The same must now be understood concerning the letter S. Among the Hebrews there are indeed three letters S: one called *Samech*, which is read simply, as though it were represented by our letter S; another, *Sin*, in which a certain hiss, not belonging to our language, is heard; and a third, *Sade*, which our ears utterly reject. Therefore, whenever it happens that the same names are interpreted in different ways, the reason is that they have been written with different letters. What we say here concerning Genesis must likewise be observed in all the books.”

By these two observations alone Jerome taught us so much about the Hebrew elements that one might have thought it superfluous to seek further evidence of his learning—had some Critics, and also Mariano Vittorio, who most recently published the works of the holy Doctor, not misunderstood them. For when Vittorio wished, according to his usual practice, to preface the *Book of Hebrew Names* with an argument, he did not pay sufficient attention to Jerome’s preceding annotations; or at least he certainly did not read what is plainly contrary to his own opinion. He says:

“No one should be surprised that the Divine Jerome explains one and the same name in this book with various meanings among the Latins. This happens not so much because of ambiguity and variety in the interpretations as because of the diversity of the elements among the Hebrews. What we, through the poverty of our alphabet, express at times with one character, the Hebrews write with different elements. For, besides our five vowels, which they have in fourfold form, from [letters illegible in the supplied text], they also have three C’s, namely [letters illegible in the supplied text]; and four S’s, *Sin*, *Scin*, *Samech*, and *Tzade*. Although these differ among the Hebrews in pronunciation and in the shape of their figures, we can pronounce them more readily than we can represent them.”

I am not surprised that Jerome explained one and the same Hebrew name with various interpretations [Col. 1532A]; but it is very surprising that Jerome’s editor did not know what the holy Doctor expressly taught concerning the three S’s among the Hebrews, both here in the *Book of Names* and in his Commentary on the Epistle to Titus, chapter III. For if he had read the cited passages with even moderate attention, he would never, relying on Jerome’s authority, have introduced three C’s or four S’s among the Hebrews. Nor was Mariano permitted to confuse the letter Heth with the element C, since in Jerome Heth is a double aspiration, not the consonant C. Jerome himself consistently mentions three S’s among the Hebrews, but nowhere does he recognize four. To make this entirely clear to us, I shall reproduce the passage from his Commentary on chapter III of the Epistle to Titus in full. It is exceptionally lucid and especially suited to our purpose:

“When he says, ‘Avoid genealogies, and contentions, and disputes that arise from the law,’ he is addressing particularly the Jews, who boast and think that they possess knowledge of the law if they know the names of individuals. Because these names are foreign, and we do not know their etymologies, we generally pronounce them incorrectly. And if we happen to err in the accent, in the lengthening or shortening of a syllable—either lengthening short syllables or shortening long ones—they are accustomed to ridicule us for ignorance, especially in pronouncing aspirations and certain letters produced with a scraping of the throat.

“This happens because the Seventy Interpreters, through whom the divine law was translated into Greek, since they could not transfer the letter Heth, Ain, and the other letters of this kind into Greek with their double aspiration, expressed them by adding other letters. Thus, for example, they said *Rachel* for *Rahel*, *Hiericho* for *Hierio*, *Chebron* for *Hebron*, and *Segor* for *Seor*. In other cases their attempt failed.

“For we and the Greeks have only one letter S, whereas they have three—*Samech*, *Sade*, and *Sin*—which possess different sounds. *Isaac* and *Sion* are written with Sade. *Israel* is written with Sin, yet it does not sound as it is written. But *Seon*, the king of the Amorites, is written and pronounced with the letter Samech.

“If, therefore, these peculiarities of names and language—ἰδιώματα—are not expressed by us in the same way as by the Hebrews, they are accustomed to raise a loud laugh and swear that they do not understand at all what we are saying. Hence we took care to correct from the authentic copies all the books of the Old Testament that the learned Adamantius had arranged in the Hexapla, transcribing them from the Caesarean library. In those books the Hebrew words themselves are written in their proper characters and rendered in Greek letters by a method of close transcription. Aquila, Symmachus, the Seventy, and Theodotion each retain their own order. Some books, however—especially those composed in verse among the Hebrews—have three additional editions, which they call the fifth, sixth, and seventh translations, following the authority of an unnamed translator.

“This immortal genius bestowed this work upon us through his labor, so that we might not greatly fear the arrogance of the Jews, who delight in loose lips, a twisted tongue, hissing saliva, and a scraped throat.”

Whoever among the Critics wishes to reread that golden Commentary of Jerome, together with the annotations previously quoted from the *Book of Names*, will immediately admit, if he is a man of integrity, that nothing in the Hebrew language escaped Jerome. Such was this holy man’s mastery of the language that no modern grammarian can be compared with him. Indeed, who in our age knows Hebrew well enough to teach us how the aspirations and sounds are exchanged in the elements Aleph and Ain, He and Heth? From what Lexicon, from what Hebrew Grammar, can I learn what Jerome means by the certain hiss in the letter Sin, a sound not belonging to our language? What is the Hebrew Sade, which sounds neither like S nor like Z, but like something else that our ears utterly reject? What shall I say of the differing accents of letters, the length and shortness of syllables, and the letters pronounced with a scraping of the throat? Which of the Hebraists will boast that he knows and can teach these things?

I shall certainly say this with confidence: there is no man, whether among the Jews of today or among Christian writers, who has attained such mastery of the Hebrew language as to be able to explain the pronunciation of the letter Sin as it was used by the ancient Jews in the name Israel—a name which among them did not sound as it was written. Moreover, what principle do we find in the Grammars for recovering the ancient pronunciation of Hebrew letters with a scraped throat, a twisted tongue, loose lips, and hissing saliva? Jerome alone learned and taught all these things. He knew the Hebrew language so thoroughly that he himself corrected whatever was corrupt in Origen’s Hexapla from the authentic books, restoring everywhere the native aspirations of the elements, which the Seventy Interpreters had altered by rendering the letters Heth and Ain with χ or γ.

Would that Origen’s Hexapla had not perished from the republic of letters [Col. 1533B]—the work in which the Hebrew words themselves had been written in their proper characters, rendered in Greek letters by a close transcription, and corrected by Jerome’s hand against the Hebrew sources. If these works had survived for us, we would indeed acknowledge the immortal genius of Adamantius, but we would acknowledge as wholly divine the genius of Jerome, together with the astonishing diligence of that mortal by which he restored corrupted readings to integrity in the Greek letters representing Hebrew words and marked them with their proper accents. It was an outstanding labor, by which the ancient Christians were so enriched that they no longer greatly feared the arrogance of the Jews, who, before the restoration just mentioned by Jerome, mocked the faithful for ignorance, especially in the aspirations and in certain Hebrew letters pronounced with a scraping of the throat.

That boasting of the Jews came to an end when it pleased the supreme God to provide his Church with the greatest Interpreter of the Scriptures. If he found among the Circumcised anything true and suited to our faith, he judged that it was not merely not to be feared but should also be claimed from them, as unjust possessors, for our use. For the Jews possessed not only false traditions and heavy burdens, which the Christian people would detest and flee, but also books and the oracles of God entrusted to the fathers, like vessels and ornaments fashioned by the Prophets from gold and silver. Jerome seized and took all these things, converting them to Christian use. Hence he wrote to Marcella:

“For a long time now I have been comparing the edition of Aquila with the Hebrew volumes, lest perhaps the Synagogue may have altered something out of hatred for Christ; and, to confess frankly to a friendly mind, I find many things that contribute to strengthening our faith.”

But let us return to the arguments proposed, which are to be drawn from the *Book of Names* in order to prove Jerome’s Hebrew learning. In column 7 he warns that certain names are to be read with aspiration, as though with the Greek Chi χ. But because that general instruction might generate an error in a reader who did not sufficiently understand it, he immediately clarifies it with these observations [Col. 1533D]:

“Cham, hot. But it must be known that Hebrew does not have the letter Chi (χ); it is written with Heth, which is pronounced with a double aspiration.”

And shortly afterward:

“Chethaeus, an excess of mind, or fixed, or cut off. But this name does not begin in Hebrew with a consonant; rather, it begins with Heth, concerning which we have already spoken above.”

Then, in column 11, he says this concerning the name Gomorrha:

“Gomorrha, fear of the people, or sedition. It must be known that Hebrew does not have the letter G; rather, it is written with the vowel Ain.”

If you compare the recent Grammars of Hebrew with these observations of Jerome, you will find many things in them contrary to or different from his teaching. Jerome teaches that Heth is not a consonant; he likewise teaches that Ain is a vowel. The Hebrew Alphabet denies both points, since all its elements are consonant letters—Heth and Ain like the other twenty. Nor do modern grammarians disagree among themselves any less over the reading and pronunciation of these elements than they differ from Jerome’s precepts. This disagreement clearly shows that they do not know the genuine pronunciation of the Hebrew elements or the Hebrew language, of which the holy Doctor was a master.

If they say that it has always been known to them that the letters we call gutturals—[letters illegible in the supplied text]—were regarded as vowels by the ancient Hebrews, let them likewise show, if they can, what distinction there was in pronouncing the first E in the names listed in column 9. Concerning this Jerome observed in the same place:

“Up to this point the beginnings of names are to be read with a short letter E; from now on with a long one.”

Thus the name Eden and those following it up to Esbel were read by the ancients with a short E; but with the same letter lengthened came the name Elissa and the next thirteen names through the letter F. Which of the Critics or grammarians will seriously teach me why the first letter of the name Elmodad—namely Aleph—was short among the ancient Hebrews, while the same letter was lengthened in Eliezer and in many others that follow Jerome’s brief annotation [Col. 1534B]? We can indeed detect the distinction between short and long vowels in certain names, as in Bethsabee, concerning which he speaks in column 57; but where the elements and beginnings of Hebrew names are equal, the distinction remains unknown and obscure to us.

Since all these matters were clear and certain to Jerome, it follows that he knew the Hebrew language, and even its grammatical intricacies, better than any of today’s Hebraists or sharp-nosed Critics. And unless I were weary of repeating the same things and copying the same annotations of Jerome three or four times over, I would reproduce in order every admonition inserted in the *Book of Names*. But I know that this is tiresome and unwelcome to the studious reader, to whom we often show consideration by omitting some arguments relevant to the question, lest his attention be disturbed by an excessive abundance of testimonies [Col. 1534C]. Whoever wishes may therefore consult Jerome and learn from the *Book of Hebrew Names* which elements are to be pronounced with aspiration, which are short, and which are long. Armed with these and similar grammatical precepts, he may himself approach as a witness to support Jerome’s learning. For Jerome is held in contempt only by the ignorant, who either rarely or never read what they are not ashamed to accuse in men like themselves.

We already know the man to be richly furnished with expertise in the Hebrew elements; several observations prove him equally skilled in the meanings of words, for he undertook to explain certain words himself. We shall select only a few examples, since the proof of the matter proposed by no means requires all of them.

In column 10 of the Book of Genesis, we read the following above:

“Deson, a strong nipple, or ‘he will tread upon it’; but this is said in the Syrian language. In Hebrew, however, it means fatness, or ashes, that is, the ashes of burnt offerings.”

If I consult the Hebrew Lexicons, they report nothing else at the root *dassen* except the two meanings properly understood and explained by Jerome. For *dessen* means fatness or ashes, that is, the ashes of burnt offerings. Hence Leviticus 1:16: “He shall cast it beside the altar toward the east, to the place of *haddesen*,” that is, “of ashes,” or “to the place where the ashes are burned.” The same name *desen* signifies fatness in Judges 9:9: “Shall I abandon my *disseni*, my fatness?”

Whatever the Hebrew dictionaries teach the reader in many words about the meaning of the Hebrew word *desen* or *deson*, St. Jerome explains in two words. If he had omitted the first etymology, “he will tread upon it,” derived from the Syrian language, the fault would have been laid upon him by the Hebraists of our age, learned and unlearned alike, as a wholly forced and unlearned explanation. But concerning this kind of derivation, see above in our scholia on the word *Deson*.

Another example of Jerome’s learning and understanding, by which he most keenly discerned what each Hebrew name signified, may be taken from the word Rachel, whose multiple etymology he explains in this way in column 15:

“Rachel, a sheep, or seeing the beginning, or a vision of crime, or seeing God. This occurs because of the diversity of accents and letters, so that names may be changed into contrary meanings.”

What kind of diversity of letters produces contrary meanings, Jerome himself clearly explained in column 114, saying:

“Raab, if it is written with Ain as the middle letter, signifies hunger; if with He, an assault; if with Heth, breadth.”

In the same way, Rachel, if written with Heth, signifies a sheep; if with Aleph, one who sees God. Again, if you understand it as formed from *raa* and *hhalal*, it means “seeing the beginning.” Finally, from *rai* and *ra*, with Ain, it expresses “a vision of crime.”

I take a third argument for Jerome’s learning from the famous name Somthonphanech, concerning which he argued as follows in column 17:

“Somthonphanech is said incorrectly; for in Hebrew we read *Saphneth phanee*, which means ‘discoverer of hidden things.’ Moreover, we have learned from the Egyptians that in their language it sounds ‘Savior of the world.’”

This annotation is extremely brief and expressed in concise words, but the more compressed it is in language, the more expansive it becomes in meaning. Jerome immediately warns that the name Psomthonphanech is read corruptly among the Seventy. He restores the genuine reading from the Hebrew source and then gives the Hebrew etymology of the true name. Nor was that great man content with this: he also carefully recorded from the Egyptians the Egyptian derivation of the word *Saphneth phanee*. When these things are joined to the same holy Doctor’s *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, chapter forty-one [Col. 1535C], where he explained the translation of the aforementioned name *Saphneth phanee*, nothing remains to be sought for a complete understanding of the word, no matter which Commentaries of ancient or recent Writers one examines. In the cited passage Jerome says:

“And Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Saphaneth phanee; and he gave him Aseneth, the daughter of Phutiphar, priest of Heliopolis, as a wife. Although in Hebrew this name means ‘discoverer of hidden things,’ nevertheless, since it is given in Egyptian, it must be understood according to that language. In the Egyptian language, therefore, Saphaneth phanee is interpreted—or, as the Seventy wished to translate it, Psomtomphanech—as ‘Savior of the world,’ because he freed the world from the destruction of the impending famine.”

Such learning shines forth, and such incomparable diligence on Jerome’s part, even in this one example, that, having become more certain through reading a recent heterodox writer, I dare to assert fearlessly that none of today’s hunters after novelty can equal the faith, knowledge, and genius of the holy Doctor, even if he employs pompous language and strives with all his strength to forge a new meaning in the sacred Books. Those who know the genius of John Clericus and how eagerly he pursues contrived and far-fetched subtleties, even from trivial arguments, will readily grant this.

For in his recently published Commentary on Genesis, an advocate of many heresies, he found nothing new with which to instruct the reader concerning the interpretation of the name imposed upon Joseph by Pharaoh. Indeed, he obscured what others had said well—especially what Jerome had presented with such learning—by his own conjectures. Thus, in his new version and continuous paraphrase, he renders Genesis 41:45 as follows.

In the version:

“And he called Joseph by a new name, Tsophnath-phahaneach, and gave him Asnath, the daughter of Potipherah, priest of On, as a wife.”

In the paraphrase:

“Then he forbade him to be called any longer by the name of Joseph, and in the Egyptian language called him Tsophnath-phahaneach, that is, ‘Revealer of hidden things.’ And, so that he might never consider returning from Egypt to his own people, he wished Asnath, the daughter of Potipherah, priest of On, to be joined to him in marriage.”

It is not the concern of the present work to warn the reader how many profane novelties are contained in such new interpretations. It is enough to observe that Joseph cannot be called *Tsophnath-phahaneach* in the Egyptian language, because that name has a Latin sound and ending, not an Egyptian one. Yet, since it is given in Egyptian, it must be understood according to that language, as Jerome taught above; and recent Critics nowhere approach his diligence.

Nor do observations of this kind escape the holy Doctor, as is readily proved by the word *Sichimorum* in column 16:

“Sichimorum, shoulders; it is the same as Sichem. But it is turned into a Latin and Greek sound.”

Apart from John Clericus’s error, by which an Egyptian is made to speak Latin [Col. 1536B], there is another, and indeed worse, in the same continuous Paraphrase: namely, where *Tsophnath-phahaneach* is said to mean “Revealer of hidden things” in the Egyptian language. Clericus invents this Egyptian derivation. Had he consulted the most ancient Egyptians through Jerome, he would have admitted that they interpreted the name *Tsophnath-phahaneach*, or rather *Saphneth-phanee*, not as “Revealer of hidden things” but as “Savior of the world,” as the holy Jerome correctly reads it according to the Hebrew.

Moreover, this too should be added: if we believe students of the Coptic language, the name *Esotem-pane* means in Coptic, or the Egyptian language, “Savior of the age.”

In the same Commentary of the recent Writer, many things that Jerome clearly explained and carefully noted are found confused with obscure opinions. Jerome expressly asserts that the Seventy wished to translate *Psontomphanech*; whereas Clericus seems to deny this in these words on p. 265 of his Commentary on Genesis 41:45 [Col. 1536C]:

“*Tsophnath-phahaneach*. [Hebrew words illegible in the supplied text], which words have been preserved intact by the Septuagint Interpreters, except that they write Ψονθομφανὲκ, as though they had read *ptsothon*—unless there is some error, which could easily have crept into a barbarous word through the carelessness of Greek copyists. Truly novel readings and unheard-of opinions.”

He says that the Hebrew words are preserved intact by the Seventy, except that they write Ψονθὸμ instead of *Saphneth*. This is precisely the same as saying that the Seventy write the Hebrew words intact, except that they represent all their elements reversed and confused, reading *Psonthom* for *Tsophnath*, and sometimes putting *Dano* for *Adon*. But who does not know that in Hebrew names and words their meaning depends so entirely upon the complete order of the letters that anyone who reverses one overturns the whole sense of the words?

Let us therefore not treat the sacred text in the Hebrew Names as a matter of indifference, but, with Jerome, acknowledge the name *Psomthom-phanech* as corruptly written and altered by the Seventy. How much harm such disturbances of the elements bring with them we can learn from Jerome himself. In Book VIII of his Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter XXVII, he appropriately observes:

“Charran, in our language, means ‘holes’; *Channe*, ‘preparation’; *Eden*, ‘delights.’ In place of this, among the Seventy we find *Edne*, a word that does not exist in Hebrew; what it means we do not know, and we ought not to seek the etymology of a fictitious name.”

How great an error was caused among the Seventy by the transposition of a single little letter? For *Eden* itself becomes *Edne* if you place the final *e* before the preceding letter. Yet Jerome calls this a fictitious name, whose etymology he disdains to seek, because the name *Edne* is not found written in Hebrew.

From these things it plainly appears how different Jerome’s diligence, genius, and study in sacred matters were from those now displayed by the Critics of our time [Col. 1537A]. But when I say this, they immediately accuse me of envy or, in their ignorance, brand me with the reputation of a bitter Writer—as though a fault changed along with the person, and as though what Clericus may freely do against Jerome, I may not do for Jerome against Clericus, an advocate of new meanings and doctrines.

If this accusation should ever arise, I have nothing to oppose in this *Apology* except the words of the holy Doctor, for whose sake I undertook it:

“Truth,” he says, “is bitter, wrinkled of brow and sad, and it offends those who have been corrected . . . . . Let truth and sincerity be in us, and bitterness will immediately follow.”

Thus he writes in Book I *Against the Pelagians*.

By the preceding arguments I have abundantly proved Jerome’s Hebrew learning and sufficiently made manifest the excellence of the holy man, the greatest of the Interpreters of Scripture, as well as his fidelity and diligence. Nevertheless, I judged that the final hand should be added to this apologetic work through two further examples that by no means ought to be omitted, since they greatly commend Jerome’s expertise and his exceptionally diligent study of interpretation.

He observes, therefore, the particular character of the language of the Syrians and Egyptians, not only in the words *Desen* and *Saphneth-phanee* mentioned above, but also in the names Javan and Bubastus. Concerning the former, we read the following written by him in column 11:

“Javan, ‘is and is not,’ or ‘dove’; but the latter is Syrian.”

The reasoning behind the etymology “is and is not” did not greatly trouble me, because, as I said in the scholia on this passage, Javan can be understood as formed from the verb *jes*, the connective particle *ve*, and the negative particle *en*. Thus Javan means “is and is not.” But for a long time I remained uncertain and not a little anxious as to the authority by which Jerome had published this etymology, even until the present.

My own conscience did not permit me to assert that Jerome derived it from the Greeks, because the name Javan is not found in the Greek Fragments or in the Origenian Lexicon. But the eighth book of Jerome’s Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter XXVII, left me no room for doubt, where Jerome himself expressly warns the reader about this same etymology:

“The Hebrews say that Greece, that is, Javan, is interpreted ‘is and is not.’ This properly refers to secular wisdom: if they discover something correct in it, it is called ‘is’; if it tends in the opposite direction, ‘it is not.’ For they themselves also discuss many good things by nature, concerning duties, continence, contempt for riches, and so forth.”

St. Jerome therefore professes to have received the etymology of Javan from the Hebrews. When, however, he adds in the *Book of Hebrew Names* that Javan also means “dove,” he provides an argument both of singular diligence and of understanding, saying: “But this is Syrian.” The name Javan, that is, is interpreted as “dove”; for in Hebrew “dove” is *Jona*, while in Syriac it is *Jauno*, or *Jaunon*, as in Sophonias 3:1, which comes closer to Javan.

As for the word Bubastus, written *Phibeseth* in Hebrew, I had no further expectation, since there is no modern Hebrew Lexicon from which the etymology of the name can be discovered by us. For in column 83 Bubastus is interpreted as “mouth” or “lip of testing.” There is no difficulty concerning mouth or lip, since *phi* or *phe* signifies both among the Hebrews. But the meaning of *beseth*, which is rendered “testing,” is entirely different. Jerome did not learn this etymology from the Hebrews; rather, he borrowed from the Egyptians what belonged to the Egyptians.

Hence in his Commentary on Ezekiel, Book IX, chapter XXX, you may read:

“Bubastus, according to the Egyptian language, is interpreted ‘testing of the mouth.’”

Without doubt, the person who wrote the following in a certain letter to the distinguished man Alix had not read this passage. Concerning the etymology of Bubastus, he says:

“It is reported by some that Bubastus or Bubastis is an Egyptian name, and that it means ‘the city of the Cat.’”

“Bubastus or Bubastis is written in two words in Scripture. Others say that this word is Egyptian and that it means a female cat, the city of the Cat; that is, ΠaΠΙΣaου (Παπισαυ).”

I thought it worthwhile to note this, so that the prudent reader might understand how much learning Jerome supplies, even concerning foreign words that far surpass the capacity of all the Hebraists.

I do not, however, wish to be convinced beyond doubt that, from the origin and interpretation of certain Egyptian words, Jerome knew the Egyptian language as he knew Hebrew. Nor can I agree with a recent writer who asserts this, although, in the present context of my Apology, I do not refuse to grant a place to the argument he employs against a foolish author who mocks Jerome concerning the etymology of the name imposed on Joseph by Pharaoh.

Thus, in the first chapter of his Dissertation on the Name of the Patriarch Joseph Imposed by Pharaoh, Guillaume Bonjour writes:

> “Certain modern writers, living in complete ignorance of the Egyptian language, cannot persuade themselves of this. Hence John Gregory, rising up against Jerome in his Notes and Observations on Certain Passages of Scripture, chapter 16, says: ‘Whoever revealed this gloss of this name, Savior of the world, to Saint Jerome imposed it upon him sufficiently.’ As though Egyptian had escaped the notice of Jerome! For the letters which Pachomius, Cornelius, and Syrus wrote to one another in the Egyptian language—and of which Gennadius makes mention in his account of Pachomius—he rendered into Latin, imitating the simplicity of the Egyptian language, as he himself testifies in the Preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius:
>
> > ‘The Thebans say,’ he writes, ‘that an angel gave Pachomius, Cornelius, and Syrus—who is said still to be living today, beyond the age of one hundred and ten—the knowledge of a mystical language, so that they might write and speak to one another through a special alphabet, concealing hidden meanings in certain signs and symbols. We have translated these letters into our own language as they are read among the Egyptians and Greeks, preserving the same letters as we found them. And since we have imitated the simplicity of the Egyptian language, the fidelity of the translation prevents rhetorical speech from altering men who were apostolic and wholly devoted to spiritual grace.’
>
> “Therefore Saint Jerome knew the Egyptian language: for the sake of fidelity in translation, he says that he imitated the simplicity of Egyptian speech. Consequently, he is a suitable witness to the meaning of the words of that language and must be preferred altogether to those who, having paid no attention whatsoever to Egyptian speech, interpret the name imposed on Joseph by Pharaoh as ‘revealer of secrets.’”

[Col. 1538B]

Since, then, we now know Jerome to have been thoroughly acquainted with the language of the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Syrians, and Egyptians—if Guillaume Bonjour is to be believed—anyone who does not admire the outstanding knowledge of Hebrew possessed by the holy Doctor will henceforth be held guilty either of ignorance or of envy, even though I have passed over a great many proofs of this learning, lest I burden the nauseated stomach of the Critics with too much food.

Every diligent reader can easily supply the evidence here omitted, if only he attends for a while to the following words in the book of Hebrew Names:

- col. 21: Jessaar;
- col. 24: Abarim;
- col. 25: Basan;
- col. 30: Moseroth;
- col. 31: Opher;
- col. 32: Salu;
- col. 33: Aseroth;
- col. 34: Gaza;
- col. 35: Sina;
- col. 36: Adonibezec, Ailon, Azaf;
- col. 37: Affara and Asara;
- col. 38: Alal, Baaloth, and Bethaphue;
- col. 39: Balath, Balathaba, and Cana;
- col. 40: Chiphara, Chermel;
- col. 46: Tyrus, Thaffue;
- col. 55: Nabal, Rachal, and Rachel;
- col. 58: Hiram, and the following three words;
- col. 61: Bethsabee;
- col. 65: Zamri;
- col. 69: Nabuzardan, Sir;
- col. 70: Theglath, Therach;
- col. 71: Coph;
- col. 72: Samech;
- col. 73: Joach;
- col. 79: Chabonim;
- col. 83: Ulai;
- col. 86: Semel, and so forth.

All these words especially demonstrate Jerome’s learning—a learning that before us no one had noticed in the book of Names, although amid the errors and obscurities of the older editions it had always appeared to me sufficiently clear.

For this reason, in this dissertation I have wished to confine myself within the narrowest limits of a single volume, so that I might more easily persuade fair-minded readers how great Jerome’s Hebrew learning was when collected and demonstrated from all his works, since so much of it is most clearly displayed and more than sufficiently proved in what seemed to be the most insignificant of all his little works.

I have therefore wished to exhibit these proofs of Jerome’s learning as though they were broad expanses of land shown upon a small map—not extending the spaces of the meanings and discussions, but signifying the infinite by certain points and abridgements.

But since learned and honorable men have sometimes asked me, in a friendly spirit, about the causes and origins of the suspicion concerning Jerome’s knowledge of Hebrew—a language in which he was commonly said among the Critics to be sufficiently unskilled—and since everything I have learned ought to be imparted to trustworthy ears, I shall briefly explain what caused some people, under the influence of a preconceived opinion, to regard Jerome as ignorant.

The principal occasion for this opinion was the enormous multitude of errors in the printed books. For Jerome’s text is found in them to be so corrupted that very few Hebrew names and words are written correctly or retain their proper etymologies—especially in the book of Hebrew Names, where, if the corruptions were removed, nearly a third of the volume would be cut away.

And lest educated readers suppose that I have stated this hyperbolically, I shall reveal the ugliness of the corruptions through a few examples.

In the book of Genesis, the first Hebrew name retains a false etymology in the previously printed books: “Assyriorum, diligentium” [“of the Assyrians, of those who are diligent”]. Yet from the singular Assur, which follows correctly, it is easily understood that one should read “dirigentium” [“of those who direct”], not “diligentium”; for *asar* in Hebrew does not mean “to love,” but “to direct,” “to proceed,” and “to be blessed.” Hence Assur means “directing,” or “blessed,” or “walking.”

Nor is it wrong to add here, together with the printed editions, “arguens” [“accusing”], since the word Assur does not signify that.

In the same place, for the name Aevila we read Amila, and for Archab, the corrupted form Archat. The etymologies joined by Jerome to these names do not correspond to the corrupt names just mentioned, but to the restored forms Aevila and Archab.

Under the same letter A, Aggea is corruptly read for Aggai; in the etymology of the word Agar, “adversa” [“adverse”] appears instead of “advena” [“stranger”]; in the etymology of Apher, “humilis” [“humble”] instead of “humus” [“earth”]; and the name Abdam appears instead of Amada. All these changes alter the meanings along with the letters.

Under the letter B, the words Beor and Bochor have especially absurd etymologies. Nor are they read in only one corrupt form in the older editions. For Beor, which is rendered “in pelle” [“in skin”], Erasmus and Marianus changed it with the verb *impelle* [“drive in”]. Then Bochor is interpreted in the Erasmian edition as “ingressus est angustus” [“he entered narrowly”], but in the Marian edition as “in ingressu est angustus” [“he is narrow in entering”].

Removing both false etymologies, we restored the genuine and Jerome’s reading, namely: “ingressus est agnus” [“the lamb entered”]. For *bo* signifies “he came” or “he entered,” and *cher* or *char* means “lamb” in the Hebrew language.

Nor did we restore Jerome’s true readings on our own authority, but on the evidence of the oldest books and the full abundance of manuscript codices.

It is unnecessary to increase the reader’s weariness by bringing every corrupted Hebrew name into view and into the light. I shall therefore offer only one further example from the names written corruptly and interpreted incorrectly under the letter M, so that learned men may judge how many corruptions and errors there are throughout the entire volume when so many obvious faults are found in only a few names:

- Mathusale: “mortis concussio” [“shaking of death”], instead of “mortis emissio” [“release of death”];
- Mesa: “aqua rara, vel evado” [“rare water, or I escape”], instead of “vel elatio” [“or exaltation”];
- Mamre: “divisio” [“division”], instead of “de visione” [“from vision”];
- Mabram, instead of Massam;
- Mabeleti, instead of Meleth;
- Masreca: “sive libans” [“or pouring a libation”], instead of “sive sibilans” [“or hissing”];
- Matraid: “percussio” [“striking”], instead of “persecutio” [“persecution”];
- Mezaab: “aquam hauriens” [“drawing water”], instead of “aqua auri” [“water of gold”];
- Mabzar, instead of Mabsar.

I say nothing of the other words that had their order reversed in the previously printed books, since I think it sufficient to have noted the corrupted names, and especially the faulty etymologies, through which Jerome was given an occasion for criticism in the book of Hebrew Names.

[Col. 1539D]

Furthermore, Hebrew words written in their proper letters in the editions of Erasmus and Marianus gave Jerome’s critics another opportunity. These editors, being insufficiently attentive to the usage of the ancients and to Jerome’s practice in transcribing Hebrew words, substitute the Masoretes for Jerome in our copies; and their editions show that they sow errors with a full hand rather than remove them.

For what we read fully and accurately written in Latin letters in the manuscript exemplars, they corrupt by introducing Hebrew characters where they were inappropriate, thereby presenting Jerome to us as utterly ignorant of the Hebrew language and stammering everywhere in it.

We took the proof of this matter above from the word *Hareb*, which, having been incorrectly written in Hebrew letters in a certain form, gave even the most learned Bochart an occasion for error. He thought that Jerome had been mistaken in the etymology of this name, although the word *Hareb* or *Oreb*, written thus by Jerome according to the difference of the reading, signifies “sword” and “dryness,” or “raven.”

All the manuscript codices that exist throughout the Christian world most clearly demonstrate this kind of corruption. Nowhere will you find an exemplar that does not plainly contradict the editions of Erasmus and Marianus.

Since I have mentioned them, it will not be irrelevant to observe what is read in the eighth book of Jerome’s Commentaries on chapter 27 of the prophet Ezekiel. He explains the fourth verse, “Your neighbors who built you,” and so forth, in this manner:

> “In place of this, I do not know with what intention, the Septuagint translated: ‘Beelim, your sons, surrounded your beauty,’ and so forth. For the word *Beelim* is not found at all among the Hebrews in this passage; instead of *Beelim* it is written *Gebulaich*, which means ‘your boundaries.’ Moreover, when they said ‘your sons,’ they were deceived by the ambiguity of the word and by the similarity of the writing, since, with a different pronunciation, the same letters are read as ‘builders’ (*Bonaich*) and ‘sons’ (*Benaich*).”

Jerome could not have explained more openly the error of the Septuagint translators arising from the ambiguity of the Hebrew word, which, according to its different pronunciation, means at one time “your builders,” and at another “your sons.” If you read *bonaich*, it means “your builders”; but if you pronounce it *benaich*, the word means “your sons.”

Yet in the books previously printed, all the Hebrew words have been copied corruptly and confusedly, and you will not find their differing pronunciation marked or distinguished in Erasmus or Marianus. For they disturb the reading by writing them in Hebrew letters in such a way as to produce *benajich* and *bnich*, *gebulejich*.

These are certainly not Jerome’s Hebrew readings, but the errors of unskilled editors or printers, whose incompetence and stammering in Hebrew matters everywhere provide material for that preconceived opinion of which we are now speaking.

Certain allegorical interpretations, and also a great many unlearned etymologies of Hebrew names, likewise gave Jerome’s critics occasion for their suspicion of his ignorance.

Anyone who has read only one passage or a small portion of some volume in Jerome, and who sees his learning and his interpretations of words differing from his own habitual understanding, immediately declares the holy Doctor ignorant of the Hebrew language and judges him worthy of contempt because of his hurried study, as he calls it, and careless observations.

We saw many such faults attributed to Jerome at the beginning of this Apology, and I refuted them sufficiently by Jerome’s own words. In them the most learned man rejects the Greek etymologies that not a few Critics rashly and ignorantly attributed to Jerome as their original author, although he was only their Latin translator. This is demonstrated especially by the words Israel, Dapheca, and others, explained in the book of Hebrew Names according to Greek etymologies, whereas in the Hebrew Questions on Genesis and in the letter to Fabiola concerning the forty-two stations of the Israelites in the wilderness, they are explained according to the mind of the most holy Doctor and restored to their proper, native etymology.

Let learned men therefore take care not to stumble against this obstacle hereafter, attributing ignorantly to Jerome what properly belongs to Philo the Jew or to Origen Adamantius, the authors of many foolish etymologies, because they possessed little knowledge of the Hebrew language.

John Clericus discovered a particular cause and occasion for a new error in criticizing Jerome in his appendix to the Commentary on Genesis. For, unlike the other Critics, he does not blame foreign errors in Jerome; rather, he censures a learned observation deserving of the greatest care and erudition, in these words, Dissertation I, p. 318:

> “The same place is called *αὐλών* (*aulōn*), that is, ‘valley,’ from the nature of the site, although Jerome incorrectly wishes the Hebrew word to be intended. ‘Aulon,’ he says, ‘is not Greek, as some suppose, but a Hebrew word. It signifies a great and level valley,’ and so forth.”

What thoughtlessness in Clericus as a critic! Jerome very carefully warns in the Hebrew Places that the name *aulon* is not here a Greek word—as some supposed—because the Greek word *αὐλών* was more familiar to the reader than the Hebrew *aulon*, *ailon*, or *ajalon*.

Jerome therefore did not incorrectly wish *aulon* to be a Hebrew word, as Clericus wrongly accuses him of doing. Rather, he supplied the reader with necessary preliminary information, lest, in the ambiguous word *aulon*, which is both Greek and Hebrew, there be room for error, when an unlearned reader of Hebrew might think that he was finding Greek names in the Hebrew Places.

To make this clearer, I shall draw another observation from Jerome’s book of Hebrew Names. In col. 36, the following is written concerning *aulon*:

> “Ailon, which above we called *aulon*: but if we wish to read *Aeglon*, it means ‘their heifer.’”

Above, however, in col. 34, under the letter E, he said:

> “Elath, terebinth, or *aulones*.”

But he expressed the very name *aulon* still more significantly in col. 19, under the letter E, saying:

> “Elon, oak, or *aulon*: concerning which we have spoken more fully in the book of Places.”

What will Clericus’s erudition and diligence reply to these observations of Jerome? The holy Doctor had written more fully about *Aulon* in the book of Places. That *Aulon* is the same as *Elon*, interpreted as “oak,” or the same as *Elath*, that is, “terebinth.”

If this is so—as indeed it is—how can Clericus’s ingenuity count Ailon, Elon, and Elath among Greek words? His comments would not be called splendid and golden unless the greatest of men were attacked in them, and Jerome’s knowledge of languages despised.

I do not say this because I venerate Jerome as though he were a sacred author, or because I have decided, for his sake, to retaliate against the Critics of the present age. I say it because a concern for truth and reverence cannot allow statements to pass unpunished when I find that they have been made falsely and rashly by malicious or imprudent writers against the greatest Doctor and the most diligent interpreter of Scripture.

Otherwise I myself learned from Jerome that one ought not to envy or reject whatever others may have said more plausibly after him concerning obscure questions of the sacred Scriptures:

> “If someone,” he says, “having meditated day and night on the law of the Lord, has possessed greater zeal, greater ability, leisure, and grace, and can say something more plausibly about the present chapter, I do not envy him or reject him. Rather, I desire to learn from him what I do not know, and I shall gladly profess myself his disciple, provided that he teaches and does not disparage. For nothing is easier than to discuss the labor and vigils of others while oneself is idle and asleep.”

Book I of the Commentaries on Micah, chapter 2.

I now come to the conclusion of the Apology. Above all, I wished to warn the diligent reader not to place credence too readily in certain writers who think themselves learned if they disparage Jerome’s genius, praise, or learning. They do not understand that the clearest proof of ignorance lies in disparaging a great man and finding displeasure in the abundance of his varied learning.

For what do Jerome’s writings fail to provide in any branch of knowledge or in the diligent pursuit of commendable studies? Certainly, if we had now undertaken a discussion of his universal learning, many proofs would be readily available by which I could establish that nothing useful can be found in other authors that is not found much more abundantly in Jerome, while many things may be read in him that are found nowhere else at all.

And although many learned men agree with me that this is so, I shall nevertheless offer one particularly striking example in Hebrew matters, since in this place I have undertaken the defense of Jerome’s Hebrew learning alone.

The Hebrew word *Taphnes*, or *Taphnis*, occurs very frequently in the sacred text of the Bible. It is the name of the wife of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, in 3 Kings 11:19, [Hebrew form], in Greek *Τεχεφενής* (*Techephenēs*).

The same name was also given to an Egyptian city, Taphnis, in Ezekiel 30:18, where it is written in Hebrew *thehhaphnehhas*, as also in Jeremiah 2:16 and 43:7 and following.

The Critics of the present age therefore interpret the word *Taphnes*, or *Taphnis*, as “hidden temptation,” or “flight,” or “covered banner”; or, from Hebrew and Syriac, “hidden miracle.”

Then, in Jeremiah, they interpret it as “covering of confidence,” or “protection,” or “hidden confidence,” or “protection.”

I find this interpretation at the end of volume VI of the Polyglot Bible, and learned men, celebrated for their reputation for erudition, join no other etymology to that name.

But when this is compared with Jerome’s treasury of etymologies, everything that is said is recognized as altogether slight and narrow. For in the third book of Kings, above, col. 65, we read *Taphnes* interpreted in this way:

> “Taphnes, ‘a covered sign’; which in Greek is expressed more significantly as *σύσσημον* [‘a secret sign’].”

Then in Jeremiah, col. 81:

> “Taphnas, ‘the frenzied mouth of a serpent,’ or ‘a covered sign.’”

Likewise in Ezekiel, col. 86:

> “Taphnas, ‘the astonished mouth of a serpent’: it must be understood from ‘mouth,’ not from ‘bone.’”

But in Jerome’s Commentaries on Ezekiel there are still other and multiple etymologies of the same Taphnis. He says in Book II of the Commentary on chapter 30:

> “Phatures means ‘the trampling of bread’; Taphnis, ‘a humble command.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “And in Taphnis the day will grow dark. Taphnae means ‘yielding to the mouth’; the mouth of the devil is understood. Those who yield to him will lose the light of truth and will change day into night.”

From all these passages it clearly appears that the name Taphnis, written differently in Hebrew, was expressed very accurately according to this difference in the book of Hebrew Names, and interpreted learnedly according to the character of the Hebrew language.

The name is especially noteworthy because it is written *Taphnes* in 3 Kings 11:19, but in the Prophets *Taphnas*, with Heth at the end in place of the penultimate Jod of the preceding form *Taphnes*.

Wishing to express this differing reading, Saint Jerome wrote *Taphnes* in the book of Names when treating 3 Kings, but in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, *Taphnas*.

He also expressed this different reading by the variety of the etymologies: he interpreted *Taphnes* as “a covered sign,” or *σύσσημον*; but *Taphnas* as “the astonished mouth of a serpent.”

In this connection I wish first to observe that the earlier etymology, “a covered sign” or “a hidden sign,” is genuinely Jerome’s and is expressed according to the character of the Hebrew language, since the Hebrew *hhapha* or *hhaphaph* means “he covered,” “he concealed,” and “he hid.”

Moreover, *nes* means “banner,” or “military sign.” Hence Numbers 21:8 has *lenes*, “for a sign.”

We know from the Greek Lexicon of Hebrew Names published by us that the second etymology of Taphnis belongs not to Jerome but to Greek writers. There we read, col. 661:

> *Τανίης, Ἐντολὴ ταπεινὴ, ἢ δροσιζομένη*—that is, “Tanies, a humble command, or bedewed.”

And immediately afterward:

> *Τάφνος, ἐξανιστάμενον στόμα ὄφεως*—that is, “Taphnos, the rising mouth of a serpent.”

Therefore what is found in Jerome as the interpretation of *Taphnas*, “the frenzied mouth, or the astonished mouth, of a serpent,” must be attributed to the Greeks. For the name is understood to have been figuratively forced from *taphal*, *hhaphaz*, and *nahhas*. These words retain letters different from those seen in the word *Tahpnas*.

We shall speak more fully shortly about the third interpretation of Taphnis. I conjecture that the fourth must likewise be attributed to the Greeks, as were the earlier ones, because they interpret *Taphne* by force as “yielding to the mouth.” Nor do I see where that etymology could arise unless it was derived from *tahhath* and from *Phe* among the Greeks, who may have taken “yielding to the mouth” to mean “lower than the mouth.”

In Syriac, too, it is said, “he became weak” and “he was cast down,” in which sense “yielding” can be understood in the present etymology.

As for the third etymology, namely, *Taphnis*, “a humble command,” I have discovered that it arose from a corrupt reading. For in the oldest manuscript exemplars of Jerome’s Commentaries on chapter 30 of Ezekiel we read:

> “Phatures means ‘the trampling of bread’; Tanis, ‘a humble command.’”

The name *Tanis*, which is read as *soan* in Hebrew, Jerome translated in the book of Hebrew Names, col. 75, as “commanding humble things,” and then in col. 86 as “a humble command.”

We have established from the Origenian Lexicon that the authors of such etymologies were Greeks. We cited its words above:

> *Τανίης, Ἐντολὴ ταπεινὴ*—that is, “Tanies, a humble command.”

It is easy for me to believe that in ancient times the name *soan* was written with Vau in a certain form, whose first syllable *so*, or *sau*, means “command.” Whether it can sound “humble” from the root *ana*, no one acquainted with the Hebrew language will deny.

Finally, since I have mentioned the word *Phatures*, the reader should be warned that its etymology is taken from the Hebrew *phath*, which properly signifies a morsel and a piece of bread, not bread itself, and from the verb *raphas*, from which comes the meaning “trampling” in the etymology of *Phatures*, although the middle radical is redundant in the root *Raphas*.

If all these matters explained and discussed by us up to this point are carefully observed, we hope that readers will encounter no delay in recognizing how deeply unjust are the prejudices against Jerome’s Hebrew learning.

For I have made it sufficiently clear that everything laid to the charge of the holy Doctor must be attributed either to the ignorance of the Greeks, or to the errors of the older editions, or to the thoughtlessness and envy of the modern Critics.

And although the arguments and examples of this Apology happened to end with the word *Taphnis* and *Phathures*, I do not think that this has made an unsuitable end to the writing. For in it we can discern nearly all the causes and origins of the preconceived opinion against Jerome: the errors of the older editions, where *Taphnis* is read for *Tanis*; the etymologies proper to the Greeks but carelessly attributed to Jerome; and finally the errors of the Critics, who do not sufficiently attend to Jerome’s interpretations and usage when, in the variety of allegories, he employs false and forced etymologies of Greek writers—etymologies which elsewhere he himself had often taught ought to be rejected.

Thus in Book IV of his Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 12, you may read:

> “But since some wish the captivity of Zedekiah, whose name means ‘the just Lord,’ to precede as a type of the Savior . . . I think that the prudent and careful reader should first be warned that we present these things lest we seem to pass over anything, but that we do not approve them. For an impious king cannot precede as a figure of him who is the example of all piety.”

And after much more:

> “We have said these things,” he writes, “leaving the judgment to the reader. For the rest, there is no doubt that it is dangerous to compare the captivity and death of an impious king with the mystery of the Lord.”

He protects himself with a similar warning against the hasty judgments of an ignorant reader or the criticism of rivals when, in the book of Hebrew Places, under the word *Elmoni*, he appropriately observed:

> “Elmoni, ‘a certain place,’ is interpreted. In its place Aquila and Theodotion translated *τόνδε τίνα*, which we may render ‘this one’ or ‘that one.’ Let the diligent reader recognize that, as I also touched upon in part at the beginning of this book, I do not approve everything that I translate. Rather, I leave certain things according to the authority of the Greek because I have discussed them more fully in the books of Hebrew Questions.”

The safest precaution for a prudent reader, therefore, will be not to attribute to Jerome, or credit him with, anything that he has not himself explained and approved in the Hebrew Questions or in another volume of his Commentaries.

For it is not the mark of a prudent man to assert as Jerome’s own everything that is read in Jerome, unless we have learned from elsewhere that the holy Doctor taught it according to his own judgment or agreed with the others.

If this rule for judging Jerome had not been unknown among the Critics of the present age and among unlearned readers, I would not have had to undertake the task of defending Jerome, nor would any apologetic burden have been placed upon me—an undertaking that, with God’s protection, I have carried through to the end, praying that he himself may bring it to its final outcome and confer from it some benefit upon his Church.

## § II. The Usefulness of the Book of Hebrew Names

Some have thought the little book of Hebrew Names utterly useless and insignificant. A certain etymologist, an acquaintance of mine, even judged that it contained quite a few absurdities; I preserve in my desk his letter to me on this subject.

I am entirely convinced that, in the books previously printed, the dignity and usefulness of the book of Names have completely vanished through the incompetence of printers or the negligence of those responsible for the older editions.

For a book whose text has been utterly overturned cannot be read with any profit when its structure is everywhere disfigured by absurd etymologies, its words universally altered and corrupted, and the order of its words reversed and confused.

I certainly do not call such a book useful when it has been published with so many errors and such great faults. I am speaking of the book of Hebrew Names, whose interpreter and editor was Jerome, and whose dignity and benefit for reading I have undertaken to commend in this discussion.

To carry out the task I have undertaken, I shall first quote the words of the greatest men—Origen, Jerome, and finally Augustine—for they commended the excellence of this book of Names in more than one statement and wished to proclaim its usefulness in more than one place.

Origen, in volume V of his Commentary on John, says:

> “And indeed, when John points out Christ, the man points out God and the incorporeal Savior, and the voice [points out] the Word. But just as in many matters the activity of names is useful—*χρήσιμον δὲ αὖ ἦν ὥσπερ ἐπὶ πολλῶν ἡ τῶν ὀνομάτων ἐνέργεια*, that is, ‘just as in many things the efficacy of names was useful’—so here too it will be useful to see what Zacharias and John signify; for it is as though someone were not contemptible with respect to the giving of a name, and so forth.”

Origen therefore teaches that the force of names, or their *ἐνέργεια*—that is, their efficacy—is not useless in many matters, not only here but even more clearly below, in volume VIII of his Commentary on the same John:

> “Gergesa is interpreted as ‘dwelling of those who cast out,’ perhaps having received this name from the prophetic event that the inhabitants of the place enacted against the Savior when they begged him to depart from their territory.
