Something similar may also be observed in the Law and the Prophets concerning names, as we carefully learned from the Hebrews when comparing our copies with their exemplars—copies that are attested by the editions of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, which have not yet been corrupted.
>
> “We shall therefore add a few things for the benefit of the diligent, so that they may attend to these matters more carefully. One of the sons of Levi is called Geson in many copies, instead of Gerson, the same name as that of Moses’ firstborn, the name being correctly given to both because they had been born while dwelling in a foreign land.
>
> “Again, Judah’s second son is called Aunan among us, but among the Hebrews Onan, which means ‘their labor.’
>
> “Furthermore, in the journeys of the children of Israel in the book of Numbers, we find that they departed from Sochoth and encamped at Buthan, whereas the Hebrew has Aeman instead of Buthan.
>
> “And why need I delay by adding more, when the truth contained in names is available to anyone who wishes both to investigate and to recognize it? Above all, we must regard as suspect those passages of Scripture in which a great many names are enumerated together, such as the passages in the book of Joshua that concern the division of the inheritance, and in First Chronicles, from the beginning in sequence up to the material that occurs at the beginning of . . . Likewise in Ezra.
>
> “Nor should names be regarded as insignificant, since useful matters are signified by them for the interpretation of places. But it is not now the right time to begin a discussion of the theory of names, leaving aside the matters already proposed.”

Thus Origen speaks of names corrupted in the Septuagint version and of the usefulness of Hebrew names, whose interpretation is particularly helpful for understanding sacred Scripture.

The author of the Questions to the Orthodox likewise regarded the interpretation of Hebrew names as not only useful but also entirely necessary, as he declares in Question 86. For when asking for the interpretation of the following words—Mna, Ephi, Nebel, Seraphim, Bezel, and so forth—he immediately adds:

> “For knowledge of both is entirely necessary for us, since both are contained in the Scriptures.”

The answer appended to the question advises that this explanation of names, so necessary for understanding Scripture, should be taken from Origen, in the following words:

> “Origen, a man skilled in the Hebrew language, has explained the interpretation of all the Hebrew names and measures found in the sacred Scriptures. If you seek it, you will find there an explanation of the names of all the things about which you have asked.”

Those acquainted with the Hebrew language will scarcely grant to Greek writers that Origen was skilled in Hebrew; but everyone will acknowledge that the book of Hebrew Names is useful and entirely necessary.

Hence Jerome, highly skilled in Hebrew letters, counts that little work among Origen’s distinguished monuments, saying:

> “Wishing to imitate Origen in part—whom, after the Apostles, no one but an ignorant person will deny to have been a teacher of the Churches—among the other splendid monuments of his genius he also labored at this: to complete as a Christian what Philo had omitted as a Jew.”

The Jew Philo had omitted the Hebrew Names of the New Testament, which he did not accept. Origen, as a Christian, collected them and published a complete volume of Hebrew Names, which Jerome translated into Latin at the urging of the brothers Lupulianus and Valerianus, but also moved by the usefulness of the work itself.

Passing through each volume of Scripture in order and restoring the old building with new care, he rightly judged that he had done what the Greeks most ought to desire: for the book of Hebrew Names was published by the Latin writer Jerome in a much more corrected, much fuller, and more accurate form than by any Greek translator or author of the book of Names.

The holy Doctor also commends this same usefulness in Book IV of his *Commentary on Jeremiah*, chapter 23:

> “From words and from the interpretation of names, things are often revealed. Thus the changed names of Abraham, Sarah, Peter, and the sons of Zebedee signify a change of circumstances. Likewise, in this same Prophet, *Phassur* is said to mean ‘terror,’ or ‘translation,’ and ‘settler,’ or ‘stranger.’”

[Col. 1546A]

For these words to be understood more easily according to the mind of Saint Jerome, the prudent reader should remember that Jeremiah 20:3 and the following verses say: “The Lord did not call your name Phassur, but Terror on every side. For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will make you a terror,” and so forth. Jerome interprets *Phashur*, or Φαχώρ, as read by the Septuagint, as “blackness of mouth”; this, however, differs greatly from “terror,” “translation,” “settler,” and “stranger.” Hence Jerome appropriately observed the following concerning the same passage of Jeremiah:

> “The name of the priest is changed so that the future punishment may be indicated by the name. You will no longer have, he says, the name ‘blackness of mouth’ and the rule of an unrighteous power; rather, you will be led captive into Babylon. For this signifies ‘terror on every side,’ or ‘around,’ so that, trembling and uncertain of your own safety, you may look about in every direction and fear the adversaries coming against you. In place of ‘terror,’ which is written in Hebrew *Magur*, the Septuagint and Theodotion translated μέτοικον, that is, ‘one who migrates’; [Col. 1546B] the second edition of Aquila, ‘stranger’; the first, ‘one who looks around’; Symmachus, ‘removed,’ or ‘gathered and compelled.’”

We should therefore not understand Jerome in such a way as to suppose that the name *Phassur*, or *Phashur*, or *Phaschor*, means “terror,” “translation,” “settler,” and “stranger.” For, understood in that way, the words of the holy Doctor would absurdly produce a meaning entirely contrary to what he wished to teach. Nor, when he had previously said that *Phassur* means “blackness of mouth,” does he contradict himself when he states that it is also called “terror” or “stranger.” For he understands that, when the name *Phassur* is changed, Jeremiah means *Magur*; and the name *Magur* can signify “stranger,” “one translated,” and “one who looks around,” or even “terror” and “dread,” according to the character of the Hebrew language, among whose speakers the root *gur* has all these meanings.

Things, then, are often revealed through the words and interpretation of Hebrew names. Hence they contribute the greatest usefulness [Col. 1546C] toward grasping the genuine meaning of Sacred Scripture, as we have attempted to establish from this passage of Jerome.

As for the authority of Saint Augustine in commendation of the book of Hebrew Names, no one among the Greeks or Latins has wished to testify so clearly to the usefulness and dignity of this volume. For in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 16, he wonderfully commends the collection of Hebrew words by Origen and Jerome, saying:

> “With translated signs, if some unknown things happen to compel the reader to hesitate, they must be investigated partly through knowledge of languages and partly through knowledge of things. For something contributes to likeness, and undoubtedly suggests a certain secret meaning, in the pool of Siloam, where the man whose eyes the Lord had anointed with mud made from spittle was ordered to wash his face. Yet, unless the Evangelist had interpreted the name of that unknown language, so great a meaning would lie concealed. Likewise, many things that have not been [Col. 1546D] interpreted by the authors of those books—the Hebrew names—must undoubtedly possess no small force and assistance for solving the riddles of Scripture, if someone is able to interpret them. Certain men skilled in that language have conferred no small benefit upon posterity by interpreting separately all such words from Scripture: what Adam means, what Eve means, what Abraham means, what Moses means, and likewise the names of places—what Jerusalem means, or Sion, or Jericho, or Sinai, or Lebanon, or Jordan, or whatever other names in that language are unknown to us. Once these have been disclosed and interpreted, many figurative expressions in Scripture are brought to light.”

To this outstanding testimony of Augustine I thought nothing should be added except the words of the same most holy Doctor found in the same work, chapter 39, section 59:

> “Just as certain men have done with all the Hebrew, Syrian, and Egyptian words and names, or with [Col. 1547A] those of any other language that may be found in the Holy Scriptures and that have been set down in them without interpretation, so that they might interpret them separately; and as Eusebius did with the history of the ages, on account of questions concerning the divine books that require its use: so, then, what these men did concerning these matters, so that a Christian need not labor over many things because of a few, I see could likewise be done, and so forth.”

Thus, according to Augustine, the interpreters of Hebrew Names conferred no small benefit upon posterity; their disclosed etymologies greatly assist in solving the riddles and translated signs of Scripture. That book of Hebrew Names offered such great assistance, especially to the ecclesiastical writers of earlier times, that without it they would have had nothing to say in the exposition of Sacred Scripture. This happened long ago to the interpreter writing on Isaiah, whom Saint Jerome recalls in Book IV of his *Commentary* on chapter 10 of that Prophet:

> “This is according to the letter. But someone, unable to find in this passage [Col. 1547B] the etymologies of the false names according to the Septuagint, and admitting that he could not find them in the book of Hebrew Names, sends us into uncertainty by saying that, at the end of the world and at the consummation of this age, when punishments are imminent, the great prince of the Assyrians will flee, and will wish to escape from the wrath of God through various places and by different journeys, and so forth. He says this because, compelled by the truth of the matter, he had nothing else to say.”

Yet although the authority of so many ancient men would not by itself suffice to prove the usefulness of the book of Hebrew Names, the hallucinations of the greatest intellects of our own age and the errors of celebrated writers clearly demonstrate that this volume ought to have been despised neither by learned men nor rejected by anyone else. For things sometimes considered contemptible and more superfluous can, in their own time, provide the greatest usefulness. I have decided to establish this by two examples [Col. 1547C], and indeed by two especially prominent examples in this field of learning, so that all students may at last be thoroughly persuaded that the book of Hebrew Names must be constantly consulted, especially by those who possess either no knowledge or only slight knowledge of that language.

Our French translator of Josephus the Jewish historian, unanimously acknowledged as most learned, is nevertheless found to be mistaken in the etymology of the name *Esau* because he did not know the character of the Hebrew language. For he rendered the Greek words of the Jewish writer in Book I of the *Jewish Antiquities*, chapter 17 or 18, into French as follows:

> “Rebecca was pregnant with two sons. The elder was completely covered with hair, and the younger held his heel when he came into the world. The elder was named Esau because of the hair he had brought with him at birth, and Isaac had a particular affection for him. The younger was named Jacob, and Rebecca loved him much more than his elder brother.”

In the index he likewise says of Esau:

> “Esau, [Col. 1547D] that is, hairy, and surnamed Edom, son of Isaac.”

If these words are compared with the Greek Josephus, one will find that the translator omitted several words, by which it is not Esau but Seir who is called hairy. For in the Greek text we read as follows:

> Ἠγάπα δὲ ὁ πατὴρ τὸν πρεσβύτερον, Ἠσαῦ λεγόμενον κατ’ ἐπωνυμίαν τῆς τριχώσεως. Ἑβραῖοι γὰρ τὸ σήειρον τρίχωμα λέγουσιν.

> “The father loved the elder, called Esau, a surname derived from his hairiness; for the Hebrews call hair *Seir*.”

Thus Isaac’s elder son was not called Esau because of the hairs with which he appeared completely shaggy at birth. Rather, Esau himself received the surname *Seir* because of his τρίχωμα—that is, because of the covering of hair, or hairy covering, of his body.

[Note: And indeed learned men maintain that in Josephus *Seir* should be substituted for *Esau*, or that the text should be read continuously, Ἤσαυον τὸν καὶ Σήειρον λεγόμενον: “Esau, who was also called Seir.”]

I nevertheless admit that Josephus’s Greek expression, Ἠσαῦ λεγόμενον κατ’ ἐπωνυμίαν τῆς τριχώσεως, can scarcely [Col. 1548A] be expressed in any other sense than that in which our learned translator rendered it into French, especially since the very words of the sacred text, Genesis 25:25—“The first came out red, and entirely hairy like a skin, and his name was called Esau”—seem to favor this interpretation to a considerable degree.

But when the order of the reading and the context of Jerome’s version are considered somewhat more carefully, it readily becomes clear that Isaac’s elder son was not called Esau because of his hair. [Col. 1548B] Rather, the younger was called Jacob because, at his birth, he had held his brother’s heel in his hand:

> “The first came out red, and entirely hairy like a skin, and his name was called Esau. Immediately the other came out, holding his brother’s heel in his hand; and for this reason he called him Jacob.”

Who has ever sufficiently admired Jerome’s diligence and acumen of interpretation in this passage of Genesis? Of Esau he said, “His name was called Esau,” and did not add, “for this reason he was called so,” because, as a man thoroughly skilled in the Hebrew language, he knew that the name *Esau* means “deed” or “making,” not “hairy” or “covered with hair,” as the French translator supposed after being misled by Josephus’s obscure words.

Speaking of Jacob, Jerome deliberately expressed the reason for the name: “For this reason he called him Jacob.” For he was called *supplanter*, that is, *Jacob*, because, as he came out of his mother’s womb, he held his brother’s heel.

These matters are perfectly clear to the reader of the book of Hebrew Names and of Jerome’s Book VIII of the *Commentaries on Ezekiel*, chapter 25, where we read:

> “That Esau, Seir, Edom, Idumaea, and Duma are all called one nation will not be doubted by anyone who possesses knowledge of the Scriptures. To say nothing of the other Prophets—Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Amos—who prophesied against Idumaea, Duma, and Edom, the Prophet Obadiah directs his entire prophecy against this nation; we discussed him long ago as best we could. Seir, therefore, is accused: because he was hairy, he received the name ‘hairy.’ Edom means ‘bloody,’ because he lost his birthright through the cooking of red lentils and received his name from [Col. 1548C] that food. Esau likewise signifies ‘deeds.’ And this must be known: in Hebrew, Idumaea is never written, but always Edom, which the Greek translation rendered as Idumaea.”

From these words it is evident that *Seir* means “hairy,” while *Esau* is interpreted as “deeds,” or, in the singular, “making”—ποίησις, as Jerome teaches more frequently elsewhere.

To leave nothing lacking for the curious reader, who wishes to understand the reason for the name Esau, it should also be observed that this name was used to indicate something entirely new. It was indeed something new for an infant to emerge from its mother’s womb hairy and entirely shaggy, like a skin covered with hair. Such a condition does not belong to human beings in infancy, but to those of robust and mature age. Thus Esau, when he was born, was *neesa*, that is, “made” and “perfected” with hair, like a child of many years; and for this reason he was called Esau. This is comparable to our saying of an adolescent, because of the maturity of his judgment, “He is a fully formed man” (*C’est un homme fait*).

Accordingly, according to the character of the Hebrew language, [Col. 1548D] Esau means “made,” or “making”; Seir means “hairy” and “shaggy”; and Edom means “red,” or “bloody,” on account of the red color of the lentils.

The following example will also show how great a stumbling-block the learned Henri Valois encountered because he did not know Hebrew. It is taken from his annotations on Book II of Eusebius Pamphilus’s *Ecclesiastical History*. Eusebius had written in chapter 23 of the book just mentioned:

> Καὶ πολλῶν πληροφορηθέντων, καὶ δοξαζόντων ἐπὶ τῇ μαρτυρίᾳ τοῦ Ἰακώβου, καὶ λεγόντων Ὡσαννὰ τῷ υἱῷ Δαβίδ.

> “And when many were confirmed by this testimony of James and glorified Jesus, saying, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David,’” and so forth.

But a Greek copyist ignorant of the Hebrew language split the name Ὡσαννὰ into two words, ὡς ἀννὰ τῷ, and thereby provided the occasion for so great an error. [Col. 1549A] Valois published the corrupt form of Eusebius’s text produced by this ignorant division and attempted to explain and confirm the copyist’s error in his notes on page 40 of his annotations on Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*:

> ὡς ἀννά. “In all our copies there are two words, ὡς ἀννά. So too in Jerome’s interpretation of the Hebrew Names: ‘Hosanna, save us,’ we say in Greek, ὡς ἀννά. Both names, however, must be read with the letter lengthened. That is, Hosanna lengthens its first syllable in both Hebrew and Greek. Isidore likewise testifies in Book VI of the *Etymologies* that Hosanna is composed of the two words Osi and Anna, with one letter elided, as happens when we scan verses. For Osi means ‘save us’; Anna is an interjection expressing a movement of the mind in a supplicating disposition. These words of Isidore are taken from Jerome’s Letter 145 to Damasus.”

This passage proves beyond contradiction that the errors of writers were multiplied by badly edited [Col. 1549B] editions of Jerome’s works. Valois had found the name Hosanna written in all the Greek copies of Eusebius with the division ὡς ἀννά. Since he saw that it had been divided into two words contrary to usage, he reasonably thought it necessary to take refuge in the book of Hebrew Names as though in a Lydian stone. But, in place of a Lydian stone, the old editions of Jerome set up a cliff against which this otherwise learned man did not know how to direct his observations.

Above, in our notes, column 92, we exposed the extremely corrupt reading of the book of Names in the editions of Erasmus and Mariano. There it is most clearly established, with the unanimous testimony of all manuscript copies, that Jerome wrote as follows:

> “Hosanna: ‘save us,’ which in Greek is σῶσον δή. Both names, however, must be read with the letter *o* lengthened.”

[Col. 1549C]

It is therefore false and ridiculous to read, “which in Greek is ὡς ἀννά,” since the Hebrew *Hosanna* is rendered in Greek as σῶσον δή.

Finally, the statement that both names must be read with the letter lengthened should not be understood, as the hallucinating Valois understood it, of Hosanna in both the Hebrew and Greek languages. Jerome’s words must instead be taken to mean that the name *Obed*, and the following name *Hosanna*, are to be read with the letter *o* lengthened.

Let the prudent and studious reader now consider how much usefulness is provided by the book of Hebrew Names, restored by us according to its original integrity and fidelity. Through it, not only the numerous errors of printed Latin books but also those of Greek manuscripts can certainly be corrected.

Regarding Hosanna as written among the Greeks, I add that in the Greek Fragments and in the Origenian Lexicon, Ὡσαννὰ is found everywhere without any division of syllables, and is always rendered there as σῶσον δή or δόξα. These observations completely remove and correct the ignorance of both Latins and Greeks.

Nevertheless, it should not be denied that among the ignorant the name Hosanna was formerly written and separated into two words. [Col. 1549D] Jerome makes this sufficiently clear in his commentary on Matthew 21:

> “Let no one, then, suppose that it is composed of two words, one Greek and one Hebrew, but that it is wholly Hebrew,” and so forth.

It was perhaps thought that ὡς was Greek and ἀννά Hebrew. The holy Doctor refutes this opinion here, warning that the name is entirely Hebrew.

I could easily demonstrate that many other errors were propagated among interpreters and modern writers through ignorance of, or faulty editions of, the book of Hebrew Names. But I believe that the examples already given, because they are more prominent and familiar, are sufficient in place of six hundred others.

Nor may I pass over in silence what the Latin translator published concerning Hosanna from the Greek *Catena* on John, at the end of chapter 8. He presented a ridiculous statement when he translated the following Greek words:

> Ἰωβὴλ γάρ ἐστιν Ὡσαννεὶ διπλασιαζόμενος, ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ Θεός. Ἰωὰ γὰρ καὶ Ἐλὰ, παρ’ Ἑβραίοις ὁ Θεὸς ὀνομάζεται.

That is, if we believe the translator:

> “Jubit [Col. 1550A] is Hosanna doubled, that is, ‘God, God’; for Jehovah and El are called God among the Hebrews.”

Anyone who has even been lightly touched by knowledge of Hebrew can easily understand how absurd and foreign to the Greek context this Latin translation is. How could doubled Hosanna be found in the word Ἰωβὴλ, and a double God—that is, the word “God” twice—in Hosanna? Neither the sharpest of rabbis nor the most stubborn of Hebraists will permit himself to explain this. Even fools can see that such an interpretation is false and utterly tasteless.

The Greek writer’s meaning, therefore, is absolutely certain: in the word Ἰωβὴλ, *Jobel*, there are found two names of God—namely Ἰώ and Ἤλ, or Ἰωὰ and Ἠλό, both of which mean “God” among the Hebrews.

Moreover, Ἰωβὴλ is a form of Ὡσαννεὶ, that is, of praise and confession, as the Greek words Ἰωβὴλ γάρ ἐστιν Ὡσαννεὶ—“Jobel is Hosanna”—plainly declare. In the Colbert manuscript, Hosanna is called glory and praise, δόξα, because [Col. 1550B] that name was once acclaim­ed as an honor to bishops and priests who were arriving.

Hence Jerome says in Book III of his *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 21:

> “Although the priests do not dare to lay hands upon him, they nevertheless bring accusations against his works; and they turn into an accusation the testimony of the people and of the children who cried, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David,’ claiming that this is said only to the Son of God. Let bishops, therefore, and however holy men may be, consider with what danger they allow such things to be said to themselves. If it is charged as a crime against the Lord, to whom it was truly said—for the faith of those who believed was not yet firm—”

We learn the same Christian custom from the *Jerusalem Itinerary* of Antoninus the Monk, page 30:

> “There,” he says, “women came to meet them with children, holding palm branches in their hands and vessels containing rose oil. Having fallen at our feet, they anointed the soles of our feet, and they sang in the Egyptian language, chanting an antiphon: ‘Blessed are you by the Lord, and blessed is your coming: Hosanna in the highest.’”

[Col. 1550C]

Here, then, you have the basis for the etymology of the word Hosanna, which appears in second place in the Colbert Greek exemplar of the book of Hebrew Names, where Ὡσαννὰ is interpreted as δόξα—not according to the character of the Hebrew language or the testimony of its letters, but according to a usage adopted among ancient Christians, who went out to meet holy men and bishops, the teachers and vicars of Christ, to whom the words “Hosanna in the highest” were acclaimed.

The book of Hebrew Names can also offer great usefulness to students in settling disputes among critics and interpreters concerning certain Scriptural words. These words, interpreted differently by different people, greatly inflame the minds of disputants, when they ought instead to have been restrained among Christian writers, who profess to seek truth through disputation, not disputation through truth, as lovers of what is right and true.

What controversy has there not been among [Col. 1550D] modern interpreters and critics over the words of Matthew, “whose winnowing shovel is in his hand”? Certain critics refuse to accept those copies containing the old Latin Vulgate of Matthew that read, in accordance with the present Vulgate, “whose winnowing shovel is in his hand,” because Cyprian read from that most ancient edition of the Gospel according to Matthew, “holding a shovel openly in his hand.”

Others may be seen who by no means accept the same words of the Evangelist translated into French as *Il a le van en la main*—“He has the winnowing fan in his hand.” For, if they are to be believed, the winnowing fan was grasped and moved by the ancients not with one hand only, but with both. Many emphatically deny this and decree, both orally and in written books of observations, that it must be marked with a critical stroke.

Amid such disagreements and conflicting opinions among learned men, if the book of Hebrew Names is placed between them as mediator, it will clearly show that among the ancients the shovel and the winnowing fan were commonly regarded as the same instrument. It will likewise show that “holding a shovel openly in his hand” in the Gospel is entirely the same as “whose winnowing fan is in his hand.”

[Col. 1551A]

If we grant that the shovel was called a winnowing fan, then our vernacular translation, *Il a le van en la main*, is excellent, because farmers hold a shovel with one hand when they are preparing to clean wheat on the threshing floor.

For, just as methods of threshing grain differ in different regions of the kingdom, so there is no doubt that farmers winnow threshed grain in different ways. In Occitania, winnowers use a sieve suspended in the middle of the threshing floor; this winnowing fan can be moved with one hand, or with both if desired.

Among our Basque countrymen, however, I have always seen grain winnowed with a wooden shovel. With it they lift the grain mixed with chaff and straw high into the air with all their strength and throw it far from themselves; when the wind passes through it, the chaff is separated and the clean, purified grains fall to the ground.

Nor have I mentioned the winnowing fan merely in passing, but briefly in commendation of the book of Hebrew Names, in which we read, [Col. 1551B] column 69:

> “Nabuzardan: he prophesied shovels, which are commonly called winnowing fans.”

Thus the present passage of Jerome has taught us most clearly that the ancients frequently possessed shovels, commonly called winnowing fans, for winnowing grain. It is well suited to settling the disputes of learned men and avoiding the errors of critics.

[Col. 1552A]

Besides the many uses of the book of Names already mentioned, it has another especially important one: it illuminates obscure expressions in the Sacred Scriptures and clearly reveals the allegorical meaning of the three writers whom it recognizes as its parents.

Many things remain closed and shrouded in darkness in the sacred books and in the commentaries of Philo, Origen, and Jerome unless the book of Hebrew Names holds before the reader a light and torch for understanding. But since it would be lengthy to list all the arguments and individual examples by which this particular usefulness might be established, and since explaining it would almost be the work of an entire volume, let it suffice to have indicated beforehand to prudent readers what it is especially useful for, and, as it were, to have painted the position of the lands upon a small tablet, showing within a narrow outline the vastness and extent of the whole world and the circuit of the ocean. Nor is it necessary [Col. 1552B] to admonish the reader repeatedly about this or to distrust his prudence and diligence.

[Col. 1551]

## Names of the Prophets and Etymologies of the Names

### Jerome

[Col. 1551C]

Hosea is interpreted as σώζων, “saving,” which we may render “one who saves.”

Joel: ἀρχόμενος, “beginning,” or “one who begins.”

Amos: βαστάζων, “bearing,” which among the Latins is called “carrying.”

Obadiah, that is, Obedia: δοῦλος Κυρίου, “servant of the Lord.”

Jonah: περιστερά, “dove.”

Micah: τίς ὡς, a name composed of two parts of speech, which among us sounds like “who is as,” or “who is like?”

Nahum: παράκλησις, “consolation.”

Habakkuk: περιλαμβάνων, “embracing,” or “wrestling.”

Zephaniah: κεκρυμμένος Κυρίου, “the Lord’s hidden one,” or “the secret one of the Lord.”

Haggai: ἑορτάζων, “celebrating a festival,” which we may call “festive” or “solemn.”

Zechariah: μνήμη Κυρίου, “memory of the Lord.”

Malachi: ἄγγελός μου, “my messenger.”

Isaiah: σωτηρία Κυρίου, “salvation of the Lord.”

Ezekiel: κράτος Κυρίου, “the strength” or “rule of the Lord.”

Jeremiah: ὑψηλὸς Κυρίου, “exalted of the Lord.”

[Col. 1551D]

Daniel: ἔκρινε με Κύριος, “the Lord judged me.”

### The Greeks

[Col. 1552C]

Hosea: σκιάζων, ἢ φύλαξ, “overshadowing,” or “guardian.”

Joel: ἀγαπητοῦ Θεοῦ, “of the beloved God.”

Amos: κάρτερος, ἢ πιστός, ἢ λαὸν ἀποσπῶν, “strong,” or “faithful,” or “one who draws away the people.”

Obadiah: δουλεύων Κυρίῳ, “serving the Lord.”

Jonah: περιστερά, “dove.”

Micah: τίς οὗτος βασιλεύς, “who is this king?”

Nahum: παράκλησις, “consolation.”

Habakkuk: πατὴρ ἐγείρων, “a father who raises up.”

Zephaniah: συνιέντα αὐτόν, “understanding him.”

Haggai: ἑορτάζοντος, “of one celebrating a festival.”

Zechariah: νικητὴς λέων, “a victorious lion.”

Malachi: ἄγγελος, ἢ σωτηρία Κυρίου, “angel,” or “salvation of the Lord.”

Isaiah: σωτήριον Κυρίου, “salvation of the Lord.”

Ezekiel: κράτος Θεοῦ, “the strength of God.”

Jeremiah: ὑψούμενος Κυρίου, “exalted of the Lord.”

Daniel: κρίσις αὐτοῦ ἰσχυρά, “his strong judgment.”

I have decided to bring the book of Hebrew Names to a conclusion with this contest and comparison between Jerome and the Greek writers, because from this opposition the supreme knowledge of the Hebrew language shines forth in Jerome, whereas there is little or none in the Greek authors of the etymologies of Hebrew names.

From this it is clear that all the strained etymologies found either in the book of Names or elsewhere in Jerome have Greek authors as their source. For wherever Jerome interprets Hebrew words according to his own judgment and by his own initiative, even the sharpest master among the Hebraists will find nothing to add to his diligence and perfect learning.

I wished to attest to this from the preface of the holy Doctor to his *Commentary on the Prophet Joel*. I copied the words of that preface as they are found in the oldest manuscript copies, for in the books previously printed nearly all the Hebrew and Greek names, apart from a few, have been corrupted.

I warned learned men of this corruption and continual degradation in our *Prodrome of Saint Jerome*. Although I know that the sincerity of my warning displeased certain petty scholars and rivals of mine, who eagerly tried to deter me from my position through numerous insults, I now pay no attention to their ignorant peevishness. Against its wishes, I decided to write a letter to the very learned Urban Chevreau, so that I might inform him of the astonishing corruption of Jerome’s old editions and demonstrate it by the notable example of the word ψυλλέα, for which they thrust upon us the most absurd ψηφιστήν in the preface of Jerome just mentioned.

[Col. 1553]

## Glosses on Certain Scriptural Passages and Interpretations of Names in the Language of the Britons

From the most ancient Colbert manuscript, no. 4951.

[Col. 1553A]

### Genesis

*Furfum*: *dun*, or *rot*; read *sursum* instead of *furfum*.

A deer is said to be “released” when it follows a doe. A horse is said to be “released” when it follows mares.

### Exodus

*Fiscellam*: a basket, *thenil*.

“You are the bridegroom of blood to me”: that is, a boy born from my blood who has been circumcised.

“Let it not make a sound”: *grennat, gillit*; because the destroyer does not harm it.

“Hoarfrost”: *brimus*.

“The price of chastity”: that is, the twelve shillings which the man who gave her to a husband must give to the girl.

“Sending hornets”: that is, *urnite*; he said this because of terror, or because of evil angels.

“Rams’ skins”: that is, without wool, like *partica*, that is, *roth loschi*.

“Hyacinth skins”: that is, without wool, or “for covering”; it is not found in Britain.

“Pins” or “brooches”: *hringan*.

“Neck-opening,” that which is around the neck: *fithalsetha*.

“Armlets”: *armbo gusbregida*, before the sleeves, and there the nails or studs are joined.

[Col. 1553B]

“Kidneys”: *levint legum*.

“Small loins”: *lenbradun*.

“Chrogillius”: a spiny animal larger than a hedgehog.

“Garula”: *rouca*.

“Newly married woman”: *nectret*.

“Larum”: *meu*.

“Bononem”: *uuof*.

“Diver”: it is called “black” from diving, that is, *dop fugul*.

“Herodian”: *uua luc*; this *fuch brucus* is similar to a locust but larger.

“Bird-catching”: that is, *fugolada*.

“Shoulder blades”: they resemble a sword; hence they are called *spadulae*.

“They pass beneath the shepherd’s staff”: that is, “his *rabbacula* ran out.”

### Numbers

[Col. 1553C]

“Signs”: that is, “place its proper sign,” namely *eribethoon*.

“Bailer”: that is, *serscufla*, resembling vessels from which water is thrown out of ships.

“Bdellium”: a plant of white color.

“Of full age”: that is, thirty years old.

“Porfilio”: *philfor*.

“Night-owl”: *nactrafan*.

### Joshua

“Arched wound”: that is, a curved wound, because the scorpion’s tail is curved, and with it the scorpion does harm.

“Postliminy”: that is, after the father’s death.

“Golden rule”: *ringam gurdiles*.

“City of letters”: because learned men are kept there.

### The Book of Judges

“Testimony,” or because they made *tistas* there.

*Uaum.*

“In the tavern”: that is, *negali sernin*.

“Whistlers”: the flatteries of kings.

“Litio”: that is, *eblit*.

“She gathered meal”: that is, *congregatio formal*.

[Col. 1554A]

“Circle of days”: that is, a year.

“Son of one year”: because of humility.

“On the day after tomorrow”: after tomorrow.

“Commentator”: one who wrote annual commentaries.

“Tipsinas”: they make them from barley; they remove the husks from the grains in a mortar—that is, in hollowed wood—and then cook them in whatever they wish.

“Pilenticius”: “it maddens minds.”

[Col. 1555]

## Explanation of the Book Concerning the Situation and Names of the Places of the Hebrews
### Explanation of the Book *On the Places and Names of the Hebrews*

[Col. 1555A] The first author of the books *On the Places of the Hebrews* was Eusebius, surnamed Pamphilus. In this little work he gathered the names of almost all the cities, mountains, rivers, villages, and various places mentioned in Holy Scripture, indicating which names had remained the same, which had afterward been altered, and which had been corrupted in some respect.

When someone scarcely initiated into letters had dared to render this book of Eusebius into Latin—but not in Latin fashion—he gave Jerome the occasion and reason to prepare a new and more learned Latin translation. Following, therefore, the scholarly undertaking of Eusebius himself, Jerome translated the volume into Latin according to the alphabetical order found in the Greek, leaving out what did not seem worthy of remembrance and altering a great many things. For in the *Book of Chronicles* also he once declared in his preface that he was either an interpreter or the author of a new work.

Thus he presented the Eusebian little work to speakers of his own language according to the alphabetical order found in the Greek, although he followed the sequence of the Latin alphabet, not the Greek one. Indeed, when writing in Latin, or converting Greek exemplars into Latin speech, he could not, with sound judgment, distort the order of our alphabet so as to place names beginning with γ, *g*, among the third letter in his Latin edition; nor could he in the same way preserve the Greek order for κ, χ, η, and ω, and similar letters, which are pronounced with aspiration or as lengthened vowels.

Therefore, so that the prudent reader may not be led into error by an obscure understanding of Jerome’s words, he should know that the holy Doctor observed the Greek alphabetical order only in this respect: he first listed the names and place-names occurring in Eusebius from Genesis, then those from Exodus, and so on, preserving the order of the sacred books.

Secondly, he imitates the Eusebian order within the individual letters. For example, following Eusebius, he begins under A with Ararat, Achad, Agai, and so forth; under B likewise with Babel, Bethel, Bala, and so forth. These names occupy a different order in the alphabetical sequence of lexicons and also in the book of Hebrew Names once compiled by our Bede, though published in volume III with his other works.

I therefore find the Greek Eusebius and the Latin Jerome in agreement, insofar as the order of our alphabet permits—an order that differs in many respects from the Greek, both because of aspirated consonants and because of lengthened vowels, which in Greek are arranged with considerable space between them; for example, κ is separated from χ, ε from η, and ο from ω, whereas among the Latins they are read under the same letter. For the vowels *e* and *o*, whether long or short, retain the same form and are written in one place.

These are the principal matters concerning the ancient writers of the book *On the Places* that we wished to set before the learned reader. Since he might perhaps let escape him what was recently written on the same subject in the Preface of Jacobus Bonfrerius to his *Onomasticon*, I thought it very useful to insert here much material excerpted from it.

“Now this book,” says Bonfrerius, “was first written in Greek by Eusebius of Caesarea, as Jerome himself testifies in the Preface to this book. Jerome thought that it ought to be translated by him into Latin for the benefit of those who take pleasure in the study of Sacred Scripture. He translated it in such a way, however, that he added not a little of his own, altered some things, and corrected certain statements that had been wrongly made, as he himself admits in the Preface, or as can be gathered from the course of the book. As a man of exceptionally keen judgment, a spectator of those regions and places, indeed one who had spent many years among them, he deserves great confidence. Nevertheless, Jerome generally professes to be performing the office of an interpreter.

“Perhaps at first Jerome had written his own additions in different characters, or had marked them with an asterisk; afterward, as often happens in works of this kind, they became fused into a single body with the words of Eusebius. Eusebius himself had indeed spent a long time in Palestine, being bishop of Caesarea in Palestine; yet many arguments persuade us that Eusebius had not acquired the same knowledge of the cities and places that Jerome possessed.

“Nevertheless, it must be admitted that several things may be missing from this book which Jerome either could not complete because he was occupied with other duties, or which he certainly did not wish to complete. Therefore we too, recently applying our hand to this work, have endeavored to contribute some small labor in this matter. Thus this book, which otherwise seemed rather confused and, because of the disorderly arrangement of the proper names, was destined to be useless to many—since the difficulty of seeking out and finding the places they wished to investigate would have turned them away from using and reading it—might be useful to all students of Sacred Scripture and sacred topography.

“I shall briefly indicate what we have accomplished in this matter. First, although the individual names in Eusebius and Jerome have been assigned to their respective initial letters, as they say—that is, all names beginning with A have been gathered together—nevertheless, since even within these groups they had been placed without order, causing those who wished to locate the places mentioned a tedious expenditure of both labor and time, we have arranged everything in such order that anyone may immediately come upon the very entry he is investigating without difficulty.”

After this and much else—not relevant to our purpose—had been set forth by the learned Bonfrerius, he finally thought that the reader ought to be informed about the Greek Eusebius in the Royal manuscript as follows:

“Until this point,” he says, “I had been dealing with Jerome alone, since I had no hope of obtaining Eusebius of the Hebrew Places in Greek. But behold, quite unexpectedly, when I had gone to Paris, a Greek manuscript of Eusebius from the Royal Parisian Library fell into my hands. Having obtained it for extraction, I formed new plans; and with Eusebius there came new cares and new labors.

“It therefore pleased me to join this Greek work—or Jerome’s Latin rendering of it—to my own annotations, so that the kindly reader would lack nothing from our labor. The chief advantage will be that it will not be difficult to distinguish what belongs to Jerome from what belongs to Eusebius, and to see what Jerome added to, removed from, corrected, or altered in Eusebius’s labors.

“Jerome did indeed add certain things not only to Eusebius’s account but also some proper place-names that are not found in Eusebius. Yet there may also be some suspicion that some of these had dropped out of Eusebius. Conversely, a few proper place-names are found in Eusebius that Jerome did not express; these may be considered to have been suppressed or overlooked by Jerome.

“Some brief remarks must be added here about this manuscript Eusebius, of which the reader ought to be forewarned. First and foremost, this manuscript Eusebius is riddled with very many errors, especially in the rendering of proper place-names. These are often expressed so corruptly that one can scarcely discern their relationship to the words found in Jerome. Nevertheless, I preferred generally to leave them with the corruption in which I found them, lest I seem to be handing down to you not so much Eusebius as my own conjectures and inventions. Nor will this be burdensome or inconvenient for the reader, since from what is found in Jerome, or from my additions, it will almost always be possible to determine clearly how those words ought to be corrected. …

“As for the remaining errors, whenever the sense, the truth of the statement, or the syntax required it, Eusebius had to be assisted and some remedy supplied: now a letter or word was added, removed, or altered. Obvious errors could not be left standing, especially when Jerome suggested the correction. Yet at times we preferred to handle the matter by a marginal annotation.

“To this I add that sometimes Eusebius gives proper place-names in a more genuine and uncorrupted form than Jerome, and that Jerome can occasionally be corrected from Eusebius. When this occurs, it will not be difficult to gather it from what we report concerning errors in Jerome’s names. I must also point out that some place-names appear in Eusebius that are absent from Jerome; but these are very few. Likewise, certain proper place-names were suppressed in Eusebius and had to be restored from Jerome.”

Thus far Bonfrerius.

I transcribed the greater part of this Preface in our Admonition, in order to show my gratitude toward the distinguished Bonfrerius; for the observations of that learned man anticipated the labor and the portion that I had undertaken. Nevertheless, for a fuller understanding both of the Greek Eusebius and of Jerome, his interpreter, and also for a complete knowledge of what we have treated in particular, certain additions to Bonfrerius’s warnings, proper to our undertaking, were necessary.

First, then, I warn the reader that I am an editor of Jerome, not of Eusebius. For that reason I had to adapt and accommodate Eusebius to Jerome, not Jerome to Eusebius. This will be demonstrated throughout the book *On the Places*. Jerome arranged the names of places according to the alphabetical order in such a way that he adapted to the Latin alphabet the order that Eusebius had adapted to the Greek; therefore we too, following Jerome’s footsteps, bring the order of the Greek letters back to the Latin order.

Thus names that have Greek X as their initial letter we have assigned, with Jerome, to Latin C; those beginning with Φ have been assigned to F. Names beginning with II—that is, with aspiration or a breathing—have been placed among those whose initial is A or E. Finally, we have endeavored to assign certain words, treated by Jerome as common nouns and translated or expressed in Latin, to their respective initial letters. Such are “Field of the fuller,” “Well of the oath” or “of the vision,” “graves of lust,” and so forth. In the Greek alphabet these have initial letters very different from the Latin ones.

Necessity compelled us to follow this order and method, since we were wholly intent upon Jerome, lest anything from his works be published by us that was not truly Hieronymian, whether in the words or in their order.

But, while providing for the usefulness of another class of readers and wishing to indicate to students who do not know Greek what was added by Jerome to the Greek Eusebius, we enclosed these additions in the Latin text in brackets, in this fashion:

“Furthermore, the Hebrews say that this is the city of Mesopotamia now called Nisibis, once besieged and captured by Lucullus, the Roman consul, and a few years ago handed over to the Persians by the emperor Jovian.”

These signs therefore indicate that the entire passage and historical observation were joined by Jerome to the entry “Achad.” Eusebius wrote nothing more about it than what follows: “Achad, a city of the kingdom of Nimrod in Babylonia.” Where Jerome’s additions are not enclosed in brackets, they can easily be recognized from the absence of the Greek text in the other column; or at any rate they will become perfectly clear in our scholia, in which we have undertaken to illuminate very many passages.

For the rest, the kindly reader must be warned not to expect from our diligence anything in the edition of the book *On the Places* that editors of Jerome could not rightly, deservedly, or fairly be expected to provide. We shall not attempt to alter the ancient topography of the Holy Land by a new system. Rather, with the greatest fidelity we can muster, we shall strive to restore Jerome’s works to their original and primitive integrity and to illustrate them with notes according to our ability.

Whoever seeks anything beyond this in our edition should recognize that his hope will be disappointed, since it demands greater and unwarranted efforts than the work and province we have undertaken appeared to require. These, then, are the matters about which the learned reader most needed to be forewarned. He will also find many other things in our brief annotations concerning the correction of the Greek Eusebius, both manuscript and printed. For Bonfrerius omitted many matters that are curious and worthy of knowledge, and many others were corrupted in his edition through the ignorance of printers. All these matters can be seen marked, restored, and supplied in their proper places.

[Col. 1557]

## More Extensive Notes on the Book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis

[Col. 1557D] In addition to our brief annotations, which we placed at the bottom margin of the pages in the preceding book, I am compelled by necessity to conclude here, in a longer discussion, several difficult matters that have already been touched upon briefly. Nor do I have much hope that the brevity of my observations will please certain critical writers—unless they should propose for renewed examination and illustration the many passages that they themselves attack in Jerome.

Let us therefore examine not those things in Jerome that abound in every commendation, but only those that recent critics wish to attribute to error or ignorance.

### I

The first insufficiently approved passage in the book *Hebrew Questions* is taken from this observation of Jerome on Genesis 1:2:

“In place of what is written in our manuscripts, ‘was borne along,’ the Hebrew has *merepheth*, which we may render ‘was brooding’ or ‘was fostering,’ after the likeness of a bird animating its eggs with warmth, and so forth.”

“Modern critics,” they say, “more correctly translate the Hebrew *merahhepheth* into Latin as ‘was borne along’ than as ‘was brooding,’ because the verb ‘was brooding’ comes closer to the speech of the Syrians than to the Hebrew idiom.”

But the judgment of the most ancient Fathers and of the most learned men concerning the interpretation of the Hebrew word and the relationship of the Syriac language to Hebrew was very different. On the basis of that relationship, the holy Fathers approve “was brooding” or “was fostering” as the closer and more genuine exposition, rather than “was borne along.”

On this matter Basil the Great must be heard, *Homily 2 on the Hexaemeron*:

“But in what manner,” he says, “will you say that here this Spirit was borne over the waters? I shall report to you not my own opinion but that of a certain Syrian man, who was as far removed from worldly wisdom as he was near to knowledge of true things.

“That Syrian said that the word used among the Syrians was more significant and clearer, and that because of its affinity with the Hebrew language it touched the meaning of the Scriptures somewhat more closely. Thus he said that the sense of this statement was as follows: they take and interpret the word ‘was borne along’ as ‘was fostering,’ and as supplying the waters with vital fecundity, after the likeness of a little bird that broods and impresses a certain vital force upon the things warmed by it.

“He declared that such a sense was signified by that word in the statement ‘over the waters’: namely, that the Spirit of God was borne over them, that is, that the Spirit himself prepared the nature of the waters for vital fecundity. Through this, therefore, what some inquire about is sufficiently demonstrated: that the Holy Spirit was not absent from the act of creation.”

St. Ambrose says the same in *On the Hexaemeron*, book I, chapter 8; Augustine likewise in book I of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 18.

This most clearly confirms Jerome’s annotation, in which he teaches the reader that in the Hebrew, instead of “was borne along,” one reads “was brooding” or “was fostering.” Because the Syriac speech is closer to Hebrew and consequently better suited to expressing Hebrew words, it retains *merahhpho*, that is, “was brooding” or “was fostering.” That interpretation therefore undoubtedly comes closer to the Hebrew source than the version of the Seventy Translators, “was borne along.”

Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that in the Latin Vulgate and in Jerome’s translation we find the verb “was borne along” written. Jerome deliberately retained it, so that he would not appear to draw an ambiguous word, understood differently by different people, toward only one meaning; and so that he might establish as the interpretation to be accepted his own understanding of what many take to refer to the wind—that is, the spirit of this world—as referring instead solely to the Holy Spirit as the creator of all things.

Moreover, the holy Doctor admitted in more than one passage that he wished to adapt his translation to the custom of the ancient interpreters where there was no harm to the meaning:

“Therefore,” he says, “we did not wish to alter what was read by the Ancients, because the meaning was the same.”

And shortly afterward:

“But here too there is no change of meaning; and, following the ancient interpretation, we did not wish to alter what caused no harm.”

In accordance with his customary practice, therefore, he did not wish to alter the word “was borne along,” because there was no harm in retaining what had been read by the Ancients. In this verse of Genesis, “was borne along” can be understood indifferently both of the wind and of the Holy Spirit.

### II

A second and more prominent passage is brought forward against Jerome, because in it he seemed to certain critical writers to be an advocate of Jewish fables.

Jerome observes, therefore, at Genesis 2:8, that the Hebrew has *mecedem*, that is, “from the beginning,” and he teaches that this meaning should be preferred to the version of the Seventy Translators, who rendered it “toward the east.” The holy Doctor again proves his opinion from the agreement of the Greek versions of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, which say that paradise was planted in Eden “from the beginning” or “at the beginning.”

“From this,” Jerome says, “it is most clearly established that before God made heaven and earth he had already created paradise, just as it is also read in the Hebrew: ‘The Lord God had planted paradise in Eden, from the beginning.’”

If we believe Augustine, bishop of Chimasium and father of the critical history of the Old Testament, Jerome defended this interpretation most badly, having been instructed or deceived by the Jews, who indulge in many ravings and maintain that seven things were created before the creation of heaven and earth, among which paradise is commonly counted in the scholarly systems of Rabbinic Kabbalists.

But I, who have always resolved to weigh the statements of holy men with a generous mind, shall gladly undertake Jerome’s defense with Salianus and Jansenius, so that I may demonstrate that the most learned Interpreter spoke from the Jewish understanding, not from his own.

Salianus, therefore, defending Jerome in the *Epitome of the Annals of the Old Testament*, defends his annotation in this way:

“St. Jerome spoke according to the opinion of the Hebrews, whose Traditions he was recording there. Jansenius wished to excuse Jerome in the same way for all readers when he wrote the following on Genesis 2:

“‘From the beginning,’ he says, ‘not before the earth was created, as the Jews fabulously claim from 4 Esdras 3:6, and as Jerome says in the Hebrew Traditions is certain—namely, according to the Jewish understanding—but from the beginning, that is, long before the seventh day. The Hebrew word is indifferent to the beginning of time and to the place that is the east, where the sun’s movement begins. Hence the Seventy translated it “toward the east.”’”

We shall readily be persuaded of this understanding of Jerome’s opinion if we compare the words of 4 Esdras 3:6, “And you led him [Adam] into the paradise that your right hand had planted before the earth came into being,” with Jerome’s Preface to the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, where he expresses his own opinion, saying:

“Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that only one book has been published by us; nor should anyone take pleasure in the dreams of the apocryphal third and fourth books. For among the Hebrews also the books of Ezra and Nehemiah are joined into one volume, and whatever is not found among them and is not among the twenty-four elders must be cast far away.”

These words are reported as having been written by Jerome around the year of Christ 392, whereas in the year 388 he had proposed a different opinion in the book *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*. Here, then, Jerome’s true personal opinion shines forth: he rejects the dreams of 4 Esdras, among which the most foolish was the planting of the earthly paradise before the earth came into being.

I could have found similar and other responses in defense of Jerome, and I could have appealed to the style and character of the book *Hebrew Questions*. For since it is a collection of Hebrew Traditions, no one should find it surprising if it reports what the Hebrews think about various matters.

“Since,” Jerome himself says, “our little work, the *Hebrew Questions*, is a collection of Traditions, let us therefore introduce what the Hebrews think about this. They say that this man is Shem, the son of Noah, and so forth.”

The most learned Doctor therefore wished to express the Jewish tradition about paradise, not his own opinion. In six hundred other passages he plainly taught that the allegories of the earthly paradise and similar Jewish ravings were to be ridiculed and despised. Whoever desires more may consult Franciscus of Messana in the final volume of the Paris edition of St. Jerome’s works.

### III

J. Drusius contends in *Hebrew Questions*, book III, question 5, that our interpreter rendered Genesis 3:18 badly: “Cursed is the earth in your work.” After Drusius, the author of the *Critical History of the Old Testament*, ever afflicted by his habitual itch to criticize others, adds the following in book II, chapter 12:

“St. Jerome further adds that by the words *in opere tuo* one must understand sin, not tillage; and he further maintains that this sense is also that of the Seventy. But he seems far removed from the true explanation of the text. Theodotion too followed this latter interpretation; and one should note that St. Jerome sometimes followed that interpreter without examining him attentively enough. This partly explains why the Vulgate often conforms to Theodotion’s translation. Aquila translated here *propter te*, in conformity with the Hebrew text as it now stands, and I do not doubt that this latter translation ought to be preferred to the others.”

Thus our critical writer censures Jerome, and with Jerome the Latin Vulgate edition, because it does not conform to the present Hebrew source and comes closer to Theodotion’s translation, which St. Jerome, he says, did not examine with sufficient care.

But St. Jerome seems to me to have been wrongly criticized by Simon, as is clear from this context of his annotation alone: “Cursed is the earth in your works. Here *works*, he says, signifies not the cultivation of the soil, as most suppose, but sins, as is found in the Hebrew. Nor does Aquila disagree, saying: ‘Cursed is the ground because of you.’ And Theodotion: ‘Cursed is *Adama* in your transgression.’” What worthy of censure can modern critics find in this most learned and exact observation of Jerome’s? However they may choose to read the Hebrew, whether *baaburecha* or *baabodecha* with *daleth*, will not Jerome’s assertion always be true: namely, that the verse of Genesis, “Cursed is the earth in your works,” is to be understood not, as most suppose, of the works of cultivating the soil, but of sins?

If, moreover, sin or sins are to be understood according to the genuine sense of Scripture, let these unfair critics say why Aquila does not agree with the Vulgate edition, or Jerome’s version. For Aquila’s rendering, “Cursed is the earth because of you,” cannot be understood in any sense other than that in which Theodotion’s version is understood: “Cursed is *Adama* in your transgression.” For those different readings or interpretations—“because of you,” “in your work,” “in your transgression”—signify nothing other than Adam’s sin, through which death is believed to have entered the world and a curse the earth, among all who are truly devout and uphold the Catholic faith. Therefore Jerome’s present annotation afforded no ground for blame, but the strongest ground for praise, had its judges been readers equally fair and learned.

### IV

Jerome’s following observation on Genesis 6:14 is altogether brief: “Make yourself an ark of squared wood. Instead of ‘squared wood,’ we read ‘coated with pitch’ in the Hebrew.” Yet it is censured at greater length by the author repeatedly mentioned above, *Critical History*, book II, chapter 12, pp. 252–53:

“On verse 14 of the same chapter, where the Vulgate reads *De lignis laevigatis* [‘of smoothed wood’], St. Jerome observed that, according to the Hebrew, it should be translated *De lignis bituminatis* [‘of wood coated with pitch’]. In this he seems to have been mistaken and to have read *Copher* instead of *Gopher*. He may nevertheless have changed the letter *Ghimel* into *Caph* in order to find a more convenient sense, although he read *Copher* in his Hebrew copy, as it is read in those of today; and the rabbis indeed do this fairly often.”

Thus, without any necessity arising from knowledge or truth, the critical author attributes the ignorant and sacrilegious audacity of the rabbis to the most faithful and religious interpreter of the divine Scriptures. No one can honestly maintain that Jerome altered letters in the Hebrew text and deliberately read *Caph* in place of *Ghimel* in order to produce a more convenient sense in his translation or his *Hebrew Questions*. How abhorrent this would have been to Jerome will be clear to the reader from his own words to Marcella, in which he defends himself against the wrong now inflicted upon him by R. Simon:

“After my previous letter, in which I had briefly touched upon a few Hebrew words, word suddenly reached me that certain petty people were deliberately disparaging me because, contrary to the authority of the Ancients and the opinion of the whole world, I had attempted to correct certain things in the Gospels. Although I could rightly despise them—for the lyre sings in vain to an ass—yet, lest they accuse us of arrogance, as they are accustomed to do, let them have this answer: I was not so dull of heart and so grossly rustic as to suppose that anything in the Lord’s words needed correction or was not divinely inspired; rather, I wished to restore the corruption of the Latin manuscripts, proved by the divergence of all the books, to the Greek source, from which they themselves do not deny that they were translated. If they dislike water from the purest spring, let them drink muddy rivulets, etc.”

He who so sharply rejects the charge of altering the Gospel text, always appealing to the sources of the sacred Scriptures—what would he now answer Simon, who shamelessly imputes to him an alteration of the letters of the Mosaic and prophetic text? The holy man was not so dull of heart or so grossly rustic as to think that anything in prophetic words needed correction or was not divinely inspired. Let that rash *Critical History*, then, fall silent, since it deliberately disparages a most learned man whose glory will always overcome all envy.

To return to the charge, I think it superfluous to write here anything else in Jerome’s defense beyond what I set down in the notes to the *Divine Library*, cols. 7 and 8, where the matter was argued as follows. When Jerome said that, instead of “squared wood,” the Hebrew reads “coated with pitch,” some thought that he had erred and read *Copher* in the Hebrew text for *Gopher*. But, with due respect to writers of this kind, it may be maintained that Jerome read *Gopher* and interpreted the Hebrew excellently as “wood coated with pitch.” For *Gophrith* is a kind of gum and bitumen, or sulphurous material. The rabbis also place *Ets-schemen*, “the tree of fatness,” among the species of cedar; and many hold that the Ark was made of cedar wood. *Gopher*, therefore, is a species of bituminous tree that exudes resin or pitch, such as fir and pine. Hence it is clear that the critical author’s false conjecture against Jerome is unjust, and quite unworthy of a man who everywhere professes skill in the Hebrew language.

### V

I pass over many things said pointlessly in the *Critical History*, so that I may more carefully refute the more serious falsehoods and the ignorant boldness displayed in certain passages. The following observation is especially unjust to St. Jerome:

“In chapter 13, verse 14, where we read in the Vulgate *peccatores coram Domino nimis*—‘sinners exceedingly before the Lord’—St. Jerome reproaches the Seventy for adding *in conspectu Dei*, ‘in the sight of God,’ which, according to him, are superfluous words. But they are in the Hebrew text and mean the same thing as *coram Domino*, ‘before the Lord.’

“It is necessary to observe, on the occasion of this criticism of St. Jerome, that this Father reported many things in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* that are inaccurate and entirely inconclusive. He deliberately opposed the Greek version of the Seventy in order to lend greater authority to the Hebrew text and at the same time to his new translation based upon it.”

These are the words of Richard Simon, in the book and chapter cited above.

It is worthwhile to refute the falsehood and ignorant slander of these words from the very context of Jerome’s annotation, which was written as follows:

“‘And the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners exceedingly in the sight of God.’ In the Seventy Translators, ‘in the sight of God’ has been added superfluously, since the inhabitants of Sodom were wicked and sinners in the eyes of men.

“But he is called a sinner in the sight of God who can appear righteous before men, as it is said in praise of Zechariah and Elizabeth that both were righteous in the sight of God. And in the Psalter it is said: ‘No living person will be justified in your sight.’”

Jerome, therefore, the diligent and accurate interpreter, observes that “in the sight of God” has been added superfluously in the translation of the Seventy. He proves this by a true and correct inference, saying: “Since the inhabitants of Sodom were wicked and sinners in the eyes of men.”

That is, the Sodomites were regarded as wicked even by men. They committed their shameful lusts with such shamelessness that Isaiah later wrote of the greatest sinners:

“They proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and did not conceal it.”

But when crimes are not concealed, but proclaimed by the criminals themselves, what need is there to say of such people that they are wicked “in the sight of God”? It remains, therefore, that in this passage, as in many others, the critical writer is devoid of modesty, judgment, and learning. He dared to attack the words of the holy Doctor, words confirmed even by a prophetic oracle and established by the context of the argument.

Nor should you think that a man possesses judgment and learning in the Scriptures who rashly indicts the most learned men while himself ignorant of the phrases and idioms of the Hebrew language. For above he said that “in the sight of God” was written in Hebrew and that it meant the same as “before the Lord.” He would certainly not have made this observation if he had not claimed for himself a knowledge of Hebrew greater than the truth permits.

In Hebrew, therefore, the following is read:

*vehhattaim laihova meod*;

or, as I read it with the learned,

*vehhattaim ladonai meod*,

that is, “and sinners to the Lord,” or “against the Lord exceedingly.”

This is how the interlinear Gloss interprets it, as do those who rendered the Samaritan text and the Arabic version into Latin. Although the Chaldean Interpreter and the Syriac may seem to favor Simonius, the question must concern the word *laihovah*, or *ladonai*: whether it means “in the sight of God,” or whether—as is more correct—it signifies “to the Lord” or “against the Lord.”

And, so that I may meet our critic on equal terms, let him say in which Hebrew copy he found the words “in the sight of God.” In Hebrew these are expressed not by *ladonai* but everywhere in the books of the sacred Old Testament by *liphne Adonai*, or *liphne Haeloim*, or *beene Adonai*.

Properly speaking, “in the sight of God” in Hebrew is *liphne Haeloim*, as in Genesis 6:11, and in six hundred other passages in another form, *liphne Adonai*, that is, “in the sight of the Lord,” as in Genesis 10:9; Exodus 28:30 and 35, and afterward 29:11, 23, and 25, and so forth.

In a third form, *beene Adonai*, “in the eyes of the Lord” or “before the Lord,” it is found in Genesis 6:8 and 38:7, and so forth.

Thus, with the single exception of Genesis 13:13, whenever the Latin words *coram Domino*, “before the Lord,” occur, the Hebrew has *liphne Adonai* or *beene Adonai*. We therefore know with certainty that the father of the *Critical History* did not read the disputed verse in Hebrew as “in the sight of God.” And what is equally blameworthy in him, he also failed to understand the government and meaning of the servile letter *lamed*, which according to all Hebrew grammarians is never rendered in Latin as “in the sight of,” but as “in” or “to.”

Accordingly, *ladonai* properly means “to the Lord,” “toward the Lord,” or “against the Lord.” By an improper usage, however, it was rendered by the Seventy as “in the sight of God.” The Chaldean Paraphrast, the Syriac interpreter, and Jerome afterward followed that interpretation in his Latin translation, which he often wished to keep in agreement with the Seventy Translators, lest excessive novelty should frighten the reader.

And it was not merely the force of indeclinable particles that our careless critic failed to understand; but—what you will find even more astonishing—he openly demonstrated through his unlearned observation that he did not know the idioms of the Hebrew language. For if he had been familiar with the idioms of the Hebrews and the Prophets, he would never have said that *ladonai* meant the same as “in the sight of God” or “before the Lord.” For, as I shall soon prove by examples, this phrase, “sinners to the Lord,” employs a superlative construction surpassing every intensification. Thus, in Jonah 3:3, to express the extraordinary size of the city of Nineveh, it is said: “And Nineveh was a great city *lelohim*, to God, or of God”; that is, an exceedingly vast and extensive city. In a similar native idiom, in Acts 7:20 the martyr Stephen expressed the exceptional beauty of the infant Moses, saying: “Καὶ ἦν ἀστεῖος τῷ Θεῷ”—that is, “And he was beautiful to God,” which among us means “most handsome” and “most graceful.” According to this manner of speech, extremely common among the Hebrews, it was said of the Sodomites that they were “sinners *ladonai*,” that is, “to the Lord” in the highest degree—namely, the most criminal and wicked of men.

Besides bearing the mark of this ignorance, he also incurs the reputation of a slanderer, when he accuses Jerome of hostility toward the Seventy Translators, as though Jerome had deliberately wished to undermine their Greek version in order to lend authority to the Hebrew source and to his own Latin translation made from the Hebrew. Jerome removed this unjust accusation from himself in the Preface to his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, where he sets forth the purpose of his work in these words:

> “It will therefore be the aim of our work either to refute the errors of those who form various conjectures from the Hebrew books, or to restore to their proper authority those things which seem to abound in the Latin and Greek codices; and also to explain, in the vernacular tongue, the etymologies of things, names, and regions that do not resound in our language . . . Nor do we, as the envious bark, censure the errors of the Seventy Translators; nor do we regard our labor as a criticism of them, etc.”

[Col. 1564B]

Why, then, does the envious author of the *Critical History* bark? Let him henceforth imitate not the envious, nor the foolish artificers of slander, but rather modest and sound-minded authors, especially James Bonfrère, who defends the version of the Seventy Translators by Jerome’s own example, saying:

> “To these men also, astonishingly, certain Catholics—too little modest or learned, in my judgment—add their voices, when on every occasion they reject the version of the Seventy Translators with I know not what superciliousness . . . Jerome certainly did not act so. Whenever something obscure occurs in that version, he frankly admits that he cannot know what they intended, as in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, at chapter 35, where he asks what among the Seventy is meant by *Chabratha terrae*; or, as others have it, *in via hippodromi Chabrathae terrae*. He corrected their translation where it contained errors, and translated certain passages from the Greek into Latin. Everywhere he clears himself of the charge that he produced his edition from Hebrew into Latin in order to detract anything from the honor of the Seventy Translators, but says that he did so for other just reasons—especially in the *Galeate Prologue*, where he speaks most humbly of himself and his version. In another preface to the book of Chronicles, he acknowledges the Holy Spirit in the Seventy Translators.”

Thus Bonfrère in the *Preliminaries to the Whole of Sacred Scripture*, chapter 16, section 4. We earnestly hope that the imprudent Critic, chastised by these words, may come to his senses.

After so many errors noted in the *Critical History*, there still remains a chronological blunder that the author’s diligence has not yet recognized. The attentive reader must nevertheless be warned about it, lest he continue to follow a blind guide. Above, Simonius had said that Jerome deliberately wished to disparage the version of the Seventy Translators in the *Hebrew Questions*, so as to secure authority for his own version derived from the Hebrew.

[Col. 1564D]

But no one is unaware that no writer has ever thought of attributing authority to a version that did not yet exist. Jerome’s Latin version of Genesis, produced from the Hebrew source, was published six years after the book of *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* had appeared. We have said that this little work was published in the year of Christ 388, whereas the Latin version of Genesis prepared by Jerome did not appear before the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 394. From this whole sequence of observations it is most clearly demonstrated that the author of the *Critical History* repeatedly departed from the truth and stood far removed from Hebrew learning and from a commendable understanding of the divine Scriptures.

But lest you think that what I say is tainted by envy, and that I am less criticizing another’s errors than allowing my own irritation to erupt against rivals, I shall willingly and gladly repeat some things that are true and learnedly written in the same *Critical History*.

[Col. 1565A]

For I have learned from holy and ecclesiastical writers that one should neither praise the faults of friends nor detract from the merits of adversaries when they possess anything honorable. Judging each matter, therefore, not by the weight of persons but by the weight of things, I acknowledge as true and excellent the following observation of Simonius, in *Critical History*, book II, chapter 12, page 251:

> “One should not imagine that one will find exactly in the observations of St. Jerome the very words that are in the Vulgate we presently use. It is enough that ordinarily the sense is the same; and there are also reasons why the remarks of St. Jerome, both in his *Questions on Genesis* and in his commentaries on the rest of Scripture, are not always in conformity with the Vulgate, although he is its author.”

And then, on page 253, column 1:

> “Thus St. Jerome, who retained in his version the word ‘window,’ shows that he paid greater attention to clarity of meaning than to expressing the Hebrew word for word. This nevertheless ought not to have prevented him from making literal and critical observations in his *Hebrew Questions*.”

In this observation and argument the critical writer has indeed touched upon the truth. His statement expressly refutes the opinion of ignorant persons who eagerly seek to prove, by arguments resembling his, that the Vulgate version is not Jerome’s, because it sometimes differs in wording from the readings that occur frequently in the *Hebrew Questions* or in the commentaries of the same holy Doctor. For if they argue from the variation of readings that the Vulgate is not Jerome’s true offspring, it will consequently be true that the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, or the commentaries on the Prophets and on Paul’s Epistles, should not be attributed to Jerome because of those same variant readings—even though he himself often acknowledges this different method of interpretation.

For example, in the commentary on Ezekiel 43, where he wished to warn the reader in these words:

> “The Seventy have again translated *geîson* (γεῖσον). Concerning this word, as I have already said, I cannot know its derivation, nor confidently say to what language it belongs. I can only advise the reader that where I have now translated it as ‘definition,’ below I have rendered it as ‘crown.’”

Let the ignorant therefore deny that the Vulgate version of Ezekiel is Jerome’s because it sometimes differs in wording from his commentaries. On the contrary, let it be established for all learned persons that the Latin Vulgate version of Genesis is no less Jerome’s than the Latin version of the sixteen Prophets, whose distinctive character no one but a fool has thought should be denied to its author Jerome.

[Col. 1566B]

## More Extensive Notes on the Commentary on Ecclesiastes

[Col. 1565]

What I was compelled to do at the end of the book of *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, I am likewise compelled to do at the end of the Commentary on Solomon’s Ecclesiastes. For Richard Simonius did not wish merely to attack the volume of *Hebrew Questions* in his *Critical Observations*; with the same method and recklessness he also dared to turn his pen against Jerome’s Commentary, upon which no stain or blemish could have been smeared except by the ignorant and false Aristarchus of our age, who more than once calls evil good and good evil. To restrain, therefore, the extreme intemperance of this kind of censor, I have thought it useful here to expose the inherently feeble, unsound, and unjust observations of the *Critical History of the Old Testament* against so learned a man. For once the ignorant falsity of these observations has been compressed and pierced by our notes, the truth attacked in them will shine forth of its own accord, and due honor will accrue to Jerome’s labors. I shall introduce the actual author of the *Critical History* as speaking, so that he may never be able to complain that any alteration has been made here, in this defense undertaken for Jerome, either to his words or to his meaning.

Thus Simonius began chapter 13 of book 2 of his *Critical History of the Volumes of the Old Testament*:

> “It is easy to recognize, from the criticism we have just made, that the Latin Vulgate, in the form in which we presently have it, is not entirely by St. Jerome, although, speaking generally, he is its author. Since there are other books in the same Vulgate that are absolutely his, and of which no one can doubt, I thought it appropriate to examine this Version further in certain places that are certainly by St. Jerome. I therefore chose the book of Ecclesiastes, of which we have the two Vulgate Versions arranged in two different columns in the works of this Father; and thus there is no reason to doubt that one of these columns, which represents the Vulgate of today, is St. Jerome’s new translation, which he joined to the old Vulgate that had been made from the Greek of the Seventy, and in which there is also some mixture of Theodotion’s version.

[Col. 1566B]

> “St. Jerome declares in the preface placed at the beginning of his commentary on Ecclesiastes the method that he followed in his new version.
