He first testifies that he did not subject himself to the authority of any interpreter, but translated simply from the Hebrew. Nevertheless, he adds that he accommodated himself to the usage of the Seventy more than to any other translation wherever they did not differ greatly from the Hebrew text. Finally, he admits that he also sometimes had recourse to Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, so that he consulted all these authors in order to produce a good version. Let us now see whether he always succeeded in the choice he made among these interpreters.”

From this turbid source of the *Critical History* innumerable errors have flowed among curious and learned men who do not shun the unreliable authority of R. Simonius. For when they believe the words of a writer who has instilled into himself a false persuasion of his own learning, they are compelled to revere countless fantasies and phantoms. Of this kind, certainly, are the following claims: first, that two Latin Vulgate translations are placed in distinct columns in St. Jerome’s Commentary on Ecclesiastes; second, that the same most holy Doctor joined his new translation from Hebrew to the old Latin Vulgate derived from the Greek when he illustrated Ecclesiastes with his Commentary; third, that he declared the method to which he had adhered in producing a new translation of the Bible; and fourth, that he sometimes followed Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion in preparing the same version in Latin.

Perhaps you are surprised, reader, that the critical writer, leaving port, immediately drove his ship upon so many reefs of error, since you had thought him exceptionally learned and extraordinarily devoted to these studies. But I, who am not surprised by a cause rooted in ignorance, find that Simonius wrote here, as in many other places, ignorantly and recklessly, and judged so badly concerning everyone else that no one could possibly judge his errors. But I shall come to the matter itself and refute the critical author’s first hallucination in a general discussion by these observations.

We do not possess, as he claimed, two Latin Vulgate Versions distinguished in separate columns in St. Jerome’s Commentary on Ecclesiastes. We have only the one modern version, joined through the rashness of contemporary scribes and editors to the Latin text of Ecclesiastes, which was for the most part rendered from the Hebrew words and illustrated by commentary by St. Jerome.

This was always perfectly clear to everyone, and indeed ought to have been clear from the precise words of Jerome’s Preface, by which he warns the reader as follows:

> “I briefly point out that I have followed the authority of no one, but, translating from the Hebrew, have adapted myself more to the custom of the Seventy Translators—only in those matters in which they did not differ greatly from the Hebrew.”

Who, amid such a light of words and truthful meanings, could calmly listen to a writer who is not wholly unlearned saying:

> “I therefore chose the book of Ecclesiastes, of which we have the two Vulgate Versions arranged in two different columns in the works of this Father”?

Simonius himself later concedes that the older Latin Vulgate version of Solomon’s Ecclesiastes was derived and taken from Greek exemplars of the Seventy Translators. How, then, can the Latin translation of Ecclesiastes placed in the first column of the published Commentary of St. Jerome be the old Vulgate expressed from Greek books, when Jerome testifies in the preface to this work that he translated from Hebrew into Latin while following the authority of no interpreter? Will this most combative writer ever be ashamed of such ignorance? Is there any trace of diligence in that observation? But, so that he may now blush at his own errors, he who did not know how to blush modestly when criticizing the errors of others, let us compare the ancient Latin version of Ecclesiastes expressed by the Seventy Translators with the Latin translation that Jerome prepared and placed before his Commentary on Ecclesiastes as its sacred text.

## Chapter One

[Col. 1567C]

### Verse 1

**According to the Seventy:** “The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Israel in Jerusalem.”

**According to Jerome:** “The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem.”

As you see, the ancient Latin version retained, according to the Seventy, “king of Israel in Jerusalem.” The text read in St. Jerome’s Commentary is therefore not the ancient Vulgate, since in the context of his translation he rejected the superfluous words “Israel” and “in,” and teaches that they were wrongly added both in the Septuagint and in the ancient Latin Vulgate.

“Moreover,” he says in his Commentary on this passage, “this must be observed more carefully: throughout the three books of the Author—Solomon—the title is different. For in Proverbs it reads: ‘The Proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel.’ But in Ecclesiastes: ‘The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem.’ For ‘Israel’ is superfluous here, and is wrongly found in the Greek and Latin codices.”

I shall certainly say with confidence that Simonius did not even read the title of the book of Ecclesiastes; or, if he read it, he understood it not at all, when he dared to assert that two Vulgate Versions, distinguished in separate columns, had been placed in St. Jerome’s Commentary on Ecclesiastes. From the single wording of the title it is manifest and certain to us that neither Latin version in Jerome’s Commentary is the ancient Vulgate expressed from Greek exemplars. Yet that father and champion of the worst *Critical History* of the sacred Scriptures foolishly insists on teaching otherwise.

### Verse 5

**According to the Seventy:** “And the sun rises, and the sun sets, and returns to its place: rising there, it goes toward the south, etc.”

**According to Jerome:** “The sun rises, and the sun sets, and returns to its place; and it rises there.”

In this verse Jerome adapted himself to the usage of the Seventy Translators, and afterward appropriately warns the reader, saying:

> “But where, following the Vulgate Edition, we have written ‘returns to its place,’ the Hebrew has *Soeph*, etc.”

He would have taught us about that usage in vain if he had always placed the Vulgate edition before his Commentary on Ecclesiastes.

### Verse 11

**According to the Seventy:** “There is no remembrance of former things, and indeed of the last things that shall be; there will be no remembrance of them among those who shall be at the end.”

**According to Jerome:** “There is no remembrance of former things, and indeed of the last things that shall be; there will be no remembrance of them among those who shall be afterward.”

The meaning of these words is clearly explained in the Commentary. There Jerome adds:

> “According to the Seventy Translators, who said, ‘There is no remembrance of former things,’ etc.”

By this he shows that his version is one thing and the version of the Seventy Translators another, and that in the two the meanings are plainly different. This would certainly not have escaped the critical writer if he had for even a short time examined the matter that he had undertaken to establish.

### Verses 16, 17, and 18

**According to the Seventy:** “I spoke in my heart, saying: Behold, I have been magnified, and I have increased in wisdom beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem. And I gave my heart to know wisdom and knowledge. And my heart saw many things, wisdom and knowledge, parables and knowledge. I learned that this also is presumption of spirit. For in the abundance of wisdom there is an abundance of knowledge, etc.”

**According to Jerome:** “I spoke with my heart, saying: Behold, I . . . , in Jerusalem; and my heart saw much wisdom and knowledge. And I gave my heart to know wisdom and knowledge, errors and folly. I learned that this also is a feeding on wind, or presumption of spirit. For in the abundance of wisdom there is an abundance of vexation, etc.”

Let Simonius now compare these two Latin versions, and he will easily learn that the ancient Vulgate differs from Jerome’s translation as greatly as the Seventy differ from the Hebrew source itself. For they differ from one another not only in meaning but also in wording and in the order of the words, as is clear to anyone who reads them. Add to this Jerome’s observation on the preceding verse, “This grievous occupation God gave to the children of men,” which the Latin interpreter expressed as “a grievous distinction.” Thus we demonstrate most clearly that Jerome’s translation placed in the Commentary mentioned above is very different from that which is called the ancient Vulgate even today, and that the opinion of the critical author must be wholly rejected and eliminated.

I could have offered many arguments of this kind from the following chapters of Ecclesiastes, in which Jerome’s version is both different from the ancient Vulgate and often contrary to the Seventy Translators. But the first falsehood of the *Critical History* that has just been overthrown is so obvious to all that I would seem to waste time and effort in continuing to refute it. We must therefore wage war against Simonius’s other errors and extinguish them as quickly as possible, since, intent upon better studies, we are very reluctant to engage in contentious disputes.

[Col. 1568D]

I have already shown, while refuting several errors of the *Critical History* at once, that the opinion by which Simonius was deceived—namely, that St. Jerome joined an old Latin Vulgate to a new Latin Vulgate, as though they were displayed in separate columns in the published Commentary on Ecclesiastes—is entirely false and ignorant. This will be utterly convincing to everyone who forms a judgment of that Commentary from ancient records or from the older editions of Jerome’s works. For in all those books there is a single text of Sacred Scripture, and indeed in handwritten copies it is written throughout in precisely the form in which it is now published by us. No one before Marianus Victorius had allowed a double Latin Version of Ecclesiastes to be printed together in distinct columns.

Finally, when Jerome explained Ecclesiastes in his Commentary, he had translated no other book of Scripture into Latin from the Hebrew besides this one. For he completed his Commentary approximately five years after he had returned from Rome to Jerusalem, that is, around the year of the Christian era 389; but he translated the four books of Kings from Hebrew into Latin before the other books of the Old Testament, in the year 392 or 391. From these chronological notes it is sufficiently clear that the modern Vulgate version of Ecclesiastes could not have been joined with another translation in Jerome’s Commentary, since the Commentary precedes the new Vulgate edition of the books of Solomon by three years.

No one who has been prepared by reading Jerome’s Preface and Commentary can fail to refute the remaining errors of the *Critical History* noted above by that reading alone. For everything written there must be referred not to the modern Vulgate version of the sacred Scriptures, but to the single text of the translation and Commentary on Ecclesiastes. Let it therefore be a settled opinion among all learned persons that Simonius is far from the truth when, through ignorance, he taught that what properly belongs to the Commentary on Ecclesiastes should be attributed to the Latin Vulgate version of the Scriptures—a version that perhaps had not yet even entered the mind of the holy Doctor.

Jerome therefore recalls Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion at times when, in the text of his Commentary, he quotes the versions of those interpreters. For example, column 387, line 38, he says:

> “Where, following the Vulgate edition, we have written ‘returns to its place,’ the Hebrew has *Soeph*, which Aquila translates *εἰσπνεῖ*, that is, ‘breathes in’ or ‘draws breath.’ Symmachus and Theodotion have ‘returns,’ because, plainly, etc.”

You now see, candid reader, what Jerome teaches when he says that he adapted himself to the usage of the Seventy Translators and that he sometimes also recalled Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion. He does both here and in six hundred other passages that follow in the Commentary. Let the critical writer therefore be ashamed of so many and such great hallucinations; and let the man who applauded himself as far superior to his peers now be compelled to admit that he often taught others many things of which he himself was ignorant.

We must now examine more carefully what he rashly wished to criticize in Jerome and in our Latin Vulgate version. In his censorious manner he does not hesitate to say:

> “Let us now see whether he always succeeded in the choice he made of his interpreters.”

Let us also see whether that censor judged Jerome’s interpretation correctly, so that, if he uses unfortunate judgment, the false and ignorant Aristarchus of our age may be condemned by everyone. Here, then, is his first observation attacking the modern Vulgate:

> “First, it does not seem to me that, even in following the rules of his method, it was necessary for him to change these words of the old Vulgate in chapter 1, verse 4: *Generatio vadit, et generatio venit* (‘A generation goes, and a generation comes’) into these others: *Generatio praeterit, et generatio advenit* (‘A generation passes away, and a generation arrives’). And although the meaning is the same in one version and the other, I nevertheless find that the old Vulgate expresses the Hebrew words better and more literally than our Vulgate; and therefore no correction was needed in this place.”

As many of Simonius’s words, so many are his hallucinations. For no judgment whatsoever concerning the method that Jerome followed when he produced the new Vulgate—that is, our present Vulgate—can be formed from the Preface to Ecclesiastes. Everything that the most holy Doctor says in that Preface belongs specifically to the Commentary on Ecclesiastes. As I warned earlier, Simonius could not, without bearing the mark of ignorance, write indiscriminately about different Jeromean translations as though the same account applied to all of them.

If anyone greatly desires to know the method by which Jerome translated the sacred books from Hebrew into Latin, let him hear Jerome himself writing to Augustine in letter 89:

> “There,” he says, “we translated the Greek; here we expressed from the Hebrew itself what we understood, sometimes preserving rather the truth of the meaning than the order of the words.”

In his new translation, therefore, he strove to preserve the truth of the meaning rather than the order of the words. He could not have carried out this task more fully than by changing the old Vulgate, “A generation goes, and a generation comes,” into another, new, and more truthful version: “A generation passes away, and a generation arrives.” Nor should we listen to the critical writer, who asserts that the meaning of both versions is one and the same, and that the old version is more expressive and literal than the new Vulgate, while also claiming that the aforementioned change—“A generation passes away,” etc.—was made without necessity.

We may readily set all such errors before the reader, both from the sacred text of Ecclesiastes itself and from Jerome’s Commentary on this passage:

> *Dor holech, vedor ba*—that is, “A departing generation and an arriving generation.”

For the immediate, genuine, and literal meaning of these words could not have been expressed more clearly than in the following Commentary:

> “While some die, others are born; and when you no longer see those whom you had seen, you begin to see those whom you had not seen.”

If “a generation goes, and a generation comes” immediately signifies “some die and others are born,” then undoubtedly the Vulgate of today, “A generation passes away, and a generation arrives,” expresses the sense of Scripture and of the sacred Author better than the ancient Latin version, “A generation goes, and a generation comes.” For in our Vulgate it is expressly stated that one generation is extinguished and perishes while a new one succeeds it; whereas in the ancient Vulgate it can be understood that the same generation goes away and afterward returns, as we shall say shortly.

This observation of ours can be reconciled with the authority of the best Hebrew lexicographers, who before us taught that the Hebrew verb *halach* is to be understood, by metalepsis, of things that vanish, perish, die away, and die. Thus in Genesis 15:2: *Et ego holech ariri*—that is, “going childless,” or, more plainly, “I am dying without children.” The Targum expressed it as *azel bela velad*, that is, “going without offspring.” The Seventy: *ἀπολύομαι ἄτεκνος*, “I die childless.” The Jerusalem Targum: *azel minni alma*, “I depart from the world.” Thus in Latin, *abitio* means death. Whoever is born comes; whoever dies departs. Festus Pompeius says: “The ancients called death *abitionem*.”

Moreover, the Latin interpreters of the Syriac and Arabic versions agree with our Vulgate and with Jerome, saying: “An age passes away, and an age succeeds.” And what deserves even more careful attention is that the Chaldean Paraphrast interprets the word *holech* here in Ecclesiastes in the same way as above in Genesis 15:2, namely, *azal min alma*, “he departed from the world.”

Confirmed, then, by the testimony of so many interpreters, the new version of Jerome, or the modern Vulgate edition, should cause that ignorant *Critical History* forever to fall silent—the work whose author had hoped that a time would come when no age would be silent about his praises.

And so that our censor may finally learn why it was necessary for Jerome to change the old Vulgate in the disputed passage of Ecclesiastes, he ought to remember that from this version, “A generation goes, and a generation comes,” an occasion and cause are supplied to the followers of Epicurus and Origen for thrusting upon us innumerable foolish cycles of the same things and endless Platonic circuits. The excellent interpreter Jerome, our Vulgate translator, wisely forestalled this danger. In place of the old Latin version he substituted a new one: “A generation passes away; a generation arrives.” This more clearly explains the genuine sense of Scripture and provides no opening for disputes, so that we might otherwise suppose that signs and wonders, and many things that occur newly in the world by God’s will, had already taken place in earlier ages; and so that Epicurus might find a place, asserting that the same things happen through innumerable cycles, in the same places and through the same persons.

For if one generation passes away and another new one succeeds or arrives, then Judas did not repeatedly betray; Christ did not repeatedly suffer for us; nor are the other things that have happened and will happen rolled back into the same cycles in the same manner. I would add more to rebuke the ignorant Critic, if I had not heard and seen in many of his little works that his character is incurable. Let us nevertheless set forth the remaining objections of the *Critical History* for refutation.

> “Secondly, in verse 6 of the same chapter, the old Vulgate seems to have translated better and more literally the words of the Hebrew text by these expressions: *Vadit ad Austrum, et gyrat ad Aquilonem: gyrans gyrando vadit spiritus, et in circulos suos revertitur spiritus* (‘It goes toward the south and turns toward the north; turning and turning, the wind goes, and the wind returns to its circles’), than they were translated by St. Jerome. I am not speaking at present about the sense that should be given to these words, which are sufficiently difficult to explain; but I am convinced that the Septuagint interpreted the Hebrew better in this passage than St. Jerome did. When a passage is obscure and can be explained in different ways, it seems that the translator is then obliged not to depart so far from the grammatical sense; and this is what the Septuagint observed here much better than St. Jerome.”

See how greatly he trusts in his own recklessness. “I am not speaking,” he says, “about the sense of those words, which is sufficiently obscure and intricate; but I am convinced that the Hebrew was better interpreted by the Septuagint than Jerome rendered it in Latin in the new Vulgate.” O splendid wisdom of the critical writer! He confesses that he does not know the meaning of a passage that is excessively obscure, yet amid such darkness he dares, in an inelegant manner, to assume the role of judge and, rejecting Jerome’s authoritative Version, pronounce in favor of the old Vulgate—already long obsolete in the Church of Christ and neglected in daily use.

Accordingly, I shall here disregard the mask of the *Critical History*, prepared to uphold the defense of our Vulgate once I see Simonius performing the office of a sound critic rather than uselessly throwing around censorious words that contribute nothing to the clarification of the matter proposed.

But lest anyone think that by this response I am avoiding the difficulty of the discussion, and that, according to the common proverb, I am applying a bad wedge to a bad knot, I shall return to the point from which the argument turned aside to this place, so that by comparing the two Vulgates I may openly establish, against Simonius’s opinion, that Jerome’s version, expressed from the Hebrew, is to be preferred to the ancient Latin translation.

In the Hebrew, then, we read the following in Ecclesiastes, chapter 1, verses 5 and 6:

*Vezarahh hasschemesch uba hasschemesch, veel mecomo scoeph zoreahh hu scham. Holech el darom, vesobeb el tsaphon: sobeb sobeb, holec haruahh, veal sebibothav schab haruahh.*

These words, if we follow the affected literalism of the interpretation, may sound in Latin as follows:

> “And the sun will rise, and the sun will enter; and, rising breathlessly toward its place, it is there. Going toward the south and circling toward the north; circling, circling, the wind goes, and the wind returns over its circuits.”

The Seventy Translators, praised above by Simonius, appear to follow this path, saying:

> “And the sun rises, and the sun sets, and returns to its place; rising there, it goes toward the south and turns toward the north; turning and turning, the wind goes, and the wind returns to its circles.”

But Jerome, following the truth of the meanings rather than the order of the words, translates it more clearly as follows:

> The sun rises, and the sun sets,
>
> and returns to its place;
>
> and there, rising again, it turns through the south,
>
> and bends toward the north;
>
> surveying all things, the wind proceeds in a circuit,
>
> and returns to its circles.

Does it not seem to you, learned reader, that such an elegant version has flowed from Solomon’s mouth speaking Latin? What meaning of the words, what eloquence of expression does not shine forth in this interpretation? For whatever the wisest Ecclesiastes recounts concerning the sun’s continual rising and setting, its return toward the east, and its oblique turn through the south toward the north, the most eloquent interpreter Jerome has expressed for us in complete Latin. For that oblique and broken line, as the sun travels through the south toward the north and thus returns toward the east, could not have been more beautifully described than in the rhythm of the four preceding clauses:

> “The sun rises, and sets, and returns to its place; and there, rising again, it turns through the south and bends toward the north.”

The remaining two clauses, which may still be understood either of the sun or certainly of the wind, Jerome translated into Latin so elegantly that we may refer them to either without any restriction of meaning.

The Chaldean Paraphrast understands the entire passage of the sun’s circuits. He says:

> “The sun rises by day from the side of the east, and the sun enters the side of the west by night; and it gradually thrusts itself toward its place and walks along the way of the abyss, and tomorrow it will rise from the place where it rose yesterday. It traverses the whole side of the south by day, and returns to the side of the north by night along the way of the abyss. It turns, circles, and travels toward the wind of the southern region during the revolution of Nisan and Tammuz, and through its circuits returns toward the wind of the northern region during the revolution of Tishri and Tebeth. In the morning it comes out through the prisons of the east, and in the evening enters the lattices of the west.”

The Syriac and Arabic interpreters interpret the final verse as referring to winds that are carried around in a circle:

> “It proceeds toward the south and bends toward the north. The wind is carried around in a circle and passes through it, and the wind returns to its circuits.”

From this great variety of interpretations it is clear to everyone that the modern Latin Vulgate—that is, Jerome’s version—far surpasses the others in explaining the ambiguous words of the Hebrew context:

“Zoreahh hu scham holec el darom, vesobeb [Col. 1572C] el tsaphon: sobeb sobeb, holech haruahh, veal sebibothav, schab haruahh”—“The wind goes toward the south and turns toward the north; turning and turning, the wind goes, and returns upon its circuits.”

Nor, I think, can a more elegant or more accurate Latin translation of this passage of Scripture be found than our Vulgate:

> “And there, being reborn, it circles toward the south and bends toward the north; surveying everything around, the spirit proceeds and returns to its circuits.”

For whether you wish to understand the sun as the spirit—because by its light and heat it animates and gives life to everything—or the aerial spirit, which is carried in a circle, driven and driven back in every direction, and thus returns to its same circuits, Jerome’s Version supplies you with this twofold interpretation, with the greatest precision of Latin vocabulary and eloquence of expression. Those who know this language will readily grant me this, provided they do not take pleasure in the stale Latin interpretation of the Hebrew words: “it circles, circling; the spirit goes; and the spirit returns to its circuits.”

Simonius proposed a third criticism, in order, against the Vulgate edition, as follows:

> “At verse 7, where the Vulgate has *Mare non redundat*—‘The sea does not overflow’—the [Col. 1572D] Septuagint expressed the Hebrew text more literally by translating *Mare non impletur*—‘The sea is not filled.’ Thus I do not see what reason Saint Jerome had for changing their translation at this point, since he professed that he would not abandon the ancient Latin Vulgate except when compelled to do so by good reasons. He also changed several other words in the same verse without any necessity.”

Before truth restrains Simonius with the overflowing freedom of his critical speech, I should like to ask him whether he understands what he himself is saying, and under what teacher he learned the Hebrew, Greek, or Latin language. Certainly, if he knows what *male* means among the Hebrews, what ἐμπίμπλαμαι means among the Greeks, and what *redundare* means among the Latins, there was no reason for him to treat the modern Latin Vulgate unjustly, nor to criticize Jerome, the father of this Version.

The Hebrew word *male* [Col. 1573A] signifies every kind of abundance and fullness. Likewise, the Greek ἐμπίμπλαμαι means “I am filled” and “I am satisfied”; hence ἐμπιμπλαμένη in the Septuagint Translators, which has the same meaning as πλημμυρεῖ in Symmachus: “it swells with flood,” or “overflows,” because of excessive fullness.

Since, therefore, the rivers continually flow into the sea and from there are rolled back again toward their sources so that they may continue to flow, and since this occurs without any flooding of the sea despite the perpetual course of rivers and torrents, that remarkable spectacle of nature could not have been transferred from the Hebrew of Ecclesiastes into Latin speech more elegantly than by saying:

> “All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from which the rivers issue, they return, so that they may flow again.”

The sea has its own *melō*—that is, its fullness—even though the rivers do not flow into the Ocean; and Scripture often speaks in the Psalms and Prophets of that fullness, or abundance of waters: “Let the sea thunder, and its fullness,” or “Let the sea be moved, and its fullness.” [Col. 1573B]

But Ecclesiastes is speaking of another fullness of the sea. He marvels that all the rivers continually flow into the sea, yet that the sea itself, though increased by so many river and rain waters, never overflows. The ancient Latin Vulgate does not express this flooding of the sea by saying, “and the sea is not filled”; Jerome’s translation, by contrast, represents it explicitly by saying, “and the sea does not overflow.” Jerome therefore had a reason for changing and correcting the ancient Vulgate; Simonius, however, could have had no reason for rashly criticizing Jerome while disparaging the modern Vulgate edition.

Now the following observations will themselves show us how little praise this critical writer grants Jerome:

> “At verse 8, where we read in the Vulgate *cunctae res difficiles*—‘all things are difficult’—the Septuagint translated *omnes sermones graves*—‘all words are weighty’; but the first translation is much better. Since the Hebrew word means both *res* and *sermo* indifferently, the [Col. 1573C] Septuagint, who often translate Hebrew too literally, and sometimes even without attending to the meaning, do not always choose the true sense accurately. They become obscure by adhering too closely to the letter, as at verse 10 of this chapter, where they translated word for word from the Hebrew, *Non est omne recens sub sole*—‘Everything new is not under the sun’—whereas Saint Jerome translated much more clearly, *Nihil sub sole novum*—‘There is nothing new under the sun.’

> “Such changes are praiseworthy in Saint Jerome, and it cannot be denied that in countless passages our Vulgate should for this reason be preferred to the ancient Vulgate. On the other hand, there are passages where Saint Jerome seems to have taken a little too much liberty. For, on the pretext of avoiding barbarism by translating the Hebrew words too literally, he sometimes restricts the meaning of the original and departs from the letter more than he ought. It is true that elsewhere his translation is admirable, and [Col. 1573D] that, without clinging scrupulously to the words, and that, without clinging scrupulously to the words, he explains his author’s thought very well. This is clear evidence that he possessed sufficient knowledge of the Hebrew language—for example, when he translates certain futures by the present and changes one case into another according to the genius of that language.

> “Thus, in verse 8 of the same chapter, he translated very well *Saturatur et impletur*—‘It is satisfied and filled’—whereas the Septuagint translated with strict literalness, *Satiabitur et implebitur*—‘It will be satisfied and will be filled.’ And at verse 11, where we read *Non est priorum memoria*—‘There is no remembrance of former things,’ his translation is much better than that of the Septuagint, who translated *Non est memoria primis*—‘There is no remembrance among the first things.’

> “In short, Saint Jerome’s translation has this merit: it removes most of the ambiguities that are difficult to avoid when one adheres too closely to the grammatical sense.”

Simonius would appear to praise Jerome and our Vulgate at length, [Col. 1574A] were he not openly accusing, in the very course of his praise, the author of a translation that he does not deny to be remarkable in several places. Yet with what dignity should we regard in the Church of Christ a censor who dares to write the following publicly about the most holy Doctor?

> “On the other hand, there are passages where Saint Jerome seems to have taken a little too much liberty.”

O singular modesty of an orthodox writer! It is not fitting for a little man to speak so contemptuously of great men. Simonius was always far more intemperate toward everyone than he ought to have been; but now he wants to teach Minerva herself, and with an impudent Muse to accuse the greatest Doctor in the interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, as though he had sometimes rendered the words of the Prophets into Latin with immoderate freedom.

Simonius came close to begrudging Jerome even his knowledge of the Hebrew language. For when he says, “he possessed sufficient knowledge of Hebrew,” he does not attribute to Jerome a complete mastery of the Hebrew idiom, but only a limited and moderate competence. Yet which passages of Scripture, he claims, were expressed by the holy Doctor [Col. 1574B] in Latin words with excessive freedom? The false Aristarchus did not dare to identify them, thereby depriving us of the opportunity to defend Jerome and the Vulgate. Let us therefore proceed to the remaining heads of his accusations.

> “At verse 15,” that writer says, “where the Vulgate has *Perversi difficile corriguntur*—‘The perverse are difficult to correct’—the Septuagint translated much better, *Perversum non poterit adornari*—‘The perverse thing cannot be put in order.’ Saint Jerome ought not to have restricted to a moral sense what is expressed generally and without limitation in the Hebrew text. What follows, *Stultorum infinitus est numerus*—‘The number of fools is infinite’—is even farther from the original, which has literally, *Defectus nequit numerari*—‘Diminution cannot be numbered.’

> “This error of translation likewise arose from restricting the meaning, because Saint Jerome did not reflect sufficiently on the style of the Book of Ecclesiastes. Its Author uses certain terms taken from natural things generally, which can then be applied to several other matters, especially to those relating to morals.” [Col. 1574C]

To refute this sort of criticism from the *Critical History*, it is enough to transcribe Jerome’s Commentary on this passage of Ecclesiastes, which we published above, column 722:

> “The perverse cannot be put in order, and diminution cannot be numbered. Whoever is perverse, unless corrected first, cannot be put in order. Straight things receive adornment; crooked things receive correction. One is not called perverse unless one has been distorted from what is straight. This is directed against heretics who introduce certain natures that do not admit healing.

> “And because diminution—that is, what is lacking—cannot be numbered, only the firstborn of Israel were numbered. The women, slaves, children, and common people who came out of Egypt were passed over without number, not as the fullness but as the diminution of the army.

> “This may also be the meaning: So great is the wickedness contained within the capacity of this world that the world can scarcely return to the complete state of goodness, nor easily [Col. 1574D] recover the order and perfection in which it was first created.

> “Alternatively: When all things have been restored to wholeness through repentance, the devil alone will remain in his error. For everything that has been done under the sun has been overturned by his will and by the spirit of his wickedness, as sins are heaped upon sins at his prompting. Finally, the number of those deceived, and of those whom he has snatched from the Lord’s flock, is so great that it cannot be comprehended by reckoning.”

The verse of Ecclesiastes, explained in so many ways, leaves no room for doubt concerning Simonius’s ignorance, since he falls into various criticisms by censuring Jerome carelessly and wrongly. Jerome had undoubtedly considered the diction of Ecclesiastes carefully when he gave it Latin form, as the Commentary cited above proves: it was composed three years before his Vulgate translation of the same book. But I recognize no considered deliberation [Col. 1575A] or knowledge of the Hebrew language in the critical writer.

For if he had wished to consider Jerome’s Version with some learned and diligent person, he would immediately have understood that the Hebrew context of Ecclesiastes,

> *Meuvath lo juchal lithcon; vehhesron lo juchal lehimmanoth*,

has been correctly expressed in Latin by:

> “The perverse are difficult to correct, and the number of fools is infinite.”

Although *Meuvath* is a singular passive participle, in this passage it is taken distributively—that is, “each perverse person cannot be put in order”—and is therefore elegantly rendered in Latin by the plural *perversi*, so as to include every perverse person.

Moreover, the other word, *lo juchal*, “cannot,” since it signifies difficulty of correction rather than the absolute impossibility of a thing, is appropriately and fully expressed by the adverb “difficult.” The same judgment applies to the other words that follow. For the Hebrew phrase, “and diminution, or what is lacking, cannot be numbered,” has the same meaning [Col. 1575B] as Jerome’s Latin Vulgate Version, “and the number of fools is infinite,” because Ecclesiastes is not speaking of every kind of defect or diminution, but of that which occurs in human beings, whom he had already called foolish a hundred times.

Thus Proverbs 10:21 says:

> “And fools shall die in lack of heart,”

*bahhasar-leb*, a concrete expression used for an abstract one; it is the same as if he had said, “fools shall die in senselessness.” Likewise, later in the same book, chapter 12:11, *hhasar-leb* means “diminished in heart,” or “witless.”

The number of these witless people is therefore infinite, and they are also difficult to correct, according to Ecclesiastes 7:14 above:

> “For who can put in order one whom God has perverted,”

or, as Symmachus has it, “whom God has diminished.”

These are the principal considerations by which we may establish that Jerome was well versed in the language and idioms of the Book of Ecclesiastes, while Simonius, by contrast, neither knew the phrases of Scripture nor could distinguish the precise wording of the translations. [Col. 1575C]

The Chaldaean Paraphrast and the Syriac translator were not like him. By common agreement they refute the *Critical History*, while agreeing perfectly with the Vulgate Version. The Syriac reads *Moroudo*—that is, “The rebellious person cannot be directed, and the imperfect cannot be numbered.” Unless you understand this of foolish and perverse people, you will foolishly teach that the rebellion of wood or stones is meant here.

Likewise, in the Chaldaean paraphrase, perverse people are indicated morally:

> “A man whose ways are perverse in this world, and who dies in them without returning to repentance, has no power to correct himself after his death,”

and so forth.

Therefore anyone who wishes to examine the Latin Vulgate Ecclesiastes with sharp and mature judgment, rather than with critical rashness, will be compelled to acknowledge its accuracy.

I am now ashamed to hear Simonius speak in the *Critical History* as follows:

> “At verse 18, [Col. 1575D] where we read in the Vulgate *Labor et afflictio spiritus*—‘Labor and affliction of spirit’—the Hebrew has simply *afflictio spiritus*—‘affliction of spirit’; and in the ancient Vulgate reported by Saint Jerome, *pastio venti*, or *praesumptio spiritus*—‘feeding on wind,’ or ‘presumption of spirit.’ These are two different translations of the same Hebrew words, [Col. 1576A] which have been joined together, as sometimes happens in that ancient Vulgate, and so forth.”

I shall demonstrate in a few words how great this critical writer’s hallucination is. The ancient Latin Vulgate, translated from the Greek of the Septuagint Translators, never contains *pastio venti*, but everywhere has *praesumptio spiritus*. Hence Jerome says in his Commentary on verse 14 of the preceding chapter:

> “Necessity compels us,” he says, “to discuss Hebrew words more frequently than we wish. For we cannot know the meaning unless we learn it through the words. *Routh* [Hebrew word uncertain] Aquila and Theodotion translated as νόμην (“pasture”); Symmachus as βόσκησιν (“feeding”); but the Septuagint Translators did not express the Hebrew language, but the Syriac, saying προαίρεσιν. Whether therefore νόμη or βόσκησις is used, the word derives from feeding. Προαίρεσις, however, more properly means ‘will’ than ‘presumption.’”

If, moreover, the following passage of the scriptural text is read in that same Commentary of Jerome:

> “I learned that this too is feeding on wind, or presumption of spirit,”

you should not, with the authority of an Aristarchus, suppose that two translations of the same Hebrew word were joined together in the ancient Latin Vulgate. Rather, attribute this variation to Jerome’s Commentary, where the great man, often following the Septuagint edition, sometimes recalls Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion.

After so many errors that we have noted thus far, [Col. 1576B] Simonius prepares the reader’s mind appropriately for the remaining discussion by prefacing it as follows:

> “For the rest, I believe that what we have now presented concerning the manner in which Saint Jerome made his new Version of Scripture from the Hebrew is sufficient to make known in particular the method he followed in so great a work. We shall add only to what we have already observed a few general reflections, which will make us understand this same method of Saint Jerome even more fully.”

What we have previously noted seems sufficient to nullify the hope of the critical [Col. 1576C] author, who, deceiving himself, carelessly supposes that he can deceive others. The preceding and subsequent observations of the *Critical History* have taught us nothing that contributes to understanding the method by which Jerome translated the Hebrew Bible into Latin. For whatever the holy Doctor prefaced in his Commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes belongs specifically to that work, and is no more relevant to the Vulgate translation of Scripture than to his exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew.

A prudent reader will therefore rightly reject all the observations of the *Critical History*, because the writer of this work, flowing forward with great vehemence of speech like a muddy torrent, everywhere pours forth turbid discourse and repeatedly—or rather continually—forces falsehoods upon us as truths.

I have been compelled to protest these insults of Simonius on behalf of the authentic Latin version of the Roman Church and on behalf of Jerome, the greatest interpreter of the divine Scriptures. Otherwise, I am prepared to be reconciled with that critical writer, [Col. 1576D] provided that he himself does not wish to return to his own temperament.

[Col. 1575]

# Catalogue of Manuscript Codices Against Which Martianay Collated Both Other Works and, Especially, the Works of Saint Jerome Contained in This Third Volume

[Col. 1575D] The abundance of manuscript codices whose authority I used in editing the present volume is so great that I would scarcely have dared to state their number, had it not been easy for me to call each by its proper name and designate it by its own number. I therefore list them, distributed into distinct [Col. 1576D] classes: more than one hundred different books, written out in ancient times in different places and periods.

## Gallic Manuscript Codices: Seven Royal Codices

These belong to the library of the Most Christian King of France: [Col. 1577]

Greek Codex 2282, containing the book of Hebrew Names and Places, which I copied in full in my own hand, translated into Latin, and published with innumerable notes.

Another very ancient Greek codex, containing the Expositions on the Psalms and Origen’s Letter on the *Diapsalma*, not yet published; I discussed it in one of Jerome’s letters to Marcella.

Latin Codex 3998, copied in the year of Our Lord 887.

Codex 3999, another collection of Jerome’s Letters, copied in the year 1114.

Three others—3629, 3993, and 3994—containing the books of Hebrew Names and Places, the Hebrew Questions on Genesis, and Jerome’s Critical Letters.

## Colbert Codices: Twenty

One Greek codex, 4124, containing a Lexicon of Hebrew Names, which I copied in my own hand and translated, as I did the Royal codex above.

The Latin copies that I used for the edition of this volume are the following: 455, 464, 635, 893, 1038, 1128, 1248, 1335, 2397, 2430, 2471, 2504, 2599, 2807, 2852, 4354, 4436, 4951, and 5216.

## Our Corbie and Saint-Germain Codices: Seventeen

The oldest and best-quality manuscripts, many of them copied more than a thousand years ago in uncial or Lombard letters, bear these numbers in our library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés: 9, 126, 127, 132, 133, 134, 137, 138, 143, 147, 276, 281, 374, 580, 596, 660, and 675, together with others whose numbers have now escaped me.

## Codices of Other Monasteries of Our Congregation: Fourteen

These are: Saint-Remi of Reims, 193 and 194; Saint-Thierry near Reims, one and another; Sainte-Marie de Crasse in Occitania, one; Saint-André near Avignon, one; Saint-Michel in Peril of the Sea, two; several from the monasteries of Saint-Evroul and Saint-Martin of Sées; two from Fécamp and Jumièges; and one from Sainte-Marie de Pratellis.

## Cluniac Codices: Thirteen

Ten from the celebrated Abbey of Cluny, containing nearly all the genuine and spurious works of Saint Jerome; and three from the Paris monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. All these codices are of ancient and excellent handwriting.

## Codices of the Monastery of Saint-Cyran: Five

These are contained in as many volumes, in which are found, written in excellent hands, Jerome’s books of Hebrew Names and Places, the Hebrew Questions, all his Letters, the Commentary on Ecclesiastes, the spurious Commentary on the Psalms, and likewise the remaining Treatises and Commentaries on all the Prophets.

## Sorbonne and Navarre Codices: Nine

One is Greek-Latin, containing Jerome’s Letter to Sunnia and Fretela together with a threefold Psalter: the Hieronymian, the Roman, and that of the Septuagint Translators. The last of these is Greek written in Latin letters.

Seven others contain Commentaries on the Psalms, on Solomon’s Ecclesiastes, and on the Major and Minor Prophets; and two contain Jerome’s Letters.

One Navarre codex contains the Letters of Saint Jerome, which we recently cited and described in the *Prodrome* of this new edition.

## Memmian Codex: One

This belongs to the library of the illustrious president de Mesmes. It was copied at the command of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans—that is, at the end of the eighth or the beginning of the ninth century. We have said more about this codex in the Prolegomena to the preceding volume, or *The Divine Library of Saint Jerome*.

## Occitan Codices: Three

One belongs to the church of Carcassonne, of which I spoke in the *Prodrome of Saint Jerome* and in Volume I of this edition.

The second is from Toulouse, belonging to the convent of the Friars Preachers. At its end I found the following written:

> “Lord Bernard, bishop of Albi, caused this book to be written in the year of Our Lord 1294.”

That codex contains the Book of Names and Places and the Hebrew Questions on Genesis.

The third codex belongs to the monastery of Fontfroide, situated not far from the city of Narbonne.

## Roman Manuscript Codices: Nine

The following belong to the Vatican Library: 38, 341, 342, 343, 344, 348, and 349.

Then two belong to the Palatine Library: 133 and 135.

These contain the Critical Letters of Saint Jerome; the books of Names and Places; and the Hebrew Questions on Genesis, the Books of Kings, and Chronicles.

## German Codices of Murbach: Four

One is Greek, containing David’s Psalms, written in uncial letters—that is, majuscule letters—as was customary a thousand or nine hundred years ago.

The second is a Latin codex of Saint Jerome’s Letters, copied in the third year of King Childeric, under Abbot Amicus.

The third contains the Commentary on Ecclesiastes, and the fourth the books of Hebrew Names and Places.

All these manuscripts were collated with singular diligence and care by Monsieur Hyacinthe Alliot, whom I praised at the end of the Prolegomena to this volume.

The total number of all the manuscript codices is one hundred and three books, after adding the manuscript copy of Jerome’s Letters belonging to the Church of Ancy, which I omitted from the list.

Apher, one of Abraham’s descendants, led an army against Libya and settled there after defeating the enemy. His descendants called Africa by the name of their ancestor, 344.

All waters and torrents return through hidden channels to the womb of the abyss, 316.

Hot waters burst forth at Amantha, 147.

Arbee, in which four were buried: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam himself, the first prince of the human race, 340.

All who wrote barbarian histories remembered Noah’s ark, 126.

The burial mound of Archelaus, king of Judaea, was shown near Bethlehem, 167.

## B

[Col. 1580] Balaam, of the stock of Buz, is called Elihu in the Book of Job: at first a holy man and prophet of God, but later, through disobedience and desire for gifts, he is called by the divine name, 339. He was from the city of Fathura, 214.

Balsam and dates grow near the city of Balam, 167.

Baraciba, a Doctor of the Hebrews, whom the Jews especially admired in Jerome’s time, 424.

The Samaritans who had crossed over from the region of Babylon built Benith, 179.

Mount Beris in Armenia, where certain traces of Noah’s ark were found, 126.

Betharam, called Bethramtha by the Syrians and Libias by Herod in honor of Augustus, 172, 174.

Bethlehem in the tribe of Zebulun, and Bethlehem in the tribe of Judah, 177.

A city more august than Rome, 381.

Bethphogor, a mountain of the Moabites, 214.

They removed bitumen from the remains of Noah’s ark and used it in their purification rites, 126.

The collars or chains of the condemned were commonly called *boiae*, 43.

All good and truth are enclosed within a definite limit; wickedness and falsehood, however, are without limit, 496.

According to God’s arrangement, each thing is good when it is needed, 412.

What good God has given human beings in this life, 449.

## C

[Col. 1581] By what sign did Cain know that Abel’s offerings pleased God? 310.

He wandered about the earth, homeless and fugitive, 312.

**Calamity.** Those who are unjustly oppressed by the powerful cannot find a comforter, 418.

To trample earthly things is a mark of wisdom, knowledge, and virtue, 405.

Callirrhoe, a city from which hot waters burst forth and flow into the Red Sea, 321.

Wounded she-goats seek dittany, 444.

The mountain of the Cardueni in Armenia, 126.

Carthage is thought to be Tarshish, 286.

True charity, violated by no envy, grows both in number and in strength, 422.

Christ’s birth takes its beginning from shadow, 523.

Called a Nazarene from Nazareth; but among the ancients we too were called Nazarenes, as though in reproach, whom they now call Christians, 255.

God’s mercy is shown when the sinner is visited here for his crime, 315.

The Latins pronounce *codrans* through the letter Q as *quadrans*, 89.

The heavenly realms were closed until Christ opened the gates of paradise with the thief, 416.

**Thoughts.** Among many diligent people who labor in daily meditation, a pure thought, worthy of the name of man, is scarcely found, 449.

Corojatha, a village flourishing with Christians throughout, 183.

Cyprus and Cypricittium, 194.

## D
David, displeasing to Saul’s daughter, pleased God more, 409. The tomb of David and Jesse, 167.

**Declamator.** It is a sign of folly, both in the one who speaks and in those who hear a declaimer in church, to stir up applause with a certain coaxing charm and elegance of words, 467.

The fifth dialect of the Greeks is called Aeolic, 318.

Ancient foreign writers remember the Flood, 126.

The Dioscuri are Castor and Pollux, 100.

The Hebrew language has diphthongs, 58.

**To discern.** It is difficult to find someone able to distinguish a wise man from those who seem to be wise, 450.

**Disciples.** After much silence, we ought to become teachers from disciples, 412.

**To displease.** Everything under the sun is vain, while we displease one another over the boundaries of good and evil, 393.

It is the worst kind of sickness to be tormented in thought over riches and, amid sadness, groaning, and quarrels, to acquire perishable wealth through futile labor, 431.

**Teacher.** A false teacher flatters and deceives; he does not seek the conversion of his hearers, but applause and praise, 437. He teaches what pleases the people to hear, flattering sinners in their vice and provoking the uproar of his listeners, 478. He acquires riches, food, and possessions through enticing promises, ibid. He prepares his hearers for the future fire and binds them more tightly in the chains of sin, 437.

**Learned.** Even a learned man disputes with heretics not without danger, 473. The learned in the Church seize the wise of the world in their own cunning, 400.

The Lord is holy with the one who is holy, but he is perverted in the presence of one who has already been perverted by his own will, 441.

Our Lord was handed over in the torrent, dedicating our regeneration and the sacrament of Baptism, 346.

**E**

The doctrine of the Ebionites and the habitation of Hebrews of this kind, 190.

In Greek, *Ecclesiastes* means one who gathers an assembly—that is, a church—which the Latins call a preacher, 383. It is the book of Solomon doing penance, 392. Some wrongly think that this book summons us to pleasure and luxury, 385. He would never have preferred mourning’s sadness to the festivity of a banquet if he had thought that drinking and eating were of any importance, 433. An ecclesiastical man, instructed in the heavenly Scriptures, always desires to learn, 434.

Eden, the site of the sacred paradise, toward the east, 199.

Origen discovered the fifth edition on the Actian coast and discussed it fully and openly, 499.

H is regarded by most people as an aspiration, not a letter, 34. Grammarians do not think it should be counted as a letter, 91. Three names are read with H, 106. The Hebrews read the letter *he* as *a*, and conversely. See A.

The Hebrew letter *heth* has a double aspiration and is represented by the Greek χ (*chi*) in the Septuagint, 7, 317, 366.

Every heretic and defender of a false doctrine has an impudent expression, 450. Heretics who acquiesce in false doctrines promise themselves happiness and prosperity, 396. They express in the feminine gender what we usually call absolutely and neutrally, 449. The Hebrew language does not have the Greek letter χ (*chi*), 7.
