To wrench the club from Hercules’ hand requires great strength, 301.

Hieria, a region of India, 199, 258.

Jerome’s infancy occurred in the time of the emperor Constantius, 195.

Jerome’s Hebrew teacher, under whose instruction he read through the Holy Scriptures, 393, 412, 424, 428, 438, 459, 466, 470, 471.

Jerome does not approve the exposition of his Hebrew teacher, 428, 459. He often did not approve what he translated into Latin, 195, 207. Against his own conscience, he refused to follow the little streams of opinions while abandoning the fountain of truth, 381. So as not to deter the reader’s zeal by excessive novelty, he sometimes followed the ancient interpreters, ibid. He does not criticize the errors of the Septuagint translators, 303. He adapted himself to the usage of the Septuagint translators in matters that did not differ greatly from the Hebrew, 381. At Rome he had read Ecclesiastes to the holy Blesilla, to urge her toward contempt of this age, 381.

The swallow knows how to treat its young by means of its own eye-clearing plant, *chelidonia*, 444.

**Human being.** Human life after the Flood was not shortened to one hundred and twenty years, 315, 318. The human being was not created by God as insensible and stupid; rather, free choice is left to him for choosing good and avoiding evil, 442. For this purpose the human being was born: that, understanding his Creator, he might revere him with fear, honor, and the practice of his commandments, 496. The human being was given as a tenant and guest of the world, so that he might enjoy the brief period of his life and, with the hope of a longer age cut short, regard everything he possesses as though he were departing for elsewhere, 412. The inner human being arises within us after the fourteenth year of puberty, 424. The foolish person never thinks about the future but delights in present and fleeting things as though they were great and everlasting, 425. Human beings, swept along by the error and whirlwind of the age, do not understand the ruin caused by their sins and exult in things more deserving of lamentation, 396. We must not care what people say about us, 446.

*Hormiscus*: a torque or necklace, 515.

The place of Topheth, watered by the springs of Siloam, provided the delights of gardens, 300.

It is said hyperbolically that birds and walls report to us what they have heard when we speak, 479.

**I**

Idols are said to have first been made in the time of Enos, 312, 313.

**Enticements.** The enticements of vice are found where there was thought to be a covering of virtues, 477.

**Imprecation.** Ecclesiastes curses those who do not have the fear of God and wishes that they not be long spared from punishment, 455.

Everything among human beings is now uncertain, and it is uncertain whether they endure through love of God, like Job, or through hatred, like the majority of sinners, 457.

**Hell.** Before Christ’s coming, it made little difference whether one perished with the body or was detained in the darkness of hell, 416.

The human race is ungrateful for benefits received, 466.

**Interpretation.** In interpreting the Scriptures, we must not sew together scraps of opinions according to our own will; rather, we must preserve one text, one order of argument, and the same meaning, 429. Simple understanding requires no interpretation, 427.

The envious bitterness blazed up against the most learned men, 301. It also found those who were hidden, ibid. Nothing is more vain or unstable than people who do not weep over their own miseries or mourn their own sins, but envy those who are better, 420. The envious person is tormented by another’s happiness, and the celebrated person is exposed to ambushes, 420. The more someone envies his brother, the more he himself wastes away and perishes, ibid.

**Anger.** Anger is assigned in place of correction and instruction toward inferiors, 439. Anger is always joined to pride; and if a wise man is angry, he is judged foolish, ibid. When raging and recent anger has been postponed, it is more easily calmed and can be removed, ibid. We should be angry with ourselves when we sin, and angry with others as well, because through the sadness of the face the mind becomes better, 437.

Isaac was born at Gerar, not by the oak of Mamre, 337. Either at the ninth hour or before sunset he offered spiritual sacrifices to God and devoted himself to prayer in the field, 343.

Ishmael, playing with Isaac, was either making idols or, in jest, claiming the birthright for himself, 335.

Itabyrium is Mount Tabor in the great plain, 235.

**J**

Why Jacob was called Israel, 357.

Jericho: the first, second, and third, 230, 231.

Jerusalem is itself also Salem, and so forth, 231.

Jethira had all its inhabitants as Christians, 234.

Job was not of the stock of Esau, as some wrongly think, 339. His house was at Carnaim-Astaroth, 182. He is said to have reigned after Balac son of Beor, 195.

Jobab is thought to be the same as Job, 365.

The relics of John the Baptist were buried in a town of Palestine called Sebaste, 271.

The Jordan River rises from the springs of Paneas and flows into the Dead Sea, 139. It bursts forth from the streams Dan and Jor, which signifies “river,” 195, 230. Dan and Jor are the springs of the Jordan, from which it also received its name, 328.

Joseph’s bones were buried at Shechem, 274. His mausoleum could still be seen at Shechem in Jerome’s time, 374.

Joshua’s tomb was shown near Timnah, 223, 283.

The tribe of Judah, rich in the most warlike men, held the leading position among all the tribes, 174. They boast in vain of the repose of the Sabbath, 307.

**Judgment.** Many have been judged in this life before the day of judgment, 444. God does not now judge piecemeal and individually, but reserves judgment for the future, so that all may be judged together and there receive according to their will and works, 415. In the judgment, when the Lord begins to judge, truth will then exist; now injustice rules in the world, ibid.

Jupiter Enyalius signifies Mars, 266. Jupiter Gamelius, ibid. The beloved and catamite of Jupiter used to hand the cup to Jupiter himself, 356.

Justice has rest; iniquity has labor, 421. That justice is inhuman which does not forgive the frailty of the human condition, 443. Justice and piety ought to precede the light of knowledge in us, 407. The scale of justice is a great one: to assign to each person what, how much, for how long, and of what kind, whether in action or in counsel, 446.

The just person does not have a left cheek in himself; everything in him is right, 469. The things that ought to happen to the impious frequently happen to the just, while the impious live so happily in this world that you would think them perfectly just, 456. Because of the uncertain and slippery condition of this life, the just person falls and the sinner rises, 418. The just and the sinner will by no means have the same outcome, because the one will go to refreshment and the other to punishment, 404.

**K**

Among the Latins, K is considered a superfluous letter except in *Kalendae*, 34. It is represented by C, 91.

**L**

**Labor.** The greatest vanity among human beings is that one person enjoys the labor of another, and that the sweat of the dead becomes the delight of the living, 405. We are permitted to have tears only in calamities, when we are oppressed by the more powerful, 418.

**Lactantius.** In his excellent work of the *Institutions*, he mentions the letter Y and discusses most fully the right and left sides—that is, virtues and vices, 469.

**Joy.** Not only bodily joy but also spiritual joy is a temptation for the one who possesses it, so that he needs a correcting spur lest he become exalted, 396. In the joy of a banquet, if we seemed to possess any fear of God, we lose it, 436.

**Snare.** Everything is full of nets: the devil has filled all things with snares, 529.

It is the nature of ghosts to frighten little children and chatter in dark corners, 303.

Health-giving baths at Betoanea, 151, 175.

**Praise.** Many are frequently praised in the Church after death, and people are publicly proclaimed blessed for things they had not plausibly done, either by their successors or by the peoples, 454.

The Roman legion called the Tenth was stationed at Aila, at the extreme boundaries of Palestine, 130.

The ancient Law, rigid and unkind, sparing no sinner, kills the one who sins. The grace of the Gospel shows mercy and summons to repentance, 409.

The Hebrews assign the names of books from their opening words, 306.

Countless books are called one Law and one Gospel, 495.

The books that people compose with the greatest labor they often hand over to the lazy and those numb with idleness, 404.

The danger of unrestrained speech, 479.

The Hebrew letters *aleph*, *he*, *heth*, and *ayin* alter their aspirations and sounds; the Greek letter χ (*chi*) is not found among the Latins, 190.

Luke, as a proselyte, did not know the Hebrew letters, 371.

**Mourning.** The sinful people are described as mourning in dark garments, 462.

Lucullus, the Roman consul, besieged and captured Nisibis, a city of Mesopotamia, 126.

The moon stood still while Joshua prayed at Ajalon, 143.

Libya is called Put by the Hebrews, 319. The Laabim are called Putites, 320.

**M**

The tombs of the Maccabees were at Modi’in. Nevertheless, their relics were displayed at Antioch, 247, 250.

We must follow the footsteps of our ancestors and not depart from their authority, 495.

We must not burst into curses or detraction against kings and rulers, 479.

Manaim is interpreted as “camps,” 356.

Manasseh was restored to his kingdom after the captivity and lived for a long time thereafter, 443, 456.

What *mannus* is, 471.

Marcion and Valentinus say that they are of a better nature than the Creator, 450.

Marcion and Mani tore apart the ancient Law with rabid mouths, accepting only the Gospel, 480.

Among the Hebrews, “sea” denotes every gathering of waters, 306. In the Scriptures it is used for the west, 326.

The tomb of Mary, the sister of Moses, was shown at Kadesh, 183.

The idol of Mars was called Ariel at Areopolis, 162.

The martyrs and Maccabees, for the Law of God and justice, seemed to perish in their own righteousness, 442.

A cake made from fresh figs is called *debelath* among the Hebrews and *palatha* among the Greeks, 27.

In what year Methuselah died, 314.

Daily meditation and frequent reading are usually more a labor of the soul than of the flesh, 495.

According to the opinion of the Hebrews, Melchizedek was Shem, the son of Noah, 328.

Milcom, the idol of the Ammonites, 250.

Mesopotamia is so called because it is enclosed by two rivers, the Euphrates and the Tigris, 102.

Metallophon, a place near the Golden Mountains, 199, 211. The same as Fenon, or Finon, ibid.

**Merits.** There is no recompense for merits in the present age, but in the future, 465.

**Miracle.** One of God’s signs in Egypt softened the hearts of believers and hardened those of unbelievers, 441.

Both are miserable: the one who is endangered because of wealth and the one who is exhausted by poverty because of lack, 420.

**Moriah.** The Temple is believed to have been built on Mount Moriah, 337. From Gerar to Mount Moriah—that is, the site of the Temple—was a journey of three days; but from the oak of Mamre to the same mountain the full journey was scarcely one day, 338.

**Death.** The present corpse of the dead reminds us of our condition and human frailty, 436. Why the day of death is better than the day of birth, ibid. Wherever we fall, overthrown by the storm of death, there we shall remain forever, 480.

Moses, first when God was angry and afterward when he inspired him, received the law, 494.

**Woman.** Women are the source of all evils, 447. All women lead not to virtue but to luxury, 448. In the ruin of the human race, woman is more easily led to a fall, ibid. The body of holy women is not stained by force but by the will, 324.

The world consists of diverse things, and human life on earth is constituted in the same way, 442. Such great wickedness moves within the capacity of this world that it cannot receive the order and perfection in which it was first created, 394.

**N**

Nabau, or Nebo, the mountain on which Moses died, 251.

Nazareth, an idol of the Assyrians, 253.

Nimrod was the first among the people to seize an unfamiliar tyranny, and he reigned in Babylon, 320.

**Naphtali.** In Naphtali, hot springs were born, 377.

Nineveh, a city of the Assyrians, and Nineveh, a Jewish city in a corner of Arabia, 251.

Nisibis was handed over to the Persians by the emperor Jovian, 128.

Summer snows were brought from Mount Hermon to Tyre for its luxuries, 143.

Noah was not righteous according to perfected righteousness, 315.

**Name.** Four men in the Old Testament were called by their names before they were born, 332. Hebrew names change into various meanings according to differences of accents and letters, 15, 33, 36, 88, 98, 100, 114.

Certain heretics introduced natures that do not admit healing, 384.

The heretics wanted nothing new under the sun except what had existed in past ages before it came to be, 391.

Many harmful things were created in the world, so that by avoiding them we might be instructed in wisdom, 395.

The singular number is always understood in relation to good, the dual in relation to evil, 421.

**O**

*Obryzum*, a kind of gold that the Greeks call tawny, 81.

It is the nature of oil both to nourish a flame and to relieve the labor of the weary, 463.

Ommei, or Ommim, a powerful people in Save, 267.

On, in Greek Heliopolis, had been built before Jacob entered Egypt, 258. On, or Aun, a city of Samaria, ibid.

Ophir, a region of India, so called from Ophir, one of the descendants of Eber, 258, 275.

**Works.** Permission should be granted to a new work, 303. The perverse take the seeds of heresies from the best works and slander the labors of others, 405. The error of certain people concerning the works of the dead, 459. After death people can perform no good work, ibid.

Or, the mountain on which Aaron died, 258.

Origen is called the teacher of the Churches after the Apostles, 4. In his Homilies he followed the common edition; in the volumes on the Hebrew language he sought aids, 303. In the book of Hebrew Names he supplied what Philo the Jew had omitted, 3. He surpassed everyone in the other books; in the Song of Songs he surpassed himself, 499.

Idleness and sloth are the rust of wisdom, 473.

It is reported that Italian and Mesopotamian sheep have one and the same nature, 355.

**P**

The Hebrews do not have the letter P. Their names are written abusively with F among the Latins, 96, 101.

*Palae* were commonly called winnowing-fans, 96.

Israel grew weary of heavenly bread and desired the meats of the Egyptians, 138.

Paradise is said to have been created before heaven and earth, 307. What should be thought about Paradise and its rivers according to Sallustius, the most reliable author, 202.

The sparrow is never read in Scripture in a negative sense, 489.

**Passions.** All disturbances of the mind are included under anger; under the wickedness of the flesh, all bodily pleasures, 486.

**Father.** In Scripture, those who depart from ancient authority and despise the hoary precepts of their parents are called young men and fools, 476.

**Patience.** Patience is necessary not only in hardships but also in more joyful circumstances, lest we become exalted beyond what is fitting, 439. It is fitting for the just person to possess a little simplicity and, because of excessive patience, to seem foolish while reserving vengeance for God, rather than to exercise malice immediately while taking revenge under the guise of prudence, 468. God’s patience is hidden: it allows the saints to suffer now and does not visit sinners according to their crime, so that he may restore eternal goods to the just and inflict perpetual evils upon sinners, 443.

The etymologies of all the patriarchs’ names are given, 350.

**Paul.** The clearest prophecy about the apostle Paul occurs in the blessing of Benjamin, 379.

**Sin.** It is one thing to sin in thought and another to sin in deed, 470. Sin has the odor of something foul; virtue breathes perfumes, 505. Because of one sin, many acts of righteousness perish, 468. Whoever has sinned and done evil is dead; for in the very act of sinning he has immediately died, 454. The sinner, ignorant of spiritual contemplation, shuts his heart off from true delight, 402. God’s anger toward the sinner is that he gathers wealth day and night and, never using it, leaves it to those who are righteous in God’s sight, 406. Because sinners are not immediately rebuked and corrected, they think that judgment will never come and persist in crime, 453. The remedy for sinners arises from good conduct, not from inflated and excessive dignity, 470.

**Money.** Because of the ambiguity of the Greek language, *argyrium* may also be translated as “money,” 430. Those possessing money are said originally to have been called *pecuniosi* because they possessed more *peculia*—that is, cattle—ibid.

Among the perfect and those perfected in love, teacher and disciple are equals, 385.

The perverse person, unless corrected beforehand, cannot be adorned, 394.

Petra, a city of Arabia, surnamed Jectael and called Rekem by the Syrians, 259.

Philo is called the most eloquent of the Jews, 1. In the book of Hebrew Names, as a Jew, he omitted the names of the New Testament, 3.

Although the philosophers sought truth with every effort and thought they had grasped wisdom, they could not reach the light of truth, 475. They try to assert the falsehoods of their doctrines through the variety and multiplication of their arguments, 499.

Jerome the Egyptian wrote the antiquities of the Phoenicians, 126.

**Piety.** There is a time for hatred in martyrdom, when piety, hostile to us, attacks us for confessing Christ, 411.

The office of cupbearer was not considered an ignoble duty among the ancients, but was of the highest dignity among barbarians, 365.

The Sheep Pool—that is, the pool for animals—is elegantly described, 182.

We must mourn at present so that afterward we may dance, with that dance with which David danced before the ark of the covenant, 409.

**Applause.** If by the arrangement of words or by the devil’s prompting we arouse the applause of the people, we believe that we know, against our conscience, what we were able to persuade others of, 411.

The medicine of repentance has been offered to sinners, 444. God gladly receives the penitent, 462. God does not immediately avenge human crime but postpones punishment while awaiting repentance, 453. At the voice of a bishop or presbyter, sinners rise through repentance, 489. When all have been restored through repentance, the devil alone will remain in his error, 394.

Porphyry’s slander, by which he accused the Evangelists, is refuted, 307.

This is our portion and everlasting reward, if we labor here for virtues, 402. It is our part to rejoice in our study and labor, 432.

**Commandment.** We must not investigate why God commanded each thing, but whatever we see to have been commanded, we must hasten to fulfill with a devout mind, 451.

**Preacher.** Whoever preaches the word of God only at a time when the people willingly listen and a favorable breeze of popular rumor is blowing is a negligent sower and a lazy farmer, 482. The words of the wise prick rather than flatter; they do not handle wantonness with a gentle hand, but inflict the pains of repentance and a wound upon those who err and are slow, 494.

**Foreknowledge.** Through God’s foreknowledge and predestination, the things that will happen have already happened, 391. This does not abolish free choice but indicates that causes precede each event, explaining why each thing happened, 435.

What true rulers and judges are like, 476.

**Progress.** We ought to live so that each present day is better for us than the days that have passed, 439.

**Promise.** It is better to weigh an uncertain judgment for a long time than to be ready in words but difficult in action, 428.

**Prophets.** The Prophets and all the saints are clouds, able to rain down the precepts of instruction, 481.

The book of Proverbs does not contain, as the simple-minded think, obvious precepts, but something like gold hidden in the earth and a kernel within a shell, 493.

**Providence.** Everything happens by God’s arrangement, not by accident or chance, 461. All things are arranged not without God’s will, and God does everything for the benefit of human beings, 452. The outcome of events must be entrusted to God’s providence while we labor in good works, 482. God commanded the elements to serve human uses, so that people, seeing these things, might understand that there is providence, 413.

Psalm 64 and Psalm 71, according to the historical sense, were written about Solomon, although they pertain prophetically to Christ and the Church, 386.

There are fifteen Psalms of Ascents, through which we are first instructed in the Law, 480.

What does *Psomthom-phanech*, or *Saphaneth phanee*, signify? 367.

Ptolemy was a follower of Plato. For this reason he esteemed the Jews highly, because they were said to worship one God, 303.

The Punic language is adjacent to the Hebrew language, 362.

The doctrine of the Pythagoreans is to remain silent for five years and afterward to speak as learned people, 410. That decree concerning five years of silence was borrowed from the book of Ecclesiastes, where it says: “A time for doing, and a time for speaking,” ibid.

**Q**

No language other than Latin has the letter Q, 44.

The oak of Mamre was celebrated with superstitious devotion until the time of King—or Emperor—Constantius, 130, 195.

The pronoun “who” in Scripture always signifies not the impossible but the difficult, 417.

**R**

Res and Daleth are distinguished by a small mark, 452.

Natural reason, which God also implanted in sinners as its author, leads them to seek wisdom and trample folly underfoot, 397.

Rekem, the king of the same city that is also called Petra, was also called king of Midian, 262. There was another Rekem in the tribe of Benjamin, ibid.

The books of the Law and the Prophets are called the kingdom of God, 433.

Remman, the house of the idol of Damascus, 263.

The rejected sometimes have God dwelling within themselves, 423.

Rhinocorura is a word added by the Septuagint translators because of their knowledge of the place, 263, 298.

The Rhodians are called *Rodanim* or *Dodanim* in Hebrew, 15.

Laughter dissolves the one who laughs; anger seizes and corrects him, 437.

**S**
## S

**Triple S among the Hebrews:** how it is read, 16, 266. **Hebrew ṣade** sounds neither like our *s* nor our *z*, 92. **The Sabbath** was abolished at the beginning, 307. **The word Sabee:** its various interpretations, 337. **Priest.** Among the Hebrews, the firstborn exercised the priestly office before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood, 348. **Sacrament.** The mystery of the Christian Church does not consist in sacrificing irrational victims, but in the offering of bread and wine—that is, the Body and Blood of the Lord Jesus Christ, 329. **Age/world.** Every good thing of the present age is confusion; that of the future age is perpetual strength, 477. **Salem** is called both Shechem and Jerusalem, 358, 359. **Solomon had three names**, 383. He was wiser—not than Abraham, Moses, and the other saints, but than those who had preceded him in Jerusalem, 394. According to the number of his names, he published three books, in which he teaches the little ones, men of mature age, and the perfect and fully completed, [Col. 1589] 384. Solomon did not have a son like himself in Rehoboam, 404. Many of Solomon’s writings became obsolete and did not remain in memory, 496. **Salvation.** The simpler sometimes attain the salvation that the more learned lose, 417. **Salutaris.** Which province in Palestine was called Salutaris, 337. **The Samaritans:** from whom they took their origin, 278. **Samson and Delilah:** where they came from, 277. **The saints.** Before Christ’s coming, all the saints were held in hell; but not after the Lord’s resurrection, because they are with Christ, 464. **The wise man.** In Scripture the wise man labors and composes books that come into the hands of fools and are frequently exposed to slanders, 405. Whoever is wise always thinks about the future age, which leads to the right hand; the fool, however, thinks about the present, which is placed on the left, 469. Why the wise man with riches is better than one who is merely wise, 440. The wise man goes to the house of a man who will rebuke him when he sins, so as to bring him to tears and prompt him to weep for his own sins, 437. What the grief of the wise and the perfect is like, 395. By the example of many it is proved that sometimes the wisest men are in need of necessities, while the most ignorant flourish in the Church and consider themselves prudent, 465. It is characteristic of a wise man to follow wisdom going before him and not to consider empty rumors, 446. The perfect wise man needs no rebuke and is disturbed by no slander, 438. The more someone has attained wisdom, the more he is indignant at being subject to vices and far from the virtues he seeks, 395. Wisdom comes to us through certain torments and intolerable labor, by continual meditation and study, 395. It lies hidden in a secret and profound place and does not present itself to minds as light does to sight, ibid. It is proved in seeking good things and avoiding evil ones, ibid. It is the tree of life; unless it is planted in the midst of the virtues, the other trees will dry up, 398. In distress it can provide more help than any very great powers, 445. **Mount and desert of the Saracens:** Pharan, 191. They wander about with no fixed dwellings, attack all peoples, and are attacked by everyone, 330. **Sarai:** her name was changed to Sarah. The Greeks’ errors concerning the change of this name, 331. **Satan** is interpreted as “adversary,” 347. Under Saul, Jerusalem was not yet ruled as a kingdom, 390. Nothing that we secretly think is hidden from the knowledge of God, 479.

**To know.** We believe more than we know what is true, 401. Excessive care and anxiety, tormenting people in various ways, were given by God so that they might desire to know what they are not permitted to know, 393. We are commanded not to wish to know more than Scripture has attested, 435. A human being cannot know the wisdom of the Creator as clearly and purely as the one who is its maker knows it, 403. The more we seek to know, the more we display our vanity and superfluous words, 435. Divine Scripture is compressed into a short compass: as far as it expands in meaning, so far is it constricted in language, 495. The true food and drink taken from the Word of God is knowledge of the Scriptures, 413. Knowledge of them is the riches of Christ, 303. Wisdom must be followed, and knowledge of the Scriptures joined to it as though in marriage, 463. Knowledge of the Scriptures cannot be possessed together with worldly riches, 303. We cannot know the meaning of the Scriptures unless we learn it through their words, 394. Although there are many who say that they can unlock the hidden things of Scripture, rare is the person who finds the true solution, 450. We do not learn any of the arts without a teacher; only the teaching of Scripture seems so cheap or easy to many that it requires no instructor, 411. All difficult things are learned through great labor, contrary to those who think that knowledge of Scripture comes to the idle and to those who merely make requests, 390. The poverty of the historical sense, or the literal understanding, must not be passed over while we pursue the anagogical meaning in Scripture, 406. It is the custom of Scripture, although there are many books, to call them one volume if they do not disagree among themselves and are written about the same subject, 495. They use the imperative mood in place of the optative, 506.

**Secure.** No one ought now to consider himself secure; rather, he must handle weapons in this time of warfare, so that, once victorious, he may one day rest in peace, 411. **Mount Seir:** from whom it was named, 348. **Old age.** Good works must be done at every time, both in advanced age and in youth, because youthful frugality is of no benefit if old age is spent in luxury, 483. We ought to pursue meanings more than words, 495. **The number seven** is complete and perfect, 461. **The Seventy Translators** did not wish to disclose the mysteries of Scripture to King Ptolemy, 303. Jerome did not accuse them of these errors, ibid. They rendered only the five books of Moses into Greek, ibid. Those books agreed more closely than the others with the Hebrew, [Col. 1590] ibid. Jerome vindicates them, 340. **Sellers of tombs** are chastised by the example of Ephron the Hittite, 340, 341. **Discourses.** If someone’s speech does not prick but merely delights the hearers, it is not the speech of a wise man, 494. Why the end of a discourse is better than its beginning, 438. Slaves, sometimes puffed up by a dignity suddenly bestowed by the devil, trample the public roads with their mules, while every noble and prudent person, crushed by poverty, walks along the road, performing the office of slaves, 471. **Sikera** among the Hebrews means anything that can intoxicate, 96. **Sychar or Shechem** is Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans, 541. **The shekel**, in Latin *siclus*, is called *secel* in Hebrew and weighs an ounce, 341. **The tribe of Simeon** lived in the midst of the tribe of Judah, 174. Simeon and Levi did not receive a separate inheritance, 375. **Images** derive from resemblance, and the Latin noun *similitudo* (“likeness”) derives from the Hebrew *Semel*, 86. **Sin**, the hissing letter of the Hebrews: Isaac slightly altered it and pronounced *samekh* in its place, 348. **Mount Sinai** is sometimes called Mount Horeb, according to Jerome, 191. **Soccho** was founded by the Samaritans, 274. **The sun** daily indicates the world’s destruction by its rising and by its setting, 387. When it travels through the south, it is nearer the earth; when through the north, it is raised higher, 389. One and the same operation of the sun melts wax and dries clay, 441. The cause of anxiety and distraction is not in God but in the one who previously sinned of his own will, 407. Whoever believes in dreams gives himself over to vanity and foolishness, 426. **Sonthomphanec, or Saphaneth Phanee,** was interpreted by the Egyptians as “savior of the world,” 17. See *Psomthomphanech*. **Spirit.** Among the Hebrews, both “spirit” and “wind” are called *ruha* in the same way, 439. The Holy Spirit was from the beginning the giver of life, Creator, and God, 306. How we are joined in the embrace of the divine bridegroom, 319. To be without folly is the first wisdom; but no one can be without folly unless he has understood it, 395. Folly wages war against wisdom and, stimulated by jealousy, rejects whatever prudence it sees in a learned man, 474. Fools judge everyone by their own character, 469. A fool considers himself learned in whatever he multiplies words, and considers himself wise in the same respect, 475. In this age fools are lifted up before the face of the devil, while princes enter into the degradation of slaves, 395. **Pride.** Nothing in this world is worse or emptier than a proud person pleased with himself, who approves nothing except what he himself has done, 435. Some maintain that the Syrians were called *Assurim*, 344. **Syrtis** received its name from its drawn-out stretch, according to Sallust, 104.

## T

**Temple.** Entering the house of God is not a matter of praise, but entering without offense, 426. **Terence** used to place the prologues of his comedies on the stage in his own defense, 301. Luscius Lanuvinus accused him as though he were a thief of the public treasury, ibid. **Testament.** How the Old and New Testaments should be read, 483. We are commanded to believe in both Instruments—that is, the Old and the New—with equal reverence, 480. Eternal punishments are prepared for those who in no way join the two Testaments together, 482, 483. Christ and the Apostles produce many testimonies from the Old Testament that are not read in the codices of the Seventy Translators, 303. **Tabor**, a mountain in Galilee, 283. See *Itabyrium*. **Tarshish**, a region, 286. Every sea is called *Tarshish*, 299. **Tarsus**, the metropolis of Cilicia, glorified by the apostle Paul, 318. **Teman** among the Hebrews denotes every southern region, 282. **Theodotion** agrees in many things with the Seventy Translators, 396. **Teraphim**, images or figures, 70, 355. **Theristron**, a kind of Arabian garment with which the women of that province are veiled, 343. **Frankincense** arises among the Sabaeans, 319. **The Tigris and Euphrates** rise in Armenia, 202. The Tigris was so called because of its swiftness, 279. **Fear.** There are two kinds of fear and fear of God: that of beginners and that of the perfect, 497. Whoever fears God is neither lifted up by prosperity nor crushed by adversity, 445. As an imitator of his Creator, he hastens to do good to everyone without regard to persons, 444. A stream in Scripture, without an added qualification, is nowhere read in a favorable sense, 389. **Trachonitis and Ituraea** are the same region, 279. Though we are confined by various tribulations, we must speak nothing blasphemous and think nothing impious, 479. [Col. 1591] The confession of the Trinity among Christians, 460. **Tullius**, king of orators and illuminator of the Latin language, is accused by the Greeks of extortion, 301. **Tiberias** was built by Herod in honor of Tiberius Caesar, 191. It had knowledge of the Law and therefore was called a well-watered field, according to the opinion of the Hebrews, 378. **Tyre** is called *Sor* in Hebrew, 46, 93. See *Sor*.

## U

**Oil/perfume.** It is the custom of the Hebrews to call a good perfume “oil,” 436. **Use.** It is a gift of God that such a mind be given to a just man that he himself may consume what he sought through cares and vigils, 406.

## V

**Vau and yod**, Hebrew letters, differ only in size, 366. See *Yod*. All things are vain until what is perfect comes, 386. Nothing in this world is emptier than for the earth, which was made for human beings, to remain while the human being himself is suddenly dissolved into the dust of the earth, 387. We ought not eagerly desire things that perish while they are possessed, 385. We shall have to render an account for every idle word, and everything that does not edify the hearers turns into danger for those who speak, 497. We behold truth through a narrow opening and through certain dark caverns, 488. [Col. 1592] The spring season of the year is the chosen season, 360. Why Eve was called *Virago* (“woman”), 308. **Virgil** was called a compiler of the ancients, 301. He was both philosopher and poet, 469. Among philosophers the virtues are placed in the middle, and everything excessive, whether above or below, is considered a vice, 443. They are in the middle, and every excess is a vice, 469. They follow one another, and whoever has one has them all, 468. There is no rivalry among the virtues, 509. They make the days good for one who lives virtuously; vices make them bad, 439. They breathe forth perfumes, 509. Whoever restrains himself after vices and becomes a follower of the virtues is praised by Ecclesiastes, 398. **Life.** This is our portion and the fruit of our labor: if only in this shadowy life we may be able to find the true life, 463. Through our own fault we slide daily into worse things, 448. **Will.** It is better to do everything according to understanding, which is the eye of the soul, than to follow the desire of the heart, 435. Pleasure and desire are compared with drunkenness, which overturns the vigor of the mind, 397. Past pleasure does not help the present, and what has been exhausted does not satisfy, 396. As riches and pleasures increase, so wisdom is lacking among human beings, 397. People give themselves entirely to luxury and pleasures and seek riches that do not free them in necessity, 467.

## Y

**Y**, the philosophers’ letter: what it signifies, 424, 469.

# Order of the Contents of This Volume

## Volume II of Jerome’s Works

[Col. 1591C] **Preface**, 9. Notice concerning *The Lives of Paul, Hilarion, and Malchus*, 13.

**The Life of St. Paul.** — Jerome narrates, in a style somewhat lowered for simpler readers, the life of St. Paul, from whom the inhabitation of the desert first began; he shows that Paul, about sixteen years old, sought the desert under Decius and Valerian in order to escape the persecution raging against Christians, and that he lived there for ninety-eight years with remarkable abstinence and holiness, until, visited by the great Antony after Antony had been divinely warned, he met his final day. He dedicates the history to Paul the Elder of Concordia, his namesake, 16. Prologue, ibid. The Life begins, 19.

**The Life of St. Hilarion.** — Jerome describes at length how Hilarion, a monk born at Thabatha, a village of Palestine, and a disciple of the great Antony, lived with what abstinence and holiness, and by what miracles he became famous even in solitude; in him he sets forth a model of the perfect monk, 29. Prologue, ibid. The Life begins, ibid.

**The Life of Malchus the Monk.** — He places before readers the life of Malchus, a monk from Maronia, a village of Syria, a life harassed by various dangers and misfortunes and oppressed by captivity, 33.

Notice concerning the Rule of St. Pachomius, translated into Latin by St. Jerome, 59.

**Latin Translation of the Rule of St. Pachomius**, 61. Preface, ibid. Beginning of the Precepts, 65.

**Institutes of St. Pachomius.** — How the assembly is to be held and the brothers gathered to hear the word of God, according to the precepts of the elders and the teaching of the holy Scriptures, so that they may be freed from the error of the soul, glorify God in the light of the living, and know how they ought to conduct themselves in the house of God without ruin or scandal; so that they may not be intoxicated by any passion but stand within the measure of truth and the traditions of the apostles and prophets; and so that they may observe the order of the solemnities, imitating their conduct in the house of God, and complete fasts and prayers according to custom. For those who minister well follow the rule of the Scriptures, [Col. 1592C] 77.

**Precepts and Judgments of St. Pachomius**, 81.

**Precepts and Laws of St. Pachomius**, 83.

**Admonitions of St. Pachomius**, 85.

**Letters and Mystical Sayings of Fathers Pachomius and Theodore**, 87.

**Letter I of St. Pachomius.** — Writing to Cornelius, who was father of the monastery of Mochanseos, he speaks in the language that had been handed down to both men by the angel, ibid.

**Letter II of St. Pachomius.** — He writes to the Syrian, father of a monastery, who had himself also received, together with Pachomius and Cornelius, the grace of the angelic language, ibid.

**Letter III of St. Pachomius.** — He writes to Father Cornelius of the monastery called Mochanseos, 88.

**Letter IV of St. Pachomius.** — He writes to the Syrian father of the monastery of Chnum and to John, superior of that same monastery, 91.

**Letter V of St. Pachomius.** — He writes to all the monasteries so that all the brothers may gather at the greater monastery called Bhnum during the days of Easter, and there may be one solemnity for all, 95. [Col. 1593]

**Letter VI of St. Pachomius.** — He writes to the Syrian and to John mentioned above, 95.

**Letter VII of St. Pachomius.** — He commands all the monasteries that all the heads of the monasteries and superiors of the houses gather at the monastery called Bhum on the twentieth day of the month called Mesore by the Egyptians, so that the remission of all sins and deeds may be properly completed, 96.

**Letter VIII of St. Pachomius.** — He writes to the brothers who were beating goats in the desert, from whose hair sackcloth is woven, 97.

**Prophecy of St. Pachomius.** — In a vision he instructs the brothers in the monastery of Mochansi concerning what would happen to them and concerning what the heads of the monasteries would either do or suffer, 98.

**Letter of Theodore.** — He writes to the monasteries concerning Easter, 99.
